Toys for small children where multiple activities are included in one toy. Each activity helps develop motor skills and hand-eye coordination. Examples of activities are a bead maze, shape sorter, musical toys, and abacus.  Activity toys can take multiple forms. Modern versions may be electronic.

Time that is measured by direct observation of the Sun, by a sundial, astrolabe, or directly by another device. It differs from "mean solar time," which is keyed to time zones and kept by most clocks and watches. Apparent or true solar time is particular to the very site at which it is observed. Thus it remains distinctive and critical for various reasons, including the observation of Islamic rituals.
Scribes, composers, or other writers whose works may be identified by the distinctive style of their handwriting or calligraphy. May be anonymous or named.
The ensembles of chessboard and chessmen needed to play the game of chess.

Species of flowering rainforest tree having original distribution original distribution was in the central areas of the Deccan plateau, as well as the middle section of the Western Ghats regions. It is important to the cultural traditions of the Indian subcontinent and adjacent areas.

A rose cut fashioned with 24 facets on the top side and a flat bottom side. This particular cut originated in Amsterdam in the 17th century, hence the name. The name, however, is only commonly used from the 18th century. The cut is to be distinguished from an 'Antwerp rose cut'.

Yámù are one of the many burial forms in traditional China. They are excavated from the hillsides and cliffs near rivers and are generally located within the Sichuan Basin in southwest China, including in Sichuan, Chongqing, and Guizhou provinces. Yámù usually contain a tomb passage, a tomb door, a front chamber and one or more side halls and burial chambers. Some yámù are furnished with carved stone coffins, stoves, and niches, which are architecturally integrated into the caves. Some tombs also have architectural elements resembling timber buildings and walls decorated with carved images. The burial objects are largely the same as those found in brick or stone chamber tombs from the same period (Luo 1988, Fan 2006). However, the distinction between these cliff tombs and cliff burials in more central and eastern areas of China has not been given enough academic attention.
Any forms or styles used in the fashioning of gemstones.

Renewing or strongly improving products or services or the processes by which products and services are created. It is the change of a technical or scientific nature made to the good or service offered by a company or organization, in the processes developed within it. This is usually done in order to achieve greater competitiveness. Innovations in technology influence values ​​within a society and often raise ethical questions.

Journeys at sea for the purpose of hunting whales for their meat, baleen or whalebone, and blubber. Practiced as an organized activity as early the first century CE, by the 16th century whaling voyages as part of the industry of whaling became commonplace in the Basque region of Europe, and then the world. Whaling voyages peaked in the 19th century when the needs of industrialized society demanded whale oil in vast quantities, in advance of the development of fossil fuels. Recognition of the near-extinction of certain species of whale has caused the almost complete cessation of whaling and whaling voyages, except those allowed for by indigenous peoples in some parts of the world.
Motility or other conditions that limit a person's movements, senses, or activities in a conventional sense.
Persian wool carpets made in Herat, characterized by a wine red field color, and a border of clear emerald green and asymmetrical knotting; often made of silk.

Species of tree endemic to the tropical arid savanna of the African continent, but also relatively well distributed in parts of Asia having a tropical or subtropical climate. Long-lived, majestic tree revered in Africa for its medicinal and nutritional value.
Men who row a boat using oars.
Genus containing over 600 species of flowering plants, such as the morning glory, water convolvulus, and sweet potato.

Pictorial narrative device featuring two or more successive actions from the same story or related stories within one setting. Term may be confused with "simultaneous representation," which has to do with point of view, not with sequential episodes depicted in one scene.

Tanzanite is the blue and violet variety of the mineral zoisite (a calcium aluminium hydroxyl sorosilicate), caused by small amounts of vanadium. Tanzanite belongs to the epidote mineral group. Tanzanite is only found in Tanzania, in a very small mining area (approximately 4.3 mi long and 1.2 mi) wide near the Mererani Hills.
Reprographic machines that produce copies from a stencil, operated manually, and that use a particular type of ink and chemistry.

Genus containing three living species of tropbirds.

Species endemic to New Zealand, but extirpated everywhere except Little Barrier Island; it is being reintroduced elsewhere.

Star systems in which two or more stars orbit each other, bound by gravitational attraction.

The term angxing shuatou refers to any shuatou made into the shape of an "ang," which is usually an oblique or angled element. The term originated from Liang Sicheng's descriptions of buildings and has been widely adopted by scholars as the mainstream name for describing this type of shuatou (Liang 1955, 105-28). The earliest image of an angxing shuatou appears in the wall paintings of the High Tang (ca. 8th century) Cave 172 at Dunhuang (Yu 2017; Xiao 2003, 232). During the Song dynasty, the angxing shuatou was already widespread in northern China, but not in the south. The term does not appear in the 1103 CE Yingzao fashi (Zhang 2015).

Pairs of shoes or slippers with handmade beaded faces, typically worn by Peranakan communities in various Southeast Asian countries. The intricate designs of the beaded faces are handsewn using specific coloured glass or metal seed beads onto fabric stretched over a wooden frame. Common decorative motifs for kasut manek include florals, birds, and geometric patterns. “Kasut manek” are typically worn with the sarong-kebaya and on special occasions such as weddings, as part of the Peranakan wedding outfit. Kasut manek may be closed or open-toed and could also be designed with heels.

Describes text that appears on Web pages that provides an equivalent of what would be presented by an image. This appears in HTML as the 'alt text' label. Alternative text can be provided at the same time as images when building Websites. Screen readers may read 'alt text' aloud, and present text when images fail to load.

Liujin douke is one of the bracket set (dougong 斗栱 or douke 斗科) types used in Ming and Qing dynasty official architecture. According to the Gongcheng zuofa (1734) the term liujin douke refers to a bracket set that connects the eaves purlin (yanheng 檐桁) to the interior purlin (jinheng 金桁) via one or more slanted timbers (chenggan 秤桿). Literally meaning “flowing gold bracket set,” it can be used in any of the three eaves bracket sets types, i.e. the inter-columnar bracket set (pingshenke 平身科), the corner bracket set (jiaoke 角科), and the pillar-top bracket set (zhutouke 柱头科). Here the word jin 金 refers to the interior purlin (xiajinheng 下金桁), while liu 溜 can be understood as a verb meaning “to slide”. It might also be understood as “a row" (pai 排). The slanted timber bar echoes the form of the Song dynasty ang 昂, but it functions less for roof load transfer and more as a stabilizing component locking the eaves to the interior structure. Modern scholars have used the term liujin dougong 溜金斗栱 to refer both to the liujin douke and tiaojin douke 挑金斗科.

Refers to the refractory molds used in the lost-wax casting process or to the material used to make that mold. It also denotes the process of coating or embedding the wax model in this material and is applicable to clay-based, plaster-based, and ceramic shell molds. In all of these, the first layers have a special, fine consistency that is designed to pick up the detail and avoid problems during casting; the later layers are coarser. Clay-based investment may also be referred to as “loam.” The investment is destroyed in the process of casting.

In the Pinuyumayan culture, end-of-year festivals involve a series of December rituals starting from Mangayangayaw (or Basibas) for boys coming of age, Mangayaw (or Amiyan) featuring hunting, then all the way to the new year celebration. The festivals underline the significance of connecting, border-crossing and purification. Mangayangayaw (“monkey-shooting”) is held for members of takuban who age from thirteen to eighteen years old. Every December, people refurbish the roof of the takuban, hold purification ritual at the house of ancestral spirits and security ritual (known as semalikid) at the border of the tribe’s territory. Afterward, people would set up a stage for Mangayangayaw. The boys who are about to attend Mangayangayaw should use the leaf of hardy banana to sweep their household as a purifying act (known as alabakabakay) at the ceremony’s eve. At the ceremony, their courage and determination shall be tested by shooting monkeys. At the hunting ritual, adults ranking higher than miyabetan (senior rank of the junior hall) enter the mountainous territory for ceremonial hunting and related rituals. With seniors chanting a hunting hymn known as pairairaw, young adults should stand guard over the hunting camp. At the end of the hunting ritual, which takes up a number of days, the hunting party returns by passing the tribe’s arch of triumph known as laluwanan and men will be crowned with garlands by women awaiting them. The senior members are to announce the end of mourning period for those who have been put on mourning. Subsequently, the end-of-year celebration will last numerous days with singing, dancing and evening puazangi.

Used by Native North Americans that are part of the Midewiwin medicine society to hold medicinal plants and other ceremonial items.

Particles of silver that have a typical size of 10–100 nm and can exhibit a wide variety of shapes. The synthesis of AgNPs is commonly performed via the reduction of silver salts with reducing agents such as sodium borohydride in the presence of a colloidal stabilizer, including polyvinyl alcohol, bovine serum albumin, or citrate. Silver nanoparticle is known for its antimicrobial properties and exhibits chemical stability, good conductivity, and excellent optical properties.

Board game played by two players in which counters, 15 per player, are moved on a specially-marked board or table; the object of the game is to race to a goal, with the movement of the counters being controlled by the throw of two dice. For the similar, older game of French origin, use "tric-trac."

General term for calendars used in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, many modern communities in the Guatemalan highlands, and states of Veracruz, Oaxaca and Chiapas, Mexico. The essentials of the Maya calendar are based upon a system which had been in common use throughout the region, dating back to at least the 5th century BCE.
Glyphs or symbols that represent the name of a place.

Japanese books having a support comprising a long strip of paper with writing on one side, folded in a concertina fashion where each written page faces another written page. A cover may be attached to the front and back of the book; holes may be pierced to allow the book to be laced. Glossy mulberry torinokogami paper is often used. Based on a style of binding known in China during the Tang period.

Cultures and styles of the Amis people lived in Taiwan. The Amis people refer to themselves in two ways: Pangcah meaning “we people” is used in regions north of Taitung, and Amis meaning “northerners” is used in the south. The denomination has to do with routes of migration and interaction among tribes. The Chinese term came to adapt Amis. The Amis territory stretches from the Qilai plain to the Hengchun peninsula, where the Amis people develop an agrarian culture intricately rooted in the low lands of Taiwan’s eastern valley and coastal plains. The Amis has the largest population of aboriginals in Taiwan.There are three subcategories of the Amis people based on geographical and cultural-linguistic differences: The Northern group of “Nanshi” Amis, the Middle group of “Xiuguluan” Amis and coastal Amis, and the Southern group of “Falangaw” Amis and Hengchun Amis.The property inheritance of the Amis is matrilineal and traditional matrimony follows the rule of mikadafo which marries Amis men into the brides’ homes. The Amis tribe is co-governed by clan chiefs, who assign responsibilities and tasks to male members of different age classes. The Harvest Festival, known as Malalikid, is the most important celebration which unifies traditional beliefs, social structure and tribal identity.

Wooden, conical-shaped hats and visor, often made of bentwood and decorated with ivory carvings and feathers. Used to conceal one's head while hunting. Made and used by Yup'ik and other Alaska Natives.

Groups of stacked stones or boulders in a figural form, constructed by Inuit individuals. Inuksuit are constructed to act as waypoints, message centers, spiritual veneration, or as hunting decoys. The oldest inuksuit date from 2400 to 1800 years ago.
Species of bamboo found in southern North America; may grow in large monotypic colonies.

Originally a type of messenger's badge that was an attribute of a messenger at Dutch government institutions that was intended to collect posted messages. Worn on the belt these appeared as a shield bearing the coat of arms of the body representing the messenger. These imparted privileges to the bearer, such as free transport. Over time, these evolved into often elaborately decorated badges worn by representatives of city governments.
Retail establishments that sell books and other bound materials or recordings of books.
Any of various hardware that can be used to keep framed works of art or similar objects secured on walls in the event of shock or unintentional movement.

In traditional classifications, gulls are arranged in this subfamily, Larinae. Gulls comprise more than 40 species of long-winged, webfooted, heavily built seabirds of the gull and tern family Laridae, distributed all over the world. Adult gulls are mainly gray or white, with variable head markings.

Subfamily of small burrowing insectivorous mammals found throughout temperate Eurasia and North America. They usually have very poor vision, velvety fur, and short limbs with clawed toes adapted for digging the underground passages in which they live.
Large, oceangoing earless seals ranges over the Pacific coast of the U.S., Canada, and Mexico. mainly on coastal islands off California and Baja California.
Genus containing species of salamanders endemic to North America.
Salamander of the family Ambystomatidae (order Caudata), notable for its permanent retention of larval features, such as external gills. It is found in lakes near Mexico City.
A ritual festival celebrating Nahua deities and one of the eighteen periods of twenty days in the Xiuhpohualli (solar Nahua calendar).

Bubbles that range in diameter from 0.1 micrometers to 10.0 micrometers. MNB technology has been used in bioremediation, water treatment, aquaculture and plant cultivation, and as cleaning technology in the field of conservation.

The hard exoskeletal components composed of chitin that covers the wings of a beetle (Coleopter). Elytra provide protection from heat, wind, and moisture evaporation allowing beetles to live in adverse conditions, such as a desert environment. Beetle elytra often have bright jewel-tone colors and an iridescence due to the interference of light between the multiple layers of chitin. They have been used as applied decoration on textile and other cultural artifacts.

A specific division of works that involves applying polychrome painting to architectural surfaces, categorized in the Yingzao fashi (1103). The Yingzao fashi details several schemes of polychrome painting works that can be largely divided into two types: (1) zhuangluan 裝銮 (lit. harness bells), which are images and/or patterns painted on components such as bracket-blocks, bracket-arms, cross-beams and pillars, as well as on wall surfaces; (2) shuaran 刷染 (lit. brushed-on colors), which entails less complicated designs and is limited to two or three colors used on the aforementioned surfaces as well as on doors, windows, balustrades (goulan 勾欄), pale fences (chazi 叉子) and other places not specified in the text.

"丁" cross beams" or dīngfu run parallel to the roof ridge and form a "T" shape with cross beams perpendicular to the roof ridge. In traditional Chinese timber-frame architecture, the dingfu refers to cross beams used on the gable sides of a building with a hip and gable roof (jiuji 九脊 or xialiangtou 廈兩頭; later xieshan 歇山) or the "hip" side of a building with a hip roof (Song dynasty si'e 四阿 or Qing dynasty wudian 廡殿). In historical texts, we have only found this technical term used in the Yingzao fashi (e.g. Chapter 5, 7b). Modern architectural historians use this term to describe cross beams on the gable sides of buildings dating from the Tang to the early Ming dynasties.

First coined in the 1980s (Su Bai 1982, 141-142), yingzuo mugou is a modern term adopted by archaeologists and art historians referring to painted representations of timber architectural components in underground architecture (e.g. tombs and reliquary chambers beneath pagodas). The meaning of yingzuo here as a “painted representation of something” has departed from its original context in the Yingzao fashi. Similar appropriations appeared in 1950s (Su Bai 1957), such as in painted representations of door lintels (yingzuo men’e 影作門額), and painted representations of bracket-sets (yingzuo puzuo 影作鋪作).
A type of concave or plate tile, one variety of roofing tile.

A type of roofing tile. Term used in the Qing court architectural manual, the Gongcheng zuofa (1734), to describe the type of barrel tile (tongwa 筒瓦) which is used to cap the end of covering tiles at the eaves. A goutou is the barrel tile at the bottom of each tile row used to cap the ends (Liang 1981, 78). This term is commonly found in Ming and Qing dynasty texts. An earlier term for this element is "wadang."

Condition of fabrication for items made to an individual's specific order, often in referencing items of clothing. For items made for an individual request, but based on only a given set of possible designs, prefer "made-to-order."
Use to describe items of clothing made in advance for sale to any purchaser.

A diagnostic method based on electromagnetic measurement of the permittivity of the material under investigation, such as brick, plaster, and stone. The theoretical concept is based on the measurement of the dielectric contrast between water and the host material in the microwave frequency range, and is successful up to 2 cm in depth. In conservation, this method has been usefully employed for determining by non-invasiveway the moisture and salts content inside materials.
Wood boring beetles in their larval and adult states. As larvae, commonly known as woodworms. Termites, though wood eating, are not beetles and thus not wood borers.
Private orgainizations or other people who care for collections of art, library materials, or other items.
People who touch up or edit digital photographs or traditional photo-chemical photographs.
Negatives that depict other works, usually other photographs, that are used to strike copy prints.
A deciduous broom of western Europe that is widely cultivated for its bright yellow or partly red flowers and that has become naturalized in North America. It has been used as textile dyestuff.

Digital microscopes that combine three-dimensional image capture, image stitching, and modelling data. These scan an object through multiple focal planes and compiles this data into a three-dimensional image.

Citang is a type of building for performing sacrificial rituals to family ancestors, well-known people, religious figures, and nature spirits in traditional China. Citang 祠堂 is a compound word, in which ci means “sacrifice” and can be used as a verb, while tang is a noun indicating a type of building. The term citang as a whole means “a building used for worship” and was first found in the Western Han dynasty (206 BCE-9 CE) history Han shu (Ban 1962, 2948; 3085).
Utensils designed for eating pastries or other desserts. These normally have three or four tines, sometimes with the leftmost tine being wider to help cut into the pastry.
Long-handled spoons made from ca. 1880's through about 1910. The original use is disputed, thought to either stir claret, or retrieve fruit from claret pitchers or to place fruit on dishes.
The reputation, essence, and impression imparted to the public and employees by a corporation, especially as shaped by public relations programs.

Strings of characters that uniquely identify a location on the internet or other network to which email can be sent; the email address is typically a point of contact for a particular individual or organization.
Racks of mesh for laying out herbs to dry for use.
Official documents that indicate an award of distinction, such as achieving an academic diploma or an award.

Words or phrases indicating the certainty with which art or other creative work can be attributed to a known individual creator or group, used when the attribution is uncertain, is in dispute, when there is more than one creator, when there is a former attribution, or when the attribution otherwise requires explanation. For qualifiers that may be more broadly applied, not only for creator attributions, see "information handling functions."

Describes a type of dance characterized by elaborately decorated regalia, including feathered bustles and roaches, and fast-paced movements. Commonly performed at powwows by Native North American men. Popularized at powwow events in the 1960s, though  has origins in 19th century Plains dances.

This instrument functions as a seismograph. It consists of a cast-iron ring suspended by a lead weight, which is fastened with a single bolt through two metal disks and rubber tubes that must be connected to stethoscope earpieces to hear sounds transmitted through the earth. The geophone needs to be placed on the ground to receive the energy transmitted as wave motion through the earth. It then transforms the seismic waves of the ground into sound waves, which can be heard through the earpieces.
Refrigeration systems that lower the temperature of a building, or of machinery, industrial spaces, and process fluids by removing heat from the system and transferring it somewhere else.
Objects that are worn by individuals that are meant to indicate authorization or confirmation of personal identity within a predermined locale or context.
Equipment developed and used in the early 19th century to synchronize images and sound.
Objects or components originally created as accessories used in the transportation of people or goods above the face of the earth. Included are objects created to be parts of aircraft or spacecraft.
Administrative centers for parks.
Pins with words or images displayed on them that provide some mental or spiritual influence.

Measurement for internet connection speeds; preceded by a numerical value, denotes the download and upload speeds of digital data passing through a data transmission system, one megabit being equal to one million bits.
Unit of speed and velocity, comprising distance in feet traveled or displaced, divided by the time in seconds.

Priests in the Shintō religion of Japan. The main function of the shinshoku is to officiate at all shrine ceremonies on behalf of and at the request of worshippers. He is not expected to lecture, preach, or act as spiritual leader to his parishioners; rather, his main role is to ensure the continuance of a satisfactory relationship between the kami (god or sacred power) and the worshipper through offerings, evocation of the kami, and mediation of the deity’s blessing to the parishioners.
The action of taking someone away by force, deception, or otherwise without the full, informed consent of the person or his or her legal guardian. In historical usage, the term also implied rape.

A European shrub of the olive family, now also growing in North America,  having cordate ovate leaves and large panicles of fragrant pinkish, bluish purple, or white flowers. Syringa vulgaris (lilac or common lilac) is a species of flowering plant in the olive family Oleaceae, native to the Balkan Peninsula, where it grows on rocky hill
Genus of plants native to Mexico, Central America, Caribbean, and South America, and naturalized in other places.
Species of shrub native to northern South America, Central American, and Mexico, and cultivated worldwide. Used as a source for food and pigment.
Genus containing shrubby evergreen plants.
Genus of onion- or garlic-scented bulbous herbs of the amaryllis family (Amaryllidaceae); species are found in most regions of the world except the tropics and New Zealand and Australia.
Species of bulb-forming plant in the amaryllis family, widely cultivated for its trumpetlike flowers. Daffodils are native to northern Europe and are grown in temperate climates around the world.
Genus containing around 105 species of flowering shrubs and trees, native to the tropical and subtropical regions of Central and South America and to New Zealand and Tahiti.
Species of hardy biennial plant that is grown as a vegetable. The leek is an ancient crop and is native to eastern Mediterranean lands and the Middle East.
Genus containing around 5 species of evergreen woody vines or shrubs in the ginseng family (Araliaceae).
Genus of flowering plants containing between 525 to 600 species.
Species of flowering plant, with the native range from India to China (S. Yunnan), Jawa to Lesser Sunda Islands (Bali); the source of a natural red dye and used for medicinal purposes.
Species native to the Mediterranean, the Middle East, India, Pakistan, and Central Asia. Noted as the source of the blue-purple colorant "turnsole."

A natural yellow dyestuff obtained from the wood of the smoketree, Cotinus coggygria (formerly Rhus cotinus). This small tree, also called Venetian sumac, is native to southern Europe, the Middle East, India and China.
Genus of around 100 species of flowering plants native to Southeast Asia, southern China, the Indian Subcontinent, New Guinea, and northern Australia.

Species of  perennial, rhizomatous, herbaceous plant native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, valued for its root-stock, which is used as a spice, as a yellow dye, as a chemical test for alkalinity, and also medicinally.
Species of flowering plant native to southeastern Europe and adjacent parts of Asia.
Fields in the building and construction industries requiring specialized knowledge. These fields may include carpentry, masonry, electricity, heating, ventilation, and plumbing.
Pools, usually lined with soft padding, filled with small balls. Common feature at playgrounds or childrens' activity centers.
Shallow bowls or dishes used to scoop and pour water over the recipient's head at a baptism. Often in the shape of a sea shell.
Keys used to wind clockwork mechanisms.
Ribbons, often made of silk, historically used to bundle cigars in groups. These are usually imprinted with a brand name, and have been traded as collectibles since the late 1800s.
Tongs designed specifically for serving salads often designed to have one end that is a scoop and another that resembles a fork, some are pivoted to open and close.
Describes where an individual has carried out significant actions or primary locations of activity.
People having sexual attraction or sexual relations with people of the opposite sex.
Females having sexual attraction or sexual relations with other women.
Those who specialize in the carpentry and making of the structure of altarpieces, which are objects set upon the altar of a Christian church.

Lacework carpentry associated with Mudéjar Spain and Portugal, and as such often called Mudéjar carpentry. Geometric and decorative, this type of structural woodwork is often seen in framing, paneling, and roofing.
Those who engrave or etch designs or patterns on glass.
Refers to craftsmen who create gold leaf. Generally considered a trade separate from goldsmiths.
Metalworkers who specialize in working with silver, especially in the making of jewelry, flatware, and tableware.
Those who specialize in shaping iron by cutting, using specialized tools.
Building commissioner working for the church.
The hard wood-like endocarp of a cherry, the fruit of a cherry tree.
Sculptors who create works in iron metal.

Holiday in Mexico, honoring dead loved ones and making peace with the eventuality of death. Also observed to a lesser extent in other areas of Latin America and in the United States. The holiday is derived from the rituals of the pre-Hispanic peoples of Mexico. Led by the goddess Mictecacihuatl, known as “Lady of the Dead,” the celebration lasted a month. After Christianity was established in Mexico, this feast was merged with All Souls' Day and All Saints Day on the Catholic calendar, November 1 and 2. An example of celebration is for families to adorn grave sites or altars with candles, marigolds, and the favorite foods of deceased relatives. Today, the festivities are often characterized by black humor. Toys and food, including breads and candies, are created in the shape of symbols of death such as skulls and skeletons.
Species of large scallop that is native to the Pacific and Gulf coasts of California, the Baja California Peninsula, Mexico, down to the western coast of Peru.
Genus of edible and ornamental plants in the amaranth family.
Works made from sugar or chocolate in the shapes of skulls and skeletons, for the Day of the Dead celebrations.
Pan dulce that is traditionally baked in Mexico for the Day of the Dead celebration and formed or decorated appropriately, such as with a crucifix or bone-shaped decorations.
Prints made by exclusively using the process of screen printing, whether originated by hand or photographically.
Starchy edible tubers of the Solanum genus, particularly Solanum tuberosum, native to the Peruvian-Bolivian Andes and cultivated among the world’s main food crops.
Order of flowering plants, containing some 5,489 species.

Family of flowering plants comprising between 300 and 400 genera of plants distributed principally in the north temperate regions. Most members are aromatic herbs with alternate, feather-divided leaves that are sheathed at the base. The flowers are often arranged in a conspicuous umbel (a flat-topped cluster of flowers). Many species are poisonous.
Genus containing around 25 species of herbaceous plants found worldwide.
A species of white, flowering plant in the family Apiaceae, native to temperate regions of Europe and southwest Asia, and naturalized to North America and Australia. Cultivated for its edible root.
Perennial plant of the nightshade family (Solanaceae), grown for its edible fruits. Eggplant requires a warm climate and has been cultivated in its native Southeast Asia since remote antiquity.
A Nahua constellation also known by two other Nahuatl terms, Yohualteuctli and Yacahuiztli. Scholars have argued for various identifications with known asterisms.
Species of small, gray Australian parrot. It has a yellow head, red ear patches, and a heavy beak used to crack nuts. The species is bred as a pet globally, with several established color mutations.
Men of noble birth or rank. For female counterparts, use "noblewomen."
The right of women by law to vote in national or local elections.
Racks on which wet laundry is hung for drying or airing, typically an upright wooden frame standing upon legs, with horizontal bars on which clothes are hung.

Boards with a dark, usually black or green, surface for writing or drawing with chalk or a similar material. Examples of use include as a teaching aid in classrooms, and in shops, restaurants, or elsewhere for displays, usually words, that may be easily altered.
Divisions, notes, or other areas of information in cataloging or other information recording configurations.
Note recording the abstract, a short description of the work or other entity.
Any remarks associated specifically with a provenance event, as they appear in a collection record.
Titles in fielded data that are formatted to sort in a particular way for display in a list or group, usually alphabetically, by the first word after an article, i.e.: "title, the".
The Japanese art of folding paper into intricate decorative designs and objects.

Japanese art of paper cutting to create stencils, using awls, punches, and small knives. In the traditional Japanese craft of katagami, paper stencils are carved by master artisans for use in decorating textiles. Documented since at least the sixteenth century, the technique developed out of methods originally devised for embellishing leather armor.
Genus of edible, herbivorous gastropod mollusks, having around 100 or more species, depending upon the classification system. The shell is valued for its iridescent nacre.
Genus containing one species of recently extinct New Zealand bird. The last living birds were seen in the 1960s.
Extinct species of wattlebird, formerly endemic to the North Island of New Zealand.

A unique Māori variation of whatu (twining); may be used to weave the colorful, intricate borders of cloaks. Māori weavers developed tāniko by introducing coloured horizontal threads to the whatu twining technique. They worked out that they could combine full and half twists to bring one or another colour to the front. In this way, they could create intricate geometric patterns.
Order of flowering plants including 7 families of trees and shrubs and around 85-90 genera. Most of the species are tropical and subtropical, though a few genera reach the temperate zone.
Genus containing up to 2,000 species of shrubs, llanas, and herbs, the number varies depending upon the classification system.
Species of small tree containg several subspecies endemic to New Zealand on North Island, Lord Howe Island, Norfolk Island, and the Kermadec Islands.
Species of densely branched, brittle, woody climber native to New Zealand; leaves are used in Māori weaxing.
Species of shrub-like plant, know in several cultivated varieties; having white to rose-red flowers and gray-green to brownish leaves. The stems are used in basketry.
Coastal sedge endemic to New Zealand; its fibers are used by Māori in weaving.
Representations of only the head and shoulders of a figure.
Genus of conifers distributed in Africa, Australia, Centeral and South America, and the South Pacific.
Species of medium to large podocarp tree endemic to New Zealand throughout the North Island and northeastern South Island in lowland, montane and lower subalpine forest at elevations of up to 600 m.
Implements used in the process of cutting branches or twigs from trees, shrubs, or vines in order to promote flowering and fruit production.

Books intended for children, which contain interactive content such as games, puzzles, quizzes, pictures to color and other elements that involve writing or drawing in the book itself. Specific types of activity books include colouring books and puzzle books. A book is normally referred to as an activity book if it combines a variety of interactive elements and does not fall into one of these more specific categories.
Print advertising that is designed to be viewed within the pages of magazines or journals.
Equipment used to apply loops of material around paper or other printed materials to hold them together. Materials used range from metal to plastic.
Knives designed to separate orange or other citrus segments from the pith, or knives for peeling oranges.

Inflatable, air-tight bags of rubber, plastic, paper, silk, or similar lightweight material, of varying shapes and sizes that are imprinted with slogans or names of candidates or measures that are up for election; used as promotional items.
Badges or ornaments of varied materials, generally round or rectangular that bear an inscription or a design. These are designed  to fasten to clothing, used to show support or presence at an event.
A sheath typically of very thin rubber, worn over the penis during sexual intercourse to prevent contraception or sexually transmitted disease.
Prosthetics that are created to replace natural joint structures in the body when they become worn out.
Instruments for corporal punishment consisting of a bundle of supple twigs bound together and used to strike the offender's bare skin.
Heated pointed implements used in the art of decorating wood, leather, or other materials by burning designs on the surface.

Antitank lightweight artillery units or man-portable launchers that are designed to eliminate recoil by allowing part of the propelling blast to escape to the rear of the weapon. These may only be used at short range.
Poles with red and white, or red, white, and blue spiral stripes used as signs for barber shops.
Small, light work tables with one or two drawers, the lower of which forms a frame from which is suspended a bag for needlework.
Ornaments applied to shoes, made of varying material such as fabric or plastic.
Machines or other devices used to cast votes, varying in size and design. Relies upon mechanical components to record votes.

Wall brackets of a particular style distinctive to Venetian interiors; they typically were used to hang household items or clothing. There was often a piece of damask or other textile placed behind the bracket.
Tools used to prepare shrimp for eating by removing a vein.
Shuttleless looms that utilize thin metal shafts, or rapiers, to carry single picks of weft through the warp shed from stationary supply cones.
Devices outfitted with mirrors which, when turned clockwise, direct the sun’s light in a particular direction.
Straight-handled tools that have a knife blade attached, and that may be retractable, used to cut pieces of wallpaper for hanging.

Articles of furniture, comprising a flat surface made of wood or another sturdy material reinforced by fold-out metal legs, used to support strips of wallpaper while they are being covered in paste before being applied to a wall. To flatten the wallpaper and keep it from unwanted curling during the pasting process, its ends are typically tucked under a string tied loosely around the table's fold-out legs.
A device consisting of a wooden beam worn as shackles placed around the neck to restrain enslaved people.
A type of decoration or signage made from plastic film that adheres to the surface of a window by means of static electricity so that it is easily removeable and reusable.

Mill devices used to separate chaff from grains after the threshing; an example would be a large shallow container with a mesh or perforated wooden bottom, or sliding panels, that winnow the grain when turned manually by a metal crank and hand grip.
Workbenches used in the trade of barrel-making.
Frameworks or overhead structures of beam or timber; used as a working platform or as a means of support equipment.
Flat mats placed on desks or other writing surfaces, both to protect the surface and to facilitate writing.

Tablets with two distinct sides joined by hinges, variously made of plastic or metal. One side holds paper and the other contains shallow holes that form the basic six dots of a braille cell. Individuals use a stylus to poke the paper to form raised braille text.
Boards of wood or other material bearing a spring-clip at one end for holding papers.

Mechanized devices, comprising a system of automated pullies and carrier rolls, used to wind strings of yarn into tight balls. These machines are built in various sizes depending on the desired size of the yarn ball, and are often arranged with a double screw to produce two yarn balls simultaneously.
Spherical projectiles of stone or iron, usually solid, made to be fired from cannons. For the solid bullets of spherical or conical shape fired from small arms, use "balls (bullets)."
Amplifiers that increase the power levels of audio equipment.
Containers used for the protection and transport of audio equipment.
Buttons that cause a corresponding bell to ring, usually used for summoning people or calling elevators.
Filters that purify liquid specimens by passing the liquid through Seitz discs, composed of asbestos filters.
Small tools with a hinged cover and fitted with a rasp, used to store and grate nutmeg.

Mechanized devices, comprising a double-sided frame equipped with a long row of spindles carried by ring rails, designed to convert pure roving into yarn and strengthen the yarn by twisting the roving in a simultaneous and continious process. After receiving roving from an intermediary simplex machine or fly frame, these devices expose the roving to a drafting process through which it is transformed to a desired thickness. The drafted roving is then twisted and wound onto a ring bobbin for packaging. The most commonly used devices in the yarn manufacturing process, these frames are small, accessible, and simpler to use than other methods of cotton spinning.

Receptacles intended to receive the expectoration of tobacco chewers. These may appear in a variety of forms and materials, but the term is frequently applied to circular bent wood containers made the Shaker religious community specifically for this purpose. These resemble other types of Shaker nesting boxes with the addition of wood or metal reinforcing rims, and lack fitted lids.
Devices used to steam rice, usually electric with a timing capacity.
Stills used to produce arak, which is an anise-flavored spirit popular in the Middle East and elsewhere.
Belts containing a concealed compartment for money.
Metal implements comprised of a long handle culminating in a blade or scoop for the removal of ash from fireplaces or wood stoves.

Mechanized devices designed to use compressed air hoses to blow polyester and similar filling materials into pillows, quilts, and other products. These devices typically operate on a continuous cycle, allowing them to stuff large quantities of pillows or other products consecutively without stopping.

Syringes having an extended tube for intrauterine administration of holy water, refined in the 19th century. The devices were used to baptize a fetus in utero prior to a spontaneous abortion, or when it was othewise feared the unborn infant would die in delivery.
Horizontal platforms surrounded by ultraviolet light-emitting bulbs that cause the appearance of a suntan on human skin.
Devices that specifically play back tape housed in cassettes, and do not have a record function.
Devices for controlling the temperature, humidity, and sometimes the purity of the air in an interior space.

Specialized combs, typically made of wood, comprising a flat surface covered by iron nails, wire teeth, or other sharp objects designed to manually disentangible the fibres from textile materials prior to spinning.

Mechanized devices designed to remove superfluous moisture from fabrics by passing fabric materials through the device's rollers in vertical loops without tension, and exposing the materials to hot air. These devices typically comprise a series of rollers, a continuously moving conveyor belt, a series of large drums, and fans blowing hot air. The characterizing feature of these devices is the fact that it carries fabric materials vertically, not horizonally, through the rollers.
Disks, balls, or devices of other shape having holes or a shank by which they are sewn or secured to an article and that are used as fasteners by passing through a buttonhole or loop or a trimming.

Automated open-width devices specifically designed to apply a finishing solution or material coating to the backside of a fabric, enhancing its appearance, functionality, and/or stability. As variants of the padding machine, these devices include large rollers that treat wet fabric in batches using a roller coating technique, and are typically utilized for continuous fabric processing.
A narrow trimming made by a variety of techniques such as tablet weaving or braiding. It comes in a variety of fibers and weights, but is heavier than ribbon and flatter than cord.
Containers, often made of soft canvas and comprised of multiple fold-out pockets, designed to store loose crochet hooks and other related tools.

Devices used for producing bobbins that are evenly covered with yarn, used to wind thread or yarn around a bobbin. These usually include a fixed shaft that is rotated continously, distributing the thread uniformly onto the mounted bobbin.
The protective and ornamental coverings that support and enclose a clock movement and dial.
Devices that use cold water to cool lard after the process of rendering.
Full-length black robes worn as court attire by barristers or advocates in the UK and some Commonwealth countries.
Printing presses requiring hand operation.
Apparatus, fixed or portable, whose primary purpose is to produce artificial light.

Flat pieces of metal, usually made of zinc or aluminum, used in offset printing. Plates are treated with a photosensitive substance and then exposed to light to create a printing surface. Used as the first printing surface which transfers the image to a rubber medium; the image is then transfered from the rubber to the final substrate.
Sheds to shelter sheep.
A house, other than an inn or hotel, in which rooms are rented.
Large bags in which mail is carried, either shoulder bags used by postal carriers, or bags or pouches used to transport mail in bulk, as from central post offices to branch offices, or city to city.
Receptacles used in the process of maple sugar or syrup, after it has been heated to concentrate the sugar content.
Machines that automatically close bags or sacks, typically of animal feed, seed, or fertilizer.
Implements usually of marble or glass rounded at the top and flat on the bottom, used for grinding pigments against a fixed grinding slab.

Self-contained painting kits that allow users to gradually reveal a pre-designed picture on a canvas or board by applying specific paint colors to the canvas's corresponding numbered sections. Often cheaply purchased at drug or art supply stores, these boxed sets became a popular leisure activity for middle-class Americans beginning in the early to mid-1950s. The original invention is credited to Dan Robbins and Max Klein of the Palmer Paint plant in Detriot, Michigan, who began marketing the kits in 1951. The inspiration for the invention is said to originate from Leonardo, who assigned numbered portions of his paintings to his apprentices for easy completion.
Pieces of bent wire or plastic used for holding several sheets of paper together.
Passenger aircraft operated by commercial airline companies.
Molds, often metal or earthenware, for baking cakes in distinctive shapes, such as in the form of animals.
Accessories for machinery comprised of a blade that smooths, guides and spreads asphalt.
Percussion beaters consisting of a group of metal wires attached to a handle, used to strike drums and cymbals.
Circular, lidded containers made to hold contact lenses, often made of plastic.
Loops or bands of fabric, usually colored black, worn around the upper arm to commemorate one or more deceased individuals.

Various articles of jewelry worn in memory of a deceased person during periods of mourning; especially such jewelry preserving hair of the deceased or bearing motifs such as a weeping willow, lyre, or broken column.
Benches intended for use by the player or an organ, sometimes made en suite with the instrument with which it is sold.
Benches intended for use by the players of musical instruments.

Electronic devices that are specifically attached to acoustic instruments, such as acoustic guitars, to amplify sound vibrations, for passing the signal through to an amplifier or for recording purposes.

Tubes, often made of tin, with two diaphragms of pierced tin where several fifes can be stored; the cases have lids which lock the fifes in place, and early examples are decorated with the insignias of military regimens.
Whistles that emulate the chirping of birds by passing air through a reservoir filled with water.
Enclosed receptacles used for the storage of small, thin, rigid pieces of metal with sharp points used in needlework.
Usually hard-sided containers with hinged lids and a handle used for storing pins for needlework.
Devices of varied design used to secure fabric to a frame as it is being worked into a quilt.
Receptacles made of flexible material closed in on all sides except at the top, that are intended for storing tools and materials for needlework.

Holding devices or structures, typically made of wood, plastic, metal, or other similarly durable materials, designed to keep fabric taut and secure for embroidery and other needleworking tasks. These devices often comprise sets of laterally moveable bars, on which strips of webbing are nailed and to which the work is sewn, as well as sets of stationary bars with holes pierced at regular intervals for receiving pegs, clamps, or pins to keep the parts in place. These devices are often used in conjunction with fixed stands or trestles to hold them upright for easy use.
Contrivances used for holding or supporting spools for thread for needlework.
Two circles of wood, metal or plastic that fit one inside the other, and that can be tightened with fabric stretched over the inner hoop to keep it taught while being worked.
Collections of tools and materials that are kept together in a receptacle for use by sailmakers.
Prefabricated models or designs for the construction of quilts.
Frameworks that incorporate rails, bars, or pegs, in or on which safety pins may be placed or suspended for access.

Holding devices or structures, typically made of wood, plastic, metal, or other similarly durable materials, designed to keep fabric taut and secure for needleworking tasks. These devices often comprise sets of laterally moveable bars, on which strips of webbing are nailed and to which the work is sewn, as well as sets of stationary bars with holes pierced at regular intervals for receiving pegs, clamps, or pins to keep the parts in place. These devices are often used in conjunction with fixed stands or trestles to hold them upright for easy use.
Utensils in the form of a flat board with a raised rim, or a shallow box without a lid, made of a variety of materials in various sizes and shapes that hold pins for needlework.

Small tools, typically operated by hand or as an attachment to sewing machine foot peddles, designed to ensure regular spacing and sizing of manually-applied buttons onto sewn textile materials. These tools are marked with a set of templates and size labels, allowing the user to accurately measure both the distance between and size of the buttonholes according to desired specifications.

Bundles of small, square paper held together by an adhesive binding at one side. Used for note-taking or other informal writing; each sheet is pulled off after being written on to be discarded or adhered to another surface. Post-It (R) is a registered trade mark for a commonly used product that exemplifies this concept.
Pleats or gathers of fabric used to trim a garment or soft furnishing.

Protective envelope-like containers for phonograph records, usually of heavy paper or cardboard and often printed with images and information relating to the record, such as important information about a performance or illustrative material.
Discs, tapes, filaments, or other media on which sound has been recorded.

Modified Gregorian telescopes that contain Cassegrain reflectors, designed to reflect and focus light toward their primary light-gathering mirrors. Designed in 1672 by French priest Laurent Cassegrain, the improvement was rediscovered in the late 18th century as it was proven to reduce spherical aberration.
Refracting telescopes that utilize achromatic lenses, which prevent chromatic aberration (inability to focus, and the refracting of light into its constituent colors).
Benches with raised iron pins in the form of a comb, so that one or two people can manually remove seed bulbs from flax or hemp stems while seated.
Devices used in hearth-cooking, consisting of vanes on a shaft attached to a spit. Updraft from the hearth fire turns the vanes, which then rotates the spit.
Light-tight bags designed with holes for the insertion of the user’s arms to manipulate photo-sensitive materials without the use of a darkroom.

Transparent, flexible plastic material, usually of cellulose acetate or polyester, on which a light-sensitive emulsion is coated, or on which an image can be formed by various transfer processes, used for still photography and cinematography. Also, a thin coating of collodion or gelatin spread on photographic paper or plates, or used by itself instead of a plate.
Sacklike removable and washable coverings for pillows, often matching bolster cases and sheets.  For decorative coverings enclosing or laid over pillows use "pillow shams."
Plate armor pieces for the left hand and arm, protecting the hand and forearm up to or slightly beyond the elbow. They were used from the 15th through the 17th century, particularly in jousts.
Small tents for children to play in. These usually consist of textile materials and are available in different shapes, such as an Indian tipi.
Promotional objects issued during the course of an electoral campaign that promote a cause or individual.
Promotional objects issued during the course of an electoral campaign that promote a cause or individual. These are designed to be affixed to clothing.
Promotional objects issued during the course of an electoral campaign that promote a cause or individual. These are designed to be pinned to clothing.

Pieces or lengths of fine fabric, such as silk or satin forming a narrow strip or band that are imprinted with images or text that advocate for a political cause or person in the context of an election, usually pinned or otherwise affixed to clothing.
Receptacles for storing flour.
Covered containers of varying form intended primarily for storing biscuits.
Receptacles for storing flour.
Containers typically made of metal, and often cylindrical in form intended to hold grease for cooking.
Canisters, made of a variety of materials, but typically of tin or ceramic, designed to hold coffee and maintain its freshness.
Covered containers of varying form intended primarily for storing cookies.
Frames used to support and organize spices.
Devices used to keep hot food at temperature via infrared radiation.

Shallow dishes placed alongside a dinner plate for the bones and other remains of an elaborate meal. Often included as part of a standard place setting in the 19th century; often having a crescent shape.
Tight-fitting undergarments designed to smooth and shape the body
Machines used to sort produce into grades.

Movable stands used to transport a coffin and often upon which corpses or coffins containing corpses may be placed during viewing and religious services before burial. They often have long handles at either end to be carried by or placed on the shoulders of the pall bearers.
Coverings that are used for soft furnishings.
Textile coverings used to protect the tops of cupboards, typically embroidered, made of damask, or made of carpet.
Long narrow strips of cloth placed along a table for decoration or to protect the surface when placing objects upon it.
Lengths of narrow textile materials used to cover the tops of bureaus.
Wooden bars or staffs, sometimes tapered at the ends, employed as an apparatus for heaving or lifting, as a lever.

Greeting cards that are sent or given as expressions of goodwill at Christmastime. The first Christmas cards were made in the 1840s in England. The tradition is followed in all English-speaking countries and the practice is growing in many others.
Wide ornamental underskirts of sumptuous cloth often supported by hoops. Worn from the late 15th to the 17th century, especially by Basque and Spanish women.
Pads woven from palm fronds to be put under a hot pan to protect the surface on which it rests.
Pin-backed buttons of varied materials that signify membership in a fraternal organization. These display symbols or emblems that identify the member's affiliation.

Articles of jewelry designed to be suspended, such as from a necklace, brooch, or earrings that symbolize membership in a fraternal organization. These feature emblems affiliated with the organization.
Small buttons or badges meant to be affixed to clothing that indicates membership of the wearer in a fraternal organization. These display emblems unique to the organization.
Round shields featuring various designs used in military action and ceremonies of Nahua peoples.

Three-dimensional polyhedra meant to illustrate or demonstrate mathematical or geometric principles, or as models for drawing exercises. These are normally in sets containing various solids such as cones, spheres, cubes, cylinders, triangular pyramids, etc.
Machines for separating grains from their husks, using a current of air.
Devices or systems of devices that distribute water and heat uniformly to wheat kernels when being processed, allowing the maximum extraction of flour.
Mechanical devices that use high-speed hammers to grind dry corn and other grains to create feed for livestock.
Mortars with a flattened end used for processing grain.
Devices used by bakers to determine the expansize properties of gluten in flour.
Devices used to separate crop seeds by size. Used for sorting mixed seeds of different sizes or to separate broken or low-quality seeds from high-quality seeds.
Mechanical devices used to clean and remove foreign objects from grain, such wheat, corn, barley, etc.
Slabs of stone or metal, on which printed material or stereotype plates are arranged before printing.

Devices for carrying lightweight tree trunks, telephone poles and similar. The version designed for two persons consists of a pair of hinged chisel-bill hooks used as pincers mounted on pivots at the middle of a wooden pole, which is grasped at either side of the object being carried. The weight of the log forces the hooks to sink into the wood. There are verions for single-person operation with a number of interconnected levers between handle and hooks and is used for carrying relatively short pieces.
A double egret-feather device inserted in the hair. Part of the array of several deities such as Tezcatlipoca or Huitzilopochtli and worn by warriors of central Mexico during the Postclassic period.
Circular ties made to hold hair in place. Usually made of bunched fabric, often colorful.
Containers made to store hairpins, often rectangular in shape.
Ornamental hairpins or sticks used to hold hair in place, or simply for decoration.
Hand fans made from palm fronds.
Articles that overlie soft hats of the type usually tied under the chin and having a front brim, with the effect of protecting, enclosing, decorating, or hiding them.
Accessories used to protect hats from rain and other elements, usually made of plastic or other flexible materials. Covers the hat entirely.
Feathers, bunches of feathers, or other like materials such as horsehair used to ornament hats.
Pronged utensils for turning fish cooking by the heat of a fire.
Heaters for the burning of coal. May be for industrial or domestic use.
Forks with several long metal tines, slightly curved and pointed, fixed to a crossbar and attached to a wood or metal handle, generally with a hand grip. Used to fill bags of coal.
Apparatuses used for heating, usually of cast iron, designed to burn charcoal efficiently.
Butchers' tools consisting of curved rods of wood or iron used to support a carcass.
Machines used to cut thin sections (3 to 5 micrometers thick) of plant and animal tissue for microscopic examination.
Instruments use to determine the fat content of milk by measuring their specific gravity.

Portable milking machines for dairy cattle, consisting of four metal tubes attached to a bucket. The tubes, attached to a pulsator, mimic the squeezing action of nursing or hand milking. Herbert McCornack of New Jersey invented the surge bucket milker in 1922.
Small pails, usually wooden, with one long stave used as a handle, used as a milking pail.

Spherical objects that may be made of a variety of materials, and that may be either solid or filled with particulate matter, especially made for throwing and catching in the air for recreation or for spectator entertainment.
Knives with blades designed to separate the pith and flesh of grapefruit.
Devices for weighing meat, usually to price a portion for sale.
Bowl-shaped strainers having one handle and a wire-mesh or perforated bottom; intended primarily for straining gravy or clarifying soup stock.
Racks used to dry objects on, especially washed kitchenware.
Machines used to wrap cut portions of butter. For flat-headed wooden devices used to pack butter into storage containers, use "butter tamps."
Data cables that are connected to networked computer systems and interfaces.
Data cards with notches punched along their edges, representing data.

Modems that connect to telephone systems and convert digital data into sound signals, which are then transmitted through telephone lines. Historically, for acoustic couplers to connect to telephone systems, telephone handsets would rest in soundproof enclosures which have loudspeakers and microphones that are close to the earpieces and mouthpieces of the phone handsets.
Devices that convert data and other information found on punch cards directly to magnetic tape.
Sleeves that protect computer disks.
Devices whose purpose it is to convert data. May include devices for early computing and data processing, including card-to-tape converters.
Devices that punch identical data into decks of punch cards.
Devices that prepare multiple punched cards from a punched card source, copying all or part of the data from the sourced punch cards.
Pliers used to enhance crown form contours to improve gingival margins, customizing orthodontic bands, or other purposes.
Artificial replacements of one, several, or all of the natural teeth especially ones not permanently anchored in the mouth.
Chemistry in dry granulated form for developing sensitized photographic materials. Generally this is mixed with water to create an aqueous solution, or very rarely used in its dry state.

Mechanized devices, typically comprising a series of revolving rollers covered with steel napper wires or teasels, designed to raise the naps or pile fibers on a fabric's surface to create a velvety, soft finish. As fabric is passed through the device's cylinders, its loose surface fibers come into contact with the napper wires or teasels; these sharp mechanisms lift the fibers from the fabric's weft yarns to the its surface to form naps. This process, which increases the fabric's warmth, is often applied to woollens, cottons, spun silks, and spun rayons, amongst other knitted or woven materials.

Devices for electrical or electronic musical instruments that, when activated, often via a footswitch, add auditory effects to a signal. These are most commonly intended for performing with electric guitars.

A brand and type of electronic musical keyboard instrument developed by Harry Chamberlin in conjunction with a London-based manufacturer, which incorporated a selection of electromagnetic tape samples, as looped recordings played by pressing the keys of a keyboard. The prototype, the Mellotron Mark II, was available in 1964, and was used by numerous pop and rock groups, such as the Beatles and the Moody Blues.

Timepieces, often worn on the wrist, which display information in the form of individual numerical digits rather than using hands or pointers on a dial, typically by means of an LED or liquid crystal display, or by any other means.
Devices that are capable of stamping raised braille alphabet figures onto paper or other supports for use by people who are blind or visually impaired.

Semiformal evening suits consisting of a dinner jacket and trousers, the trousers having a stripe of material, such as silk or faille, down the outside of the legs. May also include a bow tie, cummerbund, and a shirt.

Hand-held tools, typically comprising two blades made of lightweight stainless steel or aluminum mounted on identical finger rings, designed to easily cut through fabric freehand. Unlike paper scissors, which are often equipped with dull blades, these scissors are equipped with sharpened blades so as to make long, crisp cuts in textile materials that span the entire length of the blades.
Tools comprising a metal ruler or hem guide on which various widths are marked, as well as a bulb with marking power, designed to mark, measure, and press up even hems on a variety of garments.
Small pointed instruments for piercing holes in cloth.

Hand-held tools designed to facilitate detailed stitching of embroidery floss, thin yarn, ribbon or other fine threaded materials, often for embellishment purposes. These tools comprise a perforated metal tip and a hollow channel through which the thread or yarn runs, mounted on a handle for easy gripping. Due to its sharp needle, this tool effectively pierces most tight-weave fabrics. After piercing thread or yarn through tight-weave fabric backing material, the tool's perforated tip leaves a loop of thread remaining on the backside of the fabric to create aesthetic patterns and designs.

Hand-held tools comprising two long, sharp stainless steel blades, one of which is bent at an angle and one of which is rounded, mounted to two different-sized finger rings. These tools are specifically designed to cut long swaths of fabric, oftentimes straight from the bolt; they are most often utilized to craft dresses or other types of clothing. The bent-angle blade, which is controlled by the user's thumb, helps to keep the fabric flat on the cutting surface for more precise cuts.

Mechanized devices used to measure the burst strength of, or force required to break or rupture, fabric materials. To measure a fabric's burst strength, these devices first utilize clamps to hold fabric samples in place. The devices then subject the samples to hydrostatic pressure via an elastic or rubber diaphragm, which automatically inflates and expands toward the sample thus applying increasing physical stress to the fabric until it ruptures. Typically, both sides of a fabric sample are measured using a burst tester; the results of both sides are averaged to calculate the fabric's overall burst strength.
Type of pliers used to repair and maintain hard wire fencing. These have features such as cutters to cut through hard wire, and gripping jaws to bend and manipulate wire.
Rectangular dividers, often made of card stock or plastic, used to separate and organize documents such as medical charts.
Cylindrical containers with corresponding lids used for holding film, particularly that wound onto cassettes for 35mm still photography.
Devices, usually metal, comprising vertical elements and often a horizontal bar, supported by legs, and used to support logs in a fireplace. May be used with a "fireplace grate."
Flash lamps consisting of a gas-filled tube activated by a discharge of electric current.
Gauges that measure the forward speed of an aircraft in any of several units, knots being the most common.

Devices or systems that present a user with the impression of operating aircraft, excluding space flight. These create an illusion of manned flight, applications of flight controls, the effects of other aircraft, and environmental factors such as air density, velocity, turbulence, wind, cloud cover, precipitation, for example. These are used for training, aircraft design and research.
Corkscrew-like tools used to break up dried fruit packed in casks or or receptacles
Relatively small, covered containers for dry tea used on a tea table or other surface, in conjunction with a teapot and a kettle.

Devices used to carry whole cheeses from the pasture to market. One type of cheese carrier is made of wood and consists of a platform to hold the cheeses, which rests on carved legs attached to two arms, called 'horns'. To carry it, the ‘horns' are placed on the shoulders, with the platform resting on the head. Other types of cheese carriers consist of a platform to hold the cheeses, suspended by cords carried in the hands.
Casks used aboard ships, designed specifically to store bread during long ocean voyages.
Domed screens placed over dishes of food to protect them from insects and debris.
Stencils, placed on the top layer of cakes, over which a decorating material, such as powdered sugar or powdered chocolate is sprinkled in order to make a decorative pattern.
Utensils, often wire or iron, which hold ears of corn for the process of drying.
Any of various culinary devices used for grinding food, such as grain, vegetables, or meat.
Machines that automatically fill and pack barrels, typically with grain, feed, or flour.
Wooden paddles used to stir apple butter to ensure proper consistency.
Stones with nut-sized pits or depressions, used to crack nuts.
Cases or coverings into which the blade of a kitchen knife is thrust when not in use.
Boards for preparing shaping, or decorating sweets.
Small stick-like devices inserted into a cake during baking in order to determine its doneness, which is determined if the tester comes out clean.
Cheese-making implements used for stirring curd, which may take a variety of forms.
Shallow troughs used for curing meat with salt.
Shovel-like tools used to retrieve ice from a large container.
Small, hand-operated carts equipped with beverages and other items, such as glasses and napkins, used for serving, most typically on airline flights.
Small cloth pouches used to store and protect napkins.
Rectangular trays with sides; one common design includes hinged sides of curved profile that may be folded up to form sides for the tray; may also have attached folding legs or an accompanying stand.
Culinary tools used to shape butter into fluted scrolls.
Devices used to cut fruit into slices.
Chambers used for preserving fish by exposing them to smoke.
Devices used to sort apples by weight, shape, or color.
Plastic bags with a self-sealing opening made of a thick plastic suitable for storing food in a freezer.
Any of various containers for shaking cocktails in order to mix ingredients; usually lidded, made of glass or metal, and of a tall shape designed to be conveniently held and shaken by hand.
Boxes used to store jewelry.

Cards distributed by merchants or manufacturers to advertise or promote their business or product; their use may have been as "premiums." For small printed sheets or cards bearing tradesmen's advertisements from the 17th through the 19th century, use "trade cards." For cards made later, bearing the name and address of a business concern and the name of its representative, and intended more for information than for advertising, use "business cards." For cards made later and issued primarily to be collected, with or without advertisements on them, use "collecting cards." For cards intended to be posted as public advertisements, use "posters" or its narrower terms.
Printed or lettered objects that are intended to be posted in open spaces, particularly yards in public places or on private property.
The simplest of propeller designs, associated with light, piston engine aircraft. The angle of attack of fixed pitch propellers is set at installation and cannot be changed during aircraft operation.
Fabric that has been cut on the bias into strips and folded to form a finished edge along a seam. This material is available commercially or may be home-made.

Bookbinding machines that apply a coating of glue to the back of the book, and additional adhesives to the strips either over the entire surface, the center portion to secure the back of the book, or over the edges which are to be secured to the end papers.
Biospecimens that are taken from humans or animals, that are used for research or storage.

Mechanized devices designed to measure, mix, and homogenize a compound of one or more products, including but not limited to various types of flours, textile materials, and seeds. These devices typically comprise oval or semi-circular chambers inside of which a rotating reel is housed. As the products to be blended are feed into the chamber, the reel's rotation works to mix the various ingredients to form a uniform and amalgamated product.
Walls having a modified board and batten arrangement of horizontal and vertical surface boards.
Devices for determining phosphates in boiler water consisting of a slide with incremental or gradiated standard measurements.
Cases that are used to protect or transport compact discs.

Mechanized devices that utilitize a pneumatic conveying process to compress webs of cotton fibers into a sliver or roving, as well as to remove dirt or dust from the cotton lint. The devices project a current of cotton laden air against screens made of mesh fine enough to prevent the passage of small fibers. Extraneous matter is extracted from the materials without the loss of valuable fibers, while a suction fan allows for the transport and cohesion of the fibers. Fiber webs are also cut into ribbons by condenser bands, which are then rubbed into round strands of fibres or roving.
Disposable bags used to contain meat while it roasts in an oven.
Forks comprising a long shaft and ending in two prongs, used to turn meat on a barbecue.

Devices, traditionally made of iron, having two palettes designed so that batter may be placed between them for baking. Historically, the devices had two long, lever-like handles for placing the iron in a fire or in an oven. Modern baking irons may operate as separate electrical appliances. The palettes are often stamped or molded with a pattern or design that is transferred to the baked item.
Coolers specifically designed to store beer at the perfect temperature for serving and pouring.
Double-handled blades for shaving wood in the shaping of staves in the construction of barrels, usually shaped in a scoop for shaping curves.
Devices used to can fresh produce, meat, etc. in order to preserve it.
Containers used to hold soldiers' personal effects.

General term for baskets made by Native North Americans across the United States used to carry personal items or foodstuffs. Made of varying woven plant fibers and come in variable shapes and sizes. Examples include baskets made by Apache women notable for attached hanging decorations or white oak baskets and tumplines made by Cherokee women.

Temporary, heat-resistant, cohesive, porous molds that capture the fine impression of a model to be reproduced and forms the void into which a molten material will be cast. Investment, green sand, and ceramic shell are examples of refractory molds.

Items of costume worn below the waist and behind the wearer, specifically while performing sacred or ceremonial dances. The use of this term is most often applied to objects of Native cultures of the Americas, and these are most frequently constructed primarily of feathers arranged in a circular or fanned manner.

Noisemakers, usually comprised of a handle and a rectangular wooden rattle. Used as part of Purim celebrations; during the reading of the ‘Scroll of Esther,’ children are encouraged to rattle gragers each time Haman, the chief minister of the Persian King Ahasuerus, is named. This act is symbolically meant to drown out his plot against Persian Jews.
Small, hand-held devices resembling an apple corer, used to extract a small plug sample from the center of the cheese wheel, in order for it to be evaluated for taste and texture.
Collections of objects used to analyze the contents or purity of water.
Instruments designed to measure carbonic acid in a mixture.

Devices worn over the shoulder or on the back, made of fabric or other materials including bark, used to support and carry an infant. These have been used throughout human history and into the present day.
Wedges or fittings, usually of wood or hard rubber, that are insterted between the front of a mast and the front of the mast gate to fill the available space on a ship’s mast.
Keys used to loosen and tighten the chuck holding the bit on a drill.
Mills used to grind apples for the making of cider.

Containers intended primarily for holding cigars, especially covered boxes of varying shape, similar to but larger than cigarette boxes, meant to be placed on a table, desk, or the like. For flat containers used to carry cigars, use "cigar cases." For airtight containers for cigars, use "humidors."
Accessories worn on the collars of garments; usually clips are attached to each end of the collar, holding the fabric ends closer together.

Color correction filters used to compensate for the temperature of the prevailing light for photography. These filters adjust the orange-yellow quality of tungsten lighting to match the blue of daylight.

One-piece, tight-fitting main garments that extend from neck to ankles or feet, usually made of knitted material; designed for everyday wear rather than for physical activities; dating from the second half of the 20th century. Distinguished from "leotards," which are designed for physical activities such as by acrobats and dancers.
Dissecting tools used to hold structures such as nerves or vessels, while dissecting with probes or needles.

Stones, slabs, or pillars of any material, set by the side of a road to mark distances between one point and another; most often distances between cities. The term "milestones" does not necessarily refer only to the unit of measurement called a "mile"; it may be used to describe objects that denote measures of the kilometer or other units.

Overhead receivers, accumulators, reflux drums, and condensers including ejector-condensers used to receive and collect condensed liquid material from a distillation unit and from which the condensed liquid is pumped to larger storage tanks or other process units.
Rigid tubes with removeable caps at the ends used to store or transport large documents such as maps, blueprints, or any large format document that may be rolled up.
Doll furniture consisting of a cot, a mattress and bed linen. These may be made from a variety of materials, such as wood, metal, reed or plastic.
Instruments used to draw the arc of a circle without using a central point.
Loose-fitting knee-length or ankle-length garments, often tied with a belt, usually of a warm absorbent material, worn before and after bathing or informally around the house.

Machines that make copies of print originals by scanning an image, or receiving a digital signal from a computer, and burning a 'master' or stencil onto a photosensitive polyester resin film bonded to thin fibrous paper, which is mounted on an ink drum, through which ink passes onto a paper support. For machines that make a similar type of print from a manually created stencil, and that do not have the scanning stage, use 'duplicators'. For similar machines that use a specific type of chemistry and ink combination, and that are manually operated, use 'mimeographs.'
