Small loudspeakers worn on the head for listening to music or for communications purpose; may have speakers for one or both ears, attached to the head by a band.

Round, broad-brimmed ecclesiastical hats with low crowns made of felt or beaver hair. Prelatial hats are black, except those worn by the pope or cardinals. A silk band or cord with tassels encircles the crown, with the color indicative of the wearer's rank.
Devices for shining a light through eggs to allow an observer to determine the egg's quality.
Small, electric appliances that combine the functions of a toaster and an oven. Typically these are used for toasting bread, reheating food, and small batch baking.
Projectiles tipped with metal points, as shot with a crossbow.
Glasses with graduated markings.
Thermometers used to make candy, and determine the correct stage in cooking sugar syrups.

A silvery white metal, with symbol Ca and atomic number 20, the fifth most abundant element in the earth's crust, occurring in many compounds. Its uses include as a nutritional supplement to assist the growth of bone and teeth, as a dehydrating agent for organic solvents, and to remove gases from molten metals prior to casting.
A white crystalline powder occurring naturally chiefly as the minerals calcite and aragonite.

Optics using lenses comprising arrays of small hollow glass tubes that guide the x-rays to one small point. The array is tapered so that one end of the capillaries points at the x-ray source and the other at the sample.
Conically shaped devices used in conjunction with polycapillary optics to collimate and guide divergent x-rays.
An order of moss.
A family of moss with only one living genus Sphagnum
Genus containing 150-350 living species of mosses. The taxonomy of Sphagnum species remains controversial, with various botanists accepting quite different numbers of species.

Tree that grows in parts of Africa, Central and South America, the West Indies, and extreme southern Florida. It is used as an ornamental, for traditional systems of medicine, and for its fruits that are used as vessels.
Order of flowering plants containing around 14 families, whose members produce glucosinolate (mustard oil) compounds.

Gourd family of flowering plants, containing 98 genera and about 975 species of food and ornamental plants. Members of the family are annual or perennial herbs native to temperate and tropical areas and include cucumbers, gourds, melons, squashes, and pumpkins.
Genus of herbaceous vines native to the Andes and Mesoamerica, known for gourd-like fruits.
Genus of gourd-bearing vines, containing six species.
Places at which coal is separated from impurities or dust by washing in water or other liquids.
Nonmetallic chemical element (O). It is a colorless, odorless, tasteless gas, the most plentiful element in the Earth's crust; its most important compound is water.

Oxygen in its atomic form as it exists at altitudes over 12 miles above Earth's surface. It is the result of photo dissociation of molecular oxygen enabled by the ultraviolet radiation found in space. Atomic oxygen comprises 96% of low Earth orbit atmosphere. In conservation, an atmospheric atomic oxygen beam is effective in removing through oxidation organic materials that are typical of graffiti or other contaminant defacements which may occur to the surfaces of paintings.

A silvery-white metallic element of the lanthanide series, atomic no. 60, which was discovered as a component (with praseodymium) of the supposed element didymium and is used in mischmetal and some other alloys.

Strontium (symbol: Sr) is a soft silver-white metallic element that turns yellow when exposed to air. Strontium is used commercially in luminous paint, fireworks and television tubes, and the compound strontium-oxide serves as a non-toxic replacement for lead in ceramic glazes. Paleontologists study strontium levels in human and animal bone for information about ancient diet.
Family of comb jellies.
Genus of comb jellies.
Boxes on the deck of a ship near the helm, in which compasses are kept.
Sets for the game known as Backgammon, including the game board, along with the pieces for each player, and dice. These are often stored in a folding case that forms the board itself.

Tobacco prepared for chewing, produced in a variety of forms such as compressed cakes, braided ropes, shredded leaves, and loose leaf ends, and usually flavored with substances such as licorice, spices, honey, or rum.
Three-dimensional constructed objects that mimic the appearance of flowers and foliage. Materials may include porcelain, carved wood, ivory, silk, and paper.
Lights on an aiming post that serve as an aiming point during night survey or in night firing.
Small transparent vessels with straight sides, suitable for holding a sample in a laboratory instrument.
Shapes made of fabric or paper, in modern times often tissue paper, used as guides to cut out sections of fabric that can be stitched together into articles of clothing.
Status occurring when items are left unsold and remain the property of the owner at an auction because there are no bids on a lot, or the bidding did not reach the reserve price.
Painters who created art conforming to the official standards and principles of taste of European and American art academies.
Instruments used to measure the percentage of alcohol contained in wine.
Data processors that operate on continuously variable data rather than digital input.
Machines and devices that perform arithmetical operations, often more complex than can be performed on adding machines.

Blankets comprising a cloth or velvet covering with cloth ties on the underside made to cover the front and sides of a dog's body. Usually richly decorated in floral beadwork and cloth fringe, with bells placed along the center cut of the blanket. Used to protect sled dogs and to herald the sled's arrival. Originated with the Métis and later spread to Athabaskan communities.

Hollow projectiles containing harmful agents such as shrapnel, explosives, or incendiary or poisonous chemicals, designed to be fired from artillery. For the explosive weapons, including both projectiles and stationary devices, which incorporate both a detonating mechanism and explosives or other harmful agents, use "bombs."
Weapons that serve ceremonial or symbolic functions, for instance as symbols of office, public regalia, or signs of personal status.
Containers for storing solid paints or pigments, such as watercolors or tubes of liquid paint, that typically contain one or more small pans for mixing and blending paints.

Telescopes that are mounted with one axis pointed toward the celestial pole, and the second axis parallel to the earth’s equator, allowing the telescopes to follow a celestial body by moving along the polar axis.
Dedicated devices that play audio in digital formats. These usually consist of internal storage, either a hard drive or flash memory, designed to retrieve content using an interface for navigation.
Various models of machines that are used for the recording of human speech for transcription purposes (such as Dictaphones).
Sets of pouches, sleeves, or other protective wraps bound together for the storage of sound recordings in the form of magnetic tapes.
Sets of pouches, sleeves, or other protective wraps bound together for the storage of sound recordings: most commonly laquer or vinyl discs, and sometimes magnetic tapes.
Small magnetic tape recorders that use tape wound on spools housed in cassettes, and that are meant to be easily transported. Most have a handle incorporated in their design.
Machines that close bags, typically of grain and flour, by means of sewing.
Containers used to collect voting ballots. Often made of cloth, plastic, or other flexible material.
Horizontal circular metal hoop supporting a net through which players try to throw a ball in the sport of basketball.
Laboratory baths that are used to dehydrate specimens or tissues.
Padded coverings for the hands of boxers in the form of gloves with a single undivided section for the fingers.
Skewers used to hold the carcasses of animals or other such pieces of meat while being butchered.
Machines that perform the mechanical operations involved in creating and providing billing records or invoices, such as calculations, typing, and duplication.
Filters that are attached to camera lenses to correct for the quality of ambient light or for other artistic purposes.

Glass, plastic, or gelatin light filters that accentuate the appearance of clouds in the sky. These may be tinted in a variety of ways to achieve a particular effect depending on the type of camera or film used.
Containers for transporting cups.
Genus of extremely slow growing, spineless, button-like cacti native to Texas and Mexico; the various species grow low to the ground and they often form groups with numerous, crowded shoots.

Species of small, spineless cactus native to Texas and Mexico. Peyote contains the hallucinogen mescaline. The plant is ingested for its psychoactive properties, having a long history of ritualistic and medicinal use by indigenous North Americans.

Written or oral compositions characterized by condensed language chosen for sound and suggestive power as well as meaning, and by the use of such literary techniques as structured meter, natural cadences, rhyme, or metaphor.

Formalized exhibitions that include works made by more than one person. This describes most accurately contemporary exhibitions that are devoted to visual works made by individual creators rather than historical or thematic exhibitions devoted to a broad subject.
Cloth book bindings that have an illustration or other image applied to or in the fabric of the binding.
Stories that focus on or deal primarily with animals, plants, natural features, or natural phenomena.
Popular literature from Northeastern Brazil. Usually, woodcuts illustrate cordel booklets, which are hung on a piece of string by vendors.

Adornments, embellishments, or ornamentation used to decorate the itnerior or exterior of a church, chapel, temple, city plaza, or other location, or the bier or coffin, where the deceased is laid out and honored during funerary rites. For ornaments worn by the deceased or attendees of the funeral, specifically designed for this purpose, use "funeral ornaments (personal ornament)."
Sexual activity in which the male organ of a partner is sucked or licked.

Family of saurian reptiles, small lizard-like creatures, distinguished by a prehensile tail, long tongue, eyes moving independently, and covered each with a single circular eyelid, having the characteristic of changing the color of their skin.
Genus containing herbivorous lizards that are native to tropical areas of Mexico, Central America, South America, and the Caribbean.
Italian black letter script that is more rounded than in northern centers.
Islamic architectural masonry style in which alternating light and dark courses of stone are a design element.
Meaning "at the abode of," in publishing refers to the publishing house.
Glass ware made of glass having a decorative mesh pattern or patterns of fine glass threads embedded inside.
Type of watermark, known in many variations, comprising a head in profile wearng a fool's cap and collar. Known from as early as 1580; found in paper from many European nations.
Early sound films that included synchronized dialogue; usage is usually reserved for films dating from the 1920s through early 1930s.

Aztec vestments comprising articulated pieces of iridescent shell sewn in a pattern on a textile support. Derived from Nahuatl for "joined mother -of-pearl." Many examples are made from the Pacific mollusk Pinctada mazatlanica.

Style of writing in inscriptions or other texts in which lines are written from right to left and from left to right in alternate lines. From the Greek boustrophēdon, meaning literally “to turn like oxen” (in plowing).
People who take part in card games.
Paper cups that were first used in ancient China; for serving of tea, often colorful and decorated.
Cups, usually disposable, designed for cold liquids.
Genus which contains about 50 species of flowering shrubs. It belongs to the Thymelaeaceae family and is native to Eurasia.

Fixed bridges that extend without hinges or joints across three or more supports, making them capable of resisting bending and shearing forces at all sections throughout their length; continuous bridges are firmly supported in the perpendicular direction by piers and abutments.
Metal implements consisting of a blade bent at a right angle extending from a handle. Used to clean off dough from a dough trough or to cut it into smaller portions.
Computer generated renderings of architectural structures that are interactive with the viewer.

In the Catholic church, churches having been bestowed an honorific assigned conferred by papal brief and including a certain precedence before other churches along with the right to display the conopaeum (a baldachin resembling an umbrella).
Veneer made from tree excrescences that are typically in the form of flattened hemispheres. For example, one type of burl veneer is made from the stumps of walnut trees.

In traditional Indian art and dance, a pose of ease and relaxation, with the figure having one leg folded on the seat while the other is pendant, hanging or extending downward, sometimes resting on a stool or other support. posture of royal ease.
Family of freshwater flatworms.
Order of free-living flatworms.
Genus of flatworm.

Bovid species equiped for living at high altitude, having large lungs, a high red blood cell count, and higher concentration of hemoglobin than most other bovids. Domesticated populations differ from the wild species, Bos mutus, in having shorter legs, broader hooves, more varied pelage coloration, and weaker horns which sometimes can be absent altogether. was probably domesticated in Tibet but has been introduced wherever there are people at elevations of 4,000-6,000 metres (14,000–20,000 feet), mainly in China but also in Central Asia, Mongolia, and Nepal.
Family of marine gastropod mollusks (sea snails).
Genus of very large marine gastropod mollusks (sea snails, having an operculum.
Genus of very large marine gastropod mollusks (sea snails), having an operculum (aperture cover). Found in the western Atlantic Ocean.
Order of bivalve molluscs; most are saltwater molluscs, although some are freshwater molluscs.

One of the largest family of marine bivalve mollusks comprised of over 200 species. The two valves of the shell are symmetrical, and range in colour from brown to red or yellow. The outer shell surface of many species can be smooth; others have ridges that radiate from the hinge area between the shells.
Species of marine bivalve mollusc, a member of the pearl oysters. It is found in shallow tropical waters on the Pacific coast of Central America; its shell was highly valued by Precolumbian cultures.
Genus of marine bivalve mollusks (saltwater oysters).
Family of medium-sized to large marine bivalve mollusks (saltwater clams). Some members of this family are noted for producing pearls.

Units of measurement of electrical current in the International System of Units, and defined as the intensity of the constant current which, when maintained in two parallel straight conductors of infinite length and of negligible cross section placed one metre apart in a vacuum, produced between them a force equal to 2 × 10−7 M.K.S. units of force per metre length. Defined by the International Weights and Measures Congress in 1948. It replaced the international ampere which had been defined in 1908.
Memory components of computers held on chips that retain data and instructions in a quickly accessible state that bypasses the usage of the computer's CPU.

Artificial compilations of sheet music that has been collected by an individual and bound into a single volume. The most common examples of these date to the early-mid-19th century, created when the owner, often a woman, had a personal collection bound for posterity. Many scholars consider the peak of this activity to be 1830-1880, though volumes of manuscripts or printed material are known since at least the 16th century. Binder’s volumes were most common in the 19th century because of advances in printing technology and the rise of a middle class. Around 1880, publishers began offering printed collections of music that could serve the same purpose as an individual’s binder’s volume, initiating the obsolescence of this object genre.
Korean gates used to mark the entrance to sacred sites such as royal tombs; having a light design comprising red columns and simple wooden rods arranged vertically.

Tamarix, also known as salt cedar, is a deciduous, flowering shrub that historically has been used for windbreaks, ornamentals, and erosion control. Tamarix is highly invasive and affects water drainage systems in North America.

Style of sculpture dating ca. 4,000-2,000 BCE in Anatolia, characterized by figures that have flat bodies, schematic features, detailed with light engraving and painting. Examples are highly stylized standing nude females with flipper-like arms and a bulbous head. The type is named after the village in Turkey where the first examples were found.
APIs or application programming interfaces are sets of standards, communication protocols, and tools for building software.

Computer interfaces in which software, files, or other data are represented by visual display with graphical symbols, icons, or menu items. These can be manipulated to allow functions to be performed without the use of a command language.
Subdiscipline of fluid mechanics that predicts the behaviour of fluids and of the effects of fluid motion past objects by numerical methods rather than model experiments.

Cryptocurrency comprising a digital payment system that has its own unit of account. It was devised in 2009 by an entity known as 'Satoshi Nakamoto,' which is presumed to be a pseudonym for one or more unknown persons.
Stamp art made specifically with rubber stamps.
Vascular plant genus in the flowering plant family Phyllanthaceae, with diverse growth forms including herbs, shrubs, climbers,etc. Most all exhibit phyllanthoid branching.

A deciduous tree of the family Phyllanthaceae. A few of its uses include its edible fruit, as a “green," nontoxic antioxidant, a rust removing agent of akaganeite from steel, and as a mordant for textiles.

Vacuum tubes for television cameras, using a photosensitive surface located in the image plane, of the television camera object lens; having a storage surface on which electronic charge is accumulated, and a scanning electron beam that discharges the target to produce the amplitude modulated video signal.

Small television camera tubes of a particular kind, in which the image is formed on a transparent electrode coated with photoconductive material, the video signal being obtained from the variation in the current flowing to or from this as it is scanned by a beam of (usually low-speed) electrons.

Unmanned underwater robots used for survey missions such as detecting and mapping submerged wrecks, rocks, and obstructions (with the use of sensors) that can be a hazard to navigation for commercial and recreational vessels. They complete these missions without operator control. For similar devices controlled by an operator remotely, use 'remote submersibles.'
Domain-specific language used in programming and designed for managing data held in a relational database management system, or for stream processing in a relational data stream management system.
Tree that is cultivated throughout the Old World tropics, notably in India and Southeast Asia. Used as a source of timber and medicinal oils and resins.

A whitish, malleable, metallic element from the alkaline earth group, occurring primarily as a sulfate (barite) and less often as a carbonate (witherite). Salts of barium are used as pigments in paints, ceramics, glass, plastics, and rubber, as fillers, as pesticides, and to produce the green color in fireworks.
Any compound joining fluorine to another element or to an organic group.

An element with atomic number 7 and symbol: N.  It is an odorless, gaseous element that makes up 78% of the earth's atmosphere, is a constituent of all living tissue, and is nearly inert in its gaseous form.

A soft, waxy, light, extremely malleable, silvery-white, unstable metallic element of the alkali group. It has the symbol Na in the periodic table and the atomic number 11. Sodium is the most common alkali metal and the sixth most abundant element on Earth. It appears only as a compound with other elements in nature. It has a strong affinity for oxygen and other nonmetallic elements. It is highly reactive, burns with a yellow flame, oxidizes in air, and reacts violently with water. Sodium provides the chief cation (positive ion) of extracellular body fluids. It is an essential nutrient in animals; it helps to maintain blood volume, regulate the balance of water in the cells, and keeps nerves functioning.
Substances composed by the chemical union of sulfur with additional elements.
Visual works in any medium that depict a landscape as a highly idealized version of nature and natural forms with references to Classical mythology.
The dried or partially dried fruit of the plum tree.
Species of flowering plant native to tropical South America, but cultivated widely for its edible seeds.
Drying houses built or used for drying fruit and vegetables specifically, fitted with shelves to lay out whole fruits or cut pieces fruit or hangers from which to suspend branches of fruit.

The function or method of signalling using flags to convey a code or using an apparatus, such as flag-like devices mounted on a tower. Semaphore conveys messages by a code whereby the arms are placed successively in certain positions in a vertical plane relative to the body, often with a flag in each hand.
Covers or shutters fitted in grooves to slide open and closed over a relatively small window or similar opening, such as on a ship or wall.
Small to massive colonial forms of coral. Lower parts of polyps fused into a fleshy mass; oral ends protrude. Internal skeleton of isolated calcareous spicules. Primarily tropical.
A family of corals.

Genus of corals having separate male and female colonies, and from the few reports of reproduction, it is believed that fertilization is internal, and therefore depends on free-swimming sperm from male colonies reaching the polyps of female colonies.

Species of coral that lives in the Mediterranean Sea and adjacent Eastern Atlantic Ocean on subtidal hard substrates. Corallium rubrum is a long-lived gorgonian coral that has been commercially harvested since ancient times for its red axial calcitic skeleton and which, at present, is thought to be in decline because of overexploitation.

Genus of bivalve mollusks, characterized by foliaceous spines. They are used for edible meat and for their decorative shells. Although some common names include the word "oyster," they are not closely related to true oysters (in the family Ostreidae).
Species of bivalve mollusk; noted for having decorative and symbolic value for Pre-Columbian cultures.
The larger of two species of elephants existing in Africa.

Lacquer discs were the most common type of instantaneous recordings. These consisted of a coated substrate with grooves cut into the coating, allowing for playback. The format replaced wax matrices used for recording and mastering in the mid-1930s and was the dominant format for making original, or master, recordings before the advent of magnetic tape. Lacquer discs are often incorrectly referred to as acetate discs, or acetates, though they are composed of a nitrocellulose lacquer layer applied to an aluminum, glass, or steel base. The thin lacquer layer on new discs was soft enough to be inscribed with grooves by a cutting stylus and resilient enough to survive several playbacks and were used to record radio programs, field recordings, and other live events. Those made by radio networks and others for professional purposes were often 16 inches in diameter, while those recorded for personal purposes were more often 7 to 12 inches.

Optical, machine readable codes, usually representing numbers, rendered as black and white bars of varying width that carry information; used for entering data or making data legible to a computer system. Bar codes are often used to identify, for pricing, organizing, or distinguish information about one thing, person, or other entity from others.
Species of evergreen tree native to Africa.

Describes conservation activities that are accessible by or visible to the public, usually in museums, archaeological sites, or other cultural heritage settings. As a form of public outreach, these activities are typically intended to promote education and raise awareness of heritage conservation.

In a controlled vocabulary hierarchy, an ancestor record that provides a broader context for the record at hand, and that is defined as the primary ancestor record in the event of there being multiple ancestors in a polyhierarchical structure. The status of being the preferred parent may be defined by multiple parameters as indicated by the guidelines of the database or the hierarchy itself.
Plier-shaped punches with several different-sized heads mounted on a wheel, for punching holes of different diameters. The punching is accomplished by squeezing the handles of the tool together.

Genus of primarily herbaceous flowering plants, valued for their ornamental flowers. Included are common wildflowers and others that have been extensively cultivated and hybridised for hundreds of years.

Species of flowering plant native to western and southern Europe. Distinguished by having broad leaves and short leafless stems, each bearing a solitary pale yellow flower; pink and reddish varieties are found in nature and in cultivation. Numerous cultivars were popular in the 19th and 20th centuries in garden planting. The primrose is one of the earliest spring flowers in much of Europe, thus the common name is derived from  medieval Latin "prima rosa," meaning "first rose," although the plant is not closely related to the rose family.
Genus containing around 120 species of shrubs or small trees native to warm temperate and tropical regions of the Northern Hemisphere, in eastern and southeastern Asia and South America.
Annual European Alpine event, comprising the herding of cattle and other animals from the summer pastures to lower latitudes;  takes place in late September or early October.
The herding cattle over a significant distance.

Groups of electors in a political system, by whom leaders are chosen for a particular office. Examples are the electoral college of United States presidential elections and the electoral college of cardinals who elect a pope.
Moveable bars carrying the reed of a loom that strike home each filling thread as they are interlaced with the warp by the passage of the shuttle.

Entoprocta is treated as a class of phylum Kamotozoa, rather than as a full phylum. Group of small, aquatic invertebrate animals composed of about 150 species and subdivided into four families. Entoprocts occur throughout the world, primarily in marine habitats, although one genus is a freshwater form.
Initial letters formed from figures of human, animal, or hybrid creatures.
Plays in which the dialogue is written in verse lines.
People who are expert in or students of Asian history, art, culture, etc.

Compositions of tunes, melodies, or other pieces of music or song in which a single melodic line predominates, and which has little or no distinctive accompaniment; if a song, may have simple or unobtrusive accompaniment.

Academically oriented study of theater, comprising theater criticism, history, aesthetics, and the study of drama as a specialized form of literature. For the professionally oriented study and practice of theater, use "theater (discipline)."

The discipline having to do with ballet, which is artistic dance in which stylized poses and steps are combined with light and flowing figures and movements, such as leaps and turns; often combined with music, scenery, costume, and sometimes pantomime or speech to convey a story, theme, or atmosphere to the audience.
Discipline involving the study of the theoretical aspects of music and its notation, typically as opposed to actual performance.
Operas in which the subject matter and characters are usually treated light-heartedly and humorously, the ending is happy or conciliatory, and a large part of the dialogue is spoken.
Expositions of a given subject delivered before an audience or class, especially for the purposes of instruction.

Important form of classical Japanese dance drama that has been performed since the 14th century. It is often based on stories from traditional literature with a supernatural being transformed into human form as a hero telling a story. Noh integrates masks, costumes and various props into a dance-based performance, Emotions are mainly conveyed through stylized conventional gestures.

The art of tumbling, balancing, and jumping presented as performance, often with the use of such apparatus as poles, unicycles, tightropes, trampolines, and trapezes, and typically performed at fairgrounds, circuses, and theaters. For the competitive sport involving physical exercises of strength, agility, and balance, use "gymnastics."
Method of acquiring property through bidding at an auction.
Recording the entry of items into a collection in the order of acquisition.
Method of acquiring property for use over an extended period of time, but without transferring ownership to the second party.
Seals stamped on books and prints indicating that the work has been approved by a censor for publication. Prime examples are censor's seals on Japanese prints dating from the 18th-19th centuries.

General designation for the ethnicity, styles, culture, and heritage of people of sub-Saharan African origin or descent in places outside Africa, or of members of any dark-skinned group of peoples, including those of  Australian Aboriginal origin or descent. Exceptions for usage include when black people are the majority in a particular country, unless they are treated or considered as a separate group, as was the case in South Africa under apartheid.
General term for the culture and styles of ancient Jews, up to the Medieval period, including culture that does not have strictly to do with religion per se.
Nationality, style, and culture of Jewish people living in Baghdad, Iraq.
The cultivation of fresh water and marine species of fish, shellfish, and aquatic plants; the aquatic equivalent of agriculture.

Cloaks worn by the Aboriginal people of certain areas of Australia, made from the skins of Australian possums (members of Phalangeriformes), sometimes together with other small pelts such as from flying squirrels, sewn together; the cloaks were used as a garment to cover the back and shoulders, as a blanket, and as a sling for carrying infants.
Family of nocturnal marsupial mammals native to Australia, New Guinea, and parts of Indonesia; according to some classifications, the family includes 6 genera containing 28 species.

Body of laws that are derived from canon law and civil law, administered by ecclesiastical courts. Ecclesiastical laws govern the rules and doctrine of a specific church. Examples are the laws of the Anglican church.
Development rights to the space above a piece of real estate; the owner of the land may sell or lease these rights to another party.
Offerings to a deity, for the purpose of propitiation or homage, usually something of value, material or immaterial; human, animal, or other living agent or object.

System of law concerned with private relations between members of a community rather than criminal, military, or religious affairs. Examples are systems developed from the Roman law,  influenced by Germanic, ecclesiastical, and purely modern institutions.
A system of ecclesiastical law, especially of the Roman Catholic Church as promulgated in ecclesiastical councils and by the pope.
Breast ornaments worn by Jewish high priests. Traditionally comprising a folded piece of embroidered linen worn on the breast, and adorned with twelve precious stones, representing the twelve tribes.
Large packages consisting of cloth or leather wrapped around a human cadaver or sacrificial animal and other objects. Prime examples are funerary bundles of the indigenous cultures of the Americas.
Funerary bundles of the indigenous cultures of the Andes, containing the mummified remains of sacrificial victims or other people.
Ceremonial packages in which a symbolic object is wrapped in skins or textiles that gives concrete expression to the presence of a deity in postclassic central Mexico. Literally, "wrapped thing."
Even-weave textile of long, strong cotton or linen fibers, used as a needlepoint foundation.

Conventional costumes worn by ballerinas, composed of fine tarlatan or other light-weight materials that often expose the dancers' knees. Traditionally consists of a tutu, bodice, basque or peplum, and waistband.

Religion of the Aztec culture. It was based on earlier belief systems, filtered down from the Olmecs, Teotihuacan, Monte Alban, Mayan, and fellow Nahuatl-speaking Toltec peoples; was typically Mesoamerican in terms of cosmology, the emphasis on the sun, and even particular deities.

The general method used to sample or scan a surface using laser technology. Controlled deflection of laser beams to perform analysis or provide insight.  Uses are many, including in laser printers, in laser shows, stereolithography machines, barcode scanners, in rapid prototyping, in machines for material processing, in laser engraving machines, in ophtalmological laser systems, and in many other uses.
Process of scanning a three-dimensional real-world object or environment to analyze and collect data.

Skirts, usually made from felt, falling to the knee or just below, with a nipped waist and full silhouette. These were popular in the United States during the early 1950s. So-called because they often included an appliqué of a poodle, though variations of the applied image were common, and were often personalized. The original invention is credited to Julie Lynn Charlot, who sold pre-made skirts as well as patterns for home construction.
Lingerie shorts popular from the 1920s. Originally made for dancing, but more popularly worn as an undergarment.
Miniature versions of clothing meant to be worn by figural toys.
Distinctive uniforms worn by servants or other classes of people.
Button-down, collared outer garments worn by hunters for convenience and warmth. These traditionally featured poacher's pockets for storing small game.
Special clothing used for performances of dance.

Tailored costumes, made of durable material such as linen or wool, worn by cyclists predominately in the late 19th century. Typically comprised of a matching set of garments including trousers or a skirt, a short button-up jacket, bloomers, leggings, and a cap,
Flat, stand-up collars, starched, wired, or otherwise stiffened, especially those commonly worn by men and women in the 17th century.
Genus of tropical flowering plants, including around 200 species, several of which are sources of the drug cocaine.

General term for any of four varieties of plants of the genus Erythroxylum that are indigenous to western South America and cultivated in Africa, South America, Southeast Asia, and Taiwan. The leaves are used with powdered lime, as a masticatory, appeaser of hunger, and stimulant of the nervous system.
Double-hulled voyaging canoes.
Referes to traditional bungalow home style native to Portland, Oregon.
In language, words or lexical units that modify the meaning of a verb, adjective, or another adverb, expressing manner, place, time, or degree.
Language of an Anatolian people contemporary with the Hittites, known from hieroglyphic and cuneiform inscriptions.
In some classifications, a large branch of the Romance languages.
Group of related Romance languages, including Spanish, Asturian-Leonese, Aragonese, Catalan, Portuguese, French, Franco-Provençal, Gascon, Provençal, Gallo-Wallon, Romansh, and Ladin.
Group of related Romance languages that developed on the Iberian Peninsula, comprising modern Spain, Portugal, Gibraltar and Andorra, and in southern France.
Branch of Romance languages that includes Castilian, Astur-Leonese, and modern descendants of Galician-Portuguese.
Languages that include Castilian Spanish and its closest relatives.

Romance language spoken by Sephardic Jews in Israel, the Balkans, North Africa, Greece, and Turkey. It combines a very archaic form of Castilian Spanish with Hebrew, along with elements from Aramaic, Arabic, Turkish, Greek, French, Bulgarian, and Italian. Ladino originated in Spain and was carried to its present speech areas by the descendants of the Spanish Jews who were expelled from Spain after 1492.
Inexpensive machine-made oriental paper.
Coin-like tokens not intended as legal tender that celebrate notable people or events.
Family of sea turtles containing 5 extant genera.
Genus containing only one extant species.
Species of sea turtle, critically endangered; was primary source of the material tortoise shell for hundreds of years.
Flexible slender branches, stems, or twigs of willow, specifically Salix viminalis, or common osier, used for tying, binding, or weaving, especially in basketry, or to construct furniture.
The variety of Spanish spoken in Basque Country; not to be confused with the Basque language, which is not related to Spanish and is not a Romance language.
Refers to the variety of Spanish spoken in the Antilles; it is largely of Andalusian derivation.
The variety of Balearic Catalan spoken on the island of Mallorca, along with Mallorcan Spanish.

East Asian language spoken primarily in Japan. Held by many modern scholars to be a member of the Japonic (or Japanese-Ryukyuan) family of languages, while others maintain that it is a language isolate.
Rods or slips of wood designed for personal reading, used for following words on a page; may be highly decorative and of a type used in the Early Christian and Medieval periods.
Currency issued by the French revolutionary government between 1789 and 1796, in the form of paper money and based on the security of the state lands.

Paper money representing standard monetary units in the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, historically from states in the USA, and other places; each equal to 100 cents. Originally from a silver coin that circulated in many European countries.
The built-up or elevated parts of the soles of shoes or boots, that support the heel of the wearer.
Chief Buddhist priests of the Tibetan territories.
In Buddhism, dedicated mendicants or religious devotees.
Genus of South American rodent containing one extant species.
Species of rodent endemic to a wide variety of habitats in central Chile.
In Hinduism, mother-goddesses, seven in number.
Species of aromatic herb cultivated for its pungent leaves; native to the Mediterranean region.
In Japanese folklore, tools or household objects that have acquired a kami or spirit.
Beings who hold up the weight of the world or planet earth; examples are Atlas in Classical mythology and the Diggajas in Hinduism.
A measurement unit of frequency, equal to 1000 megahertz (MHz). Used most often in reference to computer processing speeds.
Photographs created specifically to promote products or services to the public. These are often commissioned or produced by advertising agencies.
The activity of creating photographs to promote products or services to the public. This is often commissioned or produced by advertising agencies.
In Hinduism, planetary divinities, nine in number.
Monstrous men with two heads but only one body, literally, "one who has two heads" in Nahuatl. One of the omens predicting the arrival of the Spaniards.
Masks used by actors in Ancient Greek and Roman theater, having many standard variations, representing comical or silly expressions.
Deities or supernatural powers who are protectors, guardians, or patrons who watch over a particular person, place, or thing.

Shortened versions of a name or title, using abbreviations instead of spelling out words. Applied only to titles or names using abbreviations to a significant extent, typically not when a single word is abbreviated. For personal names, use abbreviated names.

In book cataloging, a parallel title is the title proper of an edition in a language or script other than that of the original title. For example, if the original Chinese title is translated into English for cataloging purposes.
Identifying codes for world languages or language families, living and extinct, maintained by the International Organization for Standardization.
Expressions of words by letters that are incorrect.
An order of Agaricomycetes containing over 1300 species of diverse fruiting body types. Most members are saprobic, primarily found on the wood of fallen trees or in the soil at the base of trees.
Rights to property that is destined for the support of ministers of Christian religion or of an ecclesiastical office.
Decorative items worn inserted into a hole in or near the lip.
Species of tree native to tropical America, from which cocoa and chocolate are prepared.
Fruits of a tree native to tropical America, the seeds of which are used to prepare cocoa and chocolate.
Boletes with red tubes and pores, a red-dotted yellow stem and blue staining flesh.
Species of perennial grassland herb; noted in Classical literature as used for medicinal purposes.
Prints of a film provided to a movie theater or other venue for exhibition.

Sun rooms, usually located at the back of a dwelling, equipped with a bar or other furnishings to allow preparation of beverages and entertaining of guests. Traditionally, Florida rooms have tile floors.
In Indian architecture, the quality of being two-sided.
Dishes passed around a congregation, used to hold offerings. Made of various materials. For flatter, plate-like containers, use "offering plates."

Nahua tlahuiztli (insignia) in the form of large umbrella-shaped feathered structures worn on a back-frame. These were prestigious gifts presented to nobles made in a variety of colors, and was frequently topped with an effigy head of the deity Xolotl; hence its name, "Xolotl-head." This insignia also represents the altepetl of Tepeticpac, Tlaxcala.

Works of folk art made from sugar and other ingredients, of distinctive types and known in Mexico and elsewhere in Latin America and the United States. These types of works originated in sugar figures made for religious celebrations in Italy; they spread to Spain and in the Spanish colonies were enriched with indigenous art styles.

The non-living bodies of animals, and sometimes of humans, with an emphasis on the structure of the body rather than death or corruption. With butchers, it refers the whole trunk of a slaughtered animal.
Characters known from legend and stories, whether or not there is a counterpart in recorded history.
Graffiti pieces that are regarded as being of exceptional quality, as judged by other graffiti artists. To ‘burn’ is to outdo the work of others.
Larger and more involved graffiti art 'pieces' that involve several artists working together. These are achieved legally, where permission has been granted or the work commissioned.

The first month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendars, containing 31 days and falling before February. It was named after Janus, the Roman god of all beginnings. January replaced March as the first month of the Roman year no later than 153 BCE.

The day following Saturday and preceding Monday, observed by Christians as a day of rest and religious worship, traditionally regarded as the first day of the week, and usually considered (together with Saturday) as forming part of the weekend. In English and other languages, the name refers to the Roman Sun’s-day. In Romance languages, name refers to the Lord's day.
A combination of adverse circumstances or events occurring by chance; a person's apparent tendency to have ill fortune; misfortune.

A genre of animated film or television entertainment distinctively Japanese or in Japanese-style, characterized by a visual style involving stylized action sequences and usually featuring characters with distinctive large, staring eyes, and typically having a having themes of science-fiction, fantasy, violence, or sexually explicit material.

Wood trays used to hold moveable type. These are 32 inches long, 17 inches wide and two inches deep and are divided into compartments of various sizes to accommodate letters that occur more or less frequently. California job cases are arranged such that capital letters are at the right and lower-case are at the left. Special characters such as dollar signs or parentheses are in the top row.

Edicts, laws, announcements, or narrative histories, usually issued by a sovereign to his subjects, and carved into rocks for posterity and for display to the public; rock edicts may be carved into cliff rock, onto pillars or stelae, and in caves.

Shallow trays made to hold moveable type for hand-type setting. These are divided into compartments for each letter in a font of type, and typically are laid out with capitals to the right and lower-case characters to the left.

Coachmen in colonial Latin America, usually depicted stereotypically as black men, usually slaves, who drove calesas, or carriages. Their extravagant uniforms and ornamentation were indications of their owners' wealth. In Cuba, caleseros are distinctive characters of the colonial period and are usually portrayed in images as garishly dressed dandies.

Species of shrub or small tree found in regions of Africa, the Americas, southern Asia, and Australasia. extremely tough and durable. In New Zealand its heavy wood is traditionally used by the Maori for making weapons, ax handles, walking sticks, and for other purposes.
Compositions comprising a musical farce with songs.

The state of being physically or psychologically habituated to a substance or practice to such an extent that its cessation causes severe trauma. For the long term or excessive use or misuse of narcotics, alcohol, or other substances, use "substance abuse."
Species of gram-negative, rod-shaped coccobacillus that can infect humans via the oriental rat flea, causing infection that takes three main forms: pneumonic, septicemic, and bubonic plagues.

Genus containing ovoid- or rod-shaped bacteria of the family Enterobacteriaceae. Yersinia are gram-negative bacteria and are described as facultative anaerobes, which means that they are capable of surviving in both aerobic and anaerobic environments.

Family of gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacteria that do not form endospores. Its organisms are distributed worldwide with some being saprophytes and others being plant and animal parasites. Many species are of considerable economic importance due to their pathogenic effects on agriculture and livestock.
Order of gram-negative bacteria containing one family, Enterobacteriaceae.
A group of the proteobacteria comprised of facultatively anaerobic and fermentative gram-negative bacteria.

Family of RNA viruses containing four genera, some of which are noted for causing influenza in humans. Orthomyxoviridae have enveloped virions (virus particles) that measure between 80 and 120 nm (1 nm = 10−9 metre) in diameter. The nucleocapsid, which consists of a protein shell, or capsid, and contains the viral nucleic acids, has helical symmetry. The orthomyxovirus genome contains eight segments of single-stranded negative-sense RNA (ribonucleic acid), and an endogenous RNA polymerase is present for the transcription of the negative-sense strand into a positive-sense strand to enable protein synthesis. The lipoprotein envelope of the virion contains two glycoproteins, designated hemagglutinin (major antigen) and neuraminidase.
Insignia in the form of shields that identify membership in a fraternal organization.
Epidemics of infectious disease that are extremely widespread, for example have spread to many countries, often to more than one continent, usually affecting a large number of victims.
Culture at Chiripa dating from 1500-1000 BCE, based on calibrated radiocarbon dates from 1992 and 1996 excavations.
Whistles or other simple instruments for imitating the song of birds, in order to attract or decoy them.
Groupings into which items are divided to be sold at an auction.
The act or function of using lots, which are bits of wood, paper, or another material, to make decisions based on random selection.
A type of layered composite wood board made from the shavings and flakes of wood that are generated at saw mills.

Fiberboard that is typically made of wood fibers left over from processing of hard woods or soft woods; distinguished from medium-density fiberboard and low-density fiberboard by density of fiber and strength.
Common term for the transparent larvae of members of the Chaoboridae family.

Formerly considered a separate phylum; now generally classified as an order of annelids. Contains primarily marine invertebrate sausage-shaped organisms, that have lost their segmentation, found in sand and mud of tropical and subtropical seas. A flattened extension of the head is curved along its lateral edges and sometimes shaped like a scoop or spoon to form a nonretractable anterior proboscis. Some respiration probably takes place across the body wall, but the hind gut is often utilized as a respiratory organ by drawing water through the anus.
Magnifying devices designed for individual direct viewing of backlighted filmstrips.
Dress associated with a culture defined by or named for a nationality.
Descending troughs partially filled with constantly moving water through which people may ride or slide, usually terminating in a pool of water.
Cathers provided with a small balloon to enlarge passages or openings as in a blood vessel.
Memorials mounted to a wall or pillar of a church consisting of a framed stone or wooden slab bearing an epitaph.
Series of defenses covered by flooding. This type of defense was practiced in the Netherlands with its many waterways and polders.
Cookstoves fueled by alcohol.
Windmills in which the caps are turned by a winch inside the cap itself.
Type of eel traps comprising a container, often woven, with funnel-shaped openings; used for catching eels.
Post mills having a shorter central post, and developed specifically as sawmills.

Flexible, sterile tubes that pass throught the urethra and into the bladder to drain urine. These feature two separate channels, one to drain liquid, and one to keep the catheter in place through the use of a balloon filled with sterile water. This type of catheter was developed by the urologist Frederic E.B. Foley in the 1930s.
Genus having one extant species.
Species of plant native to temperate forests of central and southern Chile and Argentina; known for leaves that can mimic leaves of various other nearby species of plants.

General term for Nahua ornaments worn on the ear. The term refers to a wide variety of designs made from many materials, including simple earplugs and larger earflares to more complex pendant ornaments in the form of vegetal or animal elements.

Circular, silver ornaments applied to belts, riding tack, jewelry, and clothing; often decorated with stamped inlay and semi-precious stones such as turquoise. Originated in the mid-1800s amongst Navajo (Diné) and Pueblo silversmiths.

Plaques designed to be worn on a belt or as part of belt assemblage; may be decorative and functional. Examples are found in many cultures, including Chinese cultures and Precolumbian cultures, such as used for Maya rulers. Usage sometimes overlaps with "belt plates," although items made of stone are typically called "belt plaques"; for items dated to the 18th-century and later, usually metal, worn on belts to signify military rank or affiliation, always use "belt plates."

Animated films in which a viewer travels through and around architecture and related environments. May refer to a stand-alone film focused exclusively on architecture, or footage included in a larger film. For computer-generated programs rather than films, in which the viewer is moving through an architectural space and surroundings, whether or not the user can interact with the space, use "architectural walkthroughs."
Animations depicting a built work or urban space, as if the viewer were floating or flying through the space. Such works are used for architectural models and for other purposes.

A theoretical tenet for conserving cultural heritage. The theory maintains that what is old acquires a value of its own due to age, therefore the signs of age, such as patina, should be retained and not corrected or hidden. Based on the philosophy of Viennese art historian Alois Riegl (1858-1905).
Long, tapering, knitted caps.
Racks for the towels on which a priest dries his hands after washing them before celebrating Mass.
Processional torches or other lamps used by a given guild and marked by the insignia of that guild.

Qualifier used for attributions to express minor to moderate uncertainty regarding the attribution to a known creator, as when the work's provenance, style, or physical characteristics strongly suggest a given creator, but the attribution cannot be validated with absolute certainty (e.g., attributed to Frans Hals (Dutch painter, ca. 1581-1666)).

Qualifier used for attributions of works by an unknown creator working under a master's name, generally in a system of apprenticeship common from ancient times through the mid-17th century (e.g., workshop of Gislebertus).

Qualifier used for a work by an unknown creator whose style is strongly influenced by the named artist or architect, and who is living at the same time as or shortly after the named artist, but is not necessarily his or her pupil (e.g., follower of Hokusai).
Qualifier used for a work by an unknown creator who has created a copy of a known work of the named artist.

Actions or processes resulting in the change of form in an animal or its parts, during post-embryonic development. The term is used for the process of transformation from an immature form to a different adult form that many insects and other invertebrates, and some vertebrates (e.g., frogs), undergo in the course of maturing.

In modern usage, reproduction from a gamete without fertilization, occurring most commonly in invertebrates and lower plants, but also occasionally in some vertebrates, such as birds and reptiles, that normally would require sexual reproduction. The term was formerly also used for asexual reproduction, as by fission or budding.

Transcriptions focusing on the pronunciation of the transcribed words or text. Examples include the use of phonetic symbols as an abbreviation for a phonetic description; some of the allophones may be represented by specific symbols, or some of the phonemes may be designated by the symbols for a more restricted set of categories.
Electronic storage media used especially in digital cameras and mobile phones in the form of small, removable flash memory drives.
A type of non-volatile memory storage that does not require moving parts such as spinning magnetic or optical platters, and that stores data in blocks rather than bytes.

Raised cushions, stools, or boards for kneeling, often attached to pews or having an elbow rest or desk attached. Kneelers are found in churches, but also in private chambers, including chapels, bedrooms, and studies.

Certificates verifying the authenticity of a relic, which is a part of a body or an item that was in contact with a holy person or deity. In Roman Catholic tradition, the certificate for the relic of a saint will attest to the relic's being what it is claimed to be, so far as is known or believed by the signees; it will include the status of the relic as first, second, or third class, defined by the immediacy of association with the saint.
Technique of laying masonry of squared stones in courses that are not continuously of even height, as distinguished from "range work."

Devices used for detecting the explosive gas methane in the context of mining operations. A firedamp detector is hung at the mining face or in other work areas to monitor methane levels and sound an alarm when they reach a dangerous concentration.

General name for a number of computer operating systems for personal computers; several unrelated microcomputer disk operating systems had "DOS" in their names. An example was MS-DOS, which dominated the IBM PC-compatible market between 1981 and 1995.
Dates or dating offering a choice or another possibility to the primary or originally assigned date.

In reference to visual works, the main or front surface of the work. For the back or secondary surface, use "side B." Examples include extend indications for ancient Greek vessels and other such works.

Identification of years as Before Common Era or Before Current Era or Before Christian Era. BCE uses the same numbering as BC (Before Christ) and corresponds to the Gregorian Calendar. "CE" and "BCE" are placed after a year number, and BCE is now most often used instead of BC especially in scientific writing.

Lunisolar calendar of Assyria and Babylon, having years consisting of 12 lunar months, each beginning a new crescent moon on the western horizon at sunset. It was based on a Sumerian calendar, dated at least to ca. 21st century BCE.
Status of recognition and protection for a structure, area, or thing. An example is the status assigned by the U.S. National Register of Historic Places.
Years, or spans of time, periods, seasons, during which something lasts; the duration or term of existence or during which something happened or is to happen.

Dating system based on a year consisting of synodic months, which are complete cycles of phases of the Moon. In every solar year (or year of the seasons), there are about 12.37 synodic months. Therefore, if a lunar-year calendar is to be kept in step with the seasonal year, a periodic intercalation (addition) of days is necessary.
The provision, serving, or preparation of food, particularly regarding the industry concerned with this.
Boards upon which one writes directly, usually of a size larger than handheld. For smaller board-like objects for writing, use "writing tablets (writing equipment)."
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 303/304-347; ruled by the Li family of the Ba ethnicity.

Numeric, alphanumeric, or other identifying codes assigned when an art object, book, or other item enters the collection of a museum, library, or other repository. Such codes are unique within the set of codes, and specifically identify the particular item at hand. The numbers may be marked on the objects or not.
Unique resource locators that, in addition to identifying a resource, provide the address of the internet document according to one of a variety of protocols.

Technique using a silver wire or rod to draw on a prepared surface, usually paper or parchment; when a silver mark is made on the ground, the metal particles tarnish to form a black mark of silver sulfide.

Drawings made by using an implement comprising thin, sharpened rods of silver, usually in a holder, on a support of paper, parchment, or wood treated with a prepared wash or gesso. Ivory may also be used as a support. The silver lines oxidize quickly, making the drawing more distinct, but still delicate and fine.
Movement and positioning of limbs, hands, or body as a means of intentional expression. For positioning of the body primarily for artistic effect, prefer "pose."
Alternative names for a person, corporate body, place, or thing; possibly but not necessarily false or assumed names; they may be simply variant forms of proper names.
Surnames composed of two or more proper names, usually joined by a hyphen, preposition, or conjunction.
Sets or group of initial letters used as an abbreviation for a name or expression and pronounced as a single word.
Designations for streets, highways, roads, or other thoroughfares, either proper names or numeric indicators.
Nicknames indicating a diminutive or affectionate reference. In English, often made with the addition of a "y" or "ie."  An example would be "Annie" used for "Ann."
Pseudonyms adopted by members of the Bentvueghels group, also called Schildersbent; it was a 17th-18th century association of mainly Dutch and Flemish artists living in Rome.

Information that is formatted and presented in a form that is easily legible and understood by users, often allowing expressions of uncertainty and nuance. Display information is often used in conjunction with "indexing information."
Built works transmitted inter-generationally within a society and that are invested with significance in that society.

The urban area understood as the result of a historic layering of cultural and natural values and attributes, extending beyond the notion of “historic center” or “ensemble” to include the broader urban context and its geographical setting, including social and cultural practices and values, economic processes, and the intangible dimensions of heritage as related to diversity and identity. The recommendation on the Historic Urban Landscape was adopted on 10 November 2011 by UNESCO’s General Conference.
In Indian architecture, a lion-throne.
Refers to an architectural order characterized by capitals composed of foliate echini derived from the Corinthian order superposed by volutes derived from the Ionic order.

Dipan is an architectural term seen in Yingzao fashi (1103) and Luban yingzao zhengshi (1465-1505), but is also used in texts related to building activities such as Zhuzi yulei (1270), and Yangzhou huafang lu (18th cen.). Interpretations of the term and its relevant images in the Yingzao fashi are under debate. Some scholars suggest it concerns the plan of puzuo (corbelling) seen at a vertical position above the pillar top (Chen Mingda, 2010), either understood as reflected ceiling plan (Chen Mingda 1981), or the view looking downward from above (Zhu Yongchun 2016). Others interpret the term as a ground plan showing pillar positions and, in some cases, the layout of puzuo (Pan Guxi, He Jianzhong 2005). Recently Ren Sijie has shown how this term was likely directly related to the building foundation Ren Sijie 2016).
A group of writing systems that are descended from the Brahmi script of ancient India, and now used throughout South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, and formerly in Japan.

The process or activity of writing, marking, or delineating a date on something, usually indicating when the thing was created, and usually with the intention that the inscription will be conspicuous or durable.

A Postclassic Nahua garment design, literally of "eyes on the edge." It was composed with white circles on a black background in a band at the hem. As a prestigious design added to capes, it was typically worn by tlahtohqueh (rulers) and pipiltin (high ranking noble men), and occasionally appeared on women's clothing. The design may also be correlated with the deity Tezcatlipoca.

The only genus in the flowering plant family Paeoniaceae. They are native to Asia, Southern Europe and Western North America. Boundaries between species are not clear and estimates of the number of species range from 25 to 40.
According to many taxonomies, a subfamily of Nymphalidae butterflies that includes the morphos, the owl butterflies (Caligo), and related lineages.
According to many taxonomies, a tribe of the nymphalid butterfly subfamily Morphinae.

Genus containing a large number of species of neotropical butterflies found mostly in South America, Mexico, and Central America. Many speices are distinguished by metallic, shimmering shades of blues and greens color on the dorsal side of the wings, with the ventral side brown with eyespots.
General term for any of four or more species of moths in genus Morpho having blue wings.
Genus of moth having species found primarily in North and South America.
Species of moth found widely in North, Central, and South America. There are several subspecies.

In plants, the process or series of processes through which energy of light is absorbed by chlorophyll and utilized by the plants for the synthesis of complex organic compounds from carbon dioxide, with the accompanying oxidation of water to form oxygen. In animals, any of various similar processes by which the energy of light is converted to chemical energy for biosynthesis in bacteria, often involving alternative sources of carbon and not resulting in the generation of oxygen.
In Pre-Columbian Mexico, small T-shaped hachuelas or axes used as money or a unit of exchange in markets. In Africa, full size objects in the shape of an ax and used as currency.
The application of the principles of mechanics and hydraulics to engineering problems dealing with soil as an engineering material.

In geology, the discipline that studies and predicts the nature and operation of the forces by which the earth's surface are affected, as distinguished from the existing condition of the surface and the order and characteristics of the strata.
Large houses or estates in Spain, Portugal, and Latin America in the country or on the outskirts of a town; may be associated with vineyards or cattle ranches.

Species of vulture that ranges from southern Mexico to Argentina, where they soar singly or in pairs over tropical forests. Noted for distinctive color: the head and neck are red, yellow, and bluish; the eyes are white with red eye-rings; the body is buff above and white below; and the neck fringe is gray. Wingspan is about 2 metres; the body is about 80 cm (31 inches) long.
Females whose job or activity is to milk cows or sometimes goats, usually employed in a dairy.
A preparation or extract of the root of an aconite (genus Aconitum), used as a drug or as a poison.

Genus containing aropund 250 species of evergreen shrubs and trees native to East Asia. It is best known for a few ornamental flowering species and for Camellia sinensis, the source of the beverage tea.

Species of evergreen shrub or small tree native to Asia, but today cultivated widely in tropical and subtropical regions. It is known in several varieties. The leaves and leaf buds are used to produce the beverage tea.
General term for lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender / transsexual / transvestite attractions or behavior.

Contemporary outdoor paintings, drawings, or three-dimensional works on walls, sidewalks, or street surfaces in public thoroughfares of urban environments, sometimes intended to draw attention to urban issues.
Area or linear space in the natural world or built environment that  is or in the past has been considered important or revered in a religious or spiritual context.
Rhythmic movements of the body, usually to the accompaniment of music; as a performative work, or as part of tradition or ceremony.
In Christian tradition, prayers or offices appointed to be said at the seven stated canonical hours or times of the day allotted to prayer.

Bell-shaped jars, placed open-end down on a base and usually sealed, for display or storage of artifacts, natural specimens, dried flower arrangements, figurines, objets d'art, or other decorative items. For bell-shaped glass covers used to protect living plants, use "bell glasses (horticultural containers)."

Flowers, often with stems attached, and other plants that are treated so as to remove moisture and in order to preserve them. Methods of drying flowers include hanging to dry, covering with a desiccant such as glycerin and silica, or pressing between paper, a textile, or another absorbent, wicking material.

Metal racks, usually comprising a round metal band supporting multiple hooks, that were hung from the ceiling or another support and used to hang meat. The racks are usually historical. Antique crown meat racks are sometimes used in modern kitchens as pot racks
Iron component of a scratch plow attached to the colter, with a sharp and pointy edge to cut the earth while plowing.
Hard, fine-grained siliceous sedimentary rock composed of the remains of radiolarians, single-celled organisms that sink to the seafloor and form this rock, or radiolarian earth.
Rosaline lace with a little pearl in needle lace added to the heart of the rosaline-flowers.
Mixed lace from Milan with a ground in needle lace on which motifs made from mechanically made tape are applied; these motifs most often depict flowers.
Frames with dark slides used to hold flexible photosensitized cut film.
Covers that fit over the nails of the fingers or toes. Examples include caps used for decorative purposes or in burial rituals.
The undersurfaces of shoes that elevate the foot at approximately the same height over their entire length. These may be solid or constructed from discontinuous components such as stilts or wedges.
Small hollows or dents formed in a surface.

Annual 15-day festival in China and Chinese communities around the world that begins with the first day of the first lunar month, which occurs sometime between January 21 and February 20 according to Western calendars, and lasts until the following full moon. The festival originated in ancestor and deity worship rituals in the Shang Dynasty (ca. 16th to 11th century BCE); it was firmly established in the Western Han Dynasty (206 BCE-8 CE). Activities associated with the festival include cleaning the home, worship of deities and ancestors, family reunions, preparation of special foods, receiving cash in red envelopes, posting poetry, lighting candles, and setting off firecrackers, symbolizing wishes for a happy new year and a fortuitous future.
Festivals celebrated in China and other Asian countries, and elsewhere by people of Asian ethnicity or descent.
Webs that are spun by spiders, made of spider silk as interlaced threads of viscous protein fluid that solidify on exposure to air.
Research, study, teaching, publication, and other dissemination of information in the field of art history using digital technologies.

Term used to designate a diverse assemblage of spirit and ancestor cults constituting the traditional religion of the Fon and Ewe peoples residing in Dahomey (modern-day Benin). Vodún is a decentralized religious and social system united by common elements including ancestor and spirit veneration, deity ceremonies, and the use of animal sacrifice. It is widely understood as the original ancestor of the African diasporic Vodou and Voodoo religions, which were syncretically developed as enslaved Vodún practitioners encountered and integrated New World practices and cosmologies during the Atlantic slave trade. Vodún continues to thrive as the most practiced traditional African religion in Benin. For the Afro-Creole religion of Haiti, use “Vodou.” For the Afro-Creole religion of the Mississippi River Valley, use “Voodoo.”

Religious movement beginning in the 19th century based in Plateau Native North American spiritual practices. Smohalla, a Wanapum prophet and leader, developed the faith after receiving visions on how to remove white settlers from the Columbia River area. Followers believed adherence to traditional practices and peaceful opposition to colonization would revert society back to their pre-contact lifeways. The Dreamer religion continues to be observed today, with revival of Native culture and protection of the environment as major themes.

Species of shrub shrub that is an annual, biennial, or perennial, depending upon the climate. It was an original source of indigo dye. It is naturalized to tropical and temperate Asia and Africa, and cultivated elsewhere for centuries; its location of origin is uncertain.
Species of herbaceous, thistle-like annual plant; commercially cultivated for vegetable oil extracted from the seeds and for red colorant produced from its petals.
Species of flowering plant native to the steppes and deserts of Central and Western Asia. It is the source of blue dye; it was cultivated in England, France, Greece, Italy, Egypt, and China.
Species of narrow-leaved plant that grows 60 cm (2 feet) tall and bears purple flowers in coiled sprays.

Subspecies of buckthorn plant found in Mediterranean European countries. The berries historically have been used as medicine and to produce a yellow-green dye; in export it was often named for a French origin. In some classifications, R.infectoria is considered a synonym of R.saxatilis rather than a subspecies; in other classifications, it has been considered a separate species.

A semiconducting material that can be used as an additive for thermo conductive, superconductive, glass, ceramics and sensing materials. Copper oxides exist in two different forms: cupric oxide (CuO) and cuprous oxide (Cu2O), depending on the valence state of copper.

Ornamental deciduous tree species native to Japan, Korea, China, and Taiwan. In Japan its durability and easy working properties have led to its popularity as a building timber and as a wood for carved objects.
People having the profession or task of inspecting residential and commercial buildings during various stages of construction and remodeling.

Relatively large side tables, some of which may have tops attached to the wall, which are used in a dining room for serving food or displaying dishes. For case furniture used to serve food and display, use "sideboards (furniture)."
Variation of Art Nouveau found in Slovenia.

Finnish variations of Jugend and Art Nouveau, including elements of Finnish nature and national culture, such as folk poetry, folk life, mediaval Finnish ecclesiastical architecture, Carelian folk, architecture, among others.

Swedish variation of Jugend and Art Nouveau, more restrained than eleswhere in Europe. Characterized by a more naturalistic ornamentation, inspired by the Swedish flora and fauna; in later years, exhibited more geometric design.
A Hungarian variation of Art Nouveau.

Variation of Art Nouveau in Switzerland, relating to the aesthetic production of the pupils of Charles L’Eplattenier in La-Chaux-de-Fonds ca. 1900/1910. The ornamental expression was based on regional flora of the canton Jura, deriving from pine-tree, Carline thistle, and Alpine gentian.
Variation of Art Nouveau found in Croatia.

Norwegian national style inspired by 11th-century Norse ornamentation and stave churches in Norway. Mostly used in architecture, furniture design, and silverware. Often used in combination with Jugendstil elements.
Spools used to wind lengths of photographic or motion-picture film for projection, processing, or storage.
In Japanese printing, format having dimensions ca. 33 x 22.7 cm.

Sections cut out of other works or documents; in art, primary examples are illuminations or other sections from a manuscript. For cuttings of newspapers and journals, use "clippings (information artifacts)."

Process or technique of using individually shaped stones of varying colors used to make a composition, often but not always low-relief rather than flat. Often used for small objects, such as focal pieces in a piece of jewelry. Although usage may overlap, for the process used to make larger works, such as table tops, from shaped stones, prefer "pietra dura (process)."
In Christian churches, the condition of a vacancy occurring in the leadership of an episcopal see, the papacy, or another office.
The condition or event of no pope being in office, usually the period during which the papal election is taking place.
That which is placed in position number one of a sequence.
Compound of copper containing up to 0.5% arsenic which, at elevated temperatures imparts higher tensile strength and a reduced tendency to scaling.
Pairs of works that match and are intended to be used together. For works intended to be displayed side by side, prefer "pendants (companion pieces)."

Large condor native to South America, having a wingspan of over 10 feet; only living member of the Vultur genus. The exact taxonomic placement of the Andean condor and the other 6 species of New World vultures remains. The New World and Old World vultures evolved from different ancestors in different parts of the world and are not closely related.
State or condition of existing or moving in the air above the earth, usually within the atmosphere of the planet.
Indication of a named or generic event that is related to a person, place, or thing. An example of usage is in data modeling.
Information indicator used when a work is about multiple subjects, rather than a single coherent subject.
Toward the fore-and-aft center line or within the sides of watercraft, aircraft or machines.
Formal or ceremonial robes of varying color and trim meant to convey status in an academic context. These have evolved from what was once everyday attire for scholars and clerics.
Violent attacks against civilians as part of a systematic effort to create a general climate of fear in a population, usually for political, religious, or social ends.
To wrap, protect, or place items of any kind in a container for transport or storage.

Files or sets of files, which may contain text, images, video or audio recordings, or other types of information. Data is copied from the main source, whether the internet or computer, and transferred to a peripheral device.

Long narrative poems celebrating on a grand scale the adventures and deeds of one or more heroic figures, ordinarily concerning a serious subject significant to a culture or nation. Classical epic poetry employs dactylic hexameter and recounts a journey.
Buildings in which money or other valuables are stored, usually of relatively modest size and used for historical buildings. Examples are found in Classical Greece and Rome.

Headgear comprising circular or U-shaped garlands made from the leaves and branches of the laurel tree. An example is as worn by Roman commanders during the triumphal procession after a martial victory.

The second epoch of the Quaternary and the most recent geologic interval of time. It extends from about 10,000 BCE to the present. It coincides with the late and post-Stone Age history of the human species.

Sets which consist of a kettle and a pot usually with a perforated flat lid used by people from cultures that dine using their right hands, to wash their hands before and after meals. The kettle sits on the perforated lidded pot and is placed at the dining place. The kettle is filled with water and diners pour the water over their hands into the perforated lidded pot to wash their fingers. Hand washing kettles come in different designs and shapes, ranging from simple to elaborate and are made from materials such as stainless steel, brass or plastic. These are common to Southeast Asia and other parts of the world.

A surface designed for relining of oil paintings patented by art restorer George T. Oliver in 1937. Instead of ironing a new canvas onto the old one, the most practiced method to date, this technique bonds the two canvases, which have been coated with a molten adhesive, on a hot metal plate. A pump evacuates oxygen between the canvases and adhesion occurs upon cooling.
X-ray absorption spectroscopy technique that analyzes the modelling of the dominant edge feature, and its pre-edge, that occur at the frequencies that correspond to transitions between atomic levels.
