Deciduous shrub common to the Mediterranean region whose gray-green rush-like shoots are used in basket-making and provide a fiber employed in products as cords, coarse cloth, and canvas.

Iron instruments similar to waffle irons, composed of two palettes that come together with the aid of two handles acting as a lever; designed to create Eucharistic hosts for Christian liturgies. A Christian symbol is typically engraved in the iron bed and stamped onto the hosts. Early examples produced hosts of around one-fourth inch thickness; later examples produced wafer-like hosts. The existence of host irons is established as early as the ninth century, although the earliest surviving example dates to the twelfth century. Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century host irons have been preserved in large numbers, and are quite similar to those now in use.
Distinctive pointers used during the liturgies of certain Christian churches to indicate to the congregation which text will be read.
Genus of plants native chiefly to the east coast of North America.
Christian ceremonies in which a person first receives the eucharist. In many denominations, those receiving the first communion are typically children.

A natural orange-yellow colorant widely distributed as pigments in plants and animals and converted in the livers of many animals into vitamin A. In plants, carotene imparts yellow, orange, or red colors to flowers (e.g., dandelion, marigold), fruits (e.g., pumpkin, apricot), and roots (e.g., carrot, sweet potato). In animals they are visible in fats (e.g., butter), egg yolks, feathers (e.g., canary), and shells (e.g., lobster). These pigments are unsaturated hydrocarbons (having many double bonds), belonging to the isoprenoid series. Carotene occurs naturally in three isomeric forms, the most common being beta-carotene. As a colorant, it is sensitive to light and air; soluble in fats, oils and other substances, insoluble in water.
Species of tree native to western Africa, prized for its reddish, striped wood.
Species of tall grain-bearing tropical plant native to Southeast Asia; it is cultivated elsewhere as a garden annual.
Museums that specialize in the history, objects, vehicles, and other materials associated with flight and space travel.
A sulfite having a base that is alkaline. Examples of uses include in a chloride extraction treatment to stabilize corroded marine cast iron, and in wood pulping.
Ionic compounds or salts that contain a negatively charged sulfide ion.

Egyptian holiday with ancient origins, celebrating the natural cycle of the Nile; it is held during two weeks annually starting August 15. In Ancient Egypt, the flooding was associated with the tears of Isis for Osiris, her deceased husband. In the Coptic Church the ritual includes ceremonially throwing a martyr's relic into the river. With the construction of High Dam at Aswan, the annual flooding cycle in Egypt came to an end in 1970.
General term for the period and culture of the Middle East as described in the Biblical Old Testament.
Genus of tropical Old World shrubs in the Lythraceae family having tetramerous flowers and a four-celled capsular fruit.

Tropical shrub or small tree of the loosestrife family, native to northern Africa, Asia, and Australia. The plant bears small opposite leaves and fragrant, white to red flowers. It is the source of dye used for temporary tattooing and to dye skin, hair and fingernails, as well as fabrics including silk, wool and leather.

Refers to the cultures associated with human community-building prior to the development of farming, where groups were sedentary and took advantage of plant and animal food sources native to the area.
Large liquor cabinets having spaces designed specifically for holding bottles of liquor, wine, glasses, other utensils, ice, and a shelf or surface needed for making and serving drinks.
The medical condition of low oxygen in the blood or tissues of a human or other animal.

An an early, widely used 3-D printing technology. It is a process that builds 3-D objects by converting liquid materials into solid parts by curing them using a light source, which causes chains of molecules to link, forming polymers. The process is used for creating models, prototypes, patterns, and production parts. A typical method uses a UV laser to create cross-sections of the object within a vat of liquid photopolymer. The process was first developed in 1986. The process is valued to create accurate parts with repeatable dimensions; applications include engineering assemblies, jewelry casting, and dental repairs.

The Miocene is the fourth epoch of the Tertiary period, or the second of the more recently designated Neogene, following Oligocene and preceding Pliocene. It extends from about 23 million to 5 million years ago. The epoch is marked by the expansion of grasslands and the development of modern grazing mammals.

On the geologic time scale the second epoch of the Tertiary period of the Cenozoic era, or the second of the more recently designated Paleogene. It extends from about 55 to 34 million years ago and is marked by warm climate, the proliferation of many modern groups of organisms, especially mammalian families and molluscs, and the emergence of what is now the Himalayan range.

On the geologic time scale, the period preceding the Proterozoic Eon, spanning about 1.5 billion years, in which the Earth's atmosphere was probably of methane, ammonia, and other gases, and the surface cooled enough that rocks and continental plates began to form.
Devices in the form of a wheel, sometimes spiked, used for torture or execution by breaking the victim's bones or tearing flesh; in use from antiquity into early modern times.

Sheet music that has been bound. The sheets may have been assembled and bound for a variety of reasons, including professional musicians’ volumes, music bound for publishers, music stores, or door to door sales, or as keepsakes, assembled primarily by women of the middle- and upper-classes during their formative years of musical training. For volumes of music that were created as bound volumes, use "music books."
African tree cultivated as a source of oil in West and Central Africa, where it originated, and in Malaysia and Indonesia, and as an ornamental tree in many subtropical areas.

Cities designed on an urban plan having a series of functionally specialized parallel sectors, such as a zone for railways, a zone for educational and cultural institutions, a residential zone, a park zone, an agricultural zone, and a green zone buffering the city from the highway. Such cities were ideally placed parallel to a river and so that winds would blow industrial air away from residential areas. The idea was developed by Arturo Soria for Madrid, Spain in the 19th century; other experiments took place primarily in Russia and Germany.

Species in the Sapotaceae family that grows up to 70 feet tall with dark brown outer bark, and pink inner. Inflorescences bear up to five flowers. Fruits are ellipsoid, up to 1 inch long. Named for the Italian naturalist Odoardo Beccari. Endemic to Borneo.
Portuguese expression of the Art Nouveau movement.

Sets of decorations for the tops of fireplace mantels usually made up of a clock and two matching vases. First popularized in 18th century France and common in the United States and Britain during the 19th century; out of fashion by early 20th century. For matching sets of vases, use "garnitures (vases)."
The activity of exiting a water conveyance, particularly to go on shore from a boat or ship.
The activity or condition of being employed as a servant attached to a household.

Distinctive culture of ancient Sardinia, dating 1900-400 BCE. It is characterized by, among other things, thousands of truncated conic structures made of huge blocks of basalt taken from extinct volcanoes; it predates the Phoenicians, who arrived here ca. 800 BCE.
Belonging to the ethnicity and culture that existed in Estonia and Latvia.
The school of philosophy and logic founded ca. 400 BCE by Euclides of Megara.
Scissor-like clamps with tapered ends that are often curved. These are used during surgery to temporarily close off blood vessels.
Tools capable of gouging grooves of various depths, which can be altered by turning the guide ring on the handle.

Large clocks placed in towers, turrets, or in other prominent locations on public buildings. Usually the dials are set at a distance from the movements. Display of the time is viewable from long distances. These are usually also fixed with chimes that sound the hour, half-, or quarter-hours.

Broad-brimmed felt hats with strings on opposing sides bearing a formation of 15 tassels each. Red galeros are worn by cardinals in the Roman Catholic Church, while other colors may signify clergy of other ranks.
Gynecological tools used by doctors during pelvic exams. Made of metal or plastic, and hinged and shaped like a duck's bill.
Keys with bittings on opposing sides of the shank, allowing either or both wings to operate the tumblers of a lock.

Chairs of various designs, positioned at the front of certain Protestant churches and used by the preacher during services. For chairs having a tall back surmounted by a lectern and used as a  pulpit, use "preaching chairs."
Devices composed of two flat wood sticks attached at one end by a leather strap or metal hinge. Used to collect lard by compressing a cloth bag containing rendered fat between the two sticks.
Side altars in Catholic Churches or chapels that venerate the Virgin Mary, often patronized by the wealthy of a particular community.

Genus of deciduous tree in the family Paulownaceae or Scrophulariaceae, native to east Asia. Bears large heart-shaped, usually hairy leaves. Cultivated for its lightweight and fine-grained timber, and as an ornamental with massed sweetly-scented violet to cream-colored, trumpet-shaped flowers that appear in Spring.

An Asian species naturalized in eastern North America. It grows to 35-50 feet high. Leaves are five to ten inches long and deep green. Flowers are lavender or purple with yellow stripes and appear at branch tips before leaves sprout in Spring.
Tree species native to a limited area in Central Africa.
The teeth of a shark, which is any fish of the order Selachii. Sharks continually shed and replace their teeth during life, thus some may shed up to 35,000 teeth in a lifetime.
Sharp, slender modified hairs projecting from the body of an animal.

Edible seeds of the legume plant, Arachis Hypogaea; classified as a grain legume and also as an oil crop, because peanut oil is a primary product. Peanut pods develop and ripen underground, which is unusual for crop legumes.
Long, showy feathers of the peacock, male of the Pavo genus. In art, used for decoration, as a material, and as a design motif.
Small immature leaves, or the individual segments of a compound leaf.
The edible roots of Daucus carota; these roots are large, tapering, and in cultivation are bright orange-red, fleshy, and sweet.

Species of bush or small tree of Asia; it is 16 or 23 feet in height, has elliptic to lance-shaped, bright-green leaves, long and handsome axillary orange-red flowers borne toward the ends of the branchlets, and a red fruit, which is a calyx is tubular and persistent and has five to seven lobes.The fruit is the size of a large orange. While the pomegranate is considered indigenous to Iran and neighbouring countries, its cultivation encircled the Mediterranean and extended through the Arabian Peninsula, Afghanistan, and India in ancient times. It is commonly cultivated in the Americas from the warmer parts of the United States to Chile.
Family of large, flightless birds having only one remaining genus.

Genus containing several species of large flightless birds of the Australo-Papuan region. They stand about five feet high; the wings are of no use for flight, but are furnished with stiff featherless quills, like spines, which serve for combat or defence
Species of large, flightless bird of Australia; it is the sole living member of the family Dromaiidae, several other forms having been exterminated by settlers.
Sisters of a one's parent or wives of one's parent's brother.
Sons of a one's brother or sister.

Women who cohabit with a man without being his wife. The term today has a negative connotation, and is generally only used in the context of certain historical periods, particularly in Asia or ancient times.
Group containing around 26 species of medium-sized wading birds.

Term for all members of the subfamily Threskiornithinae that do not have a spoonbill. They are medium-sized wading birds who inhabit shallow lagoons, lakes, bays, and marshes and use their slender, down-curved bills to feed on small fishes and soft mollusks.
Genus of perennial plants of Eurasia, containing over 250 species.
Aromatic vegetative products such as ginger root, black pepper, and nutmeg, added to food as a flavoring or condiment.
The yellow citron fruit of the Citrus medica plant; used ritually in the Sukkot, or the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles.
Migratory species of slim dove native to Africa, Asia, and Europe.
Old World genus of songbirds.

Eurasian garden and field bird; it gathers in large flocks in the Autumn for migration to northern Africa and the Middle East. The bird's common name is French, from the Latin "hortulanus," meaning the "gardener bird."
Family of bony fish having only one living genus.

Genus of freshwater fish; the only living genus in the family Esocidae, which were endemic to North America, Europe, and Eurasia during the Paleogene through present. They are distinguished by an elongate body, small scales, long head, shovellike snout, and large mouth armed with strong teeth. The dorsal and anal fins are far back on the tail.

General term for various species in the Charadriidae family, generally distinguished by being small to medium-sized, short-billed, gregarious, and typically feeding beside water but sometimes frequenting grassland, tundra, and mountains.
General term for various species in the family Scolopacidae, characterized by having a long straight bill, and by frequenting marshy places.
Species of flowering plant native to central and eastern Russia, Kazakhstan, Mongolia, and northwestern China.
Species of conifer native to Japan; the only species in its genus.
Small marine gastropod that flourishes in the Indian Ocean, having a porcelain-like shell that is used as money in some parts of Africa and Southern Asia.

Species of evergreen flowering plant. Formerly cultivated for a red dye, alizarin, that was obtained from the ground-up roots of these plants. Also used for medicinal purposes and as food plant for the larvae of the Hummingbird hawk moth and other species.
Family of flowering plants.
Genus containing around 40 species, primarily  herbs, covered with bristly hairs, cultivated in Europe, North Africa, South Africa, Western Asia, and North America.
A plant found chiefly in the Mediterranean and West Asia. A red natural organic dye may be prepared from the root.

Members of a group of bacteria that differ in certain morphological, physiological, and genetic features from the eubacteria. One of the three major divisions of living organisms. They do have some features in common with the eubacteria, suggesting to some researchers that the two groups shared a common ancestor early in their evolutionary history. The two groups of bacteria are as different from each other as they are from eukaryotes (plants and animals). Archaea are microbes and most live in extreme environments requiring excesses of heat or salt for survival, and neither sunlight nor oxygen. They absorb carbon dioxide, nitrogen, or hydrogen sulfide and give off methane gas as a waste product the same way humans breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Archaea could survive in environments such as those on Venus and in the past on Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn, and Jupiter's moon, Io.

Small song bird native to the Canary Islands, the Azores, and Madeira. Wild birds are yellow-green with brownish streaking on the back. The species in captivity exists in a several color varieties, most commonly yellow.
Species of large bird in the hornbill family,  found in the Malay peninsula, Sumatra, and Borneo.
Class of bacteria.
Order of bacteria.
Family of bacteria.
Genus of rod-shaped, gram-positive, aerobic or, under some conditions anaerobic, bacteria widely found in soil and water.
Ancient family of cartilaginous fish, abundant in the fossil record, with the sharks their closest living relatives; they branched off from sharks 400 million years ago.
Family of rays having a long flat rostrum lined with sharp transverse teeth.
Mushroom-forming; parenthesomes imperforate or perforate (spore caps have openings); includes subclasses Agaricomycetidae and Phallomycetidae; contains 17 orders.
Genus of scale insect, including several species from which a red dye, kermes crimson colorant is obtained.

term: inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry
definition: Emission spectroscopy that uses the inductively coupled plasma to produce excited atoms and ions that emit electromagnetic radiation at wavelengths characteristic of a particular element. The intensity of this emission is indicative of the concentration of the element within the sample.

Optical emission spectral analysis technique in which excitation employs glow discharge, a plasma created by passing an electric current between metal electrodes in a tube containing a gas. In GD-OES a sample located in the cathode is bombarded by a glow discharge lamp. Sputtered neutral atoms excited in the plasma give off characteristic light in deexcitation which is collected by a spectrophotometer.
In Chinese landscape painting, perspective created through a view past high mountains into the distance.
Genus of plants including food crops such as cabbage, cauliflower, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, and some types of seeds, including mustard.
Species of plant containing the various varieties of cabbage.
The conclusion of the transfer of ownership via sale from one entity to another, where all actions to resolve the sale have been achieved.

A spectrometer-based OCT technique using a broadband light source and an interferometer. A low-loss spectrometer measures the spectrum of the interference pattern of light returned from the reference and sample arms of the interferometer. SDOCT has been used in a conservation science context for noninvasive and noncontact assessment of varnish layer thickness and structure on easel paintings.

Hosts, which are pieces of consecrated bread in Christian liturgies, that are small, very thin, and wafer-like, typically round with a meaningful Christian symbol stamped upon them. They are created in a special wafer iron. Communion wafers have been common in the western churches for hundreds of years. The first reference to small, round hosts, but not necessarily as thin as wafers, is mentioned in the eighth century; the small, regular hosts were seen as advantageous in eliminating the need to break up a piece of bread that could crumble easily. Eventually the hosts became very thin wafers that were widely adopted in the west. With the Second Vatican Council of the Roman Catholic Church, other forms of bread have again become increasingly common for consecration as hosts, as a reference to the original, ancient Christian practices.

Small portable altars, most often made of terracotta, but also of stone. These usually have a square or rectangular shape with varying dimensions. Arulae are considered too small to have been used for animal sacrifice, and are commonly decorated with moldings at top and bottom and with molded reliefs on one or more sides. Characteristic products of South Italy and Sicily from the the second quarter of the sixth century through the Roman period. They have been found in sanctuaries, near or inside graves, and in habitation sites.

Any natural, treated or man-made material with the appearance but not the composition, structure or physical and optical properties of a diamond. Use "synthetic diamonds" when referring to the artificial product with the same physical and chemical properties.

Any of various materials used to replicate gold leaf. Genuine gilding has been imitated since medieval times by using a transparent yellow glaze over silver or tin leaf. In the 19th century, bronze leaf was also used as a gilding imitation. Currently, imitation gold leaf is typically made from tinted sheets of aluminum or white gold (palladium and platinum).
Shallow drinking cups or bowls, with curved sides and flattened bases, typically made from forest glass. Often decorated with ribs or moderately high bosses or prunts.
Distinctive clothing worn by members of monastic religious orders, by which their membership is typically identified.
Implements for cutting dough, having a rotating wheel with a fluted, jagged, toothed, or otherwise shaped edge; used to cut, crimp, or decorate pastry or dough.
Military uniform service coats intended for wear in warm climates, having short or long sleeves and of a breathable fabric such as linen or cotton.
Robots and robotic systems with the appearance and/or behavior similar to that of humans. To refer to machines with human parts, use "cyborgs."
Large curtains hung in front of the altar during Lent to conceal it from the view of the congregation. The veils are often decorated, for example, stenciled or embroidered.

Vessels reserved for the eucharist, used to hold the hosts for distribution to the faithful during a liturgy; often taking the form of a cup with an arched cover. The term may also be used for vessels taking the form of a temple or tabernacle, sometimes suspended from the roof of ciboria (structures). For shallow or deeper bowls used to hold the hosts for distribution to the faithful in place of the ciborium, use "communion bowls."
Metal devotional medals that depict Christian figures of veneration including Jesus, saints, or the Virgin Mary.

Traditional accessory for the celebration of the Eucharist, consisting of a straw, which is a very narrow tube, through which the consecrated wine may be sipped from the chalice; typically made of silver or gold. The purpose of the straw was to prevent spillage of the consecrated wine; it is known from ancient times, when methods of sharing the wine included spoon, straw, and tube.
Spoons intended to commemorate the birth of a child, typically given as gifts.
General term for political entities that are typically but not always independent, usually nations or empires, and considered of the highest order or level in a political hierarchical arrangement.

Refers to an optical technique which enables interferometric measurements of surface displacements. When laser light is scattered by a rough surface it generates a random intensity distribution known as a speckle pattern.The technique allows visualization and measurement of the three dimensional distribution of displacement and strain/stress on the object.

Decorative wreaths for the display of Advent candles, typically made from evergreen foliage and set upon a table or other surface. There are usually four candles, three purple and one rose-colored. One candle is lit on each of the four Sundays of Advent, optionally with a fifth, white candle lit on Christmas Eve.

Refers to decorated trees, typically an evergreen tree of pine, balsam, or fir, decorated with candles, lights, and ornaments as a part of Christmas festivities. It is rooted in the use of evergreen trees, wreaths, and garlands to symbolize eternal life, customary among ancient Egyptians, Chinese, and Hebrews. In addition, tree worship was common among the pagan Europeans; Scandinavian and German customs surrounding evergreen branches and trees during the midwinter holidays survived their conversion to Christianity. The modern Christmas tree originated in western Germany, around a popular medieval play about Adam and Eve, in which the 'paradise tree' was a fir tree hung with apples, representing the Garden of Eden. The Germans set up a paradise tree in their homes on December 24, the feast day of Adam and Eve. The custom became popular in Victorian England; the symbolism was expanded to include ornaments that referred more directly to Christ's birth. The tradition was taken up by many countries in the Western world. In today's use, it has often lost its original religious significance.
Cabinets of relics that are divided into days, weeks, and months with relics of a saint, martyr, deity, or other holy person mounted or displayed within.

The  Phanerozoic is the current eon in the geologic time scale. It extends from approximately 542 million years ago until the present and is marked by the rapid expansion and evolution of life forms allowed by the development of plants carrying out photosynthesis, thus releasing oxygen into the atmosphere. It contains the Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic eras.

The youngest era of the Phanerozoic. It follows the Mesozoic,  extending from about 65 million years ago to the present. During the Cenozoic, flora and fauna evolved toward their present state and the continents assumed their modern configuration. The Cenozoic comprises two periods: the Tertiary (with its five epochs) and the Quaternary.

Composite mixture of pigment having a pinkish hue, often available pre-mixed, and intended for use as a flesh color resembling Caucasian flesh tones. Typically used only in western art prior to the early 1900s. Types and proportions of the pigments used for this mixture varied. For the technique of painting to resemble flesh tones, particularly Caucasian, use "encarnacione (technique)."

The earliest period of the Paelozoic, extending from about 542 to 488 million years ago. It is characterized by rapid diversification of marine life. Cambrian rocks are the first to contain an abundance of fossils.
The last period of the Mesozoic, extending from about 145 to 65 million years ago. The sudden extinction of the dinosaurs occurred at the end of the period.

The second of three divisions of the Cenozoic Era encompassing the interval between 23 million and 2.6 million years ago and including the Miocene and the Pliocene epochs, preceded by the Paleogene period. Marine and terrestrial life of this time were more closely related to each other than to those of the Paleogene. The Neogene and Paleogene periods are new additions to the geologic time scale and together represent what was formerly referred to as the Tertiary period.
The older of the two epochs belonging to the Cretaceous period on the geologic time scale. It extends from about 146 million to 100 million years ago.
Salishian (or, Salish) language with several dialects spoken on southern Vancouver Island.

Used to distinguish the variety of Spanish spoken in Spain, on the Iberian Peninsula, from other forms spoken elsewhere. To refer specifically to formal varieties of Spanish as spoken in Spain, use "Castilian Spanish."

Subgroup of the Uto-Aztecan languages, now considered a division of the Corachol-Aztecan subgroup of Southern Uto-Aztecan (also called Sonoran). The Nahuan languages include Pochutec and Nahua (made up of Pipil and Nahuatl). The Nahuatl language has many dialects and is spoken throughout Mexico; the Mexican government, Ethnologue, and Glottolog, recognize up to 30 varieties of modern Nahuatl as distinct languages.
Tropical evergreen tree native to rainforests of Uganda and West Kenya named for its scarlet-orange flowers which resemble tulips in shape.
Relatively short, stout nonferrous nails having a cut shank, designed to avoid splitting the underlying planks of wood when nailing down slates to slate roof.

Dovetail seams in sheet metal, for joining collars to flanges, where the seam has a bead formed by means of a beading machine. This bead acts as a stop for the flange to rest upon and the tabs are bent over to hold the flange in place.

Species of tree native to eastern Asia, northern China, Manchuria, Korea, Ussuri, Amur, and Japan; invasive in America. It is a major source of an important substance used in traditional Chinese medicine

Species of small deciduous tree having prickly branches with leaves and brush-like inflorescences; native to semi-desert regions of Sub-Saharan Africa, Oman, Pakistan, and northwestern India. It is the source of gum arabic considered to have superior properties over other sources of gum arabic. Formerly classified in genus Acacia.

Species of small tree with pale greenish or reddish bark and feathery leaves having two thorns at their base, native to Africa from Egypt to Kenya, west Senegal, and in the Sahara. It is a source of gum arabic. The wood was used in Ancient Egypt to make coffins; it is noted in the Bible as the material out of which the Ark of the Covenant was made. Formerly classified in genus Acacia.

In wooden barrel-making, bung borers designed to allow the boring of the bunghole and tap hole in one step, rather than the two-step process of a drilling pilot hole and then enlarging the pilot hole to the correct size with a tapered reamer.

Punches designed specifically for punching holes in paper; usually reserved for the types of punches that are office tools used to punch holes in sheets of paper so that the sheets can be inserted into binders.
Louvered shutters having deep louvers, over 2 inches wide; typically installed into the casement of a window.

Exterior shutters, usually louvered shutters or jalousies, characterized by being hinged at the top and opening from the window like an awning instead of horizontally. They are designed to provide protection from severe storms.

Rubbed or scuffed areas caused by a gradual loss of material on the surface due to rubbing, wearing, or scraping of an object or material against itself or another usually harder object or material. Abrasion may be a deliberate attempt to smooth, clean, or polish a surface. It may also be a deteriorative process that occurs over time as a result of weathering or handling.
Condition is the overall state of an object, being, or environment, including physical characteristics such as appearance, pristineness, level of damage, completeness, working order, or quality.

Family of flowering plants containing 16 genera and about 770 species, mostly in the tropics or warm temperate regions of the world. The affinities of Vitaceae have long been uncertain, with no obvious close relatives to the family

Genus containing around 60 species of vining plants, predominantly from the Northern hemisphere and important as the source of grapes. Usually having a woody vine, climbing by means of tendrils (modified branches) and producing juicy fruits in clusters.
Species of evergreen perennial plant native to New Zealand and Norfolk Island. The Maori grew many varieties for specific purposes: for clothing, fishing nets, bindings, baskets, mats, and medicine.

Cutting wand that operates by punch-tip action, cutting by perforating paper rather than slicing it. Designed for use in children's arts and crafts; used as well by paper conservators for preparing hinges, inlays, and fills.
Books containing rulings, rules, or regulations.
Large family of related languages, including around 300 living languages and dialects.

Established systems of spoken or written communication, distinct from other such systems and used by a particular nation, culture, people, or community, typically consisting of words used within a regular grammatical and syntactic structure. The concept may include established sign languages as well. For the general concept of verbal or non-verbal communication, use "language (general communication)."
Writing systems using alphabets, which represent the basic phonological structure of the language, the phonemes being the constituent parts of syllables.
In postclassic central Mexico, a Mexica military commander whose role is both to start the war and to lead the fight. Associated with the Tlacateccatl warrior and more generally with Huitzilopochtli.
Species of elepahnt distributed in southeast Asia from India to Borneo.

Dramatic entertainments consisting of dance and mime performed to music. Ballets are characterized by stylized poses and steps that are combined with light and flowing figures and movements, such as leaps and turns; often combined with music, scenery, costume, and sometimes pantomime or speech to convey a story, theme, or atmosphere to the audience.
Theatrical dances in which a formal academic dance technique of the "danse d’école" is combined with other artistic elements such as music, costume, and stage scenery.
The art and practice of preparing and cooking foods. For art works incorporating edible materials, prefer "edible art."
The process of preparing food, a dish, or a meal, typically by combining and heating ingredients.
Specialization of photography focused on architecture as subject.

The principal performer or bullfighter who both works the capes and performs the task of killing the bull by means of a sword. Matadors are almost exclusively male, but there have been female 'matadoras.'
Something milled such as flour, usually referring to ground maize meal. Literally, "ground thing" in Nahuatl.
The flesh of fish used as food.
Discipline having to do with the culture and history of Africa.
The fatty substance obtained from cream by churning; used chiefly for spreading on bread and in cookery.

An alcoholic beverage obtained by the fermentation of malt from cereal grain (or another saccharine substance), flavored with hops or other aromatic bitters. Formerly the term was used as distinct from "ale," with beer being hopped; now "ale" is used to describe a type of beer. May also be applied as a generic reference to other fermented liquors of various kinds, flavored by various ingredients such as ginger.
Crisp, thin wafers containing or intended to contain ice cream; usually conical or having a truncated cone-like shape.
In the APG IV system (2016) for the classification of flowering plants, denotes a clade (a monophyletic group), common examples of which include the forget-me-nots, nightshades, and potatoes.

Order of flowering plants, consisting of the single family Vitaceae, which contains 16 genera and about 770 species, mostly in the tropics or warm temperate regions of the world. It is a basal member in the rosid group of the core eudicots in the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group III (APG III) botanical classification system.
Family of dicotyledonous flowering plants containing 14 genera and around 910 known species.
Genus containing around 60 species native to the north temperate zone, including varieties cultivated for table fruit, dried to produce raisins, or crushed to make grape juice or wine.
Genus of weevils.
Beetle that feeds on cotton buds and flowers. Thought to be native to Central America, it migrated into the United States from Mexico in the late 19th century.

Clownfish or Anemonefish are fishes from the subfamily Amphiprioninae in the family Pomacentridae. Thirty species are recognized, one in the genus Premnas, while the remaining are in the genus Amphiprion. In the wild, they all form symbiotic mutualisms with sea anemones. Depending on species, Clownfish are overall yellow, orange, or a reddish or blackish color, and many show white bars or patches. The largest can reach a length of 18 centimetres (7.1 in), while the smallest barely can reach 10 centimetres (3.9 in).
Military excercises that involve that part of a military force consisting of horse-mounted troops.
Facilities where vehicles that navigate through the air are manufactured.
Artists involved in mapmaking, primarily in the addition of color or painted decorative elements, such as vegetation and sea creatures.

A form of pyrolysis mass spectrometry in which the temperature of the sample is raised gradually to separate compounds in the evaporation phase from those in the crosslinked fraction of the pyrolysis phase. It is used to provide qualitative views of the broad-band molecular-level characteristics of complex organic samples.

A technique for materials analysis that uses an ion beam to excite atoms in a target, and visible light emitted from the target material is analyzed with a fiber-optic spectrometer. Since visible light results from outer-shell transitions, IBIL can give information about the nature of chemical bonds in materials.
Order of comb jellies, distinguished by having spherical or oval bodies and branched, retractable tentacles.
Family of marine invertibrates containing three genera.

Genus of gelatinous, planktonic marine invertebrates, now generally considered to contain one living species that manifests in three different ecological forms.The sea walnut resembles the sea gooseberry morphologically, but as in many ctenophores the body is prolonged into eight lobes.
Genus of sea snails.

Species of predatory sea snail, native to central and western parts of the Mediterranean Sea, the Indian Ocean, and South China Sea. It was used to make expensive purple dye since Antiquity; it produces  a milky secretion that turns into a powerful and lasting dye when exposed to air.
Species of predatory sea snail, native to the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic coasts of Europe and Africa. It was used to make expensive purple-blue indigo dye since ancient times.
Species of perennial herbaceous plant native to Europe and Asia. Traditionally used as a cough suppressant.
Species of common Eurasian thrush; the male has black plumage and a yellow bill and is noted for its melodious song, and the female is dark brown.
Genus containing  medium-sized water birds; they are close relatives of coots.

Ceramic ware produced by the Kirkcaldy pottery of David Methven and Sons, decorated in an imitation of Wemyss ware. The Kirkcaldy pottery is near the Fife Pottery which produced Wemyss ware. Abbotsford ware may indeed have been decorated by artists from the Fife Pottery.

Drawn-glass beads with an internal structure of multiple, pleated layers in different colors, creating a two-dimensional star-like pattern of chevrons around the central hole, and stripes on the sides.

General term for a popular type of paper that is blue in color and historically was used primarily as artists' drawing paper and for some other uses; first documented in 1389 in Europe. The dyes used to create the blue or purplish color vary by place of manufacture. The term is often reserved for Western drawing papers produced prior to the introduction of aniline dyes in the late 19th century.
Bunches or arrangements of cut flowers.
Arrangements of flowers, ribbon, or other materials, carried by the bride in wedding ceremonies.

Communities of animals or plants that are temporary or in a constant state of flux. Examples include groups of animals that stop temporarily during a migration, or communities of plants that appear and disappear with changing climate.
Costume of any kind, made primarily or entirely of fur.
Its origin was Gallia Narbonensis.
Structures or complexes serving as a base of operations for rangers or other wardens of a forest, and typically also accessible to the public.

Smaller cities on the outskirts of larger metropolitan areas that are independent of the larger city's jurisdiction but dependent on its economic and social orbit. Satellite cities may be planned as such or they may result from ad hoc growth. For planned communities designed to be socially or economically independent of larger metropolitan areas use "new town."

Types of Roman planned settlements that were designed as regional market towns having a forum, basilica, and facilities for administrative and economic management. They were distinguished from settlements that arose ad hoc around military garrisons.
Communities, relatively large in size, that are the location of a cathedral, which is the principal church of a Christian diocese and seat of the bishop, archbishop, primate, or patriarch.
Consolidant used to treat deteriorated limestones, sandstones, and marbles.
Coating designed to prevent the corrosion of metals, particularly the rusting of iron and steel.

A synthetically produced aluminum oxide, a white or nearly colorless crystalline substance that is used as a starting material for the smelting of aluminum metal, as the raw material for a broad range of advanced ceramic products, and as an active agent in chemical processing. Alumina is derived from bauxite, a naturally occurring ore containing variable amounts of hydrous aluminum oxides.
Tectonic plates that are comprised of continental lithosphere (as opposed to oceanic plates).
Genus of the New World vulture family containing a single species, Gymnogyps californianus, the California condor.

Vulture species formerly common in the mountains of the western United States. Once nearly extinct, the species has been sustained by breeding in captivity. A carefully controlled conservation program has led to inreasing numbers of birds released into the wild.
Areas that are historically documented or otherwise surmised, but are now gone or the location is unknown.
Underwater, flat areas of a seafloor, usually appearing adjacent to continents and covered with a layer of sediment.

Sculptural works that incorporate sound; used especially in reference to sculptural instruments for performance, such as those created by François and Bernard Baschet, Robert Rutman, Charles Mattox, and Harry Bertoia, among others.
Vast landforms that are connected or continuous mainland. Often used when referring to the continents of modern geography, but may also refer to former continents.

Forests of cold-tolerant evergreen conifers with needle-like leaves, such as pine, fir, and spruce, located between 50 and 60 degrees north latitudes in the broad belt of Eurasia and North America, including Siberia, Scandinavia, Alaska, and Canada. They are characterized by seasons divided into short, moist, and moderately warm summers and long, cold, and dry winters. The length of the growing season in boreal forests is 130 days.

Tropical forests characterized by dense canopies of broad-leaved trees and other vegetation that form three different layers; located in areas having no dry season; an example is the Amazon rainforest in Brazil.
Temperate forests of coniferous trees that dominate higher elevation zones in areas having low precipitation. Examples are in the northern Rocky Mountains.

Category of grasslands having scattered individual trees, found in warm or hot climates where the annual rainfall is 51 to 127 cm. Rainfall is concentrated in six or eight months of the year, followed by a long period of drought when fires can occur; if the rain were well distributed throughout the year, many such areas would become tropical forest.

Biomes surrounding desert environments occurring where rainfall is less than 50 cm annually. Most deserts occur at low latitudes, although cold deserts occur elsewhere. Most deserts have a considerable amount of specialized vegetation, as well as specialized vertebrate and invertebrate animals.

Biomes that have cold, long, snowy winters, and warm, humid summers, with well-defined seasons and at least four to six frost-free months; temperatures range -40 to 20 degrees C, and rainfall is 300-900 mm per year. They are characterized by coniferous-evergreen trees and are located in North America, Europe, and Asia.
Depressions in the earth that are filled with water, smaller than an ocean or sea and ranging in size from just a few square meters to thousands of square kilometers.
Marine areas surrounding coral reefs, which are formed by the growth and deposit of coral.

Deserts along coasts, having cool winters followed by moderately long, warm summers. The average summer temperature ranges from 13-24 degrees C; the average rainfall measures 8-13 cm annually. The soil is fine-textured with a moderate salt content.
Tundras located on mountains throughout the world at high altitude where trees cannot grow. The growing season is approximately 180 days.
Features that contain water and are man-made rather than natural.
Stars in the center of a solar system around which planets orbit.

The regularly repeated, typically elliptical courses of a celestial object, satellite, spacecraft, or other object, around a more massive body to which it is bound by gravity. Examples are the orbits of planets around the sun.

Formerly classed as a species of hibiscus, now assigned to the genus  Abelmoschus: an edible leafy green malvaceous plant closely related to okra (Abelmoschus esculentus). It is native to tropical Africa, Asia and northern Australia. In cooking, its seedpods are fried or used to thicken soups and stews. The roots of Abelmoschus manihot are used for cordage and are also the source of a mucilaginous substance used as a dispersion aid in traditional papermaking in East Asia.
Devices used to measure the acoustic oscillation of the eye to detect and treat glaucoma.

The rigid, calcareous material that is white in color and forms the skeleton of vertebrates; primarily composed of calcium hydroxyapatite with smaller amounts of calcium carbonate, calcium fluoride, magnesium phosphate, and ossein, a high molecular weight protein. Bones have a concentric structure with central lymphatic canals surrounded by a spongy lamellar region protected by a dense outer cortex. Bone has been carved and used since ancient times for many purposes, including fish-hooks, spear heads, needles, handles, and art objects. Bones were also burnt to produce bone black and boiled to produce bone glue. Bone can be distinguished from ivory by being generally whiter, more porous, and less dense.
Parts or components of joints.
Features above sea level that are man-made rather than natural. Included are large mounds and other features that resemble natural features; excluded are buildings and bridges.
Features comprising communities of plants that are grown by man rather than being natural.

A spectroscopic analysis based on a luminescence phenomenon that provides the differential emission intensity of right and left circularly polarized light, thereby providing information on the excited state properties of the chiral molecular systems.

Points on the earth characterized by coordinates that are determined by observation of celestial bodies. The expression is usually used in connection with positions on land determined with great accuracy for survey purposes.

In geology, the fundamental units of lithostratigraphy comprising distinctive assemblages, layers, or units of rock in an area, characterized as being of homogeneous origin and appearance. The designation and limits of a given geological formation may vary, depending upon the criteria imposed by the cataloging body.
The varieties of Catalan spoken on the Balearic Islands.
Language of the Tonkawa people, considered by some to belong to the Coahuiltecan family of languages and by others to be a distinct linguistic stock in the Macro-Algonquian group.
Generic term for a variety of languages, dialects and language groups, most of which are found in the lower Himalayas.
The varieties of the Dutch language spoken historically in Flanders and today in Belgium.

General term for the varieties of English spoken primarily in the United States. The chief differences between British and American English are in the pronunciation of certain individual vowels and diphthongs, and the spelling of certain words.
Refers to dialects of the French language generally spoken in Canada.
Extinct Germanic language that was spoken by the Goths. It is known primarily from the Codex Argenteus, a 6th-century copy of a 4th-century translation of the Bible.

The variety of German language that developed after ca. 1100 CE, based on the upper German dialects Alemannic and Bavarian that had begun to arise in the southernmost part of Germany. Middle High German was the language of an extensive literature that includes the early 13th-century epic "Nibelungenlied."

Language documented by at least 15th century CE and now the present-day republic of Albania. It presumably continues one of the very poorly attested ancient Indo-European languages of the Balkan Peninsula, but which one is not clear.

Group of related languages derived from Vulgar Latin within historical times. The major languages of the family include French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, and Romanian, Catalan, Occitan and Rhaetian dialects, Sardinian, and Dalmatian, among others.
Korean language expressed in the Hangul writing system.
General term for the forms of Latin used in ancient Rome, as distinguished from Latin used from the Medieval period onwards.

The earliest recorded form of Low German, spoken by the Saxon tribes between the Rhine and Elbe rivers and between the North Sea and the Harz Mountains from the 9th until the 12th century. A distinctive characteristic of Old Saxon, shared with Old Frisian and Old English, is its preservation of the voiceless stops.
Family of tonal languages of the Otomi people inhabiting parts of central Mexico.
Variety of the Portuguese language used primarily in the nation of Angola.
An apparatus for supporting the physical functions of infants that are born prematurely.

Term applied to digital art works that emphasize the computer’s role in thier creation and apprehension. Specifically used for artworks that employ computer terminals or technology for display, distribution, or interaction, so that the machinery is an integral part of the work.

Visual works created or modified using a computer or other digital medium. These products are exhibited in a variety of ways: statically or as interactive concepts that may reveal or obscure their computer origins. For works that use computer machinery intrinsically as a part of the work, use "computer art."
Artists who specialize in creating any in a range of artistic works that use digital technology as an essential part of the creative or presentation process.

Natural arches that have been formed by a current of water, often leaving a formation that resembles a bridge. For similar structures that were not formed by a current of water, use the broader "natural arches."
Hand-stitched embroidered needlework pieces from South American Andean countries, used as wall hangings or to make quilts, handbags, pillows, or various other objects.
Style and culture of the city of Athens. For the culture of the larger region of Attica, use "Attic."

Areas of dry or relatively dry land or islands surrounded by water or low wetland; island groups considered archipelagos are characterized by compactness and adjacency. The original Greek meaning referred to the water in which such islands were located.

Small, shallow terrestrial depressions or basins located in arid and semiarid regions that contain ephemeral bodies of water from periods of rainfall, leaving residual deposits of salt, sand, or mud.  Distinct from "dry lakes."
Porcelain ware made of clay mixed with bone dust or phosphate of lime, having walls that are pure white and translucent.
Ceramic ware to which a vitreous glaze has been applied.
Features that are located in the sea under sea level and are made artificially rather than being natural.
Seamounts with flat tops.

In geography, the perimeters of each continent and the associated coastal plain; now, during the current interglacial period, submerged under relatively shallow seas. Much of the continental shelves' area was exposed during glacial periods. In international law, under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the "continental shelf" is defined as the stretch of the seabed adjacent to the shores of a particular country to which it belongs.
The four largest moons of Jupiter (Io, Ganymede, Europa, and Callisto), discovered in 1610 by Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei.
Muslim dynasty of Turkic origin that ruled over the Delhi sultanate in medieval India, beginning in 1320.
Anchorages located near shorelines that are less safe than harbors, but where ships may safely ride at anchor.
Manmade islands composed of shells, usually shells that were discarded from human consumption of seafood over many years. Examples are in the Florida Keys.

Buildings that house educational facilities with higher education curricula specifically designed to train rabbis; for schools providing training in Talmudic law generally, but not necessarily specifically for the rabbinate, use "yeshivas." For schools providing education for the priesthood, use "theological seminaries."

Spiritual places in the Inca religion. Included are Pre-Columbian Inca tombs or temples, usually a truncated pyramid of stone, and often of immense size. Huacas could also be caves, springs, special rocks, and man-made shrines.

During the Iron Age, settlements were the settings for ritual activities which included the making of special deposits. A series of rectangular ditched enclosures known as Viereckschanzen is concentrated in the temperate regions of central Europe. Many include deposits of iron weapons and tools in the ditches.
Natural or artificial caves used as a burial places for one or multiple deceased, often with carved or constructed elements.

Complexes or structures having as a main purpose the launching of vehicles or rockets into the atmosphere or space, or having other functions having to do with space or air travel, for example designing testing space vehicles.

General term for political entities considered of the highest order or level in a political hierarchical arrangement, but where the entity is historical and no longer exists. Examples are former nations, states, or empires, such as the Byzantine Empire.

Streams or distributaries that no longer carry flowing water but whose trace is still evident due to lakes, wetland, topographic, or vegetation patterns along their former course. For watercourses that no longer exist, use "lost watercourses."
Features that comprised physical geography, but now no longer exist or are changed from their earlier form.
General term for areas of a country forming the border, particularly applied to the regions at the edge of settled or inhabited regions.
Societies or groups of people who once existed and were characterized by common ideas, customs, or social behavior within a particular nation or people and period.
Communities of any size that formerly existed but are now disbanded or abandoned. For communities for which the location is unknown, use "lost settlements."
Cities that are the official seat of government.
Settlements enclosed by walls, particularly used for early settlements that have only rudimentary walls, but not heavy or sophisticated fortifications.
Communities of relatively large size that have been buried due to volcanic eruption, landslide, accumulation of sediment, etc.; often refers to an archaeological site.
Communities of relativelly small size that are located near a body of water and have economies centered on fishing.
Ports that are located inland, on rivers.
Communities of modest size in which a prison and activities supporting the prison are primary industries.
Places where caravans stop to rest.
Places, whether inhabited or not, that serve as a focal point of worship, gathering, or other activity of a particular cult.
Settlements whose primary concern is military; may also be used for settlements upon which military considerations have had a considerable formal or economic influence.
Relatively small settlements that grow up around farming activities; usually refers to early farming settlements.
Communities of very small size that hold a market, typically agricultural centers in a rural area.
Communities of modest size that have tourism as an important industry.
Communities, relatively large in size, that are the location of a university, which is a type of degree-granting institution.
Communities, typically small or medium-sized towns or cities, that have economies centered on a college and the college population.
Designates industrial settlements purposely built by factory owners to attract workers to isolated or otherwise undesirable locations with a minimum of services.
Designates industrial settlements in which the primary employment is in factories for the manufacture of, for example, paper, steel, or textiles.
Towns where the principal industry is the mining and refining of precious metals.
Towns located along a coast.
Settlements situated on a hill.
Towns situated near or on a river.
Distant or overseas settlements established for punishing criminals by forced labour and isolation from society.
Areas inhabited by primarily indigenous peoples. The term is used particularly in Australia, but may also apply to other areas.

In a hierarchy, an ancestor is any record that is broader context for the record at hand, including parents, grandparents, and all other broader contexts at higher levels; any node in the succession of parent nodes on a path all the way up to the root.
In a thesaurus, an alternate descriptor is a variant form of term that is the descriptor; usually a singular form or a different part of speech than the descriptor.
Slips or sections of paper redeemable for specifically named articles, services, or funds and often attached as a group in book form or incorporated individually within larger printed matter.
Sections of oil pipelines where two or more pipelines join together.
Political entities that worked or governed together, but are historical and no longer exist. Examples are Etruria and the Hanseatic League.

Statistical geographic entities representing permanent and/or seasonal residences for Alaska Natives who are members of, or receiving governmental services from, the defining Alaska Native Village located within the region and vicinity of the Native Village's traditional and/or historic location.

Works that are auxiliary or an accessory to the primary work; the concept may apply to a wide variety of disciplines. An example would be a heating system that is ancillary to the primary architectural work.
Collected components that work together to store and manage data and assemble it into intelligible information.
Systems for describing and indexing works or images, particularly in a collections management system or other automated system.
Smart materials that have the capacity to clean themselves. Examples are silicone-based architectural coatings.

In astronomy, moons or other natural satellites having a distant, inclined, eccentric, and retrograde orbit around a planet. Irregular satellites were likely captured by their parent planet rather than having been formed in situ.

Fine terra sigillata that was produced in the province of Africa Proconsularis, the area corresponding to modernTunisia and other terrritory. It is distinguished by a thick-orange red slip over a slightly granular fabric. Interior surfaces are completely covered, while the exterior can be only partially slipped, particularly on later examples.
Gradual gravitational downslope movement of water-saturated seasonally thawed soil and other surface materials over permanently frozen subsoil; a type of mass wasting.
Traditional Hawaiian residential structures to which women of a household retire during menstruation; often containing a shrine.
Occasions when the Moon is obscured to observers on Earth by the Moon passing through the Earth's shadow.
Chemical oxidant; a solution of hydrogen peroxide and iron sulfate used for in-situ oxidation of organic contaminants such as trichloroethylene.
Denotes a rash or any pox-like outbreak on the skin.
Genus comprising up to 200 species of plants, many climbers; found throughout the tropics and subtropics of South Asia and the western Pacific Ocean.
Family of flowering plants native to the tropics and subtropics of the Old World, containing four genera in about 900 species.
Non-invasive neutron diffraction technique that characterizes the size distribution and surface characteristics of various substances at a scale of about 1-1000 nanometers.
Species of small deciduous tree native to northern Somalia. Noted for resin that is used as incense.

Species of aromatic grass found in North America and northern Eurasia, noted for its distinctive sweet scent. It is used in herbal medicine, in the production of distilled beverages, flavoring, and in ceremonial observations. Examples include in Europe, where the grass is laid at the church entrance on certain saints days. It was widely used by North American indigenous peoples, considered a sacred plant used as incense in peace and healing rituals. In some classifications, part of the genus Anthoxanthum.
An artificial pigment made by heating lead and tin oxide together and is a reddish hue of lead-tin yellow (type I), which frequently occurs in European painting before the 18th century.

Species of flowering tree native to southern Mexico and northern Central America. The leaves and bark are used in various medical applications. It was long a natural source of reddish and bluish dye, still an important source of haematoxylin used in histology for staining.

Oriental Orthodox Christian religion based in Armenia, which was the first country to adopt Christianity as its official religion in 301 CE. By tradition, it originated in missionary work of the apostles Bartholomew and Thaddeus in the first century.

The style and culture of the confederacy of tribes that spoke Aramaic (a North Semitic language) and, between the 11th and 8th century BCE, occupied Aram, a large region in northern Syria. In the same period some of these tribes seized large tracts of Mesopotamia. The first mention of the Aramaeans occurs in inscriptions of the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser I (1115-1077 BCE).

Refers to the world religion and culture that developed in the first century CE, driven by the teachings of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. Its roots are in the Judaic tradition and the Old Testament. The tenets include a belief in the death and redemptive resurrection of Jesus. The religion incorporates a tradition of faith, ritual, and a form of church authority or leadership.
Everyday items that connect a curtain to curtain rings or a curtain rod, enabling the curtain to hang.

Paintings in which the primary subject is an animal, generally a dog, horse, or other prized pet or livestock, or an exotic wild animal. The subject genre was highly developed in 18th-century European painting.

Paintings that depict multi-figure narrative scenes of real or legendary events, especially those in the academic style and with subject matter intended to convey a noble sentiment. The term is especially applied to paintings that were common from the 17th through the 19th century.

Languages characterized by having gone extinct in ancient times, thta is, more than a millennium ago. Ancient languages are identified by having a distinct literature and as treated distinctly by the scholarly community.
Wheeled, assistive walkers, used to improve mobility for the disabled.
Hunts arranged for royalty or other rulers. Prime examples were ritual hunts in Europe and Asia.

Irregularly occuring phenomenon in which a southward current of warm equatorial water displaces the northward Peru or Humboldt Current. It is characterized by unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean and its disruption of the ocean-atmosphere system in the Tropical Pacific has important consequences for weather and climate worldwide.

Hand gesture indicating divine protection, approachability, and dispelling of fear. The right hand is represented palm outward, raised to shoulder height, with the fingers upward. The gesture is ancient, probably originally demonstrating that the hand is empty of weapons and indicating peace. In Buddhism it represents the absence of fear of death. In Indian art, a hand gesture of assurance or protection.

Artists who create digital art works that emphasize the computer’s role in thier creation and apprehension. Computer artists devote themselves specifically to employing computer terminals or technology for display, distribution, or interaction, so that the machinery is an integral part of their work.
Those who create art works in the medium of cut paper.
Artists who specialize in painting images of animals, generally cats, dogs, horses, or other prize pets, livestock, or exotic wild animals.
Painters who specialize in architectural subjects, which include buildings, gardens, and other items of the built environment.
Artists who produce history paintings, which are multi-figure narrative scenes of real or legendary events.
Artists who specialize in painting scenes of daily life of common people, such as market scenes and domestic settings.
Artists who specialize in painting inanimate objects such as bowls of fruit, bottles, and flowers, which are often arranged in an aesthetic composition.

In the United States presidential election, people who are chosen by each state, usually through an election by individual voters, to represent citizens of the state in casting a vote for leaders; this system is contrasted to an election determined by direct popular vote.
People or corporate bodies who make harpsichord, which are zitherlike chordophones having a keyboard which operates a plucking mechanism.
People who specialize in creating pargeting, which is ornamental relief plasterwork stamped or carved between the studwork on the outside of half-timber houses.
Artists who specialize in designing or making tapestries, particularly tapestries containing depictions.
In Medieval Spain, individuals who were in charge of overseeing construction works, either as master builders or master masons.
General term for orgainized groups whose members are artists.
Body of ministers responsible for the administration of a country or state.
Offices, businesses, agencies, or departments for the transaction of public business, having a specified function and often coordinating related activities and the distribution of information.
General term for organizations or establishments that provide instruction.

An acquired defect of cellular immunity associated with infection by species of human immunodeficiency viruses. Criteria as defined by the CDC in 1993 include a CD4-positive T-lymphocyte count under 200 cells/microliter or less than 14% of total lymphocytes, and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections and malignant neoplasms. Clinical manifestations also include emaciation and dementia.
A vapor phase inhibitor used in steam generation and distribution systems required for heating or humidification to protect the ferrous components of these systems from corrosion.
Regional styles belonging to Papua New Guinea cultures.
A poisonous evergreen shrub in the genus Daphne with dense, narrow, dark green leaves. It is a native of the Mediterranean region.

Sodium chloride that occurs naturally as, or obtained mechanically from, a mineral deposit and sold as large crystals. Rock salt is used to melt ice, as a food preservative, and for the production of soda ash by the glass industry. To refer to the mineral composed of sodium chloride, use "halite."
An Egyptian and Roman glass with a blood red color created by the dispersion of cuprous oxide crystals in black glass.

An art movement that prevailed in Taiwan in the 1970s, roughly concurrent with the Nativist Movement in literature and other spheres that reflected on Taiwan’s local identity in the face of political crisis and rapid industrialization. Under the influence of publications such as Lion Art, many artists shifted their fascination with Western modern art in the previous decade to the local and the traditional. Four trends can be identified within the multifaceted movement. First, the naive style of suren artists (artists without formal training) such as Hung T’ung and Ju Ming earned high esteem. Second, typical scenes and objects of Taiwan became popular subjects, usually depicted in Nostalgic Realist or Super-realist style. Third, major artists from the period of the Japanese rule regained attention and recognition. Finally, there was a surge in the study of folk art and a growing concern about preserving traditional architecture and other forms of heritage. The movement marked a major shift in Taiwanese modern art history and is thought to have played a significant role in the formation of Taiwanese identity.
A water-soluble white crystalline compound used predominantly as a fertilizer, as a fire retardant, or as a stone consolidant.
Refers to the style, period, or culture of the Arhab area in Yemen.
Printing establishments that issue small editions at the pleasure of the owner, often finely printed, perhaps on a hand press.
Married men who manage their own households, especially as their principal occupation. The more commonly accepted term for people of either sex performing this duty is the broader "homemakers."
People who hold an office, function, or mandate within the government of a city, town, district, or municipality.
Architectural elements found on Indian religious buildings.

The long, fine hair from any breed of Angora rabbit. The white French rabbit is favored for its high-quality, soft hair. Angora dyes readily, but is difficult to spin because of its fine texture and it does not felt like common rabbit hair. It is usually mixed with sheep wool or other fibers for weaving.
In Indian architecture, a Prakrit form of caityagṛha.
Ghantas, ritual handbells, having a vajra ritual scepter or club at the other end of the handle.
Artists whose primary creations are painting, sculpture, or graphic art with subject matter that does not include forms that represent objects from the visible world.

The fruit of Piper nigrum, the pepper plant, dried and typically ground into powder to use as a condiment. It has a hot, pungent flavor and is most frequently paired with some form of salt. The ground spice appears in two forms, the more pungent black pepper, produced from black peppercorns, and the milder white pepper, produced from white peppercorns.
The daughters of one's son or daughter.
The father of one's parent.
A brother-in-law is the brother of one's spouse, or the husband of one's sibling.
A stepbrother is a male child of a step-parent who has married one's parent after thier natural parent's death or divorce.
A stepdaughter is a female child of one's spouse, whom one has married after the child's natural parent's death or divorce.

Artists who specialize in the marketing of products and other sales, including typography, advertising, packages, television commercials, mailings, and other visual materials having to do primarily or exclusively with sales, including design for the Internet and social media.
People who create the visual arts, such as painting, sculpture, graphic arts, or others, as a pastime rather than as a profession.

A thermally-induced physical separation process that utilizes heat to increase the volatility of contaminants such that they can be removed from a solid matrix. Options used to manage or treat the resulting contaminant-laden gas stream may consist of condensation, collection, or combustion.

Very thin biomaterials made of pure cellulose from various species of wood or plants, with a neutral pH. In conservation, it is used for various treatments including the conservation of paper-based objects made of translucent or transparent supports.
In Indian art and architecture, a composite fantastic animal; griffin, chimera; mythical fabulous creature; varāla; virāla; viḍāla (Oriyā); griffinic monster.
A creamy white or golden colored limestone dating from the Miocene period that is quarried in Lecce, a city in the Salento region of South East Italy.

Assortments of various items, often consisting of clothing and accessories, tools and products such as neutralizing chemical agents, often contained in a box, bag, package or bottle made of different materials, such as metal and plastic or glass, and of different shapes. Used to protect clothing, to decontaminate and to handle spills.

The repair or re-equipping of an object. In an archaeological context this refers to identifying flakes and other pieces of broken objects or chipped stones and, if possible, reassembling them on a lithic core in order to learn more about the process of making stone tools.
In chemistry, an organic compound in which one or more hydroxyl functional groups (-OH) are bound to a carbon atom; the carbon center should be saturated, having single bonds to three other atoms.

A toxic and reactive reddish gas, NO2, nitrogen dioxide  is an atmospheric pollutant (as in photochemical smog) produced by combustion of fossil fuels. Exposure to nitrogen oxide can cause fading of dyes and organic colorants in paints, textiles, and photographs, as well as deterioration of calcareous stone.
Refers to all polymerized siloxanes, especially the silicones.
Nondestructive technique for determining the surface topographical features of three dimensional objects by means of laser triangulation.

A family of anionic polysaccharides that are obtained by alkaline extraction from some species of red seaweeds. There are three major types of carrageenan, which include iota-carrageenan (i-carrageenan), kappa-carrageenan (κ-carrageenan), and lambda-carrageenan (λ-carrageenan). In conservation, it is used as a hydrogel in paintings consolidation, among other uses.
Refers to the style of artistic production in colonies of the Republic of Venice featuring a combination of Venetian and native characteristics.
Type of emission spectroscopy in which electrical energy in the form of a spark or an arc is used to excite the analyte prior to measuring the intensity of emitted radiation.
Porosimetry which uses mercury as the non-wetting liquid pressed into the pores of a material by the porosimeter.
Refers to DNA recovered from ancient specimens. Ancient DNA is studied by the newly established subdiscipline of archaeology, archaeogenetics, also known as ancient genomics.
Refers to any of the various double stranded nucleic acids found in chromosomes of higher organisms which store and transfer genetic information.
Endoscopy assisted by a video camera on the tip of the endoscope.
A thick, white, smooth adhesive made from starch and used especially on paper and paperboard.

Table tops, usually relatively simple, that are placed upon pedestals, saw horses, or other supporting structures to form a table. They may be stored separately from the base, and assembled as needed.
Processes having to do with the carving and working of stone, particularly in the context of building.
Structures designed or used for the isolation of women giving birth from the rest of the social group.

Carbon dioxide held at or above its critical temperature and pressure in a fluid state. Like all supercritical fluids, its properties are intermediate between those of gases and liquids. Supercritical carbon dioxide has numerous applications as a cleaning, protecting, and consolidating agent in the conservation of materials such as paper, waterlogged wood, stone, and deteriorated textiles.

A complex calcium phosphate, a naturally occuring mineral form of calcium apatite,  that serves as an important component of tooth enamel and vertebrate bone. In an archaeological context,  hydroxyapatite from human and animal remains is studied to reconstruct ancient diet.

Devices consisting of a biological component (such as an enzyme or bacterium) that reacts with a target substance and an electrochemical or optical component that detects the resulting products or by-products and emits a signal.
Any of the silicates found in the earth’s crust, such as clays, micas and feldspars, in which aluminum replaces some of the silicon.
Models that provide a rough idea of the form of the building or urban space, including massing, distribution, and arrangement of volumes and spaces.

The gradual increase over time of the average temperature of the entire earth's lower atmosphere. Global warming has occurred in the distant past as the result of natural influences, but the term is most often used to refer to the warming predicted to occur as a result of emissions of greenhouse gases directly and indirectly caused from the burning of fossil fuels. An increase of the earth's temperature by only a few degrees results in dramatic climate change, loss of habitat and species, sea-level rise, and alteration of the oceans' currents.

A variant on traditional electrophoresis, capillary electrophoresis (CE) is designed to separate particles by species. A sample is placed in a capillary tube subjected to a high-voltage charge which separates the constituent ions by differences in size, shape, and charge.

General term for an ailment. Although often translated as smallpox, it can be used to refer to any widespread plague or pestilence. It is often the designation for the infectious illnessess that spread in Indigenous communities in Mesoamerica from contact with Europeans in the sixteenth century.

The culture and style of the Brittonic-speaking peoples originally inhabiting all of Great Britain south of the Firth of Forth, and Brittany in northern France, before and during the Roman occupation.

A colorless crystalline compound of the composition HNO3 used in the production of explosives and fertilizers. As nitrate runoff from agricultural land it is a toxic pollutant which may cause eutrophication.

Display cabinets having many openings or drawers, that were originally designed to hold and display multiple relics of a saint, martyr, deity, or other holy person. Later the term came to mean similar cabinets intended to hold historical artifacts or curiosities of any kind, usually modest in size and having a common theme.

A pharmaceutical substance made of zinc oxide with small amount of fenic oxide (to give faint pink color), and containing after ignition, not less than 98% and not more than 100.5% zinc oxide. Commercial calamine may be distributed as a pink lotion, used as a skin protectant and salve.
General term referring to destinations designated for data storage.

Craftsmen who practice “dancheong,” the traditional Korean decorative coloring done on wooden buildings and structures. In South Korea, they are considered living national treasures and classified as National Intangible Cultural Heritage 48 by the Cultural Heritage Administration.
Technique for determining measurement of the size distribution of granular material.
In Maori culture, skeletal remains.
Priestesses, priests, or votaries of the Roman god Bacchus or the counterpart Greek god Dionysus. Typically a male/female distinction is made through spelling, bacchant vs. bacchante.

Radiometric dating method which measures the age of igneous calcium carbonate materials. The technique calculates the degree to which radioactive thorium-230 isotopes within a sample have reestablished secular equilibrium with their parent uranium-234 isotopes.

Micellar electrokinetic chromatography (MEKC) is a separation mode of capillary electrophoresis (CE).  Its separation principle is based on the differential migration of the ionic micelles (surfactant molecules) and surrounding aqueous buffer solution under electrophoresis conditions and on the interaction between the analyte and the micelle. Unlike conventional CE, the solution contains a surfactant at a concentration that is greater than the critical micelle concentration  MEKC is a useful technique for the separation of small molecules.

A colorless corrosive gas, the hydride of fluorine and an extremely powerful halogen acid, hydrogen fluoride is used as a catalyst and a fluorinating agent. Its chief use is in making fluorine-containing refrigerants such as freons.
