The Confucian ideal was most popularly expressed in scenes of filial piety while Taoist artists favored landscapes and folk legends. Secular artistic traditions also underwent changes, particularly in the realm of painting. Gu Kaizhi, considered the father of Chinese landscape painting, was active during this period. Noteworthy advances in ceramics in southern China were also made, most notably in the green-glazed stoneware called Yueh-yao or "Yueh ware," a durable ceramic that was eventually exported to places as distant as Egypt and the Philippines. It was during this period that gentlemen-painters and calligraphers and great private art collections first emerged in China. Literary and art criticism also developed.

Transducers whose operation is based on magnetostriction, the change of length of a ferromagnetic substance when it is magnetized. They are used for the reception and transmission of high-frequency sound.

Refers to at type of tall and mainly concave-sided lekythoi that developed in the 5th century BCE. It is a common form in black-figure. It features a mouth and neck resembling an old-fashioned chimney pot.

Style of a sub-group of Veneto-Saracenic metal wares that includes the bulk of such objects. Related to late 15th-century Mamluk metalwork, their designs are organized centripetally or in concentric bands. The motifs, which are typically Mamluk, include alternating knots, twisted ropes, and trefoiled trelliswork derived from calligraphy. None of the objects in this group is signed, but many bear north Italian, and specifically Venetian, coats of arms. Although they do not provide precise enough information about ownership, they are nonetheless evidence of the close diplomatic and commercial ties between the Mamluk and Venetian states.
Pottery decorated primarily with slip that is black in color. Examples are from 12th-3rd century BCE Nepal, 3d-2nd century Praeneste, ancient Gaul, and other places.
Head-vases consisting of two different heads back-to-back.
A black-figure cup type that is unusual in that one large picture fills the interior of the bowl.
Refers to a type of skyphos consisting of a thin-walled cup with delicate handles and a ring foot. The form originated in Corinth.

Visual effect in motion pictures in which one scene fades in to another. Both shots are seen briefly superimposed. The dissolve was first used to imply geographic or temporal transitions. Later, the optical nature of the dissolve was used for more tonal effects, such a character's state of mind, fantasy, or flashback sequences.

A system of marking locations using an electronic device or “marker,” which is buried at a site. Locators are used later to transmit a signal to the buried marker, which returns a signal that indicates the marker’s exact position. Originally developed for utility companies to quickly and accurately locate buried features such as power, water, gas, and fiber optic lines, the technology has potential for use in cultural resource management.
Portable video cameras with a built-in video recorder-playback machine and other features, such as for editing, picture magnification (zoom), on-screen titling, and low-light recording.
Styles belonging to Bahral Ghazal region cultures.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Chad and Niger.

Carved wooden masks of the Songye people of the Democratic Republic of Congo in Africa, existing in both "female" and "male" types; the female type is used in burial rituals and the consecration of new chiefs, while the male type is used to impose discipline among the ranks of the circumcised.  In form they are distinguished by prominent facial features, often including a crest, and stripes of black, red, and white. They embody attributes of the human, the animal, and the spirit.
Dispersions of a people from their original homeland. Examples are the diaspora of Jewish people from Israel and the disapora of African people from Africa.

Flat stones that have a shallow depression in the upper surface for holding maize or other grains to be ground with manos, of the type used by Native Americans, especially in areas conquered and colonized by the Spanish.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Somalia.

Refers to a system of projection generally used in cartography and named for Gerardus Mercator, who introduced this projection on a map in 1569. It is generally classified as a cylindrical projection, even though it is actually derived mathematically. It is characterized by having parallels of latitude represented as straight horizontal lines and meridians of longitude represented as vertical straight lines at right angles to the equator. It is often used for navigation charts because any straight line is a line of true bearing that allows navigators to plot a straight-line course; it often considered impractical for world maps because the scale is distorted and areas farther away from the equator appear disproportionately large.

Refers to a projection generally used in map-making, where a section of the surface of the Earth or other heavenly body is depicted so that a straight line drawn from the center to any other point represents the shortest distance and can be measured to scale. This type of projection is often used to show distances and directions from a particular city, and measurements are accurate only when taken from the selected central point.

Refers to a system of projection generally used in creating large-scale map series, where each map is depicted as part of a cone tangent to the globe at the particular latitude.  The projection is based on the concept of a series of concentric cones being placed over the sphere so that each cone is tangent to a different latitude, where only the section of each unrolled cone that lies along a common central meridian of longitude and forms a strip on both sides of the line of tangency is represented. In this system, all parallels of latitude are arcs of nonconcentric circles, and the meridians of longitude other than the central meridian are represented by curved lines.

Generally refers to a rather rough imitation of incised Coromandel lacquer made in England in the 17th century. In 17th- and early 18th-century literature the term sometimes refers to the genuine article as well.

Modern term for a type of embroidery made in various places, including Italy, since the 16th century. The pattern in Assisi work is reserved in plain linen and the rest of the ground is covered with long-armed cross stitch in red or other colors. It was supposedly first produced in convents in Assisi although this is unlikely; the term instead probably derives from the fact that such embroidery has been made in Assisi in recent times.

Sewn boats of East Africa origin, about thirty or fourty tons, and having a long curved prow, and rigged with a square sail of coarse matting. No longer used, mitepe were mainly engaged in traffic along the section the Swahili Coast that lies between Zanzibar and the Lamu Islands.
Refers to needlepoint in which the design is worked on a canvas or cloth that has around 7 to 16 mesh holes per linear inch, allowing stitches that are relatively large and bold.

Refers to needlework created by working a design between the prongs of a large hairpin or another implement shaped like a hairpin. Loops are passed around the prongs to hold the piece in place as it is created, and the piece is slipped off the hairpin when it is finished. It is characterized by having large open loops at the sides, and it may be tied together to form rosettes or attached to other pieces of hairpin lace. It is typically used to make edgings, trimmings, headwear, or other apparel.
Refers to works of delicate knitting in which, instead of yarn, much finer threads are used.
Appliqué in which cut pieces of fabric with embroidery stitches are applied to a secondary ground fabric, or in which the embroidery itself acts to attach the applied material to the ground.

Pieces of ornament or entire textile works created by applying shapes or patterns in one material onto another material. The works are typically further decorated with embroidery that is used to secure and embellish the design. The term may refer to a single cutout decoration that is intended to be fastened to the larger piece of material, or to the material having the piece attached. Works may be intended to be framed or formed into apparel, hangings, bed linens, or other household items. Appliqué, along with embroidery, are among the most ancient and universal types of decorated textile works.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting southeastern Cameroon.

Refers to a darned net worked in silk or flax on an open, woven gauze ground. It is a variant kind of filit lace and one of the earliest types of lace. It is characterized by a twisted net background running in one direction and single thread running in the other direction; designs are sewn over the square grid.

Broad designation for areas of endeavor, physical and mental actions, discrete occurrences, systematic sequences of actions, methods employed toward a certain end, and processes occurring in materials or objects. Activities may include branches of learning and professional fields to specific life events, from mentally executed tasks to processes performed on or with materials and objects, from single physical actions to complex games.

A colorless hydrocarbon gas, the simplest of the alkynes, also called ethyne. Acetylene burns much more brightly than other gases and was used for stage lighting before electric lights were introduced. It burns with an intensely hot flame and is widely used as a fuel in oxyacetelene welding, soldering, and cutting of metals.
A serpentinite from the Italian Riviera having a red color.

Colorless, odorless, highly flammable gas, the simplest alkane. Methane occurs in natural gas, as firedamp in coal mines, and is produced by decaying vegetation and in the guts of ruminants. Methane is used as a fuel, and as a starting material in manufacture of chemicals. Methane carried into the stratosphere by rising air acts as a greenhouse gas and degrades the ozone layer.
A thicker and slightly stiffer form of railroad board; six-ply and eight-ply are the common thicknesses. Poster board is typically covered on only one side with either white or colored paper.

A generic term for a group of polysaccharides that are located in the cell walls of all plant tissues. Pectin is composed of methoxylated galacturonic acids joined in long chains. The main commercial sources of pectin are citrus peel and apple pomace. Pectin dissolves in water to produce viscous stable solutions. They are mainly used for food products (jams and jellies) but are also found as sizing agents in paper and textiles.
The smallest particles in which the elements combine either with themselves, or with each other, and thus the smallest quantity of matter known to possess the properties of a particular element.

Ions that have gained one or more electrons and thereby carry a negative electric charge, so-called because when an electric current is passed  through a conducting solution the negative ions present in the solution are attracted to the anode.

Hollow cylindrical molecules in the form of tubes measuring nanometers in diameter and composed entirely of carbon atoms. Carbon nanotubes have many potential commercial applications. They possess extraordinary strength and unique electrical properties, and are efficient conductors of heat. Nanotubes are already used in many common products, such as bicycle frames, automobile bodies, and tennis rackets.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Algeria, Mauritania, and Morocco.
Style and culture of the Iwellemmeden group of the same name inhabiting Mali and Burkina Faso.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a subgroup of the Kel Ayr living in Nigeria.
Describes works created by the Bedouin people of the same name living in Nefzaoua region, Tunisia.

Refers to a Protestant denomination that arose out of the 16th-century Anabaptists of Holland and Switzerland, particularly from the so-called Swiss Brethren. The name comes from one of their leaders, Menno Simons, a Dutch priest who consolidated and institutionalized the work begun by the moderate Anabaptists. Mennonite doctrine includes the practice of baptism upon confession of faith and adherence to the Confession of Dordrecht (1632) and the teachings of the New Testament. Mennonites, who are pacifists, have a policy against holding public office. Although Mennonites can be found in many parts of the world, most live in the United States and Canada.

Refers to one of two branches of the modern Islamic movement of Ahmadiyya. This branch regards Ahmadiyya's founder, Ghulam Ahmad, as a reformer rather than as a prophet and thus stays closer to mainstream Islam. The Lahori, like the Qadianis, are known for their preaching although they are more concerned in gaining converts to Islam in general than to their particular sect. They are also active in liberalizing Islam and in English- and Urdu-language publishing. The Lahori were led by Mawlana Muhammad Ali from its inception in 1914 until his death in 1951. The sect, which has spread widely, established the Woking mosque as it center in the United Kingdom; its main center is in Lahore, Pakistan.

Blotters bearing advertisements. Some, advertising mainly school supplies, were issued to school children in France from the late 19th century up until the 1960s. In mid-20th century,  Esquire Magazine was advertised by blotters featuring movie star pin-up drawings and photos. Customized advertising blotters are still produced today.

Christian Pentecostal denomination formed in Canada and the United States in the early 20th century out of previously independent Pentecostal churches. The Assemblies of God are in the Baptist tradition and specifically believe that speaking in tongues is evidence of baptism by the Holy Spirit. The denomination promotes missionary work all over the world.

Celebrations of the eucharist by a number of priests at once. Together the priests say the eucharistic prayer or the words of consecration over the same bread and wine. The practice died out in the West except at ordinations, but it was revived in the Roman Catholic Church by Vatican II. It is sometimes used as a way to allow priests and congregations from churches out of communion with one another to have a eucharist together.
Large meteors in which the meteoroid explodes as it passes through the Earth's atmosphere, creatng the effect of a brilliant ball of fire.
Notebooks commonly used in educational contexts. These normally come in a standardized format.
Bohisattvas who serve as otherworldly guides of souls.
The experience of a series of eidetic images, ideas, and emotions occurring during sleep.
Describes techniques for creating three-dimensional objects with malleable or hard materials, such as clay, wood, stone, bronze, ivory, and found objects.

In the Christian church, a day commemorating all the saints of the church, both known and unknown, celebrated on November 1 in the Western churches and on the 1st Sunday after Pentecost in the Eastern churches.

A Jewish festival and holiday commemorating the first and most momentous event in Jewish history: the liberation of the Hebrews from bondage in Egypt and the "passing over" of God of the houses of the Isrealites during the tenth plague of Egypt (when the first-born children of the Egyptians were killed). Passover begins on the 15th and ends on the 21st or 22nd day of the month of Nisan (March or April). On these seven (or eight) days, also called the Festival of Unleavened Bread, all leaven is prohibited, and only unleavened bread (matzo) may be eaten. The matzo symbolizes the Hebrews' suffering while in slavery and the haste with which they left Egypt during the Exodus. After the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem, Passover celebrations became home-based. The first night of Passover is particularly celebratory, with a special family meal called the seder. Symbolic foods commemorating the Hebrews' liberation are eaten at the seder and prayers and traditional recitations are performed. Custom also calls for a place to be set for Elijah, the herald of the messiah. Though Passover is one of great rejoicing, strict dietary laws must be observed, and there are certain restrictions regarding work at the beginning and end of the festival.
Description and study of seas, lakes, and other bodies of water.
Those who study seas, lakes, and other bodies of water, especially those who make hydrographic surveys or construct charts of the sea and its currents.

A branch of the medieval Cathars in Southern France; its main center was at Toulouse but another place of activity was Albi, hence its name given by the Council of Tours in 1163. The sect was regarded as a serious threat by the Catholic Church: Pope Innocent III (1198-1216) failed to convert these Christian dualist heretics and Simon de Montfort led a savage Crusade (the Albigensian Crusade) against them until 1218. The Dominican Inquisition also sought to eliminate the sect.

Reformed branch of the Carmelite order that became its own order in 1593. Perceived laxity and abuses within the Carmelite order led to the reforms of St. Teresa of Avila and later of St. John of the Cross. The term 'discalced' refers to the practice of the reformers of wearing sandals instead of shoes and stockings. Discalced Carmelites focus on parochial and missionary work.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting South Africa.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Kalahari desert of Botswana.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a subgroup of the Kel Ataram living in eastern Mali.

Domestic architectural style of the Cape provinces of South Africa, developed mainly in the period from 1652 until the end of the rule of the Dutch East India Company in 1796 and for a generation further, some examples being built as late as 1874. Characteristic elements include front and end gables, steep thatched roofs with a span of about six meters, and thick rubble, clay, or soft-brick walls, plastered and limewashed.

In Buddhism, the final nirvana or nirvana-after-death, which occurs upon the death of the body or ultimate departure from the conventional realm of a person who is an awakened being, having attained nirvana during his or her lifetime.
Amusement devices or toys comprising a box and images, often a reel of images, that are viewed through a hole cut into the box.
Containers, usually decorative, for storing board gamesor other gaming pieces. The boards for the games may form part of a lid or other surface integral to the box.
Graffiti works that cover subway cars from one end to the other.

Medieval picture bibles that are composed of paraphrased passages translated into French, including passages from the "Historia Scholastica" of Petrus Comestor, or of biblical passages juxtaposed with passages from Comestor.

The Hindu festival of lights, an important festival celebrated throughout India for four or five days in October/November (from the thirteenth day of the dark half of the lunar month Asvina to the second day of the light half of Karttika). The festival, honoring Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and good fortune, is observed with particular enthusiasm by merchants who begin new account books at this time (the goddess Kali is worshipped in Bengal). Worshippers place small earthenware oil lamps in rows along the parapets of temples and houses; the lamps are also set adrift on rivers and streams. This commemorates the return from exile and coronation of Rama, an incarnation of the god Vishnu. Ornate patterns of lotuses are drawn on the floor near the doors of houses as a way of inviting Lakshmi in. During the festival, people visit one another, exchange gifts, feast, and wear new clothes. The fourth day of the festival marks the beginning of the new year according to the Vikrama calendar.

Refers to an important Jain festival that ends the ritual year. The lights of the Hindu festival of the same name are reinterpreted as a commemoration of the passing into nirvana of Mahavira, the most recent of the Jain Tirthankaras, or saints. The lighting of the lamps is seen as a material substitute for the light of holy knowledge that was extinguished with Mhavira's death. The festival occurs on the full-moon day of the month of Karttika (October-November).

A wooden war canoe. Described in the Florentine Codex, it was used on the lake of Texcoco and its canals by the Mexica during battles with the Spaniards. The term also refers to a quadrangular, canoe-shaped shield, part of the array of the detiy Totoltecatl.

Maskers, primarily of African descent, who masquerade as Native Americans for Carnival parades in various cities and nations including New Orleans, Toronto, London, Brooklyn, Brazil, and Haiti and other island nations of the Caribbean. They are renowned for their elaborate, vividly-colored, hand-made costumes.
The characteristic of having an angular, V-shaped bottom.
Motif of an almond-shape with a circle in the middle, representing a human eye seen frontally. It was first used in Ancient Egypt; generally was a symbol of protection and power.
The impressions or marks of human feet, shod or unshod.
Secular lantern festivals of Senegal and Gambia.

Reinterment. In conservation context, refers to reburial of human remains or cultural artifacts unearthed or exposed during excavation. Motivations for reburial may be ethical in nature (as with regard to what was purposely buried) or protective (e.g. the reburial of an ancient mosaic pavement exposed to the elements). For the filling in of earth removed, use "backfilling."
Small cylindrical or flat bottles used to contain snuff, often carried on the person. Often highly decorative and made of a variety of materials.
Prehistoric structures consisting of a large flat or flattish unhewn stone resting horizontally on three or more stones set upright.
Core styles belonging to Mande cultures.
Refers to a combination of cels intended to be shown together, for example a cel with a design and a background cel.
Any chemical such as copper sulfate used as a preparation to destroy algae.

Describes human and other animal figures other then fish having legs depicted as fish bodies, usually holding in his or her hands the fish tails or two other animals in an aggressive, dominant attitude.

Major executive or administrative units within an organization. For major autonomous or semi-autonomous units within an organization, use "divisions (organizational units)." Use of these terms in literature, especially with regard to the official titles of organizational units, is idiosyncratic and often no consistent distinction is made.
Undergoing a change in color, or changing from transparency to a bright color, upon the passage of an electric current. A typical material manufactured to have this property is window glass.

The arrangement and layout of spaces inside architectural structures or parts of structures that are the result of conscious construction, are of practical use, are relatively stable and permanent. The term typically excludes the moveable works located within the space, such as furniture or accessories.
Levant said to be of the best quality, from South Africa and made from the skins of large Cape goats. It was used by French master binders for very fine bookbindings.

The skin of an adult female deer, leather made from which was used in early bookbinding. For the soft, suede-like leather made from the flesh split of kidskin, sheepskin, or goatskin, use "doeskin (leather)." For leather made from doeskin (skin), combine "doeskin (skin)" + "leather."
A vegetable secretion of shrubs and trees, consisting of a resin mixed with gum mucilage. Gum resin is generally insoluble in water, but dissolvable in alcohol.

A natural hydrocarbon polymer formed from the resinous latex of trees of the  Hevea and Parthenium genera. To prepare natural rubber, the latex is collected from a cut in the bark, precipitated with acid, then washed and dried. Rubber is very elastic and was used for bowls, shoe soles, adhesives, and bouncy balls. However, when cooled, rubber becomes brittle and when warmed it becomes sweaty and tacky. Prior to the development of synthetic resins, unvulcanized rubber was used for adhesive tapes and crepe shoe soles. In 1839, Charles Goodyear discovered that rubber can be hardened with the vulcanization process in which sulfur is used to initiate crosslinking of the hydrocarbon strands. Higher sulfur content produces a harder, denser material. Vulcanized rubber is used to make rubber bands, foams, fabric coatings, small objects, combs, pens, and musical instruments. Vulcanized rubber, however, will emit sulfur when exposed to light or heat causing the rubber to degrade and become brittle. Since the 19th century, small amounts of wax have been added to the rubber during vulcanization. The wax slowly migrates to the surface and provides a thin layer of protection from oxidation.
Aldehyde tanning done by exposing leather to smoke, which contains aldehydes. Usually done in combination with oil tanning.
Setting out by hand leather or parchment, done when the skin is very thin and delicate or when an exceptionally smooth grain side is required, as with vellum.

The practice of painting on the fore edge of a book, either with the edge solid so that the resulting image is visible with the book closed, or, in the more usual sense of the term, with the edges fanned out so that the image is visible only when the book is open. The edge may also be gilded or marbled in the usual manner.

The technique of painting two separate images on the fore-edge of a book, one done with the leaves fanned one way, the other with the leaves fanned the other way, so that the two images are visible independently.
Two separate images painted on the fore-edge of a book, one done with the leaves fanned one way, the other with the leaves fanned the other way, so that the two images are visible independently.
Patterns tooled onto the spine of a leather-bound book, consisting of a fillet, usually double, running from head-to tail alongside the joint, with horizontal lines intersecting it at intervals.
Tools made of agate used for fine burnishing, such as for gilding and for other purposes.

A pile of vellum or parchment paper leaves together with laminae of gold leaf, which are to be beaten in the first stage of beating to produce gold leaf by hand, before being transferred into the "shoder" packet.
Refers to the culture and styles native to the area and islands along Adriatic coast, both historically and in modern times.

Having the shape of a horseshoe, that is generally U-shaped but with the arms of the "U" turned inward to varying degree. Named for the protective narrow iron plate that is bent to the outline of the horse's hoof and nailed to the animal's foot.
A woven jadeite collar. An attribute of Quetzalcoatl in postclassic central Mexico.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in northwestern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Cameroon.
Refers to a type of pâte de verre that is characterized by being especially translucent. It was developed by Gabriel Argy-Rousseau, a famous Art-Deco glass designer of the 1920s and 1930s.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a subgroup of the Berber living in the High Atlas Mountains.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a Berber people living the Middle Atlas region of Morocco.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a Shluh subgroup living in the Moroccan High Atlas and the Sahara.
Building complexes focused on a church.
In Indian art and architecture, a makara head motif.
The enclosed form of the maṇḍapa that may be connected to the shrine of a temple or stand separately.
Documents comprising texts that are relatively short in length, sometimes but not always abbreviated versions of longer texts.

Refers to the styles associated with the peninsular region of Thailand. The styles are driven by the region's geographical location characterized by maritime trade and transpeninsular river passages that encouraged cultural exchanges. In architecture, the style reached fruition during the 8th through the 13th century and is evidenced by the Wat Kaeo featuring a cruciform structure with central cella, shrines that housed five Jina Buddhas, large stone pillars, colonnettes, and miniature decorative arches reminiscent of Cham (ninth and tenth centuries) and Srivijayan architecture. In sculpture, the style features bronze Mahayana Buddhist figures and clay votive tablets depicting Buddha and bodhisattvas in post-Gupta Indian style.
Technique of applying paint to the back of a sheet of glass in reverse order, that is, with details and highlights first and background last. The finished picture is viewed from the front.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in northern Ghana and Burkino Faso.

A dark, shiny glass formed in nature by the rapid cooling of lava. Obsidian is widely distributed and has been used since Paleolithic (before 3500 BCE) times for mirrors, weapons, tools, and jewelry. Obsidian is often black in color but may also be red, brown or green. It produces conchoidal fractures when cleaved. Sources of obsidian include Anatolia, Armenia, Ethiopia, Greece (Milos), Italy (Lipari, Eolie), Iceland, the U.S. (Wyoming), Mexico (Teotihuacan), Guatemala (Tikal), and Peru. Obsidian changes into pumice when it is melted.

Describes motion picture film that is 16 millimeters wide. In silent films it is perforated on both sides; in sound films only on one side, the other being used for the sound track. It was introduced in 1923 for the amateur market, and evolved into the common medium for home movie makers and filmmakers whose work was not intended for general theatrical release. Film of this size is typically used for independent films, documentaries, and films made for educational purposes.

Introduced in 1971, Super 16mm motion picture film has a picture area 40-46% larger than standard 16mm film. It is often used with the intention to blow the film up to 35mm for theatrical release, as Super16mm production costs are less expensive.
Having the form or outline of a decagon, which is a plane figure with ten sides and ten angles.
Having the shape or outline of a circle, which is a plane figure bounded by a single curved line which is everywhere equally distant from the center.
Having the form or outline of a rectangle, a plane figure with four sides and four right angles.
Having the form or outline of a square, a four-sided plane figure with four equal sides and four right angles.

Low-budget motion pictures made usually to accompany major features on double-bills. In the 1930s, "B" was the designation given to a motion picture shown in a U.S. theater as the second half of a double feature. Typically they have lower production values and less well-known or unknown actors compared to major features. The term is still used although the practice of showing two features for a single admission price no longer applies to new releases.
Short segments from longer, finished motion pictures, often inserted into a compilation of like segments or into another motion picture or television program.

Early motion picture genre, made prior to 1910. It consisted of silent films of very short length showing people and events from everyday life as they happened, usually authentic but sometimes manipulated.

Type of cutout animation in which flat silhouettes, often highly intricate, cut out of paper or other stiff material are silhouetted with back lighting, minutely readjusted, and each position photographed with single frame exposures. The technique was first developed by Lotte Reiniger in Germany during the 1920s.

Animation involving pliable modeled clay figures which are moved very slightly, filmed a few frames, moved again, filmed again, and so on. When the film is projected at normal speed, the figures appear to move and change expression.

Collectively, all the processes and techniques employed in the creation of motion pictures on film or videotape, including directing, performing, producing, filming, editing, writing and design. Specifically refers to the activities of film or video directors and producers.

French term meaning "putting into the scene," originally used to describe the arrangement of visual components on a stage.The term was later used in film criticism to include discussion of camera position, the relationships between objects, people, and masses and how they collectively affect the work. Results of this technique are often montage sequences, careful editing, and careful composition within and individual film frame. The has been, but is rarely used outside of a film context.
Special effects achieved by combining or altering film or video images, generally done after shooting by means of special optical or computer technologies.

The production of sounds other than speech or music, naturally or artificially reproduced, to make desired effects in a motion picture, video recording, radio or television program, or live theatrical stage presentation.

Style and culture of the people of southern Nigeria noted for their production of fine bronzes and carved ivories, particularly of the inhabitants who predated the modern nation of Bénin. For the style and culture of the modern nation, use "Beninese."
The style and culture of the city of Marrakech, the chief city of central Morocco.
Describes books the edges of which have been hand cut with a knife to remove the bolts after the binding process is finished, usually by the bookseller or purchaser.
Soft, durable, fine-grained, nonporous colored leather, vegetable-tanned and curried, made originally solely from the outer layer of horsehide rumps, later also from goatskin and pigskin.
Smooth, thin vegetable-tanned sheepskin leather, usually tanned with oak bark and grained in imitation of other leathers, softer than roan, and popular for inexpensive bookbindings.

Soft, pliable oil-tanned leather originally made from the skins of the chamois, Antilopa rupicapra, a small deer; now made from the skins of lamb, sheep, goat, or from the flesh split of skins or hides.

Leather made from skin from deer or deer family animals from which the grain has been removed. Generally treated with animal oils, formaldehyde, or a combination of both. For unprocessed skin, use "deerskin."
The folded or doubled edges of paper at the head, fore edge, or tail of the sheets of an uncut book; usually intended to be cut open.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in northern Nigeria.
Styles belonging to Luba region cultures.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Botswana.
Term used to describe works produced by members of the pan-ethnic group of people speaking the language of the same name, living in central, southern, and eastern Africa.
Style and culture of the Bantu-speaking African ethnic group of the same name living in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The planning discipline concerned with the physical environment and any and all human involvement with it, with the general objective of assuring proper habitat for people, animals, and plants and the resources upon which they depend. For the branch of architecture that deals with the design of the scenic environment, including green spaces, accompanying structures, and roadways, with the aim of creating a natural setting for human structures and settlements, use "landscape architecture."
Persons who are offered membership in an association as a sign of distinction, because of their merits, and usually without obligations.

Skiver, usually sheepskin, that has been coated with a thin paste or glue wash, which, when it dries, causes the skin to shrink and draw up, forming an artificial grain pattern which is then enhanced by boarding.

The concept of using found materials to resolve problems and create things. The idea was first described in a 1969 publication by the social anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss, drawing an analogy between how a bricoleur, or man-of-all-work, uses whatever tools and materials are at hand to construct projects, and how primitive human beings, when presented with new problems, did not think up new concepts but reordered and adapted existing ideas to accommodate a new set of circumstances. The concept has been borrowed  by thinkers and writers in other disciplines, such as education, art theory, law, and economics, in discussions of how creative artists, teachers, and others make adaptive reuse of existing ideas, materials, and practices to deal with new situations.

An ancient Greek vessel type used in connection to marriage. It is generally thought to hold water for the ritual bath taken by the bride, and perhaps the groom, before the wedding.  Another theory is that it was a container for the couple's food; there may also have been funerary uses as well. Pictures of a wedding procession or women preparing for marriage often appear on such vessels.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Kenya.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northeastern Namibia.

Refers to the period in the southern Levant from about 5000 to 4500 BCE, named after the site of Wadi Rabah. The period is characterized by the continued production of pottery, particularly bright red-or glossy black, burnished vessels, and the introduction of maceheads and biconical sling bullets.
Continuous, unbroken decks from stem to stern.
Short, deep keels in the shape of a fin, used typically by racing yatchs to improve winward sailing and increase transverse stabilty under sail.
Process of transmitting and recieving information to and from one's place of employment via telecommunication systems, such as microcomputers and modems.
Plays intended to be acted by children.

In Indian architecture, a miniature corner "cogged wheel" marking the symbolic storey in the vēṇukōśa of Kaliṅga temple śikhara; karṇāṇḍaka (Western India); corner "cogged wheel" marking the storey of a North Indian spire.
Cannons of a particular type, invented in 1877, designed to project a rope from the shore to a stranded ship to facilitate salvaging and rescue operations.

Treating unhaired hides or skins with a solution of pigeon or hen manure in order to remove undesirable constituents and impart a quality of softness and flexibility to the final leather. For a similar process using dog manure, use "puering."

Treating skins or hides with brain tissue which contains phosphorous compounds that oxidize oils to aldehydes. The process is not considered true tanning, as it is reversible, and the shrinkage temperature of the resulting material is not raised above that of the original.
Very light buffing of the grain side of leather with an abrasive, often sandpaper wrapped around a revolving cylinder, to remove slight grain defects.
Short pieces of timber supporting the planks of a mason's scaffold, one end supported by the scaffold, the other inserted in a putlog hole left in the masonry wall.
An ideographic script developed and used by the peoples of the Cross River region.
Ritual killings of humans as an offering to deities or other supernatural forces.

A method of curing hides and skins, generally employed in the larger abattoirs, prior to transportation to tanneries. After flaying, and a thorough washing and brushing to remove hair and flesh, the hides or skins are hung in pits or large paddles in a very strong solution of sodium chloride, causing salt to penetrate the material. Distinct from "pickling," a beamhouse operation following bating, in which hides and skins are soaked in a solution of 12% salt and 1.2% sulfuric acid.
The branch of grammar that studies the smallest meaningful units of languages and their formation into words, hence, also the structure of words.

African American male maskers, usually of the working class, who sing, dance and parade in unofficial associations or "tribes" in New Orleans's Mardi Gras and St. Joseph's Day parades. Their costumes are comprised of large feather headdresses, moccasin-style boots, and aprons with patterns sewn in such materials as sequins, rhinestones, glass beads, ribbons velvet, and ostrich plumes.

Sharp edged or pointed implements used in Pre-Columbian Mesoamerican cultures to kill victims or simply shed blood as sacrifices to the gods; they take a variety of forms, including manmade objects such as knives and sharp spikes with handles, and natural objects such as thorns and stingray stings.
Refers to the period and dynasty of the two legendary Etruscan kings of ancient Rome named Tarquinius.

Portable and collapsable frames, typically made of wood, designed to help wind/unwind skeins of yarn during the hand-spinning and weaving processes. This type of swift is equipped with various umbrella-like ribs that expand and/or fold in to accomodate variously sized yarn skeins.
Smoking equipment with a long flexible tube attached to a water reservoir through which the smoke is drawn and cooled; used for tobacco and narcotics.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name. A traditional autonomous kingdom, today they are an important ethnic subgroup of the Ovimbundu people of Angola.

Indigenous furniture typically produced by anonymous craftsmen and based on either traditional practices or high-style prototypes that may follow the original closely or display a range of modifications, such as a simplication of form and the use of local materials and techniques.

The use of children as a labor force in industry or business. Now widely considered inhumane, it has been rendered illegal in most developed countries, though it was common until the early 20th century.
The process of gilding the edges of a book with a piece of paper laid over the gold and the burnisher rubbed over the paper, resulting in a dull finish.
Desk-top or portable computers, based on a microprocessor and meant for a single user.

A system that incorporates components that allow recording, editing, mixing, storing, performing and outputting digital audio. Generally these include three components: a computer, software, and some kind of hardware interface for the connection of microphones or musical instruments.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Bénin and Nigeria.

A set of standards proposed by the World Wide Web Consortium to promote common data formats, including a semantic component, in order to convert currently unstructured web documents into a shared framework and a web of data that can be processed by machines.
Pieces of work or activities concerning work done, emphasizing the activity rather than the profession, although jobs are done as part of one's regular profession.

Glories that comprise a circle, disk, series of lines, or rays of light with which the head of the sacred personage is surrounded. In Hellenistic and Roman art, halos are worn by the sun-god Helios and Roman emperors often appear with a crown of rays. The imagery was picked up in Christian art.

In linguistics, phonetically distinct variants of a phoneme, usually distinguished from other variants by its position in the word or by its phonetic environment. Speakers of a language often have difficulty in hearing the phonetic differences between allophones of the same phoneme, because these differences do not serve to distinguish one word from another. In English, examples would be the "t" sounds in the words "hit," "tin," and "little."

The branch of forensic science dealing with the study of fingerprints to establish the identity of the person who made them or from whom they were taken. For the method or technique of analyzing and identiying fingerprints, use "dactyloscopy."

A dense, crystalline or microcrystalline limestone that was formed by the evaporation of river or spring waters. It is named after Tivoli, Italy ("Tibur" in Latin), where large deposits occur, and it is characterized by a light color and the ability to take a good polish. It is typically banded, due to the presence of iron compounds or other organic impurities. It is often used for walls and interior decorations in public buildings. It is distinguished from "tufa" by being harder and stronger.
In libraries and book collecting, the exchange between or among individual authors, libraries, or other institutions of their own publications or of those institutions with which they are affiliated.

Audio recordings or multimedia files formatted like radio programs, but distributed as digital files online. The user may play these back at his or her convenience on a computer or digital music player. Most often podcasts include interviews, music, or tutorials. The term was coined in 2004.
Works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Ghana and northern Togo, formerly part of the Ano and inhabiting Côte d'Ivoire.
Describes works produced by the African people of the same name living in the Ngamiland region of Botswana and Namibia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting southwestern Ethiopia and southeastern Sudan.

Funerary pottery style from the Akan region of southern Ghana in Africa, exemplified by terra cotta heads and ritual pots found in burial or funerary contexts dating from the 17th ceentury and later. They come from the Akan region of southern Ghana of Africa where the pre-colonial state of Twifo was located; Hemang refers to the place near whch these ceramics were discovered.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in central Côte d'Ivoire.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Ghana.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Ndop plain in the Northwest province of Cameroon, in the Cameroon Grassfields.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Tanzania.
Style and culture of the many African ethnic groups who inhabit this highland area in western Cameroon and who share similar stylistic characteristics, forms, and motifs in their art.
Describes works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name living in eastern Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, and western Guinea.
Stone or concrete mintadi, used as grave monuments erected on tombs of high-ranking persons among Kongo peoples and in Angola.
Wooden sculptures to which medicines are added and activated during oath-taking rites, sometimes by driving nails, blades, or wood points into the sculpture's surface.
German drinking glasses that are tall, cylindrical, and decorated in enamel with mountain landscapes.
Type of moss commonly found in the southern United States, characterized by tufts of grey strands on the trunks and branches of trees.

Islamic writing boards used in Qur'anic schools upon which pupils write verses from the Qur'an as a means of rote learning. Also used as devotional objects, and by diviners in magical practices involving inscriptions and symbols written upon the boards, both Qur'anic and from other sources. Typically they have crescents carved at the top.

Style and culture of the historical group that dwelled in the Horn of Africa from the 11th century, comprising mostly Christian, Semitic-speaking peoples in a territory including Eritrea, Tigray, Gonder, and parts of Gojam, Shewa, and Welo in the territory of the modern nation of Ethiopia.
Styles and culture belonging to modern East Africa.
Sculpture styles belonging to modern Makonde cultures.
Style of modern Makonde sculpture depicting devils or folk spirits, featuring distorted, exaggerated, or abstract forms.

A type of chevron bead carried by the Spaniards for trade to the New World, and first identified in an archeological site in Venezuela, from which they derived their name "Nueva Cadiz," an island which was a prosperous port from 1498-1545. They are usually made from three twisted layers of blue glass.
Style and culture of an African people living in South Africa, part of the southern Nguni cluster.

The absence of clothes in which the absence implies embarrassment at being deprived of clothes or in which the depiction of the nude is intended to cause embarrassment or salacious feelings in the viewer.
Technique in ancient Roman construction, using hydraulic-setting brick-faced concrete; most used during the late Roman Republic and the Roman Imperial period.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northern Nigeria.

Style and culture of the Afar ethnic group, who speak the Afar Cushitic Afro-Asiatic language and live in the Horn of Africa, primarily the Afar region of Ethiopia, northern Djibouti, and southern Eritrea
Works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name residing in Cameroon, Congo, and Central African Republic.
Describes varieties of patterns produced artificially through embossing into book-cloth and used for publisher's binders.
Book cloth grain with bead-like pattern.
Trade name for a book cloth made by the Winterbottom Book Cloth Company of England, made of linen and finished with a grain pattern resembling that of leather, most often straight-grain morocco.
Sterns in which the bottom edge of the transom is above the waterline.
Buildings that house justice centers used for the custody and treatment of juvenile offenders.

Used to describe works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Swaziland and South Africa. Mahlalela was the name of a formerly independent chiefdom, and of their chief, within the nation of Swaziland.
Combination-tanned leather that has first been chrome-tanned, then retanned by a vegetable tanning process.
Wraps, typically made of wool, covering the head and body, and worn in northern Africa.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Cameroon.

Components of some belts, especially those that formed a part of early medieval dress: rectangular plates placed behind the buckle. These were found on belts that would have included a buckle, a counter plate that was placed opposite the buckle, and sometimes a rectangular back plate placed in the middle of the belt at the back for decoration.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, living in a kingdom of Dyula origin in Burkina Fasso.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in Ghana, a subgroup of the Nzema.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Burkina Faso.
Standard model boats, either sail or power, designed to be produced in quantity.

Floating objects in fixed positions used by ships or boats for mooring in deep water. Their design incorporates a weight fixed in the bottom of a body of water that acts as an anchor holding the buoy in its position. These are often used in areas near coral reefs to save the reef from damage by the use of ships anchors.

Any of a variety of sweet, relatively rich quick breads, shortened or unshortened, typically made with flour, sugar, leavening, liquid, and flavoring, and usually shaped by the tin in which it is baked.

Spherical seed beads, often made of glass and usually no bigger than 1/8th inches in diameter. Commonly used in Native North American beadwork; were brought to North America by European traders in the 18th to 19th centuries.
Beads, usually manufactured from conch shell or animal bone, commonly worn by Plains Native people from the 1800s to present. Used as components for breastplates, bracelets, and hair ornaments.
Refers to strings of beads or knots for counting prayers, one third of the length of a rosary.
Snake masks made of turquoisean attribute of Xiuhteuctli. Also designates a snake mask pattern on capes in postclassic central Mexico.

Visual works where architecture is depicted in outdoor views and interiors and where the architecture is the predominant focus of the painting. In European art, architectural paintings exist as an independent genre developed in the 16th century in Flanders and the Netherlands, and reached its peak in 17th century Dutch painting.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the lagoon region of Côte d'Ivoire.
Half models used specifically as guides in the construction of vessels.
Carved staffs bearing heads shaped like double-headed axes, carried by devotees of the Yoruba god Shango and used in ceremonies as dance wands.

Builder's models comprising alternating strips of constrasting colored wood glued edge to edge to create a checkerboard effect when carved, and to distinguish the sectional lines of a proposed vessel.
Relatively short-shafted spears designed to be thrust instead of thrown.
Small cloaks covering the shoulders of the child or adult being baptized; often decorated.
Hairstyle of Nahua women composed of two horn-like tufts wrapped around the head in postclassic central Mexico.
Metal repoussé icon cover, often serving as an icon frame.
Examples of script or type forms considered to be fine quality examples of typography or calligraphy.
Sequence of illustrations containing a story or stories (called "comics," because some are humorous), often serialized, published in booklet form.
Comics in which the story or action is basically adventurous, often set in exotic locations and involving the main characters in travel.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in the Central African Republic.
Musical performances, typically public and consisting of a series of separate songs or pieces; may include a number of singers or musicians.
Stationary members or tracks in a slipway, upon which the sliding ways, supporting a vessel, travel.
Parts or components of shipyard structures.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in Burkina Faso and Ghana.
Shield-like aprons worn by Mangbetu women of Africa to cover the buttocks; usually made of woven fibers and often decorated with geometric patterns.

A rare light blue corrosion product found as a contributing factor to the greenish chromatic degradation of azurite in mural paintings, and in the patina of outdoor bronze monuments such as the horses of San Marco in Venice.

Typically refers to Persian rulers. The term is derived from a Persian title meaning "Great King" or "Emperor." The term is usually used to refer to the shah of Iran, but it may also refer to the Sultan of Turkey or to the Great Mogul of India. Before 1948, it was also used in India to refer to the sovereign of Great Britain. It is occasionally used in Asia to refer in a more general sense to monarchs of Europe.

Events comprising presentations that instruct in, explain, or illustrate the practical operation or results of methods, processes, products, devices, or theories to others, such as students or prospective clients.
Genus containing one living species of flying lemur.

Members of an order of marine invertebrates having a flat, disk-shaped body, lacking the spherical symmetry of other echinoderms, but having five- or six-rayed markings on their surface; living on the sandy sea bottom of coastal North America south of the Arctic.
Members of a genus containing over 1,000 species of ant large ants that create nests in dead, damp wood or hollow out sections of trees. They may infest buildings made of wood.
Hand-held personal fans printed with information advertising companies or products, usually distributed for free as promotional items.

Shoulder belts worn across the breast that hold ammunition within pockets, loops, or cases or from which a wallet might be suspended at the side; also, decorated straps worn over the shoulder and across the breast by North American Indians. For bags with attached straps worn by North American Indians over the shoulder and across the breast, use "bandolier bags."
Those who ride bicycles.
Bivalves separated by some into a subclass based on shell structure.

Waist-length army jackets of a particular style and khaki color, resembling jackets worn by U.S. General Dwight D. Eisenhower during World War II. The jacket became standard issue for U.S. troops beginning in November 1944.
Military decoration of an orange and blue lanyard presented to Dutch soldiers of the Princess Irene Brigade who took part in the Normandy landing in 1944: also worn by the Dutch Fusiliers.

Cords, usually braided, ending in aglets, worn looped under the arm and sometimes across the breast on military uniforms; worn especially by aides-de-camp, but also by other officers. Distinguished from "fourragères," which are braided cords worn as an honorary military decoration.
Complexes within an enclosure, comprising single or multi-unit family dwellings with communal spaces, adjacent outbuildings or structures. Examples are in Africa.

Places designed for those with decreased cognizance from conditions such as Alzheimer's disease. These combine residential, commercial, and “public” buildings where residents live and associate with others in environments resembling pre-industrial small towns that include pedestrian-friendly navigation routes, family-centered houses, and shared communal spaces. Healthcare facilities are often disguised.

Self-contained districts within or near a city that is hosting the Olympics sporting events, providing accommodation and amenities for competitors and other people who have an official connection with the Olympic games. Self-contained districts within or near a city that is hosting the Olympics sporting events, providing accommodation and amenities for competitors and other people who have an official connection with the Olympic games.

A type of small communal housing development, designed and managed by the occupants, in which each resident family owns a home and shares with the group common facilities, such as kitchens, child care centers, and laundry rooms, and their associated tasks. The modern method of cohousing originated in Denmark in the 1960s.
Beltlike devices, worn by women especially in the Middle Ages, designed to prevent sexual intercourse.
Long, square spikes used in heavy timber construction.
Early Iron Age culture, partially identified by characteristic ceramic ware from East Africa.
Cooperatives that provide agricultural products such as grain, milk and meat.
Larvae of butterflies, moths, as well as larvae of some other insects that are hairy, such as the saw-fly.
Parts or components of stalls.
Shelf-like projections attached to the undersides of hinged seats in choir stalls; when the seats are lifted, they give support to a person standing in the stall; often ornamented.

Wild species that was transformed to the domesticated form, B. mori, over many centuries, and the continuing artificial selection by humans to maximize the quantity, quality, and diversity of silk, as well as the creation of infection-resistant strains.

Women who narrate, chant, or sing histories, especially genealogies, of individuals, families, and communities, often accompanying this with instrumental music, acting, and mime. Originally used with reference to West Africans, now applied to such people in other cultures and geographic areas.
West African harvest festivals held to celebrate the yam crop.
Relatively large, enclosed buildings with facilities for housing and breeding a large number of swine under one roof.
Photovoltaic cells that convert sunlight directly into electricity.
Parts of ancient Greek houses used only by men. For those sections set aside for women, use "gynaecea."
Women's apartments in ancient Greek or Roman houses. For the sections of Greek houses set aside for men, use "andra."

Commercial spaces in museums or separate buildings staffed by museum personnel and selling primarily museum-specific souvenirs and related merchandise, the proceeds of which help to support the operating museum.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northeastern Madagascar.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the northwestern Ituri forest in Democratic Republic of Congo.
A Chinese marble with markings created by fossil content; when the stone is cut sectionally, the markings resemble the shape of a pagoda.
Refers to the temporary cessation, interruption, postponement, or withholding of a right, statute, legal proceeding, or legal decision or its effects, such as a prison sentence.
Artists who specialize in painting altarpieces, which are objects in a Christian church, usually framed and either set on the rear part of the altar or hung on the wall behind the altar.
Legal actions brought to court by one or more parties against another or others to enforce, redress, or protect private rights.

Use generally for any proceedings in court brought by one or more persons against another or others, or by the state against a person or persons, to enforce a private right, redress or prevent a private wrong, or to punish a public offense.

Sharp pointed implements used in Pre-Columbian Mesoamerican cultures to prick the flesh and draw blood to offer as a self-sacrifice to the gods; includes both manmade implements resembling daggers or spikes with handles, and natural objects such as thorns or stingray stings.
Bevelled, wedge-shaped boards of varying sizes usually made of wood and sometimes faced with metal, used in a lying press when backing a book.

The technique of sewing a text block, usually by hand and generally on cords or tapes, in which one length of thread passes through each sewing station within a single gathering, from kettle stitch to kettle stitch.

Bookbinding stitching technique in which stitches pass close to and over the binding edges, creating gatherings which are then sewn all along. In addition to sewing through the fold, the first and last signatures of a book are overcast to strengthen them against the volume's opening and closing.
To mend by covering a hole or weakened area on a surface with a patch.
Large, round sprays of feathers worn as headdresses or back devices by warriors in postclassic central Mexico.
Spiral cone shell disks worn as ornaments and prestige objects by the Shona people of Zimbabwe and Mozambique, taken from the base of the shell of the marine snail species Conus.

Persons trained in the feudal Japanese art of ninjutsu or a modern equivalent. Collectively, a mercenary force that specialized in spying and executing attacks. Originally these agents had differing names in each region of Japan based on tasks they performed. In most historical Japanese texts they are referred to as 'shinobi'.
Equipment used to measure and cut paper or printed material into specific formats.
Hairstyling process in which hair is parted into rows and braided firmly on the surface of the scalp into various patterns.

Tubular trade beads of West Africa, known from the 15th century, of different and variegated colors though the most highly prized were blue with a greenish translucence. Their manufacture and component material is uncertain.
Snake-shaped ear ornaments of postclassic central Mexico. One of the attributes of Huitzilopochtli.
Tools used to smooth glued surfaces or fold and layer printed material. Made from bone or plastic and comes in two forms; a straight, rectangular tool or a curved tool ending at a point.
Equipment, usually a type of keyboard, used to generate typed characters and titles which are inserted or superimposed onto a video image.
Enclosures, left open in front and usually of wood, housing the pipes of an organ.

The process of preserving bodies of human beings or animals, resulting in a mummy, whether it occurs by chance (natural mummification) or is intentionally pursued through embalming or treatment for burial using preservatives.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name, a subgroup of the Mongo inhabiting northwestern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Sculptures of the Fon people of Benin, Africa, consisting of a staff surmounted by a disc-like platform decorated with a tableau of cut-out or forged metal figures, often with pendants hanging from the edge; they function as commemoratives to deceased relatives, and are prayed to and offered sacrifices in ceremonies of mourning and ancestor worship.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name, a Sarwa people living on the northern fringe of the Okavango Delta.

Carved heads or faces, usually having fierce expressions, exagerated features, and bulbous eyes. Examples are faces of ancestors located on Maori meeting houses. For faces carved with a more realistic appearance, used for gables of houses or canoes, use parata.
Use to describe objects, including structures, or components of objects designed to perform a complete rotation around an axis.

In geology, the cementing of rock sediments or remains of microscopic marine organisms by the precipitation of minerals (silica, carbonate, iron oxide), which are deposited as microcrystals into the pore spaces. It is the final stage in the formation of sedimentary rock.
Chewing tobacco produced in the form of a flat cake.
One of two families containing anteaters.
Family containing the three-toed sloths.
A type of trough or long narrow open container that holds water or food for animals.
Headgear with which a horse is governed and restrained, usually consisting of a headstall, bit, and reins.
The curved parts of harnesses, shaped to fit around a draft animal's neck, against which it exerts its weight to move a load.
Raised back parts of some saddle seats, which provide support and keep the rider in the saddle.

Members of a species of hominid found only in lowland rainforests of the Congo river. They differ from the other extant species of the genus Pan, Pan troglodytes, in being more slender, with longer limbs, a narrower chest, a rounder head with a less-protruding face, descending from trees only to move between trees, and having different behaviors and dynamics in social groups. In older classifications, the bonobo and the common chimpanzee were classified as one species.
Short whips, usually made of braided leather, used by equestrians.

Carrying devices or frames carried across a person's shoulders that consist of a length of material, usually wood, sometimes shaped to accommodate the neck and shoulders of the user, though this is often a simple rod. Suspended from this support are two buckets that can transport liquid or other materials by one person.
The parents of one's parent.
Any of a number of systems employing prerecorded audio messages to inform visitors to museums or other exhibitions.
Undergarments that reach from the waist to the ankles, usually worn to keep the wearer warm in cold weather.

In the context of materials, material comprising a tendon taken out of an animal body and used for some purpose, especially as a cord or thread, as a string in a musical instrument, or for another purpose.
A mixture of gases comprising the earth's atmosphere generally understood as that which is essential to the survival of land animals and plants.

General term for a material that has the ability to take up another material without any chemical bonding, or that takes up energy. Examples include materials that take up and dissipate radiated energy, or a material that takes up moisture or odor.

Straight bars or clips which are generally made of the same metal as a medal; they have engraved data on their surfaces that are allusive to the decoration and complement it. These may be located on the decoration itself or the ribbons from which the decorations hang.

Refers to symbols or other marks made by masons, generally incised into the stone. They were used to indicate a mason's responsibility for a building or sections of a building. They were often very elaborate marks, sometimes used in conjunction with a signature. The term may also refer to marks incised on stones to indicate in which part of the building they belonged.
Unit tools cut in flower or leaf designs.
Bindings structured so that two books share a lower board, fore edges facing in opposite directions.
Any substance that absorbs ultraviolet radiant energy then dissipates the energy in a harmless form; used in plastics and rubbers to decrease light sensitivity.
Study of topographic irregularities on a very small or microscopic scale.
French registers, usually made of silk.

Furniture designed to be erected and dissasembled easily and quickly, produced for officers to be taken on military campaign.  Despite these requirements, campaign furniture is typically luxurious and crafted from quality materials.
News agencies that distribute news reports and photographs to subscribers by telecommunications.
Flageolets that have an attached third pipe, sometimes a bass pipe, enabling players to create three-note chords. Purported to have been invented by William Bainbridge of London, ca. 1820.
Businesses that offer services in advertising, branding, marketing, and promotion.
Groups of buiiness enterprises of the same kind or function, such as restaurants, stores, theaters, or hotels, linked together into a single system under a single ownership, management, or control.

Business enterprises owned and operated by members who use the enterprises' services and share the financial benefits. The first consumer cooperative store was established in Rochdale, England, in 1844, and most are still modeled after the original principles.

Categorization designating a group or individual comprised of more than one distinct differentiated people based on socially defined characteristics, ethnicity, language, or culture. People of mixed race may have differing opinions about which terms are considered  derogatory or acceptable, depending on region, country, or personal preference.

Rented compartments in officially designated post offices in which all mail is placed and held until called for by the renter. For outdoor public and private boxes for pickup and delivery of mail, use "mailboxes."

A type of faïence parlante, generally plates and jugs, that features inscriptions and depictions of the French Revolution, its ideology, or other national political events. The first examples appeared around 1745 and featured the Royalist fleur-de-lis. Republican themes soon appeared, including the Phrygian cap, the Gallic cock, plows, oak trees, draped flags, the Bastille, and slogans and scenes related to liberty, the rights of man, the Third Estate, and agriculture.
Wooden or bamboo structures attached to the back with a carrying strap connected to a front band. Used to transport goods in Mexico.
Clutch bags with a fold-over flap, of leather or other materials; made to resemble an envelope.
Trumpet-shaped megaphones.
Painting styles belonging to Christian Nubian cultures.

Style of Nubian fresco and panel painting that, among other stylistic characteristics, makes great use of the colors violet and steel gray, dating from the early 8th century until the mid-9th century.
Moored, floating devices, employed as aids to mariners, marking navigable limits of channels and their fairways, or hazards such as sunken dangers, rocks, mines, torpedoe grounds or telegraph cables.
Pivoted sighting devices or pointers that can be aligned against a circular scale of degrees and is typically a component of an astrolabe, plane table, or similar instrument.
Describes the surface of the leather from which the inner subcutaneous flesh and fat have been removed.
Equipment for the recording, transmission, reproduction, and amplification of sound.

An individual person's conscious sharing of some kind of essential character with one or more groups of other people, such as a race, nation, social class, profession, or body of people organized into a group at some particular time for some particular purpose.
Devices that play audio, whether on removeable media or integral drives that hold digital information.
In Indian architecture, an image-frame, often bearing retinue of subsidiary figures panelled or otherwise.

Artists who create in order to express an often intense and very personal vision or aesthetic, and whose work is usually unmediated by the standards, traditions, and practices of the culture of the art world, as embodied by the international art markets and established art institutions.
Devices intended to eliminate impurities in the air.
Codes used specifically to disguise the content of a message, involving a rule defined by a secret key known only to the transmitters and legitimate receivers of the message.

Refers to hand sewing characterized by techniques more elaborate than used in plain sewing. It includes embroidery, smocking, and quilting, and other works done with a needle and thread. The purpose of fancy sewing is generally to create decoration rather than to bind pieces of material together.

Containers in Christian churches, made in the form of a dove and designed to be hung by chains over the altar. They had a door, sometimes hidden under a wing or on the back, that concealed a small cavity once used to hold the eucharistic bread. Eucharistic doves were formerly part of the standard liturgical furnishings for churches that could afford them. They were typically made of gold, silver, or another metal with enamelwork.
Linens used in setting a table for dining, such as tablecloths and napkins.

Uniform bindings produced wholesale and in quantity (often machine-made case bindings), applied to books expected to sell rapidly and in quantity; used from the mid-18th century onwards; distinguished from small quantity "trade bindings," which are simple bindings of sheep or calf commissioned by booksellers from the 15th to the 18th century.

Blocking without the use of gold leaf, silver leaf, or color, usually involving a heated block or frame. In bookbinding, distinguished from "blind stamping" in which a hand tool is used instead of a machine.
Fishing lures that are designed to imitate the underwater swimming motions of bait used to attract fish.

Lightweight composite panels consisting of two sheets of aluminum bonded to a polyethylene, polyurethane, or other core, and cut to standard measurements. These have been used as exterior cladding as well as for interior surface applications, and signage. Aluminum composite panels are increasingly used in museum storage and exhibition applications as a non-VOC-emitting material, safe to use around all museum object materials. For the material that aluminum panels are formed from use "aluminum composite material."

General term for structures or other accommodations designed or adapted for residential occupancy, as contrasted to business occupancy. For hotels or other buildings intended for use by transients see "public accommodations" and its narrower concepts. For the locale which constitutes the center of an individual's domestic life, personal relationships, and interests, together with the feeling of comfort and satisfaction that it conveys, use "home (concept)." For the collective concept referring to types of living arrangements of a particular group, use "housing."
A brick that has been shaped with an ax and not trimmed when laid.
Key plates with a pivoting pendant attached that drops to cover the keyhole.
Blankets made or used for covering horses, dogs, or other animals
Parent companies whose activities are confined to owning stock in and supervising the financial, managerial, or marketing functions of their subsidiaries.
A genus of hornbills.

Use with reference to sculpture, architectural decoration, ceramics, and various ancient artifacts that have been decorated with more than one color. For the process of so decorating, use "polychromy."
Members of a species of seabird native to the Arctic and northern coasts of the Atlantic that nests in burrows, and has black and white plumage and a very deep and brightly colored bill.
Seats in postclassic central Mexico, usually made of mats made of thick reeds. Used as a metaphor for the power and authority of the ruler.

Refers to the aggregate of high-end audio-video equipment, usually with large-screen television receivers and surround-sound capabilities, designed and arranged to provide theaterlike environments; may also be used for rooms designed to accommodate viewing images offered by such equipment. For domestic spaces whose focus is a home entertainment system, with video, music, and games, use "media rooms."

A branch of landscape archaeology which emerged during the 1980’s in the context of historical restoration. Garden archaeology investigates diverse questions, from studies of natural history and rural economy to recovery of ancient garden layouts. Excavations at Castle Bromwich Hall Gardens in Birmingham and at the Privy Garden of Hampton Court are examples of garden archaeology.

Culture or style of a North American Indian tribe of Algonquian linguistic stock who lived during the 19th century along the Platte and Arkansas rivers of what are now the U.S. states of Wyoming, Colorado, Nebraska, and Kansas. Their oral traditions suggest that they once had permanent villages in the Eastern Woodlands, where they engaged in agriculture. Because of pressure from tribes to the east, the Arapaho gradually moved westward, abandoning farming and settled life during the process. They split into northern (Platte River) and southern (Arkansas River) groups after 1830.

A fluorescence microscopy technique that obtains higher resolution images of very small objects than conventional optical microscopy. Rather than flooding the entire specimen evenly with light, which causes simultaneous excitation of all parts and results in a large out-of focus background part captured by the microscope's photodetector, confocal microscopy uses a condenser lens to focus the light  from a pin-hole onto a very small spot on the plane of the specimen. An optical system rapidly scans the object in synchrony with the illumination. The reflected and emitted rays entering the collector lens are focused onto a plate which generates a signal that forms a display of the image.
Mechanisms built into some keyboard instruments, such as organs, reed organs, and harpsichords, to vary the volume of tone.

Boxlike chambers within an organ or reed organ housing a set of pipes or reeds, and having on one side a movable lid, shutter, or set of shutters or slats that can be opened or closed to increase or diminish the tonal volume of the pipes or reeds within.
Assemblies or bodies of people convened for consultation or to administer rules or advice.
Translucent overglaze fired at very low temperatures.
Reworking large painted areas either to cover damage, mask unwanted features, or change color and design. For similar work done on paintings by conservators, use "inpainting" or "overpainting."
