Courts in Great Britain and in some American states that administer specifically the law of equity and proceed according to the forms and principles of equity, as opposed to the common law or statutory law.
Way of life characterized by cyclical or seasonal movement from place to place which is necessary for the subsistence of the group, resulting in lack of a continuous permanent abode.

Literary or oral fiction genre in which a crime, often murder, is committed under mysterious circumstances and then solved by the central figure of a detective, using keen observation and rational analysis of clues and evidence.
Phrases, sentences, or inscriptions in which certain letters, usually distinguished by size or other means from the rest, express by their numerical values a date, year, or epoch when added together.

Printed periodicals with or without text in which the essential information is conveyed through a collection of photographic images. These may be authored by one or more artists or photographers, or arranged by an editor. Generally the images in a  photo zine are meant to be viewed in context, as parts of a larger whole. These often are produced in inexpensive formats, usually with small circulation. For similar singular publications bound as books, use 'photobooks.'
Ringless binders that hold sheaves of documents via a spring-or clamp device built into the spine.
Bookbinding cords that have been placed in grooves sawn into the back of the sections of a book.
In the context of armor, plate arm guards protecting the arm from the humerus to the wrist, of the style used in Italy and elsewhere during the 14th-17th century.
In Indian architecture, a tall plinth with additional special mouldings for larger temples; tall socle with additional set of upper mouldings, usually vēdībandha, for sāndhāra temples.
The top edges of books trimmed smooth and gilded, implicitly leaving the two other edges ungilded and either rough cut or uncut.
Organizations engaged in the free assistance of the poor, the suffering, or the distressed.

Double-ended surfboats, 26 feet long, with ten rowing stations, centerboard, rudder, and lug-rigged sail; designed by the United States Coast Guard in 1934, sometimes used as gigs, and named after Monomoy Island, Cape Cod, Massachusetts.

Organs of government belonging to the judiciary established by law to hear cases, petitions, and other causes, and publicly administer justice, whether military, ecclesiastical, or relating to the statutory or common law of the land.

Heavy buckram in tan shades, so colored as to resemble sheepskin leather. Used as book cloth, it superceded the more expensive leathers "law calf" and "law sheep" as a common binding material for law books in the 20th century.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Chad and Central African Republic.

Parabolic, dish-shaped reflectors for receiving primarily television or other video programming via satellite; often found on or near residences; may also be used in non-residential contexts and for some data and voice reception.

Prehistoric shaft-hole axes with symmetric cutting edges at each side of the shaft. Found in stone, copper and bronze. The double axe was a common religious symbol in Minoan Crete and was also used as a votive object.

Refers to a type of dagger-axe, or halberd, used for display by Shang elite in Bronze Age China. They are single- or double-edged blades with short hafts, though length, shape, and motif varied and evolved over time. Many bronze ge were functional weapons, while later examples are ground from materials such as nephrite and are presumed to be purely ceremonial. Bronze ge may have been among the first objects created in Chinese foundries.
Small plastic or metal tabs inserted underneath collar tabs to keep them from curling.
Length of existence of anything in its present form.

Waste material produced by the process of coal mining, that may include coal gangue found in mining heaps, the light gray, washed waste produced during coal preparation, the red-colored burnt coal gangue caused by pyrite oxidation, and a high percentage of coal itself.
Books kept at the headquarters of a military unit, such as a regiment or company, in which orders received from higher authorities are recorded.

Interleaves, often made of highly sized paper, or glassine paper, inserted into a book to prevent the transfer of ink from an illustration or plate onto the facing page. Guard sheets are also frequently used to elucidate the accompanying illustration. They may be loose, or bound, and are often made of inferior paper, which may transfer acidity to the facing leaves.
Branch of electronics dealing with the study, manufacture, and use of electronic circuits and devices of very small size, especially integrated circuits involving semiconductors.

Masquerades particularly for children. Primary examples are masquerades performed by young African boys, either as part of initiation rites or as entertainment; they are sometimes considered as training for adult masquerades.

Refers to the overall management of urban areas, encompassing the setting of objectives for urban life, the establishment of policies, and the planning, development, operation, and maintenance of the urban environment and services. For the field of planning concerned with designing and improving the spatial organization and content of urban areas, use "urban planning."

Education, usually at the postsecondary level and taken on a part-time or short-term basis, sometimes noncredit, designed to advance or update adult learning for personal, academic, or occupational development.
Postsecondary education leading to a formal degree or certificate.
Desk or floor lamps employing a movable, projecting support or arm of great length to support the lighting element.

Tracts of land set aside for the propagation of wild animals for hunting. Early hunting parks in Europe and Asia were wooded, but later parks in European colonies in Africa may include savanna or other types of land.
Buildings housing businesses specializing in the sale of cigars and related tobacco products and smoking accessories.
Refers to carved wooden figures, usually life-sized, set up as advertisements in front of or just inside of cigar stores; popular in the United States from the early 19th century until the 1890s.
Cigar-store figures representing American Indians; popular as cigar store advertising signs from the 1850s until the 1890s.
Those trained and working in the science that deals with the physical history of the earth, the rocks of which it is composed, and the physical changes which it has undergone and is undergoing.

Distinctive visual works composed of individually shaped stones of varying colors used to make a composition. The works may be low-relief or flat. An example is as used for a pendant or gem, where the commesso work is often coupled with enamel, gold, and gems. Although usage may overlap, for larger works, such as table tops, using a similar technique, use "pietra dura (visual works)." For works utilizing differently colored layers of a single material to create the design, use "cameos."
Froth produced by yeast that forms on the top of fermenting malt liquors; it is used to leaven bread and to cause fermentation in other liquors.

Two-masted fishing schooners with long narrow bows, straight keels, and a draft limited to 10 to 12 feet due to shoal slips used by them in Gloucester, Massachusetts, harbor; generally found from around 1900 to the 1930s, and used for banks and market fishing.

Flemish vessels used in the estuary of the river Scheldt for fishing, particularly of shrimp. Typically these had their home port in Antwerp and are mentioned by the 18th century. They disappeared from shipping by 1920. These usually were no longer than ten meters and had a rounded keel with a curved, upright bow, with a hold extending from the prow to the the mast.
Describes fishing watercraft that engage in the capture of marine life through dredging, specifically digging or pulling out with a dredge.

Style of ceramic made in China during the Qing-period (1644-1911) by commercial kilns for the domestic and export markets. It is characterized as overglazed enamel porcelain having a delicate rose pink derived from colloidal gold, in addition to a wide palette that facilitated a meticulous style of painting. For ceramics made in this style but manufactured elsewhere, use the broader term, “famille rose.”
Adventure stories following the model of Robinson Crusoe featuring exploits of persons stranded in difficult circumstances, surviving through resourcefulness and ingenuity.

Literature written by travelers, typically describing interesting or exotic places, the inhabitants, and adventures; often illustrated. The genre differs from "travel guidebooks" in not necessarily advising about lodging, food, and sights to see.
Trademark for a type of commercially produced aramid, a synthetic textile material which is lightweight, nonflammable, and has a high impact resistance.
Reference works on coats of arms, heraldic bearings and devices, or the subject of armory (the devising and regulating of emblematic representations according to established convention).

Refers to a religious order following the Rule of St. Augustine that was founded by the medieval mystic St. Bridget of Sweden (died 1373). After the death of her husband, Bridget dedicated her life to prayer and experienced visions, one of which was to found the Order of the Most Holy Savior.  Shortly after Bridget's death, her daughter, St. Catherine of Sweden, became the first abbess of the original monastery in Vadstena, Sweden. Other monasteries followed, each with no more than 60 nuns. Attached to each was a parallel community of monks who shared the same liturgical life under the governing of the abbess. Brigittine contributions to Scandinavian culture include one of the first printing presses, located at Vadstena Abbey. The order, emphasizing humility, simplicity and contemplation, flourished until the Reformation and was banished from Sweden in 1595. After this time there were no more Brigittine monks but four autonomous houses of nuns survived: one in England, another in Bavaria, and two in Holland. Elisabeth Hesselblad founded a new branch of the old order in 1911 and went on to revive the order by founding houses in Sweden, Italy, England, India, Switzerland, and the United States. Although the order has an ancient history, it is modern in its efforts regarding monastic revival and ecumenical concerns.

Woolen bonnets, typically having a crease in the crown from front to back, short ribbon streamers at the back, and often a badge in the front; introduced for wear by the Highland units of the British army and then adopted for Scottish traditional dress.
Tall military caps of fur, usually bearskin, worn primarily by European and Canadian military personnel, especially grenadiers and foot guards, from the 17th century.
The set of characters used for writing the Arabic language. It is the second most widely used alphabetic system in the world. Distinguished from the scripts used to render the alphabet.
Type size, standardized at 12 point, often used for type or plate areas.

Members of a common species of rat known worldwide. The brown rat may be brown or gray. As the black rat, the brown rat has exploited human food resources, moved all over the world with humans, and is often considered a pest because it has killed small livestock and native species, and spread certain diseases among humans; it has also been used in laboratories worldwide for medical, genetic, and basic biological research. It is thought to have originated in northern China; it is now the dominant rat in Europe and much of North America.
Ancient subclass (or order) of which Nautilus is the last surviving genus; ancient specimens are important in paleontology for dating the strata in which they appear.
Genus containing the meerkat.

Term used in a general sense to refer to any animal or plant that eats animals, as opposed to a plant-eating herbivore or an omnivore, that has a diet of both plant and animal material. For members of the mammalian order Carnivora, use "Carnivora" or the alternate descriptor "carnivores (order)."
Species of sheep of many breeds, descended from the wild mouflon of Europe and Asia. Sheep were among the earliest animals to be domesticated. They are raised for fleece, meat, and milk.
The male of several animals, including deer, rat, sheep, squirrel, weasel, and others.
Main buildings, typically located in a resort or park, and primarily serving tourists or sportsmen specializing in fishing.
People who belong to the cabinet, comprising the confidential advisors and policy-makers of the head of state of a country, and who usually head government departments, as in the United States.

Comprising or involving more than one people that shares identity, distinctiveness, or significance based on linguistic group, religious belief, nationality, cultural tradition, and sometimes perceived physiological characteristics.
People in colonial Latin America who had the authority and power to replace another person in a given position, as a deputy.
Water in the upper surface of the earth which forms the water table that supplies springs and wells.

Members of a genus containing five species of gregarious, colony-forming rodents that live in extensive burrow systems in grasslands of plains, high plateaus, and montain valleys in North America, and have a call resembling a dog's bark.

Members of a species of giant-sized, stocky, North American burrowing ground squirrel, common in the northeastern and central United States, north to Alaska and southeast to Alabama. According to popular legend in the United States, the woodchuck emerges from hibernation to predict the coming of warm weather each year on February 2, designated as Groundhog Day and corresponding to the older Christian feast day, the Purification of the Virgin Mary, and to more ancient ceremonies marking the mid-point between the solstice and equinox.

Branch of bioengineering dealing with medical problems, such as implantable devices, artificial limbs and organs, physical aids for the handicapped, and instrumentation used in research, diagnosis, and treatment.

Those working with techniques of modification or manipulation of organisms, which may involve the processes of heredity and reproduction, motor function, implantable devices, artificial limbs and organs, physical aids for the handicapped, and instrumentation used in research, diagnosis, and treatment of disease or physical disability.
The young of any bird, especially the young bird still in the egg or only just hatched.
Speakers, or speaker systems, that are connected to jukeboxes, either built-in or as satellites of the main cabinet.
Text that appears on the title page of documents, usually books or scholarly papers, inclusive of author, title, publication, or other information such as indications of patronage or mottoes.
Fighting bracelets furnished with one or more projections, either blunt or sharpened.
Christian religious societies or fraternities.

Originally, those who managed the property such as a steward, tax collector and domestic concerns of a large household; now, by extension, applied to those who manage matters concerning personal service, stores, and catering for a variety of organizations and commercial businesses.

Groups of religious, generally Christian, Muslim, or Buddhist, who follow a common rule of life, engage in a specific kind of work or schedule of devotions, and submit to the directions of superiors, often though not exclusively living within a cloistered or restricted space such as a convent or monastery.
Genus containing the furniture beetle.

Family containing around 300 species of venomous snakes, characterized by short fangs fixed in the front of the upper jaw. Terrestrial elapids generally resemble the more abundant colubrids, whereas aquatic elapids may possess paddle-shaped tails and other structures adapted to marine environments. Most species lay eggs; a few, chiefly in Australia, bear living young.

Military groups of the Fante of Ghana, constituting the primary defensive units of the Fante states. They also serve political, social, and religious functions. They are widely known for the colorful flags that represent them at important festivals.
General term referring to any of numerous species of stony corals (order Madreporaria or order Scleractinia) that are round or polygonal in shape and contain conspicuous radiating septa.
Genus of large scallops that often have attractive, strongly colored, thick shells.
Refers to districts or other divisions into which a larger area is divided for the purpose of conducting a census.
Candy or sweets having a chocolate or fondant coating and fondant center that sometimes contains fruits and nuts.

Architectural features of some Mesoamerican buildings, consisting of a horizontal rectangular panel (tablero) cantilevered over an upward-sloping apron wall (talud); often found repeated on stepped pyramids after around 300 CE.
Standards incorporating the chi-rho and a wreath, used in the standard of Constantine the Great and other contexts.

Refers to tangible objects capable of being moved or conveyed from one place to another, as opposed to real estate or other buildings. The term is borrowed from legal jargon. Art and other cultural works may be classified in two broad categories: movable works and built works. Movable works, which are typically located in a repository, have a repository identification number, have a provenance of former locations, and other characteristics that do not apply to built works.
Keys for adjusting the nuts and bolts of a bedstead.
Field concerned with the design and creation of productive, low-maintenance agricultural systems and urban environments which have the diversity, stability, and resilience of natural ecosystems.
Parachutes designed specifically to deliver goods and machinery via drop from airborne vehicles.

Buildings housing indoor swimming pools, particularly large buildings or complexes containing multiple pools, and occasionally also an area of a sea, lake, or other outdoor body of water suitable for swimming.
Pottery technique in which the piece is built up from ropelike coils of clay, without the use of a potter's wheel.
An adornment in the form of a hammered gold disk.
Technique of activation analysis induced by neutrons to determine chemical elements.

Technique of elemental analysis funamentally similar to and most often practiced in conjunction with particle-induced x-ray emission (PIXE) with the difference that gamma rays are measured instead of x-rays.

Literary works of 20th-century poetry, particularly of the concrete poetry movement of the 1950s and 1960s in which language elements are arranged freely, not necessarily in linear syntax, and meaning is derived from spatial, pictorial, and typographic characteristics of the work, as well as from the sense of the words. For pre-20th-century works of poetry in which letters, words, or lines are arranged to form a shape or image, usually related to the meaning of the words, use "pattern poems."
Mournful, melancholy, or plaintive poems, especially funeral songs or laments for the dead.

White crystalline salt found naturally as mineral alunogenite; made synthetically by treating bauxite with sulfuric acid. It is used as a dye mordant, in tanning, as a flocculant in water purification, and for sizing paper.
Deep-learning models that are intended to generate high-quality text, images, and other content based on the data on which they were trained.
A mixture of cod oil and tallow used to incorporate oils and fats into leather during the hand stuffing or currying process.

Items comprising relatively short lengths of rope or cord, designed to be used in various contexts, including but not limited to the following: to hold a whistle, knife, or other item around the neck of a person, to wear as a symbol of a military citation, to attach something to a costume, to attach a sign or name tag to an item, to fasten something on a ship (particularly rope passing through deadeyes to extend shrouds or stays), or to fire a cannon, sound a whistle, or activate some other system.
The study of ancient or extant wood charcoal macroremains from archaeological sites, including researching the ways communities used the plants and trees around them.
Genus containing 23 species of bats.
Remainders of animals, regardless of the stage of decomposition or preservation, including fossils.
People who work in the arts, a handicraft, or a skilled trade, particularly when utilizing traditional or non-mechanized methods. Typically not applied to makers of fine arts.
Those who study of the structure of metal and alloys.

Chronologies in graphic linear form, either vertical or horizontal, listing important events or other phenomena, such as dominant styles, for successive years or periods within a  defined historic period, often limited to a particular culture or region.

Those who specialize in arranging time into periods or divisions, and placing events in the sequence in which they occurred, either at a defined point or period in time, or in relation to an established time sequence.
Refers to people who make embroidery, which is needlework in which decorative designs are stiched into cloth, leather, or paper.

Early silent motion pictures, made prior to 1910, usually of very short length, recording people and events from everyday life as it happened. They were usually filmed direct from life but sometimes manipulated.

Japanese gardens, traditionally associated with Zen Buddhist temples, that have no water. Sand and rocks are used to represent streams and waterfalls. Literally "dry landscape" or "withered mountains and waters." This term is usually used to refer to gardens of the Muromachi (1392-1573), Momoyama (1373-1615) and Edo periods (1615-1868).

Structures created by animals other than humans, most commonly by various mammals, birds, insects, and arachnids, occasionally by fish, reptiles, amphibians, crustaceans, mollusks, annelids, marine filter feeders, and others. Building materials may be collected material or self-secreted material. Animals create structures primarily to make protected habitats for thermo-regulation and safety from predators, to trap prey, and for display between members of the same species.

Shoes or overshoes having a platform sole, often but not exclusiely for women, usually with a mulelike upper; the high platform sole was made of cork or wood. Worn from the 14th to 18th century to increase height and protect the feet from cold, wet, and dirt. For mulelike footwear with thinner soles used as slippers or overshoes, use "pantofles."
Light footwear made for indoor wear, generally without means of fastening and made to be easily slipped on and off the foot.
Low-heeled, slip-on shoes of adapted moccasin-type construction with a slotted strap stitched to the vamp. Also, similar shoes decorated on the vamp with a metal chain or tied tassels.

Small educational buildings, generally consisting of one major teaching space, and often built to resemble meeting houses, churches, or dwellings. Use when emphasizing the size or form of such buildings; when emphasizing the function or location of some early examples, prefer "rural schools."
Columns erected in honor of a naval triumph and ornamented with the rostra or prows of ships.
Sloping boards or frames upon which hides are worked in tanning.
Artificially dwarfed trees and shrubs that are grown in containers and pruned so as to resemble mature, full-sized plants.

Crucifixes that are specifically designed to be permanent adjuncts to the altar in a Roman Catholic church, traced back to at least the 13th century. They are prescribed to be placed at the middle of the altar between the candlesticks, of a size large enough to be conveniently seen by both the celebrant and the congregation.

Liners for helmets that create a web-based system to create a small amount of space to absorb energy and separate the interior shell of the helmet and the wearer's head; typically comprising intersecting straps and a headband that rest directly on the head.

Refers generally to processes that complete an object, treatment, or work, including the chemical, electrolytic, and mechanical application of finishes. In the context of bookbinding, refers to that sequence of processes carried out on a book and its binding after forwarding, up to the point of attaching its cover. In case binding, where the cover is attached prior to the application of lettering or decoration, the attachment of the cover is part of the forwarding, not the finishing. In the context of leather manufacture, all the processes carried out on the leather after tanning. In the context of papermaking, all the processes carried out on the paper after it leaves the papermaking machine.
Devices placed in the ears to aid deafness, and meant to amplify sounds.

Species of orangutan living on Sumatra island, they differ from the Bornean orangutan in being smaller and shorter, having lighter and longer hair, a longer face, and flanges that are covered in small white hairs.

Species of intelligent, social hominid, the largest living primate, having a large head, broad chest, long arms, a flat nose with large nostrils, and fur that is black with a silver saddle on the back of adult males. The eastern gorilla differs from the western gorilla in being larger, darker, lacking an overhanging tip on its nose, having a more robust body, being less arboreal, and typically living in a larger family group of up to 40 individuals. In some classifications, both the Eastern Gorilla and the Western Gorilla are classified as a single species.
Analysis employing microscopic techniques to determine how a tool was used and what materials were worked on by examining its wear.
The right or condition of permanent and absolute tenure of land or property with freedom to dispose of it at will; examples include freehold in fee simple, fee-tail, or for term of life.

Refers to the culture, style, and movement of Mexican Americans in the United States, particularly as beginning in the 19th century, characterized by artistic and political discussions addressing social issues relevant to Mexican and Chicano communities. The movement is driven by a rediscovery of Pre-Columbian indigenous styles, the development of mural painting, and by cultural studies focussed on bi-culturalism and ethnic heritage and identity. The movement also reveals strong regionalist elements, promoting vernacular forms and techniques to expound traditional and contemporary iconography.

Refers to the apse or chancel of a basilica, usually in the context of ancient or Early Christian basilicas or meeting places, synagogues, or Eastern Orthodox churches. In modern times it most commonly refers to an elevated platform in a synagogue on which the Torah reading stand is placed; in the Ashkenazi (German) ritual, the Torah and Haftarah (a reading from the prophets) are read on the Sabbath and festivals. In the Sephardic (Spanish) rite, the entire service is conducted from the platform. At an earlier date, when the bimah was positioned in the center of the synagogue (as it still is in Sephardic and many Orthodox Ashkenazi synagogues), the attention of the congregation was divided between it and the Ark of the Law.
In Indian architecture, a dais; platform; prastara; adhiṣṭhāna-type; adhiṣṭhāna type without kumuda.

Phylum of about 600 recorded species, all of which are parasites in vertebrates (usually fish) as adults and in arthropods as juveniles. They are named for their proboscis, or snout, which bears hooks.

Ritual washing of the feet, derived from hospitality customs of ancient civilizations in which a host would provide water and often a servant to wash the feet of the visitor. Owing to the general use of sandals in Eastern countries, the washing of the feet was almost everywhere recognized from the earliest times as a duty of courtesy. The principle modern example is the ceremony performed by Christian denominations on Maundy Thursday during Lent, following the example of Jesus in Biblical passages.
Meshed textile made of sheer silk, nylon, or rayon with a hexagonal mesh; used for hats, veils, ballet costumes, and women's dresses.
Groups of animals of one kind, feeding or traveling together; in modern usage, specifically applied to an assemblage of birds, sheep, or goats.

Animals that have been tamed and live with or are cared for by humans; typically limited to animals that have been altered through selective breeding to modify the behavior and often the appearance of their wild ancestors, such as dogs, domestic cats, horses, and cattle. The term excludes wild species of animals cared for by humans in a zoo, park or other place, even if the animal has been bred and raised in captivity.
Any living organisms, including human beings; may be real or fictional, including mythical or legendary creatures.

Inflatable, air-tight bags of rubber, plastic, paper, silk, or similar lightweight material, of varying shapes and sizes that are imprinted with text or images that advertise goods, services, or brands.

Class of solitary, free-swimming tunicates found throughout the world's oceans, characterized by being filter feeders, and having a form superficially resembling tadpole larvae, retaining the juvenile discrete trunk and tail in adult life (pedomorphism).

Order of eel-shaped, scaleless, soft-skinned aquatic primitive vertebrates with paired thick barbels on the end of the snout, a tail fin (but no paired fins), no jaws, cartilaginous skeletons, mouths comprising round or slit-like sucking openings with horny teeth, poorly developed eyes buried under the skin, a single nostril at the end of the snout, and five to 15 pairs of gills used for respiration. They are found in cold seawater, habitually lie buried except for the tip of the head on soft bottoms and in burrows.
Family of hagfishes distinguished from the family Myxinidae of hagfishes by having gills that open separately on the surface rather than on each side.

Order of amphibians characterized by larvae lacking true teeth and external gills, adults being tailless and having elongated hind limbs modified for jumping, and a single frontoparietal and no lacrimal bone in skull. Dates from the Middle Jurassic to present, including two extinct and 28 or more extant families with over 5,400 living species.
Subclass of gastropods that includes marine snails.
Subclass containing mites and ticks.
Water-cooled nozzles through which air is forced into a forge or blast furnace.
Portable, cordless telephones for use in a cellular radio network.
Compact, portable radiotransmitter-receivers for very high frequencies that have a limited transmitting power and are usable within a limited area.
Modified microtomes used to cut ultra-thin sections (20 to 100 nanometers thick) of plant and animal tissue for electron microscopy.

Beverage of Asian origin derived from unfermented leaves, cut and steamed, of the plant Camellia sinensis; used for many medicinal applications as well as for refreshment. ‘Black tea’ is derived from the same plant. It is produced by allowing the leaves to oxidize. In the context of conservation, green tea catechins have been used as environmentally friendly formaldehyde scavengers.

Cylindrical projectiles that can be propelled to a considerable height or distance by the combustion of the contents and the backward ejection of waste gases, usually giving a burst of light and used for signalling, in maritime rescue, for entertainment, and as a firework, typically giving a brilliant visual display at the apex of its ascent. For weaponized rockets, use "missiles (weapons)."
In Indian art and architecture, a circular medallion as decorative motif.
Closed-circuit television system where programs are transmitted via coaxial or fiber-optic cable (as opposed to airwave transmissions) to connected subscribers.

Cupboards intended for the storage of food and other donations for impoverished people or others in need. Primarily used in historical contexts, for such cupboards on the premises of churches, hospitals, guilds, private estates, or other establishments that distributed alms.

The recruitment, transportation, transfer, harbouring or receipt of people through force, fraud or deception, with the aim of exploiting them for profit. It is the trade of humans for the purpose of forced labour, sexual slavery or commercial (sexual) exploitation for the trafficker or for others. Men, women and children of all ages and from all backgrounds can become victims of this crime.
Telecommunication system with transmission and reception of electromagnetic waves from 10 to 80 meters in length, and frequencies larger than 3000 kilohertz.

Animals with distinctive shaggy white hair and backward curving horns. Mountain goats are native to mountainous regions of northwestern North America from southeastern Alaska south to the Columbia River in Washington; east into Idaho and western Montana; and north to southern Yukon. They are part of the antelope family, rather than true goats.
Male domestic fowls.

Members of a genus containing about 10 living species of herons, which are long-legged wading birds. Most egrets have white plumage and develop long ornamental nuptial plumes for the breeding season. The term "egret" is sometimes used to refer to birds of similar appearance in other genera.

General term referring to around 18 species in different genera of parrots, having in common that they are large, colorful, native to tropical America, have a very large beak that is dark in color, and have a relatively featherless, light colored, facial patch.
Genus containing four living species of Eurasian grouses.

Large wading birds belonging to the family of the Ciconiidae and occurring in Sub-Saharan Africa. Mainly gray and white with a naked pinkish head and neck with an inflatable throat pouch. They survive on carrion, competing with vultures. The soft white downy feathers from the wings or tail of the marabou stork are frequently used for trimming on hats or other garments.
Species of ox-like grazing hooved animals native to North America; sometimes divided into subspecies based on their habitat: the plains bison and woodland bison.
Largest of the wild pigs, native to forests ranging from western and northern Europe and North Africa to India, the Andaman Islands, and China.
Castrated adult male cattle, typically used as draft animals.
General term for several species of wild goats inhabiting the Asia, Africa, and the Alps and Apennines of Europe.

Extinct order of obligate bipedal or quadrupedal, beaked, herbivorous dinosaurs characterized by a pelvic structure like that of birds, a beak-like structure in the front part of the mouth and grinding teeth in the rear, a four-branched pelvis, toes that often have hooflike structures., and often having heavy armor and horns. Dating from the Upper Triassic to Upper Cretaceous, existed in five major groups: ornithopods, pachycephalosaurs, stegosaurs, ankylosaurs, and ceratopsina dinosaurs.
Breed hound that is trained and used for fox hunting; bred for a strong hunting instinct, energy, and keen sense of smell. There are variations of the breed in America and Britain.

One of two living species of camels. It has two humps and is native to the steppes of central Asia. It has been widely domesticated. It is thought that the Bactrian camel was domesticated sometime before 2500 BCE in the area of modern Iran. In some classifications, Camelus ferus is used to refer to the wild form.

Breed of horse characterized by a distinctive head shape, high tail carriage, fine bone structure, concave profile, arched neck, a comparatively level croup, and known for speed, stamina, beauty, intelligence, and gentleness. It is believed to be one of the oldest horse breeds, with archaeological evidence dating to 4,500 years before present.
Domesticated descendant of the wild ass. Donkeys resemble horses and are characterized by their large head, long ears, and cow-like tail.
Genus containing one living species of Asian elephant.
Members of a genus containing around eight species of slender, agile, furry, bushy-tailed, forest-dwelling mammals of the weasel family.

Martes foina, more commonly known as stone martens or beech martens, are found across Europe, and Central Asia. They are weasel-like carnivores that are more generally found in deciduous forests or on rocky hillsides.

General term referring to any of more than 30 species belonging to the genus Lepus and sometimes used for species of other genera of the family Leporidae. They have long ears, a divided upper lip, and long hind legs adapted for leaping, but are distinguished form rabbits by significantly longer ears, longer hind feet, a shorter tail, longer body, and having young are born fully furred and with eyes wide open and seeing. The common names of species containing the word "hare" and "rabbit" are not strictly indicative of the genera to which the animals belong.

General term referring to any of several breeds of domesticated rabbits having long hair. The Angora rabbit is native to Asia Minor, domesticated by the Trelicians in the 6th century. It has been bred in France, England, and elsewhere in Europe since the early 19th century.
Members of a species of small rodent native to Eurasia but introduced worldwide; now  living in most parts of the world in close proximity to humans.
Small metal rods used as fasteners having a head and often helical threading and being usually secured by a nut or by riveting.
Flexible plates or leaves joined by a pin so as to allow swinging motion in a single plane of one of the members to which they are attached, such as a door or gate.
Finish hardware used to secure objects.
A fuming liquid soluble in benzene, chloroform, and ether; used for dye manufacture and in organic synthesis.
Mixtures prepared according to a particular formula to create materials or preparations for specific purposes.
Metallic element having symbol Ce and atomic number 58; a gray, ductile metal, a lanthanite, cerium is the most abundant of the rare-earth group.

All chemical elements possess one or more types of unstable as well as stable isotopes. The former are known as radioisotopes or radioactive isotopes. Their nuclei dissipate excess energy as alpha, beta, and gamma rays. This radioactive decay forms the basis for the measuring processes of radioactive dating.

Structurally distinct forms in which a chemical element may occur. Some chemical elements may exist in two or more different forms, in the same physical state. Allotropes are different structural modifications of an element; the atoms of the element are bonded together in a different manner.
A colloidal system such as a mist or fog, in which the dispersion medium is a gas.
Refers to the group of studies or branches of knowledge concerned with facts and phenomena of the observable or quantifiable world, systematically arranged and showing the operation of general laws.
Fields of study relating to sciences that address the health of humans and animals.

Study of medical concepts and practice throughout human history in a global, social, cultural, and scientific context including theories, diseases, health care, individual practitioners, special branches of medicine, and medical professions such as nursing.
Theoretical models of systems in any discipline, constructed using a graphed network of relationships between concepts, used to represent a subject. These may be textual or physical.
Traps designed to catch wild animals, originally bears, with a distinctive pair of metal jaws with jagged teeth, which snap shut around the leg when a trigger is stepped on.

Airtight chambers that can be filled with steam under pressure or surrounded by another chamber for the steam and that are used for sterilizing, cooking, or other purposes requiring moist or dry temperatures above 212 degrees Fahrenheit without boiling.
Machines employed for blending the constituents of materials such as concrete, grout, mortar, or paint.
Cloth armbands, often with braiding or tassels, worn around the upper arm, as by military personnel to signify a particular group or regiment.
Long, iron bars equipped with sliding shackles and a lock, used to confine the ankles.
Shackles for the feet of a human being or animal.
Surgical tools for removing glands, particularly the adenoid glands.
Equipment for dressing a wound in the field or battle.

Automated machines, typically comprising various lattices and rollers, used to separate and loosen the fibres of raw cotton bales before they are mixed into yarn, cloth, or other usable fabric. After being manually fed through the machine's conveyors, the bales encounter multiple sets of rapidly rotating rollers which reduce them to a more malleable state for mixing.
Pointed tweezers for lifting knots from wool, so that their luster is not lost by handling them.

Simple looms with the warp threads stretched between parallel sticks, one of them attached to a post or tree, the other to the weaver's body by a strap around the waist by which the weaver controls tension in the warp.
Weaving shuttles having a canoe-shape, often with an opening in the center.
In Indian architecture, the seat-slab positioned above the vēdikā-dado that is found in a hall or balcony.
Thermal storage walls consisting of south-facing, glass-fronted, thick masonry walls with circulation vents that pass heated air, stored during the day in the walls, into rooms during the night.
The providing of advice and sometimes other services by professionals in the field of their special expertise.

Metal and plastic identification tages, often worn in pairs, by military personnel around their necks, carrying such information as name, rank, serial number, religious affiliation, and blood type; so-called because they broadly resemble the common tags used for pets. Modern tags may include digital information.
General denomination for the fossils of certain bivalve molluscs. Distinguished from the family of living cockles comprised of over 200 species.

Sets of Catholic liturgical objects designed to fit in a case for traveling, including bottles for anointing oil and holy water, a chalice, crucifix, a stole, etc. These are used to perform mass outside the church or to perform rites for the seriously ill.
Document folding method comprising a pleated series of alternating folds to create three or more panels.
Paper or cardboard covers that form illustrated slip-cases for records, such as a seven-inch 45 rpm phonograph record, or slim  books, to protect and to advertise the contents of the book or record.

Traditional Korean decorative coloring done on wooden buildings and structures, such as royal palaces and temples. Its usual function was to cover design defects and prevent cracks in wooden buildings, in addition to repelling pests and protecting from rain and wind. Since dancheong is based on yin and yang and the Five Elements Theory, blue is placed to the east, red south, yellow center, white west and black north, in addition to green. In South Korea, the color pigments with specific color index numbers are standardized by the state.

The actions of declaring a status or state void or invalid. A common example is when a marriage between two people is annulled, returning each person's status to single, never married, rather than having been married and divorced.
Parties held to introduce young women, generally those of the upper class, into the adult social life of their class.

Persons who specialize in cooking by dry heat acting by conduction, and not by radiation, hence either in a closed space such as an oven, or on a heated surface. Their typical products include breads, cakes, cookies, and pastries.
Military uniforms for formal wear.
Long-stemmed, ornamented pipes used by Native North Americans on ceremonial occasions, especially as a token of peace or friendship.

Doors or closures of cast iron or another material, often decorative objects in their own right, used to cover the opening of a stove, oven, or furnace. In modern usage, may refer to any door constructed, as a component of a device or architecture, so as to enclose fire or to protect an area from fire.

A complex natural carbohydrate, or polysaccharide, composed of long, connected chains of glucose molecules, forming the primary component in the cell walls of plants. Pure cellulose is an odorless, tasteless white powder. Cellulose exists in three forms: alpha, beta and gamma. Cellulose is used to manufacture paper and textiles, and as a raw material in rayon, cellophane, cellulose acetate, and celluloid.

Glossy transparent material made from regenerated cellulose, typically in the form of thin sheets, usually moisture-proofed and sometimes dyed; impervious to dry gases, grease, and bacteria, and used as packaging or wrapping for food and other merchandise, envelope windows, and bags for dialysis.

Shadow theater is a type of puppetry involving the use of flat shadow puppets manipulated behind a blank translucent screen or sheet onto which light shines so that the shadows of the puppets are cast on it. The audience views the shadows of the puppets as they act out the story. There is difference in scholarly opinion as to its origins, but either Egypt or eastern Asia is a likely place.
Prows on Maori boats.
Constructions on the upper decks of sailboats or motorboats, often equipped with a door and windows, which serve to accommodate crewmembers or passengers or ship material.
Walking long distances, especially through rural areas, as for pleasure, exercise, or military training.

Wind catchers consisting of a tall tower, generally square in plan with X-shaped panels set diagonally across the interior from corner to corner, open at the sides near the top to funnel and accelerate incoming breezes down one channel to cool spaces below creating by convection an updraft in the opposite channel which draws warm indoor air out; Persian in origin, found in Iran and the Gulf countries.
Assembly of rails, ties, and fasteners over which rail vehicles travel.
Short railroad tracks connected by switches or points at one or more places with the main track and used especially to enable trains to pass each other.
Short tracks that are parallel to, and join, main tracks.

In the visual arts, refers to views or pictures that depict a place, episode, situation, incident, series of actions, or events, or objects. It is derived as a metaphorical use of "scenes" in the theatrical sense of a subdivision of a play.
Devices of various styles for carrying a baby or small child; an example is a carrier designed to be worn over the shoulders with the baby supported on one's back, hips, or chest.
Rooms or spaces in theaters where tickets are reserved, sold, and distributed.
Those parts of complete rounds of ammunition, either cartridges or shells, that encase the charge, primer and, usually, the projectile.
Mills where oil is extracted from olives.

A locale that constitutes the center of an individual's domestic life, affectional relationships, and interests, together with the feeling of comfort and satisfaction that it conveys. For the buildings or portions of a building designed for residential occupancy by one family, use "dwellings."
In archaeology and related disciplines, the location where an object, artifact, or another thing or things were found.
The distinctive character or atmosphere of a place that impresses itself upon the mind.
Motifs of female masks having a ruff around the head and under the chin, popular in 18th-century French decorative arts, especially Régence.

Safety indicators styled as signs or panels marking pipe- or transmission lines and ropeways along flight paths usually on or near an airfield. These carry information, usually numbers, intended to read from the air.
Waterspouts carved into grotesque figures and projecting from the roof gutters of buildings.

Variations in the color or growth of crops or other vegetation on the surface of the ground, usually patterns or other recognizable shapes that reflect the shapes of buried walls, ditches, or other remains; used, for example, to locate ancient sites on aerial photographs.
Lightweight silk of plain weave.

Fabric made of undyed wool, noted for being extremely soft, light in weight, graceful in draping, and formerly commonly used as a material for ladies' daytime dresses. Although it was originally left in its natural color, it was later dyed in various colors.
Riding whips with short rigid handles to which one or more leather lashes are attached.
Buildings housing museums that specialize in the history, objects, vehicles, and other materials associated with flight and space travel.

Refers generally to the style of art, architecture, and material culture created by the Islamic North Africans, including the colonizers of the Iberian Peninsula and their descendants of North African and mixed North African and Iberian lineage. The style predominated approximately from the eighth to the 15th century in Spain and the region of Mauretania in North Africa (now comprised of Morocco and part of Algeria), though it persisted in a smaller way after that and elements are still used today. For the style created and used by the people of the modern West African nation, the Islamic Republic of Mauritania, see "Maure".

Refers to the Islamic culture, art, and architecture associated with the Tulunid dynasty, a dynasty founded in 868 by Ahmad ibn Tulun, a governor of Egypt who extended his control over Syria as well.  The dynasty was prosperous but short-lived, being deposed in 905 by Abbasid forces. Outside the capital at Fustat, Ahmad built a mosque known as the Mosque of Ibn Tulun, considered one of the masterpieces of medieval Islamic architecture.The art of the Tulunid dynasty also included carving of wood, rock crystal, stucco,  production of ceramics and textiles.
Rugs woven in the Beliksir area of northwestern Turkey.

Refers to the art and architecture of the Islamic dynasty of the same name that ruled Iraq and Azerbaijan from 1336 to 1432. The architect of the early Jalayirids continued in the manner of earlier local styles with an emphasis on geometric brickwork, stucco decoration, and fine inscriptions. The major building of this period is the funerary complex built from 1356-1359 built by Mirjan , the amir who governed the city. Manuscript illustration also flourished during this period, particularly under the patronage of Ahmad (reigned 1382-1410). These works saw a fusion of Chinese and Near Eastern pictorial elements along with a new formula for depicting space.

term: Central Persian textile styles after the Mongols
definition: Textile styles after the Mongols belonging to Central Persian cultures.

Generally, the style and culture of the Bakhtiari ethnic group occupying the plains and mountains in western Iran; they are one of the nomad peoples of Iran whose chiefs have been among the greatest tribal leaders in Iran and have long been influential in Persian politics. Specifically, the textiles, particularly rugs, produced under the influence of the Bakhitiari people in certain villages southwest of Esfahan in central Iran. Bakhtiari rugs are symmetrically knotted on a foundation of cotton, with bold coloring and patterns. The field is usually divided into compartments that may be rectangular or produced by an ogival lattice. Occasionally there are tree or medallion decorative schemes. The palette tends to be darker than is found on most Iranian rugs, with much use of yellow.

Style of handwoven floor coverings made in the region of Khorasan, in northeastern Iran, including the classic Herat carpets. From the late 18th and early 19th centuries there are carpets in the herati pattern, probably made in villages of the district. They show a repeat pattern of a lattice that peeps through a maze of blossoms and leaves, with a characteristic border showing pairs of smoothly curved split arabesques. These carpets are usually woven in jufti asymmetrical knotting (upon four warps) on a cotton foundation. The designs of room-sized carpets made in Meshed (Mashhad), Birjand, and villages nearby are characterized by medallions that are often unusually round, grounds that revive the coiling stems of the Herat classic carpets, and borders that show an unusual number of narrow stripes. Most of these carpets, too, are jufti knotted. Reds are dyed with cochineal, which, with the significant amount of blue used in the rugs, gives the carpets a purplish cast. The combination of soft wool and the inadequacies of construction has reduced their durability.
Generally, the style and culture of the nomadic Afshar tribe in southeast Iran. Specifically, the style of textiles, particularly rugs, handwoven by the Afshar.
Style of textile, particularly carpets, from Arak (formerly Sultanabad), Iran.
Pottery styles belonging to Ottoman cultures.

Photographic films on which additive color images are created using a screen process. This process uses a screen of red, green, or blue filters to record the relative intensity of each hue on a panchromatic, black-and-white emulsion which is processed to form a transparency on film. When viewed through a similar filter, each filter contributes its hue with its intensity modulated by the silver image.
Painting styles belonging to Il-Khanid cultures.
Pottery styles belonging to Il-Khanid cultures.
Describes groupings of cloth coverings produced and worn by inhabitants of Africa or those of African descent.
Finely woven, often intricately patterned, Spanish American style blankets, woven longer than wide and worn wrapped about the shoulders.
Northwest Coast Native American blankets with totemic designs outlined in buttons, often of abalone shell or pearl, used ceremonially to indicate status and power.
Textile styles belonging to Caucasian cultures.
Textile styles belonging to Central Caucasian cultures.

Style of handmade thick knotted carpets or rugs, usually with a floral but occasionally an animal pattern, originating in the Karabakh region, in modern southwestern Azerbaijan and eastern Armenia, just north of the present Iranian border. Karabagh designs and color tend to be more like those of Persian rugs than do those made in other parts of the Caucasus; they may be very similar to designs of Karaja, Iran. Certain Karabagh rugs also resemble those of Shirvan to the north in Azerbaijan. They are characterized as being typically stout and comparatively coarse, made of wool and have longer pile than rugs found elsewhere in Caucasia.

Style of handwoven floor coverings made in the vicinity of Baku, Azerbaijan, a major port on the Caspian Sea. Rugs have been woven in this area since at least the 18th century and probably long before, although it is difficult to determine which were woven in the city and which in such nearby villages as Surahani and Chaildag. The so-called Chila rugs were almost certainly woven in this area. The earliest examples are larger than most Caucasian rugs, ranging up to 12 feet in length (3.6 metres). Most of these rugs have a blue field, and characterized by either an avshan (scattered floral sprig) or harshang (crab) design. Examples from later production may have some cotton in the wefts and are more likely to show a boteh (pear-shaped motif) design, often with a small medallion.

Style of floor covering handwoven in Azerbaijan in or near the city of Genje and characterized by simple, angular designs and saturated (intense) colors of blue, dark blue, and madder red. Genje carpets most often have designs composed of octagons, stars, or three geometric medallions arranged on the carpet's longitudinal axis.
Painting styles belonging to Uzbek cultures.
Culture and styles of the Central Asian polity that existed in the historical region of Khwarezm in Central Asia from 1511 to 1920.

Style of textiles, particularly rugs, characterized by a higher pile than other Shirvan rugs. They are flat and tightly woven with a red ground color and the central field dominated by three large hooked octagons, the middle one of which is almost invariably white.
Small, folding stools with a detachable seat of canvas or leather.
Light folding chairs, usually with canvas seats and backs.
Style of Turkoman carpet from Yarkand (Shache) in Xinjiang, China.
Historic painting styles belonging to West Turkestani cultures.

Material that contains shorter length grain boundaries than a fine-grained material. Grain boundaries restrict slip transmission to neighboring grains. A coarse-grain material has a lower tensile strength and is softer than a fine-grain material.
Style of textile, particularly carpets, from Bukhara, a district now in south-central Uzbekistan.

Generally refers to the style and culture of the Chiadma ethnic group in Morocco, who dwell mainly on the Atlantic coast between Safi and Essaouira. Specifically, may refer to a style of pile rug by the Chiadma tribal weavers noted for a unique mixture of medallions, borders, and motifs.

Refers to the style of carpets manufactured in Northwest China in the 19th century. The style is characterized by knotting with four-ply wool and simple floral decorations, typically lotus flowers and promegranates.
Feraghan style carpets made in India.
Weaving process in which no pile, hand-knotting, or hand-tufting is used, typically with reference to rugs, towels, or other textiles that typically may be expected to have a pile.
Style of textiles, particularly carpets, of the region of Agra in the west-central Uttar Pradesh state, north-central India.

The simplest form of weft wrapping technique in which weft elements repeatedly cross first over or under two or more warp ends, then back under or over half the number one or more, thus progressively encircling all warp ends one or more at a time. The technique is one of the oldest known, identified among charred 7th-century-BCE fragments excavated at Gordion, near Ankara in Anatolia. Widely associated with the flat woven rugs known as "soumaks," although the term has come to be associated with this basic weft wrapping technique wherever found.
A class of planes used for reducing, leveling, and smoothing wood.
Tapestry-woven rugs depicting one of many Navajo ceremonial sand paintings.
Children's chairs with long legs, a feeding tray, and a footrest.
A size of card photograph on a mount measuring 8 1/2 by 5 1/2 or 8 1/4 by 5 inches; popular from the 1870s to 1890s.
A photographic process usually used for reproducing technical drawings. The image is formed using aniline dyes and appears blue-black.

The sport involving the racing of automobiles, which are self-propelled vehicles, for competition, on specially designed tracks, city streets, or roads. The first organized automobile race took place in 1887 in Paris.
Bowling sports played using a bowling alley.
The action or an act of cutting down a tree or trees.
The action of using a pole to propel a waterborne vessel by pushing against the bottom of a waterway.
Boat racing, commonly with dinghies, during late fall, winter and early spring.

Alpine ski racing for speed on a course marked by gates formed by paired poles, set at least 26 feet apart, through which the racer must pass. The racer who completes the course in the shortest time, without missing any gates or knocking down any poles, is the winner.
Detachable buttons with a shank or eye on the back that are inserted through one or more eyelets or buttonholes in a garment that display insignia or emblems of a fraternal organization.

Clasps, often richly ornamented, used for various purposes. They are often in the form of a hook sewn to one side of a garment or armor, to be attached to a loop or ring sewn on the other side. Also, an agrafe may be a pin or badge worn -- often on a hat -- in recognition of a pilgrimage to a sacred site.
A lozenge twill with a small weave unit which has an interlacing forming a spot in the center of each lozenge.

Precolumbian Mesoamerican ritual ball game. The game was played on a court shaped like a capital I with serifs and oriented north–south or east–west; it represented the heavens. Players, wearing heavy padding, used elbows, knees, and hips to knock a solid rubber ball into the opponent’s end of the court. A version of the game is still played today.
Physical activities that are performed in the air.
Hunting of game or other animals by pursuit. Usually the hunting animals are greyhounds or other sight hounds, who catch the prey by speed, using sight rather than scent.
Bunching folds of textile together by pulling on a thread stitched through it for this purpose or on one or more of its constituent filaments, to create fullness.

Refers to any process or technique done with a needle and thread, such as sewing, stitching, smocking, quilting, and embroidery. In common usage, the term is sometimes used to refer to decorative work rather than plain sewing; however, to distinguish more decorative work from plain sewing, it is less ambiguous to use "fancy needlework" or a specific needlework technique, such as "embroidery."
Textile construction involving the interlocking of looped stitches, employing a single cord or strand of yarn and a single hooked needle.

Tools used in weaving to beat the weft fiber tightly against previous rows of weaving. Also used in basketry work. Beaters may be of  various shapes, sizes, and materials; may be handheld or incorporated into the mechanism of a loom.
Preparing relatively short fibers for spinning by cleansing, disentangling, and collecting them together using a card.
Process of copying written or printed text or images by radio or telephone transmission for exact reproduction elsewhere.

Any of the processes for making photographic prints that employ materials which yield a positive image when exposed to a positive and then processed, or a negative image when exposed to a negative and processed.
Small, squarish pieces of colored marble, glass, stone, or tile used in making mosaics.

A crystalline form of lead monoxide, the oxidized product of molten lead that has been stirred or atomized to incorporate air then cooled and ground to form the yellow powder. It is used as a drier in paint and varnish, for the fluxing of earthenware, and in the manufacture of glass. Litharge tends to be slightly more orange than massicot, another crystalline form of lead monoxide, due to the presence of small amounts of red lead oxide.

Pure metallic element having symbol Cr and atomic number 24; an extremely hard, silvery white metal with a bluish tinge. Use also for the metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials, notably stainless steel, heat-resistant alloy, high-strength alloy steel, and for wear-resistant electroplating.

Pure metallic element having the symbol Cu and atomic number 29; a reddish brown, ductile metal that is present in the earth's crust, occurring as a native metal and as ores of sulfide, sulfate and carbonate (azurite, malachite, etc.). It was the first metal used by humans, probably from about 8000 BCE, in the regions of Mesopotamia and India. By about 3800 BCE copper was made into bronze for weapons and knives. Today, copper is one of the most widely used metals because it has high electrical and thermal conductivity, can be easily fabricated, is ductile and polishes well. In moist air, copper forms a protective green film of basic carbonate. Metallic copper combines well with other metals to form alloys, most commonly brass and bronze. Copper and its alloys are used for wire, electrical devices, pipes, cooking vessels, ammunition, ornamental trim, roofing, grillwork, coins, musical instruments, jewelry, and sculptures.
A copper-aluminum alloy with aluminum as the chief alloying element.

Pure metallic element having symbol Au and atomic number 79; a soft, inert, shiny reddish yellow metal that is very malleable and ductile. Gold has been highly valued and found in artifacts dating to before 5000 BCE. Native gold, found in quartz veins (vein gold) and alluvial deposits (placer gold), generally contains some silver and copper. Gold is purified by dissolution in mercury or cyanide solutions, by melting, or by electrodeposition. The purity of commercial gold is expressed in karats which is the number of parts of gold in 24 parts of the alloy. Today gold is primarily used for monetary systems and for jewelry.

Pure metallic element having symbol Pb and atomic number 82; soft, dense ductile metal of a dull gray color, shiny when freshly cut, occuring naturally most often as a sulfide in the mineral galena. Other lead minerals include anglesite (lead sulfate) and cerussite (lead carbonate). Native metallic lead was found and used from about 3600-2600 BCE when the technique for obtaining lead from roasting the sulfide ore (galena) was discovered. Lead was used to make small cast items such as coins and statuettes, plumbing pipes, spires, statues, cisterns, gargoyles, pigments (lead white, litharge, orange mineral, etc.), as a component in pottery glazes, for roofing, flashing, stained glass windows, as a soft solder, and as radiation shielding.
Alloy of mercury with another metal.

Pure metallic element having symbol Ni and atomic number 28; a silvery white metal with a yellowish cast, resistant to corrosion and to most acids except nitric. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials.

Pure metallic element having symbol Ag and atomic number 47; a malleable, ductile, white metal with characteristic sheen, considered a precious metal. Silver is widely distributed throughout the world, occurring rarely as metallic silver (in Peru, Norway) but more often as silver-gold alloys and silver ore. Today silver is obtained as a byproduct in the refinement of gold, lead, copper, or zinc ores. Silver was smelted from the ore galena as early as 3800 BCE. As a pure metal, silver is second to gold in malleability and ductility, can be polished to a highly reflective surface, and used -- typically in an alloy -- in jewelry, coinage, photography, mirrors, electrical contacts, and tableware.

Pure metallic element having symbol Sn and atomic number 50; a soft, pliable, silvery white metal. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials.
Describes groupings of discrete tangible or visual things that are inanimate and given form by human activity.

Constituent parts of a larger object. A component differs from an item in that the item can stand alone as an independent work but the component typically cannot or does not stand alone. Examples are a panel of a polyptych or a discrete architectural component such as a dome.
Personal articles, such as furnishings, equipment, or dress, especially those belonging to a soldier, but excluding weapons.

The aggregate of physical things, conditions, and influences surrounding and affecting an organism, object, or structure. For the branch of biology dealing with the relations and interactions between organisms and their habitat, use "ecology." For the earth's major animal and plant communities, use "biomes." For the concept of the perceived external world, including the forces at work in it and the nonhuman life inhabiting it, use "Nature."
In Indian architecture, a row of lamps.

Refers specifically to sets of armor pieces designed as a whole to possess particular physical characteristics, usually to suit a particular purpose. For the general meaning of all costume designed to be worn or carried to protect the body in combat, either entire sets or individual pieces, see "armor."
General term for ensembles of ball game artifacts.
General term used for stamps that are grouped, such as in panes or sheets.

Refers to parts added onto an object or structure. In architecture, if a modification does not substantially increase a structure's volume, use "alterations." With regard to printed matter, use "addenda."
Parts or components of materials.

Pure metallic element having symbol Zn and atomic number 30; a bluish white crystalline metal. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials.

Pure metallic element having symbol Fe and atomic number 26; metallic iron is silvery in color, lustrous, soft, ductile, malleable, and slightly magnetic; it rusts when exposed to moist air. It is rarely found as a native metal (telluric iron) except in meteorites (meteoric iron). Iron is most often found throughout the world as iron oxides (hematite, magnetite, limonite, and siderite) mixed with other ores.
Mixture of the unmelted raw materials, such as sand and cullet, properly proportioned and ready for fusion into glass.
Parts and components of electrical systems.
Mechanical and electrical systems that relay information within buildings.
Networks of equipment that provide nonstructural services, such as HVAC or electricity throughout a building or complex.

Computer science concept of a place within the collective memories and interconnecting networks of computers filled with virtual 'stuff' and populated by people with virtual bodies. Distinguished from "virtual reality" which is an immersive virtual physical environment with user interfaces.
Parts or components of fire alarm systems.

Copper-nickel-zinc alloy, typically 20% zinc, 18% nickel, and the balance copper, used as a base metal for plated silverware, for springs and contacts in electrical equipment, and for corrosion-resistant objects.
Soft solder of eutectic composition, possessing the lowest melting point of any type of solder; constituted in proportions of 60% tin and 40% lead.

Chiwei is a tile component used at both ends of a building’s roof ridge (zhengji 正脊). The term appears in the statutory documents of official histories where the types and grades of buildings that can use chiwei are regulated; thus, it would have been a marker of high status. Provisions for the size, manufacture, labor, and other regulations for the use of chiwei on different types of buildings are outlined in the Yingzao fashi, Chapter 13, 5a-b. The names of specific shapes include owl or hawk tails (chiwei 鴟尾), dragon tails (longwei 龍尾), and beast heads (shoutou 獸頭). Different names for this feature were also used over time, including sea-beast tails (chiwei 蚩尾), shrine tails (ciwei 祠尾), owl or hawk beaks (chiwen 鴟吻), central lips or jaws (zhengwen 正吻), and great lips or jaws (dawen 大吻). Before the mid-Tang dynasty, chiwei were usually simple tails arching inwards and decorated with fin or feather patterns on the outer edge. In the mid-Tang (ca. 790-820) we see the added pattern of a beast head with an open mouth, and the tail gradually transitioning into that of a fish. Beginning in the Yuan dynasty (1279-1368), the chiwei tail arched outwards instead of inwards. In the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties, the beast's head opened its mouth around the ridge, the tail curved outward, and the ends (duanbu 端部) changed from bifurcated (fencha 分叉) to curled (juanqu 卷曲). Furthermore, dragons and swords were attached to the body of the beast and its shape was squared off. During the Ming and Qing dynasties, chiwei were commonly called chiwen 鴟吻, wenshou 吻獸, or zhengwen 正吻.
Bamboo- or cane-colored porcelain biscuit, invented by Wedgwood. For objects made from woven or carved bamboo, use "bamboo work (visual works)."

Towers or other elevated buildings located at large and medium-sized airports and from which the movement of aircraft and other surrounding traffic is controlled by radio or other means. The control tower structures generally rise high above other buildings at an airport and have windows, tilted outward to avoid glare, circling the entire top floor to allow a clear view for air traffic controllers. They contain necessary equipment, such as radios, radar displays, computer systems for meteorological information and flight data, controllers' headsets, telephone systems, light guns for communication with aircraft via aviation light signals, and wind and pressure gauges.
Organized units of documents grouped together in an overall arrangement or plan.
Buildings housing interdisciplinary museums that present the history and heritage of a particular community or region in the context of its society, culture, and natural environment.

Structures enclosed by glass or other transparent material, and devoted to the cultivation and protection of plants. These are usually free-standing but may be attached to another building. Greenhouses may vary in size, from small sheds to very large buildings, depending on their intended use. For rooms attached to houses and used as sun lounges or for growing indoor plants, prefer "conservatories."
Small, usually hand-held electrical appliances that dry hair by emitting a stream of warm air.
People having the historical rank overseeing the artillery, particularly in German and the Austro-Hungarian armies.
People who have withdrawn or secluded themselves from the world for religious reasons. Examples are the recluses of the East in the early Christian centuries.
Painters who paint the surfaces of industrial facilities.
Painters who specialize in landscapes.

Refers to the ancient Roman emperors from the time of Augustus Caesar (born 63 BCE) to the fall of Constantinople. The term is taken from the surname of the Roman dictator Caius Julius Caesar, and was transferred as a title to succeeding emperors. From the time of Hadrian (died 138 CE) it was also used as a title of the heir-presumptive of the emperor.
Those who specialize in portraits in the medium of paint.

Those who preach or otherwise spread a religion or religious ideas, usually by speaking but may be in written works. Examples include the writers of the Christian gospels and modern Protestant occasional preachers having no fixed pastoral charge.
Individuals who were elected pope in opposition to a pope held to be canonically chosen. Primary examples are those who resided at Avignon during the "great schism."
Containers in which cocktails or other mixed drinks are blended by shaking.

Rugs made in India in the 17th century incorporating design motifs borrowed from 16th-century Persian rugs, such as elaborate vine-leaf floral palmettes and scrolling vines in the field design; typically made with a red ground.
Radical partisans of the lower classes during the French Revolution; term refers to a man shabbily dressed, not wearing the breeches of the middle and upper classes of the period.
Planters for ferns. For structures or outdoor areas devoted primarily to ferns, use "ferneries (greenhouses)."
Tools and equipment used for conducting an examination or inspection to achieve a comprehensive view, as of a place, a situation, or an area of study, or to ascertain condition or value.

Those who hold a position of authority or command in the armed forces, specifically those holding it by commission. For those holding positions of trust and authority within a civil, governmental, or private context, see "officers (administrators)."
Leather bags, used primarily in the Americas, to contain personal items; designed to be attached to a horse's saddle or to the frame of a bed.
Valves used for controlling the flow of beer.

Technique used in computer imaging to counteract the jagged effect seen in curved or diagonal lines, caused by pixelation. It involves the interpolation of intermediate colors where differing colors meet on computer monitors and printouts.
Semirigid colloidal system of a liquid in a solid.

Techniques used to create images that display a higher luminous dynamic range than is possible with a single conventional exposure. This may be achieved with a series of conventional exposures captured with differing values, or via a laser scanner with high dynamic range (HDR) texture compression that records a range in excess of what normal digital imaging techniques allow.
Images created using a binary numerical system electronically stored in the form of encoded picture elements, or pixels.

Compounds having highly basic properties, specifically any of the soluble hydroxides of the alkali metals; a general term now used for any basic material (pH greater than 7). In general, alkali compounds will react with fatty acids to form soaps; turn litmus paper blue; dissolve in water to form alkaline solutions; taste bitter and are irritating to the skin. Alkaline solutions are used in deacidifying and buffering paper. Alkalis also act as fluxes in ceramics and glass production.

The degree to which an image is distinct in its details as a function of the spacing of individual optical elements, such as grains of light-sensitive chemicals in a photograph or pixels in an electronic image; an important factor affecting image quality.
Pentagonal knotted-pile woven rugs made in pairs to decorate the flanks of a camel.
A complex gül in which a quartered diamond is nested either within a rectangle or stepped diamond, which in turn is nested within another diamond, which is nested within a rectangle.
Rigs in which the principal sails are set parallel to the keel.

Refers to a process of planning and managing construction projects from inception of a facility to its eventual demolition through digital information models (e.g. 4D CAD) placed in shared knowledge resources.
Rigs consisting of a single gaff and boom mainsail set on a mast stepped close to the stern and carrying no headsails, found on catboats and other watercraft.
Metalworkers who apply a protective or decorative coating of one metal to another by means of an electrolytic bath.
Generally, style and culture of the area near the city of Kairouan, Tunisia. Specifically, the style of rugs from this area.

Japanese palanquin of basketwork slung on a pole and carried on the shoulders of bearers; type of litters used as a means of human transportation by the non-samurai class in feudal Japan and into the Meiji period.
The use of digital technology to overlay visual real-life representations, usually provided through video, with computer-generated data.
Dress for daytime social functions.
Tools employed in stretching materials for mounting, such as canvas onto a stretcher or screen onto a printing frame.
Tools or appliances used to cut the areca nut for preparing betel-chew.

Impressing an image into a surface using a tool that is cut intaglio with a complete design, resulting in a relief image. In bookbinding, distinguished from "blind blocking" in which a machine is used instead of a hand tool.
Districts within a city, town, or other community marked out for specific governmental or administrative purposes, such as for electoral, school, or police services.
Refers to people employed by fire departments to fight fires, rescue persons, and perform other emergency-related duties.
People who have traveled in space as crew members on board a spacecraft or on a space mission.
Concepts related to the study of human beings and their ancestors through time and space and in relation to physical character, environmental and social relations, and culture.
advertising via the broadcast media of radio or television.
