Refers to the process by which a computer is used as a tool in designing architecture, landscape design, cities, transportation infrastructure, engineering projects, automobiles, computer chips, or other objects of any size. The process uses a computer program to provide an interactive drawing tool, with an interface to allow simulation and analysis. In architectural design, the computer typically allows the user to virtually walk through three-dimensional spaces, to view the architecture in position on the proposed site, and to test aspects of stress and support. It is also used to reconstruct ruined buildings and cities, and to depict archaeological sites at different periods of time.
Persons who contribute to the production of an animated cartoon or other animation, as by making drawings.
Brushes for smoothing and styling the hair.
Loosely woven gauze-like cotton cloth, used primarily in cheese making, but also used for a wide variety of cooking techniques, such as making small sachets for herbs.
Assistants to priests and deacons, who generally perform duties such as lighting and bearing candles. The term is also used, by extension, in a general sense to refer to any novice or assistant.
Synagogue officials who sing or chant liturgical music and lead the congregation in prayer.
High-ranking clergy in Islam.
Hereditary Zoroastrian priests of the ancient Medes and Persians.
Articles, furnishings, or other physical resources utilized for or with animals.

Those who study or practice a form of chemistry and speculative philosophy practiced in Europe mainly in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, and concerned principally with discovering methods for transmuting base metal into gold and with finding a universal solvent and an elixir of life.
Men who engage in business as their primary occupation or function.

Public officers who examine publications, motion pictures, correspondence, or other forms of public or private communication for the purpose of suppressing any material in them deemed objectionable on moral, political, military, or other grounds.
Clasps or catches used to fasten the ends of a belt, sometimes ornamented with designs.
Two buttons, one larger than the other, connected by a shank, inserted into shirt neck buttonholes.
Strings used to lace up corsets, able to tighten them in place or to loosen them to aid in their removal.
People who specialize in the engraving of dies for stamping.
Refers generally to the process of striking something repeatedly.
To catch something or someone or to take prisoner.
The activity of going by boat or of rowing, especially as when an amusement rather than as a necessity.
Recreation, sport, or mode of transportation that involves moving over the ice by means of a pair shoes fitted with a metal blade.
Tools constructed so as to allow a single motion to inscribe multiple lines at once, usually parallel lines.
Members of an American, British, Foreign, or other Legion, though in modern times the term refers particularly to members of the French Légion étrangère.
Those who play the harpsichord.
Those who play the banjo.
Those who play on bagpipes.
Source works of art or documents from which copies may be made, or works otherwise distinguished in general from reproductions or other types of copies.
Radar allowing accurate measurement of the depth in the ground of certain target objects; used, for example, in archaeology.
Those who play the drum.
Those who play the kettledrum.
Those who play the timpani in a Western orchestra.
Stencils cut from sheets of stencil film to be used for blocking out nonprinting areas in screen printing.

Countries that are economically, politically, or militarily dependent on a more powerful country or empire. The term is one of several terms with overlapping meanings used to describe the subordination of one state to a more powerful state in international affairs. Examples of client states are Cappadocia as affiliated with the Roman Republic and Poland as affiliated with the Soviet Union.
Areas outside the boundaries of sovereign states in which they have settled communities of their own people and which remain subject to or closely connected with the parent state.
Illustrated cards that celebrate an event or person of note.

Refers to Medieval monumental crosses, usually of stone, used to mark an outdoor place, typically a sacred place, a burial spot, or an assembly point in the Celtic lands of Ireland, Scotland or elsewhere. They are generally inscribed or decorated in low relief in the Celtic style, influenced by Viking art. The form is typically the Latin cross with a ring around the point of vertical and horizontal intersection; however, some of the oldest examples are single stone pillars that have been decorated and inscribed.

Unglazed ceramic material that has been fired only once; generally producing a grainy texture; frequently used for modeling ornament or making small statues, dolls, or vessels. Distinct from "parian (porcelain)," which is silky in texture and marblelike in appearance.
Boards covered with flannel or felt on which images or cut-out figures can be attached as a teaching aid.

Sequences of DNA immobilized on a solid support such as a membrane or glass slide. DNA arrays are used in the identification and sequencing of a sample and to measure the expression of many genes simultaneously.
Visual works that depict marine scenes, specifically of harbors.
Designations for locations, either physical or virtual, where a person, corporate body, physical object, Web site, or other thing may be contacted or found.
Sticks with which the conductor of an orchestra or similar ensemble beats the time.
Electronic devices or systems capable of automatically performing prescribed sequences of operations on digitised data to achieve a desired end result.

Devices with which pages of a book or other materials can be turned without the use of hands. With variations in design these may be used to assist reading for the disabled, for musicians reading musical scores, or to photographically duplicate books.
Competitions of speed in which horses are run, usually mounted or pulling a conveyance with driver, in which the horse that finishes first is the winner.

Vessels capable of continuous, extended underwater voyages under their own power without surfacing; often naval combatant vessels. For vessels capable of complete submersion for only limited amounts of time and which may or may not move under their own power, use "submersibles."
Artifacts, usually flexible, often textiles, used to cover or conceal interior spaces, surfaces, or furnishings, especially for protection, warmth, or embellishment.

Refers to aluminum honeycomb-core solid support panels. These may be used in various capacities including as an auxiliary support for paintings on fabric in the conservation field: they supply an alternative to bonding to another piece of fabric as method of consolidation.

Protective boards or other heavy paper with an opening or openings cut in order to reveal photographs. These typically comprise two pieces, the bottom piece supports the print while the top piece has a window through which the photograph may be viewed. The boards may be hinged together to form a protective folder.
Members of the nobility.
People who shoot with bow and arrows, whether used in hunting, competition, or war.

Devices used to ring bells, often decorative and comprising long, narrow embroidered textiles attached to a bell-wire, hanging against an interior wall. Used to ring servant bells, and later as purely decorative objects hung on walls or laid over furniture.
Cushions filled with air rather than stuffed with material.
Portable inflatable bladders that are used as temporary head support while sleeping or resting.
Large, often mace-like batons wielded by a drum major to keep measure in marching bands.
Districts under ecclesiastical control.

Domains of the admiral under the Real Hacienda, royal tax office, designated by the king of Spain. These domains contain their own jurisprudence and certain rights and responsibilities. Almirantazgos have the right to a significant percentage of the profits obtained from fleets that remain in the harbor. The profits from this percentage also included all activities relating to ships that arrived at the harbor including shipping cost rights, anchoring rights, entrance and exit fees, and loading and unloading fees.
Grids of fine opaque lines or other fine opaque patterns through which images are photographed to break up tonal areas into fine patterns for creating tonal areas in printing.
Halftone screens consisting of a grid of fine lines.
Officers of the highest rank in a navy.

Officials of monasteries and other religious communities in charge of provisions and supplies, especially of food, of the running of the kitchens, the work and conduct of servants and lay members, the purchase and delivery of goods, and all aspects of the management of the establishment that are not specifically assigned to others.

Those licensed and appointed to steer ships while arriving or departing a port, or through local waters until those ships reach their destination or open sea. The license issued to maritime pilots is specific to particular areas.
Makeup used to emphasize the contour of the eyes, coming in many forms, most commonly a pencil or a brushed-on liquid.
The action of adjusting or adapting to a new temperature, climate, environment, or situation. In conservation, usually used in the context of object testing or treatment.
Spectacles of any kind that end in a point on the upper outside rim. Initially popular for women in the 1950s and 1960s, the shape goes in and out of fashion.

Eyewear that protected the eyes from gas and other irritant agents; developed during WWI. Following the introduction of the Small Box Respirator, anti-gas goggles were considered obsolete and their use declined.
Sunglasses designed with a wire frame and large lenses, similar in shape to those worn by early aviators to accommodate face masks.
Dental hygiene devices, usually battery operated, fitted with a vibrating or oscillating brush for cleaning teeth.
Commanders of private bands of mercenaries who sell their services to warring states or rulers, especially those active in Italy and other regions of Europe from the 14th to the 16th century.
Covers for floors, intended to protect the floor from soiling or wear, to provide warmth or a more comfortable walking surface, or for decoration.
The collective bodies of religious and lay counselors, officers, courtiers, family members, and attendants constituting the retinue of a pope. For the judicial bodies of popes, use "papal tribunals."

Refers to male heads of the house of Habsburg. The title of archduke Palatine (in German, "Pfalz-Erzherzog") was first assumed by Rudolf IV, Duke of Austria, with the goal of gaining for the dukes of Austria an equal status with the electors of the Holy Roman Empire. The term was also used to refer to the Bourbon kings and queens of Spain, even though they were not descended in the male line from their Habsburg predecessors. The term may also be used to refer to rulers of other Continental European states, including Lorraine, Brabant, and Austrasia. For the wives and daughters of archdukes, use "archduchesses."
Daughters of the former Habsburg emperors of Austria or Austria-Hungary, and for the wives or widows of archdukes.
Use specifically for women who dance in classical ballet.
Objects designed to fit over the hand that are made of slightly abrasive textile materials, used for the purpose of exfoliation while bathing.
Devices with a hole over which a sharp, thin blade moves to cut the top of a cigar.

Optical devices for use with both eyes consisting of two small telescopes fitted together side by side on a single frame and containing an erecting system usually with both focusing tubes simultaneously adjustable by means of a single screw.
Includes the making of or working on or with glass or glass articles.
Process of manufacturing glass vessels around a core of material made in the shape of the desired vessel.
Devices used to protect image areas of a printing plate or stone from contact with the hand during drawing.
Metal frame used to hold and secure matter for printing.
Tools, such as rollers or dabbers, used for applying ink to a printed surface.

Transparent sheets of tints that consist of dots, which are used to apply texture to artwork and designs. The name derives from Benjamin Day, a New Jersey printer, who sold shading mediums in the 19th century. Ben Day dots were made famous through their use by Pop artist Roy Lichtenstein.
Stencils used in screen printing.
Rectangles of piano felt or foam rubber used between the paper and the roller on a rolling press.
Term of Japanese origin for smooth, flat, round, or oval pads with handles used to press a sheet of paper against the face of a relief printing block to form an impression.
Machines for composing type that do not employ hot-metal casting at the time of composition.  Includes those that assemble foundry type mechanically and those that do strike-on composition.
Railroad trains capable of traveling at speeds greater than 200 km per hour on their own dedicated track.
Type cast in relatively hard metal by type founders and sold to compositors.
Machines for strike-on composition of type that are essentially typewriters, sometimes with limited memory capacity.
Those composing machines that produce a hot-metal slug for each line of type.

Early Spanish carpets with three major types of ornamentation derived from Persian or Anatolian rugs, an octagonal-hexagonal design, stepped lozenges design, and star and lozenge design; they are often embellished with coats of arms, and incorporate non-Islamic motifs such as animal or human figures.

A term originating in the mid-20th century, originally to distinguish strike-on composition of type from hot-metal methods; later extended to include photographic methods. Use another term when possible.
Method of mechanical type composition in which type is cast as single full lines, each as one slug.

The composition of text, using electronic and photographic methods. Images of type characters are projected from a film or disk onto photosensitive film or paper; the resulting page is used to produce, usually, an offset plate.
Division of the natural sciences, consisting of those sciences that deal with the organic world, including all aspects of living beings and the systems that sustain them.
The state of discomfort or discontent with the physical or social aspects of one's own sex.
Railroad passenger cars with seating areas on two levels, the upper of which may or may not extend the full length of the car.
Passenger train cars in which travelers' luggage is carried.
Freight cars whose bodies can be tipped for discharging loads.
Bases of Ionic columns following a pattern developed in Asia Minor, with an upper torus surmounting a disk generally composed of shallow scotias, both elements being usually horizontally fluted.
Decorative parts or areas that are attached or applied to the surface of an object after the object has been formed.
Light aircraft specially equipped for agricultural applications, such as crop dusting.
Use generally for manned orbiting space probes and specifically for the portion of space shuttles containing the crew and payload.
Spherical feet, used mainly on tables and case furniture in the second half of the 17th century.
Tool handles, such as those of axes, hatchets, or hammers.
Handles in the form of a single bar mounted on one or more brackets.
Describes handles in the form of small masses, usually rounded, which are intended to be mounted on the door of a cabinet.
Vertical take-off and landing aircraft whose engine pods or rotors tilt 90 degrees from a horizontal position for horizontal flight to a downward position for vertical flight.
Aircraft designed or equipped primarily to transport cargo.
Trophies consisting of the whole bodies or portions of game animals or fish taken in hunting, preserved as souvenirs usually by being taxidermized and mounted for display.
Airplanes with two sets of wings, one above and usually slightly forward of the other.
Aircraft whose wings are so designed that they can be moved backward or forward in flight to optimize aerodynamic performance at widely differing speeds.

Fossilized shark's teeth that since the Renaissance were regarded as petrified tongues of dragons or snakes; thus referred to as "tongue stones" or "glossopetrae." They were considered talismans against poison or toxins, and were used in the treatment of snake bites. Noblemen and royalty are known to have worn them as pendants or kept them as charms. They were also incorporated into utensils. For the material derived from the animal that may or may not be fossilized, use "shark teeth."
Small passenger aircraft operating either on a scheduled or nonscheduled basis, along short routes normally not serviced by airliners.

Refers to coarse lace or fringe made by knotting cords or thick threads in a geometric pattern. The term comes from Turkish "makrama," meaning "napkin," or "towel." It was a specialty of Genoa, where towels decorated with knotted cord were popular in the 19th century. The predecessor of macrame was the 16th-century technique of knotting lace known as "punto a groppo." In the 1960s macrame became a popular craft and creative art technique in America and in Europe. It has been used to create lampshades, plant hangers, hammocks, window coverings, and wall hangings.
Contrivances for connecting one thing to another mechanically in series, either permanently, or temporarily.
Small, lightweight, low-cost, low-horsepower aircraft with a maximum take-off weight of 12,500 pounds; usually fixed-wing, single-pilot, privately owned aircraft.
A Persian term for long, relatively narrow rugs measuring approximately 6 by 4 feet, or 2 zars.
White-ground Anatolian rugs with an endless repeat of stylized angular leaves.
Objects or materials concerning characteristics of American civilization or culture.

Refers to painted or carved image-bearing objects in a Christian church. Altarpieces are characterized by usually being framed and either set on the rear part of the altar abutting the back of the altarblock or hung on the wall behind the altar. Altarpieces may be set on both the central high altar and side altars. The subject of the image is typically a religious figure or figures, often included in a narrative or didactic scene; it may also include a patron of the church.

Objects that are venerated within a particular system of worship; for those that are, or contain, images, use "cult images." Use especially with regard to extinct cultures and religions; for objects venerated in still-living religions, prefer "religious objects," and if those objects retain their sacredness in their present context, use "sacred objects."
Solid spheres made of transparent quartz crystal or glass. Examples are those used variously by fortune tellers, clairvoyants, and in certain faiths.
Guides used to set out brick work or block work accurately.
Object wielded by a medium to make wise statements or communicate with divine beings on behalf of individuals of the populace.
In the context of Christian churches, guards, usually comprising a wooden or metal strip, used to protect the altar frontal from injury or wear.
Blocks of wood cut parallel with the grain and used for woodcut.
The outer boundary of an object or shape, especially when it suggests volume or mass.

Black-figure kylikes characterized by decoration in a band, generally in the zone of the handles. The rest of the vessel is black. Decoration consists of figures, ornaments, or inscriptions, often the potter's signature.

Kylikes with a handle zone decorated with a chain of buds, the next zone usually decorated with upside down silhouettes of animals or other figures, and the base of the bowl decorated with rays and separated from the zone above by stripes.

Explosive devices typically consisting of a paper case containing combustible material, an oxidizing agent, and, if desired, a metal salt as a coloring agent; used for signals and celebrations. For such celebratory displays of light, sound, or smoke, use "fireworks (visual works)."
In the social organization of Nahua culture, a city-state or political entity with a shared ethnic identitity and other ideological and economic characteristics.
Cylinder presses in which the printing surface lies horizontally.
Material, usually a chemical compound or a mixture of compounds, produced for the purpose of causing an explosion.
Printing presses for offset printing.
The process of making printing plates by using a mold of another printing surface, such as a wood engraving or set type, and electroplating with copper.

Groups of people organized for a purpose, typically characterized by a more or less constant membership, a body of officers or functionaries, and a set of regulations governing their activities and conduct.

The process, involving various procedures done by hand or machine, of securing leaves or gatherings, usually within covers, to form a book. In book production, the process of assembling the finished book; the concept of securing the leaves of sections of a text so as to keep them in proper order and protect them

The process of attaching individual boards to a text block, usually by gluing the tapes and spine-lining material to the inside of single boards or between split boards, or by the lacing-in of the cords through holes or grooves in the boards. For the attachement of a previously made case to a text block, use "casing-in."

Tools used in printmaking for engraving metal plates or end-grain wood blocks, consisting of a small steel rod, of square or lozenge section, with a sharpened point, and having a half-round wood handle that fits in the palm of the hand. In the context of archaeology, a specialized flake or blade with a chisel edge; used to carve or engrave softer materials such as bone, wood, or antler. For various tools for chasing or engraving metal or wood, use "gravers."
Watertight, usually metal, boatshaped containers hauled on a line between a wrecked vessel and the shore; used for marine rescues from 1849 until ca. 1910.
Vessels fitted with machinery for deepening or cleaning and improving waterways, especially harbors and river channels.

Single-masted lightly armed cutters with fire lines built for governments expressly to prevent smuggling and to enforce customs regulations; in use mostly from the late 18th to the early 19th century.
Small open boats used for carrying supplies and provisions to sell to ships lying in harbor; also employed to take garbage ashore.

Ships' boats assigned to flag officers, especially since 1750; generally smaller and lighter than launches and longboats, usually having more than 10 oars, and often decorated and fitted out with accommodations for the assigned officer.
Describes vessels that operate on the water's surface.
Describes vessels designed to achieve buoyancy by displacing a volume of water equal to their weight.
One or more animal skins inflated to serve as a vessel for water crossing, in parts of Africa and elsewhere.
Refers to any of various motorized watercraft fitted with planes or foils beneath their hull to lift the vessels clear of the water when traveling at high speed.
Small or medium-sized vessels engaged in coastwise navigation; generally merchant vessels maintaining trade and communication among smaller ports and between major entrepôts and the hinterland.
Watercraft designed for use on canals generally long and narrow with bow and stern often nearly vertical for increased cargo capacity.

Watercraft of various pre-Columbian South American civilizations constructed from woven reeds of the Totora bullrush. The form and size may vary, including small fishing boats and large transporting vessels.

Double-ended, log-bottom boats or later flat-bottom, shallow-draft boats of similar shape, but built plank-on-frame, with two masts raking aft carrying a jib and triangular sails; used for offshore fishing and general cargo transport in the Chesapeake Bay area.

Small- to medium-sized watercraft built on a log bottom, either as extended dugouts or, less commonly, in log-canoe fashion, typically with an open central hold and propelled by sails, oars, or poling; common to the southeastern United States and South and Central America.
Small, broad round or roundish skin boats of various constructions used for river or coastal transport in ports of the Near East and Great Britain in ancient and modern times.
Describes watercraft powered by human activity.
Describes watercraft propelled by the rotation of oars in water and powered by human beings.
Describes watercraft propelled by oarsmen positioned on one level.

Oared fighting ships, principally of the Mediterranean, in operation from the Early Bronze Age until the 18th century CE; most commonly with numerous oars on one or several decks and equipped with a ram with which to damage and sink enemy vessels. For post-18th century steamships equipped with an armored prow as a primary weapon, use "rams."

Pulling boats developed in the 1820s near Whitehall Street, New York City, and used originally in large harbors as workboats by chandlers, pilots, shipping agents, and other businesses, and later for recreation; usually 14 to 22 feet long with one to five rowers sometimes with pail and centerboard, and distinguished by a plumb stem and wine glass-shaped stern.
Ancient Mediterranean warships propelled by oarsmen arranged in two levels.
Relatively light, fast, oared warships used by Roman navies of the Imperial period to patrol sea lanes and pursue pirates.
Describes watercraft that can be powered by an external source, such as an internal combustion engine, added to the vessel.
Vessels with smaller sail area than typical sailboats plus a motor as means of propulsion.
Describes watercraft powered by a heat engine that derives its heat from fuel consumed outside the cylinder.
Watercraft powered by naphtha-burning engines.
Boats propelled by inboard or outboard engines.

Speedboats with a light hull and equipped with one or more marine engines. Built primarily between 1900-1910, the name "autoboat" originated in France, where the first high-speed motorboats had automobile engines.
Steam-powered watercraft propelled by a pair of paddle wheels mounted amidships or by a single paddle wheel at the stern; developed in the late 18th century.
Motorboats propelled by outboard motors.
Boats having sails as their primary means of propulsion.
Describes watercraft rigged with fore-and-aft sails on their main masts.

Catboats developed in the 1870s around Cape Cod and Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts, and generally characterized by a 1:2 beam to length ratio, high freeboard, large cockpit, perpendicular square stern, and large outboard rudder; first built for fishing and later used as pleasure craft. Distinguished from "Great South Bay catboats" which have a lower freeboard, narrower beam, and a counter stern.
Square-rigged vessels having two masts.
Two-masted vessels square-rigged on the foremast, but primarily fore-and-aft-rigged on the mainmast, although some vessels carried square topsails on the mainmast.
Brigs having a gaff-rigged spanker or trysail set on a small auxiliary mast, called a spencer mast or trysail mast, just abaft the mainmast.

Finely woven rugs intended for a sophisticated, urban clientelle. They typically duplicate specific patterns and are woven to standards that are enforced in a workshop setting under the guidance of a master weaver, often employing a cartoon that carefully depicts knot counts and colors.

Artists' implements having a flattened surface of various forms and made of various materials; used by painters and other artists, particularly as used to mix, spread, or transfer ink or paint, or for other purposes. For spatulas comprising blades of flexible metal used in creating art, usage overlaps with "palette knives (painting equipment)."
Instruments utilizing a prism to project an accurate image of an object onto a flat surface for the purpose of tracing.

Optical instruments for projecting kromograms, which are prepared sets of photographic images; the instrument accurately combined and projected three-separation color images. Invented by Fred. E. Ives and first demonstrated in 1896.

X-ray diffraction technique which uses x-ray optics to focus an excitation beam to a small spot on the sample surface so that extremely small features on the sample can be analyzed at much higher resolution than with conventional XRD.
Broad, flat-bottomed boats with bulging sides, used for coasting and fishing.
Cutting a raw block of glass that has not been previously cut to shape, using a rotating wheel fed with water.

Refers to large wing-handled lusterware vases found at the medieval Islamic palace of Alhambra in Granada, Spain. Averaging 125 cm in height, they are the largest lusterware pots ever made. They were probably produced in the coastal town of Málaga. These amphora-shaped vessels fall into two stylistic groups. Vases of the first group, dating to the late 13th and early 14th centuries, are more bulbous in shape and have short necks, monochrome luster, and bold, angular inscriptions. Vases of the second group, dating to the late 14th and early 15th centuries, are more elongated and are decorated in cobalt blue and gilding; they also have less conspicuous inscriptions. As they are unstable, they would have been displayed on tripods or set into holes in the floor.
A type of mold-blown glass blown in full-size molds that usually consist of three parts, but occasionally the term is used to describe glassware made in two-, four-, or five-part molds.
Tin glaze with a blue to grayish blue or lilac-gray stain; used to decorate ceramics, especially Italian maiolica.
Refers to a whiteware specially compounded to serve an electrical insulator. Often used as an insulator in spark plugs and power lines.
Oblong rugs designed to encircle a column or post in Lamaist temples, they have no side borders and their design is not complete unless the edges of the rug abut.
Tibetan rugs with a length double the width, the primary function is for sleeping or sitting.
A type of rug that served as a door at the entrance to a Turkoman tent.
Karabagh rugs with a pattern which consists of one or more medallions containing motifs which resemble the cloud whisp motifs of Chinese art.
Multicolored spotted rugs produced in ancient southwestern China.
Refers to any carpet made in India, Turkey, Iran, or elsewhere that copies the original carpets made for use at the Ardabil shrine; and any contemporary carpet made in the area of Ardabil.
Turkish rugs with a design element consisting of a tomb and trees.

Early Spanish rugs characterized by a woolen pile tied with Spanish knots to an undyed woolen foundation, generally somber in color, often with a red ground and geometrical design motifs reminiscent of Classic Anatolian rugs.

Refers to a distinctive type of bobbin lace that was sold in and exported from England during a particular period of history. It refers both to genuine Brussels lace that was secretly imported to England in late 17th century, and to lace produced in England that was comparable to fine Brussels lace in thread quality, technique, and design. In order to encourage the lace industry at home, in the 1660s both England and France enacted laws prohibiting the importation of the wildly popular Brussels lace. To circumvent these laws, merchants often smuggled Brussels lace to England and France, selling it as lace made in England. Scholars still debate whether surviving examples were actually made in England or Brussels, or both.

Refers to lace made in Armenia, Cyprus, Turkey, and the Greek Islands, and characterized by the use of a single needle and traditional techniques and stitches. Designs and stitches vary in different regions, but in general it is characterized by extreme delicacy and intricacy of design. It often is made with silk thread and includes gold threads and is decorated with pearls and various precious gems. It was particularly popular in the 17th century, and was used in lace borders on apparel, as chalice covers, and on other liturgical linen. Some scholars believe that Venetian lace has its origins in 16th-century Armenian lace.
Textile woven by Igbo women of Nigeria, featuring intricate weft-woven patterns in cotton or rayon over a ground weave in cotton; only commercial machine-woven yarn is used.
Yoruba indigo dyed cloth.
Asante stamped cloth.
Provision of fixed soft coverings for furniture, especially seating and reclining furniture. Originally referred to the provision of all textile components of a room.
Fastening an upholstery covering and padding in place by the use of buttons, usually in a pattern such as a diamond or square for a decorative effect.

Textile weaving technique in which a pattern is formed or the ground enriched by the use of more than one series of warp ends; the patterning is done using either a supplementary or complementary warp.

Finishing process in textile manufacture using controlled shrinkage to produce a thicker, more compact, and firm cloth. In heavily fulled textile, both the structure and the individual component strands are entirely obscured, giving the appearance of felt. For the application of heat, pressure, and moisture to fiber to cause it to mat together, use "felting."
Traditional textile painting technique practiced in parts of India which combines hand painting and block printing through the medium of vegetable dyes on prepared cotton fabric.
Trimming made by twisting silk, worsted, or cotton thread around a core thread or wire, resulting in a flat openwork braid.
Territories or other administrative bodies that are subject to the control of another nation, while yet remaining outside the official boundaries of that nation.

Entities that share sovereignty in constitutional federal union, and have transferred a portion of their sovereign powers to a federal government. Federated states may be called provinces, states, Lands, cantons, or other terms, depending upon usage within a particular nation. Examples of federated states are in the United States, Brazil, Canada, and many other nations. For entities retaining complete sovereignty, use "sovereign states." For territories within a federation that do not share sovereignty, use "federal territory."
Sovereign states consisting of a city and its contiguous dependent territories.
Administrative bodies subject to an archduke or archduchess.

Fast, powerful seagoing watercraft, usually schooner- or brig-rigged, with fine entrance, long run, moderate to pronounced drag, and strong deadrise; built in the first half of the 19th century and often involved in illegal trades, either as smugglers or slavers, or as revenue vessels trying to catch smugglers.
Single-hulled watercraft especially when contrasting them to multihulled watercraft.
Describes watercraft with a flat hull, often used to traverse shallow bodies of water.
Barge-like, flat-bottomed sailing ships common to the Netherlands from the Middle Ages to the end of the 19th century, used for fishing and river and costal transport.

Inland waterway vessels, typically flat bottomed and designed to carry cargo; generally towed by animals or people for certain parts of the journey, although modern versions may be fitted with motors.
Hydroplanes that ride on two forward sponsons and a point at the stern, which may be suspended by propellor alone; almost always raceboats.
Chesapeake Bay watercraft with V-bottom hulls.
Describes watercraft in which each end of the vessel is distinctly shaped.

Large, ancient Roman merchant vessels of the western Mediterranean having a curved sternpost, but a projecting, ramlike cutwater at the bow; such vessels tended to be longer and narrower than "corbitae," the other major Roman merchant type.

Small to medium-sized vessels, with plain head and square stern, originally developed as lateen-rigged coastal fishing vessels in Medieval Portugal, but eventually used as exploratory vessels in Iberian voyages to the New World in the late 15th and early 16th centuries; vessels of exploration were often square-rigged for more efficient ocean-going travel.
Watercraft with both ends coming to a point or ending in a full stem and sternpost.
Lightly built, slender, open craft of shallow draft that are paddled and not rowed and normally double-ended; may have sails.
Small craft with flat rockered bottoms, flat sides, and broad square ends, commonly but not exclusively found along the New Jersey coast.
Engine-powered launches with high glass-sided cabins, which provide easy standing headroom and may be three feet or more higher than the basic hull.
Mass-produced three-island vessels of 10,500 deadweight tons built to a specific design in the United States during the Second World War to carry general cargo and military supplies.
Watercraft having a primarily ceremonial or ritual purpose.
Watercraft, usually highly decorated and propelled by oars or paddles, used for transporting important persons, either alive or dead, on state occasions or for ceremonial visits.
Watercraft engaged in fishing.
Small, Chesapeake Bay centerboard boats of bugeye type about 40 feet long, half-decked, with two masts and leg-of-mutton sails; used for oyster tonging.
Small (under about 25 feet) V-bottomed boats, both power and sail, chiefly used for crabbing on Chesapeake Bay, with handliners or trotlines in summer; may be used for oyster tonging in winter.
Fishing craft in which handlining is carried out from dories.
Pulling boats used in menhaden fishing to drive the fish into nets, usually 12 to 13 feet long and carried aboard menhaden steamers to the fishing grounds.

Small otter trawlers of various types and sizes, which engage in shore fishing along the Atlantic Coast of the United States, usually within 50 miles of the coastline; introduced in the mid-20th century.
Two-masted, spritsail-rigged, half-decked, square-sterned lobsterboats developed in Kingston on Massachusetts Bay; after ca. 1880s slightly altered for racing and recreational use.

Dory-type waterfowling boats with wide stern found on the Susquehanna Flats of the upper Chesapeake Bay during the late 19th and early 20th centuries; generally having a hole in the transom for a sculling oar.
Whaling vessels specifically designed for processing whales as they are caught; usually accompanying whale catchers. For the facilities where whales are processed on shore, use "whaling stations."
Describes watercraft used for sporting or competitive activities.
Open outboard-powered boats in the 15- to 18-foot range, configured especially for freshwater sport fishing.

Light, bevel-lapped double-ended guideboats from New York State's Adirondack region, ranging from 13 to 18 feet long, fitted with a carrying yoke, having a flat bottom board, and planked over natural crook frames in the style of dories; planking is usually smooth or carvel.
Sailboats sufficiently alike or having differences under sufficient restrictions to enable them to race against each other as a class without the necessity of handicap allowances.
Racing sailboats built to a rule which allows hull and rig variations, but still allows boats built to the rule to race without handicap.
Watercraft designed primarily to transport cargo.
Vessels either designed for or engaged in the trade of carrying coal in bulk.
Passenger ships taking extended cruises, often with intermediary stops along the way.
Ships providing service and support to naval operations.

Unarmed ships staffed and equipped to provide hospitalization for wounded military personnel or to evacuate wartime casualties; marked according to standards of international law to allow for safe passage.

Naval vessels carrying war horses or cavalry mounts to overseas military campaigns; such vessels are usually specifically modified to stable, support, and feed horses, and may additionally be constructed for rapid loading and unloading.
Warships designed to transport and land troops, equipment, and supplies, often with the aid of helicopters.
Warships equipped or designed for laying mines in or under the water.
Warships acting as floating mobile air stations with facilities for the takeoff, landing, and servicing of aircraft.
Naval submarines carrying ballistic missiles.
Describes vessels that provide assistance or support to other watercraft.
Vessels built or equipped to carry out salvage work: i.e. the retrieval of a sunken ship after the cargo has removed. Usually equipped with heavy duty pumps, lifting equipment, winches and cables.
Vessels fitted for laying and repairing underwater communications cables.
Vessels equipped with pumps and other apparatus for fighting fires on or from the water.
Ornamented barbed darts thrust into the neck and shoulders of the bull during a bullfight.

Biologically mediated deterioration that includes molecular changes to a material such that characteristic properties of the material are no longer evident. For loss of utilitarian or physical characteristics of a material caused by bacteria or other microorganisms, use 'biodeterioration.'

Throwing axes with a short handle and a long arched blade widening toward the cutting edge and ending in a prominent point at the top back corner and often at the bottom one as well. They had become the characteristic national weapon of the Franks by the 6th century and were used by other European peoples at least into the 9th century.
Bluish or grayish discoloration of timber caused by the growth of several types of moldlike fungi on the surface and in the interior of the sapwood.
A nonreversible condition whereby the fibrous structure of leather breaks down partially or completely, becoming extremely powdery.
Streams of electrons or positrons emitted from an atomic nucleus in a certain type of radioactive decay.
The destructive formation of a soft powdery mineral on copper or any of its alloys caused by the presence of chlorides and moisture.
Sites located under bodies of salt water, particularly in oceans or seas.
General term for engineering concepts that are related to the stress that physical structures can withstand.
The ability of materials to resist stress without yielding or fracture, especially as described by the stress level at which it fractures or fails.
Physics concepts dealing with the properties of sound.
Luminous bridges of electricity formed in a gap between two electrodes.
The condition of being safe, free from danger.

In the context of property loss from fire, defensible space is a buffer between a structure and a surrounding landscape. Adequate defensible space acts as a barrier to slow or halt the progress of fire that would otherwise engulf property by clearing plants or objects from the perimeter of a structure. It also helps ensure the safety of firefighters.

The process by which a liquid, or a mixture of gases and liquids, is drawn into and tends to fill permeable pores in a porous solid material; usually accompanied by a physical change, chemical change, or both.
The loss or migration of colorant due to contact with liquids, especially water; also in painting the diffusion or migration of coatings or the pigments in them into surrounding layers or surfaces.
The husbanding and efficient use of energy resources so as to extend non-renewable supplies or to make the most cost-effective use of renewable supplies.
The action or process of becoming smaller, shorter, or pressed together.
Disturbance of soil and sediment by flora or fauna; in an archaeological context, bioturbation serves to displace and move buried artifacts such as grave goods.
The joining of two surfaces by means of a generally viscous, sticky composition such as an adhesive or through physical or chemical force.

Methods by which masonry units, such as bricks or stones, are interlocked or joined through adhesion of mortar to the bricks. Bonds may be identified and referenced by the pattern on the surface of the masonry. For the process focusing on facing patterns, often in reference to ancient patterns, use children of "masonry facing (process)," although meaning overlaps.
Reduction or decrease in number, size, or strength, also wearing down, often by rubbing or friction.

Any or all of those processes involved in the manufacture of leather or rawhide that follow curing and precede tanning or tawing of skins or hides. The objective is to rid the skins or hides of substances not wanted in the finished leather, and to put them in the proper chemical and physical condition for tanning or tawing.

Marking the surface of an object by pressing onto it, by means of a machine such as a printing press, a block, plate, or frame containing the elements that make up the printing surface, often having a raised design. In bookbinding, distinguished from "stamping (marking)", in which a hand tool is used instead of a machine.
Process in which heat converts a liquid into its gaseous state at a fixed temperature for that liquid known as the boiling point.
Devices for testing the strength of gunpowder by igniting a measured quantity, causing an indicator to move along a numbered scale against which the relative strength of the powder is read.
The functions involved with producing or maintaining certain humidity levels.
Shoelike devices or platforms that attach to shoes, are fitted with a metal blade or blades, and are used for gliding across ice.

Ice skates for competitive speed skating designed with short boots having no ankle support attached to a long, straight blade with an essentially flat bottom. Made to be thin and light, the top part of these blades are often hollow. Speed skates may have asymmetric blade placement on the right or left boot, or have provisions for customized blade placement.
Any of various heat-resistant containers intended primarily for baking.
Large usually rectangular boards at sports venues used primarily to display the score and other relevant facts, figures, or images of the game in progress.

Applied low-relief decoration made by free-hand brush application of gesso before gilding. Works with aggetti designs are commonly described as pastiglia, but the techniques are very different. Use aggetti for works designed using free-hand brush application. For works designed using the application of a mould, use "pastiglia."
Plant material used for binding and weaving, from Ripogonum scandens plants native to New Zealand.

Soft red ocher that is a natural mixture of hydrated silicate clays colored with red iron oxide. Since at least the 17th century, it has been used as a foundation for gold leaf and as a red earth pigment.

Leading staffs with heads imitating those of various other staff weapons, but most commonly having a broad, pointed blade with a rounded base, often with two pointed lugs like a partisan or a crossbar like a boar spear. They were used in Great Britain and Continental Europe from the 18th into the mid-19th century by infantry subordinate officers, particularly English sergeants.
Square-ended artists' brushes with shorter bristles than flats.
Long, slender, hair brushes that come to a shaped chisel tip, used for lettering and for precise lines or bands.

A scaraboid is a seal, setting in a ring, or other object in the general shape of a scarab--that is a ovoid domed shape with a flat bottom--but lacking the details that identify it as the scarab insect. Scaraboids may be decorated with designs unrelated to the original insect.
Mesh attached to basketball hoops, used to slow the passage of the basketball through it when scoring.
Jousts developed in Germany that were fought with lances having a blunted, often pronged, head.
Bottles fitted with a pump or bulb that can deliver liquids such as scent in the form of a fine spray.

Persons trained in the theory or science of agriculture. Those engaged in the formal study, administration, or practice of the science of cultivating soil, harvesting crops, and raising livestock. For those who primarily work the land or raise livestock as a means of making a living, prefer "farmers."
Egyptian peasant farmers living in the Nile River Valley.

Men typically of noble birth, who, under European feudalism, held their rank, privileges, and landed estates from higher ranking individuals, in return for service as armed and mounted warriors or for providing another to fulfill this service in their stead. Use also for those who receive the title as a mark of honor and social distinction.
Female slaves in a harem.
Italian stuffed quilting technique worked in smaller and narrower areas, creating almost the appearance of corded quilting.
Upholstering technique in which furniture is provided with deep stuffed upholstery.
Pleated tufting done in a diamond pattern.
Form of buttoning originating in the Victorian period, producing deeply puckered, comfortable upholstery.
Close nailing in which the nails are set in two parallel rows.
Gathering cloth by drawing it together with duplicated rows of alternating short and long stitches, to produce even parallel folds; used especially in women's dresses.
Automata that operate by hidden clockwork and play out biblical or other inspirational scenes, often at given times of day; the art form flourished in medieval northern Europe.
Finished edge of a cloth article, such as a skirt, sleeve, or curtain fashioned by rolling up or folding back an edge and stitching it down.
Synthetic yarn with reflective properties made of aluminum filaments coated with plastic. It is used in Nigeria and other parts of West Africa to weave shiny, glittering cloth-like material.
Yarn produced by twisting together two or more strands of plied yarn; the final twist is opposite to that of the plied ends.
Yarn in which the twist of its component fiber follows the direction of the central bar of the letter S.
Cloth made from the fibers extracted from sheaths of the banana tree.
Textile forming the back of something, or placed at or attached to the back of something to support, strengthen, stiffen, or protect it.
Textile made for blankets and similar items, woven by the yard.
Yoruba narrow-strip woven cloth made on a horizontal loom.

Balls or pellets, usually of lead, used as projectiles in muzzle-loaded long guns known as muskets. Musket cartridges consisted of black powder, and a ball, wrapped in paper. This was then torn open and manually pushed into the barrel of the musket for firing.
The collective body of courtiers, family members, counselors, officers, and attendants constituting the retinue of a sovereign or high dignitary.
People or corporate bodies who specialize in making scientific instruments, which are crafted instruments used for scientific purposes and research, in all branches of science.
Chrome-tanned calf traditionally dyed black and boarded in two directions to produce a grain of rectangularly crossed lines. Distinct from "willow calf" which is boarded in only one direction.
Tea services designed to fit into a special box or carrying case, intended to be portable.
A lightweight fiber usually made from polyester used as a filling material for cushions and insulation.
Brocade done in high relief.
Use to describe firearms in which the firing mechanism, including the hammer, is completely inside.
Use to describe firearms that are loaded at the rear end of the barrel.
Light carriages with low wheels, having a removable folding hood or top. In Canada, a two-wheeled, one-seated vehicle, usually without a cover, with a seat for the driver on the splashboard.
Specially designed or modified automobiles for racing.
Lightly armored, highly mobile, fully tracked vehicles primarily for transporting personnel on and off the battlefield; usually fitted with light armament.
Self-propelled vehicles designed primarily to transport passengers over ordinary roads.

Strong vehicles, having two or sometimes three wheels and without springs. Usually animal-drawn and built for utility purposes, used in farming operations, and for carrying heavy goods. Some varieties were designed as sporting vehicles or for personal transportation. For utility vehicles having four wheels, use "wagons."
Overland self-propelled devices for conveying people, materials, or goods or designed for specific transportation operations.
Sled-like vehicles for the transport of barrels that may be pushed or pulled by a person or pack animal.
A cut velvet with very long pile.
Land vehicles with armorplated bodies and extra strong doors, locks, and windows, such as trucks for carrying money and valuables or automobiles specially designed for dignitaries.
A double-woven textile with a quilted appearance, utilizing a wadding weft to increase the relief.
Low-profile platforms on casters that allows a user to recline and slide under a vehicle to perform maintenance.
Bookbinding morocco, often levant, that has had its grain flattened before it has been attached to the book boards, then, after it is on the boards, polished very smooth.
Pile that is both cut and uncut, forming a pattern; produced by raising the pile warp threads over two wires, a cut and uncut pile wire.
Pile weave in which the pile is produced by a supplementary pile warp.
Wide, sharply pressed pleats, arranged in a row, evenly spaced and all turned in the same direction. For narrow pleats of a similar nature, use "knife pleats."

Heavy, two- or four-wheeled, horse-drawn freight carriers, generally without sides, having flat, level floors or loading beds, with or without springs; primarily for use by industry in and around cities; distinguished from horse-drawn trucks by having straight and level loading areas and rear wheels smaller than trucks so that they fall below the floor level to allow the hauling of large items.
Road vehicles licensed or registered to transport goods or materials, other than passengers, for gain or reward.

Loosely woven wool or cotton tabby, finished with a long nap to imitate felt and dyed in solid colors. Used as a protective covering for furnishings, as well as for costume, especially the lining of outerwear.
Any form of twill woven using more than one binding system.
Automobiles that are fully enclosed, as opposed to automobiles such as convertibles, that have open bodies.
Long, luxury automobiles distinguished by a larger than normal compartment for the passengers and typically a separate compartment for the driver.
Automobiles with tops that may be removed or folded open.
Automobiles used by police officers, usually equipped with radiotelephones for communication with headquarters.

A secondary warp that binds weft floats. In weft-faced compound woven textiles, the binding warp binds the weft. In woven textiles with more than one weft, the binding warp's primary function is to bind specifically the brocading weft or pattern weft, thus making a supplementary binding.

Textile fabric having a very long, soft pile, which may imitate fur, made of plant fiber or synthetic fiber. The textile may occur in any color, not necessarily resembling the coat of a mammal, and is typically used for fashion and interior decoration.
A discontinuous supplementary weft which does not travel from selvage to selvage, but rather is limited to the area where it is required by the pattern.
A type of weft-loop weave in which uncut pile is used sparsely for patterning, sometimes in contrasting colors. Popular in many countries, especially for bed coverings and similar items.
Weft pile weave with cut pile ribbed in the direction of the warp, usually made of cotton.
Fine, loosely twisted, two-ply, worsted yarn used in embroidering.

Firearm safety catches found on dog locks, consisting of small pivoted hooks located behind the cock which engage in a notch in the cock's heel to hold it at half cock, enabling the firearm to be safely carried ready-loaded and primed.
Refers to the initial act or instance of burning and for the chemical processes in which light or heat are produced by the vigorous union of various substances with oxygen.
Detachable trailers for hauling freight with wheels at the rear and with the front end normally supported on the rear of a truck tractor.
Equipment, accessories, and instruments used in air and space transportation, not including vehicles.
Land vehicles pulled by horses.

Large, sliding rondels that  protect the inside of the elbow,  the armpit, or another joint. They are usually round or oval, attached by straps, rivets, or laces to upper body armor such as pauldrons, spaudlers, and vambraces.

A pattern of crackle in paintings occurring after all layers have dried, often penetrating the ground as well, resulting from subtle movements in the support, such as from changes of temperature or humidity.
Totally enclosed boxlike freight cars, with floor, roof, sides, and ends, usually with large doors on the sides or sides and ends.
High-speed ground transportation vehicles traveling along guideways using superconducting devices of various configurations, generally with the aid of magnetic forces and linear induction.
Self-propelled, nonrevenue rail vehicles designed to convert electrical or mechanical energy into tractive effort to haul railway cars.
Locomotives used for shifting or switching railroad cars from one place to another in yards or terminals.
Locomotives in which power is developed by oil-burning internal combustion engines driving electric generators that supply power to electric traction motors for propulsion.
A term derived from the Nahuatl for a device used to amplify the propulsive force of spears or darts used in both hunting and warfare across the North American continent.
Banking machines capable of automatic processing of various transactions between depository institutions and customers; may be on or off the premises of the depository institution.
Weft patterning technique of weaving raised patterns on a woven textile. For the process of stitching decorative designs into cloth, leather, or paper by hand or machine, use "embroidering."
Tapestry weaving technique in which different color weft threads are turned alternately around a common end.
Hopper cars with a permanent roof, roof hatches, and bottom openings for unloading bulk commodities.

A unique Māori technique of twining; characterized by having two groups of threads – the aho (weft, or horizontal threads) and the whenu (warp, or vertical threads). The threads are usually made from muka (flax fibre). From a basic warp and weft base, the weaver builds a cloak, row by row, in a meticulous process that can take months or years to complete.
Transit railway vehicles used in an urban transit rail system.

Street railway cars drawn by horses, operating from the 1850s until the 1890s. For horse-drawn public street vehicles not operating on rails and generally accommodating fewer passengers than horsecars, use "omnibuses."

Electrically powered rail rapid transit vehicles with a control cab at one or both ends, two or more double doors on each side, and designed to operate singly or in multiple units and for fast boarding at high-level platforms.
The tubular hollow interiors of the barrels of firearms.

Sliding breechblocks incorporating a firing pin, cartridge case extractor, and one or more lugs to lock them into firing position, found in bolt action, automatic, and semiautomatic breechloading rifles, machine guns, and submachine guns with blowback action. They guide ammunition into the chamber and rotate to lock the breech mechanism.
Mechanisms for opening and closing the breech of a breech-loading firearm.
Movable metal blocks fitting into the breeches of firearms, serving to close and seal the breech opening of the barrel during firing.
Surveyors' measuring devices consisting of 1-inch-long steel links joined in a chain 100 feet long; succeeded surveyors' chains, but now obsolete.

Communication by means of a system that allows computer users to exchange messages in electronic format on a network, often but not always comprising messages from one individual to one or many others via telecommunications links between computers or terminals.
Timetables listing the arrival and departure schedules, routes, and names of the stops for a transportation service.
Use to describe firearms with two barrels, one above the other.
Flat beveled or triangular bars, usually of wood or plastic, with a variety of graduations so that scale drawings can be drawn and measured.

In archaeology, refers to deposit sites formed at the bottom of or along the shores of depressions in the earth that are filled with water, and that are smaller than an ocean or sea and ranging in size from just a few square meters to thousands of square kilometers.
X-ray scattering technique that characterizes solution structures of biological macromolecules and synthetic nanoparticles at a scale of about 1-2 nanometers.
Rules used to measure the distance from one base line of type to another and marked off in various units, usually point scales and picas.
Measuring devices, usually in the form of flat sticks, bearing various scales for computing board feet.
Woodworking rules graduated into eighths of an inch along one edge and sixteenths of an inch along the other edge and usually made of maple or hickory with brass tips; may also be metrically divided.

Portable containers of wood, horn, metal, leather, or ceramic used to hold the priming powder or gunpowder for firearms. They normally terminated in a metal nozzle which also served as a powder measure, closed by a plug or spring cap, and are often highly decorated. Prefer "powder horns" for those made from the horn of a cow or oxen.
Things conferred or bestowed as a reward for merit, including a prize, reward, honor, document, or remuneration.

The formation of biominerals by a living organism as in bone, teeth, and shell. In conservation context, the process may be induced through introduction of biomineralizing agents into deteriorating stone, an intervention known as "biomediated reinforcement."
The chemical analysis of materials by the separation of the constituents and their estimation by weight.
Light meters that convert measured data into readings that allow photographers to adjust lens apertures and shutter speeds on cameras.

Analysis and measurement of minute quantities of radioisotopes in materials, using a particle accelerator. It is used in fields such as archaeology, anthropology, toxicology, radiochemistry, and climatology for purposes such as dating, identifying, and describing materials.
Objects originally created as ornaments for hair, as implements for securing a hairstyle, or as artificial substitutes for hair.
Pointers that indicate the hours on clocks or watches.
Shoes designed to be worn for optimal play in the sport of basketball. These often reach over the ankle to provide additional support.
Small round boxes that store detachable collars for men's shirts.
Pieces of luggage; usually rectangular, rigid, and flat; especially for carrying clothes while traveling.
Priming powder, especially for firearms ammunition, derived from fulminic acid.
Concave or convex mirrors designed to start fires by focusing rays of sunlight.
Mirrors contained in frames that have strong architectural features, often including side columns and pediments.
Specially designed ropes with handles at the ends used for exercise or in games.
The practice of identifying and describing terrestrial objects pictured in aerial photographs.

Method for capturing 3D data of large areas using an airborne laser illuminating device to scan successive narrow strips of the ground, producing a picture of the terrain over which an aircraft is flying.
Objects designed as a set and used in Christian baptism, including vessels for the sacred oil and holy water, among other possible items. Baptism sets may be portable.

Technologies, processes or measures implemented to protect computers, networks, and data from unauthorized access, vulnerabilities and attacks administered via the Internet or in other ways. Cybersecurity is most commonly intended to protect against viruses or fraud.
Single-use bulbs that give a single bright burst of light, triggered by a camera, and synched to the shutter.

An alternative to ethyl silicate surface treatments for consolidation of stone which involves sealing the object or architectural element, dehumidifying it, evacuating the air from around the object, and introducing the agent, which then permeates the stone surface in a vacuum.
Refers to use of an ultrasonic humidifier to apply extremely small, finely controlled, amounts of dilute solutions to a material. In conservation this is typically an art object or artifact.

Microfadeometry is a recently developed technique that measures color changes and evaluates light stability in individual objects of art that are sensitive to light exposure. A microfade tester (MFT) uses a powerful xenon arc lamp and filters to focus a beam of very intense light through a fiber optic onto a tiny spot on the surface of the artwork.  A second fiber optic collects the reflected light and delivers it to a miniature spectrometer.  As the lamp fades the surface of the artwork, the resulting color change is monitored by the spectrometer.
Portable or transportable weapons that can discharge long burning streams of liquid or semiliquid fuel under pressure.

A barrier layer, or coating, is a reversible bond applied as a film between an irreversible adhesive and the surface it is mated to. In paper conservation, for example, a barrier layer is a thin film, such as gelatin or methylcellulose, deposited between the original paper surface and inpainting media applied to compensate for loss or damage. Such barrier layers allow for reversibility of the inpainting treatments.
The properties of sound, especially the sound properties of built environments, materials, and sound devices, such as reverberation and absorbency.
Use to describe things pertaining to anodes, especially phenomena taking place in the vicinity of anodes or materials formed by such phenomena.
The degree of heat as measured on a relative scale.
Generally used for any type of quilted soft armor.
Use to describe materials having no stratification or crystalline structure, or, more generally, things having no pattern or structure.
The quantity of two-dimensional space that is contained within given limits. Area is typically measured in square units, for example square meters or  square miles.
Coat armors of cloth or leather having metal plates riveted on the inside, widely used in 14th-century Europe.
Groups of 64 yōginī figures, that from around the 10th century, appear in open-air temples dedicated to them.
Use to describe things constructed in vault form or things covered or closed by a vault.

A measure of digital resolution as determined by the number of bits used to render each pixel or sample. Higher bit depths indicate a higher tonal range or fidelity. Bit depth for color defines the amount of color available to each of the pixels in digital image processing and display. This is derived from the number of bits used to define color within a digital image as determined by its file format. Audio bit depth is defined by the amount of bits in a sample in digital audio, which directly corresponds to the resolution of the sample and the dynamic range of the resulting sound produced or recorded.
Calculating devices of the slide rule type, but having a circular rather than straight form; they comprise disks that form circular scales located in one plane.
Baking dishes, sometimes having a cover, in which food may be baked and served.
Pans, often metal, intended primarily for baking bread; made in varying size and form.
Spoons having a broad deep bowl, sometimes silver gilt and may be pierced or embossed with fruit motifs; used to serve berries and other juicy foods. Often made by altering plain tablespoons.
Surveys which assess the condition of a set of historic buildings and prioritize preservation and repair.
Broad, flat forks with four or five tines used to serve hot or cold asparagus.

Ahtlatl of turquoise (in mosaic or color) in posclassic central Mexico. Also known as a xiuhcoatl. This device used to amplify the propulsive force of spears or darts, in hunting as in warfare, is associated mainly with Xiuhteuctli, but also with Huitzilopochtli and Tezcatlipoca.
Toy banks in which a coin is deposited by a mechanical process that is usually activated by pushing a lever.

Firearms in which, after initial manual or mechanical loading, the process of firing, extraction, ejection, and reloading continues without intermission as long as the trigger is pressed and the supply of ammunition lasts. To describe firearms which reload automatically after firing but require a squeeze of the trigger for each shot, use "semiautomatic."
Parts and components of arrows.

“Green” surfactant obtained by the dehydration reaction between glucose hemiacetal hydroxyl and fatty alcohol hydroxyl in the presence of acid catalyst. Its raw materials are the vegetable oil and starch which are the natural renewable resource and low cost, and its biodegradability is very excellent.

Small decorative cases for carrying visiting cards, which were small cards bearing the name, and sometimes the address of a person or married couple for presentation; prime examples date from 19th-century western nations.

Small, miniturized, or compact sets of items intended to allow the convenient transport and distribution of the Christian communion to the sick, dying, battlefield, or others outside the church building.

A game played on a court, typically indoor over a net with rackets and a shuttlecock. It is a combination of the children's game of battledore and shuttlecock. It is believed that the modern game was developed by British army officers in India, and was so name after a version of the game was played at Badminton House in 1873 by officers on leave, although there is no evidence of this. Versions of the game, however, were popular among the British in India by 1873.
The frequency, intensity, and distribution of earthquakes in a given area.
Use to describe materials, solutions, or treatments that involve water.

The state or characteristic of having a high degree of distinctness in an image. Examples are images achieved through the spacing of individual optical elements, such as grains of light-sensitive chemicals in a photograph or pixels in an electronic image.
Keyboard instruments combining a harpsichord with an organ.
Structural sheet of iron, usually galvanized for weather resistance, shaped in alternating ridges and grooves; used as roofing, siding, and the like.
Very abbreviated two-piece bathing suits with the bottom half cut below the waist.
Frames with carved moldings and decorations of small mirrors and flowers interrupted by plain areas, named after the 18th-century Venetian painter Giovanni Antonio Canaletto.

Uniform frames selected by an owner so that all the works of art in the owner's collection might be framed alike. Such frames identified ownership and status and for this reason frequently changed, sometimes every generation, to keep up with fashionable styles and taste.
Frames designed by artists, usually for specific works they have done.
Region of space subjected to the influence of magnetism typically due to magnets, current-carrying conductors, and electromagnetic waves.
Moldings, often of metal, wood or fabric covered wood that are placed between the frame and painting when the painting has shrunk from the frame or the frame is slightly larger than the painting.
The flipping back and forth between two spin directions of electrons in a magnetic field when electromagnetic radiation of the proper frequency is applied.
Frames that sit upon the altar during mass, containing the words for parts of the mass; used to aid the priest during recitations.
Refers to the condition of being impervious to air penetration, or nearly so.
Act of leaving something immersed in a liquid for an extended period of time so as to saturate it.
The act of purification, clarification, or distillation of a substance or product, by a series of industrial processes. Examples may include the processing of sugar, crude oil, or metals.
The technique of reinforcing with a framework, for example in painting conservation to reinforce wooden panels, or in architecture to support an arched or coved ceiling.
Process of comparing photometrically the relative intensities of light absorbed, reflected, or emitted by a microscopic specimen in different parts of a spectrum.
Gas chromatography technique using an open tubular column to convey the gaseous sample. Adsorption occurs on a medium spread on the walls of the capillary tube.
Wall mirrors having hooks for hanging hats and other small items.
Frames which incorporate architectural features.
Ambient sound makers with strings, usually tuned in unison, which are sounded by the natural wind blowing across them.
Handheld megaphones that contain combined microphones and loudspeakers.
Curved Roman brass aerophones of conical bore, their range limted to a few notes of the natural scale and filling primarily a signalling function.
End-blown trumpets of Tibet, made from a conch shell usually fitted with a metal mouthpiece and bell, commonly played in pairs during Buddhist rituals.
Clearing snow from areas where it is not wanted.

Surface elemental analysis technique widely used for identification and characterization of pigments in conservation science. It is an x-ray fluorescence technique in which an incident beam strikes a sample below the critical angle of external total reflection for X-rays resulting in nearly total reflection of the excitation beam photons.

Reedpipes of ancient Greece, consisting of two separate slender cylindrical pipes of wood or metal each with a reed, single or double; the pipes were held at a divergent angle and both reeds held in the mouth together.
Zitherlike chordophones with a stick string bearer and a gourd resonator of the Malagasy Republic. Formerly played by male slaves, they are now made for tourist sale.
Treatment of objects under elevated temperature and nitrogen atmosphere by high energy electrons for various purposes including cross-linking of polymers and sterilization.

European zitherlike chordophones consisting of a heavy gut string attached at each end to a long wooden pole and passing over an inflated pig's bladder which serves as a resonator. They are sounded with a notched stick or horsehair bow, to provide a droning accompaniment to folksong or dance.

Folk instruments from the Appalachian region of the United States, usually consisting of a long figure-eight shaped box, a fretted fingerboard set centrally along its entire length, and from three to five metal strings tensioned by lateral pegs. For the American chordophones of similar construction, but struck with hammers instead of plucked, use "hammer dulcimers."

Manuscripts distinguished by having a support formed of a long strip created by feathering together individual deer hides or pieces of maguey (agave) or bark (amate) paper to form a smooth continuous surface and coated with a white gesso. The strip is folded back and forth to create individual pages on which the figures and symbols are painted. In prime examples, made by Pre-Columbian American cultures

Distinctive clothing worn by clerics and members of religious orders; the term often refers primarily to Christian religious orders, but it may apply to habits used by any religious group. For the ceremonial garments worn of priests and others officiating at religious rituals, use "vestments."

Dress suits for men, worn at formal dinners, evening weddings, dances, receptions, and other ceremonial events.These consist of a dress coat with tails, a waistcoat, a starched shirt with upstanding collar, a bow tie and a black pair of pants with the outer seam trimmed with satiny material. As a dress code, also referred to as 'white tie' or 'cravate blanche', in contrast with 'black tie'.

Feathery edge at the border of a sheet of hand- or mold-made paper, caused by the deckle or frame which confines the pulp to the mold; also on some machine-made papers, caused by the rubber deckle straps at the sides of the paper machine, or made by artificial means.

Long formal trains, made of luxurious materials that were compulsory wear for women at royal court from the beginning of the 19th century. Worn with a court dresses, these may be attached from the waist, or with straps around the shoulders, or both. The decoration of court trains was controlled by protocol according to the station of the wearer.
Mechanisms by means of which the strings or pipes of a keyboard instrument are sounded when a key is depressed, or, in harps, that alter the pitch of strings when a pedal is depressed.
In piano actions, a hammer is a slender wooden shank with a padded wooden head that strikes the strings when the corresponding key is pressed down.
The science dealing with crystallization and the form and structure of crystals.
Broad class of coating applied specifically for decorative purposes.
A photographic coating composed of layers of gelatin and tannic acid introduced by Louis-Désiré Blanquart-Évrard in 1857 to resolve the problem of image impermanence.
Refers to members of the most commonly used group of non-aqueous liquid solvents, organic compounds that contain carbon atoms.

In Indian culture, literally "Eight Auspicious Symbols," endemic to a number of Dharmic Traditions, which may vary slightly. Examples are in Sanatana Dharma, Jaina Dharma, Buddhadharma, and Sikha Dharma.

Refers most often to characteristics of individual objects, items, or entities, mostly expressions used to describe the thing. Often readily apparent though not quantifiable by an established standard.
State of partial undress in which the individual is without shoes or other foot coverings, in a circumstance where shoes may be expected.
Technique in microanalytical chemistry in which a finely focused electron beam is used to excite an x-ray spectrum.

A technique for observing the temperature, direction, and magnitude of thermally induced transitions in a material by heating or cooling a sample and comparing its temperature with that of an inert reference material under similar conditions.

Printed pieces such as notices or advertisements, usually in the form of single sheets or leaflets, intended for wide distribution to the general public. For similar pieces intended for distribution by hand and often doubling as posters, use "handbills."

Armors designed as costumes, rather than having a significant protective function. Prime examples were designed for pageants in pseudoclassical dress, which were popular in Europe, 15th through 18th centuries.

Double pieces of plate armor for the pauldron, worn to reinforce the lower three-quarters of the front of the pauldron and attached to it by pins, pegs, or rivets; first appeared in the early 15th century.
Miquelet locks in which the external mainspring operates on the cock by pressing downwards on its heel.

Application of electron diffraction in the backscattering mode as used in analysis of crystallographic structure of textured materials that show a preferred orientation of crystalline components. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) is based on the measurement of the diffraction pattern formed by the electrons backscattered toward a phosphor screen positioned at an angle from the sample surface.
