The visible lines generated by the impinging electrons are called Kikuchi bands; thus the technique is also known as backscatter Kikuchi diffraction (BKD).
The activity of using a scanning electron microscope, which is designed for directly studying the surfaces of solid objects, utilizing a beam of focused electrons of relatively low energy.

Form of scanning electron microscopy that provides electron imaging at a relatively high degree of sample pressure. It allows the option of capturing photomicrographs of wet or uncoated specimens by offering a gaseous environment within the specimen chamber.

A set of care guidelines or techniques used to minimize and prevent damage to collections due to pests. IPM encompasses aspects in a cultural institution's setting and encourages a less chemical-based approach.

Mechanisms on breechloading firearms featuring a manually operated cylindrical bolt with an external lever which the shooter pulls back to open the breech and extract the empty case of a fired cartridge and pushes forward to push a fresh cartridge into firing position and close the breech.

In firearms, metal tubes closed at one end that hold the projectile and the propellant charge and, utilizing the explosive force of the charge, act as the path for the projectile. They may be smoothbore or rifled.
Containers for cream and other liquids in the form of a cow, with an opening in the back for filling, a spout in the form of a mouth, and a curved tail as a handle.

Containers with a tight-fitting lid, and often an insert with separate wells, used to poach eggs. Also, various contrivances used to poach eggs, often consisting of a stand, with a long vertical handle and a number of smaller containers, meant to be placed in a pan or skillet of water. For vessels used coddling eggs, use "egg coddlers."
Woven Persian salt bags.
Use to describe things having the structure or appearance of a honeycomb.
A colorless gas used commerically as a fumigant and disinfectant.
Combination weapons consisting of a small arm combined with either a different weapon or with some tool or article of everyday use, such as a walking stick.
The property by which a material is able to take up a liquid or a gas by capillary, osmotic, solvent, chemical, or other means.
Large, deep wall bags, used primairly in tents, suspended from the trellis structure.  The fronts are pile woven and the backs done in a weft-faced plain weave.

Large bags of leather or fabric hung from one side of a saddle or laid over the back of the horse, mule, or donkey behind the saddle and commonly one of a pair united by a band or strap. Also, similar bags hung on each side of the rear wheel of a bicycle, motorcycle, or the like.
Walking sticks, especially those with a curved handle and made of cane or bamboo.
Clothing intended for wear at the beach, possibly but not necessarily intended for sports. Beachwear could include bathing suits, coverups, sun hats, flip flops, and other items.
Dresses which hang straight from the shoulders, sometimes tapering slightly at hips.
Garments worn by wedding participants invited by the bride, generally consisting of a bodice and skirt.

Long staffs often having a pointed lower tip and topped by a knob or hook onto which was attached a gourd (pilgrim's gourd), a cloth tied into a sack, or other item. Used as an aid walking on pilgrimages; some were decorated with religious inscriptions and images.
Shorts popular in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Often made of luxurious fabrics, such as leather or suede, and sometimes made with straps or a bib.
Beachwear for bathing, dating from the 19th century to present.
Small, long-tined forks designed to pierce a strawberry, dip it into sugar or cream, and place it into one's mouth.

Sensitivity to blue and green light, but not to red: usually designates black-and-white negative photographic materials that are low in red and high in blue light sensitivity. 'Panchromatic' designates sensitivity that is more equal between the red, blue, and green parts of the spectrum.

Dolls that are typically used for play by boys rather than girls, or as collectibles for adult males, characterized by being representations of comic book characters, military people, sports figures, movie or television characters, or other characters who take part in heroic or adventurous activities. The figures are usually male, although they may occasionally be female. They often have unnatural, overdeveloped musculature; they may have movable joints that allow the characters to hold various weapons or strike various poses. The term was coined by Hasbro corporation in 1964 to market  a "G.I. Joe" military-themed doll to boys. The legal case "Toy Biz v. United States" determined that for purposes of tariffs, action figures produced by Toy Biz/Marvel Comics were toys, not dolls, because they represent "nonhuman creatures."
Stoles used for the Christian sacrament of confession, purple in color; may be shorter and narrower than stoles that are used with the chasuble and intended for masses, funerals, and other rituals.
Gun mounts featuring a block made of two rigidly joined triangular or trapezoidal side panels, supporting the trunnions on which the gun barrel rests.
Toys designed to be pulled along the ground.
Russian plucked lutelike chordophones consisting of a triangular body with a flat back and slightly arched belly, a long neck with frets, and three strings; it is made in six different sizes.
Pear-shaped, short-necked Japanese lutelike chordophones made of wood, commonly with four strings and a pegbox sharply angled back from the neck.
Balloons anchored to the ground and grouped as protective screens to prevent or hinder operations by enemy aircraft.
Fixed-wing airplanes that perform observation and collection of data such as measurements, photography, etc., usually in the context of military intelligence.
Specially designed unmanned spacecraft intended to maintain an orbit around a celestial body. For unmanned spacecraft designed for nonorbital missions, use "space probes."
Vehicles capable of flight both within and outside the sensible atmosphere.
Lines that secure aircraft to a mooring point while on the ground in the event of wind or other weather conditions that could threaten the aircraft's stability.
Boosters used to launch spacecraft into orbit or into space.
Light aircraft used for business, usually seating fewer than ten passengers.

Long guns used in England in the late 16th century for military purposes, as they can be fired without rest. They were a newer form of the harquebus, but were not used after the Civil War. They were generally sized larger than the harquebus and smaller than the musket.

Use only for puzzles consisting of maps mounted on pasteboard or wood and cut out into irregularly shaped pieces to be reassembled as an educational exercise; invented in the mid-18th century and popular through the early 19th century, especially in England and the United States.
Mechanical puzzles consisting of plane or solid figures cut into various shapes, the goal of which is to reassemble the pieces into a prespecified form; known since the 3rd century BCE in Greece.
Solid geometric puzzles composed of interlocking notched rods of wood or plastic whose final assembled form is highly symmetrical.
Black-faced grotesquely dressed male dolls with a shock of fuzzy hair, usually featuring pop eyes and a large red mouth; based on a character in children's books of the 1890s.

Handles, usually of leather though very rarely of wood, riveted to the back of a shield and used to hold it. Commonly each shield has two, a fixed loop held with the hand, and an adjustable strap buckled around the arm.
Acts that engage with cognitive processes.
Artillery having its rifling in the barrel and is loaded from the breech at the rear of the gun.
Artillery designed to fire at enemy aircraft in flight.
Artillery specially designed for defending coastal areas.
Guns that operate using the propulsive power of compressed air.

Projectiles generally consisting of a straight, slender shaft with a sharp point or carrying a sharp edged or pointed head of stone or metal, shot from a bow. More developed versions also have flights near the butt to stabilize their trajectory.
Shooting arrows with a bow, as for hunting, battle, or sport.
A gambling game of cards played by a banker and 2 or more punters or players who bet against the banker.

Variation of baccarat played by up to 12 players in which two hands are dealt and the winning hand is the one that comes closer to but does not exceed a count of nine on two or three cards. The name refers to the French railroad and is so called for its speed.

Dice game, played on a special table and layout, where all bets are made against the house. A player signifies his bet by placing chips or cash on the appropriate part of the layout before all rolls, and it is required that the dice be thrown in such a way that they strike a wall of the table and bounce back. In a version known as bank craps, the player or shooter, throwing the dice, or anyone wishing to bet that the shooter will win, places his bet "on the line," in the areas marked "Pass," "Come," or "Win." Anyone betting against the shooter, places his bet in the areas marked "Don't Pass" or "Don't Come." The shooter is said to win if he throws seven or eleven on his first throw and lose if he instead throws two, three, or twelve (craps). Bets are then paid off. If the shooter's first throw is four, five, six, eight, nine, or ten, that number is his point, and he continues to throw until he rolls the same number again and wins or throws seven (misses out, or craps out.

A game played with rectangular pieces or tiles, usually 28, having various numbers of pips marked on the pieces; players position ends of tiles having the corresponding number of pips in contact with each other as long as this can be done; the player who has the lowest number of pips on his or her remaining tiles is the winner.

Game, probably of English origin, played with billiard cues and nine balls on an oblong board or table varying in size from 6 by 1.5 feet to 10 by 3 feet with nine numbered cups at its head, eight arranged in a circle and the ninth in its center. Of the nine balls used, one is black, four are red, and four are white. The black ball is placed upon a spot about 9 inches in front of hole number one. A line called the balk, is drawn across the board, from behind which any number of players shoot. Each player plays all eight balls up the table, with no until a ball has touched the black ball. The object of the game is to play as many balls as possible into the holes, the black ball counting double. The game is decided by the combined score made in an agreed number of rounds.

General term for a group of games that are played on a rectangular table with a designated number of small balls and a long stick called a cue. The table typically has a cushioned railing and is topped with a felt-like covering.

Game that developed in the 19th century as a game of skill, using a cue ball for each player and a red striker ball. The object of the game is to use your cue ball to push the striker ball into your opponent’s cue ball. A billiards table does not have pockets.
Athletic games played on a court with a ball.

Game of ball between two nine-player teams usually played for nine innings on a diamond-shaped field with an infield, home plate, and three other bases 90 feet apart. This forms a circuit that must be completed by a base runner in order to score against the central offensive action, being the hitting of pitched balls with a wooden or metal bat, the winner being the team that scores the most runs.

The action or practice of ascending in balloons, which are flexible spherical bags made of a lightweight material inflated with heated air or a gas that is lighter than air. It is both a recreational activity and competitive sport.

Game played on a lawn, in which wooden balls are driven by means of wooden mallets through wickets or 'hoops' fixed in the ground in a particular order. The object is for a player to put the ball through as many wickets as possible before turning play over to the opponent.
A game derived from the sport of golf, where golf balls are hit with clubs over a novelty putting course, typically set with colorful and whimsical hazards.

Bowling game played on a standard tenpin lane but with slender, cylindrical pins about 15 inches tall and tapered at both ends. The ball is 4.5 inches in diameter and weighing 2 pounds, 7 ounces. Three balls are bowled in a frame but knocked down pins are not removed until the frame is completed.
Bowling game mostly popular in the United Kingdom and Canada that is played on an indoor carpeted rink.

French ball game played between two players or teams, who take turns throwing or rolling a ball or boule, usually made of steel, as close as possible to the target ball, called the jack, or cochonnet. If necessary, the player will use his ball to knock the opponent's ball away.

Game similar to lawn bowls, but played on ice, and consisting of two teams of four players, the lead, second, third, and skip. Each player slides a round stone, concave on the bottom and with a handle on the top, across a natural field or rink of ice toward the tee, or button, which is a fixed mark in the center of a circle, called the house, marked with concentric bands. The object of the game is for each side to get its stones closest to the center. A distinctive element of curling is the use of a brush, or broom, to clear the ice of debris in front of the sliding stone. The broom also provides balance for the curler during delivery of the stone and by the skip to direct aim.

Sport that evolved during the late 19th and early 20th centuries in the mountainous terrain of the Alps in central Europe. Modern Alpine skiing is competitive, divided into speed events (downhill skiing and the supergiant slalom, or super-G) and technical events (slalom and giant slalom).

Sport in which ice skaters, singly or in pairs, perform graceful movements of jumps, spins, and lifts. The name is derived from the patterns or figures skaters make on the ice, a required part of the sport until recently. There are various kinds of figure skating, including freestyle, pairs, and ice dancing. Rules of competition, as well as the moves and techniques of the skaters, vary for each category of skating.

Recreational activity comprising traveling by skis in open country over rolling, hilly terrain as distinguished from traveling downhill on skis. The activity developed in Scandinavian countries as a means of travel as well as recreation. Cross-country skiing differs from downhill skiing in that the skis are longer, narrower, and lighter, the bindings allow movement between the heel of the skier's boot and the ski, and the ski poles are longer than those used in Alpine skiing.
The ensembles of balls, mallets, and wickets needed to play the game of croquet.

An soft, whitish, absorbent powder derived from the siliceous skeletons of microscopic water plants called diatoms, composed of 88% silica. It is used as a poultice, a desiccating insecticide, a decolorizer and filtration aid for purifying oils, fats, and waxes, an inert pigment, a filler in paper, paint, brick, floor tiles, ceramics, linoleum, plastic, soap, and detergent, an insulation for boilers and blast furnaces, as sound insulation, and as a very mild abrasive in metal polishes and toothpaste. It reduces gloss, acts as a suspending agent, increases viscosity, and absorbs dyes well, thus is used as a base for lake colors.

Figural toys made in the likeness of specific real persons or animals or human, humanoid, or animal fictional characters; use "character dolls" for the narrower category of figurines representing only specific real people or human or humanoid fictional characters.
Firearms, usually shotguns, used in skeet shooting; normally autoloaders with more weight toward the front end of the gun than in field guns.

Rifles specially designed for particular target shooting matches in which artificial supports were not used, originating in Germany in the 15th century and popular in the United States from the early 19th century until the First World War. They are characterized by long, heavy octagonal barrels, often with extra weight at the muzzle, palm rests, double set triggers, thick stocks, and very high quality, accurate sights.
Any of various natural polymers; long chained macromolecules occurring as DNA, protein, cellulose, etc.

Boxlike devices containing a lamp, reflectors to concentrate the light, and, usually, lenses to reduce or expand the light designed to project images painted on glass transparencies slowly drawn across the lens; first developed in the mid-17th century.
The proportion of pure precious metal in an alloy.
A basic defect in glass caused by an imperfect proportion of ingredients, particularly an excess of alkali, and consisting of a fine network of cracks and the formation of moisture on the surface.

Māori kites, having wooden or rush frames, and covered with bark, leaves, or other material; thought to have been used for recreation, for divination, for communication, and in celebration of the Maori new year.
Morphology on an extremely minute scale.

Paddles made from laminated wood covered with rubber on one or two sides. The official Internation Table Tennis Federation term is "racket," but in the the US "paddle" is generally preferred. In European and Asian countries, "bat" may be used. There is no regulation size or shape.

Use both for groups of merchant or naval auxilliary ships traveling under armed escort and for groups of motor vehicles organized for the purpose of control and orderly movement, with or without escort protection.
Vehicles for transporting people or objects above the land, either in the atmosphere of the earth or above the atmosphere and in outer space.
Watercraft generally smaller and less seaworthy than ships and generally not designed to cross large open waters.
Refers to the slightly undulating wooden surface finished with an adze, a type of axe with the blade set at right angles to the handle.
Microscopic traces of wear on artifacts; used especially in reference to archaeology.
Chaises of the lightest construction capable of rapid speed; rarely with tops, frequently without dashboards.

Large, covered freight wagons distinguished by their curving boat-shaped profile with flaring endgates and side panels of planking with a series of short uprights; usually pulled by six horses and used between the mid-18th and mid-19th century in the areas of Ohio, Virginia, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. For similar wagons but characterized by mostly straight lines and linen tops and used across the western prairies and plains to carry freight and emigrants, use "prairie schooners."
Two-wheeled freight vehicles pulled by a person or by a pack animal, intended for the transport of beer barrels or beer crates.
Two-wheeled vehicles drawn by an ox or oxen.
Fenders comprising wooden beams, cables, inflatable rubber, or another material that are hung along the outside of a boat or ship to protect against damage when docking.
The action of sprinkling a liquid (water or blood) on objects or people as part of a ritual in postclassic central Mexico.

Heavily armed and well-manned merchant ships of the Dutch East India Company, or Verenigde Oostindische Compagnia, VOC. These were specifically designed for the long roundtrip, or 'retour,' voyage from the Netherlands to the East Indies. These vessels were also repeatedly used as warships.
Handcarts propelled mainly by pulling the vehicle by hand. These appear as two- or four-wheeled vehicles often with a cross-handled beam to pull from.

Microbially mediated stabilization of degraded or weakened areas of works, usually of stone, that are affected by chemical, physical, or biological weathering phenomena. In situ cementation of ornamental materials occurs via microbially induced biomineralization. Bioconsolidation may occur naturally on surfaces where microorganisms aid in the formation of cementing phases such as oxalates and carbonates, and biofilms.
Gaff-rigged, stern-steering iceboats usually with long booms and gaffs; developed between the 1860s and the 1880s for racing on the Hudson River.

Automobile-drawn, wheeled recreational vehicles providing a temporary dwelling or shelter while camping outdoors, often incorporating a folding shelter of canvas or other fabric. Distinguished from "motor homes," which are larger.
Cation-exchange capacity (CEC) is defined as the quantity of nutrient cations a soil can adsorb and exchange.

The measure of unsaturated fatty acid in a fat, oil, or wax obtained by counting the number of grams of iodine absorbed by 100 grams of the material. The more saturated the substance, the smaller the iodine number will be. Relatively unsaturated oils, waxes, fats will have a higher iodine value.
Manned spacecraft consisting generally of a reusable orbiter that touches down on a landing strip after each mission, reusable boosters, and an expendable fuel tank.
Oxidation caused by the atmosphere or self-catalyzed and spontaneous.
A method of removing or reducing the acid content, usually of paper, that uses water as the solvent carrier of the alkaline.

Creation of graft copolymers, a special type of branched copolymers in which long chains have occasional branches comprising repeat units different from those of the main chain. Such copolymers are created for a variety of diverse applications including enhanced tensile strength, controlled wettability, better pigment dispersion, and enhanced thermal stability.
The decomposition of a molecule with the addition of the elements of an acid to that molecule.
Any of the techniques of chemical ionization which takes place at atmospheric pressure used to evaporate solvent and ionize the compounds injected for mass spectrometry.
The phenomenon whereby electron waves scattered by the regularly spaced atoms of a substance produce diffraction patterns characteristic of that substance.
Aircraft that are supported by giving the surrounding air a momentum in the downward direction equal to the weight of the aircraft.
Aircraft, usually light aircraft, used for private business, sports, or recreation.

Vehicles that are supported and propelled by a cushion of air ejected downwards against a surface close below it, and that may travel over any relatively smooth surface such as a body of water or flat land without direct contact.

Military aircraft designed to be used primarily against surface targets and equipped to carry and drop bombs, generally characterized by long range, low maneuverability, and large weapon-carrying capacity.
Aircraft with unpowered horizontally placed rotors which provide lift, akin to those on helicopters, and conventional engine-driven propellers that pull the vehicles forward, as on airplanes.
Announcements paid for by an advertiser and broadcast on radio or television.  For other public notices or paid announcements, especially those in print, use "advertisements."
Shortened forms of words, names, or phrases that are not words themselves but stand for the original; often created by the omission of letters or the replacement of several letters by a symbol.

An image sharpening technique introduced in Germany in the 1930s that increases the perceived acutance of photographic images. This is achieved through the use of an intermediate positive that is slightly blurred coupled with the original negative. When light is projected through the in-register negative and positive, some information is cancelled from the negative. The original photomechanical process has been reproduced in digital image processing to achieve a similar effect.
Books containing benedictions, which are solemn invocations of blessedness officially pronounced by an ecclesiastical functionary; often for liturgical use, especially by bishops.
Collections of choice extracts, from the writings of one author, or various authors, and usually having a common characteristic such as subject matter or literary form.

Books with blank pages used for assembling and presenting a collection, or any unpublished sets of pages that are bound or loose-leaf and have other materials affixed to them or writing or other images made on them. The volume may have been constructed with blank pages that were intended to have materials affixed, or it may have been assembled after having had materials affixed to separate pages.
Cards that contain manually or mechanically recorded data; used historically with information processing.

Mass communication materials or means that call public attention to a product, service, or event and to elicit a specific response, particularly to acquire, use, or participate in the product, service, or event that is being advertised.
Illustrations, diagrams, etc. that are printed along with the text of a book for the purpose of clarifying or illustrating the text of a book.
Tanning hides or skins with chromium salts or chromic acid, used chiefly to produce light leathers.
Loose-fitting underpants for men, having short, trouserlike legs rather then leg openings.
Cords, narrow bands, or the like worn at the waist, especially those worn as an ecclesiastical vestment.
Decorative items, usually composed of flowers that are meant to be affixed to the wrist.

Refers to the various types or classifications of documents, which are typically physical or digital representations of a body of information that is designed with the capacity to communicate. For the broad meaning of documents as a separate concept in itself, use "documents."
Devices that distribute individual cups to users from a stored stock of cups.
Costume accessory worn around the head, comprising a wreath of leaves, or resembling a wreath of leaves but made from other materials, such as gold.

Refers to pharmaceutical ceramics or glass that typically take the form of medium-sized jars, often cylindrical with short necks and glass stoppers although other shapes and sizes are found. Drug jars are made to hold medicine, spices, herbs, pigments, or other ointments, powders, and liquids. The term can sometimes refer specifically to sets of four or more jars originally sold to an apothecary and labeled with the name of a standard medicine.
Large low narrow containers for supplying water to livestock.
Artworks combining oil painting with mother-of-pearl inlay. These are particular to colonial Latin America and may have been influenced by goods imported from Asia.

Method of rock fragmentation which employs pulsed power in short, high power bursts of electrical energy to create high internal tensile stresses which fracture materials along grain boundaries. Electric pulse disaggregation (EPD) is an efficient method for separating a rock's constituents with applications that include separation of single crystals for isotopic measurement, and fossil preparation.
Textile coverings for communion vessels, used in the Orthodox Eastern Church.
Large textile coverings used by the Orthodox Eastern Church to cover both chalice and paten together.
Cover in the liturgical colour of the day that completely covers the Missal stand.
Mechanical devices for igniting the propellant charge in firearms.
The striking arms holding the gunflint in flintlocks, snaphances, and miquelet locks.
Melody pipes on bagpipes; they may be of conical or cylindrical bore and be fitted with either a single or a double reed.
Pipes that are constituent parts of other aerophones, have no fingerholes, and are used to sustain single notes. For Australian aboriginal instruments use "didjeridus."
Padded coverings for food or for containers containing food, used to retain heat.

Xylophones of the Manding people of West Africa, having wood keys thinned on the ends and undersides for tuning and with a gourd resonator beneath each; they are played exclusively by male professional musicians, using a rubber-tipped hammer in each hand and often with bells strapped to their wrists.
Special ceremonial cloths, often decoratively woven or embroidered, used to wrap funerary bundles of the indigenous cultures of Mexico, Central and South America.
Turkish woven squares used for wrapping or sewn into baglike containers with one side left unsewn, to be folded like an envelope.
Palls, usually of black, purple, or white velvet, used during the funeral ceremony to cover the coffin, hearse, or tomb. May be decorated with commemorative inscriptions or funerary portraits.
Cloth coverings for altars often with decorative edgings and individual embroidered motifs.
All upholstery components under the final top covers, including stuffing, springs, and other component parts.
Layer of coarsely woven, heavyweight textile used in upholstery, fixed over webbing to form a seat cavity and to keep the stuffing from falling through.
Photographs or other images that are converted to digital form through scanning or another mechanism.
Iranian darabukkas, often carved from a single block of wood and decorated with an inlay design, constituting the principal percussion instrument in classical Iranian music.
Small brass or copper pots with long handles, used to make coffee.
Small coupes.

Small, wooden vessels shaped like buckets but which have one extended stave to serve as a handle. Also glass, silver, or other dishes of this form, especially those used for butter, sugar, milk, or cream.
Small trunks designed to be kept at the foot of a bed, especially to contain a soldier's personal effects.
Traveling bags, especially ones made of or simulating carpeting; of a type and style popular in the 19th century.
Small containers often ornamental or mechanical for holding coins.
Money purses, may be made out of a mongoose's skin or having a weasel's head. In Indian iconography, may be held by Kubēra.
Coaches hung on berlin undercarriages, employing two light perches instead of a single heavy one to connect the front transom with the rear axle.
Four-wheeled carriages generally characterized by high outside seats for the driver, passenger seats with either folding or fixed tops, and coachlike lower quarters and undercarriage.
European two-wheeled carriages pulled by a single horse and having bodies resembling nautilus shells.
Gigs without tops, devised in the early 19th century; distinguished from "tilburies" by their suspension and the addition of extra luggage space under the seat.
Sleighs originally designed by James Gould of Albany, New York, and generally characterized by sweeping lines and rounded, or swelled, bodies; often with colorfully decorated panels.
Large wagons, often built high for visibility, and sometimes ornate, that are capable of carrying a band of musicians in a procession, such as in a circus parade.

Silver or gold boxes or caskets, usually rectangular in form but sometimes circular or oval, which are given to a person granted the freedom of, for example, a city, town, or college. Usually engraved, chased, or enameled with the coat of arms of the recipient and donor, and often an appropriate inscription.
Small versions of refrigerators, containers which maintain cool temperatures to preserve food, designed to be portable.
Refrigeration units that have a vertical orientation for a tall storage space, sometimes with shelves for organization.
Insulated box-like chests designed to contain ice and used to cool and preserve food or other perishable items.

Riding habits for women, in fashion from the early 18th century, used specifically for riding sidesaddle. Variously described as tailored masculinized ensembles that may include long skirts that cover riding pants, fitted jackets, top hats, and gloves.
A form of pajamas in which exposed panties match the fabric of a hip-length top.
Refers to loose garments worn over main garments for protection while working, especially coarse linen garments worn by peasants or lower-class workmen over their nicer coats or in the fields.

Waistcoats that are woven, usually woolen, and that open the full length of the center front. An example is the short woollen waistcoat with sleeves, formerly part of the garrison uniform worn by U.S. and British troops ca. WWI.
Aircraft that derive lift from the motion of air over aerodynamically designed surfaces that are rigidly and permanently attached to the fuselage.

Self-propelled and steerable lighter than air vehicles dependent on the displacement of air by a lighter gas for lift; generally composed of a streamlined hull, usually prolate ellipsoids, with one or more cells, a cabin for crew and passengers, and a propulsion system.

Large silk or cotton handkerchiefs or scarves that usually have a solid ground of red or blue with simple figures or geometric forms in white or yellow resulting from a mode of dyeing in which the cloth is tied in different places, to prevent the parts from receiving the dye. From a Hindustani word for this process.
Refers to old style typefaces based closely upon humanistic scripts.
Horse-drawn vehicles designed to transport people, that have four wheels.
Heavy driving vehicles with a high driving seat and no body designed for training horses for carriage driving or for exercising or breaking horses; not used for pleasure driving.
Sleds used specifically for freight transport. These are pulled by a person or a pack animal with slides for the transport of loads.
Game sets for activities that involve the moving of game pieces across a gameboard.
Flat boards or boardlike game accessories marked such that the progress of play can be tracked.
Large towels used to dry the body after bathing, typically made of an absorbent material such as heavy cotton.
Linen coverings for the credence, often matching the altar cloth.
Hexagonal leather pouches suspended by long straps from the sword belt of a cavalry officer; also, fashionable bags in a similar shape.

Fingerwoven sashes worn by Métis and First Nations individuals. Also known as assumption sashes due to their production in L'Assomption, Québec in the 19th century. Patterning varies, but often features an arrowhead design using red, green, yellow, blue, and white colored yarns. Currently, the sash has become a symbol of Métis identity.
Devices used for roasting whole apples, typically one to be placed in front of a fire, and comprising a tin frame, shelf, and reflective canopy to heat the side of the apples not facing the fire.
Glass bowls intended primarily for the keeping of live fish.
Sarangis of the Langas of Rajasthan, smaller and higher in pitch than the classical version, with one drone and three melody strings and 23 sympathetic strings.

A red colorant extracted along with purpurin from the roots of the madder plant; it is one of ten distinct isomers of dihydroxy anthraquinone. It has been used as a dye and pigment since ancient times. The colorant was first isolated in 1862 by Colin and Robiquet in France; For the synthetic colorant first produced in 1869, use "synthetic alizarin."

Wine decanter stands, or coasters, usually of silver, which are mounted on wheels with a swiveling handle and joined with a coupling. The decanter wagon was developed in England during the reign of George IV to avoid the need of dinner guests on either side of the king to rise and pass the wine.
Breast-shaped bust forms.
Tongs intended primarily for serving individual portions of asparagus; having either narrow or broad blades and made either as U-shaped sprung tongs or as scissorlike devices.

Balls thrown or batted in the game of the same name; usually 9 to 9 1/4 inches in circumference, weighing about 5 ounces, and consisting of a cork center wound round with twine and covered with white leather.
Long, elongated, and usually wooden clubs of various sizes and shapes used to strike balls in certain sports, such as baseball and cricket.
Game sets in which game pieces are moved and game pieces are usually captured from the opponent.

Small Japanese barrel drums with two projecting heads of deerskin, mounted on hoops and laced to each other across the shell. They are set horizontally on a low stand and both heads are played with drumsticks.
High-speed passenger trains used on some routes in Japan.

In current usage, refers to light two-wheeled motor vehicles with a small engine. designed to provide economical and relatively safe transport with minimal licensing requirements. Their features and capabilities are defined slightly differently in different licensing districts. For example, in English law, a moped must have weight not exceeding 550 pounds (250 kg), with a maximum speed not exceeding 30 mph, and an engine capacity of not more than 50 cc. The term originally referred to motorized pedaled bicycles; for that concept in current usage, prefer "motorized bicycle."

A naturally occurring metallic element with symbol K and atomic number 19. Potassium is a soft, silvery-white metal that rapidly oxidizes in moist air. It does not occur in nature in the free state because it is highly reactive. It is found mainly as potassium chloride (sylvite) and in clays (orthoclase, microcline). Major potassium salt deposits include the Great Salt Lake and Salduro Marsh in Utah and the Dead Sea between Israel and Jordan. Potassium salts are used to make fertilizer and hardened glass.
A potassium carbonate in the form of a white alkaline granular powder. It is used in glass manufacture, soft soap, and wool washing.

Light, simply constructed, four-wheeled carriages with or without collapsible tops and usually accommodating only one or two passengers; developed in England in the late 18th century; may also be used for early automobile designs with similar body styles.

Flatcars having a portion of the floor set lower than the deck to accommodate special loads with oversized vertical dimensions; in use since the early 20th century. For flatcars in use since the mid-20th century with larger depressed central sections designed primarily to accommodate intermodal containers, use "well cars."
Pilot-adjustable propellers that may change blade pitch during flight. The blade angle can thus be adjusted to its optimum value for the phase of flight, be it takeoff, climb or cruise.
Automobiles designed and built especially for straight line sprinting or drag racing.
Artificial orbiting vehicles designed to reflect or relay electromagnetic signals among communications stations.
Schooners having three masts, all nearly the same height.
Dutch clinker-built watercraft with a well and an open hold. Its rigging consisted of a mainsail and a jib.
Small half-decked skipjacks in the 24- to 30-foot range, from the lower eastern shore of Chesapeake Bay; may also be used for recent motorized versions.
Small flat-bottomed rowing, sailing, or outboard skiffs, usually with two-planked sides, whose cross-planked bottom is in the shape of a household flatiron.
Elegant sleighs with enclosed bodies; term used in New England from the mid-18th century until the end of the carriage era.
Vertical wheels by which motion is communicated to the rudder of a waterborne vessel, through the medium of a tiller-rope or other device.
Electric streetcars propelled by current through trolley systems connected to overhead wires or wires located between the rails.
One-wheeled vehicles with an open loading surface and an upright front panel, exclusively for the transport of stones and roof tiles.
Material that contains neither hydrocarbons nor any of their derivatives.

Slender poles or sticks, usually with a point at one end and a handle or loop for the hand at the other end and a disk near the lower end to prevent their sticking in the snow; used when skiing on snow to gain momentum, maintain balance, or execute certain jumps or turns.
Seats for a rider, made of various materials including wood, leather or textiles, which may be secured to the back of a camel by means of a girth passing under the body.
Cables that extend from watercraft to devices designed to bury themselves in the beds of waterways in order to restrict movement.

Sloop-rigged fishing vessels, 20 to 40 feet long, with a deep keel, counter stern, clipper bow, strong sheer, and gaff topsails and double headsails; originally designed in Friendship and Muscongus Bay, Maine; often converted to power yachts.
Jet aircraft in which additional propulsive thrust is gained by extending a portion of the compressor or turbine blades outside the inner engine cases.
Seaplanes supported on water by one or more floats, usually attached to the fuselage and/or wings.
Small children's velocipedes with two wheels at the back and one at the front. These usually lack brakes or gears and use frontwheel drive via cranked pedals.

Wooden two-wheeled vehicles with steering mechanisms; propelled by the rider pushing from the ground with each foot. The first two-wheeled rider-propelled machine was the draisienne, invented by Baron Karl von Drais de Sauerbrun of Germany, in 1817. Denis Johnson of London purchased a draisienne and patented his model as a “pedestrian curricle.” Many buyers were members of the nobility, and caricaturists called the devices “dandy horses.”
Decorated miters, lacking jewels, worn by Christian officiates. For miters decorated with gold and jewels, use "mitra pretiosa." For miters of simpler materials, use "mitrae simplex."
Ornamental embroidery or other decorative panels on certain ecclesiastical vestments. It is a medieval term that was revived in the 19th century.
Tall, pointed crowns to hats, often cone-shaped.
Headcloths of crochet work, lace, or the like, worn by women in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Contemporary term for multiweapon bombers carrying non-nuclear payloads.
Fighters designed and equipped to remove hostile aircraft from a given volume of airspace and so establish control of the air without prohibitive interference from enemy aircraft.
Small motorized pleasure craft used for such activities as day fishing or recreational outings.
Paddles designed for moving a canoe on a body of water.
Small novelty promotional items of varied form given away with packaged tobacco products from the late 19th-early 20th century generally.
Hydrophilic organic monomer used in the manufacture of flexible contact lenses. In conservation used as a water-absorbing poultice.

Small thin pliable lames or tongues of metal, used in a number of contexts, such as attached in overlapping rows onto leather or fabric supports to form armor, as yarn, and as the principal sounding element in lamellophones.

Buffer of an alkaline substance added to materials such as paper to counteract the formation or introduction of acid. The alkaline reserve is intended to neutralize future acidic components that may otherwise accumulate. As cellulosic materials are very sensitive to acid degradation, an alkaline reserve is sometimes added to archival papers and treated papers to minimize acid produced embrittlement, yellowing, and deterioration.
Long slender throwing spears of hard wood, usually with an iron head, used by peoples of southern Africa.
Round, flat caps with the crown projecting on all sides.
Close-fitting caps with a visor, generally having a gored crown with a button on top.
Long, knitted caps, made from a bag tapered at both ends and having one end turned inside another; traditionally worn for winter sports by Canadians.
Imperial Roman cuirasses constructed of about two dozen curved iron lames held together by a complicated system of leather straps and buckles.
Men's hats made from beaver-fur felt; worn from the 17th to the 19th century.

Percussion instruments in the form of a very shallow circular metal vessel, of varying size, usually with a turned-down rim, either nearly flat or with a central boss. Sounded by being struck with a beater midway between center and edge, or on the boss when present; they vibrate most strongly at the center and weakest at the rim.

Double-reed instruments used as practice instruments by musicians before eventually playing the Scottish Highland bagpipes. They have a narrow bore and a less stiff reed than traditional bagpipe chanters, thus their sound is about one octave lower.
Visors with deep horizontal ridges, used in the late 15th and early 16th centuries.

Shoes intended as streetwear for women or girls that have a deep instep opening, and that are derived stylistically from ballet slippers. These feature a sturdier leather or plastic sole and typically have no heel or a very low one.
Low-pitched single-octave gender of Java, played with one hammer only.
Gong chimes of Southeast Asia, in which the gongs are arranged in double or single rows in L- or U-shaped frames. They constitute an important element of the gamelan.
Low boot, generally made of leather or synthetic material, covering the ankle. It may have a zipper closure, be laced or simply slipped on. Used to protect the foot from the elements.
Boots, generally of ankle height with a lace closure, designed to walk or hike in outdoor settings or uneven terrain.

A type of full, baggy knickerbocker, typically worn for field sports, especially golf. The name connotes the length of the pants leg that extends 4 inches below the knee. These were popularized in the 1920s and remained in fashion until the late 1930s.
Technique of activation analysis induced by gamma rays to determine chemical elements.
The branch of science which measures intensity of incident radiant energy by the speed of a photochemical reaction with the aid of an actinometer.
Size exclusion chromatography technique that uses electrophoresis to resolve and separate large biomolecules; also known as electropherography.

Refers to an enhanced technique of liquid chromatography developed in the late 1960s in which stationary phase particles are smaller and packed more densely than in traditional liquid chromatography. The mobile phase solvent is then forced through the dense adsorbent by means of a pump. The technique was initially known as "high pressure liquid chromatography" (HPLC). The acronym remains but with a shift in emphasis to the high performance the method attains.
Process by which substances may be crystallized again. The process may be initiated by dissolving crystals in solvent, whereby crystals reappear in the resulting concentrated solution.
Refers to cleavage of the bonds that hold a polymer chain together, as in rubber as a result of heating.
Waist-length jackets or capes worn in bed.
Ornamental plugs for the nose.

Gold disks of the Akan people of Africa, often elaborately worked, usually worn as pectoral pendants, but known to be worn occasionally attached to caps or the hair or tied to the ankle. Their original function, especially among the Asante,  was to mark the wearer as the "akra" or "soul washer" of a king, responsible for cleansing the king's soul in ceremonies of purification or soul renewal. Later on akrafokonmu became multifunctional, worn by kings, chiefs, sword bearers, heralds, sub-chiefs, war leaders, junior officials, and young girls at puberty ceremonies.
Small seals or charms, intended to be worn from a watch chain.

Tabs or decorative objects attached to a chain or ring supporting one or more keys. In modern usage, it can refer to such tabs incorporating a small electronic device for locking and unlocking a vehicle or performing other tasks remotely.
Words or phrases, often in Latin, inserted in the inscription of an artwork to designate the activity performed by the creator, such as the role of the artist or designer.

Yellowish white ornamental material with a vibrant, brownish-red coating traditionally used for carving in China and other Asian countries. It is derived from the solid keratin casque atop the beak of the helmeted hornbill (Rhinoplax vigil).
Refers generally for all lutelike instruments having a soundbox and played with a bow.
Sticks with a horse's head on one end, meant to be ridden by children; for riding toys consisting of animals mounted on rockers or springs, use "rocking horses."
Two connected posters or signboards that hang in front of and behind a person and usually bear a message such as an advertisement, notice, or exhortation.
Promotional media that appears as a physical object such as a lettered or pictographic display on flat or dimensional structure or board.

Panel paintings installed in churches with religious texts appropriate to the the guild responsible for sponsoring the panel. These often have an ornamented frame bearing references to the guild itelf.
Posts, usually mounted on the roadside or at intersections, bearing a sign or signs for the guidance of travelers.
Use broadly for signs identifying places of business.
Signs that indicate a trade by rendering a particular shape or symbol that is unique to the trade, or is an agreed upon non-textual indicator of a particular trade.
Jewelry specifically worn on the head, such as ear ornaments.
Decorative or ceremonial plates or panels worn over the breast. Examples are breastplates of Pre-Columbian cultures. For breastplates used as armor, prefer "breastplates (body armor)."
Tightly woven and relatively deep baskets seldom made larger than 2-quart size; most are a quart or less in capacity.
A dense, black, semiprecious form of lignite that takes a brilliant polish and is used ornamentally, particularly in Victorian mourning jewelry.
Instruments for practicing violin playing, consisting of four strings stretched across a curved board with a normal violin fingerboard.
Wood reedpipes with a double reed and a conical bore which doubles back upon itself like a hairpin.
Large squares of cloth, often edged with lace or embroidery, which were wrapped around a swaddled baby during a baptism.

Small cards produced since the 19th century bearing the name and address of a business concern and one of its representatives, and intended more for information than advertisement. For small printed sheets or cards bearing tradesmen's advertisements from the 17th through the 19th century, use "trade cards." For cards made later and distributed for advertisement, use "advertising cards."
Staffs, clubs, or truncheons carried as symbols of office or authority or used as weapons.

Prehistoric artifacts of uncertain function. Formed from short lengths of reindeer antler with a pierced end, and often decorated. 'Bâtons de commandement' was the term initially used for this class of artifacts, but made an assumption of function; bâtons percés, the more recent term, is descriptive of form rather than any presumed function.
Pastoral staffs in the Eastern Church, where the crosier terminates not in a crook but in a tau (T), the ordinary form of a crutch.

Cards containing pictures of birds, baseball players, celebrities, or other popular culture subjects packaged by manufacturers of cigarettes with their product during the 19th and early 20th centuries.
Long zithers of Thailand, shaped like crocodiles.

The dark, porous, carbonized residue left after the destructive distillation of bituminous coal, petroleum or coal tar pitch. Coal can be converted to coke by heating it in an airless oven to drive off all volatile components. Coke was once made in large quantities as a byproduct when coal was burnt to produce methane. Coke is useful in metallurgy because it burns hotter than coal; it is used primarily as a fuel or as a reducing agent in the iron and steel industry, primarily in blast furnaces. The process for using coke in smelting was developed in the 17th century. In the 18th and 19th centuries coke aided in the expansion of the cast iron and steel production. Coke can also be converted to graphite.

Any of various solid or semisolid mixtures of hydrocarbons that occur in nature or that are obtained as residues from the distillation of petroleum or coal. For the blackish hydrocarbon portion of asphalt, use "asphaltic bitumen."
Loose, sleeveless mantles traditionally worn by Arabs.

Asphalt mixture of 13-60 percent bitumens with finely pulverized mineral fillers, usually limestone. It differs from natural asphalt by the presence of paraffin and a greater content of petroleum oils.
Windup toys using the mechanisms and workings of clocks to move all or parts of the toy; popular since the mid-19th century, especially in the United States.

Carbon-rich material that most often occurs in stratified sedimentary deposits. It is one of the most important of the primary fossil fuels. It is characterized by being solid, hard, opaque, black, or blackish, found in seams or strata in the earth, and largely used as fuel; it consists of carbonized vegetable matter deposited in former epochs of the world's history.
Uniforms designed to be worn by firefighters while performing their duties.
Guideway vehicles that do not operate on rails.

Shirts made from brightly colored printed fabric depicting images of the Hawaiian Islands: palm trees, outrigger canoes, fish, flowers, surfing, and hula dancers. Usually sold to, and worn by, tourists. First made in the 1930s from inexpensive fabric imported from Japan, the popularity of the garment peaked during the 1950s.
Spacecraft occupied by and capable of sustaining one or more persons, who normally have control over the vehicle's movement.
Close-fitting helmets with a rounded skull, large hinged cheekpieces overlapping on the chin, and a pivoted visor, in use from the 15th to the 17th century.

Rattles, occurring in pairs and worn around the ankles; usually made of box-turtle shells but tin cans or milk cartons are also used. Affixed in dense clusters so the shells frequently shake and collide with each other. Worn by Southeast Native North Americans, such as the Chickasaw, Cherokee, and Yuchi, usually during stomp dances.
Refers to aged wheat starch paste, a traditional adhesive used to bond layers of paper and/or silk in the mounting of Japanese scrolls.
Sheaths or tubular coverings for the fingers. Examples include gold finger stalls used in Egyptian burial practices, and finger stalls used for medical purposes.
Describes watercraft employed during combat to land and support ground forces entering enemy territory.
Aeronautical lights specially provided on an aircraft.
Relatively small, navigable submersibles designed for exploring ocean depths.
Bicycles or tricycles designed to carry heavy loads, specifically those with large, integrated containers or platforms that can hold cargo or additional passengers, pets, or children.
Digestive enzyme that breaks down starch by hydrolysis into its basic sugars. In conservation, used for removal of starch adhesives.
Square, boxlike, unassuming buggies having two or more movable seatboards set at the same level as the driver's seat.
Buses with two levels of seating, one above the other, connected by one or two stairways.
Canoes whose outer skin is bark; originally built by North American Indians.
Vessels designed to carry dry bulk cargoes, such as grain, coal, or ore, loose in large compartments.
Wheeled hand-drawn vehicles with built-in shelves that are used to transport books, usually in a library context.
Ancient war or racing chariots drawn by two horses abreast.
Communications satellites that transmit television signals directly to home receivers.

Roughly constructed fore-and-aft-rigged workboats built in the Bahama Islands and used for fishing and interisland transport; usually 13 to 20 feet long with a single mast stepped forward, loose-footed gaffe sail, outboard rudder and sometimes with an outboard engine.
Straight-sided, narrow-sterned, and almost double-ended dories developed in the 1790s by fishermen in North Atlantic waters, and typically employed aboard fishing schooners.
Emergency land vehicles designed and equipped for conveying the sick or injured to medical facilities.

Main portions of land vehicles on or in which the passengers or loads are contained; excludes those components necessary to make the vehicles move. For similar main portions of watercraft, use "hulls," and of aircraft, use "fuselages."
Railroad trains comprised of freight cars.
Large or heavy typefaces used for such elements as headlines, title pages, or advertisements, often defined as type of 24 points or larger.
Collectors' term used to describe pressed glass with a stippled background and usually a scroll-and-flower design; made from the mid-1820s to the mid-1840s.
A lime glass in which soda is used.
A sodium potassium feldspar mixture containing albite and orthoclase.
A type of snaphance incorporating the flintlock's combined steel and pan cover but with a laterally, not vertically, operating sear working on the cock through an opening in the lock plate.
The topmost components of adzes, often made of bone, stone, or metal. Adze heads are attached to the shafts of the adze.
Sports and athletic equipment used in games that employ balls.
Educational toys produced and used in a series for teaching Friedrich Froebel's system of kindergarten education. There are 10 gifts, each comprising one or more geometric shapes and colors.
The flat vertical surfaces at either end of basketball courts to which the baskets are attached.
Narrow, and relatively long, wooden or steel beams set horizontally several feet above the floor and upon which performers demonstrate balancing acts and gymnastic moves.
Cubical objects of wood, plastic, or other material having letters of the alphabet on most or all sides and used as teaching toys.
Heavy, sturdy sleds having two pairs of runners, a brake, and steering mechanism that enables the front rider to direct the sled down steeply banked chutes; found in two- and four-rider versions.
Bowling pins similar to tenpins but used in the game of ninepins.

Fertility figures, usually female, of abstracted form, with disk-like heads with high oval foreheads and most often having horizontal arms, cylindrical torso, breasts, and navel; among Asante of West Africa believed to ensure conception and successful birth.
Children's scale baby carriages for use with dolls.
Flat jumping jacks, usually of pasteboard, popular in France in the 18th century.

Toys in which two or more mirrors at one end of a tube create, when rotated, ever-changing symmetrical patterns by reflecting bits of glass or metal contained within the tubes or other objects sighted outside the tube.
Objects used for voting, comprising small clay or glass balls; to vote, in one utilization, marbles are placed into a particular slot or hole in specially-made ballot boxes.
Dolls that by means of a bellows or other mechanism in the inside are able to emit the sounds of speech.
Children's books intended for use in the bath, with plastic or vinyl waterproof leaves, often filled with foam sponge so that they float; usually pictures predominate over text.

Books, whether unique items or multiples, made or conceived by artists, including commercial publications (usually in limited editions), as well as unique items formed or arranged by the artist. For texts written by artists for the sake of their informational content, use "writings." For artists' books that emphasize the physical book as a work of art rather than the content, use "bookworks." For works that look like or incorporate books but do not communicate in the ways characteristic of books, see "book objects."
Pins used in the game of skittles.
Parallel bars having the two bars set at different heights.

Animated peepshow machines based on the flip-book principle; popular from the 1890s until around 1910. These early motion picture devices, upright and typically coin-operated were designed for individual viewing. As the handle of the mutoscope is turned, photographs placed around a central hub inside the device flip to give the illusion of continuous motion. For the cylindrical slitted viewer, use zoetropes.
Group of typefaces, originating in France in 1698, characterized by such features as vertical emphasis, strong contrast between thin and thick strokes, and unbracketed serifs.

Detachable, flexible coverings for books, usually of paper cut flush with the covers, folding around the binding with the ends tucked in between the cover boards and the free end paper. For attached outer sheets or boards, use "covers (gathered matter components)."
Games in which hands or fingers manipulate objects, often one or more balls or rings in a cavity, a recess, or around a stick.
Bindings for albums used as a presentation format for traditional East Asian painting.

Early gold-tooled bookbindings made in Venice and other locations in northern Italy. Stylized arabesques or a small trefoil leaf called an 'Aldine fleuron' often decorate the angles. Simple geometric strapwork or rectangular panels of gold fillets with the book's title or author's name stamped in the middle are typical decorations on these bindings.
Vaulting horses fitted with pommels, which are knob-like projections rising from the surface; may also be fitted with two graspable arch-like handles.
Small rackets made of parchment or rows of gut stretched across wooden frames.
Stuffed toy bears, usually with a plush outer material, having an upright body and straight forearms; first appeared in 1903.
Inertial toys of skill consisting of a double-cone-shaped object and two sticks, one attached to each end of a length of string on which the double cone rolls.
Jewelry for wear with current fashions usually made of inexpensive materials (metals, shells, plastic, wood) often set with imitation or semiprecious stones.
Large circular discs or trumpet-like objects that are placed in or on the ear. Examples are Precolumbian works that may be part of or a type of earspool.
Rectangular boards with low feet used for step aerobic exercise.
Small platforms designed to skim over the water when towed at high speed by motorboats and upon which riders stand during certain aquatic sports.

Disk-shaped objects, over 7 inches in diameter, thicker at the center than at the edges and having a metal rim permanently attached to a wooden body and with a central weight; to be thrown for distance in a field event.

Air-tight bags of rubber, plastic, paper, silk, or similar lightweight material, of varying shapes and sizes, usually brightly colored, which, when inflated with air or lighter-than-air gas, becomes lighter or nearly as light as air. Small ones that can be handled by children are intended as toys or as decorations.  Largr-than-life examples, often representing lifelike or fictional beings and objects, are used in parades and other public displays.
Small disc provided with holes, through which a string runs. The string is wound by rotating the disc. When one pulls the string apart, the disc rotates quickly and makes a buzzing sound.
Construction toys that are architectural or architectonic in form or purpose.
Figurative toys or animal toys with a mechanism or a mechanical device.
Toys, most often animal representations or dolls, filled and covered with soft materials.
Refers to any of a variety of pieces of mourning jewelry.
Chess pieces that move as bishops are designated to move.

Quarter bindings featuring a flat, gilt-lettered, green or brown calfskin leather spine, dark red cloth or paper covers on the boards, gilt top edge, and rough-cut or deckle side and bottom edges. This type of binding was originally used for publications of the Roxburghe Club, an association of bibliophiles founded in England in 1812 and named after the Duke of Roxburghe.
Adhesive bindings produced in the mid-19th century using a rubber solution to glue the leaves together. They ceased to be made years later when it was discovered that  rubber turns brittle over time.

Bindings in which a closely-spaced number of holes are drilled or punched through the leaves near the binding edge to take a spiral-twisted wire or plastic coil which is drawn through the holes to secure the leaves.

A labret with a hanging ornament in the shape of the broad leaf of a type of aquatic plant. Worn by Otomí in postclassic central Mexico, while Nahua tlahtohqueh (rulers) wore a golden version for dancing.
A type of mourning jewelry that incorporates human hair in its manufacture. Usually refers to intricately woven or braided strands, set in gold and made into bracelets, necklaces or watch fobs.

Disc-like, saucer-shaped targets, about 4 1/2 inches in diameter and 1/2 inch thick hurled through the air from a trap in the sports of skeet and trapshooting; first developed in the 1860s and made of baked clay, now usually a mixture of river silt and pitch.
Flat ornamental objects that  are inscribed with insignia identifying membership or affiliation with a group.
A type of flat Japanese fan that does not fold, comprising a disc or other shape attached to a handle.
Four-sided tops with the Hebrew letters non, gimmel, hé, and shin one on each side and used in a children's game traditionally played during the Jewish festival of Hanukkah.
A variety of toy guns that utilize caps, which are small charges of gunpowder, to imitate the sound of real pistols.
Coverings for the feet that sometimes extend above the ankle; generally made of durable materials. Distinguished from "hosiery," which is primarily leg coverings.
Ornamental or symbolic pendent scarves or veils attached to knights' helmets or ladies' headdresses such as hennins.
Bands, sashes, or belts, usually richly ornamented, worn diagonally from shoulder to hip to support a dagger, bugle, sword, or drum.
Trousers cut with fullness on both the outer and inner seams to give a flare at the hem. This style was popular in the 1960s and 1970s.
Manufactured electric fans attached to ceilings.
Hosiery that covers the calf and thigh, having ties or garters attached at the top to hold them up at the level of the waist or crotch, worn especially in Medieval and Renaissance Europe.
Elaborate shawls worn by Native North American women, decorated with beadwork, ribbonwork, fringes, and/or metal jingles. Used for the Fancy Shawl Dance performed at powwow gatherings.
Belts having loops or pockets used to carry ammunition and sometimes other equipment.
Mittens worn over thinner mittens or gloves as extra protection for extreme weather conditions.
Short gaiters worn over the instep and usually fastened under the foot with a strap; worn especially in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Overshoes of rubber or other waterproof fabric, especially those that extend above the ankle and that often have buckles or other fasteners. Use "rubbers" for overshoes without buckles or fasteners that are cut below the ankle.
A script developed in Luxeuil, in Burgundy, which was a particularly important center in the development of a Merovingian cursive style during the 7th and 8th centuries.

Collars worn to signify the status of an acolyte, who is an attendant, assistant, or novice, usually in a ceremonial context, religious order, etc. The collar is distinctive in color and style; it may be worn over another garment.
Neckties of thin cord fastened in front with an ornamental clasp or other device.
Neckcloths with broad ends usually looped and tied under the chin and sometimes secured by a stickpin.
Very long, elliptical neckpieces made of feathers, fur, or similar fluffy materials, especially popular in the 1890s.
Open ruffs, embroidered or lace, popularized by women of the Medici family. The collars are wired or stiffened to curve from the back of the head to the throat, giving it a fan-like appearance.
An Insular book hand derived from half uncial, characterized by a broad, round ductus, short ascenders and descenders, and wedge-shaped finials.
A formal script developed in the 15th century in Italy based largely on Caroline minuscule.

A serpentinite that may be white, yellow or gray but is rarely green or red. It is so flexible that the ancient Romans were said to have used it to make shrouds so that the ashes of the dead did not mix with those of the fuel.
Mixtures of surfactants, cosurfactants, electrolytes, hydrocarbon, and water.

A type of intimate mixture in which is embedded polymeric molecules, resulting in high viscosity. Other materials, such as solvents or chelating agents, may be added to the dispersion to increase its efficacy. Its texture can be described as that of a peelable gel. In conservation, it has been used in the cleaning of paintings and removing adhesives as it leaves no residue. An example is an HPVD made of polyvinyl acetate (PVAc) molecules crosslinked with borax.

Refers to the various costumes worn by university and collegiate faculty, administrators, and graduating students at graduation ceremonies and other special occasions. The most common element of academic costume is the gown, a tradition dating to the Middle Ages. Decorative hoods and various caps, including the mortarboard, are other common elements of academic costume. Trimmings of various colors may be used to refer to different disciplines of study.
White cotton or linen robes worn by orthodox Jews on certain holy days; also used as a shroud.

Ornamented or embroidered forms of amice worn over the alb, having a circular shape with a round hole or slit in the center so that it can be placed over the head and extend just over the top of the shoulders to fall in a semicircle in front and at the back in the manner of a short cape. From the 8th through the 12th century it is documented as having been worn by several orders of the clergy; in the later centuries it has become restricted to the pope alone. In order to distinguish the papal garments from the earlier garments, use the narrower term "papal fanons."

Chasubles, which are sleeveless outer ecclesiastical vestments, that are designed for travel. Examples include lightweight, unlined chasubles and chasubles that are reversible in two different liturgical colors.
Cinctures or belts for the alb.

Voluminous cloaks worn by higher Christian prelates, typically bishops and cardinals. In design, it is often circular, of purple or red color, having a large hood, and so large that the back trails on the ground, and the front is draped over one arm to allow free movement of the feet. This very full form did not develop until the 14th century.

Christian vestments comprising tunics of the form of a dalmatic, but of silk or another fabric that is lighter weight than a dalmatic. They have been worn by bishops, abbots, and cardinals under their chasubles during pontifical masses. In earlier periods, the garments were of linen and white in color.
Bracelets made out of coyote hair or skin, with cut paper hanging from it of postclassic central Mexico. Compared in colonial sources to a Christian maniple. Worn by Huitzilopochtli.
Short-sleeved, waist-length version of the surplice with a square-cut yoke at the neck.
Rectangular pieces of white cloth, usually linen, worn around the neck and partly under the alb; designed to protect other vestments from perspiration.
Very deep, turned-back cuffs on a man's coat; they frequently reached the bend of the elbow.  Fashionable from 1727 to the 1740s.
Short uniform jackets designed to be worn under military jackets or coats, or worn alone when the outer jacket is not necessary.
Decorative emblems worn by firefighters on their uniforms to identify their affiliation with a specific company or firehouse. These are usually embroidered with symbols such as ladders, flames, etc.
Small pockets made in the waistband of breeches, cummerbund, and other clothing, usually men's clothing or clothing made to imitate menswear, used for carrying a watch, money, or other valuables.

Long loose sleeves with a slit through which the arm can emerge. Also, long false decorative sleeves attached to the back of the armhole. Worn by men, women, or children especially from the 15th through the 18th century.
Brassieres in the form of a narrow band of fabric worn tightly around the bust, usually without shoulder straps; the term may refer to any women's strapless top in a similar style.
Briefs that reach to the hips or below.
Women's one-piece garments consisting of a camisole and bloomers.

Bell-shaped crinolines of whalebone or steel worn in the mid-19th century. Use "hoops (shaping garments)" for 18th-century shaping garments consisting of a series of concentric hoops of whalebone or bamboo.
Drawers with full, loose legs gathered above or below the knee; worn by women and children.
Slips with a foundation included in the bodice portion.
Women's underbodices usually worn over corsets or brassieres, reaching to or just below the waist. Usually cut straight across the bustline, with straps structurally separate from the garment body.

Men's unlined, close-fitting, collarless undergarments, worn as undershirts or jerseys in the 18th and 19th centuries. Also refers to sleeveless, athletic tops and unlined waistcoats. In the context of modern costume, the term may refer to single-pieced outfits worn by wrestlers. For lined waistcoats, use "doublets."

Underskirts fashioned from cloth attached to a series of elongated, concentric hoops made of whalebone or cane. Typically worn under a petticoat and/or gown to create a dome-shaped, small-waisted silhouette. Popular women's fashion in the 19th century.

Boned corsets, made in one or two pieces, with or without shoulder straps, that assume a conical form when fastened. Boned corsets, made in one or two pieces, with or without shoulder straps, that assume a conical form when fastened.
Girdles with a crotch.
Supporters for the genitals worn by men participating in sports or strenuous activities.
Rectangular pieces of cloth wrapped around an infant and pinned in place or bound with swaddling bands, to keep the arms fixed by the sides and the legs straight.
A precious stone associated with the specific month of a person's birth.
Infants' soft hats with hood-shaped crown fitted to the head with a frilled surround, tied under the chin.
Low, folding fur caps made of astrakhan fleece, worn by artillery regiments and others.
Term coined in the 19th century for cocked hats with the brim turned up flat against the front and back to form two corners.
Crash helmets that completely enclose the head, and that usually have transparent full-face visors; especially worn by motorcycle riders.

Grayish white poisonous powder once commonly used as an herbicide and insecticide but retired due to its high toxicity. It is currently used for preservation of color in zoological and botanical specimens; in taxidermy, as ingredient in soap used for cleaning and sterilizing hides.
A compound in which nitrogen is paired with a more electropositive element, such as silicon, boron, and most metals.

Compound that is a salt with the sulfate ion SO4 2-, or an ester of sulfuric acid. Sulfates comprise an enormous group of chemicals that contain the element sulfur. Sulfates are used in a variety of common products and processes.
Describes groupings of armor piece sets designed as a whole to possess particular physical characteristics, usually to suit a particular purpose.

Armor made in the style of ancient Roman armor, as understood by the maker and patron based on depictions on Roman monuments. The armor was usually ceremonial rather than functional, most of it made in the Renaissance for ceremonial parades and tournaments.
Supplementary pieces of armor attached to pieces of a basic set in order to reinforce the protection and suit it for other purposes.
Long cylindrical armor plates to protect the forearms and upper arms, either partially or completely encircling them; they were generally worn in pairs, linked at the elbows by cowters.
Armors designed to be worn by humans mounted on horses. A primary use equestrian armors is for contestants in equestian-related tournaments. For armor worn by horses, use "horse armor."
Armors designed for use in a joust, which is a competition in which two contestants are mounted on horses and armed with lances.

Coarse hairnets, often very decorative and used to confine the hair at the back of the neck or in a bun; sometimes attached to the back edge of a hat. For close-fitting netted caps or hairnets usually of gold, silver, silk, or wool thread worn during the 13th through the 16th century, use "cauls (headgear)."
Typefaces that are a thicker version of the same typeface style.
Devices used to agitate cream in a churn, with the purpose of separating the fat from the cream to produce butter.
Long-handled wood scoops used to remove butter from a churn.
A network of fine fracture lines in a coating layer, such as a ground, paint layer, varnish, or glaze.
Orchestral percussion instruments, consisting of one or two metal bars mounted on a resonating frame; occasionally, they are actual blacksmiths' anvils.
Generally, all lip-vibrated aerophones of predominantly cylindrical bore.
Simple end-blown aerophones of Scandinavia and the Baltic region, made of goat's horn, having three to five fingerholes and a mouthpiece carved integrally at one end of the horn.

Concert pitch, nontransposing aerophones of conical bore, constructed in circular shape with three piston valves and the bell directed either upward or forward, usually played at 9 foot C pitch; invented around 1870 by one of the English Distin family, and intended for use by amateurs.

Historic harps of Ireland characterized by brass strings, an outward-curving forepillar, and a resonator hollowed from a single block of willow wood. The term is also used for small, gut-strung harps with a hand-operated device to alter the tuning, developed in the 19th century.

Zitherlike instruments in the form of a rectangular box with a keyboard set in the long side. Strings, usually two per note, run from hitch pins on the left over a bridge to tuning pins at the right. Brass tangents on the rear portion of each key strike the strings from below to produce sound.
Keywork for the clarinet developed by the Belgian instrument maker Eugène Albert around 1860.

The mode or fashion of personal attire and dress, including the way of wearing the hair, style of clothing, jewelry, crowns, scepters, and other accessories of personal adornment, belonging to a particular nation, class, period, or special occasion, including all items worn or carried by people for warmth, protection, embellishment, or symbolic purposes. In English, generally expressed in the singular.

Men's loose-skirted wraps worn informally from the 17th to early 19th century; so called from their resemblance to similar garments worn by Banyans, a caste of Hindu merchants. Also refers to women's garments based on the men's banyan.

Hooded pullover hip-length garments made of weather-resistant material often with zipper closure at neck and drawstring hem; may be lined and have a front-center pocket; worn for sports. For hooded jackets or pullover garments reaching to the thighs or knees made of skins or hides or water-repellent or windproof fabric, use "parkas."
Garments worn over main garments for protection and sometimes ornamentation. Usually cover the front of the body and tie at the waist with strings, but may have a bib or shoulder straps.
One-piece, skin-tight garments made of knitted or stretch material, usually covering the feet, legs, and torso, and sometimes arms; worn under other clothing.

Women's close-fitting underwear worn for bust support and varying greatly in style, ranging in width from a band to a waist-length bodice, made with or without cups or straps and often boned or wired for additional support or separation.
Items that do not form the primary articles of clothing, but are instead the smaller articles of dress, and that are carried, as opposed to worn on the body.
