Small, medium, or large-sized soft or rigid receptacles, intended for carrying personal articles and usually used as ladies' costume accessories. A bag is closed in on all sides except at the top, where also it generally can be closed, and usually having handles or straps for carrying on the shoulder or in the hand.

Main garments for the upper body, usually lightweight and loose-fitting, made with or without sleeves and worn over or tucked in the waistband of a skirt or trousers. Examples include loose garments worn by workmen, peasants and artists, as well as women's upper body garments of various designs.

Short or long main garments consisting of panels or shields made of hides, skins, cloth, or woven fibers suspended from or near the waist with attached strings or cords; often decorated and usually indicating age or marital status. May cover the front or the back of the body; worn by women and girls in Africa.
Soft, socklike footwear, usually knitted or crocheted.
Bands encircling the arm, sometimes worn for decoration, identification, or to signify mourning.
Medieval pouches or bags suspended from the girdle and worn by nobles.
Neckwear consisting of two white, downward-hanging bands of fabric. These are typically worn as part of the professional regalia of lawyers, judges, and university professors.
Brimless head coverings, often made with a visor.
Upright plumes of feathers of an egret or heron arranged as a hair ornament or in a turban. Also, similar ornaments, often jeweled, in the shape of feathers, especially those worn on the head.
Archaeological term for bracelets or armlets, especially those worn by royalty and sometimes as part of the coronation regalia.

Ornaments worn around the neck, usually in the form of chains or strands of beads, pearls, stones, or decorative or precious materials, and often including a suspended ornamental pendant. Use "chokers" for short, narrow necklaces worn close to the throat. Use "dog collars (necklaces)" for wide ornamental bands worn tightly around the neck.
Ornamental bands, rings, or chains worn around the ankle.
Decorative items, similar in appearance to a brooch, but attached to a garment with a spring fastening. For jewelry made in a variety of forms fastened by a pin, uses "brooches."
Leather leg bands worn around the calf by high-ranking military personnel in postclassic central Mexico.
Gold rings with thorns described as having the shape of toes hanging from the serpentine nacochtli (earspools) of Huitzilopochtli in postclassic central Mexico.
Decorative items worn in, on, or about the ear.
Endleaves made of paper, often decorated.
Long-handled, paddle-like instruments, usually wooden, metal, or polypropylene, used to stir or rouse beer at various stages of its production.
Skimmers specifically used to remove cream from the surface of milk.
Spatulas with a bent blade. The bend in the blade allows the user to grasp the handle safely while using the blade on hot surfaces or delicate foods, such as frosting.
Phenomenon of visual perception which occurs when interlocking areas of contrasting colors are combined on the retina and perceived as a mixed color.
A chain-lattice clay mineral, also a group name for lightweight fibrous clay minerals characterized by their bleaching and absorbent qualities.
A dioctohedral clay mineral of the smectite group.
Massive form of sepiolite used especially for tobacco pipes.

An exceptionally tough, compact, fine-grained greenish or bluish mixture of actinolite and tremolite; it is a calcium magnesium silicate with traces of chromium and nickel, which produce its color. With jadeite, it is one of two minerals commonly called "jade." Nephrite has an oily, lustrous appearance when polished and is sometimes variegated in color that can incorporate white, yellow, brown, gray, and black. Nephrite has been used since Neolithic times for small utensils, decorative carvings and jewelry. If heated to about 1025 C, nephrite changes mineral forms to diopside.
An intense blue or violet-blue feldspathic mineral of the sodalite group; it is the principle constituent of lapis lazuli.
Short uniform jackets, distinguished by a particular breast panel and cut. First worn by lancers in the First French Republic and used in various countries until World War I.
Double-breasted overcoats of a type originally worn by British army officers.
Overdresses with a decoratively draped skirt.
Raincoats of rubberized cloth; use especially for those made with India rubber following a technique invented by Charles Mackintosh (1766-1843).
Robes worn for ceremonial or official occasions, usually with significant details of trim or color.
Suits for small boys consisting of a shirt and shorts made of matching or coordinating fabric and held together by buttons at the waist.

Long, full, close-sleeved garments worn by Chrisitan clergy and as secular garments in Greco-Roman and later times, often white in color. Albs are worn by Christian priests and occasionally by consecrated kings, often beneath other vestments. They are white in the Western Church and of varying colors in the Eastern Church. Albs were sometimes decorated with richly embroidered apparels at the wrists and along the bottom. For loose, sleeveless or full-sleeved garments, prefer "dalmatics."

Shirts worn for formal or semiformal occasions usually with a stiff or pleated front fastened with studs. often heavily starched and pleated in the front. The forms of such shirts have changed over time, and once featured detachable collars and cuffs. Evening shirts formed part of full evening dress. The cuffs are most often held closed with cuff links.
Loose-fitting overblouses with a sailor collar.
Pullover garments of knitted cloth with short or long sleeves; may be a sweater, shirt, or tunic.
Pullover sweaters having a neckline following the curve of the collar bone; high in the front and back, wide at the sides, and ending in shoulder seams.
Long, loose greatcoats which have large buttons and one or more spreading collars called capes.
Garments worn as loose skirtlike loincloths, the fabric wound around the waist and passed between the legs and tucked in at the waist from behind.
Very full, ankle-length petticoats of gray or white horsehair, worn to hold out the skirt before and in place of the cage crinoline.
Pull-on, loose-fitting, fairly short shorts, usually with an elastic waistband.
Circular-shaped skirts that are slightly gathered or pleated at the waistline and often supported with crinoline petticoats to maintain their flared shape.
Armor pieces protecting the throat and lower part of the face, worn either independently or attached to the helmet skull by pivoting rivets.
Flared and pleated skirts of cloth, often velvet or brocade, or of mail or plate metal, worn over or in place of tassets in early 16th-century Europe.

Devices attached to the right side of the breastplate, generally consisting of a small base plate to which is fixed or hinged a short, stout, projecting arm on which to rest the lance. They served to distribute the shock of impact.
Plain quilted or padded coats of textile or leather, often sleeveless, worn either under metal armor or as the sole protective garment, in use from at least the 12th to the early 15th century.

Term used in the glass trade for a type of art glass first produced by the New England Glass Company in 1886, characterized by a glossy mottled surface created by first coating the object with metallic stain and then spattering it with a volatile liquid; the finish is fixed by a light firing.
Sandglasses for which one hour is required for the given quantity to fall from the upper to the lower vessel.
Copy, either artwork or text, ready to be photographed for reproduction without further alteration.
Glass with very deep, complex, and polished cutting.
Glass with a red color due to the presence of copper.
Sets of armor consisting of a full field armor plus a large number of double pieces to form sets for the tilt, barriers, and foot combat, with a full bard.
Material comprised of living organisms.

Water-soluble and alcohol-soluble protein obtained from egg, blood, or milk; used in adhesives, finishes, coatings, varnish, as a clarifying agent for tannin, and in oil emulsion. The spelling with "i" is typically reserved fro this broader meaning. Use "albumen (egg white)" (spelled with an "e") for egg-white protein in the context of food preparation or photography.

The gas and aerosol envelope that extends from the ocean, land, and ice-covered surface of a planet outward into space; used especially in reference to the earth where it is held by the force of gravity.

Coins generated through a minting error which produced the same design on the obverse and reverse, one in relief and the other incuse; the coins are created when a preceding coin remained in the die and consequently left its impression on the next coin.
Culinary tools used to form butter into decorative shapes.
Of musical instruments, being the smallest and highest in pitch of their families.
Term, chiefly of British usage, used to refer to children's voices and to certain older European musical instruments, such as viols and recorders, of the soprano range.
Figured flasks depicting a variety of historical subjects such as portraits of presidents or other famous individuals, emblems, or slogans.
Narrow-necked stoneware bottles, globular or pear-shaped, ornamented with a bearded mask and often a coat of arms; of a type made in the 16th and 17th centuries.

Bottles, usually glass or ceramic, designed to hold medicines in an apothecary's establishment, often having matching glass stoppers or cork stoppers. The name of the contents was written on the bottles, on labels or molded into the glass. For vessels used to store medicines by an apothecary, but having wider necks and often made of ceramic, use "drug jars." For smaller bottles used to store smaller household quantities of patent medicine or other medicine, use "medicine bottles."
Drums with hemispherical or egg-shaped bodies and a single tensioned head.
Kettledrums used as the left hand drums of the tabla, in India.

Light half armor worn by heavy infantry from the early 16th to the mid-17th century in Europe, at first comprised of a gorget, spaudlers, breastplate, backplate, tassets, vambraces, gauntlets, and an open helmet, but no legharness. In the 17th century, arm defenses were usually omitted.

Conspicuously painted poles, usually with alternating red and white bands, roughly 7 to 8 feet high with metal points at one end used by surveyors to mark points of reference. For similar devices marked with numbers, use "leveling rods."
Objects that bear insignia that are worn by individuals to identify an affiliation with a group such as a branch of the military, fraternal organization, or law enforcement.
Term used in the glass trade for a type of art glass molded in ornate patterns, made in various shades of pink.
Stickers intended to be placed on the bumpers of motor vehicles, usually bearing messages such as slogans, witticisms, or advertisements.

Percussion vessels consisting of a hollow object, usually of metal but in some cultures of hard clay, wood, or glass, which when struck emits a sound by the vibration of most of its mass; they are held in position at their vertex, the point farthest from their rim, and their zone of maximum vibration is towards the rim.
The collagen in bone; used to make glue and gelatin.
Instruments used when preparing and cooking food.
Cloth bags in which flour or meal is shaken as a means of sifting.
Knives with a long blade and a serrated or scalloped cutting edge. Similar in form to "cake knives," but having larger teeth set further apart.
Culinary accessories in the form of charms, placed on a glass, and typically used for personal identification.
Small, narrow, usually three-pronged forks made with short tines and a long handle, intended for eating appetizers or small pieces of seafood or oysters; often resembling a trident.

Small knives with a wide but dull blade used as a place piece by an individual diner to spead butter on bread, rolls, or similar foods. For similar knives used as a serving piece to cut or serve butter from a butter dish use "butter knives."

Silver spoons with the top of the handle surmounted by a small statuette of an apostle. Apostle spoons were intended for personal use at table and were highly popular in England ca. 1490-1675; they were also made on the Continent, especially in Germany. Sometimes apostle spoons were made as sets of thirteen, a dozen featuring the apostles and another topped with a figure of Jesus Christ, a so-called master spoon. Spoons featuring small statuettes of saints have also been called apostle spoons. In the 16th and 17th centuries apostle spoons were seemingly popular as christening presents. Silver-plated versions were made in the 20th century for use as demitasse spoons.

Small printed cards on coated cardstock having a glossy surface resembling porcelain, usually bearing tradesmen's advertisements and often images. They may be lithographed or printed in combination with hand painting for metallic details. Production ceased in the late 19th or early 20th-centuries because the materials contained lead, which was toxic to the printers and painters who made the cards.
Forks designed for a toddler to feed itself. The traditional design includes a short handle and short, relatively blunt tines.
Term applied to a wide variety of special-purpose utensils designed to serve cake and similar foods, especially those with a flat wedge-shaped surface. May be accompanied by a cake knife.
Devices used to extract juice from firm fruits, usually consisting of an auger set in a receptacle with a hand-turned crank.
Paddle-shaped wooden tools used to pack sauerkraut into jars.
Books, usually for children, in which elements of a picture spring out at the reader when the pages are opened or a tab is pulled.
Renting or hiring something for exclusive use, typically a boat, airplane, or bus.
Utensils of varied design for agitating cooking apples in the process of making apple butter.
Tools used in the process of fermenting fresh apples into an alcoholic cider beverage.

Tabernacles, which are receptacles for sacred items representing the essence of the deity (for example consecrated hosts in Christian contexts), that are not fixed within an architectural structure and of small enough size to be portable.
Whisks used to agitate cream until it thickens.
Instruments or containers that measure, for example, extent, quantity, capacity, mass, or position in terms of a standard unit or fixed amount.
Sheets of lightweight paper, bearing an official postal stamp imprint, that are folded to form their own envelopes and can be sent via airmail at a special, low rate.
Designs applied to the skin by means of transferring temporary ink or dye from a decal.
Diviners who work by means of signs derived from configurations of earth, such as from a handful of earth thrown upon a surface, or from arrangements of dots jotted down on paper at random.

Divination by means of signs derived from configurations of earth, such as from a handful of earth thrown upon a surface, or from arrangements of dots jotted down on paper at random. It was popular throughout Africa and Europe in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.

Kitchen appliances consisting of a container with a fixed propellerlike blade at the bottom which rotates at different speeds to chop, mix, purée, or whip foods, and that have bases designed to rest on a fixed stable surface such as a kitchen countertop.

Devices intended primarily for mixing ingredients and kneading bread dough; used especially with reference to pail-like containers with large, hand-cranked kneading paddles or blades; also, for electrical devices that mix, knead, and bake bread dough.
Denotes Chinese base-metal cast coins with a square hole in the center issued from the 7th to the 19th centuries.
A type of gold coin (adopted from "denarius").
A script developed in South Italy in the 8th century and in use until the 13th century.
Arabic script, originally developed in the Ottoman Empire, and frequently used for scrolls and inscriptions.
Use generally for weapons using the power of exploding gunpowder to propel a projectile.
Self-propelled explosive devices that are intended to be launched from an airborne vehicle to hit targets that are also airborne.
Pairs of wooden paddles, typically grooved or cross-hatched, used to work butter into shapes.
Wallpapers decorated with simple patterns or stripes, usually printed with only one or two colors and often lacking a ground color.
Explosive devices designed to be dropped from the air into water or onto land which detonate when activated by something passing over or near it.
Wallpapers with texture produced by means of powdered textile fibers glued into place on the paper surface.
Wallpapers designed for use on ceilings, often with tiny repeating patterns or astronomical motifs.
Embossed paper wall coverings which were painted after being hung; made by a process patented by T. J. Palmer in 1887.
In the context of the modern military, projectile containers that hold an explosive for the makeup of bombs.

Bulleted breech caps are a variety of .22 caliber rimfire ammunition. The original design of 1845 was a percussion cap without a well-defined head loaded with a .22 caliber ball designed for use in Flobert rifles for low velocity indoor target shooting.
Ancient Roman cast bronze coins, usually in the form of ingots, and in circulation before 300 BCE, preceding the aes grave.
Designates cumbersome, heavy, bronze Roman cast coins, generally of the 3rd century BCE.
Artillery shells designed to be fired from the ground at flying aircraft.

Cartridges containing an explosive propellant but no projectile, designed to produce a loud noise on firing and used for signalling, training, firing salutes, or to mimic the effect of real gunfire in theatrical performances.
Valances hanging from the lower edge of a bed or bedcover; used decoratively to conceal the base of the bed.
Protective bed curtains, running on a separate outer rod, enclosing beds and their hangings when not in use.
Inner and outer bed valances which allow curtains to be drawn between them, thus concealing curtain hardware both to the interior and exterior of the bed.
Base valances with floor-length ruffles.
Wall coverings of various materials, including paper, which are characterized by embossed patterns.
The inner of two sets of bed valances, which conceals curtain hardware to the interior of the bed; often less richly decorated and perhaps shorter than the outer valances.

Small washable mats, often crocheted, used in the 19th century to protect the backs and arms of upholstered seating and reclining furniture from the stains caused by Macassar oil or other hair preparations. In the late 19th century, these were replaced by "tidies."

Sacklike removable and washable coverings for a bolster. If used on sleeping furniture, they often match pillowcases and sheets; if used on seating furniture, they often match other slipcovers. Textile coverings for long stuffed pillows or cushions used to support a sleeper's head in a bed.
Any of various coins valued at one-hundredth part of the monetary unit of several Spanish-American and Portuguese-speaking territories.
Irregularly shaped and uneven gold or silver coins struck in various parts of the Spanish Empire between the 16th and 18th centuries.
Long spears used in hunting bears.

Short swords, hangers, with short cross hilts, often elaborately decorated and made of fine materials such as carved bone or ivory or cast silver, sometimes with a chain linking the forward quillon to the pommel; some but not all were designed for hunting. They first appeared in the second quarter of the 17th century and became quite common in the 18th.

African bearing swords with long iron blades, symbolizing the power of the rulers of Benín; one has traditionally been carried on public occasions by a swordbearer accompanying the oba, or king, and sometimes other certain designated chiefs. Historically they were also used as executioner's swords.
Sheets for a bed, having boxed corners to fit the mattress.
Official nickname for a type of tube-shaped smoothbore portable rocket launcher, held atop the shoulder when fired, introduced as antitank weapons during the Second World War.
Horn-shaped portable containers for carrying priming powder or gunpowder, especially those made from the horn of a cow or ox.
Knitted or crocheted throws composed of strips or squares sewn or crocheted together.
Flexible steel tapelines or ribbons of steel used for accurate measurement of horizontal distances and which generally coil up into a special casing when not in use.

Panels or hangings for the front of a Christian altar, pulpit, or lectern; may be carved, painted, embroidered, or otherwise decorated. Antependia are of various materials including wood, ivory, precious metals, and embroidered textiles. The exposed position of precious antependia meant that they were sometimes moved on top of the altar for safety, thus becoming retables. If the coverings are continued around the sides and back they are called "paraments" or paliotti.

Special cloths placed over a Christian altar. Chrismales altar cloths are impregnated with wax to make them impermeable. They are placed directly on the brick or stone, under the other altar cloths, for the purpose of preventing chrism or other oils used in the consecration of the altar from seeping into the other, upper altar cloths.
Papers produced or used for lining containers or storage spaces such as boxes, trunks, or drawers, often decorated.

Heavy, woven textiles used as wall hangings, curtains, upholstery, or to hang from windows or balconies. Tapestries are characterized by decoration that may include ornamental or pictorial subjects; they often have details that are painted or embroidered. They are usually of wool and hand-woven on a tapestry loom by a process that differs from cloth-weaving in that the weft travels only to the warp at the edge of a particular color or pattern in the design, rather traveling from edge to edge of the entire piece of fabric. Various techniques are used in mixing and overlaying colors to create shading and patterns. The term also refers to machine-woven imitations of hand-made hangings.
Strips of textile or other material that hold bed curtains out of the way when they are not needed.

The basic unit of many quilt tops which, sewn together or to setting blocks or sashes, create the design. Blocks are composed of one or many patches, either pieced or appliquéd. Blocks are commonly square, but can also be in other geometric shapes such as hexagons or circles.
Blocks of material sometimes used to join together the sections of a quilt.
Upholstery that is built up over the seat rails.
The topmost fixed cover of upholstery.
Upholstery webbing that results in a tightly interlaced upholstery foundation component; often associated with French furniture.
Curtains, occasionally embroidered, which cover the aumbry.
Small mats, often crocheted, laid on furniture for protection or decoration, used especially to keep heat or scratches from polished surfaces.
Long narrow strips of textile material that rest on the surface of furniture items for decoration or protection.
Very narrow strips of decorative textiles that are meant to rest on the surface of furniture.
Decorative and protective textile coverings placed along the front of an upright piano.
Bed coverings used as the topmost cover of a bed during the day.
Small tablecloths for use on card tables.
Decorative covers for bolsters, often with an added flange.
Pieced quilts composed of a single design unit of a given size set together in rows.
Relatively narrow tapestries designed for the space between two windows or doors.
End panels of Turkmen bag faces and rugs which are located outside of the main borders.
Sound devices that create atmospheric or natural sounds.
Parts or components of aerophones.
Electric devices that, when activated, produce short, relatively high-pitched tones, at regular intervals over a period of time, as in portable pagers or animal tracking collars.
Ensembles that either play related groups of instruments, such as all brass, or which serve a particular function, such as for rehearsals, dances, or parades.
Upright grand pianos with straight bass side, the treble side usually curving over to form a scroll at the tail, made from about 1798 to 1850.

Large double-conical drums of West Africa with a tubular open foot at the base, played upright, usually in pairs, each being of a different pitch; one of the pair often has a jingle suspended across the drum head. They serve as talking drums on ceremonial occasions, and as accompaniment to ritual singing and dancing.
Gaming counters used when playing poker.

Scripts used for writing several languages of Asia and Africa, including Arabic, Persian, and Urdu. The Arabic script is written from right to left, in a cursive style, and includes 28 basic letters. Because all letters usually stand for consonants, it is classified as an abjad. After the Latin alphabet, it is the most widely used alphabet.
Scaled-down versions of tall case clocks, usually 2 to 5 feet high, with 8-day brass movements, and having pendulums; popular in the United States in the early 18th century.
Dessert glasses for serving an individual portion of custard, sometimes set on a stem and may have a single handle.
Small sweetmeat glasses, usually about 4 inches high, used for serving dry sweetmeats or confections.
Books of blank pages, usually ruled, used for taking notes, especially by pupils and students for taking class notes or writing or drawing exercises.
Tone in a halftone image in which dots are eliminated, thus printing white.
Large bass-range chordophones of the violin family, made in 19th-century New England primarily for accompanying church choirs.

Method of attaching leaves together to form a text block. Slots or holes are cut or punched through the folds of a gathering,  thin adhesive is forced through the holes to adhere the leaves of the gathering together, then a second, thicker adhesive is applied to the back of the stack of  gatherings to create a text block.
Group of script typefaces based on Gothic cursive hand-written scripts.

An imaginary imprint used for the purpose of evading legal and other restrictions, to mask piracies, to protect anonymity of the author, etc. An imaginary imprint used for the purpose of evading legal and other restrictions, to mask piracies, to protect anonymity of the author, etc.
The recording, storage, and manipulation of images in computer systems in the form of electronically encoded picture elements.
Refers to large scale digitizing projects, usually of books digitized in order to create a digital library.
Placards carried or otherwise displayed by people engaged in picketing.

A type of composite centerpiece, often tiered and quite elaborate, consisting of a metal frame with dishes, vases, or candleholders of silver, glass, or porcelain intended to hold fruits, flowers, candies or the like, and used for service or decoration.
Chants that are monophonic, or unison, and accompany the Latin mass and canonical hours of the Ambrosian rite. The word Ambrosian is derived from St. Ambrose, bishop of Milan (374-397).
Notebooks in which photographers note important details of the creation of a photograph whether in the field or the darkroom.

Novels of a traditional German genre that focuses on the spiritual development or formative years of an individual. Now in broad use to refer to this type of novel written in any language or in any culture.

Refers to one of the main service books of the Byzantine Church; it contains the text and rubrics for the Orthodox Christian liturgy of the eucharist, fixed parts of the daily office, and the other sacraments and minor rituals. The term sometimes refers more generally to collections of prayers or prayer books.

Bookbinding boards with the back or binding edge either split open to a  shallow depth or, in the case of laminated boards, left unadhered. The boards are attached to the text block by the tapes or flanges being inserted into and adhered within the split edge.
Words or phrases made by transposing the letters of other words or phrases.
Collections of psalms, anthems, or verses to be sung responsively.
The bottom margins of pages in Medieval manuscripts, often used when illuminations appear in that area.
Water recreation complexes including clubhouse, marina, and associated boating facilities.

Type of saltcellar used to hold salt for individual use at the table and which rests on a flat base without legs or feet. They occur in many shapes with one, two or three wells for salt and are often made in sets.

Refers generally to comic books produced in Japan. Although the term manga is often used to refer to the Japanese form of animation known as anime and much anime has been based in manga, it is a separate art form. Manga themes include sports, romance, historical drama, comedy, soap operas, fantasy, mystery, sexuality, and horror. It is often produced in black and white, with the cover or the first few pages in color, with emphasis on exaggerated facial expressions and large eyes.
A type of lip on a container that extends to a point.
Objects that are placed or that naturally overlie or overspread another object, with the purpose or effect of enclosing, hiding, or sheltering the second object or its contents.
Devices used for closing or sealing a bottle, typically made of metal and fitting tightly over the mouth of a glass or plastic bottle, held in place by crimped edges.
Stoppers for uncorked bottles that have decorative or whimsical tops. The object may have a shaft of cork or another material; modern stoppers are often made of metal and plastic.
Balances for measuring small gravitational, electrostatic, or magnetic forces by determining the amount of torsion on a slender twisted wire.
S-shaped crooks on bassoons and English horns that carry the mouthpiece and double reed.
Bowls used in many cultures for soliciting food or other alms.

Artisan or merchant class of people that lived in urban areas and are associated with the production of much of the art, music, literature and drama in Japan during the Edo period (1615-1868). This class includes both wealthy financiers and wholesale merchants as well as low income artisans, peddlers, and day laborers. The term is often translated as "townspeople" or "townsmen".
People or institutions that share in the ownership of an object, land, or other entity.
Bevor components constituting the lower portion, protecting the chin and throat.
Gears that drive the hands of timepieces or some other visual indicators of the time.
Grills with metal racks on which food is broiled directly over a fire.
Small hand-held devices for storing and grinding peppercorns.

Hangings for windows, doorways, or other openings, usually of cloth, plastic, or another such material, that are generally finished with hems, casings, pleats, or ruffles and hung by the top edge; used for privacy, control of light and drafts, or decoration.
Blinds with narrow slats that become practically invisible when positioned horizontally, giving an unobstructed view to the outside.
Shades with narrow, sharply pleated folds, resembling the musical instrument. For shades that pull up in wide horizontal pleats, use "Roman shades."

Devices, known since antiquity, used to batter through the walls or gates of a fortified place, basically consisting of a large beam with a heavy metal head, mounted on a wheeled carriage or a frame from which it could be swung back and forth, or carried by people.
French and English staff weapons used between the 12th and 14th centuries, having a pointed head with a scythelike blade and a fluke on the back.

Curtains, often in pairs, made of straight pieces of cloth with rings and cords running diagonally on the back of each from bottom center to outer top. When the cords are pulled, the cloth is gathered up and to the side in two swags, with points or tails hanging down to either side.
Large bore, single-shot shotguns mounted on a punt or specially designed boat, used to shoot waterfowl sitting on the water.
Firearms for firing harpoons, usually furnished with a swiveling gun mount and typically used on whaling ships.
Air guns with rifled bore.
Smoothbore spring air guns designed to fire BB shot.

Pistols made expressly for formal personal combat, usually in pairs and furnished with a case, and generally characterized by high technical quality with only modest decoration. They commonly date from the late 18th to the mid-19th century.
Pistols with a flaring muzzle like a blunderbuss, intended to be loaded with shot for use at close range. They were extremely popular from the mid-18th to the early 19th century.
Curtains which close the stage of a theater from the auditorium in case of fire, preventing the spread of flame and smoke; usually fabricated of woven asbestos and steel wire.
Valances draped in soft, billowing, crescent-shaped folds, sometimes with tails at the ends.

Glass curtains, usually shirred, stretched taut between lightweight top and bottom rods, or sometimes hanging loose at the bottom; popular for doors, casement windows, and lower window sashes, which require curtains that will not interfere with their opening and closing.
Curtains that can be drawn to the side, especially those that slide back and forth on a rod or track through a system of cords and pulleys operated either by hand or electrically.
Long curtains, reaching to the floor.
Percussion locks in which the priming powder is held in a bottle-shaped pivoting magazine.

Firearm accessories that replace the stock on a semi-automatic firearm. The recoil from the weapon in addition to a springing mechanism to generates motion that allows the rifle to bump the trigger against a shooter's finger, enabling rapid firing without the shooter continuously pulling the trigger.

Projectiles or stationary devices containing both a detonating mechanism and a harmful agent such as an explosive, poison gas, biological poison, or incendiary substance, set off by a time fuse or by impact. For the hollow projectiles containing shrapnel, explosives, incendiary or poisonous chemicals, or other harmful agents, designed to be fired from artillery, use "shells (ammunition)."
Bombs designed to be dropped from aircraft, first seriously developed during the First World War.
Explosive devices lacking propulsion of their own that are intended to be launched from an airborne vehicle to hit targets that are also airborne.
Grenades specifically designed to explode into and scatter fragments, used against personnel rather than mechanized vehicles, installations, or structures.
Small ladles intended primarily for serving cream; generally smaller than gravy ladles. Sometimes made en suite with a cream pail.

Polariscopes of a particular type; instruments for measuring the degree of polarization, determining the amount of rotation of the plane of polarization by a substance through which polarized light passes.
Instruments designed to measure rain amount; includes recording, nonrecording, and rain-intensity gauges.
Special utensils of wood or metal, often with ornate forms, and particularly associated with Berber or Tuareg peoples, used to break or cut up pieces of sugar to sweeten tea.
The placing of consecutive numbers one on each folio of a book; may also refer to the overall configuration of the numbering in the book.

Navigational instruments designed by the Englishman John Davis in 1594. This instrument measures the height of the sun by the projection of a shadow. In this case the observer stands with their back to the sun, hence the English name 'backstaff'. Instead of the cross of the Jacob's staff, the Davis quadrant features two arcs to which sliding vanes are mounted. By taking the horizon as the starting point, the observer can measure the shadow of the vane on the first arc using that of the second arc. The Davis quadrant was originally made of wood with ebony or ivory quadrants.Brass or steel predominanted after about 1775.
Any instrument used to measure the intensity of radiant energy, especially of the sun.

Instruments designed to demonstrate the mothion of rotating bodies, consisting essentially of a rotating wheel mounted in a ring, with its axis free to turn in any direction. With modifications or in conjunction with other equipment, these may be used as navigational devices, or to stabilize ships and mono-rail vehicles.
Devices used to measure the rate of flow of air or gas.

Chambers encased in thick, fireproof vaults of clay, brick, or stone; particularly suited for baking bread.  The bake oven was sometimes built in a separate structure, outside the living quarters of the home; some bake ovens were communal.
Copy prepared for photographing to make a printing plate, consisting of such elements as text, titles, and artwork that have been arranged, pasted, and marked.
In churches in the Netherlands, distinctive funnels used for transferring the collection money into bags or boxes

Preparation of copy in a form suitable for printing or for making printing plates, whether by hand, by mechanical devices, or by computer, including casting off and the arranging of type, spacing, and other material. For the specific process of arranging type, use "typesetting."
Generally, methods of character assembly for printing that employ a computer. Can be directed toward exposure of the characters on photosensitive film or paper, or output from a computer printer.

Folded books comprising a series of accordion or concertina style pleats and attached at one or both ends to stiff covers. The name leporello most likely comes from the manservant Leporello in Mozart’s opera Don Giovanni, a famed rogue who keeps a tally of his conquests on a long accordion style list. In the late 19th century, leporello were common travel souvenirs consisting of depicted scenes or photographs of a region’s tourist attractions.
Layouts marked on a card or paper, used as guides for motifs for weaving or lacemaking.
Devices that use electricity to open cans with a rotating blade that cuts around the edge of the can's lid.
Group of typefaces based on Gothic bastarda script, especially common for, and surviving into the 20th century in, Germanic-language printing.
Large, spatula-like tools used to slide pizzas or other foods into a hot oven and to retrieve them when done.
Devices that use an electric heating element to pop corn.
Ceramic griddles used to bake tortillas.
Small balls of perforated metal or other material in which tea leaves are placed to be immersed in hot water to make tea.
Headings in newspapers indicating subject matter and set in larger type than that of the copy.
Literary works in which action, physical danger, and suspense are key elements.

Objects bearing special or distinctive marks and worn for decoration or to signify affiliation. Originally, badges were heraldic symbols worn as identifying marks by a knight and his retainers, e.g., a badge of arms. In later use, the term refers to any distinctive device, emblem, or mark worn to indicate a person's affiliation, rank, office, name, or membership in an organization or support for a cause, particularly objects that comprise small pieces of metal, card, plastic, etc., that bear a distinguishing design or words.
Plays written chiefly to amuse the audience.
Hagiographies devoted to the life of a single saint, and often containing additional material such as liturgical texts, letters, or music.
Mechanical pitters designed specifically to remove stones from cherries.
Utensils for toasting cheese on bread before an open fire.
Any of various devices used for straining beer; in southern Africa they take the form of long basket-like strainers with a tubular form and narrow base.

Circular, perforated plate sieves, typically made of wood and parchment, having raised sides. They are designed especially for the preparation of communion wafers for liturgical use; the sieves are used for separating the wafers from the edge remnants.
Devices used for winnowing flour, often having a mechanical action for forcing flour through a mesh screen.
Metal graters for making bread crumbs.
Wire whips, typically wide at the top and coming to a rounded point at the bottom, designed to give maximum lift to a batter.
Mills used for grinding corn into grain.
Devices for reducing dried herbs to small particles for use in cookery.
Mills used for extracting the juice out of sugar cane.
Mechanical devices with multiple blades designed to finely chop or grind meat.
Shaped devices, generally of sheet metal, used for cutting biscuits from rolled dough.
Tools used for removing caps on bottles.

Machines used for sifting, especially flour. These consist of revolving sieves or spinning cloth screens, which are housed in enclosures. The screens have varied mesh sizes, from fine to coarse. The flour enters the bolter at the end with the finest screen, where the lightest part of the flour is separated out. Gravity carries the remaining flour, separating out the finer endosperm from the germ and bran of the wheat.
Spits made with a central basket formed of thin iron strips.
Standing cups, generally made in silver or gold, with a bowl made of a coconut shell. Of a type which dates from the 15th century.

Jugs with a perforated neck and from three to eight spouts along the rim that make ordinary drinking or pouring impossible. One can drink or pour without spilling only if certain holes along the rim and under the handles are covered with the fingers.
Large transverse flutes used in Hindustani or North Indian classical music.
System of writing or printing for the use of the visually impaired in which combinations of dots or points are used to represent characters and are read by touch.
Open vessels meant to be filled with boiling water and into which other containers are placed to warm or cook food.
Those styles of handwriting designed for legibility and used in transcribing manuscript books.
Sedimentary conglomerate of calcareous sand and chalk formed in intertidal zones of beaches in tropical and other areas.
Refers to those derringers actually made by Henry Deringer, the Philadelphia gunsmith who first developed the type.
Instruments that measure minute amounts of electromagnetic radiation by determining the changes in resistance of a conductor caused by the heating effect of the radiation; used in meteorology.
Rain gauges capable of measuring very small amounts of precipitation.

Machine guns first developed by Dr. Richard J. Gatling in 1861, featuring a cluster of revolving barrels equally spaced around a central shaft, a magazine to feed them, and an action by which the cartridges were chambered and fired. Early models were powered by a hand crank, later ones by electricity or gas, attaining a firing rate of up to 3000 rounds per minute.
Sclerometers that measure the rebound of a standard ball dropped onto a material from a standard height.

Clocks with a running duration of eight days. They are either longcase or bracket in form. The interval for winding is seven days, but the additional day is to enable a day's delay in winding. They can often be identified by winding squares on the dial.
Bullets designed to penetrate hard targets such as armored vehicles, generally consisting of a hard core inside a casing of softer metal.
High-impact ammunition designed to stay in one piece on contact expanding about 1.5X to 2X caliber. The limited expansion reduces area friction, intended for use in hunting large game.
Inert cartridges containing no explosive components, used in the armed forces for practice loading and manipulation of firearms.
Component of a complete round of ammunition or use in detonating an explosive charge, that ignites the propellant.
Self-propelled submarine missiles that carry explosives and are launched from a torpedo bomber aircraft into water, where the weapon propels itself to the target.
Refers to kantharoi that are also head-vases.
Rhyta of a particular type in which a half-head of a ram is joined with a half-head of a boar or donkey.

Refers to a type of hydria featuring a neck forming a continuous curve with the body. This shape also features a smaller mouth and narrower neck than the shoulder hydria. It was the most common form of hydria for red-figure. Although the kalpis was introduced after the invention of red-figure, there are some red-figure kapides. Many kalpides were also made in bronze in addition to terracotta and, unlike the metal versions of other shapes, a good number survive.
Nolan amphorae featuring double handles, each composed of two cylindrical sections.
Small pointed-neck amphorae used for scented oil (perfume).
A type of continuous curve amphorae characterized by flaring and slightly concave lips, flat handles with flanges, and feet in two degrees.
Red-figure kraters in the form of an inverted bell with handles placed high on the body.  The rim is offset and the foot is stepped.
Late red-figure lekanai on which a bride and groom, accompanied by others and in the presence of wedding vases, are depicted.

Refers to one of the most common forms of oinochoe. This type is usually red-figured and features a trefoil (three-spouted) mouth and bulbous body continuously curved from neck to foot. The chous was a standard unit of measure, equivalent to about 3.28 liters. The chous was especially associated with the Anthesteria, an Athenian festival celebrating wine, the wine god Dionysos, and the dead. The second day of the festival was called 'Chous.' It was customary during the festival to drink from choes and to pour libations from them at tombs. Miniature red-figured choes, decorated with scenes of children at play, were probably festival gifts to children or gifts offered at a child's grave.
Refers to a rare vessel type of hybrid form; most examples are neck amphorae. An amphora-psykter functioned like a double-walled krater.
A type of phiale that lacks the omphalos of phialae mesomphalos.
Ancient Greek and Roman storage vessels of many variations usually having a large oval body with a narrow neck and two or more handles extending from the mouth or neck to the shoulders on the body.
A rare variation of the basic pelike featuring an offset neck and less globular proportions.
Ancient Greek vessel type named after the potter Nikosthenes. It features a domed lid with finial, a body shaped like an inverted bell set on a short stem, and a flaring foot for support.
Small urinary containers for female use; design may be of compressed elliptical shape with an incurved rim on the front end. Generally made of ceramic or occasionally silver.

Ashtrays mounted on a low pedestal stand generally used along side of a sofa. Distinct from "smoking stands" which are small stands or cabinets with zinc-lined compartments used to store smoking supplies.

The most common shape of loutrophoros; it resembles a tall neck amphora but differs in its narrow proportions and elongated handles, with the space between the neck and handles occasionally partly filled in.
Welsh hornpipes, known in Medieval times, consisting of a single or double cylindrical pipe with a beating reed, terminating in a cow horn bell and having a cow horn mouth bell protecting the reed.

General purpose bags carried by North American Indians with attached shoulder straps worn over the shoulder and across the breast. Usually made of wool, muslin, or buckskin and heavily decorated with beadwork, quillwork, or embroidery. For shoulder belts worn across the breast from which wallets, small bags, or pockets often containing ammunition are sometimes suspended, use "bandoliers."
Vases in the form of masted ships.
Early Bronze Age Aegean two-handled drinking cups.
Bowls used to make batter, such as for bread or pancakes, typically deep in form and having a spout and handle.
Serving vessels in which sauces are kept warm by hot water, or sometimes embers, contained in an internal chamber.
In Indian architectural contrexts, relatively small reservoirs or tanks in which rainwater is collected for drinking.
Vessels having a dish-shape and intended primarily for baking.

A kind of magnetometer used in aerial surveys consisting of one or more high-magnetic-permeability cores surrounded by primary and secondary windings. The signal picked up by the latter represents the direction and magnitude of the external magnetic field.
Structures, troughs, drinking fountains, or containers for clean water, particularly when intended to be consumed by animals or people in isolated places.
Gauges that are used for measuring changes in air pressure, velocity, or flow. These can measure extremely small differences in pressure of both gas and liquid.
Instruments used to measure the masses of small, electrically charged particles.
Mass spectroscopes that record mass spectra on photographic plates.
Meteorological instruments that automatically record temperature and pressure.
Devices used to measure respiratory function, particularly the volume of air moved during breathing.
Clocks that audibly mark periods of time by striking or playing musical notes.

Laser-based instruments operating on the time of flight principle for determining the distance from an observer to particular objects; used for topographic measurement as used, for example, by space probes to profile the surface of Mars.
Any of various instruments for measuring and recording vibrations in the earth.
Tools used to affix dates to surfaces using ink and a rubber medium. The rubber stamps are often on a rotating wheel to allow for a variety of dates to stamped.

18th-century printmaking process that imitates the appearance of chalk lines; employs etching, with the ground having been marked with a roulette, and sometimes the addition of directly engraved stippling.
Planographic printing process in which a design is deposited on a stone or plate with a greasy substance and the surface is chemically treated to accept ink only in the greasy areas.

Printing from wooden blocks, as in block books before movable type, or from wood or occasionally metal blocks on textile. Sometimes used loosely with reference to relief printmaking processes; there prefer "relief printing."
Printing technique in which color is applied to specific areas of the plate with a pad or rolled piece of felt.
Thermometers whose sensing element is an electrical resister, the resistance of which is an accurately known function of temperature.
Thermometers used to indicate mean temperature, consisting partly of a clock mechanism whose speed is a function of temperature.
Surveying instruments, comprising an electronic theodolite integrated with an electronic distance meter. The data they record in the field can be downloaded directly to a computer.

Japanese or Japanese-style boxes comprised of individual compartments, and used to store or transport packed meals, typically lunches or a picnic. Named after a Chinese dialect word meaning ‘convenient,’ bento boxes can vary in style and material from the simple to the very ornate, the more decorative type often made of wood or painted lacquer.

The largest type of tureen, said to have been used originally to serve a  particular kind of Spanish stew; they are commonly  of round body resting on feet or a pedestal, with two handles and a cover, usually made of silver but sometimes of porcelain; most examples date from the 18th century.
Tools for determining the alcohol content of a solution of alcohol and water.
Flat pieces of stone, ceramic materials, or iron used for baking.
Articles of flatware having a handle with a shank terminating in two or more tines, used to manipulate food especially in serving and eating.
Scissor-shaped tongs used to break a lump of sugar from a sugar loaf.
Cranked, but not necessarily geared, devices of wood or iron for mechanically paring apples.
Devices that remove hulls from nuts.
Instruments that record the duration of sunshine and provide qualitative measurements of the amount of sunshine by the action of the sun's rays on blueprint paper.
Frames of parallel metal bars used for broiling food over coals or an open fire.  Also, wood gratings or racks for the same purpose.
Mould for making chocolate bars, truffles and hollow chocolate figures.
Small tubes with a strainer at one end used in drinking maté.
Utensils consisting of concave containers fitted with long handles intended primarily for lifting liquids, such as drinking water.
General term for items used in conjunction with accessory tables.
Photometers designed to measure the intensity of light reflected at various angles from a surface.

Utensils with a hemispherical end used to serve ice cream and similar foods; may have a mechanism which moves a blade around the inside of the scoop to loosen ice cream from the sides. For utensils which have a relatively large flat surface of varying shape used to serve ice cream use "ice-cream servers."
Containers built to hold ancillary items for equipment or personal adornment.

Coffins made of cast iron, particularly those that were manufactured in the early through mid-19th century in the United States, used to transport and preserve corpses. Usage declined after effective embalming became prevalent. The primary manufacturer was Almond Dunbar Fisk in Providence, Rhode Island.
Covers of documents, made of paper or other materials, and often with padding of some kind to protect contents while being shipped.

Portable files for holding and organizing documents that expand via accordion-style folded sides. These appear in a variety of styles and materials, some with hard covers, latches or locks. Common contemporary versions are often made entirely of paperboard or reinforced paper. These may include dividers with or without indexing tabs.
Escapements in which wedge-shaped pallets of an anchor-shaped component engage an escape wheel causing the wheel to recoil slightly at every release.

Small bottles for perfume made in a variety of forms and materials. They generally have a tiny orifice to retard the flow of perfume and usually have a stopper or screw cap. Sometimes made as double or triple bottles, each to contain a different perfume. May be part of a toilet set.

Navajo shoulder blankets, woven wider than long and worn horizontally, characterized by a simple weft-banded design in weft-faced tabby weave, perhaps with tapestry-woven rectangles or diamonds. Not associated with rank.
Producers of film, television, or another work, who supervise other producers; they may be involved with other activities such as  funding. They may own the rights to the screenplay.
Blankets with depictions of recognizable figures, objects, or scenes.
Mechanical clocks run by a series of weights and wheels.
Coverings for mattresses that are intended to protect it from moisture or pests, and that remain under the fitted sheet.
Bedspreads, usually white and generally of cotton, with raised designs done either in weft loop weave or needlework, using a heavy thread resembling the wicks used by candlemakers.
All-white cotton coverlets with distinctive geometric designs in weft loop weave. Originally made in Bolton, England, and copied in North America.
Rag coverlets in the Scottish tradition.
Quilts made of identical, repeating patterned units.
Quilts made to commemorate events ranging from international to local significance, for example wars, political campaigns, or centennials.
Particularly fine album quilts made by a group of women living in the Baltimore area in the mid-19th century.
Quilts constructed of blocks, made and signed by a number of different people as a remembrance, as would be the pages of an autograph album. Often pieced or appliquéd with pictorial motifs.
Quilts made to commemorate a two-hundredth anniversary.
Mourning quilts made from clothing of the deceased.
Quilts depicting flags or incorporating real flags.
Patriotic Hawaiian quilts depicting the Hawaiian flag, sometimes with the royal coat of arms or other royal symbol at the center.
Instruments consisting of a rectangular soundbox bearing one metal string, furnished with a projecting keyboard and terminating in a small oval body set on folding legs.

Small free-reed instruments consisting of a grooved rectangular metal box on which free reeds are mounted, played by moving it back and forth in front of the player's mouth while inhaling or exhaling.
Scrap quilts theoretically composed of 999 different printed cottons, no two of which could be alike. Always done in one-patch designs.
Crazy quilts constructed of square blocks, long strips, stars, or diamonds, or having some other regular format.
Quilts decorated with the letters of the alphabet, sometimes illustrated with appropriate objects, such as an apple with the letter A.

Small perforated containers used for sprinkling sugar, salt, mustard, or other spices, especially at the table. Casters may be of varying shape and material either made as one piece, with holes in the top and filled through a corked or otherwise plugged hole in the bottom, or made as two pieces, with a threaded stopper or screw cap. Casters of various types and for various purposes were historically made in a set, often fitting onto a tray and set upon a table during dining. Casters were often made for use with a specific spice, sugar, or salt, but the forms are often very similar or identical, so that attributing a particular caster to its intended use may be difficult.
Vessels used to contain or receive water that is used in practices involving washing the body of oneself or of another, or of a thing; common in many religions, or as cultural practice.

Afro-Cuban drums, generally single-headed and with nail tension, approximately cylindrical or barrel-shaped and open at the bottom; they are played with two drumsticks. For the snared double-headed cylindrical drums of the Yoruba people of Nigeria, see "bembes."

Large cylindrical drums, usually double-headed, with a rather shallow body, the diameter always being greater than the length. When played, each head faces sideways and is struck close to the rim with a padded stick.
End-blown flutes of the Maori, made of wood, clay, or whale tooth, with conical bore, usually three fingerholes, and terminating in a short upturned snout.
Individual copies of books or other publications, including prints, made for presentation by the author, usually a gift.

Receptacles used in Roman Catholic services to burn the coals needed for censing, and to light the Paschal candle on Holy Saturday, usually on a tripod, or a three-footed stand of varying height. The brazier is typcially accompanied by liturgical tongs and a scoop.
Footed dessert dishes having a wide but shallow bowl.

Ceremonial tea bowls of various designs used for preparing and drinking tea in East Asian tea ceremonies. They are traditionally small earthenware vessels without handles, often glazed in muted tones and characterized by an aesthetic of irregularity or imperfection.
Instruments designed to measure the percentage of ammonia in an aqueous solution.
Recording hygrometers.
Tools comprised of a conjoined hygrometer and thermograph, which record temperature and relative humidity conditions in which sensitive objects are displayed or stored.
Instruments for measuring atmospheric pressure.

Drinking vessels, usually in the form of a cylindrical cup but sometimes slightly tapering, having a flat base with a low foot ring and one vertical handle; especially those made of silver or pewter in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Small lidded vessels, almost always cup-shaped and sometimes having handles, used to wash the celebrant's fingers in the context of a Christian communion service.

A large type of urn with a wide lip used for funerary purposes in ancient Etruria, particularly during the 10th-8th centuries BCE. Early Villanovan burials were often characterized by the use of such urns; one handle would be knocked off in a ritual destruction of the vessel. Biconical urns often stood as a shorthand for the body of the deceased and were often capped by a military helmet.
Receptacles for smokers' tobacco ashes, made in a great range of sizes and designs.
Moorish Revival architecture seen primarily on the Iberian Peninsula and in Ibero-America.
Cases or coverings into which pointed iron or wooden tools used in nautical contexts for rope splicing and other functions.

Shallow containers designed to be used for urination or defecation by persons confined to bed. For containers found in a bed chamber, but not necessarily designed for use in the bed, prefer "chamber pots." For portable vessels for urine, prefer "urinals (containers)."
Pocket-size containers, such as bags or rolls of cloth, for carrying small articles such as thread, needles and scissors.
Bell-shaped glass domes placed over delicate plants to protect them from the weather and to force their growth.
Instruments for measuring the length of curved or straight lines on maps or plans.
Inkwells in a stand or structure that also includes one or more candlesticks.
Spanish water vessels of porous, unglazed earthenware used for cooling water by evaporation.
Disposable containers, made of food-safe paper, used to cook food in ovens.
Small tray designed for supporting or carrying ampollae and other small bottles or flasks, often having a handle mounted vertically in the center of the tray.
Containers made of palm fronds to preserve dates.
Drinking glasses that have a complex, often twisting and intertwined, stem. The glasses may be flutes, goblets, wine glasses, or of many other forms.
Vessels used for preparing and serving alcoholic beverages, such as glasses, decanters, and cocktail shakers. May also include other utensils used at a bar to prepare drinks.
Incense pot, usually clay, widely found in Gambian homes and used to burn incense in order to provide protection from spirits.
Flowmeters for measuring and recording the amount of gas moving through a pipe, as for calculating household consumption.
Recording actinometers.
Acidmeters, ranging from small hand-held devices to larger stationary devices designed to sit on a work bench, used test the pH levels in cheese.
Hydrometers for the determination of the alcoholic content expressed in Gay-Lussac degrees. The device was invented by French physicist and chemist Louis Gay-Lussac.

Scales with a horizontal bar pivoting about a central fulcrum, creating equal-length arms; suspended from the ends of the arms are pans or baskets, in one of which is placed the item being weighed and in the other, a premeasured weight.
Instruments for determining the weight of objects or substances.
Instruments for determining the weight or density of air or other gases.
Oceanographic instruments for measuring the depth of water.

Chinese spike fiddles having two strings, a long neck of hardwood with two tuning pegs at the upper end, and a tubular, hexagonal, or octagonal resonator covered at one end with snakeskin. They are played with a horsehair bow which passes between the two strings.

Instruments that measure and indicate the passage of time, especially by mechanical means producing a regularly recurring action and indicating, usually by hands or changing numbers, the hours and minutes; not designed to be worn or otherwise carried about on a person. For wearable timepieces, see "watches."
Timepieces used to register the time of an event or graphically register specific time intervals, such as for the duration of events.
Devices that take conformations of things, especially human heads for hat-fitting.
Small cheaply made high-pitched fipple flutes, usually made of metal or plastic and having six fingerholes.
Thin glass globes used to measure the density of gases by weighing the globe in the gases.
Cake pans with a hinged or clamped side that can be unfastened to facilitate releasing the cake when done.

Small crucibles used for cupellation, made of a porous, refractory material such as bone ash and used to melt small amounts of metal, usually silver, for the extraction of lead, or gold, for assaying.
Coasters for holding a bottle of wine on a table.
Any device used to determine the strength of an acid. Refers to an electronic instrument in more recent use.

term: Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints
definition: Refers to the largest denomination and principal body of the Mormon religion. By the late 20th century it had more than 9,700,000 members. Its headquarters are in Salt Lake City, Utah. An important leader of this denomination was Brigham Young (1801-1877), who led the trek to Utah in 1847, founding Salt Lake City.

Instruments that consist of a metal plate, two heel abutments opposite to each other and an adjustable ball joint abutment with a sliding pointer and sliding indicators with number and letter markings for the length, width and arch length of the human foot. Used to measure a person's shoe size.
Instruments designed to measure the numerical aperture of microscope objectives.
Precision instruments with a spindle moved by a finely threaded screw that touches the object to be measured, usually for recording thicknesses.
The scientific study of human history in its biological, linguistic, and social aspects.
Navigational compasses consisting of a pivoted compass card, usually with 8, 16, or 32 equal divisions, set in a gimbal-mounted nonferrous metal bowl.
Instruments for measuring and indicating a horizontal reference direction relative to magnetic north.
Instruments designed to observe the positions and measure the altitude of celestial bodies; used from the 2nd century BCE, until superseded by sextants.
Instruments for measuring variations in the gravitational field of the earth by detecting small differences in the weight of an object of constant mass.
Devices for measuring the direction of a magnetic field relative to astronomical or survey coordinates.
Instruments that measure and record the amount of exposure to nuclear radiation over a given period.
Instruments for measuring the optical effects of color.

Photoelectric instruments equipped to measure the absorption of nearly monochromatic light in the visible range by a gas or liquid and so determine the concentration of the absorbing constituents in the gas or liquid.

Coverings for pamphlets, each cover consisting of two boards connected by a cloth hinge to which an additional tape or strip of material is attached. The pamphlet is then sewn or adhered to the strip.
Clocks with a bell or buzzer that can be set to sound at a particular time, as to awaken someone.
Large, circular, dishlike vessels upon which money, collected in church from the congregation in smaller containers, is assembled and presented at the altar.
Devices for measuring the velocity and attenuation of sound waves in a gas or liquid by studying the interference pattern set up by two waves generated from the same source.

Glasses having tall, narrow conical-shaped bowls designed expressly for champagne and other sparkling wine. Used especially for modern glasses with this form, where the bowl is not typically not as tall as early flutes.

Embedded air pockets used as decoration of glass, comprising large, intentionally created air bubbles or tears, arranged in a decorative pattern, often in criss-crossed diagonal rows or spirals. Often seen in the stems of 18th-century and later wine glasses, particularly English.
Containers used for the rearing or breeding of livestock.

Type of knop with flat sharp edges which occurs along the stem or which joins the bowl or foot to the stem of stemware. For other encircling rings on stemware or other vessels, use "collars (container components)."
Items that cover, protect, or close a container or other object, usually by fitting around a cylindrical rim or collar.
Type of spout that is attached to a pouring vessel by a horizontal bar or decorative ornament.
Term generally applied to any textile used to cover a bed.
Blankets with an inner wiring system and thermostatic control, which provide constant warmth.
Coarse, heavy lap robes used by passengers aboard ship.
Trade blankets made for the Hudson's Bay Company, of various weights and colors, often patterned with broad weft bands and points.
Sarapes with slits in the center, allowing them to be slipped over the head.

Objects with the same weight, and sometimes design, as specific coins in general circulation and usually of brass or other base metal, rarely of glass, created to insure proper metallic content and weight; known in antiquity, but used especially from the 4th century CE to around 1800.
Keyboards that can be worn around the body, especially popular in the 1980s. Handles are similar to the necks of guitars and feature controls for pitch, modulation, and volume.
In ancient Rome, an incense box, usually made out of precious metal but also sometimes of wood or marble, used in sacrifices.
Containers used for the transport and protection of audio recordings.

Liturgical containers, often in the shape of coffins, that hold sacred earth or ashes from Ash Wednesday that are meant to be buried in the coffin of a deceased person, so that the dead is considered buried in consecrated ground. This practice dates from a period in which Catholics were forbidden to perform religious rites in Dutch cemeteries. In Old Catholic parishes this practice is still in use.
Baskets or basketlike containers intended primarily for carrying laundry; often oval or rectangular and generally with a pair of handles at the rim.
Boxes or enclosed places used to hold or store coal.

Small ancient Greek or Roman vessels for holding oils, ointments, or perfumes; usually elongated in form, almost cylindrical, and rounded at the bottom. Some footed examples also exist. They either have no handles or one small handle at the side. Alabastra are small enough to be held in one hand or it could be carried by a string looped around its narrow neck or passed through smal lugs on the shoulder. The shape originated in Egypt, where it was made in glass, faience, or alabaster (it takes its name from this stone).
Titles stamped or lettered on the spine of a bound volume by the binder, as distinct from the cover title on the publisher's edition and the title printed on the title page.

Native American duct flutes traditionally made of wood or cane, in which the bore is blocked by a partition which forces the airstream out through a hole where an external block, normally of wood tied on to the tube, channels the air along the exterior of the tube to a second hole where it impinges on the voicing edge; traditionally used as a man's solo courting instrument.
Gothic scripts employed especially in the 14th and 15th centuries that combine characteristics of the Gothic cursive and the more formal textura.
Five-string pluriarcs of Gabon and western Angola.

Short cylindrical Japanese reedpipes with double reed and conical bore, having seven front fingerholes, two rear thumbholes, and a ring of cane guarding the reed. Originating in China and known in Japan since the 8th century, they were formerly made of hardwood, bone, or horn, but now usually of bamboo lacquered on the inside.

Reedpipes with double reed and cylindrical bore, with a wind cap covering the reed, a body curved at the lower end and slightly flared at the opening, one thumbhole, seven fingerholes, and one or more ventholes in the curved lower section; modern versions often have a key above the top fingerhole.

Generally all reedpipes with single reed and essentially cylindrical bore. May also refer specifically to those reedpipes with single reed used as solo and orchestral instruments in Western jazz, classical, folk, and band music.
Teakettles made en suite with a stand which has a heating device.

Casting bottles designed and used to sprinkle fragrance, usually rosewater, in a room or for guests or others to sprinkle lightly on their fingers or elsewhere on their person. Important examples are rosewater bottles traditionally used in the Middle East to sprinkle rosewater.
Bell-shaped glass jars or covers for protecting delicate instruments or natural or fabricated objects from dust or damage. Also, vessels for containing gases or a vacuum in chemical experiments.

Kettles that boil water using electricity; specifically, electric kettles have within them heating elements that contain electrical resistance, such as coils, and the resistance turns the electrical energy flowing through the coils into heat.
Aerophones consisting of a spatulate piece of wood, bone, stone, or similar material, tied to a string and sounded by being whirled through the air by the player holding the free end of the string.

Concussion instruments consisting of a pair of small shallow cup-shaped pieces of hardwood, strung together, hollow sides facing each other, on a cord which loops around the player's thumb. The two pieces are clicked together by the fingers. Usually two pairs are played together, one higher-pitched than the other.

Idiophones invented in the 1920s consisting of a small flexible steel blade or lamella suspended in a wire frame ending in a handle. As the player waves the instrument, the blade is struck alternately on each side by wooden or rubber knobs on the end of wires fastened to the frame. For instruments whose sound is produced essentially by plucking lamellae, use "lamellaphones."
Percussion idiophones made by cutting, burning, or gouging a slit in the wall of a hollowed-out piece of wood, used for musical or signaling purposes.
Clusters of small bells or metal discs, usually referring to such bells arranged on a strap, loop of wire, or handle, and sounded by shaking or striking.
Instruments consisting of a series of rattling objects hung from a frame.
Brazilian scrapers, made of a bamboo tube with transverse notches, which the player scrapes with a small stick.
Latin American instruments consisting of a long gourd or similar tubular object with notches cut in its surface which are scraped with a stick.

Keyboard instruments having the form of a small upright piano in which metal plates (usually steel) suspended over resonating boxes are struck by hammers and sustained in a manner similar to piano action.
British copper, bronze, or tin coins equal to one fourth of a British penny; introduced in the 13th century and withdrawn in 1961.
Flutes sounded by the player blowing against the sharp rim of a hole in the side of the tube.
English silver or cupronickel coins valued at twelve pence and minted from the mid-16th century until 1970.
Extreme dryness.
The phenomena associated with electric and magnetic fields and their interactions with each other and with electric charges and currents.
Resting bells of Afro-Cuban origin. They are struck, and clapperless. In some locations, they are multiple bells.
Suspended bells sounded by a swinging clapper attached inside.
Bake ovens having a shape resembling a beehive.

Silver standing cups of which the bowl and cover together are in the form of an acorn and generally with a trunklike stem; of a type made in England in the late 16th century and early 17th century. Acorn cups are similar to gourd cups and reflect the taste of the time for natural forms.
Distinctive type of Japanese drums set on the stand horizontally and played by tapping the right drumhead with a narrow stick held in each hand.
Literally, a "blood banner." Generally surmounted by a flint in the iconography of postclassic central Mexico, this red painted banner was an attribute of warriors and the deity Huitzilopochtli.
Long narrow flags, scrolls, or streamers, often with a cleft end, flying from the mast-heads of ships, carried by hand, carried in battle, and for other uses.
Refers to a forked or triangular double-sided pennant; a standard carried to identify a military unit.
Near Eastern double clarinets with one melody pipe with six fingerholes and one drone pipe, very much longer and with several detachable extensions to vary the pitch.
Devices specifically for measuring the space between two points.
Devices for measuring forces in physical nature, such as gravity and magnetism.
Devices used to measure the shapes formed by two line segments that meet at a common point.
Any instruments for making recordings, either continuously or intermittantly, of the successive values of a number of different physical quantities, such as heat, light, and moisture.
Mechanical pressure-measuring instruments employing as sensing elements a curved or twisted metal tube, flattened in cross-section and closed.
Devices that measure electricity, such as those that measure current flow, electrical resistance, and electrical consumption.
Instruments for measuring the strength of electric current flow, amperage, in amperes.
Instruments for measuring the rate of evaporation of water into the atmosphere.
Oceanographic instruments that measure and record temperature at various depths in the ocean; often used by ships underway.
Light measuring devices specifically for measuring color and color properties.
Instruments for measuring, indicating, or recording accelerative forces, such as those imparted by gravity or aeronautical devices.
Instruments that measure the inclination of the wind from the horizontal plane.
Astronomical clocks that indicate sidereal time.
Graduated rings designed to fit over compasses, compass repeaters, or similar direction finders and often equipped with sighting vanes for measuring azimuths.
Long, fine, usually spiral, springs used to determine the time of oscillation of balance wheels of timepieces.
Precision balances with a sensitivity of 0.1 to 0.01 mg.
Instruments that measure the angles at which x-rays, neutrons, or electrons are diffracted by matter; used to study atomic crystal structure.

Barometers that depend on neither hydrostatic equilibrium nor the laws of gases but instead on measurement of force exerted by the atmosphere on some component of the mechanical system; often calibrated for use as altimeters.
Aneroid barometers equipped with an automatic recording mechanism.
Crossbars of balances, from the ends of which the pans or baskets are suspended.

Various processes performed with type and typefaces, including setting type and creating layouts with type for printing. For the process of designing type used in the practice of typography, use "type design."
The spacing of words and letters within a line of type so that all full lines in a column have even margins on both the left and the right.
Calipers that may be used as either inside or outside calipers or as dividers.

Devices intended for use in a laboratory environment primarily in reading levels of a liquid in a capillary tube to determine surface tension, or for determining the changes in the liquid level during a chemical reaction.
Instruments that measure and indicate the altitude of an object above a fixed level, such as sea level or ground level.
Instruments that measure the optical density of areas of photographic film or paper, for color saturation and to calibrate print equipment, and generally to make adjustments for quality control.
Extremely accurate electronic clocks regulated by the resonance frequency of atoms or molecules, such as cesium or ammonia.

Refers to a Chicano and Latino subculture or lifestyle associated with a particular set of dress, behavior, and worldview that originated in Los Angeles.
