Cholo was once a derogatory term for people of mixed-bloodheritage in the Spanish Empire in Latin America and its successor states, but was reclaimed by Chicano youth in the 1960s and emerged as a popular identification in the late 1970s. Cholos/cholas are often stereotyped and unfairly associated with criminal behavior and gang activity. The cholo/chola subculture has spread to cities in the United States with large Chicano or Latino populations, including New York.

A water-soluble, tasteless colloidal form of processed collagen obtained from bones, hooves or skins and used as a dispersing agent, sizing medium, adhesive, or coating for photographic films, and stabilizer for foodstuffs and pharmaceutical preparations. Is high in molecular weight after processing, as opposed to more vigorously processed collagen which results in animal glue.

Prepared outside membrane of the large intestine of cattle used primarily to separate individual gold leaves during the final stages of preparing gold leaf. Occasionally used for the repair of skin artifacts and as the moisture-sensitive element in hygrometers.
Pelt of any of the fur seals prepared for use in clothing or other artifacts.
Emergency coinage of various denominations issued in 1689 and 1690 in Ireland by supporters of James II of England and made from any available brass or brasslike objects, including cannon.
The white and black variety of marble from Marmara Adasi, Turkey.
Unintentional variations in the color of a rug caused by irregular dyeing of the yarn, or by using yarn from a different dye lot.

General term for the cultures and styles, regardless of period, of the westernmost protrusion of Asia, which makes up the majority of the modern Republic of Turkey. To refer to the ancient cultures of this region, use "Anatolian," although there is overlap in usage. To distinguish the nationality of the modern nation of Turkey, use "Turkish."
Idiophones consisting of a lamella carved in the surface of a nut, fruit shell, or other globular object which serves as a resonator; the lamella is plucked by the player's thumb.
Adhesive postage stamps already canceled in advance of mailing.
Postage stamps authorizing the delivery of mail by air.
Sliding rattles found in Indonesia. They are constructed from bamboo tubes with cut-back tongues, inserted into a frame; when the frame is shaken, the tubes slide back and forth.
Sheets of stamps or large portions of sheets as issued for sale by a postal service.

Historically a form of paper currency used in Europe from the late Medieval to the early Modern period often as credit among merchants. Now refers to written orders to pay a specific sum of money on demand or at a specified future time; used with reference to foreign transactions; for similar orders to pay usually restricted to domestic transactions, use "drafts (negotiable instruments)."
Credit instruments specifying the drawer's intention to pay at the date of maturity; generally applied to drafts and bills of exchange.
Matter prepared or to be prepared for printing, often referring to both text and images, sometimes to the text as distinguished from the images.
Advertising materials for those selling books.
Badges worn as identifying insignia by beggars. For example, as found in the early 15th century in Great Britain and Ireland.
Highly detailed or finished layouts, especially for one-page pieces; for more extensive detailed layouts, including representation of the arrangement of pages, use "dummies (printed matter)."
Open harps in which the neck makes a sharp angle with the resonator.
Harps having a string for each semitone, and thus able to play a full chromatic range without the need for tuning devices such as pedals or hooks.

Experimental musical instruments in the friction idiophone family invented by Hans Reichel ca. 1980s. These are made of wood, and consist of a 'tongue' that is fixed in a block that contains one or more contact microphones. The tongue is bowed with a conventional stringed instrument bow while simultaneously pressing down on the the tongue with another piece of shaped wood called a 'dax,' thus achieving various tonalities or notes. The tongue can also be excited by plucking. The shape of the tongue, and the type of wood also influence the sound.
Books or similar documents that recount, describe, and depict a coronation and associated festivities and events.

Single-headed frame drums of Ireland, with a membrane of animal skin and a criss-cross arrangement of cord, sticks, or wire over the open end by which they are held with one hand; they are struck by the free hand or alternately by the knobs at each end of the stick.
Single-reed reedpipes of conical bore, with the shape of a bassoon.

A class of electronic devices that alter the sound of a musical instrument or another electronic audio source through audio signal processing. These are most commonly used either in recording or performance contexts.
Pages covered with intricate ornament, sometimes with a central cross motif, as in certain Insular manuscripts, sometimes composed of minute script, as in certain Hebrew manuscripts.
Coverings of a book which hold the sheets together to provide protection, and collectively all the parts of books applied in the process of attaching the leaves and covering them.
Pieces of material adhered to the back of a text block prior to casing-in, or used to line the inside of the cover along the spine.
Two-manual five-octave electronic organs made by the Hammond Organ Co., with electronic tone generation.

Fretted electric stringed instruments based on the same principle as the electric guitar, invented by Emmett Chapman in the early 1970s. It is most commonly strung with 10 to 12 strings and is played by tapping and fretting the strings instead of plucking. There are many variations of the instrument, including bass models.
Marks or symbols, particularly those that are incised or inscribed.

Standardized ideogrammatic symbols used to represent concepts, emotional states, or other information wordlessly and succinctly in electronic communications such as text messages, e-mail, and social media. Originally Japanese, from e: “picture, drawing” and moji “letter, character.”
The symbols 0, 1, 2, and so forth, derived from Arabic numerical notation in the late Middle Ages in Europe.

Device having one or more bells mounted to a wheel, the turning of which rings the bells, usually clapper bells. The devices may be of various sizes and used for various purposes. One use of the device is as a sanctus bell during the Catholic mass.

Genre of visual poetry, particularly of the concrete poetry movement of the 1950s and 1960s, in which language elements are arranged freely, not necessarily in linear syntax, and meaning is derived from spatial, pictorial, and typographic characteristics of the work, as well as from the sense of the words. For pre-20th-century works of visual poetry in which letters, words, or lines are arranged to form a shape or image, usually related to the meaning of the words, see "pattern poetry."
Group of typefaces characterized by heavy faces and angular outlines, based on Gothic hand-written scripts.
Animal or vegetable refuse from the shipping, processing, or preparation of food.
Italic typeface having exaggerated serif, terminal, tail, entry stroke, or other flourish or flourishes. Capital swashes are often used as the first letter of a word beginning a paragraph.
A type of basket woven from palm fronds.

Cases or covers, often of cloth and decorated, used to hold the afiqoman, which is a piece broken from the second of the three matsot, set before the leader of a Seder and put aside to be eaten at the end of the meal.

Containers or receptacles of leather, cloth, paper, or other flexible material, often capable of being closed at the mouth. For ladies' bags intended to carry personal articles, use "bags (costume accessories)." For large containers of cloth or plastic for carrying, transporting, or storing produce and other items, use "sacks."

Cloth or velvet bags usually richly decorated with beadwork, made distinctive by its bottom terminating in eight separate arms. Created by Métis and First Nations communities  to carry ammunition, fire starters, and/or tobacco. Likely originated in the early 1800s amongst the Métis and spread to other Native North Americans across Canada and the United States.
Large casks or barrels; especially ones of a capacity between 63 and 140 gallons.
Large casks of varying capacity, but usually 80 gallons.

Pressurized kegs, made of a wide variety of materials, including wood, plastic, and aluminum, and now made predominantly of stainless steel, used for storing, transporting, and dispensing beer. Although standard beer kegs featured the curved sides mimicking barrel staves, most contemporary beer kegs are straight-sided cylindrical containers..
Casks, tuns, or other vessels used for storing water, beer, or other liquids.
Small pouch containers for sacred, protective, or lucky items.

Refers to many varieties of relatively large drinking vessels without handles, cylindrical or conical in shape, with a flat base in the form of an open cup or goblet. Specifically, in archaeology refers to the tall wide-mouthed vessels produced by the Bell Beaker culture and found in certain early Bronze Age graves.
Any of several laboratory testing techniques based on the binding of antigen to antibody that are used to detect or measure biochemical substances involved in immunological reactions.
Use both for bronze coins of the Roman Republic and for copper coins used during the Roman Empire from the 1st century BCE through the 3rd century CE.
Small, silver Greek coins originally equivalent to six obols and issued from the 6th century BCE; usage continued by the Parthians and Sassanians until the 7th century CE.
Refers to the lower of two dies between which coins are struck.

Chalices used in some Christian rites for ablution or rinsing; the ablution chalice holds unconsecrated wine or water, which is used after the eucharistic ceremony to rinse away the remains of the consecrated host.
Classes of letters and other visual symbols that represent a phoneme or cluster of phonemes, which are unit of sound in a language.
System of shorthand used in ancient Roman and early Medieval writing.

A technique of decoration employed in Spain for tiles and other wares which superseded the cuerda seca method. It involved impressing the pattern on tiles to form ridges which prevented the colored glazes from intermingling.

Titles of works or major divisions of works, such as parts or chapters, when they appear at the beginning of the first page of the text, often though not always set below the normal level of the first line of the page. Use also for the titles of musical scores when they appear immediately above the opening bars of the music.
Refers to the adjoining inner margins of two facing pages of type.
Headbands worked on two cores, usually one being smaller than the other and placed either above, or below and in front of the other one.
Light that falls across a surface at an acute angle, often revealing irregularities of the surface.
Lighting techniques in which 90 to 100 percent of the light is directed toward the surface to be illuminated; usually downward light.
The quality of having different characteristics, as properties or dimensions, along different axes.
The structure of a cell revealed by electron microscopy.
Coins or medals without any inscriptions (legends).
Documents that confirm that the bearer is authorized to board a commercial conveyance such as passenger aircraft.
Describes currency manufactured from paper originating in Asia, used from the 8th century.

A waxy, odorous substance of marbled ashy color produced in the intestines of the sperm whale, and often found floating in tropical seas, or on the seashore. Formerly used as an ingredient in perfumery to prevent evaporation, more recently it has been replaced in this function by synthetic substances.
Bodily waste discharged through the anus.
Excrement of animals, rarely of humans, particularly when used to fertilize the soil or, when dried, as a building material.

Refers to fermented urine, formerly exploited for its ammonia content in various industrial applications. Lant was once commonly used in the textile industry as a scouring agent for wool and as a dyebath with indigo and other dyes.

Remanence that is being examined or analyzed with regard to archaeological remains. When examined with regard to geologic materials, especially those predating human civilization, prefer "paleomagnetism."
The capacity of a material to retain its shape and resist change to its physical size under set conditions.
Medals that are formed by two halves that screw together to form a shallow, medal-shaped box.These usually contain one or more images on the inside surfaces.

Material derived from eggs, which in the context of art materials are usually the ellipsoidal shell and embryonic contents produced by birds. For paintings, the egg contents are used as a tempera medium. The whole egg, yolk, or white may be used sometimes mixed with oil and/or resin. The egg yolk is a stable emulsion of an aqueous liquid with an oily, proteinaceous medium which dries quickly into a hard, insoluble film. Egg white has been used as a medium for illuminated manuscripts. It is also used as a size for attaching gold leaf. Albumen is the adhesive substance of egg white. As a pure film, albumen is clear, brittle, and water soluble. Water solubility can be decreased by heating or adding tannin. For the exterior of a bird egg comprising the brittle shell composed of keratin and calcite, use "eggshell (animal material)."

Material comprising or processed from the hard exterior covering of eggs, usually eggs of chickens or other birds. The thin, brittle shell from an egg is primarily composed of keratin and calcite. Eggshell may be decorated and valued intact or as a component of a cup or other object. Eggshell is also used as pigment and in grounds for silver point drawings. For preparation, the shells are washed, crushed and boiled in water with some quicklime. The sequence is repeated until the eggshells form a fine, white powder.
Paper money made legal tender by government decree but that is not based on nor convertible into coin.
Generally describes objects that can be moved into a variety of proper positions, shapes, or configurations appropriate to a specific use.
The bony frameworks or supports of an animal body considered as a whole.
Bones in the hindlimbs of tetrapods; in humans, the bone that articulates with the acetabulum of the pelvis at the hip, and with the tibia and patella at the knee.
Use to describe objects or structures when emphasizing that they have been designed by architects.
The function, quality, or activity of having instruction or teaching as a primary or ulterior purpose.

Refers to style and movement associated with a group of Polish painters and sculptors that worked between 1917 and 1922 and who were primarily known as Polish Expressionists from 1917 to 1919. The Formists exhibited works for the first time in Kraków in 1917, endeavoring to form a distinct national style in alliance with the ideologies behind Polish modernism.

Material made from antlers, which are paired deciduous outgrowths of bone projecting from the frontal bones of ungulates of the deer family. Distinguished from "horn," which is modified skin tissue or compacted hair.

Material made from hard, bone-like structures grown in the mouth of vertebrates; distinguishable from other bone by its structure. Animal teeth, such as from hippopotami, whales, lions, dogs, boars, bears, and humans have been used to make jewelry, gaming pieces, buttons, and and other items.

Intensely hard calcareous substance covering the dentin, that is, part or all of the crown of the tooth in mammals. Enamel, when mature, consists predominantly of apatite crystals containing calcium and phosphate. Enamel is the hardest tissue of the body; it is not living and contains no nerves. The thickness and density of enamel vary over the surface of the tooth.

The modified form of dentin derived from animal teeth. The most common example is from the tusks of mature elephants; similar material is obtained from any tusked or large-toothed mammal such as a walrus or narwhal.
Material comprising or processed from the hard exterior covering of an egg of the emu, an Australian flightless bird. An emu eggshell is dark green in color.
Hard outer covering of invertebrate creatures, composed of calcareous or chitinous material.
Weathervanes in the form of roosters.

Term used to describe pigments or dyes that fade or change color due to the action of light. It does not refer to color changes caused by chemical reactions with the atmosphere or surrounding materials.
Christian religious season lasting from the fourth Sunday before Christmas until Christmas, observed by some as a period of prayer and fasting.
Paper money issued by the French revolutionary government between 1789 and 1796.
The first national paper money of the United States, authorized for issue in 1775.

Styles originating in or expressing ideals supported by the post-World War I review "Zenit," which supported a strong ideology promising a brighter future, a new man, and a new society expressed in free artistic forms and Expressionism, including free verse and new typographic and graphic forms.
Works, particularly artistic or written works, produced relatively early in the maker's career.

Subgroups within a larger cultural or social order that are distinguished from the majority and each other by their national, religious, linguistic, cultural, or sometimes racial background. For groups that are the objects of prejudice or discrimination from the majority, use "minorities."
Groups of spectators, listeners, or viewers.
Recognized groups of persons of appromimately the same age in a community, especially common in Africa.
The practice and activity of breeding, raising, feeding, and tending animals, especially but not exclusively domestic farm animals.

Leather made from the skin of a ray fish and characterized by a covering of pearl-like papillae usually ground flat leaving a pattern of tiny contiguous circles which are further emphasized by dyeing.
Roof-like coverings, usually of canvas or metal and often adjustable, placed over windows, doors, or decks to provide protection from sun and rain.
Form of farming in which crops are grown reliant upon the varying residual moisture in delta areas and other floodplains.
Glue made from degraded or denatured collagen obtained from bones.

A flexible insulating material composed of loosely felted fiberglass fibers, used for thermal or acoustical insulation and available in precut, standard lengths, usually one inch thick and 17-36 inches wide. A long, continuous roll of batt insulation is also called blanket "insulation."
Part of hide or skin consisting of fibrous connective tissue. The layer of hide or skin from which leather is made.

A fine, lustrous, natural fiber obtained from the catepillar cocoons of silk moths, such as the domesticated Bombyx mori. Silkworm silk is composed of a heavy and light chain of core proteins called fibroins, which are coated by sericin, a collection of sticky, glue-like proteins.  Microscopically, raw silk appears as two strands that are held together with sericin protein. According to legend, silk was discovered by Chinese Empress Si-Ling-Shi when a cocoon fell in her tea. China maintained a monopoly on the production of silk fabric for almost 3,000 years.The worms were first cultivated in Japan about 195 CE and in Europe about 555 CE.
Material derived from the bill of a bird or similar horny mouthpart in other animals, such as the squid.

Chitosan is the deacetylated form of chitin, the chief component in the exoskeletons of crustaceans, insects, and beetles. It is used in horticulture and agriculture as a biopesticide, and plant growth enhancer; and in medicine as a coagulant. As a sprayed coating, cyanoethylated chitosan is used to protect historic paper material. Chitosan is also found as an organic component incorporated into polymer materials to form a self-healing coating which promises to render the painted surfaces it is applied to scratch-free.

Material comprising the cylindrical filaments that grow from follicles embedded in the skin of mammals. Hair is a column of overlapping, fused cells that are composed of the protein keratin; hair is composed of three parts: the innermost column is the medula, the surrounding live cells (the cortex) contain pigment, and the outermost dead transparent cells are the cuticular scales. The portion of the hair outside of the skin is called the shaft. Fine, closely spaced hair that covers most of an animal's body is called fur. Dense, soft, curled hair is called wool. Coarse, stiff hairs are called bristles, spines, or quills. Horsehair and cattle hair have been used for brushes, plaster binders, haircloth, and upholstery stuffing. Rabbit hair, often called rabbit fur, has been used to make felt hats.
The inner deep or center part of a structure, such as of a hair.
Structural and decorative elements at the bottoms of columns upon which the columns are supported. Column bases may aggregate plinths, sub-plinths, and column mouldings.
Foliate or clawlike ornaments that project from the round base of a column toward a corner of a plinth.

Aerophones in which the sound is produced by metal or cane tongues which vibrate through a closely fitting frame, moving freely at one end and held down at the other; the pitch is determined by the length and mass of the tongue.

Apparatus of glass or metal formerly used in distillation. They are in the shape of an inverted bowl with an internal gutter along the rim into which the condensed vapor descends and from which extends a long horizontally sloping tube to the receptacle for the distilled liquid.
Artists' brushes made of hog, pig, or boar bristle.
Double-ended metal spatulas that are heated and used to burn in colors in encaustic paintings.
United States copper or bronze coins minted at various times between 1793 and 1857 and valued at one half of a cent.
Silver or cupronickel coins valued at 100 cents; originally from a  silver coin that circulated in many European countries, from the German "thaler."
The first distinctive Australian coins, created by overstriking Pieces of Eight from which the center had been punched out; issued between 1813 and 1829 and valued at 5 shillings.
Periods of time devoted to rest, relaxation, or recreation.
Typewriters, the movement of which is governed by electrical power.
Addiction to alcoholic beverages.

The long term or excessive use or misuse of narcotics, alcohol, or other substances. For the state of being physically or psychologically habituated to a substance or practice to such an extent that its cessation causes severe trauma, use "addiction."
Those who are addicted to narcotics or other drugs.
Excessive use or misuse of drugs, causing physical, emotional, mental, or sensory injury or impairment. For addiction to narcotics or other drugs, use "drug addiction."
Those who are addicted to alcoholic beverages.
Affixing the initials of one's name to something.

The process or activity of preparing beer from barley or other grains. The brewing process can be divided into four steps: mashing, separating, boiling and fermentation. Different approaches to the brewing process lead to variation in beers and beer types.
Refers to 18th century chair stretchers that combine balusters or other turned elements with blocks.
The earliest developmental stage of a living being.
People who are afflicted that an illness or disease so serious that there is no chance of recovery.

Refers to paintings, photographs, or art in other media in which the subject is a female nude in a suggestive pose or other erotica. It generally refers specifically to pictures dating from the 17th through 19th centuries in Western art, when such pictures would have typically been displayed in a smoking room, study, or other domestic room frequented primarily by men. The female subjects commonly assumed traditional poses known from older, more traditional art, such as the reclining nude originally depicted in iconography of the mythological characters Venus or Diana.
Stage of early childhood, commonly considered to be the period before being able to walk.

Stage of physical development at which living beings first become capable of sexual reproduction, marked by the maturing of the reproductive organs and the development of secondary sexual characteristics. In human beings it usually occurs between the ages of 10 and 15, and in North American common law it is defined as the age of 14 for boys and 12 for girls.
Stage of adult life between young adulthood and old age; in humans, commonly defined as extending from 45 to 65.
Fighting with fists, usually with gloves over the hands, and often as sport.
State of well-being of an organism or part of one, characterized by normal function and unattended by disease.
Concepts related to the physical and mental growth of human beings.

Condition manifested by subnormal intellectual functioning that originates during the developmental period. This has multiple potential etiologies, including genetic defects and perinatal insults. Intelligence quotient (IQ) scores are commonly used to determine whether an individual has an intellectual disability. IQ scores between 70 and 79 are in the borderline range; scores below 67 are in the disabled range.
Any aberrant or maladaptive patterns of behavior that are sufficiently severe to warrant the attention of counselors or therapists.
Groups of prints related in theme or technique and usually issued together.
Concrete containing fibers of such materials as glass, asbestos, wood, steel and plastic in order to reduce weight and increase tensile strength.

Lay honorary officers of a parish or district church who manage the secular affairs of parish or district churches, particularly those relating to the building and other property.  Formerly, they acted as the sole representatives of the laity of each parish in matters of church business. The term is use particularly in Episcopalian and Anglican churches.
Broad area of commercial or mercantile activity involving the exchange of commodities, services, or financial resources.

Selecting the quality standards required for a project, and monitoring the properties of the finished work to assure compliance with those standards. For the concept of inherent merit, worthiness, or excellence in the context of aesthetic judgment, use "quality."
Alloy of silver and mercury.
Refers to earth spirit figures, made by the Baule people of West Africa, which serve as intermediaries to contact blolo spirits.
Frames incorporating architectural elements consisting mainly of a pair of columns or pilasters that flank the object, support a frieze and pediment, and rest on a base.
Convicts conditionally released from prison prior to the end of their sentence.

Principally used in Classical architecture, the lowest of the three main parts of an entablature that rests on the abacus of a column, comprising a horizontal beam that spans the columns or piers in the manner of a lintel. The other two parts of the entablature are the cornice and the frieze. For the architrave-like molded frame that surrounds a door or window, use "architrave trim." For the ornamental moldings around the exterior curve of an arch, use "archivolts."
Flat strips on Ionic and Corinthian architraves. For boards nailed across the ends of rafters in wood construction, use "fascia boards."
Lithographic printing in colors by means of separate stones or plates for the various colors, with some colors printed over others, of a type used commercially in the latter half of the 19th century.

Surfaces or portions of objects that are opposite to those regarded as fronts or to the most important or useful surfaces. For the adjective describing the location of something at or near the back of something, use "rear." For the parts of seating furniture that supports sitters' backs, use "backs (furniture components)."
Refers to the back, underside, or subordinate surface of coins, medals, seals, or currency notes. Use "versos" for the reverse or subordinate side of sheets of paper.
Refers to the front, top, or principal surface of coins, medals, seals, or other two-sided objects. Use "rectos" specifically for the principal side of sheets of paper.
In Indian architecture, refers to a side; often joined in words, for example in as "dvayasra" or "caturasra."
In heraldry, the top one third of a shield.
Objects created by 3-D printing, whether reproductions or original works.
Table supports of Medieval origin, consisting of two or more inverted T or Y shapes braced by a stretcher or brackets.
Short cylindrical sections of aerophones which couple the mouthpiece to the rest of the tube.

Planar trusses of various configurations in which the diagonal members are in compression and the vertical members are in tension; when the diagonals are in tension and the verticals are in compression, use "Pratt trusses."
Parts and components of drums.
Works that present the illusion of movement and that may be created by a number of techniques including successive drawings, photographing positions of puppets or models, or using computers.
Images so executed as to give a distorted shape to the object represented but which, if viewed from a certain point or using a curved mirror or other instrument, show the object in true proportion.

Pictorial images, usually drawings, that are humorous or that use wit and satire to comment on contemporary events, social habits, political trends, or other topical subjects, often executed in a broad or abbreviated manner. Originally referred to full-page illustrations in a circulating paper or periodical, especially when comical and relating to current events.

Art works, including performance art, designed specifically to interact with an existing work, structure, environment, or situation, be it another artwork, the audience, an institution, or in the public domain.
An art form popular in the 1950s consisting of layers of posters with parts torn away; for the process or art of making them, use "d00ecollage."
Strings which produce a single low tone when played.
Works of art in any medium in which an animal or animals are the primary focus; includes real and imaginary animals.
Consisting of more than one individual crystal having various orientations.
Refers to the aggregation of all playing cards employed in a game.
Recovery and reuse of materials and energy from waste.
Thin flat clappers of bone, ivory, or hardwood played in pairs, usually a pair in each hand.
Short-term, usually three-to-six-month, negotiable instruments that arise from commercial, as opposed to speculative, investment, or real estate, and public or private transactions.
Checks that certify that the signature of the drawer is genuine and that the depositor has sufficient funds on deposit for payment.
Monetary tokens used in the United States, primarily in the 1930s and 1940s, to pay sales tax when coins of proper denomination were not available.

Tokens distributed by any civil, church, or parish council to needy citizens or parishioners. These could be exchanged for clothing, food, fuel, drink or a coffin, all according to the symbol, letter or text it bore.

Tokens entitling the bearer to a portion of bread; usually minted from non-precious metals. Historically these have been issued at different times for various reasons: examples include bronze tokens issued in ancient Rome to citizens to exchange for 'panis civilis,' and in later times, tokens issued to the needy, for example on the occasion of a person's death, often nobility, at their requiem mass.
Coupon that is exchanged for a specific product that is in short supply, often food or fuel.
Lighting of an object or work plane primarily from a specific and preferred direction.

Printing an image so that it extends to the edge of the paper or other printing surface. Distinguished from "bleeding (trimming)" which refers to trimming printed material so that portions of the illustration or text are removed.
A popular genre of spiritual autobiography that proliferated during the last two-thirds of the eighteenth century within the context of the Evangelical Revival in England.
The maintenance policy applied to buildings or sites to uphold their structural integrity, yet preserve their ruined appearance. May also be applied to objects.

A form of damage to photographic prints, typically those with a gelatin layer, that occurs when a print is exposed to water or a high relative humidity while in contact with a smooth surface. The gelatin swells and reforms in the shape of the surface it is in contact with, causing the gloss of the print to be non-uniform. The term 'blocking' refers to the same cause, but that causes stacks of prints to adhere to each other.
In etching, the condition where an area of the printing plate is too deeply bitten and lines fuse together.
Technique of submerging a printing plate in acid in stages to produce subtle tonal gradations or other effects.
Brush strokes found in traditional Chinese painting. These wedge-shaped strokes resembles the cuts made by an ax.
The field of education that trains professional architects.
Fighting men on horseback, typically of upper class background, especially those who fought on the side of the Royalist party in 17th-century Great Britain's civil war.

Actions involving the falling upon with force, and usually with arms; actions involving the commencing of a battle or making another offensive operation. In common military situations, attack is the opposing action to defense. For a personal actions involving falling upon with force or arms, use "assaults (personal life events)."
Combat in and on seas, oceans, or any other major bodies of water, using combatants in boats or ships. The first naval battles date to more than 3,000 years ago.
Symbolic garments worn by members of a fraternal organization, most commonly the Freemasons. These may be embellished with decorative symbols.

Material things that can be perceived by the senses. In the context of art history or art information, the term may be restricted to works of art or cultural heritage, including architecture, art works such as paintings, drawings, graphic arts, sculpture, decorative arts, photographs, and other cultural artifacts. An object may be a single item or it may be made up of many physical parts.

Structures or parts of structures that are the result of conscious construction, are of practical use, are relatively stable and permanent, and are of a size and scale appropriate for--but not limited to--habitable buildings. Works of architecture are manifestations of the built environment that is typically classified as fine art, meaning it is generally considered to have aesthetic value, was designed by an architect (whether or not his or her name is known), and constructed with skilled labor. For the art or science of designing and building structures, use "architecture (discipline)."
Large rectangular coverings of thick but soft material, used especially for warmth.
A name of convenience used to designate rugs with a repeating pattern composed of two main elements: an octagon with an outline of angular interlace and a cross-shaped motif of arabesque forms.

Describes objects that are or have been in the ground and covered with, often in direct contact with, earth. For structures intentionally built below the earth's surface, use "underground structures." With regard to the effects of being buried, use "underground environments."
Any of various synthetic materials resembling grassy turf, used especially as a playing surface for sports.
Mats woven from palm fronds.

The act of shaping, marking, or decorating wood, stone, or another material by cutting or incising, typically using tools such as chisels and other blades. It refers to this process as it is applied to small-scale objects or to objects that are not considered art. "Carving" may also be considered a sculpture technique that is employed in the creation of art.
Technique in which stone is chiseled to the approximate shape of the finished work.

A white powdery crust formed by extraneous salts evolving on the surface of stone, plaster, ceramics, or another material as the result of water migration and subsequent evaporation. Typical efflorescence on masonry surfaces, mural paintings, and frescoes occurs when moisture dissolves water soluble salts, then migrates to the surface, where the water evaporates leaving a salt residue. Efflorescence crystal growth can result from fluctuations in water vapor pressure that occur with changing humidity and temperature. The salts most commonly found in efflorescence are sulfates, carbonates, and chlorides of sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium, and iron.
The greatest stress, especially in tension, that a material, such as a fiber, can withstand without rupture.
Parts or components of curtains.

Knots of rugs tied on pairs of warp strands, looping under one strand and then over and around the other, the ends of the knot coming up individually between each single warp strand to form a pile. They can be tied so that the knot ends come up either to the right or to the left of the encircled warp strands.
Textiles, often of Baluch style, sewn in the form of a grain or storage bag, often used as a cushion.
Hearth rugs which have conical formations at both ends of the central field.
Rugs that are made from the hide of an animal or a synthetic material resembling such.
Decorative rugs which define a living space in a room by providing an often colorful focus.
Carpets that cover the entire floor in an area and are tacked or otherwise attached to the floor.
Refers to prayer rugs with a columnar motif on either side of the mirhab.
Objects, natural or human-made, unaltered or only slightly altered, presented by an artist as works of art in themselves or used as parts of works of art.
Hooked rugs popular in the early 20th century with designs inspired by Native American rug motifs.
Late-19th-century ingrain carpets which were woven in one piece, with border and fringe. They could be used as crumbcloths, and were easy to move and clean.
Knotted pile carpets originally produced in Axminster, Devon, England. They are woven in one piece with weaving of high quality.
Pile carpets woven in the manner of a Wilton carpet but with yarn of lesser quality.

Brussels carpets that are heavy and multiframed, with all of the colored worsted pattern yarns carried along with the body or structure of the carpet, to be picked up into the pattern as the design requires.

Tapestry carpets of the type in which the loop has been cut so as to form an upright, velvety pile. The pile is typically slightly higher than a tapestry carpet. Velvet carpets may resemble Wilton carpets, but the pile of the velvet carpet is not so rich or thick as a Wilton carpet, and the two types of carpet are produced by different methods.
Reliquaries believed to contain a part of the body of a saint or other holy figure. They may be, but are not necessarily, speaking reliquaries, which take the form of the body part.
Popular risings against authority or for some common purpose, usually not as organized as an insurrection and may involve marches, riots, damaging of property, etc.
Designation given to many types of rugs of Anatolian, Iranian or Indian origin, based not on the style of rug but a descriptor of the animal motifs on the rugs.
Male siblings.
Refers to floors of fireplaces and the immediately adjacent floor areas.
That part of a hearth on which the fire is built.
Term of convenience for Polonaise carpets used in the ointment ceremonies of Danish kings.
Ink used in the printing of lithographs.
Places at which a bus makes a regular halt.
Wax formed into an edge around a printing plate so that the plate may be bitten before immersion; used especially for extra-large plates.

Any of several waxes obtained from animal sources, found in small deposits in many parts of the animal. Animal waxes, such as from a mammal, typically contain no glycerides; they contain sterols (cholesterol) and other long-chain alcohols. Also included are the waxes from insects such as the lac insect which produces shellac. Any of several waxes obtained from animal sources, found in small deposits in many parts of the animal. Animal waxes, such as from a mammal, typically contain no glycerides; they contain sterols (cholesterol) and other long-chain alcohols. Also included are the waxes from insects such as the lac insect which produces shellac.
Sets, which are assemblages of scenery, props, and lighting and sound systems, that are designed or used for films.
Skaters who glide over ice, as a pastime or as a means of exercise.

Refers to modern-day Zoroastrian high priests. Dasturs oversee the liturgical lives of the important fire temples with which they are associated, assisted by a team of mobeds. This rank of priest is akin to that of the bishop in Christianity. The dasturs have a strong tradition of learning, especially among the Parsis in Bombay.
Limestone slabs used in lithography.
The activity and function of teaching animals specific responses to specific conditions or stimuli.
Prostitutes who draw their clientele from a court or from the upper classes, and whose services often include social entertaining as well as sexual activity.
Measures taken to forestall criminal or delinquent acts.
Ceramics styles belonging to modern Dutch cultures.

Refers to the style of hard-paste porcelain produced by the factory of the same name from 1784 to 1820. The style is characterized by the use of high-quality styles copied from Meissen and painted in polychrome enamel, typically in brown or other tonal colors.

Objects and other material culture found in contexts of archaeological research, typically reserved for those unearthed from periods before usually the 19th century and from extinct cultures. For objects originating in any culture still living or known through relatively recent history when those articles are the concern of ethnographic or ethnological study, prefer "ethnographic objects."
Gifts that are placed in or near graves to pay homage or as offerings to the deceased.
Striplights hung upstage of a border for illuminating the stage.

Lamps used to inspect ovens, commonly either of tin with a long oval font and tubular handle at one end and a whale oil burner at the other, or a cast iron cup-shaped font with a wick channel, attached saucer base and usually a hinged lid.
Ballasts specially constructed to have certain prescribed characteristics for use in testing electric discharge lamps and other ballasts.

Hanging light fixtures, especially those designed to hang from the ceiling. Usually refers to such fixtures having only one to four lights; for suspended ceiling fixtures having a larger number of lights, use "chandeliers."
Lighting devices mounted on a vehicle for the purpose of indicating the overall width and height of the vehicle.
Tubular electric discharge lamps in which ionization of mercury vapor produces radiation that activates the fluorescent coating on the inner surface of the glass.
Projectors whose lamp may be moved toward or away from the reflector to vary the beam spread.
Emergency lights above exit doors.
Headlights in which the reflector and lens are hermetically sealed together with the filament in a single unit.
Lamps in which light is produced by an electric arc between two electrodes in an ionized mercury-vapor atmosphere; they give off a bluish-green light rich in ultraviolet radiation.
Mercury lamps which come in two types: those that use just mercury, and those that use a mixture of mercury and metal halides.
Sodium lamps in which light is produced by radiation from sodium vapor.
Aeronautical beacons used to indicate the location of an airport.
Aeronautical ground lights indicating a desirable line of approach to a landing area.
Runway lights placed to indicate the longitudinal limits of that portion of a runway, channel, or landing path usable for landing.
Taillights that are illuminated as the driver of a vehicle steps on the brake pedal to slow down or stop.

Lamps with usually one or two vertical wick tubes projecting from a tightly closed reservoir. From the patent of John Miles of Birmingham, England, 1787; so called because the fuel is protected from spillage when agitated.
Supports for candles which attach to a wall; the supporting arm may be jointed or rigid.
Mechanical lamps which have a spring-driven pump to maintain a uniform flow of oil to the top of the wick. Developed in France by Carcel in 1798.

Lamps having a shallow font of oval or pear shape with a wick support attached to the bottom of the font at the narrow end, usually partly or fully covered by a hinged or sliding lid and often a half-bail support at the end opposite the wick support with an attached halbred hook and wire wick pick.
Gas burners having a domical top pierced by a narrow slit across it, producing a fanlike sheet of flame.
Slide fixtures, usually for chandeliers, that adjust by sliding the rod in and out in overlapping cylindrical sections.
Pendant lighting fixtures having a T-form rod suspended from the ceiling connected to two or more gas burners.

Areas that were bound in the past by culture, economics, topography, or another characteristic, and that have historical importance. For administrative areas that are officially designated by a governmental or preservation body as of historic importance, use "historic districts."
Technique which involves the application of flat color over an area too large to be covered by a single brush stroke.
Aircraft aeronautical lights designed to illuminate a ground area from the aircraft.
Generally, a period before a war. Specifically refers to a period or activity before the American Civil War (1861-1865).
Catastrophes caused by man-made events such as war, explosions, terrorism, or airplane crashes.

Light sockets having one or more parallel slits or L-shaped slots, a longer side parallel and the shorter side perpendicular to the axis of the socket, along which a projection from the bulb slides in such a way that when fully inserted, locks into place so the two parts cannot be separated by a simple longitudinal movement.
Globular or hemispherical glasses used to protect the light source within, diffuse or redirect its light, or modify its color.
White crystalline powder used in electric batteries, in printing, as a soldering flux, and in making other compounds.
Type of bronze powder made from pure aluminum or an aluminum alloy, commonly used as a pigment in industrial paint, ink, plastic, and caulking compound, and as a textile coating.

The short downy hairs or fuzz adhering to the cotton seeds (removed by a machine called a linter), which is unsuitable for spinning into yarn and is used as a source of celluloseu. Linter is useful in papermaking and upholstery.
A white or other colored crêpe made of artificial or raw silk fiber in plain weave with normal chain and weft of alternately two right and two left twisted yarns.
Etching ground which is applied to a warm printing plate and hardens upon drying.
An alkoxysilane used as a consolidant in treatment of stone and waterlogged wood.
Fiber-reinforced plastic using glass fiber, produced so as to have the characteristic of being opaque to the passage of light.
Trimming consisting of small glittering objects or tiny glittering bits.

A compound constituting the essential part of woody cell walls of plants in which cellulose fibril aggregates are embedded in a matrix material consisting of hemicelluloses and lignin. Lignocellulosic biomass is used as fuel and is the feedstock for the paper and pulp industry.
Paint consisting of brass powders. Often used to create decorative surfaces, and in low-quality restorations of gilded objects.

A rubberized cloth made by coating two fabric layers with rubber dissolved in naphtha and then pressing them together. This double cloth was the first coated cloth and was developed by Charles Macintosh in Scotland in 1823 for rainwear use.

Hydrous sodium carbonate found in nature as evaporative residues. Used widely as a silica source in early glass manufacture; in ancient Egypt used as well as a bleach for linen, a preservative in mummification, and as an ingredient of incense.
The amino sugar derivative of the monosaccharide hexose in which the hydroxyl group is replaced with an amine group.

Aqueous paint composed of pigments held together by animal glue or casein. Distemper has been used since ancient Egyptian times for wall painting, house decoration, and the painting of theatrical scenery. It has only occasionally been employed for easel painting.
Prehistoric art, especially Paleolithic, found in caves, including paintings, carvings, and certain artifacts.
Series of representations of the Passion of Christ, usually beginning with the Entry into Jerusalem and ending with the Descent of the Holy Ghost at Pentacost.
Any light specially provided as an aid to air navigation, other than a light displayed on an aircraft.
Geometrically planted, pruned, low-growing boxwood shrubs sometimes on a base of colored earth, rubble, shells or lawn, interspersed with space for other garden elements.

Assemblages of joined metal rods, tubes, wires or other materials such as wood that provides a structural framework for a sculpture and usually attaches to a base. Though generally internal, these may also include external supporting components that are eventually removed. In a lost-wax bronze, the armature is created to support the model, whether it is hollow or solid. In the case of a hollow cast, it will further help support the refractory mass of the core during the pour. Armatures may also be used in the assembly of a sculpture that was cast in parts, and in the repair of sculptures that have been structurally damaged. For the structural frames used to sustain or reinforce buildings or other structures, use "armatures (structural frames)."

Chinese works comprising slabs of stone carved and engraved with figurative images or decorative patterns, associated with tombs. The designs on the stones were traditionally copied by rubbings and dispersed to a wider audience. This plastic and graphic art form developed in the Han Dynasty (206 BCE-220 BCE).
Tall Mahafaly wooden sculptures in Madagascar, placed in small groups at tombs, carved with human and animal figures and geometric openwork.

Literally "mirror lid", these netsuke carvings contained a metal mirror, usually of copper, silver or an alloy of copper and gold, set on a bowl of ivory, wood or other material. They were devised after the prohibition against carrying swords in 1876 as an outlet for swordsmiths.
Central African reliquary figures of the Kota culture that are placed as protective devices on baskets containing bones of ancestors.
Direct, literal events carried out by artists, especially in Germany and Austria, attempting to destroy barriers between art and life; often brutal and obscene.

Abrasive wheels or disks used for cutting or smoothing materials such as metal, glass, plastics, or clay. They are distinguished from grinding stones, which are of different design and typically for culinary use.
Millstones made of the siliceous rock known as buhrstone.

Various means of reproducing identical copies of graphic matter in a fixed form. Processes by which an image, pictorial or textual, is transferred, usually to paper or cloth, most often by means of a plate, block, stone, or screen. Use also for the making of photographic prints and, with computers, for the production of a paper copy of stored data. For the production of prints in a fine arts context, prefer "printmaking."
Automatic devices that give an alarm when such items as doors, windows, or safes are tampered with or opened without authorization, as by burglars.
Roofs in which the loads are carried by cables.
Technique of pattern bond in which a course of full-length headers occurs at regular intervals, usually every five or six courses; other courses are composed only of stretchers.
Pigment that is violet in color, contains no carbon, and is ultimately not derived from vegetable or animal sources.
Refers to abbozzi when in the context of French painting.
Refers to an altarpiece or other polyptych with five panels.
Devotional images, especially from the Late Gothic and Renaissance periods, intended to inspire meditation and usually emphasizing subjects of grief and suffering.

Small items, often in the form of a disk or resembling a coin, having a religious or devotional subject imprinted, carved, cast, or otherwise marked upon them. They are found in Ancient, Christian, Hindu, and other religious contexts. The tokens may be considered holy in themselves, conferring luck or grace upon those who carry them.
Prints made using the process of lithography, which is a planographic printing process in which a design is deposited on the stone or plate with a greasy substance which will accept ink.
Marks made in paint by the action of the painter's brush.
In a painting, a colored glaze, size, or wash applied on top of a white ground, to provide the initial tone for the design layer.
Japanese handscrolls, containing text, artwork, or both, and displayed horizontally.
Prints made using the process of intaglio printing, in which recessed areas of the plate or block have been cut or etched away in order to hold ink.
A process of relief etching, usually on zinc plates, used in the 19th century to reproduce existing printed material, including drawings and pages of type.
Russian popular prints of the 18th and 19th centuries.
The process of combining photographic images, or photographs along with other materials or images, such as architectural drawings, usually arranged into a somewhat unified image.

Refers to the act of rendering large, colorful, and stylistically elaborate works of graffiti art that require a greater amount of time and expertise to create, and that dominate an entire surface area such as the wall of a building.

Heavy color, or zhongcai describes a style of painting popular in medieval-era China that relies on a dispersion of mineral colors that are opaque and solid. Artworks created with this technique are characterized by a fine, precise definition of volume and the layering of pigmented hues. Having risen to prominence in the Tang Dynasty, the practice of heavy color or zhongcai later waned. Unlike free-flowing ink paintings, the technique displays meticulous brushwork with lifelike effects, while the lightweight texture of the paint differs from the thicker, denser effects produced by oil painting.

Screenprint where a light-sensitive resist applied to a screen is exposed to a photographic image which has been broken down by a dot screen. It is then exposed to light, and a photo stencil is created. Unexposed sections are washed away, and the ink is forced through the mesh to create the image.
Shelflike platforms or other similar sleeping spaces on board transportation vehicles, such as boats, trains, or travel trailers.

A planar product manufactured from polymeric material used with soil, rock, earth, or any other geotechnical engineering related material, as an integral part of a man-made product, structure, or system.
Any permeable textile used with foundation, soil, rock, earth, or any other geotechnical engineering related material, as an integral part of a man-made product, structure, or system.
Wood of the Arbutus menziesii tree, which is generally located in the Pacific Northwest of North America.

Marbled ware produced by mixing pottery clays of two or more colors to produce ware resembling agate. Agate ware was made in ancient Rome and was later very popular in England in the 18th century, when it was made by Staffordshire potters such as Whieldon and Wedgwood.
Use with reference to photographic and electronic images, usually pertaining to the clarity of details, often relating to the degree of resolution.
Reflectance that is not specular.
Reflection in which a significant portion of the light is reflected in many different directions.
Analyzing the potential loss, failure, injury, or other damage involved in or resulting from any activity or project.
Spectroscopy involving the study of radiant energy by free atoms.
Technique for measuring small absorptions, applied when small concentrations molecular species must be detected in the presence of other components at high pressure.
Burners used for controlled burning of acetylene gas.
Kerosene burners with a spring-loaded lever to secure the chimney within the rim of the base plate and hold the loose dome-shaped deflector; of a type patented by Edward F. Jones in 1858.
Burners for oil lamps consisting of a thin metal disc mounted on a cork through which one or more wick tubes protrude.

Works of art, architecture, and any objects that occupy space, are perceived by the sense of sight, and are created or arranged, rather than naturally occurring. Of special interest are those objects conveying a symbolic or expressive meaning or an aesthetic experience, although visual works are not limited only to such works. Visual works generally exclude the intangible, however, designs for works never constructed may be included. Visual works include pictorial and sculptural works, as well as time-based works such as performance art. They also include utilitarian or ceremonial objects of the type collected or valued by museums, cultures, or individuals. Visual works do not include the performing arts.
Lamps or candleholders that are attached to, or suspended from, some form of bracket by which they can be hung on a wall or that is affixed to the wall.
Lights shown at night by a vessel at anchor.
Cylindrical masses typically of tallow or wax containing a wick or loosely twisted linen or cotton threads burned to give light; made by dipping or casting in a metal mold.
Lighting devices consisting of rush, with most of the outer skin or cortex peeled off, dried and saturated in hot grease or fat, and burned for light.
Devices which hold splints while they burn, usually simple wrought iron U-shaped grips, some with spring or pincer action.

Lights consisting of an open flame emitted from a stick-like handle, usually carried by hand or mounted on a wall or pole. Torches originally consisted of a stick of resinous wood or bundles of fiber soaked with pitch, wax, resin, tallow or other flammable substance. In later usage, includes other sorts of lamps on poles that are designed to be carried like torches.
Lighting devices designed for use over a billiard table.
Lighting devices designed to be affixed to a bicycle when riding in dark locations. These may be powered by batteries, a dynamo attached to a wheel, or historically by burning fuel in a lantern.
Candle brackets having a base with a spike or peg positioned vertically so that the candle is held in place by pushing the spike into the bottom of the candle.
Lighting fixtures attached to or suspended from the ceiling.
Lighting fixture allowing more than one method of illumination, typically gas and electric fixtures, gas and oil fixtures, or gas and candle fixtures.

Burners employing a circular wick mounted between two metal tubes through which a current of air rises to feed the inside of the wick; also used for gas burners with multiple holes arranged in a circle with a hollow center providing a central draft.
Floodlights, usually fixed, consisting of a lamp in an ellipsoidal or paraboloidal reflector.
Lights, often in elevators, that display floor numbers.
Hand lamps with very small fonts of blown glass with drop or cork disc burners, or of metal on saucer bases with slender whale oil burners.
Incandescent lamps, made in R and PAR shapes, which contain a reflective coating on the inside of the glass envelope, giving the entire lamps accurate light beam control.

Powerful spotlights having a plano-convex lens thinned by reducing the convex side to a series of concentric rings of approximately the same focal length and producing a smooth, soft-edged beam of light.
Wooden tops with a wooden or metal peg at the bottom on which the top rotates; may be spun by hand or by pulling a wound string.
A type of miner's lamp consisting of a shallow metal pan with an attached half bail terminating in a usually rounded hook; a shield is mounted at the point of attachment of the bail to the lamp.
Night lamps having a base and shade of glass, burning a short, thick candle with a self-snuffing rush wick.

Small hanging lamps made of iron or earthenware having a handle at one end and a pinched spout for a wick at the other, utilizing a round bowl (called a "cruse") of about 3 inches in diameter to contain fuel, typically hard fat. The cruse lamp developed from the floating-wick pan lamps used by Mediterranean peoples in pre-Christian times.
Man-made stepped waterfalls, whether naturalistic or architectural in form. For similar natural or highly naturalistic features, use "waterfalls."

European staff weapons having a long blade with one cutting edge, convex or of flattened S-shape, divided at the top into a vertical spike and a forward curving hook, and with a horizontal fluke in the center of the back. They were used from at least the middle of the 13th until the 17th century, and were one of the most widely used foot soldiers' weapons.
Serial impact printers in which the font is formed on the end of spring fingers that extend radially from a central hub.
Digitizers that derive data from the scanning of opaque or transparent images.
People who report on, write about, analyze, or evaluate architecture, usually contemporary works.
People who study or work in any of the disciplines dealing with the institutions and functioning of human society and with the interpersonal relationships of individuals as members of society.
People employed in an official capacity, often by a city or governmental agency, as experts to certify the safety and compliance of built works in the jurisdiction.
Those who study the history of Christian Churches and their sects and branches.

Displays that transmit and reflect visible information from a computer or device to a human viewer. There are varying forms of flat-panel displays due to changes in technology or innovation, such as the liquid crystal display (LCD) or the plasma display. These displays may be found on a variety of portable computers, from televisions to digital watches.

Persons concerned with the acquisition, arrangement, description, preservation, interpretation, and making available for reference archival materials, which are public records and documents of historical significance.
People whose profession has to do with communications.
Conceits or techniques used in literature and other arts.
The study of the history of book production and the description of books as physical objects, including study of the relationships of varying texts or multiple editions of a work.
Generally, figures sent on an errand; messengers. Specifically used in the context of Christian iconography to refer to the 12 witnesses sent forth to preach the words of Jesus Christ.
The uncovered binding edges of text blocks, formed where and when the back edges of the gatherings are attached together. For the portions of covers that enclose the back, use "spines."
Cylinders into which a medium such as a rod of graphite or silver is inserted and held by various means.
Anything that can be owned, tangible or intangible.
Real or notional lines marking the limits of an area, territory, etc.
Extreme regularity of balance achieved by the correspondence of identical compositional units on either side of a central axis.
Buildings housing prisons administered by a federal government, in the U.S., those managed by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Prisons.

Decorative patterns of stylized foliage characterized by a continuous stem which splits regularly, producing a series of counterpoised, leafy, secondary stems. Used also generally for allover patterns of fanciful foliate scrollwork.

Carefully selected and situated collections of original buildings designed to illustrate not only the architecture and building forms of a given geographical area and period, but also to recreate the atmosphere and lifestyle.
Towers used specifically for defense purposes.

Houses in the country as opposed to an urban area, especially houses that are large, have substantial property, and are used seasonally. For the entire residential estate, including the house, outbuildings, and properties, use "estates (residential complexes)."
Structures specifically designed for the business of a railroad or railway.
Public notices or paid announcements, especially those in print. For announcements paid for by an advertiser and broadcast on radio or television, use "commercials."
Buildings or other facilities where in which the founding of metal or glass is carried on, meaning these materials are cast or poured into molds.

Buildings, groups of buildings, or spaces within buildings where works of art are housed and displayed for public benefit. For stores in which works of art are displayed for sale, see "art galleries (buildings)."
In Indian architecture, buildings where people live, such as a house, an abode, a dwelling.
Square-back Windsor chairs with two turned rods across the top, the upper rod either capping the back posts or framed between them.

The habit, power, state, or faculty of being able to locate, gain entry to, and use something, such as a building or a database. In computer-based information retrieval, access is the method by which a computer refers to records in a file, dependent upon their arrangement.
Sliding receptacles, fitted into furniture, that can be drawn out horizontally.
The visible fronts of drawers, on which drawer pulls may be mounted.
Large elevated lecterns that may be pivoted, usually found in the choir of churches.
Athletic fields designed or used for playing baseball.
Natural dikes composed primarily of peat.

Public accomodations having an orderly array of individual cabins set alongside a highway and having an internal system of driveways, parking spaces, and a clearly visible and distinctly articulated office near the complex's entrance; especially popular in the United States from the late 1920s to the early 1950s.
A verd antique from Genoa, Italy that was first used by the ancient Greeks and Romans and continues to be used in modern times.

Those trained or working in the field that studies the chronological record of events, such as affecting a nation, community, individual, object, or place, based on a critical examination of source materials.
Refers both to those specializing in the field of linguistics and to those who are fluent in several different languages.
People who study codes as a discipline, and who may also write in code or decode.

Persons responsible for the intellectual content of books or other writings, namely those who write or otherwise compose books, articles, poems, plays, or other works which involve literary composition. The works are often, but not always, intended for publication.

People who alter or amend a text to make it suitable for another purpose. An example of an adapter is one who adapts an earlier text to better agree with a philosophy other than that intended by the original. Other examples are those who adapt a written work for another medium, such as film, broadcasting, or stage production.
Those who engage in the scientific study of human history in its biological, linguistic, and social aspects.
Entries for books or other bibliographic material in the collection of a library, etc. that are printed and bound in book form.
Firescreens with a shelf or slide attached, to be used for writing before the fire.

Any ties that are designed to be broken off at a specified depth, for example after the concrete slab has hardened. Typically, snap ties are metal wire ties for concrete or other materials that combine the function of the traditional tie and wooden spreaders, comprising a metal tie rod and tie holders.

Refers to the early phase (ca. 4800-4300 BCE) of the Neolithic Yangshao culture. It is named after a Neolithic village site near Xi'an in Shaanxi province. Banpo architecture already includes the traditional Chinese orientation of the entrance towards the south and the use of wooden roof support frames. Banpo was a major site for ceramic production; a kiln has been excavated. Vessels were usually shaped by hand but were sometimes coiled or formed in molds. Basins and bowls with contracted bases are typical vessel shapes. Vessels were decorated with impressions or with a black or grey slip and were burnished. Geometric patterns predominate; human masks are an unusual motif sometimes used. A series of about 20 different marks incised on the rims of vessels may be a primitive means of recording events.
Those whose occupation is to shave or trim the beard and to cut and dress the hair of their primarily male clientele.
Approach to art education based on and integrating the four disciplines of decorative arts, art criticism, art history, and aesthetics.

Refers to the period of the Singhasari empire (1222-1292 CE) in Java. In general, the art of the period is characterized by the blend of Hindu, Buddhist, and indigenous iconographic styles. Artistic production from this period is distinguished by the prevalence of demonic sculpture and masks and skull designs based on religious concepts in Tantric texts. Examples of artistic production from this period include the Bhairava figure, a demonic rendition of Shiva adorned with skulls and accompanied by buffalo in twisted positons, and Ganesha statues decorated with skulls. Temples in this period reflect the styles of Tantric magic temples in Nepal and feature tiered, slender constructions.

Designates the period that began with the pacifying rules of Harivarman IV (1074-1081 CE) and Jaya Indravarman II (1113-1145 CE) and flourished from the 11th to the mid-12th century. In architecture, the period features distinct kalan groups known as the Silver Towers, the Gold Tower, the Ivory Towers, and the Copper Tower, constructed along hill terraces and exhibiting redented plans and silhouettes much like the Khmer prasat. Other architectural features in this period include projecting spearhead arches often tripled above doors or false doors, plain pilasters, moldings, colonnettes engaged vertically against rows of foliate ornamentation, and friezes decorated in carved stone with the 'woman's breast' motif. Later in the period, prevailing stylistic simplification yields the clarification of kalan structures and structural masses. In sculpture, the period features images of mythical animals such as the makara used as corner pieces, serpents, elephants, and garuas and lion figures used as atlantids with fangs.
Bergères with concave backs; distinct from bergères with flat backs, which are called "bergères à la reine."
Devices designed to be attached to a wall to support the implements in firesets such as pokers, tongs, shovels, and brooms.
Compact, fitted dressing chests intended to hold a gentleman's fashion accessories.

Sheet metal seams comprising interlocking turnings on each of the two pieces, made in a manner so they lock together at the bottom. Such a seam is used to fasten bottoms to cylindrically shaped articles such as pails, tanks, and other items.
General term for the wood any of several species of yellow pine tree.
Masonry joints formed without tools, as excess mortar is squeezed out from between the bricks. In appearance, rustic and textured.
Disciplines concerning arts that depend upon performances presented to the attention of observers through the live or recorded actions of the artists, such as actors, musicians, poets, etc.
Chairs designed for and used at a dining table, intended for use while eating meals.
The decorative repeating pattern created by the bookbinder's finishing tool, called a roll.
Refers to patterns of scrolling stems and leaves, especially of acanthus and in classicizing decoration. For other leafy scrollwork, use "scrolling foliage."
Structures that house and protect equipment needed operate substations or other facilities for electricity, water, or other utilities.
Half gables, such as those that close the end of a penthouse roof or the roof over a side aisle of a church; may be scrolled, curved, or otherwise ornamented.

In Indian architecture, the recess between major moldings. Examples are often found between kalaśa and kapōtapālī in pīṭha; also, may be inserted between two courses of kapōtapālī in varaṇḍikā/prahāra below the śikhara. May be decorated with the kuñjarākṣa pattern.
Ceramic basins pressed into walls as ornament.
Duchesses chairs made in two or three parts, each of which can be used separately as a seat.
French 18th-century chairs that stood in the center of a room and could be moved. Distinct from "sièges meublants" which were largely decorative and were positioned against the wall.
Stools designed as seats at dressing tables; introduced in the 18th century.
Refers to stools, which are armless and backless seats for one person, characterized by often having a cloth or leather seat and a frame that may be folded or collapsed for transportation or storage.
High stools that are usually one of a row of such stools standing in front of a bar, often taking the form of a rounded seat fixed on a central post.
Refers to benches on which stonecutters place blocks of stone in order to dress and prepare them.

Benches designating the location where food and other donations for impoverished or unfortunate people are distributed. Primarily used in historical contexts, for such benches on the premises of churches, hospitals, guilds, private estates, or other establishments that distributed alms.
Larger organizing principles and classifications used by archaeologists in researching and understanding the past.
Infants' beds, especially those with a hood over one end.

Low tables, often with a raised rim around the edge, intended to support a cabinet, chest, or other piece of case furniture. Intended to stand against a wall, and thus usually undecorated on one side.
Steps used to climb into a bed.
Tripod, often tilt-top, circular tables whose top has a scalloped, molded rim resembling the edges of a pie.
Relatively small tables, originally designed to seat customers in ice-cream parlors.

Tables of various designs whereby the table top may be folded partially or entirely from the support, or where the legs may be folded under the table top; folding is done for ease of storage or otherwise to make the profile smaller.
Corners on furniture that have wide chamfers at the junctions of front and sides.
Doors concealing cubbyhole spaces found in case furniture such as fall-front desks, secretarys or escritoires, and often fitted with a lock. They are frequently decorated with carvings or marquetry.
Ends of furniture panels or tabletop elements that have a rounded, convex section.
Feet, in the shape of claws, on a piece of furniture.
Groups of shelves, used for storage. Shelving units can be fixed or movable (on tracks), and made of wood, metal, or another material.
Ceremonies at which degrees or diplomas are conferred by an educational institution.
A synthetic rubber which is a copolymer of isobyutylene, and 1 to 3% isoprene.

Light spongy rubber made by mechanically whipping air into the rubber latex prior to curing. It is used for mattresses, cushions, and insulation. Foam rubber turns yellow and becomes powdery when exposed to sunlight.
Declarations made by the master of a vessel before a government official, indicating that any damage incured during a voyage was due to sailing conditions rather than neglect or misconduct.
Documents attesting to the fulfillment of the terms or conditions of a contract.
Ancient Greek sacred cult songs.
Songs with rhyming verse and a narrative; some ballads are slow, romantic songs.
Machines that utilizes several parallel saw blades which can cut all of the boards of a log in one pass.
Motif of fruit, flowers, and foliage in three-dimensional friezes, particularly as used by architects and carvers in the 17th-18th centuries.

Refers to the parts of seating furniture that support sitters' backs. For the rearmost surfaces or portions of objects in general, use "backs (portions)." For supports that are used to rest one's back, either separate pieces of furniture or attachments to backless seating, use "backrests."
Plastic that becomes soft when heated and hard when cooled, no matter how often these processes are repeated, because of little or no cross-bonding between molecules.
Resin formed by the reaction between dibasic acid and dihydroxy alcohol.

Thermoplastic polymer of the polyester family made by condensing ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid. It is used to make textile fibers, disposable beverage bottles, photographic film, and magnetic recording tape. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) was the first commercially marketed polyester, sold as Dacron (TM) in the U.S.
Communities that were of a relatively large size, but are now abandoned by their occupants.
Mechanical contrivances that are the result of devising, inventing, or artistic endeavor, and that have a particular purpose.

Machines capable of automatically carrying out a complex series of movements, especially one that is programmable. In historical usage, as depicted in science fiction, inspired by the mass-produced workers in a play by Karel Čapek, robots were intelligent artificial beings typically made of metal and resembling in some way a human or other animal.
Atomizers resembling fountain pens with attached reservoirs, used for applying a fine spray of paint or another coating by compressed air.
Describes apparatuses or tools used to produce an image transfer print.
Tools consisting of a long drill bit which pierces a spool-shaped object; used in conjunction with a bow to drill holes in brass, iron, and steel. Most often used by clock- and watchmakers.
Portable, hand-held, motor-driven tools used to turn a bit for boring holes in a material and powered either by direct or alternating current.
Wheeled or tracked vehicles resembling tractors with a front-mounted bucket or scoop; used in construction to load or move heavy, loose materials from one place to another.
General term for intials that incorporate ornament or other decoration, in contrast to the simpler forms of other letters on a page. May refer to manuscripts or in reference to printed texts.
Tools which take a variety of forms; used for cutting threads in metal pegs to make bolts.
Pieces of blotting paper in various sizes and formats, including individual sheets, gatherings of sheets, and large sheets inserted or built into desk pads to protect desk tops from ink stains.
Encompasses various tools involved in the creation of technical drawings, including drawing boards, T-squares, french curves, etc.
Machines devised to make diazo prints of technical drawings or other images.
Nations, parties, or leaders in armed conflict or waging war, particularly when recognized by the law of nations.
