Computer storage devices involving no moving parts in which data is stored in non-volatile memory. Information can be written and retrieved to flash drives more quickly than electromechanical hard drives.
Output devices for translating information from computers into pictorial or graphic form on paper or a similar medium.
Flat surfaces, usually consisting of a grid of wire set in a substrate, that can be placed on a desk and used together with a mouse or stylus for the input of data to a computer graphics system.
Any devices that make use of mechanical impact to print characters or images onto paper.
Furniture for supporting flax bales.
Mechanical equipment specifically used for cutting materials.
Large chest-like freezers with a hinged lid that opens from the top.
Stoves heated by gas generated from alcohol.
A simple form of damask having a rectilinear pattern formed by the contrast of warp and weft faces, with numerous warp floats on the surface as in satin; much used for simple linens.
Paper to which any abrasive substance has been adhered, typically used for finishing surfaces.
Equipment used for cleaning or removing surfaces by a controlled stream of pressure-ejected material consisting of sand or manufactured grit.
Furnaces where metal is heated before shaping.
Hammers used in woodworking.

Information indicator for any combination of a variety of materials plus the associated techniques, used in the making of a single work of art. In printmaking, use when more than one technique, such as both etching and engraving, are used in one print. For the painting technique of laying oil paint glazes over tempera paint or tempera paint glazes over oil paint, use "mixed technique." For a general term for a variety of artistic or communicative forms used in a given work or works, such as contemporary works that employ both sculpture and music, use "multimedia." For the concept that certain contemporary works merge known art forms to inaugurate a new type, use "intermedia."
Books listing names with residences, usually in alphabetical order.
Administration by a local political unit, such as a city, town or village.
A disruptive often luminous charge around or over the surface of an insulator, usually due to high voltage.
Any tools which are operated by and guided by hand.
In structural engineering, quantification and rating of damages and potential damages to structures; for example, measures of seismic damage potential based on ground motion records.
Portable tools with power-driven, abrasive-coated continuous belts, used to smooth surfaces.
Records schedules governing specified series of records common to several or all government agencies.
Sworn statements in writing; especially made upon oath before an authorized magistrate or officer.
Any materials representing, in whole or part, the earth or any celestial body at any scale.
Without columns or pilasters or without the repetitive use of them in important locations or as influential elements of design; used especially with reference to facades.
The act of following the formal rules and traditions of literature and art.
The quality of being genuine or original.
The last brick, block, stone, or tile laid in a horizontal course; may be either a complete unit or one trimmed at the site.
Refers to the use of a buffering agent to stabilize acidity or alkalinity. In the context of conservation, this action is often applied to prevent damage due to acidity.
Exceptionally intelligent or talented people, particularly those having an intelligence quotient greater than 140 on the Lewis Terman scale.
Objects or sets of objects that separate, keep apart, demarcate, or serve as deterrents.

Perforated lattices or screens of stone, usually marble; use especially with reference to Indian architecture of the Mughal period. For Islamic windows filled with turned wood screens or grills, use "meshrebeeyehs."
Log-frame houses, common in Northern Russia, primarily rural, but found in urban areas until the 17th and 18th centuries.

Telecommunications towers that are cellular-enabled mobile device sites where antennas and electronic communications equipment are placed to transmit and receive cell phone signals over one or more cells in a mobile phone system.

Wood of any of several varieties of the species Fraxinus excelsior. The wood is whitish to pale brown in color with a pink cast. It is a dense wood that is tough and elastic with a straight grain and slightly coarse texture. It is moderately durable but susceptible to insect attack. The timber is used for ladders, tool handles, oars, poles, wheels, boats, weapons, furniture, gymnasium equipment, tennis racquets, and hockey sticks.

Wood log construction technique of layering tightly fitting timbers one on top of the other. Used since the Neolithic period, particularly in Europe and Asia. Either round logs or squared timber beams may be used. The combination of a block enclosed in a frame is called "plank construction."
Drainage structures that extend across and beneath roadways, canals, embankments, or traveled ways other than bridges.
Facility where livestock are slaughtered, processed, and packed as meat products.
Military installations or reservations, or defense-related industries.
Buildings or groups of buildings used for manufacturing beverages.
Inns, hotels, or private homes offering a room for the night and breakfast the next morning for one inclusive price.
Plastics with additives applied to their formulation, usually adhesion promoters combined with particulate filler for reinforcing molding compounds, or fibers for reinforcing composite materials.

Maps, usually maintained in the public works or engineering departments of a city, showing information such as street and rail rights of way, location of bridges, and grade separations; used for planning and executing engineering work in a locality.

Chairs designed for use at the beach, having a hood for protection from the sun and wind. May be made of wicker, wood and cloth, or other materials. Originally made of wicker in the 19th century, based on wicker armchair furniture with covered high rising hoods that had been created by basketmakers for centuries.
Bidets with legs made to screw off and tops made to lock, popular in the 19th century. Use "traveling bidets" for those made to rise out of a chest.

Refers to the movement within American Scene painting, concentrated in the rural midwestern United States in the 1930s and capturing the flavor of life there in a literal painting style.(PDAT) For the concept of a general consciousness of and loyalty to a distinct subnational or supranational area, use "regionalism."
French form of standing desk, sometimes having a pupitre.
Open shelves for holding books; distinct from "bookcases" which generally have several shelves enclosed by doors.

Ornamental areas of distinct pattern, material, color, or shape around the edge or boundary of something.  With regard specifically to tapestries, refers to the areas around the central field outside the inner guard and within the guard that edges the outer sides of the tapestry. For the narrow surfaces showing the 'thickness' or smallest dimension of thin, flat objects, as distinguished from the broad surfaces, see "edges (object components)."
Motif representing Lakṣmī with a pair of elephants performing lustral  ceremony; in architecture usually a tutelary image at the "lalāṭa" block of the doorframe.

Stylized ornamental motif used especially in architecture and decorative arts, based on a characteristic Mediterranean plant with jagged leaves, Acanthus spinosus. It was first used by the Greeks in the 5th century BCE on temple roof ornaments, on wall friezes, and on the capital of the Corinthian column, such as at Temple of Olympian Zeus in Athens. Later the Romans used the motif in their Composite order, in which the capital of the column is a three-dimensional combination of spirals resembling rams' horns and full-bodied acanthus leaves. The acanthus leaf has been a popular motif in carved furniture decoration since the Renaissance.
Decorative pattern imitating an arcade, as on a piece of furniture.

Carved tripod stand that was popular as a type of furniture, particularly in Neoclassical French design. Often used as a washstand. It was based on the style of the metal tripod on the choregic monument of Lysikrates and also found in Herculaneum. The form was reconstructed by James Stuart as a motif at Kedleston Hall, Derbyshire. The form is also depicted in a painting by Joseph-Marie Vien, "La Vertueuse Athénienne" (1763), and thus the name is derived.

Protection measures intended to eliminate and reduce the hazard and damage that could result from avalanches, including issuing bulletins to the public, planting and maintaining stands of trees, building defensive structures, and preventatively clearing areas of loose snow by using controlled avalanches.

Pattern comprising a zigzag of contrasting colors, imitating flame stitch embroidery in certain upholstery at the Bargello Museum in Florence. Examples of the pattern are found in upholstery, wallpapers, and parquet floors.
A type of openwork pattern originating in Chinese art and adapted to Chinoiserie in Europe in the 18th century.

Structures built of ice, often elaborately decorated, furnished, and lit, erected for festivals, exhibitions, and sporting events; popular in 18th-century Russia and then throughout the northern latitudes during the mid-20th century.
In Indian architecture, the motif of a series of lotus petals.
Decorative motif comprised of diagonally rising steps and ending in an angular curved hook.
Mirrors having curved, rather than flat, reflective surfaces.

Small freestanding mirrors, usually supported on a standing frame within which the glass can be adjusted, designed to be used on a dressing table. Dressing glasses are sometimes made with a boxlike base fitted with small drawers.
French chairs with open arms.
Curved, tapered cone-shaped blades with a handle and a hook on the tapered end; used to enlarge the hub-holes of wheels.
Files with rounded edges and tapered or parallel sides; used to clean and shape the spaces between gear wheel teeth and pinions.
The positioning of communications cables, electric cables, or other cables, whether underground, undersea, or aerially.
Irons used to mark a barrel with the emblem of the maker, akin to a branding iron.
Large pocket knives whose blade or blades fold or shut into the handle.
Transparencies having images composed of gray tones, black, and clear areas; may include one hue as a result of process, toning, or discoloration.
Photographs made by the Autochrome process.
Workbenches used the prepare or fabricate the ropes, chains, wires, and associated fittings used to support and operate a sea vessel's masts, sails, derricks, booms, etc.
Groups of families and households, the heads of which claim descent from a common ancestor.
Refers to the application of paint to a surface with a revolving paint roller covered in an absorbent material. The technique allows for rapid coverage of large areas.
Supports, usually comprising pairs of legs in an X-shaped configuration with a crossbeam; often used to support a log while being sawed or for other purposes.
A term referring to the social relationship of a group, rather than its territorial demarcation, in regard to its support of community life in each tlaxilacalli (neighborhood) of Mexico-Tenochtitlan.
The process of lining by adding a new or additional lining material.
People who play keyboard instruments.

Originally, make-up or costume intended to imitate the appearance of a black person, particularly as part of a performance. By extension, any practice of stereotyping dark-skinned people in an exaggerated fashion. Though not exclusive to the United States, blackface was associated with minstrel shows in the US from the 1830s until the mid-20th century; and is widely regarded now as an offensive example of racism. Blackface was adopted by some African American performers in minstrel shows from ca.1840 as a means to earn a living in venues that were otherwise denied them in mainstream show business.
Conjunction of the Sun, Moon, Earth, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. It was considered a sign of imminent disaster.
The long-term total of atmospheric variations at a specific geographical location. Regarding shorter-term atmospheric conditions, use "weather."

A type of collodion process in which the binder was dried before exposure or contained a hygroscopic agent to retain sufficient moisture to allow processing after an extended period of time; an improvement on the wet collodion process because it alleviated the need for a portable darkroom. Used to produce negatives and lantern slides.
Cloth woven in lengths, to be sold by the yard.

A type of stiff pasteboard that is thicker than 0.006 inches, typically consisting of good-quality chemical pulp or rag pasteboard, and varying greatly in type and stability. High quality archival cardboard is made from rag pulp and has a low acid content, used for mounting prints, drawings and watercolors. Other grades of cardboard is used for cards, signs, printed materials, and high-quality boxes. Inferior grades of cardboard, such as corrugated board, are made from coarsely ground sulfite treated wood pulp; for this board, use "corrugated board." The first carboard box was produced in England in 1817. Corrugated cardboard was patented in 1871.
Earthy or mineral residue that remains after combustible substances have been thoroughly burned.
Rough board reclaimed from barn structures or that resembles this either through natural weathering or manufacture.
Semi-cylindrical roofing tiles, usually clay, that are laid in interlocking columns alternating with one column having the convex side facing up and the next column having the concave side facing up.
Tile which fits like a saddle on the ridge of a roof, forming a crest.

The tiles that bridge the open joint between rows of tiles in a roof. For example, in ancient Greek architecture, the roof tile (imbrex) of terracotta or marble, usually semicircular (Laconian) or triangular (Corinthian) in section, bridged the open joint between two rows of flat tiles or pantiles (tegulae).
Cutting machines consisting essentially of a single heavy blade that descends between vertical guides to cut or trim paper, metal, or other materials.
Machinery designed to pierce or bore a hole or passage into anything, including earth and rock for wells of water or oil.

Tools, usually having a straight or tapered shank, designed for piercing, perforating, or making or enlarging a hole, especially when piercing by means of a rotatory movement; common examples include tools for boring through rocks or through wood. For tools used for piercing or making holes, but having a fluted or spiral shank, use "drills (tools)."
Machines or tools which grind with abrasives; used to cut hardened or tempered metals and to develop a smooth finish as on metal, wood, stone, or concrete.
Electrical devices, usually located in sinks, used for grinding up garbage.

Scraping implements, usually consisting of a straight-edged blade of rubber or similar material, attached to the end of a long handle, for removing water or other material from a surface, such as window glass.
Tools for sweeping. Originally made of twigs fixed to a handle; now refers to handled tools with bristles made of any material.
Mechanical devices that mount two rollers in close proximity to a crank and gear, through which wet textiles are passed to squeeze out excess moisture.
Support beams with recesses for shoulders and with centrally placed hooks for attachment to a beer barrel. Used for the transport of barrels over a short distance by two people.
Motor-driven machines, such as endless belts or a series of rollers, used for the continuous transport of material.
Devices that shape materials by forcing them through a specially designed opening.
Machines for graduating or dividing a circle into a number of equal parts, or for cutting the circumference of a wheel into a number of teeth.
Power-operated saws used in grooving uncured concrete, to prevent cracking, or in cutting hard concrete slabs.
Refers to large power-driven machines mounted on wheels that ride on steel pavement forms, and also for portable machines with large paddles used to float and finish concrete floors and slabs.
Furnaces used to apply heat to change a material’s strength and hardness, relieve internal stresses, and provide increased ductility.
The anniversary of the storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789, celebrated as a national holiday in France.
Tools used for removing burrs from pipes.
Journeys or trips that involve stopping at a series of ports or places.
Lathes designed to work metal materials or objects. Metalworking lathes were introduced early in the Industrial Revolution, around 1800.
Stereoscopic photographs in which the two images are in contrasting colors and produce a three-dimensional effect when viewed through colored filters.
Pincers with gripping jaws used for working metal.
Machines for welding that use a power supply to create an electric arc between an electrode and the base material, in order to melt metals at the welding point.

Lathes used for working wooden materials or objects. In its early form, woodworking lathes consisted of two holding cemers with the suspended stock being rotated by an endless rope belt; one person pulled on the rope while a second person cut while holding a hand lathe.
Tools with a round, semicircular, or spade-shaped blades often socketed and mounted on a wood handle; used for stripping bark from logs.

Optical devices invented by Carlo Ponti in 1860, and patented in 1861. These were used to view photographic transparencies or prints. It was claimed that stereoscopic relief was obtained from a single photograph, though the stereo effect was due to the nature of an illusion caused by the single viewing lens of the alethoscope.

Viewers for full-plate Daguerreotype stereo pairs, designed and patented by Southworth & Hawes, ca. 1853. A large cabinet mounted on a cast-iron base could display ten stereo pairs in succession by means of a crank.
Structures, often tower-like, from which signals are sent to control the movements of railway trains. They typically house the control equipment for signal apparatuses and switches.
Solid figures of which the base is a circle, and the summit a point, and every point in the intervening surface is in a straight line between the vertex and the circumference of the base.
Float valves incorporating a spherical float; used to control the height of water.

Hangers used for heavy exterior sliding or rolling doors, consisting of two pulleys secured to the top of the door in tandem, connected by a heavy metal strap. The door is moved by rolling along a horizontal track which either hangs from the lintel or is anchored to a parallel member projecting slightly from it.

Borehole heat exchangers are used to extract heat stored in the ground by means of a vertical borehole with a “closed loop” collector installation with the help of a geothermal heat pump. A collector hose filled with a carrier fluid is installed in the borehole which is drilled into a geothermal aquifer. This circulating carrier fluid absorbs heat from the surrounding bedrock, which is then extracted by the heat pump for use in space-heating via piping connected to the heat exchanger.

Economic system characterized by private or corporate ownership of capital goods, by investments that are determined by private decision rather than state control, and by prices, production, and the distribution of goods that are determined mainly by competition in a free market.
Refers to earthenware covered with a transparent lead glaze in imitation of English creamware. The term is a misnomer because the ware is not faience, given that it is not tin-glazed.
Portable slabs or flat surfaces used for throwing or hand-building clay objects, or supporting works in a kiln; may be attachments to potter's wheels.

A type of warping usually associated with wood when one face of a length of lumber shrinks more than the other, resulting in a bowed curvature. Less commonly this process may occur in stone such as marble, due to residual stresses, anisotropic thermal expansion of calcitic grains, variation of fluid contents, and dissolution processes.

Generic name for any of a class of compounds formerly used as a fire-extinguishing agent. When exposed to flame, these chlorofluorocarbon gases release halogen atoms which interact with hydrogen atoms, suppressing combustion in the process. They also deplete the earth's ozone when exposed to solar ultraviolet light and have consequently been withdrawn from use. Included in the group are Halon: dichlorodifluoromethane, CCl2F2; Halon 1211: bromochlorodifluoromethane, CBrClF2; and Halon 1301: trifluorobromomethane, CBrF3.
Any material used in laying a floor.
Culture of the Mouride brotherhood found in Senegal and Gambia.
Process in which images are transferred by painting a wet acrylic medium on a paper print and subsequently rubbing the paper away, leaving only the colorant, toner, or ink embedded in the acrylic.

Technique for the transporting of images from one surface to another, such as the separating of a paint film from its mount and moving it to a new support, and for processes of precisely copying or reforming an image on another surface, as in pouncing.
Correspondents who report from abroad.
Reduction of data needed for storage or transmission. Data is reduced in volume by means of encoding information to require fewer bits to be stored than the original.
Publishing content on the internet.
Systematically examining records in a file or collection for the purpose of locating specific data or records.
Technique of decorating glass in which a painted, drawn, or gilded image is executed on the underside of the glass and backed with metal foil, usually gold or silver.
Experts in one or more of the arts or matters of refined taste, competent to pass critical judgement in relation thereto..
Refers to various photomechanical processes that use a daguerreotype to make the printing plate.
A planographic photomechanical process that uses the same principle as lithography, the repulsion of oil and water, but uses a photographic process to transfer the image to the plate.

The process of relief printing by which an image is photographically transferred to a plate for printing in such a way that either the light or the dark areas become susceptible to attack by an etchant. As contrasted with photogravure, the non-printing areas are etched.

An early photo reproductive process developed around 1890 in France, using a negative; it was abandoned in favor of simpler halftone screen techniques as they became available. In the typogravure process, the printing plate was cast from a photosensitive gelatin relief, formed when exposed to sunlight through a negative and then washed out. The cast contained many raised peaks of varying sizes from where the gelatin was washed away in relationship to the amount of exposure it received. These peaks could be rolled with ink in the letterpress manner, creating a series of dots that gave the illusion of continuous tone.
Those who study the structure, function, and development of the cells, tissues, and organs constituting the animal body.
Those that advocate or engage in vigorous action, persuasion, or campaigning related to political or social causes.

Transit systems consisting of overhead wires, cables, or rails supporting and towing suspended cabins along a, usually, closed-loop circuit; generally for transporting passengers up steep gradients, or over deep valleys or bodies of water.

Designates rail systems operating on private but not necessarily exclusive right of way, at street level or grade separated, generally on electric power, at medium speeds (10-30 miles per hour), and generally making frequent stops at low platforms or directly at grade-level stations.
Irrigation or piping network within a structure that conveys sewage, rainwater, or other material from point of entry to point of disposal, such as a public sewer.
Transit systems that utilize buses on fixed routes, running on regular schedules to transport people in or around metropolitan areas.
Free-wheeled transit systems consisting of buslike vehicles, whose power comes from overhead cables to which the trolleybuses are attached, and of routes that intermingle with general street traffic.
Rapid rail transit systems linking suburban districts with central city terminals; generally not operating on exclusive rights of way.
Includes rail transit systems serving primarily urban areas.

Broadly refers to any sulfide of copper, more specifically to the blackish crystalline sulfide CuS used in textile dyeing and as a black pigment in ancient painting. The presence of copper sulfide on the surface of ancient bronze artifacts has generated much debate over whether it should be seen as symptomatic of copper corrosion or as an intentional patination technique.
Metalworking tools formed as an angle with conical points intended to enlarge drilled or punched holes.
Refers to male human beings from birth through adolescence.

Marks on a fixed and enduring object, indicating its elevation above sea level and serving as a reference in topographic surveys and tidal observations. In a more general sense, the term may also refer to any point of reference from which measurements may be made.
Refers to groups of artists working in a studio. In modern usage, it generally refers only to fine arts studios, and often only to artists' studios in France, or in Britain after the 18th century.

Fired clay in various shapes and thicknesses and with a variety of uses, as for surface covering, drainage, or construction. For general flat, solid, and relatively thin durable material used primarily for surface covering and of various materials, use "tile."
Type of sandstone having a light warm-beige to a rich golden brown hue. Often used for paving, wall cladding, and decorative elements. Prime examples are found in Indian architecture.

Material comprising the seed of a plant, which is the nutrient material for development after germination that is enclosed in a protective coat. Seeds may be processed in various ways for use as materials, or they may be used whole as elements in a design.
Material comprising a seed vessel of long form, usually dry and dehiscent; strictly used only of leguminous and cruciferous plants, but often extended to other long fruit.

Paper coated on one or both sides with a mixture of a binder and pigment. The coating provides a smooth, enamel -like surface for writing and printing, producing a brighter appearance, either glossy or matte, and improved printability by preventing ink absorption. A type of coated paper was used as early as 450 CE in China. Uniform machine-made coated papers have been used for over 100 years to provide optimum surfaces for printing. Some of the white pigments used in the coatings are barium sulfate, calcium carbonate, calcium sulfate, calcium sulfite, clay, diatomaceous earth, lead white, satin white, talc, zinc sulfide, lithopone, zinc oxide, and titanium dioxide. Over the years, the binders have changed from the early use of starch to include the use of linseed oil, gums, glues, and waxes. Recently, synthetic resins such as polyvinyl acetate, acrylic, and styrene-butadiene. The coatings are often burnished or calendered to produce a glossy finish.

Quadrilateral figures in which both pairs of opposite sides are parallel to each other, especially used for such figures in which the sides do not intersect at right angles. For four-sided figures having right angles, the terms "square" or "rectangle" are more commonly used.
The curves that are formed from chains or rope that hang from two fixed points, though not in the same vertical line. Derived from the Latin "catena," meaning "chain".
Soft, unctuous clays of various colors, used as pigments and in the ground for gold leaf.
A kind of ceramic clay of exceptionally small particle size and, consequently, very good plasticity. Used to impart plasticity to other clay bodies.
Building materials comprising cut, carved, shaped, or molded units of stone, ceramic brick or tile, concrete, glass, adobe, or other similar material.

Groups of persons, commonly formed as business enterprises, considered in law as legal persons having an existence and rights and duties distinct from those of the individuals who form them. For unincorporated groups of persons contractually associated as joint principals in business, use "partnerships."
Partnerships of two or more persons who carry on business under a common name.

People called on for professional advice or services regarding matters in the field of their special knowledge or training, usually for specific projects or problems. For persons who give advice either professionally or nonprofessionally, usually on an ongoing basis, use "advisors."
Etching needles ground to an oblique face to obtain swelling lines; first used by 17th-century artist Jacques Callot.
Tools similar to rounding adzes, but used for rougher work, including, but not limited to, cross-cutting bungs and stock for bungs.
Augers having a wood stock with a shell or nose bit; turned by a wood bar passing through a hole in the top of the stock.
Single-cut files which are half-round on one side and flat on the other.
Tools used by coopers to insert a cooper's flag between the head and staves of a barrel after the head is in place.
Iron rods which terminate in a flat surface on which is a device or letter set in relief; used after heating to mark livestock, tools, or manufactured goods with indelible evidence of ownership.
Flat brushes with long coarse bristles set in a wood handle; used by artists and draftsmen to sweep away eraser crumbs from work being done on a drawing board.
Awls having a half-moon or bent shape, often in the form of an eye-pointed needle and designed for use in sewing horses' collars or similar items.
Large lathes used for turning heavy work such as locomotive and railroad car wheels.
Small scissors having a form specialized for cutting appliqués and other small, negative shapes; often has one round-backed blade against a short, straight blade.
German variety of the board chair.
General term for wood of any species of horse chestnut native to North America.
Includes authorizations granting the power to perform a task or duty and documents appointing or hiring someone to perform a task.

Refers to earthenware decorated in a freehand manner with raised clay slip designs. The slip may be applied through slip trailing or piping. The technique was first employed on Rhenish pottery prior to the 3rd century BCE, replacing molded decoration. The slip was applied by piping to decorate the edges of flat dishes with small flowers and other designs. The technique was again used in the mid- and late 1800s, but it was not popular because firing difficulties caused the slip to flake off easily.

Refers to a very distinctive style of Black-figure pottery, most of which comprises hydriai dating from around 530 BCE to around 500 BCE, found in Etruria, and very probably made at Caere (modern Cerveteri, near Rome, Italy). The drawing style is of very high quality, the painting style is remarkably colorful, and the form and decoration of the hydriai differ from contemporary examples produced elsewhere in the Greek world. Decoration typically includes lotus, ivy wreaths, palmette friezes, and mythological scenes.

Refers to the styles and cultures that developed in the area of Gaul, in modern France and south and west of the Rhine river, under the influence of Roman rule and culture. The term is also used to refer narrowly to the style and culture that developed among Gallic people in Gaul, under Roman influence.
Canopy beds having an upper portion in the shape of a dome over the bed, from which the curtains are suspended.
One of the two principal sects of Jainism; meaning "sky-clad," referring to the male ascetics possessing no clothing.

Religion that draws upon Taoism, Confucianism, and Buddhism as sources for its doctrines and practices. It is a school or sect of religious Taoism founded by Wang Ch'un-yang (1112-1170) in 1163 after he met a hermit claiming to be an incarnation of two of the immortals and from whom he received secret teachings. Ch'uan-yang drew on classic Tao sources as well as on sources outside the Taoist tradition, particularly from Zen Buddhism. Every disciple of this school has the objective of realizing Tao in experience, through understanding his own mind and nature in relation to Tao. The school was favored by the Mongols and its second patriarch, Ch'iu Ch'ang-ch'un, was invited into Central Asia to preach to Genghis Khan. The school was immensely popular and its establishments of celibate monks continued to be active into the 20th century, with the famous White Cloud Monastery at Beijing as headquarters. This particular monastery is of the Lung-men (or Dragon Gate) school, one of the most important of several movements that came out of Ch'üan-chen tao.
Cupboards containing bookshelves and closed with doors usually of glass or sometimes fitted with grilles.
Visible, functional hardware that has a finished appearance and is often treated as part of the decorative scheme on objects such as furniture, architecture, and book bindings.
Hardware used for the control of awning windows, allowing the window to swing out and open.

Accounts detailing the process of probate including inventories, final expenses, and the dispensation of property. Historical probate accounts were mostly filed by women and therefore these accounts provide unique information on women's experience in handling property and the history of property relations between men and women.

Refers to clients or patrons of a library, information center, or information retrieval service. For persons who themselves use products or services of the information industry to provide information services to clients or patrons, prefer "users."

In ancient Roman religion, the signs of the gods that were inscribed in nature and meant to be deciphered. Auspicia were seen as affirmative or negative answers to proposed courses of action. Auspicia often came from the sky as thunder, lightning, and different kinds of birds although there were other kinds as well. Public auspicia were taken by magistrates or augurs in the sacred space of the templum.

A declaration of forgiveness of sins. In Christianity it refers specifically to the formal remission of sin imparted by a priest or minister either in private after confession or as part of the liturgy in public worship. In Catholicism it is part of the sacrament of penance.
Use with respect to air quality inside buildings.
Term used by Chippendale and others for fret-back chairs incorporating Chinese frets.

Large French desks popular in the late Louis XV and the Louis XVI periods with a roll top in the shape of a quarter cylinder. This type was occasionally imitated in other countries, besides France, particularly in Germany and Scandinavia in the last decade of the 18th century and virtually every western country during the 19th and 20th centuries.

The transparent, gem-quality variety of olivine, which is a magnesium iron silicate mineral characterized by an olive green color. Peridot was known in ancient Greece and in Egypt; many of the green stones known to be worn by Cleopatra were peridot. Peridot was called "evening emerald" because it appears to lose its yellowish cast at night. It has sometimes been misidentified as emerald and as green glass. The main old world source for peridot was the island of Zabargad on St. John's Island in the Red Sea. It is also found in Brazil, South Africa, Myanmar, Norway, British Columbia, and Arizona and Hawaii in the USA.

Refers to Christian orders or communities of men or women following the Rule of St. Augustine, consisting of instructions for religious life written by the theologian Augustine, bishop of Hippo (354-430). The Rule places an emphasis on union with others in a common love of God. The earliest to follow the Rule were the Canons Regular, Augustinian (or Austin) Canons, approved 1059-63. Specifically, the term often refers to one of the two main Augustinian branches, the mendicant order known as the Augustinian Hermits. The Augustinian Hermits came about in 1256 when disparate orders of Italian hermits were united. The Premonstratensians and the Jeronymites are other notable orders that adopted the Rule. Augustinians have been responsible for many missions, monasteries, schools and well-known hospitals all over the world.

A Christian monastic order that resulted from 10th- and 11th-century reforms within the Benedictine order. The order is named after the town of Cluny in Burgundy, site of the celebrated abbey of the same name that was founded in 910 by Duke William the Pious of Aquitaine. The new order returned to strictly observing the rule of St. Benedict during a time of general monastic laxity. The Cluniac reforms were imitated by other monasteries and a succession of abbots gradually built up an impressive network of monasteries throughout western Europe that followed the strict Cluniac customs. The Cluniac order, free of feudal control itself, sought to eliminate feudal warfare; it supported the Truce of God and the Peace of God, which respectively restrict fighting and range of conduct. Cluniacs are also credited with integrating monks and society. The most important Cluniac abbots were St. Odon of Cluny (879-942) and St. Hugh of Cluny (Hugues de Semur; 1049-1109). St. Odo gained for Cluniac houses (called priories) exemption from all but papal authority, a centralization previously unknown in the Benedictine order. Under St. Hugh medieval monasticism reached its apogee and Cluny gained fame as a spiritual center of Western Christianity. While Hugh was abbot almost 2,000 more monasteries were founded in Italy, England, and Spain and in 1055 he founded the first Cluniac convent.

Monastic order founded in 1529 by Matteo da Bascio (1495-1552) as a reform movement. It is an autonomous branch of the Franciscans and prescribes a very strict rule emphasizing austerity and poverty. In seeking to return to the greater simplicity of early Franciscans and their literal observance of the rule of St. Francis of Assisi, Matteo wore the pointed cowl or hood (capuce) of St. Francis and he introduced aspects of the solitary life of the hermit. Despite opposition from established groups of Franciscans and near-suppression when their vicar-general became a Protestant in 1542, the zeal and preaching of the Capuchins made them powerful during the Counter-Reformation as they appealed to common and country people. In 1619 they officially became an independent order. Matteo and his followers devoted themselves to caring for victims of the plague from the 16th to the 18th century; they are also noted for their missionary and social work.

Amphorae, usually Campanian, having a body close to that of a neck amphora, but where the handles have been replaced by a single handle arched over the mouth. Mythological scenes on these amphorae are rare, while funerary scenes around a stele are common.
Gun carriages consisting basically of a central beam flanked by two lateral supports, its back end resting on the ground and its front end attached to an axletree for the front wheels.
Handwear made to be discarded after use, such as in medical or preservation contexts. Commonly made of nitrile or latex.
Producing visible forms primarily by delineation, usually by the direct application of material or instrument to the surface of the support.
The art or process of making photographs, which are pictures produced by means of the chemical action of light on a sensitive film, glass, paper, metal, or by digital means.

The art and practice of applying pigments suspended in water, oil, egg yolk, molten wax, or other liquid to a surface to create an expressive or communicative image. Paint is usually, but not always, applied with a brush. For the application of paint primarily to protect a surface or add a general color, use "painting (coating)."
Setting people in a new place or a new way of life.
Refers to buildings or rooms for long-term storage or depositing of archives or documents.
Organizations, either commercial or nonprofit, which provide information or documents (in any media), or facilitate access to them.
Saints chosen or regarded as a protector of or intercessor for a person, place, occupation, etc., which normally carry the name of the saint.

Information services which provide access to documents in a specific subject field or fields by means of abstracts and indexes issued periodically on paper, in microform, or as machine-readable databases, available by subscription or fee.

Automated reference services which provide direct answers to users' queries, or provide direct access to electronically stored databases containing the needed information. For automated information services which provide data either directly or in the form of citations to data sources, use "information retrieval services."
Optical instruments of various form used to view distant objects, particularly in the context of nautical navigation.
Fretsaws having a very deep frame and a short blade; used for inlay work.
Refers to any of various hard, brittle, heat-resistant and corrosion-resistant materials made by shaping and then firing a nonmetallic mineral, such as clay, at a high temperature.
Actions causing the infliction of the punishment of death in pursuance of a judicial sentence.

Wells bored into a confined aquifer which overflow the wellhead, because the water level of the aquifer lies above the level of the wellhead; the water rises under its own pressure through the borehole.

Term used from the 17th to the 19th centuries in England for chapbooks, usually of eight pages and sometimes with a woodcut title page, containing songs, poems, nursery rhymes and tales. The word "garland" often occurred in the books' titles.
Annual or multiannual commemorations, often occurring on the specific calendar date of the event remembered.
Refers to any rock or mineral from which iron can be extracted.
Those who specialize in creating miniatures in the medium of paint.
Those from whom a person is descended, usually considered to be those more remote in the line of descent than grandparents.
Partners in wedded or parental relations, most often applicable when the person holds certain titles, such as Queen-Consort, the wife of a king, or King-Consort, Prince-Consort, etc.
Men at the time of their marriage, or during the times just prior to or immediately after marriage.
Women at the time of their marriage, or during the times just prior to or immediately after marriage.
Female offspring.
Photomechanical prints produced by the process called heliotype.
Prints made from half-tone blocks that were prepared by photoengraving using negatives.
Photogravures differing from the ordinary type in that they are made using an aquatint grain and only one density of etching.

Photomechanical prints produced by photolithography in which the printing plate is prepared using a bichromate process, gelatin, and greasy ink, which is held in the characteristic wormlike patterns of cracks.
People who are fully grown and developed, commonly considered to be those aged 18 years or older.
People in the later stage of life, commonly considered as 65 years of age and older.

Dualistic Christian sect that thrived in Bulgaria from the tenth to the seventeenth century and more widely in the Byzantine Empire in the 11th and 12th centuries. It was founded in Bulgaria in the mid-tenth century by a priest who took the name Bogomil. The sect can be described as a fusion of dualistic, neo-Manichaean doctrines imported from the Paulicians and a local Slavonic movement aimed at reforming the recently established Bulgarian Orthodox Church. The central belief was that humanity and the visible, material world were created by the devil. Bogomils were hostile to most aspects of the Orthodox church as well as to civil authorities. The sect advocated a rigorously ascetic lifestyle, rejecting sex, marriage, possessions, and the eating of meat. Bogomils influenced the later Cathari of Europe.
A process of making deep cuts in wood so that it may be bent.
The act of freeing from restraint or bondage.
Judging how well a building performs its functions, through an understanding of the building's purpose, present use, environment, and history.
Obtaining something by the payment of money or its equivalent.
Limestone that is rich in carbon.
Modifier describing a color of high intensity and high to medium value.
Chairs usually with arms and having full-length leg rests, designed for lounging outdoors. Use "chaises longues" for similar forms used indoors.
Upholstered seats with interior springs of coiled wire.
Surgical reconstruction or replacement of a joint.
Refers to that part of the architectural design process in which requirements, conditions, goals, and methods of a building project are defined and documented.

Cushioned steps or detached cushions for the step located in front of or around an altar, used at a Mass or other Christian service. An example of usage is by kneeling acolytes, deacons, and sub-deacons during solemn segments of the worship.
The undertaking of the responsibilities and duties of an office or position.
The creation or alteration of valued objects or documents with intent to deceive.
Short poems or prose compositions in which text is arranged so that the first letters of each line form a word, phrase, or motto.
Written recognitions of acts or achievements.

Nonprint materials, such as slides, transparencies, motion pictures, or filmstrips, that make use of sight and sound to convey information; refers especially to such materials when used for instruction.

Strings or other physical combinations of specific objects such as kola nuts, cowrie shells, pieces of textile, chalk, or bark, conveying highly allusive encoded messages. These are used  by the Yoruba of West Africa in a symbol communication system.

Branch of social anthropology that studies the culture history of specific peoples using historic oral, pictorial, and textual documents as the major research sources. Refers also to the study of a people's own telling and interpretation of its history.
The science of poisons including their effects, antidotes, and detection.

Refers to maps of the surfaces of planets other than Earth, or the surfaces of moons, suns, or other celestial bodies. Modern maps of this kind are based on coordinate systems analogous to latitude and longitude used on Earth. In most cases, such modern maps are compiled from photographic observations made with Earth-based equipment or with instruments carried aboard spacecraft. The term is also used to refer to charts of stars and the heavens, where its meaning overlaps with "astronomical charts"; however, "astronomical maps" is most commonly used for all such depictions derived by modern technology.

Transcribed collections of names indicating tallies of the action or fact of being present, in answer to a summons, or to take part in public business, entertainment, instruction, worship or any other purpose.
Lists documenting persons or organizations from which a repository or institution has received gifts or donations.
Documents created or amassed by those who keep a  merchant’s books or accounts in pursuance of its legal obligations or in the transaction of business.
Observing, honoring, or commemorating with ceremonies, festivities, or wide public praise.

Actions or procedures followed to produce some end, and for the actions or changes that take place in materials or objects. When emphasis is on the manner or method by which actions or procedures are performed, use "techniques."
Photographs of a person's face or head and shoulders; most specifically portrait photographs used to identify actors, models, or other professionals.
Positive-image photographs produced in the camera without the intervening use of a negative, or produced by a positive-to-positive process.
Refers to negatives whose images are composed of gray tones, black, and white or clear areas; may include one hue as a result of process, toning, or discoloration.

Type of glass negative where the glass plate is first coated with a mixture of albumin and potassium iodide. This is then dipped in a silver nitrate solution. Albumen glass negatives were not widely used and are difficult to visually distinguish from wet collodion glass negatives.
Photographic prints having images composed of gray tones, black, and white; may include one hue as a result of process, toning, discoloration, or the use of a colored support.
Photographic prints having albumen as the binder; always black-and-white, though they may be toned to a monochrome hue.

Photographs taken of celestial bodies or astronomical phenomena. For photographs taken from beyond the earth's atmosphere, use "space photographs." For photographs of the earth taken from aircraft, use "aerial photographs."
Devices that include the full display of armorial bearings: the escutcheon plus its adjuncts (helm, crest, mantling, motto, supporters).
Modifications to shields or coats of arms for supposed misconduct or dishonor.
Notations indicating on a drawing the elevation of each point indicated by a datum mark.

Prints made from the photographic process in which the developed silver in a gelatin print is used as a catalyst to tan the gelatin, and the untanned highlights are used as a resist to a greasy ink. The original plate may be the end product or may be used as a master for transferring the image to another support. Resulting prints resemble etchings or lithographs. Though the process was originally described ca. 1907, prints may be made in this way using modern enlarging papers.

Photographic recording of a light field, rather than of an image formed by a lens, used to display a three-dimensional image of the holographed subject. Processes create three-dimensional appearing images by laser light; when properly viewed, the interference pattern recreates the pattern of light originally reflected by the subject. Allows multiple perspectives such that images in the background are obscured and revealed by those in the foreground as the angle of view changes.

Process of creating mosaics using tiny pebbles set over three foundation layers: the bottom layer of large pebbles set on packed soil, second, of stone and gravel, crushed terracotta and Santorini powder from lava, and the top being a mixture of brick powder and fine sand that sets the pebbles.
Stoles worn by a British king at his coronation.
Miniature puppets fitting over and manipulated by one finger.
Large masks enveloping the wearers' torso, and often the head or arms as well. Known particularly among the Yoruba and Makinde peoples of Africa.

Refers to the making of chronophotographs, recording motion or change with a still camera of a series of photographic images, either discrete photographs taken sequentially or a single exposure capturing movement, with a blurred effect on the images of the people and objects moved. Not to be confused with "cinematography," which is the photography of people and objects in motion with a motion picture camera.

Refers to the activity of taking photographs from aircraft. The term may also be used to refer to any photography from the air, including photographs obtained by cameras mounted on aircraft, rockets, or Earth-orbiting satellites and other spacecraft. The purpose of photography from airborne or spaceborne vehicles is generally to provide information on ground features for military and other reconnaissance, or to record the dimensional disposition of such features for surveying or mapmaking. To refer specifically only to photography taken from beyond the Earth's atmosphere, use "space photography"; for photography of celestial phenomena, use "astronomical photography." When emphasis is on the view achieved by photographing from aircraft or other high locations, use "aerial views."
Branch of aeronautics which includes the design, production, and operation of aircraft, particularly heavier-than-air aircraft.
The process of finishing or refinishing so as to give the appearance of age to an object.

Digital optical discs formatted to enable recording, rewriting and playback of high-definition video (HD), as well as storing large amounts of data. Discs in this format offer more than five times the storage capacity of previous DVDs and can hold up to 25GB on a single-layer disc and 50GB on a dual-layer disc. The name Blu-ray comes from the fact that the laser beam which reads the data from Blu-ray and Ultra HD Blu-ray Discs is blue, instead of the red beam used in DVDs and CDs.
Charitable relief given to impoverished people or others in need, including money, food, clothing, or other material gifts.
Closed social classes rigidly sanctioned by custom, law, or religion and based on heredity, that determine their members' prestige, occupation, and social relationships, especially marriage.
Dictionaries that provide terminology and definition in two languages.
Volumes composed of biographical sketches, arranged alphabetically, of people that share a common cultural context or origin.
Brief summaries that provide the essential points of written works, such as the content of a publication or of a journal.

Spaces in urban environments designed as passages for pedestrians, and as social spaces, not as clearly delimited as parks, but sharing some of the same characteristics. Often these function as utilitarian connecting spaces between buildings, or simply as an open area designated by a municipal authority, but without the amenities or formality of a park.
Areas of gardens or lawns demarcated from their surroundings and devoted to the cultivation of a particular group of plants.

Diffusion transfer process in which color dyes migrate from the negative to a sealed film unit and residual materials used in the internal development are rendered harmless and invisible once processing is complete. Generic name for the Polaroid SX-70 (TM) process.
A photographic process employing silver in a gelatin binder on a glass photographic plate.

Small paintings that depict peasant genre and street scenes, such as Roman street life, rustic taverns, travelers, street vendors, brigands, charlatans, and carnivals. Originally created in the 17th century by Northern artists living in Italy, who were known as the Bambocciati, after Pieter van Laer, who was nicknamed ‘Bamboccio.’
Ancient Roman couches, used for dining and therefore generally lacking head and foot boards.
Tusche in semi-solid paste form used to make washes of various densities in lithography or silkscreen processes. It is known for producing desirable reticulation effects.
In Jewish tradition, wooden coffers containing the Tables of the Law, kept in the holiest place of the synagogue.

Additive color screen films introduced by Agfa Company on the German market in 1916. There are two generations of this additive color screen process on film: Agfacolor-Film (1932-1934) and Agfacolor Ultra (1934-1938).

Photographs of the earth taken from aircraft. For photographs taken from beyond the earth's atmosphere, use "space photographs." For photographs of celestial bodies or astronomical phenomena, use "astrophotographs."
Structures with raised platforms and terminating in or shaped like crosses, set up in town marketplaces and used for public addresses.
Bergères with flat backs; distinct from bergères with concave backs, which are called "bergères en cabriolet."
Chairs whose splats are pierced to form a cypher with the initials of their owners.
Stools or other types of simple seats in the choir of a church, used by acolytes or other assistants of the celebrant.
Refers to the context of or associated specifically with the modern political entity of the United States of America.
The art or practice of taking and/or processing photographs whose images are composed of gray tones, black, and white, and sometimes one hue, which may result from toning or aging.
Photography that represents humanity in its natural condition, often with the intent of social critique or with the purpose of reforming social ills.

Refers to the movement in American painting, centered mainly in New York, that flourished in the 1940s and 1950s. Incorporating theories of Surrealism, Synthetic Cubism, and Neo-Plasticism, styles ranged from spontaneous, gestural compositions that paid attention to the qualities of the painting materials and stood as records of the painting process, to contemplative, near monochromatic works featuring large areas of color.
Radiographic images made by using a plane beta source to produce an image on a radiographic film. Examples are images of watermarks taken with beta radiography.

Refers to the activity of taking photographs using cameras mounted on satellites orbiting the Earth or another planet. Its purpose is generally to observe ground features and activities from high orbits above the Earth, as for military reconnaissance, mapmaking, and monitoring weather phenomena. The cameras may also be focused on space, and the photographs could reflect celestial objects or phenomena covered by the concept "astronomical photography."
Holograms lit from the front, reflecting light toward the viewer, often imitating the effect of a painting or photograph.
Color instant camera photographs.
Gum bichromate prints in which two or more superimposed differently pigmented gum layers produce a color image.
Infrastructural elements of bridges.
Inclined obliquely from a reference line, like a straight line joining the two opposite corners of a rectangle.
Positional attribute used to describe something situated at or near the lowest or deepest part of an object. For the noun denoting these parts of objects, use "bottoms" from the Components hierarchy.
Joined, connected, or bound together in some way.
A photographic plate size, about 8 1/2 by 13 inches.
Describes buildings, particularly classic Greek and Roman temples and buildings like them in structure, that have columns at the front and rear but none along the sides.
Equipment and accessories used in any of a large array of activities that are engaged in for personal satisfaction or amusement during leisure time.
Boards marked to allow the playing of backgammon. The board may consist of two panels, usually united by a hinge, allowing for game pieces to move as determined by throws of the dice.
Small-scale models of rooms with related furniture and ornaments; usually they are collectibles made for recreation or display.

Outlaws who travel the seas in ships with the organized intention of attacking and robbing others. Pirates have been active throughout history but the term is used chiefly to describe those active between the 1500s and the 1800s.

Bureaux with two tiers of drawers flanking a kneehole recess, some forms intended to be used as writing desks, others as dressing tables; of a type popular in France during the second half of the 17th century.
Persons whose occupation is to make a staple food of flour and water or other liquid or yeast to form a dough which is then cooked, usually by baking.
Cabinet officers of king or queen.
Those engaged in the breeding of horses for show, farming, sport, or other purposes.

term: Members of the House of Representatives
definition: Refers to members of the lower of the two Houses of Congress, the House of Representatives.  They serve four-year terms representing defined districts within the states.

A butler is the chief male servant in a large household; primary responsibilities may include managing the wine cellar, overseeing dining arrangements, supervising other servants, and greeting visitors.
People who cremate the dead.
Women advocates of female suffrage, primarily in Great Britain.
Written receipts given by a carrier for goods accepted for transportation.
Drawings that are end elevations of ships, indicating curvature at certain points along the ship's length. When appearing with a half-breadth plan and a sheer plan, use "lines drawings" for the set.

Distinctive glass produced on the island of Murano, located off Venice, Italy. Murano was well-known for glassmaking by the 10th century. Even though Murano glassmakers have emigrated elsewhere, experts and commercial markets usually hold that authentic Murano glass is fabricated only in Murano. Most Murano glass is made using the lampworking technique.
Documents certified by notaries that are sealed with a seal or stamp and that are recorded by the notary in a register or protocol permanently maintained for such purpose.
Prints made by machines that operate using a stencil matrix that ink is pushed through onto a paper support, in a mechanized process similar to silkscreen printing.
Films made by visual artists.
Shape having a flattened curve between convex sections of similar flattened curves, particularly in reference to furniture pieces.

People who specialize in writing in code, or are otherwise engaged in the analysis and decoding of ciphers or codes, or in the creation of them. For people who study code as a discipline, and who may also write or decipher codes, use "cryptologists."
Gouges having a shank that is either curved for its entire length or straight for most of its length with a sharp bend near the tip.
Lathes having a turret for holding various different cutting tools.
Rasps which are half-round on one side and flat on the other.
Material made to imitate ivory; usually consisting of celluloid, a synthetic resin, or, before 1881, ceramic.

Photographic or photomechanical prints in which a grid acts as a barrier to alternately reveal and obscure parts of the image, thereby creating the illusion of movement. Photographic prints of two or three phases of a depicted motion are assembled into one print. An animated picture is produced through a striped transparent overlay across the interlaced image. The order can also be reversed, with lined paper as the bottom layer, over which a transparent film with the photo is moved. It is the predecessor of the lenticular print. Examples include the Magic Moving Pictures card by G. Felsenthal & Co or the Ombro-Cinéma toys.
Locations where nuclear devices are experimentally exploded.

Discipline that studies the chronological record of events, such as affecting a nation, community, individual, object, or place, based on a critical examination of source materials and usually presenting an explanation of their causes.

Scientific study of language as a system, covering the structure, sounds, and meaning, as well as the history of the relations of languages to each other and the cultural place of language in human behavior.

Science of human and animal mind and behavior, both healthy and unhealthy, with the focus on individuals in interaction with their environment. For the branch of medicine dealing with the treatment of mental, emotional, and behavioral disorders, use "psychiatry."
Study of the conformation of the skull as indicative of mental faculties and personal character.
The study of the ancient civilization, language, history, and antiquities of Assyria.
The practice of writing in code or symbols.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Mozambique, Malawi, and Tanzania.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.

The activity of directing the business affairs and human and material resources of an organization, project, or enterprise, involving primarily the formulation of policy. When the application rather than the formulation of policy is the primary aspect, use "management." For directly overseeing the activities of an organization or enterprise, use "supervising."
Refers to the permanent or temporary cessation, in whole or in part, of a right, legal proceeding, nuisance, taxes, debt, or other claim.
Housing built by a slow step-by-step process whereby building components are added or altered by owner-builders as money, time, or materials become available.

Refers generally to large bodies of military aircraft under the control of a ruler, state, or nation that is responsible for the conduct of air warfare. The term is extended to administrative and maintenance personnel in support of this force. Functions of air forces include control of airspace and support of land or seagoing military forces. Modern air forces of major nations have incorporated intercontinental ballistic missiles, long-range bombers, and aircraft both manned and un-manned.
Investigations to determine the practicability of instituting a larger study, program, or other proposed activity.

Ecological monitoring of air, water, land to infer quality of an environment and to evaluate the impact of factors such as pollution and other potentially harmful effects of human activity. In a preventive conservation and conservation of cultural heritage context this includes the measuring, recording, and interpretation of relative humidity (RH), temperature, ultraviolet and visible light levels, pests, and both gaseous and particulate pollutants.
Counseling people, particularly students, in choosing and preparing for appropriate careers.
Areas where a river or any linear body of water curves.
Natural depressions or courses in the Earth's surface that in the past have been filled with water but currently are not filled with water or otherwise do not exist.
Designates sloping, fan-shaped masses of sediment deposited by a watercourse at the place where it leaves a constricted course or upland and emerges into a broad valley or a plain.
Hills or ridges of sand, typically in deserts, formed by shifting winds.
Flat expanses of land which have been covered with a layer of salt, due to the evaporation of a body of water.
Salt encrusted flats or plains subject to periodic inundation from flooding or high tides.
Slopes formed by loose rock fragments piled at the base of a cliff or steep slope.

Plants having seeds inclosed in a seed-vessel possessing the distinctive feature, the flower, which is a cluster of highly-specialized leaves that participate in reproduction. There are perhaps as many as 400,000 species of flowering plants, representing arouind 80% of plants now living. The classification of angiosperms is in flux, with newer divisions called the "APG system" (organized by the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group).
Shrubs or small trees having close branches arising from or near the ground.
Designates plants that complete their cycle from seed to seed in a single year.

Edible rounded bulbs of Allium cepa, which consist of fleshy concentric leaf-bases. Onions have a strong pungent flavour and smell, and vary in color from white to yellow and dark red, and are used as a culinary vegetable throughout the world, eaten raw, cooked, or pickled.
Buildings associated with academic institutions, including the schools, libraries, and other associated buildings.
Trees which seasonally shed leaves.
Trees which form an overhanging shade or shelter.
Plants with prostrate or low spreading growth that cover the surface of the earth and that smother weeds. Generally used in landscaping in place of turf.

Plant communities that are dominated by trees and other woody vegetation. A typical forest is composed of the overstory and the understory; the understory may be subdivided into the lower tree layer, shrub layer, herb layer, moss layer, and soil microbes. Today forests occupy approximately one-third of the earth's land area. For forests in the sense of cultural landscape rather than as a plant community, use "forests (cultural landscapes)."

Land suitable for agricultural production, both crops and livestock, including planted and harvested crops  such as field crops, greenhouse crops, fruit and berry plantations, nurseries, orchards, vegetable gardens, fallow land, meadows, and natural pastures.
Man-made landscapes that are the result of a process of industrial decline.
Large, uncleared areas of plant growth or thick vegetation.
Groups of trees, often of a single species, smaller than forests in extent, growing naturally or planted in formation, and generally with little or no undergrowth.

Areas having beneficial qualities to the surrounding environment or considered as natural assets to their region, typically including wetlands, flood plains, critical habitats of endangered species, and recharge zones of sole-source bodies of water.
Land that is owned collectively, by a government, or by one person, but over which certain traditional rights are in place for certain other people or the general public, for example grazing rights.
General functions and processes that occur in agriculture.

Activities involved in deliberately conveying knowledge, skills, or social values to others. For the discipline that concerns the entire process of imparting such knowledge or values, use "education."
Settling disputes by legal process.
Emergency aid or treatment given to someone injured or suddenly ill before regular medical services arrive or can be reached.

The activity of sprinkling for religious purposes. The custom is derived from ancient Rome. In Catholic and Episcopalian churches, the congregation is sprinkled with holy water before the Mass, during other sacraments, or in processions.
A branch of tourism whose object is to provide great understanding of monuments and sites, focusing on historical authenticity, preservation, and local involvement.
Describes activities conducted to advertise across platforms and spaces.
Pillars or columns, usually monumental in scale, with inscribed proclamations, laws, or histories that have been issued by a sovereign or other authority to their subjects.

Big tops, or circus tents, were first introduced ca. 1825 by the American itinerant company of J. Purdy Brown. This innovation soon became a standard of circus performances worldwide. Where a circus is made up of multiple tents, the big top is the main tent.
Covered walkways or gallerys found in gardens. Used to connect buildings or gateways, lang also divide spaces in the manner of a standing screen.

A type of mixed lace consisting of a light ground in mechanically produced tulle on which motifs are applied in bobbin- or needle lace. These motifs may be floral or figural. The technique was common from the mid-18th century and throughout the 19th.

Refers to a strong, heavy-looking bobbin lace made from the 17th century in Antwerp. A two-handled vase is the dominant decorative motif in Antwerp lace. The term can also be used more loosely to refer to other varieties of lace produced in Antwerp.

Fabric formed in a satin weave usually from silk or a manufactured fiber. It has a lustrous face and dull, crepe back. Charmeuse is most often used for lingerie, evening dresses, blouses, and linings.
In Indian architecture, a tōraṇa-pattern above wall-niche.
Cards enclosed with invitations to Mardi Gras balls, intended to be presented for admission.
Structure or arrangement of the internal elements of a work of art, such as a drawing, sculpture, or written or musical work.
The surface or part of a composition that appears to be farthest from the viewer and against which represented objects or forms are perceived.
The season of the year which is the transition period from summer to winter, occurring as the sun approaches the winter solstice, its beginning marked by the autumnal equinox.
Slag concrete to which a chemical foaming agent has been added, resulting in a lightweight slag concrete full of air holes.
A detail within a painting that is subordinate to the main theme of the work; an example would be a still life within a portrait painting.

Sets of pottery utensils designed to fit together vertically in the form of a vase or urn, made as a gift for women during confinement; usually consisting of a broth bowl on a raised foot, its cover in the form of a plate, a bowl or cup, a saltcellar, and its domed pierced cover.  They were made in Italy during the Renaissance and subsequently in other parts of Europe, and were often elaborately decorated.
Drawings giving the information necessary for preparing a dry dock for reception of a ship. May include profiles and sections.
A type of tin brass that is widely used for products requiring high strength and a high level of corrosion resistance, particularly marine equipment.
A light tan-gray or nearly white oolitic limestone quarried in Colbert County, Alabama that contains large isolated shells and other fossils.

The first photographic positive transparency process utilizing albumen-coated glass plates for making lantern slides. Introduced by Frederick and William Langenheim of Philadelphia in 1849. The process was also used for making large glass transparencies hung in windows as decorative works.

A variant of the wet collodion process to produce a direct-positive camera original. The collodion is coated on glass, the image underexposed and then underdeveloped, the glass backed with black lacquer or black cloth, and the whole mounted in a case or frame. Occasionally, the image was made on ruby glass.
Diffusion transfer process that uses dye couplers rather than silver and produces color instant camera photographs.

A direct positive process to make photographic prints in which a physically developed, unfixed print containing exposed silver chloride is soaked in a solution of potassium iodide and is bleached in relation to exposure in the camera.

A subtractive color reversal process using a film with an integral tripack, each layer containing dyes appropriate to the color sensitivity of the layer. The image is formed by the chromogenic process.
A subtractive color process for making photographic prints and transparencies using a silver-dye bleach process. Also marketed under the name Cilchrome.

Refers to a variant of the dusting-on process in which pigment is a vitrifiable powder, available in a wide range of colors, that is fired onto porcelain, earthenware, china, or the like; more broadly refers to any process to form an image on porcelain, china, earthenware, or similar material.

Photographic process that is a variant of the oil process in which the developed silver in a gelatin print is used as a catalyst to tan the gelatin. The untanned highlights become saturated when the print is soaked in water and will resist a greasy ink, while the tanned shadows accept the ink. The original print may be the end product or may be used as a master for transferring the image to another support.
Velvet having a pattern formed by cut and uncut pile.

A general name for steel that owes its distinctive properties to elements other than carbon; types of alloy steel typically take the name of the element or elements that are most influential on their character.  Usually used for toolmaking and building.
Artificial navigable waterways.
Describes nations of the world that are considered economically and technologically advanced. Generally consider this more current and accurate than "First World."

Photographic prints made by the carbon process, which uses carbon pigment and gelatin to transfer images to a paper support. Carbon prints show a very slight relief and rarely exhibit signs of aging or image deterioration. During the last quarter of the 19th century they were widely used for book illustrations and the commercial reproduction of conventionally made photographs and prints.

UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of brownish green colors.
Slides having images composed of gray tones, black, and clear areas; may include one hue as a result of process, toning, or discoloration.

Photographic images made from a negative that had been printed on a glass plate covered with gelatin silver emulsion, characterized by the back of the glass plate having been painted with gold mixed with banana oil or with bronze powders mixed in resin to give the appearance of gold. The technique was popularized by Edward Sheriff Curtis (1868-1952).
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of bluish green colors.
Negatives that have a gelatin layer as a binder on a glass support.

Silver gelatin, or silver halide, black and white prints on a fiber base, or RC-base paper, and having a digital component. Silver gelatin paper is exposed in a photographic laser printer from a digital file, then processed in liquid photo chemistry. These may have archival qualities and a completely neutral image tone.

Refers to the technique of detecting underground water, minerals, treasure, archaeological remains, and even dead bodies by feeling the motion of a divining rod. A Y-shaped twig is the traditional divining rod, its two prongs twisting or dipping in the hand of the dowser to indicate the nearby presence of the material sought; alternatively metal rods are held parallel a few inches apart and swing across each other. The nature of the stimuli causing these reactions is unexplained, but most dowsers deny that it is a matter of divination.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of bluish green colors.

UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.
One-piece bathing suits, usually tight-fitting.
Gates serving a largely ceremonial purpose.
Buildings or parts of buildings housing firms that specialize in advertising.
Buildings or sets of buildings erected as common living quarters for groups of soldiers or workers.

Areas of land that are leased by governments for the purpose of economic development, such as for forestry or mining.
Area of ground or open space; usually, but not always, where flowers, shrubs, trees, vegetables, or fruits are grown and cultivated.
