In Indian architecture, a raised terrace in front of a door; vestibule.
Rooms and other spaces within buildings that house exhibitions.
Usually rectangular units of scenery consisting of a framework of lightweight lumber and covered with canvas, linen, or other fabric.
Theatrical platforms, visible to an audience and commonly framed by a proscenium arch, on which performances are carried out.
Parts of theater stages nearest the audience and usually projecting beyond the curtain. For the acting surfaces of ancient Greek and Roman theaters, use "proscenia."
The projecting portions of the outer wall of a fortification.
Parts of bastions that connect the curtain to the face and that are in defense of the opposite face, and the passage of the ditch.
Fortified parapets with alternate solid parts and openings.
Gaps in a fortification made by battering.

Distinct from "outline drawings" in that the lines in contour drawings also follow major spatial edges within an outline; distinct from "contour maps," which delineate contours at regular intervals of elevation; distinct from "cross-countour drawings," in which the lines follow contours across the surface of the form.

Drawings made by moving a drawing implement in one continuous line while looking at the subject of the drawing and not at the drawing itself. These are usually done as excercises in hand-eye coordination.
Parts or components of pews.
Seats hinged against the end of a pew to afford accommodation when needed in the aisle.
Walls often found in gardens, usually whitewashed, also referred to as an “undulating wall.” The top of the wall has a rhythmical, wave-like appearance, and is covered by small dark tiles.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting western Kenya.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in Tazania.

Type of farthingale chair developed by the Asante people of Africa after the European prototype, decorated with brass tacks, having a low inclined back, and often with a leather-covered seat, used only by high-ranking or honored persons.
Commodes incorporating a tier of drawers flanked by open shelves or cupboards.

Glazed boxes, cases, or cabinets, of relatively small size, used for displaying and protecting items in a store, museum, home, or other location. For large, wooden cabinets with drawers, shelves, and doors or a fall front, designed for storing rare collections and popular in the 17th century, use "display cabinets."

Refers to disks of wax bearing the sign of the Agnus Dei, which is a symbol of Christ in the form of a lamb bearing a cross with a halo round its head. The small cake of wax was stamped with such a figure and blessed by the Pope. The wax may be the remains of the Pascal candle, solemnly blessed by the Pope on the Thursday after Easter. Disks may be round or oval. Figures of saints or the name and arms of the Pope are commonly impressed on the reverse. Agnus Deis may be worn suspended round the neck, or they may be preserved as objects of devotion. In virtue of the consecration they receive, they are regarded as "sacramentals," like holy water or blessed palms.
Manufacturing using computer systems and techniques to track and control the flow of information, materials, energy, and labor throughout a factory, completely or in part.
The act or process of treating something, usually by adding or applying a substance, before proceeding with additional treatment.

The process of re-recording or adding a layer of sound to an existing soundtrack, usually for the purpose of introducing a translation of spoken dialog to a film. Also generally; to mix several tracks into a united track, or in extended use, the process of copying an existing sound or video recording in its entirety.
Joints filled with mortar and located between masonry units.
Joints between different courses or layers of bricks.
Recessed joints where a space is left between two members. An example is with joints in drywall or metal, where there is a narrow space between two adjoining panels, often allowing movement.
Heavy-guage wire U-shaped fasteners used to secure wire fencing to fence posts.
Purchasing by prepayment a series of objects, events, or services, such as a specified number of issues of a serial publication, a concert series, or cable television.
Architectural elements that are part of the structure of a building, as opposed to elements that are decorative.
Masses, usually of masonry, that support and receive the thrust of arches, vaults, or trusses.
The general classes of load-distributing devices, based on structural principles, used in built works.
Rows of columns that serve primarily to separate interior spaces.
Niches or small shrines, often intended for sculpture, or for frameworks around doors or windows formed of columns, corbeling, or pilasters, supporting a pediment or canopy.
Structures in which cables are essential to the system of support, as for example by suspension or staying.
Parts or components of arches, domes, or vaults.

Generally, any process or method involving aging, seasoning, washing, drying, heating, smoking, or otherwise treating whereby a product is preserved, perfected, or readied for use. In the context of leather manufacture, use specifically for processes such as "brining", "dry-salting", and "wet-salting" done to prevent putrifaction or other damage to hides and skins before tanning.
Architectural elements used to fortify structures.
Infrastructural elements of dams.
Parts or components on sites related to air flight or travel.
General term for architectural features that reduce heat gain or light, through designs that block the direct entrance of sun rays into buildings; may be either fixed or movable devices.

Use both for the horizontal or vertical members dividing glazing areas into lights and supporting the panes, and for the vertical members separating panels in panel doors; for the uprights that divide openings set in a series, use "mullions."
Small, thin, flat pieces of metal, leather, or other suitable material bearing a unique official identification number of a registered vehicle, to which it is to be attached.
The action of selling by auction, which is a public sale in which each bidder offers an increase upon the price offered by the preceding bidder.
Rooms adjacent to a lady's bedroom, serving as private sitting rooms and dressing rooms.
Parts of building plumbing systems that carry away waste; for sewers designed to carry away waste in larger drainage systems, use "sanitary sewers."
The removable actuating devices of locks. For hand tools used for opening and closing devices other than locks and that do not have a jaw and do not fit into screws, use "keys (adjusting equipment)."
Parts of keys which are inserted into a lock and engage the tumblers or bolt.

Flat, thick plates, usually of concrete, functioning as structural elements and capable of sustaining loads, often serving as floors and roofs; also, use collectively, for the structural systems based on such elements.
Structural portions of a flat slab that is thickened (by lowering the form) throughout an area surrounding a column, column capital, or bracket.
Plates, usually metal, set in a coffin lid bearing the name of the deceased, usually with the dates of birth and death.
The compass point that is 90 degrees clockwise from the north point, or generally the direction towards the half of the sky where the sun rises.
Beams with three or more supports. Beams with three or more supports.
Continuous foundations under the full extent of a structure.
Method for the removal of wall paintings involving the removal of the arriccio together with the wall support.
Refers to isolated masonry foundation components delivering loads to a bearing stratum; distinct from "piles," which are smaller and may be clustered.
Timber, steel, or precast concrete columns serving as subsurface supports for vertical loads; distinct from "piers (foundation components)" which are larger and are never clustered.
Portions of the foundations of some structures which transmit loads directly to the soil; used to distribute the weight of the superstructure over a greater area to prevent or reduce settlings.
Semicircular or polygonal extensions off of a larger space, such as the termination to the choir or sanctuary in a basilica. May be vaulted.
Drawings created by artists qualified to teach apprentices and to carry on their trade independently. This term is usually applied to works created before 1800.
Paintings produced by applying washes of thin, transparent watercolor, usually onto paper.
Large stone slabs set vertically as revetments at the lower part of walls. Large stone slabs set vertically as revetments at the lower part of walls.
Screws with a hexagonal recess to receive an Allen wrench.
Threaded fasteners that screw into a threaded hole rather than into a nut. Cap screws are specified by diameter, length, and thread pitch.
Heavy thumbscrews designed for securing one end of a vertical shutter.
Decorative handles that use a stylized figure of a lion’s head or body holding a movable or fixed ring in its mouth or looped tail.
Racks for holding or storing small arms; may be freestanding or attached to something else.
Hardware mounted on the exterior of the water tank of a toilet that lifts the valve inside the tank allowing water to flow into the toilet bowl.
Bars attached to the wall in a shower or near a bathtub that may be grasped to steady the bather.
Spherically shaped gate valves which provide a very tight shut-off for fluids in a high-pressure piping system.
Steel bars, usually with manufactured deformations or threading, used in concrete and masonry construction to provide additional strength.

A rock bolt is a steel or fiberglass rod used as a long anchor bolt to stabilize the roof or walls of a rock formation in underground mining and tunneling. It is inserted and anchored in a hole drilled into the rock and transfers load from the exterior to the much stronger interior of the rock mass.
Small columns with capital and base placed against the jambs of doors or windows, especially found in Medieval architecture.
Use broadly for all sorts of walls constructed to resist attack.
Easels used primarily or solely for the display or presentation of an object, rather than to support a work as it is created.
The outward upper portion of a furniture leg, especially of a cabriole leg.
Distinctive barge board supports seen in Maori architecture.
Horizontal members that tie together and stiffen two opposite rafters, usually at a point about halfway up the rafters.
Volatile, noninflammable compound of carbon and chlorine.
Mixture of liquid hydrocarbons obtained from petroleum in the form of a flammable pale yellow to colorless oily liquid used as fuel for lamps, heaters, and jet engines, and as a solvent.
Coffeepots having separate containers, often in the form of a muslin bag, in which the coffee is immersed while being boiled and usually a stand with a heating device for keeping the coffee warm.
Protection systems that provide safeguards to construction and exit facilities through the use of fire alarm, fire detecting, and fire extinguishing equipment to reduce the risk and spread of fire.

Electrical or mechanical systems, installed in a building that sound a blast or bell when smoke or flames are detected; certain alarms are engineered to trigger sprinkler systems for added protection.
Solid figures contained by six equal squares and eight rectangular solid angles; regular hexahedrons.

Sections of new construction attached to an existing built work, with the function of adding an extension or increasing the floor area or height of an existing building beyond the original building envelope.
The state of the body of pottery and porcelain after it has partially hardened in consequence of the evaporation of the moisture content.
In mechanics, the distance from the axis to a point, such that, if the whole mass of a body were concentrated at it, the moment of inertia would remain unchanged.
Regions of a member where yielding occurs as loads are increased; the regions of highest moment that develop when all fibers are fully yielded at a cross section.

Physical forces that affect the motion or equilibrium of material bodies, in modern usage including both statics and kinetics. In earlier usage, dynamics was restricted to the action of force in producing or varying motion, and thus was opposed to statics.
The deformation or movement of a structure and its flexural members (such as beams or trusses) from their original positions, due to loads and forces acting on that structure.
Quadrilateral parallelograms having four right angles.
Acts of formal coming or going into a place, often with a procession and retinue, such as a king entering a town.

Periodic programs of festive activities and cultural events with a specified focus on objects, environments, or experiences that are visual in nature, were created by the use of skill and imagination, and possess an aesthetic that is valued and of a quality and type that would be collected by art museums.

The belief systems, values, philosophical systems, knowledge, behaviors, customs, arts, history, experience, languages, social relationships, institutions, and material goods and creations belonging to a group of people and transmitted from one generation to another. The group of people or society may be bound together by race, age, ethnicity, language, national origin, religion, or other social categories or groupings.

Motion in a medium in which, when particles are displaced, a force proportional to the displacement acts on the particles to restore them to their original position. If a material has the property of elasticity and the particles in a certain region are set in vibratory motion, an elastic wave will be propagated.

Architectural term that defines the stone edges of stairways on the pyramidal bases of temples of central Mexico. They were sometimes decorated with reliefs or capped with a serpent head in the postclassic period.
Short vertical members used to support a stair handrail or coping, often circular in section with a vase-shaped outline. Used also in furniture, as on the backs of chairs.
The group of religions comprising Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, that trace their origin to the prophet Abraham.

Any of several Christian denominations that believe in the literal and imminent second coming of Christ and the imminent end of the world. These beliefs are found in most periods of history. William Miller (1781-1849) began a movement in the United States based on his prediction that Christ would return in 1843-44. Miller's followers, who formed the denomination called Seventh Day Adventists, believe that Christ's second coming is delayed solely by a failure to keep the Sabbath. Seventh Day Adventists rigorously follow laws of Sabbath observance as well as Old Testament dietary laws.

Refers to an Islamic religious movement founded in India in 1889 by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (ca. 1839-1908). Ghulam Ahmad claimed to be the Messiah Mahdi prophesied in the Koran, the Christian Messiah, an incarnation of the Hindu god Krishna, and a reappearance of Muhammad. In 1914 the sect split into two very separate branches, the Qadiyani and Lahori. Ahmadiyya is rejected by orthodox Muslims because Ghulam Ahmad's claim to be a prophet following Muhammad cannot coexist with the traditional belief that Muhammad was the last manifestation of God. Other unorthodox beliefs are that Jesus feigned death and actually escaped to India, where he died at the age of 120, and that the concept of jihad (holy war) can be reinterpreted as a peaceful instead of violent battle against unbelievers. After many years of demonstrations against the sect, its followers were declared heretical in 1974 and were officially banned from the orthodox Islamic community. The movement is noted for its missionary zeal and is active in Asia, Africa, and Europe.

Religious movement and Jewish branch espoused by Zacharias Frankel (1801-1875) that endeavors to preserve particular elements and customs of traditional Judaism while allowing for limited modernization such as the support of the secular Zionist movement. This branch of Judaism is governed by the idea that Judaism defines Jewish culture and national identity, and therefore, religious customs and traditions such as dietary laws, the study of Hebrew, and the observation of Sabbath, must be upheld.

Refers to a Hindu sect and reform movement founded by the brahman Dayananda Sarasvati in Bombay in 1875. Followers, striving for a return to the original purity of Hinduism found in the Vedas, are against image-worship, child-marriage, polygamy and meaningless ritual. Dayananda's book 'Vedabhashya' contains his interpretations of the Vedas, the earliest Hindu scriptures. Arya Samaj promotes a moral vision of kindness and goodwill to all. Arya Samaj, now a worldwide organization, is also opposed to the traditional Hindu caste system and works to remove religious and social injustices. Arya Samaj followers also introduced the novel idea of converting to Hinduism people of other faiths. In 1893 there was a split between conservative and liberal followers who disagreed on whether to advocate traditional or modern forms of education and on whether to advocate vegetarianism or freedom of diet. The movement became nationalistic and was in conflict with Sikhs and Muslims, especially in the Punjab around the time of the partition of India and Pakistan in 1947.
Sector of Catholicism of the Church of Milan, reflecting a distinctive, ancient rite, including its associated plainsong. Derives its name from St. Ambrose, Bishop of Milan (374-397).

Refers to the conservative Anabaptist sect led by Jakob Amman that separated from the Mennonites in Switzerland around 1693. The development of more liberal sects occurred after many Amish migrated to the United States, particularly in the 1870s. Only the Old Order Amish (founded 1720-1740) still maintain Amman's strict dress codes, customs, and policy of non-cooperation with the state. Today, the Amish exist mainly in southeastern Pennsylvania.
Collective term referring to the various schools of Buddhism that have flourished in China.
Constructions containing the stairs, supporting framework, balustrade, well opening, adjacent walls, and other components for a flight or series of flights of stairs.
Stairs that, as they progress from bottom to top, turn 90 degrees; for stairs with landings at which the stair turns 90 degrees, use "quarterpace stairs."
Stairs with landings at which the stair turns 90 degrees; for stairs that turn 90 degrees as they progress from bottom to top, use "quarter-turn stairs."
In architecture, upright posts supporting the handrail at the top and bottom of a stairway or at the turn on a landing; also, the main posts about which circular staircases wind.
Terminal features of newels often molded, turned, or carved in a decorative shape.
Film or video makers who present fact and real situations and people rather than fiction.
Bead moldings separated from an adjoining surface by quirks, along one or both sides.
General term for rooms or sets of rooms used as dwellings or private living quarters and located in larger buildings, such as apartment houses, private houses, or hotels.
Of a text, editing into a shortened, concise form, often by omitting the less important passages of the original.
Including or appropriating an area within the limits of a governmental unit.
Airtight spaces permitting passage between spaces of different air pressures or qualities, or between underwater and air-filled spaces.
Rooms for the accommodation of guards while on duty.
Rooms, primarily of the 18th century, in which social gatherings and balls (commonly referred to as assemblies) were held.
Rooms or structures where monarchs or other great personages formally receive visitors.
Arched or vaulted niches or similar recesses in Roman catacombs; usually meant to hold sarcophagi.
Altarpieces consisting of several painted panels or other images connected by an architectural structure.
Seats in the choir area of a church, wholly or partly enclosed on the back and sides.
Frames that are set in walls to receive and hold windows, either being boxed for sliding sashes, or solid and rebated for casements.
Particular arrangements of vertical elements of a building as seen by observers from the garden view.
Ceilings with deepened decorated panels between intersecting beams of a ceiling.
Recessed panels, usually square or octagonal, set into ceilings, roofs, vaults, or soffits.

Solid, fixed supports found under such architectural elements as columns or balustrades, or built in to hold sculpture; may also be used for freestanding furniture supports, usually for decorative objects, sometimes incorporating cabinets or shelves; usually classically divided by tripartation into base, dado, and cap.
Refers to the topmost projecting element of a pedestal classically divided by tripartation.
Framing members that cross and support the ends of joists or rafters.
Metal members having an L-shaped section.

Named for French mathematician Pierre Bézier. Use for curves rendered mathematically from cubic equations generated from a series of control points. Bezier curves are used in computer programs to create curved lines for graphics and complex paths for 3-D modeling. A Bezier curve is a form of b-spline curve.
The highest points of arches or vaults.
Designates security systems dependent on electronic devices, such as card readers.
Official recognition of an institution as maintaining standards that render them eligible for membership in an association of similar institutions.
Windows having two vertically sliding sashes, each closing a different part of the window; the weight of each sash is counter-balanced for ease of opening and closing.

Doors, usually unframed, formed of narrow vertical boards or planks held together by cross-pieces, battens, nailed to them. They may be constructed with two layers of planks, positioned on either side of the battens.
Stiles on doors to which the door hinges are attached.
Boards shaped to a tapered edge set into a frame and with a raised center section, field, or panel.
In Indian architecture, the outermost door jamb.
Unexpected happenings that occur without the intent or volition of any beings involved, especially those of an undesirable or unfortunate nature.
Sales involving works of art.
Ceremonial feasts typically held to honor or support a person, organization, or cause.

Rituals surrounding the exit from a locale or building. May involve burnt offerings, pit offerings, and broken pottery or ornaments. Examples are in pre-Columbian cultures where it was believed that living spirits inhabit inanimate objects, and that damaging or destroying the object can release the spirit.
Ceremonies joining a couple in matrimony, in which at least one of the two parties is of royal or noble birth.

Cultural gathering practiced by Northwest Coast Native Americans that commemorates the lives of deceased clan members; historically has referred to any kind of potlach ceremony but in contemporary usage refers specifically to memorial services. Gift giving and speeches are a central feature of the event.
Ceremonial excision of the clitoris, or less radical surgical procedure thereon, typically performed as a female initiation ceremony in some societies.

Contests in which the participants prepare a recipe in a fixed amount of time. Although the term has been trademarked by the Pillsbury Company since 1950, it is found without the tradmark designator in dictionaries.

Tournaments in which knights, divided into companies (quadrilles) and distinguished by liveries, are engaged in various plays and exercises; to this were often added chariot races, and other shows and entertainments.  For specific tournaments, races, or balletic exercises involving horses, use "equestrian ballet" or "horse races."
Gateways or doors; in the context of Mughal architecture, refers to grand entrances to significant buildings or complexes.
Passages through fences or walls separating two exterior spaces, or the structures or ornamental constructions enclosing such passages.

Performances that include trained animal acts or exhibitions of human skill and daring, or both. Circuses usually include a trained, traveling company or troupe of performers, various animals, and their equipage. The term "circus" refers to the circular arena surrounded by tiers of seats below which the performance occurs in a circular area called the "ring."
Refers to the final climactic day of Carnival festivities, occurring on the last day before Lent. In some places, such as New Orleans, the term is applied to the entire Carnival season.

Parades consisting of floats, vehicles, boats, or participants that are decorated or covered with flowers. Floats are usually designed to illustrate a theme or represent a group, and are often judged in a competition following the parade itself.
Processions on horseback or with horse-drawn carriages, marking a festive or solemn occasion.
Raised skylights or small lanterns with the sides mostly glazed, erected on a roof to admit light to the space below.

The concept of a supernatural force, typically a deity, causing a person to experience creative desire. The inspiration may be to the extent that the deity describes the specifications for the work to be created. The deity may be said to have expressed their wishes in a dream or vision, or in another fashion.
Days of celebration observed by followers of Buddhism.
Windows or portions of window units that are designed not to open.
Windows of a type commonly used in residential basements, usually having between one and three lights only.
Holes or crevices (as in a furnace, oven, or door) through which one may look.
Unintended imperfections on a bronze that occurs during casting and appears as a more or less subtle discontinuity in the desired form and is associated with either a lack or an excess of metal.

Small openings (as in walls or parapets), often with deeply splayed jambs, through which small arms may be discharged; for similar openings to admit light and air or to permit observation, use "loop windows."
Designates architectural drawings done early in the design process; often not to scale and may include diagrammatic elements.
Underdrawings for fresco paintings made with the red earth pigment sinopia, which is brushed on the arriccio layer of plaster and over which the intonaco is applied before painting.
Windows that have one or more top-hinged, out-swinging sashes.
Events in which men ceremonially fight with, and in most traditions kill, bulls according to formal ritual in an arena for sport and public entertainment.
Art that is created by a step-by-step procedure, often expressed and realized through computer code.

Social gatherings for dancing, especially events where people belonging to a common group, establishment, society, or profession gather and sometimes having an organized program and special entertainment.

Balls at which those attending wear costumes departing from currently conventional style and usually representing fictional or historical characters, animals, particular occupations, or the fancy of the wearer.
Games in which a ball is used in play.
Axonometric projection in which all three spatial axes are inclined, but only two are equally inclined to the plane of projection or drawing surface.

Refers to a system of projection in which principal faces of an object or structure are parallel to the picture plane, but multiple views of the object or structure are provided in order to fully represent all sides of it.

The actions of legally, or sometimes informally, taking a child or other person who is not one's offspring into the relationship of parent/child. The term may also refer to similar arrangements between people and animals or between two animals.
Murders of high public officials or other prominent persons, whether by persons acting alone or in conspiracy with others.
Executions by decapitation, or other actions of cutting off the head of a human or animal.

Refers to the penultimate stage in the formal process that leads to the canonization of a saint in the Roman Catholic Church. At this stage, the pope grants the title 'Blessed' to a Roman Catholic of exemplary faith and life who is considered worthy of public veneration after his or her death. After this stage, such a person can be locally honored. If there is evidence of two miracles then the canonization can proceed, leading to the person becoming a universally recognized saint.
Small triangular lights between subordinate arches of the tracery of a window.

Recreation involving at least some bodily exercise or hands-on activity, especially in children and immature animals as part of their process of learning adult behavior and exploring their environment.
Narrow boards placed at an angle in louvers.
General functions related to analysis.

Suspended structures used to protect the altar in a church, or to designate the altar as the place of greatest importance in the space. When an altar canopy is made of fabric, it consists of a roof with hangings and sometimes curtains.

Generally reserved for the process or function of assigning a price for a thing based on market value, insurance value, or another such means of estimation; often determined by comparing the thing to other similar things that have been sold in a recent timespan. An example is the insurance value of an item that is vouched for by a reputable antiquarian.

Examining an object, action, material, or concept in detail by separating it into its fundamental elements or component parts, reducing something complex into its various simple elements. It is the opposite process to "synthesis."
The practice of obtaining funding for a project or venture by soliciting contributions from a large number of people especially using social media and the Internet.

Collaborative, instructional Web-based seminars that do not require participants to be in physical proximity to one another. Webinars may include the ability to interact with other participants via audio or video feeds.
Rooms in barns or stables with provisions for feeding horses or other animals.
Systems whereby developers are granted concessions in exchange for providing amenities a community feels are desirable.
Curb roofs with only the two opposite sides sloping.
Small dimension stone with a flat faced surface, usually square or rectangular.
The figures or ornaments at the lower angles or apex of a pediment, generally supported on plinths.

Refers to those portions of a roof that project beyond the gable, in effect the raking equivalent of eaves; see "eaves" for portions projecting beyond the walls, at the lower horizontal edges of roofs. Refers to those portions of a roof that project beyond the gable, in effect the raking equivalent of eaves; see "eaves" for portions projecting beyond the walls, at the lower horizontal edges of roofs.
The property or characteristic of a color regarding its position in the visible spectrum.

The process of removing sections of gathered matter from within a binding with the intention that they stand alone thereafter. Where the gathered matter has been removed from the binding in preparation for rebinding in a different form, use "pulling (dismantling)." Where the gathered matter has been collated but never bound, for example a book in sheets, signatures, or gatherings, use "unbound."
Administration by local or regional authorities.
Refers to the buying, selling, and trading of works of art.
Vaults constructed by corbeling, or cantilevering, successive courses inward beyond the preceding one, until they meet and are capped at the vault's midpoint.
Tile timbrel vaults erected by the Guastavino family between about 1800 and 1950, especially in the United States since 1881.
Tapestry weaving technique in which the weft threads of two adjacent areas are turned alternately around a common end in groups of two or more.
The uppermost members of columns, piers, or pilasters.
Parts or components of pier foundations.
Stepped platforms of Classical temples.
Arches struck from a single center, such as semicircular, segmental, or horseshoe arches. Arches struck from a single center, such as semicircular, segmental, or horseshoe arches.
Official status in a hierarchical ordering of positions within an organization or social class, such as the armed forces, aristocracy, diplomatic corps, or government bureaucracy.
Wood or metal arches hinged at the two springing points.
Arches that counteract the thrust of another arch.
Arches with jambs that are not at right angles to the faces.
Arches whose intrados, and possibly the extrados, has a very slight rise; for arches with no curvature, use "flat arches."
A surface layer intentionally produced by an artist or a specialized professional on a metallic artwork to mimic a natural patina with aesthetic or practical purposes.

Theory or method that seeks to humanize modern architecture by moving away from global uniformity and unquestioning reliance on technology, favoring instead solutions drawing on regional traditions and materials, while at the same time maintaining awareness of the universal nature of contemporary culture.

Prescribed ceremonial cleansing of part or all of the body or of objects with the intent of purification or dedication, usually but not exclusively performed with water. Usually associated with a religious ritual.

Literary device based on the Latin word, allusio, meaning 'a play on words', used to insinuate, suggest, or provide indirect reference to a person, event, thing, or part of another text. Allusions are distinguished from devices such as direct quote or imitation and are based on the assumption that a body of knowledge and cultural understanding is shared by the author and reader.
Numerical quantity expressing the degree to which a substance absorbs something.
The motion and behavior of projectiles in flight.
Algorithms, often expressed in algebraic symbols.
The portions of columns, colonettes, or pilasters between the base and the capital. The portions of columns, colonettes, or pilasters between the base and the capital.
In Indian architecture, a rectilinear band or recess in the necking of columns.
The determination and measure of responsibility and liability to another.
Pulls that are designed to be installed in recessed cavities in the edges of pocket doors, and that lie flush against the edge of the door when released.
Hanging devices used to support pipes, designed to allow adjustment for pipes of various sizes.
Short sections of angle iron used to attach structural members, such as precast panels, to structural steel.
Short, headless pins with a sharp point on one end and barbs between the two ends, used largely for fastening the mortise-and-tenon joints in a window sash and for door work.
In Indian architecture, a type of beam.
The study, planning, and actions of conveying people or things from one place to another.
An area reserved for leaving vehicles temporarily.
Degree to which air is polluted, such that air quality is deemed to be high when air pollution levels are low.

Type of tax used in Spanish colonial times. Each land owner or tenant had to pay an alcabala tax to the State to be able to carry out activities of buying and selling products in their respective establishments.

Designs that are rhetorical, reflecting a theoretical or speculative architectural position on social or political issues, often considered ahead of their time, and usually not intended to be carried out; often applied, but not necessarily restricted, to designs by certain French architects of the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
In traditional Indian art and dance a standing pose in which the body has a slight bend in both upper and lower halves, through which a perpendicular axis would pass to the right of the navel.

Architectural order similar to the Ionic order, but differing in that the capital features a palmette motif rising between the two outer volutes, rather than being linked horizontally by a form at the top of the capital.
Mechanisms in a lock that automatically deadlock  the main latch bolt when the door is closed.
Refers to catches of various kinds, but usually spring bolt latches used to secure the doors of cabinets or other furnishings.
Arched pulls, typically found on furniture, where the ends of the hoop or half-ring are attached to the body of the item or to a plate attached to the item.
Large cupped pulls for heavy doors.
Natural sources of water, such as lakes, rivers, and ground water, available for use.

Drawings or works in another two-dimensional medium representing one longitudinal half of a ship as viewed from above and emphasizing the ship's lines. When appearing with a body plan and a sheer plan, use "lines drawings" for the set.

Refers to drawings or works in another two-dimensional medium, where the image is created by using axonometric projection, which is a system of portraying a three dimensional object by depicting projectors parallel to each other and generally where at least one of the three spatial axes is inclined to the plane of projection. In modern architectural parlance, the term sometimes refers only to drawings depicted as if an orthographic rendering of the object has been tilted to the plane.
Traditional Mexican cut-paper works. Multiple works may be attached to ropes and hung as banners. Used for Day of the Dead, Independence Day, and other festivals.
Door hinges each having a single joint, usually of modern design.
Recessed masonry joints formed in mortar by the use of a curved steel jointing tool; effective in resisting rain penetration.

The earth's major animal and plant communities, classified according to the predominant vegetation and characterized by adaptations of organisms to that particular environment. The number and description of biomes varies depending upon the classification used.
The condition of moisture being taken up by buildings.

A term historically applied in a general sense to the trade carried on between ports of the same country as distinguished from that carried on with foreign ports. Also called intercoastal navigation. According to the laws of some maritime nations, the term is also applied to the trade carried within the geographical limits of the foreign trade. The modern term "short sea shipping" refers to the movement of cargo and passengers mainly by sea along a coast, without crossing an ocean.

An ISO standard developed to measure and calibrate lightfastness and fading of colorants and other materials. It consists of a card that contains eight sections of blue-dyed wool cloth, each with a different lightfastness. The dyes fade at a known rate.
The conversion of outmoded or unused things, often things having historic value, to new uses or application in new contexts. Examples include reuse of buildings, objects, software, etc.
Compositions or interior design that are considered  by many to be overly crowded and busy; from the Latin meaning "fear of empty spaces."
Those trained in or practicing acrobatics.

Term used in maritime commerce to signify the damage or expenses resulting from the perils of marine navigation such as damage caused by storm, collision or cargo shifting. It also implies partial, as distinguished from total, loss. To be distinguished from 'general average' which refers to damage caused in shipsaving situations.
Originally from a funerary fire of bones, typical usage came to refer to large fires kindled in the open air for a celebration, display, or amusement.
Power-operated doors that open and close at the approach of a person or vehicle.
Two hundredth anniversaries or their observances.
Holidays associated with a particular culture or ethnicity.
The transmission of sound pressure waves from a body due to a rapid energy release in response to internal or external mechanical stress placed upon the medium.
Sound having frequencies greater than 20,000 Hz; often applied in testing and therapy techniques.
The state of low temperature or to describe processes or situations that take place under conditions of low temperatures.
The general application of science and related disciplines, typically to commercial or industrial objectives, often with the implication of mechanical, electronic, or computerized components.

The development and use of sustainable approaches to meeting human and ecological needs through the applications of scientific principles and engineering techniques as they are connected to the place, resources, economics, culture and impacts of their uses.

Of a device, instrument, information storage, or other applications, operating according to the principles or methods of electronics, such as having a transistor, microchip, or electron tube. For appliances or instruments that are powered by electricity, use "electric."

Using or devising mechanical or electronic devices, processes, or systems which take the place of human effort, observation, or decision, and which require minimal human intervention in their operation.
The rate at which the velocity of a body changes with time.
Dating of volcanic activity by studying tephra deposits, which include volcanic ash and other ejecta, especially in a stratigraphic deposit.
Concepts and devices used in artistic practice.
Purpose, design, or concept behind an artist's creative effort.
The practice or art of choosing, cooking, and eating good food.

The capacity to form or the state of forming mental images or ideas of people, objects, and situations that are not truly present to the senses, including both remembered and constructed ideas and images. In modern philosophy, imagination is the power or capacity by which the mind integrates sensory data in the process of perception.
Ideas having to do solely with the spectacular and improbable, with no or very little relationship to real people, objects, or events.
Systematic arrangement of visible energy rays by wavelength, seen as a band of rainbow colors when sunlight is passed through a prism.

Use to describe an image, or to denote the effect itself, when the image is composed of a smooth gradation of tones. Often used to designate copy that will need to be photographed with a halftone screen in order to be printed.
The condition of being understandable in two or more ways, as, for example in two or more different social or historical contexts, or of referring to two or more things at the same time.

Symbolic gesture of the body, often particularly focused on the hand and fingers, used in in Indian dance, Hindu and Buddhist ritual, ceremonies, and art, and other contexts. Also used in yoga, meditation, and other activities. Types of mudra represent various concepts, such as reassurance or meditation. These symbolic or ritual hand positions have deep roots in Indic religious tradition. Types of mudra in sculpture and other visual arts are relatively restricted in number, given that movement is necessarily not incorporated.
Property of materials having a pH of 7 or higher when the concern is that there be little or no acid present to accelerate aging or deterioration.
Properties relating to or resembling those of dielectrics, substances such as air, ceramics, or wax, that act as electrical insulators and can sustain an electric field.
The ability of a material's surface to withstand wear due to mechanical action against it such as rubbing, scraping, or erosion.
The quality or state of having both viscous and elastic properties.
The state of being rigid to a degree or in part.
The dimensional response of a material subject to crushing forces and the action that leads to it.
The measure of the level of sharpness that photographic films are able to render.
Visible fluorescence emitted by materials in paintings and other objects exposed to ultraviolet radiation.
Quality or state of exhibiting a milky iridescence like that of an opal.
The emission of light produced in chemical reaction by living organisms and the light so produced.
The ability of a paint, varnish, or other medium to completely hide or cover a surface, often in one coat.
The extent to which gases, liquids, or plant roots penetrate into or pass through a layer of soil.
The temperature at which liquid comes to a boil.

In design, the positioning of two elements set back-to-back, such as two identical figures facing in opposite directions. Examples are in heraldry and architectural ornament. For two figures facing each other, use "affronted."
The use of similar forms around a center of balance. The forms may give a feeling of equal relationships, but are varied to prevent visual monotony.

A technique of lacquer decoration where patterns are cut into the lacquered surface, more lacquer is applied and gold foil or gold dust is placed in the incised areas, becoming cemented into the designs when the lacquer dries. This technique was introduced to Japan from China, where it was known as "ts'ang-chin", during the Muromachi period (1392-1573) and became particularly popular in the 18th century.
Having the outline or form created by two intersecting regular curves, namely the shape of an oval with pointed ends, like the kernel of the drupe (fruit) of an almond tree.
In art, harmony or fitness in the adaptation of the parts of a whole to each other; often, studied elegance of design or arrangement.
The placing of something, usually a building, in relation to the sun.
The ratio of width to height of an image frame. The term is generally used in reference to motion pictures and other screen-oriented technologies including computer graphics.
Scale represented by a line or bar subdivided into units.
Range of distances, near and far, within which objects appear in sharp focus.
Visual sensation occurring after the external cause has disappeared.
The gently swelling convex curvature along the line of taper of columns, made to prevent the illusion of concavity in straight or regularly tapered columns.

Refers to a system of perspective that is based on orthodox linear perspective but exploits the extreme degradation of forms on the picture plane at very wide angles of view. It uses the optical trick of anamorphosis, in which a form depicted on the picture plane is subject to such extreme lateral stretching that it is unrecognizable from the front, but legible when viewed from a very shallow angle.

Refers to a perspective system in which rectangular forms are set at an angle to the picture plane rather than parallel to it; among possible techniques are two-point perspective and three-point perspective.

The state or quality of being composed of or bearing small grains or particles.  Regarding paint layer structure, refers to paint that consists almost entirely of pigment particles with little or no vehicle.

Refers to methods of making storage areas in openly accessible. Collections on view are often only a small portion of an institution’s total holdings. Physical objects previously hidden from view may be shared with the public through such means as glass wall bays exposing contents of storage areas; or by visitable study collections in storage space available for viewing and research by students, scholars, and the general public.
Loads or forces acting through the center of gravity of the section of structural members, therefore perpendicular to the plane of the section.
Dynamic loads created in a structure caused by the rapid movement of structural members due to seismic vibrations.
Loads added to existing loads.
Tension and compression forces that are collinear with the long axes of structural members.
The overloading or overstraining of bridges to such an extent that they can no longer perform their required functions.
Depiction or description of sexual love. For depiction or description of sexual activity in an explicit manner intended to stimulate erotic rather than aesthetic feeling, use "pornography."
Conforming to the architectural theories of the European and American academies of architecture.
Conforming to the official standards and principles of taste of European and American art academies.

Art and design that focuses narrowly on the marketing of products and other sales, including typography, layout, packages, mailings, and other visual materials having to do primarily or exclusively with sales. It may include design for the Internet and social media.

Genre of Japanese folk art conforming to the principle of the inseparability of beauty and high utility in everyday practical objects of the common people; traditional craft methods without conscious aesthetic intent govern the production of the objects of the genre. Distinguished from the utilitarian goods of the aristocracy, which consciously strove for aesthetic effect, and from the everyday utilitarian products of modern industrialization; genre defined and term used since 1920s.

Refers to a concept or idea not associated with any specific instance, and to the process of formulating general concepts by abstracting common properties of instances. It includes the consideration of a thing independently of its associations; or a substance independently of its attributes; or an attribute or quality independently of the substance to which it belongs. It is the idea of something that has no independent existence; a thing which exists only as an idea. For the modern art movement and its products, use "Abstract."
Biomorphic forms or images are ones that while abstract nevertheless refer to, or evoke, living forms such as plants and the human body.

Refers to illusionistic effects on two- or three-dimensional art works in which the appearance of wood grain is simulated. In interior spaces, pine and other inexpensive softwood paneling may be painted to imitate expensive woods such as oak, walnut and cedar. Plaster or wall paper may also be painted with a wood grain texture. The term may also refer to furniture or other objects, typically intended for use outdoors in a garden, where the objects appear to be made of branches or trunks of trees, both in their three-dimensional form and in the surface effect that simulates wood grain.

Refers to works depicting realistic situations with tones of social protest, common especially in the 1930s and 1940s. For the representational art in Communist countries sanctioned by the government, use "Socialist Realist."

Promises or undertakings of legal validity embodied in a contract under seal; also particular agreements contained in a deed or contract under seal which are incidental to the main purpose of the document.
Agreements generally running with specific pieces of land, restricting the free use of that land with reference to particular purposes or occupancy by members of a particular group.
Guarantees with reference to goods offered for sale which assure that a breach may be answered by a claim for damages.
An association formed between private and government sectors to fund and operate a venture.
Goods given in exchange for a bride by the family of the man to the family of the woman.

Beginning in the 1980s, sites designated by US Congress and administered by non-profit organizations or state governments where natural, cultural, and historic resources combine to form a nationally important landscape.

Exclusive, legally secured rights determining who may publish, copy, or distribute a work of art, writing, music, photograph, or other work. Works protected by copyright require the permission of the creator or other rights holder for their use. Some nations have the provision of fair use, which allows for limited use for educational purposes.
Right or condition of owning real property that is intended for domestic use, usually by one family.
The right of one owning waterfront land to have access to and use of the shore and water.
Sets of logical procedures for solving problems in a finite number of steps.
The shapes, or measures of the shapes, formed by two line segments that meet at a common point.
Parts of the circumference of a circle or other curve in a two-dimensional plane.

Polygons having one edge and one vertex, considered an impossible object in Euclidean geometry. In spherical geometry, a finite henagon may be drawn by placing a single vertex anywhere on a great circle; two henagons may be used to construct a dihedron on a sphere.
Parallelograms with four equal sides and four right angles.
Degree to which two or more attributes or measurements on the same group of elements show a tendency to vary together.
Sequences or series of mathematical objects or quantities, in which each entry is determined from its predecessors by some algorithm.
Gradual reduction of a financial obligation by payment of a part of the principal, contribution to a sinking fund, or the gradual depreciation of an asset.
Compensation often in the form of a fixed charge for professional services or requested exercise of talent or skill.
Fees charged to allow entry into an exhibition, event, museum, or the like.
The prices asked for or set by a seller.
Rate of rent which is sufficient to cover all costs of maintenance and operation of a building and, in addition, yield a reasonable return on the investment of the owner.
The state of being without a paying job.
A range of means of extending credit, such as small loans with no collateral, to nontraditional clients, chiefly impoverished people in undeveloped areas.
The industry providing facilities and services to people traveling for recreation.

The right to obtain full ownership of a real or other property, contrasted with or used in conjunction with legal title. Equitable title may exist without legal title, often having judged to have unwritten ownership interest or right of use which exists despite another party having legal title.
Financial assistance, usually to a business or other organization, given by the central government, as distinct from the separate units constituting it.

A need-based or merit-based financial award given to a student, usually from the funds of a school, college, or university, for the purpose of defraying the cost of education.  Distinct from fellowships in that scholarships are awarded to members of an undergraduate community, rather than graduates, and the course of study is unspecified.
Value assigned to currency by the issuing authority, which all users accept, is engraved on one side of a coin or on paper money.  Sometimes called nominal value.

Cultures surmised from assemblages of artifacts that recur as to type, general date, and places of distribution, thus often held by scholars to represent the material culture remains of a particular past human society. Use of the term is debated. Some scholars note that particular types of material culture do not always relate directly to groups or societies. However, use of the term has increased in recent years in scholarly publications.
The attitude and movement characterized by the love of practicing a craft, art, or work without direct remuneration or professional status.
The quality or procedure characteristic of a person who cultivates an art or a branch of knowledge as a pastime without pursuing it professionally.
Indianism is a current that started in Brazilian romantic literature (c.1836 - c.1881) and later in painting, in which Indian figures were idealized and represented as symbols of a nationality.
Style and cultural movement, primarily European and North American, that comprised a wide range of borrowings from Japanese art and culture, particularly in the 19th century.
The forms required by good breeding or prescribed by authority to be observed in social or official life.
Official or approved style, as of art, architecture, or costume, established at a ruler's court.

Method of expressing complex or abstract ideas in the literary or visual arts under the guise of another subject of aptly suggestive resemblance. An allegory is principally constructed from personifications and symbols. In art, allegories include combinations of personifications and/or symbols, which, on the basis of a conventionally agreed relation between concept and representation, refer to an idea outside the work of art. The properties and circumstances attributed to the apparent subject of the allegory really refer to another subject in an extended or continued metaphor. Allegories may have meaning on two or more levels that the viewer or reader can understand only through an interpretive process.
Characters or symbols with which a language is written, comprising an "alphabetic writing system"; a set of conventions for their use is not necessarily included.

Refers to the concept that a work of art must be experienced in its context or setting and that this knowledge of the work of art leads to a richer appreciation and understanding of it. Contextualism holds that not only literature, which is ordinarily appreciated contextually, but also the other arts, including nonrepresentational music and painting, should be experienced in this way. The opposite viewpoint of contextualism is isolationism.

Correspondence between two things, or in the relationship between two things and their respective attributes. In visual and literary works, a figure of speech or depiction used to cite or hypothesize a relationship of similarity and comparability between two disparate ideas or elements; often used as a point of clarification, or to elucidate an unfamiliar point or idea in terms of something more familiar and accessible. An example would be describing the correspondence between a river moving through a valley, with which readers would be familiar, and a glacier moving through a valley, which is much slower and more difficult to perceive.
Type of metaphor where an explicit comparison is made between two different things in order to create a new meaning, generally using  the words "like" or "as."
The genre of nonfiction that concerns accounts of the lives of individuals. For examples of this genre, prefer "biographies (literary works)."
Literary genre of accounts of a person's life given by themselves. For examples of this genre, prefer "autobiographies (literary genre)."

Italian 16th- to 18th-century comedy performed by companies of actors trained to improvise dialogue, gesture, and movement from a written plot built around standardized situations and stock characters.
Fiction which contains elements of autobiography, or fictionalized autobiography. The term was originally coined by author Serge Dubrovsky in 1977.
Stories handed down by tradition from earlier times, usually concerned with a real person, place, or event, and popularly regarded as historical although not entirely verifiable.

Form of poetry comprising long narratives celebrating on a grand scale the adventures and deeds of one or more heroic figures, ordinarily concerning a serious subject significant to a culture or nation. Classical epic poetry employs dactylic hexameter and recounts a journey.

A early 20th-century literary movement created in revolt against romanticism, specifically its optimism and supposed carelessness; the movement called for free verse and precise imagery. It is seen as the successor to French symbolism in the sense that it has an affinity to sculpture as symbolism has an affinity to music. Ezra Pound, inspired by the critical views of T.E. Hulme, devised its poetic ideals in about 1912.
Concepts related to perception of what is ideal or beautiful.
Principles of conduct or proper action that members of professions are expected to observe in the practice of their professions.

The state of utter confusion and disorder, where everything exists as an undifferentiated, formless mass or mixture. Derived from the original concept in ancient Greek cosmology, meaning the primevil emptiness of the universe before distinct entities came into being.
A philosophical movement or attitude associated with Albert Camus that posits that humanity's search for meaning is futile in a chaotic, senseless universe.

Refers to a philosophy developed by Plotinus in Alexandria in the 3rd century CE that consists of a modified version of Platonism combined with aspects of Judaic and Christian thought and possibly Oriental mysticism. Neo-Platonism holds that there is one source from which all existence comes from and with which an individual soul can be mystically united; it also emphasizes the plurality of levels of being, with the physical universe perceptible to the senses being the lowest. Neo-Platonism developed in a variety of forms over many centuries and it has enjoyed numerous revivals and modifications throughout history.

Belief systems that encompass various personal and institutional relationships between human beings and what they regard as holy, sacred, or divine, usually but not always a deity, or a spiritual or occult force. Participation in a religion is typically manifested in obedience, reverence, and worship, often including group activities and alliance with a leader. Elements of a religion or similar belief system include doctrine, ritual, defined parameters of morality, and a code of living, often seen as a means of achieving spiritual or material improvement.

Individual stories derived from a mythology; distinguished from historical accounts in that they are considered by current scholars to lack a determinable basis of fact or natural explanation; typically concerning a being, hero, deity, or event and explains some practice, rite, or phenomenon of nature.
Christian doctrine that Jesus of Nazareth became the son of God by exaltation that was not his at birth.
The reverence, worship, or allegiance accorded individuals identified as saints, often expressed through ceremonies, prayers, or other religious rituals.
Scientific concepts related to biology.
Physical phenomenon involving electric charges and their effects when at rest and in motion.
Light other than daylight that is produced using any of various energy sources and human-made mechanisms.
Harsh, uncomfortably brilliant, usually reflected light.
Lacking or having very little light.
The shadow of a figure or an object portrayed as it falls or is "cast" on another surface.  Often used in reference to painting or drawing.
Pressure that the air exerts on any surface in contact with it.

High-energy particles arriving from outer space that are mainly protons (often referred to as hydrogen nuclei), but also include nuclei of heavier elements. When they arrive at Earth, they collide with the nuclei of atoms in the upper atmosphere, creating more particles.
Generally, the capacity to do work; precisely, any quantity with dimensions that can be represented as mass times length squared divided by time squared.
The utilization of fossil fuels or nuclear fuel to produce energy.
The utilization of fuels so as to conserve supplies and promote efficiency.
Energy supplied by the heat of the earth's interior.
The large-scale production of electricity for industrial, residential, or rural use, generally in stationary plants designed for that purpose.
Electric phenomena and properties of the earth; used in a broad sense, also includes atmospheric electricity.
Agencies such as police, fire, or medical units prepared to respond to immediate and acute physical or sociological events that impact public health and safety.
Disposal of the solid wastes of a community.
The carrying from one place to another by way of a craft that utilizes air as the travel meduim.
The aggregate of movement including people and means of transport, specifically in the public space and context of a city.
The state or condition of having as much as one wants or more than is needed.
Breaking into and entering any building belonging to another with the intent to commit theft.

Acts of destroying, damaging, or carrying off booty in time of war or unrest. In the context of heritage management and cultural diplomacy, use "looting (social issue)" rather than the more general "theft (crime)" with reference to cultural property, often taken with the aim of illicit trafficking.
Discriminatory attitudes or practices toward people on the basis of their age.

Discrimination or exclusion based on racial or ethnic grounds, arising from systems, structures, or expectations that have become established within society or an institution. This may be applied to government, business, education, news and entertainment media, and other systems. Does not connote the intent, but rather to the structures and policies of the institution.
Acts of extreme cruelty, heinousness, savage enormity, or horrible wickedness.
Revolutions opposed to a previous revolution or reversing its results.

Violence and intimidation, either open or clandestine, employed by governments or factions within governments against citizens, other government factions, or against foreign governments or groups. An example is the Reign of Terror, a government by intimidation as directed and carried out by the French Revolutionary government during the Revolution of 1789-1794.
Wars between different areas, factions, or parties of the same nation.
Climate characterized by very little precipitation and extreme hot to cold temperatures, with great changes in daily temperature except in coastal areas.
Environments completely or mainly under water.
Noise produced by the activities of urban life, generally audible within the city or near to it, including within buildings.
Noise produced by vehicles passing along streets and highways.
Pollution of the earth's atmosphere.
Air that contains harmful or poisonous substances within a building.
Contamination or fouling of ocean or sea waters.

Form of precipitation (rain, snow, sleet, or hail) containing high levels of sulfuric or nitric acids. It is produced by the combination of atmospheric water with oxides released when hydrocarbon fuels are burned. Acid rain damages architecture and outdoor sculpture; it kills or harms forests, crops, and aquatic life.
The control and removal of pollution, specifically harmful odors and gases, from the air.
The actual quantity of water vapor present in a given volume of air.
Small, fine, sprays of precipitation that may seem to float in the air as a mist.
A wind blowing from the east.
General term for natural or administrative expanses having rough boundaries and located on the surface of Earth or another planet.
The settling of permanent residents on a certain area of land.
Departure from a place of abode, natural home, or country for life or residence elsewhere.
Withdrawing voluntarily from one's native country, especially if renouncing allegiance to it or to its government.
Migration within a country or region from rural areas to towns or cities.
A decrease in the total number of individuals of a given species or other class of organism in a defined area.
Activity of making something beautiful or repairing or enhancing its appearance.
Activity of planting and landscaping carried out along highways to improve their appearance, and to stabilize the soil, and create wind or sound breaks.
Basic development of rural regions emphasizing improvements in the standard of living and the active participation of the local population.
Activity of clearing, rebuilding, restoring, or refurbishing urban areas.
The renovation and settlement of decaying urban areas by middle- and high-income people.

Real estate development which aims to maintain the character of an older area by adding new buildings that are architecturally similar to those already there. For the insertion of material to fill a hole or area of loss, see "filling."
Refers to anything inserted into a larger whole, as a piece of cloth to a garment or a replaced portion of a drawing.
The increase in population of the suburbs of large cities, spurred on in part by the spread of highways and rail systems.
Informal or formally organized cooperative living arrangements based on ideological, religious, or political affiliation.

Marriage in which one or both parties are deceased. The custom is or was practiced in several cultures, including in the Sudan, China, France, and elsewhere. The custom often concerns property or inheritance rights of a deceased male.

One of the social classes whose income derives from the profits of commercial and industrial enterprise, especially as distinguished from the landed gentry, wage earners, farmers, and the professions.
The class of people in a society who hold exceptional rank, power, and privileges. The government in which this class is the ruling class is called an "aristocracy (form of government)."
Upper class within the aristocracy, whose titles, property, and privileges are maintained and passed on by heredity. For individual members of the nobility use "nobles (aristocrats)."
The portion of the working class at the lowest end of the social and economic scale.

A term referring to the legal separation of any religious and political orders in a nation or state. Usually applied in the context of the United States government as stated in the first amendment of the United States Constitution:  "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof."France has a similar statute regarding the separation of church and state, enacted 9 December 1905.

A course or principle of action adopted or proposed by a government to protect wildlife and endangered species and habitats, and decrease the threat to planetary systems posed by pollution, deforestation, desertification, and other effects of human activity.
A political theory aimed at maximizing personal freedom and abolition of the state and all governmental authority.

The theory adopted as the official philosophy of the Soviet communists which states that physical matter is the only true reality, that every aspect of it is subject to constant change resulting from the pressure of conflicting forces, and that mental processes are dependent on material ones.

Derived from agitation propaganda, meaning intended to inspire political action. With reference to visual art, refers to the specific art movement arising in Soviet Russia following the Bolshevik revolution.

Land tenures of a particular kind that came into use in the 8th century. By a benefice, a lord leased an estate to a freeman on easy terms; the lease normally came to an end on the death of the lord or of the tenant, though holders of benefices often succeeded in turning them into hereditary holdings.

The evaluation of building performance in terms of technical and physical aspects of structures after construction, such as structural integrity, mechanical system performance, and properties of materials.
A contracting arrangement in which a person or organization assumes responsibility under a single contract for both the design and construction of a project.
Picking out or choosing in preference to another or others.
Action or function of the determination of value of non-market properties and services, chiefly cultural and environmental goods.
Establishing, maintaining, and applying consistent spellings and forms of proper names and terms used as the descriptive and access language for collections of documents and objects.

Classification process or scheme that allows or exhibits linkages from one smaller context to multiple categories rather than to a single category. An example is in indexing a group of works or a complex work; as a whole, the group may be so diverse that it may be appropriately classified under multiple classification headings.
Changing the representation of data in a database from one form to another, as for instance changing the storage medium, data format, or the code in which the data is held.
An act of documentation via photography to record the conditon or state of an object or the status of a project. Examples include excavations or art conservation treatments.

Teaching methodology using cases as a pedagogical tool in fields such as law, business, medicine, and education. Cases may include real and imagined scenarios, critical incident analysis, case studies, vignettes, and anecdotal accounts.
The writing, assembling, and design of publications using microcomputers and word processing, graphics, and page layout software.

The study on the history of origin and evolvement of buildings, using varied research methods such as photography, study of literature and archives, iconographical, cartographical and in situ-research and the study of oral histories.
The evaluation of proposals for development or for changes to existing structures or spaces, typically by a board representing the community where the activity is to take place.
The systematic examination of land or water areas from aircraft.
The use of what was originally a picture-symbol or hieroglyph of an object or being to represent phonetically the initial syllable or sound of the name of the object or being.
Officially correcting written text or recorded data by addition, deletion, or modification.
Documenting in writing the requirements of a project.
A type of underground mining employing vertical shafts driven from the earth's surface. It is used for coal, iron, and other dense mineral deposits that are deep underground.
Techniques of dating which result in dates given in terms of calendar years.
Measures taken to create desirable conditions and limit specific undesirable factors within a given, often a closed, environment.

Occurrences taking place during a particular interval of time. The term is much broader in meaning than the scope of the facet also called "Events." While the facet includes only terms referring to general events, the actual term "events" may be used to index these as well as specific named events.
Long, severe snowstorms, often accompanied by strong winds.
Formal rites or observances in academia.

Design competitions in which entry is restricted to a small number of participants specifically invited to offer solutions; usually for complex projects or projects for which particular technical expertise is required.
Exhibitions held once per year.
Celebrations or gatherings held for the presentations of newly mounted art exhibits.

National and international fairs exhibiting the material culture and products of colonies and colonized peoples, with the general aim of promoting the colonization activities of nations or organizations; held from the mid- 19th until the mid-20th centuries, especially in Great Britain and France.
Assemblies of cardinals who have come together for the election of a Pope. In its present form, the conclave dates from the end of the 13th century.
Meetings at which academic specialists deliver addresses on a topic or on related topics and then participate in a discussion on the topics.
Extended tours; the tour is often used to refer to European tours through France, Germany, Italy, and Switzerland; formerly taken by youth of the aristocracy as part of their education.
Printed books produced in during the early development of printing that feature illustrative elements added by hand.
Bindings decorated with a sovereign's arms.
Printed matter included with or added to a text after it has been set.
Greek and Latin papyri that contain text concerning aspects of everyday life, such as letters, contracts, and records.

In type, the largest letters in a given type size. In handwritten scripts, letters modeled on ancient Roman capital letters. For handwritten scripts without ascenders or descenders more generally, prefer "majuscule."
Packaging comprising pieces of paper shaped like a cone, and twisted at the apex; used for packaging small goods such as candy or nuts.
General term referring to doers of actions, including any people, corporate bodies, animals, or inanimate things that act upon something or someone.
The characteristic of being not harmful to living organisms or biological processes; not causing a toxic or harmful response.
Diseases transmitted by a specific infectious agent between persons or other species, either directly or through an intermediate vector.
A disorder of the brain that causes periodic seizures, and sensory or psychic malfunction in an individual.

Type of insanity, described by ancient writers, in which the patient imagines himself to be a wolf, with the instincts and propensities of a wolf. Also, more generally applied to those forms of insanity in which the patient imagines himself a beast.
State of psychological well-being or adequate adjustment to society and the ordinary demands of life.
The act or process of increasing in size or substance through natural development.
The directional growth of an organism or part of an organism in response to an external stimulus.
The faculty or sense by which sound is perceived.
Partial or complete loss of sight.

Of a person, or his or her feelings: estranged, excluded, or turned away (from a person or thing); experiencing a feeling of estrangement or isolation. Also in extended use: (of a period, place, etc.) characterized by or inducing such feelings.
A subjective state of feeling defined as bad or harmful.
The feeling or expression of grief or sorrow, along with the ritual observances accompanying a death.
Conduct that departs from a society's established norms, rules, standards, or expectations.

A socially unacceptable pattern of sexual behavior in which one's preferred means of sexual arousal is the clandestine observing of others when they are disrobing, nude, or actually engaging in sexual activity.  Arousal is dependent upon the observed person(s) being unaware of their being observed.
The act or process of coming to direct knowledge or certainty without reasoning or inferring.
Sense of ease and satisfaction of bodily wants, with freedom from pain and anxiety.
Sexuality characterized by romantic love or sexual desire toward members of either sex.
State, condition, or behavior having to do with sexual attraction or sexual relations between women.
In agriculture, the removal of surplus water from land.
The running of rainfall or melted snow over land and into streams; also, the running of excess fertilizer or pesticides from farmland and into rivers.
Collecting data, usually in monetary terms, about economic activity, processing those data, and reporting them for the use of interested decision-makers.
Accounting that deals with systematically classifying, recording, analyzing, and summarizing the costs incident to production or the rendering of a service.

Public presentation of or calling attention to a product, service, event, or idea, that is openly paid for by an identified entity. Media for advertising include print and online publications, posters, television, and other media.

Communications field concerned with using photographs to document significant events, often in the context of news and related commentary through the mass media, both print and electronic. For journalism focusing on images other than photographs, use "pictorial journalism."
Science of the long-distance sending and receiving of computerized information, the term coined by Alain Minc and Simon Nora in 1978.
Branch of economics concerning the management or use of funds and credit by a government, business, or individual.
Includes activities and experiences that are intended to effect developmental changes in children from birth through the early years of elementary school.
Branch of education covering kindergarten through grade 3.
