Education for handicapped or gifted students, who have intellectually, physically, emotionally, or socially different characteristics from those who can be taught through regular methods, facilities, or materials.

A practice that addresses the role of cultural production or in the definition of physical space or its representation. The discipline of experimental geography may involve factors of human social or economic relationships rendered graphically, physically, or virtually. Products of this practice may be art objects or discursive scholarly practice, and often are a combination of these.
Branch of jurisprudence that relates to crimes.
Branch of paleography specializing in the study of certain ancient characters termed "runes" and the systems of writing that are based on them.

Study of the ways in which different societies establish and work with their political structures and government, with the goal of developing general theories concerning government based on the analysis of the differences and similarities among political units.
Branch of psychology concerned with the mutually interactive relationship between the built environment and behavior.
Branch of sociology concerned with study of the origins, stages, and laws of social life and social institutions.
The history of cities and towns, the urbanization of human life, and all aspects of urban life over time.
The branch of science that deals with the properties of air and other gases in motion and the interaction between a gas and objects moving through it.

Branch of agriculture that deals with land cultivation, soil management, and field crop improvement, management, and production. For the science concerned with all aspects of soils, including their origin, distribution, classification, utilization, physical and chemical properties, and the role of organisms in soil production and in relation to soil character, see "soil science".
Science or discipline of cultivating the soil, harvesting crops, and raising livestock.
Branch of anatomy which studies tissue structure in organisms using microscopic examination.
The branch of biology that studies airborne transport, distribution, and effects of biological materials as pollens, pollutants, viruses.
The study of botanical remains in an archaeological context, that is, how they relate to human development and culture.
Branch of ecology that studies interactions between ancient plants and animals and their environment.
The branch of molecular biology which maps and analyzes the set of proteins expressed by an organism; an adjunct to genomics.
The scientific study of insects.

Branch of engineering that deals with the design, development, testing, and production of aircraft, spacecraft, missiles, rocket propulsion systems, and other equipment operating both within and beyond the earth's atmosphere.
Branch of aerospace engineering dealing with the design, development, and production of aircraft that function within the atmosphere, and their related systems.

Professional application of scientific principles and technical practices to the management and optimum use of air, water, and land resources, with the goal of protecting the environment from the adverse effects of human activity, protecting human populations from the effects of adverse environmental factors, and improving environmental quality for human health and well-being.
Branch of enironmental engineering specifically concerned with the protection and promotion of the public health, specifically with the provision of clean air, food, water, and housing.
Branch of electrical engineering that deals with practical applications of electronics, primarily with the design, manufacture, and operation of electronic devices and systems.
The branch of engineering concerned with the daily technical and managerial operations of a factory.
Study of the structure of metal and alloys, especially such study with the microscope.
The study of metal objects, especially with regard to their manufacturing process, in an archaeological context.

Term used by the Association for Preservation Technology (APT) which promulgates structural engineering as a component of architectural conservation in the United States. Buildings preservation initially developed in this country without including engineers since older buildings tended to be relatively small and engineers were engaged in constructing large new structures. The aging of those large structures, along with public interest in preserving relatively recent architecture, recommends the development and implementation of preservation engineering.
The science, management, and cultivation of forests for recreation, timber production, conservation, and other purposes.

Branch of forestry concerned with the overall administrative, economic, legal and social matters regarding the protection and regulation of forests for wildlife, recreation, aesthetics, preventing fire, and harvesting of wood products, with the aim of balancing conservation and economics.
Raising and care of trees and shrubs, usually in gardens or for ornamental purposes. For the cultivation and study of forest trees, use "silviculture."

Study and practice of the use of selected books and other readings for therapeutic purposes to promote an individual's mental or physical health or development; often used as an adjunct to psychotherapy.
Traditional system of Indian medicine, including traditional preventive and curative health care; widely practiced in parts of Asia.

Branch of mathematics that investigates general statements of relations, using letters and other symbols to represent specific mathematics entities such as sets of numbers, values, vectors, and series.

The science that deals with the material universe beyond the earth's atmosphere, comprising the study of celestial objects and extraterrestrial phenomena, and of the nature and history of the universe.
Study of astronomical phenomena in terms of the underlying physical processes.
The study of the chemistry of living organisms and the reactions and methods for identifying their chemical substances.
Science that determines the size and shape of the earth or other celestial bodies, and carries out measurements and computations necessary for accurate mapping of the surface.

Science that deals with the land and submarine relief features of the earth's surface and seeks a generic interpretation of them using the principles of geology in its descriptive aspects and of structural geology in its explanatory phases.
Branch of geophysics concerned with the study of earthquakes and seismic waves.
The branch of science that studies climates and their phenomena.
The branch of paleontology that studies fossil traces such as footprints, trails, and burrows as evidence of animal and plant activity.
Branch of physics that deals with sound and sound waves.

Branch of mechanics dealing with the properties and behavior of liquids and gases and the ways in which they respond to and exert forces. Study of fluids in motion, or fluid dynamics, makes up the larger part of fluid mechanics, and branches of fluid dynamics include hydrodynamics and aerodynamics. Hydrodynamics is often used synonymously with fluid dynamics

Discipline that arranges time into periods or divisions, and places events in the sequence in which they occurred, either at a defined point or period in time, or in relation to an established time sequence.

The profession concerned with the application of knowledge and those principles, theories, techniques, and technologies which contribute to the establishment, preservation, organization and utilization of libraries and library materials.
The study of the capacity of machines to simulate human behavior such as reasoning, learning, probelm-solving, or the understanding of speech.
One of the three ancient categories of learning, along with the seven liberal and the seven mechanical arts; included magic, divination, and thievery.
Group of studies in the Middle Ages forming the elementary division of the seven liberal arts and consisting of grammar, rhetoric, and logic.

A form of chemistry and speculative philosophy practiced in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance and concerned principally with discovering methods for transmuting base metal into gold and with finding a universal solvent and an elixir of life.
Areas of responsibility in which activities are conducted in order to accomplish a purpose.
Naming to or placing in an office or position.

In science, business, policy, and other fields, a careful item-by-item comparison of two or more comparable characteristics, alternatives, processes, products, qualifications, sets of data, or other features in order to draw an authoritative conclusion.
Cutting desired shapes out of a material such as metal to be used for forming or other manufacturing operations.
Refers to pierced or perforated metalwork. For open work jewelery that uses threads that are soldered together use "filigree."
The final chasing or smoothing of a metal object.
Process in which the surface of a metal is coated with a protective or decorative layer through electrolytic action.
Producing a hard surface layer on steel, as by carbonizing, cyaniding, and flame hardening.

Refers to the process of combining a substance with carbon. In metallurgy. the diffusion of carbon into wrought iron at high temperature to produce steel; or into low carbon steel to increase surface hardness.
Drawing wire by forcing it through a series of progressively smaller holes.
The manufacture of metal printing type.
Ironworking specifically to make tools and other heavy iron pieces with a forge and anvil; an example is the making of horseshoes by blacksmithing.
The art of folding paper into objects or designs.
Refers to the pressing of a wet sheet of newly made paper still on the mold onto a felt.

The art of building with wood, especially in the construction of buildings and other structures, including the installation of floors, windows, and other trim work. For the making of fine furniture and intricate woodwork, see "cabinetmaking." For the broader activity of working in wood more generally, use "woodworking."
Hand carving of wood by cutting chips with a knife or other instrument usually in simple geometric designs.
Type of brush strokes used in Chinese painting to indicate wrinkles, markings, and modeling on mountains, rocks, trees, and stones.

A form of very high resolution scanning probe microscopy in which a sample in solution is moved under an atomically sharp (i.e. only a few atoms wide) stylus mounted on a cantilevered spring. A detector senses deflections of the cantilever, measuring the force between stylus and surface, and transmits this information to an electronic display system.

A technique for measuring x-ray fluorescence that involves exciting elements in a sample then diffracting the emitted radiation by using a device, such as a crystal or monochromator, in order to measure the intensity of x-rays with a specific wavelength.

Biologically mediated loss of utilitarian or physical characteristics of a material caused by bacteria or other microorganisms. Biodeterioration includes only physical disintegration and cosmetic disfigurement. For deterioration that includes molecular changes to a material such that characteristic properties of the material are no longer evident, use 'biodegradation.'
Corrosion caused by pollutants in the atmosphere.
Weathering that has been caused to proceed at an unusually fast pace, whether by special environmental conditions or by intentionally imposed testing conditions.
The action of progressive removal of material from solid surfaces such as coral or rock, by the action of living organisms.
Contracting or lessening of size, especially as a result of conditions of temperature or moisture.
The change in length or volume of a material or body due to change in temperature.
Developing a network of fine cracks in a coating layer, such as a ground, paint layer, varnish, or glaze.
Separation into constituent layers.
Branches of learning, professions, and areas of professional specialization.
Fields that are interdisciplinary.
Refers broadly to the areas of activity that encompass both performing and visual arts. With reference more narrowly to the fine arts or the fine and decorative arts together, see "art."

The discipline concerning works that are primarily utilitarian in form or function, but that have aesthetic value provided by the design, decoration, or embellishment, such as ceramics, furniture, textiles, glass, and others.
Discipline involving the study of dancing and movement, including performance.
The study and practice of recording, reproducing, broadcasting, or distributing moving visual images on magnetic tape or (in later use) in a digital format.
Genre of African-influenced Brazilian percussive music, usually performed by an ensemble, known as a Bateria.

The art or science of designing and building structures, especially habitable structures, in accordance with principles determined by aesthetic and practical or material considerations.  For a general term for the actual structures or parts of structures that were made by human beings, see "architecture (object genre)."
The study of the scientific or technical aspects of architecture as distinguished from the purely artistic or historical aspect.

Architecture that focuses on the design, renovation, and remodeling of golf courses, which are large outdoor areas where the sport of golf is played, consisting of a teeing ground, fairway, rough, hazards, and a series of greens.

Practice and discipline of designing the appearance, ergonomics, complex systems, and other aspects of motor vehicles, usually road vehicles such as automobiles, motorcycles, trucks, buses, coaches, and vans.

In traditional literature, the term ceyang is primarily used in the Yingzao fashi (1103) of the Song dynasty. Literally meaning “side appearance” (Kroll 2005 35, 534), it refers to the view of architectural frameworks or components from the side perpendicular to the roof ridge, which is then expressed in the form of a drawing (Li 2009, 5.19b, 30.6a-7a, 31.3a-6a).
The activity of drawing or painting illustrations of fashionable apparel and accessories, especially for advertisement.
Painting of the body, either in connection with ceremonies, festivals, or other special events, or for reasons of personal decoration.

Refers to techniques used to record images of subjects located outside the atmosphere of the Earth and certain phenomena associated with the ionosphere, such as aurorae and meteor showers. For photography taken from beyond the Earth's atmosphere, use "space photography." For photography of the Earth from aircraft in the Earth's atmosphere, use "aerial photography."

Motion-picture technique using single-frame exposures to give the illusion of movement to inanimate articulated figures or to animated sequences or to give the illusion of sudden appearance or disappearance of objects or performers from a scene. It is an essential technique in model animation, cutout animation,  pixillation, and special effects.
The study or practice of the analytical description, interpretation, and evaluation of architectural works.

Refers to an emerging interdisciplinary field which seeks to integrate scientific study of art into the practice of art history; and the interpretative methods of the art historian into the conservation lab. An outgrowth of the subdiscipline of art history once known as Technical Studies, the field has recently established itself within graduate program curricula.
The branch of conservation science involving treatment, preventive care, and research directed toward archaeological sites and materials.
Branch of musicology focusing on the study of music in its cultural context.

Branch of linguistics where the primary concern is the application of linguistic theories, methods, and findings to practical language problems, such as language teaching, lexicography, translation, stylistics, and speech therapy.
Study of speech communities, particularly those with no writing system, by the application of anthropological and linguistic techniques.
The study of the rules of a language governing the sounds, words, sentences, and other elements, including their structure, combination, and interpretation.

The study of similar literary works from two or more nations, periods, or languages in relation to each other, or the study of any literary phenomenon from the perspective of at least two  literatures.
Refers to museum methods of classification, description and display of objects; the practical application of the body of theory known as museology.

Appreciation or criticism of the beautiful. The term refers to a branch of Western philosophy concerned primarily with the fine arts, although it may also be used in the context of the appreciation of natural beauty. Usage of the term dates from the 18th century, although historical discussions regarding issues now called "aesthetics" date from Antiquity.
A logic based on the idea that propositions can be graded in value, rather than simply being true or false. Fuzzy logic has applications in expert systems and artificial intelligence.
Branch of systematic philosophy that deals with the character of the universe as a cosmos, combining speculative metaphysics and scientific knowledge.
Study of religious beliefs and traditions in human life and culture from the perspective of the humanistic disciplines.
Study of religion using the methods and theories of anthropology.
Critical study of the Bible and biblical writings, including such approaches as textual analysis, historical study, exegesis, hermeneutics, and literary and linguistic criticism.

Scientific study of the material remains of past human life and activities, including human artifacts from the very earliest stone tools to the man-made objects that are buried or thrown away in the present day. Archaeological investigations are a principal source of knowledge of prehistoric, ancient, and extinct cultures.
Direct observation and descriptive study of the culture and way of life of particular societies.

An autobiographical genre of academic writing that draws on and analyzes or interprets the lived experience of the author and connects researcher insights to self-identity, cultural rules and resources, communication practices, traditions, premises, symbols, rules, shared meanings, emotions, values, and larger social, cultural, and political issues.
Study of human body measurements on a comparative basis.

The application of modern scientific and technical methods to the interpretation of archaeological remains, for example the dating of specimens through scientific techniques such as radiocarbon dating and amino-acid dating.
The technique of disguising the appearance of beings or things so as to make them blend into their surroundings.
The earthmoving required to create a surface of desired grade elevation.

The act of adding biological agents to contaminated environments in order to neutralize, remove, or break down contaminants; e.g., the process of biodeterioration induced by the introduction of bacteria into an oil spill. Bioremediation is of use in stone conservation for the removal of algae and other organisms, and in collections care for nontoxic pest control.
Technique of inpainting using  small flicks or dots.
Process creating stonework or brickwork that is used as the surface finish of structures.
The reassembly of a monument or other structure using the original architectural elements to the greatest degree possible.

In archaeology, the reordering of available remains digitally to virtually reassemble something that existed in the past.This process makes a 3D model assembling surveyed fragments, present in the excavation site, with elements philologically reconstructed on the basis of historical knowledge and documentation.
Past restoration, preservation, or conservation process, especially as it affects present condition and appearance of artifacts and their future treatment.
The process of dividing something into two equal or nearly equal parts.

Application of an electric DC field for removal of the solubilized salt ions by electromigration. During the process, the concentrations of ions of salts will decrease as these ions concentrate around an electrode of opposite polarity. The electrodes are placed in or on the surface or on a poultice on a salt-infected material and the ions concentrate here. After the desalination the poultice is removed and thereby, the damaging ions.

Movement of molecules of a liquid through a semipermeable  membrane from a region of high solute concentration into a less concentrated field; a reversal of normal flow that occurs when hydrostatic pressure exceeds the osmotic pressure.

Process whereby particles intermingle and move from a region of higher to one of lower concentration, and for the transmission or reflection of light. Includes the effect of such processes, such as the softening of sharp outlines in a photograph.

Controlled drying technique introduced into printmaking and hand papermaking workshops to shorten drying time and ensure planarity of paper. To do this a material that features open air ducts that promote air exchange is integrated into the structure of the drying stack. Drying is carried out in stacks of corrugated cardboard and other paperboard materials under slight pressure. The stack is equipped with a blower that provides a continuous air-stream through the open channels. The water is removed by continuous evaporation through the moisture-absorbing board until equilibrium with the ambient air is reached.
To sift or strain by passing through a screen. In archaeology, refers to sieving of archaeological sediments to collect fossils.
The extraction of metals from minerals using naturally occurring microorganisms instead of chemical solutions.

A technique used in printing whereby a sheet of paper, originally China paper, is adhered to a heavier backing sheet as it is run through a printing press. This creates variations of color or texture under the printed image.
Refers to mechanics, aesthetics, and installation of hanging textiles, paintings, and other objects for display.
A technique for depositing a film onto a surface in monolayers by utilizing a self-limiting chemical reaction. It is a vapor phase technique capable of producing thin films of a variety of materials.
Enameling process developed in Mughal, India, which uses both translucent and opaque enamel applied over gold and silver and carved into a bas-relief.

Gilding technique in which an amalgam of gold with mercury is applied to a metal, such as copper or silver, then the metal is heated to flash volatilize the mercury and deposit a thin layer of gold. The process has been in use since at least 300 CE in China. In most regions, it was replaced in the mid-19th century by electrogilding.
Gilding on a surface coated with oil paint and size.

The hard-finish lacquering technique which utilizes many coats of varnish composed of shellac dissolved in spirit, then polished and decorated, usually Oriental in style and subject matter. Originally developed as a substitute for genuine Oriental lacquer which was popular during the second half of the 17th century.
Surrounding, enclosing, or protecting something as if in a capsule; for example, in paper conservation, the sealing of an item between two sheets of polyester film.
Creating raised letters or designs without ink, foil, or other color.
Engraving produced by short repetitive strokes of a cutting tool, especially on metal.
Refers to the specific step of corroding a material by the action of acid.
A method of decorating surfaces with patterns or pictures composed of small, regularly-shaped  pieces of colored durable material, such as stone or glass.

Intarsia technique that incorporates relief carving, developed in Bohemia, especially in Eger, and popular all over Europe from the mid-17th to the mid-18th century. It was used particularly for altar panels, furniture, and lids for game boxes and caskets.

Marquetry comprised of brass and tortoise shell, applied to furniture especially in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. The term derives from the name of the artist André-Charles Boulle and his sons, whose work was imitated widely.
In wall plastering, the creating of an insulating space of a few inches between an exterior wall of a building and the lath of the plaster wall.
Making shiny or lustrous by rubbing with a tool that compacts or smooths.
Smoothing or brightening of surfaces by means of metal pellets, balls, or other metal shapes in a rotating container.
Tooling, using implements which are usually hand-held and heated, without the addition of gold leaf, silver leaf, or color; often on leather or cloth.
Refers to the process by which materials, such as metal and glass, are softened and made workable by heating and controlled cooling.
Causing to become hardened into a solid body by the abstraction of heat.
A method of storing food and other perishables, such as photographic film, at a low temperature to prevent deterioration.
First firing of a clay object which turns the greenware into a hardened object that may be glazed.
The action or process of conveying or transporting over water, usually a small body of water.

A method for lifting and removing large or fragile objects or groups of objects from archaeological excavations by surrounding them with rigid foam or other supporting materials. The block often incorporates some of the surrounding soil, which lends extra support.

A plasma-based technique primarily used for local pre-treatment of different surfaces. With atmospheric plasma technology, gas is excited by means of a high voltage underatmospheric pressure, such that a plasma is ignited. The plasma is expelled by compressed air from the nozzle. The treatment performance can be affected in different ways by varying the process parameters such as treatment speed and distance from the substrate surface.

Refers to the technique of making pottery of the same name to produce a variety of effects. The traditional Japanese process involves low firing temperatures in which the fired piece is removed from the kiln while still hot and is allowed to cool in open air.

Process of decorating ceramics by transferring the design from prints on another material, often using heat; invented in England in the 1750s. Designs are first engraved and then printed on paper or another material using a special ceramic ink. The paper is then pressed against the surface of the ceramic, enamel, or glass and the design is thus transferred, often with the application of heat. The process is also used for enamels and glass.
Tanning hides or skins, usually sheepskins or lambskins with the grain split or shaved off, with an aldehyde, usually formaldehyde, to produce a white, washable leather.

Removing scars, scratches, and other defects from the grain side of leather by means of an abrasive or abrading tool. For the removal of defects from the flesh side of leather by similar means, use "fluffing."
The process of making objects out of brass or employing brass.

Refers to the process of joining two pieces of metal by inserting filler metal of very high melting point, such as hard solder, between them and applying heat, at temperatures ranging between 750 and 900 degrees Celsius; sometimes but not necessarily involves softening or melting the surfaces to be joined. For the similar process carried out at temperatures below 750 degrees Celsius, see "soldering." For the process of joining two pieces of metal that necessarily involves softening or melting the surfaces to be joined but not necessarily the insertion of filler metal, see "welding."
Soldering at lower than usual temperatures, typically between 130 and 180 degrees Celsius.
Brazing with an electric arc, that is, the electrical discharge between two electrodes.
Method of welding whereby a groove, fillet, plug, or seat weld is made using a nonferrous filler metal having a melting point below that of base metals.
The joining of metal parts by fusion in which the necessary heat is produced by means of an electric arc, that is, the electrical discharge between two electrodes.
The joining of metals at room temperature by subjecting to pressure.
The application of an aluminum coating such as to iron and steel sheet.
Galvanizing by a process in which the zinc is deposited by an electroplating method.
The treatment of a surface to give the appearance of bronze. In printmaking, refers to printing with metallic inks.
Technique of applying silver leaf in which silver is mixed with mercury and applied to the surface of the object; the object is then heated to dispel the mercury.
Process of plating with silver leaf on steel, iron, or occasionally brass, used especially on knives and scissors; patented in 1779 by Richard Ellis as a technique less expensive than French plating.
Aquatint process in which a salt solution is used to lift the ground, and exposes the image areas so the plate can be etched.
Techniques involving making, imitating, or altering valued objects or documents with intent to deceive. Distinguished from "copying" by the intention of deception.

A lithographic printing process achieved by drawing with lithographic chalk, also called crayon, on a grained stone roughened by fine sand. The drawing chalk or crayon adheres to the grain, making shading possible. Applied ink adheres to the chalked area, and is then transferred to paper for the final print.

A type of photolithography in which the printing plate is prepared using a bichromate process. Unhardened gelatin areas hold water and thus resist greasy ink; hardened areas accept ink and hold it in the characteristic wormlike pattern of cracks.
Transfer lithography in which drawings or writing in autographic ink, litho ink, and chalk are tranferred from autographic paper to stone or zinc for lithographic printing.

A printmaking process that uses two or more blocks, one often as a key or line block in black and others in a single colors in differing tones. Tone blocks were printed in lighter and darker versions of the same color, a characteristic of the 'camaieu' print as resembling engraved cameo stones. Early scholars distinguished two-block from multi-block processes by calling them "camaïeu," that is, the ‘monochrome method,’ distinguishing them from "chiaroscuro woodcuts," Current usage does not make this distinction, and the terms have been used interchangeably in various sources.

A reproductive process used primarily for photographs from the 1880s to the 1950s, utilizing small dots of variable size in relief to reproduce tone in the prints. The process involves re-photographing a photograph through a ruled screen, which creates a negative image made of dots of variable size. A relief halftone block is prepared by printing the negative face down on a copper plate coated with fish glue or bichromated gelatin. The unexposed areas remain soluble after development and are washed away; then the plate is acid etched and used in a printing press. From the end of the 19th century onwards, halftone was the principal means of reproducing photographs in printer's ink where long print runs are required and high quality is not of paramount importance. The principle was first suggested by William Henry Fox Talbot in 1852; it was developed commercially in the 1880s.
The process of making a counterproof, which is printing a mirror-image from an original printed or drawn work, including both art works and printed or handwritten materials.

Process used for holograms captured and processed at up to 40 frames per second, allowing video-rate holographic imaging. Potential uses for this technology include holographic video display for examination of objects, medical imaging, 3-D video conferencing, and other purposes.
Indicating on a drawing the actual dimensions of whatever is represented in the drawing.
A method of painting by means of a small, finely controllable mechanical paint sprayer; used also in the retouching of photographs.

Mural painting technique in which pigments are ground in water and mixed with lime upon freshly laid plaster. As the pigmented lime dries, the calcium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide to form a pigmented calcium carbonate layer. Such paintings have survived from the Minoan period (1700 BCE) and Pompeii (79 CE). The technique was widely used from the 13th century in Italy for interior wall decorations, particularly in churches. Noted from ancient times as the preferred method of mural painting, superior to techniques that apply pigment to dry plaster, fresco secco, or partially dry plaster, mezzo fresco.

Technique in paintings or the painting of sculptures in which gold leaf is applied to depicted costume or other textiles, or other details, in order to intensify the visual effect. The technique is seen in Byzantine, Medieval, and early European Renaissance paintings, but reached its zenith in Spanish colonial art.
The art or practice of producing creative works with acrylic paint.
The stage of encaustic painting in which the surface of a painting is heated so that the colors may be manipulated and blended.

Refers to a technique in painting, drawing, mosaics, or other media in which depicted drapery is modeled using two contrasting colors, rather than darker and lighter tones of the same color, to create an effect that simulates shot or cangiante textiles.

Refers to a projection that depicts a portion of a globe as a flattened disk. It is often used in cartography and typically represents a section of the Earth or a heavenly body as viewed from a point at the center of the globe ("gnonomic projection"), on the opposite side of the globe ("stereographic projection"), or from a point in space ("orthographic projection").
In fresco, transferring a pricked drawing onto the final plaster layer by dusting it with a cloth sack filled with charcoal powder, leaving an outline of the design on the fresh intonaco.
Stencil process for making colored prints or adding color to printed illustrations; usually where a monochrome print is colored by hand using a series of stencils.
Aerial photography using a camera mounted or held in a hot-air balloon or other large balloon traveling in the atmosphere.

Process that records the location and distribution in an object of radioactive substances, or those made radioactive in order to be detected, when radiation from these substances act on a photographic emulsion placed in close contact with the object. When used on a painting, identifies areas of pigments through elemental half lives.
Refers to the technique of taking photographs that utilize natural and artificial light sources that are present at a scene, and excludes light sources produced or supplied by the photographer.

Infrared photography technique commonly applied to a variety of techniques including aerial photography and art examination. False color infrared is preferred for vegetative and hydrologic studies. False color infrared film is sensitive to ultraviolet, visible and infrared radiation to approximately 900 nm. When the film is exposed with a yellow filter, the emulsion layers become sensitive to only green, red and infrared wavelengths. Blue radiation is absorbed by the filter; hence, the greater haze penetration ability of infrared film. In art conservation, the resulting false color images can be used as a noninvasive means of identifying the pigments that have been used in a painting or underdrawing.

Process introduced by the Eastman Kodak Co. in the early 1930s for printing color images from gelatin matrices which are prepared by exposure to separation negatives. The process is seen as a prototype for the modern-day dye transfer process.

Two-component diazo process in which both the diazonium salts and the coupler are on the base, and development is achieved by neutralizing the acidic stabilizers with vapors derived from evaporating ammonia water.
Photographic process that is a variant of the platinum process in which citrate of mercury is introduced, giving sepia tones to the print.

William Henry Fox Talbot's process to make negatives on paper; the image is formed from silver iodide coated on the base without a binder and is developed. The calotype process produced a translucent original negative image from which multiple positives could be made by simple contact printing. This gave it an important advantage over the daguerreotype process, which produced an opaque original positive that could only be duplicated by copying it with a camera. In the mid-20th century, the term was sometimes used incorrectly for any salted paper or paper negative process.

Processes for making photographic prints using a bichromate compound which, when exposed to light, causes its colloid binder to harden; unhardened areas are washed or abraded away. Pigments may be incorporated before exposure or during development. Though the expression dichromate is now preferred in chemistry, bichromate remains common usage in photography.

Printing process in which powdered carbon is used as a pigment to form an image, particularly when the process employs sensitized carbon tissue on gelatin. The process was patented by Joseph Wilson Swan in 1864, his work having been base on the work of A. L. Poitevin; it was actively exploited in England by the Autotype Company, who acquired Swan's patent rights in 1868. The process depends upon the hardening action of light on bichromated gelatin, whereby sheets of pigmented gelatin are used to transfer images to a paper support.

A variant of the carbon process to produce contact prints; the image is formed from a pigment, usually carbon black, in a colloid suspension that has been made light-sensitive with bichromates. Marketed under the name Charbon Velours.

Variant of the daguerreotype process devised by Claude-Abel Niépce de St. Victor, distinguished by the use of silver chloride to produce natural color. The image cannot be fixed, and therefore is impermanent. In the early 20th century, sometimes used to mean color photography in general.
Photography of moving objects by repeated flashes or a pulsating light source.

Photographic processing designed to preserve a print or negative for as long as possible by protecting it against deterioration due to chemical reactions. For activities involving the arrangement and description of archival materials use "processing" plus terms for the form of material being processed.

Drawing or sketching from nature, this practice was useful in the development of "yamato-e" techniques through the realistic study of nature. The term is also used to refer to the drawings or sketches that result from the activity.
The technique accomplishing the measurement of quantities of heat.

Technique of using photographs to measure, survey, or map the Earth's surface, specifically employing aerial photographs, which are photographs obtained by cameras mounted on aircraft, rockets, or Earth-orbiting satellites and other spacecraft. The technique typically uses an overlapping series of photographs taken from an aircraft following a systematic flight pattern at a fixed altitude.

Refers to measuring the sensitivity of photographic film, specifically recording the film’s response to light exposure and silver formation in development. The process entails exposing film to graduated levels of light, recording the density of produced-silver deposit and plotting this data on a graph against the logarithm of the exposure.

Mingling or combining so that the separate constituents or the line of demarcation cannot be distinguished. In painting, includes the gradation of color so that two hues or values merge imperceptibly.

The automated action or practice of creating three-dimensional objects from a digital file or other original, used for rapid prototyping, model making, additive manufacturing, etc. In an additive process, an object is created by laying down successive layers of material until the object is created; the process uses 3-D printers.

Method of bookbinding in which a hard cover is made wholly separate from the book and later is attached to it by gluing the endpapers to the inside of the boards of the case. Introduced in Great Britain in the 1820s.

A very strong method of sewing leaves or sections of books using stabbing and side sewing in which the sewing proceeds from one hole (often the center) to the next, then over the head and the tail of the spine. The sewing can also include sewing through the holes and around the back of the book. When complete, the leaves or sections are tied together with a flat knot on the outside.

A contemporary technique of creating a three-dimensional work of art by combining various elements, especially found objects; may include elements painted, carved, or modeled by the artist. Originally coined in 1953 by artist Jean Dubuffet.
Sculptural relief technique in which the projection of the forms is relatively shallow.
Knitting performed by machine.

Refers to the technique of knotting cords or thick threads to create a coarse lace or decorative fringe. It is generally performed by using a padded cushion mounted on a wooden frame to secure the knot-bearing supporting cords or the hem of a piece of fabric.  From the hem or a line of knot-bearing cords, long threads or cords are mounted by knots, and the long threads are then tied to each other with a variety of knots to form patterns or designs. Pins may be used to secure threads to the cushion while the piece is being worked. The technique was developed in 19th-century Genoa, Italy, but the term is derived from the Turkish word for "towel," because the process was inspired by decorative fringes on Turkish towels and other fabrics. It is also based on the techniques used by 16th-century Italian artisans in the creation of "punto a groppo."
Weaving strings of seed beads or other tiny beads, either on a specialized loom or off-loom.
Making a distinctive type of lace by hand by looping and knotting with a single sewing thread and a small shuttle, making varied designs of rings and semicircles.

Type of embroidery beginning in the 19th century, usually worked in worsted yarns following a colored pattern drawn on a graphed chart; named as such because early major supplies of these patterns, yarns, and canvas came from Berlin. Primarily a Victorian phenomenon.

Quilting technique in which two parallel lines of stitching are made through two layers of cloth, then heavy yarn or soft cord is inserted between the layers within the lines of stitching, making a raised linear pattern on an otherwise flat ground.

Temporarily joining two or more pieces of material together by sewing with long loose stitches in order to hold them in place until final sewing. For a slight or temporary fastening done by other means, use "tacking."
Spinning of fibers done by hand rather than by machine, often producing a less than regular yarn.
The process of augmenting the contents of an individual book by adding prints, engravings, letters, or other documents after publication, often resulting in its rebinding.
Refers to glazing that considers values including reflectivity, strength, weight, color, heat transfer, and ultraviolet absorption, for a variety of protective applications including architecture.
The installation or repairing of gas pipes and appliances.
Receptacles designed to collect surface or rainwater from open areas.
V-shaped gutters usually of wood.
Any vertical pipes, including those within a building, that convey rainwater to sewers, drains, or the ground.
Basins used as fixtures for bathing; usually in the context of ancient architecture.
Vertical pipes or stacks in a plumbing system that convey the discharge from toilet fixtures; for stacks that convey the waste from fixtures other than toilets, use "waste stacks".
Bathtubs that are not permanently afixed to the floor, but devised to be hidden in a drawer or cabinet, folded into a wall, or otherwise positioned to save space in the room when not in use.
Wash basins, often set into a decorative surround and often found in ceremonial contexts; may have more than one spout.
Toilets that are not connected to a sewage system, and which have a compartment in which waste is treated with a chemical solution for temporary storage, and for deodorization.
Traps integral with or serving plumbing fixtures and for interceptors serving as such traps.
Water heaters whose primary source of heat energy is the sun.
Systems that bring several clocks into conformity, and may ring bells or alarms at scheduled intervals.
Fire alarm systems that transmit an alarm over a municipal system to the fire station.
Equipment that detects fire in the flame stage.
Detectors of fire and smoke that work by detecting ionized particles in the air.
The process or activity of surrendering ownership or physically leaving a building or location.

Any of various assembling techniques that press additions firmly onto finished parts. In the context of bookbinding, the process of flattening the leaves or gatherings of a text block before sewing or stitching by striking them repeatedly with a beating hammer, in order to compress and flatten them, or, in rebinding, to remove the backing shoulders. Similarly, in the context of weaving or similar activities, the process of using a beater or comb to press each new weft into correct position against existing wefts.
Fixing or attaching one thing to another with a metal pin or cylinder with a head, often joined or secured with a nut.
A technique of laminating different colored metals and alloys together to produce a decorative effect.
Cleaning method that removes soil, discolorations, or coatings through the action of certain materials which impact and abrade the surface under pressure.

Minimally invasive stone cleaning treatments for historic masonry in sculpture and architecture that aim to avoid damage to surface topography of material while mechanically removing the soiling agent or coating.
The action of exposing humans or animals to the free action of water by immersion or suffusion, For recreational immersion in water, use "swimming."
To add color to a black-and-white film or other monochrome image by means of a computer or other methods.
To make or become dark in shade, value, or color; a form of discoloration: the blackening or browning of materials due to such causes as chemical process, exposure to light, the passage of  time.
Technique of dyeing threads of a fabric in different colors so as to produce an image.
Resist dyeing in which wax is used as the resist.
Inducing compaction in mortar or concrete by the use of a tamping rod.
The activity of cutting with a quick and heavy blow with a hewing, hacking instrument, such as an ax, cleaver, sword, or the like.

Trimming printed material so that portions of the illustration or text are removed. Distinguished from "bleeding (printing technique)" which refers to printing an image so that it extends to the edge of the paper or other printing surface.
Changes of color and texture of Oriental rugs or other textiles over time through wear and when different dyes have been used.
The blasting of a boulder by placing a quantity of explosives against it without confining the explosives in a drill hole.

Breakage, cracking, or slippage caused by shear stress, which is the force that tends to cause deformation of a material by slippage along a plane or planes parallel to the imposed stress. Shear failure is often in reference to geological or architectural materials.
The process of loosening rock, or other hard-packed materials, with explosives.
Process of grinding a material in a wet state, such as in preparation of paint pigments.
Refilling of an excavation with the earth removed. For reinterment of human remains or artifacts removed or exposed in course of excavation, use "reburial."
Turning, pressing, or forcing with stress concentrated at specific points in order to form angular or curved forms.

The process of making small pleats or folds in paper with a blade, a process which imparts stretch, strength, bulk, conformability, and texture similar to that found in fabrics. It also refers to the crimping or frizzing of hair or a similar treatment for rubber or thin fabric.
A method of casting by the lost-wax process using a machine in which the mold revolves so that its cavity is filled with molten metal by centrifugal force and pressure.
Any technique for forming or shaping wax into sculptural shapes, either for casting purposes or as a final work.
The process of giving paper or cloth a flat, smooth, glossy, or embossed surface by running it between rollers under strong pressure.
Shaping material, such as paper or sheet metal, between two plates, one with the design in relief and the other with the corresponding design recessed.
Technique of engraving on ivory dyed blue, green, or red. Practiced in China during the Tang dynasty, and introduced to Japan during the Nara period.
The drilling of holes as small as 2.5 mm (0.10 inch) in diameter using a high precision tool made of cobalt steel or micrograin tungsten carbide.

Refers to the process of making still images appear to move, particularly by the technique of photographing drawings or objects in progressive stages of performing an action, so that movement is simulated when the images are projected as a series in quick succession.
Collective term for the animation processes used in Japan by Japanese animation artists for anime films.
Computer graphics technology as applied to special effects for motion pictures. The term is used generally to refer to images that mimic the appearance of three dimensional objects.

The art of creating elaborate flourishes to decorate the margins or otherwise blank spaces in a work of calligraphy. Especially common in European copybooks of the 17th and early 18th centuries, the technique often resulted in images of animals, plants or human composed of a single line, or having that appearance.
Cartography in which the points and lines that comprise a map are digitized as computer data.
A drawing technique, usually employing red chalk and black chalk or charcoal.

Refers to images rendered in pixels that correspond to bits of data in computer memory, and are displayed on a screen. Pixels correspond to bits that may vary in depth: a one-bit pixel is either black or white. The higher the bit depth, the greater the number of colors that may be represented on screen. Bit maps make raster graphics possible.

Photomechanical process in which gelatin relief matrices are made by a bichromate process from color separation negatives or positives; a full-color print is then made by transferring dye from the matrices, in register, to a support.
A modified version of collotype in which the alum-hardened gelatin layer is transferred from glass to the metal plate; allows for the making of many more prints than ordinary collotype.
Stamping over old coins in a die rather than melting them down and recoining with fresh blanks.

Intaglio printing technique that uses a piece of oilcloth rather than a printing plate; the cloth is engraved with a design and inserted into a washing machine wringer or other device to print. Its best known use was by Feliks Jabłczyński (1865-1928); he used a knife and needle for scratching, engraving, and uncovering the underlying canvas; thin oil paint was used as the printing medium. The prints appear similar to drypoint and etching.

A printing process developed in the 20th century in which mezzotint-like tone is achieved by roughening the surface of the plate with abrasives. The process was developed as a way to avoid the laborious process of rocking the plate.

An intaglio etching technique in which a metal plate is sprinkled with a finely-powdered resin (asphaltum, rosin, etc.); the plate is heated to melt the resin, then cooled, and placed in an acid bath. The acid lightly etches areas not covered with the resin. The results in a plate with fine pockmarks. The process was invented in the 1760s by J.B. LePrince. Aquatints were popular until the late 1830s.

Aquatint process in which the image is drawn on the plate with a water-soluble solution; the plate is covered with a ground and submerged in water which dissolves the solution, lifts the ground, and exposes the image areas so the plate can be etched.
Elevators operating through a sidewalk, especially for the handling of goods or refuse.
Elevators that can be operated by the passengers, having at least automatic doors and leveling at landings.

Refers to continuously operating, power-driven, moving stairways used as transportation between floors or levels in subways, buildings, and other mass pedestrian areas. An inclined belt for passengers riding on cleats was invented by Jesse W. Reno of the United States in 1891; it was inclined at an angle of 25 degrees, and in the first model, the handrail was stationary. The name "escalator" was first applied to a moving stairway shown at the Paris Exposition of 1900, originally a trademark of the Otis Elevator Company.

Conveying systems having a moving surface on which passengers stand or walk and that remains parallel to its direction of travel; for similar devices designed to carry passengers or goods either horizontally or up inclines, use "moving ramps."
Building systems in which air is treated to control its temperature, humidity, cleanliness, or distribution.
HVAC systems fueled by heated water.
Fasteners used in concrete, consisting of two semicircular shields that are forced apart, to bear on the walls of a hole, as a bolt is driven into the shields.
Bolts with threads on both ends, used for securing two lengths of handrail timber or other members together.
Heating systems utilizing floor, wall, or roof panels containing electrical conductors or heating pipes.
Solar heating systems that include mechanical equipment and hardware to collect and transport heat; for solar heating systems without mechanical assistance, use "passive solar heating."

Steam heating systems that include vacuum pumps that separate air from condensation in the return main of the system, maintaining the pressure at a constant level and accelerating the circulation of steam.
Systems that use motor-driven fans or blowers to distribute heated air.
Ventilation that allows fresh air to enter a space through available or controlled openings and employs mechanical means such as fans to remove foul air from the same space.
Air conditioning systems run from one or more centralized units that provide controlled air to an entire building or complex.
Air cooling systems in which cold water is circulated between mechanical refrigeration water chilling units and remote cooling equipment.
Use with reference to the direct light of the sun; for the light of day in general, use "daylight."
Lighting systems that employ artificial light, including the arrangements and installation of such systems.
General lighting providing uniform, diffuse illumination approaching a shadowless condition acceptable for the filming of motion pictures and television programs.
Localized lighting technique designed to emphasize a particular object or area.
Supplementary lighting to reduce, soften, or eliminate shadows caused by the main source of illumination.
Lighting systems supplying light outdoors for safety, pleasure, or information, as for playing fields, highways, or advertising.
System of lights arranged for decorative purposes, as in store window displays, on Christmas trees, or on bushes.
Lighting systems comprising light sources shielded by a panel set parallel to the wall and attached to the ceiling to distribute light over the wall; generally used for visual effect.
Lighting systems for the illumination of building elements, spaces, or exteriors for visual effects.
Devices for removing pollutants from the air in a system by passing it through various screens and dry porous materials.
Outlets in an air supply duct for distributing and blending air in an enclosure, usually mounted in suspended ceilings.
Vertical noncombustible structures containing flues for drawing off into the outside air products of combustion from, for example, stoves, fireplaces, and furnaces.
Parts of air conditioning systems in which the air is freed from dust and given the desired humidity by means of a spray of water.
Any heating unit in a hot water heating system in which water is heated before being circulated through pipes to radiators or baseboards.
Designates coiled arrangements of piping or tubing used to cool by transferring heat between one fluid and another or between a space and a refrigerant.

A geothermal heat pump (also known as a ground-source heat pump) transfers energy from the ground as a component of heating, cooling, and water-heating systems. A collector hose filled with a carrier fluid (water or a combination of water and antifreeze) is installed in a borehole which is drilled into a geothermal aquifer. In colder months, this circulating carrier fluid absorbs heat from the surrounding bedrock, which is then extracted by the heat pump for use in space-heating via piping connected to the heat exchanger. During the warmer months the process is reversed: heat from the air is transferred to the heat exchanger and into the fluid. As it moves through the pipes, the heat is dispersed to the rocks, soil, and groundwater.
Small stoves used for heating finishing and lettering tools, especially in the context of bookbinding.
Furnaces in which the high-temperature heat required is produced by electricity; used especially for forging alloys and refractory materials.
Openings or recesses in chimneys or walls in which fires may be built, as for heating or cooking; may also refer to low fireproof structures erected outdoors for cooking over open flames.
Heating elements that are housed in special panels placed horizontally along the baseboards of a wall.

Refers to relatively isolated, solid supports of masonry or another material designed to sustain vertical pressure, including a square or rectangular pillar or pilaster, the solid masonry between doors and windows, the pillars from which an arch springs, or the pillars or posts of a gate or door. A pier may also be a solid structure of masonry or ironwork supporting a telescope or other large instrument.  It is sometimes distinguished from columns or posts by being more massive in size and often square or rectangular in cross section. For cylindrical uprights and for all uprights in steel and concrete frames, the term "columns (architectural elements)" is more often appropriate; for wooden uprights square in cross-section, "posts" may be more appropriate.

Structural elements, typically curved, spanning openings and transmitting vertical loads to either side of the opening; also, structural elements or freestanding structures that resemble arches or act structurally like arches.

Rounded vaults comprising spheres or portions of spheres sitting on circular, elliptical, or polygonal bases, forming the roof of any building or part of a building. They are constructed so that they exert equal thrust in all directions.
Arched structures, usually of masonry and forming a ceiling or roof.

In the discipline of architecture, refers to cylindrical or slightly tapering, vertical members made to either give support or to appear to give support. They usually comprise three sections: base, capital, and shaft. The term also refers to all uprights in steel frame or concrete frame structures. Columns may occasionally stand alone as a monument, for example in Trajan's Column in Rome or Nelson's Column in London. Columns may be used as decorative elements on furniture. For square or rectangular members, either in masonry construction or classically treated, and for massive uprights in Medieval architecture, see "piers (supporting elements)"; for wooden square uprights, see "posts." In the discipline of architecture, refers to cylindrical or slightly tapering, vertical members made to either give support or to appear to give support. They usually comprise three sections: base, capital, and shaft. The term also refers to all uprights in steel frame or concrete frame structures. Columns may occasionally stand alone as a monument, for example in Trajan's Column in Rome or Nelson's Column in London. Columns may be used as decorative elements on furniture. For square or rectangular members, either in masonry construction or classically treated, and for massive uprights in Medieval architecture, see "piers (supporting elements)"; for wooden square uprights, see "posts."

Refers to the elaborated superstructures carried by the columns in classical architecture, horizontally divided into architrave, frieze, and cornice. May connote similar features in other contexts, such as along the upper portions of walls.
The projecting, uppermost features of classical entablatures; use also for similar features crowning a window or wall.

Middle horizontal members of a classical entablature, above the architrave and below the cornice. For horizontal decorated bands in general, found on architecture and furniture, see "friezes (ornamental areas)."

In engineering, structural members such as beams, bars, or rods, usually fabricated from straight pieces of metal or timber, that form a series of triangles lying in a single plane; based on the principle that a triangle cannot be easily distorted by stress. Trusses were probably first used in primitive lake dwellings during the early Bronze Age, about 2500 BCE. The first trusses were built of timber. The Greeks used trusses extensively in roofing; trusses were used for various construction purposes in the European Middle Ages. A major impetus to truss design came in the development of covered bridges in the United States in the early 19th century. Cast iron and wrought iron were succeeded by steel for railroad truss bridges. Trusses are also used extensively in machinery, such as cranes.
The surfaces of rooms or spaces on which one walks.
Outside, overhead enclosures of buildings or other structures, including the roofing and its structural framing.
Chambers located below fireplaces or fireboxes for the collection and removal of ashes.
Refers to the horizontal portions of a sloping roof that project beyond the walls. For portions of the roof projecting beyond the gable, use "verges."
Vertical triangular portions of the ends of buildings having double-sloping roofs. Includes similar ends which are not triangular in shape, as of a gambrel roof.

Vertical architectural members used to define and divide spaces. In English, there is no distinctive term for an external wall and the internal sides of a room, but this is not universal. Many languages distinguish between the two. In German, some of this distinction can be seen between Wand and Mauer, in Spanish between 'pared' and 'muro' and Dutch 'wand' and 'muur.' These terms are all contained here, select among them according to the local context.
Generally denotes apertures or breaks in the surface of a wall or other architectural element.

Barriers that swing, slide, tilt, or fold to close a doorway, usually of solid and finished construction and usually leading to or separating interior spaces. Use also for similar features that close a container or a piece of case furniture. For barriers of less solid or finished construction, and usually separating two exterior spaces, use "gates."
Denotes openings, which contain or could contain a door, that provide access into or out of building spaces.

Barriers, often swinging or sliding, used to fill or close a gateway between two spaces or placed within a wall or fencing, often exterior and often made of a grating or open framework or forming a heavy or rough structure. For barriers of more solid and finished construction and usually leading to interior spaces, use "doors." For more substantial structures, whether or not they include an actual barrier, see various types of "gate structures."
Openings in the wall of a building, serving to admit light, usually to permit vision, and often to admit air.
Ornamental openwork of masonry found in the upper parts of Gothic style windows; also, similar motifs and forms in various materials applied decoratively, as on walls, furniture, and other objects.
Staircase units that consist of one tread and one riser, or any similar element providing a horizontal surface on which to support the foot of a person descending or ascending.
Nahua altars or earthen platform.

Receptacles that separate and retain greases, oil, dirt, gravel, and all other substances lighter or heavier than the liquid waste that bears them, such as to prevent their entrance into the house sewer.

Water distribution systems in which water is pumped to holding tanks above the points of use, thereby increasing water pressure through gravity; most often employed in tall buildings where municipal water supply lacks the pressure necessary for an upfeed system.

Works that use non-art elements, often junk and/or debris, to form a work of art. Assemblages are sculptural works created since about 1945 by the technique of assemblage, the creation of a three-dimensional work of art by combining various elements, especially found objects. They may include elements painted, carved, or modeled by the artist.  For such works created earlier in the 20th century, see "object sculpture."

Beads with religious significance that were introduced to Japan from Korea. They are found in the prehistoric graves of ancient Japan and it is thought that they were worn on the body from the beginning of Japan's recorded history up until the Kofun period (300-710). These beads were carved from jadeite, agate, talc, glass or jasper usually into comma shapes and varied in size from a few millimeters to five centimeters.

Mass-produced utilitarian objects which the artist transforms into works of art by placing them in an artistic context. The term is applied particularly to certain works of Marcel Duchamp, who pioneered the practice.
Refers to sculpture executed in relatively shallow relief.
Ornamental wood or stone projections where the ribs intersect at the apex of a vault. They may serve as the keystone; may be painted or carved.
Ancient Greek sculptures in which the extremities are made of stone and the torso is made of another material, usually wood.

Distinctive Mexican folk art sculptures of fantastical creatures, usually brightly colored and imade of wood or papier-mâche. Although inspired by elements of earlier Mexican-Spanish and indigenous art, the style of these works is attributed Pedro Linares, active In the 1930s.
Recumbent effigies as decomposing corpses.
Refers to lead-glazed Staffordshire pottery figurines of a type associated with John Astbury and Thomas Whieldon.

Figural sculptures, often with additional objects incorporated onto the surface, made and used by the Fon and other Ewe peoples of Africa in the context of voodoo, to gain protection and achieve empowerment and change for the individual.

Highly stylized anthropomorphic carved sculptures constructed from flat boards and decorated with red, black, and white paint. These figures were used to display trophy skulls within the men's ceremonial houses, on the south coast of New Guinea. The sculptures are depictions of important ancestors or founders of a clan.
Representations that visualize architectural projects in three dimensions, often including a representation of the surrounding site or context, and usually, but not necessarily, built to scale.
Distinctive dioramas as made by Cornelius Bavelaar father or son, or other dioramas in the same style.

Casts that have been created from molds taken directly from an existing work. After-casts are therefore made using the indirect lost-wax process, or in some instances by sand casting. The term is normally applied to bronzes, but may be applied to other types of casts.
Indoor installation works which incorporate materials from nature and address ecological concerns.

Dovetail joints in wood, designed so that interlocking pins and tails are concealed within the edge of the wood member and not visible when the two members are joined; often used with fine woodworking.
Bark cloth of Hawaii and other Polynesian Islands, made by pounding the bark of the paper mulberry, breadfruit, or other plants.
Twinned dead bolts projecting from a lock mechanism that engage a common opening in the strike.

Generally, bolts used with nuts to join the side rails or posts of a bed frame to the headboard and footboard. In modern usage, the term commonly refers specifically to a particular kind of bolt and nut configuration: Very long bolts are seated in a counter-bored hole in the bed posts, penetrating into the side rails. A special nut is located in a recess, usually in a round mortise, within the side rail. A special wrench is used to tighten the bolt, which draws the components together securely. This type of bolt used with special nuts is referred to as a "bed bolt," even when used to join parts of other furniture, such as tables, chairs, or other items.
Threaded bolts, usually embedded in a foundation, for securing a sill, framework, or machinery.
Refers to furniture or built-in features in the form of an upright partition that can be used to embellish, partition, shelter, and provide privacy. Screens are often highly decorated.
Hinges so designed that, when the door is closed, only a ball-type knuckle is exposed. Such hinges have an adjustment for vertical control within limited scope.
Hinges with threaded arms instead of hinge plates, each leaf extended and bent into a flange, each side of the hinge forming a cantilever with its opposite.
Mortise locks operated by a key having a wing bit, in which the keying of the lock is integral with the lock case.
Locks used on doors of psychiatric institutions providing special protection against tampering.
Threaded nuts, used for alignment of an object, that are often coupled with a locking nut to secure them in position.

Wood screws designed to attach a stop bead, which is a narrow wooden strip that is molded on one edge, located in a door or window frame, and upon which a door or window sash closes. The screw is often placed within a washer-like recessed metal adjuster, to allow for periodic unscrewing and adjustment of the stop if the sash operation becomes difficult due to seasonal climate changes, and to allow for the easy removal of the stop for painting or glazing.
Connectors used to join concrete.
Joints between two pieces of wood in which the direction of the grain of one piece is at an angle (usually 90 degrees) to the grain in the other.
Lists of additions to the holdings of a collection, usually in chronological order by date of receipt and giving the titles of the accessions.
Use with specific reference to documents, such as drawings and specifications, associated with a construction project.
Written articles appearing regularly in a series in a newspaper.
Posted texts that accompany an exhibition of art or other cultural material, including wall labels and other explanatory texts, charts, etc.

Labels affixed under, beside, or otherwise near a work in an exhibition or museum installation, noting the name of the artist, title, and other pertinent information. For the format and content of the information itself, use "tombstone (document genres)."
Projects involving planning and execution of significant engineering and construction activities.
In Indian architecture, a facetted coping piece.

Wood from the species Acacia melanoxylon, reddish brown to black in color and prized for attractive grain, appearing similar to rosewood. The strong, elastic, hardwood is used for furniture, walking sticks, and tool handles.

Door hinges that are visible when the door is open but concealed when the door is closed. Distinguished from "invisible hinges" which are completely concealed, from the outside, whether the door is open or closed.
Slender, smooth, wire nails having a small deep head used for finish carpentry work.
Nails having a tip that is blunt rather than pointed.
Mechanical fasteners designed to bridge a joint and pull the two pieces tightly together as they are driven in place.
Nails having a shank that is barbed rather than smooth, to improve the grip. Distinguished from “ring-shank nails,” which have ringlike grooves around the shank.

Roofing nails having a plain shank and a lead cap or washer, used for attaching corrugated or other metal roofing. The advantage of using lead washers is that they make a tight joint and prevent leaking and rusting at the nail hole; given that the lead washer is soft, it conforms to the curve and irregular surface of the metal.
In construction, support or anchoring hangers made of metal wire, used to attach a wooden member to a metal member.
In construction, support or anchoring hangers used to attach two steel members.
Support or anchoring hangers suspended from horizontal ceiling slabs or other members by means of tabs or clips extending at right angles from the vertical portion of the hanger.
Metal supports, wires, straps, or other hardware devices used to hang the formwork for concrete beams.
Joist hangers that allow a joist to be hung from two points.
Inserts for attachment or fastening that allow for a certain amount of adjustment in positioning.
Cords used to loop around materials to secure them in place for easy transport. Examples include tumplines and straps for bags.
Forms used by persons requesting assistance, authorization, employment, admission, or other action.
Electric conduits prefabricated in sections and containing heavy conductors for transmission of large currents at relatively low voltage.
Electrical systems temporarily produced or supplied by standby power generators when normal electric power supply fails or is interrupted.
Any of various combinations of electric, hydraulic, or pneumatic systems that convert energy into mechanical movement.
Transformers capable of stepping down the voltage of a current.
Hoisting or lowering mechanisms equipped with a car or platform used in buildings exclusively for carrying materials.
Tandem elevators with one car above the other riding in the same hoistway and serving two consecutive floors simultaneously.
Elevators designed to move large objects, such as freight.
Decanters in the form of a jug with a long neck and a loop handle extending from the rim to the shoulder.
Ewers used for ritual ablution, for example in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic rites.
Glass flasks with raised designs on one or both sides.
A type of German glass jug that is onion-shaped and has a neck or spout formed of several intertwined tubes.
Lids, usually plastic, made to cover disposable hot liquid cups, whether used for coffee or other hot drinks. Usually having an opening for drinking and a vent to allow steam to escape.

Bowl-shaped basketry pot-lids made and used by the Zulu and other southern African peoples, traditionally fabricated of grasses, or, in recent times, of colored telephone wire. They are also sometimes used as dishes to hold small items or dry foodstuffs.

Tops, sometimes decorative, for sealing bottles; they are formed by a shaft to fit into the bottle joined to a top by which to grasp the stopper. Examples include stoppers for decanters, uncorked wine bottles, and perfume.
Nonflexible bracelets that slip over the hand or which are hinged and closed by a clasp.
Brooches made in the form of a flat disc, to the back of which is attached a fastening pin.
Earrings with clip fasteners.
Necklaces made of strung beads or crocheted or stitched using beads.

Pendants in the form of discs of thin, beaten gold or silver with stamped decoration based on Roman coin or medallion prototypes or with runic inscriptions. Suspended by means of a circular attachment and intended to be worn on a thong or other support around the neck.
Ornaments given to commemorate events or as a reward for merit, taking the shape of a designed element attached to a pin.

Rings worn by students and alumni of an educational institution that commemorate the final academic year and/or graduation, generally for a high school, college, or university. These often feature a gem held in a metal setting in which a year and school is displayed.

Traditional headdresses that unmarried women may wear on certain holidays, at festivals and, finally, at their wedding. These are common to central or Northern Europe, and designs vary regionally. In parts of Europe during the Middle Ages, they were decorated with flowers, fir branches, herbs and ripe fruits. From the 17th century until today, more expensive materials may be used such as pearls, mirrors, silver and gold.
Diadems of turquoise mosaic worn by Nahuas tlahtohqueh (rulers).

Headdresses of a type worn by important figures in Tsimshian society, such as chiefs or leaders of carving societies. Consists of a wooden base with a carved frontlet, usually depicting clan crest figures, animal whiskers protruding from the top, and a train of ermine skins framing the back and sides of the headdress. Sometimes a space is carved in the frontlet to hold feathers, which would be used by chiefs to welcome indivduals during various ceremonies.

Medals with Philip II of Spain, ruler of the Netherlands, on one side and on the other two hands clasped through a beggar's pouch. These were worn as a pendants from 1566 by rebellious noblemen to mark membership of their closed group.
Hairpieces consisting of long locks of hair used to thicken or lengthen the look of one's own hair. Chiefly employed for down-hanging styles such as the long bob or pageboy bob.
In Indian culture, a wig.
Chopines (platform shoes) of exceptional height, particularly those worn by women in Venice.
Wooden clogs from the Philippines, cut to resemble the shape of feet, and painted on the sides.
Sandals used indoors in ancient Rome, typically made from one piece of leather and fastened by laces.
Heelless slippers, of Arab-Islam origin, often pointed at the toes.
Ballet slippers with reinforced toes, usually tied on with criss-crossed satin ribbons, for dancing on point.
Type of short sock that covers only the sole and heel of the foot, not extending above the ankle.

Knitted or woven stockings worn during pontifical masses over ordinary stockings by prelates who enjoy pontifical priviledges. Over the centuries they were of various colors and decoration. After the Second Vatican Council, they have fallen out of common use along with revisions of the liturgy.
Brimless, close fitting headwear with peak; made of fabric, often khaki-coloured. Worn in the field in addition to the helmet.
Various types of hats adapted from Bavarian and Austrian Tyrolean hats, usually of felt and with a brim and slightly peaked crown, often trimmed with a ribbon or cord and a feather.
Top hats made of beaver fur or of a fabric simulating this fur. Prefer "castors (hats)" for other men's hats of beaver fur made in varying form.
Cocked hats with the front side pinched to form a peak; worn in the 18th century.
Strings or bands worn around the head in order to secure a kaffiyeh in place.
Fur-lined hoods with two long ends meant to hang down in front; of a type originating in the Medieval period and worn especially by clergy.
Kerchiefs, triangular or folded triangularly, with two of the ends tied under the chin; often open at the back.
