Neck-scarves worn with combat uniforms or service uniforms. Square or rectangular shape with closures at the back of the neck. Often in a regimental color with its emblem placed centrally.
Small, round skullcaps, often brightly colored, worn especially by children and collegians.

Face veils having camouflage pattern. Examples are military-issued netting used by soldiers to hide the face and keep insects out of the eyes and nose; these were intended to be worn over the helmet to cover the face, respirator, and gas cape. Other examples are used by hunters.
Garments worn over main garments to both protect clothing and to store utensils when not being used. Generally contains a front pocket for storage.
Short-sleeved blouses with a low neckline, and often cut to expose part of the midriff, especially those worn by Hindu women in India.
Loose-cut breeches banded at the knee.
Women's capes of cloth or fur with long pointed ends hanging in front.

Long, loose-fitting overgarments traditionally worn in the Middle East and Muslim countries eleswhere. They are often made of wool and cover the entire body from head to toe;  one of the most popular pieces of modest fashion.
Cloaks or long coats of a distinctive type worn by soldiers or horsemen in the 16th-17th centuries; examples are coats worn by musketeers and gardes du corps.
Suit coats designed to be worn in the morning, patricularly a cutaway coat with long tails.

Refers to 18th- and 19th-century full-length gowns with overskirt split in front to reveal an ornamental petticoat or underskirt beneath. In two popular variations, the back may be fitted in the "robe à l'anglaise" style or loose in the "robe à la française" style.

Jackets that formed part of the military costume of the hussars, between hip and knee length. The jackets were decorated with five rows of braid frogging, looped into rosettes at the ends, with toggle closures incorporated into the frogging. Matching piping adorned the collar, front edge, bottom hem, back seams, and rear skirts.
Parkas characterized by broad shoulders and case on the back meant to carry an infant; created and worn by Inuit communities in North America. Often decorated with beadwork and fringe detailing.
Special rucksacks designed to be worn into combat and outfitted to carry basic supplies and equipment, especially pre 19th century, made of stiff material, with a waist belt.
Parasols with articulated handles that allow the shade to tilt at an angle. These were designed for use on carriage rides, and were popularized by Queen Victoria in the 1840s.
Small rectangular suitcases hinged to open into two compartments of equal size.

Umbrella-like objects carried in processions, particularly as used to distinguish important people or things in the procession, as well as for protection from the sun. Examples are found in ancient, Asian, and western traditions. For example, in Christian tradition, parasols are held in procession as a sign of veneration over monarchs, high-ranking church dignitaries, or the blessed sacrament (the consecrated host).
Maori ornamental hair combs made of whale bone.

Carved wooden ancestral poles, large in size, made by the Asmat people of the Sepik region. The figures on the sculptures represent deceased clan members who were murdered by enemy clans. A recurring characteristic of most bisj is the phallus, representing the strength of male fertility. These memorial poles were constructed for funerary ceremonies that commemorated the deceased. Designs vary depending on the area or group who constructed the bisj.

Small carved wooden or ivory sculptures consisting of a figurine, often a male equestrian or a kneeling woman, and a shallow bowl. The bowl is used to hold the sixteen sacred palm nuts used in Yoruba divination rituals. Such sculptures are works of art commissioned by patrons from the carvers.
Recumbent effigies.
Reliefs found on the face of a voussoir or keystone, so-named because they resemble the shape of a clasp or badge ("agrafe" in French).

Small reliefs made from materials having layers of different colors, such as gems, glass, ceramics, or shell, and carved so that the design stands out in one color against a background in another. Cameos may be incorporated in jewelry. For works created from different pieces of stone and other materials, prefer "commessi (visual works)."

Metal whistles traditionally used on ships by boatswain's mates to relay orders or to pipe senior naval officers aboard; they were grasped in the hand when blown, the pitch rising or falling as the hand was opened or closed.
Multiple flutes of Slovakia, consisting of two separate flutes tied together.

Late serpents appearing around the early 19th century, consisting of a conical tube about 230 cm long, generally made of copper, with six fingerholes, three or four keys, a swan-neck crook, and terminating in a widely flared bell.
Aerophones in which free reeds fitted in pipes or chambers are sounded individually or in combination by the player's blowing or sucking.

Large square-built concertinas developed by the German Heinrich Band in the 1840s. It has button keys and may have either a single or double action, though single is more common. Early models have 88 keys or more, but the average modern instrument has 71. They are best known as used by the tango bands of Brazil, Argentine, and Uruguay, but are also known in West Africa and the USA..
English guitars fitted with plucking or striking devices, to eliminate finger plucking.
Pianofortes having a horizontal wing-shaped case, with one bent or curved side and one straight side, and most of the strings running parallel to the individual keys.
Refers broadly to devices or contrivances by which people, animals, or objects are conveyed or carried.
Road vehicles propelled by electric motors, drawing their current either from storage batteries or from overhead cables.
Term used by tableware designers and glass manufacturers at the end of the 19th century for U-shaped dishes set on a high stem and intended to hold bananas.
Two handled porringers: shallow, flat-bottomed bowls with vertical sides, having two lateral handles that are level with the rim, often with a cover, and sometimes a conforming stand.
Shallow dishes for candies or other sweets; may have a lid or stem.
Frying pans heated electrically.
Plates for holding an individual serving of bread, similar to but smaller than dessert plates.

Teapots that rest on a stand usually having a warming device such as a spirit lamp. Sometimes the stand is merely to support the teapot without a heating device; such a teapot may have a rounded bottom, as it rests on the stand rather than on a flat surface.

Vessels in the form of a caster, typically in order to match the other casters in a set, but lacking a pierced lid or having an interior sleeve to protect the contents. They may have a domed lid that may be opened or removed, to allow the contents to be extracted with a small spoon.

Small casters intended primarily for sprinkling sugar, cinnamon, or other spices on hot muffins. They are typically historical objects. They may be part of a set with a small milk or cream pitcher designed to be set at table or on a breakfast tray when muffins are served, but they are usually not part of a larger set of casters in a special tray used at the formal dining table. They may be of cylindrical or baluster shape, or squatter, and made of metal, glass, or porcelain.
Double cruets, made to contain oil and vinegar, typically of glass with dual long-necked spouts facing opposite directions, and often designed as a single two-chambered vessel.

Large platters, usually circular or oval, often earthenware or metal, used for serving meat. For other, circular or rectangular dishes, sometimes of wood, on which meat or other food is carved or served, use "trenchers." For large plates set under dinner plates at table, use "service plates."

Small, low, open vessels used to hold salt at the table; made in a variety of forms and may have a flat base or rest on legs or a stemmed foot. For tall vessels used to hold salt, use "standing salts."
Term applied to lavishly ornamented standing salts, such as those used on the high table at ceremonial banquets.
Flat boards, sometimes with a low rim, used to hold offerings for religious ceremonies. Some feature a base raising the board off the ground.

Table-long centerpieces of silver or gilt that may carry flowers, fruit and condiments, as well as other items. They typically comprise a platform, often mirrored and set on feet, and upon which are typically placed two candelabras, an epergne, a large bowl on a stand, flat bowls or étagères, and other items, including flowers and various fruits, confections, and sweets displayed in a decorative manner and intended to be eaten as dessert.
Small spoons used to measure the water that dilutes the wine in the chalice during a Catholic mass.
Round-bowled spoons similar to but larger than bouillon spoons; intended to be used to consume cream soups.
Long-handled spoons, usually with the capacity of a teaspoon, used for measuring ingredients or mixing drinks.
China, glassware, and silverware, used for table service.

Thin-walled slipware vessels characterized by small rolled rims and molded decoration on the outside surface. Made from the late first century BCE until the early first century CE. These are named for the craftsman who signed his goods with “Aco”. Cups of the same shape without the Aco signature are also referred to as Aco cups.

In Peru and other areas of Latin American, cups of faience or organic materials, used especially in the colonial era to serve hot chocolate or other hot beverages. Chocolate drink was consumed by the Mayans as early as 150 BCE, and in the following centuries it became a popular beverage among many indigenous groups. To create a Western-style form of the traditional mate cup, Spanish colonists improvised by using gourds, coconuts, wood, and other organic materials already in use, to which they added European-style bases, handles, and rims made of silver.
Small coffee cups for serving strong coffee.

Glasses intended for drinking ale or beer. Early 17th- and 18th-century examples are often similar in form to elongated wine glasses with ogee or rounded funnel bowls, resting on stems of varying length; bowl capacity is usually between three and five ounces. Modern examples are often in the form of tall, thin glasses, generally of 12-ounce capacity, which taper at the bottom and rest on solid bases.
Term applied to small short-stemmed ale glasses of 3- to 4-ounce capacity, especially those made in England from the early 17th until the early 19th century.
German goblets, usually made with a cover and often made of glass or silver, usually intended for presentation or other ceremonial purposes.
Glasses intended for drinking champagne and other sparkling wine, having either a shallow saucer-shaped bowl on a stemmed foot or flute-shaped.
Stemmed glasses designed for champagne, having a shallow broad bowl.
Handled vessels used in association with a fraternal organization, or secret society. These display symbols or emblems of the organization.
Earthenware mugs intended as vessels for beer; also, glass vessels having a similar shape; commonly holding about a pint. They may be decorated with references to beer, or to a particular brewery.
German type of stoneware tankards made from the 16th century in Siegburg in the Rhineland.

Brasswork inlaid with silver or gold in knot patterns and mauresques. Azzimina was made in northern Italy, notably in Venice, and the Levant from the late 15th century to the 16th century. It is sometimes confused with damascening.

Parts of works or complete visual works employing basketmaking that uses a type of plait having two canes or willows twisted together in the same direction, so as to enclose a crossing weft at each half-turn. Examples of fitched works include baskets and backs and seats of furniture.
Works of feather mosaic created by Nahua peoples. Objects included cloaks, fans, and shields.
Designs, patterns, or images created by using scissors to remove small portions from the interior or edges of a piece of paper.

An interlacement of parts of a rope by twisting the ends about each other and then drawing tight the loops for the purpose of fastening them together or to another object or to prevent slippage. The goal is to fasten the ropes in a way they can easily be released again, without loosening themselves.
The statements, usually monthly, rendered by a bank to a depositor.
Large and small items that are attached to, or used in conjunction with, doors.
Joints of various types that join two or more wooden planks, panels, or boards by securing them with wooden batten cross pieces.

Butt-joints in which the edges of the boards are not square with their faces due to the pitch of the sides, as used to make a box having a wider top than bottom. Examples of items requiring hopper joints are hoppers, bins, chutes, and other items. The difficulty in making this joint is in laying out the pieces to obtain the proper angle for the edges to meet.
Tongue-and-groove joints in which the tongue is wedge-shaped and the groove is tapered to receive it.
Wood joints in which two pieces are each cut to half their thickness at the overlap, so that the total thickness of the system does not change.
Wood joints in which the ends or edges of both members are milled with matching rabbets and combined at right angles.
Double rabbet wood joints made by mating two rabbets in a way suitable for cladding.
In carpentry, joints created by fitting, usually at right angles, the end of a piece of wood into a groove cut across the width of another piece to a depth of half its thickness.
Intersections consisting of two pieces of molding where one is cut to fit the contour of the other.
Mortise-and-tenon joints used when two timbers are joined at an angle of less than 90 degrees.

In carpentry, right-angle joints that comprise one piece having a rabbet cut and another having a dado groove cut, produced in a way so the protruding rabbet fits into the groove of the opposing piece to form a joint.
Nonrigid airships having several balloonlike compartments.
Receptacles or formed or flexible coverings designed to hold, store, or ship objects or substances.
Relatively broad, bowl-like vessels intended to collect water used during ablution rites; used in several religions.

Containers made of birchbark wood, often decorated with quillwork, incised designs, or beadwork. Used for a variety of purposes, from souvenirs to household containers. Historically made by Native North Americans from the Northeast and Great Lakes and by First Nations communities in Canada; contemporary makers of boxes reside across North America.
Cans made of aluminum.
Cases or containers used to hold an amulet, which is an object believed to protect or bring good fortune.

Xylophones of the Ganda of Uganda, consisting of 17 (formerly 22) wood slabs set on two banana trunks and held in position by two shoulders carved on the underside of the slabs. They require up to six players and are traditionally associated with royalty.
Suspended stones that are struck to make sound, specifically used in the kivas of Pueblo Indians.
Upper surfaces of the soundboxes of chordophones over which the strings pass and which play a major part in transmitting the vibration of the strings to the surrounding atmosphere.
Banjos strung like ukeleles.

Bass citterns in use chiefly in France and Germany in the 17th and 18th centuries, patterned on the theorbo, with two peg boxes, one for the on-board strings which were stopped by the fingers, and one for the off-board unstopped strings.

Guitars with twelve strings in six courses, most commonly found in acoustic iterations, but also exist as electric guitars. The instrument likely emerged in the last decades of the 19th century and was probably inspired by other double-course instruments, such as the mandolin.
European harps composed of three sections: resonator, neck, and pillar. The pillar, by taking the tension of the strings, allows these harps to withstand far greater string tension than open harps.
Arched harps of the Teso of Uganda and Kenya, with a very slim elongated body and five or six strings.
Diatonic frame harps with a series of hooks set in the neck to permit the player to raise the pitch of each string by a semitone.
Triple harps developed in Wales in the 17th century, having a slender forepillar of nearly two meters and a steeply curving neck, with a range normally of five octaves plus one note.

Plucked harp lutes of the Manding linguistic and cultural family of Africa, having a long neck passing diametrically through a large gourd resonator covered with leather, 21 leather or nylon strings arranged in two parallel ranks perpendicular to the resonator on either side of a vertical notched bridge, and two handles, one on the outer side of each rank of strings. They are played only by male professional musicians.

Harp zithers of western central Africa, made of a stalk of raffia palm from the surface of which from three to five strings are detached and supported above the string bearer by a central, vertical, notched bridge; from one to six gourd resonators are attached to the back of the string bearer. They are played by plucking.
Harps equipped with a double-action pedal mechanism to raise the pitch of the strings by either a semitone or a whole tone during performance.

Lutes constructed so that the neck penetrates the sound box, having long thin necks and small bodies, usually covered with skin. The strings are normally lifted well above the neck by a high bridge. The form developed into "spike fiddles."
Small mandores with a very narrow almond-shaped body, short fretted neck, sickle-shaped pegbox, central soundhole with rose, frontal string fastener, and gut strings.
Large, sitar-like plucked lutes from North India. Effectively, bass sitars.
Lyres having a natural or man-made bowl for a resonator and a membrane belly.
Five-string wishbone-shaped frame lyres of the Kipsigis people of Kenya.
Large, usually rectangular but occasionally round, box lyres of Ethiopia and the Sudan with ten strings tuned in pairs in octaves, played with a plectrum.
Large mandolins of bass range.
Upright double psalteries with a trapeziform box acting as a soundboard between two rows of strings.

Hungarian dulcimers consisting of a shallow trapezoidal box with from 20 to 35 courses of metal strings crossing two bridges, played while suspended from the player's neck by a strap or resting on four legs; popular in gypsy, folk, and nightclub bands.
Large, fiddle-shaped, early form of the hurdy-gurdy, developed in 12th-century Europe, played set horizontally across two players' laps, one operating the tangents while the other turned the crank.
Keyed monochords developed in France in the 1880s, having an oval body, 29 keys set on the neck, and a single string made of horsehair.
Bass liras da braccio with from nine to fourteen strings, held between the player's legs; they were known primarily in France and Italy, from the mid-16th to the end of the 17th century.

Fiddles combining qualities of the guitar and the violoncello, being smooth-waisted like a guitar, with a guitarlike tuning and fitted with 24 frets, but of the size of the violoncello and bowed in the same manner.
18th-century small violas having five strings and played on the arm, in use from about 1725 to about 1770.
Violas d'amore made around 1780 by Thomas Perry of Dublin, with a body about the size of a viola d'amore and five pairs of metal strings.

Viols of bass range, similar to the bass viol but with ten or more additional wire strings that pass close to the belly and under the neck, which sound sympathetically and may also be plucked by the left thumb.
Small English violas da gamba, developed around the middle of the 17th century, used primarily for the performance of free ornamentation by way of varying given melodies.

Brazilian musical bows of African origin, with a single wire string and sometimes a coconut or gourd resonator, held against the chest during play. One hand holds the bow and occasionally applies a metal coin to the string to alter its pitch, while the other strikes it with a stick; normally the striking hand holds or has attached to it a rattle.
Braced mouth bows of the Shona of Zimbabwe, made from a single stick of wood and with the string looped to the bow at its center.
Goras of the Southern Sotho people of southern Africa.

Use to denote collectively the bars or strips of wood glued under the soundboard of many string instruments such as the lute, guitar, harpsichord, and piano, which are crucial to the tone of the instrument.
Lip-vibrated aerophones made of brass or other metals.
Very large keyed bugles made of metal, with a U-shaped tube of wide conical bore ending in a slightly flared bell and a cup mouthpiece.

Valved brass instruments of the cornet family of alto range, usually pitched at E flat or F, having a conical bore and medium-sized bell; the tube, about 79 inches in length, can be coiled in tuba, orchestral trumpet, or helicon shape.
English post horns, having a straight conical tube, usually of brass, sometimes of copper, with mountings of a different metal, a narrow bore, and a widely flared bell, played with a cup mouthpiece.
Early English version of the trombone, in use from Medieval times up to the 18th century.
Tubular trumpets in which the mouthhole faces the axis.
Wooden trumpets of cylindrical or conical bore, made of a young tree curving upwards naturally from the roots to form the bell, found in pastoral communities in the Alps.
Side-blown Ethiopian trumpets made of an elongated gourd or a long bamboo tube, with a copper bell attached by means of a length of curved horn so that it is perpendicular to the tube.
Valved brass instruments, essentially tenor tubas, pitched in B flat with a nine foot range, with a wide conical bore, cup-shaped mouthpiece, and built in helicon, tuba, or trumpet form.
Woodwind instruments containing reeds.
Small mouth-blown bagpipes of Brittany, with a sheepskin bag, drone pipe, and conical wide-bore chanter with seven fingerholes and double reed.

Bassoons pitched below the regular bassoon, with the tube usually, though not always, bent back upon itself several times in order to reduce the overall length and bring the keys within convenient playing position.

The most common type of cornett, made of a long section of wood, split in two and glued together after the conical tube was carved out, finished to an octagonal exterior cross-section, and covered in thin black leather. Usually the instruments curved to the right, accommodating right-handed players, but left-curving models were also made.

Double duct-flute developed by William Bainbridge of London in the early 19th century, featuring six, occasionally seven, fingerholes on each side, and one or no thumbholes. It allowed the player to play in two-part harmony with one hand on each duct.
General term for grouping flute aerophones without ducts.

End-blown flutes of the Teso and Karamojong areas of Uganda, cut off at a slanting angle at the bottom end and blown obliquely; there are two sizes, the longer having a hemispherical gourd bell attached at the lower end.
Tenors of orchestral oboes, having a pear-shaped bell with a small opening and its double reed carried on a short metal bocal.
Stopped panpipes of Romania, in raft form, composed of up to thirty pipes set into a curved pipe or stick.
Recorders that are between the soprano and tenor in size, and correspondingly intermediate in pitch.
Brass instruments in the saxophone family with a range that are analogous to the alto voice, and are tuned to E flat.
West African shawms having a pirouette, a long iron staple carrying the reed, five or six fingerholes, and a bell; the pipe and bell are made from a single piece of wood and covered with leather.

Musical glasses developed by Benjamin Franklin around 1761, in which glass bowls of graded size fitted concentrically on a horizontal rod are turned by a crank attached to a pedal as the player rubs the rims with slightly moistened or chalk-dusted fingers to produce sound. In a slightly later development, a shallow trough of water is fitted below the rod, which is mounted obliquely so that the bowls are moistened as they rotate.
Flexible sticks of wood, usually with lengths of horsehair between the two ends, used specifically to play violins.
Mutes incorporated into the piano actions, consisting of felted blocks resting on the strings to keep them silent except when their keys are pressed or when the entire set is lifted by a pedal.
Percussion hammers specifically intended for use with xylophones.

Tongues of metal or wood in various types that are components of open bells which produce the sound by striking the side of the instrument; generally they take the form of a rod, or of a ball or pellet attached to a cord.
Music boxes with two rows of free reeds worked by suction wind, two hand-cranked bellows, and strips of perforated paper fed by the cranks that actuate the bellows.
Basque tabor pipes of slightly conical bore, with two front fingerholes and one rear thumbhole.
American 19th-century clocks generally resembling an acorn in outline and available in shelf, wall, and mantel styles.
Clocks originating in the United States in the early 19th century, distinguished by slender turned pillars flanking the case between top and base and by a scrolled top.
Types of table clocks with a gallery and small cupola or in other ways in the form of two-level towers; popular in England and France from the mid-16th century into the 17th century.
British pendulum wall clocks of the mid- to late 18th century, with large dials and wooden cases, generally made for public gathering places, such as inns.
Late-18th-century bracket clocks having a round upper portion, waisted central section, and a rectangular base, with or without small feet, vaguely resembling ascension balloons.
Clocks that are powered by electricity, or that are synchronized with a mother clock.
Detachable brackets in clocks and watches that carry the upper pivot of the axis of the balance.

Sundials, of several varieties, whose dial plate is tilted so as to lie parallel to the earth's equator and whose gnomon is perpendicular to the plate at its center, pointing to the north celestial pole; the layout of the hour lines is not dependent on latitude.
Watches that display, for example, the date of the month and day of the week, in addition to the time.
Apparatuses, instruments, or other objects used to produce sound, whether musical or nonmusical.
Devices consisting of two or more musical instruments or of a musical instrument with another type of device.
Sound devices that produce their sound by using the air itself as the primary vibrating agent.
Improvised instrument played by blowing over the opening of a bottle.

Type of chordophone with strings and keys, superficially resembling a harpsichord, but functioning like a hurdy-gurdy. The strings are bowed, creating sustained tones, by means of a series of parchment-covered metal wheels that are brought in contact with the strings by pressing the keys. The wheels were powered either by a footpedal or a crank.
Musical instruments which produce audible sounds by acoustic methods and incorporate built-in microphones or pickups which amplify the vibrations.
Idiophones made to vibrate by friction.
Instruments whose sound is produced essentially by the vibration of thin lamellae or tongues of metal, wood, or other material.
Scraped idiophones consisting of a cog wheel which is either revolved by means of a handle against one or more wood or metal tongues, or twirled so that the tongues strike the cogs of the wheel.
Idiophones that vibrate when directly struck.
Concussion idiophones consisting of two or more objects in the form of sticks, plaques, troughs, or vessels of wood, bone, ivory, shell or other hard sonorous material, sounded by striking together.
Shaken idiophones made in a variety of forms worldwide, in which one or more objects strike against each other or against the inside or outside of another object.
Membranophones with a resonating cavity covered at one or both ends by a membrane, which is sounded by striking, rubbing, or plucking.
Brazilian friction drums, whose membrane is perforated by a stick which is rubbed with either the player's wetted hand or a damp cloth.
Tortoiseshell drums used by Aztecs.

Hourglass rattle drums of the Indian subcontinent, the Himalayas, and Mongolia, having a body usually made of wood or metal (in Tibet often of human skulls), with two thin skins wrapped around wooden hoops tightened by V-lacings and a central crosslacing. Two cords knotted at the ends or with pellets of wood, clay, or other hard material threaded on their ends, are attached to the central lacing; the knots or pellets strike the drum heads when the drum is twirled.
General term for keyboard instruments operated by the player’s hands and feet, in which pressurized air produces notes. Includes pipe organs, reed organs, and electronic organs.

String keyboard instrument mentioned in 14th to early 16th century texts. No accurate description exists of its construction but evidence suggests that it was a type of clavichord. It is said to have looked like an organ, but sounded by strings.The earliest known reference to it is from 1360, when Edward III of England presented one made by Jehan Perrot to John of France. References to the clavichord begin to appear around the middle of the 14th century; and as the harpsichord appeared only after 1390, it is assumed that use of the term 'chekker' indicated a struck string, rather than plucked string keyboard instrument, though documentation remains unclear.
Upright harpsichords having a vertical soundboard and a complicated action, often involving springs, in which the jacks move horizontally rather than vertically to pluck the strings.

Flemish virginals having their keyboard placed off-center to the right; consequently the strings are centrally plucked for most of the instruments' range, giving them a distinctive flutelike tone unlike that of any other type of virginal.
Loud pipe organs that were created to imitate the sound of a live band, including percussion instruments. Often used in the context of carousels and fairgrounds.
Automatic pipe organs imitating the sounds of the orchestra, employing organ pipes controlled by perforated cards, pinned cylinders, or paper rolls.
Portable reed organs consisting of an expandable bellows worked by the player's arm and a variable number of melody and bass keys.
Very small harmoniums in the shape of a large book.

Organ pipes with a flue or windway through which air is blown to issue in a flat sheet of wind striking the edge of the upper lip of the pipe mouth. The eddies of wind created at the mouth combine with the vibrating column of air in the pipe to create the tone.
Grand pianos of the smallest size.
Mechanical upright pianos devoid of a keyboard, operated by pinned cylinders set in motion by a crank, often mounted on wheels for playing in the streets.
Mechanical musical instruments in which tuned steel prongs are made to vibrate by contact with moving parts driven by a clockwork mechanism, the whole contained in a box.

Maori kinetic percussion instruments comprising light circular balls attached to a cord that is twirled with the twist of the wrists in combinations of movements, around and against the hands and body. The are used as visul and rhythmic accompaniments in Māori cultural song and dance performances.
Collections of drums or other percussion instruments, usually cymbals, arranged to be played by a single player.
A type of small kettle drum.
Snare drums carried by a person, for military or other marching purposes, usually held and played at the side of the player by a strap across the torso.
Double-headed drums from Provence in the form of a large tabor but with a long cylindrical body and a single snare on the upper head.
Single-headed open frame drums of the Yoruba of Nigeria, having an earthenware frame and either sticks or bamboo pegs for adjusting tension.

Double-headed hourglass pressure drums of the Yoruba people, held under the arm and beaten with a hooked stick. Use also for the sets of Yoruba hourglass pressure drums of which the dundun constitutes the largest member.
High-pitched kettle gongs of Java with a high central boss, played resting on crossed cords in a wooden box; they are played in sets in the Javanese gamelan.

Single-headed goblet drums of the Islamic Near East and North Africa, made of pottery, wood, or metal, with the bottom open. They are played with the fingers and palms of both hands, held under the arm or resting on the thigh.

Tubular drums with a constricted waist and lacings along its length which attach the drumheads to the body and control their tension. The player holds the drum under an armpit and presses it to affect the tuning.
Membranes stretched over the frames or shells of drums and sounded by being rubbed, plucked, or, most commonly, struck with the hands or beaters.

Children 's rattle also functioning as an amulet in the period between 14th and 19th century in Europe. Most tinkle bells are made of precious material with an object that offers protection and prosperity to the child. The tinkling bells usually featured jingle bells and the handle often incorporated a whistle. It was believed that the sounds warded off evil spirits.
Bells, especially those used in hotels and attached to signal boards, that ring when attendance is needed.

Small hand-held bells placed on or near the altar in a religious service or for a funerary altar. Altar bells may be attached to a wooden or other handle, or the handle may be cast as a piece with the bell. The device typically accommodates one or two small bells. An example of such devices is on Christian altars after the 8th century, but similar bells were known in ancient Babylonia, ancient Egypt, Jewish temples, the altars of the Romans and Greeks, and in cultures in Africa, China, and Hindustan.
Distinctive handbells or gongs, used as an instrument in Indian music and in Buddhist ritual. A ghanta may be paired with a vajra; use the more specific "vajras-ghantas."
Small pellet bells having a short, light ringing sound, or a succession of such sounds. For larger pellet bells making a louder sound, use "sleigh bells."

Small metal cymbals, attached in pairs to a hinged fork or forked sticks that can be tuned to a definite pitch. They were known in ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome and continue in use in present-day Myanmar (formerly Burma).

Large bronze gongs of Bali and Java, from about 34 to 40 inches in diameter, suspended by a rope from a wood frame and beaten softly and firmly on the central boss with a padded hammer to produce a low-pitched sound.

Cuban concussion idiophones consisting of two cylindrical hardwood sticks; one stick is held in one hand so that it crosses the cupped palm, which acts as a resonator, while the other stick, held in the other hand between the thumb and first two fingers, is used to strike the first.
Shaken instruments used for religious or ceremonial practices. Widely used across religious traditions; some examples include Native North American and African religious ceremonies.
Generic term for Brazilian shaken and struck rattles.
Gourd rattles of the Ewe of Ghana, made of a calabash covered with a mesh of string, beads, shells, and pieces of bamboo.
Japanese Buddhist wood slit drums, shaped like a stylized fish or pair of fish, struck to mark important points in temple services.
Stamping tubes made from gourds, played by the Ashanti women of Ghana.
Resonant wood blocks of Ethiopia.

Indonesian xylophones, consisting of from 16 to 21 wood or bamboo slabs laid stepwise in pitch order on a cloth over a carved wood trough and held in place by metal pins. They are played with two padded hammers.
Extensions of back legs which support the chair back.
Decorative, flattened, arrow-tipped spindles incorporated in the chair backs of Sheraton, American Federal, and some Windsor chairs.
Shaped extensions of backboards.
Decorative border of contrasting types of wood cut straight across the grain, generally used to finish edges and rims of furniture.
Posts at the foot of a bed.
Bedsprings that consist of spiral springs attached to a foundation and enclosed in a cloth-covered frame.
Portable inflatable bladders that are used as temporary bedding.
Folding testers, such as those found on a press bed.
Drawers with fronts that may be decorated but that feature no protruding hardware pulls.
Deep drawers often lined with lead that are designed to hold wine bottles. Often included in sideboards.
Drawers shaped as quarter circles that swing outward on a pivot when opened. These often contain divisions for the storage of small items such as bottles of ink.
Parts and components of furniture feet.
Ball feet with small collars at their bases.
Slender, outward-curving bracket feet.
Feet of slightly compressed spherical shape with vertical indented channels or crenellations.
A termination mainly used on cabriole legs in the first half of the 18th century (though earlier examples occur), representing a bird's or dragon's claw clutching a ball. Of Oriental derivation.
Claw and ball feet which have very sharp and thin claws.
Similar to club feet but resting on a disk.
Furniture feet in the shape of spinning tops.
Chair or table feet fashioned to resemble the paws, and often forelegs of dogs. These are represented in some of Duncan Phyfe's furniture of the 19th century.
Terminations on furniture legs having the form of a ball, which is a smooth, round object.
Triangular closed backs forming the hood or top to a tall piece of case furniture.
Vertical supports for a piece of furniture, typically used for longer supports of modified cylindrical, columnar, or pier-like form. For shorter vertical supports, use "feet (object components)."
Furniture legs comprising a molded shaft, square or lathe-turned, that resemble the form of a spindle or baluster.
Furniture support components that are designed to demount from the surface they are attached to, by unscrewing from fittings, or any other means.
Refers to hinged legs with a stretcher, which swing out to support the drop leaf of a table, such as found on gate-leg tables. For similar legs without a stretcher, use "swing legs."
Furniture leg components comprised of an inlaid or otherwise differentiated or decorated region appearing as a band or flange surrounding the leg a few inches above the floor.
Knees with carved ornament on cabriole chair legs.
Supports, usually of carved wood or scrolled wrought iron, used to support furniture legs, projecting windows, bays, bows, or other features.
The part of seating furniture on which one sits.

Chair seats that are rounded in the front and which sometimes have incurving sides, forming an outline like a horseshoe; most popular in America between the 1730s and 1760s, although in many areas persisting into the Federal period.
Chair seats shaped like the cup of a saddle with a slight center ridge at the front edge; most often used on Windsor chairs.
Frames intended to hold or encase seats.
Curved medial braces running from front to back of the seat frame.
Small slides above the slant top in desks to support candlesticks.

Figural decorative supports for various purposes that are in the stylized figure of a dolphin, originally developed in Hellenistic and Roman sculpture and revived as supports for furniture and decorative arts in later periods.

Supports of various design for the baptismal font, particularly for basin-style fonts. Examples include tabletop supports and metal supports mounted on a wall or other church architecture. For holders of baptismal fonts that rest on the floor, use "baptismal font stands."

Horizontal members connecting and supporting the legs of furniture in an X-form. This form is of Italian origin, often having a scrolled or serpentine figure with a finial in the center. Introduced into England toward the end of the 17th century.

In printing and print-making, the individual example produced by the printing of a block, plate, or type, etc., on a sheet of paper. Use when emphasizing the individual instance of printing. For printed images more generally, use "prints."

Prints in which the image has been printed onto a thin sheet of paper, such as China paper; the thin sheet is then backed by a thicker sheet of paper. These prints usually date from the 19th century. They were prized because thin China paper received the intaglio impression readily, and the product had a richer appearance than a standard print. Over time, the two types of papers age differently, and conservation problems may result.
Prints that are published to mark special occasions, often carrying inscriptions that name the event , the date, the participants, and typically depicting the event or a reference to the event.
Prints composed using only black and white, usually black ink on white paper. For black-and-white photographs, use "black-and-white prints (photographs)."
Refers to prints made by the process of crayon manner. Such prints imitate chalk drawings by means of the roulette.

Refers to prints made by combining carborundum with synthetic resin or varnish; this mixture is then hardened on a plastic or metal support and various heated tools are used to cut lines. This type of print was invented in the 1960s by the French artist Henri Goetz (1909-1989), who noticed that carborundum provided an ink-holding 'tooth.' Many corborundum prints resemble intaglio prints.
Prints made from an engraving in a copper plate.

Refers to modern prints produced by the carborundum mezzotint process, developed in the 20th century and by which mezzotint-like tone is achieved by roughening the surface of the plate with abrasives. Such prints will have the general quality of a mezzotint but will not show in the lighter areas the straight lines of the rocker's serrated edge.

Prints produced from designs created by the aquatint process, by which a printing plate is covered with a coating and etched with acid so as to create a range of tonal values, often combined with line work. The resulting print resembling a watercolor.
Aquatints made with a ground obtained by running a normally grounded plate through the press with fine sandpaper placed faced down on it.
Refers to lithographs made from aluminum plates; the term is not commonly used.
Color lithographs produced commercially in the latter half of the 19th century and later.
Chromolithographs printed with oil paint onto a textured surface and often coated with varnish; popular as inexpensive reproductions of oil paintings in the late 19th century.
Relief prints made by inking pieces of cardboard that have been attached to a base.
Prints made from plates with designs created by using dots from punches of various shapes and sometimes including burin lines.
Japanese prints on which the principal hand coloring was executed with beni, a red pigment.
Japanese prints in which colors, red (beni) and usually green, were printed rather than hand-colored.
Photomechanical prints, in color, and usually tinted relief halftones. Used in France in the late 19th century.

Color prints made using a combination printing process involving an intaglio, or occasionally lithographic, key plate which prints the image, after which color is superimposed on the print using wood blocks. The process was patented by an Englishman, George Baxter, in 1835, and was very popular up into the 1870s. The term is sometimes used to refer exclusively to prints made by Baxter himself; Baxter-process prints is a term used to describe prints of the same process made by other printers.

Instruments consisting of a flat brass bar with sights at the ends and a circular brass box in the middle, containing a magnetic needle, which plays over a graduated circle; the whole being supported on a staff or tripod.
Ancient Roman sideboards, generally having a tablelike lower member and an upper member with shelving; used to display highly prized ornaments.
Stands or racks for holding boots. Some include a drip tray for drying wet boots.
Kneehole writing or dressing tables.

Refers to English and European desks with a steeply sloping lid (usually a 45-degree angle) surmounted by a bookcase. For similar American examples use "desks and bookcases." The furniture type developed from the bureau. In the early 18th century one form of bureau comrpised drawers below a sloping writing flap, resting on cabriole legs. Many bureaus of this period and earlier were surmounted by a bookcase, often enclosed by glazed or unglazed doors. Dutch furniture makers developed the form, creating the "bureau-bookcase," which was often fitted with an ingenious combination of drawers and compartments. It became very popular, and spread to other parts of Europe.
Lady's writing desks fitted with an adjustable looking glass above.

Desks invented by William S. Wooton in 1875, manufactured by the Wooten Desk Company, and characterized by either a flat or slanted writing surface and a single or double pedestal base; the base contains a hinged or pivoted caselike section which, when opened, reveals dozens of slots, shelves, and pigeonholes.

In modern usage, generally refers to small, portable writing desks that first appeared in 16th-century Europe, and were extremely popular in France in the 18th century. They are generally characterized by having a nest of drawers enclosed in a box, often with a sloping front that is hinged along the bottom edge and may be let down to provide a writing platform. An escritoire was placed on top of a table or had its own legs. Formerly, these small portable desks were also called "secretaries"; however, in modern usage, the term "secretaries" typically refers to larger pieces meant to be placed against a wall.
Castilian name for small writing tables with hidden places for jewels and other valuables.
Bureaux plats with a set of drawers or pigeonholes along one side of the top.
Women's small writing tables with a cabinet at the back; often elaborately decorated and occasionally fitted for toilet purposes as well as writing.
French desks with a vertical fall front enclosing drawers and pigeonholes; usually with a cupboard below, but sometimes raised up on tall legs.

Refers to either a writing table incorporating drawers or a type of case furniture, generally a chest of drawers, with a hinged, fall-front writing surface. The first furniture types to be referred to by this term developed in France in the mid-17th century, the term having evolved from the medieval French word for a coarse linen cloth that was laid on a table to provide a surface for writing.  In modern usage, in Europe a "bureau" is a writing desk, usually with a hinged writing flap that rests at a sloping angle when closed and, when opened, reveals a tier of pigeonholes, small drawers, and sometimes a small cupboard.  In the United States, a "bureau" is typically synonymous with a "chest of drawers," having lost the surface for writing.

Tables supported by a fixed bracket (console) against a wall, or supported by a substructure consisting of two or more legs of console form. The term may be used for similar tables having other forms of supporting legs. May have marble tops and heavily carved substructures.
Console tables supported by an eagle bracket.
Adjustable tables, with ledges at the back and sides, used by persons in bed, usually for eating or writing. Also may refer to tables at the side of a bed.

Tables designed for a game similar to billiards called bagatelle. These tables have a semicircular area at one end in which there are nine numbered holes or cups, each number signifying the points to be scored by pocketing a ball. The table width is usually one-third of its length.
Small breakfast tables, made in early 19th century, intended to be used in ladies' boudoirs or morning rooms.
Tables intended for use in dining at special occasions; may be large and elaborate in design.
Extension dining tables invented during the Victorian period, which received their name from the slide action by which their length is varied.
Contemporary name for plain dressing or writing tables in the 18th century.

Men's or ladies' dressing boxes on a tall stand with a lid that opens to reveal a fitted interior, usually with drawers beneath. Unlike other dressing tables, it has taller legs and lacks a full case of drawers beneath.
Small Spanish tables, usually in a woman's room.
Fitted dressing tables. The most typical 18th-century form has three rising flaps, the center one being fitted with a mirror.

Gaming tables with tops marked as boards for playing backgammon. They may be similar to French "tric-trac tables," because the games are similar. Tric-trac was popular in France and elsewhere from 16th through 19th centuries. Both games could be played on either table. Backgammon tables tend to be of more recent origin.
Small card tables for playing bassette, a card game popular in Italy and France in the late 17th century and in England in the early 18th century.
Earlier iterations of ironing boards that existed in table form, originally patented in 1858. Improved design occurred in the 1890s.
Small plank top tables supported on a triangular frame with three legs.
Bedside table with a cabinet integrated beneath the table surface.
18th-century French term for any small, easily portable table.

Articles of dining-room furniture intended to dispense with the services of a waiter at table. It comprises an upright pole bearing one or more trays or shelves, sometimes revolving. On these are placed glasses, dishes, and other table requisites.
Spanish Renaissance trestle stands used to support vargueños; oblong pulls on each side of the stand support the drop-front of the cabinet.
Stands of various designs that rest on the floor or ground and support the baptismal font. For tabletop or wall-mounted supports for the baptismal font, use "baptismal font supports."
Stands or bookrests designed to hold a very large dictionary.
Refers to boxes or chests of pedestal form for the Koran; it can also refer to thrones or preachers' seats in a mosque as well as to large lecterns on which readers of the Koran sit.

French term of uncertain derivation denoting decorative candlestands; original type had a circular top and a central standard, often in the form of a Moor, or, as the taste for exoticism increased, of a negress or Indian. In Louis XV and Louis XVI periods guéridons became small movable tables.
Étagères and similar shelved stands intended to hold potted flowers, sometimes other small plants.

Small stands for washing, having a shelf or ring to hold the basin, and often shelves for a pitcher and chamber pot beneath. Drawers, towel bars, and ledges for soap and other toiltries may be included.
Basin stands designed to fit into the corner of a room.
Wash basin stands meant to be situated in spaces where walls meet, and that have closed, rather than open support structures, sometimes fitted with doors for storage.
Small movable tables sometimes with a porcelain or marble top.
Tea tables of various designs, having a raised edge or gallery to protect china against slipping off or other damage.
French 18th-century term for small tiered tables, usually of tripod form, with movable arms to support candlesticks; generally used by women both for work and for reading.
Small tables made of palm fronds.
Drop leaf tables having a pear-shaped surface, that when the leaf is dropped, resemble butterfly wings; named after a table first designed by Finn Juhl in 1949.

A more elaborate version of the Pembroke table, with a small nest of drawers which is concealed in the body and may be made to rise from the top by means of weights; of a type made in late 18th-century England.
Term used by Sheraton to describe a nest of four small tables.
Side tables of a size and design to stand in front of the pier or wall between two windows; sometimes surmounted by a pier glass.
Low tables or shelves meant to stand against a wall in the space between two windows, often surmounted with a mirror, and with a rail or shelf enclosing the surface.
Ancient Greek vessels used for cooling wine, having a body drawn in toward the base and set on a high pedestal or foot.
Furniture designed by architects or to match or accord with the architectural features of the rooms for which it is intended.
Variety of innovative furniture forms covered wholly or in part by a registered patent.
Furniture made up of modular units capable of use separately or in various combinations.
Precut furniture parts, made of wood generally used for crates, sold in kits to be assembled by the purchaser into tables, chairs, and bookcases at low cost. Designed by Gerrit Rietveld in 1934.
Furniture designed for use by children rather than for adults.
Ornamental extensions below the bottom edge of the seat of a chair, or frame of a table or cabinet.
Supports for the elbow and forearm used in seating furniture.
Chair arms having supports that sweep back in a curve between where they meet the seat and the arm rest.
Broad, flat arms on chairs intended to serve as a writing surface.
Refers to the upholstered elements of the arms of chairs. Arm pads may cover the entire arm or a small part. This term is also extended to the serpentine arms of Windsor chairs.

Form of late 19th-century commode chair, often associated with invalids, having a chamber pot concealed within a small cabinet under the seat; such cabinets usually have a door in the back so the chamber pot can be removed without disturbing the patient.
Desk chairs with deeply coved backs and usually, but not always, with a projecting central front leg; may have four or five legs. Very often carved.
Adjustable highchairs which may be converted into a carriage or walker.
Chairs used for wheeling the elderly and the infirm through large gardens.
Type of upholstered armchair intended to be used as reading chairs in 19th-century dormitories.

Chairs having a very low seat and a padded top rail, designed for female spectators of card games, who could kneel while resting their arms on the padded top rail. Males would sit astride a "voyeuse" with a somewhat higher seat, but it was considered inelegant for women to sit astride. For chairs having a very similar design but intended for prayer, use "prie-dieu chairs." Prie-dieu chairs may be made of humble materials, such as a wooden frame with a rattan seat-kneeler, or they may be upholstered; they may include a shelf for prayer books. If they are part of a set, it is usually a bedroom set. Voyeuses à genoux are always upholstered, and are generally part of a larger set along with voyeuses intended for males.
Type of elaborate wheelchairs, sometimes glassed, especially those made in England in the mid-19th century and used at spas and seaside resorts.
Chairs that are lightweight, portable, and can be folded flat for storage, typically made of wood, metal, or canvas.
Reclining chairs with a spring concealed under the seat which allows the chairs to recline and then snap into place; attributed to the American Chair Company, Troy, NY, about 1850.

19th-century American rocking chairs derived from Windsor chairs and having wooden seats that curve upwards to meet the spindles of the noticeably high, curved back with a scrolled top rail; usually grained or painted with fine ornamental detail.
Stools with the seat board hinged to the seat-rail in the form of a small lidded chest.
Box stools with a china bowl and cover. Use "commode chairs" for chairs having a chamber pot.
Footstools with a padded top which may be adjusted to support a gouty foot at the least uncomfortable angle. Made mainly in 18th-century England.
Stools for a pianist to sit on, usually adjustable and often with a space inside for storing music
Tabourets stools from the 18th-century, often lavishly carved and sometimes surrounded by a back on three sides so that they resembled the end of a miniature duchesse brisée.

Pliants having a back with finials, which were often hooked forward and made to resemble parakeets (thus the name). Came into fashion in France in the early 17th century; principally used at dining tables.
Long seats for two or more people, with or without a back, usually of wood, but also of stone, metal, or another material. A bench is distinguished from a stool by its greater length.
Seats for several people, having a storage chest below and a high back and arms. Examples include benches in the sacristy of a church.
Pews screened and enclosed by high backs and sides.
Settles with a box seat with a hinged lid which allows access to a storage space beneath.
Banquettes made to stand in the embrasure of a window.
Roman couches intended to seat two people.
Small sofas formed of two or three combined chair backs, with arms, backs, and legs similar to those of the open-back chairs of the particular period.

Sofas that are oval or round in form, with an upholstered pillar-like back located in the center of the seating area. Intended to stand in the center of the room, with seating around all sides of the sofa. The form developed in France.

Refers to S-shaped sofas with ends curving inward so two people could sit face to face. For straight-fronted sofas with small triangular seats (sometimes detachable) set outside the arms at either end, use "confidantes."
Large upholstered sofas, often convertible into beds.

Generally, the sleeping places of humans and animals. Specifically, permanent pieces of furniture comprised of a bedstead, which is the wooden or metal support, and the bedding, including the mattress and cover.
Beds with hexagonal or octagonal posts, usually thought to have been made prior to the American Revolution.
Portuguese tester beds with turned elements and carvings on the headboard; generally having turned posts and either a plain or pagoda-shaped tester. Of a type made in the 16th century.
Beds with ends of equal height and an upholstered back.

Magnificent state beds used in the ceremonial bedrooms of a noble or royal residence, coined in 18th-century French usage. Such beds were not intended to be used for routine sleeping, but for example, for the display of a royal newborn with his mother, of the sick or dying monarch, etc.
Beds for one person, especially a matching pair in a bedroom.
Any of various kinds of concealed or disguised beds first designed in the 18th century. Such beds were among the many ingenious forms of late 19th-century patent furniture.
Deception beds which fold into a dummy bookcase.

Folding beds built into cabinets that incorporate shelving for books on either side of a mid-section covered by double doors, and which were intended to be used in a dining room to make an occasional extra bedroom.
Cradles with two front wheels for transport.
Cribs, typically consisting of a cot or bassinet suspended from a upright member, designed to allow to swing back and forth as to rock a baby to sleep.

Distinctive chests, often portable, designed for the altar to be collapsible or otherwise fit into a chest, along with the other essential items required for the liturgy. The term may also apply to chests associated with a separate altar, whether or not they are portable or were intended to be hidden. Well-known examples of collapsible portable altar chests, intended to be hidden, were those used in northern Europe in the 17th-18th centuries, during times of prohibition of the celebration of Catholic Mass.
Fairly small bookcases, generally between three and four feet high, set on castors to facilitate their easy movement, of a style popular in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Case furniture consisting of a set of small drawers intended for the storage or display of objects.
Portuguese paneled cabinets on stands.
Tall, narrow, and deep cabinets intended to accommodate the elaborate bonnets peculiar to Normandy and Brittany in the 18th century.
Cabinets of drawers designed to store unbound maps, prints, posters, drawings, or any other large-format flat documents.
Cabinets with narrow shelves for holding piano rolls.

Relatively small cases of cabinet-work made to hold wine bottles. They may be lined with lead or another water-impervious material, in order to hold cold water or ice. For larger pieces of case furniture used to hold wine or other alcohol, prefer "cellaret sideboards."
Chests for the safe-keeping of valuables usually made of wood and sheathed in iron, of a type made in the ancient and Medieval periods.

Lidded boxes, often decorated, that were placed on the dressing table and contained pins, ribbons, feathers, and other adornments for dressing; they may also contain separate lidded cosmetic canisters. Often used for a lady's toilette, although men used them as well.
Cassoni that serve as wedding chests, often coming with the bride to her new home and decorated with images related to marriage and fertility.
Chests of drawers having a folding top which, when open, serves as a writing board; of a type made in 18th-century England.
19th-century term for heavy iron-bound coffers used for the storage of valuables; generally of German make and rarely dating from before the 17th century.

15th- and 16th-century brides' chests constructed in the Catalonia region of Spain. At one side of its face is a door which conceals a set of drawers to hold small articles. Both inner and outer sides of the lid are decorated.
Cupboard in which the archives are kept. An inscription sometimes indicates its function. The term is often used to refer to the archives of a church, confraternity, or a town.

Tall, three-storied cabinets consisting of a desk between two cupboards and typically decorated with inlay, built in Spain during the 17th century. The name refers to the spindled top story, which form a ventilated food cupboard for fruit, cheese, and bread.

Small pieces of storage furniture built into or hung on a wall near the main altar, in the baptistery, or in the sacristy to contain the holy oils. The door, which must be kept locked, sometimes bears the words "Olea Sancta."

Originally large closets or chests for storing arms, implements, or tools. Today refers to French-styled wardrobes for the storage of clothing or linens, with large doors opening to shelves, sometimes with drawers on the bottom of the piece, and short legs.

French case furniture consisting of two cupboards, set one above the other, each with two doors, the front and sides of the upper cupboard being recessed. They generally have an architectural framework with pilasters and a crowning pediment.

Eighteenth-century term for large chests or cupboards used to store clothes, often having sliding shelves behind closed doors. For large upright case pieces fitted with hooks, pegs, or rods to hang clothes, use "wardrobes (case furniture)."
Cupboards for storing clothes that are not as tall as standard clothes presses, often of shoulder height or shorter.
Small triangular cupboards made to fit into a corner; usually made in pairs, often to match a commode; often of ornamantal design.

Stamps that share the appearance of conventional postage stamps, including size, perforated edges, and in some cases imagery, but that are created and used by artists engaging in the practice of mail art.
Collocates tokens minted due to specific local needs by private parties, companies, or local governments otherwise barred from minting coinage.

Works that facilitate human activity and to provide for physical needs of people in or around a building generally by offering comfort, convenience, or protection. An example of usage is in distinguishing the architecture of a building from the furnishings that are placed in and around it.
Coverings laid under a table to catch crumbs and protect the carpet.

Candleholders, usually in a circular arrangement, designed to hold the four or five candles that are lit successively on the four Advent Sundays before Christmas, with the optional fifth candle lit on Christmas Eve. Advent candleholders may be decorative items in themselves, or concealed within an Advent wreath.

Candlelabra with three, five or seven candleholders on a slanting or semi-circular arm, mostly belonging to a set of two or three. Are usually set out for the midday Benediction (blessing) on Sundays.

Candlesticks designed to stand on an altar, especially as used on the altars of Christian churches. Use of candles in the context of Christian liturgies is first documented in the tenth century, when acolytes carried candlesticks to the altar, but placed them on the floor of the sanctuary or near the corners of the altar, as is still the custom in the Eastern Church. Candlesticks designed to be placed on the altar typically include five parts: the foot, the stem, the knob about the middle of the stem, the bowl to receive the drippings of wax, and the pricket on which the candle is fixed. Altars typically have two candlesticks, placed on either side of a crucifix. However, sets of altar candlesticks may comprise two, four, or six identically designed candlesticks.
Wall-mounted candelabra or other supports specifically for candles and intended to be mounted on a wall.
Ornate kerosene table lamps with a high stem dating to the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Betty lamps supported on a standard or tidy top; of a type attributed to the Ipswich region of Massachusetts.
Crusies incorporating two pans, the upper pan to hold the fuel and wick and the lower pan to serve as a drip catcher.

Spout lamps, usually made of sheet brass, having a cylindrical reservoir with a domed or conical cover and a single wick tube with a drip-catching channel immediately below, mounted on a standard with a weighted base. Of a type detailed in a painting of the Flemish school.
Lamps with a ring-shaped reservoir and central Argand burner or burners; the name was originally used for hanging lamps, thus the name astral from star.
Astral lamps with burners that have solar deflectors.
Kerosene lamps employing a central draft burner and an incandescent mantel. Based on a 1909 patent, they are usually made of metal or glass.
Describes lighting devices that can be manipulated to change the direction of light.
Hanging lamps that have a mechanism such as a chain and pulley by which they may be raised or lowered.

Beams of wood or iron between the chancel and the nave of a church upon which candles are placed, and on which the rood usually stands; the term also refers to any supports that resemble such beams in ecclesiastical settings; any T-shaped or horizontal beamlike or rail-like candle supports.
Troughs serving as a base and reflector for a fluorescent lighting unit.

Lamps equipped with containers for calcium carbide, a reservoir of water with a controlled drip, and a nozzle or burner for the combustion of the acetylene gas produced by bringing the water into contact with the calcium carbide; also lamps with acetylene burners connected to a central source of acetylene.
A German type of 12th-century hanging pottery oil lamp with a mouth or mouths for one or more wicks.

Electric lamps in which the current is made to traverse an air gap between two electrodes, usually of carbon. The air in the gap as well as the two electrodes become heated to a brilliant incandescence.

Illuminated sculptures, or lanterns, that are based on traditional Japanese lantern-making craft. Coined by Isamu Noguchi to describe the objects he designed and that are manufactured in Gifu, Japan, from paper made from mulberry tree bark; and that are considered to be a union of sculpture and functional object.
Brass or wrought iron pincers supported horizontally by a standard on a tripod, disc, or four-legged bases. The taper is coiled around the vertical shaft.

Lamps with single or multiple wick tubes mounted at the end of a pole for carrying in political parades and torchlight processions. The lamp fonts are often shaped like stars, eagles, top hats, or other political symbols.
Constructed objects that mimic the appearance of logs, used accessorize a fireplace.
Candles used during the Christian sacrament of baptism; in many customs, the candle is kept by the baptized person as a symbolic momento.

Fluorescent lamps, available in two types, with ultraviolet emitting phosphors. Used in the ultraviolet investigation of cultural materials, conservation, and in many scientific contexts. Filtered black light blue bulbs produce a dark violet glow with phosphors releasing near 404.7 nm; non-filtered black light bulbs emit a light blue light with phosphors releasing near 360 nm.
Any of various props or supporting devices used to keep books in an upright position.
Small 18th-century screens used to protect lighted candles.
Fire screens with a panel set between two standards or a frame, on four legs; distinguished from "pole screens" which have a tripod base and shaft which supports the fire screen.
Pivoting fire screens adjusted in position by a thumbscrew on a rod.
Seating furniture produced for use by one person.
Seats for one person with a back or a back and arms. Distinct from "stools" which have no back.
Term applied to a wide variety of chairs with arms, to distinguish them from side chairs which have no arms.

Armchairs developed in the mid-twentieth century, with foam rubber upholstery on the back and seat, and a characteristic "floating" seat which rests on only the two front legs and a crossbar running between the side slats. The design originated with Danish architect and furniture designer, Finn Juhl (1912-1989).

Term of convenience for a type of chair with a wide but not very deep seat, low back, and no arms, originating in England in Elizabethan times. Term may have been coined under the assumption that the chairs were designed to accommodate the wide, hooped dresses called farthingales.
Large, deep armchairs with sides and wings.
U-shaped armchairs, the upper rail of the back gently sloping down to the arms. Most popular during the Louis XV period.
Brass-studded prestige X-chairs of the Asante people of Africa, having arms, openwork backs, and legs that cross diagonally; the leg configuration is based on European folding chairs.
Chairs with open backs and usually horizontal splats with the top rail and uprights rounded to give an overall balloon shape to the back.
18th-century American turned baluster-back chairs whose crest rail has cutouts of these shapes; the period name for these chairs is not known.
French chairs with oval or medallion-shaped backs, the frames being carved in the center of the top with a ribbon bow.
Chairs or sofas of the Hepplewhite period whose back is comprised of carved or shaped veritcal bars curved to fit the shield of a shield-back chair.

Simple, wooden slat-back chairs with a seat usually of woven material, originating in Chiavari, Italy. Mass-produced chairs have been based on this design, including Gio Ponti's 'Superleggera' chair of the 1950s.

17th-century American turned great chairs styled after one that belonged to Elder William Brewster of Plymouth Colony. Such chairs have boldly turned posts and decorative spindles, but unlike Carver chairs they have spindles below the seat as well as in the back and below the arms.
Chairs having a back formed by slender members crossing over each other in a netlike pattern.

Chairs designed in Buenos Aires by Antonio Bonet, Juan Kurchan and Jorge Ferrari Hardoy, having steel frames and slinglike one-piece fabric or leather seats. Though commonly referred to as a butterfly chair because of the distinctive shape of its frame, the official name is the B.K.F. Chair, which credits its three designers. The lightweight and inexpensive chair became hugely popular in the U.S. from the 1950s, particularly on the West Coast, where it was frequently used as outdoor seating. The chair was produced by Artek-Pascoe from 1941 to 1948. Knoll Associates acquired U.S. rights to the design in the late 1940s. Unauthorized copies continue to be made.
Chairs used to seat the clients of a barber, specifically chairs fixed to the floor and incorporating a mechanical means of adjusting height, rotation, or angle of recline.

Thrones depicted in Buddhist art or used in Buddhism that are supported by lions or incorporating lions in the design; most often thrones upon which the Buddha is seated. An example is the seated Buddha in which eight lions positioned at the corners of the base or dais support his lotus throne; another example is the throne of the Dalai Lama of Tibet.
French chaise longues characterized by the foot end that is surrounded on three sides by a low curving back.

Tools, equipment, and supplies originally created to be used for hunting, target-shooting, warfare, or self-protection. This class includes firearms, artillery, bladed weapons, and striking weapons. It does not include structures designed for housing troops or supplies and objects designed for transporting troops or supplies.
Early cannons in use from the 14th to the 16th century, typically of large bore, made of wrought iron or cast bronze and firing stone cannonballs.
One of the common types of culverins in the 16th and 17th centuries, having a bore between 4 1/4 and 4 3/4 inches in diameter and firing balls of from 9 to 13 pounds in weight.
Artillery with rifle bore designed to have cross-country or road mobility for use in the battlefield.
Short squat guns or cannons used to test the strength of coarser blasting powders, used mainly 18th-19th centuries.

Small-calibre rifles used as ranging devices for other artillery pieces,  such as on artillery and antitank rocket launchers. If the spotting rifle manages to hit the target, it is assumed that the attached artillery or launcher will also.

Cutting weapons consisting basically of a relatively heavy, flat blade fixed to a handle, wielded by either striking or throwing. For axes used for other purposes, typically having narrower blades, use "axes (tools)."
Short, thick arrows fitted with flights and a head of any of various shapes, often square or blunt, designed to be shot by crossbows.
The pointed or edged heads of arrows.
Pollaxes with a very long, narrow, curved blade, elongated at the uppper end for thrusting, used primarily in northeastern Europe, particularly Russia.

Bayonets that are permanently attached to the firearm barrel, slid forward or unfolded for use by hand or some type of spring mechanism when needed, and retractable when not. They were widely used on pistols and blunderbusses in the 18th and 19th centuries and some 20th century and contemporary military rifles.
Bows, the shaft of which is composed of two or more organic materials, combined so as to enhance the elastic efficiency of each.

American weapons consisting of a band of metal, either with holes for four fingers or a single large opening to slip the main part of the hand into, leaving the thumb outside, used to increase the effect of a blow with the fist.

Javelins of the ancient Franks, Anglo-Saxons, and others, comprising a long spear with a double barb, one tongue of which is longer than the other and flame-shaped. The weapon is found primarily in grave goods of the wealthy, and is believed to have been rarely used on the battlefield.
Pikes with a long, spiked blade quadrangular in section and fitted with a disk at the base.
Heavy military swords with broad blades having a single cutting edge, a flattened back edge, and a well developed defense for the hand, usually a basket hilt or a shell guard.

Two-handed Scottish broadswords with a long, heavy double-edged blade, long diamond-section quillons angling toward the blade, and a tubular leather-covered hilt with a round pommel; they were used by Scottish Highlanders and mercenaries from the 15th to the 17th century. Use also for the one-handed Scottish broadswords with basket hilts in use in the British Army since the early 18th century.
Daggers worn in a sheath attached to the upper arm.
Stilettos having a scale for converting weight of shot into caliber engraved on the blade, issued to artillerymen in the 17th and 18th centuries for use as a weapon or tool, and as a symbol of rank.

Heavy swords of the 15th and 16th centuries, having a long rigid blade of square or triangular section, and originally a simple cross hilt with a relatively long grip, used primarily for thrusting. In the late 16th century the hilt acquired a more developed guard.

Short-bladed, slightly curved infantry sabers carried by the soldiers and officers of Napoleon's Imperial Guard. "Briquet" refers to a metal blade flint striker for lighting fires, which resembled this infantry short sword. The term for the sword was made official in an instruction of June 1806 by Napoleon's ministry of war. The two-foot blades were mostly used for utilitarian purposes, but could also inflict serious injuries during battle.
Sixteenth century two-handed swords with undulating blades resembling a flame and with a very long hilt. Used by the so-called Landsknechte, German mercenary soldiers.
General term for fighting swords carried by mounted knights attached to the belt, used for both cutting and thrusting.

African ceremonial swords of the Asante people, having a curved iron blade, broad at the point but gradually tapering towards the woden hilt which is sometimes encased in gold and consisting of two spheres at either end of a cylinder, worn or carried by Asante kings and major chiefs or their representatives.
Hunting swords having a long, straight, slender blade widening to a heavy point like a spearhead, often with a cross bar at the base to prevent the impaled prey from running up the blade.
Curving metal bands located one on each side of a sword hilt, between the quillons and the lower guard.
That part of a print-making device that transfers the medium to the substrate. Usually used to describe components of ink jet printers.

Relatively large firearms, generally having a bore of over one inch in diameter, designed to be supported on a gun mount or carriage when operated and requiring a crew of at least two people. Included are mounted guns, cannon, mortars, anti-aircraft weaponry, and other types of large-caliber firearms.

Short-barrelled shotguns with a wide bore expanding gradually throughout its length, typically terminating in a flared or thickened muzzle, and often carrying a spring-activated bayonet that folded back along the barrel when not in use. They were designed to fire a quantity of shot at once against a mass of opponents, and were popular weapons for defending stage coaches, ships, and prisons from the 17th to the 19th century.

Early firearms resembling small smoothbore cannons mounted on a wood stock or shaft, loaded at the muzzle and requiring to be primed and loaded for every shot; used in Europe in the 14th and 15th centuries.
Short firearms, either rifled or smoothbore, with the chamber made as an integral part of the barrel, designed for use with one hand.
Large pocket pistols.
Revolvers, generally breechloading, designed to fire cartridges.
Short, light smoothbore muskets with a large bore.

American-made muzzleloading flintlock rifles manufactured, mainly in Pennsylvania, from the Revolution to the late 19th century, characterized by a long octagonal barrel, maple stock, brass fittings, and ornamental openwork mounts.
