Heavy, long-range, muzzleloading rifles designed for use on the western frontier of the United States, approximately from 1800 to 1870. Typically they were unornamented, made with browned or dull metal that did not gleam in the light, and fitted with percussion locks and double-set triggers.
Firearm locks in which the entire mechanism is either set into the stock or contained within a metal boxlike frame, rather than mounted on external side plates.

Type of flintlock developed in Spain in the 17th century, involving an externally mounted heavy mainspring and cocking mechanism attached to the lock plate, which operates on the cock by pressing downward on its toe, or, more commonly, upward on its heel.

Matchlocks in which a cock or serpentine, holding the match, is held pressed into the pan of priming powder by a spring. When the firearm is cocked, the match is held up from the pan; when fired, it snaps rapidly down, igniting the powder.
Refers to firearms that hinge open at the barrel breech to allow ammunition to be loaded.
Guns designed for use in hunting.
Parts and components of edged weapons.

Traditional stone hand clubs used by the Mapuche, indigenous inhabitants of south-central Chile and southwestern Argentina; often resembling the form of a claw. They were ceremonial symbols of power; may have had a Polynesian connection.
A type of mace made of lead, sometimes with sharp pins on three sides, or having a trefoil shaped head.

Roman term for slings consisting of straps of flax, leather, or horsehair, in the middle of which was a pocket or pouch to hold the missile, used both for hunting and in warfare. They were used by Roman and allied troops in Republican and Imperial times at least into the 5th century and continued in military use in Europe into the 14th century and occasionally later.

Highly developed throwing-sticks of the Australian aborigines, known also in India, Africa, the Americas, and ancient Egypt, being basically curved or angular flat sticks designed so that they can be thrown so as to return to their starting point. They have been used in warfare, for hunting, and as recreational objects.
Objects that are used in the exchange of goods and services and in the settlement of debts, and typically assigned a specific value.

Coins of the ancient Western world from the 6th century BCE until the financial restructuring undertaken by the Franks and Arabs in the 7th and 8th centuries CE; includes Greece, Rome, and the Near East through the Sassanians.
Florentine gold coins struck from 1252 until the 16th century.
Islamic gold coins issued from the 7th to the 18th century; originally struck with legends on both sides and in the same size and weight as Byzantine solidi.

Use specifically for the United States, silver, dollar coins issued between 1873 and 1878 expressly for use in trade with Asian countries, and generally for other dollar-sized and -valued coins used for economic purposes beyond the national boundaries of the country of origin.

Coins that honor people, places, events, or institutions. These coins may be legal tender, but are generally not minted for circulation and are typically produced in limited quantity and are made available for a limited time. Distinguished from medals as coins have a stated face value.
Coins or paper money in denominations less than the basic monetary unit.

Drawings or works in another two-dimensional medium in which two or more related images (e.g., different views of the same structure, or a figure in various poses) are displayed together or fused into one. In disciplines outside architecture, the term refers to any image compiled from multiple parts, including faces constructed for forensic identification, maps, geographic diagrams, or images of planets created from telescopic imagery.
Refers to drawings, or works in another medium, in oblique projection in which the vertical plane is parallel to the plane of projection (drawing surface).
Drawings in oblique projection in which a vertical plane is parallel to the plane of projection (drawing surface), and receding planes are drawn at half the scale of that vertical plane.
Refers to orthographic drawings or works in another medium projected at an angle other than the usual plan, section, or elevation, in order to show true shape of an oblique plane.

Refers to drawings, or works in another medium, created using dimetric projection, which is a projection in which all three spatial axes are inclined to the plane of projection or drawing surface, and two of the axes are equally inclined to the picture plane.
Renderings made in projection on a vertical plane of the finished appearance of the exterior walls of structures.
Two-dimensional graphic renderings that represent half of the exterior façade of a symmetrical structure.
Orthographic plans portraying buildings, topography, plantings, roads, and other features of an area.

Drawings or works in another medium laying out the precise arrangement of a structure on a plot of land. It may also refer to plans for gardens, groups of buildings, or developments, where the layout of buildings, roadways, utilities, landscape elements, topography, water features, and vegetation may be depicted. For drawings or other representations on a horizontal surface of cities or larger areas, particularly when such representations are not part of a design process, use "plans (maps)."
Small-scale, simplified plans of a building or building site, with features or structures indicated by simple outlines or shapes.
Refers to plans indicating the layout of trees, shrubs, and other plants on a building site or for garden or landscape design.

Drawings or works in another two-dimensional medium that represent a horizontal section through a building taken above a floor to diagramatically illustrate the enclosing walls, interior spaces, doors, and windows of a building.
Floor plans taken near ground level and showing the foundation and ground floor of the building.
Scaled floor plans showing electrical layout; may include an adjacent small drawing of an elevation, or a riser diagram. For other drawings of electrical systems, use "electrical drawings."

Refers to plans representing the layout and configuration of heating facilities in a structure. They typically include the position of boilers, radiators, or other heating sources, pipes, air conduits, and the number of rooms and desired temperatures. They may include specialized symbols and conventions, such as the flow of steam or heated air depicted in red, and the return in blue.

Orthographic drawings of the exterior of a structure or object with a small portion removed to show an interior detail. When a more substantial portion is removed, use "half sections" or "sectional elevations."
Drawings of a full longitudinal section of a ship, showing internal arrangement.
Oblique sections that are intended to show true shape of an oblique plane in the structure or object.
Vertical sections of soil showing the nature and sequence of the various layers, as developed by deposition, weathering, or both.
Architectural drawings that render the exteriors of structures and give the impression of relative position, size, or distance, as the structure would if viewed from a physical vantage point.
Genre of architectural drawings, prints, or designs in other media that suggest an unlikely or impossible arrangement and projected environment that is surprising to the viewer.
Drawings required to be sent yearly from Rome to the Académie des Beaux-Arts in Paris by winners of the Prix de Rome.
Drawings preliminary to other works of art that are actually incorporated into those works.
Refers to cartoons that depict small portions of a design or other details related to the main cartoon.

Refers to drawings, generally for engineering or construction, that depict how parts are positioned relative to one another in a design or plan. They may also depict how the parts are fixed in place and how depicted mechanisms should operate.
Refers to assembly drawings that depict the complete layout of equipment. They are distinct from subassembly drawings, which show only a detail of a certain area or component.
Graphic interpretations of the drawings or other contractual documents issued by the architect.
Detail drawings made by an architectural office for reuse on more than one project.
Shop drawings depicting components and relative positions, for process of erection of a structure.
Refers to drawings of HVAC systems, which are systems for heating, ventilation, and air conditioning. For scaled floor plans use "HVAC plans" or a more specific term, such as "plumbing plans."

Animated films, tapes, or sheets comprising a series of drawings that show successive phases of an action in order to produce the illusion of movement. The drawings are typically photographed on film or drawn directly on film and projected, or manually flipped as a series of pages, with the effect of simulating movement of the objects and figures depicted in the drawings.
Drawings at the same size as the object.

Drawings of architecture and drawings for architectural projects, whether the project was executed or not. The term may also refer to any image in a two-dimensional medium that serves this same purpose, including prints and computer images.
Computer generated renderings of architectural structures that give the viewer the sensation of walking through a structure.
Metal ties or plates used to fasten together timbers or masonry.
Very small nails having a small, flat head; usually used for trim or fine finishing work.
Flat-sided nails for fastening horseshoes to the horse’s hoof, and having an extended head to allow traction in the snow and ice.
Rose headed nails made of a soft material that allows for clinching, which is bending or beating back the tip after being driven through a surface.
Tapered wooden pins or pegs that are fixed through both components of a mortise and tenon joint to lock and tighten the join.
Cloak pins used to fasten customary Maori cloaks over the shoulder; made from marine mamal ivory, and later boar tusks.
Nails having slender shanks and large, round, often decorative, heads, used to anchor upholstery and stuffing to the wooden frame of upholstered furniture.
Flat-headed tacks used especially to fasten down carpets.
Implements or mechanisms used for defense or attack in combat, hunting, or war.

Armor pieces used in jousts in the 15th and 16th centuries, consisting of large metal plates, either shield-shaped or thigh-shaped, hung one on either side of the saddle or strapped to each of the combatant's thighs, to protect the thighs and knees.

Laminated cuirasses first appearing in Italy in the first quarter of the 16th century, built up of horizontal overlapping lames joined by leather straps and sliding rivets on the inner side. They went out of fashion in western Europe by the end of the 16th century, but continued to be popular throughout the 17th century in eastern Europe, particularly in Hungary and Poland where they were used by heavy cavalry.

Specialized type of mitten gauntlet, in which the end finger lame was extended so that, when the hand was closed, it could be fastened to the cuff, thus locking the hand in its grip on a weapon; they were popular in the 16th century as double pieces for foot-combat armor.
Greaves consisting of front and back pieces, hinged together to enclose the lower leg.

Casques intended for the protection of those flying aircraft. These were initially made of leather, were fitted to the head and had earflaps that were connected via a chin strap. Some were lined with fleecy material. More historically recent models are made from a variety of materials including fiberglass and plastic, and are more typically formed into a round dome encasing the entire head of the wearer.

Heavy basnets having a hinged visor with an eye slit, a long neck guard overlapping the top of the backplate and a wide bevor, so that the weight was borne on the shoulders rather than the head. They were in use from the late 14th to the early 16th century, becoming particularly heavy and long in the late 15th century.

Helmets which are a cross between burgonets and close helmets; they are constructed like close helmets but, like burgonets, have a peak, cheekpieces, and a falling buffe instead of a visor and upper bevor.

Low-skulled helmets that curve up and out at the top to form a flattened point along the line of sight, forming a thin gap between bevor and skull which served as an eye slit. Examples date from   the late 14th to the 16th century, used in jousts rather than battle.

Deep, one-piece sallets with a vision slit cut into them, sometimes furnished with a reinforced brow and a roller on their lower front edge, designed especially for the Rennen, the German style of joust.
Use only in the United Kingdom for visors on caps and various types of military headgear, other than armored helmets.
Gutterlike pauldrons used from the mid-14th century, consisting of a series of articulated semicircular lames protecting the point of the shoulder and upper arm.
Sabatons with broad, blunt toe caps, popular in the mid-16th century.

Hard leather shields used by light calvary and designed specifically for riding riding with a short stirrup with knees bent. They were originally of a round or heart shape, then generally created in the shape of a pair of overlapping ellipses or ovals. They were originally used by the Moors, then by Spain; the form came to North America when Cortés entered Mexico in the early 16th century.
Complete sets of horse armor.
Shaffrons covering only the upper part of the horse's head, popular in Europe during the mid-16th century.
Spurs attached without straps to the heels of boots by means of an integral catch in the heel.
Horizontal inscribed tablets hung in halls or pavilions, often bearing the name of the structure or room, or a poetic verse.
Locks used principally to lock sliding cabinet doors by means of a pin extended into locked position by pushing; they are unlocked by inserting a key and pulling.
Pear-shaped pendants installed as handles or pulls on doors or cabinetry.
Devices consisting of wheels mounted to heavy doors that roll on a track or rail either above or below the door itself, designed for doors of large size and weight.
Devices mounted at the tops of doors and to door frames that allow for the door to be held open at any desired angle.

Metal plates which protect the lower part of a door from kicks and scratches; similar to kickplates but covering the door to a greater height, usually 39 inches (1 meter) or more from the bottom of the door.
Modified form of barrel bolts, in which the locking bar is shortened.
Vertically mounted bolts on the bottom of a door which slide into a socket in the floor.
Fasteners attached to an outside wall for securing a shutter, blind, or door in an open position.
Magnetic catches with an inward and outward moving strike that retract and project by means of springs on successive applications of pressure.
Butt hinges having ball bearings positioned between the knuckles to reduce friction.
Pintle-type hinges having extended pins that it can be fastened to the casing of a door.
Double-acting hinges equipped with a spring to bring the door back in line with the frame.
Door latching devices used where one side of double doors needs to be secured at top and bottom, or where a single door is attached to a panic bolt.
Heavy latches for large doors having plate-mounted pivoting bars that cross the joint of the door to engage with a strike on the jamb or opposing door.
Locks that combine heavy deadbolts with latch bolts operated by thumb handles instead of knobs.

Fastenings for French doors or casement windows that consist of sliding rods that engage with strikes or plates at the top or bottom of the frame of the portal. The rod is controlled by a handle that retracts the upper and lower parts of the bolt from the frame.
Spring bolts or magnetic latches, usually found on cabinets.
Cylinder-type locks with independent pin tumblers, both controlling the same bolt, and operated with dual keys, one a master key designed to control a set of such locks.
Mortise locks in which the cylinder is contained in the knob.
Devices permanently secured to the hasp on a door which causes the hasp to be locked as soon as the door is closed; often used in prisons.
Mortise locks each having a front turned into two perpendicular planes, used on a door with a rabbeted edge.
Surface-mounted locks in addition to the main lock on a door.
Automatic locks actuated by the closing of the door; also, time locks working on the same principle.
An electrode which has a high degree of selectivity for one ion over others present in a sample.
Metal chains used in place of sash cords to connect a vertically hung sash with its counterweight.
Window locks that require special keys or tools to open, ensuring that the windows they are mounted on stay closed until they need to be cleaned, or for any other purpose.
Hinges containing a spring for closing a compression chamber in which the liquid escapes slowly, thus retarding the closing action to prevent slamming of the door.
Hinges designed to show only the knuckle, which is shaped like an olive, when the door is closed.
Surface-mounted hinges with one leaf or both leaves elongated to accommodate additional fasteners.
Fixtures designed for hanging towels or robes in a bathroom.
Covers, often decorative and metal, that attach to the leg or frame of a piece of wooden furniture so as to hide the hole into which a bed bolt has been inserted.
Strikes with enclosed recesses to receive lock bolts.
Ornamental straps fastened to the surface of a door to render the appearance of a strap hinge.
The protruding parts of latches or locks that prevent a door from opening.
Lock hubs designed to compensate for shrinkage or swelling in a door, and subsequently to prevent the disengagement of the lock.

Machine screws that are permanently combined with a lock washer which was inserted before the thread was cut. The term probably derives from an abbreviation for “assemblies,” because the screw and washer are pre-assembled when purchased.
Screws, used for alignment of an object, that are often coupled with a locking nut to secure them in position.
Key with teeth that lifts the levers or catches in a lever tumbler lock to free the bolt to move.
Round keys with hollow barrels made to fit over drill pin components generally found in cabinet locks.
Plates that serve as mounts for knobs or pulls and intervene between them and the cabinetry to which they are attached.
Joints between two consecutive pours of concrete if the time elapsed between the first and second pours is such that the first pour has started to harden.
Joints formed where the full thickness of one member's edge or end is accepted into a corresponding housing, groove, or dado in another member.
Paintings that are applied directly to the ceiling of a chamber or hall.

Small paintings, generally smaller than two feet in any dimension, originally intended to be hung in small rooms or "gabinetti" of collectors. Typically dating to the 16th century and later; the support may be panel, ivory, metal, or canvas. The subjects depicted are of small scale, intended for viewing at close range.

Collective term for large scale Japanese paintings pasted to wall surfaces of one sort or another, such as fusuma (sliding door panels); typically treating landscape, figural or bird-and-flower themes. It is often translated as "screen and wall paintings."

Small painted wooden panels (and later, canvases) created as the covers for official documents of the Biccherna, the finance ministry of Siena between the thirteenth and eighteenth centuries. At some point in their history, the covers, which typically portrayed scenes of office life, were detached from their documents and treated as paintings which were hung on the office walls. Only 136 of these painted covers have been preserved.
Narrow lateral paintings often extending over many feet and viewed section by section; these are especially significant in Asian art.

Ancient Greek visual works comprising pottery objects on which black decoration appears silhouetted on a red ground. Details were incised into the black figures or applied in purple or white pigment. The works gave way to red-figure vase paintings. Works appeared by 720 BCE in Corinth.
Creative works in the medium of acrylic paint.
Paintings executed in oil paint that were intended as preparatory studies of a more finished, usually larger, painting.
In Indian art and culture, an image subject to worship.

Prints, photographs, or drawings that have been decorated or enhanced by affixing cut-outs of fabric or paper, using watercolor, or other adornments. Creating such works became a popular hobby in the 19th century.

Refers to combinations of photographic images, or photographic with other images, such as architectural drawings, usually arranged into a somewhat unified image. For photographs produced by printing two or more negatives as one unified image, use "composite photographs." When pieces of photographs or other relatively flat materials are pasted together into less unified images, use "collages."
Atlases that includes historical maps and charts depicting the evolving geopolitical landscape, as well ast he scope and scale of historical events and subjects.

Refers to globes that depict the celestial sphere, which is a representation of the heavens in which the stars, constellations, and planets are depicted as if the sky visible from Earth were a ball. They were used for astronomical or astrological calculations or as ornaments. They have been known since the time of the ancient Greeks. The globes are intended to depict the heavens, generally the night sky, that to an observer on Earth appears as a hemisphere resting on the horizon. The eastward rotation of the Earth on its axis produces an apparent diurnal westward rotation of the starry sphere, and the stars seem to rotate around a northern or southern celestial pole. For representations of the celestial sphere projected onto a flat plane, use "planispheres."

Skeleton models of the celestial sphere, generally having the earth at the center, consisting of a framework of rings depicting the relative position of such astronomical elements as the celestial equator, the ecliptic, the zodiac, and the planets. They were first developed by the ancient Greeks and used especially during the 14th through 16th centuries as an aid to navigation.
Globes that illustrate geographical features through the use of modeling on their surfaces.

Maps having decorative panels of views, monuments, costumed figures, or other illustrations that surround the actual cartographic representation. Illustrations were often arranged around the borders, particularly in early examples from the 16th and 17th centuries.
Maps showing boundaries of subdivisions of land, buildings, or other details for purposes of describing and recording ownership.

Refers to images depicted on a flat surface, but representing the celestial sphere, which is the stars and constellations as they are located on the apparent hollow sphere of the sky as seen from the surface of the Earth. They appeared in Europe around 1515, though simple depictions of constellations had been known since the time of ancient Egypt. They are a narrower concept to "astronomical charts" because "planispheres" are specifically early depictions of the heavens on a flat surface, where the concept being depicted is of a sphere projected on a flat plane; "astronomical charts" may refer to charts from a much wider historical range, and do not necessarily refer only to charts where the heavens were conceptually considered to exist on or in a sphere. For representations of the heavens actually depicted on a sphere, as opposed to being projected on a flat plane, use "celestial globes."

Maps of hydrographic data that may include data on coastal intertidal and shallow water zones, vegetation, contours, land use, drainage, shoreline, wetlands, or other features. These may be rendered in digital or printed form.
Geological maps which map mineral deposits and underground mines.
Maps that outline or define the drainage systems or area of a region.

Maps that depict the relief and other features of a battlefield, generally including representations of the disposition and movement of troops. It may also include references to military strategies and tactics.
Refers to maps that focus on the population patterns as described by a census, which is an official enumeration of the population of a country or district.
Maps that indicate the locations of telecommunications, power, or other types of cable that are routed underground, and act as a guide for workers that are digging into the earth.
Maps that illustrate the routes taken by buses, usually for an urban area.
Maps designed primarily for use in air navigation, giving surface features of aeronautical importance.
Maps, often global in scope, that depict airline routes, destinations and connections.
Nautical charts issued by the United Kingdom Hydrographic Office and subject to Crown Copyright.
Charts depicting accurate, measurable features of underwater terrain.
Simple maps used in cartography to show the location of a particular geographic area within its larger context.
Outline maps showing the important natural and man-made features of an area, to which specific information may be added for any of various purposes.
Maps made from an assembly of perspective photographs in which tilt and relief have been removed.

Maps showing elevation and the configuration of the ground by the use of contour lines and usually lacking other detail. For maps that use lines to show the distribution of characteristics other than elevation, use "isoline maps."
Maps of a particular region or area which maybe be defined by states, zip code, sales territories, natural landforms, demographics or any other natural, statistical or subjective criteria.
Maps created or presented by means of a computer or computer systems.
Refers to maps that are stored in digital form, which is data recorded by digits or similar discrete elements compatible with storage and manipulation in a computer.
General term for visual works produced by any number of reproduction methods, for use in construction, engineering, and other fields.
Prints made on light-sensitized surfaces that produce black lines on neutral backgrounds.

Digital databases of bibliographic records that form an organized collection of references to published literature such as journal and newspaper articles, conference proceedings, reports, government and legal publications, patents, books, etc. Records in bibliographic databases often contain abstracts, keywords, and subject classification terms.
Thin, round, flexible disks with magnetic surfaces for storing and retrieving data.
Magnetic tapes on which sound is recorded digitally.

Instruction sets or programs that are stored in ROM or programmable modules in devices such mobile phones, digital cameras, remote controls, or electronic musical instruments to control their functions.
Documents written in, and usually signed with, the writer's own hand; in certain legal instances, prefer "holographs."
Documents wholly written in the hand of the author; used especially in law with regard to wills and deeds.
Computer output produced directly onto microform, without paper printout as an intermediary.
Cards with one or more openings into each of which is mounted a frame cut from a strip of microfilm.
Segments of microfilm that are usually inserted into microfilm jackets.
Computer output produced directly onto microfiche, without paper printout as an intermediary.

In Ethiopian culture, parchment scrolls upon which various taslismanic images and texts, often prayers, are inscribed, generally by clerics in complex rituals. Their purpose is in healing ceremonies. Sick people focus on the scroll, and enter into a healing trance by which they are cured; they may wear the scrolls for a time. The images that appear on the scrolls range from Jewish, Christian, and Islamic religious symbols, the story of King Solomon, lions, birds, and abstract talismanic patterns to the most frequently depicted symbols, large, colorfully-rendered eyes.
Sound recordings on magnetic tape.
Phonograph records, invented by the RCA company in the mid-20th century, which eventually replaced 78-rpm records in terms of production and popularity.

Cartridge-based 1/4-inch analog audiotape format. The 8-track cartridge is a magnetic tape-based recorded sound format that was used exclusively for commercial releases. The tape is composed of magnetic particles or pigment, binder, and a polyester base. It was a popular format from the mid-1960s through the early 1980s.
Very small audiocassettes roughly a quarter of the size of a standard audiocassette. For audiocassettes of comparable size, but that lack a capstan drive system, use 'minicassettes.'
Compact discs on which a large amount of digitized read-only data can be stored.

Optical disks on which still images, moving images or sound are recorded in an analog format. The images can be displayed on a video monitor, such as a television attached to a videodisc player, which may be controlled by a computer. Prior to the introduction of compact disks, which also use a laser to read the data, videodiscs were sometimes referred to as "laser disks." For the digital versatile disc format specifically, use "DVDs."
Storage media intended for video recordings that are wound and played back from open reels or spools.
Consumer-level analog videocassette magnetic tape recording format developed by Sony, released in 1975.
Inscriptions that are written vertically rather than horizontally.
Personal objects, usually worn or carried, that express an individual's thoughts, opinions, convictions, allegiances, interests, or attitudes.
A script of ancient Egypt, derived from hieratic and used from about 700 BCE to 500 CE.
The identifying mark of an order or congregation, usually worn on special occasions such as a patron's day.

Small engraved or printed labels, usually found on the upper outside corner of one of the front flyleaves, giving the name and usually the address of the bookbinder; common in the 18th and early 19th centuries.
Bookplates displaying coats of arms or other armorial devices as a mark of ownership.
A watermark placed in the corner of a sheet of paper.
Marks stamped on bottles by the manufacturer.

Defacements made by authorities for the primary purpose of preventing reuse of postage stamps; for official marks bearing information about the time and place that a postal system accepted custody of a piece of mail, use "postmarks."
The letter of the alphabet stamped on silver to indicate the year in which it was made or assayed, especially in England.
Marks on objects idicating the country in which it was manufactured, typically to determine the rate of duty.

Refers to zigzag or wriggled grooves found on the underside of silver pieces (Continental or Scottish but rarely English) formed when samples of the metal were taken for assaying. The marks often resemble the letter N or Z but no significance can be attached to their form.
Shapes made of fabric or paper, in modern times often tissue paper, used as guides to cut out sections of fabric that can be stitched together into finished works.
Small pieces of material such as textile, leather, or paper, either individual pieces or groups of them bound together, especially when issued by a single manufacturer.

Seals with which papal and royal documents were authenticated from the early Middle Ages. Examples include the round leaden seals used on particular documents originating from the pope, namely those with the superscription of the pope "episcopus, servus servorum Dei."
Formal instruments attesting to the transfer of ownership of personal property.
Written demands that something be furnished; also demands or applications made, usually with authority, as a demand made by military authorities upon civilians for supplies.
Detachable portions of tickets returned to the user as proof of purchase.
Lists or invoices of cargo on a ship, usually containing marks or indication of contents or commodity, consignee, and other pertinent information for use at terminals or customhouses.
Official records or accounts related to a legal declaration of insolvency, accompanied by abstracts or reports of papers presented.

Papers filed in a court of bankruptcy by a debtor seeking the benefits of the bankruptcy act, or by creditors alleging the commission of an act of bankruptcy by their debtor and seeking an adjudication of bankruptcy against the debtor.

Bonds executed by defendants or those legally liable for debt, that state defendants will appear in court when required and that in the event defendants fail to appear, the signers of the bonds will pay to the court the amount of money specified.
Performance or surety bonds furnished by a subcontractor to a prime contractor as guarantee of payment and delivery for all associated equipment, labor, and materials for a specific contract.
Charters by which all or part of a ship is leased for a specific voyage or period of time.
Written and signed legal documents authorizing a change from the original plans, specifications, or other contract documents, or authorizing a change in the cost of the project.
Bargaining agreements as to wages and conditions of work entered into by groups of employees, usually organized into a union on one side and one or more employers or corporations on the other side.
Contracts in which the work of the job is divided into several prime contracts, such as general, mechanical, and electrical, rather than awarded to one contractor.

Standard forms of agreement, often enforceable by law, between architects and independent contractors hired to complete a project. These contracts specify the terms and conditions of the agreement, in addition to duties, responsibilities, and liabilities.
Agreements or contracts under which the contractor or the architect is reimbursed for the direct and indirect costs of performance of the agreement and in addition is paid a fee for services.
Specifications listing or describing only the materials, equipment, and methods of construction upon which a base bid must be predicated, exclusive of any alternate bids.
Written agreements between masters and minors under which a minor agrees to work for a master for a stated period of time in return for instruction in a trade by a master.
Records generated by a commercial or industrial enterprise.
Administrative and operational records of offices of upper level government officials, including presidents, premiers, senators, congressmen, ministers, deputy ministers, etc.
Executive records or documents related to the judicial process.
Parchment rolls upon which charters were enrolled at the chancery.

Records tracking the goods passing through and fees collected at customs, which is the area at a seaport, airport, etc., where goods, luggage, and other incoming items are examined and customs duties levied.
Warrants conferring authority to raise and command a body of troops; certificates conferring military or naval rank and authority on officers of certain rank.

In the United States, patents granted for the ornamental design, configuration or shape, and surface ornamentation of a functional item, such as furniture, appliances, containers, tools, computer icons, etc. (but not including fine art).

Permits required by local governmental bodies for new building, or for major alteration or expansion of existing structures. Applications, building plans, estimated costs, and a fee are usually required before a permit is issued.

Regulations issued by a governmental agency, having the force of law, to interpret or implement the provisions of a statute. For acts of a legislature declaring, commanding, or prohibiting something, and that constitute the law, use "statutes."

Laws, ordinances, or government regulations concerning fitness for habitation setting forth standards and requirements for the construction, maintenance, operation, occupancy, use, or appearance of buildings, premises, and dwelling units.
Court records limited to the daily court proceedings of a given court.
Testimonies of witnesses, under oath or affirmation, before a person empowered to administer oaths.
Documents that are a product of courts dealing with civil, rather than criminal cases.
Records generated by probate courts, which have general powers over the probate of wills, administration of estates, and, in some states, over the appointment of guardians or the adoption of minors.

Documents generated, collected, or maintained by the executor of an estate. These generally include correspondence, memos, estate and income tax returns, probate court paperwork, insurance policies, records of debt and claims against the estate, and papers related to all assets.

Lists, catalogs, accounts, or schedules, made by an estate executor or administrator of the tangible and intangible property of the estate, describing the items or classes of property so as to be identifiable and usually placing a value on each.
Lists, catalogs, accounts, or schedules, made by an estate executor, describing items of property as they appear in a particular physical environment, so as to be identifiable.
Drafts of proposed laws introduced in a legislative body.

Acts of a legislature declaring, commanding, or prohibiting something, expressed according to the forms necessary to constitute law. For regulations having the force of law issued by a government agency in order to interpret or implement the provisions of a statute, use "administrative regulations."
Statutes or regulations, especially as enacted by local government.
Ordinances that establish the permitted uses of the land in a particular district or zone and dictate such things as lot sizes and building placements.
Documents recording the procedures of the House of Representatives and the Senate of the United States.
Documents of deliberations and decisions of meetings of the United States Congress that are charged with a specific duty, rather than the general duties of Congress.

Documents accompanying measures reported from a committee of the United States Congress. These contain explanations of the provisions of the measure, arguments for its approval, votes held in markup, individual committee members’ opinions, cost estimates, and other information.
Collected documents on policy making, correspondence, investigation and reporting related to legislation, or the political environment of the House of Commons.
Texts of legislative initiatives that a Minister of the Crown submits to Parliament to be approved, and possibly amended, before becoming law.
Private bills brought from the House of Lords to the House of Commons.
Documents created by county governments including records such as bonds, census reports, court records, land records, estates, marriage records, tax records, wills, etc.

Books, papers, maps, photographs, machine-readable materials, or other documentary materials, regardless of physical form or characteristics, made or received by an agency of a federal government in connection with the transaction of public business and preserved or appropriate for preservation by that agency or its legitimate successor as evidence of the organization, functions, policies, decisions, procedures, operations, or other activities of the government, or because of the informational value of the data in them.

Agreements or contracts made between two or more states, formally signed by duly authorized representatives, and usually ratified by the lawmaking authority of the states, as treaties of peace or alliance, or commercial treaties.
Records pertaining to an exhibition of art or other cultural objects.

Certificates that record the administration of the sacrament of baptism for an individual. Where the custom is to baptize infants, in documenting biographies, baptismal certificates are often substituted for birth records that are nonexistent or unobtainable.

Records of the expenditures and activities of the churchwarden, a lay honorary officer of a parish church who manages secular affairs, particularly those relating to the church building and other property.
Lists of the real estate and belongings of a parish, including chalices, patens, altarpieces, crucifixes, other liturgical equipment, vestments, candles and wax, hymnals, etc.
Regular courses of study or training, particularly at a school or university.

Written treatises, or the records of a discourse on a subject, usually prepared and presented as the final requirement for a degree or diploma and typically based on independent research and giving evidence of the candidate's mastery of the subject and of scholarly method.

Written treatises presenting the author’s scholarly investigation or original research on a specialized subject. Examples are treatises submitted for an advanced academic degree or historical European treatises written by the praeses or primary professor and defended by the respondent or degree candidate.
Personal papers of members of a single family; usually of parents and their children, but sometimes including papers of spouses and their families as well.
Family records of births, baptisms, marriages, and deaths written on blank or printed form-like pages of Bibles.
Materials related to the office of an architect or architectural firm, including drawings, correspondence, and written documentation.
Volumes of maps, with or without descriptive text, which may be issued to supplement or accompany texts or be published independently.
Files that employ paper cards of approximately the same dimensions, on which information is recorded.

Collations of terms or names that serves as a standard for cataloging purposes, particularly electronic or physical files or other groupings of authorized cataloging entries for names, subjects, or other information. An authority file is characterized by having labeled the authoritative or preferred form of the name or subject entry for a particular entity.

Electronic or physical files or other groupings of authorized cataloging entries for names, particularly personal and corporate names, but the term could also be used for authorities containing other names, such as geographic names, titles of works of art, etc.
Files containing records with information about individuals, such as dates of birth or death, address, career information, etc.
Collections of material relating to law cases; they may include brief decisions or histories of cases.

Lists or registers of cases before a tribunal, usually kept by the clerk of the court, identifying the cases, with entries of action taken; used originally in connection with judicial proceedings, now also used in connection with quasi-judicial or administrative proceedings.
Documents representing the lineage of a person or persons in tabular or diagrammatic form.

Statistical diagrams in which numerical quantities are illustrated by rectangles of equal width but of varying length extending horizontally or vertically from a base line, and which represent frequency distributions. The rectangles or bars are ranged along an x/y axis representing two sets of variables.
Handbills put out in great numbers by lottery promoters.
Prescriptions or detailed statements of ingredients and processes used to fabricate materials.
Lists or other accounts of relics in a collection of other context.

Short for 'Web logs' or 'weblogs:' a Web site that functions as an online journal or diary, most often maintained by a single person, but also by groups with common interests. Commentary, images, sound, or video files are posted regularly with the most recent entry appearing first. Blogs may focus on a particular area of interest and contain links to content on external Web pages. Blogs usually have archives of all past entries, with links between similar items of interest. They originated in the United States in 1997 as a few online journals, and became popular ca. 2002, when software designed specifically for creating and maintaining blogs was introduced. For files storing detailed requests from Web servers use 'Web logs.'

Internet-based discussion forums in which messages are exchanged via electronic mail, rather than through a bulletin board system or newsgroup. LISTSERV (TM) is a trademarked term for a commercial software product devoted to managing electronic mailing lists. Though "listserv" is often generically used to refer to any such software application, and commonly to mailing lists themselves, "electronic mailing lists" is preferred.
Registries or other lists containing names, dates, and other information about members of a guild.
Lists of merchandise located in or belonging to a retail sales establishment.
Lists of persons traveling on a ship.
Series or lists of rates of duties imposed by a government on imported or exported goods.
Registers of the names and information on the members of a brotherhood.
Notes, often in books, kept by researchers or surveying parties while on site.

Oaths, written or verbal, concerning a renunciation of a belief, office, status, or the like. Included are oaths to depart from a realm, a repudiation of a religious, political, or other principle, or a rejection or disavowal of a claim or claimant.
Outlines of stories or plots, as for example of plays, ballets, operas, motion pictures, and television programs.
Posters intended to be placed in subway cars and buses.
Documents, such as deeds, by which title to property is conveyed from one person to another.
Official lists kept by government agencies or departments in which information concerning land ownership, possession, or rights are recorded to provide evidence of title or transaction.
Summaries giving details of title deeds and documents that prove an owner's right to dispose of land, together with any encumbrances that relate to the property.
Surveys which investigate and determine the distribution and origin of mineral deposits and rock masses.
Statements of fact, in speech or writing, in support of a proposition and advanced for the purpose of influencing another person.
Brochures, online pages, or other documents detailing or advertising the facilities or activities of a school, university, or other educational institution.
Official or formal records outlining administrative details, or events sucha as functions, proceedings, or investigations.

Official or formal records of an investigation related to an unexpected happening, in the form of documents containing presentations of facts, proceedings, investigations, or an outline of events preceding the accident.
Reports prepared each day that provide performance information for any particular project or endeavor to its management.
Official announcements.
Arrangements by which a publisher or a vendor assumes responsibility for selecting and supplying materials to fit an institution's profile, but with some right to return.

Methodological tools that have been developed by researchers to reverse engineer the casting sequence of a bronze sculpture and visually represent the separately cast parts. It is based on the evidence presented in the object and attempts to map the decisions made by a foundry regarding the number and position of separately cast pieces.
Documents containing accounts of the meetings and papers presented at a conference.

Assessments of the overall physical condition, characteristics, and completeness of a thing. Examples include reports on works of art or architecture, the state of conservation of the natural environment, and the state of roadways and waterways under various weather conditions. For assessments of groups or collections of things, use "condition surveys."

Documents describing the recurring records of an organization or administrative unit, specifying those records to be preserved as having archival value, and authorizing, on a continuing basis and after the lapse of specified retention periods and the occurrence of specified actions or events, the destruction of the remaining records.

Sets of small books planned around themes and housed together in cases. The first of this type of collection was from the English publisher John Marshall circa 1800, who issued diminutive libraries with ornamental pediments added to the boxes to give the impression of glass-fronted bookcases. Sets such as these have appeared thereafter in various forms. Miniature libraries were typically collected for children.

Documents issued by the government to ships engaged in foreign trade, establishing the nationality and ownership of a ship and entitling it to the benefits and privileges appertaining to all ships of the nation to which it belongs.
Sketchbooks in which graffiti artists develop ideas, practice tags, and acquire other artists’ signatures.
Concordance tables showing parallel passages from the four Gospels.
Statements of money owed by individuals or corporate bodies for compulsory contributions to the support of government.
Paper slips or cards indicating that the holder has paid for or is entitled to entrance or admission.

Documents outlining a proposed journey. Originally, a list of destinations in the Roman Empire with the distances between them, thought to be measured from the 'Millarium Aureum' or 'Golden Milestone' in the Roman Forum.
Official documentation concerning dates and places of persons' births, as well as parentage.
Formal documents certifying the date and place of persons' births and their parentage, as issued by an official in charge of such records.
Official documentation of burial kept by officials charged with registering interment.

Records documenting the legal separation of husband and wife, effected by the judgment or decree of a court, and either totally dissolving the marriage relation, or suspending its effects so far as concerns the cohabitation of the parties.
Records documenting additions to a collection, whether acquired by transfer under a legally based procedure, or by deposit, purchase, gift, or bequest.
Documents, often in list form, stating things to be done, as items of business or discussions to be brought up at a meeting; includes programs consisting of such items.
Records maintained by an organization regarding the action or fact of individuals being present to take part in social transactions, entertainment, instruction, worship, or in answer to a summons.
Rules made by a legislative body concerning the mode and manner of conducting its business and for the purpose of making an orderly and proper disposition of the matters before it.
Documents that outline the achievement of stated goals during a specified time period.
Recorded statements of evaluation or estimate of the market or other value, cost, utility, or other attribute of land, buildings, works of art, or other objects of property, by qualified persons.
Books in which financial accounts are kept.
Documents in which are entered debits, credits, and all other money transactions under each individual account or heading.
Individual pay records of members of the armed forces.

Formal requests to insurance companies demanding payment based on the terms of an insurance policy. Claims are reviewed for their validity by the policy grantor and subsequently paid out to the insured or requesting party if approved.

Certificates attached to bills of exchange drawn against shipments of property that empower the holder to dispose of merchandise as security for the payment of the bill if payment or acceptance is refused.

Primers of cardboard or wood, consisting of two or three pages with the alphabet, numbers, simple text, and sometimes pictures printed or impressed upon them and often varnished for protection. Distinguish from their predecessors, "hornbooks," which are primers consisting typically of a sheet of parchment or layer of paper mounted on a thin wooden board and protected by a sheet of transparent horn.
Books or treatises containing rules or instructions needed to perform methods of building, modifying, or repairing something without the aid of experts or professionals.

Books that include instructional material and also directions on how to assimilate information. Material in the textbooks is divided into units of information to be assimilated, combined with instructions on student fulfillment of assignments, additional explanations, and sections for self-testing for retention.
Books or treatises, containing rules or instructions needed to perform tasks related to building, intended to be used as reference.
Sets of information describing the contents, format, and structure of a database and the relationship between its elements, used to control access to and manipulation of the database.
Lists of the music used in a motion picture with the precise times it is meant to be played. Usually includes title, composer, and duration.
Collections of the texts of songs, but without accompanying musical notation.

Official or authoritative statements distributed to the press typically by a public relations firm or government agency. For packets of promotional material distributed to the press, use "press kits."
Books that tell one or more stories entirely through pictures without text, including both books intended for children and those with adult fictional subject matter.

Solemn blessings bestowed by the pope or his delegates, usually including patriarchs, primates, archbishops, and bishops. In locations where these prelates are unavailable, the delegate may be a local priest.
Books containing the epistles to be read at the mass; by the 13th century, generally folded into the missal.
Hebrew prayer books containing the Jewish liturgy for festivals.
Copies of plays used by a prompter, showing action of the play, cues, movements of actors, properties, costume, and scene and light plots.

Screenplays that contain all necessary visual and audio instructions in the final pre-shooting phase, including dialogue, sound effects, shots, and basic editing for all scenes in the order in which they are to be shown on the screen, subject to change only by the director.
Bibliographies with notes added to the entries to elucidate, evaluate, or describe the subject and contents of the entries.
Lists of works that themselves collect other lists that collate works on a particular theme, rather than of a particular author, printer, or country.
Lists of descriptions of individual documents in a collection or of a specified kind, usually arranged in chronological order.
Indexes recorded on cards of uniform size, arranged alphabetically, numerically, or by some other order.

Indexes in which each significant word in the entry is brought to the beginning, in alphabetical order, followed by the remaining words which follow it, and then followed by that part of the original title which came before the significant word.
Indexes of publications released annually.
Indexes to information printed in newpapers.
Indexes consisting of the names of authors.
Catalogs of works arranged alphabetically by authors' names or by other persons responsible for the intellectual content of the works, such as editors or translators.
Yearly publications, such as a book or journal published once a year.
Books published annually as a compendium, report, or summary of the statistics or facts of a calendar year and intended as reference books, limited to a special subject.
Annual publications by schools that provide information and often photographs relating to activities and the students at the school during the previous year.
Publications containing information concerning market conditions or expectations, especially those produced by firms or other financial organizations.
Newspapers or magazines containing sensational or popular stories, originally having the tabloid printing format, in which pages are half the size of those of the average broadsheet.
Periodicals that are compendiums of previously published, summarized, or condensed literary, historical, legal, scientific, or other written matter.
Religious discourses delivered by the celebrant at a funeral or otherwise in honor of the deceased.
Texts of speeches to be delivered in an academic environment.
Formal addresses or speeches given at a funeral or otherwise in honor of the deceased.

Controlled vocabularies in the form of a thesaurus, that are limited in the range of topics covered, but fit within the domain of a larger, broader, or more generic controlled vocabulary. A microthesaurus typically contains highly specialized terms that map to the hierarchical structure of the broader vocabulary at a high level node.
Addenda to wills, which explain, revoke, modify, or add to their provisions.

Bound collections of autographs, writings, paintings, and drawings collected by the owner from his or her friends and acquaintances. Thought to have developed in German-speaking Europe in the mid-16th century; the custom was spread by students traveling from one university to another. Albums were soon compiled by people other than students, particularly men and women of the bourgeoisie. Albums belonging to members of the nobility usually contained drawings of coats-of-arms.

Volumes containing reproductions of correspondence, made directly from originals through a transfer process. Using a screw-powered letter press in conjunction with a press book, a bound volume of blank, tissue paper pages. Letters written in special copying ink were placed on a dampened page. The book was then closed and the mechanical press screwed down tightly, causing the ink to be transferred to the bound page.
Publications containing titles and useful facts about books and other publications; usually annuals.
Pieces of formal stationery designed to announce a date marking a notable event, such as a marriage.
Documents advertising for bids to be submitted for a particular job.

Roman calendars, including works on parchment and also works inscribed in stone and displayed for the public; fasti indicated dates of festivals, games, days allowed for legal business, anniversaries of historical events, and other notable dates.
Documents showing the dates of Easter and the movable feasts associated with it.
Calendars that note the feast days and the anniversaries of Christian saints for each day of the year.
Cards used for sending greetings to individuals on their birthdays, often bearing illustrations and printed sentiments.
Postcards having a pictorial image on one side, often representations of a place or works of art, upon which a message can be written, then posted.
Pictorial postcards designed to be sent serially, with the completed set forming one picture when assembled. These may be arranged in a variety of ways, as a grid, horizontally, or vertically.

Certificates attesting that a thing or things are of the location of origin, provenance, creator, date, or materials which are claimed; signatures of officials or official seals are often included on the certificate to verify the claim. Examples include certificates of authenticity for art works, artifacts, memorabilia, collectibles, and software.
Charts used display the alphabet, used for teaching and learning.
Pieces of text cut out of newspapers.

Messages, intended usually for special or expeditious transmittal or delivery, such as important official messages, or news items sent with promptness by correspondents to newspapers or news agencies.
Formal and usually succinct letters issued from a business or individual requesting or delivering information, applying for a job, or addressing any other topic excluding personal communication.
Letters intended for wide or general circulation.
Letters addressed by the pope to all the bishops of the church.
Commercial or business intercourse engaged in by two or more parties. May be considered broadly to include letters and other forms of communication including electronic mail.
Documents which evidence the status of being a citizen, such as passports and birth certificates.
Statistical study of biological observations and phenomena.
Letters of the pope determining some point or question in ecclesiastical law and possessing the force of law within the Roman Catholic Church.
The last text versions of documents or other written works as they come from the authors or editors.
Excerpts of parts of a literary composition, as into another book or writing; use also for statements of market price of one or more securities.
Specialists in the use of radiation, such as X-rays, and radioactive materials in the diagnosis and treatment of disease.
Physicians specializing in the branch of medicine called ophthalmology. For those trained in the practice of optometry, use "optometrists."
Refers to those versed in the science of sound and sound waves.  Refers also to those who design, make, or repair sound devices, acoustic materials, and acoustical components of structures.

Those who use or create rope access or rappelling mechanisms, particularly for the inspection, maintenance, and repair of built works or features at high access locations. For example, rope access technicians may work with engineers, architects, geologists, or conservation professionals.
People who commit adultery, which is the voluntary participation in sexual intercourse when at least one of the parties is married.
Those who set fire to buildings, vehicles, or other property with criminal intent.

Used to describe those immigrant residents of a state or country who do not possess rights acquired through due legal process, or more specifically those not having the appropriate legal documents associated with their status. It includes people who entered the U.S. without inspection or permission from the government, and those who entered with a legal visa that is no longer valid.
People who are the subjects of portraits.

Those who, through membership in voluntary associations, support causes and institutions such as museums, libraries, and charities through donations of money, volunteer work, or public expressions of support. For those who undertake primary responsibility for causes or projects, either as individuals or in groups, use "sponsors." For those who support causes as individuals or in groups but not necessarily taking primary responsibility for them, use "patrons." Do not use for the common meaning of "friends," that is, not for persons joined to one another in mutual benevolence and intimacy.
Preservationists engaged in maintaining, rehabilitating, and preserving landmark architecture, particularly in historic districts.
Reformers who advocate the abolition of a custom or institution.
Persons employed in keeping the premises of an apartment building, office, or other building clean and free of refuse, tending the heating system, and making minor repairs.
Male police officers.

Those whose primary work is to repair or refinish shoes, boots, and other footwear, and other items such as handbags, luggage, and belts made from the materials commonly used in shoemaking and repair, such as leather, canvas, and plastic. For those who make and sometimes also design footwear as well as repair it, see "shoemakers."
Servants or attendants who work in the household, often living in the same house as the family.
Wage earners performing manual work which usually calls for the wearing of work clothes or protective clothing on the job.
People whose occupation or trade is to transport, mine, or otherwise procure or process coal.
Practical specialists in the technical details of a subject or occupation.
Workers occupied in preparing, transcribing, systematizing, and preserving written communications and records, distributing information, or collecting accounts, usually in an office environment.
Persons who engage in a particular pursuit, study, or science as a pastime rather than as a profession.
Those having the position or role of master overseeing other draftsmen and recognized as being superior in the art of draftsmanship.
Students in a national service academy, private military school, or on a training ship, or students training for service as commissioned officers in the United States Army, Air Force, or Coast Guard.
Persons who learn by practical experience under skilled workers a trade or art, usually for a prescribed period of time and for a prescribed compensation.
Children in the Yoruba culture of Nigeria  Africa, who die young and then are reborn to the same mother, only to repeat the cycle of birth and early death several times.

People with a cognitive or psychological condition that limits a major life activity in some way or requires special services. Mental disabilities can be caused by biological factors, environmental factors, substance abuse or brain trauma, that may result in an emotional, behavioral, or intellectual disadvantage that may hinder their ability to adapt to life activities.
People having any of several conditions characterized by subnormal intellectual functioning and impaired adaptive behavior that are identified during the individual’s developmental years.
People who do not have the functional use of the sense of hearing.
Men who have children, either biologically or by adoption.
Persons given or kept as a pledge pending the fulfillment of an agreement, demand, or treaty.
Class within the nobility consisting of those who are descended from or related to a monarch or line of monarchs.
People in the transitional stage of development between childhood and adulthood, commonly considered as those of 13 to 17 years of age.
Children in the earliest stage of their lives, before being able to walk.

General term for offices, departments, or other branches or representatives that have authority to oversee, direct, manage, and administer on behalf of an institution or other group. Use "governing bodies" specifically for organizations who exercise executive power.
Foundations, government agencies, institutions, or other organizations which give funds for a specific purpose.
Associations expressly formed for integrated joint action by two or more political powers, typically for a specific purpose such as mutual defense, trade, or the acquisition or sharing of power.
Governmental agencies having administrative, legislative, or judicial powers concerning the arts.
Exclusive social clubs that stage festive events such as private balls and public parades during Mardi Gras in New Orleans.
Accumulations or groupings of works of art that are acquired and assembled by private individuals or public instiutions.
Committees, usually of experts or specialists, formed for analyzing, investigating, or solving a specific problem.

Manufacturing or other commercial activity or trade that is carried out partly or wholly in people's homes, rather than in a factory or communal workshop, Often carried on by a self-employed worker and their family, possibly with the aid of a few apprentices.
Associations or bodies of people united by a common interest in the  scientific study of the remains and monuments of the prehistoric period.

Refers to religious groups in colonial Latin America that promoted Christian devotion through pious activities. They took charge of public and private activities for the benefit of the community such as paying for the mass, care of widows and orphans of deceased members, maintaining altars and images of patron saints, and processions and celebrations on holidays.

Indian state-sponsored manufactories for the production of multiple kinds of art and craft, including weaving, manuscript illumination, enameling and jewelry making. They were established during the Sultanate and Mughal periods in India; they later became vocational centers.

Types of textual, graphic, electronic, or physical items having the primary and original purpose to record or convey specific information. For forms in the sense of a document having blanks to be filled in, use "forms (documents)."

Brief explanations, translations, comments, interpretations, or definitions of a word or passage, particularly those found in the margins of pages or between lines of text in a book or manuscript. Also used for any other explanation that serves the same function.
In Indian architecture, a manual of architecture; architectural tradition.

Books of designs or plans for architecture or architectural details, circulated or published to enable widespread copying; in addition to illustrations, may describe techniques and working methods for construction.
Narratives structured in the form of dialogues consisting of the imagined speech of real people.
Dictionaries book containing versions of the same text in several languages; especially Biblical texts in several languages
Devices informing users of a building or complex about the location of or directions to individuals, organizations, or services within that building or complex.
Directories of names, addresses, and other data about former students of schools, colleges, or universities.
Publications that list manufacturers or fabricators of materials for those that seek their services.

Manuals intended to be taken into the "field," i.e., in natural environments, and containing information or pictures to aid in the identification and disambiguation of flora, fauna, and other objects of natural occurrence, such as minerals.
Records of events arranged in yearly sequence, usually without comment or interpretation by the compiler. For more connected and full descriptions of events in chronological order, use "chronicles."
Formal descriptions of badges, banners, and  flags, or in heraldry, coats of arts, which enables a person to construct or recontruct the appopriate image.

Persons who engage in the study and writing of history based on the critical examination of sources, the selection of particulars from authentic material, and the synthesis of particulars into narratives that will stand the test of critical methods. Also, persons officially appointed to write a history or to record the continuing history of a country, group, or institution.
Librarians who provide information services in governmental organizations and branches of government.
Linguist who is versed in the history and the origin of words.
Persons who study music in a sociocultural context, especially that outside the European tradition.
Those who study and write about perceptible beauty in art and nature, together with the intellectual and emotional responses to beauty.
Those versed in the study of the theistic philosophy that views creative becoming as the universal form of reality and emphasizes the relational nature of all being.
Publishers of prints, which are pictorial works produced by transferring images by means of a matrix such as a plate, block, or screen, using any of various printing processes.
People in a society who hold a special rank and position in which they read, write, and interpret sacred or special texts. Examples are the class of lector scribes in Ancient Egypt.
Those who do descriptive study, based on direct observation, of the culture and way of life of particular societies.

People who study or practice that branch of social anthropology that studies the culture history of specific peoples using historic oral, pictorial, and textual documents as the major research sources.Use also for those who study a people's own telling and interpretation of its history.
Those who specialize in the science and art of calculating and representating the earth's surface or a part of it on a flat surface. For artists who make maps, use "mapmakers."

Specialists in the study of the geographic aspects of political phenomena, including the geographical bases of the power of nations, and geographic influences on power relationships in international politics.

People who study or practice art therapy, which is the therapeutic use of images and objects to foster nonverbal communication, creativity, and physical interaction, and to uncover verbal associations and interpretations helping to identify and understand patients' emotional, motor, and perceptual dysfunctions.
Those who translate the communications of people speaking different languages; specifically those who do so orally while the people are present and conversing.

Refers to agriculturists who study and work in land cultivation, soil management, and field crop improvement, management, and production. For scientists who specialize in any or all aspects of soils, including their origin, distribution, classification, utilization, and physical and chemical properties, see "soil scientists."

Free people who support themselves by tilling the soil, either as small landholders or hired laborers. For the social class comprised of these people, use "peasantry." For those in a condition of servitude under feudalism, owing services to a lord and commonly attached to the lord's land, use "serfs."

Historically, a specialization of the fisherman occupation, harvesters of coral who brought raw coral to workshops where it would be processed in a variety of ways to sell as jewelry or for other uses in a global coral trade centered in Italy. In the late Medieval and early modern Mediterranean this was a specific occupation, often with its own guild (in places such as Genoa).
Foresters specializing in silviculture, which is the cultivation and study of forest trees, especially those raised for timber.
People who fell trees or cut timber into logs.

People who perform a variety of work to maintain and develop landscaped areas; tasks may include planting and maintaining ornamental trees, shrubs, flowers, lawns, hardscapes, as well as litter and trash removal.
Persons who tend goats that are grazing at large.
Those who engage in hunting with falcons or practice hawking as a sport.

People appointed as neutral parties to settle disputes, especially between labor and management. They are authorized to appraise the facts and arguments and to make decisions binding upon the disputants.
Arbitrators who resolve disputes between labor and management in industries.

Refers to judges of certain higher courts in the United States, Canada, and Great Britain, the exact levels of court varying from one jurisdiction to another, but generally including judges of the supreme courts of these countries.
Counsels admitted to plead cases in court and undertake the public trial of causes in the higher courts of law.

Professionals who physically handle cultural objects, including those who prepare works for shipping, transport the works themselves, or are involved in the storage or installation of artworks. For those involved in preparing art, other objects, or specimens (such as fossils) specifically for display in museums or galleries, use "preparators."

People who use cameras, particularly those who operate motion picture, video, or television cameras professionally. The term is used whether the person is male or female. For persons who oversee all the aspects of photography in a filmmaking, video, or television project, see "cinematographers."

People trained in or practicing the art of clay animation, which is animation involving modeling clay figures  moving them very slightly, filming them for a few frames, moving them again, filming again, and so on. When the film is projected at normal speed, the figures appear to move and change expression.
People who operate video cameras.
People ultimately responsible for all creative and technical aspects of a motion picture.
Actors in a play, film, television broadcast, performance art, or other performance who relate part of the plot to the audience or who speak a commentary.
Persons who transcribe music for voices or instruments for which it was not originally written, or adapt it to a style suitable to a particular performer or group of performers.
Those who lead or conduct a band of musicians, often a brass or military band.
Singers who are trained in and specialize in singing opera.
Individuals who specialize in creating ambrotypes, which are photographs produced by mounting a negative on glass with a dark backing, making the image appear as a positive.
Those who practice the skill of making images produced on photographic film by a radiation other than light, especially x-rays or gamma rays.
People who bind books, which entails using various procedures, performed by hand or machine, to secure leaves or gatherings, usually within covers.
Colorers who sprinkle reflective bronzing powder over paint or adhesive ink applied as an image to a substrate, either by hand or with a bronzing machine.
Individuals designated to pull prints in an edition from blocks, engraved or etched plates, or type.

Those engaged in the art and craft of designing type, typefaces, or fonts. For those who use type to arrange compositions to print from, use "typographers." Typographers may also act as type designers.
People having occupations in religion.
Bishops of the highest rank, who preside over archdioceses.
Cardinals of the Catholic church who gather to elect a pope.

Refers to clergymen in the Anglican Church responsible for assisting diocesan bishops in ceremonial functions and administrative work. Duties typically include general supervision of parish clergy and attention to matters of church buildings and other property. Archdeacons are styled as 'Venerable.' The office formerly also existed in the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches; in the Roman Catholic Church the role has been displaced by that of Vicar-General.
Monks who hold the office of superior of a monastery.
Nuns who hold the office of superior of a convent.

Clergymen having certain responsibilties, which varies by religious denomination: In the Protestant Episcopal Church, the clergy in pastoral charge of a parish. In the Roman Catholic Church, the clergy in pastoral charge of a college. In the Church of England, the clergy having pastoral charge of parsonages, with full possession of all rights and tithes.
The chief priests of a religion or religious group. An example is the chief priest of the ancient Jewish temple.

Female unmarried or widowed members of religious, ascetic or philanthropic lay societies, devoted to religious life, but not bound by strict vows of a religious order, and who may marry. Beguines often lived in communities called beguinages. This way of life first appeared in Liège toward the end of the 12th century, and use of the term was established by the 1230s. By this time the movement had spread throughout the Low Countries, Germany, and northern France.

People who are expert in one or more of the group of studies or branches of knowledge concerned with facts and phenomena of the observable or quantifiable world, and who employ the scientific method in their work.
Those who study or work in the statistical study of biological observations and phenomena.
Scientists who deal with the material universe beyond the earth's atmosphere.
Specialists or experts in astrophysics, which is the study of astronomical phenomena in terms of the underlying physical processes.
Scientists trained or working in the study of plant life.
Zoologists specializing in the scientific study of insects.
Chemists who analyze the value and quantity of metals in ores and alloys.
Experts in the science of natural and artificial stones, including gems.
Yoruba metalworkers who work in non-ferrous metals such as lead, silver, copper, bronze and brass.
Persons who shoe horses or make horseshoes.
Generic term for goldsmiths in Nahua culture.
