Ironsmiths who make iron into tools, horseshoes, machine parts, and other objects by heating it in a forge and hammering it into shape on an anvil.  Includes those who fit and nail horseshoes to horses' hooves.
Metalworkers who make armor or arms, or that repair, assemble, and test firearms.
Gunsmith that specializes in fitting the stocks of guns to their barrels.

People who specialize in creating engraved designs for coins. Historically, coin engravers were guild members who created coins in mints. The coin engraver creates dies for coins that incorporate engraving on the face of the die, distinguished from dies created from punches that displace the metal of the die instead of removing it.
Those who make decorative paper, such as wallpaper, printed from wood blocks and colored by hand. This was a profession, for example, in 15th-century France.
Textile workers who apply a coloring matter that is in a solution or fine dispersion so that at least some of the coloring matter is taken up by the textile.
Dressmakers, usually limited to those creating clothing of high quality and those who are also fashion designers.
Tradespeople that engage in the practice of dyeing raw silk.
Those who create art works in the medium of embroidery.

Refers to people, often women, who make articles of female apparel, particularly hats or other headgear. In older usage, the term may refer to vendors of apparel and luxury items, including hats, ribbons, gloves, and cutlery; the term originally referred to the city of Milan, Italy, which was the source of fine headgear known as "Milan bonnets" and other luxury items.
Tradespeople that engage in the process for producing single yarn of silk out of discontinuous filament of cocoon.
Craftspeople who constructed close-fitting body-garments, with or without sleeves, worn by men from the 14th to the 18th centuries.
Weavers whose work is considered art, rather than plain weaving, and may include embroidery or other needlework as well.
Woodworkers or carpenters specializing in fine art or otherwise exhibiting craftmanship of particularly high quality.
Skilled French craftsmen of luxury furniture; also French cabinetmakers specializing in veneering furniture, originally with ebony.
French joiners of the 17th and 18th centuries who specialized in small objects.

Carpenters of old Spain who practiced rough woodwork without decoration or smooth finishes. The wood they worked with served as a base for the more refined and detailed work of the 'carpintero de lo blanco.'
Persons professing a special secret knowledge concerning ceramics, especially the making of porcelain.
A broad term for any technicians, craftsmen, artists or artisans in Nahua culture who practice a skill knowledgeably.
Independent dollmakers who design and create one-of-a-kind dolls, their costumes, and other accessories, usually for individual sale to collectors.
Jewelers who create works considered to be art works.
People who, in the process of diamond cutting, split a rough diamond into smaller parts.
In colonial Latin America, potters who specialized in the creation and/or sales of maiolica earthenware, especially dishware.
People or corporate bodies in the manufacturing industry who make jigs, fixtures, dies, molds, machine tools, cutting tools, etc.
Modelers who specialize in creating models of aircraft.
Historically, those whose occupation it is to make wooden ships or  vessels watertight by driving oakum or other material into wedge-shaped seams between planks forming the hull.
Those involved in planning, organizing, directing, and controlling human or material resources to accomplish specific goals.

Refers to officials carrying this title serving in various administrative, judical, or secretarial capacities in various contexts, such as noble and royal houses, governments, the judiciary, churches, and universities.

People in an executive position in an arts organization or theater company whose responsibilities include making the final choice of the material staged in a season, the hiring of creative and production personnel, and other high level management tasks. For those in non-executive positions who formulate concepts and supervise the execution of the visual appearance of a publication or performing arts production, use "art directors."

Refers to official heads of organizations such as schools, institutions, or government bureaus, or those named to control a business. Distinct from "managers," who control a portion or project within an institution or business.
Managers whose responsibility is to direct and manage advertising campaigns or other outreach.
Specially trained workers who work with and commonly lead a crew.
Foremen of gangs of laborers.

Practitioners of the general management of urban areas, encompassing the setting of objectives for urban life, the establishment of policies, and the planning, development, operation, and maintenance of the urban environment and services.
Artists in any media who were official members of and worked for a noble court.

During the colonial period in Latin America, escribanos were public servants whose duty was confirming the validity of legal documents, such as deeds, fulfilling similar functions as contemporary notaries.

Refers to officers of this title in public services and institutions, their rank and extent of authority varying with the specific context, but generally holding authority over a group or area of activity. For military officers holding the same title, see "captains (military officers)." For captains of ships, see "shipmasters."
Diplomats of the highest rank, sent by one sovereign or state to another or to an international organization as its chief representative.
Turkish governors of a province or district.

Magistrates in colonial Latin America with jurisdiction over certain territories. They had many administrative and governmental functions such as overseeing the initial trial in lawsuits, serving as the local people’s legal representatives in their business deals and contracts, and examination of the ordinances made by the cabildos (municipal councils).
Refers to governors of large territories who have other, subordinate governors under their jurisdiction.
Certain chieftans or other leaders, originally of aboriginal peoples of the West Indies, Mexico, and elswhere in America, later also applied to European leaders in these areas.

Usually refers to the sovereigns of Iran or Persia. The term may also refer to a ruler of Afghanistan prior to the downfall of the monarchy in 1973. It is sometimes used to refer to rulers of other countries of central and southern Asia, or to the hereditary governors and heads of Sufi orders.
Princes of Germany who were entitled to elect the Holy Roman Emperor.
Archaeologists who specialize in studying the sites, structures, and artifacts of the industries and processes of industrialization of former times.
Specialists in the study of runes and runic writings.
Authors who write accounts of the lives of individuals.
Authors who write the history of their own lives. For authors who write episodic accounts of events in their lives, prefer "memoirists."
Journalists who analyze news and write columns or commentary based on personal knowledge and experience for publication or broadcast.
Those who read out the news on television and radio newscasts.

Refers to people employed by a newspaper or broadcasting company to contribute regular news reports or interpretations from a location distant from the home office. For those people or organizations who communicate with others by correspondence, see "correspondents (correspondence writers)."
People who report on, write about, describe, interpret, or evaluate literary works, usually contemporary works.
Persons who head one of the divisions, faculties, colleges, or schools of a university.
Teachers in post-secondary education institutions who rank immediately below professors and above assistant professors.
Professors with the highest ranking position on the staff of a university or college, having full rank and privliges, and in a position higher than associate professors or assistant professors.
Members of the species Homo sapiens and their close extinct relatives, as distinguished from other animals, spirits, or other entities.
General term for types of groups of people.

People or corporate bodies who perform work or provide supplies, often on a large scale, according to a legally binding contractual agreement at a certain price or rate. For example, in the building and related trades, contractors undertake construction work according to the terms of a contract.

Professionally-qualified people who record all the transactions affecting the financial status of an organization, including the collation, recording, and communication of financial information and the preparation of analyses for decision-making purposes.
People who act as architects, which are those who design and oversee the building of habitable structures, as a pastime rather than as a profession.
Architects serving as the primary, overseeing architect for a government.

Architects who specialize in the design, renovation, and remodeling of golf courses, which are large outdoor areas where the sport of golf is played, consisting of a teeing ground, fairway, rough, hazards, and a series of greens.
Persons who lay down asphalt on streets, driveways, sidewalks, parking lots, and other sites of construction.
People who build houses, or who oversee the building of houses. Usually used in historical contexts, where the person was both designer and builder or overseer, and the construction was wood frame.
Workers who attach slings to articles for hoisting.
People whose skill and profession is in thatching roofs of houses, corn or hay ricks, or other structures.
Those whose occupation it is to quarry stone.
Refers to the masons who carved the stone at their banker in the building lodge. They performed  the final preparation work on stone masonry blocks.

People or corporate bodies in the construction industry that undertake work as detailed in a legally binding contractual agreement, and whose services are limited to the construction of commercial buildings and single-dwelling or multiple-dwelling residential buildings. For contractors on a construction project whose services are unlimited, use "general contractors."
Draftsmen who execute technical drawings from others' designs.
Engineers who design spacecraft, missles, and rockets.
Engineers who design aircraft.

Civil engineers specializing in the design and production of systems, equipment, and structures that either control, transport, or generate power from water or other fluids or that derive some or all of their power from the flow of water, such as hydraulic machinery, sewage disposal plants, waterworks, dams, pipelines, and hydroelectric power plants.
Those whose occupation is the preparation of plans and specifications related to mechanical and structural water treatment.
Specialists in electronic engineering.
Those trained or working in the branch of engineering concerned with the daily technical and managerial operations of a factory.
People training or working in the planning field having to do with the establishment of objectives, procedures, and resources for architectural projects.
People who estimate or measure quantities of materials and equipment necessary to build a construction project.
People trained in or practicing architecture, which is the art of designing and building habitable structures, especially those considered to have aesthetic value.

Refers to collage artists who use torn posters to create their works. Usually the term is reserved for artists associated with the Nouveau Réalistes, who began creating similar works in the 1950s and early 1960s: François Dufrène, Jacques de la Villeglé, Raymond Hains, and Mimmo Rotella, though it is often used for others whose work involves torn and collaged commercial posters.
Painters who specialize in creating embellishments, adornments, or ornamentation, often specifically those that are temporarily put up on a stage, or for a holiday or another special occasion.
Artists specializing in a method of painting by means of an airbrush, which is a small, finely controllable mechanical paint sprayer.
Artists who specialize in painting ceilings; usage is restricted to those who paint scenes or illusionistic devices on ceilings of grand buildings, not including house painters.
Printmakers who specialize in illustrating and decorating books with  engravings or other prints, or otherwise using printmaking techniques to decorate books.
Those who engrave copper, usually artists who engrave copper plates for printmaking.
Printmakers who work in aquatint.
Those who work in chromolithography.
Artists who specialize in sculpting altarpieces, which are objects set on the altar in a Christian church.
Design professionals who work with architects and engineers in the creation and development of architectural projects and translating client needs.
Those whose occupation is to arrange the display of merchandise in a shop window, often with decorative additions for effect.
Engineers specializing in designing, building, and testing the prototype of a product.
A dealer in cloth, and by extension, other articles of textile manufacture, including clothing or dry goods.
People who make abridgements, summaries, or compilations.
Persons or corporate bodies who work on behalf of artists to sell their works, find commissions, or otherwise assist the artist in locating lucrative opportunities.
People or businesses who represent collectors and investors in locating and purchasing art.
Refers to people or corporate bodies who own or run a manufacturing plant. For those who create or construct artifacts by their own labor, especially as their craft or profession, see "makers."
Refers to people or corporate bodies who own or run manufacturing plants for making vehicles that navigate through the air.
Collectors who specialize in acquiring fine art.
People or corporate bodies that sell antiques, which are artifacts created or produced in former periods.
People who divide, distribute, deliver, or bestow books.

Refers to those who practice an occupation, trade, or pursuit requiring manual dexterity or artistic skill, typically excluding those who produce painting, sculpture, drawing, or architecture. Generally distinguished from "artists" and "architects," based on the media of their creations. For a more general term for those who construct artifacts directly by their own labor, especially as their profession or primary occupation, use "makers."

Persons who engage in carving or cutting a figure, design, or shape out of a solid material such as stone or wood. For persons who create create large or medium-sized three-dimensional works that are considered art, see "sculptors."
Refers to those engaged in carving and cutting gem stones, including creating cameos and intaglio carvings on the surface of gems.
Metalworkers who specialize in casting objects in yellow copper or brass.
Craftsmen who gild the metal mounts on furniture.
One who engages in the trade of varnishing with japan.
Persons who erect shafting, move machinery, or care for the mechanical equipment in a workshop, mill, or plant.

Those engaged in the creation of decorative veneers pieced together from wood, or other materials of varied shades or colors, especially on the surfaces of furniture, cabinetry, or decorative works. The result is a surface covered with decorative motifs, figures, or pictorial images. For artists creating similar works that may be of any material, including glass, use "intarsia artists."
People who create decoration or objects from beads, which are small, pierced objects through which a wire or string may be passed.
Craftspeople who specialize in making belts, girdles, and other items worn around the waist, as well as straps and other belt-like items.
Smiths whose work is of the quality of fine art or crafts.
Those who melt and pour glass into a mold; founders also do fusing.

Machines for the production of electrical discharge at high voltage. These commonly consist of an insulated hollow conducting sphere that accumulates in its interior the charge continuously conveyed from a source of direct current by a belt of flexible nonconducting material.
Motors that are powered by a controlled circulation of pressurized fluids.
Turbines that are powered by gas resulting from the combustion of fuels.
Instruments or machines that produce a strong current of air by expansion or contraction of an air chamber, usually used to fan a fire in a hearth.
Fire-making tools involving a bag, usually made from animal skin, with an attached nozzle and an opening that could be closed by gathering the bag material by hand to force air through the nozzle.

Matches that use sulfur as the lighting tip, often comprising wooden sticks dipped in melted sulfur. Sulfur matches were recorded as early as 577 CE in China.  By the 19th century, improvements to the sulfur match were invented, including impregnating the wood or paper with stearic acid, wax, resin, or paraffin to allow faster lighting and less offensive odor.
Furnaces that generate warm air for a heating system.
Instruments and apparatuses used for cultivating the soil, producing crops, and raising livestock.
Devices used to crush rock, usually in the context of the mining industry, either to extract ore or simply to break material into smaller pieces.

Long-handled tools with a curved blade set perpendicular to the shaft and curving inwards towards it; used for cutting or slicing away the surface of wood, such as in dressing lumber. For similar tools but used for cutting, use "axes (tools)."
Small axes for chipping wood or stone into shape.
Tools designed to pry corks off the necks of champagne bottles and/or to break open the muselet.
Power saws with a continuous piece of flexible steel running around two pulleys and with teeth on one or both sides; used primarily to cut wood, but with the proper blade may be used to cut metal.
Machinery devised to excavate holes in rigid material such as rock or earth, for mining, digging wells, or other purposes.
Blocks or wedges of wood or other material used to secure or steady an object, or to prop or keep something in position.
Steel bars that have a straight chisel point at one end, and are bent at the other end, which has a notch for pulling nails; used for general demolition work.
Screwdrivers whose head is set at 90 degrees to its shaft.
Small, usually hand-held devices that insert wire staples into two or more sheets to fasten them together.

Mechanized devices used to increase the quality of textile materials by removing impurities, blending raw materials, and untangling/cleaning textile fibers. These devices are typically fitted with sturdy fabrics embedded with wire teeth or pins, which are used to cover a series of cylinders that rotate at varying speeds. Loose fibers are separated, removed, and/or disentangled as textile materials pass through the devices' rotating cylinders and encounter the sharp wire teeth.  These machines alleviated the problem of hand carding, a task that slowed the newly mechanized production of textiles in the 18th century. Several inventors developed machines to perform carding, including John Kay, Oliver Evans, Lewis Paul, R. Arkwright, and Johann Bodmer. Mechanized devices used to increase the quality of textile materials by removing impurities, blending raw materials, and untangling/cleaning textile fibers. These devices are typically fitted with sturdy fabrics embedded with wire teeth or pins, which are used to cover a series of cylinders that rotate at varying speeds. Loose fibers are separated, removed, and/or disentangled as textile materials pass through the devices' rotating cylinders and encounter the sharp wire teeth. Mechanized devices, typically comprising a series of steel rollers, gears, and a rotating steel drum with steel bristles, designed to comb, blend, and align the fibers of raw cotton or wool in preparation for subsequent spinning processes. When passed through the device's rollers, drum, and bristles, raw materials are rid of impurities and transformed into long fleecy rolls of blended sliver. First invented in England by both Daniel Bourne and Lewis Paul in the 1740s, these devices ultimately replaced manul carding due to their speed and efficiency.
Receptacles made of metal, porcelain, wood, or stone with a cup-shaped cavity in which ingredients for cooking can be ground or pulverized with a pestle.
Implements consisting of a handle with an enlarged, rounded end used along with a mortar to grind or pulverize food.
Torches operated by compressed acetylene gas and oxygen; used in welding and metal-cutting.
Auxiliary stands or supports for holding a bag or sack upright and open, to facilitate filling with any material such as grain, or laundry.
Devices, usually of iron, bent at the ends, or of dovetail form; used to hold together structural timbers or stone.
Pincers which remove old horseshoes before re-shoeing.
Pliers with jaws having sharpened edges especially adapted for cutting.
Utensils used to handle or burn incense, particularly large pieces or cubes of incense.
Vises attached to a workbench to hold material while it is being worked.
Lifting devices operated by forced pumps of fluid with an external lever.
Brooms made from palm fronds.
Brushes designed for applying paint over large or relatively large areas as a coating. For small brushes made to be handled with precision in applying paint or ink, see "artists' brushes."
Devices or machines that compress and transport fluids, usually by pressure, suction, or both.

Screw-shaped surfaces mounted inside a pipe, used for raising water. These are among the earliest form of hydraulic machine used for lifting water from a low-lying body of water onto another surface, often for irrigation. In a contemporary context, Archimedean screw pumps are widely used in wastewater treatment plants and for dewatering low-lying regions.
Sharp metal points with wood handles; used to make small holes in wood or leather.
Axes to be used in case of fire. They are standard equipment of firefighters and are also often found in public buildings; part of the head and heft may be painted red.
Masks worn over the nose and mouth to protect from dust and other airborne particles.
Coarse camouflage nets worn over helmets.
General-purpose tapered steel files used essentially in metalwork but also in working hardwood surfaces.
Molds that measure or verifies the diameter of bullets or the size of bullets.
Stamps used to indicate that a item has been used, or is no longer valid, such as a postage stamp or check.

Tools used to pound, hammer, or tap materials to be flattened or mashed. The term is extended in particular to wooden tools used to pound the bark or bast of trees in the manufacture of bark cloth in African and Oceanic cultures.
Machines consisting of hammers that are raised and dropped to form metal on an anvil or die. For similar devices used to drive piles into the earth use "pile drivers."
Hand-held pneumatically powered drills which hammer and rotate a bit or chisel; used for drilling rock or breaking up concrete, asphalt, or paving.

Implements consisting of a heavy head, usually of wood, with a handle or stock, used in various industrial and domestic operations, and having various shapes according to the purpose for which it is used. Examples include beetles for driving wedges or pegs, ramming down paving stones, or for crushing, bruising, beating, flattening, or smoothing various materials or things.
Tools for creating gunflints, in the form of hammer-like instruments with dual heads often of pyramidal shape culminating in sharp points, or other shape variations.

In the hand working of hides and skins, convex slabs, typically wooden, sloping upwards from the floor, over which hides and skins are placed while they undergo such processes as trimming, fleshing, depilation, liming, and scudding, known as beamhouse operations.
Small tools with interchangeable heads used to scratch metal and wood surfaces.
Tools used for delicate or precision work.
Programmable machines that are capable of autonomously performing the operations of CNC machining, for example CNC routers used for turning or cutting and CNC milling machines.
Spools of plastic material used to facilitate the printing process for adding machines, printing calculations on paper.
The tapered ends of anvils.
Bits having a square tapered shank fitted into and rotated by a brace, and are used for drilling holes in wood.
Large, long, auger bits with a very open twist that may or may not terminate in a screw end.
Thin, flat metal blades, bands, or stiff plates with cutting teeth along the edges that are attached to handles to create a saw.
Handles used for carrying waterskins.
Ropes or wires used to guide and steady anything which is being hoisted in the air; or to secure or steady objects to prevent them shifting position.
Instruments employed in fabricating rope by hand, consisting of a slender rounded rod that tapers towards each end, which is made to revolve and twist fiber into rope.
Heavy-rimmed wheels used for regulating the speed of machinery via inertia.
Long bar-type clamps either of wood or metal with an adjustable stop at one end, and a screw-type stop at the other.
Somewhat lighter versions of bar clamps.
Pegs or pins partially inserted into a hole at an edge or end of a workbench to help secure a piece of work or prevent it from sliding off the bench.
Hammers with a hardened face on one end of the head for driving nails, and curved forked tines on the other end for pulling out nails.
Mallets designed for loosening or removing the bung (stopper) of a cask.

Vises having a threaded nut and flange, which is known as a "box." Early vises had built up boxes, often made by forge welding and brazing parts together; the threads were made by brazing a coil inside a tube. Later, the boxes of box vises were made in solid pieces, often with screw threads being hand turned on a lathe.
Box vises for which the threaded nut and flange "boxes" were made in solid pieces, originally with screw threads being hand turned on a lathe.
Hand tools which consist of a wood or metal bar about 2 feet long with four spirit levels set into it; used by carpenters to determine a horizontal or vertical plane or line.
Tools similar to the try square except that they have an adjustable blade which can be set at any angle.
Small shovels of varied design used to shovel ash from domestic hearths, fireplaces, or coal stoves.
Spades designed for digging ditches or troughs that feature handles on their hafts and blades that are slightly wider at the point.
A powered plow-like machine used for breaking up soil by means of rotating blades.
Cages for confining birds.
Implements resembling hoes or pitchforks, designed to dig clams out of the sand.

Small, usually metal fans typically consisting of a base with a shaft to which two arms, with a blade at each end, are attached, and which is operated by a clockwork mechanism. Used to keep flies away.
In Benin and elsewhere in Africa, distinctive fishing rafts of floating grass and vegetable matter, anchored with stakes near river bank.
Objects in the form of a fish, designed to attract other fish for capture by the harpoon, spear, or leister of ice fishermen. Unlike a fishing lure, a fish decoy doesn't have a hook attached.
Maori fish hooks, traditionally made of stone, wood, or shell, later incorporating metal.
Maori crayfish pots, used for fishing for crayfish.
Fishing nets of various types which are pulled through a body of water, or just above the bottom of the sea or a lake bed, in order to capture fish and other aquatic creatures.
Tools comprising metal blades mounted on handles, used to scrape bark from trees or logs.
Wooden levers with metal hooks on their shafts, used to roll logs; later combined with the jam pike to become peavies.
Pocket-sized cant hooks for rolling logs.

Astronomical instruments invented by M. Weighelius, a mathematics professor at the University of Jena in Upper Saxony in the 17th century, which allowed multiple people to view the same telescopic image at the same time.
Early devices, originally invented by Ferdinand Carre in 1860, which created a limited amount of ice based on ammonia’s affinity for water.
Tools, equipment, and supplies originally created for the sampling, observation, measurement, or recording of specific chemical properties in specialized applications.
Encompasses objects used in the study of sound and for transmitting sound.
Structures placed behind or over pulpits, rostrums, or platforms to reflect sound toward the audience.
Microcomputers (or minicomputers) that are specifically designed to fit into an office environment.
Electronic protection accessories that are plugged into computers or other devices to enable the use of protected software or other restricted functions.
Devices used to print barcodes that are then adhered to other items, usually by heat transfer printing.
Machines used to create a physical object from a three-dimensional digital model, typically by laying down thin layers of a material in succession.

Direct-current amplifiers in which the signal is passed through a low-pass filter, then used to modulate a carrier signal so it may be amplified as an alternating-current signal. The amplified DC output is obtained by rectifying and filtering the carrier signal.
Semiconductor lasers used in Raman spectroscopy that reverse, or flip, the direction of conduction-band electrons as they spin on an axis in the direction of the magnetic field.
A simple electron tube with only two electrodes, an anode and a cathode. For more sophisticated electron tubes housed in evacuated glass bulbs, use "vacuum tubes."
Continuous belts passing over pulleys, providing a track on which loose materials or small articles are carried from one point to another.
Nautical pulley blocks having projections at the bottom of their shells to prevent the rope that is rove through them from becoming jammed between the block and the yard.
Devices, as rods to which freely rotating pointers are attached, for indicating the direction of the wind.

Devices for changing the diverging light or other radiation from a point source into a parallel beam. This collimation of the light is required to make specialized measurements in spectroscopy and in geometric and physical optics.
Binoculars intended for use outdoors.
Magnifying glasses designed to be held in the hand.
Microscopes having one microscope for each eye, arranged so that the specimen is viewed from slightly different angles, giving a three-dimensional picture. They are widely used in surgery.

Electron microscopes designed for directly studying the surfaces of solid objects, utilizing a beam of focused electrons of relatively low energy as an electron probe that is scanned in a regular manner over the specimen. An electrical signal is obtained by collecting and amplifying secondary electrons emitted by the specimen and is applied to a cathode-ray tube scanned in synchronism with the electron beam.

Use to refer to devices that convert chemical energy into voltaic electrical current. Strictest usage applies this term only to devices of two or more galvanic cells, but American English usage is most commonly applied to the single-cell variety.

Engines that are activated through the use of animal locomotion. The animal works either in a vertical or horizontal plane to drive a central axis, treadwheel, or series of gears in more sophisticated machines.
Steam engines, common in the 19th century, in which a beam is pivoted in the center above a veritical cylinder, transmitting motion to the piston down to a crank shaft by a long connecting rod.
Tongs designed with a gap for holding around an obstruction at or near one end, usually to fit over the head of a bolt in order to grip the shank of the bolt.
Tongs to hold hammers being reforged. The prong fits into one eye of the hammer, while the bottom piece keeps the head from twisting sideways.
Portable vises used to hold pipes in the jaw by means of a chain.
Wrenches which consist of a steel bar, hexagonal in section, bent to form a right angle; used for Allen screws.
Stacks of iron rollers used in papermaking to smooth paper or to give it a glossy surface.
Devices or machines for cutting the edges of paper or cutting paper into sections, often having the mechanism of a guillotine.
Knives used by paper hangers for trimming wall paper at baseboards and around window and door frames .

Devices having a razor-sharp blade mounted with a straight edge, and so-designed to cut matboard; may be used for straight cutting or for bevel cutting of mat windows. For hand held, knife-like devices, use "mat knives."
Brushes used to smooth wallpaper as it is applied to a wall to secure the adhesive, and eliminate pockets of air.
Long tapering cones used to stretch holes in rushwork, to open the strands of a rope in splicing, or to enlarge a hole, as in leather.
Small knives with a wide blade; used for trimming a finished basket.
Sewing clamps used to keep fabric taut, usually made of bronze, and topped with the image of a bird.
Needles having rounded tips, used for sewing knits and other materials where it is desirable to shift fibers rather than piercing or snagging fibers.

Small frames or spools around which yarn is wound to facilitate knitting projects requiring regular color changes. These frames are often made of plastic, wood, cardboard or other everyday materials. They are equipped with hooks or clamps designed to secure and organize yarn color changes by minimizing tangles and eliminating the need for multiple balls of yarn.
Frames that hold the fabric support of a rug while it is being worked by hand.
Looms designed for weaving beading, using strings or threads with threaded seed beads or similar beads.
Flexible needles with a point on each end; used for knitting a seamless tube.
Any of various devices that wind thread into a bundle or onto a support for storage.
Hammers with very small narrow faces used in upholstery for show-wood or neat work.
Fine steel needles that have a butt at one end and a long flexible hook at the other that curves back to the shank of the needle.
Augers designed with a hollow cylindrical tip or shaft, to allow removal of a plug, disk, or cylinder of wood, soil, or another material.
Cylinder augers designed for removing columns of soil for study and monitoring.
Augers used for boring bung holes, which have tapered sides, in barrels; also used for boring such holes in wood for other purposes.
Tools resembling ice picks, used to make holes for brads and wood screws.
Axes used to split timber before removal of the bark. For tools used to strip bark from trees use "300411589 barking axes."
Small two-headed axes used for cutting mortises; one end is chisel-shaped and the other is a triangular knife.
Braces with a ratchet-driven chuck, permitting its use in confined spaces where complete circular sweeps of an ordinary brace would be impossible.
Chisels used in the debarking of timber.
Chisels with a short blade; used especially for setting hinges on doors and door frames.
Heavier versions of forming chisels; used for harder work and generally fitted with an iron band on the handle to prevent it from splitting.
Giant paring chisels which are pushed by the hands and shoulder rather than struck.

Coopers' tools for ploughing the groove or channel in cask staves,  for the attachment of the barrel heads; the channels themselves are also called "crozes." The tools may be mounted with a channel-cutting tooth.
Drawknives with a slight downward thrust of the handles for cutting outside curves, such as on the outside of barrel staves.
Wedge-shaped tools used for cleaving and riving staves. These have a handle in the plane of the blade, set at right angles to the back.
Two-bladed tools with the larger blade in the shape of a hatchet and the smaller shaped like an adz, as distinguished from "hatchet-adzes" in which the adz-shaped blade is the larger.
Medium-sized hatchets with a nail-pulling claw at the side of a nail-driving poll.
Adjustable stops with a projecting knife or hook that holds a piece of work on a workbench.
Planes with a moveable fence and interchangeable blades; used for a variety of grooving and molding purposes.
Large wood hand planes, the mouths of which are cut obliquely from side to side, so that they can work close to a corner.
Planes with an adjustable fence which exposes the blade in proportion to the desired width of the cut; used to cut grooves on the side nearest the worker.
Small planes whose mouths can be adjusted for coarse or fine work, used in corners and other difficult to reach places.
Small hand-held planes, either of wood or metal, with low-angled cutting blades; used for small work, to clean up rough spots, and especially to clean up end grain and miters.
Planes as large as 5 to 6 feet in length which are turned upside down and mounted on legs. The wood to be planed is slid over the plane.
General term for wide molding planes with a simple or complicated profile.
Planes having a curved cutting edge which makes bead moldings along a wood surface.
Hollow planes which produce smooth long cylindrical surfaces; used to make stair rails, carriage-wheel spokes, large furniture moldings for case pieces, and tool handles.
Steel punches with a decorative face, used for marking wood to give texture.
Small handsaws whose back edge is stiffened with a steel or brass strip; used in finish carpentry for cutting mitered joints and other joinery work.
Small backsaws, 3 to 6 inches in length, with very fine teeth and very little set; used for fine work.

Thin saws with approximately 11 teeth per inch, stiffened with a metal rib along the top to prevent buckling; used to smooth cut the edges of tenons, dovetails, or miter fittings; a modern variety of the tenon saw.
Circular saws designed to operate with a built-in wobble so that the kerf it makes is greater than the thickness of the saw; used for grooving and for other special purposes in carpentry.
Hand saws with a thin blade held in place between the two ends of a frame.
Framed bow saws with a light blade and handles at both ends.
Large pit saws supplied with frames; used to cut logs into boards or planks.
Saws with a reversible handle and a blade which has teeth on either side; one set is fine and the other coarse.
Compass saws having especially narrow blades and fine teeth.
Saws 3 to 4 feet long generally having plain teeth; used for sawing trees into logs.
Lighter or shorter ripsaws, with teeth that are more closely spaced.
Two-handed scorpers having a semicircular blade about 4 inches wide and bent to bring the wood handles in line with the blade.
Scraping tools whose blade is perpendicular to the handle and set at the end of two parallel arms.
Molding planes with simple profiles.
Spokeshaves which cut a chamfer on the edge of a piece of wood.
Wedges of hardwood, metal, or another material, used for inserting into a hole or crack and then struck, for splitting logs or firewood.

Devices, usually made of hardwood, used in carpentry to secure the work at the back of the workbench, in order to protect the surface of the workbench from being scarred or damaged by movement of the work.
Tools used for burnishing or polishing that are made of bone, ivory, smooth wood, or in modern contexts, plastic. Examples of usage include the smoothing and burnishing of paper or leather.

Tools used for inking a plate or stencil, laying an etching ground, or pressing a material into the interstices of a plate or type. Examples include a cotton pad covered with silk or leather, a piece of rolled felt, or a short-bristled brush.
Very sensitive brayers for giving a smooth distribution of ink, having a surface of gelatin.
Polished plates of copper on which a design is engraved or etched for printing.
Presses in which the type or the plates are held on a horizontal or vertical plane, and ink rollers and sheets of paper, carried by a cylinder, alternately pass over them.
Soft rubber rollers attached to wooden or metal handles; used to ink wood blocks, linoleum blocks, lithographic stones, or printing plates.

Marking tools comprising thin pieces of material, such as metal, paper, cardboard, or stencil film, into which the shapes of letters are cut so that paint or ink applied to the surface of the stencil tool will produce the image of that letter on a second surface through the cut-outs.
Potter's wheel manually operated with a foot pedal or by kicking a disc at its base.
Two- or four-wheeled conveyances, sometimes motor-driven, for transporting mixed concrete over short distances at construction sites.
Concrete mixers, usually mounted on crawler tracks, that mix and place concrete pavement on the subgrade.
Powerful stud drivers for driving a hardened steel fastener into concrete or other hard material, having the impact of a blank gun cartridge.
For glassmaking, multipartile molds with a decorative pattern; glass blown into this type of mold picks up the pattern on its exterior.

Leather-working tools used to produce two parallel surface lines or furrows on a piece of leather by means of two adjustable spring jaws set open with a screw to make guide-llines at any required distance apart.
Small double creasers with parallel edges.
Hand tools having a beveled blade used to round the edges of leather of varying thickness.
Hammers with magnetic heads that hold tacks or nails on the head of the hammer as they are struck.

Knives of various designs having a curved blade set transversely to the handle, used in leatherworking and other occupations. For such knives with a curved blade in the shape of a crescent moon, use "moon knives."
Knives with curved, spatulate blades, which may be in a half-moon or a crescent shape. These are used to cut heavy leathers.
Knives having a beveled point and used to split or pare leather.
Knives having a relatively broad squared-off point, used in leatherworking.
Leatherworking needles that have triangular tips with sharpened edges that reach to the point to prevent tearing of the material sewn.

Lacing needles designed so that the lacing his held in place on the needle by a two-pronged clip formed at one end. The lacing is then drawn through slits or punched holes made for stitching together multiple pieces of leather or other materials.
Pliers used to set eyelets into pliable materials such as leather or canvas.

Hand tools principally used for holding, bending, and cutting thin materials or small gage wire. These vary in size. The jaws are hollow on one side opposite the cutting edges, in addition to having a flat, serrated tip or nose that can be used as a grip or to twist wire ends into a splice. For similar tools with gripping surface at the nose, use "wire cutters."
Manual tools used for piercing or cutting pieces from any semi-soft material, often leather, designed so that the shank is split into an arch before it meets the cutting end.
Hand tools with multiple metal points imbedded into a handle used to impress dots into the surface of leather as a decorative motif.
A tool for grooving lines in leather where it is desired to sink stitches below the surface.
Thick and protective thimble palms, worn when using sharp tools like awls and needles to prevent injury to the hand.
Hand tools used to finish a plastered surface.
Axes having a flat face for knocking off projecting angular points and a pointed peen for reducing a surface to a desired form.
Any rugged, broad-edged stone masons' chisels.
Slender drills used for boring or drilling a blasthole in rock.
Trowels with two surfaces meeting at a right angle; used to finish plaster or concrete in a corner.
Striking tools having two cutting edges, or one cutting edge and one hammer face, used for dressing or spalling rough stone.

Mechanical tools designed to blend different paint colors or components by propelling paint cans in a rapid, oscillatory motion. Typically composed of a paint can clamp, used to secure the can in position, and a motor, these devices were initially intended to replace manual paint stirrers. For the small, hand-held tools designed to manually mix paint components, use "paint stirrers."
Hand-operated saws used for cutting stone, especially marble, into usable slabs.
Pieces of metal with a serrated edge; used to scratch plaster and create a rough gripping surface for the next coat.
Trowels having a flat, triangular steel blade in an offset handle, used to pick up and spread mortar.
Trowels used to finish inside corners.
Wooden or metal frames that hold the sand forming the mold used in a foundry.
Heavy, usually steel or iron blocks, on which metal is shaped by hand hammering or forging. Anvils are also used for working materials other than metal.
Anvils with two shaped ends.
Metal components having a square shank for insertion into a hole in an anvil.
Anvils used in conjunction with dapping punches for depressing metal.
Hammers whose head is a distinctively shaped truncated cone which is set off balance on the narrow end of its handle; used to cut teeth in files.
Gravity powered drop hammers with boards that are engaged by contrarotating friction rollers.
Hammers having a hemispherical peen, the end opposite the hammering face.
Punches mounted on a handle; often used in conjunction with square and round punches in farriers' work.
Closing machines that roll together the rims and lids of metal cans to make a hermetic seal.
Stakes or small bench anvils having a slender horn on one side.
T-shaped creasing stakes having a different surface on each of the two arms. For example, one side of the T may be grooved or notched, while the other side may be flat or rounded.
Common form of chisel with a cutting edge of 60 degrees formed of tempered steel; used for cutting metal which has not been softened by heating.
Long, cold chisels having long tapers and narrow cutting edges; used for cutting keyways and the like.
Tools used for cutting horseshoe nails.
Tools or machinery used to grind and smooth glass.
A form of turret lathe usually having a hollow spindle through which a bar can be fed to be machined into bolts, studs, and other screws.
Large shears used in sheet metal work typically having one handle bent to go into a hole in the top of the workbench so that they rest on the surface when in use.
Cylinder-shaped taps used for cutting internal screw threads.
Curved stones used for sharpening gouges with an inside or an outside bevel.
Any of several styles of pliers that can be used for cutting, swaging, or hammering, as well as for gripping.
General term for tools and equipment used for bookbinding.

Refers to the temporary framework used to support a structure under construction until it is self-supporting. Distinct from "scaffolds," which are temporary structures for holding workers and materials.
Temporary construction, usually of wood, over which arches and vaults are formed and held until they become self-supporting.
Scaffolding supported by metal brackets which are temporarily attached to a building or column.
Machines that use weight, vibration, or a combination of both, to achieve compaction.
Concussive machinery or equipment designed to set, compact or level pavers in construction.
Power-driven tools used to compact soil or other granular material.
Self-propelled or towed drumlike rollers with projecting studs that penetrate the surface of the ground; used to obtain deep compaction of fill material.
Tractors with caterpillar treads, used to push away debris for clearing an area.
Bulldozers with blades are set on an angle.
Excavating machines used for cutting trenches with a boom-mounted bucket which is drawn through the ground toward the machine.
Heavy-duty four wheeled construction machines mounted with a scoop that excavate, load and transport loose materials such as sand, gravel, or dirt.
Self-propelled, power-operated machines used to excavate or load soil or debris.
Power shovels operated by steam from an integral boiler.
Mobile loaders that use a series of small buckets on a roller chain to elevate excavated dirt or rock to the dumping point.
Buckets used on cranes or derricks for handling granular materials. Their jaw-like halves close and open by cable or hydraulic action.

Cranes used in manufacturing or assembling heavy objects, composed of a bridge spanning two overhead rails and a hoisting device which moves laterally along the bridge. The bridge can move longitudinally along the rails.
Tower cranes which are mounted on crawlers, rubber tires, or rails.
Devices consisting of a vertical mast and a horizontal or sloping boom operated by cables to a separate engine or motor; used for hoisting and moving heavy loads or objects.
A derrick whose mast is held upright by guy cables attached to the top.
Derricks without a boom whose mast can lean in any direction. Loads are raised and lowered by ropes threaded through the top of the mast.
Mechanisms or apparatus as ropes and pulley blocks; used for hoisting, lowering, and shifting objects or materials.
Open-topped motor trucks having a body that can be tilted to discharge its contents, usually loose materials, through an open tailgate.
Extension ladders capable of reaching very high places; often mounted on a vehicle such as a fire truck.

Tools, consisting of wooden or metal rollers mounted on spindles and attached to frames and handles, used to produce the illusion of natural wood grain. Typically, an imitation wood grain pattern is cut or stamped on a leather or rubber band, which is then wrapped around the roller, fed with color, and applied to a surface by hand.
Brushes with a reservoir in their handle for ink or paint.
Edged equipment used manually or by means of a mechanical device that spread and level paving materials of various types.
Clamps used to hold books in place while being bound.
Presses used for stamping designs on a book cover.
Crayons made from powdered pigments, combined with non-oily binders and pressed into finger-length sticks.
Points or styluses of copper used as drawing instruments.
Pencils with lead of finely ground, highly compacted charcoal. Less messy, but not as versatile as charcoal sticks.
Grease pencils made especially for lithography.

Pens with a writing tip made of a metal ball that is housed in a socket, which allows the ball to rotate freely when pressed against a writing surface, releasing a quick-drying ink. The ball is constantly bathed in ink from a reservoir, one end of which is open and attached to the writing tip. Commercial models of the pen appeared in 1895 and it became popular beginning in the 1930s. It was first patented by Lázló Bíró.
Roller ball or ball-point writing implements that use an ink that suspends pigment in a water-based gel.
Small stumps of tightly rolled gray or white paper, usually pointed at one end only; used to blend charcoal and pastel.

Instruments consisting of a long horizontal bar on which two movable heads slide, one of which carries a pencil, and the other a pin or tracer; used to draw large circles or arcs of circles as for full-scale working drawings, cask gauging, or carpentry work.
Tools used as guides for ruling curves through a series of points.
Dividers with two legs pointed at both ends and joined near the center by a movable pivot that can adjust along a graduated scale for proportional measurements.
Soft, crumbly erasers made of natural rubber or caoutchouc.
Templates that govern the accurate matching cuts of corresponding pieces in dovetail joints.
Artists' brushes made of any flexible animal hair, such as red sable or squirrel.
Large round brushes that fan out to a flat end, used particularly in oil painting to soften or blend edges or textures; usually made of badger hair.
Large artists' brushes usually made of hair set into a fairly flat ferrule and round at the end; they are used for applying washes.
Large, usually round artists' brushes made with squirrel or badger hair, used for applying large amounts of watercolor and to blend and soften washes.
Palettes designed to be supported by the painter's forearm and larger than palettes held in the hand.

Lightproof boxes fitted with a lens through the aperture of which the image of an object is recorded on light-sensitive material such as film, or transformed into electrical impulses for direct transmission or for video recording.
Cameras of varied form designed to shoot images on frames of strip film 35mm wide.
Cameras that record an image in half of the area of the conventional 35mm film frame for still photography. The image area usually measures 18x24mm.
Cameras using a film format smaller than 35mm.

Cameras used to photograph television broadcasts onto motion picture film media, used before the advent of videotape. Kinescope cameras were mounted before a video monitor, and synchronized to the monitor's scanning rate. The format could be either 16mm or 35mm.

Devices combining an un-manned camera and a mechanism to trigger the capturing of a still or moving image. The triggering mechanism may comprise a motion sensor, an infrared sensor, or a light beam, or it may be mechanical, as when an animal tugs at bait or passes in proximity to the camera. An example of usage  is to capture pictures of animals in the wild.
Cameras which allow the user to see the exact image formed by the picture-taking lens, by means of a hinged mirror between the lens and film.

Stereoscopic cameras that made exposures on glass plates, and that could be transformed into stereo viewers by removing the shutter panel. Introduced in 1904 and used until the 1930s. These were marketed as cheaper alternatives to Verascopes, a similar device made by the same manufacturer.
Cameras with wide-angle lenses capable of producing oversized, wide-angle images of great depth and clarity.
Photographic accessories in the form of circular mounts that allow the attachment of filters, lenses, or other pieces of equipment to a camera body or to a lens itself.
Lenses that have no chromatic aberrations.
Lenses designed specifically for the highest quality reproduction of flat, two-dimensional originals; used mostly in the printing industry.
Long-focal-length lenses which enlarge distant subjects within their narrow angle of view.
Soft camel hair brushes used in lab work, photography, and photoengraving.

German Expressionism consisted of a number of related creative movements in Germany before the First World War that reached a peak in Berlin during the 1920s. These developments in Germany were part of a larger Expressionist movement in north and central European culture in fields such as architecture, dance, painting, and sculpture. Der Blaue Reiter was a group of artists who were part of German Expressionism. The term as it is applied to cinema may be considered a separate concept.
A mid-1940s precursor of Abstract Expressionism that itself was a transitional synthesis of various forms of abstraction with Surrealist automatism.
Branch of Symbolist movement and style inspired by and borrowing from Rosicrucian philosophy, traditions, and allegory.

Very generally the term covers from late prehistory to the time when Islam became the dominant religion and way of life in those areas of the world where, at various times after the early seventh century CE, a majority of the population or a preponderance of the ruling classes converted to Islam. It covers a wide and varied range of cultures, artistic traditions, and time periods, varying with the different times when Islam came to different regions and influenced and was influenced by different traditions.

Refers to the art and culture associated with the Islamic dynasty of this name that was founded in 750, when it overthrew the Umayyad caliphate. The Abbasids were a Meccan family descended from Abbas, Muhammad's uncle. Their headquarters were in Mesopotamia and they founded the city of Baghdad in 762.  Persian ideas prevailed during this period and the Abbasids ruled in great splendor as Oriental monarchs. Encouraging intense intellectual and artistic activity, many palaces and mosques were built and the production of luxury items became an industry. A unified style of art developed, inspired by ancient Persia rather than Christian Syria. The ruined city of Samarra, occupied by the Abbasids in the 9th century, is a prime example of this influence, especially in the Sassanian construction methods. Samarra is noted for its ornamental stucco, particularly the so-called 'bevelled' manner of decoration derived from Scythian-Siberian abstract design. Highly valued Chinese porcelain was imitated by potters of the period; the results were distinctly Islamic, however, with Arabic inscriptions and designs. Abbasid textiles also assumed an identifiable Islamic character. The vast empire became unwieldy and as its central administration weakened, rival caliphates were established. Although the Abbasids continued to rule part of the Islamic world until 1258, their dominance only lasted until the mid-10th century.
Pottery styles belonging to Abbasid cultures.
Painting styles belonging to Ayyubid cultures.
Pottery styles belonging to Fatimid cultures.

Refers to the style and period that coincided with the reign of Osman I, a Turkish ruler active in northwest Anatolia at the end of the 13th and beginning of the 14th centuries. His emirate took over the declining rule of the Saljuqs of Anatolia and was based on the concept of religious warfare. Under Osman I, the state expanded rapidly to the west over Byzantine territory in Thrace and the Balkans. Little is documented regarding the art of this period.
Pottery styles belonging to Samanid cultures.

Style and culture of the Arabatchi tribe. Typical of the style are rugs  characterized by a dark brown field, a part cotton weft and alternate warps which cause the back of the rugs to have a brown and white, speckled appearance.

Describes the culture and style of Aboriginal Australians and current inhabitants of Australia, such as rock art, sculpture in wood, clay and sand, body decoration and bark painting, created both before and after European colonization.

Describes the culture and style of the original inhabitants of Australia and their descendants. Traditional art forms are currently produced in most regions, but many contemporary Aboriginal artists, influenced by globalization, have begun to utilize a variety of media.
Describes the style and culture of the Aboriginal tribe that occupied a region in central Australia. Arunta painters tend to utilize engraved dots and flicks in their backgrounds.

Describes the style and culture of the inhabitants of the Fiji islands whose settlers are well known for their Lapita pottery. Fijian men tend to utilize wood as a primary medium during art production. Specialist Fijian carpenters produce sculptures, bowls, canoes, drums, weapons, headrests and ornaments. Late 20th-century Fijian art production includes traditional objects made for the craft market and local use, and 19th-century antique reproductions, as well as tourist art products.

Describes work created by a group of inhabitants of New Britain Island. The Baining people are well known for their masks and headdresses, which continue to be used in many areas of the New Britain Islands. The masks are conical in form and made of canes, poles, and barkcloth with white, black, and red designs, and are utilized in secretive male cults.

Describes the style and culture of the inhabitants of Irian Jaya. Most of the art of Irian Jaya comes from the coastal areas. Masks, ceremonial costume, and body paint design are very important art forms.
Describes the style and culture of the inhabitants of the Massim area.
Native styles belonging to Sepik cultures.
Describes works created by the people of Ambrym Island. The most well known artwork of the Ambrym people are distinctive woven penis wrappers.
Sculpture stules belonging to New Ireland cultures.

Describes the style and culture of the inhabitants of the Bougainville Islands. The people of Bougainville represent human and animal forms in naturalistic proportions and features, however human heads are also constructed in a canine-like style with the jaw protruded outward. Surfaces are often stained black and enhanced with inlaid patterns of red and white pigments. Decorative features in ceremonial structures are well known for demonstrating excellent carving techniques.

Describes the style and culture of the inhabitants of the Caroline Islands. The people of the Caroline Islands developed various art forms, such as canoe design, architecture, personal ornament, containers, tattoo, loom weaving and plait work; mostly objects of functional need and simplicity of form.
Describes the style and culture of the inhabitants of the Chuuk Islands. The Chuuk people ornamented their wooden bowls, canoe bows, and stern pieces with stylized sea bird and fish designs.

Describes the culture and nationality of the inhabitants of the Cook Islands. The people of the Cook Islands are known for their woodcarvings and sculpture, which were primarily used during traditional religious ceremonies. The sacred nature of the objects encouraged the carver to increase their durability in order to pass them on to future generations.

Describes the style and culture of the Mangaian people of Mangaia Island. The Mangaian are well known for incising in every decorated object a K-motif, which was made up of a dense pattern of crosshatching combined with zigzags and concentric diamonds.

Describes the style and culture of the Mangarevans. Few works of art created by the Mangaveran survive today due to their destruction by orders of missionaries in the 19th century. The few surviving sculptures and fragments demonstrate that the Mangareva figures are of a rectangular frame.

Describes the style and culture of the Maori aboriginal community, native inhabitants of modern New Zealand. Some of the more specialized forms of art for the Maori were architectural ornamentation, tattooing, dog skin and feather weaving and weaponry design. Since the islands settlement, their art has experienced much change.
Sculpture styles belonging to Maori cultures.

Describes the style and culture of the Tahitian people from Tahiti Island. The Tahitian people valued elegant and simple lines in their various types of artwork. It was customary for all Tahitian people to be tattooed distinguishing designs. They were utilized to visually state age and the social ranking of individuals. The tattoo designs were simple and contained bold geometric designs. The area of the buttocks was the most frequently tattooed.

A school of Chinese Buddhism probably dating to the 6th century that combines Mahayana teachings with those of Taoism to form a belief system emphasizing a meditative rather than an intellectual approach to enlightenment. It is closely related to Zen. The term can also be used to generally refer to meditation in Chinese Buddhism.

A school of Pure Land Buddhism in Japan which focuses on the mercy and power of Amida Buddha, the Buddha of infinite light and deep compassion. It is by the grace of Amida that one can be reborn into Amida's paradise or Pure Land, and from there one can eventually attain nirvana. The school was founded in 1175 by Honen, who emphasized the practice of 'nembutsu,' the repeated calling upon the name of Amida Buddha. Jodo is the second largest school of Pure Land in Japan.

A school of Jōdo-shū Buddhism founded by Bencho, a student of Honen who built Zendōji as a center for training in nembutsu in his hometown of Kyushu. There are many subdivisions of Chinzei, with Shirahata-ryū being the strongest ongoing group. Its center is at Chion-in but Zōjōji in Tokyo is also of special importance.

Refers to one of the two main branches of Zen. It originated in the Lin Chi school of Ch'an in China and was later introduced to Japan by Eisai in 1191. Rinzai stresses spontaneous enlightenment and advocates unusual ways of achieving it, such as shouts, slaps, and the use of koans. Rinzai downplays veneration of Buddha images and reading of scripture (sutras). After it was first introduced it appealed to the aristocracy and was supported by the shoguns. Later, Soto became the more popular form of Zen. Rinzai nevertheless flourished during the Kamakura period (1685-1768) during which Hakuin, a Rinzai master, introduced reforms that led to modern Zen.

The form of Buddhism practiced in the South Asian countries of Sri Lanka, Burma, Cambodia, Thailand, and Laos. Its doctrine, relatively unchanged since the 3rd century BCE, is based on the 'tipitaka' or Pali Canon and consists of a conservative interpretation of the Buddha's teachings. Theravada's main distinction from later Mahayana is its rejection of bodhisattvas. While the ultimate goal of Theravada is to become a 'perfected saint' or 'arhat,' lay believers cannot attain true enlightenment. True enlightenment is only reached by entering religious orders and even then it is nearly impossible for anyone to become a Buddha.

Refers to the school of Buddhism said to have been founded by the Chinese monk Hui Yuan (334-417) which became one of the most popular forms of Mahayana. Pure Land Buddhism advocates devotion to the bodhisattva Amitabha, who rules over a 'pure land.' Devotion to Amitabha can ideally lead to rebirth and enlightenment in this pure land. Pure Land Buddhism spread to Japan where it broke away from the main school and goes by the name Jōdo.

Body of several self-governing churches in Greece and elsewhere within the larger communion of Orthodox Eastern Christianity. The member communities have no obedience to a central authority: they conform in general to the liturgy and discipline of the Byzantine Rite, but look to their respective Holy Synods in their home countries for governing authority and direction. They have a liturgy traditionally conducted in Koine Greek, the original language of the New Testament, and they share a common Greek cultural tradition. The current territory of these churches covers the Eastern Mediterranean region that was formerly part of the Byzantine Empire, as well as newer churches established throughout the world.

Cultural movement encompassing DJing, rap and rap music, dance and dance music, graffiti writing, and styles of dress. The movement began in the 1970s, in the South Bronx section of New York City, a depressed, predominantly African American neighborhood. The popularity of rap music in particular throughout the 1980s to the present, helped turn hip-hop into an international movement.

Refers to certain Abstract Expressionist paintings. Use "Color-field" to encompass Abstract Imagist painting and the works of the 1960s derived from it, and "Action painting" for more spontaneous, gestural works of this era and genre.

French painting similar to American Action Painting, including that of the late 1940s sometimes called Abstraction Lyrique. Use "Lyrical Abstraction" for the continuation of Abstract Expressionism into the 1960s and 1970s (e.g., Guston, Frankenthaler).
Art in which the process of destruction of objects or materials within the work is regarded as the work, and especially work created in the 1960s related to a movement founded by Gustav Metzger.
Collections of equipment, instruments, machines, tools, parts, or other items used for a particular purpose.

Refers to the style of late Anglo-Saxon art that flourished during the ninth century and is named after the Trewhiddle Hoard from Cornwall, England. The style is characterized by its distinctive decoration with interlaced, contorted beasts and leafy scrolls, and in metalwork by the preference for silver rather than bronze.

Refers to the style that marks the traditioinal beginning of Gothic style in England around 1290, when Edward I erected a number of crosses, with distinctive ornamentation and architectural elements, to commemorate the queen, Eleanor of Castille. The term was coined in the early 19th century and then referred primarily to window tracery, but is now understood to apply to the style more broadly. The style has its roots in the royal London style and French Rayonnant Gothic, and is characterized by immense glazed surfaces, rectilinear apses, thick walls instead of the Continental buttressing system, and intricate decoration composed of lively geometric and organic forms.

Refers to the earlier phase of the decorated style in the late 13th century, when window tracery was composed of geometrical patterns such as circles, arcs of circles, and cusps, but before the patterns evolved into undulating curves.

Refers to the period and style associated with the Normans, who were Norsemen from Denmark, Norway, and Iceland who raided the European coasts in the eighth and ninth centuries CE, settled in northern France in the early tenth century, reigned over the indigenous Frankish population, adopted their language, and eventually founded the duchy of Normandy. From Normandy, the Normans expanded to the British Isles, southern Italy, and Sicily. The style is particularly evident in designs of weapons and armor, the motte-and-bailey castle, and grand Romanesque ecclesiastical and monastic structures. The style is characterized by the brilliant adaptation and exploitation of indigenous local styles combined with some influences of the Byzantine east, which were introduced to the area by Norman adventurers and pilgrims.
Architecture styles belonging to German Medieval cultures.

Refers to the culture of the modern nation of the Netherlands, or in general to cultures that have occupied the same area in northwestern Europe along the North Sea. It is often used to distinguish the culture of the northern historic Netherlands from "Flemish," which is the culture of the southern Netherlands or Flanders. It may also be used to refer in general to the culture of Germanic or Teutonic peoples; however, this meaning is seldom found in modern texts.

Refers to the style of art and architecture that flourished in Portugal and her colonies, beginning in the late 14th century and lasting into the mid-16th century. The style is named afer Manuel I, King of Portugal (ruled 1495-1521), and it developed as a national style and conscious rejection of Spanish style. The style is characterized by the merging of Late Gothic style with inventive references to Portuguese voyages, particularly in symbolism and lavish ornament. New themes include lush foliate and nautical designs, and references to the exotic, including Islamic art.

Refers to the period, culture, and style of art produced between the later eighth century and early 12th century in Scandinavia and Scandinavian settlements overseas. The term is derived from the old Norse noun "víkingr," and narrowly refers to sea pirates and raiders. However, it is usually applied to the broader realm of Scandinavian culture from this time period.

Refers to the style and culture of the Asturias region of northern Spain (modern Oviedo), particularly the cultures of the Medieval eighth- and ninth-century kingdom of Asturias. It is characterized by the retention and development of classical Roman forms and architectural techniques, anticipating the Romanesque style in Europe by two centuries. This style differs from contemporary Carolingian style in its distinct architectural iconography, often including walls of "petit appareil," stilted brick arches, ashlar quoins, and timber roofs with small barrel vaults over the apses.

Refers to the style and period associated with the penitentiary pilgrimages, the Crusades of 1096 to 1291, and subsequent settlement of European Christians in the Holy Land and eastern Mediterranean area through the 15th century. The style is characterized by the joining of European Romanesque and Gothic art and architecture with the local artistic traditions.

Refers to the intellectual movement, style, and culture that originated in Italy in the late 14th century, spread throughout Europe, and culminated in the 16th century. Style is characterized by a deliberate reference to the art, architecture, literature, and ideals of Classical Rome and Greece.

Refers to a style and a period in evidence approximately from the 1520s to 1590, developing chiefly in Rome and spreading elsewhere in Europe. The style is characterized by a distancing from the Classical ideal of the Renaissance to create a sense of fantasy, experimentation with color and materials, and a new human form of elongated, pallid, exaggerated elegance.

Culture, period, and styles in the British colonies, typically featuring a combination of British and native characteristics. For works produced in the British colonies of what is now the United States, "American Colonial" is generally used.

Period, culture, and English style of architecture and decorative arts produced during the reign of Elizabeth I between 1551 and 1603.  A combination of Gothic, Italian Renaissance, Flemish and French Mannerist, and vernacular styles, it is characterized by elaborate architectural silhouettes, elements suchs as finials, pendants, and strapwork and in decorative arts, rich surface ornamentation.
Period and English architectural style during the reigns of Charles I and Charles II between 1625 and 1685 and associated with red brick and hipped roof structures prominent between 1640 and 1670.
Style that reflects the cross-cultural influence between England and the Netherlands in art, architecture, or culture, primarily from the 15th through the 17th century.
Refers to the style of artistic production in French colonies featuring a combination of French and native characteristics.

Refers to a style of painting that developed in Regensburg, Germany, and elsewhere along the Danube river during the Renaissance and Reformation. It is characterized by a renewed interest in medieval piety, an expressive use of nature, the relationship of the human figure and events to nature, and the introduction of landscape as a primary theme in art. The term was coined by Theodor von Frimmel (1853-1928), who believed that painting in the Danube River region around Regensburg, Passau, and Linz possessed common characteristics; the style seems to exist even though leading artists did not form a school in the usual sense of the term, since they did not work in a single workshop or in a particular center. Major artists whose work represents the style include Lucas Cranach the elder and Albrecht Altdorfer.

Refers to the style of 18th-century Italian architecture and sculpture associated with the Rococo and characterized as lighthearted, imaginative, elegant and decorative.  Sculpture features dramatic gestures, open poses, and sweeping drapery as with the work of Camillo Rusconi, whose sculptural compositions portray an unorthodox sense of playfulness and intimacy.

Refers to the Italian style of pottery produced in the region of Abruzzo in the 17th and 18th centuries.  Initially derivative of istoriato ware, the style developed local character with the use of naturalistic colors such as olive green, brown, and yellow, and religious, mythological, and landscape themes based on the work of Baroque artists.

Refers to the style of art and architectural ornament seen primarily in the late 17th through late 18th centuries, principally in Spain and its American colonies. The style is named after the family of Madrid architects, particularly Jose de Churriguera, though other architects also contributed to the development and popularization of the style. The style is characterized by an abundance of ornament and detail, combining various elements from earlier Mannerist and Baroque art.

Refers to the first distinct phase of of Spanish Plateresque style, starting in the late 15th century. It is characterized by a merging of Flamboyant Gothic and traditional Spanish styles. The style overlaps with Isabelline.

Refers to the early period of the Renaissance, when the style developed in Central Italy in the mid- to late fourteenth century and spread throughout the peninsula and to northern Europe in the early to mid-15th century. The style moved away from the fantastic, decorative styles of the Medieval period to place new emphasis on the idealized naturalistic world portrayed in the art, architecture, and literature of Classical Greece and Rome.
Refers generally to the beginning of the Baroque style and period, particularly the Italian Baroque from about 1585 to 1625.

Style identified retroactively to describe works of the late 17th and 18th centuries. Considered a modification of the Baroque, and often appearing in autocratic monarchies of France and Britain, where the original excesses of the Baroque are lessened and elements of classical antiquity are re-established.
Includes works influenced by the architectural style of Andrea Palladio; excludes works by Palladio himself.

Refers to a style that employs a particular type of ornament and was popular in 17th-century Europe. It is characterized by lobate scrolls, embossed relief work, and plastic, curvilinear, rippling forms that can resemble a human ear, to which the name refers. It developed in Utrecht, the Netherlands, in the early 17th century. The style may be seen in various art forms, but was most often used in metalwork. The style is derived from 16th-century graphic works of the Italian Mannerists, although the Dutch goldsmiths Adam and Paulus van Vianen are often credited with its invention.

Refers to a style of blue-and-white pottery decoration done in Italy beginning in the 15th century in imitation of Damascus wares. This decorative technique developed in response to the popularity of imported East Asian pottery. Sometimes the term is used synonymously with "alla porcellana" which is better described as a different type of decoration.

Refers to maiolica with usually polychrome decorations of historical, mythological, Biblical, or allegorical scenes painted over most of the surface. It was first produced about 1500 and is associated with Urbino. The earliest examples were decorated only in the well of plates and dishes; later the decoration extended to the entire inner surface. Images were often derived from works of contemporary artists, notably those reproduced in the engravings of Marcantonio Raimondi.

Austrian variation of Art Nouveau, derived from architect Joseph Olbrich's exhibition hall for the Wiener Sezession.  Associated mainly with architects and designers, the style reflects less the serpentine line and organic forms of the Art Nouveau and shows a more geometric quality influenced by the work of Charles Rennie Mackintosh.

Refers to the style identified with Scottish-born architect Robert Adam (1728-1792), prevalent in Great Britain from 1760-1790. Inspired by archaeological discoveries in Herculaneum and Pompeii, the Adam style is characterized by austere but refined Classical forms, symmetry, detail, and geometric precision.

Refers to the English style of architecture, interior design, and decorative arts from the 1830s to the 1860s, drawn from the Elizabethan period of the sixteenth century.  Architects adopted a range of Elizabethan architectural forms including gables, octogonal turrets and lead-paned windows, while designers applied cinquefoils, strapwork, and coats of arms to furniture, silver, and ceramics.
Style of 19th-century architecture and other art that uses elements of Elizabethan and Gothic style.
