Now refers to covered shopping malls that architecturally resemble or were inspired by Italian gallerias. The term is also used to describe areas of a department store that are designed so as to appear to contain a number of separate shops.
Buildings that house businesses that sell antiques, which are artifacts created or produced in former periods and considered to have value.
Shops or small stores where baked goods are displayed and sold; usually the items are baked on the premises, but typically out of view of the customers.

Buildings housing businesses that comprise a series of stores which belong to one firm, and sell the same type of merchandise. Series of stores which belong to one firm, and sell the same type of merchandise.

Buildings housing businesses specializing in drapery and dry goods, prevalent in the early 19th century, which, contrary to standard merchandising practices of the day, kept large stocks of goods on the premises, grouping related items together in departments.
Buildings housing sales enterprises associated with and usually owned and operated by a company for the convenience of employees, who are often required to shop there.

Built works housing small, upscale specialty businesses generally specializing in fashionable clothing or accessories or a special collection of other merchandise; may also be used for individual departments within larger stores if featuring a similar line of goods.
Facilities used for receiving and transmitting information.
Broadcasting studios designed for radio programs; for larger facilities, including offices and equipment, from which the transmissions are sent and received, use "radio stations."
Studios designed or used for creating audio recordings, such as tape and electronic recordings.
Broadcasting stations for sending and receiving radio programming transmissions; for rooms and spaces designed for the origination or recording of radio programs, use "radio studios."
Microwave communications stations capable of boosting an incoming weak signal for retransmission on another frequency.
Railroad signal towers that are of modest size and house-like in form.
Structures or other places of adode; in a legal sense, a domicile is the primary dwelling of a person, their fixed or permanent location.
Houses with steep gable roofs that extend to ground level on two sides; constructed mostly for vacation and second homes.
Masonry, corbel-domed huts found from the Medieval period in Ireland and possibly built to house hermit monks.
Ancient Roman houses or similarly styled houses containing internal courtyards with impluvia but without colonnades; for houses with internal courtyards having colonnades, use "peristyle houses."
Sloping channels through which coal can descend, either on a small scale into the basement of a home or on a large scale in an industrial facility.
In Indian architecture, a gallery; fore-hall, lobby, verandah; oblong forehall or fore-lobby.
In Indian architecture, the forehall.
Circulation spaces that run the center length of religious or secular buildings that have oblong plans. Central aisles often bisect rows of pews or seating.

Very small courts that are enclosed within the walls of a building and supply ventilation to windows. Prefer "light courts" for somewhat larger courts supplying significant light as well as ventilation, or courts supplying only light.

Stairwells equipped with a system that prevents stairwells in highrise buildings from becoming smoke-filled in case of fire. Stairwells are pressurized by using fans or otherwise forcing fresh outside air through air ducts in the building's exterior walls and down the stairwell shafts. As the system pumps increasingly more air into the stairwells, the air pressure rises until it is greater than the air pressure on the building's floors. Given that stairwell doors must open into stairwells in the direction of egress from the building interior, standards are typically in place to regulate the pressure so that it is not too great to prevent ease of opening.

Display and study spaces providing artists, especially new, emerging artists, the opportunity to exhibit their works outside the traditional gallery and museum context. These are usually small-scale, independent areas administered by artists for the exhibition of work that is often experimental and outside mainstream art movements.
Places where automobiles are displayed and sold; may include single buildings as well as complexes with sales-and-service buildings and surrounding lots.
Large rooms, halls, or apartments designed or used for festive or state functions.
Areas on military bases that serve chiefly as dining halls, rooms or separate buildings.
Ancient Greek dining halls where important guests and visitors were invited to take a sacred meal.
Rooms designed for or used to contain a bed or beds for sleeping.

Ancient Roman domestic spaces often considered sleeping chambers, but that may also have functioned as social spaces for more private activities such as polytheistic worship, study, or other personal or intimate uses of the householder.

Rooms or areas in domestic architecture set aside for the care of babies and young children, distinguished from "night nurseries," which contain only bedding and supplies for nighttime care. Day nurseries typically serve as playrooms and schoolrooms. They are also distinguished from "day care centers," which are public or private facilities for the care of groups of children, while the day nursery is in the children's home.

Relatively small, private rooms, often adjacent to bedrooms in great houses, serving as sitting rooms, rooms for dressing, study, devotion, or private meetings, and, during certain periods, often containing collections of curiosities and art objects.

Hypostyle halls, such as a palace or audience hall, typically of stone construction with columns, in Persia or other places. Examples are reception halls in the palaces of Achaemenid rulers at Susa and Persepolis distinguished by six rows of six columns and three columned porticos, each with two rows of six columns. These structures may have functioned as audience halls for the king's court and visiting foreign vassals and ambassadors.
Living spaces open in part to the outdoors.
Lounges reserved for privileged and important individuals.
Recreation rooms devoted entirely to table games.

Drawing rooms in private houses as distinguished from a 'salon de famille;' designated as a meeting place for guests and found only in houses where the primary drawing room is so large that a more intimate space is required.
Rooms or sets of rooms for the systematic maintenance and storage of records and documents.
In Indian architecture, a storeroom.
Service rooms between kitchens and dining rooms, typically equipped with counters, a sink, and storage space for china and silver.
In Indian architecture, the place for cooking food, the kitchen.
Offices spaces occupied by architects and their associates.
Spaces provided for the boilers used for heating, ventilation, or power generation.
Small buildings that contain equipment and tools and in which goods are manufactured or repaired within the context of a private domicile.
Includes spaces in rooms as well as rooms and buildings where blood or blood plasma is collected, processed, stored, and distributed.
Areas in hospitals for critically ill patients requiring especially close surveillance and special life-support equipment.
Intensive care units devoted to the treatment of burn victims.
In Indian architecture, the cloister of a mālikā.
Semicircular or polygonal circulation spaces enclosing an apse or a straight-ended sanctuary.
In Indian architecture, a sanctuary.
Small apses, especially those which project from a larger apse.
Inner narthexes where there is also an outer narthex (the exonarthex).
Sacristies in Orthodox Eastern and Byzantine churches.
Small inner rooms adjacent to or within the naos, found in some ancient temples.
Spaces in theaters used to seat or contain audiences.
Stages of ancient Greek and Roman theaters. For the stage podiums of ancient Roman theaters, use "pulpita." For the areas of modern theaters nearest the audience, use "forestages."
Floor of a building that is partially both below and above ground level, and lacking an entrance at that level.
Cellars in which beer is stored.

A general term used to refer to freestanding buildings, components of buildings, complexes of buildings, other structures, or a man-made environment, typically large enough for humans to enter, serving a practical purpose, being relatively permanent and stable, and usually considered to have aesthetic value.

Refers to constructions of any kind artificially fabricated of parts joined together in some definite manner and which may or may not provide enclosure or shelter. Includes not just buildings, but other structures, for example oil wells, bridges, docks, and railroads. The term normally applies to structures built by humans, but may also apply to those built by other species.
Painted buildings, referring to the painted design on a tecpan (palace) in postclassic central Mexico.
Structures, generally enclosed, that are used or intended to be used for sheltering an activity or occupancy.
Buildings of five stories or fewer accessible by stairs only; commonly applied to apartment houses and some commercial buildings.
In Indian architecture, a seven-storeyed structure, the quality of having seven stories.

Lou is generally understood to mean a multi-story building (two stories or more) or a loft-building (Kroll 2015, 281) elevated on a terrace or city wall. Historically, lou as a type of traditional architecture usually designates a building elevated either by means of multiple stories or man-made or natural platforms. The Eastern Han dynasty (25-220 CE) classic Shuowen jiezi defines lou as a structure with a layered wu 屋 (a roof, or a roofed structure).
In Indian architecture, a seven-storeyed (gōpura) structure.

High-rise buildings usually in tower form with apartments or offices grouped around a central circulation core; use when distinguishing from "slab blocks" which are more like rectangular slabs in form.
In Indian architecture, works that have multiple spires, in the Nāgara śikhara style.

Huts of variable plan constructed of dry-laid masonry walls and domed roofs; found in rural areas of Provence, France, of generally indeterminate date from the prehistoric period until the 19th century CE; may also have had agricultural uses.
Free-standing structures for individually sponsored exhibits at trade fairs, international expositions, or other venues such as national parks.
In Indian architecture, a rounded astragal.
In Indian architecture, a down-turned minor cyma molding.
In Indian architecture, a cyma-recta at base of adhiṣṭhāna.
In Indian architecture, a type of āliṅga band or fillet, usually carved, such as at the base of a wall or other element.
Small moldings having a rounded, convex section. The term can also loosely refer to the glazing bars of case furniture.
In Indian architecture, a type of ovolo molding.
Moldings of nearly circular cross section with narrow bands or fillets on the face.
Molded bases, in Indian architecture, a molded lower element, such as in South India, the moldings below a wall-frieze.
Ornamental treatments used over openings such as doors or windows, and composed of ogee arches the apex of which extends upward to form an ornamental finial.
Wooden strips, plain or molded, that cover joints, as in paneling.
Struck moldings which are terminated short of the end of the member into which they are cut.
Short, straight billets or portions of molding usually of rounded section forming the zigzag molding in Romanesque architecture; for the complete molding, use 'zigzag moldings.'
Brackets projecting from the intersection of two walls; when on the exterior, often to support a cornice; when on the interior, often to support a rafter.
Fixed ornamental corbels of inverted conical or pyramidal form, resembling in simple shape the bottoms of ancient lamps.
In Indian architecture, the octagonal rising towers in śikhara Hindu temples.
Ovens having a fan that circulates hot air uniformly and continuously around.
Embankments, trestles, or other structures that provide access at either end of a bridge.
The enclosed open spaces within castles; especially applied to Medieval fortifications; sometimes also used to refer to the outer walls of such spaces.
Refers to the spaces between an inner wall and a keep in a castle.

Norman keeps, usually on the sites of older structures, and consisting of a stone wall on top of a motte, or steep mound. Within this wall, or shell, other buildings were contructed, using the wall as support, leaving an open courtyard in the center. A successor to the motte-and-bailey castle.
Outworks in Medieval fortifications, such as gate towers, but more frequently an advance work used to flank the approach to a gateway.
The moats surrounding the main ramparts of fortifications.
Small ravelins.
Fountains for ritual cleansing, usually associated with religious buildings.

Low rails or barriers in front of the altar of a church, intended to separate the sanctuary of the church from the body of the church, also separating the officiating clergy from the other worshippers.
In ancient Rome, a small, portable altar where perfumes were burnt, placed before the dead.

General term for poles, staffs, or pillars located at or incorporated in the altar, used in several religions globally. Examples are wooden poles surmounted by metal toppers, used in processions to the altar and then placed at the altar during a liturgy or ceremony.
Altar rails at which communicants receive the sacrament of Holy Communion in Christian churches.

Multi-panelled sanctuary screens like those used in the Eastern Orthodox church, but on a small scale. Used in private devotion in a family chapel, in private homes, or for travel. The depiction of saints matched that of the church iconostasis.

A fixed stand with a guardrail situated at the entrance to the chancel. Often found in pairs: the one at the North side is used to read the Gospel, the one at the South side is for the Epistle. It may have one or several bookrests, and may be used as a pulpit.
In mosques, high podiums on columns from which the celebrant's assistant repeats his Koran readings and gestures for the more distant worshippers.
Short sections of road that allow vehicles to enter or exit a controlled-access roadway .
Publicly accessible receptacles into which flat mail such as letters is deposited for retreival by mail delivery personnel.
Road arrangements, resembling four-leaf clovers in plan, for permitting easy traffic movement between intersecting highways.
Road junctions that permit vehicles to pass from one road to another by a system of separate levels.
Driving lanes added beside through-traffic lanes to allow vehicles to speed up for merging.

Generally includes the HVAC and plumbing of buildings or complexes; in some contexts may also include electrical systems and electricity-based systems, such as protection systems and communication systems.
Chimneys containing a number of flues, especially when rising as shafts above a roof.
Metal lintels that support the masonry above fireplace openings.
Chimney pots of long and slender form, intended to improve the draft.
Single, large stones forming the floors of fireplaces.
Building spaces that are covered, and located on the exterior of the buildings.
Rooms in buildings specifcally used for gatherings or meetings.
Prison cells generally in the form of shafts with openings only at the top; often concealed pits below the floor.
Galleries appropriated to a choir.
Use to designate small recessed spaces off of larger rooms.
Alcoves or small room openings off the atrium of an ancient Roman house.

Complete self-contained apartment units or extensions to a house created within, or with minor exterior additions to existing single-family homes, usually with their own separate entrances and generally for relatives of the homeowners.
Booths where art works or goods are exhibited or sold.
Refers to the outer or lesser courts of mansions or castles.
Refers to the colonnaded forecourts of Early Christian churches.

Literally meaning “dew terrace” or “exposed terrace” (Kroll 285; 440), a lutai is a raised platform within a building complex. In the literature of the Han and Tang dynasties, lutai referred specifically to a structure built by Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty. The term later appeared in a large number of Song dynasty texts to indicate a space for the performance of theater, music, and dance in cities, private gardens, and temples, as well as the places at which sacrifices were made to the gods. There are also a few records that refer to the platform of the ramp of the city gate as a lutai (Li 2009,15.3b).
Porches, usually attached to residential buildings, that are enclosed with small mesh screening between the columns or pillars, to permit ventilation but bar insects.
Circular, projecting porticoes.
High stoops making a quarter turn, reached by a flight of stairs along a building front.
In barns or stables, individual compartments in which an animal may move about freely.
Separate sections of large homes that  contain the private rooms of the family.

Rooms containing a bathtub or shower, and usually a toilet and lavatory; for rooms containing only a toilet and lavatory, use "lavatories (rooms);" for public facilities containing toilets and lavatories, use "rest rooms."
Includes both passages between sections of seats and the side divisions of buildings where the interior is divided into parts by columns or piers.
In Indian architecture, a wall-pilaster.
Lesenes at the edges of a façade.
In Indian architecture, a angular subdivision of the karṇa.
Secondary, and often inconspicuous back doors or gates, especially to fortified or walled enclosures; may also be used for minor, private or side entrances.
Doors, windows, hatches, or other openings leading to the outside, usually kept closed and locked, and used chiefly for emergencies when conventional exits fail or become inaccessible.

Streams of high-velocity, temperature-controlled air which are directed downward across an opening to prevent transfer of heat across it, thus making it possible to air condition a space having an open entrance.
In Indian architecture, eight-jambed doorframe.
In Indian architecture, the intermediate band or innermost jamb of a doorframe.
In Indian architecture, a lintel, beam; door-architrave or door-lintel; pataṅga.
In Indian architecture, a threshold; doorsill; bhuvaṅga.

Sliding decorative doors or panels that are the sole entrance to a concealed area in a shoin-style building. The term literally means "sleeping-room fixture." May be used to refer to the doorways rather than the panels themselves.
Doors, usually small, opening through a finished construction, as into a duct or wall, and used to provide a means of inspection of equipment or services housed behind.
Openings in half-doors, giving entrance to a pantry and over which are served out the contents of the pantry.
Doors that slide into a recess in a wall.
Flush doors with a space between the facings that is occupied by a structure of air- or insulation-filled cells, made of wood, plastic, or other suitable material.
Frames that line or finish a doorway.
Small or relatively insubstantial gates or door-like structures.
Posts on which gates are hung.
Windows, either single or in a series, forming a bay or recess in a room and projecting outward from the wall in a rectangular, curved, or polygonal form.
Bay windows that are curved in plan.
Show-windows that project outward from the principal plane of a building.
Windows having a sash that opens on hinges attached to the upright side of the frame.
In Indian architecture, a window.
Windows consisting of a series of horizontal glass louvers that pivot simultaneously in a common frame.
In Indian architecture, a type of window opening.
Valances consisting of lengths of fabric draped around or from a rod, pole, or mounting board; used either with curtains or alone.
Windows made of composite material such as fiberglass and resin compounds or chemically–bonded blends of wood and plastic resins.
The upper horizontal cross members or decorative elements of window frames.

Window sills in a brick or stone wall, where the sill extends beyond the width of the window opening and with the ends of the sill set in the wall. Distinguished from "slip sills" which are just as long as the window is wide and fit into the walls between the jambs.
Glazing quarries, often square or diamond-shaped, having a pattern or design impressed, painted, or fired upon them.
Trim or casings around the sides and top of a rectangular opening, having a molded form similar to an architrave.

Da'e, literally "great forehead" (Kroll 2015, 73, 99) is usually used to refer to over-sized column-top tie beams often found in the timber architecture of Shanxi and Shaanxi constructed during the Yuan period (thirteenth-fourteenth centuries). As an architectural term, da’e is only recorded in the Yingzao fashi, but it is not clearly defined. Based on the context in which the term is used, it is possible that da’e is an alternate name for lan’e 闌額. This is because it is often used together with yan’e 簷額 and you’e 由額 where the term lan’e would normally appear. Still, nothing in the Yingzao fashi indicates that this so-called da’e is a larger size version of lan’e. In a seminal article, the twentieth-century architectural historian Zhang Yuhuan used this term to describe huge longitudinal beams found in Yuan timber architecture in Shanxi and Shaanxi. Since that time many modern scholars consider it to be the signature element of the so-called “da’e style” buildings of the Yuan dynasty. Da’e can be placed either under the eaves or inside the building, but must be parallel to the roof ridge as part of the zongjia 縱架. Some scholars believe that the Yuan dynasty da’e are equivalent to the yan’e in the Yingzao fashi, while others disagree.
Louvers which combine both horizontal and vertical shading, to control both high and low sun, and reflect daylight into the interior space.

Window shutters having a vertical folding blade system in a frame, designed to cover a large expanse quickly. An example of such shutters is for hurricane protection. For window coverings with lighter weight vertical slats attached only at the top, use "vertical blinds."
Openwork of molded mullions that divide a window into lights in decorative patterns; common in the Gothic style.
Tracery in which continuous compound or ogee curves predominate.
In late 13th- and early 14th-century Gothic tracery, lancet-shaped openings pointed at the foot, rounded or pointed at the head, and cusped inside.

Inclined surfaces designed to facilitate launching of an object, such as missiles or rockets; boats into the water; vehicles or goods onto boats, trains or trucks; targets for trap shooting; or the launching of any other object.
Specially constructed stairs which can be folded and swung upward into a space in the ceiling when not in use.
Stairs with one flight up from the lower floor to the landing and two flights from the landing to the next floor.
Halfpace stairs which have no well hole between successive flights; the rail and balusters of the upper and under flights fall in the same vertical plane.
Stairs in which two spiral stairs are intertwined, one of the most famous examples being the central staircase at the Château of Chambord.

Equipment that provides a means for passengers and aircraft personnel to traverse between aircraft doors and the ground or another surface outside the vehicle. These may be towed, self-propelled, or in some cases are integral to the aircraft.
Pieces of lumber protruding from a wall to support carriage pieces or strings of a wooden stair at their upper ends or at landings.
Posts located at the landing points of stairs and supporting handrails.
In Indian architecture, a semicircular ornamental step with a half-moon shape used at shrine portals. Literally, 'moonstone,' in Indian architecture; ardhacandra; moonstone; asvapada.
Steps, usually the lowest in a flight, having one or both ends rounded to a semicircle and projecting beyond the face of the stair string and the newel.
The overhanging, usually half-round, edges of the treads of steps.
Series of winders arranged so that the small ends of the steps are not much narrower than the parallel steps of the same stair.
Outer strings on stairs, usually of better material or finish than the carriage pieces which they cover; may be part of the actual construction or applied to the face of the supporting member.
Strings which have the upper edge notched, or otherwise worked to the shape of the steps, so that treads and risers are supported by and overlap the step-shaped edge.
In brickwork, raked joints used with bricks of rough texture.

Flexible mechanical joints that allow the axis of one part to be set at an angle to the other by virtue of the design of the two components. One possesses a fixed spherical shell to accommodate the ball-shaped end of the other.
Moldings which are nailed, laid on, or otherwise fastened to the work rather than cut into the solid material.
Moldings cut into, rather than added to or applied to, a member.
In Indian architecture, an inverted cyma moulding bearing lotus-petal ornamentation.
Common Norman moldings consisting of a series of billets which are cylindrical in cross section, usually staggered in alternate rows.
Beveled moldings, either having a beveled back for nailing into a corner or angle, or one whose face or profile is a cant or oblique surface.

Pavements that maintain intimate contact with and distribute loads to the subgrade and depend for stability on aggregate interlock, particle friction, and cohesion; for pavements that are more rigidly bonded, use "rigid pavements."
Meaning, literally, "without shaliangtou." See shaliangtou 厦兩頭
Roofs in which the slope is broken, the lower slope being steeper than the upper slope; may be two-sided or four-sided roofs.
Roofs formed by the junction of two gable roofs with a valley between them, resembling the letter M in section.
Roofs pyramidal in form, or with a very short ridge so as to be nearly pyramidal. Roofs pyramidal in form, or with a very short ridge so as to be nearly pyramidal.
Mansard roofs in which the lower slope is nearly vertical, the upper slope nearly horizontal. Mansard roofs in which the lower slope is nearly vertical, the upper slope nearly horizontal.
Awnings drawn over outdoor theaters or amphitheaters as protection from the rain or sun.
Exterior parts or components of roofs.

In Indian architecture, a antefix above the roof of the kapilī; forward-drawn fronton or antefix of a vimāna-superstructure (Karṇāṭan, North Indian) occurring above the kapilī-walls; antefix at the front of the superstructure.
Small, unglazed dormer windows used to provide light and ventilation in an attic or space below a sloping roof; especially used in Medieval buildings.
Gabled dormers in which the gable is treated as a pediment.
Eaves in which the supporting members are enclosed and therefore not visible.
In Indian architecture, a projection of the eave.
Finials used in Islamic architecture, typically found atop a minaret, dome, or minber, usually tipped with a crescent.

Watertight membranes, along roofs or other flat surfaces, that turn up against and cover the intersection with vertical surfaces, such as chimneys or parapets; the exposed upper edge is normally covered by counterflashing.

Gables having an underlying triangular or rectangle form with curved sides; so-named because they resemble the cross-section of a bell or a 17th-century mantle clock. If the gable is surmounted by a pediment, it is often called a "Dutch gable."
Stones which form the sloping edge of a gable built of masonry.
In Maori buildings, facing boards on the gable of a house; the lower ends are often ornamented with carving.
Octagonal spires rising from a square tower without an intervening parapet, the four angles of the tower being covered by corner segments of a pyramid seeming to penetrate the tower.
Complex spirelet with several miniature aṇḍaka-spirelets.
Parallel sloping members that support the roof covering.
In Indian architecture, a circular purlin; circular roof-covering; rafters.

Pingbanfang is a tie beam with a rectilinear section that is placed on top of the pillar top tie beam (e’fang 額枋) to support dougong 斗栱 bracket sets (Liang 1981, 77). The term pingbanfang is equivalent to the Song dynasty term pupaifang and is most commonly found in the Gongcheng zuofa (1734) and other books published in the Qing dynasty. Architectural historians use this term to describe buildings from the Ming and Qing dynasties.

Rafters which are at right angles to the eaves of a roof and extend from the plate to the ridgeboard. Rafters which are at right angles to the eaves of a roof and extend from the plate to the ridgeboard.
Jack rafters that extend from a valley rafter to a ridgeboard.

As an architectural term, caojia (literally “draft frame,” Kroll 2015 34, 194), primarily appears in technical manuals such as the Yingzao fashi(1103), Yuanye 園冶 (1631), and Yingzao fayuan 營造法原 (1959). It refers to the roof frame between the interior ceiling (the pingqi 平棊 in Yingzao Fashi and the xuan 軒 or juan 卷 in mansion-hall style architecture of Jiangnan area in Ming and Qing dynasties) and the roof, which is left rough (hence the term “draft”) because it is not visible to the viewer (Chen 2010, 259; Yao 1986, 116).
Vertical members connecting the apex of a triangular truss, as in a roof, with the base. Vertical members connecting the apex of a triangular truss, as in a roof, with the base.
Walls to which battens have been affixed.
Walls having the primary purpose of serving to that separate, keep apart, demarcate, or serve as deterrents.
Walls, usually of concrete, built as fortifications specifically to prevent the progress of armored combat vehicles.

Mamian 馬面, literally "horse face," is a defensive structure within a traditional Chinese city wall. The mamian is prominent on the outer surface of the wall and can be taller than or equal to the height of the city wall. According to literature and archeological evidence, most mamian are solid masonry. It is named for its narrow façade and long shape like a horse head. Its main function was to increase the defensive capacity of the city wall by eliminating blind corners, which were vulnerable to attacks from the side. Mamian also played a role in strengthening the city wall. Mamian were clearly defined in texts as early as the Song dynasty and remained in use through the Qing dynasty.
Steps made on the ramparts of works near the parapets, for the troops to stand upon, in order to fire over the parapet.
In Indian architecture, a corner bastion.
Chambers in outer fortification elements with openings for the firing of artillery. These are designed to be difficult to see and hard to strike from the forecourt.
Batteries flanking a part of a fortification.
In Indian architecture, a rampart; surrounding wall.
In Indian architecture, the inner or sanctum wall.
In Indian architecture, an outer wall.

Refers to façades extending beyond, especially above, the dimensions of a building with the specific purpose of giving a more imposing appearance; for façades which exceed the height or width of buildings but not with that intention, use "screen façades."

Interior walls separating one portion of a space from another; sometimes permanent inside walls that divide buildings into various rooms, sometimes designed to move aside and open up a space. For entities other than walls that divide interior spaces, often incorporating bookshelves, cabinets, or drawers, use "room dividers."
Nonloadbearing partitions made of prefabricated sections that can be readily disassembled and relocated.

Literally meaning "bay-dividing plank partition" (Kroll 2016), scholars generally agree that jiejian banzhang 截間版帳 is a room dividing partition, and some scholars believe that it is a partition specifically running perpendicular to the main roof ridge (Zhao 2005, 102). The term is only found in Yingzao fashi 營造法式 (1103; Li 2009, 6.6a), and is considered to be a type of xiaomuzuo 小木作 (fine carpentry or joinery). According to the description in the Yingzao fashi, jiejian banzhang is six to ten feet high and is composed of planks or boards (ban 版) and covering strips (yatou hufeng 牙頭護縫), which can be used on both sides of the board. These components are fixed by a board casing (nanzi 難子) between the columns. If the jiejian banzhang is more than seven feet high, column-top-ties (e’fu 額栿) along with posts (tuanzhu 摶柱), and a waist bar (yaochuan 腰串) should be added to the framework. If its width is wider (or deeper) than usual, a bay muntin (qianzhu 槏柱) should also be added.

Nonbearing walls supported by the members of a rigid frame structure, such as a reinforced concrete or steel frame, and therefore serving to enclose but not to support. Nonbearing walls supported by the members of a rigid frame structure, such as a reinforced concrete or steel frame, and therefore serving to enclose but not to support.

Curtain walls assembled from highly similar components, each combining two or more of the traditionally separate elements of windows, external finish wall, internal finish wall, and insulation. Curtain walls assembled from highly similar components, each combining two or more of the traditionally separate elements of windows, external finish wall, internal finish wall, and insulation.
Large aedicules that elevate and surround the altarpiece or altar sculptures behind the altar.
Arcades closed at the back and serving only as decorative features.
Very small balconies, usually not large enough to stand on and consisting of little more than a protective railing.

In traditional Chinese fortifications, die refers to the battlements built on the top of a city wall constructed to protect defenders from missile fire. This term already appears in the literature of the Pre-Qin period (e.g. “In the standards of city wall building, the wall should be [built to the] height of 30 feet, die should be added to the top, and the width should be ten feet 行城之法。高城三十尺。上加堞。廣十尺,” from Mozi, Chapter 14, Beiti). The element is also referred to as zhidie 雉堞, nütouqiang 女頭墻, and duokouqiang 垛口墻 in different traditional textual sources.
Bondstone which extends completely through the entire thickness of a masonry wall and is exposed on both wall faces.
In Indian architecture, a colonnade around a courtyard.
In Indian architecture, a rectilinear band, such as used in the adhiṣṭhāna (pedestal or base of a structure) or the blocking or finishing course of masonry on a wall, such as above a cornice.
Stringcourses of bricks laid diagonally so that one corner projects from the face of the wall.
In Indian architecture, a bay formed by pillars.
Two wings (usually) running at right angles to each other.
In Indian architecture, the ground floor.
Fittings or panels in a kitchen or bathroom designed to shield walls and appliances from splashed liquid or food debris.
In Indian architecture, a niche at the central offset.
In Indian architecture, an attached or appliquéd parapet.
Pediments whose lines are interrupted either at the apex or the base, or in both locations; found especially on Late Antique, Baroque, and Mannerist architecture, and on Chippendale furniture.
Broken pediments both in furniture and architecture, with s-shaped sides terminating in inwardly facing scrolls and separated at the center point often by a finial or urn.
Expanding vaults in which the smaller base is semicircular, the larger base semielliptical. Expanding vaults in which the smaller base is semicircular, the larger base semielliptical.

Vaults consisting or solid concave-sided semicones, meeting or nearly meeting at the apex of the vault, the areas between cones being flat, and the whole being given a highly decorative treatment with ribs that fan out from the vault's springing.
The ridges or edges formed by the intersection of the surfaces of two or more intersecting vaults.
The courses of vault ribs at the point where the ribs begin to spring and separate from the wall bonding; the point of the vault's maximum outward thrust.

Metal or wooden bars, rods, or framing used to consolidate and reinforce buildings or other structures. Uses include sustaining slender columns, as the supporting framework for a tent, canopy, or hanging members, and in tracery. For the skeletons or framework that support the plastic material of sculptures during modeling, use "armatures (sculpture components)."

Jianzhuzao, literally translated as "reduced-column construction" or "column-elimination construction," is a term used to describe the arrangement of interior columns in traditional Chinese architecture. This term was not used in classical literature. Rather, it was first coined by architectural historians who conducted field investigations and wrote Chinese architectural history from the 1930s to 1960s. Generally, jianzhuzao refers to buildings with fewer interior columns than those with a full interior column grid aligned with the eaves pillars (Liang and Liu 1933; Guo 2009, 786). Some scholars, in accordance with the interpretation that there were two timber-frame structural systems (diange 殿閣/diantang 殿堂 and tingtang 廳堂) defined in Yingzao fashi, argued that only buildings with fewer interior columns than these two structural systems could have "column elimination" (Fu 2002). However, Chen Mingda, who used the two timber-frame structural systems as a standard to analyze extant buildings, opposed the use of the "jianzhu" neologism (Chen 1981, 4,178-181).
Structural frames of monolithic reinforced concrete with walls and floors in the form of slabs creating a cellular appearance.
Built-up hollow beams of rectangular section, whether metal or wood.
Beams built up of structural timbers which are bolted together with a steel plate sandwiched between them.

One of the main categories of structural elements in Chinese traditional architecture; interchangeable with liang 梁. The essential features of a cross-beam are described in Yingzao fashi (1103) and Gongcheng zuofa (1734) as such: (1) the cross-beam is placed above the pillars; (2) at least one end is supported by a pillar directly or by a bracket (gong) on top of a pillar; (3) the other end can either be inserted into the body of a pillar or placed above another beam. Within extant historic buildings it is also possible to find cross-beams in which both ends are placed above another beam. With the exception of the T-beam 丁栿, a cross beam is usually located perpendicular to purlins. In Yingzao fashi, beams are usually described with the character “fu 栿,” and a beam between pillars is named after the number of rafters it spans, such as a 6-rafter-beam, or 8-rafter-beam; however, there are exceptions, including the pinpricking connector (zhaqian 剳牽), infant beam (rufu 乳栿), eaves cross beam (yanfu 檐栿), level cross beam (pingliang 平梁), and T-beam. Modern architectural historians use this term to describe architecture dating from the Tang (618-907) to early Ming (1368-1644). In Qing dynasty texts such as the Gongcheng zuofa, a cross beam is usually named after the number of purlins it spans, such a 5-purlin-beam or 7-purlin-beam.
Girders with more than two supports. Girders with more than two supports.

Transverse beams in Christian churches that span the nave at the entrance to the chancel or choir, and that separated the area around the altar from the area set aside for the laity. They are most common in the Middle Ages or early Renaissance Later, 'rood screens' developed between the beam and the floor. The rood beam may bear carved or painted portraits of the apostles, but most often is surmounted by a triumphal cross or crucifix. Rood lofts also later evolved above the rood beam.
Joists which carry a ceiling; also small beams to which the ceiling of a room is attached.
In Indian architecture, a column with attached colonnettes.
In Indian architecture, a dwarf atlantan figure.
Caryatids with baskets on their heads.
Interior posts or columns encased in finished millwork.
Upright timbers at the sides of openings.
Groups of two columns set closer together than others in a line, or otherwise forming a visual unit; for columns with interpenetrating shafts, use "doubled columns."
Engaged columns flanked by half pilasters.
Refers broadly to a range of capital designs found in the Mediterranean world prior to the Classical period and generally characterized by paired, vertically rising volutes.
In Indian architecture, a bracket-capital (Early India; South India); Types: citra, taraṅga, puṣpa.
In Indian architecture, a lotus-capital.
Uppermost members of the capitals of columns; often plain square slabs, but sometimes molded or otherwise enriched.
In Indian architecture, an abacus (pillar-part supporting pōtikā-capital/pillar-part above the capital).
In Indian architecture, a striated, multi-faceted, or polygonal necking (pillar element); necking in pillar shaft.
In Indian art and architecture, a pedestal for oblation.
In Indian architecture, a broad band, especially the projecting topmost band of adhiṣṭhāna; broad fillet.
Entablatures in which the cornice rests directly on the architrave, the frieze being omitted.
Cornices of slight projection, with plain blocklike modillions and simple bed moldings.
Overhanging vertical members of a cornice in classical architecture, supported by bed moldings and crowned by cymatia, usually with a drip to throw rainwater clear of the building.
In Indian architecture, a strut, cantilever; or modillion.
Friezes with a convex face.
Refers to the half channels on either side of a triglyph.
Half or incomplete metopes in Doric friezes, usually found at corners. Half or incomplete metopes in Doric friezes, usually found at corners.
Curved braces, usually in pairs, used to support a roof frame and give the effect of an arch.
Angle braces which support one end of a dragon beam.
Diagonal bracing in pairs between adjacent floor joists to prevent the joists from twisting.
Horizontal timbers at the bottom of the frame of a wood structure, that rest on the foundation or subfloor.
Wall plates that receive the lower ends of the rafters of a roof. Wall plates that receive the lower ends of the rafters of a roof.
Trusses having a bow-shaped top chord, often semicircular or parabolic, and a straight or cambered member that ties together the two ends of the bow.
Fink trusses with subdiagonals radiating outward from central points.
Pratt trusses with polygonal top chords.
Roof trusses which are smaller in size than the others, usually because of location, as in a hip roof.
Principal members of trusses that extend the length of the truss.

Support systems and areas of buildings or other structures located below ground level or at the lower portions of structures when distinguishing these portions from the above ground or upper levels, in which case use "superstructures." Use "foundations (structural elements)" specifically for those parts of structures, usually below ground, that transmit loads to the supporting earth or rock.
Drāviḍa-śikhara, on the superstructure of a vimāna or over a Phāṁsanā.
Specially designed structures made to span great lengths.
Sloping tops of buttresses or projecting piers.
In Indian architecture, lateral screens at the antarāla or vestibule’s entryway.

In Indian architecture, a balustrade or cloistered parapet; for example, in the superstructure, most often includes the kuta and sala aediculae. May serve as a connecting wall-segment or parapet of the upper storey. Often wrongly interpreted to be the recess between the wall-angas.

Wall assemblies or segments of walls for buildings that resist high temperatures and limit the spread of flames. These follow code to resist flames for specific amounts of time, and are constructed using materials that have high fire resistance made to withstand extremely high temperatures without combusting, and feature construction details that limit air exchange and other factors.
In Indian architecture, a lattice of gavākṣa.
In Indian architecture, a stairway banister resembling elephant trunk; stylized elephant-trunk shaped stairway-banister.
Ceilings covered with a material designed to absorb sound.
In Indian architecture, an ornate ceiling type with deep concentric cusped-and-coffered courses or bands.
Flooring systems consisting of completely removable and interchangeable floor panels that are supported on adjustable pedestals or stringers to allow free access to the area underneath.
Layers of boards or plywood sheets laid directly on joists and surmounted by the finish flooring, sometimes with a layer of underlayment in between.

Electoral constituencies that elect one member of a congress. In the United States, territorial divisions of a state from which a member of the United States House of Representatives is elected. Other nations having congressional districts are the Philippines and Japan.
Central areas or other commercial areas of a town or city, typically areas that are zoned to allow the operation of businesses.
Urban areas in which brothels are located, whether operating legally or illegally.
Historic districts established and maintained by local units, such as a county, city, village, or township.
In  India, a collection of huts, sometimes defined by the area upon which they stand as being at least one-sixth of an acre.
Use only to denote the Spanish-speaking quarters of cities or towns especially in the United States.

General term for relatively large areas, usually named but having undefined boundaries, where ancient cultures existed. For ancient administrative areas that are defined by historical boundaries, use "former primary political entities" or "former administrative divisions."
Urban areas that are historically significant and retain characteristics and buildings from an historical period or periods.
Areas designated, usually by a governmental agency, as appropriate for industrial and economic development, often to improve stagnant economies and bring employment opportunities into the region.

General term for offices, departments, or other branches or representatives that are no longer in existence, but formerly had authority to oversee, direct, manage, and administer on behalf of an institution or other group.
Counties, particularly in Hungary that act as administrative capitals, and have the responsibilities of both a county and a municipality.
Precincts, usually walled, around cathedrals and their dependent buildings.
General term for relatively small and contained places where archeological remains, old structures, or cultural artifacts are or were located.

Cleared and bounded areas, devoid of artifacts, and of unknown function found associated with hunter-gatherer camps, especially those of the North American Great Basin. Cleared and bounded areas, devoid of artifacts, and of unknown function found associated with hunter-gatherer camps, especially those of the North American Great Basin.
Lots or portions of land sufficient for and intended to be used or currently being used as the site of a house.
Junkyards for automobiles.
Refuse dumps over which layers of earth or ashes are heaped regularly to control pests and odors.
A subdivided residential, governmental, institutional, or commercial lot which contains no structures of a permanent or temporary nature.
Strips established to separate and protect one type of land use from another (e.g., industry versus housing).

Suburbs designed to incorporate large tracts of green spaces and to control internal growth and development with an emphasis on residential communities. Distinguished from "garden cities" by their smaller size and location outside urban centers.

An abundant motif in the art of the central highlands of Mexico since Teotihuacan period, generally consisting of a series of rings formed by two simple concentric circles. In pre-Hispanic palatial architecture, these rings are found in series in the upper zone or frieze of the tecpan façade.
Strengthening or supporting elements (buttresses) located at the juncture of two walls. Also used for similar elements found on furnishings.
Paired buttresses set at right angles, forming the corner of a structure.

Foundations consisting of flat reinforced concrete slabs or mats or of reinforced concrete tubs with walls turned up around the edge of the mat to create a larger volume, either designed to move with the surface of the ground without structural damage, or used when the soil is so soft that even friction piles will not support the building load. In the latter case, the floating foundation is used because it makes the building like a boat in obeying Archimedes' principle: it is buoyed up by the weight of the earth displaced in creating the foundation.
Footings that are slabs under two or more columns or columns and a wall, one of which is internal rather than on the perimeter so that the footing cannot take a beamlike form.
Concrete piles that are poured at their permanent location.
Piles formed by driving a hollow tube into the ground, excavating within the tube, and filling it with concrete.
Vertical poles stayed by guys or guylines, which are attached ropes, chains, rods, or wires.
In Indian architecture, a wall-pier flanking entry.
Piers composed of several engaged columns or pilasters grouped around a central core. For supports formed by three or more closely spaced columns in a group, use "grouped columns."
Piers produced by the thickening of walls at their termination.
In Roman and later classicizing architecture, those parts of a pier that form arch abutments and flank a central engaged column or pilaster carrying an architrave.
Round arches supported by large corbels with curved lower edges, giving the opening a bell-shaped outline.
Flat arches in which the joints of the voussoirs do not radiate but all slope outward from the center at the same angle on both sides.
Pointed arches with radii that are located within the span of the arch, whether or not the centers are above, at, or below the springing.
Semicircular stilted arches.

Arches that carry the primary thickness of a wall over an opening, usually a door or window, when the rest of the wall is carried by other means, such as a lintel, an arch of different form or size, or a decorated frame.

Architraves modified by being carried around a curved opening instead of a rectangular one, specifically the continuous curved molded or decorated bands framing the face of an arch. Examples include bands stacked in a series framing a portal.
Central wedge-shaped voussoirs in arches or central stones in vaults; often decorated or enlarged. Faux keystones may be applied as ornaments on the heads of doors or windows.
Wedge-shaped stones at the apex of masonry arches.
Cable structures in which a field of crossed cables, of different and often reverse curvatures, make up the primary roof surface.
Structures supported by a series of double cables of different curvature used in the same vertical plane and held apart by struts in compression.
Structural systems based on one-way plates given additional stiffness by folding into a series of long, narrow planes, the typical sections resembling a series of interconnected Ws or splay-sided Us.
Flat plates made of concrete and used as structural elements in architecture.
One-way structural systems in which reinforced concrete slabs are supported on beams or girders that run in one direction only.
Structural systems based on two-way concrete slabs employing no beams, drop panels, or column capitals.
Stable, three-dimensional structures consisting of members under tension that are contiguous and members under compression that are not.
Membrane structures that act as roofs.
Pneumatic structures in which closed membranes, used as building elements, are inflated; for pneumatic structures supported by pressurization of the habitable space, use "air-supported structures."

Meaning "egg," refers to the distinctive domes of Indian temples and other architecture, usually hemispherical or egg-shaped; sometimes refers to other egg-shaped elements of Indian architecture. In North Indian temple architecture, a spirelet form found in the Śekharī temple superstructure.
In Indian architecture, a lotus umbrella; loti-formed cap above the āmalaka of a Bhūmija śikhara.
Rings or chains that encircle domes in order to contain their outward thrusts.
In Indian architecture, a pendentive made up of kōla courses.
Vaults formed by the intersection of two or more simple vaults. Vaults formed by the intersection of two or more simple vaults.
Vaults divided into three vaulting cells.
Vaults shaped like a pyramid with sides that bow outward.

Compound vaults in which intersecting barrel vaults are of differing widths, the ridges of the same height but the springing lines of different height, producing a groin line of double curvature. Compound vaults in which intersecting barrel vaults are of differing widths, the ridges of the same height but the springing lines of different height, producing a groin line of double curvature.
Vaults in which the surface between the stilted wall rib and the diagonal rib is warped like a plowshare.
Vaults of plain, semicircular cross section supported by parallel walls or arcades.
Barrel vaults covering a space the plan of which is formed by the area between two concentric circles, or any portion of such a space.
Aggregations of buildings, other structures, and/or open spaces, often multifunctional, and more extensive than single built works, usually shaped over a longer period of time by more participants.
Buildings or complexes constructed for or serving agricultural purposes.
Farms, which are complexes where plants or animals are raised for livelihood or commerce, that have been deserted and are no longer functioning.
Farms consisting of many small holdings collected into a single unit for joint operation by a community under public or state supervision.
Russian collective farms.
Complexes or plots of land where bees are raised in apiaries and where their products collected for livelihood or commerce.
Ranches devoted primarily to the raising of beef cattle.
Marketplaces, usually consisting of a network of covered streets, stalls, booths, and shops, common in parts of North Africa and West Asia.
Dwellings grouped closely together to form relatively compact units, with the space between clusters usually allocated to pedestrian circulation and cooperative recreational use.
Housing that is intended to provide accommodation for residents for a relatively short period of time.
Housing provided consequent upon a sudden state of danger or calamity that has made people's regular housing inaccessible or unsafe.
Temporary settlements used for laborers during railroad construction.

Designates housing for people who are unable to purchase or rent homes through normal marketplace mechanisms; includes such options as low cost housing, low income housing, shelters for the homeless, or mobile homes.

Housing in which multiple individuals, couples, or nuclear families have some shared facilities (for example, laundry facilities or gardening services) but maintain primarily separate living spaces that have been constructed in quantity, either as multiple dwellings under one roof (such as in an apartment house) or in single units (such as a retirement community). When communal housing comprises separate buildings, the buildings typically have a uniform or coordinated appearance.

Use when referring to a semi-independent group living arrangement, usually for the elderly, where some shared common space and some support services, such as housekeeping, transportation, and social activities, but not personal care, are provided; used in the United States since the 1960s.

Public housing units, either new or rehabilitated, located on noncontiguous sites and intended to promote racial integration by placing relatively small housing units within the context of existing neighborhoods.

Grounds of colleges or universities, including the open space between or around the buildings. The term is also used to refer to the grounds of other building complexes with layouts similar to colleges.
Zoos designed for the education and enjoyment of children and young adults, often including a petting zoo, animal shows, and exhibits of baby animals.

Distinguished from "wild animal parks" by the lack of restrictions on animal movement and by the mingling of animals and the visiting public, who generally drive through the parks in their own vehicles.
Underground systems of passages used as cemeteries, generally unsystematic and irregular in plan with networks of galleries and multiple levels over extensive areas.
Necropolises consisting of inhumation graves set out from a center in long distinct rows; used during the early 5th to 7th century in Germany, France, and the Low Countries, usually along rivers.
Yards which belong to churches and are used as places for burial.
Industrical complexes focusing on extraction of minerals, oil, or other material from the earth.
Complexes comprising a coal mine and processing facilities such as a breaker or sorting machinery.
Mines where chrome ore is extracted.
Industrial parks whose facilities are devoted primarily to research and development.

Power plants using water pumped to and stored at a high elevation during periods of low energy demand, for use when demand is high, when water is released to operate hydraulic turbines to produce needed electricity.

Power plants producing electricity by utilizing temperature differentials between surface water heated by the sun and deep cold water pumped to the surface. Power plants producing electricity by utilizing temperature differentials between surface water heated by the sun and deep cold water pumped to the surface.
Steam-producing, electric power generating plants using coal as the primary fuel.
Military ranges reserved primarily or entirely to the firing of artillery, which include firearms generally having a bore of over one inch in diameter.
Bases for the operation of military aircraft.
Land-based military airbases for the military aviation division of the navy of a nation.

Military training camps for new recruits, where intensive and harshly disciplined training is carried out. Originally the term referred to United States Marine Corps training, but is extended to any United States Military initial training camp.
Naval bases that build, repair, dock, or convert warships, and are manned by civilian engineers and workers and administered by engineer duty officers.
A defensive perimeter made by arranged felled trees with their sharpened branches pointing outward.
Areas of land or property where many office buildings may be grouped together and developed specifically to attract corporate offices.
Commercially operated areas containing rides, stalls, and shows, and other entertainment attractions intended to attract a large number of visitors.
Amusement parks organized round a unifying idea or group of ideas, for example, Medieval castles or science fiction.
Aquatic recreation facilities with attractions based on fast-moving, rather than static, water.
Camps offering supervised programs focused on social, recreational, and educational activities for children. They may include day camps, overnight camps, or longer-term camps.

Resorts specializing in maintaining or improving the health or rejuvination of its clients, often including dietary and exercise instruction, bathing in mineral waters, breathing of fresh air, and formerly, extended exposure to sunshine (which was formerly considered healthy). Resorts specializing in maintaining or improving the health or rejuvination of its clients, often including dietary and exercise instruction, bathing in mineral waters, breathing of fresh air, and formerly, extended exposure to sunshine (which was formerly considered healthy).

Resorts or other facilities possessing or located near natural mineral springs or pools that are valued because of the believed restorative or curative powers of the water; also, artificial pools or other aquatic facilities containing waters believed to have restorative powers. The term is derived from the proper name of Spa, Liège province, Belgium, celebrated for the believed curative properties of its mineral springs.
Areas set aside for the propagation of game, especially in historical usage. For modern areas set aside for shooting with guns, use "shooting preserves."
Resorts specializing primarily in snow skiing.
Courses designed for the sport of miniature golf, typically consisting of a series of putting greens set with colorful and whimsical hazards.
Tracks, usually oval in shape, designed or used primarily for the racing of automobiles; surfaces may be made of dirt, asphalt, brick, or another material.

Tracks or strips of road, dry lake beds, or another flat surface used for drag racing, which is an automobile race over a flat, straight course, most commonly 1/4 mile in length.  Drag racing as an organized sport began in the 1930s on dry lake beds in southern California. Tracks or strips of road, dry lake beds, or another flat surface used for drag racing, which is an automobile race over a flat, straight course, most commonly 1/4 mile in length.  Drag racing as an organized sport began in the 1930s on dry lake beds in southern California.
Use only for military weapons testing; for small arms target ranges, use "shooting ranges" or a more specific term.
Areas designed or used primarily the sport of archery, which consists of shooting with bow and arrow at targets.
Outdoor trails equipped with a series of stations where joggers or walkers stop and perform exercises on the apparatus provided.
Heritage trails having an emphasis primarily on more ancient history, including archaelogical remains and sites. The trail itself may also be of archaeological significance.

Complexes for Indian religious communities whose members focus on religious study and meditation and lead lives of austere self-discipline. Such communities or retreats are usually secluded and center around a Hindu philosopher or religious teacher.
Designates independent and canonically erected monasteries, ruled by an abbot if occupied by monks and by an abbess if occupied by nuns.
Complexes containing facilities to accommodate people, functions, and vehicles having to do with air transportation.

Typically refers to large tracts of open, level land upon which runways, hangars, terminals, and other buildings have been constructed to allow for the takeoffs, landings, loading and unloading, and maintenance of aircraft. For smaller areas that have a runway but no or few additional facilities, see "airfields."
Landing places for helicopters.
Railroad yards in which trains are assembled from individual cars.
Railway yards that employ lead tracks on small rises over which an engine pushes single cars, or blocks of coupled cars, where they roll by gravity onto destination tracks where the cars are sorted.
Districts defined by administrative boundaries.
Areas, the boundaries of which are defined for property values and tax assessment purposes.
Hand tools that take the yarn through the canvas and bring it back to the surface; used for knotting rugs.

Resource Description Framework is a standard model for data interchange on the Web. RDF can facilitate data merging when underlying schemas differ, and supports evolution of schemas over time without requiring that all data consumers to be changed.
Prints made by taking a second impression without reinking the plate, to clear the plate of residual ink.
Filing or collecting (as records or documents) in an archive or other repository.
Species of giant aquatic herb endemic to Bolivia.

In or near a temple complex, wells or reservoirs, typically below ground level, often a Hindu temple in India. The tanks serve for ritual bathing and purification, and also function as water sources for the community. They may take any of several forms and are known by various specific terms, depending upon their form and the language.
Limestone that is white, with a slight grayish tint, from deposits near Carthage, Missouri.
Freestone from a quarry in Haslebury in Wiltshire, England.
Granite quarried near Monson, Massachusetts.
Shingles made of oak.
Masonry construction using a single non-structural external layer of masonry, and having an air space behind the veneer. Distinct from veneer attached directly to the surface, "adhered veneer."
Tile used as finish flooring.
Ceramic tiles made of terracotta.
Roofing comprising formed metal sheets with vertical ribs at the panel edges, installed by lapping and interlocking edges of adjacent panels.

Nineteenth-century architectural style that referenced Italian 16th-century Renaissance style The style first developed in Britain in about 1802 by John Nash, and it was taken up in other nations. For example, it was common in mid-19th-century North American residential architecture, which featured a low-pitched hipped roof topped by a belvedere.
Period of the second city on the site of ancient Troy, ca. 2550-2300 BCE.
Culture and style of the ethnic group primarily found in the state of Odisha.
Group of primates of which Tarsiers (family Tarsiidae) are the only living members, however, they once ranged across Europe, northern Africa, Asia, and North America.
Components of phonographs that wind a mechanism governing the movement of the turntable.

Structures at, near, over, or surrounding gateways to residences, other buildings, colleges, castles, other fortifications, walls, monasteries, towns, etc.; usually containing a gatekeeper's dwelling. For subordinate buildings on the grounds of estates or parks, that may be used as the dwellings of employees, prefer "lodges (caretakers' houses)" or "entrance lodges."
Having attributes or characteristics of two genders, particularly designating a person whose identity encompasses two genders. This term may be combined with other gender identities.
Standards to label individual frames of video or film with a timecode.
In Indian architecture, a knife-edged arris moulding; minor karṇaka.
In Indian architecture, a corner band of the spire (Orissa); karṇalatā, vēṇukōśa.
In Indian architecture, a flower-blossom (or bud) extension of pōtikā; bracket with emanating floral projection.
In Indian architecture, a vyāla with a human head motif.
In Indian architecture, a nāsī faced by gavākṣa.
In Indian architecture, a śākhā with floral pattern motif.
In Indian architecture, a maṇḍi-type made up of a circle of thickened petals simulating cobra-hoods.
In Indian architecture, a flat ceiling.
In Indian architecture, a pañjara, nāsī.
In Indian architecture, a decorative half-dormer-like form.
In Indian architecture, a patralatā, leafy scroll.
In Indian architecture, a octagonal, compound pillar-type.
In Indian architecture, a type of prāsāda having three sanctums trinity: usually Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu but Sūrya sometimes replaces Brahmā.
In Indian architecture, a jāla formed by vertical and crossbars.
In Indian architecture, a stambha, pāda, pilaster at the angle.
In Indian architecture, a upapīṭha-type.
In Indian architecture, a oversailing band of rafter-ends; dentils.
In Indian architecture, a lower ‘kampa or lower fillet of an element.
Cakvā-bird, a species of heron as a decorative motif in Indian architecture.
In Indian architecture, a kūṭa above the karṇa-bay; karṇakūṭa.
In Indian architecture, an upāna; sub-plinth moulding; base.
In Indian architecture, a kumuda moulding with three facets; tri-faced torus.
In Indian architecture, a bhūta-based column-type.
Buildings or complexes having facilities or housing institutions dedicated to the practice or study of an area or areas of science.
Groupings of structures that may or may not be intended to function together. Examples could be sets of row houses built in coordinating or similar styles in the same area.
In Mughal and other architecture, cupola-like structures typically found crowning buildings, such as gateways, pavilions, or towers; characterized by dome-shaped roofs supported by pillars.
Buildings in which courses of high school or college-level study are provided for candidates for the priesthood, brotherhood, or sisterhood.
Chapels of a church endowed for chanting of masses and other services.
Subsidiary chapels opening off the apse of churches. For chapels opening off the nave or side aisles, prefer "side chapels."
In architecture, a part or component that is set at an angle, off the axis or off center of the primary line, such as in a facade or wing.
The state or quality of having only one part; undivided.
Pens with a tubular, needlelike point for which the ink supply is controlled by a check valve and released only when pressure is placed on the point; used for drawing precise, even lines.
Paper made from the boiled and pounded inner bark of a wild fig tree. Most "amate paper" is fig bark paper.
Books with instructions for making crafts, some consist of text, while others are interactive, in which you can cut and color.
Buildings on the grounds of a zoo, including those used for displaying animals.
The ovoid, woody shell found beneath the fibrous husk of the fruit of the coconut palm tree.

A baby floor mat, also called a playmat, play gym, or an activity mat is a brightly colored, interactive mat for a baby or toddler. They come in a variety of sizes, shapes, and themes, but almost all have a few small toys, such as mirrors, rattles, jingles, or crinkle toys.

Time that is kept by most clocks and watches and keyed to timezones; that is, the solar time that would be measured by observation if the Sun traveled at a uniform apparent speed throughout the year rather than, as it actually does, at a slightly varying apparent speed that depends on the seasons.

A rose cut fashioned with 12 facets on the top side and a flat bottom side. This particular cut forms the transition between a six-facet and a full rose. The Antwerp rose originated in Antwerp in the 17th century, hence the name. To be distinguished from an 'Amsterdam rose cut'.
A gem-cut type that results in the shape of a long, narrow rectangle, bordered by four facets each step cut in the shape of an isosceles trapezoid.

Rugs or carpets produced during the period of the Safavids, the dynasty that took control of Persia (now modern Iran) in the early 16th centuryand ruled from 1501 to ca. 1739. Many consider this the high point in Persian carpet design and manufacture. No certain examples of 9th/15th-century examples may survive. Safavid rug weaving is characterized by arabesques developed initially in manuscript illumination and architectural décor. Documentary evidence indicates that these tended to rely on a large central medallion format developed in the last phase of Timurid rug production. Scholars have attributed the centers of Safavid weaving to the major cities or centers of power.
Females who row a boat using oars.

Visual works having narrative content in which one scene, episode, or moment in a story is represented, rather than several; the scene includes figures and objects relevant to that one narrative moment.

Translucent zoisite stone having a pale to deep pink color, in which manganese replaces up to 2 % of the calcium. Thulite was discovered near Telemark, Norway and named for Thule, an old name for Norway.

Generic term that commonly refers to a broad class of anthropomorphic figurines or dolls, historically made of wax, clay, lead, and other material, used as focus entities to ritually bind social and supernatural enemies. Though these figurative objects have been anachronistically linked to colonial syncretic religions such as Haitian Vodou or Mississippi River Valley Voodoo, often through the dissemination of racist popular culture in the 19th through 21st centures, the dolls are not prominent features of any Vodun-based religions. Contemporary scholars specifically locate the false equvalence between these figurative objects and Vodu or Voodoo religions in the 19th century European misinterpretation of the Kongo power figure (ir nkisi nkondi). The objects that are vernacularly termed voodoo dolls, however, more accurately evidence a wide spectrum of defensive magic rituals employed by ancient Greco-Roman and Egyptian cultures, amongst others, to control evil forces. While evidence of these figurative objects was first documented around the 7th century BC, the use of these dolls is thought to have predated the Greco-Roman period and entered the European imagination as a cultural import from the East. Traditional treatment of dolls includes twisting, burning, melting, and otherwise manipulating their limbs into bound positions; piercing the objects with pins or nails; and enclosing the dolls within sealed boxes. For the figurative binding figures used in the Kongo tradition, use the term "minkondi." For a more precise reference to ancient Greco-Roman binding figures, use the term "kolossoi." For a less pejorative  generic term for a wide range of anthropomorphic figures, use the term "binding figures."
Genus of New Zealand parrot.
Additive color screen plates invented in England in 1913 by the Paget Prize Plate Company.
In cataloging and similar contexts, an indication that a fact or data, usually a date, is less than certain, but recognized as within close proximity to the date as stated.

Defines a ceremonial dance performed by Native North American women, usually at powwows. Colorful, fringed shawls are the focus of this fast-paced dance. Was popularized in the mid 20th century, as a counterpart to the male Fancy Dance.
Broad category of flat inscribed objects of varied material such as metal, plastic, or ceramic that indicate verification or confirmation of identity. These may be fixed or moveable.
Equpment developed and used in the late 19th century as a home film projector.

Ceremonial social dance performed by unmarried Hopi women and their male clan relatives. Dances are sponsored by families or indivduals, celebrating life cycles and the place of women in Hopi society. As part of the dance, female dancers wear large wooden headdresses, or kopatsoki, and decorated mantas.
Events surrounding the sale of goods.

Defines type of pottery popularized by Nampeyo (ca. 1860-1942) and other female Hopi-Tewa and Hopi potters in the late 19th century to early 20th century. Utilizes the same techniques and visual program as historical Sikyatki pottery from the 14th to 16th centuries: a golden-hued patina due to high temperature firing and black and red curvilinear designs often featuring birds and dragonflies. Nampeyo is often credited as being one of the first to revamp this style, but other Hopi-Tewa and Hopi women were likely involved as well. Potters used the Sikyatki visual framework as a base for new works that were often traded and sold to Native and non-Native audiences in the 20th century.
Chemical elements of hydrogen having the same atomic number but different mass. Three of them are naturally occuring: 1H (protium), 2H (deuterium), and 3H (tritium).
General term for utensils used in handling or burning incense.

Indohdohan celebrates the babies born to the tribe and is one of the traditional rites of passage in the Bunun culture. It takes place at full moon between the harvest festival (known as Cin-san) and the storage festival (known as An-daza). New born babies are introduced to the members of the tribe and a blessing necklace will be put on to their necks.The necklace is called matalunas and it is made of glass beads. It is among the inventory of things that the baby’s parents should prepare before Indohdohan; other objects include home-made millet wine and puh-da (“millet cake”). The mother will kill a rooster and put the necklace on babies according to the order of their birth time. The father will invite tauta-tagus to give blessing to the babies, and invited guests are to give a round of gallantry report known as mapulau. Finally there will be a party in which people share millet cakes. The necklace will be removed and carefully preserved by nightfall.
Beggar's bowls of Sufi mystics; kashkuls are containers carried by wandering Sufi dervishes to collect money, food, and other goods. Often boat-shaped.
The act of officiating or presiding over a game, match, debate, or other competitive event.
Vehicles accommodating a small public library.
The second month of the French revolutionary calendar (introduced in 1793), extending from 22 October to 20 November.
Board game played in ancient Egypt and adjacent cultures, using game pieces and a gameboard grid of 30 squares arranged in three rows of ten.
Thuribles in the shape of a structure or incorporating architectural elements.

Cultures and styles of the Atayal people lived in Taiwan. The Atayal people live primarily in the mountains of northern Taiwan, ranging from New Taipei City, Taoyuan City, Hsinchu County, Miaoli County, Nantou County and Nantou City. Though systematic and regional variations are found in different tribes, the concept and practice of gaga and rutux unify the Atayal people as a whole. Important festivals include the sowing festival, the harvest and the worship of ancestral spirits.
Condition of fabrication for items having a predetermined design, but where the items are tailored for an individual's request; usually made in quantity.
Administrative divisions that care for collections of library materials separated from the general collection because they are rare and valuable.

Refers to tin-glazed European earthenware, particularly ware made in France, Germany, Spain, and Scandinavia. It developed in France in the early 16th century, was influenced by the technique and the designs of Italian maiolica, and is named for Faenza, Italy, which was famous for maiolica. It is distinguished from tin-glazed earthenware made in Italy, which is called "maiolica," and that made in the Netherlands and England, which is called "delftware." It has no connection to the ancient objects or material also named faience, which was developed in the Near East ca. 4500 BCE.

Diantang, a building type sometimes referred to as dian 殿 or even diange 殿閣, is arguably the highest ranking structure in the traditional Chinese building hierarchy. Meaning, literally, "palatial-type" or "rear" (dian 殿 Kroll 2015, 86) "hall" (tang 堂 Kroll 2015, 444), in historical sources diantang is likely a compound word inclusive of dian and tang-type structures, and can be used generally to refer to all main buildings in an architectural complex. When describing a single building it denotes a higher rank structure than ting 廳, 堂 tang, or tingtang 廳堂. Diantang is usually used to describe imperial buildings and the main buildings in religious complexes. The earliest use we have found for diantang is in the "Rhapsody of the Goddess" (Shennüfu 神女賦) traditionally attributed to Song Yu 宋玉 (298-263 BCE), but the compound became more common after the Northern and Southern Dynasties. Diantang is a major term used throughout the Song Dynasty Yingzao fashi building manual. Sales statements associated with a provenance event.
Clay formed into blocks and distinguished by having a white color when fired, usually made of Gault clay. Noted as a particularly hard, durable variety of brick.
