Objects that are worn by individuals that are meant to indicate authorization or confirmation of personal identity within a law enforcement organization.
Measurement for how much of a file is downloaded/uploaded per second. Distinguished from megaits per second, which refers to Internet connection speeds.

The action of one or more people upon other people with hostile intent, usually physical actions involving blows or weapons. For the falling upon, usually with arms, in a military conflict, prefer "attacks (armed conflicts)," although usage may overlap.
Species of perennial plant grown for its flavorful bulbs; native to central Asia but grows wild in Italy and southern France, and is a classic ingredient in many national cuisines.
Devices contructed by by human skill, in imitation of or substitute for the terminal part of the human arm beyond the wrist.
Species of perennial herb used as a flavoring, in confections, as a pigment, as insect repellant, and in folk medicines; native to the Middle East and southern Europe.

Exercise machines consisting generally of two parts: an elastic or fabric band and a motor to induce vibrations in the band. Built to simulate massaging the body. Invented in the early 20th century, with usage particularly popular in the early to mid-20th century.
Containers designed to hold liquids used for baptism ceremonies. Vessels vary in shape, size, and decoration.
Fixtures that mark points along boundaries.
Utensils resembling soup spoons that are designated for eating breakfast cereals.
Specialized utensils designed for immersing and retrieving morsels of food from a fondue pot or fountain.
Three-dimensional constructed objects that are meant to mimic various fruits. Often made of glass, plaster, or clay.

Numbers that uniquely identify each computer on the internet. A computer’s IP address may be permanently assigned or supplied each time that it connects to the Internet by an internet service provider.
Tools of any form that mount blades and are intended to slice wallpaper evenly.
Maori implement, paddle-like but variable in form; used for agriculture and other purposes.

Devices for separating grain from the chaff, that employ a riddle, which is a coarse-meshed sieve formed of cross pieces of wires or stiff fiber, supported on circular rim with a base shaped like a shallow drum.
Equipment designed to provide a level surface on pitched roofs while installing or repairing roofing.
Devices made to create and decode ciphers; some examples include typewriter-based machines using electrical rotors to scramble messages one character at a time.

Mechanized devices used for measuring and winding a desired length of yarn, usually a skein. These devices comprise a spoked wheel with gears attached to a pointer with a face resembling that of a clock. The user manually twists the wheel to wind the yarn and, when a skein of yarn has been wound, the pointer makes a popping or clicking sound to alert the user that the desired length has been attained. The nursery rhyme "Pop Goes the Weasel" is widely thought to refer to the clock reel's popping sound.
Cone-shaped objects used to amplify or concentrate sound waves, used in a variety of applications.
Devices that can erase audiotape for re-use, often with the ability to erase tape in bulk.
Horns that are used to announce mealtimes, usually on farms.
Filters that remove fibrin or other particles from specimens of blood serum.
Large containers, often of metal, with a wide rim or a funnel-shaped mouth, serving as receptacles for spit, especially from chewing tobacco.
Devices that use the heat of the sun to distill water.
Belts used to secure utensils to the wearer to allow for temporary storage when working.
Frames for the support of an instrument constructed to furnish a strong blast of air for stoking fires.
Instruments designed for the purpose of administering a liquid or gaseous substance into the rectum.
Vertical stalls that are fixed with ultraviolet light-emitting bulbs or a means to spray chemicals that simulate a deep suntan.
Consumer audio players that specifically play 8-track tapes housed in cartridges.
Devices used for producing or moving large volumes of air or gas with a low compression ratio; usually consisting of a rotating paddle wheel or airscrew.

Hand-held devices, comprised of long metal teeth mounted on a thin rectangular wooden base with a handle, used straighten and make uniform natural fibers. Typically, a user would employ two combs, one of which was fixed to a post by an iron rod.
Any of a variety of hooks, rings, clips, etc. used to hang or secure curtains.

Mechanized devices, typically comprising a chute, packing belt, vibrating plate, and compression roll, used to compress unprocessed fibers and form them into continuous matted sheets. These machines are designed to produce a consistent weight of fiber material required for subsequent carding processes.
A cabbage-shaped ornament similar to a fabric rosette, but usually larger, softer, and three-dimensional rather than flat; used to trim costume, coverings, and hangings.

Containers, often made of soft canvas and comprised of multiple fold-out or rollup pockets, designed with various compartments to store loose knitting needles and other related tools. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, these containers often took the form of thin, cylindrical tubes made of silver, wood, or other hard materials.
Devices either manually or electrically operated that wind thread onto spools for needlework or sewing.
The cases or outer coverings for the works of watches.
Small keys for winding up watches, particularly pocket watches.

Novelty textile inserts in tobacco product packaging made of a cotton flannel fabric and printed with designs.These were common promotional items from the late 19th century through the early 20th century.
Describes the geographic location where an individual was born.
People having sexual attraction or sexual relations with others of the same sex.
Males having sexual attraction or sexual relations with other men.

A type of carpentry in old Spain. In contrast to 'carpentería de lo blanco,' carpentry classified as 'lo prieto' is typically not decorative. It may also constitute pieces that are heavier, rough-hewn, and irregularly shaped.
People or corporate bodies who design and construct stained glass works, which are windows or other objects made of glass colored by adding metallic oxides to the molten glass.
Metalworkers who specialize in making objects out of gold, especially jewelry and tableware.
Skilled workers who produce wrought iron or steel from pig iron by melting and agitation in a bath, followed by working and forging the metal.
Building commissioner working in  a noble or royal court.

Amaranth, (genus Amaranthus), genus of 60–70 species of flowering plants in the family Amaranthaceae, distributed nearly worldwide and species are useful as food crops and are grown both for their leaves and for their edible seeds.
Edible starchy tuberous roots of various plants of the genus Dioscorea.
Family containing around 52 genera and 700 species of flowering plants including perennial herbs, trees, vines, and succulents.

Species of annual plant grown for its starchy edible tubers. The potato is native to the Peruvian-Bolivian Andes and is cultivated as one of the world’s main food crops. Potatoes are thought to have been independently domesticated several times and were largely cultivated in South America by the Incas as early as 1,800 years ago.

An open star cluster visible to the naked eye and prominent in the sky during the winter in the Northern Hemisphere. Known to the ancient Greeks as the Pleiades, the star cluster is identified as a constellation by many cultures around the globe.
Women of noble birth or rank.
Large boards having a surface upon which one may write or draw with chalk. The color may be black, green, or another color.
Data, ideas, and imaginative works that have been communicated, recorded, published and/or distributed formally or informally in any format.
The prose description of the most recent acquistion of the work.
Order of flowering plants consisting of 5 families, 154 genera, and around 3,000 species. Members of Magnoliales include woody shrubs, climbers, and trees.

Depictions in which the entire body of the person is portrayed, as contrasted to a portrait of only the face, a bust, or a half-length portrayal. The sitter may be standing or sitting in his or her entirety, and is often portrayed life-size or larger.

Devices used to clean grain consisting of a cylinder covered in mesh or with perforations. Grain passes through the cylinder as it rolls and foreign matter, such as dirt, is trapped in the mesh or perforations.
Devices for removing impurities from and grinding middlings (larger pieces of grain left over from the process of grinding grain into flour).

Revolving reels or agitators used in the process of making freshly milled flour appear whiter by oxidizing the surface of flour grains. Flour-bleaching agitators carry flour through air charged with nitrogen peroxide gas.
Devices that separate grains such as oats by grade.
Artifical or naturally-derived hair attached to the wearer's own hair to create a thicker or longer appearance.

Hair binders with two feather tassels worn by Nahua elites in the postclassic period. These were insignia of tlahtohqueh (rulers) and given as prestigious gifts to nobles and warriors in recognition of their military achievements. Several varieties were made with speicific feathers: cuauhtlalpiloni with eagle feathers, quetzallapiloni with quetzal feathers, zacuantlalpiloni with zacuan feathers, and xolotlalpiloni with yellow parrot feathers. The same term may also be used for decorations hanging from capes, sandals and other costume items.
Containers made to store hairpins, often rectangular or cylindrical in shape.
Devices that convert electrical current into heat via an element called an electrical resistor. These are of various design.
Vessels for the storage and distribution of volatile liquid fuel. These often have nozzles incorporated for pouring.
Apparatuses used for heating, usually of cast iron, designed to burn coal efficiently.
Instruments that measure the amount of butter in milk.
Props used by jugglers that appear in a variety of materials, generally with a bulbous body transitioning into a narrow handle.
Bladed tools for carving cooked ham.
Scales that are programmed to provide caloric and other qualities for a variety of foods based on weight.
Cloth bags used to strain cooked fruit, separating pulp from juice, in the process of making jelly.
Blocks of wood with slots for holding knives.
Large oar-like implements used to stir kettles of rendering lard.

Neckwear consisting of two rectangular pieces of white cloth falling from the collar and tied to the back of the neck used by barristers, lawyers, judges or any court officials in the UK or parts of the Commonwealth as part of full court attire.
Printing presses in which both the paper and the printing surface lie flat and come into direct contact with each other by closing and opening like a clamshell.
Shades placed over or around the light source of a lamp, and that are designed to diffuse or direct light and shield glare. They may be designed to perform a task or to be primarily decorative.
Molds used to shape maple sugar, usually wood; may consist of either a single, one-sided mold, or two held together with dowels.
Automatic machines, typically in the form of an assembly line, that fill, cap, and label bottles for distribution, sale, and, use.
Molds, into which cookie dough is placed, in order to make a decorative shape or design.
Containers made to hold coupons or ration books, generally taking the form of a flat, rectangular envelope or bag.

Benches intended for use at a piano, generally made with a hinged seat that opens to reveal a storage area for sheet music, books, and other such items; often made en suite with the piano with which it is sold.

Rosin intended for rubbing on the strings of musical instruments, such as violins, which would produce little to no sound without its application. Stickier, darker rosins are preferable for cellos and basses, while gold and amber rosins are preferred for violins and violas.
Toy and miniature versions of accordions intended for children's play.
Enclosing containers of varied design used for storing hinged cutting tools for needlework.
Small receptacles, usually cylindrical or rectangular, usually with lid, typically intended to contain tools and materials for needlwork.
Devices that hold a stretched quilt horizontally which enables holding three layers of the quilt (backing, batting, and quilt top) without the need for basting.
Contrivances used for holding or supporting rolls of tape used for needlework.

Devices similar to an embroidery hoop, but usually of a larger size. These are in two parts; a solid ring and a slightly larger split ring which may be expanded around the thicker layers of a quilt. These may be circular or rectangular in shape.
Devices resembling sewing machines that may have larger support surfaces and 'throat' areas to accommodate larger pieces of fabric.
Frameworks that incorporate rails, bars, or pegs, in or on which spools for thread used in needlework may be placed or suspended.

Devices comprised usually of two pieces of wood, metal or plastic that fit one inside the other, and that can be tightened with fabric stretched over the inner hoop to keep it taught while being worked.
Hand-held tools, typically comprising one or more rotary blades or other types of blades, used to trim manufactured fibers, yarn, pile loops, or other textile materials.
Ruled writing tablets of gathered paper, often yellow, that conventionally measure 8.5 by 14 inches, though other sizes exist.
Manifestations of motion pictures, stored electronically, in any media or digitized format. Use 'videotapes' to refer specifically to electronic audio-visual recordings stored on tape.
Reflecting telescopes used for studying the scintillations of stars.

Refracting telescopes named after the telescope Galileo first constructed in 1609. Galilean telescopes are each designed with one convergent and one concave, or divergent, lens, with the divergent lens acting as the ocular lens, and the convergent lens as the objective lens that creates the image.
Spring-loaded mechanical devices designed to rotate a spit over a fire in order to evenly roast meats.
Any portable receptacles or compartments for holding photosensitive film.
Sheets of glass, metal, porcelain, or other rigid material coated with a light-sensitive photographic emulsion.
Textile coverings for small pillows placed on a chair, couch, or other furniture, primarily for decoration.
Hard, sharpened wooden sticks used for loosening the soil for planting and weeding in postclassic central Mexico.
Tunnels of varied design, often collapsible, intended as play structures for children.
Print advertising that is designed to be viewed within the pages of daily newspapers or journals.
Hollow tubes often made of plastic or rubber, filled with ink. Used to transfer ink onto printing surfaces or in utensils that use ink as a drawing medium.
Instruments of punishment usually consisting of a metal framework that encased the head that included a gag or sharpened bit to restrain speech.
Devices that attach to pyrography pens that afford a variety of mark-making on wood, leather or other materials.

The  gaper or "yawner" is a typically Dutch shop sign in the form of a head carved in wood or stone. The head is almost always a sylized depiction of a Moorish man with his mouth open to receive medicine. These were displayed to indicate the location of a pharmacy.
Handiwork table of a distinctive style, having four slender legs and a deep body set with several drawers; typically used for sewing.
Fasteners attached to shoes, used for both decoration and to secure shoes to the wearer.

Looms designed to use high pressure jets of water as the primary method of inserting the weft yarn into the warp shed to efficiently  produce water-resistant, synthetic textile materials like Nylon and polyester filament.

Cutting tools consisting of two bevel-edged cutting blades and handles, specially designed to cut both lengths of wallpaper before their application and overlay wallpaper directly off the wall during the application process. The blades are longer in length and straighter than those of standard cutting tools to facilitate even trimming.
Small cup used as a measure in mixing cocktails.
Instruments for measuring the temperature of oil or another fat heated for the purpose of deep-frying foods.
Refers to both hand tools and large horse- or tractor-drawn vehicles that usually consist of a frame upon which is fastened shares, discs, or tines used for breaking up the surface of soil.
Cutting tools used in the dairy for cheesemaking, to process curd.
Cables that are used to connect devices and transmit data through computers’ parallel ports. Parallel cables have 25 wires, all of which can synchronously transmit information.
Paper cards on which machine-readable data are recorded by the punching of holes in specified positions in accordance with a predesignated code.
General term for types of computer cables or bound optical fibres, which are used to transmit data.

Devices that decode data; may also be devices with any number of input lines that carry signals and output lines with up to one carrying a signal, creating a one-to-one correspondence between output and input signals.
Plastic sheets that fit over keyboards' keys which identify the keys' functions when using software.
Devices, in computing and data processing, that can read data travelling around a network.
Keyboard-activated devices that punch holes in punch cards.
Computing devices that can play or read tape, but do not punch or record onto tape.

Monophonic, nonimitative electronic instruments, invented by Maurice Martenot in 1928. The tone is generated by the heterodyne action between a fixed and a variable radio-frequency oscillator, the latter being controlled by a seven-octave keyboard and the relative proximity of the player's hand to a horizontally stretched cord.
Devices that emboss bank or personal checks for identification purposes.

Hand-held tools, typically comprising two stainless steel blades longer than 6 inches mounted on different-sized finger rings, designed to cut straight, accurate lines in a variety of fabric materials. Unlike fabric scissors, which are equipped with equally-sized finger rings, these shears have a smaller, rounded finger ring for the thumb and a larger elliptical bow for the fingers. This design allows for the user to exert more control over the fabric and ensure that the fabric remains flat while cutting.

Specialized stencils or diagrams illustrating the arrangement or placement of pattern pieces on fabrics. To facilitate pattern marking, these stencils are superimposed onto fabric materials and subsequently arranged and traced directly on the fabric. Typically used to ensure precise cutting and tailoring procedures, these stencils assist the user in reducing fabric waste and, in turn, increasing pattern yield.
Hand-held instruments, typically characterized by a pointed mental tip and a thick wooden handle,  used to make small holes and sew seems in heavy-duty fabrics.
Punches for cutting holes in fabric to set grommets in.
Long-bladed shears for removing the nap from the surface of woolen textile surfaces after the process of fulling.

Devices used to measure the natural waviness of yarn, which results from the interlacing of the materials' warp and weft. Consisting of two clamps, one fixed in place and the other moveable, these devices fasten yarn in place while exerting tension onto the textile material until it is straightened out. Using the device's tension scale, the user can effectively measure the crimp-free length of the yarn. This measurement is subtracted from the length of the crimped yarn, and the percentage of this difference is expressed as the crimp percentage.
Levered devices used to pull wire taut when constructing fencing.
Metal or earthenware covers used to preserve and restrict hearth fires overnight, having a handle and one or more holes to permit draught.
Light sources which attach to the camera and coordinate with the shutter mechanism to provide a brief intense flash of light.

Devices or systems that present a user with the impression of operating spacecraft. These create an illusion of manned flight, applications of flight controls, the effects of other aircraft, and environmental factors. These simulators are used for training, design and research.
Implements used to break up hardened sugar consisting of a rod with a handle on one end and prongs or blades on the other.
Small bags that are intended to carry food for an individual's lunch. These may be paper or reusable.
Large casks of varying capacity, especially those used for wine, beer, or water, and formerly for salmon and shrimps.
Hollow cones of metal or plastic, with smooth or notched tips inserted onto the end of a pastry bag, used to make decorative patterns with icing or frosting.
Trays or gridded racks used for drying fruits or nuts; traditionally made of natural fibers or wooden slats woven with open spaces for air circulation, and may have a handle.
Machines, either manually or electrically operated, designed to tightly seal bottles, typically for carbonated beverages such as beer or soft drinks.
Boards used for cleaning and polishing knives, typically with an abrasive powder or other abrasive material.

Confectionary machines consisting of a spinning head enclosing a small sugar reserve bowl into which a charge of granulated, colored sugar is poured. Heaters near the rim of the head melt the sugar, which is squeezed out through tiny holes by centrifugal force. The sugar then re-solidifies in the air and is spun around a paper cone into cotton like threads
Wheeled carts with trays or receptacles for transporting dishes of food for service, or for transporting clean or dirty dishes during the course of kitchen work.
Cases that contain utensils used in food service.

Trays, typically made of metal or plastic, designed to hold food, service utensils, and vessels while dining in a cafeteria. Also, compartmentalized trays designed to hold individual portions of food.
Devices typically made of wood, but also of plastic, equipped with a lever or flat-bottomed stamper, used to press butter into a uniform shape.
Tools used to slice meats, sausages, cheeses or other products. These may be manually or electrically operated, and have adjustments for the thickness of slices.
Chambers used for preserving meat by exposing them to smoke.
Devices used to sort coffee and food beans by color into quality grades.
Receptacles for storing raw vegetables.
Airtight or nearly airtight, box-like containers, of metal, wood, or plastic; used for storing bread and other baked goods to keep them fresh.
Containers for holding lard.
Covered containers for storing flour.

Jars, often ceramic but sometimes of silver or other materials, usually of ovoid shape with flattened shoulders, an upright collar, and a dome or cap cover; of a type traditionally used by the Chinese for preserving ginger.

Devices used to keep food warm during service in a cafeteria or other similar establishment, consisting of a tank of water, heated by some form of heating element, into which shallow pans of food may be placed.
Bowls into which the dregs, leaves, and grounds of teacups and coffee cups are emptied at the table; usually made as part of a tea or coffee service.

Foot-shaped devices inserted in shoes to maintain their shape when they are not being worn. Also, machines in factories or workshops that force wooden parts into shoes to smooth out wrinkles during finishing. Distinguished from "lasts (shoemaking tools)," which may be similar in appearance.

Undergarments that consist of a stiff structure or a padding whose shape allows it to fit over the breasts. It generally fastens at the back and may occasionally be adjustable at the front. Used to make the breasts appear larger, and to improve the bust line.
Fitted coverings that protect standalone cooking grills from dust and dirt when not in use.
Pads of leather, plastic, or other materials that rest on the surface of a desk to protect it from marring.
Long narrow strips of decorative fabric intended for the surface of pianos that incidentally provide protection to the piano surface from objects resting on it.
Devices for applying hand power to lift objects by means of a screw or lever, or by hydraulic power.
Cards imprinted with greetings or messages and often suitable illustrations that are sent or given to celebrate Easter.

A category of Nahua chimalli (shield) designs that were usually paired with the Cuextecatl warrior costume. At least five basic designs are identified, the most common feature either the yacameztli (crescent-shaped nose plate) or the double rectangle motif known as "hawk scratches" that are both associated with the Huastec region.

Devices that indicate the total amount or average value of a quantity; in analog computing these may be devices whose output functions are proportional to the integral of their input functions, with respect to specific variables.
Cloth coverings of various materials cut to cover a horse's body from around the withers to the rump and, in front, around the chest; used to protect a horse or discourage growth of a heavy coat.
Weapons which are combinations of two or more different types. May also be used for weapons that are hidden in or appear to be articles of everyday use.
Telescopes that orbit around a celestial body (namely Earth) to capture and collect light from deep space.
Devices that reproduce sound by the means of a vibrating needle, or stylus, which follows the groove of a rotating phonograph recording.
Devices on which sound is recorded onto magnetic tape, and may be replayed.
Sets of pouches, sleeves, or other protective wraps bound together for the storage of laquer or vinyl discs.
Containers used for the transport and protection of audiotape.

Machines, into which bags or sacks are fed, typically consisting of a throat for receiving the upper end of the bag, and additional devices for bunching, tying, and releasing the bag from the machine.
Boxes used for depositing voting ballots. May also be utilized to draw lots, in which case small objects are drawn from it.
Inflated spherical balls bounced or thrown in the game of the same name; generally about 30 inches in circumference and weighing 20 to 22 ounces.
Laboratory baths that are used to enclose specimens or tissues in a mass using an embedding medium, such as paraffin wax.
Implements used for removing meat from the bone to which it is attached.
Machines, usually key-operated, that provide and keep records of expenditures and receipts, and perform computations and calculations in that context.
Devices used to mount cameras to keep them steady during exposure, having a single pole or foot, usually extendable.
Filters that correct for color temperature or cast for film or digital cameras and photographic enlargers.
Devices used by beekeepers for driving smoke into a hive to stupefy the bees while the honeycomb is being removed.
Devices that surround a beverage vessel and that provide insulation to keep a liquid hot or cold.
Medium sized compartmentalized boxes designed to store various items of jewelry.
Printed matter intended as promotional material for goods, services, or brands that typically appears in newspapers, journals, magazines or other serial publications.

A strong woven fabric tape made in a herringbone twill weave that is used most often as button or seam reinforcement in the construction of garments, though other uses may include binding edges or as ties or closures. It may be made from a variety of natural and artificial fibers.
Machines designed to help align sheets in preparation for cutting, punching, drilling, or binding. They are also used for aligning checks, mailers and invoices for folding and inserting.
Containers, usually used by botanists, for transporting recently gathered specimens.
Biospecimens that are taken from plants, used for research or storage.

Mechanized devices designed to blend bales of cotton or other fibers by passing layers of fibers through the device horizontally and removing them perpendicularly to produce a resulting homogenized fiber blend.
Devices or sets that allow measurement and comparison of levels of hydrogen in a material or solution.
Cases specifically used to protect and transport digital videodiscs.

Mechanized devices, originally patened in 1826 by John Goulding, used as part of the carding process to produce a continuous wool roving. These devices utilize a ring doffer and revolving tubes to separate carded wool into strips and twist the strips enough to ensure that the fibers adhere in a tubular form. These condensers benefit the carding process by both eliminating the need to piece together individual lengths of carded fibers and producing more uniform, higher quality roving.

Sacks in which puddings are cooked. They consist of tightly-woven pieces of cloth into which ingredients for a pudding may be poured or placed. The corners of the cloth are then brought together and tied with a string to form a bag, which is then suspended by a stick into boiling water.
Implements made of iron with a long handle and a paddle-like end. Used to heat wine or other liquids by placing the iron in a kitchen hearth until hot, then plunging the iron into the liquid.
Autoclaves used specifically for canning.
Bags used to keep detachable collars in after they have been cleaned. Used to describe historical objects as removeable collars are no longer a common element of haberdashery.
Scientific instruments for identifying minerals by sublimation or to measure the buoyant force that a body experiences when placed in a fluid, essentially to determine its suspended weight.
Boards or flat framework to which Native Americans traditionally and often today bind an infant.
Objects of wood, metal, or other materials, usually wedge-shaped, that can be inserted beneath a wheel to keep it from rolling out of place.
Shovel-like tools used to cut up and remove compacted mash and straw following cider pressing.
Flat, often rectangular cases, similar to but larger than cigarette cases, used to carry cigars. For covered boxes placed on a table, desk, or the like and used to hold cigars, use "cigar boxes."
Accessories worn on dresses or other garments and fastened with a clip placed on each side of the collar or on the bodice to create pleats in the material.

One-piece garments consisting of a trouserlike portion and a full top with or without sleeves worn over other garments for protection. For one-piece garments consisting of trousers with a bib use "overalls (main garments)."
Dissecting tools, usually about six inches long and inserted into wooden handles, that are used to separate and explore specimens.
Containers, often of glass, with a bulb and long downward-curving neck used for distilling liquids and other chemical operations.
Small versions of (high) chairs that are made to accommodate baby dolls.

Instruments used to render perspective drawings. These consist of three rulers joined together in a Y-shape so that a central ruler, along which lines are to be drawn, may be orientated correctly by adjusting the position of the legs that rest against two nails placed on the drawing board. As the device pivots, the main bar changes slope, resulting in drawn lines that orient to a vanishing point that would be otherwise difficult to obtain.
Dressing garments in the form of capes, long with slits for the arms.

Spirit duplicators that employ a manual printing method devised in 1923 involving a 2-ply master sheet as a plate. One layer of the master may be typed or drawn on, and the second layer is coated with wax and colorant. Marks made to the first sheet are transferred to its rear, coated side. The sheet with the transferred wax image is then attached to a drum on the machine that revolves over paper, gradually transferring the wax onto a paper support by means of a solvent. Approximately 40 copies or prints can be made in this way.
Receptacles used for transporting eggs, usually designed to help protect the delicate eggs.

Describes the discipline of theatrical or dramatic composition, representation, and research. English dramaturgy is derived from German Dramaturgie, a concept developed by the German dramatist and critic Gotthold Lessing in a series of essays entitled 'Hamburgische Dramaturgie,' published 1767 to 1769. The discipline includes researching, selection, adaptation, or development of texts, scripts, plays, operas, or films for a theater or other production company.
The aspect of the discipline of dance that involves inventing or arranging and putting together steps, gestures, and patterns to form dances, and separate dances to form a dance composition.
Discipline involving the study of singing and other vocal expressions, including performance.

Relatively short musical pieces, ranging from light instrumental compositions, to entertainments performed between the acts of a play, to elaborate comic pieces performed between the acts of 17th- and 18th-century serious operas, usually for soprano and bass.
Lengthy speeches by one actor in a film, play, or broadcast production, or a dramatic composition performed by one person.

Refers to the performing art characterized by movement, gesture, facial expressions, speaking, and intonation, which are used to create a fictional character for the stage, motion pictures, or television. The art of acting is not mimicry, exhibitionism, or imitation, but is marked by the skill to react to imaginary stimuli, a refined sensibility, intelligence, and an ability to convey the intent and feelings of a character to the audience.

The act of exchange or contract by which parties trade goods or commodities for other goods of equivalent value. Distinguished from  'selling', which is defined as a transaction of goods or property for money. Use 'exchange' in specific instances where goods are exchanged for goods or exchange media, or where 'barter' is less appropriate.

In collections management, the act by which a library, museum, documentation center, archive, or other collection receive materials, including purchase, gift, exchange, or any other means. For the methods by which acquisitions are made, see narrrower contexts of "methods of acquisition." The act of obtaining an asset or object by any means.
The status or condition of property having been taken or forfeited by a governmental or other entity in power or having authority.
The culture of the body of Jews living outside the land of Israel.
Nationality, style, and culture of the Jewish sect known as Karaites.
The activity and profession of raising bovine species.

Body of laws undertaking to provide relief for the poor. Prime examples are laws developed out of late-medieval and Tudor-era laws being codified in 1587-1598 in England and Wales, and in existence until the emergence of the modern welfare state after WWII.
Use with regard to legal protection for the work of visual artists, including copyright, protection from mutilation, and royalty payments.
Objects or monuments donated by an individual for a public place or shrine, especially in gratitude for deliverance from distress. For those that are, or contain, images, use "ex-votos."
Systems of law derived from English law based on custom and judicial precedent rather than statutes.
Very full skirts, either short or long, traditionally made of net or tulle and worn by ballerinas.

System of beliefs of the Mayans, a Mesoamerican people who flourished between 300 and 900 CE in southern Mexico and Central America; knowledge of the beliefs comes from hieroglyphic writing carved into stone monuments and from codices from the colonial Spanish.

Literary and oral genre rooted in the compressed and cogent imaginative awareness or associations of experiences, ideas, or emotional responses and arranged under an organized criterion of meaning, conscious and unconscious expression, symbolism, formal or informal pattern, sound, and rhythm. The genre encompasses narrative, dramatic, satiric, didactic, erotic, and personal forms.
Formalized exhibitions that include works by a single creator. This term is usually reserved to describe exhibitions of contemporary work by living artists, rather than historical retrospectives.
Cloth bindings made by the publisher, usually uniform bindings distinctive to that edition; as distinguished from cloth bindings added in a later restoration.
Intimate sexual contact between two individuals involving penetration.
Family containing American Arboreal Lizards, Chuckwallas, Iguanas, and Iguanids.
Styles of architecture and urban design in the Muslim world that have adapted the values of Islam as well as changes in materials and construction technology.
Meaning "composed [it]," in printmaking and other art works, indicates the one who designed the work.

Type of watermark known in many variations, comprising a fleur-de-lys in a shield, in use from 1600 through to the 19th century in papers made in Strasburg, Basle, Germany, the Netherlands, Britain, Scandinavia, Russia, and elsewhere.

The various insignia of a Nahua tlahtoani (ruler) in postclassic central Mexico, including the xiuhhuitzolli (turquoise mosaic diadem) and the xiuhtilmahtli (turquoise cape), usually tenixyoh ("with eyes on the edge").

Style of writing in Ancient Greek or Roman inscriptions or other texts where the writing is arranged vertically rather than horizontally; may include one or more characters per each horizontal position.
People who takes part in the game of checkers.
Cups, usually disposable, designed for hot liquids.
Truss bridges having the roadway or track on top of the trusses.
Devices to press noodle dough into thin sheets, then cut the sheets into noodles. Two rollers press out and cut the dough with a wringer-like action, controlled by a hand crank.
Churches having been bestowed an honorific assigned to the most highly ranked Roman Catholic churches
Seated, cross-legged posture in which each foot is placed sole upwards on the thigh of the opposite leg.

Wild bovid species that has black pelage, long hair, and otherwise adapted for living at high altitude. Domesticated populations differ from the wild species in having shorter legs and other characteristics. Wild and domestic yaks can freely interbreed, although they are still generally classified as different species.
Units of measure of exposure to light given by multiplying foot-candles by hours.
Computer memory which acts as the primary storage for programs and data.

Lingxingmen is an elaborate gateway with a form similar to wutoumen 烏頭門. Usually, a lingxingmen is used at the entrance of ritual architectural complexes, such as the Wenmiao (Temple of Literature), sacrificial altars to the spirits of Heaven and Earth, and other religious complexes. The term lingxingmen was used beginning in the Northern Song dynasty (960-1127).
The interaction between the user and computer or device using commands in the shell to access the operating system.

Remote underwater free-swimming vessels distinct from remote control vehicles that operate in the air or on land. ROVs are unoccupied, and are tethered to operators that maneuver them from vessels, floating platforms, or on land. They are common in deep water industries, underwater archaeology, and marine biology. They are linked to a host by buoyant tethers or load-carrying umbilical cables.
Compounds consisting of the chemical element barium.
General term for great variety of chemical compounds formed with flourine.
Substances composed by the chemical union of nitrogen with additional elements.
Substances composed by the chemical union of sodium with additional elements.
Compounds containing calcium.

Any of several forms of calcium oxide obtained from heating calcium carbonate (limestone, marble, chalk, and shells); when calcium carbonate is heated to about 500 C, carbon dioxide is driven off leaving anhydrous calcium oxide or quicklime. When quicklime is soaked in water, it is changed to calcium hydroxide or slaked lime. Slaked lime that is dried and ground to a fine powder is called hydrated lime or lime hydrate. Lime will eventually harden and react with carbon dioxide to reform calcium carbonate. Lime is used in mortar, cement, stucco, glass, whitewash, putty, leather tanning, papermaking, and as a water-softening agent.
Order of flowering plants containing seven families, 129 genera, and 2,295 species.
Genus of gourd-bearing vines, containing six species.
Forms of the chemical element oxygen that are different from each other but exist in the same physical state.

An allotropic form of oxygen, O3, which is a bluish toxic gas with a characteristic sharp odor, is a powerful oxidizing agent, and is produced from molecular oxygen by electrical discharge and in the upper atmosphere by ultraviolet light.
Isotopes of the element neodymium.
In an archaeological context, analysis of stable strontium isotopes in ancient objects and materials can supply information about date and provenance.  Strontium in its isotopic form.
Genus of comb jellies.

Nautical devices for the standing and running rigging of traditional sailing ships consisting of circular, laterally flattened wooden blocks with a groove around the circumference, pierced with holes through which a lanyard is reeved, used for tightening or extending shrouds.
Toys or sets in which a shuttle must be hit with special long-handled rackets. Unlike professional sports equipment, this is marketed in all shapes and colors for recreational use.
Cylinders, smaller than cigars, made of finely-cut tobacco for smoking rolled up in thin paper, tobacco-leaf, or maize-husk.
Three-dimensional constructed objects made to mimic the appearance of plants.
Supports with Y-shaped branches on one end, on which long-barrelled firearms could be steadied while shooting.

Scientific equipment to which chemical or other laboratory equipment can be fixed when in use, typically consisting of a heavy base supporting a vertical metal rod to which clamps can be attached to hold test tubes or burettes for experiments in titration or for filtering.
Devices, usually made of rubber, used to maintain the mouth open during prolonged treatment.
Status of property that was described for sale, but not necessarily offered or sold, in an auction, which is a public sale of property to the highest bidder.
Printmakers who created art conforming to the official standards and principles of taste of European and American art academies.

Metal or glass instruments resembling syringes, consisting of a tube, which may be graduated, and cone-shaped at one end, with lateral handles used to suck up a small amount of wine from a cask to taste it.
Analog computers, comprised of mechanical components, that were designed to solve differential equations.
Any set of data, facts, instructions, or other information that are broad in scope and discussion, rather than specific and detailed.

The remains of industrial culture which are of historical, technological, social, architectural or scientific value. These remains consist of buildings and machinery, workshops, mills and factories, mines and sites for processing and refining, warehouses and stores, places where energy is generated, transmitted and used, transport and all its infrastructure, as well as places used for social activities related to industry such as housing, religious worship or education.

Heritage characterized by the continuity of the original function or the purpose for which it was originally established. Such heritage maintains the continuity of community connections, continues to evolve in the form of tangible and intangible expressions, and taken care through traditional or established means.
Refers to the architectural order characterized by a capital having a bell-shaped echinus decorated with a combination of spiral and plant, usually acanthus, motifs.

Ancient alphasyllabic script, noted as one of the oldest writing systems used in South and Central Asia, dating approximately 3rd century BCE and earlier to 3rd century CE and later. Important examples of Brahmi inscriptions include edicts inscribed in stone in Northern Central India from 3rd century BCE.
Affixing one's signature to something.

Species of large, iridescent tropical butterfly of Central and South America; there are many subspecies. The males are more brightly colored than females, who also have blue on the dorsal wings, but have a much wider band of brown or dark coloration around the dorsal edges than the males.

Money that was used in parts of Africa into the 20th century, comprising unadorned copper and iron rods, bars, and blade-shaped pieces. The blades may resemble hatchets, axes, knives, hoes, swords, spearheads, arrows, or other items. Rather than value accorded by weight, these currencies are priced by length.

In architecture, engineering, and other fields, the discipline that does structural analysis to study and predict the behavior of structures as subjected to dynamic actions, such as acceleration and loading. Dynamic loads include people, wind, waves, traffic, earthquakes, and blasts.
White crystalline compound, acetylsalicylic acid, most often used  as a medicine, as an analgesic and antipyretic.

Single light, contact printed copies of film made from an unedited roll of original camera negative immediately after processing and screened to the cast and crew, used to review "dailies (motion pictures)."

Describes a complete entry-level Nahua warrior's costume consisting of a feathered encasing body suit with a conical copilli headpiece. It was the most commonly depicted type in tribute rolls of the Triple Alliance and was made in a variety of colors. Usually decorated with a double rectangular figure known as "hawk scratches" and paired with the crescent-shaped yacameztli nose plate as well as other attributes associated with the Huastecs. It was not actually included in tribute from Huastec region, but from twenty other culturally and geographically diverse provinces of the Triple Alliance instead.

Edible art of grand scale, including elaborate ephemeral architecture, sculpture, and floats made of food, particularly but not exclusively those that were designed for court and civic celebrations in early modern Europe.
The dead bodies of humans or other animals.
Characters, whether fictional or historical, depicted in literary works.
Works of graffiti art that are large, colorful, and stylistically elaborate and that require a greater amount of time and expertise to create.

The second month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendars, containing 28 days (or 29 in a leap year) and falling between January and March. It was named after Februalia, the Roman festival of purification. Originally, February was the last month of the Roman calendar.

The day following Sunday and preceding Tuesday, traditionally regarded as the second day of the week, but now frequently considered the first day of the week. Named as Moon’s-day on the Roman calendar.
A combination of favorable circumstances or events occurring by chance; success, prosperity, or advantage apparently brought about by chance rather than through one's own actions or abilities.
Italian comic operas, with dialogue in recitative and characters drawn from everyday life.
Abnormal reactions of the body produced by a sensitizing dosage of or exposure to some foreign material.
Standard carried on the shoulders of Nahua warriors in postclassic central Mexico.

Epidemics or pandemics of infectious disease that spread rapidly and have a high mortality rate, whether among people or animals. A prime example is the Black Death, an infectious fever caused by the bacillus Yersinia pestis.

Culture at Chiripa dating from 1000-800 BCE, based on calibrated radiocarbon dates from 1992 and 1996 excavations. This phase is marked by a growth in population and an early example of communal architecture in the Lake Titicaca Basin, a semi-subterranean plaza or court.
Whistles or other simple instruments for imitating the call of deer, in order to attract or decoy them.
Layered composite wood board consisting of cross-oriented thin, rectangular strips compressed and glued together with resin adhesives.

Fiberboard that is typically made of wood dust or fibers, or other cellulose left over from the processing of other products; distinguished from medium-density fiberboard and high-density fiberboard by density of fiber and strength.
Cookstoves fueled by coal.
Tools consisting of a metal head with a ball peen attached to a wooden handle. Used to forge and fit a horseshoe.

Items, usually of metal, flat, and rectangular or oval in shape, worn on the belt of a uniform or other costume. When part of a military uniform, often bear insignia of rank or unit. Includes plates worn on waist belts, shoulder belts, and sword belts. Usage sometimes overlaps with "belt plaques," which may be made of various materials, although items made of stone are typically called "belt plaques" rather than "belt plates."
Computer-animated simulations of what would be seen if one were to float or fly through a particular environment or object, either real or imaginary.
Polynesian war canoes.
In language, a small set of words that give definiteness or indefiniteness and specificness or genericness to the application of a noun.

Variety of Spanish spoken in north and central Spain; was the basis of modern standard Spanish. The dialect arose in Cantabria in the 9th century. It is the standard language used for radio and TV speakers.
Refers to Spanish spoken in areas of Argentina.
Pointers used by readers of the Torah in the synagogue to follow the text, typically having the form of a rod terminating in a hand with an outstretched index finger.
The standard unit of currency of Australia.

Enclosures, often made of plastic or recyclable material, fitted around shoes to protect them from outside wear. Also used to keep shoes from tracking material into other spaces, such as infectious materials in medical contexts.
Buddhist priests of Mongolia and the Tibetan territories of southwestern China.
The standard or base unit of frequency in the international System of Units defined as one cycle per second.
Deities associated with, or personifications of, the sun.
Monstrous men described in the Florentine Codex as the fifth omen that heralded the arrival of the Spaniards to the Mexica. Literally, "man (as) poisonous (or thorny) plants".
Stylized wooden masks covering the face of participants in gigaku, a type of Japanese dance drama. Gigaku masks are the first known masks used in Japan and among the world’s oldest extant masks.
Titles that vary from the primary title. Distinguished from "alternative titles."
Jewelry or other decorative items worn in, on, or about the nose. Included are ornaments that cover larger portions of the face, but are attached at the nose.
Grapes that are partially dried in sunlight or by artificial means. Uses include eating as is, as an ingredient in cooking, and in the production of wine
Agricultural structures in which tobacco is dried and cured, with or without supplemental heat.
Species of bivalve mollusk; noted for having decorative and symbolic value for Pre-Columbian cultures.
The smaller of two species of elephants existing in Africa.
Philosophical principles underlying and guiding approaches chosen for conservation of monuments, sites, and objects.The ethics and values regulating conservation practice fall under this heading.
Events comprising the apprehending or restraining of a person, usually under legal authority, in order to be questioned or prosecuted for an alleged or suspected crime.
A part of a loom that controls tightening and loosening the warp threads. It usually consists of a friction brake or a pawl and ratchet wheel.
Initials containing scenes or figures germane to the text.
Those who study pharaonic Egypt, spanning the period around 4500 BCE to 641 CE.

Musical pieces composed for one or more voices with instrumental accompaniment, typically incorporating a narrative and organized in a somewhat dramatic manner but not intended to be acted in movement or costume.
Genus of fruit-bearing deciduous shrubs or small trees having two extant species.
Cabinets for storing wine, usually located near the dining table, having four or more openings for bottles, often with ice to cool the wine. The type is particularly well known in Tuscany.
The condition of a person or animal having a bodily wound, hurt, sore, or loss.

On the geologic time scale, the youngest epoch of the Tertiary, or of the more recently designated Neogene, following Miocene and preceding the Pleistocene epoch of the Quaternary period. It extends from about 5 million to 1.8 million years ago. The Pliocene is marked by the change to a cooler, dry seasonal climate and the presence of essentially modern flora and fauna.

On the geologic time scale the third epoch of the Tertiary period, following Eocene and preceding Miocene, or the first period of more recently designated Paleogene.  It extends from about 34 million to 22 million years ago. The epoch is marked by the further development of mammals. The name Oligocene refers to the relatively few moder animals originating during the epoch.

The period of Earth's history that began 2.5 billion years ago and ended 542.0 million years ago, following the Archean. In this period stable continents first appeared and began to accrete, and also the first abundant fossils of living organisms, mostly bacteria and archaeans, then eukaryotic cells.
Loops tied at the end of rope usually knotted so that the loop tightens as pressure is exerted upon it with the weight of a person being executed by hanging.
The activity or condition of being active as a member of a branch of the military.
Culture of a pre-Nuraghic people of Sardinia living near what is now Ozieri.
Wrenches that are used to apply different heads to harness awls, in leatherwork.
Black round hat with a wide flat brim, with hanging black tassels on a cord that is tied around the ball.
Linear, usually pointed leaves, usually of a coniferous tree.

In botany, underground plant structures consisting of a solid thickened portion or outgrowth of a stem or rhizome, of a more or less rounded form, and bearing ‘eyes’ or buds from which new plants may arise; a familiar example is the potato.
Genus of large, flightless birds having only one remaining species.
Brothers of a one's parent or husbands of one's parent's sister.
Daughters of a one's brother or sister.

Women who have a romantic relationship with a man without being his wife. The term today usually has a negative connotation, and is generally only used in the context of certain historical periods. The mistress may be a powerful person in the household, even bearing children; it is often used when the husband is married to another person. Its usage can overlap with "concubines," although "mistresses" is typically preferred in historical periods of Europe and elsewhere in the West.
State, condition, or behavior in which a person's identity does not conform unambiguously to conventional notions of male or female gender, including transsexualism or transvestism.
Formulas of words spoken or chanted, intended to produce a magical effect; may include magical ceremonies or arts.

Peranakan Chinese covered jars which are oval with a symmetrical tapering profile. The lids (covers) commonly but not always, have a funnel-shaped knob at the top. Chupu are usually designed with Peranakan Chinese motifs which have auspicious symbolisms such as peonies, phoenixes, the eight auspicious Buddhist emblems, butterflies, and other flowers. The jars can be used for double-boiling foods such as soups. They are also used as ceremonial vessels for Peranakan Chinese weddings. Smaller ones were used to store beauty products as well.

Related to a device, instrument, information storage, work, or other application, operating according to the principles or methods using signals, information, or data represented by a series of discrete values (commonly the numbers 0 and 1), such as for electronic storage or processing.

Refers the bodies of human beings, or sometimes of animals, that have been embalmed, naturally preserved, or treated for burial with preservatives. Among the many peoples who practiced mummification were the people living along the Torres Strait between Papua New Guinea and Australia, the Incas of South America, and the Chinese. Prominent examples were created by the ancient Egyptians. The process varied from age to age in Egypt, but it always involved removing the internal organs (though in a late period they were replaced after treatment), treating the body with resin, and wrapping it in linen bandages.
Containers or detachable receptacles that may be used on analog cameras to hold photographic film, enabling exposed film to be switched out quickly.
In a surface, hollows or depressions that are longer than they are broad.

Chinese festival observed on the ninth day of the ninth month in the Chinese calendar; it is documented since before the East Han period, before 25 CE. According to the "I Ching," nine is a yang number, which is a traditional Chinese spiritual concept. According to custom, it is held that the double yang of this day is too much yang, and potentially dangerous; to protect against danger, it was customary to climb a high mountain, drink chrysanthemum wine, and wear the cleansing zhuyu plant. Other observances may include visiting the graves of ancestors, cleaning the graves, laying out food offerings, and burning incense.

Religious movement originating from William Faw Faw (Waw-No-She) (c. 1854-1924), an Otoe-Missouria prophet; became popular amongst Native North Americans in Oklahoma in the late 19th century to the early 20th century. With a focus on returning back to Native lifeways, adherents would enact complex dances and ceremonies, as well as wearing heavily decorated regalia.

Naturally occuring as tinstone or cassiterite, stannic oxide is the principal ore of tin. It can be artificially obtained as an anhydrous powder when tin is burned in the presence of oxygen, or by igniting stannous hydrate or stannous oxalate. Stannic oxide is used in the manufacture of white glazes and enamels, and as an opacifier. In its pure state is white or light yellow in color.
Swedish variation of Art Nouveau that emphasized stricter and more  geometric designs.
Flanged cores around which magnetic tape media is wound for storage and playback.
In Japanese printing, format having dimensions ca. 52 x 18 cm.
Visual works that are undone, defaced, or otherwise broken into useless or unreadable form, either through accident or intent.

Distinctive type of opus sectile ("cut work") technique, by which small triangles and rectangles of colored stones and glass mosaics are set into stone matrices or encrusted upon stone surfaces of floors, walls, or church fixtures; particularly as used in works with geometric patterns produced in Rome from the 12th to the 14th centuries. The name derives from the surname of a family of marbleworkers active in Rome, although all works of this type were not made by this one family.
That which is placed in position number two of a sequence.

Pairs of works of art that were designed, or purposefully chosen, to be displayed together, usually side by side. Examples would be portraits of a husband and wife, of the same size and scale, having the same or similar background, with the sitters arranged to face each other when hung on the wall.
State or condition of existing or moving in water.
The left-hand side of a ship, that is, the side to the left hand of a person looking from the stern towards the bows; as opposed to starboard.
Black gowns worn by ministers of the Protestant church. These are loose fitting garments with bell sleeves, sometimes embellished with velvet to indicate academic achievement.

The process of wrapping a flat, flexible work or material around a cylinder or onto itself for the purpose of storage or transport. Examples include the following: the rolling of scrolls around a rod or onto themselves; the rolling of drawn, painted, printed, or inscribed works on parchment, paper, or canvas; the rolling of textiles, film, or other flexible works or materials.
Qualifier used to refer to an attribution that had been accepted in the past, but is no longer generally held to be valid (e.g., formerly attributed to Yan Wengui (Chinese, active ca. 970-1030)).

Qualifier used for attributions of works by an unknown creator working for a named artist in a system common after the 16th century, when master artists took on pupils who were learning to be artists rather than apprentices who were learning a trade.

Qualifier used for a work by an unknown creator whose style is influenced by the named artist or architect or by the associates of the named artist, who is living at the same time or shortly after the named artist, but is not known to be a pupil or direct follower of the named artist (e.g., school of Rembrandt).

Qualifier used for a work by an unknown creator whose style seems to be a deliberate copy of the style of the named artist, but when the work at hand is not a direct copy of a known work by the named artist (e.g., copyist of Rodin).
The production by living organisms of new individuals or offspring by a process or mechanism that is either sexual or asexual in nature.
Portable, removable computer drives that operate via a type of non-volatile flash memory in which data can be written or erased only in blocks, and that connect to a computer via USB port.
Technique of constructing masonry walling made of stones laid up in regular horizontal rows or courses.
Spade-like tools for digging or excavating, having a narrow chisel-shaped blade.

Date range of years representing the earliest and latest dates for the most important or principal body of items in the group. There may be multiple sets of bulk dates for any group (e.g., 1914-1918 and 1939-1945 (bulk dates)).

In reference to visual works, the the secondary or back surface of the work. For the front or main surface, use "side A." Examples include extend indications for ancient Greek vessels and other such works.

CE, for "Common Era," and occasionally, "Christian Era," identifies years as part of a historical cultural current for recording dates used today. CE is used as an alternative to "AD" used by Christians, but the numbering is the same, with the same meaning as AD, and corresponds to the Gregorian Calendar. CE is now often used instead of AD particularly in scientific writing.
Pre-Columbian Andean-Amazonic calendar, for which the new year is still celebrated in Bolivia and other countries.

Conceptual systems for reckoning the passage of time in terms of days and years, often also with months or other such divisions. For processes by which age is determined and translated to estimated dates of creation or another event, use "dating (measuring processes)."
Dating system based on the orbit of the moon and with reference to the apparent passage of the stars across the sky.
Tools, equipment, and supplies that play a direct and essential role in the creation or transmission of written messages.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 320-376; founded by Han Chinese Zhang family.
Identification numbers assigned by the government to identify a property for the purpose of property taxes and other purposes.

Sustained posture or positioning of the torso and limbs, especially  when assumed for artistic or ritual effect, particularly as found in still images and dance. Common examples are in fashion modeling, in subjects of portraits, and in figures of other art works.
Bodies whose heads have been cut off, as a result of the neck being severed. Taking place after the enemy had been defeated, this practice was common on the battlefield in central Mexico.
Names, or words or phrases used as names, that are descriptive or connotative.
Sets or group of initial letters used as an abbreviation for a name or expression, for which each letter is pronounced separately. For initials pronounced as syllables or single word, use "acronyms."
An East Low German dialect used by Mennonite settlers to the south west of the Russian Empire starting in the 18th century.
Set of dialects of the Portuguese language used primarily in Brazil.
Refers to the varieties of Spanish spoken in the Americas. Pronunciation and other characteristics vary from country to country, and from region to region.
Sheet metal dovetail seams that are secured with a rim or collar.

Any gradual build up or enlargement due to external addition by deposition of new matter; for example, the increase in size of an inorganic mass as fresh particles are added to its surface or the physical addition to land due to deposits.

The physical results of an action, process, physical circumstances, or spontaneous physical or chemical change; usually observable with the eye, other senses, or with specialized equipment, and typically having a measurable quantity, dimension, or other measurable characteristics.

Frisbee is a trademark of the toy company Wham-O, but the name is used for all similar flying discs. Frisbees are usually made of plastic, have a diameter of about 20 to 30 cm. They are designed to fly aerodynamically and spin when thrown.
Small language family of South America, without known relationships to any other American language family.

Organized, regular methods of representing information and communicating thoughts or ideas, typically tied to a language. Writing systems use a set of visible marks, forms, or structures called characters or graphs that are related to some structure in the linguistic system. Examples containing general attributes or categories of writing systems include  alphabets, syllabaries, logographies, and others; any one system may comprise attributes of more than one category.

Writing systems in which consonant-vowel sequences are written as a unit: each unit comprises a consonant letter with a secondary vowel notation. Examples of alphasyllabaries are the Brahmic scripts of South and Southeast Asia.
Dances that have a ceremonial or ritual function. Characteristic are movements that are continuously repeated that may reflect a form or inducement of worship, prayer, visionary insights, or healing.

Japanese ceremonial dances combined with music used in Shinto, Buddhist, and Imperial court rituals and festivals. The dance and music were brought to Japan at an early date from China, Korea, India, and Southeast Asia. These dance and music forms were standardized and systematized by Japanese emperors of the 9th century. The dances are composed of stylized movements cued by the beat of a drum and the overall choreography is based on simple geometric patterns. The masks worn by the dancers are an important element of bugaku. There are two basic dance forms each accompanied by specific music: saho no mai ("dances of the left"), accompanied by togaku (derived mainly from Chinese music); and uho samai no mai  ("dances of the right"), accompanied by komagaku (music imported from Korea). The richly embroidered costumes of the saho no mai dancers are typically red while the costumes of uho samai no mai dancers are usually green or blue. A bugaku program typically starts with a selection performed by the lead dancers of both forms, followed by alternating dances from both repertoires. When the music is performed alone it is called 'gagaku.'
The discipline of extinguishing or limiting the spread of fires, as performed by members of organizations dedicated and trained for this purpose.

Discipline dealing with the study of traditional and expressive forms of culture, such as song, story, dance, ritual, handicraft, art, food, costume, custom, religion, architecture, and work skills, and of the processes and meanings that underlie them.
Edible substance consisting of the curd of milk (coagulated by rennet), separated from the whey, and pressed into a solid mass.

Sparkling wine named for the region of Champagne in northeastern France where it is traditionally produced. The term is frequently applied generically to other sparkling wines, with restrictions, outside France. In the United States, sparkling wines made in a similar manner are designated by place of origin, as in New York state champagne, or elsewhere as “champagne-style.”
In the APG IV system (2016) for the classification of flowering plants, denotes a clade (a monophyletic group) containing about 70,000 species, more than a quarter of all angiosperms.

Genus comprised of a single species: Premnas biaculeatus, which inhabits lagoons and outer reef slopes in 1 to 16 metres. Commensal with sea anemones, usually Radianthus gelam. Also reported to be associated with the anemone Entacmaea quadricolor, found mainly in protected coastal waters and lagoons. Feeds primarily on zooplankton and benthic algae.
Drills conducted by that part of an army which consists of men who march and maneuver on foot and are armed with small arms or rifles, in preparation for actual combat.
Factory buildings in which automobiles are produced or assembled.

Nondestructive ion beam analysis technique using accelerated particles in which specific target elements in the sample undergo a nuclear reaction. The emitted ionizing radiation is characteristic for this reaction and can be detected.

A method of painting with matte, opaque watercolor paint. Gouache painting employs opaque layers of color rather than the transparent washes used in the aquarelle technique, due to the differing pigment densities of the media.
Order of marine invertibrates distinguished from other ctenophores by having smaller tentacles with flattened lobes.
Genus of sea snails.
General term for several species of medium-sized water birds that are members of the rail family Rallidae, most but not all in the genus Gallinula.
Genus containing around 100 species of periennial flowering plants.
Family of ray-finned fish located in freshwater environments in temperate regions across the Northern hemisphere.
Species of Eurasian plant used to produce madder dyes and colorants from ancient times.
Genus of flowering plant native to the Mediterranean and western Asia.

Members of the group of true bacteria, which is one of two major groups of prokaryotic organisms, and one of the three major divisions of living organisms. The division of the bacteria into two groups arises from studies of their ribosomal RNA, which indicates that they are as different from each other as they are from eukaryotes (plants and animals). Bacteria and Archaea (formerly called Eubacteria and Archaebacteria) are thought to have evolved separately from a common ancestor early in Earth's history. Bacteria and Archaea differ in important characteristics, such as the number of ribosomal proteins and the size and shape of the ribosomal S unit. Use generally for unicellular microscopic protists, spherical, rodlike, or spiral in form, or clustered into filamentous colonies, reproducing by cell division, by asexual spores, or by imperfectly understood sexually processes. Various types have chemical effects, such as fermentation, nitrogen fixation, and putrefaction, or cause diseases.
Class of fungi.
A type of atomic emission spectroscopy which employs a highly energetic laser pulse as the excitation source.
In Chinese landscape painting, perspective created through a view of lofty mountains.
Genus containing around 30 species of flowering plants native to the Mediterranean region and Asia.
General term for several species in the genera Brassica and Sinapis.
Artificial products that have essentially the same physical and chemical characteristics as a diamond.
Costume indicative or characteristic of the calling or vocation of a religious community of women, especially a cloistered one, living under vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience.
Dough wheels or other utensils for crimping, and usually sealing, a pie crust by pressing together the edges of the top and base in a series of indentations
Cybernetic organisms, often depicted in science fiction works as humans with machine parts.

Christian liturgical vessels or containers, usually circular, used to hold the reserved hosts on the altar or to carry the eucharist to the sick.  For the similar small vessels found within the tabernacle, holding the host for use in the monstrance, use "custodes." For vessels used to hold the hosts for distribution to the faithful during a liturgy, use "ciboria (vessels)."  Early in church history, the word "pyx" was used in a very general sense, derived from the Latin and Greek words for wood of the boxwood tree, and intended to mean any containers of various sizes and shapes used to contain eucharistic bread.

Tubes used to dispense the consecrated Eucharistic wine. It is typically of larger diameter than a "eucharistic straw," and usually has a reservoir in which a serving of wine is held until released into the mouth of the recipient. Although the term may have overlap with "eucharistic straw," the straw typically is used for sipping. The purpose of the tube was to prevent spillage of the consecrated wine; it is known from ancient times, when methods of sharing the wine included spoon, straw, and tube.
Decorative utensils consisting of a straight handle with an enlarged and hollowed end-piece that are designed as mementos of a notable person, place, or event, rather than as functional objects.
General term for administrative divisions, usually of a nation, that represent the highest unit or level under the nation itself. Examples are the states of the United States.

Optical interferometry technique which involves study of the fringe pattern created when holograms capturing three dimensional information about the surface of the same object are reconstructed and superimposed.  After a stress is applied to the object, its new surface geometry is compared with a previously recorded state.

Refers to a representation of the events surrounding the birth of Christ. It is typically characterized by being three-dimensional and including the infant Jesus in the manger, the Virgin Mary and Saint Joseph, sheep, the ox and ass, and other attending figures, such as shepherds, magi, and angels. The term "crèche" derives from the animals' manger in which, according to some translations of the Gospel of Saint Luke, the Virgin placed the newborn Jesus. According to legend, Saint Francis of Assisi popularized the Christmas crèche in 1223 at Greccio, Italy, when he is said to have celebrated Midnight Mass in a stable where men and animals re-enacted the Nativity.

Period of the geologic time scale that extends from about 4.6 billion years ago, from the Earth's formation, to the beginning of the Cambrian Period, 542 million years ago. The Precambrian represents more than 80 percent of the total geologic record, and contains the  earliest evidence for the advent of life; microfossils that resemble algae, cysts of flagellates, tubes interpreted to be the remains of filamentous organisms, and mounded colonies of photosynthetic bacteria called stromatolites.

The middle era of the Phanerozoic eon externding from about 251 to 65 million years ago. It follows the Paleozoic and precedes the Cenozoic. It is divided into the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods. The Mesozoic is popularly known as the age of the dinosaurs.

The fifth interval of the Paleozoic Era in the geologic time scale, following the Devonian Period and preceding the Permian Period. The Carboniferous Period began approximately 358.9 million years ago and ended 298.9 million years ago, the longest period of the Paleozoic Era and the second longest period of the Phanerozoic Eon. The first reptiles and seed-bearing plants appeared during this period, accompanied by widespread coral reefs, coal-forming swamp forests, and extensive limestone deposits.

The second period of the Mesozoic era, following the Triassic and preceding the Cretaceous. During the Jurassic period, dinosaurs were the dominant form of terrestrial life and the first birds appeared.

Oldest of the three divisions of the Cenozoic Era spanning between 66 million and 23 million years ago. It includes the Paleocene, Eocene and the Oligocene epochs. This period was formerly considered a part of the Tertiary.
The younger of the two epochs belonging to the Cretaceous period on the geologic time scale. It extends from about 105.5 million to 66 million years ago.

On the geologic time scale the earlier and longer epoch of the Quaternary. The Pleistocene extends from about 1.8 million years ago to 10,000 BCE. It is best known as the time when Earth entered its most recent period of glaciation.
Vessels used in the Jewish ritual cleansing of hands, often before meals or after meals. Some cups feature two handles to allow each hand to be washed separately, while others have no handles at all.
Hand held devices that emit a very intense, narrow, parallel beam of highly monochromatic and coherent light, used as a pointer.
Special Christian eucharistic ceremonies that are accompanied by ritual and prayers outside the usual, often including the renewal of baptismal vows.
Species of tree native to western Africa, prized for its reddish, striped wood.
Museums that focus specifically on the history of space travel and astronauts.
A sulfite of copper. Uses include in herbicides applied to water to kill plants, but they are toxic to fish and other water animals.
Compounds in which sulfur is bonded to two organic groups.
The Germanic and Anglo-Saxon feast of the winter solstice, observed in December in pre-Christian Britain and northern Europe; later Christianized as Christmas.
Scientific facilities used as bases from which research is carried out or monitored.
Streams, rivers, or other watercourses that are wet and dry seasonally or otherwise flutuate depending upon rainfall, snowmelt, or other factors.
Physical features that contain water, either natural or man-made.
Tracts of land along the border of a nation, country, district, or region, including those originally established as military districts for national defense.
Capital towns or cities for administrative departments.
Artificial mounds consisting of the accumulation of debris from successive settlement levels; common in regions where mud brick is used.
Villages whose economies are based on agriculture.

Communities of relatively small size that hold a market, typically agricultural centers in a rural area. Market towns typically developed as a location to trade farm products, sometimes near fortified places.
Communities of small size where the central economic activities are built around tourism.
Communities, modest in size, that have economies centered on a university and the university population.

Communities of modest size, built mostly since the Industrial Revolution, in which the primary employment is in factories. When the primary employment is in factories for the manufacture of paper, steel, or textiles, use "mill towns." When settlements are purposely built by factory owners to attract workers to isolated locations, use "factory villages."
