Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a Shluh Berber group living in the Morocco High Atlas.

Religious complexes generally comprised of a structure of worship, such as a mosque or temple, towers, and subsidiary sancturaries or temples; characteristic of Southeast Asian, Indian, and Middle Eastern religious architecture.

In Indian architecture, a makara-shaped gargoyle; makara-shaped water chute or conduit for discharging deity’s lustral water; elsewhere in halls, at eave-cornice, etc.; torana-arch spewed from the mouths of makaras, or formed from their tails.
The hall for the preparation and distribution of consecrated food offerings in an Orissan temple.
Documents comprising a text corpus, database, or other source that is generally complete and of substantial length.

Refers to a style associated with the northern region of Thailand. Artistic production in this style primarily deals with the wood carving arts and features teak figures of Brahmanical and Hindu gods and of Buddhist images. Sculptures and carvings were often inlaid with mother-of-pearl or glass mosaics. The style is driven by the desire to intermingle animal, plant, and human life, evincing a detailed, exuberant blend of myth and realism. From this distinctive art, stylistic contradictions emerged, evidenced by sculptural figures of menacing demon entities doubling as guardian beings and by rigid geometric patterns set amidst designs of fanciful creatures on wooden relief panels. The most dramatic example in this style are the grandiose wooden royal barges and royal funeral chariots, both completely gilded constructions with mythical serpents and ornamental floral designs.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name, a subgroup of the Frafra living in northern Ghana.

A volcanic glass that contains about 75% silica and usually has a higher water content than obsidian; found in Oregon and California. Commercially, the term refers to volcanic glass that will expand or "pop" when heated to form a lightweight aggregate.

Describes motion picture film that is 35 millimeters wide with four perforations per frame on each side and having 16 frames per foot. It has been used as the standard gauge of film for professional cinematography since the earliest days of cinema.
Havng the form or outline of a dodecagon, a plane figure with twelve sides and twelve angles.

Having the shape or form of a cone, which is a geometric body for which the base is a circle, and the summit a point, and every point in the intervening surface is in a straight line between the vertex and the circumference of the base.
Having the form or outline of a rhombus, which is a parallelogram with four equal sides and the opposing angles equal, two being obtuse and two acute.
Film footage inserted into a motion picture that was originally shot for another purpose.

Films made using animation techniques, including the process of making still images appear to move, such as the technique of photographing drawings or objects in progressive stages of performing an action.

Unusual elements of a motion picture created using a variety of techniques such as computer, mechanical, makeup, pyrotechnic, optical, lighting, camera speed, weather effects, and model techniques. Generally they are used to create effects that normal camera techniques or set action cannot provide or would be too costly to shoot normally. They are often inserted into the motion picture by the special effects department after live shooting.

A transitional visual effect used to indicate to beginning of one scene and the ending of another by means of an image gradually disappearing (fade-out), while another image grows stronger and gradually comes into view (fade-in). An image fading into black typically indicates a major separation of action, while a fade to white can indicate a character's loss of consciousness or death.

Refers to combined software and hardware systems that relate and display collected information concerning phenomena associated with location relative to the Earth. They often have the ability to overlay temporal information or information related to geology, ecology, weather, land use, demographics, transportation, or other data on top of existing geographic base data. The data are typically presented in the form of maps or tables, displayed in color on a computer screen or printed out.

Hand-held, shoulder-mounted, or structurally-attached cameras using electronic components to record or transmit motion pictures and sound for television production. Color television cameras have typically used a beam-splitter to focus onto the faces of three red, green, and blue image tubes.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Central African Republic, Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Cameroon.
Refers to African people living in Darfur region of the Sudan and in Chad.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Chad.
Permanent marking of the human body, as with symbols, patterns, or other designs, by means of producing raised scars, done for social or cultural reasons or for adornment.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Ethiopa and Kenya.
Anthropomorphic basaltic stone monoliths referring to dead legendary figures and found in localized areas in the Middle Cross River region of Nigeria, Africa.

Carved heads without bodies in Maori art. The heads are often carved in a relatively realistic manner. They may be affixed to the gable of a house or a canoe. For carved heads that are less realistic, having fierce expression, bulbous eyes, etc., use "koruru."
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in Côte d'Ivoire.
Styles belonging to southern coastal Cameroon cultures.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in Zambia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Angola, Botswana, and Namibia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in eastern Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, and western Guinea.

German drinking glasses that are tall, cylindrical, and decorated in enamel with portraits of the Holy Roman Emperor with the seven Electors. The emperor can be depicted on horseback with the three spiritual electors behind him and four princes below, or the kaiser can be depicted enthroned, with three or four princes on either side.
Style and culture of the people of Algeria or Algiers, in northern Africa.

Style of twentieth-century Makonde sculpture reflecting Tanzania's national emphasis on family and unity, featuring clusters of intertwined, naturalistic human figures arranged around a central core or pole.

An ancient Roman half-timber construction technique involving either wattle work or timber with a concrete or rubble filler, sometimes plastered over. This style of construction has been found at sites such as Pompeii and Herculaneum.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in Cameroon, Congo, and Central African Republic.
Grain pattern of intersecting lines produced by boarding the leather in two different directions.
Book cloth grain with a bubble pattern, introduced ca. 1870.
Small loops that are components of belts on clothing that secure the loose end.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Angola.
Hard, saltless biscuits or bread made of flour and water; formerly used aboard ships and in the armed forces.
Trade beads, often made of Czech glass, commonly used in Native North American beadwork. Usually no larger than 7 mm in diameter. Seed beads are still used in contemporary Native beadwork.
Rings used to say the Christian rosary prayer beads. The surface of the ring is marked with a decade, ten beads or protruding knobs and a cross, to serve as counters to track number of prayers said.

Oval wooden or metal face masks made and used by the Senufo people of northern Côte d'Ivoire, southern Mali, and southwestern Burkina Faso. Representing the female element, these masks are generally slightly smaller than life-size. They are ornamented with sets of geometric projections that flank the crown of the head, upper face, and mouth, diagonal scarifications on each cheek, and sometimes a set of vertical horns.

East Asian paintings primarily depicting birds, and plants, and natural subjects. Paintings of this genre originated in China and were transmitted to Japan by the literati master Shen Nanpin when he visited there in 1731. Japanese artists further developed the genre in the Edo period.
Marks printed or impressed on a surface, in wax, or otherwise applied to a material by "seals (artifacts)," which are devices bearing a design, emblem, a letter, name, or words.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a Sidamo people living in Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the lagoon region of Côte d'Ivoire.

Ceremonial staffs associated with power. They symbolized the taking of command or the transfer of an office from one person to another in Mexico in the postclassic period, and their use has continued through the colonial period into the present day.
Builder's models comprising a plank backboard or sawn-out section of the hull of a ship with plank sections mounted onto it to represent the frames of the proposed vessel.

Short cloaks covering the shoulders and designed to be worn at night, as is required by some religious orders. Such scapulars may be of various designs; an example is joined by bands at the side and has the hood attached to it.
Hairstyles incorporating plaited, interwoven, or entwined strands of hair.
Type of metal cover for icons, typically one layer of metal ornamented, often set with jewels; oklads cover most of the depicted figure. It may also contain chambers to hold individual relics.
Comics, usually serialized and composed of a few frames, and often syndicated for publication in newspapers.
Comics, inspired by the underground comics of the 1960s and 1970s, that began to appear in periodicals from ca. 1980. Their contents are generally for a mature audience and with small print runs.
Activities comprising the tolling of a church bell or other bell, rung slowly and solemnly, to announce a death or a funeral.
Heavy timbers in a slipway, which slide down the ground ways when a vessel is being launched.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northern Ghana and Burkina Faso.

Generally, the style and culture of the people of the tribal area and town of Mediouna, near Casablanca. Specifically, the style of rugs from this area, distinguished from rugs originating in a nearby urban carpet center, Rabat, in having fewer minor borders and a wider field than Rabat rugs, and having three or more octagonal medallions on the field. Traditional Mediouna rugs are no longer woven, but the style is copied.

Said of a book of which the folded fore edges  of the leaveshave not been cut with the plough or guillotine prior to sale. Distinct from "unopened" which is said of a book sold with the folded fore edges not trimmed or cut, intended to be slit by hand by the purchaser with a paper knife.
Leather that has been tanned by forcing vegetable tanning liquor through the pores of the skin or hide. It is often dressed on the flesh side to have a fine nap like suede.

Vegetable-tanned goatskin from Nigeria. Similar to "oasis" but tanned locally and dyed in fewer colors, the most common being brick-red, green, and buff. It is highly prized by bookbinders for its high quality and grain pattern.

Smooth-grained natural- or cream-colored sheepskin leather, vegetable-tanned, usually with bark, commonly used in the 19th and early 20th centuries in binding law books, especially in England, as a less expensive alternative to "law calf." It has been superceded in that use by "law buckram."
Raw animal skins converted to leather from treatment with two or more tanning agents; i.e., a combination of vegetable matter and metal chromium.
Leather made of the skin of a calf, used especially for bookbinding.
Book edges that have been smoothly cut with a guillotine or plough, so that they are flush with each other.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name, a subgroup of the Katab living in northern Nigeria.
Ethnicity, culture, and styles of the Maniema region, Central Africa.

The collective style and culture of various African peoples whose adult males grow to less than 59 inches (150 cm) in average height, and who live in Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Democratic Republic of Congo, Congo Republic, Central African Republic, Rwanda, and Burundi. Use of "Pygmy" for a culture is considered pejorative; where possible use instead the most specific name for the subgroup.
Describes works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Democratic Republic of the Congo at the confluence of the Lulua and Kasai Rivers.

Style and culture of people speaking a Bantu language called "Mongo" and living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (formerly Zaire). This includes any of several peoples living in the African equatorial forest, south of the main Congo River bend and north of the Kasai and Sankuru rivers in Congo (Kinshasa), such as the ethnic groups Bokote, Ekonda, Bolia, Sengele, Ntomba, Ndengese, Songomeno, Mbole, Bongandu, Boyela, Nkutu, and Tetela-Kusu. They speak dialects of a common language, Mongo or Nkundo, which belongs to the Benue-Congo branch of the Niger-Congo languages.
The outermost or surface split of a skin or hide.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in the Democratic Republic of Congo south of the Kasai River between the Loange and Kamtsha Rivers, also west of the Kamtsha.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in the Central African Republic and the northwestern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Describes African people living in southern Ethiopia. They are distinct from the Hamar but live in close proximity.

Refers to the Pottery Neolithic period in the southern Levant from about 6000 to 5500 BCE. The period is characterized by pottery decorated with incised or combed patterns, clay and stone anthropomorphic figurines, and incised pebble figurines.
Straps, usually of leather or woven horse hair, that encircle the body of a horse or other animal to fasten a saddle upon its back.

Members of a species of hominid found in tropical forests and wet savannas of western and central Africa, although their habitat was formerly much larger. They are characterized by a body that is mostly covered by dark brown hair, having thumbs and its big toes that are opposable, and differing from the other extant species of the genus Pan, bonobos, in being more robust, having a more protruding face, spending more time out of the trees, and having different behaviors and dynamics in social groups. In older classifications, the bonobo and the common chimpanzee were classified as one species.
The parents of one's grandparents.
Bells used to summon attendants (such as in hotels), or to give alarms or notices of varying kinds.
Ties or bands worn to support stockings or socks.
Close-fitting underwear combining a shirt and drawers in one piece and often having a drop seat.
Region of the upper atmosphere of the Earth containing a relatively high concentration of ozone, which absorbs much of the ultraviolet radiation reaching the earth from the sun.
Material that may be in the form of a gas, liquid, or solid that binds to and forms a film or layer on other materials.

Decorations in the form of charges or devices consisting of a bar bent like two meeting rafters; multiple chevrons may be grouped together, forming inverted V-shaped stripes. Examples occur on heraldic escutcheons and as worn on the sleeve of a uniform to indicate rank.
Portable furniture intended for use outdoors.
Companies that employ one or more licensed architects to practice the profession of design and production of architecture.
Refers generally to associations of persons carrying on commercial or industrial enterprises.
Business enterprises owned and usually operated by married or co-habiting couples.

Relating to, or comprising more than two distinct differentiated peoples based on socially defined characteristics. This term is applied both to groups of people or to individuals. Multiracial people may have different opinions about which terms are considered derogatory or acceptable, depending on region, country or personal preference. The term may be perceived as homogenizing.
Vertical poles in fire stations positioned to facilitate getting firefighters quickly and safely from their sleeping quarters to their vehicles; invented in the United States in the late 1870s.

Small, decorative handbags, usually without handles, but often with an attached chain, intended as accessories for women's formal evening wear. They are typically constructed as small rigid metal boxes that hold only a few essential cosmetic items, and may have elaborate shapes, beading, metalwork or other forms of surface embellishment. The term was coined by the jeweler Charles Arpels in 1930 to describe objects of his design.
Style of Nubian fresco and panel painting that, among other stylistic characteristics, uses the color white more than had previous styles; it dated from the end of 11th century until around 1175.
Devices used in aquatic navigation that measure distance to solid objects by echo-location.
Describes the surface of the leather from which the outer layer of hair and epidermis is removed.
Sound-amplifying devices or speakers worn or held against the ear in order to compensate for impaired hearing, to listen to telephone or radio communication, to listen to music, or other purposes.
In Indian architecture, a niche frame.
Devices for charging storage batteries.

Refers to hand sewing characterized by the simplicity of the stitches and by its application, which is primarily for the construction of clothing and the finishing of household textiles. It is distinct from sewing used to create designs, such as embroidery. Plain sewing generally may include basic stitches, such as running stitches, back-stitching, hemming stitches, and seaming stitches, as well as simple embellishments to these basic stitches.
Bindings produced as unique or limited editions and intended to be works of art in themselves.
Blocking that leaves a pattern of gold on a surface, usually involving the use of a heated block or frame which is pressed on gold leaf.
Sandwich panels that provide insulation, generally from a rigid foam core, and structural stability, making them suitable as complete wall, floor, or roof units.
Brick that has been ground or otherwise produced to accurate dimensions.
Sodium copper formate acetate found as a corrosion product on objects in which copper alloys are in contact with glass.
Genus containing one living species of flying lemur.
Fans without a leaf, comprised of flat, overlapping sticks which broaden towards the outer edge where they are secured, one to another, by a ribbon or cord.
Detachable shoulder straps for military rucksacks or haversacks. Often with hooks for attaching cartridge pouches and fitted with cinch buckles.
Those who ride motorcycles.
Common term used for members of several families of clams.

Large, multistory, multiroom complex dwellings of the Ancestral Puebloan and Hohokam periods, mostly dating from 950 to 1150 CE; distinguished from "pueblos (housing complexes)" by their often D-shaped outline, cohesive planned design, and location in the San Juan Basin, New Mexico, and parts of Arizona.
Groups of houses or tents and associated facilities designed as a residence for loggers who are temporarily in a forest to cut down and transport timber.
Discrete housing complexes closed off to nonresidents by gates and fences or walls; may or may not also have guards or other surveillance and security installations.

Temporary and often spontaneously established, settlements of displaced peoples along borders of neighboring or nearby countries, generally having minimal shelter, supplies, and sanitary facilities and created without the granting of technical asylum.

Landed properties, usually of considerable extent, which typically have a grand house and outbuildings, and which may, but not necessarily must, have certain land on which a crop is cultivated; may have tenants who operate the agricultural lands. For commercial agricultural lands, particularly those similar to plantations and located in European colonial areas, use "estates (commercial agricultural holdings)."

Strips of fabric and elastic used as an accessory to one's outfit, usually worn around the waist. Sometimes decorated with beads, buttons, or ribbon. Cinch belts were particularly popular in the United States in the 1950s, replacing garter belts as a way to create a defined waist.
Long, thin nails designed to be used with a ferrule to secure gutters.
Ancient East African culture, partially identified by characteristic pottery ware found in southeastern Kenya and northeastern Tanzania.
Cooperative associations that make small loans to their members at low interest rates.
Fixed seats for the clergy with high, enclosing backs and sides.
Species that is the closest relative of Bombyx mandarina, the wild silk moth. The silkworm is the larva or caterpillar of a silk moth, used for silk fiber.
General term for places where pigs are kept or bred.
Portions of Islamic houses reserved for men, and in some countries, also considered the public sectors of houses. For the women's quarters of Islamic houses, use "harems."
Women's quarters of Islamic houses. For the portions of Islamic houses reserved for men, use "selamliks."
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in southwestern Madagascar.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Ituri forest in Democratic Republic of Congo.
Painters who work in service of the church.
Ecclesiastical tribunals for the investigation, discovery, and suppression of heresy. First organized in the 13th century under Pope Innocent III.
Machine or hand sewing of text blocks without the use of tapes, cords, or other sewing supports.
Method used in binding pamphlets of only one gathering in which wire staples are passed through the single fold.
Quetzal-feather head fan or quetzal feather device.

High-ranking military title in Tenochtitlan. Warriors were associated with a particular hairstyle, snail shell fringed necklaces and distinctive grid-like face paint. Not to be confused with the ethnic designation referring to populations in the mountains north of the Valley of Mexico.
Utensils used to create folds in paper.
Equipment used for playback of digital versatile discs (DVDs). Generally, DVD players can also play CDs, although CD players cannot play DVDs.
Refers to animals that naturally feed exclusively or nearly exclusively on the leaves and other parts of plants. Butterflies and elephants are examples of herbivores.
Adult males of cattle, oxen, bison, camel, moose, walrus, whale, seal, rhinoceros, hippopotamus, giraffe, elephant, dolphin, and other animals.

The names for subfamilies Old World deer (subfamily Cervinae) and the New World deer (subfamily Capreolinae) reflect where the deer originally evolved; however, now it is not a geographical distinction but instead derives from their different foot structures. In the Old World deer the second and fifth hand bones (metapodia) have almost completely disappeared except for proximal, terminal remnants. In the New World deer the remnants are distal.

Water drawn through taps from pipes in a dwelling or other structure. Due to its noncorrosive properties, tap water may be used in conservation of ancient stone materials in preference to distilled water.
Genus containing over 30 living species of tree squirrels, including the common, bushy-tailed squirrels in North and South America, Europe, and parts of Asia.
Adult male birds.

Fighting bracelets consisting of a single, continuous disk-shaped blade with a gap and a hole in the middle to allow them to be slipped onto the wrist, with thin sheaths of hide covering both the inner and sharpened outer edges; may also serve as cutting tools, and in some cases as ornament or signs of identity.
Genus containing the cigarette beetle.

One of the large divisions of an army; military units in the form of a headquarters and a large body of soldiers commanded by a field-grade officer. The term has been used variously in Western culture for centuries with a variety of shifts in meaning and context.

Areas, used mainly for census and federal funding allocation, having a dominant central city with a combined minimum population of 50,000 and with a surrounding urbanized community that is economically and socially integrated with the central city.
Fruits or pieces of fruits that are preserved by being impregnated with sugar.
Flags, banners, figures, or other objects that are an identifying symbol or rallying-point, and that are designed for or used in processions.
Cones of fabric with hoops at the larger end, used as brakes or drags for air- and spacecraft, or similar vehicles or equipment.
A ceramic technique in which fine cord is wrapped around a paddle and pressed against an unfired clay vessel, leaving the cord imprint.

Nondestructive technique of activation analysis induced by neutrons. The prompt gamma rays immediately emitted by the sample are measured with a gamma ray spectrometer, allowing the identification of a wide variety of neutron-capturing elements simultaneously.
A couplet is a pair of successive lines of verse, typically that are rhyming together and of the same length.
Nuptial poems or songs in praise of the bride and bridegroom, and praying for their prosperity.

Ammonium salt made from a reaction of sulfuric acid and ammonia. It is primarily produced by the destructive distillation of coal. Ammonium sulfate is a commercially important chemical used as a fertilizer, food additive, and tanning agent.

Object genre comprising items and equipment worn, carried, or otherwise used for an individual's needs, convenience, or fashion. Includes, but not limited to, costume accessors, sports equipment, and armor.
The joints that connect the foot with the leg of a human or an animal; also used for the larger area comprising the slender part of the leg between this joint and the calf.
Persons who fit together the component parts of an object.

People responsible for treatment, preventive care, and research directed toward the long-term safekeeping of cultural and natural heritage. For those engaged in making changes to an object or structure in order to prevent further deterioration, see "preservationists." For those who make changes to an object or structure so as to closely approximate its state at a specific time in its past, see "restorers."
Buildings or complexes of buildings in which each unit is individually owned and ownership of common areas and facilities is shared.
Footwear, the leg of which extends above the ankle joint.

Footwear made partly or wholly of wood, with a thick sole usually of wood, but sometimes of leather or cork; originally to protect the foot, hosiery, or other footwear. The term "clogs" may also apply to shoes in the style of wooden clogs, but made of other materials. For overshoes consisting of a sole set on bands of iron, use "pattens."
Shoes that are an element of Greek folk dress. The tip of the shoe is formed as an upstanding point, on top of which a pompom is attached.

Heelless footwear made entirely of soft leather, as deerskin, with the sole brought up to form part or all of the upper portion covering the foot, and with a back seam; worn originally by indigenous peoples of North America. Also, shoes of similar construction, with hard sole and heel attached, made of soft or hard leather or leatherlike material.

Refers to the culture of the Arikara, an American Plains Indian people who lived along the Missouri River between the Cheyenne River in South Dakota and Fort Berthold in North Dakota. The Arikara, a Caddoan-speaking people, were culturally related to the Pawnee, from whom they broke away and moved gradually northward, becoming the northernmost Caddoan tribe. Wars and smallpox epidemics severely reduced their numbers by the 19th century. To escape further violence, the Arikara joined with the Hidatsa and Mandan tribes, known today as the "Three Affiliated Tribes."

Refers to the most commonly used flourescence microscopy technique. Exciting radiation is mounted above ('epi') the specimen and is reflected downwards, passing through the microscope objective lens on its way toward the specimen.
Parts or components of swells.

Longitudinal shutters or slats built into one side of the swell box of an organ or reed organ, usually with beveled edges and linked together in sets either vertically or horizontally, and pivoted so that the organ player can open or close them as desired by means of the swell action.

Supreme executive legislatures, especially the assemblies of citizens having the highest deliberative functions in a government, currently or historically summoned by a monarch for the discussion of important matters.

Reworking small areas of a painting or photographic negative usually to cover damage or to mask unwanted features. For similar work done on paintings by conservators, use "inpainting" or "overpainting."
Describes depictions of human habitation of countryside or pastoral areas, most often including some aspect of farming.

Loose-leaf binders with either solid or sectional posts that pass through holes in the margins of the individual leaves, typically intended for pages that are unusually large and heavy, such as in a scrapbook.
Refers to the style and culture of an African people living in Chad and Central African Republic.
African ceremonial knives of the Kuba people having a pommel and a flat, leaf-shaped blade of metal or wood.
Stays, made of plastic or metal, meant to hold brassieres and other upper undergarments in place by pinning the straps to the outer garment.
The extent of a continuous passage of time.
Any solid, liquid, or gaseous by-product that is destructive to the environment or dangerous to the health of people or animals.

Masquerades held by the secret society named Gelede of the Yoruba people of West Africa, incorporating performances of songs honoring the older women of the community, and satiric commentary on community figures, events, and moral behavior; they are held all night on the opening night of the society's annual festival.
Electrical table or desk lamps with a flexible arm that permits the control of the focus of light.

Relatively large areas intended for enjoyment and amusement, distinguished by woods and other features, such as architectural fantasies and riding trails. For smaller areas having a similar purpose but with an enclosing wall and focusing on flowers, shrubs, mazes, fruit trees, pedestrian paths, etc., prefer "pleasure gardens." Later pleasure parks may include separate areas for different amusements, forerunners of "amusement parks."

Generally, scientists who study the occurrence and movement of water on and over the surface of the earth. The particular processes with which hydrologists are concerned are precipitation, evaporation and transpiration, stream flow, and groundwater flow. Their work includes flood control, supplying water for domestic and industrial purposes, irrigation, and the production of hydroelectric power.

Inlaid works in which pieces of hard, polished stone have been set into marble or another hard surface; a Florentine specialty often used for decorative table tops and small wall panels. The singular form, "pietra dura," is used within Italy to refer to works incorporating a single type of stone; but outside Italy it refers to works using combinations of stones. Pietra dura works were carved in classical Rome, and the techniques for cutting such hard stones were revived in 16th-century Florence, where a workshop established under the patronage of Grand Duke Cosimo I de' Medici produced decorative panels; the workshop was refounded in 1588 as the Opificio delle Pietre Dure. The hardstones used are semi-precious stones, typically agate, chalcedony, jasper and lapis lazuli, but do not include marble or precious stones. Stones of the requisite hardness for such work generally fall between 6 and 10 on Mohs' scale of hardness, i.e. between orthoclase and diamond (lapis lazuli being the notable exception).
Drinkable liquids; often excludes water.

Fishing vessels with covered hulls and upswept prows that are fitted with mizzen-masts and mainsails with a boom and lowering gaff. These were used in the South Holland islands in the 18th and 19th centuries. The hull was covered to provide for a livewell for keeping live fish and bait.
Describes fishing watercraft that engage in the capture of marine life using lines, as opposed to nets.

Narratives for children in which geography, together with the history, customs, and folklore of nations, is presented by means of accounts of the fictional adventures of a child, a family, or some other group.  Examples are found in the United Kingdom in the 19th and early 20th centuries.
Dictionarylike references of armorial bearings (all authorized devices including coats of arms, badges, and flags) listed alphabetically by surname.
Bonnets made with a tight-fitting headband and a very wide circular crown, usually with a pompon in the center. In British military usage, worn by Scottish ranks as field service headgear, from 1915.
Tall caps of black fur or feathers, with or without a plume or cockade and usually with a bag draped from the crown to the right.

An alphabet created by the scholar Mesrop Mashtots ca. 405 CE, with 36 original characters, and auxiliary letters added later historically. Used from the fifth century for the preservation of Armenian cultural and literary identity.
One of two families containing anteaters.
Family containing the two-toed sloths.
Devices or small structures, either freestanding or attached to trees or buildings, designed to hold and dispense feed such as seeds, suets, and sugar water, for feral birds.
The complete equipment by which draft animals are attached to vehicles of any kind; sometimes also used for riding accoutrements.
Pairs of ropes, chains, or usually leather straps with which a draught animal is attached to the splinter-bar or swingletree of the vehicle it's pulling.
Tags of metal or plastic, attached to the collar of a dog and containing information such as his owner's contact information and verification of the licensing of the dog.
Fossilized fecal material; indirect evidence of prehistoric life, particularly as pertains to ancient diet.

The actions, rites, ceremonies, or agreements surrounding a formal arrangement between a man and a woman to marry at some future time. An engagement or betrothal is a promise to wed, and also the period of time between a marriage proposal and a marriage which may be lengthy or trivial.
Brazilian coming out celebrations and ceremonies held on the occasion of a girl's fifteenth birthday.
Professional cooks, specifically head cooks in restaurants, hotels, or other food service organizations.

Military uniforms for soldiers worn when they are performing labor, training, or engaging in combat. These are typically durable, include utilitarian details such as multiple pockets, and are designed to withstand rough use. The term derives from "fatigue duty:" non-military labor assigned to soldiers.

Pipes designed to vaporize and inhale opium, consisting of a long stem and a small ceramic bowl connected by a metal fitting. The opium is heated in the bowl over an opium lamp, causing it to vaporize, after which the smoker inhales the opium through the stem.
Canopies fitted above a stove to aid ventilation, sometimes equipped with an exhaust fan and attached to a flue.
Sterns on Maori boats.
Walking with long or extended steps.

Wind catchers consisting of tall shafts rising well above rooflines and having a single large opening and a diagonally sloping top facing prevailing winds; found especially in Egypt, Iran, and Pakistan.
Parts or components of tracks.
Strong internal rectangular supports for the rails in railroad tracks.
Rubber or plastic teats made for babies or small children to suck on for comfort.

Components of shotgun shells that are used to separate the shot from the powder, contain the shotgun shot, and provide a seal that prevents gas from blowing through the shot rather than propelling the shot out of the shotgun.
The concept of one's home or native land.
Area of manufacture that is concerned with the factors that determine where producers choose to locate and the effects of the location of a piece of land on the use made of it.
The area immediately surrounding individuals which they reserve for themselves.  Also, the space allocated for normal conversational voice and friendly interactions.
Motifs of human faces surrounded with foliage, in many cases with leaves appearing to sprout from the mouth, nostrils, and sometimes the eyes.
Indicators, often married to sound-making devices, that light as a visual warning or alert as triggered by some stimuli. Often these are red but may appear in any color.
Waterspouts in the form of lions' heads.
Term generally applied to any of various tools used for fleshing skins or hides.
Vegetation that is considered less likely to combust from flame or other ignition sources. These may be damaged or killed by fire, but may not contribute to fueling the fire itself.

Crosses comprising broad, flat planks of wood on which is painted the crucified Christ, often in lifesize or monumental scale and with additional scenes or figures filling the terminations of the arms and the area above and beneath the figure of Christ. Painted crosses were particularly common in Byzantine and early Italian art, typically placed over or near the altar in churches.
The process of applying a new surface treatment, such as paint, sealer, or stain, to an object or work.
Compact electronic amplifiers worn to improve one's hearing, usually placed in or behind the ear.
Species of orangutan living on Borneo island; they differ from the Sumatran orangutan in being larger, taller, having darker but shorter hair, a shorter face, and a more solitary lifestyle.

Species of large, intelligent, social hominid. The western gorilla differs from the eastern gorilla in being lighter in color, having an overhanging tip on its nose, a more slender body, being more arboreal, having a diet more based on fleshy fruits, and typically a smaller family group.

General term for the right or condition of complete dominion, title, or proprietary right to a real or other property as allowed by law. Ownership may be private, collective, or common. Ownership may be present even in the absence of possession.
In Indian architecture, a dais; platform; prastara; adhiṣṭhāna-type;  adhiṣṭhāna type without kumuda.
Used to describe something riding on top of another thing, such as a person riding on another's shoulders or hips, but often used in the context of objects.
Islamic ablutions required before the five daily prayers, involving washing with water the face and nostrils, the head, the hands and forearms, and the feet and ankles.

Groups of wild or domestic mammals of one species that remain together, specifically applied to horses, zebra, oxen, antelope, cattle, camels, buffalo, elephants, deer, swine, whales, or certain other species.
Collectively describes living beings that reside in the ocean. This term is often additionally used to describe legendary or mythological beings thought to live in oceans or seas.
Animals that walk on two feet, usually having two other limbs terminating in hands or having wings..
Animals, typically domestic or tame, that are housed and cared for by humans for the purposes of pleasure or companionship.
Long strips of cloth bearing slogans or images that are meant to be hung in public places, which advertise goods, services, or brands,
Viruses that have DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) as genetic material and replicate using a DNA-dependent DNA polymerase.

Class of sac-like marine filter feeders characterized by a tough outer "tunic" made of the polysaccharide tunicin, as compared to other tunicates which are much less robust. They have with some primitive vertebrate features, found in all seas from the intertidal zone to the greatest depths. The tadpole-like larvae are free-swimming and have a notochord (a flexible, rod-like structure common to all vertebrates) and a nerve cord in the tail. When the larva finds a place to settle, it attaches itself with a sucker; the tail with its notochord and nerve cord is absorbed and disappears. They are commonly found on pier pilings, ships' hulls, rocks, large seashells, and the backs of large crabs. Some species live individually; others live in groups or colonies. Adults have functional male and female reproductive organs; fertilization occurs when eggs are shed into the water and come into contact with sperm from another individual.

Order containing 22 species of primitive, eel-like, jawless vertebrates that are scaleless, have a funnel-like toothed sucking mouth, no paired fins, large eyes, one nostril on the top of the head, and seven gills on each side. The animals begin life as burrowing freshwater larvae (ammocoetes), which are toothless, have rudimentary eyes, and feed on microorganisms; they transform into adults via a metamorphosis that is as radical as that seen in amphibians.
Family of hagfishes distinguished from other hagfishes by having gill pairs that share a common opening on each side.

Members of an order of amphibians characterized by having a tail, normal limbs, many cartilaginous skeletal elements, four-faceted articulation between the skull and vertebral column, incomplete maxillary arcade lacking a bony connection with neurocranium and palatoquadrate, and larvae with true teeth and external gills. Dates from the Middle Jurassic to present, with ten living and three extinct families, including more than 550 living species.
General term formerly referring to a bivalve shell-fish such as the mussel or oyster; in more recent usage, refers to any large marine snail with a spiraling shell that is pointed on both ends.

Order containing about 38,000 living species of predatory arthropods having two body segments, eight legs, no chewing mouth parts, no wings, and in many species possessing the ability to spinning webs, which are made of a thin, strong protein strand extruded from spinnerets (most commonly found on the end of the abdomen) and in which their prey is caught.They feed almost entirely on insects. In the context of art and other cultural objects, the presence of spiders in a storage area usually indicates that insects are also present. Spiders, however, do not pose any danger to artifacts themselves.
Mobile phones that have the ability to access the internet, send text messages, make calls, or store data such as music, but that lack the advanced functionality of smartphones.

A fermented tea made by incubating the kombucha culture, a symbiotic colony of bacteria and yeast. In conservation, this tea has an enzyme content that has been applied successfully in the cleaning of crystal fouling on archaeological silk objects.

Television system standard for broadcasting television signals at twice the resolution than the current NTSC (National Television System(s) Committee) standard. It employs a wide aspect ratio of 16:9.

Places for keeping victuals; variously applied to a store-closet, pantry, or cupboard in a pantry. The term was first used in the Medieval period for enclosed cupboards or storage niches enclosed by doors; often a receptacle for provisions to be given away as alms. The term remained in use chiefly for the aumbries enclosed in or hung on a wall near the altar in churches in which sacramental vessels were kept. When referring to such forms enclosed by doors from the 17th century on, use "cupboards."
Genus containing one living species, the budgerigar.
Species of ox-like grazing animals native to Europe.
General name for several breeds of various species of goat that produce fine, soft coat used for cashmere wool.

Extinct order of reptiles characterized by triradiate pelvis with the inferior pelvic elements directed downwards, a subnarial foramen, some reduction in digits, forelimbs that are usually distinctly shorter than hind limbs, and three to seven sacral vertebrae. Includes all theropod carnivorous dinosaurs and one of the two great lineages of herbivorous dinosaurs. Dating from the Upper Triassic to Upper Cretaceous, after which all non-avian saurischians became extinct.

Breed known as the fastest and one of the oldest breed of dog. Streamlined and slender but strong, the greyhound can attain a speed of about 45 miles per hour. The greyhound stands 25 to 27 inches (64 to 69 cm) and weighs 60 to 70 pounds (27 to 32 kg). In art, greyhounds appear on an Egyptian tomb dating from about 3000 BC. In a painting by Dürer, the greyhound is identified with the harbinger of the Second Coming of Christ.

One of two living species of camels. It has one hump and is probably native to the Arabian Peninsula. It is believed to have been domesticated as early as 4000 BCE in Arabia. It has been widely domesticated, with living populations that exhibit wild behavior existing only in Australia, where a feral population was introduced.

A desert breed of horse known for hardiness, stamina, and a fiery temperament. It has a powerful front end, high withers, short back, a sloping croup, and carries its tail low. It is hardy with clean legs, and small, round, sound hooves. The origins of the breed are uncertain, but it may have originated in northern Africa during the 8th century.
The genus containing of two extant species of elephant in Africa.
Genus containing 16 extant species of weasels, ermines, and ferrets.
Members of a rather rare species of the weasel family that is dark in color, agile in trees, has a slender body, pursues prey into hollow trees or burrows, and despite its name rarely eats fish.

General term referring to mammals belonging to any of several genera containing around 30 species of Leporids, having long ears, a divided upper lip, and long hind legs adopated for leaping, differing from hares in being smaller and having thier young born naked and blind.

Members of a common species of rat known worldwide. Despite its name, the black rat exhibits several color forms. As the brown rat, the black rat has exploited human food resources, moved all over the world with humans, and is often considered a pest because it has killed small livestock and native species, and spread certain diseases among humans. The black rat originated in tropical Asia and spread through the Near East in Roman times before reaching Europe by the 6th century and spreading with Europeans across the world. Today it is again largely confined to warmer areas, having been supplanted by the brown rat in cooler regions.
Order of large number of widely distributed, shallow-water cephalopods having eight sucker-bearing arms or tentacles, a beak-like mouth, and either only a vestigial internal shell or no shell at all.

term: Northeast Persian textile styles after the Mongols
definition: Textile styles after the Mongols belonging to Northeast Persian cultures.

Style of textiles, particularly rugs, handmade in the village of Joshaqan, north of Esfahan in central Iran. A great variety of rugs has been attributed by various writers to this small place, including Kerman vase carpets, other silk rugs, and rugs with pronounced Kurdish characteristics.
The style term used specifically for carpets made by the Lur people. For the more general style and culture of the Lur people, use "Lur (general style and culture)."

Style of textiles, particularly carpets, handwoven by Kurds in the vicinity of the village of Bijar in western Iran, and characterized by their weight, sturdiness, and remarkable stiffness and resistance to folding. Woven on a woolen foundation in the symmetrical knot, these carpets are said to be double-warped. This refers to the way the warps are strung closely together, and alternate weft shoots are pulled so tight that the warp lies on two levels, one almost precisely behind the other. The structure is unusual in that the weft is passed three times between rows of knots. This is also a Kerman characteristic. Many Bijar carpets have clumsy medallion decorative schemes in which the medallion and corners are ornamented but the balance of the field remains a solid red or yellow. Other examples show repeat patterns, including the herati, in which a diamond lattice peeps through a tangle of stylized flowers. From Bijar come a remarkable number of vagirehs, or weavers' samples used as models for large carpets, that show portions of several patterns and borders.

term: Anatolian Islamic pottery styles after Manzikert
definition: Pottery styles after Manzikert belonging to Anatolian Islamic cultures.

Glass or plastic supports on which images are created using a screen process. With this process, additive color images are created using a screen of red, green, or blue filters to record the relative intensity of each hue on a panchromatic, black-and-white emulsion which is processed to form a transparency. When viewed through a similar filter, each filter contributes its hue with its intensity modulated by the silver image.
Painting styles belonging to Timurid cultures.
Pottery styles belonging to Safavid cultures.
Describes groupings of cloth coverings produced and worn by individuals of Native American descent.
Blankets woven by Chilkat Tlingit communities, usually made of mountain goat wool and cedar bark. Blankets are usually comprised of black, white, yellow, and blue ovoid shapes. figures, and lines.
Parts or components of land vehicles.

The Kura-Araxes cultural tradition existed in the highlands of the South Caucasus from 3500 to 2450 BCE. By 3000 BCE, groups bearing this identity had migrated southwest across a wide area from the Taurus Mountains down into the southern Levant, southeast along the Zagros Mountains, and north across the Caucasus Mountains.
Textile styles belonging to East Caucasian cultures.

In general, refers to the styles and culture of Turkic people of central Asia, forming the basic population of Kazakhstan. Specifically, refers to the style of floor coverings woven by villagers living in western Azerbaijan and in a number of towns and villages in northern Armenia and the adjacent southern part of Georgia. Textiles are typically all wool, coarsely knotted in the symmetrical knot with a long, lustrous pile, and use strong red, blue, and ivory in bold combinations with relatively simple but dramatic designs.

Style of textiles with geometric designs, particularly rugs, originating in the Dagestan region of the eastern Caucasus in present-day Russia. Dagestan rugs are usually small, finer than the Kazakh types, but less fine than rugs from the vicinity of Kuba to the south. While many of the rugs are called "Derbent," referring to a major collecting point, much of the weaving has occurred to the south in villages around Ortasal and Kasumkent. Dagestan rugs of the 19th and early 20th century tend to use blue over red and are more likely to be all wool than the Kuba rugs from neighbouring Azerbaijan. Edges are also more likely to be of blue wool, and the backs of many of these rugs appear ribbed. Rugs marketed under the name "Zeykhur" were woven in the Tabarasan district, and many show unusual qualities of color, such as the use of pink and deep red in juxtaposition, and floral designs based on European sources. During the mid-20th century a type of Shirvan prayer rug with an ivory field and lozenge-shaped compartments of stylized flowers was mistakenly called "Dagestan."
Style of textiles, primarily carpets, from the city and plain of Lenkoran, in southeastern Azerbaijan on the shore of the Caspian Sea.

Style of rugs woven by the Baloch people living in Afghanistan and eastern Iran. The patterns often incorporate repeated motifs diagonally arranged across the field, or a maze of intricate latch-hooked forms. Prayer rugs may contain a field filled with the leaves and stems of a stylized tree, with geometric small plants in the spandrels. Baluchi rugs frequently have long aprons at both ends, decorated with stripes and bands of brocading. The color scheme of older rugs is a dark combination of reds, browns, blues, tans, and white. The fibers are typically wool, goat and camel hair, cotton for whites, and in some cases a few knots of silk. The knotting is customarily asymmetrical. The rugs vary greatly in quality, the better ones usually being ascribed to the Khorasan province of Iran. Baluchi rugs are frequently classed with the products of the Turkmen but show little relationship to them.

Folding stools having curved legs forming a wide X, no back, and low arms. They were originally easily transportable chairs for magisterial commanders in the field; over time, the seat developed a hieratic significance;  Ancient Roman folding curule stools were used by senators and magistrates. Although often of luxurious construction, the Roman curule was meant to be uncomfortable, symbolizing that the official should carry out his duties in an efficient and timely manner.

Early 17th-century English folding chairs having legs crossed front to back and having arms connected to the back and to the front seat rail; design supposedly based on a chair used by the last Abbot of Glastonbury at Wells Cathedral and term derived from collectors' use.
Historic textile styles belonging to West Turkestani cultures.

Refers to material that contains a greater length of grain boundaries than a coarse-grained material. Grain boundaries restrict slip transmission to neighboring grains. A fine-grain material has a higher tensile strength and is thus harder than a coarse-grained material.

Generally, the style and culture of the tribal area and city of Chichaoua, located west of Marrakesh. Specifically, a style of carpet produced in the Haouz plains surrounding Marrakesh, characterized by a large size (2.2 x 5.5 m maximum), and having overlapping rows of coarse symmetrical knots with red grounds and sombre decoration of triangles, squares or even figures in green, browns or orange.

Refers to the style of carpet manufactured inthe Suiyuan region of China during the 19th century. The style is characterized by motifs such as clouds, floral elements, and the shou, the symbol of longevity.

Weaving by means of warp twining on a tablet loom. Because the number of warp threads is limited by the number of tablets that can conveniently be operated, this method is normally used for narrow bands.
Style of carpets and other textiles characteristic of the city of Amristar, located in northern Punjab state, northwestern India.
Planes having a curved baseplate, either concave or convex, used for smoothing curved woodwork.
Tapestry-woven Navajo rugs depicting a center block joined to four corner blocks by zigzag lines, suggesting thunderbolts.
A size of card photograph on a mount measuring about 7 by 10 inches.
Printing process based on light-sensitive diazonium compounds, most often used to reproduce technical drawings.
Parts and components of bolts.
Parts and components of hinges.
Parts and components of securing devices.

Adenosine triphosphate is an energy-carrying chemical found in the cells of all living things. It is a nucleotide composed of ribose, adenine, and a triphosphate group. ATP captures chemical energy obtained from the breakdown of food molecules and releases it to fuel other cellular processes such as biosynthesis, ion transport, and muscle contraction.

Metallic element having symbol Cs and atomic number of 132.905. Cesium is a soft, silvery gold alkali metal with a very low melting point; it is the most reactive and electropositive of all the elements.

Complex pure substances made up of two or more elements in definite proportions with respect to the number and kind of atoms, held together by chemical bonds. They have entirely different properties from those of the constituent elements, which lose their individual character. For combinations of two or more substances in no definite proportions that are only physically mixed and within which the constituent substances retain their individual properties and are separable by ordinary physical means, use "mixtures."
A material made up of finely divided particles uniformly distributed in a continuous liquid, gaseous, or solid medium.
Fields of study that investigate the natural world based on facts learned through experiments and observation.
Study of the development over time of the discipline of conservation science.
Large bags to keep small game that has been shot.
Traps of various designs used to capture or kill birds.
Any of various instruments, similar to but smaller than a flat bladed oar, used for mixing, stirring, or beating.
Armbands worn on the upper arm made with precious feathers of postclassic central Mexico.

Heavy wooden squares made to enclose the neck of a human being, so that he or she cannot lie down, feed her/himself, or touch her/his head. They were used in the past in China and Chinese-influenced countries to punish people for petty offences. The offender's name and crime were inscribed upon the wood.
Shackles for the hand, generally consisting of a divided metal ring which is locked around the wrist; usually made in pairs of rings connected by a short chain or bar.
In medicine, hermetically sealed, small, bulbous glass vessels used to hold a solution, such as for especially hypodermic injection.

Hand tools used to pound tree bark, to soften the bast in the processing of bark cloth. These are common to many cultures, and are varied in form. Many Polynesian beaters are four-sided, with three of the sides grooved to better-pound the bast and with the last side flattened to create a smooth final texture for the textile.
Small planks or boards on which material is mended with thread.
Any looms used to weave a fabric 54 inches or wider.
Weaving shuttles of a stick shape, often having openings in the middle or on either end.
The sport or business of catching, usually killing, fish.
Sports that are played on ice.

The practice or sport of running horses in competitions of speed, in which the horse that finishes first is the winner; horses usually carry a rider astride or are pulling a conveyance with a driver. The sport is ancient, certainly predating its documentation in both four-hitch chariot and mounted (bareback) races held in the Olympic Games of Greece beginning ca. 700 BCE.
Bowling sports that are played on a green.
Activity or occupation of laying out or cultivating an area of plants, or other occupations involving horticulture.
Moving through the water by the action of wind on sails.
Fastenings that hold together parts of garments.
Any form of twill in which the diagonal lines have been deliberately broken. The binding points are not regularly set over by one end on each successive pick, but breaks occur at regular intervals.

Ceremonial ball game played by Southeastern Native North American tribes. Players utilize two long, wooden rackets to either hit a single wooden post or pass through two posts with a ball; scoring and team size vary across communities. Has origins in the Mississippian period and continues to be played by Cherokee, Choctaw, and other Southeastern tribes in the present day.
A handball game played against a wall in a three or four-sided court, in both singles and doubles teams. The game originated in England, and there are many regional variations of play.
Sports that involve moving along an area or path.
The sport or activity involving chasing or hunting game using a trained bird of the family Falconidae, usually a hawk.
Drawing loops of thread, yarn, or cloth through a supporting mesh into a pattern, usually to make a rug or wall hanging.
The forming and interlacing of loops by means of needles according to a prescribed manner or pattern, either by machine or by hand; most often used for textiles or costume.
Narrow strips of land planted with perennials, typically included in a formal garden to provide color.
Preparing fiber for spinning by cleansing, disentangling, and collecting together by the use of a comb; used to prepare relatively long fibers.

Process used especially for copying letters, invented in the 19th century, in which writing or drawing made with aniline dye is transferred to a prepared gelatin surface from which a number of copies can be made; eventually replaced by spirit duplicating.
A process employed in the darkroom to darken a portion of a print, by means of additional exposure.

Heavy yellow powder composed of lead monoxide, both the native mineral as well as lead monoxide produced by heating lead carbonate to 300 C. It is used as a drier in oil, as a low-fire flux in making ceramics and glass, as a yellow pigment in paints and glazes, in thin layers to produce iridescent colors on brass and bronze, as a filler for rubber, and to produce artificial tortoiseshell and horn.
Alloy in which chromium is the principle element.
Alloy in which copper is the principle element.
Alloy in which gold is the principle element.
Alloys in which lead is the principle element.

Pure metallic element having symbol Hg and atomic number 80; a lustrous silvery metal that is liquid at ordinary temperatures. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials.
Any alloy containing nickel as the base metal, or as the chief alloying element.
Alloy in which silver is the principle element.
Alloy in which tin is the principle component.
Designates complex assemblies of equipment and activities, arranged according to some scheme or plan, and intended to perform specific functions.

Collections of historical records and primary source documents that have accumulated over the course of an individual's or organization's lifetime, and are kept to show the function or history of the person or an organization. Documents may be tangible or digital.
Describes groupings of functional and decorative moveable objects in dwellings, places or business, or other public or private spaces.

Sets of decorative items, such as vases or candelabra, of a proper scale and design to be displayed together on a mantel. For groups of vases, whether or not to be displayed on a mantel, use "garnitures (vases)."

Modifications to an object or structure. Refers especially to the physical evidence of the change. In architecture, use "additions" if the change increases the structure's volume; "alterations" if it does not.
Parts or components of systems.
Alloy in which zinc is the principle element.
Alloy in which iron is the principle element.
Scrap glass intended for reuse or recycling.
Parts and components of frames.
Parts and components of HVAC systems.
A number of interrelated hardware and software components that work together to store and convert data into information by using electronic processing.

Refers to the aggregate of various electronic equipment, such as video recorders, television receivers, video enhancing equipment, and audio components, and often including computer equipment, coordinated for home diversion.
Composing precise, logical sequences of instructions that direct the actions of a computer or computer system.

Use with regard to types of computer interface that produce compelling sensory output in response to user selections or movements. Distinguished from "cyberspace" which is the virtual place within the collective memories and networks of computers.
Parts or components of fire extinguishing systems.

Ornamental finish, usually rhythmic and highly decorative, consisting of a regular series of motifs applied to the top of walls, roof ridges, and the like; may also be used for similar decoration on furniture or glass objects.
Structures for the shelter, service, and repair of aircraft.

Numbered groups within a series of spoken word digital audio files known as podcasts. These are usually arranged in chronological or thematic seasons. For the entire collection of grouped podcasts under a singular title, use 'podcast series.'
Buildings housing museums administered by a historical society, which is a group formed to study and disseminate information about the history of a place, usually a town, city, county, or state.
Stiff silk yarn dyed in the gum state consisting of two or three threads united without preliminary twisting, and generally used to weave crepes.
Yarn or fabric made from the fine, soft, light wool from the undercoat of the Kashmir goat.

Buildings housing museums that specialize in the history, objects, vehicles, and other materials associated with self-propelled vehicles designed primarily to transport passengers over ordinary roads.

Refers to culture, art, and architecture associated with the Islamic Nasrid court at Granada, Spain; it flourished as a brilliant center of Islamic culture for almost eight centuries until 1492 when all of the Iberian peninsula was brought under Christian control. The Alhambra, the royal city of the Nasrids, is one of the most famous Islamic buildings and is the most extensively preserved medieval Islamic palace anywhere. Nasrid architecture is characterized by glittering facades concealing structurally simple buildings; trabeate construction, heavy stone walls, and light wooden roofs are typical. Decoration includes carved and painted stucco, glazed tile, carved and joined wood, and muqarnas vaults. Other noteworthy Nasrid artworks are the large lusterware wing-handled vases known as Alhambra vases (the largest lusterware pots ever made), probably produced in Málaga.

Refers to the art and culture associated with the Islamic Turkish dynasty of this name that ruled Syria and Egypt from 935 to 969. From 946 to 968 most governmental power lay with the vizier rather than with the sons of the dynasty's founder, Muhammad ibn Tughj. The vizier, Abu al-Misk Kafur, was a patron of learning and the arts, briefly attracting the eminent poet al-Mutanabbi to his court. The Ikhshidid dynasty was the first to restore order to Egypt after the fall of the Tulunids, laying the groundwork for the new artistic developments that occurred under the Fatimids. In 969 the Fatimids overthrew the last of the Ikhshidid rulers, a grandson of the founder, while the Hamdanids drove the Ikhshidid governors out of northern Syria.

Refers to the art and culture of the Islamic dynasty of this name that ruled the Yemen as representatives of the Fatimid caliphs of Egypt from 1047 to 1138. Al-Sayyida al-Hurra Arwa bint Ahmad, the wife of the powerful Sulayhid ruler Al-Mukarram Ahmad (reigned 1067-84),  ruled after her husband's death and established a new Sulayhid capital at Dhu Jibla. There she built a palace and a mosque that notably introduced several features characteristic of Fatimid mosques in Egypt. With Arwa's death in 1138, the effective power of the Sulayhid dynasty ended although a few Sulayhid princes continued to hold fortresses until the end of the twelfth century.

Several types of floor coverings handwoven at Bandirma, a town in Turkey on the southern shore of the Sea of Marmora, usually as imitations of Ghiordes prayer rug designs. The enterprise was begun in the early 20th century, perhaps with weavers from Ghiordes, although it is usually described as an Armenian establishment. The rugs are characterized by overly elaborate areas, such as the sides of the prayer-niche design, and a differing color range from the originals they imitate, including pastel shades and opaline effects.
Long, often cylindrical, pillows or cushions that are used to support the head of a person lying on a bed, couch, or similar form of furniture.
Cushions placed under the feet of an important person, as a sign of status and holiness.
Long oblong cushions used to support the full length of a sleeper's body while lying on their side.
Administrative divisions of a church, under the authority of an archbishop.
Divisions of French departments and some French cities.
Halftone screens having a random, rather than a regular, pattern.

Officers in the military whose specific rank and extent of authority varies from one institution to another but who generally are in charge of a company of men or area of action, such as a ship, aircraft, or station. For officers of public services and institutions holding the same title, use "captains (public officers)."

Originally, high stewards of a sovereign or member of the nobility, having particular charge of the sovereign's or noble's private living quarters. Now used also as the title of officials serving as treasurers for public corporations or offices.
Cosmetic creams or powders that come in various colors that are applied to the eyelids or brows to accent the eyes.
To standardize the settings for a measuring instrument so that its readings are absolute rather than relative.
Goggles for protecting eyes and face against explosions. First developed in World War I.
Military leaders of the Cossacks; originally the Polish title for commanders in chief.
Various materials used to decorate and protect walls and other surfaces, often in the form of flexible sheets.

Refers to noblemen holding a barony, which is a large estate or a sizable section of a larger territory ruled by a sovereign and often originally awarded for military or other service. It typically refers to members of the European nobility who rank, in modern times, immediately below a viscount or a count in many countries, although the rank and status of a baron varies from country to country and in various historical periods. The term may also be used in its original sense, which in the early Middle Ages designated the tenant who held a tenure of a barony directly from the king, whatever the tenant's rank. It may also be used to refer to noblemen of low rank in Japan. The term may be used in a more general sense to signify a powerful personage or magnate. Barons are always male; female holders of a barony are "baronesses."

Refers to European noblewomen holding a barony in their own right. It may also refer to European and Japanese noblewomen who are the wives or widows of barons. In Great Britain and Japan, they occupy the lowest rank of nobility; in Continental Europe, their rank and status within the nobility vary from country to country. Refers to female holders of a barony, which is a large estate or a sizable section of a larger territory ruled by a sovereign and often originally awarded for military or other service. It may also refer to the wives or daughters of a baron.
Manually or electrically operated devices with small overlapping teeth that can cut hair very close to the skin to shape beard growth.

Three-dimensional representations of human figures, often stylized or otherwise abstracted, used by tailors, dressmakers, and sales personnel for fitting or displaying clothing. For models of the human body used for teaching anatomy or demonstrating surgical operations, use "manikins." For jointed figure of humans or animals used by artists, use "lay figures."
Hollow cylindrical devices used to hold a cigarette while it is being smoked.

Convex, dark-tinted glasses used as mirrors to reflect landscapes or objects in landscape in reduced size, muted colors, and merged detail, abstracting the subject from its surroundings, simplifying it, and presenting it in terms of light and shade. It was popular in the 17th and 18th centuries with artists, travelers, and those who simply wished to view landscapes in a different way. They were either handheld, or larger ones were mounted beside the windows of carriages. They were said to have been used by the painter Claude Lorrain, who produced similar effects in his landscapes, hence the name.
The severing of a glass object from the blowpipe or pontil rod.
Refers to people who have withdrawn from the world by living on top of high columns or pillars, particularly the early Christian ascetics.
Painters who specialize in painting marine scenes.

Sovereigns or supreme monarchs of an empire, which is a political unit that comprises a number of territories or nations and is ruled by a single supreme authority. The use of the term is often restricted to reference to such supreme authorities in only certain parts of the world, including the ancient Roman empire, the Early Christian Roman empire, and the empires of Austria-Hungary, China, Japan, Morocco, India, Asia Minor, and Germany. The rulers of conglomerate political states in other parts of the world are generally known by other titles. The term "emperors" always refers to males, while "empresses" refers to female rulers.
Clergymen of the highest order in Christian churches, usually charged with an administrative function such as the supervision of a diocese.
Utilitarian or ornamental containers intended primarily for growing plants.
Those enrolled in the military service of a government.
Saddlebags used for donkeys or mules, differing from saddlebags for horses in that the donkey or mule may not necessarily be ridden, so there is more accomodation for carrying objects and materials.
Computerized process of accentuating or exaggerating forms in an image, often used to clarify indistinct forms, as for example in photographs.

Creation of images by hyperspectral remote sensors which collect data simultaneously in dozens or hundreds of narrow, adjacent spectral bands. The images thus created are more detailed than those of other multispectral sensors with just a few relatively broad wavelength bands.

A data transfer technique that allows the user to access audio and video media via the Internet without downloading the entirety of a very large file. A host or source "streams" packets of information to the user in smaller increments as it is viewed. Unlike downloads, streaming video is not intended to be retained as a file on a viewer's computer.

Equipment (bits, bridal, chest piece, forehead fringe, halters, headstalls, neck pieces, saddles, headstalls, neck pieces, saddles, saddle blankets, etc.) used on a horse, particularly when the equipment is decorative.
A gül consisting of serrated or stepped diamonds, which may be concentric.
Rigs having a triangular sail whose forward edge is attached to a separate spar which is hoisted to a fully vertical position where it becomes an extension of the short mast.
Covered or fully enclosed litters for one person carried on the shoulders of four or six bearers, formerly common in Asia, especially India.
Regulated, formal dress for presentation to the monarch and courtly functions, including costume and the accessories required.
Devices designed for scratching one's own back; often in the form of a small hand mounted on a long handle.

Any of various international territorial divisions, typically a section of a county forming a unit of local government. In the United States, surveyed tracts of public land measuring 6 miles square and divided into 36 sections of 1 square mile each.
Male security guards or soldiers (usually officers) of the guards or household troops of a royal or noble household.
Pilots of heavier-than-air aircraft, especially airplanes, which are fixed-wing aircraft designed to lift and transport people and cargo.
Social science concepts related to economics.
advertising via outdoor locations, such as on billboards or with posters.
Use generally for computer processing activities in which the output is in pictorial form.
Those skilled in creating specialized lettering by hand.
Leather straps that loop around the root of a horse's tail and fasten to the saddle to keep it from slipping forward. For the armor protecting a horse's hind quarters, use "cruppers (horse armor)."
Cloths used in the kitchen for washing dishes.
Clergy of a large Christian church living as a community under a rule; also Medieval clergymen belonging to the chapter or the staff of a cathedral or collegiate church.
Those who use the title of respect in use since the first century BCE given by the Jews to learned doctors and teachers of the law.
Prayer leaders and officiating priests of Islamic mosques.
Designates an animal double and an individual who has the power to take on a second appearance.
Women who engage in business as their primary occupation or function.
Officials who inflict capital punishment in pursuance of a legal warrant.
Fasteners used to secure breeches to the wearer, with the buckles holding straps usually around the middle of the leg. Particularly worn in the 18th century.
Detachable buttons with a shank or eye on the back that are inserted through one or more eyelets or buttonholes, usually in a garment, to serve as a fastener or ornament.
Narrow straps, laces, or the like, used to fasten a shoe or sandal.
Garment hangers having a scale and shape appropriate for the storage or display of ceremonial robes, for example, for liturgical vestments or royal robes.
Artisans skilled in engraving on stone.
The action of moving or turning a door, gate, window, tap, lid, or other component away from its open position so as to stop or prevent passage or access.
To carry something with a strap placed on the forehead.
Railroad passenger cars constructed with raised areas in the center of the car with a transparent roof for passenger observation.
Ordinary passenger-carrying railroad cars for daytime travel.

Small, four-wheeled rail vehicles used in conjunction with track inspection and repair to transport workers and equipment; originally open platforms with manually operated propulsion mechanisms, now usually gasoline- or electric-powered.
Railroad cars, usually those employed for track maintenance and right of way inspection, that do not generate income.
Refers to column bases consisting of a scotia between an upper and lower torus, usually found on Ionic, Corinthian, and occasionally on Doric columns.

Additions to visual works, comprising canted or other wise extending outer pieces, usually but not always surrounding primarily rectangular objects such frames, altarpieces, fire backs, architectural elements, etc.
Manned spacecraft designed for repetitive missions.
Feet on furniture in the shape of a cube, generally used with square untapered legs.
Braces or bars used to hold a casement window open in any of several positions.

A form of door hardware that consists of a single knob fastened to one end of a spindle, on the other end of which is a rose or plate used to secure the knob and spindle to the closet door. Distinguished from "doorknobs," in which a pair of knobs on opposite ends of a spindle is used to release the door latch.
Aircraft designed or equipped to carry primarily passengers.

Items taken as spoils, remembrances, or proof of victory in battle. Examples are scalps taken from the fallen enemy and the piles of arms and armor collected and displayed after Greek and Roman military victories.
Fixed-wing aircraft with one set of main supporting surfaces.
Fixed-wing aircraft capable of taking off and landing vertically and cruising at forward speeds comparable to conventional aircraft.
