Ornamental metal pieces attached to an article usually of another material, such as to glass, porcelain, wood, or leather.
Fixed-wing aircraft weighing no more than 254 pounds empty and having a maximum speed of 63 mph, generally for one person; may or may not be motor powered.
A Persian term for a small rug measuring approximately 3 by 2 feet.
Small Ushak rugs with opposed niches in the central field.
Sacred objects or images that are not shaped to resemble a human or animal; rather, the works symbolize the sacred idea or entity, while not being a depiction or visual representation of something.

Wands or small rods used in a ritual, such as a coronation, or a religious sacrament to anoint a person with sacred oil or chrism. Depending upon the rules of the various rites, anointing wands may be made of simple wood or they may be more decorative, made of precious materials. The practice was known from ancient times. In modern contexts, anointing wands are used most commonly to anoint a sick or dying person in Christian rites. In some rites of the Eastern church, seven cotton-wrapped wands are used to anoint the sick or dying. In Western rites, although the anointing is usually done using the thumb, anointing rods may be used in certain circumstances, such as for the anointing of the sick with contagious diseases.
Use broadly for articles associated with or used in private religious devotions.
Long poles, often wooden, made for use in ceremonial dances.
Sharp steel bars used to split stone so that the facet angles can be measured.
Prayer sticks, usually made of wood, completed with painted designs and bundles of feathers attached to one end. Used in Hopi religious ceremonies.

Originally a pipe or reed (hence the name arundo, which means "reed") with which the celebrant of the Mass may sip the communion wine, instead of the celebrant and all communicants putting their lips to the rim of the same cup. Use of the arundo was known from the Carolingian period onwards, when the arundo was made of a precious material such as gold; for example, in the papal high mass, a golden arundo is used.
Designs constructed of curved, black lines and secondary thinner lines, characteristic of Northwest Coast Native North American works. May appear in sculpture, painting, or prints.
Black-figure kylikes characterized by having a lip and body usually covered with simple patterned bands and often with rays above the foot; generally of the 6th century BCE.

A type of kylix characterized by a deep bowl, a lip that is not offset, and a short stem and foot. This form dominated black-figure vase painting after about 540 BCE but also continued in red-figure. The ordinary type A kylix is an eye cup.
Any devices or combinations of device and material which operate to set off the main igniting charge in an explosive device or firearm.
Incendiary liquid mixture known to the Byzantine Greeks, used especially to set fire to ships in naval warfare.
The process of making printing plates by taking a mold of set type and making a cast in type metal.
In bookbinding, the process of gilding, coloring, tooling, painting, printing, or other by other means coating or marking one or more edges of a book.
Various tools for making fine, delicate engraved lines, as to create a tonal area in intaglio or wood engraving techniques.
Fine-point tool used especially in wood engraving for making curved lines.
Those who play the organ, especially those engaged to play the organ at the services in a church.
Specifically, those who play the double bass.Also refers generally for those who play bass instruments of any kind.
Those who play the bugle, including those who use it to sound signals, as in an army.
Objects that are based on or signifiantly borrow from other existing objects, rather than being original creations.

A radar system that uses the motion of the vehicle (such as a spacecraft) carrying it to simulate a system having a much larger antenna area and that is used to obtain high-resolution images of a surface (as of a planet). It requires that the radar be moving in a straight line, either on an airplane or orbiting in space.
Politically dependent territories administered jointly by two or more foreign powers.
Historic territories, colonies, or dependencies.
Cases that hold commemorative objects, and that sometimes are themselves considered commemorative objects themselves.
Visual works in the shape of a cross having the figure of Christ crucified.

A material comprising white clay, or "kaolin," and a feldspathic rock, that react when fired so the clay serves to hold the shape of the object and the rock fuses into a natural glass. In China, it includes any such ware that is highly fired enough to produce a ringing sound when struck. In Europe, it is limited to hard-fired ceramic that is translucent.
Boards on which type is placed or to which letters may be fixed.
Geological samples elected for examination, display, or study.

Depictions of a specific ship. The genre was developed to a great extent in the Netherlands, beginning in the 17th-century; but it also flourished in the art of several other western maritime nations.
Phone numbers connected to a fax machine, fax service, or fax server, rather than to a voice telephonic device.

Objects that facilitate the production of musical sound by manual or mechanical/electronic means, but do not themselves generate such sound. Included in this subclass are musical instrument components.
Computer peripherals composed of a monitor or printing device and a keyboard, which are linked together to function as a single input/output unit.

Devices that, using an access mechanism under program control, enable data to be read from or written on a spinning magnetic disk, magnetic disk pack, floppy disk, or optical disk media. "Disk drives" may be used to refer to devices that use either fixed or removable media. To refer specifically to fixed, large-capacity magnetic disk drives used to store computer data, use "hard drives." To refer to the fixed disk itself, rather than the mechanism it is a part of, use "hard disks."
Devices put between the leaves of books to mark a place. Distinguished from "registers (book components)," which are attached to books.
Racing events for watercraft, usually consisting of a group of races over short to medium distances and often having the nature of festive social occasions.

Vessels capable of complete submersion for a limited time; may or may not be able to move under their own power. For vessels capable of continuous, extended underwater voyages under their own power, use "submarines."
Artifacts, usually flexible, often textiles, that are hung to cover or conceal interior spaces, surfaces, or furnishings, especially for protection, warmth, or embellishment.

Designates given materials used to close off the reverse side of paintings on canvas. Such materials include but are not limited to simple cardboard, Perspex (acrylic), Melinex (polyester). Backboards are applied either on the stretcher or on the frame, using screws, nails, or tape.
Member of certain hereditary nobility, including duke, marquess, earl, viscount, or baron; or a person elevated to the peerage for life, without hereditary rights. Primarily in Britain or Ireland.
Those whose occupation or profession is to play games played with a ball and a bat, in which a player strikes the ball with the bat and attempts to run to one or more bases to score points.
Services intended for use in serving coffee generally consisting of a coffeepot, creamer, sugar bowl, and often a matching tray. May also include matching cups and urn, saucers, or dessert plates.

Relatively small powerful vessels used to tow ships at sea, to tow barges, or to assist in and around harbors, as during berthing; for merchant vessels employed to push groups of barges, use "towboats."
Boats of various kinds, often double-ended and human-powered or having an auxiliary motor, used for rescue or lifesaving at sea.
Lifeboats used to assist a vessel in distress and to rescue crew and passengers, rather than having been shipboard lifeboats lowered from the vessel in distress.
Vessels specially designed with reinforced bow and powerful engines for breaking navigable channels through heavy ice, especially the pack ice of extreme northern latitudes.
Boats that are carried on ships, especially those used to serve the ships; before the engine era, usually rigged for both oar and sail.
Clinker built ships' boats, usually 24 to 36 feet long, generally rowed double banked.
Collocates vehicles retrofitted with planes or stepped hulls to lift the vessels above the water's surface when traveling at high speeds.

Refers to a wide variety of watercraft that are essentially floating platforms, more or less rigid or stationary and buoyant, constructed without interior volume and in a way that cannot keep water out.
Light, high-powered vessels, often with stepped hulls, designed to plane along the surface of the water at great speed.
Collocates descriptors for watercraft used on enclosed bodies of relatively protected water, such as rivers, lakes, and canals.

Inland vessels used in the Netherlands from the seventeenth century to the nineteenth century to transport passengers on the waterways. The barge could be drawn by a horse, but it was also an option to sail. The boat was generally a stretched vessel about fifteen meters long with a falling prow, a tent, and later a wooden structure with windows that gave the passengers shelter.
Describes watercraft constructed with a bottom-based hull.
Bottom-based merchant ships of the 13th to the 15th century, clinker-built with rounded bow and stern, fore and after castles, and very broad in the beam; occasionaly used as warships.
Describes watercraft constructed by hollowing out the interior of a tree trunk.

Vessels constructed of skin, or later of tarred canvas, over a substantial wooden frame and having a distinctive narrow shape, with the bottom rising forward and a definite knuckle or break in the sheer; sometimes as large as 10m long, built in Ireland, particularly on the west coast.
Describes watercraft powered and propelled by machinery.
Describes watercraft propelled by oarsmen positioned on two or more levels.
Ancient Greek warships propelled by 25 pairs of oarsmen; such ships formed the backbone of early Greek naval fleets.
Ancient warships propelled by oarsmen arranged on three levels.
Describes watercraft powered by the combustion of fuel with an oxidizer inside a combustion chamber.
A boat propelled by steam power; especially one designed for river or coastal travel.
Describes watercraft in which movement occurs from the rotation of two or more blades.
Steam-powered vessels propelled by a single paddle wheel mounted at the stern.
Ships equipped with sails as their primary means of propulsion.
Sailing vessels on which the principal sails are set athwartships.
Relatively small, decked sailing vessels similar to sloops, with a single mast and a bowsprit with, often two, headsails, but with the mast stepped farther aft.

Distinguished from "Cape Cod catboats" by their counter stern, lower freeboard, and narrower beam; originally developed for shellfishing and later for racing in the shoal waters of Great South Bay, Long Island.
Two-masted vessels carrying a full set of square sails on each mast, although the mainmast also carries a gaff-rigged spanker or driver sail; the mainmast is taller than the foremast.
Sailing vessels of three or more masts, square-rigged on all but the aftermost mast, which is fore-and-aft-rigged.
Rugs of any design made by commission on royal or court looms, such as Moghul, Ottoman, or Safavid.
Devices for dispersing pigment in a vehicle, consisting of a rotating cylinder containing pigment, vehicle, and ball bearings or pebbles.
Rooms or boxes with a single small opening, with or without a lens, through which an inverted image is projected from outside the box onto the opposite interior wall.
Devices used to project an image of an opaque object, such as a drawing or other graphic material, onto a flat surface for tracing or viewing.
Technique applying x-ray diffraction to crystalline or powder samples in order to ascertain their structure.
Conveyor devices that use a screw or auger mechanism to move grain or similar materials.
Process of decorating glass in high relief by cutting away part of the glass between the body of a piece and its decoration, leaving an intervening open space.

Refers to a type of lusterware made by Wedgewood from November 1915, featuring decoration designed by Daisy Makeig-Jones depicting whimsical creatures in a fairyland setting, the colors having a marked irridescent appearance.
Rugs made of mats measuring about 2 feet square that have been sewn together; often placed between pillars in Buddhist temples.
Small Tibetan rugs usually smaller than 3 feet square placed as the top rug on a pile of rugs for sitting.
Knotted pile weaving suspended in a doorway from a rod about 10 inches above the threshold in order to keep out dust and animals; rug is up to 12 inches long by 35 inches wide.

Late-17th- and 18-century rugs, thought to have originated in the Caucasus, frequently characterized by a depressed two-level natural wool warp, wool wefts often dyed red, and knotted with symmetrical knots; the field pattern consists of a drop repeat directional lattice pattern made up of jagged leaf forms enclosing stylized dragons.
A name of convenience given to types of rugs thought to have been made in Isfahan or Kashan characterized by a silk pile, floral designs, and areas of gold or silver brocade.
Rugs with a large, complex star motif, so named because they appeared in a painting by the Italian Renaissance painter Carlo Crivelli.

Handwoven rugs with pile in loops, made in Spain in the Alpujarras district south of Granada and elsewhere in Andalusia and Castile. The foundation is of linen, and the coarse woolen pile material runs along with the weft, each color pulled up above the surface in loops as needed in the design. It has about 20 loops per square inch. This technique may have been in use in the area for a long time, but surviving examples probably do not date before the 18th century. The patterns can be described as folk art and the colors, usually two but as many as ten, are strong. The Alpujarra's origins are probably Moorish. The construction of these rugs makes them more suitable for bedspreads.
Box constructions enabling the artist to control the even distribution of rosin particles onto the aquatint plate.
Hand-held trays in which type is assembled before transfer to the larger galley.
Small mesh bags used to dust aquatint plates with powdered rosin.

Reprographic equipment invented in 1780 by James Watt. A sheet or sheets of copying paper would be pressed against original documents, and ink would be transferred. Letter copying presses were made in various forms: roller, bed and platen, and portable models. Presses comprising a platen and base, often a screw press, used to copy an original document. In the 18th century, the original was pressed to a dampened tissue-weight paper, producing a copy transfer; the image was a mirror image of the original, but could be read through the back of the tissue. In the 19th century, the original was often written with a special copying ink that was formulated to allow easy and repeated transfer. For presses of similar design, used to press newly bound books, use "book presses."
The apparatus used for screen printing, consisting of a fabric screen stretched on a frame hinged to a baseboard of flat wood or other material.

Thin iron frames, hinged to the tympan of a hand press, securing the sheet and lowered with it to face the form before the carriage is rolled under the platen. The frisket was covered in paper with windows cut in it where, and only where, type meets paper.

Tools used in screen printing consisting of a firm but flexible blade set directly into a straight-edged grip, traditionally of wood, used to force paint or ink through a screen onto a support. For similar implements used as cleaning tools, usually with handles perpendicular to a thinner blade, use "squeegees."
Those machines that cast type for printing as the matter is being composed, either by individual characters, such as Monotype (TM) machines, or by one-line slugs, such as Linotype (TM) machines.

Type cast as individual, single-character units, capable of being combined into text, printed, and redistributed and reused. Use especially with regard to its invention, in Europe in the late 15th century and earlier in China and Korea, and in contrast to printing numerous characters and sometimes images from one block.
Machine composition where type is cast from molten metal.
Methods of composing type in which characters are set by direct impression, as with typewriter composing machines.
Division of the natural sciences that systematically studies inanimate matter and energy apart from the vitality of living beings.

Describes the external appearance of an individual's gender identity. This may be presented through manner, clothing or other physical manifestations, and which may or may not conform to common determinations of what is masculine or feminine.
Soft, very flat brushes of fan shape, made in either sable or bristle and set in a metal ferrule, often used for blending and to produce wispy effects.
Nets used in the game of table tennis that divide the table into two halves, suspended from two poles attached to the table at a regulation height of 15.25 centimetres.
Jousts developed in Germany, fought with lances furnished with sharp pointed heads.
Those who cultivate land or crops or raise livestock as their main occupation, whether for livlihood or for sustenance.
Those who have legal title to land.
Gathering cloth by pulling it along two or more parallel lines of stitching or encased cords, by stitching it with elastic thread, or by weaving rubber threads under tension into it.

The surface produced by raising the fibers on the face of a woven textile, especially by brushing. For the raised surface produced by supplementary warp or weft projecting from the ground of a woven textile, use "pile (textile component)."
Smooth compact yarn spun with average to hard twist from long wool fibers that have been carded and combed.
Thick, loosely twisted, plied yarn, usually of cotton, used especially for embroidered bedspreads.
Yarn with no apparent twist; the direction of its fibers correspond to the central bar of the letter I.

A non-woven textile made by beating the inner bark of certain trees and bushes until it is fine and soft. Bark cloth can be painted, stamped, embroidered, or cut and sewn as patchwork although it is relatively fragile, especially when wet. Used in many places arond the globe. An example is the cloth once used in almost all of sub-Saharan Africa, being reported as early as the mid-16th century in Liberia; today it is found in Ghana and Nigeria.

Generally, textile that is woven, felted, knit, pounded, or otherwise made into a flat piece. For textile in the form of continuous strands made from filaments of fiber by reeling, spinning, twisting, or throwing, see "yarn."
Strips of protective material that cover the raw borders, seams, or edges of textiles.
Material woven by the yard to be made up into carpets.
Fine, soft, sheer cloth of plain weave made of any of the principal types of fiber, such as cotton, linen, rayon, silk, or wool.
Highly intricate tape lace that originated in Germany from about 1893 onward.

Dense, fine, plain woven black cloth with a plain or twill weave. The raw yardage is creased or folded double, with its two lists brought together, as for cloth over 54 inches wide. Historically made of wool, broadcloth is used chiefly in the construction of menswear.
Heavy weave cotton, jute, or linen textile stiffened with glue, size, or starch and used for interlinings in garments, box making,  bookbinding, etc.

Refers to distinctive printed textiles manufactured by the Oberkampf manufactory in Jouy-en-Josas, near Versailles, France, from 1760 onward. The designs were originally printed on cotton or linen from woodblocks; later works were printed from copperplates as well.  It is typically characterized by large-scale, monochromatic floral designs or figural scenes. It is often made into hangings or covers for furnishings.
Methods or practices used for upholstering furnishings or other objects.
Upholstering technique in which nails are set close together to secure the edges of the top cover, also creating a decorative feature.

Textile weaving technique in which a pattern is formed or the ground enriched by the use of more than one series of weft strands; the patterning is done using either a supplementary or complementary weft.
Process of crimping, plaiting, or fluting the edges of lace, linen, or a trimming or textile of any kind.
Dyeing cloth by repeatedly putting a resist on different parts of its pattern and placing it in successive dye baths.
Any of various gold-colored braids used especially on uniforms.
Administrative sections, of any administrative level, of larger nations, territories, or other districts as defined for political, religious, military, judicial, or other purpose.
Divisions of a political entity, of any administrative level, that formerly were in place but are now defunct.

Independent states, or regions once independent and still distinct in race, language, institutions, or historical memories. For example,  England, Scotland, and Northern Ireland are countries in the nation of the United Kingdom.

Political entities have a government in which the chief power lies in the hands of those who are most distinguished by birth or fortune. In an aristocracy, power is in the hands of multiple people rather than a single ruler.

Large, seagoing ships of the 15th through 17th century, distinguished by high sterncastle, high, overhanging forecastle, and a low waist; could be used either as a merchant vessel or warship; usually square-rigged on the fore- and mainmast and lateen-rigged on the remaining one to three masts.
Refers to watercraft, usually sailing vessels, with two hulls of equal size held apart above the water deck by rigid structural members.
Describes watercraft with a concaved V-shape hull.
Capacious, flat-bottomed vessels, usually intended to be pushed or towed, primarily for transporting cargo.
Describes watercraft in which both ends of the vessel are symmetrically shaped.
Describes watercraft with a square-shaped stern.
Describes watercraft with symmetical square ends.

Ancient Roman merchant vessels having a full hull with curved stem and sternpost; generally shorter and wider than "pontones," the other major Roman merchant craft. Corbitae made regular voyages between ports in the Red Sea and the west coast of India, as well as regular Mediterranean routes.

Small craft, traditionally clinker-built but more recently of plywood, with flat panels at each end instead of conventional posts; the panel at the bow is usually smaller than the one at the stern. For flat-bottomed, flat-sided, hard-chined inland watercraft, use "prams (bottom-based watercraft)."
Boats having a hull that is similar or exactly alike on both ends.
Any of various types and styles of boats used for waterfowl hunting.
Boats from the Chesapeake Bay rigged with hydraulic clam dredges; generally square-sterned deadrise motorboats, somewhat beamier than similar boats such as used in other Chesapeake fisheries.
Describes fishing vessels used for handlining, where a fishing line is cast and held by hand.

Screw steamboats used in the menhaden fishery to carry fishermen, seiners, and driveboats to fishing grounds, and to transport the catch to fish factories; usually 90 to 150 feet long with the forward mast fitted with a crane for loading catch, and cranes aft for hoisting and lowering seiners and driveboats.

Late-19th- and early-20th-century light shallow-draft boats designed to be poled in marshes in pursuit of various Rallidae, usually flat-bottomed, both cross- and fore-and-aft-planked, and double-ended.

Open, double-ended, round-bottomed rowing boats usually also equipped with a sail, in the 25- to 35-foot range, designed originally for the harpooning of whales; often attached to larger ships but may operate from shore.
Watercraft constructed or used for entertainment.
Small rowing boats built for professional fishing guides to take customers fishing.

Lapstrake boats 14 to 17 feet long, primarily designed for rowing and found on Maine's large western and southern lakes; examples from the 1870s to about 1910 were double-ended; later boats had transom sterns.
Any powerboats designed for racing, generally built to restrictions similar to sailing development or restricted classes.
A class of sailing yachts built from a standard design and identical in construction and rig.
Watercraft used primarily to carry passengers.
Passenger vessels operated for excursions.
Vessels built and armed for combat purposes
Tankers carrying fuel oil and fitted out with pumps, hoses, and couplings to facilitate refueling warships at sea.
Vessels carrying large numbers of combat troops and associated military supplies; may be built for the purpose but are often converted passenger liners.
Vessels specially designed or adapted for clearing or destroying mines at sea.
Light warships, sometimes relatively small boats, stationed or patrolling around the periphery of an anchored fleet to provide advance warning of or to intercept intruders or attackers.
Refers to the most heavily armored warships carrying the most powerful armament and deployed directly in the line of battle.
German subsurface attack vessels developed during the First and Second World Wars.
Describes vessels used to service communications infrastructures.

A Japanese term for Chinese style brocades where the ground is a twill weave and the design is a satin weave. These fabrics were often used for the most decorative and florid of the costumes for noh plays and so the term can also refer to the outer garment of the female costume in these plays.
Use to describe firearms, usually pistols or revolvers, in which a single pull of the trigger first cocks the firearm and then releases the hammer to fire it.
Freewheeled vehicles used for transporting freight or goods.
Land vehicles used for recreational purposes, sometimes equipped with living facilities, sometimes motorized, and sometimes for off-road use.
Horse-drawn military vehicles used in the 19th century to transport tools and materials for repairing an artillery battery's equipment.

Any of various wheeled vehicles designed primarily for carrying infants; may be pushed or pulled and are often wagonlike or carriagelike in appearance. For vehicles designed primarily for pushing small children sitting upright, prefer "strollers."
Specialized road vehicles designed with apparatus for emergency situations.
Runnered vehicles pulled by dogs, especially those used by various Arctic peoples. For similar runnered vehicles operated by hand or by gravity, use "sleds."
Wheeled stretchers, trollies, or cots used to transport patients in an ambulance or hospital.
Morocco with a small, round, tight grain pattern, popular in 19th-century bookbinding.
Pile having cut ends instead of loops.
Pile weave in which the pile is produced by a supplementary pile weft.
Wide double pleats, with the material folded under at each side. For wide double pleats having the flat fold turned in rather than out, use "inverted pleats."

Hand-propelled vehicles consisting of a vertical frame incorporating a handle, and a horizontal projecting edge, platform, or toe plate perpendicular or angled to the vertical frame, at or near its lower part. The projecting edge slides under loads for the purpose of lifting or moving. Distinguished from handcarts, which have four wheels mounted to a level platform.
A plain-weave textile with different colors for its warp and weft; one of these is usually white. Chambray is noted for its durability.
A heavy, twill-woven, warp-flush textile.
Regular production automobiles individually modified in their bodywork to give the appearance of increased power and in their engines for fast acceleration and increased speed for road use or racing.
Fully enclosed automobiles with two or four doors and seating four or more passengers in two ranges, one behind the other.

Small, light, open automobiles powered by motorcycle engines and usually with four wheels, although some had three wheels; for three-wheeled closed automobiles, usually with larger engines, use "three-wheelers."
One of two or more sets of warp that are equally part of the basic weave structure.
Fabric with a short woolen pile, usually of mohair, and resembling velvet. Used to produce tapestries, upholstery of soft furnishings, and formal dress.
One of two more sets of weft that are equally part of the basic weave structure.
Weft pile weave, often of cotton, with solid cut pile.
Equipment that is used in conjuction with land vehicles and land transportation.
Fracture lines in coating layers caused by localized, specific pressures.
Freight-carrying railroad cars consisting of a flat floor without sides or top.
Railroad freight cars, usually flatcars or gondola cars, equipped to transport one or more standardized removable containers.
Locomotives in which power developed by oil-burning internal combustion engines is delivered through hydraulic transmissions to driving rods and axles by means of shafts and gears.
Machines that separate continuous feed business forms or stationary (such as checks or currency notes) into single sheets.
Vehicles used in an rapid transit railway system.

Refers to the successors to streetcars, usually larger and faster electric rail transit vehicles capable of boarding and discharging passengers at either track or platform level; often composed of two cars permanently articulated.

Degradation of a material caused by exposure to light, specifically the chemical changes to photodegradable molecules induced by absorption of photons, especially those wavelengths found in sunlight. The process by which a material is damaged due to prolonged exposure to ultraviolet radiation.

A decay of wood caused by fungus that decomposes cellulose and the associated pentosans, leaving the lignin more or less unaltered; the resultant mass is powdery and occurs in various shades of brown.
A portion of the oily constituents of a leather that appears on the grain surface in the form of white crystalline fatty acids or as a dark gummy deposit.
Ability of a liquid metal to fill and pick up every detail of a mold.
Sites that were originally on dry land but have been submerged or flooded.

The quantitative relationship between a varying magnetic field and the electric field created by the change. This potential difference, or electromotive force, by motion of a conductor in a magnetic field is the fundamental operating principle of electrical transformers, inductors, and electrical motors. It was first observed by Michael Faraday ca. 1831, and is described by Faraday’s law of induction.
Collocates descriptors for concepts related to producing or dissolving a state of safety.
Numerical values given to materials that designate their resistance to fire.
Various processes simultaneously involving both the introduction of one or more acetyl groups into a compound and hydrolysis by means of a chemical reaction.
Any infusion of carbon dioxide into a liquid. In geology, refers to interaction of dissolved carbon dioxide with minerals, especially limestone, in water; a form of chemical weathering.
The utilization of energy resources, resulting in their destruction, reduction of supply, or transformation.
A gradual loss of color or intensity.
The increase in length or volume of a material, or a body, caused by temperature, moisture, or other environmental condition.
The process that causes blisters, which are areas bulging out from the main mass or surface, such as paint.
Fitting together various parts to make an operative whole.
Covering a surface with a layer of substance, especially a substance that is spread on.
The process of whitening or lightening the color of a material by means of oxidation through the use of chemicals or exposure to sunlight.
Hide and skin processing techniques, such as fleshing, unhairing, and scudding, performed with a piece of equipment called a beam.

Process like that of embossing, except inverted; for instance, where a relief plate is placed under a sheet of paper as it runs through a press, lowering areas of the paper as opposed to raising them.
Proccess of removing heat in order to lower the temperature.
Containers intended primarily for cooking.

Originally applied works of metal, but also used for works in plastic, glass, or other similar materials, pieces of design that are created separately and intended to be attached to the main visual work or other object. For works of textile, prefer "appliqué (visual works)."

Zitherlike chordophones with a shallow soundbox, furnished with a series of button-controlled chord bars lying across the strings which damp all strings not required for the chord being played at the moment.
Costume components that are attached to the back of dresses. Generally take the form of extended skirts or gowns that trail behind the wearer.
Parts or components that are used during keyboard actions.
Upright pieces of wood placed one per key at the inner end of every key in a keyboard action, communicating its action to the string by means of a quill, tangent, or hammer.
Sets of levers or keys actuating the sounding mechanism of keyboard instruments.
Branch of chemistry that deals with the chemical effects of radiation, chiefly visible and ultraviolet light, and with the direct production of radiation by chemical changes.
Any substance applied to a surface that is intended to smooth or produce a glossy coating or appearance.

Refers most often to characteristics that suggest how a substance, or sometimes a grouping of items or entities, will respond under certain conditions. Often quantifiable, though often not apparent without analysis or testing.
Technique in microanalytical chemistry in which a finely focused proton beam is used to excite an x-ray spectrum.

A form of thermal analysis rooted in the science of rheology, a branch of mechanics that deals with the flow deformation of materials in terms of force (stress, strain) and time. DMA is a technique in which rheological data for a particular material is generated using a rheometer and software. The material is characterized in terms of its modulus, elasticity, viscosity, damping behavior, and glass transition temperature, and the changes of these with strain, strain rate, temperature, and oscillatory frequency.

Small printed sheets usually containing a notice or advertisement intended to be distributed by hand and often doubling as posters. For small printed sheets intended for wider distribution, to the general public, use "circulars." For larger pieces, intended especially for posting, use "posters."

Armors intended for show rather than for function, including armor used in ritual or formal events rather than in battle, or armor intended for display but not worn at all. Typically, display armor is decorative, elaborate, and incorporates precious materials.

Double pieces consisting of outward-curving flanges of plate metal, either riveted to the pauldrons or forged in one piece with the gardbraces, designed to provide extra protection for the neck. Used from the mid-15th to the mid-16th century by horsemen, often they were made removable for foot combat or the field.

Elastic scattering of beam electrons from a sample in a direction approximately opposite to that of the incident radiation. Backscattered electron (BSE) imaging is a technique used in examination of archaeological artifacts to make surfaces of materials visible.

A form of electron microscopy in which the electron beam passes through a very thin sample, deflecting or scattering some of the electrons which are focused by magnetic lenses onto a screen or photographic plate. The technique is used to visualize the interior structure of such specimens as cells and tissues.
Scanning electron microscopy performed using a field-emission cathode in the instrument's electron gun, producing clearer, less electrostatically distorted images than conventional SEM.
Procedures to make a material safe from damage by moths; an example is the use of chemical agents to repel moths from textiles.

Mechanisms on breechloading firearms in which a lever, usually an extension of the trigger guard, is used to open and close the breech. In repeaters, the lever also ejects spent cartridges, loads fresh ones, and cocks the firearm.
Parts or components of firearms barrels.
Rear sections of the barrels of firearms, containing the chamber in which the charge is ignited.
Parts or components of breech mechanisms.
Surveyors' measuring devices consisting of 100 steel links each 7.92 inches long joined in a chain 66 feet long; precursors of engineers' chains.

Refers to instances of formal written messages routed by a network of radio operators. These are plain text messages, with metadata, which are relayed through a chain of radio operators, the last of which volunteers to deliver the transcribed radiogram to its destination.
Use to describe firearms having two barrels positioned one alongside the other.
Scale that is shown by a line that is labeled to represent a stated distance.
Environments located in oceans or other salt water.
Rules generally laid out in picas along one edge and graduated in inches along the other for measuring widths or margins or for centering of copy for printing.
Rules containing graduations and various data conversion tables for making measurements and calculations of use to carpenters; since about 1800 most commonly 2-foot, two-fold or four-fold rules.
Wooden rules having extra large and bold numbers; produced during the first half of the 20th century.

Honorary rewards, usually involving monetary compensation, awarded in recognition of excellence or work done, or as a fee for services rendered; distinguished from salary and other forms of payment. For the actions and functions surrounding honors in general, without the connotation of monetary compensation, use "honors."
Refers to conversion of organic material into silica; a form of permineralization.
Light meters measuring in footcandles the intensity of visible light falling on surfaces.

Evolved gas analysis (EGA) is a technique whereby temperature-resolved, volatile species generated from a sample placed within a microfurnace are analyzed using mass spectrometry. It is the most useful technique to determine the nature and amount of volatile products formed during the thermal degradation of materials.
Small containers made of fabric, often decorated with a ribbon encircling the top opening. Made to contain hair and the end of wigs to keep them from damaging clothing worn by the wearer.
Athletic shoes specifically intended for use while running.
Bags carried by hand and designed to hold a traveler's clothes and other personal articles.
Mirrors in which the center is farther away from the object than the edges and that reflect enlarged or reduced images.

Mirrors having frames partly or fully of marble and often ornamented with filigree or openwork cresting; popular in the late 18th and early 19th centuries and thought to have originated in Bilbao, Spain.
Buoyant boards held by the hands or arms of swimmers practicing kicking techniques.
An interpretation of a heritage site offered to the public through display and communication.
Sets containing three or more condiment vessels; generally accompanied by a metal frame or stand.

Small disposable cubes containing a bulb and reflector on four sides that provides four flashes in rapid succession, powered by battery and a circuit in a camera through current pulses. These have become obsolete with the advent of electronic flash.
Those materials that form an outermost coating.
Quality of being able to change or be changed so as to suit new circumstances or function in a new role or capacity.
Use to describe things pertaining to cathodes, especially phenomena taking place in the vicinity of cathodes or materials formed by such phenomena.
Use in the sense of interrupted by design. For the sense of damaged, see 'broken' (ALT of "breaking").

The element serving as the reference point in an equation or ratio of  size, dimensions, or other contexts. An example is in an equation of numeric scale, the left side of the equation is the base, 3/4 inch = 1 foot. For the right side of the equation, use "target (relationship indicator)."

Coat armors or tunics of rich material worn by men of the Middle Ages, with heraldic arms depicted on them. Today, they are known as a sleeveless garments of crimson velvet worn with a mantle. The term is somewhat ambiguous, and can also mean outergarments worn by people of rank of both sexes.
In Indian architecture, a distribution of adorning deities; deities as adornment on the temple and hall walls.
Characteristics of building elevations.
Format in which a large sheet of paper is printed on only one side, and not folded.
Circular baking dishes with low plain or fluted sides that angle out from the base to the rim.
Pans, often metal, intended primarily for baking cake; made in varying size and form.
Spoons having a round bowl used for scooping bonbons from a bowl. The bowl may be pierced, for use with bonbons in liquids.

Systematic assessment of the condition of collection holdings conducted periodically with the aim of identifying and prioritizing conservation needs. A conservation survey is a core part of a collection's long range plan.
Large and often ornamented forks used for serving meats and cold cuts.
Banks, originally made from an orange-colored clay called pygg, usually used by children for saving coins. Often in the shape of a pig.

Use to describe automatic and semiautomatic firearms in which the pressure of the propellant gas is used to force the bolt to the rear, independently of the barrel, which does not move relative to the receiver.

Carved stones that have been found at ancient and more recent North American sites. They were apparently often part of an atlatl, or spear-thrower; it is believed that a bannerstone was tied to the center of thin, willowy atlatl shafts, thus increasing the spear-thrower's flexibility and causing an efficient, whip-like action. Bannerstones were often carefully carved of decorative stone, and were probably considered sumptuary implements and symbols of status. Some bannerstones seem to have been mounted on staffs or poles to serve primarily as symbols of rank.
Metal balls used as ammunition in early cap and ball pistols.

Smooth-grained, natural- or cream-colored calf, vegetable-tanned, usually with bark, and commonly used in the 19th and early 20th centuries in binding law books, particularly in England. It has been superceded for that use by "law buckram."
Sensitivity to light of all colors in the visible spectrum.
Dolls whose expressions, proportions, and dress mimic those of infants.

Stoles worn by deacons to designate their rank. In the western church, deacon's stoles are worn over the left shoulder; historically hanging straight down, in the modern church worn across the body and tied under the right arm.
Gun mounts consisting of two small side panels, joined at the base to a center column which swivels on a fixed pedestal, enabling the weapon to be trained rapidly and to fire vertically.
Toys designed to be pushed.

Plucked lutelike chordophones of bass register, having a soundbox with a scalloped silhouette, a flat or slightly domed back, a flat soundboard with a round ornamental soundhole, and a long neck with a pegbox with usually lateral tuning pegs. They are strung with six or seven double courses of metal strings, the lowest of which are made of two or more strands twisted together. The bridge is glued in position, having a fret-like strip of brass and a row or hitch-pins along its bottom edge; a lutelike system of bars is fixed under the soundboard. They are said to have been first made by John Rose, in London, 1562, and were popular as continuo instruments in string consorts into the 17th century.

European Medieval plucked lutelike chordophones having a flat body, short neck and pegbox carved from a single piece of wood, with a bridge, one central or two lateral soundholes, frets, and usually four but sometimes three or five strings.

Unpowered round or pear-shaped airtight vessels designed to rise into the air when inflated with hot air or a gas, and which are tethered to the ground or another vehicle such as a ship. These may be manned or unmanned, and most usually used for observation, historically in a military context.
Unmanned spacecraft designed for nonorbital missions, such as flights to other planets or into deep space; for unmanned spacecraft designed for orbital missions, use "artificial satellites."
Vehicles that navigate through the air, either supported for flight by buoyancy or by the dynamic action of the air on their surfaces; usually designed to accommodate one or more persons.
Auxiliary or initial propulsion systems for aircraft, missles, or spacecraft which may or may not separate from the parent craft when their fuel has been consumed.
General aviation aircraft generally used for sport, recreation, or aerobatics and usually homebuilt, ultralight, or light aircraft.

Light, relatively short-barreled rifles and smoothbore long guns used by cavalry and lightly armed special troops, originating in Europe in the late 16th century and made in various sizes and with different firing mechanisms throughout their development down to the present day.
Puzzles for young children consisting of large puzzle pieces to be assembled on the floor.
Mechanical puzzles whose goal is assembling two- or three-dimensional pieces back together into a specified form.

Very plump dolls with topknots based on a character in serialized magazine stories of the late 19th century and since around 1912 produced in numerous materials, most often in celluloid, bisque, or plaster.

Metal bosses applied to the center of shields, serving to protect the handgrip. From ancient times they served as a reinforcement and sometimes as an offensive device to be used at close quarters; after the early Medieval period they tended to serve purely as decorative elements.

General term for large artillery pieces, developed in Europe since the 14th century, consisting basically of a long smoothbore iron, bronze, or steel barrel, cast in one piece or built up by a series of forgings, supported on a carriage or stationary mount, capable of firing very heavy projectiles.
Guns designed for use against tanks or other armored vehicles.
Artillery designed to have cross-country or road mobility for use in the battlefield.
Leather thongs, Greco-Etruscan in origin and adopted by the Romans, attached to the shafts of javelins and used to throw them with more propulsion than was possible by hand alone.

Projectile weapons consisting of two or more stone or iron balls attached to the ends of a cord, whirled and thrown to entangle an animal or human being. Bolas were used by native peoples in the Americas.
Sports or contests involving bloodshed. Examples include hunting, cockfighting, bullfighting, and ancient gladiator games.

Card game for 2 or sometimes 3 or 4 players, in which the object is to make counting combinations for points that are scored on a cribbage board, a typically wooden board having holes into which pegs are inserted to mark the score and track the progress of the players.
Tile game of Chinese origin usually played by four players with 144 dominolike pieces or tiles marked in suites,  counters, and dice, the object being to collect winning combinations of tiles.

Game of chance using cards on which there is a printed grid of numbers, a row of which constitute a win when they have been chosen at random. The chosen numbers, usually up to 75 or 90, are called out by a "banker," and the first player to achieve a card or a line in which all of the numbers have been called shouts "bingo" or "house," and collects the entire stake money, usually less a specified percentage, whatever is permitted by local law. Other variations play a card in which the central square is free, and the first player on whose card five of the called numbers appear in a row, vertically, horizontally, or diagonally, is the winner.
Table game in which players take turns shooting discs across a circular playing surface marked with scoring regions, while also attempting to knock the discs of their opponents.
Game that developed as a common man's game from billiards, that was considered a gentlemen's game of skill. Pool is played with a 15 balls and a cue ball on a table with six pockets.
A game in which standing players push or shove wooden or plastic disks with a long cue toward numbered scoring sections marked on a board on a floor or deck.
Team game played on a grass pitch, with bowling at a wicket defended by a batting player of the other team.

Cross-country game in which a player strikes a small ball with various clubs from a series of starting points (teeing grounds) into a series of holes on a course. The player who holes his ball in the fewest strokes wins. Evidence suggests that early forms of golf were played first in the Netherlands and then in Scotland.

Bowling game played on a standard tenpin lane but with pins that are 9.4 inches tall and a ball that is no larger than five inches in diameter and three pounds twelve ounces in weight with finger holes. Three balls may be rolled in each frame of the ten-frame game, but there is no bonus for knocking down all ten pins. A perfect game is 300, as it is in tenpin bowling.

Outdoor game in which a ball, called a bowl, is rolled toward a smaller stationary ball, called a jack, the object being to roll one's bowl closer the jack than that of an opponent. This is sometimes achieved by knocking aside an opponent's bowl or the jack.

Game between two teams of typically six players each, who wear skates and compete on an ice rink. The object is to propel a vulcanized rubber disk, called a puck, past a goal line and into a net guarded by a goaltender, or goalie, using a stick with a wooden blade.
Type of skiing that came out of the hilly terrain of Norway and the other Scandinavian countries, it includes cross-country skiing and ski-jumping events.
Sport of racing on ice skates on an oval track against other competitors or the clock.

Game of ancient origins in which two people with small rackets bat shuttlecocks from one to the other as many times as possible without allowing it to fall to the ground. Similar games with a shuttlecock existed in ancient Greece about 2000 years ago, and were later found in India, China, and Siam. In Europe it has been a children's game for several centuries.
Property of materials, such as paper or mat board, or processing methods that are expected to allow items to be stored for extended periods of time without loss of quality.

The state or characteristic of having a low degree of distinctness, lacking sharp focus or fine detail. For example, used in reference to a visual output, such as from a camera, television, computer screen, or printer.

Tempered steel instruments consisting of a stem with two prongs, producing a musical tone of definite constant pitch when struck and serving as a standard as when tuning musical instruments and performing acoustical experiments.
Combination instruments featuring the hammer action of the piano with the plucking jacks of the harpsichord, developed in the early 18th century.
Structural sheet of steel, shaped in alternating ridges and grooves; used as roofing, siding, and the like.
Two-piece swimsuits consisting of a bikini bottom and a top part in the style of a tank top.
Frames with simple lap-jointed back frames and entablature-derived moldings.

Ornate frames, usually gilded, distinguished by curvilinear shapes resembling ears or earlobes; based on a style developed by silversmiths in the Netherlands ca. 1600; may include shapes of masks and marine life.
Class of physical phenomena associated with magnets and the fields of force produced by moving electric currents.
Wedges of wood set at the corners of frames.
The selective absorption of electromagnetic radiation by an atomic nucleus in the presence of a strong, static magnetic field.
Frames for altar frontals (antependia), particularly frames that serve to suspend or hold textile antependia in place.
The quality or state of being conditioned or constructed or fitted so tightly as to be impervious to water.

Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) uses the techniques of gas- chromatography and mass spectrometry in tandem to identify substances in complex mixtures within a test sample. It is a standard tool of forensics. In conservation, GC-MS is employed to determine the presence and type of organic compounds in paintings and other artifacts.

Mirrors of varied form designed to fit above mantels. Generally of two main types: those made to be hung horizontally and which usually consist of three but sometimes four panes of glass, of which the central pane is about twice the width of each outer one; and those made to be hung vertically, often consisting of a single square or rectangular pane of glass, sometimes with a painting set within the frame above the upper portion of the mirror. May have attached candle branches.
Frames with moldings which have undulating surfaces.
Tops containing reeds that vibrate and hum when the tops spin. Found worldwide, they are sometimes intended as children's toys.
Instruments consisting of a tube of wood, metal or plastic, with a mirliton covering a lateral hole, played by being sung or hummed into.

Most commonly keyless, valveless aerophones with a wide conical bore, usually though not always coiled, and a cup mouthpiece, now used chiefly for military and parade use. Early in the 19th century, the addition of keys and valves lent a full chromatic scale: for these instruments use "keyed bugles."

End-blown marine shell trumpets of Japan, made of a conch shell either with a wood or metal mouthpiece fitted to the narrow end or with the pointed end snipped off and the hole polished smooth for blowing. They have been used since at least the 7th century in Buddhist ritual, and also for signalling troops in battle.

A type of x-ray fluorescence used for elemental analysis that involves exciting elements in a sample then diffracting the emitted radiation by using a device, such as a crystal or monochromator, in order to measure the intensity of x-rays with a specific wavelength.

Composite reedpipes consisting of an air-tight skin, cloth, or rubber bag which serves as the air reservoir, one or more chanters with fingerholes on which the melody is played, and often one or more drone pipes which sound a continuous background to the melody. All sounding pipes have reeds and are attached to the bag by being inserted into tubular wooden stocks which are tied into openings in the bag.

Simple zitherlike chordophones found worldwide, consisting of a flexible stick curved by the tension of a string or, rarely, several strings, stretched between its ends, with or without a detachable resonator. Different types are plucked, struck, bowed, blown upon, or played by a combination of methods.
Bowed, zitherlike chordophones of Iceland with trapezoidal bodies, and two or four horsehair strings.
Sets composed of playing cards plus other items designed to be used together in games in which the primary activity during a round of play involves the use of the playing cards.
Large pieces of woven fabric, often terrycloth, meant to be used at beachside as a mat for laying in the sand and for drying off after swimming. These often come in vibrant colors or patterns.
Small table mats on which individual place settings are laid.

Long, rectangular bands of woven fabric terminating in woven streamers or tassles, usually wrapped around the waist. Woven by using one's hands without the use of a loom, joining lengthwise and sideways threads together. Often used in Native North American and Métis regalia.
Reflector ovens specifically designed for roasting fowl, with hooks to hold the bird and a drip pan.
Compounds derived from barberry (Berberis vulgaris) bush, both from the berry and from the bark. Used as pigment and medicinally for antimicrobial properties.
Small tongs often with claw-shaped ends used for serving ice cubes.

Balls used in the game of American football, in the form of inflated prolate spheroids usually covered with leather having a laced seam where the edges of the cover meet; normally about 21 by 28 inches in circumference and weighing about 15 ounces.
Long, narrow, curved wicker baskets fitted to the end of a wooden handle with a glovelike compartment at the base used by players of jai alai to catch and throw the ball.

Sets of objects used for playing table tennis or ping-pong. Sets usually consist of paddles, balls, and a detachable net that can be stretched over the center of a table. The set may also include a foldable table, usually with wheels, that enables easy storage.

A fine, white pigment composed of calcium hydroxide and calcium, produced by slaking of lime in water or air to form a thick, white, alkaline paste. It was used for fresco painting where it hardens to form a cohesive film without the aid of a binder. It reacts with proteins, such as egg white or casein, to produce a tough, insoluble film.

Toys consisting of boxes with hinged lids from which an enclosed figure springs out when a latch is released, as by turning a small crank on the outside of the box an appropriate number of revolutions.
Rifles used for recreational purposes, especially for hunting.

Complex polymers created by combining two monomers of different species. The resulting materials may exhibit combined properties of the monomers employed; distinct from what can be achieved by a physical, rather than chemical blend of polymerized component monomers.

Optical devices that give the illusion of depth and action when viewing two-dimensional images, by the use of one or more magnifying lenses or mirrors set in a boxlike enclosure and viewed through a small opening on one end. Usually used with special prints designed for the purpose, "perspective view prints."
The state or quality of being composed from dissimilar parts, elements, or characteristics.

The alteration of the light transmission characteristics of glass as a result of prolonged exposure to visible or ultraviolet light. Deterioration can be evident as a change in the color of the glass due to a reaction between the iron and manganese oxides in the glass initiated by light. This irreversible alteration can be a deep purple color, but is more often a subtle change in hue to pink, violet, or yellow. Solarized glass most commonly seen is pink to violet because it contains manganese. Since at least the 2nd century BCE, manganese has been used as a glass decolorizer to diminish the greenish hue imparted by trace amounts of iron. However, with exposure to ultraviolet light, manganese can photo-oxidize to reform manganese dioxide which is violet in color. From the 20th century, seleium and cerium have also been used as decolorizers; when photo-oxidized they impart a yellow to golden hue.

Heavier-than-air objects designed to float on the wind, and that are intended for play or pleasure, particularly for use by children. These have a light structure of wood, cane, or plastic that is covered with a membrane of thin material that catches the wind, and is held at the end of a string or line.

Use primarily for large organizations of warships and associated forces under orders of a single commander, and, by extension, may be used for other large groups of vehicles under a single operator, such as large numbers of motor vehicles owned by one company.
Transportation vehicles capable of travel equally well in water and on land, or in water and in the air.
Watercraft generally larger and more seaworthy than boats, usually propelled by sails or engines.

Covered wagons of medium size carrying freight and emigrants across the western prairies and plains of the United States; generally characterized by mostly straight lines and linen tops; for similar wagons used predominantly east of the Mississippi River and having a boat-shaped profile with flaring ends, use "Conestoga wagons."

Single draft-animal drawn farm carts designed to tilt backwards to dump loads, typically having two broad wheels and a wide flat platform. Carts of this type could be used to carry corpses, refuse, or dung. During the French Revolution, this type of cart was frequently the conveyance used to transport prisoners to the guillotine.
Generally lightweight, two-wheeled utility vehicles meant to be pushed by hand, as, for example, used by street vendors.
Refers to any of various motorized or nonmotorized wheeled vehicles designed to transport golfers or their equipment around golf courses.
The concentration of a pigment in a coating expressed as percentage of total volume of a paint film.
Refers to light-induced oxidation.
A method of removing or reducing the acid content, usually of paper, utilizing alcohol or another nonaqueous solvent.

Technique developed by John Fenn in the late 1980s, an improved method of ionizing samples for use in mass spectrometry. Electrospray ionization (ESI) discharges a solution of a sample into an electric field that disperses the sample as fine droplets. ESI is especially useful for samples containing macromolecules, prone to fragmenting in other techniques of ionization.

The phenomenon, similar in principle to electron diffraction, whereby a beam of neutrons scattered by the regularly spaced atoms of a solid produces diffraction patterns characteristic of the solid’s crystal structure. Neutron diffraction may be used in place of x-ray crystallography.
Aircraft weighing less than the air they displace, sustaining lift by displacing the air using aerostatic bouyancy.
Aircraft designed or modified for specialized military operations.
Airplanes propelled by engines that eject jets or streams of gas or fluids, obtaining all or most of their thrust by reaction to the ejection.
Unmanned aircraft, often guided by remote control, used for strategic reconnaissance, aerial surveys or to deploy weaponry.
Aircraft in which the horizontal stabilizers used for trim and control are positioned forward of the main wings.
Refers to various heavier than air aircraft characterized by large-diameter, powered, horizontally rotating wings or blades that can lift the craft vertically and sustain their position in the air.

Versions of written works produced by condensation and omission but with retention of the general meaning and manner of presentation of the original, often prepared by someone other than the author of the original.

Regarded as the central text of the Hindu religion, the Bhagavad-gītā, written ca. 200 BCE, is comprised of eighteen sections and a total of 700 verses which form part of the epic poem known as the Mahābhārata. The verses describe a dialogue between the warrior Arjuna and Lord Krishna, on the eve of a battle between Arjuna and members of his family. It is thought that the text was written at a time when Bhramanical religion had been splintered, with Buddhism and Jainism separated. The Bhagavad-gītā teaches that there may be many ways to salvation, and can be interpreted as an endorsement of reconciliation.
Works, especially written or oral works, of unknown or disputed authorship, considered not authentic, spurious, or uncanonical.
Books of blank, mostly blank, or ruled pages, or of printed forms.
Magnetizable material in disk form, capable of storing information in the form of electromagnetic signals.

Pieces of cloth or other flexible material painted with signs or decorative designs and intended to be displayed by hanging or suspending. In heraldry, refers to square flags bearing heraldic devices. For other cloths intended to symbolize or to signal, use "flags."
Illustrations on the first page of a book, usually facing the title page.
Snug-fitting underpants with leg openings, made in a variety of styles for men, women, and children.

Physical formats, objects, digital information, or other non-material human constructs by which specific information may be recorded or conveyed. For example, books, leaflets, or audiotapes; or in computing, the primary components of an information artifact are information systems and procedures related to the artifact.
Containers or devices that hold and dispense a small paper towel or cloth, especially as used to dry the hands after washing them.

Crowns crafted for the funeral ceremony of young, unmarried women in England from the 17th through the 19th centuries.  Never intended to be worn, they consist of dome-shaped wooden frames decorated with ribbons, flowers, rosettes, and the names of the decreased.  They were either carried before the coffin or placed upon it.
Containers for keeping leeches, usually inscribed or labeled, and having some form of a pierced cover.
Small pail-like vessels used for holding and serving cream, generally made of porcelain or silver, the latter sometimes having a glass liner.
Odorless, non-flammable, highly toxic gas formerly used extensively as a fumigant.
Small wall bags, used primarily in tents, suspended from the trellis structure. The fronts are pile-woven and the backs done in a weft-faced plain weave.
Bags hung on the wall, especially in tents, and used to store personal belongings.
Long sticks carried in the hand for support in walking.
Specialized garments intended for exercise, made in a variety of forms since the mid-19th century.
Dresses of southern Chinese origin, typically having a high mandarin collar, a split skirt, and a fitted bodice with an asymmetrical closure extending from the neck to the right underarm.
Long dresses, typically elaborately trimmed with lace, beading, or embroidery, and worn by infants for christening.

Staffs carried in procession by participants, for example members of a religious confraternity, guild, congregation, parish, tribe, or a ruler's retinue. Identification of the group represented in the procession is typically affixed to the staff, including badges, the statue of the patron saint, or other items. For processional poles upon which banners, lanterns, torches, candles, or crosses or mounted, prefer the appropriate term describing the item.
Seats or covered pavilions for two or more people on the back of an elephant or camel.
Any of various devices dropped to the bottom of a body of water and designed to bury themselves there in order to restrict the movement of watercraft or other floating objects.

Centerboard sloops with mainsail and jib, usually 16 to 26 feet LOA (length overall), developed during the mid-nineteenth century around Muscongus Bay, Maine, for lobstering and fishing off the Maine and Massachusetts coasts; forerunners of Friendship sloops.
Jet aircraft with turbine-driven propellers that produce the principal thrust augmented by the thrust of the jet exhausts.
Seaplanes with a boatlike hull or fuselage providing buoyancy and the ability to plane across the water.

An early form of bicycle that was driven directly by pedaling cranks on the front wheel axle, rather than with a chain drive. The front and rear wheels were disproportionate in size to increase the distance covered for each turn of the cranks, and the rider sat almost directly over the large front wheel. Spokes allowed wheels ranging from 40 to 60 inches in diameter.
Miters worn by Christian clergy, distinguished by being decorated with jewels and other precious materials.
Armor pieces which are physical parts of or are affixed to other pieces and cannot function alone. For individual armor pieces which can be worn and function individually or in sets, see "armor."

Medieval headcloths for women usually consisting of a long linen or woolen cloth draped from one shoulder over the crown of the head, down and under the chin, and then around the back to the other shoulder, where it was left hanging.

Bombers for large-scale missions carrying conventional or nuclear weapons used generally in the protection of national policy interests or specifically to attack and destroy enemy industry, economic bases, and civilian population centers.
Fighters designed to identify and, if appropriate, engage enemy airborne objects.
An ester of methacrylic acid, methyl methacrylate is a monomer used for the production of polymethyl methacrylate resins.
Light, versatile spears with iron heads and long shafts used by ancient Germanic peoples.

Spears designed specifically for hunting, typically with wings on the blade or a crossbar just below it to prevent an impaled animal from running up the blade as well as to facilitate quick withdrawl.
Soft, flat-topped, visorless caps with a tight-fitting headband; in a military context, worn as an official item of headgear.

Loricae made of overlapping bronze or iron scales attached to a foundation of hide or strong cloth, typically arranged in horizontal rows and imbricated like roof tiles to avoid gaps. Their use was adopted by the Romans by at least the 4th century BCE and continued into the 4th century CE.
Gongs that are used and played as an ensemble.
Visors with sharply pointed or conical snouts, fitted on basnets in the 14th century.
Heavy shoes with open side flaps, especially coarse leatherwork shoes reaching to the ankles.
Gong chimes of Vietnam. They consist of three gongs, suspended in metal circles, which are attached to a wooden frame. Since the 18th century, they have been used in Vietnamese court music.
Closed-front, sometimes laced ankle boots introduced in the mid-19th century and characterized by the vamp wings being extended along either side to form a galosh.
Calf-length boots made of water-resistant materials such as rubber, designed to protect the wearer from rain and mud.
Process of comparing photometrically the relative intensities of the light in different parts of a spectrum.

Analytical technique used to measure changes in energy of a material as a sample and a reference are individually heated at a predetermined rate. Heat-generating or absorbing processes are detected as differences in electrical energy supplied to either the sample or the reference material. The heat flow into or out of the sample is due to the occurrence of a physical or chemical process  such as melting, crystallization, or ceramic firing temperature.
Chromatography of volatile substances existing in or converted to a vapor state.

In biology, a modification of a protein’s structure brought about by heat, alkalis, and other factors, which causes it to collapse into a disordered mass. The process Is irreversible for most proteins. In conservation science, the denaturation of leather and parchment is studied by various analytical techniques.

Square textile coverings used to cover both chalice and paten before and after communion. A chalice veil is placed over the chalice, paten, and purificator when the vessels are prepared for the Eucharist and placed on the altar; it is removed before the Consecration. It may be embellished and of the same color as the liturgical vestments. For stiff squares covering just the top of the chalice, use "palls (chalice covers)."
Small textile coverings used by the Orthodox Eastern Church to cover chalice and paten separately.

Textile bands used under Torah mantles to hold the scroll together. Among Ashkenazi Jews, the swaddling cloth used at a circumcision would be cut and sewn into a long strip, embroidered and appropriately inscribed, to be used later as a Torah binder.
Parts or components of firearm locks.
Small sharp pieces of flint for use in a flintlock of a firearm, to produce sparks to ignite the priming powder.
Pipes which are constituent parts of other aerophones, have fingerholes, and are used to play the melody.
Textile coverings for loaves of bread (hallot), often baked in elaborate plaited forms, used for the Jewish Sabbath and festival meals. Often of linen, and embroidered with religious inscriptions.

Calabash-resonated wood xylophones of Africa, introduced into Latin America where they took on various local forms. Also the modern orchestral instrument developed from Latin American models, having metal tube resonators and a four-octave compass.

Shrouds of Madagascar, woven of silk, cotton, bast, or raffia and often decorated with embroidery or beads, used to wrap bodies for ritual reburial. The term literally translates as "red cloth", although red is not always the dominant color.
Square textiles used in Japan to wrap presents.

Curtains hung around the altar, particularly in a temple or church. They were hung in front of, or to close off the sides of, an altar during the service. As with rood screens, altar veils were liturgical barriers marking the boundaries between the congregation's space and the holy of holies; the Lenten veil is a type of altar veil, used in Catholic and other churches in the season prior to Easter. Beginning in the early days of the Reformation, altar vela began to be used in certain Protestant churches during the entire liturgical year. In some cases, altar veils may be associated with the "altar canopy."
Parts or components of upholstery foundations.
Firmly stuffed rolls attached to the edges of upholstered seats to make the edges more durable.
Coffeepots in which boiling water rising through a tube is repeatedly deflected downward through a perforated basket containing ground beans to extract their essence.
Rectangular, usually leather, traveling bags with sides that come together and fasten at the top or open to the full width of the bag and with two straps that wrap around the bag to secure it.
Containers with one or more cylindrical channels for holding stacks of coins of identical size.

Compact, low-hung coaches with the driver's perch outside, space for two or more passengers, and generally with a straight front; may also be used for early automobiles whose form borrowed the characteristic closed carriage-style body and open driver's area.

Carriages developed in Poland and Austria in the early 19th century and eventually popular in England for long-distance travel since the interior seating compartment could be converted into sleeping quarters; often featuring a large rear-facing seat to accommodate servants.
Any of various light, two- or four-wheeled open or covered carriages, normally intended for a single person, and typically drawn by a single horse.
Gigs of the 19th century similar to stanhopes but heavier, differing in suspension, and usually lacking the extra luggage space under the seat.
American sleighs with light angular bodies seating four passengers; developed in Portland, Maine, in the early 19th century.
Four-wheeled vehicle with various loading surfaces, pulled by a pack animal, specifically designed for the transport of beer barrels and crates.
Wheeled vehicles, particularly on four wheels.

Large, ornamental cups of varying form but generally with two or more handles, used for ceremonial drinking by assembled companions. Also, similar cups given as a prize, honor, or token of friendship.
Refrigerators that have glass doors installed to allow the user to see the contents without opening it.
Wire racks used for cooling baked foods such as bread and cakes.
Riding habits, worn chiefly by women in the 18th century, which button all the way down the front and have a small collar.
Machine designed to fly by means of artificial flapping wings.

Refers to  nonporous, flexible spherical or pear-shaped bags or envelope made of a lightweight material inflated with heated air or a gas that is lighter than air and designed to rise and float in the atmosphere, usually while carrying aloft passengers or scientific instruments.
Small handkerchiefs kept in the pocket of a formal jacket as a decorative accessory.
Horse-drawn vehicles designed to transport people, that have two wheels.

Horse-drawn coaches available for public hire, usually seating between two and six passengers with the driver riding outside; in operation from the 17th to the late 19th century. For automobiles licensed to carry passengers for hire, use "taxicabs."
Simple sleds used to transport logs, stones, sticks, or other objects.
Toy guns in which pellets, often cork and attached to the gun by a string, are shot by compressed air, producing a loud pop.
Coverings of cloth, leather, or similar material worn over the ankle and sometimes lower leg.
Costume accessories worn in conjunction with hair on the head.
Small ornaments clipped to bolo ties, both to keep the tie in place around the wearer and as decoration.
Hip- to knee-length garments made in jacket or mantle form, worn by women while dressing.
Ring-shaped ornaments worn in the nose.
Small decorative or functional objects, typically attached to a chain or strap hanging from a pocket or within a purse, such as fobs for a watch or key. When decorative, they often serve as jewelry.
Small decorative fobs or functional objects attached to a chain or strap that is attached to a watch placed in a pocket. For the chains attached to the fob, use "fob chains."

Bowed lutelike chordophones of modern Greece, Bulgaria, and Dalmatia, having a pear-shaped body, wooden belly, peg disc with rear pegs, and three strings. They are played in a vertical position resting on the player's knees.
PVC or vinyl balls mounted with one or two handles, intended as toys on which children can bounce.
Boards bearing signs, especially common as tavern and shop signs.
Signs, emblems, designs, or motifs that guide users to destinations, or indicate way finding to a viewer.
Tablets hung in church that display to the congregation the numbers of hymns and readings for services.

term: jewelry worn around the neck or on the upper body
definition: Jewelry specifically worn around the neck, such as necklaces, or on the upper body, such as pectorals.
Pectoral medallions, suspended from the neck, bearing a sacred picture; worn by bishops of the Orthodox Eastern Church.
Deep, open baskets of varying form intended primarily for gathering or transporting eggs; used especially with reference to those with rib-type construction.
Broad bands of cloth, such as those wound around a baby's waist to support the back and stomach.
Wallet-sized cards that those registered for the United States draft are by law required to keep in their personal possession at all times.
A fly-whisk made of hair or feathers or a representation of same, held by figures attending royalty or respected personages in Asia, and particularly in the art of the Indian subcontinent.
Printed cards distributed to attract freight or passenger business especially for the clipper ships of the 1850s and 1860s.
Long zithers of Java, with movable bridges and tuning pegs located inside the body.

A crystalline aromatic compound (C10H8) derived from coal tar, with a molecule consisting of two fused six-membered rings and a pungent mothball smell, used in dyes, synthetic resins, explosives, insecticide, fungicide, and moth repellent.
