It is not recommended for general use as an insecticide because it may recrystallize on specimens and can discolor wool in the presence of moisture, and its actual effectiveness against insects is questionable. It fluoresces purple in mercury light.

A natural, solid, hydrocarbon substance, distinguishable from bitumen by being infusible and insoluble. When heated, however, pyrobitumens generate or transform into bitumen-like liquid or gaseous petroleum compounds. This class of natural bituminous material includes peat, lignite, and coal.
Sumptuous outergarments worn during the Renaisssance by upper-class men. Often with puffed or full sleeves, chamarres are folded back and fastened at the neck.

A composite material consisting of gravel, sand, and stone that is bound together with asphalt; it is laid down in layers and compacted. It is commonly used in construction projects such as road surfaces, airports, and parking lots. The ingredients are mixed under high temperatures and kept heated until applied to a surface.
An unconsolidated deposit of semicarbonized plant remains formed in a water-saturated environment such as a bog.
Uniforms intended for those in the armed forces.
Guideway vehicles that specifically operate on rails.

Long, loose-fitting sheer shirts worn by men in the Philippines and considered to be part of the national costume. Traditionally made from pineapple fiber, jusi (a combination of pineapple fiber and silk), or banana fabric; particularly notable for the embroidery on the front of the garment.

Helmets used in Greece from about the mid-6th century BCE on, consisting of a skull with a short neck guard and two movable cheekpieces hinged to the skull. They were often highly decorated and surmounted by an elaborate crest.

Gauntlets with a long cuff encircling the forearm up to the elbow where the edge often was cut at an angle to form a point. They were characteristic of foot soldiers' armor in the 16th century, and common for light cavalry from the 15th to the 17th century when they were worn on the left or bridle arm only.
Coverings for the hand enclosing each finger separately, sometimes extending over the wrist and arm.
Warships assigned to protect single ships or convoys of transports or merchant vessels during wartime.
Portions of sterns, typically curved, that project aft of the sternposts of watercraft.

Underwater vehicles that maneuver without humans on board. These exist in two types: remotely operated underwater vehicles (ROVs), which are tethered to and controlled by a remote operator, and autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), which maneuver independently of direct operator input.

Vehicles with two wheels in tandem propelled by the rider straddling a diamond-shaped frame mounting wheels seat and steering handle bars, with a horizontal bar as the top element joining the handlebars to the seat post. These are the basic elements of most bicycles with the exception of those that have eliminated or dropped the top horizontal bar to accommodate women's skirts. Historically some bicycles with identical structure have been marketed as either "men's bicycles" or "women's bicycles" as fashions changed.

Any enzyme which splits triglyceride fats into their component fatty acids and glycerol. Lipase, found in the body, aids in the digestion of food. Lipase, added to detergents, aids cleaning. In conservation, lipase is sometimes used for removal of oil-based varnishes from paintings and of oil stains from drawings.
Buses used to transport students to and from school.
Narrow, shallow canoes common in East Africa, made of hollowed-out tree trunks and equipped with outriggers of both sides.

Vessels designed to carry cargo packed in standardized, sealable, and reusable containers, that are made to fixed dimensions (usually either 20 or 40 feet in length) and designed to stack and lock together. They are also characterized by the lack of cargo handling gear, which is located on shore terminals rather than aboard ship. Container ships require large hatches in the deck for stowing the cargo; belowdecks typically is a cellular grid of compartments opening to the weather deck and designed to receive the containers and hold them in place until unloading is achieved at the port of destination.
Carts with two or more wheels with low beds and high side barriers, specifically equipped for the transport of cattle.
Ancient war or racing chariots drawn by four horses abreast.
Large, dorylike vessels with straight posts and flat sides; commmonly found in upper New England and Canada.
Motor vehicles with apparatus for fighting fires on or from land.
Structural lower parts of motor vehicles that include the drive trains, exhaust systems, and steering, those components that make the vehicles move and that support the vehicle bodies.
Railroad trains consisting of passenger cars, primarily hauling passengers but may include cars for associated nonfreight items, such as baggage, mail, or express.
French high-speed trains running on separate tracks and capable of speeds over 160 mph.
Small lightweight motorcycles that are very similar to a bicycle, but propelled by an attached motor. The specific features and capacity may be defined differently in various legislative districts.
Substances composed by the chemical union of potassium with additional elements.
A white or colorless crystalline solid or powder of the composition KCl, used for molten salt baths, for the heat treatment of steels, for fertilizers, and in explosives.

Gentlemen's light phaetons for pleasure or competitive show driving generally characterized by tilbury bodies set on four wheels, often having spindle-back seats and a skeleton rumble seat for grooms.
Railroad flatcars designed and equipped to transport containers or truck trailers.
Mechanical devices with a central hub and radiating blades on aircraft that provide thrust by spinning.
Artificial satellites that gather data about the earth's atmosphere and surface in order to aid meteorologists.
Refers to schooners, usually two-masted, carrying topsails on one or more masts.
Light one-horse sleighs with a single seatboard for two or three passengers; developed in the United States around 1800.
Material containing carbon, including those derived from living organisms.
Short horizontal, usually wooden, bars attached to eveners or splinter bars or crossbar shafts of vehicles and to which the traces of draft animals are attached.

Specialized brassieres that provide support to women who are nursing and that permit breastfeeding without the need to be removed by including flaps on the cup which can be opened with one hand to expose the nipple.
Type of knitted briefs worn by men or boys.
Women's one-piece garments consisting of a chemise and underpants with loose-fitting legs or a snap crotch.
Long drawers decorated at the ankles, worn by women and children in the 19th century. Also, a pair of separate shaped pieces designed to tie onto the leg and reach the ankle.
Underbodices worn over a corset with sleeves or built-up straps.

Underskirts, extending from the waist to usually just slightly shorter than the outside skirt, which provide fullness at some point. For similar skirtlike underwear which does not provide fullness use "half slips."

Short girdles, designed to accentuate a small waist, starting at the ribs and stopping above the hips, sometimes with attached supporters for stockings. For narrow elastic or fabric bands worn around the waist or hips with supporters for stockings use "garter belts."
Gowns worn by infants, having a very long skirt designed to somewhat restrict movement and to keep the baby's legs warm by being so long that he or she cannot easily kick the skirt off the legs.

Precious or semiprecious stone that can be cut, polished, or otherwise dressed for use as gems; distinguished from "gems," which are made of gemstone that has been worked or other material such as pearl.
19th-century women's bonnets, often with a soft gathered crown and a stiff brim with ribbons tied at the side or under the chin.
19th-century name for cocked hats with the brim turned up to form three corners.

White, water soluble crystalline or granular powder, commonly known as baking soda or bicarbonate of soda. It is used as a leavening agent for baking; in medicine as an antacid; as a whitening agent in toothpastes; a fire retardant; a stain-absorbing ingredient in dry cleaning preparations. Chemical formula: NaHC03.

Used in an ecological context to describe a large class of nitrogen oxide gases produced in combustion which occur as atmospheric pollutants. Colorless, poisonous gas formed when nitric acid reacts with copper or when ammonia reacts with platinum. It is produced in combustion engine processes such as automobile emissions, resulting in acid rain and photochemical smog. It is also an important messenger molecule in mammals and other animals, produced through cellular metabolism, and involved in oxygen transmission, blood pressure regulation, and other physiological activities.

A compound of sulfur with another element (usually denoted by a qualifying term). Sulfide is used to describe any of three types of chemical compounds that contain sulfur: organic sulfides, inorganic sulfides, and phosphine sulfides.
Complete costume, including garments and accessories, worn for a harmonious effect. Also, two or more garments or accessories designed to complement one another.
Alternative pieces of armor that could be exchanged with others in a set to adapt it for various purposes.

Plate armor for the shoulders and upper arms, consisting either of one large plate shaped to the shoulder or several articulated lames, extending at the front and rear to protect the armpits and often the shoulder blades.
Armors designed specifically for the Rennen, a form of joust fought with sharpened lances.
Typefaces whose characters are especially narrow in proportion to their height.
Typefaces used for the body of the text of printed matter, often defined as type of 24 points or smaller.

Pressed glass made in the 1920s by automatic machines in factories in the American mid-west; it is thought to reflect the austerity of postwar life. Some patterns are reminiscent of 19th-century designs while others incorporate the sharp corners and precise lines of Art Deco styles.
A white, gray, brick-red, or green mineral of the alkali feldspar group.

Locks in which the steel and pan cover are made in one piece and the sear operates vertically to engage in two notches in a tumbler attached to the inner end of the cock spindle, to place the mechanism in either half-cock or full cock. When the trigger is pressed, the flint strikes the steel and simultaneously the pan is uncovered, exposing the priming powder therein to a shower of sparks that ignite the charge.
The topmost components of axes, often made of stone or metal, having at least one sharpened edge. Axe heads are attached to the shafts of the axe.
The apparatus used in weightlifting, consisting generally of a bar with replaceable, disk-shaped weights fastened to the ends.

Made of ivory or metal, sometimes embellished with incised decorations of animals such as bears or seagulls. Made by Yup'ik families for their female children. Using the knife to draw in various surfaces, Yup'ik girls retell important histories, share personal experiences, or sing songs.
Special ropes, usually of four strands of selected manilla long fiber and about 1 1/2 inches in diameter, designed for gymnastic climbing or as practice for mountain climbing.
Toy blocks capable of being stacked to make simple constructions.
Specially designed brooms used to sweep the ice in the game of curling.
One-of-a-kind dolls made by hand by the original designers, together with their costumes and other accessories, such as a base.
Small versions of furniture as accessories for dolls. They are larger than dollhouse furniture and show more finishing.
The pieces used in the game of chess, in modern sets generally comprising kings, queens, bishops, knights, rooks, and pawns.
Large kite-like contrivances with wide textile canopies that are attached to a pilot by a harness in order to allow flight after jumping from or being hauled to a height.

Optical toys that create moving images, consisting of a slotted disk featuring a series of images that appear to move when the disk is spun and viewed through the slots before a mirror. Its invention is attributed to Joseph Plateau in 1833. Distinct from "stroboscopes," similar devices that employ two disks in place of the mirror.
Wind-up or battery-powered dolls that simulate walking.
Books in which the entire text and illustrations for each individual page is printed from a single carved wood block.
Loose covers for books, often of soft leather, having pockets into which the boards are inserted, used sometimes in the Middle Ages instead of binding.
Puzzles composed of several parts that pose a problem for one person to solve by manipulation using logic, reasoning, insight, luck, or dexterity.
Bindings that rely on adhesives to hold together the leaves of the volume.
Bindings decorated with arms or other devices of royalty or nobility.

Implements used for striking the ball in the sport of tennis. Consisting of a handle that supports a more or less circular or oval frame, traditionally of wood but more recently of lightweight metal, etc.; across the frame is strung a taut latticework of fine cord, catgut, or artificial fibre, and (shuttlecock, etc.) in various sports
Children's toy made from a fan of paper or plastic curls attached to the shaft of a wooden or plastic stick with a pin. The fan or wheel rotates when blown by the wind or by a person.

Pendants, brooches, or any other jewelry that has as a primary focus a devotional or religious subject or theme. Devotional jewelry has been common since ancient times, and is known in many religions, including Hinduism and Christianity. Wearing of devotional jewelry may be thought to convey blessings, health, or good luck.
Ear ornaments worn suspended from a bent wire or a thin loop passed through a hole pierced in the lobe of the ear or clipped or screwed to the lobe.
Weights consisting of two spherical ends firmly attached to a short bar serving as a handle; used as exercise and fitness apparatus.

Long, wide buoyant boards, anywhere from 4 to 12 feet long and about 3 feet wide at the maximum point and usually having slight curves, especially in the front, used for riding surf. Originally constructed of wood, since the 1960s they have most often been made from synthetic foam covered in resin-coated fiberglass.
Metal spheres, weighing about 16 pounds, attached to a long handle of steel wire having a rigid grip at the other end; meant to be thrown for distance during a field event.
Large inflatable balls used in various recreational games and activities, originally intended for the beach.
Toys intended to be used by children to play in the sand, such as at the seaside. These may include sand mold toys, toy pails, or toy shovels, often in sets.

The toy consists of a sturdy cord with two hard plastic balls at the ends. The cord is knotted to a plastic tab. This tab is held between the thumb and forefinger, so that the balls hang side by side in equilibrium. A quick up and down motion of the wrist causes the balls above and below the wrist to tap against each other, creating a click-clack sound.

Construction toys consisting of girders, nuts, bolts, motors and other parts for assembling buildings and structures; first manufactured by the A.C. Gilbert Company in 1913 and later by the Meccano Company.
Mechanical toys operated by springs or similar mechanisms that must be wound.
Chief game pieces of chess sets, the protection of which is the object of the game.
Bindings in which the back of a text block is trimmed to produce a block of separate leaves, an adhesive is applied to the area, and the cover is affixed.

Bindings created using a series of wire staples along the edge of gathered sheets of loose paper. Usually employed for speed and convenience rather than longevity. Often used for pamphlets or other slim publications rather than commercially produced books.
Large circular boards, usually of cork and having numbered compartments, used as targets during the game of darts.
Zitherlike chordophones with a box resonator and multiple strings but no keyboard, played by being struck with light hammers.

Keywork for the flute developed by Theobald Boehm in the 1830s, involving an improved placement of fingerholes and a key mechanism to provide full venting and bring all fingerholes within easy control of the fingers. Other instrument makers later adapted the system for the clarinet, oboe, bassoon, and other aerophones.
Clothing worn by participants in baptismal ceremonies.
Jackets, often made of leather with ribbed trim, resembling those worn by Second World War bomber crews.

Refers generally to that category of costume designed to be worn or carried to protect the body in combat. Armor pieces which are always physical parts of or are affixed to other pieces and cannot function alone are collocated under the guide term "<armor components>." For specifically groups of armor pieces designed as a whole to possess particular physical characteristics in order to suit a particular purpose or occasion, see "armors."
Loose-fitting, straight-hanging shirtlike underwear with or without sleeves, usually extending to the hip or knee.

Padded rolls or cushions worn around the hips as women's undergarments to accentuate the fullness of skirts, gowns, petticoats or jackets. Sources attribute their use to both the Elizabethan period and the 18th century.
Objects of precious materials and symbolic value, such as jeweled scepters or crowns, appendant to the office of a sovereign.
Cone- or funnel-shaped decorative accessories for holding flowers in the hand, often with an attached finger ring; may also be pinned or hooked to a garment.
Waist-length coat-like outer military garments, sometimes attached by buttons to trousers and often worn by soldiers and airmen.

Main garments worn by women, primarily in Africa, to cover the genitals, often consisting of pendant elements made of metal or vegetal matter that hang from a cord tied around the waist or hips; may also be made of cloth and some element may pass between the legs.
Ankle-length boots worn by women.
Rectangular bands, often made of cloth or metal, made to hold cuffs of garments in place. At each end is a button or metal pin to attach the band to the cuff's buttonhole.

Ornamental chains, usually of polished metal with various badges, medals or other symbols attached, worn around the neck and generally long enough to rest upon the chest. They are worn by officials such as mayors as insignia of office.
Round, stuffed coverings for the head with wide streamers falling from the crown; worn in the 14th and 15th centuries.

Decorative bar-shaped devices with a clasp designed to hold the hair in place, particularly such devices to hold long hair pulled to the back of the neck or a section of hair pulled to the top of the head, away from the face.
Ornamental bands or circlets worn on the upper arm. Use "bracelets (jewelry)" for similar articles worn on the lower arm.
Rings, usually of metal worn in a piercing on the nipple.
Rings worn on one of the toes.

Devices, often ornamental, used to secure the cuffs of a shirt, which is generally supplied with buttonholes or other openings to allow insertion of the cuff link. Forms include an ornamental disc or other shape attached to a toggle, or two linked ornamental buttons.
Golden leg bands worn on the calf by Nahua tlahtohqueh (rulers) in postclassic central Mexico.
General term for ornaments worn on any part of the face.

Utensils consisting of a wide, shallow perforated bowl extending from a long handle. Used to remove foam and other undesirable substances floating on the surface of a liquid or to remove food from a liquid cooking medium.
Spatulas with rubber, nylon, or similar synthetic blades, used especially for such tasks as removing soft foods from bowls.
Widely occurring monoclinic mineral, usually green in color, associated with and resembling mica but chemically consisting of hydrous silicate of aluminum, ferrous iron, or magnesium.

Single- or double-breasted fly-front coats usually of dark plain woolen fabric and often having a velvet collar.  Of a type first worn by men in the 18th century and adapted for women during the 20th century.
Loose-fitting raincoats; use especially for those of oilskin or rubberized fabric and often made in bright colors.
The deel is a traditional Mongolian garment, little changed since the 13th century, a wide, colorful, calf-length silk robe with long sleeves that buttons up the right side.
Sets of two or more garments, made from worsted, broadcloth, or other high-quality material, commonly worn for formal functions.
Tunics, short or long, and generally of linen, worn by men and women in ancient Greece.
Sleeveless garments usually worn over a blouse or a shirt, and that have no placket or fastenings.
Sweaters that open the full length of the center front, closing with buttons, snaps, or a zipper, and having a round or V-shaped, usually collarless, neckline.
Traditional loincloth of Swaziland, formerly made of leopard skin; now sometimes made of faux skin due to the endangered status of the leopard.
Petticoats of linen stiffened by gum or paste; worn in the early 18th century.
Knee-length walking shorts worn by men and women.
Short, puffy skirts that flare out from a narrow waistband and taper at the hem. First popularized in the 1950s.
Baggy pleated trousers tapered at the shins, common to both gaucho and African traditions. Customarily worn by South American cowboys when carrying out agricultural or other outdoor work.
Electric instruments that create an artificial breeze, for cooling.
Footless leg coverings usually worn over tights, trousers, boots, or the like, for warmth or as a fashionable accessory.
Distinctive shawls, usually woolen, produced in Kashmir, India.

Belts decorated with conchos, circular, silver ornaments often further decorated with stamped decoration or semi-precious stones. Originated in the mid-1800s by Navajo (Diné) and Pueblo silversmiths. Contemporary concho belts frequently contain a variety of semi-precious stones and are widely made by Southwest Native American artisans.

Overshoes consisting of a sole, usually set on bands of iron, often ring-shaped, and fastened over footwear by tie straps, worn to elevate the foot for protection from mud, dirt, or wetness. For footwear with a thick sole usually of wood, but sometimes of leather or cork, use "clogs."
A script developed by the early 7th century from the later Roman cursive and first known from charters issued by the Merovingian kings.
Deep, capelike collars, often of lace or silk, worn about the shoulders by women.
Small neckties tied in a bow knot.

Formal neckcloths consisting of long strips of fine cloth wound around the neck and tied in front into a bow or knot. Ends may also tuck inside a coat. Worn especially from the end of the 17th century through the 19th century. For long, narrow lengths of cloth worn around the neck and usually under a collar, tied in a knot, loop, or bow, and often with two ends falling free vertically, use "neckties."

Refers to collars and ruffs that were made of Venetian lace or a similar lace; they were an article of fashionable dress in 18th-century Europe and European colonies. They typically include deep, acute-angled points of lacework. The term refers to the appearance of such collars in portraits by the famous painter, Anthony van Dyck (also spelled "van Dyke").
An Insular script of angular, compressed, minuscule form, with pronounced pointed descenders, often incorporating cursive elements.
A cursive script developed in the 15th century in Italy taking some features from Caroline minuscule.

A serpentinite from the Italian Riviera, between Spezia and Genoa. It is found in two varieties: one is purplish or mottled black and dark red with some green pebbles or veins, the other is green with many white veins. It is difficult to work with but acquires a high polish. It may resemble some varieties of variegated marble from Tennessee in the United States.
Paper adornments (clothing, banners, cut-out strips). Part of the array of sacrificed victims in Postclassic Mexico.

Short, cape-shaped garments that coveri the shoulders and reach only to the elbow, with an open front, which may be fastened by means of a row of small buttons; at the neck it has a very small and purely ornamental hood. The privilege of wearing the mozzetta belongs properly to no one but the pope, cardinals, exempt abbots, abbots general, and the four prelates di fiochetti.
Armbands worn on the upper arm, usually made of gold, but also made from a range of other materials (wood, leather, etc.) in postclassic central Mexico.

Pieces of cloth that are used to envelop the hands of the celebrant when holding the monstrance during the Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament and on other occasions. It takes the place of the humeral veil, which is also used for this purpose.

Tiered sleeve ruffles of lace or other cloth that serve as cuffs; fashionable especially during the late 17th century to the mid 18th century. Also, detachable undersleeves edged with lace or embroidery, fashionable during the middle of the 19th century.
Plastic or fiber liners, often detachable, that fit inside helmets. Some varieties may worn separately, without the helmet.
Embroidered emblems or insignia worn by members of a fraternal organization to signify membership, affiliation, or rank.
Sleeves with very full tops around the shoulder and upper arms and beginning at the elbow, tapering to a tight wrist; fashionable especially during the 19th and early 20th centuries.
Parts and components of chordophones.
Electric signaling devices that produce a buzzing sound.
Organized bodies of singers.
Grand pianos having a harp contour and open strings strung vertically from just below keyboard level up to the curving harplike neck.

Armor pieces protecting the neck and upper part of the chest, consisting either of a single plate or of two main front and back plates hinged together, often with additional lames at the upper edge encircling the neck.

Pieces of mail to protect the genitals, worn attached to the center of the lower edge of a shirt of mail or appended to the fork of a plate armor skirt. They took various forms, including short skirts or breeches, and could incorporate a codpiece.

Pieces of plate armor attached to the breastplate, early in their development only to the lower half but later extending over the whole, doubling its thickness. They served as double pieces for both tournament and field armor, becoming increasingly common as firearms increased in power.
Protective armoured plates inserted into a carrier or bulletproof vest, that can be used stand-alone, or in conjunction with other armor.

Term used in the glass trade for uncased art glass developed by the New England Glass Company in 1883, which varies in shading from light amber to deep ruby, the ruby areas result when part of the glass is reheated and the gold particles in the glass develop a ruby color.
Graphic material for reproduction composed of only black and white with no intermediate tones.

Glass of a deep red color that is produced by a colloidal gold solution prepared by dissolving gold in aqua regia, sometimes including some tin or silver salts. Gold ruby glass was made by the ancient Egyptians and Romans; the ancient technique was lost until rediscovered in 17th-century Germany. Gold was also thought to be anti-toxic and to protect from poison anyone who drank from it.
Sets of armor generally consisting of a full field armor with double pieces; from this could be formed a half armor or a three-quarter armor for warfare, or an armor for tournament combat on foot.
Materials remaining after a part is taken, separated, or designated; or after the completion of a process or reaction.
Class of protective proteins, naturally present in the body or produced by the immune system, which target harmful foreign substances, called antigens, in order to remove them from the body.
Animal material, such as shell and bone, that is made out of both inorganic and organic material.
Coins that have two or more impressions of the same design on either the obverse or reverse, generally caused by movement of the coins in the die between successive hammer blows.
Molds, usually of tin or pewter, for forming candies.
Describes musical instruments pitched highest, or, if there are piccolo versions, second highest in their families. With regard to human voices, describes the highest-pitched voice.
Figured flasks bearing purely decorative designs such as scrolls, cornucopia and sunbursts.

Bottles covered with wicker, wood, or other protective material, of a 1- to 20-gallon capacity and intended to contain corrosive liquids such as acids, or distilled water. For similar large bottles covered with wicker and intended for noncorrosive liquids, use "demijohns."
Small bottles used for holding bitters and having a metal dropper. Also, bottles of varying form used for holding patent medicine or other medical products.
Drums made of earhtenware pots, having a membrane tied across the mouth.
Promotional stickers on correspondence, popular especially in the early 20th century.
Groups or collections of bells that are used together.
The calcium-binding protein in bones.
Triangular wooden trays with either a corrugated pin or wooden arm with a metal blade used to work butter.

Small knives with a wide but dull blade and often with a rounded tip used to cut or serve butter from a butter dish. For similar knives used as a place piece by an individual diner, use "butter spreaders."
Racks designed to hold a bottle, typically at an angle, and placed on a table for serving.

Forks smaller than a dinner fork intended primarily for eating desserts; generally having a short handle and three or four, but sometimes two, tines. May be accompanied by a dessert spoon; sometimes a part of a dessert service.

Knives smaller than a dinner knife intended for eating desserts; generally having a shorter handle and may have a curved and pointed blade; sometimes a part of a dessert service. Use "fruit knives" for knives with a sharp, sometimes serrated blade and often an ornamental handle used to pare and cut fruit at the table.
Small spoons with a circular bowl used to consume bouillon and other clear soups. For larger spoons with a circular or oval bowl and used to consume soup use "soup spoons."

Spoons designed for toddlers to feed themselves. The traditional design comprises a short-handled spoon with a well-balanced bowl that is broad and blunt. Another common design incorporates a curved or curled handle. For spoons designed for adults to feed babies, use "pap spoons" or "feeding spoons."
Term applied to a wide variety of special-purpose utensils designed to serve cheese.
Juicers with a rigid and pointed cone upon which a fruit half is pressed to extract juice.
Utensils of wood or metal used for pounding and thus tenderizing meat often in the form of a wooden mallet, and sometimes with large flat toothed or otherwise textured heads.
Tools used for beating, stirring, or whipping. Tools used to beat or mix food.
Specially designed curved or cylindrical knives or other circular multi-bladed devices for removing the core of a fruit or vegetable.

Tabernacles in Christian churches having multiple compartments or niches, usually two or three, each of which can be revealed or brought forward using a rotating device. The compartments typically could hold a monstrance, a ciborium, and a crucifix; the niches could be highly decorated. Rotating tabernacles were considered mechanical marvels, and were relatively rare, most common in 18th-century northern European Roman Catholic churches.
Printed matter prepared to solicit trade or contributions and sent directly through the mail to individuals.

Method of divination in which the diviner creates a pattern to interpret rather than looking for omens in nature or other existing phenomena or things. Examples of interpretive divination include casting lots and reading tea leaves.

Electrical kitchen appliances intended to whip, chop, or froth food products. These are are designed so that they may be held in the hand and immersed directly into a pan or bowl. The chopping blade is mounted at the end of a shaft.
Devices intended primarily for mixing cake batter; used especially with reference to manually operated mixers with hand-cranked gears attached across the top of a straight-sided container.
Oval Japanese gold coins of various values issued from the 16th to the 19th century.
Several varieties of ancient Chinese cast bronze coins shaped roughly like spades and issued possibly as early as the 9th century BCE until the 3rd century CE.

A script of great clarity, used in both books and documents, that combined characteristics of cursive and half-uncial; developed in Carolingian centers in the late 8th century and then predominant throughout Europe until the 13th century.
An angular Arabic script; it is a formal type of Arabic calligraphy used decoratively on buildings, textiles, pottery and other things.
Self-propelled projectiles carrying a warhead containing biological or chemical agents, explosive or incendiary materials, or inert materials intended to inflict damage.
Self-propelled explosive devices that are launched from aircraft to hit targets that are on ground level.
Culinary tools used to impress designs on butter.
Attachments for a food processor or electric mixer, for kneading dough.
Two-edged, scoop-like tools with a long handle, typically made of silver or nickel, inserted into a tub of butter in order to take a sample for tasting or examination.

Fine cracks or fissures in the surface of hardened or dried material, such as varnish, concrete, plaster, paint, or ceramic glazes; sometimes appearing opaque; usually not exposing the underlying surface.
Foot-activated percussion instruments described by the ancient Greeks. The instruments had metal plates that would have made a noise like a modern tap shoe, used in order to create a rhythm.

Idiophones composed of two clapperless hollow cylinders, usually of metal but occasionally of wood and of differing pitch, connected at their vertices by a handle. They are sounded by being struck on the exterior with a stick, and are usually used in a ceremonial context.

European lip-vibrated aerophones of conical bore, consisting of a long wooden or ivory tube, straight or gently curved, with fingerholes, and made in three main sizes: treble, small treble, and tenor.
Aerophones of conical bore with three, sometimes four valves, of nine foot range and pitched in B flat, popular as brass band instruments. Similar to but smaller than euphoniums.

Welsh harps, long recognized as the main national instrument. Occurring in a variety of shapes and dimensions throughout their history, they were initially single-strung, until the triple-strung form was adopted around 1700 and continues to the present.

Shallow decorative vessels in a variety of materials that often have ruffled or wavy edges, and usually set in a purpose-made stand, sometimes having a handle resembling a basket. These have evolved from the more ephemeral objects used at weddings to hold flowers or the bridal bouquet.
Members of common society having civic rights, includng a burgess, citizen, or any other below below the rank of a peer.
People who own the premises they live in.
Bevor components constituting the upper portion, covering the face from eye level to the chin where it overlapped the lower bevor; they often had small slots and holes for ventilation.
The gears and related works that operate the striking mechanism of clocks or watches.
Refers to the short vertical arrangement of draped fabric, with a tapered lower hem falling in a broken diagonal, often used as the center ornament of a festoon curtain.
Blinds having overlapping horizontal slats that may be opened or closed, especially ones in which the slats may be raised and drawn together above the opening by pulling a cord.
Wallpapers made to be hung as window shades.

Popular term for curtains raised or lowered by cords and rings, made in several variations and distinguished mainly by their bottom hem which, when the curtain is raised, billows in a series of graceful puffs suggesting balloons.
Small percussive weapons typically consisting of a leather-covered piece of lead or other heavy material with a short flexible handle such as a strap or springy shaft.

Air guns having a pair of flat bellows in the butt which are squeezed together by a spring or springs when the trigger is pressed, producing a strong blast of air to propel the projectile. They were popular in southern Germany and Austria in the 18th and early 19th centuries.
Very heavy pistols intended for use by big game hunters when attacked by wounded animals, and carried on a saddle or howdah.
Wheel lock, flintlock, or snaphance pistols designed to be carried in holsters on saddles.
Stage curtains that are lowered instead of drawn.
Curtains that pull straight up by means of rings and cords attached to the back.
Curtains that reach the window sill.

Weapons consisting of a container fitted with a priming charge and a bursting charge, and filled with a destructive agent such as high explosives, gas, or incendiary chemicals, propelled from firearms or thrown by hand.
Bombs fired by ships or aircraft at underwater targets such as submarines, installations, and the underwater part of unarmored hulls, detonated by water pressure, on impact, or magnetically.
Explosive devices lacking propulsion of their own that are intended to be launched from an airborne vehicle to hit targets that are at ground level.
Grenades designed specifically for use against tanks or other armored vehicles.
Crudely printed and hand-colored papers made by dominotiers and used as wallpapers, as endpapers in books, or to line boxes.
Mines placed on or just below the surface of the ground, designed to be detonated on command by electrical impulse or by the weight of vehicles or personnel passing over them.
Wallpapers with a washable surface, particularly such paper made in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Wallpapers used to cover the main portions of walls between borders.
Interior wall decorations created from specially tooled, varnished, and colored panels of gilt leather.
Shot for cannons, consisting of two spheres, hemispheres, or cylinders connected by a bar of iron, used primarily to destroy masts or rigging in naval combat.
Small pellets 0.175 or 0.18 inch in diameter, used in shotgun cartridges or for use in BB guns.
Designates Roman coins of the 3rd century CE distinguished by a radiate crown on the depiction of the emperor; originally of silver and probably a double denarius, later debased.
Early Roman copper coins.
Artillery shells designed to penetrate hard targets such as armored vehicles and warships.

Cartridges lacking the conventional metal case; instead the propellant is mixed with a binder, thus becoming a hard block which is shaped as required, with the bullet recessed into the forward end and a combustible cap fitted into the base.
Curtains on or around a bed, that can be opened or closed for privacy, control of light and drafts, or protection against dust.
Curtains at the foot of a bed that could be drawn either in two directions, to cover the lower half of the sides and meet in the center of the end, or to cover the lower half of the sides only.
Wall coverings consisting of panels of wood or other material joined in a continuous surface.
The outer of two sets of bed valances, which conceals curtain hardware to the exterior of the bed; often more richly decorated and perhaps a little longer than the inner valances.
Coverings, either decorative or protective for arm supports on chairs.
Sleeves of textile or other material such as plastic, into which upholstered cushions are inserted for protection from soil or wear.
Tubular pieces of plate armor shaped to fit the lower arm, constituting part of the vambrace.
Any of various, usually copper or aluminum, coins issued since the late 18th century by several French-speaking countries and valued at one-hundredth part of their monetary unit.
Designates various Spanish and Spanish-American gold coins issued between the 15th and the 19th centuries.
African bearing swords with a looped handle and very thin, broad blade swelling to a large oval shape at the end, carried by Benín chiefs at the royal court.
Refers to the upper sheet for a bed, often with a decorative top border, which may be turned down.
Curved sword guards, consisting of a metal bar extending from the cross guard toward the pommel, designed to give some protection to the knuckles.
Cloth or plastic coverings used to protect furniture and equipment, as during a period of nonuse.

Consecrated, square white linen or hemp cloths upon which the chalice and paten are placed when the Eucharist is celebrated. The cloths were originally large enough to cover the surface of the altar, but since the 12th century, corporals have become smaller, only large enough to contain the chalice and host. According to liturgical rules, the cloth may be edged with fine lace, and a cross may be embroidered at the front edge, but it is not permitted to have any embroidery in its center in order to maintain an even surface to support the chalice.
Textile coverings sized according to the tray and worked in any technique, so long as they are washable.
Fasteners in the form of a loop, rather than a strip, that act as a tieback for curtains. These can be chained together to create extra length.
Component pieces of quilt blocks, either pieced or appliquéd.

Boards or cloth panels used in counting houses, which were offices attached to a shop or residence of a merchant, having a checker pattern for the purpose of counting money or tokens representing accounts. The counter board was portable, placed upon a table or chest when used.
Mats that fit under pieces of furniture that protect the surface that they are resting on.
Bed coverings of cotton, linen, or the like, commonly used in pairs so that one is immediately above and the other immediately below the sleeper.
Small tablecloths for use on tea tables, especially during a meal.
Pieced quilts composed of blocks divided into two equal or nonequal parts by a seam which may be horizontal, vertical, or diagonal.

Refers to a style of tapestry design that developed in the Gobelins manufactory and flourished in 18th-century France. It is characterized by a relatively small, framed picture area containing figures or other scene, with the scene surrounded by rich borders composed of motifs such as flowers, garlands, decorative ropes, and other ornament.
Rug components which consist of intertwined parts of one or more flexible bodies (such as ropes, cords, or strips), which form lumps or knobs.
Whistles or other simple instruments used to imitate the sound of a particular animal, such as a bird or a deer; often designed for hunters or bird watchers to attract animals.
Utensils shaped like a deep spoon used for picking up a quantity of a pellet-like foods such as nuts, etc.
Small ladles intended primarily for serving gravy; generally larger than cream or sauce ladles and sometimes made as part of a flatware service.
Guages to measure solid precipitation composed of white or translucent ice crystals.
Generally, the overall configuration of the numbering in the book. The ordering of pages of a book, microimages on a microfilm, etc., by placing placing of consecutive numbers, one on each page.
Boxes usually of bronze, brass, or wood, often decorated with silver, gold, or jewels, and used for the storage of valuable books and manuscripts.
Instruments for detecting and measuring thermal radiation, especially at wavelengths longer than those of visible radiation, such as in the infrared or microwave regions.
Instruments used to measure the speed of ships.
Instruments used to measure the flow rate, discharge rate, or pressure of liquids, gases, or vapors in a pipe or other contained vessel.
Electrical devices in the form of a small hot plate, used to warm cups of liquid, and designed to be portable for travel.
Kitchen tools consisting of a cone ending in a spout, used to pour liquids or small grains into containers.
The arrangement of type or image pages so that they will be in proper sequence when the sheet is printed and folded.
The composition of type in which characters are assembled and adjusted by hand, without machine assistance.  Some photographically produced display type can be composed by hand.

Folded books developed in China and Japan, in which individual folded sheets are gathered into a text block with the folds at the back. Adhesive is applied between the sheets along the outside of the folds to attach adjacent sheets to each other; the cover is adhered to the first and last leaves but not to the spine. When the book is opened, each pair of adhered pages stands out at an angle like the wings of a butterfly, with two pages of text alternating with two blank pages.

Machines designed to cook and dispense popcorn, consisting of a kettle that applies heat to popcorn kernels, usually via steam or heated oil, and some form of receptacle for containing and dispensing the popped kernels. Early popcorn machines in the United States were on horse-drawn carts and designed for street vending.
Headings of subsections in a work, such as an outline, Web site, or book, newspaper, article, or other written text.

Literary works that employ allegory to express complex abstract ideas, for example works that employ symbolic, fictional figures and actions to express truths or generalizations about human conduct or experience. May be extended to refer to visual works or other creative works that have allegories as subject matter.

Objects signifying an honor bestowed upon an individual; usually worn on the person. For decorative forms that are an integral part of a building or object but not essential to its structure, also for decorative objects attached to or worn by humans and animals, use "ornaments."
Allegorical plays offering discourses in praise of morality between actors representing characters such as Charity, Faith, or Death.
Mechanical devices designed specifically for removing seeds from raisins or grapes.
Culinary appliances with electrically heated elements for browning bread and similar food.
Strainers that hold back solid materials such as fruit or ice from the liquid, typically used after a drink has been stirred or shaken.
Sieves having a mesh woven of hair.
Wide, tray-shaped vessels made of woven fibers. The fibers are woven with gaps to allow small objects to fall through the basket.
Tools with numerous small teeth used for grating cheese.
Rotary beaters operated by hand for aerating eggs or liquids such as cream.
Any of various culinary devices used for reducing to powder or meal such things as grain, coffee, bones, dried beans and peas, or whole spices.
Upper cylindrical or oblong hand-held stones used when grinding maize, or other food, dyes, and materials on metates, or grinding stones.
Small mechanical devices for grinding coffee beans.
Culinary machines used to cut up small bones or vegetable matter, used in the preparation of food for poulty and other livestock.
Tools with t-shaped handles mounted on a screwing device on a support used to pull bungs from barrels.
Small spits used to roasting birds.
Lavishly decorated standing cups, generally made in silver or gold, with a bowl made of nautilus shell.
Term generally applied to a variety of drinking glasses designed to challenge the skill of the drinker to carefully manipulate the vessel and drink without spilling the contents.
Baroque traversos are the forerunners of modern transverse flutes. They were commonly made of wood, and have simpler system of valves.
Components that result when sheets, as of paper, parchment, or other material, are folded to form leaves and pages, which then are usually gathered or bound together.
Parts or components of letterforms.
Very small, deep pots or pans made of metal, intended to warm brandy over a flame or heater. The vessels sometimes have a spout; often having a long handle,.
Scripts used for titles or other headings, especially when different from that used for the body of the text.
The largest rock fragment recognized by sedimentologists, a boulder is a detached rock mass larger than a cobble, having a diameter greater than 256 mm (10 in.).
Sensitive radiometers used to measure weak radiant energy and generally consisting of a thermopile supported on and connected directly to the moving coil of a galvanometer.
Rain gauges that automatically record the amount of precipitation collected as a function of time.
Solid bullets of spherical or conical shape, containing no propellant or explosive, fired from small arms. For the spherical projectiles made to be fired from cannons, use "cannonballs."

Type of expanding bullet developed at the western Bengal town of Dum Dum, derived from a rifle cartridge. The metal envelope encasing the bullet is removed at the tip, exposing the interior lead which then expands upon impact.

Devices that initiate the firing of muzzle-loading cannons. Comprised of a copper tube filled with powder attached to the vent of the cannon with its tip in the powder charge. On this tube a short tube containing a friction composition. Lying in the composition was the roughened end of a wire slider, The other end of the slider was twisted into a loop for hooking to the gunner's lanyard. Pulling on the lanyard caused the slider to ignite the composition.

Ancient forms of writing originating from Asia, dating to the Shang dynasty (ca. 1600-1046 BCE). Chinese calligraphy evolved from pictographs into the many characters that are written today. Early characters or pictographs have been discovered inscribed into pottery or bone dating back over 4000 years ago. There are five main types of Chinese calligraphy: seal script (zhuan-shu); official script know as clerical script (li-shu); block script called regular script or (kai-shu); semi-cursive script called running script (xing-shu); and cursive script known as grass script or (cao-shu).
Pendulum-driven floor clocks having cases about 6 feet high or larger, developed in England in the mid-17th century.
Short dessert glasses with a rudimentary stem or no stem intended for jellies or ices; often with a single or double handle.
Gemstone that is considered more valuable than other types, especially diamond, sapphire, emerald, ruby, and sometimes pearl.
Largest and lowest-pitched instruments of the violin family, having four, or more rarely, five strings, and varying considerably in size and shape.
Method of adhesive binding used in the mid-19th century employing a rubber solution. The method was discontinued after some years because it was discovered that rubber turns brittle with age.
In the context of libraries and publishing, refers to imprints indicating that the work was printed in Europe rather than in the United States or elsewhere.

In multispectral imaging, images simultaneously obtained of an object at different wavelengths are made into a composite that displays the discrete spectral bands as colors. The resulting color patterns can be used to identify surface features.

Composite pieces consisting of an arrangement of sweetmeat glasses or jelly glasses on a glass salver with a tall glass in the center. They were often made in three graduated tiers. For composite pieces consisting of a tall glass stand with small basketlike dishes suspended from branching arms, use "sweetmeat stands."

Liturgical chants used originally in Church of England services for singing unmetrical texts such as psalms and canticles, and characterized by a short repeating melody for each verse, with the first note extended to accommodate a varying number of syllables.
Daily records of the progress of a ship at sea, with notes on the weather and important incidents of the voyage.
Novels written by using the device of a series of letters, diary entries, newspaper clippings, or other documents.
Square arrays of integers arranged such that the sum of the integers in all rows, columns, and major diagonals add up to the same number; known for over 4000 years.

Religious books typically containing collections of prayers, psalms, readings, and rites.The form first appeared in the 11th century Christian monastic communities and among clerics, although the texts of the longer Divine Office had been established in the Roman rite by the 7th century and in Carolingian Europe by the 10th century. Although it was a complex book, it was briefer than the full Divine Office, thus known as a "breviary." The "book of hours" was developed by the 13th century as an even less complex book of prayers for the lay community. Works similar to the Christian breviary were adapted from primary texts of other faiths, including the Koran and Hindu works; these works are also referred to as breviaries. Breviaries may contain elaborate illumination.

Clubs, including the premises and grounds, that are located in or near the countryside rather than in an urban environment, and that are typically characterized by having a restricted membership and facilities for recreation and social intercourse.
Closures designed to plug an opening.
Closures which are secured by friction and are usually low and flat-topped.
Russian cups for vodka, often with a horizontal handle flush with the rim.
Drinking vessels used primarily in wedding ceremonies; may contain liquid, plant matter, or foodstuffs based on the protocol being observed.
Stone or ceramic jars in which the ancient Egyptians preserved the viscera of a deceased person usually for burial with the mummy.
Airtight containers intended to keep cigars fresh before smoking. These come in a variety of forms from cylinders for individual cigars to small cases for multiples.
Rigid sheaths made of wood, metal, or leather, used to enclose and carry edged weapons or tools, or hand weapons such as carbines and rifles.

Shallow bowls from 4 to 6 inches in diameter, with one flat handle usually flush with the rim, employed by barber-surgeons of the 17th and 18th centuries in bleeding a patient. In England the term is also sometimes applied to what in America is known as porringers.
Rectangular baskets with one side woven higher than the other and from which they were hung on a loom post to hold unused bobbins for the loom.
Containers, usually of pottery or porcelain, with a perforated cover in which cut flowers, boughs, or branches are held or displayed.
Instruments for measuring circular arcs or for recording the revolutions of a wheel and thus measuring the distance traversed.
Bottles in which ink is sold. For small vessels usually sold empty and intended for holding ink into which a pen can be dipped, use "inkwells."
Openwork, splint baskets used for making cheese.
Relatively large, deep, globular-shaped baskets, tightly twined and intended primarily for cooking food.
Meal trays of a size and designed to fit across the lap of a person sitting in bed; often fitted with legs or supports at each end.
Baskets for preserving dates or grapes or carrying crops.
Bottles for serving wine or water at the table.

Distinctive censers, suspended by chains, used for rituals and liturgies. A thurible usually comprises a metal receptacle, often with a pierced cover, containing combustible material to burn gums used as incense; swung by hand or hung on a stand.
Kantharoi with bowls in the form of back-to-back, or janiform, faces.

The standard hydria form used for black-figure vases. This substantial vessel is distinguished by a large round mouth, offset neck, broad flattish shoulder, and wide body. This shape continued in red-figure but was less common.

Neck amphorae with splaying, conical necks, high bodies, and two flat strap handles extending from the shoulders and joined into the lip. They are known mostly in black-figure. The shape was adapted by the potter Nikosthenes from a native Etruscan shape. It is thought that nikosthenic amphorae were produced especially for the Etruscan market.
A type of continuous curve amphorae characterized by a straight or slightly concave lip, round handles, and an echinus foot.
Kraters so named for their resemblance to a calyx flower. The form is said to have been developed by Exekias in black-figure; it is, however, more characteristically a red-figure shape.
Refers to a special type of oinochoe based on a narrow-beaked and round-bodied shape indigenous to Cyprus.

Refers to a rare vessel type of hybrid form. It combined the functions of a krater and a psykter, either by implanting a psykter inside the bowl, or by making the krater's body double-walled which, when the compartment between the two walls was filled with cold water, chilled the wine.

A typical form of phiale featuring a hollow knob in the middle- an omphalos- projecting upward into the bowl. The vessel was held with the middle finger tucked into the underside of the omphalos and the thumb hooked over the rim.
Ancient Greek storage vessels for wine, water, or oil, similar to amphorae but with a pointed bottom and characterized by two side handles.
A type of pyxis with a flat lid and knob and a concave-sided body. It is either footless or has a ringlike foot that is sometimes divided into three or four sections.
Urinals designed to accommodate the male anatomy.
A type of loutrophoros featuring three handles, two horizontal ones on the sides and a vertical one at the back.
Hornpipes of southern Scotland, with a tube of wood or bone, elongated wood mouthpiece, a bell of natural animal horn, and single reed.
Large, wide-mouthed, unstructured bags intended for carrying swimwear and beach gear.
Containers for holding batter, typically made of earthenware and designed to be set near a fire for rising. For containers designed to hold batter for mixing, use "batter bowls."
Small glass vessels intended for salt or sweetmeats, usually with double ogee or cup-shaped bowls.
Rectangular basins used to contain liquids used for libations at religious ceremonies. Often made of stone.
Pans intended primarily for baking.
In magnetometry, devices with multiple sensors that measure the gradient of magnetic fields.
Flasklike vessels used to carry water or other liquids as by hikers or soldiers; typically made of metal and carried in a cloth jacket.
Mass spectroscopes that identify and record the kinds and intensities of particles in a given substance.
Instruments that automatically record graphically atmospheric pressure, temperature, and humidity.
Musical clocks in which, instead of bells or gongs, sound is produced by organlike pipes blown usually by bellows.
Stamps, usually self-inking, which are used to notoarize documents and provide a notary's credentials for authentication.

The intaglio process in which the design is incised into a printing plate, usually a flat copper plate, with the aid of a graver or burin that is held in the palm of the hand and pushed against the copper to cut lines comprising V-shaped grooves. The plate is then inked up, wiped so that ink is retained in the grooves and then forced out under the pressure of the printing process to create lines on the paper. The technique was first developed in the early 15th century in Germany, probably by goldsmiths who wished to keep records of the designs they had engraved on their wares. The process is distinct from "wood engraving (process)," which is a process for relief printing; "wood cut (process)" refers to engraving wood blocks for printing. Historically, "engraving" has sometimes been used incorrectly to refer to all printmaking processes, particulalry any process employing printing plates. For the single step of incising an inscription or design into any surface, not only a printing plate, see "engraving (incising)."

A printing process that consists of painting an image onto a plate and then laying a support on top to transfer the image. Only one impression can be made, although if enough of the original paint remains on the plate, subsequent prints can be made by reapplication. These prints are called ghosts or cognates, and no two prints will be alike.
A method of relief printing in which chemicals are used to etch a metal plate on which a drawing has been made, or a similar process by which photographs are made.
Surface preparation techniques that involve biting, or corroding materials by the action of acid.
Thermometers in which the heat-sensitive element is located at a distance from the temperature-indicating element.
Small thermometers used to measure accurately the temperature of the human body.

Tiered cylindrical containers consisting of usually two to four separate containers of the same shape and size, which are stacked one on top of the other within a frame that has a handle. Tiffin carriers are used for carrying cooked food, with different dishes placed in the separate containers. Traditionally, these stacked containers are held together by the carrier handle which frame is fitted through the small side handles of each container and fastened with a catchment at the top. Presently, there are various designs of tiffin carriers. Tiffin carriers are usually made from stainless steel or enamel. Tiffin carriers, as they are called in Singapore and Malaysia, are used in other parts of Asia and have their own local names.
Small covered tureens, sometimes with a conforming stand, for serving sauce.
Box-like devices into which bottles are placed and then steamed in order to sterilize them for safe use.
Thick wooden planks, sometimes with a short one-legged support, on which cakes are baked before a fire.
Utensils consisting of a shallow bowl with a handle used for preparing, cooking, serving, or eating food.
Tools for peeling citrus fruit.
Machines used to separate the hulls from peas.
Small implements to grip pieces of cheese, comprising discs, often decorative and silver, with spikes on the bottom.

Ring-shaped extrusions or objects that are positioned below the opening of a bottle or other vessel from which a liquid is poured, on a candlestick or other object, with the purpose of impeding or stopping drips of the liquid from running down the body of the vessel. For drip catchers on candlesticks, use "bobeches."
Napkins used in bread baskets to keep bread or rolls warm.
Photometers which measure the intensity of visible light falling upon surfaces or reflected by surfaces.
Survey instruments used in mining and construction that measure and record the deviation from the vertical of, for example, boreholes or well shafts.
Instruments for measuring magnetic flux.
Radiation counters that use Geiger-Müller tubes in the appropriate circuitry to detect and measure ionizing particles.
Instruments for measuring color perception.

Instruments that measure optical density of materials or objects by measuring the intensity of transmitted or reflected light; used, for example, in photography to measure the opacity of images or to determine film speed.
Covers, as of pamphlets, of the same paper as the inside leaves.
Clocks that display astronomical phenomena, such as the phases of the moon, or clocks that show sidereal time.

Small, stoppered vessels for wine and water used in the celebration of the Eucharist. According to the regulations for the Roman Catholic service, two are always employed and it is recommended that they should be made of glass, although precious materials such as silver or gold may be employed if they are clearly marked to indicate which is water and which is wine.
Parts or components of breastplates.
Instruments for measuring and recording the acuity of hearing.
A type of flute glass intended for drinking ratafia, a liqueur flavored with almonds and fruit kernels; of 1- to 1 1/2-ounce capacity.
Containers used in the context of a pharmacy, or the dispensing of compounds and drugs.
Container covers which are circular and have a dome-shaped profile.
Type of spout which has a lip rather than a cut off end.
Period term referring to both bedcovers and bed hangings.
Large pieces of woven fabric that are padded or quilted, and that are used to protect objects from damage while they are being transported.
Inexpensive, machine-woven blankets made by the Pendleton Woolen Mills in Oregon for trade with the Indians, designed especially to suit Native North American tastes.
Finely made, intricately patterned, richly colored sarapes in tapestry weave, made in northern Mexico.
Special weights, often of decorative shape, used with scales for weighing gold or gold dust, particularly as used where gold is currency.

Keyboards, usually of organs but also found on carillons, harpsichords, clavichords, and pianos, played by the feet and connected either to their own pipes, bells, or strings, or to those of the manual keyboards.

Trays or platters, usually of circular or octagonal shape and made of various materials: wood panel upon which a scene or symbolism had been painted, ceramics having similar scenes or family crests, or metal. The trays were important symbolic gifts made on the occasion of a successful birth in late medieval and Early Modern Europe, particularly in Italy. Food, clothing, or other gifts were often presented stacked upon the tray.
Containers used to collect voting ballots, made of any material.
Boxes or chests in which a corpse is enclosed for burial.
Artificial ponds or tanks, often with glass sides, in which aquatic plants and animals are kept alive for purposes of observation and study.
Term generally applied to a variety of oval or rectangular open baskets with a single handle, intended primarily for taking products to the market or purchases home.
Small pails, generally made of metal, for holding or carrying coal, typically having a bail handle and one scooplike lip.

Relatively small ancient Greek vessels with a globular body, a short neck, a flat disk-shaped mouth with a small orifice, and a handle (or sometimes two) extending from the shoulder to the rim; used for holding oils, perfumes, and ointments. They are usually made of terracotta. Uses of the aryballoi included in funeral rituals and by athletes who wore them on their wrists, suspended by thongs or strings.
Bags or containers used to carry portable bedding and other items when traveling, including  mattresses, blankets, shoes, etc.
Massive upright ceramic jars historically used for burial in parts of southeastern Asia such as the Yeongsan River area, South Korea.
Very large folders that go inside the drawers in flat file cabinets, where large items, usually on paper, can be stored in a horizontal position.
Escapements in which there is no recoil from the shock of contact among the locking parts; introduced in the early 18th century and best suited for expensive or precise timekeepers.
Soft, loosely woven, weft-banded Navajo shoulder blankets for everyday, all-purpose use.
The people who oversee and control all aspects of the production of motion pictures. With commercial films, the producer is ultimately responsible for the motion picture's success or failure.
Blankets with a number of short bars called points woven in the corner to indicate size and weight.
Textile covers intended to be draped or fastened to headboards or the beadsted at the head of the bed.
Bedspreads made of plain textile squares folded to frame smaller squares of colored or printed textile, the total effect being somewhat like stained glass windows.
Comforters filled with the down of the eider duck.
Handloomed coverlets with weft loop weave patterning, often in colored wools, in the French-Canadian tradition.
Quilts composed of three-dimensional puffs, small silk squares slightly gathered and stuffed with batting, pieced together.
Coverlets of two layers of cloth filled with padding such as down or batting held in place by ties or stitched designs, made in an appropriate size for a child's crib.
Quilts made as tokens of friendship, often for someone leaving the community. Often with signatures, dates, and locations embroidered or inked on.
Quilts illustrating Bible stories or including scriptural quotations, adages, maxims, or proverbs conveying religious or moral precepts.
Quilts made to commemorate a hundredth anniversary.
Quilts made for the Red Cross, often in times of war, either as fundraisers or as warm coverings for soldiers or others, often with the Red Cross design.

Motuh organs of Laos and Thailand, consisting of a set of bamboo pipes grouped in two rows and graduated from longest to shortest, held together by a windchest they pierce through. The reeds of copper or silver are mounted in the pipe walls within the windchest, and the fingerholes are cut in the pipes within fingers' reach above the windchest.
Vessels, usually with a handle and a stopper, used to serve condiments; generally of glass and often made in sets of two or more.

Dishes for holding and serving butter at the table. Use "butter chips" for small dishes used by an individual diner to hold a pat or small serving of butter. Use "butter coolers" for vessels designed to serve chilled butter at the table.

Small bottles or flasks with one or two handles, disk-like or globular in form. In ancient Egypt and Rome, used for perfumes, ointments, or serving drinks. In churches, shrines, coronations, etc. for holding water or other liquids.

Small single-headed drums, Afro-Cuban in origin, with conical or cylindrical hardwood shells; they generally occur in pairs joined together horizontally, one being larger in diameter than the other. Existing in tunable and nontunable versions, they are played with the bare hands.
Double-headed drums of Cuba.
Globular vessel flutes made of clay, porcelain, wood, or plastic in oblong form with whistle head, eight fingerholes, and two thumbholes.
Shallow, circular dessert dishes, usually made of silver, with a fluted, pierced, or scalloped border.
Instruments that measure the amount of silver salt in a solution by means of finding the specific gravity or by photoelectrics.
Hygrometers that determine humidity by reading two thermometers, one with a wet bulb and the other with a dry bulb.
Instruments for measuring atmospheric pressure, and thus sometimes altitude, by its effect on the boiling point of liquids.

Concussion vessels of great antiquity, occurring in many sizes and grades of sound throughout their history. Traditionally they have consisted of a pair of round metal plates, usually slightly convex to create a resonant hollow, sounded by striking together. In modern orchestral and jazz music, cymbals are often played as percussion instruments, suspended and struck with drumsticks or wire brushes.
Sets of percussion plaques made of sonorous stone, taking the form of either horizontally arranged bars, or vertically suspended plaques.
Tubes of wood or bamboo, often hollow, which are stamped rhythmically against the ground or another object.

Long poles surmounted by a crescent and an ornament shaped like a Chinese hat from which bells and jingles and, usually, two horsehair tails are suspended, adopted by European military bands from the Turks.
Rattles in which objects slide up and down.
Metallophones of Java and Bali, consisting of thin bronze bars suspended by horizontal cords over individual tube resonators. They are important instruments in the Javanese and Balinese gamelan.
English coins valued at one half of a penny, introduced in silver in the 9th century and later issued in bronze or copper.
Flutes blown directly against the sharp rim at the upper open end of the tube.
Silver or cupronickel British coins valued at two shillings sixpence; phased out of use after 1971.
The earth's magnetic field and associated phenomena.
Boat- or trough-shaped clapperless iron bells of the Ewe of Ghana, played by being held in the palm of the hand and the lip struck with a metal rod.
Orchestral bells resembling the clapper bells hung around the necks of cows and other herd animals, but without a clapper, sounded by being struck with a drumstick.
Standing cups often having a trefoil foot, baluster-shaped stem, and an embossed cup; so named from their resemblance to the columbine flower.
Chinese drums generally having the shape of a barrel, with a drumhead on either end, tacked rather than laced to the shell; only one drumhead is struck, by two beaters.
Appliqué flags of the asafo companies of the Fante people of Ghana; they typically measure about four feet by six feet and carry mirror-image designs.
Banners that are designed for and used in processions and hung in funerary settings; known in various cultures. For coverings and curtains used in funerary settings, prefer "mourning cloths."

Small triangular flags in paper or fabric, illustrated with a saint, the church or chapel where the saint is venerated, and occasionally scenes from the life of the saint, or events occurring at the church or chapel. These were typically sold as souvenirs of the pilgrimage itself.

Any of a group of pipes or sets of pipes, usually consisting of a single piece of wood with two narrow cylindrical bores each having an idioglot single reed, less often of two pipes inserted into a common stock which holds the reeds. Some terminate in bells or are attached to bags.
Use generally for devices designed to measure or otherwise determine the size, state, or mechanical accuracy of something.
Devices used to measure the changing of place or location of any object, liquid, gas, or other substance.
Devices used to measure electromagnetic radiation.
Instruments designed to measure minute changes in distance between two reference points due to contraction, expansion, or deformation.
Any of several instruments that measure the density or specific gravity of liquids, solids, or gases.
Instruments for measuring and graphically recording variations in fluid pressure, as of the human pulse.
Devices used to measure the degree of heaviness of matter.
Devices that measure electricity by totalizing electrical quantities with time, such as watthour meters.
Instruments designed to measure and record automatically several meteorological elements, such as air pressure, temperature, and humidity.
Instruments for measuring heat quantities, such as the heat of combustion, specific heat, or vital heat in such processes as chemical reactions or changes of state.
Devices that measure the absorption of electromagnetic radiation.
Instruments for measuring the velocity of sound in water.
Instruments designed to measure the speed or force of the wind.
That part of compasses on which the direction markings are placed, usually in the form of thin disks graduated in degrees clockwise from 0 to 360 and sometimes also indicating compass points.

A quartz crystal microbalance is an extremely sensitive sensor which weighs mass per area by measuring change in the freqency of an acoustic resonator. It is composed of a specially cut quartz crystal set between two electrodes that oscillates at its resonance frequency when AC power is applied through the electrodes due to the piezoelectric effect.
Instruments devised to measure angles, especially the angles of crystal faces.
Recording barometers.
Refers to the compensating or counterbalancing weights on scales.
Methods and practices used in typography.

The setting of type characters closer together than would normally or automatically be done; for visual effect, usually to close an unsightly gap. With metal type, the body of the type is cut for a closer fit; in photocomposition, minute increments of backspacing are used.
Calipers whose legs turn outward to be used to measure inside dimensions, usually diameters.
Devices used primarily in reading levels of a liquid in a capillary tube to determine surface tension, or for determining the changes in the liquid level during a chemical reaction.
Clocks that indicate the time by a display of figures rather than by a dial.
Calibrated devices for measuring the flow of liquids in open conduits by observing differences in the heads on opposite sides of a partial obstruction.
Instruments for measuring the total intensity of solar radiation.
Devices that measure and compute the amount of acid in milk which is calculated by pouring alkali of a known strength into a measured sample of milk until the color of the milk changes.
Automatic indicating scales in which the graduations are on a rotatable cylindrical chart.
Weighing devices used in the process of determining components of a material, as in the percentage of pure metal in a specimen of ore, bullion, or alloy.
Radar or ultrasonic instruments using echo location to measure the depth of the sea.

Single-string spike fiddles of the Savanna area of West Africa, consisting of a half-kalabash resonator covered with monitor lizard skin with a hole on one side, a straight or curved wooden neck running through the resonator, a V- or Y-shaped wooden bridge, and a horsehair string.

Timepieces that measure equal periods of time by the motion of sand or other freely flowing, fine-grained substances through a narrow aperture between two triangular or conical glass bulbs arranged mouth to mouth; probably introduced in the early 14th century and used then especially for timekeeping aboard ships.

Certain types of precision time pieces. Originally referred to strongly built precision timekeeping devices especially designed for use on ships; now also used for extremely accurate wrist watches or pocket watches.

Short duct flutes with a cylindrical bore widely flared at the lower end, two fingerholes and one rear thumbhole, introduced by the blind Italian flutist Picco in London in 1856 and copied by London flute makers.
Devices consisting of a small drill or blunt indenter point under pressure and used to measure the hardness of materials, such as metals, rubber, and rock.
Circular cake pans having a hollow cone-shaped centerpiece; used for baking ring-shaped cakes.
Instruments used to determine the amount of albumin or soluble protein in liquids, especially urine.

Refers to the second largest Mormon denomination. Its headquarters are in Independence, Missouri and it had a membership of more than 200,000 people by the late 20th century. The Community of Christ came out of one of the factions that developed after Joseph Smith's death in 1844. A group of Mormons rejecting Brigham Young's leadership instead claimed that Smith's son was the rightful successor; they did not follow Young to Utah. The leaders of the denomination were descendants of the founder up until 1996. This denomination actually rejects the appellation Mormon because of the association with polygamy. Followers feel that polygamy is not in harmony with the original tenets of the church or with the teachings and practices of Smith. Many of its doctrines are similar to those of other Mormon denominations but the church can be described in general terms as more liberal and more ecumenical. For instance, the Community of Christ allows women to be ordained, rejects the practice of 'blood atonement' called for by Young, and allows the general public to attend its services.
Instruments consisting usually of a pair of adjustable pivoted legs and used for measuring, for example, thickness or diameters.
