Devices for measuring the diameter of minute particles or fibers based on a measurement of the diffraction pattern produced by them in monochromatic light.
Instruments used to measure the thickness of a material, as a sheet of paper.
Compasses that track the direction and position in which the stars rise and set on the horizon, providing knowledge needed for wayfinding.
North-seeking navigational devices containing a gyroscope and used as a vehicle's directional reference.

Simple pipes, used as complete and independent sound devices by themselves, in which the sound is produced through vibration of a single, double, or free reed; the pipes themselves may be made from reed, cane, wood, bone, or metal. For the organ pipes sounded by the vibration of a flexible metal reed, use "reed pipes."

Distinctive Spanish glass rose water sprinklers typically characterized by the body of the vessel being ovoid or pear-shaped atop a high spreading foot. The vessel is intended to be filled through the neck. Four slender upright spouts come out of the shoulder. Almorratxes were most commonly found in Catalonia.
Artists' brushes made of squirrel hair or any other fine hair.
Metal spatulas with pointed ends used to apply color in encaustic paintings.
Designates various copper, copper alloy, steel, and copper-plated zinc coins valued at one-hundredth part of a dollar or pound sterling.
United States gold coins issued between 1796 and 1929 and valued at two dollars and fifty cents or one quarter of an eagle.
Style or culture of Texans of Mexican descent. Tejano derives from Coahuiltejano, a name given to the citizens of the Mexican State Coahuila y Tejas, now Texas.
Processed intestine used, for example, for making strings for musical instruments and tennis rackets.
Emergency paper money issued during the first half of the 20th century, especially that issued by Germany and Austria during and shortly after the First World War.
A dusty gray variety of marble from the island of Marmara Adasi, Turkey.
Diagonal lines formed in textiles by the meeting points of successive rows of discontinuous wefts.
Refers to the style and culture of modern Azerbaijan.

Generic term for a type of mouth-resonated instrument consisting of a flexible tongue fixed at one end to a surrounding frame. The free end of the tongue is placed in front of the player's mouth cavity and is plucked with a finger.
Designates stamps that are affixed to mail at post offices when prepayment of postage is insufficient and that indicate the amount owed from the addressee.

Sliding rattles known in the Near East since the 3rd millennium BCE, consisting of a U- or lyre-shaped frame with a handle, fitted with loose-fitting rods or wires which jingle when shaken; small loose discs were often strung on the rods or wires to create additional sound.
Refers to the group of stamps located in one corner of a pane that contains the plate number printed on the margin; may include as few as four stamps arranged two by two.

Written orders drawn on a bank or the Treasury of the United States to pay on demand a specified sum of money to a named person, to his order, or to bearer, out of money on deposit to the credit of the writer; must be endorsed to be transferred.
Interest-bearing certificates of public or private debt, usually offered in series, constituting promises to pay the lender a certain amount of money at a fixed future date.
Unprinted, partially printed, or sketched samples of projected publications to suggest the appearance of the completed work.
Advertising materials for those publishing books or prints.
Badges won on military headgear, often as regiment insignia.
Open harps in which the strings are at one end attached to a resonator and at the other to an onbuilt neck which curves over the resonator.
Harps in which generally the strings are all tuned to the notes of a single key; often an extra string is inserted in each octave for a flat seventh or, less often, a sharp fourth.

Instruments that produce sound by rubbing aluminum rods instead of plucking strings, and which can be played vertically or horizontally. An original version was invented by John Calhoun Deagan and called an “aluminum harp.”
Books or similar documents that recount and depict tournament festivities and events.

Use generally for single- or double-headed frame drums of the Near East, Central Asia, southern Europe, and parts of Africa, South Asia, and Latin America. The various types are round, square, or octagonal in shape, and may have jingles or snares.
Single-reed aerophones with a conical bore, beaked mouthpiece, small metal bell, and 14 keys, sounding somewhat like a soprano saxophone.

Electronic instruments in the form of keyboards that either play a limited number of sounds, often those that mimic acoustic pianos or similar instruments, or that make no sound themselves, but are intended to trigger other devices through control voltage, MIDI, or other means. For electronic instruments that shape or form a great variety of sound wholly from electronic signals, either from analog circuitry or through digital means, and that may or may not have an integral keyboard, use 'synthesizers.'

Pages on the right-hand side, recto of a leaf, at the beginning of a book where the bibliographic information about the work is provided, displaying the book's title and usually the author's name, the publisher, and sometimes the date of publication. Where more than one page giving particulars of the title are present, that giving the fullest information is the title page.
Parts or components of bindings.

Raised ridges across the bound spine of a book indicating the location of the cords beneath the covering material. Distinguished from "cords (binding components)," the twisted strands of fibrous material to which the sections of a book are sewn.

Electroacoustic stringed instruments more or less in the form of guitars, occurring in two types. One has a hollow body which functions somewhat like a resonator; the other has a solid body serving solely as a mounting block for the bridge and electronic apparatus, and to bear the strings. In both types the sound is electronically amplified and its tone modified by electronic controls.

Small pictures, pictograms, or symbols used on computer displays or in graphical user interfaces meant to represent files, objects, applications, actions, or messages. These can be selected and manipulated to access data or perform functions. Icons are represented with a graphical design that indicates meaning to the user and may act as hyperlinks. Icons may change their appearance when events occur, such as files being opened.
Symbols used first in the ancient Roman system of numerical notation.

Sets of stationary hanging bells, normally for outdoor use in an open tower chamber or on a high frame, played manually from a keyboard, automatically by clockwork, or electronically by pneumatic mechanism. More extensive than chimes, their range covers two octaves or more, with all but the lowest notes forming a fully chromatic scale. They are typically played with a keyboard, by which keys mechanically activate levers and wires that connect to metal clappers that strike the inside of the bells. They are often housed in the bell tower of a church or other municipal building.

Genre of pre-20th century poetry, in which letters, words, or lines are arranged on the page to form a shape or image, usually related to the meaning of the words. For works of poetry from the 20th century on, particularly of the concrete poetry movement of the 1950s and 1960s, in which language elements are freely arranged, not necessarily in linear syntax, and meaning is derived from the spatial, pictorial, and typographic characteristics of the work, as well as from the sense of the words, use "concrete poetry."

Typefaces that slant upward to the right rather than being erect, often having cursive features derived from humanistic cursive script. Most often designed to accompany a roman typeface but sometimes independent.
Used up, worn out, or broken things that are not garbage or ash.
Small baskets made of palm fronds.
Containers of various sizes and designs built to gather donations for charity or for religious organizations.
Cylindrical containers, usually wooden, with slightly bulging sides made of staves hooped together, and with flat, parallel ends.
Receptacles made of flexible material used for holding grain.
Large casks for holding liquids, especially wine, ale, or beer.
Small kegs which originally held 18 gallons.
Drinking vessels with usually one elongated spout, but sometimes more, used for feeding children or invalids.
Roman bronze or brass coins worth two asses minted from the early third century BCE until the mid-3rd century CE.
Ancient Greek and Roman silver coins valued at two drachmas.
The upper of two dies between which a coin is struck.
Oversized chalices, bowls, or urns used for collecting ballots by a papal conclave, monastic election, or other religious institutions' election, typically when choosing a leader.
Conventional symbols, usually written or printed, representing alone or in combination simple or complex speech sounds and constituting the units of an alphabet.

Decoration technique in which outlines are drawn on the surface of wares (especially tiles) with a greasy substance colored with manganese, allowing glazes of several colors to be used without intermingling; the grease disappears during firing; found primarily in Iberia.
Words placed at the bottom of a page repeating the first word on the following page; used especially at the very end of a gathering to guide the binder in assembling the gatherings.
Headbands sewn on one core.

Titles that appear at the beginning of a chapter in a book or other publication, usually bearing some relation to the content of the division of the work. Chapters may simply be numbered or given a number and a title.

Duct flutes having a fipple, a block housed within the mouthpiece. The duct, formed by the space between the surface of the fipple and the inner wall of the mouthpiece, directs the player's breath against the sharp edge of a hole in the wall of the flute below the fipple.

Refers to cursive Gothic scripts, developed first in the late 12th century in England and first for documentary use; later used sometimes as book hands and gradually somewhat formalized to become bastarda.
Double reed pipes of Burma, with seven fingerholes and a rear thumbhole.
Cylindrical, double-reed instruments of Armenia and Turkey. They usually have eight finger holes and one thumb hole. They have a warm timbre and are used for lyrical tunes.

Reedpipes consisting of either two pipes joined together or a single piece of wood with two bores, whose air columns are set in vibration by an idioglot single reed; in some cases both pipes have fingerholes, in others only one does, the other serving as a drone; known since ancient Egypt.
In Indian architecture, an auspicious jar.
Trusses having parallel chords, vertical members in compression, and diagonal members (which slant toward the center) in tension.
Hammers or sticks, plain or with heads, used to sound struck instruments such as drums, dulcimers, and percussion idiophones.

Mechanical figures or contrivances constructed to move as if by their own power, generally by intricate hidden mechanisms; known since at least the Hellenistic period, as toys, amusements, and in clocks.

Exaggerated, distorted representations of a subject in art or literature; in art, refers particularly to representations, often portraits, that exaggerate certain features or characteristics to humorous or ludicrous effect.

Stock images used by graphic artists for decoration or illustration; traditionally on paper and clipped out with scissors to be pasted into layouts, more recently, electronic images that can be transferred into a computer application as needed.

Visual works that are usually ultimately based on ancient or traditional practices, and comprise adornment or embellishment applied to the human body. In body art in this sense, generally the body is the support upon which media are applied, either temporarily or permanently, or where the body is permanently altered. Examples include scarification, tattooing, body piercing and painting, and hair styling. For the art form that arose in the 1960s among performance artists and conceptual artists, where the human body is the medium of the artist, use "body art (performance art)."
Refers to works of art, first appearing in the late 1960s, that exploit the possibilities of compressed air, or the natural force of the wind, usually in association with plastic envelopes.
Those strings, among all those on an instrument, on which the melody of a piece of music is played.
General term for artificial plant matter, including flowers, foliage, and fruit.
Treating sewage in order to remove its objectionable constituents and render it less offensive or dangerous.
An instrument consisting of either one short wooden stick partially split in half or two sticks, sometimes hollowed out and bound or linked together at one end by a leather thong or cord.
Negotiable documents other than paper money that are supported by coin reserves and provide evidence of current or long-term debt.

Tokens bearing the name and often location of a business and exchangeable for specific goods or services at particular stores; popular especially in England and the United States since the 17th century.
Lead coins used in ceremonies surrounding the election of the "boy-bishop" during the feast of St. Nicholas in medieval Europe.

Decorated, trapezoidal pieces of copper made by Northwest Coast Native North American tribes. Usually formed into two curved rectangular pieces visually joined by a raised T-shaped border in the middle of the piece; some coppers have thin, rectangular additions on one side. Usually decorated with clan crests by incision or repoussé. Historically were created as markers of status or for giving through potlatch ceremonies.
Lighting from units that direct 40 to 60% of their emitted light upward, and the remainder downward.
An appearance or texture due to the arrangement and especially stratification of constituent particles or fibers.
Currency that does not have the name of the issuing authority in its inscriptions.
General term used to collocate terms for all paper currency of European origin.
Fluid that circulates in the principal vascular system of vertebrate animals.

Clear amber liquid (mammals, aquatic species) or grayish semisolid (birds, reptiles) excretion of metabolic waste from vertebrates. In mammals, urine is formed in the kidneys. It is a collection of water-soluble by-products of protein metabolism (urea, creatinine, uric acid, ammonia, etc.) mixed with salts and pigments. Urine has been used in cleaning, dyeing, and tanning.

Remanence that is being examined or analyzed with regard to geologic materials, such as sediments and lava flows, especially in periods preceding human civilization. When examined with regard to archaeological remains, prefer "archaeomagnetism."
In soil mechanics, the study of static and dynamic stability of soil in natural slopes and other forms of embankment.
Silver coins of Austria issued between 1740 and 1780 and then sporadically until 1961; used for trade with Africa and the Near East.

The white of an egg, which is the clear substance that surrounds the yolk; in the context of art materials, generally refers to whites of bird eggs. The whole egg, yolk, or white may be used sometimes mixed with oil and/or resin. Egg white, or glair, has been used as a medium for illuminated manuscripts. It is also used as a size for attaching gold leaf. For the egg white protein that is used in the food industry and in photographic emulsions, use "albumen (egg white protein)."
Banknotes with additional official stamps placed after issuance, by which the authority legitimized them, authorized their circulation, extended their maturity, etc.

Use to describe an activity or something produced by an activity that employs a computer to expedite some of the steps or operations required. When programming generates automatically a relatively large number of the steps between what is input and what is produced, use "computer-generated."
The parts or components of skeletons.
The bone or bones of the lower jaw in mammals and other vertebrates.
Condition of fabrication where the item is not ready-made, but is either custom made or made to order for the client.
Various forms of remote education in which the instructor and students are physically separated and communication is effected by written, audiovisual, or electronic media.
A Polish variation of Art Nouveau.
Bone derived from the bodies of human beings, used as a material.

Material comprising the primary, bone-like structure of a tooth. Dentin is hard calcareous material, with less porosity and less organic matter than bone. It is generally covered with a protective enamel layer. Layers of dentin cover animal teeth (whale, hippopotamus, boar, etc.) and tusks (ivory, elephant, walrus, etc.).
Material comprising or processed from the hard exterior covering of the egg of an ostrich, which is a large, flightless bird inhabiting open, semi-arid areas of Africa and formerly the Middle East.
Hard, pearly, iridescent internal layer of various kinds of mollusk shell, extensively used for making small articles and inlays.
Use generally for the ability to resist change, such as fading, due to light.

Jewish religious season commemorating the rededication of the Second Temple of Jerusalem after its desecration. Marked by the rite of lighting the menorah, symbolic of the Talmud story in which the small supply of nondesecrated oil, enough for one day, miraculously burned in the Temple for eight full days. Gifts are also exchanged and children play holiday games.
Circulating paper money of the United States issued by Federal Reserve banks since 1914.
Literary or artistic works produced by persons in their childhood or youth; usually used to set those works apart from later, mature works.

Smaller groups within a larger society that are the objects of prejudice or discrimination from the majority. For groups distinguished from the majority by their national, religious, linguistic, cultural,or sometimes racial background, use "ethnic groups."

Groups or movements whose religious beliefs and practices differ significantly from dominant or orthodox religions or society, typically centered around a particular deity, historic or mythic figure, or charismatic living person.
In the Roman Catholic Church, the deceased who are considered to be in paradise, but who have not yet been granted the higher designation of "saint."
Following slaughter, the extraction of meat from animals for consumption; the trade of a butcher.

Roof-like coverings of various kinds, not attached to four walls, but suspended by poles, cords, or attached on one side to a wall. Examples include coverings or hangings suspended over a throne, couch, bed, etc., or held over a person walking in procession, or an architectural roof-like ornamented projection, surmounting a niche, door, window, tomb, etc.
Form of farming in that takes place on hillsides and other upland areas, used for the raising of crops or rearing sheep, cattle, or other animals.
Glue made from the degraded collagen from fish skins and wastes. Also glue made from the swim bladders of fish, a tissue composed entirely of collagen.
Denotes flexible, lightweight, faced or unfaced thermal or acoustical insulation formed in long continuous rolls.

Integument of a large animal such as a cow or buffalo separated from the body with or without hair, whether green, dry, tanned, or dressed. For the integument of a small animal, use "skin." For tanned hide, use "leather."

Protein substance spun by spiders as thin, uniform filaments to make webs, other structures, conveyance, or to capture prey. A strand of spider silk is about 25 micrometers (0.00001 inches) in diameter. It is strong and dimensionally stable. Hummingbirds and other animals use spider silk for nest-building. Spider silk is currently used for crosshairs in optical instruments. Attempts have been made to produce fabric from spider silk, but it took an enormous number of spider webs and work to produce a fabric that was so sheer that it was of little use.
In Indian architecture, a basal-block of pillar.
Individual instances of armed conflict between two or more groups.
Broad classifications for objects, which are material things that can be perceived by the senses; also includes electronic media.

General term for the broad genre of objects, environments, or experiences (as in performance art) that are visual in nature, were created by the use of skill and imagination, and possess an aesthetic that is valued and of a quality and type that would be collected by art museums. It may refer to the study or practice of the fine arts or the fine and decorative arts together. For the discipline of art including reference to expertise of art, use "art (discipline)."
Coverings for floor or beds woven using strips of rag cloth as the weft.
A name of convenience for rugs with a geometrical design of octagons within rectangles.
Use to describe the location of something in its customary or unaltered place or position.

Waterproof floor covering material composed of layers of bitumen-impregnated felt cardboard, and provided with a printed decorative wear-resistant top layer. Sold in rolls, balatum had its greatest popularity in the middle of the 20th century as an alternative to true linoleum, as it was inexpensive and easy to apply. It was eventually replaced by vinyl products. Originally a brand name, it was manufactured beginning in 1924 at the Papeteries de Genval. The term often appears uncapitalized as a common noun to refer to any linoleum-like floor covering.
Floor coverings for use in a bathroom that prevents accumulation of water on the floor.
Manners of execution used in carving.

Sculptural process in which the sculptor forms the image by cutting away from the block of stone, generally without working from a model. The concept of the work evolves and develops during the carving process and adaptation may be made according to the character of the stone found within the block.
Ability of a material, usually in sheet form, to withstand hydrostatic pressure without rupture.
Parts or components of quilts.
In rug weaving, one knot to every two warp yarns.
Rugs intended for use as door curtains.
Single rugs woven to represent the arrangement of four rugs often used in the main chambers of important Islamic houses, composed of the mian farsh, kelleyeh, and two kenares.
Anatolian prayer rugs that are characterized by two octagonal shapes that intrude into the field design at the bottom and top, from the border.
Works composed primarily of industrial and modern consumer-culture waste, usually presented as assemblages of found objects.
Embroidered rugs named after and made in Arraiolos, Portugal. The technique is herringbone or cross-stitch on a linen cloth foundation.
Turkish term for flat-woven rugs with a particular supplementary weft structure.

Machine-made floor coverings of a particular type, having the loops of the pile uncut. All colors run with the warp, concealed, and are brought above the foundation in loops to produce the pattern. The type is believed to have originated in or near Brussels; was popular in the first half of the 19th century. They differ from Wilton carpets, which are produced by a similar process but the loops are cut, producing a soft pile surface.

Carpets created to look similar to the traditional body Brussels carpet, but produced by a cheaper method. For tapestry Brussels carpets, designs are printed on the warp yarns before the carpet is woven, rather than dyed-in-the-skein yarn used and the design produced in the weaving. Tapestry Brussels carpets may be machine printed or drum printed. One process to make these textiles involved a large cylinder or drum around which yarns were wound, then colored by a mechanism or by hand.
Reliquaries in the form of a rectangular box-shape, including the forms of a chest, coffin, or building surmounted by a roof-shaped cover.
Events involving multiple people reaching agreement or working together for an evil or unlawful purpose, such as treason, sedition, murder, or other serious wrong doing.
Rugs having a field divided into stripes, each ornamented with a pattern usually seen in borders.
Female siblings.
Parts or components of hearths.
Refers to the parts of hearths that project into rooms.

A black ink containing powdered carbon pigment, usually lampblack in a dilute aqueous solution of gum or glue. Carbon inks were used in China as early as the 3rd millennium BCE, also found on Egyptian papyrus and medieval manuscripts. Black carbon inks were replaced with iron gall inks in the 12th century. Distinguished from "India ink," which is a dispersion of carbon black in water.

Generally, inks formulated specifically for the process of printing from plates or blocks. These usually consist of pigment suspended in an oil vehicle, combined with resin, solvent, adhesive and a drier, but there are countless recipes for printing inks dependent on the purposes for which they are intended.
Ink that is invisible on paper until heat or other substance is applied to make it visible, or when the paper is held up to a light.
Medium used to create designs during lithography; when applied to chemically-treated stone plates, the wax produces areas that do not hold water, allowing the retention of oil-based inks.

White, translucent waxy material composed of a series of high molecular weight hydrocarbons, generally obtained from the fractional distillation of petroleum, shale oil, lignite, or coal. Mineral waxes are relatively pure materials that have little to none of the alcohols or esters found in plant waxes and beeswax. Examples of purified mineral waxes are paraffin, ceresin, microcrystalline, and petrolatum, which are stable and unreactive. They are used as a substitute for or extender of beeswax, and in polishes, candles, printing inks, crayons, phonographic records, and insulation.

Refers to Zoroastrian priests of the lower degree. Ervads have undertaken navar, the first of the two initiation rites for priests. In the more important ceremonies, ervads act only as assistant priests. The correlating historical term, 'ehrpats,' originally referred to religious teachers who were entrusted with the care of the fire.

Plates or surfaces that hold marks or information necessary to produce an image or text on a substrate, producing a print or reproduceable multiple, traditionally by applying ink to the matrix before running through a press, but digital files may be considered a type of matrix as well when used in the 3D printing process, for example.
The activity and state of training in the capacity of an apprentice, who learns by practical experience under skilled workers, usually for a prescribed period of time.
Activities and precautions designed to avoid an outbreak of fire, reduce the potential for fire to spread, and to safeguard persons, property, wildlife, and flora in the event of fire.
Typewriters whereby computer operators can monitor system and program operations.

Concept having to do with the state or condition of habitual reliance upon a narcotic, opiate, or hallucinogen for psychotropic rather than medicinal purposes. For excessive use or misuse of drugs, use "drug abuse."
The process of making cheese, which is the curd of milk (coagulated by rennet) separated from the whey and pressed into a solid mass, used as food.
Stretchers which connect chair legs in a continuous line.

Transitional stage between childhood and adulthood in the physical and emotional development of a living being; in humans, it extends mainly over the teen years and terminates legally when the official age of majority is reached.
One who has blisters, bumps or pustules on their skin. Characteristic of some contagious diseases.
Final stage of the normal life span, now commonly considered to be the years after 65.

Competitive athletic sport involving the skillful execution of physical exercises of strength, agility, and balance, involving apparatus such as mats, balance beams, parallel bars, vaulting horses, and flying rings. For the art of tumbling, balancing, and jumping presented as performance, use "acrobatics."
Concepts that are related to the condition of the body.
Physical or intellectual conditions that limit a person's movements, senses, or activities in a conventional sense.
General term for any emotional or organic mental impairments, manifested in maladaptive behavior, psychological problems, or impairment in one or more significant areas of functioning.
Chief officers so designated in various organizations, such as military orders of knighthood, fraternal orders such as the Freemasons, and trade unions.
Functions based around business and business activities.
In the context of Indian architecture, a figure representing a dwarf goblin; pramatha; gaṇa.
Parts of components of architraves.
In Indian architecture, an upper projecting section of a lintel; frame, line; horizontal upper facia of a beam lintel.
Refers to the lowest or deepest parts of objects. For the adjective describing the location of something at or near the bottom of something, use "bottom (positional attribute)."

The reverse or subordinate sides of leaves or sheets of paper, including the left-hand page of an open book. For the front side of a leaf, use "rectos." Use "reverses" for the back, underside, or subordinate surface of coins, medals, seals, or currency notes.

The front or obverse sides of a leaf; the right-hand pages of an open book or manuscript. Thus, refers to the principal side of sheets of paper. For the back of leaves or pages, use "versos." Use "obverses" for the front, top, or principal surface of coins, medals, seals, or currency notes, bearing the main design.
Genre of works made of twigs, rushes, thin strips of wood, or other flexible material woven together; includes baskets, other vessels, and other items.
Flared or bulbous terminals found on many open-ended aerophone tubes.
Heartwood of pine or other resinous wood cut into long slivers or splinters for burning.
Tubular or frame holders to support a torch in a fixed position.
Small metal or glass lamps frequently with a saucer base meant for use in the bedchamber.
Lamps designed to be used on a desk, usually having some means of adjusting the light source.
Brackets that can be moved horizontally.
Lighting fixtures that may be converted from incandescent to florescent bulbs, or that may be converted in another way.
Burners designed to hold two wicks.
Any lights in a theater, especially those installed in the audience area (house), except exit lights or lights on or back of the stage.
Gas-filled tungsten incandescent lamps containing a certain proportion of halogens in an inert gas whose pressure exceeds three atmospheres.
Popular name for any powerful spotlight; formerly described high-intensity carbon arc spotlights.
Toy tops meant to be spun and not whipped.
Lamps in which a wire gauze is used to screen the flame to prevent explosions; usually cylindrical and often made of brass.  Based on a lamp developed by Sir Humphrey Davy.

Relatively small grease-burning pan lamps, often used in kitchens, in which animal fat was placed in a round or spade-shaped metal cup, and wicks made of cord or rags (called "sluts," in reference to their being messy and dirty) were placed in one or two spouts at the side; the device was often attached to a large saucer to catch overflow or drippings.

Reservoirs of water used as swimming pools or fish ponds inside a Roman home, or in a public bath, where they were used for cooling plunges. In Medieval monastic communities, piscinae were used as fish ponds, when fish was a staple item of diet. Piscinae are also seen in Classicizing architecture, particularly in the 18th century. For basins having drains, used in Christian churches during the liturgy, use "piscinae (Christian fixtures)."

Short pole weapons, around 5 feet in length, having a retractable blade of either a one or three long thin points that were retracted into a hollow aperture inside the shaft. A sharp thrust of the weapon propelled the points out. The weapons were used by both infantry and civilians alike between the 16th and 19th centuries.
The physical materials that make up the mass of an archive. Distinguished from AAT "archives (groupings)."
Set of striplights at the front edge of the stage platform used to soften face shadows cast by overhead lights and to add general toning lighting from below.
Shallow pans, usually open, with the reservoir narrowed at one point to form a channel or slot for the wick; often have an attached curved half bail ending in a hook opposite the wick channel.
Lighting devices where the housing is set above the ceiling, and the lamp lens is flush or nearly flush with the ceiling.
Colored lights on vehicles intended to diminish the effect of fog, dust, or smoke in the air.
General group of electric discharge lamps comprised of a discharge tube containing the high-pressure gas or vapor enclosed in a hermetically sealed outer envelope.
High-intensity discharge lamps in which the major portion of the light is produced by radiation of metal halides and their products of dissociation.
High-intensity discharge lamps in which the partial pressure of the mercury vapor during operation does not exceed 100 Pa.
Sodium lamps in which light is produced by radiation from sodium vapor operating at a partial pressure of 01 to 1.5 Pa.
Revolving aeronautical beacons of high intensity used to indicate the course of a runway.
Aeronautical ground lights delimiting the boundary of landing areas.

Lamps with a ring-shaped reservoir with a burner or burners located in the center of the ring at the same level or below the level of the reservoir and connected to it by two tubes through which fuel is fed.

Mechanical lamps similar to Carcel lamps in that they contain a clockwork movement in the base actuating a pump which forces oil through a tube from the reservoir to the wick. The distinction between Diacon and Carcel lamps is unclear.
Gas burners where a circular row of small gas jets are emitted from a burner tip, and may be coalesced.

Extension gas fixtures, usually for chandeliers, that use water to seal the joints. Various improvements to the fixtures were invented throughout the mid- to late 19th century, attempting to solve the problem of evaporation of the water, which caused gas leaks.
Regions having human habitation.
Technique of applying diluted ink with a paint brush to create images, which may be classified as paintings or drawings and are often monochromatic.
Aircraft aeronautical lights forming the basic or internationally recognized navigational light system.

A period in United States history following the U.S. Civil War and characterized by industrialization, political corruption, globalization, mass immigration, Western expansion, and widespread cultural and artistic activity. Historians generally agree that the Gilded Age lasted from about 1865 to around 1900.

Lighting devices comprised of a housing, ballast, and connection to electrical power that mount tubular electric discharge lamps, or 'bulbs,' in which ionization of mercury vapor produces radiation that activates the fluorescent coating on the inner surface of the glass.
Catastrophes caused by naturally occurring phenomena such a flood, hurricanes, or earthquakes.

Cylinders into which the base of the candle can be inserted to keep it upright, either short to hold only the end of the candle or elongated, in the form of a tube, to hold the major part of a candle, with a lifting device to elevate the candle as it burns. Found on candleholders such as chambersticks and candlesticks, and on sconces and chandeliers.
Attachments of glass, metal, or fabric which surround the light source and reduce or deflect the light.

The anhydrous form of calcium chloride is very hygroscopic. It is used as a desiccant. Calcium chloride also exists as dihydrate and hexahydrate crystals. These crystalline forms are used in antifreeze solutions, fire extinguishers, fireproofing solutions, wood preservatives, as a gelling agent for starch size and to melt snow and ice from roads. Calcium chloride was used to speed up the rate of cure in mortar, shotcrete, and dry-mix concrete until 1973 when it was replaced by a non-chloride accelerator because it corroded steel reinforcements.
Copper or one of its alloys in the form of or reduced to powder or in fine flake form used as a pigment, or for the preparation of coatings.
A semi-transparent artificial fiber or natural silk fabric woven in plain weave with undeterred chain and weft threads, alternately two right and two left twisted.
The acid-resistant substance used for aquatint, made by dusting rosin particles onto a plate and heating.

Silane used as a crosslinking agent of silicone rubber and a coupling agent of glass fiber and  treatment agents of reinforced plastic laminated product. It is also used as a consolidant  in combination with Paraloid B-72 (TM) acrylic resin to treat deteriorated limestones, sandstones, and marbles.
Fiber-reinforced plastic using glass fiber, produced so as to have the characteristic of allowing light to pass, rather than being opaque.
Collectively used for decorative or additional material serving to finish, decorate, or complete textiles of any kind, including garments.
Paint having gold as a pigment, often in combination with another pigment of similar color.

An artificial sweetener made by a multi-step process that starts with ordinary table sugar (sucrose) and replaces three hydrogen-oxygen groups on the sugar molecule with three chlorine atoms. It was discovered in 1976 by researchers at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London, during a collaborative research program with UK sugar producer, Tate & Lyle, PLC. It is sold under the brand name Splenda (TM). In conservation, it has been used in the treatment of waterlogged wood.
Paint having water usually as the volatile phase with the various nonvolatile substances (as a linseed-oil varnish) in emulsion as the binder.
Refers to the surface of a cast object immediately after removal from a mold, before fettling and chasing.

Neolithic Chinese objects in the form of a flat disk with a hole in the center. The term bi is applied to wide disks with proportionately small central holes, made from jade or other stone, and found at burial sites. There is much speculation on the function of these objects, though they are generally thought to represent the heavens or the sun. Bi have continued to be used as a form of regalia and as decorative objects well into the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. They are often seen as related to the "cong (ceremonial vessel)," which represented the earth.

Works from the 1950s and 1960s that were unique, unrehearsed events, often combining elements of theater, music, and the visual arts. Usually nonverbal, they may incorporate visual, tactile, and olfactory responses, chance, and audience participation. The term was coined by artist Allan Kaprow.
Flat discs, made of sandstone or another stone of considerable thickness, that are rotated on an axle and used to grind, sharpen, polishing, or shape objects.
Preparatory procedures used in the printing process.

A gradation technique used in woodblock printmaking, particularly as mastered by Japanese printmakers. Bokashi is notable in the work of Hokusai and Hiroshige, and is used most frequently in depicting the sky or water and to heighten the illusioni of space. There are multiple variations of the technique.
Narratives, usually told in first person, relating the life events or experiences of the narrator.
Conditions caused under certain climatic situations that result in heat loss and unwanted heat flow in rooms and spaces.

In photography, refers to the usually unintended optical effect caused by reflected light at the time of initial film exposure, or the resulting halo surrounding the boundaries of light-emitting or reflecting sources in the image printed from this film. Modern photographic films are coated with an 'anti-halation layer' to prevent this effect.
Irregular marking of a printing plate during biting as a result of faulty grounding.
The biting of a printing plate to such a degree that the printing area becomes substantially recessed and thereby productive of sharper definition and longer runs.
Brush strokes found in traditional Chinese painting. These long, loose strokes often are used to define rock and mountain formations.
Education in art aimed at encouraging an understanding of it based on its perceptible qualities, including training students in the sensory experiencing of art.
Spanish soldiers, particularly those operating as military sorce during the Spanish conquest of Mexico and Peru in the 16th century.
The limitation of the order of inheritance of an estate to a prescribed sequence of inheritors.
Buildings housing institutions tasked to hold and detain members of the armed forces, in the U.S. particularly who have been convicted of violations of the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
A running ornament consisting of a sinuous stylization of a cloud, common in Chinese art and in Oriental rugs.

Low, circular defensive towers used, especially since the Napoleanic wars, for coastal protection; derived in name and form from the traditional Mediterranean watchtowers found on Cape Martella, Corsica.

Chief dwellings attached to farms, particularly a dwelling for the family of a family-owned and -operated farm. Modern farmhouses characteristically comprise two stories with spacious, if modest, rooms and furnishings. Earlier farmhouses were characteristically one-story.

Documents prepared primarily to confirm a government's action or perspective that was previously expressed orally. Informal in nature, aide-mémoires do not contain the markings of more formal documents; only the date of execution is visible at the end of the text.
Mills or other buildings where iron or steel is smelted or otherwise processed.
Buildings or parts of buildings that house casts; usually art musuems or study collections that house plaster casts of ancient sculptures or other works. For museums of wax casts, use "wax museums."
Square-back Windsor chairs with narrow vertical lath instead of round spindles.

Of people and corporate bodies, the state of being professionally active. A common example is in reference to dates associated with people or corporate bodies, where the specific dates, and sometimes loci, of birth and death are unknown; the term is commonly so-used in the discipline of art history for estimated life dates based on the oeuvre or other documentation of the artist. It may refer to the time of the artist's apprenticeship through old age, regardless of whether this was his or her most prolific period. For people other than artists and architects, prefer "flourished," which has the connotation of demarking that time when the person has achieved full development or success. However, usage overlaps.
Parts or components of drawers.
Narrow strips applied to the bottom edge of a drawer to provide a good running surface on the framing.
Low dikes around polders, which are areas of low-lying land reclaimed from the sea.

An Italian verd antique from Pegli, Italy that was first used by the ancient Greeks and Romans and continues to be used in modern times. It is a breccia marble consisting of deep green fragments of serpentine cemented by light green calcite.

Experts in linguistics who study the structure and historical development of a language or languages, such as when doing close analysis of literary texts in the context of cultural and political research.

Compilers of bibliographies, which are lists of books, periodical articles, and audiovisual materials on specialized subjects, annotate bibliographies with physical descriptors, and analyze subject content of materials. Also, scholars of books as physical objects and those who advise on the acquisition of materials in special subjects.
Those who study human history through the remnants of material culture, environment, and animal remains.
Catalogs, particularly of a library or other collection, in which each item is entered on a separate card and arranged alphabetically by author or title, or in another logical order.
Refers to a Chinese Neolithic culture dating to ca. 6000 to 3000 BCE. Chungwan refers to the Central Plain of China which is commonly regarded as the cradle of Chinese civilization.
People who serve alcoholic beverages at a bar.

Refers to the period of the Javanese Majapahit empire (1292- c.1500 CE).  The period is characterized by the re-emergence of pre-Hindu elements. The sculptural style in this period is most noted for the relief panels depicting the punakawan, clownish characters from Javanese poems. Prominent examples of architectural styles in the period are Candi Brahu, featuring brick construction, Candi Tikus, featuring bathing pools, Candi Wringin Lawang, featuring a gate type known as candi blntar ("split gate"), and Candi Sukuh, featuring a truncated pyramidal structure. Late in the period, temple styles evolved to include cylindrical bodies, square foundational bases, complex stepped sanctuaries, and horned banaspati head sculptures that supported the cornices.

Refers to the period associated with the Shaivite area known as Mi-son in central region of modern Vietnam. Architecture and monumental sculpture in this period is sub-classified A through H according to location. In general, the period features artistic properties from pre-Angkor, Angkor, and Indonesian works.
Upholstered chairs with slightly concave backs to fit the contours of the human body; distinct from those with flat backs called "chaises à la reine."
Brackets, usually metal, used on closed stairways, and which fasten the handrail to the wall.
Compact, fitted dressing chests intended to hold a lady's jewelry and cosmetics. Compact, fitted dressing chests intended to hold a lady's jewelry and cosmetics.

Sheet metal seams formed by slipping a cap strip, which is a narrow metal strip that has had long edges turned, over the turned edges of the two metal pieces to be joined, to form a lock. An example of use is in assembling cross seams of ducts.
Mortar joints that are flush with the faces of the blocks.

Discipline concerning physical objects that are meant to be perceived primarily through the sense of sight, were created by the use of skill and imagination, and possess an aesthetic that is valued and of a quality and type that would be collected by art museums or private collectors.

Roofs having rafters as framing; rafters are very long planks that incline from a point along a central ridge beam and meet in an intersection with the outer walls, in stick framing.The function of the long planks is to hold up the roofing frame as well as the roof sheathing. Compare to "truss and beam roofs," which use triangular forms as further support for the roof.
Technique of bond in which alternating courses of all headers and all stretchers are laid, with the headers centered on the stretchers and on the joints between stretchers.
Pigment that is violet in color, contains carbon, and is ultimately derived from vegetable or animal sources.
Refers to an altarpiece or other polyptych with four panels.
Devotional images that are two dimensional or low-relief pictures.
Refers to Latin American ex-votos, usually cast of silver and valued as a distinctive form of folk art.
Unique prints made using the process of monotype, which consists of placing a painting of an image onto a plate and then laying a sheet of paper on top to create the print.
Areas of a fresco that are executed each in one day; usually these sections remain visibly divided by a seam in the finished piece.
Transparent layers applied to a drawing or painting using diluted ink or watercolor. An example of usage is in order to create an atmospheric effect.
Chinese handscrolls, containing text, artwork, or both, and are displayed horizontally.
Prints made by the monoprint process resulting from direct painting combined with a traditional printmaking process, such as silk screen, etching, woodcut, and lithography.
The fronts or forwardmost ends of watercraft or airships.
Items that do not form the primary articles of clothing, but are instead the smaller articles of dress, such as shoes, gloves, hats, jewelry, etc.
Ferries designed to take railway passengers or freight across bodies of water. In one design, the large ferry is equipped with tracks, upon which railway cars may board the ferry.
Reflection of light, heat, or sound without diffusion such as, for example, light off a mirror surface.

A variant of XRF imaging that is based on the use of two x-ray lenses in a confocal configuration, enabling measurements of high spatial resolution in three directions, including depth (x, y, and z) in the micrometer range.
Infrared spectroscopy having the range of 10-400 inverse centimeters [cm-1].

Burners with one or more thin, tapering wick tubes extending above the burner plate but cut off immediately below it to prevent conducting heat into the font containing highly volatile fuel (a mixture of alcohol and redistilled turpentine). When there is more than one tube, they diverge from base to top. Usually small caps are attached by chains to each tube for use in extinguishing the flame and to prevent evaporation of the fuel.
Burners having a domed deflector and a simple, collarlike perforated chimney-holder attached to the base plate; believed to be the earliest flat wick kerosene burner.
Metallic discs perforated by one or two wick tubes, which rest on the opening into the font; such burners often have a small tab on the edge by which they can be lifted.
Lighting devices which produce a uniform, diffuse illumination approaching a shadowless condition; may be supplemented by other lighting.

Devices for supporting candles, having one or more candle sockets or spikes to secure candles; sometimes having drips to catch wax, push-ups, and other devices for removing the stub, or adjustable features for controlling the position of the flame. For lamps using candles as the source of illumination and containing the candle within a vessel, use "candle lamps."

Supports for rushlights, which must be held at an angle for proper burning. Usually consisting of upright pincers of wrought iron, jaws held closed by spring action or a curved arm counter-weighted by a metal ball, decorative element, or candle socket. The base may be an iron tripod or wooden block, often decoratively turned.
Low, usually three-legged stools with heavy circular tops set on round-bottomed bases.
Stools designed to placed or stacked on top of one another.
High stools that are usually one of a row of such stools fixed in front of a counter; often backless and having a revolving seat.
Small benches usually with upholstered seats; in form they resemble a tabouret lengthened and supported on six or more legs.
Seats, usually made of cast-iron and in period character, located in a garden.
Small beds for infants, usually on bends.
18th-century term for English stands in the form of a deep partitioned tray on legs intended to be placed near a table to hold plates and cutlery.
Ladders from which the upper shelves of a bookcase may be reached, often fitted into a chair, stool, table, or other piece of furniture.
Term for French tables with a deep rim or gallery around the top.
Any small tables used in relation to a couch or chair.
Term generally applied to tables intended for use in kitchens, especially those having an ample work surface and drawers or bins for storage.
Tables constructed so that the tabletop is set upon a base or stand constructed using mortise-and-tenon joints.
Corners on tables or other furniture in which the normal angle is rendered as a quarter-round inversion.
Furniture elements characterized by a concave half-round section, usually where the corner or end of a squared rectangle would be found, as on a tabletop.
Feet on baluster legs which end in a ball flanked by rings, over the beginning of another baluster facing downwards; resembling the foot of a colt.
Assemblies of members of a college or university to observe a particular ceremony, such as the opening of the academic year or the announcing of prizes, awards, and honors.
An ethylene-propylene elastomer noted for resistance to oils, ozone, weathering and heat.

Prayers intended to be chanted or sung, used in Christian worship; sources of the prayers are the Bible (other than Psalms) and other certain texts. Examples of these scriptural hymns are the Song of Moses from the Old Testament, the Benedictus from the New Testament, and the Lord's Prayer.
Saws used in large mills in which a heavy blade is tensioned in a sash frame.
In Indian architecture, a festoon formed by kīṅkaṇikās issued from the grāsa-heads.
Parts and components of furniture backs.

A polymer with strong intermolecular bonding that becomes rigid by chemical reaction and that is not remeltable. Thermoset polymers are usually insoluble in most solvents. Examples of thermoset polymers are epoxies, silicones, and phenolics along with some polyesters and polyurethanes.

A superpolymer that maintains mechanical and chemical integrity above 400 degrees Fahrenheit for extended periods and has high strength and modulus of elasticity and excellent resistance to solvent, oil, and corrosive environment.

Thermoplastic polyester manufactured from corn starch or other renewable resources. First developed for use as a synthetic fiber during World War 2 when organic materials were in short supply. In conservation used as a protective covering for stone materials exposed outdoors.
An assemblage of machines or machine parts.

Large containers, made of wood or other durable material, used by traveling painters to store essential supplies such as palletes, brushes, pallete knives, and tubes of paint. Often fitted with many compartments and drawers of various sizes for organizing tools, and partioned off at one end to accomodate long-handled brushes.
Drills rotated by a cord or string wrapped tightly around it and strung to a bow.
Hand-operated boring devices made up of a central steel tube containing a shaft. At one end is a handle and at the other a bit-holding chuck.
Equipment designed for or used for extinguishing or containing fires.
Attachments for a materials-handling or excavating machine.
Typographical ornaments having a hole in the center in which an initial letter is printed; common in early printed books.
Threading tools, many-toothed or with a single cut edge, shaped especially for cutting or finishing external or internal threads; usually used in conjunction with a lathe.

Slender, compressed cylinders of material often made from calcium sulfate in its dihydrate form, gypsum. Most often used to write on blackboards or chalkboards in classroom contexts, but also for many other marking purposes.
Crafted instruments used for drawing and measuring, such as rulers, scales, protractors, pens, pencils, etc.
Tools used for rendering mechanical drawings.

Organizations which contribute in varying degrees to a community. Community organizations may be non-profit, private-sector, or private for-profit organizations. They may have a broad constituency, such as a neighborhood council, or a more targeted constituency, such as a tenant's association. Organizations which contribute in varying degrees to a community. Community organizations may be non-profit, private-sector, or private for-profit organizations. They may have a broad constituency, such as a neighborhood council, or a more targeted constituency, such as a tenant's association.
Output devices that convert coded information from the processor into a readable form on paper.

Devices consisting of a vertically mounted shaft that can be pushed in any direction; used for generating signals that can cause the cursor or some other symbol to be moved rapidly about on a display screen.
Printers in which the image is formed without use of mechanical impact with the printed surface material.
Printers that create each character from an array of dots that are usually formed by transferring ink by mechanical impact.
People who make barometers, which are instruments for measuring atmospheric pressure.
Craftsmen and textile workers who specialize in making fringes and other trimmings.
Those who study the development over time of the human built environment.
Refers to all types of laborers employed in building construction, including skilled and unskilled workers.
Scholars or compilers of the prescribed rites of formal and public worship, typically including words, music, symbolic aids, and ritual actions.

Flat-panel video displays for computers and other such devices that utilize ionized gas, or plasma, to illuminate pixels on the screen which emits a bright light that reflects focused color and images.
Scholars of the ancient classical period or adherents of classicism in art or literature.

term: concepts relating to the creative process
definition: Artistic concepts that deal with creation of works.
Exposition or explanation, especially critical interpretation of a portion of Scripture or other text.
Persons who are extremely rigorous in the practice of self-denial, whether by seclusion or by abstinence from creature comforts, usually as a result of religious practice..
The individual sheets folded into two leaves that together form a gathering.
Cylindrical rods in which nibs or penpoints are inserted, and that form the handle of a dip pen. These may be made from a variety of materials, including wood, metal, or plastics.
Concepts related to the ownership of land.
Economic and political system in which land and capital goods are publicly owned, and the governing authorities control the means of production, prices, and distribution.

Creamware that is lead-glazed, and originating ca. 1763. It was developed by Josiah Wedgwood and named after Queen Charlotte. Its popularity eventually led to the disappearance of the English, tin-glazed earthenware industry.
Mixing machines fitted with paddles or propellers, used to prepare clay slips and glazes.
Hand tool for pressing the scutched flax into flax bales.
Tools with a blade or sharpened edge with the primary function of cutting.
Mechanical contrivances designed to remove moisture from surfaces or materials.

Gas burners used in laboratory work in which gas and air can be combined variably to control the heat output. These are named for Robert Bunsen, a German chemist who developed it ca. 1855, in partnership with Peter Desdega.
Implements consisting of bristles, hair, or the like, set in or attached to a handle; used for painting, cleaning, polishing, or grooming.
Stationary machines having a moving belt, disk, or spindle with an abrasive surface, usually a sandpaper; used for smoothing surfaces.
Presses consisting of a frame containing stationary dies; used to cut or shape metal or other materials.
General term for any machinery used in woodworking.
Hammering tools with a head and handle, of various designs, used in woodworking.

General term for a variety of artistic or communicative types of media used in a given work or works. Typically reserved for modern works. For works that are of a single type but use multiple materials, prefer "mixed media."
Publications, usually annuals, containing a variety of useful facts of miscellaneous nature, or statistical information; originally included projections of coming days, months, and holidays.
The net increase in heat within a space.
Equipment and machinery powered by hydraulics, which is the use of the motion of water or other liquids in motion to transmit energy.
A state of balance between opposing forces that is either static or dynamic.
Sanders shaped so that they can be used to smooth complex moldings.
Writing made to evidence the terms and conditions, or the fact, of an accord or arrangement.
A tabular or graphic representation of a fluctuating or dependent variable, such as magnitude, temperature, cost, etc.

Includes any manifestation of the material culture of classical Greece and Rome. With reference to the period of late 18th- and 19th-century art and architecture which featured a return to classical principles, use "Neoclassical." With reference to the period of architecture and ornament of the late 18th- to early 20th-century based relatively closely on ancient classical forms, use "Classical Revival."

The relative disposition and way of arrangement of the various parts of the body of a human, or sometimes of an animal. Includes the position and carriage of the limbs, hands, head, or the body as a whole, often as indicating a particular quality or feeling. Examples of displays of body position include in the visual arts, dance, and ritual.
Stabilizing degraded or weakened areas by introducing or attaching materials capable of holding them together.

Buildings that house archives, which are institutions that store, maintain, and care for non-active public records or other important historical documents. The facilities typically include shelves and drawers for storage of boxes, folders, and other containers or documents; areas of the facility may be climate controlled.
Those endowed with some natural faculty, ability, or talent. The talent may be a general intellectual one or a quite specific talent such as music or chess playing.
Architectural elements used to form a barrier.
Distinguished from "log houses" by being generally more crudely built of timbers left round and joined at the corners by overlapping saddle-shaped notches.
Wood from the species Fraxinus floribunda.

Meaning literally “well” “structure” (Kroll 2015, 218; 128) Jinggan originally refers to the wall of a wooden well or the railing of a well, but also indicates a construction technique, known as “jinggan method” (jinggan shi 井幹式). According to textual descriptions, archaeological discoveries, and surviving images, the jinggan method involved stacking layers of timbers to form the wall of a building, in which the ends of the timbers were fit together with mortise and tenon joinery. The jinggan construction method is still being used in some areas of northeast and southwest China that are rich in timber. The first appearance of the term jinggan 井幹 is in Zhuangzi’s 莊子 “Autumn Floods” (Qiushui 秋水) from the Warring States Period. In this text, a frog jumps into a “jinggan,” which likely refers to the wall of a wooden well (jingbi 井壁) or the railing of a well (jinglan 井欄). One of the most famous references to the jinggan method describes the architecture of the Jinggan Pavilion (Jinggan lou 井幹樓) in Jianzhang Palace (Jianzhang gong 建章宮) of the Han dynasty.
Underground conduits for carrying away waste and storm water.
Places where animals are killed for food.
Use generally in contemporary contexts for permanent centers of operations; use "military camps" for contemporary nonpermanent posts.
Factories where bricks are made.

Stations along caravan routes providing overnight accommodations and facilities for caravans and individuals and their animals; generally characterized by large central courtyards, a single entrance and, often, shops. For Islamic structures of similar function, but in urban contexts and having more mercantile facilities, use "khans."

Sheets of film material made of various types of plastic and used for drafting, in use since the 1940s, but emerging as preferred supports from the 1980s through the 2000s. Drafting films will have a matte finish on one or both sides, which gives the surface teeth to accept media or emulsion. Like other translucent supports, drafting film may be used alternately for original drawings or as a reproductive intermediate. Reproductions are typically run through a diazo machine. Stability will largely depend on composition. Acetate was used for drafting film primarily from 1939, with a decrease in usage in the 1960s. Polyester or Mylar (TM) was used from around 1950, becoming very popular after 1970.
Maps prepared primarily for fire insurance underwriters, showing information, such as type of construction, about structures in a given area.
Bidets made to rise out a chest. Use "portable bidets" for those with legs made to screw off and tops made to lock.
Ornamental enframements, such as for an inscription, monogram, or coat of arms, or ornately framed tablets, often bearing inscriptions.

Motifs representing the heads of rams or goats used in antiquity to decorate altars, sarcophagi, and funerary urns; revived as an ornamental device during the Renaissance and used to decorate furniture in the late 18th century.
In Indian art and architecture, a decorative motif in the form of a bunch of mango fruits.
A sharp edge produced by the meeting of two curved or plane surfaces in an angle; as in the edges that are produced by fluting in a column.
As an artistic concept, the state or quality of having many intricate or interrelated parts.

A zigzag pattern in which the rows of zigzags alternate colors, in which each leg of each v is often decorated with an s-motif and in which a line extends from the point of each v into the succeeding v.
Patterns consisting of repeated, linear, geometrical shapes, usually angular, in a continuous band. For similar patterns not confined to a band, especially openwork, use "fretwork."

As with the Egyptian lotus, Indian lotus motifs are also ancient and seen in Hindu iconography, but they gained widespread use in Buddhist iconography. The Indian motifs are based on the species of aquatic plant Nelumbo nucifera, having a large bright pink, white, or blue flower, in art seen in profile, in rosettes, and as medallions. Examples of use in Indic culture include as a pedestal to support figures of deities, as a molding, or as a capital. It is associated with the qualities of transcendence and grace, and appears as an emblem of Vishnu. Color variations impart various meanings.
Term generally applied to mirrors that have flat reflective surfaces, as opposed to those with a convex or concave surface.
Term used during the mid-18th century for armchairs with upholstered seats and backs, carved frames and cabriole legs.

Chairs with elaborately carved or painted backs, frequently bearing emblems and coats of arms, and having solid wood seats often with hinged lids to reveal a storage compartment. Intended for use in halls and corridors.
Running ornament in which the main element curves back and forth from one side of the band to the other.
Scrolling foliage consisting of grapevines with bunches of grapes.
Bulk delivery points for electrical power, from which it is distributed to consumers.
Representations of windows inserted to complete a series of windows, or to give the appearance of symmetry to a facade.
In Indian architecture, a recess between moldings.
Type of wall decorations consisting of vertical bands of rusticated masonry which divide the surface into panels or bays; common in 17th-century French domestic architecture.
Refers to a type of French chaise longue featuring a foot surrounded on three sides by a low curving back.

French 18th-century chairs that were positioned against the wall. Their use was governed by strict protocol and sièges meublants were usually not sat on, but rather meant to be a part of the architectural decoration of a room. Distinct from "sièges courants" which stood in the center of a room and could be moved.
Companies that own or control other companies, usually through owning a controlling portion of their stock.
Long handled adzes whose blade is beveled on the inside; later adzes have polls on the head which are used as a maul.
Augers whose points are heated to burn holes in wood and then twisted to enlarge the holes.
Coarse rounded single-cut files used for cleaning out mortises and for shaping the bed and throat of a plane.
Steel bars with a flattened, forked, or chisel-shaped end which is sometimes slightly bent; used for heavy prying, and as a lever for moving heavy objects.
Finely spiked or serrated wheels mounted at the end of a handle, used to perforate paper along the lines of a drawing in order to transfer it to another surface by pouncing.
Brushes used to clean saw dust from the teeth of rasps and files.
Awls used in making holes for stitching harnesses; some varieties have a needle inserted in a tubular shank, with a feed for thread and means of creating an interlocking stitch.
Lathes having a mandrel, which is a shaft or spindle to which work is fixed while being turned in the lathe.
Small scissors having a form specialized for cutting buttonholes; they are typically forged for strong cuts and to stay sharp for long periods.
Very small, thin files used in delicate work.
Refers to the installation of glass as a transparent barrier, as in windows or for works on display. Includes glass used in framing, display case construction, or display space illumination.
Large pocket knives.
Positive transparencies having gelatin as the binder, holding silver as the final image material.
Wood blocks cut at a right angle to the grain and used for wood engraving.
Work surfaces for sailmakers that often include holes or pouches for tools and equipment, and a flat surface on which the sail material is worked.
Groups of individuals related by blood, marriage, adoption, or cohabitation.
The action of applying a coating by adding pressurized air to a paint emulsion, and directing it onto a support through a nozzle.
Four-legged supports, usually having pairs of legs in an A-shaped configuration with a crossbar; often used in pairs to support wood while being sawed or for other purposes.
Social groups sharing a common tie or interest such as a mode of life, activity, or social context.
Attaching silk chiffon or other fine, transparent material to one or both sides of a sheet of paper in order to strengthen, repair, or preserve it.
Those who play percussion instruments.

Generally, a relatively high level of cultural and technological development in human society. Specifically, the stage of cultural development at which writing and the keeping of written records is attained.
Occurrences of rapid descent of large masses of snow or ice down a mountainside.
Parts of a fluid body of air or water moving continuously in a certain direction through a surrounding body of water or air in which there is less movement.

Photographic process that uses a collodion binder which must be coated on the support, exposed, and developed before the collodion has become dry. A silver halide is the light-sensitive agent, and the process may be used to produce positives or negatives.
The incombustible residue of something burnt.
A plywood board in which veneer layers used in the core are replaced by blocks of wood, the direction of grain of the blocks running at right angles to that of the adjacent veneer.

Roofing tile of shallow concave shape; can serve as a gutter tile or a covering tile. Eaves tiles of this type have an overhanging lip to allow water to drip away from the bottom edge. These are categorized according to decorative treatment of the lip. Two types described in the Yingzao fashi (e.g. Chapter 13) are the chongchun banwa 重唇瓪瓦 and huatou banwa 華頭瓪瓦 (lit. flower/ornamented head plate tile). Although having the same pronunciation, from the Yuan dynasty onward this term was also written: "板瓦".

The term dishui 滴水 (literally “dripping water”) as an architectural term is first found in Ming dynasty literature. The texts explain that dishui are located at the end of the eaves and that the end of the tile “hangs down,” but there is no description of the specific shape. Recent research and existing examples indicate that the term dishui can be understood in both a narrow and a broad sense. When modern scholars define dishui, they are usually referring specifically to the plate tile with a “ruyi”-shape 如意形 descending from the lowest end of the gutter tiles, especially in the context of Qing architecture. Thus, dishui can be used to distinguish Qing style buildings from Song style buildings, the latter of which more commonly employed “multi-lipped plate tiles” (chongchun banwa 重唇瓪瓦)," as described in the the Song dynasty Yingzao fashi (Liang 1981, 85; Yao 1986, 111; Pan and He 2005, 157). More generally, dishui can be used to refer to any eaves gutter tile with an end that hangs down.
In ancient architecture, a term used to describe a flat tile or tegula.  In modern usage, an S-curved roofing tile, laid so the down curve of one tile overlaps the up curve of the next one.

Machines in which work is rotated about a horizontal axis and shaped by a fixed cutting, boring, or drilling tool while being held in a chuck, faceplate, or mandrel or between centers in headstock and tailstock.
Tools used for boring.
Large machines or hand tools used for making holes in a variety of materials. Drills typically have fluted or spiral shanks.

Receptacles of a hard material, such as stone, brass, wood, or glass, that have a cup-shaped cavity in which materials are pounded or ground with a pestle. Often used to grind ingredients used in a pharmacy, painting, or cookery.

Refers to machines or mechanical apparatus, either simple or complex, for grinding or reducing a solid substance to a powder or pulp, such as corn or spice. To refer to the combined building and the milling machinery housed within it, use "mills (buildings)."

Powered machines designed to wax and buff floor finishes. These usually consist of a handle mounted to a revolving element that spins a removeable pad to either apply wax or dry polish a floor surface, as needed.
Supports in the form of paired beams used by two people to carry and move loads.

Use generally for devices that expel a material or object from one area and discharge it into another area. Use specifically in civil engineering for pumps that elevate sewage from a lower sewer into a main disposal system.
Wooden blocks in the form of a hat, used by hat makers to shape a felt or straw hat. Modern hat blocks may be made of other materials.
Machines used in goffering.
Finishing tools used on the edges of fresh concrete to provide a rounded corner.
Machines that mix cement, aggregate, and water in a rotating drum to make concrete.
Steel rods with ridged or abrasive surfaces, fixed with handles, and used for maintaining the edges on knife blades.
Trips, journeys, voyages, or excursions made for some definite purpose, often for military or scientific purposes.
Photographs originally taken as one of a pair of stereoscopic photographs but then printed or mounted as a single image.
Tongs used in metalworking.
Benches used in conjunction with drawplates for drawing long or tough lengths of wire.
Horse-powered mills used for grinding bark.
Hand tools with a handle, crank, and chuck; used for turning a bit or auger to drill a hole by hand.

Apparatuses invented by Carlo Ponti of Venice ca. 1870, for viewing large albumen photographs on thin paper, using a large lens to create the optical illusion of depth and perspective and having candles or kerosene lamps as a source of light. The photographs themselves were translucent, often colored and pierced with pinprick holes to create dramatic visual effects with backlighting, such as that of lights in a night scene.
Areas, often sheltered, located beside a railway track at a station and raised to a level convenient for passengers and freight to be loaded on and off the train, tram, or other similar conveyance.

GGeometric solid figure having two ends comprising equal and parallel circles, and the intervening curved surface is such as would be traced out by a straight line moving parallel to itself with its ends in the circumferences of these circles. If the direction of this straight line is perpendicular to the planes of the circles, the figure is a right cylinder; if not, an oblique cylinder. In modern geometry, the term is used for the solid generated by a straight line moving always parallel to itself and describing any fixed curve, not necessarily a circle. Used in common language to refer to hollow forms as well as solid.
Hangers that are suspended, supported, or anchored to ceilings.

Piping or tubing in coils, spirals, or other various configurations, employed in cooling or heating systems to serve as heat exchangers. For the any general object genre designed as concentric rings or circles, use "coils (object genre)."
The idea of survival of a person in some form after physical death. This notion is present in a wide variety of forms in different religions.

Cylinder desks, that is writing desks with a cover that rolls up into the desk top, that are designed for ladies; they are distinguished by often having a relatively delicate design and a wide space to accommodate ladies' skirts.

Refers to several Christian monastic communities of the Byzantine Rite that follow the rule of St. Basil, their spiritual father; there are five major branches of the Order of St. Basil. The Basilian monastic community has been highly influential in the Byzantine community over the centuries, comparable to the Benedictine influence within the Western monastic community. St. Basil, theologian and archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (modern Turkey), created his monastic rule between 358 and 364. St. Basil's simple yet strict rule asks followers to practice community living and advocates ascetic practices as a way to serve God more perfectly. His rule avoids the extreme asceticism of the desert hermits. Implied by St. Basil are vows of chastity and poverty, anticipating the later Western monastic systems, and aid to impoverished people is also called for. Attached to the monasteries should be schools for children in which the students can be tested for a possible religious vocation. St. Basil's rule was revised in the 9th century by St. Theodore of Studios. The Basilian order should not be confused with a Latin-rite congregation of the same name that was founded in France in 1822 but later active mainly in Canada; the members of this congregation devote themselves to educating children.
Amphorae in which the neck and body merge into a continous, unbroken curve.
Gloves intended for use while operating an automobile, and that may enhance grip on the wheel while driving. They can be made of a variety of materials including leather, rubber, and woven textiles.
Methods employed in the act of drawing, such as contouring, cross-hatching, or stumping.

Procedures by which light-sensitive materials are made to produce an image. For procedures related to how a photograph is taken or composed, or is manipulated during or after processing, use "photographic techniques." For printing processes involving light-sensitivity at one stage, but creating a final print that was never itself light-sensitive, use "photomechanical processes." For light-sensitive processes used especially to make reproductive prints of documents and technical drawings, use descriptors found under "<light-sensitive reprographic processes>."
Methods of paint application employed to create a specific effect.
Commercial or professional organizations established to provide supplies, equipment, software, and services to libraries.
