Named for the site where they were discovered, this type is charcterized by a thin but more triangular form with wide shoulders and tapering legs and feet, and precise, angular incision depicting anatomical details.

Refers to the Predynastic period in Upper Egypt around 4500 BCE. The period is characterized by pottery that is primitive in appearance which has led some scholars to believe it is earlier in date than the Badarian period. Others believe it is contemporary with the Badarian period or just an early stage of it.

Refers to the Predynastic period in Lower Egypt from about 4500 to 3500 BCE named after the site of Merimde. The period is characterizd by a fully sedentary village life with pottery and stone artifacts similar to those of Fayum A but with more variation and elaboration in the pottery.

Refers to the culture, style, and period based in the Bronze Age of Vietnamese history (around the 15th or 14th century BCE) associated with the site in northern Vietnam in the Thanh Hoa Province known as Dông-Son. The period is characterized by the high production of bronze ritual objects and bronze kettledrums reflecting strong Indonesian stylistic influences and a predilection for animal motifs. Objects produced in this period also display affinity in form and style to Chinese pottery and bronze works. In architecture, the period features houses and temples with curved roofs and support structures based on a stilts system.
Refers to the period in Egypt from about 525 to 404 BCE. During this period Egypt was conquered by the Persians and little remains of the art and architecture of the period.

Refers to the Egyptian pottery style produced during the Badarian, Amratian, and Gerzean periods from about 6000 to 2925 BCE. The style is characterized by polishd thin-walled, handmade vesels coated with a red ocher wash, with black tops probably produced by placing the vessels while hot in carbonizing organic matter.
Pottery styles belonging to ancient Italian cultures.

Refers to a Bronze Age period and culture that supplanted existing cultures on the Aeolian islands from around 1250 BCE. It is apparently of Apennine origin and is characterized by a new type of dwelling, generally of wood on stone, with an oval or square foundation. It has much in common with the contemporary Morgetian culture in Sicily.

Refers to architectural style associated with the fourth of the traditional five classical orders of architecture, that also include Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite. It is often described as a simplification of the Doric style, and it is distinguished from other styles by fewer and bolder moldings, no triglyphs or other decoration on the frieze, no decorative details on the entablature or capitals, and generally no fluting on the column, though in Neoclassical works the shafts may have rusticated bands. For the assemblage forming associated columns, "Tuscan order."
Pottery styles belonging to Roman cultures.

Refers to a style of Terra sigillata ware that developed in Italy and elsewhere in the western Roman Empire, after it had first been introduced in the Hellenistic east. It is characterized by being high quality tableware based on the typical Roman technology and design, merged with various local features.

Describes the style and culture of the inhabitants of Wuvulu Island. The people of Wuvulu Island are primarily known for their woodcarvings of human figures or heads, often containing crocodile and fish characteristics. These carvings are found on lime sticks, coconut shell ladles, eating utensils, spears, obsidian daggers, slit gongs, canoes, beds, and architectural features.
Regional styles belonging to Irian Jaya cultures.
Refers to the Paleolithic period in southwestern Turkey around 9500 BCE named after the site of Beldibi.
Refers to the period from about 1750 to 1250 BCE in the area of modern Bahrain, Failaka Island, and the eastern coast of Saudi Arabia.
A modern adaptation of sun-dried brick that contains a binder of emulsified asphalt.

Refers to a technique for representing three-dimensional objects in two dimensions by using parallel projecting lines that are perpendicular to the plane of projection or picture surface. Principal surfaces of objects are parallel to the picture plane. It does not include foreshortening, shifts in scale and proportion, or other distortions that would be caused by employing linear perspective. It is often used for technical and architectural drawings, including plans, sections, and elevations. It is also used to create azimuthal projections of the Earth or another heavenly body as seen from space.
A process in which a print, usually a photograph, is permanently adhered to a clear sheet of acrylic. This enhances the perception of color and sharpness, due to the acrylic's refractive qualities.
Rods, sometimes marked with numerals, used for making calculations in ancient East Asia.
Method used for the relative dating of bone by measuring the amount of nitrogen remaining in its collagen, which decomposes at a generally uniform rate.
Testing to determine the components of a material, as in the percentage of pure metal in a specimen of ore, bullion, or alloy.
Chemical analysis on a minute scale.
Small rooms, cubicles, alcoves, or enclosed study desks, such as in libraries, used for individual or semiprivate study.
Method of dating potassium-rich materials or objects by measuring the amount of radioactive decay in the ratio of potassium to argon.

Rooms in which efforts are made to keep contamination out, including atmospheric pollutants, by the use of air filters, mats, or other devices, as in assembly rooms for precision products or computer rooms.
Parts or components of manholes.
Hangers made of metal wire that are attached to the top of the supporting member, bending at a right angle down the face to receive the supported member.
U-shaped joist hangers forming a pocket for attaching a beam or other member, attached to a vertical surface by wings.

Hangers for steel-to-steel or for wood, comprising parallel inverted-U-shaped metal wires or bands joined at the open ends by a flat plate or bar, intended to be suspended from a horizontal member and attached to a horizontal beam or ceiling slab.
Hangers for wood-to-masonry attachments or other materials, designed so that they can be adjusted to a variety of pitch angles.
In construction, hangers designed to attach joists to supporting beams, bearing walls, or other members.
Watercraft engaged in recreational fishing; for vessels engaged in commercial hunting and fishing, use descriptors under "<hunting and commercial fishing vessels>."
Monstrances in which the circular theca is encircled with stylized rays, indicating a glory emanating from the host within. The form dates from the 16th century, and has persisted to the present day.
Parts or components of scaenae.
Refers to the facades of the stage buildings of ancient Roman theaters.
In Indian architecture, a vestibule with nine bays.
Rooms or spaces in buildings that are used for health facilities.
Portions of theater buildings that rise above the stage area and enclose the fly lofts and devices located over the stage; usually found with proscenium theaters.
Parts or components of stages.
Stage podiums of ancient Roman theaters, especially the areas rising above the orchestra. For the stages of ancient Roman theaters, use "proscenia."
Parts or components of bastions.
Entrances into bastions or other outworks of fortifications.
Componenets of battlements.
The open spaces between two merlons or solid portions of battlements or castellated parapets.
Drawings in which lines follow contours of the form across the surface of the form; distinct from "contour drawings," in which lines follow edges of the form.

Dating from the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1912) dynasties, large screen walls built of glazed bricks and tiles with reliefs of nine dragons, an imperial motif in China. These function as symbolic walls demonstrating imperial power, or screen walls, shielding the people behind it from malevolent spirits and influences.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in southwestern Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name, a subgroup of the Luyia living in Kenya east of Lake Victoria and in Uganda.
Plots of land used for the sale or hire of used cars.
Parts or components of upper stages.
Upper stage acting areas, in front of the chamber, of Elizabethan theaters.
Parts or components of tiring houses.
Refers to deep, wide defensive ditches surrounding towns, castles, or houses and usually filled with water.
Grade separations where clearance to traffic on the upper level is obtained by depressing partially or completely the grade of the lower level.
Drawing technique in which lines move in any direction across the form rather than along the edge of it.
Structures supporting a number of railroad signals for several tracks.

Construction employing a horizontally projecting member unsupported at one end. Cantilevers are employed extensively in building construction and in machines. In building, any beam built into a wall and with the free end projecting forms a cantilever. Longer cantilevers are incorporated in a building when clear space is required below, with the cantilevers carrying a gallery, roof, canopy, runway for an overhead travelling crane, or part of a building above.
The filling in of losses and lacunae in the course of virtual anastylosis and virtual restoration.

Refers to drawings, or works in another medium, that are made using oblique perspective, which is a system of linear perspective in which rectangular objects are set at an angle to the picture plane rather than parallel to it. Oblique perspectives may be two-point perspectives, three-point perspectives, or they may use another scheme. For drawings that use oblique projection, where parallel lines remain parallel rather than converging as they recede in space, use "oblique projections."
Computer output devices consisting of flat drawing tables traversed by writing-tool assemblies which produce drawings on paper or film to high-standard accuracy.
Initial or beginning specific conceptual schemes for the organization or appearance of a work or creative endeavor. For preliminary designs expressed in drawings, use "preliminary drawings."

Term used broadly for video art that uses a single electronic source with a single playback system that is exhibited on a single display. An example would be a videotape source being played on a videocassette recorder, being displayed on a single monitor.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Tanzania.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in Nigeria, historically the same group as  the neighboring Tumbuka across the border in what is now modern Tanzania.

Prints made from objects, usually inscriptions and low-relief designs found on stones, bronzes and clayworks. A source surface is washed and damp paper is tamped or pasted on and left to dry, then  blacked with a specially prepared pad imbued with liquid ink, the projecting areas of the surface becoming dark. The resulting rubbing has white impressions where the paper was pressed into the carving surrounded by a black ink field. Easily disseminated, ink rubbings were the primary means of reproducing historical data, poetry, scholastic texts, calligraphy, and imagery throughout China. Due to deterioration of original stones over time, ink rubbings are often the only evidence of a part of China's cultural heritage. The earliest known rubbings of this kind are Buddhist texts made from wood blocks in 8th century Japan. The technique may have been practiced as early as the 2nd century in China, where it was used to disseminate Confucian texts carved on large stones.
Persons that broadcast radio or television programs.

Refers to the style of German faience produced between 1661 and 1806 and largely imitative of blue and white Delft pottery. After circa 1725, pieces are characterized by blue dots applied to a white ground.

Rooms, usually above ground, intended for the protection of people from danger, such as from storms or violence. For below ground spaces for protection from tornadoes and other wind events, use "storm cellars."

In current usage, usually refers to rooms, located in offices or other public or commercial buildings, that are reserved for computer servers and have regulated temperature and humidity suited for the optimum operation and storage of computer equipment. In the recent past, before the advent of networked environments, the term often referred to rooms reserved for a number of stand-alone computers, often in a school or other facility offering training in the use of computers or computer applications; the term may occasionally have this meaning in the present.
In South Indian architecture, a vimāna with detached hāra.
Parts or components of steeples.
Parts or components of façades.
Tiered, semicircular seating areas in ancient, especially Roman, theaters and amphitheaters.
The spaces above the stage behind the proscenium, out of view of the audience, used during a performance for the storage of hanging scenery.
Altering an object by repeating a process that has already been applied to the object.
Process in which organisms or specimens are submerged in an aqueous formaldehyde solution, stabilized with methanol, containing 37 per cent by weight of formaldehyde.
Parts or components of coffered ceilings.
Parts or components of pedestals.

Refers to the middle portion of a pedestal, between the base and the cap. Use also for the lower zone of an interior wall, when given a distinct treatment, as this treatment often resembles a pedestal in appearance. Refers to the middle portion of a pedestal, between the base and the cap. Use also for the lower zone of an interior wall, when given a distinct treatment, as this treatment often resembles a pedestal in appearance.
Wood strips or boards let into the studs to add support for the ends of the joists.
Metal members having a C- or U-shaped section.
Computer drawings when emphasizing that they were produced on a plotter.
The outer surfaces of vaults or arches.
Officially attesting that something is valid or meets a standard, or, with regard to people, that a standard degree of qualification has been met.
Windows having one vertically hung movable sash and one fixed sash.
Term used in the 18th century for commodes with two tiers of drawers set on high legs; term later used for commodes with three or four tiers of drawers.
Manufacturing goods in large quantities so as to attain high rates of output at decreasing unit cost.

In analytical chemistry, sample preparation refers to the phase of scientific investigation that follows sampling and precedes measuring. It encompasses all the processes involved in readying a sample for examination, including extraction from a larger sample, and all the techniques of reduction and processing required to produce a representative test sample.
Masonry joints having no mortar, or having the appearance of no mortar.
Concealed joints in masonry.
Recessed joints designed to give a particular surface appearance of very narrow joints between members.
Parts or components of structural elements.
Supporting elements in the shape of human figures. For piers with engaged figures where the pier, not the statue, supports the entablature, see, for example, "Osiride pillars."
Architectural elements that consist of entire systems to support structures.
Structural members whose primary function is to carry transverse loads.

Series of arches on the same plane and carried on piers, columns, or pilasters; either free-standing or attached to a wall (a "blind arcade"). The term is also used to denote a covered avenue with shops on one or both sides, which originally was set within an architectural arcade. Series of arches on the same plane and carried on piers, columns, or pilasters; either free-standing or attached to a wall (a "blind arcade"). The term is also used to denote a covered avenue with shops on one or both sides, which originally was set within an architectural arcade.
Structures based on a skewed grid of archlike forms, usually wood or metal.
Boiling oil from blubber of marine mammals.

Collectively, the physical elements that constitute an exhibition, including the exhibit design, graphics, lighting, labels, audiovisual components, and exhibit cases, as well as the objects on display.
Infrastructural elements of structures that are built to support the transport of goods and people.
Structures such as a mounds, walls, or fences that act as barriers, particularly within the context of a sporting activity.
Architectural elements or components located on the surface.

Distinct portions, sections, or divisions of a surface, especially when sunk below or raised above the general level or enclosed by a frame or border. Common on walls, ceilings, and doors, and also on furniture pieces.
The business of selling and generally dealing in books.

Rooms designed to house collections of various objects, typically fossils, botanical rarities, shells, taxidermy, horns, tusks, skeletons, minerals, small artworks such as medallions and statuettes, and other items that often had been collected during exploring and trading voyages. Items were typically arranged in cabinets as well as on the walls and ceilings. Popular in 16th- and 17th-century Europe, cabinets of curiosities focused on the strange and unusual, and have been described as the forerunner to the natural history museum and other modern museums.
Plumbing systems used to pump water.
Parts or components of keys.
Keys adapted to open a particular set of locks in a group, distinguished from master keys, which are designed to open all the locks in the group.
Parts or components of structural slabs.
Plates, usually of metal, placed on doors, usually of houses, apartments, or rooms, bearing the occupant's name or other identifiers.

The compass point towards the magnetic pole, to which a compass needle points, or generaly towards or in the direction of the pole on the earth's surface that lies on the earth's axis of rotation and at which the heavens appear to turn anticlockwise about a point directly overhead.
Beams supported at each end so their ends are free to rotate.
Parts or components of spread footings.
Refers to many-storied, skylit spaces in or between high-rise buildings, common since 1960.
Drawings that are produced as a result of training under the tutelage of a master or an institution.
Paintings using gouache, which is opaque color that is ground in water and mixed with glue, such as gum and honey. Gouaches may be classified as either drawings or paintings.
Screws that in connection with wood or metal jaws may be used to provide a clamping force.
Screws each having a recessed head and an X-shaped driving indentation.
Screws that clamp a movable part when it is required to be fixed, or otherwise form a stop, which check the motion or thrust of a mechanism or determine the position to which a part may be moved.

Racks, usually with pegs, knobs, or hooks, from which to hang hats; generally attached to walls or other pieces of furniture. Less elaborate and less likely to be free-standing and furniturelike than "hat stands."
Bars, usually of metal, installed around or near a toilet, or existing as a demountable unit, and used as an assist for lower and raising the body.
Valves controlled by a float in a chamber, such as the float valve in a tank for a toilet.
Rods used as connecting members or braces, especially to counteract the spreading action of vaults or roofs.
Parts or components of defensive walls.
Large, sturdy easels for use in artists' studios.
Parts and components of furniture knees.
The vapor baths or hot plunges in Roman baths.
Grants or gifts of money or other property made by way of financial aid.
Biographies focusing on a few defining events in the life of the subject, conveying the essence and main milestones of a life.
Colors which have hue. All colors have hue except for black, white, and shades of grey.
Manually operated fire alarms, usually boxes with a handle that is pulled.
Hand-held medical tools or implements designed for insertion into and viewing within body orifices. Various forms are based on the specific use.
Generally any substance added to another to to increase its quantity, bulk, or dilution, as in paint, ink, or adhesives.
Chains that can be secured by a slide bolt between a door stile and a door jamb to allow the door to be opened slightly while remaining securely fastened.
Cylindrical bolts that are mounted on a plate having a raised case that contains the bolt and guides it into a recess in a jamb or some other suitable cylindrical socket.
Celtic and Viking interlace incorporating two- or four-legged creatures with ears, biting snout, and tail.

More finished than "preliminary sketches" and more concentrated on one portion of a design than "preparatory drawings." Not appropriate with regard to architecture; then prefer "studies (visual works)" or "detail studies."
Official placements of deceased persons within the canon of saints.
Windows or tracery lights having a curved or inclined bottom caused by, for example, the arched heads of other lights below.
Parts or components of louvers.
Functions or performances that are related to communication or the communications industry.

Roof-like ornamented projections, suspended from one wall or from the ceiling, used in architecture or furniture design, typically placed over a niche, door, window, tomb, etc., to protect it from the sun or elements, or to draw attention to the feature.
An amount of money made available by a governing or funding body of a museum, library, archives, or other agency for expenditure according to established budgetary and accounting practices.

Settlement of disputes, especially between labor and management, by a neutral party authorized to appraise the facts and arguments and make a decision binding upon the disputants. Distinguished from "mediation" in which a neutral party proposes a solution but has no authority to make a binding decision.
Providing direct material aid, most often monetary, to persons, groups, or enterprises, usually for the purpose of supporting or promoting the recipient.
Refers to relatively small instructional sessions or classes emphasizing demonstration and practical application of skills and principles in a specialized field or occupation.

Military strategic plans that are large scale, of long duration, include combat operations in a given area, and incorporate a number of military operations or battles as part of a larger conflict or war.
Upper-story storage spaces for hay in stables or barns.
Curb roofs with all four sides sloping, usually enclosing habitable spaces, and therefore having dormers.
Dimension stone with a smooth exposed face.

Rooftop pavilions intended as lookouts or for the enjoyment of a view. For unroofed platforms, use "widows' walks"; for rooftop structures that are primarily ornamental, use "cupolas," for small pavilions, in a garden setting, intended for enjoyment of a view, use "gazebos."
Ornaments at the ridge or eaves of a roof, in classical architecture and derivatives, that close or conceal the open end of a row of cover tiles.
Parts or components of verges.
Boards that hang from the projecting end of a roof, covering the gables; often elaborately carved and ornamented.

Horizontal slabs or timbers resting on the tie beams of a roof, supporting the lower ends of common rafters directly above the wall; used in cantilevered hips to support loose timbers. Horizontal slabs or timbers resting on the tie beams of a roof, supporting the lower ends of common rafters directly above the wall; used in cantilevered hips to support loose timbers.
Volatile liquid used as a dilutent in the making of butyl rubber.
A hydrocarbon petroleum distillate, used as a dry-cleaning fluid and as a solvent for varnishes and paint.
Metal coffee- or teapots of French origin with straight handles perpendicular to the reservoir.
Building systems that secure or protect a premises from unwanted intruders.
Installations of automatic sprinklers, foam distribution systems, fire hoses, and/or portable fire extinguishers designed for extinguishing fires.
Polyhedrons having one face (the base) that is a polygon of any number of sides, and the other faces are triangles with bases forming the sides of the polygon meet at a common vertex.
In Indian architecture, divisions created by walls.
Hardness of a substance measured by an indenter, such as a diamond point, that penetrates microscopic areas.
Refers to the ratios of pressure force to viscous force in fluid mechanics.

Any interaction that, when unopposed, will change the motion of an object; force may be an agency or influence (as a push or pull) that, if applied to a free body, results chiefly in an acceleration of the body and sometimes in elastic deformation and other effects. Equations differ in ancient, pre-Newtonian, and Newtonian understandings of force.
Geometric figures having four equal sides and equal opposite angles, particularly where there are no right angles, as contrasted with a square; an oblique equilateral parallelogram.
Ceremonial namings of people, animals, or things, such as ships.

The festive period of balls, masquerades, parades, and general revelry held in the pre-Lenten season, over periods of time ranging from between Christmas and Shrove Tuesday to the last few days before Lent, varying from one country or city to another. For traveling or seasonal amusement enterprises consisting of sideshows, games of chance, rides, and other similar entertainments, use "carnivals."
The sum total of ways of living, artifacts, customs, and so on, built up by a group of people and transmitted from one generation to another.
Collocates descriptors for concepts related to the nature and phenomena of electrical action.
Parapets or low screens composed of balusters and carrying a rail or other horizontal member that is usually heavy in proportion to the balusters themselves.
Railings that are intended to be grasped by the hand in order to serve as a support; may also refer to the top members of balustrades or railings.
Indigenous, traditional religious beliefs and practices of the peoples of Africa south of the Sahara, which are not homogeneous across cultures but share certain commonalities in world view.

Refers to the doctrines of the Alexandrian priest Arius (ca. 250-ca. 336), which denied that Jesus was of the same substance as God and stated instead that he was only the highest of created beings. As such, the Son was not co-equal or co-eternal with the Father. According to the Arians, Jesus was created- not begotten- by God and he achieved his divinity through his perfect obedience to God. Arius' doctrine was condemned as heretical at a synod in Alexandria in 321 and definitively at the Council of Nicaea in 325. Arianism maintained a foothold in many Germanic nations. The Arian controversy was revived at different times and was eventually superseded by Unitarianism.
Culture of a religious group in Syria that had originated in Shiite Islam but separated from other Shiite groups in the 9th-10th centuries.

Branch of Judaism that most staunchly adheres to traditional beliefs and practices, characterized by the belief in the immutability and supreme authority of the Written Law and Oral Law as the fundamental basis of religious observance, by resistance to modernization, by strict conformity to daily worship and dietary laws, by the regular study of the Torah, by the observance of the Sabbath, and by the separation of men and women in the synagogue. This branch of Judaism often disputes the legitimacy of other Jewish groups on the issues that transgress Orthodox Jewish law such as non-Orthodox marriages or divorce.

A Hindu-oriented movement that arose in the 1930s in Hyderabad out of the vivid religious experiences of a merchant named Dada Lekhraj. Lekhraj, using the new name of Prajapita Brahma, encouraged the movement's leadership to pass to female followers, where it still remains. In this millennial movement, the traditional roles of husbands and wives have been reversed. The Hindu belief in the possibility of escape from samsara is rejected in favor of a belief in a golden age that will follow our present age of decline, ending in a nuclear catastrophe. Only purified souls will continue to exist in this golden age and these souls will live as deities in a state of complete happiness. Followers recommend a lifestyle of vegetarianism, abstinence from alcohol and cigarettes, and celibacy with a large emphasis placed on meditation and yoga as ways to attain mental union with God. Their ideas are circulated in the form of messages or 'murlis' that are delivered daily at Brahma Kumari centers throughout the world. Followers have recently become active in the United Nations, for instance they inspired the Global Co-operation Movement. Current headquarters are located at Mount Abu in Rajasthan, India.

Any of the movements stemming from the more radical elements of the 16th-century Reformation that insisted that only adult baptism is valid and that true Christians should not hold government office, use force, or bear arms. Followers of these movements, also known as Rebaptizers, emphasize strict church discipline, adherence to scripture, and the separation of church and state. Anabaptists frequently suffered persecution as a result of their criticism of government; they are often considered the forerunners of the Baptists.

Name applied by followers of Mahayana Buddhism to the ancient, more orthodox schools of Buddhism predating the rise of Mahayana ideas. Although the name reflects the Mahayanists' evaluation of their own traditions as a superior model, surpassing other schools in its universal benevolence, it is not used by the conservative schools as a proper term referring to the common tradition of Buddhism. Modern upholders of the ancient Hinayana tradition are called Theravadins (followers of the Way of the Elders) and practice Theravada Buddhism.

General term for ascending series or flights of steps; utility constructions using steps and designed to bridge a vertical distance. A stairs is a construction or contrivance comprising a change of elevation consisting of one or more risers, as defined by the International Code Council.
Stairs which turn 180 degrees as they progress from bottom to top.
Stairs with landings at which the stair turns 180 degrees.
Parts or components of newels.
Turned wood collars used to lengthen the base of a newel.
Filmmakers who make motion pictures without financial backing from a major studio. Generally they retain a greater degree of artistic control over their projects than do studio filmmakers.
Successions of connected rooms, generally on one floor, that are occupied as one unit.
Roofed shelters for automobiles, often without walls; usually associated with or projecting from a separate building.
The main inner halls of Roman houses having a compluvium (opening in the roof) for rainwater and an impluvium (rectangular basin) to collect the water.

Production of a document surrogate which summarizes the subject matter or describes other essential qualities of the document. For the process of making visual forms less representational, see "abstraction."
Dividing and assigning according to some rule of proportional distribution.
Continuous recesses or grooves built into walls to receive pipes, ducts, and other elements.
General term for rooms or other accomodations intended to provide basic conveniences for day-to-day life, such as sleeping, eating, and relaxing.
Large rooms designed for formal dancing or any room in which balls are routinely held.
Rooms whose purpose is the formal reception of guests, tradesmen, and other visitors.

Rooms or entire buildings designed for a variety of activities such as would occur on a stage before a seated audience; for rooms or buildings used only for theatrical performances, use "theaters;" for rooms with fixed seating designed for lectures, use "lecture halls."
Rooms or other areas, above or below ground, that are reserved for burial, generally intended to accomodate one or a small number of bodies.
Refers to altarpieces composed of a single panel, rather than multiple panels.
Parts or components of window frames.
Particular arrangements of vertical elements of a building as seen by observers from the primary street view.
Concepts related to the universe beyond the earth's atmosphere.

Use with reference to perspective systems for the line in which the horizontal plane containing the eye meets the picture plane and for the line containing the vanishing points of horizontal planes in the picture.
Parts or components of shafts.
In columns, concave sweep where the shaft springs from the base or terminates in the capital; also, hollows or scotias beneath the echinus of some Archaic Doric capitals.
Of people or animals, the state or attribute of being quick to attack or otherwise take the offensive position.
Plates or boxes containing a handle or grip that are mortised into the edge of doors that open by sliding along a track.
Hangers made from thin strips of material.
Special clips used on the back of gypsum board in certain applications, as in some demountable partitions, to hold the board in place by insertion into slots or other receptacles in the framing.
Concepts related to the transport of people.
The passage of people or vehicles along routes of transportation. Also, vehicles or pedestrians in transit.
Colonization and contamination of surfaces, as on machinery or other structures, by a diversie array of living organisms; especially after prolonged immersion in water.
In Spanish colonial areas, taxes that were collected on products that were imported and exported through the ports.
In traditional Indian art and dance, an active, standing pose with one leg bent and the other outstretched. An example of usage is when depicting a deity trampling an adversary.
A set of orders of architecture, typically reserved for the five orders of architecture known in ancient Greece and Rome, usually including Ionic, Doric, Corinthian, Composite, and Tuscan.
Door latches whose spring bolts are operated by one or more knobs, but whose dead bolts are actuated by a key.
Small and simple lift-latches used to secure cupboards, cabinets, gates, or other doors.
Hand-forged pulls mounted with plates shaped like balls with single spear points projecting from them; similar to onion pulls.
Refers to handles used for pulling open a door or drawer. These are usually in the form of a hollow convex piece of metal, and were originally designed for use as grips on storage bins.

Drawings, prints, or other media in which the projectors are perpendicular to the plane of projection (drawing surface), that is, a three-dimensional object is shown fully frontally at all points, with no indication of recession into depth.
Occasions of shaking or trembling of earth, divisible into two major types, volcanic or tectonic, according to the major precipitating factor.
Masonry joint in which the mortar is flush at the edges, but with a concave groove is added, centered along the joint.

Describes shipping with inland navigation vessels for the transportation of goods and people on rivers, lakes and other inland waterways. Inland navigation vessels are used to transport cargo from and to sea-going ships, but also for conveyance of goods and passengers between places that are connected by inland waterways.
Standards of judgment or authority, such as a test, criterion, or means of discrimination.
Use to describe projects or buildings when there is a highly site-intensive mixture of several different, major, revenue-producing functions involved.
Describes an enclosed empty space in architecture, sculpture, or painting which makes an essential contribution to the composition.
Persons who use movement, gesture, facial expressions, speaking, and intonation to create a fictional character for the stage, motion pictures, or television.
Damage caused by bats, usually chewing damage or damage from droppings.
Doors of two or more hinged leaves which open by bringing the leaves into parallel positions.
Observances, usually celebratory in nature, marking the anniversary of someone's birth.
Holidays established by legal authority and characterized by legal restrictions on work and transaction of official business.

Structures housing entry doors that are attached to the main door to form an interlocking system of two sets of doors, or occasionally revolving doors, such as in churches, theaters, banks, clean rooms in laboratories, ships, etc. In secure systems, it is required that the exterior door is closed before the interior door is opened. Even if this security measure is not employed (such as in a church), the system serves to protect the interior from outside weather, light, and noise. It differs from a vestibule in that a vestibule is part of the floor plan, designed as integral to and attached to the architecture, while an entry cubicle is primarily separate and attached to the architectural entrance.
The vertical pieces of a door to which the lock is fastened.
In Indian architecture, a door-jamb carved with goblins/bhūtas.
Use generally for occurrences of physical combat between or among people furnished with weapons.
Public sales of property to the highest bidder, as by successive increased bids. May refer to a single sales event as well as to multiple sales over a period of time.
Formal introductions of a major work into public use with appropriate ceremonies, as the opening of a building or park, the unveiling of a statue, fountain, or other work.

Events during which parties compete for an honor, job, or the like. A prime example is in the context of art and architecture, where a competition is a formal process by which competing architects or artists submit plans, and often budgets and other information, to the same client or patron for the same architectural or artistic project. For the physical works produced by the competition, use "competitions (object groupings)."
In Indian architecture, a śālā-roof over entry; small entry-gate usually with gala-roof (Tamilnadu) or with eave-cornice (Karnataka).
Parts or components of gateways.
Performances typically involving rhythmical skipping and stepping, with regular turnings and movements of the limbs and body, usually to the accompaniment of music.
Processions associated with a funeral or memorial event, often but not always with the coffin accompanying the participants.
Glazed panels, usually set flush with the ceiling, serving to admit light to the room below.
Days of celebration observed by followers of Christianity.
Windows that swing on hinges, fixed to the sides, top, or bottom of the frame; the sash can open inward or outward.
Semicircular windows over doors or other openings with radiating bars giving the appearance of an open fan.
Any windows used or designed for the display of goods or advertising material, whether fully or partly enclosed or entirely open at the rear; may have a platform raised above street level.
Large gates or passages generally linking the inner and outer works of fortresses and suitable for the use of troops making a sortie.
Drawings done when an architectural design is more developed than at the stage of conceptual and schematic drawings but is not yet to the stage of working drawings.
Windows with sashes that open inward on hinges placed at the bottom of each sash.

Traveling or seasonal amusement enterprises, consisting of sideshows, games of chance, rides, and other similar entertainments. For the festive period of balls, masquerades, parades, and general revelry held in the pre-Lenten season, use "Carnival (pre-Lenten festival)."
Sets of visual works comprising digital descriptions for various aspects of a work of architecture or other works.
Social gatherings of guests invited to a dinner.
Game in which one player is blindfolded, and tries to catch and identify any one of the others, who, on their part, push him about, and make sport with him.
Axonometric projection in which the three spatial axes are equally inclined to the plane of projection or drawing surface.
Acts or procedures of putting a person or animal to death by fire or extreme heat, whether as a judicial punishment, sacrifice, or torture. Examples include burning at the stake.
The movement of acoustic energy, by wave motion, through a medium.
Having or characterized by a moderately low temperature, but not so low as indicated by "cold."
Concepts related to technical processes or knowledge.

The application of microelectronics, computers, telecommunication, and other automation methods or technology to the organization, storage, retrieval, and dissemination of information, including aural, pictorial, textual, and numeric information.
Refers to the underlying foundation or basic framework of a system or organization, especially the services and facilities which are an integral part of the life in an urban community.
Force that tends to impel matter outward from a center of rotation.
Origin of a work of writing, music, or art; frequently used for the profession of writing itself.

Describes a technique for creating the illusion of continuous tones or color depth by mixing dots of color from a limited palette. The term is generally used in the context of digital imaging or computer graphics, and can be applied to color or black and white images.
Critical concept relating to the tendency of thinkers, artists, architects, and writers to rebel against the perceived theories and practices of modernity and Modernism.
Hand gestures that developed in Naples and are used elsewhere in Italy; often accompanied by facial expressions, used alone or with spoken language.
The degree of acid content of a substance. Use particularly with reference to solutions having a pH value less than 7.
The ease with which an electrical current will pass through a material.
The property of being hard and rigid with little tensile strength, tending to break readily with a comparatively smooth fracture.
Any change of form, shape, or dimensions produced in a body by a stress or force without a breach of the continuity of its parts.
Having the property of color change, due to chemical impurities or optical effects.
Fluorescence stimulated by x-rays; when the emissions are examined by spectrometry, useful in determining chemical composition of a substance.
A surface finish effect that approximates the lustre of pearl or mother of pearl for decorative effect.
Luminescence produced when a substance is bombarded with cathode rays.
The temperature at which a liquid begins to cloud.

In design, the positioning of two elements set facing each other, such as two mirror-image figures facing toward each other. Examples are in heraldry and architectural ornament. For two figures set back-to-back, use "addorsed."
Balanced arrangement of compositional units on either side of a central axis.

A technique of lacquer decoration employing gold and silver foil inlay where coats of lacquer are applied over the decoration and then polished to expose the design. It was sometimes used with "maki-e". This technique originated in China, where it was known as "p'ing-t'o", and came to Japan in the Nara period (710-794). Since the Heian period (794-1185), the term "kanagai" has also been used to refer to this technique.
Having an angle or angles, sharp-cornered.
Canon of proportion based on the ratio between two unequal parts of a whole when the proportion of the smaller to the larger is equal to that of the larger to the whole.
Scale converting the units of a bar scale or numeric scale into another set of units, for example "30 palmi = 114 mm."
The quality or state in a painting or of an object due to the use of optical illusions, manipulated surfaces, or discordantly juxtaposed images.

The illusion of or erroneous perception of perspective; usually characterized by a subtly distorted depiction of three-dimensional objects, spatial relationships, and color, and by the perversion of the linear perspectival system.

Refers to the effect of suggesting pictorial depth by depicting more distant things with less clarity of outline and detail. Where color is involved, distant objects may be indicated by alteration of hue toward blue, and decrease of color saturation and value contrast.

Refers to perspective depicted by using a single vanishing point. The technique was codified by the Renaissance artist and theoretician, Leon Battista Alberti, who described a visual pyramid, the vertex of which is in the viewer's eye. The illusion of recession into space is produced by parallel lines converging at one vanishing point, which was usually at or near the center of the composition and was at that time called the "centric point." Alberti described how to determine the correct intervals for horizontal lines at progressively deeper positions in space, and how to draw objects and figures to the correct scale for their position in space.
The quality of having a surface diversified with small projections, points, and irregularities so as to be harsh or uneven to the sight or touch.

Loads applied to a structure or object from a blast wave, which is described by the combination of overpressure and either impulse or duration that causes catastrophic damage to the building both externally and internally.
The imposed force of pressure by air in motion that is supported by a structure or body.
Stress developed at the point of contact between two loaded structural members.
The overloading or overstraining of buildings to such an extent that they can no longer perform their required functions.
Genre that depicts or evokes idyllic life in the country; in works of pictorial art, often scenes of shepherds and shepherdesses in idealized arcadian landscapes.
General term for built works, often local and of nonestablished style, where the architect is unknown and typically unknowable.
Any art which deals with the final doom or ultimate destiny of the world, including that in the Biblical story of Armageddon in the Book of Revelations.

Nose art is the name given to the talismanic graffiti painted by war theater servicemen on the fuselage of military aircraft, usually located near the nose, for the purpose of individualizing aircraft.

Term coined by the architectural historian Charles Jencks to describe design which comes about, not by formulating new solutions to problems, but by combining pre-existing elements to achieve a new result.

Characterized by the use of simple geometric forms placed in nonillusionistic space and combined into nonobjective compositions, geometric abstraction evolved as the logical conclusion of the Cubist destruction and reformulation of the established conventions of form and space.

Refers to illusionistic effects on two- or three-dimensional art works or architecture, in which the appearance of marble is simulated by painting. For example, wooden or plaster columns or paneling may be painted to imitate the color and graining of marble, which would be a more costly and desirable material. It is distinguished from "scagliola," in which the effect of marbling is achieved by mixing pigment directly with the wet plaster, and then applying the plaster to the surface.
Extreme form of realism that repudiates idealization, nobility, and heroism in visual art, literature, and theater, aiming to reproduce exact descriptions or appearances of even repugnant subjects.
Strength or purity of a color, determined by the quality of light reflected from it; a vivid color is of high intensity, a dull color of low intensity.

The process of removing gathered matter from a binding in preparation for rebinding usually involving removal of covers, spine lining, and old glue, cutting the sewing threads, and separating all sections from each other. Where a discrete bibliographic item has been removed from a binding with the intention that it should stand alone thereafter, use "disbinding." To describe gathered matter that has never been bound, but rather left in sheets, signatures, or gatherings, use "unbound."
Administration by the principal division of a country.
Trade in furs. An example is historic trading in North America in which pelts were exchanged for money or goods at trading stations.
Vaults in which the rows of bricks are laid at a slight inclination, leaning against the previously laid row, thus obviating the need for formwork.
Tapestry weaving technique in which the weft threads of two adjacent areas are linked together either around a common end, or more normally between adjacent ends in either a single or double lock.
Parts or components of capitals.
Substructures supporting the columns of Greek temples.
Wood or metal arches that are hinged at the two springing points and at the crown.
Arches which deflect the weight off of another arch, opening, or other structural member located beneath.
Arches with intradoses having a greater radius at one face of the arch than at the other.

A biological treatment for copper alloys involving the conversion of existing corrosion patinas into more stable copper oxalates using the unique properties of carefully selected fungal strains. The cooper oxalate forms a protective layer that passivates the surface to prevent any exchange of copper ions and water.
Strategy of critical analysis arising in the mid-20th century, directed toward exposing unquestioned assumptions and internal contradictions in philosophical and literary language.

A term used by Spanish observers of Taino ceremonial rituals. These were gatherings that might include music, song, dance and pantomime applied to religious liturgies, magical rites, and epic narratives of tribal history, but most particularly refers to a type of call-and-response song-poem accompanied by dance.
Precipitation in the form of spherical or irregular pellets of ice larger than five millimeters in diameter.
A wind blowing from the north.
Statistical data of a population, especially relating to density, growth, distribution, and vital statistics.
Type of use of a lot or parcel of real property.
The use of a lot or parcel of real property for farming or agriculture.
Arrival into a country, area, or abode for the purpose of permanent residence.
Migration within a country or region from towns or cities to rural areas.
An increase in the total number of individuals of a given species or other class of organism in a defined area.

Support for developing countries, international organizations and non-governmental organizations to improve their ability to implement and observe goals and treaty or charter obligations. Capacity building focuses on identifying obstacles to success and developing strategies to overcome them. Capacity-building programs are generally supplied by multilateral and regional organizations, multilateral banks or bilateral programs.

Community development which focuses on minimizing urban sprawl and environmentally damaging development, promoting greenbelt protection, pedestrian and rural areas, and restoring vitality to center cities and older communites through adaptive reuse and the use of infill development.
Removing a slum by demolishing it, or altering it by correcting the conditions that caused it.
Activity of dividing an area of land into smaller parcels for lots, blocks, streets, open spaces, and public areas, and the designation of the location of utilities and other services.
Additions or details added to a work after the work was complete, usually signfying an addition that is inappropriate, superfluous, or in poor taste; generally used with architecture or sculpture.
The state or status of legal dissolution of marriage by a court or other authoritative body, or according to forms recognized by a country, nation, culture, or tribe.
The social class comprising people of gentle birth and breeding, immediately below the nobility.
A state or commonwealth's members' taking part in the political processes that lead to the selection of political leaders and determine or influence public policy.

Social, political, and economic system of racial segregation, assigning rights to classes of people based on their racial background, supremacy being granted to those of white European extraction, with laws limiting the political participation and economic advancement of those of African, Asian, and mixed race.
An appropriation or giving up of property to public use that precludes the owner from asserting any right of ownership inconsistent with the use for which the property is dedicated.
Charges upon real or personal property for the satisfaction of some debt or duty ordinarily arising by operation of law.

Movable works or built works, or parts of works, having archaeological or ethnological value to a particular culture, often subject to export restrictions of the particular country where they were created or discovered. Includes property having significant importance to the cultural heritage of a people, such as monuments of architecture, art or history, whether religious or secular; archaeological sites; groups of buildings which, as a whole, are of historical or artistic interest, works of art, artifacts, manuscripts, books and other objects of artistic, historical or archaeological interest; as well as scientific collections and important collections of books or archives.

In the US, sites that are eligible for inclusion in the National Register because of their association with cultural practices or beliefs of a living community that are rooted in that community's history, and are important in maintaining the continuing cultural identity of the community.
As related to copyright, refers to the right to perform music or another form of performance in public. The right is usually held by the creator, including a composer or lyricist, and the publisher.
Statements that each of two expressions is equal to the other.
Fixed reference lines for the measurement of coordinates.

Lines having a locus that may be conceived to be traced by a moving point, the direction of motion continuously changing or deviating from a straight line. A closed curve is a path that repeats itself, and thus encloses one or more regions; simple examples include circles, ellipses, and polygons. Open curves such as parabolas, hyperbolas, and spirals have infinite length.

In geometry, a digons are polygons with two sides or edges and two vertices; pairs of vertices connected by two edges. A digon is degenerate in a Euclidean space, but may be non-degenerate in a spherical space.
In statistics, the set of values, together with their relative frequencies, of any variable.
A series of numbers in which each number is the sum of the two preceding numbers.
The state of being under a legal process because of insolvency, or otherwise unable to pay debts.
Compensation derived from a share of profits from a whaling or fishing voyage, distributed to officers and crew.
Prices arising from a situation in which supply and demand are matched and prices stable.
A price per year or term of years paid for the right to occupy and improve a piece of land.
Used generally for city, town, borough, or village finance.

The right to own a particular property, where that ownership is regularly evidenced and capable of recognition and enforcement in a court of law. The law typically considers the legal title as resting in the last party to whom it was transmitted by descent or by purchase through a regularly connected chain of transmission from the original source of title.

The financial grants awarded to members of a college or university graduate community for a limited number of years, on condition of pursuing some specified branch of study. Distinct from scholarships in that fellowships are given to members of graduate communities, rather than undergraduates, and the course of study is specified.
Use generally for opposition to the use of idols. For more vehement movements against religious images, use "iconoclasm."
Representation of characteristics of Asian art or culture appearing in Western practice.
The practice of referring to intangible or religious concepts through architectural proportion or repetition of forms in works of art.
Objects, and sometimes animals or plants, closely associated with a specific person or deity and used in an image to identify that figure.
In recent architectural theory, the consideration of loads and stresses in architectural designs.
Literary device in which a painting, sculpture, or other work of visual art is described in detail; the work may be real or imaginary. In original usage, was undertaken as a rhetorical exercise.

Genre encompassing forms of theatre, literature, and improvisation with the basic objective to amuse, humor, and induce laughter. In general, it is often contrasted with tragedy and can be applied in the form of social criticism through satire and political or intellectual wit or applied in the form of pure spectacle through farce or burlesque.
A genre of that concerns accounts of the lives of the saints. For written examples of this genre, prefer "hagiographies (literary works)."

Form of comic Japanese theater performed since the 14th century. It developed alongside Noh theatre and often used to be performed as a light-hearted interlude, consisting of one scene, between acts of Noh. In the present, these plays are also often performed separately. This type of theater relies on mime, dialogue and fixed stereotypes of characters.
Fiction in which crime is the central theme.

Folk tales of mythical figures who are comical or deceitful; the tales are amusing yet also serve to highlight important social values. Typical characters include Br'er Rabbit, Coyote, Til Eulenspiegel, Badger, and Ananse.
Poetry in honor of a married couple and marriage; by traditional convention, composed and delivered at a wedding celebration.

Dutch literary movement of the 1880s, the members of which were young writers and poets determined to express real emotions in highly individualistic language, avoiding cliché and traditional rhetoric. Notable members included Willem Kloos, Jacques Perk, Frederik van Eeden, and Hélène Swarth.

Violation of trust or confidence or an abandonment of something committed to one's charge, such as a revelation or divulging of something which it is desirable to keep secret or a treacherous giving up to an enemy.
Ethics that have as their utilitarian end the well-being and fair treatment of the entire community.

Originally in ancient Greece, a form of logical argumentation proceeding by question and answer.  In modern times it is the idea that internal contradictions are transcended, but then give rise to new contradictions that themselves must be resolved. As a concept of evolution, it applies to diverse fields including philosophy, nature, and history.
A theory of art which maintains that the philosophy of art is separate from any other philosophy and that art can be judged only by its own standards.
Ideas and notions that are fundamentally religious.
Doctrine affirming that the existence of God is possible, but denying that there are any sufficient reasons for holding either that God does or does not exist.

Refers generally to the prescribed rites of formal and public worship, typically including words, music, symbolic aids, and ritual actions. The diverse forms of liturgy reflect the needs and attitudes of different religious communities. The term can also refer more specifically to the Christian rite of the Eucharist.
Concepts related to study of computation theory and computer design.
Energy in the process of transfer between a system and its surroundings as a result of temperature differences.
Use with reference to the natural light of day; for the direct light of the sun specifically, use "sunlight."
The perceived result of rays of light turned back when they strike a surface and are not absorbed, as from a mirror.
The points of brightest reflection of light off an object; use also for the areas of brightest value in a picture, whether achieved by brightening or by leaving white areas of the support.
Pressure exerted in every direction at any given point by the weight of the atmosphere.

Highly energetic electromagnetic radiation with a very short wavelength emitted during radioactive decay. Gamma rays are essentially very short x-rays and penetrate matter deeply. Gamma radiation is used in radiography and as an exterminant and sterilizing agent, which kills insects, molds, bacteria, or fungi.
Refers to the process of creating data models in software engineering by applying formal techniques such as probability theory and statistics.
Refers to documentary methods and techniques engaged to provide a detailed record of a particular piece of land, for example an archaeological site.

Actions required to arrive at a design. A design method is a structured approach or method for designing and building objects or structures. The techniques of a design process may include: defining problems, conducting research, brainstorming and conceptualizing, prototyping, selecting and finalizing, product analysis and improvement.

Publishing text or images in electronic machine-readable formats; included are databases, magazines, and other works published online or in other media, current or historical, including magnetic tapes, compact disks, floppy disks, etc.

A systematic approach to recording and presenting information that provides a summation of the cultural character, significance, and workings of a place. It encompasses a wide range of techniques and activities from community-based participatory data collection and management to sophisticated mapping using GIS (Geographic Information Systems).
The process by which the performance of a professional person is evaluated by a group of independent experts in the same field.
Structural examination with the aim of obtaining information on the variation of composition with depth below the initial surface.

Writing produced involuntarily, when the subject's attention is focused elsewhere, performed in a waking or hypnotic state. In the late 19th century, automatic writing was frequently attributed to supernatural forces. In the 20th century, it has been viewed as an internal phenomenon, specifically in relation to theories of the personality. The Surrealists adopted this technique with the hopes that it would assist in tapping the unconscious.
Mining method in which surface soil and rock are removed in successive strips to reveal minerals beneath.
The technique for dating that examines the relation between elapsed time and the degradation of amino acids in proteins, specifically the racemization of amino acids in collagen.

The action of managing or keeping something in good order for optimum efficiency or performance. In conservation, the care and maintenance of historic heritage sites and collections with an emphasis on preventive preservation.
Violent, destructive whirling winds, accompanied by funnel-shaped clouds, that progress in a narrow path over the land.
Rites or observances related to the construction of a building.
Design competitions offering a compromise between open and invited competitions; entry is available only to a portion of a profession, for example only to those within a limited geographic area.
Exhibitions featuring works of art.
International expositions that feature exhibits on arts, agriculture, science, and industry, with participants from around the world.
Meetings of two or more people for discussing matters of common concern, usually a formal or public exchange of views.
Formal meetings at which several specialists deliver short addresses on a topic or on related topics.
Tours in which the means of travel is walking on foot.
Notes added as comment or explanation, such as those accompanying an entry in a bibliography, reading list, or catalogue intended to describe, explain, or evaluate the publication referred to.
Greek and Latin papyri that contain literary works or fragments thereof.

The design, graphic forms, or shapes of letters or symbols, either as written by hand or as represented in a particular type font. Referenced most often in the fields of typography, paleography, calligraphy, and epigraphy.
Small cardboard folders into which paper matches are stapled or glued.
Concepts related to the the transmission and reception of information, including but not limited to science and technology.

Refers to the gradual development of living organisms over successive generations, from lower to higher forms, especially as articulated in Darwinian theory or in alternatives to or modifications of Darwinian theory.
Medical conditions or diseases that are not transmissible between people or other species.

Persistent mental disorder or derangement. The terms ‘insane,’ ‘insanity’ are commonly used informally to denote mental instability or mental illness but can be considered offensive. The medical profession favors use of the terms ‘mental disorder’ or ‘psychopathology.’ The term can be used in a descriptive or historical context, in which case the use of quotation marks is suggested.
The faculty of perception with the eyes.
Belonging to or of the nature of a hermaphrodite, combining male and female characteristics.
The doctrine that mental and moral phenomena may be accounted for by association of ideas.
A subjective state of feeling defined as good or beneficial.
The reception and accommodation of guests, visitors, or strangers in a generous and welcoming manner.

The process by which an ordered structure within input data (e.g., speech, blocks of text, images) is recognized as a meaningful array distinct from surrounding stimuli. While first recognized and studied as a mental process, pattern recognition is now most widely pursued by computer science and engineering in attempts to create artificial perceptual systems.

The bodily and emotional experience consisting of physiological and affective responses to an undesirable event. Often serves as a warning mechanism that protects an organism from the threat of injury or potential injury by stimulating a withdrawing response from harmful stimuli.
Sexuality characterized by romantic love or sexual desire toward members of the opposite sex.
State, condition, or behavior having to do with sexual attraction or sexual relations between men.
Physics concepts that deal with energy.
Power produced by converting the potential power of natural stream flow into energy, usually electricity.
Energy in the form of a stationary electric charge.
Disposal of the wastewater of a community.
Generally, transportation in urban areas, whether by transit systems or private means.

The act, process, or policy of prohibition of the production, distribution, circulation, or access to a work, or the suppression or deletion of parts of a work, on the grounds that the work contains material or is of an appearance considered politically or morally offensive by some.
Actions or instances of deceit, trickery, or breach of confidence used to acquire unfair or dishonest advantage or material gain.
The practice of stealing money or other items by stealth from another person's pockets or bags.
Economic, religious, or racial discrimination against Jews.

Systematic use of terror, violence, and intimidation against people, usually civilians, or property to create a general climate of fear in a population. The purpose of terrorism is typically to bring about a particular political or social objective.

Violence and intimidation by revolutionaries seeking the complete abolition of a national regime or political system, and its replacement with new structures. Modern instances of such activity include campaigns in the Russian revolution and by the Italian Red Brigades.
Wars characterized by hit-and-run tactics by small, mobile groups of irregular forces operating in territory controlled by a hostile regular force.
Climatic conditions of a particular geological epoch, also known as geologic climate.
Refers to the aggregates of human-made structures, infrastructural elements, and associated spaces and features.
Noise produced by land, air and water vehicles and navigational devices such as foghorns.
Contamination of the unconsolidated material on the earth's surface formed by the weathering of rock and that portion of the earth's surface that can support plant life.
Smoke-filled fog that contaminates the air, most often originating over industrial sites and cities.
Control and reduction of smoke, particularly smoke from industry, in an environment.
The ratio of the amount of water vapor in the air to the amount which would be present at the same temperature were the atmosphere to be fully saturated.

Branch of linguistics where the primary aim is to establish universal principles for the study of language and languages, and to determine the underlying structure and other characteristics of human language.
Branch of linguistics concerned with the use of computers for the analysis and synthesis of language data, as in translation, word frequency counts, and speech recognition and synthesis.
Study of writing systems and of their relation to speech.
The discipline of describing, interpreting, and evaluating literary works, including the exposition of principles, methods, and theories for the analysis of such works.
The study and practice of the administration of museums.

Field of study developed by Austrian educator and philosopher Rudolf Steiner (1861-1925) to develop a scientific and intuitive faculty of cognition and the realization of spiritual reality. Students were said to acquire ultrasensitive perception by means of a type of meditation. It was greatly influenced by the religious ideology theosophy.
The branch of metaphysics concerned with the nature and relations of being.
Branches of learning devoted to religion.

Comparative study of the characteristics of religious systems in different societies that focuses on the origin and evolution of religious beliefs and practices from earlier or less urbanized societies to modern ones, aims to develop a universal evolutionary continuum of religions, and stresses a scientific methodology. For the comparative study of religions that largely disregards evolutionary schemes and features a primarily historical methodology, use "religious history."
Study of the history of the Christian Church and its sects and branches.

The scientific, historic, or comparative study of the origins, characteristics, and functions of human cultures and societies. For the study of the history and culture of ethnic groups within a larger cultural or social order, use "ethnic studies."
Branch of anthropology dealing with fossil remains of the human species and its predecessors.
The study of animal remains, especially bones, in an archaeological context, that is in the context of human development and culture.
Business of receiving and safeguarding money on deposit, loaning money, extending credit, and facilitating the transfer of funds by check, draft, or exchange.

Refers to the profession concerned with the systematic transmission of entertainment, information, advertising, and educational programming by radio or television for simultaneous reception by a scattered public audience.

Communicaton to a mass audience of news and related commentary through prints, photographs, or other images, without accompanying text or with written material subordinate to the pictorial elements. Where the images comprise only modern photographs, "photojournalism (discipline)" is more commonly used.
Branch of education covering kindergarten or grade 1 through grades 6, 7, or 8.

Study and explanation of the spatial, organizational, and behavioral patterns of people across the natural and built landscapes; includes the methods and theories of behavioral geography, cognitive geography, economic geography, marketing and decision theory, and locational analysis. For the sociological study of individuals and their near environment, use "human ecology."
Branch of history that deals with the evolution of ideas, how these ideas were influenced by various factors, and what happens to these ideas or thoughts among people in a given society.
Field of law dealing with matters relating to the environment and environmental legislation.
Study of the geographic aspects of political phenomena, including the geographical bases of the power of nations, and geographic influences on power relationships in international politics.
Branch of psychology dealing with the minds and behavior of ethnic groups.

The interdisciplinary study of the mutually adaptive interrelationship of individuals and their near environment; involves aspects of demographics, home economics, housing, design, social services, and family behavior. For the study of the broader spatial and organizational patterns of people across the landscape, use "human geography."
Science and practice of controlled flight through the air.
Science and discipline of breeding, raising, feeding, and tending animals, especially but not exclusively domestic farm animals.
Discipline concerned with the structure, function, and development of the cells, tissues, and organs constituting the animal body.
Branch of anatomy that studies bone structure and function. In paleontology, the interpretation of skeletal remains of past populations of organisms.
Branch of biology dealing with life forms living in the sea and on shore and the features of their environment that affect them.
The branch of science that studies the use of plants and plant products in human societies.
The branch of zoology that studies reptiles and amphibians.

The study and practice of the application of engineering principles and techniques to biological and medical problems, such as the biosynthesis of animal and plant products, erosion control using live plants, and the design and production of artificial limbs and organs.

A branch of civil engineering which applies principles of rock and soil mechanics to the study of subsurface conditions. In a conservation context, geotechnical engineering is used in the monitoring and preservation of monuments and historic sites.
Study of the structure of metal and alloys as related to properties that are important in their technological utilization.
Branch of metallurgy which extracts metals from raw materials at high temperatures using processes of reduction, oxidizing, refining.

The science of planning and overseeing the preservation, maintenance, use, and development of land, often public land, including the wildlife habitats, plant and animal species, timber, minerals, oil and gas, geothermal energy, recreation areas, areas of cultural importance, rivers and other water bodies, conservation and wilderness areas, open-spaces, and construction found on the land.
The cultivation of flowers or flowering plants, especially on a commercial scale.
Study of the processes of human health and disease, giving special attention to spinal mechanics, musculoskeletal, neurological, vascular, nutritional, and environmental relationships.
Branch of medical science which treats distribution of disease in populations.
Mathematics that deals with concrete problems of data in the empirical sciences, rather than fundamental theory or principles.

Branch of physical science that deals with the composition and properties of the elementary substances of which all bodies are composed, the laws that regulate their combination, and the various phenomena that accompany their exposure to diverse physical conditions.
A branch of chemistry that generates systems of chemical interest using a digital computer programmed with mathematical models representing the essential physics that determines molecular behavior.
Science that deals with the physical history of the earth, the rocks of which it is composed, and the physical changes which it has undergone and is undergoing.
The branch of geology which studies water on or below the surface of the earth in relation to its geologic environment.
The study of invertebrate animal fossils, such as mollusks, echinoderms, and others.
Subdiscipline of petrology which describes rocks by means of microscopic examination with the goal of classification.

Field concerned with the application of techniques developed in engineering to problems in physics, and the application of new concepts developed in the basic sciences, particularly physics, to engineering problems.
Branch of mechanics which studies the generation of cracks in materials using methods of analytical and experimental mechanics.

Branch of optics that uses x-rays instead of visible light, concerned with focusing and otherwise manipulating x-rays beams for use in analysis. Since x-rays are strongly absorbed by solid matter, the optics used in the visible and near-infrared portions of the electromagnetic spectrum cannot be used to focus or reflect the radiation.

An interdisciplinary field that uses computers to extract useful information about the physical world from digital images or video, including meaningful descriptions of physical objects, to mimic the functions of human vision.
Studies comprising the trivium and quadrivium in the Middle Ages, usually arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music, grammar, rhetoric, and logic.
Group of studies in the Middle Ages constituting the higher division of the seven liberal arts and consisting of arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy.
The study that assumes and attempts to interpret and foretell the influence of the stars, moon, and planets upon human affairs.
Management of all stages of the life cycle of data assets.
Systematic, quantitative appraisal of a project to determine whether its benefits justify its costs.
The evaluation of building performance in terms of client needs and goals, including such things as environmental design, comfort levels, and mechanical systems as they affect human occupancy.
Contracting with a third party to perform all or a specific part of the obligations required in another contract.
The practice or function of casting lots in order to decide something or to forecast the future, or the implementation of divination performed in some other way.
The estimation of the price or value of property for the purposes of insurance.
Searching, locating, and accessing data from a file, database, book, or other body of material, such as data stored in a database.

Subtractive process which progressively removes base metals from a gold-containing alloy to produce a nearly pure layer of gold. Depletion gilding was used in ancient Greece, in Egypt in the second century BC, and in pre-Columbian America.
A method of joining plastic sheets or films by the simultaneous application of heat and pressure to the areas in contact.
Decorating a surface by indenting or embossing it, as in stamping of linen book bindings or gold leaf surfaces.
A technique for decorating glass, and sometimes porcelain, by scratching or stippling it with a diamond-tipped stylus.
The process of creating a nonglossy finish by exposing annealed glass to acid fumes.
Surface finishing process for concrete and mortar that embeds aggregate, removes slight imperfections, humps, and voids to produce a level surface, and consolidates material rising to the surface.
