A technique of decorating metal, usually gold or silver, by engraving it with designs that are then filled with a black inlay. Prints are sometimes made from the engraved metal before inlaying.

Decorative wood process in which the design or pattern is made by assembling small pieces of veneer in various shapes. The term, which derives from 15th-century Italy, is commonly used to describe both "marquetry," in which the entire surface is veneered, and "wood inlay," in which the pattern pieces are laid into a solid ground. The term may also be used to refer to similar works of stone, glass, or another material. Distinguished from mosaics, as pieces in intarsia work are precision-cut to tightly fit together.
Process or techinque of applying a surface with fine plaster, so as to cover or add ornament.
Producing a smooth bright surface on a metal object by immersion as an anode in an electrolytic bath.
Tooling using implements that are usually hand-held, heated, and pressed onto gold leaf leaving a pattern in gold on a surface.
Refers to a process of endothermic reaction in which thermal decomposition or a phase transition of a solid material without fusing is induced by heating it at temperatures below the melting point.

Refers to the process by which an open fire or a special firing pit is used to prepare, cure, or transform clay or another material by means of heat. It is characterized by the free circulation of oxygen, which results in the oxidation of iron and other components in the material, and a relatively low firing temperature. It differs from firing in a kiln, where the structure of the kiln allows a higher firing temperature to be achieved and the space may be sealed from oxygen.
The process of elevating or hoisting something into the air or a higher position from the ground or a lower position.
Process of weaving with split rattan such as for seats or backs of chairs.
Methods or practices used with pottery decoration.

Technique of cold transfer of an overglaze design to pottery, developed in England in the late 18th century. The process involved creating a design on a printing plate; then a bat, a thin sheet of gelatinous substance, was used instead of paper to pick up the oiled design from the plate and transfer it to the ceramic surface. Color in powder form was dusted onto the porcelain; only the oiled parts having the design retained the pigment. First designs were primarily in black, thus it is also called "black printing."
The use of two or more tanning processes, such as vegetable tanning and mineral tanning, to produce leather which possesses important characteristics of each method.

Incorporating a fatty substance into heavy leather, such as belting leather, to increase its strength, pliability, and water repellency; distinguished from "fat-liquoring," which is the introduction of a fatty substance into light leather.
Activity of working with copper, especially to create objects such as kettles, coils, tubing, and fittings.

The process of joining two pieces of metal by inserting solder between them and applying heat, sometimes but not necessarily softening or melting the surfaces to be joined; usually carried out within a temperature range of 183 to 310 degrees Celsius, with an upper limit of 750 degrees Celsius. For the similar process carried out at temperatures ranging between 750 and 900 degrees Celsius, use "brazing." For the process of joining two pieces of metal that necessarily involves softening or melting the surfaces to be joined but not necessarily the insertion of filler metal, use "welding."
Process whereby the metals to be joined are dipped into a bath of molten salt, which acts as both flux and a source of heat.
Any of a number of methods of welding that use electricity as a source of power.

A form of electrical pressure welding in which the necessary heat is produced by a flow of current through the parts to be welded. Sufficient pressure to make the weld is applied simultaneously with the flow of current.
Any method of welding that uses burning gas as a source of heat.
Arc welding in which a flux-coated metal electrode is consumed to form a pool of filler metal and a gas shield around the weld area.

A solid-state welding process in which the parts are joined by the local application of high-frequency sound waves as they are held together under pressure. This process is used in many industrial applications to join dissimilar materials. It is also used in the conservation of parchment, the encapsulation of paper objects, and in joining woven and non-woven textiles.
Coating one metal with another by means of bonding, as to protect the inner metal from corrosion or for minting coins.
The application of a protective coating to ferrous metal by dipping it in a bath of molten zinc.

Process involving the surface application of gold or another metal in the form of leaf, powder applied directly to the surface, powder mixed with a binder, electroplating, or other forms to approximate the effect of solid or inlaid metal.
Deposition of a metallic coating by a controlled chemical reduction that is catalyzed by the metal or alloy being deposited.

The process of fine detailed “cold work” after casting and fettlingthat serves to correct or enhance the cast surface by removingand/or compressing metal using hand tools by punching,engraving, and/or chiseling, and in modern times also with powerand pneumatic tools.
A type of chasing done to decorate a flat surface rather than to develop relief decoration.
Act of using a chisel and hammer to remove metal. With each strike of the hammer the tool jumps, often leaving a visible “step.” Chiseling may be part of either fettling or chasing.
The process of hammering metal into shape without the use of heat.
The art of folding paper into objects or designs.
The practice and activity of woodworking that results in the creation of  fine art or otherwise exhibits craftmanship of particularly high quality.

The technique or process of using microscopes that have a digital camera attached instead of an eyepiece and display the digitally acquired image on a large monitor. This technique may include functions such as dimension measurement, and recording of still images and moving images.

X-ray spectroscopy technique in which an intense, tunable X-ray beam of variable frequency from a synchrotron radiation source is directed at a sample and the absorption of the X-rays is measured as a function of frequency.
Dissolution into separate parts, used especially of organic materials or of such changes at a molecular level.
Corrosion that occurs when current flows between cathodic and anodic areas on metallic surfaces.
A distinctive effect of weathering, often affecting stone, characterized by a pattern of small cavities.
Rock weathering processes whose effects can be seen only at the microscopic level.
Formation of a concavity or cuplike hollow in a paint layer.
Separating into thin flattened pieces or layers.
Branches or departments of knowledge, particularly at a university.

Research into the evolution of the book and its variants (pamphlets, newspapers, broadsheets) in all aspects of its production, dissemination and consumption in relation to literary, political, economical, social and religious history. The history of the book includes subjects such as the production of manuscripts in medieval scriptoria, authorship, printing techniques, economic aspects of printing and publishing, design, printshops and publishing houses, trade, ownership and reading culture, typography, typesetting and printing techniques, and book collecting and connoisseurship. Use " literary history" Use “literary history” for the study of literary trends and movements.
Branches of learning devoted to the arts.

Discipline concerning physical objects that are that are meant to be perceived primarily through the sense of sight, are of high quality, requiring refined skill in creation, and typically using the media of painting, drawing, sculpture, and architecture.

Discipline encompassing the art and form of expression of filmmaking and motion pictures, which are produced in the media of film or videotape, on which a series of pictures are presented to the eye in such rapid succession as to give the illusion of natural movement. It may also refer to similar art created in digital media.  For the actual works created on film, use "motion pictures (visual works)."

Music in which sound is generated, transferred, triggered, or amplified by electronic devices. The creation of electronic music may involve the use of magnetic tape or digital technology and whose reproduction involves the use of loudspeakers. For works created with only natural sound sources recorded and manipulated via discs or magnetic tape use "musique concrète." For music created entirely through the use of a computer, in which the sound is initiated purely through digital means, use "computer music."

Discipline that concerns expertise or the study of objects, environments, or experiences (as in performance art) that are visual in nature, were created by the use of skill and imagination, and possess an aesthetic that is valued and of a quality and type that would be collected by art museums. It may refer to the study of the fine arts or the fine and decorative arts together. With reference to the visual and performing arts together, use "arts (broad discipline)." The meaning is broader than "works of art" or "art objects," including architecture as well. For general reference to the genre, use "art (object genre)."
The art and science of constructing architecture.

Discipline that focuses on the presentation of information using visual and written elements. Communication design is a broad concept covering various disciplines, such as advertising, branding, web design, user interface design, information design, and social media. Communication designers focus on the strategy, content, and context of their messages, and how they can influence the behavior, attitude, and perception of their audience. Communication design uses research, analysis, storytelling, and user testing to create effective and engaging visual solutions that meet the needs and goals of clients and users.

Drawing technique used to render three dimensions in a two-dimensional medium. Depth is represented by rendering all lines in the drawing so that they disappear to one or more points. This term is often used when representing architectural and spatial elements, such as buildings, cityscapes, streets, and other structures. It may also be applied to the rendering of objects in the context of industrial design.
The technique of creating illustrations that communicate information of a scientific nature by employing exploded views, cutaways, diagrams and etc.

The process of applying a protective coating and decorative painting to land vehicles, primarily those drawn by draft animals, such as carriages, wagons, and sleighs; encompasses the application of primer, ground color, and varnish, lettering, striping and other ornamentation, and the painting of pictures such as coats of arms and flower wreaths.

The art and science of photographing animate or animated beings or objects in motion, using a motion picture camera. Distinct from "chronophotography," which records motion or change with a series of photographic images shot with a still camera, either discrete photographs taken sequentially or a single exposure capturing movement, as blurred images. For terms concerning the overall process of making motion pictures and the various techniques involved, see descriptors under the guide term "<filmmaking and filmmaking processes and techniques>."
Study of the development over time of the human built environment.
Describes all interventions pursued by architectural conservators to preserve the integrity of built objects, directed toward the long-term safekeeping of architectural heritage.
Descriptive and analytical study of musical instruments.

Term that was appropriated first by the Surrealists from physiology and psychiatry, and later applied to spontaneous writing, drawing, and painting. Automatism in the visual arts includes techniques in other movements as well, such as Abstract Expressionism and others, referring generally to manual creation techniques involving chance or psychological experiences.
Type of animation in which the images are drawn or painted directly onto the film rather than photographed.
A drawing technique usually employing a combination of red, black, and white chalks on a yellowish or off-white paper; especially common in the 18th century.
Effects, usually pre-set algorithms, that are applied to a digital image to create variations.

A photomechanical process that produces continuous tone images in slight relief. A gelatin relief is prepared by a bichromate process and then used to make an intaglio plate. This plate is used as a mold and is filled with pigmented gelatin; the gelatin layer is then pressed onto a paper support. Widely used for fine book illustration from about 1875 to 1900.
The collotype process advanced by F. Joubert in France in the 1860s.
Photogravure process in which the impression is produced by a rotary press using an intaglio engraved cylinder.
Refers to the process of engraving for printing using copper plates. It was replaced in the early 19th century by the use of more durable plates, generally made of either steel or steel-faced copper.

A printing process developed in the 20th century in which mezzotint-like tone is achieved from sandpaper grain. The process was developed as a way to avoid the laborious process of rocking the plate. The plate is passed through the press several times with a sheet of sandpaper; the grains of sand physically displace dots of copper, forming ink-retaining burrs.

A printing process in which tone is added to a major part of the print by sprinkling granulated salt on the ground while it is still hot and liquid. Once the plate is cold and the salt has been rinsed away, a random pattern of pits of varied depth is left behind and will create corresponding clusters of black dots on the resulting print.
Aquatint process in which a sugar solution is used to lift the ground, and expose the image areas so the plate can be etched.

Technique for making copies of images or documents using a device called a polygraph. An early polygraph consists of a blunt stylus and a pen or brush connected by frames and springs that allow the user to trace over the original with the stylus while the pen or brush moves in parallel, copying what is traced onto a sheet of paper or other surface. The term can also be used to describe a technique for simultaneously producing two or more identical writings or drawings. Polygraphy also refers to a method of producing copies of paintings, invented by Joseph Booth, ca. 1788. Polygraphy can furthermore more generally refer to the art or practice of using any copying machine.
The process of producing color woodblock prints, usually through combining a series of blocks in precise registration that have been inked with individual hues and pressed onto one support.

In comics, the process of tracing over pencilled work to add definition to the illustration. Traditionally undertaken with pens, brushes, and ink, inking is now largely accomplished with digital drawing tablets.
Process by which a continuous tone digital image is applied to receiver materials via thermal transfer of cyan, yellow, and magenta dyes.
Color printing in which colors are laid down separately in multiple steps.
A method of oil painting in which the final effects are achieved in the initial application of paint as opposed to covering the canvas layer by layer.
Fresco technique common in the latter half of the 16th century where painting was done on partially dry intonaco, with lime added to the colors to enhance their adherence.
A monochrome painting technique that employs two or three values of a single color to create an image that varies from very light to very dark.
The art or practice of producing creative works with casein paint, which is water-based, matte paint made with pigment in a binder comprising a phosphoprotein of milk.
The technique or activity of executing the lay-in of a painting.
The technique of contrasting light and dark within a picture, especially one in which the forms are largely determined, not by sharp outlines, but by the meeting of lighter and darker areas.

Refers to a system of projection by which the points on a sphere are mapped onto a plane, maintaining a one-to-one correspondence of points. It is generally used for map-making, and tries to resolve the problem that arises because a sphere cannot be represented on a flat surface with the preservation of the proportion of all distances. Conformal projection attempts to preserve the relative shape of configurations that surround each point; that is, it preserves the magnitude and sense of angles at each point. Mercator projection and streographic projection are examples of conformal projection.
Process by which the color of a black-and-white image is altered by replacing the silver image with inorganic, metallic compounds (such as gold, sulfur, iron, or selenium).

The geometric correction of spatial distortions such as tilt and relief in aerial photographs, resulting in uniformity of scale. Orthocorrected images may be used to measure true distances; a basis of aerial photogrammetry.
A radiographic technique that uses a plane beta source to produce an image on a radiographic film.
The technique of taking photographs using a brief, brilliant burst of light, synchronized with the camera's shutter activation.
Dye transfer process invented by Dr. E. König where a single gelatin film can be treated to create multiple prints from the colored plate.
A subtractive color photographic process in which dyes present in the emulsion are bleached, leaving only those dyes that correspond to the image color.
Diazo process in which the diazonium salts are on the base and the latent image is developed by moistening with a liquid containing the coupler.

William Henry Fox Talbot's process in which paper negatives were produced by printing out a silver image. Distinguished from "calotype," in which the image is developed. In the mid-19th century, sometimes used as a synonym of photography.

A carbon process to produce photographic prints in which the carbon transfer tissue is made sensitive when placed in contact with a developed silver bromide print. Distinguished from the "carbon process" by the chemical method for hardening the carbon transfer tissue and by the use of a silver bromide print, which allows carbro prints to be made from smaller negatives.

Photographic process in which the image is formed by dusting a pigment onto a surface of bichromated colloid that has been exposed through a transparency. Areas exposed to light lose their tackiness and hold less pigment. Generally for prints on glass or ceramic, where the pigment is fired as a glaze.

Carbon printing process that creates prints by superimposition of three monochromatic carbon plates in register. Each of these register plates is in a subtractive primary color, exposed from color separations.
Technique of taking a series of photographs at set intervals to record changes that take place slowly with time, such as the growth of a plant.
Method of obtaining a glossy surface on collodion prints by pressing them between rollers.
Enumerating individual units out of a body of units to determine the total number of units concerned.
Refers to use of terrestrial photogrammetry to measure, survey, or map architectural structures, particularly historical monuments and sites.

Process of using dried palm fronds to make objects. For example, this is one of the most important and main traditional crafts in Al-Ula city, and is exclusively practiced by women. Numerous tools and products are made out of dried palm fronds to be used in housework, agriculture, and may be used in everyday life in urban zones as well. (Nasif, 1995).
The binding of identical books in quantity, using high-speed automatic equipment, usually for a publisher or distributor and usually case binding in hard covers.
Bookbinding technique in which slanted cuts are made across the back edge of the text block, through which threads are passed and secured by adhesive.
Process of using nonglare wax to polish a sculpture or painting to reduce its shine; associated with the ancient Greeks.
Relief technique in which the surface of the block is allowed to remain as background and the figures are carved with positive projections within the surface.

Type of weave, primarily used in basketweaving, that consists of alternating splints of plant fiber. Starting at the base, the splints construct one full basket before bending downward to form another basket on the outside of the first.
Trimming, furnishing, adorning, or covering textiles or objects with beads, or creating jewelry by stringing beads.
Embroidery, popular during the Renaissance, that uses black or red silk thread to design stylized patterns on garments for both women and men.

Quilting technique in which layers of cloth with no filling between them are back-stitched together under sufficient tension so as to raise the ground very slightly, thus giving the impression of filling.
Sewing by hand, as distinct from sewing by machine.

Japanese art form and spiritual discipline that involves the formal placement and arrangement of flowers, branches, and sometimes other natural objects. Those who practice ikebana organize the objects according to strict rules.

The action or process of conserving for the preservation of existence, state, life, health, safeguarding from destructive influences, natural decay, or waste. May apply to conserving a building, object, environment, species, or other thing.
The process of creating a tunnel through excavation.

Refers broadly to painting conservation treatments, such as oiling and inpainting, intended to recreate the original appearance of the design in a defect that cannot be corrected. Use a more specific term if possible.
Pointillistic single tone in-painting technique used as compensation for loss; an adaptation of the tratteggio technique.
Traditional Japanese craft and process to repair ceramics using urushi lacquer and gold or silver.

Refers to digital recreation of art works (such as paintings, sculpture) and other objects (furniture, relics, etc.) by reassembling known parts and filling in lacunae to create realistic, full-color hypothetical models.
The action of diffusing or spreading, as in particulate matter in liquid suspension.
The act or process of removing or depriving of water; though other liquids may remain.  For the process of making free, or nearly free, of liquids, use "drying."

The process of stregthening or stabilizing by use of an inner layer, usually using paper or fabric.  In conservation and other contexts, the process of reinforcing a work by applying a paper or fabric lining with an adhesive, sewing, or another method; examples include lining applied to the support of a paper or canvas support of a  work of art, or the lining applied to a garment as an inner layer of cloth.
Securing of a work of art, document, or other generally flat object within a mat for support, protection, or display.

Enameling that is accomplished by carving away troughs or cells in metal, leaving a raised line that forms the outline of the design. The enamel is laid in the cells, fired, and then filed and polished.
Parts or components of piers.
Parts or components of arches.
Parts or components of domes.
Parts or components of vaults.
Parts or components of columns.
Parts or components of entablatures.
Parts or components of cornices.
Parts or components of friezes.
Parts or components of trusses.
Parts or components of floors.
Parts or components of roofs.
Designates the back walls or linings of fireplaces.
Parts or components of eaves.
Parts or components of gables.
Parts or components of walls.
Parts or components of openings.
Parts or components of doors.
Parts or components of doorways.
Parts or components of gates.
Parts or components of windows.
Parts or components of tracery.
Parts or components of steps.
Parts or components of moldings.

Elevated platforms or constructions upon which religious sacrifice is offered or other religious or spiritual activities carried out. In a Christian church altars are platforms where Eucharistic elements are consecrated, in the ancient tradition of a sacrifice. Includes both indoor small, tablelike fixtures and larger, free-standing, outdoor structures. It consists of a horizontal part, the mensa, placed on various types of supports. For the surface at which communion is celebrated in Protestant churches, use "communion tables."

Covered pits into which raw sewage is discharged, the liquid portion seeping or leaching into the surrounding porous soil, and the solids being retained in the pit to undergo partial decomposition before removal.
Water distribution systems in which water is forced upward by pumps or pressure within a main.
Drains that lead from the trap of a fixture to another drain pipe.
Gutters installed on the uphill side of a chimney on a sloping roof; used to divert water around the chimney.
The piping comprising the plumbing of a drainage system.
Plumbing fixtures, usually in the form of tubs or basins, in which baths can be taken.
Vertical vent pipes installed primarily for the purpose of providing circulation of air to or from any part of the building drainage system.
Bathtubs in which water is sprayed down upon the bather from an overhead, usually perforated, nozzle.

Sinks used for washing the hands and face. For deep, relatively large sinks used for washing the arms and upper body, use "wash sinks"; for deep, large sinks used for washing laundry, use "laundry trays."
Traps installed in building drains to prevent circulation of air between the plumbing system of the building and the building sanitary drainage system.
Refers generally to the components of heating systems that distribute heat within rooms and spaces, usually by radiation or convection.

Formats and systems endorsed by the NTSC, which sets the television and video standards for the United States. The standard television signal set by the NTSC is composite video, which is compiled of red, blue, and green signals. The NTSC standard TV image has 525 horizontal lines per frame. Alternate standards include HDTV (high-definition television), as well as Phase Alternate Line (PAL) or Sequential Couleur avec Memoire (SECAM) primarily adopted in other areas of the world.
Fire alarm systems that produce signals on the protected premises only, primarily to notify occupants.
Electronic circuits that are used for signal processing. These may be analog or digitally based, and most commonly govern frequency selectivity of a tuning circuit, but have various applications.
Fire detectors that sense the presence of heat sufficient to indicate the presence of an openly burning fire.
Smoke detectors that work by detecting the obscuration of light by smoke.
The process of building by combining parts or elements, and also for the manner in which the buiilt work has been put together.
Causing to adhere by or as if by means of a soft plastic mixture or composition.

The process of securing a nail, bolt, or other rod-like piece that has been driven through a substance by beating back the point or end of the nail or bolt with a hammer or other tool so that the end is turned over and driven back into the substance through which it has passed. Also, the process in which the end of a bolt is beaten down and flattened upon a metal ring or washer put around it for the purpose.
Removing dirt, surface coatings, accretions, discolorations, or other undesired matter from a substrate using biological agents e.g. bacteria, enzymes, plant-based surfactants.
The washing of textile items, such as shirts and linens.
Process of applying a coloring matter that is in a solution or fine dispersion so that at least some of the coloring matter is taken up by the substance.
Making or becoming dirty, tarnished, or stained; damage to the surface or substrate of materials.
Resist dyeing technique; the threads are printed before weaving, resulting in vague patterns in the fabric. Similar to the ikat-technique.
Cutting, as metal or paper, with dies.
Trimming or cutting away the edges of gold or silver coins in order to pilfer some of the precious metal.
Smoothing a surface with abrasive paper or cloth, either by hand or by machine.
Splitting into pieces or smashing into parts or fragments, typically by a blow or stress and with suddenness or violence.
The insertion of stone chips into the joints of rough masonry to reduce the amount of mortar required, to wedge larger stones in position, or to add detail to the appearance.

Bending something over upon itself, as cloth or paper. For the parts bent over upon each other, use "folds"; for resulting ridges, use "creases." To describe objects designed to fold into a compact form, use "folding (attribute)."

Casting that uses a mixture of metal powders with a resin or gypsum base and carried out without heat, resulting in objects with the appearance of solid metal. Silicone molds are typically used for the casting.

Distinctive type of ancient lost-wax casting technique named after the Dhokra tribes, who are the traditional metalworkers of West Bengal. It is distinguished by decoration made using a pipette to squeeze out long strings of wax that are applied as coils, spirals, strips, or other designs to the mold. Among the items produced by this technique are folk deity figures, votive horsemen, lamps, dowry rice bowls, animal figures, and fish-shaped openwork brass purses.
Process of applying heavy pressure to something between two surfaces for a brief period.

A technique of pottery surface treatment in which an implement is pressed into wet clay using a rocking motion. Varied patterns may be achieved depending on the form of the tool, and direction or spacing of impressions.
The art or process of carving gems or seals.
Hinges that swing casement windows outward, the phrase often used to describe those hinges that permit cleaning the outside glass surface on an outward-swinging window sash, when opened.
Locks manufactured to fit into a circular hole in a door.
Contrivances for securing doors in closed position, often with a combination of a keyed bolt.
Plates attached to an object to which accessories or structural members may be attached by welding, screwing, nailing, or bolting.
Threaded nuts which help to create a watertight joint, as on the long thread of a pipe connector, and whose one dished side accepts a grommet.
Joints between masonry units.
Joints formed where two construction members meet at an angle.

Documents comprised of a project description, including overviews of activities or products to be realized,  and instructions for the project organization and methods, tools, and the definition of standards used.
Short articles, usually related to a long article, but separated visually on the page.

Computer drawings, digital artwork, animation, videos, films, html pages, or projects in other media that have gone through a production process and have then been formatted in a way suitable for viewing by a user. The term is used in reference to architectural projects, and to other projects as well. May also be used to refer to projects that are highly finished and ready for viewing, even if done by hand rather than with a computer.
In Indian architecture, a coping.

Hard, golden-brown wood of the species Acacia koa, native to Hawaii. The color and grain pattern of koa wood changes with growing conditions and tree age. It is a lightweight, but durable wood, that is brittle with variations in density. Koa is difficult to work or plane but carves well and polishes to a high gloss, used for carvings, boats, dugout canoes, early surfboards, veneers, musical instruments, and furniture. It was the royal wood of the native Hawaiians and was used for everything that came in contact with the royal family.
Hinges mounted on the outside of a door or hinged surface, as distinguished from concealed or invisible hinges.
Wire nails with a flaring head, used for outside finish and also for nailing floors.
Nails having a tip that is tapered on two sides to form a sharp edge, as a chisel.
Nails made of relatively soft metal or so cut that the pointed end may be bent over easily for clinching.
Nails similar to common nails with the same penny designation of length but having a shank smaller in diameter.
In construction, support or anchoring hangers used to attach a wooden member to masonry.

Tie hangers or other hangers that incorporate a coil or other mechanism to allow small amounts of vertical or lateral movement, used to suspend ceilings, floors, in bridges, and for other construction uses.
U-shaped supporting or anchoring hangers having upper ends that are bent at right angles, used to support forms for concrete work.
Joist hangers designed to allow the top of the attached joist to be flush or even with the top of the beam to which it is attached.
Inserts for attachment or fastening that provide a continuous slot for attachment.
Printed forms, characterized by a heading containing the name of a company or name and address, on which a statement of money due is recorded.
Systems of electric conductors, at least one of which is intentionally grounded, either solidly or by means of a device that limits currents.
Devices used to introduce capacitance into an electric circuit; consists of conducting plates insulated from each other by a layer of deilectric material.
Electric cables that can handle significant alternating electrical current, that connect to devices requiring electricity to function.
Transformers capable of increasing the voltage of a current.
Systems in buildings designed to horizontally move people, equipment, or goods.
Elevators with glass-enclosed cars with operating mechanisms so located as to maximize viewing area for the passengers.
Elevators operated by electricity.
Elevators whose cars or platforms move at a degree less than completely vertical.
Building system for the lowering of air temperature, as for comfort, process control, or food preservation.
Systems for heating by radiation from a surface, especially from a surface heated by means of electricity, hot air, or hot water.
Bolts designed to attach newel posts to stairway railing.

Solar heating systems that collect and transfer heat by the natural laws of convection, conduction, and radiation with little or no mechanical assistance; for solar heating systems utilizing mechanical devices to transfer heat, use "active solar heating."
Central warm-air heating systems through which air is circulated by gravity.
Systems supplying and exhausting fresh air by mechanical means.
Air conditioning systems in which units can operate independently without the need for a central distribution system.
Supplemental cooling systems in buildings that utilize ice production and storage for the purpose of reducing utility loads.
Lighting systems that employ daylight, including the arrangements and installation of such systems.
Illumination directed at a specific target area for aiding visual tasks.
Lighting arrangements to illuminate indoor spaces.
System of lights arranged to define the outline of architectural features, such as doors, windows, or rooflines.
Indirect lighting systems comprising light sources shielded by vertical or horizontal ledges or recesses attached to walls and distributing light over the ceiling and upper and side walls.
Building lighting systems that supply illumination essential to the safety of life and property in the event of failure of normal supply.
Air-cleaning filters that employ a surface covered with a viscous oil or fluid, to which dirt particles and other airborne impurities cling as the air passes through.
That part of a ventilation system which includes supply and return air ducts and plenum chambers.
Parts or components of chimneys.
Refers to a wide range of pressure vessels in which water or other fluid is heated and then discharged to supply hot water for heating or steam for heating or power generation.
Boilers that supply hot water or steam for space heating, processing, or power.
Coils designed to remove moisture from the air by condensation.
Heat pumps whose operation is at times supplemented by solar collector-storage systems.
Small portable stoves designed to contain hot coals and used to warm the feet.
Furnaces for the production of heat by the combustion of oil.
Parts and components of fireplaces.
Room heating units consisting of a heating device, often a finned tube, mounted in a metal enclosure with openings to allow the transfer of heat to the air, principally by convection.

Flasks made to be carried in a pocket and therefore not having lugs for a carrying strap. Sometimes made of heavy glass reinforced with added strips of glass or later of glass in leather or metal casings.

An ancient Greek jug featuring a squat body, a tall and narrow neck, and a beak spout. The body sometimes features rib decoration. Th name means "to pour." Most of these vessels were produced in South Italy.
Lids, usually plastic, made to cover disposable cold drink cups.
Stoppers for the openings of casks where they are filled.
Ornamental bands worn on the lower arm that are constructed with individual links or rings passing through one another.
Discontinuous, ring-shaped brooches with two terminals which are often flattened and highly decorative.
Necklaces comprised of beads sewn in rows to form a bib-like pendant that lies upon the wearer's chest, notable among ancient Egyptian jewelry.
Small pendants, usually of gold but sometimes of leather, designed as containers for amulets; use especially for those of Etruscan origin.
Rings in the form of a circular band set with a continuous row of gemstones, usually diamonds, of the same size and cut.
Crowns that are open, lacking hoops, arches, or an internal covering; typically comprising a ring or band of precious metal, often with jewels.

Bamana carved wooden headdresses representing antelopes or aardvarks. Typically, they are worn by males who perform a masquerade in pairs, with one dancer representing a male animal and the other a female.
Medals, often of brass or precious metal, that commemorate the birth of a child and are inscribed with a name and birth date.
Long, single-pronged accessories used to keep hair or headgear in place or for decorative purposes.
Small pads or rolls of hair or the like formerly worn by women underneath their natural hair to give the appearance of greater thickness.
Wigs in which the backhair was enclosed in an ornamental bag.
Traditional Japanese wooden clogs that are worn outdoors, with inverted V-straps that pass between the first two toes and with two transverse supports on the bottom of the sole.
Traditional Mexican sandals having the uppers made of interwoven leather strips and often held on the foot by loose heel straps.
Slippers often with a flexible sole and either heelless or with a low heel, intended for indoor use.
Women's hats with a wide brim, generally of light material over a framework to create an inflated crown; named in commemoration of the pioneering balloon ascent of 1783.
Narrow bands or fillets, often of soft material, worn by women to bind the hair or as part of a head-dress, particularly when tied horizontally around the top of the head, across the forehead.
Heavy knitted or crocheted hoods that cover the head, neck and tops of the shoulders; worn especially by soldiers or mountaineers.
Square headcloths, usually of cotton, often folded into a triangle and traditionally secured on the head with an agal; worn by men especially in Western Asia and parts of North Africa.
Neckwear in the form of broad tubes or loops that fit over the wearer's head and neck, worn as a scarf.
Type of skullcap, sometimes pointed, worn especially by ancient Greeks and Romans, and also by ecclesiastics.
White veils, often lace or embroidered, used in the Christian baptism or christening ceremony to cover the head of the baptized or christened adult or child.

Traditional Indonesian womenswear in the form of a light jacket or blouse, to be worn with a sarong. Often made in white or sheer material and embellished with embroidery. Depending on the region of origin, a kabaya can be long or short, open at the front or closed.
Leather bifurcated garments, with either short or long legs, usually held up with suspenders; traditionally worn in Bavaria.
Capes designed to protect the wearer from rain.

A thin or netted style of cape worn by Nahua men in the postclassic period that was typically made from maguey fibers. Also made from cotton or with designs embroidered or appliqued with precious materials such as quetzal feathers or turquoise.
Close-fitting short coats having a short skirt, flaps, or tails, including military coats and similar items of women's fashion.

Cutaways of the late 1830s to 1850 with short rounded tails, the front sloping sharply from above the waist downward to the thighs in back, single- or double-breasted, often with flapped pockets; worn for riding or as a suit coat.

Late 18th-century womenswear comprising two parts: an outer robe with a bodice cut in one piece and and overskirt that parted to reveal a matching or coordinated petticoat. The bodice lacked center back pleats, distinguishing it from a "robe à la française or open robe.
Coats worn by infant participants in baptismal ceremonies. Usually made with white or pastel fabric.
Combination umbrella and parasol for all weather, generally brightly colored but untrimmed.
Combs generally made in pairs, worn on each side of the head to hold the hair in place.

Art which makes use of the book format or the structure of the book; typically usage is limited to unique sculptural works that take the form of, or incorporate, books but that do not communicate in the ways characteristic of a conventional book, such as being experienced sequentially. For books made or conceived by visual artists, use "artists' books" or "bookworks."

Bamana zoomorphic sculptures, which serve as portable altars for the Komo association, and which are usually shaped in the form of a cow, with the insides containing materials such as animal bones, vegetable matter, honey, metal, and covered with a thick coating of earth.
General term for sculpture that is carved from or applied to surfaces of architectural members, usually exterior.

Refers to works executed by cutting a figure or design out of a solid material such as stone or wood. It typically refers to works that are relatively small in size, are part of a larger work, or are not considered art. For large and medium-sized three-dimensional works of art, use the broader term "sculpture" or another appropriate term.
Sculpture that is constructed of metal using such processes as welding, hammering, and soldering as opposed to casting.

Rocks prized by Chinese scholar-officials for their distinctive shapes and crevices, seen as suggestive of the transformational powers of nature.  Larger stones were placed in gardens as unique focal features, while smaller rocks often adorned scholars’ desks, a microcosmic representation of the natural world within the space of the study.
Refers to works in which half or more than half of the natural circumference of the modeled form projects from the surrounding surface.
Sculpture made of or covered with gold and ivory; used especially for ancient Greek figures.
Buddhist sculptures that represent the footprint of the Buddha as he walked on the earth. The sculptures originated in India and are important symbolic devices.
Sculpted human figures or heads attached to the reliquaries of deceased Fang elders, which function as a symbolic evocation of the ancestor as well as a guardian of the relics.
Igbo wooden shrine statues of male human figures representing tutelary or guardian spirits.
Drawings, prints, or statues of flayed human or animal figures, used in the study of musculature.

French term for replicas of the artist’s model (often in bronze) that is used to make molds for the production of large editions in sandcasting. In rare cases, a chef-modèle has been used in lost-wax casting.
Interdisciplinary art installations that incorporate sound into physical environments.
In carpentry, a dovetail joint having horizontal ledges or shoulders at its base.
Bolts or pegs designed to be set into holes or slots in the interior walls of a bookcase, forming an attachment or small platform on which bookcase shelves can sit.
Threaded bolts for holding together temporarily parts of a structure during riveting.
General term for any furniture intended for seating.
Hinges in two leaves, screwed to the face of a door which is not thick enough to permit the use of butt hinges.
Mouth bows of southern Africa sounded by the player inhaling and exhaling sharply on a flattened ostrich quill attached to the string.

Flexible sticks of wood, very rarely of metal or plastic, carrying stretched between the two ends a length of horsehair or other stringlike material which is used to brush against the strings of a chordophone, causing them to sound. Historically bows have been evenly curved, curved only at one end, or straight in the middle with both ends curved; modern Western bows typically have a concave curve.
Traditional name for Western orchestral or concert flutes, recorders, clarinets, and oboes.
Brass instruments of the cornet family, of alto pitch, shaped like a tuba, with medium-sized bell, three valves, and a cup mouthpiece.
Trombones that operate with a slide mechanism, as opposed to a valve mechanism.
Trumpets in which the mouthhole is located on the side, as opposed to the end.
Trumpets of the Teso of Uganda, consisting of a straight wood tube with a bottle-shaped calabash bell; they are played by men in sets of three as accompaniment for dancing.
Side-blown ivory trumpets of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Angola, used for signalling in hunting and warfare.
Large bass tubas built in circular form for convenience in carrying, first produced in Vienna in 1845.
German mouth-blown bagpipes with a single horn-belled chanter and a bass drone.
Wooden clarinets having seven fingerholes, one thumbhole, and two diametrically opposed keys, and usually a foot joint like that of a recorder.

Treble cornetts having a conical mouthpiece turned in the wood tube of the instrument itself rather than detachable; the mouthpiece thus merges with the bore without a sharp break, causing a softening and veiling of the tone quality.

The original or classic flageolets developed in France in the 16th century, featuring a narrow conical bore contracting slightly toward the foot, and commonly four fingerholes at the front and two thumbholes at the back.
Flutes in which the air stream is directed through a narrow duct against the sharp edge of a lateral aperture.
Flutes of modern Egypt and Morocco. They generally have six fingerholes.
Wooden oboes with a straight body terminating in a bulb bell, and a conical bore considerably wider than that of the usual baritone oboes, which they resemble in tone and pitch.

Panpipes of the Soga of Uganda, made of from eight to thirteen stopped pipes of bamboo, elephant grass, or other material tied in raft form. They are played in ensemble, grouped in three pairs, usually accompanied by drums.
Recorders that play an octave lower than the alto recorder, standing between the tenor recorder and C great-bass (or quart-bass) recorder.
Brass instruments in the saxophone family with a range that roughly analogous to the baritone voice. They have tapered bores, and are single-reed.

Low-pitched shawms developed in Europe between the 14th and 16th centuries, being long and slender with a narrow, slightly conical bore ending in a bottle-shaped or flared bell, six fingerholes in two groups of three, and, later in its development, at least one key.
Sticks, usually of wood, either padded with fabric or some other soft material on one end or plain, used to strike drums.
Tabor flutes of the Basque region. Txistus have two finger holes and one rear thumb hole. They are played with the left hand, while the right hand plays a drum that hangs from the left forearm.

Whistles that are attached to barrel-operated, steam calliopes. The volume of calliope whistles dictates their pitch. Calliope whistles may also be detached from the instruments, and historically were sometimes placed on trains or ships as steam whistles.
Double-duct flutes of Yugoslavia, consisting of two slightly divergent pipes bored in one piece of wood, with a beak-shaped double mouthpiece.
Upright bassoons developed in the early 19th century, made in three or four detachable sections, capped by a brass flared bell or painted dragon's head and furnished with a swan-neck crook.
Keyboard instruments whose sound is produced by freely vibrating reeds, activated by air either under pressure or suction.
Portable free-reed instruments having two hexagonal casings connected by an expandable bellows, each of which has a small button keyboard.

Small portable pianos built in the shape of a harp lying on a box and having a compass of from two to four octaves; intended for outdoor performances, they could be suspended around the player's neck or set on the lap.
Small dishes used by an individual diner to hold a pat or small serving of butter. For dishes intended to hold and serve butter at the table use "butter dishes (serving dishes)."
Cast iron frying pans originally made with short feet to stand among coals on the hearth.
Small plates, generally 3 to 4 inches in diameter, made in pressed glass and used to hold ceramic teacups while tea is being drunk from the saucer.

Vessels, usually of baluster or cylindrical shape and intended for serving dry, ground mustard flour; used especially for vessels that were historically part of a set of casters at table. A mustard caster may have a pierced, domed lid or it may be a blind caster, meaning the lid is not pierced or is blocked with an interior sleeve to prevent moisture in the air from causing the powdered mustard to clump. For vessels used to contain and serve prepared, wet mustard, usually having a cover or lid, use "mustard pots."
Platters having a depressed well at one end for holding gravy.

Vessels having a perforated top for sprinkling table salt on food. Saltshakers are made in a variety of forms and materials, including glass, ceramic, and metal. They are often paired with a pepper shaker. Saltshakers and pepper shakers may be designed in whimsical forms that are considered collectibles. For similar objects for sprinkling salt but made of precious materials and designed as part of a larger set of casters, particularly in historical or formal usage, use "salt casters."
Trays, usually made of precious metal, on which the jugs or pitchers of zeon (hot water) is are held during some Eastern Christian services.
Collectible spoons made to commemorate events or places, often intended as souvenirs. On the handle or bowl of the spoon may appear an engraved text, a scene portraying the event, or a location.
Spoons with a long, hollow handle used to stir and sip lemonade and similar drinks served in tall glasses.

Straight-sided glass vessels, often decorated, with a bulging wall that narrows slightly near the rim, resembling a club weapon. The largest of these glasses held half a liter of beer. Smaller examples were used for wine. The creation of such glasses flourished during the second half of the 15th century, particularly in the Netherlands and Germany.

Drinking glasses having a wide, flared bowl and stout, hollow stem. The glasses have a distinctive green or yellow color caused by iron impurities in the sand used for glass production. They were first introduced in 15th-century Germany and the Netherlands.

Trumpet-shaped ale glasses about 3 feet in height and which hold approximately 1 pint of ale. Made either with a flat circular base or with a rounded hollow bulb. The latter were used as trick glasses.

Small to medium-sized, stemmed wine glasses of a distinctive type used particularly in the 18th-19th centuries, and intended for drinking claret, which was originally a Rosa wine from Bordeaux but gradually came to mean any red wine from Bordeaux. Claret glasses are typically made of colorless glass, and have a relatively short stem, a relatively small bowl, and a round foot. They are often, but not always, further distinguished by having a bowl that is cut or etched and sometimes flares at the lip.
Champagne glasses with hollow stems intended to keep the champagne bubbling.
Drinking cups formed of staves of wood in the manner of a miniature barrel, hooped with wood, metal, or cord, typically having a wooden bottom and often decorated with carved and painted decoration.

Refers to the creation of decorative scrapbooks and albums, typically using photgraphs and other items mounted to colored and patterned papers, which may be cut or stamped in various ways and involving the application of decorative lettering and other embellishments.
Statements showing the income and expense accounts of a business over a stated time, the difference being the profit or loss for the period.
Joints formed by bolting a fishplate (supporting plate) to each side of two abutting rails, timbers, beams, or other members.
Butt joints in which one of the members has a bevelled cut where it butts against the other, so that there is not a right angle between the pieces.
Angle joints involving two members, each having been cut to half its thickness and lapped over the other in such a manner as to result in a change of direction.
Relatively large rabbet joints that are typically made in structural timber.
Interlocking joints formed by a flaring or fanlike tenon and a mortise into which it fits tightly.
In carpentry, mortise-and-tenon joints where the projecting tongue (tenon) of one piece is round in cross-section, made to fit into the corresponding round cutout (mortise) in the other piece.

In carpentry, right-angle joints comprising one piece having a dado groove cut, and the other having a tongue, groove, and rabbet cut, produced in a way so the protruding parts fit into the grooves of the opposing pieces to form a joint.
Airships that are held aloft via a volume of gas held in an envelope without a structural skeleton.

Basins or shallow bowls having a convex boss, umbo, or elevated point in the center of the basin, for the purpose of gathering the liquid around the rim of the basin, such as for libations, or to provide an attachment for a ewer that is fitted with a concave bottom.
Boxes that slide into openings in case furniture or shelving, used for storage but not mounted on runners as drawers would be.
Containers usually with two interlocking halves that are designed to hold reels of film, most often motion picture film, but also bulk film intended for use in still photography.

Containers made to carry and store chalices used for eucharistic ceremonies. Some are shaped in the form of a chalice while others are square in form. Made of varying material, including leather, wood, and plastic.
From 1772; describes a common shape of decanter produced by British, Irish, and American glassmakers, having an elongated neck and slightly squat, barrel shape.
Ewers used for washing hands, especially those made of pottery and used in Roman times, and metal versions, often in animal forms, made in the medieval period, used for hand washing at the table.
Clocks driven by tiny permanent-magnet synchronous motors and electronic circuitry.
Coiled springs that determine the time of vibration of balance wheels, with which they work to regulate the progress of the hands on timepieces.
Sundials that first appeared in ancient Rome, used to tell time by utilizing the moving shadow of the sun cast upon a marked surface.
Watches that strike the hours in passing; for timepieces that strike the hours at any time upon request, use "repeaters."
Musical instruments which are played by means of a keyboard.
Sound devices that produce their sound by means of vibrating strings stretched between fixed points.

Generally refers to any musical wind instrument consisting of a hollow cylinder or pipe of wood, metal, or another material, with holes along its length that are stopped by the fingers or by keys that are opened by the fingers. Although most flutes are tubular, some are globular (as with a gourd flute). A flute is sounded by a stream of air from the player's lips striking against the sharp edge of an opening, breaking the air up and vibrating within the enclosed space. The air may be blown in from an end or from the side, depending upon the type of flute. Many, but not all, modern flutes are equipped with the Boehm system of keywork.

Bowed instruments, the term for which appears in medieval Europe from the mid-12th century to the late 14th century. Its exact form seems to vary in different locations and periods, but it is related to "vièle," "fidel," and "rebec."

Musical instruments that produce sound by means of rotating tone-wheels which themselves produce no acoustic sound but create a regular fluctuation in an electrical circuit which can be converted into an audio signal.
Instruments in which elastic tongues or lamellae, fixed at one end, are vibrated either with the fingers or mechanically.
Notched sticks, usually of bore or wood, sounded by scraping with another stick or other nonsonorous object.
Idiophones that produce sounds as the result of indirect actions, such as shaking or scraping.
Concussion idiophones consisting of sticks, usually used in pairs, played by being struck together.
Idiophones having a corrugated surface that is scraped by a nonsonorous object such as a stick.
Friction drums of the Akan people of western Guinea.
Membranophones having a larger diameter at the middle than at the ends and a curvilinear body.
Earlier of the two basic models of clavichord, in which each pair of strings serves several different keys.
Trapezoidal or wing-shaped harpsichords with the strings running diagonally from left to right, at an oblique angle to the keyboard.

Mechanical pipe organs operated by a rotary handle, which both works the bellows to supply air, and turns a pinned cylinder which, as it is turned, raises keys which cause the sounding of the appropriate pipes.
Small hand organs used in training song birds.
Small European reed organs activated by wind under pressure supplied by a compression bellows.

Organ pipes sounded by the vibrations of a flexible metal reed. For the simple pipes, used as complete and independent sound devices by themselves, in which the sound is produced through vibration of a single, double, or free reed, use "reedpipes."
Grand pianos of the largest size, about 9 feet or more in length, adapted in volume, timbre, and brilliancy of tone to concert use.

Type of large upright piano invented by William Southwell of Dublin in 1807, remaining popular until the mid-19th century. It was from 6 to 6 1/2 feet in height with a large, open front panel covered with cloth.

Membranophones sounded by friction, accomplished directly by rubbing the drumhead with the hand or a piece of leather or cloth, or by means of a cord or stick which passes back and forth through one or two holes in the drumhead. In some types, the drumhead is vibrated indirectly by friction on a cord or stick in contact with, but not piercing, the drumhead.
Kettledrums whose tuning screws are operated simultaneously, by a pedal, a single master screw, or by rotation.
Double-headed hourglass pressure drums of West Africa, principally of the Hausa people of Nigeria, held under the arm and beaten with a hooked stick.
Percussive instruments originating from Mali and Guinea. Held between the legs of the musician and struck on top, djembes can be used as leading instruments or to accompany others.

Japanese hourglass drums having two heads of hide stretched over iron rings that project well beyond the body, laced to each other across the body with ropes. Players hold them by the ropes, relaxing and tightening their grip to alter the tension and thus adjust the pitch of the heads during play. Often used during performaces of Noh drama.
The bodies of tubular and vessel drums, acting as resonators.
Bells that are rung at a specific time to announce dinner, historically used on ships, in hotels, or in homes.
Small bells in the presbytery or on exterior of churches, smaller than bells mounted in the bell tower. May also refer to small bells on musical instruments.
Small handbells placed upon the table at meals for summoning attendants.
Bells attached to a sleigh or to the harness of a horse pulling a sleigh. Use also for orchestral vessel rattles consisting of a set of pellet bells strung on a hoop.
Cymbals of India, often made of brass.
Javanese bronze gongs, about 15 to 20 inches in diameter, suspended from a frame and beaten with a padded mallet.
Rattles in which the rattling objects are attached to a frame against which they strike.
Toys for very young children, consisting of a hollow object enclosing small, loose beads that strike against each other when they are shaken.

Chinese slit drums in the abstract shape of a fish, squat and wedge-shaped, carved from camphor wood and usually lacquered. They rest on the player's hand or a cushion and are struck with sticks during Buddhist or Taoist temple services.
Stamping tubes of Nigeria and northern Africa, consisting of a gourd open at the top and bottom, played by women.
Woodblocks used in temple rituals in China, Japan, and Korea.

Xylophones consisting of large wood keys or slabs resting across banana tree trunks, or a combination of straw bundles and banana tree trunks, found in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa. Commonly from two to six players interlock different melodic patterns on a single instrument.
Xylophones of the Ganda of Uganda, consisting of twelve wood slabs placed across two banana trunks and separated by tall thin sticks driven into the stems; they are played by three players.

Stones that emit ringing tones when struck. This refers to those that are found as a geological anomaly in the landscape; for those that are found and used specifically in a musical context, use 'rock gongs,' though often there is no distinction.
Resonators in keyboard string instruments, consisting of thin boards of wood or other material over which the strings are stretched.

Finger-plucked banjos fitted with five strings, four of regular length plus a fifth one positioned below the lowest string, secured by a peg halfway up the neck, on which the melody is played with the thumb while the fingers play accompaniment on the others.

Type of late cittern very popular in England from about 1750 to 1810, having a flat or slightly convex back and six courses of metal strings, the bottom two being single-strung and the upper four double.
Steel-stringed acoustic or semi-acoustic guitars, having a full body and a distinctive arched top.
Harps with no forepillar.
Large harps of the Fula and the Malinke people of Africa, with an arched neck, three strings, and a gourd resonator.
Harps equipped with a pedal mechanism which changes the string tension and thus alters their pitch.
Harps equipped with a single-action pedal mechanism, used to raise the pitch of the strings by a semitone during performance.
Plucked, stringed lutes of the Balkans, which resemble a mandolin in shape. The alto version of the instrument is known as the brac, and the tenor is the celo.
Lyres having a built-up wooden box serving as a resonator and a wooden soundboard, existing today primarily in Ethiopia.
Five-string bowl lyres of Egypt and the Sudan.
Bowed or plucked box lyres of ancient Wales, surviving into the early 19th century.
Mandolins of alto-tenor range, having from four to eight pairs of strings.
Psalteries from the Ukraine with flat, oval bodies, and thirty strings or more along the soundboard. Bandouras are sometimes played in large ensembles.

American dulcimers which, like dulcimers worldwide, are played with hammers. For the American chordophones involving strings stretched over a soundbox, but played by plucking, use "Appalachian dulcimers."
Hurdy-gurdies with organ pipework and bellows housed in their bodies, popular in France in the 18th century; players could activate either the strings or the pipes, or both together.
Fiddles of North India and Pakistan, similar to the esraj.
Small bass viols popular in 17th-century England.

Single-string musical bows of the southern United States, consisting of a length of wire attached to the wall of a frame house, which acts as a resonator; a cotton reel is often used as a bridge. They are plucked with glass bottlenecks or nails. A more portable version replaces the house with a fence picket.
Stands intended to hold books.

Stands for supporting the Koran in a position convenient for reading. May resemble a common bookstand or take the form of an X, with the book supported in the upper cradle of the crossing planks. Stands for supporting the Koran in a position convenient for reading. May resemble a common bookstand or take the form of an X, with the book supported in the upper cradle of the crossing planks.
Candlestands with a notched mechanism for raising or lowering a support for a candle and usually with a trestle base.
Stands intended specfically to hold flowers, usually cut flowers. May be small table-top items or larger stands, used for decoration or for selling flowers.
Wash basin stands that have closed, rather than open support structures, sometimes fitted with doors for storage.

Small three-legged tables or stands; also, table-like stands for tea caddies. The term is of Anglo-Indian origin, originally from the Hindu word "tepai" for tripod. From ca. 1810, the term was used specifically for small tables used to support tea caddies or tea chests, whether or not the table had three legs. Teapoys were often fitted with various compartments for storing tea. The stand may be one with, or dettachable from, the tea chest or caddy.
Work tables specifically used for sewing.
Tables with a circular top that expands on an iron frame to allow eight extra leaves to be inserted. It was patented by Robert Jupe in 1835.
Small tables with extending flaps supported on slender legs, or hinged brackets.
Dropleaf tables of the Pembroke stye, having pillar and claw supports, with legs jutting from a pillar or columns, and with feet terminating into a claw.
Relatively large vessels or basins used for chilling wine at the dinner table; usually ceramic or metal, often richly ornamented.
Term applied in the 1860s to furniture produced by firms which employed leading designers and architects. Designs tended toward simple forms with hand-carved and painted decoration.
Term generally applied to a great variety of furniture specially designed for use outdoors.
Parts and components of furniture arms.
The scroll ending on arms of certain kinds of Windsor chairs.
Rails that form some part of the support of the arms of chairs.  Found on some Windsor chairs, where the arms are a part of one continuous rail around the back of the chair.
Chair or seat rails that form the upright support of the back, often with carved details such as fluting or "ears."
Spindles split longitudinally and applied to furniture surfaces as decorative elements.
Decorative inlaid border of contrasting types of wood cut diagonally across the grain, generally used to finish edges and rims of furniture.
Frames of a bed, including bedrails, headboard, and footboard.
Posts set at the head of a bed.
Fabric cases filled with feathers used either alone as a bed or on a bedstead, or box spring.

Rooflike components generally cantilevered from the headboard as opposed to being supported by posts, and which extend over the whole area of the bed. Use "half-testers" for similar forms which only extend over the head half.
Drawers which overlap their frames, usually with molded edges that protrude slightly from the cabinet they rest in, rather than sitting flush.
Drawers devised to store paper documents. These may be of various form, to hold documents either horizontally or vertically.
The lower parts of a piece of furniture that serve to support it, usually projecting at the base or at the end of a leg.
Cabinet feet with a cyma reversa profile, found in American and some English work.
Claw-and-ball feet associated with early American furniture originating in Massachusetts.
Feet in the form of animal paws with elaborate hair, often found on chair legs, but appearing also on many decorative art objects, including andirons.
Modern American term for a band separating the leg and foot of a table or stand.
Parts and components of furniture legs.
Legs with a double curve, convex above concave, introduced about 1700.
Refers to a hinged leg, without a stretcher, which swings out to support the drop leaf of a table, such as found on card tables. For similar legs with a stretcher, use "gate legs."
Parts and components of seats.
18th-century term for seats in which the middle and front are lower than the sides.
Frames on which the seat is built.
Modern term for a melon-shaped swelling, often carved with gadrooning, used centrally on table legs, bed posts, and press cupboard supports in the late 16th and the 17th centuries.
Framing or brackets installed in chests, cabinetry, desks, or other furniture that support drawers.

Used to distinguish prints that are original creations, for example prints by Rembrandt or Dürer, from "reproductive prints," which are intended to copy a painting or drawing for mass circulation. In other contexts, for prints produced with the intention of their being works of art, simply use "prints." In the 1960s, the term "original print" was defined by the Print Council of America as those prints for which the artist alone had created the plate or other master image to print from, and that photomechanical processes were not be used. Modern printmaking techniques blur this artistic distinction, but the term is still used to make the distinction with 17th- to 19th-century reproductive prints.
Japanese prints of a standard size, about 11 by 8 inches.

Prints commemorating a marriage, often of a ruling family or otherwise of a marriage important to the community. The subject typically includes portraits and particulars of the event, or allegorical subjects referring to the couple. The genre was particularly popular in Europe from 16th-19th centuries.
Prints made from surfaces built up with liquid plastics on wood, metal, cardboard, or plastic supports. May be printed intaglio or relief.

Prints on paper incorporating impressions of a reverse design created on a printing plate, usually copper, into which the design has been incised (engraved) using burins or gravers. Historically, "engravings" has sometimes been incorrectly used to refer to all prints, regardless of the specific technique. For prints made from designs engraved on a flat wooden block, use "wood cuts"; for prints made from a plate that is etched rather than engraved, use "etchings."
Intaglio prints made from surfaces upon which shapes, textures, etc. have been glued or otherwise attached. For collagraph prints that combine intaglio and relief, use the broader term "collagraphs."

Refers to modern prints produced by the sand-grain mezzotint process, by which a mezzotint-like tone is achieved from sandpaper grain. The process was developed in the 20th century as a way to avoid the laborious process of rocking the plate. Such prints will have the general quality of a mezzotint but will not show in the lighter areas the straight lines of the rocker's serrated edge.
Prints produced by the salt-ground etching process.
Lithographs obtained by means of lithographic chalk, also called crayon. Before its application the lithographic stone was roughened by grinding fine sand over its surface.
Prints made from a design cut in linoleum-faced blocks on which a knife or gouge has been used to recess the non-printing area and leave the image to be printed in relief.
Refers to wood engravings with one or two tints from wood blocks.

Color woodblock prints in which two or more blocks are printed one on top of the other, one or more being flat tonal blocks with limited chromatic range and a line block printed last. Early scholars distinguished two-block from multi-block prints by calling them "camaïeu," that is, the ‘monochrome method,’ distinguishing them from "chiaroscuro woodcuts," Current usage does not make this distinction, and the terms have been used interchangeably in various sources.
Japanese multi-colored woodblock prints in which a separate block is carved for every color, and printed serially to create the final image.
Photomechanical prints made by the dye transfer process.

Color prints made using a combination printing process involving an intaglio, or occasionally lithographic, key plate which prints the image, after which color is superimposed on the print using wood blocks. The process was patented by an Englishman, George Baxter, in 1835, and was very popular up into the 1870s. This term refers to prints of this process not made by Baxter himself; the term Baxter prints is sometimes used to refer exclusively to prints made by Baxter.

Small, spring-driven or pendulum, wood-cased clocks intended to be placed on a bracket on the wall, set on a mantel, or carried from room to room; the brackets were often designed to match the style of clocks; generally from the 17th and 18th centuries.
American pendulum wall clocks having a circular case for the dial, a narrow tapering body, and a boxlike base, resembling a banjo; design invented and patented by Simon Willard in 1802.

Weight-driven domestic versions of tower clocks with iron movements set in openwork cases having Gothic details; primarily produced in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland in the 15th and 16th centuries, and then introduced in the United States in the mid-19th century.
Late 18th-century American chairs with pierced and intertwined slats and generally associated with Philadelphia cabinetmakers.

17th-century American turned great chairs styled after one that belonged to John Carver, Governor of Massachusetts Bay Colony. Such chairs have boldly turned posts and decorative spindles, but unlike Brewster chairs they have spindles only in the back and below the arms, and not below the seat.
Chairs with backs which may be lowered and seats that are hinged to unfold or that can otherwise be extended to form beds.
Thrones or seats incorporating lotus motifs, found in Hindu, Buddhist, and other traditions.
Chairs with adjustable backs, swivel seats, and commonly mounted with castors, designed to be used in the course of office work.
Wheel chairs, sometimes propelled and steered by turning winches on the arms, and having a foot rest designed to elevate the legs. Developed by John Joseph Merlin in the 18th century.
Easy chairs with a back and footrest adjustable up or down to comfort the user.
Popular term for mid-19th-century American rocking chairs with a high, upholstered back and seat and open arms with upholstered pads on the elbows.

16th-century English and early 17th-century American stools, usually upholstered and covered with sumptuous fabric and fringe. Term also applied to a variety of small, low stools generally with socketed legs.
Pierced wooden seats with removable containers underneath; used as a commode.
Large stuffed cushions that serve as seats or leg rests.
A Roman seat or bench for two persons, though usually occupied by only one for festivals, etc.
Pews in a church reserved for the royal family; the pews may be set up on a high platform or otherwise decorated and designated as belonging to the monarch or family.
Settles with boards across the tops of the side boards.
Term used by Chippendale for double-headed couches with a canopy.
Settees formed of three linked armchairs.
19th-century sofas with a central backrest on either side of which people can sit.
Canapés whose backs gently curve forward and downward to form the arms.

Long seating forms with a back support and one end; primarily used for reclining rather than sitting. Distinct from "sofas" which have a back and two ends and are primarily used for sitting rather than reclining.

Beds enclosed with paneling on all sides but one, where there was a curtain over the opening; usually stood against the wall and, in some cases, were built into the wall or incorporated into the scheme of paneling.

Beds with a rooflike component supported above the bed by the bed posts. For beds with testers that only cover the head half of the bed, use "half-tester beds." Use "canopy beds" when the rooflike component is suspended from the ceiling or the wall, as opposed to being supported on posts.
High-post beds with arched, or in the Federal period often serpentine, as opposed to straight canopies and whose posts are generally less than six feet in height.
Beds with two ends of equal height, with each end overscrolled.
Beds which are 54 inches wide; large enough to accommodate two adults.
Beds constructed so that they can be folded or swung into a closet; named after William L. Murphy, American inventor.
Deception beds concealed in a carcase that outwardly resembles a bureau.
Beds for infants that are mounted on pivots that allow for the cradle to swing from side to side.

Strong chests, coffers, bins, boxes, close baskets, or similar tightly covered receptacles, generally made of wood and distinguished by having particularly strong, durable, and often water-tight construction. Used to store food or articles of great value.

Bureau-cabinets typical of fine furniture originating in the 17th century that feature cabinets of drawers or pigeon holes, fronted by one or more doors, and supported on a stand from which it may be detached.
Pieces of furniture fitted with pigeonholes or compartments to hold boxes made either as independent pieces of furniture or as pieces to be placed on top of a bureau plat.
Chests with deep storage space, at least one drawer, and a hinged lid. Frequently used for the storage of blankets.

Typical Frisian money chests given by a husband to his fiancée during an engagement ritual. These are usually small and rectangular and are often made of silver. The surface of the chest is usually decorated or engraved and sometimes contains a text.
Chests of drawers with a secretary drawer at the top.

Medieval French term for portable coffers or chests used for personal luggage, covered in leather and studded with nails and usually having a rounded top. Eventually they took the form of a chest mounted on feet, used for storing goods. The current French form is a decorative high chest or cabinet with an arched or curved top.
15th- and 16th-century groom's chests with a single large compartment; made only in the Catalana region of Spain.

Italian cupboards that were originally cassoni with doors instead of a lid, but from the 16th century developed into two-tiered pieces similar to English press cupboards. Generally having massive architectural decoration, including pilasters supporting a monumental cornice; frequently made for sacristies.
