Wardrobes that are a typically American variations on the 17th-century Netherlandish kast or large cupboard; made by Dutch settlers in the Hudson and Delaware valleys about 1675-1750 and more widely into the 19th century. Generally have two raised paneled doors, and a heavy overhanging cornice with a drawer or drawers below; sometimes decoratively painted with grisaille panels and fruit.
Cupboards for the storage of linen items, including undergarments, shirts, bed linens, or table linens.
Clothes presses flanked with additional drawers and storage areas on either side of the central carcass, coined in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

Case furniture for a dining room having compartments or shelves for holding articles of table service below, and a surface for serving or preparing food. The term has been in use since the 16th century.
Racks comprising a frame with compartments for storing bottles.
Desks on frames set on high legs, of the type generally used in mercantile establishments in the early 19th century.

Desks and bookcases with a hinged one-piece round lid or cover that resembles a section of a cylinder and which rolls up into the desk top; chiefly made in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. For similar desks without a bookcase use "cylinder fall desks."
Fall-front desks that were intended for use by ladies, often of relatively delicate design and sometimes having a wide opening to accommodate ladies' voluminous skirts.

Office furniture that is a hybrid of cabinet and desk manufactured by Wooton and Company in Indianapolis in the latter part of the 19th century. These are characterized by two locking doors that themselves carry drawers and compartments for storage. When opened, a fall extends to create a writing surface facing an interior of ranged compartments and drawers.
Writing tables with a pop-up reading stand.
Small ladies writing desks with cabriole legs, mounted with drawers or compartments, and with a pull-out writing surface.
Fall-front desks having a writing surface that, when closed, folds upward and inward, forming an angle with the carcass.
Slant-front desks generally intended for a woman's use.
Tables with a single columnar support.
Tables with a slate surface covered with cloth and surrounded by cushioned rails, on which the game of billiards is played. Distinct from "pool tables" which are similar in form but have six pockets.
Dining tables with extending frames whose tops can be lengthened by inserting loose leaves.
Dressing tables fitted with mirrors, compartments for cosmetics, and drawers or cabinets enclosed by doors for the storage of clothing.
Dressing tables with two drawers in the sides which swing out and provide mirrors on a quadrant so that a woman could see herself at any angle.
Heart-shaped dressing tables with drawers springing out at each side somewhat like butterfly wings.

Tables having tops marked with a checkerboard pattern of 64 squares for the purpose of playing the game of checkers. Chess may also be played on the same board. Traditionally, checkerboards will comprise alternating black and red squares, although any contrasting colors may be used.
Large oval or circular card tables with a central support and tilt top.

Refers generally to three-legged supports of any kind. The word may be applied variously to objects such as stools, tables, light stands, stands for cameras, or pedestals. Ancient, antique, or classical forms are associated with religious or symbolic altars, or sacrificial vessels. The seat of the Delphic oracle was in the form of a tripod.
Swords designed primarily for cutting blows.

Swords carried during public ceremonies and rituals to signify the authority of the owner or wearer. They were often carried point up by a body guard or other attendant following the owner, rather than worn by him.
The metal plates or mountings of a scabbard or sheath; particularly those that cover the point.
Simple hilts in which the grip and quillons, together with the blade of the weapon, form the outline of a Latin cross.
Firearms, generally having a bore of 1 inch or less in diameter, that are designed to be operated by one person, held in one or both hands, with or without the support of the shoulder.
Light shotguns designed for hunting small game, especially birds, in use from the mid-16th century.
Firearms that can be held and fired with one hand.

Small single-shot muzzleloading percussion pocket pistols of large bore, first made by the Philadelphia gunsmith Henry Deringer in the 1840s and subsequently widely copied throughout the United States. Specifically for those actually made by Henry Deringer himself, use "deringers."
Automatic rifles developed from submachine guns during the Second World War for use with cartridges intermediate in size and power between pistol and rifle cartridges.

The earliest type of mechanical ignition system for firearms, originating in the mid-15th century, consisting of a slow-burning match or wick held in an arm which, when the trigger is pressed, lowers the match into a pan full of priming powder, the burning of which ignites the main charge.
Firearms designed for military use.
Parts or components of projectile weapons.
Throwing clubs with a short shaft and a large heavy knob at one end, originating in southern Africa and typically made of hardwood.
Coins of the early Medieval through the modern period in the Western world, from the 7th or 8th century to the present.
Islamic silver coins struck from the 7th to the 14th century.
British silver coins of various denominations given as alms during Maundy Thursday ceremonies; issued since the early Medieval period.
Government-authorized adhesive stamps, imprinted stamps, hand stamps, or meter markings issued as evidence of prepayment of postage.
Collocates tokens that provide the right to goods or services but are not redeemable for cash.
Cases or structures that surround or enclose such items as works of art, mirrors, or documents, serving as support or protection or to call attention, while leaving the items visible.
Coarse textiles which were used as inexpensive floor coverings by themselves or on top of a carpet.

Devices with a wrought iron standard, often ornate, supporting a horizontal flat ring and spring for clamping whatever is placed within the ring. May have been intended for holding a torch or link rather than an ordinary candle.
Candlesticks having one or more spherical or near-spherical shapes incorporated in the design of the stem of the candlestick or forming the body of the candlestick.
A product line of lamps with bubble shapes, originally designed by George Nelson in 1947, and manufactured by Howard Miller from the early 1950s until 1979.
Betty lamps with integral stands; the form is believed to have originated in the Portsmouth, New Hampshire, area.

Spout lamps, usually made of tin, having a cylindrical font with a domed or conical cover and one or more wick tubes. The font is fitted into a separate container to which is attached a bail handle and drip catcher.

Argand lamps fitted with a rod terminated by a plate which is positioned so that the air passing through the tube surrounded by the wick is deflected against the flame causing it to spread and become globular.
Lamps for use by architects to illuminate a work area, and which usually use a combination of incandescent and fluorescent bulbs.
Lamps designed to be suspended from the ceiling and cast light downward.
Chandeliers made to hold candles.

Lamps with fonts, either of metal or glass, which are high and narrow, generally tapering from top to bottom, and which have one to six diverging wick tubes that extend well beyond the height of the burner. Small metal caps attached by chains are furnished to extinguish the flame and retard evaporation of the volatile fuel (alcohol and redistilled turpentine or camphene).
Lamps which burn colza oil.
Lamps in which light, or radiant energy near the visible spectrum, is produced by the passage of an electric current through a vapor or a gas.

Lanterns fitted with a lens or lenses, sometimes of knobbed or faceted glass to concentrate and intensify light. May be four-sided with lenses on three sides and a handle on the fourth, or have a lens on one side and a handle on the opposite side, or be cylindrical with a hinged door on which the lens or lenses are mounted.
Devices in which the taper is wound on reels or drums and unwound and pulled up through grips as needed.
Torches used in a ceremonial context, common in many cultures globally. An example is the torch carried prior to the start of the Olympic games.
Single opaque or translucent elements which shield a source from direct view at certain angles and absorb unwanted light.
Candles made of wax.
Incandescent lamps having a constant but not necessarily known luminous intensity against which other lamps are successively compared in a photometer.

Screens used to shelter the face or legs from the full heat of a fire in a fireplace. May include a decorated panel or panels, often set into a decorative wooden furniture structure that can be moved for the convenience of the sitter. For nonflammable metal screens placed directly in front of fireplace openings to prevent logs and sparks from escaping, use "fire screens (equipment)."
Fire screens constructed of two folding leaves; many, but not all designs allow sliding of the panels to adjust coverage.
Seating furniture produced for use by multiple persons.

A seat for one person, often without a back. They were the most common type of seat furniture until the 19th century. Distinct from "benches" in that they seat only one person; usually distinguished from "chairs" in that they have no back; however, tall seating pieces at a bar or counter are called stools though they sometimes have backs. Generally made in two types; one supported on four straight legs and the other with legs arranged crosswise.
Modernist armchair design in beech and teak wood by Peter Hvidt and Orla Molgaard Nielsen, ca. 1947.
Angular armchairs with slatted seats and backs; not known to have originated in the Adirondacks. They are generally used outdoors.

Easy chairs having a semicircular back forming a single upholstered piece with the wings and arms. For chairs with a solid, rounded wooden back or those made from cutting away parts of a barrel, use "barrel chairs."

Collector's term for Italian Renaissance X-chairs with crossing assemblies only in the front and back. Their name is derived from association with the 14th-century poet Dante, although it is questionable that such chairs were actually used by him.
Use with reference to chairs with backs consisting of a series of vertical banisters between the seat and top rail; of a type first made in the 18th century.

Paintings and other adornments applied to books, scrolls, or other document types for the purpose of illustrating or decorating the text. It may take any of three forms: Miniatures, which are small pictures that are often set apart from the text and comprise a self-contained design; decorated initial letters, that themselves may contain a small scene; and decorated borders, which also may contain scenes. The media of illumination generally includes paint, ink, and precious metals on vellum, paper, or silk. Among the earliest surviving illuminated documents are papyrus rolls of the ancient Egyptian Book of the Dead. Other early examples have survived from Classical Greece and Rome, as Aztec pictorial maps, and in Mayan and Chinese codices. The art form flourished in bibles and other sacred books of medieval Europe, where the media typically were egg-white tempera on vellum and card. It also flourished in Indian and Islamic miniatures, which were produced into the 19th century. For pictures that are not painted miniatures or that accompany printed books or advertisements, use "illustrations."
Paintings -- usually on a rigid support such as wooden panel or metal, but occasionally on canvas -- that are painted on both front and back and intended to be viewed from either side.

Refers to distinctive painted wall panels, generally those from 15th- and 16th-century Italy. They were typically installed in a frieze above the wooden cornice molding, forming a separate register between the wooden paneling and the bare wall just below the ceiling. Today, they have often been removed from their original location, and are recognized by their long, narrow proportions. They are distinguished from "spalliere (paintings)," which were installed lower on the wall, just above chests or benches. Since the original context of the setting is lost once the panel has been removed from the wall, the term "spalliere" may be applied to both.
Scrolls, displayed vertically, that contain text, artwork, or both.

Ancient Greek visual works comprising pottery objects having primarily black decoration on a red ground, with figures reserved in red. Details were painted on the red of the background clay, allowing overall more sophisticated works than with black-figure vase paintings. Works appeared in Athens ca. 530 BCE.

Describes elaborately painted sheets of bark found throughout Aboriginal Australian cultures. For native Australians, the art of bark paintings was an everyday practice, but it was also utilized for ceremonial purposes.  After European colonization, bark painting production decreased.
A type of collage and painting that uses only paper to create the composition; the term means "glued papers."

Drawings or works in another two-dimensional medium in which part of an object or structure is removed to show the interior. For orthographic drawings specifically, use "broken-out sections," "half sections" (for objects), or "sectional elevations" (for structures).

Refers to drawings in oblique projection in which the horizontal plane is parallel to the plane of projection or drawing surface, and the plan is rotated to any convenient angle so that verticals may be drawn. They are characterized by typically having a higher angle of view than an isometric drawing, and orthographic plans may be depicted on the horizontal surfaces.
Drawings in oblique projection in which the vertical plane is parallel to the plane of projection (drawing surface), and all three spatial axes are drawn to the same scale.
Drawings or works in another medium showing the arrangement of vertical elements of a building, either exterior or interior, as a direct projection to a vertical plane.

Refers to drawings, or works in another medium, created by isometric projection, which is a projection in which all three spatial axes are equally inclined to the plane of projection or drawing surface.
Renderings made in projection on a plane surface of the finished appearance of the interior walls of structures.
Orthographic drawings, prints, or sketches that depict a building, or sections of a building, on a horizontal plane.

In the architecture of military fortifications, the term refers to ground plans of fortified works, including fortifications, mine fields, defensive positions, military installations, or other plans. The plans may be superimposed on a map or photograph.
Plans that show the ground surface of a building site or other site, generally including grade elevations and contours.

Plans that illustrate the configuration and location of the foundation, which comprises the supporting elements of a building, located primarily below ground level, that transmit building loads to the soil or rock underneath. They may also note the conditions that are required for the support of a specific structure.
Plans of one story of a building that has numerous stories in that form, thus illustrating what is typical or usual in the floor plans of this building.

Scaled floor plans showing HVAC layout, which is the layout for heating, ventilation, and air contitioning. They may include small drawings of an adjacent elevation. For other drawings of HVAC systems, use "HVAC drawings."
Orthographic images that depict a building, object, or site as if cut transversely.
Architectural drawings that render structural interior space and give the impression of relative position, size, or distance, as the space would appear if viewed from a physical vantage point.

Regarding the modern building trade, refers to drawings that indicate changes made during construction from the work proposed in the working drawings. For these and other drawings or copies of drawings that are kept as file records of a completed project, use "record drawings." For scale drawings of existing structures, generally, use "measured drawings"; for drawings that generally depict actual locations, use "topographical views."
Refers to full-size preparatory drawings made for the purpose of transferring a design to the working surface of a painting, tapestry, or other large work.
Drawings that are intended to show the assembly of small details of a larger construction.
Drawings of plumbing systems or parts thereof. For scaled floor plans specifically, use "plumbing plans."

Refers to drawings on sheets of clear acetate or nitrate, where the outline of the figures are applied to the front of the cel, and the color is applied to the back. The sheet is typically placed over a background image and photographed, along with a series of other animation cels that together depict phased movements of the figures.
Refers to complete drawings of whole compositions, whether as pattern drawings, working drawings, or done after a finished work.
Drawings of the mechanical systems of buildings (e.g., HVAC and plumbing systems).

Thin supporting strips, usually of wood, used to hold together boards, panels, or planks of wood in order to join them, give them strength, and prevent warping. Examples of battens are on the reverses of panel paintings and the cross boards on board-and-batten shutters and doors.
Rose headed nails having a relatively flat head.
Devices of metal or wood with rounded handles and cylindrical shafts that are inserted into holes in pinrails on traditionally rigged sailing ships to secure lines of rigging.
Tacks having an inverted U-shape or square shape, with a point on both ends. Distinguished from staple nails, which are of heavier construction.
Projectiles and propellants used to operate firearms.

Bronze cuirasses of ancient Greece, typically consisting of two pieces hinged on one side and joined by metal pins or loops on the other, and characterized by an inward curve near the waist below which the lower rim curves strongly out. They were common until the late 6th century BCE.
The earliest form of greaves, dating back to the mid-13th century, being gutter-shaped tubes of metal or hide, open on one side and covering the shin from just above the ankle to just below the knee.
Type of body armor to protect the skull, usually a particular type used from the end of the 15th to the beginning of the 17th centuries.
Helmets and helms, of various designs, intended for use in jousting rather than in battle.
Tippets of mail attached around the lower edge and face opening of helmets, commonly basnets, to protect the shoulders, neck, and part of the face; used in the 14th and 15th centuries.

Round, oval, or bilobated shields of Classical Greece and later, Doric in origin, made of layers of cow hide and large enough to protect most of the body. Early models were held in the hand; later versions had an armlet set diagonally, with a handle near the edge, and were carried on the arm.
Armor for the horse's neck, made of narrow lames articulated together, or of lames alternating with bands of mail.

Spurs furnished with a single spike for goading the horse, in common use from the pre-Christian era until the 13th century. Medieval European models generally have conical spikes or a raised molding or ball close to the point to prevent the spike from penetrating too far.

Cannons first manufactured at the Carron Iron Company at Falkirk, Scotland, around 1778 and continuing in use until the late 19th century. They were short and light in relation to their bore, had no trunnions, and were used mainly on ships for firing broadsides at short range.
Small culverins about 7 feet long and of about a 3-inch bore, firing shot of approximately 4 pounds. They were in use during the 16th and 17th centuries.
Edged steel weapons resembling daggers or short swords, designed to be attached to the muzzle end of a firearm barrel.

Flat wedge- or fin-shaped appendages fixed to the rear of the shaft of an arrow or dart to enhance the range and accuracy of their flight. They have been made from a number of different materials, typically bird feathers but also parchment, cuir bouilli, wood, and plastic.

A type of long-handled battle axe of the Ottoman Empire, Persia, Armenia, India and surrounding regions and cultures having one or two broad crescent-shaped blades and thin handles measuring from three to seven feet.
Detachable bayonets with a grip and sufficient breadth of blade to allow them to be used as knives or daggers.

Bows basically consisting of a curved stave mounted crosswise on a center shaft by means of a system of cord or gut bindings or metal bands, the string being drawn back, held, and released by some mechanical means such as a windlass or a rotatable nut. They were in use as early as the 11th century and continue to be used contemporarily for hunting and recreation.

Weapons of Africa worn on the wrists and designed for close combat, consisting generally of a metal disk with a central hole and a gap to allow them to be slipped onto the wrist, the outer edge of which is either sharpened like a knife blade or furnished with one or more projections for clubbing or slashing an opponent; sheaths may be worn on both edges. They are used in both actual and ceremonial combat, and worn as signs of manhood or status, or as ornament.

Roman javelins of Etruscan origin, issued to Roman soldiers from the Republican period to the 4th or 5th century CE. Their form and weight varied over time, but usually they were characterized by a long, narrow head attached to the staff by a flange or socket, and a weight attached to the staff below the head to improve balance and trajectory.
Pikes with comparatively short, stout staffs, used as weapons aboard warships from the 16th into the 20th century either when boarding a ship or to repel boarders.
Long, straight-bladed swords with a grip long enough to allow them to be grasped by one hand plus two or three fingers of the other, used in the 15th and 16th centuries.

Broadswords with a distinctive basket hilt and, usually, a double-edged, pointed blade, named after the Slavonian bodyguards of the Doge of Venice who used them; surviving examples date from the late 15th to the late 18th century.
Indonesian, asymmetrical daggers with a wavy blade, often made from precious materials such as gold, ivory of rare types of wood. The kris is often associated with power, dignity and mystical powers.

Reproductive prints of architectural plans, maps, mechanical drawings, and other technical drawings, characterized by having white images on blue backgrounds and produced by the blueprint process. For blue images on white backgrounds, use "blueline prints." For blue-toned photographs produced by the blueprint process, use "cyanotypes."
Prints made on light-sensitized surfaces that produce blue images on neutral backgrounds. For white images on blue backgrounds, use "blueprints."
Collections of images, usually, but not always, held in electronic format for retrieval by computer. Image databases may contain images of works of art, documents, medical CAT scans, or other images.
Software that combines more than one primary function.

Ancient manuscripts generally taking the form of the modern book: bound leaves of paper or parchment with information inscribed on both faces, attached at a center fold. For books that are printed rather than inscribed, before 1501, use 'incunabula.'

Flexible, transparent sheets of film bearing a series of microimages on a flat sheet of film, usually arranged in a grid pattern, to be read by magnification on specially designed equipment; normally having an identifying strip legible without magnification.
Microfiche with a reduction ratio greater than 90 times.
Computer output produced directly onto microfilm, without paper printout as an intermediary.

Works having the form of a scroll and depicting a wide panoramic view, such as of a map, city, landscape, military battle, other historical event, or narrative. Examples include Chinese panoramic scroll paintings and prints of cityscapes popular in Europe.

Sound recordings invented by Thomas Edison in 1877. They were the earliest form of phonograph record, and were marketed commercially. Sound would be funnelled through a horn and against a diaphragm, which would vibrate. The resulting vibrations were transmitted to a stylus, which followed a helical path along a surface, usually wax, which coated a rotating cylinder. The resulting cylinder could be played by a cylinder phonograph.

Phonograph records played at 78 revolutions-per-minute, the standard playing speed for records until the mid-20th century. The maximum length of play per side was 4 1/2 minutes, and they appeared most commonly in ten-inch and twelve-inch formats.
Cassettes of audiotape. According to international standards, the tape is usually 0.15 inches (3.8 millimetres) wide and can carry 4 to 8 tracks.

Small audiocassettes that are approximately one quarter the size of a standard cassette, and that use only the reels to achieve tape transport. For audiocassettes of roughly the same size but that use a capstan transport system, use 'microcassettes.'
Recordable compact discs. CD-Rs have a light-sensitive layer which can be recorded onto, or "burned," by a CD-recorder.
Magnetic tapes on which visual images are electronically recorded and played back, with or without sound.
Cassettes containing recordings on videotape.

Describes videotape one-half-inch wide, for professional use, with higher resolution than standard VHS, Super-VHS or other, earlier analog video types. Originally developed by Sony and introduced in 1982.

Painted marks on ancient Greek vases, usually found on the foot of the vase. Less common than graffiti, dipinti were typically painted in red ocher and the vase after firing. The relatively fewer dipinti done in black gloss were painted before firing. Like graffiti, dipinti usually consist of a single letter or linked letters, numerical notations, and, less frequently, words, phrases, and sentences. Most are probably forms of trademarks; they are mostly found on vases intended for export.

term: coats of arms and coat of arms elements
definition: Coats of arms and coat of arms elements.
A script of ancient Egypt consisting of abridged forms of hieroglyphics, used by the priests in their records.

Insignia of warriors in Nahua culture reflecting the person's rank and experience in battle. Generally used to refer to the feathered suits that encased the body, arms, and legs, however, the term also applies to various accoutrements including headdresses, large emblems carried on a frame worn on the back, as well as banners and shields.
Ceramic plaques pierced with holes to hang from wine barrels and inscribed with the names of the contents.
Bookplates that are usually printed or engraved with an area reserved for additions in handwriting, for the purpose of noting to and by whom a book was given.

Marks in paper produced by placing a stereo in bronze, rubber, or other substance, on the press roll of the papermaking machine and so leaving a design in the paper where it was more compressed. Technically, they are not true watermarks but are made to serve the same purpose.

One or more marks made to deface something in order to indicate a change in its status, such as through a pottery factory mark, indicating the piece is defective or outmoded, or as across a printing plate, assuring that no prints are produced beyond a limited edition.
Contemporary term sometimes applied to any marks placed on the underside of any ceramic object but strictly applicable to only such marks made with rubber stamps.
Cylinders of hard material engraved in intaglio upon the curved surface, used especially in ancient Mesopotamia to roll an identifying impression on wet clay.

Tablets produced for a variety of functions, as souvenirs for pilgrims, icons for portable shrines, models for artists, or for insertion into images or stupas to enhance their potency. These may incorporate carved images of deities or inscriptions.
Small pulleys or wheels which facilitate and direct the movement of a sliding barn (or other) door by rolling along a horizontal track or rail.
Small frames that attach to a door surface for insertion of a name card or plate.
Sliding bars that move in opposing directions, mounted at the top and bottom of a door. The bars engage with strike plates or openings in the door frame to secure the door.
Catches whose strike holds a communicating projection or finger by means of the pressure exerted by one or two spring-loaded balls.
Door hinges that can be separated by lifting. The door can thus be removed without unscrewing the hinges.
Door hinges containing one or more springs that may automatically close or otherwise restrict movement of the door.
Locks designed for doors that separate connecting rooms, often incorporating  knob latches and thumb bolts.

Fastenings for French or casement doors that consist of long rods, often hooked, at the top and bottom of the sash and that operate with a handle in the center. These use a round or square bar, distinguished from the half-round bar of a cremorne bolt.
Keyed locks designed for use on cupboards or boxes.
Master-keyed locks, often with a latch bolt and one or two dead bolts, designed for use by both a guest in a rented room and for a maid’s use.
Locks set into a cavity, hole, or recess of a door or window frame and requiring a special faceted or slotted shank key.
Prison-type locks designed to be built into the masonry of the door jamb, the bolt when locked being projected from the jamb and engaging with the door.
Locks having a case that requires a bored, round hole rather than a rectangular mortise. The face plate and the lock case are fastened together as a unit.
Time locks constructed to lock by the action of a clock at a predetermined time subsequent to and irrespective of the time of the closing of the door.
Ropes connecting a sash with its counterweight in a double-hung window.
T-shaped, surface-mounted hinges. The cross arm of the T is fixed to a doorframe or post while the length of the T supports a door or gate.
Heavy hooks and eyes, generally used on marine installations. Distinguished from "cabin hooks," which are generally used on cabinets.
Fastenings on a door frame into which a bolt is projected to secure a door.
Strikes with a spring plunger that completely fills the hole when the door is open.
Enlarged, protruding, cylindrical parts of a hinge through which the pin is inserted.
Pieces of hardware that act as protective covers on keyholes or lock cylinder mechanisms that may restrict intrusion of foreign bodies or incorrect keys.
Keys having a special faceted, splined, or slotted shank. An example of use is for mortise rack bolts.
Escutcheons cut for both knob and keyhole or cylinder.
Interfaces or meeting surfaces between two successive pours of concrete.
Wood joints of various types that are held securely in place through the shape of the lock, having one or more pieces that join to corresponding pieces in the opposite member.
Any writing made or proposed as an addition to or improvement of some principal writing; in legislation, refers to modifications or alterations in a bill or enacted law.
Formal requests submitted to an institution or individual as part of a selection process for a paid position, employment, or post.
Outlines of work or goals expected to be achieved during a projected time period.
Final reports following formal examinations of accounts.
Documents in which monies or goods received and paid or given out are recorded in order to permit periodic totaling.
Lists, sometimes recorded in book form, of those entitled to receive compensation at a given time and of the amounts due to each.
Documents by which one party (the insurer) in consideration of a premium, engages to indemnify another (the insured) against a contingent loss, by making a payment in compensation.
Documents showing items supplied, together with the prices charged for each; also, itemized bills or accounts.
Concise statements of the arguments of a party to a case in dispute, submitted to the court or other body hearing the case.

Surety bonds executed by the bidder on a construction project that serve as a guarantee that the bidder will enter into a contract within a specified time and furnish any required bonds ensuring completion of the work.
Legally binding instruments between a property owner and a hired contractor for a construction project.
Documents, enforceable by law, embodying agreements between two or more competent parties to do or not to do something, and specifying the terms and conditions of the agreement.
Contracts by which one conveys land or other property for a specified time usually for compensation or rent.

Legal instruments for government procurement detailing funds spent on supplies, services, and interests in real property by and for the use of a government through purchase or lease, whether the supplies, services, or interests are already in existence or must be created, developed, demonstrated, or evaluated.

Contracts based on payment by an agency to a contractor of reasonable costs incurred in the contract performance. These contracts may not require completion of a project, but rather the best efforts of the contractor.

Detailed and exact statements prescribing materials, dimensions, and workmanship for something to be built, installed, or manufactured, stipulating the use of proprietary products or processes without provision for substitution.
Documents attesting to acts of registering.
Records maintained by or relating to a particular church and its activities, such as baptisms and burials.
Records of a tribunal established for the administration of justice.

Documents amassed in the course of a presidential term that may include diaries, letter books, general and special correspondence, speeches, executive orders, press releases, scrap books and other miscellanea.
Records of the writs authorizing delivery of money out of the treasury.

Orders or regulations issued by the President, or some administrative authority under his direction, for the purpose of interpreting, implementing, or giving administrative effect to a provision of the Constitution or of some law or treaty. May also include similar state documents issued by governors or upper-level management in business.

Documents giving permission to one or more military persons to travel unimpeded, although usually with some restrictions, in a territory occupied by a military force; issued to a person or persons living in, or visiting in, the occupied area, by the commander of the military force in control thereof.
Permits granted by public officials authorizing the wrecking or destruction of property, especially by the use of explosives.
Systematically arranged and comprehensive collections of laws, or, more generally, systematic collections of regulations and rules of procedure or conduct.
Legislation that exhaustively covers a complete system of laws or a particular area of law.
Conclusions or resolutions reached after consideration by a judicial body.

Any forms of attestation, written or verbal, by which persons signify that they are bound in conscience to perform an act faithfully and truthfully; also affirmations of the truth of a statement given before testifying, as in a court of law.
Documents that are a product of courts dealing with criminal, rather than civil cases.
Formal documents issued by probate courts that serve to appoint an administrator of an estate.
Laws or statutes passed by a legislature.

Collective term for various documents presented to the House of Parliament. These consist of annual reports from government departments, or of organizations created by an Act of Parliament, regulations made by any Minister of the Crown under the authority of an Act of Parliament, and miscellaneous letters, typescripts and photocopies of documents presented by members with the House’s permission during the course of debates or other proceedings in the House.
Collected documents on policy making, correspondence, investigation and reporting related to legislation, or the political environment of the House of Representatives.
Collected documents on policy making, correspondence, investigation and reporting related to legislation, or the political environment of the House of Lords.
Records in which documents from various governmental jurisdictions are represented.

Registers that record the administration of the sacrament of baptism to members of a community. In historical usage, these registers also served as important civic documents, in that they recorded the approximate date of birth and names of new babies, their parents, and baptismal sponsors in the community.
Records of districts or churches under the jurisdiction of a bishop.
Formal documents conferring some honor, degree, or privilege, especially those bearing record of graduation from or a degree conferred by an educational institution.
Papers, research results, or other documents presenting the author's research and submitted in support of candidature for a Master's Degree.
Papers, research results, or other documents presenting the author's research and submitted in support of candidature for a doctoral degree.

Materials relating primarily to individual visual artists, artist collectives, collectors, art historians, and curators, including announcements, architectural drawings, photographs, auction catalogs, biographical information, books, brochures, correspondence, exhibition catalogs, institutional publications, interviews, invitations, manuscripts, memorabilia, negatives, newspapers, official records, oral histories, pamphlets, postcards, posters, press releases, price lists, and any number of other types of materials related to artists.

Refers to graphic or photogrammetric representations of the Earth's surface or a part of it, including physical features and political boundaries, where each point corresponds to a geographical or celestial position according to a definite scale or projection. The term may also refer to similar depictions of other planets, suns, other heavenly bodies, or areas of the heavens. Maps are typically depicted on a flat medium, such as on paper, a wall, or a computer screen. For similar depictions on a sphere, see "globes (cartographic spheres)."
Atlases of a particular nation.

Refers to spheres that bear a map of the Earth on their surface. They were first devised by the ancient Greeks, who had calculated that the Earth is a sphere. Modern terrestrial globes are typically mounted on an axle that permits rotation and is tilted 23.5 degrees from the vertical in order to simulate the inclination of the Earth relative to the plane in which it orbits the Sun.
Instruments, in the form of glass globes, which depicted the position of the earth in relation to the fixed stars.
Highly abstracted, simplified maps, which demonstrate a single idea or a specific type of data, often statistical, in a diagrammatic way.
Small-scale maps keyed to an atlas or series of maps showing how the total area has been divided up by the individual maps.
Maps that chart the extent of past incursions of water on land, showing possible patterns that may occur in the future.

Plans that depict defensive installations of a town or fortress, while the interior of the town is often left as generic built space. They were used as building plans as well as for the management, inspection, maintenance, and defense of towns. The topography around the fortress or fortified town may also be represented.
Maps depicting the locations of natural gas pipelines.

Maps designed and used primarily for plotting courses and traveling on water in a ship or other vessel or in an aircraft or spacecraft. It is sometimes used also for maps specifically designed and used for traveling with motor vehicles.
Charts showing the depths of water, nature of the sea bottom, contours of the sea bottom and coastline, tides, and currents in a given sea or sea-land area.
Nautical charts used for navigation close to shore, such as for entering or leaving bays and harbors or for navigating inland waterways.
Maps comprised of assemblies of overlapping aerial photographs whose edges have been torn or cut and matched to form a continuous photographic representation of the earth's surface.

Refers to maps where the relief of physical features is physically raised in three dimensions. They were first mass produced during World War I by a process in which an aluminum sheet that had a map drawn on it was worked with the repoussé technique of tapping the reverse in order to raise the physical features in relief on the obverse. The metal sheet was then used to shape maps printed on plastic sheets.
Maps depicting a particular nation.
Originals of compiled maps, drawn but not printed; loosely, any map drawn by hand.
A serial publication issued by an organization or society, especially a short account, alert, or report of public news or events issued by authority.

Periodicals for enthusiasts of aspects of popular culture such as pop music, comic books, and other specialized interests, especially science fiction and fantasy works, often inexpensively produced and with small circulation.
Thesauri consisting of sets of terms in a single language.
Books, loose-leaf binders, or other volumes containing blank leaves, on which persons have written sentiments, quotations, or signatures.
Pieces of printed matter that formally declare the bestowal of a symbol of merit.
Forms, furnished to bidders, on which to submit their bids.
Charts or mechanical devices that indicate the day of the week corresponding to any given date over a period of many years.
Calendars that provide religious or spiritual readings for each calendar day. They may contain daily prayers or themes on which to meditate.
Cards of standard dimensions that are used to record information and filed in card catalogs.
Greeting cards that offer an expression in a complimentary way gratification at their success, fortune, or happiness.
Cards sold by the post office with postage stamps already printed on them.

Postcards bearing a picture, a stamp bearing the same picture or one similar in image content, and usually a postmark related in some way to the picture. They are made and sold as commemoratives or collectors' items, or created by collectors themselves.

Documents officially certifying that premises conform to provisions of the zoning ordinance and building code and may be used or occupied; granted for new construction or for alteration or additions to existing structures.
Cards often imprinted with messages and suitable illustrations, sent or given on special occasions or holidays.
Letters intended for circulation, either widely or throughout a particular group.
Correspondence on the topic of any legal proceeding, as between a lawyer and a client regarding an impending trial.
Documents issued to freed slaves, attesting to their status.
In chemistry, application of statistical and mathematical methods to chemical data and experimental design.
Rough or preliminary proposed texts of documents, not yet in definitive form, usually subject to review, revision, rejection, approval, or adoption.
Files where items, usually ephemeral and topical in nature, such as newspapers and magazines, are kept for information and reference, usually in folders in vertical files and arranged systematically.

Records kept by public officials or other persons relating to their official duties, but not necessarily readily available to the public. For private documents belonging to individuals, use "personal papers."
Electronic or physical files or other groupings of authorized cataloging entries for terminology appropriate for subject indexing.
Collections of files in which each file relates to a specific project, action, event, patient illness, legal proceedings, or other subject.

Collections of files in which each file is related to one particular project, including but not limited to an engineering or architectural project. The term is also used to refer to electronic files related to a project.
Charts or lists showing lineage, especially those showing the ancestors of purebred animals.
Diagrams in the form of a circle divided by radii into sectors proportional to relative magnitudes, quantities, or frequencies of a set or to the number of data values in a corresponding class.
Sets of directions with a list of ingredients for making or preparing something, especially food.

Listings of items, goods, or raw materials that are available, usually kept on the premises, of a shop or other establishment. Stock lists may be kept locally or published. Examples are stock lists of prints by print dealers and print publishers.
Books in which noteworthy literary passages, cogent quotations, poems, comments, recipes, prescriptions, and other miscellaneous document types are written.
Lists of items located in a warehouse, often with location noted.
Registers, usually in volume form, of copies of charters, title deeds, and other documents of significance belonging to a person, family, or institution.

Notes that are included in a document for the use of an administrator, editor, or other manager, rather than a general viewer, usually including details about the structure or function of the document.
Oaths, verbal or written, usually mandatory, affirming the loyalty of the takers, such as to a government, ruler, constitution, or set of principles.
Cards displayed in movie theater lobbies to advertise motion pictures; usually 11 by 14 inches and issued in sets of eight.
Brief outlines or explanations of the features comprising a particular musical performance. These usually include the names of participants, titles of pieces, and other relevant criteria.
Books in which official copies of deeds are collected.
Deeds embodying a mortgage.
Surveys of the surface configuration of an area, including natural and man-made features.

Documents that outline formally and in detail a project or endeavor, and that are submitted to an entity capable of bestowing funding to realize the project described. The intended audience may be a government agency, a private foundation, or other corporation. Grant proposals are written on behalf of individuals, non-profit organizations, charities, companies, or educational institutions.
Official documents that collect facts about a particular subject or event, and often draw conclusions based on these facts.
Documents that state the mission and revenues of a corporation for the inspection of the public and shareholders alike.
Reports prepared monthly that provide performance information for any particular project or endeavor to any agency of its management.

Organized, detailed proposals that are comprehensive in scope and lay out strategies and schemes of action for something to be done. Examples include land use control law, zoning, and urban redevelopment omnibus plans of cities or towns for housing, industry, commercial, and recreational facilities and their impact on environmental factors.

Plans that outline the significance of a heritage asset, such as a church or other built work, and that outline the course of its conservation and management. Plans set out in the CMP include its significance for future use, along with a description of repairs or alterations. The compilation of a CMP involves the collaboration of various professions and stakeholders.
Systematic assessments of the condition of a group, collection, or system, for example, the contents of a library or archive. For reports on individual items, use "condition reports."
Refers to schedules that show specific times at which certain events are expected or intended to occur.
Printed documents containing the names, descriptions, and wage information of every member of a ship's company, including the master's name and the ship's name, destination, and tonnage.
Tables for changing the values of units, typically of measure or weight, into equivalants in different systems of measure.
Documents filed with a state or local agency used to calculate income tax or other taxes. Tax returns are normally prepared using forms created by the taxing authority.
Tickets authorizing free admission, as to events or transportation.

Official documents issued by a government that certify the identity and citizenship of individuals and grant them permission to travel abroad; includes permits issued by foreign countries allowing goods to be transported or persons to travel within that country.
Official records of deaths kept by public officials charged with registering deaths.
Official lists of recorded births, including details considered sufficiently important to be formally noted, and maintained in a regular manner.
Certificates issued by public officials stating that a person has died; often include the cause of death and the signature of the attending or examining physician.
Certificates which serve as evidence of marriage, and are executed by the persons officiating at the marriage.
Records that relate to budget, personnel, supply, and similar facilitative operations within an organization.
Biologists trained or working in the field dealing with life forms that live in the sea and on shore and the features of their environment that affect them.
Zoologists who specialize in the scientific study of fish.
Scientists trained or working in the chemistry of living organisms and the reactions and methods for identifying their chemical substances.

Geologists who deal with the land and submarine relief features of the earth's surface and seeks a generic interpretation of them using the principles of physical geography in its descriptive aspects and of structural geology in its explanatory phases.
Physicians who specialize in the treatment of mental, emotional, and behavioral disorders, especially as originating in endogenous causes or as resulting from problematic interpersonal relationships.

Scientists who study the physical forces acting on, and particularly within, the earth. Their work concerns phenomena such as the study of earthquake waves, geomagnetism, gravitational fields, and electrical conductivity using precise quantitative principles.
People who pursue hazardous, risky, unscrupulous, or questionable enterprises and activities, either to gain wealth, power, or social position, or for the sake of excitement.
Criminals who make fraudulent copies of paper documents or coins. May also generally refer to criminals who imitate with intention to deceive.

Those who use their means or influence to benefit individuals, institutions, or causes; especially those who support the work of artists and writers, and including those who commission and pay for individual works. For supporters who assume primary responsibility for projects or activities, use "sponsors." For supporters who give voluntary work, money, or public expressions of support through membership in a voluntary association, use "friends."
Those who advocate the extension or granting of political suffrage to those lacking it, either universally or to specific groups within the population.
Women police officers.
Refers to itinerant workers who move from place to place in search of work, especially agricultural work.
Persons who act as subordinates to another or as an official in a subordinate capacity.

Those, usually in Japan, who are trained in and carry out the preparation and consumption of green tea, according to strict rules of ceremony, as an expression of Zen Buddhist philosophy. They are often monks.
Students in institutions of higher learning that provide general or liberal arts education leading to degrees.
Students at any level in a professional field, such as medicine, who are getting practical professional experience under the supervision of experienced practitioners.
Those who are addicted to an activity, habit, or substance.

People who have a physical impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, or who have a history or record of such an impairment, or those who are perceived by others as having such an impairment. Although ’handicapped’ is widely used in both law and everyday speech to refer to people having physical or disabilities those described by the word tend to prefer the expressions 'disabled' or 'people with disabilities.' The often-repeated recommendation to put the person before the disability would favor 'persons with physical disabilities' over ’physically disabled persons.'
Those subject to psychiatric disabilities, psychiatric illnesses, emotional disorders, or mental disabilities,
People having no sight or very limited vision.
Women who have children, either biologically or by adoption.
Persons imprisoned for political activity.
People in the earliest developmental stage of life.
Young people attending elementary school or of an age to attend elementary school, typically including those from age 5 to 13.
Commercial organizations or certain administrative units of government that provide a service.
Organizations of artists who have come together due to common a common cause or interests.
Corporate bodies that collectively manage a company’s affairs. Decisions are made via majority vote, or delegation of authority to one or more members of the board.
Clubs which promote civic beautification, conservation, and historic preservation. Historically organized by women.
A collection of books in a library or bookshop.

Formally structured organizations, establishments, or associations created for the promotion of a specific benevolent public objective, usually a charitable or educational objective, such as schools or colleges, hospitals, or museums.
Associations of professionals or amateurs united by a common interest in the study or preservation of built works.
Notes or symbols written or printed in the margins of pages. For scenes or figures in the margins or decorative borders of a page of text, use "marginal illustrations."
Books or publications with detailed maps of city streets, accompanied by an index of street names linked with coordinates or page numbers where the streets can be found.
Directories lisitng names of and information on businesses.
Guidebooks designed for pilgrims, who are people who travel to sacred places as an act of religious devotion.
Accounts of the chronological development of cases of disease or conditions of individuals, with details of symptoms.
Manuals or guides for instructing through a series of questions and answers, especially for religious instruction.

Children's primers consisting typically of a sheet of parchment or layer of paper mounted on a thin wooden board and protected by a sheet of transparent horn and having on it the alphabet and other rudiments such as the digits and often the Lord's Prayer.
Works containing material for instruction and practice in reading.
Documents in any format  describing, comparing, and contrasting the benefits of products for the benefit of consumers.
Books, pamphlets, or other documents containing instructions needed to control the proper functioning of a machine, process, or system.
Books containing collections of hymns, usually to be sung in church.

Children's picture books produced primarily in Britain in the mid-19th century. Typically comprising six or eight large, nearly square pages printed on one side only with color illustrations accompanied by a minimum of text.

Brief formal prayers used in Western Christian worship that vary with the day. The term reflects the original 'collecting' of the petitions of the worshippers into a single prayer. Collects consist of an invocation, a petition, and a pleading of Christ's name or ascription of glory to God. The collect precedes the readings in the eucharist. The collects in the 'Book of Common Prayer' are partly written by Thomas Cramner and partly adapted from Latin service books. According to the 'Book of Common Prayer,' two invariable collects follow the collect of the day at morning and evening prayers.
Books containing the four Gospels, or readings from the Gospels arranged for the liturgical year; by the 13th century the gospels were generally folded into the missal.
Jewish prayer books containing both Hebrew and Aramaic prayers used chiefly in the daily liturgy.
Texts for a broadcast announcement, talk, play, or other productions intended for radio.

Final approved screenplays, with full dialogue, all necessary technical instructions for shooting, and usually broken down into individual scenes with shots numbered consecutively in chronological order, for the use of the director and sometimes also the actors during production.
Bibliographies comprising citations for works about a given person, or containing biographical information about the author or authors in the bibliography.

Bibliographies of books or other written records relating to a geographical area smaller than a county, which typically include those written by and about people born in the area, as well as books  concering the area's geography, natural history, or architecture.
Finding aid in catalog form.
Book indexes which give descriptions or definitions of the words indexed as well as their page numbers.
Indexes in which each significant word in the entry appears in a fixed position within the entry and is arranged with other entries in alphabetical order in a column.
Indexes to published materials that have cited a particular work; often includes subject and author indexes as well.
Scales or listings of colors, often with each color listed assigned a name and number that reflect its composition, chemical class, and shade.
Arrangements of records for library materials by subject or topic.
Persons who buy and sell furs or fur products; also persons who make, repair, alter, or clean fur garments.

Trade- or craftspeople who created cloth by weaving threads together. Wool would be gathered from sheep, cleaned, carded, dyed, and then spun into thread. Weavers would then use a loom to weave the threads together to form fabrics. This generally refers to a trade active from the Middle Ages through the Industrial Revolution when the process was taken up by machine looms.
People who specialize in smoothing or levelling a surface, particularly in a woodworking context.
Ceramicists who specialize in majolica, which is  tin-glazed earthenware.
People whose craft it is to cut and polish diamonds.
Naval officers supervising the construction and repair of ships.

Refers to officials or members of an administration divided into separate areas of responsibility or bureaux. Perjoritively, refers to such officials who work inflexibly by routine, without exercising independent intelligence  or judgment.
Persons who hold a high position of administrative or managerial responsibility in a private business.
Directors of commercial art galleries or public art museums.

Appointed or elected heads of groups, states, or organizations. Included are elected officials serving as both chief of state and chief political executive in a republic having a presidential government. Also included are the heads of organizations such as banks, clubs, and corporations when used as the official job title for those positions.
Managers of building projects who oversee the construction.
Makers of fine furniture and other woodwork in the service of a noble or royal court.
Public officers responsible for keeping the public peace and for certain petty judicial duties.

Ambassadors or other diplomatic representatives of the pope, vested with both political and ecclesiastical powers and accredited to the court or government of a sovereign nation, or assigned to a definite territory; primary duty is safeguarding the interests of the Holy See.
Refers to legislators of the United States who are elected to one of the two Houses of Congress as representatives of one of the states or of defined districts within a state.

Refers to the elected magistrates of this title of Republican Rome who performed some of the duties of the consuls, to whom they were subordinate. Refers also to chief magistrates or mayors in 17th- and 18th-century Italy who bore this title.

Term used in various parts of Europe at different times from the Roman Empire to the early modern era, and in some European colonies in America, to designate high-ranking officials or nobles who either directly served or represented their monarch in certain spheres, such as the military, the judiciary, or the royal household, or who exercised royal power in a division or dependency of the realm.

Name referring to secular and religious leaders of Muslim communities who are seen as successors of Muhammad; it derives from the Arabic 'khalifa' meaning 'successor.' The term is primarily used in historical reference following Turkey's abolition of the caliphate on March 23, 1924.
Monarchs who are also esteemed as warriors, often confirming the right to rule through prowess.
Authors who specialize in writing for an audience of children.
Authors who write biographies of saints.
Persons who write comments on topics of reader interest to stimulate or mold public opinion, usually in accordance with the viewpoints and policies of the publication they work for.
Reporters in a war zone who are assigned to a military unit and who travel with that unit.
General term for the whole teaching staff of a college, university, or school.
In general, those who give directions or instructions on a particular topic or activity. Specifically, college teachers who are inferior in rank to a professor.

Those trained or working in the field of history.concerned with topics that are distinctly localized in subject matter and source materials, generally covering specific neighborhoods, communities, counties, or other specific subdivisions of larger geopolitical bodies.
Those whose occupation is to compile alphabetical lists of terms denoting names or subjects.
Libraarians who manage and work with  the circulation procedures and policies of a library.

Those who study or practice in the field of grammar, the study of the rules of a language governing the sounds, words, sentences, and other elements, including their structure, combination, and interpretation.
Those who study the nature, origin, limits, and validity of human knowledge.

Scribes who execute rubrics, which are headings, catchwords, or marginal index words printed or written in red (the remainder of the text being in black), or otherwise distinguished in lettering, as guides to the contents of pages.
Those who engage in the scientific, historic, or comparative study of the origins, characteristics, and functions of human societies and cultures.
Specialists in bibliotherapy.
Those whose business or occupation is to catch fish or shellfish.
People who practice the art and science of horticulture, or the cultivation and growing of gardens.
Professionals concerned with the planning, cultivation, protection, and management of urban forests.
Persons who guard, tend and herd flocks of sheep grazing at large.
Muslim theologian who is expert in the religious law of Islam.
In colonial Latin America, oidores were ministers of justice of the Real Audiencia of the Spanish court, who listened and passed judgment on civil cases.
In the United States, lawyers appointed or elected by a city or county as full-time, official defenders to represent financially disadvantaged citizens in criminal cases at public expense.

Persons who superintend or manage the collections, exhibitions, research activities, and personnel of a museum, art gallery, zoo, or other place of exhibit; also, the superintendents or managers of a single collection or subject of study in such an institution.

Generally, the leaders of dramatic choruses in ancient Greece. Specifically,  individual citizens of ancient Athens who sponsored one of the choruses appearing in a dramatic festival, selecting the members, providing space for their practice, and paying for all expenses relating to their performance, including costumes, training, and meals.
Native North American dancers, usually male, that perform fancy dances at powwow events and other ceremonies. Dancers are defined by their elaborately colored and decorated regalia.

Masked, comic actors referred to as "gossips" in farces adopted from Greek Middle Comedy plays and especially popular in southern Italy in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE. Known principally from vase paintings, these are grotesque figures meant to satirize aspects of everyday life, or as burlesques of mythology.
Members of a band of musicians.
Those who direct and train choirs.

Persons who oversee all the aspects of photography in a television, video, or filmmaking project, especially the lighting; they are particularly charged with achieving the photographic images and effects desired by the director. For operators of motion picture, video, or television cameras, use "cameramen."

People who make physical books, including bookbinders, printers, and others. The term does not generally include authors, who write the intellectual content of books, although it may include artists who make books by hand, including writing or drawing the content by hand. Do not use for a broker who accepts wagers from gamblers.
Persons who set type according to copy and operate a cylinder or automatic platen press to print complete job orders.
The clergy of Buddhism.
People having princely or noble rank who also hold the authority of a bishop.
Heads of monasteries or convents in the Eastern church; comparable to abbots in the Western church. Occasionally used to refer to superiors of groups of monasteries.
Nuns governing their own houses (priories) or nuns ranking next below an abbess in an abbey in a position similar to that of a claustral prior.
Ancient Egyptian clergy who recited spells and hymns during temple rituals and official ceremonies.

The term derives from the Latin "frater," the title by which early Christians customarily addressed each other. From the end of the 13th century, it referred to the members of the mendicant orders. Friars are distinguished from "monks" in that friars focus on a sacred ministry of preaching, mixing with their fellow men in the world, soliciting alms, and moving from place to place, while monks live in seclusion in a fixed place; in addition friars' orders originally could possess no fixed revenues, but lived upon the voluntary offerings of the faithful, while the orders of monks could possess property and revenues, although the individual monks took vows of poverty. The orders of friars are usually divided into two classes, the four great orders mentioned by the Second Council of Lyons, Dominicans, Franciscans, Carmelites, and Augustinians, and the lesser orders.
Those who write computer software or programs.
Mathematicians specializing in the properties, relationships, and computation of real numbers, involving chiefly addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
Scientists trained or working in the study of living organisms.
Receptacles generally made of stone, metal, or wood, sculpted or shaped into a pattern, and equipped with risers. Used to contain molten metal and give it a shape while it solidifies.
Stamps, usually engraved, used for impressing a design upon a softer material, as in coining money, medals, and printing banknotes.

Hand tools having a hard solid head, usually of metal or stone, set transversely on a handle. They are used for driving nails, beating, breaking, or other applications involving pounding or striking. The term may also refer to machines in which a heavy block of metal is used for the same purpose.
Heavy-duty combinations of hatchet and hammer with a broad blade with a notched under part for pulling nails; used to chop off hardened plaster and to do other heavy work.
Long-headed wooden mallets used for driving caulking irons.
Hand tools consisting of a metal head flattened at one and usually pointed on the other end, mounted on a relatively long handle.
Scaffoldings or other supporting structures, decorative or purely functional, for bearing fireworks during a fireworks display or from which fireworks are shot off into the air.

Leather finishing tools consisting of a stone or a blunt blade of metal, glass, or plastic set into a wooden handle, used to gently scrape, smooth, and remove excess moisture from very thin and delicate leather or parchment, or to produce an exceptionally smooth grain side on leather. They are also sometimes used to work dubbin into a skin.

Refers to tools, implements, vessels, or articles of furniture that are relatively small and are useful or necessary in a kitchen, dairy, or elsewhere in a household. It also refers to such items designed for use by an artisan, mechanic, or farmer, or used in the services of a church, temple, or other place of worship.
Power-operated machines, such as lathes, used for general cutting and shaping of metal and other substances.
Parts and components of anvils.
Tool components that fit into a brace or drill that are bent at one end into a semi-circular form.
Arched handles in the form of a hoop or half-ring that extend over the top of a vessel or other container, and are either fixed or swivelling.
Hoist components usually consisting of looped lines used to hold securely something to be hoisted, lowered, carried, or suspended.

Rods, usually tapered at both ends, used as axes in hand spinning. Fibers are drawn and twisted onto the spindle from a mass of wool or other material that is gathered on the distaff. The image of the spindle and distaff has been associated historically with feminine power or virtue. For the similar cylindrical objects used to gather or accumulate thread after it has been spun, and for use in weaving, use "spools."
People who work for another person or corporate body, particularly when employed for wages or a salary under an employment agreement.
Persons trained in mathematics and statistics whose business it is to calculate insurance and annuity premiums, reserves, and dividends.
Licensed architects or architectural firms that are  responsible for the design and construction documents for a building project.
Construction workers whose work is blasting with explosives.
Carpenters who are of a level of master in skill, accomplishment, and responsibility.
Those whose occupation or craft it is to build with hardened clay bricks. For those who lay any combination of stone, blocks, or bricks, use "mason."

People or corporate bodies who are responsible for most of the work at the construction site, including that performed by the subcontractors. The services of a general contractor are unlimited as to the type of work which he or she may do for the project. For contractors whose services are limited to the construction of commercial buildings and single-dwelling or multiple-dwelling residential buildings, use "building contractors."
Draftsmen who do rendering, especially those who produce drawings of architectural designs in accurate, representational perspective to show what the project will look like when built.
Professionals who apply the principles of engineering to the planning, design, and construction of buildings and other structures.
People who design systems to protect public health and promote clean air, food, water, and housing.
Those who study or work in the field of environmental design.

Persons who formulate concepts and supervise the execution of the visual appearance of a publication or performing arts production, including layout, illustrations, designs for art work and copy, etc. for visual communications media, such as magazines, books, newspapers, online publications, posters, packaging, television, film, theater, video games, and other visual media. Art directors are typically not in an executive position. For executives of a theater company or arts organization who choose the material staged in a season, the hiring of creative and production personnel, and other management tasks, use "artistic directors."
Painters who specialize in decorating façades.
Painters who work in enamel as medium.
Refers to people who create humorous, satiric, obscene, or gang-related writings or drawings that are executed anonymously in public places, usually on walls and typically illegally.
Printmakers who do relief printing in which chemicals are used to etch a metal plate, ususally upon which a drawing has been made.
Engraving printmakers in the service of a royal or noble court.
Etchers who create plates depicting other works, from which it is intended to print reproductions in relatively large numbers.

Those who engage in lithography: the photomechanical process that uses the same principle as lithography, the repulsion of oil and water, but uses a photographic process to transfer the image to the plate.
Sculptors who specialize on works carved from or applied to surfaces of architectural members, usually exterior.
Those who design ceramic objects, often in a studio or manufactory, working separately from those who execute the design and create the cermic works.
People whose profession is the selection and organization the surface coverings, draperies, furniture, and furnishings of architectural interiors, usually of existing spaces.
Refers to those who make public offers, solicitations, or promotional declarations by means of paid advertisements or commercials, whether produced by themselves or purchased from others.

Individuals or companies that act as middlemen, who for a fee or commission negotiate contracts of purchase and sale between buyers and sellers. Distinct from "commission merchants" in that they do not take physical possession or control of the merchandise.
Individuals or companies that act as middlemen between buyers and sellers of stock, usually for a commission.
People or corporations who invest in and accomplish the building of railroads, which are transportation systems comprising tracks upon which trains are run.

Refers to people or corporate bodies who own or run manufacturing plants for making devices used in a domestic context that facilitate such tasks as food preparation, food storage, cleaning, and grooming.
People who are experts on books, and often collect books.
People or corporate bodies that represent artists and engage in the buying and selling of works of art.
People who buy and sell books, including proprietors of bookshops.  In contexts before about 1800, refers also to those responsible for issuing books, later called "publishers."
Retailers who own and operate small to medium-sized stores.

Persons who engage in the process of making casts or of shaping in a mold; usually refers to those who pour liquid material, such as metal or glass, into a mold, as distinguished from pressing a material into a mold.
Craftsmen who carve, engrave, or cut designs into glass.
Metalworkers specializing in casting bronze, which is an alloy of copper with trace amounts of tin or zinc.
Artists who specialized in gilding and painting, particularly those skilled in applying gold leaf and paint to sculpture over a gesso ground. Typically used in historical references.
Creators of an indegenous American art form using the bark of the birch tree. In one example, the artist will bite on small pieces of folded birch bark to form intricate designs.
Those whose occupation is to grind and smooth glass.
Persons who dress and color leather after it has been tanned.
Metalworkers who make metal objects shiny or lustrous by rubbing with a tool that compacts or smooths.
Workers who melt and pour metal into a mold.
Metalworkers who work in brass. For metalworkers who work primarily in bronze, prefer "bronze casters" or "bronzeworkers."
Artisans who cut out and produce metal elements, usually for architecture, such as fittings, lattices, and gates.
People who make marbled paper. Examples were those who created marbled wallpaper, as was popular in 15th-century France.
Tool used to pull hay towards sickle.
Long-bladed knives with heavy, rounded serrations on the edge of the blade, used for cutting portions off of haystacks or other compact bundles or piles of hay by hand.
Traps or fykes of varied construction; typically provided with conical funnels leading to a chamber in which eels are trapped and retrieved.
Contrivances of various forms designed for luring and trapping flies or other flying insects.
Gaffs with a large iron hook at the end for securing large fish.
Long-handled nets used to retrieve fish from water while fishing.
Tools which combine the jam pike and the cant hook; used by lumbermen to pry and roll logs.
Generally, instruments used for measuring the specifics of celestial bodies, such as diameter.

Devices, dating from the 19th century, that were used in place of dissecting knives; operators would breathe into the blowpipes to inflate and scrutinize parts. The pipes were outfitted with valves that would prevent the backflow of unwanted air or bacteria into the pipes.
Artifacts originally created to be used in the observation, measurement, and recording of atmospheric phenomena.

Pieces of wood or another material, used to receive the blow of a hammer or other device for the purpose of producing sound. An example is the disk-shaped striking block used with a gavel (ceremonial mallet) in courts, as when a judge bangs a gavel to start a session.
Microcomputers so compact that they can be operated while resting on the user's lap.
Any devices that transfer data, programs, or signals into a processor system.
Computer output devices that produce a line of print per cycle of its operation.
Printers that form images by projecting droplets of ink onto paper or other media.

Amplifiers in which small electrical currents and voltages are amplified before they can operate devices, where the current flows in one direction, rather than with alternating current in which the direction of the flow of electrons switches back and forth at regular intervals or cycles.
Tools for examining or testing doubly-refracting crystals or gemstones.
Small, usually compact, binoculars intended for indoor use, as at the opera,  theaters, or concerts; includes those made with a detachable stick or handle for holding.

Microscopes that have a digital camera attached instead of an eyepiece and display the digitally acquired image on a large monitor. In addition to observation, these can also have various extended functions such as dimension measurement, and recording of still images and moving images.
Machines that compress a refrigerant gas; used in air conditioning and refrigeration.

Internal-combustion engines in which a spray of fuel introduced into air compressed to a temperature of approximately 1000 degrees Farenheit (538 degrees Celsius), ignites at a virtually constant pressure.
Devices that convert heat energy directly into electric energy using the Sabbatier effect, via thermocouples.
Turbines powered by moving water.

Instruments comprising a long pole or handle to which is affixed a wick or other lighting mechanism, used to light the candles located above convenient reach in a church. A candle snuffer is sometimes attached.
