The interrelations between clans are clearly defined and there are rigid regulations imposed on incest.Traditional Bunun farming has developed sophisticated skills in rearing millet in highlands corresponding to a calendar with set rituals. The Bunun material culture emphasize function and simplicity, while the Bunun people value dynamic harmony between hanitu (“soul; spirit”) and is-ang (“heart”) as the ideal for personal development. This not only sets up the undertone of the Bunun religious life, but also motivates individual to achieve what the individual’s talents and recognition point toward, forming an egalitarian sense in the Bunun society.

Fine tin-glazed earthenware produced in Italy. The term originally referred to the island of Majorca (or an alternate theory has it referring to Malaga), and designated only Hispano-Moresque lusterware; but since the 16th century it has been used to refer to Italian tin-glazed ware and imitations of the Italian ware. It is characterized by painted decoration of high quality executed in several colors on the dry but unfired tin glaze, generally with a final coating of clear lead glaze. The range of colors is typically limited to cobalt blue, copper green, manganese purple, antimony yellow, and iron red, with white provided by the tin-glaze material. When white is used for painting, it is applied onto a bluish-white glaze or blue ground. The luster is typically a golden color derived from silver or a mother-of-pearl effect.
Halls dedicated as a memorial, particularly to those lost in war. Purposes of the halls vary; often found at universities.
Clay formed into blocks and distinguished by having a yellowish color when fired, due to the clay having a relatively high lime content.
Limestone quarried in the US state of Wisconsin, known for a wide color range.
A fine-grained, even-textured sandstone that is reddish-brown in color, quarried near East Longmeadow, Massachusetts. Used extensively for buildings in New England, United States.
A type of seam-face granite quarried in Weymouth, Massachusetts.
Roofing shingles made of redwood.
Masonry construction using a single non-structural external layer of brick.
Tile designed to be used for areas of pavement.
Tiles made of concrete.
General term for the recent art made between the aftermath of World War II and the early years of the 21st century.
Period of the third city on the site of ancient Troy, ca. 2300 -2200 BCE.

Historically, foil that is used as a recording surface and wrapped around cylinders during the recording process. Phonograph foil was used prior to the invention of wax cylinders, where vibrations were cut directly into the wax.
In Indian architecture, a gatehouse; gateway.
State, condition, or behavior in which a person's identity corresponds to his or her biological sex at birth.
Time time measured by Earth’s rotation relative to the Sun.
In Indian architecture, a wave (bracket-type/pōtikā-type).
In Indian architecture, a lion headed composite fabulous animal; gryphon; lion-vyāla motif; leonine vyāla-type.
In Indian architecture, a large gavākṣa front of a vaulted, apsidal structure.
In Indian architecture, a śākhā carved with śrīvṛkṣa pattern.
In Indian architecture, lotus; inverted cyma-recta moulding with (or without) lotus-petal pattern as decoration; loti-formed mandi-type;  lotus-shaped cupola-cap; lotus motif
In Indian architecture a pañjara projecting from a sālā (kōṣṭha).
In Indian architecture, the nāsī of the bhadraśālā.
In Indian architecture, a jāla-screen formed by intercrossing uprights and transoms.
In Indian architecture, a column bearing Nandi figure at the top.
In Indian architecture, a upapīṭha-type.
In Indian architecture, a kūṭa-niche; kūṭa and sālā together; niche having a kūṭa as its crowning member.
In Indian architecture, a kalaśa moulding; circular kumuda.
In Indian architecture, a tetragonal column-type of South India.
Buildings arranged around a space or a courtyard that is usually rectangular in plan. Common examples are in universities and palaces.
Pavilions that represent a nation at an international fair or exhibition of art.
Buildings in which the study of religions, doctrines, practices, histories, and relationships of the world's religions is facilitated.
Rooms or separate structures devoted to funeral services in funeral homes. For chapels intended to permanently contain individual or family tombs, use "sepulchral chapels."
Subsidiary chapels opening off the center of the apse of churches, on an axis down the center of the plan.
The state or quality of having or hving been divided into eight parts.
Refers to a paper made from a beaten bark material or from the lengua de vaca plant; was made by the Maya.
Books having content related to the topic of science or a particular branch of science, often with illustrations, graphs, and charts.
Material comprising the hard or woody pericarp enclosing the kernel of a nut.
Toys for babies and toddlers specially made to hang in or above a crib. They usually have a suspension system like a mobile or play arch, or can be attached around the edge like a play spiral.
An early rose cut fashioned with six facets and a flat bottom side.

The most common style of cutting for both diamonds and colored stones. The standard round brilliant consists of a total of 58 facets: 1 table, 8 bezel facets, 8 star facets and 16 upper-girdle facets on the crown; and 8 pavilion facets, 16 lower-girdle facets, and usually a culet on the pavilion, or base.
Visual works having subject content in which multiple scenes, episodes, or moments in a story, or multiple stories, are represented.
Flat tools with smoothed curves at both ends, typically made of metal, wood, or plastic, designed to pull warp threads through the reed of a loom.

Utensils used when eating corn on the cob, allowing the user to keep hands away from the hot ear of corn. Corn or cob holders, as they are called, typically consist of a holder with a heat resistant, knobbed end that has two protruding shafts.

Specialized kitchen utensils used to dispense viscous liquid such as honey or syrup from a container. These are usually made of wood or plastic, and have a handle terminated with a concentrically-grooved bulb.
Addresses, not necessarily street addresses of the home or workplace, to which mail for a particular person, family, or corporate body is to be sent.
In cataloging and similar contexts, an indication that a fact or data is less than certain, but recognized as within the range of possibility. Indicates a level of certainty less than "probably."

Tools used to lift newly printed sheets from a press to transfer somewhere else, usually a drying rack. These are usually small metal tong-like implements. The purpose is to minimize contact with the printer's hands and clean printed paper.

Defined as an energetic ceremonial dance performed at Native North American powwows by men. Possibly has origins in the Omaha Oska society dance and the Pawnee iruska dance. Dancers typically wear regalia with long fringes and feathered roaches.

Dance performed by the Chickasaw, Koasati, Yuchi, and other Southeastern Native North American tribes. Likely originated with the Chickasaw, the dance is often performed in conjunction with Green Corn Dances. In some cases, garfish teeth are used in a purification rite during the dance, while in other variations dancers carry garfish effigies.

Describes type of pottery created by Hopi potters from the late 14th century up to the early 1600s. Production is associated with Hopi pueblos formed after 14th century migrations from scattered villages across northern Arizona and New Mexico to consolidated towns. Distinguished by the clay's golden yellow lustre after firing with large amounts of coal. Frequently decorated with black and red pigmented designs featuring birds, dragonflies, feathers, and abstract, curvilinear motifs. Production particularly associated with Hopi Mesa communities in Arizona, namely Sikyátki which gives the pottery its name. Often created for export to other Native communities, with sherds being found as far as Kansas. Decline in production occurs in tandem with Spanish colonization in the 17th century and with the abandonment of Sikyátki and Awatovi towns.
Instruments, often in the form of a comb or board, with sharp pins or teeth for the manual disentanglement of scutched hemp or flax fibers.

Two-part fasteners for a coat, jacket, or other garment usually made of a looped braid or cord in an ornamental design on one edge of the garment that attaches around a knot, toggle, or similar device on the other side.

High-speed mechanized devices used to tighten the weave of linen materials and produce the fabrics' characteristic sheen and lustre. These devices are comprised of a heavy frame supporting a large quantity of hardwood faller stamps, metalweights, mallets, or hammers that are operated by cams attached to a horizontal shaft. The linen is typically dampened then wound on an iron cylinder directly beneath the hammering devices, which rapidly pound the fabric to prepare it for washing, calendising, and/or dyeing. These devices constitute the last major step in the linen manufacture process.
Rosettes, knots of ribbons, or similar ornaments worn usually on a hat as a badge of office or party, as part of livery dress, or as decoration.

Popular novelties or premiums given away with commercial tobacco products in the late 19th-early 20th century made of a variety of fabrics that were polychrome printed with images and usually the name of the tobacco company. These came in various themes and formats
Describes the physical location where a collection was amassed.
Metalworkers who specialize in making objects out of iron.
Large boards with a white surface for writing or drawing.

Element for describing the organization or filing sequence of the records, particularly in the context of archives. May be used to record the logical or physical groupings within a hierarchical structure and their relationships. This includes how the described materials have been subdivided into smaller units, e.g., record groups into series. May also indicate the filing sequence of the described materials, for example chronological or alphabetical arrangement.
Representations of persons from the head down to the waist only.
Small discs or knobs designed to be attached to clothing, and that bears the insignia of a law enforcemnent agency.
Actions or processes that stop respiration of a human or other living creature by compression of the air-passage, especially by a sudden and violent compression of the windpipe.
Short, stiff, boards used for surfing; riders typically lay on top of the board.
Cases designed to hold a ciborium, which is a vessel used to hold the hosts for distribution in the Eucharist.
Stones that commemorate political, cultural, and artistic days, acts, individuals, or events at the local, regional, or international level.
Devices used during the process of harvesting cranberries to separate firm, saleable cranberries from poor quality soft cranberries.
Round, square or rectangular containers equipped with a lid, and often handles, and used to store cakes and keep them fresh.
Small box or container, usually made of metal, designed to store sugar.
Devices that heat plates to a desired temperature to keep food warm until being served.
Small bowls into which tea bags are deposited after steeping.
Panties that offer body-shaping and smoothing benefits resulting from elasticated material, aside from being worn as standard underwear.
Protective coverings for lighting devices.
Cloth, often decorated with embroidery, used to protect the top of a dresser from scratches or other damage.
Long narrow strips of usually decorative fabric that are meant to be draped over the length of tables.

Devices for securing or grasping bulky or heavy articles while being lifted or lowered, generally in the form of a belt, rope, or chain formed into a loop and fitted with hooks and tackle that can attach to a hoist.
Greeting cards that are sent or given as expressions of goodwill during the celebration of Hanukkah.

Nahua chimalli (shield) design composed of a large number of feather-down balls in postclassic central Mexico. Distinguished from tehuehuelli chimalli which featured only five of these down-balls in a quincunx pattern.
Machines used to remove smut, a fungous blight, from grain, in the process of cleaning.
Devices that create an electric current through which a stream of air is passed in order to electrify it. Used to age and bleach flour.
Devices used in the process of grain cleaning to separate out impurities.
Term generally applied to various types of ornaments, such as hairpins and combs, worn by men or women.
Small vessels for use at a dressing table, of varied shape, with a lid with an opening for depositing hairpins after use.
Metal tripods for use in large open hearths that suspend pots or other cooking vessels over the fire.
Electric heaters that incorporate a fan to blow air past the heating element to distribute warm air.
Devices used to clean ducts or other parts of furnaces used for heating.
Space heating stoves that burn flammable oil as fuel.
Devices used to test the purity of milk, providing information on quantities of chalk, lime, or water found in the tested milk.

Tools consisting of a straight blade, with or without hollows, and a handle, used in culinary applications. Santoku knives differ from chef's knives in that the straight edge of the blade only allows for a vertical chopping motion, whereas chef's knives feature a curved blade that can be rocked.
Devices for weighing out spices.
Wire racks used to support and store cooling pies.
Presses for rendering lard.
A clothes line is any type of rope, cord, or twine that has been stretched between two points, outside or indoors, above the level of the ground.
Headpieces worn by barristers in the UK and commonwealth countries as part of court attire. These are traditionally made from horsehair and are styled distinctively.
Vessels, usually consisting either of metal or of wooden staves affixed by a hoop to a flat wooden bottom, designed to be used in conjunction with a sap spout to collect sugar sap from maple trees.
Devices, typically in the form of a hydraulic press, outfitted with a cradle for holding lids known as can blanks, and a lever, which when pressed down, seals the cans.
Tools used to form uncooked dough or batter into doughnut-shaped rings prior to baking or frying.
Semicircle-shaped, lidded containers, often made of plastic or other lightweight materials, made to contain dentures when not in use.
Stands onto which drums are placed; many, such as snare drum stands, have adjustable cradles or baskets where the drums rest.
Toy and miniature versions versions of drums, scaled for use by children as playthings.
Usually hard-sided containers with lids used for storing spools for needlework.
Usually hard-sided enclosing containers of varied design that are used for storing materials and tools for needlework.
Contrivances used for holding or supporting thimbles for needlework.

Writing utensils containing permanent color dyes, paints, or inks, used to transfer notations, designs, or markings onto fabric materials. The color dyes employed by these tools are especially designed to mantain their color over time after the dye has dried, without significant fading during wash or wear. Also refers to a class of measuring tools or devices used to trace or illustrate textile alteration patterns with onto fabrics, typically with ink or chalk, in preparation for subsequent alteration activities.
Sharp blades used to slice off the exposed part of a length film for processing, to avoid processing an entire roll of film, for testing or other purposes.
Implements or machines for planting or for sowing seeds.
Tools used to imprint symbols or numbers on materials; for example, placing symbols to prevent the alteration of numbers after printing.
Flogging instruments made from stretched bull penises that are stretched, twisted, and dried to form whips for corporal punishment.

Traditional signs displayed by Japanese merchants from the 17th-20th centuries to call attention to their shops and that graphically depict the products or services offered within. These are created from a variety of materials including wood, bamboo, iron, paper, fabric, or stone, and sometimes rely on visual puns.
Ornaments fastened to the tops of shoes by means of a clip.
Tools for joining seams of wallpaper that are comprised of a free-spinning wheel mounted on a handle. They may come in various widths.
General term for mechanical devices for separating grain from the chaff; may be hand-operated or use another source of power.
Devices that automatically affix signatures to documents such as checks.
Devices designed to wrap loose yarn onto a cylindrical or conical bobbin in preparation for weaving.
Devices placed on turntables that allow records with different spindle hole sizes to be played; particularly those adapters that allow 45 rpm records to be played, which have larger spindle holes.
Whistles used to mark the beginning or end of work days at a factory.
Sharp implements used to break coal into pieces for burning.
Electric devices designed to emit ultraviolet light for the purpose of suntanning.
Tape players where magnetic tape is carried on two separate reels mounted on spindles, wound from one reel to the other.
Devices that record sound onto thin, magnetized wire, and can later reproduce those recordings.
Containers meant to hold phonograph records.
Large supports of varied design used for dressing game.

Calculating machines, now historic, that were able to produce tables of values for arithmetic functions. The machine was designed by English inventor and engineer Charles Babbage in 1822, and a working model was built in 1853 by George and Edward Scheutz.

Hoods mounted around ground glass focusing screens of certain cameras that block ambient light from falling across the screen, allowing for a clearer view. These may be fixed or removeable, but are frequently designed to fold flat when not in use.

Directional filters that when positioned at a certain angle pass only light polarized in the direction perpendicular to reflected light, which is absorbed. This absorption diminishes glare reflected from reflective surfaces such as glass or water, or suppress atmospheric glare in the light of the sky. The rotational orientation of the filter is adjusted for the preferred effect.

Printed matter or objects devised to advertise or promote products, causes, or other concerns, especially those items given away to prospective consumers, clients, or contributors. Not used with reference to items produced before the late 19th century.
Bookbinding machines, typically hydraulic, into which books are fed for the purpose of binding their components together.
Devices or sets used to test and compare materials, often liquids, against a standardized scale of color, gradations, or other criteria.
Cases specifically used to protect and transport floppy disks.
Mechanized devices that use tape strips to both divide the wide fiber web from a woolen card into a series of strips and rub the strips into slubs or slivers.

Devices consisting of an iron shaft ending in a decoratively shaped form. The form is covered with batter, and then the iron is quickly plunged into hot oil, creating a fried pastry in a decorative shape, sometimes called a rosette.
Wide-mouthed funnels, typically of metal or plastic used to fit into jars, and used duing the canning process.

Bags of varied sizes and shapes, often made from flexible materials, such as polyester or nylon, which seals the bag against the infiltration of moisture. These are used in outdoor activities, such as kayaking and canoeing, to protect personal belongings from getting wet.
Used for measuring moisture content in solid materials.
Presses for expressing juice from apples; used to make cider.
Built objects used for scraping the mud off of one's boots. Typically located in front of a house, particularly in wealthy areas.
Scissors specifically used for blunt dissection, transection, and cutting during the dissection process.
Instruments used by draftsmen to render cone shapes.

Draftperson's triangles that include an adjustable arm to eliminate a  need of multiple triangles with fixed angles.  A protractor placed between the adjustable arm and the place where it is hinged assesses the angle of the clamped triangle.
Men's or women's loose, informal garments, often coat-like, worn when partly or fully undressed. Generally warm and often full-length; may be worn with a rope belt.

Machines that make prints using special stencils that allow ink to bleed through onto a support. The stencil is mounted onto a drum containing the ink, which is pushed through the stencil onto a support, usually paper.
Pressurized tools used to create circular perforations in an eggshell to remove interior material.
Thermometers designed to be inserted into meat during cooking in order to measure its internal temperature.
Fork-like tools used in the dairy in cheesemaking to process curd.

Cables that are usually used to connect devices (such as printers or mice) through computers’ serial ports and by using serial communication, or the transmission of data one bit at a time. Serial cables have nine wires, although multiple types of serial connectors exist, including 9-pin connectors and 25-pin connectors.
Panels with numerous electrical sockets that are used for cables that transmit data, both incoming and outgoing.
Devices that convert digital input signals to analog output signals, with the resulting output signals representing the same information contained in the input signals.
Flat pads on which computer mice are used, producing corresponding movement of pointers on monitor screens.
Devices, processing systems, or software that represents certain features of the behavior of a physical or abstract system.
Devices that punch one hole at a time into punch cards (or other data media).
Hard chalk or soapstone used to make eradicable marks on fabric for tailoring or cutting fabric.

Specialized tools, comprising two plates between which fabric is inserted as well as a single punch element, designed to clamp and perforate a variety of textile materials. Typically operated manually, these tools often feature punch elements that allow for variable and adjustable punch sizes.
Hand tools used to make holes in the fabrication of sails.
Scissors with zig-zag edges to make jagged cuts. Used to cut edges of fabrics to prevent fraying and unraveling.

Accelerated aging testing devices designed to measure a fabric's color fastness or resistance to color fading caused by exposure to strong light, ultraviolet rays, or other damaging external light sources. These devices expose dyed textile samples to a carbon arc, which emits an intense actinic light that mimics the effects of natural light, for extended periods of time. Although the device's actinic light does not directly duplicate the effect of natural light exposure, it is the most effective indicator of a textile material's light stability.
Devices that dispense or unroll tension wire for fencing.
Low often ornamental fences of iron or brass set before a hearth to confine coals and ash.
Devices that may be attached to a camera to hold and operate flashbulbs.
Basket-like objects intended to carry foodstuffs for an individual's lunch.
Small casks containing a quarter of a barrel or half a kilderkin for liquids, fish, butter, or other foods.
Culinary tools used for cake decorating.
Kitchen appliances for drying food, typically consisting of a heater, a fan, and several perforated trays which allow the circulation of warm air around the food to be dried.
Devices, hand-held or secured to a work bench, typically consisting of a lever, that when pressed down, firmly inserts a cork into a bottle.
Boxes or trays for holding knives, often divided into two or more compartments.
Rolling units used for collecting or storing food service trays.
Containers with compartments for organizing flatware.
Devices in which dough is inserted in a chamber and extruded by means of a plunger, through one of a number of interchangeable plates to form shaped cookies.

A composite wood board made from small wood chips mixed with a water-insoluble adhesive, then compressed into a dense solid panel. Particle boards were originally made in 1915 as wallboards. The most common adhesive in particle boards is urea formaldehyde glues are used which release volatile formaldehyde. Some particles boards are made with polyurea or phenolic resins. Particle boards are water-resistant, insect resistant, and dimensionally stable during humidity and temperature fluctuations. Particle boards are commonly used in the construction of inexpensive furniture, cabinetry and mobile homes.
Cookstoves fueled by electricity.
In language, uninflected words used to connect clauses or sentences, or to coordinate words in the same clause.
Language spoken in the Amazon areas of Peru, Brazil, and Colombia.
The variety of Spanish spoken in Catalonia; not to be confused with the Catalan language, which is not Spanish.
Refers to several varieties of Spanish spoken in Bolivia, which may be divided into two main groups: varieties of the Andes and of the lowlands.

Currency of Austria and Liechtenstein between 1919 and 1925; from after the dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian Empire until the introduction of the Schilling and the Franken, respectively. Intended to replace the Austro-Hungarian Krone, it was prone to hyperinflation and was replaced by the Austrian Schilling.
Decorative elements applied to shoes, vary in size, form, and material.
Unit of frequency representing one thousand cycles per second (hertz). It is used mostly to measure the transmission speed of electronic devices.
Masks used by actors in Ancient Greek and Roman theater, having many standard variations, representing serious or tragic facial expressions.

In book cataloging, the second part of a title proper that consists of two parts, each a title in itself, connected by the word "or" or its equivalent in another language (example: The Female Quixote, or, The Adventures of Arabella). Distinguished from "alternate titles" and "subtitles."
Small ornamental piercings worn through the tongue, often made of metal.
Series of numbers, key letters, words, or symbols used for identification of an entity, often in place of a name or title or used to stand for a longer word or concept.

Governing principles that serve as guidelines for decision-making and action in preservation and conservation of cultural heritage. Concept covers collection materials in institutional context as well as governmental policy set at civic, regional, or national level for built objects and other historic landmarks.
The acts of coming to a place, such as landing on a shore or in a country.

Automated devices used to facilitate the initiation of new fabric designs onto a loom by threading yarns from new warps through the eyes of the loom's heddles and the dents of its reeds. By reducing the labor time required to carry out the drawing-in process, which consists of both drafting and denting tasks, these devices allow more frequent re-drawings or establishment of new design patterns in fabrics. H.D. Coleman is credited with inventing the first automated drawing-in machine in 1904 based on the principle of manual warping.
Initial letters that contain figures of human, animal, or hybrid creatures.
Experts in or students of the German language, literature, history, or culture.

Musical compositions that are free in form and inspiration, usually for an instrumental soloist. Examples include 16th- and 17th-century English fugal compositions (i.e., based on melodic imitation) for consorts of string or wind instruments, and earlier 16th-century works for lute or keyboard consisting of short sections based on one or more musical motives.
Serious or tragic operas, particularly those with elaborate arias that were prevalent in the 18th centurey and usually based on a classical or mythological subject.
Formal addresses or speeches, especially those given on special occasions.
Performing arts genre concerning rhythmic movement, creating visual designs by a series of poses and tracing of patterns through space in the course of measured units of time.
Method of acquiring property by transference or bestowal following the death of a benefactor, by means of the last will or other method.
The preparation of archival materials for use.

The status or condition of a thing or site having been obliterated or ravaged to such a state as to be rendered useless or reduced to rubble. For lesser states of severe damage of architecture or sites, prefer "ruined."
The activity and profession of breeding and raising horses.
Laws that regulate expenditure, typically with a view to restraining what is perceived by the lawmakers or society as excess in food, dress, equipage, etc.

The right, action, or eligibility to cast a vote or votes in an election; includes the collective right of a group of people, such as the subset of a nation's citizens eligible to vote in a political election.
Systems of ethical and moral codes taught by religious traditions. Types of religious law include Jewish halakha, Christian canon law, Islamic sharia, and Hindu law.

Form-fitting, one-piece combination garments made of stretchable fabric that covers the body from neck to feet, comprising elements of both a leotard and tights in one article of clothing. Worn, for example, by gymnists and dancers. For one-piece, skin-tight combination garments that leave the wearer's legs either fully or partially exposed, use "leotards."
Meaning "delineated [it]," in printmaking and other art works, indicates the one who drew the design.
The military equipment of the Mexica soldiers in postclassic central Mexico.
Style of writing of inscriptions or other texts in which only capital letters are used, in reference to the ancient Latin alphabet of capitals.
People who take part in the game of chess.
Kitchen utensils having several parallel wires bent in a semicircle and secured by a handle, used especially for cutting shortening into flour to make pastry dough.
General term for both wild and domestic species of yak.

Units of illuminance measured as the degree of illumination that falls upon the interior of a sphere with a radius of one foot from a uniform point source of light of one candle and equal to one lumen per square foot. In the metric system, a lumen is measured by a square meter or a lux. Thus a foot-candle is equivalent to approximately 10 lux or 10.57 lux.
Computer memory that contains fixed information, such as a program, that does not change, and cannot be written to, only read from.
Chinese ornamental gateways of one, three, or five openings, usually commemorative or triumphal.

The tools and commands that connects the user to a computer or device. It allows the user to control operations and input commands or data. The design for the user interface can range from graphic to command-driven.

Chemical element that, when pure, is a pale-yellow, toxic gas. Fluorine occurs naturally in the form of mineral fluorite, cryolite, and fluorapatite. Fluorine is the most electronegative and reactive element known. Henri Moissan of France received a Nobel Prize for first isolating fluorine in 1886.
Isotopes of nitrogen: nitrogen-14 and the uncommon isotope, nitrogen-15.
Compound formed by interaction of free calcium and phosphate. Calcium phosphate is a component of bone and tooth enamel and the chief source of calcium in bovine milk.

Order of dicotyledonous flowering plants in the Rosid I group among the core eudicots. The order comprises 4 families (Fabaceae, Polygalaceae, Quillajaceae, and Surianaceae), 754 genera, and more than 20,000 species. However, more than 95 percent of the genera and species belong to Fabaceae, the legume family. Fabaceae is the third largest family of angiosperms, exceeded only by Asteraceae (aster or sunflower family) and Orchidaceae (orchid family). Along with Poaceae (the grass family), Fabaceae is the most important plant family in the production of food for humans and livestock, as well as in the production of industrial products.
Stable oxygen atoms that have the same atomic number as the element oxygen, but differ in atomic weight. O-17 and O-18 are examples of stable oxygen isotopes.
General term referring to either of two cosmopolitan genera of invertebrate marine animals in the Pleurobrachiidae family, the Hormiphora and the Pleurobrachia.

Small hard balls used in cue sports, originally made of varied materials including ivory, now made of polyester or resin. These come in a variety of colors and a few sizes determined by the games that they are intented for.
Compact rolls of tobacco leaves for smoking, one end being taken in the mouth while the other is lit.
Removable dental appliances that provide a flat biting surface that covers the functional surfaces of the teeth; used to prevent the direct contact of the tooth surfaces.
Status of property that was presented for sale, but not necessarily sold, in an auction, which is a public sale of property to the highest bidder.
Sculptors who created art conforming to the official standards and principles of taste of European and American art academies.
Devices that measure fermentation in liquids.
Devices that analyze periodic functions to find their harmonic components. Early examples measured the harmonic components of sound waves.
Weapons featuring a sharp edge or point for cutting, thrusting, clubbing, slashing, or various combinations thereof.

Telescopes used for photographing the sun, developed in the mid-19th century in Europe. The first photoheliograph was developed by astronomer Warren de la Rue and constructed in London by Andrew Ross, and was completed in 1856.
Machines that reproduce recorded content from magnetic tape. Most often this content is audio recordings.

General term for administrative divisions, usually of a nation, that represent the second highest unit or level under the nation itself, under the first level subdivision. Examples are the counties of the United States.

A technique based on the Doppler-effect for determining vibration velocity and displacement at a fixed point. It uses a two beam laser interferometer measuring the difference in frequency between a test beam and an internal reference beam.

Eggs created for and consumed at Easter. They are often gaily painted or dyed eggs (usually hardboiled or blown) decorated for Easter as gifts, or display pieces, or the objects of an Easter egg hunt. By extension, egg shaped trinkets of wood, porcelain, or other materials, sometimes bejewelled.
An era following the Palaeozoic era, comprising both the Mesozoic and Cenozoic (Cainozoic) eras.

An interval of the Paleozoic Era that followed the Silurian Period and preceded the Carboniferous Period, spanning between about 419.2 million and 358.9 million years ago. This period featured diverse and abundant aquatic life. Forests and marine organisms known as ammonites appeared early in the Devonian, and later amphibians appeared, the first vertebrates on land.

The first period of the Mesozoic, extending from about 250 to 208 million years ago. Following the mass extinctions of the Permian, many new forms of flora and fauna emerged in the Triassic including ocean reptiles and terrestrial vertebrates such as dinosaurs. The first mammals, small shrew-like creatures, appeared in the late Triassic.

The Quaternary is the second major division of geologic time in the Cenozoic era, following the Tertiary period. It extends from about 1.8 million years ago to the present. It is divided into Pleistocene and Holocene epochs.
Institutions that specialize in the history, objects, vehicles, and other materials associated with self-propelled vehicles designed primarily to transport passengers over ordinary roads.

The magnesium salt of magnesium sulfite in sulfurous acid appearing as colorless crystals or white, crystalline powder. It oxidizes to sulfate on exposure to air and loses all its water at 200 degrees fahrenheit. It is used as an adsorbent and absorbent, as an agricultural chemical, in the manufacture of paper pulp, as a wastewater treatment, and etc.
Sulfides that occur when the sulfur atom reacts with organic phosphines.
Condition of suffering severely or perishing from malnutrition or hunger.

On the geologic time scale, oldest of five epochs of the Tertiary period, or the last of the more recently designated Paleogene period of the Cenozoic era. The Paleocene extends from about 65 million to 55 million years ago. It followed the Cretaceous period and preceded the Eocene epoch. It is marked by the rapid proliferation and evolution of mammals, including the first primates, and by the formation of the Rocky Mountains.
Instruments or equipment used to punish or restrain.
The activity or condition of being employed or otherwise working as a primary endeavor in the government or other public function.

Devices used to cut patterns into leather or other materials, originally parts for the uppers of boots and shoes, but now typically for any material intended for garments. These now are in the form of hand or hydraulic presses fixed with dies.

Dramatic or mimic representations, usually of a light or humorous character, such as was commonly introduced between the acts of the long mystery-plays or moralities, or exhibited as part of an elaborate entertainment.

A Peranakan Chinese bulbous, tub-like container with a dome-shaped lid that usually can be found in Peranakan households. The bodies of the kamcheng may have small handles, and the lids, may be topped by an auspicious animal design. Kamcheng can be found in a range of sizes. Kamcheng are usually designed with Peranakan Chinese motifs which have auspicious symbolisms such as peonies, phoenixes, the eight auspicious Buddhist emblems, butterflies, and other flowers. The term “kamcheng” in Hokkien (a Chinese dialect) means “covered jar”. It is an important ware in Peranakan Chinese wedding ceremonies. On a day-to-day basis, a kamcheng is used for serving and storing different types of food such as pickles and rice. Smaller kamcheng have also been used to store cosmetic products.

Hides or skins that have been stripped from a dead animal, with hair, wool, or feathers attached; the legs, tail, and head may also be attached. For skins with hair that are used as a material, prefer "pelt (animal material)." For pelts mounted and represented as a three-dimensional animal, use "taxidermy mounts."

Frames used to hold inflexible photosensitized plates made of glass, rigid plastic, metal, or other materials. These are components used in medium and large format cameras for dry or wet plate photography.

Chinese festival celebrated on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month, primarily focused on prayers by women for dexterity in needlework and a happy marriage. The festival has its origin in astronomical rituals of early Chinese people, particularly the Western Han Dynasty (206 BCE-8 CE). The stars Altair and Vega came to represent the legendary lovers Niu Lang (the Cowherd) and Zhi Nu (the Weaver Girl). Observances include offering fruits to the goddess, threading seven-hole needles, watching stars in the sky, and laying clothes to dry in a tower.

Religious movement that spread across Plateau Native North Americans during the late 19th century to the early 20th century. Founded by Klickitat prophet Jake Hunt, also known as Titcam Nashat. Focused on returning pre-contact lifeways to the Klickitat and other Native participants, accomplished through specific dress requirements and ceremonies. Placed emphasis on Eagle spirit veneration, with eagle feathers featuring in religious regalia.

Oxide appearing as an olive-brown or blue-black anhydrous powder when stannous oxalate is heated out of contact with the air. Uses include manufacturing of other tin compounds, as a reducing agent, and as an ingredient in creating ruby glass.
In Japanese printing, format derived from a large sheet, ō-ōban, around 26.5 x 19 cm.
Works of art, architecture, or other objects that have been taken apart or fragmented, either through damage or intentionally.

Process of creating works in which pieces of hard, polished stone of varying shapes are set into marble or another hard surface to form a pattern. It differs from "mosaic" in that the pieces are not of uniform size.
That which is placed in position number three of a sequence.
State or condition of existing or moving in the heavens, usually meaning above the atmosphere of the planet, but also including the area of heaven, the doctrinal concept.
The right-hand side of a ship or aircraft, as distinguished from the larboard or port side. Traditionally, the side upon which in early types of ships the steering apparatus was worked.

Flowing floor-length robes with wide sleeves, made of silk or similar material. These are worn by judges while sitting at the bench in courts of law in the United States and elsewhere. Judicial robes in the United States are usually black but may vary in slight detail, as there is no official source or design, in the United Kingdom there exist color variations based on the court in which the judicant sits.

Placing goods in a transportation vessel such as a ship, airplane, or automobile. The concept may be extended to fixed locations such as warehouses. In general this is done in a manner that takes up the least space for economic reasons and that limits the risk of damage.
Qualifier used to express minor uncertainty regarding the attribution, generally indicating a slightly stronger probability than "attributed to."

Qualifier used for attributions of works by an unknown creator working for a named studio that called itself an atelier, generally reserved for those studios located in France, or in Britain after the 18th century.

Qualifier used for a work by an unknown creator who appears to be associated with the named artist, he or she is living at the same time as the named artist, and probably had some contact with him or her, but not is necessarily his or her pupil.
Qualifier used for a work by an unknown creator whose style is strongly under the influence of the style of the named master (e.g., style of Raphael).
Masonry construction using a single non-structural external layer of masonry, typically brick or stone.

Date range including earliest and latest dates of items in a group. For example, dates for the subjects contained in the archival materials, used particularly when the subjects do not correspond to the dates when the group or series was created. For example, a series created in the 1970s about the 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor would have a coverage date of 1941 and inclusive dates of 1970-1979 (e.g., 1941 (coverage), 1970-1979 (inclusive dates)).
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1799 to 1700 (or 1800 to 1701) Before Common Era.
Calendar system used by the Aztecs and other Pre-Columbian peoples of central Mexico.
Dating system based on the mutual relations of the sun and moon, or taking account of their combined action.

Hand-held board-like objects used for writing or drawing, either written upon directly or used as a support for paper or another material. For artifacts rather than equipment, particularly artifacts upon which something has been written, use "writing tablets (information artifacts)." For larger boards for writing, use "writing boards (writing equipment)."
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 351-394; founded by Fu Jian, of the Di people.
Numbers used to identify an individual publication within a classification or location in a library.
Names or titles given to products, techniques, or concepts by the inventor, maker, or distributor and legally belonging to the inventor, maker, or distributor.
The first letters of each word in names, as of a person or organization, used as an abbreviation for or to stand for the names.
Information that is formatted, stored, and linked in a way to allow efficient retrieval. It is often used in conjunction with or distinguished from "display information."
Refers to the architectural order characterized by columns generally without bases, relatively simple capitals, and a frieze composed of alternating triglyphs and metopes.
An alphasyllabary script used for writing Sanskrit, as associated with the Gupta Empire of India; descended from Brahmi script.

Currencies based on knives or knife-shaped objects as a means of purchasing or exchange. Examples are the obsidian knife currencies of Pre-Columbian America, the metal and stone knives used as currency in ancient Asia, and knife-shaped blades used as currency in Africa.

Medicinal concoction of varying ingredients and preparations, formerly believed to be a universal antidote to poison or a panacea. According to legend, was first formulated by Mithradates VI Eupator of Pontus in the 1st century BCE; one of the most highly sought-after drugs in the Middle Ages and Renaissance periods.

Projection prints that are of very high quality and made for screening at special events, such as gala premieres. Usually printed directly from the composited camera negative onto a higher quality of print stock than is usual for mass-production release prints.

Feathered encasing body suits awarded to a Mexica warrior after taking his second captive in battle. The feathered suit was worn over ichcahuipilli (quilted cotton body armor) along with other elements of the Cuextecatl (Huastec) warrior costume. They were made in a variety of different colors, and frequently decorated with a motif consisting of pairs of black rectangles known as "hawk scratches" that are also associated with the Huastec region.
Characters featured or depicted in religious or mythological works.

Graffiti art works produced with spray paint, that spell out the artist's name in rounded letters. Usually these are rendered in two colors, one for the body and another for a contrasting outline. These are intended to cover as much surface area as possible in the shortest amount of time without regard to style or technical proficiency.

The third month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendars, containing 31 days and falling between February and April. It was named after Mars, the Roman god of war. Originally, March was the first month of the Roman calendar.

The day following Monday and preceding Wednesday, traditionally regarded as the third day of the week, but now frequently considered as the second. In English and other language, named from Tiu, or Tiw, the Anglo-Saxon name for the Norse god of war, one of the sons of Odin, or Woden. In Romance languages, named for the Roman Mars’s-day.

French operas in which spoken dialogue alternates with self-contained musical numbers. The earliest examples of opéra-comique were satiric comedies with interpolated songs, but the form later developed into serious musical drama distinguished from other opera only by its spoken dialogue. The opéra-comique developed in the early 18th century out of the comédies de vaudeville, farcical entertainments performed at fairs.
Any of various diseases afflicting one or more joints.
Chiripa style and period dating 800-100 BCE, marked by more elaborate common structures, domestic architecture, and more sophisticated gardening practices.
Artists who specialize in making altarpieces, which are painted or carved image-bearing objects set upon an altar in a Christian church.
Artists formally attached to a university, college, community, or other organization, usually for a specified period.

East African rectangular cotton textiles printed in bold designs and bright colors, with borders that frame the panel that often contain Swahili inscriptions. They are variously used as main garments, skirts, shawls, hoods, and even occasionally as tablecloths.

Generally, all ware made of ceramic, which is any of various hard, brittle, heat-resistant and corrosion-resistant materials made by shaping and then firing a nonmetallic mineral, such as clay, at a high temperature. In specialized usage, it typically does not include porcelain, which is a type of ceramic ware made of a refractory white clay, or "kaolin," and a feldspathic rock, that react when fired so the clay serves to hold the shape of the object and the rock fuses into a natural glass.

Rivers, streams, creeks, or any other type of watercourses that formerly existed but no longer do, or that currently exist for some distance but then disappear into an underground channel or dry up in an arid area.
Physical features located on land, particularly those above sea level;  either natural or man-made.
Capital towns or cities for administrative districts.
Centers or sites having religious sanctuaries as a primary focus.
Communities of relatively small size that hold a market, typically agricultural centers in a rural area.
Tracts of land set aside, usually by the United States government or a single US state's government, for the use of one or more native North American peoples.

In a hierarchy, a descendent is any record that is a narrower context for the record at hand, including children, grandchildren, and all other narrower contexts at lower levels; any node in the succession of parent nodes on a path all the way down to the tips (leaves) of the hierarchies.
In a thesaurus, a descriptor is the term recommended to represent the concept in displays and indexing. In the AAT, terms in each language may have one descriptor.
Written orders or promises to pay money that may be transferred from one person to another by delivery, with or without endorsement.

Works that are based upon one or more pre-existing works, such as a translation, musical arrangement, dramatization, fictionalization, motion picture version, sound recording, art reproduction, abridgment, condensation, or any other form in which a work may be recast, transformed, or adapted.

Ceramics made of the distinctive type of clay found in the Arita area of Japan; first manufactured in the early 17th century. Characterized by early unglazed blue and white porcelain to colorful enamel ware perfected in the 1640s. Arita ware was produced in large quantities in the 17th century and mass-produced by the Meiji period (1868-1912).

Works comprising precious or semiprecious stones or other materials such as amber or pearl, cut, polished, or otherwise dressed for ornamental purposes to be used in jewelry, seals, or amulets; distinguished from "gemstone" which is precious or semiprecious stone that has not been worked.

Heaps or piles of wheat sheafs, typically arranged in fields at harvest time. The stacks comprise sheafs of grain, primarily to be used for bread. The stacks protect the sheafs from rain until the grain can be separated from the stalks by threshing. For stacks of grass to be used for an animal food, prefer "haystacks."
Living organisms that are unique to geographic locations and cannot be found anywhere else on earth.
Clothing made of wool or chiefly of wool.

Small communities that were typically built to accommodate the workforce of a large employer, often providing a relatively high standard of housing. Prime examples are those constructed from the late 18th century onwards by industrialists to house their workers near the factory site.

Any liquid polymerized siloxane with organic side chains. It has good weatherability (including resistant toward extreme temperatures), and is waterproof and environment friendly. Silicone oils are primarily used as lubricants, heat transfer oil or hydraulic fluids. In conservation, it has been used as a consolidant.
Genus of large condor native to South America, having only one known species. The fossil record of the genus is slight.
Gently inclined slopes rising from the deep ocean towards the foot of continental slopes.
Landforms smaller than a continent, completely surrounded by water at high water. Islands appear in oceans, seas, lakes, or rivers.

Forests with varied vegetation, depending upon whether they are tropical or temperate, but having in common a high annual rainfall of between 98-180 inches. Tropical rainforests are found closer to the equator and temperate rainforests are found farther north near coastal areas.

Forests located near the equator, within the area bounded by latitudes 23.5 degrees N and 23.5 degrees S. Tropical forests include the rainforest, the cloud forest, and the dry forest, such as the pine savanna and others. One of the major characteristics of tropical forests is their distinct seasonality: winter is absent, and only two seasons are present, rainy and dry. The length of daylight is 12 hours and varies little. Of all earth’s environments, they harbor the greatest diversity of species.

Tropical forests of coniferous or broad-leaved trees that lose their leaves during the dry season; trees do not grow close together and there are few climbing plants. Seasonal rainforests are found in areas having short dry periods in an otherwise very wet tropical region. They are located between the tropical rain forests and the tropical savannas.

term: moist conifer and evergreen broad-leaved forests
definition: Temperate forests of conifer and evergreen broad-leaved trees, located in areas having wet winters and dry summers; rainfall is concentrated in the winter months and winters are relatively mild.

Biomes surrounding freshwater environments, defined as having a low salt concentration of less than 1%. Plants and animals in freshwater regions are adjusted to the low salt content and would not be able to survive in areas of high salt concentration.

Biomes that go through four season: leaves change color in autumn, fall off in the winter, and grow back in the spring; this adaptation allows plants to survive cold winters. Temperatures range -30 to 30 degrees C, with annual percipitation 750-1500 mm. Vegetation includes broadleaf trees, shrubs, perennial herbs, and mosses.

Large category including areas of land characterized by poor drainage, standing or slowly moving water, and as a result, an almost constant state of water-saturated soil. Wetlands include swamps, marshes, and bogs.
Category of marine body of water comprising the main water areas of the earth, lying in basins; for shallow salt water areas lying on the margins of continents, use "seas."
Deserts having seasons that are generally warm throughout the year and very hot in the summer; winters usually bring little rainfall.

The physical universe beyond the earth's atmosphere, consisting of near vacuum with small amounts of gas and dust. Usage often excludes celestial objects, but includes the expanse in which celestial objects are situated.
Electronic devices for generating oscillatory electric currents, or for generating electromagnetic waves by means of such currents, particularly in the audible frequency range.
Geographic latitude is the angular distance north or south of the equator, measured along a meridian. Parallels of latitude are equidistant circles drawn around the globe parallel to the equator.

Variety of the Dutch language used in the Netherlands for public and official purposes, including instruction in schools and universities. Standard Dutch is characterized grammatically by the loss of case endings in the noun.

Refers to the variety of English traditionally the official language of England and the usual spoken language of educated people in London and southeastern England. It is codified in the British Received Pronunciation (RP).
Informal term referring to the most common variety of the French language spoken in France, Andorra, and Monaco.
A vernacular dialect of German, spoken in much of northern Germany; it is more closely related to Dutch than to Standard German.
Now extinct, Anatolian languages were spoken during the 1st and 2nd millennia BCE in what is presently Asian Turkey and northern Syria. The best-known Anatolian language is Hittite.

Form of the Latin language used in the Roman Rite of the Catholic Church for liturgical, documentary, and legal purposes. It is distinguished from Classical Latin by a simplified syntax, lexical variations,new idioms and words, and Italianate pronunciation.
Variety of the Portuguese language used primarily in the nation of Cape Verde.
Variety of Spanish spoken in Morocco; it includes elements of Arabic and French.
The simplest variety of dovetail seams in sheet metal, where tabs are cut from the sheet of metal and folded or bent over the collar to form a seam; usually used for joining collars to flanges.

Digital distortion that occurs when a sampling frequency is too low, as in jagged stair-stepping in curved lines or transitions in images. In sound, aliasing occurs when the sampling rate drops below 40 kilohertz (Khz).

An early projection photocopier created in the decade of the 1900s by the Commercial Camera Company, which became the Photostat Corporation. The "Photostat" name, was originally a trademark of the company, later became genericized, and was often used to refer to similar machines produced by the Rectigraph Company.
Language family of indigenous North America, including the Algonquian family of languages of the area from the Rocky Mountains to Atlantic Canada, and the Yurok and Wiyot of northwestern California.

Writing systems that represent the consonantal value of a syllable while ignoring the vocalic element. Such systems have graphs for consonant sounds but not for vowel sounds, with the result that a certain amount of guesswork is involved in determining which syllable is being represented.

Avant-garde dances having a style that originated in Japan. The first Butoh performance was given by Tatsumi Hijikata in 1959. As practiced by various groups and individuals, Butoh may incorporate elements of dance, theater, and performance art. Butoh performances typically incorporate grotesque imagery and physical endurance.
The whitish-yellowish layer that floats to the top of milk, comprising 18 to 40 percent butterfat.
A fermented liquor made from maize and other plants by the indigenous peoples of South America.

Industrial facilities dedicated to the large-scale production of food products prepared by moistening, kneading, and baking flour or meal into bread or similar products. For buildings or parts of buildings where bread and other baked goods are prepared, and that may include a space for the retail sale of baked goods, use "bakeries."

A form of ion beam analysis named for Lord Ernest Rutherford. It yields information on the thickness and elemental composition of a sample by detection of the backscattered protons from crystalites or other particles of the analysed sample.

Genus of predatory sea snails of the Indo-Pacific region. The genus Murex was defined by Linnaeus to include many taxa that are now placed elsewhere in the superfamily Muricoidea, particularly those from which the red dye Tyrian purple was made.

One of the three major divisions of living organisms; includes plants, animals, and all living things other than Archaea and Eubacteria. Although members in this group differ greatly, all members of the group have eukaryotic cells with a nucleus that contain genetic material within chromosomes.
In Chinese landscape painting, perspective created through a view across a low, broad expanse.
Genus of plants including food crops, such as mustard and various greens.
Robotic applications that work with detailed precision in controlled environments, such as manufacturing.

A term meaning “averter of evil,” and applied to lion-like mythological Chinese guardian creatures. Stone sculptures of bixie are often placed along spirit roads to protect tomb occupants from evil influences.
Collections of preserved web pages.

In historical western fashion, particularly in the 18th and 19th centuries, attire worn near the end of the period of mourning, when colors of mauve and lavender and more sumptuous fabrics are appropriate.

Belgian art movement in painting that is associated with the group ‘Vie et Lumière’ formed around the artist Emile Claus in 1904. Typical are works with light-infused impressionist Flemish landscapes, often depicting the countryside in the surroundings of the river ‘Leie’.
In Indian architecture, a miniature simulacrum of a pillaret within a recessed moulding; vertical partition in the gala; vertical block at intervals inside the gala; gala block-projection.

Mythological beings known in Vedic, Zoroastrian, Hindu, and Buddhist sources. Described in Indian texts as powerful superhuman demigods with good or bad qualities; defined by their opposition to the devas or suras.
Materials with names given by the company responsible for their production and sale to provide distinction and recognition between similar materials.
Japanese events involving a picnic meal and enjoyment outdoors, usually taking place during the annual appearance of cherry blossoms.

Syriac script that appeared around the 8th century CE, taking on a more cursive appearance than Estrangela. By 700 CE, Serto adopted Greek vowel letters, modifying them with diacritics typically written above the consonant letter that the vowel follows. In cases where the consonant letter takes up a lot of vertical space, the vowel diacritic can occur under it.
The sport of pitting domestic dogs to fight each other; now illegal in most countries.
In architecture, the sum of all areas on all floors within the outside faces of the exterior walls of a built work, including vertical penetration areas that connect one floor to another.
Time units equal to a 10-year length of time.
Metric measurements of length equivalent to 10 centimeters or 0.1 meter.
Units of volume, in which one cubic inch corresponds to the volume of a cube that measures 1 inch × 1 inch × 1 inch.

Metric units of mass equal to about 2.205 pounds. One kilogram is approximately equal to the weight of 1000 cubic centimeters of water. The kilogram is the base unit of mass in the International System of Units (SI) (the Metric system); defined as being equal to the mass of the International Prototype of the Kilogram. It is the only SI unit that is still directly defined by an artifact rather than a fundamental physical property that can be reproduced in different laboratories.
The hair grown on the sides of a man's face extending the hairline along the cheeks.
Tuft-like beards grown underneath the lower lip, resembling the beard style of the French emperor Napoleon III.
Long bristly moustaches sagging down at the ends, similar to the moustaches of walruses.
Side-whiskers; more specifically, large and worn with moustaches. Named after the U.S. Civil War general Burnside who popularized this style.

The most common variety of Maori pounamu stone that comes in many shades, from strong rich green to dark green; often a translucent nephrite. It is often characterized by small dark inclusions, which is considered an addition to its character.
Instruments comprising a small gourd with holes, which is attached to a string and twirled to create a sound like that of birds.
General term for clothing designed for or suitable for either males or females.
General term for clothing designed for or worn by young females.
Fiber or fiber-like material made wholly or in part from silver.
Existing, constituted, or carried on within a given nation.
A sweet-tasting, white, crystalline amino acid that is a constituent of many animal proteins; found in sugar cane, animal glue, and gelatin.
Multivariate statistical technique that reduces variables in a large data set to a smaller number of determining factors underlying otherwise loosely related data.

Electromagnetic radiation emitted by high-energy particles following a curved path at close to the speed of light as in the variety of particle accelerator known as a synchrotron. It is also produced naturally by charged particles moving through magnetic fields.
Nanomaterial composed of a hydrogel (a hydrophylic polymer network) used for varied applications including medicine, DNA sequencing, and in conservation as a surface coating and protectant.
An organic compound made synthetically or obtained from peppermint or mint oils with flavoring and local anasthetic properties. In conservation, it has been used as a temporary consolidant.

A polysaccharide, gluten-free additive produced from a fermented bacterial secretion that is used in cosmetics and food as a thickener or stabilizer. In art conservation, it can be used to make oil-in-water emulsions for non-water-miscible solvents.

Electron energy loss spectroscopy measures the energy of scattered electrons reemitted from surfaces after bombardment by an electron beam, thus determining the distribution of energy loss. Provides data complementary to Auger electron spectroscopy which operates according to the same principle but uses a different process to produce the electrons.
Adhesive made from flour containing 70% starch and 12% gluten. It is clear, and reversible with water.
Traditional Hawaiian residential structures set aside as eating places for women.
Instruments used to measure sensory discrimination.
Models that illustrate the design of the interior space of a built work; focusing on form, space, and function; may also include colors, materials, lighting, and furnishings.
Electrophoresis in which the migration of proteins occurs under an applied electric field through a gel medium having a pH gradient towards a region where they are isoelectric.

The style and culture of the ancient Gallo-Germanic Belgæ tribes living from the 3rd century BCE onward in northern Gaul, between the English channel and the west bank of the Rhine. They were later found in Britain and Ireland.

Drugs or other substances that cause hallucinations, which are apparent perceptions, usually by sight or hearing, of an external object or activity when no such object or activity is actually present.
Mechanism for managing and storing digital content in order to manage and preserve it.

Priestesses in ancient Roman religion who tended the state cult of Vesta, the goddess of the hearth; the cult existed from ca. 7th century BCE until it was banned in 394 CE by Theodosius I. Each vestal virgin served for 30 years, during which time she remained chaste and tended to the rituals of the temple, such as tending the perpetual fire in the Temple of Vesta, fetching water from a sacred spring, preparing ritual food, and officiating at the annual Vestalia festival. The virgins lived in the House of the Vestal Virgins on the Roman Forum, near the Temple of Vesta.
The activity or sport of riding a bicycle or any cycle.
To speak or reason in opposition, to raise objections, contend, or dispute as a way to prove, evince, or show weighty reasons for supposing a proposition or for refuting another’s position.
Inordinate desire of acquiring and hoarding wealth, greediness of gain.
The personal state of pleasurable contentment of mind, typically including contentment with or resignation to one's circumstances.
Styles and Islamic culture on the Indian subcontinent.
A dry, nonchemical photocopying process in which an electrostatic image remains after exposure and is developed by the deposition of toner.
Species of small deciduous tree native to  Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Andhra Pradesh, India. Noted for resin that is used as incense and as medicine.

Oriental Orthodox Christian religion in Eritrea, which has had a large Christian population since the 4th century. It is in dispute whether or not the Eritrean Orthodox church is a division of the Ethiopian Orthodox church.

Refers to the monotheistic religion of the Jewish people, central to which is the belief that the ancient Israelites experienced God's presence in human events. Jews believe that the one God delivered the Israelites out of bondage in Egypt, revealed the structure of communal and individual life to them, and chose them to be a holy nation of people able to set an example for all humankind. The Hebrew Bible and Talmud are the two primary sources for Judaism's spiritual and ethical principles. The religion, which traces its origins to Abraham, places more emphasis on expressing beliefs through ritual rather than through abstract doctrine. The Sabbath, beginning on sunset on Friday and ending at sunset on Saturday, is the central religious observance; there is also an annual cycle of religious festivals and days of fasting. Judaism has had a diverse history of development over almost 4000 years, with a number of resulting branches in modern times, namely Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform.
Horizontally mounted rods from which curtains are hung, sometimes with the aid of curtain rings.
Languages used in communicating with, querying, or programming computers.

Hand gesture indicating touching the earth; used for seated figures, usually the Sakyamuni Buddha in his victory of Mara. The right hand, palm inward and extending downward, touches or gestures in the direction of the earth.
Printmakers who specialize in the subject matter of architecture and architectural components.

General term for acute viral infection of the upper or lower respiratory tract that is marked by fever, chills, and a generalized feeling of weakness and pain in the muscles, together with varying degrees of soreness in the head and abdomen. May be caused by any of several closely related viruses in the family Orthomyxoviridae (a group of RNA viruses).

Sodium chloride crystals prepared for use as a food seasoning and preservative. Table salt contains sodium chloride with small amounts of a free-flowing agent (calcium silicate or magnesium carbonate), an anti-caking agent (sodium ferrocyanide), an iodizing salt (potassium iodide or sodium iodide), and an iodide stabilizer (sodium carbonate and sodium thiosulfate).

Refers to a painting genre during period of Japanese occupation in Taiwan. In Japanese, 'toyo' broadly refers to a geographical area that includes India, Taiwan, China, Korea and Japan while 'ga' means painting. The earliest official record of the term toyoga came with the Toyoga Section of the first ‘Taiwan Fine Arts Exhibition’ held in 1927. While borrowing from a broad sweep of expressive forms, from Japanese nihonga and nanga to Chinese style ink painting, toyoga in general also incorporates native Taiwanese elements.
Style or culture of the of the people of the city in southwestern Yemen.
In Indian architecture, a pile of tiers on which mūlamañjarī of the Anēkāṇḍaka śikhara sits.

Artists in any medium whose primary subject matter is architecture, including buildings, gardens, or other aspects of the built environment. The term may be used to distinguish those who design architecture as art, rather than designing only constructions having purely a functional purpose.
A father-in-law is the father of one's spouse.
A stepfather is a man who has married one's mother after their natural father's death or divorce.

Large tree that is a natural hybrid between the big-leaf linden (T. platyphyllos) and little-leaf linden (T. cordata). It was frequently planted in towns and parks, thus known by the name "common lime" since the 17th century. It is easily propagated by layering.

Family containing 243 genera and at least 4,225 species of herbs, shrubs, and trees, common in the tropics but found in all but the coldest regions. Economically, the most important member of the family is cotton (Gossypium). Several species of Hibiscus produce fibers that are of lesser importance. The green fruits of okra (H. esculentus) are cooked and eaten, and the mucilage secreted in tissues of some species has been used in certain confections and for other purposes. Genera now included in Malvaceae were long thought to be very closely related, but, until DNA studies were done at the end of the 20th century, they were placed in four different families: Malvaceae, Bombacaceae, Tiliaceae, and Sterculiaceae, this group of families alone constituting Malvales for some earlier botanists. DNA evidence has shown that many of the genera in these families are interdigitated, a finding used for including them in a larger, single family rather than maintaining artificial lineages (ones that do not share a common ancestor).

Genus containing around 20 species of large trees found in tropical areas of Mexico, Central America, South America, the Bahamas, Belize, the Caribbean, West Africa, and Southeast Asia. Formerly was placed in the now defunct family Bombacaceae; now generally placed in family Malvales, subfamily Bombacoideae.

Species of large deciduous tree native to southeastern Europe but widely cultivated as a large shade and street tree; it grows to a height of 30 meters (100 feet). The Champs-Élysées in Paris is lined with rows of horse chestnut trees.
Family containing two or three genera of trees and shrubs. Some classifications include members of the Hippocastanaceae, along with members of the Aceraceae, in an enlarged family of Sapindaceae.

Species of small, deciduous, fruit-bearing tree that originated in China but is now cultivated throughout the temperate regions of the world. The scientific name includes a reference to Armenia, where it has been cultivated since ancient times. The common name is derived from an Arabic word, dating to the Moorish occupation of Spain. The tree has also been cultivated in Persia and Egypt since ancient times. Seeds or kernels of the apricot may be substituted for almonds; the oil pressed from these kernels is called "oil of almond"; the Italian liqueur amaretto and amaretti biscotti are flavored with extract of apricot kernels rather than almonds. In Europe, apricots were long considered an aphrodisiac, as mentioned by Shakespeare. A clear, water soluble gum exudes from open cuts in the bark; the gum contains arabinose, galactose, mannose, and glucuronic acid. In modern agriculture, apricot cultivars are usually grafted on plum or peach rootstocks.

Species of large, deciduous tree native to the Himalayas, Iran, Lebanon, Asia Minor, and Greece, and growing in Britain and elsewhere since about the middle of the 15th century. It reaches heights to 35 meters with a trunk up to 2 meters in diameter. It has a short trunk and broad crown, though taller and narrower in dense forest competition; it thrives in full sun. It is a valuable timber tree; other portions of the tree also have commercial value. The nut kernels are used for cooking and the pale yellow fast-drying oil expressed from the nuts is used for artists' paints. Tannins and dyes are extracted from the nut hulls and shells that produce a brown color. Ground nut shells have been used as a soft abrasive and a plastic filler.

Species of tree found in moist areas of the eastern U.S. from Maine south to the Gulf Coast and westward to Oklahoma. Its wood is light and soft, but tough. The black gum is sometimes grown as an ornamental, prized for brilliant scarlet autumnal foliage. The bark dye has good washfastness and fair lightfastness.

Species of tree native to Sri Lanka, India, and Malaya, used as medicine, as an anti-bacterial, as an anti-coagulant, for reddish dye called brazilin used for dyeing fabric as well as making red paints and inks, and for its wood, which is somewhat lighter in color than Brazilwood.

Family containing 44 genera and around 760 species of primarily herbaceous plants, but the family also includes some woody shrubs and a genus of small tropical trees. All species in the family have bisexual, regular, dish-shaped flowers with one superior pistil (female structure) and many stamens (male parts). The buds and flowers are usually large and often nodding.

Species of chestnut native to China. Nuts of the tree have local importance as food and are exported in large quantities. When cultivated close to other species of chestnut, it readily cross-pollinates to form hybrids. This species has evolved over a long period in coexistence with the bark fungal disease chestnut blight, and it has evolved a very successful resistance to the blight; although it is not immune, it typically sustains no more than minor damage when infected. This is in stark contrast to the American chestnut, which had no resistance to the blight, and was nearly wiped out after its introduction from Asia to North America in the early 20th century.

Species of ebony tree found in abundance throughout the flat country west of Trincomalee in Sri Lanka. The tree is distinguished by the width of its trunk and its jet-black, charred-looking bark, beneath which the wood is pure white until the heart is reached. The heartwood excels in fineness and in the intensity of its dark color. Although the center of the tree alone is used, reduced logs 30 cm to almost 1 m (1 to 3 feet) in diameter can be obtained.

Family containing 28 genera of herbaceous flowering plants. The family has been variously circumscribed, and some classifications include over 50 genera. In any case, although worldwide in distribution, most species grow in temperate and colder regions of the Northern Hemisphere, and many are Arctic or Alpine. These annual or perennial herbs have simple leaves, often with a toothed margin; their flowers are borne in groups on leafless stalks and have a tube with spreading lobes, the stamens being attached to the tube. The fruits are capsules.
Species of elm native to China but now found throughout the world as an ornamental, having small, lustrous leaves and interesting mottled bark.

Tree species of Western Australia grows up to 130 feet high with a trunk up to 9.8 feet in diameter. Growing in gray sand, clay, or sandy loam, on hills or rises.The species exhibits a rough, gray-brown, vertically grooved, fibrous bark. The leaves are often curved, 3.1–5.1 inches long and 0.59–1.18 inches wide, shiny dark green above and paler below, with a light colored border. Its flowers roughly half an inch in diameter, are white or cream to pink, and appear in clusters, blooming in spring and early summer. The fruits are ovoid, 0.35–0.63 inches long and broad.

Family of dicotyledon plants, placed within the order Myrtales. Myrtle, clove, guava, feijoa, allspice, and eucalyptus belong here. All species are woody, having essential oils and flowering parts in multiples of four or five.
Family of flowering plant containing one genus, Paeonia, the peonies.

Species of medium-sized tree native to North America, having bright green elm-like leaves with three prominent veins arising from the base of the blade, and edible pea-sized purplish-black fruits attractive to birds. The bark is sometimes covered with wartlike bumps. It is easily cultured and common as a street tree, attaining heights of 12-30 meters (40-100 feet).

Genus of 7 species of large tropical trees, deciduous or evergreen depending upon the species. The leaves are harvested as animal food; the bark and other parts used for medicinal purposes; the swellable gum is used for many purposes; and the wood, which resembles true mahogany of the genus Swietenia, is harvested for dugout canoes, furniture, and many other purposes.
Species of tree in North America, 21 to 27 m (70 to 90 feet) tall. It is an economically important timber tree, also having many cultivated varieties.

Large family containing around 275 genera and around 7,500 species of flowering plants, including herbs, shrubs or trees, and succulents that resemble cacti.
