Ship builder's models comprising layers of horizontal planks designed to be removed and measured as a guide in determining the waterlines of a proposed vessel.
Scapulars of cloak-style or small scapulars worn by Christian penitents, typically under clothing; they may be made of rough wool and decorated with the crucifix and instruments of the Passion.
Hairstyles incorporating a large coil or mass of hair wound around itself or a form and positioned on the nape of the neck or back of the head.
Metal covers for icons, made of numerous thin pieces. The riza usually covers only certain parts of the icons.
Comic books or strips in which the pictures are photographs with balloons containing the speech or thoughts of the characters. Most are of the romance or soap opera kind.
Comics that tell stories intended to be entertainingly frightening, usually featuring such things as monsters, violence, and the supernatural.

Performances encompassing two distinct minor genres, evolved from courtly entertainment: operas and serenatas. They are of abbreviated length and generally concern events such as royal weddings or birthdays. The focus is on drama, spectacle, and chorus, rather than elaborate musical composition.

Generally, the style and culture of the people of the tribal area and town of Mediouna, near Casablanca. Specifically, the style of rugs from this area, distinguished from rugs originating in a nearby urban carpet center, Rabat, in having fewer minor borders and a wider field than Rabat rugs, and having three or more octagonal medallions on the field. Traditional Mediouna rugs are no longer woven, but the style is copied.

Said of a book sold with the folded fore edges of the gatherings (bolts) not trimmed or cut, intended to be slit by hand by the purchaser with a paper knife. Distinct from "uncut" which is said of a book of which the folded fore edges have not been cut with the plough or guillotine prior to sale.

Vegetable-tanned leather made originally of shaved cowhide, later of calfskin, goatskin, sheepskin or horse hide, tanned with willow and other types of bark, then curried on the flesh side with birch bark extract to give it a pleasant but relatively short-lived odor in imitation of Russia calf.  Its uses included for upholstery and for binding blank books.

Vegetable-tanned goatskin leather imported in a partially-processed state from Nigeria or South Africa. Similar but distinct to "Niger (leather)," in that its final tanning and dying is processed elsewhere, usually England or France, and is available in a wider range of colors.
Sheepskin leather that has been tanned by forcing vegetable tanning liquor through the pores of the skin or hide. It is often dressed on the flesh side to have a fine nap like suede.
Strong, rigid leather used for durable items such as powder flasks, pots, or armor, made by tanning skin in a hot tanning solution and molding, pressing, or stamping it to shape.
Leather made from the skin of any of several species of very small deer-like mammals of Asia and West Africa, used in England in the Medieval period for "chemises," a type of loose book cover.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name, a subgroup of the Katab living in northern Nigeria.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in the central Democratic Republic of Congo.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Democratic Republic of Congo.
The field of planning concerned with development, resource utilization, and environmental preservation and amelioration in rural communities.
The split of a skin or hide between the grain and the flesh split.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Republic of the Congo.
Describes African people living in southern Ethiopia.

Refers to the Pottery Neolithic period in the southern Levant from about 5500 to 5000 BCE based on the site of Munhatta. The period is characterized by the continuation of cultural traits of the previous Yarmukian period, particularly the production of pottery.
Marine crustaceans and molluscs which bore into wood in water.
The young of cattle, oxen, bison, dolphins, elephants, giraffes, hippopotamuses, moose, rhinoceroses, whales, and yaks, and other animals.

The names for subfamilies Old World deer (subfamily Cervinae) and the New World deer (subfamily Capreolinae) reflect where the deer originally evolved; however, now it is not a geographical distinction but instead derives from their different foot structures. In the Old World deer the second and fifth hand bones (metapodia) have almost completely disappeared except for proximal, terminal remnants. In the New World deer the remnants are distal.

Members of a genus containing large, bushy-tailed, stocky ground squirrels native to mountainous areas such as the Alps, Carpathians, Tatra, and Pyrenees in Europe, the Rockies and the Sierra Nevada in the United States, and Northern Canada.
Adult female birds.
Genus that includes the death-watch beetle.

With reference to the military, refers to large army units regularly organized with officers and enlisted men, able to conduct major operations independently. Also refers to various tactical units devoted to particular services, such as medical, engineering, and communications, or to some branches of the armed forces of various countries, such as the marine corps of the United states and Great Britain.
Tiny sweetmeats made of breath-freshening seeds such as caraway, coriander, or anis, or fruit or root, coated and preserved with sugar.
Flags, banners, figures, or other objects used as symbolic representations during religious ceremonies. Examples include standards carried during religious processions.
Parachutes designed to slow the descent of persons falling from aircraft, specifically in a military context.

A technique of forming pottery by hand, in which a mass of wet clay is flattened to a slab with a rolling pin. The slab may be beaten into various shapes, joined to other slabs with slip, or paddled over a wood form.
Technique of activation analysis induced by protons to determine chemical elements.

Brief narrative poems in dactylic hexameter of ancient Greece, imitated by Romans and others. Usually dealing with mythological and romantic themes. They are characterized by lively description, miniaturistic attitude, scholarly allusion, and an elevated tone similar to that of the elegy.
Poetry intended to be funny or cause mirth in the reader. Poetry that is primarily funny or displaying humor.

A sulfate of copper, blue crystals in hydrous form, white when dehydrated. Copper sulfate is used as a preservative for wood, leather and paper; as a mordant and dye for textiles; as a biocide, and for a wide range of other purposes.
Paired deciduous outgrowths of bone, projecting from the frontal bones of ungulates of the deer family.
People who gather together physical items into a larger assemblage or other whole. Examples include people who compile albums or other sets of works.
Shoes or boots made with an extremely long pointed toe and worn in Europe in the 14th and 15th centuries. May also refer to toes of such footwear.
Footwear worn over shoes for warmth or protection.
Shoes of various styles made of wood.
Refers to the style and culture of the Assiniboine, an indigenous people primarily residing in central Canada, as well as parts of the United States.

Fluorescence-lifetime imaging microscopy or FLIM is an imaging technique for producing molecular images based on the fluorescence lifetime (the average time that the molecule spends in the excited state) from a fluorescent sample.The lifetime of the fluorophore signal, rather than its intensity, is used to create the image in FLIM. The fluorescence lifetime can function as a molecular stopwatch to observe a variety of events.The technique is thus particularly suitable for live-cell imaging.

The assemblies of citizens having the highest deliberative functions in a government, as in ancient Rome and other ancient states, the free cities of Medieval Europe, and the upper and smaller branches of the legislatures of, for example, the United States, France, and Italy.

Organs of the papal government that historically could hear cases, petitions, and other causes, and administer justice in civil, criminal, and ecclesiastical matters in the Vatican and other territories under papal dominion. The jurisdiction of the papacy in modern times is limited to ecclesiastical matters.
Loose-leaf binders in which two or more rings of metal or other durable material, attached to a back, pass through holes in the margins of individual leaves.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Lake Chad region of southern Chad.
Peruvian sacrificial ceremonial axes or knives.
Currently or actually existing, particularly, continuing to exist despite the passage of time and/or other circumstances.

Festival of dancing and masquerades held every two years in March by the Yoruba people of West Africa to promote the fertility and well-being of the community, and to honor important people and events in community history.
Flexible lamps, usually mounted and equipped with brackets, which allow for movement of the lamp, and for adjustment of the direction of light.
Those who follow the study of atmosphere and all of its varied phenomena.
A clear liquid broth derived by straining water in which meat or vegetables have been reduced by boiling. This then may be used as a base for soups.

Dutch marine fishing vessel used on the North Sea, particularly for herring and coastal fishing. These were flat-bottomed and blunt at both ends, and were fitted with sails. A bomschuit could be moved to and from the shoreline using oxen during low tide to account for the lack of good harbors in the Netherlands. In common use from ca. 1700 until 1918 and originated from the 'pink' type of ship.
Describes fishing watercraft that engage in the capture of marine life using nets.
Heraldic reference sources in which coats of arms are arranged in some methodical order by the designs they contain (the charges).
Alphabet of written Russian, Slavic, and some non-Slavic languages, originally based on the 38 Greek uncials and including later additions.
Feeders designed to dispense a blend of grain, cereals, and poultry feeds, free flowing in any desired proportion.
Bars that rest on the shoulders to allow drawing, plowing, or load carrying.
Straps, or pairs of straps, usually of leather, and attached to the bridle or bit of horses or other animals, used by riders to direct their locomotion.
People who have children, either biologically or by adoption.
Bells, gongs, buzzers, or sets of chimes that ring inside a building when their control, usually a button located adjacent to an entrance, is activated.
Men's garters, worn at the knee to hold up socks that are below-knee in length; the term is currently used in the United Kingdom and historically was used in North America.
Furniture sold in units which can be packed flat and easily assembled with a screwdriver.
Business enterprises involved in the buying and selling of art works on behalf of artists or otherwise engaged in art sales between two parties.

Enterprises or organizations, usually commercial, in which two or more parties jointly undertake the enterprise, but otherwise retain their distinct identities. It differs from "partnerships (companies)" in that a partnership generally involves an ongoing, long-term business relationship, whereas a joint venture is based on a single business transaction or project.
Companies controlled by another company that owns more than 50% of its voting shares.
Bill- or coin-operated machines that automatically play pre-recorded music, furnished with a variety of recordings for listener selection, housed in cabinets that are often colorfully illuminated.

Small removable cases that are part of pickup arms on phonographs, gramophones, or record players. Cartridges contain styluses and mechanisms for translating stylus motion into changing electrical voltage.

Simple bindings in sheep or calf, rarely lettered, commissioned in small quantities by booksellers from the 15th to the 18th century. Distinguished from uniform "edition bindings" produced wholesale, (often machine-made case bindings), applied in quantity to books expected to sell rapidly and in quantity, from the mid-18th century.
A term applied to any brick handmade with the aid of a brick stock, a wooden board on which a frame was placed to contain the clay; it is also used to describe the ordinary brick of a locality.
Blankets worn draped over the shoulders.
Hand held fans commonly used in churches.
Those who ride tricycles.
Taxonomic subclass of marine bivalve molluscs (saltwater clams).
Stiffened, generally rectangular pieces of cloth worn on military uniforms at the shoulder that bear the insignia of rank; worn primarily by United States military personnel.
Designates the dwelling, land, and outbuildings, if any, where a family lives.
Commercially developed real estate tracts commonly consisting of one- to four-unit dwellings.
The dwellings or buildings of Fourierist communities. The dwellings or buildings of Fourierist communities.
Belts that conducted electrical current to the body; advertised in the 19th and 20th centuries as curative instruments, though without scientific evidence.
Large spiked hooks, usually square-angled, that are driven into the rafter during roof thatching in order to secure courses of thatch as the thatcher works.
Ancient Greek folding stools without a back and having crossed legs.

Refers to a specific design of folding chair first created by Giancarlo Piretti in the 1960s, characterized as a folding chair that could be easily stacked and opened with one hand, composed of a steel or aluminum frame with a press-molded transparent plastic backrest and seat.

Refers to alloys that contain intermediate grain boundaries between fine-grained material and coarse-grain material. Grain boundaries restrict slip transmission to neighboring grains. A medium-grain material has a higher tensile strength and is harder than a coarse-grained material, and offers a practical balance between hardness and toughness.
Generally, the style and culture of the Rehamna ethnic group in Morocco. Specifically, the style of carpets produced by the Rehamna tribal weavers, noted for unique free-form designs.
Refers to the style of carpet manufactured in the Suiyuan province of Inner Mongolia in China. The style is characterized by all-over repeating patterns.

Refers to the process used to create tapestries, which are heavy, woven textiles characterized by ornamental or pictorial designs and used as wall hangings, curtains, upholstery, or to hang from windows or balconies. The process is performed on a tapestry loom and differs from cloth-weaving in that the weft travels only to the warp at the edge of a particular color or pattern in the design, rather traveling from edge to edge of the entire piece of fabric. Various techniques are used in mixing and overlaying colors to create shading and patterns. Details of the design are often painted or embroidered.
Style of carpets and other textiles produced in India as an imitation or interpretation of Persian Sarouk rug or carpet style.

Coffin-shaped planes, similar to smoothing planes except that they are round in both planes on the bottom, with a 2-inch single or double iron made in different sizes to fit the barrel it is cleaning and smoothing.
Tapestry-woven Navajo pictorial rugs depicting yeibichai, Navajo dancers impersonating the yei, or Holy People.
A size of card photograph measuring about 4 by 8 inches on a mount measuring 7 1/2 by 13 inches or larger.
Copying process employing silver halides in which both a positive and a negative copy are produced simultaneously.

Any member of a class of organic compounds that contain the carbonyl group (in which a carbon atom is doubly bonded to an oxygen atom), and in which the group is bonded to at least one hydrogen. With the exception of formaldehyde, a gas, aldehydes are acrid, volatile liquids. Their chief use is as chemical intermediates in polymer production for manufacture of solvents, dyes, resins, plasticizers, and pharmaceuticals.
Any of the group of metallic elements whose oxides are classed as rare earths. These include the lanthanide series, yttrium and scandium.

Simple chemical substances composed of only one type of atom and not able to be broken down, changed, or decomposed by ordinary physical or chemical means. They are the basic chemical constituents of compounds and ultimately of all tangible matter in the universe.
A hard or brittle external coating or covering on a material or object.
Study of scientific concepts and practice throughout human history in a global, social, and cultural context.

Hunting tools used by Alaska Native and Inuit communities. Consists of a carved wooden handle, usually in the shape of an animal's paw, terminating in several carved points imitating the appearance of claws. Often, claws of other animals such as seals are lashed to these points with fiber. Sometimes a bead or circular depression is placed in the middle of the paw shape, relating to pierced hand designs common in Alaska Native and Inuit material culture. Used to imitate the sounds of seals scratching the ice and attract the attention of seals when hunting.
Snares that catch the feet of animals in hunting or trapping, or in the context of warfare.
Implements having a flat elongated form with various modifications of shape and size, used for a variety of purposes, such as mixing, stirring, spreading, lifting, or examining.
Poles to which people, judicially condemned or not, are bound and then executed.
Shackles attached to the neck to prevent free motion.
Strips of woven material used for protecting, covering, or immobilizing injured parts of the body.

Metal frames on which multiple bobbins, or cylindrical spindles for winding yarn or thread, are fitted and wound parallel to one another. These frames often incorporate manual or automated yarn tension devices arranged between each bobbin fixing shaft, which help standardize the yarn's directional path and tension to overcome friction and facilitate subsequent yarn processing and warping.
Smooth shapes, often in the shape of an egg, over which fabrics are stretched for repair.
Small flat instruments used to create a kind of knotted lace from thread, which is wound around an element of the shuttle. These may be made of metal, wood, plastic, or other materials.
Tags or labels attached to luggage, containing an identification of the owner and his or her contact information.
Microscopic fossilized remains of organisms usually less than 2mm in size. Subject studied by micropaleontology.
Groups of items to be used for sewing and typically gathered in a box, basket, tin, or other container. May include thread, needles, thimbles, scissors, and other items.
The ceremonies or procedures used to dissolve a marriage contract between a husband and wife, either by process of law or otherwise through ritual or other agreement of the society.
Latino coming out celebrations and ceremonies held on the occasion of a girl's fifteenth birthday.
Boards that fit over the range of a stove to create a working or protective surface.
Rolled steel bars, commonly T-sections, designed to be laid end to end, usually in pairs and in parallel lines, to provide the running surface for certain transit vehicles.
Rings, historically made of ivory or bone, now usually of plastic, used by infants to chew on when teething.

Structural devices that are lightweight carriers into which a subcaliber projectile is centered to permit firing the projectile in a larger caliber weapon. The sabot fills the bore of the weapon from which the projectile is fired and is normally discarded a short distance from the muzzle.

Places that are imagined but do not exist in the real world, and have not existed in the past; typically derived from religious or literary traditions, including more modern video game materials. For places that are generally agreed to have existed, but for which the coordinates are unknown, use "lost settlements."

A space or area within the lived world of daily experience, perceived as distinct and unified, and possessing emotional, purposive, and social connotations along with physical features and characteristics. For the concept of purely physical position precisely definable in terms of geographic or astronomic measurement, or situation relative to geographic or astronomic features or elements of the built environment, use "location."

Visual signaling devices used primarily in military applications, and most particularly between ships in close range. These constitute a bright, focused lamp that incorporates the ability to create intermittent bursts of light. These were used to transmit coded messages without the use of radio to remain undetected by enemies. Named for its inventor A.C.W. Aldis.
In Indian architecture, an elephant-trunk; fluted design of praṇāla; water spout.
Knives of various forms and materials, designed and used in the skinning of an animal.

Trees symbolic of freedom or liberty, especially those in revolutions of 18th century Europe, modeled on the historic elm, Tree of Liberty, in Boston, Massachusetts dating to the time of the American Revolution.

The right or condition of vsible power or control over real or other property, defined by the intention to use or to hold it against others, typically as distinct from, or at least not synonymous with, lawful ownership.
In Indian architecture, a dais-like moulding supporting figure-bearing niches on the wall frieze; pedestal-like moulding in the lower section of a temple-wall.
Groups of marine mammals, partricularly a small herd or family group of whales or dolphins.
Birds that frequent bodies of water or inhabit the margin of lakes, rivers, seas, or other water. May be used to specifically refer to only larger swimming birds, such as ducks, geese, and swans.

Animals without a backbone or spinal column, including all soft-bodied animals without a rigid internal skeleton for the attachment of muscles, but often with a hard outer skeleton, comprising the great majority of all animals (such as insects, mollusks, and crustaceans). Apart from the absence of a vertebral column, invertebrates have little in common. The taxonomic term Invertebrata, formerly used in contrast to Vertebrata (still a valid subphylum name), is not used in modern classifications.
Badges designed to be affixed to clothing that carry text or images intended to promote goods, services, artists, brands, etc.

Small class of marine tunicates that are free-floating for their entire lifespan; they have an atrial aperture directed toward the rear of each zooid, and asexual buds that form from a ventral stolon. Sometimes classified as an order instead of a class.

Order of serpent-like amphibians, having a compact skull for burrowing with many compound bones, limbs or girdles, a persistent notochord, typically having naked skin (although some have scales), complete metamorphosis like frogs and toads, a compact skull, and  lidless tiny eyes nearly hidden by the skin. Dates from Early Jurassic to present, with six extant families and about 170 living species.
General term used to refer to many families and species of gastropod that have coiled shells in the adult stage.

Members of an order including around 1,400 species of arachnids having a pair of large nippers and a general resemblance to a miniature lobster; they inhabit tropical and warm temperate countries in both hemispheres.

Any of various telephonic devices enhanced with computer technology; specifically mobile phones capable of operating computer applications. These now usually feature touch-screen interfaces, cameras, and the ability to access the Internet.
One piece cupboards, usually with two drawers over one or two doors, used to store foodstuffs, particularly when used to store canned or preserved foods.
Genus containing one extant species of small Australian parrot.
General term referring to several species of carnivorous dinosaurs that walk on two legs, including Velociraptor, Deinonychus, Oviraptor, Dromaeosaurus, Gigantoraptor, among others.
Breed hound that is trained and used for hare hunting; the breed resembles the foxhound, but is smaller.

Breed of heavy draft horse characterized by a thick muscular neck, small head, powerful shoulders and quarters, short legs, and having a sorrel (chestnut) coloring with a lighter mane. It is an old breed descended from the Flemish 'great horse,' the medieval battle horse native to the Low Countries.

Extinct genus of the elephant family that lived from the Pliocene epoch (5 million years ago) into the Holocene (5,000 years ago) in Africa, Europe, Asia, and North America. They were characterized by having long, curved tusks a coat of long hair in colder climates.
Members of a genus containing two living species and one recently extinct species of semi-aquatic, carnivorous mammals of the weasel family.
Order of marine cephalopod mollusks characterized by having eight short arms and two usually longer tentacles; they differ from the related squid in having a calcified internal shell.
Recreation, sport, or mode of transportation that involves moving over snow by means of a pair of long, flat runners called skis, attached or bound to shoes or boots.
The action or practice of chasing, and usually killing, game or other wild animals, for sustenance, profit, or sport.
Ornamental clasps primarily for fastening a cope.
Any form of twill in which the direction of the diagonal lines is reversed over groups of picks, or over groups of ends.

A handball game with play similar to American handball and with scoring resembling tennis. It originates in the Northern Dutch province of Friesland. The game is played on a rectangular grass court by two teams with three players each. A hard leather ball is served from a box to a receiving zone. When the ball falls from a rally the spot is marked by a small wood block called a kaats, from which the game derives its name.
Describes the act of interlacing or tying linear material to form knots, which in succession can produce decorative patterns.
The processing of flax, hemp, cotton, or another fiber by separating the fine fibers from the impurities such as the seeds, straw, and woody stems.
Describes copying processes that employ light-reactive chemicals or electronics to reproduce graphic materials.
The technique of printing one photograph using images from more than one negative. For the technique of recording more than one image on a single sheet or frame of film, use "multiple exposure."
Compounds consisting of the chemical element lead.
Compounds created by combining silver with another material.
Refers to groups of archaeological artifacts found in association with each other, as from one level, activity area, or site, regardless of their material or type.
Costume artifacts that are related but discrete and are treated as a unit.
Matched sets of furniture, especially those comprising the basic furniture necessary for one room.

Parts or additional items, such as documents, separate from the main item but fastened to it in some way. The term is usually applied in the context of documents, but it may be used in other contexts as well. Examples are an appendix paperclipped to a main document, and a subsidiary electronic document linked to a primary document.
Collocates records for elements developed originally or primarily as portions of built works, including architecture, landscape architecture, engineering, and the like.
A glob of molten glass before it is tooled or fully shaped.
Parts and components of furniture.
System components that support systems of public works of countries.

Building systems or devices designed to move people, equipment, or goods through a building or complex; for networks of equipment designed to move similar items through and between settlements, use "transit systems;" for machinery designed for the continuous transport of material, use "conveyors."
Creating and manipulating data in machine-readable form by means of computers, including inputting, storage, conversion, editing, and printing.
Parts or components of security systems.
Ornaments which terminate the point of a spire, pinnacle, or other vertical member; found on furniture as well as architecture.

Series of spoken word digital audio files that a user can download to a personal device for easy listening. These are usually arranged in chronological or thematic groups, the entire collection being the series. For subgroups of podcasts within the series, use "podcast seasons".
Houses with historical importance locally, regionally, or internationally that have been restored and opened to the public as museums.
Horticultural facilities where trees, shrubs, and plants are grown for sale and transplanting elsewhere or for use as stocks for budding or grafting.

Sheer, crisp fabric made with a loose plain weave; usually made from silk or synthetics such as rayon, nylon, acrylic or polyester. It is fine to leightweight, strong, stable, and durable. It is distinct from organdy, which is made from cotton.
A wool textile that is thick, heavy, and waterproof; used especially for outerwear.
Buildings that house and display horse-drawn carriages and related objects or documents.

Refers to the art and architecture associated with the Islamic dynasty of this name that ruled in Morocco from 789 to 985; it was the first Islamic dynasty to establish an independent state in Morocco and played an important role in making Morocco an Islamic country. Islamic urban culture began to make its appearance in Morocco during the Idrisid period. Idris I, a descendant of Muhammad, founded the dynasty as well as the city of Fès. Fès became the capital during the reign of his son, Idris II, and flourished as a trade, religious and intellectual center under Idris II's patronage. The Idrisids were responsible for the layout of the old city center and the division of the city into two distinct areas (the Kairouanis and the Andalusians) separated by the River Fas. Unfortunately, physical remains from the period are limited. The Idrisids built what is now the Qarawiyyin Mosque in Fès but only its core preserves Idrisid elements. The tomb of Idris I at Moulay Idris near Volubilis (made the capital of Idris I after 788) and that of Idris II in Fès are considered the holiest shrines in Morocco; both tombs were completely rebuilt in the 18th century.

Refers to the art and culture associated with the Islamic Berber dynasty of this name that ruled in Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia) from 909 to 972 and in Egypt from 969 to 1171. The Fatimids, of the Shi'a sect, traced their ancestry back to Fatima, the daughter of Muhammad. The Fatimids had many rivals to contend with as well as the challenge of the Crusaders. Fatimid art is noteworthy for its internationalism: it bridges the east and west of the Islamic world and it was open to the Hellenic heritage of the Mediterranean and to some ideas from Christian powers to the north. Although Fatimid artists continued to use materials and techniques developed by the Tulunids, the abstraction favored by the Tulunids was replaced by an interest in exploring the tradition of figurative representation inherited from Iraq. Painting, book illustration, wood and ivory carving, and glass, ceramic and textile design bear figurative decoration unparalleled in contemporary Islamic art. An interest in naturalism is also evident. The iconography of Fatimid art is often indebted to Abbasid court art. Just as figural traditions were being developed, so were designs based on infinite systems of linear pattern; this form of ornamentation became one of the most successful forms of abstract Islamic art. Figural art was inappropriate for religious buildings, which were instead decorated with a vigorous new style of stone carving typically featuring elegant inscriptions in a distinctive form of kufic script elaborated with foliate and floral elements. A conch shell motif known from late antiquity was popular with the Fatimids, as seen on the façade of the mosque of al-Akmar. Nothing has survived of the two Fatimid palaces that stood in the center of Cairo but accounts of them attest to their magnificence.

Refers to the style and period associated with the reign of the Islamic dynasty that began to rule in Anatolia in 1281 until the promulgation of the Constitution of the Turkish Republic in 1924. Under the support of Ottoman sultans, a distinct architectural style developed that combined the Islamic traditions of Anatolia, Iran, and Syria with those of the Classical world and Byzantium. The result was a rationalist approach that favored spatial unity and clarity, the most important structure being the kulliye, a building complex combining religious, educational and charitable buildings. The main architectural theme of this complex was the domed square unit and combinations of varying spatial and architectonic expressions. The mosque, and in some cases the mosque-convent, was the crowning achievement. Under the conquest of Constantinople and the establishment of new administrative palaces across the empire, the relationship between Ottoman patrons and the artist became centralized. A corps of court architects employed architects of different ranks, and controlled all building activity throughout the empire. A community of craftsman brought together societies of artists and craftsman, forming the imperial design studio where illuminated manuscripts, tiles, woodwork, carved stone, jade, and metal objects, along with carpets and textiles were produced. These works typically chronicled the important events of a sultan's rule. During the 18th and 19th century, Ottoman art was increasingly westernized in style, often incorporating elements of European Baroque style.

Style of textiles, particularly village floor coverings, that are handwoven in the vicinity of Bergama, western Turkey, or brought there for market from the interior of the country. Although most Bergama carpets date from the 19th and 20th centuries, rare examples survive from the 17th century. They are characterized by bold, highly varied patterns often in red, blue, and white. Typical designs include rows of panels or central medallion designs, preserving the fashions of much earlier centuries. The format of Bergama carpets is usually more nearly square than other Turkish types, and the few known prayer rugs tend to be unusually small. The red dye used in this area sometimes causes the pile to erode and look as if it had been cut in relief.

term: South Persian textile styles after the Mongols
definition: Textile styles after the Mongols belonging to South Persian cultures.
Style of textiles, primarily silk, created since Sasanian times in and around the city of Yazd, Iran.

Generally, the style and culture of a Turkic-speaking people living around Shiraz in Persia. Specifically, a style of carpets handwoven by the Qashqa'i people, who have the reputation of making the best rugs from the Shiraz district of Iran. The coloring of the carpets employs rich blues and reds, with limited use of golden yellow. Usually the designs are geometric, sometimes with a row of three diamond medallions against a background replete with tiny forms of all kinds, including stylized animals and birds. The designs are often based on Persian urban sources. The carpets are asymmetrically knotted on an all-wool foundation.

Style of textiles, particularly floor coverings, from the Farahan district, northeast of Arak in western Iran, produced in the 19th or early 20th century. Ferahan rugs are prized for sturdy construction and design, most having a dark blue ground showing an endless repeat of the herati design, in which a diamond lattice peeps through a tangle of blossoms and leaves.

term: Anatolian Islamic textile styles after Manzikert
definition: Textile styles after Manzikert belonging to Anatolian Islamic cultures.

Style, particularly of carpets, from the area around the city, Kermān, in southern Iran. Sophisticated carpets with elaborate, organized designs have been woven in Kermān since the 16th century. The best known Kirman carpets include a wide variety of 16th- and 17th-century vase carpets, rugs with rows of shrubs, arabesque carpets, fine garden carpets, and a group of medallion carpets with animals. All have asymmetrical knotting on cotton warps, with stiff, heavy woollen wefts pulled straight, and silk or cotton wefts between left relatively slack. The result is a double-warped carpet, the warps of one level lying almost directly behind adjacent warps. The color schemes of older carpets are among the richest and most varied found in Persian carpets. Vase carpets apparently continued to be made in the 18th century; a revival of carpet weaving came about in the late 19th century, with a variety of successive styles and fashions, including copies of French carpet styles, French paintings, architectural scenes with mosques and minarets, and symbolic and personage rugs similar to those made at Kashan and Tabriz. Cream shades are often used for the ground in modern carpets; the foundation is now all cotton, but the knotting is still asymmetrical.
Painting styles belonging to Safavid cultures.
Describes groupings of cloth coverings draped on the body that are stylistically Spanish-American.

Wearing blankets manufactured by Navajo weavers and frequently traded with Plains Native North Americans and to a lesser extent Euro-American settlers. Defined by alternating horizontal bands of indigo, white, red, and black wool. The earliest first phase chief's blanket dates from 1750; blankets continued to be produced in this style until the 1860s. Not associated with rank; "chief blanket" refers to their value assigned by Navajo and Plains communities.
Parts or components of watercraft.
Textile styles belonging to South Caucasian cultures.

Style of textile, particularly carpets, made in the city of Derbent, Dagestan, in southwestern Russia. Carpets are typically characterized by the use of fine-spun yarn and short pile, with the two wefts between each row of knots being barely visible on the back of the carpet. Many, often complementary, colors are used, with blue being the most common. Motifs are quasi-representational and of graduated sizes, and patterns are intricate.
Style of textile, particularly carpets, from the area of Moghan, now in Iran.
Painting styles belonging to East Turkestani cultures.
Period of the dynasty that ruled the province of Diyarbakir in northern Iraq (now Turkey) 1098-1232, and again 1104-1408.

Style of handwoven floor covering that was once marketed through the ancient city of Samarkand in Uzbekistan, but is actually produced by Kyrgyz or Uzbek tribeswomen or in the towns of Khotan (Hotan), Kashgar, and Yarkand in Xinjiang, China. Except for their coloring, the general effect of these rugs is more Chinese than Middle Eastern.

Style and culture of a people originally of Iranian stock, closely related to the Scythians. The Sarmatians migrated from Central Asia to the Ural Mountains between the 6th and 4th century BCE and eventually settled in most of southern European Russia and the eastern Balkans.
Players of the lutelike chordophone known as a fiddle, especially those who do so for hire in the context of live entertainment.

Political entities of any size that are dependent upon another country or power. These political units are generally regarded as territories that are fully or partially subject to the other state. Examples of dependent political entities are American Samoa and Guam, which are dependent on the United States, and Bermuda and the Virgin Islands, which are dependent on the United Kingdom.
Ceremonial certificates that mark an event such as a birth, but that are not considered official documents.
Crosses with short handles that are held in the hand, used in Christian rituals or devotions; they may be used in religious processions but are smaller than processional crosses.
Zoological, botanical, or mineralogical samples chosen for scientific study or display.
Identifying numbers assigned to a telephone or group of telephones; the numbers are dialled in order to make a connection to telephonic devices.
The physical components of a computer system or device as opposed to the software required for its operation.

Devices that house a fixed (non-removable) hard disk for storage and retrieval of digital computer data. To refer to the disks themselves, use "hard disks," to generally refer to mechanisms that use magnetic media for storage on disks, either fixed or removable, use "disk drives."
Relatively small rods used as pointers, usually handheld, for following the words or text while reading.
Devices used to prevent wood panels from warping and cracking, consisting of a system of wooden ribs attached to the back of the panel.

Those whose occupation or profession it is to engage in a game played indoors or out of doors with a large inflated ball, which is thrown from player to player, the object being to score by casting it into one's opponents' goal, a basket fixed ten feet above the ground at each end of the field of play.

Place settings or other combinations of cups, saucers, and plates that were given as a traditional gift on the occasion of a person's first solemn communion, which was a rite of passage among young adults in some Christian denominations. The items are typically made of porcelain or silver. The dishes are distinguished by decoration or text commemorating the event.
Bags or similar containers made typically of cloth, leather, or rubber stuffed with a resilient material and used to give support or ease to the body while sitting, reclining, or kneeling.
Japanese floor cushions for sitting or kneeling; relatively large, flat throw pillows. The Japanese word zabuton means "sitting mat."
Cushioned headrests for the deceased in a coffin.
Areas of jurisdiction of a deacon.

General designation for any autonomous place within the sphere of a larger adminisrative entity. Specifically, the term is given to certain divisions within a nation that have a degree of independence, administer their own affairs, or are otherwise self-governing to some degree. In this context, the precise definition of "autonomous area" varies from nation to nation, and is assigned to the area by the nation rather than being assigned by an outside body. Examples of autonomous areas in this sense are in Russia.
In Greek and Roman history, the title of a military commander of 1000 men.
Stewards of British manors, whose responsibilities include the day-to-day supervision of tenants, administration of rents, leases, and agreements, and the maintenance of the buildings.
Fine black powder composed of antimony used as a cosmetic to darken eyelids and eyebrows.
Adjusting a musical instrument or other sound device to the correct or desired standard of pitch, or an audio signal receiver to the frequency of the desired signal.
Goggles of various form designed for the use of pilots or flight crews, usually in a military context.
Artifacts, often textiles, that are hung on walls, especially for protection, warmth or embellishment.

People in medieval Germany and later who were appointed as the judicial and military representatives of the king in a burg, which was a fortified town. Eventually the title became hereditary and was associated with not only the burg but also the surrounding domain.
Continental European noblewomen holding a countship, English noblewomen holding an earldom, or the wives or widows of counts and earls. They rank after duchesses and marchionesses.
Mechanical devices of various form designed for rolling cigarettes in bulk or individually.
Thin lenses of glass or plastic which fit over the cornea and correct vision defects.
The process of shaping glass, making facets, grooves, and depressions, by grinding using rotating disks of various materials, sizes, and shapes and a stream of water with an abrasive.

Refers to female sovereigns of empires, which are political units that comprise a number of territories or nations and are ruled by a single supreme authority. The term may also refer to the wives and widows of emperors.
Ecclesiastical officials of the Roman Catholic Church who constitute the Pope's council, or the Sacred College, and who retain the right of electing future popes.

Ornamental containers of various designs, usually relatively squat, for holding or growing plants or flowers. For containers that are not particularly ornamental, use "flowerpots." For ornamental containers for holding or concealing a flowerpot, use "cachepots." .For vase-shaped containers for cut flowers, use "flower vases."

Generally refers to those belonging to an army, whether that of a sovereign state, a faction or division within a sovereign state, or of an individual leader. Specifically refers to military personnel of enlisted rank, as distinguished from commissioned officers. For those trained for or engaged in the physical combat of warfare and sanctioned in that function by the society or group for which they fight, irrespective of actual membership in an army, see "warriors."
A class of probabilistic, iterative, and generative models that turn noise into a representative data sample used by AI to create high-quality images.

A computational imaging technique that creates a virtual three-dimensional digital surrogate of a subject that can be interactively relit from any direction. An RTI file is a composite of multiple images of a subject photographed from a fixed position for which a light source has been repositioned at a constant radius from the subject, thus creating a hemisphere of positions.
Woven trappings covering the chest of a camel during Turkoman marriage rituals.
Motif comprising a heavy-armed cross with a lighter-armed X-shape over it (that is, an eight-armed figure), with the heavier arms typically terminating in a ram's horn motif.

Rigs generally characterized by a single mast, a triangular sail whose forward edge is sharply raked aft and is attached to a right spar or yard which in turn is attached to the mast, and a boom that extends forward of the mast.
Mode of dress for a fashionable women in the 19th and 20th centuries; dinner dress is less formal than evening wear, ensembles often include sleeves, or open decolletage.
Objects used to warm a bed. Traditionally refers to a covered pan with an extended handle filled with hot coals.
Marking an object with a postal or other mark to waive the charge for, or otherwise facilitate, its passage.
Female security guards or soldiers  of the guards or household guards.
Professional or paid drivers of motor vehicles such as automobiles or limousines.
Social science concepts related to law.
Advertising in publications such as magazines or newspapers.

Construction of digital, virtual objects or structures based on historic, archaeological, or other similar evidence. Includes manipulation via software of digital copies of damaged objects to effect a virtual restoration.
A commercial artist who renders lettering.
Short, cylindrical brushes, with long, soft bristles, used to lather the face before shaving.
Towels for drying dishes.

Refers to any Christian clergy officially attached to a household or institution. It includes, for example, the clergy for the house of a sovereign or lord, for a castle, ship, garrison, regiment, or any group in an army or navy, for a college, school, workhouse, prison, cemetery, legislative chamber, or other public institution. The term may also be used in its original sense, in which case it refers to the priest or other clergy assigned to or in charge of services in a chapel.
Learned teachers of the religious law and doctrines of Islam.
Tools and other equipment used to prepare food.
Those who study or practice the art that assumes and attempts to interpret and foretell the influence of the stars, moon, and planets upon human affairs.
Refers to those who organize, manage, and usually own a business entreprise, assuming the risks of profit or loss.
People tasked with gauging measures and weights, an exciseman who inspects dutiable bulk goods. The function was established in the Middle Ages and existed until the beginning of the 19th century.
Rodlike buttons of wood or other material, attached to cord, leather, or chain loops and designed to be passed through another loop as a fastener on a garment.
Ties or laces, as of leather or ribbon, finished with metal tabs or aglets at the ends. Originally used to fasten together parts of costume; later, tied in bows and used for trimming.
Hangers of various designs used for the storage of neckties.
To abuse or use wrongly someone or something.
The action of cutting open a person's chest, a ritual killing.
The work or industry of capturing, killing, and rendering seals.
Collocates descriptors for vessels used to transport troops or horses to overseas locations.
Seagoing vessels that are specially built and equipped to carry out hydrographic and other nautical surveys such as observation of currents and winds in coastal waters and on the high seas.

Sailing warships carrying one or more heavy mortars or howitzers mounted on specially constructed platforms or in heavily reinforced pits; often ketch-rigged to give mortars a clearer field of fire forward and used in bombarding coastal towns or fortresses.
Vessels that provide assistance or relief during emergency situations.

Lifesaving boats designed for launching and beaching through the surf, and generally double-ended, with marked sheer, high ends, an outboard rudder, and sometimes a sailing rig; early models were rowed, later ones had auxiliary power.
Small self-propelled boats fitted with tanks used in harbors for supplying fresh water to vessels and having pumps and hoses for discharging their cargo.
Small open boats carried on or towed by larger watercraft as lifeboats, tenders, or workboats; may be rowed, sailed, or driven by outboard motors.
Vessels constructed for travel or transport below the water's surface.

Belgian barges with a gaff rig, used as market ships and primarily intended for navigation on canals. The largest types are built with a helm port transom. The mast is rigged with a long gaff that carries the gaff sail.
Relatively small simple boats with flat, rockered, keel-less bottoms, high bows, and flaring clinker or plywood sides, widely used by fishermen.
Small Chesapeake Bay sailing craft built up from three to five logs bolted together and carved to shape.

Specifically used for single-seat native arctic North American canoes with watertight skin covers over a light wooden framework propelled by a double-bladed paddle, and generally for small boats resembling these made commercially of a variety of materials and used in sports. For similar North American skin boats but larger and seating more than one person, use "umiaks."
Small watercraft of conventional, not elongated, form, propelled by oars; may be used for work or recreation.
Ancient warships propelled by oarsmen grouped somehow into units of four on at least two levels; exact arrangement of oarsmen unknown.
Ships propelled by steam engines.

A wide variety of lateen-rigged watercraft used for trading along the East African, Arabian, and Indian coasts; generally having long raking bows and fuller sterns. This is a European term derived from the Swahili and is not used by most of the people who sail such vessels.

Catboats generally characterized by a deep keel, raked stem and transom, and loose-footed gaff sails; sometimes with bowsprit and jib and usually 20 to 24 feet long; originally built around the point at Newport, Rhode Island.

Two-masted vessels, square-rigged on both masts, with the mainmast forward of and taller than the mizzen; in use between the late 17th and early 19th centuries. For similar two-masted vessels, but with fore-and-aft rigs and in use since the mid-19th century, use "ketches (fore-and-aft-rigged vessels)."
Vessels of three or more masts, square-rigged on all masts.

Rugs woven within a tribe or group, typically woven by nomadic or pastoral people for their personal use rather than for commercial purposes. They are characterized by the use of traditional geometric motifs, a lower knot count than the tightly woven rugs produced in urban centers, and often use of a wool foundation with plant based dyes and hand-spun wool thread; they were originally woven on wooden looms that could be dismantled for traveling and reassembled.
Ink-soaked pads used for applying ink; examples include a pad in a shallow box used for inking a rubber stamp or taking fingerprints, as parts of typewriters, or automatic numbering machines.
Manually-powered cinematic apparatuses developed in France by the Lumière brothers at the end of the 19th century, which functioned as motion picture cameras, film projectors, and developers.
Projector which projects an image onto a vertical screen by passing light through a transparency that is positioned horizontally, then through lenses positioned above the transparency.
Devices for conveying bales of hay or other bales into a loft or barn.
Large Tibetan rugs that were woven on commission and used for a variety of purposes.
Knotted pile weavings that hung around the door of a Turkoman tent; also may have served as an animal trapping for Turkoman marriage rituals.

Kazak rugs named after the historical province Loru Pambak, a mountainous region of Armenia that borders Georgia in the western Caucasus. Since ca. 1800, the rugs have been largely produced by Armenians living in this area, although earlier examples may have originated with the Persian Lori or Azeri. The style is distinguished by a central medallion containing a rough cross-shape in which two opposing arms are square with zigzag terminations, and the other two arms are stylized tulips.
A name of convenience for a group of Persian rugs probably woven in Kirman at the beginning of the 17th century; motifs commonly include medallions, real and mythical animals, or human figures.
A name of convenience for rugs with a specific, endless repeat pattern of hooked octagons.
Rugs woven in India with Persian design motifs.
Describes tools used for preparing a printing plate, including engraving, cleaning, and inking.

Historically, a collection of type consisting of all letters, numerals, punctuation marks, and other symbols belonging to a single design and point size, and not including other sets of characters such as the bold type of the same design family. In photocomposition and desktop publishing, a font is the set of characters and other symbols of one style available as a unit, such as through a strip of film or a program module.

Engraving tools powered by electricity, in contrast to engraving done by a hand-held burin. In the field of art, such  tools are typically designed for and used for printmaking or metalworking; however, similar tools are used in other disciplines, such as dentistry, medicine, and archaeology.
Describes tools that directly cause or facilitate the transfer of an image, such as to pull pigment through a screen or to form an impression.
The mesh that is stretched over a frame for screen printing.
The flat component of a platen press that brings the paper to the inked surface and presses them together.
Composing machines that project images of type characters onto photosensitive film or paper, producing camera ready copy from which a printing plate is made.
Any of various railroad cars used for inspecting track and right of way.
Railroad vehicles carrying passengers or hauled on passenger trains.
In Indian architecture, a pillar base; pot motif on jagatī.
Parts or components of electronic images.
Feet formed by cutting sections from sideboards.
Handles or pulls of various shapes intended for doors on public spaces. These often have a large surface area to grasp.
Knobs that attach to doors, but that do not turn and have no working parts. Often used on closet doors or double doors.

Small rugs of approximately 3 by 5 feet, often with a design that incorporates some depiction of a mihrab; originally intended for Islamic prayer, although some motifs and inscriptions indicate not all were made for this purpose.

Ushak rugs with an oval medallion in the central field and a composite starlike medallion of 16 points which appears at the sides of the carpet. Both types of medallions are filled with compositions of arabesques and plant ornaments, with finials projecting from the ends or sides. The ground is covered with a pattern of stems, leaves, and flowers.

Artifacts created or produced in former periods. The term was traditionally applied primarily to works of fine or decorative art and furnishings, but is currently employed for any type of man-made object of a past era. U.S. customs laws define antiques as artifacts whose date of initial purchase was at least 100 years before the present. In common usage with respect to automobiles, the term includes those at least 25 years old.

Refers to Buddhist, particularly Tibetan, paintings portraying the endless process of birth, death, and rebirth (samsara) as a wheel. The many pictures on the wheel represent the conditions of samsara as well as the moral and mental factors that cause an individual to remain within samsara. The wheel is clutched by a demon monster, symbolizing death and impermanence. Bhavacakras are usually found on tankas or painted in the doorways of Tibetan temples. The earliest surviving example is a 6th-century fresco at Ajanta. The drawing of the bhavacakra was originally developed, supposedly by the Buddha himself, as a pedagogic device that could be used to teach the non-literate about Buddhist truths. The term, which is Sanskrit, translates to the 'wheel of existence.'
Refers generally to objects associated with or used in the rituals of public worship, especially of the Christian religion.

Use broadly for objects associated with or used in funerary practices of any culture. Sometimes defined more narrowly as only those placed with individual human remains either at the time of death or later as part of a death rite or ceremony.
Small mallets with heads of malleable iron.

Instruments, usually of metal attached to an absorbent material, for the sprinkling of holy water. In the Western church, the aspergillum is composed of a handle surmounted by a perforated ball, sponge, or brush-like end to hold water. Some have sponges or internal reservoirs that dispense holy water when shaken, while others must periodically be dipped in "aspersoriums (vessels)." The tool was originally made of branches of hyssop, palm, or boxwood, wisps of straw, or the tail of a fox (in Old French the fox was called "goupil"). By the 13th century the aspergillum assumed the modern Western form of a handle surmounted by a rose-shape covered with bristles; the handles of the sprinklers came to be very richly ornamented. In the Greek Orthodox Church the aspergillum is a standing vessel with a tapering lid perforated with holes for sprinkling; in the Russian Orthodox Church, it is a whisk made of cloth, hair, or sprigs of basil. The tool was derived from ancient sources, where branches were used to sprinkle water, blood, or another liquid in rituals. Such tools were used in ancient Rome, the Middle East, ancient Norse rituals, and elsewhere.
As an artistic concept, strokes or marks, long in proportion to breadth, traced upon a surface or implied through imaginary joining of points in a composition.

Black-figure kylikes of type A, generally of the 6th century BCE, decorated on the outside with a pair of large eyes on each side, often with figures painted between the eyes and sometimes under the handles as well. On some rare eye cups, moldmade male genitals substitue for the wheelmade foot.
A type of kylix characterized by one continuous curve from lip to foot and a broad and relatively shallow bowl. It was the most common red-figured cup, supplanting eye cups by about 500 BCE.

Incendiary substance developed for military purposes in 1943, consisting of gasoline thickened by a mixture of aluminum naphthenate and aluminum palmate to form a gel, used particularly in flamethrowers and incendiary bombs.
Those who play the piano.
Locomotives whose motive power source is electricity generated on board or obtained via overhead wires or a third rail.
Devices that place punch cards into pockets based on the hole patterns punched into the cards.
Weft-faced compound tabby weave with a plain weave and an added weft system.
In polymer science, refers to the molecular deterioration of polymers caused by overheating.
Refers to a type of decomposition of timber by fungi.

In casting, interfaces where two streams of metal come together in a mold but do not fuse properly, often due to premature cooling of the metal in the mold. A cold shut may also describe a hole or void in a cast caused by premature cooling. The cooled metal edges will be rounded in profile.
Physics concepts related to the function of machinery.
Voltage gradient at which a particular type of ion or other particle passes equally easily in either direction across a cell membrane.
Unavoidable dangers or risks, or things causing such dangers or risks, though often foreseeable.
Refers to various processes involving the introduction of one or more acetyl groups into a compound by means of a chemical reaction.
Describes processes that transform the color of an object.
Available supplies or means of producing energy, whether natural, such as fossil fuels or hydro-electric power, or manmade, such as nuclear fuel.

The process or condition of growing in bulk or size, as for example by inflation or accumulation of fluids. Refers also for the distended, protuberant, or thickened portion of something, such as the entasis of a column, the thickened portion of a gunstock, or the extra thickness on the back of the text block of a book caused by the sewing thread or extreme guarding.

The swelling of clay objects during firing as gases are released in the vitrification process; sometimes caused by overfiring and occurs either generally or in small areas; generally considered a defect in pottery but sometimes desirable in nonbearing bricks for construction.

Includes the process of binding or tying, usually by lapping one unit over another, as various masonry units, and holding or adhering together firmly by means of a binder or bond, as the fibers in paper.
Decorative technique for the application of precious materials like gold to the surfaces of objects, or the application of marble or other materials to the surfaces of built works.
Drilling or cutting out material left between adjacent holes in a row of closely spaced drill holes; process used especially in mining and quarrying.

The process of enhancing or modifying the grain on a piece of leather by folding it grain side to grain side and working the fold across the leather back and forth either by hand with a board or  by means of a boarding machine.
Producing raised letters or designs on a surface, typically by means of stamping or molding.
Process of adding heat in order to raise the temperature.
Decorative border of contrasting types of wood cut at varying angles to the grain, such as for finishing the edges and rims of furniture.
Flat artists' brushes with rounded corners, usually made of bristle.
Those who practice the laying out or cultivating an area of plants, either professionally or as a hobby.
Those who occupy or use land, buildings, or any other premises owned by another in consideration of some condition, typically the payment of rent.
The raised surface produced by supplementary warp or weft projecting from the ground of a woven textile. For the surface produced by raising the fibers on the face of the textile, use "nap."
Tufted yarn made by cross weaving a textile with warp ends in groups, then cutting it into narrow strips along the length between the groups.
Yarn in which the twist of its component fibers follows the direction of the central bar of the letter Z.

Term used in ancient times for a fiber (and by extension, fabric) highly prized for its fineness, which was once the basis of a small textile manufacturing industry centered around the Italian Mediterranean. 'Byssus' was used to describe a variety of substances, leading to confusion and controversy over its proper denotation. Some scholars view byssus as simply a generic term covering a host of fiber proteins and products manufactured from them; others insist that the term specifically describes shellfish derived 'sea-silk'. Usage extends to both.

Textile having the characteristic that it can be stretched without permanent alteration of size or shape. Examples include yardage or strips of textile material comprising threads or thin strips of rubber or other another elastic substance covered by a woven material.

Textile material produced for use in covering book bindings, typically woven cotton or linen subjected to processes to stiffen, color, and pattern it and enhance its durability, such as bleaching, dying, sizing, impregnating, glazing, and embossing.
Textile used for bed sheets, pillowcases, and similar items, woven by the yard.
Heavyweight plain- or twill-weave cloth of worsted, cotton, wool, or other fibers, singly or in combination, first made in Bedford, England, characterized by heavy, warpwise cords or stripes.

Needle lace produced in Brussels since the 15th century. It was originally inspired by Spanish and Venetian lace. It is characterized by a fine flax thread produced in Brabant, and a simple open buttonhole background, generally without bars or brides, upon which was worked a thick cordonnet and other raised work in floral or other designs.
Textile produced by brocading, typically richly figured and incorporating metal thread, often of silk.

Originally an Indian patterned textile, usually cotton or linen, painted and/or printed in multiple stages of dyeing, mordanting, and resist-dyeing. Later imitated with industrial processes, usually cotton or linen, dyed in a number of colors and usually glazed.

Refers to large sheets of heavy linen or another fabric on which a design has been painted. They were originally used for tapestry cartoons in sixteenth-century France, and then hung as though they were tapestries. A large collection survives at Reims. The term also refers to  eighteenth-century French cloth that is inspired by these painted designs, but created by printing with copperplate engravings. It may also refer to any fabric done in the style of 18th-century copperplate designs.
Fitting of upholstery foundations with springs.
The process of raising fibers on the surface of a textile to give a pilelike surface, especially for softness, warmth, and increased absorbency.

States that are allied with another, usually larger power by a Compact of Free Association or other agreement, by which the states retain international sovereignty and control over their territory but receive benefits, such as protection or economic cooperation. An example is the Marshall Islands, associated with the nation, the United States.
Administrative sections of larger nations, territories, or other districts as defined for political purposes.
States that are recognized in law, but who in reality (de facto) have little or no control over their territory.

Refers to large estates or sizable sections of a larger territory, which itself is typically ruled by a sovereign. A barony is held by a baron and was often originally awarded for military or other service to the monarch, and thereafter was generally handed down from father to son.

Fast ocean-going sailing ships generally characterized by sharply raked stern, a long and low hull with the draft deeper aft than forward, an inclined, overhanging counter stern, and a large spread of canvas; developed in the mid-19th century as cargo vessels, but their speed lent the vessels to other uses; typically having three masts and square rigs.
Refers to watercraft with a prominent central hull and flanking subsidiary hulls.
Flat-bottomed boats with a straight falling stern and a short forecastle. These are known to be used as fishing vessels on the Schelde River from the thirteenth to the 19th century.

Northern European seagoing ships of the 16th through 18th century, usually Dutch built and less than 700 tons burden, having a long, narrow hull with full ends, considerable tumblehome, ship rig, and a false transom or lute stern over a full sternpost.
Small, flat-bottomed boats with shallow draft and square ends propelled by poling along shallow rivers and streams.

Any small pleasure or service watercraft, where the foredeck is raised to be flush with the top of the cabin in a conventional trunk cabin type. The flush deck is carried across the full width of the boat to the stem.
Watercraft, often wide flat-bottomed boats, outfitted as floating dwellings and not normally designed for rough-water use.
Vessels engaged in some aspect of whaling.

Single-masted sailing vessels built with deadrise construction, decked, with a cabin and generally carrying a triangular mainsail and jib, set on a sharply raking mast; a few two-masted, or three-sail examples were built; introduced onto the Chesapeake Bay in the mid-19th century and usually used for oyster dredging.
Vessels rigged for longlining, a mid-20th-century fishing technique, characterized by one or more winches or drums to handle the lines, often several miles long.
Boats used in fishing with seines, nets hung vertically in the water and having floats on their upper edges and sinkers on their lower edges.
Waterfowling boats built to hide gunners inside and able to float partially submerged.
Small, engine-powered ocean-going vessels used to hunt and kill whales; generally used in conjunction with whale-oil factory ships.

Sail- or power-driven watercraft of various kinds, usually light and used for racing or for recreation. In early use, yachts were fast and often used for the conveyance of royal or other important persons; in modern use, recreational yachts are luxury vessels.
High-speed planing powerboats, often with accommodations, capable of going offshore and specially equipped for rod and reel sport fishing.

Double-ended, lapstrake rowing boats, using a single thole pin and oar with hole to fit over it, ranging in length from 16 to 23 feet, originating in the mid-19th century on the St. Lawrence River; larger examples may have sailing rigs, and are sailed without rudders.
Oceangoing passenger ships.
Printed matter or handbills that promote candidates for public office, platforms, referendums, or other campaigns to potential voters.
Detachable reinforcing pieces of plate armor shaped to cover the bent left elbow. They served as double pieces for tilt armor.
Electon scanning microscopy using a focused beam.
Mechanisms in breechloading firearms in which a sliding handgrip below the barrel is pulled back to open the breech and extract the case, and pushed forward to reload.
Messages sent by telegraph.
Flat beveled or triangular straightedges, usually of wood or plastic, graduated in multiples of ten parts per inch allowing drawings to be drawn or measured to scale in decimal values.
Rules for measuring the height of capital letters for copy fitting and layout, often of a transparent material and usually graduated in points, picas, and inches or centimeters.
Measuring devices, usually in the form of flat sticks, 3 to 6 feet long, bearing various scales and tables for estimating the amount of sawn timber to be obtained from unsawn logs.
Measuring devices combining rulers with calipers having one jaw fixed to or integral with a graduated straight bar on which the other jaw slides.
Light meters that measure in metric units called lux the intensity of visible light falling on surfaces.

A surface analysis technique which measures the elastically scattered ion created when a primary ion beam is directed at the sample surface. The kinetic energy of the reflected primary ion depends on the mass of the surface atom involved in scattering, thus revealing information about the sample surface.
Ornaments worn in hair, often decorated with varied materials or shaped in different forms. Attached by two grips.
Pointers or other indicators that mark off the seconds on clocks or watches.
Athletic shoes specifically designed for playing tennis.
Mirrors in which the center is closer to the object than the edges and that reflect reduced images.
Full-length adjustable mirrors suspended on four-legged frames.
Light frames, usually wood, covered with a thin material to be flown in the wind at the end of a long string; known from at least the 3rd century BCE in China.

Sets of articles used for the eucharist or distribution of communion, including at minimum a chalice or communion cup and a paten. For sets smaller in scale than those used in a church, use the narrower term "portable communion sets."
Mechanical or electronic equipment used to create sudden, brief, and bright illumination for use in photography in situations where there is insufficient illumination or to freeze action.

Use to describe things produced by human action, as opposed to by natural causes, usually those things intended to substitute for their natural counterparts. For things produced by human action but not substituting for natural counterparts, use "man-made." For things produced specifically by synthesis, use "synthetic."
Powered by electricity, operating by means of electricity.
Use to describe a material having a structure composed of cells, whether biological cells, as in wood, or open cavities otherwise generated, as in some bricks.
The measure or distance of the extent across a surface. For the length of a straight horizontal line extending from one side to the other of a form, prefer "width," although usage overlaps.
Refers to series of visual works depicting events and unified by a common topic, not necessarily a sequence in a single story line.
Characteristics of the layout of buildings.
Measurement for describing the resolution of a printed image,  referring to the number of dots that can be printed per linear inch on a support.
Small dishes in which food can be baked and served.
Large flat pans on which cookies are baked.
Small spoons, often decorative, intended primarily for removing and measuring dry tea from a tea caddy.

Surveys which gather geophysical data for a location systematically. In archaeology, refers to prospection techniques, such as ground penetrating radar and magnetic survey, used to locate artefacts and map subsurface archaeological features.

Large, broad four-tined forks used with a fish slice or with a serving knife to serve fish. For forks having three or four tines, generally used with a conforming fish knife, use "fish forks (place forks)."

Describes automatic and semiautomatic firearms in which the pressure of the propellant gas is used to force the barrel forward from a standing breech to open the action and eject the fired case. A spring brings the barrel back to firing position and also reloads and cocks the firearm.
Parts or components of firearms.
Calf that has been tanned by forcing vegetable tanning liquor through the pores of the skin or hide. It is often dressed on the flesh side to have a fine nap like suede.
Use to describe firearms which are loaded from the front end of the barrel.

Freewheeled land vehicles, often with open sides, usually with a permanent or removable top, furnished with benches or long seats all facing forward, typically used for sightseeing. Early models were horsedrawn, later ones were motorized.
Motor vehicles in which the rear end is supported on caterpillar tracks and the front is supported on wheels.
Vehicles with two wheels in tandem propelled by the rider straddling a frame which holds the wheels and handlebars for steering.
Any of a variety of animal-drawn, all-purpose wagons designed for farms and generally characterized by square-box bodies mounted without springs.

Sleds that serve to support a plough during transport to and from the field through mud or earth. These consist of parallel rails connected by beams. The sliding rails are often covered at the bottom with an iron belt or runner. Variations may include dividers covered with planks to form a deck or an open support surface of dividers.
Flat frames or shallow boxes used for transporting materials over short distances. These are generally dependent on two people to move.

Traditionally a  high-quality morocco from the Middle East with a distinctive large grain pattern. In recent years it refers to vegetable-tanned or semii-chrome tanned goatskin leather from Africa, particularly South Africa.
Pile produced not by knotting, but by wrapping supplementary weft strands around the warp and then cutting them, so that they stand out above the ground of the textile.
Small cylindrical pleats arranged in a row, thus resembling a military cartridge belt, used decoratively to give a military effect to costume and hangings.
Two-wheeled vehicles for the transport of felled trees, usually pulled by tractors.
Coarse, strong linen or cotton twill in various weights and with a warp face; used for durable clothing and furnishings.
Automobiles that have open bodies, such as convertibles, as opposed to automobiles that are fully enclosed.
Automobiles with an open body, a single seat for two or three passengers, and a large trunk or rumbleseat.
Warp supplementary to the main warp, which creates a pattern or texture in floats above the ground of the textile.
Warp pile weave with uncut loops on either one or both faces. Often in cotton or linen, and used for its absorbency in towels, bathrobes, and the like.
The principal, or only, weft in a textile.
Woven textile material with main or supplementary weft pulled up to form loops on the face.

A pattern of crackle in paintings produced by shrinkage in a rapidly drying upper layer over a slow drying lower layer, characterized by a complex branching in which apertures are abnormally wide and disfiguring.
Open freight cars, commonly with low sides, for transporting bulk goods, as coal or steel, not requiring weather protection.
Multilevel freight cars for carrying new automobiles and trucks.
Rail guideway vehicles that are part of a transit system.
Statements, transcripts, or recordings of conversations in which one person obtains information from another such as for research purposes, publication, or broadcast.

Written works or works derived from written works, where the second work is an alteration or amendment a text to make it suitable for another purpose. An example of an adaptation is a version of an earlier text made to better agree with a philosophy other than that intended by the original. Other examples are written works adapted for another medium, such as film, broadcasting, or stage production. For visual works adapted from another work, use "adaptations (derivative objects)."

Refers to books, scrolls, rolls, or other document forms containing the sacred scriptures of Judaism or Christianity. Bibles may also contain illuminations, which are painted scenes or decorations.
