Instruments for the measurement of the specific gravity of liquids.
Drinking cups designed with a lid that fits over the vessel. Usually refers to traditional cups of glass, ceramic, or metal, rather than to modern plastic or metal vessels with screw-on tops.

Small unspouted cups with two vertical handles and usually a cover with a finial used to drink caudle; especially popular in the late 17th and the 18th centuries and typically made of silver. Formerly known as posset pots or in England as porringers. For similar forms having a spout, use "spout cups."
Vessels holding or intended to hold the ashes of cremated bodies.

Covered boxes of varying shape, similar to but smaller than cigar boxes, meant to be placed on a table, desk, or the like to hold cigarettes. For flat containers used to carry cigarettes, use "cigarette cases." For open cylindrical containers used to hold cigarettes, use "cigarette holders (containers)."

Portable bowls kept in a bedroom and used for the discharge of urine, excrement, etc., especially at night. Usually having shaped convex sides, a flat bottom, and a single loop or scroll handle; some have covers.
Describes a variety of receptacles designed to store materials and tools used for needlework.
Relatively tall containers with a narrow mouth intended primarily for holding one or a few buds or flowers.
Instruments for measuring distances.
Stands for holding inkwells, pens, sand, and other writing equipment.
Boxes, typically made of wood, used to contain food stuffs, such as vegetables or ice, while being chopped.
Partitioned cases constructed to hold a specific number of square wine bottles, made especially during the late 18th and 19th centuries.

Covered, spouted vessels for preparing and serving hot chocolate, often similar in form to coffeepots but invariably having a provision for inserting a molinet and often having a handle placed at a right angle to the spout.
Indigenous Mexican effigy braziers that functioned as receptacles for copal incense that, when burned, produced a thick, musky smoke that rose through openings in the figure.
Ancient Greek silver coins worth three drachmas.
Chalices, usually unconsecrated, that are used by Christian seminarians when learning to say mass. The vessels are typically of non-precious materials, such as common metal or wood.
Writing signs that correspond to individual syllables of a spoken language.

Meaning “seven colors”, a term used to describe a technique of painting on glazed tiles to create tile-work crafts that can be found in ornaments of many architectures and shrines of Iran and can be traced back to the Seljuk dynasty. It features black lines that delineate the tiles' design. The high maturing temperature of this line prevented the low-temperature coloured glazes run together during the firing.
Main divisions or sections of a book, typically designated in some way, such as with a special heading, title, number, or layout.
Headbands that are attached to the text block by means of glue or other adhesive.
Titles printed or impressed on the cover of a publication as issued by the publisher, which may be a shortened form of the title proper.

Duct flutes similar to recorders but having fewer finger holes and, from the mid-18th century on, furnished with a slender ivory mouthpiece connected to a small chamber holding a sponge to absorb breath moisture.
Formal Gothic book hands, characterized by lateral compression, angularity, and the identical treatment of all vertical shafts.
Use generally for reedpipes with double reed and conical bore. May also be used specifically for those reedpipes with double reed played in Western orchestral, chamber, and solo music.
Reedpipes of Thailand with cylindrical bore. They generally have six front fingerholes.
Reed pipes with single reeds, terminating in an upturned bell made of animal horn. They occur in various forms, some having fingerholes, or more than one pipe, or are furnished with a bag.
Jars used to draw or carry water.
Percussion instruments that consist of a series of tuned metal bars arranged in a single or double row.
Sets of tuned metal tubes hung vertically in a frame and struck with hammers, commonly used for bell effects in the orchestra and on the operatic stage.
Rattles consisting of rattling objects strung on a bar or ring.
Metallophones consisting of a series of tuned steel bars arranged in rows and played with two knobbed beaters.

Old style English coins, originally of silver, name derived from Roman denarii; issued from the late 8th to the 17th century; then of copper or bronze from the 18th century until 1967, when they were replaced by a new decimal bronze penny. For equivalent French silver coins introduced in the 8th century, use "deniers."

Flutes with a globular body, made of clay, porcelain, wood, or a natural vessel-shaped object such as a gourd or coconut, in which the air stream is directed against the sharp edge of a round blowhole.
Use only for those British large silver coins struck sporadically from 1551 to 1937 and valued at five shillings, and for British cupronickel coins of the same value issued from 1937 to 1965.

The magnetic flux that remains in a magnetic circuit after an applied magnetomotive force has been removed. When remanence is examined and analyzed with regard to archaeological or ancient geologic materials, use "archaeomagnetism" or "paleomagnetism."

Bells used in Christian services to mark the most important parts of the service, the eucharistic celebration. Sanctus gongs are located on or near the altar; they have a louder, deeper tone than altar bells, and are often struck with a mallet from the outside rather than with a clapper on the inside of the bell. In modern services, the altar bells are often used universally for all alerts during the Mass rather than using different bells for different purposes.

Ancient Japanese bronze bells of the Yayoi period, elliptical in cross-section with pointed ends, and in profile a tall trapezoid with a flat top, surmounted by a wide metal loop for suspension. They were cast in one piece, were highly decorated, and are believed to have served a ritual or symbolic rather than strictly musical function. A few surviving examples show signs of having held clappers.
Cups of identical form which fit together, rim to rim, sometimes having, when joined, the appearance of a barrel, its staves bound with hoops of wire bands.
Tall wooden drums used by Aztecs. Instead of using mallets, players strike the tops of the huéhuetls with their fingers or hands.

Flags hung from a crossbar or frame mounted on a pole, often having two or three streamers or tails or else square in shape, historically used as standards in battle or in processions by military leaders, princes, cities and republics, particularly of Italy, guilds, and groups associated with the church; also used in the present day by trade unions.
Flags or banners on which prayers are inscribed. Prominent examples are known in Buddhist practice, especially in Tibet.

Double clarinets of India and Ceylon, consisting of two parallel pipes each with a single beating reed and a regionally variable number of fingerholes, fitted into a globular gourd made airtight with wax which acts as both blowpipe and wind chamber. Usually the right pipe serves as a melody pipe and the left as a drone pipe with its holes plugged as required.
Devices for measuring portions or amounts.
Devices for measuring types of physical force or compression.
Devices used for measuring atmospheric phenomena.
Devices that measure horizontal distances or lengths.
Devices used for measuring bodies of matter.
Instruments designed to measure the differences between two fluid pressures, generally consisting of two-legged columns of liquid.
Devices that measure magnetic attraction or magnetic phenomena.
Instruments calibrated to measure very low voltages without drawing appreciable current.
Instruments carried aloft by free, unmanned balloons and equipped with devices for measuring temperature, pressure, and relative humidity and automatically able to transmit the data by radio.
Instruments for the precise measurement of the absolute or differential boiling points of solutions.
Devices that measure the intensity of light falling on a surface (illuminance), or reflected by a surface (luminance), or emitted by a light source (luminous flux or luminous intensity).

term: liquid or gas movement measuring devices
definition: Devices that specifically measure the movement of liquid and gas.
Instrument components that detect a fluid pressure and then produce an electrical signal related to the pressure.
Balances in which the weight of the sample or the exertion of a force is balanced and thus measured by the extension of a spring.
Devices consisting of spirit levels set within metal or wood bars and used for determining or setting the horizontality or verticality of objects or surfaces.
Barometers that measure atmospheric pressure by measuring the height of a column of mercury that the atmosphere will support.
Receptacles on scales designed to hold the weights or the objects or substances to be weighed.
The practice of designing type, typefaces, or fonts. For the process of using type in the production of printed or reading matter, use "typography."
Spacing out the letters of a word or line, spreading them slightly and uniformly, for visual effect.
Calipers whose two legs turn inward toward each other used to measure exterior dimensions, as the diameter of an object.
Automatic devices for measuring and recording cloud heights.
Extremely accurate electronic clocks using the natural frequency of vibrations of quartz crystals to regulate the clock's movement.
Instruments designed to measure the relative speed of fluids and consisting of a narrow tube, with one end facing upstream, connected to a pressure-indicating device.

Scales with fixed counterweights at one end of a horizontal bar, a movable fulcrum which allows for changes in the ratio of the lengths of the arms, and a single hook from which to attach the item to be weighed; for scales of similar form, but with a fixed fulcrum and a movable counterweight, use "steelyards."
Household accessories, usually portable, meant for persons to stand on in order to ascertain their weight.
Any of various mechanical instruments used to measure the depth of water and usually consisting of a reel of wire, a weight, and a recording device.

Spike fiddles of the Tuareg of North Africa, consisting of a large gourd body covered with goat skin, a skin handle, and a single horsehair string which passes over a bridge to a notch in the end of the handle; it can be either bowed or plucked.
Instruments that indicate approximate time of day from a shadow cast by a gnomon in sunlight onto a graduated surface.
Electronic devices for measuring extremely short intervals of time with great accuracy, such as for determining the velocity of projectiles.
End-blown fipple flutes of the Andes, made of cane, bone, or wood, with a regionally varying number of fingerholes.
Instruments for measuring the density or specific gravity of liquids.
Devices that measure the quantity of alcohol in a liquid.
Instruments for measuring the size of the skulls of living beings; for instruments that measure the skulls of deceased beings, use "craniometers."

Devices used to measure the diameters of circular objects to specified tolerances and consisting of cylindrical steel rings whose inside diameter matches either minimum or maximum allowable dimensions.

Science of society, social institutions, and social relationships; specifically the systematic study of the development, structure, and function of human groups conceived as processes of interaction or as organized patterns of collective behavior.
Tokens used to pay a fare on public transportation, toll bridges, or toll roads.
Tokens engraved with name of a person and date to commemorate the baptism. Early tokens are of brass or precious metal; later examples may be made of various materials.
Tokens, often small round disks, that replace coins when games are in progress and which may be reconverted into cash.
Lighting techniques providing substantially uniform levels of illumination throughout an area exclusive of special local requirements.
The state or quality of having equal physical properties along all axes.
Very thin, usually silver, coins struck with an obverse die only so that the design shows through on the reverse; used in Germany and neighboring territories between the 12th and 18th centuries.
Money manufactured from paper and originating in multiple places around the world.
The flesh of animals used as food.
Waste matter discharged from the body.
Magnetic domains within iron minerals that have been heated to above the Curie point and then cooled.
Resistance to permanent changes in property caused solely by heat.

Material comprising the yellow spheroidal mass of stored food that forms the inner portion of the egg, usually a bird's egg. The whole egg, yolk, or white may be used sometimes mixed with oil and/or resin. The egg yolk is a stable emulsion of an aqueous liquid with an oily, proteinaceous medium which dries quickly into a hard, insoluble film.

Paper money issued as a substitute for standard money by, for example, businesses, military organizations, or local, rather than national, governments; normally in denominations less than the basic monetary unit.

Use to describe something that is produced by a computer, especially when the programming generates automatically a relatively large number of the steps between what is input and what is produced; included are visible forms, audio forms, data, and other products.
Bony framework of the head, enclosing the brain and supporting the face.
Use to describe wooden watercraft hulls in which the edges of planks are set flush resulting in a smooth exterior surface.

Directly instructing others in knowledge, attitudes, or skills. For the acquiring or imparting of specific skills relating to particular functions or activities through instruction or practice, use "training."

Style focusing on artistic iconoclasm and the breaking down of the traditional boundaries of academicians, abandoning realism in favor of methods intended to cause an intuitive response in the perceiver. The style was influenced by the philosophy of Henri Bergson, son of a Polish Jewish musician. The style in art, writing, and music was explored in the journal Rhythm, founded by John Middleton Murry.
Refers to the property of a dye or a material to retain its color and resist fading or discoloration by washing.

In the Western Christian church, a period of penitential preparation for Easter that includes 40 weekdays extending from Ash-Wednesday to Easter-eve, observed as a time of fasting and penitence in imitation of Jesus Christ's fasting in the wilderness. In Eastern churches Lent begins Monday seven weeks before Easter and ends the Friday 9 days before Easter. This "Great Lent" allows that Saturdays and Sundays are relaxed fast days.
Former United States paper money issued by the federal government for general circulation between 1865 and 1933 equal to and redeemable for gold at a stated value.
Works, particularly artistic or written works, produced relatively late in the maker's career.
Groups of people whose members have one or more social characteristics in common.
Groups of players of musical instruments and/or singers, ranging from two people to entire orchestras.
Those who are consecrated, hallowed, holy, including those consecrated by a religious rite or ceremony.
Action, practice, or system of the operation of a farm, including the cultivation of the soil to produce crops.
In Indian architecture, an eave-cornice, or awning.

Farming in which large planting areas are located on raised platforms or raised fields, allowing farmers to better regulate or avoid flooding. Examples are the raised field agriculture of some Pre-Columbian cultures.
Animal glue made from degraded collagen obtained from skin and hide.
Consists of loose, granulated materials such as rock wool, cork, or other material poured or packed between framing members.

A material providing high resistance to heat flow; usually made of mineral wool, cork, asbestos, foam glass, foamed plastic, or diatomaceous earth, fabricated in the form of batts, blankets, blocks, boards, granular fill and loose fill.

Integument of animals such as sheep, calves, or goats, separated from the body, with or without hair, whether green, dry, tanned, or dressed. For the integument of large animals use "hide." For tanned skin, use "leather." For dried and stretched skin, use "parchment" or "vellum."
A horny keratinous material derived from the mouth of whales.
Reeds in the form of a stretched band or ribbon, stretched taut between two points, against which an air stream is directed.

Regional or indigenous Latin American ceramic vessels, usually Incan, having a pointed base, globular or cylindrical walls, and a long, narrow neck; often have handles. They are named after, but distinguished from, Greek vessels "aryballoi," which may have similar shapes. distinctively shaped Inca vessel is a symbol of the Inca Empire. Arybalos are found in every territory that the Inca conquered, with regional variations in decoration.
United States silver or cupronickel coins valued at three cents and issued during the mid-19th century.
Five-dollar gold pieces issued by the United States between 1795 and 1916 and again in 1929.

The skin or hide of an animal that has been tanned to render it resistant to putrefication and relatively soft and flexible when dry. For composite material made from scrap leather pieces, use "maril."
Emergency coins or paper money issued by authorities of a besieged town and thus cut off from the standard money supply.

The effect of graduated or shaded color in textiles, created through the weave or by dyeing. The effect may be monochromatic or polychromatic. The term is most often used for textiles, but may also be extended to painted or colored surfaces that display a graduated shading effect.
The nationality, style, or culture of Bahrain, an archipelago and small island country situated near the western shores of the Persian Gulf.

Lamellaphones originating in Africa, consisting of tuned metal or split-cane tongues fitted to a wood board or resonator, so that the tongues can vibrate freely at one end; they are played by depressing and releasing the free ends of the tongues with thumbs and forefingers.
Postage stamps with special designs, having a value indicating an extra fee in addition to regular postage, and affixed to mail to ensure special, usually speedier, delivery.
Orders issued by a company and drawn upon its bank or banks for payment of a dividend to a named shareholder or stock holder.
Unconditional written promises to pay on demand, or at a fixed or determined future time, a certain sum of money to, or to the order of, a specified person or to the bearer.
Plans prepared for or by printers to show the arrangement of the matter, type faces, sizes of type, and positions of illustrations and captions for pieces of printing.

Distinctive badges, devices, or marks bearing a crest, heraldic bearing, coat of arms, or other mark worn by a person or company or attached to property, particularly such devices intended to denote ownership of property or affiliation of retainers to a noble house, whether the retainers bore arms or not.

Wood friction idiophones of New Ireland, consisting of a curved block with three (rarely four or five) crosscut slits. The flat upper surface is thus divided into tongues; the player rubs the surface with rosined hands to produce tones.

Books or similar documents that recount and depict nuptial festivities and events, chiefly of royalty, nobility, or famous persons, and which may also include literary works offered to the principals, such as epithalamia or the Italian "per le nozze."
Small single-headed drums with a shallow shell, played in sets, normally of seven.  They are tuned by rotation on a fixed, threaded spindle, or by pedal mechanism.

Single-reed instruments, commonly of brass, with wide conical bore and slightly flared bell; built in several sizes from sopranino to contrabass, all but the two smallest are bent back in a U-form with the bell tilted forward.

Electronic keyboard instruments designed to imitate the tone of conventional pipe organs, and, like pipe organs, are able to sustain the tone indefinitely, play chords, and decrease or increase sustained tone.
The row of small twists or rolls at the base of a hand-sewn headband formed by passing one thread over the top of the other.

Conventionalized pictures or symbols that stand for an idea or thing, and not precisely the thing pictured; often not corresponding to one particular word in the language written. Examples are Chinese characters.

Sets of tuned stationary bells, and struck to sound. They are less extensive than carillons, having a range limited to within two octaves. The term is always used in the plural. For a single bell, see "cymbal."
Poetry that is combined with images to create a completed work.
Typefaces, in Latin or non-Latin characters, that exhibit some form of embellishment or decoration.

Baskets constructed of baleen that is coiled around an ivory base. Often includes a lid topped with a carved, ivory finial; these finials are usually figurative, taking the forms of various Arctic animals. The first baleen baskets were woven by Inuit men in the 1910s following tourist interest.
Footed bowls or shallow dishes of varied design used in Greek Orthodox or other Catholic churches to distribute bread that is blessed but not consecrated to those who cannot receive holy communion.
Containers made of twigs, rushes, thin strips of wood, or other flexible material woven together.
Containers, often made of animal hide or fabric such as yarn, used to carry materials necessary for religious ceremonies. Commonly used in Native North American traditions.
Capacious vessels for beer or ale usually of tar-coated leather, dating from the Medieval.
Roman copper or bronze coins valued at one fourth of an as and issued from the early Republic through at least the 2nd century CE.
Sets of procedures leading to the production of printed images or text, usually each including its special techniques of preparation or transfer.

A deterioration of photographs, occurring when silver is attacked by any of a wide variety of oxidants that convert metallic silver atoms to highly reactive and mobile silver ions. It is the most common cause of fading of silver images.

In the context of typesetting by hand, the condition of the pieces of type having been sorted into the wrong compartments of the case and any errors appearing in the resulting printing due to this condition. Signs of foul case typically include letters of the wrong size or wrong font, or spelling errors.

Printmaking technique in which the plate is painted directly with acid, so that the artist is drawing with acid rather than ink; the acid is washed off when the desired effect had been achieved. Technique is typically used with etching, rather than as the sole technique.

Brush strokes found in traditional Chinese painting.  Associated with the Northern Song dynasty painter Mi Fu (1051-1107), after whom they are named, these wet, inky strokes create a misty, atmospheric effect.
Generally, refers to instruction in and study of one or more of the visual arts at any and all levels, including the teaching of both amateurs and professionals, and of art teachers.

Specialized soldiers who were physically the most powerful and used to lead the charge on a battlefield or in the storming of a fortificaitons in siege warfare. Originally, as the name implies, grenadiers were the troops who threw grenades in battle; although in later usage, refers to the strongest, largest soldiers who led the charge, whether or not grenades were employed.
Encounters or fights, often armed, between two persons, parties, animals, or machines.

Generally, objects or other things made or modified by humans, typically manually portable products of human workmanship, such as tools, utensils, objects for personal adornment, or art, as distinguished from natural remains. In archaeology, an artifact is an object made by a human culture and later recovered by an archaeological endeavor. In the context of museum objects, use "cultural artifact." In the context of technical and medical research, for a spurious result that is a product or effect resulting from the experimental technique or procedure itself, use "experimental artifact."
Embroidered coverings or hangings produced by using the colcha stich.
Material that is intended to fit under carpets to add a cushion of support, or to prevent slippage.
Protective coverings on which a mattress or bedroll can be laid, for protection or comfort.
The maximum amount of axially-directed pressure a material can withstand before being crushed or fracturing.
Parts or components of rugs.
Asymmetrical knots, woven over four warp threads.
Rugs characterized by a coarse, long pile and decorated with bold, abstract patterns; thought to have been made by nomads from the central Zagros Mountains. Commonly used as sleeping rugs.
Machine-made carpets woven on a wide loom, usually measuring 54 inches or wider.
Prayer rugs with multiple niches or arch designs, used for family or group prayer.
Tapestry- or flat-woven rugs made in southern France, used as floor coverings or wall hangings.
A type of flat-woven rug usually made of cotton, produced in India.

Carpets or rugs made using knots, in the most common method of creating pile carpets; knots are formed by tying yarn around two warp strands to form a knot on the surface of the textile. After each row of knots is created, one or more strands of weft are passed through the warp strands. Then the knots and the weft strands are beaten with a comb securing the knots in place. The number of knots per square inch determines the appearance and texture of the rug.
Boxes or other containers that hold the relics inside larger reliquaries.
Sudden and great changes in the government carried out violently or illegally, usually by a small group within the existing state establishment.
Two siblings conceived, carried in the womb, and usually born at the same time. They may be identical, as when one fertilized egg splits, or fraternal, as when two eggs are individually fertilized.

A carbon ink made from burning tung oil with a low oxygen component. Originally in the form of a solid, imported to Europe as compressed sticks. Also, fluid consisting of the pigment suspended in a medium such as water combined with a glutinous binder.
Slabs of ink used in lithography to obtain soft tones.

Resinous preparation of shellac and turpentine, or of beeswax and Venice turpentine with coloring matter, that is plastic when warm and used for sealing letters, attaching impressions of seals to documents, and sealing batteries and jars.

A synthetic wax made by catalytic polymerization of low molecular weight, high-density ethylene. It may be used as a reversible protective coating in many applications including the conservation of outdoor sculpture.
Refers to Zoroastrian priests that rank above ervads and below dasturs within the priestly hierarchy.

Blocks, usually of wood, that either are cut to print an image, whether on paper, fabric, or other material, or that support other materials that form the actual printing surface. Use a more specific term when possible. For metal printing surfaces, prefer "printing plates."

Conditions under which aspiring artists learned or learn their skills. In Europe, before the establishment of the state art academies in the 17th and 18th centuries, training as craftsmen took place in the workshop of experienced masters, controlled by the guilds. Gradually the teaching programme began to include more theoretically-based disciplines, set up in art schools/academies.
Automatic typewriters that utilize magnetic cards about the size of punch cards (as opposed to punched paper), and are linked to computers.
The process of making wine, which is the fermented juice of the grape used as a beverage.
X-shaped horizontal braces or rails connecting and supporting the legs of chairs, tables, and case pieces.
Stage at which a living being is fully grown or developed.
The action of tossing and catching a number of objects continuously, keeping at least one of them in the air while handling the others, usually as a form of entertainment.

An abnormal, pathological condition that affects part or all of an organism, affecting the functioning of one or more of an organism's systems, parts, or organs. It is often construed as a medical condition associated with specific symptoms and signs.

Refers to state officers or servants, either of prominent households or individuals, who carry messages and announce proclamations, and often also keep the family's genealogical records and regulate the depiction of its coats of arms. Applies particularly to officials in Medieval and modern Europe who arranged ceremonial events, particularly tournaments, at which they had special charge of conveying challenges and regulating the use of coats of arms by combatants. From the 19th century onwards, the office's duties consist mainly of regulating a family's or organization's coat of arms and often of doing the blazonry of those arms as well. For visual artists whose works consists solely of depicting coats of arms, see "blazoners."
Refers to spirit spouse figures made by the Baule people of West Africa, representing a man. For spouse figures representing a woman, see "blolo bla".
In Indian architecture, an architrave of the entablature (South India); lintel, beam.
Areas of objects where converging lines or surfaces meet.
Works or miscellaneous collections that are created from a diverse range of materials or sources; generally reserved for literary, musical, or visual works, such as sculpture or architecture.

Detachable lengths of tubing inserted into aerophones, either permanently or for a specific playing occasion, for the purpose of either changing the sounding tube length, or to carry the mouthpiece where it is within easier reach of the player.
Trusses in which the members are arranged three-dimensionally rather than in only one plane.
Refers to small objects, of any shape or material, pierced so that they may be strung or hung or attached, as by sewing.
Panoramic picture painted on a cylindrical wall surface designed to afford a viewer in the middle of the room a 365 degree view of the painting seen in natural perspective.

Works that are designed to be displayed or used together, usually referring to a relatively small number of such works. For larger numbers of works, or works that are often of matching pattern, prefer "sets (object groupings)."

Painted decorative coatings on surfaces and objects, including clothing, utensils, boats, and chariots, created using polychrome colorants. In Chapter 14 of the Yingzao fashi (1103), the craft of applying polychrome painted decoration on architectural surfaces (caihuazuo 彩畫作) is categorized as a specific division of architectural works.
Visual works made of woven, coiled, inscribed, or carved bamboo, which is material derived from woody or treelike tropical and semitropical grasses of various genera.
Strings designed to sound by vibrating in sympathy with bowed or plucked strings.

In Hindu art, anthropomorphic or personified depictions of a divine weapon, often a partial incarnation of their divine owner. The noun is masculine or feminine, depending upon the gender of the word for the weapon in Sanskrit.
Systematic administration of activities that provide for collection, processing, and disposal of solid wastes, including the recovery of materials and energy.
Clappers of Bali and Java. They consist of two metal objects shaped like bananas on stalks, and with concave surfaces, which are then clapped together.
Written, negotiable instruments that contain orders for payment.

Areas used for the game of football (American or gridiron football), in professional play having standard official dimensions of 360 x 160 feet (109.7 x 48.8 m), with a goal line near each end of the field, 100 yards (91.4 m) apart. Areas used for the game of football (American or gridiron football), in professional play having standard official dimensions of 360 x 160 feet (109.7 x 48.8 m), with a goal line near each end of the field, 100 yards (91.4 m) apart.

A soft Italian verd antique from Prato, Italy that is deep olive green with dark green spots and veins of clear green and white. It was first used by the ancient Greeks and Romans and continues to be used in modern times; it was notably used for much of the exterior decoration of the cathedral in Florence.
People who assemble items of information into reference works such as dictionaries and encyclopedias, typically by selecting and putting together matter from the works of various persons or bodies.
Experts in criminology, which is a branch of sociology devoted to the scientific study of offenders, of crime as a social phenomenon, and of the criminal justice system.
Subject catalogs in which entries are arranged by the class numbers of a classification schedule.
Complete, systematic, and critical listings of all the known works of a single artist, providing comprehensive information, including provenance, for each work.

Refers to a Chinese Neolithic culture dating to ca. 3300 BCE to the beginning of the Bronze Age. It geographically covered western Shaanxi province, Gansu and Qinghai provinces, but since the most striking pottery comes from sites in Gansu, the culture takes this name. Gansu culture falls into three major phases: Majiayao (ca. 3300-ca. 2100 BCE), Banshan (ca. 2800-ca. 2300 BCE) and Machang (ca. 2000-ca. 1800 BCE). These were followed by the Qijia (ca. 2000-ca. 1600 BCE), Xindian, and Shajing phases. The finest Gansu ceramic vessels are thin-bodied and light, with a variety of boldly painted decoration. Clay was carefully selected and prepared and painted decoration was done in earth pigments probably applied with a soft brush. The most notable vessel type made during this period was the funerary urn with a wide shoulder and narrow base.
People, animals, or other beings who carry, bring, or transport something, particularly something heavy or cumbersome; may be used in actual or figurative contexts.

Refers to the period of the Mataram kingdom from the seventh to the tenth century. The styles of this period are driven by religious ideological struggles between the Shaivite Sanjaya dynasty and the Mahayana Buddhist dynasty of the Shailendras, which resulted in sweeping building programs of Hindu candis and Buddhist temples throughout the Javanese region. Later, the resurgence of indigenous ancestor and spirit cults that flourished alongside Shaivism resulted in synthesized styles that incorporated Buddhist, Hindu, and indigenous elements into textile production, weapon design, manuscript panting, and calligraphy.

Refers to the period in Champa associated with the royal monastery complex Dong-Duong founded by King Indravarman II (875-889 CE) and prevailing in the region from the ninth to the early tenth century. Architectural features from this period are based on the Dong-Duong complex and include brick construction, sanctuaries grouped within inner enclosures, pillared halls, interior and exterior piers supporting the stupa, multi-story brick kalan, columnar structures known as stambahs similar in shape to Buddhist tower-stupas, a long hall known as a vih'ra containing Buddha images, and altars restrictively placed against walls. In sculpture, the period is driven by the religious trend of Mahayana Buddhism and features Buddha figures draped in the Chinese manner, dv'rap'las figures with fierce expressions, thick lips, stylized ears, and close-cropped short side whiskers, bronze sculptures of Buddha cast by the lost-wax process, bas-reliefs decorating tympana and altars, exhibiting various royal personages in stylized actions, and elephant statues with the hind legs bent and with the head turned forwards or trunk raised. Shaivite heads and female images of Tara produced in this period feature strong frontality and exaggerated features.
Fauteuils with concave backs; distinct from "fauteuils à la reine," which have flat backs.
Wall hardware that projects at ninety degrees and that supports members for supporting curtains or other hangings.
Sheet metal seams comprising interlocking turnings on each of the two pieces, in a manner so they fit firmly together at a corner.
Vertical joints in brickwork made by laying the brick in a bed of mortar and shoving the brick toward the last brick laid.

Roofs having trusses rather than rafters, and beams or purlins, meaning the frame comprises a triangle-based webbing having the function to support the roof and tie the outside walls. Truss roofs may be wood or steel.
Technique of bond in which headers and stretchers alternate horizontally and vertically, each header being centered with regard to the stretcher above and below.
Violet pigment that is derived artificially from an inorganic source.

Christian devotional prints made primarily for wide public distribution, depicting a saint or events in the saint's life. Such prints date from the Middle Ages and later. They were sometimes distributed as mementos for accomplishing a pilgrimage to a sacred site associated with the saint.

Letterpress prints characterized by soft edges and a range of tonalities accomplished in a single run. The print is made by placing a flexible, layered matrix behind the printing sheet which is then fed into the grippers to pull an impression from a type-high, inked surface. The matrix performs as elaborate make-ready that applies more pressure in thicker areas and less in thinner. Often, pressure prints introduce visual noise around the central image.
Layers in a painting, usually an oil painting, that are between the ground or primer and any protective coating.

Paint applied to a painting over already dry areas. Sometimes used to include the original artist's glazes and scumbles; sometimes, especially in conservation, used to mean only later restorers' work. For restoration work that only fills in lost areas without covering original paint, use "inpainting."

Images produced by processes that involve a photographic process (that is, employing light-sensitivity) to transfer an image, and then a separate process to produce the print, which was never itself light-sensitive.

Enclosed rooms or compartments either aboard watercraft partitioned off by bulkheads and designed as private accommodations for officers, crew, or passengers. These may also be aboard aircraft and spacecraft designed for crew, passengers, or cargo.

Coverings for the torso, limbs, hands, feet, and head for warmth, fashion, or to cover nudity. It generally excludes other items of costume such as jewelry, crowns, and other accessories that are purely decorative or symbolic and have no practical function.
Type of ferry known in the Netherlands, operating on rails at the bottom of a canal or other shallow body of water. Comprises a platform on wheels elevated above the water level.

Technique that quantitatively measures the amount of electrochemical corrosion resistance provided by a coating to a metal substrate. In conservation science it is used extensively for evaluating the anticorrosion performance of coatings to metal works of art.
Infrared spectroscopy having the range of 400-4,000 inverse centimeters [cm-1].
Burners for the combustion of gas, usually with various arrangements of holes through which gas issues.

Burners consisting of metal discs with vent holes and one or two, sometimes three, tinned wick tubes 1/4 inch or less in diameter soldered upright and a wick slot in the side. The wick tubes extend farther below the disc, into the font, than above.
Lighting devices designed to hang from the roof or ceiling having two or more branches, holding candles, burners, or lamps; often ornamental.
Lights, electronic apparatus, or other devices that emit identifying signals related to their position to guide or warn navigators or pilots of aircraft or ships.
Lighting designed to provide illumination for workers inside factories; also includes exterior lighting of factories, particularly in the context of discussions surrounding environmental impact.
Lamps on tall standards, designed to rest on the floor.
Lighting fixtures that use electricity to provide illumination.
Burners designed to hold a flat ribbon-shaped wick. Commonly used for burning kerosene but also found on some oil and lard lamps.
Lighted signals mounted on tall poles used to indicate the presence of waterways or channels.
Tops designed to be spun by slapping at them with whiplike objects, as opposed to tops meant to be spun by hand directly.
Designates artificial areas of water, usually of geometric shape, specifically designed and located so as to mirror buildings or other structures.

Staff weapons having a three-pronged head with a central triangular double-edged blade, often with a strong medial ridge, with two shorter blades radiating from its base or curving up like the prongs of a trident. They were used from the 15th to the 17th century, mainly in France and Italy.
In Indian architecture, an ornament, image, picture.
Fixtures (usually chandeliers) having devices allowing adjustment of height.
Lights mounted on the front of a vehicle to provide illumination ahead of it.
Lamps consisting of exhausted glass tubes filled with neon gas that is ionized and conducts an electric current through the tube.

High-intensity discharge lamps, highly efficient in terms of lumens produced per watt of current consumed, with one-color light (orange) making them unsuitable for general use; often used for street and highway lighting.
Aeronautical beacons used to indicate the location of natural or man-made landmarks used by pilots as an aid to navigation.
Aeronautical ground lights along the sides of a channel of a water airport.

Lamps with a burner that has a cylindrical wick sandwiched between two metal tubes that admit a current of air to the inside of the flame and a chimney to enclose the flame and direct air to the outside of it; use especially for such lamps with a separate fuel reservoir from which fuel is fed to the font and burner on the bird-fountain principle. Argand lamps were invented ca. 1782 by Aimé Argand in Geneva and were manufactured in England by Boulton, in the United States by Cornelius & Co. and in France by Quinquet, after whom they are sometimes named.
Mechanical lamps designed to burn without a chimney, having a spring-driven blower in the base to provide a draught.  Patented by Robert Hitchcock in 1868.
Gas burners that have three apertures and emit three jets of flame from a burner tip.
Use with reference to projects sponsored by any of the United States government programs established under the New Deal administration and operating at various times between 1933 and 1943.
Occasions of the severe damage or loss of a boat or ship at sea.
Light sockets designed so that a cylindrical termination of a bulb may be attached by rotating the bulb along helical or spiral threading lining the interior of the socket.
Refers to the calcium salt of phytic acid. In conservation, used in a solution to inhibit iron gall corrosion on manuscripts.

Finely granulated copper with numerous metallurgical applications produced by various techniques such as electrolysis, atomization, hydroscopy. Each method of manufacture yields a powder with its own inherent characteristics.
Etching ground containing grease so that it does not harden.
Refers to very thin plates or sheets, spangles, strips, or threads of gold or silver. It may also refer to imitations made of copper, brass, or a gold- or silver-colored alloy.
Paint containing metallic silver as the primary pigment component, for use in art, for covering a surface, or for conductive purposes.

Crystalline sugar, a disaccharide, stored instead of starch in some fungi, algae, and insects. Industrially manufactured trehalose has been used in combination with lactitol as a sugar-alcohol saturation treatment in the conservation of archaeological waterlogged wood.

A matte, opaque water-soluble paint typically having gum arabic, gum senegal, or dextrin as a binder. Gouache differs from watercolor paints primarily through the addition of white fillers, such as chalk or baryte, which give it a higher opacity and matte surface quality. Gouache was used for miniature paintings in the 16th-18th centuries, for decorative paintings on interior walls, and for printing wall paper patterns. The term originally had a different meaning, referring to oil applied on top of tempera painting.

Repairs consisting of a localized cast of molten copper alloy to fill cavities or other casting defects. Cast-on repairs may fill a void in a sculpture or secure a separately formed patch or element to the cast.
Incised brass plates serving as memorials to the dead, typically found in Western art on tomb slabs or otherwise near burial sites, and often showing a portrait or coat of arms.
Works, dating from the 1960s, that incorporate people and usually movement but imply a close relation to static figure sculpture.
A pair of circular stones used for grinding grain or other substances, which are typically fed through a central hole in the upper stone.
Venetian wall mirrors of the first half of the 16th century that usually also have a shelf and pegs; frequently ornately carved and may be gilded or painted; used primarily in bedrooms.

Chairs made from looped and twisted iron wire, usually having circular oak seats. Chairs of this type were patented in the early 1900s. A number of manufacturers made such wire chairs; the name derives from their use in public restaurants and cafes.
Running ornament in which forms are attached to a central feature that runs down the center of the band.
Buildings where electrical power is generated for distribution, often as part of a larger power plant complex.
Layers of masonry units running horizontally in a wall or, much less commonly, curved over an arch. Layers of masonry units running horizontally in a wall or, much less commonly, curved over an arch.
In Indian architecture, the wall and entablature of the upper floor, or the area between the cupola and the entablature.
Ornamental features, usually in relief and triangular in form, resembling pediments and located over doors or windows.

Low, bench-like seats or kneelers used for prayer or meditation. Known in many cultures, including in Christianity and indigenous African cultures. For specifically Western Christian prayer furniture, 'prie-dieu (benches)' and 'prie-dieu chairs' are sometimes called 'prayer stools.'
Stools having very tall legs or other supports, designed for sitting at a counter or other high table-like surface.
Long stools located near or extending from a fireplace fender. Popular in the 18th century.

Italian wood benches with a chest under the seat, in the form of a large cassone with back and arms added to form a settee or sofa with storage below. Loose cushions were used for comfort. The form was popular in Florence.
Benches, generally without padding and upholstery, often made en suite with chairs or hall mirrors and intended for use in halls and galleries.
Small bedsteads with a high enclosure and usually slatted sides for a child.
Stands with two or more tiers or stands for maximizing surface area.
Tables designed to stand against the wall, generally with one side undecorated.
Tables that can perform a variety of functions by rearranging or removing its parts such as the top and drawers, for example, to transform from a dressing table to a writing desk.
Rounded elements or outlines which break the square corners of cabinetry, picture frames, or other furniture. The form is derived from classical architecture.
Popular motif used as the terminal ornament on chair feet and table legs in the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries.
Synthetic rubber made from ethylene, propylene, and a diene comonomer that enables crosslinking via sulfur vulcanization. Used in many applications.

Religious or contemplative songs of a particular type; may be monophonic and more or less extended (as Gregorian chant: see Gregorian, or else short and formulaic, usually harmonized, and adjusted to the syllables of a prose text.
Machines which utilize the up-and-down motion of a straight saw blade, but which depend on clamps to hold the saw blade stiff.
In Indian architecture, a net or festoon of hanging miniature bells.
Plastic based on polyether or polyester resin.
Devices for applying mechanical power, often for the purpose of replacing or assisting manual labor.

Brushes made for use by artists from animal hair or synthetic material in a variety of shapes and sizes, but generally small enough to be handled with precision. The term pencil was used until the 19th century to describe small pointed sable or camel hair brushes. For larger brushes made for applying paint over large areas, especially as a protective coating, see "paintbrushes."
Describes apparatuses or tools used for preparing a printing plate.
Manual rotary drills which have an attachment for applying pressure with the chest; used by carpenters for drilling horizontal holes.
Percussive power tools for breaking up hard surfaces such as concrete through repeated blows of a bit driven by compressed air.
Jackets intended to keep people afloat in the water in emergency situations.
Machines for lifting men or materials on a platform at the end of an extendable boom, usually mounted on a carrier with wheels to provide mobility.

Refers to special ornate capital letters in illuminated manuscripts marking the beginning of a section of text such as a verse or paragraph. In modern calligraphy the term is applied to capitals built up by inking between pen strokes and having serifs in the form of long, thin, straight lines.
Equipment used for the making of glass, or the working on or with glass or glass articles.
Tools used for cutting the threads of bolts, pipes, or other metal objects.
Black crayons made of charred twigs of wood, usually willow or pieces of vine, or sticks of compressed charcoal.
Organizations and associations dedicated to the preservation and conservation of cultural heritage.
Hand-held, pen-shaped computer devices which are light sensitive so that when they are held to a point on a video screen they allow the computer to modify data or drawings.
Persons who make, sell, clean, and repair hats.

Artists identified as the creator, performer, or originator of a work. Typically based on the attribution to an individual based on the style or other characteristics of their works. The person may be named or anonymous, known only by the attribution to their oeuvre of works. May also reference writers, composers, actors, or musicians.
People who report on, write about, analyze, or evaluate works of art, usually contemporary works.
Individuals, companies, or corporations engaged in the development and improvement of land for construction purposes.
Persons who circumcise male infants in accordance with Jewish ritual.
Those engaged in the study and interpretation of ancient inscriptions, including writing, pictures,  and random scratchings, incised on stone, clay, metal, or other hard surfaces.
Those who are responsible for the education of other people.
Artistic concepts concerned with form, as opposed to content.
Describes the collective production of films within a particular time and place.

Superhuman beings of infinite wisdom and compassion; Buddhist saints who, having only one birth to undergo before attaining Nirvana, consent to be reborn for the sake of suffering mankind. In Mahayana Buddhism, the spiritual ideal. In Theravada Buddhism, the term is exclusively used to identify historical Buddhas in their previous lives.
Handles for holding chalk, crayons, or charcoal, consisting of a split metal tube, usually double-ended, in which the material is secured by a ring that slides over the split end.

The legal or practical methods or means by which property of some sort is bought, acquired, or transferred. An example is the means by which an art object entered the collection of a particular museum.
Buildings that house prisons administered by the state, particularly a state in the U.S.
Mansions belonging to, or used by, the lord of a manor.
Intermediate stopping places along lightrail tram routes.
Printed, spoken, or published statements or notices that inform the reader of an event or other news.
High towers, usually round, in which shot is made by dropping molten lead from an upper story into a cistern of water.
Buildings housing museums that focus on peoples, societies, and cultures.
Fancy Windsor chairs of square-back based on Sheraton's designs, and found in the region of Mendlesham, England in the early 19th century.
A generic relationship between one entity and another, used when no more specific alternative is available.
Tools used to smooth the surface of a hole or finish holes which have been drilled in either wood or metal.
Club-shaped instruments of a hard material with a round end used for crushing, pounding, or grinding herbs, spices, drugs, pigments, or other materials in a mortar, which is a cup-shaped receptacle.
Small sharpening machines that utilize a horizontal, flat metal plate that is turned by means of a gearing system. The knives are held in specially designed clamps.
Pieces of woven material intended as tools to remove dust from surfaces.
Machines or structures in which solid, semisolid, liquid, or gaseous combustible wastes are burned, sometimes at high temperatures leaving little or no residue.

Utensils consisting of an inverted cone with a narrow tube at the apex, used for conducting liquids or other substances from one container to another, usually with a narrower opening; sometimes combined with strainers.
Portable mechanisms used for moving loads short distances by means of force applied with a lever, screw, hydraulic press, or air pressure.
Devices of various forms that mechanically maintain a correct positional relationship between a piece of work and a tool, or for positioning parts of an object during assembly.
Sets of two parallel rulers joined by a circular joint, marked with degrees, that combine the functions of a protractor and a set square.
Pumps that force premixed concrete through a hose to a desired location.
Holiday taking place on the first day of May or another day near that date, traditionally marked by springtime festivals and later in many countries also celebrated working people.
Tools, usually made of steel, used for sharpening knives.
Trips taken by newly wedded couples.

A stereoscopic print or transparency in which a three-dimensional illusion is achieved through the use of alternating strips of images taken with a stereographic camera. The array of strips is covered by a grating that allows the right and left eye of the viewer the see only corresponding right or left image fragments, which creates the perceptual illusion of three dimensions. A stereoscopic print or transparency in which a three-dimensional illusion is achieved through the use of alternating strips of images taken with a stereographic camera. The array of strips is covered by a grating that allows the right and left eye of the viewer the see only corresponding right or left image fragments, which creates the perceptual illusion of three dimensions.
Vises designed to hold metal material or objects for metalworking.
Machines used especially in pulp mills to remove bark from logs.
Pieces of hardwood against which a workman presses his breast in operating a breast drill or similar tool.
Receptacles with slotted intervals that hold individual mounted slides together in a group for storage, with some designed to be a component of a projector.
In the context of railroads, revolving platforms that turn on a central pivot laid with rails connected to adjacent tracks; used for turning railway vehicles.
The two portions of a sphere cut off by a plane through its center.
In refrigeration systems, the heat exchangers that remove heat from the refrigerant and transform a hot gas under pressure into a cool liquid.

The theory or doctrine that society can be organized according to a cooperative model, a system based on non-profit credit and voluntary association for the exchange of services. Mutualism originated in the the writing of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon.
Perforated metal plates through which clay is forced to mold it into a desired shape.

Tools of various designs used for cutting glass by scoring a line on a piece of glass. The scoring makes a split in the surface of the glass, allowing the glass to be snapped or broken along the score.
Externally driven device for breaking rippled seed bulbs.
Machines or rooms used for freezing and preserving items such as food.

Pans, often with legs, that are used to safely move hot coals from one location to another, or that fit under the grate of a coal stove and double as ash catchers. For small pails, generally made of metal, for holding or carrying coals, use "coal hods." For similar equipment that allows the containment of coals but also the heating of a room or the cooking of food, use "braziers (cooking, heating equipment.)."
Any of various devices used for polishing or buffing.
Tools designed to carve, plane, or otherwise shape or work pieces of wood or wooden objects.
General term for woodworking tools used for striking, such as mallets and hammers.
Information indicator used when a work contains media that are unconventional or may vary. An example of use could be to index collection containing conceptual, minimalist, and video art.
Books or other media containing collections of moralized fables, especially as written in the Middle Ages, about actual or mythical animals.
The net decrease in heat within a space.
Tools powered by electric motors or by gasoline engines.
An undesired oscillation in a part of a machine or structure under stress.
Power hand tools that have a rotating, circular abrasive disk; used for smoothing or polishing a surface.

Written agreements embodying the purposes or other conditions of the association of a number of persons for the pursuit of a joint enterprise; especially those duly executed and filed with a state's administrative authorities so as to have the force of a charter under general incorporation law.

Graphic designs intended to explain rather than simply represent. For example, in geometry, a diagram may be a figure composed of lines, serving to illustrate a definition or statement, or to aid in the proof of a proposition. In other contexts, a diagram may be any illustrative figure which, without necessarily representing the exact appearance of an object, gives an outline or general scheme of it, so as to explain or exhibit the shape and relations of its various parts.

Approach or practice of selecting the best elements from different doctrines, methods, or styles to apply them in a new creation. In the specific context of art or architectural criticism, use to mean borrowing from a variety of visual sources in the creation of a work.

Characteristic of belonging equally to more than one, of being possessed or shared alike by all or most of the people or things in question. An example of usage is in indexing groups of works or complex works, for subject or material terms that apply to all items in the group or all aspects of a work that has multiple aspects.
Making a material or object firm, stable, or stationary.

People who have a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, or who have a history or record of such an impairment, or those who are perceived by others as having such an impairment.

Wood of Fraxinus americana, native to Canada and the United States. It is a lightweight wood that is stiff, strong, and resilient. The sapwood is white and the heartwood ranges in color from light brown to reddish-brown. It is used for boat frames, church pews, sports equipment (baseball bats, hockey sticks, skis, paddles and oars, and tennis racket frames), and tools (handles of shovels, hammers, spades, hoes, and rakes as well as ladder rungs), and other products.
Building technique using short firewood-sized logs set in piles perpendicular to the length of walls and held in place by mortar or wooden frames.

In contemporary military contexts this refers to groups of huts, tents, or other shelters set up temporarily for troops. In historical contexts the term connotes permanent or semipermanent places of encampment. Use "military bases" for contemporary permanent installations. In contemporary military contexts this refers to groups of huts, tents, or other shelters set up temporarily for troops. In historical contexts the term connotes permanent or semipermanent places of encampment. Use "military bases" for contemporary permanent installations.
Lodging places providing a variety of amenities for travelers and often maintained by a religious order.

Lightweight and buoyant polymers containing uniformly dispersed air pockets, like a sponge. They are made from most types of polymers (rubber, polyethylene, polystyrene, epoxy, polyurethane, vinyl resins, silicone resins, and others). Steam, air or an inert gas is mechanically added or chemically produced in the plastic resins during manufacture to form a cured open cellular structure. They may be soft and spongy (foam rubber, polyethylene, etc.) or rigid and strong (polystyrene, epoxy). Closed-cell foams have individual non-connected bubbles while open-cell foams have an interconnected tunnels formed when the incorporated gas or steam escapes during cure.

Maps used by insurance companies and emergency management agencies such as FEMA in assessing risk to property. In conservation and heritage management contexts, maps used in vulnerability analysis, assessing risk to cultural heritage areas.
Small racks with partitions intended to hold sheet music, books, or loose papers.
Areas of visual works having pattern, image, or other elements of primary interest, as distinguished from neutral areas or background.
In heraldry design, human or animal figures that hold or support the coat of arms.
In Indian art and architecture, a decorative motif in the form of a sprout or bud.
Enrichment consisting of a line of tiny beads; common on silver and furniture.

In art, refers generally to a pleasing, orderly, and consistent arrangement of the parts of a whole. The concept of aesthetic description in which architectural proportion or artistic design displays congruity.
Protective measures against floods, including relief channel and reservoir construction, afforestation, and bans on building in flood-prone areas.

Use with regard to specialized procedures related to how a photograph is taken or composed, or is manipulated during or after processing. Use "photographic processes" for the procedures by which light-sensitive materials are made to produce an image.

On-going essential services provided by government relating to the protection and maintenance of the lives and property of community members as a whole. For the actual enterprises, use a more specific term such as "public utilities," "public works," or "social services."

Organizations or agencies that serve as central bodies for the collection, organization, storage, and dissemination of information and documents. They may also perform referral services for researchers.
Events comprising the indiscriminate and brutal slaughter of people; indescriminate butchery of animals or people in in large numbers.
Wells sunk to extract water from a zone of saturation.
Wells constructed by driving lengths of pipe or other conduits into the ground with percussion equipment or by hand.
Celebratory occasions, either joyous or solemn, at which elaborate or ritual meals are a central feature.
Facilities that pump oil through pipelines.
Generally, collateral relatives more distant than a brother or sister. Specifically, the sons or daughters of one's uncle or aunt.
Male partners in a marriage relationship.

Photomechanical prints, usually illustrations, characterized by having tonal gradation simulated by a pattern of small dots that vary in size. They are typically printed from a block in which the tones were broken up into dots of various sizes by the interposition of a glass screen, ruled with fine cross-lines, between the camera and the object, usually another photograph.

Refers to color photomechanical prints produced as lithographs from photographic negatives. The technique was developed in the 1890s in Switzerland by Hans Jakob Schmid at the company Orell Gessner Füssli, also known as Photoglob Zurich. The technique was introduced at the World Exposition in Paris in 1898 and it was used until ca. 1930s. The technique was one of the more successful attempts preceding color photography to produce color images; indeed, photochroms looks deceptively like color photographs unless viewed with a magnifying glass. A black and white image served as the base and a form of photolithography with as many as sixteen colors was used to make the final image. Photochroms are distinguished from chromolithographs by their hard clear coating. The patented process was licensed to firms in England and America; most photochroms are scenic views of the American West, Europe, and the Middle East. William Henry Jackson and the Detroit Publishing Company were responsible for a large number of photochroms. Captions are often in gold lettering, on the lower portion of the recto, identifying the view and sometimes the maker. The process was labor intensive and time consuming and was replaced by faster and easier techniques.

A Christian sect founded in Richmond, Virginia in 1848 by John Thomas (1805-71), who had previously been a follower of Thomas and Alexander Campbell. John Thomas wanted to return to the beliefs and practices of the earliest disciples, hence the name meaning 'brothers of Christ.' The name was adopted during the American Civil War to justify the follower's pacifism. The doctrines of the Trinity and of the pre-existence of Christ were rejected by Thomas. Christadelphians believe in the complete accuracy of the Bible. At the center of Christadelphian belief is millennialism. Specifically, it is believed that Christ will come again to establish a theocracy based in Jerusalem. Christadelphians do not agree on whether all people will be resurrected although it is most commonly believed that anyone other than a true believer will go to oblivion. Adult followers must be baptized by immersion. There are no ordained ministers and local congregations are called 'ecclesias.' Christadelphians do not take part in military service, politics, or voting.
Nonstructural, outer, exterior wall covering of buildings.

Technique of transferring pictures and designs from specially prepared paper onto a surface, such as glass, and the Surrealist painting technique in which one freshly painted or inked surface is pressed against another to form an image.
Converting to machine-readable form data records from a manual or non-machine-readable file that are not converted in day-to-day processing.

Process for producing a photographic printing plate, using a particular method developed by William Henry Fox Talbot. This process for producing a printing plate from a photograph was patented in 1858.  After coating a copper plate with bichromated gelatin, Talbot exposed the plate to light under a positive transparency.  It was then dusted with powdered resin and heated evenly to distribute the resinous particles. The plate was then etched in an acid solution that dissolved the gelatin and etched those same areas.  After cleaning, the plate was inked, wiped, and printed on paper. He coined the term photoglyph from the Greek for "carved light."

Those whose medical practice is focused on teeth and associated structures of the mouth, involving the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of disease, injury, or malformation of the teeth, gums, and jaws.
Adherents of the movement inaugurated by Austrian Rudolf Steiner (1861-1925) and devoted to the development of the faculty of cognition and the realization of spiritual reality.
Transit systems comprised of small, automated, self-propelled vehicles, usually with rubber wheels running on concrete rails, within their own separate guideways.

Systems for communicating at a distance, often a collection of individual communications networks, transmission systems, relay stations, subsidiary stations, data terminal equipment, and other facilities for disseminating information. Examples include telephone, telegraph, radio, television, optical communications, internet, etc.
Transit systems, usually of low average speed (under 15 miles per hour) and making frequent stops, located locally within portions of cities, towns, or neighborhoods.
Monosulfide of iron found in nature as pyrrhotite and troilite. It is synthesized to use in generating hydrogen sulfide.
Describes people whose gender expression is other than conventional expectations of masculinity and femininity.
Diamond-shaped tablets or panels exhibiting the coat of arms of a deceased person, displayed upon their death.
A soft sandstone containing red iron oxide, having a reddish-brown color.

Paper having having a smooth, glossy, glasslike finish. The gloss is obtained by treating the paper with a substance, including starch, glue, wax, or synthetic resins, followed by heat-pressing between rollers. Examples of glazed papers are as used for book covers, pages of books, advertisements, decorative wrapping paper, and bags.

Geometric plane figures produced when a cone is cut obliquely by a plane taking a smaller angle with the base than the side of the cone makes with the base; the form is symmetric about its horizontal and vertical axes.
Native clay selected for its fineness, plasticity, absorbency, and other qualities that suit it to various ceramic uses.
A red indurated clay from the upper Missouri region historically used by Native Americans for tobacco pipes and other carvings.
Building blocks comprising extruded clay shapes having substantial depth that may be laid as other masonry.
Groups of two or more persons contractually associated as joint principals in business. For business enterprises considered in law as legal persons, use "corporations."
Short-handled adzes used for splitting wood.
Files having a blade-like cross section, with a sharp edge; used to finish narrow grooves.
Prying tools with a double-hooked head used in caulking barrels with flags or for removing barrel heads.
Bags made of a porous material filled with a fine powder of charcoal, chalk, or pipe clay; used in pouncing.

Small brushes with soft, often long bristles of camel hair, straw, or other natural fibers set into round, elliptical, or curved bases of wood, metal, ivory, or other material. These often have a long stem-like handles. Used to revive the pile of velvet and felt hats or to brush lint and dust away.
Long, slender pointed awls used to regulate the stuffing in collars and saddles or for leveling thread.
Primitive lathes in which the cord passing around the work to rotate it is fastened at its ends to the treadle and to an elastic pole above.
Small scissors with two sharp points designed for precision cutting of thread ends and other purposes.
Round tapering files, 4 to 20 inches long, used for enlarging holes and shaping curves.
The act, work, or trade of joining pipes together.
Small pocket knives, usually with only one blade.
Blocks of material that are carved or incised with designs; these designs are later impressed onto paper or other mediums to create a reverse of the carved image.
Workbenches intended for shaping and building with wood. These often incorporate vices or other appurtenances for holding pieces of material while it is worked.
Extended Māori kinship group, in which members share distant common ancestors.
X- or Y-shaped wood devices used to support logs during sawing.
Groups comprising two people united by love, marriage, betrothal, or sexual union. To specify people joined by marriage, use "spouses." For people who cohabitate, use "domestic partners."
A painting conservation technique where a deteriorated canvas is strengthened by affixing a strip of canvas to its outside edge.
People who play stringed instruments.

General term for symbols, sounds, or gestures devised according to a system and used to represent something else. An example is in translating a piece of information in a source language, such as a symbol, letter, word, or phrase, into a target language according to a strict rule, in order to achieve some purpose, such as disguising the message or facilitating its transmission or reception.
Differential movements of the earth's crust or parts of its surface, or elevations or subsidences of land.
Water droplets condensed from the air, usually at night, onto cool surfaces.
Partially fused product from a kiln, which is ground and used for cement.

Boards made of wood, but from flakes or chips of wood rather than from full lengths of lumber. Composition wood boards are usually classified by fiber size (largest to smallest): waferboard, oriented strandboard, flakeboard, particleboard, and fiberboard, which may be made of cellulose fibers other than wood.
Roofing tiles that are flat, plate-like in shape, rather than barrel-shaped; usually made of concrete.

In ancient Greek architecture, the flat tile or pantile with a decorative nosing used on the eaves (with antefixes) as a substitute for the sima (terracotta or marble gutter of a building).  In modern construction, tile, usually shorter or plainer than other roofing tile, used in the first course of tile along the eaves of a building.

Special type of roofing tile made with perforations to permit the passage of air and sometimes light. Ventilating tiles are typically set into a span of regular roof tiles; they usually have a raised, curving profile in which the ventilation holes are situated.
Blades that are used to prepare specimens for viewing under microscopes.

Gameboards of 64 squares arranged in eight vertical rows called files and eight horizontal rows called ranks. These squares alternate between two colors: one light, such as white or beige; and the other dark, such as black or green. The board is set between the two opponents so that each player has a light-colored square at the right-hand corner. Chessboards are identical to checkerboards except for the colors, which tend to be black and red in checkerboards.
People, usually women, employed by a family to care for one or more children for an extended period, typically living in the household and attending to the children day and night.
Documents used in common carrier transportation, setting out the route of the vehicle, details of goods or passengers, and revenues received.
Drawings representing a side elevation of a ship and emphasizing the arrangement of the rigging.
Motion pictures produced primarily for children.
Having a central section that projects in front of the side sections, especially used in reference to 18th-century bookcases or cabinets.
Those who transcribe in shorthand, or who operate shorthand writing machines.
Gouges sharpened both outside and inside; the larger outside bevel is used for hardwoods, and the smaller inside bevel for softwoods.
A synthetic material prepared to simulate the appearance of wood.
Use to describe photographs, usually daguerreotypes, ambrotypes, or tintypes, mounted in sturdy, boxlike cases.

The study of pharaonic Egypt, spanning the period around 4500 BCE to CE 641. Egyptology began when the scholars accompanying Napoleon Bonaparte's invasion of Egypt (1798-1801) published "Description de l'Égypte" (1809-1828), which made large quantities of source material about ancient Egypt available to European scholars.
Study of the history of a particular word or element of a word, or of historical linguistic change.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Malawi.
Giving sanction to an action or object, as done by a valid authority.
Taking human life under judicial order.

Housing units available to occupants whose income does not exceed certain maximum income limits set by local housing authorities. Distinguished from "low cost housing," which refers to the subsidized low rent of the units rather than the low income of the occupants.
Refers to large organized land forces armed for war and regimented in some manner for deployment. Applied both to independent organizations or to groups under the control of one nation or ruler.
The activity and status of rule by a monarch, usually associated with a defined period of time and delimitation of the area ruled.
Documents that are concerned with the description of antiquity or antiquities.
Papers, drawings, plans, letters, and other documents, either hard copy or digital, having to do with the construction of buildings, usually originating in an architect's office.

Items comprising a collection of leaves of paper, parchment, wood, stiffened textile, ivory, metal tablets, or other flat material, that are blank, written on, or printed, and are strung or bound together in a volume.
Charts used for navigation beyond the earth's atmosphere, including interplanetary or interstellar space.

Lists of books, documents, and other bibliographical items, often all related by author, topic, or another criterion. Bibliographies are arranged in some logical order giving brief information about the works, such as author, date, publisher, and place of publication.
Lists or rolls of the collective body of members, as of a society, at a given time.
Documents related to insurance policies including explanations of benefits, claims, bills from medical offices, notices of supplemental insurance programs, or premium payment notices.
Diverting or amusing someone; causing someone's time to pass agreeably.
Opaque photographs, usually positive (i.e., reproducing appearances without tonal reversal, otherwise use "negative prints"), usually on paper, and generally, but not always, printed from a negative.
Negatives made by drawing through a prepared ground applied to a glass plate (a subtractive process), or painting directly on a glass plate (an additive process).

Photographic prints made on a gelatin-silver chloride photographic paper introduced commercially in 1867 by the Munich-born chemist Johann Baptist Obernetter. This was considered the first industrial ready-to-use photographic paper print process. Aristotypes are composed of a paper layer, a layer of baryum sulphate in gelatin, and a layer of emulsion containing silver chloride suspended in a binder. The baryta layer made purer whites possible. As this was was a printing-out-paper, aristotypes are exclusively contact prints.
Photographs made to sell clothing and accessories or show them to advantage.
An accessory formed of clothlike folds or scrollwork depicted behind or above a heraldic achievement.
Photographic prints made by transferring oil prints that are still wet to a secondary support.
Floor mosaic technique characterized by the insertion of irregular fragmented slabs of polychrome marbles and stones in a monochrome opus tessellatum field.
