Prints made by relief printing in which chemicals are used to etch a metal plate on which a drawing has been made; examples are illustrations, maps, or other designs printed from a plate prepared by a chemical process such as a zinc-etching process.

Prints made from an etched printing plate, which is a metal plate on which a design is made by coating the plate with an acid-resistant substance, creating a design in the coating, and then exposing the plate to acid, which etches the plate where the metal is exposed. For designs incised directly into a copper plate using a burin or graver, use "engravings (prints)."
Relief prints made from surfaces upon which textures or objects have been attached. For collagraph prints that combine intaglio and relief, use the broader term "collagraphs."

Prints made using the process of line engraving, which is the printing process that produces images in line and with little tonal quality because the slight burr produced by the engraving process is scraped away.
Prints produced by the sand-grain etching process.
Relief prints taken from an engraved metal plate; made chiefly in the 15th century.
Photomechanical prints of the mid-19th century made by an etched daguerreotype process.
General term for sheets printed in chromatic colors by any process. Examples would be relief prints made from metal blocks.
Standing clocks that are positioned on floors.
Decorative wall clocks originating in France in the early 18th century; usually spring-driven and set in gilt-bronze or carved wooden frames coming to a point at the bottom.
Small metal clocks whose case is an openwork frame resembling lanterns; popular in England and France in the 17th century as successor to Gothic clocks.
Clocks whose recurring motion depends on mechanical, as opposed to electronic, devices, such as escapements, the swing of a pendulum, or the oscillation of a balance wheel and spring.
Wheels that oscillate against the tension of balance springs to regulate the beats of clocks or watches.

Timepieces, usually worn on the wrist, that are powered with a "resonance drive," in which a tiny tuning fork driven electrically provides the motive power. First produced in 1953, the resonance drive type, properly called an electronic watch maintains accuracy since it operates at a frequency higher than that customarily used with balance-type watches. When the battery is too weak to operate the tuning fork, the watch simply stops, without deterioration. Power is provided by miniature high-energy-density batteries.
Musical instruments in which the sound is produced automatically or mechanically, usually without a performer although some instruments involve a degree of human participation.
Musical instruments that produce vibrations which must be passed through electrical circuits ending in loudspeakers before they are heard as sound.
Large gourd used as a musical instrument, which is played by blowing over the opening at the top.
West African chordophones in which the plane of the strings is at right angles to a soundbox; the strings pass over a notched vertical bridge.
Musical instruments that incorporate electronic circuitry as an integral part of the sound-generating system.
Sound devices made to vibrate by being struck.
Tubes, often made from an animal's horn, with notched or corrugated edges, sounded by scraping with a nonsonorous object.
Concussion idiophones made of hollowed-out objects.
Instruments in the shape of two springy arms connected at one end and touching at the other. The arms are forced apart by a little stick, to jingle or vibrate on recoil.
Friction drums of the Zulu people in South Africa. They consist of spherical clay pots covered in goat skin, and they are played with a friction stick.
Struck drums that have a bowl shape.
Later model of clavichord in which each key is served by its own pair of strings.
Small harpsichords that are usually rectangular in shape, and having one keyboard and with the strings running at right angles to the keys.

Organs involving a set of graded whistles operated by steam or compressed air, played by means of a keyboard, pinned cylinder, or paper roll. Producing a great volume of sound, their typical use has been outdoors, such as at circuses, fairgrounds, and on steamboats.
Portable American reed organs in the form of a deep rectangular box held across the player's lap, with a keyboard of ivory buttons on the upper surface and a double bellows worked by one hand.
Upright pianos having the string length of a regular horizontal grand piano but with the strings running from below keyboard level upwards to the top of the case.
Drums in which the vibrations of a plucked string are transferred to a membrane, thus producing sound.
Small kettledrums of Medieval Europe, more or less hemispherical in shape, usually played in pairs suspended from the player's waist in front and often furnished with snares.

Goblet drums of Bulgaria and Yugoslavia, with a shell of baked clay and a single head of animal skin attached with fine hemp string, usually held under the left arm and struck with the fingers of both hands.
Strings of gut, metal, or wire-covered silk stretched over that head of a drum which is not struck, tensioned so as to give a crisp, brilliant tone to the drum.
Bells used to mark the beginning or end of work days at a factory.

Bells that are used in a carillon, which is a set of stationary hanging bells. Carillon bells are typically cast bronze, thick sided, cup-shaped bells, which are serially played to produce a melody, or sounded together to play a chord. They are typically played with a keyboard, by which keys mechanically activate levers and wires that connect to metal clappers that strike the inside of the bells.
Finger cymbals of the ancient and modern Islamic world, still played today in southeastern Europe and Turkey.
Southeast Asian metal gongs, usually bronze, with a deep, curved rim and a flat surface often ornamented, suspended by handles and struck with beaters.
Rattles in which the rattling objects are mounted together and shaken to strike against each other.
Latin American rattles consisting of a natural or synthetic round or pear-shaped gourd covered with a network of beads and finishing in a short handle, sometimes also containing rattling pieces.
Mesoamerican slit drums made from a hollowed-out log with an opening cut in the form of an "H" on the top.
Xylophones of Burma. They usually consist of 17-23 slats which are tuned by wax that has been applied underneath each slat, and they sit above a trough which acts as a resonator.
Log xylophones of the Gwere of Uganda, with six slabs supplemented by a drum, placed on two banana stems and separated by sticks; the drum is played as though it were another slab.

Slabs of rock that emit pitched tones when struck, sometimes giving varied pitches from different places on their surfaces, and that are used intentionally as percussive instruments. For similar stones found in the landscape, use 'ringing stones.'
Resonators of plucked and bowed chordophones.
Large wire-strung citterns popular in the 17th century, with slanting bridge and frets, tuned like the lute and interchangeable with it in much of the music written for either.
Version of the bajo sexto with 10, instead of 12, strings.
Five-string arched harps of the Masa people of central Chad, having a skin-covered soundbox and tuning pegs; played resting either on the ground or on the shoulder of the player.
Chairs in the form of a four-legged stool to which a back has been added. The term first appeared in the 16th century and was sometimes used in the 17th and 18th centuries for a chair without arms.
Upholstered armchairs, differing from other armchairs in being upholstered between the arms and seats.
Chippendale's term for high-backed easy chairs stuffed all over and upholstered in wool fabric.

Collector's term for Italian Renaissance chairs with numerous crosspieces linked up along the sides. Named for the 15th-century reforming monk, although it is questionable that such chairs were actually used by him.
Early 18th-century chairs with or without arms, having a vase-shaped splat in the back which was curved to give comfortable support to the back.
Chairs of greater than usual height, often with a front ledge to be used as a foot rest, designed for spectators' use at billiards games.

Ancient Greek throne-like chairs, usually ornamented, having an elevated seat, often a high back and arms and either legs ending in animal feet, turned or rectangular legs, or with solid sides. Used by people of wealth or prominence and seen in depictions of the Greek gods.
Chairs mounted on wheels that may either be pushed or propelled by the occupant by means of hand rims attached to the two large side wheels.
Chairs having legs mounted on curved supports, usually bands of wood or metal, which allow the chair to be rocked back and forth.
Rocking chairs which move upon a stationary base instead of rocking on curved bends.
Applies to a variety of small stools, such as footstools, generally having splayed legs.
Footstools with thickly padded upholstered tops.
Long, low, upholstered seats of Turkish origin usually without backs or arms.
Settles having a hinged back so that it can be let down to rest on the arms and thereby forming a table.
Term used during the Greek Revival era to describe the form of couch produced with scrolled ends reminiscent of Greek and Roman furniture designs.

Settees with high backs and hinged arms that may be upright or sloped out from the seat, named after the unique early specimen at Knole Park, Kent; popular for rich suburban furnishings in England in the 1920s and 1930s.
Late 18th- and early 19th-century sofas having a high-pitch back.

Extended chairs, generally without arms, used for lounging with one backed end usually made to tilt; often supported on a stretcher frame with six or eight legs. Also, long, wide, sofalike seats, often with two low ends that somewhat resemble headboards or footboards, that can be used for sitting or sleeping. Daybeds are typically designed for one person to recline on and were historically sometimes used for the formal reception of visitors. They are generally placed against the wall or in a niche.
Beds for two people with one sleeping place above the other in the manner of tiered bunks.

Beds having dome-shaped testers supported by rods, often of iron, curving up from the corners of the head boards, with the rods being hidden by the bed hangings. Developed in the 18th century, such beds were often meant to stand in a deep niche in the bedroom of the main apartment of a palace or mansion. In other installations, the bed are often placed with one side lengthwise flush against a wall.
Term generally applied to beds larger than double beds but smaller than king-size beds.
Deception beds that fold into dummy cabinets.
Cases for holding books generally having several shelves enclosed by doors; distinct from "bookshelves" which are open shelves for holding books.
Cabinets designed to fit into a corner of a room, usually by being triangular.
Cabinets, often with glass fronts and sides, used to hold and display china.
Simple chests constructed of six boards butted, lapped, nailed, and hinged together; an economical alternative to joined chests.
Two-part chests of drawers, one stacked on top of the other.
Wood boxes, often covered in leather and tooled in gilt or bound with iron, which were used as traveling trunks to store papers, valuables, and clothes; of a type made in the late Medieval period.
Ancient Roman cupboards, generally having a rectangular case, mounted on feet, with doors reaching approximately from top to bottom, a gabled or flat top, and interior shelving.
German wardrobes for the storage of clothes and linens; generally with two paneled doors and sometimes having one side with drawers and shelves and the other side an open space for hanging clothes.

Large, but fairly low, cupboards with both the upper and lower sections containing enclosed storage space; of a type made in 16th- and 17th-century England and 17th-century America. Distinct from "court cupboards" which have an enclosed storage cabinet above and an open shelf or shelves below.
Sideboards with a place at one end to hold bottles of wine and at the other end either a plain drawer or a drawer lined with lead, in which glasses could be washed.
Rods secured horizontally, usually in closets or armoires, for the purpose of hanging clothes on clothes hangers. They may be removable or permanent fixtures.

Desks with a hinged one-piece round lid or cover that resembles a section of a cylinder and which rolls up into the desk top. For similar desks surmounted by a bookcase use "cylinder desks and bookcases."
Large flat-top writing tables, usually with drawers in the frieze.
Writing tables with fire screens to protect the writer from the heat of the fire.

Spanish fall-front writing cabinets, taking the form of a rectangular chest supported on a decorative pie de puente or trestle stand. The interior is often elaborately decorated and generally contains tiers of drawers which may be supplemented with pigeonholes and a small cupboard. The name is a late 19th-century name that erroneously suggests that this type of writing cabinet was made in the Toledan village of Vargas.
Popular term for American slant-front desks.
Term applied to tables with legs jutting from a pillar, regardless of their form, and with feet terminating into claws.
Tables used in bookbinding.
Tables having semi-circular or "U" shaped surfaces, designed for and used while eating meals in large formal dining rooms.
English and American 18th-century tables made to provide the facilities of the modern bathroom, with provisions for a basin, bottles, bidet, and other toilet equipment.
Term applied to a variety of French dressing tables designed for women.
Tables with tops marked with a gameboard divided into 64 squares of two alternating colors, for playing chess.
Small, three-sided tables, with pits in the top to hold counters.

Small freestanding racks, poles, or stands, either plain or elaborately carved with symbols, made and used in Africa for supporting bows, with or without arrows; traditionally functioning as symbols of office for chieftains and symbols of honor for great heroes and hunters, though in some regions may be owned by any man.
Inclined, sometimes foldable supports, made of wood or metal, on which a missal or other liturgical book is placed on the altar.
Small tables or tall stands intended to hold bouquets of flowers in decorative vessels.

Small ladies' work tables. In their classic form, may have galleries around its top and the shelf joining its legs to provide shallow receptacles into which one could place chiffons (scraps of ribbon and cloth) and other needlework materials; either square or circular in form and generally having three drawers, the uppermost sometimes fitted with writing equipment.
Joined tables with three legs; of a type made in 17th-century England.
Tables whose flaps are supported by jointed gates which swing out from the central section.
Furniture built into the walls or overall structure of a building. This can include, chests, cabinets, corner cupboards, bookcases, beds, and seating.
The board or boards that make up the back of a piece of case furniture and sometimes extend above the top.
Upholstered furniture arms that retain an open space between the back and seat, rather than being closed by the upholstery itself.
Vertical or curved uprights supporting the front end of chair arms.
Up-curved ends of a crest rail; usually on Chippendale chairs.
Decorative inlaid border of contrasting types of wood cut along the length of the grain, generally used on the edges and rims of furniture.
Upright supports on a bedstead, such as those which support the tester on a high-post bed.
Foam pads, sometimes in a case of fabric used either alone as a resting or sleeping surface, or supported on a bedstead, or box spring.
Rooflike components, generally cantilevered from the head posts, which extend over the head half of the bed.
Helmets worn by motorcyclists, air crews, automobile racers, and others, to protect the head in the event of an accident.
Parts or components of bevors.
Small shields with an internal grip, held in the left hand during foot combat; they were used from the 13th to the 17th century.

Plate metal or leather armor protecting a horse's hindquarters, in complete form consisting of three heavy oblong plates covering the top of the rump and sides and back of the hind legs. Lighter versions consist of several leather straps, often metal plated, which run along the spine to the tail guard, down either side of the horse's flanks, and horizontally below the root of the tail. For the leather straps looping around the root of a horse's tail and fastened to the saddle to keep it from slipping forward, use "cruppers (tail straps)."
Spurs furnished with a spiked wheel revolving on an axle fitted into the stem of the Y-shaped spur frame. They came into wide use in the 13th century.

Use generally for solid or nearly solid projectiles of stone or metal, containing no explosive charge themselves, fired from artillery or firearms. Use specifically for the small solid lead or steel pellets of various sizes, usually housed in a cartridge, fired from shotguns in multiples with each firing. For the small metal projectiles designed to be fired from small arms singly with each firing, use "bullets."
Term used from the 15th to the 17th century for cannons especially long in proportion to their bore.
Small culverins used in the 16th and 17th centuries, designed to fire projectiles of less than 1 pound in weight.

Weapons comprising thin, razor-edged rings of flat steel; as traditionally used by Sikhs. Primarily used as a throwing weapon, but can also be used hand-to-hand. For symbols of the wheel of the law or the symbol of dharma, see "chakras (motifs)."
Maori adzes, used for war, ceremonial purposes, or for building.
The earliest form of bayonet, consisting of a narrow, daggerlike blade with a grip tapered to fit into the muzzle of a firearm, thus converting it for use as a thrusting staff weapon.

Fist weapons designed for hand-to-hand combat at close quarters, consisting of a finger ring with a single sharp, metal hook; also used for personal use or adornment; found primarily in the Great Lakes region of East Africa.

Macedonian infantry pikes having a very long shaft of from 16 to 24 feet, a short leaf-shaped iron head, and an iron point on the butt end which could be plunged into the ground to withstand an enemy onrush.
Term applied from at least the 17th century to heavy military swords with a large, straight, double-edged blade and a basket hilt or shell guard, designed primarily for cutting.

Daggers having a hilt shaped like a capital H on its side (becoming more like a capital I over time), usually worn at the girdle by civilians. The form originated in southern Germany or Switzerland in the late 13th century and remained in wide use throughout Europe until the late 15th century. Some types are as long as short swords.
Sabers with strongly curved blades tapering to a sharp point, traditionally associated with the Near East.
Blunt swords designed specifically for the sport of fencing.
Devices fixed to the handles of edged weapons to protect the user's hand.

Hilts characterized by a cup- or bowl-shaped guard in front of the quillons, covering the user's hand and the arms of the hilt, developed in 17th-century Spain and those parts of Italy under Spanish influence. They are most often found on rapiers.
Use to refer to firearms that are fired from the shoulder, primarily rifles and shotguns.
Pocket pistols designed to be held in the palm of the hand and fired by closing the fist.

Most common type of European hunting rifle from the late 17th to the mid-19th century, typically with a short octagonal barrel of large bore, a heavy stock, and brass fittings. Originally fitted with flintlocks, after 1820 they commonly were fitted with percussion locks. They were popular in the American colonies until superseded by American long rifles after the Revolution.

Firearm ignition mechanisms in which a fulminate or gunpowder priming powder is struck and explodes, thereby detonating the propellant. The most developed versions feature a percussion cap, fitted over a nipple screwed into the breech and pierced by a small hole that connects with the propellant; when struck by the hammer, the cap sends a small jet of flame into the propellant, igniting it.
Small arms, especially short-barreled shotguns, often fitted with an attachment for a bayonet, used in guard duty or to disperse rioters.

Clubs used throughout Europe mainly from the 11th to the 17th century, made either entirely of metal or of a wooden shaft with a metal head, the head having longitudinal grooves or flanges and sometimes surmounted by a spike.
Money in the form of coins originating from Asia.
Coins the design, metal, or denomination of which has not yet been approved for issue and have been produced primarily for inspection.
Stamps required to be affixed to certain products or documents before they change hands to indicate that a tax has been paid.
Collocates tokens of fixed value that are redeemable for cash, though often expressed in other terms.

Movable or fixed objects or equipment, which may be either functional or ornamental, particularly objects for sitting, reclining, or storage, such as chairs, beds, tables, cabinets, etc.,  in a dwelling, business, or public space.
Devices holding two to four candles and made of gilt brass with an adjustable painted metal shade.

A low, portable candleholder of a design reserved for a pope, cardinal, bishop, and certain abbots and other high-ranking prelates; usually made of silver, with a wide drip pan and ring or a long handle, which may store a spare candle. It is used to illuminate the liturgical books during pontifical services, and may bear the coat of arms of the pope.
Lamps fitted with from one to four lenses to concentrate and intensify light, most commonly made of pewter or of tinned sheet iron with a separate glass font.
Spout lamps, usually of cast bronze, often having three or four wick tubes and a font adjustable for height on a vertical standard; of a type used in Mediterranean countries.

Argand lamps usually of brass or bronze with one or two burners on arms connected by tubes to a reservoir that feeds fuel to the burners on the bird-fountain principle, often ornamented with prisms hung from rings around the reservoir and burners. The name derives from their common use singly or in sets of three on mantels.
Lamps, usually mounted on the ceiling or on a dental chair, and for the purpose of illuminating the oral cavity for precision work.

Electrical lighting fixtures designed so that the bulb housing and electrical supply may be inserted into a flat surface such as a ceiling or wall, the opening for the light source being flush with the surface.
Lamps designed to burn rectified turpentine, having an Argand burner without a separate reservoir, and a button-shaped deflector to spread the flame.
Lamps which burn fish oil, usually simple lamps such as pan lamps and crusies.
Electric lamps in which light is produced by a tungsten filament heated to incandescence by an electric current.
Protected lamps or lanterns, fixed or removable, used on coaches or carriages.  Commonly made of brass, they often were fitted with reflectors as well as red lenses to serve as tail lights.
Holders for the slender wax candles known as tapers.

Torches of tow or cotton wicks saturated with resin, coated with wax; often four wicks were joined and coated again to increase the size of the torch. Also, torches carried for pyrotechnical display, as in public parades.
Devices used with an electric discharge lamp to obtain and maintain the necessary circuit conditions, such as voltage, current, and wave form, for starting and operating.

Candles used for the Christian feast of the Epiphany on January 6, which celebrates the recognition of Jesus by the three Magi. These candles are used in homes and liturgies. Example of design include a candle terminating in three upper branches (shaped like a trident) and a large candle encircled by three crowns.
Incandescent or fluorescent lamps whose artificial light aproximates daylight.
Designates ornamental plants grown indoors, other than in greenhouses, and adapting to less than ideal environmental conditions.

Refers to screens comprising two or more panels in a frame which has hinged sections that can be folded to adjust coverage. They are often decorated. Early examples include the Chinese form, mentioned as early as the 2nd century BCE. The earliest surviving examples date to the Ming dynasty. Folding screens were introduced to Japan from China in the 8th century; such screens were often designed in pairs in Japan. From the early 17th century eastern folding screens were imported to Europe and the form was soon adopted by European craftsmen.
Fire screens of various designs, characterized by being adjustable or extendable to cover alternatively a smaller or largerspace as necessary.
Rolled textual objects, variously made of plant fibers or animal skin, upon which are written prayers or petitions to the deity.
Discs (formerly cylinders) of shellac, polyvinyl chloride, or other substances so prepared that sound is reproduced when played on a phonograph player.

Phonograph records that are made from flexible materials, usually vinyl sheets, though variations have been paper-backed. The most well-known version was introduced commercially in the US in 1962 as the Eva-Tone Soundsheet, in Europe as Lyntone Recordings. Flexible records using materials other than vinyl predating Soundsheets include Marconi Velvet Tone records of 1906, made of a paper-based core laminated between two sheets of celluloid, the Hit Of The Week label in the US, and the Durium label in the UK, which made flexible records with a cardboard backing. From the 1950s in the Soviet Union, discarded X-ray film was used to engrave recordings to distribute music outside official channels. Vinyl flexi discs were used to bind sound recordings within printed publications. From 1980 to 1982, Flexipop! magazine in the UK included colored flexi discs with each issue. Versions of the flexi disc concept have been included as elements of product packaging such as cereal boxes.
Describes audio sound recording materials comprised of magnetic particles embedded in a binder layer on polyester, acetate, paper, or PVC bases, wound onto tape reels for storage and playback.
Compact discs on which large numbers of photographic images can be stored and viewed.
Digital videotape format for digital video recording and playback with excellent resolution.
Inscriptions, that have as a theme the donation of an object.
Devices that signify an individual rather than a family or organization, usually composed of a design and a motto, popular especially in the Renaissance.

Labels affixed to a book to indicate ownership and often its location in a collection. They may be printed or engraved, frequently with a distinctive design, pasted or tipped into books on the inside of the upper cover.

Refers to detailed watermarks produced by a relief sculpture on the paper mold. The technique was supposedly invented in 1848 by the Englishman William Henry Smith. The light and shade watermark created more detail than the wire watermark. It is often used in paper money to make counterfeiting more difficult.

Refers to marks or characters punched or stamped into previously made coins. They were often applied by a Chinese assayer to silver trade dollars and other precious metal coins as an indication that the coins had met his test for purity and weight. They were widely used between 1750 and 1920.
Inscriptions threatening harm to anyone who would steal or damage a book or manuscript.

Thin disks of dried paste, gelatin, adhesive paper, isinglass, or similar material with added coloring matter and typically bearing an identifying mark, used to seal letters or other documents or to attach papers.
Tablets made for writing, usually of wood or bone, covered with wax which was written on with a stylus; used especially in ancient Rome and during the Middle Ages.
Plates with a cuplike inset used to facilitate opening sliding doors.

Metal strips or plates attached to the bottom rail of a door for protection against marring, as by shoes; also, plates, usually metal, used to create a lip or ridge at the open edge of a stair platform or floor, or at the back edge or open ends of a stair tread.
Devices for locking together upper and lower leaves of a Dutch door.
Hardware fasteners  incorporating a hook, designed to hold blinds in place while in a closed position.
Types of butt hinges mounted on the third leaf of three-ply shutters, designed to allow the leaf to enter a recess in the interior jamb of a window without jamming.
Locks built to secure French doors.
Locks adapted to fasten rolling or hinged desk lids.
Locks which are fitted into and flush with the rabbet on a rabbeted door jamb.
Devices attached to a sash rail by which the window may be raised or lowered; may be flush-mounted cups or surface-mounted bars or hooks.
Small hooks and eyes, generally used on cabinets. Distinguished from "cabin door hooks," which are generally used on marine installations.
Strikes mortised into the edge of a door jamb and surrounding a deeper recess in the frame.
The long rods that pass through a hinge's knuckles to keep the two halves of the hinge joined together.
Lock housings.
Keys so constructed that the bit or portion that actuates the tumblers may be detached from the shank or handle of the key for convenience in carrying.
Flush escutcheons for one or more keyholes.
In concrete work, a joint cut into hardened concrete by means of a special blade, generally not through the full depth of the member.
Wood joints of various types that are not locked or housed, but for which the edges of two members meet in various configurations.
Full-face portrait paintings placed on Egyptian mummies of the Roman period (2nd and 3rd centuries CE), most coming from Faiyum; usually in encaustic paint on panel.
Life-size paintings of figures, usually people, occasionally animals, on thin panel cut out to give a lifelike effect; popular in the 17th and 18th centuries.

Painted wall panels of a distinctive type produced in Tuscany in the 15th and early 16th centuries. Today, they have typically been removed from their original setting and are characterized by their size and shape: Their length is two to three times longer than their height, and they are larger than cassone panels and proportionally higher. The term originally meant "backrest [for a piece of furniture]," and referred to decorative panels positioned in wall panelling at head or shoulder height, above the backrest of a piece of furniture such as a cassone, bed, or or a high-backed bench with a chest below the seat that doubled as a narrow bed (a "lettuccio"). It may also refer to any panel paintings that were set into the wall as an integral part of the wainscoting. They are often distinguished from "cornice pictures," which were installed higher on the wall in a frieze above the wooden cornice molding, forming a separate register between the wooden paneling and the bare wall just below the ceiling. Since this distinction may be lost once the panel has been removed from the wall, the term "spalliere" is often applied to both.
Paintings for which canvas is the support, typically using canvas stretched over stretcher bars or another secondary support.
Collages in which photographs dominate the composition.
Drawings or works in another medium that show the components of a structure or object disassembled and spaced apart, but remaining in their proper relation with respect to their assembled positions.

Oblique drawings, or works in another mediu, in which a vertical plane is parallel to the plane of projection, and receding planes are drawn at a scale that is somewhere between the same scale as and one-half the scale of that vertical plane.

Refers to drawings or works in another two-dimensional medium where the work is created using multiview projection, which is a system of projection in which principal faces of an object or structure are parallel to the picture plane, but multiple views of the object or structure are provided in order to fully represent all sides of it.

Refers to drawings, or works in another medium, created by oblique projection, in which parallel lines remain parallel. Typically two spatial axes are parallel to the plane of projection or drawing surface, and a third axis is projected at an angle other than 90 degrees to the plane. For drawings in which objects are depicted at an angle to the picture plane but parallel receding lines converge, use "oblique perspectives."
Drawings of elevations arranged around a plan as if the walls had been laid flat.
In shipbuilding, drawings and works in other two-dimensional media showing the layouts of decks.
Site plans containing landscaping information, such as site grading, and location and description of plantings, sprinklers, or lighting devices.
Plans that illustrate the beams and girders of each floor of a building and how they are connected. They typically use a simple system of symbols and drafting lines rather than detailed drawing.
Refers to scaled floor plans showing plumbing layout; may include an adjacent small drawing of an elevation, or a riser diagram. For other drawings of plumbing systems, use "plumbing drawings."

Orthographic drawings in which a symmetrical object is cut away so that one half of it is shown as an exterior elevation and the other as a section. For buildings thus represented, use "sectional elevations." For drawings of an incomplete section alone, use "partial sections."
Perspective drawings of portions of the exterior or interior of a structure.

Drawings done to express proposed designs in a competition, which is a formal process by which competing architects or artists submit plans to the same client or patron for the same architectural or artistic project.
Drawings that are used to communicate information about buildings, specifically the mechanics of their construction, and used by the team tasked with erecting an edifice.
Refers to assembly drawings that depict only part of the equipment or design. They generally indicate how various components should operate.
Refers to original drawings that are created by an animator as a model from which animation cels or other animation will be made.
Drawings of construction or design details. For minute parts of a larger structure, object, or image, use "details." For preparatory studies of pictorial or design details, use "detail studies."
Rose headed nails having sharp points and flat shanks.
Half-round metal strips bent into a pinlike shape whose ends can be flared after insertion through a slot or hole.
Tacks with broad heads meant to be pressed with the thumb.
Light armor made from quilted cotton cloth in postclassic central Mexico. Typically a type of sleeveless vest worn on the upper body that was particularly effective protection from arrow strikes.
Official lists that record ownership of property, mortgages, and other instruments that relate to real property, kept in official record books provided and maintained for such purpose.

Written or spoken language that is eloquent, elegant, or ornate, particularly when expressed in terms calculated to persuade. In usage, may be intended as depreciative, referring to language characterized by artificial, insincere, or ostentatious expression; inflated or empty verbiage.
Organized and often detailed proposals that lay out strategies and schemes of action for something to be done.
Forms or other documents in which physical damage is recorded.
Reports produced at three-month intervals.
Organized and often detailed proposals that lay out strategies and schemes of action for development and maintenance of a city or municipal area.

The principle treatment document for cultural landscapes and the primary tool for their long-term management. Management and treatment decisions are based on the character of the land, its historical significance, and the anticipated challenges to preservation. Typically interdisciplinary in nature, the CLR can be used for maintenance, interpretation, and planning.
Registration documents issued by the United States government to vessels of twenty tons burden or more engaging soley in domestic or coastal trade or the fisheries.

A standardized chart of the chemical elements laid out in sequence by atomic number, arranged in horizontal rows and vertical columns, called periods and groups, so that elements with similar properties are in the same column.
Books which record the collection of unpaid taxes and the seizure and sale of property due to unpaid taxes.
Official endorsements made on passports by proper officials denoting a passport has been examined and the bearer is permitted to proceed.

Documents kept by a state, city, or town official which are permanent records of marriages and which include the names of the spouses, the maiden name of the wife, their addresses, and the date of marriage.

Official lists of recorded deaths, including details considered sufficiently important to be formally noted, and maintained in a regular manner for a community; typically including the names of the deceased, dates of death, living relatives, and often location and cause of death.
Licenses granted by public authority to persons who intend to marry, usually addressed to the authorized person who is to perform the ceremony, and usually a legal prerequisite to the marriage.
Records documenting the design and construction of buildings or other structures.
Sheets of paper, cards, or other devices used to cast a vote or announce a slate of candidates.
Brief records of one's personal history, career, qualifications, and experience, such as that submitted with a job application.

Chronological registers that define working hours, shifts, or time frames applicable to proposed undertakings or creations, and that are used as input to the planning process for developing a schedule.
Books held by depositors in which a bank enters a record of the depositor's transactions.

Statements of the financial condition, as of a corporation, at a given date showing the equality of total assets to total liabilities plus net worth, or of total liabilities to total assets plus deficit.
Books in which hours spent on a job by workers are recorded.
Collections of data gathered and examined for the purpose of formulating insurance policies.
Documents authorizing a vendor to deliver materials or equipment, or to perform services, which upon acceptance constitutes a purchase contract.

Documents asserting a right, including titles to debts, privileges, or other things in possession of another; also includes titles to anything which another should give, concede, or confer on the claimant.

Guarantees provided by a bonding or surety agency to the principle shareholder of a construction project on behalf of a contractor. These bonds cover payment for equipment, labor, goods and services in the event that the contractor fails to pay for them under the terms of a contract.
Detailed and exact statements of particulars, especially statements prescribing materials, dimensions, and workmanship for something to be built, installed, or manufactured.
Agreements by which one person undertakes to secure another in the possession or enjoyment of something, such as an expressed or implied assurance of the quality or performance of goods purchased.
Contracts made between owners and builders other than general contractors for the construction of portions of a project.

Traditional Jewish marriage contracts, traditionally written in Aramaic and signed by witnesses, setting out reciprocal duties of husband and wife, including the husband's obligation to pay the wife a certain sum in the event of divorce, and the wife's property rights upon his death.
Types of contracts in which the buyer agrees to pay the seller a definite, predetermined price.
Detailed and exact statements of particulars describing materials, dimensions, and workmanship for the manufacture or installation of commercial products.
Records evidencing the creation or existence of a corporate body, such as charters or articles of incorporation; also used generally to refer to records growing out of a corporate enterprise.
Records originating with or maintained by a government and available for access by the public.
Records documenting deliberations and decisions of a legislative body.
Official records containing the names, dates of entry, ages, occupations, and other information about immigrants to a country, typically taken at the point of entry.
Lists of troops actually present, made on the day of muster or review of troops in order to take account of their condition; used as the paymaster's voucher for the pay he issued.
Commands to appear at a certain time and place to give testimony upon a certain matter.
Written communications from a court, usually a probate court, or an officer informing an executor of his appointment and authority to execute the will of the testator.
Collected documents on investigation and reporting related to legislation, policy making, correspondence, or the political environment of the U.S. Senate.
Records made or received by the governing body of incorporated localities.

Particular types of formal documents issued by the pope and sealed with a bulla (a round, usually leaden seal) or sealed with a red-ink imprint of the device on the bulla. Papal bulls were originally issued by the pope for many kinds of public communication, but since the 15th century have been reserved only for particular types of solemn written communication in which the pope refers to himself as "episcopus servus servorum Dei," meaning "Bishop, Servant of the Servants of God." Scholars may use the term to describe any elaborate historical papal document issued in the form of a decree, privilege, and sometimes in the form of a letter.
Any of various records kept by the parish, including lists of members, activities, and expenditures.

Collections of materials including teaching material, publications, conference papers, research files, information about grants, curricula, and other materials related to the scholarly and teaching activities of the faculty at a given school or university.
Papers or other documents presenting a student's research on a particular topic and submitted as a qualification of completing a semester or other term of school or college.
Maps, charts, or plans that show the location, boundaries, and ownership of individual properties.
Medieval marine charts, used before compasses, and for Medieval navigation manuals, illustrated with charts and showing the location of ports and other navigational information.
Globes that are both celestial and terrestrial.
Maps in which aerial distribution is shown by distinctive colors or tints; most geological, soil, and political maps are of this type.
Maps that show the actual routes and types of construction of wire circuits in an area.
Maps which show the spatial distribution of water balance components and water resources.
Maps indicating the location of watermains in a building or buildings.
Charts or maps showing the movements or progress of a ship, submarine, airplane, or other craft.
Charts of the sea, especially those used for navigational purposes.
Maps on which relief is made to appear three-dimensional by the use of graded shadow effect.
Maps depicting all or most of the surface of the Earth.
Maps made by superimposing cartographic data on an aerial photograph.
Prints made on light-sensitized surfaces that produce white images on brown backgrounds. For brown images on neutral backgrounds use "brownline prints" or "sepia prints."

Prints made on light-sensitized surfaces that produce brown lines on neutral backgrounds. For white images on brown backgrounds, use "brownprints." For brownline prints on translucent paper, use "sepia prints."
Programming whose source code is open to all rather than proprietary.

Manuscript volumes comprising two or more works, whether referring to only the content combined or to the combination of physically separate leafs or gatherings that are sewn or tipped in to form one volume.
Transparent films bearing microphotographs of documents, images, etc, to be read on specially designed equipment. The support is typically a fine grain, high resolution film in roll form.

Criminals who make fraudulent fabrications with intent to deceive (of artwork, of documents, etc.). For people who copy with the intent of making a surrogate or other replica for study or another non-criminal reason, use "copyists."

People or corporate bodies who pay for or plan and carry out projects or activities, or otherwise assume primary responsibility for them. For those who support individuals, institutions, or causes but do not necessarily take primary responsibility for them, use "patrons."  For  those who contribute volunteer work, money, or public expressions of support through membership in a voluntary association, use "friends."
Workers possessing skills in a limited range of activities that demand less training, experience, and independent judgement than is required of skilled workers.
Those who have been awarded a bachelor's degree.

Students in educational institutions providing the first stage of compulsory education, generally extending from grade 1 through grades 6 or 8 and teaching the rudiments of learning; may house a kindergarten.
Those who have entered into an alliance with others, including both individuals and organizations such as sovereign states.
People unable to produce oral speech or to produce oral speech that is easily understood by others, due to physical, biological, or psychological condition, or because of choice.
Those taken by capture or surrender into the power of the enemy during war, especially military personnel.
In ancient Greece, young male citizens of around 18-20 years of age, who were taken from their homes and occupied chiefly with garrison duty.
Young children within the first year or few years of being able to walk.
Refers in the aggregate to military, naval and air forces of any nation.
Associations of artists, wherein members of each group collaborate in a formal manner.
Organizations that regulate, promote, supervise, or protect commercial or business enterprises.
A club in which the subscriptions are expended in the purchase or borrowing of books for the common use of the members.
Accumulated groups of objects or materials having a focal characteristic and that have been brought together or are maintained by a corporate body.
Interrelated systems or organizations that operate for the satisfaction of an important social need or function, such as family, economy, health, or education.

Associations of people, usually men, joined for mutual help, support, protection, or action. For social fraternities, which are local or national organizations of male college students and which typically have names composed of two or three Greek letters, use "fraternities"; however, usage may overlap.

Refers to notes, scribbles, sketches or doodles made by the artist outside the design on a plate to be printed. The practice started as a way of testing the strength of the acid on a plate about to be etched before risking the biting of the image. Remarques were usually burnished away before printing, though occasionally some marginal marks were deliberately left in some printed editions to exploit the collector's desire for rarities. See also "remarque proofs."

City directories usually contain an alphabetical list of businesses and residents for a municipality. Names of heads of households are included and in some cases, death dates, partners in firms, or forwarding addresses. Often these also include advertisements, information about schools, churches, and social organizations.
Published alphabetical lists of post offices in particular regions, often will additional information on staff and administration.
Guidebooks aimed at those involved in the transportation of cargo.
Histories in which events are described in chronological order. For records of events in yearly sequence but less connected or filled out by commentary or interpretation, use "annals."

Books or documents given to employees by an employer that gather information about the employer’s policies and procedures regarding full or part-time employment, benefits, conduct and discipline, performance reviews and other relevant details.
Books or booklets containing the text or words of an opera or similar extended musical composition.
Blessings for the home, including cards and plaques, often displayed near the entrance of the home. Common to several cultures.
Written forms of stories prepared for motion picture productions, including description of characters, details of scenes and settings, dialogue, and stage directions.
Includes bibliographies that list all the books and other publications published or distributed in a particular country and bibliographies that list publications about a particular country.

Includes finding aids that give a general account of the holdings of one or more archives, including background history, usually arranged by record group, thereunder by series; also, finding aids that describe the holdings of one or more archives relating to particular subjects or to specified types of documents.
Indexes in which each significant element of a multiword index entry appears as a filing element.
Indexes in which each significant word in an entry is separated from the entry on separate lines of their own, with the full entry in original order under them.
Indexes which combine separately published indexes into one sequence.
Lists of subject terms that provide access to a classification or the contents of a publication, catalogue or collection.
Single-leaf forerunners of newspapers. For similar items consisting of more than one leaf, use "newsbooks."
Photocopied or offset-printed limited edition serial publications featuring graphic arts, designed and produced by one or more artists.
Thesauri consisting of sets of terms in multiple languages.
Books in which to keep records of a child's birth and development through infancy, usually in the form of an album to hold pictures and other memorabilia as well as text.

Documents that announce the birth of a child. Often these include the parents' names, and sometimes physical details of the child. This term may be extended to printed cards, newspaper listings, electronic mailings, or other historical forms.
Offers to perform a contract for work and labor or to supply materials or goods at a specified price.
Calendars that highlight religious events and activities for specific days.
In Christian churches, the lists of dates for liturgical feast days and days of fasting for each year.

Cards issued singly or in sets since the 19th century, primarily to be collected, bearing a wide variety of types of images, such as sports figures, movie stars, or flowers. If cards include advertising, use also "advertising cards"; if cards accompany a product, use also "premiums." For cards bearing tradesmen's advertisements, and sometimes a variety of images, produced from the 17th through the 19th century, use also "trade cards."
Printed cards intended to be exchanged between people to express romantic interest.
Postcards that have on one side an image produced with light-sensitive materials directly on the card.
Certificates attesting to the country of manufacture of a commodity, often required by the customs office before importation.
Graphic representations of symbols connected with lines showing the successive steps in a procedure or systems.
Pieces of correspondence that are somewhat more formal than memoranda or notes, usually on paper and delivered.
Letters, memorandums, or postcards which are printed and stocked in advance of actual use and usually contain prepared spaces for insertion of information.
Correspondence, typically written letters or notes, from one person to another.

Refers to a set of statistical techniques that analyze data sets with more than one variable when there is inherent interdependence between them. Techniques of multivariate analysis include cluster and factor analysis. Multivariate analysis is often used in archaeology, e.g. to aid classification of artifact compositional data.

Collections of materials, such as pamphlets, cuttings, and pictures, which are ephemeral in nature. The documents are often of varying sizes and typically unbound, stored in drawers or on their edges in special supports that allow vertical rather than horizontal storage.
Collections of sheet or folded maps, that are often large and flat, requiring shelves or drawers with special dimensions and allowing flat storage, as opposed to upright storage.
Graphic diagrams that plot the relationship between two variables. The relationship is plotted by points against these, the points joined by a broken line to illustrate fluctuation in variables.

Refers to books containing the daily, personal accounts of the writer's own experiences, attitudes, and observations. Use "journals (accounts)" when referring to an individual's or an organization's account of occurrences or transactions.
Registers of brand designs belonging to various livestock owners.
Notes made in the course of scientific inquiry conducted in a controlled environment.
Promotional print media intended to highlight a music concert, recording, or artist. These often combine text and images.

Guides, usually printed, to the motion pictures or other features composing a motion picture theater presentation. These often include the credits of a motion picture, as well as coming attractions and other advertising.

People with the skill or ability to detect the presence of water, minerals, treasure, archaeological remains, and even dead bodies located underground by means of a divining rod. Dowsers grasp the rod by its two prongs and appear to receive transmissions from the hidden substance or object that cause involuntary muscular contractions, which in turn make the rod bend, twist, or quiver violently. Some dowsers claim to be ableto detect buried substances merely by passing a divining rod over amap of the area where the substance lies hidden. This ability has as yet no scientific explanation, but dowsers generally deny that divination is part of the process.
Artists who specialze in carving depictions, whether in relief or in the round.
Those who make casts in the medium of plaster; examples are in creating stuccowork and casting forms.
Persons who engage in ceramic arts, manufacturing, or technology.

People or corporate bodies who make objects of glass, which is an inorganic substance made by fusing silica (silicon dioxide) with a basic oxide, generally transparent but often translucent or opaque.
Persons that finish leather.
Metalworkers who do decorative work by chasing, which is the process of adding detail or ornament on metal by indenting with a hammer or other tools without cutting edges.
Metalworkers whose work is considered art or high crafts.
People who knit, which is the creation of handmade works or material created by interlacing loops of a long or continuous piece of yarn or thread by means of two needles.
Tradespeople who weave cotton cloth, historically speaking, before the advent of the Industrial Revolution, beginning in the Middle Ages.
Those whose occupation it is to saw timber into planks or lumber roughly prepared to sell.
Makers of vessels, tableware, vases, and other ware out of ceramic.
Craftsmen who specialize in making chests and other relatively simple case furniture.
People who assess the characteristics of diamonds such as weight, cut, color, and clarity to be noted on diamond certificates.
Administrators of a commandery, usually associated with a medieval religious military order, such as the Knights Hospitallers.
General term for people having a job or position where others are subordinate to them. They may be in charge of a particular activity or function within an organization.
People who manage and oversee the operations of a manufactory, which is an operation that makes articles primarily by hand.

The principal ministers of a sovereign, ruler, or state. In modern contexts, the head of an elected government who is the chief officer of the executive branch of government in countries which have a parliamentary system.
People who are the top-level administrators for an administrative department.

In modern contexts, refers to officers having this title and appointed by or with the authority of a government to reside in a foreign country in order to represent the interests of citizens of the appointing country. Also refers to the chief magistrates of Republican Rome and of the First French Republic, 1799-1804, who bore this title.
Legislators elected to represent constituencies within the provinces or major subdivisions of their country in its primary governing body.
Those who assume the position of head of a monarchy in the minority, absence, or disability of the monarch.
Refers to rulers or leaders of clans, tribes, or other groups. The term typically carries the connotation of rulers who are also military leaders.

Authors who write or compile detailed and continuous registers of events in order of time; especially those in which the facts are narrated without philosophic treatment, or any attempt at literary style.
People who observe and bring back an account of a news event or situation, usually also writing or narrating the account for broadcast, newspapers, journals, radio, television, or online.
Reporters for law reports and journals, who write summaries of the decisions of a court of record.
People who are members of the faculty at a college, university, or other institutions of post-secondary education.
Those whose principal occupation or training is in military history.

Persons who administer libraries and perform related library services, including acquiring and processing library materials, and furnishing reference and other services to patrons. Also any other persons employed in a library with professional qualifications.
Librarians who manage the reference collection of a library and assist library patrons to find the information they seek in it.
Experts in orthography, which is the art of correct or proper spelling according to standard accepted usage or convention.
Refers to those who study the values relating to human conduct, with respect to the rightness and wrongness of certain actions and to the goodness and badness of the motives and ends of such actions.

Painter-scribes who created codices in Aztec society. They were responsible for recording important historical events, religious knowledge, dynastic genealogies, and cultural landscapes. Codices were typically made using carbon and other pigments applied to gessoed amate paper, deer skin, woven cotton, or other materials. After the Spanish Conquest, the tlahcuilohqueh continued producing codices, but created a mixed system that combined glyphic writing, pictography, and the Latin alphabet.
Those who specialize in the comparative study of human physical evolution, variation, and classification, especially through measurement and observation of living people as well as human remains.
Those who delineate, chart, or survey the topography of a geographic area.
Those professionally engaged in the field of horticultural therapy.

People who supervise the development, care, and management of forests or forest parks, including officers in charge of public forests and those who look after the growing of timber on an estate. For people who hunt, use "hunters (people)."
Persons with authority to decide in a contest or competition or to arbitrate disputes, advise counsel, jury, litigants, or court personnel, and administer judicial systems.
Public officials who institute legal proceedings against someone, particularly in a legal case against a defendant in a criminal court.

American term used to refer to people, often volunteers working without pay, who conduct guided groups through a museum, art gallery, historical home, or other place. Also refers to teachers or lecturers in American universities who are not on the salaried staff, often post-graduate students.
Creators of dances and dance movements.
Dancers, usually young females, who perform any of various styles of dance from north India.
Those who create musical pieces.
Those who lead or direct the singing of the choir or congregation in a church, monastic establishment, or cathedral, especially officials of that title in certain churches.

Individuals who specialize in daguerreotypes, which are created by using an early photographic process (invented by L.J.M. Daguerre) that produces a direct positive image on a silver-coated copper plate.
Highly skilled printers who work very closely with artists to produce editions of the artists' work.
Religious officials or functionaries authorized to perform duties in accordance with Christianity.
Members of a monastery or friary who devote themselves only to manual labor and other secular affairs, remaining exempt from the studies and choir duties required of the other members.
Mathematicians specializing in the measurement, relationships and properties of points, lines, curves, angles, surfaces, and solid figures.

Scientists trained or working in the branch of physical science that deals with the composition and properties of the elementary substances of which all bodies are composed, the laws that regulate their combination, and the various phenomena that accompany their exposure to diverse physical conditions.
Those who are expert in the branch of biology that deals with micro-organisms such as bacteria, viruses, and fungi.
Zoologists trained or working in the scientific study of birds.
People who are experts in the chemical composition of the earth.
Geologists who specialize in the study of minerals, including their formation, occurrence, properties, composition, and classification.
Those who perform manual or operative procedures to treat diseases, injuries, or deformities.
Physicists specializing in deducing the consequences of established physical theories using mainly the method of mathematical solution.
Internal combustion engines driven by a mixture of gaseous fuel and air.
Turbines in which the rotor is driven by fluid jets impinging directly against the blades.

Tools consisting of a either a flat rectangular blade, made of metal or rubber; or of a series of wire or rubber bristles attached to a long wooden or metal handle that are used to suppress a fire by beating out flames in brushes or crops.

Air-blowing tools of varied design but that share an attached pair of bowl-like chambers with long ducts emerging from the base of each. A diaphragm is fitted over each chamber, and these are manipulated to draw and force air from the bellows.
Refers to the hardware required to display or use audiovisual materials such as filmstrip viewers, projection equipment, videocassette recorders, and compact disk players.

Cutting tools that consist of a relatively heavy edged, squarish head fixed to a handle, the edge or edges being parallel to the handle so as to be suited for striking, hewing, cleaving, or chopping, trees, wood, ice, or another material. For axes used as weapons, typically having wider blades, use "axes (weapons)." For similar tools that are smaller and lighter, use "hatchets." For long-handled tools with a curved blade set perpendicular to the handle and used for dressing lumber, use "adzes."

Hand-held implements having a long shaft mounted with a curved metal head with a sharpened point at one end and an adze-like blade at the other; for similar implements, but lacking the adze-like blade, use "pick-axes."
Knives designed for the kitchen or cookery.
Lightweight metal-cutting hand saws with a narrow fine-toothed blade retained in an adjustable metal frame.

U-shaped fasteners, with a pin or bolt passing through holes in the two prongs, allowing for it to be bolted on to another object to form a loop to which tackle may be attached. Clevises are used in a variety of applications including for farming, sailing, automotive, aircraft and construction industries.
Screwdrivers that are operated by the reciprocating motion of the handle which enables the user to drive a screw easily.

Mills that employ cylinders or are in the shape of a cylinder. Examples include cylindrical containers built to varying length-to-diameter ratios and are partially filled with flint stones, iron or steel balls, or other grinding bodies that tumble under the influence of gravity by revolving the container. Other examples include devices that grind grain or other materials by means of two counter-rotating roughened cylinders turning at different speeds.
Mortars made specifically for use with a pestle for grinding tobacco into snuff. The object may be a combination container and mortar and pestle.
Handheld devices that throw flame using kerosene as fuel. These usually have a tank for the accelerant, and facilities for adjusting the oxygen flow.
Mechanical devices commonly used to hold items together or firmly in place while other operations are being performed.

Instruments used for seizing and holding objects or delicate tissues such as blood vessels, mainly in surgical operations, but in extended use as tools with a variety of purposes. They have long handles with grips like manicure scissors, a provision for clamping into fixed positions, and curved or straight tips.
Pliers with long, narrow, flat jaws.

Carrying tools for moving railroad ties. The jaws are wide enough to engage a tie, the sharpened ends reaching under or into the side of the tie. The arms move away from each other so they automatically clamp when the tool is lifted, and requires two people to handle.
Clamps used to hold wire while it is filed and hammered into a rivet head.
Utensils that are intended to sweep ashes from in or around fireplaces, often designed as part of a set of fireplace tools.
Automatic pumps that use the kinetic energy of descending water to raise the water above its original height.

Relatively slender, pointed instruments used for piercing, picking, scratching, engraving, or for other purposes.Common uses of needles include to draw thread or other fiber through cloth, leather, paper, skin and tissue, or another flexible material; as hollow, to inject a liquid; for engraving or etching metal. Historically, needles have been made of bronze, iron, bone, glass, steel, and other materials.
Hoses used to convey water to extinguish fires. These are usually made to withstand high pressurization.
Steel stamps with a positive impression of designs to be reproduced in reverse on dies to make coins or medals.
Prehistoric hammering implements consisting of rounded stones.
General term for small- to medium-size hammers having a cross peen which tapers down to a narrow edge and if forked for drawing nails; used for general purposes by a variety of tradesmen.
Mallets or hammers used to make noise, for commanding attention or confirming an action; often used with a striking block. Examples are as used by a judge or presiding officer, or by an auctioneer.

Relatively large hand tools having a chisel or pick head, used for breaking up rocks; operated by swinging the tool with the arms. For similar but much smaller tools for breaking up rocks, use "rock hammers."

Framing or form made of wood, steel, or plastic that serves as a support during construction, particularly as used to support the load of an arch, vault or dome during construction, for the pouring of liquid concrete in a foundation, and in other contexts.
Scrapers with a wide flat blade; used primarily for cleaning walls of wallpaper.
Tools powered by the compression or exhaustion of air.
Continuous bands of tough, flexible material such as leather, fabric, rubber, or wire; used for transmitting motion and power from one pulley to another or for conveying materials.
Bits used to inscribe, smooth, and cut out circles from thin bone plates in the production of buttons.
Handles in the form of relatively small masses, usually rounded, and projecting from a surface or extremity.
Persons authorized to examine and verify accounts.
Architects working with other architects in a temporary agreement or partnership of joint venture.
Persons employed in the construction of boats.
Masons who place the great blocks of stone accurately into position in a building.
Contractors who have contracts directly with an owner.
Those trained or working in bioengineering.
Engineers who design bridges, dams, buildings, and other structures.

Those trained and working in the field of study and practice that falls between and overlaps architecture and urban and regional planning, and whose concern is the specific design and contextual integration of urban buildings and spaces; includes expertise in, for example, landscape architecture, urban sociology, environmental psychology, and law.
People who produce work in the visual arts. For those in the performing arts, see "performing artists."
Painters who paint human figures, whether as the primary subject of the painting or as subsidiary elements of the composition.
Painters who use the medium of encaustic paint, a paint created by mixing dry pigments with molten, refined wax and resin.
Printmakers who create collotypes, which are prints made by a particular photomechanical process.
Printmakers who work in mezzotint, in which a plate is roughened with a rocker and lighter designs are created by smoothing the rough areas.
Those who etch on stone.
Lithographers who create plates depicting other works, from which it is intended to print reproductions in relatively large numbers.
Manufacturers or modelers of terracotta, particularly the makers of figurines or architectural detail in ancient Greece.

Persons engaged in designing clothing, accessories, and ensembles intended to create an appearance characteristic of a particular period, person, place, or thing, especially (but not exclusively) for theatrical performances.
People authorized to represent or act on behalf of someone else, particularly in business transactions.
Agents of an insurer authorized to negotiate contracts of insurance.

People or corporate bodies that produce artillery, which are firearms generally having a bore of over one inch in diameter, designed to be supported on a gun mount or carriage when operated, and requiring a crew of at least two people.
People who acquire books and other bound materials in order to establish a collection.
Professionals who engage in the buying and selling of diamonds.
Merchants selling second-hand books, leaflets, and prints of little value, such as those working outdoors alongside the Seine River in Paris.
Refers to those who sell food or small goods from temporary positions on the street.  For those who move about selling small goods from door to door or on the street, see "peddlers."
Handmade papermaking tools which consist of a removable rectangular frame that forms the raised edge of the wire cloth of the mold and holds the stock suspension on the wire.
Devices comprising a clamp and a cutting plane, used for cutting stacks of books, folios, or other paper.
Knives used for cutting rushes or weaving them.

Hand-held, sharp, and hollow instruments used in the production of wool rugs, wherein the wool passes through a canvas backing to create a tufted surface. These instruments, typically comprising a hollow shank, wooden handle, and needle eye, are used to push woolen fibers through the backing fabric; when the needle is removed, a length of tuft in continuous loops is left on the surface of the backing.
Handlooms used for weaving long strips of braid.

Hand sewing tools used to weave loose ends of yarn back into a hand-knitted item when completing a knitting work. These are long needles with two ends that taper to a semi-point at each end, which also include a single eye with a beveled edge that extends through the length of the needle. Due to their design features, these sewing tools can make use of shorter lengths of yarn more easily than conventional needles, and can finish large knitted items or items with multiple colors more rapidly than conventional needles.
Small wood tools used to give tension to the webbing which forms the foundation in most types of upholstery.
Sharp-pointed steel instruments used for laying out work, especially on hard wood.
Axes having a large, broad blade bevelled on one side, used for the rough dressing of timber.
Chisels with straight sides which flare rapidly at the blade, forming a fan shape.
Long narrow chisels used for mortising.
Hardened steel plates containing holes of various diameters; used to cut dowels by driving pegs through the holes to remove excess wood.
Drawknives used to cut an oblique surface.
Tools having a hatchet blade and a hammer face; used for cutting and nailing wood lath.
Two-handled curved knives used in woodworking; similar knives may be used in other occupations. The knives are utilized by pulling them toward the user.
Tools with a sharp edge and used for reducing, leveling, and smoothing wood.
Planes whose iron is set on a skew; used to cut grooves across the grain of wood.
Planes in which the mouth and edge of the iron are obliquely across the face.
Bench planes with a slightly curved blade; used for smoothing flat surfaces of rough boards.
Two-man, two-handled planes used to make the edges of boards smooth and square in the joining of long staves.
Any kind of large complex molding plane which is pulled.
Short steel bars, square in section, with one end tapered to a chisel point and bent slightly backwards; used for tightening the nuts of handrail bolts.
Power-driven saws, usually hand-held, with a protruding arm that carries an endless chain into which the cutting teeth are set.
Small backsaws, about 9 inches in length, with thin blades, fine teeth, and straight handles; used for accurate work, as in cabinetmaking and patternmaking.
Curved saws supported on a frame on a fulcrum, which can swing back and forth, cutting as it does.
Light hand saws with a narrow blade mounted in a U-shaped frame with a handle; used to cut curves in wood. The blade may be rotated to keep the frame away from the work.
Large saws whose teeth are filed and set to cut across the grain of wood, providing more of a knife action in the cutting than ripsaws; designed for either one or two people.
Type of compass saw with teeth at the heel edge that are set out at 90 degrees to the blade; used to cut corners.
Special tools used to grip and insert brads in an inaccessible location.
Clamps in the shape of the letter C in which force is applied by rotating a threaded shaft through one jaw of the C to force the work against the other jaw; frequently used in carpentry and joinery.
Hammers used with the a driver to drive hoops tightly down onto the cone shape of a barrel in coopering.

Mallets whose head is a well-rounded truncated cone mounted upside down on a short handle. The shape enables the carver to strike the chisel from any angle without altering the hand's position on the tool.

Trowels made for incense, used for scooping, burning, or cleaning. Examples are ritual objects in the Jewish religion, recorded as having been used in the Temple of Jerusalem to clean the lamps of the menorah.
Maori spades or digging sticks, used for lighter cultivation work.

Kites used in the activity of fishing, in which the kite supports a drop line attached to a lure or bait. The kite is flown over the surface of a body of water, and the bait floats near the waterline until taken by a fish.
Specialized monitoring devices that utilize a sex pheromone attractant to lure a particular insect to the trap.
Bent or curved devices with one or more, usually barbed points, tied to one end of a line for catching fish.
Large nets having one edge provided with sinkers and the other with floats that hangs vertically in the water and encloses fish when its ends are brought together or drawn ashore.
Poles with a sharply pointed end and a hook, used by lumbermen in river driving and by tracklayers in aligning railroad ties.
Containers that are used to protect and transport astronomical instruments.
Instruments that measure rates of plant growth; they consist of levers with two arms (long and short), which are attached to plants.
Artifacts originally created to be used in the observation and recording of light, including general-purpose optical equipment.

Handheld computers first developed in the late 1980s and early 1990s, that had a miniature keyboard and handwriting-recognition software. Originally meant to perform simple tasks such as calculation and organizing, they have since become more advanced. Most PDAs now have the ability to act as a mobile phone, surf the Internet, and run more advanced software.
Devices that enable data to be transmitted between computers, generally over telephone lines but sometimes on fiber-optic cable or radio frequencies.
Printers that print complete pages of output in one cycle.
Electrophotographic printers in which a laser is used as the light source.
Devices that increase the physical vibrations of sound, whether by mechanical or electronic means.
Motor-driven machines employing an endless chain or parallel chains transmitting the pull from a driving unit, and used for the continuous transport of material.

Devices that generate electromagnetic radiation in the ultraviolet, visible, or infrared spectrum, in the form of a very narrow continuous or intermittent beam. Originally an acronym for "light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation;" the first functional laser was built by Theodore H. Maiman (1927-2007), and demonstrated in 1960. Lasers have multiple applications: they are used as components in information retrieval and transmission devices and systems, cutting, measuring, and medical tools, and as entertainment devices.

Microscopes in which a beam of electrons is focused by means of magnetic and electrostatic lenses onto a specimen and scattered by it to produce an image. The resolving power and the magnification of an electron microscope are much greater than can be obtained with an optical icroscope. microscope. The specimen must be examined in a vacuum, which necessitates special techniques for preparing it, and the electrons are usually focused onto a fluorescent screen (for direct viewing) or onto a photographic plate.
Machines for producing a physical effect, usually the conversion of energy into motion or propulsion.

A school of Japanese Buddhism founded by the militant Japanese Buddhist reformer Nichiren (1222-1282). Nichiren rejected other forms of Buddhism, and believed that the 'Lotus Sutra' contained the ultimate truth and asked the Japanese people to convert to this true Buddhism. Today there are almost 40 sub-sects, with Nichiren Shoshu being the largest and most important.
Articles or physical resources used to array, dress up, rig out, equip, or otherwise provide with what is requisite for efficient action by a person or animal or for a thing.
