(Sometimes also used for building ships.). Dry docks are known in the historical record as early as the 10th century in China.

Structures extending from the shoreline out over the sea or tidal river, to protect or partially enclose a harbor and form a landing place for vessels, or to serve as a recreational or entertainment place. A pier may also be a projecting landing stage or jetty on the bank of a river or lake.  For structures built along or parallel to the shoreline serving as landing, loading, or unloading places for vessels, use "wharves" or "quays."
Buildings designed or used to test, for example, nontraditional construction methods, new materials, or new building system technologies.

Structures built for festivals, ceremonies, processions, and funerals, particularly when referring to such structures dating to the 17th and 18th centuries in Europe. They may take many forms, including the form of a monument, building, or sculpture. Although macchine may be portable, for more modern portable structures used in parades, use "floats (vehicles)."
Buildings or collections of buildings and facilities for carrying out forest management.

Detached structures in domestic contexts containing one or more seats and a pit serving as toilets; distinguished from "latrines" which are similar structures in public contexts. For rooms that are within buildings and have such simple facilities, use "privies."

Refers to caves that are utilized, generally having been excavated or otherwise altered, for sheltering humans or animals, or for use as storage, worship, or another use. This term may overlap in meaning with "rock-cut architecture," but cave architecture is not necessarily rock-cut, and rock-cut architecture is not necessarily designed around a cave.
Long ridges of earth, rocks, or gravel primarily constructed to carry a roadway; if built to retain water, use "levees" or "dikes."
Sloping cut surfaces through hills or ridges caused by excavations for roads.
Large mounds of earth or debris that were constructed for ceremonial purposes, usually built by ancient peoples and sometimes with an unknown purpose.
Refuse heaps which mark ancient settlements, often containing bones, shells, potsherds, and stone implements.
Former man-made watercourses.

In the United Kingdom, buildings placed on the Statutory List of Buildings of Special Architectural or Historic Interest. Such buildings are deemed to have unique architectural or historical importance, as identified through periodic surveys; they are protected from  demolition or alteration.
Gardens designed to require little or no watering, typically containing ornamental rocks and stones, or plants that thrive in dry conditions.
Formal gardens that employ a geometric design.

Gardens designed for use by the handicapped or the elderly that include such features as easliy accessible and well-marked paths, raised beds, rest areas, and plants with enhanced fragrance and textures. For gardens designed to improve and maintain the pysical and mental health of the ill or injured, use "healing gardens."

Gardens, situated on rooftops, typically in urban areas above private houses or commercial buildings. The depth of soil is limited to keep the weight low and the plants are usually set in tubs or similar containers, but elaborate roof gardens have been constructed with small pools and beds.
Gardens in which primarily vegetables are grown; normally of modest size, although may be extensive.
Planned spaces that are open to the public, usually located outdoors, and focused on plants and other natural or landscaped features.

Nature reserves inhabited by indigenous peoples of Australia that have been designated as protected by the Australian Government. Traditional indigenous owners of the land enter into voluntary agreement with the Govenment to establish the boundaries of the area, in order to promote biodiversity and to preserve cultural resource conservation. An IPA is considered part of the National Reserve System of Australia.
Historic sites where significant battles are memorialized; used specifically in reference to Civil War battlefield sites in the United States, some of which are also National Parks.
Recreational parks that are open to the public.
Open outdoor spaces adjacent to school buildings used for free or regimented play, or for other purposes.
Roads for which points of entrance and exit for traffic are controlled by limiting the number of access roads.
Limited access highways located within a park or parklike setting and intended for only passenger cars and noncommercial traffic.
Accessways for cars and pedestrians that end in a court or courtyard area.
Roads that are dug out of the surrounding landscape, having a path lower than ground level.

The term chidao, literally “speed” and “way” (Kroll 2015, 51, 79), was first used in the Qin dynasty (221-206 BCE) to refer to national expressways for the emperor's tours and military affairs. The roadways were first established in the Warring States Period (475-221 BCE); in the Qin dynasty, the First Emperor (Qin Shihuang) expanded them from Xianyang to all parts of the country. New roads were built during the Han, Sui, and Ming Dynasties. Chidao were very wide and were divided into three lanes, with the middle lane being exclusively used by the emperor. After the Eastern Han dynasty (25-220 CE), chidao had two meanings. (1) Chidao located near the imperial palace were strongly associated with imperial authority and the term was gradually used interchangeably with “middle road” (zhongdao 中道), “imperial road” (yudao 禦道), and “defensive road” (yulu 禦路). (2) Between cities and counties, the military and transportation functions of chidao were emphasized. During the Ming and Qing dynasties and into the twentieth century, the term chidao was used generally to refer to common roadways (Ban 1962, 2242, 2888; Wei 1974, 68; Zhu 1984, 705; Wang 2012).
An unpaved, or earth, road.
Small public squares in towns or landscaped pedestrian spaces adjacent to office buildings or parking areas.
Covered outdoor walkways.
Expanses of land, paved or green, owned by the community as a whole.

Distinctions among villages, towns, and cities are relative and vary according to their individual regional contexts. Generally, cities designate large or important communities with population, status, and internal complexity greater than most towns in the region.
Settlements in which almost all the habitations are confined to a defined area. The nucleus is usually surrounded by agricultural land.
Late Iron Age and Roman period native settlements in Europe, often hillforts or otherwise lightly fortified, located as centers within the territory of local tribes.

Refers to certain cities, towns, or colonies in the Roman Empire and Republic, or later on the Italian peninsula, originally where citizens assumed communal obligation in exchange for the privileges and protections of citizenship. Eventually two orders of municipia developed, one where citizens had the right to vote and other rights if Roman, the other with lesser rights if they were tribal centers under Roman control.
Designated places, may be settled but not necessarily so, where people gather to exchange goods or produce. Emporia that are not settlements are often found in rural or in historical contexts.
County seats in Louisiana.
Inhabited places established as an outpost or for another reason on the frontier of a nation, empire, or other ruling entity.
Villages, towns, or cities located on or near the water, around a marina.
Physical locations, such as a city or district, regarded as constituting a central point for trade or some other activity.

Urban areas or communities within them whose design incorporates innovative attempts at solving specific social and physical problems; often applied to the redesign of existing settlements in the 19th and 20th centuries. For 19th-century cities built with prescribed forms to fulfill specific military or economic ideals, use "ideal cities."

Rural settlements occupied primarily by artists in environments perceived to be sympathetic to creative endeavors; historically, formed especially to escape urban life or to be near nature or simple country life.
Shantytowns in or near cities in Brazil.

Systems that supply water to and between buildings and other structures or to or from locations within communities or agricultural landscapes; use "plumbing systems" for water distribution systems within buildings.
Telecommunication system whereby sound and code signals are transmitted through space without wires by means of radio frequency electromagnetic waves.
Mexican artificial fields made arable by piling onto the planting areas silt dredged from a criss-crossing series of irrigation canals plus organic wastes.
Streams contributing its flow to a larger stream or lake. For streams flowing away from a larger stream, use "distributaries (streams)."
Facilities that maintain statistics and provide information about poisoning, overdoses, and exposure to toxic substances, typically including where to find treatment for poisoning.
Hospitals specializing in the treatment of diseases and injuries of children.

Long-term residential care facilities providing as their primary and predominant function round-the-clock skilled nursing care for the elderly or chronically ill. Distinguished from "rest homes" which have less emphasis on comprehensive nursing care and are residential, rather than institutional, environments.

Urban buildings for the housing and care of homeless, lost, or abandoned animals, primarily dogs, cats, and other pets. Typically the animal is kept at the shelter until it is reclaimed by its owner, adopted by a new owner, placed with another organization, or euthanized.
In Indian architecture, an almshouse.
Buildings designated to receive all or selected government publications, with the provision that public access to the collections be provided.

Buildings or spaces housing collections of books that are available to the public and typically maintained by public funds, as distinguished from libraries available only to a certain group or individual.
Military buildings used for social functions.
Enclosure walls, usually fortified, around Irish castles and some Irish houses.

Fortifications consisting of a wooden or stone keep built on a mound of raised earth and a bailey, surrounded by a palisade and ditch. This type of castle was used in Northern Europe from the 10th until the end of the 13th century.

Fortress-monastery complexes in Bhutanese and Tibetan architectures. The dzong served as a stronghold against enemies in the past, and it now plays an important role as a combined administrative center and monastery.
Defensive enclosures comprised of ramparts and ditches encircling a fortified structure on a central prominence; common in Bronze Age and Iron Age Europe.
Underground structures hardened against attack and designed for the storage and firing of missiles.
Buildings for the shelter or accommodation of military guards, sometimes in which prisoners are temporarily detained under guard.
Buildings or monuments commemorating those killed in war, often specifically for those from the local area and from one particular war, and frequently inscribed with the names of the fallen.

Christian religious monument in the form of a column and dedicated to the Virgin Mary, erected as a gesture of public faith, as a plague column, or for another purpose. Common in Catholic countries of Europe, especially in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Structures shaped like crosses.

Tall, upright megalithic stone monuments found in Europe, Africa, or Asia, and dating to prehistoric or very ancient times. The term typically refers to stones that occur singly, though it is may be used to refer to individual stones within a row, circle, or other configuration.

Malls or other arrangements of multiple corporate offices, generally for different companies, designed with pedestrian access between offices, and typically having only one story or a small number of stories.
Built works designed for or used for live performances, as distinguished from movie theaters.
Cinemas with ornate architecture and interior decoration, emerging in the 1920s. The exterior of the movie palace is often outfitted with a marquee and an upright, showcasing the cinema's name.

Large, luxurious, and well-equipped hotels featuring distinguished architecture, which are designed to present travelers with an experience reminiscent of the ambiance of life in European palaces. Usage is generally restricted to buildings erected from the mid-19th to early 20th century.
Inns that receive all guests, in contrast to inns that received only upper classes of guests; typically only used in reference to ancient Greek, Roman, and Middle Eastern structures.

Houses, sometimes family homes or other relatively small buildings, that offer for a fixed fee apartments or rooms and sometimes meals. Rooming houses typically differ from boardinghouses in that a rooming house offers fewer amenities and less social contact with the family or other operators. However, in nineteenth-century American usage, the term may overlap in meaning with "boardinghouses."
Buildings that may be adapted to many types of events such as concerts, meetings, or sporting events.

Entertainment buildings, often public, for meeting, dancing, and general recreation, often with eating and drinking facilities, music, and game rooms; pleasure houses or summer houses. For similar buildings equipped with gambling devices, use "gambling casinos."

Oblong enclosures curved at one end and built for horse and chariot racing, usage is typically restricted to such structures in Greek cities of the Hellenistic, Roman, and Byzantine eras; meaning overlaps with similar structures in ancient Rome itself, "circuses (Roman arenas)." For sports structures used for horse racing in more modern contexts, use "horse racetracks."

Use both for buildings providing enclosed and unobstructed space adaptable for various physical education and recreation activities, such as track events and basketball, and for buildings housing equipment and dressing facilities for athletes; often located at or near athletic fields.
Amusement park rides having a gravity train that moves along a closed loop on a sharply winding trestle built with steep inclines that produce sudden speedy plunges for thrill-seeking passengers.
Courts marked for playing American handball and that include at least one smooth wall.

Large bath structures filled with hot aerated water, originally made of wood but more frequently constructed with plastic or fiberglass impregnated with resin. Typically used for recreation or physical therapy.
Monumental ancient Roman bath buildings. For public or private ancient Roman baths or bath buildings of ordinary size, use "balnea."
Inclined courses or tracks of ice or snow designed, maintained, or used for certain winter sports activities, as bobsledding or toboganning.
In Indian architecture, a hall of worship.
Hall churches whose aisles are filled with galleries.

In a general sense, refers to any large church built to receive large numbers of pilgrims. In specific use, refers to churches built or remodeled in the 11th century, and designed for crowds of pilgrims along the main routes to the shrine at Campostela, Spain.

Protestant church buildings erected for persecuted believers as a result of church reductions in the territories of Upper and Lower Lusatia, which had belonged to Saxony since 1635, Protestant Brandenburg, and religiously tolerant Poland. Other border churches were erected in the Piast Principalities of Liegnitz, Wohlau, and Brzeg, and in the Podiebrad Duchy of Oels.
In Indian architecture, a shrine conjoined at the bhadras of the hall.
Siamese stupas tapering from a round base to an attenuated finial.
Jaina temples with an entourage of 24 dēvakulikās containing 24 Jinas.
In Indian architecture, a bhavana is a temple, devotional place, or house of God. It is one of commonly used names for a temple, as found in Vāstuśāstra literature such the Mayamata and the Mānasāra.
Buildings or parts of buildings set apart for, and equipped with instruments for making, observations of natural phenomena, typically astronomical, meteorological, or geophysical phenomena.

Laboratories focused on analysis and experimentation with chemicals. The building will be optimized for the necessary equipment for preparation of samples and analysis of liquid and solid samples, housing equipment such as glassware, fume hoods, furnace, centrifuge, mill, and oven.
Facilities having equipment to measure earthquakes and other seismic phenomena.
Buildings, usually run by a charity, where people who have no home can stay for a short time.

Vernacular British structures of uncertain construction and purpose, possibly temporary and made of wood with an earthen floor and used for storage of produce, equipment, or animals, popular from the 16th to the 19th century.
Tanks used to store oil, but not used to supply the oil to the equipment for which it is intended.

Maori storehouses, typically raised off the ground; used to keep preserved food, seed, mats, weapons, agricultural tools, fishing equipment, or other goods;, Often decorated, the carvings on the storehouses serving as elaborate designs that advertise the village wealth.

Buildings housing facilities that provide electrical power to transportation systems. For buildings that gather or distribute electricity to businesses and homes, use "power plant buildings (utilities buildings)."

A building or group of structures, generally a railroad facility, where freight is handled either using a physical track connection to a trunk line railroad or in an isolated location removed from the trunk line. There may be carfloat service, in which flat-topped barges are used, and freight storage facilities.
Buildings erected in coastal areas to house men, lifeboats and equipment to aid shipwreck victims; usually maintained by volunteers or government agencies.

Structures or other places that are people's house or abode, the fixed residence of a family or household, or otherwise the physical seat of domestic life and interests. For the abstract concept of the center of an individual's domestic life, personal relationships, and interests, together with the feeling of comfort and satisfaction that it conveys, use "home (concept)."
Designates a class of simple dwellings, circular in plan and with beehive domes.

Type of traditional gardens and large houses, where the house surrounds a courtyard garden; the garden is typically symmetrical in plan with a central fountain. Generally in Morroco or based on the Morrocan style.
Houses having two rows of rooms in each story of the floor plan, often with a corridor between the two rows.
Designates lines of dwellings situated on a sloping, terraced, or similar site.

Side-gabled vernacular buildings of simple massing, normally having their front walls moved inward to make an integral porch under a single steep roofline; the form was originally brought to Louisiana by French Canadian (Acadian) immigrants with a knowledge of long-span roof framing techniques.
Designates often palatial buildings of the Italian Renaissance located just outside of town, suitable for spending the day but usually without bedrooms.
Self-contained residences generally set in forests or other wilderness areas and designed for temporary, short-term use during special events, such as while on hunting or fishing excursions.
Use only for individual freestanding urban dwellings. For attached urban dwellings each having its own private entrance, use "row houses."
In Britain, Europe, and European colonies, a great house is the grand dwelling of a landed proprietor, usually the largest or principal house in the district.

Farmhouses typical of the Eiderstedt peninsula in Germany. These have square floor plans and a wooden framework on which rests a pyramid-shaped reed roof. Hay is stacked in the central space of the building, surrounded by the living quarters, stalls and other storage areas.
Homes built on ledges or dug into the rock in the vertical sides of mesas, bluffs, or cliffs. Examples are those of the ancient American Southwest.
Eskimo houses usually made of sod, wood, or stone when permanent or of snow blocks in the shape of a dome when built for temporary purposes.
Residential structures for an emperor.
Residences located at a distance from a monastery or convent and used by the monks or nuns as asylums in times of war and as pied-à-terres in times of peace.
Large, stately, or ornamental tents or tent-like coverings, usually rising to a central point rather than a ridge. Originally referred to tents used on military campaigns or at jousts.
Multiple dwellings composed of row houses whose facades in plan follow the concave arc of a circle or ellipse.
Ground-floor apartments with access to gardens, or the two- or three-story apartment buildings with communal gardens generally located in the suburbs.
Palaces in India, especially those of the Islamic period.
Temporary or permanant structures built or used for a fair.
Buildings in which monkeys are kept for show, especially in zoos.

Buildings or parts of buildings designed or used for the hygienic temporary storage of corpses prior to disposal. A morgue typically contains large refrigerated drawers or other areas for storage of individual bodies, and tables and equipment for the identification and examination of the corpses. The term derives from the proper name of a particular building in Paris in which the bodies of the dead were kept until identified.

Monuments comprising rectangular or trapezoidal tumuli or earth mounds, often believed to be collective tombs. They are found at Neolithic sites in the British Isles and at later sites of Celtic, Slavic, and Baltic cultures of Northern Europe.
Stelae marking the grave of, or otherwise in tribute to a deceased person.
In nations with a federal system, buildings that house local offices of various federal government departments and agencies.
Council houses in Roman municipalities.

Structures serving as housing or temporary location of lifeguards, who are water safety experts with medical training who watch and assist bathers who get into difficulty at a beach, swimming pool, or other body of water.
Buildings or spaces housing the meetings of chambers of commerce, which are associations formed to promote and protect the interests of the business community in a particular place.
Enclosed chambers with gates at each end connecting higher and lower sections of artificial waterways for transferring watercraft from one level to another.
Dams that resist water pressure by their own weight.
Watertight enclosures from which water is pumped to expose an area in order to permit construction or repairs.

Dams built using materials that are excavated, transported, and placed by hydraulic methods. Coarse materials of the slush settle at the outer edge and finer materials settle towards the center, forming an impervious central core. Compaction is not done, and poor drainage and settlement may cause failure of this type of dam.
Protective walls, pipes, or other structures designed to allow water to flow away from an area in order to avoid erosion of the soil.
Sewers into which empty the dry-weather flows from several branch sewers or outlets and which also may receive a certain amount of storm water.
Walls built as breakwaters specifically to protect land from erosion or other damage due to wave action.
Embankments built to prevent flooding of low-lying land. For embankments built to control or retain flood waters of rivers or seas, use the more "dikes."
Buildings for water storage and distribution.
A formalized pool or reservoir. Derived from 'Bi'r' meaning well, cistern or water reservoir.
In Indian architecture, a well structure.

Facilities for receiving waste, usually raw sewage, from surrounding homes and businesses for the purpose of removing contaminants and other materials that could damage water quality and the environment.

Refers to a building or group of buildings with the function of housing the action or process of making goods or producing anything, whether before or after the Industrial Revolution of the mid-19th century.
Facilities of relatively large size where the printing of books or other materials takes place.
Mills operated by the tidal currents.
Windmills, often tower mills or smock mills in form, distinguished by having an exterior platform or gallery wrapped around the circumference.
Facilities or location where the harvesting of fish, shellfish, and sea mammals is carried out as a commercial enterprise.
Places where metal and other substances are cut and shaped by machine tools.
Long cylindrical kilns lined with refractory, inclined at a slight angle, and rotated at slow speed.
Closed refractory chambers in which coal is converted to coke by carbonization.
Structures of relatively simple design, erected to aid in the drying by flowing air of, for example, food,  textiles, hops, or bricks.
The physical tops, or mouths of mine shafts.

Buildings that house places of confinement operated by a local government both for temporary detention of sentenced and unsentenced individuals and for persons serving sentences of less than one year; for longer periods of confinement and more secure than lockups, but less confining and for shorter confinements than prisons.
Buildings that house schools formed by the merging of two or more public schools, usually at the elementary level and often in rural areas.
Buildings housing academic enterprises that teach art.

Buildings that house schools representing the second stage of a three-tier educational system, falling intermediate between an elementary school and an upper, senior, or high school, differing by school district in grades included.
Buildings housing federated divisions of a university where a particular field of academic activity is located together, often with residences and shared meals.
Ancillary buildings used in support of health care facilities.
Sloping channels for the transfer of clothes and linens requiring laundering from upper floors to laundry rooms located on lower floors, either in a home or commercial hotel.

Entrance halls or porches through which one enters a Japanese building and is greeted by the host, removes one's shoes, etc. Historically, this term referred only to alcoves found in Zen temple buildings, but now the term is used to refer to any entry alcove. These areas are often decorated with screen paintings.
In Indian architecture, an inner enclosed ambulatory, often without windows or other sources of exterior lighting.
Aisles that flank the length of the naves of religious or secular buildings, and that are often lower and smaller than the central aisle.
Shafts designed to admit light to the interior rooms of a building.
Spaces set aside, as in museums, for the display of objects in a collection.
Showrooms in hotels specially arranged for the display of merchandise by traveling salesmen.
Small rooms for the morning meal; usually, but not always, adjoining the chief dining room; in northern climates often specially arranged with an eastern exposure to catch the morning sun.
In Indian architecture, a dining hall.
Rooms in dwellings set aside or otherwise intended for temporary use by guests and usually not regularly used by household members.
Public lounges or similar rooms in such places as hotels and colleges.
In Indian architecture, an offering hall.
Rooms or closets, usually having a cool temperature, for storage of wine, liquors, and originally also butter and cheeses.

Rooms and spaces designed for the origination or recording of radio or television programs; for telecommunications buildings containing facilities for sending and receiving microwave transmissions, use "broadcasting stations."
Workspaces in the home set aside exclusively for income-producing businesses; for reading and writing spaces used for household accounting or recreational purposes, use "studies (rooms)."
Divisions, floors, or rooms of hospitals for a particular type or group of patients.
Intensive care units designed for newborn infants under the age of one month.
Designates holy areas around shrines in Islamic architecture.

Spaces in Christian churches containing the high altar and reserved for the use of the clergy. Includes the choir when present. Use "choirs" for the spaces in Christian churches, generally between the altar area and the nave, reserved for choristers.
In Indian architecture, a sanctuary.
Refers to apses situated opposite other apses.
In Indian architecture, a cella (womb); sanctum sanctorum; sanctuary; womb house.
Cellars that are accessible from wharves.
Buildings over nine or ten stories and served by elevators, especially when such buildings stand out in a skyline.
In Indian architecture, a three-storeyed structure.

Modern high-rise buildings whose main mass rises, with the tall slender proportions of a tower, from a larger low base. For usually detached or isolated buildings or other structures high in proportion to their lateral dimensions, use "towers (single built works)."
In Indian architecture, a type of structural unit, such as a shrine, ālaya, or prāsāda.
Small, poorly constructed, or very humble dwellings.

Buildings that replaced the pagoda in some temple complexes of Esoteric Buddhism; literally "many-jewelled pagoda", "pagoda of many tiers", or "multi-treasure tower".  These were introduced to Japan during the Heian period (794-1185) and are characterized by a white, plaster hemisphere rising from a square substructure. A famous example of these is the Ishiyamadera Pagoda in Otsu near Kyoto, erected in 1154.
Towers having the primary function to contain and prominently display a clock or clocks.
Lofty detached bell towers, particularly such towers found adjacent to certain Italian churches.
In Indian architecture, an apsidal śikhara, vimāna-type.

Buildings, usually churches, mausoleums, or baptistries, having a cross plan with four apses. Usually the arms of the cross form a Greek cross plan, with arms of equal length. The design was common in Byzantine architecture.
Particularly known in English architecture from Tudor period onwards; pavilion-like buildings for eating and other entertaining, often accessible through the gardens from the main residence.

Agricultural buildings with large, usually sliding doors, prominent roofs, and predominantly open spaces on the interior, primarily used as storage buildings for hay, grains, and farm equipment and shelters for livestock; does not include those structures, often termed barns, used for the processing of food and other agricultural produce, such as hop barns and tobacco barns.
Rectangular, gable-roofed barns divided on the interior into three roughly equal bays arranged widthwise rather than lengthwise, the center bay comprising a passageway entered from the long sides.
Distinguished from "stables" by their barnlike appearance and their use as housing primarily for farm stock, feed, and associated maintenance equipment.

Agricultural complexes used for growing lemons. Composed of high perimiter walls and interconnected pillars often with with movable shutters, opened or closed in correspondence to warm and cold weather. Limonaie are chiefly associated with the area surrounding Lake Garda in Northern Italy.
Enclosures, often resembling houses, built as resting, nesting, or feeding places for birds; distinguished from "aviaries" by the lack of emphasis on confinement and by their relatively small size.
Relatively small shelters for chickens, usually chickens raised for laying eggs, who are brought into the shelter for safety overnight.
Structures for storing hay, with roofs that can be raised or lowered for protection from the elements. Some are set on skids to be moved wherever they are needed.
Wire fences designed to give a shock upon touching.
Retaining walls prevented from overturning by their own weight.
Houses owned by a church, especially a building next to a church in which social events and meetings connected with the church are held.
In Indian architecture, an assembly hall; school or college building.
Buildings housing learning environments for young children, preparing them for the elementary education system.
Buildings that house facilities and resources, and offer information and programs, for promoting and educating on topics of international cultures and history.
Buildings designed or used by those who are engaged in trade or commerce, specifically professionals involved in the exchange of goods for profit.

Public refreshment places with more emphasis on drinking, normally alcoholic beverages, than on eating, especially in the style of the 18th to early 20th century US; use "pubs" for similar facilities in other times and places; use "taverns" for such establishments offering overnight accommodations as well as food and drink.
Designates informal eating facilities with plated table service, a limited food-oriented menu generally of simply prepared items and coffee, and a social atmosphere emphasizing bustle and noise.

In modern usage, buildings that house banks that specialize in the exchange of stocks and securities. The term historically refers to buildings in which the merchants of a town assemble for the transaction of business.
Buildings that house banks that belong to the Federal Reserve System, which is the central banking system of the United States.
Commercial buildings located regionally that combine large warehouse facilities with sales and office spaces.
Relatively large structures designed or built to house a market, often either under a single large roof or positioned between and around a colonnade in open air.
Covered market spaces where meat is sold.
Structure or series of structures, either under a single roof or in open air, designed to house multiple retail outlets and to allow free passage of pedestrians on one or more levels.
Buildings that house businesses that sell art, whether the merchandise is actually displayed in the shop or stored elsewhere, with images used to communicate with the buyers.

Built works housing relatively small retail outlets located primarily near residential areas, maitaining long hours, and typically carrying a limited line of high-turnover packaged food and other products at high prices.
Buildings used for telecommunications business or activities.
Microwave communications stations set up to send and receive transmissions between other installations.
Horizontal strips, usually of wood, affixed to walls at a height which prevents the backs of chairs from damaging the wall surface.
In Indian architecture, a niche for a divinity.
Pediments with a top in the form of a segmental arch.
Pilasters, which span two (or more) storeys.
Decorative elements directly above doorways.
In Indian architecture, a doorframe.
Uppermost, horizontal members of a doorframe; also horizontal projections above a door.
Two single doors or door leaves hung in the same frame.

Doors protecting the window-like openings in grain storage buildings, attached by pins on each corner, allowing them to swing open. In African culture, granary doors are often decorated with fertility symbols, and images of people and animals, the lizard being a common motif.
In Indian architecture, an entrance-gate with  śālā-śikhara.
Windows occupying the full width of a bay and divided into a large fixed sash flanked by a narrow movable sash on each side.
Describes the compartments of windows or window sashes through which daylight may pass; for the divisions of openings each consisting of a single plate of glass, use "panes (architectural elements)."
Frames or curbs, around an opening in a roof or floor, raised above the surrounding level to prevent the flow of water into the opening.
In Indian architecture, a lintel or architrave facia.
Shutters comprising vertical planks or boards held together by horizontal or diagonal battens.
Tracery hanging from the intrados of an arch.
Tracery in which the central mullion splits in half to form a Y shape.
Platforms or boardwalks erected over unfinished building sections to provide access for workers and material carriers.
Stairs constructed without the use of newels at the angles or turning points.

Stairs within buildings so designed that they are relatively secure from the effects of fire in a building and thus are designated as an emergency escape. Use "fire escapes" for stairs located on the outside of buildings to provide a means of escape in case of fire.
Continuous series of steps with no intermediate landings.

Danbi, literally meaning “cinnabar steps” or “cinnabar platform” (Kroll 2015, 74-75; 20), generally refers to the steps of palace buildings, and in some contexts, to the open platform in front of a main palace hall.The term danbi originated from the practice of painting the steps of palace buildings with cinnabar. The earliest evidence of the use of danbi comes from the Lingqijing, which is traditionally dated to the Western Han. During the Ming and Qing dynasty dynasties, danbi became part of mainstream architectural nomenclature and was used in conjunction with danchi 丹墀, where danbi referred to the platform (yuetai 月台) outside the hall, and danchi referred to the ground in front of the danbi. However, danbi is also commonly translated as "steps." In literature before the Ming and Qing dynasties, danbi was not used for buildings other than palace buildings, while in the Ming and Qing dynasties, the scope of reference broadened to include Confucian temples, government offices, and other types of buildings.
The horizontal parts of steps.
Plumbing joints sealed with the use of a blowtorch.
The uppermost moldings, as on an interior wall, the top of a cornice, or a piece of furniture.
Moldings with bird, animal, or human heads biting a roll molding as the ornamental motif; used in Norman architecture. For fillet moldings with the front portion pendant, use "beak moldings."
Concave moldings that are similar to scotias but less deep; used especially with reference to frames.
Moldings of double curvature where the uppermost surface is concave and the lowermost is convex.
In Indian art and architecture, a fillet or band depicting cavaliers.
Bold projecting moldings, convex in shape, generally forming the lowest member of a base of a column over the plinth.
In Indian architecture, a ovolo-shaped moulding below kapōta.
In Indian architecture, a constituent molding of a principal architectural member.

Chagong 插栱, which cannot be found in traditional Chinese literature, is a term translated by Liang Sicheng from the Japanese sashihijiki 挿肘木. Sashihijiki refers to the bracket arms of the outer eaves of the South Gate of Todaiji Temple in Nara, Japan, which are directly inserted into the pillar shaft (Tanabe, Liang (trans.) 1932).
Enclosed chambers, heated by electricity, for baking food.
Tower constructions that operate a vertical-lift bridge over a water passage, equipped with counterweights to lift the bridge, deck or gate.
Passages, as a paved apron or channel, for surplus water over or around a dam or similar obstruction.
Fixed platforms on which artillery is mounted.
Designates horizontal tunnels constructed in order to listen for and intercept and destroy attackers' undermining efforts.

Use generally for partitions set up in religious and Roman Imperial buildings or outdoor areas between sacred and profane spaces or between certain Imperial and public spaces; use specifically in Jewish contexts for partitions in front of Torah shrines, especially in Byzantine and earlier periods, and in Christian churches for partitions separating the chancel from the body of the church, particularly when the chancel does not also include a choir. Use "choir screens" for the screens around the choir when the choristers are seated in the chancel area. For screens separating the sanctuary from the nave in Orthodox Eastern churches, use "iconostases."

Large basins or other vessels, often made of stone and with a cover, set in or on the ground or fixed on a pedestal; intended to catch the runoff water used during the baptism ceremony. As used in certain denominations, the basin must have a drain so that the baptismal water can flow directly into the ground.
In Indian architecture, altar stones.
Shelves or ledges above and behind Christian altars, on which the altar cross, altar candlesticks, reliquaries, and similar liturgical objects may be placed.
Niches, chambers, or slabs in mosques, indicating the direction of Mecca.
Crossings of two highways, or of highways and pedestrian paths or railroads, utilizing an underpass or overpass.

Public or private containers for pickup or delivery of mail. For rented compartments in officially designated post offices, use "post-office boxes." The term formerly referred to boxes in which the mailbags were placed on a mail coach or steamer. In British usage, "mailboxes" typically refers specifically to such containers placed on a pole or post on a person's property, while "letter-boxes" typically refers to the larger boxes located in public places.
Highway lanes restricted to vehicles transporting a driver and multiple passengers. Used as a tool for traffic management.

Uppermost cornices of masonry or other noncombustible material atop chimneys, either as an ornament or as a cover; for extra components specifically intended to cover flue openings, use "chimney hoods."

Galleries or lofts in which an organ is located, often in a church and intended mainly for use by the organist and choir. It is often connected to the organ, with which it may form a single architectural-decorative structure.  In some regions, the organ loft is very large, often consisting of several superimposed levels, and is reserved for men attending Mass. It is usually made of wood or stone, supported by ledges with a parapet and sometimes grilles that conceal the members of the choir. It is usually located in the western portion of the nave, above the main entrance to the church, sometimes supported by the inner door. It may also be located in other parts of the nave, in the arms of the transept, or along the walls of the choir.

Boxlike enclosures having openwork of bars, wires, or the like used to confine or protect its occupant, or to admit light or ventilation. Typically reserved for large or small enclosures of this type used for animals, or for freestanding barred enclosures for humans. For such rooms in prisons, particularly if the room is enclosed within walls and having only a limited area of bars, prefer "prison cells."
In Indian architecture, a recess between two vertical bays; salilāntara.

One-floor apartments, usually modest, each having an outside entrance; may also be used for buildings having a small number of such units and usually dating from the late 19th or early 20th century. Generally American usage.
A mechanically ventilated appliance to enclose use of spray paint and to confine the escape of spray vapor, exhausting it safely.

Danchi, meaning literally “cinnabar staircase or courtyard” (Kroll 2015, 74-75; 50-51), generally refers to the surface of the platform extending in front of the main hall of a palace or the surface of the courtyards in a palace, and is one of the main areas where ceremonies were held. It originated from the practice of painting the steps with cinnabar in the Han dynasty, which may have been inherited from the Zhou dynasty (Yang 2001,163, 214). Over time, the locations of danchi changed. During the Han dynasty danchi usually referred to the ground or floor inside a hall. After the Tang and Song dynasties, danchi was usually associated with the platform in front of a hall. In the Northern Song, it referred to the ground of the topmost platform in front of a palace building, and, together with longchi 龍墀 and shachi 沙墀, it constituted the sanchi 三墀 system. In the Liao dynasty and after it referred to the ground below the platform, which is on the same level as the courtyard ground. During the Ming and Qing dynasties, danchi also referred to the ground below the platform of the main hall in Confucian temples, government offices, and other types of buildings.
Decks or flat roofs intended for sunbathing.
In Indian architecture, a four-pillared entry porch; pillared entrance-porch; porch.
Rooms containing a sink and toilet, but neither tub nor shower.
Open spaces in a structure intended to allow placement and operation of an escalator.
Circular cyma-shaped architectural members placed between āmalaka/āmalasāraka and crowning kalaśa in Indian architecture; padmacchatra; karparī; khapuri (Oriyā).

Pingliang refers to cross beams that span two rafters and are located on the highest layer of the roof frame. This term is used in the Yingzao fashi (1103), where it is also called pingfu 平栿. In extant architecture, shuzhu 蜀柱 and chashou 叉手 are joined into the top of the pingliang (Liang 1983, 142; Chen 2010, 114). In official Qing dynasty architectural terminology, the beam in the location of the pingliang is called sanjialiang 三架梁, meaning a beam that spans three purlins (and two rafters), or taipingliang 太平梁.

Trusslike joists having an open web whose component parts are either hot-rolled structural shapes or cold-formed light-gauge steel shapes. Trusslike joists having an open web whose component parts are either hot-rolled structural shapes or cold-formed light-gauge steel shapes.
In Indian architecture, a split or engaged column or pilaster.
In Indian architecture a, female atlantean figure; nāyikā (in decorated ceiling); citraputrikā (at pillar-bracket) (Karṇāṭa); kanyā (Oriyā).
Posts that raise a structure above ground or water level.
Columns that are split longitudinally or partially built into a surface, not freestanding.
Capitals having interlaced bands resembling the weave of a basket; found in Medieval and Byzantine architecture.
Ornamental stalks rising between the leaves of a Corinthian capital, from which the volutes spring and upon which the fleurons are sometimes supported.
In Indian architecture, a lotus pedestal.
Cornices below the eaves of a roof
Bands of small, rectangular, toothlike blocks, usually along the underside of a cornice; a characteristic ornament of classical and classicizing styles.
The characteristic ornaments of the Doric frieze, consisting of a slightly raised block of three vertical bands separated by V-shaped grooves.
Members placed across the inside of an angle in a framework to add stiffness to the framework, as between roof members and wall members.
Braces, such as struts, which strengthen a structure or framework against the wind.

Trusses whose upper and lower chords are both curved in the same direction but with different radii of curvature, so that they meet at the ends, giving a crescentlike appearance. Trusses whose upper and lower chords are both curved in the same direction but with different radii of curvature, so that they meet at the ends, giving a crescentlike appearance.
Bridge trusses supporting loads on their lower chords and having lateral bracing between their top chords.
In Indian architecture, a five-peaked superstructure.
Structures that do not undergo appreciable changes in shape under the actions of loads.
Flat surfaces with parallel sides, of more length than breadth, running across or around an object.
Lengths of gridded wire used elements of fences or other barriers.
In Indian architecture, a perforated screen with figure(s).
In Indian architecture, a type of ceiling in the shape of an eight-petalled lotus.
In Indian architecture, a recess carved with figures in a ceiling.
Flat floors, generally raised above an adjoining floor surface.
In Indian architecture, a pavement (in compound or on platform).

Chuji 出際 is the name of a roofing structure used in both shaliangtou (hip-gable) and bushaliangtou (overhanging gable) roofs in which the purlins extend beyond the wall plane so that the roof overhangs at the two gable ends. Meaning, literally, "protruding beyond the limit" (of a gable wall), chuji can also refer to the part of the roof overhanging beyond the gables, and in that use it is synonymous with the term wufei 屋廢 (lit. “roof end”) (Chen 2010, 126; Pan and He 2005, 61). The term chuji is only found in the Yingzao fashi. In the Qing dynasty, the distance at which the roof protruded from the gable walls was usually determined by the length of the entire purlin rather than only the part extending beyond the gable wall surface. Perhaps as a consequence, the term chuji was no longer commonly used.
Roofs in which one or more of the hipped sides (usually two) are surmounted by gables.

Wudianding 廡殿頂 (also wudian 廡殿), literally the roof of a royal hall (Kroll 2015, 481, 86), is usually translated as a “hip roof”. It is a type of roof which consists of a central ridge, four sloped ridges, and four sloped surfaces, and is typically covered in ceramic roof tiles. This form of roof was mostly used for palace or other large-scale buildings. The term wudian is first seen in documents of the Qing dynasty. In the Tang and Song dynasties, this roof type was called si`e 四阿. According to the Yingzao fashi 營造法式, "si`e palatial halls"（si’e diange 四阿殿閣）can also be called "five-ridge halls" (wujidian 五脊殿) as well as "Wu halls" (Wudian 吳殿). The Yingzao fayuan 營造法原, which discusses the architectural practices of the Jiangnan region during the Yuan and Ming Dynasties, used the term "siheshe" 四合舍 for this kind of roof (姚 et al. 1986, 37). Metallic cables or rods extending from the highest point on a roof to the ground that protect the building should lightning strike, by providing a direct path to the ground.
Dormers with a roof terminating in a gable. Dormers with a roof terminating in a gable.
In Indian architecture, a curved and ribbed eave or awning; kūṭacchādya.
Boards that are nailed across the ends of roof rafters, sometimes supporting a gutter.
Finials, attatched to the top most portion of a lamp, typically by way of a screw, and often used to secure a lamp shade.

Metal flashing used at the intersection of a wall and a sloping roof; the upper edge steps up to follow the general inclination of the roof. Metal flashing used at the intersection of a wall and a sloping roof; the upper edge steps up to follow the general inclination of the roof.
Gables with curved sides and surmounted by a pediment.
Short posts located at the peak of a gable into which the bargeboards are fixed.

Slender spires rising from the ridge of a roof, most commonly from the roof intersection over the crossing of a church; use "crossing towers" for more substantial structures such as a lantern between spire and roof.
In Indian architecture, a spirelet; aṅga-śikhara (Oriyā).
Parts or components of horizontal roof frames.
Rafters placed at the juncture of the inclined planes forming hip roofs.

In decorative, open-timber roof trusses, short posts set against the wall, bearing at bottom on a stone corbel or capital and supporting, generally with the aid of a curved brace, the wall end of the tie beam, or hammer beam of the truss. In decorative, open-timber roof trusses, short posts set against the wall, bearing at bottom on a stone corbel or capital and supporting, generally with the aid of a curved brace, the wall end of the tie beam, or hammer beam of the truss.
Refers to pairs of vertical, or near vertical, symmetrically placed tie beams in a truss. Refers to pairs of vertical, or near vertical, symmetrically placed tie beams in a truss.
Walls whose whole surfaces are unbroken by windows, doors, or other openings.
Artificial surfaces designed to facilitate practicing rock climbing techniques, providing the climber with varying surface textures, grips, scale, and inclination.
The strong outer works of a fortification, usually low enough to permit defensive fire.

Yangma wall (yangmacheng 羊馬城) literally meaning “goat and horse fortification," first appeared in Tang dynasty records and then also in Song dynasty textual sources. It refers to a wall built either between the city wall and the moat or around a beacon tower. It is usually smaller than the city wall. The yangma wall forms a closed circle around the city wall or the beacon tower, or may be located in certain parts of the city wall to form a closed circle together with the city wall. Yangma wall serves as a defensive line between the city wall and the moat in order to prevent the enemy from invading. It was also used for the temporary placement of goats, sheep, and horses when residents outside the city entered the city for protection. A second term, yangmaqiang 羊馬墻, literally meaning “goat and horse wall" also survives in Tang and Song records and the two terms are interchangeable in texts until the Qing dynasty. Yangma wall serves as a defensive line between the city wall and the moat in order to prevent the enemy from invading. It was also used for the temporary placement of goats, sheep, and horses when residents outside the city entered the city for protection. A second term, yangmaqiang 羊馬墻, literally meaning “goat and horse wall" also survives in Tang and Song records and the two terms are interchangeable in texts until the Qing dynasty.
Dams built into walls across the ditches of a fortification, with a sluice gate than can regulate the height of water in the ditch at will.
In Indian architecture, a wall; bāḍa (Oriyā).
End walls having a gable.
In Indian architecture, a central, projecting face of a recessed bhadra.
In Indian architecture, the aedicule of the wagon-vault building, located above the vimāna-wall’s bhadra in the hāra-parapet.
Arcades or porticoes in Islamic architecture. Riwaqs serve as transitions between interior and exterior spaces.
Includes colonnades surrounding a building, such as a Greek temple, and Roman courtyards surrounded by a colonnade.
In Indian architecture, a foundation course of masonry, such as the substructure or course below the base.

In stone masonry, stringcourses set at window sill level; commonly differentiated from the wall by their greater projection, their finish, or their thickness. In stone masonry, stringcourses set at window sill level; commonly differentiated from the wall by their greater projection, their finish, or their thickness.
See xinjian 心間.
In Indian architecture, a pavilion on the sky storey.
Use to designate stories wholly or partly underground. For similar spaces used solely for storage, particularly food, prefer "cellars."

In general, areas or large, open structures used for burial or entombment. Specifically, typically refers to relatively large public parks or grounds laid out expressly for the interment of the dead, and not being the yard of any church. Originally the term was derived from the Latin "cœmeterium," referring to Roman underground cemeteries or catacombs.

Farms of wealthy landlords employing the latest and best agricultural techniques and technologies and designed by architects, often built as exemplars for local farmers; found, especially in England, from the late 18th century to the mid-19th century.
Farms chiefly devoted to the raising of dairy cattle and the production of milk, butter, and cheese.
Housing provided by an industry to its employees.
Complexes of schools, usually ranging from kindergarten through high school or two-year college, that draw students from a metropolitan area and are intended to minimize the effects of segregation.

Zoos in which many or all of the animals have access to open-air enclosures that resemble the animals' natural habitats, in contrast to early zoos where most animals were confined to relatively small cages. Zoos in which many or all of the animals have access to open-air enclosures that resemble the animals' natural habitats, in contrast to early zoos where most animals were confined to relatively small cages.
Gardens commemorating the dead, especially those killed in wars  or those who have been cremated.

Complexes of buildings and other structures with machinery for generating electricity from various types of fuel, such as fossil fuels, nuclear, biomass, geothermal, and solar thermal energy sources. For individual buildings in which electricity, or other forms of power, are generated for the operation of machinery or vehicles, or supplying power to other buildings in a complex, use "powerhouses."
Excavations from which gravel or sand is or has been obtained, particularly excavations where the holes have been dug vertically into the surface.
Mines from which the primary extraction is copper, which is an element and reddish metal that is very malleable.

Facilities that harness and distribute energy derived from the sun's radiation by producing heat, causing chemical reactions, or generating electricity in any of several methods, including but not limited to the following: by the using direct solar radiation to heat air, water, or another carrier fluid; by using arrays of lenses or mirrors as solar collectors to concentrate sunlight to produce high temperatures in a solar furnace; or by using solar cells (photovoltaic cells) to convert solar radiation into electricity when a small electric voltage is generated in the solar cell as light strikes the junction between a metal and a semiconductor (such as silicon) or the junction between two different semiconductors.
Power plants using steam generated by geothermal sources, such as geysers, hot springs, or volcanoes.
Military bases for the storage and deployment of guided missiles, which are self-propelled projectiles used as weapons, including but not limited to long-range ballistic missiles.
Encampments formed by troops for long stays while on a campaign, especially during winter.
Camps providing care and activities for children during daylight hours, usually including outdoor activities during warm seasons, but not including overnight housing.
Resorts located on the seaside or beach.
Buildings and other facilities used for the Olympic games.

Racetracks designed or used for horse racing. For ancient Greek or Roman oblong structures designed for horse and chariot racing, use "hippodromes (Greek sports buildings)" or "circuses (Roman arenas)" respectively. Racetracks designed or used for horse racing. For ancient Greek or Roman oblong structures designed for horse and chariot racing, use "hippodromes (Greek sports buildings)" or "circuses (Roman arenas)" respectively.

Areas or facilities designed or used primarily for shooting guns at targets, whether for sport or as training. Typically the area includes various ranges or distances marked off between the respective firing points and the targets.

Semicircular range designed or used primarily for the shooting of skeets, a sport involving clay-pigeon targets projected at a variety of shooting angles. Semicircular range designed or used primarily for the shooting of skeets, a sport involving clay-pigeon targets projected at a variety of shooting angles.

Footpaths through nature reserves or other area of countryside for the observation of plants, animals, and natural phenomena, frequently marked by posted signs and discussed in associated descriptive literature.

In common usage, the word "convent" is used for the facilities of a company of women living together in the discipline of a religious order and under one superior. For facilities for a company of males, use "monasteries."
Religious houses for communities of both men and women, dwelling in contiguous establishments, united under the rule of one superior.
Complexes built for use related to water transportation.
Territorial divisions formed for administrative or electoral purposes.
Distinct territories that are surrounded by foreign dominions.
Districts of cities in which members of a minority racial or cultural group live, especially because of social, legal, and economic pressure.
Tracts of land or regions of ice or ocean in the Arctic region of the earth, characterized by distinctively polar conditions of climate, plant, and animal life, and other physical features.
Collocates descriptors for organizations consisting of a governing authority together with a population and an area of land which are under its jurisdiction in some or all respects.

Sites comprising scattered artefacts visible upon the ground surface that indicate past human activity. This can include ceramics, lithics, animal bones, shell middens, metal implements, coins, glass beads, or natural objects used for cultural purposes such ascowries.
An alignment of at least five neolithic sites in less than ten miles.

Archaeological or anthropological contexts for accumulations of refuse associated with human occupation. These accumulations may include discarded artifacts and food remains such as bones and shells. They are often used as valuable sources of archaelogical data.
Elements resembling buttresses, but supported by corbels rather than having separate foundations and therefore not serving as true structural buttresses.
Buttresses extending at about a 45-degree angle from the corner of a building.

An alternative to a slab foundation, comprising a concrete pier reinforced with steel rebar to form a strong cage within the pier. The piers are set atop a concrete pad that also has been reinforced with steel rebar.
Piles (usually sections of pipe spliced together) which are forced into the ground to a bearing stratum, jacking it against a building or structure above, used primarily for underpinning.
Piers, such as would include several columns or pilasters, that are thickenings of or projections from a wall.
Arches constructed on the principle of the catenary, the shape assumed by a cord suspended at its ends from two supports in equilibrium under given forces.

Pointed arches in which the length of the voussoirs increases toward the center, so that the arch of the extrados has more vertical proportions than the arch of the intrados. For similar arches when rounded, use "Florentine arches."
Arches built across a nave or hall that support walls rather than vaults; for such arches when they support vaults, use "transverse arches."
Stones, usually with the shape of a truncated inverted pyramid, placed between capitals and the arches that spring from them.
Blocks of stone that close the intersection of arches at the apex of a vault, such as a ribbed vault; may be covered by a round, decorative boss.
Designates structural systems in which the structural elements or the roofing elements are hung from cables or in which the roofing is supported by cables.
Structural systems based on concrete slabs in which loads are transferred in two directions.
Structural systems in which the primary reinforcing steel runs in one direction only; may or may not include one-way supporting beams.
Two-way, flat concrete slabs supported by beams spanning between columns in both directions; the slab and beams are poured to be monolithic.

Membrane structures in which fabric is stretched across or supported on masts or poles, with or without the aid of guys. Membrane structures in which fabric is stretched across or supported on masts or poles, with or without the aid of guys.

Denotes hemispherical, caplike domes; the term applies to small semidomes lacking a drum or lantern, small shallow domes used in the ceilings of rooms to increase headroom, small domes not pierced by oculi, and domelike plaster surfaces suspended within double-shell domes and often decorated.
Vaults divided into six vaulting cells. Vaults divided into six vaulting cells.
Vaults of approximately quarter-circle profile, such as would cover an aisle in a church.
Denotes ribbed barrel vaults covered by squares set on the diagonal so that the diagonal ribs cross adjacent bays and so that by the resulting network of ribs the autonomy of individual bays is lost.
Capitals of piers or shafts that appear to support vaults or ribs of vaults. Capitals of piers or shafts that appear to support vaults or ribs of vaults.
Frameworks usually designed to carry both lateral and vertical loads and that are transverse to the length of a framed structure.

Decorative ware, typically those produced in the19th-century, characterized by in thick lead glazes and loosely based on Italian 16th-century maiolica. It was first introduced at the Minton Ceramic Factory in England.

Tingtang is a building type of lower rank than diantang 殿堂 (dian 殿 or diange 殿閣) in the traditional Chinese building hierarchy. Ting itself can refer to a reception hall in government and domestic building compounds (Kroll 2015, 454). Tingtang is a combination of, or general term for, ting and tang and is one of the most important terms in the Song Dynasty Yingzao fashi. Tingtang was also widely used for main buildings and could describe buildings in houses and gardens as well as ancestral shrines.
Basic wooden shingle made from split logs.

Type of tile used for roofing, usually of fired clay, slate, metal, concrete, asbestos cement, or plastic; available in many configurations and types such as plain tiles, single-lap tiles, and interlocking tiles.
Tile that is coated with a layer of enamel or liquid glass before firing, creating a smooth, protective layer.

Style that refers back to the original Symbolist movement, characterized by a complex synthesis of psychology, mystical and occult practices, and linguistics used to challenge traditional relationships between representation and meaning.
Period of the fourth city on the site of ancient Troy, ca. 2200 -1950 BCE.
Cone- or trumpet-shaped accessories attached to early gramophone players and phonographs, that collect and amplify the sound reproduced, or the sound that is to be recorded.
Describes the state or condition relating to anatomy that matches the biological sex binary, that is, not intersex. A dyadic state may be any gender identity, including transgender.
In Indian architecture, a pillar-bracket adorned with wave design.

In Indian architecture, a large gavākṣa dormer (South India); large nāsī; dormer at the cardinal and sometimes subcardinal points of the śikhara; cardinal nāsi; facial larger dormer of a śikhara-cupola; figuring also at the śukanāsa-front in Karṇāṭan vimānas.
In Indian architecture, a jamb bearing diamond pattern; faceted śākhā.
In Indian architecture, a maṇḍi-type.
In Indian architecture, a pañjara-pattern or motif.
In Indian architecture, nāsī-pattern on kapōta.

In Indian architecture, a wall; wall-pilaster, pillar; squares in a maṇḍala-grid; Types: Brahmakānta, Viṣṇukānta, Indrakānta, Rudrakānta, Īśakānta; Ajapāda, Bhūtapāda, Citrakhaṇḍa,  Mēṣapāda, Nāgapāda, Padmapāda, Siṁhapāda, Vyālapāda, etc.
In Indian architecture, a upapīṭha-type.
In Indian architecture, a turret of Latina or Anēkāṇḍaka form.
In Indian architecture, a square column-type with panelled bands often interspersed with cubical sections.
Pavilions, typically opulent or ornamental one, used as a place of relaxation or shelter for personal use; may be associated with or connected to a palace.
Buildings that house schools providing education in theology.
Chapels located in a hospital or clinic.
Small chapels set above and behind the high altar and usually visible from the nave of some Spanish churches of the 16th to the 18th century.
The state or quality of having or being divided into four parts.

Push toys, or walkers, are used to help children to develop balance and steering. These may have two or more wheels, and come in many forms, usually a base with wheels attached to an upright handle for grasping and pushing.
An early and simple rose cut, fashioned with 3 facets and a flat bottom side. Often used on very flat stones.

Gem cut in the shape of a square with rounded corners and small facets on the top (table). A gem cut in the shape of a cushion is often compared to the princess cut because of their square appearance.
Devices used to create loops in a fabric support to create tufted or hooked rugs.

Utensils specially designed to retrieve and spread jelly or other foodstuffs from a jar. These are designed to reach the bottom surface of a vessel, having a curved edge, often culminating in a point.
Vessels used primarily for ornamental purposes, made of varied material such as glass or ceramic and often decorated.
In cataloging and similar contexts, an indication that a fact or data is less than certain, but recognized as likely to be true. Indicates a level of certainty greater than "possibly."

Describes a type of dance that is often performed at powwows across North America. Unlike other powwow dances, intertribals are open to all dancers and powwow participants and vary in types of songs, drums, and regalia used.

Ritual group dances performed by Native Americans in the late 19th century, as part of a religious movement to promote the return of the dead, the restoration of Indian lands, food supplies, and way of life, and generally rehabilitate the traditional Indian culture.

New Year of the Thao people happens every August in the Lunar calendar, and Lus’an is held in honor of apu (“the ancestral spirit”) during the period. If the tribe has a lotsu or pariqaz, the new year would assume a large-scale celebration lasting up to an entire month; if no, the small-scale celebration of the new year last from three to five days. Lus’an entails a series of religious observance, led by shinshi and leaders from different ulalaluan units.
The fourth month of the French revolutionary calendar (introduced in 1793), extending from 21 December to 19 January.

Game for two players played on a special board; players have fifteen markers each, which they move around the board according to rolls of the dice. It evolved from other "tables" games in France ca. 1500.  While the boards are similar, tric-trac differs from backgammon in that racing is not such a significant part of the game.
Thuribles having a body that is spherical or globular in form.

Cultures and styles of the Hla’alua people lived in Taiwan. The Hla’alua people was officially recognized as distinct from the Tsou people in 2014. As it consists of four tribes – Paiciana, Vilanganu, Hlihlala and Talicia – it used to be called by the Han Chinese as the “four-tribe huan.” Under the Japanese rule the Hla’alua people used to be perceived as a Tsou branch by the colonial official. They primarily live in Taoyuan District, Kaohsiung City. Patriarchic clans are core of the Hla’alua social organization, and their major festival is Miatungusu.
Machines for writing in characters like those produced by printers' types, by which steel dies strike a paper through an inked ribbon.
Hand reels used to skein and measure yarn, consisting of a bar with shorter horizontal bars at either end  around which spun wool is wound in a figure-of-eight movement.
Brushes that are specifically made to remove dust and static from phonograph records.
Horns, first introduced in 1749 in New York, used by fire department officers in order to amplify their voices.
Metal scoops of varied size used to gather or transport coal.

Large swinging devices used for fanning rooms. Made up of cloth covered frames hung from ceilings and moved by servants or machinery. Used primarily in India. May also refer to large, hand-held fans, particularly those made of palmyra leaves.
Devices with raised iron pins through which fibers such as flax and hemp are drawn to strip them of sheaths, dirt, seed bulbs, etc.

Metal or plastic ringlike devices that provide a reinforced hole in a material, such as cloth or leather, that might otherwise tear from the stress on the hole when a fastener or other device is passed through it or attached to it.

Mechanized devices used to treat textile substrates with chemical bleaching agents, including chlorine, sodium hypochlorite, and hydrogen peroxide, thus removing any natural coloring matter responsible for diminishing the fabrics' whiteness. Fabrics are first fed through a guide roller and immersed in the bleaching solution by an immersion roller before being squeezed out and, oftentimes, steamed. These devices are typically comprised of three kiers, or vats, into which the substrates are fed and treated.
Trimming consisting of long or short lengths of straight or twisted thread, cord, or tassel; often grouped or knotted in various designs.
Describes the physical location where an individual died.
List, note, or other recording of the bibliography for a work or other entity's documentation.
Representations of the heads of humans, animals, or mythical or legendary beings.
Pieces of textile material that bear the insignia of a law enforcement agency.
United States and British imperial customary units of speed comprising the number of statute miles traveled in one hour.
Small electrically-powered vehicles, usually brightly colored, with rubber padding on all sides. Amusement park attraction; riders maneuver their vehicle to either bump other riders or avoid them.
Containers used for administering materials part of communion ceremonies.
Wheels either smooth or serrated, used to transfer pattern markings to fabric.

Devices that utilize the vibroscope method, based on the principle of string vibration, to measure the linear density of textile fibers as determined by the tension and length of fibers vibrating at resonance. By measuring the natural vibration frequency of fibers to determine the amount of fibers present in a cross-section of yarn, these devices are additionally able to evaluate the fiber's porosity and filtration resistance.
Metal devices attached to a fireplace to suspend a hook from a generally moveable arm.
Lamps providing a brief, brilliant burst of light, synchronized with a camera's shutter activation.
Small containers, usually of metal or plastic and with handles, for carrying one's lunch from home to school or work.
Large casks of varying capacity used especially for wine and oil.
Funnel-like bags which are squeezed to force soft food mixtures, such as icing, through a pastry tube making ornamental spreads and decorations.

Devices designed to dry leafy herbs and other plants, usually consisting of single or stacked trays with bottoms made of mesh or screen to allow for air flow. These are often designed to be suspended from a support.
Mechanical devices comprising a stationary filling tank and connecting nozzles adapted to receive and discharge liquid into bottles..
Heat-resistant gloves used to safely handle hot cookware.
Instruments used to measure the temperature in culinary applications.
Kitchen utensils used to sprinkle flour, consisting of a usually cylindrical container with a perforated lid.
Carts in which wine, in casks or bottles, is conveyed for serving, sale, or another purpose.
Trays, of glass or ceramic, for serving ice cream; sometimes made in sets with matching shallow bowls.

Hollow, often decorative forms, where mixtures are placed and left to sit, in order for them to retain the shapes of the decorative forms.   Hollow forms or matrices, often in decorative shapes into which food mixture is left to set to assume the shape of the mold.
Devices used to sort potatoes by size.
Boxes or cases for holding cheese.
Canisters, made of a variety of materials, but typically of tin or ceramic, designed to hold tea and maintain its freshness.
Shallow plates or dishes that are intended for the deposit of food waste.
Covers for the rings of plastic or wood fitting the top of a toilet bowl.
Covers, often made of cloth, used over tables.
Lifting or hoisting devices for moving objects that operate by force created by pressure on a liquid inside a cylinder that moves a piston upward.
Greeting cards given at the time of the new year.

Shield design of the Spartan army consisting of a large letter lambda (Λ) painted in the center of the shield. The lambda refers to the first letter of either the Lacedaemon ethno-political group or the geographic region of Laconia. The shields feature prominently in the description of the Peloponnesian War by Herodotus.
Machines that utilize water to wash wheat to separate sand or grit or  reduce contamination from pesticides or bacteria, in preparation for milling.
Devices that feed flour as it comes off the line at a mill, where bleaching and oxidizing chemicals are added in order to hasten the whitening process.
Machines that separate and grade grain by tumbling it through mesh sieves of different sizes. Used in the process of flour milling.
Swatches of hair worn in addition to the wearer's natural hair, either to cover bald areas of the head or to supplement hair for a more elaborate hairdo.
Metal implements used in hearth cooking to reflect the heat of the fire towards a piece of roasting meat.
Various contrivances for imparting heat that burn natural gas, propane, or other types of gas as fuel.
Receptacles, usually resembling an open-ended, U-shaped trough that is made of metal, canvas, or other materials and that is equipped with a handle and is used to hold and carry logs.
Biofuel stoves that burn biomass solid fuel in pellet form to generate heat. Examples of biomass solid fuel include: corn kernels, wood pellets, and cherry pits.
Devices used to measure the amount of dirt or other contaminants in a given quantity of milk.
Frames used to hang kitchen utensils, such as pots and pans; often wall- or ceiling-mounted.
Metal vessels used to heat lard in order to render it.
Shallow vessels used to concentrate the sap obtained from maple trees into a syrup. Sap is boiled in the pan until the sap reaches the desired concentration.
Packaging machines that form cartons, inserts a product inside, and folds and seals the carton closed.

Wood molds in which the dough for gingerbread or speculaas cookies is formed. The dough is pressed into the mold, forming the entire biscuit, unlike similar molds that are meant to be repeatedly pressed into the dough in series.
Lidded containers made to store epaulets; some are deep, rectangular boxes while others are formed in a bow-tie shape so that the epaulets can lay flat when stored.

Objects that are pressed against the strings of a guitar while playing. Typically these are worn on a finger of the fretting hand, creating a glissando effect without touching the frets. Guitar slides can be professionally made, or they can be household objects, such as bottlenecks. They appear in many forms, and differ based on the type of guitar used or the style of the player.

Toy and miniature versions versions of pianos. These are constructed with chimes or pieces of metal struck to make sound when the keys are depressed rather than strings, as is the case in conventional piano instruments.
Enclosing containers of varied design, used for storing thimbles for needlework.
Contrivances used for holding, containing, or supporting materials or tools related to the practice of needlework.
Specialized tools designed to create holes or apertures in textile materials.
Brushes with soft bristles, often of camel hair or sable that are used to clean dust from the surface of a lens.
Equipment used to fold printed material together into bound sheets.

Corporal punishment tools consisting of nine narrow straps or ropes tied at the end with buttons, lead pellets, or iron nails. Served to whip the back and loins. The name is derived from whips with nine knotted lashes that were an authorized instrument of punishment in the British navy and army until 1881. For similar whips or scourges, but not necessarily having nine straps, use "knouts."
