In the second deal, three cards are similarly passed to the right, and in the third, they are passed to the player sitting opposite, and in the fourth there is no passing, and each person must play with their remaining cards. This four-deal cycle then repeats itself. The ultimate winner is the player with the lowest penalty score when one or more players have reached 100 penalty points. Penalties are scored at the rate of one point for each heart, and 13 points for the queen of spades in a trick, thus, there are 26 penalty points in each deal.

Board game, held to be one of the oldest and most popular, played by two opponents on a checkered board with specially designed pieces of contrasting colors, commonly white and black. Players alternate turns in accordance with fixed rules, each player attempting to force the opponent's principal piece, the King, into checkmate, which is a position where it is unable to avoid capture. It first appeared in India in the 6th century CE; by the 10th century, it had spread from Asia to the Middle East and Europe. It remains popular and the focus of popular amateur and professional competitions.
A table-top game, or sport, that is loosely based on association football. A vast number of different table types exist.
A game combining elements of tennis and handball, played on a court approximately half the size of a regular tennis court with a lower net, with a rubber ball and wooden or plastic paddles

Bioreceptivity is defined as the ability of a material to be colonised by living organisms. In the context of conservation this concept is extended to water repellents and consolidants applied on stone objects.
Frames with protrusions, often disc-shaped, from the face at each corner.
Moldings nearest the framed object.
Frames which have a structural, as well as decorative, function, in that they physically support the panels they surround and may serve to connect from two to dozens of panels in a larger structure.
Frames having moldings of S-shaped profile; especially popular in the mid- to late 19th century.
Instruments shaped like a flute with one open bell-like end, the other being closed by an onion-skin membrane protected by a removable cap, played by being sung or hummed into.
Bronze aerophones of the Celts dating from early second century BCE shaped like long trumpets and held vertically, with a bell styled in the form of an animal head: often a boar's head or a dragon.
Bowed, zitherlike chordophones of Iceland.
Zitherlike chordophones of the Konjo people of Uganda. They are stick zithers which have three strings and three frets carved out of their bars.
Thin flexible strips of wood that exert a pulling action and transmit motion from one place to another. In pipe organs, they are connected to and activate the valves beneath the pipes.

A technique used to visually determine the shrinkage temperature (Ts) of skin and leather, as an indicator of the collagen’s hydrothermal stability. A prepared sample is covered with distilled water, placed on a Kofler hotbench, then heated at the appropriate heating rate.
Small printed sheets that advertise a trade or service, meant to be delivered by hand or posted for general consumption.

Sets of armor, consisting of a field armor plus reinforcing and alternative pieces which could either be integrated with or substituted for the regular pieces in the basic set, thus converting it into various forms for use in warfare or tournaments. They were invariably made for important persons according to a precise design for specific types of events.
Large, heavy pieces of plate armor shaped like a wing or shell, attached to the lower cannon of the vambrace, worn with tilt armor to protect the elbow and armpit.
Written messages that are transmitted electronically, typically restricted to short, keyed messages sent from one mobile phone to another or via the Internet.
Rules having graduated sliding attachments that are extendable for taking linear measurements and inside dimensions between objects.
Things offered to be competed for, or sometimes won by chance; may include objects, privileges, money, honors, or tokens.
Method of chemical analysis in which the sample is subjected to pyrolysis and the pyrolysate is then analyzed by mass spectrometry.
Open-meshed nets made of human hair, silk or synthetics, worn over the hair to keep it in place.  Also includes those studded with pearl-like ornaments.
Athletic shoes specifically designed for track sports.
Modern term for mirrors with a carved eagle surmounting the frame.
Recreation apparatus primarily designed for use by children in playgrounds or playgroundlike settings.
Sets of two to five cruets generally accompanied by a cruet stand or a small tray.

Historical devices of varied design, but usually with a handheld tray intended to hold magnesium flash powder that would be ignited at the moment of exposure of a photographic plate. These were used before the advent of flash bulbs and later electronic flash devices.
Use to describe things shaped like domes, or things having domes.

The measure of the possible full content of a vessel or other container, if it were filled with liquid, grain, or other substance. For example, the capacity of a bottle could be one liter. For the measure of the mass of an object, use "volume."

Groups of works brought together such as to exemplify the work of an artist or student. Also, groups of art works or other visual materials (often by one artist) such as photographs or prints, issued or housed together in a portfolio; they often include a loose title page or text introduction.
In architecture, the general arrangement or distribution of moldings.
The state or quality of being very thin or slender, said for example of fibers or wire.
Circular dishes with vertical sides in which a soufflé is baked and served.
Baking pans with four or more cuplike depressions used to bake muffins and similar foods.
Small spoons intended primarily for serving jam, jelly, or preserves from a jam pot or jar. The handle may be decorated with images of fruit.
Documents, often maps, which record the measuring and marking of land.
Forks used to spear a lemon slice or wedge, generally considered a serving utensil, but sometimes included with each place setting.
Banks that do not have mechanical components.
Use to describe automatic and semiautomatic firearms that utilize part of the gas from the explosion in the barrel to unlock the bolt and actuate the loading mechanism.

Small pieces of hard material such as hardwood, horn, metal, or plastic, found at the rear tip of arrow shafts, the tips of bows, and on the center shaft of crossbows, that carry a notch for holding the bow string.

Antidrag wires oppose the drag wires running from an inboard aft location on an aircraft to an outboard forward point in its bay. These anti-drag wires oppose forces in the reverse to the direction of flight.

Narrow, removeable boards of wood or metal lowered through the bottom of watercraft to increase stability. For similar, pivoting boards mounted in a casing or trunk located amidships, use "centerboards."

Vehicles with two wheels in tandem propelled by the rider straddling a frame mounting wheels seat and steering handle bars. These are the basic elements of most bicycles with the exception of those that have eliminated or dropped the top horizontal bar to accommodate women's skirts. Historically some bicycles with identical structure have been marketed as either "men's bicycles" or "women's bicycles" as fashions changed.

An enzyme that catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide into oxygen or hydrogen peroxide. It works as an antioxidant, and has also been used to catalyze the peroxidation of various compounds and as a scavenger of carbon radicals in carbonized silk fabrics.
Large canoes built to carry several passengers used to launch attacks.
Vessels designed to carry cargo packed in road or rail vehicles that are loaded and unloaded under their own power, rolled on and rolled off, via a ramp built into one or both ends of the ships.
Two-wheeled suspension vehicles pulled by a pack animal used for the transport of goods on a road, rather than for farm or field work.

Vehicles designed to carry ladders and other gear that does not fit on the main firefighting engines, historically horse-drawn but now motor vehicles, usually tractor-trailers, equipped with long extensible ladders.
A caustic deliquescent solid of the composition KOH, used as a bleach and in the production of liquid soaps and detergents, oxalic acid, matches, and many potassium compounds.
Manual or electrically operated air pumps that are designed to inflate tires, often with guages attached to measure pressure levels.
Pillowlike saddles made out of skins and stuffed with animal hair, used by Plains Indians.
Utensils employed to remove water, typically from watercraft.
Parts of a garment that cover the rear half of the girth of the body, often comprising a panel or series of panels of material.
Headcloths, often of fine fabric, worn wrapped around a woman's head and usually tied on top of the head, often with ends hanging loose; worn as part of women's traditional dress in West Africa.
Staff weapons used both in warfare and tournaments, consisting of a long shaft with a steel head, carried by mounted knights or light cavalry.
Scottish caps of varying forms, but without brim or visor, usually of knitted wool; originally worn by people in the military.
Soft caps worn for lounging or as nightwear.

Shoes decorated with rows of perforations, in imitation of untanned leather shoes from Scotland and Ireland originally fastened with thongs; may also be decorated with stitchings or pinkings and may have closed or open tabs.
Footwear of any design in which the upper extends above the ankle joint and that covers the leg up mid-calf.
Rigid boots securely fastened to the foot by various means such as laces, buckles, or hinges, and which lock into position in a ski binding.
Chromatography using two phases in contact with each other, the mobile phase being a liquid.

Consecrated, relatively small stiffened squares of linen used to cover the top of the chalice. The purpose of the pall is to keep dust and insects from falling into the Eucharistic elements. For larger, softer coverings over both chalice and paten in transportation, use "chalice veils."
Flat metal plates on which the locks of firearms are carried.

Originally a term for hangings behind or on the backs of either seats or altars. Today a term referring to curtains behind or on the backs of altars. For wall hangings above and behind an altar and containing religious images, use "altarpieces."
Second layer of stuffing in double-stuffed upholstery foundations.

Bags used to collect money, often made of cloth or leather, usually mounted on a support having handles; a primary example is in collecting money from members of the congregation during religious services.

Reduced-size coaches, generally having curved fronts, designed for compactness or to improve appearance yet retaining the elegance of the original, larger enclosed vehicles. For smaller, low-hung coaches, built generally with straight fronts and not based on larger prototypes, especially in the United States in the late 19th century, use "broughams."
Four-wheeled half-coaches lighter and less expensive than full coaches; popular luxury vehicles from the mid-17th century until the development of broughams in the mid-19th century.

Light, two-wheeled carriages, open or hooded, akin to gigs and chaises but, instead of having shafts, equipped with traces and a center pole to be drawn by two horses abreast; popular in England and the United States from the mid-18th to the mid-19th century, although production continued into the early 20th century.
Four-wheeled vehicles originally designed to carry bulk commodities and heavy loads, and which are covered.
Land vehicles that are fitted with runners.
Insulated cabinets or boxes having a compartment for ice and used for refrigeration of food.
Aircraft supported in flight partially or wholly by rotating airfoils.
Decorative, embroidered towels made to hang over everyday towels; produced by Pennsylvania Germanic women, primarily between 1820-1850.
Heavy table covers of knotted pile, tapestry or needlework.

The principal yellow colorant contained in extracts from the leaves and twigs of the gambier, cutch and kino resin. Noted as lightfast and washfast; used on wool, silk and cotton to obtain a dark brown color and in tanning leather.
Tongs used to serve pasta, especially spaghetti.
Mesoamerican solid rubber balls used in ballgames, burned as sacrifices, buried as votive offerings, and for other purposes; first appeared before 1600 BCE.
Any of various long, thin-handled shafts with relatively small heads used to strike the ball in golf.
Figural dolls that are used for play.
Pistols used for target shooting, now usually semiautomatic and .22 caliber.
Thermoplastic resin, used for its strength and durability. Due to its high level of weather resistance, ETFE is frequently used in construction and architecture.
Revolving dishlike devices that smoothly rotate on a central spindle and that have a series of equal-sized compartments on the inside made to catch a spinning ball during the game of roulette.
Recreational equipment that is used with games and activities that do not involve competition.
Two or more rail transit vehicles physically connected and operated as a unit.
Vessels that can float and are constructed for travel or transport on the water, such as a boat, ship, or raft.
Motor vehicles with revolving treads in the rear and steerable skis in the front, for traveling over snow.
Aircraft designed or equipped to train pilots, general air service personnel, and flight crews in the operation of aircraft or related equipment.
Military aircraft used to observe an enemy or potential adversary visually or by radar or photography; may be specifically designed or be modified fighters or bombers.
Written texts of stage plays, screenplays, and radio or television broadcasts.
Preliminary or tentative versions of documents.
Illustrated Biblical commentaries first produced in France in the 13th century, characterized by pairs of medallions containing depictions of the Biblical story and its moralization.
Serial publications produced by artists or their supporters. Examples are those popular in the 1960s through the 1980s as alternatives to the mainstream art press and commercial gallery system.
Books or other gatherings of orations and other speeches.
Data storage devices in disk form that use lasers to write and access data. The data may be stored in an analogue format such as a videodisc, or in a digital format such as a compact disk.
Printed or graphic material intended for promotional or publicity purposes, such as small printed works describing the features or amenities of a place, an organization, or other concern.
Illustrations that are printed separately from the text they accompany, often on different paper; may be bound in with the text, tipped in, loose in a pocket, or bound in a separate volume.
Type of underpants for women and children extending from the waist or hip to any portion of the leg above the kneecap.
Devices that dispense plates, usually in cafeterias or self-service food establishments.
The state or quality of being composed of or like crystals.
Pre-knotted ties that are attached around the neck with a strap, or to a shirt's collarband by a metal clip. These can be either bow-ties or long neckties.

Men's preformed neckcloths in the form of broad bands, soft or stiffened, usually fastened at the back. Also, similar neckcloths worn by men and women as part of formal riding attire and similar forms, sometimes made of leather, worn by military personnel as an item of uniform.

An extremely heavy sepentinite having the form of a flattened sphere, its name deriving from the Greek word for kidney. The rocks were used by the ancient Romans as standard weights and were also supposedly tied around the necks of condemned Christians before they were drowned, explaining why it is sometimes referred to as martyr's stone. It is most commonly jet black with small specks of gray and a metallic texture.
In the Netherlands, distinctive uniforms or clothing worn by those who collect for charities or in churches.

Items comprising two quadrilateral segments, or later discs, connected to each other by two strings or bands in such a manner that, when the bands rest on the shoulders, the front segment rests before the breast, while the other hangs down an equal distance at the back. The segments may contain various images or symbols. These small scapulars developed from the larger cloak-like scapulars. Small scapulars are worn by various religious orders and laity; they may be worn over clothing or under, against the skin.
An upper armband with quetzal feathers.
Outer, sleeveless, floor-length garments, cut simply in the front and full from a shoulder blade yoke in back; generally made of scarlet or black silk; always worn over a rochet.
Sleeves worn usually hanging loosely over other sleeves, often of fur and sometimes made to match a collar.
British sleeveless underbodices, usually front-buttoning, of knitted cloth reinforced with woven fabric strips; introduced in  1908 and formerly worn primarily by young girls.
Bonnets made with a wide brim slanting forward from a small crown to frame and shadow the face.
A white crystalline solid, usually encountered as a powder, used as a bleach for wood pulp, and as a versatile reducing agent which converts ketones and aldehydes to the related alcohols.
A colorless gas used chiefly as a refrigerant, as a preservative, in bleach, and for making other chemicals; it is also a component of acid rain.
Costume comprised of one or more pieces of matching or coordinated fabrics, especially those designed for a particular activity or occasion, such as a tennis outfit.
Typefaces having relatively light, thin lines; used especially to distinguish from boldface.
Glassy form of orthoclase in which sodium may replace up to half of the potassium.
Short, usually hollow cylindrical sticks or rods carried by each member of a relay race team, which is passed to succeeding runners.
Equipment used for playing the sport of basketball.
Steel or wood bars, usually about 1 inch in diameter, held horizontally and suspended from 2 to 7 1/2 feet above the ground and used for various gymnastic exercises.
Discs used in the game of ice hockey. Modern hockey pucks are black disks of vulcanized rubber with slightly beveled edges.

Dolls used as decorations on beds and divans, often with elaborate or outrageous costuming and presentation; not intended as children's toys. Made in France, Italy, and the United States from 1915-1940.

Small polyhedral objects, usually cubes, that are marked on each face with dots, symbols, or numbers, used as game pieces, for casting lots, and for other purposes. An example is dice marked on each face distinctively with from one to six dots such that opposite faces add to seven; may also be used for similar cubes marked with other numbers or symbols specially created for gambling or certain other games.
Optical devices consisting usually of two lanterns arranged so that one projected image appears to dissolve as the next image is forming.
Handmade books whose pages are folded in a variety of decorative ways.
Beautifully printed books issued by a private press, usually in a limited edition.

Group of typefaces, originating in the mid-18th century, characterized by such features as bracketed serifs, retained from old style, and the strong contrast of thin and thick strokes associated with modern.
Bindings for albums used as a presentation format for traditional East Asian painting.

Spool-like toys consisting of two small thick disks connected at their centers by a short dowel around which a string is attached by which the yo-yos can be whirled; of ancient Far Eastern origin, popular in the West only from the 20th century on.
Ear ornaments in the form of studs, frequently with decorative elements, worn through a hole pierced in the lobe of the ear.
Bottle-shaped, originally metal or wooden, clubs swung for arm exercise.
Heavy metal spheres propelled, or put, for distance in field competitions.
Wheeled toys, usually meant to be pulled, in which bells or chimes ring as the wheels turn; popular since the 1860s.
Toys that challenge children to make something creative, ranging from crafts, handicrafts, stringing beads to making mosaic figures.
Games or toys that are modelled on pinball machines but tailored to children. These may consist of a rectangular sloped box in which balls or marbles are shot up upwards from a sprung lever.
Receptacles for holding sand usually large enough for children to play in.
Chess pieces, in sets of eight of one color, moving as pawns are designated to move.
Targets consisting of objects mounted on poles or on movable crossbars set on posts and used for lance practice or during tilting in the Medieval period.
Devices outfitted with metal cleats designed to be strapped onto boots or shoes to prevent the foot from slipping on the ice or snow.
Any covering for the head.
Flowers or small bouquets worn, usually by a man, in the buttonhole of the lapel.

Crescent-shaped nose ornaments made from gold. Postclassic Nahuas of central Mexico associated this symbol with the Huastec region and with deities of octli (pulque), an alcoholic beverage made from fermented agave sap.

Articles of jewelry designed to be suspended, such as from a necklace, brooch, or earrings. Examples include Renaissance pendants fastened to the sleeve and articles of devotional, magical, or mourning jewelry concealed under clothing.
Bowed lutelike chordophones, having a long neck which passes diametrically through the soundbox to protrude as a spike or stub at the lower end to which the strings are attached.
Toy horses or other animals mounted on rockers, gliders, or springs; for toys with a horse's head mounted at the end of a short stick for riding, use "hobbyhorses."
Signs that confirm destinations; for smaller, less public identifying notices, use "labels (identifying artifacts)."
Clothing or other apparel having a primarily ceremonial or ritual purpose, or as a formal indication of station, rank, or membership.
Identifying cards issued by lending libraries to individuals or organizations that authorize the user to withdraw materials.
Symbols of office consisting of a bundle of rods bound around an axe, with the axe blade projecting, carried before Roman Magistrates as a symbol of their power.
Long zithers of Korea.
Mantles with a sleeve cut all in one with the side piece and hanging loose; sometimes made in the form of a sling.
Asphalt mixture that includes and additive to liquify the material for easier blending and applicaiton.
Uniforms for servants, of various historical design, informed by the employer's tastes and job requirements.
Overshirts with hood and front pocket for one's hands, often made of cloth or animal skin and intestine. Worn and made by Alaska Native communities

Helmets, generally ogival or egg-shaped with a pointed apex, and often fitted with an aventail and a hinged or pivoted visor, usually a pig-faced visor; used from the 13th to the 15th century. In the 15th century they became more globular and the aventail was replaced by gorget plates.

Armored gauntlets of hourglass form, popular in the 14th and early 15th centuries, characterized by a short, flared cuff and a back consisting of a single plate embossed to the shape of the knuckles and the base of the thumb.
Coverings for the hand which leave the fingers partially uncovered, especially those which extend to the elbow or above and which are made of lace, net, or the like.

A smooth round bead formed primarily within the shells of two distantly related groups of molluscan bivalves or clams, including the ocean-dwelling pearl oysters and the freshwater river mussels. Pearls are used in jewelry and for other ornamental puposes; they are considered a gem.

The fibrous, extracellular matrix protein in skin, muscles, tendons, ligaments, and bone. Collagen is composed of repeating units of glycine-proline-hydroxyproline that form linear polypeptide chains; three chains are then twisted and interlocked with hydrogen bonding to form a rigid helix structure. Collagen-containing materials, such as hides, bones and fish, have been used to make animal glues since ancient times. Collagen will irreversibly hydrolyze, or denature, in hot water, forming a water-soluble gelatin.
A compound comprised of a metal attached directly to a carbon.
Tools used to shape mixtures of ground meat and other ingredients into "cutlets" resembling drumsticks, ham shanks, pork chops, etc.
Describes human voices and musical instruments pitched below alto but above baritone.
Free-blown bottles so named for their form which ranges from an often flattened globular shape to a completely round globelike vessel; a type known in both German and American glass.
Bottles of a distinctive shape, used to hold champagne or other sparkling wines. These have deep punts that prevent the bottle from shattering during the second fermentation of the contents.

Perforated metal conical strainer with extremely fine mesh used to strain custards, purees, soups, and sauces. It can also be used to dust food with a fine layer of powdered ingredient. The chinois is similar to the china cap, but creates a much smoother product. Both the chinois and the China cap often are used with a cone-shaped pestle.
Knives with a curved blade used for cutting cheese. For large spatulas used to break up the curd for cheesemaking, use "cheese knives (food preparation tools)."
Cradle-shaped stands, typically made of wood, used to support casks of wine or beer for either serving or storage.
Type of small fork, usually with three tines, used to hold a piece of fruit while it is being pared or cut with a fruit knife.

Knives in a formal place setting, designed for use with the entrée, including cutting meat. The entrée knife is located on the right side closest to the plate, and is usually larger than the other knives in the setting. Usage and appearance may overlap with "table knives," which have general purpose use at meals with less formal settings. For knives with serrated edges, made of more modest materials and used for cutting meat in informal dining, use "steak knives."
Small spoons, similar in size to chocolate spoons, used to stir coffee served in demitasses or small coffee cups; often ornamental and made in sets.
Bottles with a rubber or soft plastic nipple attached, from which an infant sucks milk or other liquid.

Term applied to a wide variety of special-purpose utensils designed to serve ice cream and similar foods, especially those with an oblong spadelike bowl. Often made as part of flatware services, particularly in the 19th century. For utensils with a hemispherical end used to serve ice cream, use "ice-cream scoops."
Containers in which milk or cream is stirred, beaten, or agitated by a plunging or revolving dasher, or by shaking, in order to separate the oily globules from the liquid and thus obtain butter.
Devices for removing the stones or pits from fruit.

Envelopes, postcards, or other postal items of reasonable size with a new stamp or stamps bearing the postally applied marking 'First Day of Issue' and indicating the date and place of first official issue.
Devices designed to mix drinks within a glass, usually featuring a shaft mounted with an agitator.
Gold or silver coins of India issued from the late 16th to the mid-19th century.
A group of scripts, including book hands and documentary scripts, and formal and cursive styles, predominant in Europe from the late 12th to the 16th century, and in some areas still later.
Arabic script invented by Vizier Ibn Muqla, translated to mean strongly expressed and tightly woven; characterized by downward curving, broad strokes.
Self-propelled explosive devices that are intended to be launched from an airborne vehicle to hit targets that are on the surface of bodies of water.
Slabs, typically of marble, placed onto a countertop and used to cut and shape candy.
Short-handled scoops intended for coffee, typically sized to hold a specific measure, in order to brew coffee consistantly.
Idiophones composed of plaques of hard material, usually stone or metal, which are played by being struck.
Idiophones consisting of sonorous tubes, usually of bamboo, wood, or metal, used individually or in sets, sounded by being struck by strikers or other hard objects.
Trumpet-like aerophones of conical bore and fitted with keys, usually five, first made in Vienna in 1801 and popular until the 1840s.

European instruments consisting of a rectangular soundbox bearing a variable number of strings which are struck, all at the same time, with a small stick; frequently played in conjunction with a one-hand flute by the same player.
Keywork in general use on European aerophones, in which the fingerholes stand open when not in use.
Full garments reaching to the knees or ankles with sleeves or with sides that drape over the shoulders and arms; worn primarily by men in the Sahelian zone of West Africa, often over trousers.
Sleeveless outer garments of varying lengths, fastening at the neck and falling loosely from the shoulders that function as either separate garments or attach to longer coats or cloaks.

Protective coverings for the wrist used in archery, fencing, and various ball games, especially those worn by archers on the bow arm as protection from the recoil of the bowstring, generally taking the form of a band, bracelet, or plate.
Rectangular pads, generally filled with horsehair, stitched into the top back of the skirt to act as a bustle.
Items that do not form the primary articles of clothing, but are instead the smaller articles of dress, and that are worn on the body, as opposed to being carried.

Implements used to produce a current of air for individual use; also objects in the form of such implements, but intended to serve as ceremonial or decorative accessories; may be rigid or collapsible. The operation of the fan may be done by oneself or the fan may be held by another to benefit the recipient.
Women's or girls' close-fitting, sleeveless tops, often elasticized and usually having boning or facing to give shape and bust support.
Wide trousers that form the exterior silhouette of a skirt. May have a panel to cover the joint between the legs.

Long, narrow ornamental bands generally with fringe at either end, worn over the left arm near the wrist by priests, deacons, and subdeacons. Originally it was a cloth of fine quality used to wipe away perspiration, or an ornamental handkerchief, generally carried in the hand as an ornament. Ornamental handkerchiefs or cloths of this kind were originally carried by people of rank in ordinary life.

Appendages in the form of a flap or bag worn at the position of the genitals on close-fitting hose or concealing an opening in the front of men's breeches or armor, worn by men from the 15th to the 17th century; often conspicuous and ornamented. Also, similar appendages of female attire, worn on the breast.
Ceremonial chains worn to signify membership in a specific guild or order; often incorporating various forms of links and shields or plates. They may be attached to a textile support.
Ear coverings worn as protection against the cold.
Bands or fillets used to confine the hair; worn for functional or decorative purposes.

Small circular bands worn on the finger; typically circlets of real or simulated precious metal, and frequently set with precious stones or imitations of these, intended for wearing upon the finger either as an ornament or as a token.
Long neck chains worn loosely from the shoulders and usually extending below the waist.  May have a pendant or tassel suspended at the bottom.
Metal accessories attached to lorgnettes for ornamentaion, sometimes embellished with semi-precious stones.
The tendency of two colored surfaces that appear alike when viewed under one kind of light to differ from each other when viewed under another.

Mineral originally found on the Isle of Mull and used as refractory material for firebrick and furnace linings. It occurs naturally as fused argillaceous sediment inclusions in the mineral buchite, but this is rare, and as a result, it is produced artificially.
Full-length or three-quarter-length overcoats, usually made of fine fabrics, worn for formal or semiformal occasions; popular especially during the early 20th century.
Traditional costume of Korea, normally consisting of trousers or a skirt and an outer jacket or a coat.

Long, wide-sleeved tunics of the type worn as Christian liturgical vestments, or as secular dress in earlier periods, with or without a belt. In modern times it has been sometimes worn by kings or emperors. In the western church, the dalmatic is the outer liturgical vestment of the deacon, worn by bishops under the chasuble at solemn pontifical Masses, and by priests only with permission and on certain occasions; normally priests wear chasubles and subdeacons wear tunicles.
Sweaters characterized by intricate allover patterns carried out in yarns of several colors, originally hand-knitted on Fair Isle, off the coast of Scotland.
Skirts comprised of a large, rectangular cloth wrapped around the lower body and tied at the waist, worn by Indigenous women of Mesoamerica.
Knee-length trousers commonly worn by men and boys in the 17th, 18th, and early 19th centuries.
Sheer stockings woven in one with panties. For heavy, opaque stockings woven in one with panties use "tights (opaque stockings)."
Belts designed to carry a sword, generally worn around the waist or diagonally across the chest.

Collars worn to signify a member of the clergy. The most common forms are white stiffened linen or linenlike independent standing collars or tabs inserted in a black collar and worn by certain ordained Roman Catholic and Protestant clergy with a suit or liturgical robes.

Woven, wide-mouthed baskets used along with a pestle in the manner of a mortar, to grind corn and other grains. These baskets were created and used by Native American tribes in the western United States.
Hand-operated kitchen devices that force foodstuffs through a pierced grate or grill, used for puréeing fruits and vegetables.
Tools used in the process of butchering meat.

Culinary implements with, on one end, triangular heads used for piercing the tops of beverage cans, and on the opposite end, rounded heads used for opening bottles. The term is slang, and may be also be used as a synonym for both can openers and bottle openers.
Spits equipped with an adjustable hook or group of hooks suspended by a cord, the winding and unwinding of which provides the turning movement, assisted by two fly weights at the top of a metal stem.

Small transverse flutes, historically of cylindrical bore and keyless, with six fingerholes; they have a sharp, shrill sound and are traditionally used in military music and signalling. In the 19th century a new model was developed, having a conical bore and a seventh fingerhole for E flat, often with a key.
Systems of musical notation that use letters, numbers, or other symbols instead of conventional staff notation.
Containers suitable for deep frying; usually deep and often with a mesh or perforated compartment in which the food is exposed to the fat.
Pieces of hard, glassy material formed of sand or other sediment fused by lightning; commonly elongated and hollow.

Small arms projectiles, including bullets and cartridges, containing a substance that ignites at the point of impact, designed to penetrate and set fire especially to aircraft, vehicles, buildings, and installations.
Mobile or fixed complete supports for artillery, generally consisting of a platform or vehicle and a gun mount.

Refers to any scripts written with a running hand, so that the characters are rapidly formed by raising the pen very little, and in consequence characters have rounded angles and become slanted, and letters or strokes are often combined in a continuous stroke (a ligature).
Alto members of the violin family tuned a fifth below the violin; it is structurally identical with the violin but of longer body and string length.

In bookbinding, method of holding pages of a book together with glue, using no stitching or sewing. The back of the volume is trimmed to produce a block of separate leaves, the back edges are roughened, adhesive is applied, and the case is attached.

A 3D imaging and laser scanning technique which records millions of 3D points when a laser beam is swept over a scene or object. These measurements can be imported into CAD or 3D application and displayed on a monitor as a “point cloud” with photographic qualities portrayed in one-color, gray-scale, false-color or true color. The files can be viewed, measured and analyzed as 3D models.
Latin liturgical chant from southern Italy in use from the 7th century until the 11th, when it was suppressed.
A pejorative vernacular term for cheaply produced publications dedicated to sensational or morbid themes. The term is chiefly applied to literature of this type created in Victorian England.
Puzzling questions or statements, written or oral, worded so as to exercise one's ingenuity in answering or discovering their hidden meaning; frequently used as a game or pastime.
General term for books used in church services containing the chants of the Latin liturgy.
Typographical ornaments (as bullets or stars) used typically to call attention to an opening sentence or to make a break between paragraphs.
Recreation complexes where golf is played, comprising golf courses, clubhouses, and associated facilities and often restricting use to members.
Caps with interior threading which screw on and fit securely over the threaded finish of a vessel.
Wide, shallow, often decorative bowls meant for display on a side table or in a hallway, for example.
Social class ranking between upper and lower classes.
Those who hold other human beings as property in forced servitude, whether by capture, purchase, or birth.
Cooking devices consisting of a rack or grille positioned over a gas flame.
Vertical arrangement of fabric with regular folds that appear to fall one over another, with a tapered lower hem falling in a broken diagonal to one side.
A combination of café curtains across the lower part of an opening and tieback curtains, usually ruffled, across the top.

Weapons consisting of a stout handle at the end of which are attached, by means of a chain, two or more iron-clad balls, a short iron-clad bar, or a wooden rod with iron spikes. They date back to at least the 13th century.
Air guns in which the blast of compressed air is released by means of a spring-operated piston which must be recocked between shots.
Curtains that hang on the outside of other curtains, to provide added protection from the sun or cold, or as decoration to frame the window opening.

Explosive weapons used in the 17th century and later, consisting of a large case, usually of bronze, filled with fine gunpowder and placed against a door or gate to blow it in, or against a wall to breach it.
Aerial bombs filled with incendiary substances, either liquid, jellied, or solid, and fitted with instantaneous fuzes, designed to kindle fire at their objective.
Grenades filled with an incendiary substance such as white phosphorus, designed to kindle fire at their objective.
18th-century term for imported Chinese wallpapers.
Embossed wall covering made of molded canvas which provided a textured surface for paint and gilding.

Cannon shot consisting usually of two balls linked by a length of chain or wire, or sometimes of a single ball with a length of chain attached on opposite sides, used from the 17th to the 19th century to inflict damage on fortifications and most especially on the sails and rigging of ships.

Cylindrical cases containing a charge of powder and a bullet or quantity of shot for a single shot from a firearm, first appearing in the late 16th century. Early types had cases of paper, pasteboard, or linen which were ignited externally, while more recent ones have metal or plastic cases holding their own means of ignition, such as a percussion cap, at one end.
Billon or copper coins of the Roman Empire issued from the mid-4th century.
Ammunition rounds, or bombs, shot from man-portable, muzzle-loaded cannons, or mortars. These are made in a variety of forms.
Inoperative cartridges or facsimiles used for training in the handling of firearms or to test a firearm's functioning.
Single stationary hangings at the head of a bed, generally matching the bed curtains. For side curtains at the upper end of a bed, use "head curtains."

Wall coverings comprising fabric. In traditional wall-upholstering, fabric is attached to the wall by a series of clips, tacks, or tracks that hold the fabric tautly in place. Another method calls for the mounting of fabric on light frameworks of wood or another material, often fitted with an infill layer of batting. The latter method in particular is used to provide acoustical panels.
Lightweight textile coverings that are casually draped or laid over chairs, primarily as decoration.
Cases of usally textile material that cover a pillow for protection, used beneath a standard pillowcase.
Silver Catalonian coins, a form of the gros tournois, struck between the late 13th and the early 18th century.

Spanish and Spanish-American dollar-sized silver coins valued at eight reales and produced approximately between 1500 and 1900; used predominantly as trade coins; generally for a number of coins minted by Spanish-speaking countries, use "pesos."

Plate guards of a Japanese sword that separate the blade from the handle. Typically, tsuba are round or kite- shaped, having a central opening for the tang of the blade and occasionally surrounded by a smaller perforations. They vary in size from about 8 to 15 centimeters, depending on the length of the blade. While tsuba were a functional part of the sword, they also evolved into an art form in their own right around the late 15th century and peaking in the 19th century. Materials can range from iron, brass, and steel to gold and silver, and rare ones of ivory or wood.

Coverings and curtains, usually black in color, placed over sculptures, paintings, mirrors, and other elements at an altar or elsewhere in a church, or in another public or private building; used to signify mourning, such as during a requiem service or during a mourning period. For similar coverings designed particularly for the Lenten season, prefer "Lenten veils." For banners used in procession or hung in funerary settings, use "mourning banners."
Long linen coverings used to cover altar rails during the communion service. Formerly also a long linen towel held in front of the communicants at the celebration of the Eucharist.
Long linen altar cloths, as wide as the altar top and hanging over the sides, upon which the eucharist is celebrated.
Refers to the top layer of a quilt, often left unfinished, without backing, filling, or quilting. Distinct from "summer spreads," which have finished edges and seams.
Coverings, often textiles, laid on furniture for protection or decoration, used especially to keep heat or scratches from polished surfaces.
Pieced quilts composed of blocks divided by one main horizontal and one main vertical seam to form a grid of four squares of equal or nearly equal size.
Parts or components of keyboard instruments.
Two string quartets, often arranged antiphonally.
Upright grand pianos in the form of a truncated pyramid, developed in the 18th century and remaining popular until the early 19th.

Plate armor for the thighs, usually attached to the poleyns at their lower end. Introduced during the 14th century, they evolved from a single plate covering the front of the thigh to articulated lames encircling the entire thigh.
Pieces of armor protecting the front of the torso, consisting either of a single contoured plate, or of two or more plates or lames overlapping.
Term used in the glass trade for a type of art glass developed by the Mt. Washington Glass Company, shaded from pink to yellow with pink at the top caused by the presence of gold and uranium.
Boxes, usually cylindrical, of pasteboard or thin wood for holding light articles of attire such as ruffs, collars, and hats.

Coffins made of stone or terracotta, generally ornamented with sculpture or carving and of a size large enough to contain the entire body. Antique examples were often extensively decorated with relief sculpture, which were highly influential on Renaissance artists. Many sarcophagi were also produced in the Baroque and Neoclassical eras. Pliny explains that the derivation of the word ("flesh eating" in Greek) refers specifically to coffins of limestone from the Troad (the region around Troy), which was believed to cause rapid dissolving of the body; more probably, the term refers to various religious and folkloristic ideas that resulted in calling any coffin a body eater. The word came into general use as the name for any large stone coffin in imperial Rome, and is now generally used to refer to large, ornate stone coffins from any period or place.
Clock or watch movements in which the balance wheel is connected to the escapement by a lever attached to a roller.
Term used from the mid-19th century onward for a variety of bedcovers, especially those which are large, lightweight cloths that cover the full bed and pillow and often extend to the floor.
Coverlets woven with a weft of recycled cloth strips.
Quilts in which the pattern is organized in strips running the length of the quilt. May consist only of unpieced strips, or of unpieced strips alternating with pieced strips.
Quilts made to raise money for favored causes, often by groups; often in the form of signature quilts.

Quilts, rarely of more than two colors, consisting of an allover symmetrical design cut from unpatterned folded cloth, appliquéd to the center of a plain background cloth, which is often white. Frequently made in Hawaii and in North America, especially by the Pennsylvania Germans.

Mouth organs of China having a bowl-shaped windchest of wood or metal with a short blowpipe extending out from the side, and bamboo pipes of varying lengths, usually 17 in number, arranged in an incomplete circle and mounted through holes in the top of the windchest. A free-beating reed of copper or an alloy is attached at the bottom of each pipe within the windchest.

Vessels having a perforated top for sprinkling ground pepper on food. Pepper shakers are made in a variety of forms and materials, including glass, ceramic, and metal. They are often paired with a saltshaker. Saltshakers and pepper shakers may be designed in whimsical forms that are considered collectibles. For similar objects for sprinkling pepper but made of precious materials and designed as part of a larger set of casters, particularly in historical or formal usage, use "pepper casters." For devices used for storing and grinding peppercorns, use "peppermills."
Containers for storing and serving cheese, generally consisting of a flat dish with a dome cover. Use "cheeseboards" for boardlike trays use for serving cheese.

Bronze Age terracotta or earthenware vessels with a series of smal cuplike forms attached, either clustered in the center or around the upper edge of a bowl. The receptacles probably contained foodstuffs of various kinds or perhaps of flowers, intended for ritual offerings. Although the kernos was used in widely disparate regions during the prehistoric period, particularly impressive examples have come to light in the Cyclades.

Afro-Cuban drums having a long tapered or barrel-shaped shell up to about 90 cm deep and a single head about 25 to 30 cm in diameter, usually played with the hands; they are generally though not invariably played in pairs.
Double-headed drums of Korea that have lacquered bodies.

Refers to cups for chocolate beverages, no matter in which culture the cup originates. Examples in Europe are ceramic, usually relatively large, with two side handles, often a cover, and a saucer; popular in 17th-19th centuries.

Flat, usually rectangular containers similar to but smaller than cigar cases, used to carry cigarettes. For covered boxes used as containers for cigarettes and meant to be placed on a table, desk, or the like, use "cigarette boxes."
Small oval cups that have a rim curved to fit the orbit of the eye. Used to bathe the eye or for applying liquid remedies.
Baskets intended primarily for holding sewing notions; generally small, round, and usually with a cover. May have a cloth liner.
Ornamental containers for holding and concealing a flowerpot.
Instruments for measuring the focal length of lenses or other optical systems.
Small vessels for holding ink into which a pen can be dipped. For bottles in which ink is sold, see "ink bottles."
Wooden trays in which food is chopped.
Baskets or basketlike containers for holding bread or rolls in temporary storage or for passing around the table at a meal.
Wooden staved tubs with close-fitting tops used for butter storage or sale.
Decanters with a pouring lip and handle used for wine.
A type of kantharos featuring handles smaller than type A, rising only to the rim of the bowl, as well as a torus (tire-shaped) foot with very short or no stem.

Refers to amphorae that were filled with olive oil from the sacred trees of Athena, given as prizes in the Panathenaic Games. They were neck amphorae with a large, broad body sharply tapering downward and a relatively thin neck. The standard decoration included images of Athena on one side and the contest at which the prize was won on the other, usually in the Black-figure technique.

A type of late Roman amphora that feature a tapered body with the maximum diameter occurring at the shoulder and a height from 44 to 64cm, rim diameter of 4.5 to 11cm, maximum body diameter of 28.4 to 39cm and upper part height of 16.4 to 33cm.
Kraters from the ancient district of Messapia (now Apulia and Calabria) in southern Italy.
Refers to a type of oinochoe with a narrow-beaked spout. The body usually resembles that of shape 1.

The nestoride is a vessel type of native southern Italian origin. The name "nestoride" was devised by 19th-century scholars attempting to identify a vase with the cup of nestor. Nestorides are a continuation of a previous vessel type known as the trozzella which was named after the disks attached to the vessel's horizontal handles. The nestoride is a distinct form because of its tall side handles. Images of nestorides on southern Italian red-figure vases suggest that nestorides were used primarily as storage vessels like stamnoi or amphorae but there were also smaller nestorides that were similar in function to kantharoi in that they served as drinking vessels. Nestorides were most commonly made in Lucania and Apulia.
Aryballoi of the later style, having a relatively tall shape with a more pointed base than the globular or spherical styles.
A type of pyxis with a convex lid and a concave-sided body like the pyxis type A, but more shallow and broad. It is only found in red-figure.
Handbags that resemble a bucket in shape, often with a drawstring around the mouth to secure the contents.
Wooden bowls in which food is chopped.
Shallow vessels made in the form of an open basket with a high, bail handle; presumably for serving cakes and cookies.
Plasticized cardboard boxes with protective lining, often packaged with a plastic straw that can be inserted through a foil-covered hole in the top. Used to carry and consume drinks, generally juice.
A process in which an object, as a leaf or piece of lace, is pressed into a plain surface, as of soft metal, to make either a direct printing surface or a matrix.
A broad term applied to various printmaking processes used mainly by French engravers in the late 18th century, and which imitated the look of ink, gouache, or watercolor drawings.

Letterpress printing technique that utilizes a flexible, layered matrix that is placed behind the printing sheet to pull an impression from a type-high, inked plate. The plate is most often a solid, uncut surface.�

Printmaking process for making relief engravings on metal, called dotted prints, using dots from punches of various shapes and sometimes including burin lines; common in the second half of the 15th century. For later, intaglio processes employing directly engraved flicks or dots for tonal areas, use "stipple engraving."
Thermometers without scales.
Large-bulbed alcohol thermometers used to measure low air velocities or the cooling effect of particular atmospheric conditions.

Culinary utensils that have a cutting edge, especially various forms of knives used for cutting, carving, dividing, or serving food. Sometimes used to embrace all types of flat culinary utensils; however, prefer "flatware" when referring to forks, spoons, and similar culinary tools without a cutting edge.
Flat-headed wooden devices used to pack butter into storage containers.
Spoons having a long handle and a large deep bowl used for basting food.

Long, thin utensils used to extract marrow from a marrowbone, having one end channeled in the form of a long narrow scoop, but sometimes having both ends channeled and of two widths so as to fit different bone sizes.
Boardlike trays for serving a variety of cheeses. Use "cheese dishes" for containers for storing or serving cheese, generally consisting of a flat dish with a dome cover.
Photometers that measure the relative intensity of radiant energy of specified wavelengths that is transmitted or reflected by a given substance.

Large ladles intended primarily for conveying punch or other beverages from punch bowls to punch cups; similar to soup ladles but generally having a longer and narrower handle and a smaller, lipped bowl.
Instruments for measuring the direction, intensity, and duration of earth movements.
Receptacles, usually metal or terracotta, having a base designed to hold live coals, and sometimes with a grate or pierced top, used for heating a room or for heating or cooking food.
The making of flat pieces of metal from which textual or pictorial images are printed.
Single sheets of paper which are cut and folded to form books.
Literary works in which an animal or animals are the primary characters.
Pieces of cloth or other flexible material, usually attached along one side to a pole or cord, intended for such purposes as symbolizing a nation or organization, or as a means of signaling.
Dramatic performances that follow the Passion of Jesus Christ from the Last Supper to Crucifixion.
Long-handled forks used for cooking or toasting food over an open fire.
Any of a variety of handheld devices with a part made from a fine mesh of metal wire, or textile, though which food or other material may be passed to puree it.
Devices for crushing ice.
Double reed shawms of Tibet used in Buddhist rituals. They have a conical bore, seven fingerholes,  and a mouthpiece with pirouette.

European Renaissance and Baroque reedpipes with double reed, consisting of a short cylindrical body in which a number of parallel cylindrical channels were bored up and down, connected alternately at top and bottom to form one long continuous tube. The double reed, partially enclosed by a pirouette, was inserted into the center channel at the top of the body.
Solid wooden boards that are struck with a hammer or other implement to produce sounds.
Rattles composed of small objects such as shells, seeds, or hoofs, strung on cords or tied in bundles.

High-pitched metallophones of Thailand and Cambodia with a range of three octaves, consisting of a rectangular box-shaped trough resonator mounted on four short legs, with 21 iron or steel bars supported on narrow wood tracks along the tops of the sides of the resonator and tuned by filing away some of the metal on the underside. They are struck with two beaters, either hard or soft. For the Thai and Cambodian xylophones of the same range and tuning, use "ranat ek."
English silver or cupronickel coins valued at six pennies or half of a shilling and issued from the 16th century until 1971.
English gold coins issued between 1663 and 1813 and valued at 20 or 21 shillings or 4 crowns; replaced by sovereigns.
Double clapperless iron bells of the Ewe of Ghana, held by a tine at the top and struck with a stick, often in pairs, to accompany dancing.
Standing cups having a shallow but broad bowl with vertical sides, low trumpet feet, and an almost flat cover.

Classical drums of southern India, of elongated barrel shape with two heads of different diameters, fastened to hoops and laced to the body. The heads are tuned by tension wedges and the application of paste to the membranes, the larger, left head being tuned an octave below the right.
Tapering flags.

Banners carried at the head of a procession, usually mounted upon a long staff or handle. They are usually rectangular, but may be triangular or of another shape. They are usually suspended at the top edge, but may be fixed on a stiff frame on all sides. They may be painted or richly embroidered; used in religious processions, royal processions, and for other occasions. They may carry the identification of a confraternity, congregation, or parish.
Double clarinets of the Near East, consisting of two parallel cylindrical pipes of the same length and having the same number of equidistant fingerholes, usually four to six.
A device which operates as a feedback control system, emitting a signal that measures or detects a physical stimulus such as heat or motion to which it responds.
Devices to measure properties of sound energy, such as levels and frequencies.
Any of various optical or radio wave-based instruments for determining the distance from an observer to particular objects, as for sighting guns or focusing cameras.
Instruments used to measure the consistency or resistance of materials, such as soil, by measuring the depth to which a standard needle penetrates the materials.
Devices used to measure energy existing in atomic nuclei, or energy produced during nuclear fission or fusion.
Instruments for detecting an electrical charge on an object, and that indicate its magnitude based on the mutual attraction or repulsion of metal leaves or plates.
Instruments that measure the duration of direct sunshine.
Devices for measuring the physiological effects of cooling by comparing results against effects on a copper sphere maintained at a constant temperature equal to the deep body temperature of humans.
Instruments for measuring or indicating the polarization of light or for examining objects in polarized light; often used to study stresses and strains.
Devices that specifically measure the speed, direction, intensity, and other aspects of the movement of objects.
Parts or components of scales.
Balances in which the weighing surfaces are small flat platforms or shallow trays with little travel and set above the beam; used with conventional weights or a side weighing beam.
Instruments designed to measure all the angles necessary for determining elevations and distances.

Barometers of the type in which the column of liquid in the tube has above it a body of confined air or other gas (instead of a vacuum as in the mercurial barometer), so that the pressure of the atmosphere acts against the weight of the liquid and the elastic pressure of the gas; a thermometer is attached for correction of the readings according to the expansion or contraction of the gas with changes of temperature.
Inserting an extra space between words, usually in order to justify a line.
Calipers with an attached vernier scale and adjusting screw or sliding scale for very fine measurement.
Surveying instruments used to determine relative elevation, generally comprised of a telescope rigidly attached to a vertical spindle, thus capable of only horizontal rotary movement.
Instruments for measuring the rate of flow of liquids and consisting of a tapered tube into which a small float is forced until its weight balances the fluid force.
Scales generally characterized as having a large dial on the front of a box containing the mechanism, on top of which is mounted the weighing surface.
Scales used to weigh butter.

Spike fiddles of the Near East, originating in Iran, with a spherical body, a circular belly of animal membrane or fish skin on which the bridge rests, and from one to four strings, traditionally of silk, though in modern times usually of metal. The instruments are held vertically and turned to present the strings to the bow during performance. Spike fiddle of Iran, Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia.
Timepieces small and convenient enough to be carried about on a person.

Clocks or watches with striking mechanisms that, upon request, will strike a sequence of bells, gongs, or chimes to indicate the time in hours, quarters, and sometimes, minutes. For watches that strike the hours in passing, use "clock watches."

Family of fipple flutes that originated in Europe, traditionally made of wood, recently sometimes of plastic, with seven fingerholes and a thumb hole. Recorders may be made in several sizes, including the following: garklein, sopranino, Soprano, alto, voice flute, tenor, bass, great bass, contrabass, sub-great bass, and sub-contrabass.
Containers whose volume is precisely known; used to measure the density or specific gravity of liquids.
Devices for measuring either the quantity of alkali in a solid or liquid or the quantity of carbon dioxide formed in a reaction.
Instruments for measuring the external dimensions of the skulls of deceased beings; for devices to measure the skulls of living beings, use "cephalometers."

Compasses for measuring horizontal angles during surveying with reference to the direction of a magnetic needle; usually capable of fastening to tripods or other firm supports and equipped with sighting apparatus.
Calibrated wooden rods with sliding crosspieces used for measuring the altitude of celestial bodies; forerunnners of modern sextants.
Instruments that measure color changes and evaluate light stability in individual objects of art that are sensitive to light exposure.
Small, portable clocks introduced in the 16th century for use when traveling; usually set in a brass, rectangular case with glass-paneled sides and having a hinged handle on top.

Circular or oval, movable receptacles used alone or placed inside the baptismal stand or support, used to catch the runoff of holy water during the sacrament of baptism by aspersion. They may be ornamented or unornamented; they may have a hole for draining.
Pieces of armor that cover or protect the neck of the human or animal wearer.
Instruments designed to measure noise and sound levels, usually consisting of microphone, amplifier, output meter, and frequency-weighting apparatus.
Small holes, usually near the base of a container, through which liquid can be poured; usually found in rundlets and water coolers.
Covers, designed to fit around canteens, and typically including a strap, so the canteen can be worn.
Coverings for objects that facilitate human activity and provide for physical needs of people in or around a building generally by offering comfort, convenience, or protection.
Woolen blankets traded to Native North Americans in exchange for furs or other products.
Containers made to store documents, taking various forms. Some examples include boxes with lids while others take the form of bags.
Sepulchral monuments containing the heart of a deceased king.
Baskets having a cover which does not come off but which is slotted to slide up on a rigid handle; of a type intended primarily for holding feathers.
Containers for the disposal of dry waste or garbage.

Containers for holding matches; used especially with reference to wood or metal containers, sometimes lined with a fireproof plasterlike material, usually having a striking surface on one side and often made to be hung on the wall. For small boxes intended for holding matches in a pocket or purse, use "matchboxes."

Accessories for carrying cosmetics on the person. Usually made of metal or plastic and can be quite decorative. Interior most often contains a mirror in the lid of one half and face powder in the other half, but may also have compartments for rouge or lipstick or a fitting for the attachment of a lipstick case.

Trusses with parallel chords between which the braces and ties are set at the same angle so as to form a series of isoceles triangles, the diagonals of which are alternately placed either in tension or compression.
Peasant paintings or needlework of long, narrow profile on linen or paper used to decorate farmhouses in Sweden.
Refers to images, in any medium but usually referring to painting, drawing, prints, photography, or digital works, that are recognizable as representations of visible entities.

Studies, drawings, illustrations, or other representations used to convey an idea for use in visual works such as animation, films, video games, comic books, or other media. The term was originally coined by Disney in the 1930s.

A broad genre of visual communication placed on surfaces, usually in urban environments; term reserved for works that are considered art or artistic, rather than casual notations or scribbles, which are called "graffiti." Examples of graffiti art include works expressed in a signature form, in either a stylized monogram or as large colorful murals. Examples may include works that are not in graphic media or are not created directly on the surface, but created and then applied to the surface. Graffiti art has occasionally been created as paintings on moveable supports. Contemporary graffiti art emerged in the mid-1970s in New York City, rendered in spray paint on subway train cars and walls. Originally graffiti art was illegal, applied to unauthorized public space or property by individuals or groups, though now it may also appear as commissioned work.

Works made from the inner bark of the lime or linden, which is cut into strips and coarsely plaited. Examples include costume and decorations. The term is also applied to works made of similar flexible fibrous barks or similar materials.

Distinctive Christian visual works having the hortus conclusus (enclosed garden) iconographical theme; best known from the late medieval period through the 17th century, often in female monastic settings. They typically took the form of low-relief panels or assemblages, for example with a central sculpture and elaborate textile or wax flowers, embroidery work. They portrayed the Virgin Mary, Crucifixion, or other sacred figure surrounded by flowers and plants. They developed in the southern Netherlands, but were found in northwestern Germany and elsewhere.
The process of reusing waste material to create a product of higher quality or value than the original, with the goal of reducing the need for additional raw materials.
Clappers of China, made of six pieces of wood and tied at one end with cord.
Written, negotiable documents that contain promises of payment.

Small tokens, of various metals and in various shapes, used as vouchers for members of a Christian denomination who had received confession or otherwise qualified for receiving the Christian sacrament of communion. Examples were found in the Lutheran, Calvinist, and other Christian traditions.
Inscribed counters or tokens used for reckoning accounts since the 13th century; often copies of contemporary coins; used after the 16th century mostly as souvenir pieces.
Method of distributing light to produce sharply defined shadows.
The structure of a material on a minute scale as revealed by a microscope or other means.
Coins made of metals with little value, such as copper, iron, lead, or tin, covered with a thin layer of precious metal, that imitate pieces of gold or silver.
General term used to collocate terms for all paper currency of North American origin.
Sweet viscous fluid produced by bees from the nectar collected from flowers.

In the age of forgeries, banknotes were submitted to banks for authentication using stamps (either dry or ink), which indicated their legitimacy. This method was commonly used during the 19th century.
Describes objects designed to bend over onto themselves into a compact form. For the activity of bending something over upon itself, use "folding (process)."
Small calcareous or siliceous bodies occurring in and serving to stiffen and support the tissues of various invertebrates, particularly mollusks, soft coral, and sponges.
Use to describe wooden watercraft hulls in which the lower ends of each plank overlaps the top end of the plank below it; the point of overlap is usually pinned, nailed, or riveted.
The actions, functions, or state of acquiring or imparting specific skills through instruction or practice. For directly instructing others in knowledge, attitudes, or skills, use "teaching."
Art Nouveau movement in Poland including the visual arts, literature, and music. The group of artists involved in the movement were active ca. 1890/1918.
Material comprising the bone of whales.

Religious season in Islam, the ninth month of the Islamic year, marking the time during which the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet. Muslims are enjoined to fast from dawn to dusk during this month and the observance of the Ramadan fast is one of the five 'pillars,' or basic duties, of Islam.
Federally issued United States paper money authorized as legal tender since 1862, originally with dark green ink on the reverse and not backed by gold or silver on deposit.
People or other animals who are in a state of sleep or who tend to sleep frequently.
In theology, those who are doomed to or undergoing eternal punishment, condemned or consigned to hell.
The activity of reaping, gathering, and sometimes storing an agricultural crop, such as corn another ripe crop.

Canopy-like arrangments of precious fabric, often consisting of celures, testers, and at least one set of valences. They were often used with chairs of estate, foot stools, and cushions, and could be raised onto a dais for added formality. For simple hangings of precious fabric placed behind a person, use "cloths of honor."
Form of farming that relies upon flooded soils to cultivate a crop, usually rice. This form of farming conserves soil's organic matter and nitrogen from biological sources.
Material made from tendons, the tough cords or bands of fibrous connective tissue forming the termination of the muscle by which it is attached to the bone or other part.
Material comprising stiff, lightweight, often colorful, keratin structures that are the principal covering of birds.

Small ancient Greek flasklike vessels with a circular body, wider than high, with a convex top and an arched handle extending from one side across the top to a spout on the other side; used for pouring perfumed oil. Askoi were often grave offerings and sometimes shaped like birds.
Minor coins of the United States and certain other former British territories, generally composed of 25% nickel and 75% copper in the United States, and valued at one twentieth of a dollar.
United States gold coins issued between 1795 and 1933 and valued at ten dollars.

Translucent or opaque material made from calf, sheep, or goat skin which has been limed, dehaired, scraped, and dried under tension to produce a thin, strong material for writing, bookbinding, or other uses. For finer quality calf parchment, use "vellum." The terms parchment and vellum sometimes have been and still are both confused and used interchangeably.

Fabric surfaces with a soft, napped quality, similar to the skin of a peach, created by brushing the face of a dense twill or satin weave. This surface may be found on fabrics in silk, cotton, or other artificial fibers.
Refers to the style and culture of the Chechen ethnic group, living primarily in the modern Russian republic of Chechnya in the North Caucasus.

Written orders drawn by one party ordering a second party to pay a specified sum of money to a third party (who may be the first party); usually restricted to domestic transactions. For similar orders to pay used for foreign transactions, prefer "bills of exchange."
Refers to trial sheets of printed matter that are checked against original manuscripts and on which errors can be corrected and alterations made.
A French fashion, originally a court jewel, which was derived from the pilgrim badge and worn on a hat. It was meant to convey the personal ambitions of the wearer.
Sets of tuned glass vessels played by rubbing or, more rarely, striking, producing sounds like bowed stringed instruments.

Small single-headed frame drums of Near Eastern origin, consisting of a shallow ring, usually of wood, covered on one side with a stretched membrane of parchment, animal skin, or plastic, usually furnished with jingling metal discs or small bells called jingles placed in slots or otherwise attached around the circumference. It is played by shaking, striking with the knuckles, or drawing the fingers across the parchment. The earlier name for this instrument, as mentioned in translations of the Bible, was "timbrel."

Hungarian reedpipes with a wood body and conical bore. Older types, traceable back to the 13th century, were played with a double reed and pirouette; the present day model is played with a single reed and clarinet-type mouthpiece.
Electronic percussion instruments developed in the 1930s, involving a series of rotating wheels that interrupt beams of light to produce complex rhythms very precisely, controlled from a keyboard.

Items of hardware, often made of brass or silver, including screwposts, brads, book clasps, hinges, book closures, coverplates, etc., that are added as functional and decorative finishes at the end of the bookbinding process.
Signs composed of two or more letterforms joined into a single graphic configuration.

Large group of typefaces based generally on 15th-century Italian letterforms, that is, using the Latin alphabet and neither black letter nor distinctly script forms. A roman typeface, in this sense, may include an accompanying italic face. For roman as the opposite of italic, use "roman (upright typeface group)."
Open fire baskets used to bend staves during the construction of wooden barrels.

Envelope-like cases formed from two squares of stiffened material or of cardboard lined with fabric; used to carry and hold the folded corporal (altar cloth). In Roman form the burse is ordinarily made of two juxtaposed pieces about twenty-five centimeters (or ten inches) square, bound together at three edges, leaving the fourth open to receive the corporal. The fabric of the case is of the liturgical color appropriate to the liturgical calendar. The use of the burse is relatively recent. When the corporal reached its present small dimensions, it was carried to the altar in the Missal or in a bag (burse) or box. For the larger box-like containers used to carry or store corporals, use "corporal cases."
Rigid, often rectangular containers usually with a lid or cover in which something nonliquid is kept or carried.
Traditional Māori receptacles made of kelp and tōtara bark; used to carry and store food, fresh water, live shellfish, and other substances or items.
Drinking vessels in the shape of a cup for drinking brandy, similar to but usually larger than a dram cup.
Ancient Roman silver or copper coins originally valued at two-and-one-half asses or one-fourth denarius, later at 4 asses, and issued from the late 3rd century BCE until the mid-3rd century CE.
Ancient Greek coins worth four drachmas, originally of pure silver but gradually debased over its lifetime from the mid-6th century BCE until about CE 300.
Large chalices having two handles, particularly those of the style favored in the Middle Ages, resembling loving cups.
Application of a second glaze to a piece of pottery.

Vertical lists of items or vertical sections into which the text of a manuscript or printed page are divided, separated by rules or blank spaces. For texts written from side to side across the page, use "long line format."
Wide headbands worn by women in ancient Rome to bind the hair in a neat fashion and to suggest modesty. Vittae can be plain or adorned with jewels to signify wealth.
Titles of books printed on the recto of the leaf preceding the first page of the text of a major division of the book, sometimes with the number of the division.
Duct flutes of Slovakia. They are large, wooden flutes, held vertically, and have a large stopped tube attached to a smaller tube which contains the mouthpiece.
Lighting for gardens; modern garden lights are often solar powered.

Kerosene floor lamps consisting of a three- or four-legged stand supporting a vertical rod which can be adjusted for height. At the top of the rod is a bowl-shaped false font, containing the oil pot with its burner, chimney, and shade.
Lighting fixtures fitted with gas burners.
Lights placed so that they mark the limits of the shore. For buildings or other substantial structures housing lights on or near the shore or nautical hazards, prefer "lighthouses."
Refers to a series of intertwined or chained pools channeling falling water down stepped inclines; often elaborately sculpted, especially as found in Italian, 16th-century formal gardens.

Medieval weapons consisting of a crescent-shaped blade mounted on a long staff, often with the lower tip or occasionally both tips of the edge attached to the staff, and a sharp thrusting spike on top of the staff. They were used by foot soldiers.

Objects originating in any culture still living or known through relatively recent history when those objects are the concern of ethnographic or ethnological study. For objects from earlier periods found in contexts of archaeological research, prefer "archaeological objects."
Small lights on a vehicle used to indicate its presence when parked.

Lamps in which light is produced by an electric arc between two electrodes in a quartz bulb filled with xenon gas. They give off a constant high intensity light and are used in motion picture projection, flash photography, and serve as light sources in accelerated aging chambers.
Beacons marking an obstruction or hazard as an aid to navigation.
Aeronautical ground lights supplementing an airway beacon, used to indicate the direction of the airway and to identify by coded signal the location of the airway beacon with which it is associated.

Lamps, usually of painted metal but also found in brass, with a cylindrical font in the shape of a tubular column containing a T-shaped wick tube which supports a flat wick and a rack-and-pinion wick raiser. A flat oval reservoir to the side feeds fuel to the font through a tube. Used with a cylindrical glass chimney and a painted sheet iron shade. Invented about 1800 by Count Rumford.

Mechanical lamps which have a spring-loaded piston in the reservoir which forces oil up through an elaborate control mechanism to the burner. These lamps may be identified by the large flat key below the burner used to compress the spring.
Gas burners in which two jets of gas issuing from two holes inclined toward each other meet to form a fan-shaped flame when ignited.

Yellowish-brown powder that absorbs moisture from the air to form green crystals soluble in water. Copper chloride is used as a fixative in dyeing and printing fabrics, as a wood preservative, and in refining of copper, gold, and silver.
