Refers to the movement in Latin America in the early 20th century advocating a new social and political role for the indigenous peoples of regions formerly dominated by European elites. The movement became influential with the presidency of Lßszaro Cßsrdenas (1934-1940) and sought to revitalize Indian heritage through art and revolutionary movements, such as Aprismo, a social movement in Peru whose members proposed to rename Latin America, "Indo-America".
In Indian architectural contexts, a circularly disposed group of bh01utas.
Refers to the cultures of the continent of South America, which is bounded by the Pacific Ocean, the Atlantic Ocean, Central America, and the Antarctic region.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of of the U.S. state of Arizona.
Nationality or culture of the Canadian province of Manitoba.

Yards or enclosures attached to a farmhouse or surrounded by farm buildings, used for airing livestock and other purposes. Yards or enclosures attached to a farmhouse or surrounded by farm buildings, used for airing livestock and other purposes.

A tendency identified in New York in the early 1960s that was in direct defiance to the prevailing trend of Abstract Expressionism, and was concerned with combining figurative forms with a new non-traditionalist outlook.
Roofs supported by pairs of queen posts.
General term to refer to the period or style of an area when it was recently colonized by a foreign power; usually refers to European colonization from the 16th-19th centuries.

Having to do with the style or culture of the south polar region of the earth, which comprises the continent of Antarctica together with the seas and islands of the Southern Ocean. Also refers to the flora, fauna, geography, oceanography, or climate of the region.
The style and culture of Andorra, an ancient principality located in the Pyrenees between France and Spain.
Rails attached to walls which are usually adjacent to stairs.

Beliefs and practices of the ancient peoples and civilizations of what is now Turkey and Armenia, including the Hittites, Hattians, Luwians, Hurrians, Assyrian colonists, Urartians, and Phrygians. Until comparatively recent times, the pre-Christian religions of Anatolia (Asia Minor) were known only through the works of classical writers. For the Greeks and Romans, Asia Minor was above all the home of the religion of Cybele, the Great Mother of the Gods, whose cult was centred in Phrygian Pessinus.
Religious followings that are Christian. Distinguinshed from "Christian orders."

A sect of Islam that emerged in early Islamic history as a political faction that supported the rule of Ali, son-in-law of Muhammad and fourth caliph of the Muslim community. It This branch of Islam advocates the idea of rule in the Muslim world based on lineage; only descendants of Ali could rule. Adherents to this branch of are often associated with militant Islamic fundamentalism. It is distinguished from the larger Sunni branch.

A 19th-century Hindu reform movement that has its roots in the Hindu apologist and reformer Rammohun Roy (1772-1833) who was impressed by Western achievements but believed that Indian spirituality was greater. The theistic movement, influenced by Islam, Christianity, and modern science, sought a return to the purity of Hindu worship through a rejection of idol-worship, an emphasis on monotheism, and a reform of Hindu social practices. Roy's most important reform was to convince the British that sati, the practice of widow burning, was not part of original dharma and should be banned. The movement continued, with much division, into the 20th century, but quickly lost members and influence.

Refers to a system of theology based on the doctrine of the Dutch Reformed theologian Jacobus Arminius (1560-1609). Arminius and his followers opposed the Calvinist doctrine of absolute predestination and instead believed that man's free will and God's sovereignty are compatible. The beliefs of Arminianism were the subject of fierce controversy but were ultimately widely influential. Arminianism was especially influential on English theologians.

Refers to the version of Buddhism that originated in India and spread to Central Asia, China, Japan, mainland Southeast Asia, Java, Sumatra, and Sri Lanka (Abhayagiri monastery). It is often characterized as the pan-Asiatic form of Buddhism, involving widely-accepted basic shifts in the original Buddhist doctrine and approach. This form of Buddhism discredits the existence of the self and the presence of dharmas, and challenges the idea that the Buddha comes exclusively from an elite lineage (arhat), substituting in its place the idea of the bodhisattva, someone who possesses the innate tendency to become Buddha, a disposition inherent in all persons. This form of Buddhism values benevolence and service to others above all else and advocates the struggle for internal peace and supreme wisdom (prajna) through the nullification of the self and struggle toward an ultimate reality.

Areas or constructions comprising one or more flights of stairs, with the necessary landings and connecting platforms to form a continuous and uninterrupted passage from one level to another, as defined by the International Code Council.
Stairs which turn 270 degrees as they progress from bottom to top.
Uncovered wood or metal platforms, usually attached to structures and often raised off the ground or on rooftops.

The process or function of evaluating a thing or person against a scale, standard, or other criteria for quality, condition, value, extent, fitness, or other characteristics. Examples are the assessment of the habitable condition of a building or the academic value of a written work. For the estimation of the overall monetary value of a thing, generally prefer “appraising” or “valuation.”
Extension of political and economic control over an area by a foreign occupying state that usually has organizational and military superiority.
Small spaces provided in a building in order to be able to gain access to plumbing, wiring, and other equipment.

Rooms or areas set aside and furnished for babies and young children, especially those located in a house and serving as a bedroom or playroom. A nursery differs from a nursery school or day care in that the latter house private or public institutions for the instruction of young children, while a nursery is typically in a private home or an orphanage and facilitates the care of babies in addition to young children.

Any physically defined areas intended for or devoted to the display of organized, usually named, temporary public displays of works of art, crafts, natural history, science, or other items of cultural interest. Exhibition spaces may be enclosed, in defined outdoor areas, built for this purpose or claimed from structures used for other purposes previously, and may be considered either permanent or temporary.
Rooms designed or adapted for the holding of conferences, with the room usually focused around a large table and chairs.
Burial chambers, chapels, or oratories within tomb spaces such as catacombs or crypts attached to churches.

Refers to relatively large ornamented walls, screens, or other structures located above and behind the high altar of a Christian church, often holding the sacred tabernacle. A reredos may be placed against the apse wall, directly behind the altar, or may form part an altar screen. Its form evolved from the dossal, a tapestry or painting on the wall behind the altar. In church design, It may serve as a screen between celebrant and the congregation or between the choir and the retrochoir. In Spanish churches the reredos grew to be as wide as the nave and reaching to the vaulting of the roof. The reredos may be made of precious materials and heavily decorated, often with carvings, niches, sculptures, paintings and tapestries. It is distinct from a 'retable'; while the reredos typically rises from ground level behind the altar, the retable is smaller, standing either on the back of the altar itself or on a pedestal behind it. Many altars have both a reredos and a retable.

Horizontal members laid across the bottom of an unfinished opening to act as a base during construction of window frames or door frames. For the horizontal members that rest on the foundation at the bottom of a wood structure, use "sill plates."
Rolled or extruded structural metal beams having a cross section resembling the letter I.
Projecting bands, usually of masonry, that support or decorate domes or vaults.
Commodes which consist of a single drawer set on tall legs presumably intended to stand beneath a mirror.
Joints comprising the spaces between bricks, concrete blocks, or glass blocks, that are filled with mortar or grout. Mortar joints can be made in a series of different fashions.
In masonry construction, any mortar joints on the face of a brick or stone wall, above the ground level.
Rigid stays, usually of wood or metal, and commonly in compression.

Beams or other lements that project horizontally or nearly horizontally into space, and are fixed at one end and carry a load distributed along the length or at the other, such as a diving board. The upper half of the thickness of such a beam is subjected to tensile stress, tending to elongate the fibres, the lower half to compressive stress, tending to crush them. Beams or other lements that project horizontally or nearly horizontally into space, and are fixed at one end and carry a load distributed along the length or at the other, such as a diving board. The upper half of the thickness of such a beam is subjected to tensile stress, tending to elongate the fibres, the lower half to compressive stress, tending to crush them.

In Indian architecture, a superstructure type composed of corner and intermediate pillarettes supporting miniature Latina śikhara and having a vertical jāla-spine at the bhadras; superstructure type with corner and intermediate vertical bands made up of shrine-models above pillarets
All the members of buildings or structures required to transmit loads to the ground.
Parts or components of pile foundations.
Furniture, ornament, windows, and other objects that are fastened in position and form part of a religious building, usually the interior, but are not an integral part of the architecture itself.
In architecture, a general term for a part or significant component of a built work that is seen as or considered as distinct within the overall design.
The compass point lying midway between north and west.
In Indian architecture, the space occupying the āditala or ground level.
Fastener similar to a bolt but with a fine thread and a slotted head for use with a screwdriver. Often used to join sheet metal parts.
Boxes or receptacles of varied design that are engineered to release a small amount of liquid or powdered soap, usually intended for use in handwashing.
Valves connected to water faucets in hospitals or other sanitary environments that control the flow of water without the use of the hands.
Swimming pools usually found in the palaestra of large bathhouses.
Written accounts of the lives of saints. For the genre regardless of medium, prefer "hagiography (genre)."
Collocates names for general color names that are used in the literature but do not consistently correspond to precise colors.

A pasty building material that sets to form a hard, infusible solid. Most mortars are mixtures of lime, plaster of Paris, or cement with sand and water. It is used to fill the joints of brick and stone masonry and for other purposes.
Beveled spring bolts usually operated by a knob, handle, or turn.
Heavy cane shaped bolt with the top beant and right angles. It is used on the bottom of doors.

A method of mounting a flexible support such as paper or textile onto a solid support such as a wall or panel, whether before painting or afterwards. May be extended to lining a painting with another canvas to strengthen it.
Generally, any electronic calculator that is small enough to be carried in a pocket or bag.

Organized examination and evaluation of built works, usually by a qualified professional. May involve a visual inspection along with testing various aspects of the building using equipment and technologies.
Chemical analysis aimed at determining the proportions of the substances present in a sample of a material.
Rooms in clubs, libraries, hotels, or public institutions especially adapted and appropriate to reading and study.

A chamber designed to create a vacuum environment by removal of air and gasses with a pump. In conservation science practice, vacuum chambers are used for such purposes as drying, degassing, fumigation, resin impregnation.
In ancient theaters, projecting structures or wings flanking the stage on either side, and with the scaena, or background, enclosing the stage on three sides.
Any of the equipment effecting movement on the stage, including groove systems, devices for flying figures, etc.
Protruding angles of bastions or other fortifications, where the faces (i.e. the angle sides directed towards the attacker) converge.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Kenya.
Construction utilizing various different building materials and for the use of more than one type of construction method in a structure, such as a masonry building with a laminated wood beam roof.

Construction of dwellings that follows a standard for energy efficiency, particularly construction that is certified to meet criteria for heating, cooling, and other energy demands in addition to airtightness. These standards often include reliance on solar heating and insulation to create low-energy buildings.

Refers to drawings, or works in another medium, created by parallel perspective, which is either a system of perspective in which primary subjects are parallel to the picture plane or a system in which parallel projecting lines do not converge as they recede into space.
Planned works, such as works of art or architecture, that were never physically produced. For architecture more specifically, use "unbuilt projects."

French term meaning "deceive the eye," applied to images so realistic that they may fool the viewer into thinking that the represented objects, scenes, textures, or points of view are real rather than images. The term is generally used to refer to Western art, generally to two-dimensional art or bas-relief. It was seen in ancient Greek art, refined by the ancient Romans, and was popular in the Renaissance and later in Europe and America. Effects include painted textures of wood or marble on walls or columns, realistic portrayals of views framed by painted faux windows, false frames from which the contents of a still life or portrait appear to extend into the viewer's space, and depictions of shelves or cupboards with various articles seen through half-open doors. In the late 20th century, the exteriors of entire buildings have been painted in trompe l'oeil.
Central administration by a system of government in which several states form a unity but remain independent in internal affairs.

Thin vaults of one or more layers of terracotta tiles laid flat edge to edge and deriving their rigidity from cohesion and curvature rather than from massiveness or compression; can be erected without centering.

Arches in which neither intrados nor extrados has any curvature, yet is composed of voussoirs arranged so that lateral thrusts are generated from vertical loads; for arches with very slight curvature, use "camber arches."
Doctrine or theory that emphasizes psychological conceptions outside the field of psychology.
The technique of storytelling, particularly in the visual arts.

Refers to the angle at which a liquid or vapor makes contact with a solid surface. Contact angle quantifies the ability of a liquid to maintain contact with a solid surface. It is used, for example, as a measure of comparison for water droplets deposited on a flat stone surface before and after a water repellent coating has been applied to it, the difference in contact angle supplying information about surface hydrophobization.
The convex fillings of the lower part of some flutes of classical columns or pilasters.
Actions or displays of daring, courage, valor, or fortitude.
Metal or plastic clips in the form of a partial circle, worn around the ankles, to protect the trousers from tangling in the cycle chain while riding a bicycle.

As used in the in the Yingzao fashi (1103) to define a building component, the fang 方 is a structural timber whose cross-section measurement is based on a single standard modular unit (dancai) of the larger building. Its application is relatively flexible, and the term is often modified by the names of locations where it is used within the building. In the Qing dynasty the character fang 枋 encompasses the architectural use of the character 方.

Any alteration in regional or global climate as during the five glacial periods of the past 450,000 years. The term is often applied to the recent changes in global climatic patterns, attributed to emission of greenhouse gases, also known as global warming.
Immobile bodily postures, seen in Buddhist, Hindu and other traditions and in the practice of yoga.
Architectural order characterized especially by the use of rusticated columns and introduced by the French architect Delorme
Door locks with a spring bolt that cannot be operated from the outside except by a key.
Spring latches or deadlocking latches that have a 3/4-inch throw and an antifriction retractor.
Pulls, for drawers or doors, having a disk shape.
Handles or grips designed to fit the fingers, and used to open or close sliding receptacles in furniture or cupboards.
Joints in a masonry wall which have the mortar raked out to a specified depth while it is still soft.
The level corresponding to the surface of the sea at mean level between high and low tides, used as a standard for the measurement of heights.
Standards of behavior, job performance, and work habits considered to be characteristic of professionals.

The preservation of natural or cultural resources through managed use. For example, as an ecological concept, the preservation of natural resources through responsible use and stewardship; a component of sustainable development. In context of conservation, preserving cultural heritage resources through maintenance and limited use.
Performers who amuse their audience by telling jokes or acting comically.
Damage caused by fire, including burning and ash residue.
Doors of several hinged horizontal sections, that slide up along tracks to end in a horizontal position over the space to be entered; common in the United States as garage doors.
In Jewish tradition, the anniversary of the death of a parent or other close relative.
Holidays that are observed throughout a nation.
Smooth surfaced doors having faces which are plane and which conceal their rails and stiles or other structure.
In Indian architecture, a doorframe having four śākhās (jambs).
Postmortem examinations, such as inspections and dissections of bodies to determine the cause of death.

Relatively small classes for advanced students taught by a person of distinguished expertise, usually also involving practical demonstration and exercises in the skill being taught; especially common in the performing arts.
Confirmation ceremonies held in a synagogue on the occasion of a Jewish boy having reached the age of thirteen, regarded as the age of religious responsibility for males.
Events, usually competitive, focusing on the act of chasing wild animals for the purpose of catching or killing them.
In Indian architecture, a gateway with a tall upper storey.

Activity involving the execution of precise movements by a horse in response to its rider, where the horse has been trained in specific types of obedience and deportment. Horse and rider are expected to precisely and harmoniously execute a wide range of maneuvers, ranging from the simplest riding gaits to the most intricate and difficult airs and figures. Classical dressage is believed to be an ancient art that evolved from cavalry movements and training for the battlefield. From this, competitive dressage developed into a modern equestrian sport.
Processions that take place on water, using boats and rafts rather than horses or wheeled carts for transportation, marking a festive or solemn occasion.
Openings in a roof, glazed or filled with other transparent or translucent material, serving to admit light to a space below.
Days of celebration observed by followers of Hinduism.
Windows having a louver or louvers which fill all or part of the opening.
Windows externally located in a wide band of trim just beneath cornices; found on Greek Revival houses.

Spectacles in ancient Rome that included chariot races and various kinds of theatrical performances, held at regular intervals in honor of any of several gods. They are distinct from the gladiatorial contests.

Works made with and existing in the context of networked systems, meant to be accessed via network protocols. This term is not used to refer to reproductions of art made in other media that is represented on Web sites or online media. 'Web art' is considered a separate concept, as net art may use protocols other than the World Wide Web. Some argue that net art is independent of technology, and is defined only as work that uses systems or social situations as the medium, but the majority of these works exist in the context of computer networking systems.
Parties or formal social gatherings, particularly after a wedding, at which a person or persons are honoured or welcomed, and at which guests may be formally received.
Games played with playing cards, which are cards made in sets and marked in specific ways.
Refers to axonometric projection in which the three spatial axes are unequally inclined to the plane of projection or drawing surface, and the ratio of foreshortening is different for all three axes.

Endeavors to gain the attention, favor, or affection of another being, usually with the intent of establishing a relationship of further intimacy or marriage; the period during which such activities take place.
Actions causing death or torture by shooting the victim with arrows, as from a bow and arrow.

General term for all ornamental canopy-like coverings of cloth, stone, wood, or metal used in a Christian church, such as to crown an altar, tabernacle, throne, pulpit, or statue. Examples are the structure covering an altar, formerly fitted with curtains and supported on four pillars; the covering suspended over the throne occupied by dignitaries of the Church or princes; the covering under which the Blessed Sacrament is sometimes borne in processions; or the parasol-like object sometimes placed on the north side of the altar in a stand.
Offering a specific sum as the price one will pay or charge.

Generally, reviewing a practice or set of practices to certify that they are being conducted in accordance with established principles. In the context of financial matters, the periodic or continual assessment of the financial assets and liabilities of an organization.
Rooms in or attached to a horse barn or stable for the storage and maintenance of riding tack and often of stud records or for the display of prizes or other honors of the stable.
Structures projecting from a sloping roof usually housing a window or ventilating louver.
Ornamental cresting on the top of a screen or cornice, usually formed of leaves, Tudor flowers, or miniature battlements; found especially in English Late Gothic architecture.
Longitudinal members at the apexes of roofs that support the upper ends of the rafters.
In Indian architecture, the divisions or apportionments in the plan and elevation of the structure.
Acts or rites of setting aside something or someone to a special use or purpose, or to the memory of particular people or events.
Festivals held to celebrate the gathering of crops, usually expressing thanks for a successful harvest.
Energy-related concepts dealing with light.
The fluctuations that occur in the numbers of individuals in plant and animal populations in time and space.
Activity of solving or ameliorating a community's social and economic problems, organized and controlled mainly by the community itself.
Unplanned development of, usually commercial, buildings built side by side or adjoining, and stretching in continuous strings along both sides of a roadway.
The state of being related by common ancestry.
Personal liberties that belong to each individual due to his or her status as a citizen of a particular country or community.
A political outlook that values and seeks to conserve established institutions, respects traditions as embodying the accumulated wisdom of the ages, and generally opposes liberalism and socialism.

The condition or role when a party, entity, action, or situation has a direct causal relationship with another party, entity, action, or situation. For example, an action may be proven to have caused a situation.
Aggregate of property or liabilities of all kinds that a person leaves for his or her disposal at death.
Mathematical concepts related to geometry.
Degree or amount of separation between two points, lines, surfaces, or objects in geometrical space.
Two-dimensional geometrical configurations.
Plane figures having four angles and four sides.
A value in an ordered set of quantities above and below which fall an equal number of quantities.
The acts or processes of adding.
Stock market conditions characterized by the rising price of stock, as opposed to bear markets, when they are falling.
Payments made to inventors or creators for the right to reproduce or perform their works.

Prices that are established for certain goods or services and cannot be negotiated. Examples are fixed prices for a certain meal on a restaurant menu, prices set at a bazaar where it is otherwise customary to haggle a lower price, or prices for a market commodity that are set rather than flutuating based on demand.

The retention or imitation of what is old or obsolete, especially the use in language, art, and other cultural areas of the characteristics of an earlier period. It often is based on the belief in the innate value of the earlier model coming from a simpler, purer golden age,  and that the revival of these forms will encourage a revival of the imagined quality of life of those former days.

Drawings of a pointing hand that were used as symbols in marginalia for marking noteworthy passages in texts, particularly during the 12th through 18th centuries in the Western world. In modern use, the manicule is a typographical symbol employed for similar purposes in texts, the Internet, as bullet symbols, and other contexts.

A figure of speech or visual work that implies comparison between two unlike entities, in which a word, phrase, or idea is applied to something to which it is not literally applicable in order to suggest a resemblance. Metaphor is the fundamental language of poetry, although it is common in all kinds of language and in visual works. An example is the title of the Tennessee Williams play, "Sweet Bird of Youth," which implyies that the time of youth seems to fly, i.e., pass quickly. For an explicit comparison signaled by the words "like" or "as," use "simile."
Biographies employing fact and some invented elements with the intent to both inform and entertain.
Poetry composed and delivered in honor of a person, extolling the person's character or accomplishments.
An ordered and harmonious system that comprises the world or universe.
The condition in which each thing is clearly distinguished and properly disposed with reference to other things, and performs its proper function.
Philosophy incorporating essential features of the thinking of Aristotle.

Refers to the practice of self-control and self-denial as an act of religious devotion and a means of achieving greater spiritual awareness; it is found in different forms and to different extents in all religions. Ascetic practices include fasting, a solitary life, meditation, celibacy, the renunciation of possessions, and the mortification of flesh.
The introduction or condition of having unwanted biological, chemical, physical, or radiological substances or matter.
Stored capacity of a body or system to do work by virtue of its configuration and position.
Light waves made to vibrate in a single plane.

Emission of light through a means other than heat, as contrasted to light emitted from incandescent bodies, such as burning wood or molten iron. Luminescence may be seen in neon and fluorescent lamps, television, radar, in organic substances such as luminol or the luciferins in fireflies and glowworms, and in natural electrical phenomena such as lightning and the aurora borealis.
A given space filled with a gas at pressure below atmospheric pressure.

That portion of the electromagnetic spectrum visible to the human eye, having a wavelength in the range from about 4,000 (violet) to about 7,700 (red) angstroms and may be perceived by the normal unaided human eye. It ranges from the red end to the violet end of the spectrum, with wavelengths from 700 to 400 nanometres and frequencies from 4.3 x 1014 to 7.5 x 1014 Hz. Like all electromagnetic radiation, light travels through empty space at a speed of about 186,000 miles per second (300,000 km/sec). In the mid-19th century, light was described by James Clerk Maxwell in terms of electromagnetic waves, but 20th-century physicists have shown that it exhibits properties of particles as well; its carrier particle is the photon. Light is the basis for the sense of sight and for the perception of color.
The degree of height or depth of a musical tone or other sound, depending upon the relative rapidity of the vibrations by which it is produced.
Usually restricted to references to the weather, season, or climate, indicating a persistently moderate state of warmth: neither too hot nor too cold; of mild and equable temperature.
The effective working together of standardized independent units, especially in an electronic system.
Includes both the quantity that is a measure of the amount of energy in a system not available for doing work, and the ultimate state in the degradation of matter and energy in the universe.
Skill of producing work of high quality.
Includes the range of color which an artist uses, the typical color range of a school or group, or the range of colors possible when mixing a prescribed group of colorants.

The practice of borrowing pre-existing forms or images to form a new art work, particularly when done in order to bring into question issues of originality in art, for example, in certain Post-modern art.
The quality of having a pH value greater than 7 or of having the properties of an alkali.

The power or property of resistance, especially the reciprocal of electrical conductivity. The opposition offered by an object to electrical flow; the degree to which something impedes passage through it of a current. In conservation, means of maximizing such resistance are sometimes sought to protect materials; as with highly impermeable resin coatings to steel in order to strengthen electrical resistance to current corrosion.
Slow, continuous deformation or movement of structures and landscape features under sustained pressure or downward pull, such as by gravity.
A measure of the stiffness of a material, its resistance to bending; the ratio of stress to strain in flexural deformation.

The percentage of light reflected by a given surface. The highest brightness value, 100%, is a brilliant white and 0% is black. When referring to the degree of lightness or darkness of a color, use "value (color)."

Emission of electromagnetic radiation, usually visible light, caused by excitation of atoms in a material, which then reemit almost immediately. The initial excitation is usually caused by absorption of energy from incident radiation or particles, such as X-rays or electrons.
A property usually acquired by applying a finish to fabric or other substance that prevents the spread of flame.

Use when referring to the manner in which contiguous shapes are joined or formed in architectural or decorative designs or in works of art; also, the clarification of an architectural design by emphasizing certain elements of the structure.

Decorative technique in which thin pieces of gold and silver leaf that have been shaped into squares, strips or lozenges are applied to lacquerware, paintings, and sculptures. Originally introduced to Japan during the Nara period (710-794), the technique was popular from the Heian period (794-1185) through the Kamakura period (1185-1333).
The shape, in full or in outline, of a cross section of an inverted cup or bell with flaring rim and convex crown; an example is in mathematics, the bell curve of a Gaussian function.
Scale represented by numbers and text, for example "3/4 scale," "4 feet to 1 inch," "1:50."
Lines that represent the ground plane in an image.

An optical effect manifested as a series of alternating light and dark colored bands; generally caused when one piece of glass with a curved surface rests on another with a flat surface, resulting in an interference of light waves. Named for the English physicist Sir Isaac Newton who first investigated their properties.

Refers to a perspective system that indirectly uses two vanishing points, but is empirical rather than scientific. It was primarily used in Western art prior to the codification of one-point perspective in the Renaissance. In bifocal perspective, two vanishing points are placed at the same height at the left and right margins of the picture plane. From these points are drawn diagonal lines to points along the bottom or top margins of the picture plane; the points at which these diagonal lines cross are used to draw a floor or ceiling grid which resembles a grid drawn with a single central vanishing point and gives the illusion of recession into space.

Refers to linear perspective in which there are three vanishing points, generally in the context of rectangular forms depicted so that none of their sides is parallel to the picture plane, but instead each of three groups of parallel lines recede to their own vanishing points. This technique was made popular in 17th-century European stage design. It may also refer to depictions in which there are three points of view, as was also often used in Chinese hanging scroll landscapes, in which the viewer sees the foreground from above, the middle ground at eye-level, and the highest objects from below.
Tactile and sometimes visual quality of a surface given to it by the size, shape, arrangement, and proportions of its minute parts, such as granules, particles, threads, or brushstrokes.
Loads acting on a very small area of a structure.
Bending or twisting stress in a structural member combined with direct tension or compression.
Ideas, facts, or allegations spread deliberately to support one cause or individual or to damage another.

Architectural designs that are eccentric, outrageous, or unconventional, that jolt or excite the viewer, and that are generally characterized by an unusual juxtaposition of shapes or materials; may be spontaneously constructed, incomplete, or unbuilt.

Art utilizing photography, graphic design, or other art forms to design logos, advertisements, illustrations, books, brochures, signs, posters, animation, Web pages, or other displays to promote sale or acceptance of products, services, or ideas.
A key concept for Futurist artists concerning the representation of movement and the persistence of images.
Use generally for all education beyond the high school or secondary level.
Branch of geography that deals with the exterior physical features and changes of the earth in land, sea, and air.
Branch of history concerned with any and all aspects of seafaring in any context, such as commerce, exploration, warfare, and culture.

A branch of law that deals with the organization of government, the responsibilities of public agencies and officers, and the relations between a government and its citizens, as well as those of sovereign states to one another.

Branch of political science dealing primarily with the planning, operation, and supervision of government agencies, programs, and functions, as well as the determination and implementation of public policy.
Study of how people are affected by others and by their social environment.

Refers to the branch of sociology that studies the relation between thought and society, particularly the social processes and structures that produce or condition the forms and the content of knowledge.
Study of phenomena related to computers, including the construction, operation, programming, and applications of computers.

Branch of agriculture that aims at increasing or maintaining productivity at levels that are economically viable, environmentally sound, and culturally acceptable, through the efficient conservation and use of resources, while protecting the environment and the health of humans and animals.
The scientific study of all plant life, including their structure, properties, and biochemical processes.
The study of the structure and function of large molecules associated with living organisms, particularly proteins and the nucleic acids DNA and RNA.
Study of pollen grains, spores, and other microscopic plant materials, whether living or fossilized, especially their dispersal and applications in stratigraphy and paleontology.
Branch of zoology that deals with birds.
Branch of engineering concerned with the development, production, and application of ceramic and ceramic products.
Branch of civil engineering dealing primarily with the design and construction of structures such as bridges, buildings, and dams.
Interdisciplinary science and technology of interactive sliding surfaces. The three chief branches of tribology are lubrication, friction, and wear.
Branch of horticulture concerned with the cultivation of ornamental trees, shrubs, flowers, and other plants, primarily for landscape amenity and not food-producing purposes.
Treatment of disease by exposure to the sun.

The science concerned with the use of radiation, such as X-rays and radioactive materials in the diagnosis and treatment of disease. For the application of techniques producing radiographic images, use "radiography."
A method of calculation and especially one of several highly systematic methods of treating problems by a special system of algebraic notations, as differential or integral calculus.
The sciences concerned with the nature, origin, evolution, and behavior of the solid earth, its waters, and the air that envelops it, including the geologic, hydrologic, and atmospheric sciences.

Study of the chemical composition of the earth. It involves estimating the abundance of the constituent elements and their isotopes, as well as their distribution in the lithosphere, atmosphere, biosphere, and hydrosphere, and in the rocks and minerals that make up the earth.
Field of study surrounding the earth's topologic features above sea level, especially the measurement and mapping of land features.
The scientific study of minerals, including their formation, occurrence, properties, composition, and classification.
The branch of paleontology which studies processes of decay and preservation of plant and animal remains, including fossilization.

The branch of physics encompassing the study of the behavior and control of electrons. Includes the design and application of devices and systems whose operation depends fully or partially upon the characteristics and behavior of electrons flowing through semiconductors, vacuums, or gases.
The study and application of medical knowledge to questions of civil and criminal law, especially in court proceedings.

Study and practice of ritual activities intended to control or influence human or natural events through the invocation of external and impersonal mystical forces beyond the ordinary human sphere; typical ritual activities include the manipulation of special objects and the recitation of spells.

The implementation of disaster planning, incident preparedness, a disaster recovery plan; and a subset of business continuity. In conservation context, interventions on behalf of structures and artifacts affected by man made or natural disaster.
Analysis that measures how spending associated with an event flows through a regional economy as measured by positive changes in aspects of the economy such as profits, wages, and jobs.
Area of information management concerned with achieving economy and efficiency in the creation, use, handling, control, maintenance, and disposition of records.
A geophysical technique of surveying involving the measurement of distortions of the earth's normal magnetic field; used in archaeology especially to locate buried remains.
Art of writing, particularly the creation of beautiful, elegant letters or flourishes by hand with a pen, either in unjoined characters or in cursive writing.
Gardening based on soil management practices that do not include artificial or potentially toxic fertilizers, pesticides, or herbicides.
Measuring techniques used to date bone.

Generally refers to the activity of keeping people and things safe from harm or deterioration. For actions taken to prevent further changes or deterioration in objects, sites, or structures, use "preservation". When such actions are taken on buildings or other structures specifically for cultural, aesthetic, or historic reasons, use "historic preservation."
Storms in which falling rain freezes as soon as it touches any object.
Ceremonial events that are related to culture or background.
Design competitions available for students, sponsored usually by a school, foundation, or sector of the business community, for which prizes are awarded.
Exhibitions that lay out facts and examples to tell a story or explain an issue.
Meetings or sessions in which testimony, evidence, or arguments are presented in a formal setting, usually before an official.

Enclosed white spaces issuing from the mouths of cartoon or photographic characters in comics, generally used to express dialogue or thoughts but also a variety of signs and symbols, such as punctuation, to express emotions. Speech is indicated by a solid line, arrow, or tapered cone linking the balloon to the speaking character, while thought is indicated by a series of bubbles linking the balloon to the thinking character.
In type, a set of capitals smaller than and distinct from the regular capitals of a font.
Physical strength, might, or vigor.
Sense by which the flavor or savor of things is perceived when they are brought into contact with the tongue.
Psychological concepts related to behavior and mental disorders.
A high or excessively high opinion of one's own worth or importance, which gives rise to a feeling or attitude of superiority over others.
The process of receiving and interpreting sensory impressions attained by sight.
The state or experience based on the endurance of pain, distress, loss, or damage.
The use of the sun's energy to provide heating or to generate electricity.
Care of children or others unable to be left by themselves by persons other than their parents, family, or guardians on a partial or full day basis.

In criminal law, the action of assault in which a person or people have sexual intercourse with another person without that person's consent. The term formerly referred to abduction for this purpose; it was used for the action of carrying off a person, usually a woman, and typically for the purpose of sexual violation.
Discriminatory attitudes and denial of rights, privileges, or choice because of race.
Wars that involve most of the leading political and military powers of the world or most of the earth's territory.
Climate characterized by mild winters and hot summers. Rainfall patterns vary considerably throughout the subtropics which include deserts as well as humid forests.
Noise in the environment which is harmful, or irritating.
Water condensed from atmospheric vapor and falling in drops.
A wind blowing from the west.

The physical position that is precisely definable in terms of geographic or astronomic measurement, or situation relative to geographic or astronomic features or to elements of the built environment. For the concept of a space or area within the lived world of daily experience which possesses emotional, purposive, and social connotations along with physical features and characteristics, use "place."

Various styles and methods of binding performed for libraries utilizing machine or hand methods, or a combination, and executed to provide optimum durability. Included are the first-time hardcover binding of loose periodical issues, case binding of paperbound publications, the rebinding or repair of older volumes, and the prebinding of new publications specifically for high-volume circulation by public libraries.

Sculpture construction technique where cloth is soaked with lacquer and then draped over a mold that is removed once the lacquer has dried. The technique was introduced to Japan from China in the 8th century and is still used. For hollow dry lacquer technique, see "dakkatsu kanshitsu"; for wood-core dry lacquer technique, see "mokushin kanshitsu."
Technique in which a design is impressed into a soft surface, such as unfired clay, by using a mold or other implement.
Weaving on a loom or other device operated wholly or partly by hand or foot power.
Embroidering a design by laying down a thread and fastening it with small stitches at regular intervals.
Quilting technique in which designs outlined with stitching are heavily stuffed from the back with filling to give a raised effect.
Trimming or finishing edges or seams with tubular strips of textile or leather.
The process of placing sheets of paper or tissue, usually blank, between leaves of text or illustrations for protective or decorative purposes or for taking notes.
Strengthening elements of the built environment against attack, providing them with some means of defense, or protecting them with fortifications or fortification elements.
The process of removing historical restorations. A common reason is that the old restorations are now considered bad practice.

The process of passing a liquid or other material through a filter or porous medium in order to remove  or separate solid particles or impurities. May also refer to the process of passing an electrical signal or other signal through a filter to remove excess noise or undesired frequencies.
Removal of liquid from a material under reduced air pressure, allowing a lower temperature of drying than under normal pressure. In conservation, used in mass drying of waterlogged objects.
Addition of a structural element to something, usually in another material, for the purpose of improving its strength or stiffness.
The process of supporting a structure or part of one temporarily upon shores.
Gilding when the surface is not burnished or polished.
The process of cutting or engraving glass pieces using a wheel or grindstone.
Traditional Venetian flooring process in which colored marble chips are set in polished mortar and honed, creating a smooth surface.
Refers to a method of drying materials or objects in a frozen state.
Refers to the firing of ceramics at relatively high temperatures, as with porcelain, which is fired at a temperature up to 1280 degrees Celsius.
Process of transporting goods sending goods to people, stores, or other destinations.
The process of making works primarily of feathers; usually feathers are either adhered to a solid support or tied individually to a woven support.

An expensive and difficult method of decorating porcelain in which designs are painted in successive layers of white porcelain slip applied in slight relief on vessels or plaques of unfired clay and lightly carved with metal instruments before first firing to achieve a cameo-like effect. The pieces are then glazed and fired again. The technique developed at Sèvres in the mid-19th century; it was most effectively practiced there and at the Minton factory by Marc-Louis-Emmanuel Solon.
Penetration of hides or skins with oil or other lipid-rich substances to produce a durable, soft-napped leather such as chamois.
Removing defects from the flesh side of leather by means of an abrasive or abrading tool.  For the removal of defects from the grain side of leather by similar means, use "buffing (leather process)."
The process of fashioning things from iron.
Methods or practices used with metal decoration.
Brazing method where heat is developed by electricity in a heating coil and induced into the parts to be brazed.
A process by which thermoplastic materials are softened and welded together with heat produced by friction.
The process of coating an object with a thin adherent layer of gold, silver, or other metal.
The act or process of covering with silver.

A process of plating copper, also sometimes brass or iron, with silver leaf, as used by French platers from the early 18th century, and later by English platers, to repair imperfectly plated copper pieces or to refinish exposed copper on worn pieces. Similar to "close plating"  but costlier.
The technique of engraving and decorating metal with an overall pattern of continuous, encircling, and contiguous narrow grooves, usually of a wavy character.

Refers to the process of striking metal with a hammer or other instrument in order to create a vessel or other shape, or to create decoration. The oldest technique may have been to create a thin disk of metal by hammering it into a hollow carved in a block of wood. A vessel may be slowly raised by being struck on the outside surface using a specially shaped hammer and anvil. Embossing or repoussé work use hammering to create a design or pattern in a metal object, usually by hammering from the back of the piece.
Forming the shape of a metal object by heating and hammering.
The use of or investigation with a fluorescence microscope.

A form of spectroscopy in which photoelectrons excited by a beam of monochromatic x-rays are measured in order to find the characteristic binding energies of electrons at particular levels of the sample, thus identifying elements present there.
Dissolution into separate parts, losing intactness or solidness.
Deterioration of rock caused by salt crystallization, or haloclasty, salt hydration, or thermal expansion of salts in rock pores.

Condition where a surface or material has cracked due to pressure, differential in temperature, or other strain of some kind. An example is in glassmaking, where fissures develop in the body of a vessel caused by internal strain resulting from inadequate annealing and/or accidental thermal shock.
Disciplines as taught in Medieval universities, such as grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy, physics, metaphysics, and moral philosophy.
The study of language in general or of particular languages other than the students' native tongue, for the purpose of acquiring some degree of facility in the use of those languages.

Music, often improvisational, originally developed around the turn of the 20th century by African Americans from elements of blues and ragtime, with syncopated rhythms and a European harmonic structure. Jazz consistently evolved throughout the 20th century with numerous phases, from a New Orleans style or swing, to "free jazz," for example, which emerged in the late 1950s. Therefore, jazz itself has no precise definition, however it has rarely been a completely composed music.

In general, refers to the visual arts as opposed to literature, poetry, or other writing. In a narrower sense, it sometimes refers to all visual arts concerned with three-dimensional objects, but not two-dimensional visual arts. For works made of the material plastic, use "plastic (organic material)."

Branch of architecture concerning the design of the scenic environment, including the development and planting of all types of planned outdoor green spaces, often with accompanying structures and roadways, outdoor public areas, landmarks, and structures with the aim of creating a natural setting for human structures and settlements. For the planning discipline concerned with the physical environment and any and all human involvement with it, with the objective of assuring proper habitat for people, animals, and plants and the resources on which they depend, use "environmental design." For the development and decorative planting of gardens and grounds in particular, use "landscape gardening."

Designing clothing, accessories, and ensembles for personal wear. For the design of clothing, accessories, and ensembles intended to create an appearance characteristic of a particular period, person, place, or thing, especially (but not exclusively) for theatrical performances, use "costume design."  For the concept of a prevailing, usually short lived custom, usage, or style in clothing, cars, restaurants, and other personal possessions and services, use "fashion."

The activity of painting relatively small paintings, originally using an easel or other device in the process. The term is used to refer to the process used by artists in the west, dating from the 16th century and later, when art was considered valuable in its own right, and to distinguish paintings on panel and canvas from mural paintings, manuscript illuminations, or decorative painting on objects.
Photography using digital cameras, which are cameras that acquire images via an electronic sensor and storing them as digital information on a memory device.

Study of the visual arts within a historical framework, from from prehistory to the present, including stylistic development, use of art in communication and decoration, and the aesthetic and intellectual value of art. It first became a dedicated field of study in the 19th century Western world.
Conservation aimed at preventing future deterioration of materials or artifacts, including providing suitable environmental conditions.
The study of language as it functions in society, and of the interaction between linguistic and social variables.
Branch of linguistics that deals with the relation of language to the rest of culture-determined behavior.
The theory, art, or study of the nature and function of poetry and with identifying and describing its types, forms, and techniques.
Branch of philosophy that studies the nature, origin, limits, and validity of human knowledge.
Branch of religious study in which religious thought, experience, and behavior are studied using the concepts and methodology of psychology.

The science or teachings concerned with last things, such as the end of history or of the present world, the fate of the soul after death, the final judgment of individuals, and the creation or restoration of a perfect world.
Scientific study of offenders, of crime as a social phenomenon, and of the criminal justice system.
Study of the nature and essence of humankind.
Field of archaeology that deals with the culture and artifacts of the ancient Greek and Roman civilizations.

The action of transferring property to another for custody with the expectation that the recipient will sell, rent, or loan this property to a third party, for the mutual benefit of the consignor and consignee.
Joist hangers designed to hang a joist at a corner or recess.
Inserts used to attach furring to a wall or ceiling, typically plates or formed metal sections inserted in concrete or masonry walls.
Preformatted forms on which a consumer may indicate a required product or service. This form is subsequently consulted by the supplier of the product or service.
Reusable electrical devices for discontinuing current flow during abnormal conditions.
Small self-contained systems with a platform that rises vertically, usually only one story or less, to transport a wheelchair or merchandise.
Elevators in which the motion of the car is obtained by means of friction between the traction sheave and the hoisting cable, as is usually the case in contemporary installations.
Continuously moving belts designed to carry passengers or goods either horizontally or up inclines; for similar devices moving only horizontally, use "moving walkways."
Systems supplying heat and hot water by the capture and conversion of radiant energy from the sun.
Includes Chinese heated masonry beds and similar Chinese heating systems employing ducts in walls.
Systems in which a refrigerant is compressed, condensed, and expanded as a means of removing heat from a cold reservoir; the heat is rejected elsewhere at a higher temperature.
Lighting by fluorescent lamps. Lighting by fluorescent lamps.
Illumination of a subject from directly above; used to produce highlights.
Devices for removing undesirable gaseous or solid particles from ambient air.
Outdoor structures frequently placed on roofs, through which warm water is circulated to cool it by evaporation and exposure to the air.

Architectural components, generally in passive solar systems, designed to store heat energy, usually radiated back into spaces as ambient temperature drops; derived from and may also be used for the amount of potential heat storage capacity available in a given component or system.
Artificial channels by means of which liquid or other matter is drained or carried off.
Drains intended for conveying rainwater, subsurface water, condensate, cooling water, or other similar discharges, but not sewage or industrial waste, to points of disposal.
Exposed, open gutters in the valleys of roofs.
The principal supply pipes that feed all branches of a plumbing system.
Plumbing fixtures consisting of a water jet and often a shallow basin designed to provide potable water for human consumption.

Large, deep sinks used for washing the arms and upper body and more commonly encountered in factories and hospitals than in houses; for smaller sinks for washing the hands and face, use "lavatories (sinks)."
Systems which include equipment that supplies a television signal to a building or complex.
Fire alarm systems in which the alarm signals are transmitted to an off-premises station, and then to a fire department.
The practice or method of using AI to generate, create, or produce something such as images, texts, codes or the like.
Process by which objects are joined to handles, especially the blades of cutting or piercing tools such as knives or sickles.
Mounting or fastening with a hinge.
Removal of fat or grease from material by various means. In a conservation context, the concept chiefly refers to the cleaning of skeletons and skins.

The practice of painting or decorating in several colors; a term used mostly regarding sculpture, architectural decoration, ceramics, and various ancient artifacts. For the attribute describing the result of this process, use "polychrome."

Paste-resist dyeing technique for textiles associated with Japanese folk art tradition. The resist is a rice-flour paste usually applied through a stencil to create a pattern or design. The dye is absorbed anywhere that the resist is not applied.
Cutting with blows of a heavy cutting instrument.

Use generally for removing or reducing a layer or edge of a material or object. Use specifically in the context of bookbinding for the process of cutting away or shaving the flesh side of leather used to cover the boards, or of beveling the edges of such leather to provide a neat turn-in over the boards.
The act or result of intentionally inflicting damage on the surface or outer appearance of buildings or objects.
The placing of fill composed of solids, liquids, and usually water. After placement, the liquid eventually drains, leaving the solid fill.
The act or process of making casts or of shaping in a mold; usually refers to pouring liquid material into a mold, as distinguished from pressing a material into a mold, for which prefer "molding."

A traditional jewelry casting technique. The elliptical back plate or cuttlebone of the ordinary squid serves as the mold material. The desired pattern is carved into one half of the divided cuttlebone. The two halves are attached and heated metal is poured through a rounded channel cut into the top of the bone.
The process of carving away and shaping the layered gesso covering the carved ornament on a wooden picture frame so as to sharpen and, often, add detail prior to the gilding of the frame.
The art of making characters or designs in or with wax.

Type of animation in which cutout pieces of artwork made of paper, wood, cardboard, metal or other material are laid out on a background under an animation camera, moved by hand, and shot incrementally to create the illusion of motion when the film or video is projected at normal speed.

Technique in which wet, inked lines on non-absorbent paper were folded along a hinge and pressed against a second piece of paper, transferring the inked lines. The technique has been associated with the early commercial artwork by artist Andy Warhol.
Computer graphics employing series of lines as the display elements, storing a list of the coordinates for the starting and ending points of each line.
Photomechanical processes in which images are printed from flat surfaces.

Printing process that produces images in line and with little tonal quality; the plate, usually of copper, is incised using a burin, the slight burr produced is scraped away, and the plate is inked for intaglio printing.

Printing process in which the ground is mixed with a soft substance, such as tallow, allowing the rendering of textured lines and areas when the plate is etched. Sometimes, paper is placed over the grounded plate and drawn on, to pick up the ground.
The process of making replicas or copies of art images, art objects, decorative arts, built works, or other valued images or objects, made without intent to deceive.

Printing method in which an image is created by lithographic technique, using the disaffinity of greasy and watery substances, and is then transferred from the stone or plate to an intermediary, such as a rubber blanket, and then offset onto the final surface. If this transfer process is used but the original image is other than lithographic, use the more general term "offset printing."
Applying paint or ink so as to cover a surface with irregular, sparse patterns of fine specks. Use "splashing" when the paint or ink more randomly covers wide areas.
Printing processes in which the image prints from ink held in the recessed areas of the plate or block, which have been cut or etched away.
Chinese painting technique having outline and definition, giving shading, depth, and texture to the work using ink alone.
Technique used in Spanish painting which involves working a painted surface to create a pattern; used to embellish the robes of carved and painted figures.
Painting technique that explores luminosity through the use of fluorescent paints which reflect absorbed ultraviolet energy as visible light.
Shading or modeling with fine, closely laid parallel lines.

Refers to a system of projection used to transfer information from a globe to a flat surface. It is generally used in cartography where a portion of the Earth or other heavenly body is represented as if it were transferred to the surface of a cylinder and then unrolled as a plane on which parallels of latitude are horizontal lines and meridians of longitude appear as vertical lines.
A radiographic technique that uses secondary electrons emitted from a thin lead foil (100 to 250 micrometers) to produce an image of the examined object on a radiographic film.

A process to make photographic prints using a colloid emulsion of bichromated gum arabic as the binder and pigment as the final image material. The image is formed as the emulsion hardens in relation to exposure and is developed by washing away the unhardened emulsion to reveal the support, forming the highlights and midtones.
Refers to the darkroom procedure in which a photographic image is magnified by being projected through an optical system; generally used for making prints from small negatives.
Measurement of the intensity of transmitted or reflected light by means of a densitometer in order to measure the optical density of a substance or object.
Photogrammetry performed using digital image capture.
Decorative hardware used on chests and trunks.
In construction, joints in which two building elements are not butted up against each other, but are overlapped, part of one covering part of the other.

In carpentry, joints made by cutting a set of complementary cuts, usually three or more, in two pieces of wood, in such a way that they interlock when joined. A common use of finger joints is to form long pieces of lumber from shorter boards.
Airships constructed with partial frameworks consisting of rigid, or partially flexible keel frames along the long axis under an aerodynamic hull envelope.

Vessels probably used for carrying water for bathing or washing, since the name is presumably derived from the Greek word for bath. Louterion also seems to be the ancient name for a laver or washbasin on a pedestal. Today the name is more commonly, although uncertainly, applied to two additional shapes. The first is a large, broad basin featuring a spout and two upright handles. It is primarily an early black-figure shape and is relatively rare. The second shape is known in black- and red-figure but is also rare. It is similar to a lebes gamikos but differs in its spouted rim and high, upright flat handles with looped adjuncts. The latter shape may be connected to funerary rites; it may have held water for an offering to the dead or for the ceremonial bathing of the corpse.

Containers that feature quillwork as a primary motif; created primarily by Native North Americans for personal use, for the tourist trade, and for art markets. Derived from pre-contact storage and personal containers. A prominent feature of Great Lakes Native art.
Cans made of tin.
Cases that are used to protect and transport computer equipment.

Double-walled vessels designed to regulate the temperature of liquids stored within. Originally invented by Sir James Dewar. Use 'Thermoses (TM)' for the brand name examples of these. With a lowercase initial 'thermoses' is frequently applied loosely to 'vacuum flasks' in general.

An ancient Greek and Roman vessel type often used to pour wine; it was particularly popular in the Hellenistic period. It features a narrow neck, swelling body, broad shoulder, long neck, and horizontal handle. The lagynos form originates in eastern Greece. At least two places where it was manufactured in the Mediterranean are known.
Devices, often made of rubber, that prevent liquid from escaping a contained area such as a sink or an oil tank.

Brooches in the shape of a ring, with a movable pin that may extend beyond the diameter of the ring; usually of metal and often ornamented. Used to fasten costume and worn especially during the Medieval period in Europe.

A general term in Mexico for ornaments worn at the neck such as a necklace or collar. By extension, the term refers to jewels, round beads, and items of jewelry. It also includes the concept of preciousness as in the difrasismo "in cozcatl, in quetzalli" (the necklace, the quetzal's feather), a metaphor referring to children.

Pendants made of shell, stone, or metal, often having pierced holes that allow them to be strung on cords and hung from the neck. These may be found in Native American cultures where they are symbols of status.
Ornamental jewelry made in a variety of forms fastened by a pin. For decorative items, similar in appearance to a brooch, but attached to a garment with a spring fastening, use "clips (jewelry)."
Finger rings that are composed of two, or sometimes three, separate hoops linked together, having the shank split lengthwise so that the hoops can be fitted together unnoticeably as one hoop.

Crowns having a circlet surmounted by one or more arched bands that connect opposite points on the circlet. The hooped crown seems to have first developed in Carolingian states in the 8th century, perhaps derived from a hooped helmet. Hooped crowns may have two or more arches that intersect, or the hoops may comprise half-arches, often with an orb surmounting the intersection. Hooped crowns are generally royal or imperial crowns.

In postclassic central Mexico, conical headdresses commonly integrated into the Cuextecatl (Huastec) warrior costume. These were worn by the deity Quetzalcoatl. In colonial sources, it is described by the conquistadors as a miter. This term is also occasionally applied in colonial sources to the xiuhuitzolli, or turquoise diadem.

Medals having a religious or devotional subject, found in Christian and other religious contexts; often having a loop to allow the medal to be worn on a necklace or otherwise attached to clothing. To specifically distinguish small medals without a loop, intended to be carried in a pocket or pouch, use "devotional tokens."
Term applied to wigs popularly worn from the 17th to the early 19th century.
Plaited straw slippers worn by women in ancient Greece.
Straw hats with a low crown and a wide brim.

Decorative headgear or bands worn on the forehead or just above the hairline, described variously, and evolving from the Middle Ages through the 16th century. These may be ornamented with pearls, gems, or other similar decoration.
Hoods that are components of cloaks or cowls, particularly of Capuchin monks.
Heavy scarves worn around the neck, sometimes shaped and with an attached closure.
Skullcaps worn by ordained officiates in the Catholic Church. The color varies according to rank: white is for the pope, red for cardinals, violet for bishops, and black for all others.
Veils worn by women while receiving communion in the Catholic Church.
Blouses made of sheer and revealing material.
Women's hooded cloaks that resemble the habit of a Capuchin friar.
Suit coats with tails and a front that is cut away from near the waist in front and curving downward to an area in the back above the knee.
Men's coats designed to be worn for shooting.

Lightweight semi-tailored jackets usually made with a notched collar, patch pockets, and sometimes an insignia on the breast pocket. So called because originally made in brilliant colors or striped to distinguish schools, colleges, teams, or the like.

Wooden sculptures made and used by the Buluñits people of central coastal Guinea, in the form of a long, beaked head mounted upon a long, thin neck mounted on a spherical base; the heads may be carved in the shape of human heads or those of birds, crocodiles, horned animals, or D'mba figures. They are used primarily as shrine figures representing both the supreme god and the lineage protector; other uses include as dance headdresses and as divination objects for various rituals such as male and female initiation ceremonies, harvest and healing rituals, and judicial and funerary ceremonies.
Ivory diptychs with relief images presented by ancient Roman consuls to the emperor, Senate, and influential friends, to mark the commencement of their term of office.

Geometric or figural engraving into the bark of living trees. The carving is typically executed using a metal instrument. Dendroglyphs are a distinctive form of sculpture of the Aboriginal Australians made to mark ceremonial grounds or the graves of notable individuals.
Sculpture fabricated by assembling and joining a number of separate parts rather than by traditional sculptural processes such as modeling, casting, or carving.
Sculptures, either relief sculptures or in-the-round, that are ceramic and have a vitreous glaze.
Casts taken of a person's face after death.
Twinned brass images, one male, the other female, joined by a chain, usually around the neck. The edan serve as a main sculptural form of the Yoruba Ogboni secret society in Africa.
Figures, dolls, or statues designed to be contained under a bell jar, which is a bell-shaped jar turned upside down on a base.

Models that are intended to represent how something, as a building, a ship, or a city, looked at a previous time. For drawings or full-scale new objects or structures made with similar intent, use "reconstructions."
Specialized bolts of various types used for installing handrails on staircases.
Threaded bolts having a round smooth head; prevented from rotating in their holes by a square neck directly under the head.
Hinges mortised into the edge of a door and the edge of the jamb against which the edge of the door will butt when closed.
Hardware that allows the swinging motion of the doors mounted on insulated cabinets or boxes having a compartment for ice and used for refrigeration of food.
Locks in which the keyhole and tumbler mechanism are contained in a cylinder or escutcheon separate from the lock case.
Locks made of bronze for use on ships, usually of heavy construction.
In masonry work, brick or metal ties used to bind the angles or corners of the walls together.
Nuts provided with winglike projections to facilitate turning by fingers and thumb.
Connectors used to join two or more pieces of wood.
In carpentry, joints formed by the meeting of a number of adjacent heading joints occurring in a line with each other. An example is as used in connection with the laying of floor planks.
Projects designed and carried out by students as part of a learning or training experience.
Nails each having a large flat head, round shank, and long flattened point; used on sheet metal and dry wallboard.
Screws that are driven with a hammer and removed with a screwdriver.
Nails used for the wooden decks of ships or decks attached to buildings, usually having a neat square or round, flat head that beds in flush with the surface of the plank of wood.

Distinctive hand-wrought nails of various designs made in historical China, typically characterized by having no head or with a head that is created by down pounding a finished nail, rather than being manufactured with a head using a head tool.

Inverted-U-shaped metal wire tie supports or anchors used for the purpose of hanging concrete slabs or other materials on a ceiling. The ties are called "snap ties" because they are designed to be broken off at a specified depth below the exposed surface, for example after the concrete slab has hardened.
Straight wire hangers that may be cut to appropriate lengths, used to support forms for concrete work.
Prints made using the process of lithographic engraving.
Refers to color relief prints where the printing surface has been taken apart for separate inking and then reassembled for printing.
In China, wood block prints produced during the Lunar New Year as traditional domestic decoration. Prints typically summon good fortune and may also be pedagogical in nature.
Clocks designed to rest on mantels, generally squat, heavy, and lacking handles.

Wall clocks elaborately carved and decorated, usually with floral motifs, that announce the hours by a sound like the call of the cuckoo; often with exposed weights and pendulum. Introduced in the mid-18th century in the Black Forest region, the earliest examples had wooden movements.
Clocks rewound automatically either by a system of weighted levers or by electric motors.

Watches that use a clockwork mechanism to measure time with a  mainspring which gets wound and holds force which then goes on to power the balance wheel. The gear train transmits the force and also calculates the swings totaling the seconds, minutes and hours.
Instruments played either by shaking, or by striking either a membrane or a plate or bar of wood, metal, or other hard material.
Any instruments that yield sound by their own substance, being stiff and elastic enough to vibrate without requiring a stretched membrane or strings.
Aerophones that produce sound from air caused by vibrations made by the lips.
Chordophones consisting of a resonator and a neck, between which a series of parallel strings are stretched vertically or diagonally in a plane perpendicular to the resonator.
Vessels having a notched or corrugated surface which is scraped by a nonsonorous object.
Instruments sounded by being struck either with a nonsonorous body, such as a stick or hand, or against a nonsonorous object, such as the human body or the ground.
Friction drums of the Pedi people of South Africa, usually played by women. They are built with staves, are shaped like a bowl, and have goatskin membranes.
Drums whose diameter is larger at the middle than at the ends and whose body is rectilinear with an angular profile.

Small organs housed in a compact, furniture-quality wood cabinet, usually with one manual and no pedal keys, the wind being pumped into the pipes by the player's foot. Popular for domestic use in Europe and North America from the 17th to the 19th century, they were often made to resemble other pieces of furniture, such as tables, bureaus, and desks.
Small American reed organs with a single keyboard and one or two sets of reeds, activated by wind supplied by a suction bellows rather than pressure; they are often ornately decorated.
Drums that are played either by striking the membrane directly or by shaking membranophones that have objects inside them.

Kettledrums of the Islamic world, the Caucasus, and Central Asia, made of silver, copper, brass, wood, or pottery with skin heads, usually though not always played in pairs tuned to different pitches.

Special bells reserved for the death knell, which in monasteries and Christian settlements was rung originally to announce that a member of the community was dying. Later it was used to announce a death and solicit prayers for the soul. In some traditions, the tone of the ringing could be varied to distinguish between the death of an adult or child, and the number of strikes was used to indicate if the person was male or female.

Large bells, often in a set of bells, hung in the tower of a church and rung for various purposes, including the following: to call people to worship services; to mark an event such as a wedding, funeral, festival, etc.; or to mark the hours of the day, in order to keep time for the community. For handbells used at an altar in a church, use "altar bells."
Term of Malayan origin used for gongs played in Western orchestras and rhythm bands.
Rattles enclosing small objects that strike against each other or the walls of the rattles when they are shaken.
Traditional idiophones comprising  a medium-sized gourd with seeds, used as a musical instrument by shaking.
Wooden slit drums with two keys, and shaped like logs or barrels, used by the Aztecs.

High-pitched xylophones of Thailand and Cambodia with a range of three octaves, consisting of a boat-shaped trough resonator mounted on a pedestal, with usually 21 bars of bamboo or hardwood strung on cords suspended on hooks set into the end-boards of the resonator. Tuning paste is applied to the underside of the bars and they are struck with two beaters. For the Thai and Cambodian metallophones of the same range and tuning, use "ranat ek lek."
Xylophones of the Zande of the Congo, consisting of a variable number of hardwood slabs laid over two trunks of banana tree and kept in position by wedges.

Simple bronze conical tubes attached to the inside of a guitar’s sound hole that accentuates the instrument’s bass register and directs the sound towards the listener. It is a standard component of many guitars built in the 19th century, but has fallen from use in contemporary guitars.
