12-stringed rhythm-bass instruments with deeper acoustic boxes and shorter necks than the traditional 12-string guitar. Common in tejano and conjunto music.
Five-string arched harps of the Barma people of southern Chad, having tuning-pegs and small clapper bells attached to the bridge and soundbox.
Seven-string bowl lyres of Kenya and Uganda.

Wooden lyres of northeastern Europe, in use from pre-Christian to Medieval times; they had two upright arms, hollowed out for part of their length, extending up from the soundbox to merge with a curved yoke.

Traditional Finnish plucked psalteries of irregular trapezoid shape, with two long sides that almost meet at the bottom and a diagonal upperside where the tuning pegs are inserted. Originally furnished with fine horsehair strings, they now may have up to thirteen metal strings.

Chinese dulcimers introduced there from the West, having a trapezoidal body, two sound holes, two bridges, and from 14 to 20 courses of two, three, or four strings, played with two springy bamboo hammers.
Short-necked, bottle-shaped fiddles of Ossetia in the Caucasus, carved of a single piece of wood. There are two to three strings, and the neck may be fretted or not.

Single-string musical bows consisting of a flexible stick stuck in the ground with a string stretching from its free end to a soundboard of bark, leaf, or similar material secured above a small pit in the ground which acts as a resonator.
Zulu mouth bows consisting of a short, wide, flat bow and a single string of metal, gut, or fiber, which the player strikes with a steel wire.
Movable nuts or pressure bars used in fretted chordophones and pianos to exert downward pressure on some or all of the strings, thereby shortening their speaking length.
European brass valve trumpets of tenor pitch, invented in 1837, having a narrow bore and three valves; their primary use was in French and Italian military bands in the 19th century.

Tubas in elliptical shape with a conical bore that widens steadily throughout its length, terminating in a small bell, and having four rotary valves and a French horn mouthpiece. They were originally made to the specifications of Richard Wagner for use in his opera cycle "Der Ring des Nibelungen."

Single-reed bagpipes of eastern and southeastern Europe and Asia Minor, taking a variety of forms from one region or culture to another, with varying numbers of pipes and being blown either by mouth or bellows.
Small flutes; generally in historical usage, and referring to various types of small flute.
Small Maori flute; open at both ends, ductless and notchless, with  three to six fingerholes.
European alto oboes with a bulbous, pear-shaped bell.
Recorders having the lowest note of middle C.
Quadruple-reed pipe of Cambodia.
Brass instruments in the saxophone family with a range that is analogous to the tenor voice. They have tapered bores and are single reed.
Folk shawm of Spain, with conical bore. The same instrument is also known as a bolingozo in the Basque region.
Percussion beaters consisting of sticks with knobs or padded heads with which such instruments as xylophones, tubular bells, and certain types of dulcimers are struck.
Multiple flutes consisting of a number of pipes of graduated lengths, joined together in the form of a raft or bundle. The pipes have no fingerholes or mouthpieces, and are blown across their tops.
Upright serpents used in military bands in the 19th century.

Pianos whose individual notes have been changed in terms of timbre, pitch, and dynamics by means of placing various objects, such as rubber erasers, screws, bolts, and short sticks, at particular points between or on top of the strings. The idea came from American composer Henry Cowell, though the first prepared piano was created by American Minimal composer John Cage around 1940.
Dishes that are broad, round, open, and have a flat bottom, with straight or concave sides that are deeper than a plate but not so deep as a basin or bowl.

Plates for holding an individual portion of the dessert course of a meal, similar to but smaller than dinner plates. Distinguished from "dessert dishes" in that dessert dishes have shallow raised sides.
Casters of metal, glass, or porcelain, having finely pierced or meshed openings, intended for sprinkling powdered sugar.
Utensils used to ladle incense into censures.
Utensils usually shaped like pestles for crushing and stirring, especially used for making mixed drinks.

Silver or pewter cups traditionally used for mint juleps, a drink popularized in the American South and made with mint, bourbon, sugar, and water. The cup is a beaker in shape, having no handle and held only by the bottom and top edges of the cup, allowing frost to form on the outside of the cup when filled with the icy beverage. Mint juleps are today often served in various types of glass vessels.
Small drinking glasses for cocktails, with a foot, stem, and bowl, which varies in shape and size but is often funnel-shaped.

Tall, extremely narrow drinking glasses with a conical-shaped bowl that rests on a stem; typically used for drinking sparkling wine and historically also for beer. The form was developed in the 17th century in northern Europe, with some forms reaching up to a yard in height.
Fire screens designed with two hinged leaves.

Chair design by Mies van der Rohe for his German Pavilion at the Barcelona Exposition of 1929. Only two chairs were made for this purpose, but the design proved popular and has been in almost continuous production since 1929.

Armchairs designed to sit in a corner, having a back continuing around two sides of the seat and over three legs, with the fourth leg placed under the middle front of the seat. The back is typically rounded, and the occupant may sit facing forward, or to either side. The form was popular in 18th-century Britain, Europe, and North America.
Easy chairs with exaggerated wingbacks that protect the sitter from noise or drafts.
Medieval Spanish type of X-chairs, often with inlaid decoration.
Chairs that have backs that are rounded inward.
Chairs having a primarily ceremonial or ritual purpose.
Chairs that may be stacked on top of each other, usually for space-saving purposes.
Any Windsor chair with the legs supported on bends for rocking.
Low stools used in churches in Scotland before pews were introduced.
Seats suspended from a steel framework by links or springs; generally used on porches.

Couches having raised head ends and various distinctive styles of legs, used in ancient Greece chiefly for sleeping and dining but also for laying out the dead during ritual mourning and in their tombs. The earliest depictions are in funerary scenes on Geometric vases.
Term used, from the 19th century on, for a small upholstered sofa or settee designed to seat two people.

Types of sofas or settees that were developed in France in the 18th century and picked up by Thomas Chippendale and other furniture makers in Europe and North America. They are distinguished by having a rather delicate and curvilinear style, carved and polished exposed sections of the wood frame, with stuffed backs and seats, arms that may or may not be stuffed, and elegantly carved exposed legs.
Swinging couches or beds usually made of netting or canvas and slung by cords from supports at each end.

Beds with suspended canopies, rectangular, cone-shaped, or domed, which support curtains that may encompass the head half or the full length of the bed. Use "tester beds" for beds having a rooflike component supported on posts.
Term used by Thomas Sheraton for a fanciful design which incorporates two twin beds sharing a common tester and having a passageway between the beds to allow easy access for servants.
Term generally applied to beds measuring between 76 and 78 inches wide and between 80 and 84 inches long.
Deception beds that fold into a piece of case furniture that looks like a chiffonier.

Case furniture consisting of a set of shelves, small drawers, or pigeonholes, fronted by one or more doors, and intended for the storage and sometimes the display of small objects. Also, similar built-in or fitted cases often designed for specific purposes, as in a kitchen or bathroom.
Cabinets of various form that are designed to be fixed to the surface of a wall, and that have no floor support.
18th-century French cabinets with small drawers designed to house a collection of shells; fashionable between 1730 and 1750.
Popular name for low chests of drawers having handles on each end for lifting.
Chests of drawers which sit on a framed stand.
Freestanding, built-in, or hanging cupboards made to fit the shape of a room's corner.
Cupboards that are constructed in three levels, the lower two levels closed by doors and the upper level opened for display.
Refers to sideboards with a cupboard. For small, low chests of drawers, use "chiffonnières (low chests of drawers)."
General term for racks or stands of various forms for the temporary storage of coats and other garments, having pegs, hooks, bars, or projecting arms on or over which clothing may be hung or folded.
Compact writing tables fitted with drawers.

Writing tables with a low superstructure consisting of two or three tiers of small drawers rising from the back and curving around the sides. Presumably named in the late 18th century after the Prince Regent's Carlton House.
A variant form of trestle table with an X-shaped trestle at either end.
Furniture designed for fastening material into groups, such as for tying flax or other plant materials into bundles.
Dining tables, or tables used for other purposes, having pillar and claw supports, with legs jutting from a pillar and with feet terminating into a claw.

Term generally applied to a variety of dressing tables which are fitted with a mirror and have drawers to hold toilet articles. For ladies' dressing tables having drawers on the side which swing out and provide mirrors on a quadrant, use "Rudd tables." Use "toilettes" with reference to French dressing tables designed for women.

Gaming tables, often French, incorporating a tric-trac board; the board typically has twelve holes along the base of each side, used for scoring.The table may also include a chess board and surface for the playing of cards. Although similar, "backgammon tables" tend to be of more recent origin and different design. Tric-trac was popular in France and elsewhere 16th-19th centuries. Both games could be played on either table.
Circular card tables with a depression in the center for the cards and for a candlestick.
Portable stands with a very small top intended to hold a candle or lamp; usually having a round or shaped top supported on a central pillar and with a tripod base.
Ornamental receptacles on an elevated stand, used for growing plants and flowers, sometimes having a lead-lined top. For receptacles not associated with a stand, use "jardinières (containers)."
Ladies' work tables with tray tops and sometimes shelves; from "tricoter," meaning to knit, but used for a variety of needlework forms. A 19th-century term used mainly for 18th-century pieces.
Tables with flaps which may be drawn out from beneath the top to extend the length. Late 16th-century and early 17th-century hall tables are often of this type.
Tables with a triangular top and one triangular folding leaf that, when raised, converts it to a square-top table; intended to stand in corners.

Furniture, typically made of flexible, airtight material such as plastic or vinyl, designed to be inflated by air. Inflatable furniture can be uninflated when not in use and stored conveniently stored in small spaces.
Upholstered furniture arms that curve out and away from the back and seat, creating the effect of a curl. Common to Chippendale sofas.
Portions of furniture arms that are meant to be gripped by the hand.
Shaped projections that rise from the back rails of chair seats, into which the base of the splat is socketed.
Boards supporting the bedsprings, usually extending from side to side of a bedstead.
Trade term for mattresses made of half wool and half hair.
Fall-front drawers often incorporated in bookcases or as the upper drawer in chests of drawers to provide a level surface convenient for writing.
Components of claw-and-ball feet that are modeled on the talons of birds.
X-shaped legs based on Roman chair design, used on Federal and other classically inspired furnishings.
Seats that have been covered and stuffed.
Horizontal members connecting and supporting the legs of furniture.

Prints created to serve as copies of a painting or drawing by another artist, particularly popular in 17th- to 19th-century Europe. The print is considered a reproductive print if the primary intention was to record artistic heritage, even if the personality of the printmaker has been asserted to a small extent. The term is usually reserved for prints that reproduce another two-dimensional art work; however, occasionally it is also used to refer to prints that portray sculpture or decorative arts, if the printmaker’s primary intention was to record the original art works for a mass audience. Prints depicting architecture are not considered reproductive prints. Prints in which another art work is incidentally depicted as part of a larger subject are not reproductive prints. Reproductive prints are valued because they map the dissemination, reception, and historiography of original works. They were popular in Europe from the 17th through early 19th century, and fell out of fashion with the invention of photography.

Literally meaning "narrow format", this term refers to small format Japanese prints. The standard size was approximately 330 x 145 mm or 11.8 x 5.9 inches. This format was employed extensively for actor prints in the 18th century until it was replaced by the "oban", larger format prints.

Devotional art in the form of prints on parchment, paper or linen sold at sacred sites; often recognizable as such by a text or inscription referring to the place of pilgrimage. These are known in both European and Asian cultures. Woodblock prints of this type became popular in nineteenth century Japan as travel became more accessible, and prints from multiple temples were collected and adhered together on scrolls or screens.

Prints made by collagraph printing, using a printing surface created by gluing objects to a support; can be relief or intaglio, and is often a hybrid of the two in that ink can be held and printed from recesses or the surface of the matrix.
Prints made from the photoglyphic engraving process, which was William Henry Fox Talbot's improved process for producing a printing plate from a photograph, that was patented in 1858.
Prints made from dimensional plates comprising assembled metal scraps, wire, mesh, and the like; coined by artist Rolf Nesch to describe his prints.
Prints made using the mezzotint process, in which the surface of the plate is methodically roughened with a rocker to produce a dark background; areas may then be lightened using various scrapers.
Prints made using the process of soft-ground etching.
Creative works in the medium of casein paint, which is water-based, matte paint made with pigment in a binder comprising a phosphoprotein of milk.

Refers to drawings, sketches, prints, computer graphics, or works in other media depicting a building or any object viewed from above, geometrically represented as projected on a horizontal plane. The term is particularly used to refer to drawings or other images showing the relative positions of all the parts of a building, or of the parts of any one floor, roof, or other part of a building in horizontal section; it is thus distinguished from vertical sections or elevations. The term can also be used collectively to refer to sets of drawings or other images for a project, including plans per se as well as other drawings, such as sections. For general reference to depictions or photographs showing structures or sites seen from directly above, use "plan views." For representations of portions of the Earth's surface use "maps" or "plans (maps)."

Refers to drawings created by trimetric projection, which is an axonometric projection where the three spatial axes are unequally inclined to the plane of projection or drawing surface, and the ratio of foreshortening is different for all three.
Elevations of only part of a structure. For drawings showing a structure as partly an exterior elevation and partly an interior elevation, use "sectional elevations."

Ground plans that represent a horizontal section of a building, a site, a city, or occasionally, of an object. The term is used particularly in the context of 16th- to 18th-century drawings, and the meaning of the concept overlaps with "ground plans" and "plans (maps)."
Refers to plans for the brick, concrete, or stone foundations, walls, and piers of a building.
Sections taken along the principal organizational axis of a structure or object.

Drawings that form part of a contractual agreement and on the basis of which the contractor, architect, or artist is legally obliged to produce the drawings, building, painting, or other commissioned work.
Working drawings that are usually produced by the manufacturer of a building element, and approved by the architect.
Drawings, usually in watercolor, in which the design is derived from an accidental mark or blot. This was originally described by the watercolor painter Alexander Couzens in 1786.
Drawings of electrical systems or parts thereof. For scaled floor plans specifically, use "electrical plans."
Thin pieces of split wood, usually hazel, roughly 2 to 3 feet long and bent into a U shape with pointed ends designed for fastening thatch onto roofs.
Pins used to fasten diapers.
Tacks with very sharp points and flat or decorative heads used for upholstery or other purposes.
Generic term used for several types of cuirasses worn by Roman soldiers, made of leather, bronze, or iron plates or scales, or of mail.
Helmets worn by firefighters having a high domed crown and a brim extended at the rear to serve as a neck guard.

Metal plates on some sallets and armets, curving down over the skull to the line of the eyebrows and serving as extra protection for the forehead. Early forms first appearing before the middle of the 15th century consisted of a single heavy contoured plate, cusped and pointed, riveted to the skull; in the late 15th century a detachable form made of two plates was introduced and remained in use on German jousting helmets until the mid-16th century.
Circular or oval shields of leather or bronze covered with metal plates or a sheet of bronze, used by Roman heavy cavalry from the late 8th to the 4th century BCE.
Oblong plates hung in pairs, one on each side, from under the saddle to protect the horse's flanks.

Use specifically for the subprojectiles, usually small lead or steel bars or balls, contained in certain artillery shells designed to explode in midair, scattering the contents in every direction. May also be used generally to include the fragments of the cases of exploding shells, antipersonnel grenades, mines, or bombs.
One of the common types of cannons in the 16th and 17th centuries, varying in weight and in the size and weight of shot fired from it, but generally of a bore between 6 and 7 inches in diameter.
Culverins in use from about the mid-14th to the late 17th century, between demi-culverins and minions in size, firing shot weighing from 5 to 6 pounds.
Dart-like projectiles intended to be launched by crossbows. These are generally shorter and have greater weight than arrows shot from bows.

Native American fighting hatchets used for striking blows and for throwing, consisting of a short wooden shaft and a head, originally of stone, later of metals such as iron and steel, with a blade usually narrow in proportion to its length. They were also used as tools, and sometimes combined with a tobacco pipe, the bowl being on the back of the blade. North American troops of colonial times and later often carried them in place of swords.

Bayonets furnished with a socket handle which fitted over the muzzle and locked in place with a slot and stud, holding the bayonet parallel to the barrel; the firearm could still be fired when the bayonet was fixed. Introduced in the last quarter of the 17th century, they became the most popular form, continuing in use until the late 19th century.
Early type of simple bow, of which the shaft is made from a single stave of one material, usually wood.

African finger rings to which sharp, curving or crescent-shaped blades are attached, often with a tiny sheath to protect the wearer, used primarily as weapons, sometimes also as cutting implements. Examples with smaller than normal blades may be carried concealed in the palm of the hand.
Short, heavy cutting swords with a curved, single-edged blade. From the late 17th century onwards, the term has been used specifically for this type of sword as worn and used by navy personnel.

Heavy civilian daggers or short swords of 15th- and 16th-century Italy, characterized by a broad, flat double-edged triangular blade measuring five fingers in width at the hilt, a pair of short, arched quillons, a grip formed of two flat pieces riveted one on each side of the tang, and a pommel that is simply an arched cap fitted over the base of the grip. The blades are fluted and often elaborately decorated on the wider parts.
Swords designed specifically for hunting.
Light swords worn by European and American military officers as part of dress uniform, beginning in the 18th century.
Handles on edged weapons such as daggers, swords, and knives, typically consisting of the grip and the guard or guards, if any.

Sword hilts in which the knuckle guard extends or splits into one or more bars that sweep down in an S-shaped curve to link with the arms of the hilt. They were commonly made for rapiers in the 16th and 17th centuries.
Locks in which a spring-operated cock holding a piece of flint or pyrite strikes sparks from a piece of steel pivoted vertically over the pan of priming powder, igniting it.
Clubs consisting of a stick with a handle and often a strap, typically carried by the military or law enforcement personnel.
Coins used during Islamic reigns.
Stamps used for the payment of charges on telegrams.

Objects originally created to provide illumination. This class includes lighting accessories such as candlesnuffers and wick trimmers, general purpose portable lighting devices such as kerosene lanterns, and specialized fixtures such as streetlamps and theater lighting devices.
Small, glass, cup-shaped containers that hold oil and a float wick or candles, used especially for outdoor decoration and illumination.
Large candlesticks designed to stand in the choir of a Christian church, often at the choir stalls. For the large candlesticks used for the Paschal candle, use "paschal candlesticks."
Lamps with fonts that are pivoted so that, as fuel is consumed, the lamp will tilt, automatically or manually, feeding more fuel to the wick.
Lamps with Argand burners and ring-shaped reservoirs of wedge-shaped cross section designed to cast as little shadow as possible.

Special lamps that are lit with the intention of expressing devotion for a religious purpose. Devotional lamps have existed since ancient times; they are found in many cultures, including in Hinduism, Judaism, and Christianity. Examples are lamps that burn before images or statues in Christian churches. To distinguish lamps lit specifically in recognition of a vow, prayer, or desire, use "votive lamps."
Lighting devices attached along a narrow wall- or ceiling-mounted track through which current is conducted.
Chandeliers having a height-adjustable central burner which can be lowered to increase illumination when necessary, as at dinner or for reading.
Lamps using candles as the source of illumination and containing the candle within a vessel.  For devices that hold a candle or candles from their bases use "candleholders."

Lamps that burn olive oil, which is oil extracted from the fruit of the olive tree. They are often characterized by being relatively small, portable, and on the top surface having an opening for adding the oil and a smaller opening from which a wick extends.
Any lantern with means of closing off light without extinguishing the flame.
Small candlesticks used for holding tapers to light candles, specifically for use on tea tables.
Torches formed from lengths of rope or the like impregnated with wax, tallow, resin, or tar.
Sets of adjustable flaps, usually two or four, that are attached to the front of a luminaire in order to partially control the shape and spread of the light beam.

Candles used during a marriage ritual and/or in commemoration of a marriage, in the later case often with the date and names of the couple inscribed. The ritualistic use of candles during a marriage has roots in the ancient "taeda," essential in ancient Greek and Roman marriage ceremonies. In more modern western usage, several traditions exist: Included are carrying the candle in the bridal procession to the church; the solemn presentation of the candle to the bride by the bridegroom; the lighting of the candle in the home of the newly married couple; or in the liturgy, the couple may each have separate candles, which they extinguish to allow the single marriage candle to remain; or the couple may each contribute to lighting the marriage candle.
Lamps in which electricity is the source of light.
Small, heavy objects of glass, metal, or the like placed on papers to keep them from scattering.

Refers to semi-permanent screens sliding in tracks that are characteristic features of traditional Japanese architecture. They can be open and closed or removed altogether to alter the dimensions or character of a room. Location determined the materials from which they were made: wood was typically used for screens near the exterior of a building, while screens made of wooden lattices covered with translucent paper, painted or upainted, were more often used for interior rooms.
Indexes of the deceased by name, typically those that have appeared in obituaries of a newspaper or other publication over a designated period of time.
Official lists of marriages, including details considered sufficiently important to be formally noted, and maintained in a regular manner.
Documents related to performing a contract for work and labor, or to supply materials or goods at a specified price.
A periodically published official return of the deaths (later, also of the births) in a certain district.
Statements of revenue and expenditure, financial proposals or schemes for a public body or the domestic accounts of a family or individual.

Books in which entries of transactions or occurrences are made as they take place, usually pending their transfer to permanent record books; such as a police blotter or general merchandise store blotter.
Cards, either maintained by each employee or stamped by a time clock, recording the arrival and departure of an employee each day.

Documents serving as evidence or proof, specifically, a receipt or statement attesting to the expenditure or receipt of money, usually accompanied by bills or other evidence of indebtedness or expenditure.
Official statements of awards to independent contractors on project bids. These outline funding, bidders, contract amounts and other pertinent details related to the project at hand.
Surety bonds submitted by a contractor that guarantees payment of all sums owed to its employees, suppliers, and subcontractors.
Treaties and other agreements of a contractual character between different countries.
Contracts for construction where all work is contracted under the responsibility of a single or prime general contractor.
Specifications prepared as a standard for a particular type of project.
Documents concerning the real or personal property of a person or group of persons.

Service records are collections of electronic or printed material that provides documentation of a person's activities and accomplishments while serving as a member of an organization, often within a government body or the military.

Originally, letters granted by a sovereign authorizing an individual to seize the subjects of a foreign state, or their goods, by way of retaliation or reprisal for injuries; later, specifically, any license or extraordinary commission granted by a government to a private person to command an armed vessel at sea to take an enemy's ships and merchandise.
Documents containing directives or commands issued by a military superior to a subordinate.

Instruments delivered by a sheriff or other appropriate party, notifying a person that a court action has been commenced against the person and that the person is required to appear in court on the day named to answer the complaint.
Records made or received by an agency of the government of a nation-state and maintained in the conduct of national business.
Lists of dates and locations of burials within a church, convent, or other institution.

Records of the deliberations, decisions, and expenditures of the vestry board, which is an assembly of parishioners who originally met in the vestry of the parish church and ruled on certain temporal affairs of the parish.
Books used by teachers to record marks indicating students' grades, levels of accomplishment, or quality of academic work.
Atlases of a particular region.

Refers to maps representing relatively large regions, such as countries or continents, on a small scale. Chorographic maps may include the natural configuration and features of a region, in addition to political boundaries and major towns. They are distinct from "topographic maps," which depict a smaller area.
Refers to long, narrow maps that illustrate the course of a road and the places adjacent to it.
Charts having lines that connect places of equal magnetic declination or variation.
Charts depicting rivers and the features of rivers, especially those used for navigation.
Thematic large-scaled maps of cities or neighborhoods or environs within them.
Rough, freehand maps of the principal features of a locale, as one drawn from memory.

Copies of documents created simultaneously with the original manuscript or typescript by the use of an intermediate sheet of paper coated with carbon. Copies of documents created simultaneously with the original manuscript or typescript by the use of an intermediate sheet of paper coated with carbon.
The collection of software that directs a computer's operations, controlling and scheduling the execution of other programs, and managing storage, input/output, and communication resources.

Handwritten manuscripts that have been decorated with gold or silver, brilliant colors, designs, or miniature pictures. Although prevalent in Islamic and Asian societies, the longest tradition of illuminating manuscripts was in Christian medieval Europe, from the 6th-16th centuries, when the art was superseded by printed illustrations. Generally, the manuscripts were both 'historiated', or decorated with relevant paintings, and 'illuminated' in its original sense, meaning decorated with calligraphic initial capital letters using gold leaf. Over time, the term 'illuminated' came to refer to any illustration or decoration in a manuscript. Illuminated manuscripts played a major role in the development of art, partly because of the manuscript's portability in carrying artistic developments from one region to another.
Opaque cards or strips bearing microphotographs of images, pages of a book, periodical, etc.

Scrolls on which the Pentateuch is inscribed by hand in Hebrew. These are composed of many sheets of parchment or vellum sewn together and mounted on wooden rollers. They are carefully prepared by qualified scribes, or sofers, and are used for public readings during services on Sabbaths, Mondays, Thursdays, and religious festivals.

Visual records or representations of sound created using Fourier analysis, particularly speech, with colors or densities corresponding to time, frequency, and energy comprised in the sound. Created by a sound spectrograph. Sound specrography was developed at Bell Laboratories in the 1940s.
Phonograph records made of wax.

Standard size and format for consumer-level analog recording on videotape cassettes. Describes a videotape one-half inches in width (12.7mm); this videotape format, known primarily as VHS (Video Home System), was developed in the 1970s for use with home videocassette recorders. It contains 240 lines of horizontal resolution.
Inscriptions on statues, buildings, or other structures.

Devices in any form that identify a person or object as belonging to a group or organization, and sometimes denoting rank or office. For devices that are specifically symbol- or picture based,  designed for ready recognition to identify a product, company, or organization and sometimes used as trademarks, see "logos."
A bookseller's ticket records the name and address of the bookseller as a modest advertisement.

Refers to watermarks that are darker than the surrounding area on the sheet. A shaded watermark is produced by a depression in the sheet mold wire; when wet pulp flows into the recesses, the design is formed as different gradations of tone. The intaglio design, as opposed to a relief design, results in a thickening of the sheet at the point of contact, creating an opaque, or "shaded," design. It is a rather rare type of watermark; it has been produced since the early 19th century.

Marks, often stamped in ink or embossed, that are affixed to drawings, prints, or other artworks to indicate ownership. These appear in many forms and may be used by private collectors or institutions such as museums.

Stamps applied to bricks, containing information about their manufacture; they were used as an indicator of quality. Brick stamps have been known since ancient Egyptian and Roman times, where they noted the location and important people, such as the land owner, associated with the manufacture of the bricks.

Hand-held, flat objects used for writing or drawing, either directly, or as a flat, rigid support for another surface such as paper. If written upon directly, the tablets are typically coated with a substance such as clay, plaster, or wax upon which the characters or depictions are incised with a stylus.
Devices placed on the wall or floor behind a door to limit the swing of the door.
Plates applied to doors to protect them against soiling and wear when being pushed open or during the operation of locks.
Flush bolts whose heads connect to the operating mechanism via a rod which is inserted through a hole bored in the door.
Door latches employing a spring-loaded steel ball. The loaded ball holds the door closed but rolls free when the door is pulled.
Door hinges fabricated with a slope on the knuckle which causes the door to rise when opened. Rising hinges are used when there are obstructions along the door's bottom edge, such as carpeting.
Locks designed for the main entrance doors of public or residential buildings that usually have dead bolts and latch bolts, controlled by keys, knobs, or thumb-lift latches.
Securing devices consisting of a dead bolt or system of bolts and that are operated by a key adapted to secure sliding receptacles fitted into furniture.
Narrow rods inserted through holes drilled into both upper and lower sashes so that the lower sash may be held partly opened yet immobile.
Hooks that fasten to the ceiling or to the underside of shelves.
Strikes projecting slightly beyond the face of a door jamb.
The housing containing the tumbler mechanism and the key way, which can be actuated only by the correct key.
Keys having a bow or handle pivoted to the shank so that it may drop or fall parallel with the surface of the door.
Plates placed around the holes made for light switches.

In concrete finishing, a space or break of about 1/8 inch made at regular intervals, particularly over expansion joints, to allow for contraction and expansion in the topping layer of sidewalks, driveways, and similar structures.
Painted decorations or scenes that dominate a wall (or ceiling) surface. For works in other media that dominate a wall (or ceiling), use the more general term "murals (any medium)".

Paintings executed on an easel or other portable device, having either canvas or panel supports; generally restricted to those painted from the 16th century forward. The term implies not only physical aspects of creation, but also inherent concepts associated with the increased secular use of art from the 16th century and with the identification of paintings as objects of worth in their own right.
Photographers who primarily use digital cameras, which are cameras that acquire images via an electronic sensor and storing them as digital information on a memory device.

People who assemble, set, proof, and generally prepare type and illustrations for printing. For those engaged in the specific process of arranging type from copy for printing or making printing plates, whether by hand, by mechanical devices, or by inputting to computer, see "typesetters."

People who project the image on a photographic negative onto light-sensitive print paper and chemically develop it into hard copy prints; typically used for people who are using the negatives created by other visual artists.
Religious officials or functionaries authorized to perform duties in accordance with Islam.

Members of a religious brotherhood who are devoted to a discipline prescribed by their order. Monks take vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience. Performance of religious duties and contemplation are traditional priorities. Monks typically live apart from society in communal monasteries, but some live alone (hermits or anchorites). Monks are distinguished from "friars" in that for the monk retirement and solitude are undisturbed by public ministry, except in exceptional circumstances. Some of the more prominent orders of Christian monks include the Benedictines, Cluniacs, Cistercians, Trappists, Carthusians, the Premonstratensians, and Camaldolese.

Those who make historical sense of the natural sciences by employing textual, ethnographic, and social scientific methods to investigate how the sciences work in practice, and how they relate to larger intellectual, cultural, social, and political trends and changes.
Mathematicians who deal with the collection and arrangement of numerical facts or data,whether relating to human affairs or natural phenomena.
Scientists trained or working in the science of the phenomena related to computers, including the construction, operation, programming, and applications of computers.
Students, specialists, or experts in mycology, which is a branch of biology devoted to the study of fungi.

Scientists who specialize in the branch of chemistry that deals with the chemical effects of radiation, chiefly visible and ultraviolet light, and with the direct production of radiation by chemical changes.

Physicists specializing in the structure of atomic nuclei and their interactions with each other, their constituent particles, and the whole spectrum of elementary particles provided by very large accelerators, with particular reference to the generation of nuclear energy.
People tasked with giving money, clothing, or food to impoverished people or others in need.
Individuals who work on huacas (sacred sites), particularly those who clandestinely excavate for the purpose of obtaining marketable antiquities.
People who act as presiding officers of organizations, boards, committees, or events. May also refer to the administrative heads of academic departments.
Students in educational institutions for the third level of (usually compulsory) education for children, entered after elementary school and middle or junior high school.
Assumed characters or roles serving as secondary or alternative personalities of the original person.
Groups who work to promote or accomplish stated goals, provide opportunities, or promote art and artists through projects or other activities.
Organizations of people having a common interest in the areas of activity that encompass both performing and visual arts.
Groups of individuals that have been appointed or elected to supervise the affairs of a private or public institution such as a university or art museum.
Designates the documents created or accumulated and used by a particular individual, organization, or other entity that are kept together within a larger collection.
Organizations whose primary purpose is to advance social well-being and serve the public interest or common good.

Directories that provide government information and services for state employees, local government, and the general public. The directory services include state employee information, state agency information, and a State Government Organization Chart.
Directories listing the names of and information on professional individuals.
Guidebooks aimed particularly at tourists or other leisure travelers.
Accounts or histories of the descent of persons, families, or other groups, from an ancestor or ancestors; enumerations of ancestors and their descendants in the natural order of succession.
Books in which copies are written or printed for pupils to imitate.
Manuals containing sets of words, formulas, verses, or incantations that are supposed to possess occult or magical powers, cast spells, invoke demons, and achieve other occult purposes.

Original and entire drafts or transcripts of musical compositions or arrangements. Typically having the parts of all the different instruments or voices written on staffs one above another, so that they can be read at a glance.
Liturgical prayers consisting of phrases recited by a leader alternating with responses by a congregation.
Written texts of television productions or broadcasts.
Bibliographies that list only a selection of the literature of a subject.

Finding aids, whose normal unit of entry is the series. Usually include a brief history and description of the organization that produced the records, descriptive lists of each record series, and sometimes supplementary information, such as selective indexes.

Indexes computer generated by ABACUS (AB Atomic Energy Computerized User-oriented Service), the result of a collaboration between the Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm and AB Atomenergi, Sweden.
Indexes to one or more volumes of a periodical.
Newspapers or other serials that are issued or published every day, or every week day.
Periodicals produced by an organization, especially a commercial or industrial enterprise, and intended for primarily internal dissemination, or for distribution to customers.
Albums or notebooks used by the bride to plan a wedding, including notes, lists, photographs, fabric samples, and other information regarding wedding planning.
Announcements informing customers of news concerning a business, such as the opening of a new branch, change in management or address, or the introduction of a new product.
Documents outlining the procedures for preparing and submitting bids.
Calendars of the Eastern Orthodox Church recording the festivals honoring saints and martyrs, together with brief accounts of their lives.

Printed cards used in several Christian denominations, either given by a minister or deacon to identify those of proper status in the church to receive the eucharist, or given at the time of a person's first communion, serving as both documentation of the event and as a commemorative token.
Greeting cards that express concern and well wishes for the health of the recipient.
Pictorial postcards that may include hidden pictures, jigsaw puzzles, or any card which includes a puzzle to solve.
Certificates that attest to the copyright status of a thing or idea.

In general scientific use, charts that consist of several lines marked off to scale and arranged in such a way that by using a ruler to connect known values on two lines with a straight line, an unknown value can be read at the point of intersection with another line. Used specifically in the notation of Minimal music to establish new relationships between notes.
Documents recording information used for internal communication.
Letters by which the drawer of a bill of exchange notifies the drawee that the bill has been issued and is forthcoming.
Collections of files in which each file relates to a single order for a customer or patron, such as in a library or commercial sales business.

Documents in which are recorded household expenditures such as for food, utilities, and domestic help, maintained in a journal or other book; also includes classed or chronological files of the bills and receipts for household goods and services.
Registers of the watermark designs of various paper makers.
Notes made with reference to a lecture, both those from which the lecturer speaks, and those taken by people in attendance.
Posters measuring approximately 27 by 41 inches.
Programs produced and distributed to mark special events, usually more lavishly designed and printed, and with more detailed contents than regular programs.
Documents, usually executed under seal, containing a conveyance, especially of real estate.
Records of meetings, conferences, learned societies, or other organizations, usually published, and frequently accompanied by abstracts or reports of papers presented.
Documentation summarizing the activities of an organization over the course of a year.
Organized and often detailed proposals that lay out strategies and schemes of action for development and maintenance of a relatively large region.
Documents required by state and federal law that contain an analysis and report of the effects of major projects or programs on the quality of human, plant, or animal habitats.
Tables giving daily predictions, usually a year in advance, of the times and heights of the tide for one or more places.
Architects who work on projects for the community, usually as contrasted to military projects.
Workers who conduct the secondary process that can enlarge or finish preexisting holes after they have been drilled. For workers who conduct the primary process used to create holes, use "drillers."

Refers to workers skilled in stone work associated with architectural construction, first documented in Medieval Europe. They are distinguished from other masons in that they were extremely skilled and well-trained in fine and complex work. They were often itinerate, moving wherever large or important buildings were being erected. They were noted for having a system of secret signs and passwords, which they learned from other freemasons and were used as evidence that they were competent and had been properly trained. By the 16th century, the term was often used as a complimentary synonym of "mason," implying that the workman had superior skill.
Individuals or companies that undertake work under a contract that is part of or subject to a larger contract on a larger project.

Refers to people employed in the design and development of the processes of creating chemicals and in the operation and requirements of a chemical plant. They are concerned with data and predictions that often have to be obtained or confirmed with pilot experiments. Their activities differ from chemists in that chemists deal with the research of and actual creation of chemicals.
Engineers who design streets and roads to allow the smooth flow of traffic.

Those who specialize in designing and improving the spacial organization and content of urban areas. For those who work in the overall management of urban areas, encompassing the setting of objectives for urban life, the establishment of policies, and the planning, development, operation, and maintenance of the urban environment and services, use "urban managers."

People who create artistic drawings and plans for the construction or creation of something according to aesthetic or functional criteria; those who create plans or concepts for subsequent implementation of graphic works, objects, structures, systems, or conceptual schemes.
Painters specializing in scenes of the hunt and hunters.

Artists or craftsmen who paint directly on fabric with the goal of decorating drapery, banners, or another textile. The term does not refer to artists who create oil paintings or paintings in another media on canvas or another fabric, where the goal is to create a scene or other work of art that will be displayed in a frame or hung on a wall.
Printmakers who specialize in drypoints, intaglio prints using a process whereby a sharp needle scratches the plate creating a burr.
Engravers who create plates depicting other works, from which it is intended to print reproductions in relatively large numbers.
Sculptors in the service of a noble or royal court.
Persons who plan and design displays to decorate streets, fairgrounds, buildings, and other places for celebrations, fairs, and special occasions.
In Medieval Spain, officials who were in charge of weights and measures, especially for comestibles.
People who organize advertising and publicity in the media on behalf of an organization or well-known person.
Refers to people or corporate bodies who own or run manufacturing plants for making automobiles, which are self-propelled vehicles designed primarily to transport passengers over ordinary roads.
A dealer in tapestries.
Tradespeople who, since the Middle Ages have owned cloth manufactories or wholesale businesses that trade in cloth.

Refers to those skilled or practiced in incising marks on the surface of a hard material, such as glass or metal, with a sharp tool, when the designs or images created are for their own sake and not to be printed from. For those who practice the printing process of engraving, see "engravers (printmakers)."
People who specialize in creating objects that are carved from or incised on ivory, which is dentine from tusked or large-toothed mammals.
Gold casters, literally "those who blow gold" in Nahua culture.
Those who engage in enameling or creates enamel works, including the application of a vitreous coating by fusion to metal, ceramic, glass, or other surfaces.

Craftsmen who specialize in staining glass, which is coloring glass by adding metallic oxides to the molten glass. To distinguish those who design and create the stained glass windows or other works, use "stained glass artists." For those who paint details on stained glass or othewise paint on glass, use "glass painters."
Persons who remove animal hair, especially wool, from hides in preparation for leathermaking.
People who work metal by employing a forge to heat it and then hammering and beating it into shape.
Founders, casters, or makers of bells.
Those who do needleworking, especially as an occupation.
People who specialize in carving in the medium of wood, making objects or ornament in wood. For those who make woodcut blocks or prints from them, use "woodcutters."
Ceramicists who join the various separately cast or molded parts of a figure or other ceramic object into completed form.
People or corporate bodies who make furniture, which includes movable or fixed objects or equipment for sitting, reclining, storage, etc. in a dwelling, business, or public space.
People who engage in the process of transforming rough diamonds into finished gems.

Government officials in charge of a department or bureau of the public service. The term may also refer to government representatives in a district, province, or other unit, often having both administrative and judicial duties and powers.
Persons in control of a division, project, or phase of an institution or business. Distinct from "directors (administrators)," which denotes official heads of entire organizations.

Refers to the official heads of museums, which are institutions that maintain places where objects of value such as works of art, antiquities, scientific specimens, or other artifacts are housed and displayed for public benefit.

Those executives having the oversight and charge of an institution, department, place, or operation, generally having the chief governing power there, when used as the official job title for those holding such responsibility.
People who oversee, coordinate, and otherwise projects, generally as a professional position.

Refers to officers, appointed or elected, in various administrative bodies, that hold the chief governing authority. In the United States, refers to the executive heads of each of the states. In the British Commonwealth, refers to the representative of the Crown in a member nation or dependency.

Members of a governing legislative body called a Senate, in ancient Rome and other states in antiquity, in some cities of Europe from Medieval to modern times, and in some modern nations such as the United States, Canada, France, and Italy.
Absolute rulers, particularly as applied to rulers of dependent or tributary provinces.
People who create and transmit literature, whether orally or in writing.
People whose profession is to collect, write, edit, or deliver the subject matter of televised news.
Those whose job or function is to impart or convey the knowledge, or to give instruction or lessons in a subject, especially in a school.
People who are in charge of classrooms and teach at a school.
Those who practice that branch of history in which historical information is recorded or histories are presented in the form of audible speech or song.
People who are experts in the implementation, design, configuration, and customization of metadata, which is data that describes other data and provides a structured reference.
Librarians who work in contexts outside the traditional public, private, academic, and school libraries, including corporations, non-profit organizations, and governmental organizations.

Specialists in phonetics, the study of the production, transmission, perception, classification, and physical or acoustical properties of speech sounds and how they are organized in language. For specialists in the study of the sound patterns and systems of languages, use "phonologists."

Those who work, study, or are skilled in that branch of philosophy concerned with the forms of thought and methods of correct statement in all areas of inquiry, especially with inference, deduction, induction, and scientific proof.
Anthropologists who study human cultures, especially with respect to social structure, language, law, politics, religion, magic, art, and technology.
Those whose work is occupational therapy.

Public officials who enforce the game laws of a jurisdiction. For those privately employed, as on estates or game preserves, to provide an environment for game, prevent poaching, and assist the employers or other authorized persons in hunting, use "gamekeepers."
Those versed in the law, such as scholars, professors, writers, or practitioners.

Generally, lawyers who do office work and can represent clients in some courts, but who by and large do not themselves represent their clients in court. Specifically, lawyers for city, town, or other governmental bodies or departments.

Exhibition curators are the creative leaders that conceptualize and mount exhibitions, and are distinguished from curators in general, who manage collections in museums, galleries, libraries, and other repositories.
Persons who make, sell, or rent costumes, as for stage or fancy dress events.
Persons who conduct an orchestra, chorus, or other group of musical performers.
The longest of the bench planes, ranging from 2 to 3 feet; used to level long boards that are to be joined together.
Planes with the profile of ogee molding.
Planes whose blades cut a quarter of a circle, or a cove; used for cutting the under edge of a table leaf or to produce decorative moldings.
Short steel rods, usually tapered; used to drive a nail or brad below, or flush with, a wood surface.
Thin steel disks, with teeth on their periphery, that rotate on a power-driven spindle; used either as hand tools or are table-mounted.
Circular saws suspended from and moving along a cantilevered arm mounted above the saw table.
Large frame saws used to cut straight or slightly curved pieces of wood; often used by wheelwrights and furniture workers.
Thick, long, taper-bladed, two-man instruments without a frame, with an upper handle and a lower adjustable handle; used for cutting boards from the lengths of logs.
Tools used in forming veneer to the shape of a curved surface.
Clamps used to join corners during gluing.
Large hammers, weighing as much as 32 ounces, with a long handle and a claw which is relatively straight; used in house framing and construction work.
Mallets whose heads are filled with lead shot so that there is no rebound to the blow.
Drafting instruments having straight edges that may be set at any desired angle with the edge of a drawing board.
Spades fitted with longer hafts than the normal length of 14-22 inches, and a wider blade rounded to a point.

Reaping tools with L-shaped wooden handles and a blade. Siths allowed the user to stand upright, holding the crop with the mathook in the left hand, and cutting the crop with the sith in the right, which was different than with scythes.

Equipment comprising pieces of openwork fabric made of twine, synthetic fibres, strong cord, or another material that forms meshes of a suitable size; they are placed in the water and used for catching fish. Fishing nets are among the oldest known human technologies.
Devices made of buoyant materials, tied onto a line or net when fishing to gauge the depth of the fishhook or net.
Mirrors used in the place of lenses in astronomical instruments; they may be large, they do not absorb radiation, and are often aspheric to reduce aberrations.
Instruments, dating from the late 19th century, used for the examination of microscopic bacteria.
Crafted instruments used for scientific purposes and research, in all branches of science.
Computers intermediate in size between a laptop and a smartphone that use a touch-activated screen.
Computer components with a screen for viewing data at a computer terminal.
Conveyors consisting of fixed-location rollers over which materials are moved by gravity or propulsion.

Optical instruments consisting of a lens or combination of lenses that allow the viewing of objects that are too small to be seen with the naked, unaided eye. The term may also be used for various types of instruments that use a stream of electrons (electron microscope), electromagnetic radiation (x-ray microscope), or other means other than light and lenses to magnify images of small objects.
Microscopes that employ polarized light that vibrates in a single plane so that light can be transmitted through the specimen. It is used to examine thin sections of rocks  and minerals.
Mechanical or electromechanical devices that convert mechanical energy into electrical power, as alternators producing alternating current or dynamos producing direct current.
Engines driven or worked by steam.
Turbines that are driven by the pressure of steam which is discharged at high velocity against the turbine vanes.
Devices, considered a derivative of bow drills, specifically used to produce fire by friction.
Bellows in which the draft is supplied by the action of a piston.
Equipment used to aid the process of securing leaves or gatherings, usually within covers, to form a book.

Terminology used by prehistorians for a class of microlithic blades with one edge blunted by a secondary retouch. It is assumed that this was so that they could be held more easily. Backed blades first appeared in the early Upper Paleolithic.
Tools consisting of a long shaft mounted with a curved metal head with a sharpened point at one end, used for breaking up earth or rock.
Knives used for precise cutting and scraping, particularly as used in mechanical drawing for erasing ink lines from tracing paper or cloth; usually made of steel.

Electric devices that provide continuous heat to melt thermoplastic glue, which is typically inserted into the device in solid form, melted, and pushed through the gun by a mechanical trigger mechanism. The device is often hand-held and gun-like in shape with barrel and hand grip. Another form of the device may allow heat to be applied directly to the thermoplastic adhesives that have been placed in solid form onto the surface to be glued.
Screwdrivers having a blade that rotates with respect to the handle, as the handle is pushed inward toward the blade; permits a screw to be driven easily and with speed.
Torches using oxygen and acetylene; used especially for welding.
Instruments in the form of pincers used for grasping or manipulating objects, often in the context of surgery.
Devices used for holding loops/eyes in the end of cables while clamping or splicing them. Otherwise known as a triangle vise or splicing vise.
Screw or hydraulic-type jacks used as a cross bracing in a trench shoring system.
Small brooms with a short handles; used especially as a clothes brush or for light cleaning.
Reciprocating pumps used for drawing up liquid, especially crude oil from deep wells.
Small, pointed instruments for making eyelet holes.
Large rakes fitted with tempered teeth or serrated blades, for use in fighting wildfires. An example of usage is to establish a fire break in the brush.
Devices that apply numbering in sequence to documents. These are usually self-inking for continuous operation.
Hammering tools of modest size, having a handle and relatively large head, usually of wood but sometimes of other materials. Often used to drive another tool, such as a chisel or a gouge.
Tools made from a flat board attached to a handle, often studded with nails, coins, or the like, used for pounding, driving, and dressing the reeds or straws into place during thatching.
Tools used to secure type pieces by hitting them into place.

Devices comprising a frame usually of two upright posts and a transverse beam, particularly such a device employed in executing criminals by hanging. The term may also refer to any similarly constructed support, such as an iron support for a pot over a kitchen fire.

Power tools used for boring holes or setting screws. Generally used for hand-held tools that are operated electrically via alternating or direct current, this term may also be extended to large machinery used to dig tunnels for mining or transportation purposes.
In archaeology, stone tools from which flakes have been removed from both sides or faces of an edge.

A Japanese school of esoteric and mystical Buddhism which was brought to Japan from China in 806 by Kukai. A key text of Shingon is Kukai's 'Jewel Key to the Store of Mysteries (Hizoboyaku)' in which spiritual attainment through Shingon is seen as fulfilling nine other spiritual paths found in Buddhism and other religions. Shingon places importance on the Vairocana Buddha, the Buddha of infinite light, and on mandalas and other forms of sculpture and painting. There are over forty schools of Shingon in Japan today and aspects of Shingon have been adopted by other forms of Japanese Buddhism as well.
Style or movement characterized by the adoption of aggressively unconventional and often bizarre, violent, or shocking appearances and the defiance of social norms of behavior.

Long poles made of varied materials used for reaching, hooking and pulling. These are tipped with sharp metal spikes or hooks, and are variously used in boating, construction, firefighting, and other contexts.

Machines used for driving piles, which are columns serving as subsurface supports for vertical loads, usually by repeated blows from free-falling or driven "pile hammers." Pile drivers comprise a framework for holding and guiding the pile, a hammer, and a power source.
Scaffolds erected so as to bridge the ridge of a roof; usually used during chimney repair.
Equipment used in the removal of earth.
Modular devices for heavy-duty earth-moving machines used for gripping and handling bulk materials.

Cranes consisting of a rotating superstructure with power plant, operating machinery, and boom mounted on a base equipped with crawler treads for travel; used to hoist and swing loads at various radii.
Devices or vehicles used to transport and lift objects that are stacked, for moving loads from one location to another, usually in the context of warehouses, factories, or markets.
Stationary hoisting machines having a rotating drum around which a cable, rope, or chain is wrapped.
Small trucks with enclosed drivers' areas and rectangular, open, low-sided bodies, capable of light hauling.
Firemen's scaling ladders consisting of a pole with crossbars for rungs and a hook at one end.
Machines used to sew sheets and bands of books together.

Heavy vertical presses used for pressing newly bound books, pressure being applied by lowering a platen by means of a long central screw, today used primarily for hand-bound books. A larger version (nearly twice the size) was formerly used to squeeze the moisture out of large sheets of newly-made paper; today most paper is pressed with hydraulic presses.
Oil paint in crayon, or stick, form.
Thin rods of silver, often supported in a holder, used to produce delicate drawings, usually on specially treated paper.

Pencils with a drawing material made of graphite. The terms 'lead pencil' and 'graphite pencil' are often used interchangeably as earlier forms, known as graphite pencils, used pure natural graphite without clay additives. 'Graphite pencil' technically refers to pencils in which pure natural graphite is used without the addition of a clay binder.

Instruments composed of a pen attached to a wheel with interchangeable cogs used in conjunction with a straightedge to produce a stippled line of dots, dashes, or both; used for technical and working drawings.
Folding compasses consisting of faceted legs that contain hinged reversible inserts providing ink, pencil, and plain points.
Round, stiff, artists' brushes with blunt tips used for stippling and stenciling.
General term for photographic equipment specifically used for viewing.
Cameras capable of acquiring still or motion pictures via an electronic sensor and storing them as digital information on a memory device.

Cameras that focus by means of a coupled or un-coupled rangefinder device. Though many cameras may be fitted with a rangefinder including some press or view cameras, this term is most commonly used to refer to cameras that rely solely on the rangefinder for composing and focusing, rather than a through-the-lens reflex system.

Hard-sided cases usually equipped with handles or straps, and that most often incorporate interior compartments for storing and transporting cameras. For similar soft-sided containers use camera bags.
Symmetrical lens design created in 1866 by Steinheil, which formed the basis for most general-purpose lenses until the early 20th century.
Devices used to secure photographic paper as it is being exposed to light in a darkroom or elsewhere. Often these have movable elements that accommodate varied sizes of paper.
Bookbinder's burnishers used heated to polish leathers, crush down leather grains, and eliminate blisters on cloth covers.
Plates used for color printing, being the one plate for a given image that carries the most detail and serves as a guide to register the other plates.
Presses used in intaglio printing in which the plate, paper, and cushioning blankets pass between cylinders that exert pressure, forcing paper into the grooves of the plate which holds the ink.
Compass-like mechanisms for cutting circles of leather.

In the strictest sense, very specialized blades that are disc-shaped, with a hole in the center for gripping, used in leatherworking primarily to thin the leather. For semi-circular or other rounded blades set transversely in a handle, but not fully round sharpened dics, use "head knives" or "moon knives." For rotatable sharpened discs set into a handle or device, use "rotary cutters."
Hand tools used for making holes in sheet materials, particularly leather. These consist of dual jaws, one fitted with a hollow punch and the other a flat die against which the punch presses.
Tools used inside a pipe or culvert to remove excess mortar or deposits.
Stonecarvers' chisels having a straight cutting edge used for finishing rough areas to make smooth surfaces.
Plastering tools such as carpet or cork floats; used for texturing plaster.
Heavy hammers having flat faces, with one blunt end and one cutting end; used for rough dressing of blocks of quarried stone.
Plastering tools with long wirelike teeth; used to scratch the surface of unset plaster providing a sufficient bond for the next coat.
Plasterers' hand trowels on which the edges are turned up; used to finish plaster in corners.
Coarse sieves used for separating and grading granular material.
Tools similar to punches; used to open up punched holes, smoothing and shaping them at the same time.
Specialized anvils having a shape and design to allow making of nails.
In blacksmithing and other metalworking, blocks of various designs used to guide or receive the impact of a punch.
Combination tools taking the form of an iron hammer, often including an open wrench, a screwdriver, or the like.
Tapered punches used to align holes for bolting and riveting.
Sharp-edged stakes on which to bend sheet metal.
Hand tools consisting of a frame with a cutting wheel and drive wheels; used for cutting pipe and tubing by forcing the cutting wheel into the pipe material and rotating the tool around the pipe.
Shears constructed on the principle of the lever, where a lever is used to apply pressure to lower the blades. Used to cut sheet metal and in various other applications.
Tongs with one straight jaw and one crooked jaw; used by blacksmiths.
Wrenches with one adjustable jaw which moves vertically along the shaft.
Machines used for macerating rags into pulp for papermaking. Named for their country of origin, they appeared in Germany as early as 1710.
Clippers used for cutting off the ends of cane.
Needles with a very large eye and a sharp point, used for making embroidery with chenille yarn.
Handloom used for weaving rectangles of fabric, used vertically. Yarn is wound across nails in the frame, and weaving sticks are used to form sheds.
Axes used for chopping or “listing” barrel staves to a rough shape.
Steel chisels having a broad blade and a long shank; especially used for ripping up floor boards.
Steel chisels having a heavy body with a socket shank; used for cutting mortises.
A variety of double handled blades used in the construction of barrels.
Hatchets with flared blades and nail-driving polls; used to split and nail wood roof shingles.
Shoemakers' knives used to even the heel of a clog on the inside. It consists of a long, double-edged blade curved upwards at the end and a straight wooden handle.
Small planes, approximately 4 to 6 inches long, with the sole curved along the longitudinal axis like a compass plane.
Four- to 6-inch planes with the front edge open so that the iron can cut at the very nose of the plane; used for trimming in hard to reach places.
Style or culture having aspects of ancient Egyptian and Greek cultures.

Refers to the first of three great period of Egyptian civilization from about 2650 to 2150 BCE comprising the Third Dynasty to Sixth Dynasty; some sources begin with the Fourth Dynasty about 2575 BCE and extend through the Eighth Dynasty ending about 2134 BCE. The period is characterized by royal monuments of the highest quality including the pyramid complexes of the Fourth Dynasty which symbolize the absolute sovereignty of Egypt's kings and the continued use of artistic conventions introduced in the Early Dynastic period. The end of the period is characterized by a general decline in the arts reflecting the political circumstances of the time.

Refers to the period in Egypt from about 2325 to 2150 BCE. The period is characterized by internal problems in the royal family and the decentralization of power seen in the general decline of the arts and an increase in provincial tomb building.

Refers to the period in Egypt from about 2080 to 1970 BCE. The period is characterized by the continuation of Ninth Dynasty power based at Heracleopolis as well as the lack of information about the art and architecture of the period.

Refers to the period in Egypt from about 1630 to 1532 BCE during which a second branch of Asiatics took control of part of the Delta at the same time as the Hyksos of the Fifteenth Dynasty. Little is known about the art and architecture of the period.

Refers to the period in Egypt from about 1190 to 1075 BCE. The period is characterized by a continuation of Nineteenth Dynasty artistic traditions particularly in royal sculpture and relief decoration.
Refers to the period in Egypt from about 950 to 730 BCE. The period is characterized by a revival of stone architecture and the development of fine metalwork.

Refers to the period in history and the style of art that developed after Severan rule in the Roman Empire. It includes the period when Diocletian shared his power in a Tetrarchy and the subsequent period marked by the conversion of Constantine and the Empire to Christianity. This period overlaps with the Early Christian and Early Byzantine periods.

Refers to the period and style of art, predominantely sculpture and architecture, reigns of the emperors Vespasian (69-79 ), Titus (79–81 CE), and Domitian (81-96 CE), that coincided with the dynasty established after the death of Nero in 69 CE. The style is charcterized by a greater emphasis on depth, pictorial illusion, the use of light and shade, and the construction of large-scale buildings such as public baths and ampitheaters.

Refers to the style of wall painting that developed after the earthquake in Pompeii in 62 CE, and was made fashionable by painters working for Nero in Rome. The style is charterized by elaborate architectural schemes, trompe l'oeil, genre scenes, still lifes, and juxtapositions between painted and actual moldings.
Used to describe styles of the regions of Europe.

Refers to the revival of Byzantine style and western influence that evolved after the Crusades in Byzantium and eastern Europe in the late 13th century. Architecture of the period is remarkable for multi-colored materials, decorative details, and the variety of types, generally variants on old themes. In manuscript illuminations, mosaics, wall painting, panel painting, ivories, and luxury arts the style is characterized by strong color, more naturalistic depictions of light on forms, and often imaginative compositional and stylistic solutions.
Use with reference to the period c.1250 to as late as 1500 where the terms "Gothic (Medieval)" or "Late Gothic" are not appropriate.
The Gothic style of architecture and sculpture as practiced in France from 1140 until about 1500.

Refers to the style that developed in the British Isles after the relaxation of imperial Roman authority, generally from the fifth century CE. The style is seen in sculpture, metalwork, and other arts, notably in ornamental manuscript illumination that developed in monastic centers in relatively inaccessible sites. The style continued until the 13th century, and also influenced styles on continental Europe. For the scripts developed in this period, see "Insular scripts."

Refers to the style of artistic production in Spain and its colonies during the reign of Isabella I, from about 1480 to about 1510.  Influenced by the presence of northern European craftsmen and architects, the style reflects a combination of Gothic and Mudéjar forms and motifs.  In architecture buildings are elaborately decorated and are characterized by rich carving, star vaults, coats of arms, stalactite cornices, and cimborio.  The same term is used in the field of Spanish historiography to refer to the reign of Isabella II (1833-1868), though this usage is not applied to art.
Styles belonging to Southern European Medieval cultures.

Refers to the style and period of architecture, visual art, decorative art, music, and literature of western Europe and the Americas from about 1590 to 1750.  The style is characterized by balance and wholeness, often with an emphasis on spectacle and emotional content, and a tendency toward contrasts of light against dark, mass against void, and the use of strong diagonals and curves.
Architecture styles belonging to Renaissance-Baroque cultures.
Style of art in England during the Baroquer period, in England dating from the late 17th century.

Period, culture, and English style in architecture and decorative arts during the reign of William III and Mary II between 1688 and 1702.  Viewed as a transitional period between the Restoration and reign of Queen Anne, Restoration forms and motifs continue but become light and more elegant under French influence.

In Dutch history, regarded as the century from the conclusion of the Twelve Years’ Truce in 1609 until either the death of Prince William III in 1702 or the conclusion of the Peace of Utrecht in 1713. It was an era of political, economic, and cultural growth during which the Netherlands became one of the most powerful and influential in Europe and the world.
Ceramics styles belonging to Italian Renaissance-Baroque cultures.

Refers to the style and period dating from the early 16th century through the early 19th century, in areas colonized by Spain, particularly the Americas. The style is mainly seen in paintings, sculpture, and in ecclesiastical and military architecture. The style reflects the tastes of aristocratic landholders and the church, and generally imitates styles current in Spain, the Netherlands, Italy, and France, with some limited influence from native traditions of design and representation.

Refers to the style of domestic architecture but also of furniture in England and the United States in the late 19th century.  Drawn from the architecture of Queen Anne's reign (1702-1714) and mixed with features found in 17th century Dutch architecture, buildings are characterized by asymmetrical or irregular plans, the use of red brick and stone dressing, broken pediments, sash windows, and shaped gables while furniture features cabriole legs.
Refers to the 19th century English revival style in architecture and decorative arts that combines characteristics of both the Elizabethan and Jacobean periods.
Modern ceramics styles belonging to British cultures.

Refers to the styles of a disparate group of artists working around the coastal town of Saint Ives, Cornwall, England. Although there was a group of painters in St Ives active from the late 19th century, that group of artists was part of a landscape and plein-air tradition. Today, the term 'St Ives School' is most associated with the modernist school of painters active in Saint Ives from the mid-20th century. Notable artists in the St Ives School include Barbara Hepworth, Naum Gabo, Terry Frost, Peter Lanyon, Bryan Wynter, and Patrick Heron.
Style of architecture and decorative arts that began in Britain in the 19th century, evolving into Victorian styles that incorporated Gothic elements.

Refers to the Victorian style, mainly in architecture and decorative arts, produced from about 1870 to about 1901.  While the Gothic Revival still dominated, architecture and decorative arts reflected a renewed interest in Classical, Baroque, and vernacular forms and encompassed new influences such as the Queen Anne and the Beaux Arts styles.  In decorative arts, the influence of Japanese art objects, the Arts and Crafts movement, and the Aesthetic movement simplified the Victorian tendency toward heavy ornamentation.
