A class of pigments where a variety of both inorganic and organic compounds may be present. Historically, comparatively little is known about which materials were used as black pigments, and in treatises on painting technique, the terms black earth, black chalk and black stone were used interchangeably, whether discussing black pigments or drawing materials. In current technical literature, black earth is generally assumed to be a black shale or chalk, but other bituminous materials and minerals have been identified.
Non-standardized name for various organic black pigments, including vine black, cork black, and others.
A form of carbon black that is an aniline pigment, in which a primary aromatic amine, aniline, is converted into a diazonium salt that is an intermediate in the preparation of dyes.

A dark grayish blue or gray pigment mixture generally composed of ivory black with small amounts of white and blue, namely synthetic ultramarine blue, Prussian blue, or phthalocyanine blue. The pigment is used for watercolors.

Unstandardiized pigment name for several materials, including the synthetic copper carbonate (blue verditer), pigment produced from grinding the copper carbonate mineral azurite, smalt pigment, and others.
A type of dye ranging from purple to red in color, obtained from certain lichens growing, for example, on rocks in Scotland and the north of England.

Chinese purple (also called Han purple) is a synthetic barium copper silicate pigment developed in China at least 2,000 years ago. Chinese purple fades and decomposes over time, particularly in contact with acids or heat.

Any of several deep blue pigments consisting chiefly of ferric ferrocyanide; first developed in Berlin in 1704 by Diesbach. It is made by adding ferric chloride to a boiling solution of hexacyano ferrate. Prussian blue has deep blue, finely divided particles that are transparent in watercolors; it has high tinting strength and is stable to light, although it turns brown in the presence of alkalis or heat. It is used as a colorant in cyanotypes, blueprint paper, laundry blue, linoleum, leather, plastics, paper, cosmetics, and formerly as a textile dye for silk, cotton, and wool, where it was mordanted with ferric oxide.

Refers to a fine grade of Prussian blue, having a finer luster and a bronze sheen, favored in printing inks. It is also used in paints, enamels, and lacquers. Considered one of the three best grades of Prussian blue. Chinese blue (BaCuSi4O10) is more stable in chemical structure and fades less easily than Chinese purple.
A deep brownish purple pigment made by carefully roasting or charring carmine.
Material derived by bonding stainless steel and aluminum alloy, for example, through diffusion bonding, friction welding, explode bonding,  or using semisolid aluminum alloy.

Alloy of copper and beryllium containing usually not more than 3% beryllium. The alloy has a bronzelike, crystalline structure and is unsurpassed in its ability to withstand fatigue, wear, and corrosion and in its electrical conductivity at high temperatures.
Brass containing iron and manganese which, because of its hardness and crystalline structure, is named as a bronze.
A gold-copper alloy, of wide range of composition and color, resulting in a lower melting point than either contributory metal; widely employed in Central and South America.
Pewter of the 16th century containing 91% tin and 9% antimony.

Pure metallic element having symbol Cd and atomic number 48; a silver white crystalline metal, very ductile, and which can be rolled or beaten into thin sheets; resembles tin but is harder. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make objects and materials, including pigments.

A thin layer of gold or other metal that has been applied as a decorative surface finish, whether the metal was applied as a thin leaf, by electroplating, or as a thin paint layer. Examples of gilding include that applications on paintings, furniture, frames, sculptures, and the edges of pages of books.

Refers to sheets of gold that have been hammered or rolled very thin (typically around 0.1 micrometer, or 4 millionths of an inch, thick). In art, gold leaf has been applied to paintings, sculptures, manuscripts, and decorative arts since around 1500 BCE. In the 1920s, the process of creating gold leaf was successfully automated.

A base metal, usually silver, copper, or bronze, that has been coated with a transparent orange-red lacquer to produce a rich gold-colored finish that appears to be gilt. Vermeil was common in the 19th century but rarely used today. For gold-plated silver, use "silver gilding."
A matted mass of long, fine steel fiber, especially used for cleaning and polishing surfaces.

Colorless-to-white crystalline potassium aluminum sulfate; has a wide range of uses, including in treatment of leather and textile, in sizing paper, as a mordant in dyeing, and as a water-purifying agent.
A variety of beryl that is rose pink owing to the presence of lithium.
A pink to light violet variety of garnet; is used as a gemstone.
A magnesium-rich mineral of the mica group; it is usually yellowish brown to brownish red and usually occurs in crystalline limestone as a result of dedolomitization.
The yellow variety of crystalline quartz, closely resembling topaz in color.
An apple-green variety of chalcedony valued as a gem.

A type of granular acid igneous rock intermediate in composition between quartz diorite and quartz monzonite, containing quartz, oligoclase or andesine, and potassium feldspar, with biotite, hornblende, or, less frequently, pyroxene, as the mafic components. Granodiorite is the intrusive equivalent of rhyodacite.
A coarse-grained igneous rock, largely granite, sometimes rich in rare elements such as uranium, tungsten, and tantalum.
Granite quarried at Aswan, Egypt with a mineral composition that results in a rose color. It is the type of granite most used in Egyptian architecture.
Igneous rock similar to diorite, predominantly composed of ferromagnetic minerals with crystals visible to the eye; has the same mineral composition as basalt.

A dark purplish-red rock, first quarried in ancient Egypt, containing relatively large crystals in a fine-grained igneous matrix. One of the hardest rocks, it takes a high polish and is valued as a durable sculptor's material and as a decorative architectural material. It is considered the best material for the muller and slab used for grinding artists' colors.
Igneous rock formed at great depth by crystallization of magma and/or by chemical alteration, as contrasted with volcanic rock. Typically of granitoid texture and medium- or coarse-grained.

Fine-grained, dense sedimentary rock consisting of interlocking crystals of quartz approximately 30 microns in diameter. Chert and its varieties, such as flint, are non-gem varieties of cryptocrystalline-granular quartz. These stones chip very easily and thus may be fashioned into tools with a sharp edge; they are also used for building.
A clayey mud that has been hardened by pressure of cementation or heat with the composition and texture of shale but is much less fissile.
A recrystallized limestone composed largely of calcite and brucite; named for a locality near Predazzo, in the Tyrol.
Limestone containing many small, rounded particles, which are concentric layers of calcium carbonate deposits.
Fossiliferous limestone composed of fragments of corals.
Limestone that is streaked or marked with a different color or colors.
Sandstone containing mica.

A siliceous sandstone, from Saint Lawrence County in New York, containing a small amount of iron oxide, giving it its red or reddish-brown color. Although soft enough to work economically when first quarried, it becomes incredibly hard upon exposure, making it an incredibly durable building stone.
A hard, coarse, rubbly or shelly sedimentary rock that weathers with a rough irregular surface, such as a flaggy sandstone or limestone; used primarily as a building stone.

General term for several varieties of hard and soft, fine-grained rock composed of jadeite, nephrite, serpentine, or other mineralogically related materials; usually having a color ranging from dark green to green-white. Jade takes a high polish and has been used since prehistoric times for jewelry, small utensils, carvings, vases, and other ornamental objects. Some processing techniques have been used to enhance the color of inferior stones: B-jade has been bleached to remove brown stains, while C-jade has been impregnated with resins to increase its translucency; A-jade is untreated.
A white, medium-grain marble composed of greater than 90% calcium magnesium carbonate. Dolomitic marbles were quarried in Cape Vathy on Thasos from antiquity to about the 5th century CE.
Marble of the purest white and of finely crystalline form used in architecture and sculpture.

A breccia marble that is typically grayish violet with striking bright red or golden yellow streaks as well as oblong white, yellow, or red fragments. It originates from the island of Scyrus and is named for Septimius Bassus, who in antiquity had a villa sumptuously decorated with it on the Via Tusculana in Rome.

A shell marble which is usually either light purple or reddish brown in color. Its name means 'peacock's eye' in Italian, the eye referring to the presence of petrified oyster shells. There are two columns made of this marble in the Vatican Library.

A compact variety of calcite that has dark layers of impurities and polishes to a high gloss, resembling onyx in appearance. It is typically used as a decorative or architectural material or for small ornamental objects.
Egyptian marble colored black by carbon.
Marble, from the island of Melos on the Nile, that is dusty black in color with faint streaks and spots of gray.

Reddish-brown to cherry red limestone with gray, blue and red streaks and veins or spots, derived primarily from the province of Hainaut, and used extensively as material for furniture and architecture in Paris in the 16th-18th centuries, and notably at Versailles.

The name applied to a number of Italian marbles, generally containing various hues and patterns of red and brown although other colors such as white and purple are often present. The modern species are coarse and often considered unattractive; the ancient Romans quarried cottanello of superior quality about forty miles from Rome in the Sabine hills, near the town after which the stone is named.

A fine-grain marble quarried near Marble in Gunnison County, Colorado. Colorado Yule marble is usually pure white but can have pale gray clouds and/or creamy veins. Some regions of the marble belt have a pale blue-gray color. Colorado Yule has been used for statuary and was used for the exterior of the Lincoln Memorial.
A type of fine-grained, platy serpentine that is mottlish yellow with dark gray or black patches. The name refers to its resemblance to a snake's skin.
Refers to large flat sections of slate used for paving and also bluestone cut for this purpose.

Stone, generally of impressive bulk or size, used for erecting any variety of monument, but particularly for tombs or tombstones. The term can also refer to stone used to carve monumental statuary or for constructing monumental architecture.
Chalk that has been ground and washed for use in paint, ink, and putty.
An organosulfur compound with antioxidant properties used as a chelating agent. It has been used for the removal of arsenic- and mercury-based pesticide residues in museum objects.
Water that is free from dissolved salts and such metals as calcium, iron, or magnesium.

Generally, water dedicated to sacred uses and used for ritual purification of persons and things. More specifically,  water blessed by a priest and used in various rites and devotional acts, such as baptisms and blessings.
General term for certain mineral inflammable substances that are native hydrocarbons, more or less oxygenated, whether liquid, semi-solid, or solid. Examples include naphtha, petroleum, asphalt.
Animal material that contains fibrin.

Material derived from the hard, hollow shaft of a feather that attaches into the skin of the bird. The quill portion of the bird feather does not have any lateral branches; quills from ducks, geese, eagles, swans, and other large birds have been used as tips for pens and as ferrules for artists' brushes.
Material made from the hair of camelids, especially South American camelids such as llama and alpaca. For fiber made from camels, use "camel hair."
One of the long projecting hairs or bristles growing near the mouth of an animal.

Skin of a deer or other member of the cervid family, used especially for clothing, moccasins, and bookbinding leather. In early bookbinding, before the 16th century, the skin was either processed with lime or alum-tawed to make it white in appearance. For processed deerskin, use "buckskin" or "doeskin (skin)."
Material comprising the dentin of whale teeth.
Elongated, seed-bearing fruits formed from a single carpel that splits along the sides on ripening.
Pulpy fruits covered with fairly thick skins from the genus Citrus.
In Indian architecture, a circumambulatory path.

In ancient Roman settlements, open spaces used as marketplaces or general public meeting places and places for judicial and public business. For similar spaces in ancient Greek settlements, use "agoras."
Small administrative districts of many countries, especially in Europe. A distinct form of government is implied by the term, for example, government by a mayor and municipal council.
Towns which invent or reinvent themselves on a particular theme in order to attract tourism. Generally, residential areas of such towns do not incorporate the adopted theme.
Ancient Greek cities or city-states.
Places where multiple facilities are situated.
Communities, usually small in size, located outside urban areas in isolated or undeveloped areas.
Communities of varying size, located in a fertile region of a desert and with productive land.

Inhabited places noted for cultural institutions and activities, such as museums, performances of music and dance, etc., particularly when the places serve as the hub of cultural activity in an area or region.
Settlements or urban or suburban environments of any size that are developed according to a single plan, usually on a previously undeveloped site.
Inhabited places where craftsmen's work is a significant industry.
Communication system that transmits sound between distant points

Shifting cultivation plots of the Arawak people that formed a part of their agricultural system. These were selected and controlled by individual families to grow starchy and sugar-rich foods such as tubers.
Designates small mountain lakes, often with no apparent inlet, usually formed in a blocked bowl-shaped depression eroded by ice.
Buoyed channels of sufficient depth for the safe navigation of vessels.
The summits or rounded tops of a mountain or hill.
Configurations of two or more islands that are related by proximity.
Rock debris deposited by a glacier.
Extensive, generally grass-covered plains of South America.
Designates waterlogged areas with pondweeds, reeds, and rushes and in which peat is accumulating but the water remains alkaline. Distinct from "bogs," in which the peat has reached a higher acidity.

Ornamental designs, usually on a flat surface or in relief and composed of repeated or combined motifs. Distinguish from "motifs" which are distinct or separable design elements occurring singly as individual shapes.
In Indian art and architecture, a decorative motif comprising a half-diamond or split-diamond.
Motif consisting of two or more circles engaged with each other by partial overlapping or interpenetration.
Motifs consisting of a curved segment of a circle, often suggesting a crescent moon.

Zodiac symbol of a goat, roughly based on the constellation of the same name. The zodiak signs have survived from classical Greek and Roman decoration, were popular in Northern European Romanesque and Gothic churches, and often found in Medieval psalters and books of hours symbolizing each month in which the sun enters the related constellation. They have also been used as decoration on ceilings, maps, timepieces, and astronomical instruments.
Refers to Latin crosses, the center of which is surrounded by a ring or circle.

Running patterns consisting of a series of simple scrolls, each spiralling out from the center of the preceding one. For patterns consisting of wavy lines or other series of generally wavelike forms, use "wave pattern."
In Indian architecture, a split; fluted.

Generally, any prefabricated ornamental border that serves to frame an image. Specifically, a mat of paper, cardboard, or other material with an opening cut out of the center that readily accepts printed matter for display.

Of a plane figure or a solid, a set of points containing all points in a line joining any two constituent points, for example, the rounded outward exterior curve of a circle or sphere. In a convex polygon, every internal angle is less than or equal to 180 degrees.

Colorless, pungent gas composed of nitrogen and hydrogen (NH3) in the simplest stable compound of these elements. It was the first complex molecule to be identified in interstellar space. Gaseous ammonia was first isolated by Joseph Priestly in 1774. It is used in the following ways: as a starting material for the production of many commercially important nitrogen compounds, such as in the manufacture of explosives and fertilizers; and as a vapor phase neutralizing/alkalizing agent where it neutralizes effectively but provides no residual alkaline reserve. Ammonia is most often sold as an aqueous solution of ammonium hydroxide.
Cement reinforced with alkali-resistant glass fibers.
A cement used in general construction where moderate heat of hydration is required.
Similar to Keene's cement with borax instead of alum as a setting accelerator.

A cement formulation used to adhere and waterproof stained glass or leaded glass in windows. It consists in a combination of calcium carbonate, Plaster of Paris and boiled linseed oil thinned with mineral turpentine and and colored with lamp black.
Refers to prevously burnt, finely ground pottery that is added to terracotta clay in order to open the pores.
Brick having special shapes for use in capping the exposed top of a wall.
Brick made of clay mixed with only enough water to produce plasticity, and extruded through a die.

Variety of porcelain material comprising a soft or hard paste, white, fine, and vitreous, often resembling statuary marble; developed in England in the 1840s and used for figurines, especially dolls, and for art objects, ornament, and tableware. For unglazed porcelain or earthenware that has been fired only once and used for similar types of objects, but producing a grainy texture, use "biscuit (porcelain, material)."
Potters' term for pottery in a stage of the creation process where it has not yet been fired. For unfired clay as a medium that is not intended to be fired, use "unfired clay."

Hard, dense, white stoneware developed in England during the 18th century as a cheaper substitute for bone china and originally highly decorated, but used most extensively as plain white inexpensive tableware throughout most of the 19th century.
Any of a series of tiles covering a wall and overlapped like shingles.

Mass concrete in which large stones, each weighing 100 lb. (45.4 kg) or more, are embedded when the concrete is laid. The stones, called pudding stones or plums, are typically less than 6 in. (15 cm) apart and farther than 8 in. (20 cm) away from any exposed surface.
A construction material composed of cement, sand, or crushed slag and water forced through a pneumatic gun.
A lightweight concrete mixture containing little or no fine aggregate.
A cast imitation marble produced with Keene's cement.
General term for Venetian glass often yellow or smoky gray in color unless formulated with the decolorizing agent manganese, which gives the glass the appearance of rock crystal.
A glass fiber, .001 inches in diameter.
Glass, especially types invented in the 19th century, that incorporated newly developed techniques for producing colors and surface textures.
Glass which appears to be a different color when viewed in transmitted or reflected light; often achieved by the addition of colloidal gold to the glass batch.

Visual works, often windows, or components of visual works or architecture, made of bits or pieces of glass, often chipped along the edges to resemble faceting, set in a matrix of concrete or epoxy resin. The first glass in concrete windows appeared ca. 1929 in Europe; the technique is now used to create other objects as well. For cement reinforced with glass fibers, use "glass reinforced cement."

Iron alloy of fibrous nature made by melting white cast iron, passing an oxidizing flame over it, and rolling it into a mass; valued for its corrosion resistance and ductility. When describing objects produced or shaped by beating with a hammer, use "wrought."
Steel having a carbon content in excess of 0.5%.
Security structures used by the military.
Monuments that serve as guides to direction, position, or route, or that mark a boundary or limit.
Signs or posts used to indicate the distance to or between a specific point.
Stones carved with runic inscriptions. Usage extends to small stones used for divination as well and monumental standing stones.
Places of historic, scenic, or scientific interest set aside for preservation, usually by presidential proclamation.

Refers to the Fante Asafo military associations' meeting places, rallying points, and ritual centers for the groups' events; originally functioning as shrines, now also acting as storage facilities, civic symbols, and advertisements of community strength.
Theaters located at a college or university; usually affiliated with the curriculum.
Platforms or booths set up in a town square or other public location, often on market day, to accommodate traveling players or street performers.
Refers to early movie theaters, usually small and simple, where motion pictures, and sometimes variety shows, could be seen at inexpensive prices, usually a nickel.
Revitalized industrial architecture used as hotels, or hotels having a design imitating industrial design.

Ancient Roman inns that served cooked delicacies and full meals, usually having a narrow, long floor plan and vaulted ceilings, with serving boys attending and the proprieter sitting on a raised platform at one end. They were better-class establishments, distinguished from the lower-class inns, "cauponae."
Structures containing large, bounded, smoothly surfaced areas for skating.

Ancient Greek or Roman buildings for training in wrestling or other athletic endeavors. Palaestrae were often part of public gymnasia, although some functioned independently. The floorplan of palaestrae was standardized, usually comprising a rectangular court surrounded by colonnades with adjoining rooms devoted to activities such as undressing, bathing, socializing, observation, instruction, and storage.
Tennis courts enclosed within buildings or other structures.
Establishments containing special enclosures for cleansing or refreshing oneself in a bath of steam.
Area and facilities comprising the terrain and supporting infrastructure where skiing and other snow sports take place.

Buildings for public Christian worship that are distinguished historically from chapels and oratories, which are buildings that are in some respect private, or not public in the widest sense. Church architecture generally somewhat follows standard models, which vary depending upon the date, location, and characteristics of the congregation.
Churches used temporarily as cathedrals, as, for instance, during repairs or during creation of a new diocese.

Churches that are the principal church of a diocese, serving as the seat of the bishop, or of the archbishop, primate, patriarch, or pope of the diocese. They are generally grandiose structures and house the "cathedra," which is the throne of the bishop.
In Indian architecture, a shrine surrounding a Bōdhi tree.
A type of ancient mudbrick building, often a temple, in the Sudan; possibly the term derives from a Nubian term for a fortified mudbrick building.
Worship place of the Chinese folk religion Shenism, where people revere ethnic Chinese gods and ancestors. The term is now generally considered pejorative.
Natural caves used as temples or other places of worship.
Laboratories focused on designing, constructing, and testing computers and computer programs. For centers housing computers and service for computing, use "computer centers."
In India, large open-sided shelters, comprising upright poles supporting a roof usually made of bamboo matting.
Top-loading, bottom-discharging funnels or storage bins, as for crushed stone, sand, or food stuffs.
Buildings specifcally used for purposes related to railroad transportation.
Terminals that are used for the purpose of transferring, transporting, storing, or processing oil.
Towers or other structures equipped with a powerful light or lights (originally a signal fire) at the top, erected at important or dangerous points on or near the coast for the guidance of mariners.

Use only to refer to buildings or other structures placed at the endpoints of bus routes; use "bus stations" only for intermediate stops along bus routes; use "bus shelters" for structures at bus stops affording weather protection but having no sales or service facilities.
Houses or other buildings designed or used primarily for the collection of tolls or dues.

Bridges linking two or more settled areas by means of a continuous or discontinuous row of buildings that accommodate different functions, such as domestic, cultural, social, or recreational uses, and are set upon or clustered along the transport route.
Drawbridges that open and close to river craft by rotating around a central pier.
Tunnels used to transport water in water supply systems.
Structures that house signals of various types, usually in service of transportation systems; examples include such structures on seashores, canals, or along railroad lines.
Structures that float on the water and can be partly submerged to permit a ship to enter it and afterward floated to raise the ship high and dry as in "dry docks."

Substantial, man-made banks or landing stages, typically built of stone, lying alongside or projecting into water for loading and unloading ships. For structures that are not man-made banks, but built in similar locations and for similar purposes, use "wharves"; use "piers (marine landings)" for lighter structures that extend out over the water.

Buildings designed with foundations floating in water or on platforms floating in water, rather than on foundations dug into the earth on dry land. Examples include houses with foundations on a river bottom constructed so that -- if the water level rises to flood stage -- the house and the foundation will float up with the water level; and various types of buildings constructed on floating platforms or islands in a body of water, such as a lake or sea.
Structures, generally enclosed, that are used or intended to be used for sheltering an activity or occupancy, and that are intended to be non-permanent.
Structures usually associated with or located in gardens or similarly landscaped grounds.
Outbuildings used for cooking, particularly during hot summer months, when it was desirable to keep the heat of the stove and oven physically separated from the rest of the house and living quarters.

Buildings and other architectural structures constructed wholly or primarily of earth. For engineering works, such as trenches, created in the earth, use "earthworks (engineering works)." For structures built on a hillside rather than into it, use "hillside architecture." For structures built under the surface of the ground, but not made primarily of earth, use "underground structures."

Drawings on the earth's surface; specifically geometric or zoic symbols constructed by altering the arrangement of gravel. To refer to those made by the Nasca (Nazca) people and found on the southern desert plains of coastal Peru, use the specific term "Nazca lines."

Long, narrow, usually steep-sided cuts into the earth, as to receive pipes, wires, or footings; may also be used for defensive cuts, especially when the excavated earth is heaped in front as a barrier. For defensive cuts in which the earth is not used as added protection, use "fosses" or "moats."

Artificial earthen mounds, usually burial mounds, that are round and dome-shaped, sometimes with a very narrow, pointed top. Such mounds were especially prevalent with early indigenous inhabitants of midwest North America.
Facilities that formerly stationed police.
Dutch-style gardens, distinctive geometric and symmetrical designs, especially prominent in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries; found also in countries other than the Netherlands.

Gardens designed to improve or maintain the physical and mental health of the ill or injured, including gardens serving as clinical tools in horticultural therapy. For gardens designed for use by the handicapped or the elderly, use "enabling gardens."
Formal gardens or portions of gardens that by design are set at a lower level than their surroundings.

Areas of land whose natural growth is protected by legislation and where recreation and industrial use are restricted; for wild and uncultivated regions left untouched in a natural state with no human control or interference, use "wilderness."
Parks, usually over 20 acres in extent, offering a wider range of activities and considerably more open space than "neighborhood parks."
Parks owned or maintained by the state, particularly a U.S. state.
Designates special play areas set aside for children, particularly pre-school age children.
Divided, multilane highways with full grade separation and total control of access; can be freeways or turnpikes.
Roads surfaced with macadam, a type of broken stone named after J. L. MacAdam (1756-1836), the Scottish engineer who invented it.

Timber framed, one or one and a half story, side-gabled houses, with a central chimney, steeply-pitched roof, and typically clapboarded or shingled siding. These were small houses found in colonial New England, particularly Massachusetts, during the 18th century. The Cape Cod house also became popular in the United states as a revival style in the 20th century.
Houses or other buildings that slot into a tight space between two older buildings.
Small 18th- and 19th-century Philadelphia row houses generally comprised of one room per floor for three floors.
Designates Roman country houses located near the city and serving recreational, not agricultural purposes.
Houses built to demonstrate to the consumer the layout and features that will or could be included in manufactured houses, often in a subdivision.
Groups of similarly designed houses located in subdivisions; used to distinguish from those houses that are custom designed and built.

Country or suburban retreats offering comfort and simplicity, combining the design of town houses with the needs of country living; less elaborate than châteaux; popular in 17th- and 18th-century France.
Distinguished from "log cabins" by being generally larger and better built of carefully hewn timbers neatly notched at the corners.
Houses or parts of houses occupied by enslaved people, who are people treated as the property of another person, whether by capture, purchase, or birth.

The official residences of foreign ministers. When such residences include offices for ministers appointed primarily to oversee and protect the home country's economic interests in a host country, use "consulates," but use "embassies" when the offices and residences are for ministers called ambassadors appointed to implement items of international foreign policy in a host country.
Tents made of sewn together skins, typically that of goats.
Buildings containing rental apartments that are in large cities, occupied by poorer people, generally built to minimum standards of sanitation, safety, and comfort, and often in run-down condition.
In Indian architecture, a royal residence.
Buildings used for display or sale of art works or other items.

Buildings housing facilities for the care, planning and preparation of human remains for burial or cremation. While the meaning may overlap in common usage with "funeral homes," generally mortuaries have more extensive facilities for preparing the body and funeral homes have a parlor or other area for formal viewing of and services for the deceased. In modern usage, the term "mortuaries" may also refer to facilities that prepare the bodies of pets for burial or cremation.
Ancient sepulchral mounds, particularly those created by the Bronze Age Tumulus culture evident in Europe from around 1600 BCE.
Small crosses displayed together in a designated area, usually a church, each intended as a remembrance of a deceased person.

Buildings housing the body of government officers known as "ministers," typically ministers of state or secretaries of state, who are high level officials responsible for the administration of a country or state.
Legislative buildings in countries with parliamentary forms of government.
Headquarters for the police of a particular district, from which police officers are dispatched and to which persons under arrest are brought.
Refers to the chief public administration buildings of a city, generally housing the mayor's office and legislative chambers.
Barriers built across waterways to turn aside all or some of the flow from its usual course into a pipe, trench, or channel, as to bypass construction work.

Dams in which the embankment is constructed in successive mechanically compacted layers, using sheepsfoot rollers or heavy pneumatic-tired rollers to compact the fill. Rolled-fill is the most commonly used method of earth dam construction.
Dams, canals, and other structures designed to protect an area from flooding.
Sewers that discharge into branch or other sewers and have no other common sewer tributary to them.
Structures in riverways that regulate flow and play key roles in flood control and water utilization.

Structures that enclose fountains, most often leaving one side or section open for viewing. These may be simple columned porches or more elaborate structures and usually include sculptural elements. The term is most often applied to such structures in classical Greece.
Roman water distribution structures, usually reservoirs, constructed at locations where water delivered by an aqueduct is diverted to various points in town.
Builtings or structures designed to contain assemblies of interrelated equipment designed to provide heat to other buildings and  structures.
Facilities established or used to transform, alter, or treat a product or other thing by using a special process or technique, including operating upon the thing mechanically or chemically.
Windmill used to power the pumping of water from a polder, which is low-lying land reclaimed from the sea, to a drainage network.
Textile mills in which thread is spun.
Buildings equipped with machinery for grinding grain into flour.

Kilns, often used for mass-produced ceramics, consisting of a continuous conveyor belt or railcar operation with the ware traversing the kiln and gradually being heated from room temperature, through a hot zone, and back down to room temperature.
Ovens for drying and seasoning cut lumber.
Structures or other shelters designed or used for the storage, drying, or curing of lumber.
Buildings housing educational institutions, usually elementary or secondary schools, where classes are held only on weekdays and that do not provide any boarding facilities.

Buildings that house schools devoted to the professional study of the organization and management of commercial enterprises, usually at the baccalaureate level and above. For buildings that house schools devoted to training students in the clerical aspects of business and commerce, use "business colleges (buildings)."
Buildings that house schools intermediate between elementary school and high school, differing by school district in grades included.
Buildings that house colleges that are financially supported by a state government, either the government of a U.S. state or the national government of certain other nations.

Buildings or open air structures housing facilities for patients or clients undergoing medical treatment by bathing and similar remedial agencies, usually with a large communal bathing area, or a series of cubicles or apartments arranged for bathing.
Facilities, either permanent or temporary, where vaccinations are distributed.

Clinics that are located in vehicles or are otherwise mobile, typically intended to provide outpatient treatment and dispensing of medicine in rural areas or other areas that do not have access to regular nearby medical facilities.

Hospitals specializing in the care of people recovering health and strength after illness or injury, typically including provision for full medical care as needed, including professional doctor and nursing staff and diagnostic facilities.

Long-term care facilities in a residential environment for elderly persons who require some degree of personal assistance with the activities of daily life, such as dressing, bathing, or mobilization; offers a middle ground between independent living and supervised nursing care.

Buildings used as refuges for the sick or destitute who need care rather than medical treatment; for institutional facilities treating the mentally ill, use "psychiatric hospitals" or "psychiatric clinics," and for those treating the chronically ill, use "sanatoriums."
In Indian architecture, a free feeding-house, an alms house.
Buildings housing privately owned libraries established to meet the needs of the members or staff of the owning institution.
Buildings housing archives of films and other moving image materials.
Buildings housing libraries maintained by state funds.
Military structures used for the purposes of training.
Buildings or groups of buildings intended primarily to serve as a fortified residence of a prince or nobleman.
Arabic castles or fortified palaces.
Generally small ancient Near Eastern fortresses used from Syria to Egypt especially along borders and near oases or important road junctions.

Forts having a polygonal shape, which varied according to the site and requirements. Although they existed by the middle ages, prime examples of polygonal forts were those constructed resist the fire of rifled artillery and heavy mortars in the late 18th through 19th centuries.
Buildings for the storage and distribution of ammunition, weapons, military vehicles, and equipment.

Altars of any faith or culture that are not connected to or supported by a building or other structure. The term typically includes outdoor altars, and altars that are placed within a building but are not architecturally attached to the walls or structure of the building. Note that in some cases, particularly in certain periods of Catholic architecture, it may at first glance appear that an altar is attached to the wall, but it is in fact freestanding in keeping with the ecclesiastical prescription that the high altar must stand free on all sides, although the backs of smaller altars may be built against the wall.
The upper, horizontal surfaces of altars, especially the top slabs; may be arranged or placed upon supports in various ways.
Pulpits in mosques, having a small stand for the speaker, parapet, canopy, narrow stairs, and usually a gate at the foot of the stairs.
Channels at the side or in the middle of a road or street, for leading off surface water.

Cylindrical outdoor sidewalk structures used as supports for printed advertising for theatrical and other entertainments. The invention is  attributed to Gabriel Morris ca. 1868 in the city of Paris, though earlier advertising pillars were erected in Berlin in the 1850s, created by printer Ernst Litfass.
Refers to masonry on either side of a fireplace opening that supports the mantel and upper chimney construction.

Substantial interior spaces at the level of an upper story that overlook the level below and usually extend the full length or width of a room. For railed platforms projecting from the exterior walls of buildings or small, similar interior features, use "balconies." For floor levels in a church above the aisles and open to the nave, use "tribunes (stories)" or "triforiums."

In Japanese architecture, an interior space that may have evolved historically from the private altars of Zen Buddhist monks, used for the display of devotional objects; then later as elevated seating for warriors or dignitaries. The most recent use of  the space in Japanese houses is for the display of flower arrangements and scrolls that set the mood of the tea ceremony, or other art objects.

Apartments that offer all the amenities of a normal domestic apartment but in radically reduced size. These have open space for sleeping, working, cooking, and eating. These are typically part of housing projects that are six stories high with 40 units each.
Small enclosures or structures, often temporary, used for casting votes.
Rooms equipped with lockers, often having showers and toilets and sometimes used as dressing rooms, as in clubhouses and gymnasiums.
Relatively narrow spaces designed to provide access; usually interior spaces.
Slides, especially found in apartment blocks or offices, where mail is sent to a main repository.
Areas specially equipped for loading and receiving items onto and from motor vehicles or railroad cars parked adjacent.
In Indian architecture, a half-hall articulated with the vimāna or maṇḍapa; tyically in South India.
Rooms or buildings containing a systematically ordered collection of preserved plants; for gardens of herbs, use "herb gardens."
Self-service establishments providing prepared food and drinks from long counters for on-premise or immediate consumption.
Rooms, suites of rooms, other enclosed, domestic interior spaces having the primary purpose of sleeping and relaxing.
Small, private, informal rooms in houses or apartments used for work, reading, or relaxation.

In a royal palace, castle, large manor house, or hall house, the largest and central room of the house, often used for receptions and banqueting in the Middle Ages. In the country houses of the 16th and early 17th centuries, the great hall was also used by the family for eating and relaxing.
Rooms, often wholly or mostly below ground level, used for storage of food and often other items; for similar areas serving utility purposes or as living spaces, use "basements."
Offices or other spaces staffed and equipped to handle large numbers of telephone calls, using computer technology to assist in the management of calls and supply of information.
Offices spaces occupied by lawyers, experts in law, and their associates.
Control centers for on-call nursing staff in health facilities.
In Indian architecture, a space around the sanctuary.

Rooms or small buildings that serve as sanctuaries or places of Christian worship; often having an altar. A chapel may be used for private worship in or attached to a church, palace, house, prison, monastery, or school. The concept includes both freestanding chapels and rooms or recesses serving as chapels in churches or other buildings. The Latin "cappella" or the French-derived "chappelle" or "chapelle" are occasionally used for "chapel" in English texts. In its original meaning, the term referred specifically to the shrine in which the kings of France preserved the cape (cloak) of St. Martin.

The sanctuaries of Indian temples. The term may be used for earlier Indian temples as a whole, including sanctuary and attached porches. In Dravidian, Karṇāṭan as well as early Indian architecture, the main temple-structure or shrine or prāsāda in a temple complex.

Types of apses designed with special areas for officials or speakers. either a raised platform or a dome, or both. In a Roman basilica, the tribune is semicircular apse with a raised platform, where a presiding magistrates (tribunes) sat in an official chair. In Medieval and later ecclesiastical architecture, the tribune is a designated area circumscribed by a vaulted or semi-domed apse.
In Indian architecture, a temple hall containing stūpa.
Rooms in which wine is stored, in bottles or barrels, usually fully or partially below ground level.
In Indian architecture, a screened structure with balikkal.
Native round huts of southern Africa, usually built of mud and thatch.
Towers, turrets, lighthouses, or similar structures in south and east Asia.
Towerlike structures holding bells in Buddhist monasteries.
In Indian architecture, a four-storeyed śikhara (or building).
Three-apsed buildings, usually having a cross plan in which one arm of the cross is a flat-ended narthex and the remaining three arms terminate in apses.
A building or complex of buildings devoted to a particular activity or concern.

Farm buildings, generally of the 17th to early 19th century, where dairy products are made and stored, usually supervised by country ladies. Distinguished from "dairy plants" by their lack of mechanization. For subsidiary agricultural buildings devoted primarily to the care of milk, whether mechanized or not, prefer "milk houses."
Historic barn design that flourished between the late 19th and early 20th centuries in the United States and Canada. Round barns were built in a variety of shapes: octagonal, polygonal, or circular.

Barns constructed or used for the housing of sheep, usually having a pen or pens large enough to contain several sheep or a flock, smaller pens for lambing (giving birth), and areas for shearing, feeding, and watering.
Greenhouses designed to shelter through the winter tropical, and often ornamental, trees such as orange trees, and usually with southern exposure and heating systems.
Built structures or dwellings for accomodating cattle.
Buildings or rooms equipped with heated lamps and other equipment used to facilitate the incubation and hatching of chickens' eggs outside the environment of their mothers' nests.
Tall, usually cylindrical, structures in which animal feed is stored and which are normally sealed to exclude air and promote fermentation of green fodder (silage) without spoilage.
Enclosures composed of vertical posts and horizontal connecting members used to enclose all or part of a garden space.
Buildings serving as meeting places for certain groups or factions associated with a church.
Center focused on training and performance of music.
Buildings housing offices and often the printing presses for a printing and publishing enterprise.
Eating facilities where quick, light meals, refreshments, or snacks are served, usually at a counter.
Small, usually inexpensive, restaurants with a limited menu of light meals served at counters or tables.

Originally referred to buildings that house banks with offices or branches located in vehicles that may be set up in changing locations. The term more recently refers to buildings that house banks that allow financial transactions to be made over mobile devices, such as a cell phone.

Buildings or outdoor areas where trade is conducted, often optimized for a gathering together of people for the purchase and sale produce and livestock. Markets typically have booths or stalls for individual merchants, either in open air or under a single large roof.
Refers to structures designed or used specifically to house markets; the term is usually reserved for relatively small, traditional structures in the historical center of a town or city.

Relatively buildings or sets of buildings containing a relatively small number of retail units with interconnecting walkways, generally having only one or a small number of stories, often located outdoors in a suburban area, and typically arranged in a single row facing a shared parking lot. For larger, more elaborate structures housing a larger number of retail units, often under a roof with indoor walkways, use "shopping malls."
Buildings or parts of buildings where bread and other baked goods are prepared; it may include a space for the retail sale of baked goods.
Built works housing retail outlets that are owned and operated by consumers for their mutual benefit based on open consumer membership.
Buildings and other structures used for tracking satellites in orbit.

Individual dwellings designed to be occupied by a single tenant or family. May also refer to a building for human occupation, for some purpose other than that of an ordinary dwelling; with this usage, "house" is generally prefaced (e.g., "cowhouse," "almshouse").
Systems of bars laid at road level designed to prevent cattle and game from entering or leaving a designated area, while allowing the passage of other traffic.
In Indian architecture, an elephant eye; perforated screen (jāla) with holes, looking like geometricised "elephant eye."
Ceilings of semicylindrical shape.
In Indian architecture, a cusped and coffered ceiling with a central lambana-pendentive.
Floors which span the entire distance between end supports without additional intermediate support.
Roofs that are circular in plan and that rise to terminate in a point, the whole forming a regular cone in shape.
Roofs with two sloping sides meeting at a ridge, and gables at one or both ends.
Short wood framing members nailed to the sides of joists or rafters to extend a roof or floor beyond an exterior wall line.
Dormers with hip roofs.
Eaves with visible supporting members.
In Indian architecture, an eave-strut; cantilever of a faceted, lotus-stalk form; usually a faceted lotiformed cantilever.
Rounded finials.
Small ornamental gables, usually not roof gables but rather a decoration over a buttress or opening.
A hipped gable peak in which the small hip does not engage the roof structure but cantilevers from the gable surface.
Roofs of four steeply pitched faces, forming a spire; the four ridges rise from the peaks of four gables, the roof faces being set diagonally in relation to the gable faces.
Vertical parts or components of roof frames.

Rafters that do not extend from the roof plates to the ridgeboards; employed in hip roofs to reach from roof plates to hip rafters. For rafters spanning between valley rafters and ridgeboards, use "valley jacks." Rafters that do not extend from the roof plates to the ridgeboards; employed in hip roofs to reach from roof plates to hip rafters. For rafters spanning between valley rafters and ridgeboards, use "valley jacks."
Walls made of concrete masonry units.

In building construction, fire-resisting walls, enclosed stairways, and other similar obstructions for preventing the spread of fires in buildings. In building construction, fire-resisting walls, enclosed stairways, and other similar obstructions for preventing the spread of fires in buildings.
Enclosing walls connecting bastions or towers in fortifications.
The vertical wall, circular or polygonal in plan, that carries a dome. The vertical wall, circular or polygonal in plan, that carries a dome.
Outer sides of buildings, opposite the main facade. In early modern castles often open to the garden.
In Indian architecture, a four-sided, square kūṭa-type aedicule.
In Indian architecture, a square colonnade.
Courses of bondstones that affix the facing masonry to the backing masonry. Courses of bondstones that affix the facing masonry to the backing masonry.
Literally meaning a “bright” or “open” space (Kroll 2015, 309; 196), mingjian usually refers to the central bay of a building.
Risalits achieved by increasing the wall thickness, but which does not change the floor plan inside the building.
In Indian architecture, literally "earth", ground, tala, level; a floor or storey of a prāsāda; symbolic storey in Latina śikhara.
Concave surfaces located at the junction of a wall and ceiling.
In Indian architecture, a shrine-formed niche.
In Indian architecture, a single candraśālā pediment; major pediment of interlinked candraśālās; complex gavākṣa-pediment.
Pilasters in composite order.
In Indian architecture, a doorframe having two śākhās/ jambs; two-jambed doorframe.
The vertical members forming the sides of doorways.
Doors consisting of two separate leaves, one above the other; the leaves may operate independently or together.
Hinged doors that cover the mouths of ovens.
In Indian architecture, a hall-formed gate attached with a temple’s compound wall.
Windows designed to meet the requirements of school buildings, usually featuring large multipaned glass areas.

Shelflike passive solar devices usually set near the ceiling projecting from either the interior or exterior of windows to allow daylight or direct sunlight to bounce deep into buildings without glare or strong modulation, to enhance interior lighting conditions.
Vertical members at either side of doorframes, window frames, or the like.
Sets of shutters are vertically mounted one above the other within the same opening, allowing each set to function independently.
Tracery whose openings are or seem to be pierced through slabs of stone; used especially in Early Gothic windows.

Inclined planes or slopes that are constructed of earth, stone, cement, metal, wood, or another material and used to connect two different levels, or to connect one level to the air or water. Examples include sloping floors or walks in architecture, sloping construction used in highway engineering, movable sets of stairs used when boarding or leaving an airplane, and movable slopes to allow access to a bus or other type of vehicle.
Stairs constructed with newels at the angles to receive the ends of the strings.
Refers to flights of steps, found in India, that lead down to the banks of rivers or other bodies of water.
The platforms between flights of stairs, or at the termination of a flight of stairs.
Steps in a straight flight of stairs, each tread of which is of uniform width.
In plumbing, joints packed with oakum and finished with molten lead.
Used to designate moldings formed by a series of regularly spaced cubical or short cylindrical projections; found in Romanesque architecture and usually appearing in multiple rows.
Moldings having a profile of double curvature.
Moldings of double curvature where the uppermost surface is convex and the lowermost is concave.
Fillet moldings with the front portion pendant; for moldings with a beaked head ornamental motif, use "beakhead moldings."
In Mayan architecture, tripartite facade moldings consisting of a central vertical band framed on top and bottom by flaring members; characteristic of Puuc architecture.
Projecting, scroll-shaped architectural members serving as brackets or corbels. Often used to support entablatures and cornices over doorways and windows.
In Indian architecture, a śikharikā-turret placed over the karṇa in the Anēkāṇḍaka śikhara.
Devices that use the solar power to heat a chamber to the temperatures required to cook food. These devices may vary in construction and methods used to concentrate the solar power.
Depressions in a channel or reservoir deep enough to reduce the turbulence or velocity of the flow.
Chambers, often vaulted, in ramparts, bastions, or other outer fortification elements with openings for the firing of artillery.
Refers to the outer slopes of encircling defensive ditches; for the inner slopes, use "scarps."
Architectural elements found on Christian religious buildings.

Spaces in a church marked by an arch, usually as the entrance to an apse or chapel, coinciding with the part of the building containing a font for the baptismal rite. The open space beneath the arch may be spanned by a gate, grillwork, or door.
Residential treatment centers, often in a rural setting, which provide medical and counseling services for children with emotional problems.

Facilities where fish eggs are hatched and the fry raised, especially to stock lakes, streams, and ponds. Facilities where fish eggs are hatched and the fry raised, especially to stock lakes, streams, and ponds.

Single-household living arrangements in which two or more individuals who are unrelated or members of an extended family (in contrast to a nuclear family) share a single dwelling unit as a long-term occupancy; typically each resident or nuclear family unit has a private bedroom or other personal rooms, but share a common kitchen, dining area, bath room, laundry, and other facilities.

Complexes or groups of buildings that house degree-granting institutions which may typically include liberal arts undergraduate colleges, graduate schools, and undergraduate or graduate professional schools. To distinguish a single buildings in the context of being part of a complex, prefer "college building."
Cemeteries characterized by open expanses of turf with flush markers, particularly those dating from the late 19th-century.
Outdoor areas set aside for caskets or urns containing ashes.
Designates areas where a large number of high-capacity storage tanks are located, usually used for crude oil or other petroleum products.

Excavation or systems of excavations, including pits or tunnels, made underground for the extraction of metals, metallic ores, coal, salt, precious stones, building stone, clay, or another substance, or an open-air excavation for the extraction of such substances.
Underground excavations made for the extraction of diamonds.
Power plants in which the prime movers, usually turbines, connected to the generators are driven by steam to produce electricity.
Facilities that create and distribute power obtained from nuclear reactors, which initiate and control a self-sustaining series of nuclear fissions.
Area naval commands normally including a seaport, which integrates shore activities that provide local logistic services to the fleet.
Permanent ancient Roman military encampments laid out on a grid; may also designate later castles, forts, or fortified towers.

Temporary short-term habitation complexes, with permanent recreational facilities and often offering a structured program of activities. Temporary short-term habitation complexes, with permanent recreational facilities and often offering a structured program of activities.
Permanent or temporary camps where inhabitants engage in indoor and outdoor recreational activites without the restriction of clothing.
Resorts that operate seasonally during the summer months.

Typically oval courses or tracks on which races of any kind are held, including foot races, bicycle races, horse or dog races, and automobile races. Typically oval courses or tracks on which races of any kind are held, including foot races, bicycle races, horse or dog races, and automobile races.
Arenas designed or used for bicycle racing; modern velodromes comprise a steeply banked oval track having two 180-degree circular bends connected by two straight passages.
Downhill paths on a mountain or large hill that are maintained for snow skiing, snowboarding, or other mountain sports,  usually marked, patrolled, and graded according to difficulty.
Buildings and other facilities for friars, a community of men who focus on the sacred ministry of preaching, moving from place to place (in contrast to monks).
A type of religious complex that houses Buddhist monks and serves the greater community during festivals and other occasions.
Districts created for the administration of elections.
Divisions or areas designated for the management, utilization, and conservation of forests.

Areas of a city in which courtesans are available, separate from the rest of the city, sometimes walled. Primary examples are the pleasure quarters of the Ming dynasty in China and of the Edo era of Japan.
Areas or districts on or near the border between two countries or districts. An example is the border area district between England and Scotland.
Locations where a hostile meetings of opposing military forces in the course of a war have taken place.
Sites that are underwater and where archaeological excavations or exploration takes place. Included are shipwrecks, harbor and dock remains, fishing structures, and flooded land sites.

Piles of fused refuse or dross separated from metal in the process of smelting; also refers to piles of unwanted tailings or refuse that are the by-products of mining ore, coal, or other substances. Piles of fused refuse or dross separated from metal in the process of smelting; also refers to piles of unwanted tailings or refuse that are the by-products of mining ore, coal, or other substances.
Buttresses set back slightly from the corners of buildings.
In Indian architecture, a corner-buttress, angle-bay.

Foundations consisting of concrete, brick, or stone piers which deliver the load to a support stratum; the piers are usually more substantial than piles and are not clustered. Now commonly produced by excavating within a caisson.
Reinforced concrete piles manufactured in a casting plant or at the site prior to placement in their final positions.
Arches which have cusps or foliations worked on the intrados.
Pointed arches whose curves are struck from centers farther apart than the span of the arch.

Arches carried on piers, particularly the arches which divide nave from aisles in basilican churches. Arches carried on piers, particularly the arches which divide nave from aisles in basilican churches.
Projecting members, often molded, on which the ends of an arch rest.
Two-way slab systems, with the slab reinforced by ribs running in both directions, creating a waffle pattern.
Structures consisting of numerous similar, light, straight-line elements (usually in tension) which form a grid in the shape of a dome.
Ribbed vaults divided into eight vaulting cells.
Barrel vaults having their two springing points at different levels.
Vaults whose rib patterns suggest a star.
Compartments between the groins or ribs of a vault.
Wooden building frames that use diagonal bracing between full-height corner posts and the plates; generally found in construction with timbers heavy enough to be mortised.
Beams enclosed in finished millwork.

Rufu 乳栿, literally "infant beam" or "nursling beam" (Hanyu dacidian; Kroll 2015, 391), refers to cross beams that span two rafters, usually with one end located above the eaves puzuo 鋪作 and the other end inserted into an interior pillar. Liang Sicheng suggests that a rufu might also have both ends layered at the top of the puzuo (Liang 1983, 142; Chen 2008). Chen Mingda notes that a rufu should be located on the lowest level of the roof frame (Chen 2010, 196).
In Indian architecture, a joist, joist-end.
Columns resembling balusters, composed of a base, a potlike element, a bulbous shaft, and a capital.

Vertical architectural wall elements comprising wooden posts; used often, but not exclusively, in interior roof construction. For posts carried on corbels or other elements partway up the wall in open-timber roof trusses, use "pendant posts"; see also "crown posts."  For solid supports of masonry or another material that extend the full height of the wall, and that are designed to sustain vertical pressure, use "piers (supporting elements)."

Three or more closely spaced columns which form a distinct group. When two columns form a distinct group, use "coupled columns" or "doubled columns." For supports consisting of several columns engaged around a central core, especially in Medieval contexts, use "compound piers."
Capitals whose basic form is shaped like a bell or an inverted bell; may be enriched with carving.
The convex moldings supporting the abaci of Doric capitals and appearing between the volutes on Ionic capitals.
In Indian architecture, an image pedestal; pedestal (usual for an image or liṅga); pedestal for Śivaliṅga.
In Indian architecture, a roll-cornice awning.
Pendant ornaments in the form of truncated cones found on the underside of mutules and regulae of Doric entablatures.
Horizontal wood members between the principal timbers of half-timber construction for lateral support, especially when nogging is used.

Refers to a variety of symmetrical trusses: those in the form of three isosceles triangles with one triangle in the center with its base along the bottom chord and each of the outer two triangles having its base along the sloping side at an upper chord, or those in the form of triangles with diagonal members forming W-shapes, or those in the form of rectangles with few verticals in proportion to numerous diagonal web members of different lengths.
Designates light, wood, roof trusses, usually prefabricated and often used in residential construction.

In Indian architecture, a complex multi-spired superstructure-type; Anēkāṇḍaka śikhara Variation of spire in Northern Indian temples. One or two rows of half spires are on either side; miniature shikharas adorn the base and corners.
Structures having no more than three unknown reactions, so that the reactions can be found through simple application of the basic equations of statics.
Overhead surfaces of interior spaces, sometimes constructed to mask building systems or structural elements.

Describes a dance performed at powwows, originating in Anishinaabe/Ojibwe communities in the late 19th to early 20th centuries. The dance is now performed at powwow events across Native North America. Largely performed by young women wearing specialized regalia, the dance consists of bouncing footwork and careful turns.

Equipment consisting of a film transport mechanism, an optical projection and enlarging system, and a translucent screen. It was designed to handle roll film on reels and can be equipped with motorized drives or operated manually. Additionally, the readers include on/off and focus controls.

Describes a dance performed by Southeastern Native North American communities during the Green Corn Ceremony, including the Cherokees, Creeks, and Seminoles. The dance was performed frequently up until the late 19th century, with revivals occurring in the contemporary period.

Maho is a festival dedicated to the ancestral spirits after the harvest of millet. The name of this festival varies from region to region, and people have different concepts on the nature and time of occurrence of the festival. When the crops of millet are stored, the chief would preside over a council to decide when to hold the festival; the preparation of marinated meat, millet rice cake and millet wine is then scheduled according to the date. On the day of Maho, members of the tribe gather to the venue for worship to observe a rite led by the chief to thank the ancestral spirits and pray for harvest.
The fifth month of the French revolutionary calendar (introduced in 1793), beginning on 20, 21, or 22 January and ending on 18, 19, or 20 February (depending on the year).

Cultures and styles of the Kanakanavu people lived in Taiwan. The Kanakanavu people attained official recognition as distinct from the Tsou people in 2014. In the Qing dynasty the Han Chinese referred to the Kanakanavu people as kanavu-huan; and, the Japanese grouped them under the rubric of Tsou. The Kanakanavu people primarily live in Namaxia District, Kaohsiung City. The society is dominated by patriarchy, running the Mikong festival and the river festival as major celebrations.
In universities and colleges, large buildings set apart for the instruction or residence of students.
Tile, often glazed, designed to be used as a facing on a wall.
Tile is classified as weighing over more than 5 pounds per square foot.
Period of the fifth city on the site of ancient Troy, ca. 1950-1750 BCE.
Spindles found on cylinder phonographs, around which cylindrical records (usually made of wax) are made to revolve.
Having chracteristics, qualities, attributes, or actions associated with the female sex.
In Indian architecture, a wave-bracket.
In Indian architecture, a śākhā showing vidhyādharas.
In Indian architecture, (inverted) dish-shaped maṇḍi-type; a banner.
In Indian architecture, a type of pañjara.
In Indian architecture, a large flanking or lateral gable-nāsīs of a bhadraśālā-aedicule; lateral nāsī.
In Indian architecture, a square pillar-type; Brahmakānta.
In Indian architecture, a kūṭa with miniature Phāṁsanā (tiered pyramid); aedicula with tiered, pyramidal roof; tiered pyramidal aedicule.
In Indian architecture, a sixteen-sided column.

From the pre-Qin to the Ming and Qing dynasties, the form, structure, and function of ting have undergone significant changes. During the Eastern Zhou, ting referred to a three-zhang (roughly 30 ft) high military fort. In the Eastern Han, it functioned as a station house (yizhan 驛站). It could also be a government compound serving both military and registration purposes. In literature relating to the southern part of China in the Six Dynasties period, ting were built in high places and were often recognized as landmarks or gathering spots for literati and aristocrats. During the Tang dynasty, ting were built in fortified palaces (gongcheng 宮城 or "palace-cities"), were used as residences, and were enclosed by walls. They did not have to be high buildings or placed in elevated areas. After the Song dynasty, ting were often found in gardens and used for leisurely activities. In the Yingzao fashi, the ting is considered a non-essential structural form and tingxie, referring to this structural form in conjunction with its platform beneath, is an architectural type coined in the Yingzao fashi. Its form and location became even more flexible in Ming private gardens, though it was mainly a simple and open freestanding structure. Regardless of its transformation through time, the ting’s close connection to the appreciation of natural beauty persisted from the Wei, Jin, Northern and Southern Dynasties period through the Qing dynasty. The modern definition that ting is "a building with a roof but without enclosing walls" (He, et al. 2015, 210) is closest to the use of ting in Ming private gardens.
Major chapels dedicated to the Virgin Mary, usually located in the axis of a church at its east end.

A type of Roman Catholic chapel constructed in 16th century colonial Mexico, consisting of a chancel that opens to the atrium at ground level or raised to allow better visibility. Existing examples include the open chapels in Teposcolula and Calimaya. Recintos abiertos dedicados al culto, creadas en el siglo XVI, por frailes españoles en América, para dar solución al gran número de asistentes a las misas y a su vez mantener la modalidad de uso del espacio exterior sacro, habitual entre los indígenas.
The state or quality of having or being divided into five parts.
Inverted buckets or pieces of solid wood with loops attached and on which children can walk.
The variety of faceted shapes in which diamonds or other transparent gemstones can be cut.
Semi automatic hooks used to speed up work on looped rugs.

Information artifacts meant to be attached to clothing or personal items that have the form of a small flat surface with images displayed on the surface, and which are backed with a pin as a fastener.
General term for containers made to hold water consecrated by a priest or other religious figure. Examples include holy water fonts located outside of Christian churches.
Any long-handled ladles for serving food, of varied design.
Figurative dolls used for ornamental purposes, not for play.

Devices designed to assess the ignition resistance of textile fabrics against heat and flames. To evaluate the flammability of textile fabrics, these devices measure the fabrics' combustion rates according to time when exposed to a small flame directed at the textile samples from various angles.
Pronged instruments designed as tools to stoke or tend fires.
Flash devices for photography that are designed to be held in the hand or mounted on a bracket rather than on the camera itself.
Covered baskets, often with a hinged lid and two folding handles, intended primarily for carrying food and dining paraphernalia to a picnic.
Small barrels for storing and dispensing rum that have previously held rum, to enhance flavor.
Rolling pins with carved designs which are pressed to cookie dough to transfer their designs.
Devices that insert or pack food into packaging.
Tools consisting of an absorbent material, such as lamp wicking, fastened to a handle, used to apply oil or grease to baking pans.
Small trays used as a receptacle for teaspoons.

Funnels with stoppers used in candy making. The funnel is filled with warm, liquid candy, and the operator uses the stopper to dispense the appropriate amount of candy into a mold or onto a flat surface.
Large boxes with compartments for containing rations of food, tobacco, or beverages; used by troops on the march.
Greeting cards sent to a sweetheart on Saint Valentine's Day.
Lightweight shields made of vegetal matter used in many central Mexican cultures.
Devices for mixing together flour of different grades of quality to achieve a uniform grade ready for sale.
Machines that pass grain over a series of sieves in order to clean it. Used in the process of milling flour.
Head coverings of artificial hair knotted into a shaped net foundation.
Mechanical devices used to turn spits or hooks in order to evenly roast meat over a fire.
Devices that burn kerosene as fuel to create heat.

A traditional European heating system by which a stove is covered completely with glazed ceramic tiles. Tile stoves usually burn wood, and the radiant heat that occurs is absorbed by the tiles and is slowly and evenly diffused through the spaces in which they are installed.
Instruments used to estimate the purity of milk by comparing its color to a provided color chart that represents the colors of cream, normal milk, diluted milk, etc.
Annular objects specially made for throwing and catching in choreographed movements. They are created in varied sizes, colors, and materials.
Objects for hanging or resting kitchen pans in to store them when not in use.
Devices for cooling hot lard, consisting of a rotating metal cylinder cooled by water or brine. Hot lard is poured on the surface of the cylinder and scraped off once cool.
Pipes with a tapered end which are driven into sugar-maple trees in order to draw their sap.
Devices, either hand held or hydraulic, typically consisting of a bottle holder and a cork driver, that when a compressor is shifted, a cork is inserted in the bottle.
Receptacles that store hairpins when not in use.
Containers specifically crafted to store, transport, or protect musical instruments.

Enclosing containers of varied design that are used for storing thread for needlework.
Frameworks that incorporate rails, bars, or pegs, in or on which tools or materials of needlework may be placed or suspended.

Small ruler-like tools with graduated holes, often indicating both metric and imperial sizes, designed to identify the size of knitting needles and crochet hooks. These tools are especially useful for identifying the size of double-pointed needles, interchangeable needles, vintage needles, or other types of needles that are not labled for size.  Unmarked needles are inserted into the gauge's various holes until the most similarly sized gauge hole is found and the needle's measurements are determined.
Very thin, lint-free, fibrous material designed specifically for cleaning the delicate surface of lenses.
Devices used to punch patterned holes in printing tape representing information or text; that information is then printed onto the desired surface.

Tools for trimming or cutting back plants in gardening, flower arranging, and tree cultivation. There are various blade designs, which may incorporate two sharpened blades or one blade that meets a flat surface.

Corporal punishment whips or scourges consisting of narrow straps or ropes, often tied at the end with buttons, lead pellets, or iron nails. For similar devices having nine straps, use "cat-o'-nine-tails."

Hand-held electric devices, comprised of a water tank, a steam generator, a water pump, and an open-faced steam plate or pan, used to loosen wallpaper from a surface to ease the wallpaper removal process. Once steam is produced in the water tank, it passes through a narrow bore tube to the plate which is then applied directly to the wallpaper; as the steam from the device comes into contact with the wall, it saturates and begins dissolving the paper for stripping.
Flat containers, usually baskets, used in agriculture and ritual to separate grains from other plant material such as chaff.

Devices used to transfer filling yarn from spools and cones to light, tapered tubes (quills or bobbins) made of wood, cardboard, fiber, or metal for use in weaving cloth. These devices comprise a large wheel with a peg or handle on one of the spokes to facilitate rapid manual turning.
Cleaners, either in liquid or brush form, used to remove dust from phonograph records.

Trumpets, usually historic, that were used to amplify the voice, particularly aboard ships during the 19th century. They were used specifically for communication between ships, or to issue orders to the crew.
Hand-held implements used for carrying hot embers, usually comprised of a handle attached to a lidded dish, box, or other type of vessel made of brass or other metal.
Slotted planks, usually used upright and often fitted to a base used with a bat to remove broken straw while scutching flax by hand.
Groups of mechanized devices, which use a series of rollers to mix various grades of cotton fibers together into a uniform blend.
Narrow ornamented band, tape, lace or braid, often with metal thread, and often with both edges scalloped, used as trimming or binding on costume and textile furnishings.
Describes the geographic location where a group or corporate body was dissolved.
Statement or account that describes the buyer in an acquisition event, listing characteristic features, or significant details.
Figures depicted in a clearly seated position, often with the chair or other seating furniture visible; may depict the full figure seated, or from the lap upwards.

Qualifier used for attributions of works by an unknown creator working for a named manufactory or factory, which is typically larger than a studio or workshop, and typically produces porcelain, tapestries, furniture, and occasionally fine art.
Masonry construction using several wythes (layers) of brick, and having header bricks to bind them them together. Distinct from more modern methods that use "brick veneer."
Span of time including years of the earliest and latest dated works in the group (e.g., for a folder of drawings, 1911-1951 (inclusive dates)). .
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 7999 to 7000 (or 8000 to 7001) Before Common Era.
General term for the set of lunisolar calendars used primarily in mainland southeast Asia; based on an older version of the Hindu calendar.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 304-329; a Southern Xiongnu state.

Numeric, alphanumeric, or other identifying codes assigned when an art object, book, or other item is described or listed in a catalog, usually a published catalog. An example is an exhibition catalog. The numbers are typically not marked on the object itself. For numbers given to objects when they are acquired by a repository, prefer "accession numbers."
Names or titles formed by joining two or more other names or titles. Names or titles may be joined with a hyphen, conjunction, preposition, or parentheses.
