Titles of courtesy, professional titles, military rank, adjectives, or other words used before a personal name. Examples are words to indicate gender, marital status, social position, or included for another purpose, such as the following words and abbreviations: Mr., Mrs., Miss, Ms., Dr., Sir, and Rev.
Words or verbal units chosen to indicate or represent the content of a larger document, text, record, etc., in an index, catalog, or database. Keywords may be used in a search expression.
Refers to the architectural order characterized by unfluted columns, torus bases, unadorned cushion capitals, and plain friezes.
A brilliant feather ornament.
Works in public space comprising knitted or crocheted adornments, usually installed without institutional oversight.
The fifth month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendar, containing 31 days and falling between April and June. It was named after Maia, a Roman fertility goddess.

The day following Wednesday and preceding Friday, traditionally regarded as the fifth day of the week, but now frequently considered as the fourth. In English and other languages, named for Thor, the Norse god of thunder. In Romance langauges, named for the Roman Jupiter’s-day.
Refers to illnesses and ailments that seem to be induced in occupants of a building by conditions inside the building.

General non-taxonomic and historical term referring to the virus thought to cause AIDS. Since 1991, HIV was no longer considered an official species name; instead, two species were designated HIV-1 and HIV-2. The geographical, biological, and chronological origins of the viruses have been debated since the discovery of AIDS as an emerging disease in 1981.
Cookstoves fueled by kerosene.
In language, the non-finite parts of a verb, used either in compound verb forms with an auxiliary verb expressing tense and voice, or as an adjective.
Refers to Spanish spoken in Colombia.
Currency of the Austro-Hungarian Empire between 1892 and 1919, when it was succeeded by the Austrian Krone.

Titles that are shortened versions of another title, designed for convenience to identify the work in certain brief displays, such as for captions, wall labels, in an entry in Web navigation displays, or in text. In book cataloging, called the short title.
Unique and persistent identifiers for digital objects, compliant with the Handle System developed by the Corporation for National Research Initiatives.
Theory of conservation technique with emphasis on practical application; for theory of ethics and conservation science, see conservation philosophy.
Acts of interment, usually but not necessarily ceremonial, including preparation of the corpse and its placement in the grave, and all accompanying ritual practices, if any.

A stick, used with a frame loom, to which every other thread of the warp is attached. The heddle rod can either be lifted away from the frame loom to open the shed, or it holds one shed still while a shed stick is moved to create the shed.
People who are expert in or students of the history, art, culture, etc. of the Middle East.
Musical compositions for instruments, usually for the pianoforte, in several movements, commonly three or four movements.

Operas comprising semi-dramatic performance in which song and dialogue alternate, popular in Germany in the latter part of the 18th century. Usually comic in tone. The earliest singspiels were light plays with dialogue interspersed with popular songs; rose to great popularity in the late 18th century.

Performing art focusing on sleight of hand or tricks involving various types of illusion for purposes of entertainment. For the occult science that claims to use charms, spells, and supernatural power, use "magic (occult science)." The performing art may make superficial reference to the occult science in its performances.
Method of acquiring property by request from the creator or producer.
Lending items from a collection to outside users and keeping records of such loans.
The status or condition of a thing or site for which the location is unknown or which no longer exists.
The rearing of silk worms for the purpose of producing silk fibers.
Meaning "directed," indicates the master in charge of the artistic endeavor, not necessarily the hands-on creator.

Sacred or honorific gateways made of wood or stone, comprised of two uprights with one and three crosspieces, or arched, found in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain architecture. Gateway; archiform gateway-pattern; auspicious garland-like motif; decorative arch-way/gateway (early Indian); decorative auspicious arch.

Order of flowering plant containing 5 families with more than 1,100 genera and nearly 17,000 species. Many are ornamental plants or producers of drugs. Members are characterized in part by leaves that are opposite or whorled (two or more per node), with simple blades. The leaves are usually accompanied by stipules (small leaflike appendages at the base of the leaves).

Multiplayer games where each player has a form or card with numbers. The numbers can be crossed out or indicated when the number drawn by the game master is on this form. There are also variants with colors and figures instead of numbers.
General term for accessories and instruments used for dental procedures.
Status of items that are removed from bidding prior to the auction or at the auction when there is a failure to reach sufficient bidding.
Weapons designed to cause combustion at a specific target or destination, including those composed of generally noncombustible materials.

Telescopes that use multiple glass lenses which refract light; the objective lenses are the first lenses through which light passes, and the eyepiece lenses are located behind the focal plane, allowing for viewing of the magnified images. Today, refracting telescopes are used for viewing objects in the solar system that are closer to Earth.
Implements used to scrape the small hairs off hog hides which removes some bacteria and gets the hide ready for the next step in meat processing.
Machines, equipped with a guilotine-like blade or blades, used to trim the edges of books.
Devices for cooking waffles that consist of two metal parts hinged together so as to shut upon each other and impress square, round, or oval surface projections on the waffle in baking.

Type of food packaging made from a laminate or flexible plastic and metal foils, that allows for the sterilization of a wide variety of food and drink by means of aseptic processing. It is used as alternative to traditional industrial canning methods.
Sacks, usually made of canvas or other fabric, used to carry newspapers when being delivered or sold. Sometimes the sides are emblazoned with a particular newspaper's title.
Instruments for measuring the blanching power of chloride of lime and potash.
Boards made of wood or other materials affixed between buttons and the fabric they are attached to protect the material.

One-piece, skin-tight combination garments with short or long legs and with or without sleeves that leave the wearer's legs either fully or partially exposed. Worn, for example, by acrobats and dancers. For heavy, opaque pantyhose, use "tights (opaque stockings)." Distinguished from "cat suits", which are designed for everyday wear.
Drafting and drawing instruments for copying or tracing the contour of solid objects, such as sculpture profiles and moldings; invented in 1841 by Robert Willis, Cambridge University.
Protective outer garments worn by patients at a hospital, either in preparation for surgery or as a loose general purpose garment worn usually during an extended stay, to facilitate examinations.
Scissors with toothed blades used to cut the top off of an egg cooked in its shell.
Thermometers designed to read temperatures within an oven.
Tools used for stirring curds in the process of cheese-making, consisting of a toothed, rake-like bar and a handle.
Devices that receive electronic data packets and routes them to the appropriate computer systems or networks.
Devices that encode data; in early computing, refers to devices that have input lines (one of which carries signals), and output lines (any of which may carry signals).
Devices that read information that has been recorded by sequences of perforations or magnetized areas on computer tape.
A preparation of powdered plant material, most often, but not always tobacco, for inhaling through the nostrils, or sometimes taken orally.
The process of the cessation of life, while still living.
The action of asking earnestly; specifically for alms, performed by indigent people or mendicants.
Emotional and psychological state generated from the resentment and awareness of an advantage enjoyed by another joined with the desire to possess the same advantage.
The state of desiring a person, thing, or event.
General term for the Islamic cultures of Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, and Mauritania.
Oriental Orthodox Christian religion based in the Indian state of Kerala, by tradition tracing its origins to St. Thomas the Apostle in the first century.

Languages that have developed from the mixing of two or more parent languages, where the combined new language has become the first language of a community. Creole languages often arise as the result of contact between the language of a dominant group (historically often a European colonizer) and that (or those) of a subordinate group (often the colonized people, or an enslaved population). For languages developed from two or more languages, but where grammar and vocabulary is simplified and the language used only in temporary contact situations, prefer "pidgins (language, general)."
In sculpture or architectural figures, the mudra or posture of administering a slap.
Lesions on the skin such as pustules or blisters. It is a term that is often translated as smallpox because it was a term used by Nahuatl writers to describe certain epidemic diseases.
Artists in any medium whose primary subjects are battles and war.
A sister-in-law is the sister of one's spouse, or the wife of one's sibling.
A stepsister is a female child of a step-parent who has married one's parent after thier natural parent's death or divorce.
Artists who specialize in assemblages, which are three-dimensional works of art created by combining found objects and other elements.

Describes participants at The Bauhaus, founded in 1919 in the city of Weimar by German architect Walter Gropius (1883–1969). The term represents a kind of Bauhaus citizenship inclusive of faculty and students and reflects the idea of egalitarianism implicit in the institution. The term is not generally extended to those associated with the New Bauhaus in Chicago, with the exception of those associated with the original Bauhaus in Weimar, and later Dessau.
Cambodian silk textile hangings in temples. These temple hangings are pictorial and are placed above and behind images of the Buddha.
Decorated ceramic ware that, rather than being hand-painted, has a design that has been transferred to the ceramic item from a printed design on paper, gelatinous bat, or another substance.
Creeks or other channels in a coastal wetland that are subject to bi-directional tidal currents.
Physical features that may be considered part of another larger feature.
Capital towns or cities for administrative provinces.

A guide term is a record represented by a term or phrase that is created as a hierarchical level to provide order and structure to thesauri by grouping narrower terms according to a given logic. Guide terms are not used for indexing and are often enclosed in angled brackets or otherwise distinguished from other terms in displays (for example, <photographs by form>).

Multiple-word terms or names that are arranged in the form used in back-of-book indexing or other similar situations. Examples are Wren, Christopher and buttresses, flying. Distinguished from natural order terms or names.
Slips of paper or cardboard serving as evidence that the holder has paid a fare or admission or is entitled to some service.

Works that are the main focus or most important in a complex work or project; used to distinguish primary works from auxiliary or accessory works; the concept may apply to a wide variety of disciplines. In cataloging, the work is typically assumed to be a primary work, requiring clarification only when there is also an ancillary work. An example would be an office building, which is a  primary architectural work having as an ancillary work the heating system. The concept may also refer to the status of separate, independent works, which may be grander or more important than other separate, independent "secondary works."
Sigillata from the area of the Black Sea.

Early Minoan pottery named for a site near Phaistos, characterized by extensive use of painted lines instead of the earlier scored or burnished patterns and is known in two iterations. In the earlier phase, design typically was made of parallel or crosshatched painted red lines that swept around the curvature of buff clay vessels. In the later phase, painted red decoration was more formally designed, did not relate as much to the round form of the vessel, and typically was composed of crosshatched triangles or other simple geometric designs applied to the upper shoulder of jugs and jars, and to the interior or exterior of bowls and cups.
Handmade powdered glass beads made in the Mauritanian town of Kiffa, decorated with molten colored glass in various colors.
Features that were formerly above water but are now underwater.

Tracts of land with trees, often acting as boundaries or barriers, but otherwise minimally utilized; smaller and less wild than forests. For landscapes dominated by trees and having various uses, prefer "woodlands."
Temperate forests of primarily coniferous evergreen trees, located in areas having mild winters and high annual precipitation of greater than 200 cm.

Biomes surrounding marine environments surrounding oceans, coral reefs, and estuaries. Marine algae supply much of the world's oxygen supply and take in a huge amount of atmospheric carbon dioxide; the evaporation of the seawater provides rainwater for the land.

Cavity resonators designed such that a nozzle with an annular slit is located at the exit of the nozzle near a cavity a short distance away. Air blown through the slit passes over a circular knife edge at the near end of the cavity. A micrometer is used to adjust the depth of the cavity and another adjusts the distance between the slit and knife edge. The device makes it possible to generate ultrasound in air over a wide range of frequencies. Named for Sir Francis Galton who invented it in the mid 1800s to test human and animal hearing.

Designations that represent significant aspects of an administrative place or physical geographic place, including its role, function, political anatomy, size, or physical characteristics; may include references to culture.

Baltic and Slavic languages are here groped into a single branch due to the exclusively shared features; developed in the early Common Era with Baltic and Slavic tribes occupying a large area of eastern Europe, including much of present-day Poland and the states of Belarus, Ukraine, and westernmost Russia. The earliest Slavic texts, written in a dialect called Old Church Slavonic, date from the 9th century CE; the oldest substantial material in Baltic dates to the end of the 14th century.
Latin as used since the late 14th century by authors emulating classical rather than medieval models from the beginning of Italian Humanism.
Variety of the Portuguese language used primarily in the nation of Guinea-Bissau.
Variety of Spanish spoken in the Philippines; it includes characteristics of European Spanish and Latin American Spanish.
Swellings on a surface, often bubble-shaped, frequently caused by nonadherence or by separation of an applied substance.
Prints made from Fujifilms Pictrography Photo Printers.
Language family comprising two closely related Papuan languages.

Writing systems that use logograms, which are written or pictorial symbols intended to represent a whole word. Writing systems that make use of logograms include Chinese, Egyptian hieroglyphic writing, and early cuneiform writing systems. No known writing system is totally logographic; all known systems have both logograms and symbols representing particular sounds or syllables.

Japanese ritual dances with music, the Japanese word meaning 'field entertainments,' in reference to the agricultural folk religion of medieval Japan (ca. 11th-17th centuries). Dengaku was performed in the rice fields either at New Year's or during the planting season in early summer. The dance and music were meant to entertain the kami (Shinto gods) in the hopes of plentiful crops and to relieve the boredom of the workers. In the 14th century some forms of dengaku were taken to the cities and performed as court entertainment; through this exposure dengaku came to influence some of the classical performing arts such as the Nō drama.
Dairy product created from cream, flavorings, and sugar, which is stirred slowly while freezing to prevent large ice crystals from forming, resulting in a smoothly textured semi-solid.

A clear liquor distilled from malted grain mash and flavored with juniper berries. This term is used to designate the spirit manufactured in the Netherlands and Belgium as distinct from the British and American versions of this, called 'gin.' Only liquors produced in the countries of Belgium, the Netherlands, and some districts in France and Germany may carry the name 'jenever', 'genièvre' or 'genever.'
Buildings that house glass manufactories.

General term for administrative divisions, usually of a nation, that represent the fourth highest unit or level under the nation itself, typically under the third level subdivision. Examples could be townships in the United States, which are smaller than counties, the third level subdivisions.

The final period of the Paleozoic Era. The Permian Period began 298.9 million years ago and ended 252.2 million years ago, following the Carboniferous and preceding the Triassic. Glaciation was widespread in the early Permian, but the climate warmed throughout the period resulting in hot and dry conditions that caused a crisis in marine and terrestrial life.
Transliteration of varieties of Greek used in Eastern and early Western Christianity; often but not always Koine Greek.
Leatherworking tools for rounding off the sharp edges of thick leathers.
General term for the creation and conceptual arrangements of music into works to be performed.
Frames with darkslides used to hold flexible photosensitized sheet film.

Festival celebrated in China and other Asian countries, and elsewhere by people of Asian descent; it marks the last day of the lunar New Year celebration, on the first full moon night of the 15th day of the first lunar month. The festival has its origin in the religious rituals of the imperial palace, dating to the Han Dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE). In time, the festival merged with other folk customs, such as lighting candles to honor Buddha or to pray for blessings on the holy birthday of Tian Guan. Customs observed in this festival symbolize family reunion and a blissful life.
Widespread indigenous religious movement among North American Indians, entailing the use of peyote, which produces hallucinogenic effects.
In Japanese printing, format having dimensions ca. 69/75 x 12/13 cm.

Visual works that are incorporated into another work. The original work may be incorporated in whole, or in part. Examples are older buildings that have been incorporated into a larger, newer building.
That which is placed in position number five of a sequence.
State or condition of existing or moving in the water of a sea or ocean.
Genus containing about 90 species of ornamental and timber evergreen conifers in the family Pinaceae.
Genus containing 2 species of extinct deer, the Giant Deer (Megaloceros giganteus) and the Sardinian dwarf deer (Megaloceros cazioti).
Genus containing several species of brocket.

Genus containing around 30 species of medium sized trees native to coastal and mildly temperate regions of the Old World, from western Europe, north Africa, and Asia. It is one of the most important fruit trees of the world and is cultivated in all temperate-zone countries of both hemispheres. Valued for fleshy edible fruit (a pome), typically having a broad base and tapering or constricted towards the stalk, and having sweet taste, soft texture, and distinguished by the presence of hard cells in the flesh, the so-called grit, or stone cells. Pear trees are relatively long-lived (50 to 75 years), may reach considerable size unless carefully trained and pruned, and are valued for timber.

Family containing 15 genera of trees and shrubs distributed primarily throughout temperate regions, having watery sap and leaves that alternate along the stem. The leaves usually have toothed edges and often are lopsided at the base. The flowers lack petals. Male and female flowers are borne together or apart on the same plant. The fruit, a samara, may be winged, fleshy, or nutlike. In earlier classifications, the family was placed in the former order Urticales.
Genus containing around 25 species of tall, reedlike Central and South American and New Zealand grasses.

Detached clouds in the form of white, delicate filaments, mostly white patches or narrow bands. They may have a fibrous (hair-like) and/or silky sheen appearance. Cirrus clouds are always composed of ice crystals, and their transparent character depends upon the degree of separation of the crystals.
Beings that are partly of divine nature, such as when having resulted from the intercourse of a deity and a mortal, when a human is raised to divine rank, or referencing a minor or inferior deity.
Genus containing around 70 species of annual and perennial flowering plants native to South America.

The figwort family of flowering plants, the order Lamiales, containing species with worldwide distribution. Notable for many ornamental garden plants, such as butterfly bush (Buddleja), Diascia, Nemesia, and many others. Some, such as the mullein (Verbascum), are troublesome weeds.

Species of Eurasian tree around 30 m (100 feet) in height and having a grayish-white trunk and wavy-margined, wedge-shaped leaves up to 15 cm (6 inches) in length. It is sometimes classified as a subspecies of Fagus sylvatica, to which it is closely related.
Large genus of flowering plants containing over 400 species.
Genus containing around 200 species of evergreen trees and shrubs distributed primarily in tropical and subtropical regions of Central America, South America, the West Indies, and Africa.
Genus contains a single species: Spathodea campanulata, of the evergreen family Bignoniaceae.
Genus of flower plants.

Species of fast growing, short-lived, ornamental, shade, and timber tree native to northern and central North America, typically around 18 meters (60 feet) in height, with a brown bark that whitens over time and peels into paper-thin layers marked by narrow horizontal pores or lenticels. On the copper-colored inner bark, the pores are bright orange. Short, pendulous branches and numerous flexible twigs create a lacy silhouette in winter. The close-grained, almost white wood is used for turned articles, flooring, furniture, woodenware, pulp, and fuel. North American Indians used the thin, water-impervious bark for roofing, canoes, and writing material (thus the name "paper birch"). It is a pioneer species after fire. The sap is boiled down to produce birch syrup. The tree is known in several varieties.

Genus containing around 50 species of shrubs native to most subtropical areas of the world, long cultivated for fiber and oil. Many varieties of cotton have been developed by selective breeding and hybridisation of various species. Cotton cloth was made as early as 5000 BCE in India; by 3000 BCE, cotton fabrics were being woven in Egypt, China, and Peru. Cultivation of cotton became widespread in Europe in the Middle Ages.
Species of medium-sized horse chestnut native to the Ohio Valley and Appalachian Mountains of the Eastern United States.

Family family of woody shrubs and trees (and a few herbaceous perennials) and consisting of around 160 genera and 1,700 species distributed throughout the world, especially in warm temperate and tropical regions; the largest numbers are found in Africa and Australia, often in semiarid woodlands. Many members are valuable as sources of edible fruit and as ornamentals.

Species of small cherry tree native to much of Europe and southwest Asia, closely related to the wild cherry (P. avium) but having a fruit that is more acidic. Cultivated sour cherries were apparently selected from wild specimens from around the Caspian and Black Seas; they were popular in Persia and known to the Greeks by the 4th century BCE. The Romans introduced them into Britain by the 1st century CE. In Britain, their cultivation was popular in the time of Henry VIII; by 1640 over 20 named cultivars were recorded. English colonists to Massachusetts brought the sour cherry to America.
Species of ebony tree native to India and the Andaman Islands, valued for heavy, durable wood.
Family containing around 10 genera and around 160 species of trees and shrubs, found in the Northern Hemisphere in warm temperate and subtropical regions.

Species of elm native to the northeastern United States, similar to American elm in general appearance, but more closely related to the European wych elm, which has a very similar flower structure. It has a gluelike substance in the inner bark, which was formerly steeped in water as a remedy for throat ailments, powdered for use in poultices, and chewed as a thirst-quencher.
Species of forest tree native to New South Wales, Victoria, and Queensland, Australia. It is used as a timber tree and for its nectar in honey production.
Family of flowering plants containing around 50 genera and 900 species, varying according to different classifications.
Species of shrub or small tree native to eastern North America, but very uncommon north of the Ohio River; designated as threatened. Found in dry upland habitats.
Genus of flowering trees having pinnate or bipinnate leaves and axillary panicles of white or purple flowers.

A family of flowering plants comprising about 2000 species in the eudicot order of Malpighiales. Found in the tropical to warm temperate regions, many in the south temperate zone, and a few ranging as far north as the middle of the north temperate zone.

Species of  large tree native to the eastern United States and southeast Canada, growing up 27 meters tall and living to 200 years. Mature trees are recognized by their rough shinglelike bark; young trees have smooth bark.
Genus containing over 525 species of tropical evergreen trees and shrubs.

Species of small, thorny tree or spreading bush producing an edible fruit; the acidic fruit that is botanically a many-seeded pale yellow oblong berry. Its young leaves have a decidedly reddish tint; later they turn green. In some varieties, the young branches of the lemon are angular; some have sharp thorns at the axils of the leaves. The large flowers have a sweet odor. Reddish-tinted in the bud, the petals are white above and reddish purple below.
Genus containing around 160 species of flowering plant native to tropical North and South America, but cultivated in West Africa and elsewhere for their edible starchy tubers.

Species of deciduous shrub or small tree native to Japan, North Korea, South Korea, China, Mongolia, and southeast Russia; reaching 10 meters in height and typically an understory plant in shady woodlands. The tree may have multiple trunks joining close to the ground. Many different cultivars of this maple have been developed; even in the wild, seedlings from the same parent display remarkable variation in color and shape of leaves.

Species of evergreen oak native to the eastern Mediterranean and southwest Asia. It was historically important as the food plant of the Kermes scale insect, from which a red dye called crimson was obtained.
Family consisting of one or two genera containing around 15 perennial species native to wet habitats. The taxonomy under this family is under debate and is likely to change.

Portions of a plant consisting of the seed and its envelope, especially the latter when it is of a juicy, pulpy nature. In its strict botanical sense, the fleshy or dry ripened ovary of a plant, enclosing the seed or seeds, such as apricots, bananas, and grapes, as well as bean pods, corn grains, tomatoes, cucumbers, and (in their shells) acorns and almonds, are all technically fruits. Popularly, however, the term is restricted to the ripened ovaries that are sweet and either succulent or pulpy. The cultivation and processing of fruits are major industries worldwide.
Mass deacidication process using magnesium titanium alkoxid developed by the Battelle Institute, Switzerland.

Species of cottonwood poplar native to much of North America; it is known in three subspecies. It is one of the largest North American hardwood trees, growing to nearly 30 meters (100 feet) in height. It has thick glossy leaves and bark that is silver-white and smooth, becoming darker and deeply fissured on older trees. Due to the flat stem of the leaf, the leaf has the tendency to shake from even the slightest breeze. This is one of the identifying characteristics.

Genus containing around 250 species of shrubs and small trees, native to temperate and subtropical zones. All sumacs have a milky or resinous sap, which in a few species can cause a contact dermatitis. The sap is used for tannins, dyes, medicines, the leaves for smoking, the fruits for beverages and ground as spice in Middle Eastern cuisine, and the trees as ornamentals, soil binders, and cover plants valued for brilliant Fall color.
Species of hardwood tree found only in Brazil, from Bahia to Rio de Janiero. Threatened by habitat loss.
Species of willow native to northern and western North America, occurring in wetland habitats. Known in at least three subspecies.

Genus of rattan palms native mainly to the tropics and subtropics of southeastern Asia. The stems are harvest for their cores, which is used for canes and furniture. The fruits of certain species produce a red resin that is one source for "dragon's blood," used for medicine and varnish. The seeds of some species are harvested for the production of Buddhist prayer beads.

Genus containing 120 to 300 species (depending upon the classification) of annual or perennial aquatic, grasslike species growing in ponds, marshes, and lakes. They bear solitary or small clustered spikes. Their stems are often used to weave strong mats, baskets, and chair seats. Bulrushes may act as a filter, absorbing poisonous metals and toxic microorganisms, thus helping to reduce water pollution. The taxonomy of the genus is complex and currently under review, which will likely result in some species being moved to other genera. In English translations of the Bible, the term "bulrush" is mistakenly used to refer to the papyrus plant, Cyperus papyrus. In Britain, the term "bulrush" is sometimes used to refer to species of genus Typha.
A registered trademark for a paper produced by the ARJOMARI company that comprised competing paper mills, ARches, JOhannot, MArais and RIves, merged; it existed 1956-1991.
Genus of flowering plant native to Asia and Europe, but cultivated elsewhere.

Family containing 16 genera and around 635 species of herbs and shrubs, native primarily to temperate and subtropical regions. Members typically have 6-segmented flowers and 3-chambered capsular fruits, occasionally berries. The leaves usually have parallel veins and are clustered at the base of the plant but may alternate along the stem or be arranged in whorls. Most species have an underground storage structure, such as a bulb.

Diverse order containing 33 families, 692 genera, and around 11,000 species of trees, shrubs, lianas, mangroves, stem or leaf succulents, annuals, and even insectivores. Nearly half of the families are very small, with less than a dozen species each. Many members of the order are ecologically specialized to tolerate salty or desertlike environments. Some have distinctive physiological adaptations to cope with these habitats, including carnivorous digestion.

Mythical creatures represented in ancient Middle Eastern art as a lion or bull with eagles' wings and a human face. Regarded in traditional Christian angelology as an angel of the second highest order of the ninefold celestial hierarchy.
Refers to a Belgian variation of Art Nouveau, so named for the "coup de fouet" or whiplash motif common to the style.

Architectural ornaments, formed of two or more interwoven bands which wind around a series of central points, often left blank. This type of decorative frieze is characteristic of Greek and Roman architecture and borders of Roman mosaics.
Evil, malignant beings of superhuman nature.
Preservatives with names given by the company responsible for their production and sale to provide distinction and recognition between similar products.
Meals that are less substantial and less ceremonious than dinner, taken usually in the early afternoon; also a light meal at any time of the day.
Measures for land used in viceregal America, divided into four parts; corresponds to the modern "manzana."
Periods of existence or duration; may apply to animate or inanimate things.
Old measurements of length equal to 6 feet or about 1.83 meter. Specifically used to measure the depth of water. Also used as measurements of volume equivalent to 6 cubic feet.
Measures of capacity for liquids and grain or other dry substances consisting of small particles, in Britain equal to 277 1/4 cubic inches and in the United States 231 cubic inches.
Units of weight equal to 1/16 of a pound avoirdupois (approximately 28 grams). Originally equaled 1/12 of a pound in troy and apothecaries' measure, equal to 480 grains (approx. 31.1 grams).
Pointed shortly-trimmed beards named for the Flemish painter Van Dyck.
One of a group of organic compounds containing carbon-silicon bonds.
Structures designed for the isolation of menstuating women from the rest of the social group.
Models that illustrate a design of a built work, ship, or other object in section, as if the work were cut transversely.
An archaeological culture of the 2nd and 5th centuries CE in a wide area of Eastern Europe, deemed to be multiethnic mix of Sarmatian, Slavic, Gothic, and Geto-Dacian populations.
Shell of any of numerous marine gastropod mollusks of a family widely distributed in warm seas; beautifully polished, often brightly colored, and much used for ornament or as money.
Order of ray-finned fish including the cod and its allies.

General term referring to members of hundreds of  species of small, conical-billed, seed-eating songbirds belonging to several families in the order Passeriformes, including true finches of the Fringillidae family, as well as waxbills, buntings, American sparrows, and Darwin's finches of the Galapagos islands, from the Emberizidae, Estrildidae, Carduelidae, and Ploceidae families. Although not closely related, finches are very similar-looking and typically have patches of bright color.
General term for several genera of mid-sized birds in the Galliformes order, in the families Phasianidae and Odontophoridae.
General term referring to members of  27 living species in two families of large herbivorous rodents having body and tail covered with sharp defensive spines composed of modified hair.
Division of primate taxonomy containing 2 infraorders of 9 living families containing 41 living genera; 8 fossil families contain about 50 fossil genera; included are tarsiers, monkeys and apes.
Family containing two living genera of large mammals, with short, stumpy legs, and barrel-shaped bodies and several extinct genera.

Family containing 11 species in four genera including skunks and stink badgers, having moderately elongated bodies with reasonably short well-muscled legs, long front claws for digging, a striped coat, and extremely well-developed anal scent glands used to produce noxious odors to deter threats.

Subspecies of lion that became regionally extinct in the 20th century; some individuals of this subspecies have been proven through DNA analysis to survive in zoos. Distinguished, among other characteristics, by the males' thick, extensive, dark mane.
Extinct family containing two recently extinct genera and three species from Madagascar, all extinct within the past 2,000 years. Developed in the Holocene.
Family containing four genera with 29 or more living South American species, plus three fossil species in two genera dating from the Middle Miocene to Holocene.

Genus of ruminant, hollow-horned mammals containing seven to nine species, including the wild goat, ibexes, the markhor, and the subspecies of domestic goat. The classification of goats is in flux based on new DNA research, and in some older classifications includes Ovis (sheep) and Ammotragus (Barbary Sheep), which are separate genera in other classifications. The Rocky Mountain goat is a separate genus, Oreamnos.

Members of an order including 1,800 species of insects that are characterized by large membranous hindwings that lie hidden under short, leathery forewings. The name earwig is derived from the Anglo-Saxon word meaning "ear creature," probably because of a widespread ancient superstition that earwigs penetrated the head by crawling into the ears of sleeping people.
Members of a particular superfamily including clothes moths, bagworms and relatives.

Family containing up to 700 species in four genera of beetles, including the larder beetle, hide or leather beetle, carpet beetle, and khapra beetle, among others. The wormlike larvae of members of this family are the only beetle larvae that are covered with hair.

Extinct order of fossil marine reptiles characterized by a broad, flattened body, often a small head often on long flexible neck, a short tail, and four large, paddle-like limbs, dating to the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.

The culture of any group of the Hominidae family, generally referring to cultures of the hominid relatives of humans. To distinguish the cultures of humans, particularly very early cultures that overlap with other hominid cultures, use "human (culture)."
Genus containing slim, small to medium-sized species of birds in the dove family.
Range of greenish gray or bluish gray colors, resembling the color of ashes, which are the earthy or mineral residue that remains after combustible substances have been thoroughly burned.
A broad range of brownish, yellowish, or reddish colors resembling the colors of pigments called "earth color," which contain iron oxide and other substances.
Variable green color resembling the color of pigment ground from the chrysocolla mineral.
Variable reddish orange colors resembling the color of Indian red pigment, which is a synthetically produced brick red color iron oxide.
Variable color name referring to bright bluish reds similar to those created by rhodamine dyes.
A range of purplish colors resembling the purple color of lithographic ink.
Variable red colors resembling the color of some cherries, fruit of numerous trees and shrubs of the genus Prunus.
A range of yellow colors resembling the color of aureolin pigment, made of potassium cobaltinitrite.
Variable dark or blackish color resembling the color of the hardwood, ebony.

Standard comprising descriptions and names of 267 color blocks devised by the Inter-Society Color Council (ISCC) and the the United States Department of Commerce's National Bureau of Standards (NBS) (now called the National Institute of Standards and Technology).
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of whitish colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of red and grayish colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of purple colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellowish green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellowish brownish green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of brown colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of orange colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink and gray colors.
Data included in fields reserved for spans of time. These may be formatted in various ways.

Software used to create computer graphics, or edit and otherwise manipulate existing graphics; examples include raster graphics software, which is used to edit two-dimensional images; vector graphics software, which is used as a drawing tool to create graphic layouts; and 3-d graphics software which creates simulations based on given viewpoints.
Physical or virtual repositories comprising accumulated groups of objects or materials having a focal characteristic and that have been brought together by an individual or organization.
Libraries containing collections specifically geared towards the needs of children.
Museums that are administered by the county, an administrative subdivision in the U.S., the U.K., and other nations.

Educational institutions in Britain or in a system based on or similar to Britain's, where students in the last two years of secondary school study for entry into advanced schools, including preparation for qualifying exams such as A-levels, GCSEs, etc.
Ship-board official bodies empowered to punish minor infringements or more serious cases of naval law, and to make important decisions regarding the ship's activities.
Studios in which one or more master designers create designs, supervise assistants, and instruct pupils.

Chinese calligraphic script developed by the Northern Song dynasty emperor Huizong (1082-1135). Slender Gold script is characterized by taut, angular lines which expand or contract depending on their place in a stroke. Highly controlled, it projects an air of studied elegance.

Trademarked commercial name for a synthetic thermal plastic resin that does not embrittle or discolor over time, having a liquid density of 8.3 pounds per gallon, a flash point of 60 degrees Fahrenheit, and a viscosity of  3700-6200 cps. It is widely used in conservation treatments, and in clear and pigmented coatings, aerosols, printing inks, product finishes, and specification lacquers. Formerly called Acryloid B-72 (TM) in the United States.
Refers to the style and culture of the Stz'uminus First Nation and its members, a Coast Salish people whose traditional territory is located on east Vancouver Island.
Educational institutions associated with Christian churches and mainly for children, in which religious instruction is given on Sundays.
Institutions focused on the worship of a deity or deities.

Institutions of a local government having facilities for both temporary detention of sentenced and unsentenced individuals and for persons serving sentences of less than one year; for longer periods of confinement and more secure than lockups, but less confining and for shorter confinements than prisons.
The Iris family of perennial herbs is worldwide in distribution, numbering more than 2000 species. It includes many widely cultivated plants such as freesias, gladioli, and crocuses.

Genus containing around 7 species of ornamental trees native to Eurasia and North America, having a shaggy, scaly bark and thin, translucent, green leaves with hairy leafstalks. The hoplike, green fruits are composed of many bladderlike scales, each bearing a small, flat nut.
Species of alder found in the United States, native to three distinct areas: Oklahoma, Georgia, and in Maryland and Delaware on the Delmarva Peninsula.
The latter part of the day, usually the time from about sunset until bedtime.

Species of North American fir tree native to the mountains of southwest Oregon and California. It is a high altitude tree, typically occurring at 1,400-2,700 m (4,600-8,900 feet) altitude, though only rarely reaching tree line. The name red fir derives from the bark color of old trees.
Genus comprising around 1100 species of flowering plants, native from Africa and Madagascar through southern Asia east through the Pacific.
A dense, narrow pyramidal evergreen tree native to the mountains of Europe and Asia. Swiss stone pine has been used extensively for wooden sculptures and buildings.
General name referring to various species of cedar, pine, and sequoia of the cypress family, including the coast redwood, dawn redwood, giant sequoia, Japanese cedar, and Scotch pine.
Genus of conifer containing one species; native to Japan.

Species of medium sized evergreen spruce growing at high altitudes in western North America, from Idaho and Wyoming to Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico, United States. The blue spruce has a light bluish-gray tone to its needles and is commonly used for landscaping and gardens. Its weak and brittle timber is used locally for log cabins. Occasionally the name blue spruce is incorrectly used for black spruce trees.
Enterprises that specialize in making tapestries.
Embroidered laid stitches sewn in an alternating or uneven lengths to create a rough, woven-looking surface, often sewn using crewel or Persian yarn.
In Indian architecture, a colonnaded cloister.

Refers to a type of lace that developed from flat Venetian lace.  It is characterized by a raised pattern created by outlining scrolls or leaf designs with a cordonnet, which is a relatively heavy thread or bundle of threads; the design is then worked over with buttonholing so that scrolls and leaves stand out in relief.
Proofs that meets the standard used for editions that are intended for distribution to specific groups of artists or craftspeople.

Christian religious articles comprising a string of 10 or more beads woven in a ladder-like formation to allow a bead to be slid up and down the string to count sacrifices, good deeds, and prayers throughout the day. The string typically has a medal of St. Therese on one end and a crucifix on the other; modern sacrifice beads may be in the form of a bracelet. According to tradition, the beads originated in the childhood of St. Therese of Lisieux, who was said to have used a string of prayer beads for this purpose.
Money made and used in Central Africa, in the form of sand-cast copper-alloy ingots, typically in the shape of a cross, an X, or an H.
Medium of exchange consisting of shells.
Describes the culture and style of the inhabitants of New Britain Island.
Covering a surface with tiles, generally in some sort of fixative with as grout or mortar.

Refers to the culture, style, and period of the southern Chinese dynasty of the period 557 to 589 CE that was the last of the Six Dynasties. The dynasty was founded in 557 when Chen Baxian deposed the Liang emperor but the territory controlled by the Chen was smaller than that of its dynastic predecessors. Jiankang, the capital of the Six Dynasties, was a great cultural, political, and religious center to which merchants and Buddhist missionaries travelled from Southeast Asia and India. Painting, calligraphy, music, and poetry flourished with the help of Chen imperial and aristocratic patrons. The development of literary and art criticism is seen in the works of Yao Zui and Xie He. After consolidating power in the north, General Yang Jian, Duke of Sui, took Jiankang in 589, establishing the Sui dynasty and reuniting all of China.
Projectile points having a form where notches for hafting have been struck in the sides of a blade near its base.
Marbled paper where colors are not raked within the prepared bath, and instead combed to produce a whorl effect. A curl pattern may be made of one color only.

Screens in Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches that separate the sanctuary from the nave, usually pierced by three doors and, since the 14th or 15th century, covered with icons. The function of the iconostasis is modeled on the Temple in Jerusalem, where people other than the priests were separated from the holiest area.
Secondary ribs springing from the main springer or central boss of vaults and leading to the ridge ribs.

Book format created when a sheet is folded to form 12 leaves or 24 pages. Typically made by inserting a smaller sheet into a larger sheet, as opposed to creating the size by creating two parallel folds and two right angle folds in one sheet.
A size of drawing and cartridge paper measuring 28 × 23 inches.

Kingdom comprising organisms with a relatively simple organization that are regarded as intermediate between or distinct from animals and plants, especially unicellular eukaryotes. They may share certain morphological and physiological characteristics with animals or plants, or both. They may be either free-living or gathered into simple colonies, and having diverse ways of nutrition and reproduction.

Members in this phylum are subject to being moved to other phyla, due to research done in the 1990s that resulted in an improved understanding of relationships of fungi traditionally placed in the phyla Chytridiomycota and Zygomycota.
Clade including crustaceans, insects, and myriapods, all having  mandibles on the third head segment that are modified for feeding.

General term referring to various trees and shrubs that form dense thickets in muddy coastal swamps and tidal estuaries in tropical and subtropical regions, marked by their ability to tolerate salt water and by their possession of different forms of aerial roots. The term is applied chiefly to species of the genera Rhizophora and Bruguiera (family Rhizophoraceae), Avicennia (family Avicenniaceae), Laguncularia (family Combretaceae), and Sonneratia (family Lythraceae).
Order containing more than 1,000 species in 18 families of mouse-like quadrupeds capable of flight with the ability to navigate at night by using a system of acoustic orientation.

Members of a genus of primates characterized by a relatively large cranial capacity, limb structure adapted to a habitual erect posture and a bipedal gait, well-developed and fully opposable thumb, hand capable of power and precision grips, and the ability to make standardized precision tools, using one tool to make another. Together with modern man, Homo sapiens, the genus includes the extinct species H. habilis, H. erectus, and H. heidelbergensis as well as the extinct Neanderthals (H. neanderthalensis) and the early form of H. sapiens called Cro-Magnon.

Members of the species to which all modern human beings belong. Homo sapiens is one of several species grouped into the genus Homo, but it is the only one that is not extinct. The name "Homo sapiens" was applied in 1758 by Carolus Linnaeus, who distinguished humans from their close cousins, the apes. The large fossil record now contains numerous extinct species that are much more closely related to humans than to today's apes and that were presumably more similar to us behaviorally as well.
Genus of one 1 species of wolf-like canid of South America.
Species of North American wolf somewhat smaller than the gray wolf.
Genus of three primarily Central and South American species, including the little spotted cat, margay, and ocelot.
A distinct population or subspecies of Felis silvestris found in Europe.

General term referring to animals from several evolutionary lines and thus not properly a taxonomic group. The term refers to aquatic animals found in the fresh and salt waters all over the world, characterized by being cold-blooded, living and breathing primarily in the water throughout their lives, possessing gill slits, a notochord or skeletal supporting rod, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, a tail, scales covering the body, and two sets of paired fins and several unpaired fins. Living species range from the primitive jawless lampreys and hagfishes through the jawed fishes with cartilaginous skeletons such as sharks, skates, and rays to the abundant and diverse bony fishes.
Phonographs that can be easily carried.
Chinese bronze ritual vessels used for holding wine.
Unit of measurement for computer file storage. Equal to 1,048,576 bytes.

Class containing around 200 species of cup animals, including some jellyfish. Life histories commonly involve alternation of a very small polyp with a medusa that develops from an ephyra released by the polyp. They are divided by four longitudinal septa producing tetramerous radial symmetry; gonads are endodermal. They have marginal sensory structures (rhopalia) with statocysts and/or ocelli. They are most abundant in coastal waters, but oceanic species exist.

Members of an order of nearly 2,900 species placed in about 35 families of bony fishes, characterized by certain distinctive features of the skull and swimbladder. Species vary widely in size and behavior, but most species have prominent barbels. They are sometimes classified in the same order as characins, carp, and minnows; their taxonomy is currently in flux as more research in molecular relationships is undertaken.

Large subclass of reptiles characterized by overlapping scales, no bipedal specializations, two complete temporal openings, a complete palate, being egg-laying, and a male lacking a penis. They include tuataras, lizards, snakes, and amphisbaenians.
Extinct genus of small horses known from North American Oligocene fossils.
Ass found in Iran and Turkmenistan.

Hooved animal. Original populations of Equus caballus were once found in the steppe zone from Poland to Mongolia. Now domesticated, horses occur throughout the world and in feral populations in some areas. Three of the several early breeds of horse - Przewalski's horse from central Asia, the tarpan from eastern Europe and the Ukrainian steppes, and the forest horse of northern Europe - are generally thought to have been the ancestral stock of modern domestic horses. According to this line of thinking, Przewalski's horse and the tarpan formed the basic breeding stock from which the southerly 'warm-blooded' horses developed, while the forest horse gave rise to the heavy, 'cold-blooded' breeds. All modern breeds are divided as light, fast, spirited breeds typified by the modern Arabian, heavier, slower, and calmer working breeds typified by the Belgian, and intermediate breeds typified by the Thoroughbred. They are also classified according to where they originated (e.g., Percheron, Clydesdale, and Arabian), by the principal use of the horse (riding, draft, coach horse), and by their outward appearance and size (light, heavy, pony).
Powerful horses used to carry men, usually in armor, in war.

Describes material or content created in electronic form and saved as digital data, having had no initial or interstitial state as an analog or physical product. Usually used to refer to electronically produced drafts of text, correspondence or visual works such as photographs created with digital cameras. This material may be written or saved on personal computers, floppy disks, CDs, DVDs, hard drives, or any mode of digital storage media.

The most common technique for converting analog signals into digital form, involving sampling. Pulse Code Modulation is not a universally accepted standard, but rather a technique used in a variety of applications from telephony to CD production. CD quality music is sampled generally at 44.1 kHz at 32 bits per sample.

An HTTP-based published standard or protocol for adaptive bitrate streaming originally developed by Apple Inc. to distribute live or pre-recorded audio and video with low latency over the Internet. It allows a receiver to adapt the bit rate of the media to the current network conditions in order to maintain uninterrupted playback at the best possible quality. The protocol has been implemented in media players, web browsers, mobile devices, and streaming media servers. While HLS started as an Apple proprietary streaming protocol, it has become an open industry standard.
Natural depressions or courses in the earth's surface that contain standing or flowing freshwater, including rivers and lakes.

Areas of level land that flank hills, ridges or mountains, where slopes rise on one side, and descend on the opposite level. More specifically can refer to bedrock platforms bounded by steep slopes that overlook bodies of water.

Educational institutions devoted to the professional study of the organization and management of commercial enterprises, usually at the baccalaureate level and above. For buildings that house schools devoted to training students in the clerical aspects of business and commerce, use "business colleges."
Eaves or awnings projecting from a Hindu temple buiding.
In Indian architecture, a ceiling showing lotuses or lūmās; adhiṣṭhāna type.

Planetary-mass objects that are neither a planet nor a moon. As defined by the International Astronomical Union (IAU), a dwarf planet is a celestial body in direct orbit of a star, massive enough for its shape to be controlled by gravitation, but it differs from a planet in that a dwarf planet has not cleared its orbital region of other objects.

Technique used to create images of objects, structures, or other features located underground at relatively shallow depths, by bouncing sound waves off the features from several different positions, collecting and processing the signals to get a number of partial views, then focusing and combining these partial views to create a complete image; developed by Alan J. Witten between 1984 and 1987.

Microphones that respond to air velocity rather than air pressure of sound waves. This is accomplished via a ribbon of corrugated aluminum held between two magnets. Ribbon microphones were used extensively in radio and television broadcasting during the mid-20th century due to their broad dynamic range.
Fixed aperture settings on some photographic lenses referred to by a numbering system that is a ratio of the diameter of the aperture to the focal length of the lens.
Hereditary names shared by members of the same family, as distinct from a given names for the individual. In modern western culture, family names are usually the same as the "last names."

General term for a medium-sized citrus fruit of several species, distinguished by having a rind with an orange color (reddish-yellow) and an acidic, juicy pulp that is sweeter than a lemon, grapefruit, or lime. The species most commonly intended by this term is Citrus sinensis.
Oval drupe, or stone-fruit, of the olive tree. The edible olive has been cultivated since approximately 3500 BCE, generally in warm climates. There are hundreds of named varieties.
Any of various fleshy fruiting bodies of fungi consisting of a stalk and a cap. Forms deviating from the standard morphology usually have more specific names.
Windsor chairs with sawn back posts of gunstock shape; common in the mid-19th century.

Computer system programs, procedures, and associated documentation concerned with the operation of data processing systems, and which require hardware for use to be made of them. For individual collections or sequences of code provided by a user to perform a particular task, use "programs." For programs that serve a particular purpose and that may be packaged and sold by a manufacturer use "applications."

A tough, flexible, transparent, moistureproof polyvinyl acetal resin made from polyvinyl alcohol and butyraldehyde; used, among other things, as the interlayer in safety glass and other laminated products.

Plastic or glass elements used to change the direction of light by bending or refracting the rays in a specified pattern over an area, achieved by covering the surface of the lens with prisms that are arranged in a pattern designed to achieve the desired effect.
Eyeglasses with colored or tinted lenses that protect the eyes from the glare of sunlight.
Tools with one to four blades connected to a handle used to mince and chop meat, vegetables, or other foods. Blades may be straight or curved, the latter for use in a chopping bowl or tray.
v
Nahua warrior recognizable by his hairstyle characterized by a tonsure, associated with the Otomi rank.
Equipment used to play magnetic tapes, sometimes including recorders, but without speakers. Can also refer to components in audio or video systems.
Describes the culture or style of an African people living in Ethiopia.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting western Cameroon.

Style and culture of the people of the modern nation of Botswana. To refer specifically to the style and culture of the Bantu people living chiefly in Botswana and western South Africa who speak or are descendants of those who traditionally spoke the Twana dialect of the Sotho language, use "Tswana."
Roman masonry facing method in which the techniques of opus reticulatum and opus testaceum are combined to form a hybrid surface pattern.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living mainly in Djibouti, but also in Somalia and Ethiopia.
Grain pattern embossed on leather in imitation of the grain of pigskin.
Book cloth grain pattern imitating the appearance of a diagonal beaded line.

Components of some belts, especially those that formed a part of early medieval dress: a counter plate was placed opposite the buckle. These were found on belts that would have included a buckle, and sometimes a rectangular back plate placed in the middle of the belt at the back for decoration.

Category of paintings derived from a description by the French Academy in 1717 of Antoine Watteau's variations of the "fête champêtre" genre. Fête champêtre ("rural festival") paintings portray costumed figures in an idealized, poetic setting, while fête galante ("courtship party") paintings are usually small in scale, and show groups of aristocratic men and women in pastoral settings engaged in amorous play.

The marks made on copperplates by steel tools when engraving or etching. Tool work can sometimes be identified (such as stipple work), however, most tool work cannot be specifically identified when examining prints.
Nahua hairstyle of postclassic central Mexico in which some or all of the hair on the sides of the scalp is shaved.
Comic booklets produced from the 1930s to the 1950s, containing parodies of popular comic strip characters in explicit sexual adventures. Typically issued in 3x4 in. booklets of eight leaves.

Comics whose stories are set in distant times and lands, either past or future, featuring heroic persons, magicians, and mythological figures battling evil forces, typically in face-to-face combat with swords, axes, hammers, and other hand-wielded weapons, and often involving magic.
Performances including music for voice and optionally instruments, generally relatively brief in duration, containing words.
Leather tanned without removing the hair from the skins or hides.
Leather derived from lizards, which in common usage refers to reptiles of the genus Lacerta as well as any other reptiles resembling these in shape and general appearance.
Book edges that have been decorated with a spattering of color or colors, usually earth pigment dissolved in a non-spirit solvent.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northern Nigeria.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Democratic Republic of Congo north of the Lukenie river.

Planning and management of traffic routes and speed and other regulations with the goal of achieving calm, safe, and environmentally improved conditions on or near roads and streets, and in the community or region as a whole.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Democratic Republic of Congo, on the left bank of the Kasai River.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Removing the grain surface of a skin or hide by chemical or mechanical means to allow penetration of tanning oils.
Spears used for ritual purposes, rather than as fighting and hunting weapons.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in northern Ghana and Burkino Faso.
A palindrome is a word or a sequence of words that reads, letter for letter, the same backwards as forwards.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting eastern Ghana.
Ceremonial structures that are related to or concerned with religion.
Refers to cels actually used in the production of the animated work, for example, a cartoon.

Toxic substances used to eradicate fungi that damage crops or ornamental plants or endanger the health of animals or humans. Most fungicide is applied topically but systemic fungicides may be applied that are distributed throughout living tissues to eradicate or protect against disease. Fungicides may also be impregnated in textiles, paper, leather, or wood as well as painted on masonry and plaster.
Representing or imitating animal forms, as in decorative art or symbolism.
Complexes of built works surrounding a temple or temples.

In Indian architecture, a diminutive of maṇḍapa; temple-type with pillared walls and usually Muṇḍamāla (flat or without superstructure)/with only a "vēdī" superstructure; pandal; small pillared structure; pillared pavilion; small pavilion.

Describes motion picture film that is 8 millimeters wide, the narrowest gauge available for such film. Introduced in 1932 for use by amateur filmmakers and for home movies, 8mm film was also taken up by filmmakers of the avant0garde and the underground, due to the comparatively low cost of the film stock and the processing. Since the mid-1960s, standard 8mm film has been generally superceded by the Super 8 type.
Having the form or outline of a hexagon, which is a plane figure with six sides and six angles.
Shape comprising a solid of which all the plane sections through one of the axes are ellipses, and all other sections ellipses or circles.
Motion picture material shot for a larger work but not used in the final edited version.

Genre of film obsessed with bringing to the screen sexual, exploitive, and typically horror-oriented subject matter. Grindhouse films are typically bloody, low-budget, and aimed at a young adult audience.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name inhabiting the Kurdufan region of Sudan.
Distinctive masks of the Igbo people, worn by men to appease the spirits of beautiful girls.
Distinctive lacquerware made with lacquer mixed with powdered red cinnabar, applied in thick coats and carved to produce boxes, jars, figures, panels, beads, and other objects, particularly in China.

Refers to works decorated with cross-stitching, which is a type of needlework in which designs are created with tiny crosses or "x" shapes made by crossing two stitches. The works may be executed on fine fabrics, such as linen, or on heavy canvas or carpets.

Refers to a fine, openwork ornamental textile work formed by looping, interlacing, twisting, plaiting, or braiding threads of linen, cotton, silk, hair, metal, or another fiber to form designs or patterns. Lace may be made with a needle or with bobbins. Embroidery may be added. Modern lace may be made by machine. Openwork fabrics made on a loom and ornamental openwork knitting are generally not classified as lace. Lace is often white or monochromatic. True lace developed in the fourteenth century in Europe and the Middle East, although ornamented openwork fabrics were known in ancient cultures, including the Egyptian culture. Lace may be used as a border, edging, or insert on linens or apparel; it is also formed into large pieces of cloth used for hangings, draperies, apparel, or other items.
Any atom or group of atoms that bears one or more positive or negative electrical charges.
The activity of using one's mind to produce thoughts.
Christian feast day celebrated on August 15 in the western tradition. The feast honors the corporeal taking up into heaven of the Virgin Mary at her death.

The Jewish autumn festival celebrated in September or October (15-21 Tishri) as a festival of thanksgiving. Sukkot is one of three Jewish pilgrim festivals. In biblical times the festival was associated with the agricultural year. Following the tradition established in Leviticus (23: 42), 'booths' or temporary shelters are built in homes, gardens, and synagogues in memory of the huts used by the Israelites after leaving Egypt.

Bibles which generally contain only illustrations, sometimes with short pieces of text. In the past, they were used to spread knowledge of the Bible to the uneducated. Numerous examples exist from the Middle Ages, although picture Bibles dating to the 11th and 12th centuries, as well as those dating as late as the 16th century, have been discovered.

The cycle of death and rebirth experienced by all unawakened beingsover potentially infinite eons consisting often of six destinies: (1) divinity, (2) demigod, (3) human, (4) animal, (5) ghost, and (6) hell dweller in Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism. Although debated, the concept is probably of non-Vedic or heterodox origin.
In Buddhism, realms of individual bodhisattvas who have attained awakening; may have varying spiritual climates or degrees of perfection, either pure or mixed.
Bag-shaped fish traps with cork floats, towards which fish are directed by means of a leader, such as a line of netting; used in rivers and sheltered waters.
Hand tools for raking flax waste, used in an indoor context, such as a shed.
Instrument placed around the neck, used to restrict the freedom of enslaved men and women and prevent escape attempts.
Tubes that are temporarily placed in the body to absorb bodily fluids, to administer drugs, or to enlarge passages.

Mechanized devices, comprising a series of rollers equipped with wavy ridges or protruding knobs called buttons, designed to lessen the stiffness of and soften excess starch in textile materials. Originally designed to increase the pliability of silk goods, these devices can be used to soften many types of stiffened textile materials after they have been exposed to finishing and drying processes. As textile materials are passed through the rollers, friction exerted by the fabric prompts the rollers to rotate and expose the fabric's surface to the protruding buttons. In order to achieve the desired softness and pliability,  fabrics can be passed through these devices multiple times if desired; the more a stiffened fabric comes into contact with this device's buttons, the softer the fabric's surface will be.
Frames, often made of wire, used as a fitting model in making dresses. Often custom shaped to the person for whom the dress is designed.
Looms on which the heddles operate on cords revolving over rods or pulley with or without heddle-horses for support.
Sets of tools, especially those kept for a particular purpose, usually in a special bag or box.
Ceremonies or rites held in connection with the burial or cremation of the body of a deceased person.
Lids or plates, often iron, which are placed over burners on a stove.
The interpersonal behavior regulator, which covers the defining of a space, and the creation of visible and invisible boundaries to that space.
Pyrotechnic devices, usually handheld or used with a launcher, producing intense light, sometimes in combination with smoke or sound, used for signaling, identification, or illumination.
Animals that have four feet and walk using four legs.

Objects of a variety of form that are marked with text or images meant to promote goods, services, brands, etc., and are normally given away as a form of advertising. These may be utilitarian items such as pens, fans, hats, etc.

Extinct order of order of highly specialized snake-like amphibians with a small skull with large orbits, large fenestrae, reduced or absent bones at the back of the skull, and an extremely elongate body. Dating to the Carboniferous and Early Permian.
Common name for any of numerous terrestrial slow-moving pulmonate gastropods or land-snails in which the shell is rudimentary or entirely absent.

Freestanding cupboards, particulary with reference to cupboards in use in the mid-16th century in England for freestanding cupboards used for the storage of food and drink, generally in the form of a two-tier cupboard with pierced or spindle doors for ventilation. Use "aumbries" with reference to similar forms made before, after, or during the Medieval period.
Breed of dog, now extinct, that was introduced to New Zealand by Maori during their migrations from East Polynesia in the late 13th century.
General term referring to members of around ten species of small carnivores with very elongated, slender bodies.

Order of deepwater squid-like cephalopods containing only one extant member; distinguished by possessing a distinctive buoyancy organ, which is a chambered internal shell. In some classifications, they are a family of Sepiida.
Animals that typically acquire food by actively hunting or lying in wait to kill and eat other animals.

The male deer, especially of the red deer; specifically a hart or male deer of the fifth year of its life. Also used to refer to a male animal castrated when fully grown, as with cattle, a boar or hog, and other animals.
Subfamily containing the genus Muntiacus.
General term referring to 122 species in 22 genera of tree squirrels.
A soft sweet confection made originally from the root of the marshmallow plant and later from albumen, gelatin, sugar, and other ingredients.
The process of making a ceramic object on a potter's wheel.

Literary works in the form of poetry that tells a story, often making use of the voices of a narrator and characters as well. The story may be written in metered verse, but not necessarily following rhythmic patterns.

Satirical poems that critique or poke fun at living people, including personal acquaintances or political figures. Examples are found in the novel Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes and in popular culture associated with the Day of the Dead celebrations.
A white salt used medicinally as a laxative and anticonvulsant. In conservation science it is encountered as a salt weathering deposit on stone.

Stiff, projecting oral structures of certain animals, including some invertebrates (e.g., cephalopods and some insects), some fishes and mammals, all birds and turtles, and many dinosaurs. Many beaked animals, including all modern birds and turtles, lack teeth.

People who design, make, form, set up, or bring into existence an art work or other thing or activity, particularly where the creation is imaginative or inventive. For makers who execute the designs of other people, use the more general "makers" or the specific "executors (makers)."
Shoes, boots, or sandals with an unusually thick sole.
Shoes meant to be worn submerged in water or in otherwise wet environments. These are often made of materials that are water-resistant or water-proof.
The duration of a dramatic performance, film, musical work, song, or similar activity, excluding any intermissions or interruptions.

Religious masquerades of the Igbo people of Africa, performed in the northcentral Igbo region on very special occasions, such as yam festivals and major events associated with kingship. It features monumental mask costumes in the form of a huge cylinder or cone bearing a complex tableau of miniature human, animal, bird, and spirit figures made of brightly-colored cloth stuffed with grass.

Scientists who specialize in any or all aspects of soils, including their origin, distribution, classification, utilization, physical and chemical properties, and the role of organisms in soil production and in relation to soil character. For agriculturists who study and work in land cultivation, soil management, and field crop improvement, management, and production, see "agronomists."

Foodstuff made from sugar or other sweet, edible substance. Includes a wide variety of forms, from hard lozenges of crystallized sugar made by repeated boiling and slow evaporation, to soft filled sweets, such as chocolate-covered bonbons.
Schooner-rigged vessels used for fishing.
Describes fishing watercraft that engage in the the capture of marine life using trapping devices.
Alphabet of Semitic origin, borrowed from the Phoenecians in first millennium BCE, and modified by the Greeks to include characters representing both vowel and consonant sounds.
Ropes, straps, clogs, or other contrivances used on the legs of a horse or other animal to limit its movement, to prevent it from straying or kicking.
Ropes, cords, or straps used as harnesses to guide or restrain mount or pack animals.
Cloths put over the back of a horse or other riding animal under the saddle and extending out behind it.
Refers to a combination of devices designed to transmit, amplify, and reproduce sound, so as to make it audible to an audience in a public space.
Personal decoration as a token of affection or recognition of services, which may be awarded by a knightly order or by the state.
Businesses which hold sales, often public, where items such as artworks are sold to the highest bidders.
Devices that are designed to record onto read-only compact discs.
Fans that do not fold or close, with a decorated area attached to a handle.
Distinguished from "trailer camps" by being only for infrequently moved prefabricated structures designed for year-round living.
Belts that are designed to store and carry small objects for the wearer while active.
Early Iron Age culture, partially identified by characteristic pottery of the interlacustrine region of East Africa.
Enclosures for pigs that include a low shed and covered fore-court.
Painters who specialize in painting decorations, scenes, or figures on façades, particularly in historical contexts.
Die cut in brass, typically in a design or letters of the alphabet, used by a bookbinder's finisher in lettering book covers.
Method of hand sewing a text block in which two gatherings are sewn together by a single length of thread; the thread passes between them at alternate sewing stations.
Texture mapping is the application of a two-dimensional image file containing texture, color, or surface detail to a 3D model or computer-generated graphic.
Güls characterized by a hooked stepped polygon; usually found in an endless repeat format on rugs, but sometimes also on saddle rugs and other Turkoman weavings.
Manner of dressing required by custom or etiquette for formal or semiformal evening occasions.
Personal use equipment for caring for children.

The activity of impressing official stamps (hallmarks) onto articles of gold and silver for security and decoration. Traditionally, hallmarks have been applied manually with steel punches. Laser hallmarking is used as an alternative, in particular to avoid bruising items.
People who keep, protect, or defend prisons and the inmates of prisons.
Those trained in or who practice navigation, especially on ships or aircraft.
Scientific concepts related to psychology.
Computer software technique for rendering virtual models of three-dimensional terrain.
