People skilled in the arrangement and use of type in creating printed matter, including the setting and arrangement of type to be printed from. The role of the typographer may also extend to designing typefaces themselves, but for those who design type exclusively, use "type designers."
Articles or physical resources related to the science and practice of breeding, raising, feeding, and tending domestic animals.
Thick flexible pads, as for example of quilted or crocheted textile, used to protect the hands against hot cookware or utensils.

Christian clergy whose defining official function is to hear the confessions of others, prescribes penance, and grants absolution. Prime examples are the private spiritual directors of a king or other great personage.

Those who study and practice ritual activities with the object of controlling or influencing human or natural events through the invocation of external and impersonal mystical forces beyond the ordinary human sphere; typical ritual activities include the manipulation of special objects and the recitation of spells. Distinct from "magicians (illusionists)", who create illusions and perform sleight-of-hand, conjuring tricks, and other types of stage magic.
Refers to partners in or owners of professional practices who are legally responsible for the activities of their companies, especially in architectural or design-related companies.
Public officers charged with the duty of collecting taxes legally due to the government of the political administrative body they serve.
Fasteners made of one or more metal wires encased in paper or plastic, used for closing or securing something, such as a plastic bag, by twisting the ends together.
The action of performing or executing work or labor, particularly as one's paid employment,
Concealing one's body or face.

The activity of a person or animal propelling themselves in the water by natural means of progression, such as floating and kicking or paddling the limbs. For the activity of cleansing, prefer "bathing (hygienic activity)."
The collective actions or processes of felling trees and sawing them into short lengths to be transported to a sawmill.

A ball sport invented in Holland ca.1901 with similarities to netball and basketball. Intended as a mixed-gender sport, two teams of 8 members must field four female and four male players. The objective is to throw a ball through a bottomless basket that is mounted on a 3.5 m (11.5 feet) high pole. Players are allowed to run only when they are not in possession of the ball.
Activity involving ascending mountains or other steep terrain, usually for adventure or sport.

Handicraft characterized by simple meshes of thread or cord joined by knots. It is of ancient origin and known in most cultures of the world. When produced under tension, it creates a stable fabric. In making the net, the thread is wound on an elongated shuttle or large needle; a mesh stick or gauge is used to maintain a uniform size of mesh. As the thread is looped round the gauge it is passed through a secondary loop to form a fisherman's knot or other non-slipping knot. The net can vary greatly in weight, shape, or size. It is used to make utilitarian objects, such as fishing nets, snares, and apparel, and as a foundation upon which to apply ornamentation, such as in the creation of lace or other textiles.

Refers to an early stage in the process of turning flax or similar plants into yarn in which the material is steeped in order to soften and separate the fibrous core of the plant from the outer layer. Basic methods include dew retting and water retting.
Printing process utilizing master sheets that release color through type indentations when a colorless chemical fluid is applied.
Printing techniques in which light is obstructed or reduced in selective portions of the image, lessening exposure (and resulting density) in those areas.

Physical works, such as drawings and written documents, that were the result of a competition, particularly an artistic or architectural competition in which various applicants vie for a prize or for the assignment of a contract to create the finished work. For the event of the competition, use "competitions (events)."
Describes groupings of objects affiliated with activities for leisure, entertainment, and pleasure.
Rims or bands that surround and hold a stone or other ornament, such as on a ring or snuff box, or a crystal, such as on a watch case or clock, or a glass or plastic covering, such as on a headlight.
Parts or components of furnishings.
Parts or components of protection systems.
Network of electrical components constructed to supply, transfer, and use electric power.
Converting, sound, motion pictures, images, or other analog data to binary form to be stored or altered with a computer.
Capstones of pyramids or obelisks, themselves having a pyramidal form.
Buildings housing museums dealing with the sea in general, navigation, or shipping, as distinct from "naval museums," which deal with navies, warships, or ships in general.
Textile made from untreated silk fibers as reeled from cocoons.
Wool textile with a rough, homespun surface effect.

Refers to the culture associated with the Islamic dynasty of this name that ruled in parts of North Africa and Spain and was an active patron of art and architecture between 972 and 1152. Zirid architecture was open to outside influences: the ruins of the palace of Ziri at Ashir suggest that it was modeled on an early Fatimid palace at Mahdia and the extensive ruins of the palaces at the Qal 'at bani hammad show similarities with Fatimid architecture in Egypt and Norman architecture in Sicily. There are several Zirid buildings in Granada, including a palace (1052-6) on the site of the Alhambra erected by Yusuf ibn Naghrallah, the Zirid's Jewish vizier. The only remains of this splendid palace are 12 white marble lions, reused in the 14th century for the central fountain in the Palace of the Lions. Zirid patrons also furnished religious buildings; for example, a carved wooden minbar was given in 980 by the Zirid ruler Buluggin to the mosque of the Andalusians in Fez. The most important example of Zirid woodwork is the heavily carved maqsura ordered by al-Mu'izz ibn Badis for the congregational mosque at Kairouan; a carved inscription is outlined by a distinctively Zirid raised bead. Bookmaking also flourished during this dynasty and the ruler himself was the author of an important treatise on the art of the book.
Dynasty which ruled over Egypt, what is now upper Iraq, part of Syria, and Yemen from the late 12th to early 13th centuries CE.
Style of carpet and textile design from the area of Demirci,  Anatolia.

Style of textile, particularly carpets, handmade in any of a group of villages near the town of Heriz, lying east of Tabriz in northwest Iran. Heriz carpets are often room-sized, stout, serviceable, and attractive to markets in Europe and the United States. They are apparently an offshoot of the Tabriz carpets, a country version of city styles. The smooth curves and flowing lines of a sophisticated Tabriz medallion system are translated into hard, geometric angles and broken contours. Repeat patterns occur less frequently, and a jagged vine and rosette border is characteristic.
Transparencies used in conjunction with a negative or another transparency to alter color or contrast.

term: Iranian Islamic painting styles after the Mongols
definition: Painting styles after the Mongols, belonging to Iranian Islamic cultures.
Southwestern Native American blankets in the Rio Grande pattern of narrow brown, blue, and white weft bands.

Style of textiles, particularly short-napped rugs or carpets, from the region of Shirvan, Azerbaijan in the southeastern Caucasus. With the exception of a group of rugs woven in the vicinity of Baku, most Shirvan rugs are small, with examples from the southern part of the area around the town of Saliani more likely to be in the long, narrow format described in the West as runners. The area around Maraza has produced many prayer rugs, including a well-known type with boteh (leaf-shaped) figures on a blue field. Most small Shirvan rugs are not specifically identifiable as to village source, as they share a range of geometric field designs and borders. They are generally less finely woven than rugs from farther north in the Kuba district, although they are finer than the Kazakh-type rugs made in western Azerbaijan. Shirvan rugs are usually all wool, but some may show cotton wefts and cotton edges.

Refers generally to the period and styles of a number of Turkish principalities in Anatolia from the last years of Saljuq family rule at the end of the 13th century to the final incorporation of Anatolia in the Ottoman family state in the late 15th century. While some Beyliks achieved only a brief independence, others were quite durable.
Textile styles belonging to Uzbek cultures.

Folding stools used by worshippers to sit or kneel, especially those used by the sovereign during coronation. For chairs used by bishops or other prelates in the chancel of a church, use "faldistories." For the French form of folding stool used at court or domestically after the 17th century, use "pliants."
Progressive encircling or wrapping of warp ends by the weft. If the weft, in addition to encircling one or more ends, passes through a loop of its own part, forming a knot, prefer "knotting."
Long planes, up to 36 inches, used in making floorboards; distinct from "jointer planes" in their size and use.
A size of card photograph on a mount measuring about 3 1/2 by 5 inches.
Generic term for the class of electrostatic copying techniques.

Aluminum compound used in solution to stabilize deteriorated leather. The basis of this treatment is cross linking of aluminium ions with the collagen in the degraded leather and the introduction of an alkaline buffer.

Elements found in minute quantities in minerals, not essential to their composition but found in their structure or adsorbed on their surface, conventionally held to constitute significantly less than 1.0% of the mineral. Use also for elements found in plant and animal tissue in concentrations of 1.0% or less, which are physiologically essential to the organism.

The systematic distinguishing, classifying, and naming of type groups of organisms, objects, and phenomena within a subject field, especially as applied in biology to living and extinct animals and plants. Also refers to the study of the theory, rules, and methods of systematic classification and nomenclature per se.
Sovereign states typically originating with a large group of people associated with a particular territory and possessing distinct ethnic, historical, or cultural characteristics.

Refers to the offices, reigns, or dominions of caliphs. The caliphate, a political-religious state, became a Muslim institution after the death of Muhammad in 632. Through conquest the caliphate grew rapidly for the first few hundred years but ultimately ceased to exist after the defeat of Baghdad by the Mongols in 1258. Even when declining in power, the caliphate remained a symbolic focus of Muslim unity and there have been attempts to revive it.

Cargo vessels or warships of the Middle Ages through the 16th century usually having a curved stem, straight sternpost after about 1200, clinker planking, and castles at the bow and stern; earlier vessels were relatively small, but 15th- and 16th-century examples could exceed 500 tons deadweight capacity; originally developed in northern Europe, but were eventually widespread.
Any of various small flat-bottomed craft of the Far East, propelled by a single sculling oar or sail.
Small craft, more or less canoe-shaped but wider, usually less than 6 m long, with round bilges, and exactly symmetrical ends; originated in New England but no longer confined to that region.
Vessels with tubular or rounded topsides, creating a convex deck which allowed seas to run freely over the hull; form originated on the Great Lakes in 1896.
Ships, typically anchored in a specific location where a lighthouse would be impractical, and equipped with lights and various warning devices serving as aids to mariners.
Semisubmersible torpedo boats built and used by Confederate forces during the American Civil War; steam driven, with a small, protected opening at the top of a long, spindle-shaped hull.
Vessels, usually old warships or cargo vessels, converted for use as stationary work platforms, for accommodation, or for storage.

Relatively short and wide watercraft used for navigation of inland waterways in South-Holland, Zeeland, Brabant and the Scheldt/Rupel basin. A notable feature is the inward turned prow. These were mainly meant for cargo but occasionaly also for passenger travel.
Any of various boats small and light enough to be rowed or sailed by one person.

Flat-bottomed, flat-sided, hard-chined inland watercraft common in northern Europe from the Middle Ages onward; sides usually clinker; similar in structure to dories. For small craft, traditionally clinker-built, use "prams (square-based watercraft)."
Ancient Greek warships propelled by fifteen pairs of oars.
Indonesian vessels with a very large triangular, usually lateen, sail and a substantial loadbearing outrigger.
A white, vertical, flat surface on which images are projected, made of reflective material. Generally used for motion picture, video, or photographic slide projection.
Caucasian rugs which depict eight large pointed stars.
A name of convenience for rugs with a specific endless repeat pattern of arabesque forms, so called because they appear in a painting by the Italian Renaissance painter Lorenzo Lotto.

Broadly, rugs woven in Iran, in brightly coloured patterns of animals, plants, figures, or geometric shapes. The history of Persian carpet manufacture is divisive, and many assumptions are made without historical evidence. Scholars disagree on many aspects of their production. Particular styles are most often identified by the region in which they were made.
Oblong trays with upright sides to hold set type.
Engraving tools used in creating plates for printmaking.
Rubber mats used to transfer images from metal or other surfaces to the printed substrate.
Passenger train cars for daytime travel having more comfortable seats and more amenities, such as smoking compartments, buffet bars, or tables, than coaches.
In Indian architecture, hōma; basal-block of pillar or pilaster.
Parts and components of motion pictures.
Flattened ball feet, used on furniture from the mid-17th century.
Handles used for pulling open a door or drawer.
Handles in the form of small rounded masses that project from the interior surfaces of movable screens that cover portals, especially windows.
Small rugs which are approximately twice as long as they are wide.
Objects collected by fanciers, such as toys, miniatures, spoons, or various other items, but generally not applied to collections of art, stamps, coins, or furniture.

Images, either two-dimensional pictures or three-dimensional, used in private piety or other religious purposes in a place of worship or home, intended as recipients of prayer or aids to meditation; distinct from images that serve the liturgy or are primarily didactic.

Objects that symbolically represents a flail, which is an implement having stout handle at the end of which are attached ropes or chains for whipping. Examples include flails used by Ancient Egyptians during religious and funerary ceremonies, often consisting of a staff with three rods attached by a ring.
Tools of bone or other materials used to press off flakes of stone in making stone implements.
Pitchers used during the Eucharistic service to contain the sacramental wine, which will be poured into the chalice and consecrated.
Visual boundaries of a form, without regard to internal features; distinct from a "contour," which may bound a form within an outline.

Black-figure cups named after the chief subject chosen for their decoration, namely revellers (komasts). Komast cups feature narrow, offset lips, deep bowls, and short, flaring or conical feet. The komast cup was one of the forms to predominate in black-figure until about 540 BCE.

Kylikes with a lip which curves slightly outward and is clearly tooled off from the body. It also features a reserved bowl and black handles, stem, and foot. Figures were often painted on the lip and/or an inscription, often the potter's signature, is written in the zone between the handles.
Those methods for bookbinding that rely on adhesives to hold together the leaves of the volume, so that single leaves are held together using an adhesive rather than a sewn attachment.
Those who play the harp.
Those who play the oboe.
Territories for which jurisdiction is in dispute between two or more powers.
Plates, usually of ceramic, that are emblazoned with an image of an event, place or person of note. These are generally meant to be collected or hung as decoration rather than as functional items.

Crosses or crucifixes mounted on staffs and carried in Christian religious processions. Such crosses seem to have been in general use from very early times, given that it is mentioned in the Roman "Ordines" as to suggest that such a cross belonged to each church.
Revolving cylinders found in computers that have magnetized surfaces where data is stored.

Pieces of protective boards or other heavy paper with an opening or openings cut in order to reveal a two dimensional visual work. Mats typically comprise two pieces, the bottom piece supports the print or other work, and the top piece contains an opening through which the work may be viewed. The boards may be hinged together to form a protective folder. Mats are used for prints, watercolors, pastels, other works of art, documents, or other generally flat objects.
Persons who takes part in fighting with the fists, especially for sport.

Services intended for use at dinner by a number of diners, generally consisting of numerous dishes, plates, and cups of different sizes, and sometimes other vessels such as tureens, platters, casters, or decorative articles such as vases and épergnes, as well as flatware and glassware.
Fabric cases filled with foam material used to support the head or other parts of the body while reclining.
Districts under the jurisdiction of a church.

Designation given to certain districts within a nation that have a degree of independence, administer their own affairs, or are otherwise self-governing to some degree. The precise definition of "autonomous district" varies from nation to nation, and is typically assigned to the district by the nation, rather than being assigned by an outside body. Examples of autonomous districts are in Indonesia.
Commissioned officers in various navies, ranking immediately below captains. For chief officers in command of a military force, place, or station, see "commanding officers."
A cosmetic preparation for darkening, lengthening, and thickening the eyelashes and (occasionally) the eyebrows, usually applied with a small brush.
Goggles designed especially for use while skiing to protect the eyes from glare and wind.
European noblemen holding a duchy, ranking highest in the peerage.

Sovereign duchesses of certain Continental European states called grand duchies, also for the wives and widows of grand dukes and the daughters of the Czars of imperial Russia; ranking immediately below queens.

Implements having a row of teeth on one or both edges or sides, used for adjusting, distangling, or cleaning the hair. For such tools that are intended primarily to be decorative and displayed in the hair, use "combs (hair ornaments)."
Mechanical devices in various forms used to uniformly roll the binder leaf evenly around the filler tobacco of a cigar.

Devices to compensate for defective vision or to protect the eyes from light, dust, and the like, consisting usually of two lenses set in a frame that includes a nosepiece for resting on the bridge of the nose and which may also have two sidepieces extending over or around the ears.
A method of coloring glass by dipping clear glass, while still pliant, into a bath of molten glass of a deep color, or by fusing a thin piece of dark glass to a thicker one of clear glass.

Monarchs who reign over a kingdom, which is a major territorial unit or government ruled by a single person. The term may also refer to rulers of smaller entities and may include tribal rulers or rulers of petty states who are by tradition called "king." If kings rule over a territory that is contained within an empire, kings are typically subordinate to the emperor. Kings are always male; female rulers of kingdoms are called "queens."
People holding the rank of head of the Roman Catholic church and bishop of Rome. Also, the Orthodox patriarchs of Alexandria.
Mirrors, often circular and convex, with elaborately carved and gilded frames that are fitted with branched candleholders.
Long sticks with a pair of footrests about 1 foot from the bottom attached to a powerful spring at the bottom and used for standing on and leaping.
Portable sets of equipment, bandages, and medications used for treating minor ailments or for administering aid a sick or injured person until full medical treatment is available.
Electronic devices that trigger electronic flashes remotely. These may be connected to the flash units via wire or wireless means, usually radio frequency.
The maximum amount or number that can be received or contained, or the ability to receive or contain.
Characteristics and qualities of form, that are figure-derived.
The length of a line that bounds a circular plane surface, equal to pi times the diameter.
Prints collected and grouped together, and that are usually related in theme.
In Indian architecture, relative unit of measurement for establishing the proportions of the maṇḍapa.
Use to describe images, or other single graphic elements that cover a whole page, or nearly so.
Earthenware or similar fireproof vessels in which food is baked and served.
Small pans for baking little pies, commonly referred to as patties.
Small spoons intended primarily for serving prepared (wet) mustard from mustard pots; usually have an elongated bowl and a long, thin handle.

Surveys involving the gathering of basic information about records regarding the quantity, physical form and type, location, physical condition, storage facilities, rate of accumulation, uses, and similar data for the purpose of planning acquisition and disposal programs, microfilming operations, new facilities, and related archival activities.
Small long-handled forks usually with two short tines used to serve olives. For similar forks with three or four tines use "pickle forks."
Use to describe automatic and semiautomatic firearms that utilize recoil to throw back or unlock the bolt or slide and actuate the loading mechanism.
Pieces of hard material, typically stone or metal, sharpened to have a cutting edge or penetrating point for use as projectiles or the heads of projectile weapons.

Red or reddish-brown calf originally produced in Russia and introduced into western Europe in the 17th century, vegetable-tanned with willow, poplar, or larch bark and curried on the flesh side with extract from birch bark, which gave it a characteristic pleasing odor thought to repel insects. It was often finished with a diced pattern. Between 1780 and 1830 it was highly prized for bookbinding, "Russia leather" was made in imitation of it.
Attribute of firearms designed to fire several shots in succession without reloading.
Decorated platforms, either built on a vehicle or towed behind a vehicle or horses, often bearing a display or tableau and drawn in a parade or procession for a festive or solemn occasion.
Lightly armed and armored reconaissance vehicles, either wheeled or half-track, without turrets, and adapted for high-speed operation on either hard roads or for cross-country missions.

Covered, nonmotorized animal-drawn vehicles equipped as traveling living quarters, particularly those used in the 18th and 19th centuries by small itinerant groups or individuals, such as gypsies, tinkers, or traveling salespeople; for motorized counterparts use "motor homes."
Wheeled vehicles designed to carry bodies to gravesites.

Light vehicles on parallel runners, usually having seats and usually open and horse-drawn, for carrying passengers over snow and ice. For similar, but simpler, vehicles for transporting goods or passengers by animal locomotion or gravity, use "sleds."
Oblong pieces of wood, plastic, or aluminum mounted on roller-skate wheels on which riders stand and propel themselves.
Wide double pleats, with the material folded over at each side. For wide double pleats having the flat fold turned out rather than in, use "box pleats."
Soft twill with a slightly napped surface, made in various weights of wool or soft cotton yarn, often in combination with synthetic yarn.
Supplementary warp used to create a pile on a textile.

Warp pile weave, typically silk, with a short, soft dense pile produced by a supplementary warp that is raised in loops above the surface of the textile through the introduction of rods during the weaving; the loops may be cut or left uncut.
Weft supplementary to the main weft, passed from selvage to selvage to enrich the ground or to form a pattern.
Railroad freight vehicles whose bodies are tanks for transporting liquids, gases, or granular solids.
Railroad freight cars designed to carry livestock, generally equipped with slatted sides and doors.

Locomotives powered by onboard internally fired boilers through which hot exhaust gases flow from a firebox in the rear to a smokebox and stack at the front and in which high-pressure steam expands within cylinders to drive two pistons; often having coal or water tenders coupled behind.
Devices for sorting and counting paper money or coins.
A decay of wood caused by fungus that attacks both cellulose and lignin; the resultant mass is spongy or stringy, usually white, but sometimes yellow, tan, or light brown.

A common type of casting flaw that includes a group or area of cavities caused by shrinkage or trapped gases. Porosity may vary considerably in dimension and may or may not break through thesurface of the cast object.
Exertion of force per unit area.
The taking up of the molecules of gases, dissolved substances, or liquids by the surfaces of solids and liquids with which they are in contact.
In glass, the loss of transparency caused by crystallization or deposition of one or more of its ingredients.
The supply of electric power to the human built environment or to tools and equipment.

Describes a process of weathering in which the outer shell of rock becomes more resistant to erosion than its interior. Case hardening occurs by strengthening the exterior shell of the rock or by weakening of the rock's interior. In materials such as sandstone a greater accumulation of cements holding individual grains together at the surface causes shell strengthening. Case hardening in crystalline rock takes place when bonds are broken in the interior through chemical weathering.

To make, arrange, compose, or construct a written work, art work, or other work, by arrangement of materials collected from various sources. It may refer to the arrangement of content only (as in a literary work), or of physical pieces.
The action, process, or result of constructing artificial waterways to conduct water for drainage or irrigation, or for the navigation of boats or ships.
Processes that follow the tanning or tawing of hide or skin, or the stretching and drying of skin that is to be made into parchment, in order to modify it to meet specific needs.
The process and technique of producing, forming, or tracing a pattern, text, or other usually linear motif by cutting, carving, or engraving.
Process of melting previously frozen object.
Decorative forms created when pieces of a material are inserted into similar-sized openings in a surrounding material so as to create a design.
Artists' brushes that are about the same length as flats. They are round and have tapered points, useful for sketching, outlining, and for fine detail.
People who reap or gather crops, either as part of their occupation as farmers or as seasonal workers.
The longitudinal edge of a piece of textile closed by weft loops, often distinguished by warp ends differing from those in the body of the textile and sometimes by a change in the binding.
Yarn deliberately raveled off of a finished textile for the purpose of being reused.

Cloth exported from India as a product that could be traded by European merchants in exchange for African goods. Broadly covers a wide range of cheap, brightly colored fabrics, often striped, checkered, or plain.

A continuous ribbon or band of loose, untwisted fiber that is used to spin yarn. A sliver is created by carding or combing fiber and drawing it into parallel strips that are then ready for drawing, roving, or slubbing.
Extra layer of material placed between a textile and its lining for strength, warmth, shaping, or to improve the hang of the finished product.
Closely woven textile made in various weights, usually of flax, hemp, jute, or cotton, used especially for sails, tarpaulins, awnings, upholstery, bags, and as a support for oil painting.
Elaborate needle-knotted lace, often with three-dimensional flower motifs used as edging on garments and textiles.
Ottoman fabric comprising voided silk velvet woven with gold, gilded silver, and silver metallic threads.
Cloth dyed or marked with a mud solution, as made by the Bamana people of Mali.
Technique of weaving and attaching strips of cloth, typically canvas, to the seats of furniture for support.

Nations whose residents, or some portion thereof, exercise self-government, and usually but not always hold sovereignty over the territory. To specifically designate independent nations having sovereignty, use "independent sovereign nations."
Unsprung four-wheeled vehicles pulled by a pack animal with an open platform for the transport of flax bundles.
Land vehicles equipped with continuous roller belts over cogged wheels for moving across rough terrain.

Machines consisting of a can within a tub used for making ice cream. The cream mixture is poured into the can then frozen and stirred as the can is rotated, either manually or by power, within the ice- and salt-filled tub.
Small, and sometimes pre-moistened pieces of material used for personal hygeine, particularly for washing hands.
Cloths for covering the top of a table, especially during a meal.

A red natural transparent lake colorant that has poor lightfastness and fades in strong sunlight. It is prepared from the bodies of the female scale insect, Dactylopius coccus, native to Mexico, the Canary Islands, and Central and South America. Cochineal dye was used by the Aztec and Maya peoples of Central and North America, adopted by Europeans. The pigments are extracted from the dried bodies of insects using water or alcohol. The substance contains about 10% carminic acid, 2% coccerin wax, and 10% fat: the crimson color of cochineal dye is attributed to cochinealin or carminic acid. Cochineal is also used in medicine as an antispasmodic.
Tongs designed for serving steaks or other cuts of meat.
The balls used in the game of softball, generally in the form of spheres, softer and larger than baseballs and composed of a wound yarn core wrapped in kapok covered with smooth-seamed leather.
Wooden implements, generally with long handles and short striking heads set perpendicular at one end, used to hit balls in certain sports, such as croquet and polo.
Toys, usually representing fat squatting figures, often clowns, that are rounded and weighted at the bottom so as to rock and right themselves when pushed.
Recreational rifles used for target shooting.

Any of a class of synthetic aluminosilicate materials, chains or networks of mineral molecules linked with covalent bonds, used in concrete-polymer composites as an alternative to Portland cement; in resins and binders; and as a decorative cast stone-like material.
Coin-operated gambling machines, activated by various mechanisms, usually a single lever or button, in which the final alignment of predesignated symbols determines the amount of payoff.
Recreational devices for entertaining the public.

Nonmotorized wheeled vehicles intended to be towed by a passenger automobile or small truck to provide a place to sleep while traveling, in some jurisdictions having dimensions designated by law as not exceeding 8 feet wide and 32 feet long.
Aircraft designed or equipped to carry cargo or passengers.
Motorless heavier than air aircraft using air currents to soar from lower to higher altitudes and gravity to descend.
Document genre for the texts of public addresses or talks.
Documents or records that have been written out in a fair, large, or legal character.

Books containing the prescribed order of prayers, readings from the bible, and rites for the canonical hours; often illuminated and intended for the lay community. For books containing the Divine Office for clerics or monastic contexts, use "breviaries."
Small books or pamphlets, usually cheaply printed and containing such texts as popular tales, treatises, ballads, or nursery rhymes, formerly peddled by chapmen.
Books for the visually impaired that are printed using a system of embossed printing, perfected by Braille in 1834.
Tapes made of paper and used for representing data by means of punched holes.
Paper strips that surround the bodies of individual cigars that carry the imprint of the cigar maker. These are used as a means of promoting the maker's brand.
Containers or devices that give out individual straws.
The state or condition of having low moisture content.

Form-fitting one-piece costumes worn as the standard competitive wear for female skaters. Typically consists of a short skirt attached at the waist to a tight bodice and a pair of trunks that are partially revealed under the skirt. Often designed to complement the intended aesthetic or theme of the skater's performance.

Long garments for women, typically cut with flowing lines. Examples include semi-fitted women's dresses worn from the Middle Ages forward, and more formal dresses of modern times. Use "robes" for long, loose garments that tend to be one piece and open down the front, not necessarily women's fashion.
Informal garments made of breathable material, designed to allow their wearers unhindered leg mobility. Typical attire for walking, working, or engaging in other daytime activities.
Dolls with bodies of cloth or cloth stuffed with various materials, as rags, sawdust, or papyrus leaves.
Long-necked lutes of Greece, generally with fixed metal frets, three or four double courses of metal strings, and played with a plectrum.
Plucked lutelike chordophones with a short neck and two strings of the Bisa people of Upper Volta.
Balloons used to carry meteorological instruments, especially radiosondes, aloft; for balloons carrying self-registering instruments aloft for general atmospheric research, use "sounding balloons."
Devices that propel unpowered aircraft aloft by creating lift force and velocity sufficient to keep them airborne on their own.
Heavy, smoothbore military long guns of large caliber, usually muzzleloading, furnished with varying types of firing mechanism throughout their history.

Puzzles consisting usually of irregularly cut pieces of pasteboard or wood that when fitted together form complete pictures; historically, the images would not include maps nor would they purport to have an educational emphasis. For similar puzzles of maps, with an educational function, popular from the mid-18th to the early 19th century, use "dissected maps." For puzzles with tightly interlocking pieces made with a jig or jigsaw, use "jigsaw puzzles."
Early type of artillery, commonly used before breech-loading weapons became common. Projectiles and powder charge are loaded via the muzzle, rammed down the barrel, and then fired at the target.
Heavy artillery mounted on and fired from rail-borne gun carriages.

Short straight, angular, or curved sticks, flat or cylindrical in form, thrown by hand as a hunting or, more rarely, war weapon. They occur in various parts of the world, including ancient Egypt and Australia.
Various types of competitions in which speed in traveling between two or more points is the deciding criterion.

American card game typically played by three players acting alone or four players in two partnerships. The name means "eyeglasses," and refers to the scoring combination of the queen of spades and the jack of diamonds, because the game originated with a deck of cards in which these characters were depicted in profile, having one eye apiece and therefore two eyes in combination. Pinochle is played with 48 cards, with two cards of each rank and suit with aces high through ten, king, queen, jack, and nine low. Tricks as are taken and a table lists storable card combinations in simplified scoring system.

Game for from two to six players, derived from Halma, which is a checkers-type board game invented about 1880. In Chinese checkers, players attempt to move a number of pieces, usually 10 or 15 marbles, on a board in the shape of a six-pointed star that has holes instead of squares. It was introduced in the United States in the 1930s.
Game similar to outdoor tennis played on a table with small paddles and a hollow celluloid or plastic ball.
Game, originated by Native Americans, in which two ten-member teams attempt to score by putting a small ball into each other's netted goal with a crosse, a stick with a netted pouch at the end.

A ball game for two players (or two pairs of players) occupying the same playing area in a four-walled court, in which the ball is directed with a racket against the front wall, points (in the modern game) being won by the server if the opponent is unable to return the ball successfully within the laws of the game. Rackets is distinguished from the more recent game, squash, in particular by the use of a solid, harder ball. Rackets is now played in covered indoor courts, but rackets is known to have been played in open outdoor courts before the 19th century, though the exact nature of the original game is uncertain.
Frames with overlapping moldings and corner embellishment, often carved to imitate wood bark, popular in the 19th century and named for American artists Nathaniel Currier and James M. Ives.
Frames that incorporate microclimate systems to reduce fading and preserve sensitive works of art, particularly photographs and works on paper.
Frames having their highest moldings on the sight edge.

Sound modifying devices which incorporate mirlitons set in vibration by the human voice, and used to disguise the voice of the user; in Africa they are often employed in the context of masquerades, ceremonies, and rituals.

Valveless brass aerophones with conical bores. These were used mostly in the military to give signals to the infantry. Now chiefly used to refer to trumpet-like instruments of this kind in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, distinguished from modern "bugles."
Wing-shaped bowed zitherlike chordophones with a fingerboard along the left side and two strings stopped by means of buttons.

Zitherlike chordophones of France having a long, slightly tapered shallow soundbox with one heart-shaped and one roseate sound hole and five strings, two of which are melody and three are drones. The melody strings, running over fixed frets, are stopped in unison by a small stick held in the left hand as the right hand strums all five strings.
A technique that chemically analyzes a substance by measuring changes in its weight due to increasing temperature. It can be used to study the stability of materials.
Armors, typically of elaborate workmanship and highly decorated, made for wear in ceremonies, on state occasions, and at other special events.

Double pieces to reinforce the visor, consisting of a plate shaped to the lower half of the visor and to the chin, attached to the helmet by a strap around the neck and buckled at the back. Designed for armets and close helmets, they were used in jousts and tournaments.

A method of correspondence developed during World War II that allowed US civilians and military personnel abroad to communicate. The system was based on letter-sheets designed to fold into envelopes, and which allowed only for brief texts.  After mailing, V-Mail letters were reviewed by censors, photographically reduced on microfilm, and sent to processing centers overseas where facsimiles were reproduced at one-quarter their original size. These facsimiles were then delivered to the addressee. The system allowed for the reduction of shipping space needed for war materials, and speeded delivery by air rather than by sea.

Rules with proportioned graduations for measuring or making scale drawings. The term refers to a graduated strip of metal or wood used for measuring length as well as to a rule drawn or otherwise indicated on an architectural drawing, map, or other work.

Rulers composed of light strips of wood joined so that the individual pieces fold and usually pivot in more than one plane; most commonly in 2-foot lengths with four folds. Historically superseded by zigzag rules, which are generally longer and have strips that all fold, zigzag fashion, in a single plane and by metal tape rules.

A form of mass spectrometry commonly used for surface analysis. When a primary beam of accelerated ions strikes a solid surface, secondary ions are among the elements displaced in a process called sputtering. These ions may be directly studied to gain information about the target material.
Single- or multi-pronged pins used to hold hair or headgear in place or for decorative effect.
Bonnets of fabric or straw having a wide brim to shade the face, often a ruffle around the front and sides, and sometimes a capelike extension in the back to protect the neck.

An anhydrous grayish-white, odorless, water-soluble powder, NA2CO3, usually obtained by the Solvay process and containing about 1 percent of impurities consisting of sulfates, chlorides, and bicarbonates. It is used in the manufacture of glass, ceramics, soaps, paper, petroleum products, as a cleanser, for bleaching, and in water treatment.
Sulfur dioxide dissolved in water.
Matched sets of ornaments intended to be worn together, either jewels or trimmings for costume, usually a collar and cuffs.

Long, straight, poles of metal or wood, usually circular in section, that constitute the main bodies of staff weapons, serving as handles and to carry the heads. For the smaller objects of similar form constituting the main bodies of arrows, use "shafts (tool components)."
Handheld objects of generally round shape made of clustered fibrous or metallic material, used by cheerleaders in their routines.
Gameset containing skittles and balls for bowling. Dimensions and materials vary.
An apparatus consisting of two long, parallel wooden bars set on pairs of uprights adjustable in height and width and designed for vaulting, balancing, and swinging gymnastic exercises.
One- or two-person low-slung sleds specially tailored to fit the rider, generally about 51 inches long and with a maximum weight of 44 pounds, and used to race down chutelike courses.

Small to medium-sized figures comprising a carved or molded bust or half-figure, set upon a cage, which may resemble a cage crinoline or may be of simpler design. The cage is usually made of wood or metal. The figures are designed to wear clothing, with long skirts covering the cage. Many cage dolls are religious statues, representing the Virgin Mary, angels, or saints, including but not limited to such figures in the Hispanic tradition of "santos." Another use of cage dolls was as "fashion dolls," to display dresses in miniature in order to allow the customer to choose a fashion. For porcelain or wooden objects representing a figure, often female, from the waist up, intended to be sewn or attached to a base or lower body but not to a cage, use "half dolls."

Flat, rectangular blocks, usually of bone, ivory, or wood and occurring in sets of 28, the top face of each being divided transversely into two equal parts by a line; each part is either blank or bears from one to six pips or dots, so as to present all the possible combinations from double blank to double six. Sometimes the pieces have more pips, and are more in number accordingly.

Optical toys consisting of disks with different images on each side which, when the disks are spun rapidly, tend to merge together as the strings on which the disks are mounted are pulled by the fingers; developed in the 1820s.
Books having an extra covering of leather allowing the book to be hung from the girdle and read while still attached.
Books printed before 1501.
Bindings in which the cover of the book is made completely before it is attached to the text block.

Weights used in athletic training, as depicted in classical Greek sculpture and vase painting. Two shaped weights joined by a leather strap are swung by a long-jumper to increase momentum. The weights themselves have been depicted in various forms from half-moon to cylindrical hourglass shapes.
Lightweight solids, usually cubical and often of wood, plastic, or similar material, occurring in sets and designed as children's toys.

Toys and games that require dexterity and practice. Dexterity toys often involve a physical activity, such as hula hooping, juggling, and jumping rope or can involve precision and aiming such as shooting games, marbles and throwing games.
Toys, usually wheeled, that are designed to be either pulled or pushed.
Play apparatus consisting of a plank 10 to 14 feet long and supported and balanced in the middle upon which two children, one seated at each end, can ride up and down.
Chess pieces that move as queens are designated to move; the most powerful of chess pieces.

In Scotland, a pair of straps or pieces of string tied around the leg just below the knee to secure the trousers of farmworkers; used to keep the bottom of trousers lifted clear of dirt to keep them clean.
Metal devices worn on helmets that indicate rank or unit.

Decorative attachments resembling suspenders, with shaped straps which pass over each shoulder, and sometimes connect to a matching waistband. The straps are sometimes connected by horizontal bands across the chest or back.
Loose shirtlike garments, often knee-length, worn for sleeping.
Hanging nose ornament in postclassic central Mexico. It could be worked in gold, decorated with stones or painted. Usually worn by slaves destined for sacrifice.
Use to distinguish those signs that convey general information from those that are "direction signs," "identification signs," or "regulatory signs."
Jewelry specifically worn on costume, as opposed to worn on the body.

Cloths or clothing, usually white, worn to cover the chrism, which is a holy material comprising oil and balsam, used in various rituals and sacraments, especially Christian baptism. Examples includes white strips of fabric or cloths wrapped around the heads of the newly baptized, over the place where the chrism had been applied. Other examples are long white-hooded robes in which the newly-baptized were clothed for several weeks.
Cards that mark a place reserved for occupancy.

Carved wooden staffs of the Akan people of Africa. They are surmounted by carved finials of various figures, often covered in gold leaf, representing at least one proverbial saying. Held and displayed by the chief counselors of paramount chiefs at public events, they serve as the badges of office of those counselors and their proverbial subject matter refers to the continuity and political dominance of chief and state, the responsibilities of the chief, and the appropriate and wise behavior of the chief's subjects.
Long zithers with a slightly convex soundboard and flat bottom, having 13 silk or nylon strings each passing over its own movable, V-shaped bridge; it is considered the national instrument of Japan.
Wool mantles worn by women and men in ancient Greece.

An emulsion of asphalt cement and water, that contains a small amount of emulsifying agent. The amount of asphalt in emulsion will depend upon the grade and type, but is typically 55-65% by volume. Uses include surfacing floors, painting pipes, and waterproofing concrete walls.
Uniforms worn by sports teams and athletes.
Shirts made for expectant mothers, typically fashioned from loose fitting or stretchy material.

Light open helmets of ogival or hemispherical form, commonly furnished with a comb, a pointed peak projecting over the eyes, gorget plates on the lower part of the falling buffe, and hinged cheekpieces or earflaps. They were worn by infantry and light cavalry during the 16th and 17th centuries.

Gauntlets consisting of a tubular plate cuff, a single plate or several articulated lames covering the back of the hand, and lames covering the fingers, with only the thumb being allowed independent movement. They were popular in German-dominated Europe from the 15th into the mid-16th century.
Small muffs or fingerless mittens that cover the wrist and part of the hand. Most often these are knitted or crocheted. For handwear with finger holes, use 'mitts (fingerless handwear)'.

Steam-driven warships of the 19th and early 20th centuries equipped with an armored prow to be used as a primary weapon against other ships; for rowed warships equipped with ramming prows, use "galleys (watercraft)" or a descriptor under "<multilevel rowed watercraft>."
Wires in the plane of the outer cover of an aircraft for locally reinforcing this cover in that part of the airship and reducing fluttering in flight die to air pressure or other factors.
Platforms extending part-way or all the way from side to side of a vessel, forming a covering for the space below and itself serving as a floor.
Vessels engaged in transporting human beings for sale as slaves, sometimes designed specifically for the purpose.

Animal-drawn carts used historically to transport heavy materials such as manure. These may be considered particular to parts of Belgian and the Netherlands, though the general form of the two-wheeled cart is familiar to many places. These consist of an axle mounted to two wheels supporting a load-bearing platform. The distinguishing feature of the earth cart is that the mounts or beams for pulling the cart are separate hinged pieces attached to the support of the load platform so that the platform may be tilted while still mounted to a pack animal.
Four-wheeled, usually horse-drawn, firefighting vehicles mounting large reels for carrying fire hoses.
White, highly deliquescent opaque crystals or powder that is soluble in water and alcohol and decomposed by heat. It has a low toxicity and a pungent saline taste.
Saddles on which a rider sits with both legs to one side of the horse, designed originally for female riders in skirts.
Posts mounted in pairs on the decks of a ship, for fastening mooring lines, cables, or ropes.
Lace or ribbon flounces attached to the back of a bonnet to cover a lady's neck for modesty or to prevent sunburn.

Rectangular pieces of fabric wrapped from the back of the head and either tied or tucked behind the head so as to expose the face. Head wraps in the United States have been associated with slavery and servitude of African American women. In recent years some women have reclaimed the garment to assert their heritage.
Obsidian-bladed weapons of postclassic central Mexico.
Knitted wool cylinders that are pulled over the head and fashioned into caps by rolling up one end of the tube. Cap comforters evolved from informal British military headgear.

Caps that are worn by the Pope, larger than a skull-cap and having flaps over the ears. They are often made of red wool or velvet and ornamented with red satin, having swan's down trim or lined with ermine. It is white during the week in albis. The name means "camel-skin cap"; incorporated in the Papal wardrobe since the 12th century.
Rope-soled shoes often with canvas or cotton upper, sometimes laced across the vamp and around the ankle.

Low boots of a type first designed for Roman military use and later adapted for other uses. They are first known by the time of Augustus. The soles comprise several layers of leather, which may be nailed all around with hobnails for traction; the uppers may be cut in open latice work for ventilation, giving the boots a sandal-like appearance. For Christian liturgical footwear known by a homograph, use "liturgical stockings."
Chromatography with paper strips or sheets as the adsorbent through which the solution flows by gravity or is sucked up by capillarity.
In matchlocks, snaphances, and wheel locks, small, shallow receptacles for holding the priming powder.

Carved, painted, embroidered, or otherwise decorated panels or hangings that cover all four sides of a Christian altar, as distinct from an antependium which covers the front alone. The term may also refer to similar hangings or ornaments of a room of state. The term formerly referred to both the vestments worn by the celebrants of Christian services and the hangings around the altar; over time it has come to mean only the hangings and panels.
Loosely woven textile covers for upholstery foundations, used immediately under the top covers, usually to cover springs or layers of stuffing.

Slotted boxes or other containers used, often in churches, for receiving offerings or donations. They may be portable, or fixed to a part of the building or a furnishing. Portable collection boxes typically have a handle used to pass around in order to collect donations.

Coaches used for public transportation along scheduled routes having intermediary stops to change horses; in use by the mid-17th century. Forms having an oval body, outside driver's seat, and single door in each side were popular in the United States from the early 19th until the early 20th century.

Lightweight, open-front, four-wheeled horse-drawn carriages intended for families, particular to the United States, and obsolete after the mid-19th century. These had long bodies with seating for multiple passengers, and were suspended on straps or springs.
Light, two-wheeled carriages generally pulled by a single horse, hung by braces from the springs and used for pleasure driving; mostly of the 18th and 19th centuries.

Insoluble, white, fibrous protein comprising the filaments of raw silk, secreted along with sericin by the insect. Unlike wool, silk is composed mainly of non-sulfur containing amino acids. The primary amino acids, glycine, alanine and serine, are contained in dense, highly crystalline regions of the fiber. The amorphous regions are composed of tryosine, tryptophane, histidine and phenylalanine.
Unconsolidated material on the earth's surface formed by the weathering of rock and that portion of the earth's surface that can support plant life.
Hollow, decoratively shaped forms into which warm gelatin is poured to cool to create a gelatin dessert in the same shape.

Describes human voices and occasionally musical instruments pitched lower than tenor,  but higher than bass. For some instruments, such as the oboe, it refers to the deepest voice of the instrument family.

Bottles covered with wicker and holding from 1 quart to 10 gallons; intended to contain noncorrosive and bland liquids. For similar large bottles covered with wicker, wood, or other protective material and intended for corrosive liquids, acids or distilled water, use "carboys."
Bottles containing holy water or oil used in the christening or baptismal ceremony; may be inscribed with a commemoration of the occasion.
Filters, typicallly made of paper, but also made of metal, used in coffee brewing to separate the coffee grounds from the water.
Large knives with a broad blade of varying form used to cut and serve ice cream and similar frozen desserts.
Tray-like supports with handles used for serving and transporting dishes such as casseroles. Also frame-like holders, often of a decorative metal, used for more formal serving.
Forks for eating ice cream and similar foods and having a bowl or spoonlike end terminating with three or four small tines.

Small knives with a flat blade, often decoratively shaped and lacking a sharp edge but having a sharp tip; designed to remove the backbone of the individual serving of fish and with a conforming fish fork to eat fish.
Spoons intended for eating desserts, intermediate in size between a teaspoon and a tablespoon. May be accompanied by a dessert fork; sometimes a part of a dessert service.

Spoons having a fairly large carrying bowl and a rounded end, designed for feeding pap, which is liquid or semi-liquid grain meal moistened with water and suitable for babies or invalids. The pap is sipped from the bowl or poured from the bowl into the mouth. The bowl is somewhat larger than that of a baby spoon or feeding spoon, the bowls of which are designed to fit entirely within the baby's mouth. These spoons were popular in the 19th and early 20th centuries. They are often of silver and given as gifts, intended to be kept as a memento of infanthood.
Term applied to a wide variety of special-purpose utensils designed to serve lemon slices, especially those which have an ornately pierced surface.
Hand tools intended to mix and divide dough. These usually appear as tools carved from wood with a shovel-like end and handles of various lengths, though they can be made of any material.
Culinary tools used to remove hulls from grain, nuts, or fruit.
Cards on which a message may be written or printed for mailing without an envelope, usually at a lower rate than that for letters in envelopes.
Electric food mixers that are designed such that the beaters are mounted in a stand that can accomodate a bowl, leaving the user's hands free.
A book hand derived from later Roman cursive and used from the 5th to the 7th century.
An Arabic cursive script from which modern Arabic writing descends.
Self-propelled long-distance weapons that are directed either by remote control or automatically, to detonate like devices in the air.
Devices, ranging from simple sheet pans to electrical machines, used for coating sweets (comfit), with chocolate, nuts, or sugar.
Large long-handled forks used to lift meat as from the pot or pan in which it was cooked.
Idiophones consisting of sonorous sticks, used individually or in sets, sounded by being struck against a hard object or another stick.

Percussion idiophones made from the ends of oil drums, cut to a relatively shallow depth, made concave, subdivided by grooves, and hammered so as to create up to 30 segments, each of which produces a tuned pitch when struck with a rubber-headed stick.
European lip-vibrated aerophones of bass register, consisting of a serpentine wood tube about seven feet in length and of conical bore, with a long crook carrying a cup mouthpiece.

Aerophones of conical bore with a widely flared bell, funnel-shaped mouthpiece, and slender tube which curves into wide circular coils; today it is furnished with valves, which are usually positioned to be played by the left hand while the right hand is placed in the bell for stopping. Commonly used in the brass section of Western-style orchestras as well as smaller ensembles and in solo work.
Keyboard instruments outwardly resembling grand pianos but with a different, simpler action, involving tangents being pushed against the strings, rather than hammers striking them.
Keywork developed for the flute in the 18th century, most often using eight keys.
Veils covering the body from head to foot, typically made of sheer black cotton or silk, and worn by Swahili women of Zanzibar, Pemba, and the coastal cities and towns of Tanzania and Kenya.

Long, full, and usually hooded cloaks or overcoats made of a rough cloth or skins; use especially for those worn during the Middle Ages or later by travelers and soldiers as part of a military uniform.
Leather leg coverings held together at the top by a belt or lacings, worn over trousers when horseback riding.

Close-fitting, usually knitted underwear made of natural or synthetic fibers and consisting of drawers and a shirt with sleeves that usually reach the wrist; may be in one or two pieces; worn to retain body heat or wick moisture off the body.
Frames of varied construction worn at or below the waist in the back to distend the garment backward at the hips.
Pieces of cloth, usually square, varying in size and material, carried for usefulness or as a costume accessory.

Close-fitting waist-length or hip-length garments with or without sleeves worn by men from the 15th to the 17th century and for similar garments reinforced by mail and worn under armor. Also refers to sleeved, hip-length garments worn as part of military uniforms by the Scottish units of the British army after 1855.

Garments comprising a leaf or a cluster of leaves, often resembling the leaves of the fig tree, used as a cover for the genitalia. Typically depicted in art works of nude figures; for example, on a statue or painting of the Biblical subject Adam and Eve.
Weights sewn or fastened to the bottom of the large sleeves to make them hang well.
Wide sashes worn around the waist, often horizontally pleated; worn with tuxedoes and as part of miltary uniforms.

Neckwear that resembles a short chemisette, meant to cover a woman's neck and chest. Often white, and made in a variety of fabrics. For headwear that envelops the head, chin, sides of the face, and neck, and retained as headwear by nuns, use 'wimples'.
Ribbons, strings, or narrow bands of any material used for binding the hair, or worn round the head to keep the headdress in position, or simply for ornament.
Hair accessories made of rope, ribbon, or fabric. Made of knots with two loops and two ends. Sometimes affixed to clips, headbands, or pins.
Ornaments consisting essentially or partly of a pointed penetrating wire or shaft.
The phenomenon through which the same color can reveal different hues, depending only on the colors surrounding it.
A material of white to light gray or light yellow color, extremely lightweight, absorbent, and compact, that is found in Asia Minor and is used for making tobacco pipes and ornamental carvings.
Overcoats made from animal or artificial fur.
Men's two-piece casual suits consisting of trousers and a matching jacket styled like a shirt.

In the Nahuatl language, refers to the loose and boxy, often colorfully embroidered blouse worn by Indigenous women of Mesoamerica. Traditionallly formed from a single rectangular piece of cloth with a slit in the center for the head, folded in half and sewn up the sides leaving openings for the arms. Associated with the skirt called cueitl.
Fulls skirts gathered or pleated on a tight waistband.  Also, similar parts of dresses.
Women's casual trousers with a tapered leg that ends above the ankle which often have a vertical slit at the outside bottom edge.
Hosiery that covers the foot and extends to somewhere below the knee.
Full, circular plaited collars worn in the 16th and 17th centuries by both men and women. Usually made of stiffened lace or linen or of muslin and frequently trimmed with lace.
Very narrow neckties usually tied in a bow knot.

A serpentinite whose predominant color is usually a shade of green although there are a few purple varieties. It often bears a strong resemblance to granite; the best serpentina comune comes from Liguria, Italy.

Clothing worn by Catholic boys and girls during the ceremony and often integral day of their first Communion. The outfits are from the 1830s very similar to wedding clothes: light-colored dresses and accessories for girls and a suit or uniform for boys.
Shawl-like garments, often of wool or silk, with fringe at the four corners; worn around the shoulders by Jewish males usually during the morning service.
Golden armbands worn on the upper arm by tlahtohqueh (rulers) in postclassic central Mexico and also given as gifts of prestige.

Long, semi-circular cloaklike garments fastened at the neck with a morse; worn by ecclesiastics in processions and on other ceremonial occasions. Also, similar garments worn as coronation or processional robes by laymen.
Half- or three-quarter-length funnel-shaped sleeves that flare at the bottom to resemble a pagoda roof; fashionable especially during the third quarter of the 19th century in Western cultures.
Thermometers having a bulb that is kept moistened.

Culinary utensils that are basically flat, such as forks and spoons, and have no cutting edge. Distinguished from "hollowware" such as drinking vessels and bowls. In modern usage the term embraces all types of flat culinary utensils with or without a cutting edge; however, prefer "cutlery" when referring to culinary utensils with a cutting edge, especially various forms of knives used for food. Flatware is now usually made in sets having on the handles similar or related decorative patterns.
Shallow, flat-bottomed, wooden vessels with sloped sides, used to contain the pressed butter for further processing with a butter paddle.
Long handled three-tined forks used for cooking meats or poultry and or other kitchen uses.

Spoons of teaspoon size having a bowl pierced in a decorative pattern and long handle with a pointed end. The bowls of mote spoons were used to strain tea and to skim leaf particles and dust motes from the surface of a cup of tea. The thin pointed handle was used to clear clogged spouts of pots. For spoons of similar size with pierced bowls but lacking pointed handles, used specifically to serve olives, use "olive spoons."
Implements used to cut clusters of grapes into small portions.

Apparatuses used to slice cheese, typically comprising a board and an attached knife or wire for cutting the cheese. One example comprises a guillotine-style metal blade equipped with a wooden handle attached to a wooden turnstyle cutting block.
Small ladles intended primarily for serving sauces; generally smaller than gravy ladles and sometimes made as part of a flatware service.
Boxes intended primarily for packing goods for transport or storage.
Instruments on land or water vehicles that measure and indicate the rate of travel; usually graduated in miles, kilometers, or knots per hour.
Devices used to broil meat, fish, poultry, or other foods.

Refers to the specific process of arranging type from copy for printing or making printing plates, whether by hand, by mechanical devices, or by inputting to computer. More generally, for the preparing of copy, casting off, arranging type, spacing, and other material, use "composition (printing preparation)."

Short, pithy statements of principle or precepts, often of known authorship; distinguished from "proverbs" which are statements repeated colloquially and which often embody the folk wisdom of a group or nation.
Words or phrases preceded by a hash symbol to identify and categorize messages about a particular subject. Created on and primarily used on social media.
Plays produced for schools, colleges, universities, or any educational institution, for any academic grade or level.
Pierced bowl-like strainers or specially designed pails used to strain milk.
Any of various devices or machines for cutting or shaping food or expressing liquids from food by means of applied pressure.
Stone tools used, along with a poi board, to beat taro root into a staple Hawaiian dish known as poi.
Machines used to grind grains into flour.
Devices used to slice butter.
Devices used to remove corks from bottles. It typically consists of a body affixed to a surface, and a lever that inserts a prong into the cork. When the lever is pulled back, the cork is extracted.
Flutes in use primarily in 18th-century Europe, ranging a minor third below the standard range.

Sets of printed characters, comprised of alphabets, numerals, and other symbols, that share certain characteristics of style or design. For the rectangular pieces, usually metal, having a character on one side, from which text is composed and set to be printed, use "type."
Containers consisting of two pots, one of which fits partway into the other; water is boiled in the lower pot to warm, melt, or cook the substance in the other.

Refers to rock in its original environment, as opposed to having been quarried. It typically refers to rock that is carved or otherwise used in situ, often to sculpture or architecture carved in situ.

Muzzleloading rifle bullets with a conical head, cylindrical body, and a three-grooved hollow base which, upon firing, expanded to fill the barrel rifling. They were developed in the mid-19th century by Captain Claude-Étienne Minié, among others, but rapidly grew obsolete with the increasing use of breechloading firearms and practical fixed ammunition in the late 19th century.

Devices or assemblies of devices designed to support artillery and heavy small arms such as machine guns. They range from simple tripods to complex supporting, pivoting, and elevating mechanisms on gun carriages.
Ancient Egyptian writing, and certain other scripts, such as Mayan, composed of characters that are for the most part pictographic.

Chordophones with a viol-like body but unfretted, held and bowed like the viola; it has seven playing strings which pass over the top of the bridge and seven sympathetic strings which run through the bridge and under the fingerboard into separate pegs in the pegbox.

In technical examination of artifacts, use of light-sources, such as light-emitting diodes, to excite pigments to emit infrared radiation as luminescence in the visible range. The emission is recorded by a digital camera equipped with suitable filters.
Chants of musical verse or incantation known in various versions throughout the Buddhist world.

Rolls containing texts for the celebration of Easter, including the Exultet hymn, and having illustrations, placed upside down in relation to the text; when the roll was draped over the lectern, the images appeared right side up to the congregation.

Facilities for the congregation of the team and other members of a polo club, which is an association involved with the equestrian team sport of polo. Facilities for the congregation of the team and other members of a polo club, which is an association involved with the equestrian team sport of polo.
Bowls designed with a cover that may be removed.
Social class, especially of Europe prior to the Industrial Revolution, comprised of persons that till the soil to support themselves. For individual members of this class, use "peasants."
Horizontal cloth hangings fixed across the top of an opening; generally used as decorative headings to conceal the tops of curtains and their hardware.
Symmetrical pairs of curtains.
Curtains hung in doorways or archways to separate spaces, prevent drafts, or serve as decorative elements.
Small explosive shells that were designed to be rolled down the rampart of a fortification to harass the besieging enemy.
Wallpapers decorated with a pattern of alternating vignettes framed by vertical stripes, flowers, or foliage. Used also for the individual vignettes.
Artillery ammunition in which the projectile is permanently attached to a case containing the primer and propellant, so that it is supplied ready for loading as a single unit.
Ancient Persian gold coins possibly introduced by Darius I in the late 6th century BCE and in use until the early 4th century BCE.

A type of rimmed, cylindrical ammunition used specifically in shotguns, which are filled with metal shot, or pellets, powder, and primer. The case is usually of paper or plastic fitted into a brass base that contains the primer cup.

Historically, specially treated cases of linen in which a charge of powder and shot for firearms is made up. These were developed in 1852 by American inventor Christian Sharps as part of his Sharps rifle. The added strength of the linen cartridge was an improvement on paper cartridges. The rear of the linen cartridge had flash paper attached for ignition. The linen used was treated with starch for stiffness and other chemicals to make the linen more combustible.
Tentlike hangings designed to be suspended over a bed or cradle.
18th-century wall coverings made in Germany and neighboring areas of textile saturated in molten wax and oil then painted.

Loose covers for furniture, often tailored and close fitting, but easily slipped on and off. Used to protect the finer upholstery materials beneath from soil or wear, to conceal shabby upholstery, or to enhance the decorative scheme of an interior.
Decorative coverings enclosing or laid over pillows when they are not in use.  For sacklike coverings for pillows use "pillowcases."

Widely circulated small, silver French coins introduced in the mid-8th century; appear in debased form until the French Revolution. For comparable English coins, also derived from Roman denarii, use "pennies."
Rich pieces of cloth spread upon or over something.

Curtains located behind the royal door of an iconostasis, separating the nave from the sanctuary. Some Eastern churches have only the curtains without the iconostasis.  In Christian theological interpretation, the New Testament reference to the rending of the temple curtains at Jesus' death came to signify his passing through the heavenly boundary, thus the curtain was continued in certain liturgies.
Coverings of cloth or other material used to decorate or cover the gradine or altar ledge of the altar in Christian churches.

Curtains that hang in front of or behind the doors of the Torah ark in a synagogue, often richly embroidered. They are based on the curtains in the ancient Jewish temple, which were used to conceal the Holy of Holies from the people; no one was permitted to enter the area except the high priest once per year on the Day of Atonement.
Pieced quilts composed of blocks divided by two horizontal and two vertical seams into a grid of nine major areas.
Devices that emit an audible repetitive tap to regulate musical tempo. Many different forms exist, most commonly the small clock work-driven pyramidal devices with a beating rod in front.

Leverlike mechanical devices attached to or forming an integral part of a musical instrument or other sound device, functioning either as part of the direct sound-producing mechanism, as when admitting air to a pipe or causing a string to be struck or plucked, or, when on a confined aerophone, as devices governing those tone-holes that are out of reach or too large for the unaided finger.

Ensembles of Southeast Asia, consisting of various combinations of gongs, metallophones, xylophones, drums, bowed and plucked chordophones, flutes or double reed aerophones, small cymbals, and singers. They accompany dances and religious and ceremonial events.
Armor pieces worn in both foot and mounted combat to protect the upper part of the buttocks, consisting of one or more articulated lames.

Armored sleeveless jackets used by infantry from the mid-14th century to the beginning of the 17th century, consisting of small rectangular metal plates, overlapping in vertical strips, mounted on a fabric or hide support in parallel rows, the whole being sewn to a quilted jacket which gave the garments their final shape.

A type of art glass characterized by large air bubbles of various sizes combined with larger unsifted glass particles, and cased with heavier clear glass. Cluthra glassware is made from a lump of crystal glass on a blowing iron, which is rolled across a marver that had been sprinkled with powdered glass of any desired color. It was developed at Steuben Glass Works before 1930 as a variation on the very similar Clutha glass.
Pulsed radar devices for measuring the vertical height of ionospheric layers.
Instruments for measuring, and often also recording, the amount of water passing a specified point in a piping system.
Scales in which the balance pan for loads is a platform mounted on a balanced beam or series of levers; usually used for heavy goods, often in bulk.
Scales, in use predominantly from the 13th to the 18th century, for weighing coins to prevent the circulation of pieces that were light or clipped.

Japanese spike fiddles having a long neck, square body, parchment belly and back, and from two to four strings. They are held vertically by the kneeling players and rotated to select the appropriate string to be sounded by the bow, which always follows the same path.
Ancient devices for measuring the passage of time that depended upon the regular flow of water into or out of graduated vessels.
Devices that automatically time a process or event or activate an operation or another device at a preset time or times; may or may not give an audible signal at the end of the timed interval.
Fipple flutes played in ensemble with the small drums called tabors, held and played by the left hand while the tabor is played by the right.
Instruments used to determine the hardness of materials by measuring the pressure needed to scratch, indent, or pierce the materials.

Instruments for estimating the percentage of butter fat in milk. The instrument comprises a cylindrical bottle that tapers off at one end to a graduated tube with a conical bulb termination. It is often used with instruments gauging the purity of milk, "lactometers."
Devices used for measuring the height and diameter of trees using principles based on the relation of the sides of similar triangles.
Instruments that measure vertical angles by taking a sight and reading against a vertical pendulum or by measuring the angle between the earth's magnetic field vector and the horizontal plane.
Timepieces that indicate the difference between mean solar time and apparent time (usually based on Greenwich mean time).

Ecclesiastical drinking vessels for eucharistic wine having a stem, often with a central knop, and a foot; often made of precious metals and usually accompanied by a paten. Use "communion cups" when referring to similar but generally less ornate ecclesiastical drinking vessels used in the Protestant Church during or after the Reformation.
Instruments for measuring the frequencies of tones or exact pitch, as a set of graduated tuning forks.
Object components which are used to cover or close a mouth or other openings on containers.

Standard closed, often lightproof, covers or containers used to hold film, microfilm, magnetic audio tape, or video recording tape, having  both supply and take-up spools enclosed, and so designed that the cassette needs merely to be inserted into a suitable tape recorder, camera, computer, or video recorder to be ready for use. Such cassettes are usually made of made of plastic or lightweight metal and are flat and rectangular in shape.
Simple, utilitarian blankets.

Plates commemorating a child's baptism or christening, of metal or ceramic and often having decorations or an inscription. Examples would be particular types of plates of brass, ceramic, or tin that were common in the 17th-18th centuries in Gelderland, the Netherlands; these plates were sometimes used as offertory plates for well-wishers of the child, often given by the godparents to commemorate the baptism. The tradition grew, in part, out of the earlier tradition of the "birth trays." Modern christening plates may be both commemorative and utilitarian, used by the child to hold food for consumption.
