Rectangular, flat containers made of flexible material that is folded to produce overlapping seams that are adhered together on two or three edges; often with a flag closure, and intended for small objects or documents.
Cases fitted closely to a swathed mummy usually having the face area modeled and the body portion covered with ritualistic emblems.

A sack filled with feed that is tied onto the head of a horse or other livestock. Printed cotton feed bags were recycled as inexpensive women's wear and quilting during the US Depression in the 1930s.
Dishes used during meals in medieval times to discard food fragments and other waste.
Tanks designed for safe storage of oil used for fuel. Often made of metal.

Small containers designed to store cosmetics and other personal hygiene materials. Cosmetic boxes are found in the form of a cube, disk, or other shape, generally having a lid. Best known as works from ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, and Asia, dating from the Late Bronze age, made from materials such as wood, ivory or bone.
Containers or pouches for the storage and organization of belts.
Clock and watch escapements in which the pallet axis is set at right angles to the axis of the escape wheel; probably the earliest type of escapement and now obsolete.
Warm, heavily wadded bedcovers usually consisting of three layers (top, backing, and filling) which are often tufted or tied rather than quilted.
Quilts with tops made of a single textile, with neither pieced nor appliquéd designs, decorated solely with quilting. A different textile may be used as backing or border.
Quilts worked by the bereaved during a period of mourning, often black, white, or gray, with appropriate patterns or motifs.

Quilts made of blocks constructed of strips of fabric arranged in a way that simulates the construction of a log cabin; usually done by press piecing, tied rather than quilted, and rarely containing batting.

Mouth organs of Japan, descended from the Chinese "sheng", having a lacquered wood bowl for a windchest, a short mouthpiece, and 17 bamboo pipes arranged in a circle in symmetrical order, two of which are silent, with neither reed nor fingerhole.

Containers shaped like deep, lidded glass jars, designed to serve pickles. Pickle casters were typically placed in a silver or silver-plated frame with a handle, sometimes in pairs; often with matching tongs or forks, which hang from the frame.

Dishes, often covered, that are designed and used to serve the main course at table. Entrée dishes are usually fine silver dishes, intended for formal use, and often date to the 17th-19th centuries. They may have a means of keeping the food warm, such as having a space for hot water or a candle. For more modern dishes used for keeping food warm at table or at a buffet, use "chafing dishes."

Drinking vessels of varying form but usually bearing a Hebrew inscription, used for drinking wine in Jewish religious ceremonies, on special occasions such as weddings, or in the benediction before the evening meal preceding each Sabbath or holy festival.
Single-headed bass drums with a very shallow shell, suspended by straps from a frame.
Double-headed drums of India, usually played in a horizontal position.

Type of banded wine cup common throughout the Mediterranean in the sixth and seventh centuries BCE. The designation is something of a misnomer as the cups were made in several parts of the Greek world including Sicily and Southern Italy. Nonetheless, they are ultimately dependent on an East Greek model.
Decorative cups presented to infants or their parents on the occasion of their baptism or christening; often of silver or other precious material.
Open, usually cylindrical containers used to hold cigarettes on a table, desk, or the like. For covered boxes used to hold cigarettes, use "cigarette boxes."
Rubber bags or earthenware bottles for holding hot water; used for local application of warmth to the body.
Boxes intended primarily for holding sewing notions.
Open baskets with upcurving sides to which is attached a large handle; of a type intended primarily for gathering flowers or herbs.
Accurate surveying instruments that use electronic-optical devices that measure distance on the basis of the velocity of light.
Narrow trays designed or used for pens, often forming part of an inkstand.
Baskets, often coiled baskets, in which dough is set to rise.
Shallow receptacles used to serve bread at the table; often rectangular with upcurving sides.
Ceramic vessels of simple, rough construction, made by hand, and used as containers for liquids or solid food.

Covered spouted vessels for preparing and serving coffee. The term is often reserved for a decorative vessel made of ceramic, silver, or another material and used to transport and serve the coffee at table after it has been prepared in another vessel. Coffee pots typically have a handle and sometimes small feet.
A type of kantharos featuring handles as in type A, a continuously curved bowl, and a torus foot with a very short stem.

A type of neck amphorae found in large numbers in Etruscan site in Italy, and not in Greece, so that they were originally thought to be Etruscan-made, Tyrrhenian being an old name for Etruscan. It is now know that they were made in Athens specifically for export to Italy. Komasts (dancers) and the adventures of Herakles are among the most popular subjects for Tyrrhenian vases. The artists to whom these vessels are attributed to are known as the Tyrrhenian Group.

A type of krater of an early-black figure shape (but invented earlier, in the Late Geometric period) with the bowl resembling a large skyphos, with separate lid and stand, high horizontal handles, and a simple torus foot.
Refers to one of the most common forms of oinochoe. It was popular in both black- and red-figure and features a trefoil (three-spouted) mouth, offset neck, and bulbous body.

Ancient Greek pear-shaped storage vessels with a broad mouth forming a continuous curve with the body; introduced into Attic black-figure pottery at the end of the 6th century BCE, though painted primarily in the red-figure technique. They were principally used for storage of liquids although they were suitable for other commodities. From ca. 450 BCE, pelikai were also used as a container for the ashes of the dead. The shape is related to that of amphora type C.
Aryballoi having a round shape that is spherical rather than ovoid.
A type of pyxis with a body similar to the pyxis type B, but with a smaller, caplike lid rather than a slip-over lid. It is found only in red-figure.
Small bags suspended from a belt or waistband; popular from the mid- to the late 19th century.

Vessels with spouts, generally with lids and handles, used for preparing coffee or another beverage on the stove top or on a fire. They they are used to boil the beans or grounds in water, typically by forcing boiling water through a hopper that holds the beverage grounds. Coffee boilers are most often made of iron or enamelware.
Platelike vessels from which cake and similar food is served.

Containers intended primarily for storing or serving honey. They usually have a cover, may have an indentation for the handle of a serving spoon, and sometimes a saucerlike stand. Often made to resemble a beehive.
Printing process whereby material to be printed is stored in an electronic archive, and copies are produced as required by the end user.
Printing from raised and inked type, distinguished from lithographic or intaglio printing, particularly in the context of book and other text printing.

Bamboo clappers of Hawaii made by cutting most of a length of bamboo into narrow longitudinal strips, stopping short of one end with a natural node which serves as a handle. They are struck against the palm of the free hand or other part of the body like a switch, struck in pairs against each other, or shaken like rattles.
Tokens distributed at funerals, often guild funerals and particularly in the Netherlands and Belgium, as evidence of attendance.
Lighting achieved by directing 90 to 100% of the light toward a ceiling, wall, or other reflecting surface, rather than directly at the area to be illuminated.
The structure of a molecule.
Coins that have undergone the intentional alteration of some of their formal elements, for example, in their inscriptions or motifs.

Semi-transparent liquid obtained from the gall bladders of cattle. Used in cleaning, painting, and formerly for medicinal purposes. Contains sodium choleate salts (taurochloate and glycochloate) with some cholesterol, lecithin, and other substances. Examples of use include as a wetting agent in watercolor, in marbling, engraving, lithography, textile dyeing, and as a plasticizer in glue-paste mixtures.
Banknotes that were withdrawn from circulation using various methods: circular drilling, cutting with scissors, and stamping.
Designed to be filled or distended with air or gas in order to be functional.

Describes the practice, craft, and business of fashionable custom-made women's clothing, especially in Paris where a couture house is registered as such with the Chambre syndicale de la couture parisienne. This practice originated in Paris in the course of the 19th century, and is characterized by the utilization of high quality materials, and half-yearly or quarterly collections of original designs of garments.
National Polish style of art and design, inspired by vernacular folk art forms, techniques, and motifs; based on work of Stanisław Witkiewicz and the Zakopane region.
Paper money issued as legal tender by specified national banks; also, certain paper currency of the United States issued between 1863 and 1935.

Any individual or group with a stake in an organization or enterprise  who may be vitally effected by its actions and should be consulted or considered. Includes stockholders, financially invested parties with a governing interest, but also employees of a business and the community at large. Usage applied by practitioners of fields such as archaeology and heritage management.
Populations who have spread or become dispersed beyond their traditional homeland or point of origin, by either voluntary or forced means.
The activity of cutting and drying grass for hay.
Includes small projecting covers serving to carry off the fumes from stoves, fireplaces, or laboratory benches.
Form of farming in which nearly all of the crops or livestock raised are used to maintain the farmer and the farmer’s family, leaving little, if any, surplus for sale or trade.
Material made of the scales of fish, which are hard or rigid structures produced from the mesoderm skin layer of most bony and cartilaginous fishes.

Rare red-figure vessels in the shape of knucklebones. The ancient name of the vessel is unknown. The Greeks and Romans used sheep knucklebones as gaming pieces and it has been suggested that the astragalos may originally have been used as a container for them.
United States silver coins valued at five cents and minted between 1794 and 1805 and between 1829 and 1873.
United States gold coins issued between 1849 and 1933 and valued at twenty dollars.
Material comprising the hide or skin of an animal, usually a mammal, with the hair or wool left on.

Refers to a textile effect produced by weaving warp threads of one color and weft threads of a contrasting color, so that the fabric, often silk or other lustrous fabric, changes in color when viewed from different points of view.

Culture of the Arabic-speaking esoteric ethnoreligious group. The Druze faith incorporates elements of many others including Shia Islam, Gnosticism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, Buddhism, Hinduism, etc. Druze people inhabit Syria, Lebanon, Israel, and Jordan.

Use both for letters addressed by a bank to a correspondent certifying that a person named therein is entitled to draw upon his credit up to a certain sum and for letters addressed by a banker to a person to whom credit is given, authorizing that person to draw on the issuing bank.

Official indicators of a firefighter's service, used as identification at fire scenes, and a mandated part of a firefighter's uniform. They usually indicate identification numbers, and the company of the firefighter.

Blunt hand saws which are played as musical instruments, one end being held between the player's knees while the other is grasped and flexed by the left hand; the edge is bowed with a violin or cello bow.
Single-headed circular frame drums of the Near East, North Africa, and as far east as Malaysia, usually with metal jingles.
Aerophones of tenor range, resembling small bassoons but with a single reed; known in the 19th century, they are now generally considered obsolete.
Electronic hardware or software instruments used to create digital representations of audio waveforms, process them, and replay them in a musical context.
Stiff upper and lower covers of books comprising stiff, thick cardboard or other material, often covered with leather, cloth or another material.
Signs or characters representing words.
Typefaces that are within the large class of roman style typefaces and are the more upright, nonitalic characters. For the large class of roman typefaces, use "roman (typeface style group)."

Coiled baskets woven by Washoe Native North Americans, defined by a globular shape and tightly-coiled weave. Often made with willow, sedge, and other plant fibers. Well-known Washoe weaver Dat-So-La-Lee, also known as Louisa Keyser, (1835-1925) is often credited as repopularizing the degikup.

General term for various articles, usually of silver or gold, intended for ecclesiastical use. Examples include patens, chalices, alms dishes, censers, or any other items that are made of or plated with silver or gold.
Containers, racks, or other devices for holding, organizing, or storing items.
Small or moderate size bags for carrying small articles, often having drawstrings, a flap, or closure hardware.
Russian ceremonial drinking vessels, globular in form and sometimes having a cover and a low foot ring; usually of silver and sometimes richly enamelled or ornamented with gems.
Roman silver coins originally valued at ten asses, later debased in value and purity; in use from the late 3rd century BCE until the mid-3rd century CE.
Ancient Greek silver or gold coins valued at eight drachmas and issued from around 500 BCE, in northern Greece, through the Hellenistic period, especially in Egypt.
In ceramics, the application of color to the surface of a clay body before application of a transparent glaze.
Notes set into the text of a page, the type being set around them on three sides; usually set in smaller or heavier type.
Headbands sewn directly onto the text block.
Titles of a book as printed, in full or in brief, on the recto of a leaf preceding the title page; usually in a smaller font size than the font in which the title proper is printed on the title page.
Flutes blown with breath from the nose rather than the mouth; widely distributed but particularly common in Southeast Asia and Oceania.
Brass instruments of wide conical bore ending in a flare, played with a double reed.

Low-pitched metallophones of Thailand and Cambodia with a range of just over two octaves, consisting of a rectangular box-shaped trough resonator mounted on four short legs, with 17 iron or steel bars supported on narrow wood tracks along the tops of the sides of the resonator, which are tuned by filing away some of the metal on the underside. They are struck with two beaters, either hard or soft. For the Thai and Cambodian xylophones of the same range and tuning, use "ranat thum."
British gold coins originally valued at 20 shillings, one pound sterling, and issued first in 1489; 21-shilling and 30-shilling versions appeared from the 16th century.
Standing cups that are highly decorated.
Double-headed Japanese drums, resembling large taikos. Often played on a stand, although they may be played horizontally as well.

Official banners authorized by the United States Department of Defense for families who have members serving in the Armed Forces. These have a white field, red border and blue and/or gold stars representing each family member in service.
Instruments, machines, or other apparatus used for determining weight, which is the amount of force exerted on an object or substance by gravity or the amount of force needed to support it.
In Indian architecture, a cord for measuring curvature of śikhara.
Instruments for measuring the pressure head of fluids, as of water in wells.
Devices used for measuring energy that travels as electromagnetic waves.
Instruments for measuring the frequency of alternating currents.
Instruments for measuring high temperatures by measuring the radiation emitted by hot objects.
Instruments used to measure the index of refraction of substances in any of several ways.
Measuring device accessories used in surveying.
Weights to be suspended from one end of plumb lines to determine verticality or to aid in locating points on the ground during surveying.
Objects of known mass for use on scales during weighing.

Prints made using a process of relief printing, in which the nonprinting areas of the block or plate are carved, engraved, or etched away, leaving the original plane surface raised so that ink is deposited and transferred to paper.
Revolving shafts with radiating blades used to propel craft through air or water.

Qualitative and quantitative element analysis made by applying X-ray to the sample and then analysing the re-emitted element characteristic fluorescent X-ray. Examples of use are in chemical, electronic, food, and refinery industries.

Method of obtaining infrared spectra absorption, emission, photoconductivity or Raman scattering solids, liquids or gas by first collecting an interferogram of a sample signal using an interferometer, and then performing a Fourier Transform (FT) on the interferogram to obtain the spectrum.
Burners using oil to produce heat.
Vessels, usually made of iron or earthware, used for holding burning oil, pitch, or other flammable substances for lighting.
Any lights designated for use during a power outage or other emergency; often required by municipal regulations in public buildings.
Lamps designed to be suspended in foyers or entries, often with the font and burner inside a shade.

Lamps with a relatively short stem making them suitable for standing on tables and other furniture. The term is especially used in reference to late 18th-century lamps designed to burn whale oil and burning fluid compounds, which generally maintain the traditional stemware divisions of top, stem, and foot and often resemble stemmed drinking glasses of the same period.

Complete lighting devices consisting of light source and ballast, where appropriate, together with accessories, such as globe, reflector, and housing and usually mounted on poles or posts by brackets along roads.
Staff weapons having a large sharply pointed blade resembling that of a sword or dagger, often with a short false edge near the point.
Commodities, merchandise, or materials shipped, sent, or otherwise transmitted from one country to another for use, sale, reprocessing, exchange, or reexport.
Lights indicating the presence and overall length of a vehicle.
Aeronautical devices used to indicate visually the direction designated for landing and take-off.
Glass table lamps with twin fonts and burners on a single standard and base.
Gas burners masked by ceramic or opaque glass sleeves to resemble candles.
Material used as an ingredient of mordants in the production of etchings rather than nitric acid due to its ability to produce more selectively vertical lines.

Metal rods, nails, or wire that is embedded in both the core and the outer mold of a cast that serves to secure the core in place during a pour. Core pins have traditionally been made of copper alloys, iron, or steel, and today are generally made of stainless steel.

Conical, solid pottery funerary sculptures that were placed in the walls at the entrances of Egyptian tombs, almost exclusively at the Theban necropolis. The flat, round bases of the cones were stamped with hieroglyphs stating the name or title of the deceased, or longer texts such as prayers.
General term for works, particularly contemporary works, that integrate sound and the visual arts.
Process of printing new matter over, or on the same sheet as, already printed matter, including one color over another to produce a mixture of the two.
A symptom of oxidative-reductive deterioration in photographs.
Excessive biting of a printing plate.
Soldiers armed with a harquebus.
Acts or processes of entering or making a hostile incursion into a country or territory as an enemy with armed force.

Depictions and representations on a surface in two dimensions or low relief, or digital, whether the optical counterpart exists in reality or only in imagination. For example, the term may refer to a depiction as distinguished from its support, as when referring to a drawing as distinct from the paper upon which it is drawn. For a representation of an object as opposed to the tangible object itself, as when distinguishing between a photograph or digital image and the art object depicted, use the descriptor "visual surrogates" or the UF "images (visual surrogates)." For three-dimensional works, use "objects" or a more specific term, such as "sculpture (visual works)."
Large resist painted and dyed cotton panels made in India, often with the flowering tree pattern, used in Europe and America especially as bedcovers and hangings.
Heavy pieces of cloth painted to imitate carpet, tile, or some other floor covering.

Pads that are generally used on a floor surface to provide a modicum of protection against a hard surface for sleeping, resting, or reclining. These may be constructed in various ways, often with foam, or air inflation.
Bruising the surface of stone by striking with a blunt tool.
Resistance of a material to fracture by a blow expressed in terms of amount of energy absorbed before fracture.
Parts or components of upholstery.

Knots made by using a temporary rod along the width of the carpet, placed in front of the warp; the long yarn is placed around two warp threads and then around the rod. When the weaver is done with the entire row of knots the loops around the rod are cut to create the knot.
Carpeting that can be used either indoors, or outdoors where it will be exposed to weather conditions.
Rugs of some size whose primary use is to cover a flat surface; carpets constitute the largest and most familiar group of rugs.
Any of various rugs woven without a pile.
Persian term for covers made of assembled strips of warp faced fabric.
Generic name for French pile carpets, usually large; not always made at the Savonnerie workshop.
Reliquaries representing the saint whose relics are contained within, made in the form of a bust, which is a representation of only the head and shoulders of a human figure.
Revolts against a government that are less organized than an "insurrection" and smaller than a "revolution," and that are not recognized as beligerency.
Drawing material prepared by binding carbon particles in gall extract (from an abnormal growth on oak trees), that when applied to paper darkens by oxidation.

Training or retraining designed to prepare individuals for gainful employment in recognized or new and emerging occupations, assist them in making occupational choices, and upgrade or update those already working in an occupational field. It encompasses both secondary and postsecondary programs, public or private, and usually involves both classroom and field work.

Automatic typewriters, first introduced in the early 1960s, that utilize magnetic tape cartridges as opposed to punched paper, and are linked to computers. This allowed data to be recorded on tape, re-typed, and corrected.
Physical training or body toning involving the use of weights. For the lifting of standard weights as a competitive sport or conditioning exercise, use "weightlifting."
The status or attribute of living a long lifespan.
People holding posts to which they have been legally elected or appointed and exercising government functions.
In Indian sculpture or architecture, an umbrella-bearing female figures.
The extremities of long, thin objects. For the adjective describing the location of something at or near the end of something, use "end" from the Attributes and Properties hierarchy.

Object genre including visual works and other articles made of ceramic, which is any of various hard, brittle, heat-resistant and corrosion-resistant materials made by shaping and then firing a nonmetallic mineral, such as clay, at a high temperature. Ceramic ware, earthenware, porcelain ware, and brick products are examples of ceramics.
Use to denote collectively the various mechanical contrivances devised to supplement the fingers in controlling the fingerholes of aerophones.

Objects made of brick, particularly those having a design or image impressed, carved, or painted upon them. For brick used in construction and having a purpose basically utilitarian rather than decorative, prefer "brick (clay material)."

Allegorical pictures, often inscribed with mottoes, common especially in Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries. Emblems combine both words and images, the interpretation of which requires intellectual effort and results in the communication of a moral lesson. For the simpler symbol that represents an idea, use "emblems (symbols)."
Digital content, often humorous, and the viral spread of its various iterations.
Textile art made using resist dyeing in which wax is used as the resist.

Visual compositions incorporating content from a particular Buddhist text, usually taken from descriptions in sutras having to do with transformative experiences. Examples include birth in a Buddhist paradise, the intervention of bodhisattvas in human affairs, and images of hell. These are ritual works, not only illustrative.
Discarding or throwing away unneeded or excess material including equipment, products, or materials in any form including oils, chemicals, gases, or liquids.
Factories in which coke is produced, usually by burning coal or distilling coal gas.

Public houses of lodging for strangers and travellers, typically distinguished from an inn or hotel by being inexpensive and providing communal accommodations, with several beds in a single room and shared bath facilities.
Maps designed primarily to meet specific requirements.
Built-in staggered, asymmetrical shelves commonly found in shoin style decoration. This style first because popular at the end of the Muromachi period (1392-1573).

Ground or area on which patterns or other designs or images are located, as on rugs or flags; the ground of each division of armorial flags and shields on which the charges are placed; and the blank areas on either the obverse or reverse of coins, tokens, or medals not occupied by the central design or the legends or inscriptions.
Stylized images of birds or birds' heads.
Motif consisting of three- or four-petal flowers, usually nearly closed over a ball, frequently occurring in hollow moldings in English Gothic architecture.
Closely spaced parallel grooves used to ornament columns and pilasters and in the decorative arts in woodwork, metalwork, glass, and ceramics.
As an artistic concept, the absence of intricacy or excessive ornament in form, structure, or appearance.
The practice of rescuing or protecting lives from danger of death, typically from drowning or fire.
Crossing or interlacing lines or series of lozenges, forming a net- or weblike pattern.
Low-back chairs with wide seats; intended to be used in the embrasure of a window.
Elements imitating doors, but not meant to pass through, inserted to complete a series of doors or to deceive.
Boards which are used as trim on the external corner of a wood frame structure and against which the ends of the siding are fitted.

Benches that were historically seats for the deacons in early protestant church services; the style is now commonly seen in homes. The forms vary, but they are typically long enough for two or three sitters, with a wooden seat, often with a wooden back; the seat may comprise a hinged cover that opens to reveal storage.
Benches with desks, usually attached, designed for the seating of two or more students in a class room.
Terminal for chair legs in the form of a cloven hoof; first used by ancient Egyptians, and popular in 17th- and 18th-century Europe.
Elastomer which is highest in resistance to oxidation, chemicals, oil, solvent, and heat; typical applications are brake seals, O rings, diaphragms, and hose.
Songs of praise in honor of gods, countries, famous people, or other objects of high esteem, especially settings of metrical strophic nonbiblical texts intended to be sung at religious services.
In Indian architecture, a looped bell-garland.
Devices used for cleaning artists' brushes, or to prevent them from drying out.

Cord drills of a style unique to the Maori; used to create holes in hard materials such as basalt, pounamu (New Zealand greenstone) or bone. The holes were made by applying downward pressure and a twirling motion by pulling cords, creating friction at the drill point to bore through solid material.
Life-saving devices resembling and operating similarly to firearms, designed to shoot a rocket or other projectile with a line or rope to a stranded vessel.
Appliances or apparatuses designed to lift, transfer, or load construction materials from one location to another.
Equipment and tools specifically used in metalwork, such as in the act or process of shaping things out of metal or of decorating with metal.
A generic term for any drawing material made in stick form. Common examples are pigments in a wax binder, available in stick form.

Institutional forms that function under a system of rules to achieve some goal and that maintain a technical and material organization, constitutions, staff, etc., and that joins members that share citizenship of one nation, and some common interest.
A computer interface that behaves as both an input and output device. The surface of the monitor screen is overlaid with sensors of various types that allow the user to trigger software tasks.
People who make or trade in bows.
Those who write, invent, promote, investigate or propound a theory or theories about the visual arts.

Persons trained in a branch of engineering. In some jurisdictions the designation is legally restricted in technical use to persons who have completed a prescribed course of study and complied with requirements concerning registration or licensing.
Those who study the comparative history of the nature and structure of the world's religions and their diverse manifestations over time in different societies and cultures.
People who study or are expert in heraldry.

Persons who engage in the study and activities concerning the nature, collection, dissemination, and retrieval of data and information, especially in automated environments, or who design information systems.
The principles derived from the analysis of literature, and by extension, art and culture.
Religious officials or functionaries prepared and authorized to conduct religious services or attend to other official religious duties.
Text, image, diagrams, etc. drawn from a book, presented as an example of the larger work, but that does not present the totality of the work itself.
The legal, physical, historical, or other state or condition of property, usually with reference to physical objects or sites.
Patterns of or pertaining to flowers.
Primary living quarters for a ranch, which is a large farm, especially in the western US and Canada, where cattle or other animals are bred and raised.
Documents conveying formal statements intended to create, preserve, assert, or testify to a right.
Facilities where steel is processed and rolled into sheets.
Buildings for any of a wide variety of museums where collections are amassed and typically presented to give a chronological perspective of the history of a city, town, region, group of people, etc.
Square-back Windsor chairs with a single turned rod across the top usually capping the back posts.
The state or activity of recording, or sometimes of being recorded in, a census, which is an official, usually periodic, lists of persons or property with varying degrees of descriptive detail.
Refers to the entire playing areas upon which lacrosse is played.

People who assemble, revise, correct, or arrange the contents or style of literary, artistic, or musical work or data for publication or presentation, particularly when the work was compiled largely by others. Includes those who edit electronic documents and records.
Those who study or work in the field concerned with the production, distribution, and consumption of money, goods, and services.

In general, refers to catalogs of any type available on or compiled using a computer network, including catalogs for library collections, for shopping online, or for any other purpose. Specifically, refers to online catalogs for libraries, comprising references to materials held by a library or group of libraries that are available to the public. It can typically be searched in various ways, such as by keyword, author, title, subject, or call number, to find out what resources a library owns.
Documents that enumerate and describe items, events, or presentations relevant to a festival, such as a film festival, art festival, or music festival.
Hotel or club employees who escort guests to rooms, assist them with luggage, and run errands.

Refers to the period before the eighth century associated with the site Tra-Kieu. Artistic production in this period features elements of sensuality and intricacy of detail with an emphasis on feminine images and motifs, such as the female breast and smiling female dancers, and on images of movement such as a high relief sculpture depicting Hindu gods on their galloping mounts.
General term for projecting support devices (brackets) attached to a wall, usually an interior wall; examples are used stands or supports for a lamp, ornaments, or shelving.

Sheet metal seams comprising one sheet turned and placed over the bent edge of the second sheet. To prevent the elbow from breaking at the joint through handling, the elbow seam is closed using a special machine or with a mallet over a bench stake.

Mortar joints that are angled in cross-section, recessed increasingly from the bottom to the top of the joint. The effect is a straight, inclined surface that catches the light and gives the brickwork a neat, ordered appearance
Technique of pattern bond using only stretchers and in which the vertical joints of one course fall midway between the joints of the courses above and below.

In general meaning, images that portray a sacred entity and that are themselves regarded as sacred. In specific meaning, the term is typically used particularly for Christian images produced in the Eastern Rite churches, since the 6th century, according to prescribed formulas of subject (Christ, the Virgin, saints, and the great feasts) and composition, for devotional use in the church or home. Most commonly comprising tempera on panel, but they may be in any two-dimensional or relief medium, including fresco. Christians who venerate icons make the distinction between veneration and worship, although in actual practice the distinction is blurred. For a non-Christian image that is sacred or embodies a deity, use "idol" or "cult image."
Areas in a fresco completed at the same level of a scaffolding leaving rectilinear seams in the finished work; generally appear in large Roman, Byzantine, and 13th century frescoes.
A paint layer that is opaque yet allows the color underneath to show through by being applied either thinly or irregularly.
Hindu sacred wells, reservoirs, or tanks, located below ground-level, often stepped, and associated with Hindu temple architecture.

Victory celebrations of ancient Rome, held in honor of generals and admirals, or in Imperial times of emperors or members of the imperial family, who had won a complete victory over a foreign enemy. Typically, the celebration consisted of a victory procession including the honored commander, his army and spoils of war, execution of the chief prisoner, sacrifices at the Temple of Jupiter, and a public feast.
Outdoor poles installed by utility companies to support telephone, electric, or other cables.
One's relatives who are related by marriage rather than by blood.
Christian society and sect that began in Germany in the 18th century as a reaction to Lutheranism, and migrated to the United States.

The process of removing a mosaic or pavement from its original location to a new support and often to a new location. The process involves temporary facings, lifting or removal of the mortars, stabilization of the tessera or panels, and other issues; for various reasons, lifting is used rather than in situ stabilization treatments.
Practitioners of traditional medicine.
Persons who advocate conservation of natural resources.
Basic service systems required for developed areas; for the government-regulated enterprises providing such services, use "public utilities."

Insoluble black compound that occurs naturally as galena, the chief ore mineral of lead. It can also be synthesized by reacting a soluble lead salt with hydrogen sulfide or sodium sulfide. When crushed, lead sulfide becomes a powder which is used in photoconductive cells, and as a pigment in ceramic glaze.

In India and elsewhere in South Asia, this term may describe people who are intersex, androgynous, transgender, or who have been born male, but adopt a female gender identity. Hijra people may be considered non-binary, that is neither male nor female, not associating themselves with a specific sexual orientation.

Graphic images that are designed for ready recognition of a product, company, or organization and sometimes used as trademarks, and that are word- or letter-based, derived from the name. For those graphic images similarly used but more symbol- or picture-based, use "logos."
Paper having a smooth finish created by running the sheets through a series of heated metal cylinders.

Geometric plane figures having the shape of an elongated circle, bounded by a smooth curve having no concave parts, longer along one axis and rounded at each end. An oval differs from an elliptical shape in that it is not necessarily symmetric about its horizontal and vertical axes.
Clay possessing a high absorptive capacity; it is extensively used as an absorbent in refining and decolorizing oil and fat.
Units for masonry construction made primarily of concrete; the most common types are concrete bricks and concrete blocks.
Two-bladed tools having the larger blade in the form of an adz and the smaller in the form of a hatchet; distinguished from "adze-hatchets" in which the hatchet blade is larger.
Augers for boring holes in logs, so that they can be pinned together as rafts.
Devices in the form of a handle with jaws and an extendable shank, used for pulling nails out of wood. For handtools with a forked end used for similar purposes, use "tack pulls."
Instruments used for scoring a variety of materials.
Lathes designed especially for turning locomotive and railroad car wheels.
Blocks used for printing color woodcuts, being the one block for a given image that carries the most detail and serves as a guide to register the other blocks.
Supports consisting of two crossed wood clubs; used to support logs that are being sawed.
Levels in human populations distinguished by degree of wealth or privilege, modes of labor, way of life, or other social, economic, or cultural factors.
Broadly refers to the quality of coexisting harmoniously.
Events or processes resulting in a species or multiple species dying out and having no living representatives. Extinctions may be natural events or the result of human activity.
A period of abnormally dry weather sufficiently prolonged that a serious hydraulic imbalance occurs, such as crop damage or reduced water supply.
Substances formed as a result of the process of corrosion.

A material, typically used for building, composed of 100% wood fibers. Fibers are usually obtained from wood chips, sawdust, and board trimmings; they are broken into fine particles by grinding (dry process) or by steam (wet process). The interfelted fibers are consolidated with heat and pressure (at least 31 pounds per cubic foot) to form a dense, rigid sheet that is held together by naturally occurring lignin with no additional adhesive. Hardboards range from a dark brown to a light tan in color and have one very smooth surface; the reverse side has a wire screen impression. Some hardboards contain a small amount of oil on the surface either as a residual lubricant or as an additive to increase weather resistance; these oils may hinder the adherence of paint or gesso and may be removed with acetone.
Single-lap roofing tile of two types used in combination: a flat, tapered undertile having flanges, and a half-rounded, tapered overtile.
A tile which is curved in section, used to cover the ridge of a roof.
Mechanical equipment used for upkeep, such as equipment used for cleaning.
Plates on which heated irons may rest when not being used so as not to damage surfaces.
Flexible tubes for the conveyance of liquid materials from one place to another.
Wheels having grooved rims for carrying a rope or other line and turning in a frame.
Tools used in the process of making molds from melted metal.
Holiday in the United States and some other countries, intended for giving thanks for a good harvest and other blessings.
Chisels designed to shape, form, or otherwise work metal.
Journeys, usually long, undertaken as acts of homage or devotion, often to a shrine, birthplace, or sacred site.
Stereoscopic photographs on tissue paper mounted between sheets of glass or in a cardboard frame.

Chisel-like tools designed for use in plumbing, typically having a blunt end and curved blades, pushed ans struck with a hammer to force lead and oakum in the collars of pipes to make them watertight.
Machinery used to saw wood, typically for sawing planks or boards.
T-shaped tools with a steel shank and a wood head, used to make small holes in wood so that it is easier to start nails or screws.

A stereoscopic viewing device that uses a wheel or reel of slides to present two images, isolated for each eye, that together create a three-dimensional optical effect. Invented by William Gruber in 1938 as an educational device, it has been marketed as a children's toy since that time under the trademarked name "View-Master." For the device used to view individual stereo cards, popular in the 19th century, use "stereoscopes."

A geometrical figure comprising the set of all points in three-dimensional space lying the same distance (the radius) from a given point (the center), or the result of rotating a circle about one of its diameters.
Long-handled forks used for placing glass in kilns.
Devices to apply pressure to glass in a mold while in a plastic state.
Wooden mallets, often having ribbed striking surfaces, that are used to crush, break down, and flatten stalks of flax, hemp, reed, or another plant, as part of the process of producing fiber.
Devices for supplying or maintaining humidity.
Fittings, attachments, or auxiliary objects related to devices that impart heat.

Implements with a hard smooth rounded end or surface, used for smoothing and polishing. It differs in material and shape according to the purpose and trade. In printmaking, burnishers are used to smooth rough areas of an intaglio plate.
Includes indexes to the location of words or phrases in a text and finding aids, in two columns, establishing the relationship between the past and present reference numbers of individual items.

The ratio of the amount of work performed by a heat engine in one cycle to the amount of energy input required to operate the engine over one cycle. This ratio may be applied to the ability of an object, machine, or structure to maintain temperature parameters measured against the energy expended to control that temperature.
The phenomena by which a force causes the body to which it is applied to rotate about a point or line.
Sanding machines in which the sandpaper is carried on a small-diameter vertical drum located on the work table of the machine.
Documents issued by the Secretary of State or other state official, establishing a corporation.
Condensed, orderly arrangements of data, especially those in which the data are arranged in columns and rows.
In Indian architecture, two-storeyed.

Doctrine or practice that emphasizes practical utility or functional relations in the design and construction of structures, objects, and systems. Use also when referring to the contemporary design philosophy, relating chiefly to architecture and furnishings, holding that form should be adapted to use, material, and structure.
The status or characteristic of a structure or other thing having been devoted to a saint, deity, patron, or other person or cause, or otherwise officially and ceremonially set apart.
Buildings set apart to contain books for reading, study, or reference, typically with shelves containing books and tables and seating for users of the library.
Velvet having certain areas of the ground weave left free of pile. In these areas the pile warp is not lifted over the velvet rods but is woven in with the ground weave.
Steel coated with a thin layer of zinc to prevent corrosion. The application may be effected by electroplating or spraying the steel with molten zinc, or by coating the heated steel with zinc powder.

Ceremonial stools common to the Taino culture carved out of wood or stone and are typically made with zoomorphic and anthropomorphic design elements. The stools were used by the higher ranking tribe members during community rituals and activities.
Refers to an Italian painting movement of the 1950s, co-founded by Enrico Baj, Sergio Dangelo and Gianni Bertini to promote a style of gestural painting relevant to the post-War nuclear age.
Infrastructural components of systems that allow for the movement of large numbers of people.
Being at right angles to a given line or plane.

Positional attribute used to describe something situated at or near the forward or most important part of something. To refer to those parts themselves, use "fronts" from the Components hierarchy. For the sense of facing the viewer, as a figure in a picture, use "frontal."

Refers to objects either that have become separated or disconnected from objects to which they were an integral part, as ticket stubs, or, especially with reference to buildings, that are standing apart with no walls in common with other structures. To refer to sculpture or architectural and infrastructural elements that stand alone, prefer "freestanding."
A photographic plate size, about 3 1/4 by 4 1/4 inches.
Describes buildings, particularly classic Greek and Roman temples and buildings like them in structure, having a row or rows of nine columns at one or both ends.

Boards that generally consist of two panels (usually hinged), used with game pieces that are moved as determined by throws of the dice. The boards typically have twelve holes along the base of each side, used for scoring. Similar to "backgammon boards."

Drawings that are broadside elevations of a ship, emphasizing the ship's lines. When appearing with a body plan and a half-breadth plan, use "lines drawings" for the set. For more detailed broadside elevations, use "outboard profiles."

Films created by cutting and splicing film clips from pre-existing motion pictures or library footage. Often done with nonfiction footage to make documentaries, or with clips from old motion pictures for entertainment. May have new footage by way of introduction, comment, or closing.
Having a front that is convex in the center and concave at both ends, used with reference to case furniture.
Gouges with a deep channel; used for making flutings.

Any material that is not the fine, soft, thick, hairy coat of a mammal, but resembles genuine fur. To refer specifically to the fashion textile having a very long pile, prefer the narrower term "fake fur fabric."
Photographic prints made by interfacing a negative and a sheet of photographic paper and exposing the paper with raw light.
The study of family history and ancestry.
Theory and study of signs and symbols dealing especially with their function in languages, including syntax, semantics, and pragmatics.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Malawi, Tanzania, and Zambia.
Refers to any venture in which individuals or organizations work together, especially in an intellectual endeavor.
Taking legal action; carrying on an action by judicial process.
Housing built or renovated by nonprofit groups or single families whose labor is counted as part of the homeowner's equity.

Military or naval forces that enforce a nation's maritime laws, assist vessels wrecked or in distress on or near its coasts, and in some countries maintain aids to navigation, prevent smuggling, and in wartime augment the regular navy.
A fine grain white limestone quarried in Val Gallina near Verona, Italy.
Modifier describing a color of moderate to light intensity and dark value.
Chairs, often reclining, for use outdoors in garden areas or on lawns.
The event or status of having control, government, or dominion.

Registers of days or other contrivances for reckoning days, months, years, etc., such as a table showing the division of a given year into its months, weeks, days, years, or other divisions of time. A calendar may include important astronomical data, ecclesiastical or other festivals, and other events belonging to specific days. For calendric systems of dates, see children under "<dating systems by specific type>."

Plates, usually metal, fixed to a manufactured item and displaying information about the item. May be used for train locomotives, other vehicles, marine vessels, bridges, other works of engineering, stoves, other appliances, and other things.
Rectangular pieces of stiff paper or plastic, usually of standard dimensions, used as a support on which information is typed, written, or transcribed.

Hand-sized wooden boards covered with beads, shells, and carvings, created and used by the Mbudye secret society of the Luba people to recall their genesis myth and other complex information about the history, organization, and functioning of the society.
Maps that display the geographic distribution of climatic variables, usually in monthly or annual values.

Transcribed collections of numbers, names, or other text listing events, biographies, milestones, or other items in serial temporal order relative to given dates or time periods. Used to represent textually those events, biographies, etc.
Statements or lists of the prevailing prices of merchandise, stock, or other items for sale.
Negatives having gelatin as the binder, holding silver as the final image material; may be on glass ("gelatin dry plate negatives") or on film.
Photographic prints made using a solution of gold chloride. Developed by Sir John Herschel.
Photographs produced from a frame of motion picture film. For other photographs of the action, actors, or production of a motion picture, use "film stills."
Pavement mosaic technique using ceramic elements, usually of the same size and rectangular shape, arranged in a herringbone pattern.
Puppets operated, usually from below, by a main control rod with or without subsidiary rods.

Masks designed to cover only, or primarily, the eyes for fashion, disguise, ritual, or another purpose. For articles used to cover the eyes for the purpose of blocking light for sleep, use "eye masks (blindfolds)."

Refers to techniques used to produce the appearance of three-dimensionality in photographs by using two images made at slightly different positions, mounting them side by side, and viewing the pair through a stereoscope or other device. This type of photography was extremely popular in the Victorian period. The process was described in 1832, but the techniques were perfected only after 1856, when a twin-lens camera was designed to take two pictures of the same scene simultaneously. The viewpoints of the photographs were 2 1/2 inches apart, which is approximately the normal distance between human eyes.
Photography that takes place in an indoor setting, often employing lighting of some sort.
Gifts, usually of money, given over and above what is due in return for or in anticipation of some service.
Photographs produced in small, automated picture-taking enclosures; usually requiring automated payment of a small fee to initiate the photographic process.
Wood of the tree belonging to the genus Aesculus glabra.
Documents which grant a person the right to do something not forbidden by law but not allowable without such authority.

Generally, lead or tin-glazed, relief-molded and decorative earthenware manufactured principally in Germany from 1350 as insulating tiles for stoves. The term is also used to describe vessels with figurative decoration, usually of religious or mythological scenes, created by stove makers beginning in the 16th century. From ca. 1500 polychromatic glazes appear. From the mid-1600s, lead glazes are replaced by tin. Nürnberg is considered the center of Hafner ware manufacture, though it was made in Switzerland and elsewhere in Central Europe.

Beds, particularly those created in Europe prior to the 16th century, of various designs having a high wooden frame suspended over the head half of the bed, from which curtains may be hung in a tent-like fashion. Sparver beds typically do not have bedposts, but the frame may be attached to the wall or ceiling.

Case furniture of the 18th century, often in the "Chinese style," which incorporate bookshelves behind glassed-in or trelliswork doors over chests of drawers.The design is epitomized in plate XXI of Ince and Mayhew's "Universal System of Household Furniture" (1762).
Pieces of hardware, usually metal, that form a right angle and are used to secure or reinforce the corners of a picture frame, a window frame, furniture, or other object.
Actions and status of a dvinity's retributive justice by which the destiny of people or other creatures is decided, typically according to their merits and demerits.
Concepts related to the doctrine of Buddhism.

A Roman Catholic religious order that originated in the 12th century from hermits on Mount Carmel who sought the way of life of the prophet Elijah. When the Crusades failed, the Carmelites migrated to Europe where they flourished as mendicant friars. Solitude, abstinence, and prayer are strictly practiced. In 1452 the friars were joined by Carmelite nuns (Sisters of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mt. Carmel), the Carmelite Second Order. The Carmelites do not have a founding figure as do many orders, but they consider Elijah and Mary, both central to Carmelite consciousness, as their founders. Important reform figures are St. Teresa of Avila, reformer of the female order in 1562, and St. John of the Cross, who similarly reformed the male order later in the century. The reformed branch became its own order in 1593 and is referred to as the Discalced Carmelites.
Amphorae characterized by pointed or knob-feet and requiring stands. In its unpainted form it was the standard container for commercial transportation of wine and oil.
Hand coverings worn for work tasks, protecting the wearer. An example are rubber work gloves worn by fishermen to protect from water and sharp tools.

Organized assistance provided by public or private agencies and organizations to individual community members. For essential on-going services provided by the government relating directly to the protection and maintenance of the lives and property of community members as a whole, use "public services."
Organizations or departments of organizations that provide direct answers to users' queries or refer them to sources of information that will satisfy the queries.
The act of dying by one's own hand. The act of dying by one's own hand.

The aesthetic quality of the permanent, essential, or eternal character of appearances or other phenomena, which is rooted in an idea of perfection or archetype. It is ultimately derived from from Plato's "Theory of Ideas," which holds that perfection is a concept that is only mirrored imperfectly in real life. This perfection was the ideal to which artists sought to strive in certain periods, styles, or contexts. The concept was particularly evident in various periods of antique art, the Renaissance, and in the 17th- and 18th-century art academies throughout Europe.
Material comprising flowers, which are the reproductive portion of any plant in the division Magnoliophyta (Angiospermae).

UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying whitish colors, such as the color of snow or milk. More specifically, white is the absence of color. It is the color produced by reflection, transmission, or emission of all kinds of light in the proportion in which they exist in the complete visible spectrum, without sensible absorption, being thus fully luminous and devoid of any distinctive hue.

Devices used to help shape uniformly-sized ravioli, a type of filled pasta. Ravioli presses consist of a tray with evenly-spaced divots separated by raised cutting edges. A sheet of pasta dough is laid across the tray and the divots filled with ingredients before being topped with another sheet of dough, which is then pressed with a rolling pin, cutting and shaping the ravioli.
Landed estates administered as units and consisting of the main residence (manor house), demesnes, and the land over which the lord has privileges.
Usually paved strips for taxiing at an airport.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink and yellow colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of red.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of orange colors.

Narrow exterior pedestrian passageways or alleys between buildings, where the passageways lead from the street to the dwelling houses, outhouses, stables, a common stair, courtyard, or other common area.
Altars standing in the center of a Greek theater orchestra.

Describes photographs that capture current events, human interest, or cultural or social issues that are timely or of immediate interest, and which are intended to be published in the context of a news periodical in any format. These are distinguished from documentary photographs, which represent general themes of ongoing human or natural activity.
Card photographs that measured approximately 4 inches by 8.5 inches.

Simplified versions of carbon prints. These use silver bromide paper to make a contact print. These prints were then placed against pigment paper and through a chemical developer and warm water, and a pigmented print was created on the bleached original carrier. A double transfer, used for carbon printing, was no longer necessary.

Photographs made by dissolving light-sensitive bitumen in oil of lavender and applying a thin coating over a polished metal plate, or other substrate. The process was invented ca.1822 by Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, and is considered the first process to produce a permanent photographic image from a camera projection.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of brown colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of brown colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
Housing designed or used by military personnel.
States that are governed by tribal authority, often physically located within a larger sovereign state.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of bluish green colors.

Use broadly for the capture and transmission of information by detecting devices located at a distance from the receiving device and for the detection of information beyond the reach of normal human capacity.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellowish green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellowish green colors.

In the context of ancient Roman architecture, this term usually refers to passageways that allowed for closure at either end. Originally these structures functioned as bridges or as crossings of the pomerium. The term was later applied to gateways and over time post-and-lintel doors were replaced by arches. Later jani were often vaulted as well. There were several noteworthy jani in Rome, most notably the Janus Geminus, the most important shrine of Janus in the city. The closed gates of the Janus Geminus signaled that Rome was at war and open gates meant that it was at peace. It is not known if all jani were considered sacred in some sense but the term certainly has some religious connotation.
Buildings or parts of buildings housing interns, usually the interns of a hospital or other health facility, interns being the assistant resident physicians, usually students or recent graduates.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of greenish blue colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.
Areas where military exercises are performed.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of purple colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of violet colors.

Core or central areas of cities or towns that are either the oldest areas of the city or the core business areas. The term is thought to derive from these areas, as the oldest areas, having the lowest street numbers; alternatively, term may derive from the development of New York City, where the oldest section is in the south, at the bottom of a map.
Buildings or spaces for museums that are owned or administered by representatives of a nation, or that specializes in exhibitions from a given nation.
A range of orange colors resembling the color of orange pigment.
In Indian architecture, a central raised platform for dancing in the hall; slightly raised nave-platform in hall, for dancing.

Decorative vases or urns used to decorate gardens. These are created in a variety of materials including marble, ceramics, stone, or iron, and may exhibit applied decoration including handles, leaf motifs, or masks.
Geomorphic features of the earth's surface that are located underwater, but not undersea. For features under the surface of the ocean, use "undersea features."
Irregular, partially obstructed, fast-flowing areas in rivers or streams.

Division of the plant kingdom containing conifers, which are gymnospermous exogens (stem grows by deposit on its outside), comprising trees and shrubs bearing cones; most are evergreen, with leaves that are needlelike, scale-like, with a single vein or, less commonly, strap-shaped with multiple veins.
Trailing or twining plants, whose stems require support.
The buildings used by an institution, which is a formally structured organization, establishment, or association created for the promotion of a specific benevolent objective.

Landscapes considered in the past or present as consecrated or important to a deity or a religion particularly including natural features, such as springs and caves. Also natural areas used for spiritual inspiration and to guide their contemplation of the divine.
Areas of low-lying land reclaimed from the sea, a river, or other body of water, and enclosed by dikes. For a piece of marshy or boggy land, use "marshes."
Functions concerning the industry of food.
Legally removing a person or persons from the premises.
Generally, the act of making a request in a humble manner. Specifically, the act of addressing a deity or spirit with supplication, adoration, confession, or thanksgiving.
Instructing others in, or explaining or illustrating to others, the practical operation or results of methods, processes, products, devices, or theories.
General term for buildings or rooms primarily used for performances, which are the executions of a literary, artistic, musical, theatrical, or other creative work.

Refers to imitations of hand-made lace created by machines. The term may also refer to lace that is worked by hand on top of machine-made netting. The latter was produced in England beginning in the 1770s. Early machine-made netting is often characterized by looped stitches, which tend to run; machine-made netting dating after 1808 may be characterized by an imitation of the simple twist of Lille lace. Machine-made nets may be decorated by machine with chain stitching or needle-run patterns. Machine lace dating to the 1840s or later may imitate bobbin lace. Machine laces are generally characterized by a lack of the clearly woven structure of bobbin lace.

Refers to a type of bobbin lace created in Brussels, Belgium (formerly Flanders) in the 17th and 18th centuries that was very expensive and favored at court. It is characterized by a distinctive mesh composed of a hexagon with four twisted sides and two sides plaited four times. Alternatively, portions of the design may be joined by a background of bars, or brides. Designs typically comprise large curved forms, bold, sweeping floral and plant designs, and landscapes and figures in narrative scenes. Individual motifs or small sections of the pattern were sometimes made separately and joined to the net ground. It was noted for being made of high quality thread from local Brabant flax. The term also refers to imitations of Brussels lace made later and/or in other locations.
In Indian architecture, a tōraṇa-gate around the door.
In pictorial arts, that part of the composition between the foreground and the background.
Sets of tools, equipment, and other items, often contained in a box or bag, provided for some necessity or to be assembled.
A fine-grained French oolitic limestone that is cream in color and easily carved.
Photographic processes in which collodion is the binder. A silver halide is the light-sensitive agent, and the process may be used to produce positives (ambrotypes, tintypes) or negatives.
Of or belonging to the nation of Brazil or its people.

Artistic aesthetic developed by John Weichsel, influenced by the writings of the German art historian Wilhelm Worringer, and steeped in anarchist philosophy. The Cosmist aesthetic was put into practice by such artists as Elie Nadelman and Adolf Wolff.
Roof systems in which the cross framing members are some form of light wood truss.

Period and styles of painting, sculpture, graphic arts, and architecture dating from the recent past and present. It differs from modern art in that the term 'Contemporary art' does not carry the implication of a non-traditional style, but instead refers only to the time period in which the work was created. 'Modern' and 'Contemporary' are inherently fluid terms. The term 'Contemporary' is sometimes more narrowly used to refer to art from ca. 1960 or 1970 up to the present. To refer to the current time period without reference to style of art, use "contemporary (generic time frame)".

In the context of art and culture, the culture of the indigenous peoples of the northern polar region of the earth, including the Arctic Ocean and the northernmost parts of Asia, Europe, and North America. The term may also refer to the animals, plants, climate, geology, geography, and oceanography of the area.
Nationality or culture of the modern nation of Armenia, a mountainous country in the South Caucasus region of Eurasia.

Refers to the culture of the modern principality of Wales, or in general to the cultures that have occupied the wide peninisula on the western part of the island of Great Britain. The term formerly referred specifically to the native British population of England in contrast to the Anglo-Saxons.
Refers to the culture of the modern nation of Norway, or in general to the cultures that have occupied the western part of the Scandinavian peninsula in northwestern Europe.
Affiliation or culture of the Hanseatic League, or Hanse towns, a historical association of northern German trading towns.
The nationality, style, or culture of the region of Calabria, Italy.
Culture and style of the region of Cordoba, in Spain.

Soft-paste porcelain ware that was first produced by the factory at the Palazzo di Capodimonte in 1743 under the auspices of Charles VII of Naples and continued until 1758 when Charles became the king of Spain, dismantling the concern and reestablishing it as the Real Fábrica del Buen Retiro near Madrid. The style was developed by chief modeler Giuseppe Grieci from prototypes by Meissen.

A  trend in post-revolutionary Soviet art in the 1920s and 1930s that promoted a fusion of artistic practice and industrial production. Productivists believed that in the socialist society there had been no need in art as an autonomous practice. Art was to deal with the pragmatic and utilitarian tasks such as design of objects, training of practical skills or organization of the living environment. For productivists an artist was akin a producer and an engineer. Though Productivism is often conceived as a movement associated with the particular theorists, artists and institutions (e.g. journals Lef and Noviy (New) Lef), it was rather a broader trend followed by many artists and art collectives across the USSR, including Central Asian republics. Institutional self-organization of numerous artistic collectives into “art-factories” in which the artistic production was organized as in an industrial plant was one of the most emblematic expressions of the productional view of art.
Nonpolar hydrocarbon solvent, used in the production of corn oil.
A solvent added during chemical processing to an original solvent, the two, thanks to synergism, forming a mixture with solvent powers more than the sum of its parts.
Refers to the style and culture evident in areas held by Burgundian rulers of Flanders, particularly during the 14th and 15th centuries.
Buildings housing the legislative bodies of a government.

Architectural and interior design popular in Europe and North America in the 1970s. In architecture, the style is characterized by the use of sleek lines, space-age materials, and pre-fabricated parts, with the purpose of exploring the limits of technology.

Publications in any medium issued in successive parts bearing numerical or chronological designations and intended to be continued indefinitely, such as periodicals, newspapers, annuals (reports, yearbooks, etc.), journals, memoires, proceedings, transactions, etc., of societies and numbered monographic series.
People who create rapidly executed freehand drawings, usually portraits, for various purposes, including forensic identification, courtroom renderings, and entertainment.
Styles belonging to Italian Renaissance-Baroque cultures.

Refers to the style of architecture and decorative arts during the reign of Louis XIV from 1643 to 1715.  Luxurious yet formal and reflecting Classical and Baroque forms and motifs, the style is associated with the King's patronage and with the furniture, tapestries, and decoration created for his palace at Versailles.
Openings in vertical surfaces, such as walls, parapets, curbs, or bulwarks, to allow the runoff of excess water from horizontal surfaces.
In Indian architecture, a cavity within moon-window motif; recess/cavity of gavākṣa.
In Indian architecture, a central cavity of a nāsī.

School of painting that flourished in the mid-16th century in eastern Tibet; it was begun by Jamyang Khyentse Wangchuk (b. 1524). Attention to detail, continued Chinese influence, and a new way of treating the background are hallmarks of this school.
Leaves indicating the beginning of distinct, major portions of books, bearing the divisional title or number of  the portion on the recto. The verso is normally left blank.
Limitations placed, usually by the government, on the vertical distance from the base to the top of structures.

Objects such as cloths, screens, curtains, or canvasses, used to provide suitable background behind the subjects of photographs, paintings, or other pictorial media, or behind the actors and props in a theatrical stage or setting.
Thin, flat, rigid objects, of considerable length or breadth compared to thickness, most often of wood, paperboard, or composite fiber materials.

Refers to the style inspired by the building of the temple of Banteay Srei during the mid-tenth century in Angkor and partly reflects the revival of the pre-Angkor sculptural styles of the seventh and eighth centuries. The temple features pink sandstone construction, small-scale and elaborate jewel-like relief decoration, tympanum reliefs of large and small deities enveloped in swirling foliage, sophisticated narrative relief panels that portray Shiva, Vishnu, and Krishna placed at staggered levels, and wall paintings. Sculptural figures display slimmer bodies, more naturalistic proportions, narrower heads, more youthful demeanors, and garments that lack narrow vertical pleats and cling to the body.
Refers to art and culture of the Karen, or Kayin, people, members of a Thai-Chinese ethnic group dwelling mainly in southern and southeastern Myanmar and in northern Thailand near the Myanmar border.

Nationality, styles, and culture of the modern nation of India, or more broadly to cultures that developed on the subcontinent of India, which is bounded by the Arabian Sea, the Indian Ocean, the Bay of Bengal, and the Himalayn Mountains. It may also refer even more broadly to cultures of India, the East Indies, and the former British Indian Empire. It was formerly used less specifically to refer to any Oriental or Asian culture. Do not use this term to refer to the indigenous populations of North or South America; see "Native American" or other appropriate terms.

East Polynesian religious structures of various forms from small stone platforms, to simple stone enclosures. The most common patterns of marae are found on Society Island.  to templelike structures. For similar structures from Hawaii, see "heiaus."
Inhabited places established in areas that are newly colonized or under the rule of a colonial power.
Military settlements established by the Spanish in America often as garrisoned forts or outposts.
Ports on a seacoast.

Tombs that are excavated from hillsides or cliffs. These may contain  tomb passages, and sometimes multiple chambers, carved stone coffins and niches, which may be architecturally integrated into the caves.
Stations along or at the terminals of a tram line where trams load or unload passengers.
Establishments for making wine, which is the fermented juice of the grape used as a beverage.
Secure mooring facilities primarily for yachts and other recreational small craft.

Styles and cultures originating in the southernmost region of the African continent, comprising the modern countries of Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. The island nation of Madagascar is excluded because of its distinct language and cultural heritage.
Sculpture styles belonging to Japanese culture.

Works of art that incorporate several different styles or are made up of parts drawn from a variety of sources. May also refer to other artistic works, such as works of music or literature, that piece together fragments from various sources or that closely imitate the style of another work. A pastiche typically selfconsciously borrows its style, technique, or motifs from other works of art, yet is not a direct copy of any work; it is often deliberately exaggerated and satirical. The term may also be applied in a derogatory sense, implying that the creator was unoriginal.
Industrial structures built to support mining activity.
Plan of a building or city that radiates from a central point, often symmetrical.

Built works or groups of built works housing entities providing higher education that include space for training technicians in business, industry, and commerce for an immediate local area, having fewer residence facilities, and offering more part-time classes than "universities (building complexes)." For buildings housing educational institutions emphasizing training in agriculture or specific trades, use "vocational schools."
Buildings housing businesses where meals or refreshments are sold and eaten.

Visual time signals, generally including a ball that is mounted on a tall pole or rod set up on a tower or other prominent location and that is arranged to drop suddenly at a predetermined moment, such as noontime; used, for example, by ships at anchor.
A small house, usually of only one story.

Raised structures, often canopied, on which the coffin or effigy of a deceased person lies or is carried in state. It is distinguished from a "bier," which is much smaller and simpler, and from a "castrum doloris," which is a structure that shelters the bier or catafalque.
Structures, often wooden, with platforms that are topped by small towers or huts, with pitched roofs. These structures are used by hunters to spot deer.

Instruments developed by the Institute of Applied Physics of the CNR of Florence (Istituto di Fisica Applicata del CNR di Firenze) that are based on evanescent field dielectrometry (EFD). These instruments work in the microwave range (1-1.5 GHz), ar portable, and allow real-time non-invasive measurements of sub-surface moisture content and the detection of soluble salts (salinity index).
Areas equipped with distance markers, clubs, balls, and tees for practicing golf drives.
Buildings that house prisons populated by prisoners who can be reasonably trusted to not to try to escape; the term is often used in British prison systems.
In Indian architecture, an elephant band in base.
Joints used to separate extremely long buildings into a series of adjacent volumes to resist earthquake damage.

Refers to wooden or metal posts on a ship, whale-boat, quay, or pier, used for securing ropes. Bollards made of concrete may be used to prevent passage by automobiles into pedestrian spaces. For indicators sited in roadways that may indicate wayfinding or obstructions, use "traffic bollards."
Vertical members in woodwork or furniture, such as in a door, a sash, or a chest of drawers, into which secondary members are fitted.
The compass point in the direction of that part of the earth or heavens which is directly opposite to north.
Small enclosures or stands, permanent or temporary, and freestanding or not, used for selling goods or to afford privacy to their occupants.
Screws that enable two objects to be secured together without a nut. These are usually in the form of shanks that are continuously threaded along their length.
Racks on which to hang neckties.
Devices for regulating the flow of liquid, usually water, in a pipeline, and providing for the regulation of temperature through the controlled combination of hot and cold sources.
Rooms in the Roman bath or gymnasium between the laconicum, sudatorium, or stove, and the caldarium or warm bath where athletes retired to remove sweat from their bodies.
