Elements of low conductivity placed between two conductive materials to limit heat flow; for use in metal windows of curtain walls that are to be used in cold climates.
The state, quality, or condition of being inaccurate, incomplete, defective and/or displeasing in some way.

Material made of excrescences produced on trees, usually the oak species Quercus infectoria in Europe and the Near East, and on the sumac species Rhus semialata in China and Japan, by the action of insects, chiefly of the genus Cynips. Galls are formed when gall-wasp eggs are deposited on tree branches in nut-like pockets; the gall grows until the larvae are completely enveloped. The mature insect bores a hole through the gall in order to escape. All galls contain 36-60% tannins; the bluish-green galls, gathered before the insect escapes, are richest in gallotannic acid. The tannins have been used for centuries for vegetable tanning of leather. When galls are combined with ferrous sulfate, a black dye is produced; alone, they produce a gray dye. Gall extract was also used as a mordant in the preparation of writing inks.

Kitchen utensils designed for extruding food, especially cooked potatoes, by pressure through a perforated container so that the resulting product emerges as strings about the diameter of a grain of rice.
Facilities for producing fertilizer.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink and yellow colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of red.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of orange colors.
Streets open only at one end. For alleys open only at one end, use "blind alleys."
Art in the medium of photography.
Photograph introduced in 1875 as a variation of the cabinet photograph. Measuring approximately 9.5 centimeters by 19 centimeters, the size was meant to allow for photos of standing figures.
Direct positive photographs produced by the process called Hillotype.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of brown colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of brown colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
Housing, typically dormitory-style facilities, provided for students at a college or university.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of bluish green colors.

The process of discovering an archaeological site to be excavated by aerial photography, remote sensing, or by other means such as statistically predicting archaeological sites from environmental variables.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellowish green colors.
Structures with equipment and facilities for the washing, waxing, and polishing of motor vehicles.
Group dwellings on or near hospital grounds providing dormitorylike housing for nurses or nursing students.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of greenish blue colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.
Designates large, open Islamic prayer areas built to accommodate the entire population of a town; often with the mihrab as the only architectural feature.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of purple colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of violet colors.
Refers to the usually older and more densely populated central sections of cities.
Museums administered by, and located on the premises of, a unversity.
A range of pink colors resembling the color of pink pigment.

Platforms used for public speaking. In Ancient Rome, a platform elevated in the Roman forum, decorated with the prows or rostra of captured ships, and used to deliver orations or pleadings to the Roman populace.

Vases designed for or used to hold offerings of food, libations, or flowers at a grave or tomb. Examples include those from ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, and China, where they were often designed in pairs. They remain common as flower receptacles in modern cemeteries.
Plants collectively, usually referring to plants or vegetal growths in a defined area. For the kingdom of plants, use "Plantae (kingdom)."
Small streams only a few inches deep, either man-made or formed by rainwater.

Regions of land, usually bordering rivers, streams, or lakes, which are subject to excessive rainfall and short-term flooding of flat portions. Regions of land, usually bordering rivers, streams, or lakes, which are subject to excessive rainfall and short-term flooding of flat portions.

Gymnosperms that are related to the conifers but resembling palms and having affinity with tree-ferns. Characterized by a crown of large compound leaves and a stout trunk; examples exist in tropical and subtropical regions today, but they flourished in great variety and abundance during the Jurassic Period.
Landscapes considered to have picturesque features and a pleasing appearance, generally including natural features and vegetation, with or without manmade structures.
Use to designate the physical environment of the streets including such elements as structures, open spaces, and vegetation.
Land available for building but not currently developed and lacking any improvements or utilities.
Turning over a criminal suspect to another state or province in the country, the national government, or a foreign country.
The act of delivering a sermon or religious address.
Affecting the actions, behavior, opinions, or work of others, possibly unconsciously. For the effect produced by someone or their work upon the creative thought or work of others, see "influence."
Type of lace reuniting elements and motifs from bobbin and needle lace to form a harmonious piece. It can also contain mechanical elements such as tape and tulle.

Refers to lace made at Chantilly, Oise departement, France, since the 18th century. It is characterized by being delicate, made of silk or linen, and having a six-sided mesh ground and a distinctive floral or scrolled design. Later designs include ribbons, naturalistic flowers, and other designs on a dotted background. Chantilly lace dating from the 19th century was produced in three colors: white, black, and "blond," which was the natural beige color of silk.  It was made into large items such as veils, shawls, other of apparel, and household dresser covers and draperies. Chantilly lace was copied in machine lace from 1840 on.
In Indian architecture, a image’s (or niche’s) frame crowned with tōraṇa.
An element placed in the immediate foreground of a pictorial composition to direct the spectator's eye into the picture.
Sets of two individual things of the same or similar type that are associated or complementary in use, purpose, or position.
Oolitic limestone, quarried in the vicinity of Clipsham, Leicestershire, England; used primarily as a building stone.
In film photography, the use of chemicals intended for developing one kind of film (e.g. color) and applying them to another (e.g. negative), and vice versa.
Artificial passages of wood or masonry, a dam or embankment, used for impounding the water of river, stream, or canal, and fitted with a valve or gate for stopping or regulating the flow.

Chairs designed for the use of the priest or other celebrant presiding at a Christian mass or other service. The chairs are usually of substantial size and having arms, placed in the choir of the church. For a set of three chairs or seats on a recessed bench for the celebrant, deacon, and sub-deacon, use "sedilia." For the chairs of a presiding bishop, use "cathedrae (bishop's chairs)." For chairs specifically for a presiding Protestant preacher, use "preacher's chairs."

Refers to the Italian art movement of the 1970s that was analogous to the Minimalist and Conceptual Art movement in North America. The style is characterized by the use of intentionally humble and worthless materials, and artistic expression through happenings and installations, with often obscure or conflicting meanings.
Arranged or having parts arranged like rays around a central axis.

Describes individually discrete things raised in relative position to other places or things, especially above the ground or other surface. For the form attribute describing something protruding above a surface to which it is attached or is a part, use "raised".
A photographic plate size, about 1 3/8 by 1 5/8 inches.
Describes buildings, particularly classic Greek and Roman temples or buildings like them in structure, having a row or rows of six columns at one or both ends.

Roughly assembled visual and audio workprints of each day's shooting of a motion picture production, shown that same day or the next for the director and others involved in the filming process to judge the results.
Long thin woodworking gouges, the cutting edge of which is beveled on the concave side.
Any metallic alloy used as a substitute for gold.
A term for a type of photographic portrait popular in the years before the First World War. Usually oval, finished with liberal airbrushing and colored with pastels.

Field of knowledge dealing with coats of arms and armorial insignia, including their depiction and use, determination of who is entitled to display them, the genealogy of families having coats of arms, and the maintenance and interpretation of heraldic records.
Causing discrete agents or agencies to work together.
Condemning to penalty or punishment.
Groups of soldiers armed, trained, and equipped to fight on foot.
Modifier describing a saturated color of high intensity and medium to dark value.
General activity, condition, or employment of a domestic servant, a public servant, or in the military.
Documents giving authoritative recognition of a fact, qualification, or promise.
Pieces of material removed from punched cards during the punching process.

Materials for the packing or protective wrapping of products that contain information or otherwise convey a message about the product. For material used to protect, cushion, or brace objects for safe shipment or storage, carrying no information or message about the objects, use "packing material."

Refers to maps of a given region, intended to chart the areas covered by forests and other vegetation. They typically record the boundaries of the forest, the relief of the area, assessments of timber volume and expected growth rates, and features or projections related to concerns such as animal or human inhabitants and ecological matters.
Selective or complete lists of sound recordings, which can be compiled by composer, performer, or group of performers, or of a particular genre or recording label.
List of recommended books, periodical articles, or other information forms, typically as part of course which students are expected to read.

Photographic negative transparencies that are designed to be developed immediately after exposure via an integrated packet of chemistry when pulled from a special film holder or camera that enables the integrated developer chemistry to be squeezed through rollers and onto a light sensitive emulsion. This method of image-forming was developed as a commercial product by the Polaroid corporation, and sold as individual plates that would yield both a positive print and a printable negative transparency, known as Polaroid 55.
Photographic prints having collodion as the binder.
Photographs of recently deceased persons taken as part of the mourning and memorialization process.

Standard mosaic process and technique using small cubes of uniform size known as tesserae, made of hard materials such as stone and glass, applied to a ground to form ornamental patterns and pictures. While opus tessellatum was initially a cheap substitute for finer mosaic work executed in the more complex technique of "opus vermiculatum," it eventually became the dominant technique and remained so throughout the Middle Ages.

Flat puppets of leather or another material, often elaborately painted, originally developed in Java to cast shadows on white screens during dramatizations in shadow theater. They are often, but not always, animated with rods.
Masks that are worn on the face and cover most of it. Examples are masks worn for protection or during ritual dances in African and other cultures.
Photography of distant objects using either a telephoto lens or a telescope.
Photography that takes place at night, typically outside, and often with emphasis on the existing light, such as neon signs, street lights, or stars
Gratuitous grants or transfers of property that have been promised, but as of yet are not delivered.
Dictionaries dedicated to terminology related to particular arts, crafts, or industries and their unique technical vocabularies.

Lines of closely spaced hedges typically interspersed with trees, usually planted on a low earthen wall or base and trained to form a barrier or mark the boundary of an area, particularly in fields or between properties.
Photographs of minute objects, usually taken through a microscope. Distinct from "microphotographs," which are images reduced to minute size.
Wood of the species Aesculus pavia.
Directions or orders of remedy for a disease or illness.

Refers to a type of earthenware first developed around 1850 by the Thomas Minton factory in England. It is characterized by a richly modeled surface with thick, colored glazes. It is typically used for large objects such as umbrella stands, fountains, jardinieres, and figures.

Book furniture comprising bookcase units surmounting a cupboard support. These are of various design, but often with a center double-doored unit with two wings with single doors. The doors are often glassed or have a screen to allow viewing the contents within.
Various items used to furnish doors functionally including kick plates, garment hooks, roller latches, bolts, stops, numbers, and letterbox plates.
Religious concepts related to doctrine.
Concepts related to the doctrine of Christianity.

A Roman Catholic monastic order founded by St. Bruno of Cologne in Chartreuse (north of Grenoble, France) in 1084. The Carthusians combine the solitary existence of hermits with a communal life within the monastery. The monks or nuns live in individual cells and only come together at specific times of the day and at special feasts; strict abstinence is practiced. The Carthusians spread slowly, but, by 1521, the order numbered 195 houses in every Catholic European country. They played an important role in the monastic-reform movement of the 11th and 12th centuries; it is itself, however, the one form of communal religious life that has not experienced reform. Houses are found in many parts of Europe although membership is relatively small. A famous liqueur is made at 'La Grande Chartreuse,' the order's mother-house, with profits donated to charity.
Amphorae with a shape like a Panathenaic amphora, but with subject matter and painting that is not characteristic of Panathenaic amphorae.

Constructions of India, often architecturally embellished, with steps deeply cut down to a water-drawing area; used also as shelters from the heat. Below ground water reservoirs having stairways down to the water level. Most common in India and Pakistan, the structures may be decorative, elaborate, and multistoried.
Generic term to refer to either gender, where the relationship to oneself is the child of one's sibling.

Christian sect originally founded by Charles Taze Russell in the late 19th century. Russell's successor, Joseph Franklin Rutherford, adopted the name Jehovah's Witness in 1931. The sect believes that Jehovah (Yahweh) is the true God, and that Jesus Christ is the son of God. The sect's goal is to establish what they consider to be God's Kingdom, which they believe will emerge following an apocalyptic Armageddon. Generally, Jehovah's Witnesses have no association with other denominations, and shun secular governments. They do not vote, celebrate religious or national holidays, and members refuse military service. Members engage in door-to-door proselytizing, selling their publications, "The Watchtower" and "Awake!", which is published in 80 languages.
A technique used by sculptors to reproduce a clay or plaster model or to copy a finished work through measurements.
Those who are trained or work in hygiene.
Those who take part in a revolution opposed to a previous revolution or reversing its results.
A silver ore, also known as argentite, acanthite, and silver glance, used in niello work and as a colorant in ceramic glazes.

People that are born with both male and female sex organs. Historically the term 'hermaphrodite' has been used in this context, but now prefer 'intersex people'. Reserve use of the term 'hermaphrodite' for the context of organisms that can produce both gametes associated with male and female sexes.

Standardized symbols, notations, or other markings applied to objects during or after creation, conveying information such as the object's origin or maker, its authenticity, or a change in its official status. For lettering marked on something for documentation or commemoration, use "inscriptions." For marks inherent in the paper support, not applied as part of the image or work, use "watermarks."

Paper, typically hand-made, produced by laying the pulp on a wire screen that leaves parallel and perpendicular translucent lines in the finished product. The parallel lines in one direction are heavier and more widely spaced than those in the orthogonal direction. There is often a watermark pattern incorporated into the screen. The look of handmade laid paper may be simulated by using a dandy roll to transfer a similar pattern. Laid paper is distinguished from "wove paper," which has a crosshatched or even appearance.
Symmetrical open plane curves formed by the intersection of a cone with a plane parallel to its side, resembling the path of a projectile under the action of gravity.
Clay from the Gault Formation, deposited in a calm, deep water marine environment during the Lower Cretaceous Period. When raw, a stiff blue clay, when fired, white in color.
Lightweight building material composed of solid gypsum, used for building lightweight, fire-resistant, non-load bearing interior walls.
Adzes with a blade gouge-shaped in cross section and designed for hollowing.
Long augers whose end terminates in a notched spoon blade with one projection sharpened to form a nose, and the other projection bent upward to clear and hold the shavings from the hole.
Hand tools consisting of a steel or other metal head pointed at one or both ends and mounted on a handle or wood or another material; used for loosening and breaking up compacted soil or rocks.
Pointed instruments used to mark lines in wood, metal, or brick.
Pieces of linoleum, often mounted on a wooden block on which is cut an image to be printed.
Devices comprising a timber or other narrow surface that is suspended by a rope or attached by hooks to a roof that is being thatched, to serve as a platform or foothold for the thatcher.
Dealing with or offering comparison between two or more different cultures or cultural areas.
Risings and overflowings of bodies of water, covering land not usually underwater.
Water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the air in sufficient concentration to appreciably reduce visibilty.
Powdered debris produced by insects in the course of feeding and boring, often including excrement and food remains. In art conservation, frass may be an indicator of insect damage.
A channel-shaped, tapered, single lap, roofing tile.
Tile used for roofing, distinguished by being shaped and laid to form a valley.
Tools used for upkeep, such as cleaning tools.
Cleaning instruments consisting of a pole or stick attached with a thick bundle of loose strings, yarn, or other absorbent material; used to soak up liquid in cleaning floors and other surfaces.

Jointed figures of humans or animals able to assume a variety of poses to serve as substitutes for living models for artists. For three-dimensional representations of human figures used specifically for fitting or displaying clothing, use "mannequins." For models of the human body used for teaching anatomy or demonstrating surgical operations, use "manikins."

Tools consisting of a broad blade or scoop used for taking up, removing, or throwing loose matter, such as earth, snow, or coal. Hand-operated shovels typically have the blade or scoop attached to a long handle. For long-bladed tools with shorter hafts and t-bars or handles to grasp, use "spades."

Tools or instruments used for gilding, which involves the surface application of gold or another metal in the form of leaf, powder applied directly to the surface, powder mixed with a binder, electroplating, or other forms to approximate the effect of solid or inlaid metal.
Cutting devices of various kinds used in metalworking.
Journeys or excursions, either for business, pleasure, or education, that include visiting numerous places in a sequence.
Tools with a pistol grip and a small electrically heated bit that reaches operating temperatures rapidly; used to solder electrical components.

Wood-handled tools having a steel head flattened at one end suitable for striking or driving; formed at the other end into a wide sharp blade used for chopping. The underpart of the blade may be notched for pulling nails.
Ceramic objects used to separate wares during firing.
Hard, flat surfaces of stone, wood, or metal on which a mass of molten glass gathered on the end of a blowpipe or pontil is rolled and shaped in glassmaking.
Any of various toothed devices used in handling or ordering textile fibers.
Insulated enclosures in which conditions such as temperature and humidity are tightly controlled to regulate growth of living things.
Furnaces, ovens, or heated enclosures for drying, charring, hardening, baking, or burning various materials.
Handheld devices that extrude caulking material from a disposable tube mounted on the gun itself. Squeezing the handle forces material from the tube, usually through a narrow tip on the tube.

A controlled vocabulary is an organized arrangement of words and phrases that are used to index content and/or to retrieve content through browsing or searching. It typically includes preferred and variant terms and has a limited scope or describes a specific domain. Controlled vocabulary is a broader concept than authority file, encompassing authority files as well as other controlled lists of terminology.
Design of a beam that is proportioned to carry at ultimate capacity the design load multiplied by the safety factor.

Documents, usually sealed, granting specific rights, setting forth aims and principles of a newly established entity, and often embodying formal agreements and authorizing special privileges or exemptions.
In Indian architecture, five-storeyed/superstructure.
General theory that emphasizes the importance of history as a standard of value or as a determinant of events.
The condition of having elements that are different, varied, or unlike. Used often to describe organizational or social groups composed of different types of people with varying perspectives.
Facilities for crushing stone, minerals, or other materials.

Buildings where travellers or tourists are provided with overnight accommodation, meals, and other services; often distinguished from inns and other forms of temporary lodging for travellers by their larger size and range of facilities, in modern times often equipped with a restaurant, bar, conference rooms, and leisure facilities.

Maps intended to introduce a region or locality to tourists, who are visitors to an unfamiliar place, particularly those who travel for pleasure or culture, usually to visit a number of places with the goal of experiencing places of interest and scenery.
Open hanging shelves for displaying china, often with lattice work on the sides.

Extended horizontal bands decorating architecture, furniture, or other objects and containing figures, scenes, inscriptions, or ornamental motifs. For the specific parts of classical entablatures, see "friezes (entablature components)."
Motifs representing the head or skull of an ox, often garlanded, common in classical style friezes.

Motif in the form of a stylized bellflower of the family Campanulaceae. Examples of the motif include northern and eastern European folk art and Japanese tiles. For motifs on 18th-century furniture and other items resembling strings of husk or bellflower shapes nestled together in a festoon, use "husk (motif)."
A decorative pattern formed of a series of convex ridges.
As an artistic concept, the appearance or condition of oneness or wholeness.
A pattern in which a series of small right angles produces a steplike edge, usually proceeding a few steps up and then down again.

Mirrors made from polished obsidian, which is a dark, shiny glass formed in nature by the rapid cooling of lava. Such mirrors were used since Paleolithic times. In ancient Mesoamerica and elsewhere, they were often used as instruments for seeing.

Stones forming part of corners or angles in walls, especially when lying at the foundation of a principal angle. These may also incorporate the date of or inscription about the structure's construction.
Long benches without a back.

Benches located on the stoop of a residence or other building in an urban environment; usually of modest size and fixed in place. For benches, swings, chairs, and other furniture on the porch of a residence, use "porch furniture."

An Italian word meaning design or drawing, referring broadly and theoretically to the conception of a work of art, incorporating the idea that drawing was the foundation of art; the theory was expounded in Renaissance Italy, particularly in Tuscany. By extension, in Mannerist art theory the term refers to the work of art in ideal or Platonic form which could exist only in the artist's mind. The term is contrasted to "colorito" or "colore," which is the application and use of color in a work.
Feet carved to represent an animal's paw; used on chairs, sofas, and case pieces, especially in the 19th century.
Fluorocarbon elastomer-based synthetic rubber.
Songs or soothing refrains sung or chanted, usually to children, to quiet or lull the listener to sleep.
Large sheets, made of paper, plastic, cloth, or other absorbant material, which are typically spread on or near a painter's workstation to protect the area from unwanted paint drippings or splatter.
Resources or machinery used for arranging characters comprised of alphabets, numerals, and other symbols.
Primitive drills in which the shaft is revolved by working up and down a bar carrying a cord attached at the center to the upper end of the shaft.
Folding, umbrellalike fabric devices with cords supporting a harness or straps for allowing objects to float down safely through the air.
Equipment used in the cutting or weaving of weaving of rushes.
Devices which attach to a drawing table and combine the functions of a straightedge, T-square, triangle, and protractor; used by draftsmen, designers, architects, and engineers.
Those whose occupation is brewing beer and other malt liquors.
Those who make, process, or handle ribbons, including those who attach them to garments.
People who write or give orally critical reviews of motion pictures and the art of filmmaking for broadcast or publication.
Those trained or working in any of the planning fields, which have to do with the establishment of objectives, procedures, and resources.
Those who collect or study coins, tokens, medals, paper money, and objects closely resembling them in form or purpose.
People who study, practice, or are otherwise active in the field of law.
Ecclesiastics or lay attendants who carry a cross in a procession.
Foliate decoration, derived from leaflike forms.

Authoritative orders, edicts, laws, ordinances, or judicial decisions that are set forth by a civil or ecclesiastical authority, typically having the force of law and often settling a disputed issue or doctrine.
Buildings that house museums with exhibitions and other holdings documenting the history and artifacts pertinent to the written word and other literature.
Square-back Windsor chairs with a slat across the upper back framed between the back posts.

A continuous flow of space linking the parts of a building or buildings, or through any series of interior or exterior spaces. Used often with reference to traffic patterns through areas or buildings, including the means of travel through a building, such as doors, corridors, stairs, or elevators.

Outdoor or indoor areas of turf for play of the equestrian sport of polo. The outdoor polo field has dimensions of 300  x 160 yards, with goals located at each end between two vertical goal posts that are 24 feet apart and light enough to break in case of collision. Outdoor or indoor areas of turf for play of the equestrian sport of polo. The outdoor polo field has dimensions of 300  x 160 yards, with goals located at each end between two vertical goal posts that are 24 feet apart and light enough to break in case of collision.
People skilled in the practice of exegesis, which is exposition or explanation, especially with regard to the critical interpretation of a portion of Scripture or other text.

Those trained or working in the social science dealing with the earth and its life, especially the description of land, sea, air, and the distribution of plant and animal life, including human beings, their activities and territorial organizations.

Catalogs in the form of comprehensive or selected lists issued by a library or group of libraries of the books, periodicals, maps, and other materials in their collections, arranged in systematic order.
Generally, people whose work or business is cleaning, especially of building interiors or of clothing and linens.

Sheet metal seams used primarily with light material, distinguished by an offset along the side of the seam. To make a grooved seam, the edges of both pieces are turned and hooked together; a grooving machine or other roller is run over the seam, creating an offset in the upper sheet, securing it so the seam does not come apart. Examples of uses for this seam are for joining two flat sheets, making longitudinal seams in round pipes, and vertical seams in articles having a flaring or cylindrical surface.
Technique of purely pattern bond with no overlapping of units, so that all vertical joints are aligned.
Paintings or other art works that serve as a reminder of the inevitability of death, usually due to the depicted subject.
A preliminary layer in a painting in which drawing, composition, and tonal values are worked out, or an area in one color which is then to be worked with glazes.
Prints made by using stencil printing, which employs plates or screens having holes to allow ink or paint to be pushed through to form a design or image.
Movable control surfaces used to impart direction to craft when in motion; usually located at the rear of vehicles.

Spectroscopic technique that measures the absorption of infrared radiation by a sample. A molecule with a dipole moment, that is one end with a positive charge and the other end a negative charge, can absorb infrared light, but only at certain fixed frequencies. Hence, an infrared spectrum of light reflected from the surface will show absorption peaks which are characteristic of the molecule and its method of bonding to the surface.
Infrared spectroscopy having the range of 0.9 – 1.7μm, but can also be classified from 0.7 – 2.5μm.
Small devices consisting of a glass container filled with spirit alcohol and a wick used for heating small vessels.

Lighting devices having a vessel to contain fuel used as a source of illumination, such as grease or oil. The term also refers to relatively small -- of a size to be placed on or beside a desk or table -- household or office lighting devices that incorporate a vessel of glass or some similar material that encloses the source of illumination, whether a candle, oil, gas-jet, or incandescent wire inside a light bulb. The lamp was invented at least as early as 70,000 BCE, originally consisting of a hollowed-out rock filled with moss or some other absorbent material that was soaked with animal fat and ignited. To refer to the glass bulbs used as a component of electric lamps, use "light bulbs."
Lights which soften or eliminate the shadows created by strongly directional lighting.
Glass vessels of vase shape with a wide flaring neck, bulbous body having a flat base or trumpet-like stem hung for use in a mosque.

Any lamp (lighting device) intended to be hung on the wall. Use "brackets (lighting devices)" for wall lamps attached to or suspended from some form of bracket, by means of which it can be hung on the wall.
Rows of small floodlights mounted on trough reflectors and used for theater borderlights, footlights, and general stage illumination.

Automata, water jets, or other devices designed to spray, soak, and surprise unwary onlookers in gardens; generally activated by hidden, usually pressure-sensitive, levers, springs, or similar triggers; popular especially during the Renaissance.

Staff weapons widely used in warfare in the 15th and 16th centuries, having an axlike blade with a short fluke on the back and a spike at the top of the staff. After the late 16th century they increasingly came to be used solely as ceremonial weapons, in which capacity they survived well into the 19th century.
Goods in transit, whether by land, air, or water.
Lights, usually red, mounted at the rear of a vehicle to serve as a warning.
Aeronautical ground lights indicating the presence of an obstruction.
Burners designed to assure an even flow of gas to the individual jet.

Salt formed by adding hydrochloric acid to lithium. Lithium chloride is the compound used to produce lithium metal by electrolysis. Thanks to its hygroscopic capacity, it is used for controlling relative humidity within a sealed environment. It is also used as a soldering flux, and to produce red colors in pyrotechnics.

Those portions of refractory molds that define the internal spaces in  hollow bronze sculptures. These may be formed in a variety of ways and are usually (but not always) made of similar material as that used for the outer portion of the mold. The term is also used as shorthand to refer to the material it is made of. A core is generally solid but may be hollow.
Japanese clay or terracotta cylinders surmounted by modeled figures or heads, placed in a fencelike position around burial mounds.
Works of art that employ video technology, especially videotapes. For the study and practice of the art of producing such works, use "video."
Preparatory techniques used on printing surfaces, such as plates.

Tone reversal in photographs caused by massive overexposure of the photographic emulsion to light. True solarization rarely occurs in modern emulsions, and is most commonly seen in early daguerreotypes. For the similar effect that occurs with exposure of negatives or emulsions to bright light during development, rather than at the moment of camera exposure, as was used by the Surrealists, use "Sabattier effect."
Use when, in printing, not all successive plates or blocks were positioned accurately.

The technique of dropping or painting acid onto an aquatint ground to allow localized and controlled biting. To control the acid application, traditionally, a clean brush was coated with saliva, dipped into nitric acid, and brushed onto the ground.

Type of heavily armed foot soldiers of ancient Greece in use from ca. late 8th century BCE, specializing in close-formation fighting. Prior to the appearance of hoplites, individual combat between heroes predominated in warfare. New, heavier armor and the thrusting sword, rather than throwing spear, gave the hoplites stronger protection as foot soldiers, enabling the formation of a compact phalanx that was very successful. Greek hoplites were renowned as the best fighters in the Mediterranean world and in great demand as mercenaries in ancient Lydia, Babylonia, and Egypt.
Revolts or rebellions of a substantial number of soldiers, sailors, prisoners, or others against those under whose authority they are expected to serve.
Object genre including equipment, tools, vessels, apparatus, utensils, instruments, apparel, small furnishings, and other things employed in any trade or used in executing a task or work.
Heavy woven textiles used for a variety of utilitarian purposes essentially in the form in which they left the loom. In Western societies they are used primarily as floor coverings.
Sheets of impermiable material meant to be layed on the ground as a base for a portable mattress or other sleeping mat, usually in the context of sleeping outdoors.
Straw matting used as a floor covering in Japan.
Peel strength is the measure of the average force required to separate two bonded materials.
Rugs that are utilized as tablecloths or otherwise to protect the surface of a table or other furniture.
Long, narrow, Persian carpets whose lengths are generally two to three times their widths; usually headpieces in the traditional carpet arrangement of Islamic rooms.
Scandanavian closely tufted, handwoven rugs.
Tapestry-woven rugs produced in the Islamic lands of western Central Asia, the Middle East, the Balkans and North Africa.

Strictly speaking, floor or table carpets, rugs, and kilims of Turkish design; however, in historical sources the term may be used imprecisely to refer to any rugs having Oriental designs, not necessarily only those of Turkish manufacture or design.

Receptacle, typically of gold, silver, or another precious material, intended for the preservation of relics, which are the physical remains of a holy person or an object of particular veneration. Reliquary monstrances are distinguished by having an opening or transparent covering, sometimes a horizontal cylinder of glass, crystal, etc. through which the venerated object may be seen. For receptacles specifically for the display of the sacred Host, use "monstrances."
Organized oppositions to authority; risings in arms or open resistance against established authority or governmental restraints.
Rugs that include rectangular compartments, each containing some floral or botanic motif, designs possibly representing the layout of Persian gardens with flower beds and streams.

Artist's ink made from the brown pigment derived from the ink of cuttlefish, an invertebrate related to the octopus and squid. The cuttlefish uses the natural ink defensively. To make artist's ink, the animal's ink sac is extracted, dried, then dissolved in dilute alkali, and further processed. The resulting pigment is chemically inert and fairly permanent; it is used primarily as a drawing ink and to apply washes. Sepia ink has been used at least since ancient Roman times. It was particularly popular as a drawing medium from the Renaissance onwards, and in the late 18th and 19th centuries generally replaced bistre as a medium for making wash drawings.
Mechanical typewriters that operate via movement produced entirely by the operator without electrical power.
A broad term that includes all aspects of an organism's physical condition; often reserved for abnormal conditions, including diseases, disorders, illnesses, and injuries.
Refers to high executive officers or ministers in a Muslim government, particularly in the Ottoman Empire.
A figure of a female lamp-bearer, in Indian architecture or sculpture tradition.
Portions of objects that are torn, broken off from, or dislocated from their original whole.

Visual works and other objects made of more than one material; for example, an object made of bronze, terracotta, and amber. The term is used in archaeological conservation and other disciplines. For modern works where the artist employs multiple materials, use "multimedia works."
Mostly metal parts of a single-reed instrument used to keep the reed in place against the mouthpiece, without obstructing its vibrations when played.

Works in which three-dimensional objects, often figural sculpture, in the foreground blend with a realistic painted background. The entire work is usually enclosed in a case or niche and is viewed from a distant, darkened vantage point.
Occasional printing, used for advertisements, letters, flyers and visiting cards. The type is reduced and consists of formulas; the production period is very short.

Refers to decorations in any medium that dominate a wall (or ceiling) surface; most often refers to works executed on the wall, but may also refer to works done separately and affixed to the wall. For paintings specifically, see "mural paintings."
Visual works comprising designs, patterns, or other arrangements of beads, typically stringed or attached to textile supports.

Paintings or prints that depict beautiful women. This term, which literally means "pictures of beautiful women," was most likely coined in the Edo period (1615-1868) or the Meiji period (1868-1912). Before this period, these pictures may have been called "onna-e" or "bijin-e".
Clappers made of two slabs of wood hinged at one end and clicked together.

Decorative discs that are baked into or otherwise affixed to baked goods; today typically limited to cakes for children, particularly in the southern Netherlands, but formerly also in Britain and elsewhere. Patakons were formerly ceramic, now may be edible. The tradition probably derived from an original practice of placing a coin in the baked item.
Use to designate the apparent principal source of illumination of a subject or area, especially in relation to photography and film.
Structure, especially in the context of semiconductors, that is an arrangement of molecular dimensions, or nanometers.
Small, usually thick coins that may have been created by removing circular pieces from other, larger coins, as in the case of holey dollars.
Moisture excreted through the pores of the skin of most mammals, usually as a result of physical exertion or heat, in order to cool the body.

Use to describe two-way systems involving feedback from a viewer or user, to obtain data or commands and to give immediate results or updated information. Generally used to describe computer-based systems, but may have broader applications as well.
Describes ceramic or objects of ceramic fashioned from a mixture of clay and crushed rock.

Refers to the style and movement founded by Leon Chwistek in the 1920s after the disintegration of the Formists and is based on the philosophical theory of painting that entails the grouping of elements of similar shape and color into 'zones'.

United States paper money issued between 1878 and 1963 in several denominations from 1 dollar to 1000 dollars, equal to and redeemable for silver at the stated value, replaced by Federal Reserve notes.
The original, or earliest known, inhabitants of a colony or country.
Groups of two or more people or animals functioning as a collaborative unit in some joint action, such as a sport, game, project, or task.
Persons atypical due to disabilities or giftedness.
The activities of moving and tending of sheep, cattle, reindeer, or other domesticated herd animals.
In Indian architecture, a ribbed cyma-awning; khuracchādya.

Form of farming that uses steps or terraces on an upland area, to  maximize arable land area by creating horizontal, flat plots for crops. A prime example of the practice was in Pre-Columbian cultures.
Material derived from the horny covering that protects the end of the digits of certain animals such as horses or deer.
Open, rounded vessels of greater width than depth, with sloping or curving sides, used for receiving running water or holding water and other liquids, especially for washing purposes.
Silver and cupronickel decimal coins of the United States and certain other former British colonies issued since 1796 and valued at one tenth of a dollar.
Untanned skin or hide which has had the flesh and hair removed and allowed to dry into a desired shape.
Nationality and culture of the United Arab Emirates, which is diverse, including heritage from the Arabian Peninsula, East Africa, Iran, Baluchistan, India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.
Credit instruments ordering the payment of a specified amount of money, usually issued and payable at a bank or post office.
Gilt crescent-shaped badges suspended from the neck or on a uniform, derived from an article of medieval armour designed to protect the neck and throat, and formerly worn by officers on duty.

Bowed friction idiophones, consisting of a circular flat wood resonator with a set of nails or iron pins of varying heights driven into its sides, which were sounded by being rubbed with a rosined bow. Sympathetic strings were added to some models.
Frame drums of Indonesia, made of heavy wood, they have an open bottom and goatskin membrane.

Electronic instruments made in a wide variety of models differing considerably in size, appearance, and manner of operation, though generally their output must pass through external amplifiers and loudspeakers to produce sound.

The twisted strands of fibrous material to which the sections of a book are sewn. Distinguished from "thongs (binding components)" which are the narrow strips of rawhide or processed animal skin used for the same purpose before the latter part of the 16th century, and from "tapes (binding components)" which are flat strips of closely woven cloth that perform the same function. Also distinguished from "bands (binding components)" which are the raised ridges across the spine of a bound book that indicate the location of the cords beneath the covering material.

Refers to the written or printed characters that denote units in a numerical sequence. For the abstract units belonging to a mathematical system and subject to specified laws of succession, addition, and other functions, use "numbers."
Typefaces that imitate cursive handwriting.

Baskets created with doubleweave techniques, where one basket is woven outside another separate basket. Typically made of plant fibers such as rivercane (Arundinaria gigantea); splints are often dyed to create varying patterns on the sides and lids of the basket. Manufactured by various Southeastern Native North American tribes, but the Cherokee are most well-known for their doubleweave basketry.
Box-like containers used to carry or store corporals, which are altar cloths. For envelope-like containers of stiffened material used to hold the corporal, use "burses (corporal)."
Cylindrical or rectangular containers usually of lightweight metal, plastic, or laminated pasteboard used for holding dry products.

Drinking vessels distinguished by having two spouts: a short one for filling and a long one through which the liquid is poured into the mouth without the spout touching the lips of the drinker. Well known examples were developed in Catalonia, Spain; they are also known in former colonial areas of Spain in Latin America, and among indigenous people.
Ancient Greek silver coins worth ten drachmas, struck in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, primarily in Sicily.
Images or texts designed to occupy two facing pages.
Titles or abbreviated titles of a book, or section of a book, repeated in uniform style at the head or foot of each page or verso.
Flutes with two finger holes and one thumbhole. Usually played in tandem with a drum. A full diatonic scale could be achieved by over-blowing and many folk tunes and dances were thus playable.

Reedpipes with double reed, conical bore, and characteristically a pirouette, distributed worldwide. They were the precursors of the oboe in Europe, introduced there from the Near East in the 12th century.

Javanese metallophones consisting of thick bronze or iron slabs, usually six or seven but varying regionally, set on top of a wood trough or cradle, often elaborately carved, and struck with hammers of wood or horn. They exist in three sizes, and are important instruments in the Javanese gamelan.

Japanese barrel drums with two heads, only one of which is struck; the size and ratio of diameter to length vary greatly, and the membranes are either tacked to the body or laced on, sometimes lapped over metal rings and then laced. Taiko have a legendary origin in Japanese folklore, but historical records suggest they came to Japan in the 6th century CE through Korea and China.
Devices for measuring and recording the passage of time.
Devices of various kinds for measuring size in various contexts.
Instruments for measuring pressure, normally of gases or liquids.
Instruments for measuring small electric currents.
Devices of various kinds for measuring characteristics of the wind.
Small pyramid or cone shaped made from various refractory materials and intended to melt at different temperatures; used in kilns where temperature is not automatically regulated.
Parts or components of timepieces.
Cords, strings, or other lines which, when used in conjunction with plumb bobs suspended from one end, are used to determine verticality or to aid in locating points on the ground during surveying.

Straight poles graduated with numerical marks that are held upright and used with leveling instruments to measure heights and elevations, especially during surveying. For similar poles having numerical and various geometrical markings suited for measuring horizontal distances with other stadia equipment, use "stadia rods."
Scales designed to weigh parcels in preparation for calculating shipping costs.
Small scales used for measuring the weight and therefore the market size of eggs, usually one by one.
Ethiopian single-string bowed spike fiddles, having a tuning-peg, bridge, and parchment-covered diamond-shaped soundbox.
Small clocks or large watches mounted in folding cases and meant to be used when traveling.
Devices for measuring the amount of lime in soils.
Instruments consisting of a rule that slides through a crosspiece and is inserted to measure the depth of holes, grooves, or other similar small depressions.

Reflecting navigational instruments used for measuring the altitude of celestial bodies and having an arc of 1/8 of a circle, but due to their reflecting properties can measure up to 90 degrees; invented in the 1730s and used into the 19th century when superseded by sextants.
Devices that tell the time.

Ecclesiastical drinking vessels; the term is particularly used in reference to those cups used by the Protestant churches since the Reformation. The communion cup may take the form of a goblet wine cup or beaker. For other ecclesiastical drinking vessels, particularly those used by the Catholic churches and often more ornate, use "chalices (liturgical vessels)" or "communion bowls (vessels for wine)."
Parts or components of shields.

Containers in which aromatic pastilles may be burned or liquid perfumes evaporated. Often in the form of a covered vase with holes on the shoulder or cover, or with pierced or openwork decoration. Sometimes made in the form of a tripod, especially an athenienne. For other containers of varying form used to hold burning incense for the purpose of scenting a space, use "incense burners." For covered vaselike containers intended primarily for potpourri, use "potpourri vases."
Containers used for ceremonial celebrations or eulogies.
Boxes in which papers, letters, or other documents are arranged in convenient order for storage or reference.
Containers for bones of the dead.
Tall ovoid or egg-shaped baskets, often without handles; of a type traditionally used for holding geese while plucking their feathers.
Large metal vessels, sometimes lined with white porcelain, used for boiling clothes.

Containers for the safe storage of articles; use especially for boxlike receptacles, generally of steel or iron construction and having one or more securing devices, that can be freestanding or built into a wall or vault and which are used to protect money and other valuables against fire or theft. Prefer "kitchen safes" for ventilated cabinets in which food is stored. Prefer "strongboxes" for lockable boxes which tend to be smaller and more portable.

Small flasks of glass, stone, or another material, designed to store cosmetics. Best known as works from ancient Egypt, elsewhere in the Middle East, Greece, and Rome. Usually distinguished from cosmetic tubes by having a foot.
Storage containers for areca nut and other ingredients like slaked lime and betel leaves that were used in betel chewing.
Term formerly used for a variety of bedcovers, especially those woven of cotton or wool; from the mid-19th century onwards generally replaced by the term "bedspreads."
Quilts expressing patriotic sentiments, usually decorated with such elements as flags and other national symbols, portraits of national leaders, or political slogans.
Quilts with depictions of recognizable figures, objects, or scenes.
Containers for holding table salt; made in a great variety of forms, styles, sizes and materials.  Whenever possible use a more specific term.
Large, shallow dishes, usually oval and having a ledge and a well, used for carrying other dishes.

Copper alloy vessels cast by the lost-wax process and used by the Akan peoples of Ghana to hold valuables such as gold dust or beads, and to serve several ritual purposes; of various forms and styles and often with a hinged lid.
A Mesoamerican upright tubular drum made of wood with a skin membrane.
Tubular drums of South Africa, made from hollow logs and two skins which are laced together.
Ancient Greek drinking vessels in the form of a broad, shallow bowl set on a high foot or pedestal with two upcurving handles.
Cups, with one or two handles, or sometimes with none, intended primarily for drinking coffee; often accompanied by a saucer.
Airtight containers for cigars. For boxlike containers used to hold cigars use "cigar boxes."
Waterproof bags designed to hold ice and used for local application of cold to the body.
Large, footed baskets, of a type thought to be used for the cleansing of raw wool prior to spinning.
Bases or holders which sit in water and are used to hold flower arrangements in place.
In Indian culture, a straight line marked by a measuring cord; straight cord; line for measuring.
Small boxes with perforated lids formerly used to contain pounce or fine sand sprinkled on wet ink to blot it; sometimes made as a unit of an inkstand or desk set.
Boxes or troughs, which may have lids, in which dough is mixed and kneaded.
Receptacles consisting of a tray upon which to rest a napkin and having along the rear end a box divided into two or more compartments for eating utensils and spices.
Partitioned boxlike containers intended for use by travelers and military personnel to carry flatware, cutlery, and other articles for eating and drinking.

Vessels intended to hold or dispense coffee, either urnlike or in the form of a coffeepot and having, instead of a spout, one or more taps and a spigot; usually supported on legs or a stand and may have a heating device. May be part of a coffee service. Prefer "hot water urns" for urnlike vessels intended to hold or dispense hot water in connection with the serving of coffee and which may also be part of a coffee service.
A type of kantharos featuring handles and bowl as in type C and a small torus foot with a very short stem.
Kraters with volute-shaped handles extending from the shoulders to above the rim. They are rare in black-figure but common in red-figure.
Refers to a type of oinochoe similar to shape 2 and featuring a round mouth (also called a flat mouth).
Large ancient Greek earthenware storage jars, spherical in form and having a wide mouth, for bulk storage of liquids and solids.
A type of pyxis that has a lid with finial and a bowl-shaped body supported on three concave slab-like legs.
Bags without handle or strap, but usually with a clasp, of a size that is suitable to be carried in the hand; made of various fabrics or leathers.
Regional or indigenous Latin American containers used to ferment the type of chicha that is obtained from a variety of pumpkin called guada.

Vaselike containers, typically made of glass, intended to be used on the dining table for serving stalks of celery. For relatively low and narrow dishes intended for serving celery, use "celery dishes." For similar vaselike forms also used on the dining table but which often have a scalloped rim and are intended to hold spoons, use "spoon holders." For vaselike forms which are often made of glass but sometimes made of wood or bone and which are usually kept near a fireplace or oil lamp, use "spill holders."

Lidded, roughly cylindrical containers with one or two handles used for holding, cooling, and transporting milk, holding varying quantities and generally of stainless steel or tin-coated galvanized steel.
Processes that involve a photographic process (that is, employing light-sensitivity) to transfer an image, and then a separate process to produce a print that was never itself light-sensitive.
Printing process that uses engraved linoleum, which may or may not be mounted on a wood block as the plate for printing or stamping a design or composition.
Implements used to shelter or enclose food.
Wide, sometimes circular- shaped spatulas, typically with an off-set blade, designed to turn or flip cakes.
Small flat brushes used to coat pastry with butter, eggs, or the like.
Forks that are used as part of a place setting; all forks used for consuming at table and not for serving food.

Vessels having a single, high looped handle that function as ladles for serving wine out of a krater. The kyathos is teacup-shaped and thin-walled. It is primarily a black-figure form and was originally copied from an Etruscan shape.
Devices used to cut into large round cheeses, often consisting of a revolving base and an attached cutting arm.
Small boxes, which may be made of varied materials, used to carry one or more seals.
Instruments used for observing motion or measuring vibration frequency, by means of flashes of periodic, interrupted light from a stroboscopic lamp.
Coffee making devices similar to espresso machines, but equipped with a spout for steaming milk to make cappuccinos.
Genre designating works containing references to or portrayals of short popular traditional songs that normally frame a narrative element.
Codes or numbers used for identification.

Deep hemispherical pierced bowls having two long side handles or one long side handle and a hook at the other side in order to rest on the rim of a punch bowl. Used for straining orange or lemon juice squeezed directly into the punch bowl.
Devices used to press sausage meat into casings.

Hand-operated mills typically consisting of a slab with a slightly concave upper surface and  a smaller, smooth, rounded stone, used for grinding or pulverizing grains or other food materials. They are distinguished from grinding wheels, which are abrasive disks used for cutting or smoothing materials such as metal, glass, plastics, or clay.
Rectangular pieces of wood with one or several diagonal blades used to cut or shred cabbage.
Tools with a pointed spiral piece of metal attached to a handle, used for drawing corks from bottles.
Transverse flutes of Japan.

Traditionally, large pots heated by surrounding the pot with fuel, and placing hot coals on the lid; often made of cast iron, having a tight-fitting lid, and placed in an open fire. May have legs and two side handles as well as a bail handle, used for cooking or baking. The term is also used for modern pots having a similar design, but heated by placing in a conventional oven.

A rock fragment, generally rounded by abrasion, larger than a granule and smaller than a cobble; it has a diameter in the range of 4 to 66 mm, or a size between that of a pea and that of a tennis ball.

Bullets containing a chemical mixture that ignites when the bullet is fired, producing a trail of colored flame or smoke, making the flight of the bullet visible. Their most common use is in machine gun ammunition, spaced at intervals with the regular ammunition.
Containers or reservoirs in which ammunition is stored before loading, one charge at a time, into the firing chamber of a firearm; they may be detachable or an integral part of the weapon.
Scripts related to conventionalized pictures or symbols that convey an idea or thing.

The soprano members of the violin family, having a hollow, resonating body with an incurved waist, arched top and back, and two F-shaped holes cut in the top, a neck terminating in a pegbox and scroll, a bridge, and four strings.

Liturgical chants that are monophonic, or unison, used in the Greek Orthodox church during the Byzantine Empire (330–1453) and down to the 16th century; in modern Greece the term refers to ecclesiastical music of any period.
Service books containing the musical portion of the mass sung by the choir.

Pictures or diagrams that clarify or provide an example or visualization. They usually accompany a text; the term is most often used to refer to pictures in books or published journal. For works that explore a subject or are preliminary to a separate, more finalized work, use "studies (visual works)." For paintings in manuscripts, use "illuminations" or "miniatures (paintings)."
Complexes designed to board horses and accommodate equestrian events such as competitions, dressage, and recreational riding.
Broad category of vessels with rounded profiles that are set upon an integrated supporting member.
That social and economic class that ranks above the middle class.

Flexible or removable devices used to obstruct or regulate vision or light consisting of flexible panels or of horizontal or vertical slats that can be opened or closed, often with the angle of the slats adjustable to admit varying amounts of light. For heavier coverings, often of wood, permanently affixed to buildings, use "shutters." Prefer "shades (coverings)" for flexible screens, usually of paper, cloth, bamboo, or similar materials and sometimes mounted on a roller, used to obstruct or regulate vision or light.
Curtains, especially long curtains of heavy fabric, usually hung in carefully arranged folds at the sides of openings, either in a straight or draped fashion, sometimes used over sheer curtains.
Short, broad-bladed Maori weapons used to jab an opponent in the body or the head; a symbol of chieftainship.
Waterproof curtains, or curtains with waterproof liners, to be hung across a bathtub or shower stall opening to contain splashing water.
Grenades designed to be fired by a small arm firearm with a special barrel or discharge cup, requiring a separate propelling device loaded separately.
Wallpapers decorated with only a single solid ground color.
Clusters of small iron balls, usually nine in number, held together by means of cast iron circular plates at top and bottom with two rings and a central connecting rod, used as cannon shot.
General term for types of Ancient Greek and Roman coins in drachma denominations.

A type of small arms ammunition made from paper that contained shot, wadding, and powder, used before the evolution of metallic cartridges. Construction of gun cartidges from paper evolved to include linen and later metal and other materials with more strength.
Textile covering stretched over an open tester frame.
Lightweight textile coverings that are casually draped or laid over sofas, primarily as decoration but often also for warmth.
Cloth cases, usually of ticking, for a bolster, mattress, or pillow, containing feathers, hair, straw, or other materials used for stuffing.
Western World coins with dollar values.

Envelopes or other simple coverings for relics, which are the remains of a saint, martyr, deity, or other holy person, or their personal items; known in many cultures. Relic covers are made of materials such as paper, leather, silk or another textile; often inscribed, stamped, embroidered, or otherwise decorated. Relic covers may themselves be considered holy from having been in contact with the relic; relic covers may be swapped out and the used cover distributed to the faithful for veneration or perceived healing properties. For more substantial containers for relics, often made of precious materials, use "reliquaries."

Huge textile coverings for the Ka‘ba at the Great Mosque in Mecca, used during the period of pilgrimage, with quotations from the Koran either inwoven or embroidered. Replaced each year, they are cut up after the ceremonies and their pieces distributed as relics.

Relatively small, rectangular linen cloths used by the celebrant for wiping the Eucharistic vessel after each communicant has drunk from it and to wipe the chalice and paten after the ablutions that follow Communion.
Long, narrow textiles used as furniture coverings, to protect polished surfaces and as decoration. Shorter and narrower than scarves for furniture.
Sound-producing apparatuses whose primary function is to play music.
Membranes used in musical instruments and other sound devices to modify the sound made by that device or by the human voice; their vibrations color the tone with a buzzing nasal timbre.

Organized groups of instrumentalists consisting of players of bowed string instruments, to which may be added any number of wind and percussion instrument players; normally there is more than one player for each musical part.
Pieces of armor protecting the front of the abdomen below the breastplate, made originaly of mail, later of plates.
Jackets, sometimes sleeveless, made of leather, worn in 16th- and 17th-century Europe either under a cuirass or as an independent protection against edged weapons.

Term used in the glass trade for an opal glass which has been acid finished and had various ornate designs embedded in the glass in shades of brown and beige. A type of art glass, developed by the Mt. Washington Glass Company.
Describes human voices and musical instruments pitched lower than baritone.

Spheroidal, bulbous shape, pear-shaped, or flattened vessels with a narrow neck and a small mouth, usually of glass, ceramic, metal, animal skin, wicker, or another material and used for various purposes. Also used specifically for distinctive narrow-necked vessels, usually of glass, having a rounded body, used in laboratories.
Containers made to hold water dedicated for sacred uses, made of various materials.

Bowl-shaped or conical devices with perforated or pierced walls, used for draining and straining foods; usually set on a base or on legs. For other culinary tools used to filter foods, use "strainers (culinary tools)."
Containers to hold coasters.
Forks having a small head and tines, used for eating oysters and similar shellfish, often slender with a long handle and three or four pointed tines.

Small knives with a sharp, sometimes serrated, blade used to pare and cut fruit at the table. Often with an ornamental handle and sometimes with a folding blade such as on a penknife. For other small knives with a short handle and sometimes a curved and pointed blade, use "dessert knives."
Spoons having a hinged stem allowing them to be folded for storage or travel. Of a type made from the 15th century. Later often made in sets with knives and forks.

Utensils having a handle and a concave, blunt pushing surface designed for use by toddlers to push food onto their forks or spoons. Popular in the 19th and early 20th century, often collected in a set with a pap spoon, baby spoon, and a baby fork.
Utensils often with a flat triangular blade used for cutting and serving pies and pastries.
Wooden implements used to stir large quantities of liquids consisting of a flat blade on a long handle.
Tools for extracting juice from fruits and vegetables.
Paper for writing letters, often having a letterhead or decorative design, and often accompanied by matching envelopes.
Hand-held electrical appliances having one or more beaters and used in mixing, beating, or creaming food.
Scripts developed in 15th century Italy in humanist circles, largely to replace the Gothic scripts and revive features of Caroline minuscule.
Script developed in Persia in the 14th century, combining elements from both the nashki and tal'iq scripts. Its main features are groups of connecting letters that slope downwards.

Long-distance self-propelled weapons that deliver explosive materials to a target. These are rocket-powered only in the initial phase of flight, then follow an unpowered trajectory that arcs upward before descending to a target. Ballistic missiles can carry either nuclear or conventional warheads.
Short-handled scoops intended for flour, sometimes sized to hold a specific measure, such as one cup, and made with a partial cover.
Percussion instruments consisting of a steel rod bent into the shape of a triangle open at one angle, and struck with a metal beater.

Percussion instruments known primarily in Africa and New Guinea which employ water as a resonator. The African instruments consist of a half-gourd floating upside down on water within a larger vessel; the floating gourd is struck by spoons, sticks, or the hands. The New Guinea instruments have an hourglass-shaped hollow body open at both ends, sounded by being stamped against the surface of water.

Use specifically for aerophones of generally conical bore and a wooden body made from or bound with birch or other bark, with fingerholes, a cup-shaped mouthpiece, and a bell of horn at the other end; examples are known to have been made in the early 1930s by Teppo Repo, a native of the Ingria region of Russia who brought the instrument to Finland. Used also very generally for a variety of wooden horns of Finland, usually made of or covered with birch bark, with or without fingerholes, some resembling trumpets or cornetts, others having a single reed.
Valved brass instruments of conical bore in circular form, designed to replace the French horn in marching bands.
Loose garments covering the entire body and having a veiled opening for the eyes; worn by Muslim women.
Sleeveless outer garments which fasten at the neck and fall loosely from the shoulders to cover the entire body; may have a yoke or some shaping from the neck to the shoulders.
Long, lightweight coatlike overgarments worn in the early 20th century to protect the wearer from dust, especially while riding in automobiles.

Underwear usually made the length of the garment under which it is to be worn, thereby taking the place of a lining. Usually applied to full slips with a bodice and shoulder straps made in dress length. Prefer "half slips" for skirtlike underwear extending from the waist to near the hemline of the garment with which it is worn.
Bands of tape, webbing, or elasticized fabric arranged in an oblong panel which may be slightly curved over the bustline. Worn to compress the breasts.
Type of eyeglasses, often more decorative than functional, hand-held to the eye and usually mounted on a long ornamental handle.
Garments having a strap encircling the neck and supporting the front of the bodice, leaving shoulders and most of the back bare.

Close-fitting trouserlike garments, often with a strap that goes under the foot or shoe at the instep; includes those made to match a coat or jacket and worn outdoors by children. Also, leg coverings, usually extending from the ankle to the knee but sometimes higher, worn for protection.
Bands made of a variety of materials, worn around the wrist as ornament or for protection.
Harnesses designed to hold flags in front of the wearer's body; consisting of at minimum one strap worn over the shoulder and one strap around the waist, with socket attached to the waist strap.
Detachable, made-up cascades of soft fabric, often lace, worn at the center front of the neckline over other garments.
Shaped coverings for the head having a brim and crown, or one of the two.
Long, rectangular pieces of fabric used as hair accessories, often tied in a bow.
Device comprising two buttons, usually decorative, joined to allow its use in closing sleeves or cuffs, which are fitted with button holes or other openings to allow insertion of the sleeve buttons.
Effect produced by slightly changing or adding a color to a thing, making the thing a lighter or darker shade of color.
Any of a group of expanding-lattice clay minerals, the chief constituent of bentonite and fuller's earth.
Heavy, oversized overcoats originally having fur lining.
Men's two- or three-piece suits of matching material, worn in the United Kingdom for informal occasions from the 1860s.
Sleeveless tunics that open at the chest and reach below the waist of postclassic central Mexico.
Ankle-length, black underskirts worn by acolytes in the old Dutch Catholic Church; worn under the cassock when the young man had outgrown it.

Originally a pair of pants for men, made in different lengths throughout history, which closed in the front with a flap the wearer can button to the waistband. Developed from the braguette, or codpiece, around 1600. Common garment for men around 1800.
Hosiery that covers the foot and extends to the knee or above; can be heavy or lightweight.
Upstanding collars originally derived from Chinese costume that do not roll over. Structurally, these are essentially bare collar stands with no fall. Shapes and method of attachment may vary.

A light or dark green massive serpentinite, commonly with veinlets of calcium carbonate and magnesium carbonate.  It is capable of being polished and is commercially considered a marble; it is also considered to be among the highest-quality serpentinites.
Costume worn by members of a court of law.
Garments worn by priests or other ecclesiastics during divine service, such as performing mass or other rituals, as appropriate to the rite and indicative of their hierarchical rank.

Liturgical vestments comprising a shield-shaped panel of embroidery, artificially stiffened and sometimes adorned with a fringe, attached to the back of the cope. Cope shields evolved from the cappa or hood on the oldest form of copes.
Sleeves used in armor, made of mail, which is a metal fabric consisting of iron or steel rings, riveted or pressed together.

A crystalline compound, NaCl, found as colorless, cubic crystals that naturally occur in ocean water at concentrations of 2.6% and in the mineral halite. Sodium chloride is widely used for flavoring and preservation of food, for curing hides and skins, in electrochemical reactions and mordanting, in the precipitation of photographic emulsions, and for many other purposes. For any substance resulting from the combination of negative ions from acids and usually metal ions, use "salt (inorganic material)."

Any of several gaseous compounds of sulfur and oxygen, most importantly sufur dioxide and sulfur trioxide. Sulfur oxides are responsible for about 18 percent of the total average pollutant content of air.
Circular steel plates attached to lances in front of the grip to protect the hand, in use from the 14th to the early 17th century.
Long, usually wooden, sticks with various types of heads used to propel balls or disks in some games, such as billiards and shuffleboard.
The club-shaped or candle-shaped wooden or plastic targets set up for the various games of bowling.

Floor-supported gymnastic vaulting horses, for jumping across the width of the horse rather than the length. For the type with two graspable curved handles set a little distance apart along the top at right angles to the length, use the narrower term "pommel horses."
Long, narrow, flat-bottomed vehicles with upward and inward curving fronts used recreationally for coasting over snow.
Human figures outfitted in traditional national or ethnic dress.
Refers to th small objects, often of metal and with six prongs, needed in the game of jacks.
Optical toys that create moving images, consisting of a revolving slitted drum with a paper band of successive images mounted within the drum and facing inward; developed in the early 19th century.
Books bound in stiff covers.
Books set in type larger than normal, generally over 16-point, usually for the benefit of readers with visual impairments.
Bindings designed so that the book could be chained to a fixed feature such as a shelf or desk.

Highly decorated bindings, usually covered in red morocco, tooled in gold with elaborate Rococo-style borders, areas of criss-crossed or dotted lines, and exotic motifs of animals, plants, and human and mythical figures. Motifs inspired by Chinese and Chinese export porcelain, such as dragons, flowers, and birds, are also common.
Large, solid, heavy, leather-covered balls used for conditioning exercises, generally weighing 6 to 9 pounds, and measuring about 18 inches in diameter.
Small balls made of an elastic material such as rubber or silicone. After the ball has been thrown with some force, the ball bounces several more times.
Toys and tools with which children can draw creatively. Examples are (magnetic) drawing boards and spirographs.
Toys designed to be ridden upon.
Smooth sloping boards or troughs down which children can slide.
Chess pieces designated to move as rooks may move during a chess game.
Coverings for the leg from ankle to knee consisting of a narrow cloth wrapped spirally around the leg or a fitted leather legging secured by a strap, catch, or laces.

Plumes made of feathers, often three, used as an ornament on top of a helmet, hat, or cap or as a headdress. Common also as a heraldic device and as an ornamental motif on furniture and other objects.

Lightweight garments intended for women as outerwear, prevalent in 19th century Europe. Originally the name for Regency era spencer jackets made of silk or kerseymere, specifically designed to be worn with an evening gown. These later evolved into shawl- or blouse-like garments with or without sleeves, often with lacework incorporated into the design. Many of these were made from muslin or cambric, but the style of varied in material and form. For cropped jackets from the Regency era worn by both men and women, use "spencer jackets."
Loose-fitting one- or two-piece garments consisting of short or long trousers and a shirt or pullover top, worn especially for sleeping or lounging around the house.
Signs that are intended to regulate behavior, displaying such information as prohibitions or rules of order or conduct.
The dress of an actor or actress who is representing a character on stage or in film, or of any other person who is playing a role or impersonating a character, as during Carnevale or Halloween.

Small cards containing the name and contact information for a person, similar in design to a business card, but used by an individual unaffiliated with a particular commercial concern. For personal cards used when formally visiting a home, particularly among the upper classes in historical usage, prefer "visiting cards."

Bands, usually of gold or silver, worn in the manner of a wedding ring by some orders of nuns in the Roman Catholic and certain other faiths, signifying the nun's fidelity and betrothal to the Church and to God. The ring may be given when the nun professes vows at her first profession or at her final profession of vows.
Long tube zithers of Myanmar (formerly Burma) and Assam carved to represent a crocodile, made of wood and lacquered, with three metal strings and from eight to eleven movable frets.
Mantles made of pelts, worn traditionally by peoples in southern Africa, especially by chiefs and young male initiates, and as war dress.
