Species of small horse chestnut tree or bush having long clusters of pink to dark red tubular flowers; native to the southern and eastern United States.

Family containing around 135 genera and 1,600 species occurring mainly in the tropical areas of the world, especially abundant in the American tropics. Species range from trees and shrubs to lianas or herbaceous vines. The family is found throughout the wetter tropics and subtropics, extending north to Japan and south to New Zealand.

Species of small tree or large shrub that probably originated in the region around the Caucasus and the Caspian Sea. According to the earliest writings in which the plum is mentioned, the species is at least 2,000 years old. It has a fruit that is a fleshy drupe of variable size, usually having purple, red, or yellow skin with a dull powdery bloom when ripe, a sweet pulp, and a flattish pointed stone.
Large ebony tree attaining 18-24 m in height and a circumference of 3 m, with irregular branches and oblong leaves; native to India.

Family of flowering shrubs and trees  native to temperate and tropical regions of both hemispheres, including several ornamental plants, one that is the source of tea. The number of genera belonging to this family is debated, numbering from 7 to 40, depending on the method of circumscription.

Slow-growing species of elm native to North America from Ontario and Quebec to Tennessee, Kansas, and Minnesota, having hard, heavy wood used for various products, and twigs that often develop corky ridges.

Species of large tree native to Australia, distinguished from other eucalyptus by having rough bark half way up the trunk, where white smooth bark appears, and leaves of a glossy dark green. It is a koala food tree, is cut for timber, but is mainly used commercially for its abundant, pungent oil, used in pharmaceuticals, as an antiknock agent in gasoline and for the manufacture of menthol. The common name, blackbutt, refers to appearance of the type specimen collected in 1794, which had a black base after fires.

Genus of evergreen trees from tropical America including at least 3 species, which hybridize easily when grown in proximity; thus the species are poorly defined biologically. The trees have a hard wood that turns reddish brown at maturity, valued as timber. The leaflets of each large leaf are arranged like a feather, but there is no terminal leaflet.
Family of 16 genera and around 120 species of tropical and subtropical flowering plants.
Species of hickory tree native to south-central North America.
Genus containing around 80 species of perennial scrambling or climbing herbs and shrubs native to Europe, Africa,  Asia, and America.
Species of small evergreen tree or shrub, cultivated in Mediterranean countries and the West Indies for its fruit.

Species of large maple tree native to central Europe and western Asia, but introduced into Britain in the 15th century. On young trees, the bark is smooth and grey but becomes rougher with age and breaks up in scales, exposing the pale-brown-to-pinkish inner bark. It is an important timber and shade tree in Europe, having many ornamental varieties. For other trees sometimes called simply "sycamore," use "Ficus sycamorus" for the sycamore fig and "Platanus occidentalis" for the American sycamore.
Species of medium to large tree native to the central and eastern parts of North America. It is used for timber and as an ornamental, valued for its colorful autumn foliage.

Outgrowths, usually green and flattened, that extend from the stem of a vascular plant. Botanically, leaves are an integral part of the stem system, and they are initiated in the apical bud along with the tissues of the stem itself. Leaves manufacture food for plants, which in turn ultimately nourish and sustain all land animals, directly or indirectly.
A gear-driven drilling instrument which inserts a three-millimeter-diameter probe into a tree, and graphically or digitally records resistance to the probe; used to detect decay and defects.
Species of cottonwood poplar native to southwestern North America.
Genus of South American trees, most of which produce hard wood.
Species of small to medium tree endemic to China. Used for wood and in folk medicine. Listed as a threatened species, now confined to Hainan Island, known only from stands of coppiced individuals.

Species of medium-sized tree native to eastern North America. It has been used for timber, as a substitute for quinine, and to make a bitter tea with similar chemical compounds to aspirin. The young branches and twigs were used by Native Americans to make baskets.
Monoecious trees with large leaves, having two accepted species.
Trademarked name for moisture-sensitive silica beads used as a humidity controlling sorbent for paintings, paper, textiles and other materials.

Genus of flowering plant native primarily to North and South America. The common sunflower is an annual herb with a rough hairy stem 1–4.5 metres (3–15 feet) high, broad, coarsely toothed, rough leaves 7.5–30 cm (3–12 inches) long, and heads of flowers 7.5–15 cm wide in wild specimens and often 30 cm or more in cultivated types. The disk flowers are brown, yellow, or purple; the ray flowers are yellow. The oval hairy leaves are arranged in spirals. The sunflower plant is valuable from an economic as well as from an ornamental point of view.
Order of Liliopsida including four families of flowering trees and shrubs, native mainly to tropical regions of the world.
Order of flowering plants containing about 600 species. Plants within Cornales usually have four-parted flowers, drupaceous fruits, and inferior gynoecia topped with disc-shaped nectaries.
Unreal creatures of the imagination; grotesque monsters, formed of the parts of various animals.
In Indian architecture, a curvilinear vertical band of śikhara, usually bearing jāla-web (mesh) pattern; central jāla-section of a Latina Nāgara śikhara vine; creeper.
Deities or good spirits in Hinduism and Buddhism.

Meals eaten out of doors, especially when part of an excursion to the countryside, coast, or other outdoor location. Originally, a meal for which each guest contributed a share of the food; this may be true of contemporary picnics, but is not necessarily so.
Imperial and U.S. customary units of area, defined as the area of a square with sides of one foot (12 inches) in length..
Time periods of 1000 years; more specifically, of the Christian era.

Standardized linear units of measure made up of twelve inches, 1/3 of a yard; equal to 0.3048 meters. It was a unit of length in both the imperial and US customary systems of measurement; since 1959, both units have been defined as the same by international agreement. Originally the unit was based on the length of a man's foot, varying in exact length at different periods and in different countries.

In avoirdupois measure, standardized units of weight and mass equal to 16 ounces (7000 grains, exactly 0.45359237 kg). The pound was originally made up of 12 ounces, as in the system of troy weight which is still used in stating the weight of precious metals.
Triethanolamine (TEA) is a yellow viscous organic compound used as a surfactant and emulsifier. It is both an amine and a triol, a class of alcohols that have three hydroxyl groups per molecule.
Traditional Hawaiian residential structures set aside as eating places for men; often containing the family shrine; taboo to women.
Models that describe the structural design of a built work, without including the full form; used to work out and illustrate issues having to do with structure and space for architects and engineers.
The nationality, culture, and style of Dacia, an ancient country of southeastern Europe.

Drugs, products, or agents that are consumed for pleasure, and that stimulate bodily functions, consciousness, elevate mood, feeling, or cognizance. These may be found in certain foods or plants, and include caffeine, nicotine, and amphetamines.
The action of ingesting food into the mouth, chewing, and swallowing.
In the context of graffiti, bombing denotes prolific and repeated renderings of a single 'tag' in a given physical area in order to attract recognition.
The state of alarm and urgency; apprehension toward a potentially harmful experience.

Emotional and psychological state based on strong affection, loyalty, and benevolence for another arising out of kinship, as in maternal love; arising out of sexual attraction and emotional affinity, as in affection and tenderness felt between lovers; and arising out of respect and admiration, as in the valuation and appreciation among friends.
Sytle and culture of Islam in Spain, particularly during the period 709 until 1614.

An Oriental Orthodox Christian religion based in the Eastern Mediterranean. By tradition it derives from an early Christian community established in Antioch by St. Peter the Apostle. It uses the oldest surviving liturgy in Christianity, the Liturgy of St. James the Apostle, which is celebrated in Syriac, a dialect of Aramaic spoken by Jesus and the apostles. The church is led by the Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch. The group has historically been called "Jacobites" after St. Jacob Baradaeus, bishop of Edessa, who organized their community in the 6th century; however, they reject that name because they trace their beginnings instead to St. Peter.

Languages that are no longer spoken by native speakers. While the term may have overlapping usage with "extinct languages," an extinct language typically is limited to languages having no descendents. For example, Latin is a dead language but not extinct, because it has several descendent languages and is read and even spoken by scholars and in the Vatican.
Hand gesture indicating teaching, the turning the wheel. Using both hands held at chest level, the hands touch each other in any of several ways.
Artists who specialize in accurate depictions of plants and their parts for use as illustrations.
A son-in-law is the spouse of one's child.
Artists who specialize in creating batik, a type of resist dyeing of textiles in which wax is used as the resist.

Designation used for painters in 14th- through 18th-century northern and southern Europe who specialized in decorative work or minor works rather than painting the main subjects of primary paintings. It was defined within the painters' guild of St. Luke; it also included house painters and varnishers. Coarse painters were considered of lower status than "artist painters."
Textile works with figural or other representational subjects depicted. An ancient art form; some of the earliest references to this type of visual works are in Iliad and the Odyssey.
Term generally applied to ceramic products that are usually but not necessarily white, and which consist typically of clays, feldspar, potters' flint, and whiting.
Physical features located in the oceans below sea level, whether natural or man-made.
Capital towns or cities for administrative regions.
The highest levels of hierarchies, from which all branches descend.
Multiple-word terms or names that are arranged in the form used in speech or written text. Examples are Christopher Wren and flying buttresses. Distinguished from inverted terms or names.

Designates substitutes for money that move within a limited universe, usually not in general circulation, may be exchanged for particular goods or services, and are made from hard substances whose intrinsic value is always less than the stated value.

Reference to the status of separate, independent works that are less grand or considered less important than other separate, independent "primary works." An example would be in a country estate, the country house may be considered the primary work, and the surrounding cottages may be considered secondary works. For works that are part of or integrally associated with primary works, use "ancillary works."
Pottery created by the Bandkeramik Central European Neolithic culture. It is characterized by decorations of incised bands of lines, strokes, and indentations.

African cylindrical or biconical beads made of a type of reddish brown stone after which they are named, made by the Yoruba, particularly in Ilorin, Nigeria. They are no longer made though they are still used.
Gradual slopes, typically with a smooth surface, such as those found around island groups and seamounts.

Temperate forests of broadleaf trees (e.g., oaks, maples, beeches), shrubs, perennial herbs, and mosses in areas that go through four seasons. Examples are in the Eastern United States, Canada, Europe, China, and Japan.
Biomes characterized by hot, dry summers, and cool, moist winters and vegetation comprising aromatic herbs (sage, rosemary, thyme, oregano), shrubs, acacia, chamise, and grasses.
Instruments for measuring the harmonic relation of sounds, or musical notes.

Particulars of the place where a person, organization, building, or monument can be found on a street or other thoroughfare; typically consisting of a number, street name, the name of the administrative area (a town or district). May also include a postcode, as the street address may also be the "mailing address."
English as spoken from ca. 1700 through the present.

Languages of the Celts; in the first millennium BCE, these languages were spoken across a wide area of Europe and Asia Minor. Surviving Surviving Celtic languages are now spoken in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Brittany, Cornwall, and the Isle of Man, and Cape Breton Island.

Refers to the forms of non-Classical, nonstandard Latin from which originated the Romance group of languages. Aside from the numerous inscriptions found throughout the empire, there are many longer texts in Vulgar Latin.
Variety of the Portuguese language used primarily in the nation of Mozambique.

A waxy, cloudy or powdery haze that appears on the surface of paint, varnish, leather, ink, metal, plastic, or other materials. Bloom may be due to the deposit of atmospheric pollutants such as ammonium sulfate; for varnish, it may be caused by trapped or condensed moisture often due to varnish application in humid conditions, or due to wax-based media; for paint it may be caused by exudation of organic salts formed by reactions of the oils components with pigments or driers; for plastic, rubber or ink, it may be caused by exudation of additives or unreacted monomers; for leather, it may be caused by ellagic acid crystallization after tanning with some pyrogallol type vegetable tannins; for metal, it may be caused by  trace impurities that crystallize on the surface after casting; for a photographic plate, it may be caused by dried residues from tap water. It is distinguished from "blanching" which is the milky appearance of resinous or oily film following application of a solvent.

Proprietary name for a type of television camera tube similar to a vidicon, but in which the photoconductive layer of the signal plate is of lead monoxide; noted for their ability to form images in low light. The plumbicon allowed the development of the color television camera.These have been used in cameras intended for surveillance.
Language families comprising two groups of indigenous languages of the Andaman Islands.
General term for systems used to visually represent music through written words or standard notations.

Choreographed dressage performances by mounted riders and typically set to music, particularly popular in Europe in the 16th-18th centuries. It grew out of cavalry maneuvers and Medieval tournaments. Equestrian ballets were performed outdoors or in large arenas. Costumed horsemen rode horses in patterns and conducted intricate maneuvers, including leaps and acrobatics. One of the earliest known equestrian ballets was performed in Paris for the wedding of the Duc de Joyeuse in 1581.
White or yellowish white fluid secreted by the mammary glands of female mammals.

A beverage consisting of an infusion of hot or cold water and the leaves or leaf fragments of various herbs, dried or fresh, sometimes with ground spices added. It is often used for medicinal purposes as well as refreshment. For the beverage made from infusion of the leaves of the tea plant, Camellia sinensis, use "tea (beverage)."

Facilities for making margarine, allowing for the processes of emulsifying a blend of vegetable oils and fats, which can be modified using fractionation, interesterification or hydrogenation, with skimmed milk.
General term for administrative divisions of a city or other inhabited place.

In the geologic time scale, the third period of the Paleozoic Era. It began 443.4 million years ago and ended 419.2 million years ago, following the Ordovician Period and preceding the Devonian Period. It is characterized by a rise in sea levels and a proliferation of fish species. Vascular plants colonized coastal lowlands but continental interiors were mostly devoid of life.

Objects of varied design used to treat the raw edges of heavy leather. These are sometimes in the form of small wheels, with a groove in them to receive the edge. The leather is dampened and the slicker is rubbed rapidly along the edge of the leather to burnish the surface.
Dramatic or theatrical performances staged by actors before an audience; acted representations of an action or story.

Harvest festival celebrated by ethnic Chinese and Vietnamese peoples on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, near the autumnal equinox. The festival has roots in ancient Chinese religious rituals celebrating the harvest. It may also have ties to ancient moon-worshipping rituals. Observances included worshipping Tudi Gong (the earth god) or Tai Yin Jun (the moon god) and references to other myths and legends incorporating the moon. It is customary to have a family reunion during the full moon, to eat moon cakes, and to appreciate the beauty of the full moon.
In Japanese printing, format comprising strips of paper derived from a large sheet, ō-ōban, around 33 x 15 cm.
Works of art, architecture, or other objects that have been previously taken apart or fragmented, either through damage or intentionally, and that are subsequently put back together.
That which is placed in position number six of a sequence.
State or condition of existing in or comprising mountains.

Qualifier used for attributions of works by an unknown creator working as an assistant to a named artist, architect, or other creator whose staff is relatively small in number and do not call themselves a studio or an office. Also use for an assistant who worked in a studio or office, but in a special, close relationship to the named artist or architect.
Technique of constructing masonry walling made of stones laid up in a random pattern, without regular horizontal rows or courses.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1099 to 1000 (or 1100 to 1001) Before Common Era.
Gaulish Coligny calendar used by Celtic countries to define the beginning and length of the day, the week, the month, the seasons, quarter days, and festivals.
Culture, style, and period a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 386-403, during the Jin Dynasty in China; founded by the Lü family of the Di ethnicity.

Identification numbers associated with objects or documents that are assigned by an individual collector, rather than a numerical system applied by a repository. These numbers may appear on the backs of paintings, and occasionally appear in stock books along with other descriptions of an object.  These are similar to collector’s marks but without a stamp, and may be numeric or alphanumeric.
The legally recognized words or phrases under which a corporate body or institution is known and engages in action.

Appellations, words, or phrases that follow a personal name. For example words or numerals denoting family relationships, usually between members having the same first name, such as the senior and junior of two indicated persons.
Quetzal feather banners of postclassic central Mexico.
The sixth month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendars, containing 30 days and falling between May and July. It was named after Juno, the Roman goddess of childbirth and fertility.

The day following Thursday and preceding Saturday, traditionally regarded as the sixth day of the week, but now frequently considered as the fifth, and also as the last day of the working week in western culture. In English and other languages, named for Frigg, the wife of the Norse god Odin, representing love and beauty. In Romance languages, named for the Roman Venus’-day.
Small cookstoves that can be powered by a variety of fuels, meant be used for outdoor activities, such a camping.
In language, indeclinable words or particles governing (and usually preceding) a noun, pronoun, etc., and expressing a relation between it and another word.
Refers to the variety of Spanish spoken in Costa Rica.
The standard unit of currency of Belgium prior to adoption of the Euro.
Titles applied to collections, which are accumulated groups of objects or materials having a focal characteristic and that have been brought together by an individual or organization.

Numeric, alphanumeric, or other codes assigned to a thing, concept, person, or other entity in order identify it and distinguish it from other similar entities. Often a sequence of integers or characters arbitrarily devised.
Systematic courses of aggressive activities designed to persuade or establish power over others.

In weaving; refers to the cords, wires, or steel strips that the warp passes through in a loom after passing through the reed, that allows the warp threads to be separated, allowing the shuttle to pass through the weft. Heddles are considered a major advance in the development of weaving technology.
Musical compositions, generally short, containing words.

Genre of performing art that expresses or conveys action, character, or emotion without words, and using only gestures, facial expression, and movement. In Classical times, works of mime were simple, usually farcical dramas characterized by mimicry and the ludicrous representation of familiar types of character.
Method of acquiring property with the expectation that the recipient will sell, rent, or loan this property to a third party, for the mutual benefit of the consignor and consignee.
Gathering things in order to retain them.
To get back or regain possession or restoration of something by judgment or law.
The activity and profession of breeding and raising sheep.
Meaning "from the original," in printmaking and other art works, indicates the original work from which the work at hand was copied.
Gateways to Shinto shrines, generally composed of two columns and two horizontal spanning members often with slight upward curvature at their ends.
Order containing about 16,000 species of diverse flowering plants divided into 32 to 42 families.

Sets for board games for 2 to 6 participants that is played on a square or hexagonal (star-shaped) playing field with a set of marbles. The variant with a hexagonal (star-shaped) playing field is called Chinese checkers or sternhalma. Halma boards often feature both boards on the front and back.
Trays used to hold instruments required by a dentist during procedures.
Weapons that are used to strike or hammer.

Telescopes that have both reflecting and refracting elements to produce magnified images. Schmidt telescopes were invented by Bernhard Schmidt of the Bergedorf Observatory in Hamburg, in 1930. Each Schmidt telescope has a spherical primary mirror which then passes light through a spherical corrective lens, thus eliminating spherical aberrations from the mirror.
Bars that support hooks for hanging meats for a variety of purposes.
Bookbinding machines used for making the cases or covers of books, which typically includes the embossing of the book's title.
Air-tight lids with rubber gaskets designed to screw on glass jars for home canning.
Cloth sacks made to store pajamas when not in use, generally for children. Often in the form of animals or cartoon characters.
Instruments designed for the estimation of phenol.

One-piece garments consisting of trousers with a bib and having straps extending from the bib to the back. For one-piece garments consisting of a trouserlike portion and a full top with or without sleeves worn over other garments for protection use "coveralls."

Drafting tools with two adjustible arms: one fixed with a drawing implement, normally a sharpened piece of graphite, the other with a pivot post with which the center of a circle is defined on a drawing.
Women's dresslike garments made in various lengths, worn informally around the house.
Any of a number of devices used to clean eggs to ready them for sale.
Implements used in cheese-making to scoop curds out of a curd mill.
Mechanical, automated devices that instruct pupils with teaching programs. Most models allow progression based on correct answers to questions.
Small microscopes used for counting the threads in linen fabrics. These devices typically comprise a square or round opening through which the threads can be magnified and viewed.
Fireplace components formed of frameworks of metal bars, intended as supports for flammable materials, used in place of, or with, andirons.

Photographic electronic flash devices that have the facility to ignite repeatedly in sequence to make multiple exposures on while the shutter of a camera remains open, allowing the capture of motion in one frame.
Strong light casks used for transporting and dispensing drinking-water, often in the context of ships at sea or where potable is not otherwise available.
Machines that automate the various parts of the process of packaging a product for sale.
Funnel-shaped tools used to support and vent pie crusts during cooking.
Utensils for sampling food as it is being prepared.
Trays that accommodate tea services. Some examples may be components of a tea table, detachable from the base or legs.
Teaspoon-like utensils with rounded scoops at one or both ends of a handle. These are used for scooping the pulp out of melons, potatoes, or other fruits and vegetables.

Storage containers of bent wood, most common to the 19th century to store dry items like sugar, cereals, and spices in the pantry. These are now considered decorative objects. Often these incorporated handles and could be used to transport products to and from a market.

A shield design of postclassic central Mexico composed of five tufts of down in a quincunx pattern, literally a "people-destroyer shield" in Nahuatl. Part of the array of Huitzilopochtli and other deities.
Devices used to hold and fill grain bags, consisting of a tube- or funnel-like top to which a bag can be attached.
Machines used to clean grain using a strong current of air and screens that remove dirt and other unwanted objects.

Collar-like devices with vents that fit over the top of a lamp chimney or a collapsible circular wire rack with two or more prongs protruding from the center fixing it to the top of a lamp chimney. Used to support various objects, such as curling tongs, and liquids to be heated by a lamp.
Closed boxes or vessels of earthenware or most commonly metal, which may be portable or fixed, in which heat is produced by combustion of wood for use in heating applications.
Frames, of a variety of designs, used to store a set of spits.
Large vats in which rendered lard is allowed to separate from any water left over from the rendering process.
Devices used to reduce the liquid content of sweet sap or juice, such as the juice of sugar cane, until concentrated into a dense syrup.
Containers made to store womens' slippers for safekeeping.
Supports specifically for use while playing musical instruments.
Utensils in the form of a flat board with a raised rim, or a shallow box without a lid, made of a variety of materials in various sizes and shapes that hold materials and tools for needlework.
Paired needles made of steel, wood, bone or other material, used for knitting.

Devices used to steady the head of photographic sitters when long exposures are necessary for formal portraits, to prevent blurring the image. These have been rendered mostly obsolete as photographic technologies have advanced.
Tools used to cut the leads and slugs in letterpress printing. Usually consisting of a single handle attached to a blade and a platform to measure and hold up printed material before being cut.
Punishment devices consisting of a wooden frame mounted on a post with holes or rings for restraining the head and hands of persons to be subjected to public ridicule or assault.
Revolving devices used in winding yarn or thread into hands or skeins consisting usually of a light frame with radial arms on a central axis.
Rollers with moistened cloth that are used on the surfaces of phonograph records to remove both dust and static electricity.
Devices that create specific imitative sounds, or simulate an environment of sounds, such as a battlefield.
Cast iron grates that fit in the bottom of a coal or wood-burning heating stove to allow air to flow into the fire and ashes to pass down to the ash pan.

Hand-held devices, typically comprising small teeth mounted on wide wooden, plastic, or metal heads, designed to facilitate the weaving process by emphasizing the weftfaced structure of textile materials and regulating the yarn's density.

Mechanized devices used to bond multiple fabrics together and produce reinforced nonwoven fabric. These devices vary greatly and include stich-bonding machines and seamless bonding machines. The former utilize warp-knitting to stich-bond base materials like yarn layers, non-woven fabrics, or base material webs. The latter use adhesive tape that is heated and melted to bond fabrics together.
Ornamental braid or lacing of various patterns in gold and silver, used to trim coats, particularly elements of uniforms. For similar trimming material with scalloped edges, use "galloon."
Harvesting machines used to separate grain from the stalk of a plant.
Describes the geographic location where a group or association was formed.
An indication of the level of cataloging represented by the record, based on the physical form or intellectual content of the material, such as item, group, volume.
Depictions in which the figure is cut off below the waist, usually mid-thigh or just below the knee.
Forks used in harvesting barley and other short-stemmed grains, having a guard where the handle joins the prongs.
Standardized attire worn by members of a law enforcement agency when engaged in their duties.
Small sculptures used for embellishing baked goods. Variously made of organic (sugar) or inorganic material.

Cloth garments of a particular type, decorated with metal cones or beads. These cones are usually sewn in rows on the skirt of the dress, but can also appear across the entire garment. Used as part of powwow and medicine dances, originating with Anishinaabe/Ojibwe Native communities in the late 19th to early 20th centuries.
General term for landscaping, structures, water features, and other built works in a garden.

Defined as a dance performed at Native North American powwows, primarily by men. The dance consists of movements and steps close to the ground to mimic hunting or tracking movements. Likely originated in the 19th century from the Omaha Dance performed by Omaha, Ponca, Kaw, Kiowa, and Pawnee communities.
Dance often performed at powwows by Native North Americans, consisting of manipulating several wooden or plastic hoops that encircle the dancer's body.

Malah tangia takes place in April and May every year and counts as the largest festival co-organized by the Bunun’s clans bearing different family names. When the millet tassels bend with weighty grains, men would go hunting in the mountains and women would start brewing wine in preparation for the upcoming rituals. In the early morning of malah tangia a family should fire their fusil if there is a boy born to the family recently. Then men would initiate the ritual with the fire-lighting mapatus, roast and distribute the game and use a plant called bauvan to tell the fortune. Post-prandial proceedings involve drizzling the remaining wine on the bones and fusil-firing as an invigorating act. Subsequently, men should gather in the leading family’s house through a fire-crossing ritual called daugkav sapuz to attend a party of valor known as malastapan. In malastapan attendants should announce their family name and enumerate the achievement in hunting and fighting over the last year. Sons of the attendants are brought to the party to participate in malah tangia in which they are to shoot arrows at a deer’s ear. Adults utilize the occasion to go through mapa-ip taiga and mapis-lai as a ritual to augment the spiritual power of their weapons.
The sixth month of the French republican calendar, introduced in 1793, extending from 19 Feb. to 20 Mar.

Cultures and styles of the Kavalan people lived in Taiwan. The Kavalan people primarily live in Yilan. The word Kavalan derives from the place of the people’s landing form the sea. The word can also be traced to Kuvarawan (“people of the plain”) as opposed to Pusoram (“people of the mountains”). In the eighteenth century the Kavalan people was driven south to the Qilai plain in Hualien by agrarian settlers, and they were forced again to move to the coasts and the valley with the Qing invasion near the end of the nineteenth century. As a result of a long-term cohabitation of the Kavalan people with the Amis people, the Kavalan culture has borrowed some aspects from the Amis and the process involved a certain degree of mutual assimilation. Yet distinct Kavalan character can still be discerned from the Kavalan language and rituals, which serve as important markers of the Kavalan identity throughout the campaign.
Tile is classified as measuring greater than 15 inches on any side.
Period of the sixth city on the site of ancient Troy, ca. 1750 -1300 BCE. Probably the period associated with the Troy of Homeric literature.
Tools used to cut, shave, or sharpen needles that were used with early phonographs and gramophones.

The state or condition of identifying outside a male/female gender binary, specifically people who do not identify with a single fixed gender; having or expressing a fluid or unfixed gender identity or fluctuating between gender and expressions.
In Indian architecture, an (inverted) dish-shaped maṇḍi-type; banner.
In Indian architecture, a pañjara.
A diminutive form of nāsī.
In Indian architecture, a square pillar with two recessed corners.
In Indian architecture, round column-type; Rudrakānta.
Rooms or buildings for worship: oratories, that are attached to places of residence for a community living under religious vows.
In Greek churches, side chapels, or small added churchlike spaces, separate from the cathedral or principal church of a monastery.
The state or quality of having or being divided into seven parts.

Toys in which three-dimensional geometric figures must be sorted into holes in a cube or sphere with the same shape dimensions. The object can also take other forms.The toddlers manipulate the shapes to correctly fit into their holes and then once the container fills, they dump them back out again.

A type of rectangular gem cut in which the corners are cut off. Mainly used for emeralds, but can also be used for other gemstones and diamonds. In comparison to a baguette cut, the emerald cut has more horizontally broken facets and also facets in the corners.

Small metal spikes or hooks designed to secure and stretch the edges of wet woven cloth as it dries after being exposed to fabrication processes such as washing, beating, and fulling, amongst others. Hundreds of these hooks are positioned in close rows around a wooden tenter frame to hold the fabric taut and prevent the damp piece of cloth from shrinking and warping out of shape during the drying process. Widely used in Europe beginning in the 15th century, this term's meaning later evolved and was abstracted in the 16th century to mean the expansion of one's consciousness and uncertainty about one's future.
Four-centered pointed arches.  Four-centered pointed arches.

Pointed bulbous domes characterized by a distinctive tapering bulb or onion shape that has a diameter greater than the drum upon which it is placed, and typically having a height that exceeds its width. Onion domes first saw widespread use in Islamic architecture in about the 8th century, when they often topped minarets or were placed over the central space or on the corners of mosques and domestic buildings in the Middle East and India. They were then used in Russia, Spain, Austria, Bavaria, and Eastern Europe by the 18th century; use spread to other Western styles and locations in the 19th century. For small domes, often resembling overturned cups or pointed, and placed over a turret, use "cupolas."
Structures based on upright posts or columns supporting horizontal beams or lintels; these exclude balloon frames and platform frames, in which support is by stud walls.
Used to describe both beams reinforced with one or more tie rods and beams in the form of trusses, braced by vertical posts and supported by inclined rods.
Small or slender columns. For small Medieval columns, usually attached to architectural features, use "shafts (Medieval columns)."
Columns set within angles formed by the features of a building, as where the jamb of a doorway meets the external face of a wall.

Capitals of the Corinthian architectural order, characterized by having a bell-shaped echinus decorated with a combination of spiral and plant, usually acanthus, motifs; may be either two rows of acanthus leaves or one row of acanthus and one row of palm leaves, volutes, and a fleuron atop an abacus.
In Indian architecture, an echinus; Types: pāli, padma, nāgadala.
Trusses having two vertical posts between the rafters and the tie beam; the upper ends of the vertical posts are connected by a straining piece.
Thin, impervious material placed in construction to prevent water penetration and/or provide water drainage; generally located between a roof and a wall and over exterior door openings and windows.
Protective elements placed at dangerous points, as along the edges of roads or on stair landings.
Areas of a town or city zoned for or used primarily for single- or multiple-family dwellings.
Defined areas in which the stationing or concentrating of military forces, or the retention or establishment of military installations of any description, is prohibited.
Any place where burials have taken place, generally restricted to human or other hominin burials.
Architectural elements used to move people through spaces.

A platform of sticks where Huitzilopochtli's ixiptlah, made of dough of amaranth seed, was seated in postclassic central Mexico. Used during the installation of the deity, it was made of huitzitzillacotl or "hummingbird sticks" and nacaztlacotl "ear sticks," describing the shape of the wood.
Arches in which the curves are carried below the springing line so that the opening at the bottom of the arch is less than its greatest span.
Groupings of educational buildings and other facilities; if possible, use a more specific term.
Farms devoted to the cultivation of fruit or nut trees.
Large elaborate cemeteries of ancient cities or ancient or prehistoric burying places.
Refers to cemeteries set aside for the burial of pets or other animals, usually domestic animals. Refers to cemeteries set aside for the burial of pets or other animals, usually domestic animals.
Buildings for 'trying' or extracting oil from blubber.
Pits, tunnels, or open-air excavations originally made for underground extraction of metals, metallic ores, coal, or another substance, that are now not used or abandoned.

In the context of amusement parks, exhibitions, fairs, etc., the central avenues along which the chief exhibits or amusements are placed. In the context of amusement parks, exhibitions, fairs, etc., the central avenues along which the chief exhibits or amusements are placed.
Camps providing recreational and sporting facilities during the summer holiday period, usually intended for children and often including overnight accommodations.
Monastic complexes of the eastern Mediterranean in which hermit monks live in a loosely organized group of cells around a common central complex.
In Indian architecture, a monastery.
Areas defined for the purposes of designing or controlling of urban or economic development. Areas defined for the purposes of designing or controlling of urban or economic development.
Any built structure used as a lookout station that affords observation of a surrounding area.
In Indian architecture an oblong śikhara without lateral gables, miniature model of; khākharā-muṇḍi (Kaliṅga).

Spaces between the outer and inner doors to buildings, or for sheltered spaces, recessed in the mass of the building, just outside the outer doors. For spaces just inside the outer door but not separated from the building interior by any barrier such as a door, use "entrance halls."
Corridors or galleries in Roman architecture with windowlike openings, whether subterranean or above ground.
Rooms or buildings devoted to the display of merchandise for sale.
In Japanese domestic or nobles' architecture, a sitting or reception room or area having a raised floor.
In large residences, relatively large, long rooms used by the family for eating and relaxing.
Rooms for pedagogical use that do not conform to a typical school instruction structure. Use 'classrooms' for similar rooms that are located in schools.

Part of the outworks of a fortress, built in front of the glacis, consisting of two converging faces forming a salient angle, forming an arrowhead shape.Similar to a redan, but with faces forming an acute angle.
Architectural elements found on Japanese religious buildings.

Cross-shaped fixtures or painted marks in Catholic churches, most often on the walls or columns at the places consecrated with chrism during the consecration of the church. The symbolism for the crosses is laid out in liturgical treatises, such as the "Rationale" of Durandus; there are twelve consecration crosses to symbolize the twelve apostles.
Altars upon which offerings for the dead are displayed in Mexico and related cultures, in homes or cemeteries, particularly for Day of the Dead celebrations.
Poles or posts made of various materials used to indicate an obstruction or to regulate traffic, usually mounted on median strips or refuge islands of a roadway.

Metal, masonry, or ceramic extensions which continue the flue on top of chimneys to improve draft or appearance; for extensions that protect chimney openings and may serve to block rain, use "chimney hoods."
Spaces or rooms used to store equipment.
Apartments with rooms on three levels.  For buildings comprised of three dwelling units, use either "triplexes (multiple dwellings)" or "three-deckers (dwellings)."
Refers to the court toward the back of a Roman house, commonly with a small garden surrounded by a colonnade.
Areas or spaces located in ancient Roman baths.
A broad fillet; complex of kampa and paṭṭa fillets.
Elaborated details projecting laterally at the corners of door and window frames.

In the Yingzao fashi (1103) this term refers to squared beams (fang 方) carved with bracket-arms in low relief and layered within the wall plane above pillar tops. It can also refer to the entire composition of square beams and bracket-arms within the wall plane above pillar tops (Cheng Mingda 2010; Xu Yitao 2005). Also called “shadow bracket-arm(s)” (yinggong 影栱).
Small towers, especially when corbelled out from a corner.
Secondary trenches in the bottom of a moat or ditch, serving as a drain, and as an extra obstacle to possible attackers or to keep the ditch ice-free.
Boxes, usually elongated, containing soil and used for growing ornamental plants, placed on a window sill or at the level of a sill.
Individual plates of glass in windows or other openings; for the compartments of windows or window sashes, use "lights."
Shutters, typically made of wood, mounted on the inside wall of a house, covering a window.
Stairs which rise in one direction only, without turns.
In Indian architecture, a stairway.
Inclined boards that support the treads and risers of a stair.
In Indian architecture, a series of steps; stairway.
In sheet metal, the joints between two parts whose preformed edges engage to form a continuous locked splice.
Moldings enriched with a series of starlike, raised pyramidal forms; common especially in Early English Gothic architecture.

Crowning finial components in the shape of a pot, pitcher, or ewer appearing in Hindu temple architecture. In Indian architecture, a pitcher; torus moulding; jar-shaped pinnacle of śikhara; pitcher-finial; ghaṭa; vase-finial; pot; stūpī, stūpikā (southern); also torus in a vēdībandha group of mouldings (northern and upper southern).
Indian architecture, a cyma-eave/cornice; flexured minor cornice of a base/entablature.
In Indian architecture, a pediment of interconnected gavākṣa-dormers/caitya-dormers (candraśālās); triangular pediment, usually formed by  gavākṣa-dormer mesh
In Indian architecture, a cantoning pilaster.
Stepstones at the threshold of a door.
In Indian architecture, a six-jambed door-frame.
In Indian architecture, a crest figure, central (figural, rarely floral) symbol on door lintel; tutelary deity over a door, carved on a lalāṭa-block.
Doors consisting primarily of glass panels. May refer to doors that are entrances to architecture (e.g., an office building door) or components of furniture (e.g., a door on a cabinet).
Defensive gratings, of massive iron or timber, movable vertically in retaining grooves cut in the jambs of fortified gateways.
Semicircular windows divided by two upright mullions.
In Indian architecture, a circular/curved rafter.
Combination walls in which the masonry facing and the backing are so bonded as to exert a common reaction under load.
Walls which support no vertical load except that of their own weight. Walls which support no vertical load except that of their own weight.
Artificial mounds used as a lower rampart, located in front of the main rampart of a fortification.
Refers to the top platforms or horizontal surfaces behind the parapets of ramparts.
In Indian architecture, a sanctum wall.
In Indian architecture, a miniature square structure on corner of superstructure; corner aedicula, see kūṭa; kūṭa-turret placed above the karṇa-bay of a wall.
In Indian architecture, a sub-plinth course.
Use to designate second or sometimes third stories given greater apparent height or prominence on the exterior and a higher ceiling within, and containing the principal rooms of a building.
Narrow shelves or rails located along the upper part of the walls of a room and constucted with a groove to hold plates or decorations.
In Indian architecture, a slit-niche.
In Indian architecture, a window carved with perforated mesh design; grille-window.
Ceilings formed by or suggesting open-timbered roofs, often higher than the ceilings of the other rooms in the building.
In Indian architecture, an eave, cornice, or tier in the form of a stepped, pyramidal roof.
Sloping roofs placed either against buildings so as to create smaller substructures (such as a sheds or outhouses) or over doorways or windows to protect from the weather.
Structures appended to roofs.

Dormers whose eaves lines are parallel to the eaves lines of the main roof instead of being gabled; provide more attic space than gabled dormers. Dormers whose eaves lines are parallel to the eaves lines of the main roof instead of being gabled; provide more attic space than gabled dormers.
Gables having an overall tall, rectangular form; may be capped with a broken pediment or other form.
Thin spires rising from the center of a tower roof, well inside a parapet, protecting a pathway upon which scaffolding could be erected for repairs.
Semi-permanent anchorages consisting of a heavy anchor, chain, mooring buoy, and pennant.
Buildings that incorporate computerized building management systems which automatically control HVAC, security, and other systems.

Churches having a centralized, circular plan; examples are the round churches popular in Scandinavia in the 11th and early 12th centuries. For churches with a round floorplan but that are in the form of a tower, use "round-tower churches." For churches having a centralized that is polygonal rather than circular, use "polygonal churches."
Churches, other than cathedrals, endowed for a chapter of canons, or, as in the United States and Scotland, churches joined together and served by a joint pastorate.
In Indian architecture, a shrine-type.
In Indian architecture, a temple-type resembling a terraced stūpa (discussed in Viṣṇudharmōttarapurāṇa).

Buildings that house clinics specializing in outpatient treatment, including counseling and the dispensing of medication, for relatively mild or controllable mental illness that does not require overnight admittance.
Hospitals that are not restricted to patients suffering from one particular class of disease or to those of a particular sex or age-group.
Health care facilities for the chronically ill.

Temporary residences of former convicts, drug users, or mental patients that serve as a transition environment between confinement and a return to society; for long-term residential environments, which reproduce the circumstances of family life for persons requiring continuing supervision due to special needs, use "group homes."

A form of building often found in gardens, its location and function similar to those of multi-storied buildings, but usually smaller in size.  It is often built on flat land, but occasionally found against hillsides or on the edge of water.
Library buildings having collections focused on the study and application of medicine and healing.
Redoubts formed by a number of re-entering and salient angles, the sides of which flank each other.
Refers to freestanding structures having approximately the form of columns, with capital, shaft, and base, but without a full superstructure and erected as memorials.

Refers to megalithic prehistoric structures comprising two monolithic upright stones topped by a monolithic lintel. For smaller structures formed by two or more large standing stones capped by monolithic horizontal slabs, use "megalithic chamber tombs."
Refers to public establishments equipped with pool and/or billiard tables.
Ancient Roman structures adapted to ball playing.

Sikh places of worship and community gathering that may include a dining hall, medical facilities, a library, nursery, classroom, meeting rooms, and recreation areas. Gurudwaras are open to people of all faiths and religions.the name; the term literally translates to "door to the guru" or "gateway to the guru," in Punjabi. It is the site of a copy of the Adi Granth (“First Volume”), of the sacred scripture of Sikhism.

Impermeable, rigid barriers built out from a bank of a river or stream diverting the current to prevent or encourage scour. For similar structures located at the seashore, use "groins (erosion protection works)"; when such structures are built to control shoaling, use "jetties (erosion protection works)."
Installations with equipment for raising water in water distribution systems to a higher elevation; may be used for similar structures in sewage systems.
Reservoirs, typically but not exculsively of water, located below the surface of the earth.
Built works used to house radioactive waste.

Small, primitive windmills designed for drainage of plots of land or at peat digging sites as they are easily moved. Most often identified as a Frisian design, these are found in other Dutch provinces, and Northern Germany. Characterized by a single shaft supporting the sails on one end and an Archimedean screw on the other, allowing for a gearless action.
Places at which material such as wool, ore, coal, or crushed stone is separated from impurities or dust by washing in water or other liquids.

A furnace with an inner chamber to keep objects from exposure to direct flame; a low temperature oven used to apply overglaze colors on objects. Temperatures usually range from 700 to 900 degrees Celsius.

Buildings that housed places of confinement and labor for those unable to pay debts, common particularly during 17th-19th century in Europe and America. For buildings housing similar institutions intended to provide punishment and reformation of the criminal, use "houses of correction (buildings)." For welfare buildings providing charitable care for low income individuals, use "almshouses (buildings)."
Buildings that house schools for training horses and teaching people how to handle, breed, and manage horses. For buildings that house schools teaching equitation, use "riding schools."
Buildings that house schools devoted to training dentists.
Buildings designed to meet the needs of continuing education programs, which focus on postsecondary instruction designed for adults.
Health facilities specializing in the treatment of and rehabilitation from illnesses and injuries that require prolonged care over an extended period of time.
Buildings housing the central switching point for telephone communications.

Houses that are generally two-story, one-room deep, and which have a thin profile. Prominent in England, they became particularly popular in the American mid-Atlantic states from 1700-1915, and symbolized rural prosperity.

Designates ancient rectangular dwellings consisting of a large main space and a shallower front porch framed by projecting antae; may be used for similarly shaped central features within more complex ancient buildings.
Dwellings used by occupants on the weekends or other periods of time away from weekday life, such as country residences for those who work during the week in a city.
A type of house built with stone walls.
Refers generally to houses seeming to be inhabited by ghosts or other apparitions.
In the ancient Roman Empire, the official residences of provincial governors.
Ancient Roman tenements or apartment houses.
Palaces that provide summer, generally rural, retreats for rulers and their courts.

Buildings housing devices for projecting celestial images onto the interior of a dome for public viewing; may also be used for the projecting mechanisms. For mechanical models of the solar system, use "orreries."
Markers or memorials of any kind that designate the site of a grave, ranging from the ephemeral, such as special flower arrangements, to the permanent, such as tombstones.
Municipal buildings in France and other French-speaking countries.
Dams oriented in the direction of the flow of a river, as protection for hollow river banks or of bridge piers, or for limiting the river's normal width.
Irrigation canals, pipes, pumps, and other structures and equipment for distributing water.
Establishments where dogs or cats are bred, raised, trained, or boarded.
Fences formed of a series of vertical posts, stakes, or rods, sometimes sharpened at the upper end, which are joined together by horizontal rails.
Premises that house facilities for the spare-time activities of young people, often those belonging to a given social club for youths.
Buildings or building complexes providing wholesalers with a single location having display spaces for product vendors of various trades, such as apparel, furnishings, or business equipment.
Buildings housing businesses where the primary retail trade is the sale of ready-to-wear clothing and accessories.
Very large retail stores, often specializing in a particular genre of product.

Use broadly to refer to buildings associated with any aspect of the various activities and business relationships of industry and trade; when referring to structures associated with the purchase, sale, or exchange of goods in business, use "mercantile buildings."
Buildings comprising large, deep, and narrow storage bins and mechanical conveying systems for the receiving, weighing, storing, and discharging of large quantities of grain.
Use primarily for large greenhouses with plants and facilities for public entertainment, popular in the 19th century; may also be used for areas planted for winter display.
Rooms or spaces from which tickets are sold, as for films, travel, or sporting events.

Refers to distinctive chambers in temples or churches. In ancient temples, the chambers were the apartments of the "pastophori," who were an order of priests who carried the shrines of the gods in procession. According to tradition, the Temple of Jerusalem also had such chambers, thus the term is applied to apartments that imitate these chambers and are typically located on either side of the bema in ancient churches or modern Greek Orthodox churches.

Enclosed spaces composed of a garth and surrounding walkways, which are generally arcaded on the courtyard side and walled on the other. Cloisters are often found in Christian monastic building complexes, but may be found on university campuses or elsewhere. The term is used for such features in secular buildings only when closely resembling the monastic prototype.
The open vestibule in front of the naos or cella of a temple.
In Indian architecture, a single-spired structure.

An easily worked yellow-brown fossiliferous limestone quarried in the Berici Hills south of Vicenza. It has been used since ancient times as a building and ornamental stone; the cathedral of Padua is a pietra di Nanto construction.
Refers to a type of rock consisting of clayey, or argillaceous, slate or schist containing scales or flakes of mica.

Stone quarried in the vicinity of the Isle of Purbeck peninsula, Dorset, England; used primarily as a building stone. It is actually a hard semi-metamorphosed limestone formed from the shells of snails. Given that the stone is hard enough to take a fine polish it is called "Purbeck marble," even though it is not fully metamophosed marble.
A coarse breccia marble of sharply angular red, pink, and white fragments in a dull red-brown matrix.
Metal fabric consisting of iron or steel rings, riveted or pressed together, typically used in armor.

A laminated leaf, resembling gold leaf, was made by placing a thin sheet of gold over a similar sheet of silver (or tin) and hammering the two together. The gold-silver laminate was used instead of gold leaf, but it had the undesirable characteristic of tarnishing, since the thin gold layer cannot protect the silver below.
Discarded metal, often fragmented, that is suitable for reprocessing.
Steel, rolled in a variety of shapes, such as beams, bars, or sheets, and used as load-bearing structural members.

Ankerite is a carbonate mineral, a member of the dolomite group in which the magnesium is replaced in substantial part by iron, with or without manganese. Ankerite occurs in deposits of iron ore and is also found in thin veins in coal seams.
Glass that absorbs heat because it is opaque to infrared radiation; it nevertheless retains a reasonable degree of transparency to most other radiation.

Decorative glassware in which metal particles, precious stones, or other materials are embedded in the glass. Particularly used to describe ancient Roman glass. For a distinctive kind of ornamental glass, similar to millefiore, made by fusing together rods of variously colored glass and then cutting the fused rods into cross-sections, use "mosaic glass." Also, although the names are similar and sometimes confused, murrhine glass differs from “Murano glass."
A copper alloy containing copper (89%), aluminum (5%), zinc (5%), and tin (1%).

Brass (a copper-zinc alloy) that is rich in zinc; it is easy to cast, is ductile, and has a golden color. It was notably used by the ancient Greeks and Romans. According to legend, it was mined in Atlantis in ancient times. It used for jewelry and, according to Plato, to line the outer walls of the Temple to Poseidon on Atlantis. By Roman times, the alloy was used for coinage and jewelry. It is likely that references to the material have historically referred to various yellow metals or alloys, for example, perhaps to a naturally occurring alloy of copper and gold.
Bronze containing phosphorus, or which has been deoxidized by the addition of phosphorus in its final processing stage, little or no phosphorus remaining in the final alloy.
Ancient pewter containing 70% tin and 30% lead, with other elements such as iron present as impurities.
Bricks made of refractory ceramic material which will resist high temperatures; used to line furnaces, fireplaces, and chimneys.
Pottery covered with a lead glaze and fired at a very low temperature, leaving the body soft and porous; originally developed in Japan.

Green-glazed stoneware manufactured in the kilns of Zhejiang province in southern China, with production concentrated in Shangyu, Yuyao, and Shaoxing. Developed during the Six Dynasties period, it was the first recognizable ware type in China. Yueh-yao was a highly durable ceramic often used for bowls and jars. Its popularity led to its eventual exportation to places as distant as Egypt and the Philippines.
Concrete that has been poured into a form or structure rather than being the material from which construction blocks have been made.
Concrete for delivery to a site in an unhardened state for immediate use.

Inexpensive glass, commonly of greenish or brownish color, which is caused by the presence of impurities, notably iron. It is often used to make bottles or windows. The term is derived from its resemblance to forest glass, which is also called "green glass."
Pressed glass with an orange gold iridescence made with a colored spray rather than by the presence of metallic oxides.
Inert noble gas with symbol Ar and atomic number of 18, used in metalworking and as a filler for electric incandescent and fluorescent light bulbs.
Magnesium oxide mixed with water, often with the addition of asbestos fiber; used to cover such things as steam pipes and furnaces.
A type of cement composed of an even mixture of portland cement and fine granulated blast-furnace slag.

Multifunctional ritual and pictorial modes in which deities occupy purified geometric precincts. They are represented as geometric motifs, often circular and symbolic of the Universe, capable of innumerable variation and meaning in a variety of media.
In Indian architecture, a bud (conical decorative motif, usually shown in suspension).

Zodiac symbol of a pair of scales, roughly based on the constellation of the same name. The zodiak signs have survived from classical Greek and Roman decoration, were popular in Northern European Romanesque and Gothic churches, and often found in Medieval psalters and books of hours symbolizing each month in which the sun enters the related constellation. They have also been used as decoration on ceilings, maps, timepieces, and astronomical instruments.
Crosses having arms ending in a shape resembling three knobs or bud-like projections, similar to a trefoil leaf.

Small rural centers which contain basic community, education, and religious facilities and which generally do not exceed 250 residents; may also refer to the smallest incorporated units of a municipal government.

Use only for large communities established in space or on natural extraterrestrial bodies. For smaller manned installations established on natural extraterrestrial bodies for specific functions, use "extraterrestrial bases." Use "space stations" for manned artificial satellites placed in a fixed orbit and serving as a base for specific functions (e.g., scientific observations or the refueling of spaceships).
Places or areas that are no longer occupied, modified, or inhabited by communities of human populations.
Tracts of land set aside by a government for aboriginal, tribal, or native populations.
Refers to networks of autonomous sensor nodes monitoring environmental or physical conditions at diverse locations that pass their data via wireless technology to a central location.
Land under cultivation or capable of being cultivated.
The hollow bed of a stream.
Continental islands that are attached to the mainland by dry land, often forming peninsulas, at low tide.
Marshy or reedy pools, ponds, small lakes, backwaters, or inlets.

Objects or motifs formed in a smooth, convex circular, or oval shape that is flat on the bottom. Refers specifically to the shape of unfaceted gems, architectural ornament, and details of furniture, particularly during the 16th and 17th centuries and revived in kidney shape on the cabriole knees of chairs and tables in the mid-18th century.

Structures built on sloping sites, as on the sides of hills or mountains. For architecture built of earth or primarily into the earth, prefer "earthen architecture." For architecture created from caves, prefer "cave architecture."

Holes, pits, or other generally vertical excavations cored, bored, drilled, or otherwise constructed in the earth for purposes of drawing out various liquids, such as water, brine, or petroleum, or natural gas.
Artificial earthen mounds with a flat summit, intended to support a structure or activity. They were particularly prominent in the Pre-Columbian American cultures.

Structures, which are constructions of any kind artificially fabricated, that are deemed significant in the history of architecture or engineering, or that played significant historic roles in local cultural or social development. Includes not just buildings, but other structures, for example oil wells, bridges, docks, and railroads.

Gardens or plantings that are on a steep slope, on a stepped pyramid or ziggurat, on the top of a wall, on a roof, or otherwise situated so as to hang over the ground below or to appear to float. The most famous example was the hanging gardens of Babylon, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world.
Private gardens established primarily for growing vegetables and herbs for domestic consumption.
Areas containing properties and buildings of historical significance, and extending to include significant natural features as well.

More recently, refers to roads over which mail is carried. Historically, roads with stations providing for horses for postriders, mailcoaches, or travelers. More recently, refers to roads over which mail is carried. Historically, roads with stations providing for horses for postriders, mailcoaches, or travelers.
Narrow walks or ways, typically not constructed like a road, and intended to be traveled by foot.

Ribbons of protected lands and waters, primarily within or near cities, established to provide the public with access to open spaces that mitigate the hard edges and overdeveloped landscapes of urban areas.
Temples dedicated to all the gods.
In Indian architecture, a temple type.

Rooms, buildings, or groups of buildings where people conduct studies and tests on the behavior and control of electrons and the design and application of devices and systems whose operation depends upon the behavior of electrons.

Refers to modest outbuildings used for shelter or storage. A shed is usually one story, typically has one or more open sides, and may be covered by a lean-to roof with one high pitched plane covering the entire structure. It may be leaning against a permanent structure or standing alone. The special purpose of the shed is typically  indicated by a defining word prefixing (e.g., "cowshed," "woodshed," "train shed").
Transportation buildings, or stations, which are usually built to act as a terminal point for airlines, a railway, a bus service, or another type of transportation.

Relay stations or rest stops set along ancient Roman and Byzantine roads (through the 7th century) and providing for the minimal needs of travelers. For stopping places for overnight stays along these ancient routes, use "mansiones."
Bridges containing more than one span, typically with a superstructure comprising a row of elongated single-span girders arranged end-to-end and supported at their ends on vertical support columns.
Refers to polyester polymers used as fibers woven into fabrics.

Composite material used for molding objects; made of repulped or pulverized paper and a liquid adhesive binder. May also comprise strips of paper, sometimes reinforced with textiles, stuck together with a wet adhesive, and used to form an object. The object becomes solid when the paste dries; the object may then be sanded, lacquered, and painted. Such objects are very durable; they first developed in Asia and were common in Europe and elsewhere since the 17th century.
Sheer, lightweight, crisp, semitransparent cotton fabric. It is a plain woven cloth of fine combed yarns.
Soft, dense, light-brown wooly undercoat of the musk ox.
General term for Japanese lining papers made from the inner bark of mulberry trees of the genus Broussonetia. Kozo papers are often used for backing when Asian scrolls are relined.
Embossed, decorative paper produced using woodblocks and stencils, that is embellished with a metallic finish.
A turquoise colored pigment used in ancient Egyptian and Mediterranean wall painting, Egyptian green is similar in chemical composition to Egyptian blue with which it is sometimes confused.
A blue pigment composed of Prussian blue mixed with synthetic ultramarine blue.
Green pigment prepared as a mixture of blue and yellow, often indigo and orpiment, and used as an alternative to verdigris by Medieval painters and for illuminated manuscripts.

Green crystalline copper carbonate prepared as pigment by selection, grinding, washing, and levigation of the malachite mineral. Coarsely ground malachite gives a dark green color while finely ground particles give a lighter more transparent tone. It is a lightfast, but sensitive to acids and sulfur fumes. Basic copper carbonate can also be made artificially by coloring chalk with copper sulfate, then called "green verditer." Natural malachite was occasionally used in tempera-based paintings before the 16th century and later, green verditer was used for both distemper and oil based interior house paints in the 19th century.

A very poisonous copper-based bright green powder that is used as a pigment and  insecticide; it is mixed acetate and arsenite of copper, discovered about 1800, and first commercially manufactured in Schweinfurt, Germany in 1814. It is lightfast but is decomposed by acids and warm alkalis and darkens in the presence of sulfur. In the 19th century, it was used for oil paints, coach paints, watercolors, pastels, wax crayons, and pencils. In the early 20th century, it was also used as a colorant in wallpapers, fabrics, linoleum, and toys. Marketed as Paris green, it was used as an insecticide, fungicide, and rat poison. Emerald green is no longer used as a pigment due to its toxicity.
An unstandardized name for many red pigments, included but not limited to Indian red, Persian Gulf oxide, light red, and a variety of chrome red colors.
An earth pigment containing red iron oxide, originally obtained from Spain. It is a coarse grain, an inexpensive colorant, having a dull red color, and used in industrial paints.

Heavy, opaque, orange-red pigment composed of lead tetroxide. Although chemically equivalent to the mineral minium, red lead pigment has been synthetically prepared by roasting lead white (480 C) since before the 5th century BCE. Red lead has been found as a pigment on early objects from Egypt, China, Japan, India, Persia, and Rome; it is no longer used as an artist's color because is has poor light stability and poor working properties, although it is still used to color glass and ceramic glazes. Pliny called it "secondarium minium." It was widely used in illuminated manuscripts, and with its use, the term "miniare" came to mean "to color with red lead," giving rise to the term "miniature." Red lead paint was used as an anticorrosion primer for structural iron and steel until the late 20th century.

A natural dark pink madder colorant extracted from madder roots with an acid, then the precipitate, primarily pseudopurpurin, is redissolved in alum then reprecipitated with calcium carbonate to produce a pink lake. It became popular as an artist pigment after the madder plant was imported to Holland in the 16th century.
Zinc sulfide coprecipitated with barium sulfate; it is used as a dense white pigment in house paint and industrial coatings.
White pigment containing CaCO3, made of carbonate of lime or limestone, and arragonite, as well as other material.
Lake pigment extracted from small berries from various a buckthorn  plant, Rhamnus infectorius.

Lumber that is intended for use in building where allowable properties are required. The grading of structural lumber is based on the strength or stiffness of the piece as related to anticipated uses, such as lumber that is 5 inches or more in both thickness and width.

An exudate from several species of shrubs of the genus Astragalus, especially Astragalus gummifer, found in the dry regions of Iran, Iraq, Syria, and Turkey. The use of gum tragacanth dates from pre-Christian times. It used for textile sizing, printing, pastel crayon production, leather curing, furniture polishes, as an emulsifying, suspending, and thickening agent, pharmaceutically as a demulcent (coating) and as a binding agent in pill manufacture, and in processed foods.

A transparent, resinous exudation, red in color, derived from several plants in 4 genera, having in common the primary red coloring component dracorubin. Dragon's blood is available as red sticks, cakes, or as a powder, and was traded as early as Roman times. It is used medicinally as an astringent, as a red colorant in medieval manuscript illuminations, to stain varnishes for violins, as a colorant for plaster, marble, and paints, and as a resist in photoengraving to protect zinc plates from acid. The red color is fugitive when exposed to light and air, but may be partially protected by a resin film layer.

An aromatic, thick, viscous exudation obtained from several Central European fir trees, including Abies alba. Strasbourg turpentine contains about 57% resinous acids, 28% terpenes, and 13% resins. It is similar to Venice turpentine and has been used since the 16th century as an additive to oil paints, mastic, and other varnishes.

Aromatic, yellow gum resin obtained from various African, Arabian, and Indian trees of the Commiphora genus. Myrrh contains approximately 25% resin (mostly triterpenoids), 60% gum, and 15% volatile oils. Translucent yellow resins have been used for incense and perfumes since ancient times. Myrrh has also been used for its healing properties in traditional medicines.
The root of an East Indian herb that yields a red dye.

Any of a class of wash-fast sulfur-containing synthetic organic dyes dissolved in a heated alkaline bath of sodium sulfide and then absorbed by cellulose fibers to which they are applied; they are made insoluble within the fibers by oxidation upon exposure to air.  They are the dyes most commonly used for cotton.
Pigment having the color red, which is produced by light having a spectrum dominated by energy with a wavelength of about 630–700nm.
An unstandardized pigment name used for Bremen blue, azurite pigment, cupric sulfide, and others.
Wood of the Cryptomeria japonica tree, an evergreen native to eastern Asia. It is reddish brown, soft, fragrant, and used for construction, furniture, and ornamental carving.

General term referring to wood from several species, including Chamaecyparis thyoides (Atlantic White Cypress), Cupressus lusitanica (Mexican White Cedar), and Thuja occidentalis (Eastern Arborvitae).
Wood of Abies alba, an ornamental and timber species tree native to the mountainous regions of central and southern Europe and Asia, much used in carpentry.
Wood of the Pinus parviflora, native to Japan.
Wood from the Picea smithiana.
Hard, central wood of the trunks of dead trees. Usually, heartwood contains tannins which make it aromatic and dark in color.

A type of structural lumber product composed of a wood core with several layers of wood veneer bonded to the front and back by durable adhesive known as laminating stock. Glue-laminated timber beams are used as an alternative to steel beams in construction due in part to the relative energy-efficiency of their manufacture which produces far less greenhouse gas emissions.
Wood of the species Fagus orientalis, native to Eurasia.

Wood of the species Betula pendula found throughout Europe, including the British Isles and Scandinavia. It is characterized by having no distinct heartwood, with whitish to pale brown, fairly straight-grained wood. It is used for plywood, furniture, dowels, fittings, brooms, and turnings
Wood of any tree belonging to the genus Nyssa, found in North America and Asia. It is soft, light, and tough and is used in the manufacture of bridge and pier decking and construction.

Wood of the Carya laciniosa, native from Ontario to Minnesota, Florida and Mexico. It has a white sapwood, and brown heartwood, and is used for tool handles, sporting goods, turnery, vehicle bodies, veneer, fuelwood, charcoal, and bent wood.
General term referring to any of several species of mahogany from South and Central America. Was mistakenly called "cedar" by Jesuit missionaries.
Hard, strong, fine-grain wood of the species Acer rebrum, soft red in color.

Refers specifically to the wood of the species Quercus prinus (also called Q. montana), used in making furniture. The term "chestnut oak" is also used informally as a general term referring to any of several species of oaks having leaves similar to chestnut trees.

Wood of the species Populus deltoides, native to the lower Mississippi Valley. It has a soft, pale color, fine grain, uniform texture, works easily, and stains well; however, the wood has a tendency to warp. It is used for millwork, musical instruments, paneling, packing boxes, paper pulp, and excelsior.

Wood of the tree from the genus Tsuga. The bark contains tannin, used in the tanning industry, and the timber is mostly light in color with a pinkish tinge, and the soft, and coarse-grained, used in construction of boxes.
Fur from a European polecat, dark in color. It is used in the fur trade. It is also used in paint brushes, valued for its elasticity.
The hide of jaguar (Panthera onca).
Berry developed from an inferior ovary, with a hard outer rind and numerous seeds attached to parietal placentas. The characteristic fruit of the gourd family.
Material derived from the stalks of rivercane plants; while there are three species of rivercane, Arundinaria gigantea is most often used.
Mass noun for the fruits or seeds of plants of the Oryza genus, forming one of the most important food grains of the world.

Wood of trees belonging to the genus Malus. It is a pinkish buff wood that has a straight grain with a fine, even texture that polishes well; used for turnery, inlay, veneers, carving, handles, pipes, and cabinetry.
Marble that is streaked or marked with a different color or colors.
A jet black marble with irregular white veins, occurring in Virginia, that is considered the best American black marble.
A marble of argillaceous limestone containing dark coloring matter so distributed as to resemble forests or landscapes.
White marble with grey/black veins or speckling quarried in Val Venosta, Alto Adige, Italy.
Slate that has a component of hematite, causing a reddish color.
In Indian art and architecture, this term refers to stone.
