The maintenance of objects as closely as possible to their original condition through appropriate environmentally controlled collection maintenance, repair, and physical treatment. Refers to actions taken to prevent further changes or deterioration in objects, sites, or structures. When such actions are taken on buildings or other structures specifically for cultural, aesthetic, or historic reasons, see "historic preservation." For changes that return an object or structure to a state of historical correctness, see "restoration (process)." For actions taken to return to sound condition an already deteriorated structure, see "rehabilitating." For the activity of keeping people and things safe from harm or deterioration generally, see "protection." More generally, for the treatment, preventive care, and research directed toward the long-term safekeeping of cultural and natural heritage, see "conservation."
Long, narrow bands, typically of a different color.
Plaster or stone tablets set into the outer walls of buildings and carved with images depicting the profession of inhabitants or text to identify the building.
In Indian architecture, a heron, ruddy goose (Anas Casarca), or Cakva-bird as a decorative motif placed on kapōta.
Facilities housing operations by which raw foodstuffs are made suitable for consumption, cooking, or storage.
Relatively small public buildings that offer for a fee rooms for sleeping and a tavern for food and beverages.
Maps delineating the boundaries of districts which, along with the zoning text, comprise the zoning ordinances.
Open-tiered shelves for displaying small objects; often with a mirrored back and sometimes having drawers or a cabinet below.
In Indian architecture, a band showing haṁsas and cakravāka birds.
Reference sources containing alphabetical lists of words with information given for each word; generally including meanings, pronunciation, etymology, and often usage guidance.
The planning and construction of a structure that is involved with its ability to maintain its intended position and orientation during earthquakes.
Any items, such as deeds, bonds, or monies, held in trust by a third party to be turned over to the grantee upon fulfillment of a condition.
In Indian architecture, nine-storeyed.
Includes references to or interest in hidden, mysterious, or supernatural powers, as manifested in all fields of human endeavor or creativity. Excludes occult sciences themselves.
Action or state of something having been incorrectly done through ignorance or inadvertence; a mistake, miscalculation, or bad judgment.
Containers or spaces maintained at a low temperature by means of ice or mechanical apparatus for the purpose of preserving its contents, especially food or drink.

Gradient-heated devices used to determine the melting point of a substance designed by Ludwig Kofler, usually to be used with a microscope. These feature stainless steel surfaces which are electrically heated at one end, resulting in an approximately linear temperature gradient along the top surface.

Steel tools resembling chisels, most often characterized by a large, thick, flat blade cast as a single piece with a narrower handle and striking surface; used in conjunction with a caulking mallet to drive various materials into seams and crevices to make joints water- and airtight.
Equipment and tools used specifically for painting.

Any of various types of electronic instruments for detecting the presence of metallic objects by means of their effects on an electromagnetic field. Examples include portable devices with a search head that is swept over the ground to locate buried metal objects, a hand-held or walk-through security device for locating concealed weapons, and a device for checking for the presence of extraneous pieces of metal in food.
Files, usually of metal, used for filing metal materials or objects.

Courses of sailing or navigation other than by land, usually by sea or water from one place to another, specifically to a distant place or country. By extension, this has been applied to journeys into space or to extraterrestrial bodies.
Tools for joining metals with solder, having a wedge-shaped metal bit, usually of copper, which is heated.
Heavy, round iron rods about 3 to 6 inches long, curved round at one end nearly at a right angle; used by coopers.
Devices with a rotating flat disc or turntable on which clay may be shaped to create symmetrical forms; the process of forming clay objects on a potter's wheel is throwing.
Solid iron rods onto which a partly made molten object is transferred from the gathering iron or blowpipe for the final shaping and decoration.
Externally driven machine with percussion hammers or rollers for deseeding flax stems.
Periods when large areas of Earth were covered with ice; glacial episodes.
A deposit of minute ice crystals formed when water vapor condenses at a temperature below freezing.

Extremely small particles and droplets suspended in air. They may include organic chemicals, acids, metals, and dust or soil particles. Also known as particle pollution, particulate matter is used as a measure of air pollution. The EPA  groups inhalable pollutants which pass through the throat and nose and enter the lungs into two categories: “inhalable coarse particles” (between 2.5 micrometers and 10 micrometers in diameter); and “fine particles” (2.5 micrometers in diameter and smaller).
A flat clay tile used for roofing.
Tools consisting of a large rubber suction cup on a wood handle; used for clearing plumbing traps of minor obstructions.
Refers to male human beings from young adulthood through old age.

Ornamental arrangements of the initials or letters of a name, often used to indicate ownership or patronage. In numismatics, it typically refers to the mint mark, the assayer, or the individual responsible for the issuance.

Paper made on a machine that allows pulp to flow onto a moving and vibrating mesh or belt, thus forming a continuous strip that may be dried and pressed before being wound onto a roll for storage. Machine-made paper may exhibit laid lines, chain lines, and watermarks that mimic those of handmade paper.
Geometric plane figures having three or more straight sides and the same number of angles.

Hydrated aluminum silicate clay. It is used for making porcelain for china and chemical porcelain for valves, tubes, and fittings, as a pigment and filler in paint and plastic, an abrasive powder, and in paper to yield a glossy surface.
A masonry unit, laid so that its ends are exposed, overlapping two or more adjacent wythes of masonry and tying them together.
Adzes whose blade edges are turned upwards on each side to give a trenching cut, a square rather than round channel; also used to cut scores or notches across the grain at intervals.

Small tools used for the removal of staples from materials such as paper or upholstery. These are of two basic designs, either a single wedge used as a lever, or a hinged pincer device with teeth that grasp the staple and pull it out.

Printing surfaces, usually rectangular in shape and made of wood, used to print designs onto wallpaper. The surface is first engraved with the design, covered with ink, and then pressed into the printing surface.

The adoption of the practices or aethetics of one social group or society by another, more dominant social group or society, in ways that are exploitative, offensive, and/or disrespectful. These customs or aethetics may include cultural traditions, clothing, and general behavior. The term is most commonly used to refer to the adoption of non-Western aesthetics by people in Western cultures.
Ceramic vessels that were used to transport wine or other liquid, and are characterized as being plain and  unglazed.
General term for people who have an unspecified familial relationship, either by blood or marriage.
Components of aerophones which are placed in or against the player's mouth and which, together with the player's lips or the reed, form the tone generator.

Works comprising pairs of panels hinged together. They were used by the ancient Romans for writing tablets, often having images on the outer surfaces. In Medieval and later times, they were used primarily to support images for altarpieces and other purposes, most often composed of carved ivory or of painted wood panels, with the primary images on the interior surfaces.
Works of art that employ words and letters primarily as formal elements, often without regard to their verbal meaning.
Works used as test-pieces, often by apprentices, and presented to a guild to determine whether the makers were qualified to rank as masters.

Visual works that are derived directly from nature, including formerly living organisms and non-organic objects, and that have been processed, prepared, or altered only in such a way as to preserve or minimally enhance the appearance of the natural object or living organism. For natural materials, see the specific term in the Materials hierarchy.

Inlaid works comprising an alloy of copper, lead, tin, and zinc, used as a ground for inlaying with gold and silver. The handicraft originated in Bidar, Karnataka, India in the 14th century CE, during the rule of the Bahamani Sultans.

Carpets woven with loops like Brussels carpets but different from them in being heavier, having velvet cut piles, being generally of better materials and having designs adapted from Oriental rug patterns.

Reliquaries designed in the shape of the relic they were ostensibly intended to contain, which may be a piece of clothing, an object or fragment of an object, a body part, a saint's blood, or other artifact.
Mass meetings of people for the purpose of showing support for a cause or protest.
Typewriters that read punched paper tape, decode the punched data, and then print corresponding texts in human-readable form. Used especially in early information and data processing.

The systems of physical and breathing exercises, typically combined with meditation, practiced as an activity or discipline for mental and physical health benefits. For the orthodox system of Indian philosophy, use "Yoga (philosophy)."
The process or state of restoration of a person or animal to a healthy or normal condition, or to consciousness, as from the cure or healing of an illness or wound.
A lamp-bearing maiden in Indian sculpture or architecture.

Surfaces or portions of objects that face forward or are regarded as the most important or useful. For the adjective describing the location of something at or near the front of something, use "front" from the Attributes and Properties hierarchy.
Imprints of the edges of the plate on intaglio prints.
Insufficient biting of a printing plate.

Mercenary soldiers of a certain class in the German and other continental armies in the 16th and 17th centuries. The term originally applied to the serfs brought into the field by the nobles within the territories of the Empire, in contradistinction to the Swiss mercenaries. In time this distinction became obsolete, and the designation connoted a soldier armed with a particular kind of equipment, of which a lance was part.
Actions of taking, or the conditions of maintaining, possession or control of a land, country, building, etc., typically by military force.
The aggregate of physical objects produced by a society or culturally cohesive group.
Commercial name for central Asian floral embroidered panels, usually large in size, used as hangings and bedcovers.

Durable floor coverings made primarily of linseed oil, with a filler of cork dust or wood flour, and flax, with pigments added to create the desired colors and patterns; also, similar floor coverings made with substitutes for the linseed oil or filler or both.
Traditional woven mats, particularly those forming the basic floor coverings in Maori structures.
The maximum shear stress which a material or soil is capable of sustaining.
Long, narrow runners used to protect stairs, typically characterized by fitting only the central portion of the stairway, leaving the wood of the treaders and risers visible.
Two narrow carpets placed on either side of the mian farsh in the traditional carpet arrangement of an Islamic room.
Heavy knitted mats with a shaggy pile of short strips of fabric that are inserted as the knitting progresses.

Pileless, handwoven floor coverings made in most of the rug-weaving areas of the Middle East, with usage of the term varying in different locations, including slit-tapestry kilims in the Caucasus, woven fabric in eastern Iran, and large rugs with a diamond grid and narrow borders as woven by the Turkmen Yomut, Tekke, and Ersari tribes.
Lighting units consisting of one or more lamps in a metal hood with a reflector or inner reflecting surface; used to illuminate large areas diffusely.

Devices that are a combination of a dark lantern, night light, heater for food, milk, or shaving water, candleholder (in handle), and tinder box, usually made of tinned sheet iron. Based on a patented design of William Howe of Boston, 1812. Use also for earlier European examples partially or wholly of ceramic.
Stage lights, usually spotlights or striplights, mounted at each side of the stage.

Light European staff weapons, about 6 1/2 feet in length and with a head that is usually more decoration than weapon, carried by infantry officers in the 16th and 17th centuries as an insignia of rank and to give signals when leading their men.
Objects, often valuables, deposited with a corpse, in or near a grave.
Aeronautical ground lights arranged along a runway indicating its direction or boundaries.
Gas burners having a single round hole, producing a long, slender flame. Used primarily in modified form as burners for gas candles.

White crystalline salt that occurs in nature as the mineral magnesite and may be prepared artificially by precipitation. It is used in pigments, inks, glass, ceramic glazes, and dentifrice. Magnesium carbonate has also been used as a sorbent powder for water-free (dry) cleaning of jewelry, doll hair, and other items. Aqueous solutions of magnesium carbonate are used for neutralization and alkalization of paper.

Describes a variety of metal or other features that reinforce or support the core during the casting process. This term is used in different ways depending on the context. In industry, it is applied to metal inserts or spacers that hold the core in place during the pour; therefore, core pins, chaplets, and mold extensions are examples of core supports. In cultural contexts, the term is applied to internal wires or rods that help strengthen the core during assembly of the casting model and/or during the pour. Generally reserved for smaller wires in projecting limbs, or wires and rods used to strengthen joints between separately molded wax sections in the indirect lost-wax process. For clarity, when the second definition is intended, the term “internal core support” should be used.

Disc-shaped objects made from papyrus, stuccoed linen, bronze, gold, wood, clay or resin, placed by ancient Egyptians under the heads of the dead. The disc, which was inscribed with images, symbolized the eye of Ra or Horus, and was related to the idea of resurrection.
The technique of creating tone in lithography by splattering lithographic ink on the stone or plate using a stiff brush and mesh screen or sieve.

Sheet metal seams having a bottom plate with a turned edge that is inserted inside the side plate; the seam may be secured by welding, soldering, or riveting at the overlapping joint. For bottom seams having the bottom plate with a turned edge that overlaps the side plate rather than being inserted inside it, use "lap bottom seams."
In Indian art or architecture,  a sacred image or depiction of a deity.
Wheels used as the primary means of maneuvering vehicles.

Spectroscopy technique concerned with the spectrum between the visible and the short-wavelength microwave. Infrared spectroscopy can detect the internal vibration of molecules. The field was traditionally broken into near-, mid-, and far-infrared spectroscopy, although with the development of Fourier-transform spectrometers, this distinction of areas has blurred and the more sophisticated instruments can cover from 10 to 25,000 cm-1 by an interchange of source, beam splitter, detector, and sample cell.

Lighting devices, fixed or portable, designed to protect and enclose the light source, usually with sides of glass, horn, pierced metal, paper, or other material, allowing light to emerge and often having a supporting frame, hanging device, or carrying handle. They may be purely utilitarian or decorative, sometimes having ceremonial significance.
Buildings for repositories devoted to the art, history, and technology of motion pictures, television, and video.

Square-back Windsor chairs with a cross panel capping and usually extending beyond the top of the back posts. Such chairs can have backs consisting of long spindles, cross slats, one or more cross slats with short spindles, or a vertical back splat.
A thing, writing, moneys, or other contribution added to to a common fund, stock, collection, database, or literary work.
Refers to the entire playing areas upon which rugby is played.
Persons who research information about words that make up language and write and review definitions for publication in a dictionary.
Those who study aging and the special capabilities and problems of the elderly.
A listing of items that are offered in a lottery.
Persons officially entrusted with guarding and keeping things, such as property, artifacts, or records, or with custody or guardianship of people, such as prisoners, inmates, or wards.

Outer sheets or boards that are part of, or are attached to, groups of leaves, whether a substantial block or a single gathering; sometimes simply the first page of a document, as for example of a leaflet, if it is designed as distinct from the body of the document. Designed to protect the text block or gathering within, and often carrying information about it such as the title, and decoration.

Proclamations or orders concerning a law, decree, or other authoritative command, usually having the force of law. Edicts are the proclamations, as distinguished from the formal, finalized laws, decrees, ordinances, etc. that are referenced by the edicts.

Artisans who make tapestries, which are heavy wall hangings or other textiles characterized by ornamental or pictorial designs and woven by a process that differs from cloth-weaving in that the weft travels only to the warp at the edge of a particular color or pattern in the design, rather than traveling from edge to edge of the entire piece of fabric.
People who are expert in the history of filmmaking and critical analysis of motion pictures.
Those who examine or inspect in order to achieve a comprehensive view, as of a place, a situation, or an area of study, or to ascertain condition or value.

Persons engaged in professional or voluntary service of a specialized nature concerned with community welfare and family or social problems such as arise from poverty, mental or physical handicaps, or maladjustment.
Beings holding the estate or rank of a god or other supremely divine entity.
Quilts pieced from thousands of squares or rectangles the size of postage stamps.
Dishes intended primarily for serving vegetables, usually shallow and sometimes made with one or more interior dividers. May have a cover or feet or sometimes both.

Vessels used during libation rituals: the pouring of a liquid as an offering to a god. These vessels often have a significant shape which set them apart from secular vessels, though libation vessels appear in varied forms.
Single-headed drums of South Africa. They are made with two handles and an open bottom.
Double-headed Japanese drums with deerskin heads, used in Japanese court music.
Ceremonial containers used in the context of funerals or burials.
Folded sheets of light cardboard used to cover or hold papers, letters, or other flat documents, as in a file.
General term for secure chests or arks intended to contain the remains of the deceased, used particularly for such chests from ancient Greek, Etruscan, and Egyptian cultures.
Open boxes or troughs in stables, barns, stalls or pens, that contain hay, grass or other fodder for farm animals.
Tubs for use in washing clothes, linens, and the like, often used with a washboard or mangle.
Large baskets used for storage; used especially with reference to covered baskets with square or round bases and rims.

Small jar-like vessels designed to store cosmetics, typically made of stone, ceramic, or glass. Best known as works from ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, Asia, and in Europe and North America through the early 20th century.

Containers made of two long rectangular pieces of flexible material, usually leather or textile, sewn together on the two short sides and one long side and open on the remaining long side, designed to carry paper money. The billfold is usually only slightly larger than the bills and is folded in the center. Billfolds are typically men's accessories, carried in the pocket of the trousers or a jacket.
Containers having a primarily ceremonial or ritual purpose.
Fiddles of Mongolia, generally square-bodied, with two strings and a carved horse's head at the top of their necks.
Instruments for measuring the carbon content of steel.
Devices used measure diameters.
Instruments for measuring altitudes, usually consisting of a graduated arc of 90 degrees, a pair of sights, and a plumb bob.
Dials with gnomons used for showing the hours of the night by moonlight.

Dishes or shallow or deeper bowls used to hold the consecrated hosts during their distribution during the Christian liturgy. This bowl or dish is used for the distribution of communion in place of a ciborium. For bowls, often two-handled, used to hold consecrated wine, use "communion bowls (vessels for wine)."
Parts or components of vambraces.
Encircling bands on containers and other objects. For flat, sharp-edged collars or knops on stemware, use "mereses."
Discrete sections or texts found or entered in an itemized work, such as an account book, record, database, dictionary, encyclopedia, catalogue, index, or other such work.
The titles impressed on the outside of the front cover of a book, or written or printed on a label pasted to the cover, sometimes a shortened version of the title proper printed on the title page.
Duct flutes of Burma, made of bamboo and with seven fingerholes.
Treble shawm of Spain, played usually in Catalonian ensembles.

Metallophones consisting of tuned, graduated metal bars arranged in two rows suspended from a metal frame with tubular resonators suspended below them; motor-driven spinning discs fixed above the open tops of the resonators produce the unique vibrato characteristic of the instrument.
Devices used for measuring distances on a vertical plane.
Device that measures the flow of viscous liquids in response to applied force.
Instruments for determining the amount of water in materials, as timber or soil, commonly by measuring its electrical resistivity.
Tools for gathering and measuring features or substances present in the air.
Devices for determining true horizontal or vertical angles by the centering of a bubble with a glass tube or circular case filled nearly to capacity with alcohol or ether.
Instruments for measuring the smoothness of surfaces by amplifying minute variations in vertical deviations of the surface.
Scales in which measurement is based on the deformation of some elastic material.
Covered vessels, usually circular in shape, used by Christian churches for storing unconsecrated hosts.
Sealed metal containers for food or beverages. Also, other containers for holding or carrying liquids, such as oilcans, and metal or plastic containers for holding film on cores or reels.
Cylindrical drinking vessels with a generous capacity that rest on a flat base with a single handle, used to drink coffee.
Any one of two or more layers of a skin or hide separated from each other by a mechanical splitting process.
Refers to the style and culture of modern Georgia, in the Caucasus region of Eurasia.
Identifying objects that are worn to indicate a person's affiliation, rank, office, name, or similar information. these may display insignias or symbols.

Electronic instruments played by the performer's hand moving back and forth at different distances from an antenna rising vertically from the instrument; the pitch of the single tone produced varies with the distance of the hand from the antenna.
Small lengths of material, such as vellum, catgut, leather, straw, or paper, around which headbands are sewn.
Individual written signs that correspond to separate speech sounds or to syllables in a spoken language.
Maori woven baskets or bags made of flax.
Flat-bottomed, cylindrical vessels usually with a pouring lip, especially those used by chemists and pharmacists.
Coins issued in various metals and valued at twenty-five cents.
Clappers of the Thonga peoples of South Africa. They consist of rectangular pieces of wood which are worn like gloves to increase the sound of clapping.
Small squares of various hard materials used by the ancient Romans possibly for such purposes as reckoning and gaming.
Lighting technique that distributes illumination over a relatively limited area or confined space without significantly altering the illumination of its general surroundings.

Coins, often a United States penny, pressed into an oval or elogated shape by being rolled between steel dies with a design impressed on one or both sides.  Elongated coins are typically souvenirs and are not used as currency.
Viscous, colorless, somewhat opalescent secretion that is usually slightly alkaline in reaction and which contains water, mucin, protein, salts, and often starch-splitting enzymes.
In a form that can be fed directly into a computer, such as electronic bits on a disk drive, diskette, or magnetic tape.
Successions of rulers from the same family, line, stock, or group, during a particular period of time; extended to include all the people and culture surrounding this succession of rulers.
People who are famous or had significant roles in history; also, those who are not necessarily famous, but whose existence is recorded, as distinguished from those who are fictional or legendary.

The activity of breaking up or loosening the surface of the ground, dislodging weeds, or covering plants with soil using a specialized agricultural implement that has a thin, flat blade set transversely at the end of a long handle.

Cantilevered or suspended roofs over the entrances to buildings, of metal or metal and glass; in the 19th and 20th centuries, common over the entrances to theaters, casinos, and hotels to advertise entertainment. For smaller, often ornamental, rooflike structures at entrances, use "canopies (structural elements)."

Material comprising horns, the hard, semitranslucent, proteinaceous structures that grow from the head of some mammals, such as cattle, sheep, goats, and antelope. Horn, like nails, claws, and hooves, is composed of epidermal cells known as keratin. Rhinoceros horns are formed from matted hair. The colours of horn range from a light cream to black. Horn can be cut, engraved, or carved, and has been used since ancient times for tools and ornamentation. The thermoplastic material is softened with steam or boiling water then pressed into numerous shapes. In the 18th century, London was the center of the horn molding industry, primarily making snuff boxes and decorative containers. Distinguished from "antler (material)," which is the fast-growing bone of deer.
Representations in any medium of Gautama Buddha.

Media containing any content that is represented in digital form, meaning it is encoded in an electronic format that uses a series of discrete values (commonly the numbers 0 and 1) to record data and render it machine-readable. Digital media include, but are not limited to, digital audio and video tape, floppy discs, and portable hard drives.
Hand or rifle grenades containing a smoke-producing chemical mixture, used for signaling or screening. Different types produce either white or colored smoke.
Wallpapers with colors blended in subtle gradations, particularly in the ground.
Artillery ammunition in which the case containing the primer and propellant is not permanently attached to the projectile; the two units are assembled into one at the time of loading.
Ancient Roman copper coins of the 3rd and 4th centuries, replaced by centenionales.

Cartridges characterized by a detonating pin projecting from the base which, when struck by the hammer, detonated the priming powder in a small cap inside the cartridge case, thus setting off the main charge.
Decorative or protective covers for backless seating furniture.
Use only for gold coins struck in Venice from the late 13th through the 19th century and for similar Austrian and Czechoslovakian coins issued in the early 20th century.
Refers to a piece of cloth in which a corpse is wrapped for burial.

In churches, cloths and coverings used to conceal paintings, sculptures, and other items of luxury and beauty during the solemn Lenten season. For the curtains used to conceal the altar during Lent, use "Lenten veils."
Scripts developed in India or South Asia, typically associated with the Indian branch of the Indo-Iranian languages, Indo-Aryan.

Large four-stringed instruments of the violin class; a bass violin tuned an octave below violas. They are structurally similar to violins but differ in having relatively deeper ribs and a shorter neck. They are often referred to simply as 'cellos'.
Liturgical chants of the Chaldean rite, historically associated with the Assyrian Church of the East.

Collections of homilies or sermons, which are discourses usually delivered from a pulpit, based upon a text of scripture, with the goal of giving religious instruction or exhortation. Homiliaries are often arranged according to the ecclesiastical year for reading at services.
Ornament filling the ends of lines in illuminated manuscripts.
Buildings or rooms occupied by associations formed to combine the operations of persons interested in the promotion or playing of tennis.
Bowls used to contain liquids used for libations at religious ceremonies. Examples include paterae used in Ancient Rome.
Class of persons employed for wages, usually at manual labor.

Objects originally created to cover or adorn a window, door, or doorway. This class does not include relatively permanent structural parts of buildings such as canopies, exterior shutters, and window sashes.
Narrow curtains fixed at the side of an opening, used purely for decoration as they do not have enough width to be drawn across to cover the intervening space.
Weapons consisting of a large, heavy, metal head studded with spikes that is either directly mounted on a shaft or attached to it by a length of chain.
Stage curtains that open in the center by being pulled diagonally up and to the sides.
Sharp knives or hatchets used to cut candy into suitable pieces; typically used for hard candy or taffy.
Tools or devices for loosening screw lids of jars.
Transverse flutes of the Pedi peoples of Southern Africa.
Shallow, metal pans with a relatively long, single handle used for frying foods; sometimes made with a lid.

A large, loose residual mass of stone left after the erosion of a once continuous bed or layer; often used to specifically refer to one of the large sandstone blocks scattered over the English chalk downs.
Rods of wood or metal used from the 15th century to drive the ball and powder charge into the breech of a firearm barrel or to clean it.
Artifacts in card form that contain information about, or related to, the cardholders.
Spoons with pierced bowls used to separate solids from liquids when serving or eating, or to skim liquids.

Apparatuses consisting of a hopper with a crank handle operated grinding mechanism at the bottom, the whole fixed to a lidded receptacle or a base equipped with a clamping device. Used to grind nuts finely.

Protective boxes with a hinged top, shaped like a thick book, for storing books, prints, pamphlets, and documents; developed in the 18th century for the storage of botanical specimens and later for the storage of books, prints, and documents.
Instruments that measure revolutions per minute or the angular speed of rotating shafts.

Dishes supplied with a heat source (such as a fuel lamp or candle) used for cooking or keeping food warm. The term is sometimes applied to vessels containing charcoal or other fuel and upon which another container with food may be placed.
Written solemn invocations of blessedness, for the purpose of being officially pronounced by an ecclesiastical functionary.
Process invented in the late 20th century by Jon Cone, where special, monochromatic inks are used in conjunction with software to produce black and white inkjet prints using consumer printers.
Printing using the surface of a potato that has been sliced and carved.
Tools used for canning, typically consisting of a canning funnel, ladle, and jar lifter.
Long-handled tools with a curved blade for taking potatoes out of the coals.
All spoons used for eating and not for serving food at table; all spoons used as part of place settings.
Spoonlike utensils with a deep bowl and a relatively long handle used for lifting, conveying, or serving cream, soup, punch, or other liquids.
Devices or surfaces that are designed to keep food or drinks warm over a period of time, usually as a prelude to being served, as at a buffet.

Ladles similar to but smaller than punch ladles and used for serving hot toddy from punch bowls to drinking glasses. Term used especially with reference to those made in Scotland during the early and mid-19th century.
A type of black-figure kantharos featuring a single handle.

Refers to a type of oinochoe featuring a narrow-beaked (narrow-spouted) mouth with the neck and upper body concave and curved outward. The lower body is either straight-sided or concave and curved inward.

Vaselike forms which are often made of glass but sometimes made of wood or bone and intended to hold spills, small pieces of wood or twisted paper used to light a fire. They resemble celery glasses in form although they were not intended for use on the dining table, but rather near a fireplace, oil lamp, or similar lighting device. For similar vaselike forms typically made of glass and used on the dining table for serving celery, use "celery glasses." For vaselike forms with a scalloped rim and used on the dining table for holding spoons, use "spoon holders."
Bags, often similar in style to purses, used to hold and carry diapers.
Bowls, usually set on a high footed stem and sometimes having a cover, used to serve fruit, compotes, nuts, or sweets.
Containers of various designs used to store molasses, which is a thick, brown, uncrystallized syrup drained from raw sugar.

Covers that encircle the body of disposable hot drink cups in order to protect the hand from the heat generated by the hot liquid through the cup. The term is used whether or not the hot liquid is coffee.

Containers for holding and serving cream, especially a small pitcher that may be accompanied by a sugar bowl. Sometimes made as part of a tea or coffee service. For containers designed for holding and serving milk, especially medium-sized pitchers, use "milk jugs."
Ancient Greek two-handled cups shaped like a woman's breast. The shape is principally known in black-figure and white-ground.
Drinking bowls, almost always having two handles and footed base, used in Christian eucharistic liturgies to hold consecrated wine.

Carrying cases used for storing and transporting tobacco and smoking pipes; commonly made and used by Plains Native North Americans. Due to tobacco's importance in many Native North American ceremonies, pipe bags are considered a spiritually charged object. Often held in one's left hand instead of being attached to the body.
Boxes, usually shallow and often round, for holding pills.
Boxes for holding instruments and materials for work, especially needlework.
Any of various containers in which plants are grown or placed for decorative purposes.
Surveyors' distance measuring devices consisting of interconnected metal links of precise length.
Small pots with perforated covers used to contain pounce or fine sand sprinkled on wet ink to blot it; sometimes made as a unit of an inkstand or desk set.
Reservoirs for processing food items, usually for salting or marinating.

Small, shallow platelike containers or mats, usually circular, used to protect a surface from being scratched or damaged by heat or moisture. Formerly referred to a low round tray or stand for a decanter.
Woven bedcovers, especially those made of a single piece of fabric, usually of wool and cotton.
Quilts made by members of a community as a gift for a minister, teacher, or mayor who was retiring or moving away. Often in the form of album quilts or signature quilts.
Separate sleeves of light material worn under the sleeves of a main garment and visible through it or extending beyond it.
Chlorine compound commonly used as a bleaching agent for textiles and paper.

Sulfuryl fluoride (SO2F2) is a toxic inorganic gas used as a structural fumigant insecticide to control dry-wood termites. It was developed by Dow Chemical Company in the late 1950s and sold under the trade name "Vikane." It more recently has been used as a post-harvest fumigant for dry fruits, nuts, and grains, sold for this use under the trade name "ProFume."

In various team sports, upright posts, typically a pair, which form part of the demarcation of a goal line. Goalposts are typically joined by a crossbar and in some sports with a net or covered framework behind, which form an area or space into or through which players attempt to send the ball, puck, etc., as a means of scoring.
Any equipment or clothing used to play the game of table tennis.
Flexible inclined boards for springing from to increase the height of leaps in vaulting and tumbling exercises.
Human figures or dolls created to illustrate or promote specific fashions in clothing, textiles, and hair styling; especially popular from the 16th to the 18th century in Europe.
Thin, shaped strips of ivory, bone, wood, or plastic, or tapered sticks used in the game of jackstraws.

Devices of the 18th century for viewing "perspective view prints," which are pseudo-stereoscopic images. These table-top viewers consist of a wooden stand supporting a hinged mirror and lens, used to view a flat image placed on the table next to the stand. A perspective effect is created through a combination of image design and lens and mirror properties. Surviving examples are elegant and highly collectible pieces of mahogany furniture, designed for the drawing rooms of affluent homes.
Sleeveless knitted pullovers or buttoned garments worn over a shirt in the manner of a waistcoat or vest.
Loose, billowy skirts gathered at the waist and hem, resembling garments traditionally worn by the inhabitants of a harem.
Calf-length fashion pants with flared legs, inspired by the traditional garments worn by the cowboys of the South American pampas. For the baggy pants worn by South American cowboys, see "bombachas."
Japanese ankle-socks, usually of cotton, with a separate stall for the large toe, worn by both sexes. Often with a thick sole, and worn alone or with wooden clogs or 'geta.'

Wide collars, usually on coats or day wear in the style of coats, that lie around the shoulders, often tapering to the waist, resembling a stole. For wider, capelike collars, use "berthas." For neck liners of ecclesiastical stoles, use "stole collars (liners)."
A serpentinite from Ponsevera, Italy, near Genoa. It is usually green with white veins, the green ranging from light green to metallic green to bluish green.
Costume associated with or used by officiates of the rituals of public worship, especially of the Christian religion.

Vestments worn in some Eastern Orthodox churches as a sign of authority or rank. These are made from a stiff, lozenge-shaped or rectangular cloth, and hang on the right side of the body, below the waist. These may have a cross or other image embroidered on it, and are suspended at knee height by a ribbon attched to the girdle or shoulder.
Small umbrellas used as a sunshade or simply carried as a fashionable accessory.
Short coats for the upper body made in various forms and lengths, but usually no lower than the waist or upper hip; worn indoors or for light warmth and protection from the weather.
Cloths worn around the loins, often as the sole article of clothing in warm climates.
Strips of cloth passed from front to back between the legs, attached to and supported by a cord or band around the waist.
General term for cloths of varying form worn at the neck.
White cloth coverings for caps, incorporating a flap hanging over the neck. Worn by soldiers as sun protection.
Long, rectangular hairpins used to hold up and decorate hairstyles. Often decorated, either with figurative elements or with incised details.
Ornamental metal clasps that secure by tension the two ends of a necktie to a shirt front.
The variation of color produced by changes in intensity or value.
A group of micaceous clay minerals closely related to chlorite and montmorillonite; vermiculite is derived from the alteration of biotite and phlogopite in the zone of weathering.

Loose-fitting, long overcoats or cloaks with elbow-length, often detachable cape and close-fitting collar, may be belted; originally from Inverness, Scotland, and fashionable especially during the second half of the 19th century.

Style of men's suit consisting of either a matching ensemble composed of a single-breasted cutaway coat, vest and trousers, or a black single-breasted cutaway coat paired with striped trousers and a complementary vest. Morning suits were originally adopted by men in the early-19th century for wear during the morning hours when they would go riding. It gained popularity near the end of the century for morning and daytime business activities in addition to riding, supplanting the frock coat. Edward VII (1842-1910) popularized the acceptability of the morning suit for daytime formal occasions, which it has maintained to the present day.
Protective guards worn over or on the face, often made of transparent materials, usually plastic.
Bodices worn next to the body or under other bodices or garments.
One-piece garments combining a brassiere and a corset or girdle.
General term for ornaments of various types worn at or on a belt.
Arabic script similar to muhaqqaq, though smaller.
Projectiles provided with means for altering their direction after being launched, either by remote control or as directed by equipment carried in the weapon.
Mechanisms that use rotating helical screw blades used to move or dislodge materials for food processing.

Percussion instruments found worldwide in a variety of forms, consisting basically of a set of two or more tuned bars of wood, bamboo, or synthetic material, supported at two nodes of vibration and struck with sticks or hammers; resonators are often included, either for each individual key or for all keys as a set.

Chromatic horns developed in the 19th century, incorporating several different lengths of tubing in the form of fixed crooks and various devices such as plungers, sliding shutters, and valves to bring any desired tube length into play.

Long, coatlike garments, fastened at the waist with a sash, having extra long sleeves.Originally men's garments worn in Turkey and other eastern countries, but later became fashionable garments for men and women in the west.
Loose-fitting unisex pullover shirts derived from African design and made from African fabrics or Africa-inpired fabrics. Dashikis became part of the wardrobe of black activists in the 1960s.

Machines used on dairy farms and in factories for separating and removing cream from whole milk, consisting of a centrifuge in the form of a rapidly revolving bowl containing a set of disks and mounted on a spindle. Milk enters the bowl at the top, and as the bowl revolves, the heavier skim milk  is thrown to the outer sides and led off through openings while the cream concentrates in the interior and is led off through a cream outlet at the center.

Knifelike utensils with one long straight edge shaped like a sharp-edged half-cylinder, or fitted with a friction-driven rotating brush inside a housing, used to remove crumbs from a tablecloth or similar surface.
Forks, smaller than a dinner fork, used for eating salad and generally having three or four tines.

Sharp knives in a place setting that are intended primarily for cutting meat and similar foods; usually having a serrated steel blade and often a handle of wood, bone, or plastic.The steak knife in modern usage will typically take the place of the normal dinner knife, although it may appear in addition to a duller dinner knife.
Spoons similar in size to teaspoons but having a bowl that tapers to a point and often a serrated edge; used to eat sliced grapefruit.
Utensils, usually designed as a pair of large spoons or forklike objects intended to grasp and serve salads onto plates while dining.

Culinary utensils or appliances having one or more beaters and used in mixing, beating, or creaming food. For tools used for blending food consisting of a container with a fixed propellerlike blade, use "food processors."
Small, sharp-pointed implements used for extracting the kernels from nuts.
Self-stick slips of note paper with a re-adherable adhesive strip on the back.
Devices used to mix malts and milkshakes, usually designed with a base that mounts a paddle at the end of a long shaft that can be immersed in a tall mixing vessel.

The distinctive book hands employed in the British Isles and occasionally on the Continent between the 6th and the 9th centuries, for some texts to the 13th century, and for Gaelic texts to the present day.
Long, broad textiles used as furniture coverings used either to protect surfaces or as decoration. Longer and wider than runners for furniture.
Any of several types of devices, such as horns, rattles, or clappers, used to make noise. Examples of usage is at celebrations or other public occasions such as sports events or political rallies.

Spool-shaped cylinders that rotate within music boxes. The cylinders have protruding pins in locations that correspond to the locations of notes on the “combs” of steel prongs, thus plucking the notes on the combs, which also correspond to specific, timed pieces of music played while the cylinders rotate.
Four voices or instruments, particularly when having four stringed instruments.

Plate armor for the lower legs, consisting of one contoured plate or two hinged together. Rare in Asia, they were worn in ancient Greece and Rome, and in the rest of Europe from the late 13th to the 17th century.

Garments worn on the torso as protection against bullets. Contemporary bulletproof vests commonly incorporate plates of steel, aluminum, fiberglass, or ceramic, or numerous layers of heavy-weave polymer fiber cloth.

Trademark name for a type of glass developed by Tiffany and Company with an iridescent surface simulating that of excavated ancient Roman glass; this effect was produced by spraying the surface of the glass while hot with metallic salts.
Describes musical instruments pitched lower than bass.  It does not exist for all families of instrument.
Bottles consisting of two flattened oval bottles joined at the base and with two curved necks pointed in opposite directions.
Novelties consisting of one or more items sealed inside a glass bottle. The earliest examples date from the 18th century and featured miniature ships inside.
Firearms having a rifled bore and designed to be fired by one person from the shoulder.
Artillery pieces having a rifled bore.

Historical military engines of various designs for discharging darts, stones, or other missiles. A typical design consists of a long upright arm with a spoon-shaped or slinglike holder to carry the projectile at the upper end.

Sports that includes running, walking, jumping, and throwing, usually on a running track and a grass field. Winners are those who complete the event in the shortest amount of time, throw the longest distance, among other parameters.
Card games in which players compete to collect four matching cards.

Board game for two players of East Asian origin, popular in China, Korea, and especially Japan. It is said to have originated in China about 4,000 years ago, and brought to Japan about 500 BCE. Traditionally, go is played with 181 black and 180 white, flat, round stones called go-ishi on a square, wooden board called a goban, checkered by 19 vertical lines and 19 horizontal lines to form 361 intersections. More recently it is played electronically. Each player takes turns, black moves first, conquering territory by completely enclosing vacant points with boundaries made of their own stones.

Books popular in the 18th and 19th centuries, originally often depicting harlequins, in which folded parts of pages are lifted to reveal new pictures, fitted neatly onto the remaining parts of the previous pictures.

Small emblems that are meant to be worn on the uniforms of firefighters that signify various aspects of service such as rank, years of service, etc. These may be customized to identify specific fire departments, mottos, or achievements.
Containers or devices that give out individual toothpicks.
Property of materials indicating solidity and firmness in substance or outline.

Loose-fitting garments for the upper body, often long-sleeved and collarless, of a soft, absorbent fabric such as cotton jersey, with ribbing at the collar, cuffs, and waistband. Made in pullover or cardigan style and sometimes hooded; often worn with sweat pants to form a sweat suit.
Dresses worn about the house, typically while doing cleaning. For similar garments functioning as dressing gowns, use "housecoats."

Any of various large- to medium-sized, horse-drawn vans or wagons designed to carry ice for sale on a street-delivery basis; generally enclosed boxlike vehicles, with roof overhangs, covered driver's seat, and platform springs.
Products meant to protect primarily wooden table surfaces from damage caused by spills, heat, scratches, and sunlight exposure. These may be used beneath tablecloths.
A lake pigment colorant made from archil.
Utensils, often of wood, consisting commonly of two pieces that are joined at one end or near one end by a pivot or spring, and that are used to retrieve hot toast from a toaster.
Inflated, leather-covered, laceless balls used in the game of volleyball and generally 26 to 27 inches in circumference.
Polymers containing relatively few monomers, usually less than five.

Recreational artifacts designed as amusements or diversions by presenting constructional difficulties to be solved by ingenuity or patient effort. For word or number diversions to be solved, see under "<word and number puzzles and games>."
Excerpts or short promotional works in any time-based media, particularly audio, that act as a preview of a longer broadcast.
Brief statements condensing substansive points in a longer document.

Texts having to do with devils, devil-lore, or the description or representation of devils. The term may refer to any representations in words or pictures of black magic or of dealings with the devil.
Works containing in a smaller document the substance or general principles of larger works, often serving as a supplement to the larger work.
Tall conical paper hats made to be worn by schoolchildren as a form of public humiliation for misbehavior or mistakes.
Footwear in which the uppers extend below the ankle joint, and that fastened to the foot with laces.

A thick-soled boot reaching to the middle of the leg, worn by huntsmen and men of upperclasses in ancient Greece and Rome, also by tragic actors in Athenian drama. They often took the form of calf-high laced boots, sometimes with a cork wedge to increase the wearer's height.
Chromatography in which glass plates coated with thin layers of alumina, silica gel, or cellulose are used as an adsorbent.
Locking or cutoff devices which, when applied, prevent accidental discharge of firearms.

Valancelike hangings at the front edge of an altar, often embroidered to match the altar frontal. For large superfrontals hung above and behind an altar and containing religious images, use "altarpieces."
Bronze drum-shaped vessels, often elaborately decorated with relief or free-standing animal figures, fashioned to contain cowrie-shell money in the ancient Dian kingdom of southwestern China.
Four-wheeled carriages of simple construction in which passengers sit astride a narrow bench extending between axles; found primarily in Russia.

Two-wheeled, one-horse, covered carriages originally having the driver's seat perched high on the roof, later with the seat set high at the rear and generally characterized by high wheels and low-hung bodies with easy front access for two passengers; distinguished from "cabriolets (carriages)" by the location of the driver and the much lower bodies.
Strips of fabric placed over the head of a swaddled baby and pinned to its shirt.  Intended to keep the head straight and to support the neck.
Short, barbed spears used in bullfighting.
Hats of varied form, usually tall, round, and pleated, of starched fabric or paper, worn by chefs. Different heights may indicate rank within a kitchen.
Covers worn on the fingernails. Examples include those worn by women on their fingers to protect their fingernailsl, in some cultures also used as a status symbol.
Devices used to suspend and release mines or torpedoes from aircraft.
Main structural members running for and aft along the bottom of a ship or boat, to which the frame of the vessel is attached.

Dutch cargo boats with full boughs, flat bottoms and shallow drafts, originally intended for the transport of goods on inland waterways and sometimes coastal shipping under sail, but now frequently fitted with engines and used as pleasurecraft or houseboats.
Wheeled vehicles used to assist with food service.
Bars used as levers, often made of wood and tipped with iron; typically used on board a ship for maneuvring heavy objects such as artillery.
Thin strips, as of whalebone, steel, or wood, worn in front of a corset or stays for stiffening.
Any of various garments, as loose blouses, jump suits, caftans, or sarongs, worn over a swimsuit, exercise clothing, or the like.
Small cards bearing the name, and sometimes the address of a person or married couple for presentation, as when formally calling or visiting.
Spheres surmounted by crosses, symbolizing kingly power and justice, sometimes held in the hand as part of regalia, or placed as an ornament on top of a scepter or crown.

Chinese long zithers of great antiquity, consisting of a slightly convex, shallow, lacquered box over the length of which are stretched seven silk strings of equal length, each twisted from a different, fixed number of threads. Thirteen discs of ivory or mother-of-pearl are inlaid along one edge to indicate the string divisions. They are traditionally the most honored of Chinese musical instruments, having strong associations with court and Confucian ritual, philosophy, and scholarship.
Very short mantles, often trimmed with lace or fringe.
Asphalt obtained from the refining of petroleum; the heavier or more viscous portions of certain crude oils are asphalts.
Long-sleeved shirts decorated with silk ribbons on the front and sleeves, commonly worn by Native North American men. Often worn at powwows and other important events.

Closely fitting helmets with visor, bevor, and often gorget plates, enclosing the head and face; all main elements work on a common set of pivots at the temples. They were widely used from the 16th to the mid-17th century.
Toys with an educational or teaching component.
Toys with moving or mechanical parts set in motion as sand passes through them.
Metal goads attached to a rider's boot heels, used to drive the horse on.

Collapsible shading devices made of a series of cane half-hoops covered with silk and attached to the front of a woman's bonnet that provide protection from the sun; worn especially in the British Isles during the mid-19th century. In Scotland, may also refer to entire protective bonnets made of cotton stretched over half-hoops.

Accessories or main garments used to fill in the open or low-cut bodices of dresses or worn under jackets, made of fine material and with or without sleeves; worn especially from the 19th to the early 20th century. For narrow pieces of cloth worn especially during the 17th to the early 19th century, use "tuckers."
Signs that call attention to conditions that are potentially hazardous.
Books issued in paper covers, having adhesive bindings and covers most often of heavier stock than the book's leaves.
Books which have had imperfections, such as missing leaves, made good by the insertion of portions from copies of similar editions.
Bindings that combine two or more books into a single unit.
Bookbindings that use cloth, generally wrapping a board cover.

Large inflated or stuffed bags, usually of leather and suspended from a horizontal board, to be hit with fists to strengthen arm and shoulder muscles and practice specific boxing or martial arts moves.

A toy car is a toy in the form of a car that is specially made for children to play with. They are rarely scaled and show less detail. Toy cars can come in a variety of sizes and materials, from wood to plastic. For small cars that are true to life and with great detail, use miniature cars.
Boats that convey pilots to and from large ships.
Shallow-draft vessels for passage on rivers.
Coastal transport and trading vessels of the Mediterranean, lateen-rigged on one or two masts and also having oars.
Describes textiles that are printed or stamped.
A finish containing resins, also called durable press, applied to fabric to stabilize its shape and make it crease-resistant. By extension, fabrics so finished.

Nations whose residents, or some portion thereof, exercise self-government and hold sovereignty over their territory. Examples are the nations listed by the United Nations as having undisputed sovereignty.
In the context of international relations, states controlling the foreign relations of a vassal state, but allowing it sovereign authority of its internal affairs.
Landed estates or groups of estates belonging to a military religious order of knights and placed under the charge of a member of the order, titled a commander.
New England watercraft, usually of colonial or later date, having raking posts, moderate to fine ends, and bulwarks that extend outside and abaft the head of the sternpost in a pink stern.
Watercraft designed primarily for use in warfare, either in combat operations or to provide services and support for such operations.
Large, Byzantine two-banked galleys, with one or two sails and usually equipped with flamethrowers for use with Greek fire.
Continuous strands, either single or compound, made from filaments of fiber by reeling, spinning, twisting, or throwing.

Ritual African cloth associated with the men's association known as Ekpe found among the Igbo and other peoples of the Cross River region of southern Nigeria. Indigo dyed and covered with symbols, including nsibidi, it is usually worn as a wrapper and is the prerogative of the highest grade of Ekpe.

Medieval Mudéjar textile type, a two sided non-reversible silk fabric with a herringbone twill ground with patterned motifs such as lozenge shapes, fleurs-de-lis, or lions. It is a complex silk weave with one warp system and two equal weft systems. Cloth of Aresta is preserved in many European churches as well as Las Huelgas, Burgos.

Textile having a weave structure that involves more than two sets of elements. Examples would be one or more warp sets, plus two or more weft sets, which are manipulated through different pathways to create a pattern.
Removing unwanted tanning by-products from tanned skins or hides.
The process of marking a surface with a monogram.

Applied decorative works made of cast paste or gesso applied to wooden moldings. Use pastiglia for works designed using the application of a mould. For works designed using free-hand brush application, use "aggetti."
Those engaged in the methodical breeding of cattle, for sale, farming or scientific purposes.
In some textiles woven on simple equipment, the transverse edge closed by warp loops. It resembles a true selvage and may occur at one or both ends of the textile.
Synthetic yarn that will stretch under tension and contract when released; usually made from thermoplastic filaments, and used especially for hosiery.
Woven textile, usually brocaded, incorporating flat metallic thread, often gold or silver.
The condition of being firmly fixed in a surrounding mass of some solid material.
The placing of lath in forming walls, or other building elements.
Removing dirt, surface coatings, accretions, discolorations, or other undesired matter from a substrate.
Process of becoming brittle; includes the loss of flexibilty or elasticity.
The separation of small pieces or fragments from an object or surface. May refer to accidental activity or process, or to intentional activity, as with the making of arrowheads.
Spoons designed to serve soup, stews, or similar dishes from a porringer, which is a small bowl or basin, typically with a handle.
Wide forks with short tines, often having between five and seven tines, used to serve sardines.

Chrome-tanned calf traditionally dyed brown and boarded in one direction head to tail to produce the characteristic long pattern termed 'willow.' Distinct from "box calf" which is usually dyed black and is boarded in two directions to produce a rectangularly crossed pattern.
Land-based, wheeled, military transport equipment; does not include aircraft, spacecraft, or watercraft.

Wagons, originally horse- or mule-drawn and later motorized, usually square-box in shape with a detachable top or trap-door at the rear which may be used as a luggage rack. Used for passengers or cargo.

Hand-operated utility vehicles usually fitted with a shallow, open receptacle, a wheel or wheels in front, and two unwheeled supports in back and lifted and pushed using two horizontal shafts extending outward from the rear.

Boards used for recreational snow sports, first developed in the 1960s. These are long narrow boards, most often with upturned ends, and fitted with transverse bindings for boots, on which the rider coasts down slopes of snow in a modified form of snow skiing, but with performance elements that evolved from skateboarding and surfing.

Narrow triple pleats having a center stitch drawn tight to make a pinched waist, pressed flat and produced at regular intervals in a row. For triple pleats which are not pressed flat, use "French pleats."

Enclosed, boxlike vehicles with high sides originally intended for carrying light cargo or for trade use; motorized versions often have side and rear doors and may have seating for passengers; generally the driver, passengers, and cargo are all enclosed within the body. Use "panel trucks" for light delivery vehicles with high sides in which the driver's cab is separate from the cargo space.

Durable twill, of worsted or with the warp of worsted and the weft of another wool yarn, with a clear finish and a flat diagonal rib; often used for tailored garments such as suits, coats, and dresses.
A thick warp inserted into a textile to produce relief and give added weight.
A thick weft inserted into a textile to produce relief and give added weight.
A dull, discolored surface film caused by chemical deterioration, such as the film of silver sulfide that commonly forms on silver.

The condition characterized by a total depletion in the level of oxygen or an oxygen level at or below 0.1%. Absence of oxygen in atmospheric or aquatic environments normally results in the death of living organisms. In a conservation context, anoxia may be deliberately induced as a means of insect control, by sealing objects in oxygen-free environments that are then purged with non-oxygen gas. For a low oxygen condition, use "hypoxia." For a medical condition characterized by lack of oxygen in the blood, use "anoxemia."

Length of a straight line measured downward from a plane or surface, or inward from a plane or surface. For the measurement or extension through or between opposite surfaces, prefer "thickness," although usage overlaps.

In Indian architecture, a tiered, pyramidal roof-type; wedge; tiered pyramidal superstructure; tiered pyramidal roof invariably crowned with Brahmacchanda śikhara (Upper Drāviḍades) or fluted ghaṇṭā (northern India).
Being more ample or extensive than usual in quantity, spatial extent, or transverse dimensions.
Sets comprising a ewer and basin, particularly such sets intended to wash hands at table. The items may be composed of fine porcelain or silver plate.

Attribute or physical configuration where sides or edges converge or meet, forming angular extremities or projections. Examples are the walls of a building, the sides of a box, the angular meeting of boundaries on a map, or the angular formation of a natural physical feature.
Attribute of something reaching the floor, often drapery or clothing.
Form of football played between two fifteen member teams, where players may carry the ball, block with hands and arms, and tackle, and is characterized by continuous play and no substitute players.

Singles or doubles game played in a four-walled court with a long-handled strung racket and a small rubber ball. The game is played on the same principle as rackets, but in a smaller court and using a softer, slower ball.

The ability of a material or object to resist mechanical wear or decay and to last over time. With regard to long-term situations or to nonmechanical properties existing over a long period of time without significant change, prefer "permanence."
A type of Dutch gilded frame with elaborate relieflike decorations in either an Auricular or naturalistic style or both. Named after the 17th-century silversmith Johannes Lutma.
Framing for two-dimensional visual works; picture frames may or many not use glass to protect the work, depending upon the type of work framed.
Natural horns played with the player's hand in the bell.
Zitherlike chordophones of the low countries and Scandinavia. Their frets are under the strings, which are plucked with a plectrum.
Wooden rods 1 inch square and 10 feet long marked along the length into feet and inches; used by builders and carpenters.
Method of ionizing atoms with low ionization potentials for use in mass spectrometry by contact with the heated surface of a metal.
Any of various objects consisting usually of a seat or seats suspended from above, by ropes, chains, or poles, so as to swing freely, and designed for recreation, as those found in playgrounds.

Two-dimensional figures that can be dressed in corresponding garments, intended for children's play. These are most often made of paper or cardboard, but may be made of other materials, such as vinyl.

Large lutelike instruments, popular in Europe from about 1590 to 1655, with six double courses of stopped strings over the fingerboard and eight unstopped bass strings, about twice the length of the stopped strings, to accomodate which the neck is greatly extended beyond the pegbox of the stopped strings. Its primary use was to accompany the solo singing voice.

Family of plucked lutelike chordophones with a fingerboard, pegbox, and rounded body, which is either carved from a single block of wood merging smoothly into the neck and pegbox, or is built up in a lutelike construction.

French stools with folding crossed legs; distinct from "tabourets" which have fixed upright legs, and used in domestic environments. For folding stools with ecclesiastical origins generally, use "faldstools." For folding chairs used by bishops or other prelates in the chancel of a church, use "faldistories."
A traditional Québequois weaving technique that uses old cloth torn into rag strips as weft; used to create textiles for either beds or floors.
An iron process largely used for reproducing technical drawings; produces an image in black. The image is developed out with gallic acid and is fixed by washing in water.
Parts or components of costumes.
Refers to systems that gather or manipulate geographic information.

The process of converting data into code, to conceal information or prevent unauthorized access. May be used to refer to schemes for this purpose in print or electronically transmitted, but is increasingly used to refer to digitized, or computer data.
Buildings housing museums that primarily house weapons, armor, uniforms, ammunition, documents, maps, photographs, and other records and artifacts of military forces, leaders, wars, and battles.
Textile made from silk fibers produced by wild silk worms. Given that the fibers are usually brown in color, the textile, when dyed, is typically dyed dark colors.

Refers to the art and culture associated with the Islamic Berber dynasty that ruled in North Africa and southern Spain (1130-1269). This period is notable because it was the first time the whole Maghrib was united under one dynasty. The Almohads rose up against the Almoravids in 1121 and conquered Marrakesh in 1147. The dynasty declined in power when it was defeated by Alfonso VIII in 1212, losing Andalusia, and in 1269 when they lost Marrakesh to the Berber Marinids. The Almohad courts at Marrakesh and Seville were centers of Islamic art and learning, especially philosophy. Almohad architecture is known for its juxtaposition of puritanically simple design with ornate decoration. Enormous congregational mosques were built in Seville, Rabat and Marrakesh. Simple interiors are relieved by voluptuous, lobed arches and other details. Repetitive use of an architectural unit such as an arcade or bay to create directed vistas and a deep sense of space is another typical feature. Austere exteriors strongly contrast with the richly decorated, gigantic square minarets (late 12th century) of the three mosques. These minarets are elaborately fenestrated and each face has different latticed designs done in raised stonework. The mosque of Tinmal, with its characteristically Maghribi T-shape, is considered to be an Almohad masterpiece. The location of the minaret behind the mihrab is an important innovation at Tinmal. Almohad mosques tend to be enlarged at the expense of their courtyards. Other arts such as bookmaking, metalwork, and luxury textiles flourished as well. Several copies of the Koran reveal that paper began to replace parchment during this period. A binding on a magnificent multi-volume Koran (1256) is the earliest dated example of gold tooling. Textiles, like bookbindings, show a taste for geometric patterns.
Movement and style, particularly in Egypt, when rulers commissioned grand architectural projects and other fine artworks were produced.

Style of textiles, particularly floor coverings, handwoven in imperial workshops founded late in the 19th century at Hereke, Turkey, east of Istanbul. Large carpets and prayer rugs with pile of wool or silk were for palace use and for gifts presented by the sultan. Antique carpets of various kinds were copied or patterns were created following Western fashions. Usually a tiny cartouche hidden in the design identifies the carpet's origin.
People skilled in magic and the occult arts.
Fast, labored breathing.
The work or industry of capturing, killing, and rendering whales.

Game played by two teams, usually of six per side, in which players use their hands to bat a ball back and forth over a high net, trying to make the ball land in the opponents' court area before it can be returned. A team is allowed to touch the ball only three times ball before it must be returned over the net.
Activity or process of moving to and inhabiting an area as colonists or new-comers; the act of peopling or colonizing an area.
Textile process involving twisting two or more active strands of the same set together as they interlace with another set of strands laid in parallel.
Post WWII, Eastman Kodak introduced verifax copiers intended as an office reprographic tool. The process produced poor quality reproductions that were prone to fading, and required special paper.

Archival groups are aggregates of items that share a common provenance. Archival groups may range in size from several thousand items (e.g., the entire body of drawings, models, and written documents from an architect's office) to just a few items (e.g., a handful of surviving drawings from one architectural project). Group-level cataloging focuses on the description of coherent, collective bodies of works. The description emphasizes the characteristics of the group as a whole, and highlights the unique and distinctive characteristics of the most important works in the group. Groups are usually defined by repositories, and may have several subgroups that are established by archival principles of provenance. The catalog record for a group normally corresponds to a physical group as it currently exists and is stored by the repository; however, historical groups may also be described. Groups may be divided into subgroups.
Sets or ensembles of visual works.
Rounded, cuplike, hollow parts of objects, such as the body of a stemmed vessel or the part of a pipe in which tobacco is burned.
The process of shaping glass by blowing air through a blowpipe into a glob of molten glass and forming it with tongs and shears or by rolling it against a hard surface.

Refers to female monarchs and rulers of kingdoms, which are major territorial units or governments ruled by a single person. Queens may also be the wives or widows of kings. For male monarchs who rule a kingdom, use "kings."
Formal daytime dress for men; also, during the 19th century, women's dress appropriate for wear in the morning.
People employed to keep watch or stand guard.
People who consign or receive goods for transportation.
Concepts that deal with the study of human society.
Various techniques of manipulating images in a computer environment, whether by program or by adjusting individual pixels or areas of the image.
Articles or physical resources designed and utilized for animals that perform tasks that aid human labor or activities.
Subordinate officers in a Christian church who assist priests or ministers in administrative, financial, and pastoral duties. In many churches, deaconesses are a separate order of parish assistants.
Sovereign dukes of certain Continental European states called grand duchies, also the sons or grandsons in the male line of the Czars of imperial Russia; ranking immediately below kings.

Noblewomen in Europe and Japan, specifically those of the second rank of the nobility of various European countries, or the wives or widows of marquises, ranking immediately below duchesses and above countesses.
Powders, lotion, lipstick, rouge, or other preparations to be applied to the human body for the beautifying, preserving, or altering the appearance of a person.
Smoking equipment used for cleaning the inside of pipes and usually consisting of flexible wire over which tufted fabric is twisted.
Devices that contain magnifying lenses arranged for viewing engravings, photographs, etc.
General term for sets of utensils for use when dining at table, particularly for formal dining; may include silver plate items as well as porcelain.
Small pillows placed on a chair, couch, or other furniture, primarily for decoration.
The provinces or jurisdictions of a patriarch.

Designation given to certain regions within a nation that have a degree of independence, administer their own affairs, or are otherwise self-governing to some degree. The precise definition of "autonomous region" varies from nation to nation, and is typically assigned to the region by the nation, rather than being assigned by an outside body. Examples of autonomous regions are in China, Finland, Papua New Guinea, India, Iraq, Italy, Mexico, Greece, the Philippines, and several other places.
Metal devices consisting of dovetail tenons; used to hoist heavy units of masonry.

Decorated fans in the form of a disk or other shape made from precious feathers, metal, leather, parchment, or silk, mounted on a pole or handle, and used to keep flies and other insects away from liturgical sacrifices. They were first used in pre-Christian sacrifices and were then taken up by the Early Christians. Use was continued in the Latin Church to about the 14th century, and in the Greek Church to the present day. Flabelli in the shape of a fan, later morphing into an umbrella or canopy, were also used historically to designate the ranks of bishops and princes in ceremonies. Two fans of this kind are used at the Vatican whenever the Pope is carried in state.
Black-figure kylikes characterized by the shape of their handles which resemble wishbones.

In bookbinding, the process of sewing and shaping the spine of a sewn textblock, whereby the back edges of the gatherings are splayed outwards from the center of the back, thus shaping a ridge or shoulder on each side; it is done at the same time as or just after rounding.
Those who play the violin.
Territories, usually non-self-governing, that lie outside the borders of the nation to which they are bound, but typically not so distant as overseas territories
Program-controlled devices that read data from or write data onto a magnetic tape which moves past a read-write head.
Secondary surfaces on which works, often drawings, photographs, or other works on paper supports, are pasted, taped, or otherwise attached.
Those who engage in the sport of fencing.
Any of various devices used to assure that successive printing plates or blocks for the same image are positioned accurately.
Parts or components of photographs.
Feet on carved furniture legs that flare out and flatten, resembling the tip of a shoe or hoof.
Rounded or spherical projections onto which curtain tiebacks can be affixed.
Small household items valued as curiosities or rarities, particularly articles of this kind from China, Japan, and elsewhere in the Far East.

Pieces of bread that are consecrated and form one of the principle elements of the Christian eucharistic sacrament. In modern western rites, the hosts are often thin wafers of unleavened bread. Most eastern churches use leavened bread. Early in Christian history, loaves of bread and wine for the eucharistic sacrifice were brought to the altar by the faithful, each contributing his or her share. Eventually, the hosts were prepared under controlled conditions, assuming a round form of moderate thickness, often stamped with a cross or another significant religious emblem. In modern western rites, hosts are often so thin as to be wafer-like. The term "host" derives from Latin "hostia," meaning the victim or host for a sacrifice, which is symbolized by the consecration of the bread.

Broadly, ceremonial objects that retain their sacredness in their present context.  Sometimes defined more narrowly as only those needed by a present-day culture to practice their religion. For objects that are used primarily for a religious ceremony or function, but are not necessarily in themselves considered sacred, use "religious objects."
