The rectangular pieces, usually metal, having on one side a letter or other character, from which text is composed and set to be printed. For sets of printed characters that share certain characteristics of style or design, use "typefaces."
Sharp steel points mounted in holders used to scratch crayon or tusche drawings on the lithographic stone in order to create white-line effects in the print.

Seen in the Yingzao fashi (1103 CE), specifically in the text (Chapter 14) and plates (Chapter 34) concerning the polychrome painting works (caihuazuo 彩畫作), yingzuo refers to images of bracket-blocks (sometimes emerging from painted lotus blossoms) with a “neck” and two “feet” (sometimes decorated with floral motifs), painted on the wall surface above the forehead tie beams (eshangbi 額上壁 or gongyanbi 栱眼壁).In current art historical and archaeological scholarship, the term has a broader meaning that described in the Yingzao fashi, and is often used to describe painted representations of timber-framed architecture, such as that found in tombs, cave temples, and reliquary chambers.
Hairstyles worn on the face.
Describes works created by the African peoples living in the region of the Lower Niger River, including the Delta.
Skin of sheep converted to leather from treatment with ingredients found in vegetable matter.
Cattle- or horse-hide leather, one side of which is covered with a flexible waterproof film having a lustrous and highly glazed surface produced by successive coats of daub, varnish, and lacquer.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Mokango is a singular form; Bakango is a plural form.
Bookbinding tools used to make holes in the spinefolds of books in order for them to be sewn.
Videotape recorders which may either be reel-to-reel recorders, or cassette recorders.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the ethnic group of the same name, a subgroup of the Mongo living in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Style and culture of the people of Burundi.
Businesses that specialize in calligraphic works, which are works composed primarily of beautiful, elegant letters or flourishes.
Stands upon which microphones may be mounted for performance or recording.
Hand held, flat objects used to produce a flow of air, usually for the purpose of cooling oneself.
Fabric sleeves slipped over shoulder straps on military uniforms that bear insignias of rank or service division. For similar objects made of stiffened material, use 'shoulder boards.'

Residential or commercial building developments purchased or built with the purpose of reselling or renting, having no confirmed buyers but speculating that there will be need or interest in the properties.

Military belts of heavy cotton woven fabric with metal fittings to carry equipment in the field, introduced during the First World War and later adapted for civilian use. Also, light cotton belts worn at the waist under military tunics or sashes to which sword slings may be attached, introduced around 1900.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Madagascar.
Painters who use their feet to manipulate brushes or other tools to make paintings, due to paralysis or other loss of conventional use of limbs or hands.
Masquerades of the Lunda, Luvale, Chowke, Mbunda, Bakangala, and Luchazi peoples of Africa associated with the circumcision ceremony Mukanda.
Sets of comestibles that have had the water removed from them so as to preserve and reduce their bulk. These constitute full meals that can be reconstituted when needed.
Tools used to shape or smooth the rough edges of the hooves of farm animals after trimming.

Straps with looped ends that are components of bridles attached to the headpiece. These are mounted on a horse's forehead between eyes and ears so that the bridle remains secure. Brow bands may also be decorative.
Rugs designed specifically to be used under or on top of a saddle.
Small replicas of objects signifying an honor bestowed upon an individual; usually worn on the person. These correspond to an original honor decoration and are used on certain occasions and uniforms.
Extinct order of order of amphibians characterized by a spool-shaped bony cylinder around the notochord. Dates to the Lower Pennsylvanian to Middle Permian.

Breed of dog that originated in China, and was introduced to England by Dutch traders at the end of the 17th century. The pug has a short muzzle, a black mask on the face, tightly curled tail, large head with prominent, dark eyes, and small, drooping ears. At maturity, it stands 10 to 11 inches (25.5 to 28 cm) and weighs about 14 to 18 pounds (6 to 8 kg). Its coat is short and glossy with the color ranging from apricot or silver fawn to black. In art, the pug can be found alongside sitters in portrait paintings, and as porcelain objects.

Heavy draft-horse breed that is agile, powerful, mostly grey or black with a fine coat, clean-limbed, and docile. It originated in the Perche region of France. The breed probably stems from the Flemish 'great horse' of the Middle Ages; modified by Oriental blood to develop a coach-horse type, it was changed again in the 19th century by introduction of draft-type blood to produce animals for heavy farm work.

Order of cephalopods containing only one extant member; considered to be a possible connecting link between the Teuthida and the Octopoda. They are purplish-black gelatinous animals with one or two pairs of paddle-shaped fins at various stages of growth; they have eight arms and two small retractile filaments.
Animals that typically feed on prey that has already been killed by another animal or that has died by accident or natural causes.
Baby goats.
Sweet comprising an almond with a hard coating of sugar or icing.
In poetry, units comprising four lines of verse.
Lyric poems of exalted emotion devoted to the praise or celebration of its subject; often employing complex or irregular metrical form.
The complete physical forms of humans and other animals. Includes the outer appearance and constitution, as well as internal features, such as organs.

Professional fabricators participate in producing a finished product; they are responsible for a step or process, for the creation of parts, or for assembling parts into a finished product. In the creation of artworks, fabricators are artisans or other people involved with producing large or technically difficult artworks, where resources are required beyond an individual artist's to produce the work.
Shoes consisting essentially of a sole fastened to the foot by straps, strips, or cords.
Refers to the style and culture of the Crow or Apsáalooke, an indigenous people of North America who reside primarily in the present-day state of Montana.

Devices, both mechanized and manual, used to weave geometric and regular pattern sequences at a rapid rate by utilizing a dobby mechanism to control the warp threads. Similar to, but distinct from, Jacquard looms, these floor looms comprise a series of lattices into which pegs are inserted to facilitate the lifting of heald shafts in accordance with pre-established patterns. While Jacquard looms lift individual warp threads, dobby looms incorporate dobby mechanisms to simultaneously lift shafts or sets of shafts.
Ceremonies formally admitting someone into a community, organization, or other group, or investing them with a particular role or status.
Moveable plates in stovepipes that control the flow of air to fire. A wide-open damper will increase the amount of air reaching the fire and improve combustion, or closed will starve the fire.

Hand-held devices consisting of square flags on two short poles used in a semaphore system for conveying information at a distance by means of visual signals. The flags are held in any of eight possible positions to signal letters of the alphabet and numbers.

The largest phylum in the animal kingdom; includes lobsters, crabs, spiders, insects, centipedes, and millipedes. Diverse in structure, lifestyle, and habitat, about 84 percent of the known species of animals are members of this phylum. Arthropds are characterized by the presence of a skeletal covering composed of chitin, a complex sugar, bound to protein. This nonliving exoskeleton is secreted by the underlying epidermis, similar to the skin of other animals. The body is usually segmented with jointed appendages, from which the name arthropod or "jointed feet" is derived.
General term referring to all aquatic invertebrates having an outer shell, especially those which humans eat.
Small objects meant to be affixed to clothing with an attached pin that advocate, advertise, or otherwise promote something such as a brand, musician, goods, or services.

Wheels located on the side of a sewing machine, designed to manually control the movement of the machine's take-up lever and needle bar, as well as move the fabric in the sewing machine from front to back. Used as an alternative to a sewing machine's foot pedal, these wheels offer more precise regulation of the needle, better ensuring that it will not break or get stuck in the fabric.

Flexible material made by bonding together two or more layers of materials with adhesive. For resin-impregnated laminate, such as paper or fabric, use "plastic laminate." For thin sheets of layered plastic, use "laminated plastic."
Traps of various designs used to capture insects or other arthropods for pest control or other purposes.

Devices that utilize emery-covered rollers, amongst other types of rollers, to clean and sharpen the wire teeth of the card clothing fitted to a carding machine. These devices are designed to restore sharpness and height uniformity to worn wire teeth, as well as to remove any waste stuck between the teeth.
Bicarbonate salt of the ammonium ion. Often used in baking as a leavening agent and as a cleaning agent in conservation.

Refers to the style, culture, and period of the Persianate Sunni Turkoman tribal confederation that ruled 1378-1503, under an Islamic dynasty in eastern Anatolia, Iran, and Iraq. Rising to power by supporting Timur, Akkoyunlu princes were patrons of architecture, metalwork and book arts.
Style of textile, particularly a type of coarse-woven carpet made in Maḥallāt and villages near Arak in Iran.

term: Persian textile styles after the Mongols
definition: Textile styles after the Mongols belonging to Persian cultures.
Salish blankets, done in twill and weft-twined tapestry weaves, worn by the aristocracy.
A style and culture of Greco-Bactrian Central Asia.

Web pages designed so that multiple users can add to or edit their content. Wikis are typically not monitored by a single editor: the community of users itself determines the veracity or trustworthiness of the information contained therein. Use of the term dates to 1995.
Knives with slender, flexible blades used to fillet fish.
Small cell-like shrines containing sacred images that are subsidiary components of some north Indian temples.
In Indian architecture, a adhiṣṭhāna type.
Interplanetary particles or chunks of stony or metallic matter that survive the passage through the Earth's atmosphere and strike the ground, or that strike any other planet.
Solid shaped pieces of transparent material which gather and select light rays reflected from a subject so that they enter the camera and form an image of that subject on the film.

Names that were used for an entity in the past, but are now no longer used; may include personal names, corporate body names, place names, or other names. For titles or names of works of art or architecture, prefer "former titles."
Educational institutions having facilities and programs that are closely connected with the life and needs of, and may be shared by, the whole community.
Small depressions, hollows, or valleys found in sandy terrain, caused by wind or wind erosion.

Large and varied class of vertebrate animals characterized by being warm-blooded, having mammary glands that secrete milk to feed the young, bearing live young (with few exceptins), hair (although it has largely disappeared in some adult animals, such as whales), a lower jaw that is hinged directly to the skull instead of through a separate bone (the quadrate) as in all other vertebrates, three tiny bones that transmit sound waves across the middle ear, a muscular diaphragm separating the heart and the lungs from the abdominal cavity, a left aortic arch, and mature red blood cells lacking a nucleus.
Chinese bronze ritual vessels of the Eastern Zhou used for holding water. Has a low, rounded, cauldron shape and no legs.
Extinct order of small lizard-like terrestrial reptiles dating to the Lower Permian to Upper Triassic.

Asiatic wild ass. Among other characteristics, it may be distinguished by the color, which is lighter than the African ass, ranging from reddish to yellow-gray. The term "kulan" is sometimes used to refer to this species, although it is often reserved for the race, Equus hemionus hemionus.
A unit or circuit that converts audio or video information to and from analog and digital form, for storage and use.
A platform-independent tagged file specification, or structure, that allows multimedia to be stored in a common format.

Hardware and software standard established in 1983 that provides both a physical means of interconnecting electronic musical instruments to each other and to computers, and the code to transmit data that controls variables such as notes, timbre, duration, velocity, and a variety of effects.
Natural underground water reservoirs in limestone sinkholes. Examples are in the Yucatán.
Members of a class of around ten orders of extinct fossil marine arthropods with a distinctive three-lobed, three-segmented form.
Members of this order are now under Rosales.

Order containing around 60 species of carnivorous marsupials in two families, plus the third recently extinct family of the Tasmanian wolf. Living memebers include the quolls, dunnarts, tnumbats, Tasmanian devils, and the recently extinct Thylacine (Tasmanian wolf).

Genus containing two living species of orangutans native to Indonesia and Malaysia; they are large hominids that are intelligent, primarily arboreal, having very long arms, reddish-brown hair, and having males that exhibit two modes of physical development, dominant males being flanged (with large cheek pads) and other males being unflanged. Flanged males hold and protect territory, while unflanged males look and behave more like juveniles and females.
Genus of one species of dog-like canid of Asia.

General term for members of four species of medium-sized canids found in Africa, Asia southeastern Europe, filling an ecological niche of predators of small to medium-sized animals, scavengers, and omnivores, similar to the coyote in North America.
Genus of four species, including the bobcat.

Proofs with the same printing elements as the edition, but they may differ because of the color variance, or added or deleted elements. Color trial proofs may have been pulled during the proofing period.

C-shaped metal bars (usually of copper or copper-alloy) of varying weights used as money in West Africa; originally imported from Europe, later alter cast (or re-cast) and used as a medium of exchange locally in West Africa.
Beads used as exchange media.

Describes the culture and style of the inhabitants of the Papuan Gulf. The peoples of the Papuan Gulf were well known for the agiba or skull shrines, which consisted of stylized anthropomorphic forms adorned with openwork and relief carving, and decorated with red, black, and white paint. The inhabitants of the Papuan Gulf produced a variety of masks and architecture, which varied from group to group.

A flint projectile point from the Stone Age, typically of triangular or leaf-shaped form, with a small projection at the base for the secure attachment to a wooden shaft and two kerfs of different depth and length.
Marbled paper where colors are mingled with a wired comb within the prepared bath, which produces "scallops" of colors, as opposed to "veins".

Screens, partitions, or railings serving to enclose or shut off a space in a building, particularly such structures located in a church, where they are designed to exclude nonworshippers from a chapel or shrine.
Ribs, usually decorative, located where a vaulted space abuts a wall.

Uncommon book format with 18 leaves and 36 pages, used in bookmaking from 1770-1840, but rarely used today. The most common method of creating the size is to fold a sheet in an accordian-fold, followed by an envelope fold, and a right angle fold.
Paper size, generally used in Great Britain, standardized at 22 or 22 1/2 inches by 30 inches.
Styles and cultures belonging to the Lake Chad region in Chad and northeastern Nigeria.
Distinctive ceremonial masks of the Chokwe people, in the form of an ideal of feminine beauty, including traditional scarification, but worn by men who also weare false breasts and a skirt.

Refers to works created in linen or another fabric on which a design is produced by drawing threads out of the body of a piece of material to create a mesh, and then stitches are worked on the mesh. It was highly developed in Italy and preceded the development of needle lace in the 16th century. It continued to be created in many nations, and commonly appears as a standard needlework type on embroidery samplers from the 17th century onward.

Refers to a work created by the process of sewing, which is the stitching, fastening, attaching, or joining together of layers or pieces of textiles, leather, or other materials by passing thread, cord, or other filament through the material by means of a needle or awl. It may also refer to materials intended to be sewn or to the stitches or seams of anything that is sewn.
Particles between 1 and 100 nanometers (nm) in size with a surrounding interfacial layer.

Refers to the Christian feast and festival observed on December 25 to celebrate the birth of Jesus Christ. Its observance is first documented in Rome in 336. The practice of celebrating on December 25 began in the 4th century in the Western church as a Christian replacement for the pagan festival held on the winter solstice to celebrate the birth of the unconquered sun. The East originally gave the date of January 6 for the nativity but the date of December 25 was generally accepted by the 5th century; the Armenian Church, however, still celebrates on January 6. Christmas took on the festivity (i.e. decorations and gift-giving) of the Roman Saturnalia and other pagan festivals of that time of year. Christmas has continued to accumulate traditions over the centuries; many of the customs associated with the holiday are of non-Christian origin. Evergreens, for example, are symbols of survival and have been associated with Christmas ever since the European Middle Ages. Christmas is traditionally regarded as a festival of the family and of children. In many countries presents are exchanged in the name of or in the spirit of the holiday's patron, Saint Nicholas, or Santa Claus.
In Hinduism and Buddhism, a type of profound meditation; the penultimate (seventh) stage of yoga.
Embroidery stitches consisting of satin and brick stitches, and arranged to form repeated zigzag or interlocking patterns of different colors.
In Indian architecture, a central stamenal tube of a ceiling.
Toxic or lethal substances used to kill insects.
In Indian architecture, a pavilion for Śiva’s sacred bull, Nandī.
Having the form or outline of an octagon, which is a plane figure with eight sides and eight angles.
Having the shape or form of a hemisphere, which is one of two portions of a sphere cut off by a plane through its center.

Filmed shots of various subjects stored in a film library and used in other productions. They tend to be general scenes such as busy street scenes, scenes which are difficult, costly, or impossible to replicate, such as of natural disasters or historic places and events, and, especially in the case of serials and television series, shots which are frequently used, such as shots of the ouside of a building the characters live or work in.

Film genre originally applied to plays with plots with moral issues where good versus evil were the main focus. Later, the films of D. W. Griffith, such as "Way Down East in (1920),  the personal and social problems of women are portrayed in particularly melodramatic way, and the emphasis become more on characters themselves. In films like Stella Dallas (1937) or Douglas Sirk's "All That Heaven Allows," the happy ending plot gives way to the female character sacrificing everything to a more noble cause.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting southwestern Ethiopia.

A beamhouse operation, following bating, in which dehaired hides and skins are soaked in or saturated with 12% salt and 1.2% sulfuric acid to either prepare them for chrome tanning, or to preserve them to be stored for later tanning. Distinct from "brining", which is the soaking of hides and skins in strong salt solution to cure them before transportation to tanneries.
Swords that play a part in public state or civic ceremonies or rituals, being variously worn, carried, or presented, as symbols of honor or power.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Ghana.

In linguistics, units of sound in a language that cannot be analysed into smaller linear units and that may distinguish one word from another. For example, element "p" in "tap" separates that word from "tab" and “tan."
Roman facing technique in which square-faced pyramidal stones are arranged in regular, net-like patterns over a concrete wall.
Book cloth grain pattern imitating the appearance of a diagonal beaded line.
Components of buckles: pins, often in metal, secured to the frame of the buckle, that passes through the holes in the belt in order to keep the belt secured.

Family containing 55 genera and more than 1,000 species of deciduous or evergreen shrubs and trees. The family is most common in the tropics and grows worldwide, except for New Zealand, and only a few species are found in Australia. Classification is disputed.

Species of hickory tree native to the United States; most abundant of the hickories and very long-lived, sometimes reaching 500 years in age. Used for hard, durable wood and for its bark to produce a color-fast dye, giving a dark yellow (cotton) to golden (wool) color using an alum mordant. With a chrome mordant, it will give a brass color to wool and cotton.

Species of medium-sized subtropical citrus tree known for its large, globular, bitter fruit. The grapefruit probably originated in Jamaica as a hybrid of C. grandis. It became well established as a fruit for home consumption in the islands of the West Indies before its culture spread to the American mainland.

Species of maple native to eastern North America, growing to 27 m (90 feet) in height and having leaves that turn bright red in autumn. It is known in many cultivars and often planted as an ornamental in cities, because it tolerates compact soil and urban pollution. The wood of the red maple is used in furniture, flooring, and veneer. The bark and leaves produce a dye that colors cotton and wool a cinnamon color with an alum mordant and a black color with an iron mordant. Syrup can be prepared from its sap. Seeds and shoots are food for squirrels, rabbits, and deer.

Species of medium-sized oak tree with a round crown native to the southeastern United States, but found from New York to Florida, Missouri, and Texas. It is a timber tree, and the bark is a source of tannin. It may occasionally form hybrids with other red oaks in the region.
Structures containing the seeds of a flowering plant.

Species of large coniferous evergreen tree native to the west coast of North America, growing to 70 m tall and capable of living 700 years or more. It is the largest living spruce species and among the largest trees in the world of any genus.
Genus containing 14 species of coniferous evergreen trees native to North America and central and eastern Asia.
Genus containing 3 species of deer.
Genus containing the pampas deer.

Large, complex genus of several hundred species of flowering shrubs, many of which produce edible fruit. The fruit is not a true berry; botanically it is termed an aggregate fruit, composed of small drupelets. The genus is believed to have existed as early as 36 million years ago.

Genus containing several species of perennial rhizomatous grasses known for their sweet scent; found in temperate regions in the Northern Hemisphere. In some classifications, Hierochloe is considered a section of the genus Anthoxanthum.

Detached, generally dense clouds and with sharp outlines that develop vertically in the form of rising mounds, domes or towers with bulging upper parts often resembling a cauliflower. The sunlit parts of these clouds are mostly brilliant white while their bases are relatively dark and horizontal.
Female superhuman persons or other beings who are worshipped and believed to have power over nature and the fortunes of mankind.
Genus of legume having 15 or more species.
Educational institutions having four-year programs of courses for the training of primary and secondary school teachers and granting bachelor's degrees and often advanced degrees.

Groups comprising a master metalworker and his or her assistants, who specialize in shaping things out of metal or of decorating with metal. For structures that contain industrial metalworking operations, use "metalworking plants."
Brush-written specimens of Chinese calligraphy. The term is also used to refer to rubbings of calligraphy from steles and woodblock prints of calligraphy.
Trademarked name for an acrylic resin used in solution as a consolidant and adhesive in painting conservation.
Refers to the style and culture of the Tsartlip First Nation, located on the Saanich peninsula on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.

Educational institutions that are either Hebrew-English day schools providing both secular and religious instruction, usually operated under Orthodox Jewish auspices, or schools providing training in Talmudic law and which may ordain rabbis. For educational institutions specifically devoted to the training of rabbis, use "rabbinical seminaries." For buildings that house day schools operated under Reform or Conservative Jewish auspices, use "Hebrew schools."

Generally refers to prisons for those convicted of major crimes. The term derives from the type of prison authorized by the British 1779 Penitentiary Act, enforcing strict discipline and hard labor intended to reform as well as punish. Given that, in modern systems, most prisons include reformatory or correctional functions, the original distinction is lost and the term "penitentiary" often refers to any "prison" in common usage. In the United States, penitentiaries are state or federal prisons that are reserved for the detention of convicted felons.
Species of alder native to west coastal North America.
The period between sunset and sunrise, especially the hours of darkness.

Species of pine known in several subspecies, growing as an evergreen shrub or tree, native to western North America. The name "contorta" refers to the twisted forms of some individuals growing at the coast.
Genus containing 60 to 70 species of aromatic evergreen trees or shrubs.

Software that, on a broad level, protects computer networks, personal computers, and other devices such as smartphones, from intrusion by outsiders. Some examples of this protection might be antivirus software, firewall software, encryption software, or VPN software.

General term for institutions overseeing facilities in which people accused or convicted of breaking the law may be confined and which may or may not attempt some form of reform or rehabilitative correction of offenders.
In Canada and the United States, libraries designated to receive all or selected government publications, with the provision that public access to the collections be provided.
Institutions that display collections focused on peoples, societies, and cultures.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of purple colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellowish green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of greenish gray colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of brown colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink colors.
Data type that represents a number or quantity denoting one or more whole things or units; a whole number or undivided quantity.
A range of brownish yellow colors resembling the color of bitumen, the organic, or hydrocarbon, portion of asphalt.
Refers to a range of gray colors resembling the color of the mineral, graphite.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
A range of brownish colors resembling the color of the synthetic iron oxide pigment known as "Mars brown."
Refers to a range of bright medium greens to dark bluish green colors resembling the color of emerald, a mineral used as a gemstone.
Variable purplish or reddish colors resembling the color of madder colorant, extracted from plant roots.
A range of purplish colors resembling the color of the synthetic iron oxide pigment known as "Mars violet."
A range of purplish red colors resembling the color of crimson lake colorant.

Family containing around 1,450 species of moths; many are native to the tropics, but species are found globally. They are distinguished by being moderate to large in size, having rapid, sustained flying ability, narrow wings and streamlined abdomens.

Family of around 900 species of beetles having mandibles (jaws) that are greatly developed in the male and resemble the antlers of a stag. In many species the elaborately branched and toothed mandibles may be as long as the beetle itself.

Style of architecture, interior design, furniture, or other works that evokes factories, machinery, or other elements of industry, particularly applicable when the work itself does not serve an industrial function. It is often nostalgic in sensibility, including elements of the turn-of-the-century industrial era or the mid-20th century factories, such as distressed wood, exposed bricks, building systems, industrial lighting fixtures, and exposed concrete.
Colors in a range of clear light blues, usually with little or no yellow overtone; so-named because it is often the color of clothes used for male infants.
The shell of the pearly nautilus, Nautilus macromphalus, native to the tropical Pacific and Indian Oceans, used to make decorative objects such as cups, salts, and jewelry, and as carving material.

Members of an order containing around 600 species of bony, oval-shaped, flattened fishes, such as the flounder, halibut, and turbot. In many species, both eyes lie on one side of the head, either the left eye or the right eye (depending upon species) having migrated through or around the head during development.

General term referring to members of several species in various families of Old World flycatchers and thrushes, having in common that they all frequently sing at night as well as during the day. The term has been used for well over 1,000 years.
Infraorder containing various species of lemurs.

General term referring to members of many species in the order Artiodactyla, including well-known large grazing mammals such as cattle, goats, sheep, deer, antelope, camels, and llamas. Ruminants digest food by regurgitating semi-digested cud to re-chew it in order to extract the maximum possible food value. Ruminants are often divided into suborders Ruminantia and Tylopoda. Other other large grazing mammals such as kangaroos and horses are not strictly ruminants, although they have similar adaptations for surviving on large quantities of low-grade food.
Family containing one species, characterized by being semi-aquatic, having prominent tusks, whiskers, great bulk, being relatively long-lived, and social.

Genus containing about 12 species and more than 50 recognized forms of graceful antelopes found on open plains and semideserts from Mongolia westward to the Atlantic coast of North Africa and throughout eastern and central tropical Africa. Three members of the genus Procapra are also commonly referred to as gazelles.
Members of an order of containing approximately 800 species of small primitive wingless insects, considered by some entomologists to have features similar to ancestral insects.
Drupes, or stone-fruits, from several trees of the genus Prunus. The plum usually has red, purple, or yellow skin, and when ripe, a powdery bloom.
Order of large, flightless birds having only four extant members, three species of cassowary and one species of emu.
Windsor armchairs with a low back that terminates at arm level and usually is comprised of a three-piece sawn arm rail that follows the outside curve of the seat.
Qualifier used for attributions of works by an unknown creator working with a named creator, where the relationship is between two peers rather than between a student and teacher.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 10,999 to 10,000 (or 11,000 to 10,001) Before Common Era.

Writing systems that use pictures and drawings having a communicative aim. These pictures and drawings (called pictographs) are usually considered to be a forerunner of true writing and are characterized by stereotyped execution and by omission of all details not necessary for the expression of the communication.
Dances of popular origin that may originate as ritual among inhabitants of a region and that are transmitted through generations.
Beverage comprising a bitter infusion made from yerba mate leaves, consumed as a stimulant; it is greenish in color, containing caffeine and tannin.

Based chiefly on the Attic dialect, Koine was a fairly uniform Hellenistic Greek spoken and written from the 4th century BCE until the time of the Byzantine emperor Justinian in the mid-6th century CE. Used in Greece, Macedonia, and the parts of Africa and the Middle East. The divergences of the Koine from Classical norms gave rise in the 1st century to a purist movement known as Atticism, which had little effect on the everyday spoken language although it influenced the written language, causing it to have archaizing tendencies.
Type of technical pen, having a trademarked brand name of a German company.
Family of languages spoken in western Brazil and Peru.
Points on the earth whose position has been determined by triangulation, typically marked by a concrete pillar.
The English language as spoken ca. 900-1066, it is the final stage of the English language leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the subsequent transition to Early Middle English.

Languages that developed in the middle of the 1st millennium BCE with Germanic tribes who lived in southern Scandinavia and northern Germany. Their expansions and migrations from the 2nd century BCE onward are largely recorded in history. The oldest Germanic language is the Gothic of the 4th century CE. Other languages include English, German, Dutch, Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, and Icelandic.
Variety of the Portuguese language used primarily in the nation of  São Tomé and Príncipe.
The condition, as it applies to optical phenomena and images in any medium or on any support, of being visually indistinct or hazy in outline or detail.
Biomes surrounding tundra environments, which occur in frost-molded landscapes, having extremely low temperatures, little precipitation, poor nutrients, and short growing seasons.
Devices used to create tones and tone combinations in the service of acoustic or psychological research.

Small sliding beads that were used to suspend the inro, tobacco pouches and money purses from the wearer's belt. These beads were made out of a variety of materials such as glass, bone, wood, lacquer, jade and ivory. They sometimes featured intricate carved designs or were carved into the shape of animals or human figures.
Underwater elevations, typically located on a shelf, covered by  relatively shallow water, but sufficient for safe surface navigation.
Artists who voice dissent, generally in response to politics or religion, often in a totalitarian state.
Features comprising communities of plants, whether natural or artificial.
Capital towns or cities for administrative states.
In a thersaurus, a so-called "narrower term" is a record to which another record or multiple records are superordinate in a hierarchy.
Terms or names that are used as coequal forms of access but not desingated as the "preferred term" in a given context.
Works of art or architecture that are depicted in another work of art. Examples would be a painting depicted in a reproductive print or an architectural work depicted in a drawing.

Pottery first created in the late 18th century by the merchant Numani Rozan near Kuwana in Ise and later continued inTokyo; now manufactured in and around Yojjaichi, Mie Prefecture. Productions typically include tea ceremony wares, dishes, bowls and candlesticks covered with a pale yellow milky glaze and decorated with a three-color design mostly of red, green and blue or purple.
Artists who specialize in creating art on billboards, which are large flat surfaces typically designed for advertisements and displayed in public areas.
The vice of excessive eating.
A very strong, controlling, or overpowering emotion or impulse, particularly lust, other desire, hate, or fear.
The Islamic culture and style of Syria.

Forms or varieties of a given language that are peculiar to a specific region and differ from the standard or literary form of the language regarding vocabulary, pronunciation, idiom, or other characteristics.

Refers to “elephant trunk” and represents one of the four Elirkai gestures, as defined according to texts dealing with śilpa (arts and crafts), known as śilpaśāstras. Comprised of hand gestures (hasta, mudrā or kai-amaiti), stances/poses (āsanas) and inflexions of the body (bhaṅgas). When the hand is stretched straight out, and the palm slopes downward from the wrist, with the fingers bent gracefully like tendrils on a creeper, this regal mudrā reminiscent of an elephant’s trunk, is called gaja-hasta.
Artists who create representations, often portraits, that exaggerate certain features or characteristics to humorous or ludicrous effect.
The action of clasping in one's arms, usually referring to one person holding another person as a sign of fondness or friendship.
Traveling about from place to place without a particular destination.
In Indian architecture, a base for Śiva’s phallic emblem; base of liṅga; pīṭhikā.
In theology, evil or unclean spirits. In Christian theology, includes Satan and other fallen angels.
Evening meals, typically light or informal meals. For more formal and substantial evening meals, use "dinners."
Units indicating one-thousandth of a second (usually a second of time, less often a second of arc).

Units of length in the imperial and United States customary systems of measurement, the twelfth part of a foot, 1/36 of a yard. Derived from the Old English ince, or ynce, and from the Latin unit uncia, one-twelfth of a Roman foot, or pes.
Measures of capacity for liquids and grain or other dry substances consisting of small particles equal to 1/8 gallon.
Units of weight, in Great Britain legally equal to 2240 lbs and in the United States and elsewhere, equal to 2000 lbs.

A colorless crystalline organic compound that is a product of protein metabolism in mammals. Urea can break hydrogen bonds and destabilize collagen. In conservation practice, this interaction reduces hardness and deformation in parchment, leather, and related materials.
Architectural models made to help clarify and visualize aspects of a project during the design process.

The prehistoric cultures of the regions surrounding the Danube river and beyond, particularly the agrarian societies in central and eastern Europe, from the Balkans to the Low Countries and the Paris Basin. In addition to establishing the distinctive pottery traditions of Linear Pottery culture, stroked pottery culture, and Rössen culture, the early phases of Danubian peoples cleared forests, cultivated fertile loess soils, kept domesticated cows, goats, pigs, sheep, and dogs.
Genus of flowering plant, the sap of which is used as medicine, insecticide, and for rubber.

Order containing more than 18,000 species of monocotyledons (flowering plants having a single seed leaf). The order consists of several lineages that have traditionally been recognized as groups, the members of which have often migrated from one group to another. The major groups included in Poales are the grass group (families Poaceae, Restionaceae, Anarthriaceae, Centrolepidaceae, Ecdeiocoleaceae, Flagellariaceae, and Joinvilleaceae), the cattail group (families Typhaceae and Sparganiaceae), and the sedge group (Juncaceae, Cyperaceae, and Thurniaceae). In addition, Poales includes families Xyridaceae, Eriocaulaceae, Bromeliaceae, Mayacaceae, and Rapateaceae.

Order containing 45 genera and about 1,100 species of flowering plants, which are distributed worldwide but centred mainly in the Northern Hemisphere. The delimitation of families in this order is currently disputed.
General term for legendary or mythical animals that combine features of multiple known animals.
Species of tree native to the northeastern United States, growing to 18 metres (59 feet) in height and having relatively large somewhat rounded, coarse-toothed leaves.
Genus of woody trees, shrubs, and vines that produce the skin-irritating oil urushiol, which can cause a severe allergic reaction and is used for lacquer.
Species of tree native to Central America.

Multistemmed shrub typically found in wet environments near ponds or streams. It may grow from 10 to 20 feet high, and has long branches with green or gray bark and long, narrow leaves. Native range extends from Europe to Asia, but is cultivated widely. The tough pliant branches are commonly used in basketwork.
A genus of palm having one species.
Brand name of a floor or grounds covering made of vinyl and nylon made to resemble turf. Used primarily on athletic playing fields and on outdoor patios.

Genus consisting of three species of deciduous trees and shrubs disjunct between eastern Asia (S. tzumu and S. randaiense) and eastern North America (S. albidum), and one extinct species.  They are commercially known for their fragrant oil that is used in perfumes, root beer, and tea. The soft, lightweight wood is used for lumber. A rose-brown to gray color textile dye with good color fastness is extracted from the wood.

Short-lived species of deciduous tree native to North America, ranging from Ontario to Nova Scotia, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey, with disjunct populations in Indiana, Virginia, and North Carolina. It prefers poor, dry upland soils, but is also found in moist mixed woodlands. It is a common pioneer species on abandoned fields and burned areas, thus the name "oldfield birch."Gray birch grows quickly to 7 to 9 m tall and 0.3 m trunk diameter
Genus containing around 350 species of herbs, shrubs, and trees native to warm temperate and tropical regions. Several are cultivated as ornamentals for their showy flowers.

Species of small deciduous tree native to the Middle East and South Asia, widely cultivated in Europe, east Africa and California. The fruit and oil from the sweet almond variety are used for food while the oil from the bitter almond variety is used for flavoring. Botanically, the fruit of the almond is not a true nut, but a drupe, consisting of an outer hull and a hard shell with the edible seed inside. Although the tree is grown commercially for its fruit and oils, the wood is also used. The water soluble gum that exudes from wounds on the tree has been mentioned as a watercolor binder. Almond trees are closely related to cherry trees.
Wood of the species Diospyros texana, native to Texas and Oklahoma in the United States, and northeastern Mexico. The sapwood is yellow, while the heartwood found in large trees is ebony black.
Species of Eucalyptus native to southeastern Australia, Tasmania, and Victoria. One of the tallest tree species in the world, reaching 100 meters (330 feet) in height.
Genus containing 5 species of trees in the mahogany family Meliaceae, native from Afghanistan south to India, and east to North Korea, Papua New Guinea and eastern Australia.
Large wooden containers bound by wood or metal hoops used for maturing whiskey. Different woods and treatments are used in these to impart a variety of flavors, as well as the re-use of the cask.
Patches of soft metal used to repair leaky pots.

Culinary appliances with interchangeable blades or other rotating tools within a closed container into which food is inserted for mixing, slicing, shredding, mincing or otherwise processing at various speeds.
Small pair of paddles for making butter into balls or other fancy shapes.
Insulated boxes in which milk bottles or cartons are left in home delivery.
Devices that treat grain for the maximum extraction of flour, and that may cool and air out grain in order to help preserve it, or introduce water and heat to separate constituent parts of the grain.
Devices of wood, metal, or plastic inserted into footwear to maintain their shape when they are not being worn.
Play and sports outfits made for women and children, often consisting of a one-piece suit combining shorts and shirt and an overskirt; introduced in the early 20th century.
Hand-held instruments for drafting in ink or other fluids.
Women's light dressing garments or negligée.
Large, strainer-like receptacles used for separating curd from whey in the process of cheese-making.

Devices that calculate or tabulate test scores. An early example was IBM’s “Test Scoring Machine” developed in 1928, which used the electrical conductivity of graphite pencil marks to interpret correct and incorrect answers.
Devices used to measure the average number of neps, or small entanglements/knots of fibres, in a fiber mass, as well as the average size of the neps.
Bookbinding machines into which books are fed for the casing-in or pasting of a book into its cover.
Tongs used to handle hot jars and lids during the process of home canning.
Containers used to carry personal gear. Some examples are suspended by a long strap worn over the shoulder, while others are worn on the back.
Instruments that determine the composition of gases contained in  carbonic oxide, hydrogen, etc.
Weapons that launch projectiles toward targets.

Telescopes, either reflecting or refracting, specifically made for observation of the features of the sun, including sunspots or prominences. They are often used in conjunction with coronographs or spectroheliographs.
Large hooks used to suspend meat carcasses.

Wutoumen refers to a type of elaborate gateway used in high ranking buildings through the Song dynasty, after which it declines in use. As we can tell from paintings and extant examples, the shape, size, and structure of wutoumen vary considerably. However, all wutoumen employ tall pillars flanking the gate. The name is likely derived from the black ceramic tube-shaped finials on the top of these tall gate posts (Cefu yuangui 冊府元龜, 1013). Detailed records of wutoumen exist in the Song dynasty Yingzao fashi (1103, Li 2009, 6.2a-4a).

Order of mostly of woody plants, consisting of 10 families, 338 genera, and about 6,000 species. The plants grow in various habitats throughout much of the world, and a number of members are important commercially.
Machines or devices used to mix components for a dental amalgam, which is a mixture of mercury with silver, tin, copper, and other trace metals.

Large sandstone blocks with holes for inserting a wooden stick, used in looms; the sticks are used to arrange warp threads when setting up a vertical loom. Examples of use are the Hopi and other southwestern Native Americans.
Elaborate orchestral compositions in three or more movements, originally developed from the operative overture similar in form to a sonata, but usually of grander scale and broader style.

Performing arts genre having to do with the combining of vocal or instrumental sounds in measured time to communicate emotions, ideas, or states of mind, usually according to cultural standards of rhythm, melody, and, in most Western music, harmony.
Method of acquiring funds or property through transference of ownership from one party to another as a free gift.

Building a coherent and reliable collection over a number of years by the selection and acquisition of material, and establishing criteria for decisions on the material to be included or excluded in that collection.

Describes the location change of an object in a collection, usually that of a museum,  from a safe place, or housing that is designed to take into account the unique needs of the object with a long range outlook for its health, to another, whether for temporary storage during a renovation or other practical reasons.
Meaning "released [by]," in publishing refers to the publisher.

Compound titles for a work that contain reference to both the part and the whole, or to two parts in a single title. In library cataloging, a collective title may be the title proper of a bibliographic item containing several works by one or more authors issued in a single volume or uniform set of volumes, each with its own title distinct from that of the whole. Also refers to the title assigned by a bibliographic cataloger to a group of separately published materials cataloged collectively.

Events demonstrating grateful or happy satisfaction or honor, marked by festivities, refraining from ordinary business, or other deviations from accustomed routine. For events serving specifically to call someone or something to remembrance, use "commemorations."
The standard unit of currency of Brazil.
In language, words that can function as a noun phrase when used by itself themselves or to someone or something mentioned elsewhere in the discourse.
Refers to the Caribbean language variety of Spanish spoken in Cuba.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 384-417; founded by people of Qiang ethnicity.

Numeric, alphanumeric, or other identifying codes assigned to an art object, book, or other item by the creator or producer of the work. The number is usually inscribed or otherwise marked on the work. For numbers assigned at the time of accession by an owner or repository, prefer "accession numbers."

Names for people, places, or things that are the fullest version of the name. For personal names, includes the first name, one or more middle names, one or more family names and last names, suffixes, and honorifics.
Appellations indicating honor or nobility, attaching to an individual or family rank, function, office, attainment, or the possession of or association with certain lands.

A Nahua military insignia of postclassic central Mexico formed from a compressed fan of quetzal feathers worn as a back device. It was part of dance and war costumes of rulers, and paired with the xicalcoliuhqui (stepped-fret) design chimalli (shield). This insignia also designated troops from the altepetl of Quiyahuiztlan in Tlaxcala.

The seventh month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendars, containing 31 days and falling between June and August. It was named after Julius Caesar in 44 bce. Its original name was Quintilis, Latin for the “fifth month,” indicating its position in the early Roman calendar.

The day following Friday and preceding Sunday, traditionally regarded as the seventh day of the week, but now frequently considered as the sixth, and, together with Sunday, forming the weekend. Name refers to the Roman Saturn’s-day.
Cookstoves fueled by wood, typically made of cast iron or sheet steel.
Calendar enumerating the seasonal round of ceremonies practiced by the Cherokee people, comprising 12 months and 13 cycles or phases of the moon.
Factory buildings in which ammunition is made.

Extremely small, metabolically inert microorganisms composed of a short strand of either DNA or RNA within a protein coat, and, in some, a surrounding envelope; they replicate only within the cells of living hosts, primarily plants, animals, and bacteria, taking over the nucleus and directing it to produce viral proteins and DNA or RNA. They frequently cause disease in their hosts. Viruses occupy a special taxonomic position: they are not plants, animals, or prokaryotic bacteria (single-cell organisms without defined nuclei), and they are generally placed in their own kingdom. In fact, viruses should not even be considered organisms, in the strictest sense, because they are not free-living, meaning they cannot reproduce and carry on metabolic processes without a host cell.
General term for names or other designations for political and geographic administrative entities.
Manually or electrically powered devices that punch small round holes in leather or cloth, and that set a reinforcing ring insert for laces, string, rope, rings, or the like to pass through.
Reverent petitions composed for presentation to a deity or other spiritual entity, whether orally or mentally expressed. For documents containing prayers, use "prayers(document genre)."

Chinese solar festival focused on honoring ancestors, that starts on the 15th day after the vernal equinox. It originated from the custom of offering sacrifices to ancestors; observances include the veneration of ancestors, honoring their teachings and virtues, sweeping their tombs, having picnics, and placing willow branches on doors. Ancestor worship flourished after the Tang Dynasty (618-907 CE). Because the date of the Qingming Festival was close to the Hanshi Festival (Cold Food Festival) and the Shangsi Festival (Double Third Festival), customs of these two festivals have been adopted in the retained in, Qingming Festival, including the banning of fire, eating raw food, sweeping tombs, and spring outings.
In Japanese printing, format having dimensions ca. 58.4 x 30.4 cm.
Visual works that are repurposed for use other than the original use. Examples are warehouses that are converted into dwellings.
That which is placed in position number seven of a sequence.
State or condition of existing or moving on the surface of the earth, as contrasted to in the air, heavens, or water.
Vases used to hold liquids used as libations at rituals of various cultures. Examples are found in Ancient Greece, Ancient Egypt, and elsewhere in the Middle East.

Figurative animal sculptures, often brightly colored and decorated with ornamental saddles and bridles; used in carousel amusement park rides. Includes a seat and a pole affixing the sculpture to the top and base of the carousel.
Small quantities of material kept as specimens to be referred to in a controlled environment.
Trimming consisting of small shiny objects, such as spangles, beads, or jewels, applied in loosely designed clusters on clothing or accessories.
Describes a location depicted in a visual work.
References to bibliographic sources, unpublished documents, or individual opinions that provides the basis for the information recorded.
Devices that burn flammable oils as fuel to create heat.
Objects for hanging or containing kitchen utensils while not in use.
Implements used to agitate lard during the process of rendering lard.
Tools for dispensing maple syrup.
Small lidded boxes made to hold clothing studs used for personal adornment.
Long clips that hold sheet music and scores in place.
Implements fastened to a belt or waistband, used for supporting the stationary knitting needle while knitting; usually made of wood or ivory and often carved.
Backdrops intended specifically to appear behind the subjects of photographs. These may be elaborately painted, or simply fields of texture or color, and appear in a variety of materials.
Tools used in offset printing, consisting of an illuminated flat surface with a light source built in or underneath. Used to treat photosensitive plates to prepare them for printing.
Simple vices, sometimes with protruding studs on the interior surfaces, designed as a torture instrument. The victim's thumbs or fingers were placed in the vice and slowly crushed.
Devices used to transfer yarn from bobbins to spools, or cylindrical tubes with rims at each end.
Pipes through which conversation can be conducted, such as between different rooms of a building.
Removable handles used to lift lids in a kitchen range or stove.

Mechanized devices designed to interweave three or more strands of yarn, wire, or other material to create complex braided structures such as rope, reinforced hose, power cords, and lace. While these devices can take many forms, they commonly comprise a central column and/or rotating disk around which carriers and bobbins are arranged. The device's carriers and bobbins move in a circular pattern, interlacing the strands of material. Though commonly used in the textile industry, these devices have various additional applications in the medical, aerospace, automotive, and electronics industries, amongst others.

Metal, often cast-iron inserts designed to fit fireplace openings. Some are made to provide an alternative to wood burning, with gas, electricity, coal, or other fuel. Others burn wood but increase heat efficiency. Historically these have appeared in a variety of forms, often ornamental.

Rooms or other relatively small places set aside for worship by an individual, family, or small group, where no public services are provided. A private chapel may be within the confines of a larger church, home, or other larger building; it may also be a free standing structure.
Refers to recesses, in effect chapels, used for preparation of the Eucharist by the clergy, and located on the north side of the bema in Greek churches.
The state or quality of having or being divided into six parts.
Toys where rings, blocks or other figures may be stacked on top of one other, often from large to small sizes consecutively. In this way babies and toddlers learn to stack and count.
The heart cut creates a diamonds or other gems shaped like the traditional symbol of love, an idealized heart. It is a so-called 'fancy cut'.

Describes a series of dances performed at Native North American powwows. While the schedules and type of dances performed change based on the host nation, most powwows consist of a set of core dances: Traditional/Straight Dance, Grass Dance, Fancy Dance, Jingle Dress Dance, Fancy Shawl Dance, and intertribals.

Malalikid is a major Sakizaya festival. Pre-ritual welcoming of the ancestral spirits such as minahanah practiced in the Maliyun tribe and padongi’ in the Sakur tribe is essential to the Salizaya way of worship. Other proceedings include visiting the mourning families and tribe forum foreground the importance of mapalaway i.e. the Salizaya priest. Another practice that distinguishes the Maliyun tribe in Ruisui Township from the Amis around Xiuguluan River is that they hold bihkac, a bird-catching ritual. In miliwliw, a ritual in which the Salizaya youth is summoned, shows how the social organization based on age class known as masaselal occupies a central place in collective mobilization in preparation for annual festivals.According to report of the Sakizaya scholar, Hong Qingyi (2008), members of the age class system are to gather rattan and butcher a hog to collect its liver and heart for ceremonial purposes. On the first day of the festival, men bring game and meet at dabek (men’s hall) for a purging dance; the welcoming of spirits and announcement take place in the morning on the following day, and all men are to have lunch with their age class fellows in a banquet. Guests are feasted on the third day with continuous singing and dancing. Finally, people go through pakelang (“collective fishing”) and group chat to reflect on the undertakings to mark the end of celebration and return to everyday life.
The seventh month of the French revolutionary calendar (introduced in 1793), lasting from 21 March to 19 April.

Cultures and styles of the Paiwan people lived in Taiwan. The Paiwan people primarily reside on the hills in Pingtung and Taitung. They used to be perceived as identical to the Rukai people. Paiwan contains two divisions, the Raval and the Butsul. The Paiwan society consists of a caste system ruled by aristocratic families, and the basic social unit is an “umaq” and its members. Maljeveq is Paiwan’s most renowned festival.
Tiles made of metal, generally copper, tin, aluminum, or stainless steel.
Period of the seventh city on the site of ancient Troy, ca. 1300-1050 BCE.
Devices used to manually wind early phonographs.
Suitable for, applicable to, or common to both males and females, not specifying gender.
In Indian architecture, an (inverted) dish-shaped maṇḍi-type; banner.
In Indian architecture, nāsī-front on of a pañjarakōṣṭha.
In Indian architecture, a ram-based column-type.
Cylindrical, flat-bottomed vessels that are used for ornamental purposes, not for drinking. Made of various materials, often with decoration.
Areas of land or water set apart for the protection of natural landscapes or wildlife, or for the rearing of game or fish; in some preserves, limited hunting is permitted.
Distinguished from "mobile home parks" by being only for the temporary parking of travel trailers, camping trailers, motor homes, or the like, for recreational purposes.
Monasteries or convents in pre-Islamic India; usually Brahmanical, sometimes Jaina.
Religious houses that rank immediately below abbeys and are presided over by a prior or prioress.
Usually electrically operated signals (as a system of colored lights) for warning and controlling traffic.
The narrowest portions of a chimney flue, between the gathering, or upward contraction above the fireplace, and the flue proper; often where the damper is located.
Rooms such as shelters, or other spaces specifically for protection from outside forces or elements.
Enclosed Roman courtyards with porticoes on all four sides.
In Indian architecture, a minor cyma-eave.
In Indian architecture, an arris moulding on pillar capital or in the  pīṭha; knife-edged moulding in a base.

The earliest known use of the term huagong 華栱, literally, “blossoming bracket-arms” (Kroll 2015, 167 (huā), 135) or “flower arms” (Fu 2017, 357), is in the Yingzao fashi (YZFS 4.2b-4.3a). As an architectural term, huagong refers to any bracket arm in the bracketing structure that projects away from the wall plane.
Architectural towers designed to allow a through flow of fresh air or to divert polluted air outdoors. They may employ wind turbines or use wind-induced natural ventilation.
Decorative mouldings, usually mass-produced, for placement above windows.
Those portions of jambs of an opening or recess which are visible from the face of the wall back to the frame or other structure which may be placed between the jambs.
Shutters having fixed slats that slope upwards from without, so as to exclude sun and rain, and admit air and some light. For similar shutters having movable slats, use "louvered shutters."
Arrangements of steps, rungs, or frameworks of bars and steps, contrived to allow passage of a person over or through a fence, while maintaining a barrier to the passage of sheep or cattle.
On a staircase, members which are fixed to the upper edge of a closed string to receive the balusters.
Solid steps, as those worked from one piece of stone, having more or less the section of a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse forming part of the sloping soffit of the flight.
General term for metal junctions between two edges.
Moldings enriched with egg-shaped ornaments alternating with dartlike ornaments.
In Indian architecture a 'neck' recess between mouldings; kāṇṭhi, kaṇṭi (Oriyā); recess in adhiṣṭhāna or upapīṭha.
In Indian architecture, a pilaster; bhittistambha; wall pilaster; engaged column.
Decorative members over a doorway or doorframe, such as pictures or carved panels.
In Indian architecture, a doorframe with jamb-divisions.
In Indian architecture, a projecting central part of ornate threshold (doorsill), usually round, rarely square.
Doors that are flush with and treated in the same manner as the surrounding wall so as to be concealed and have no visible hardware.

Barriers used to close sluices, which are artificial passages for water fitted with a valve or gate for stopping or regulating the flow. Often taking the form of a "wicket (architectural element)," which is a gate or door set into a larger gate or door.
Two windows, one outside the other, as storm windows, used to provide improved thermal and noise insulation.
Rafters directly along the valley, at the intersection of two sloping planes of a roof. Rafters directly along the valley, at the intersection of two sloping planes of a roof.
Freestanding exterior walls, generally of brick, having buttresses joined by curved walls, forming a scallop-shaped footprint.
Walls that are constructed to resist lateral loads, such as walls that hold back banks of earth.

Main fortified areas of Japanese castle complexes, literally "main circles", that contained the "tenshu". These areas were the most protected parts of the castle and, in some cases, were used as the residences of the castle owners during wartime.
In Indian architecture, a wall of the grīvā.

In Indian architecture, a square aedicula of prāsāda; spirelet; miniature kūṭāgāra; superstructure-type; square-domed aedicule; square aedicule of a Dravidian vimāna: of caturvarga, rarely ṣaḍvarga type.
In Indian architecture, a miniature cusped segment of ceiling; boar; decorative, semi-circular coffered ceiling course.

Refers to panels of oak or other wood that is used to line the walls of a room. It often refers specifically to the decorative or protective facings applied to the lower portion of an interior partition or wall, whether of wood or another material. The term originally referred to a superior quality of oak from Russia, Germany, and Holland, that was used primarily for fine panel-work.
In Indian architecture, a niche on the karṇa.
In Indian architecture, a mesh, lattice, screen; perforated window.
Designates roofs with one or more surfaces that have a pitch greater than 10 degrees from the horizontal.
Roofs with sloping sides but a substantial flat area on top. When such a roof is hipped, it will resemble a truncated pyramid.

Thin boards, usually wooden, that span the trusses and support the rest of the roof. Typically oriented face-grain (strength axis) perpendicular to the roof framing, providing maximum stiffness and load capacity.
Gables each side of which is multicurved.
In Indian architecture, a major spire; minor spire.
Domes with inner surfaces continuous with the surfaces of their pendentives.
Columns of the Corinthian style that is seated on a base and usually fluted.
Capitals having a series of crockets.
The part of a column between the bottom of the capital and the top of the shaft, or the molding or moldings located here.
Trusses used to support a pitched roof; the ties cross each other and are connected to the opposite rafters at an intermediate point along their length.
Networks of small light bars of wood, metal, or other material crossing at regular intervals, usually diagonally.
Districts having boundaries defined by religious groups or religions.
Areas set off by a governing body for specific use, such as residential, commercial, or industrial.
Areas that are distinguished by historical or other criteria, but not by political administrative boundaries. An example is the Middle East.
Sites that are used for ceremonial purposes; often an ancient site, sometimes the purpose of which is unknown.
Arches turned upside down, so that the intrados is below the springing; used, for example, to distribute loads in foundations.
Complexes of strucutures comprising or surrounding a fort or fortification.
Areas in the sea where oysters are cultivated for human consumption.
Cemeteries placed within a large rural landscape, planted and laid out with winding paths.
Public burial places for paupers, unknown persons, and criminals.
Mines from which the primary extraction is iron, which is an element and lustrous, silvery, soft metal.
Stations or inns along a route that is a thoroughfare for coaches or riders in a postal service, especially stations where fresh post horses are kept.
Bridges surmounted by pavilions; may be found in gardens and used for water-viewing.
Structures or devices used to allow the transportation of a boat, goods, etc. over land between navigable bodies or stretches of water.
Buildings that have a light or airy construction, such as those using plywood, plasterboard, steel studs, or frames without walls.
Churches having the form of a tower; examples are the tower churches popular in England and elsewhere in the 10th century.

Grace churches are Protestant churches that came into being due to the Treaty of Altranstadt, and the Wroclaw Execution Trial (1709). At that time, the Lutherans in Silesia were granted six so-called grace churches, which were allowed to be built outside the city walls, but in stone and with a bell tower. Still in the tradition of peace churches, three wooden grace churches were built (Militsch, Freystadt and Sagan), and three others were erected as solid constructions (Hirschberg, Landeshut and Teschen).
In Indian architecture, a temple or shrine.
Temples whose sanctuary spaces are wholly or partly open to the sky.
Facilities for clinics, either free-standing buildings or part of hospitals, where minor surgery is performed on an outpatient basis.
Facilities specializing in the care of the dying or the incurably ill.

Buildings that house establishments, often charitable institutions, for the reception, housing, and care of pilgrims, travellers, or the needy. The term was originally reserved for the similar establishments of the Knights Hospitallers.
An ornamental pavilion or recreational structure, usually situated at an elevated point in a park or garden.
Buildings housing libraries containing  paper and electronic books, newspapers and magazines, and multimedia materials such as videos and sound recordings.
Large, permanent, heavily fortified, defensive military positions, sometimes including a town. Larger and stronger than "forts."
Vertical structures that are monuments or memorials.
Main halls of temple complexes which usually housed the primary statues of buddhas or bodhisattvas. For the main halls of some early Buddhist temples (into the 8th century), use kondō.
Artificial ponds or lakes where water is accumulated and retained until needed.
Reservoirs for water storage, best known in India and Pakistan. step-well, sometimes with pavilions within; tank; stepped well
Industrial establishments where employees are underpaid and overworked usually under unsanitary or otherwise barely tolerable conditions.
Windmills having the form of a masonry tower, atop which are positioned a rotating cap and the sails.

Buildings or rooms built or used for the containment of smoke, usually such buildings or rooms where meat or fish is dried or cured by means of dense smoke. Also, rooms or structures in a tannery that are heated by smoldering bark and used to unhair hides.

Buildings that house schools that train people for careers in the armed forces and for private schools organized following the discipline and dress codes of military life; both offer courses in military training and both are generally at university level with degree-granting programs.
Buildings housing academic enterprises that teach art.
Buildings housing a learned society called an "academy," which exists for the promotion and education in art, literature, science, etc.

Designates asymmetrically massed, one-story houses with low-pitched roofs and rambling shapes; may also be used for the main dwelling on ranches. During the late 1940s and 1950s, the ranch house became associated with the work of architect Cliff May (1908-1989), who often used open plan buildings with large areas of glass. The designs became popular and were assimilated by other architects after the publication of two architectural pattern books by "Sunset" magazine, "'Sunset' Western Ranch Houses (San Francisco, 1946) and "Western Ranch Houses by Cliff May" (Menlo Park, 1958).
Houses that are very narrow in floorplan, often designed to fit in a small footprint between larger buildings.

Buildings that use a frame structure of large posts and beams that are joined with pegs or by other types of decorative joinery; the beams may be visible in the finished structure, or hidden beneath the surface walls.
Dwellings built for or inhabited by the president of a nation.
Large, rectangular, multifamily dwellings housing related families in separate compartments entered off long corridors; equipped with individual or communal hearths.
Palaces, generally rural, that provide retreats from winter weather for rulers and their courts or others.

Sepulchral monuments in the form of freestanding pillars; distinguished by being taller and generally having less breadth than a tombstone or a stele, but often having more depth. Grave pillars were common in several ancient cultures and continue in modern usage.

Municipal buildings in some English towns where moot cases are, or once were, discussed. Historically, the term was used to refer to town halls, or assembly spaces such as courtrooms, or council chambers.

Barriers or dams across waterways to regulate water level or divert or measure water flow, for example, to drive a mill wheel or as constructed on a canal or navigable river to retain the water and prevent overflow.
Simple structures for sheltering or housing livestock.
Fences of posts and usually two or three split rails.
Small restaurants or snack bars serving light daytime meals or snacks that are ready to serve or quickly prepared.
Cairene commercial buildings offering lodging, storage, and commercial space for merchants and sometimes serving as brokerage houses; similar to khans and often built with unconnected housing above.
Buildings housing businesses where sweet food items such as candy, cakes, light pastries, icing, and ice cream are produced or sold.
Buildings housing businesses by which personal movable property is deposited in exchange for money at interest and where unredeemed property is displayed and sold.
Built works used for the purposes of communications, including telecommunications.
Storehouses or other repositories for grain, especially after it has been threshed or husked; sometimes also used to store corn.
Spaces in another building or stand-alone, used for prayer. Examples are the musallā prayer halls in mosques.
Rooms or buildings used for secret or nonconformist worship.
Passageways between the walls of the cella of a classical temple and the columns of the peristyle.
In Indian architecture, structures having a form shaped after elephant's back.

North Indian mono-spired śikhara-type with curvilinear vertical bands (latās) usually bearing jāla-pattern; rēkhā-deul (Oriyā), North Indian curvilinear superstructure; single-spired Nāgara superstructure.

Entrance spaces of historic Dutch houses or farms that provide a transition from the exterior to the interior of a house. Most span the entire front width of a house, and serve as both a reception point and connection between the street, entry, stairs, and private inner rooms.
Passageways through the exterior walls of buildings and open to the outside through small-scale or slender arcades; found in Italian and German Romanesque architecture.
Small chambers or studies in private homes housing collections of art works or biological or geological specimens, popular during the Italian Renaissance.
Small dining areas, usually extensions of kitchens or pantries; for such areas when they are extensions of living rooms, use "dining alcoves."
In Indian architecture, a central hall.
Small side-rooms or recesses in a structure, usually having a door, built or used for storing clothing, utensils, or provisions.
Rooms intended for the preparation and cooking of food.
Slopes used for defense against attack; may be natural or artificial.
Architectural elements found on Japanese religious buildings.
Niches having a shelf or flat surface, found in churches and used for the placement of vessels used in the Eucharist prior to use and immediately afterwards.

Altars that are of relatively small size and transportable, often fitting into a container along with other items for worship or services. In Christian contexts, examples include consecrated altar stones set in a case or otherwise mounted, used by priests who travel from location to location saying Mass where a permanent consecrated altar may not be available. Specifications included that it should be a solid piece of natural stone of a type and size resistant to fracture, consecrated by a bishop, large enough to hold the host and chalice, and designed so that it may be inserted in or placed on a table convenient for the service. For transportable versions of Christian painted or carved image-bearing objects of the type displayed on or above an altar, use "portable altarpieces."
Paved or planted strips of ground dividing highways into lanes according to direction of travel.
Any member of a group of organic compounds, -COOH, in which a carbon atom is doubly bonded to an oxygen atom.
The hair or hair plus skin of the goat, which is a ruminant quadruped of the genus Capra.
The skin, usually of a young goat, occasionally a young lamb or related young animal, which when tanned, tawed, or manufactured, commonly finds use in the bookbinding and garment trades.
Berry of the tomato plant, which is cultivated as a garden vegetable in temperate and tropical lands. The fruit varies in color from red to yellow.
Material comprising the leaves and pithy or hollow stems of grasslike plants of the genus Juncus, found in wet or marshy places and used since ancient times to make baskets, mats, and chair seats.

Wood of any of several trees belonging to the genus Fraxinus, having distinctive growth rings with very large open pores beside small, tight pores. The wood is light in color, dense, elastic, and having a straight grain that is moderately durable but susceptible to insect attack and moisture degradation. The tough, heavy timber is used for ladders, tool handles, oars, poles, gymnasium equipment, and hockey sticks because it produces a smooth surface that rarely splinters. Ash was also popular for furniture (especially Colonial pieces), wheels, and carriage frames, and is used for decorative veneers.
Marble with a mineral composition resulting in a predominantly white color.
A deep blue-black marble with short white veins that is found in Saint Anne, Belgium.
A marble of Northern Italy having a coarse network of dark veins on a white or grayish ground.
A marble characterized by its cloudy mixture of pure white, pale brown, lilac gray, and pink on a yellow ground; it originates from Corinth.
