A type of white marble with a medium fine texture from Lee, Massachusetts. It can sometimes be light gray in appearance. A small band of Lee marble was used in the Washington Monument in Washington, D.C. but it proved too costly; it was, however, used to build parts of the Capitol in the 1850s.
Refers to massively large stones, especially those very roughly worked or left as found; used in various ancient monuments.

Soluble red or purple-brown powder extracted from the dried female scale insect Dactylopius coccus. The percentage of acidity changes the color of Carminic acid from a bright red to yellow or deep violet. It is the primary ingredient in cochineal dyestuff and is used in paint pigments, color photography, and textile dyeing.
A light, porous, siliceous sedimentary rock composed almost entirely of sponge spicules. Spongolite was much used as a building stone in medieval Bohemia.
Limestone that is rich in silica, particularly as free silica as opposed to silicates.
A durable, fossiliferous limestone quarried near Verona, Italy; used as a building material since ancient times.

A metamorphic rock composed largely of granular quartz which is cemented by silica forming a homogeneous mass of very high tensile and crushing strengths; especially used as a building stone, as gravel in road construction, and as aggregate in concrete.
A breccia marble consisting of cream-colored pebbles on a lilac ground tinged with yellow.

Generally, a layer of metal deposited upon a metal base, for purposes of decoration or to impart desirable physical or chemical properties. Distinct from "plate (object genre)" which refers to objects made of high quality solid silver or gold. The term is used more correctly for silverwork alone, but sometimes used loosely for goldwork as well.
Filament or slender rod of drawn metal.

Naturally occurring mineral of calcium fluor-phosphate; numerous deposits are found in Germany, Spain and North America. It is colorless when pure, but impurities can give it a white, green (asparagus stone), blue (moroxite), yellow, or violet color. Bones are composed of hydroxyapatite, mixed with protein (ossein) and small amounts of other minerals, such as calcium carbonate. Apatite is commercially used as a fertilizer.
Glass, usually borosilicate, with a low coefficient of expansion making it resistant to thermal shock.
Glass objects that have a function in everyday life and are not explicitly made as an artistic expression.
A nontarnishing alloy typically used for making jewelry, which exhibits the natural color of gold. It is composed of copper (90%), aluminum (7.5%) and gold (2.5%).
Brass having a reddish tint due to a high copper content.
Bronze with a smooth, reddish surface, generally composed of 7 to 10% tin, 1 to 3% lead, and the remainder copper; used, for example, to make statues, plaques, and hardware.
German utensil alloy, contains 88% to 92% tin, up to 3% copper, and 6% to 7.5% lead.

The metallic element having the symbol Co and atomic number 27; it is a hard, ductile, white metal, resembling nickel but with a bluish instead of a yellow tinge. Cobalt was first identified by Georg Brandt of Sweden in 1735. It has an abundance of 0.001-0.002% in the earth's crust and is found in the minerals smaltite, cobaltite, chloanthite, linnaetite, and erythrite. Metallic cobalt is added to alloys to increase hardness at high temperatures. It is also ferromagnetic. Cobalt oxides and salts are usually blue and they are used as pigments in paints, glass, and ceramic glazes
Smooth, dense brick which is highly resistant to abrasion; used for finished floor surfaces.

A general term for wares decorated predominantly with one or more clay slips of greater or lesser iron content than the body clay. The slip clays fire to a contrasting color or shade from that of the body. Slipware can be decorated by pouring, dipping, painting, daubing or trailing slips on to the unfired, or sometimes once-fired, body. After it is applied, the slip can be manipulated by twisting the piece, by combing or feathering the slip into more regular designs or, after drying to a tacky consistency, can be carved in the sgraffito technique. Dipping, trailing, and marbling are other common techniques used for slip-decorated ceramics. The application of slip almost always precedes glazing.
Form of concrete reinforced by broken stones or brick.
Concrete that contains embedded reinforcements, typically steel bars, in order to increase strength.
A dense opaque glass of a red or black color made at the glassworks of Count von Buquoy in southern Bohemia in the 19th century.
Glass formed of two or more fused layers of different colored glass.
A grayish-white element with symbol As and atomic number 33, having a metallic luster, vaporizing when heated, and forming poisonous compounds.
Cement produced by taking finely pulverizing calcined argillaceous limestone and heating it to complete decarbonation, which is the process of removing carbon dioxide.
A portland cement low in tricalcium aluminate; has a reduced susceptibility to attack by dissolved sulfates in water or soil.
A term used to describe large thin bricks used in medieval England.
Figures composed of more than five lobes or arcs, separated by cusps.
In Indian architecture, a wish-fulfilling tree (decorative motif).

Zodiac symbol of a fish, roughly based on the constellation of the same name. The zodiak signs have survived from classical Greek and Roman decoration, were popular in Northern European Romanesque and Gothic churches, and often found in Medieval psalters and books of hours symbolizing each month in which the sun enters the related constellation. They have also been used as decoration on ceilings, maps, timepieces, and astronomical instruments.
Stylized crosses with relatively short arms that are all shaved to a point, resulting in a form resembling a star with four arms.
Small to medium-sized settlements or groups of buildings that are constructed in long, narrow area, typically to follow a transport route, such as a road, river, or canal, or a coast.

Compactly developed or developing, usually residential, areas on the outskirts of a central city; distinguished from central cities by their more homogeneous socio-economic and physical character, although rarely is there an identifiable boundary between suburbs and central cities.

Designates once-flourishing settlements recently abandoned primarily due to dramatic economic decline or exhaustion of local natural resources; generally the buildings remain standing but in a state of deterioration.

Settlements established for the purpose of containing prisoners or other detainees and punishing them through forced labor, whether overseas or within the boundaries of the founding state. For inhabited places containing prisons, but not necessarily established as settlements for penal purposes, use "prison centers (inhabited places)."
Areas of shrubs and grasses that are used for grazing.
Pieces of soft, miry, or muddy ground, particularly areas of thoroughfares that are filled with wet mud or mire and impassable by vehicles, horses, etc.
In Indian architecture, a dormer-window decorative motif.

Buildings or complexes, often found at an international expositions or fairs, devoted to a theme but not representing by itself the identity of a single nation or geographic area. Each single building or complex structure has homogeneous characteristics that identify it as a discrete item.

Structures built in relation to water in general, especially seaward of the high-water line of the major water bodies (oceans, seas, bays); use "offshore structures" for construction built on continental shelves.
Buildings that are constructed consciously in violation of building and zoning codes.

Gardens created following the Shinto, Buddhist, or Zen philosophy of the relationship between nature and people and generally characterized by simple asymmetrical designs, dominated by clipped evergreens, often incorporating bridges, rocks, stepping stones, raked gravel, and stone lanterns to create an environment for contemplation and meditation.
Tracts set aside for recreation and located on land in contact with the sea, in submerged areas, along sea beds, or on emerged land areas near the sea coast.
Roads that comprise the principal arteries through an area; originally indicated specially surfaced routes intended for vehicles.
Open public areas, walks, or plazas, often lined with trees, shrubs, or shops, reserved for use by pedestrians.

Delimited portions of land, usually as lawn, plantings, or left natural surrounding and belonging to a house or other building. Grounds serve chiefly for ornament or recreation. Grounds may be enclosed; they may include gardens.
In Indian architecture, a main temple.
Laboratories focused on designing, constructing, and testing engines and machinery, or on structures such as roads and bridges.

Tanks used temporarily for containing fuel or another substance, usually liquid or gas rather than solid. The tanks are not intended to be linked to the equipment for which that fuel or other substance is intended.
Centers offering connections for transportation lines, could include local and express bus lines, light rail, and others.

A tertiary alcohol found in linaloe oil and other essential oils. It is used in perfumery and is a common component of flower odors. In conservation, it is used as a mild antifungal agent on paper, silver photographs, and leather.
Visual works or parts of works made of iron, generally reserved for decorative forms fashioned in wrought or cast iron.
Material which is an electrical insulator or in which an electric field can be sustained with a minimum of dissipation in power.

Any substance introduced into a deteriorated or otherwise fragile material where it strengthens and stabilizes parts into a whole, solid, or compact mass. In the conservation of sculpture, stone that has lost cohesive strength must be reinstated by the introduction of a consolidant. Materials used in this context may include epoxy, silicates, or acrylics.
Material used in masonry walls, comprising an impervious horizontal layer used to prevent upward capillary movement or downward seepage of water.
Roofing system that uses a waterproof membrane of synthetic rubber, thermoplastic such as PVC or similar material, or modified bitumen.
Shingles laid to produce uneven, wavy courses.

Pale green, volatile oil obtained from the rinds of the lime fruit. Lime oil is normally prepared by steam distillation; its components are limonene and citral. It is used in flavoring, perfumes, insecticide, antiseptic, cleaning products, aromatherapy, and as a source of vitamin C.

Oil to which an equal amount of water has been added, perhaps salt water, shaken, and exposed to the sun in a glass jar or tray for a few weeks. The vessels are typically loosely covered to exclude dirt, but permit air. The oil and water must be recombined every day for the first week. Length of exposure time to the sun varies according to the season and to the intended consistency and color desired. At the end of the treatment, the oil is separated from the water by means of a funnel.

Eroded matter from preexisting rocks which is carried and deposited by water, wind, or ice, forming layers on the Earth's surface and fluvial deposits. Sedimentary rock.is composed of consolidated sediment.
Polymer composed of macromolecules in which a small but significant proportion of the constitutional units has ionic or inonizable groups, or both.

Any solid semi-inorganic polymers based on siloxanes, obtained by the action of concentrated hydrochloric acid on calcium silicide. Silicones were first discovered by F.S. Kipping in England in 1904, but were not commercially produced as polymers until 1943 by Dow Corning and 1946 by General Electric. They were called silicones because their empirical formula (R2SiO) is similar to that for ketones (R2CO). Silicones can be liquids, gels, and elastomers as well as solid thermoplastic or thermosetting resins. In general, they have excellent heat and chemical resistance and are water repellent. Silicones are used as adhesives, lubricants, protective coatings, release agents, paints, rubbers, coolants, implants, and insulation.
Water distilled from roses or scented with essence of roses, used as a perfume, scenting a room, flavoring, in medicinal preparations, or for other purposes.
Photographic film formulated and formatted for use in motion picture cameras, or to make prints from camera-original film used in motion picture cameras.
A substance, often metal, intended for or undergoing assaying analysis or testing.
Handmade paper that is produced in a centuries-old traditional manner in Japan from the fiber of gampi tree bark, kozo (mulberry), the mitsumata shrub, bamboo, hemp, rice, or wheat.
Paper, prepared as thin strips, containing a reagent that indicates the presence of a specific chemical compound by changing color.

Photographic paper used in salted paper processes. Paper is impregnated with a solution of salt (sodium chloride) dissolved in water; it is then coated on one side with silver nitrate thus forming light-sensitive silver chloride on the surface.
Stiff cardboard faced with decorative paper, foil, or cloth, sometimes also having a textured surface; used for matting two-dimensional art work or documents.
Yellow oil derived from the kernels of seeds of Jatropha curcas, native to Central America. This oil is used in cooking, soap, and as a strong purgative.
Cadmium yellow pigment of a light variety, but not so cool as cadmium yellow lemon.
Fiber from the species Wikstroemia canescens, used in papermaking.
Synthetic fiber made from regenerated cellulose.
A writing material prepared from thin strips of the pith of the papyrus plant laid together, soaked, pressed, and dried.

Sheer, thin, heavily-sized open weave cotton, used for linings and as a wiping cloth in printmaking. Use also for a type of muslin brought from India to the United Kingdom in the 18th century, and produced in Scotland in the 19th century, commonly for ball gowns.
Raw wool sheared from live sheep.

Paper made from thin layers of pith cut from two species of rice paper trees cultivated in China, Japan, and Thailand. Often erroneously referred to as 'rice paper,' which is misleading since it has no relationship to rice itself. The pith is cut in spirals to form long ribbons, the exposed cellular structure of the pith giving the paper a unique spongy structure. Pith paper is stretchy when wet and brittle when dry; it will crack when heated and is easily damaged by abrasion. Among other uses, pith paper was used for 19th-century Chinese watercolor paintings and artificial flowers. For handmade paper having long fibers from the paper mulberry, gampi, or mitsumata plant, use "Japanese paper." For soft, fine-textured paper of bamboo fiber originating in China, use "China paper."
Paper of a weight that is thicker and stiffer than writing or printing paper, but thinner and more flexible than paperboard.

A synthetic green-blue pigment made by fixing barium manganate on a barium sulfate base. It is an inert pigment that can range in color from a clear azure blue to a bright emerald green. Manganese blue was first discovered in 1907 but not patented until 1935.
A water soluble variety of Prussian blue; used in for printing lines on ruled paper.

Pigment name for a variety of green pigments, originally referring to green created from a mixture of blue and yellow colors prepared by Paolo Veronese, a 16th century Venetian painter. It is also used for any pigment resembling that color, including green earth pigments, copper-based emerald green, viridian, and other pigments of similar color.

Unstandardized term referring to several green pigments, including malachite (natural copper carbonate), Bremen green (synthetic copper carbonate), and Scheele's green (copper arsenite), among others.

Copper carbonate pigment that is green in color rather than blue, counterpart to natural malachite pigment. It tends to have regularly sized particles with rounded edges with a paler color than natural malachite pigment. Natural malachite was occasionally used in tempera-based paintings before the 16th century and later, green verditer was used for both distemper and oil based interior house paints in the 19th century.
An unstandardized name used for Pozzuoli red, Tuscan red, and dragon's blood.
A bright red pigment prepared by depositing an organic red dye, such as alizarin, on a red iron oxide base.
An unstandardized name for various red pigments, including iodine scarlet as well as for other fugitive synthetic organic colorants.
An unstandardized name for whitish pigment made from bismuth nitrate,  bismuth oxychloride, or from a calcium carbonate powder obtained from pulverizing and calcining mother-of-pearl.
Pigment made of white clay materials and used in China clay material.
A rich, transparent yellow, quercitron-based lake pigment.
Synthetic arsenic trisulfide, made since the 18th century and valued because it is purer and less expensive than its natural counterpart, opriment.
Lumber up to 5 inches thick intended for general building construction.

Gum produced from grinding the seeds of the carob tree to a fine powder, which dissolves in hot water and cools to form a stable gel that is an excellent film former. The gum is used as dye thickener, and as size for food, cosmetics, textiles, and paper. Locust bean gums have been detected in the wrappings of Egyptian mummies.

A soft, sticky, fragrant resin derived from trees of the family Burseraceae. Elemi is used in lacquer, lithographic inks, textile coatings, paper coatings, perfume bases, and waterproofing. It has been used as a plasticizer in varnishes, but the components responsible for its initial malleability (mono- and sesquiterpenoids) evaporate and it eventually hardens to a brittle film. The term was imprecisely used in the 17th and 18th centuries to describe many oleoresin mixtures.

A thick, brown oleoresin obtained from Myroxylon balsamum var. balsamum trees that are native to the high plains of Venezuela, Columbia and Peru. Tolu balsam is used for perfumes, chewing gums, as a dark brown transparent glaze for paintings. It is similar to Peru balsam and derived from a variety of the same species. A thick, brown oleoresin obtained from Myroxylon balsamum var. balsamum trees that are native to the high plains of Venezuela, Columbia and Peru. Tolu balsam is used for perfumes, chewing gums, as a dark brown transparent glaze for paintings. It is similar to Peru balsam and derived from a variety of the same species.
Refers to the gum extracted from perennial grass of the genus Triodia. Australian Aborigines harvest and produce the resin for use as an adhesive.

A vegetable dye created from extract from the bark of chestnut trees, having a dark color that was used as a dye in 19th century Italy and southern France to make an inexpensive fast blackish dye for silk. Tannin of the chestnut bark produces a firm, heavy leather with a pale, reddish color. Chestnut extract is usually mixed with other tannins, such as quebracho, mimosa, or myrobalans.
Purpurin has been manufactured synthetically by the oxidation of alizarin since the 1920s.
Various kinds of carbon black that is produced by burning plant material.

International Klein Blue (IKB) is a powdery ultramarine pigment created by Yves Klein in 1956 and patented by the artist in 1960. He used the color, symbolic of purity of spirit, exclusively from 1957 on.
Wood of the genus Juniperus, evergreen shrubs or trees, of which numerous species are found variously in the northern hemisphere; used in joinery.
Wood of Cedrus libani, having a light brown heartwood and a pungent cedar odor and fairly knotty grain. It is typically used for joinery, garden furniture, gates, fences, and doors.

Wood of the Chamaecyparis thyoides tree, found along the Atlantic coastal plain from Virginia to Texas. Wood is reddish-brown, fragrant and used for shingles, mine timbers, fence posts, and other supporting structures.
Wood from the Pinus jeffreyi, native to the area from southwest Oregon to northern Baja California in Mexico.
Wood of Picea glauca, native to North America. It is a soft, pale-yellow wood that has a straight grain used for lumber, millwork, and pulp wood.

Thin, narrow, flat pieces of wood used for many purposes, such as in constructing lattices of trellis work, Venetian blinds, or to form a groundwork upon which to fasten the slates or tiles of a roof or the plaster of a wall or ceiling. For groundwork of any material upon which plaster or another such material is applied, use "lath (grounding surface)."
Wood impregnated with thermosetting resin then subjected to heat and pressure to provide both resin curing and compression.
Wood of the species Nothofagus fusca, native to cooler regions of the southern hemisphere. It is used in the making of flooring, toys, and tool handles.

Wood of the species Betula lenta, native to the southern Appalachians. It is similar to yellow birch and is not separated from it commercially, but it is denser and deeper in color. It is used in the making of veneer, flooring, furniture, doors, plywood, and vehicle parts.

Wood of the species Swietenia macrophylla, native to areas in southern North America, Central and South America. It has been introduced for cultivation in Asia. The wood is used for cabinet-making and other purposes.
Wood of the species Acer saccharinum, native to eastern North America and widely cultivated elsewhere. It is a soft wood, used for crating and inexpensive furniture.
Wood of the species Quercus muehlenbergii, native to the eastern half of the United States and was early valued for railroad ties and heavy construction timbers.

Soft, yellowish-white wood of the species Populus tremula, native to Europe and Asia. It is easy to work, but weak, prone to warping, and produces a disagreeable odor when wet. The lightweight, spongy wood is generally used for matches, excelsior, fruit crates, and paper pulp.
Styles of pottery belonging to Pre-Columbian Pueblo cultures.
Styles belonging to West Coast Mesocamerican cultures.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in central Tanzania.
Ethnic, cultural, and regional styles in that region of North Africa historically known as Morocco. For the style of the nation of Morocco, see "Moroccan."
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a Bedouin group living in Eritrea and Sudan.
Style and culture of the Berber people of the same name living in the African region of Mauritania.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting scattered areas of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Ethiopia.
Style and culture of an East African people who speak a Bantu language, also called Haya, inhabiting the northwestern corner of Tanzania between the Kagera River and Lake Victoria.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Tanzania.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in eastern Gabon.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Angola.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Nigeria and Cameroon.
Culture and style of people in the Adamawa state of Nigeria.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Cameroon.
Styles belonging to Ogowe River area cultures.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Central African Republic and Cameroon.
Styles belonging to Kru-speaking peoples cultures.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Kolda region of Sénégal.
Refers to the African people of Southern Ghana; formerly they constituted one of the pre-colonial Akan states.
Fine arts styles belonging to Yoruba cultures.
Style and culture of the people of the African language group of the same name living in Nigeria.
Style and culture particular to one of the five geographically based subcultures of Igbo-speaking people.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting western Cameroon and Nigeria.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northeastern Nigeria.
Pictorial representations using circles and squares so positioned as to represent an operation in set theory.
Refers to depictions with a point of view from in front of the subject, as contrasted to depictions taken from the side or back.
Landscapes featuring areas of trees or woodlands.

Representations in any medium of identified people, where the representation does not necessarily reflect the actual appearance of the person. Conjectural portraits may be based on an estimation of what the person looked like, for example, based on a written description of their appearance. Alternatively, a conjectural portrait may be a representation that is purely imaginary, but intended nonetheless to depict or stand for the person in the context of the art work. For estimated portraits based on forensic or archaeological evidence, reconstructing the appearance of the person based on the skull or other remains, or by using DNA, prefer "forensic facial reconstructions."

A type of still life depicting simple foodstuffs, such as fish, ham, fruit, cheese, or bread, with a glass of beer or wine. Though ontbijtje is Dutch for "little breakfast," paintings categorized as such do not necessarily depict items of a typical Dutch breakfast; the foodstuffs depicted are those that would be consumed at a light meal at any time of day. Ontbijtje were especially popular in the Netherlands during the 1620s and 1630s.

Culture of the body of people who were displaced from their African homeland, and their descendants. Examples include those who traveled in ancient migrations and those who were involuntarily transported due to slavery.
Refers to archaeological sites in present day Sudan which date from 4900-3000 BCE, and are divisible into Early (4900-3800 BCE) and Late (3800-3000 BCE) periods.
Nationality, culture, and styles of the historic Western Sudan region in the northern part of west Africa, from the Atlantic to the basin of Lake Chad.
Describes works produced by the African people of the same name living in the Central African Republic, Cameroon, and Chad.
Thermosetting plastic coating applied to metal, resulting in a hard and resistant finish.
A mixture of naturally occuring mineral material used by the Maya in the preparation of plasters and mortars. It has been employed as a building and paving material in Mesoamerica since antiquity.
Varnish used for stopping out areas of a printing plate.
Paint that is applied as an atomized mist, through dispensers such as an aerosol container of compressed gas or a spray gun.
A type of black face paint composed of carbon-black. Literally, "face covered in lamp-black."
Paint that contains a varnish which produces a glossy finish.
Opaque glaze containing an oxide of tin or tin ashes and of a white color, unless other color has been added.
An opaque claret red to brownish red reduced copper glaze developed in China during the Kanxi period and used chiefly in porcelain ware.
Refers to the period between about 1600 and 1100 BCE when Mesopotamia was ruled by the Kassite dynasty.
Culture of the Persianate Mongol Jalayir dynasty in Iraq and western Persia after the breakup of the Mongol khanate of Persia in the 1330s.

Refers to a Bronze Age style and culture defined by artifacts from the type site near the village of Lefkandi, on Euboia island, Greece. This term generally applies to the culture prior to the influx of refugees fleeing the destruction of Mycenaean palaces, which took place around 1200 BCE, and not to the later rich culture at Lefkandi.
Style and culture of the region of Attica. For culture particular to the capital of Attica, Athens, use "Athenian."

Refers to a regional school of Pahari miniature painting centered around the Hill State of Kulu, one of the most remote states of the Punjab Hills. It developed out of the Basohli school when Basohli artists migrated to Kulu in the late 17th century. Emphasis is placed on decorative patterns instead of naturalistic landscapes and colors are less bold than in Basohli painting. The "Shangri Ramayana', a series of 270 paintings, is a central Kulu work dating from about 1690 to 1710.

Refers to the culture and period that flourished from the 7th to the mid-15th century in the region known today as Cambodia and later migrated to other regions in Southeast Asia. The style of this period is complex and developed in different sub-phases, and is driven by animistic beliefs, Theravada Buddhism, and Indian Hinduism. Artistic production in this period is diverse and reflects Indian and other regional influences in sculpture, architecture, and the decorative arts. In architecture, the period features Hindu and Mahayana Buddhist temples in laterite, sandstone, or brick constructions.

Refers to a Mesolithic tool culture named after the site at the "big bog," "magle mose" in Danish, near Mullerup, Denmark, and evident in northern Europe from about 9,000 to 5,000 BCE. It was created by a forest people who settled along rivers and lakes as the glaciers retreated, and there developed new tools to deal with the changing environment, including stone microliths, axes, bows and arrows, fish hooks, wooden paddles, canoes, and fishnets. Artistic activities included the creation of designs on tools and decorative objects, including amulets and pendants.
Neolithic culture and style of the Körös people, who lived in the area of modern Hungary and the Czech Republic. Their culture is related to the Cris culture.
Refers to the style of sculpture developed by the artist Unkei (1142-1212). The style is characterized by realistic, sensitive portraits of Buddhist priests.

Refers to the style found on the island of Sumba. Textile production in this region reflects Sumatran and Indian influences, featuring large mantles known as hinggi patterned in warp ikat, Indian patola design elements, and ceremonial sarongs displaying warp patterning. Popular regional motifs in textiles  include human figures, horses, deer, snakes, and lions. Colors signify class distinction with Turkey red dye being the most luxurious and rare. In lapidary design, the style features the use of garnets, crystals, pearls, amethysts, rubies, red coral, ivory. Decorative arts in this style feature elaborate bead necklaces and headbands.

Refers to the Eneolithic culture established in the steppes of the Minusinsk basin by Mongoloid peoples probably of Northern Siberian descent, from the beginning of the 2nd millennium BCE. Tombs have revealed a variety of stone sculptures.
Culture of Tibetan-related ethnic group historically living at the terminus of the Silk Road in what is now northwestern China. The Tangut kingdom of Xixia flourished from 1038 until 1227.
Styles, culture, nationality, and period belonging to European colonies in India.
Styles belonging to Japanese cultures.

Refers to the style of Shinto architecture that developed during the Nara (710-794) and Heian periods (794-1185). The style is characterized by a type of shrine that is small in size and constructed in a two-bay by three-bay system upon a earthen mound. The roof or canopy sweeps down on the long side of the building, covering the stairs and providing shelter for worshippers.
Japanese painting style influenced by Chinese painting from the Yuan and Song periods, imported into Japan from the 13th century.
Refers to the style of unglazed pottery manufactured at kilns in the Mie Prefecture 16th-17th centuries.
Textile styles belonging to Chinese cultures.

Refers to a Chinese Neolithic culture of the middle Yangzi River basin dating from ca. 4400 to ca. 3300 BCE. Its name comes from a site at Daxi Wushan in Sichuan province; other important Daxi sites are Guanmiaoshan Zhijiang and Honghuatao in Hubei province and Sanyuangong in Hunan province. Ceramics are the most distinctive Daxi artifacts, with hand-built red wares predominanting. The techniques of painting, stamping, cord impressions, incising, appliqué, and openwork are all used; chevrons, flower petal designs, and intertwined curvilinear and triangular designs are common motifs. Upright vessels such as deep-bowled dou and ring-footed bowls, plates, and cups are the most important Daxi vessel forms.  Stone tools and ornaments such as rings and necklaces made of jade, bone, stone, and shell have been found at Daxi sites.
Refers to the culture, style, and period of Chinese history dating from 265 to 581 CE that encompasses six dynasties in the south and five in the north.

Refers to the culture, style, and period associated with the late Ming Dynasty, 1567-1572. The period is so short that no specific decorative style can accurately be associated with it. The blue and white and enamelled polychrome wares of the preceeding period continued without interruption.
Refers to the culture, style, and period associated with the reign of T'ung Chih, 1862-1874.  The style is characterized by the revival of Kangzhi wares for export, and  varying styles for court use.

An art trend prevalent in Guangdong Province, China during the first half of the 20th century. Lingnan, literally meaning ‘south of the mountains,' refers to an area including Guangdong and some other southern provinces of China. The key figures of the trend were the brothers Gao Qifeng and Gao Jianfu as well as Chen Shuren. In coordination with the popular ideas of reforming China with western ‘science and democracy,' the artists aimed to create a new Chinese art that defined the nation through a synthesis of East and West. Since many artists studied in Japan, they incorporated western realism as interpreted by Japanese nihonga painting into Chinese ink painting. After the Communist revolution of 1949, the trend diminished in People’s Republic of China but further developed in Hong Kong, Taiwan and some overseas Chinese centres in Southeast Asia and North America.
Refers to the style of porcelain made in the Kiangsi province of China during the Yuan dynasty characterized by a pale or sky blue color.

Culture of indigenous Ona South Americans, who once inhabited southern Argentina and Chile, including the island of Tierra del Fuego. They were hunters and gatherers who subsisted chiefly on guanaco, various small animals, shellfish, cormorants, and berries. They were historically divided into two major subdivisions: Selk'nam and Haush. They spoke different dialects and had slightly different cultures.

Refers to the style of architecture, interior design, and decorative arts that prevailed in the United States, ca. 1870 to ca. 1925. As a result of the ever widening influence of the Arts and Crafts Movement in England, the Craftsman style was also based on the rejection of historical styles in favor of a traditional simplicity. Many of the same types of people were involved, such as social reformers, teachers and women's organizations, architects, and designers, as well as the prophets of the movement, John Ruskin and William Morris. In architecture, the style is characterized by modest homes, such as the bungalow, and simple treatment of materials.
Style of Western architecture that invokes or incorporates elements of architecture of non-Western cultures, such as Egyptian, Chinese, Moorish, or others.

Nationality, culture, or style of the modern nation of Mongolia. For the historical Central Asian ethnographic group of closely related tribal peoples who live mainly on the Mongolian Plateau, use "Mongol (culture or style)."
An indigenous peoples of South America, primarily in Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Argentina, Chile, and Colombia. They are bound by shared customs and language, although their ancient origins may vary.

Culture of the most numerous group of Indians in South America, inhabiting the Central Valley of Chile, south of the Biobío River. A smaller group lives in Neuquén provincia, west-central Argentina. Historically, the Mapuche were one of three groups of Araucanians as identified by Spanish ethnographers -- Picunche, Mapuche, Huillich. All Araucanians now identify themselves as Mapuche. In the pre-Spanish period, the Mapuche lived in scattered farming villages throughout the Central Valley. Each settlement had a cacique, or chief, whose authority did not generally extend beyond his own village. The Mapuche cultivated corn (maize), beans, squash, potatoes, chili peppers, and other vegetables and fished, hunted, and kept guinea pigs for meat.

The style and culture of a populous North American Indian group who live primarily in New Mexico, Arizona, and Utah, speaking an Apachean language which is classified in the Athabaskan language family. At some point in prehistory, the Navajo and Apache migrated to the Southwest from Canada, where most other Athabaskan-speaking peoples still live; although the exact timing of the relocation is unknown, it is thought to have been between 1100 and 1500 CE. These early Navajo were mobile hunters and gatherers; after moving to the Southwest, however, they adopted many of the practices of the sedentary, farming Pueblo Indians near whom they settled.

Style and culture of one of the six Northern Tewa speaking Rio Grande Pueblos. Habitation of the historic Pojoaque Pueblo area as early as 500 CE with a large prehistoric population in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries.
Styles belonging to Native Caribbean cultures.

Culture and style of an Eastern Algonquian Native American tribe that inhabited in the Hudson River Valley and New England prior to the 17th century. Due to the American Revolutionary War, many Mahican migrated westward to join the Iroquois Oneida in central New York. Many Mahican descendants were later moved to Wisconsin.

Refers to the culture of the Ojibwa, Algonquian-speaking Indians who historically lived along the northern shore of Lake Huron and both shores of Lake Superior from what is now Minnesota to the Turtle Mountains of North Dakota, as well as from southern Saskatchewan to Quebec in Canada. Today, Ojibwa communities exist in several different tribes across the Great Lakes region in the United States and Canada, thus they are considered Native American in the United States, and First Nations in Canada.
Style and culture of a Lushootseed-speaking Native nation. Their ancestral territories are the land in and around Seattle, Washington.

The seventh of the seven main chronological phases recognized in Andean archaeology, generally dating 1476-1534 CE, during which the Inca established an empire controlled from Cuzco, which eventually reached from central Chile to southern Colombia. The period ends in 1534, the year marking the fall of the Inca empire after the Spanish conquest.
Style and culture of an ethnic group of central Peru, in the Valle del Mantaro. They probably originated in the Huari culture.

Refers to the style and culture of a little-known group of pre-Columbians who lived in the northern Peruvian cloud forests. They are known primarily for tombs placed high on the mountainsides, containing mummies and stone and mahogany carved figures. The culture flourished flourished 800-1536 CE.
Cultures and styles of Northwest Coast Indigenous Americans.
Describes works created by the Tuareg people of the same name living in the Air region of Niger.

Applied broadly to the cultures of native peoples of North America, Central America, South America, or the West Indies; typically used in anthropological and linguistic contexts. For the native cultures of North America, excluding Inuit and Aleut peoples, use "Native American (culture)."
Historically, instruments with two inscribed cones used for observing the stars. In contemporary use, the term may refer to any astronomical telescope.
Use for biological instruments that lack other descriptive or generic names or if the specific name of the instrument is unknown.
Punches used to stamp decorative scallop decorations on metal, for example on jewelry, silver plate, gold leaf of panel paintings, wrought iron items, and many other items.
Tongs whose jaws are bent at a right angle.
Adjustable wrenches with long tapering steel handles terminating in an open-end wrench at one end; used primarily in plumbing to tighten large square nuts and to align holes.

Sewing needles designed to allow easier threading. One design includes, in addition to a regular eye, a V-shaped opening and slit in the top end from which the thread can be inserted and pulled into the eye.
Simple looms in which four stakes driven into the ground hold the tension on the breast beam and warp beam, with no other frame.
Axes with a long blade, up to one foot, with a flared-shaped cheek and no poll; used for paring and trimming masts and spars.
Chisels with a sharp cutting edge cut at an oblique angle and having beveled sides.
Small planes used to hollow out scoops and shovels.
Wood or metal planes which are flat across the sole, in which the cutting iron extends to the extreme edge on one or both sides;(SALAM) used to cut a rabbet along the grain at the edge of the wood.
Planes with a convex blade for cutting hollow molding patterns; usually paired with hollow planes in sets.
Saws having a handle like that of a knife, being usually long enough to be used by two hands.
Long-handled tools which terminate in an iron spike; used by lumbermen to pry logs. Later combined with the cant hook to become a peavey.
Any lens whose focal length is appreciably greater than the diagonal of the negative in the format in which it is used.
Shallow trays made of various materials including plastic or enameled metal used to hold photographic chemicals, most often developer, stop, and fixer for processing sensitized paper or film.

Small knives comprising a blade mounted on a pivot, often having a saddle for a finger-rest. Such knives are used most often in leatherworking, but also in other occupations, including historically in surgery.
Straight-edged devices used to shape and define angles in plastering.
Tools used to break up rock.
Slate cutters' hammers which have a point at the back of the head; used for making nail holes in slate.
Diamond-shaped trowels used in pointing or repointing masonry joints.
Blocks of various types, usually of metal, stone, or wood, used as a surface upon which metal sheets, or other metal components, are laid for punching or working.

Describes the style and culture of the inhabitants of Tikopia Island. The people of Tikopia are most well known for their carved wooden artifacts and personal ornaments. The Tikopia neck-rests were exceptionally carved with a crescent outline.

Describes the style and culture of the inhabitants of the Republic of Marshall Islands. The Marshall Islanders are recognized for the creation of the outrigger canoe. Originally, three forms of canoes were created: the walap, a sailing canoe with the capability of carrying up to 100 passengers; the tipnol, carrying up to 20 passengers; and the korkor, a small canoe to be used within a lagoon. Other artworks produced by the Marshall Islanders include woven or plaited products for the craft market or domestic use and various tattoo designs.
Describes the culture and nationality of the inhabitants of the Society Islands. The focus of most of their elaborate art forms was their cheif and the traditional religious ceremonies.
General term for styles and periods from post-1945.
Handheld devices used to locate framing studs beneath a wall surface, usually drywall. These operate via electrical or magnetic action to detect changes in density, or the presence of fasteners.
Rounded, heavy, metal or concrete demolition devices swung on a cable from the boom of a crane to break through concrete or masonry constructions.
Tractor-drawn devices with protruding teeth; used to penetrate and disrupt the earth's surface up to 3 feet in depth.
Cranes that consist of a rotating superstructure and boom mounted on a base or car equipped for travel on railroad tracks; used to hoist and swing loads at various radii.
Portable sets of flat broad steps or treads, with a frame hinged to the back for steadying.

Implements that use a reservoir of ink to make a mark or marks. A marker may have pointed or blunt tips, usually of fiber. It is distiguished from a felt-tip pen in that it typically makes a thicker mark than a pen and is more often used for labeling or marking rather than writing or drawing.

Cameras that generate developed images by means of chemicals integral to the film medium itself. Invented by Edwin Land and the Polaroid Corporation, which had patents for these processes and became synonymous with them, but instant cameras have been marketed by other brands.

Magnifying devices intended to be used with photographic equipment, particularly on the ground glass of large format view cameras to achieve critical focus. These are also typically used to view exposed film.

Refers to the style and period that coincided with the rule of Bayazid II, 'the Pious,' 1481 to 1512. Bayezid oversaw the construction of two riverbank complexes, the Amasya complex completed in 1486, and the Edrine complex, probably built by Hayreddin in 1488. The latter, with its contrasting golden and red sandstone ornamentation and dark-gray lead roof, presents one of the most effective examples of Ottoman classical architecture at its early stages of development. Also under his patronage, the Ottoman narrative painting style began to take form. Bayezid also brought Syh Hamdullah from Amasya to Istanbul where the tradition of this great Ottoman calligrapher lasted well into the 18th century.
Nationality, style, and culture of a poeple that habitate near the Sepik River on New Guinea.

Refers to the style of English architecture and interior design in the first half of the 19th century and again in the early 20th. Drawn from domestic architecture of the Tudor period dating 1485-1547, architectural forms and decorative motifs include diapered brickwork, half-timbering, stained glass, and Tudor roses, which were often combined with Gothic elements.

Term for variations of Art Nouveau in the Netherlands; characterized by ornament instead of construction, and function or material as the basis for design. Characteristics are stylized or abstracted motifs from nature and a two-dimensional treatment of surface. The style flourished in The Hague and Delft.
Refers to the movement in European painting begun circa 1918 as a response to the decorative quality in Cubism and characterized by clear, delineated geometric forms and pure color.
Refers to a German variation of Art Nouveau, named after the work of Belgian artist Henry van de Velde. As a result, the term is often used in conjunction with "Veldesche."
Use with reference to certain Italian sculpture of the mid-19th century.

Refers to the style of architecture and decorative arts in Europe and the United States from the 1750s to ca. 1840, characterized by the use of Classical Greek forms and ornament. Inspired by 18th century archaeological discoveries, it attempted to closely follow original models.

Historicist architecture style developed from the latter 19th century and onwards. Adopts neoclassical ornamentation from the Louis XVI period (1774-1792), such as oval medallions, laurel and fasces motifs.

Refers to the movement in 19th-century Western art that developed in France and rejected traditional academic teaching and attempted to use science regarding the physics of color to achieve exact representations of color, tone, and light. Impressionist art is characterized by the use of small touches of pure color, painting out-of-doors in order to catch the essence of a fleeting time of day, and an objective depiction of contemporary life.

Refers to a style of Greek vase painting that developed from the Black-figure style. It appeared in Athens around 530 BCE and spread to other areas of Greece, southern Italy, Etruria, and elsewhere in the Mediterranean area, until it disappeared in the third century BCE. The style is characterized by a particular technique, which involves the use of refined slip and a two-phase firing process to create a black ground through sintering, with figures reserved in red. The details of the figures are more fluid than in the Black-figure style, and are typically drawn with a brush, using both a defined, black relief line and a more dilute line that varies in color from dark gold to black.

Refers to the Greek style of sculpture produced by Praxiteles during the 4th century BCE.  Identified with female figures, especially the Aphrodite of Cnidos, it is characterized by more slender proportions, sinuous curves, and smooth modeling producing shadows that cast a soft haze over the planes of the figure.

Refers to the last of three great periods of Egyptian civilization from about 1540 to 1075 BCE comprising the Eighteenth Dynasty through the Twentieth Dynasty. The period is characterized by a flowering of the arts including the introduction of colossal statues, a new interest in painting, a high degree of craftsmanship in both royal and private sculpture, and elegant decorative and luxury arts. Notable architectural works include chapels, rock-cut tombs, and monumental stone temples for worship of the gods attesting to the rising power of the priesthood. A brief revolutionary episode especially in representational art occurred during the reign of Akhenaten in the Amarna period when many existing conventions were reversed and more freedom of expression was allowed.

Refers to the period and style of art, predominantly sculpture and architecture, that coincided with the reign of Septimus Severus from 193 to 211 CE and his successors in the mid-3rd century CE. In sculpture, the style reflects changes in fashion such as close-trimmed beards and corkscrew curls. The period also witnessed extensive building projects, such as the Baths of Caracalla.

Refers to any English-Viking cultural interaction during the middle ages. Anglo-Scandinavian also more narrowly denotes the period and style in York, England between the death of Eric Bloodaxe in 954 and the arrival of the Normans in 1068 during which Viking influence coexisted with English rule.

Styles and periods of art and architecture during the late Renaissance; flourished at the royal palace at Fontainebleau. Describes work in a variety of media, including painting, sculpture, stuccowork and printmaking produced from the 1530s to the first decade of the 17th century, primarily in France.

Refers to the Early Bronze Age period and culture that developed in Wessex, England. It is characterized by distinctive burial mounds over inhumations or cremations, and rich, varied grave goods, notably decorated pottery, metalwork, weapons, including daggers, and personal ornaments made of non-local materials.

Refers to the culture of Armenia roughly corresponding to the area of modern Armenia and central and eastern Turkey, particularly between the 4th and 7th centuries during the so called classical period of Armenian art.
Nationalilty, style, and culture of an ancient district of southern Asia Minor.

Culture and styles of a bronze age people who existed from 2600-2000 BCE in what is now the United Arab Emirates and Northern Oman; named after the island of Umm an-Nar. The culature is known for collective, monumental, circular graves sometimes decorated with reliefs characterized by their simplicity, as well as for decorated soft stone vessels with parallels in Mesopotamia and Persia.
Periods related to Levantine cultures.
Albums made up of mounted photographs, with or without identifying information.
Announcements required by law to be given for a specific purpose or case; typically required to be published in a newspaper or posted in a court house.
Formal letters recommending a person as worthy or suitable or merely as introduction.
Groups of persons delegated to consider, investigate, or take action upon and usually to report concerning some matter or business.
Groups of sovereign states and their dependencies associated by their own choice and linked with common objectives and interests. For the concept of nations or states, use "nations."
Commissions which are in charge of maintaining local parks.
Collections owned and maintained by private individuals, outside of the public domain.
Organizations who purpose is to advance the propagation and study of cultivated plants.
In the traditional Indian caste system, members of the highest group of castes, originally that of priests and scholars.
Artists or craftspeople who have completed apprenticeship but have not attained master status in a guild.
Clerics who observe a simple rule embodying the common duties of and afford mutual assistance to their ministry, but who make no profession and follow no religious rule.
People who serve as hosts of yaksas nature spirits.
Those who study or specialise in technology.
Scientists trained and working in the field dealing with communication processes and automatic control systems in both living organisms and machines.
People washing themselves with water, or immersed in water. For people actively propelling themselves through the water by natural means, use "swimmers."

Members of an academy or other learning institution, particularly teachers or scholars belonging to a body of higher education or learned society dedicated to the promotion of art, the humanities, or science.
Writers of short literary compositions on single subjects, often presenting the personal view of the author.
Experts in the science of communication studied through the interpretation of signs and symbols as they operate in language and other fields.
Those who trap or snare wild animals, usually for their fur, as an occupation or trade.
Islamic legal scholars solicited by judges to weigh in on cases. Although non-binding, the muftis' reponse is considered authoritative and upheld in most instances.
Persons who create written records for the objects in a museum collection in order to identify the object and to record information about them such as provenance, condition, or value.
Groups of people, specializing in different crafts, creating motion pictures.
Photographers whose work is primarily art, not primarily documentary.
Refers to people in the commercial printing trade. For artists who make prints, see "printmakers."
Founders, casters, or makers of barrels and other metal parts for guns.
Those whose occupation is to create, co-ordinate, or promote the fashions or designs for a firm's commodities, usually in the context of the retail clothing industry.
People employed by a national government or ruler to conduct official negotiations and maintain political, economic, and social relations with other nations or international organizations.
Chief magistrates of a city or borough.
Leaders, including Saracen or Arab princes, who were governors of a province; also military commanders.
Persons who sharpen tools by grinding them, or who grinds metal, glass, or stone to shape or smooth it.
Those who apply a glaze to things, such as pottery, leather, bricks, or fur.
Persons who coat or plate articles with a film of metal, usually of silver or gold.
Metalworkers who form items of platinum, a lustrous, malleable, ductile, silvery white metal.
Those who, in an auction or competition for a contract, offer a specific sum as the price they will pay or charge.
People or corporate bodies who own or run manufacturing plants for making furniture.
People who sell jewelry, which comprises personal ornaments made of precious materials.
Architects or engineers who specialize in designing fortresses; typically used in historical contexts.
Artisans who paint surfaces in imitation of woodgrain.
Persons engaged in lithography, in which the design is deposited on a plate or stone with a greasy substance that will accept pigment for printing.

People or corporate bodies who design the plan and features of gardens, which are open space where flowers, shrubs, trees, vegetables, or fruits are grown. Garden designers may be amateurs or professionals. For those who practice the branch of architecture dealing with the design of the scenic environment, including plants and surrounding roads and structures, use "landscape architects."
Bits used to sink blind holes in timber.

People whose profession focuses on the arrangement and layout of spaces and architectural details inside architectural structures or parts of structures. For people whose profession focuses on the designs, colors, and placement of moveable works located within buildings' spaces, such as furniture or accessories, and perhaps also on the design of the space itself, prefer "interior designers." For those who focus exclusively on the color, textures, furnishings, accessories, etc. of interior spaces, use "interior decorators."
Persons who build or work with concrete.

Devices used to secure a metal cap-like plate with pins, which is typically marked with the identify of the vinyard or other information, over the bung of a wine barrel so that it is sealed and ready for transport. The device is usually spring-loaded.
Joined tools with a pair of jaws and handles; used to grip objects.
Large heavy hammers that are usually wielded with both hands and used especially for driving stakes and breaking stone.
Temporary elevated platforms or structures for supporting workmen, materials, and tools.
Disks of hard felt or other fiber materials meant to be mounted on a revolving driver such as a drill for the purposes of polishing or buffing a surface.
Metal hand tools with a cutting edge at one end, driven by a hammer or mallet; or now often electrically driven, used in dressing, shaping, or working wood, stone, or metal.
Knives that are designed to be used primarily or entirely as weapons.
Any devices intended to collect solar radiation and convert it into energy.
Implements used for stirring up a fire.
Devices of varied design used to compress cork stoppers and insert them into the necks of bottles. These normally also vacuum the air from the bottle as the cork is inserted.
Any clamps set by means of a screw; especially those used in woodworking which have two parallel jaws for holding together work to be pressed.
Hammers having a round face with a chamfered neck and a cross peen which tapers to a rounded tip; used as a general-purpose hammer.
Oblong cases with slat sides and funnel-shaped net used as a trap for catching lobsters.
Long slender tapering rods to which lines are attached for angling.
Sofas that can be converted into beds.
Beds, generally of the 19th-century, which when folded closed, looked to be an exact representation of another piece of furniture, such as a bureau, a dresser, or a cabinet.

Cases or shelflike surfaces, usually of a height convenient for a person standing before them, as in a kitchen or store, or sitting on stools in front of them, as in a restaurant or bar. For small tables or chests with the top marked for counting money, sometimes with a cupboard below, use the more specific "counter tables."
Popular term for tall kitchen cabinets mass-produced during the early 20th century; usually oak, with such features as an enameled work surface, storage bins, and a flour sifter.
Chairs having interlaced ornamental backs, and that may be perforated or cut in low relief, usually in geometric patterns.

Chairs designed to be used in dentists' offices that allow the patient to be positioned in various ways for dental work. These are usually accessorized with various appliances. Modern dental chairs are equipped with pneumatics for raising or lowering the chair itself.

Candles held by members of a group in processions. Processional candles may be of various designs and sizes; the term includes both the candle and the fixtures that secure them, usually with candles mounted to a hand grip or pole, often within a protective shade or glass shield.
Electrical lamps with increased voltage for sustained illumination while taking photographs.
Refers to small decorative screens, usually Chinese or Japanese, made to stand on tables. Table screens can be either single-panel screens or folding screens.
Large, soft frameless chairs resembling a beanbag; typically a clothlike plastic shell filled with plastic chips, that molds itself readily to the contour of the occupant.
Lamps with a wick supported on a small platform, such as cork or wood, which floats on the surface of the oil.

Lamps designed for use in mines; especially cast iron lamps often with a circular lidded font containing a single wick channel or tube and a D-shaped bail on pivots terminating in a spike or shallow pans with wick channels or supports and half bails terminating in hooks or spikes; also coffeepot-shaped spout lamps of tinned sheet iron worn on miners' caps.
Gas light chandeliers supported by one or more hollow rods, through which gas may be fed to the burners.
Lamps that use animal fat or lard as fuel for illumination.

Cap- or hood-like devices, usually of brass or glass and with openings in both ends, that fit onto the top of a candle. As the wax melts the candle follower retains the wick in a central position and keeps the wax from dripping down the side of the candle.
Hunting weapons consisting of a fixed or detachable barbed head mounted on a staff, thrown by hand or fired from a harpoon gun, used against large fish and marine mammals.

Fencing swords, lighter than épées, having a light, very flexible, quadrangular blade with a button on the end, generally used for practice or for recreational and competitive fencing. Since the 1930s, the button has been made as a spring-loaded contact device acting on pressure to score hits by means of electrical signals. Formerly, the term was used for all swords with blunted points.
Describes ancient or Bronze Age forms of one-edged dagger, having long, heavy blades.
Parts or components of staff weapons.
Long-handled wooden Maori clubs or fighting staffs that have a sharp tip at one end with carved or feather decoration.
Candleholders with a single candle socket set on a flat saucer or traylike base. For candleholders with a single candle socket mounted on a support with a widened base or foot, use "candlesticks."
Candleholders with a hook and a spike so that they could either be hung or stuck in a timber or wall of a mine.

Fasteners made of two or more parts, often of metal, and consisting of separate interlocking hooking and catching elements that hold together two or more objects or complimentary parts of the same object.
Pins used to fasten garments, resembling a large safety pin with an enlarged catch plate; often elaborately ornamented.

Lightweight helmets of pith or cork covered with cloth with a round crown and fixed brim that slopes downward; worn in tropical regions as a protection against the sun. First worn by the British army in India in the mid-19th century and made with the pith of the sola plant.
Round bronze shields furnished with a sturdy boss, used by Roman mounted troops from the 7th or 6th century BCE.

Armor pieces for the front of a horse's or camel's head, often with side plates to protect the cheeks and often decorated to match the armor of the rider. Known in classical Greece and from the 12th century on throughout Europe, the Middle East, Turkey, North Africa, and Japan, they were commonly made of either steel or leather, though the Japanese also used papier-maché and wood, the Ottoman Turks copper, and the Sudanese mainly brass.
Cannons in use from the 15th to the 17th century, produced in various sizes and calibers but typically long in relation to their caliber and longer and lighter than bombards.

Refers to paintings on wooden supports, including smaller portable paintings and medium-sized paintings, such as altarpieces, for which several planks of wood were joined to form a larger panel. The term is typically used to refer to paintings on a wooden support in Western art, generally dating from ancient Greece and Rome through the Renaissance, after which time canvas became the standard support for paintings in this size range. Panel paintings are still common today in Greek and Russian Orthodox icons.
Paintings made by the technique of fresco painting, which is a mural painting technique in which permanent pigments, dispersed in water, are painted on freshly laid lime plaster.
Sections that are set apart from, but adjacent to, a main view of the structure or object through which the section is taken.
Drawings done early in a design process for art or architecture. They are typically more finished than sketches.
Drawings executed in chalk, which is a fine-grained limestone, or soft, earthy form of calcium carbonate.

Appendages, usually of iron or brass, fastened to a door and hinged so that it may be made to strike against a metal plate or the door itself, to attract the attention of those within. Door knockers are usually placed on exterior doors.
Devices on the interior surfaces of cabinet doors that employ the attraction of magnets to secure the door in a closed position.
Describes knobbed locks designed for doors opening from corridors into interior spaces.
Ornamental gravitating catches used to hold opened shutters back against the exterior surface surrounding a window.
Hooks mounted in fireplaces on which pots or kettles may be suspended over an open fire.
Parts of strikes that project at an angle beyond the face of the door jamb to receive the beveled latch bolt and conduct it into the strike's recess.
Keys that operate auxiliary locks that have a spring bolt operated from the outside by the key only and from the inside by a knob.
Illusionistic paintings of the 16th to 18th century that appear to extend the actual architecture of an interior, usually on ceilings, sometimes on walls.
Documents which evidence the time, place, and court before which an alien is admitted to the rights and status of citizenship.
Books with blanks on which those attending a funeral may sign their names and condolences.
Discourses advancing an original point of view as a result of research, especially as a requirement for an academic degree.

Maps displaying the distribution of a characteristic, such as precipitation, vegetation, or another feature, by using lines that connect points of equal value. They are distinct from "contour maps" in that they typically do not show the distribution of elevation of the landscape.

Prints made from a direct-process duplication technique using gelatin. The gelatin process uses a master or transfer paper upon which the image to be duplicated is rendered with a special ink or ribbon. This master is then pressed against a moist gelatinous plate, to which the image is transferred in reverse. Sheets of paper pressed against this ink-imbibed gelatin receive the image. This may be achieved either manually on the plate or flatbed or a rotary machine. Multicolored prints may thus be produced in one operation. Prints pulled in this way usually number under 200.
Manuscripts written on papyrus.
Engraved inscriptions inside rings, often short poems.

Labels applied to crates, usually wooden produce crates, to identify the contents and the grower, maker, or distributor of the fruit, vegetables, nuts, or other produce contained in the crates. Crate labels typically employ art and graphic design; they are often considered valuable by museums and collectors. The art of crate labels flourished in the late-19th through mid-20th century.
Unique marks stamped in ink on the unsigned prints and drawings remaining in an artist's studio after her or his death, to legally authenticate them as works of the artist, in preparation for sale.
Posters of approximately 41 x 81 inches, corresponding to three of the original one-sheet posters.
Documents pertaining to money matters.
Certified reports by election officers on the outcome vote in an election.
Rough or approximate calculations of cost or value, such as statements of price for which certain work will be done by one who is willing to undertake it.
The records relating to the authorization, computation, distribution, and payment of wages and salaries.

Documents that give expression to a legal act or agreement, for the purpose of creating, securing, modifying, or terminating a right, or for the purpose of furnishing evidence of a right. For documents having legal relevance in general, use "legal documents."
Specifications, often accompanying preliminary drawings, that briefly list the materials and finishes to be used in a building project and serve as the basis for preliminary cost estimates.

Documents maintained by or relating to a particular mosque and its activities, including for many public functions; religious, political, social, and educational. Schools and libraries and courts of justice were attached to mosques until the introduction of secular law into many Islamic countries in modern times, so records of these functions may be included.
A list of questions and answers posted on a web site or included with computer software for users to consult. Originally used by newsgroups to prevent repetitive postings of information.
Documents comprised of collected instructions designed to inform the performance of specific tasks.

Letters, reports, or other brief written communications that communicate news, particularly those written by societies or buisiness organizations. Historically referred to serial publications consisting of one or a few printed sheets containing news and information of interest to the general public or to a special group.
Periodicals in an electronic format that use the Internet as a publication method.

Maori feather cloaks, distinctive by a style using feathers all over the cloak, popular in the latter half of the 19th century. Feathers had previously been incorporated into the weaving of cloaks, but usually only in the borders.
Sleeved coats, sometimes made of leather. Persian in origin and worn there by males of high social status, in ancient Greece kandys are reserved for women.

African sculptures that are in the form of a mask, but smaller in size, not intended to be worn on the face, and found predominantly among groups in Liberia and the Democratic Republic of Congo. For miniature versions of masks, use "miniature" + "masks".

Models or replicas of an artist’s model around which a mold is formed for bronze casting. It is made by the foundry in order to preserve the artist’s model. A foundry model may also be used as a reference for the finishing of a bronze for the purpose of quality control.
Refers to a type of 17th-century jug in the form of two rings which cross one another at right angles. They are made of Rhenish stoneware. The term literally means 'sausage jugs.'
A neck ornament or chain worn around the neck, similar to a torque.
Long, straight pins with a decorative head and sometimes a sheath for encasing the point.
Finger rings made with a signet or seal and used from the earliest times for the utilitarian purpose of authenticating a document by impressing the seal, or later for ornamental wear.

Headdresses worn by Haudenosaunee men, consisting of a structure of wood and leather fitted to the head with a variety of feathers attached to the top. Haudenosaunee Confederacy members arrange these feathers differently to represent their specific community. For example, Seneca men have one feather pointing upwards from the rest of the assemblage. Sometimes a band of beads or wampum is also included across the brow of the headdress.
Medals bearing images that satirize public figures or events.
Men's hats of varying form made of beaver fur; especially used for those worn from the 17th to 19th century. Prefer "beavers" for men's top hats made of beaver fur.

Paper-thin golden diadems of various shapes worn by elite Nahua men and women in postclassic central Mexico. They also adorned the mortuary bundles of tlahtohqueh (rulers). They are mentioned among the golden items melted down by the Spanish during the invasion of Tenochtitlan.
Pronged sticks or round or thin unpronged flat sticks made of wood, metal, or plastic and used to stir mixed drinks.

Beakers characterized by having a stem or protrusion at one end but no foot, so that when they are empty they must rest on their side or on the rim like a rhyton or stirrup cup; of a type found in various forms in Germany and the Netherlands.

Low drinking glasses having a short thick heavy stem and a heavy foot, and made with bowls of various shapes. They were used in private clubs, drinking societies, and at ceremonial occasions. So called from the custom of rapping the foot of the glass on the table which, in concert, sounded like gunfire.
Tall, thin wine glasses with a small conical bowl, a very thin stem, which can easily be snapped between the fingers, and a stemmed foot.
The protective plates that surround keyholes, light switches, and doorknobs, for example.
Wood joints of various designs where members overlap or interlock end-to-end; often employed when structural elements are required in longer lengths than the available material.

Large musical bows of the Yowabu of Benin, having a half-calabash resonator which rests on the player's chest. The single string is plucked with the right hand and stopped by a rectangular plaque held in the left hand.

The projecting handles of chordophones such as lutes, violins, viols, and guitars, carrying the fingerboard and held by the player with one hand as the other plucks or bows the strings. They may be separate pieces attached by glue or nails, or integral to the body of the instrument.
Maori wooden trumpets; made from a long, hollowed piece of wood, having a bell-shaped end; held together with vine.
Small bagpipes of France, especially those of aristocratic design which achieved popularity among the French nobility in the 17th and early 18th centuries.

Vertical flutes of the Katanga people of Zimbabwe. They are made with stopped canes, which are fit into a hollow nsala fruit shell. The cane has two finger holes, and the flute is played by blowing across a hole in the shell. Different from "khumbgwes," which has three finger holes.
German Renaissance double-reed wind instruments; wind cap shawms in the soprano range with a reedy tone.
Shallow, usually circular dishes from which food is eaten.

Plates of a special form used by the ancient Greeks, having a central depression and sometimes a turned-down rim, used for serving fish. The central depression was used to collect the juice or sauce in which the fish was served. Such fish plates may be made of stone, ceramic, or another material. They may be decorated with highly accurate representations of fish and other marine life. They were popular in Greece and its colonies in South Italy from the 4th century BCE. Athenian painters always oriented the bellies of the fish toward the rim of the plate while southern Italian painters positioned them with the bellies towards the center. Some fish plates have depictions of seafood arranged around a central dip for sauce. Androkydes of Kyzikos was one of the few fish plate painters to sign his work.
Spirally grooved, conical pulley and chain arrangements in timepieces designed to counteract the diminishing power of uncoiling mainsprings.

Timepieces, with one or more sweephands that can be started and stopped at will, used for precise measurement of elapsed time. To refer to timepieces that tell the time of day in addition to these functions, use "chronographs."

Musical instruments designed for recording purposes by Augustus Stroh of London around 1901. The body consists of a long, narrow piece of wood or aluminum plate, the top of which serves as a fingerboard for the strings, and a flexible membrane to which a metal bell like that of an aerophone is attached, mounted at one side of the bridge; concert models occasionally have two bells.
Drums consisting of a membrane stretched across a number of poles stuck in the ground and beaten with a stick.
Small portable organs in which the sound is produced by one or more sets of beating reeds, supplied with air from a pair of bellows and played from a keyboard.
Small floor-standing reed organs invented in England in the early 1830s.
Golden bells. The term also refers to a leg band with many bells. Part of the array of several Nahua deities including Huixtohcihuatl, Tezcatlipoca, and Quetzalcoatl in postclassic central Mexico.

Metal percussion instruments, often in bronze or brass, used on ships to give signals for the timing of watches, in case of fog, during anchoring maneuvers, or as a general alarm. Traditionally these have the name of the ship they are used on engraved or cast on their surface.
Rattles in the form of elaborate wood or bronze staffs from the Benin kingdom and other Edo peoples in Nigeria.
Large and fretless acoustic bass guitars with six strings, predominant in mariachi music.

Mechanically bowed portable chordophones having a set of melody and drone strings, a resin-coated wood wheel rotated by a crank to bow the strings, and a keyboard with tangents that bear on the melody strings when depressed.
Top rails of chairbacks that are shaped like yokes.
Boards forming the end of anything, especially a bed.
Tapered furniture legs that are square in section.
Japanese prints of a standard size about 15 3/4 by 10 1/2 inches.
Small Japanese prints produced in luxury editions to present to friends to commemorate special occasions.

Prints made by the "steel engraving (printing process)," in which plates of steel or steel-faced copper are used, having replaced the use of less durable copper plates in the early 19th century. Steel engraving was introduced in 1792 by Jacob Perkins, an American inventor, originally for banknote printing. They are often distinguished by the use of engraving, etching, and the roulette. For documents produced in long runs with precise replication, use "siderographs."

Refers to lithographs made from zinc plates by the process of zincography. The term is adopted from the French who make a distinction between lithographs made on stone and those made on zinc; the two types of print can rarely be distinguished from their appearance and so the distinction is rarely made.
Prints made using the process of white line engraving.
Photomechanical prints produced by the process called Woodburytype.
Clocks designed so that as much of their movements as possible are visible; devised in France in the mid-18th century and popular in England during the 19th century.
Upright postlike stands, usually of wood or metal, having pegs or hooks around the top from which to hang coats, hats, or other clothing.
Semicircular tables, generally used as dining tables.
Describes furniture made in related units, so that pieces such as wardrobes, chests, cupboards, bookcases, or writing desks, made in standard sizes, may be conveniently added to and rearranged.
Inclined platforms fixed to the top of lecterns, and sometimes on altars, writing desks, or other furniture on which an open book may be supported.
Small writing tables of various forms, designed for women. They may have a relatively delicate form and distinctive features, such as a wide opening to accommodate ladies' skirts when seated.
