Weavings done as a sample to display types of borders, patterns, and colors.
The principal or central rug as arranged in the traditional manner on the floor of the main chambers of important Islamic homes.
Rugs with an uncut loop pile often at different levels to give a sculpted effect.
Rugs made with a rag or list weft, often woven in strips and sewn together.
Lighting devices which emit strong directional light. Often used in photography and filmmaking to illuminate the subject.

Staff weapons having a broad, tapering triangular blade with two upturned lugs or wings at the base, used as thrusting and cutting weapons but also extremely popular as ceremonial weapons from the 16th to the 19th century, and still occasionally used as such today.

Object genre including a wide variety of items used in a domestic environment, excluding large furniture. Can include draperies, rugs, decorative items, small furnishings, wallcoverings, and many other types of things, both decorative and functional.

Any of the salts of magnesium and phosphate, which may appear in  monobasic, dibasic, or tribasic form. Deposits of magnesium phosphates bobierrite, newberyte and struvite are found in ivory artifacts and excavated mammoth and elephant tusks.

Ridges of excess metal that can occur when molten metal enters cracks in the refractory mold (both outer and core). Flashing most often rises perpendicularly to the inner or outer wall of bronze, although a gap in consecutive layers of the mold material may result in thin flanges of excess bronze that spread parallel to the metal wall. This type of feature can appear on the cast’s internal or external surfaces (respectively called “core flashing” and “mold flashing”), and in the latter case is often removed during fettling. Flashing may also occur along seam lines of an ill-fitted piece mold.
Funerary figures, similar to the cloth-covered funerary figures of the Bwende, known as niombo, but smaller in size and not as widely used.
Process in which matter printed by letterpress is dusted with powder and heated to make the lettering rise, thus giving an engraved appearance, as on business cards and stationery.

Sheet metal seams having a bottom plate with a turned edge that overlaps the side plate; the seam may be secured by welding, soldering, or riveting at the overlapping joint. An example of a lap bottom seam is the seam at the bottom of a tin or steel can.
In Indian art or architecture, a dramatic figure-composition.
Rubber cushions, usually filled with compressed air, which fit around the wheels of a vehicle.

Spectroscopic flow visualization technique that uses ultrashort pulse lasers for the study of dynamics on extremely short time scales;  fluorescent markers are excited by a laser beam; used to make visible disturbances that occur in fluid flow.

Containers, generally rectangular and shaped like a box, incorporating a translucent screen illuminated from within, typically used for tracing or for viewing or displaying transparencies and films such as slides and  x-rays, or for the shadowless illumination of small objects for photography or another purpose; portable light tables.

Buildings housing museums containing collections dealing with the properties of natural objects, plants, or animals, such as preserved specimens of birds, mammals, insects, and plants; rocks, minerals, and fossils.
The state that an information object possesses in the present; that is valid in a present context.
Those who study literary trends and movements over time, as well as the development of various branches or genres of literature.
Catalogs listing items in a collection or highlights of a collection in a museum.
Rectangular small cards placed in between documents, used to label collections of papers.
Ornamental geometric pattern in Persian and Islamic art, comprising a knot-pattern having many symmetrical axes, with star-shaped knots surrounded by geometric figures of various types.
Includes articles in publications expressing the opinions of their editors or publishers and statements on radio, film or television expressing the opinions of a station, network, or individual.
People who make decorative trimmings, and often apply them, to costume, upholstery, or other items.

People who report on, write about, analyze, or evaluate music, which is the art concerned with the combining of vocal or instrumental sounds in measured time to communicate emotions, ideas, or states of mind.
Those who study and work in the field dealing with the care, reading, and interpretation of ancient documents written on papyrus.
Members of Muslim religious fraternities.
Drills with one or more spiral cutting grooves; used to drill holes in metal, wood, and plastic.
Protective or restraining belts.
General term for the tools, equipment, and supplies used to facilitate the preparation of materials made from fibers and woven fabrics.
Devices that with a mould or stamp create concave or convex areas in a surface, often paper.
Refers to a type of oinochoe featuring a wide-beaked mouth, offset neck, and ovoid body.
Ancient Greek vessels for the storage of liquids usually having an ovoid body with high shoulders, a short neck, wide mouth, two side handles, and sometimes a cover. Generally smaller than amphorae.
Smaller version of any bag in fashion, usually beaded, sequinned, or embroidered, or of some glamorous fabric such as kid, silver, bronze, or gold.
Vessels used to contain foods or seasonings that add additional flavor.
Small boxes intended to hold comfits, which are tiny, strongly scented sweets used as breath fresheners.
Storage containers for food.
Type of bottle that preceded the decanter and was used to bring wine to the table from the cask; made in a variety of forms and materials such as stoneware, delftware, and glass.
Ancient Greek cups similar to mastoi but with a narrow flat foot, flaring lip, and one, two, or no handles.
Cups intended for one use and then to be thrown away. Materials are typically paper or plastic.
Receptacles, often cylindrical, and with or without lids that are intended to hold pipe cleaners or other tools for smoking pipes.
Lidded containers made to store medication until a particular time, set using a dial. These are often circular in shape.
Spherical containers used to hold cut roses and othe rflowers, sometimes having a pierced cover or a removable wire mesh through which the stems are inserted.
Instruments attached to wheels for measuring distance traveled, as of vehicles or surveyors' instruments.
Containers of varying form but having a perforated top, used to contain and dispense the fine sand sprinkled on wet ink to blot it.
Wooden buckets, typically with a drainage or bung hole in the bottom, used to pickle food in brine.
Fitted material cases that go on a mattress for protection under sheets.

Quilts consisting of a variety of patterns, the idea being to show as many as possible. Sometimes the work of a notable quilt maker who wished to pass on samples of her best or most difficult designs.

Quilts incorporating a large number of names, autographs or signatures. Often made in order to raise funds for a church or charity, with the subscriber paying a small fee to have his or her name embroidered or inked on the quilt.

Tall and slender vessels with an elongated neck and a flaring mouth, usually in the form of an amphora with two handles, but sometimes in the form of a hydria with three handles. It was often given as gifts at weddings since it held water used for a bride's ritual bath before her wedding. The term is Greek for "bath bringer." Since many girls died before getting married, the loutrophoros symbolized the wedding that she missed and so was often used as a grave marker. The form was common in black-figure pottery of the late 6th century BCE.
Double-headed drums of Uganda. They are found in different sizes, and although they are double-headed, only one side is played.
Boat-shaped containers, sometimes partly covered by a lid, for holding incense before it is placed in a censer.
Hinged plastic cases used to store compact disks.

Boxes used to house Egyptian funerary ushabti figures in tomb settings. Evolving from miniature coffins, ushabti boxes became larger during the New Kingdom, housing multiple figures, and were decorated with funerary scenes.
Relatively small, portable bags or cages used to transport small animals such as domestic cats, lap dogs, miniature pigs, ferrets, chickens. etc.
Standing baskets or basketlike containers for wastepaper and small items of trash.
Any of various types of receptacle used for storing loose items, components, or foodstuffs.
Small palettes designed to mix cosmetics. Usually made of stone or ceramic. Best known as works from ancient Egypt, elsewhere in the Middle East, Greece, Rome, and Asia.
Improvised bundles containing clothes and possessions, particularly bed-rolls carried by itinerant people. Likely an altered form of "bundle."

Bottoms of glass cups or bowls decorated with designs in engraved gold leaf backed by a protective layer of fused, sometimes tinted, glass; they were first made during the Roman Empire from the third to the early fifth centuries.
Refers to any container specifically designed for protecting and/or transporting chemical instruments.

Scales having a fixed fulcrum and a movable counterweight whose distance along a horizontal graduated beam is moved to balance an object suspended from a point, usually on a pan or hook, set off-center; for scales of similar form but with a fixed counterweight and movable fulcrum, use "desemers."
Devices to weigh letters or packages to determine the postage due.
Single-string spike fiddles of the Fula people of the Gambia, having a hemispherical wood resonator with one or two holes in the back.
Instruments used to measure the amount of dew formed on a given surface.
Devices for measuring thermal expansion and dilation of liquids or solids.
Astronomical instruments used for measuring angular distances, especially the altitude of celestial bodies, in order to determine the longitude and latitude of ships at sea.
Clocks that play notes or tunes at set intervals or on request.

Small plate or saucer-shaped item, often having or mounted on a handle and made of precious metal, used in Christian services during the distribution of the eucharist to prevent crumbs from the host from falling to the ground as the celebrant places the host in the mouth of the faithful. For the general term referring to any type of metal objects used for the liturgy, use "church plate."
Networks of horizontal and vertical lines used to guide the layout of graphic material.
Titles written or impressed on the spine of a volume, sometimes a shortened form of the title appearing on the cover. Distinguished from "binder's titles."

Bamboo duct flutes of Indonesia, open at the bottom and closed with a natural node at the top; a notch is cut in the node and in the tube just below it, and a narrow bamboo ring is tied over the upper end to guide the player's breath.
Devices that use changes in the electrical resistance of wire to measure pressure.
Instruments used for measuring electrical resistance and calibrated in ohms or megohms.

Devices partially composed of a differential thermometer and used to calculate variations in conditions of the sky, particularly solar radiation, and the resulting changes in temperature. Invented by Sir John Leslie.
Instruments for measuring temperature by utilizing the variation of the physical properties of substances according to their thermal states.

Precision surveying instruments for measuring horizontal and sometimes vertical angles and consisting of a sighting telescope mounted so that it is free to rotate horizontally and vertically and accompanying graduated scales to measure the angle of rotation.

Wooden rods cut to the proposed clear height between finished floors and ceilings of buildings and often marked with subdivisions to aid in the laying out of, for example, door trims, masonry courses, or stair risers.
Liurgical containers designed to serve as receptacles for a liquid or other substance.

Cardboard or plastic boxes used typically for storage or shipping, especially those which are relatively small and that when filled with merchandise are enclosed in a larger or stronger container for transport.
Funnel-shaped drinking vessels, of varied manufacture, often of ceramic material as well as glass.

A feebly basic compound (C5H4N4O2) allied to uric acid, found in various organs and secretions of the animal body and from plants, that forms a lemon-yellow compound with nitric acid. It is derived from guanine and hypoxanthine, and yields uric acid on oxidation.
Culture of the the Semitic tribe or nation that is, according to tradition, descended from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. In modern usage, it refers to the culture of the Israelites.
Badges or plaques, often metal, attached to the pole of a processional lantern, bearing the heraldic device or other emblem to identify the participants in the procession.
Decorative protective metal pieces attached to the corners of the cover of a book.

Highly simplified or conventionalized pictures that stand for the thing pictured; may be used as writing signs corresponding to individual words or phonetic elements in a language. Use also for certain prehistoric pictures and linear designs whose meanings are uncertain.
Baskets created with lids that cover the opening.
Material comprising the hollow, sharp spines of a porcupine, echidna, or hedgehog. Used in Native American ornamental embroidery and other decorative purposes.
Lidded vessels used for boiling or heating, usually oval or rectangular and often made of tin-lined copper.
Silver or cupronickel coins valued at fifty cents and issued since 1794; found predominantly in the United States and Canada.
Clappers of Naples, Italy, which consist of three mallets inserted into a wooden frame. The center mallet is fixed so the others can strike it on either side.
Coinlike objects made of wood, originally produced as emergency money then only for commemorative, souvenir, or advertising purposes.
Lighting technique providing additional quality and quantity of illumination to supplement the general lighting system.
Utensils used to transfer food items from one container to another.

Valve bugles introduced by Adolphe Sax of Paris in 1843 and patented by him in 1845, having a moderately conical bore and medium-sized bell; made in nine different sizes from sopranino to contrabass, they have retained their popularity as band instruments to the present day.
Ankle-length garments of various types, but usually having long, narrow sleeves; worn especially members of the clergy and others participating in church services.
Long, loose-fitting garments with hoods and usually long sleeves, worn over other garments, traditionally by men, chiefly in Morocco.
Devices for removal of magnetic iron metals from inert materials such as foodstuffs.
Receptacles with crossed arms, often adjustable and usually with a spirit lamp in the center, used to support dishes and keep them warm while protecting the surface below from the heat.

Utensils combining the functions of a fork and spoon having one end with tines and the other with a small shallow bowl. Of a type known in the 16th through 18th centuries and used for eating preserved fruits and sweetmeats.

Knives in a place setting that are designed and used for consuming the main meal, typically excluding dessert. For similar knives in a more formal setting, in which there may be a number of other knives of various design and for various purposes, use "entrée knives" for the knife intended for the main course.
Spoons distinguished by their bowls, which are either oblong or of conventional shape with a flat base; used to eat ice cream.
Utensils with a spatula-shaped blade and no cutting edge, used for serving meat from a platter.
Implements with a round or oval bowl affixed to a handle, used to stir food or transfer it between vessels.
Mechanical devices for removing the shells from nuts.
Physical manifestations of messages sent via telex transmissions, printed by teleprinters that recieve messages via public telecommunication lines.
Devices consisting of a rotary beater and a vessel intended for making mayonnaise.
A script of cursive minuscules in use as the everyday Roman script beginning in the 3rd century and persisting in some areas until the 8th century.

Sound device in which a photoelectric cell is used to scan a text, which then produces electric signals that are converted into audible sound. The instrument today is generally used to enable the blind to read, although the device had its origins with the inventions of Austrian artist and Dadaist Raoul Hausmann in the 1920s, who was preoccupied with unifying the senses, and changing light into sound. It was patented in 1935 as a "calculating device".

Flat metal discs, shaped like phonograph records, which have pins partially punched out of them and bent at right angles. They are used in disc-playing music boxes which became popular from the late 19th century.
Bands, originating in Trinidad and Tobago, featuring steel drums.
Sets of armor for the leg.

In the glass trade, a type of art glass developed and produced by the Württembergische Metallwarenfabrik, Göppingen, ca. 1930, characterized by decorations created through inlaid patches or strips of color, often in combination with patterned air bubbles.

A natural fibrous protein that is the primary building block for epidermal tissue. Keratin contains all of the common amino acids, but has higher amounts of cystine than other fibrous structural proteins. Soft keratins are found in the external layers of skin, wool, hair, feathers, while hard keratins are the major components of tortoise shells, nails, hoofs, scales, bills, and claws. In addition to usage in their natural form, since the mid-1600s keratin has been molded into buttons, combs, and buckles.
Hollow vessels into which pastry may be pressed in order to give it the form of the vessel.
Black- or green-glass bottles of quart and pint sizes, used primarily for beers, porter, cider, spring water, and other popular potables.

Bottles of varying size, shape, and style made to contain medicine, particularly those intended to be taken home by customers of an apothecary or sold elsewhere; examples include collectible patent medicine bottles. For bottles used to store larger quantities of medicine, as used in an apothecary and labeled with the names of standard medicines, use "apothecary bottles."
Hand or rifle grenades containing a filling which generates a gas or smoke that causes tears, sneezing, and nausea in the victims, used primarily for riot or crowd control.
Wallpapers decorated with large nonrepeating scenes, usually of landscape, literary, or mythological subjects, which create a panoramic effect.
Solid spherical projectiles lacking explosive charge that are launched from guns of any size.
Thin silver coins issued by Constantine in the 320s, used until the late 4th century, and reintroduced during the Byzantine period between about 700 and the early 11th century.

Small ornamental mats used from the late 19th century onward to protect the backs and arms of upholstered seating and reclining furniture from wear or soil. For earlier similar mats, use "antimacassars."
Refers to any of various French gold or silver coins issued from the 13th through the 18th century, bearing the figure of a shield.
Body-length, baglike coverings designed for one or two persons to sleep in, especially out-of-doors; lined or padded, with closure and often with water-repellent outer covering.
Liturgical music of the descendants of ancient Egyptians who converted to Christianity prior to the Islāmic conquest of Egypt in the 7th century.
Liturgical books containing the fixed musical chants of the mass.

The arrangment of various visual components for a page or pages, including drawings, graphs, photographs, or other illustrations used as supplementary to news, stories, or other text in a newspaper, magazine, brochure, online page, or other publication.
Bowls used to commemorate marriage ceremonies. Sometimes also used for ceremonial cleansing during the event, holding water so participants can wash hands, symbolizing union.

Screens used to obstruct or regulate light passing through a window, or obstruct the view from within or without. Usually flexible and made of paper, cloth, bamboo, or similar materials; sometimes mounted on a roller. Prefer "wndow blinds" for flexible or removable devices used to obstruct or regulate vision or light consisting of horizontal or vertical slats that can be opened or closed.

Curtains characterized by soft, billowing, crescent-shaped folds produced either by pulling a single curtain straight up, or by pulling a single or divided curtain diagonally up and to the side, by means of rings and cords attached to the back.

Medieval European weapons consisting of a long staff of wood, from about 6 to 9 feet in length and round in section, often tipped with iron at both ends; they were wielded with both hands, one hand holding the middle and the other grasping the staff at one quarter of the whole length from the end. They were especially popular as civilian weapons in England. For weapons used for ceremonial purposes, use "ceremonial staffs."
Curtains hung over the opening of a doorway, or at another threshold.

Forks used to hold meat and similar food as it is carved, generally having two long tines which may be slightly curved and which sometimes have at the base of the handle a projection on which to rest one's forefinger and thumb. May be accompanied by a carving knife.

Japanese transverse flutes of the No theater, made from three to six short lengths of bamboo joined together. They resemble the "ryuteki" in that they have seven fingerholes, a balancing weight in the upper end, a red-lacquered bore, and a wrapping of bark or twine, but are distinct from them in having a short tube inserted in the bore between the mouth hole and the nearest fingerhole, a metal ornament embedded in the upper end, and the inner red lacquer showing on the outside of the mouth hole and fingerholes.
Shallow pans with sloping sides and a long handle intended primarily for use when cooking omelets; includes those with two hinged sections.

General term for rock that has been cut, shaped, crushed, or otherwise formed for use in construction or other purposes. Includes the specific archaeological and anthropological sense of individual stones which may be decorated or ornamented and which may be used in ritual contexts. These are usually not carved or dressed, and so differ from sculptures made from stone.
Mechanical or optical devices on firearms, for aiming them or for positioning an artillery piece in position.

Small plates of metal or other material that are affixed to belts, helmets, or other articles of clothing or uniform that bear insignia identifying the wearer as a member of a particular group, particularly the military.

Strainers through which tea, or sometimes coffee, is poured in order to catch the loose leaves or grounds. For culinary tools which enclose tea leaves, or sometimes coffee grounds, within a cup or pot of water while the beverage brews, use "tea infusers."
Simple, hand-operated mills consisting of two circular stones; used to grind grain.
Long-handled utensils used when stir-frying in a wok to add liquids, moving ingredients, or for serving.
Large cases for storing objects or other goods or materials to protect or prevent damage.
Cooking devices consisting of a pan or box-like container with a lid attatched to a long handle, used to roast chestnut over a fire.

A semivernacular medieval Chinese literary genre often featuring Buddhist content; the term means "transformation text." The genre developed as a popularization of Buddhist doctrine through storytelling, pictorial representation, and performance.
Cans or pitchers used in the kitchen to collect or distribute cooking oils or grease.
Printing from glass plates, using either intaglio or planographic methods, developed and popularized from 1974 on primarily by Harvey K. Littleton.
Printing process in which the plate is etched, but unlike in most etching, the design is relief printed rather than intaglio printed.
Equipment, containers, utensils, dishes, cookware, cutlery, and other items for kitchen use, excluding appliances.
Tools used to remove a sample of a cheese wheel to test the taste, aroma, texture, and color for maturity.
Any of various tools used in connection with fire, especially metal disks or plates heated and held over food (such as pastry or puddings) to brown the top of it.

Distinctive wooden spoons of the Middle East and North Africa, used for drinking the beverage sherbet; the same term is also used for such spoons intended for soup, rice, or pickles. Often having leaf-shaped bowls. Exquisitely carved spoons were a sign of status for the well-to-do. They were featured prominently at dinner gatherings, where they were the only utensils used. For drinking sherbet, the spoons were placed in ceramic basins full of the beverage, with their handles balanced on the side and their bowls floating atop the sherbet. A guest would drink from the spoon, then place it back in the basin for the use of the other guests. Spoons may appear in various sizes, depending upon the food item or beverage intended for consumption. The largest spoons were reserved for sherbet.

Utensils with a trowel-like or otherwise shaped bowl, sometimes partially covered to form a receptacle, and used for cutting out portions of soft food or fruit or for serving up, dishing out, or conveying grains or mashed foods.
Refers to kantharoi that are also plastic vases.
Military undress caps in a great variety of forms.

Low-heeled shoes with closed toes and one or more straps around the ankle or instep. Commonly these are made of patent leather and were originally designed as footwear for girls. The name is derived from a character in the 20th century comic strip Buster Brown.

High-heeled boots of leather or leatherlike material often having decorative stitching, trimming, or tooling, generally extending to mid-calf and usually having external boot straps. Traditionally worn by ranch hands, especially in the American West.
Those parts of firearm locks that engage the hammer to hold it at full or half cock, until released by the trigger.

Textile coverings for the tabernacle, which holds the consecrated host and is located in, on, or near the high altar of a church. The tabernacle veil is often of a prescribed liturgical color, based on the period of the church calendar.
Bags for money.

Refers to cut-down versions of landaus seating two passengers facing forward and covered by a folding hood, and, by extension, for automobiles having a convertible top over the back seat, the front seat being either roofed or open.
Light two-wheeled open horse-drawn vehicles used especially in Ireland with lengthwise seats, usually to accommodate four persons, formerly more, placed face-to-face or back to back.

Thin and lightweight coverings worn over the head or face, and sometimes extending to the shoulders, for ornament, protection, or concealment; also, similar coverings made as component parts of headgear.
Instruments or weapons having three prongs.
Close-fitting caps made in a variety of shapes and sizes and worn at various periods by men and women, sometimes surmounted by a hat or headdress.

Flight instruments used for measuring the angle of drift of an aircraft. These have sight wires that rotate until objects on the ground appear to travel parallel with it so that from the position of the wire the drift angle may then be read directly from a calibration chart.
Nautical equipment used to change the direction of a rope, clew, or halyard.
Handcarts specifically designed for the profession of a traveling blade or scissors sharpener, fitted with a grinding wheel.
A gray, crystalline mass that forms potassium hydroxide; it is soluble in water, alcohol, and ether. Toxic and corrosive to tissue, it used as a chemical reagent and intermediate.
Large ropes or small cables midway between the size of a cable or a tow-line, and 5 to10 inches in circumference; used in warping and mooring.
Close-fitting extensions of the hose which cover the leg below the kneecap; worn by men during the Elizabethan and Jacobean periods.
Clothing designed for riding non-motorized cycles.
Originally the banner of St. Denis used by early French kings; more recently any banner or similar device that serves as a rallying point or symbol.

Chinese long zithers having a rectangular soundboard with a convex surface and, usually, 25 strings, traditionally of silk, each of which is supported by a movable triangular bridge which functions as a fine tuning device, each positioned relative to adjoining bridges in a diagonal row across the soundboard.
Large, rectangular mantles worn by men in ancient Greece and Rome.

Popular name for pullover shirts with short sleeves and a round or V-shaped collarless neck. Usually made of a lightweight machine-knit textile. For similar garments worn as underwear, use "undershirts."

In modern warfare, helmets for military use, especially those intended for the battlefield. Originally of metal, today also of Kevlar; usually provided with a suspension system or liner and chin strap.
Sets of miniature toys that together form a farm. These may include scaled down buildings, equipment or animals, intended as playthings for children.
Costume accessories comprising circular bands of flowers, foilage, or ornamental work worn or bestowed as a mark of honor or victory or worn for purely decorative purposes.
General term for various objects worn to protect the chest.
Books of other than a conventional rectangular shape, such as circular, triangular, or irregularly polygonal books.

Books, with or without text in which the essential information is conveyed through a collection of photographic images. These may be authored by one or more artists or photographers, or arranged by an editor. Generally the images in a photobook are meant to be viewed in context, as parts of a larger whole. Most often used to refer to mechanically reproduced and commercially distributed works. For albums made up of mounted photographic prints, with or without identifying information, use "photograph albums."

Historical bindings the structure of which originatied in Coptic monasteries in Egypt, known to have been made from the 4th to the 11th centuries CE. They feature boards made of wood or pressed papyrus, leather covers, gatherings sewn through the folio usually by chain or kettle stitches without sewing supports, and lined spines with flanges and headbands. They make up the oldest known family of leather bookbindings and represent the ultimate source of all decorated leather bindings.
Bookbindings having decorations on the four corners of the front cover, and sometimes on the back cover.
Refers to the exercise apparatus consisting of a sliding seat, foot rests, and two oarlike handles attached to mechanisms whose resistance simulates that of water.

Elastic cords of 3 to 5 meters long tied into a circle, used in a game of Chinese jump rope, or elastics, involving jumping patterns for 3 or more people. Traditional Chinese elastics are different rubber elastics tied together, but many types of commercial elastics exist.
Sodium dehydroacetate is the sodium salt of dehydroacetic acid. It is a preservative and antimicrobial agent that has been used as a food additive and in aqueous deacidification of manuscripts.
Sports and athletic equipment used in conjunction with gymnastics.
Various small hooplike, arched wire, or constructed rectilinear targets at which balls are aimed in such sports as croquet and cricket.
Padded, somewhat cylindrical, floor-supported gymnastic apparatus resembling side horses but without the handles and used solely for vaulting.

Figures made of porcelain, wood, ivory, or another material, usually representing a female and only from the waist up. The object typically has a punched hole other feature near the bottom, intended to allow the half doll to be sewn or otherwise attached to a solid base or to a lower body made of a cheaper or softer material. For similar objects attached to a cage-like base, use "cage dolls."
Little balls of various materials, such as glass, clay, agate, and porcelain, used in a variety of games.
Modified forms of zoetropes used to project a series of images of animals or other subjects in order to display movement.
Pullover sweaters with a high, close-fitting band collar, which is often rolled or turned down.
Very narrow skirts, narrower at the bottom than at the knee, causing the wearer to walk with short, mincing steps.
Low slung, usually close-fitting trousers that rest on the hips.
Heavy, opaque stockings woven in one with panties. For sheer stockings woven in one with panties, use "pantyhose." For one-piece, skin-tight combination garments, use "leotards."

Neckwear comprising narrow strips of fabric, typically white in color and sometimes trimmed with lace, that are basted as liners inside the neck of an ecclesiastical stole or other similar non-ecclesiastical garment to protect it from soiling due to contact with the skin. For medium-sized to large outerwear collars that resemble fashion stoles, use "stole collars (outerwear collars)."
A serpentinite of varying yellowish green hues, often with fine markings of black or gray; it is named for its frog-like markings.
Special clothing worn by royalty, in part intended to designate their position and stature.

Long mantles worn at formal but non-liturgical occasions. The color of the garment indicates the rank of the cleric, black for secular priests, purple for bishops, and scarlet for cardinals. The pope does not wear a ferraiolone.

Refers to the square cloths used for wiping the face, carried by the upper classes in Ancient Rome. Examples are cloths venerated as relics, believed to be parts of the cloth carried by Saint Veronica, which according to legend, was used to wipe the face of Christ and on which his features were impressed.
Main garments, usually made without a placket or similar opening, that must be drawn over the head to be put on.
Maori garments worn by tying at the waist, including garments similar to kilts, aprons, or loin cloths.
Accessories or objects of adornment worn to support stockings.
Decorative or ceremonial objects that surround or are affixed to the neck; these may also cover the shoulders and bust.
Bands worn around the head, made of cloth, leather, metal, or various other materials, typically worn to keep the hair in place, for decorative purposes, or as a sign of status or rank.

Fabric cord, ribbon, or rope worn as a decorative hair ornament; sometimes decorated with added features such as fabric flowers, bows, beadwork, or colored fabric. Usually has the decorative element placed in the middle or at the ends of the fabric, with the rest of the item secured to hair.
Ornamental pins, made with a wide variety of decorative heads, whose point pierces and holds a necktie to a shirt and fits into a receiving snap or button on the underside.

Overcoats worn by Euro-Canadian settlers and Cree men during the 18th and early 19th centuries. Adapted from pre-contact animal hide coats worn by Cree tribes. Usually made from animal hide with painted decoration and quillwork ornameting the shoulders. Coats from Northern Cree communities include further painted decoration on the spine, hem, and front of the coat. Were usually anufactured by Cree women.
Suits incorporating a Norfolk jacket with either knickerbockers, trousers, or a skirt of matching fabric.
Protective hats made of strengthened, rigid materials with a shock-absorbing lining, often yellow; worn in hazardous working conditions for protection and visibility.
Dresses worn beneath another; use especially for those underdresses designed to be seen.

Smoothly fitted undergarments extending from or below the bust down to the waist or below, stiffened by strips of steel or whalebone, or with casing for a busk, sometimes limbered by elastic goring, sometimes tightened by lacing, and fastened by hooks. It is usually worn by women for support and molding of the figure including the ribcage and possibly the hips.

Flexible straps or bands generally encircling the waist or hips or passing over the shoulder and usually having some type of fastener, such as a buckle; worn for decoration, support, or to carry such items as weapons, tools, or money.
Arabic script that is a smaller version of the tawqī' script. Invented by Muhammed ibn Khazin ca. 11th century CE.
Self-propelled airborne explosive devices that are intended to be launched from the ground to hit targets that are airborne.

Medium-sized vessels travelling at regular intervals between two ports, originally for the conveyance of mail, later also for goods and passengers; used particularly in Europe and North America in the 18th and 19th centuries. They could be ocean-going or used on rivers and canals. Merchant vessels plying regularly along fixed routes, especially on rivers or along coasts, to carry mail but also for cargo or passenger transport.

Use both for naval ships of the late 18th and early 19th centuries generally fully rigged on three masts and armed with guns on one or two decks and designed for various battle functions, and for a contemporary class of small, medium-speed warships designed primarily for escort duty and having antiair, antiship, and antisubmarine capabilities.
General name for textile woven from the spun fiber of the flax plant.

Lightweight textile made of various types of fiber, having a crinkled surface obtained by using hard twisted thread or yarn, by printing with caustic soda, by weaving with varied tensions, or by embossing.
Woven figured textile with one warp and one weft in which the pattern is formed by a contrast of binding systems, and appears on the face and the back in reverse positions.
Producing a variegated effect on the surface of a material.

Applied decoration comprising tinfoil pressed into a mold to create a surface of lines and patterns that suggest brocaded fabric. Warm wax or wax resin-based paste was then applied to the surface. This resulted in a pattern which was gilded and painted and then roundly cut with the foil. The molded product was then applied to the surface of a painting or sculpture.
People of either sex whose job or activity is to milk cows or sometimes goats, usually employed in a dairy. Usually used for male milkers; females typically called by the narrower term, "milkmaids."
In weaving, the threads that are extended lengthwise in the loom, usually twisted harder than the "weft," with which these threads are crossed to form the web or piece.
A process occurring in such materials as paper, paperboard, vellum, or cloth in which the material becomes wrinkled, puckered, warped, or rippled.
Applying heat, pressure, and moisture to cause fiber to adhere and mat together. For the controlled shrinking of textile in order to make it thicker and more compact, use "fulling."

The technique in which small pieces of specially shaped wood, or sometimes other materials such as ivory, are incorporated into a suface of decorative veneer. Distinguished from "inlay," where decorative pieces are set into a solid ground; in marquetry, the entire surface is veneered.

A subtractive manufacturing process which typically employs computerized controls and machine tools to remove layers of material from a blank, and produces a custom-designed part. The basic process includes designing the CAD model, converting the CAD file to a CNC program, preparing the CNC machine, and executing the machining operation. It is suitable for a wide range of materials, including metals, plastics, wood, glass, foam, and composites, and encompasses different operations including mechanical, chemical, electrical, and thermal processes.
Serving spoons with wide, round bowls for scooping potatoes, often designed with dual flares on the bowl near the handle.
Large forks intended primarily for serving food from platters, bowls, or the like; sometimes made en suite with a serving spoon.
Use to describe firearms that must be loaded by hand for each shot.
Land vehicles whose primary purpose is to convey travelers.
Two-wheeled vehicles similar to bicycles but larger and heavier with engines set low on the frame; usually seating one or two riders.
Road vehicles equipped with mechanical apparatus for hoisting and pulling, used to tow other vehicles that have become disabled, stalled, or wrecked.

Devices enabling the wearer to walk across deep snow without sinking and consisting generally of a light racket-shaped frame strung with a network of thong or hide straps and attached to the wearer's feet.

Heavily constructed four-wheeled vehicles, usually designed to carry bulk commodities and heavy loads, primarily in agricultural and commercial contexts; generally characterized as boxes set on running gear and more substantial than carts. Known since the 3rd millennium BCE. During the early 19th century some versions were adapted for passenger travel.

Textiles woven in different colored yarns to produce a multicolored crossed-linear pattern, often of woolen or worsted twill. Although the type of textile pattern existed in many early cultures, among the best known are the Scottish tartans, for which distinctive designs and colors signified a Highland clan and were worn only by members of that clan.
Catalytic reaction produced by the product of a reaction that was itself catalytic.
The length of a straight line passing through the center of a circle or sphere, terminated at each end by its circumference or surface.
In Indian architecture, a curvature of śikhara.

Formats of paintings, prints, photographs, sculptures, or other works or other things that fall within a large range of size for the norm. For example, the term is used for film format in photography, usually reserved for sheet film formats 4x5 inches and larger, but may be extended to describe the fields of related imaging detectors, or spectroscopic equipment.
Sets of vessels intended for use on a washstand generally including a basin and ewer, but may also include a soap dish and chamber pot.
The distribution of something per unit area; can be, for example, the measure of the mass of a substance per unit volume, or the number of dwelling units per acre.

The configuration of a work, objects, books, or data, including technical formats, or the conventional designation for the dimensions or proportion of a work. For bibliographic works, the shape, size and general makeup of a book, periodical or other publication. In the context of computer science, the physical layout of a data storage device or the logical structure or composition of a file. Designations of format may overlap with designations of standard size.

Football as played under Association rules, where two teams of 11 players each may use any part of their bodies except their hands and arms to maneuver a round ball into the opposing team's goal. Only the goalkeeper is permitted to handle the ball and may do so only within the penalty area surrounding the goal.

Game in which two opposing players or pairs of players use tautly strung rackets to hit a ball of regulated size, weight, and bounce over a net on a rectangular court. Points are awarded to the player or team whenever the opponent fails to correctly return the ball within the prescribed dimensions of the court.
Use generally for the ability to support, or high capacity for, combustion.

Frames which have a continuous ornament design, usually repeated foliage motifs, along the inner part of the molding. Of a type popular in the 17th and 18th centuries and named for the Italian painter Carlo Maratta.
Valveless lip-vibrated aerophones of conical bore, made in many shapes, originally used as signal instruments during the hunt.
Chordophones of Uganda, made of several individual single-string zitherlike instruments of millet stalk; they are held in the player's open palm and plucked in an upward motion by the index finger.
Graduated sticks 1 yard long used for measuring.

A surface-sensitive mass spectrometry technique in which an ion's mass-to-charge ratio is determined by a time measurement. Particles removed from the atomic monolayers of a surface are accelerated into a flight tube and their mass is measured by the time it takes them to reach the detector.
Pedal-driven devices with a single wheel and a seat mounted on an adjustable-height shaft ridden and steered by body balance.

Posable recreational toy or character dolls that are intended to be dressed in a variety of outfits reflecting contemporary or collector trends. Contemporary fashion dolls are usually made from plastic or vinyl, and are mass produced, though many variations exist. The current versions of this type of doll emerged in the mid-20th century and were based on a German doll called Bild Lilli, the design of which was acquired by American company Mattel, that then marketed it as Barbie. Many imitations and

European wire-strung plucked lutelike chordophones played with a plectrum, very popular in the 16th and 17th centuries, having a wedge-shaped body with a curved bottom and straight shoulders narrowing towards the neck, and a low flat bridge held in position only by the strings it supports. Their most characteristic feature is a long, fretted neck which is half cut away from behind the fingerboard on the bass side, making a channel along which the player's left thumb can slide to facilitate very rapid shifts to and from high positions.
Short-necked bass lute, known to be played in Thrace, and by Greek refugees in Turkey.
Smoothbore long guns that usually fire charges of shot rather than single projectiles.
Artillery mounted on vehicles that have their own motive power.
Historical military engines used for throwing stones and other missiles, including incendiaries; consists of a lever arm held and released under tension in a wooden frame.
Any number of various card games for two, three, or four players, each typically being dealt seven, nine, or ten cards, in which the object is to match cards into sets and sequences.

Ancient French board game, popular in Europe during the Middle Ages, though said to have been derived from the Greeks. It was played with counters on a board depicting a jardin de l’oie (goose garden) and divided into compartments, in some of which a goose was depicted; other emblems included an inn, a death’s head, a bridge, and a labyrinth. The object of the game was to land one’s counter on number 63. The game was usually played for a stake, and special fines were exacted for landing on certain spaces. At the end of the 18th century, a variation of the game was called jeu de la revolution française (game of the French Revolution).
Books that include visual images to explain, augment, or embellish the text.
Printed pieces such as notices or advertisements intended for distribution by hand or by mail. For those intended for posting, use "posters."
Dome-shaped or cylindrical containers with a small opening at the top used to contain and dispense twine or string.

Cotton or wool dresses worn by Southwest Native North American women, primarily Navajo and Pueblo (Hopi, Zuni) communities. Often richly embroidered along the hem of the dress. Used in ceremonies such as the Basket Dance and the Butterfly Dance.

Summer garments made of sheer cotton, muslin, linen or other lightweight material, typically worn outdoors for warm weather. Often white, off-white, or pastel in color and heavily decorated with embriodery, lace, ruffles, appliqué, and ribbons. Popular in Europe and North America throughout the early 20th century.

A type of large historical agricultural wagon with sides consisting of horizontal ladders attached to the loading bed for hauling hay, grain, or other materials. The sides could be removed to suit other purposes.
Light textile throws used as decor on tabletops.
An unstandardized name for various red dye colorants.

A polymer featuring ether functionality, perfluoropolyether (PFPE) refers to one branch of a family of synthetic lubricants developed by DuPont, the oil form of the line commercially known as Krytox (TM). In a conservation context, it is used primarily for waterproofing stone. Its repellent powers also recommend it as an anti-graffiti agent.
Written versions of oral language or music, or written copies made of other written documents, either in longhand or on a machine.
Texts used in the context of rites or rituals having to do with the deceased and dying.
The bodies or complete collections of writings or the whole body of literature on any subject.

Style of carpets produced in the village of Sarāb, Iran; this is the name under which a particular phase and subvariety of Heriz carpet production was sold in the West. It is characterized by a light, rather bright color scheme.

Navajo wearing blankets characterized by horizontal bands of indigo, red, black, and white wool and rectangular motifs often placed in the center and sides of the work. Produced by Navajo weavers from the 1850s to the 1870s. Not associated with rank; "chief blanket" refers to their value assigned by Navajo and Plains communities.
Style and culture of the Pashto-speaking people living in southeastern Afghanistan, northwestern Pakistan., and surrounding areas. They constitute the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan.
Culture and style related to Kuva (Quva), now in Uzbekistan, which was a medieval hub of culture and art. Style is particularly associated with pottery, jewelry, and metalwork.
Planes with a semicircular shape when viewed from above; used to smooth and level the ends of the staves of barrels after the barrels have been assembled.
Systems that supply the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning to buildings and complexes.
Compilation of data in one particular arrangement of data or characters.
Describes buildings housing museums that specialize in the history, objects, vehicles, and other materials associated with transportation.

Refers to art and architecture associated with the Islamic Hafsid rulers of Tunis who were one of four regional powers to emerge in the Maghrib after the collapse of the Almohad empire in 1212. The Hafsids ruled in the eastern area of North Africa. Important centers were the coastal cities of Tunis, Sousse, and Sfax. Hafsid culture is a meeting of east and west: the many Spanish refugees in the region brought their artistic traditions with them and the Hasfids also maintained close ties with the Mamluks of Egypt. The Hafsids were responsible for introducing the madrasa to the Maghrib and many were built as well as numerous mosques. The Hafsids, who saw themselves as champions of the Islamic faith, also commissioned many noteworthy religious manuscripts.
Style of textiles, particularly carpets, from the area of İsparta, Turkey.
Adherents of or experts in occultism, which is the belief in or study of hidden, mysterious, or supernatural powers, as manifested in all fields of human endeavor or creativity.
Describes activities that occur in relation to a body of water.
Accumulations of objects purposely buried or otherwise hidden as a group; may contain artifacts of any material or of different materials.
Describes groupings of objects that augment or allow for the transfer of media.
Any of various devices or pieces of material used to reduce shock, friction, or damage due to the contact between two surfaces.
The process of heating pieces or rods of manufactured glass over an open flame, then shaping them by blowing or tooling.
Kings or sovereign rulers of Muslim states, especially those of the former Ottoman Empire.
Clothes or draperies customarily indicative of bereavement, often donned during a period designated for the conventional or ceremonial manifestation of sorrow.
Textual statements used to initiate the creation of a process by a system, especially the creation of images or other content by Artificial Intelligence.
Hand held cutting devices similar to scissors, designed to cut the woolen fleece from sheep. The earliest examples date to Bronze Age Crete.
Refers to various Christian officials but most often to senior clergymen (after bishops) in cathedral chapters or dioceses. The term originally referred to monks in charge of ten novices.
In the armed forces of various nations, commissioned officers of the highest rank or of second or third highest rank overall, varying from one nation or organization to another.
Men identified by a particular honorific, historically designating the lowest rank of Dutch nobility.

Implements intended to spoon, scoop, and sometimes also to store, cosmetics. Best known as works from ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, and elsewhere. These spoons were made from various materials such as wood, alabaster or ivory, and were often elaborately sculpted or decorated with symbolic imagery.
Devices consisting of a tube with a bowl at one end and a mouthpiece at the other; used for smoking tobacco, opium, and other substances.
Small magnifiers of the type used by watchmakers or jewelers.
Areas of jurisdiction of a prince-bishop, who is a bishop of noble rank.

Designation given to certain divisions within a nation that have a degree of independence, administer their own affairs, or are otherwise self-governing to some degree. The precise definition of "autonomous republic" varies from nation to nation, and is typically assigned to the division by the nation, rather than being assigned by an outside body. Examples of autonomous republics are found in the successor states of the Soviet Union, including Azerbaijan, Georgia, Tajikistan, Ukraine, and Uzbekistan.
Long-handled metal tools terminating in a small cup; used to dip stone-dust from drilled holes.
Sets consisting of a stand holding a holy water bucket, censer, and incense vessel.

Black-figure kylikes whose bowl and lip are usually separated, often by a painted line creating two horizontal zones. They either have two separate types of decoration or decoration exists primarily in the lower zone but may overlap into the upper zone. Siana cups are named for the village on the Greek island of Rhodes. The siana cup was one of the forms to predominate in black-figure until about 540 BCE.

The process of securing the text block and attached endpapers into a case that was produced as a separate operation.  For the process of attaching individual boards to the text block and end papers, if any, use "board attachment."
Refers to both those who play the viola and those who play the viol.
Colonies and other possessions in Africa and Asia of the defeated powers of the First World War, which were placed under the control of various different victor nations by the League of Nations.

Objects in a variety of forms designed to hold photographs for presentation or storage. These range from simple folders that incorporate a passe-partout to more elaborate frame-like constructions, or bindings.
Fighting men of ancient Rome, either professionals or slaves, captives, or condemned criminals, who fought to the death with other men or with wild animals as a form of public entertainment.
Engraving tool shaped like a club with sharp points projecting from the head, set in a long, round wood handle.  Used to produce marks similar to chalk lines.
Instruments or devices used to produce screen prints.
Bases of large altarpieces decorated with images related to the main panels above. Formerly used to describe the platform on which the priest stood and an altar was placed.
Furniture feet common in the Renaissance characterized by horizontal side-bars connecting the front and rear legs at the floor.

Physical or digital representations of a body of information designed with the capacity to communicate. In its broadest sense, "documents" include any item amenable to cataloging and indexing, that is, including nonprint media. For the activity of gathering and recording information, see "documentation (function)." For specfic types of documents, see concepts under "document genres."

Images of a deity used as a focus for worship; the term is usually used specifically to distinguish a non-Christian item from Christian images. For a Christian image that is itself considered sacred, use "icon." For an ancient Greek or Roman sacred image, use "cult image."
Strips of white bark paper used as adornment. Liquid rubber was poured on them and they were used to decorate ixiptlah.
Strips of metal used for spacing. Also, a line of type cast by a Linotype machine.
Watercraft equipped or designed for oceanographic study or exploration.

Ships' boats smaller than launches or longboats, usually the second boat in size when a number of boats are carried; ranged from to 24 feet to 37 feet, but most commonly under 30 feet; equipped with small steam engines in late 19th century.
Decked sailboats, usually 14 to 15 feet long, with metal runners and no rudder, steered with mainsail and jib and capable of sailing over ice and patches of water.
Sailing vessels common especially to the seas of China and Java, having flat bottoms, high sterns with a square bow, and two or three masts.
Cutting tools consisting of a heavy blade with a hooked point fitted with a handle and used in pruning, clearning heavy brush, and maintaining hedges.
Cloth, usually cotton, that has been coated with compounded rubber and passed between rollers under pressure; the resulting cloth is waterproof and flexible.

The process of decorating fabrics by applying a thick paste of dye or pigment. Major methods of textile printing include: block printing (design raised in relief on a flat surface); stencil or screen printing (cutting the design through a flat sheet of paper or metal); roller printing (engraved printing rollers, one for each color, are pressed against the fabric). In each, the dye or pigment is first applied, and then fixed, usually by steaming or heating; at which point  excess color is removed by washing.

Territories belonging to or recently having belonged to one political entity, but through military occupation or other provisional control are held by another political entity without the volition of original entity.
Political entities havin democratic governments in which a nonpolitical monarch acts as head of state within the boundaries of a constitution.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, originally of Fulbe origin, who have assimilated culturally and linguistically with Mande peoples, specifically the Bamana and Maninka.

Refers to any of several commercially prepared oxygen absorbing powders to be deployed in a sealed environment for insect eradication and oxygen-free storage in museums and archives; they are also used to extend the shelf-life of commercial food items. All contain a chemical compound the active ingredient of which is a finely divided iron oxide.
In Indian architecture, a short entry-hall.
Having the form or outline of a pentagon, a plane figure with five angles and five sides.

Shape comprising the open surface generated by revolving a hyperbola about either of its axes. If the tranverse axis of the surface lies along the x axis and its centre lies at the origin and if a, b, and c are the principal semi-axes, then the general equation of the surface is expressed as x2/a2 ± y2/b2 − z2/c2 = 1.
Captions that transcribe or translate the dialogue spoken in a motion picture. These usually appear at the bottom of the screen image.

Film movement began in Italy near the end of World War II, typified by the use of both professional and non-professional actors, ordinary settings and themes, and the rejection of the happy-ending story. The films tend to focus on social issues and the everyday problems of its characters.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living mainly in Ethiopia but also in Kenya.

The beamhouse operation of treating unhaired hides or skins with a solution of fermented dog manure to remove undesirable constituents and impart a quality of softness and flexibility to the final leather. It is a similar process to bating, which involves pigeon or hen manure, but faster, as the solution is more powerful, and also possibly more damaging to the hides or skins.
Decorated sticks that record coups attained by Plains Indian warriors. These are carried to touch armed enemies as a way to demonstrate bravery.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Ghana.
Small groups or collocations of words expressing a single notion, or entering with some degree of unity into the structure of a sentence.

Describes works produced by the African people of the same name living in the Sudan. Historically they founded the Funj kingdom centered at Sinnar, which controlled the eastern Sudan, including southern Nubia, and flourished from the fifteenth to the nineteenth century.

Facing technique producing a mixture of square and rectangular stones or bricks. The term is also sometimes used for any of several other patterns of laying flat masonry in what was considered the 'Roman manner.'
Book cloth grain which became popular in the 1830s.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living around the coastal lagoons of Côte d'Ivoire.

Hairstyles in which the hair is gathered and fastened at one point on the back of the head, or on either side of the head, but otherwise unfastened, so that it hangs down to somewhat resemble a horse's tail.
Culture and style of the Nok people of northern Nigeria that appeared ca. 1000 BCE and vanished due to unknown reasons around 300 CE.
A reddish-brown leather usually made from sheepskin that is vegetable tanned. A decorative pattern is applied by sandwiching the leather between a heated metal plate and a mold.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Kinshasa region in Congo.
Machines used in the process of bookbinding, which include those that implement gluing, stamping, ruling, cutting, other functions.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting northeastern Kenya.
Style and culture of the African peoples of the independent chiefdom of the same name, located in the Upper Cross River region, just west of the Cameroon Grassfields.
Style and culture of the nation of Cameroon, lying at the junction of western and central Africa.

Ribbons of various widths, colors, and compositions from which medals and decorations hang. These complement the decorations and orders and may indicate being awarded the same distinction more than once.
Business partnerships of two or more persons working under a common name in the area of construction, which is the process of creating something by combining parts or elements.
Devices that are designed to receive two or more separate audio signals from sources such as microphones or instruments, and combine them into one output.
Pads, usually semicircular or triangular in shape, stitched or otherwise attached to the inside of a garment to shape, raise, or widen the shoulders.

Belts worn to control a diver's buoyancy underwater onto which slotted lead weights can be slipped according to the diver's body size and weight and having a quick-release buckle for emergency discarding.
Describes works created by the African Malagasy people of the same name living in eatern Madagascar.

People who create icons, which are images that portray a sacred entity and that are themselves regarded as sacred. Iconographers intend to translate revealed scripture and divine truths into visual images.

Masquerade of the Igbo people of Africa, performed in the northcentral Igbo region during the annual dry season festivals and at the burial festivals of respected men. It features massive mask costumes surmounted by horns, representing masculine physical strength and spiritual power.
In the context of a formal or casual meal, the last course, consisting of a sweet food, such as fruit, sweetmeats, cake, ice cream, or the like.
Cutting devices operated manually or electrically intended for grooming horses.
Parts of the tack that attach the backband to a horse's chest, preventing it from sliding.
Seats made over a frame and placed on an animal's back for carrying riders; may also be used for similar, but smaller, seats used on some other vehicles, such as bicycles.

Extinct order of order of amphibians characterized by vertebrae in which large fan-shaped hemal arches grow directly downward from the middle of each caudal centrum. Dates to the Lower Pennsylvanian to Middle Permian.

Breed of dog that is large, powerfully built, with a massive head and drooping ears, standing a minimum of 25 inches (63.5 cm), and weighing up to 200 lbs (91 kg). Its coat is red-brown and white or brindle and white and may be either short and dense or medium-long. They are bred as pathfinders and rescue dogs at the hospice founded by St. Bernard of Montjoux in Great St. Bernard Pass in the Pennine Alps.

Breed of horse characterized by being tall, slim, most notably used for racing and jumping. It was developed in England; the origin may be traced back to records indicating that a stock of Arab and Barb horses was introduced into England as early as the 3rd century.
Organisms that feed upon wood, as an insect larva, or boring into and destroying wood, as a mollusc or crustacean.
Poems with six stanzas of six lines each. The last words of the first stanza are repeated, in a different order, in the other five stanzas.
General term used to reference various components of a body, usually restricted to the human body. Included may be external parts or internal parts, such as organs.
In the context of archival description, the original person, people, deparment, or other corporate body who created or assembled the group, collection, or other arrangement of records.
Footwear with a relatively stiff sole and heel, and generally covering the foot at or below the ankle joint.
Any of various looms or weaving devices operated wholly or partly by hand or foot power.
The actions of separating or parting. A common example is the parting of a couple who are married, but who have not gone through a divorce.
Pipes of large diameter usually of sheet steel used as a chimney or to connect a stove with a flue.
Lamps used to illuminate colored roundels on a semaphore signal at night.

Phylum of wormlike invertebrates, mostly of microscopic size, characterized by a body cavity, the pseudocoel, that arises in the embryo in a way different from that found in more advanced animals and that has no epithelial lining.

General term referring to members of several invertebrate phyla of various disparate groups, including the entire phylum of annelids. They have in common soft, elongated bodies lacking a hard outer covering.
Short strips of of often satin-finished ribbon emblazoned with text or images that promote a person, brand, cause, etc. These normally are worn on clothing.
Viruses in which the genetic information is stored in the form of RNA (ribonucleic acid) as opposed to DNA.

Device to iron hats, for example men's silk hats, during creation and as part of maintenance in the owner's wardrobe. One use of the device was to lay down the nap on the fabric of the hat. The hat iron may be used for other tasks in sewing, beyond hat creation.

Mechanical combinations of two or more substances in no definite proportions, within which the constituent substances retain their individual properties and are separable by ordinary physical means. For complex pure substances made up of two or more elements in definite proportions which lose their individual properties and are held together by chemical bonds, use "compounds."
Describes devices that either trap a live mouse which can later be released, or those that kill mice attracted by bait.

Multi-purpose medical instruments of Roman antiquity consisting of a long shaft with an olivary probe terminating one end and a spoon on the other. The spoon and the shaft are sometimes decorated. These were used for a variety of medical and cosmetic activities such as applying and measuring medicaments or the removal of medication from flasks.

Four-legged bench, typically made of wood and asymmetrically built with one side raised higher than the other, designed to facilitate the manual textile carding process. One textile card, or sharp surface fitted with wires, is slipped into a slot on the bench's raised side, while the second card is manually manipulated by a user straddling the bench. The user is forced to change the grip on the lower card as they work the fibers between the two cards. A wooden drum is often attached to the bench's lower side, around which the smoothened wool gathers after it encounters the cards.

Process in which photographically produced dye images are physically transferred from a light-sensitive matrix to a receiving sheet; developed by Eastman Kodak Company and marketed with the trade names Verifax, Readyprint, and Ektalith.

A white granular solid that is soluble in water and slightly soluble in alcohol. It is used as a corrosion inhibitor, a mordant for printing cotton fabric; a mild cleaning agent for various metals, varnish and coated painted surfaces, and for removal of sulfate crust from stone.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellowish green colors.
A range of colors resembling variations of olive pigment.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of brown colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of orange colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink colors.
Inverse labels for information units in a data system that are meant to be read by the end user.
Variable yellowish colors resembling the color of cadmium yellow pigment, which is made of cadmium sulfide.
Refers to a range of dark gray or blackish colors resembling the color of black ink, which is a liquid material used for writing, drawing, and printing.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
A range of brownish colors resembling the color of the mummy brown pigment, formerly produced by grinding Egyptian mummies.
Refers to a range of dark green colors resembling the green colors of the deep forest or, for the Scots, the green associated with the costume of Robin Hood in ballads.
A range of orange colors resembling the color of the synthetic iron oxide pigment known as "Mars orange."
Variable dark purplish color resembling dyes made with nigrosine, which is derived from coal tar.
Variable red colors resembling the color of dragon's blood, a colorant derived from resinous material from the fruit of several types of palms.
General term for flying insects with colorful wings in Papilionoidea (superfamily), Nymphalidae (family), or Hedyloidea (superfamily).

Members of a family containing 90 species of small beetles ranging from reddish brown to black in color, and having larvae that bore through seasoned wood, reducing it to a dry powder. They do not enter varnished, painted, or treated wood. The holes left behind by this and other species of powderpost beetles are often erroneously considered to be evidence of the antiquity of a wooden object.
Style of fashion, decorative arts, and architecture that invoke elements of miliary design and architecture.
A range of blue colors resembling the color of Berlin blue pigment, which is any of several deep blue pigments consisting chiefly of ferric ferrocyanide.
Shell of an oyster.
Order containing one living family of trout and salmon.
Family containing the stitchbirds. Although the birds resemble members of the honeyeater family Meliphagidae, genetic analysis has recently proven they are not related.
Infraorder containing various species of lorises and their close relatives.

Family containing 14 species in seven genera comprising sea lions and fur seals. They are adapted to a semi-aquatic lifestyle, feeding and migrating in the water but breeding and resting on land or ice, having small but visible external ear flaps, larger foreflippers and pectoral muscles than true seals, and the ability to turn their hind limbs forward and walk on all fours. With true seals and walruses, arose in the late Miocene (10-12 million years ago), descended from a common ancestor most closely related to modern bears.
Subspecies of lion closely related to North African lions and West African lions. Today they survive in the wild only in India's state of Gujarat; listed as Endangered.

Refers to members of the genus containing 5 or more species of ruminant (cud-chewing) mammals, including domestic sheep. Sheep are typically distinguished from goats by being stockier, having horns that more divergent in form, having scent glands in its face and hind feet, and the males lack the beards of goats. In all wild species of sheep, the outer coat is hair overlaying a short undercoat of fine wool; the fine wool has been developed into the fleece of domesticated sheep. Sheep were first domesticated from wild species of sheep at least 5000 BCE, and their remains have been found at numerous sites of early human habitation in the Middle East, Europe, and Central Asia. Domesticated sheep are raised for their fleece, milk, and meat.

Members of an order of containing 240,000 species of insects possessing a single pair of wings on the mesothorax and hind wings that have developed into a pair of halteres on the metathorax. Insects in other orders may have the word "fly" in their name (e.g., dragonfly), but they are not true flies.

Order containing around 370 species in 17 families including plovers, jacanas, stilts, avocets, thickknees, terns, and murres, having three basic body plans: waders (shorebirds) that usually feed on small animals in mud or water; web-footed dense-plumaged water birds that feed by plunging into water for fish, robbing other birds, or scavenging; and dense-plumaged, web-footed, marine, wing-propelled divers that feed on fish or invertebrates.
Windsor armchairs with a horizontal U-shaped arm rail and back of medium height consisting of spindles contained within a curved bow anchored in the arm rail.
Tools consisting of a blade fixed to a handle. Used to prepare food.
Fluted bell-shaped structures used as finials in pyrimidal roofing of Indian temple architecture.
In Indian architecture, a type of adhiṣṭhāna with prati-kaṇṭha moulding at its upper end.

Interplanetary bodies of relatively small size that enter the Earth's atmosphere at high velocity, burn and heat the air around themselves causing a resultant luminous phenomenon that is called a "meteor." If such an object survives its plunge through the atmosphere and lands on the ground, it is called a "meteorite."
Mechanisms used in cameras that allow light to pass through an aperture and expose a frame of film.
In China, Korea, and elsewhere in Asia, names given to members of the same generation to distinguish them from adjacent generations.
Educational institutions formed by the merging of two or more public schools, usually at the elementary level and often in rural areas.
Flat areas at high altitude that are covered with large angular rocks.

Class of acquatic animals (fish) characterized by possessing a skeleton at least partly composed of true bone (as opposed to cartilage) and typically a swim bladder (an air-filled sac to give buoyancy), a single pair of gills, gill covers over the gill chamber, bony platelike scales, a skull with sutures, and external fertilization of eggs. Modern bony fishes represent over 20,000 species in more than 400 families. In some classifications it is listed as a superclass instead of a class.
Chinese bronze ritual vessels used for drinking wine. These have two symmetrical and pointed spouts for pouring. This vessel type appeared during the Shang and lasted until the Western Zhou.
Extinct subclass of fishlike marine reptiles characterized by a spindle-shaped body, high tail fin, triangular dorsal fin, and paddlelike legs.
Herd animal that formerly occurred in vast herds in the Karoo regions of Cape Province and the southern part of Orange Free State. It is recently extinct.

Locations on the Internet or any network that may contain sub-domains, and that are defined by a unique address. A domain is maintained by an individual or organization. A "domain name" is the part of the domain address that identifies any part of it as belonging to the domain. A "domain name server," or DNS, is the computer that contains the programs and files that populate the domain.

SPARQL is a recursive acronym for SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language. It is an RDF semantic query language for databases able to retrieve and manipulate data stored in Resource Description Framework (RDF) format.

Feature that is relatively long and narrow and axially located in relation to the waterway, such as used to designate the deepest part of streambeds where the main current runs, or stretches of sea between two land areas and linking two seas.
Order that contains a single family with two genera and two living species of flying lemur.
Genus of one 1 species of fox of Africa.
General term applied to members of various large, wild species of Canis, particularly those of North America and Eurasia that hunt in packs.
Genus of two Southeast Asian species.

Impressions taken from a print, drawing, or printed or handwritten textual work, by pressing the original against a sheet of damp paper, often by passing it through a rolling press. Some of the ink of the original is transferred to the damp paper; the resulting image appears in reverse and may be fainter than the original. The original may be damaged in the process. Counterproofs are often made as part of the working process and are used as aids in correcting for the final version. In some cases, counterproofing was used to produce the finest quality copperplate printing; the second print consisted of delicate lines, and lacked the beveled impressions seen in the original print. Counterproofs are sometimes created as forgeries of valuable prints and drawings but the mirror image gives such copies away. For images or marks that result from an unintentional transfer of ink or other medium, use "offsets."

General term for items or materials that were used as money, but were not representative of actual currencies. Examples are ingots of gold or copper, which were carried from place to place in Bronze Age Europe, the owner using a chisel to remove a bit of the metal to buy goods.

Describes works by the New Guinea Aboriginal people located in Sepik. Sepik art works are created using a wide range of materials, techniques, and forms that are often orchestrated into a single event. Sepik people have varied architectural styles. The male cult houses are the most distinctive structures and contain carved structural elements, ornamentation, and furniture.

Standard tall lykythoi of cylindrical shape, typically white-ground, and used primarily in funerary rituals, which is known from their excavation from cemeteries and the subjects depicted on them. Late in the fifth century some massive examples of the shape were produced, serving perhaps as equivalents for stone grave markers.
