Marbled paper prepared in a similar fashion as the spotted technique used in antique marbled paper, but spots are in blue.
Refers to screens surrounding or placed in front of confessionals in order to shield penitents from public view.

Book format which holds 24 leaves or 48 pages. The most common method used to produce a twenty-fourmo is to fold two separate sheets with two parallel folds in thirds. This is followed by a right angle fold, a parallel fold, and then inserting the second sheet within the first.
Paper size, generally used in Great Britain, measuring 16 1/2 by 21 inches.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in southern Chad in the region of Gounougaya in the Chari River valley.

Refers to works created with a needle and thread on fabric or a mesh of canvas. The works are characterized by designs that are executed by using the grid of the fabric to count out the desired position of various stitches or colors in the design.
Refers to stitches or an ornamental pattern formed by embroidering or shirring parallel gathers or regularly-spaced, round tucks of fabric.

Refers to a Christian feast and festival commemorating the origin of the eucharist and in honor of the presence of the body of Jesus Christ in the eucharist. The Latin term means 'body of Christ.' It is usually celebrated on the Thursday after Trinity Sunday in the Western church. Its origins lie in the Middle Ages when there was increased devotion to the Blessed Sacrament, especially after the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215. In 1246, Robert de Torote, bishop of Liège, first celebrated the feast in his diocese after being persuaded to do so by Blessed Juliana, prioress of Mont Cornillon near Liège (1222-58), who had experienced a vision. The feast did not spread until Jacques Pantaléon, formerly archdeacon of Liège, became Pope Urban IV; a bull of 1264 commanded its observance. Over time it became more accepted and in the 15th century it became, in effect, the main feast of the church. Corpus Christi has been celebrated by carrying the host in procession since the 14th century. The feast's procession became a pageant in which sovereigns, princes, magistrates, and guild members took part. In the 15th century the procession was often followed by performances of miracle plays and mystery plays by members of guilds. The feast was suppressed in Protestant churches after the doctrine of transubstantiation was rejected during the Reformation.

The chain of causation that drives all phenomena, in which virtuous actions lead to future happiness and evil acts the opposite. The sum of a person's actions in one of his successive states of existence, regarded as determining his fate in the next. Among symbols for karma is the endless knot. Karma is a key concept in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism, and Taoism.
Embroidery stitches in which the thread is wound several times round the needle and taken back through the fabric at the same spot to create a tiny raised dot.

In traditional Chinese timber-frame architecture, leveling pillars are the two eaves pillars framing the central bay on the sides of the building parallel to the roof ridge. Leveling pillars are used as a standard height for calculating the height of other pillars across the façade, as they increase in height from the center towards the corners of the building, allowing for an upward curvature of the eaves (生起 shengqi). The term appears in the Yingzao fashi (1103) and in other official documents written by officials during the Song Dynasty (960-1279) to describe the architecture of mausolea. Modern architectural historians use this term to describe central-bay pillars on all sides of a building dating from the Tang (618-907) to early Ming (1368-1644) dynasties. In traditional Chinese timber-frame architecture, refers to two eaves pillars framing the central bay on the sides of the building parallel to the roof ridge (typically the front side). Leveling pillars are used as a standard height for calculating the height of other pillars across the façade, as they increase in height from the center towards the corners of the building, allowing for an upward curvature of the eaves (shengqi). The term appears in the Yingzao Fashi (1103, Siku quanshu edition., 5.4b) and also in documents written by officials during the Song Dynasty (960-1279) to describe the architecture of mausolea. Modern architectural historians use this term to describe central-bay pillars on all sides of a building dating from the Tang (618-907) to early Ming (1368-1644) dynasties.
Capital towns or cities for administrative subregions.

In the context of thesaurus construction, a qualifier is a word or phrase used to distinguish a term in a vocabulary from otherwise identical or similar terms that have different meanings. A qualifier is separated from the term, usually by parentheses.

Terms or names that are designated among all synonyms or lexical variants for a concept, to be used as the default term or name in displays and other situations; distinguished from "nonpreferred terms."
Two-color pottery excavated in Palestine, Cyprus, and Coastal Syria; generally assigned to the 15th-16th century BCE.
People who create building information models, often architects or engineers, or working for architects or engineers.
The state of deep and poignant distress caused by bereavement over an unfortunate outcome or event.
Languages that are still in use, but are at risk of falling out of use because speakers are dying out or shifting to speaking another language.
Hand gesture indicating a threat, warning, and wrath. Pose comprises a raised index finger in a menacing attitude, with other fingers locked in a fist.

Persons who draw pictorial images using wit to comment on such things as contemporary events, social habits, or political trends, usually executed in a broad or abbreviated manner. For people who make cartoons in the sense of studies for a fresco, use "draftsmen."
Nationality or culture of the Frisian tribe or the Friesland area along the North Sea, corresponding to the modern northern Netherlands and northwest Germany.
Losing consciousness, due to a drop in blood supply to the brain. Also, a weakening or decline.
The activity characterized by rhythmical skipping and stepping, with regular turnings and movements of the limbs and body, usually to the accompaniment of music.
In Indian architecture, a central band (at the bhadra) of Latina (North Indian curvilinear superstructure) śikhara; central spine of northern Indian śikharas or of a few Karṇāṭan superstructures.
Personal spirits in some West African religious beliefs.

Meals or social serving of refreshments at which tea is featured, usually a light, informal afternoon or evening meal, at which the usual beverage is tea, but sometimes cocoa, chocolate, coffee, or other substitute may be served. In modern usage in the UK, a light meal in the late afternoon, but locally in the northern UK and in Australia and New Zealand, a cooked evening meal; in Jamaica, tea is the first meal of the day.
Units of time equal to 60 seconds or 1/60 of an hour.
In the metric system, units of length containing 1000 meters, equal to  3280.89 feet and nearly 5/8 mile.
Measures of capacity for liquids and grain or other dry substances consisting of small particles equal to 1/4 gallon or 2 pints.
The standard system of weight in ounces used for precious metals and precious stones; one troy ounce is defined as exactly 31.1034768 g.
Colorless liquid that polymerizes in light and that is used to make polyvinyl acetate. Used to make adhesives, paints, and plastics.
Models made using software, used to distinguish them from models in physical form.

Genus containing around 50 species of annual herbs; native to southwestern North America, tropical America, and South America, but cultivated elsewhere. Noted for feathery foliage and flowers in various shades of yellow, orange, and maroon. It was regarded as the flower of the dead in pre-Hispanic Mexico, and is still widely used in the Day of the Dead celebrations. A few species are cultivated in Nepal, India, and Thailand, used in garlands and decoration for weddings, festivals, and religious events.
Order of flowering plants including familiar members such as  ginger, cardamom, turmeric, bananas and arrowroot. It evolved 80 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous.

Large, diverse order of dicotyledons (flowering plant having two cotyledons or seed-lobes), such as tea, persimmon, blueberry, Brazil nut, and azalea. In some older classifications, families in this order were distributed in various separate orders, such as the Ebenales order.
Living or animate beings, including animals or people that are fantastic or of anomalous or uncertain aspect or nature.

Species of medium-sized, deciduous tree native to native to Europe, southwest and central Asia, and northwest Africa. Known in three or four subspecies. It has oval, fine-toothed leaves; is long-trunked, and grows to 35 meters (115 feet) in height. The timber is primarily used for paneling and other purposes. A yellowish dye can be extracted from the fresh leaves. On wool, it produces a brass color with a chrome mordant and a yellow-brown color with an alum mordant. The extract does not dye cotton.

Species of hardwood tree native to the Indian subcontinent, primarily found growing along river banks. It is best known internationally as a premier timber species of the rosewood genus, but used locally to make the kartaalsan percussion instrument, as an important fuel, and for shade and shelter.

Genus containing 14-19 species of palms, depending upon the classification system; occupying diverse habitats, native to northern Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia, but naturalized in other regions worldwide.

Trademarked variety of pulp composite wallboard made from wood pulp or waste paper. It became a popular interior finish wallboard because the boards were available in many types of finishes, such as pebble-surfaced, and could be painted or decorated with stenciled designs instead of wallpaper.

Species of birch tree abundant throughout northern Europe, Iceland, northern Asia, and Greenland. It is a deciduous tree growing to over 60 feet tall (18 m), with a slender crown and a trunk, having smooth dull gray-white bark finely marked with dark horizontal lenticels. It is closely related to, and often confused with the silver birch.
Genus containing balsa.

Species of small tree or large shrub native to middle and southern Europe, western and central Asia, and northwestern Africa. It produces a small thin-fleshed cherry-like drupe, the kernel of which is used in perfumery and as a flavoring that tastes like bitter almond. It is also used in dye-making. The hard wood is used for small objects. The fruits are strung as beads in Africa and Asia. The tree is also used as dwarf stock for grafting branches of cultivated edible cherries.

Species of small or shrubby tree native to North America, from New England to the Midwest, to the South Atlantic and Gulf states. The wild tree has been cultivated for its fruit and wood since prehistoric times by Native Americans. The fruit is round and orange in color. In the American South and Midwest, the fruits are referred to as simply "persimmons," used in cooking and for making brandy. Folklore holds that the fruit is inedible prior to the first frost, but this is untrue. The peculiar astringency of the fruit is due to the presence of a tannin.
Species of evergreen eucalyptus grown commercially in Morocco for the bark, which contains tannin valued for the soft, dark red color achieved when used for tanning leather.

Species of medium-sized subtropical citrus tree having a juicy fruit with a rind that is orange in color (reddish-yellow). Believed to have originated in southeast Asia and cultivated in China by 2500 BCE; it is probably an ancient hybrid of the pomelo (Citrus maxima) and mandarin (Citrus reticulata). It is the most widely distributed fruit tree having the most popular fruit in the world today.

Species of rapid-growing shade tree, native to eastern North America and widely cultivated elsewhere. It grows to 18 m (60 feet) in height. Its wood is soft, but used for crating and inexpensive furniture. It can produce syrup, but is low yield. It drops branches and produces numerous shoots, making it problematic as an ornamental, although several useful varieties have been produced.

Species of medium-sized oak tree native to the western coast of North America, from British Columbia to southern California. Particularly common in the Willamette Valley, it hosts gall wasps and mistletoe.

In botany, the parts of a plant normally underground, having the primary functions of anchorage of the plant, absorption of water and dissolved minerals and conduction of these to the stem, and storage of reserve foods.

Species of large evergreen spruce native to the western Himalaya and adjacent mountains, from Afghanistan to Nepal, 44 m in height and growing at altitudes of 3,600 m in forests together with deodar cedar, pindrow fir, and blue pine.
Genus containing 4 species of deer and sambar.
Genus containing two species of pudu.

Genus containing various annual grasses of the family Poaceae (Gramineae), many producing edible grain. Barley was cultivated in Ethiopia and southeast Asia since prehistoric times. From biblical times through the Middle Ages, barley was the primary grain for producing unleavened bread and porridge throughout Europe, the Middle East, Egypt, and some parts of Asia. The grains are also been used to make malt beer. The residual stems, or straw, were used in Europe and Asia to make straw hats. The straw has also used used as a packing material, particularly for shipping glass and as an animal feed.

The continuous rain cloud. Resulting from thickening Altostratus, This is a dark gray cloud layer diffused by falling rain or snow. It is thick enough throughout to blot out the sun. The cloud base lowers into the low level of clouds as precipitation continues. Also, low, ragged clouds frequently occur beneath this cloud which sometimes merges with its base.
Masculine superhuman persons or other beings who are worshipped and believed to have power over nature and the fortunes of mankind.
Genus of prickly shrubs and small trees of the Caribbean region.

Institutions that provide tertiary education but do not have full or independent university status, often part of a larger university. The designation varies from place to place, but in British and formerly British educational systems, such an institution of higher learning does not have the authority to award its own degrees. Students enrolled at a university college ordinarily receive their degrees from a recognized university. In due course, a university college may be granted university status.
Studios in which one or more master painters create works, supervise assistants, and instruct pupils.

A registered trademark for a milky white aqueous emulsion of ethylacrate/methyl methacrylate copolymer. Plextol® B-500 is used as a dispersant, thickening agent, and sizing agent in inks, paints, adhesives, textiles, and papermaking.

Institutions having facilities where people are legally committed as punishment for a crime or while awaiting trial. In North America, the term specifically denotes a facility run by the state or federal government for those who have been convicted of serious crimes, in contrast to a locally run facility for those awaiting trial or convicted of minor offences. Use "jails (institutions)" for facilities for offenders sentenced either for lesser crimes or relatively short terms.
Species of aromatic-leaved green alder native to western North America and far northeastern Siberia. In some classifications, a subspecies of Alnus viridis.

Twelve o'clock in the day, or the time when the sun reaches the meridian. Originally, referred to the ninth hour of the day, reckoned from sunrise according to the Roman method, or about three o'clock in the afternoon.

Species of pine native to the eastern highlands of the island of Cuba. The closely related Hispaniolan pine (P. occidentalis), native to the neighboring island of Hispaniola, is treated as the same species as the Cuban pine in some classifications.

Genus of conifers represented by a single living species, Metasequoia glyptostroboides, from central China. Fossil representatives, such as M. occidentalis, dated to about 90 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Period, are known throughout the middle and high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere. Climatic cooling and drying that began about 65.5 million years ago and continued throughout the Cenozoic Era caused the geographic range of the dawn redwood to contract to its present relic distribution. The leaves are arranged in pairs on deciduous branchlets, and this deciduous character probably accounts for the tree's abundance in the fossil record. Metasequoia is closely related to the Sequoia and Sequoiadendron genera.
Software used for creating and editing spreadsheets, the electronic documents with columns and rows for organizing and analyzing data.
Refers to archival repositories of digital materials that are made accessible to individuals
Museums specializing in the history of and objects associated with fishing.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of red colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blackish colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of purple colors.
One-piece garments with gathered leg openings and buttons or snaps closing the crotch.
Sets of drafting instruments that usually include compasses, ruling pens, nibs, graphite points, etc., usually held in a carrying case with a compartment for each item.
Mechanical devices, usually in the context of punch cards or tape data, that check the correctness of data by comparing against additional sets of the same data, or original sets of data.

Mechanized devices designed to measure a dyed fabric sample's sublimation color fastness, or degree of discoloration, fading, or stain when exposed to heat sources. To measure sublimation fastness, these devices comprise two electric heated plates between which a dyed fabric sample is placed for a fixed period of time. When the sample is removed from the device, it is compared with a gray scale to appraise the grade of color dyeing sublimation-endurance.
Bookbinding machines used to coallate pages to ensure that all sheets are present and in the correct order.
Devices used to assist with opening sealed lidded jars.
Containers consisting of a bag backed with a diagonal strap, usually worn sideways around the torso.

Devices which decompose a material or gas in a catalytic reaction  such as odors, volatile organic compounds, and automobile exhaust and suppressing their emission, particularly VOC gasses containing volatile organic compounds.
Tools with serrated blades used in the process of butchering meat.
Order of flowering plants composed of 14 families, 380 genera, and about 11,000 species distributed throughout the tropics and warmer regions of the world.
Sets consisting of a dart board and darts or arrows. The game is played by throwing the darts at the dart board.
Instruments used to transfer amalgam alloy to a tooth cavity; comprising a hollow working end at an angle to the long axis of the instrument through which amalgam is expelled by a plunger mechanism.
Any of variously shaped objects usually made of stone, clay, or metal used in conjunction with a loom as a counterbalance.

Genre of unconventional musical works that combine elements of music, drama, and sometimes dance in new ways that result in works distinct from traditional forms. Works of music theater are often small in scale and primarily dating to the 20th century or later.
Method of acquiring property, usually indirectly by using money or income that has been provided by a benefactor.
Describes the maintenance, preservation, and conservation of collection materials.
The status or condition of being greatly damaged or spoiled, with the original appearance invisible. Often used to refer to settlements and architecture.
Meaning "out of the workshop [of]," in publishing refers to the workshop from which the work was published.

Titles or names that have been supplied by the cataloger in cases where supporting information or description of a work lacks a title. Constructed titles may be derived from other text in or on the work or invented as a descriptive title or name by the cataloger. In book cataloging, an example is when a title proper is not included on a title page.

Formal acts or series of acts, especially those conducted elaborately, solemnly, and as prescribed by the ritual or protocol of religious, state, court, social, or tribal procedure. For events serving to call someone or something to remembrance, use "commemorations."
The standard unit of currency of Canada.
In language, the words or lexical units by which an assertion is made, or that serve to connect a subject with a predicate.
Refers to the variety of Spanish spoken in the Dominican Republic; and among the Dominican diaspora.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 384-407/409; a Murong–Xianbei state.
Names or appellations that are given to a person, animal, or place as a familiar or humorous replacement for, or addition to, the proper name.

Elite Nahua military insignia in the form of a whole quetzal bird covered with feathers and supported by a frame worn on the back. An item sent to Tenochtitlan from the tributary province of Tochtepec, they were worn by tlahtohqueh (rulers) and pipiltin (nobles)  in postclassic central Mexico. They were also used to identify Tlaxcalan military units of Ocotelolco.

The eighth month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendars, containing 31 days and falling between July and September. It was named for the first Roman emperor, Augustus Caesar, in 8 bce. Its original name was Sextilus, Latin for “sixth month,” indicating its position in the early Roman calendar.

The lunisolar calendar traditional for China and oversees Chinese communities; it reckons years, months, and days according to astronomical phenomena; it lists the dates of traditional Chinese holidays and guides for selecting lucky days for personal activities, such as travel, weddings, funerals, or beginning a business.
Factory buildings in which pharmaceutical drugs are produced.
General term for administrative divisions, usually of a nation, that represent the fifth highest unit or level under the nation itself, typically under the fourth level subdivision.
Small sharpening steels held between the fingers by a currier to sharpen the blades used in scraping hides.

Addresses or discourses having a more or less formal character and composed for the purpose of delivering the content orally to an audience or assembly. For texts that record the speech, use "speeches (documents)."

Traditional festival in ancient China, focused on prayers for a good harvest. The date of the festival falls approximately on the fifth Wu day after Li Chun (Beginning of Spring), which is near the vernal equinox. The observance of Spring Sacrifice flourished particularly during the Tang and Song dynasties (618-1279 CE). Differences concerning the date on which to carry out ritual sacrificial ceremonies developed between the official and the civil communities in the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644 CE). From then on, official rituals were held according to the calendar of the Tang Dynasty, while civilians held ceremonies on the second day of the second lunar month. Observances included earth god worship, community feasts, and eating spring rolls. The tradition has waned in modern times.
In Japanese printing, format having dimensions ca. 23 x 16.5 cm.
Visual works, including architecture, that have been begun by the makers but was not completed.
That which is placed in position number eight of a sequence.

Qualifier used for attributions of works by an unknown creator working under a named creator, where the relationship is apparently close, probably a student/teacher relationship; implies the unknown artist is probably younger or less experienced than the named artist; synonymous with student of.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1499 to 1400 (or 1500 to 1401) Before Common Era.

Writing systems that use a set of written symbols used to represent the syllables of the words of a language. Writing systems that use syllabaries wholly or in part include Japanese, Cherokee, the ancient Cretan scripts (Linear A and Linear B), and various Indic and cuneiform writing systems.
Indian ancient and medieval dance-form, perhaps of foreign (Śaka?) origin.
Beverage made in Mexico and some parts of Central America from the fermented sap of the agave or maguey.

Trademarked term for a particular type of digital duplicating machine made by the Riso company that employs soy-based inks. Copies are created by scanning an image, burning it to a laser-etched stencil that is wrapped around a drum containing ink that rolls over continuously fed paper to create copies very rapidly.
Small language family of central Chile and neighboring areas of Argentina; some scholars classify the languages as divergent dialects of a single language isolate, rather than members of a family.

The English language in the period between Anglo/Saxon and Modern English, usually considered spoken between 1066 and 1485 CE (or more broadly, ca. 1100/1150-1450/1500). Middle English is characterized by a reduced system of grammatical inflections, an increased lexical borrowing from other languages, especially French and Latin, and great dialectal diversity in writing.

Language, known in numerous dialects, but which has been a single language throughout its history. It has been spoken in Greece probably since the late 3rd millennium BCED. The earliest texts are the Linear B tablets, some of which may date from as far back as 1400 BCE.
Variety of the Portuguese language used primarily in the nation of Timor-Leste.
Reflections of a light source captured in a subject's eyes in a photograph, painting, film, etc.

Instruments that give visual representation of sounds, consisting of  tubes closed at one end by a taught membrane with a small mirror attached to its centre, which vibrates in response to sound entering the tube at the open end, causing a spot of light reflected by the mirror on to a screen to vibrate with varying amplitude and frequency.
Armatures or frameworks of metal or another material in which a jewel is mounted or set. The purpose of a setting is to protect the jewel or to allow it to be worn or displayed.
Depressions on the sea floor.

Painters who produce many works in quick succession for profit or otherwise to meet market demand, particularly as applied to Dutch painters in 17th-18th centuries. The term may carry overtones of works having mediocre quality or being of a duplicative nature.
Stones of a particular type, used in ceremony or ritual; usually comprising fulgerite, which is a natural tube, clump, or mass of vitrified sand caused by lightning strike.
Fitness equipment consisting of a horizontal bar with two supports attaching it to a wall or doorway. Used for lifting exercises.
Collections of significant items wrapped in animal hide or other materials, which hold cultural or ceremonial importance for Indigenous peoples, particularly in the Plains region of North America.
Toys for babies and toddlers that are water resistant and used for playing in the bath tub.
Fancy trimming used on furnishings and costume, such as braid, cord, fringe, gimp, or tassel, often in combination.
Describes the physical location where a specific activity or work was realized.
Indication of the placement of a work of art or architecture within a classification scheme that groups other, similar works together on the basis of similar characteristics
Heaters that generate heat using radiation, usually infrared. Radiant heat heats objects not the air, and are more effective in outdoor environments.
Devices for pressing refuse meat and other offal from slaughterhouses.
Capsules that contain toothbrushes to keep them clean while traveling or for other purposes.
Seats, usually chairs or benches, that are specifically intended for use of the players of musical instruments.

Small pillows or cushions, commonly designed to rest on a user's knee, utilized as a stable surface to facilitate the fabrication of handmade bobbin lace. After outlining a lace design onto the pillow/cushion with pins, the user draws and interlaces thread around the pins using the pillow/cushion as support.
Containers specially designed to protect and transport one or more items of photographic equipment.

Wheels for winding yarn or thread typically consisting of an expandable cage that swivels on a verical shaft and a finial cup, designed to be free standing on its own legs, attachted to the lids of sewing baskets or designed to be clamped on to the edge of a table. A skein of yarn is placed over the cage and turned, swiveling to order to wind a neat ball of yarn.
Whistles that produce sound from jets of steam, and which are generally attached to a steam boiler.

Mechanized devices, equipped with air-jet chambers, used to increase the thickness and volume of yarns or fibers, thus creating air spaces in the fibers for increased abosrbancy, ventilation, warmth, and softness. To initiate the air entanglement process, of which these devices are a primary example, yarns or fibres are fed through machine guides and over feed rollers into the air-jet chambers, where they are subsequently entrapped and subjected to air at high pressures. The air movement causes the fibers to interlock and tangle, increasing the thickness of the fibers or yarn.

Small rakes used to tend domestic hearths, fireplaces, or coal stoves. They often form part of a set of fire irons. For larger hand-held rakes used in fighting wildfires, use "fire rake ( firefighting equipment)."
Types of barrels used in winemaking to vary the qualities of wine as it ferments. These are usually made of oak
Flexible tubes that can be placed on a rolling pin for the purpose of applying a pattern to rolled-out dough or to prevent dough from sticking to the rolling pin.
Devices that count down cooking time.
Carved boards which are pressed into sheets of cookie dough to transfer their designs. The designs are then cut out from the dough.
Lidded containers of various forms and materials in which salt is kept. The term is used especially with reference to those which hang from the wall.
Receptacles of a hard material with a cup-shaped cavity in which grains are pounded or ground with a pestle.
Private chapels for a royal court.
Subsidiary chapels opening off the rounded apse of a church, having a footprint resembling petals or rays extending from the rounded apse.
The state or quality of having or being divided into three parts.
Objects such as teething rings designed for a baby to bite on during teething.
Cut having a boat-shaped profile with pointed ends. A variant of the 57-facet brilliant-cut.

Defines a ceremonial dance performed by Southeastern Native North American tribes, including Cherokee, Chickasaw, Yuchi, and Creek (Mvskoke) communities. Often performed as part of the Green Corn Dance, but can also be interspersed throughout other ceremonies. Consists of dancers who follow a lead dancer in a circular motion around a fire. Dancers' motions are often accompanied by turtle shell shakers worn at the ankles.

Malalikid is held by the Amis people from July to August every year; it has different names and sets of practice from the north to the south. The festival is known as Malalikid in the north, Ilisin or Milisin in the middle region and Kilima’an or Malikoda in the south. The festival generally involves the welcoming, entertaining, feasting and bidding farewell to the ancestral spirits across regions, characterized by lengthy and majestic dancing and chanting. In recent years, the celebration is evolving in an urbanized context that expects festive glee combined with a tinge of historical authenticity – its cultural importance is thus confirmed as a moment foregrounding social identity, cultural symbols and the socio-ethical value of the age class system.
The eighth month of the year in the French revolutionary calendar,  introduced in 1793; it extended from April 20 to May 19.

The Pinuyumayan social organization is characterized by the men’s hall system composed of different age class. Before coming of age, boys are required to enter junior’s hall known as takuban and they will enter adult’s hall known as palakuan when they are mature. A mature man is allowed to marry and should contribute to the tribe’s work force. The Pinuyumayan secular power is held by a number of families in corporation with religious leaders.The acknowledgement that the Pinuyumayan is a matrilineal society used to be a firm one, since the husbands are married into the brides’ house, the Pinuyumayan children belong to the maternal side and the Pinuyumayan daughters are heir to the family property. Traditional Pinuyumayan rituals can be conducted by psychics or priests. The psychic is able to purify the patient and deal with diseases, while the priest’s responsibility is to hold rituals to ensure collective protect. Both psychics and priests are important to personal rite of passage and annual festivals.
Tile having rounded edges.
Period of the eighth city on the site of ancient Troy, ca. 1300-1050 BCE.

Refers to the plates of gramophones or record players on which the recorded discs rest and are spun to draw the grooves of recorded sound under a stylus, at fixed speeds, to enable reproduction of sound. Usage of the term is frequently extended to the totality of the machinery or housing of this plate.
Describes the state of people who do not subscribe to conventional gender distinctions, but identify with neither, both, or a combination of male and female genders.
In Indian architecture, a lateral nāsī-dormer.
In Indian architecture, a nāga-based column-type.
Documents or objects conferred as a reward for merit. These are normally of symbolic or commemorative value.
Stairs or steps communicating between any water level, as of a river, lake, or harbor, and the land, for convenience of embarkation or debarkation.

Portions of stair handrails that are curved in both the vertical and horizontal planes, which occur where the handrail changes direction and slope; may also refer to strings of similar shape and location.
Steps, more or less wedge-shaped, whose tread is wider at one end than the other.

Joints used in construction and woodworking comprising intermediate construction pieces that join two or more pieces of wood or another material. Rigid joints, typically made of metal or wood, are usually overlapping or placed between, and attached to, the pieces to be joined.
In Indian architecture, a basal-band showing frontal posture of elephant figures in file; base-moulding bearing elephant figures in series.
In Indian architecture, a complex of khura and kumbha mouldings.
In Indian architecture, a pilaster with pot at base and pañjara motif on top; vṛttasphuṭita variant.
Rails or panels stretching from the lintel to the sill of doors, dividing the doorframe into two parts.
In Indian architecture, a doorframe with seven jambs; with seven śākhās.

Long timbers on a Maori threshold, usually having the front surface carved. The paepae roa extends across the front of the porch with a piece usually cut away in front of the door to facilitate access.
Doors fitted to an opening in a horizontal or nearly horizontal surface, as a floor or roof, through which a person ascends head first and descends feet first.

Restraining structures incorporating a barrier that is raised or pushed aside at the start of a race, to ensure a simultaneous start for all competitors or to ensure consistent timing of each competitor. Examples are used in horse racing, foot races, downhill skiing, and other sports.
Window openings closed with cloth or translucent paper instead of glass.
Interior walls made up of standardized moduals or units which are the basis for construction and allow for flexible arrangement.
Rigid planar surfaces that inherently resist lateral thrusts of shear. Rigid planar surfaces that inherently resist lateral thrusts of shear.

Celtic late Iron Age defensive walls, generally constructed of thick lines of stones, held together and reinforced by a core of timber frames fastened with iron nails, and covered with a sloping earth rampart; sometimes faced with cut stone and topped by a parapet.
Walls having two interior faces and existing entirely within the exterior walls. Walls having two interior faces and existing entirely within the exterior walls.

In Indian architecture, a rectangular chamber, room, or hall; nave; rectangular hall with wagon-vault roof; miniature śālā-shaped aedicula in the hāra; aedicule of wagon-vault vimāna (or hall); oblong hall; rectangular barrel-vaulted aedicule.
In Indian architecture, a "thrown"; projected cusped course in ceiling.
In Indian architectural context, a floor, or storey.
In Indian architecture, a ornate frame or niche.
Tower-like structures placed atop dams or fortification walls to block passage across the wall or dam.
A perforated screen made up of intertwining cobras (nāgas and nāginīs) in half human form.
Ceilings divided into compartments or panels separated by moldings or ribs, particularly those in which the compartments or panels are not all uniform rectangles.
Gable roofs in the form of a pointed arch, with a gently sloping convex surface. Gable roofs in the form of a pointed arch, with a gently sloping convex surface.
Pitched roofs with only one slope.
Strips of wood or metal covering the ridge of a roof.
Gables having a triangular profile that is broken, usually at only one point on each side, with a step-shape.
Small spires as those found on pinnacles or turrets.
Domes having ribs; also, domes, usually of wood or metal, with vertical members converging at the crown, intersected by horizontal members.
In Indian architecture, a banner-staff; composed of the Ashtamangala, the "eight auspicious symbols". This may take the appearance of a high column (dhvaja-stambha) erected in front of temples.
Cubic capitals with their lower angles rounded off, to make the transition to a round column; found in Medieval architecture.
Refers to the rolls, faced at either end with volutes, forming the sides of an Ionic capital.

Trusses of closely spaced intersecting diagonal members, usually of wood, following a design patented by Ithiel Town in 1820. Trusses of closely spaced intersecting diagonal members, usually of wood, following a design patented by Ithiel Town in 1820.
Administrative areas having their own board and power of taxation and serving as the smallest units for administration of a public school system.
Inhabited areas that are directly under an adminisrative division but typically not within a city. Examples are in the Netherlands and Egypt.
Locations that were or are the site of a concentration camp internment center.
Arches composed of two intersecting arcs of a circle, struck so that the apex of the arch is a point.

Complexs comprising a forum and adjacent basilica, forming the civic administrative center of a Roman community. A typical plan included a rectangular open marketplace surrounded on three sides by rooms, and basilican great hall and with a rear range of rooms.

Farms attached to education facilities either for the purpose of teaching agriculture or providing meats and produce to the parent institution. Farms attached to education facilities either for the purpose of teaching agriculture or providing meats and produce to the parent institution.
Refers to burial sites specifically for victims of a battle.
Excavations or systems of excavations for the extraction of lead, which is a soft, dense, ductile metal of a dull gray color.
Buildings and other facilities located in a  scenic, sporting, or other desirable area, and providing lodgings, entertainment, and other amenities for vacationers.

Built complexes for religious retirement or seclusion from the world for monks, who are people living a celibate life according to the rule of a particular religious order and adhering to vows, especially of poverty, chastity, and obedience.
Temples, sanctuaries, or shrines dedicated to the Greek goddess, Hera.
In Indian architecture, a flat-roofed temple-type; temple sans superstructure; flat-roofed temple (or hall).
Hospitals designed or used for the care of women immediately before, during, and after childbirth and for the care of newborn babies.
Buildings that house facilities for the housing and care of orphans, who are children whose parents are either dead or otherwise unable to care for their child.

Refers to artificially constructed garden features, common since the 16th century in French and English landscapes. A grotto is characterized by being an excavation or structure made to imitate a rocky cave, often adorned with shell-work, colorful stones, etc., and serving as a place of recreation or a cool retreat. For natural features, use "caves" or "caverns."
Buildings housing collections of photographs, sometimes including other visual resources in various formats and media, usually within larger libraries, archives, or collections.

Permanent fortifications for troops, often surrounded by such elements as ditches, parapets, and ramparts and often used as advance posts in or near hostile territory. Smaller and less heavily fortified than "fortresses."

Christian religious monuments in the form of a column and erected in thanksgiving for surviving the plague. They may be dedicated to the Holy Trinity, the Virgin Mary, a saint, or with another dedication. They were common in Catholic countries of Europe, especially in the 17th and 18th centuries
Buildings used for assemblies of Muslims to gather during Muharram.
Structures or areas forming a central collection point where silt- or debris-laden water flows or is pumped to allow the particulates to settle at the bottom.
Elevated reservoirs, usually in the shape of towers, into which water is pumped to maintain desired pressure throughout a distribution system.
Industrial buildings used for public services.
Mills designed to grind trass, a kind of rock which when ground is used for making mortar or hydraulic cement.
Refers to a facility devoted to the production of high-quality sugars from remelted raw cane sugar or from remelted and recrystallized lower-grade beet syrups.

Buildings that house children's schools with facilities and structured program activities devoted to play, often convening only in the summer; established as an emergency measure during World War I; used both as places for children of working parents and as places for parents and teachers to study the playing habits of children.
Buildings housing academic enterprises that teach the theory and practice of engineering.
Buildings that house schools providing education between primary or elementary education and the higher or university level education, differing by school district in grades included.

General term for rooms or buildings having equipment for physical work outs, such as weights, treadmills, and the like. To distinguish facilities having work out equipment but also other amenities and classes, prefer "fitness centers."
Denotes houses with two stories in front and one in back and with an asymmetrical gable roof where the rear slope is longer than the front slope.
Urban dwellings attached in a series of three or more. For individual freestanding urban dwellings use "town houses."

Term applied to a group of Frank Lloyd Wright's small, single-family houses constructed during the late 1930s and early 1940s and generally characterized by low cost, natural materials, open planning, and a close relationship between the building and the site and climate. The term was coined by the architect.

Subordinate buildings on the grounds of estates or parks used as the individual dwellings for employees, such as caretakers or gatekeepers. For structures located at the entranceway to the grounds, and which may or may not contain habitation spaces, use "gatehouses."
Official residences of a president, who is an appointed or elected head of a group, state, or organization.
Multi-unit dwellings for seniors, often providing some common facilities for residents, as for social activities and meals.
African stone palaces. The outer walls and cattle kraals were built of dressed stone while the main buildings within the walls were of mud and wattle construction.

Posts used to mark the location of a grave and in commemoration of the deceased; known in many cultures. They were originally made of a single timber, often decorated with totemic emblems or other iconography. Grave posts may also be made of materials other than wood, but in form resemble the tall, verticality of a tree trunk.
Italian municipal buildings, often combining the housing of the local ruler and the offices of  the community government.

Structures constructed for or used to shelter poultry, which are usually domestic chickens, ducks, geese, turkeys, etc., but excluding game birds. An example of a humane poultry house could have either a large open space provided with food, water, and roosting areas, often with an accessible opening to the outdoors; in large commercial facilities, there may be a series of small pens where two or more animals are confined and raised for meat or to produce eggs.

Restaurants designed or utilized for dining outdoors at tables surrounding the building, often with tables placed in a patio or on a sidewalk in an urban area, sometimes with a protective roof or umbrellas sheltering the tables. Outdoor seating may be offered only seasonally as weather permits, with additional seating available indoors.
Buildings housing businesses that specialize in objects of art or bric-à-brac, valued as curiosities or for their rarity.
Buildings housing businesses where goods are sold directly to the ultimate consumers.
Built works used for personal or family purposes, in contrast to architecture used for commercial purposes.
Structures built for the drying, baling, and storing of hops.
Special rooms with sound recording and reproducing equipment for use by students studying languages.
May be used broadly for any consecrated place in ancient Roman or Christian architecture, but more specific terms are preferred, such as "chapels," "shrines," "sacristies," or "sanctuaries."
Small galleries like the boxes of a theater, often inserted into the choir wall of Baroque churches.

A building or architectural element shaped like an elongated pyramid. Used to describe structures with upright and tapered form that do not fall under any other technical term. For monolithic pillars with this shape, use "obelisk."
In Indian architecture, a structure having a curved spire (modern); curvilinear spire; see Latina, Śēkharī.
Ancient Roman entrance passages leading from the street into buildings, usually houses.
Small dining areas when they are extensions of living rooms. Use "dinettes" when referring to similar spaces that are extensions of kitchens or pantries.

Rooms in contemporary residences used for entertaining guests, reading, watching television, or other activities, generally more formal than a den but serving a wider range of activities than a 19th-century parlor.

In Indian architecture, a great columnar hall; large hall attached to ardhamaṇḍapa (term not found in texts); outer large maṇḍapa, usually open; gūḍhamaṇḍapa; sometimes also raṅgamaṇḍapa; piriyamaṇḍapa (old Kannaḍa).
Rooms kept at low temperatures for the storage of perishable items, such as food, or other items prone to deterioration or pests, such as film or archival materials.
In military architecture, outworks of two half bastions connected by a curtain and joined to the main work by two parallel wings.
Fixtures found on religious and ceremonial buildings of the Pacific Islands.
Shelves found in churches and used for the placement of vessels used in the Eucharist prior to use and immediately afterwards.

Monumental altars having a superstructure resembling a portico, originally including two or more pillars and a pediment, usually with a sculptural group or altarpiece. The Christian form developed from ancient altars, such as the Pantheon; it was most common in the Renaissance and Baroque periods.
Elements of the cultural landscape designed for the convenience and safety of pedestrians.
The sides of chimneys above the fireplace opening that close in toward the chimney throat or damper opening.
Typically refers to interior courtyards of mosques.
Rooms or areas equipped with several showerheads or shower stalls for use by a number of people at the same time.
In Indian architecture, a minor cyma moulding with lotus-petal pattern (in Dravidian architecture); minor padma moulding
In Indian architecture, a minor fillet.
Rounded usually beaded convex moldings placed under the echini of capitals in the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders.

Literally meaning “pretend” or “simulated” ang, jia’ang refers to a bracket arm that appears to be a xia’ang visually, but does not function as a xia’ang structurally. Architectural historians have used jia’ang as a term in traditional Chinese architecture since the 1930s (Liang 1933，26). Usually it refers to a huagong in an eaves bracket set (waiyan dougong 外簷斗栱) with a shape of ang mouth (angzui 昂嘴) on the outside. In most cases, there is a carved huatouzi 華頭子 underneath the jia'ang.
Towers incorporated into a protective wall, such as the wall around a city or castle.

Meaning, literally, “resisting platform” (Kroll 2015, 82, 440), ditai is a platform structure used for lookout and defense. Based on location and function, ditai can be divided into three categories: ditai in city walls, ditai in the Great Wall, and freestanding ditai. Although the forms and development of these three types of ditai differed, they affected each other to a certain extent. According to the current historical documents, the term ditai first appeared in the Ming dynasty (1368-1644) text Ming Taizong Wen huangdi shilu 明太宗文皇帝實錄 (Zhongyang yanjiuyuan lishi yuyan yanjiusuo 1963, 125.5a).
Movable screens, covers, or similar contrivances to close an opening, especially a window or door.

Window or door shutters having louvers, which are horizontal slats that are movable and may be angled to admit light and air, but to keep out rain and snow. The louvers are set into a frame to make a shutter.
Wood of the species Fagus crenata, similar to European beech with cream-colored sapwood and brown heartwood. It is used for tool handles, flooring, joinery, plywood, and furniture.

Wood of the species Betula alleghaniensis, native to the northeastern part of North America, with light yellow sapwood and reddish-brown heartwood. It is similar to sweet birch and is not separated from it commercially. It is used in the making of fine furniture, joinery, spools, bobbins, and plywood.
Wood of Cedrela odorata (a mahogany, not true cedar) used in the United States for cigar boxes, furniture, carving, and interior trim.

Hard, fine-grained wood of the species Acer saccharum, native to the United States and Canada. It is light reddish-brown in color and tends to have bird's eye patterns. It is used for furniture, cabinetry, flooring (dance floors, bowling alleys), musical instruments, and veneer.
Wood of the species Quercus petraea, native to Europe and the British Isles, Asia Minor and North Africa. Used for tight cooperage.
Hair from the manes and tails of horses, used chiefly as a brush fiber, for musical instrument bows, and for making haircloth.
The skin of a lion, generally with hair including mane attached.
Material comprising the leaves and stems of various species of grass of the Saccharum genus.
Common term for the wood of several trees, most in the genus Populus (poplars).
Marble that is predominantly yellow in color.
Tradename of a coarsely mottled marble from Malletts Bay on Lake Champlain.
A yellowish white marble with ashy black stains and large conspicuous crystals; it originates from the island of Lesbos in Greece.
Building stone that has a smooth finish.
Colorless and odorless acid found in the juices of most fruits, as well as other plants, many animal tissues, and fluids.
Siliceous or calcareous material deposited at the mouth of springs or geysers, along streams, or on lake bottoms or shores.
Porous, fossiliferous limestone, yellowish white in color, quarried near Verona, Italy; used as a construction material.

General term for a group rocks, the constituent minerals of which have assumed a position in more or less closely parallel layers due to metamorphic action. They comprise layers of lamellar minerals, such as mica, chlorite, talc, hornblende, and graphite. Quartz is often present as a secondary mineral. Schists are formed at high temperatures from shale, clay, or mud. They cleave easily along the foliated planes. Schists are usually named for their predominant mineral constituent, such as mica schist, hornblende schist, chlorite schist, and talc schist. The exception occurs when a schist is named for an unusual mineral constituent such as garnet schist, tourmaline schist, and glaucophane schist.
A coarse breccia marble containing fragments of pophyry, basalt, quartz, and granite in a greenish or purplish ground.
Metal rolled to any given thickness between 0.06 and 0.249 inches and cut into rectangular sections.

Aragonite is a widespread mineral, a crystalline form of calcium carbonate that is found in deposits formed at low temperatures near the surface of the earth, occurring as stalactites, in sediments, iron-ore deposits, and basic rocks. It is also commonly found in pearls, coral, and shells. It was used in antiquity for beads and other decorative artifacts.

Glass that has been heat treated to induce surface compression in order to add strength. On breaking, it breaks into sharp pieces, but smaller than pieces of broken annealed glass. It does not dice, as does tempered glass on breaking. It is intermediate in strength between annealed glass and toughened glass. It is used in the curtain wall design as spandrel glazing of multistoried buildings. It is usually polished plate glass or patterned glass on one surface of which is fused a colored enamel.

An alloy of about five parts of copper with one of zinc that is used as imitation gold. It is similar to brass but contains more copper. It was invented by a London watchmaker named Christopher Pinchbeck, ca. 1740. Pinchbeck was often used in clock making and the production of inexpensive jewelry and snuffboxes, particularly by craftsmen in London.
Copper-zinc alloy with a small amount of tin which improves corrosion resistance.

A hollow brick used for furring or lining the inside face of a wall; usually the size of an ordinary brick and grooved or scored on the face to afford a key for plastering; it carries no superimposed load.

A type of pottery midway between earthenware and porcelain being made of clay and a fusible stone. It is fired to a point where partial vitrification renders it impervious to liquids, but, unlike porcelain, it is very seldom more than faintly translucent. The vitrification makes it unnecessary to add a glaze, but for reasons of utility and appearance decorative glazes are sometimes used, such as salt glaze and lead glaze.
Relatively lightweight concrete made with blast-furnace slag as the coarse aggregate.

Glass containing a high proportion of lead oxide and having a relatively high refractive index, with poor acid resistance and low rigidity; used in many optical components, neon-sign tubing, and light bulbs.

Refers to a type of glass in which colored glass is mixed with white glass, to create an opalescent effect that resembles clouds. It is often used to create decorative vessels. It is similar in appearance to "reamy glass" and to "Clutha glass," which means "cloudy glass."
In masonry, a pure cement uncut by a sand mixture.
Brick fired at the nominal dimensions of 4 by 4 by 8 inches.
Figures composed of four equal lobes separated by cusps.
In Indian architecture, a wish-fulfilling vine as decorative motif.

Zodiac symbol of an archer, often a centaur,, roughly based on the constellation of the same name. The zodiak signs have survived from classical Greek and Roman decoration, were popular in Northern European Romanesque and Gothic churches, and often found in Medieval psalters and books of hours symbolizing each month in which the sun enters the related constellation. They have also been used as decoration on ceilings, maps, timepieces, and astronomical instruments.
Crosses with each arm terminating in a stylized fleur-de-lis.
Settlement areas encompassing a central city and surrounding municipal or political jurisdictions.
Region of land or settlement that has self-government, typically having a mayor and city council.
Settlements or temporary stations featuring ports or harbors that are a safe place for pirates to dwell, repair their vessels, resupply, or avoid capture.
Land covered with grass or similar plants and used for grazing livestock.
Tracts of lowlying ground in which water collects, particularly wetlands partially or intermittently covered with water, often dominated by woody vegetation.
In Indian architecture, a wheel; Viṣṇu's discus.

Concatenates a variety of constructions that embody a theme for a spectacular event such as an international exposition or trade fair. For semi-permanent structures in similar contexts that may be larger-scale and/or inhabitable by groups of people use 'theme buildings.'

Refers to structures excavated into living rock. This term may overlap in meaning with "cave architecture," but cave architecture is not necessarily rock-cut, and rock-cut architecture is not necessarily designed around a cave.
Buildings that do not comply with current laws, codes, or ordinances, but that were lawful at the time that they were built, under the regulations then enacted.
Gardens designed as quiet spaces for meditation, often having landscaping that includes paths, water features, and isolated spaces conducive to meditation.
General term for parks that preserve areas associated with military history.
Roads that are privately owned and maintained.
Open places for walking or strolling; examples are paved or wooden public walk along the seafront at a resort.

Parcels of land with fixed boundaries occupied or capable of being occupied by one building or use, including accessory buildings, and not divided by any public highway or alley. Distinguished from "plats (land)," because plats tend to be somewhat larger than lots and are often in the countryside, while lots are typically smaller and located within a settlement.
In Indian architecture, refers to a temple, or a broader sense represents a devotional place.

Rooms, buildings, or groups of buildings where issues regarding the natural  environment are studied and tested, including issues surrounding effective resource use, resource conservation, and environmental protection.
Buildings in which goods are stored.
Buildings used for functions related to water transportation.
Stations providing electrical power to electric vehicles.
Bridges having only one span, being anchored only at each end with no supports in the middle; the longest single span bridges are suspension bridges.
Large watertight enclosures in which the water is maintained at the level of high tide so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
Buildings of several floors with large areas of unobstructed space, originally rented for light industrial purposes and now frequently converted to residential occupancy.
Wood churches with walls of vertical planks, used from at least the 9th century, especially in Scandinavia.
Churches incorporated into hospitals, especially in complexes of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, as with S. Maria della Scala, Siena.
Styles belonging to Kwa-speaking peoples cultures.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Guinea-Bissau and Senegal.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in southwestern Ghana.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting the plateau region of Nigeria.

Diagrams for setting up shaft looms to construct particular weaves. Traditonally drawn up on point paper or some other kind of paper with preprinted lines, they show at least one weave unit of the cloth to be woven. A complete set of them instructs the weaver how to plot the drawing in of the warp, connect the shafts and treadles, the order in which the treadles are to be used, the interlacement of warp and weft, and the transverse section of the weave.
Refers to photographs or other representations of the inside of a building or other structure or object that has interior and exterior space.

Portraits of the donors of a work, depicted in the work depicting a narrative or other scene. The donors may be depicted as themselves, or they may take on the character of one of the actors in the narrative.

Refers to a type of still life that features smokers' accoutrements such as tobacco pipes, smoldering hemp wicks, and braziers of burning coals. Jugs of beer or glasses of wine are also typically depicted. The term tabakje is translated from the Dutch as "little tobacco."
Refers to archaeological sites in present day Sudan which date from 8000 BCE to 4900 BCE.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Chad.

A solution or dispersion of a colorant in a vehicle that renders it capable of penetrating a material such as wood or fabric, but not capable of forming a protective surface. Also, a reagent used in microscopy to make visible minute structures. Typically, the transparency and fluidity of a stain will allow the base texture of the object to remain visible.
Plaster having crushed blast-furnace slag as the aggregate.
Paints incorporating synthetic resin, such as acrylic, which is a synthetic polymer used in latex or water based paints.
Any paint that glows in the dark.

White, sweet-tasting, crystalline sugar alcohol which occurs naturally in many plants and algae. Mannitol is used widely as a dietary supplement and dietetic sweetener. In conservation, mannitol is used in tandem with sucrose for impregnation of waterlogged wood.
Visual works or parts of works made from lead, particularly sculptural, ornamental, or architectural objects. Usage may include plumbing or glazier's work.

Substances that conduct electric current resulting from positive and negative ions discharged at terminals (cathode and anode) of an electric circuit, specifically the conducting fluid used in a battery.
A catalyst or other kind of substance that reacts with another to activate or hasten the process of curing, as in two-part resins.
Material, such as plaster or mud, used with wattle as a building material.

Roofing systems that use metal sheets or tiles, used for longevity, corrosion resistance, water impermeability, and fire resistance. Metal roofs are noted for durability, and can last 50 years or more.
Roofing shingle material made of wood.
Essential oil used for its effects on spirit varnish and for its ability to retard the drying of paint.
Oils prepared by natural thickening in sunlight. This is most often a linseed oil. Sun-thickened oil is similar to stand oil, but is prized for is fast-drying properties as a painting medium.
Fine white clay mixed with lime; used chiefly as building and plastering material, and for sculpture.
Composite material in which the separate materials are arranged in layers. An example is foam board, where smooth outer skins are adhered to an interior layer of fine-cell foam.

Negative photographic materials that are sensitive to violet, blue, green, and yellow, but not to red, light. Formerly used for general photography, but now employed mainly for photographing of phosphor screens, such as cathode-ray tubes, and for other purposes requiring green, but not red, sensitivity.
An unsized, absorbent white paper saturated with litmus and used to test for acidity.

A photographic paper used for developing or printing out black and white prints; developed in the 1880s, and still used for this type of chemically-based printing process. The paper is coated with a gelatin emulsion containing a silver bromide salt. The sensitivity of the paper allows photographers to make contact prints and enlargements from positives or negatives with artificial light. The prints may fade, yellow, or develop a dark iridescent appearance with age if not properly processed.
A stiff, heavy cardboard primarily used for book covers.
Aromatic oil found in uncombined form in various parts of plants and employed for flavoring, perfume, disenfectant, and medicine.

Fiber derived from the stalk of the species Cannabis sativa. Fibers range from 1-2 m in length and are yellow to brown in color. They have a high cellulose content with little lignin. Hemp is lustrous, strong, and durable with good resistance to water, salts, light, and insects; used for cordage, fish lines, sailcloth, canvas, burlap, packing, and as a fiber for paper or for plastic filler.

Materials produced by weaving, felting, knotting, twining, or otherwise processing natural or synthetic fibers so that they cohere into a form or unit; traditionally excludes fiberboard, paper, papier-mâché, and papyrus, which, though also fiber products, are considered as separate types of material. For generic reference to the genre, see "textiles."
A loose-weave cotton fabric, used especially to shade growing tobacco plants.

Paper made of 100% linen or cotton fiber. The general process of making rag paper involves boiling, shredding, and beating the rags to separate the fibers; the resulting smooth pulp is run over a fine screen in a thin layer and then dried and pressed. Rag paper is considered the finest paper support for paintings and similar works of art.

Soft, thin, unsized, fine-textured, highly absorbent paper of bamboo fiber originating in China, usually of a pale yellow color. It is typically used for steel engraving, woodcut proofs, and as lithographic transfer paper, because it absorbs ink without smearing. Although it is also called "Indian proof paper," it is distinct from "India paper," which is softer and looser in its fiber bond.
Greenish blue pigment found on wall paintings and painted objects from several Maya sites, determined in 1967 to be composed of indigo absorbed on a clay substrate.

General term referring to a modern blue pigment that is chemically similar to Egyptian blue, but tends to be purer and finer than the ancient pigment, or to commercial products containing a dye of the same hue.
A specific variety Prussian blue that is a high quality grade.

An unstandardized term for various green pigments, including malachite green dye, pigment mixtures of lead chromate and Prussian blue, mixtures of zinc yellow and Prussian blue, of zinc chrome green and hydrated chrome oxide, of viridian and zinc yellow, and a ceramic color that is chemically the same as vernalis.

An unstandardized name for pigment having a yellowish-green color; originally used for mixtures of green (viridian and later phthalocyanine green or chromic oxide) with yellow (cadmium yellow) pigments. Another recipe for permanent green is made by mixing Prussian blue with zinc yellow.

An orange-red mineral, found as soft lumps consisting of arsenic disulfide, having a resinous luster; it is found in eastern Europe, Asia, and western North America in lead and silver ores along with orpiment (arsenic trisulfide). Realgar was once widely used as a pigment because of its bright rich color in works from China, India, Central Asia, Egypt, and Europe. However, it is extremely toxic, not stable, and can deteriorate badly in oil paint films.

Any of several bright, transparent, synthetic azo-type organic red pigments. Toluidine reds are made using the reaction of beta-naphthol with 2-nitro-4-toluidine. Toluidine red was first synthesized in 1904 in Germany, and reached its peak of popular use in the 1970s. Toluidine reds have fair lightfastness and weather resistance: they are used in industrial coatings for air-dried and baked enamels and auto finishes, in wax crayons, pastels, and watercolors; however, they have a tendency to bleed in oil paints. It is a suspected carcinogen.
Stannic oxide, used to produce an opaque white in ceramics.
White pigment that is used in industrial products, such as white casein wall paint.

A natural yellow dyestuff obtained from the wood of Cotinus coggygria, having poor lightfastness. The primary coloring compounds are fisetin and myricetin. It was used for textiles and shading during the Middle Ages, but was rarely used after the 16th century. This is not the same dye stuff as "fustic" ("old fustic").

Yellow pigments composed of lead stannate that were used in European painting from the beginning of the 14th century until the early years of the 18th century, when it was largely replaced by Naples yellow (lead antimonate yellow). Two distinct varieties are known, both made by heating together lead and tin oxides in a furnace, with one type having sand (silicon dioxide) introduced. Both pigments are stable, used as opacifiers, colorants in glass and ceramic glazes, and in all paint media. Lead-tin yellow was often used in mixtures with other pigments such as lead white, vermilion, azurite, verdigris, and indigo.
Gum from some species of Astragalus or Penaea, mentioned in ancient writings and also in English 18th- and early 19th-century painting recipes.

A modified natural resin made from rosin that has been esterified by heating with a polyhydric alcohol, such as glycerol. Ester gum contains the glyceryl, methyl, and ethyl esters of rosin acids. Ester gum is lighter in color than rosin and have a higher softening point but lower acid number. It is not used in artist paints or varnishes although they have been tried for wax-resin linings. It is used instead of copal, dammar, or kauri in making enamels, paints, nitrocellulose lacquers, and tung oil mixtures.  A modified natural resin made from rosin that has been esterified by heating with a polyhydric alcohol, such as glycerol. Ester gum contains the glyceryl, methyl, and ethyl esters of rosin acids. Ester gum is lighter in color than rosin and have a higher softening point but lower acid number. It is not used in artist paints or varnishes although they have been tried for wax-resin linings. It is used instead of copal, dammar, or kauri in making enamels, paints, nitrocellulose lacquers, and tung oil mixtures.

A thick, viscous exudation from the Austrian larch tree, Larix decidua, containing 63% resinous acids, 20% terpenes, and 14% resins. It has been used since the 16th century in small amounts to produce an enamel-like surface that is non-yellowing. However, it is not used as a varnish because it quickly becomes dark and brittle when exposed to oxygen and light. It is also used as a mounting medium for light microscopy and as a plasticizer in glue paste linings. A thick, viscous exudation from the Austrian larch tree, Larix decidua, containing 63% resinous acids, 20% terpenes, and 14% resins. It has been used since the 16th century in small amounts to produce an enamel-like surface that is non-yellowing. However, it is not used as a varnish because it quickly becomes dark and brittle when exposed to oxygen and light. It is also used as a mounting medium for light microscopy and as a plasticizer in glue paste linings.
Yellow dye produced from the bark of the Chinese buckthorn, historically exported to Europe and elsewhere in small square cakes or crystals. It was also used in medicine.
Pigments having white color, which is a total reflection of all frequencies of visible light.

Wood of the genus Larix, native to cool and sub-Arctic parts of the Northern Hemisphere. Most larch timber is coarse-grained, hard, and heavy, and is used for the construction of telephone poles, mine timbers, and railroad ties.

Wood of the Thuja plicata species, having a reddish to dull brown heartwood with a faint, sweetish odor. The wood is used for shingles, boat making, and other purposes for which resistance to moisture, decay, and insect damage is important.
Wood of the Chamaecyparis nootkatensis tree, ranging from Alaska to Oregon. Timber is pale yellow in color and is prized for joinery, doors, window frames, greenhouses, shingles, and cabinet work.
Wood from Pinus virginiana, a dwarf pine of North America.

Wood in the form of broad, thin, flat or sometimes curved pieces that serve as a support for media in visual works; examples are paintings on wood. In architecture and other constructive arts, use "panels (surface components" to refer to a panel, whether of wood or another material, that is typically a compartment of a surface either sunken below or raised above the general level, and set in a molding or other border, as in a frame, sometimes of different color or material.
The unhewn portion of a felled tree, including a length cut off for use as firewood, construction, or another purpose.

Refers to the style of porcelain made in China at the Imperial factory at Ju Chou, Honan province, during the Sung dynasty from 1107 to 1127. The style is characterized by a buff-colored body covered with a fine glaze of pale lavender which is closely crackled.

Refers to movement in America that flourished from around 1785 to 1820 based on the revival of Roman architectural styles in the design of government buildings. The movement, endorsed by Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Latrobe, is driven by the metaphorical concept of the United States as analogous to the Roman Republic in its grandeur and political philosophy.
Style of American architecture inspired by built works of the Italian Renaissance.
Style or culture associated with the Picunche, Mapudungun-speaking people living to the north of the Mapuches or Araucanians in what is now Chile.
Style and culture of a North American Indian group native to the northern Mexican border state of Sonora.
Style and culture of one of the dozens of Pueblo cultures than once dominated the Rio Grande Valley.
Style or culture of an inhabitant of Tepotzohtlan.

Style and culture of Native American people of southeastern North Carolina, descendants of the pre-Columbian Neusiok tribe. Fought alongside American colonists during the Revolutionary War. Achieved state recognition in 1917. Today, the Coharie Tribe is concentrated in Sampson and Harnett counties.
Style and culture of the Algonquian-speaking, Native American people who inhabited the seacoast from Niantic Bay to Connecticut River.

Style and culture of a North American Indian group who speak Ute, and who at one time occupied what are now southern Utah, northwestern Arizona, southern Nevada, and southeastern California, the latter group being known as the Chemehuevi. Although encroached upon and directed into reservations by the U.S. government in the 19th century, the Southern Paiute had comparatively little friction with settlers and the U.S. military; many found ways to stay on their traditional lands, usually by working on ranches or living on the fringes of the new towns.

Refers to the style and culture of the Peoria, an Algonquian-speaking people whose ancestral land was located east of the Mississippi River and north of the Ohio River. They were assigned land in "Indian Territory" after the Omnibus Treaty in 1867; today they are a federally-recognized tribe with headquarters in Miami, Oklahoma.

The Pre-Columbian style and culture from the central region of what is now province of Veraguás in Panama. The area extends from the Pacific to the Caribbean coast and includes a number of islands. The climate here is mainly humid and tropical, and the landscape includes wooded areas and valleys suitable for agriculture, as well as high mountains, hilly areas, and coastal lowlands.

Pre-Columbian culture and period of the Central Andes, marked by the expansion of irrigation on the coast and and development of a lake-agricultural-livestock economy; focused on southern shore of Lake Titicaca, and population center at Chiripa, Bolivia. The culture is temporally located between the between the Initial period and Early Horizon period.
Culture of Nazca society that developed during the Early Intermediate Period phase 1, 100 BCE-1 CE.

Pre-Columbian culture which developed during the middle Horizon and late intermediate period (before 900 to 1350 CE) in the far south of Peru and Northern Chile, reaching its zenith of population during the 13th and 14th centuries.

Indian peoples who inhabit, or formerly inhabited, the North American Great Plains, which is a vast grassland between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains and from present-day provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in Canada through the present-day state of Texas in the United States. The area is drained principally by the Missouri and Mississippi rivers; the valleys of this watershed are the most reliable sites from which to obtain fresh water, wood, and most plant foods.
Describes works created by the Tuareg people of the same name living in southern Niger.
As a general term, belonging to Spanish-derived culture, especially referring to those of Spanish origin in North, Central, or South America.

Prehistoric culture of the American Southwest, which flourished from the mid-thirteenth through sixteenth centuries, and was centered in the Tonto Basin of southeastern Arizona. A farming and trading people, the Salado lived in walled adobe compounds, practiced burial (rather than cremation) of their dead, and created distinctive polychrome ceramics.
Inhabitants of Xochimilco.
The style and culture of the country of Tunisia in North Africa, of its capital Tunis, of the former Barbary state of Tunis, that preceded it, or of speakers of the demotic speech of the area.
Style and culture of the Berber people of the same name living on the island of Jerba, Tunisia.

Gunda Gundé style takes its name from the location of the Stephanite monastery of Dabra Garzen, noted for its manuscript illuminations. It is characterized large, exaggeratedly rounded backs of the figures, almond-shaped eyes, dotted motif employed in their clothing, extreme stylization of the figures, and geometric regularity.

Describes works produced by the African people of the same name living mainly in Burundi and Rwanda, but also in Uganda, Tanzania, and Democratic Republic of Congo. The Hutu came into the Great Lakes region around 1000 to 500 BCE. Among the resident Twa pygmy peoples, they established an agrarian society based on the family unit. They were gradually dominated by a feudal system headed by the aristocracy of the nomadic Tutsi people in the 14th or 15th century. The Tutsi monarchy in Rwanda was overthrown 1959-1961. The European colonial period created tensions between the two groups that remain problematic.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Equatorial Guinea, comprised of many Kombe-speaking sub-groups.
Describes works produced by the African people of the same name living in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
