Projecting roofs or porchlike structures that shelter vehicles and passengers at the entrances to buildings; also for short vehicular tunnels through buildings, sheltering an entrance.
Items that are necessary to attach, anchor, hold, or join components of systems that convey water or gas.
Theological or religious opinion or doctrine maintained in opposition to the official or orthodox doctrine of a given church, creed, or religious system.
The quality or state of being divine; the nature or essence of God.
Lists of names of registered voters, typically including demographic information, some vote history, and campaign contribution history, used for polling purposes.

Color prints produced through three black-and-white separation negatives. In this process, yellow, magenta and cyan gelatine films sensitized with silver bromide are transferred to a common support after exposure through the three negatives. The Duxochrome system is an improvement of the Pinatype. The materials were on the market from 1929 to 1963.

Digital images of all or part of what is displayed on a computer screen or mobile device, captured at a particular moment in time and saved on a drive as an image file, for documentation or other purposes.
The art of turquoise mosaic work in Nahua culture.
Masks that enclose the head entirely or in part, especially those worn during African ceremonies and masquerades.

Refers to the practice of making photographs with a pinhole camera. Light-sensitive film or paper is exposed through a tiny, lensless aperture: the resulting images have very great depth of field, but lack critical sharpness.
Formally arranged flower beds, planters, or boxed sections of gardens, often set with raised borders and in different shapes.

Photographs taken from beyond the earth's atmosphere. For photographs of the earth taken from aircraft, use "aerial photographs"; for photographs of celestial bodies or astronomical phenomena, use "astrophotographs."
Folded printed sheets, such as circulars or schedules, having printed matter that generally does not cross the folds.  For sheets printed to be read unfolded, use "broadsides."

Printed works that are created to meet an array of immediate needs, usually transitory in nature not intended to be saved. Examples cold be broadsides, posters, leaflets, pamphlets, programs, postcards, tradecards, labels, tickets, handbills, sale notices, and valentines.
Maps showing the existing uses of a given area.
Lists of addresses, usually kept by an organization or business, used when sending postal matter. May also refer to electronic-mail addresses.
Specialized books containing information pertinent to the collecting of particular types of artifacts.

The function or activity of making considered decisions or to arriving at conclusions or opinions, particularly when the conclusions are resonable and based on available information, employing critical faculty; discernment, and discrimination.
Modifier describing a color of light intensity and light value; may be overlapping in meaning with the modifier "pale."

Structured sets of data held in computer storage, especially those that incorporate software to make them accessible in a variety of ways. A database is used to store, query, and retrieve information, typically comprising a logical collection of interrelated information that is managed as a unit, stored in machine-readable form, and organized and structured as records that are presented in a standardized format in order to allow rapid search and retrieval by a computer.
Fixed standard sizes of card photographs.
Of a building, particularly an ancient Greek or Roman temple, that has columns at the front but none at the rear and sides.
Films that are based on or are adaptations of a previous film or script, usually with the roles played by different actors.

Material resembling pearls, often inexpensive. Imitation pearls, first made in the 19th century, were constructed by injecting hollow beads of glass with a mixture of aqueous ammonia and fish scales; this deposited a layer of guanine crystals as an iridescent film on the interior surface of the beads. In the 20th century, another process made imitation pearls by coating the exterior of solid glass beads with the fish scale mixture; the nacreous coating was sealed with a protective varnish layer.

Color stereographic photographs made by using two similar prints, one treated with dammar varnish to make it transparent, the other painted with washes of color; the former is laid over the latter and the two bound together with a glass and backing, achieving a three-dimensional effect.
Study of coins, tokens, medals, paper money, and objects closely resembling them in form or purpose.

Positional attribute used to describe something situated at or near the highest or loftiest part of something. To refer to those highest or loftiest parts, use "tops (portions)" from the Components hierarchy.
Level with the surface.

Lace in which the pattern is made using strips or tape set in a background of either thread bars (brides) or net. The quality is judged by whether the tape lies flat and curves continuously (which can be achieved only by using bobbins) or is ready-woven, in which case the tape is gathered at the bends and corners, and inevitably puckers. The best Genoese tape lace of the 17th century is bobbin-made; among the ready-woven tape laces are the Belgian and French laces of the 1880s, such as so-called Renaissance lace.

A type of symmetric, thick and sturdy bobbin lace with very dense motifs. It was made in the 17th century in Flanders to be sold on the Dutch market. It is sometimes referred to as "Brabant lace" but is not to be mistaken with the lace made in Brussels from the 18th century onwards.
Sets of implements, vessels, and other articles intended for use at one's toilet; generally including a variety of small boxes and bottles.
An oolitic limestone widely used for building in England, particularly in London; it is quarried on the Isle of Portland, off the coast of England.
Creation of images by alteration to the electrical properties of the senstitive material as a result of the action of light.
Richly or splendidly decorated chairs used on ceremonial occasions by a monarch or other person of high rank. Generally less grandiose than "thrones."

A contemporary art form that adapts scientific methods and draws inspiration from the philosophical, societal, and environmental implications of recombinant genetics, molecular biology, and biotechnology. It features interdisciplinary relationships that blur distinctions between art and science. It may involve biological entities as media.
Water issuing naturally from the rock or soil upon the land or into a body of surface water.
In regions of southwestern Asia and northern Africa, a valley or ravine which becomes a watercourse during rainy season.

Gymnospermous plants with lineage dating back only to the early Cretaceous; widely considered to be the closest extant relative of the flowering plants. Plants are trees, shrubs, lianes, and stumpy turnip-like plants.

Places, usually small in size, where man-made features in a transportation network are located, including stations, docks, platforms, and other spot features; excludes roads and tracks. For large communities that are hubs for transportation, use "transportation centers."
Functions or performances that are legal in nature.
The action or function of putting a person in a jail, prison, or other place of confinement, usually, but not always, according to legal procedures.
Attempting to influence or sway public officials toward a desired end.
Photographs produced by the wet collodion process directly on lacquered metal, usually iron.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
The process of conducting an examination or inspection in order to achieve a comprehensive view, as of a place, a situation, or an area of study, or to ascertain condition or value.
In Islamic architecture, monumental gateways or portals, especially ones with a rectangular screen wall rising above the roofline of the building beyond, usually mosques, madrasas, or caravanserais.
Commercial establishments where laundering of clothing, linens, and other personal or household textiles is done.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.
Permanently dedicated recreation areas, often open to the public and generally characterized by their natural, historic, or landscape features; often administered by governmental agencies.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of violet colors.

Areas of cities or towns that are residential or more prosperous areas, but still remaining within the central urban boundaries, not the suburbs. The term is thought to derive from these areas, in historic times, having been laid out radiating away from the older business center, thus having higher street numbers than the older areas; alternatively, the term may derive from the development of New York City, where the historical newer residential sections were in the north of Manhattan Island, at the top of a map.
A range of yellow colors resembling the color of yellow pigment.

Vases intended to contain offerings or to themselves serve as an offering in a religious or funerary context. Examples exist from ancient times and in many cultures, including the following: ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome; Asian cultures; the Pre-Columbian Americas; and in modern western culture.

Aesthetic concept or expression, arising in Europe first in painting of the 18th century and later in architecture of the 19th century, characterized by rough, curious, or irregular forms; it applies particularly to rustic landscapes and crumbling buildings having neither the awe-inspiring grandeur of the Sublime nor the order and regularity of beauty.
Material comprising leaves, which are the expanded, usually green organs borne by the stem of a plant.
Mechanical presses for expressing juice from grapes; used to make wine.
Fields where wet rice is grown.
Scottish narrow streets, lanes, or alleys that are usually curving in their course and lead off of main thoroughfares in towns or cities.
Structures where coal is unloaded from mining cars by means of a tipping device.
In Indian architecture, square without bay-proliferations on plan.

Bridges in which the roadway is suspended from cables, ropes, or chains attached to natural or constructed supports. The term applies both to primitive and massively engineered structures that share this basic principle.

Portable residential units that possess their own chassis with wheels, are designed for year-round living, are infrequently moved, and are larger than travel trailers; use "travel trailers" for portable vehicles designed for travel and recreational purposes and for frequent towing. For motorized trucklike vehicles equipped as traveling living quarters, use "motor homes."

The three outer extremities of the folded gatherings of books, usually cut at some stage so that the book can be opened and sometimes also trimmed; they may be decorated by gilding, painting, sprinkling, or some other manner.

Patterns that occur naturally on the surface of materials, such as cloth, leather, wood, or stone, caused by the arrangement of their constituent fibers or particles. Also, patterns, produced artificially, as for instance by embossing, on the surface of materials such as book cloth, in order to give them the appearance of having a particular grain; these may be either imitative of natural grains, or artificial designs such as a diaper pattern. Distinct from "grain (structure)" which refers to the actual arrangement and stratification of a material's constituent fibers or particles.

Information advisories in any form on the content of information artifacts such as audio-visual recordings or printed matter that may contain presentations unsuitable for all users. These may appear as labels, printed matter, or preambles within the content itself.
Those who specialize in musicology, which is the study of the history and theory of music.
Those who collect or study postage stamps, revenue stamps, stamped envelopes, postmarks, post cards, covers, and similar materials relating to postal or fiscal history.
People belonging to or working for a Christian church.

Large strong nets intended to protect construction workers, circus acrobats, or others from falling to the ground from heights, or to protect people on the ground from falling debris or construction materials.
Equipment used for working wood into desired forms.
Devices, such as pieces of rubber or cloth, for removing marks made with pen, pencil, chalk, or the like.
In Indian architecture, a broad recess between mouldings; generally a taller recess between upper and lower sets of basal mouldings.

Bench-like pieces of furniture for the use of a person at prayer, consisting of a kneeler with a narrow upright front surmounted by a ledge for books or for resting the elbows, and often a shelf below this for storing books. For similar pieces that are in the form of a low chair, use "prie-dieu chairs."

A method of interpreting the meaning of a work of art by synthesising iconography with the full historical context. Iconology is a broader approach than iconography to analysis of meaning in the visual arts, taking account of the tradition of pictorial motifs and their historical, cultural, or social meaning. In a more narrow sense, refers to the study of icons and their specific subjects.

A class of elastomers  that is notable for performance at low temperatures, resilience, and abrasion resistance. Used for shoe heels and soles, gaskets, and belting. Combined with other rubbers to improve their resilience and flexibility at low temperatures.
Sailor's rhythmic songs, especially those sung while undertaking labor aboard ship; for example, shanties may be sung when a group is manipulating heavy sails by means of ropes.
Steel tools with curved ends designed to pry open a paint can's pressed-in lid. Sometimes also used to scrape excess paint from hard-to-reach places.
Image of a flower of Michelia Campaka, or Magnolia champaca plant as a decorative motif.
Ornamentation composed of parallel convex moldings, particularly popular in the late 18th and early 19th centuries for furniture and silverwork.
As an artistic concept, the characteristic within a composition that causes one area or quality to stand out among others.
Branch of site management dedicated to the safeguarding of cultural heritage and other sites; including natural environments such as park lands and aquifers.
Lines or bands composed of a series of chevrons.
Crescent-shaped or semicircular areas on a wall or vaulted ceiling, framed by an arch or vault; includes openings or windows in such areas.
A geometricized image of a woman with her hands on her torso.
Plants where heating and illuminating gas are manufactured.
Main buildings of some resorts or public parks containing accommodations and other public facilities.
Raised platforms or similar work surfaces situated in the middle of a room, especially a kitchen, permitting access from all sides.
In Indian architecture, a haṁsa-band in the base.
Books, set of books, or disks, containing informational articles on subjects in every field of knowledge, or limited to a special field or subject, usually arranged in alphabetical order.
The distance between the supports of a transverse structural member or between the abutments of an arch.
Legally binding agreements between two or more parties in two or more originals or copies. Also, contracts binding one person to work for another for a given period of time.
In Indian architecture, with, or having seven offsets (pañcāṅga in Western India).

General term for a quality of art works in which the depiction is based on or seems to be based on the direct observation of the external world, including or even emphasizing flaws and imperfections rather than the beauty or idealized characteristics. Although a work may be both realistic and naturalistic, naturalism may somewhat idealize the flaws or ugliness of the subject depicted. For the formal style and period displaying the general characteristics of realism, such as in the painting of Gustave Courbet, use "Realist (modern European fine arts styles)."
Indication in texts, databases, tables, and lists when information for the instance at hand is applicable in a former iteration or earlier scholarship.
Vessels in which metals or other materials are melted and mixed.

Hand tools that usually take the form of a triangular blade at the end of a shaft; used to make conical depressions for recessing the head of a bolt, nut, or screw so that it is flush with the surface.
Electrical appliances for cleaning objects or surfaces by suction.

Tools comprising thin pieces of material, such as metal, paper, cardboard, or stencil film, into which is cut, inscribed, or otherwise indicated a pattern, in such a way so that paint or ink applied to the surface of the stencil tool will produce a corresponding pattern on a second surface through the cut-outs. For large drawings into which holes are pricked in order to transfer designs to a large surface, prefer "cartoons (working drawings)"; for smaller drawings used for transferring designs, use "pounces (pricked drawings)."
Forms or models, made from a variety of materials, cut to the size or profile of the finished article and used as a guide during its construction.
Blacksmith's or craftsman's tools used for measuring circumferences, normally of wheels.
Hand pincers with cutting jaws that meet parallel to each other rather than at an angle; used for cutting wire, thin metal rods, or the like.
Electrically driven devices with various bits; used for cutting grooves and channels in wood.

Refers to a type of potter's tool; ribs are curved pieces of wood or bone, characteristically having one flat and one curved edge. Ribs are used for shaping, curving, smoothing, trimming, or opening wet clay; they give the profile of the outside of a plate or pot. One hand presses outwards and upwards on the inside of the worked clay, while outside the rib is used to create a smooth surface.
Knife-like tool used to stretch lead when joining glass pieces or for bedding glass in wooden rebates.
Mats or boards on which textiles are laid for cutting. Often these have self-healing surfaces that allow the use of rotary cutters.
Facts, processes, conditions, occurrences, or changes caused by the natural physical environment or creatures, in contrast to occurrences created by humans.
The conditions of atmosphere in a small area or confined space.
The black carbonaceous particulate substance formed by the incomplete combustion of coal, oil, wood, or other fuels.

A type of ceramic roofing tile with a semi-circular (or greater) cross section. Usually used as a covering tile to prevent water from seeping between two rows of concave/gutter tiles (banwa 瓪瓦). Also written 㼧 (tong (lit. convex tile)).

The names, symbols, figures, letters, words, or other marks adopted and used by a manufacturer or merchant in order to designate his goods and to distinguish them from any others; usually registered with a governmental agency to assure its use exclusively by the owner of the mark. For devices similarly used but identifying services rather than products, use "service marks." For specific graphic images derived from trademarks, use "logotypes" or "logos."
Plane figures consisting of half of an ellipse bisected by one of its diameters (usually the transverse).
Calcareous clay containing up to 40% calcium carbonate.
Bricks cut in half lengthwise, parallel to the wide face of the brick.
Very broad, flat adzes having a spur or punch on the back of the head which can be used as a nail set.

Augers made in the form of a tapered, conical half-funnel, with one or both of the exposed edges side-sharpened to cut laterally. They are used to cut conical holes for coopers, ladder makers, wheelwrights, chair makers, and for other purposes.

Broad term for a Roman Catholic religious order comprising several divisions; founded by St. Francis of Assisi (1181-1226). The rule emphasizes the vow of poverty, theology, preaching, and aid to impoverished and sick people. Different schools of thought among followers developed over the years; St. Bonaventure (1257-1274) founded a moderate interpretation of St. Francis' rule that bridged many of the differences. The independent branches of the order are the First Order of Franciscans: the Observants, the Conventuals, and the Capuchins; the Second Order comprises nuns established by St. Clare under the guidance of St. Francis, known as the Poor Clares; and the Third Order comprising religious and lay men and women, including the Third Order Secular (living in the world without vows) and Third Order Regular (living in religious communities under vow).
Individuals having a common parent or parents.

Originally used by the Syrian Monophysites and Nestorians, and later Muslims, to refer to Eastern Christians who remained faithful to the ruling of the Council of Chalcedon of 451 (affirming the two natures, divine and human, of Christ) when most Christians became Monophysite. The name was originally a pejorative one, referring to fact that they theologically agreed with the Byzantine emperor (Melchites meaning 'Royalists' or 'Emperor's Men'). In later use, the term refers to those orthodox Eastern Christians who follow an Arabic version of the Greek ritual, and particularly to those who are united to the communion of the Roman Catholic Church while retaining their separate organization.
In multicolor printing, the precise aligning of the plates or stencils, usually by means of registry marks so that each color successively printed will be aligned with the others.
People concerned with the preservation, improvement, and restoration of the natural environment, as well as the policies and politics associated with environmental preservation.
Documents giving authority to do something; especially used in civil and criminal law for the arrest of persons or for their production in court as witnesses.
Clocks controlled by a pendulum.
Small vessels, in which a sacred object is kept or carried; particularly in the Christian Church, a vessel or box used for holding or carrying the Eucharist, such as a pyx or ciborium.
In Medieval manuscripts and early printed books, small letters placed in spaces left blank for initials, to guide the illuminator or rubricator.
Short, usually high-pitched duct flutes having no fingerholes, or no more than one; the body may contain a captive pellet to add a roll to the sound.
Instruments for measuring longitudinal stress, as in wires or beams, or for measuring the negative pressure, or surface tension, of liquids.

Measuring devices for determining and graphically recording or indicating the waveforms of changing quantities of electrical energy. In general, these are considered the same instrument as an oscilloscope, except that the oscillograph may be capable of creating a permanent record of the measurements, while the oscilloscope provides only visual feedback.

Surveying instruments designed primarily to measure horizontal and vertical angles and generally consisting of telescope, spirit level, graduated plates, verniers, various leveling screws, and often a compass.
Devices for measuring the height of tides; may consist of a graduated rod for visual observation or elaborate electronic devices making a continuous graphic record over time.

In the context of Christian liturgical accessories, the holders that secure the host in the monstrance. Originaly lunettes were crescent-shaped clips made of gold or silver-gilt, used for securing the host in a monstrance. In more recent centuries, the host is enclosed in a pyx the same size as the host, with two glass faces, and this pyx is itself is inserted into the apperture of the monstrance. This newer-style holder is also called a lunette, although it is no longer crescent-shaped.
A receptacle, holder, box, chest, bag, sheath, or covering fitted to contain or enclose something else; typically used for transporting or protecting the enclosed item or items.

Open bowl-shaped vessels, used chiefly for drinking, often having one handle, but sometimes two handles or none, generally on a low foot-ring; also includes similar bowl-shaped vessels, generally without handles, resting on a stem and supported by a spreading foot. Occasionally made with a lid.
Culture or style from the Hejaz region, in Saudi Arabia.
Badges bearing a shield with the coat of arms of the body representing the messenger, for identification.
Ornamental inside linings of book covers, sometimes leather, which take the place of the regular flyleaves or pastedowns.
Conventional symbols or characters used in punctuation.

Cylindrical baskets used by Hupa Native North Americans in the Jump Dance ceremony (Xay-ch´idilye). Generally made of plant fibers such as maidenhair fern and spruce, formed into a long, cylindrical shape.

Material made from the thinly-sliced horny plates covering the shells of some turtles and tortoises; the finished material is finely colored gold and brown, translucent, and glossy. It was popular in the 19th-century for inlays, jewelry, hair combs, and other ornaments, but its use is banned today. It differs from "turtle shell" in how it is worked and in the finished appearance; tortoise shell is worked upon like horn, and is usually softened or rendered plastic by placing in boiling water. The most common sources of tortoiseshell are Hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), which provides the finest scales, the Loggerhead (Thalassochelys caretta ) and the Green turtle (Chelone mydas).
Vessels having a neck and mouth considerably narrower than the body, used for packaging and containing liquid and dry preparations. For vessels having wider necks and mouths, use "jars."
Coins or medals in which each of their sides corresponds to different issues. It can be attributed to minting misstrikes or forgeries.
Refers to the dried perspiration of sheep that is deposited on the wool.
User for objects capable of being drawn or pulled back in, such as aircraft landing equipment, roofs or components of roofs, and other mechanical devices and equipment.
Use to describe items made, contrived, or assembled at home, or otherwise nonprofessionally, sometimes implying poorly done.
People who have little or no money, goods, or other means of support.
The activity of cutting down a grass or grain crop or stand, such as wheat, corn, a grassy lawn, etc. by using a scythe or machine operating with a similar cutting action.
Representation of a male flywhisk-bearer figure as acolyte.

Surfaces of objects that are not fronts, backs, tops, or bottoms, but located on lateral ends. For the adjective describing the location of something at or near the side of something, use "side" from the Attributes and Properties hierarchy.
Use generally for any metal pieces worked to a predetermined shape by one or more of such processes as hammering, pressing, rolling, or upset forging. Examples of forgings are machine parts.
Small pieces of metal, usually gold, silver, or bronze and bearing a relief design on one or both sides and having a commemorative purpose; resembling a coin, but not used as a medium of exchange.
Refers to pictures composed of several separate sections that can be combined in various ways so as to produce different scenes.

In Chinese culture, certain objects placed in tombs for the use of the deceased or as the vessels for spirits. Included are figurines of people and animals, buildings and tools, and replicas of objects in life made of precious materials, such as jewels.
Works of the visual arts that are designed for specific locations, especially those that exploit or incorporate aspects of their sites.

Refers to works produced since the 1960s that employ the artists own body, or other people's bodies, as the medium of expression. May be in the form of performance art or conceptual art, where the artist uses his or her own body as a focus or theme. For visual works that are body modifications based on traditional or ancient practices, such as scarification or tattooing, prefer "body art (visual works, adornment)."
Replacements of one governing administration by another. In later usage, often used as a euphemism for the removal of an illegitimate or hostile government by military force.
Rugs with depictions of recognizable figures, objects, or scenes.
Professional soldiers hired into service in a foreign or private armed force.

Events taking place over a prolonged period and comprising open and declared hostile armed conflict between nations or parties within a nation. For individual instances of armed conflict, use "battles."
Protective floor coverings, such as those made of a coarse material intended to protect the floor, or those made as a resilient or padded covering to protect athletes during practice or performance.
The stress, calculated on the maximum value of the force and the original area of cross section, which causes fracture of the material.
Shaggy pile-woven rugs used as sleeping mats.
Irregularly shaped carpets.
A machine-made, loop-pile rug which resembles an Axminster carpet in appearance.
Caucasian flat-woven rugs with supplementary weft patterning.
Narrow-beam lighting devices consisting of a high powered lamp; used as spotlights or directed floodlights.

Float lamps used especially in churches or temples, having a cup or vase-shaped reservoir of colored glass or metal. By tradition and eccliastical dictate, it is mandatory for Jewish temples and many Chrisitan churches to have a constantly burning oil lamp in the sanctuary, in the vicinity of the tabernacle.

European staff weapons featuring a head with an axlike blade balanced behind by either a sharp, slightly curved fluke or a flat, ridged hammerhead, a short spike surmounting the staff, and metal reinforcement protecting the upper part of the staff, with a rondel just below it as a hand guard. They were popular in foot combat in both warfare and tournaments in the 15th and 16th centuries.
Commodities, merchandise, or materials brought into one country from another for use, sale, reprocessing, exchange, or export.
Refers to the magnesium salt of phytic acid. In conservation, used in a solution to inhibit iron gall corrosion on manuscripts.
Supports below sculptured busts or heads, such as those found on terms or herms, which take the form of quadrangular pillars that narrow toward the base.

Hollow wooden memorial poles that were used by the ancient Yolngu peoples of Central and Eastern Arnhem Land to store the bones of the deceased during mortuary ceremonies. Modern artists produce new larrakitj to educate Indigenous and non-Indigenous people. Larrikitj are often painted with designs and symbols representing clans or relationships.
Generally, people who dig in the earth as an occupation, including laborers. Specifically, an archaeologist who uncovers artifacts according to controlled methods.

Sheet metal seams having a bottom plate with a turned edge that overlaps the side plate; the seam may be secured by welding, soldering, or riveting at the overlapping joint. An example of a lap bottom seam is the seam of the bottom of a tin or steel can.
In Buddhism, objects or images considered "auspicious images," for example, an image of the Buddha that had a miraculous appearance or characteristics considered to be a sign of divine favor.
Illuminated lamps that are attached to vehicles.

Spectroscopic techniques using laser sources; include Raman laser spectroscopy; laser induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS); laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA–ICP–MS); laser induced fluorescence [LIF]; lidar; time-resolved absorption spectroscopy; laser desorption ionization mass spectrometry.
Lighting devices fixed in place, such as those attached to a ceiling or wall.
Buildings housing museums specializing in the history of postage stamps, revenue stamps, stamped envelopes, postmarks, post cards, covers, and similar materials relating to postal or fiscal history.
The process or state of sinking to a weaker or inferior condition, a gradual loss of power, decay, diminution, or deterioration of a state, person, corporate body, etc.
Refers to the entire playing area upon which softball is played.
People who study myths and mythology; also, people who write myths.
Those who study the principles, institutions, and conduct of politics and government, including the political behavior of individuals and organizations.
Hollow forms, often elaborately shaped, into which ingredients for a pudding may be poured or pressed before cooking in order to shape the pudding.

Bottles or other glass vessels having the neck divided into two or more tubes, causing them to make a gurgling noise when poured. The type has Roman antecedents; it was notably produced by German glassworkers in the later Middle Ages, and among Venetian and façon de Venise glasses of the 16th and 17th centuries.
Bottles intended for poison, varying in shape, but often with a rough texture or other external features so as to be recognized by touch.

Curtains that hang below or under the main curtains, usually at a window. Examples are thin, often sheer or lace, curtains positioned under the main curtains to soften light and give privacy. For flat-hanging undercurtains fitted against the glass of a window or door, or immediately over a shade, use "glass curtains."
Small silver coins struck in several areas of the ancient Greek world from the 6th century BCE and generally worth one sixth of a drachma.
Spanish gold coins issued beginning in the early 16th century; later, these and similar Portuguese coins; and, more recently, various coins of Spanish- and Portuguese- speaking countries.

Coverings, originally sheets of canvas coated or impregnated with tar to repel moisture, used to protect objects beneath them. The term is often applied to other kinds of waterproof cloth, made from polyurethane or polyethylene.
Script used by the Minoan population of Crete in the period 2000 to 1500 BCE, not yet deciphered.
Songs or chanted poetry in Nahua culture, frequently performed during public ritual ceremonies as well as more private rituals and those related to healing.
Books containing the extracts (pericopes) from scripture appointed to be read at public worship; by the 13th century usually incorporated into the missal.
In printing, general term for decorative designs, not usually part of a type font.
Bowls for mixing food or other substances, generally made of metal, glass, ceramic, or plastic. They are sometimes made in sets and then often graduated in size so as to nest together.
Sheer ruffled curtains hung on double rods so that one curtain overlaps the other; always with ruffled tiebacks, and often with matching ruffled valance.

Use specifically for European percussive weapons having a heavy head, typically with a blunt or cusped face and at least one blade or spike at the back of the head or on top of the staff, various forms of which were in use from the 13th to the 17th century. Also used very generally for hammers used as fighting weapons in nearly all parts of the world since the Stone Age.
Small knife-like scrapers used to clean meat casings in prepariton for making susages.
Small flutes sounding an octave higher than regular orchestral flutes, having the same fingering and keywork.
Small metal or earthenware straight-handled pots or pans used chiefly in cooking.
The combinations of frame and handle that contain or join together the various other components of a firearm so that it can be handled, aimed, and fired.
Ornamental textiles that are attached to clothing that bear insignia identifying membership or affiliation with a group such as a fraternal organization.
Devices that grind grain by use of rotating cylinders, or rollers.
Strongly made, lockable boxes or chests for safeguarding valuable possessions, as money, jewels, or documents.
Stories paraphrasing Biblical texts or closely based on Biblical events.
Vessels made for domestic preservation of meat and fish, usually for short periods of time, and often covered with a layer of fat or butter.

Generally used for processes of preparing a printing surface on a zinc plate, either for lithography or etched for letterpress printing. When possible, use two expressions: the specific process term, such as "lithography," and "zinc" plus "printing plates."

A relief printmaking process derived from woodcut, but using stone blocks as the plates into which a design is carved. This technique may be exclusive to Inuit printmakers living in the Cape Dorset area,  an Inuit hamlet located on Dorset Island near Foxe Peninsula at the southern tip of Baffin Island in the Qikiqtaaluk Region of Nunavut, Canada. Stone is used here as it is a more plentiful resource than wood in the Arctic. Use of the process only dates from the early 1960s.

Articles, collectively, that are generally used for serving food at the table, including various types of flatware, cutlery, hollowware, plates, and accessories, such as coasters and napkin rings, but not necessarily constituting a service.
Vats, typically round in shape and made of steel, in which cheese  curd is formed and cut or broken in cheese making.

Pinlike utensils of wood or metal for fastening meat in a specific form while cooking. Also, similar but longer utensils used to pierce and hold food while cooking, as over a grill, or dipping in sauces, as fondue. Use "spits" for pointed rods for holding large pieces of meat and other food while cooking.
Tubes, usually of paper, metal, or glass, for sucking up a beverage or other liquid from a container.
Term used for serving utensils which are not knives, forks, spoons, tongs, or scoops. They generally have relatively large flat surfaces of varying shape and are used to serve solid food.
Kantharoi decorated with panels containing a distinctive pattern of bands having geometric and floral patterns painted with black and added white.
Refers to a type of oinochoe closely resembles the modern one-handled mug, but often has two handles. It was used as a dipper for serving wine and a cup for drinking and measuring.
Jars, sometimes airtight, used for storing food or any other items.

Purses, usually with handles or straps, that are designed to be carried in the hand or on the arm and intended as ladies' accessories. Handbags are large enough to carry banknotes, coins, and everyday personal items.

Any of various broad, relatively shallow, open vessels with a flat bottom, concave sides, and nearly level rim, sometimes having a cover; made of pottery, glass, metal, wood or another material and used especially for holding or serving food. In modern usage it is typically reserved for vessels at a dining table used for serving or holding food other than the round, flat or very shallow object used by the person dining, which is called a "plate"; however, formerly the plate was also called a "dish."
Accessory containers for serving food that are comprised of multiple components.
Containers designed to transport food for individual or small group consumption, particularly for informal meals such as a lunch, or to eat outdoors.
Decorative bottles, often with a stopper, used to store or serve beverages, especially wine or liquor.
Drinking vessels, often cylindrical, resting on a flat base without a stem and having a single handle and sometimes a lid.

Small shallow cups, often holding approximately a dram of liquid (1/8 of an ounce), usually with two loop handles and often flat bottoms and slightly rounded sides, typically used for drinking distilled spirits.
Devices for holding and storing tobacco pipes.
Small bottles or vials for holding smelling salts or perfume bottles filled with smelling salts or a scent.
Instruments used for measuring the length of curved lines, as on maps.
Trays with molds to be filled with water and then frozen.

Bedcovers consisting of three layers (top, backing, and filling) joined by quilting, which is stitching that typically forms decorative patterns or designs. The term is also used loosely to refer to similar bedcovers joined by other means. Quilts are distinguished from "comforters," which are warmer, heavily wadded bedcovers on which the design of the stitching is not as elaborate or decorative. In addition to serving as bedcovers, quilts may also be used as wall hangings or for another purpose.
Quilts made principally for warmth, not as show pieces. Made of anything from old clothing to feed sacks, often filled with homegrown cotton or wool, an old blanket, or a worn quilt.

Quilts, usually comprised of cotton or polyester fabrics, that features an eight-pointed star motif. This motif is frequently placed in the middle of the blanket, with a fabric border sometimes included around the quilt's edge. Commonly made by Plains Native Americans; traced to the late 1800s/early 1900s as a replacement for buffalo robes that were formerly constructed by Lakota and Dakota artisans. Used as powwow regalia, funerary clothing, and as gifts in give-away events.

Ceremonial vessels used for holding fresh water during tea ceremonies. The water was used for washing the tea bowls and filling the kettle. Mizusashi are typically made of ceramic or lacquerware, but wooden and glass ones are also used.
Tubular drums of Japan, generally used in kabuki theater productions. The drums have two laced heads, and are played with sticks.
Ceremonial containers associated with or used in the rituals of public worship.

Devices used to draw lots or generate random numbers; for example, picking members for a jury. A common form is an octagonal container suspended from two posts; attached handle allows the container to rotate.
Covered baskets, usually with an ovoid mouth and rigid handle, intended primarily for transporting live pigeons.

Boxes, usually of medium to large size, intended for the storage of linens, clothing, books, food, artifacts, or any other item. They are usually lidded or have flaps that allow the box to be closed. They may be made of cardboard, wood, metal, plastic, wicker, or another material.

Small tubes of glass, metal, stone, or another material, designed to store cosmetics. Best known as glass works from ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome. The cosmetic was extracted with a cosmetic stick or other device. Modern examples are made of pliable metal or plastic, and the cosmetic is extruded when pressure is applied.

Cases, often elaborate or decorative, meant to hold bodkins: needle-like objects used for lacing up garments. Decorative bodkins and bodkin cases were popular personal items in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Slightly projecting rings on the bottoms of vessels on which they stand.

Portable containers typically used by campers for storing a variety of equipment associated with a camp kitchen, such as cooking pots, pans, plates, utensils, and cleaning items.. When packed up, it looks like a large box, and when unpacked, the front and sides fold down to reveal its contents arranged into specifically designed compartments, shelves, drawers, and racks. In the contexting of scouting, chuck boxes are also known as patrol boxes.
Scales designed for use in market shops or marketplaces.
Spike fiddles of Indonesia and Malaysia, with two or three strings and varying in size and shape of soundbox and length of neck from one region to another. In Java and Bali they are used in gamelan.
Extremely sensitive gas chromatography detectors that allow man-made chemicals to be detected in low concentrations through the attachment of electrons via electron capture ionization.

Measuring devices with two legs movable on a joint or pivot, similar in form to drawing compasses but with two metal points and used, for example, to divide lines, transfer dimensions, or lay off circles or arcs.

Soft headcloths, especially of linen or silk, wrapped around the throat and passing under the chin from one side of the head to the other, and pinned to a band, hat or the hair. Of a type originating in the Medieval period and retained by nuns of various religions to the present day.
Military caps having a distinctive square plate on the crown. Originally Polish, the style was later adopted by other European armies, including that of Napoleon.
Emergency escape seats for propelling an occupant out and away from an airplane.
Two-wheeled vehicles without suspension pulled by a pack animal with a fixed, non-tilting body, used for the transport of goods.
A dark purple crystalline compound of composition KMnO4, used in deodorizers and dyes and as an oxidizing agent and disinfectant.

Long slender shafts, usually wood, shaped to a round handle or grip at one end and flat-tipped blade at the other; for rowing. For similar but shorter devices with round-tipped blades for propelling small boats, use "paddles (watercraft equipment)."
During the 18th and 19th centuries, term used to describe soft crowns found on bonnets or caps.
Clothing designed for, or used for, dance.
Rings worn to signfiy the office of a bishop, pope (the bishop of Rome), or certain other high ranking members of the clergy in the Roman Catholic church and some other Christian churches.
Narrow Chinese long zithers with from 12 to 16 strings of silk or metal, each supported by a movable bridge that functions as a device for fine tuning.
Loose mantles of undyed woolen cloth worn by men and women of ancient Rome. Also, similar loose wraps made of various fabrics and worn in various historical periods.

Helmets consisting of a single plate of bronze, shaped to cover the cranium, nose, cheeks, and chin. The most widely used type of military helmet of Classical Greece, it had spread to Italy by the beginning of the 6th century BCE.
Tracks on which marbles roll from top to bottom, often with switches, levers, loops, jumping jacks, etc.
Separate or detachable shirt fronts, often with a collar, worn under another garment.

Books that are illustrated by mounting original photographs on the printed page, dating to after the invention of photography in the late 1830s but before photomechanical illustrations became the standard for print media later in the 1800s.
Bindings for albums used as presentation formats for traditional East Asian painting.

A style of binding introduced in the early 20th century featuring a miniature painting inset in gold-tooled leather on the front cover.  Historically the term refers to bindings commisioned by J.H. Stonehouse, manager of Henry Sotheran, a London bookseller, usually using the binding firm of Rivière and Son. The style is named after Richard Cosway (1742-1821), an English miniature painter who had nothing to do with the bindings themselves.

Apparatus used for body strengthening and corrective exercises consisting of a series of normally wooden uprights about 8 feet high, secured to the wall at about 3-foot intervals, and joined by horizontal wooden bars set about 5 inches apart.
Toys with or without interlocking pieces that are designed to be put together to create various structures or other forms.

Sodium dithionite (also known as sodium hydrosulfite) is a reductive bleaching chemical. Usage includes iron stain removal, and occasionally to treat corroded copper and silver artifacts in object conservation. It can also be used for purification of water and gas and as a sulfonating agent or a sodium ion source in industrial processes.

Skaters' gloves worn in the game of ice Hockey to help prevent player's hands from being injured or burned from the ice. Padding and a shell thumb is provided as protection from hockey pucks and sticks.

Japanese ritual dolls made of clay or porcelain and dressed in real clothes that are used at the girls' festival, Hina Matsuri, held annually in March. A number or dolls representing the emperor, empress, and their court are displayed on a stepped altar. Girls of ages 7 to 17 visit each other's collections and refreshments are offered to their majesties, then to the guests, in a ritual more than 900 years old.

Game pieces used in the game of the same name that originated in Belgium The piece comprises a sculpted wooden bird, often decorated, with a metal pin in the beak, that is suspended from the ceiling or a cross beam by rope. The bird is aimed at a target by players, not unlike a game of darts.
Pullover sweaters with a V-shaped neckline.
Trousers of heavy, twilled fabric, especially cotton denim.
Hosiery worn by European men in the 16th and 17th centuries, covering the upper leg, thighs and buttocks.

Tabua are pierced and braided whales teeth, originally taken from the lower jaw of sperm whales found stranded on Fijian beaches.  As whale strandings were relatively rare, so were whale teeth more valued as a result. Tabua are considered by Fijians as a kavakaturanga or ‘chiefly thing’. They are not worn but are presented at important ceremonies, including weddings, births and funerals. Ceremonial tabua have holes drilled through the tip and the butt, and a braided sennit cord is attached.  To make tabua, the whale teeth are polished and sometimes rubbed with coconut oil and turmeric to darken them.  In some cases the teeth are smoked in a small tent-like structure covered in bark cloth to turn them a rich tobacco colour.
A piece of fabric worn on a Bishop's lap during High Mass and ordinations.
A string of beads, usually carried on one's person and manipulated by the fingers as a means of occupying one's hands to relieve worry or tension.
Military uniform coats that are typically mid-hip-length and designed to fit under an overcoat if necessary; usually single-breasted and often belted.

Wraparound garments first worn by the indigenous people of French Polynesia and the Cook Islands, and later adopted in other South Pacific islands including Hawaii and in other cultures (popularized as beachwear). Originally bark cloth, these are now usually a single straight piece of brightly patterned printed cotton cloth resembling Malaysian sarongs.

Sashes of varying widths and sometimes stiffened, tied around the waist in intricate patterns of bows and knots usually at the back, but also in front, worn over a kimono; also, similar sashes worn for fashionable dress.
Ornamental pieces, often fur, which are worn at the neck; frequently trimmed with heads and tails of the fur-bearing animal.
Term generally applied to various cloth coverings for the head.
Supports made to secure watches, usually made of metal. Some examples have a fastener or clip at the end to attach them to one's clothing.
Overcoats of waterproof or water-repellent material worn as protection from the weather.
Any of various forms of protective coverings for the head, usually made of a hard material, including the outside steel layer of helmets that consist of inner and outer parts.
Garments worn next to the body and under main garments having leg openings or short or long legs.
Petticoats originally made with a stiff, woven fabric of horsehair, linen, cotton, or wool. Later often used in conjunction with hoops of whalebone or steel.
Applied clothing accessories that may be made of rope, ribbon or fabric. These consist of knots with two loops and two ends, fixed into decorative elements attached to clothing or other objects.
Arabic script used primarily in modern day Iran and Afghanistan. Shikasteh, translating roughly as 'broken' or 'broken form', is a dense script with a lack of diacritical marks.
Self-propelled airborne explosive devices that are intended to be launched from the ground to hit targets that are also on the surface of the earth.

Long-handled, flat paddlelike utensils used chiefly by bakers to place and remove bread, pies, and similar foods in an oven. For utensils with two long prongs used to place or remove food in an oven, use "pie lifters."
Valved brass aerophones with a wide conical bore terminating in a flared bell, played with a cup mouthpiece; they are used as the bass or contrabass members of band or orchestral brass sections.

Cloaks in the shape of a semicircle, with a part tossed over the head. Although chadors have front openings, they are worn closed. Chadors are in greatest use among Muslim women who wish to reflect Islamic modesty.
Untailored outer garments of Madagascar worn by both men and women wrapped around the shoulders and sometimes the upper torso.
Devices for separating the yolk from the white of the egg.
Cylindrical, or spool-shaped rings with pierced or openwork sides, or stands used to support hot dishes and protect the surface below.
Forks in a place setting, larger than the salad fork, that are used for consuming the main course of a meal.
Spoons used to stir iced tea and similar beverages served in tall glasses, having a bowl similar in size to a teaspoon and an elongated handle.
Term applied to a wide variety of special-purpose utensils designed to serve tomatoes, especially those which have a flat and round surface which may or may not be pierced.
Utensils with a long handle and sometimes a spoon end for stirring food and drink.
Devices for removing seeds, pits, or stones from fruit.
Utensils that consist of a steel tank mounted with mixing paddles attached to a crank, used for preparing meat for sausages.
Alphabetic scripts whose letters are confined between head and base lines with no ascenders or descenders.
Sound devices that produce sound for the purpose of conveying information.

Rolls of paper meant to be used as scores for mechanical instruments such as player pianos and fairground organs. Perforations are made on the paper which allows the mechanical keys of the instruments to create sound via air flow though the perforations.

Plate armor for the knees, appearing first in the 14th century, consisting of a main cup-shaped piece fitting over the kneecap, often with additional articulated lames above and below it and a side wing on the outer side.
Pieces of defensive armor in the form of a coat, covering the upper part of the body, having interlaced rings or overlapping plates of steel, usually over a quilted linen or leathern jacket.

A type of art glass developed and produced by the Württembergische Metallwarenfabrik (W.M.F.) by Karl Weidman ca. 1926. It is characterized by the use of colorless, raw glass made iridescent by a silver stain and then matte fired, resulting in a shimmering metallic surface.

Gelatinous protein that cements silk fibers together in the cocoon. Sericin is secreted along with fibroin by the insect. It is usually removed, by boiling the raw silk in soap and water, during fabric manufacture.

Two-masted, fore-and-aft-rigged sailing vessels with the smaller, mizzen, mast set forward of the rudder post; in use since the mid-19th century. For similar craft, but square-rigged on both masts and in use from the late 17th century until the early 19th century, use "ketches (square-rigged vessels)." For similar fore-and-aft-rigged craft with the mizzen set abaft the rudder post, use "yawls (sailing vessels)."

Political entities of any size that are partially dependent upon another country or power, but typically have a significant extent of control over internal and external affairs. An example is Macau, which, by agreeement, may operate with a high degree of autonomy from China until 2049.
Administrative bodies subject to a count or countess.
Any vessels engaged in the smuggling of liquor.
Textile with linen warp and woolen weft, usually homespun and handwoven, and later also with a cotton warp.

Durable, closely woven textile of plain weave, made formerly of linen but now usually of cotton, made in various weights; very similar to canvas but finer and lighter. Common uses are for tents, belts, and clothing.
Figured woven textile having a damasklike appearance, with contrasting luster in the pattern and ground.

Process of creating three-dimensional imagery by sewing bundles of caribou hair onto a backing surface, usually animal hide or cloth. Backing stitches are pulled tight to shape the hair and then knotted. Hairs are sometimes dyed to create particular images or patterns. Originally manufactured by pre-contact Athabaskan and other First Nations communities, caribou tufting is now practiced by M%00etis and First Nations tribes across northern Canada.
Decorating a surface with rough and irregular indentations.
Ornamentation on glass, as on wine decanters, consisting of narrow applied bands of glass forming parallel ribs.
The aggregate of transverse strands of a textile, woven through the warp. Specifically for individual strands of weft, prefer "picks (weft)."

The deterioration of metal or other substances by chemical or electrochemical reaction resulting from exposure to weathering, moisture, chemicals, or other agents, causing the metal to change from a metallic state into a chemically more stable mineral compound known as a corrosion product.
Inserting material into a hole, crack, or cavity. In the specific context of mosaic conservation, the application of mortar or other material into an area of loss of the mosaic surface.
The process of coating, treating, or combining with a metal.
Making incisions with a sharp-edged instrument, thus removing material or dividing something into parts.

The process of becoming gelatinous. In conservation this may refer to a chemical deterioration of parchment and leather tanned with condensed vegetable tannins, where collagen turns into water-soluble gelatin. This occurs as a reaction to substantial fluctuations in temperature and moisture or when parchment and such materials are stored under acidic condition.
Miniature spoons intended primarily for serving salt from a saltcellar or dish.
Horse-drawn passenger wagons used in the American West for excursions into rugged terrain, fitted with multiple bench seats and heavy suspension; used from the mid-19th to the early 20th century.

Long, slender boardlike devices attached to specially designed boots and used for gliding over snow; known for over 5000 years and originally of animal bone secured directly to footwear, now made of various hard, durable materials and with a taper and upturned forward tip.

The scattering of radiation, such as x-rays, in a direction approximately opposite to that of the incident radiation and due to reflection from particles of the medium traversed; sometimes produced and examined as a technique for analyzing materials.
Extent or distance in measured in linear feet; may refer to a part or to the greater whole. Examples of things for which footage is relevant include pipes, electrical wires, and film.
In Indian architecture, six members; or six constituent mouldings.
Dimensions of a work that are the size of life, or, with reference to visual representations of something, equal in size to the original.
Boxes or other portable containers formerly used for holding medications to treat ailments or accidents while traveling. For modern portable kits containing medical supplies, prefer "first aid kits."

The ratio of the distance between highest and lowest values of a quantity. This is most often applied to recorded sound and light signals in audio recording and photographic contexts. It determines the range of intensity that may be reliably transmitted through any particular system.
The state or quality of having a strong affinity for water.
Frames with a profusion of overlapping and intertwining scrolls and volutes, popular during the 16th and 17th centuries and named for Venetian architect and sculptor Jacopo Sansovino.

Lip-vibrated aerophones furnished with curved sliding crooks called inventions, inserted prior to play in the center of the body between the circular portions of the tube, making it possible to change pitch without changing the length of the tube.
Zitherlike chordophones of Norway. They are fretted, and rectangular.

Rules comprised of short strips of wood joined at their ends by rivets so that the pieces are foldable, in a zigzag manner, in parallel planes; most usually the strips are in 6-inch or 1-foot lengths, and the rules are 6 feet or 8 feet long when open; also of similar lengths in metric units. Distinct from "folding rules" which tend to be shorter and have sections that usually pivot or fold in more than one plane.
Hand-held dolls or doll-like figures mounted on sticks with a covering, usually of cloth, concealing musical mechanisms underneath that play music when the sticks are twirled.
European lutelike chordophones, popular in 17th-century Italy, having a very long, narrow neck with up to 24 movable frets, a small pear-shaped body, and two or three strings played with a plectrum.

Short-necked lutelike chordophones of China, with a pear-shaped body, four silk or nylon strings, and from ten to twenty-four frets on the neck and belly. They are held upright resting on the lap or thigh, and plucked with the fingers.
Short-barrelled long guns, held at the shoulder or in the hands, using pistol ammunition and capable of fully automatic fire.
Artillery with multiple single-shot barrels that fire sequentially or simultaneously, though they lack automatic firing such as with machine guns.
Large siege engines used by the ancient Roman army for propelling rocks at an enemy.
Card games played with tarot cards, especially the central European game played with 22 Greater Arcana tarot cards and up to 56 regular modern playing cards.

Strategy-based board game played on a checkered board of 16x6 squares that can be played by two or four players. The number of game pieces and rules of play vary based on the number of players. The game was invented ca.1880 by George Howard Monks.
Books, usually intended for children, the leaves of which include or consist of press-out jigsaw puzzles.
Political pamphlets or booklets that lampoon a public figure, particularly such works from France under the Ancien Régime.
Property of porous material which is measured by the rate by volume at which a fluid passes through a cross section of the material.
Women's suits worn for walking and other similar physical activities, dating from around 1900, usually consisting of a coat or jacket and long skirt.
Dresses with long skirts.
Dresses made for expectant mothers, typically loose fitting or adjustable in the waist area.
Trailed multi-wheeled vehicles with long beds designed to haul lumber or timber from one place to another.

A natural dark blue colorant obtained from the tropical Indigofera tinctoria plants. The use of indigo was first mentioned in Indian manuscripts in the 4th century BCE; it was first exported to Europe in Roman times. The natural material is collected as a precipitate from a fermented solution of the plant, where the coloring component, indigotin, is extracted as a colorless glycoside that turns blue with oxidation. Indigo is a fine, intense powder which may be used directly as a pigment in oil, tempera, or watercolor media. Since the exposed pigment can fade rapidly in strong sunlight, it is rarely used in art or fine textiles today. However, it is still used to dye jeans, where its fading and uneven coloring have become favorable characteristics.

Light-sensitve polymers that change structurally with exposure to radiation such as ultraviolet light or heat. These materials may appear in various forms including films or liquids, which have applications as printing plates, in photoresists, stereolithographic printing, imaging circuit boards, and the manufacture of paints or enamels.

Written, printed, or typed copies of an original text or of words originally spoken, such as of court proceedings, broadcasts, or oral histories. Transcripts are extremely accurate copies with any editorial explanations or notations clearly distinguished from the original, including indications of misspellings or editorial omissions. For less formal copying, or for short documents or single words such as in a vocabulary, use "transcriptions."
Religious texts used for varied rites.

Collections of writings in the form of a volume of learned articles or essays by colleagues, students, and admirers to honor a scholar, other person, institution, or society on a special occasion or anniversary. Festschriften are usually complimentary or memorial publications in the form of collected essays, addresses, or biographical, bibliographical, scientific, or other contributions, often embodying the results of research.
Visorless, folding, textile caps worn as part of a military uniform.
Heeled shoes or slippers with only a vamp, or front portion, and no quarters or back portion.
Boots reaching to the hips, worn especially by fishermen.
The S- or Z-shaped moving arms in matchlocks which hold the slow-burning match and, when activated, lower it down to ignite the priming powder.
Any of various boxlike containers intended primarily for holding stamps.

Relatively heavy, four-wheeled carriages with coachlike lower bodies and tops constructed in two sections either of which could be lowered independently; may also be used for early carriage-style automobiles with convertible driver or passenger areas, and, by extension, for later sedanlike automobiles with a short folding rear top.
Light, two-wheeled, one-horse carriages, similar to chaises, but with space for only one person and generally driven by men; some varieties are used as exercise or show carts and in harness racing.

Cast iron rectangular plates which, when bolted or otherwise assembled together, form part of a five-plate, six-plate, or ten-plate wood stove. Stove plates intended for the front and sides of stoves were often decorated in low relief, especially with Biblical scenes or text.

Signaling apparatuses consisting of an upright post with one or more arms that can be moved in a vertical plane, different positions of the arm or arms representing different letters or messages. Semaphores were often placed on towers in lines across the landscape, sending messages for distances prior to the invention of the telegraph.

Bottom-dwelling marine invertebrates characterized by being covered by two valves or shells, with one valve covering the dorsal or topside and the other covering the ventral or bottom side; commonly known as lamp shells because they resemble early Roman oil lamps.
Tools used for laying gold thread, or other metallic thread; one design is flat on one end and pointed on the other.
Any brick, tile, stone, or other material fabricated in shaped units and used for paving.
Traps typically consisting of a string with a running noose by which an animal may be caught.
Rakes of various design, intended to gather and distribute manure, or for clearing debris from ponds or waterways.
Instruments, tools, and equipment used to care for teeth.
Beams onto which cloth is rolled as it is woven.

Process used to duplicate maps and technical drawings employing a ferric salt to insolubilize a gelatin master selectively by light exposure, making the image areas receptive to ink. Allows production of exact copies having sharp lines in printing ink.
Colorless, crystalline compound of ammonia and phosphoric acid. Ammonium phosphate is used as a fire retardant, in fertilizers, and as a flux for soldering.

Style of textiles, particularly floor coverings, handwoven in the village of Saruq, north of Arak in western Iran. The early carpets are characterized as being of very good quality and having short pile and a variety of designs. The medallion decorative schemes that were introduced in the early 20th century are sometimes awkward. Saruk carpets that were produced on a large commercial scale are characterized by a longer pile and rose-colored fields filled with disconnected floral sprays and plant forms. Saruk carpets are asymmetrically knotted on a cotton foundation. Mahal and Muskabad are trade names for village carpets of varying quality that come from the neighborhood of Arak.

Navajo wearing blankets produced from in the mid-to-late 19th century. Declined in production because of the introduction of European aniline dyes and yarn at the end of the 19th century. Defined by terraced diamond designs and horizontal bands of indigo, red, black, and white yarn. Not associated with rank; "chief blanket" refers to their value assigned by Navajo and Plains communities.
Period of the first of the Anatolian beyliks frontier principalities founded 1260/1290.
Weaving technique with a simple criss-cross checkerboard pattern in which two or more filling yarns, or a single heavier yarn, pass over and under two or more warp yarns.
Planes with a serrated blade mounted nearly vertical; used to roughen a surface prior to application of a veneer.
Parts and components of weapons.
Networks or systems that support the public works of a country, state, or region.
The process of moving software or processing activities from one computer system to another.

Style of textiles handwoven at the city of Cuenca, Spain (located between Madrid and Valencia), especially floor coverings from the 17th and 18th centuries. Carpets are generally coarser and heavier bodied than Alcaraz carpets, with a foundation of bast fibre. In later examples the symmetrical knot may be used instead of the Spanish knot, which encircles only a single warp. Usually the color range is limited and muddy, as if several hues had proved fugitive; later rugs may show bold coloring. A good red dye did not appear in these rugs until the 18th century, when a bright cherry red was sometimes used.

Floor coverings handwoven in or around the city of Kayseri in central Turkey. The best-known rugs from this district are those produced in the 20th century, largely for sale to tourists and undiscriminating collectors.
Those who practice sorcery, which includes magic, enchantment, witchcraft, or other occult arts.
Playing a resonant musical instrument with breath under pressure.

Groups of all copies printed at the same time. A single impression in publishing includes all of the copies of a book produced during one printing, or print-run, or an additional press-run made without revision of text.
Describes aggregates of objects that store and convey information.

The body or main structure of a constructed work, such as ships or built works, to which surface materials or fixtures are applied. For the body or framework of furniture, prefer "carcases (furniture components)."
Refers to the process of assembling pieces of glass together by inserting their edges into cames, for example to form windows or lampshades.
Regional dress expresses geographic identity, and can also indicate social, marital, and/or religious status.

Predecessors to horseshoes used in the north-western parts of the Roman Empire from the mid-first century CE. The hoof was enclosed in an oval cup of thick metal, fastened by metallic clips and leather laces.
People appointed to perform liturgical duties or other services in a Christian church, or who hold authority by virtue of their rank within a Christian religious order or similar organization.
General term for all glassware and equipment used in laboratories.
Officers, for example in ancient Rome, whose functions were to attend upon a magistrate, bearing the fasces before him, and to execute sentence of judgement upon offenders.

Refers to nobles in Europe and Japan, specifically those of the second rank of the nobility of various European countries, ranking immediately below dukes and above earls or counts. It may also carry its original meaning, denoting counts or earls who held a march, or mark, which is a frontier district.
Stick-like implements intended to apply cosmetics or sticks composed of a cosmetic. Best known as works from ancient Egypt, Asia, and elsewhere.
Tools with a flat round end on an often ornamented handle, usually made of brass or silver, used for pushing down tobacco into the bowls of pipes.
A device comprising a handle and a lens, usually of glass, that increases the apparent size of an object viewed through it.

Designation given to certain sectors within an administrative division that have a degree of independence, administer their own affairs, or are otherwise self-governing to some degree. The precise definition of "autonomous sectors" varies from nation to nation, and is typically assigned to the sector by the nation, rather than being assigned by an outside body. Examples of an autonomous sector is found in Guinea-Bissau.
Bricklayers' tools having a cutting edge on each side; used for cutting, trimming, and dressing brick or stone.
Liturgical objects in the form of small lances or spears, used in the Greek Church used in the preparatory rite of prothesis, during which the host is separated from a loaf before consecration.

Kylikes in which a central picture on the inside is surrounded by a ring-shaped figured zone, or in which one picture occupies the entire surface. Examples of both black- and red-figure zone cups are known. The largest known kylikes, up to 22 inches (56 cm), are zone cups.
The sequence of processes involved in binding a book following the sewing or stitching of the text block up to and including covering.
Those who play the violoncello.

Administrative departments outside the borders of, but under the jurisdiction and sovereignty of a primary political entity, such as a nation or empire. An example is the overseas department of France, French Guiana.
The thin, flat pieces of glass on which specimens are mounted for the purpose of microscopic examination.
Athletes whose occupation or profession is to play the game of golf.
Curved dentate blades used in mezzotint to roughen the surface of the plate.
Sheets of paper inserted between printed sheets as they are printed to prevent offsets.
Parts or components of sculptures.
Furniture feet in the form of a tight scroll, especially those found on mid-18th-century English chair legs.
Items created, manufactured, or used for a specific, limited use; typically intended to be used for a short period and discarded thereafter, although ephemera is often actually collected.
Images believed to possess supernatural powers or abilities such as healing, moving, or secreting substances resembling, for example, blood or tears.
General term for objects used in preparation for or during wedding ceremonies.
Original, rudimentary plows without mouldboards that are pulled by pack animals. It turns up but does not invert the soil, as opposed to the later turnplow.
Shallow wood trays intended to store moveable type. These are divided into compartments to store the various characters in a font.

Relatively small warships armed with one or more guns; such vessels are most commonly used for local defense and inland patrol, but gunboats of the late 19th and early 20th centuries could be quite substantial.
Small vessels employed either to attend larger ones, as for taking ashore or bringing aboard passengers, goods, and stores, or to attend coastal facilities, such as lighthouses and canneries.
Ships' boats carried on stern davits of fishing vessels, especially coasters; became engine-powered in the 20th century.

Extinct class of vertebrate jawed fish-like animals known mainly from fossils of the Silurian and Devonian periods, having the head and pectoral region encased in broad, flat bony plates. Characterized by jaws supported by both cranium and hyoid arch, a partly ossified cranium, a head and trunk with armor that is jointed at the neck, often pelvic fins, pectoral fins or finlike structures, and gill arches.
Chinese ritual vessels, usually bronze, that are among the earliest forms of spouted wine cup, used from the Erlitou to the middle Western Zhou.
Extinct order of extinct flying reptiles of the Mesozoic order characterized by having a fourth digit of each forelimb prolonged to a great length to support a wing membrane for active flight.

Striped equine found in dry upland plains in Namibia and a few scattered areas in western South Africa. Although it has been proposed that the Cape mountain zebra (Equus zebra) and the Hartmann's mountain zebra (Equus hartmannae) are two distinct species, recent genetic evidence indicates that they are a single species, in spite of their now inhabiting non-overlapping territories and typically differing in the width of the black stripes and variations in sexual dimorphism.
A type of local area network based on the principle of collision detection. It is used for connecting computers and their peripheral printers, servers, workstations within the same physical location.

Extensible Markup Language, or XML, is a markup language and file format for storing, transmitting, and reconstructing arbitrary data. Based on SGML, it allows the mark-up of electronic documents, and can aid the exchange of data via the World Wide Web, and allows users to customize tags.
Denotes small rounded indentations in a coastline, smaller than bays and generally characterized by a narrow entrance.
Paper size, generally used in Great Britain, measuring 18 by 23 inches.

Order of North and South American marsupial mammals, containing 70 or more species in only one family. Usually semi-arboreal omnivores, having a very full jaw of teeth, moving with feet flat on the ground (plantigrade) and hind feet with an opposable digit with no claw, and a prehensile tails. The name "opossum" is based on a term in the Powhatan language meaning "white dog-like creature."
Genus of five species of South American foxes.
Genus of three South American species, Geoffroy's cat, kodkod, and pampas cat.
Copies of printed matter, or three-dimensional objects, created specifically for the presentation by the artist and/or publisher.
Money, made of metal rods, used as a medium of exchange.

Marbled paper prepared one of three ways: "blue", which shows a network of blue with small to medium white spots, "four veins", which contains red, yellow, green and blue, and "hair vein marble", which contains a ground color (black), which is driven into tiny veins using water or another substance.

Chancel screens surmounted by a cross or crucifix, and which evolved from 'rood beams.' Rood screens are often richly adorned and are sometimes double with vaulting between and a rood loft on top. The French term of 'jubé' derives from the Latin phrase Jube domine benedicere ("Let us bless the Lord"), which is often said by Catholic priests before the lesson while standing in front of the screen; some jubés have a balcony or platform from which to preach to the laity.

Uncommon book format consisting of 64 pages or 32 leaves. Although it may be formed by making 5 right angles from the original sheet, the process is hampered by trapped air and buckling. Instead, the book format is created by folding an entire sheet with parallel folds, and folding a half sheet with two parallel and two right angle folds, and inserting the folded half sheet into the former.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Chad, Libya, and Niger.

Textile works, typically fine cloth embroidered by women or girls in various stitches and intended to be framed. They were usually created as demonstrations of a beginner's skill and featured a combination of stitches, motifs, letters, verses, and often the date of completion and the stitcher's name.

A type of notion used either to repair a piece of fabric or garment, or that may be purely decorative, or both. These may be embroidered, come backed with adhesive, or intended to be sewn onto a support.

Refers to the principal festival and feast of the Christian church in which the resurrection of Jesus Christ is celebrated.
