Amongst the most distinctive pilgrim badges are the scallop-shell badges from the shrine of St James in Santiago de Compostella, a badge sold as early as the 11th century. Badges were usually made of metal and were usually worn pinned to a hat. Badges also provided practical benefits, by marking the wearer as a person entitled to aid, hospitality and safe-conduct, for example; there were also supernatural benefits since badges were normally allowed to touch the shrine they commemorated and were thus thought to be transformed into secondary relics. Pilgrim badges were especially popular in the Middle Ages in Europe, particularly in the 14th and 15th centuries, but declined after the Reformation of the mid-16th century. However, there are a few instances of sites that continue to use associated badges in the present day.
Units of usually two leaves, the flyleaf and the pastedown, placed in the front and back of a book between the covers and the text block.
Characters used in certain ancient scripts, especially in Scandinavia and Britain, and in the Orkhon River area of Mongolia.
Containers made of woven materials used to hold offerings for religious ceremonies, varying in design. Examples include the Ancient Greek kaunon.

Material derived from the shells of certain turtles and tortoises, sometimes utilizing the entire shell. Differs from the material "tortoise shell" in the way it is prepared and its finished appearance; also often derived from different species than is "tortoise shell."

Rounded vessels that are generally wider than they are high, usually hemispherical or nearly so. A bowl may have a spreading base or foot ring and sometimes two handles or a cover. Distinguished from a cup, which is rather deep than wide.
Coins that consist exclusively of inscriptions (legends).

Fluid secreted by the lacrimal apparatus. Tears, along with other secretions, help form the protective, precorneal film on the exterior of the eye. Tears can be reflexly secreted in response to a variety of stimuli (bright lights, etc.). The secretion of tears as a result of emotional upset is called psychical weeping.
Use to describe objects including structures, designed to move incrementally around an axis.
Use to describe artifacts fabricated primarily by machine, usually to distinguish from those made by hand.
The activity of setting or placing a seed, bulb, seedling, or other plant in the ground so that it may take root and grow; establishing a garden, orchard, field of crops, woods, etc.
Representations of fly-whisk-bearing female figures.
The outermost layers or areas of objects, such as the portions of the exterior in contact with the air.
Fireworks or other visual works using fire or explosives as a medium.

Wood or metal discs, cylinders, or cup-shaped attachments located below the double reed in some European and most non-European double reed instruments, serving as a lip rest. The reed is taken into the player's mouth and the lips pressed against the pirouette.
Ancient Greek votive images on plaques. The supports may be terracotta, wood, marble, or bronze; images may be cast, impressed, sculpted, or painted.

Refers generally to pictorial representations with very broad horizontal ranges of view. The term is also used specifically for photographs that show a wide view produced by a panoramic camera or by joining photographs together.
Small, often quite highly finished versions of larger paintings or sculptures, made to be shown to the patron in order to indicate what is intended, or a highly finished drawing serving that purpose.
Refers to the dominant, usually central, images on either side of coins, medals, or tokens.
Actions of resisting, opposing, or withstanding someone or something, including organized or covert opposition to an invading, occupying, or ruling power.

A name of convenience for a type of rug characterized by maritime scenes in the corners, so called because the ships appear to be European manned by seamen in Portuguese or Dutch style clothing; the rugs are made with a cotton foundation with asymmetrical and some jufti knotting.
In Indian architecture, haṁsamālā-haṁsa figures on rafter-ends.
People belonging to a militia, which is an organized body of part-time, volunteer citizen soldiers.
Long, narrow floor coverings used especially in halls, narrow passages, and on stairs.

In mechanical engineering, the load at which a solid material that is being stretched begins to flow, or change shape permanently, divided by its original cross-sectional area; or the amount of stress in a solid at the onset of permanent deformation.  Britannica Online.
Small rugs that can be randomly placed.

Term of convenience for certain handwoven or hand-knotted pile rugs originally produced in certain regions of Asia, Africa, and Europe; prefer a more specific descriptor or the name of the place or culture of origin.

Flat-woven rugs from Turkey, elsewhere in the Caucasus, and surrounding areas; patterned by supplementary wrapping wefts. They are typically heavy and stiff; they may be distinguished by their pattern, which is visible from only from one side with the reverse often having threads of yarn left hanging on the back. The technique is one of the oldest known, identified among charred 7th-century-BCE fragments excavated at Gordion, near Ankara in Anatolia.
Two or more lights in the same horizontal direction used as an aid to nautical or aeronautical navigation, such as those lights indicating a channel or marking the end of a runway.
Light sources of various design, intended to throw bright, even illumination for conducting work in a workshop or similar environment.
Staff weapons of the Maori.

Objects relating to Jewish life, religion, and culture, especially but not limited to those of a literary, historic, or artistic nature, or pertaining to ritual. For individual types of items, see appropriate hierarchies.
Refers to any salt or ester of nitrous acid.
Joins between two metal parts that are undertaken using molten metal. Examples of metallurgical joints include those made using welding, brazing, soldering, and interlock casting.
Carved figures, usually of steatite, produced by the Kongo peoples of northern Angola and lower Congo, for the purpose of serving as watchmen over the deceased.

Those privately employed, as on an estate or private game preserve, to provide a natural environment conducive to the health and propagation of game, prevent poaching, and assist the employers or other authorized persons in hunting. For public officials who enforce the game laws of a jurisdiction, use "game wardens."

Distinctive sheet metal seams made with one sheet edge turned, double-bent, and locked onto a sheet having a simple bend; usually created using a special Pittsburgh lockforming machine. An example of use for the seam is at the corners of elbows and square or rectangular pipes of ducts.

Work comprising a series of fourteen devotional pictures or carvings recalling the passion of Christ from his condemnation to his burial. The devotional exercise of visiting and praying in front of each of the 14 stations originates from the practice of early Christian pilgrims who visited the scenes of the events in Jerusalem and walked the traditional route from the supposed location of Pilate's house to Calvary. The Stations of the Cross are the subject of personal and private devotions during Lent and Passiontide in Roman Catholic and some Anglican churches. The images are typically mounted on the inside walls of a church or chapel but may also be installed in such places as cemeteries, hospitals, religious houses, and on mountainsides. The Franciscans popularized this form of devotion in the late Middle Ages.

Luminescence spectroscopy is a collective name given to three related spectroscopic techniques dependent on emission of light from a substance. They are: molecular fluorescence spectroscopy; molecular phosphorescence spectroscopy; and chemiluminescence spectroscopy.
Flexible tubes containing two solutions in separte chambers, which emit light as a result of the chemical reaction that occurs when the tube is bent and solutions combine.
Formal specifications of the duties and responsibilities related to occupations or positions of employment.
Buildings housing museums focusing on the history, tenets, writings, music, architecture, or objects associated with religion, either of one particular religion or on the general topic of religion.
The action or condition of causing an organization or group of people to cease to exist. Dissolution may involve official documents and usually occurs on a specific date.
Those who study the nature and function of poetry, identifying and describing its types, forms, and techniques.

Those who study or practice the science of human and animal mind and behavior, both healthy and unhealthy, with the focus on individuals in interaction with their environment. For those who deal with the treatment of mental, emotional, and behavioral disorders, use "psychiatrists."

Slips or leaves bearing a list of corrections to typos, omissions, or other errors that occur in the printed text of a book  They are inserted loose, tipped in, or, rarely, bound in with the pages, usually in the front matter, less commonly at the back.

A pattern or ornament of interlaced curving bands in the form of two or more bands or strings twisting over each other, so as to repeat the same figure, in a continued series by the spiral returning of the bands; sometimes giving the effect of a braid, but most often in smooth curves forming circles. Sometimes considered a type of fret or a type of interlace. Named after the French engineer Guillot, who invented a machine that could scratch fine patterns and designs on metallic surfaces.

Those who write, invent, promote, investigate or propound a theory or theories about music, which is the art concerned with the combining of vocal or instrumental sounds in measured time to communicate emotions, ideas, or states of mind.
Certain church officers or leaders.

Stands, supports, or flat devices, usually with long or short feet, often three, but sometimes with none and which may also have a handle, used to elevate a vessel in a hearth while cooking or to protect a surface, as of a table or counter, from being damaged by the heat of a hot object, such as a cooking vessel or flatiron.
General term for tools used to cut, shape, sew, or otherwise work leather.
Thin shields used when erasing to avoid erasing the surrounding work.
Those whose trade is to process the flesh of animals for sale as food. Butchers may slaughter animals, but in common usage the term denotes someone who deals in meat products in a retail context.
In Indian architecture, a minor angle.

Benches designed to allow the detainment of prisoners or others. The benches may be enclosed or open, and may be designed to allow the attachment of restraints. The purpose of the benches varied in periods of history and various contexts: purposes include as a temporary means of detainment prior to imprisonment or trial, to shame the citizen in a public place, or to allow the detainees to attend a religious service or other event.
A manner of composing pictorial narratives. The expression usually refers to Renaissance and Baroque paintings.
Polymeric substance prepared from derivatives of ethylene that are capable of recovering their original shape after being stretched to great extents.

Cylindrical containers, often made of plastic or metal, used to package ready-mixed paints, varnishes, lacquers, stains, and other industrial or retail products. Typically resealable and temperature tolerant to facilitate the paint product's reusability and preservation.
A naturalistic or geometricized motif derived from the species Dianthus caryophyllus, commonly used in Oriental carpets, especially in Turkey.
Lengths of material, usually cloth, hung at a window; often hung in pairs at either side of the window.
Roman silver coins of several valuations, originating at one-half denarius, produced beginning in the late 3rd century BCE; later also of gold or bronze and issued until the 3rd century CE.

General term for a number of gold or silver coins based on the Florentine original gold coin. Originally, florins were Florentine gold coins struck from 1252 until the 16th century; to refer specifically to the Florentine coins, prefer the narrower term "fiorini d'oro."  Examples of florins include Hungarian gold coins introduced in the early 14th century, Austrian silver coins of the 19th and 20th centuries, and English two-shilling silver coins issued in the 19th century.
Curving metal bands attached to the underside of a rocket launcher or the stock of a firearm, vertically enclosing the trigger to prevent accidental discharge.
Script used by the Mycenaeans after about 1500 or 1450 BCE, apparently recording an early form of the Greek language.

Monophonic liturgical music in use in the Ethiopian national church; chants are sung in the Geez (Ethiopic) language. Although the liturgy of this church is eclectic with particularly strong influence from the Egyptian Coptic Church, the chant repertory is almost exclusively of indigenous Ethiopian heritage.
Books containing all the Roman Catholic prayers and responses necessary for celebrating the mass throughout the year.
Bowls or lidded bowls used to hold offerings for religious ceremonies. Made of varying material, including wood or brass.
Curtains made of any transparent or very lightweight material, usually plain white, often used as undercurtains. For sheer curtains fitted against the glass in an opening, use "glass curtains."
Instruments consisting of an often rigid handle and a flexible lash or lashes made of cord or leather, used for disciplinary action, torture, or weapons against animals or humans.
Devices by which molasses is processed from sorghum cane, which is stripped of leaves and fed through the rollers of the mill.
Large spatulas used to break up the curd for cheesemaking. For knives with a curved blade used to cut and serve cheese, use "cheese knives (serving utensils)."

Japanese transverse flutes used in court music and some folk dances, made from a single tube of bamboo. They resemble the "nokan" in having seven equidistant fingerholes, a balancing weight in the upper end, a red-lacquered bore, and a wrapping of bark or twine, but are distinct in having a patch of ornament embroidered on a red ground on the upper end and in lacking the nokan's characteristic tube inserted into the bore between the mouth hole and nearest fingerhole.
Any container with a tight-fitting lid used to poach food.

Pieces of paper, leather, fabric, or small tablets inscribed and affixed to something for identification or description. In the context of bookbinding, refers specifically to paper or other material separate from that used to cover a book, on which the author's name and the title are printed or engraved and glued to the spine or front board. For larger, more public identifying notices, use "identification signs."
Boxes or cases, usually lidded, in which tools are kept.

Devices for roasting coffee beans, one type consisting of a cylindrical metal receptacle with sealable opening, attached to a long handled rod. This is placed over a fire to roast the coffee beans. For mechanized coffee roasters, typically electric, use "coffee roasting machines."
Written accounts of the lives of individuals. For the genre regardless of medium, prefer "biography (general genre)."
Vessels for holding drinking water that is cooled and drawn off by a faucet or spigot.
Procedures used during the intaglio process, where images are printed from ink held in the recessed areas of plates or blocks, which have been cut or etched away.
Relief printing processes in which the nonprinting engraved lines form a white image on a black background. Most often used in reference to wood engraving and the dotted manner.

Coffee brewing device containing a plunger made of fine mesh with which the grounds are pushed to the bottom of a carafe when the coffee is ready to be poured. It is known by a wide variety of names including French press, cafetiére, cafetière à piston, and coffee plunger.

A type of kantharos featuring handles and bowl much as in type B, a small torus foot with no stem, and a bowl usually decorated with patterns rather than figures. The name comes from the botanical term 'sessile' denoting something sitting directly on its base.
Refers to a type of oinochoe featuring a round mouth and a bulbous body continuously curved from neck to foot.
Bags with single straps worn over the shoulder and across the chest.

Cylindrical containers, often metal, with a close lid perforated with a number of coarse or fine holes for sprinkling flour, sugar, or spices especially when cooking. Typically undecorated, except for some horizontal molding, and often having one simple scroll or ring handle.
Trays or small receptacles for holding two or more small bottles or other vessels for ceremonial liquids or for oil, vinegar, spices, mustard, other condiments at meals.
Vessels of a cylindrical form, often of wood, wider in the middle, and of greater length than breadth, formed of curved staves bound together by hoops, and used to store foodstuffs.

Ceramic vessels decorated with exaggerated facial features, usually on one face of the jug but multiple faces have also been used. Originated in the American South in the mid-19th century amongst enslaved and freed African potters. The production of face jugs continued into the 20th century with the development of African American potteries and with white potters adding face jugs to their offerings. Several potteries in southern U.S. states such as Georgia continue to make face jugs in the 21st century.

Double-headed cylindrical drums characterized by having several gut, nylon, wire, or wire-covered silk strings (snares) stretched across the lower head; the snares vibrate sympathetically with the lower head (to which vibration is transmitted from the upper, or batter, head by air vibrations inside the drum), causing a snappy, penetrating, relatively high-pitched sound. The use of snares on drums was known in ancient Egypt.
Cups having a guard behind the rim to protect the mustache while drinking; a 19th-century innovation.
Handled cups with spouts attached to the bowl used to feed invalids too weak or ill to sit in an upright position.
Containers of any size or shape made for holding snuff.

Containers of various designs used to hold urine, usually portable as for travel, in a sick bed, or a bed chamber; may be appropriately shaped for male or female use. They may have a handle. For portable containers intended for both urine and excrement, and usually found in bed chambers, prefer "chamber pots"; for such containers found in sick beds, prefer "bedpans (containers)."
Containers, chiefly or wholly enclosed, for growing and displaying plants and/or animals.
Instruments that record the number of paces taken when walking or running and, when adjusted for an individual's pace length, can provide a rough measure of the distance traveled.
Lightweight bedcovers for warm weather, especially those which are similar to quilt tops but have bound edges and finished seams.
Quilts similar to log cabin quilts in design and technique, except for the use of irregular shapes and a more random design.

Vessels used for one or more particular ritual activities, often for sacrificial offerings or consumption of food and wine as part of a ceremony. In some disciplines, this term is preferred over the slightly less descriptive "ceremonial vessels," but in other disciplines the meanings overlap and the distinction is moot.
Racks in which letters and papers are kept, typically located on a desk or mounted on a wall.
Cylindrical containers that store liquids or other materials, usually in large capacity.
Vessels in which the feet are bathed.

Oval boxes of light wooden-splint construction used to hold delicate finery or trinkets. Popular in the 18th and 19th century, bride's boxes were given as a marriage gift to brides to hold small items in the bride's trousseau such as linens, lace, and ribbons.
Vessel rims usually pierced which extend horizontally a short distance outward from the vessel body then vertically upward, often providing a support for a cover which rests within.
Scales or balances designed for weighing the ingredients of medicinal and other formulas prescribed by physicians and dispensed by pharmacists.
Bowed spike fiddles of Senegal and Gambia, with a heart-shaped calabash body, membrane belly, and single string held taut by a tuning ring.
Apparatus for measuring gas and for calibrating other gas-measuring devices.

Hardened steel blocks having two flat, parallel surfaces with the parallel distance between the surfaces marked to a guaranteed accuracy of a few millionths of an inch; used in manufacturing processes as a precise measuring standard.

Clocks of great accuracy containing a deadbeat escapement and temperature-compensated pendulum used for the regulation of other timepieces; usually tall case clocks in form. These were initially used in observatories and clock and watch shops as the standard of accuracy during repairs, synchronization, and manufacturing.

Tubes of various dimensions used to dispense consecrated wine, or wine and bread, at communion. Used occasionally up until the sixteenth century; use contintued by the Pope and his deacons up until the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965) during papal Masses.
In the composition of pages, matter set apart from the text as a title or a summary of the text that follows.
Devices for measuring the air pressure in tires.

Devices in which the variations in a fluctuating electrical quantity appear temporarily as a visible wave form on a display screen. These plot the relationship between these variations, with the horizontal axis normally being a function of time and the vertical axis the voltage generated by an input signal. The German physicist Ferdinand Braun developed the first cathode-ray oscilloscope in 1897. In general, these are considered the same instrument as an oscilloscope, except that the oscillograph may be capable of creating a permanent record of measurements, while the oscilloscope provides only visual feedback.
Devices used for for measuring angles between lines on horizontal planes.
Wooden coffers in which are stored the sacred altar tablets of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church; they also at times serve as altar tables.
Barrel-shaped containers, especially those stronger and larger than barrels, made of staves, headings, and hoops usually closely fitted together so as to hold liquids.
Vessels intended for an individual to use for drinking wine, water, or other beverage.
Pertains to the style and culture of modern Iran. Although modern Iran was known as Persia until 1935, art and architecture of ancient Iranian civilizations dates back to prehistoric times.
Translated versions of a text.
Lists, catalogs, histories, or accounts of religious martyrs.

Works which recount aspects of funeral and memorial activities relating chiefly to royalty, nobility, or famous persons, usually illustrated and containing descriptions of processions, services, attendees, caskets, church decorations, and other funeral furnishings and structures, and often including sermons, eulogies, and other textual testaments to the deceased's virtue and importance.
"New fathers" indoor cap, usually decorated and plumed. Traditionally worn in the Netherlands for nine to ten days after the birth of a child. No equivalent in English language or culture.
Shoes with an upper having a portion cut out to expose a toe or toes.
Stiffened, or jacked, heavy leather boots of varying lengths, often worn for riding, especially by cavalry during the 17th and 18th centuries.
Chemically treated cords that burn at a uniform rate, used to fire the powder charge in matchlock firearms and some cannons.

Any of various light, four-wheeled carriages generally characterized as seating two, having a folding top, and being owner-driven; popular sporting vehicles after their introduction in the mid-18th century; may also be used for automobiles of similar characteristics.
Caps, often made of wool, with a visor in the front and in the back, and with earflaps usually raised and tied on the top of the hat; use especially for those worn as hunting caps.
Wires used on members or structures whose primary function is to produce a smooth outline and to reduce drag, specifically on aircraft.
Arrangements of ropes, wires, and chains used for securing or supporting masts, yards, and for hoisting, lowering, or trimming the sails.
Two or three-wheeled vehicles, non motorized carts for the transport of liquid manure with fixed, semi-fixed, or separate hoppers.
White to yellow mass of amorphous crystals, with the chemical structure K2O2; used as an oxidizing and bleaching agent.

Relatively short, slender shafts,usually having with a handle at one end and a flat round-tipped blade at the other, used by people pushing the device through water in a vertical manner in order to propel small boats; may be double-ended; for longer but similar devices with flat-tipped blades, use "oars."
Headwear comprising bands of cloth or another material tied around the top of the head and under the chin. Examples are women's headwear in Medieval Europe and men's headwear in ancient Persia.
Articles of clothing suitable for casual wear during the day, in contrast to formal wear suitable for evening events.
Large crosses pinned or worn suspended from a chain or cord on the chest by the Pope, archbishops, and bishops.
Tall metal or leather helmets worn by cavalry soldiers, with combs surmounted by pompons or tails made of various materials such as horsehair, and front and rear visors.
Toys with which children can make music as a form of play.

Shaped pieces of absorbent and rubberized or plastic-coated materials often padded or occasionally filled with deodorizing herbs; attached to or placed inside a garment, as in the underarm of a dress or blouse, to prevent the garment from being soiled by perspiration.

Books produced and published by private presses. For manuals provided to theater owners, especially in the 1930s and 1940s, advising them on how to promote a particular motion picture being shown in their theater, use "pressbooks."
Japanese bindings consisting of folded sheets stitched together so that the folded edges form the fore edge.
Characteristic design of book covers, developed by Samuel Mearne, binder to King Charles II, in which the covers were ornamented to resemble cottage gables.
Belts worn for support during weight lifting.
Toys consisting of a stick with a cuplike top and a ball attached to the stick by a string long enough for the ball to swing freely and be swung up and caught in the cup.

Colorless, odorless, crystalline salt used in very dilute solutions to fluoridate water and treat tooth decay. In higher concentrations, sodium fluoride is used as a fumigant, and a preservative for zoological specimens, paint, plaster, wood, and masonry.
Long flat pieces of wood with slightly curved heads at one end used as a striking implement in various hockey sports.

Hopi, Pueblo, or Zuni dolls of various forms and materials that represent a dancer's ritual reenactment of a Kachina spirit, typically taking the form of animals, plants, objects, or persons; often given to children at the end of special ceremonies. Other tribes, such as the Navaho, produce kachina dolls as collectibles.

Short, pleated, wraparound garments usually of tartan, developed in the mid-18th century in the Highlands of Scotland as a simplified version of a full plaid. Later adopted by the Highland regiments of the British army as an item of uniform. Worn by men and boys in Scotland as part of the national dress. Also, similar plaid skirts worn by women and girls.

Trousers cut full over the hips and thighs and tapering at the knee to become tightfitting from knee to ankle, especially those worn with boots for horseback riding or hiking. For trousers cut wide around the thighs and extending to the calf, use "riding breeches."
General term for ceremonial costume worn by kings, pelates, sacrificial victims, or other people for religious or other ceremonial or ritual purposes.

Vestments comprising long, oblong veils or shawls used in the Roman rite, worn over the shoulders of the celebrant; generally made of silk. They are most often used during the Exposition and Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament. The ends of the humeral veil are used to envelop the hands of the celebrant when he holds up the monstrance, as a mark of respect for the sacred vessel. The item grew out of the tradition of sudaria cloths in ancient Rome.

Generally refers to various types of main garments for the upper body, made with or without sleeves and worn over or tucked in the waistband of a skirt, trousers, or the like. Usually having a collar, which may be detachable, often a front opening, and sometimes pockets. Specifically often refers to an article of male attire with long sleeves terminating in wristbands or cuffs. It originally referred to undergarments for the upper part of the body, made of linen, calico, flannel, silk, or other washable material; originally always worn next to the skin.
Round or cone-shaped covers, often of gourd, wood, or hides, worn on the penis, especially by men in southern Africa, particularly after circumcision.

Womens' fashion accessories comprising clamps, typically metal and decorative, that were attached to long, trailing skirts to hold them up off the floor; used particularly in the later 19th century. The skirt lifter was often attached to a cord or ribbon that was hung from the waist by a chatelaine. The wearer used the skirt lifter when necessary, such as when walking up stairs or dancing.

Rather long, narrow lengths of soft material worn about the neck, usually under a collar, tied in front into a knot, loop, or bow and often with the two ends falling free vertically. For neckcloths of fine cloth wound around the neck, usually over the shirt, and tied in front into a bow or knot, use "cravats."
Elaborate coverings or objects for the head, especially those worn for ceremonial or ornamental purposes.

Double- or single-breasted three-quarter length or full-length fitted overcoats with flared skirts, sometimes open in the front to reveal garments underneath, usually with large collars and lapels; worn especially by men and women during the 18th and 19th centuries, originally made with short shoulder cape. For dresses open in front to show an underskirt or with a front gore of contrasting material, use "redingote (dresses)."

Boys or girls' suits inspired by French or British marine-uniforms: blouses or jackets and trousers or skirts in white and blue, adorned with stripes in the contrasting color. The upper-body garment is also characterized by a flat collar that forms a rectangle down the back.
Protective coverings for the knees used when working or crawling at floor level, or when kneeling for support.
Padding woven or inserted into the calves of stockings to produce the appearance of more rounded calves of the wearer; patented in 1788 and worn in the 17th, 18th and 19th century.

Bands resembling chains, made of linked metal loops with points, usually blunt rather than sharp; the band is tied or otherwise secured on an arm, leg, waist, or other area of the body so that the points are against the skin. Used in some religious traditions to induce some degree of discomfort or pain as a sign of repentance and atonement.
Script with rounded forms and an exaggerated horizontal stroke, dating from Persia in the 9th century CE.
Missiles containing an explosive charge, designed to be launched from ships, submarines, or aircraft into water, where they are self-propelled and usually directable.
Utensils with two long prongs and a handle used to place or remove pies from an oven. For flat paddlelike tools also used to place and remove food in an oven use "peels."
Piston-valved aerophones with a wide conical bore, usually coiled, and with a cupped mouthpiece. For bugles with keys that lent a full chromatic scale, use "keyed bugles."

Main garments usually fitted to the upper body, extending below the hip line, open at the front or side and generally having sleeves. Also, similar outer garments worn for warmth or protection from the weather.
Short, usually double-breasted and belted, coats or jackets made of a thick, woolen, often plaid, material.
Vessels designed to separate gravy or another liquid from solid fat.
Specialized utensils which have a long, narrow channel on one end and a scooplike bowl on the other; used to remove the marrow from bones, typically at table.
Small, usually wire kitchen implements used for hand beating of foods such as eggs, creams, or potatoes.
Devices used to clean shrimp before cooking and eating them.
General term for various distinctive styles of writing of the pre-Carolingian hands of France that were derived from Latin cursive script.
Devices used to tune instruments.
Devices used on sound devices to soften the tone, usually decreasing the volume in the process.

Armor pieces for the foot existing in various forms in Europe from Medieval times to the 16th century, comprised of mail or plates enclosing the ankle and lames covering the foot, plus a plate toecap. Some types had a detachable long point for the toecap.
Armor protecting the front and back of the torso, variously made throughout their history of layers of linen or leather, metal scales, lames, or plates, or combinations of leather and metal.
Trade name for an art glass made to imitate the appearance of the peach-bloom glaze on Chinese porcelain.
An alcohol soluble protein from maize, analogous to gluten, used in making textile fibers, plastics, adhesives, coatings and sizes.
Decoratively shaped hollow vessels into which rice (or other foods) may be pressed in order to take on its shape.
Flattened, gourd-shaped bottles with one or two pairs of lugs at each side through which might be passed a strap whereby they could be slung over the shoulder.
Bottles for holding pressurized water that is driven out through a siphon by the pressure of the gas when a valve in the tube is opened.
Towels on which a priest dries his hands after washing them before celebrating Mass.
Refers to the process of attaching headbands to the head and tail of a text block.

Provinces outside the borders of, but under the jurisdiction and sovereignty of a primary political entity, such as a nation or empire. A historical example was Portugal's Overseas Province of Angola.
Wood frames for the support of canvas or other textile that do not have expandable corners. For similar frames having expandable corners, use "stretchers (framing and mounting equipment)."

Small wheels used to indent or perforate surfaces such as paper, pottery, or metal plates for printmaking. Use if this term encompasses tools with revolving heads of hardened steel on which a dotted, lined, or irregular pattern is incised; used in intaglio processes, especially mezzotint, and other objects such as short lengths of fiber or wood rolled into wet clay to create decorative motifs.
Letters, symbols, or ornament tranferred from a backing sheet to a working surface, either by burnishing or by hand placement of cut-out self-adhesive characters and figures.
Lateral parts or appendages of a work of art, such as those found on a triptych.
Pointed and elongated feet found mostly on Queen Anne furniture.

Generally, may refer to showy unsubstantial objects, especially a useless ornament. Specifically, typically refers to mechanical contrivances or scientific apparatuses that are collectible but of little utilitarian value.
Huichol artworks, most often employing yarn, representing the spiritual world or acting as a portal to it.
A staff with a heart affixed to the top. Part of the array of the Nahua deities Chalmecacihuatl, Xochipilli, Ixtlilton, Macuilxochitl and the other Macuiltonalehqueh.

Ship-rigged warships of the 17th through early 19th century, carrying many heavy cannon and intended to fight in a line-of-battle formation; in the Royal Navy, ships of the line were those warships carrying more than a minimum number of guns, rising from 30 in the 1650s to 80 in the 1840s.
Open boats, typically less than 20 feet in length, used for general service applications.
Small warships' boats, carvel-planked, 16 feet to 26 feet long, and rowing eight oars or fewer.
Single-masted, fore-and-aft-rigged sailing vessels, with one or two headsails.
Electrically or mechanically driven device for tying stems such as flax into bundles.
Political units, such as nations, that exercise and are recognized internationally as possessing sovereignty.

Political entities have a government in which people either rule themselves or elect representatives to rule in their interests. Elections, to be democratic, must be held regularly, be secret, and provide a choice of candidates; the elected assembly must also be free to legislate and criticize government policy.
Ships built or operated for the purpose of teaching crew members or students seamanship or other subjects; many navies operate such vessels for their cadets.
Textile made with cotton, silk, or linen warp and wool, mohair, alpaca, or some other glossy hair fiber as weft in order to produce a lustrous surface.

A twill or pile fabric with a raised nap on both sides. Originally made of wool, it is most often now made of cotton or other synthetic fibers, and often used as a light-absorbent cloth in theater or film productions.
Self-patterned textile with a small rectilinear pattern formed by contrasting the weave's warp and weft faces.
Technique of decorating a surface with a pattern consisting of small depressions produced by use of punches.

A type of decoration on Dutch and German glassware and ceramics popular in the 17th and 18th centuries. This was created with a sepia enamel that had been used in stained glass techniques, and adapted to various wares either alone or in combination with other enamels or gold.

People who tap trees for sap or juice, which involves boring holes into the trunk, tapping a metal or wooden spile into the hole, and collecting the exuded sap the sap or juice without killing the tree. Examples include those who tap maple trees and rubber trees.
Fracturing in a material or object, usually along a single or branched path.
The application of a substance, as to textiles or stone, so that the substance interpenetrates, fills, or saturates the material.
The action of administering a fine mist, especially for the purpose of moisturization.
Process of removing calcium or calcium compounds from a calcified material such as bone, soil, mortar.
The action or method of inserting intermediate elements in a series, in that the quality of the new elements is ascertained by the known elements surrounding it.
Spoons intended primarily for serving food from a bowl, dish, or the like; sometimes made en suite with a serving fork.
Cars, carriages, or other nonmotorized wheeled vehicles that include a chassis and are primarily intended to be towed by other vehicles.

Refers to horse-drawn public street vehicles intended to carry a large number of passengers, generally having rear entry, longitudinal seats facing each other, and paneled sides; for horse-drawn rail vehicles usually accommodating more riders, see "horsecars."

A variety of conveyances for one person consisting generally of canvas or similar material stretched or laid across a frame for transporting the sick, wounded, or dead. For more elaborate conveyances carried on poles by people or animals, use "litters" if boxlike in form, often enclosed by curtains, or "sedan chairs" if in the form of portable chairs.
Self-patterned twill with a rectilinear pattern formed by the contrast of warp and weft faces.
Enzyme-catalyzed synthesis of complex molecules from simpler ones in cells of living organisms.
The dimensions of area or surface space occupied by a form on a horizontal plane.
In Indian architecture, six divisions: base, wall, entablature, vertical recess, cupola, finial.

In Indian art and architecture, the measurement of the length of the body, including vertical measurements such as the distance fro mthe hair-limit to the eye-line, from that point to the tip of the nose, the length of the arms and of the legs and so on. These measurements constitute the six kinds of iconometric measurements as applied to standing, seated an reclining images.
Sets of vessels for serving drinking water, usually consisting of a pitcher and matching drinking vessels and sometimes a tray.

Refers to the state or quality of having little or no affinity for water, especially on the molecular level. To describe materials or articles having surfaces resistant, but not impervious, to water, use "water-repellent." To describe materials or surfaces impervious to water, use 'waterproof' (ALT of "waterproofing").
An English variation of the Lutma frame, but having more pronounced ornamentation; named for Althorp Lord Sunderland.
Exceptionally long metal trumpetlike aerophones of West Africa, of conical bore and made in two sections, used in ceremonial music and usually associated with kings and emirs.
Zitherlike chordophones having a long rectangular soundboard or tube resonator with a slightly arched surface and usually, though not always, movable bridges, played by plucking with the fingers.
Dolls with mechanical movements.
Plucked, long necked chordophones of Bengal and other Indian states. They are fretless, made of wood, and generally four-stringed.

Short-necked, fretless lutelike chordophones of the Arab world, the direct ancestors of European lutes, strung in double courses and played with a plectrum. The large soundbox is built of ribs of lightweight wood with a strongly rounded back and flat belly, one large or two or three small sound holes, a bridge on the lower part of the belly, and a piece of fishskin, leather, or shell above the bridge to protect the belly from the strokes of the plectrum.

Throwing weapons consisting basically of a strap of leather, fabric, or similar flexible material, widening into a pouch at the center to hold the projectile. They are held by the two ends and swung round rapidly, then one end is released to hurl the projectile.
Trick-taking card game developed in England, which is seen as a early form of bridge, only without bidding.
Board game in which a leader draws numbered disks at random and the players cover the corresponding numbers on pre-printed cards, the winner being the first to cover a complete row.
Books, usually for children, having mechanisms that move, or are moved by the reader.
Signs or notices, usually of stiff paper or cardboard, posted in public or carried in public, for example by picketers or demonstrators.
The ratio of the volume of the interstices of a material to the volume of its mass.
Close-fitting suits made of a material, such as sponge rubber, that water will go through but that retains body heat; worn by a water skier or diver, especially in cold water.
Dresses of intermediate length. They are longer than mini dresses but shorter than maxi dresses, usually extending to mid-calf.
Dresses with an abbreviated bodice usually exposing the shoulders, arms, and back.
Wagons with closed bodies of medium height mounted on platform springs and outfitted with numerous shelves or compartments for carrying the wares of traveling merchants.

Colorant made from kermesic acid that is extracted from the dried bodies of female kermes insects. Kermes dye was used since ancient times. It contains 18-32% tannins and is used for making a dark color leather.
Colorless liquid polymer used as a a water-repellent synthetic resin varnish and barrier coating.

Material objects contrived for amusement rather than for practical use by children or pets, or intended as collectibles by adults. Toys are generally miniature versions of real beings or objects that lend themselves to imaginative or imitative play. Toys may also be items for use in games. Among the earliest toys were dolls and balls.

Ceremonial weapons of the Fon people of Dahomey, generally in the shape of an axe or crooked club with a sculpted wooden handle, and, in those of axe shape, an elaborately carved metal or wooden head. They serve as symbols of power, either of the gods of Dahomey or of its king, and are used in various secular and religious ceremonial contexts.
Expressions of words with letters, in wrting or verbally.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Sudan.
In Roman masonry, a wall-facing technique using fragments of broken tile embedded in concrete.
Book cloth grain pattern imitating the appearance of a dotted line.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the lagoon region of Côte d'Ivoire.
Hairstyles in which long hair is gathered and wound into a knob of hair on the crown of the head.

Leather finished by buffing on an emery wheel, usually on the flesh side to produce a napped surface.   Distinct from "rough calf" which is always finished on the flesh side and not polished with an emery wheel.
Rags, typically soaked with olive oil, and used to remove surplus gold from surfaces of bookbindings after tooling.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name, a subgroup of the Mongo living in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in the Northwest Province of Cameroon, and seasonally in Nigeria.
Nationality, styles, and culture of the people of the nation of the République centrafricaine.
Businesses in the construction industry that undertake work as detailed in a legally binding contractual agreement.
Painters who use their mouths to manipulate brushes or other tools to make paintings, due to paralysis or other loss of the use of limbs or hands.
Masquerades of the Bini and Edo peoples of Benin in Africa, referring to the creation of the Benin royal dynasty by the mythical king Oranmiyan.

Any liquid that may be ingested for assuaging thirst, or as nourishment. For prepared or flavored liquids drunk as refreshment, or for pleasure, including alcoholic drinks, but excluding plain water, use 'beverages,' though these concepts overlap in meaning and usage.
Staffs, often having a hook at one end, for managing sheep, goats, and herds of other relatively small livestock.
Long leather reins attached to a bit on both sides, used by drivers to lead their horse drawing a cart or wagon and keep the pace under control.
Metal, wooden, or leather devices with a flat foot rest and bow-shaped section attached to the saddle by a stirrup strap, used to support the rider's feet.

Works of Japanese verse consisting of thirty-one syllables, the first and third lines containing five and the other three lines seven syllables. The tanka has historically been the basic form of Japanese poetry.
Parts of a human's or animal's body enclosed by the ribs and breast bone, forming the upper part of the trunk, and containing the heart and lungs.

Devices incorporated in special looms to control individual warp yarns via a system of punched cards. This invention, by Joseph Marie Jacquard, and first demonstrated in 1801, enabled looms to produce fabrics with complex patterns and images such as tapestry, brocade, damask, and matelasse.
Vigils held over the dead prior to burial, often accompanied by festivities.
Elements or components that raise a stove from the surface of a floor.

Widely distributed, aquatic, invertebrate animals whose members form colonies composed of numerous units called "zooids," hence the term Polyzoa or "many animals." They inhabit both fresh and marine waters. Until the mid-18th century, bryozoans, like corals, were regarded as plants and were referred to "moss animals." Seventy-five years later, the bryozoans were distinguished from the cnidarians, and the characteristic structure of the zooid was first described.
Cases for holding sewing needles.

Flat, solid, and relatively thin durable items of various materials, generally used for roofing, flooring, or wall and ceiling covering; often rectangular or squarish in shape. For fired clay materials of varying shapes and thicknesses and with various uses in addition to covering, prefer "ceramic tile." For visual works, such as painting or sculpture, on a tile support, use "tiles (visual works)"; for visual work compositions comprising multiple tiles, use "tile work (visual works)."
Implements used in the harvesting of onions.
Medical or surgical instruments used to dilate or distend an opening, passage, or organ of the body.

Hydrostatic devices, comprising iron plates and a pressing board, used to give woolen and worsted cloth a smooth and lustrous finish. Once arranged in regular folds on the device's pressing board, the cloth is sandwiched between hot plates with applied pressure until the plates cool. Cold iron or hollow plates are used in conjuction with the hot plates to moderate the temperature and prevent the heat from scorching the cloth.
A primary combination of arsenic with another element, for example hydrogen or a metal, or an organic radical.

Style of textiles, particularly a variety of sophisticated, finely-woven Persian rugs, made by Kurds in and around the city of Sanandaj (formerly usually spelled Sehna), Iran. The Sehna pile rugs and kilims are prized for their delicate pattern, coloring, and fine weave. The designs usually use a repeat pattern (diaper) such as the herati, in which a diamond lattice pattern peeps through a tangle of blossoms and leaves or through intricate versions of the boteh, a leaf with curling tip. The entire field may show such a pattern, or a medallion scheme may introduce a hexagonal centerpiece and straight-arched ends. The borders are full of fine detail, often featuring paired arabesques known in the trade as "turtles." The finely woven Sehna kilims are slit tapestries of the highest quality. Their small-scale borders are carried around the ends, as they are typically in pile carpets but rarely in such weavings. Sehna also manufactured saddle cloths, those in pile usually provided with a two-slope arch. Although the town of Sehna has given its name to the asymmetrical Persian knot (see "asymmetrical knots"), it is the Turkish, or symmetrical, knot, that is actually used there.
Textile weaving technique with an added weft system of which the threads run the whole length or width of the fabric, forming a pattern of simple, small decorations such as flowers or dots.
Parts or components of ammunition.
Arrangements and installation systems of lighting devices for particular effects.
Translation of data from one particular arrangement of data or characters to another.

Style of textiles, particularly handwoven floor coverings, usually in a prayer design and made in Kırşehir, a town between Ankara and Kayseri in central Turkey. The typical Kirsehir prayer rug of the 19th century has an elaborately stepped arch above a prayer-niche design, often  fringed with tiny carnations in profile and with a smaller, concentric niche similarly outlined but having a contrasting color. The color scheme mya include rich cherry red, yellow, violet, light blue, prominent greens, terra-cotta, and black-brown. Some of the later rugs show influence of the French Empire style, and the palette was altered by the use of harsher aniline dyes.
Exercising physical force on a body or thing to move it by force.

An ancient fabric creation technique that predates knitting and crochet; it involves braiding parallel threads with fixed threads on a frame. The term refers as well to the net-like fabric so produced. Sprang headgear, belts, and other artifacts dating from Bronze age onward have been found at archaeological sites in Scandinavia, Europe and Egypt.

Refers to a collection of prehistoric objects or implements of approximately the same age or era found at one or several related archaeological sites and used as evidence of the origin of the technique that was used to create similar objects.  For the style and technique used to produce the implements, use "industry (technique)."
The metal interior of a coin. Especially in clad coins, the core is usually made of a lower-value metal (copper or bronze) covered by a higher-value metal (gold or silver).

The process of rolling and shaping a gather of molten glass on a marver in order to make it symmetrical, to center it on the blowpipe or pontil, or to imbed applied threads into the surface as decoration.
Clothing meant for travelling. Particularly in reference to clothing from the 19th century onwards; the clothing typically reflects what is suitable for a particular means of transportation.
Openwork guards, most often of leather or metal, placed over the snouts of animals, usually dogs, to prevent them from opening their mouths, biting, or eating.
Ordained, professional Christian clergy who conduct worship, administer the sacraments, preach, and assume responsibility for the pastoral care of a given congregation or parish.
Equipment of various kinds intended for use by one person, including but not limited to equipment for the safety and comfort of the person.

Commissioned military officers ranking above brigadier generals and below lieutenant generals. Major generals command military units called divisions, which are made up of 7,000-22,000 troops, and their insignia are two stars.
Any of various pins, clasps, rollers, or appliances on which locks of hair are wound or clamped for curling.
Small spoons, made of silver, bone, ivory, or wood, used to bring snuff from a container to the nose, or from a larger container to a smaller.
Those who ride horses in races.
Places or districts under the jurisdiction of bailiffs.
In cement masonry flatwork, the wood or metal straightedges used to strike off or level newly placed concrete.
Libraries responsible for films and other moving image materials, including stock footage, films, film clips and/or videotapes; some may include microfilm as well.
Museums administered by a historical society, which is a group formed to study and disseminate information about the history of a place, usually a town, city, county, or state.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of red colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blackish colors.
A range of colors resembling variations of yellow and green pigments.
A range of colors resembling variations of orange pigment.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink and whitish colors.

Unique assets, comprised of a collection of metadata defining a digital object verified within a blockchain that certifies that these are unique and not interchangeable, and which provides a means of sale, authentication, and provenance. NFTs may be bought and sold, but have no tangible form of their own, and point to digital content such as photos, video, audio, games, or any other media that is storable digitally. Even though the content may be available freely in infinite duplicate, an NFT guarantees ownership of the work, but not necessarily copyright of the content.

A range of bright greenish yellow colors resembling the color of chartreuse, a distilled French liqueur flavored with herbs, named after the Grande Chartreuse monastery located in the Chartreuse Mountains.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of gray colors.
ASTM Standard name for a range of blue colors with greenish overtones.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
A range of reddish brown colors resembling the color of the pigment, iron oxide red.
Refers to a range of dark green colors resembling either the colors of the leaves of the hemlock plant, a poisonous herb of the carrot family.
Various tones of pinkish yellow, referring to the color of the stain of the juice of the fruit of the peach, a low spreading tree of the rose family that is widely cultivated.
A range of bluish or reddish purple colors resembling the color of skin of the ripe fruit of the plum tree.
Variable red colors resembling the color of geranium red pigment, a synthetic organic pigment made from the deposition of eosin on a alumina trihydrate base.

Family containing around 30,000 species of beetles characterized as being stout-bodied, having bright metallic colors, clubbed antennae, and front legs are broad and adapted for digging. The family includes the scarab, species Scarabaeus sacer, considered sacred in ancient Egypt.

A style that belongs to or resembles a style or fashion of an earlier time. The term refers not to an absolute time frame, but is relative to the period being discussed, not to the present. For example, a style popular in 1710 may in 2010 be said to have been "old fashioned" in 1750. "Old fashioned" differs from "retro" in implying that a style or object is antiquated, outdated, and sometimes unfashionable in form or character, while "retro" implies reference to a previous style (usually from the mid-20th century) that is still considered desirable and popular for its nostalgic value.
Refers to various blue colors resembling those made with cerulean blue pigment, especially the color of a cloudless sky or a pure deep blue.
General term referring to unrelated brownish birds with red breasts, one a thrush, the American robin (Turdus migratorius), and the other a flycatcher, the European robin (Erithacus rubecula).

Superfamily containing five families of primates that are found in the tropical regions of Mexico, Central and South America: Callitrichidae, Cebidae, Aotidae, Pitheciidae, and Atelidae. About 40 million years ago, the Simiiformes infraorder split into the parvorders Platyrrhini (New World monkeys in South America) and Catarrhini (apes and Old World monkeys in Africa).

Family containing 18 species in six genera including includes the raccoons, coatis, kinkajous, olingos, ringtails, and cacomistles. Characterized by being  tree-climbing, omnivorous, having poorly developed carnassial teeth, and being closely related to bears.
Members of an order containing over 680,000 living species of insects that develop wings inside the body and undergo an elaborate metamorphosis involving a pupal stage.
Order containing over 300 species in one family of fast-flying birds with pointed wings and weak bills, feeding on seeds and fruit.
Term introduced in the 19th century for any Windsor chair, with or without arms, of a square or nearly square back.
Strong short-bladed knives for opening the shells of oysters.
Crowning, altar-like superstructures railing the summit of a stupa's cupola, and enclosing the pole representing the world axis.
In Indian architecture, an adhiṣṭhāna-type; flower band (decorative pattern).

General term for bodies in space that are low enough in mass so that they do not generate nuclear energy in their interior (as a star), and are large enough so their shape is primarily determined by gravity. Examples would be planets, moons, asteroids, and satellites in the outer solar system.

In the context of modern western personal names, the names that are hereditary and common to all members of a family, placed at the end of a string of names for an individual; used with a first name to distinguish an individual from others with the same first name. In other cultural traditions, last names may not be hereditary family names or they may not be used at all. Before last names became common in western tradition, personal names were qualified with the addition of epithets, place names, ancestors' names, or terms for professions; these were added to a first name on an individual basis, not necesssarily hereditary for a family.
Institutions or companies that teach dance in a school setting.
Craters, usually measuring kilometers across, formed by the collapse of a volcanic mountain.

Class of air-breathing vertebrate animals characterized by being tetrapods (although some, such as snakes, have evolved modified skeletons), cold-blooded, having an ossified skeleton, usually having scales or horny plates covering their body, and laying eggs with embryos surrounded by an amniotic membrane. Living reptiles include over 8,700 species of turtles, tuataras, lizards and snakes, and crocodiles. Birds (class Aves) share a common ancestor with crocodiles, thus some classifications would group them as technically one lineage with reptiles; more commonly, but they are treated separately. Excluding birds, there are over 8,700 species of living reptiles.
Chinese bronze ritual vessel type used for holding wine.
Extinct subclass of mammal-like reptile characterized by a lateral temporal opening.
Hybrid offspring between a female ass and a male horse; mules, the offspring of a male ass and a female horse, are larger.
An abbreviation of "file transfer protocol:" a standard for the transfer of electronic files between two computers, especially via the Internet.
Designates inlets of the sea that are long, deep, and narrow and have steep walls; usually formed by glacial erosion.
Paper size, generally used in Great Britain, measuring 18 1/2 by 14 1/2 inches.

Order containing 115 or more species in 10 families and a number of extinct species. Distinguished by a pair of large procumbent incisors on the lower jaw (diprotodont) paired with typically three pair of upper incisors and no lower canines, and the fusing of the second and third digits of the foot up to the base of the claws which leaves the claws themselves separate (syndactyly) and with the fifth digit usually absent and a greatly enlarged fourth digit.
Genus of one 1 species of dog-like canid of South America.
Genus of one South American species.
Series of proofs showing the image development of the finished print. Each printing element is shown singly in black, regardless of their color in the edition.
Salt used as a medium of exchange, in the shape of bars, blocks, cones, or in bags.

Marbled paper usually prepared with five colors and then drawn with a rake or comb, and later drawn again with a fine wire comb. This produces a scalloped pattern. Dutch marbled paper is a variant of nonpareil marbled paper, with a slightly different color scheme.

Book format where a sheet is folded to form 48 leaves or 96 pages. It is formed by folding a sheet five times to form 32 leaves, and then a half sheet is folded to form 16 leaves, which is inserted into the former.
Needlework done in white on a white ground.

A festival celebrated on January 6 that is one of the three main and oldest festivals of the Christian Church (the other two being Christmas and Easter). The festival originated in the East where it originally celebrated both the birth and baptism of Jesus Christ. Since the 4th century when December 25 became the date of Christmas, the festival in the East has remained the celebration of the manifestation of Christ's divinity at his baptism. The festival spread to the West in the 4th century where it became more associated with visit of the Magi to the infant Christ and specifically the manifestation of Christ to the Gentiles in the form of the Magi. The festival also commemorates Christ's first miracle at Cana in Galilee. Gifts are exchanged on Epiphany instead of Christmas in some countries. The eve of Epiphany is called Twelfth Night in the West.

Concept of state of deep inner freedom and peace, the supreme goal of Hinduism and Buddhism. Reaching nirvana means liberation from samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. In Buddhism, nirvana represents freedom from attachments and individual consciousness and the attainment of tranquility and purity. Nirvana is conceived somewhat differently within the various schools of Buddhism. In Hinduism it furthermore means that union with God or the Absolute is possible.

Stitches commonly used in Native North American beadwork. Formed by stringing successive rows of beads one at a time, usually around another object such as a fan or gourd rattle. Often used on beadwork for fans and rattles used in Native American Church ceremonies.
In Indian architecture, a lathe-turned bed-stead like round-shafted pillar; Rudrakānta or Īśakānta (Karṇāṭan version); lathe-turned column with inverted pot member (of Karṇāṭa temples).
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name currently inhabiting Sierra Leone.
In Indian architecture, a open/semi-open type of pillared hall/colonnaded hall; raṅgamaṇḍapa; assembly hall; audience hall, pilgrims’ hall.
Having the form or outline of a polygon with three sides and three angles.
Flat, two-dimensional shape that is situated in or forming a plane or parallel planes.
Documentaries or other forms of film that profile an individual or individuals.
A pre-tanning process of loosening the hair on skin or hides prior to depilation by placing them in a warm environment and allowing controlled putrefaction to occur.
Digital currencies operating independently of central banks, using encryption techniques to regulate the generation of units of currency and verify the transfer of funds.
Refers to the variety of Spanish spoken in Honduras.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 400-421; founded by the Xiongnu Juqu family.
The name by which an individual person is identified or known, as distingushed from names for corporate bodies or other entities.

Nahua "toe" or "claw" military insignia rendered as an elongated droplet-like shape and topped by a feather crest, usually of quetzal feathers. Worn on a back frame, it was manufactured in yellow, green, and red varieties and paired with a feathered bodysuits of the same color. It was given to high-ranking warriors and as a tribute item in the postclassic period across central Mexico.

The tenth month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendar, containing 31 days and falling between September and November. Its name is derived from octo, Latin for “eight,” an indication of its position in the early Roman calendar.

Ancient Egyptian calendar having a year of 365 days and 12 months of 30 days each, plus five extra days at the end of the year. The months were divided into three decans of ten days each. The Egyptians may have used an earlier luni-solar calendar.
Implements like vises, used to hold pieces of leather together while they are being stitched.
In Japanese printing, a large sheet of paper that is half of ō-ōban, around 53 x 39 cm.
That which is placed in position number ten of a sequence.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 499 to 400 (or 500 to 401) Before Common Era.

Dances of a particular type from the Republic of Congo and nearby areas, probably originally associated with initiation rites. Today the dance has become popularized and secularized, forming part of the Congolese folkloric traditions and performed on state and other national festival occasions. The dancers wear or hold kebe-kebe masks or heads.
An alcoholic beverage of Spanish origin, composed of red wine diluted with fruit juice or various other ingredients; sweetened and served chilled.

Proprietary name for an analog videocassette format developed by Sony in 1969, using 3/4" tape with a running speed of 3.75 inches per second. The format was popular in semi-professional industrial, educational and broadcast contexts from the 1970s until the advent of digital video technology.
Language family containing two poorly documented indigenous South American languages, both of which are nearly extinct and appear to be only distantly related.

A language containing lexical and other features from two or more languages including English, characterized by simplified grammar and a smaller vocabulary than the languages from which it is derived.

Languages that were once spoken in the Apennine Peninsula (modern Italy) and in the eastern part of the Po valley. The principal language of the Italic group is Latin, originally the speech of the city of Rome and the ancestor of the modern Romance languages: Italian, Romanian, Spanish, Portuguese, French, and so on. The earliest Latin inscriptions apparently date from the 6th century BCE, with literature beginning in the 3rd century BCE.

The condition or status of prohibiting access and being blocked. Typically relating to an object or environment that has both an open and closed state, such as a book, box, vessel, garment, gate, window, room, or the like.
Acoustic research instruments that focus the vibrations of a given sound wave onto a diaphragm from which they are transmitted graphically onto a moving film.
Narrow, steep-sided depressions located on the ocean floor.
Artists who make themselves available to be engaged for work on particular assignments or projects, rather than being engaged on a long-term or permanent basis by a single employer.

In a thersaurus, a sibling is a record that shares the same immediate broader context (one level higher) as other records. Siblings are subordinate to the same broader concept and are at the same hierarchical level.
Used to flag terms in a data base, data model, or data extraction where the term and associated qualifier (gloss) are expressed as a single unit, often with the qualifier in parentheses.
A type of pottery found in many parts of India which is black on the inside and around the rim and red on the exterior surface. Generally dated to the Chalcolithic through to the Iron Age.
Those who depict coats of arms in proper form and color.
Unrestrained desire, appetite, or inclination for something or someone, usually sexual, and contrary to a culture's moral sense.

Languages characterized by being distinct from any modern languages, even languages that are descended from it. For example, Old English and Middle English are distinct from modern English. A criterion is that the language has a literature that is treated distinctly by the scholarly community.
A boon-giving hand-gesture, representing bestowing of gifts. The hand is extended downward with the palm outward, as if offering something to a devotee; an object of offering may be held in the hand.
People who specialize in creating images of coats of arms.
Nationality or culture the Gascony historical region in southwestern France.
Describes the action of giving or supplying food to another. For the intake of food by oneself, use "eating," "drinking," "suckling," or another appropriate term.
The act of guiding the movement of a vehicle or animal.
In Indian architecture, a wide band or belt, projecting topmost band of adhiṣṭhāna.
A celestial minstrel In Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism, Gandharva is a class of celestial beings whose males are divine singers and females are divine dancers from Gandhara region.
Measurements of time equal to 1/60 part of a minute or 1/3600 part of an hour.

Historical unit of measurement in France and other places, prior to the adoption of the metric system in the late 18th century. Equal to 1/12 pouce, another historical French measurement. In modern systems, equal to 2.2558 mm or .0881 inch.
Genus containing one species of perennial herbaceous plant native to Europe and Asia.
Legendary one-eyed giants in ancient Greek mythology.

In botany, a stamen is the male or fertilizing organ of a flowering plant, consisting of two parts, the anther, which is a double-celled sac containing the pollen, and the filament, a slender footstalk supporting the anther.
Section of the poplar genus that includes the aspens and the white poplar, Populus alba.

A range of gesso products that is formulated with a combination of compressible, chemically inert fine grained mineral powder, a pH buffer, oxidation inhibitors, UV stabilizers, and BEVA resins. In conservation, it has been used as a filler.
Genus containing around 20 species of small understory trees native to the tropical forests of Central and South America.

Species of deciduous, fruit-bearing tree of North America, found in forest areas from Ontario to Florida and from the Dakotas to Texas. Valued for dense, close-grain wood and its gum, a water-soluble carbohydrate that has been used as a medium for watercolor paints.

Species of medium sized oak tree growing to 20 meters in height, native primarily to the Midwestern and southern United States, typically growing in uplands with good drainage, but occasionally at lowland streams. Its leaves are shaped like laurel leaves. The fruit is an acorn that is an important food source for squirrels and birds. The common names comes from its use in making making shingles and clapboard siding for houses.
Genus containing one species of giant sequoia.

Genus containing 7 to 20 species that are often cultivated to produce an edible starchy cereal grain. It is generally an annual plant, but in tropical areas it can survive as a perennial. Many cultures have evidence of early rice cultivation, including China, India, and the civilizations of Southeast Asia. However, the earliest archaeological evidence comes from central and eastern China and dates to 7000-5000 BCE. With the exception of the type called upland rice, the plant is grown on submerged land. Seedlings are transplanted to a submerged field or paddy for the growing season. The most common species used for food in the modern world is Oryza sativa.

A generally gray cloud layer with a uniform base which may, if thick enough, produce drizzle, ice prisms, or snow grains. When the sun is visible through this cloud, its outline is clearly discernible.
In the Roman religion, numerous tutelary deities of cultivated fields and of households.
Genus of legume in the Fabaceae family. Wood of any of several species of the Centrolobium genus.
Studios in which one or more master printmakers create works, supervise assistants, and instruct pupils.
Trademarked name for group of alcohol ethoxylate nonionic surfactants.
Prisons administered by the state, particularly a state in the U.S.
General name for any of several species of green alder that grow in North America.
The apparent descent of the sun below the horizon, signaling the closing of the day.
Species of pine tree native to the southeastern U.S., growing to 30 m (95 feet) in height. It is named "slash pine" is named for its habitat of swampy overgrown land, called "slashes."
Computer software stored on a server and typically accessible via a web browser.

Formally structured organizations, establishments, or associations primarily involved with education, which is the imparting of knowledge, attitudes, skills, or socially valued qualities of character or behavior.
Mesh made from knotted material, hung between posts or from a frame. Made for playgrounds or other recreational areas, allowing users to climb from one area to another.
Devices used to drive points into wood frames for mounting glass in windows or for framing fine art.

Tubular strip of textile, usually bias-cut, which may or may not enclose a cord, used for trimming the edges and seams of costume, coverings, and hangings. May be of matching or contrasting fabric, sometimes also in leather.
Describes the physical location where a work was prepared, printed, or otherwise made available for distribution.
Terms that have been manually validated and inserted into a term bank or thesaurus, for the purpose of controlled indexing.
Lidded containers made to store wigs when not in use. Some examples are cylindrical to accommodate wigs and wig forms, while others are rectangular.
Objects used to hold needles for security or storage, often made of textile or leather. For cases used to store needles, often made of bone or metal, use "needle cases."
Passive devices used in photographic studios to control and direct light through reflection. These often incorporate adjustable screens and some kind of moveable support or stand.

Devices designed to support a skein of yarn while it is being unwound during use and/or wound into a ball for future use. These devices traditionally comprised a circular board nailed to a piece of oak to be handled manually, but are now electric and equipped with automated pre-selection counters for setting the desired yarn length.

Mechanized devices designed to perforate the punch cards used in Jacquard looms to facilitate the automatic weaving of specified patterns and designs in cloth. Each row of perforated holes in the punch cards corresponds to a row of textile pattern used to control the weaving process. These devices, along with the Jacquard loom's punch-card technology, influenced the development of modern computer programming.

Mechanized devices designed to measure the variations in a sliver's mass by compressing the sliver through a pair of rollers. In measuring the sliver's mass, these devices are built to analyze the degree of evenness characterizing a sliver's structure.

Protective screens made of woven or linked metal or other nonflammable material, placed in front of fireplace openings to prevent logs, sparks, or embers from escaping. For furniture used to protect occupants of the room from the full heat of the fire, use "fire screens (furniture)."
Metal hangers with slender arms on which skewers for cooking may be hung.
Kitchen utensils used for crushing food by pressure.
Devices that extract honey from honeycomb, usually by centrifugal action.
Small bags or packets, especially small bags containing a perfumed powder that is used to scent costume as in drawers, closets, or trunks.
Flat templates, usually made of transparent plastic, in the shape of a triangle, cut into specific angles, most commonly with 90 and 45 degree angles.
Containers for holding liquid dairy products.
Bookbinding machines equipped with blades used to create round corners to the edges of books.
Collections of objects that together form the means of performing chemical tests. Inclusive of the equipment and the container in which it is kept.
Cutting tools that consist of a relatively heavy edged, squarish head fixed to a handle that are intended for the slaughtering of animals for their meat.
Order of flowering plants including citrus, maples, horse chestnuts, lychees and rambutans, mangos and cashew, frankincense and myrrh, mahogany and neem.
Toys with which children can play hopscotch. Sets can include tiles and a marker.
Cups in which dental compounds are mixed.
Components of a loom, comprising sticks inserted close to the heddle rod of a frame loom. By pushing down or pulling up on the shed stick, the weaver forms a countershed.
The performing art of puppet shows or other performing with puppets, which are representations of figures, animated by strings, by hands inside the figure, or another manual method.
Refers to the property having been collected at an archeological site or other site.

Superintending or managing the collections, exhibitions, research activities, and personnel of a museum, art gallery, zoo, or other place of exhibit; also, the superintending or managing of a single collection or subject of study in such an institution.
The status or condition of property having been obtained by theft.
Meaning "drew [it]," in painting and other art works, indicates the one who designed the work; may refer to the design of figures, but not necessarily so.
