For art cataloging, titles or names by which the work has been known in exhibitions, particularly when different from titles by which the work is normally known. This term does not refer to the names of exhibitions themselves.

Chapels or other room-like spaces, or small freestanding structures, adjacent to or near the tomb in a funerary site. Examples date from ancient Egypt, where offering niches developed over time into rooms, where families of the dead could visit on appropriate days of the year, to eat meals or make offerings in accordance with Egyptian funerary cults. For chapels that hold the remains of the dead, use "sepulchral chapels."
Subsidiary chapels opening off the transept of a cruciform-plan church.

A gem cut named for its creator, Vincenzio Peruzzi, a 17th century Venetian lapidary. He applied a brilliant form of cutting, i.e. with 56 facets, a table and a culet. It was seen as an improvement over the earlier Mazarin cut.

Mayasvi involves a number of rituals: welcoming the gods, homage to solidarity, bidding farewell to the gods, a procession in the streets to pray for safe travels and family worship. The date of Mayasvi is not set in stone; on the contrary, whether the Mayasvi is to be held is decided by the incumbent chief of hosa judging from the current circumstances. Occasions in favor of having a Mayasvi include: relief efforts after a major epidemic or battle involving injury and death in order to fend off misfortune, foreigners and noxious spirits; celebrations for warriors returning from headhunting or battles in honor of their valor; a renovation project for the kuba is proposed to ensure the good fortune of the tribe and the Tsou compatriots. Moreover, male babies are brought to Mayasvi to make their debut in the kuba; rites will be conducted for lads coming of age during Mayasvi as well. The most important message of Mayasvi is not only to inspire patriotism so that the Tsou people will protect the whole tribe on their lives and soul and pray for the favor of war god, but also to unify the social, ethical protocols and augment general morale.
The tenth month of the French revolutionary calendar (introduced in 1793), lasting from 19 June to 18 July.

Cultures and styles of the Saisiyat people lived in Taiwan. The Saisiyat people primarily live in Wufeng Township, Hsinchu County; Nanzuang Township and Shitan Township, Miaoli County. The Saisiyat society is composed of patriarchy and clans bearing different sinraehoe’ (“family names”). These clans form into different sets of Pas-vakean as the basic religious unit with which the traditional Saisiyat rituals proceed. The Saisiyat culture is famous for Pas-taai (“Ritual to the Short People”).
Having chracteristics, qualities, attributes, or actions associated with the male sex.
In Indian architecture, a siṁhavaktra; lion-head nasi-top.
In Indian architecture, a round column-type (South India); Īśakānta column.
Plates passed around a congregation to collect money or other offerings.
Small, freestanding structures either open or partially enclosed, where merchandise is displayed, advertised, or sold.
Rooms designed for or used to induce sweating by the occupants through the introduction of hot steam into the space, which is often located in a bath, spa, or gym.
In Indian architecture, a closed hall; entry hall.

Rooms in private houses or public establishments in which dinner and other principal meals are taken and which are furnished for this purpose. For particularly large rooms or separate structures for dining, prefer "dining halls."
Sitting rooms, sometimes reserved for women, used during the early part of the day; popular from the early 19th century to the early 20th century, especially in England.
In Indian architecture, a hall for theatrical purposes.
Rooms or closets where food is stored; originally storage spaces primarily used for meat, particularly bacon, from which the term is probably derived ("lard room").
In military architecture, projecting outworks forming a salient angle beyond the main ditch and in front of the curtain wall.
Recesses with tomb chests, usually placed in the north wall of a chancel, to hold the reserved consecrated wafers and sometimes a cross or effigy of Christ.
Turn-outs along roadways used as public rest stops; often having shade trees or shelters, toilets, picnic tables, and trash cans.
Passageways constructed to control drafts in and carry away products of combustion from fireplaces and furnaces.
Booths, stalls, rooms, houses, or small buildings for the retail sale of merchandise or services. Originally referred to spaces where the goods were made or prepared for sale and also sold.
In Indian architecture, a shoulder moulding; flat upper platform/terminal cyma moulding of śikhara; visama/bisama, kāndhi (Oriyā).
In Indian architecture, a broad band.
Projecting moldings carried over door and window openings, sometimes to deflect rainwater from the openings; common in Medieval architecture. For rectangular hood moldings, use "labels (moldings)."
In Indian architecture, a cusped and downward projecting miniature pendentive or recessed cusp (ceiling ornament), whose series is often arranged around the central lambana.
Openings located in fortresses or fortified structures.
The visible bordering elements around a central piece, such as a door, window, or other opening.
Window or door shutters having panels rather than louvers set into a frame.
Series of steps or stairways having stone as the primary material.
Moldings carved to resemble leaves separated by darts.
In Indian architecture, framing split pilasters, paired pilasters, dwarf niche-pilasters.
Refers to the central uprights placed in the center of large doorways to support the lintel.
In Indian architecture, a door with three jambs.
Pairs of tall casement windows closing against each other with no frame between them, allowing access to the outside or to another room. For single tall window-like doors, use "French doors."
In Indian architecture, a half-leaning spire in Anēkāṇḍaka śikhara.

Freestanding exterior walls that curve back and forth regularly along their length. Typically made of brick, the zig-zag or serpentine configuration does not have buttresses, thus differing from the superficially similar "garland wall"; the strength of the serpentine walls derives from the wavy configuration, allowing them to be only one brick thick. This Dutch form was introduced in Britain in the 17th cedntury when Dutch engineers drained the fen country; it was taken up elsewhere in Europe and North America. Often used to enclose gardens.

Walls specially constructed to have a high capacity for collecting and storing heat or cold and then slowly releasing the stored energy through convection into a building space; usually designed as part of a passive solar system.

Barriers that surround a camp or settlement, or reinforce a defensive wall. They are typically composed of strong branches of trees placed upon a rampart, or they are made of a palisaded bank or mound, or a rampart of earth, sod, or stones.

In Indian architecture, a wall projecting in front of the sanctum framing; walls enclosing a vestibule in front of the sanctum, sometimes connecting the prāsāda to a portico or maṇḍapa; gainthiāla (Oriyā); junction wall encompassing antarāla-vestibule between vimāna and the hall; exterior walls of antarāla.
Courses of brick or tile built into masonry walls for bonding and leveling purposes.

Stories in basilican church interiors that correspond to the level between the vaulting and the aisle roof, or the vaulting of the tribune and the tribune roof; may or may not contain a small passage. Distinct from "tribunes (stories)," which always have substantial passages.
In Indian architecture, a niche; also equivalent to sālā.
Barriers which rotate on an axis and are usually so arranged as to allow the passage of a person through an opening only in one direction, one person at a time.
In Indian architecture, a grille made up of pillarettes.
Ceiling-area lighting systems comprising a continuous surface of transmitting material with light sources mounted above it.
Roof systems that have a number of parallel roof surfaces of triangular section with a profile similar to the teeth in a saw; usually the steeper side is glazed.
In Indian architecture, a tier resembling pent-roof; roof-tier somewhat resembling a spade-shape; pent-roof variety (of chādya-cornice or a constituent of a tiered roof).
Devices used to prevent snow from sliding off a roof. Devices used to prevent snow from sliding off a roof.
Gables having a triangular form with a rectangular protrusion at the apex; so-named because the form resembles a cross-section of an inverted funnel or spout.

Domes consisting of an irregular triangular mesh of hinged bars, as introduced by Schwedler in Berlin in 1863. Domes consisting of an irregular triangular mesh of hinged bars, as introduced by Schwedler in Berlin in 1863.
Columns of the Doric architectural order, having no bases and relatively simple capitals.
In Indian architecture, a vase, pot; temple-type discussed in Bṛhatsaṁhitā and other śilpa texts; cushion-shaped pillar-part (above laśuna) in a Dravidian column.
Durable coverings laid down to form the surface of a road or other outdoor area; by extension, hard floor coverings in large interiors, such as public halls or churches.
Districts encompassing tin mines and tin works, and governed by special laws in historical Britain.
Settlement areas characterized by country life or agriculture.
Refers to open spaces, buildings, or other structures that are of historic or environmental significance and threatened with development or demolition.
Arches in which the impost on one side is higher than the impost on the other.
Buildings or complexes providing housing and related facilities.
Farms or areas of forest used to raise trees, typically managed in a way that ensures the regular production of trees to replace those extracted for timber or other purposes.
Mines used to extract minerals from stream bed deposits.
Various types of paths or tracks worn by the passage of persons or animals travelling in a wilderness area, or deliberately maintained for passage through various outdoor environments.
Use only for dervish monasteries; for rest houses for Islamic pilgrims, use "hospices."
A vitrified brick, especially suitable for use in pavements where resistance to abrasion is important.

A name given to a type of glass developed in 1864 by William Leighton as a substitute for lead glass in making inexpensive bottles. Calcined limestone, or lime, is used to produce a glass whose advantages are that it is inexpensive, lightweight, cools quickly, and is less resonant.

An element with atomic number 35 and symbol Br belonging to the halogen family. It is the only nometallic element that is liquid at room temperature. Bromine is extracted from sea water by reaction with chlorine and is used in dyes, fumigants, and other applications.
Mixture of water, hydraulic cement, aggregate, and a monomer or polymer; polymerized in place when a monomer is used.
Bricks which can be laid to modular dimensions; bricks sized so that the brick plus the mortar joint will form a 4, 8 or 12 inch increment, or module.
Triangle-shaped figures formed of three interlaced arcs or loops.
In Indian architecture, a wish-fulfilling vine; kāmalatā; kalpalatā.

Zodiac symbol of a bull, roughly based on the constellation of the same name. The zodiak signs have survived from classical Greek and Roman decoration, were popular in Northern European Romanesque and Gothic churches, and often found in Medieval psalters and books of hours symbolizing each month in which the sun enters the related constellation. They have also been used as decoration on ceilings, maps, timepieces, and astronomical instruments.

Crosses having two crossbars, either of the same size or with a lower one of longer length. In the version with a shorter one crossing above the center and a longer one below the center, the cross often signifies the Free French during WW II. In the version where both crossbars are of the same length, the cross denotes the rank of cardinal in the Roman Catholic church, or the Duke of Lorraine.
Small divisions of land in Ireland and parts of Scotland; the system is of Gaelic origin. A townland typically covers a few hundred acres.
Sites known by archaeological evidence of hominind activity, but not known to be a settled community. Distinguished from "inhabited places," which are known to be communities.
Motif of wheels, circles or discs represented in Buddhist art as the wheel of the law; and in Hindu art as a symbol of dharma, the circles of existence.
Buildings designed to be built or located mostly or totally under the surface of a lake, river, sea, or ocean.

Built works that have been damaged, lost, or destroyed, then built or heavily restored at a later time according to the same design, usually but not always on the original site. Includes built works that have been physically reconstructed, as well as the subject matter of drawings, models, or other media illustrating a surmised reconstruction.
Denotes generally hilly gardens buttressed by or built up of cut blocks of peat with terraces for plantings.

Gardens, whether public or private, intended for enjoyment and amusement. Pleasure gardens may focus on flowers, shrubs, vegetables, and fruit trees, together with pedestrian paths, water features, mazes, vistas, etc.; typically enclosed by a wall or hedge. For larger areas having a similar purpose but without an enclosing wall and including woods, use "pleasure parks." Later pleasure gardens were sometimes open to the public and charged a fee for admittance.
Generally refers to parks that are smaller than national parks and providing a wide range of recreation facilities with less emphasis on the landscape value of the area.
Minor roads of a class and condition lower than that of main roads.

Denotes generally enclosed and climate-controlled pedestrian walkways or networks of them consisting of bridgelike structures over streets, second-story corridors within buildings, and various activity hubs connecting retail and service establishments, usually in a downtown area; for the individual bridgelike structures over streets, use "skybridges."
Enclosed open spaces in front of and preceding the entry to European churches.
Rooms, buildings, or groups of buildings where tests and studies are done in the area of medicine or on specimens from patients at medical facilities.
Storage facilities specifically built to house vehicles.
Stations or inns located on a stage route that provide change of horses for couriers and provisions for passengers.
Foot bridges comprising a series of stones across a shallow body of water, swamp, or other area.
Buildings designed to be movable rather than permanently located.
Buildings for gatherings of a Sufi brotherhood, to serve as places for spiritual retreat, and as hospices.
In Byzantine or Greek Orthodox monasteries, principle churches with a baptistry.
Structures forming the heart of a shrine complex, connected to the rest of the shrine although raised on a higher level; protected from public access, sacred spaces where the deities reside.
In Indian architecture, a temple without ambulatory; without pradakṣiṇāpatha.
Hospitals where formal medical training takes place, usually affiliated with nursing or medical schools.
Places providing job training and vocational rehabilitation for the disadvantaged, whether due to physical handicap or lack of experience or education.
Spaces or structures with fountains embellished with statues, pools, or plants and used for relaxation.
Library buildings having collections focused on rare books, manuscripts, and the like.
Designates ancient Roman fortified frontier boundaries or defense zones.
Upright stone slabs, plain or decorated, used as commemorative markers.
Areas or structures where storm water runoff is captured.

Small buildings that house educational facilities, built in sparsely populated nonurban areas to provide public, usually elementary, education to local residents. Use when emphasizing the function or location of such buildings; when emphasizing the small size or form of some early examples, prefer "one-room schools."
Buildings that house Islamic theological or law schools, especially when associated with a mosque, or generally for places of study.
In Britain, buildings housing the class of schools founded in the 16th century or earlier for the teaching of Latin, later secondary schools.
Health care facilities providing uncomplicated medical and nursing care for residents or members of an institution or other facility.
Distinctly vertical dwellings, built for defensive purposes, usually of stone and with at least three to four stories.
Houses consisting of only a single room, or pen.
Houses of the Native Americans of the region of the Great Lakes and eastward having typically an arched top and consisting of a framework of poles overlaid with bark, rush mats, or hides.
Residences of heads of state or other public officials.
Residences built for or inhabited by royalty.
Multiple dwellings comprised of three housing units set one above the other; for dwellings having three housing units set side by side on one level, use "triplexes (multiple dwellings)."

Altars for which the mensa rests on a sarcophagus containing relics. These developed from the Early Christian practice of celebrating the Eucharist slabs placed directly on the tombs saints. The creation of sarcophagus altars flourished in the 16th-17th centuries.
Principal public administration buildings of towns and villages housing offices for transaction of government business and places for public assembly.
Mazes of interconnected underground rabbit burrows, including natural habitations for wild rabbits or habitations on a piece of land set aside by humans for rabbit breeding.
Facilities for meetings, study, or recreation, reserved for the faculty of an educational institution.
Restaurants, usually located below street level, patterned after basements or cellars in German city halls where wine and beer are sold.
Buildings housing retail businesses that include a pharmacy and often sell other articles, such as toilet requisites, stationery, magazines, newspapers, and light refreshments.
Buildings housing businesses that carry a deep assortment within a narrow line of goods, such as furniture stores, florists, sporting goods stores, and bookstores.
In Indian architecture, a rectangular vaulted roof without gables; rectangular, keel-roofed śikhara-type (without gable-ends).
General term for buildings in which fine arts instruction is carried out or in which fine arts are displayed; examples are found at universities or at a worlds fair.

Buildings, often partly or wholly underground, in which ice, often ice collected in winter, is stored for use throughout the year. Examples were specially insulated and ventilated agricultural buildings, increasingly popular after the mid-19th-century rise in dairy production, for the storing of ice blocks.
Spaces or rooms located in temples.
Subterranean rooms or entire stories in churches, often serving as places of burial.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living primarily in southwestern Chad, with smaller numbers in Cameroon.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting northern Nigeria.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Cameroon Grassfields.
Styles belonging to Upper Zambezi River region cultures.
Styles belonging to West Atlantic cultures.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in Senegal.
Refers to dipictions with a vantage point above the subject, such as from the ceiling of an interior, but not so high as in a bird's-eye view or an aerial view.

Likenesses, portraits, or images, especially sculptured or low relief representations, that stand for the person or animal represented. Examples are sculptures of deities and certain images of rulers on coins.

Style and culture of the great Songhai trading state of West Africa (flourished 15th-16th century), located on the Niger River in what is now central Mali, and eventually extending west to the Atlantic coast and east into Niger and Nigeria.

Refers to a finish applied to bronze by using heat and a combination of copper nitrate, ammonium chloride, iron nitrate, or other chemicals. Depending upon the combination of chemicals used, the effects are dark brown, blackish, greenish, bluish, or reddish.
Paint consisting of gypsum or whiting with some zinc oxide, with water as the vehicle and glue as the adhesion.
Paint containing either liquid crystals or leuco dyes which change color depending on the temperature of the surface to which they have been applied or the immediate atmosphere.
White, sweet tasting, crystalline alcohol found in berries, fruits, algae. This simple sugar is used as a humectant in conservation of leather, paper, vellum, and other materials.
Objects made of pewter, which is an alloy of tin and lead, antimony, and copper.
Materials that create a barrier against heat sources, to protect against damage or to insulate.
Material, often a compound of lead, iron, manganese, or cobalt, used for increasing the rapidity of the drying of paint and varnish.
Material such as shingle, siding, or flooring, applied as a final surface on or within a structure.
Roofing material comprising rolled sheets of mineral surfaced oil-based asphalt; known as thinner, less durable, and less expensive than asphalt shingles.
Agents used to protect plants and crops from natural enemies, such as insects or fungus.
An essential oil obtained from the bulb and stem of the garlic plant.  This has many uses, including as a nontoxic biocide against fungal degradation of paper artifacts in conservation.
Thermoplastic polymer group which includes nylon and other synthetic resins.

Material in the form of threads or cords that surround the interstices of a net, netting, screen, or sieve, including any woven, knitted, or knotted material with an open texture and evenly spaced holes, including textiles and interlocking metal links. The size of a net or screen may refer to the spaces rather than to the threads that bound the spaces, for example, indicated by the number of openings per inch or another linear unit.
Film used to produce a positive image from a positive, or a negative image from a negative.
Paper on which music is written, typically ruled with the musical stave of five or more lines.

Film or photographic paper that allows the image-bearing emulsion to be removed intact from the base material, usually for transfer to another, more substantial or transparent, support. The first major gelatin-emulsion stripping film was Eastman American film, offered in 1885.

A relatively thin cardboard made from recycled paper; it is clay-coated or surfaced with white paper. Railroad board is often made water resistant to prevent buckling when waterborne paint is used or because of handling with wet hands. Four and six-ply are common thicknesses and it is typically found in black, white, or one of several lackluster, dyed colors.
Oil obtained from the seeds of the hemp plant. Used as a substitute for linseed oil.
Cordage fiber derived from the stems of a few species in the Garcinia genus of evergreen trees and shrubs, particularly in tropical Africa and Brazil.

Tree bark employed historically as writing material for important manuscripts in Assam, India. To write on Sanchipat, a waterproof ink was used, prepared with Silikha seed, Kehraj (a type of grass),ashes and minerals and applied with a bird’s feather. The material and associated technique are now rarely used.
A particular blue pigment that was distributed in drop form.

A coarsely ground blue potassium glass containing small amounts of cobalt oxide, which provides the source of the blue color. It is used as a blue colorant in paints, glazes, glass, bluing paper, laundry blue, starch, textiles, and rubber. Although it was intended as a substitute in painting for natural ultramarine blue, which was very expensive, it was discovered that smalt blue discolors when placed in an oil-based medium.

Pale green pigment that is an intermediate product in the manufacture of synthetic ultramarine blue; sodium sulfate or carbonate, clay, silica, sulfur, and charcoal are heated in a reducing atmosphere to create a melted mass that is green in color, then ground, washed, and dried.

Synthetic pigment composed of red mercuric sulfide, chemically the same as the natural mineral cinnabar. There are two methods for preparing vermilion, a dry-process and a wet-process. The dry-process method, adding mercury to molten sulfur, was invented by the Chinese then imported to Europe ca. 8th century, seemingly via the Islamic world. The wet-process method, placing the ground black mercuric sulfide isomorph into a solution of ammonium sulfide or potassium sulfide, was developed in the late 17th century in Germany. Vermilion is a dense pigment with excellent hiding power, used in oil, watercolor, egg tempera, and fresco paintings. When exposed to ultraviolet light and oxygen, or chloride ions, vermilion can change from its normal red crystalline form to gray or black, resulting in dark discolorations.

A bright white, permanent, opaque, nontoxic pigment made of zinc oxide and other components. Zinc white exists in various grades: white seal (>99% zinc oxide, but with poor covering power), green seal (> 99% zinc oxide with good covering power),  red seal (slightly less pure, generally used for grounds), gold seal (also less pure, used for grounds), and  gray seal (contains some metallic zinc). Zinc white pigment is used in many media, including pastels, watercolor, and goache.
Finely ground pigment made from pumice vocanic stone, used to make a clear glaze for ceramics.

The thick, resinous exudation from the species Pinus pinaster of southern Europe, especially France. Galipot is similar to Venice turpentine (a balsam) and can be distilled to produce oil of turpentine.
A vegetable juice, red in its natural state, used in the Middle Ages as a coloring; probably obtained from the turnsole plant.
Wood from any of the various trees of the genus Prosopis, commonly found in arid regions of the southwestern United States, Mexico, and elsewhere.
Wood from the Pinus contorta, found in western North America.

Wood derived directly from forest trees, such as lumber, posts, poles, pulp, plywood, particleboard, fiberboard, excelsior, and others, including items such as furniture and woven wood baskets that made directly from tree saplings.
Boards that have a tongue cut along one edge and a groove along the opposite edge, so that one board can be fitted together with similar board.

Hard, fine-grained wood of the species Swietenia mahagoni, native to southern Florida, the Bahamas, Cuba, Jamaica, and Hispaniola. It turns reddish brown at maturity and takes a good polish. This is the species for which the term "mahogany" was first coined, derived from a Native American term. The wood is used for cabinet-making and other purposes.

General term for any maple wood having distinct, strongly contrasting, irregular light and dark lines; the lines actually represent distorted growth, and run across the grain. Much used for musical instruments, such as violins and guitars, and fine furniture.

Wood of the species Quercus robur, having a coarse but straight grain that is usually a rich brown color. Flat sawn timber has a distinctive figuring while radial cut lumber has silver grain lines. The wood has a high gallic acid content that will corrode iron and other contacting metals. English oak is widely used in furniture, paneling, railway sleepers, cabinet, musical instruments, and ship building.

Any of several organic compounds composed of carbon, fluorine, chlorine, and hydrogen. Developed during the 1930s and manufactured under the trade name Freon, CFCs found wide application after World War II as aerosol-spray propellants, refrigerants, solvents, and foam-blowing agents. CFCs have been found to pose a serious environmental threat, greatly contributing to ozone depletion. In the stratosphere, the CFC molecules are broken down by the action of solar ultraviolet radiation and release their constituent chlorine atoms. These then react with the ozone molecules, resulting in their removal.
The hair or hair-and-skin of the moose.
Skins of rabbits, usually including fur, used for apparel or other purposes.

A reddish hardwood obtained from any of several trees of the genus Pterocarpus native to Sierra Leone and the west coast of Africa. For the wood of the genus Baphia, which is similar in appearance, use "camwood."
A breccia marble from Lydia in present-day Turkey; its color ranges from bright or brownish red to various hues of purple and it typically contains white pebbles or spots.

A white or drab yellow marble with purplish veins, it was supposedly favored by the emperor Hadrian. The word pavonazzo means peacock blue, violet, or purple in Italian. The ancient marble is also known as Phrygian marble because it is believed to have come from Phrygia in Asia Minor.
An ancient, coarse-grain, white marble quarried from the Greek island of Naxos. Naxian marble was used for sculpture between the 7th and 6th centuries BCE.
General term for stone that is used as derived from a natural source; distinguished from "engineered stone," other composites, or "artificial stone."

A carboxylic acid found naturally in ants and stinging nettles, formic acid is used industrially in textile dyeing, leather tanning, and in the manufacture of insecticides and other products. Formic acid is also encountered as a corrosive agent, deleterious to metals.
A red, nodular limestone; a Jurassic sedimentary that crops out in the Trento Plateau in the Southern Alps. It is a common building stone in Northern Italy.

A very fine-grained, foliated, non-layered metamorphic rock, generally produced by metamorphism of shale under relatively low pressure and temperature. It occurs in many varieties, including clay, hornblende, mica, talc slate, and others, all of which have the common property of splitting readily into thin plates.

A commercial term for any of several fibrous magnesium silicate minerals readily separable into thin, strong fiber that is flexible, noncombustible, heat resistant, and chemically inert; used in a wide variety of industrial products. It was used by the ancient Greeks, Egyptians, and Chinese as a fireproof material. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, asbestos was used for fireproofing and insulating houses: small asbestos fibers were mixed with binders and compressed into boards, paper, pipe covering, ironing board covers, shingles, tiles, and sprayed onto ceilings. Long asbestos fibers were woven into fabrics for used in brake linings, heat-resistant shields, gloves, and fireproof garments and blankets. Health concerns have limited the use of asbestos since the early 1960s. In the U.S., it was declared a hazardous material in 1986.
Traditional Japanese alloy of copper and gold. It is often subjected to a chemical process that produces a blue-black patina. Shakudo has historically been used for ornamental fittings as on katana.

Semi-metallic element having symbol Ge and atomic number 32. A silvery gray metalloid, germanium occurs in sulfide ores and is used as a semiconductor, in alloys, and in the manufacture of infrared transmitting glass.
Ancient and medieval culture and style of people in what is today Armenia and eastern Georgia.

Refers to the style of art and architecture found in the region of Lycia in the southwestern corner of Anatolia in antiquity. The style is characterized particularly by monumental tombs widespread over the region from about 500 BCE to 200 CE that exhibit Greek, Persian, and Roman influences.
Refers to the style and culture of the area of Palestine, located between the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea and the Arabian desert.
Pottery styles belonging to Mesopotamian cultures.

Refers to an ancient Greek style and period that begins around 480 BCE, when the Greek city-states defeated the Persian invaders, and ends around 323 BCE, with the death of Alexander the Great. It is characterized by the rebuilding of cities after the Persian wars, the flourishing of philosophy, drama, architecture, sculpture, painting, and the other arts. In the visual arts, it is known for the mastery of the human form and sophistication of architectural design.

Refers to a regional school of Pahari miniature painting associated with the Nurpur state of the Punjab Hills. It was a less isolated state then other Punjab Hill states and its rulers were generals and governors of the Mughal empire during the early 17th century. While stylistically distinct, the Nurpur school was indebted to Mughal painting, particularly in regards to portraiture. A bolder style was used for other genres. These two styles coalesced in the early 18th century: facial features are less exaggerated, color is more controlled, and landscapes are stylized. 18th-century Nurpur painting was influenced by the painting styles of Guler and Jammu, with more naturalistic and delicate results. A vertical format is favored and tall, graceful female figures with small heads are common. Court life in Nurpur diminished in the second half of the 18th century as did its painting.

Refers to the period named for the city and ruler Û Thong based in the Suphanburi Province of western Thailand. The style of the period came into fruition with the Khmer withdrawal from central Thailand in the second quarter of the 14th century. The period is generally classified under sub-sculptural styles known as groups A, B, and C, that combine Mon, Dvaravati, Haripunjaya, and Khmer elements in various ways. Group A features Buddha images with prominent foreheads, almond eyes, straight noses, and tiny conical curls. Images in Group B exhibit stronger Khmer influences as revealed in the square face and austere, impersonable facial expression. Group C features Buddha images reflecting Ayutthaya and Sukhothai influences as shown in the oval face, elongated body, smiling expression, and notched design on the robe flap over the left shoulder. Most Buddha images in all three groups are seated in the hero position on a pedestal with hands in the gesture of subduing Mara.

Refers to the style and culture that is named after the site at Swidry, Poland, and existed in the areas of Poland, Romania, Russia, and elsewhere. It developed in the late Paleolithic Period, though it continued and flourished in the Mesolithic. It is particulalarly characterized by distinctive flint tools, including small, assymetrical tanged blades, arrowheads, and tranchet axes. It seems to be related to the Campignian culture that flourished further south.

Refers to a Neolithic culture and style that was contemporary with the Rössen culture, but was located in Hungary, the Czech lands, and eastern Germany, lasting into the late fifth millennium BCE. It followed the relatively homogenous Bandkeramik culture, and is distinguished by the emergence of strong local traditions and styles.

Refers to the Eneolithic culture established in the Minusinsk Basin between the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE. Notable artifacts from the period include examples of the Scynthian-Siberian Animal style on bronze and gold, and clay funeral masks portraying faces with a two-color decoration.
Nationality, style, and culture of one of the largest Indian scheduled tribes, found in the Indian state of Jharkhand.

Refers to the style of Shinto architecture that developed around 300 BCE. The style is characterized by a type of shrine that is said to have been derived from a simple two-bay by three-bay system typical of prehistoric granaries and storehouses. The shrine is surrounded by a continuous deck with stairs leading to the entrance on the long side.

Refers to the work of a school of Buddhist painters who worked for the Kasuga shrine at Nara during the mid-13th century. The style is characterized thin wire-like lines, flat surfaces, and bright colors such as orange-red, deep blue and green.

Literally "gold brocaded", these overglaze-enamelled wares, mainly bowls, were most likely produced in China in the 16th century chiefly for export to Japan although some may have also been manufactured in Japan during the 19th century. They became very popular in the West as well. The dominant color was usually red or white, with lesser amounts of red, yellow and green and they were embellished with gold, generally in a floral scroll pattern.

Refers to a Neolithic Chinese culture and period active from ca. 3300 to 2250 BCE. The most notable Liangzhu artifacts consist of ritual jades; flat disks of varying sizes and segmented hollow columnar objects have been found in graves. The columnar jades feature angled corners worked with what are among the earliest representations of the human form in this part of the world. Later ritual manuals identify the objects as 'bi' (the flat disks) and 'cong' (the tubular objects) and explain their role in the worship of heaven and earth and as markers of hierarchical rank; although the jades were certainly bearers of meaning, the later texts may not be relevant to the Neolithic context.

Refers to the culture, style, and period of a Chinese dynasty of the period 618 to 907 CE, a time considered one of the most brilliant in Chinese history. China flourished as a stable, consolidated empire and the resulting prosperity and patronage created a Golden Age of Chinese painting, metalwork, ceramics, music, and poetry. Chang'an, with its masterful urban planning, remained the main Tang capital and a world center. Taizong (reigned 626-649) and Xuanzong (reigned 712-756) were important Tang rulers and patrons. Buddhism remained influential although it suffered periods of persecution during the Tang dynasty. Paintings from the caves at Dunhuang and stone pagodas such as the Great Wild Goose Pagoda (ca. 652) and the Small Wild Goose Pagoda (ca. 707) in Chang'an have survived. Monumental stone sculpture of the northern provinces displays the new tendency toward fuller, more sensual figures. This tendency also found in secular Tang sculpture, both stone and ceramic. The merging of Indian and Chinese sculpture styles is seen at the cave at Mt. Tianlong, created under the patronage of Empress Wu Zetian (reigned 690-705). Painting, which flourished during the Tang, was dominated by the secular landscape tradition. Li Sixum and Li Zhaodao, father and son, and Wang Wei are three painters' names known to us; probable copies of their work exist. Wang Wei's work, influential for later artists, was intimate and melancholy while the work of Li Sixum and Li Zhaodao features the bright greens and blues of many Tang landscapes. Chinese portrait painting, begun in the Han dynasty, was refined in the Tang by such artists as Wu Daozi. Tang ceramics include sancai earthenware figurines and vessels, typically used as tomb objects, white porcellanous wares such as the well-known Xing ware of Henan province, and the jadelike Yue celadons of Zhejiang province. The use of metal oxides in underglaze decoration was developed in Hunan and Sichuanh provinces and porcelain, although not fully exploited until later, has its origins in the Tang period. Tang decorative arts were influenced by Middle Eastern and other foreign trends during the Tang dynasty, leading to new styles in ceramics and metalwork. For instance, colorful glazed earthenware objects such as ewers and rhytons were made to resemble Persian silverwork and Persian weft patterning were introduced to Chinese textiles. China, in turn, exported its pottery, silk, and printing and paper technology. The Tang dynasty was succeeded by the Later Liang dynasty.
Refers to the culture, style, and period associated with the reign of the last emperor of the Ming Dynasty, 1628-1643.

An art movement that took place in Hong Kong and Taiwan in the 1960s and the 1970s. In the 1960s, Lui Shoukwan, pioneer of modern ink painting in Hong Kong, brought a modernist spirit into Chinese painting while adapting the techniques of earlier masters, which became a point of departure for many of his students. In the meantime, a group of young artists in Taiwan also started to innovate ink painting, blending traditional Chinese painting theories with modern Western art.  In 1971, modern ink artists from Taiwan and Hong Kong co-organized a Chinese Ink Painting Exhibition that toured from Taiwan to Hong Kong. In the same year, Liu Kuo-sung, a seminal figure of modern ink painting in Taiwan, moved to Hong Kong and taught many students until his retirement in 1992. His students held exhibitions since 1975 and founded Hong Kong Modern Ink Painting Association in 1977, the latter of which continued to promote experimentation with ink art. After the opening up of China in the late 1970s, modern ink painting had a strong impact in the People’s Republic of China as well.

Refers to the style of porcelain made in China for the Imperial court during the Yuan Dynasty (1280-1368). The style is characterized by a combination of the pale blue-green of Qingbai porcelain, with a thicker, more solid glaze that results in heavier and stronger wares.
The culture of Americans of German descent.

Style and movement inspired by the architecture and iconography of pre-Columbian Mesoamerican cultures. Most works date to the 1920s and 1930s; examples include architecture, mosaics, and other works.
Culture and styles of historic Turkestan, a region in Central Asia inhabited by Turkic and other peoples.
Culture or style of the Páez Native South American peoples of the southern highlands, Colombia. They speak a Chibchan language very closely related to that of the now-extinct Pijao and Coconuco.

Style and culture of a Native American tribe of North Carolina; origins stem from the Nansemond and Tutelo tribes, as well as Tuscarora and Saponi members. Name derives from the North Carolina counties Halifax and Warren, where most tribal members currently live.

Style and culture of the Native American people who inhabited the upper James River valley of Virginia,  or the present-day group in Amherst County, Virginia, claiming descent from these people. Distinct from the "Algonkin" who share the same original Algonquian language heritage, but inhabit Northern Ontario and Quebec along the Ottawa River in Canada.

Style and culture of the Native North American people of the Great Basin region who made their home around Lake Tahoe in what is now California and Nevada. The culture has existed for an estimated 9,000 years in the Lake Tahoe Basin and adjacent east and west slopes and valleys of the Sierra Nevada Mountain Range.
Refers to the style and culture of the Gitxsan, a First Nations indigenous people living in northwest British Columbia.
Cultures and styles of Southeastern Indigenous Americans.

Refers to the culture of the Eastern Mono, a Native American group from central California who speak a language belonging to the Numic group of the Uto-Aztecan family and are related to Northern Paiute. The Eastern Mono, along with Owens Valley Native communities across the crest, are similar to their neighbors from the Great Basin. Historically the Eastern and Western Mono traded with one another.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Tanzania.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting southern Tanzania and northern Malawi.
Culture of a Berber sultanate mid-13th-15th centuries in present-day Morocco.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Ethiopia.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Kenya.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name, closely related to the Yaka, and inhabiting the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in southeastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Used to descibe works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Congo.
People who practice bodybuilding, which is the process of developing the muscles and physique of the human body through exercise and diet, sometimes for competitive exhibition.
Persons who compose text for opera, musical plays, or extended choral works, or who adapt text to accommodate the musical requirements of composers.

Cowboys, or horsemen of the South American pampas, specifically Argentina, as well as Uruguay, Brazil, and Patagonia. Historically, gauchos were migratory horseman of the 18th-19th centuries who engaged in cattle work. They have become folkloric or iconic figures in the same sense as North American cowboys.

People who create conceptual schemes for the organization or appearance of lighting for theater, television, or film productions using color, form, surface, and space to create a visual language capable of communicating ideas relevant to the production.
People who specialize in making tintyptes, which are variants of the wet collodion process producing a direct positive image on a thin sheet of lacquered metal (usually iron, never tin).

People engaged in the specific process of arranging type from copy for printing or making printing plates, whether by hand, by mechanical devices, or by inputting to computer. More generally, for the people who prepare copy, do casting off, arrange type, set spacing, and other tasks in the printing process, see "compositors."
Those whose occupation is to make, repair, or fit locks.
People who do weaving, which is the process of interlacing strands or textile or another material to make materials or objects such as cloth, wicker, baskets, etc.

Usually refers to the wives of presidents of the United States. May also refer to women chosen by presidents to act as hostesses at the White House or to the wives of the heads of any country or jurisdiction.
People having this title of leadership; from Turkic and Mongolian languages, combining the title "khan" with the prefix "il," to signify a khan of the people or of the nation.
People who sell, and may also make, saddles, which are seats made over a frame and placed on a horse's or other animal's back for carrying riders.
Persons who fabricate, assemble, or repair machinery; also craftsmen skilled in the use of machine tools.
Artists and craftsmen who insert small pieces of one material into a larger piece of another so as to create a design.

Metalworkers who join two pieces of metal by softening or melting both surfaces to be joined by the application of heat, with or without inserting filler metal and with or without the application of pressure.
Metalworkers who specialize in working with tin, particularly in the production of tin utensils.

Refers generally to those who obtain title to or an interest in property through purchase. Refers specifically to employees in mercantile businesses who have charge of the selection, buying, pricing, stockkeeping, and display of goods for resale to customers.
People or corporate bodies who make carpets, fabrics, costume, or other works made of textile materials, which are natural or synthetic fibers.
Senior rig workers on an oil drilling crew who guide stands of drill pipe from a position at the top of a derrick.
Engineers who design systems having to do with mechanics, thermodynamics, and material properties.
Artists who specialize in creating paintings on a wooden support, including altarpieces, portraits, and other art works.

Persons who engage in photoengraving, which is the production of relief prints for which an image is photographically transferred to a plate for printing in such a way that either the light or the dark areas become susceptible to attack by an etchant.
Those professionally engaged in the field of industrial design.
Bits with a projecting lip or notched blade which allows wood shavings to accumulate in the spoon or hollow portion of the bit.
Architects who work on projects for the military, usually as contrasted to projects for the community.
Spring-driven guns used to drive staples.

Flexible fiberglass or bamboo sticks used braced against a frame to provide clamping pressure, used in a traditional Japanese method that applies controlled pressure during the consolidation of objects or when adhering parts into position.
Devices with adjustable jaws used for centering and holding a cutting bit or a drill bit.
Prehistoric biface stone tools, usually u-shaped, large and oblong, with transverse cutting edges. Thought to be used for heavy digging, the slaughter of animals, skinning game, and bone breaking.
Large heavy knives with a single-edged blade, used for cutting cane and clearing plant growth; also used as cutting weapons.
Devices, usually in the form of rotating discs that are attached to plants, which are used to study tropisms, such as light and gravity.

Apparatus for producing rotary motion by the weight of men or animals treading on a succession of moving steps or a belt that forms a kind of continuous path, as around the periphery of a pair of horizontal cylinders.
Devices used to detonate explosive or flammable materials or fuel. These may be chemically, mechanically, or electrically initiated.
General term for equipment used for processing of data for analysis.
Clamps of various types used in woodworking.

Clamps consisting of two double-cranked arms with swivel shoes connected by a system of levers actuated by a central threaded rod which also carries a round shoe; usually used for corner-clamping large mitered frames.

Ancient instruments originally designed by Huguenot inventor and pastor Jacques Besson in 1567. Cosmolabes resembled astrolabes, used to measure distances between celestial bodies. However, they could also be, according to Besson’s design, used in navigation, cartography, surveying, and when not in use could be folded into a reading desk.
Iron tongs used for a variety of purposes, but usually used to hold heavy, round metal objects while they are being forged.

Small, portable devices that use warps threaded through the holes of perforated tablets to create decorative bands. The device's tablets rotate as the warp is threaded, creating patterned sheds through which the weft thread is passed. These looms were commonly used during the Roman and Byzantine eras, but originated in Egypt around the 1st millennium BC.
Small, narrow V-shaped gouges used in woodworking.
Molding planes in matched pairs used for making rule joints on the flaps of folding tables or desks.
Lenses which are constructed to allow continuously variable focal lengths within a specific range. The effective aperture and focus settings remain unchanged throughout such adjustments.
Apparatuses for producing prints by projecting a negative or transparency onto sensitive paper; often allowing for the production of prints both larger and smaller than the original.
Devices which use a penetration test to measure the difference between initial and final setting times of cements and mortars.
Tools used to hold nail rods while making nail heads in wrought nail making.
Describes works created by the inhabitants of the Tuvalu Islands. The artwork of the Tuvalu primarily consists of tattoo and canoe design.
Nationality, culture, or styles of Tuvalu, a Polynesian island in the Pacific Ocean.
Cranes with a horizontal arm supported from a wall or columns of a building. The arm may also support a trolley.

Pens such as fountain pens and others that hold a reservoir of ink in the handle, holder, or other receptacle, as distinguished from dip pens that require frequent dipping of the pen point in ink, such as lettering pens, quill pens, reed pens, and others.
Cameras used to prepare images for printing.

Refers to a period (660-730 CE) during which that the foundations of Islamic society and civilization are considered to have been established; it is named after an aristocratic family of Mecca that ruled the Islamic empire from Syria for over 90 years. The craftsmen were Syrians, Egyptians, and Persians as the Arabs did not have a developed tradition of craftsmanship at this time. For these reasons, the earliest Islamic art and architecture is noticeably eclectic and it is difficult to establish an identifiable Islamic style. Nevertheless, three separate elements are typically found in Umayyad art, often in the same work: the naturalism of Syria where the Hellenistic tradition was still strong; the more decorative Coptic style of Egypt; and the Sassanian style of Persia which combined Hellenistic elements with aspects of the earlier Achaemenid period. Surviving Umayyad art is mostly in the form of architecture and its decoration, supplemented by some textiles, metalwork, ceramics, ivory, and coins.
Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the regin of Selim II. The Selimiye Mosque was built for him by Sinan between 1570 and 1574.
English variation of Art Nouveau, used primarily to describe mass-produced goods of many types, typically furniture.
Refers to a French variation of Art Nouveau, so named for the style's imagery and emphasis on the fantastic as seen in the writings of author Jules Verne.
German term for a variation of Art Nouveau; named after an English publication which promoted the works of the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society.

Style of architecture and the decorative arts employed by some artists in Spain and its colonies in the 19th century. It was based on the medieval work of Spanish mudajjan, denoting Muslims living under Christian rule.

European avant-garde doctrine or school of art that existed between 1932 and ca. 1960. The musicalists attempted, influenced by the works of František Kupka and Auguste Herbin, to ‘compose’ abstract paintings, and incorporated musical concepts such as ‘harmony’ and ‘resonance’ in their compositions. Characteristic for their works are vibrant colours and rhythmic lines. The driving force and main theorist behind the movement was French artist Henry Valensi, other associates were Charles Blanc-Gatti, Louise Janin, Marcel Lempereur-Haut and Gustave Bourgogne. The musicalists often held expositions in the Galerie Renaissance in Paris.
The culture or period of the Holy Roman Empire, a multi-ethnic complex of territories in central Europe during the medieval and early modern periods until its dissolution in 1806.
Small tables designed at such a height to be used for writing while sitting on a sofa.

Small tables on which vessels and dishes are placed pior to serving in a dining room. They differ from "credenzas (sideboards)" in that they are smaller and their form is of a table rather than case furniture. They may be designed so that they back flush against the table or a wall. The term originates in the custom at courts for food to be tasted and proven trustworthy before being served to the monarch. For similar tables used in churches near the altar, prefer "credence tables (religious building fixtures)."
Chests made to commemorate or anticipate a wedding; usually incorporating names and dates in their decoration.

Tall case pieces generally having seven or more drawers, and divided by a cornice into two sections, consisting of a lower case resembling an enlarged dressing table and an upper case resembling a chest of drawers. For equivalent English pieces, use "tallboys (furniture)."
Open-front cupboards on wheels, used in front of a fire to warm plates of food.
Racks for storing and/or displaying newspapers.
Desks constructed so that two people may work face-to-face; generally taking the form of a large writing table or desk with drawers on both sides.
Early form of footstool that was reproduced in great numbers during the 19th century. Thebes stools generally have concave tops, with flared legs and cross bracing.
Beds converted from sofas, settees, and other forms of seating furniture usually by folding out a concealed mattress and springs.
Cabinets of various designs, intended for the storage and display of medals; popular in 18th-19th centuries.
Chairs with backs consisting of two crescent shapes, one inverted above the other.
Chairs by means of which an electric current can be passed through a person sitting in it, especially those in which convicted criminals are executed by electrocution.

Candles lit in recognition of a vow, prayer, or desire. Examples are those found in churches, often housed in glass containers. Any candles housed in glass containers that resemble the votive candles originally found primarily in churches and other religious contexts.
Ultraviolet lamps that radiate a significant portion of their radiative power in the UV-A and UV-B bands.
Chair designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe ca. 1929-1930 having a cantilevered construction of chromed steel and leather or parchment upholstery. Prized as an example of Bauhaus design.
Lamps supported on a contrivance that permits them to move freely in any direction yet remain upright; often used on ships.

Wick channel hanging oil lamps with six or eight channels radiating from a central support, drip catcher suspended below, of brass or other metal; lighted in Jewish homes at the beginning of the Sabbath.

Lamps that burn lard or lard oil, employing some method to deliver the semi-solid fuel to the wick, either heat to liquify it so that it will flow, or pressure or gravity devices to force it to the wick; especially those of tinned sheet iron, painted or plain, dating to the 1840s and 1850s.
Devices used to control the flow of gas to a burner or lamp.
A long single-edged Japanese sword traditionally worn by the samurai class of feudal Japan, commonly referred to as a "samurai sword."
A type of dagger originally originally one with which the coup de grâce was given.

Candleholders used during Kwanzaa celebrations; term is derived from a Swahili word meaning "candleholder." Holds seven candles to represent the Seven Principles which are celebrated during each day of the Kwanzaa holiday. Examples include "Imani" (faith) and "Umoja" (unity).

Candlesticks consisting of a helix which is wound from a wrought iron strip or rod forming the stem of the candlestick mounted on a wooden base. A sufficient space is left between each turn of the spiral to allow a cup or disc containing the candle socket with a side projection to be raised or lowered by rotation within the spiral.
Plates used to connect members of a truss together or to connect several steel members at a joint.
Metal pins used in masonry work to support a horizontal string or line. The mason positions the line and then uses it as a guide in maintaining proper alignment of the work.
Small metal rods attached to the visor or the right side of the helmet to allow the visor to be raised, in use from the late 15th to the second quarter of the 17th century.
Small and light round shields carried by medieval foot soldiers to protect themselves in battle. The reduced size allowed soldiers to move freely and swiftly.

Paintings that were initially exhibited in the official Paris Salon of the 18th and 19th centuries, where members of the Academie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture would exhibit recent works. Salon paintings are most often academic in nature, and are reflective of the forum in which they were exhibited; i.e.: a competition for public and private commissions.
Circular paintings. For circular two-dimensional motifs, use "medallions (ornament areas)"; use "roundels" for circular panels in architectural contexts.

Works created by using a resist material, such as tempera, gouache, waxy crayon, or another material, to create a design on a support, usually heavy watercolor paper. The design is covered with ink, allowed to dry, and the ink is washed off. In areas where the underlying material was omitted or thinly applied, the black ink pervades; in areas where the underlying material was more thickly applied, its color and texture remain.
Finished drawings presented by the artist to a friend or patron; usually used with regard to the Renaissance-Baroque period.
Visual works that focus on the delineation of form in two dimensions and that are created using a computer, software, and input hardware.
Marks made on the hide of a living animal to identify its owner; usually made by freezing or searing with hot irons.
Objects of various form, but usually rubber buttons inserted into the metal frame of a door that cushion the door so that the audible impact of door closure reduced .
Mortise latches operated by knobs, levers, or thumb pieces from the inside, and from the outside by these same means when the stop works are not set, or by key when the stop works are set.
General purpose household hooks used for storage, especially in garages, sheds, utility rooms, or outdoors. Use includes for hanging bicycles, yard equipment, or sports gear, or for other purposes.
Keys with large parts of the bit filed away to enable it to open low-quality locks as master keys.
Broad term for principles, rules, or laws designed to control or regulate behavior of individuals, corporations, or other entities.
Refers to maps in which pictures are used to note the distribution of features, including physical features, flora, fauna, settlement patterns, or other characteristics.
Documents produced by a duplicating machine operating on the stencil principle; includes any documents produced by an ink bleed-through stencil.

Labels, often having an adhesive backing, bearing the name and address of the intended recipient of mail or packages, to facilitate the dispatch of the items by a postal service or other delivery agent.

Official stamps affixed by guilds or assay offices upon articles made of gold or silver as evidence of the quality of the metal. Distinguished from "makers' marks" which are stamped on articles of gold or silver for the purpose of identifying the craftsman or workshop of origin.
Correspondence that is intended to pass on to a third party information concerning another, as a referral for consultation or other purposes.
Cards containing advertisements displayed in store windows.
Records in which are entered sequential data, especially about activities or transactions that occur in a system.
Documents that itemize and describe the detailed contents of shipped packages, containers, or pallets.

Documents expressing the conveyance of property upon condition, such as that money will be paid or a duty will be performed, which operates as a lien, so that the issuer may, under certain conditions, take possession and foreclose the property upon default.
Private documents belonging to an individual. For records kept by public officials or other persons for their private or personal use but relating to their official duties, use "office files."
Any of various societies, the members of which are sworn to keep the rules, activities, and purposes  secret from nonmembers.
Information in the form of outlines of procedures, as directions or commands.
Periodicals published at regular intervals four times per year.
Albums designed to be dedicated or presented to a person or organization.
Short reports of the latest news or events, usually in a television or radio broadcast context, but these also may appear as printed matter.
Printed cards made on the occasion of a person's death, usually distributed at funeral ceremonies. Often the name and life dates of the deceased are printed along with a religious text and image.
General term for bodies of electors or voters, that is, those qualified for or participating in an election.

Assemblies of people, either ancient Roman citizens in the provinces who gathered for purposes of administration and justice, or in monasticism, groups of people of either sex belonging to a religious order and living together.
Government bodies charged with the oversight of land or property use, defined by zoning codes, within distinct geographical or urban areas.
A collection wherein the constituent parts have in common a general subject, heading, topic, or composition, as distinguished from collections that reflect a common provenance.
Individuals who are killed, wounded, or injured in a battle, natural disaster, or other event.
Those who have been awarded a master's degree in any field.

Individuals, companies, or corporations engaged in the development of software, which includes computer system programs, procedures, and associated documentation concerned with the operation of data processing systems, and which require hardware for use to be made of them.

Students, specialists, or advocates of eugenics, which is a science that deals with improving the hereditary qualities of the human population, especially through social control of human mating and reproduction.
The application of a first coating, such as size, ground, paint, or varnish, to a surface that is to be painted.

Technique in which paint, usually water-based, is applied directly to textiles, such as linen or silk, with only a very thin glue preparation or no preparation. The result was a subdued tonality and matte surface; however, the advantages were that it was less expensive than other contemporary painting techniques and this technique allowed the work to be rolled and transported. Examples include works by German, Netherlandish, and north Italian artists during the 15th and early 16th centuries. For the technique preferred in Spain and its colonies, where the ground was a thin layer of gesso, prefer "sarga (technique)."
The darkening of areas of a picture to indicate shadows.

Radiography by secondary electron emission, an imaging technique. An example is for technical examination of painting, that records differences in intensity of electron emissions from adjacent pigments.

In photographic processing, the technique of combining auxiliary transparencies with the original negative or positive transparency to adjust contrast, tone, or color in the exposure, and the technique of covering parts of a negative while exposing it.

A technique for studying turbidity which records the decrease in intensity of a light beam resulting from its passage through a suspension of particles. A detector, the nephelometer, measures the scattered light and may thus indirectly measure the size and concentration of particles in the suspension.

The technique of using a metal rod, usually in a holder, to write or draw on a surface, often paper, parchment, or wood that has been covered by a ground. Ivory is another common support. As the point moves across the surface, it leaves behind a thin layer of the metal, which quickly oxidizes. For example, lines from silver points becomes the brownish grey of tarnished silver and lines from lead points becomes very dark.
Technique achieved by applying paint using the digits of the hand rather than a brush. Examples range from prehistoric image-making, modern art-making techniques, and children's art.
Cleaning to such an extent that the original finish, patina, or surface layers of an object have been damaged or removed.

Cutting excess or irregular material, thereby reducing the size of an object. In the context of bookbinding, refers to the removal of a small amount of excess material from the edges of a book, either to remove the bolts and produce cut edges, or simply to make the page edges roughly even. For cutting or scraping away layers from the surface of something, use "shaving."
Shaping something, as a gem, glass, or ceramics, so that it has a series of relatively small, regular, flat surfaces that reflect light.
The art or process of casting gold in Nahuatl culture.
The technique of decorating surfaces with cut-outs of paper, linoleum, plastic, or other flat material, over which a finish is applied.
Grilles with damper assemblies covering the outlets of air distribution systems.

Automatic apparatuses for regulating temperature, particularly such a device in which the expansive force of metals or gas acts directly upon the source of heat, cooling, ventilation, or the like, or controls them indirectly by opening and closing an electric circuit.
Receptacles in plumbing or drainage systems, other than traps, intended to receive or discharge liquid or waste.
Devices that treat water, usually by removing chemicals and contaminants. Water conditioners are directly applied to showers, heaters, and and other appliances.

General term for devices that convert incoming television signals into the original images and their associated sounds. The receiver contains an amplifier and demodulator of the radio signal; in modern televisions, the receiver may be housed in a unit separate from the monitor
Process of furnishing, sustaining, or strengthening with a buttress or support.
Wood joints made by notching each member to receive the other. An example is in notched joints of two structural timbers.
Wrought nails with a faceted head, for example, cone-shaped or gem-shaped.
Flat-sided nails of soft iron for fastening horseshoes to the horse’s hoof.

Nails having a broad, round or rose head with a flat, rectangular shank and spear-like point, designed for easy clinching. So-named because they are well adapted for nailing and clinching together the oaken bars of portable hurdle fences.
Models or mock-ups of garments, most often made from muslin, and used for fittings or for making copies.
Bolts having a bend or perpendicular projection from the body of the bolt that is made to engage with a strike or keeper.
Hinges that use internal friction to hold a door or window in a selected position.

Locking systems intended for use in a series, each lock of which may be actuated by two different keys, one capable of operating every lock of the series, and the other capable of operating only one or a few of the locks.
Anchors for bolts and screws used to secure structural wood parts to masonry or concrete walls.

Sculpture serving as cult objects associated with the Cult of the Hand of the Bini people of Africa; they are made of cast bronze or carved wood in cylindrical form with a projection from the top, relief sculpture around the sides, and figures on the flat top.
Works from the mid-20th century and later that are sculptural and are installed on a wall surface.

Models created by stereolithography, which is a form of 3-D printing technology. Examples include models based on data from computer scans, e.g., as used to create replacement parts in restoration of art works or to create anatomical models for medical or paleontological purposes.
Temporary sculptural forms created in wet sand, usually at the seashore, and resembling the form of a castle.

Carved ‘serpent stones’ commissioned by Indian women that evoke symbolic properties of the tree and the serpent. These are set beneath sacred trees, and are thought to bestow fertility, especially to the barren. Stone or terracotta nāgakals bearing Shaivite or Vaishnavite symbolism may be found side by side under the same tree-shrine. Most often these are carved by local craftsmen.
Sculptures or statues in the United States that represent U.S. soldiers from World War I. The sculptures were commissioned around the country and are nameless.
A veil worn by some Muslim women to obscure the face, while leaving the eyes revealed. It is worn in combination with a separate headscarf or other head covering, such as a khimar or hijab.
Traditional Maori cloaks or mats made of flax and decorated with black twisted thrums or tassels that could be worn by both men and women.

Men's coats for civilian or military dress, having a shaped upper body of waist length in the front and from which longer tails extend at the back. The fashion is sometimes adopted for women's wear as well.
Traditional hip- or knee-length long sleeved kimono-like jacket originating in Japan. Both men and women wear haori; women’s are typically longer than men’s.
Sculptures of very large size, usually but not always sculpture in the round, often but not always outdoors. For large sculptures of figures of extraordinary size, use "colossi."
Necklaces with graduated diamonds or gemstones of the same variety, usually individually set and without other ornamentation.

Traditional crown-like headdresses worn by Russian girls and women. Originally elements of folk costume intended to support a veil, they developed into diadem-shaped tiaras that were part of the official court dress for royalty and ladies-in-waiting in the 19th century.
Hats with a tall conical crown and a moderate brim, especially fashionable from 1560 to 1620.
Drinking glasses with a large bowl, of various shapes, resting on a stemmed foot.

Cups or covers attached to the feet of furniture, to protect as well as to allow easy movement. Distinguished from "castors (finish hardware)" which are wheels set in a swivel and added to the feet on furniture to allow easy movement.
Joints made by fitting a projecting rib on one piece into a groove in another. If the pieces are metal, the joint may also be welded. For plastic or wood pieces, the joint may be glued.
Metal covers, often gold or silver, used for the veneration and preservation of icons or similar devotional images.

Inlaid decorative and protective wood, plastic, or other material placed along the edges of a chordophone's belly, back, or fretboard. The term is usually used chiefly to refer to such edging on violins or guitars.

Trumpets with a slide mechanism, much like the slide trombone which was developed later. Slide trumpets were popular during the Renaissance and Baroque periods, as well as in England during the 17th-19th centuries.

Irish bellows-blown bagpipes, dating in their present form back to the 18th century, having a double-reed chanter, three single-reed drone pipes in one stock, and three or four keyed double-reed pipes for playing chords. The instruments are played sitting with the drones lying across the player's knees.
Vertical bamboo flutes of Japan with a notched lip, four finger holes, and one thumb hole.
Shawms of Yugoslakvia, with a conical shape and six fingerholes.
Dishes used for presenting food, especially on a table for serving to people.
Small plates intended primarily for serving an individual portion of salad.
Clocks designed to be mounted on walls.
Flat discs or strips of metal or wood between which are held the movements of clocks and watches.
Drums in which the membrane is struck by enclosed pellets, pebbles, or other small objects or by an attached outside pendant as they are shaken or twirled.
Primitive guitars of African peoples, particularly Hottentots and Bushmen. They usually are unfretted, have a belly made of skin, and three or four strings which are finger-plucked.
Small, unfretted fiddles, generally with four strings, made in a great variety of shapes and played from the 16th century to the 19th.
Long, narrow horizontal members of wood or metal that connect the headboards and footboards of beds.
Japanese prints made to give an effect similar to stone rubbings.
Compact, fitted dressing chests which stand on four tapering legs, and are intended to hold cosmetics and jewelry.
Relatively small, easily movable tables.
Reinforcing blocks glued, nailed, or screwed into the corner of a chair or sofa frame to hold the leg and seat rail together.
The action or power of moving from one place to another, including progressive motion of a person, animal, or inanimate body by natural or artificial means.
The action or state of deceiving, concealing of the truth in order to mislead, fraud, cheating, or false dealing.
The three types of perspective found in Chinese landscape painting, comprising “level-distance,” “high distance,” and “deep distance.”
Structural loads that fluctuate in strength.

Structure design that is specifically environmentally conscious, taking into account construction methods and materials that are locally available as well as the building's efficient use of resources, including systems of heating, cooling, power, water, and waste. Provides affordable, adequate shelter with minimal negative effect on the local and global environment; may be replicated and locally maintained.
Art having a primary or secondary purpose of teaching, such as art intended to convey a moral theme or other truth to the viewer.
The number of calories required to raise 1 gram of a material 1 degree Celsius in temperature.
Use with reference to works of art and architecture regarding the design of visual elements such as line, mass, shape, or color.
Having a shallow, concave form or outline, like the shape of a shallow dish.
The quality of original and productive creativity. Use with reference specifically to art theory, especially during the Renaissance, to mean the selection and utilization of subject matter.
Color rendering that replaces normal, human- percievable color with assigned colors to highlight the visual display of phenomena, or to enhance contrasts.

Circulation, transmission and exchange of knowledge, views and theories between countries, regions and people from different cultures by means of contact and encounter and how this has (mutual) impact on the cultural and artistic production.
The quality of being composed of or containing a salt or salts; also the concentration of a salt or salts in a solution.
A phenomenon by which the effects in a property lag behind the changes in the forces acting upon it such as magnetizing force or stress.
Theory according to which a whole cannot be analyzed without residue into the sum of its parts or reduced to discrete elements.

The worship of one god, particularly when it is recognized that other deities exist. In such a system, one god has a central and dominating position, although the principle of polytheism is not abandoned.
The time-rate at which any physical process takes place; a scalar quantity. For example, the rate at which an object covers distance.
Tendency toward viewing alien cultures with disfavor; also the resulting sense of inherent superiority.
Poems and linguistic experiments in sound symbolism and language invented by Russian Futurist poets.
Chance or luck, when regarded as a cause of events and changes in human affairs.
Property owned by an individual person or group and kept for their exclusive use.
Systems of writing or expressing numbers.
In algebraic geometry, smooth vector bundle maps.
Plane figures having eleven sides and eleven angles.
A decline in value or reduction of worth.
Violation by a subject of his allegiance to his sovereign or to the state.

Sense of national consciousness exalting one nation above all others and placing primary emphasis on promotion of its culture and interests as opposed to those of other nations or supranational groups. For love of one's country and devotion to its interests in general, use "patriotism."
The condition or role when a party, entity, action, or situation does not have a direct causal or other direct relationship with another party, entity, action, or situation.
The sum of all chemical and physical processes within a living organism and also the energy made available for various forms of work.
The way people act in response to their environments and to others.
Filling beyond what is usual or comfortable.
Refers to all non-technical analysis of artifactual objects and art works according to precepts of such critical approaches as typology, morphology, or connoisseurship.
The placing of numerals on something, usually a series of like things given consecutive numbers.
