Method of dating by measuring the direction and intensity of the paleomagnetism in materials and comparing the results to known records of fluctuations in the earth's magnetic field.
Exhibitions staged in the open air instead of in an enclosed space.
Meetings at which participants are the leaders and members of a given labor union.

Emblems or devices with text added to the end of some manuscripts and incunabula by the author or scribe to provide the title of the work and the name or initials of its author or scribe. For similar closing statements in later printed books, use "colophons." Explicits were eventually incorporated into or completely replaced by the colophon, which included information about the printer, printing materials, and typeface, and, often, the printer's emblem.
General term for the activity of buying, selling, or bartering commodities.
Broad category of sciences and professions that deal with the health of humans and animals.
The scientific study of animals, including their anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, genetics, ecology, evolution, and behavior.
Branch of engineering that deals with the construction and operation of the power plant and other mechanical equipment of seagoing craft, docks, and harbor installations.

Medical specialty concerned with the prevention, control, diagnosis, and treatment of injuries and diseases affecting the health of domestic and wild animals, including the prevention of transmission of animal diseases to other animals and to people.
Branch of physics that deals with the properties, relationships, and interactions of elementary particles, especially those produced in collisions involving very high energies.

Business process of planning, developing, launching and managing a product or service. It covers the entire life cycle of a product, from conception to development and marketing. An important goal of product managment is ensuring that a product meets the needs of its target market and contributes to business strategy. The product manager manages a product or products through all phases of the product life cycle.

Traditional Igbo women's art and practice of painting on the body and the walls of shrines and houses, using primarily indigo and earth pigments, and featuring curvilinear abstract, occasionally figurative designs; now also incorporated into contemporary Nigerian art.

Amateur or professional photography that regards anything living and growing on the earth, generally with the exception of human beings. Subject matter is extended to plants, animals, and the places in which they live. Landscape and underwater photography may be considered distinct categories.

The disciplines of philosophy, logic, and cognate subjects, particularly as included in the course of study for a degree in the ancient school of Literae Humaniores. Often seen as counterparts to the "arts."

Study of human physiological and psychological capacities, limitations, and needs in relation to the human environment. In modern usage, the term is used particularly to refer to the workplace, regarding the the spaces, objects, and systems that people use.
The study and pursuit of archaeology, which is the study of human development and culture, using the methods and theories of geology.

Drawing a piece of leather or rawhide over a stationary rigid edge, either by hand or by machine, to soften it and render it more pliaable. Distinct from "perching" in that the leather moves and the tool is stationary.
Refers to the act of hitting of a blank in order to make an impression, as in making coins.
An electroanalytical scanning probe technique capable of imaging substrate topography and local reactivity with high resolution.

Discipline concerning the principles and rules of composition for persuasive speech, particularly as formulated by ancient critics and interpreted by classical scholars for application to discourse in the vernacular.
Discipline and activity of designing ornaments such as bracelets, necklaces, and rings for personal adornment.
Describes the activity of creating and repairing devices that indicate or measure time. See “watch making” for making or repairing timepieces worn or carried as personal accessories.

A manner of arranging stones in Asian-style gardens, in which rocks are scattered to accentuate the surrounding environment. A number of stones frequently are placed together to form a group, or used to enliven the surroundings in conjunction with other objects.
Process of insulating a space to prevent the passage of loud or disturbing sound or noise.

Process of making changes to objects, especially buildings or other structures, with the intention of improving their physical condition and returning them to a good state of repair. When such changes intend to return a building or structure to a state of historical correctness, use "restoration (process)." Distinguished from "rehabilitating" which refers to improving deteriorated structures. To relay the implication that the building is updated for the purpose of making it more sustainable, use "refurbishment."

Temporary structures for protecting the open grave immediately prior to interment or immediately after burial; typically having the form of a canopy, ramada, or tent. For structures of similar form, a ramada or shed but intended to exist for months or years rather than hours or days, prefer "gravehouses." For raised, canopied structures under which the coffin or effigy of a deceased person lies or is carried in state, prefer "catafalques."
Structures built and used for the purpose of swimming or other water recreation.
In Indian architecture, a waist; wall (early synonym for jaṅghā).
Areas, often of undefined boundaries. that are typically directly under the administration of a city. Examples are in the United States.

Graves consisting of deep, rectangular or round vertical or angled tunnels or shafts, or such shafts located above larger burial chambers. Examples are found at ancient Greek, Mycenaen, Egyptian, other Middle Eastern, Pre-Columbian, and Asian sites. The custom particularly flourished in the late Bronze Age (ca. 1600-1450 BCE), when the Greek mainland came under the cultural influence of Crete. To refer exclusively to the graves at Mycenae and other Bronze Age Greek sites, use "Shaft Grave period."

Refers to the hybrid style and culture of the Philippines reflecting the region's influx of trade and exchange with Chinese, Islamic, and Hindu cultures. Domestic folk arts of the archipelago nation reflect Indianized geometric motifs in textiles, weapons, and containers. Pre-colonial architecture featured megalithic monuments similar to late Tantric east Javanese tjandis. Painting and sculpture in the region reflect Indian erotic imagery, Buddhist images, and ornamental, curvilinear designs. Ceramic styles were often imitations of Chinese Sung Dynasty designs. As a result of Spanish colonialism from the 16th to 19th centuries, art later predominantly reflected Spanish Christian iconography in painting and colonial churches and cathedrals in Neo-Byzantine and elaborate, flamboyant designs. Secular art gained prominence in the later 19th century and followed European or international business aesthetics.
Buildings built or used for religious ceremonies or other functions having to do with a particular religion.
Architecture style espoused by Sol LeWitt and Giuseppe Terragni.
General term for various types of small openings with a grate or door, set within larger ones, including wickets set into doors, gates, or windows.
Objects used to lure or attract another into a trap.

Objects consisting of a long shaft with a bent or hooked end, usually of wood or metal, that are used to catch or hold another object, especially those used to restrain livestock or to gather hay while reaping. Employed in some cultures as a symbolic or ritual object, such as those used by the Yona Society of the Dogon people, in Mali.
Solvent that contains a hydrogen and carbon compound.

Refers to the culture of a Germanic people who in the early centuries of the Christian era lived in the area of modern Schleswig and along the Baltic coast, and who occupied Germany and the coasts of Gaul and Britain during the 5th and 6th centuries.
Refers to the culture of the Slavonic people who now inhabit Lusatia in eastern Saxony, but who formerly occupied most of Northern Germany.
Nationality or culture of Genoa, Liguria, Italy.

Refers to the loosely-organized movement in the 1920s characterized by subtle, quiet detachment and dedicated to the depiction of sharply defined forms such as the urban or rural skyline, the industrial landscape of buildings and machinery, or the bucolic landscapes of barns and fields. Artists in this style include Charles Demuth, Preston Dickinson, and Charles Sheeler.
Designating the latter part of the last Quaternary glacial period, immediately preceding the current postglacial period, marked predominantly by the retreat of glaciers.
Refers to the style and culture of the Bashkir people of modern day Russia, specifically the republic of Bashkortostan.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Florida.
Culture and style of the Faliscans, an ancient people of southern Etruria in Italy who, although Latin in origin, were culturally closer to the Etruscans.

Refers to the pottery style found in the northern Levant from about 6600 to 6000 BCE. The style is characterized by vessels formed by coils made from a composite of lime and salty gray ashes that when dried and fired turned into a hard white material.

Culture, style, and nationality of Haiti, a country in the Caribbean Sea that includes the western third of the island of Hispaniola and several smaller islands. The population is largely descended from enslaved Africans; the country won independence from France in 1804.
In Indian architecture, a rafter.

School or style of woodblock printmaking named for the Japanese port city. It offered glimpses of the customs and appearances of recently arrived visitors and large foreign resident population, usually produced for a Western audience.
Culture and nationality of ancient Thrace, which occupied territory now shared by Turkey, Southern Bulgaria, and the modern region of Thrace in Northeastern Greece.

The vernacular building technique in which the spaces between the heavy supporting timbers are filled with brick, wattle and daub, or other material. The term is also used to describe buildings with a false-timber frame attached to the outside wall to give the appearance of half-timber construction.
General term for large, open rooms in a residence or public building. In homes, the halls surpass in size and importance the private rooms or bowers, circulation spaces, or storage spaces.

Digital Image Correlation (DIC) is an optical image analysis method, based on gray value digital images captured by an optical sensor at a rate of 1,500 images per second. It employs tracking and image registration techniques to measure deformation, displacement, and strain on almost any material.
Absolving from the consequences of a fault or the punishment of a crime.
Rooms designed or used for showing films on a large screen for a private audience, usually for a small audience.
Designates a framework of open bins filled with rocks or other pervious materials and used as retaining walls or to support a construction.

In architecture and engineering, the divisions, parts, extent, distances, or spaces between supporting elements; for example between the abutments of an arch, the supports of a beam, the piers of a bridge, or the walls carrying a roof or dome.

The general term for types of Christian faith originating from the Reformation. Although the early forms of Protestantism were those who followed Luther, Calvin, and Zwingli, the term now includes most non-Roman Catholic or non-Orthodox denominations. Protestants want to be closer to the style of faith of the early Church which they feel has been obscured in Catholic practices. The term derives from the word 'protestari' which means not only to protest but to avow or confess. Common characteristics of Protestantism include the justification by faith alone, the authority of scripture, and the priesthood of all believers, in which not only the clergy are able to hear the confession of sin.

A Protestant denomination emphasizing a close personal relationship with God, the importance of the Holy Spirit, and a strong belief in the historical doctrines of Christianity. A simple and egalitarian form of worship in which ministers and laymen cooperate is advocated, as is work done on behalf of impoverished people. Methodism was started as an evangelical movement within the Church of England by John Wesley in 1739 and it became a separate denomination in 1795. The movement flourished as Wesley and other evangelical leaders traveled in England and to the American colonies. The main Methodist doctrine is laid out in Wesley's sermons, his notes on the New Testament, and his Articles of Religion.

Structures that are largely open and designed to provide shade, typically comprising four posts with a roof; may be roughly roofed with brush or branches or may have tent-like canvas or roofing of another material. The structure may be temporary or more permanent. For similar small, decorative structures in gardens, prefer "gazebos" or "pergolas."
The process or function of introducing new material; usage may overlap with "adding."

Refers to an indigenous religion of Tibet that is, along with Buddhism, one of the two main religions of the country. Many aspects of Bon were mixed with the Buddhist traditions introduced from India in the 8th century and gave Tibetan Buddhism much of its distinctiveness. Disagreement amongst the ruling class of Tibet in the 8th and 9th centuries resulted in the noble families choosing Bon and the ruling house choosing Buddhism. The religion became organized around the 11th century largely thanks to the Buddhist concern for written works. Besides surviving in many aspects of Tibetan Buddhism, Bon continues to thrive in the northern and eastern frontiers of Tibet. It is unclear how much continuity there is between ancient and modern Bon. The features of ancient Bon are hard to determine because all early description are Buddhist and what is known of Bon today is heavily influenced by Mahayana Buddhism. Ancient Bon seems to have featured animism, shamanism, and the practice of magic rites. The Bon gods of the atmosphere, the earth, and subterranean regions were incorporated into the Buddhist pantheon as lesser deities. There is evidence of a cult of divine kingship in which the kings are seen as manifestations of the sky divinity; this belief may be the root of the reincarnated lamas of Buddhism. Bon oracular priests have as their counterpart the Buddhist soothsayers. Aspects of Bon doctrine are virtually identical to that of Tibetan Buddhism, including doctrine of buddhahood and the bodhisattva ideal. Particularly noteworthy are the dzogchen beliefs of Bon that are shared with the Nyingma school of Tibetan Buddhism; these beliefs hold that there is an ineffable state beyond all Buddhas and all manifestation. The Bon monastic system is also almost identical to that of the Geluk school. Nevertheless, believers in Bon rigorously guard their non-Buddhist image. Shenrab is considered the founder of the religion and the historical Buddha Shakyamuni is said to be a manifestation of him. Bon scriptures are of one of two groups: the 'Kanjur,' containing myths, doctrines, and biographies of Shenrab; and 'Katen,' containing commentary and ritual and iconographic works. The name Tibet is derived from Bon.
Identifying the condition of a person, object, or structure.
Ornaments in the form of finials that surmount roof hips or gables.
In Indian architecture, an angular subdivision of the bhadra.
Risking money or other valuable stakes on the outcome of contests or other events whose outcome involves chance and is thus uncertain.
Events involving testing, tempting, or enticing to certain behavior, especially to illegal or evil activities.
Undertaking or offering to undertake, of one's own free will and without compensation, service to others or to some cause or institution, especially in a community context.
Sending out or apportioning something from a central source to a group, community, or individuals.

Rites or sacraments administered as a reaffirmation of a particular religious faith. Examples are the rites administered to baptized persons in various Christian churches, intended to bestow a special grace upon the recipient that confirms or strengthens their Christian faith.
Performances by a soloist or a small group, typically referring to musical recitals of a single musical piece or a selection of music, but may also refer to similar performances of dance or drama.
In Indian architecture, a triple bend of human figure.
Refers to pulls designed to be either completely or partially mortised into a door or drawer.

Spiritual clowns that perform during Puebloan ceremonies in the American Southwest; performers provide humor, personify important spirits, and teach cultural values through their dances. Often dressed in distinctive black-and-white striped clothing or bodypaint. Some kachina dolls take the form of koshares.
In Indian architecture, a śākhā in the form of a mālā; jamb in the form of a garland.
Activities that cause the reduction of a corpse to ashes, generally as a way of disposing of it.

Most architectural scholars agree that eaves tie beams (yan'e) refer to a structural element positioned atop the eaves pillars, which runs parallel to the roof ridge and spans at least three bays. The use of this element indicates a structural system where the roof is supported by a timber frame parallel to the roof ridge. This stands in contradistinction to the more commonly seen system where the timber-framing elements perpendicular to the roof ridge (support the roof. Scholars are in disagreement about whether the element referred to as the “eaves tie beam” must project from pillars at the corners of the building. The term is primarily used in the Yingzao fashi (1103). However many questions are still unsettled, including the precise definition of the yan’e as used in the Yingzao fashi, the relationship of the yan’e to the mei 楣 (an earlier term used to refer to a lintel), the relationship of the pillar top tie beam (lan’e 闌額), and to the “large-lintel style” (da’e shi 大額式) of structure commonly seen 13th-14th century architecture in Shanxi and Shaanxi, remain unsettled. They usually fall into one of two groups: (1) Scholars who believe that yan’e are lintels that extend through pillars at the corners of the building, following the description in the Yingzao fashi, Chapter 5, 4a. They look to the Linshui ting 臨水亭 of the Jidumiao 濟瀆廟 in Jiyuanxian, Henan, the main hall of the Guanwangmiao 關王廟大殿 in Dingxiangxian, Shanxi, and the Guanyinge 觀音閣 of Kaihuasi 開化寺, in Gaoping municipality, Shanxi as examples. (2) Scholars who emphasize the comment in the Yingzao fashi stating the dimensions of the yan’e regularly exceed those of other timbers used in this location argue that the large individual horizontal timbers on top of eaves pillars that extend the full breadth of the façade are yan’e. They look to the Yuan period Yuwang Hall 禹王殿 in Hancheng municipality, Shaanxi, and the main hall of the Guangsheng Lower Monastery 廣勝下寺大殿 in Hongtong, Shanxi, as examples.

Phenomenon whereby the surface and the lower atmosphere of a planet are maintained at a relatively high temperature owing to the greater transparency of the atmosphere to visible radiation from the sun than to infrared radiation from the planet. It is so-called because the heating of Earth's atmosphere is loosely analogous to the glass of a greenhouse letting light in but not letting heat out. The term is often used to refer specifically to the increased magnitude of this effect occurring in the modern age in the context of global warming: Gases from the burning of fossil fuels and other sources, including water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, and chlorofluorocarbons, absorb infrared radiation and prevent its energy from leaving the Earth, resulting in the increasing mean global surface temperature.
The ability of a structure to maintain its intended position and orientation.

Legal instruments authorizing one to act as the attorney or agent of the grantor, either generally for the management of a specified enterprise or, specifically, for the accomplishment of a particular transaction.
Refers to the approach to visual art, literature, theater, and music that emphasizes the emotional, dramatic, or exotic.
Including, participated in by, involving, or affecting, all, or nearly all, the parts of a specified or implied whole; completely or approximately universal within implied limits.
General term for chambers used for baking, heating, or drying; for heating equipment used to harden or char various specific materials, use "kilns."
Fabric coated with red iron oxide marketed in sheets and used for polishing metal.

Tools consisting of two perpendicular arms, usually made of wood, metal, plastic, or a combination of these materials, fixed together so as to form a right angle; used for marking right angles or testing the squareness of sides, edges, or surfaces.
Tool or machines for cutting screw-threads.
Wood or iron tools used to cut threads on wood screws or pegs.
Cuplike devices with a quill spout through which slip is poured to produce trailed decoration.
Boards made of soft material such as cork on which cord may be pinned and worked into knotted designs.
Violent disturbances of the atmosphere attended by wind and usually also by rain, snow, sleet, or hail.

State of the atmosphere with respect to such factors as wind, temperature, cloudiness, moisture, and pressure. For the long-term total of atmospheric variations at a specific geographical location, use "climate."

Glazed, patterned, or textured paper produced by pressing or sliding objects into a wet, often colored paste or starch mixture that has been spread on the paper; frequently used as decorative endpapers or cover papers.
A type of fine white clay used to make tobacco pipes and fine earthenwares.
Curved adzes with a strong blade; used for hollowing the insides of wheel rims or the curved parts of coach frames. May also be used for hammering.
Systems of money, usually those in general use in a particular country. For the paper bills, coins, or other monetary items as objects, use "money(objects)."

A Roman Catholic order for men founded in 1540 by St. Ignatius of Loyola, a Spanish soldier who experienced a religious conversion while convalescing from a battle wound. It is a non-contemplative order requiring strict obedience, compliance with Ignatius' Spiritual Exercises, and special loyalty to the pope. The Jesuits abandoned many medieval practices including obligatory regular penances or fasts; a common dress; and the choral recitation of the liturgical office. Other innovations include their very centralized form of authority with life tenure for the head of the order; gradation of members; a probationary period of many years before final vows; and lack of a female branch. Jesuits carry out many kinds of missionary work with special emphasis on education; the order has founded many colleges and universities throughout the world. The Jesuits have been leading apologists for the Roman Catholic Church, particularly during the Counter-Reformation. In more recent times, the order has been highly influential in modernizing the Church.
Relatives who are bound to one through the marriage of a blood relative to another person after the death or divorce of the spouse of that blood relative.

Christian sect originating in Asia Minor and Syria that follows the beliefs of Nestorius, a 5th-century bishop of Constantinople whose doctrine was considered heretical by the established church. Nestorius stressed the independence of the divine and human natures of Christ and, in effect, suggested that they were two persons loosely united. Current members live in Iraq, Syria, and Iran.
A method for transferring a drawing to another surface on a different scale, especially to a larger surface that is to be painted, such as a canvas or a wall.
Practitioners of medicine with a doctorate in any of its branches, especially those licensed by the proper authorities.
Those who advocate feminism, or the study of ideas related to women or female gender issues in general.

Refers to double pictures of the same scene that produce the effect of three dimensionality when viewed through a stereoscope. They were first envisioned in 1832 by the English physicist Charles Wheatstone, who described this as a uniquely photographic art form, since a draftsman could not draw two scenes in exact perspective from viewpoints separated only 2 1/2 inches, which is the normal distance between human eyes necessary for the three-dimensional effect. Wheatstone's mirror stereoscope was not practical for use with photographs, and the invention was not popular until the 1850s, when Sir David Brewster, a Scottish scientist, designed a simpler viewing instrument. The introduction of the collodion process, which simplified exposure and printing techniques, allowed three-dimensional photographs to become a popular craze. They may be daguerreotypes, negatives, or other forms of photographs. For images in the form of photographic prints on cards, use the more specific term "stereographs."

Refers to a distinctive pottery that was produced in Bologna, Italy, and elsewhere, primarily from the 15th through the 18th centuries. It was created by dipping the earthenware body into clay slip and covering it with a lead glaze. Designs were incised into the slip, sometimes in conjunction with the application of green and manganese glazes. The technique was copied from certain Chinese and Korean objects, and it was practiced by Byzantine potters in Constantinople before appearing in Italy about 1500. Though it superficially resembles true "maiolica," or tin-glazed earthenware, it is distinct from maiolica in that lead glaze is used instead of tin glaze, designs are applied by incision through the slip to reveal differently colored clay beneath rather than by painting, and the colors tend to run during firing.
All the devices, fittings, or assemblies necessary to operate a window, such as catches, sash cords, fasteners, hinges, handles, locks, pulls, pulleys, and sash weights.
The psychological process of experiencing devotional feelings in a private sphere, whether or not encouraged by the church authorities, often with the aid of texts, figurines or images.
Infinite time, which has neither beginning nor end.

Photographic prints made using a light-sensitive emulsion of a ferric salt and silver nitrate. When developed, a metallic silver image is formed; various developers can produce black, brown, purple, or maroon tones.
Portraits taken in a professional photographer's studio, often making use of backdrops or props.
African masks characterized by animal horns, whether real or imitation, projecting from the top of the mask.

Refers to technique that induces a viewer wearing spectroscopic glasses to see a pair of two dimensional images of the same object captured from slightly different angles as a single entity existing in three dimensions in space.
Level paved or planted areas, usually elevated above surrounding terrain and adjacent to buildings or parts of garden complexes, or if in a building, in the upper stories or on the roof.
Representations of the Earth, heavens, or another planet in the form of a ball.
Books containing coupons that entitle the holder to a fixed allowance of a rationed item.

Refers to maps that depict a polar projection, which is an azimuthal projection drawn to show Arctic or Antarctic areas. Such a projection is based on a plane perpendicular to the Earth's axis in contact with the North or South Pole, and is limited to around 10 or 15 degrees from the poles. Parallels of latitude are depicted as concentric circles and meridians are radiating straight lines.
Official lists of entries of any information considered sufficiently important to be exactly and formally recorded, typically maintained in numerical or chronological order in a regular manner.
Documents containing sets of tables for calculating astronomical events and movable dates on the calendar such as feast days; sometimes also recording the rules governing the tables.
The discipline dealing with the translation, interpretation, and care of ancient documents written on papyrus, which is of prime importance in Egyptian, Middle Eastern, and Classical archaeology.

Functions including organizing, supervising, and carrying out the activities of a person, group, organization, or enterprise, and controlling its human and material resources, involving primarily the application rather than the formulation of policy. When the formulation of policy is the primary aspect, use "administration."
When used with a color term, refers to a lustrous appearance, resembling the sheen of a metal surface.
Information electronically recorded that requires a computer or other electronic device for display, interpretion, and processing.
Describes buildings having engaged columns or pilasters along the sides and rear and freestanding columns along the front.

Motion pictures created by independent filmmakers, without financial backing from a major studio and with generally a greater degree of artistic control in the hands of the filmmakers than is the case with studio films.  Major studio distribution systems may handle their release to theaters.
Photographic prints made to resemble miniature paintings on ivory.
The position or condition of being inside relative to a reference point.

A non-continuous lace named for a town in East Devon, where it is thought to have originated from around the 18th century. Inspired by Brussels lace, typical motifs are roses, thistles and cloverleaves.
Photographic processes that record the effects of interference patterns of wavelengths of light as they interact with surfaces or filters.
Ceremonial chairs or seats occupied by a monarch, prelate, or other high dignitary, especially on state or other special occasions; usually placed upon a dais and covered with a canopy.

Refers to the expressionistic style inspired by children's art characteristic of a group formed in 1948 by artists from Copenhagen, Brussels, and Amsterdam. The formalized group is often referred to as a movement, though technically it is a corporate body made up of founding members, rather than a generalized movement with unaffiliated members.

General term for natural courses of water flowing continuously along a defined bed on the surface of the earth, forming a river, rivulet, brook, etc. The term is not used for canals or other artificial watercourses.

Vascular plants such as  conifers, cycads, ginkgo and others that reproduce by means of an exposed seed or ovule, as opposed to an angiosperm or flowering plant, which have seeds enclosed by mature ovaries or fruits. Gymnosperm seeds develop either on the surface of scale- or leaf-like appendages of cones, or at the end of short stalks. In early classification schemes, Gymnospermae were regarded as a taxonomic group, although modern classifications recognize that the fossil record suggests that angiosperms are nested within gymnosperms (thus living gymnosperms are not actually a clade).

Designates wild and uncultivated regions that have been left untouched in a natural state by humans, with no human control or interference; distinct from "nature reserves" in which plant and animal communities are protected and controlled; distinct from "wilderness areas" which are lands where natural growth is protected by legislation, and recreation and industrial use are restricted.
Events involving groups of people and friendly interaction.
Sending out official or legal instruments and documents such as warrants, writs, and licenses.

Conducting moral reflections with 'the good' as a criterion. In the European cultural climate from the 16th century onwards, bourgeois morality increasingly influenced Christian morality. Moralizing paintings emerged in which messages advocating for forms of morality can be read.

Four-square structures with two intersecting passageways and four façades. The axes are each symmetrically framed by columnar or arcuated architecture. The term is usually used in the context of monumental ancient Roman architecture. Quadrifrons were often built at right-angled crossroads and typically stood free. Quadrifrons could be triumphal or honorific in nature. Quadrifrons were particularly popular in North Africa. Notable examples are the Arch of Marcus Aurelius at Tripoli and the Janus Quadrifrons in Rome. The term can also refer to a sculptural form most often used as architectural ornamentation consisting of four faces or fronts looking out in four directions.
Buildings or parts of buildings housing firms that specialize in making arrangements for the transport and  accommodation of travellers.
Open spaces designed for public use or are accesible to the public, often designed to foster a sense of community.
Vases, commonly made of porcelain or ceramic, made to decorate religious altars. Examples include Yuan-period porcelain vases used for Buddhist altars.

Aesthetic and poetic ideal particularly important in the Japanese tea ceremony and haiku poetry which advocates taking pleasure and finding tranquility in the old, tarnished and imperfect for their own sake. It is sometimes used synonymously or in conjunction with the concept of "wabi".
Material comprising or made from the flowering plant structures containing the seeds.

Plan of a building or city that is shaped like a Greek cross, with a square central mass and four arms of equal length. The Greek cross plan was widely used in Byzantine architecture and in Western churches inspired by Byzantine examples.
Thin strips of material such as leather, card, or board, attached to the back of a text block before it is covered; done to books with a hollow back binding to imitate the appearance of true bands.
Baskets of varying form used to transport goods on animals or humans; includes those with one flattened side made to conform to the contour of the body.
The shell of the hawksbill sea turtle, which is a critically endangered sea turtle, used for decorative purposes. When processed, a type of tortoiseshell.
Typically, round wooden vessels for drawing water from a well; also, any comparable vessel for catching, holding, or carrying liquids or solids.
Coins that are incorrectly struck.
Use to describe objects which, in contact with another surface, move tangentially in a smooth, continuous, gliding motion by means of gravity or momentum.

Use to describe things produced by human action, as opposed to natural causes, but not intended to substitute for natural counterparts. For things produced by human action and intended to substitute for their natural counterparts, use "artificial." For things produced specifically by synthesis, use "synthetic."
The activity of making furrows in and turning up soil with a plough, generally as a preparation for sowing or planting.

Compositions focusing on fanciful characters involved in pranks, capers, or other imaginary activities, or on buildings or architectural features grouped in arbitrary, imaginary arrangements or in a fantasy setting. Use especially with reference to 18th-century Italian paintings and prints. For views that are realistically conceived but the topography or architectural elements are unrealistic and imaginary, use "vedute ideate."
Indicates the highest or loftiest parts of objects. For the adjective describing the location of something at or near the top of something, use "top" from the Attributes and Properties hierarchy.
Genre of written works published or otherwise available in printed form, usually on paper.

Thin elongated pieces of cane, wood, metal, plastic or other material, found in various musical instruments; they are set into vibration by the air stream created by the player's breath or by bellows, thus producing sound.

Painted or carved works consisting of multiple panels. They are typically altarpieces, but may be objects with other functions as well. The polyptych normally consists of a central panel with an even number of side-panels, which are sometimes hinged to fold, and a predella. Although any object with two or more panels may technically be called a 'polyptych,' the word is typically reserved for anything larger than a triptych. In early usage, the Greek term 'polyptycha' referred to multiple-panel writing tablets and calendar icons.
Portraits cut from paper and mounted on a contrasting background; also, by extension, images showing no interior detail set against a contrasting background.
Refers to scaled or lifesize representations of objects, structures, beings, or other subjects, usually three-dimensional.

Works for which identification with a particular physical work, either movable work or architecture, is ambiguous. For example, the name "Totocalco" was associated with both a storehouse and an aviary in ancient Tenochtitlan.
Designs or arrangements comprising fired brick, sometimes glazed or otherwise decorated, arranged using bricklaying, especially arrangements in patterns or images.
Occasions of sweeping change in established patterns of government or social organization.
Rugs with one or more mihrabs, arch-shaped designs, toward one end of the field; so called since many were intended for use by a Moslem for daily prayers. Commonly of small size.
Depictions that are specifically and primarily of the human form.
Soldiers armed with rifles.  Formerly used specifically for superior marksmen armed with the best models of rifles and formed into specially trained companies.
Rugs having loops or tufts extending above the foundation or ground to form a raised, thick surface.
Early 19th-century American rugs woven in broad lengthwise stripes with a heavy homespun wool yarn, the width was suitable for stair coverings or they were seamed together to make room-sized rugs.
Lighting devices designed to produce an approximately parallel beam of light, mounted on a fixed or movable platform.

Simple staff weapons having a sharp-pointed head and no auxiliary blades or points, used both in warfare and hunting since ancient times in many cultures and regions. Various forms have been designed for thrusting or throwing or both.
Art objects acquired unjustly or without sanction. This may include objects stolen, confiscated, sold by force, exchanged or renounced during armed conflicts, revolutions or in a colonial context.
A salt or ester of oxalic acid.

Bridge or spacer made of refractory material between a core and the outer mold in casting. It serves a double function as core support while also providing better air flow into the core to aid in its drying before the bronze is poured.
Akan terracota heads used in Africa in funerary and burial contexts.

Tradesmen who buy and sell in in large quantities (i.e., in the gross), particularly food items, including spices, dried fruits, sugar, etc., and other articles of domestic consumption, often excluding products sold in specialty stores.
Sheet metal bottom seam in which only the bottom edge is turned, and then locked into an opposing sheet with a simple bent edge.
One of the long bars between a pair of which an animal is harnessed to a carriage or other vehicle.
A variation of XRF imaging that allows visualization of the distribution of elements in a flat, macroscopic sample, up to several square meters, in a non-destructive manner.
Period term for lighting devices, such as chandeliers and candelabras, made of glass or ornamented with glass pendants.
Formal statements that recognize the unique and enduring relationships that exist between indigenous peoples and their traditional territories.
Buildings housing museums containing collections dealing with the development and application of science, scientific ideas, technology, and instrumentation.

The action or condition of causing something, such as a group or society, to exist. Examples include establishment through the granting of legal status or by an official gathering together of members of a group.
People who compose written material, often as an occupation or profession, whether or not they are responsible for the underlying intellectual content.
Experts in sexual behavior.
Sheets or cards, usually with tabs, used for keeping files organized in file containers.

Various types of patterns that consist of interweaving lines or bands. If these are rectilinear, use "frets (patterns)" or "fretwork," if they form a very regular series of near circles, use "guilloche."
Persons whose actions or attributes are characterized, influenced, or prompted by excessive or mistaken enthusiasm especially in religious contexts.
Tools or equipment for working fibers, generally restricted to fibers other than textile fibers.
People or corporate bodies engaged in the making of rugs and carpets, which are textiles having the primary purpose of covering a flat surface, usually a floor.
In Indian architecture, a hollow chamber within the śikhara; cavity in the śukanāsa; basal plinth-moulding.
Long seats of two basic types: a low-back bench with arms and a bench with a high, usually solid, back and with arms and wings. For settles with hinged seats use "box settles."
A German word meaning 'art wish' that is used to refer to artistic intention.
Isoprene polymer which includes the main constituent in natural rubber.

Mechanised tools, composed of two or more parallel rollers that rotate toward eachother at high speeds, used to crush colored pigments or paste into a homogenous consistency for the manufacture of paint products.

Motif resembling knotted, gnarled branches of a young crab apple tree, used as the form for handles and spouts that developed on 18th-century English stoneware, particularly that made by the Staffordshire, Leeds, Liverpool, and Derby potteries.
Ornament in the form of a series of small convex curves; often used as an edging.
As an artistic concept, the characteristic within a composition where a form, line, color, or other compositional element is repeated to cause unity or for another purpose.
Protective measures such as rejection coatings and filters intended to eliminate and reduce deleterious effects of ultraviolet radiation.
Shallow piers or rectangular columns projecting only slightly from a wall and, in classical architecture, conforming with one of the orders. Common also on furniture.
Lion pouncing on elephant decorative motif; kari-kumbha-vidari.
Structures comprising the buildings, machinery, apparatus, and fixtures required to shape or process metal into products on an industrial level.

Overnight public accommodations for motorists generally characterized by long low-rise buildings consisting of rows of attached individual sleeping quarters and having direct access between the rooms and parking spaces without an intervening lobby.
High chests of deep drawers used for keeping priest's vestments, often with a table so that the garments can be laid out, and a mirror so that the priests can see that they are properly attired.
In Indian architecture, a "convolution of caterpillar"; convolving/undulating pediment-border.
Documents, published or unpublished, listing or describing a body of records within a records center or archives, making them more readily accessible and comprehensible to the user.
Scripts some of whose letters have ascenders or descenders above or below a general base line and top line.

Use generally for any of several types of levers, operated by the foot and used on sound devices for a variety of purposes such as to change tuning, operate a bellows, strike a drum head, produce expressive effects, or function as keys in a pedalboard.

Armor pieces for the foot existing in various forms in Europe from Medieval times to the 16th century, comprised of mail or plates enclosing the ankle and lames covering the foot, plus a plate toecap. Some types had a detachable long point for the toecap.

Protective garments consisting of overlapping plates of steel, aluminum, or bonded fiberglass attached within a nylon jacket. They were developed during the Second World War to protect aircraft crews against fragments from antiaircraft shells, and are now also widely used by ground combat personnel.

Term used in the glass trade for a type of art glass made by the New England Glass Company in 1885, consisting of clear glass enlarged by repeated mold blowing and decorated with a network of acid etched lines, or having a mottled surface created by rolling the vessel in an acid resistant substance and then acid bathing.
Hollow forms of a circular or tubular shape into which food may be poured or pressed in order to shape it into a decorative ring.

Vessels, having a relatively stout shape, sometimes called "jars" or "bottles"; distinguished by having a double-branch/single-spout form that resembles a riding saddle stirrup. The form was known in Precolumbian art for 2,500 years. It has been suggested that the peculiar spout was used to prevent evaporation of the liquids contained in the vessel.
Bottles, usually glass and cylindrical, with sloping shoulders and a medium-length neck. They are designed to be plugged or capped, and intended to contain carbonated beverages.

Roman bronze coins valued at one-half as and issued first as cast and then as struck coins from the Republic through the 2nd century CE, and then for gold coins valued at one-half solidus issued in the Eastern Empire from the 4th through the 8th century CE.
Any of various coins issued in France and French-speaking territories since the mid-14th century.
Graduated scales attached to the rear sights of firearms, most often rifles, by which the shooter adjusts the sight to allow for the effect of wind.

Written or pictorial symbols intended to represent a whole word. Writing systems that make use of logograms include Chinese, Egyptian hieroglyphic writing, and early cuneiform writing systems. No known writing system is totally logographic; all such systems have both logograms and symbols representing particular sounds or syllables. In phonography, a logogram is a word-letter or a single stroke which, for brevity's sake, represents a word.

Works of church music written to be sung as a single vocal line in free rhythm and a restricted scale, in a style developed for the medieval Latin liturgy. It is monodic and does not need instrumental accompaniment although this may be provided. Gregorian chant is named after Saint Gregory the Great (ca. 540-604) who is said to have standardized it. Gregorian chant refers to a Roman form of early plain chant as distinguished from the Ambrosian, Galliean, and Mozarabic chants, which were similar, but were gradually supplanted by it from the eighth to the eleventh century.
In the Roman Catholic Church, books of directions for all services throughout the year, without the actual texts. In the Church of England, service books for the consecration or ordination of clergy.
Curtains consisting of straight panels of cloth tacked to the top of the window frame or sometimes suspended from rods by rings or loops attached at the top of the curtain.
Small mills for grinding spices, usually hand-operated.
Device used in cheese- making for breaking cheeses in into smaller pieces.

Refers to a Ukrainian woodwind, a small transverse flute resembling a fife with six to ten fingerholes; by extension may refer to a variety of woodwinds of the flute family played by Ukrainian folk instrumentalists.
Metal pots or skillets with three feet and a long straight handle.
Flat, often rectangular or oval, plates bearing a usually printed or engraved name of, for example, a person or company.
Mechanized coffee roasters, typically electric, into which coffee beans are placed and slowly roasted. For hand-held devices used to roast coffee over an open fire, use "coffee roasters."
Literature having to do with plants and botany.
Globe-shaped bottles with applied handles made from 1815 to 1875 and used both as containers for store-bought whiskey and as decanters at home.
Procedures used in the planographic process, where images are printed from flat surfaces.

A relief process in which the design is cut into and printed from the plank side of a wood block; distinct from "wood engraving (process)," which is a relief process using the grain end of a wood block.
Any of a number of cooking utensils made of iron, such as a waffle iron, designed to enable the user to place food in or over a heat source.
A type of kantharos that is a variant of type D. It is named for the potter Sotades.
Oinochoai with a continuous S-curved slender body and a high handle which extends above the round mouth. They were used for pouring wine or water. Olpai were popular at Corinth and also in Athens.

Knitted or crocheted bags popular from the 19th century. They are often tube-like and narrower in the middle, with rounded or squared ends. Miser’s purses were usually gender-specific in the first half of the 19th century. Short purses 4 to 6 inches in length were for women and long purses 7 to 10 inches long for men. By the mid-19th century, all were the larger size to accommodate larger coins. They would triple in length by the early 20th century. They are most typically opened via a slit in the middle, held together by rings. Often they are embellished with beadwork motifs.
Vessels used for drinking liquids.

Wooden boxes with slots where cutlery of various sizes is stored. These often bore decoration, and the more elaborate examples may exhibit exterior carving, marquetry, or inlays, and interiors lined with silk or velvet.
Tall pouring vessels which have a single handle and a hinged lid with a finial and thumbpiece. Usually without a lip or spout; intended to be used for serving wine.
Small round shallow drums, usually with one or more snares, played in ensemble with tabor pipes; they are played with the right hand while suspended from the player's neck or left arm.
Cups made of paper, often made leak-proof by a coating of plastic or wax; typically intended for one use. First documented in imperial China by 2nd century BCE.
Cups used to contain liquids used for libations at religious ceremonies; vary in shape and size but generally have a low foot-ring and a handle.
Containers intended to receive expectorated material, usually for the use of tobacco chewers.
Small receptacles to contain scented vinegar, formerly used by women, and sometimes men, to ward off faintness.

Ceramic vessels that have multiple spouts emerging from the body volume. Designs vary from pyramidal multi-piece stacking structures to smaller single-piece forms. These first appeared in the Netherlands in the 17th century and were decorated in the style of Delftware with its typical blue-on-white surface mimicing Chinese decoration.

Straight-edged strips or cylinders of medium size, usually of wood, metal, plastic, or ivory and having demarcations to indicate units of measurement, used for measuring and for guiding a pen, pencil, or other marking-instrument in forming straight lines upon paper or another material. They are used in geometry, drafting, drawing, carpentry, building, interior design, crafts, and other disciplines. For very long bars or strips of wood or metal having straight and true edges and used for a variety of purposes, including cutting or establishing the evenness of surfaces, use "straightedges."

A type of ancient Greek incense burner or small incense altar made of bronze, silver, or terracotta; the perfumed smoke of the incense would escape through decorative openings. Thymiateria were functional objects but may also have been placed in tombs as funerary offerings.

Binders, books, albums, or other collections of pages that permit the withdrawal and insertion of pages at any desired position by means of rings, posts, cords, or some other type of fastener securing the margins of the individual leaves.
Articles designed to serve as receptacles for keeping or storing liquid or other substances.
Containers for holding hair collected from the owner's hair brush, especially bowls with covers which have a hole in their center.
Flat, flexible rectangular containers with a handle used for carrying books, papers, or the like, and often made of leather. For flat, rigid, rectangular containers use "attaché cases."
Indentations in the bottom of a drinking glass or in the base of any glass object; when in the bottom of a drinking glass or bottle, they add to the stability but reduce capacity.
Weighing devices especially designed for weighing railway equipment, either empty or loaded, singly or coupled.
Cambodian spike fiddles with two strings.
Cylindrical or tapering graduated vessels calibrated in fluid ounces or milliliters for measuring the volume of liquids.
Devices for measuring the area of any plane surface by tracing the boundary of the area.
Clocks that strike time according to the system of bells used on ships.
Bowls made of human skulls, used in Hindu and Buddhist rituals, often containing offerings to deities.
Instruments designed to measure torque.
Instruments for measuring differences in electrical potential.
Devices used for for measuring angles between lines on vertical planes.

Christian liturgical vessels in which the Host (the bread consecrated in the Eucharist) may be displayed through an opening or through a transparent material; used either on an altar or in processions. It is usually made of gold or silver and is often decorated with precious stones. From the Baroque period onwards the Host is typically surrounded by a sunburst design. Modern usage has limited the meaning to vessels intended for the exposition of the Host; however the term was originally applied to all kinds of vessels of goldsmith's or silversmith's work in which glass or crystal were used to allow the contents to be readily visible, whether the contents were the Host, a relic of a saint, or another object. Distinguished from "pyxes," which are vessels used to hold the reserved Host on the altar or to carry the Eucharist to the sick.
Large or strong containers used especially for transporting goods.
Drinking vessels made of horn, especially those elaborately mounted in bronze or silver.
Refers to the style and culture of modern Iraq.

Ancient single-string instruments, first mentioned in 5th century BCE Greece, used variously throughout history as a musical instrument, a device for measuring and demonstrating musical intervals, and an organ tuner's and piano tuner's adjunct.

Dolls dressed in traditional clothes and representing people in various positions of society, created by native people in a Christian mission; particularly carved wooden dolls created by Chinese women and children in British Christian missions in China during the 1920s.
Long necked lutes of the Middle East and Central Asia, usually with 15 movable frets and 2 strings.
Short necked lutes of China. Yüeh ch'in have a circular body, four strings, a flat back, and metal tongues inside their bodies.
Y-shaped sticks with a band of plastic, leather, or other elastic material attached between the prongs, used to propel small stones in hunting or play.

Strategy board games for two players dating perhaps to the Roman Empire. The game has many variations based on the number of pieces, and corresponding variant names. The playing surface consists of a grid with intersections or points. In the most common form, each player has nine pieces in contrasting colors. Players attempt to form correspondences of pieces aligned to allow a player to remove an opponent's piece from the game. A player wins by reducing an opponent's number of pieces to a minimum, or to allow no possible moves.
Books that contain actual samples, not just illustrations, usually of merchandise available for purchase.
Promotional material located in, at, or on retail establishments that is provided by the manufacturer or their agent.
The ratio of the mass of a given volume of a substance to the mass of the same volume of water at 4 degrees Celsius.

Tight-fitting combination garments worn as the standard uniform for competitive wrestlers. Typically made of nylon, lycra, spandex, or other smooth fabrics that cover the torso and thighs while leaving the arms exposed. The form-fitting nature of this garment is designed so that officials can easily detect a wrestler's bodily contact with the mat when awarding points.
Short dresses with hemlines that extend to mid-thigh; fashionable from the 1960s onwards.

A deep red natural colorant made from secretions of the larvae of the lac insect. Lac dye is a byproduct produced during the shellac purification process; its primary colorant is laccaic acid. It was an important dyestuff used since ancient times, giving a lightfast tint to silk and wool, similar in color to dyes obtained from cochineal and kermes. Now synthetic colorants have replaced the use of lac dye.

Any of a family of water-soluble polymers that range in viscosity from liquid to wax-like solid. They are present in organic solvents for dyes and resins; and used as wetting agents, emulsifiers, and plasticizers.
Letters or characters from one alphabet displayed or exchanged for those of another that represent similar sounds in another language.

Pieces of parchment inscribed on one side with the required Pentateuchal texts and on the other with the divine name Shaddai, enclosed in a container and attached to the doorpost of a Jewish house in fulfilment of religious law.
Unpublished works, including documents not formally published or commerically available, including reports, internal organizational paperwork, or theses.
Academic caps consisting of a close-fitting cap surmounted by a broad, flat projecting square top from which a tassel hangs.
Closed tab, usually laced shoes, with the front opening stitched under the vamp.
Footwear of varied design in which the upper extends above the ankle joint and that covers the leg up to the knee.
The pivoted steel plates from which sparks are struck by the flint in a snaphance. For the hand-held tools used to strike a piece of flint to produce sparks, use "firesteels."
Four-wheeled carriages carrying both passengers and mail; used during the 18th and early 19th centuries.
Soft, cloth caps with a gathered crown, worn indoors by women in the 18th century.

The complete central structures of aircraft, to which the wings, tail assemblies, and engines may be attached. In the early 20th century, the term was taken from French specifically to refer to the framework of the body of an airplane, particularly the girder-like backbone employed in airplane design; it has since come to mean the entire central structure of the aircraft.
Devices on the gunwales of boats, usually U-shaped, for holding an oar in place and forming a fulcrum for the oar in rowing.

Rolling metal carts, usually used in commercial contexts that provide a method of transporting large, unweildy materials like plywood. These usually have rails to keep things upright, and are designed to accommodate a variety of materials such as drywall and pipes.
White crystalline compound that is soluble in water and insoluble in alcohol. Its uses include: reducing agent in photography, oxidizing agent, antiseptic, soap manufacture, and desizing of textiles.

Transparent cases, usually of glass and brass that provide a source of light for use on seagoing vessels. Traditionally these would contain a liquid fuel and flammable wick, and were used for a variety of purposes including signaling or ambient lighting.

Straps for securing helmets or hats under the chin. For ribbons or strings used to tie on hats under the chin, particularly when they are decorative, use "chin ties." For bands of cloth or another material tied around the top of the head and under the chin, use "chin bands."
Clothing and coverups used while making one's toilet and dressing.
Protective helmets for the benefit of fighter pilots. From the advent of jet aircraft these have been equipped with visors and provisions for communications, breathing, or other equipment.
Toys that are intended for outdoor play.
Type of traditional shawl or wrap worn by women, particularly in 19th century Netherlands, often held in place with silver clasps.
Books won or offered as a prize; usually special books of very high quality and having content thematically related to the event or accomplishment for which the prize was awarded.
Bindings having a space between the spine of the text block and the spine of the cover.
A scarf tied round the knees to assist in practice of yōga.
Accessories used in connection with doll-playing. Toys or miniature objects that accompany figurines representing humans or animals.

The salt of formic acid, sodium formate is used as a neutral buffering agent. It sometimes appears spontaneously as a layer of white crystalline efflorescence on sodium-rich glass artefacts exposed to the pollutant gas formaldehyde.
Specially designed horseshoe-shaped objects made of various hard durable materials and used for the game of horseshoe pitching.

Toy consisting of a set of wooden dolls of decreasing size placed one inside another. A set of matryoshkas consists of a wooden figure, which separates at the middle, top from bottom, to reveal a smaller figure of the same sort inside, which has, in turn, another figure inside of it, and so on.The smallest, innermost doll is typically a baby turned from a single piece of wood.
Small boy's suits with high-waisted trousers which button at the waist of the accompanying jacket or waistcoat; of a type worn in the late 18th and early 19th century.
Extra long skirts that usually extend to the ankle. Also, similar components of a dress, coat, or the like.

Close-fitting trousers that fit over footwear and strap under the sole, worn especially as part of a military uniform or for horseback riding. Use also for loose-fitting trousers worn over breeches or other bifurcated garments as protective wear by military personnel and others, especially during the 18th and 19th centuries.
Sleeveless knee-length vestments worn by cardinals, bishops, and certain other high-ranking ecclesiastics.The color of the garment indicates rank.
Very short jackets or sweaters with sleeves cut in one with the body.

Sheathlike coverings that encase the penis; may be attached to a belt or girdle. Often made of plaited plant material, animal intestine, or hides or skins and decorated; worn especially by African men.
Items having a certain weight, that are sewn onto, clipped onto, or inserted into the hem or lower edge of a garment in order to improve the drape, causing the fabric to hang down properly.
Articles that overlie articles worn on the head with the effect of protecting, enclosing, decorating, or hiding them.
Thick, heavy cloaks or coats worn by seamen, soldiers, or watchmen when on duty in bad weather.
Protective outerwear suits of jackets and trousers, made of oiled waterproof cloth.
Skirts worn beneath another; use especially for those underskirts designed to be seen.
Supports in the form of hoops or padded rolls, worn beneath a skirt to add fullness; of a type worn in the 16th and 17th centuries.

Ribbons or sashes, usually white in color and tied in a bow, formerly worn by both boys and girls in some Christian churches when they received their first communion or their solemn communion. The item was often retained as a souvenir of the event. Where this practice is continued today, the bow is often smaller and attached to a sleeve.
Arabic script possibly invented by calligrapher Ibn Muqlah in the 9th century CE, and based on the thuluth script.
Self-propelled airborne explosive devices that are intended to be launched from a source under the the surface of a body of water to hit targets that are on terrain.
Devices consisting of wire loops on a handle used to lift hot plates.
Main outerwear garments that cover the body above and below the waist and are bifurcated. For a similar undergarment, use "combinations (underwear)."
General term for a form of outerwear of differing lengths and having some shaping.

Utensils used to hold food out of its cooking liquid, usually oval, but sometimes circular, consisting of a pierced plate that rests in a deeper and wider serving dish. Often of silver with elaborate pierced work, sometimes depicting a net holding fish.

Elaborately decorated metal feet and stems onto which ordinary glasses can be clamped thus forming an elegant vessel. They were made as prestige objects to adorn the table. In the 15th century glass holders were often commissioned by city councils and aristocrats. By the 17th century, wealthy burghers had acquired a taste for these objects, although the fashion declined after 1650. Most glass holders were made of bronze, silver or silver gilt. The clamps often incorporated a human figure, a sea-horse or an animal head.
Tweezer-like tools, often with indentations or holes in the rounded tips, used to remove the green leaves from the tops of strawberries.
Equipment, such as remedies and bandages, used to dress or cover a sore, wound, or other lesion.

Mechanized devices, comprising a series of rollers supported by an asymetrical frame, used to stretch, smooth, and lengthen tubular knit goods or cloth materials. The device's frame is typically constructed to be wider at one end, gradually decreasing in width towards the other end, so that one roller is at a higher elevation than the rest. The cloth or knit goods are spread over the frame and the rollers, sometimes equipped with bristles, are rotated in unison; when the rotating rollers come in contact with the fabric, their pressure pushes the cloth outward from its center to its edges. The fabric is ultimately stretched to a width equal to the widest part of the frame, which can be adjusted depending on desired stretch.
Chemical compound applied to contact paper in order to indicate the presence of iron ions in test samples of materials adversely affected by iron such as textiles, paper, or parchment.

Floor coverings handwoven in or near the city of Konya in south-central Turkey. Early carpet fragments attributed to the 13th century ruling Seljuks in this style have been found in the Ala al-Din Mosque of Konya. More recently rugs from the region have used design motifs found widely distributed throughout the country. Often the Konya rug is of a fleecy wool with a loose weave.

Style of textiles, particularly floor coverings handwoven in the Sarāband area, southwest of Arak in west-central Iran. The rugs are characterized as dating from the 19th and early 20th centuries, being of sturdy construction, and having a distinctive pattern known commercially as the "mir" design, which comprises small, complex leaf (boteh) or leaf forms in diagonal rows with tips pointed alternately in opposite directions. A geometric vine with similar leaf forms usually occupies the principal border stripe. There may be geometric cornerpieces or a small, similarly geometric central medallion. The ground is red, dark blue, or ivory; the knotting is symmetrical on a cotton foundation. Large Seraband rugs are narrower than room dimension.
Period of the dynasty that ruled during the Early Ottoman Empire in the 14th century.

Process of preparing the warp by calculating the appropriate length, winding off the appropriate number of warp threads, and removing the warp from the winder in a way that ensures the threads to not get tangled.
Parts or components of measuring devices.

The systems within a building that supply water to the occupants and carry off liquid or liquid-suspended wastes; includes pipes, traps, vents, and fixtures, but not sources or destinations outside the building such as wells or septic tanks.

The representation of the behavior or characteristics of one system through the use of another system, especially a computer model; often used to forecast or predict the behavior of a dynamic system when real world experimentation is not feasible.
Launching projectiles (arrows or darts) with an atlatl or bow.
A pattern formed on a fabric, especially velvet, by burning the pile away with acid.

All examples of a set number or amount of multiples, such as coins, notes, stamps, prints, copies of a newspaper, books, periodicals, etc. that were issued at one time or otherwise sharply distinguished in pattern, design, color, or identifying numbers from those issued at another time.

Counterbalancing weights in various contexts, used to stabilize or otherwise affect the weight or position of another member. Examples of use are in cranes and other construction equipment, and in mechanical devices, such as elevators.
The blowing and shaping of glass without the use of a mold.
Informal or ordinary dress not usually worn in public.

Implements carried to brush away flies; in a ceremonial context, especially in Africa, also serving as a symbol of high position or authority; usually made of flexible fibers mounted on a handle. For instruments used to kill insects, usually consisting of a flat piece of perforated material or wire mesh attached to a handle, use "fly swatters."

Hammers used by farriers to shoe horses. Most often these feature compact solid metal heads with a flattened face on one end of the head for driving nails, and curved forked tines on the other end for pulling out nails.
Clergy who occupy offices of high rank and authority in the Christian Church.
Refers to portable lab equipment used by scientists for in situ analysis.
Military officers serving as the chief political executive of an area under military government.
People who climb mountains or other steep terrain, usually for adventure or sport.
Boroughs or districts, in Germany.
Anvils used in roofing, with specialized slater's axes or hammers, to trim slate tiles to size.
The process of evening up and squaring the edges of a text block by tapping it at the head and spine.

Territories outside the borders of, but under the jurisdiction and sovereignty of a primary political entity, such as a nation or empire. Examples include territories held by Australia, Denmark, France, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Devices or appliances for expanding a material making it taut, removing wrinkles, or the like; used especially with reference to frames upon which canvas or other textile is stretched for painting, having mitered corners that can be forced apart by wedges or keys. For frames that support canvas or other textile and do not have expandable corners, use "strainers (framing and mounting equipment)."
Utensils used to prepare printing surfaces by incising designs on the matrix surface. Also used to subtract tones and layers from photographs.
Popular in the late 17th century, feet in which the scroll turns under, towards the back.
Surviving objects having interest by reason of their age or association with the past.
Tablets, sometimes of silver, or boards, usually decorated with a Christian religious representation, that is kissed first by the priest and then by members of the congregation.
Objects that are believed to have an origin in the supernatural world, not the natural world, or that may be used to contact the spirit world.

Two-masted, fore-and-aft-rigged vessels in which the foremast is larger than the mizzen mast and is set abaft the rudder post; for similar fore-and-aft-rigged vessels, but with the smaller, mizzen, mast set forward of the rudder post, use "ketches (fore-and-aft-rigged vessels)."
States or principalities under the rule of a despot.

Stout mohair or worsted cloth produced in the 18th and 19th centuries in closely woven plain weave with thicker weft than warp, giving it a slight rib that made it suitable for watering and embossing; in the 19th century, often woven with a cotton warp.

Textile constructed usually of wool and fur fiber often mixed with natural or synthetic fiber by the interlocking of the loose fiber through the action of heat, moisture, chemicals, and pressure without spinning, weaving, or knitting.

Dobby weave is an allover figured fabric made on looms having a dobby attachment, with narrow strips of wood instead of Jacquard cards. Dobby weaves are limited to simple, small geometric figures, with the design repeated frequently, and are fairly inexpensive to produce.
The process of producing designs or pictures (as on wood or leather) by burning or scorching with hot instruments.

Threads or strands applied to an object as decoration, used especially with reference to glass threads used principally to decorate the necks, stems, and rims of drinking glasses and other objects. Threading is distinguished from "trailings" in that threading creates an independent, partially free-standing, decoration attached to the vessel, whereas trailings are simple lines of decoration on the surface of the glass.
The process of creating a crease or creases.
The forceful introduction of a fluid or other, typically liquid, substance into an object or structure to cure, stabilize, consolidate, or repair.
Application of a penetrating liquid to fill pores, to isolate coatings, or to make surfaces suitable to receive coatings.
In metallurgy, removal of carbon content from metal, usually steel.
The process of weathering or hydrothermal alteration by which minerals, especially feldspars and micas, are converted to kaolin.
Spoons intended primarily for serving granulated sugar from a sugar bowl or sugar box; similar to a teaspoon but having a larger bowl. The bowl may be in the form of a seashell.
Light three-wheeled, hooded vehicles that serve as taxis. Originally found in southern and eastern Asia, now popular elsewhere. The form grew out of the rickshaw, which was pulled by men on foot.

Wheel-less drags consisting of two or more poles framed into an A-shape, bridged by thongs, twigs, or plants, and hauled by a single person or animal; used by North American Native Americans for carrying goods or the sick or elderly.
The process of altering, injuring, or consuming something by fire or heat. For events where something is totally or partially consumed by fire, whether intentionally or by accident, use "fires."
The length of a straight vertical line extending from the bottom to the top of a form.
In Indian architecture, places of juncture on temple exteriors where successive temple halls connect with each other: a coupling-area.

Formats of paintings, prints, photographs, sculptures, or other works that fall within a medium range of size for the norm. For example, the term is used for film formats encompassing 120/220 and 70mm roll sizes and sheet films to 3.25 x 4.25 inches.
Characteristics and qualities that are inherent in electric currents and magnetic fields.
The tendency of a substance to absorb or attract water from the air.

Circular frames in which the dominant molding consists of a festoon that continues around the full circle, or of an ornamental fillet, often set off by a flat molding or decorative staves on the inside and outside edges.
End-blown trumpetlike aerophones dating from the Nordic Bronze Age, consisting of a conical tube two to three meters in length curved into a twisted S-shape and terminating in a flat ornamental disc.
Former suborder that included the primitive primates: lemurs, lorises, and tarsiers.

Family containing nine species in six genera, characterized as being large, short-tailed, having stocky legs, a long snout, shaggy hair, and plantigrade paws with five non-retractile claws. Bears are generally omnivorous, but some bears are entirely carnivorous (like the polar bear ) or vegetarian (like the panda).
Members of an order of containing various species of insects known for their extremely short adult life spans, ranging from 30 minutes to one day, and emergence in large numbers in the summer months.
Regarding personal names, last names held by a woman prior to marriage, at which time she may adopt her husband's last name.

Order containing around 211 species in ten families including hornbills, bee-eaters, rollers, hoopoes, todies, and motmots. They are a heterogeneous group of hole-nesting birds, many with long pointed bills and blue or green in plumage, and all having two toes joined at base.
Any Windsor chair having one shaped, flat leaf, in lieu of a standard arm, used as a writing surface.
Small short-bladed knives for peeling fruits and vegetables.

Raised plinths, or platforms on which temples and their attendant shrines are placed in Indian architecture, a plinth, platform; basal moulding of adhiṣṭhāna (South Indian); platform supporting a temple (with its hall) (northern Indian usage); vertical moulding at the base of adhiṣṭhāna.
In Indian architecture, a type of adhisthana with ornamentation of bands and fillets with medallions, diadems, diapers, and other decorative motifs.

Large natural objects that orbit a star or a stellar remnant. Planets are not radiating energy from internal nuclear fusion reactions, are not a brown dwarfs, and are bigger than an asteroid. Planets are large enough to have become round due to the force of their own gravity, and dominate the neighborhood around their orbit, and are thus distinguished from dwarf planets.
Educational institutions, usually elementary or secondary schools, where classes are held only on weekdays and that do not provide any boarding facilities.
Land areas, more prominent than a point, projecting into the sea and marking a notable change in coastal direction.
In indigenous American cultures, containers that are very small versions of containers of normal size; for ritual use, where the small item stands for the normal-sized object.
Extinct subclass of reptiles characterized by single temporal opening on area of cheek.

Hybrid offspring produced by the mating of a female horse and a male donkey. The less-frequent cross between a female ass and a male horse results in a hinny, or hinney, which is smaller than a mule. Mules were beasts of burden in Asia Minor at least 3,000 years ago and are still used today in many parts of the world because of their ability to withstand hardships and perform work under conditions too severe for many other draft and pack animals. Mules are usually sterile.
The method of structuring and presentation of digitized information in various formats; audio, video, text, linked together non-sequentially in the same manner as hypertext.
Hydrographic features, including grounds, banks, or other watery areas, where fishermen go to catch fish. For places on land where fishermen gather, use "fishing spots."
Paper size, generally used in Great Britain, and standardized at 15 1/2 by 19 inches. When folded, a half sheet of post forms the quarto letter-paper.
Order containing around 21 species in one family possessing several thousand short, smooth spines that  densely cover a short, stocky body except for the underside, legs, face, and ears.
Genus of two species of North and South America, one of which lives only on the Channel Islands off the California coast.
Genus of one Asian species.
Series of proofs that illustrate the image development of the finished print. Each printing element is shown singly in color.
Threaded beads made of shells and used as money by North American Indians.
