Small cast metal reliefs, produced as multiples and used for a variety of decorative purposes; usually blank on the reverse; especially common in the Renaissance period.

Golden necklaces worn as adornment of high ranking nobles in postclassic central Mexico and part of the dance array of Nahua tlahtohqueh (rulers). They could also be given as gifts or wagered in gambling.

Headdresses worn by Hopi young women and girls during the Butterfly Dance. Usually made of wood and decorated in vivid colors with designs representative of the wearer's clan and sometimes their dance partner's clan. Can also be seen carved on katsinam.
Wide-brimmed hats with a large soft crown of the type worn by ranch hands in the American West.

Drinking glasses designed to be as difficult as possible to drink from without spilling the alcoholic beverage within, often including a tube that served as a straw. The goal was to amuse the onlookers at the expense of the imbiber: in drinking competitions, the drinker had to guess how to drink from the vessel; if any liquor was spilled, he was required to start again with a full glass.
Handles comprising hardware applied to finished products and often decorative as well as functional; particularly, but not exclusively, on furniture or cabinetry.
Joints at the edges of wood boards, formed so that a corresponding indented and projecting V meet.
Cases or coverings for the blade of a sword, dagger, or other instrument to which it fits closely.
Supportive rests, most often used by violin and viola players, which allow freedom for the bowing arm when playing.
Natural trumpets in elongated crescent shape, built in Europe in the early 19th century and designed to accommodate the hand-in-bell playing technique.
Italian mouth-blown bagpipes with sheepskin bag, blowpipe, two conical chanters (for separate hands) and two drone pipes, all inserted into the same stock and all fitted with double reeds.

Vertical flutes of the Han Chinese, made of a bamboo tube with a notch cut into one end, against the edge of which the player blows. Known since ancient times, they have existed in various forms with differing numbers and arrangements of fingerholes.

Shawms of southern Asia, particularly Kashmir, consisting of a wood pipe of conical bore with an integral bell, seven fingerholes and one thumbhole, a metal staple to carry the reed, and a pirouette. The reed is held in the mouth when played.

Dishes of varying forms and materials used for serving sweetmeats; includes those suspended from the arms of sweetmeat stands. For stemmed dessert glasses used for serving sweetmeats, use "sweetmeat glasses."
Small plates of concave form, usually circular, either for eating food or as a stand for a cup. Generally, those for use with a cup have a slight depression in the center in which to place the cup.
Mechanical arrangements of toothed metal lever and snail-shaped cam designed so that the hands of striking timepieces can be advanced without waiting for the striking to be completed.
Drums that are beaten in such a way that certain features of an unvocalized text can be recognized by a listener, these features acting as clues to the meaning of the words being drummed.
Small-bodied guitars with six strings and bodies deeper than the standard acoustic guitar. Requintos are especially popular in Mexico and mariachi music.

Italian Renaissance fiddles, having a body shaped like a violin, a wide fingerboard, relatively flat bridge, a leaf-shaped pegbox with frontal pegs, five melody strings on the fingerboard, and two off-board drone strings.

Rooflike components supported above the bed by posts and covering the whole area of the bed. Use "flying testers" for rooflike components generally cantilevered from the headboard and extending over the whole area of the bed. Use "half-testers" for similar forms which only extend over the head half of the bed. Use "canopies (structural elements)" for rooflike components suspended over the head of the bed by means of a cord or chain attached to the ceiling.
Japanese prints in which the outline block is faintly printed in color, giving an effect of extreme delicacy.
Stands or small tables fitted for or of a size and shape appropriate for bottles and glasses, such as the horseshoe-shaped tables popular in the 18th century.
Spanish and Portuguese Colonial very small, low tables generally having flat carving and heavy aprons.
Writing tables often with a leather-covered slide and sometimes with an adjustable hinged panel for reading. Distinguished from "bureaux plats" by their much smaller size.
Tables designed for and used while eating meals in a dining room. Distinguished from kitchen tables, which are intended for less formal meals in a kitchen.
Chests made from a hollowed log or tree trunk, and used primarily in the Middle Ages. Frequently used as safes.
Tall wooden chest of drawers, generally with seven or more drawers, divided in two sections resting on each other, the bottom one being slightly wider and resting on legs. Used to store clothing.

Term of Medieval origin generally applied to tall cupboards with doors and shelves for storing linens, clothing, and kitchen utensils. For presses with sliding shelves behind closed doors, use "clothes presses."
Shelves designed with a row of hooks or pegs beneath, for the hanging of hats, clothing, umbrellas, or other items.
Desks having a flat top and two boxlike supports either containing cupboards or drawers.
Stools of varied height consisting of a horizontal plank of varied shape supported on three or four turned or shaved legs, frequently braced by stretchers, which socket directly into the plank.
Beds with two or four posts approximately six feet in height which often, but not always, support a tester.

Large wooden cabinets having subdivisions, drawers, shelves, and usually doors or a fall front, designed particularly for housing rare, precious, or interesting items. For small, private chambers designed for this purpose, use "cabinets of curiosities."
Cabinets used to house various data storage media formats. May also refer to cabinets that house and sometimes conceal multimedia support equipment.
Chairs whose backs are oval shaped.

Spanish Renaissance type of armchair with a rectangular leather hung seat and with a leather or velvet back; generally having a broad front stretcher, which is often carved. Sometimes hinged to allow for folding and easy transportation.
Lamps which radiate a significant portion of their radiative power in the ultraviolet part of the spectrum.
Chairs with a stuffed oval or cartouche-shaped back; of a type popular in the late 18th century.
Lamps with a large globular glass shade open at the top.
Lamps incorporating any of various features designed to make the burning of volatile fuels safe.

Ornamental electric lamps that consist of a transparent chamber housing a liquid, usually water, in which brightly colored blobs of wax are suspended. The wax moves and changes shape due to heat supplied by an electric bulb.
Ring-shaped attachments to lamps, usually of brass, which surround the opening of the font, and are threaded inside to receive the screw of the burner.

Traditional one side edged swords of various tribes in Indonesia. Initially intended as a cleaver, and later used as a weapon. Dutch troops in Indonesia also called their modified cutlasses by this name.
European daggers with light blades, square or triangular in section, and a reinforced beadlike point, in use primarily during the 16th and 17th centuries as parrying daggers in swordplay.
Candleholders with upright spikes for impaling the candle.
Candleholders with stems that slide in and out in overlapping cylindrical sections for height adjustment.
Hardware used in supporting or connecting members of similar or different material as, for instance, a beam hanger for supporting the end of a beam or joist at a masonry wall.
Tacks or pins with a head that is easy to grasp; used to affix papers or pictures to notice boards, to mark points on a map, and for other purposes.
Metal tubes fitted to helmets and shaffrons, typically covered by a small decorative plate, rondel, or shield, to support a plume.

Long shields originating in Italy and used by Roman heavy infantry from the 8th century BCE to the 5th century CE. They were rectangular or oval in shape, originally of wood or wicker, later of leather-covered wood with a central metal boss and a longitudinal spine up the back.

Works made of transparent or semi-opaque colored glass, generally in the form of a window, autonomous panel, or lampshade, in which the design is meant to be observed through refracted light and its effect is greatly dependent on the quality of the light. Generally the glass is primarily made of "stained glass (material)" as opposed to painted glass, but there may be painted details. The stages of manufacture were described in a manual written in the early twelfth century by the monk Theophilus and the process has hardly changed since then. The window or other item is made by cutting pieces of colored glass based on a full-scale cartoon and holding the pieces together by strips of lead. Details may be painted on the surface of the pieces of glass and fired in a kiln before piecing the glass together. The method of weatherproofing and fixing the glass in a window is often highly decorative and forms an important element of the design. The highest achievements in stained glass are thought to be those of the Gothic era in Europe and those of the Gothic Revival of the nineteenth century.

Refers to objects made from translucent materials that are illuminated by transmitted light. Used for the decoration of royal festivals, marriages, funerals, or processions in the Baroque period, transparent paintings became an art form in their own right from the end of the 18th century.
A critical concept concerning the qualities of congruence among the elements of a work of visual art, literature, or theater, and good taste in the work's relationship to external reality.
Ability of cement paste, aggregate, or mixtures thereof to resist attack by dissolved sulfates in water or soil.
Property of being capable of deformation by compression without rupture.

In philosophy, a theory that affirms that mind or the spiritual ideal archetype is of central importance in the interpretation of experience. It holds that the world or reality exists essentially as spirit or consciousness, and that abstractions and laws are more fundamental in reality than sensory things. Idealism is thus directly opposed to materialism, which is the theory that the basic substance of the world is matter and that it is known primarily through and as material forms and processes. Idealism is also opposed to the philosophy of realism, which holds that in human knowledge objects are grasped and seen as they really are in their existence outside and independently of the mind.

The religious ideology that there is only one god, as opposed to polytheism and pantheism. Whereas facets of earlier cultures, such as the Egyptians, worshipped one god, a full long-term doctrine of monotheism developed first within Judaism and it remains a central part of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Muslims and Jews think that Christianity's belief in the three aspects of God, the Holy Trinity, denies monotheism.

The branch of dynamics concerned with the action of forces in producing equilibrium or relative rest, and with the forces acting on systems and structures in equilibrium. Formerly, statics referred to  weight and its mechanical effects, and with the conditions of equilibrium resulting from the distribution of weight; it was considered in opposition to dynamics, as dynamics was previously defined.
Interest in or adoption of the exotic.
The state of a person or situation distinguished by admirable or commendable qualities, worthy, estimable, fine, charitable, kind, avoiding bad behavior. The antithesis of "evil."
Property owned by a state or other governmental body but dedicated to use by the public.
The values obtained by dividing one number by another; often used for comparison.
Polygons having twelve sides and twelve angles. In regular dodecagons, all sides and all angles are equal.
Severe and prolonged lowering in quality or vigor in commercial trade, financial markets, and industrial activity; more intense and prolonged than an economic recession.
Rights deemed by a society to be possessed by all humans, typicaly a set of entitlements held to be critical by virtue of being human.

Totalitarian movement led by Adolf Hitler as head of the Nazi Party in Germany; characterized by intense nationalism, mass appeal, and dictatorial rule that shared many elements with Italian fascism. However, Nazism was far more extreme both in its ideas and in its practice; it was an anti-intellectual and atheoretical movement, emphasizing the will of the charismatic dictator and including racist nationalism, national expansion, and state control of the economy.
The quality or status of being free from wrong-doing, illegal acts, sin, guilt, evil, or moral wrong.
Concepts that are found in the sciences.
Characteristic of being mortal or subject to death.

In psychological studies, refers to the condition based on pseudo-hallucinations that occur when feelings of fear or anxiety are projected onto external objects and experiences, or are imagined, invented, or wrongly ascribed.
The condition of having little or no wealth or material possessions.

The application of testing methods to materials or objects in order to analyze their composition and manufacture. In a conservation science context, this may refer to movable art works and artifactual objects in a conservation lab. For a broader range of testing methods, prefer "scientific analysis."

The practice of writing with the pen, often in a particular style or following certain rules. Penmanship was, and in certain cultures remains, a skill emphasized in children's education. Distinguished from calligraphy, which is typically an art form.
Method of dating by measuring, on an exposed surface of quartz, the thickness of the hydration layer caused by the natural intake of water on that surface from the atmosphere.
Exhibitions, usually focusing on one individual maker, that demonstrate the development of a body of work over a span of time.

Discrete bibliographical items which though once part of a larger whole (e.g., a periodical issue) have been disbound in order that may stand alone. Distinguished from "excerpts" and  "offprints" which are printed separately, in that extracts were once physically part of a larger whole.

Heritage science refers to all applications of science for the general study of cultural heritage, tangible and intangible; a cross disciplinary research domain including humanities and sciences, such as the natural, social, and formal sciences. In particular, heritage science focuses on issues such as promoting access to cultural heritage, its interpretation, conservation, and management.
Study and application of the principles of mechanics, thermodynamics, and material properties.
A branch of physics that deals with the properties and applications of photons especially as a medium for transmitting information.
The theory and practice of planning, organizing, coordinating, and leading a project in order to meet specific goals and objectives in a timely and cost-efficient manner.

The process and technique of creating two-dimensional decoration on pottery by using paint made of metallic oxides or other pigments held in suspension in slip or another medium.The pigments are typically applied to a fired body by using a brush or other tool. The painted object is typically fired again to fuse the pigment. The term is often reserved for Ancient Greek red- and black-figure works. See also "porcelain painting (image making)."
Photography of (potentially) identifiable individuals, groups of individuals, or animals.
Philosophical study of finality, especially as it pertains to design or purposes in the processes of nature.

The study of the history and culture of ethnic groups within a larger cultural or social order. For the scientific, historic, or comparative study of the origins, characteristics, and functions of human cultures and societies, use "ethnology."
Archaeology that explores the emergence of the Modern World, from around 1400 CE to the present.
Methods or practices used with pottery production and creation.
Finishing the cross section of a metal item to size or shape.

Analytical technique which combines properties of thermal analysis and microscopy to enable the solid state characterization of materials as a function of temperature. A sample substance is placed on a metal strip with a temperature gradient, a melting-point apparatus known as a Kofler bench, thereby revealing its thermal behavior at the temperature at that point when studied with a suitable polarized-light microscope.
Design of paper structures and mechanisms, such as pop-up elements in books and greeting cards, cut-and-assemble paper models, and various types of paper containers.
The construction and repair of wooden vessels formed of staves and hoops, such as casks, buckets, barrels, and tubs.

The process of building a roof with dry vegetation such as straw, reed, sedge, rushes, or heather; the vegetation is layered so that rain water is shed away from the inner roof. Thatching is an ancient roofing method, found in both tropical and temperate climates.

Process of making materials or surfaces impervious to water. To describe materials or articles having surfaces resistant, but not impervious, to water, use "water-repellent." For the state or quality of having little or no affinity for water, especially on a molecular level, use "hydrophobicity."
Restoring to a whole by replacing a part or putting together what is torn or broken, or otherwise restoring to sound condition.
Applying fine-grain, sieved sand to create a textured surface.
Technique of emphasizing shadows, darkness or night effects within a painting; generally the use of such shadowing obscures figures within the painting.
Techniques to photograph subjects that can be viewed only with the aid of a microscope or other magnifier. For the production and use of microforms generally, use "micrographics."
Measurement of the intensity of odors produced by a gaseous substance using an olfactometer; used, for example, to evaluate the success of applied methods of odor reduction on used polyolefins.

A technique that is a hybrid of drawing and printmaking. The oil transfer drawing technique is achieved by covering a surface, often a sheet of paper, with oil paint or printing ink, laying a clean sheet of paper over it, and drawing on top with a mark-making tool; the pressure of the tool causes the ink or paint from below to transfer to the back of the top sheet. The technique was used by both Paul Gauguin and Paul Klee, but predates them both.

Chinese painting technique in which the brush is applied quickly across the paper, which separates the hairs of the brush, leaving streaks of untouched white background, giving the design a light and airy quality. Most frequently used in bamboo and bird and flower paintings.

The application of a poultice, which is a substance with a soft, absorbent, or pasty consistency. For cleaning, the poultice is applied to an area in order to draw out a stain or remove other substances in a controlled manner. Poultices are also used in medical applications.
Making flat, as in removing wrinkles or folds.
Process used to reconstruct the three-dimensional structure of blood vessels by replacing the blood with low viscosity resin; the vascular architecture may then be removed from surrounding tissues.
Devices designed to replace stagnant air with pure air.

An apparatus that produces a blast of air to a furnace or a forge by means of falling water, and that separates the air and water at a secondary stage. Specifically, a blowing apparatus with no moving parts used in Italian, Spanish and other Mediterranean countries' metallurgical plants until the 19th century. A blast of wet air is supplied to a furnace through the action of falling water, which carries air downward by means of the Venturi effect to a barrel where the air is separated and sent through a pipe, or "tuyere," to the furnace.
Water harvesting vessels that are used to collect rainwater (especially from roofs) for future use.

Electronic devices used for viewing and hearing television broadcasts, or as computer monitors. Includes various models over time, from the 1920s mechanical tuner, display, and loudspeakers unit; to the boxy electronic form using cathode ray tube (CRT) technology; to the 2010s flat-panel televisions incorporating liquid-crystal display (LCD) technology, often LED-backlit LCD technology. The television receiver may be incorporated in the television viewing device or housed in a separate unit.
The action of heaving down a ship to one side with tackles, pulling up the keel from under the water, usually for cleaning, caulking, or repairing.
Joints made by deforming the members in order to make the connection.
Nails having two points, with the shank bent in the shape of an inverted-U.
Nails having a thin shank and a flat head, designed for attaching laths, which are narrow strips of wood, upon battens.

Small wood nails with a tapered shank designed to avoid splitting the wood. Jobent nails are typically used for nailing thin plates of iron to wood or another material, for example when nailing small hinges on small chests or small cupboard doors.
Special devices to interrupt electrical current where a weak electrical loss or ground occurs.
Three-dimensional models that demonstrate the shapes, features, and elevation of a part of the Earth's surface.

Bolt and nut assemblies used to fasten objects to a hollow wall or a wall accessible from only one side. The nut has pivoted wings that close against a spring when the nut end of the assembly is pushed through a hole and open on the other side.
In Indian architecture, a frieze of dwarfs; see bhūtamālā and gaṇamālā.

Self-sustaining frontier or outpost settlements created by a body of persons sent out by a religious organization to evangelize abroad, and often to aid in the administering of colonial wilderness enterprises. They are sometimes established under the protection of a government, as with the Spanish settlements of America. Missions typically include buildings for housing the people and activities of the group, including a church.
Communities of any size that are dependent on or engaged in the harvest or processing of fish.
Circular masonry tombs, primarily of Mycenaean Greece, constructed with a corbeled dome, entered via a long walled passageway, and covered by a mound.
Nationality or culture of Singapore, a Southeast Asian island.
Structures or large furnishings in which devotion is paid to a statue, picture, saint, deity or other holy objects. For containers for safeguarding the relics of a saint, use "reliquaries".
Movement in architecture that uses structure as the fundamental expression, endorsing structural and material changes enabled by the industrial revolution; term was coined by Kenneth Frampton.
Articles, substances, or procedures that conceal the identity of or alter the appearance of an object or person.
Shapes, forms, or figures cut from, or intended to be cut from, pieces of material such as paper, cardboard, wood, or cloth.
Nationality, culture, or style of Latium in central western Italy, now having Rome as its capital.

A colorless, somewhat cloudy alkaline solution of slaked lime used medicinally as an antacid and as an ingredient in calamine lotion. In art, limewater is used in buon fresco technique to impregnate fresh plaster before application of secco colors, a process related to whitewashing.

Refers to the styles and cultures of the the Medieval principalities that developed along the Danube river in central Europe. For the prehistoric culture in this area, use "Danubian (prehistoric)" or  "Bandkeramik."
Nationality and culture of the historical Federal Republic of Germany (founded 1949) before reunification, excluding the Soviet-occupied parts of Germany.
Of or belonging to the nation of Peru or its people.

Art movement lead by American painters Morgan Russell and Stanton Macdonald-Wright in the early 20th century. The style is distinguished for its focus on abstract, rhythmic color arrangements and submerged forms.

The culture, style, and period in the development of a peoples when they begin using very small stone tools, often combined with wood, bone, resin and fiber to form a composite tool or weapon, such as the points of spears and arrows. Microlithic culture developed at different times in different places throughout the world.
Refers to a style region encompassing the regions where Islam is prevalent.
Refers to the culture of the Basque region in the western Pyrenees, spanning the borders of modern France and Spain, which is inhabited by a people of unknown origin who spaek a non-Aryan language.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Georgia.
Refers to the style and cultures that developed on the Italian peninsula in places where Etruscans came into contact with Greek culture through Greek colonists and their art.
In Indian architecture, five-storeyed or five-floored vimānas.

General term for modern construction techniques used for buildings of nine or more stories, usually with elevators, employing structural systems to carry both vertical gravity loads and lateral loads caused by wind and earthquakes.
Rooms or divisions of rooms that are semicircular in plan.

A numerical method used in computing the stresses and displacements of a large number of small particles such as grains of sand. Often used in combination with the finite element method to address engineering questions involving granular and discontinuous materials in continuous physical systems.
Serving in a legislative body by authority delegated by persons subject to the laws enacted by that body, usually by election, to represent their wishes and interests.
Rooms in a palace or great house, often splendidly decorated and used for official and State entertaining.
Supporting structures composed of ribs of any material that intersect diagonally.

Meaning literally to prop and rotate (Kroll 2015 453, 479), the term tiao‘wo, as most scholars believe, is a noun that refers to a component in the timber frame structure, used in the interior of a building with an open-frame roof structure (cheshang mingzao 徹上明造; i.e. without a ceiling). Tiao'wo appears in the Yingzao fashi (1103) four times (YZFS 2009, 1.8a, 4.6a, 6.9b, 18.7a). There are two types of tiao'wo. (1) As a part of a component, tiao'wo refers to the upward end of a xia'ang in a bujian puzuo. This kind of tiaowo is also called angwei tiaowo 昂尾挑斡 by some scholars. Sometimes it can also refer to the upward end of a shuatou. (2) As a separate component, tiaowo refers to an oblique element without pointed shape, a particular form of xia'ang. Some scholars believe this is the angting tiaowo mentioned in Yingzao fashi (Zhu 2018).

Walls that project from or are separate from a building; the term is reserved for substantial constructions of masonry, lumber, or another such material. Examples of a freestanding walls could be a wall used as a room divider or a wall used as a privacy fence. For walls used to resist lateral loads, use "retaining walls."

Refers to the branch of Christianity characterized by a uniform, highly developed ritual canon and organizational structure with doctrinal roots based in the teachings of the Apostles of Jesus Christ in the first century, in the Alexandrian school of theology, and in Augustinian thought. In this religious branch, faith is considered an acceptance of revelation; revelation appears as doctrine. In juridical terms, it refers to the branch of Christianity distinguished as a unified, monolithic sacramental system under the governance of papal authority. Throughout much of its history, the seat of the Pope has been in Rome, thus "Roman Catholicism" is often used to distinguish this concept from the Orthodox Catholic church.

A Protestant denomination with evangelical beliefs stressing a Christ-centered philosophy and advocating non-violence. The Moravians believe strongly in missionary activity and, because hymns are important to Moravian worship, they printed the first Protestant hymnal in 1501. Its roots are found in an association of Brethren in Bohemia in 1457; this group was driven out of Bohemia in 1722 and they reformed in Saxony under the name 'Moravian.' The movement spread across Europe where it was influenced by pietism and later, in 1732, it was established in North America, where most of its current members reside.

The act of soliciting ideas and labor from a group of people outside one's organization or institution. This primarily online exchange draws on collective knowledge to accomplish a task, and the work is typically undertaken for free or for minimal payment.
Formal ceremonious introductions of a person to an assembly or to another person, especially of superior rank, such as a head of state.

Refers to the philosophy and religion based on the enlightenment and teachings of the Buddha Gautama in the early sixth century BCE in the northeastern region of modern India. Playing dominant roles in the art and culture of Southeast Asia and East Asia, this religion is based on the transcendence of human suffering and pain through the acceptance of the limitations of individuality, the surrender of worldly desires and cravings that cause disappointment and sorrow, and the deliverance from the impermanence of living and individual ego based on wealth, social position, or family through the process of enlightenment (nirvana). The religion also centers around 'anatman', or no-self, the idea that the self is in a state of action or a series of changing manifestations rather than in a state of fixed, metaphysical substance. The structure of the religion is based on the Triratna ("Three Jewels" of Buddha), a tripartite schematic for living based on three elements: Buddha (the teacher), dharma (the teaching), and sangha (community).
Determining qualitative or quantitative worth or significance.

Meaning “ornate” (or “blossoming”) “end,” huafei 華廢 refers to the covering of the verges, the part of the roof beyond the vertical ridges of a gable end, with roof tiles, whereby the capping tiles (huatou tongwa 華頭㼧瓦 and chongchun banwa 重唇瓪瓦) are aligned to be perpendicular to the vertical ridges and parallel to the roof ridge. The term is found in texts as late as the Song dynasty (960-1279) (Li 2009, 13.2a; 13.4b) and is written huafei 化廢 (lit. “transforming the end”) in some literature (Guo 1368, 1.8b). Modern scholars are generally of the opinion that the tiles aligned perpendicular to the vertical ridges outside the two gables should be called huafei 華廢 (Liang 1983, 256; Chen 2010, 298).
In Indian architecture, a division of the wall forming a central offset.
Games in which the outcome is strongly influenced by some randomizing device and upon which contestants frequently wager money. Skill may also be involved in games of chance.
Experiences in which a person, thing, or event appears vividly or credibly to the mind, although not actually present.
The sequence of steps involved in moving from the beginning to the end of a working process.

Act or practice of manufacturing a variety of products, selling a variety of merchandise, or investing in a variety of securities, for example, so that failure in or economic slump affecting one of them will not be disastrous.

Formal dedications and settings apart by a cleric or other religious dignitary of buildings, plots of land, or objects for ceremonial or religious purposes. For the bestowings of a sacred office upon a person, use "ordinations."
Theatrical entertainments, often plays, in which actors or puppets appear as shadows cast upon a screen placed between the stage and the audience.

Pose in Asian art and dance comprising a standing body position characterized by three-bends, often with the weight on one leg, tilted head, and the body curved in opposite directions at the waist and neck to form an "S" shape.
Pulls for components of furniture or doors that incorporate hanging rings as their main graspable element.
People concealed in masks or costumes who perform or participate in rituals or other public ceremonies. They typically impersonate known legendary characters, stock  figures, or spirit beings.
In Indian architecture, a śākhā/door-jamb bearing couples (sometimes erotic).
Acts that are forbidden by law, or the omission of duties that are required by law, which make the offender liable to punishment by that law.

Gases that contribute to the greenhouse effect, including water vapor, carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), ozone (O3), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), halogenated fluorocarbons (HCFCs), and perfluorinated carbons (PFCs).
Correspondence of sound between words or the endings of words, especially when these are used at the ends of lines of poetry.
The concept of a residential environment in which inhabitants can enhance the quality of their lives, while providing security for their families, neighbors, and friends.
Lines that define an unimpeded field of vision,(RHDEL2) as within rooms or open spaces or along city streets.
Structural loads that move.

Broad term for any architecture built of local materials to suit particular local needs, generally constructed outside any academic tradition and without professional guidance. It is often of unknown authorship and makes little reference to established styles or theories of architecture. Most architectural works in the world are vernacular architecture.

The quality possessed by a sculpture, building, or other structure that is designed to be viewed from directly in front; in pictorial compositions, the quality possessed by figures that face directly out of the picture.
Shape, usually two-dimensional rectangular or three-dimensional cuboid, having a rounded top, somewhat resembling a dome.
Something that serves as an ideal, a pattern to follow or copy, or source of inspiration to a creator.
Lines of pilasters.
Motif of an elephant head.
Facilities used for improving the metal content of ore by concentration.
Structures used for the shelter or rest of travelers.
In Indian architecture, a rectangular belt bearing vine design, occurring below kumbha (Kaliṅga); khura.
Extravagantly illustrated books about flowers.
Documents by which a dispute is referred to arbitration pursuant to an agreement between the parties.

Concept in early 20th-century visual art, theater, and literature regarding the expression of multiple awareness of things happening in different places at the same time or extended in time, challenging the traditional idea of unity of time, action, and place.

Describes particular styles or categories of works of art. Genre designates the style or technique of the intellectual content of textual materials or, for graphic materials, aspects such as vantage point, intended purpose, characteristics of the creator, publication status, or method of representation.
Pointed iron or wooden tools used in nautical contexts for rope splicing and other functions.
Portable or fixed apparatuses that furnish heat for warmth or cooking, commonly using coal, oil, gas, wood, or electricity as a source of power.
Leather-finishing tools, often used by shoemakers, that consist of one or more small wheels with a crimped edge mounted on a handle; the wheels are rolled over the leather to create a broken line.
Instruments for stamping, such as dies or tools for impressing or marking a design or pattern on metal, paper, sand, or other soft or absorbent material.
Hard stones used for sharpening edged tools.
Carpenters' tools used for shaping curved edges, consisting of a blade set between two handles and used as a drawknife or planing tool.
Rubber bottles with narrow spouts, used for trailing lines of slip or glaze in patterns.
Periods when the climate of Earth was warmer than average.
Moving air, especially a natural and perceptible movement of air parallel to or along the ground.
Imitation marbled paper, produced by spotting various colors on paper with a brush. Often used for lining boxes.

A rosy red volcanic clay that has been used as a pigment and a component in cement; pozzolana itself possesses little or no cementitious value, but in finely divided form and in the presence of moisture, it will chemically react with calcium hydroxide at ordinary temperatures to form compounds possessing cementitious properties. Pozzolana is mined at Pozzuoli near Naples, Italy. It has been used since ancient times by the Romans.
Usages, practices, or conventions that regulate social life.
Monastic order founded in 1313, abiding by the Rule of Saint Benedict.
Generic term to refer to either gender, where the relationship to oneself is either the sibling of one's parent, or the spouse of the sibling of one's parent.

Dualistic Christian sect founded in Armenia and eastern Byzantine Empire in the mid-7th century by an Armenian named Constantine. Other than a brief period when it found favor with the iconoclast emperors of the 8th and 9th centuries, the sect was persecuted and it consequently allied itself with Muslims. The sect was particularly influenced by the dualistic beliefs of Marcionism and of Manichaeism, which recognize an evil God and a good God with the former being the creator and ruler of this world and the latter of the world to come. While Paulicians honored the gospel according to St. Luke and the letters of St. Paul, they rejected the Old Testament, the letters of St. Peter, and the sacraments, worship, and hierarchy of the established church. The Paulicians influenced the 10th-century neo-Manichaean Bogomils. Small Paulician communities were found in the early 19th century in Russian-occupied areas of Armenia.

The process of detaching a fresco painting from the wall by removing the pigment layer and a layer of intonaco. Cloth is glued to the painted surface and, when dry, the cloth, painting, and plaster are stripped from the wall.
Loosely organized political group during the French Revolution. The Girondists advocated for the overthrow of the monarchy; ultimately they were supplanted by their rivals, the Montagnards.

Refers to pottery characterized by feathering, branching decoration that resembles the markings of moss agate (mocha stone). It was developed in England around 1785 and was popular through the 19th century. It is typically seen on mugs, jugs and other pottery used in taverns or to measure or store dry goods, although it may appear on other items as well. The ornament was made by dabbing the body, either green ware or covered with slip, with a liquid pigment that then spread out through capillary action or by use of a blowpipe. The pigment often included tobacco juice, urine, and metallic oxide; it was generally greenish, brown, black or pink. The body was sometimes first painted with a horizontal banded design in brown, blue or gray slip. The body was generally made of creamware, white or cane-colored earthenware, or pearlware.
Of, relating to, or characteristic of the teachings of rabbis that constitute the Talmud.
Act or state of wholeheartedly and steadfastly believing in the existence, power and benevolence of a supreme being.
Photographic prints made by the palladium process.
Photographs produced using the technique of capturing images directly from television screens with a camera, as a document, or as a source of found images.
Refers to body masks made entirely or in part from leaves and other natural fibers. Leaf masks may have a crested headpiece, and are prevalent among the Bwa people of Burkina Faso in Africa.

Refers to the activity of creating photographic images covering a very wide angle of view. In the digital realm, it has been applied to the construction of  virtual reality; as with panoramic exhibits of cultural heritage.
Trees or shrubs pruned and trained into various geometric, zoomorphic, or fantastic shapes.

Narrow strips of wood or bamboo that typically carry a single column of brush-written text each, with space for several tens of complex ancient Chinese characters. For longer texts, many slips may be bound together in sequence with thread. Each strip of wood or bamboo is said to be as long as a chopstick and as wide as a pair.
Extracts from a larger or previously printed source.

Refers to maps that show the patterns of populations of people or animals, often within the context of political administrative boundaries. Indications of various demograhic characteristics may be included, such as the life-conditions of communities of people, as shown by statistics of births, deaths, diseases, etc.
A list of signatures attached to the end of early printed books.
Specific specimens of a given written or printed work; may be issued in multiples as an edition.
Study and collection of postage stamps, revenue stamps, stamped envelopes, postmarks, post cards, covers, and similar materials relating to postal or fiscal history.
Planning and establishing a sequence or system of actions, events, or instructions.
Modifier describing a color of middle intensity and medium value, often overlapping in meaning with the modifier "medium."

Artistic genre that flourished in Europe particularly in the 16th and 17th centuries, focusing on a motto and an image representing that motto. Each emblem generally consists of three parts: a short, often Classical, motto (lemma, inscriptio), a pictorial representation or icon (pictura), and the explanation of the link between them in an epigram (subscriptio). The earliest known and most influential emblem book is the "Emblematum liber," by Andrea Alciate, published in Augsburg in 1531. The format and definiton of emblem books are typically derived from the example of this work; however, the emblem itself remained an ambiguous concept that covered a variety of connections between word and image.
Of buildings, particularly classic Greek and Roman temples and buildings like them in structure, having a row or rows of four columns at one or both ends.

Prepared sets of photographic images, sold for viewing in an accompanying viewing instrument, the kromscop, that accurately combined and projected three-separation color images. The individual images were photographed and re-presented through color filters. These images were also frequently stereographic. This was of particular importance in the development of full-color projection. Developed by Frederic Eugene Ives. Some of these early prints are preserved in the Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C.

Existing or situated within the limiting surface or boundary of something. An example is the portion of a building within the walls and under the roof, as opposed to those parts in contact with the outdoors.

Refers to a distinct type of bobbin lace created in Lille, which is now in France but was formerly in Flanders. It was created primarily during the 16th through 19th centuries. It also refers to imitations of Lille lace made later and/or in other locations. It is characterized by a very fine net background formed of a hexagonal mesh in which the thread is twisted rather than plaited. The designs typically include curving flowers and scrolls, and small, square dots scattered over open areas of mesh.

Photographic processes based on the photosensitivity of certain iron compounds. Usually require intense light and thus employ contact printing. Do not use when iron sulfate is used to develop a silver image.
Rivers located beneath the earth's surface, such as those found in caves.
Small primitive photosynthetic, nonvascular plants growing in wet places and resembling green seaweeds or leafy mosses. Formerly classified with Bryophyta.
Refers to areas reserved for natural woodland, often in the context of urban growth or in landscape design.
General functions related to the administration of justice.
Attempting to reach an agreement through discussion.

Two-storied main gates of a Zen temple complexes; literally "enlightenment gate," "mountain gate," or "triple gate." The size of the gate could be equated with the status of the temple. These gates can contain three passages and are seen also as symbolic barriers between the profane and the sacred.
Breeding areas for colonies of birds or seals.
Certain combinations of lines, colors, and spatial elements that excite pure aesthetic emotion; term coined by art critic Clive Bell.
Material comprising fine, powdery, yellowish grains or spores, sometimes in masses, which are the fertilizing element of flowering plants.
Plan of a building or city that is arranged within a hexagon (six sides of equal length), usually a centralized plan.
Large stones on which to rest a coffin momentarily at the entrance of a cemetery.
Recreation structures built to be used for activities surrounding winter sports.
One-string spike fiddles with a tube-shaped resonator, usually of wood or animal horn.
Instruments that measure the amount of water vapor in the air and thus indicate relative humidity.
Proportional measuring gauges consisting of two straight, metal bars hinged at one end and graduated for measuring; used in clockmaking.
Clocks that designate periods of time audibly by using a striking mechanism on a bell or gong. If the sounds are musical, prefer "chiming clocks."

Distinctive vessels in certain Protestant churches that are used to contain monetary offerings by the congregation; usually having a slotted lid. Vases of this type were formerly used to contain notes for those receiving communion.
The first letter of a text or section of text when it is emphasized, usually by making it significantly larger than the following text.
Wrenches that measure and indicate the amount of turning and twisting force being applied, as when tightening nuts or bolts.
Refers to an instrument used to determine the presence of electrical current.
General term for vessels or boxes used to hold offerings for religious ceremonies, appearing in various forms and materials.
Large baskets, usually having a cover or lid, for packing, storing, or transporting food, laundry, or other articles.

Silver, ceramic or glass drinking vessels, customarily used in the Netherlands during the 17th 18th century to toast pregnant women. When the cup is filled, the figure of an infant appears from a chamber.
For the modern nation, use with reference to post-1948 things, people, and events.

Strips of material, often the waste ends of the back lining or endsheets, their width extending from the book shoulder onto the board a short way; they are adhered to the boards as a means of board attachment.
Circular and shallow all-purpose baskets.
Vessels decorated by undercutting so that the surface decoration stands free of the body of the glass, supported by struts. The vessels appear, therefore, to be enclosed in an openwork cage.
Coins manufactured with previously issued coins used as planchets.
Use to describe objects designed to be easily carried or conveyed.
The activity of cutting branches or twigs from a woody plant, such as a vine, tree, or shrub in order to regulate growth and promote flowering or fruit production.
Genre in the visual arts in which the interior of churches is depicted.

Vessels  made from the dried, hollowed-out shells of the fruit of the calabash tree or of various types of gourd. Included are containers such as bottles and drinking gourds, utensils such as bowls and ladles, and musical instruments or components thereof such as drums and rattles. They are made and used throughout the world, particularly in Africa, Central and South America, and Polynesia.
Objects or parts of objects that are formed on a lathe.

In brass instruments, U-shaped segments of cylindrical tubing fitted over two straight segments of tubing in such a way as to be able to slide easily in and out, thus changing the instrument's effective total length, and with it, its fundamental pitch during play.

Visual works comprising small panels or tablets with images or text, especially miniatures painted on small wooden panels or images or ancient texts carved or engraved on stone or metal panels. Examples include small panels with miniatures used for various purposes, including as book covers. Common in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.
Japanese prints or paintings employing Western-style perspective.

Shrines that are small in size and intended for personal use. Included are personal shrines for traditional ritual and religious devotional purposes, dating from ancient through modern times in many cultures. Also included are modern works made in the form of devotional shrines: examples are personal shrines made according to New Age aesthetics and shrines designed as craft objects in themselves, made to display small trinkets or other objects without religious meaning. For large shrines, use "shrines (structures)." For relatively small shrines containing sacred relics, such as the relics of a saint, use "reliquaries."

Works, either movable works or built works, that are known by name in literature or otherwise doscumented, but not firmly associated with the corresponding physical work. For works in collections for which the purpose and thus work type are unknown, use "unidentified works."

Process, typically taking place according to customary or legal principle, by which one person, or sometimes multiple people or a state, succeeds another in the occupation or possession of a throne, land, or estate. The act or fact of succession typically binds the successor legally to the rights and liabilities of the predecessor.
Figural representation of Gaṅgā.
Members of a ship's company below the rank of officer.
Types of carpet or area rugs having deep, plush pile and long, fluffy fibers.
Tufted carpets with relatively few tufts per inch, of exceptionally long pile which falls at random in all directions to form the surface.
Strip carpets having a worsted warp concealing the weft; usually striped.
Lighting devices with a lens or lens system which produces a concentrated, sharply defined beam of light.
Objects of art or architecture that are known to have existed, usually through written documentation, but are no longer accounted for.

Colorless double salt first prepared in La Rochelle, France, and thus also known as Rochelle salt. It is used as an analytical reagent, as a laxative, and in making mirrors.In conservation science, it is used in saturated solution as a cleaning agent on bronze and other metal objects.

Decorative element resting on the surface of a sculpture via any of a variety of attachment methods, including solder, adhesives, cements, and/or rivets. Overlay materials may include a range of materials, among them metals, glass, stone, or bone.

Eastern Han artifacts, money trees were good luck charms placed in tombs; so named because of their cast bronze branches laden with leaves made of coins. The branches also contain mythological figures and objects important to Han belief.
Those hired to lead or accompany others, such as travelers, tourists, and hunters, through areas unknown or unfamiliar to them.
Seams, in sheet metal and roofing, made by turning up two adjacent edges and folding the upstanding parts over on themselves.
The supporting structures and other parts that are underneath the body of vehicles.
A technique in which localized regions of a sample are examined with spatial resolution on the micrometer scale.
Hanging oil lamps consisting of a flat metal ring suspended by three chains, the ring having apertures to hold a number (three to six) of light cups or cone-shaped beakers.

Buildings housing museums that specialize in works made from wax, often realistic duplications of actual objects or sculptural portraits of people, especially historical characters. Human figures in wax museums are often dressed in real clothing and posed as if carrying out representative activities.
The state or action of being subject to an external influence.

Paintings done on the fore edge of a book, either with the edge solid so that the resulting image is visible when the book is closed, or, in the more usual sense of the term, with the edges fanned out so that the image is visible only when the book is open.

Literally "Chinese floral motifs" or "Chinese flower designs", this pattern characteristically merges intricate floral motifs into geometric, frequently circular or diamond-shaped, designs. It was introduced to China from Japan as early as the Nara period (710-794) and is sometimes used interchangeably with "karakusa", meaning "Chinese grass motif".
Persons who obey or are guided by the opinions or teaching of another; an adherent, disciple, pupil, or devotee frequently used with religious or philosophic connotations.
People who make candles, which are cylindrical objects composed of tallow or wax containing a wick that is set afire to create illumination.

Refers to blocks of stone placed in masonry walls under girders or other beams or trusses in order to distribute the load; for shaped stones placed on sloping walls to support the copings of gables, use "kneelers (gable components)."
Benchlike seats for the use of a church congregation. They are often fixed in place in rows, have backs and often walls, and are accessible by aisles.

Refers to the rationalist model of the ideal building type based on the construction of the hypothetical first dwelling and its use of materials in response to function and climate; used as a basis for various architectural theories since the 18th century.

Synthetic rubber formed from a salt or other compound which contains two or more sulfur atoms bonded together as an anion or group that are capable of recovering their original shape after being stretched to great extents.
Tools with thin, very flexible, tapered and sometimes diamond-shaped blades, used for applying paint, especially impasto, and for scraping paintings in progress.

A decorative feature in Gothic architecture, carved in a variety of leaf shapes and projecting at regular intervals from the angles of spires, gables, or capitals. A decorative feature in Gothic architecture, carved in a variety of leaf shapes and projecting at regular intervals from the angles of spires, gables, or capitals.
A pattern of short, irregular wriggling channels imitating worm tracks, used as a surface decoration on stone, wood, or another material, to create a rusticated effect.
As an artistic concept, the characteristic of differences between surfaces in a work, or of the appearances of surfaces in two-dimensional works.

Japanese book bindings in which thread is stitched through four equidistant holes in the joint between the spine and the sides of the book, creating a diamond pattern similar to that of a tortoise shell.
Bookbindings having raised letters or designs on the surface.
Toys in the form of human or animal figures.

Amorphous sodium polyphosphate used as water softener (marketed in powdered form as Calgon T and other copyrighted names), sequestering agent, and corrosion inhibitor. In conservation, sodium hexametaphosphate is used in the cleaning of wood, stone, textiles, and ceramics.
Red cloths attached to a stick, used by a matador during the faena.

Dolls found in ancient Egyptian graves, typically carved out of flat pieces of wood, roughly in the shape of a paddle, and decorated with paint and hairmade of strips of clay or wooden beads. Their function may have been as toys but also as protective figures for the deceased in the afterlife.

Generally two-piece tailored women's suits, with a formal jacket and matching skirt of the same material. These have evolved from the end of the 19th century, when they were worn for walking or other types of leisure. From the 20th century skirt suits have become common professional womenswear.
Trousers worn as an extra layer of clothing made of waterproof or other protective material.
Circular bands of white wool with pendants of the same material in the front and the back; worn in the Latin rite by a pope and conferred by him on archbishops as a symbol of office.

Main garments formed by wrapping a strip of cloth around the lower part of the body. Worn chiefly by men and women of the Malay Archipelago and the Pacific Islands. Also, similar often preformed garments worn by Western women.
Accessories added to headwear for decorative or ceremonial purposes.
Pants worn over another pair to protect them, or to provide protection to the wearer from extreme cold.

Undergarments or garmets worn around the anatomical waist and up onto the chest, to which petticoats and drawers are buttoned. They are lightly boned or unboned, usually made of sturdy fabric, with shoulder straps and buttons at the side for attaching to a lower body garment; usually worn by children and women.
Women's underwear, often partly or entirely of elastic or boned, for supporting and shaping the appearance of the abdomen, hips, and buttocks.

Spiral disks made from the base of the shell of the marine snail species Conus. and worn as ornaments or to indicate status, especially in Africa. Use also for similar disks of ceramic or glass made in imitation of these disks.
Arabic cursive script first used in the 7th-8th century CE. Highly decorative, it is generally used for inscriptions and mosque decorations, as opposed to Korans.
Devices with two or more arms that terminate in hooks designed to lift a hot pot out of the hearth by its handles or lip.
Main garments for women, children, or infants consisting of a bodice and skirt made in one or more pieces.
Woolen shawl-like outerwear, usually gray-checked, commonly worn by shepherds in southern Scotland.

Meshed or perforated devices or utensils through which dry loose material (as flour) is winnowed or refined, material containing liquid is strained, or soft solids (as hard-boiled eggs) are comminuted by forcing (as with a pestle).

Flat pieces of material, often with decorative elements, which are placed on surfaces as protection from hot objects; most often vessels containing food. These may be considered a type of trivet, but are not intended to be used over a flame for cooking.

Spoons with circular or oval bowls, used to consume soup and similar foods, especially when served from soup plates. For similar but smaller spoons with a rounded bowl and used to consume bouillon or clear soup, use "bouillon spoons."
A script in fluidly written capitals in use as the everyday Roman script into the 3rd century.
Parts or components of percussion instruments.

Armor pieces consisting of a single plate or a series of lames flexibly connected by straps and rivets, hung in front from each side of the fauld or breastplate to protect the upper part of the thigh.

Protective garments of cloth or leather, covering the trunk and thighs, usually stuffed or quilted. Commonly used from the 12th to the 14th century in Europe, worn either over or under metal armor or as an independent defense. They were often made of rich fabric and embroidered with heraldic devices.

Refers to a type of modern cast glass that is made by pouring molten glass into molds, creating a thick glass that may have a chipped or faceted surface. It is used primarily in construction, for example, to create floors or windows set in concrete, sometimes resembling stained glass. It was invented in France around 1900 as a form of paving.
Forms into which liquid sugar may be poured to allow it to cool and crystallize into a particular shape. May take a variety of forms, including that of a cone.
Small glass vessels, usually with a neck that narrows towards the bottle’s opening. Commonly found in ancient Greek, Egyptian, and Roman archaeological sites, especially tombs.

Ancient Near Eastern coins, especially from Judea, issued during the 1st and 2nd centuries CE; also silver or cupronickel decimal coins of Israel. For Persian coins of the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, use "sigloi"; for coins issued in Sidon and Tyre from the 4th century BCE, prefer "tetradrachms."
Genoese gold coins struck from 1252 until the early 15th century; for similar coins issued in Florence at the same time, use "florins."

Celtic script used in inscriptions in the Irish and Pictish languages, dating from the fourth century and found in Britain and Ireland. Its alphabet consists of 20 characters represented by notches or straight or diagonal strokes, varying in number from one to five and drawn or cut to the left, right, or directly through vertical lines or the edges of the vertical stone monuments on which they were carved. Besides stone monuments, they are traditionally said to have been used on shields and wooden staves, and occur in at least one 14th-century manuscript.
Chants and movements of indigenous Hawaiians, that once honored the gods, or akua, then transferred after the arrival of Christian missionaries to rituals honoring the surviving ancestral gods.
Books containing the forms for sacraments and rites performed by a bishop.
Tools having a stretched wire used as a cutting edge, or trowel-like tools with a central slitlike blade, used to slice cheese.
Transverse flutes of the Venda peoples of South Africa. They are made of river cane, have two to four fingerholes, and are played by boys who herd cattle.

Lidless kettles intended primarily for boiling fruits and their syrup for preserves; made of tin, brass, or enameled ware, but never iron or aluminum as both metals are affected by the acid of the fruits.
Blocks of stone that may be heated in order to cook food.
Literary works that ridicule either through the treatment of a solemn subject in an undignified manner or by applying an elevated style and manner to a trivial subject.

Procedures used in the relief process, where the nonprinting areas of blocks or plates are carved, engraved, or etched away, leaving the original plane surfaces raised so that ink is deposited and transferred to paper.

A relief process in which the design is cut into and printed from the grain end of a wood block; distinct from "woodcut (process)," which is a relief process using the plank side of a wood block. The process is considered engraving due due to the use of a burin to carve the image, though the result is a relief printing process like woodcut.
Vessels used to pour liquids, having one handle, a large body, and a nib-like neck.

Objects that can function both as muffs and as receptacles for personal items. Often these are designed as handbags with an opening in the back in which the hands can be inserted, or conversely, muffs with an appended pouch.
Small, usually semi-ovoid cups with an often stemmed base, made in a variety of materials and used for serving individual boiled eggs in the shell.
Receptacles made of twisted wire for holding one or more eggs while boiling them and then serving them at the table.
Flat-bottomed, round or truncated conical, wicker container equipped with handles used to store dry food ingredients.

Vessels intended to hold or dispense hot water in connection with the serving of tea or coffee, often urnlike in form and having one or more taps and a spigot near the base; usually supported on legs or a stand and often having a heating device. May be part of a tea or coffee service. Prefer "tea urns" for similar vessels intended to hold or dispense tea and which may be part of a tea service. Prefer "coffee urns" for similar vessels intended to hold or dispense coffee and which may be part of a coffee service.

Cylindrical, wooden drums that are similar to snare drums, but do not have snares. They typically measure 35cm in height and 45cm in diameter. Tenor drums have historically been associated with military and marching bands, though they sometimes appear in classical orchestrations.
Ornamental cups in the shape of a pineapple, often made of silver, or silver-gilt.

Small cups intended for drinking punch or similar beverages served from a punch bowl, having a flat bottom or stemmed foot and usually a single handle. Generally made in sets accompanying and conforming to a punch bowl.

Containers, usually made of animal hide, made by Native North Americans to store tobacco. Often decorated with quillwork, beadwork, and sometimes pigment. Designs typically refer to cosmological or spiritual themes, as tobacco is a central aspect of many Native religious traditions.
Containers for water, typically of metal or plastic and having a spout with a perforated nozzle, for watering or sprinkling plants.

Straight poles graduated with numerical and geometric marks that are held upright and used with transits or other surveying instruments equipped with stadia hairs to measure horizontal distances. For similar poles graduated with numerical marks for measuring heights or elevations, use "leveling rods."
Cases or bags for keeping maps, often in the context of military campaigns, but also used by travelers.
Bins, boxes, or the like, for storing wood fuel.

Vessels with dual openings, originally used in Buddhist ceremonies for sprinkling water for purification. The form originated in India and was later transmitted to China and Korea. The kundika is one of the usual attributes of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara. Scholarship notes that Brahmanical hermits used these vessels to dispense water for their personal use.
Small, flat boxlike containers used to carry small cards, typically personal or business cards.
Protruding ornaments, often globular, found on the stems of vessels or the shafts of objects such as candlesticks. For similar protruberances in terminal positions, use "finials."
Hand axes, with heads made of stone or metal, designed to chip and shape stone.
The process of attaching boards to a text block by passing the bands or cords on which the text block is sewn through holes cut into the boards.
Areas outside the official boundaries of a sovereign nation but which are subject to and considered as the property of that nation.
Tools used to measure the thickness of printing plates, such as electrotyping plates.
Furniture feet in the form of a tapered square block, much used in the second half of the 18th century.

Works, usually sacred objects or images, that resemble a human or animal figure, rather than abstract in design. Commonly dedicated to divinities or as memorials; may be executed according to a fixed or conventional type.
Beads arranged in strings and used in praying, such as the beads of a rosary.

Instruments pierced with a hole, used in pre-Columbian times for the purpose of "seeing". Literally, "That by which one sees". Attribute of several deities such as Tezcatlipoca and Xiuhteuctli. According to the sources, could have been made of gold, in mosaic of feathers. Sometimes compared to a mirror.
Describes vessels built and armed for combat purposes and travel or transport below the water's surface.

Refers to fore-and-aft-rigged sailing vessels with two or more masts, especially those with only two masts in which the aftermast is taller than the foremast; for two-masted sailing vessels in which the aftermast is the shorter one, see "ketches (fore-and-aft-rigged vessels)" or "yawls (sailing vessels)."
Devices designed to clear unwanted vegetation from a landscape.
Autocratic governments ruled by a dictator, without effective constitutional limitations.

Refers to fabrics engineered with nanofibers having a width of less than 1000 nanometers. These have many applications thanks to such advantageous properties as extreme water-resistance and elasticity. There has been concern expressed regarding environmental and health effects of nanomaterials in nanotextiles released into air, soil, or groundwater or in direct contact with wearer.

Strong cloth woven in a variety of patterns, in common use for bedding and lining for clothing from the 17th to the 19th century. Prior to the 17th century it was made of worsted, then pure cotton or mixes of cotton and linen became common; today generally a cotton twill with a short nap.

Heavy textile consisting of two separate textiles woven simultaneously, one above the other. The warp is composed of two series of ends, and each interlaces with its own weft, or with a common weft which works with each series in turn. In patterned double weave, the two textiles change position as required by the pattern.

The process of cutting spiral grooves in the surface of a firearm projectile or the bore of a firearm barrel, also for the system of grooves so cut. The grooves impart a spinning motion to the projectile, thus equalizing its balance in flight and stabilizing its trajectory.
The uniting superposed layers of one or more materials, typically the fusing of thin sheets of plastic to the surfaces of paper or cardboard by means of heat and pressure.
Scattering a substance in drops or particles on a surface often resulting in a surface covering of small specks, spots, or splotches.
Removal of chlorine from water or another substance.
Decay in plants and plant-derived materials such as timber marked by deterioration of tissues and caused chiefly by fungi and bacteria. By extension, decomposition of stone, leather, textiles.
Large spoons, with a capacity three times the size of a teaspoon, used for serving or consuming foods and as a standard unit of measurement in recipes.
Light two-wheeled hooded vehicles having springs and two shafts, drawn by one or more men. First used in Japan ca. 1870, but now common in other parts of the world.
Conversion of carbon-containing organic matter into carbon or carbonic residue. The formation of coal is an example of carbonization.

Measurement indicator referring to the open space or gap lying between two things or two parts of the same thing. An example of usage is with repeating characteristics, such as pattern repeats in textiles or chain lines in paper.
In Indian architecture, a śikhara’s curvature having seven segments in vēṇukōśa.
Use to describe objects and beings of a reduced size or scale compared to the average or normal range for its kind.
Characteristics and qualities that are electrophysical.
Having or relating to the three dimensions of length, width, and height, plus time, or another spatial dimension.
The state or quality of materials of being incapable of being mixed.
Frames with fluted reed moldings, a trademark of 19th-century painter James Abbott McNeill Whistler.

Lip-vibrated aerophones of conical bore made from marine shells, usually conchs. They may be furnished with a mouthpiece, or simply have a hole bored in the tip, if end-blown, or in the spiraling part of the shell, if side-blown.

Plucked zitherlike chordophones consisting of a raised wood soundboard or shallow soundbox with sound holes, with strings stretched parallel to the board or box and attached at either side by wood pegs or metal pins.
Dresses worn by brides during the wedding ceremony, in many styles and colors, often having a train.
Use both for two-dimensional representations of human figures cut from paper or cardboard and for connected series of doll-like figures cut from folded paper.
Long necked, plucked chordophones of India. They generally have a single string, which passes through a gourd used as a resonator.

Devices for throwing a spear or dart, consisting of a stick or board with a groove or hollow on their upper surface and a hook, thong, or projection at the rear end to hold the projectile in place until its release.

Indian board game for four players in opposing partnerships of two in which game pieces are moved around a cross-shaped track. Moves are determined by throws of cowrie shells or dice, and each player begins with four pieces, at the center and moves down the middle track counter clockwise around the outer track of the board. The partnership whose pieces first complete the course by returning to the centre space is the winner.

Books, generally intended for children, in which the pages feature illustrations with blank spaces on which to place adhesive stickers; the stickers come with the book either as separate sheets or on leaves of the book.
Badges that advocate for a political cause or person, usually pinned or otherwise affixed to clothing.
Long, loose-hanging dresses, usually brightly colored or patterned, worn especially by Hawaiian women. Also, similar dresses worn as housecoats.

A blackish blue or blood red natural colorant extracted from the logwood tree, Haematoxylon campechianum, of Central America, Mexico, and the West Indies. It was formerly used to make black ink, and is still used to dye textiles black.

Polymerized methyl methacrylate is a compound having a hard and glasslike appearance, with softening temperature from 105-125 C. Classified as bioinert. As a resin, widely used as a glass substitute (e.g., Plexiglass (TM)) and a bonelike material for prosthetics. First commercially sold in 1933 as a glass substitute.

Intermediate versions of screenplays, written between the synopsis and the first draft of the screenplay in the sequence of development, generally including a full narrative covering all the principal situations and actions, brief descriptions of the characters, and possibly some key sequences of dialogue.
Various liturgical books containing readings concerning the sufferings of the saints or of Christ.

Limited edition books, traditionally handcrafted from fine materials, richly illustrated with original works of graphic art by well known artists. Often includes artists' visual counterparts to a piece of poetry or prose. The tradition began in France in the mid-nineteenth century and has spread elsewhere.
Cloth caps primarily intended to be worn in bed.
Footwear with uppers that extend above the ankle joint, and that have closures that involve lacing through eyelets, grommets, or other means.

Use specifically for the parts of the firing mechanisms of small arms that initiate firing when pressed or moved by the finger, typically a hinged metal lever acting on the sear in the lock. Use also in the general sense for any mechanical or electronic devices activating a firearm or crossbow by a press of the finger.

Four-wheeled, covered carriages with either paneled or curtained sides, with or without perch, mounted on elliptic or platform springs, having a driver's seat included in the body proper and generally with a common roof projecting over the driver's area; could be drawn by one or two horses; popular in the United States in numerous body styles; introduced in the 1830s.
Close-fitting, cone-shaped caps with a flat crown usually of felt and often trimmed with a long tassel; of a type originating in Turkey.
Barriers of ablative material to protect a spacecraft from heat on its entry into an atmosphere.

Projecting spars with floats, such as a log, rigged out from the side or sides of a vessel to maintain stability; may also refer to vessels so rigged. For canoes rigged with outriggers, construct from "outrigger" and "canoes."
Handcarts, often wire-framed in which mail and packages are carried for delivery, usually in an office environment.
Ribbons or strings attached to hats in such a way that they may be tied under the chin, in order to secure the hat on the head.
Articles of clothing suitable for formal wear during the evening, often as opposed to the more casual styles of day wear. For garments worn to bed, use "nightwear."

Iron and bronze staffs or scepters of uncertain origin and age, possibly made by the Soninke, Fulani or Fula people. They have been found in Guinea-Bissau and Sierra Leone. They date possibly to the 17th century.
Massive helmets, reaching to the shoulders, worn in the 12th and 13th centuries, sometimes a smaller close-fitting ones.
Toys that are intended to reenact a religious ritual. In the Catholic context, for example, altars, monstrances and habits were made for children.

Braided cords, worn around the shoulder on military uniforms, awarded as an honorary decoration. Also, similar cords adopted as trim on women's garments. Distinguished from "aiguillettes (cords)," which are usually braided, end in aglets, and are worn especially by aides-de-camp and sometimes other military officers.

Books that are valuable due to their actual or prospective rarity, specifically books distinguished by an early publication date, limited issue, historical interest, or a special characteristic of the edition or binding, for example having been signed by the artist or containing special illustrations. This designation typically includes books that are collected by a special collections department, archives, or museum, as opposed to books that are available to casual readers on the shelves of a public library.
Coined by Ted Nelson in 1965. Generally, hypertext is any collection of written or pictorial matter that may be experienced non-sequentially, specifically used now in relation to the World Wide Web.
Shallow parts of rivers, or tracts of shallow water in general, which can be crossed on foot or by vehicle.
Paper size measuring 15 by 12 1/2 inches. Originally, pott paper bore the watermark of a pot.

Members of the order containing six species in one family. Living members are primitive hoofed herbivorous mammals of the family Procaviidae, the only surviving members of the order Hyracoidea, being small thickset, herbivorous quadrupeds, about the size of a large domestic rabbit, similar to guinea pigs in appearance, with tusk-like incisor teeth, and native Africa and the Middle East.
Genus of four Asian, African, and South and Central American species, including the jaguar, lion, leopard, and tiger.
Proofs of line or halftone engravings. The proofs should ideally be pulled on the same paper as that on which the job is to be printed. In the 19th century such proofs might be signed "engraver's."

Objects used for exchange or purchase and having the shape of a weapon or that are weapons or parts of weapons, such as projectile points. Weapons used as currency are known from many historical periods globally.
Marbled paper prepared so that the color spots have shell-like rings, darker in the center than around the edges, which is produced by adding oil to the color.
A book format derived from folding a sheet of paper into 128 leaves, resulting in 256 pages. Often notated as 128mo.
Celebrated on October 7, in commemoration the victory of the combined Christian fleet against the Ottoman fleet in 1571.
In Zen Buddhism, satori refers to a sudden personal enlightenment analagous to the original moment of spiritual rebirth experienced by the Gautama Buddha.
Basic tapestry stitches worked in two journeys, first carrying the thread diagonnally over a double thread of canvas from left to right, then vertically transversing the double thread.
In Indian architecture, a attic pillar.
Describes works produced by the African people of the same name living in Sudan and Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea-Bissau. Term is used both for the works of this Mande subgroup and as synonymous with "Mande" itself.
In Indian architecture, a hall for festivities.

Having the shape or form of a pyramid, which is a polyhedron having one face (the base) that is a polygon of any number of sides, and the other faces are triangles with bases forming the sides of the polygon meet at a common vertex.
