American motion picture genre typically featuring a comic battle of the sexes in which the hero and heroine are caught up in a romantic pursuit or patching up a marriage, involving a rapid sequence of improbable events and a surrounding group of eccentric characters. The dialogue is generally fast-paced and witty, and romantic love triumphs in the end. The hayday of the screwball comedy was from the mid-1930s through the 1940s.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the African collective cultural-linguistic group of the same name living in Ghana and Burkina Faso.
Single distinct meaningful elements of speech or writing.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Côte d'Ivoire.

Relatively small vertical presses used to apply quick uniform pressure; consisting of a fixed iron or steel base and a moveable platen that is raised and lowered by means of a long vertical screw. Originally designed to copy letters, but also used for other purposes.
Style and culture of the state of Comoros, comprising the islands of the Comorian archipelago in the Indian Ocean, off the coast of East Africa.
Relatively large retail businesses selling many different kinds of articles, which are arranged in sections or deparments.
Painters serving the personal requests of a ruler or other important person. Generally used to distinguish from "court painters" or other painters associated with the same court.
Narrow strips of deep-fried potato, generally eaten as side dish, or as a snack.
Parts of a bridle that prevent a horse from opening its mouth wide enough to lay its tongue over the bit. It also keeps the bit stable.
Metal loops attached to a horse's bit, which guide the reins and prevent them from becoming tangled or snagged on the harness.
The ashes of a cremated person or animal.

Specialized looms designed to facilitate the weaving of pile or plush fabrics, such as velvet, terry towel, chenille, and pile carpets, which have tufts or loops of fibres that stand up from the base fabric. These looms consist of a Jacquard-type power loom with an attachment that introduces wires at intervals to create false wefts around which warps are bound. The threads of each warp are thus lifted at different times so that they pass over the wires to form a row of standing loops.

Phylum that includes common vertebrates such as fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals, as well as the tunicates and lancelets. With few exceptions, chordates are active animals with bilaterally symmetric bodies that are longitudinally differentiated into head, trunk, and tail. The most distinctive morphological features of chordates are the notochord, nerve cord, and visceral clefts and arches.
Devices for threading needles; designs vary, but most have a pointed end to push the thread through the eye of a needle.

General term for a solid marking substance in the form of a slender rod, which is then enclosed in a cylinder of wood, metal, or plastic to form a "pencil (drawing and writing equipment)." Common examples of materials used in "pencils (drawing and writing equipment)" are graphite, lead, and pigmented wax.
Masks fitting over the nose and mouth through which oxygen or oxygen-enriched air is supplied.

Perforated cylinders that utilize a pneumatic conveying process to extract airborne fibers, such as dust and dirt, from cotton lint and other non-woven fabrics. Also used to compress a web of fibers into long strips of parallel fibers, thus converting the web to a sliver or roving. These devices generally contain two chambers in between which is a spinning barrel. The flow of material and air enters the vacuum chamber, which is then pushed to the next chamber by the barrel at atmospheric pressure.
Benzotriazole (BTA) is a heterocyclic compound with many applications. In conservation, the silvery powder is chiefly used as a corrosion inhibitor for copper and its alloys.

Style of textiles, particularly floor coverings (often prayer rugs), handwoven in Kula, a town east of Izmir in western Turkey, popular with collectors in the 19th century and beyond. The designs are often characterized by a low, straight-sided arch (indicating the direction of Mecca), columnar sides of the prayer niche often comprising broad, ribbonlike pendant forms, and often having elaborate central motifs. Early Kula prayer rugs have strong reds and blues, but in most later examples the red has been exchanged for an assortment of muddy browns and yellows.

term: Iranian Islamic styles after the Mongols
definition: Styles after the Mongols, belonging to Iranian Islamic cultures.

Rugs woven by the nomadic Shahsavan of Northwestern Iran, typically wool-on-wool, symmetrically knotted pile rugs, characterized by relatively simple field and border designs, occasional use of camel hair in the pile and cotton in the wefts, and red and salmon color in the wefts.
Parts or components of containers.
Systems designed to alert for and protect against various hazards, such as fire and security systems.
The use of computer graphics to make large amounts of complex data comprehensible.
General term for articles or physical resources used to equip vehicles.
Launching rock projectiles in combat, hunting, or protest.

Fabric predecessor to needle lace originating during the 15th century. The mesh ground was formed by drawing warps and wefts from fabric at regular intervals, or by cutting out areas of embroidered fabric and introducing stitching to the void.

Individual objects or works. Most works in museums are cataloged as items. A stand-alone architectural work should generally be cataloged as an item. An item may be composed of multiple parts or components, and it may be desirable to catalog the parts separately, linking the records for the components to the record for the whole. An item differs from a component in that the component cannot stand alone as an independent work.

Sections made by a plane cutting anything transversely, especially at right angles to the longest axis. In conservation, cross-sectional analysis is employed in a variety of contexts, including examining paint layers and fiber analysis.
Process of reheating glass after it has cooled in order to develop color or opacity.
A cloth covered bag containing an electrical element used for applying heat to the body.
Objects that are used for breeding, caring for, and study of animals kept on a farm for use or profit, especially cattle, sheep, and pigs.
Manicure tools used for removing of the dead skin that adheres to the base of fingernails during the nail growth process.
General term for all personal equipment, tools, and accessories having to do with individual use of tobacco or smoking herbs.
Those who run, particularly athletes engaged in competitive short or long-distance footracing.
Incorporated, primarily urban divisions whose population and, usually, territorial area are smaller than those of cities.
Instruments for projecting images of sound waves directly on a screen.
Steep to perpindicular slopes on the sea floor.
Non-professional painters, sculptors, or other artists who have not had formal training and are often self-taught; also, artists who are formally trained, but who create works in naive style.

Fine white translucent porcelain with a thick white glaze made at Dehua (Te Hua) from the late Ming period and exported to Southeast Asia and to Europe from the 18th century.Characteristic forms were small figures depicting Buddhist deities and dignitaries, cups, and vases. The term is also used for similar ware produced elsewhere in Japan and Europe, such as in Saint-Cloud, France and Chelsea and Bow, England.

People who specialize in applying decoration, modification, and embellishment to the human body for purposes of cultural identity, beautification, or self expression. Their art includes such forms as scarification, tattooing, body piercing and painting, and hair styling. Body artists in this sense are typically practicing techniques that are based in ancient and traditional body modification; they thus differ from "body artists (performance artists)" who arose in the 1960s and whose art is closely related to performance art and conceptual art.
Deep regret, guilt, or sorrow for having done something morally wrong or otherwise considered incorrect.

Technical or specialized parlances of a specific social or occupational group that others outside the group cannot understand well. The term originally indicated unstable rudimentary hybrid languages.

Hand gesture representing explanation, exposition, or discourse. The hand is presented with palm outward, the fingers upward, and the thumb and index finger forming a circle. A hand-gesture of exposition.

Artists who create publications consisting of comic drawings in the form of sequential juxtaposed panels, often accompanied by descriptive prose or written narrative, with dialog between characters often in the form of word ballons.
The culture of ancient Latium or the ancient Latini tribes.
The activity or function of restoring a person or animal to health, to aid in treatment of wounds, recovery from sickness, or otherwise curing.
The activity of leaving or escaping an area or situation with stealth or speed.
In Indian architecture, a pearl-cable arch.
Buddhist or Hindu celestial beings or spirits who are part human and animal, either horse or bird.
Units of time equivalent to nearly 365.25 days, 12 months, or the period of one full circuit of the Earth around the Sun.

Units equal to one meter in a straight line; used to measure the amount of shelf space occupied by archival materials within a specific collection, as well as piping, wiring, and other things that are linear in orientation.
Order of flowering plants.

Mythical monsters, represented as a huge and terrible reptile, usually combining ophidian and crocodilian structure, with strong claws, like a beast or bird of prey, and a scaly skin; it is generally represented with wings, and sometimes as breathing out fire. The heraldic dragon combines reptilian and mammalian form with the addition of wings.

Species of hardy, medium-sized poplar tree native to cool temperate regions of Europe and Asia, including the British Isles. The bark is pale greenish-gray, smooth on young trees with dark grey diamond-shaped lenticels. It turns darker and fissured on old trees. The leaves are especially liable to the tremulous motion common to all poplars, thus the name of the species; leaves have an unpleasant taste that discourages denuding by fallow deer. The wood has large, evenly-distributed pores that produce a soft fibrous texture, making it valuable for only limited use.
Construction membrane used for roofing.

Species of small, slow-growing deciduous shrubby tree native to the dry, sandy areas of the southeastern United States, on the coastal plain from Delaware to Florida and Louisiana. It reaches 10 meters in height, has deeply incised leaves with 3-7 slender lobes, and acorns that take 18 months to mature. It hybridizes easily with southern red oak (Q. falcata), bluejack oak (Q. incana), laurel oak (Q. laurifolia), and water oak (Q. nigra). Its name "turkey oak" is derived either from the turkey-footprint shape of its leaves or from the fact that wild turkeys eat the acorns.

Genus containing 5 species of resinous, evergreen ornamental and timber conifers of the cypress family (Cupressaceae), native to North America and eastern Asia. The genus is monophyletic and sister to Thujopsis or false arborvitae. Arborvitae are trees or shrubs, usually pyramidal in habit, with thin, scaling outer bark and fibrous inner bark, horizontal or ascending branches, and characteristically flattened, spraylike branchlet systems. Each branchlet has four rows of tiny, scalelike leaves. Juvenile leaves are much longer and needlelike and in some species may persist along with the mature foliage. Male and female reproductive structures (cones) are borne at the tips of different branchlets of the same tree, the male cones rounded and reddish or yellowish, the female very small and green or tinged with purple. They are commonly known as arborvitae (from Latin for tree of life) or thujas; several species are widely known as cedar but they are not true cedars (Cedrus).

Genus containing 6 to 40 species (depending upon the classification) of perennial grass cultivated for its juice in tropical regions. Sugar cane products include table sugar, falernum, molasses, rum, cachaca, bagasse, and ethanol. Most present-day commercial canes are hybrids of the species Saccharum officinarum, which was developed from a wild cane species, Saccharum robustom, and cultivated by native peoples of southern Pacific Islands.
In Greek and Roman mythology, goddesses regarded as presiding over and inspiring learning and the arts, especially poetry and music. Often, but not always, numbering nine.
Genus containing 43 species of annual and perennial herbs native to Middle East and Asia. It is best known for the widely cultivated member, C. arietinum, chickpea.

Studios in which one or more master textile artist creates works, supervises assistants, and instructs pupils in creating textiles or works made of textiles, which are works that use plant, animal, or synthetic fibers to construct practical or decorative items.
Species of North American pine related to Ponderosa Pine, found in the area from southwest Oregon, United States, to northern Baja California, Mexico.
Enterprises, whether businesses or institutions, that focus on the display or sale of art works or other items.
Any of a wide variety of museums where collections are amassed and typically presented to give a chronological perspective of the history of a city, town, region, group of people, etc.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of yellow colors.
A range of colors resembling variations of red pigment.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of whitish colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink colors.
Forms of data whose expected content is the URI of a referenced entity expected to follow a specific independent data schema.
A range of yellow colors resembling the color of gamboge, a resin from an Asian tree.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of gray colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.

A cool brownish color with overtones of violet or olive color, varying from light to moderate value, originally referring to the color of sepia ink, which is derived from cuttlefish and used in pen and ink drawings.
Refers to a range of greenish colors resembling the color of ivy, which is a climbing or trailing evergreen plants with shiny dark green leaves.
Variable reddish orange colors resembling the color of quinacridone red pigment.
Flesh-colored, carnation, pale red or pink, but also used for various shades of crimson or blood-red.  That is, the color of either a European person's skin or of animal flesh (meat).

Style of architecture, interior design, or other works that evokes elements of plantation houses of the American south or of Hawaii or other island colonial settlements. Particulary appropriate when the work is not affiliated with a plantation, but only the style is appropriated.
Range of light, strong shades of blue.
Members of a family containing around 80 species of small, dark-barred brownish birds with a short bill slightly downcurved, short rounded wings, and a short cocked tail.
Division of primate taxonomy containing 3 infraorders of 6 families with 4 fossil families; included are lemurs, galagos and lorisids.

Family containing 35 species in 20 genera of civets and related species resembling long-nosed cats, having retractile or partially-retractile claws, a baculum (penile bone), and an anal scent gland. They are among the most primitive families Carnivora, with skeletons very similar to those of fossils dating back to the Eocene 50 million years ago.
Members of an order of containing a single family of icebugs.
Personal names that include last names acquired by a person, usually a woman, through marriage; distinguished from "maiden names."

Order containing 141 species in two families including anis, roadrunners, and the hoatzin, with one species extinct since 1600. They are long-tailed birds with rearward or sideward facing toes, feeding on both fruits and small animals, most are arboreal but a few are terrestrial, and some are brood parasites.
Tools consisting of large, flat squares of metal, sharpened on the edge opposite the handle. Used to divide bread and pastry dough or scrape dough off of a working surface.

The sections of wall of Indian temples located above but not including moldings, and below the tower or spire.  In Indian architecture, a wall; wall-frieze between vēdībandha and śikhara; kaṭi (older synonym); jāṅgha (Oriyā).
In Indian architecture, a adhiṣṭhāna-type.
Relatively large celestial masses that are gravitationally coupled to a larger mass. Examples are the Earth, which orbits the Sun, and the Moon, which orbits the Earth.

Educational institutions devoted to training dentists, who are those whose medical practice is focused on teeth and associated structures of the mouth, involving the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of disease, injury, or malformation of the teeth, gums, and jaws.
Large, subterranean, naturally formed chambers, with entrances from the surface.
Pre-Columbian ritual libation vessels, comprising two chambers.

Extinct order of aquatic reptiles with slender elongate jaws filled with long pointed teeth, a tail as long as or longer than the body and flattened side to side, well developed limbs, and enlarged paddlelike hind feet.
General term referring to any of four living species of equines having black-and-white-stripes over all or most of their bodies.

A concise description of the date or range of dates associated with the creation, design, production, presentation, performance, construction, or alteration of the work or its components, presented in a syntax suitable for display.
Devices that put fabric under tension so that it can be worked with thread, usually for a variety of decorative techniques including embroidery.

Mechanized devices designed to apply a layer of textile strength carrier, such as polyurethane, polyvinyl chloride, acryclic resins, natural or synthetic rubber paste, or similar chemical solutions, to one or both sides of a textile substrate. Unlike traditional chemical finishes, during which chemical treatments infiltrate the substrate's fibers, the coating facilitated by these devices produces a chemical layer in the spaces between the fibers; this coating produces a new chemical structure to strengthen textile materials and promote increased corrosion, thermal, and abrasion resistance. Depending on the type of substrate being coated, these devices can incorporate interroller pressure, knife-spread, dip, spray, powder, extrusion, or UV-cured coating technologies.

Precision instruments, comprising two identical tubes placed side by side, designed to determine the color of a sample of any substance and record it in terms of an arbitrary unit. To determine the sample's exact color, the device's first tube is filled with the sample to be examined; tinted glasses, which are graduated on a scale of color density, are inserted in the second tube and manipulated by the user until the colors in both tubes exactly match.  Based on the observed correspondence between the sample color and the tinted glasses, the user is able to determine the degree of impurity or purity for the given substance of a certain color. The tintometer's invention is credited to Joseph W. Lovibond, who obtained a patent for the device in 1886. Though Lovibond initially created the tintometer to control beer quality by matching each batch to a color standard, his invention has since been applied to the textile industry, amongst other applications.

Freestanding supports for implements in firesets, frequently designed as a tray mounted with a vertical rod terminated by an open ring, or hooks, used to contain the handles of tools such as shovels, pokers, tongs, etc.

Small dishes on which spoons or other cooking utensils may be placed during cooking to keep the cooktop or other surface clean. May be designed to hang on the side of a pot or placed flat on a surface.
Racks used to hold meat during cooking or for storing meat.
Stones used to mill grain into flour. The handstone is held by the operator and used to crush the grain against a larger, stationary stone.
Boards or multipurpose tables, usually relatively small in size, on which paper or canvas can be placed for drawing.
Scales made for weighing dairy products, typically designed to withstand the moisture found in a dairy and having platforms that accomodate large quantities of milk cans, butter, or cheese.
Bookbinding machines that apply a layer of paste to the outer edges, or books.
Analog devices used to compare different transcriptions of the same information to verify the accuracy of the data, to verify arithmetic functions, or to verify storage.
Concussive instruments used to stun animals in the course of slaughtering and butchering them.
Meaning "invented [it]," in painting and other art works, indicates the master designer.

Order of flowering plants consisting of 2 families, 27 genera, and about 300 species. Members are herbs or shrubs, rarely hemiparasites, and largely restricted to tropical or temperate arid or saline regions. The flowers are showy and possess oil or nectar glands for bee pollination.

Jokari is a paddle ball game principally for two players, but it can also be played solo, for example against a wall. The game consists of a rubber ball attached to an anchor by means of a long elastic band, which makes the ball come back when you hit it. Jokari is played with wooden paddles.
Anvils used to form and shape dental appliances or to make dental tools.

Mechanized devices designed to expedite mass fabric production by tying each warp yarn on the existing loom beam to the associated yarn on the replacement loom beam. By automating the loom beam replacement process, these devices eliminate the need for a new warp beam to be drawn-in when the pattern is not changing. Portable tying-in devices were widely introduced in 1910, replacing previously popular stationary machines.

Genre of performing art characterized by the skillful production of musical tones by means of the human voice. Singing requires a physical technique in which the lungs supply air to the larynx, which acts as a reed or vibrator; the chest and head cavities function as amplifiers. The tongue, palate, teeth, and lips articulate and impose consonants and vowels on the amplified sound. In the art of singing, refined skill is required to coordinate these various anatomical mechanisms and their interaction upon one another. Singing is distinct from speaking in the way in which the breath is expended to vibrate the vocal cords and by the control required in the movement and reflexes of the larynx.
Hereditary succession to property, quality, or immaterial possession. When the inheritance is transferred by a legal document such as a will, regardless of familial relationship, use 'bequest.'
Listing items on hand.
Titles that are the most complete or longest versions of the title, as distinguished from shorter versions of the title. In legal writing, called the long title.

Unique numeric, alphabetic, alphanumeric, or other codes that identify or reference a thing, concept, or record, and that are reliable and longlasting. An example of a persistent identifier is as used for digital objects. Persistent identifier systems include "persistent object identifiers" (POIDs) and "digital object Identifiers" (DOIs).
Events intended to entertain audiences.
The standard unit of currency of Germany prior to adoption of the Euro.
Refers to the variety of Spanish spoken in Nicaragua; it is influenced by indigenous languages and creole dialects.

Short-lived dating system that was adopted in 1793 during the French Revolution and which was intended to replace the Gregorian calendar with a more scientific and rational system that would avoid Christian associations.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 397-414; founded by the Tufa family of Xianbei ethnicity, considered relatives of the Tuoba imperial house of Northern Wei.

General term for false or ficticious names or appellations used instead of personal names, place names, and other names. When adopted for personal names, pseudonyms may be used to conceal the real identity of the person, for example, as used by authors and artists.

The twelfth and final month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendars, containing 31 days and falling after November. Its name is derived from decem, Latin for “ten,” indicating its position in the early Roman calendar.
Tools with serrated jaws, designed for gripping leather. In shoemaking hey are used for straining leather uppers over the last.
In Japanese printing, a sheet of paper that is in portrait format (height is greater than width).
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 99 to 1 (or 100 to 1) Before Common Era.
Dances particular to one or more Native American cultures.
Beverages comprising primarily water into which carbon dioxide gas under pressure has been dissolved, either naturally or artificially. Soda may contain flavorings or other additives.

A proprietary magnetic disk digital storage format marketed by Iomega from ca.1994-2003. The system consisted of a drive mechanism and sealed 'superfloppy' magnetic disks originally with 100Mb, then 250Mb, and 750Mb capacities.
Large language family of continental Southeast Asia, in isolated areas of India, Bangladesh, Nepal, and the southern border of China.
In Indian architecture, an octagonal column/pillar/pāda type.

The princess cut is a combination of a brilliant-cut variation with a square or, less often, rectangular outline. The design evolved to increase the brilliance of square and rectangular gem cuts by increasing the number of facets on the crown and pavilion. There is no standardized arrangement although the majority have 76 facets.

Miatungusu is a major festival of the Hla’alua people after the harvest of rice. It is traditionally held once every two to three years, now it is an annual event. The festival is devoted to takiarʉ (“the sacred shell”), a sacred being left by the kavurua people. The ritual includes welcoming the gods, initiation, hog sacrifice, wine offering to takiarʉ, expelling evil spirits and the distribution of game. It is believed that through pleasing the sacred shell harvest and prosperity can be brought to the Hla’alua people.
The twelfth month of the French revolutionary calendar (from Aug. 18 to Sept. 16); the revolution which took place in that month in 1797.

Cultures and styles of the Seediq people lived in Taiwan. In 2008 Seediq was officially recognized as an ethnic group distinct from the Truku people. The Seediq people primarily live in Renai Township, Nantou County and Hualien County. The Seediq language is constituted by three dialect clusters: Tada, Tgdaya and Truku. The traditional life centers on gaya (waya) and the belief in utux, while their social protocol has evolved through the encounter with the modern state and Christianity.
Encompassing all kinds of sexuality; not limited or inhibited in sexual choice with regards to biological sex, gender identity, or sexual practice.
Cards upon which prayers are inscribed or written.
Small pieces of paper, usually multicolored and sometimes cut in various shapes, ceremonially thrown at various events, such as weddings or parades.
In Indian architecture, a vyāla-based column-type.

The radiant cut produces the optical effects of a brilliant cut from a cut-cornered square or rectangular stone gem cut. There are various facet combinations with no set standard. The average number of facets is 70.

The festival of Mikong is the Kanakanavu people’s celebration of millet harvest in honor of their millet god, tamu vinaʉ. Today, the festival is held in October on an annual basis. The festival takes place after the millet harvest, proceeding from family prayers, making rice cakes (“pepe”), presenting offerings to the millet god to bidding farewell to the millet god. Once the family ritual is over, each family is to bring their home-made pepe, wine and fish to cakʉrʉ (“tribal meeting place”) to attend tribal worship.

Cultures and styles of the Tao people lived in Taiwan. The Tao people take residence on Orchid Island off the coast of Taitung. They primarily live on the subsistence of fish and taro crops, which are core to the Tao material culture. The Tao society is marked by monogamy and bilateralism. Their major festivals revolve around the traditional economy such as the crops of millet and taro and the annual catch of flying fish. Miyaron (“flying fish festival”) is their most renowned celebration.
Embodying multiple genders.
General term for candlesticks used primarly in a religious or ceremonial context.

Headgear used to protect and to provide a steady supply of oxygen for the user. Used for both shallow-water and deep-water diving. Early examples from the 19th century were commonly made of metal and featured several portholes for viewing, covering the entire head. Contemporary helmets are made of various materials (metal, plastic, fiberglass, etc.) and provide a single transparent viewer to aid sight.
Ornamental textiles that are attached to clothing that bear insignia identifying membership or affiliation with a group.
Sets of objects with which children may discover chemistry by performing experiments with supplied materials and labware.
18th-century term for ornamental trimming in the form of bands or stripes on a robe or gown.
A concise description of the location where the creation, design, or production of the work or its components took place, or the original location of the work.
Devices that use a current of air to remove bran from middlings (pieces of grain left over from the process of milling grain into flour).

Hand-held tools, typically made of bone, ivory, steel, or wood, used to weave and repair mesh nets. Though these tools vary in appearance, they often include a smooth, well-rounded stick with a uniform thickness throughout its length. This allows for equally-sized loops to be knotted around the stick in the production of mesh. The size of the tool determines the size of mesh materials produced.

Mechanized devices that use fixed quantities of wet heat to smooth, relax, and fix the strain on undyed woven material so as to avoid severe creasing and felting at the subsequent dyeing stage. These devices are also sometimes used to smooth and level dyed fabric. Dyed or undyed woven materials are wound dry and level on the device's rotating cylindrical roller that is partially imersed in hot water for a specificed amount of time. The device then subjects the steamed fabric to cold water, before reversing the fabric and completing the process on the backside.

Devices used to measure the exact level of twist, or the spiral arrangement of fibers around the axis of yarn, inside a spun yarn sample. To calculate this measurement, these devices work to remove the twist by mechanically rotating a yarn sample held between two moveable clamps with a defined tension rate. The number of rotations needed to untwist the yarn's fibers are then calculated. The higher the twist measurement, the stronger the yarn is determined to be.
Stiff straight metal rods, one end of which is fitted with or made into a handle, for poking or stirring a fire.
Mechanical devices used for making pasta.
Containers used to transport milk bottles.

Heavy-duty stitching machines designed to stitch or staple books using rolls of wire, and in bulk, as well as stitching other products. These are often used by binderies, print shops and high volume production facilities.
Devices for measuring rates of diffusion.
Knives used to kill hogs by severing an artery and allowing the animal to bleed.
Meaning "painted," indicates the person whose role was painter of a work. May be applied to a place name as well, meaning painted in a given location.

Sets of 144 domino-like pieces or tiles marked in suits, counters, and dice, used to play the tile game of Chinese origin, mah jongg.Mahjong is a tile-based game that was developed during the Qing dynasty in China and has spread throughout the world since the early 20th century. It is commonly played by four players. The game and its regional variants are widely played throughout Eastern and South Eastern Asia and have also become popular in Western countries. The game is played with a set of 144 tiles based on Chinese characters and symbols, although some regional variations may omit some tiles or add unique ones.
Instruments in the form of a brush or other shape used to apply etchants, sealants, bonding agents, hemostatic agents, or other materials to teeth or dental work.

Rotatable rollers horizontally attached to the back end of a loom on which warp threads are wound, ensuring that they are evently spaced, in preparation for weaving. These rollers, and the warp threads they hold, are manually tightened or slackened by means of a wheel controlling the tension of the beam.
Genre of performing art focused on poetry or another composition intended to be spoken aloud before an an audience.
Method of acquiring property for temporary use, with or without the payment of interest.
The process of affixing an identification number, tag, or label to an object in a collection or stock of merchandise.

Titles or names for works that consist of the work type or otherwise are very generic. For example, if a chapel has the generic title "Chapel" rather than a more specific title, such as "Chapel of St. Mary."  In book cataloging, generic titles may be constructed by the cataloger to collect works by a prolific author (e.g., "Speeches" as a title for a group of works by William Shakespeare).

Numbers or codes that uniquely identify a record or entity within a given area of a system. Such numbers are typically system-generated; the values may comprise sequential numbers or codes algorithmically constructed. A goal may be to ensure uniqueness across multiple systems, such as UUID or GUID.

Refers to days on which custom or the law dictates a suspension of general business activity to commemorate or celebrate particular events. Originally derived from "holy days," which are in modern usage called "religious holidays": for religious feast days or holy days that are specified for religious observance, use "religious holidays."
The standard unit of currency of the Netherlands prior to adoption of the Euro.
Refers to the variety of Spanish spoken in Paraguay.
Varioius dating systems used regionally by early Germanic peoples; names for the months varied by region and dialect.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 398-410; founded by people of of Xianbei ethnicity.
Distinguishing identification numbers or codes assigned to either a plot of land or a batch of items, such as at an auction.

Words or phrases, often descriptive or evocative, used to identify or provide reference to a work, including physical works, performances, literary works, and conceptual works. May apply to individual items or works, or to groups or series of items, in any medium. Titles may also be initials, numbers, or symbols. Examples are titles or names of works of art and architecture. For numeric or alphanumeric IDs or codes for uniquely identifying a work, prefer "identification numbers." To refer specifically to titles printed or inscribed on a book or other object, such as on the title page, prefer "titles (partial documents)."
Models of the foot made of wood or metal, and in modern times plastic, of varous sizes, upon which boots and shoes are shaped during making or manufacture.
In Japanese printing, a sheet of paper that is in landscape format (height is smaller than width).
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 999 to 1 (or 2000 to 1) Before Common Era.
General term for various styles of dance from north India, chiefly performed by professional dancing girls.
An intoxicating drink holding a prominent place in Vedic ritual and religion.The plant from which the drink was derived is not certain.

Proprietary storage drives marketed by Iomega from ca. 1994-2003. The system consisted of a drive mechanism and sealed 'superfloppy' magnetic disks originally with 100Mb, then 250Mb, and 750Mb capacities.
Large language family found dispersed throughout Maritime Southeast Asia, Madagascar, and Pacific Ocean islands, with a few members on continental Asia.
Historical instruments created by Etienne-Gaspard Robertson ca. 1810 for imitating the sound of the human voice, housed in an automaton.
Undersea mountain systems, including subordinate ranges, basins, and plateaus.
Artists who who perform official artistic duties as a representative of a family, government, organization, or other entity.
Early Roman pottery that is characterized by having a fine, hard, and thin fabric, generally made of reddish clay that may be fired brownish gray and may contain some mica.
Artists who specialize in bookworks, which are art works that exploit the book form or alter its physical structure as part of the content of the work.

The painful emotion arising from the consciousness of something dishonoring, ridiculous, or indecorous in one's own conduct or circumstances of being in a situation which offends one's sense of modesty or decency.
Groups of languages deriving from a single ancestor or parent language.
Artists who design for logos, advertisements, illustrations, books, brochures, signs, posters, animation, Web pages, or other displays to promote sale or acceptance of products, services, or ideas.

Nationality, culture, and style of ancient Pannonia, a region and a province of the Roman Empire, area east of the Adriatic Sea and west of the Carpathian Mountains, corresponding to early-21st century western Hungary, parts of eastern Austria, Slovenia, and northern Yugoslavia.
Activities and principles for preserving or promoting health.
Forms of competitive play, usually involving an element of strategy, especially to interfere with an opponent's play; may or may not require physical skill.
In Indian architecture, a principal spire in Śēkharī/Anēkāṇḍaka śikhara; mūlaśṛṅga; principal tower; central spire of an Anēkāṇḍaka (Nāgara) śikhara.
Hindu semi-divine beings that are half human and half serpentine. They are often associated with waters, such as rivers, lakes, rain, and seas.

Order containing 7 families, 199 genera, and 4,445 species of flowering plants. Members of the order range from annual and perennial herbs to herbaceous or woody vines, shrubs, and, in a few cases, trees. Ranunculales is part of a group of families and orders informally called the basal eudicots. One of the main characteristics that distinguish these families and other eudicots from the monocotyledons (species with one embryonic leaf in their seed) and basal angiosperms is the pollen, which typically has three openings (colpi) instead of one. They also lack ethereal oils, which characterize many orders among the basal flowering plants. In Ranunculales, the petals seem to have evolved from staminodes (sterile stamens) rather than bracts (floral leaves), and the carpels are unfused in most members of the order.
Winged gods associated with love and sex in Greek mythology.

Species of tall, fast-growing tree native to cooler areas of North America. The name refers to the tendency of leaves to tremble or quake in even a slight breeze due to their flattened petioles. It is most easily distinguished from a similar European species, P. tremula, by the shape of its leaves, which have more pointed tips, and by growing via root suckers: it propagates itself primarily through root sprouts, and extensive clonal colonies are common. The leaves are food for various insects. A substance in the bark was extracted by Native Americans and the pioneers of the American West as a quinine substitute. The soft, weak wood is used as paper pulp and for other purposes.

A type of structural plate glass that is ground to true plane surfaces; used for storefronts, countertops, tiling, and paneling. It is made in many colors in thicknesses from 11/32 to 1 1/2 inches (0.86 to 3.81 cm) or laminated to give different color effects.

Species of medium sized oak tree native to the southeast of the United States, from coastal Virginia to central Florida to Texas, growing 20-25 m (65-80 feet) in height, and having a large, circular crown.

Genus containing around 25 species of coarse grasses, many with with reddish to purplish-black panicles, growing to 2 m in height. These grasses are cultivated for food and forage worldwide, but some species have escaped cultivation and are troublesome agricultural weeds in temperate to tropical regions throughout the world.

Deities of the Yoruba people of southwestern Nigeria, including numerous minor gods and spirits invoked or worshipped by the Yoruba people and their diaspora and descendants in Cuba, the West Indies, and the Americas.
Genus of flowering plants, some members of which are important for resin production.

Species of pine native to the mountains of Oregon and California, United States, and Baja California, Mexico. It is one of the largest species of pine, 40-60 m (130-200 feet) in height. The species is prominent in the Achumawi First People creation myth, in which the creator drops a seed from the tree to make one of the first people.
Data types that are a sequence of symbols or linguistic elements in a defined order.

Institutions, groups, or other corporate bodies who oversee the finances, management, and maintenance of a garden, which is an open space where plants are cultivated; generally reserved for those managing a large public or private garden.

Libraries maintained out of federal government funds and serving the nation as a whole. Their broad function is to collect and preserve the books, periodicals, and newspapers published in the country.
Museums located in industrial buildings or complexes that have been expressly converted into a museum.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of gray colors.
A range of colors resembling variations of brown pigment.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of pink colors.
A range of yellowish colors, typically with undertones of red or brown, resembling the color of the lustrous metal, gold.
Variable color term referring to any whitish or light gray color resembling an oyster shell.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.
A warm brownish red color of various values, originally referring to the color of sienna pigment, which is derived from soil and used as a pigment in oil and watercolor painting.
Refers to a range of greenish colors resembling the color of jade, which is a gemstone composed of nephrite or jadeite.
Variable reddish orange colors resembling the color of lead red pigment, lead tetroxide.
Variable red colors resembling the color of kermes colorant, derived from female Kermes insects.
General term designating a culture, style, or period occurring or existing before the colonial period of a country. Often used in reference to indigenous cultures prior to European colonization.
A range of purplish blue colors resembling the color of the blooms of cornflower plants or the blue colorant obtained from the petals of the cornflower plant, Centaurea cyanus.
Members of a family of 305 species of songbirds in 20 genera, including birds that are called thrushes, bluebirds, robins, and others.
Infraorder containing one living family of tarsiers and the Eocene to Early Miocene families Anaptomorphidae and Omomyidae.

General term for any of 32 species of web-footed aquatic mammals that live chiefly in cold seas and whose body shape, round at the middle and tapered at the ends, is adapted to swift and graceful swimming. There are two types of animals often called by this term: the earless, or true, seals (family Phocidae); and the eared seals (family Otariidae), which comprise the sea lions and fur seals.

Order that includes around 50,000-80,000 species of cicadas, aphids, planthoppers, leafhoppers, shield bugs, and other bugs, ranging from 1 mm (0.04 inches) to around 15 cm (6 inches) in length, all having a common arrangement of sucking mouthparts.

In the context of personal names, particularly in western culture, names that are positioned between a first name and a last name, possibly comprising an additional familiar name or a maternal family name. In other traditions, such as Islamic tradition, the middle name may be the primary personal name (analogous to the first name in western tradition) or another sort of name.

Order containing at least 9 extinct species of flightless birds native to New Zealand. Recent genetic studies reveal that their closest relatives are the flighted South American tinamous. According to Māori tradition, moa were swift runners that defended themselves by kicking when cornered. Early Polynesian peoples hunted moa for food and made spear points, hooks, and ornaments from their bones and water carriers from their eggs.
Knives that are used for cutting and spreading by a person while eating, rather than for serving at table; all knives used as part of a place setting.
Moldings in Hindu temple architecture that resemble roll-cornices, or overhanging cornices; curved cornices of basement or walls.
In Indian architecture, a sub-plinth moulding; bottom adhiṣṭhāna moulding.

Large groups of stars, existing as two primary types: globular clusters are tight groups of hundreds to millions of old stars which are gravitationally bound; open clusters are loosely clustered groups of generally young stars, containing fewer than a few hundred members typically.

Natural openings in the earth large enough for human exploration, the largest and most common being those formed by a chemical reaction between circulating groundwater and limestone or dolomite bedrock.
Chinese bronze ritual vessels used to hold water during ablutions. These are in the form of a shallow basin resting on a ring support.

Extinct order of two or three families, ten or more genera of small to moderately large terrestrial reptiles, ranging in appearance from lizard-like to sprawl-limbed and cow-like. They had dermal sculpturing of large tuberosities and deep pits on skull, well developed limbs, often possessing a robust limb and trunk skeleton.

Fast external serial bus standard for the connection of computer peripheral devices such as cameras, hard drives, and video recorders. It was developed by Apple Computer, and has been licensed to other manufacturers. The term "FireWire" is trademarked, thus the technology is implemented by other manufacturers under various names.
Very large bodies of ice moving slowly down a slope or valley or spreading outward on a land surface.
Paper size, generally used in Great Britain, measuring 20 by 25 inches.

Order containing around 87 species in two families, having a superficial resemblance to rodents in some ways. Characterized by long ears, a short tail, and strong hind limbs, or by shorter, rounded ears, no external tail, and less-well-developed hind limbs associated with scampering locomotion. Members of the order Lagomorpha, which includes rabbits, hares, and pikas.

General term referring to various members of the family Canidae, especially those of the genus Vulpes, such as the red or common, fox (V. vulpes), which lives in both the Old World and the New World. Several other foxes belong to genera other than Vulpes, including the North American gray fox, the Arctic fox, and the the bat-eared fox, and the crab-eating fox. Foxes resemble small dogs, with pointed snouts, large ears, and bushy tails.
Genus of one Southeast Asian species.
Proofs of letterpress type pages that include illustrations to be reproduced.
Metal money in the form of metal wire, often copper or brass, cut in lenghts and stored in bundles or loose, introduced into Africa by European traders as trade money.
Marbled paper with light and dark waves that diagonally cross the marbled pattern. Occasionally the paper is folded or creased in squares or diamond shapes before staining to increase the effect.
A size larger than normal sizes, such as a book or other object too large to be housed in its expected place or sequence.
Christian holiday celebrated on December 8, honoring the status of the Blessed Virgin Mary, who was held to have been born without original sin on her soul.
In Buddhism, a ūrṇā is a tuft of hair, conventionally depicted as a bump or jewel, in the middle of the forehead; one of the physical marks identifying a buddha.

A basic knitting stitch made by putting the needle through the front of the stitch from left to right, so that each loop is drawn through other loops to the right side of the fabric. The loops form vertical rows, or wales, on the fabric face and crosswise rows, or courses, on the back.
In Indian architecture, a mortar-based pillar.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living mainly in northwestern Uganda and southern Sudan, but also in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
In Indian architecture, a Nandi-pavilion; Nandi-maṇḍapa.
Right rectangular prism shape; a shape having all angles that are right angles, and opposite faces that are equal.
Film genre in which the humor is derived from pratfalls, physical confrontation, chases, and other violently energetic activity.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in the Ubangi River region.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Uganda.
Style and culture the African ethnic group of the same name living in northern Ghana.
Book cloth pattern which resembles plant fronds.

Instruments for cutting or trimming the edges of books or paper, consisting of an adjustable wooden frame that holds a blade which is run back and forth along a groove or guide-rail in the cutting-press. Used to hand-cut the bolts from the uncut edges or to trim the already cut edges of books while they are held in a lying press.
Nationality, styles, and cultures of the Republic of the Congo.

Business partnerships of two or more persons working under a common name in the area of design, which is the discipline comprising the creation of conceptual schemes for the organization or appearance of graphic works, objects, structures, or systems.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Madagascar.

People who apply color to sculpture or other carvings, including adding details, shading, and decorations. Medieval and Renaissance polychromers were considered artists who could be as important as the sculptor.
A conserved food substance made by boiling fruit and sugar to a thick consistency.
Leather thongs used to restrain the wings of birds to prevent them from bating.
In saddlery, straps that pass under the horse's throat, securing the bridle in position.
The food matter in the cytoplasm of an ovum or a cell, as distinguished from the active or true protoplasm.
Textile weaving looms operated by mechanical power, associated with the advent of the Industrial Revolution.

Phylum of aquatic invertebrates typically having a simple tube-shaped or cup-shaped body, which includes sea anemones, hydras, jellyfish, and corals. There are over 9000 species living today.  More or less radially symmetrical marine invertebrates having a single internal cavity serving for digestion, excretion, and other functions, and usually a circle of tentacles around the mouth for catching prey, some provided with paralyzing stings.
Small cushions into which pins are stuck until needed.
Storage vessels in which oxygen is kept under pressure in a gas cylinder. These are used for a variety of purposes in medical or exploratory contexts such as mountain climbing.
Tools used for holding prepared fibers in a carefully arranged manner so that they require the minimum of manual regulation during spinning.
A class of binary boron-hydrogen compounds; a derivative of such a compound.

Style of textiles, particularly handwoven floor coverings, usually in a prayer design and made in or near Lâdik, a town in the Konya Plain of south-central Turkey. Ladik prayer rugs have either a high, stepped arch design or a triple arch with a dominating central portion. In a separate panel above or below the prayer-niche motif, a group of five or more flower stalks project upward from a band of crenellation. Although a few date to the late 18th century, most Ladik carpets were made in the 19th century.
Style and culture of carpets and textiles characteristic of Tabriz, a city in northwestern Iran, that traditionally incorporate a rich decorative medallion pattern.
The style and culture belonging to the Shaybānid dynasty; after moving into Transoxiana, they were called "Uzbek," although that term has broader meaning.
Parts or components of sound devices, or instruments designed to make music.
The arrangement and associated installation systems of seats in places of assembly.
General term for devices used to cast votes, varying in size and design. Relies upon computerized screens and/or computerized ballot counting to record votes.

Sitting, settling or reclining on a mattress or a seat. In postclassic Mexico, both linguistic and gestural expression signify the taking of power, the accession to a function of a ruler or the installation of a deity on the occasion of the ritual feast that was dedicated to him.
Complete outfits of clothing and equipment for a newborn infant.
Methods of decorating glass.
Objects consisting of decorative fobs or objects fastened to a key ring with a chain.
Thread-like material often coated with wax or other substances that is designed to be drawn between the teeth for cleaning.
Object used for grating tobacco into snuff.
Constituent political and administrative divisions within some European nations under a federal system, such as Switzerland.
Chisels for chipping, smoothing, or otherwise working stone or masonry.
Process in the hand binding of books in which the material covering the spine is pressed and shaped over the bands with band nippers to ensure proper adhesion.

General term for dependent communities, nations, or territories that are under the protection or domination of a foreign power, but where this relationship is not necessarily defined by international treaty. To distinguish such entities that are bound by international treaty, use "protectorates."
Blocks of wood used to set type; mallets are used to strike the planers onto type blocks to level and set them.
Furniture feet having the form of three connected lobes.

Objects produced by industrial technology. These may include such things as machinery, transport vehicles, or military equipment, and mass-produced consumer goods. These are often constructed of hybrid materials which may include metal and plastics.
In the context of Buddhism, revolving cylindrical boxes inscribed with or containing a mantra, used as aids to meditation, each revolution considered to be equivalent to the recital of the text.

Objects comprising upright wooden sticks with folded paper attached, forming a zigzag pattern on each side. The type of folding and paper varies based on the type of gohei and its related religious functions. Feature of Shinto practices; often placed in Shinto shrines or temples, either as an offering or as an indication of a deity's presence.
Administrative bodies subject to a duke or duchess.
Brand of strong vinyl-coated cloth made to look like leather.
Raw or unfinished textile prior to bleaching or dying.

Plain-woven textile, originally of silk, now made also of wool, cotton, and synthetic fibers, characterized by slight, flat ribs in the weft; used, for example, for women's suits and dresses, hats, trimmings, and interior furnishings.
The act or process of marking with lines, scratches, or notches.
Pressing or twisting into a compact mass of irregular folds or wrinkles.
Forming or arranging in layers.
The process or technique of applying veneer, which comprises thin sheets of wood, metal, ivory, or another material.

Removal or deprivation of color. In discussion of textiles, decolorizing refers to removal of a dyestuff, whether by physical separation methods such as washing, or by chemical means such as bleaching.

Refers to impregnation of matter with salt. In the ecological context, refers to a land degradation process caused by excessive soil salinity in arid regions. The accumulation of salts in soil layers close to the surface produced by various causes (e.g., capillary transport of salts in the water table; fertilizers or excessive irrigation precipitating salts in the soil) can inhibit crop growth and may result in eventual desertification.

Large, wooden, serving spoons with carved handles, typically in the form of a human head, domestic animals or ornament, used by the Dan and neighboring peoples in Liberia in association with feasts, and serving as a symbol of hospitality and generosity.
Light carts for one or two passengers drawn by a single horse or pony; popular during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
The addition of carbon dioxide or a carboxyl group into an organic molecule or compound, thus forming carboxylic acid or carboxylate.
The dimension of a straight horizontal line extending from the left side to the right side of a horizontal form. Usage may overlap with "width."
In Indian architecture, a śikhara’s curvature of six segments in vēṇukōśa.
Size that is very large, solid, and imposing; comparable to a monument in massiveness.
Characteristics related to fabrication.
Having a form that is loosely or irregularly structured.
The state or quality of a substance of being incapable of being dissolved in another, usually specified, substance.

Medieval end-blown ivory aerophones made from elephants' tusks, finely carved and prized by the wealthy classes mainly as tokens of land tenure or by churches as reliquaries, rather than as sound devices.

German plucked zitherlike chordophones with one to four melody strings and several drone strings stretched over a slender rectangular soundbox with frets fitted to its long left side and tapering to form a pegbox at the upper end.

Dolls in the form of saleswomen hawking household items from their aprons or from tables and dressed in traditional working class costume; popular especially in England in the 18th century into the early 19th century.

Plucked lutelike chordophones with built-up ribs, gently-waisted body, fretted neck, flat peg disc, rear or machine tuning pegs, frontal string holder combined with bridge, and large circular soundhole. Their size, form, and number of strings can vary.

Medieval military weapons consisting basically of a lever with a great weight attached to the short arm and a basket, box, or sling attached to the end of the long arm to hold projectiles. When the weight is permitted to fall, the projectile is hurled with great velocity. Distinct from "biffas" in which the weight is attached flexibly to the longer arm and is movable.

Peg solitaire is a board game for one player involving the movement of pegs or marbles in and out of holes. The standard game uses a board with 37 holes with each hole containing a ball, peg, or pin, except in the middle hole, which is empty, the aim being to remove balls by steps until the board is empty but for the central hole, though there are variations of the method of play, and the size and shape of the board and number of pegs.

Handwritten documents, particularly books and other documents created before the invention of the printing press. May also be used to distinguish certain documents from published or otherwise printed documents, as in the cases of typed personal letters or a typescript from which printed versions are made.

Books having leaves that are relatively rigid, and that may be in non-traditional forms. Often used to refer to board books or books whose leaves are glued together as part of the binding process, though the concept of board books is distinct.
Small flat plaques imprinted with images or text that advocate for a campaign for a cause or person, usually pinned or otherwise affixed to clothing.
The property of a fluid that resists the force tending to cause the fluid to flow.
Dresses worn over another, especially ones designed or draped to show an underdress.

A natural organic colorant extracted from the roots of any of several species of the genus Rubia, having a reddish color. Madder has been used as a colorant for dyeing textiles since ancient times in India, Persia, and Egypt. It has been largely replaced as a dye and a pigment by synthetic alizarin. Used for dye and lake pigment preparation.
Refers to any polymerized olefin. Polypropylene and polyethylene are the two most common polyolefins.
Set of books with directions to confessors in form of prayers, questions, and lists of sins with penance.
Headwear that is designed to protect the heads of small children that are learning to walk from injury caused by falls. Of varied design historically, some are quilted or padded.
A Scottish term for laced shoes made out of the untanned hide of an animal, with the hair facing to the outside; molded to the foot when the hide is still pliant.

Soft boots of sealskin or other animal skins or hides, in moccasin construction, developed by indigenous peoples of the North American Arctic and Subarctic regions; use also for other similar boots, often of heavy-duty cotton, with a soft attached sole and worn with linings, adapted by other peoples.
Tools for cocking the mechanism of wheel lock pistols.

Four-wheeled pleasure carriages having two or three seats seating two or three passengers each, with or without doors, with or without a separate driver's seat, occasionally open or with an umbrella or half top; popular in the early to mid-19th century.

Round, wedge-shaped caps with low, flat, soft crowns, with a short visor in the front. These are usually made of wool or tweed, but can be found in a variety of fabrics, and slight variations in styling. These are thought to originate in 15th century Northern England, though versions appear elsewhere in Europe, with variations in shape. They were originally worn and were associated with working class men, and became popular in the United States from the 19th century, introduced by immigrants from Ireland and England. They have gone in and out of fashion to the present day, with both men and women in many social contexts. Usage of the term has been extended to include caps of various shapes and styles appearing in portraiture, but should be reserved for the modern style and its obvious historical antecedents.
Structures underneath aircraft that are designed to support the aircraft on the ground and to absorb the shock of landing.
Enclosed spaces on the deck of a ship, housing the steering wheel and other navigating devices.
Wheeled vehicles adapted to carry and distribute containers for milk.
Purple bands which ornamented Roman tunics, running up and over each shoulder from hem to hem, and indicated the rank of the wearer. Also, bands of this type and color used on vestments.
Traditional apparel expressing the regional, national, community, or ethnic identity of a population. Folk costume may be reserved for ceremonial events or be found in everyday use.

Staffs culminating in an ornament such as a pine cone and sometimes decorated with ivy or wine leaves. In Greek mythology, the staff belonged to Dionysos and his followers. These were used as sacred instruments during religious rituals and celebrations.

Heavy helmets completely enclosing the head and face, originally flat-topped, later having a conical or rounded top; used in warfare from the late 12th to the mid-14th century, and continued in use in tournaments until the mid-16th century.

Toys that children usually use on the beach or in the sandbox. Sand molds can have all kinds of shapes. By pressing sand into the shape, then turning it over and removing the shape, three-dimensional shapes are created in the sand.
Plain or decorative strips of material worn to fill in a low neckline, especially on a dress.
Especially strong and durable bindings on books intended to withstand heavy use; may be original or rebinding of a work.

Bindings featuring cloth covers, usually of velvet, silk, or canvas, embroidered with gold, silver, or silk thread. The art of making this type of binding peaked in Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries.
Thematic sets of toy figures with accessories.

A white, deliquescent, water-soluble solid, NaOH, usually in the form of lumps, sticks, chips, or pellets, that upon solution in water generate heat. It is used for the manufacture of other chemicals, rayon, film, and in medicine as a caustic.
In athletic endeavors such as fencing, shields or pads worn to protect the chest.

Very small dolls made of bits of cloth, bone, and wood generally produced in Guatemala but probably having originated in the Maya culture utilizing scraps of fabric left over from making clothing. Children and adults confide their worries or troubles to the doll, and it is believed that the doll takes on the troubles so that the user can sleep in peace.
Skirts worn over other skirts and draped, usually to the side, to show the skirt below.

Long, wide-legged fashion pants that flare outward from the midriff to the floor. Often fashioned from lightweight, breathable materials such as silk or crêpe. Popularized by Coco Chanel in the 1930s. For calf-length fashion pants with wide legs, use "guachos."
Ecclesiastical cloaks worn by clergy of the Eastern Church.
General term for clothing worn on the upper part of the body, above the waist, excluding outerwear and underwear. Typically not used in reference to men's clothing.
Exposed bifurcated garments extending from the waist or hip to any portion of the leg above the knee.
Soft, supportive lining placed inside headgear to protect the wearer from injury.

Infants' garments worn over a diaper, usually triangular wrappers made of flannel, boiled wool, or tightly knitted wool, used in Western nations until the 1890s when more waterproof materials such as rubberized cloth were available. In modern usage, the term is sometimes used to refer to colorful pants lined with plastic or other waterproof material and used to cover infants' diapers. The term also refers to earlier outer garments for adults, made of animal skin with the fur turned inside and used as a lining.

18th-century shaping garments consisting of a series of concentric hoops of whalebone or bamboo; worn to add fullness to a skirt. For bell-shaped shaping garments of whalebone or steel use "cage crinolines."
Devices made to contain real or artificial flowers that are attached to the clothes of the wearer. Sometimes these are fitted with a receptacle for water to keep real flowers fresh.
Forklike utensils, often used in pairs, which penetrate large pieces of meat to turn while cooking, or to prepare for serving.
Coats worn over a suit or other main garment; use especially for those worn in cold weather.
Devices or utensils of fine mesh used for winnowing powdered or granulated substances and often with a contrivance, as a rotator, to aid the action of sifting.
Small, low utensils for supporting the blade of a knife at the dinner table, sometimes made a part of a flatware service.
Small spoons, with a capacity one third the size of a tablespoon, used for stirring tea, coffee, or the like served in cups or mugs and used as a standard unit of measurement in recipes.

Script associated with Western Europen manuscripts of the 12th century. It is a transitional script between late Carolingian and Gothic textura that assumes an oval aspect and some lateral compression of minims.
Containers specifically used for the protection and transportation of phonographs.
Laminated armor pieces shaped like long, flared funnels, covering the body from waist to knees, a characteristic element of some types of foot-combat armor.

Body armor, similar to gambesons; close-fitting military garments from ca. 14th century that are worn under body armor or hauberks. Generally considered the forerunner to doublets, gipons extended to the knees and were sometimes belted. There is some ambiguity with this term and the term 'jupons', which have been defined as types of surcoats. There is also ambiguity as to whether gipons had sleeves or were sleeveless.

Bottles of varying size and shape intended primarily for storing or serving wine. Often made of glass, which may be clear or colored, and sealed with a cork. For decorative bottles usually plugged with a stopper and used to store or serve wine, use "decanters."
Silver coins of ancient Persia equal to one twentieth of a daric and struck from about 515 to 331 BCE.
English silver coins originally worth four pennies and issued between the 13th and 17th centuries, and occasionally later.
Methods of handwriting that use simplified strokes, abbreviations, or symbols to facilitate rapid writing.
Chants and mantras of Hindu tradition.
Books containing litanies, hymns, and other materials for use in religious processions.
Screens formed by a set of strings threaded with beads, usually hung in a doorway.
Thick, often large blocks of wood on which food is placed for cutting, trimming, chopping, and the like.
Covered pans for roasting meats or similar foods, often in the form of oval enameled pans with two handles on the side and a domed cover.

Objects bearing designs, emblems, letters, names,  words, etc. in intaglio that are used for stamping a flat surface or for making an impression in relief on some soft, tenacious substance such as clay or wax. They may be flat or cylindrical, the impression made by rolling the seal over the surface. Seals may be used to authenticate documents or for decoration.
Large, flat stones used to cook food over a heat source, in a manner similar to a griddle.

Stories, verses, or writings usually intended for children, admonishing or warning of the consequences of misbehavior or foolishness; also, in various disciplines, refers to writings warning of possible methodological pitfalls.

Printing technique created by a combination of direct painting with screenprinting, lithography or other traditional print matrix. For single prints painted on a plane without the use of a print matrix, use "monotype (planographic process)".
Oinochoai having a trefoil-mouthed shape.
Flat pouches of fabric with a bound slit in the outer surface, which is worn suspended from ties which fasten around the waist.
Metal vessels in which a mixture of melted cheese and other ingredients is kept warm over a heater or flame. These are used communally, as users dip bread into the pot with a fork.
Small bowls, usually of glass, for holding water to rinse fingers at the table.

Vessels designed for holding and serving milk, especially for medium-sized pitchers having a handle and a spout or lip and sometimes a lid; usually made as part of a tea service; originating in the early 18th century. For containers for holding and serving cream, especially small pitchers, use "creamers."
Sets of two or more double-headed vertical cylindrical drums tuned by tension rods, used in Western rhythm bands since the 1920s.
Drinking cups, usually footed and having two handles but sometimes only one handle; typically refers to ancient vessels of this type. They are distinguised from kylikes by having deeper bowls.
Cups, usually accompanied by a saucer, intended primarily for drinking hot tea.
Boxes used for storing or carrying smoking or chewing tobacco; the covers may be unattached and fitted or hinged. For similar boxes intended for snuff, use "snuffboxes."
Instruments for measuring the distance between an observer and an object of known height by measuring the angle subtended by the object.
Flat, portable containers used to carry papers, maps, or drawings, usually consisting of two covers joined together at the back and usually tied in the front and the ends.

Small cologne boxes hinged in two halves and that contain a sponge soaked in perfume water. The lodderein box differs from other silver boxes in that its shape is always higher than wide, this to prevent the perfume from evaporating too quickly. The name lodderein is a corruption of "eau de la reine (de Hongrie)," a special type of perfume, related to eau de cologne.
Bags used to transport personal items on the body, usually with handles or straps to facilitate this.
Generally, concealed vessels which fit snugly within others which isolates the contents from the holder.
Measures used in mixing drinks and holding usually one and one half ounces.

Measuring devices usually about 2 feet long, used to measure human feet for shoes. They are roughly in the form of caliper gauges with one adjustable toe stop and a fixed heel stop, and calibrated either in shoe sizes or inches.
Devices used to cause multiple clocks or other timekeeping units to coincide in time, or to operate simultaneously.

Shallow saucer-shaped plates used in Christian liturgy on which the large host rests on the altar at times before and after consecration. For a dish or bowl used to hold the hosts during distribution to the faithful, use "communion bowls."

Refers to the extra spacing between lines of metal type, in addition to that provided by the shoulders of type sorts. For the space allowed for each line of type when produced by means other than metal type, use "line spacing."
Instruments that measure the absolute gas pressure in vacuum systems.
Calibrated instruments for measuring differences in electrical potential; usually graduated in volts.

Containers for safeguarding or exhibiting relics, which are personal items or parts of items, or parts of a corpse of a holy person, saint, or deity. Reliquaries vary in small boxes to large objects, sometimes in the shape of the enclosed relic. For places in which devotion is paid to relics or holy objects, use "shrines (structures)."

Metal receptacles of a standardized volume, sealable and suitable for re-use, designed to be stacked and secured together for shipping. These are suited to various modes of transport including marine, railroad, and trucking.

Very large cylindrical beakers or steins, usually made of glass but also ceramic or metal, often decorated with enamel or engraving. They were used for drinking beer and wine, made in Germany from the 16th century onwards.

Refers to the style and culture of modern Jordan. Following the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire, Britain created this semi-autonomous region of Transjordon in the early 1920s, which gained its independence in 1946 and was named Jordon in 1950.
Refers to the leaf of a book's endleaves that is not pasted to the cover.

Baskets made by Plateau Native North American communities, such as the Wasco and Wishram. Baskets usually have a cylindrical form with flexible rounded sides, constructed of plant fibers. Often have woven designs decorating all sides, ranging from geometric patterns to animal and human forms; less frequently, beadwork is used to create these designs. Used historically as a gathering basket, production of sally bags continues in the 21st century.
Large, open vessels, especially those used over an open fire.

Coins with one or more holes. This characteristic is a post-minting alteration that does not respond to an official typology of a central hole. These perforations may respond to a process of demonetization (withdrawal from circulation) by the State or may be of a ritual, transforming the piece into an object of adornment or amulet.
Denotes the attribute of a material or object being prepared or created in advance of an action or use.
The activity of cutting and usually gathering a grain or similar crop, originally by using a sickle or scythe.

Refers to creative works that depict settlements that may be considered cities, which are large or important communities with population, status, and internal complexity greater than most towns in the region. For creative works depicting towns, use "townscapes (representations)."

Works composed primarily of beautiful, elegant letters or flourishes that are typically created by hand with a pen, either in unjoined characters or in cursive writing. May also refer to similar works created by computer or another means.
Devices applied to aerophones, primarily to brass instruments, to alter their tube length by a fixed amount during play.

Visual works for which tile is the support, such as painting, or for which tile is the medium into which a relief is pressed or carved, or encaustic design is created. For visual works comprising multiple tiles, whether or not individual tiles are decorated, use "tile works (visual works)." For tile as a material in roofing, etc., use "tile (material)" or a more specific narrower context.

Depictions of places or things seen from a distance, with a range of sight distinct from other information forms such as diagrams, working drawings, or verbal descriptions. Generally reserved for two-dimensional media such as prints, drawings, paintings, photographs, or bas-reliefs.

Refers to souvenirs acquired at pilgrimage sites that served as tokens of accomplished pilgrimage. Such souvenirs include badges and ampullae sold at pilgrimage sites, and even more valuable objects taken or presented as gifts from the shrine.

Works that cannot be, or have not yet been, identified as to the object type and other information. Term may be applied to movable works or built works. The term is most often used for works currently known or in collections, but for which the purpose of the work is not known and thus work type is not known. For works known by name in literature or otherwise doscumented, but not firmly associated with the corresponding physical work, use "unidentified named works."

The event or condition of an office, post, or tenancy, usually a political office, post, or tenancy, being, becoming, or falling vacant. Vacancies occur by the voluntary act of the incumbent, by circumstances such as a death, or by compulsion.
Rugs that incorporate into their field design the motif of tigers or tiger pelts.
In Indian architecture, a fanciful figure (Kaliṅga).
Members of a class of military retainers of the daimios in feudal Japan, or any members of the Japanese military caste.
Caucasian flat-woven rugs with dragon forms in the shape of the block letter S.
Lamps, often light bulbs set in a cylinder or other container, placed on the floor so that a beam of light is directed upwards.

Movable, tangible property having more or less intimate relation to the person of the possessor; generally includes such objects as clothing, jewelry, furnishings, personal collections, books, vehicles, and appliances.
