This element might also be called “initial-cut head” (qieji tou 切幾頭) when the end is cut into a basic rectangular shape (Pan and He 2005, 84).
The strongest and securest parts of a castle, usually a great tower used as the residence and situated in the innermost court or bailey.
Horizontal members across a window or door opening near the top.
Window or door shutters consisting of a number of horizontal slats hinged together and configured so they may be raised by rolling them onto a roller; operated by hand or motorized.
Moldings carved to resemble a ribbon spiraled around a stick.
In Indian architecture, a plank-moulding of the temple base and hāra.
In Indian architecture, paired nāsīkōṣṭhas.

Double windows of Dutch origin; windows are divided in four sections, with the lower halves covered by shutters or doors and the upper halves glazed. A related design is seen in "kloosterkozijns," resembling one-half of the kruiskozijn.
In Indian architecture, a mālikā-cloister; wall around the cuttambaiam.
Masonry courses which project beyond the courses below; when referring to projecting structural elements, especially when used in a series to form arches, domes, or vaults, prefer "corbels."
Barriers of varied form that attached to windows, or to the outside of them, usually of metal, but sometimes of other materials.
In Indian architecture, a class of ceilings decorated with grouped pendentives; ceiling type bearing luma-pendentives.
In Indian architecture, a pyramidal roof.

Roofs with a square, octagonal, or other base and steeply pitched slopes rising to a peak. May include Russian and Victorian wooden structures as well as membrane and thin shell structures comprising roofs of modern structures and actual tents. For such roofs in the specific context of Russian architecture, use "saters."
Gables having a triangular form, like a pediment; the term is often used to distinguish the simpler triangular form from more complex gable forms.
Domes formed by a spherical section rather than a hemisphere, so that their vault rises are less than the radius of the hemisphere.
Columns, having bases, of the architectural order characterized by capitals with volutes and richly carved moldings.

In Indian architecture, a vase-shaped part of pillar capital (at the upper part of the shaft); ridged; or faceted and fluted; sinuous, often vase-shaped, shoulder-part of a column-shaft below the capital members.
The underside of a part or member of a building (as of an overhang, ceiling, staircase, cornice, or entablature).
Areas within city limits or closely linked to them by common use of public utilities or services.
Exposed forests on the earth's surface that have been fossilized by geologic activity.
Arches having only one half of their sweep developed. Arches having only one half of their sweep developed.

Self-sufficient, rural built complexes centered on iron production; prevalent in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. They were often located near iron ore deposits and near forests for fuel. The structures served all aspects of ironmaking for the community, from mining to smelting and manufacturing. They typically included dwellings for the community members.
Mines comprising vertical shafts driven from the earth's surface; examples include mines for coal, iron, and other dense mineral deposits that are deep underground.
In Indian architecture, a niche with pañjara top.
Slender windows with lancet arches at the top, common in Gothic architecture.
In Indian architecture, enclosing walls interspersed by parivāra shrines.
In Indian architecture, a moulded course.
Metal protective grilles, often of elaborate, decorative character.
In Indian architecture, a ceiling showing the central pendentive surrounded by padma-lūmās.
Arched roofs erected over platforms with a single pitch on each side of a central ridge.
Half-round or keel-shaped culminations of an outer wall of a church building in Russian architecture. It may also refer to rounded gable heads in English architecture.
Melonlike ribbed domes (either exterior or interior), found especially in Islamic architecture.
In Indian architecture, a pillar-shaft.
Capitals resembling a lotus bud, common in ancient Egyptian architecture.
In Indian architecture, an adamantine seat.
Parcels of land with historic significance due to historic events, architectural, engineering or archaeological activities, etc.
Arches with intradoses that are full semicircles.
Complexes typically comprising a jail, police station, and courthouse, which provide services such as educational classes and treatment programs as means of reform.
Mines from which silver is obtained.
Wood from the species Quercus laurifolia.
One of a group of complex organic substances formed in the living cells of plants and animals; it is a necessary catalyst for the chemical reactions of biological processes.
Material comprising the skin of an unborn, prematurely born, or aborted animal, especially a calf, having very fine fibers and used for high-grade parchment and suede.

General term for wood of any of several trees having either dark red wood, or having reddish wood and red sap, particularly including some belonging to the genus Eucalyptus from Australia, but also to trees of the genus Gordonia from Jamaica, the genus Lagerstroemia from India, or various genera from South America.

A coarse variegated marble, quarried on the island of Proconnesus, present-day Marmara Adasi, Turkey, that is either gray, white, or white with gray stripes. Large quantities of this marble were imported to Greece to be carved into sarcophagi. Also called Cyzican marble because it was used extensively in Cyzicus, present-day Belkis, as it was in Constantinople as well.

A famous Greek marble quarried at Mount Pentelikon near Athens. It is pure white but may turn yellow after long exposure to air; a few miniscule veins of talc sometimes cause a faint greenish tint. It was used in antiquity as early as the 6th century BCE and continued to be popular for both sculpture and architecture; both the sculptural decoration and the architectural members of the Parthenon are made of Pentelic marble.
Pulverized stone used to fill the spaces between irregular stones and produce a stable surface.

A highly corrosive, caustic, and toxic water solution of hydrogen fluoride that dissolves most metals, except gold, platinum, glass, ceramics, and organic material; used for etching glass and cleaning metals.

Triclinic borosilicate mineral group comprised of  Axinite-(Fe), Axinite-(Mg), Axinite-(Mn), and Tinzenite. Axinite without a sub-designation is not recognized as an individual mineral species. The group has its name after the generic name axinite first introduced in 1797 by the French mineralogist Rene Just Haüy.

Bluish white, fiery, opalescent, translucent glass that has been made white by the addition of calcium phosphate (bone ash) and opalescent by the addition of fluorides (fluorspar, cryolite, or lepidolite) and/or arsenic. Red tones appear in transmitted light. Opal glass was used for windows, bowls, light shades, table tops, and cosmetic jars.

Pure metallic element having symbol Ir and atomic number 77; a hard, brittle silvery-white metal of the platinum family. Iridium is the most corrosion-resistant metal and the second densest chemical element.
Brick whose nominal dimensions are 2 2/3 x 4 x 12 inches.
An opaque glass that has the appearance of white porcelain.

Flat pane glass made by blowing a bubble of glass, transferring it from a blow-pipe to a rod, cutting it open, then rapidly rotating it until, by centrifugal force, it is spread into a flat disk. Can be either small individual panes with so-called bulls-eyes in the centers or large disks that are annealed and cut into pieces. Crown glass is thin and brilliant with a slight convexity and concentric wavy lines. Known to the ancient Romans throughout the Empire; found in windows of medieval cathedrals.
A fine-grained limestone, or soft, earthy form of calcium carbonate; used chiefly in putty, crayons, paint, rubber products, linoleum, and as a pigment and abrasive.
An artificial cement with hydraulic properties that is made by grinding together granulated blast-furnace slag and hydrated lime.
In Indian architecture, a lotus petal motif.
Crosses that have arms terminating in roundels or knobs.
Cities or other administrative areas having the rank of an administrative division higher than other cities. Examples are in South Korea and Lithuania.
Pairs of towns, usually in different countries, that have established official links.
Settlements whose inhabitants are squatters.
Motifs consisting of two wavy lines set beneath three balls arranged in a triangular shape.
Systems in which plants grow on a vertical surface such as a building facade.
Rooms, buildings, or groups of buildings where tests and studies are done in the area of veterinary medicine or on specimens from animal patients at veterinary facilities.
Buildings, lots, or other facilities where where goods are transferred between trucks, or between trucks and railroad cars or ships.

Bridges that employ trusses, which are structural members comprising straight pieces of metal or timber forming a series of triangles lying in a single plane, thus making the structure unlikely to be distorted by stress. Wooden truss bridges, in the form of covered bridges, were common in the United States from the 1870s to the 1930s; carefully fitted timbers were combined with iron rods for tension. Later, railroad bridges and other bridges were constructed of cast iron and wrought iron, which were eventually succeeded by steel in truss bridges.

Buildings, monuments, and other structures that are intended to be non-permanent, sometimes transportable. Erected for festive or sporting events or to provide access to or protection or support of facilities under construction.

Pillared halls or porch structures of Southeast Asian origin. For example, in Thai culture, mandapas are elongated meeting halls that lead to a Buddha image at one end; usually featuring a square roof and accompanied by a wihan outside near the entrance. Mandapas are incorporated into northern Indian Hindu temples; they may connect to the shrine directly, lead to intermediary spaces, or be completely detached from the shrine itself.

Churches belonging to a monastery or having their origin in a monastery, which is a place of religious retirement or seclusion from the world for monks, who are people living a celibate life according to the rule of a particular religious order and adhering to vows, especially of poverty, chastity, and obedience.

In Indian architecture, a minor shrine(s) located at the corners of the temple; kōṇa-vimāna(s) subsidiary shrine placed at the corners of a pañcāyatana (5-shrined) complex; miniature temple situated at the corner of the main temple.
In Indian architecture, a temple having inner ambulatory passage around the sanctum/cella; with ambulatory.
Designates small buildings for the Japanese tea ceremony.
Dense plantings used as fortifications. The best known examples are barriers used as defensive walls in North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, Moorish Spain, and elsewhere.
Buildings that house schools, generally associated with universities, sponsoring degree-granting programs in a broad range of subjects pertaining to the field of music.
Built works housing schools that award general education degrees in a wide variety of subjects that are not part of graduate education.
Buildings, other structures, and complexes of structures whose primary function is mental health care.
Buildings or outdoor sites set up for purposes of trade, especially in frontier or other a region not fully developed.

Sculpted figures in mourning displayed on sepulchral monuments or tombs. Based on Antique examples, they became popular as small figures, often family members, in niches on European sepulchral monuments in the 13th century. By the 14th century the first representations appear of the heavily cloaked and cowled professional mourners who were normally employed to follow the coffin in a funeral procession. In later centuries, weeping or fainting angels or female figures became common.
Built structures or dwellings for accomodating swine.

Buildings or large rooms associated with a parish church, that are used by the congregation or by the local community for social or charitable activities, though not necessarily associated with the litergy.
Buildings housing businesses that sell food and some nonedible household goods.
In Indian architecture, a wagon-vault roof; Valabhī; rectangular, wagon-vault śikhara.

Buildings that are significant in the history of architecture, that incorporate significant architectural features, or that played significant historic roles in local cultural or social development; may or may not be officially designated. For buildings that are abandoned but not considered necessarily historic, use "abandoned buildings."
Subterranean spaces of larger structures where raw milk is put to separate from the cream layer. For dedicated structures designated for similar purposes use "milk houses."
The quarters assigned as working space for media personnel, as at sporting events and political conventions, and usually equipped with communications facilities.
In monastic architecture, rooms, groups of rooms, or separate buildings where monastic rule was relaxed.
Freestanding structures with a single-pitched roof leaning against two posts or trees. For similarly roofed minor structures built against the side of buildings use "appentices."
In Medieval halls, the spaces between the screens (which act as visual barriers) and the doors to the service rooms (buttery, kitchen, pantry).
Rooms found in large houses and hotels intended for meals that are part of late evening entertainments.
Rooms for sitting and relaxation, often located adjacent to bedrooms and generally more private than living rooms or parlors.
Grand reception halls. In gardens, tang are generally located in  central, public areas.
Rooms or larger areas devoted to the storage or display of fine art prints.
Containers for the eucharist that are suspended above the altar; they may also hang from a ciborium (structure), an altar canopy, an altarpiece, or a reredos.
Either of the two edges or borders along a road, especially that portion on which vehicles can be parked in emergencies.
In Indian architecture, a prati-kaṇṭha of a base bearing end-makaras and vyāla figure(s) between.
In Indian architecture, a basal plain moulding of vēdībandha, below kumbha; kumbha proper (in Oriyā).
In Indian architecture, a pillar bracket.
Steep mounds, a main feature of certain 11th- and 12th-century castles.
Strips fixed to the sill of an external door or window to resist the penetration of water.
Shutters of various types, designed or used to provide protection for doors and windows from severe wind and weather.
In Indian architecture, a vēdī-moulding with vyāla figures.
Any convex, rounded molding which has a partly cylindrical form; commonly used to refer to Gothic or Romanesque rather than classical forms.

Refers generally to the ceramics produced in and around the city of Kyoto, with the exception of raku ware, made from the 8th century to the present. Productions from the 8th century are typically three-colored, lead-glazed ware and monochrome green wares from the 9th to the 11th century. By the mid-17th century, productions have polychrome glazes with decorative motifs often comprised of built up layers of enamel, giving a three-dimensional effect.
Refers to the culture and styles of West Turkestan, which covered present-day Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and the southern part of Kazakhstan.

Refers to a Chinese Neolithic culture and period spanning ca. 2500 to ca. 2000 BCE. It is named after a site at Chengziyai, Zhangqiu county, in Shandong province; the site was excavated by Johan Gunnar Andersson in 1930 to 1931. Longshan is chiefly known through its pottery; the pottery style has been found in the region reaching from southern Manchuria through Hopei, eastern Honan and Shatung, and as far south as Chekeing. The style is characterized by black, burnished, often incised wares in a wide variety of shapes.

Refers to a Chinese dynastic culture, style, and period dating 1115 to 1234, an empire formed by the Tungus Juchen (or Jurchen) tribes of Manchuria. The empire covered much of Inner Asia and all of present-day North China.

Refers to a group of painters working primarily in Shanghai from the mid-19th century to the early 20th century. Although not a school in the Western sense, the painters associated with it shared subject-matter, styles, techniques, and the patronage of Shanghai merchants. After the devastating Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864), four professional painters surnamed Ren moved to Shanghai: Ren Xiong (1820-1857), his brother Ren Xun (1835-1893) and his son Ren Yu (1853-1901) from Xiaoshan and the unrelated Ren Yi (1840-1896) from Hangzhou, both in Zhejiang province. The four Rens, of whom Ren Yi was the most influential and successful, formed the nucleus of the emerging school. Shanghai school painting was made to please its merchant patrons. The paintings, typically displayed in the merchants' offices and homes, were mostly decorative, and their subjects often contain auspicious symbolism pertaining to longevity, good fortune, or prosperity. The hanging scroll format was particularly popular, as was the folding fan format. The works typically feature bold coloration and accessible and everyday subject-matter such as figures, birds, and plants. Landscape usually had a minor role in Shanghai painting. Shanghai flower painting was popularized by Zhao Zhiqian (1829-1884), who is known for his large, decorative scrolls of flowers painted in broad brushstrokes of rich, opaque color. The Shanghai school attained its height in the early 20th century under Wu Changshi, arguably the best of the Shanghai artists.

The contemporary music and fashion style, originating in Seattle, Washington, among alternative hard-rock bands and by the 1990s influencing national fashion trends, based generally on the flannel shirt, torn jeans, and combat boots ensemble of urban youth.

An American architectural style developed in the early and mid-20th century by the US National Park Service (NPS). Goals were to standardize buildings in their parks, with an emphasis on harmonizing the architecture with the natural environment and existing historical architecture of the site.

Style and culture of a Native American tribe of North Carolina; their origins are disputed, however the tribe believes they are descendants of the Cheraw and related Siouan-speaking tribes of Native Americans originally inhabiting the coastal regions of the state of North Carolina.

Refers to the culture of the Nanticoke, a confederacy of Algonkian-speaking Indians who have lived along the eastern shore of what are now Maryland and southern Delaware. Their culture is related to that of the Delaware and the Conoy. The name Nanticoke means Tidewater People. Today, the Nanticoke are known today as the "Nanticoke Indian Tribe" in Delaware and the "Nanticoke Lenni-Lenape Tribal Nation" in New Jersey.

The style and culture of the Iroquoian-speaking peoples of North America who emerged as a tribe around the north shore of Lake Ontario; believed to have been the most populous confederacy of Iroquoian-culture indigenous peoples of North America.

Refers to the Hailhzaqvla, or Heiltsuk language-speaking people that inhabit the area around Bella Bella, British Columbia. Historically, the people that inhabit Bella Bella have been referred to as "Bella Bella Indians." The correct term to refer to the larger culture, and to describe the art and artifacts of this people, is "Heiltsuk."
Style and culture of a group of First Nations people located in Saskatchewan, Canada.
Refers to the style and culture of an African people living in Tanzania.
Style and culture of the Berber people of the same name living in Nefusa Jabal in southwest Tripolitania, Libya.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Kenya and Tanzania.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting central Tanzania.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Democratic Republic of Congo.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Central African Republic and Sudan.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northeastern Nigeria.
Describes an African people living in Cameroon.
Describes works produced by the African people of the same name living in Chad.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Guinea-Bissau, Senegal, and Gambia.
Depictions as if from the point of view of the subject, looking backwards. For depictions of the back of a subject, use "back views."

Estimated portraits of identified or anonymous individuals based on forensic or archaeological evidence, for example, reconstructing the appearance of the person based on the skull or other remains, or by using DNA.
Visual works or portions of works fashioned in silver, especially fine, decorative work.
Material, such as the aggregate in a concrete mixture, that does not enter into a chemical reaction.

Treatment added to laundered fabrics to make them softer. Historical softeners were typically based on water emulsion of soap and oils. Contemporary softeners are primarily based on quaternary ammonium salts.
Material comprising thin, usually rectangular, pieces of slate and other varieties of stone which split readily into laminae, used especially for the purpose of covering the roofs of buildings.
Solid or liquid material used to whiten or remove color from other materials; created with various mixtures of chemicals.
Oil extracted from the root bark sassafras trees, native to North America and Asia. Sassafras oil is used as an odorant in fabrics, a flavorant, and an ingredient in soaps and medicine.

Amorphous, high-temperature, yellowish or transparent thermoplastic developed in 1982 with a molecular weight of Tg = 215C. Characteristics include resistance to ultraviolet and gamma radiation. May be used as reinforcing fiber or as fire-resistant material in electrical components, jets, and automobiles. Resistant to aliphatic hydrocarbons, alcohols, and dilute bases.
Refers to the gaseous products of burning materials, especially of organic origin, made visible by the presence of small particles of carbonaceous matter.

Film that can be developed in chemistry that is integral to the media itself. There are various means to achieve this, but generally, after exposure, chemicals are released across the surface of light-sensitized film where development and fixing takes place. See also 'diffusion transfer prints.'
Strong, thick paper treated with wax or oil and used to make stencils.
Generally, an oil that is extracted from the kernel or pit of a fruit.

Warm yellow pigment containing lead antimonate that has been used as a colorant for glass, ceramic tiles, and paint for at least 3500 years. It is probably named after the its resemblance to the yellow minerals found at Mount Vesuvius near Naples, Italy, although it not well documented that the pigment was first made in Naples. The specific color of the pigment depends on the method and temperature of manufacture. It came into widespread use in the 18th century, replacing lead-tin yellow as the pigment most often used by artists in Europe. The term is also used loosely to refer to other pigments imitating Naples yellow but produced by mixing together pigments such as cadmium yellow, zinc white, ochre, and Venetian red.

Fiber from the species Hibiscus cannabinus. It is light colored, resistant to water, soft, elastic, and silky. Kenaf was unknown in the West until late in the 18th century, when cordage and sacking made from the fiber were brought to Europe. It was used as a substitute for jute fiber in WW II; also used as a substitute for hardwood fibers in papermaking.

Paper made from chemical wood pulp, which is pulp in which lignin has been removed from the wood, making the cellulose less likely to yellow and embrittle with aging. For paper that contains no free acids, use "acid-free paper."
A thick paper, historically hand-made in Japan, with a smooth finish produced as an imitation of vellum parchment.

The end-product of the refining process that is used to produce natural ultramarine blue pigment from lapis lazuli, ultramarine ash remaining after higher grades of ultramarine blue have been extracted. Ultramarine ash contains small blue particles mixed with a large proportion of colorless materials, such as calcite and silicates; it has been used for glazing.
A mixture of zinc yellow and a variety of Prussian blue. This composite pigment is permanent to light but not to alkali or water.
Any of the range of synthetically polymerized organic compounds suitable for use in ion exchange.

A yellow dye made from the flowering stems of the yellow larkspur plant (Delphinium semibarbatum). Yellow larkspur was one of the main sources of yellow dye in central Asia before the adoption of synthetic dyes in these regions and was used in the silk and silk-and-cotton ikats of the Uzbeks, Tajiks, Turkmens and Jews.
Wood from numerous trees of the genus Pinus. Pine is used largely in the construction and paper industries, although it is also a source of turpentine, resins, and oils, among other products.
Wood of any of dozens of species of pine, particularly those having particularly resinous wood.

Wood processed and used as a raw material for manufactured items, including paper products, wooden furniture, doors, decorative paneling, siding, moldings, knobs, toys, musical instruments, laminated beams, tool handles, and others. Distinguished from "primary wood," which is wood derived directly from forest trees.
Timber formed into long, cylindrical sections, the approximate diameter at breast height being one foot or less.
Books or pads that gather receipts for payments made.

Books or treatises, often compendious, containing rules or instructions needed to perform tasks, operations, processes, occupations, arts, or studies, and intended to be used as reference while the task or study is performed.
Albums in which excerpted verse, drawings, pressed flowers, and other items were added; particularly such albums popular in the 19th century.
Cards displaying samples of small merchandise items, such as beads and buttons.
Organizations or institutions established by endowment or otherwise established with provision for future maintenance.

Refers to sworn confraternities, brotherhoods, or associations formed for the mutual aid, protection of its members, or for the furtherance of professional interests. In the context of art and related disciplines, it refers to associations of artists, craftsmen, tradesmen, or merchants, which flourished in Europe between the 11th and 16th centuries and formed an important part of the economic and social fabric of this period. Most guilds were associated with a particular town or city. Guilds often monitored training, standards of production, and the welfare of their members. Guilds also provided significant patronage of the arts.
The inhabitants of a colony, either those who moved there or were born there. For those who take part in the initial founding of a colony, use "colonists."
People regarded by others as an example to be imitated.
Scientists who specialize in the science of numbers, magnitudes, quantities expressed symbolically, and forms and figures, including their interrelationships and the operations performed on them.
Refers to people who follow and provide services to military camps or armies, but who are not in official military service themselves.
Persons who write original plays, such as tragedies, comedies, or dramas, or adapt themes from fictional, historical, or narrative sources, for dramatic presentation.
Those skilled or specializing in the art or practice of music, such as composers, conductors, and performers.
Persons who cut steel letter punches for type founders in the first stage of making metal type.
Women, typically of noble birth, who attend upon a queen, princess, or other royal female.
German rulers, originally counts having jurisdiction over a territory, and having under him several inferior counts; later, the title of certain German princes.
Civilian provisioners to a military post, typically having a shop in a garrison town and selling merchandise primarily to soliders.
Persons skilled in the construction, operation, or repair of machines or vehicles run by machines.
People who specialize in cutting latticework.

The discipline and practice that concerns the art departments on films and television productions, including the design of sets, costumes, lighting, and makeup. For the discipline concerning the design of sets, costumes, etc. in the theater, use "scenography."

Officials charged with attending fairs and markets to carry out any or all of the following duties: to regulate the standard of weights and measures, to punish misdemeanors, to collect market dues, and to inspect the items displayed at the market. Typically relevant in historical contexts.
Persons who work on a structure, such as a steel building or bridge, by assembling fabricated parts.
Those whose occupation is the preparation of plans and specifications related to municipal infrastructure, including streets, lighting, waste management, parks, and other public works.
People who create ceremonial designs using sand and other natural materials such as minerals or pollen.
Those who make prints with the use of silk screens.

Bits having a sharp spiral cutting edge which may be square, half-round, half-round and hollow, or five- to eight-sided and with tapered ends; used for enlarging existing holes or to remove burrs from the inside of pipes.
Architects designated to manage their firms' services related to given projects.
Cutting tools with a blade hooked at the tip; used for marking outlines on wood or metal.
Parts or components of computers.
Machines that cut metal or paper dies; they may be flat-bed die cutters, where dies are cut with a reciprocating motion, or rotary die cutters where dies have circular shapes.
Devices, often automated, that are used to count biological agents (such as counting bacteria colonies in cultures).

Pieces of wood, paper, cord, cloth, or another material dipped in melted sulfur, phosphorus, or another composition that is readily ignited by friction with a flint or when rubbed against a roughened surface, or when brought into contact with a chemical reagent. Sulfur matches were recorded in China by the 6th century. The first modern, self-igniting match was invented in 1805 by Jean Chancel.

Instruments which forecast solar and lunar eclipses across the globe. Two types exist; one invented by Scottish astronomer and mathematician James Ferguson, which incorporates a globe, and the Bibliothèqe Nationale has an example in their collection made by Ole Rømer (1644-1710), which is styled like a planetarium.
Tongs with an overlapping bent bit designed to hold flat strips of iron from the side,  parallel to the tongs.
Three-legged supports for stabilizing a camera while permitting it to be tilted, turned, raised, or lowered.

Frames, usually of metal, designed to hold sheets of film as they are immersed in a tank of developing solution, used so that the surface of the film does not come into contact with any other surface.
Wood or metal containers, usually V-shaped with a long handle and having one end open, used in masonry work to carry plaster or lime putty to the mortarboard.
Hand tools used in making sheet metal joints or seams.
Video cameras that are connected to or are integral to a computer so that its output may be viewed online.

An anti-modernist movement in early to mid-20th century Germany that focused on an idealized German past in order to combat a perceived threat stemming from French Impressionism, and other influences deemed as "foreign". The movement was exploited by Adolf Hitler for purposes of propaganda.

Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Ahmed I, from 1603 to 1617. During his reign, The Ahmediye Mosque was built by Mehmed Agha. It is known as the Blue Mosque from the color of its interior tiles.
Style of interior architecture and design using elements of English country houses, including elegant furnishings combined with country-themed textiles and other details.

Refers to the style of painting centered in Pont Aven between 1886 and 1890 whose proponents advocated the simplification of form and painting from memory in order to create meaning.  Accordingly, the style is characterized by simple, strongly contoured forms, flat, unmodeled color, and the arrangement of color and forms into harmonious patterns.

Specifically refers to the work of the "Lukasbrüder," a group founded in Vienna in 1809 by Friedrich Overbeck, later derisively called "Nazarenes." The style is anti-academic and emulates techniques of the late Medieval and early Renaissance period, particularly Dürer and Perugino, and places an emphasis on Christian values and morality in art over technical virtuosity.

Refers to the style in 19th-century European and American architecture and decorative arts initially inspired by the Italian Renaissance, or related Renaissance styles in other European countries; characterized by pilasters, rustication, and classical motifs. Later, it includes Renaissance styles based on regional or national variations such as the Elizabethan and Jacobean revivals and the French Renaissance revival.

The culture and ethnic group of the traditionally itinerant people who originated in northern India but live in modern times worldwide, principally in Europe. Most Roma speak some form of Romani a language closely related to the modern Indo-European languages of northern India, as well as the major language of the country in which they live. It is generally agreed that Roma groups left India in repeated migrations and that they were in Persia by the 11th century, in southeastern Europe by the beginning of the 14th, and in western Europe by the 15th century. By the second half of the 20th century they had spread to every inhabited continent.
Refers to the culture that developed in antiquity in the geographical area of modern Iran.
Culture and style of ancient Pergamum, in northwest Anatolia.

Confederation of tribes, primarily aggressive seafarers, who invaded eastern Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Cyprus, and Egypt toward the end of the Bronze Age, in the 13th and 12th centuries BCE. They may be associated with the Philistines, among other groups.

Refers to a period from about 2125 to 2025 BCE in Mesopotamia associated with the rules of Gudea of Lagash and the Third Dynasty of Ur. This style is charactersized by a combination of technical achievements developed in the previous Akkadian period, a revival of Early Dynastic traditions, and the establishment of artistic conventions.
Culture and styles of ancient Epirus, located in modern northwestern Greece and southern Albania.

Refers to the style and period associated with the reign of King Suryavarman I (1002-1050 CE), generally considered the first Buddhist ruler of Angkor. The period is characterized by prolific building programs that included sandstone constructions of minor temples and of the Royal Palace that featured the first fortified wall encompassing a palace in Angkor, storehouses and treasuries known as Khleang, and a single central tower-sanctuary rather than the more commonplace five towers in quincunx configuration. Examples of other architectural and sculptural innovations of this period exist on the site of Preah Vihear where series of courts and gopuras are set on a longitudinal axis rather than in concentric enclosures.

Refers to the period associated with the city Thonburi established in 1767 by the military leader Taskin after defeating invading armies and seizing political power. The style of this period is driven by the renewed sense of military might and political unification. In painting, the style features murals depicting Buddhist subject matter, Thai landscapes, and details showing the plans and construction of buildings. Wall paintings usually decorated the interiors of royal buildings or temples. In this period, temple and palace building programs prospered, featuring the Chakri Maha Prasat and the Wat Arun, a Chinese-inspired temple featuring bell towers and porcelain-covered tympana and also distinctively Thai details such as domestic teak dwellings for monks. In sculpture, the period is seen in large statues of Buddha in royal attire made of gilded and lacquered stucco and bronze and decorated with inlaid mother-of-pearl. Giant guardians such as mythical half-human, half-bird figures and apsarasas and Chinese stone statues embellish temple courtyards of this period.
Refers to a Neolithic style and culture named for the site near Syracuse, Sicily. It is characterized by distinctive pottery in a wide variety of forms, generally with incised designs.
Painting styles belonging to Indian cultures.

Refers to the style of porcelain made in China during the T'ang dynasty (618-907 BCE). The style is typically characterized by pure white, simple shaped bowls and dishes, and more rarely in elaborately carved vessels.

Refers to the style of Japanese residential architecture designed  for tea ceremonies, which reached its peak in the Momoyama period (1568-1600).The style is characterized by an emphasis on simple, austere interiors with almost no ornament, columns made of rough hewn tree trunks, and earthen walls.
Japanese painting style, also known as the "boneless" technique, which refers to painting without outlines.

Nails designed to attach metal mesh lath to a wood or masonry support, either having a short shank and broad head, or having a hook head, which is an offset top at a right angle to the shank of the nail.

Diodes with a cylindrical anode surrounding a coaxial cathode in which the flow of current is controlled by a magnetic field applied parallel to the axis; and now usually designed to produce microwaves.
Door hinges each having one plate surface-mounted on the jamb and the other plate mortised into the door stile; the opposite of half-surface hinges.
Locks designed with a push button or a turn-locking outside knob. When so locked, there is no entrance by key from the outside.
Anchors made of sheet steel or other metal, cast into a surface with a chase narrower at the surface than at the base into which shaped metal tongues are inserted.

Carved portrait figures of kings of the African kingdom of Kuba, typically depicted sitting cross-legged, wearing royal regalia, and grasping a knife; at the front of the base is a small carved object serving as the unique symbol identifying the particular king.

Sculptural works, vessels, or structural forms made from terracotta, a fairly coarse, porous clay product that when fired typically assumes a reddish or orange brown color, and often is left unglazed. When possible, for indexing use a more specific term, created locally by combining the material term plus a more specific object name, such as "terracotta" + "figurines."

Three-dimensional, free-standing sculptures that are smaller than life-size and usually but not always figural. They are often reduced versions of larger works. While the term may be used interchangeably with "figurine" in certain situations, it differs in that a statuette is always free-standing while a figurine may be part of a larger work, such as a decorative detail on a candelabra or mirror. Also, a statuette may represent objects other than a figure, while a figurine always represents a human, animal, or mythical figure.
African monkey figures of the Baule people, characterized by open hands or small offering cups for sacrificial offerings.
Simple square or rectangular cloaks made of coarse wool and worn by the Roman military, but also by the ancient Gauls, Germans, and Spanish.
Men's close-fitting, formal or semiformal jackets extending to the waistline and partially or fully open at the front. Originally part of military uniforms, now worn by civilians as well.
Two or more sculptures that are designed to be displayed together.

Headdresses worn by Yup'ik communities, usually made out of animal hide and caribou hair. Consists of a headband with animal hair attached to one half of the band, forming a crown-like shape above the wearer's head. Sometimes the headband is decorated with beadwork, both on the band and hanging underneath, placed in front of the wearer's eyes. Worn as regalia for Yup'ik and intratribal dances.
Headgear worn by members of a priestly class, not necessarily as part of an array of vestments, but sometimes as indication of rank.
Tall drinking glasses intended primarily for lemonade; of a type which first appeared in the late 19th century.
Finish hardware used to hold or support other objects.
Fiddles of India with the soundbox in the shape of a peacock, the long tail forming the neck.
Pegs around which the strings of a stringed instrument are passed, and by turning which they are tuned to the correct pitch.

Technically, any trumpet fixed with valves for keyed playing, specifically modern Western band, concert, and orchestral trumpets, having a wide mouthpiece, a narrow bore, valves, and a medium-sized bell throat and bell flare.

Shawms of the Arab world and areas of Europe and Asia influenced by Islam, taking many regional forms but commonly consisting of a wood pipe with conical bore, seven front fingerholes and one rear thumbhole, a flared bell, and a small reed with a metal pirouette below it.

Large dinner plates, typically decorative and measuring 10-13 inches in diameter, that are placed on a formal dining table prior to dinner participants being seated and before food is served. The service plate remains at the place setting, with the bowls and plates of the dinner service placed on top of it, until the main entré is served, or until dessert is served; service plate use and etiquette varies by location and time period. For ceramic or metal platters for serving the meat course, use "chargers (platters)."
Any of the adjustable screws, usually in sets of four, in the rim of watch balance wheels used to bring the watch to time.

Drums with two membranes, one of which is beaten, the other forming part of the lacing device. They are generally cylindro-conical in shape, with parallel straight sides on the upper part, the remainder taking the form of a truncated cone. They are common in Uganda and adjoining parts of East Africa.
Smaller acoustic guitars, introduced in the 1920s, that have four strings and are tuned like tenor banjos, an extremely popular instrument of the period.

Prints, especially from the 15th century, made by impressing a plate onto paper coated with a paste, producing an embossed image; sometimes printed with ink, with tinted paste, or with gold leaf pressed into the paste.
Stands constructed to hold caskets or other funerary remains; examples include table-like structures consisting of a base and flat surface.

Tables having a single slab as a top surface, usually having a slab of stone, typically marble or slate but also granite or another type of stone, or of concrete or heavy wood. The slab is set upon a plinth or frame, usually of stone, wood, or metal. The slab top is not enclosed or encased in a supporting structure. For 18th-century tables having a marble top, use the more specific "marble slab tables."
Lidded troughs on legs or stands in which dough was mixed and left to rise and kneaded on top.
Small chests fitted for bottles and intended to hold medical supplies; of a type made in the 18th and early 19th centuries.
Chests of drawers having seven drawers and intended to hold a week's supply of clothing; of a type originally made in 18th-century France, Italy, and elsewhere.

Early American furniture for holding buckets. The furniture developed in Pennsylvania German communities in the 18th century, spread throughout the eastern United States and beyond by the 19th century. Early forms comprised a bench-like piece for holding buckets, but soon the form added shelves or cupboards with closed doors for holding water or milk buckets, cleaning supplies, or other kitchen or bathing supplies. May also be used for reproductions of this furniture form.
Pieces of furniture consisting of risers and treads, typically used indoors in place of ladders.
Desks or stands designed with a slanted front and ledge for the positioning of an open book for comfortable reading.
Beds with frames in three sections equipped with mechanical spring parts that permit raising the head, foot, or middle as required.

Originally a chest or coffer in which things were stored, including a  box-like pen in which an animal was confined. Today the term typically refers to a dining room case piece with a surface surmounted by an enclosed cupboard or open shelves, generally resting on either a relatively solid base or taller legs.
Spanish Renaissance variation of vargueños, used for storing papers. They are usually smaller than vargueños and lack a writing lid; generally they have turned feet and may be bound with iron.

Chairs featuring an ornamental design pressed into its back. This effect is created by the use of a sharp steel die stamp mounted on a roller, passed over the chair with great pressure, resulting in a perfect impression of a design that was literally pressed into the wood, giving the illusion of hand carving. Press-back chairs were popular in the late 19th-early 20th century.
Term generally applied to a variety of different chairs with low seats.
Small, low armchairs, or backstools, often upholstered, which have a wide front, a very narrow back, and a trapezoidal seat.
Small lamps in which the font usually forms the bottom of the lamp, and having one or more handles for carrying.

Lamps with fonts or reservoirs marked to indicate the passage of time by the falling level of fuel, usually either pewter Cardan lamps with a glass reservoir, or small glass kerosene lamps with cylindrical fonts bearing the hour markings.
Lamps designed to burn oil as fuel, typically with a reservoir for holding the oil and an opening from which a wick can be extended.
Devices to redirect or scatter light from a source, primarily by the process of diffuse transmission.
Single-edged pointed war knives of ancient Greece with a convex curving blade, used by both infantry and cavalry, as well as for slaying sacrificial victims and some domestic uses.

Small, decorative daggers typically worn hanging from or through a sash or belt, often as part of a ceremonial costume or military uniform, and as a symbol of rank or custom; may feature an ornate handle and blade design.

Candleholders, usually of painted sheet iron or brass, for one or two candles with shades mounted on a rod supported by a weighted base. The holders and shades are independently adjustable on the rod.

Series of iron or brass rods, usually six, set upright in a circle into a wooden base, joined at the top by a flat iron ring. A lower ring with finger loop and candle socket slides vertically on the rods to adjust height.

Fasteners that consist of two components that are attached to opposing surfaces to be fastened. One component features tiny hooks; the second features smaller loops. When the two are pressed together the hooks catch in the loops and the two pieces bind temporarily.
Pins in the form of thin pieces of short wire having a head and a sharp point.

Works in which paint is applied on a textile support with only a thin gesso preparation. The works were flexible, often rolled and transported as banners or for other purposes. Popular in Spain and its colonies. For similar works on textiles having a thin glue preparation, popular in northern Europe and Italy, prefer "Tüchleins (visual works)."
Refers to drawings intended as experiments rather than designs to be executed and that are not so speculative as fantastic art or architecture.

Drawings of figures that are characterized by rapid execution, either in a studio setting, from public observation, or as purely imaginative renderings of figures in motion. Typically these are not considered finished works but as excercises, preparatory works, or studies.
Abbreviations, monograms, or symbols placed, usually unobtrusively, on coins to indicate the mint at which the coins were made.
Keys capable of controlling a subordinate group of master-keyed locks, each having a different key of its own, but all in turn controlled by the main master key.
Papers carried by a vessel on a voyage, in order to furnish evidence of its national character, nature and destination of cargo, and of compliance with navigation laws.
Maps, as those published by the United States Geological Survey, which show tracts of a country on a series of sheets and according to a specified scale.

General term for copies produced by photocopying, that is, in a machine employing a light-sensitive process, and usually at a one-to-one scale. In the early to mid-20th century, used regarding copies made by various specific processes; since the mid-20th century, most often refers to xerographic copies.
Labels, usually of a stiff or adhesive material, attached to a thing or person and bearing some information relevant to the thing or person.
Requests or agreements issued to a manufacturer or supplier to produce a specific quantity of items or materials within a certain timeframe.
Formal expressions of the opinion formed by some superior authority on matters referred to its decision and forwarded to inferior authorities for their instruction and government.
Games that are played individually or in a group and which are intended to teach or practice a language skill.
Providing direct cash support to another person or organization.

Christian ceremonies or sacraments involving of the consecration of bread and wine by the minister or priest and its distribution to the worshippers. The term 'eucharist' derives from the Greek 'eucharistia' meaning 'thanksgiving.' It is the central act of worship for most Christian denominations, commemorating the Biblical story of the Last Supper, when Jesus referred to the wine and bread as his blood and body.
Performances and displays on a large scale that are specially prepared or arranged for viewing, usually by the public, with the intent of forming an impressive or interesting show or entertainment.
A yogic seated posture.
Those who manipulate puppets in performances.
In Indian architecture, a pearl-cable jamb.
The acts of leaving a place, such as exiting a country.
The action or state of disharmony or disagreement between people, mutual antagonism, dissension, contention, or strife.
The persistent presence of pests, especially in large numbers.
Collocates descriptors for concepts related to the nature and properties of non-living matter and energy.
Surface characteristics perceptible by touch.
The force of the flows of vehicles, persons or objects along a specified route that is supported by a structure or body.
Collective term used to refer to all art works which employ electronic media or technology.
The property of shining in the dark, or luminescence without sensible heat or combustion.
The practice of arranging and modifying proportion so that the heads of figures are aligned at nearly the same horizontal level; particularly prevalent in Greek reliefs and friezes.
Havng the form or outline of an egg, that is of an oval with only one with axis of symmetry.
The effect conveyed by some works of art of skillful execution done without apparent effort.
System of chronological notation, characterized by the numbering of years from an event or some other particular point of time.
The property of being firm or devoid of flexibility.

In philosophy, a theory that affirms that the basic substance of the world is matter and that the world is known primarily through material forms and processes. It is opposed to idealism, the theory holding that spiritual and ideal is of central importance in the interpretation of experience.

Refers to the religious beliefs and practices of religions outside of the so-called 'major' religions. Pagans are sometimes defined as those who are not Christian, Jewish, or Muslim; occasionally the term is more narrowly used to described any non-Christian, sometimes even Jews.
The tendency of a force applied to an object to cause the object to rotate about a given point.
The most flourishing period in the history of something, the time of highest achievement or greatest development.

Philosophical concept central to Navajo aesthetics and culture. Advocates for individuals to be balanced and in harmony with other spiritual and material aspects of Navajo life (landscape, community, etc.) In Navajo material culture and art, beauty is achieved through this balance. This concept can be seen expressed in textiles and pottery through their balanced compositions and in sandpainting in its illustrations of interconnected, harmonious relationships between people, animals, spirits, and the land. Also is applied to contemporary art made by Navajo artists.
Property having an officially registered title, title plan, and other pertinent documents, which are held by an official agency, such as in a governmental land registry.
A number, numerical quantity, or element in a field.

In economics, significant disparity in the distribution of income between individuals, groups, populations, social classes, or countries. Income inequality is a major dimension of social stratification and social class.

The interaction of persons or groups of persons representing various nations in the pursuit of a common goal or interest; international cooperative activities with or without the participation of governments
Political and economic doctrines advocated by the populists, including representation of agrarian interests, free coinage of silver, and government control of monopolies.

Usually restricted to usage in criminal law, the state or circumstance occurring when two or more parties agree or conspire to take some action, not necessarily for profit, but which makes all participants liable for an accident, crime, or debt arising out of the activity. Distinguished from "joint venture (economic concept)."
The five faculties by which stimuli from outside or inside the body are received and felt.
The mental capacity or faculty of retaining and recalling facts, events, impressions, or recognizing previous experience.
The degree of well-being felt by an individual about his or her lifestyle, often defined in terms of social indicators, such as nutrition, air quality, crime rates, etc.
Methodically analyzing the visual impact of a development project or planning policy on a community or area.
The process of making a copy of a work in writing.

Method of dating, based on the known half-life of carbon-14, by measuring the amount of low-level radioactivity of carbon remaining in ancient and dead material of organic origin and thus determining when a plant or animal had died.
Exhibitions occurring once every three years.
Opening phrases of a manuscript or early printed book, or a section of same, sometimes containing details of its production.
Science of numbers, magnitudes, quantities expressed symbolically, and forms and figures, including their interrelationships and the operations performed on them.
Development and manufacture of objects 100 nanometers or less in size, or the manipulation of individual molecules and atoms.
Seeking out and enlisting people for an enterprise, usually for a stated period of time, on either a paid or volunteer basis.
The discipline of design for the stage, including design of all visual aspects of a stage production, such as scenery, properties, lighting, costume, and makeup.
The activity of producing photographs that document or illustrate scientific phenomena.
Study of aging and the special problems and capabilities of the elderly.
The study of cultural landscapes and their features through archaeological fieldwork and analysis.
Covering entirely or partially with a liquid, a foam, or sometimes dust by means of a sprayer.
The activity and process of working in stone.
Activity of cutting, sewing, and creating ladies clothing, particularly dresses, coats, and shirts.

A technique of creating scenery in gardens by piling up stones.  Instead of using the stones to form a hill, they are placed at key points to enhance the scenery and draw attention to these locations.  Rocks selected are chosen for their interesting shape, or for the effect they generate when grouped together.
Application of coatings and other means pursued to render impervious to weather.

The process of making changes to an object or structure so that it will closely approximate its original state or other state at a specific time in its history. For changes not considering historical correctness, see "remodeling" or "renovation." When changes are made to prevent further deterioration, see "preservation." More generally, for treatment, preventive care, and research directed toward long-term safekeeping of cultural and natural heritage, see "conservation."
Reducing the density of a negative or print by dissolving some of the silver forming its image.
Refers to the technique of making measurements by using photography. It usually refers to this technique as applied to mapmaking, measuring site elements, and surveying.

Drawing technique in which charcoal or, less commonly, pastel crayon is used on a board painted white and coated with marble dust, which gives the drawing a sandpaper-like sparkle and texture, and effects of light and dark similar to an engraving. Popular in mid-19th century United States.

Technique of painting a mural in which an aqueous pigment slurry, often pigments mixed with egg as a medium, is applied to dry plaster. It produced a painting of shorter longevity than buon fresco. Fresco secco was sometimes applied over buon fresco painted regions to correct mistakes or to add details.
The action of washing or wiping with a sponge.
The making of knurls, small protuberances, or knobs.
Covered pits with open-jointed linings through which the septic tank effluent seeps or leaches into the surrounding soil.
Devices that permit both the transmission and reception of audio messages.
Collocates descriptors for processes that alter the condition of an object or structure; some descriptors collocated here are both such a process and the resultant effect on the item.
Scarf joints between timbers with their ends fashioned to lock together positively and resist tension.

The process by which a fresco is detached from a wall, used when the plaster on which it is painted has greatly deteriorated; the color layer is removed by a strong glue without removing excessive amounts of plaster.

Medical experts whose practice concerns the prevention, control, diagnosis, and treatment of injuries and diseases affecting the health of domestic and wild animals, including the prevention of transmission of animal diseases to other animals and to people

Members of a loosely constituted youth movement originating in the United States in the 1960s, rejecting the established conventions and structure of society, and advocating universal love, peace, communal living, and simple, idealistic values.

British lead-glazed earthenware with a cream-colored body, painted, stippled, or sponged with high-temperature colors, mainly a brownish ochre, dull blue, and green, and featuring relief decoration; made from 1790 onwards until about 1830. Associated with and named for the pottery factory of William Pratt in Staffordshire, it was made by other local potters in Staffordshire, the north of England, and Scotland.
Acts or thoughts that are transgressions of the divine law and an offence against God, or are a deliberate violation of some religious or moral principle.
Place or state of eternal bliss and ideal relationship with God or the gods, usually accorded as the reward for virtue and true religious faith.
Lists of the holdings in a library, records center, or archives, arranged in the order of the contents of each shelf.
Photographic prints made using an iron process in which a mixture of platinum and palladium is reduced from salts to form an image.
Wooden headdress, in the form of a female bust, with four base posts, worn on top of the head, with the base posts encircling the wearer's chest. Found among the Baga and Nalu peoples of Africa.

Designates passive reflective or dynamic elements in the cultural landscape that incorporate water as the primary design feature; for naturally occurring areas of water use the descriptors under "bodies of water."

Stone documents used as records of land grants to vassals by the Kassites in Babylonia between the 16th and the 12th century BCE. Akkadian for "boundary," the original stone would be kept in a temple and a clay copy, which was used as a boundary marker.
Use to designate evidence of authority, status, rights, entitlement to privileges, or the like.
Controlling according to rules, laws, or requirements.

Printed materials illustrating the prevailing style or a new style of dress, including both plates in a magazine and independent sheets; often serving as advertisements for a dressmaker or dress shop.
Multi-episodic films, presented one chapter at a time.

Photographs in which the image is near life-size or larger. Distinct from the term "enlargements," which only indicates that a photograph has been produced from a smaller photograph. For photographs taken through a microscope use "photomicrographs."
Describes things situated on, directed toward, or coming from the side of some other thing or the viewer.
Broad category of bobbin lace made in 16th and 17th century Flanders.

Photographic processes in which images are formed using pigments rather than silver or other metal. Common pigments included lampblack, watercolor pigments, oil paints, and oil-based inks. The pigments themselves are not light-sensitive; the photochemical action of another transparent agent makes a support bind, attract, or receive pigment.

Style and movement that grew out of Constructivism; it emphasizes underlying structural forms and processes; it views the world as being internally created through constructs, or internal models, often uses naturally occurring proportional systems and rhythms to underpin geometrical art. Refers especially to certain work in Britain in the 1950s; can also refer to certain American and European works of the 1930s and 1940s.
Perpendicular or very steep descents of the water of a stream. May be used for artificial waterfalls only if highly naturalistic in form and context; otherwise prefer "cascades" or "fountains."
Activity or state of conferring or having conferred to an outsider the rights and privileges of a native subject or citizen.
Openly expressing objection, disapproval, or dissent.
The appreciative sensibility of observers who experience delight when disinterestedly observing or experiencing  certain natural and manmade objects and events.
Material comprising the juice or circulating fluid of a plant.
Plan of a building or city that is arranged within an octagon (eight sides of equal length), usually a centralized plan.
Houses with the amenities of domestic dwellings that are of very small size, often on less than a 12 x 24 foot footprint.

Structures, usually in cemeteries, designed to temporarily store the bodies of the deceased prior to interment in a permanent grave or tomb. They may include chambers dug into hillsides or free standing structures. Examples are receiving vaults used during winter months in climates where the ground may be frozen. For rooms or structures used for the hygienic temporary storage of corpses, not designed for visitation by mourners, prefer "morgues."
In Indian architecture, a band of makaras.
Towns or other locations where formal conferences or councils convened, especially an assembly of magnates.
Communities that acted or continue to act as trading centers for fur.
Used to designate ancient Roman funerary structures of several stories usually rising from a stepped square or rectangular base and topped by a pyramidal, domical, or flat roof.

Genre of objects having the form of a broad shallow container, with a flat bottom, concave sides, and nearly level rim, made of earthenware, glass, metal, wood, plastic, bone, or other materials, used for food, cosmetics, storage, transmission equipment, and for other purposes.

Refers to the cultures that developed in the region situated along the eastern coast of the Indochinese Peninsula known as modern North and South Vietnam. Artistic production in this region features a broad scope and an intermingling of styles, featuring dynastic temple construction that included variations of tower shrines, sanctuaries, porticoes, molded capitals, and recesses, and grandiose and refined sculptural programs featuring monster figures that decorated corners of architraves, figures of lions, solid snake-like ornamentation reminiscent of Indo-Khmer foliage motifs and Dong Song styles, and large icons and relief panels carved in sensual styles suggestive of Chen-la works. From the 15th through 18th centuries, architectural planning incorporated Confucian and Taoist elements and sculptural styles of this period feature elaborately-colored woodwork based upon the dragon-and-cloud decoration of the Ming and Ch'ing Dynasties of China.

Buddhist relic mounds of earth, brick, or stone, dominated by a hemispherical or bulbous dome set on a square or circular base and topped by a small pavilionlike structure and a spire. Stupas often serve as pilgrimage sites and symbols of the Buddha or his teachings. solid hemispherical tumulus symbolizing Buddha’s or Jina’s nirvāṇa
Things made, usually visual works or writings, chiefly in order to practice or display a specific technical point or aspect, especially by students.

Nationality, culture, or style of the Lucani, a branch of the Sabelline race that inhabited ancient Lucania, which is coextensive with the modern Italian region of Basilicata. For the culture of the city of Lucca, use "Lucchese."
Solvent that does not contain water.
Nationality, styles, and culture of Suriname, in northern South America.

Basic reference to 'after the colonial" condition, periods, and cultures of peoples, states, and societies that have been through a process of formal decolonization. Since the 1980s the term is used to also refer to the trend to question Western knowledge, categories, and assumptions.
Cultures and styles of various regions in Oceania, comprising islands scattered throughout the Pacific Ocean (generally excluding Japan, Indonesia, and the Philippines), but including Australia.
Refers to the culture of Belgium, usually the modern nation established in 1830 and defined as the Netherlandish provinces watered by the Meuse and Scheldt rivers.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Indiana.
Periods related to Italian Bronze Age cultures.
of the West Indies islands or nation of Saint Kitts and Nevis
In Indian architecture, a temple having offsets.

Meaning, literally, to raise and build up, jujia is the method of positioning the purlins within the roof frame, layer by layer, in order to determine the pitch of the roof. The term mainly appears in the Gongcheng zuofa (1734) and Yingzao suanli edited by Liang Sicheng, so it can be considered part of the official practice of the Qing dynasty. Different from juzhe 舉折 described in the Song dynasty Yingzao fashi (1103), jujia is the process of determining the height of the roof ridge based on the heights of the purlins as calculated from the bottom (eaves) to the top (ridge). Here jugao 舉高 refers to the height that a purlin is lifted relative to the one below it. The jugao of each purlin is determined by the percentage of the distance of bujia 步架, the distance between two adjacent purlins. For instance, “65 ju” ( 六五舉) means that the height of jugao is 65% that of the bujia 步架. The first step is to determine the height between the top of the neighboring pillars, guazhu 瓜柱 post, or tuodun 柁橔 brace. Then add the appropriate height of pingshui 平水, and this will result in the appropriate position for the purlin. As outlined in the Yingzao suanli, the calculation of jugao differs according to the number of purlins in a given building. Few actual buildings correspond exactly to the method of jujia outlined in the Gongcheng zuofa and Yingzao suanli, indicating that the height of the purlins could be increased or decreased according to specific circumstances rather than always rigidly following a single standard that was documented in these texts.
Posts usually supporting outdoor lamps or lanterns.

Large upper-level floor spaces directly below the roof of commercial buildings or warehouses, originally unpartitioned but often modified for secondary use; may also be used for domestic sleeping or storage platforms set close to ceilings or roofs and open to and overlooking a living space below. For enclosed spaces under sloping roofs, between the roof and the ceiling of the uppermost story, especially in houses, use "attics (interior spaces)." For substantial interior spaces at the level of an upper story, usually extending the full length or width of rooms, use "galleries (upper level spaces)."

The movement of charged, heterogeneous particles in a suspension gel under the influence of an electric field created by electrodes of opposite charge set on either side of the suspension; used as technique for analysis of macromolecular substances such as DNA and proteins.
Regulating land use for stated purposes.

Parts of structures, usually located below ground level, that transmit building loads to the soil or rock underneath; when specifically distinguishing the support systems and areas of structures below ground, including the foundation, from the above-ground portions, use "substructures."

One of the main Protestant groups that arose out of the 16th-century Reformation. Generally speaking, modern Presbyterian churches trace their origins to the Calvinist churches of the British Isles, the European counterparts of which came to be known by the more inclusive name of Reformed. The term presbyterian also denotes a collegiate type of church government led by pastors and lay leaders called elders or presbyters. Strictly speaking, all Presbyterian churches are a part of the Reformed, or Calvinist, tradition, although not all Reformed churches are presbyterian in their form of government.

The process or function of gathering and recording information, especially to record facts or characteristics or to establish evidence or testimony. For the organizing and controlling of information, use "information management." For the records of information, use "documents."

Religious beliefs and practices of the ancient Celts, an ancient Indo-European people, peaking during the 4th century BCE, extending across the length of Europe from Britain to Asia Minor. The religion included many male and female deities, some of whom were venerated only in a small, local area, but others whose worship had a wider geographical distribution.

Testing a hypothesis or model. In science and related fields, refers to testing systematically under controlled conditions in order to discover the qualities, behavior, or effects of the subject of the experiment.

Ornamental pieces made of metal or wood that were used in traditional Japanese architecture to cover the wooden pegs necessary to secure the crossing of the lintel and uprights. They were also used on doors to conceal the heads of large nails.

Particular arrangements of vertical elements of a building, either exterior or interior. For the external areas of buildings, not necessarily restricted to surface features, use "fronts (architectural)." For the features of a primary front, restricted for the most part to surface elements in a single plane, use "façades."
Instruments for measuring the amount of dust in the air, as in mills or mines.
Devices used to measure the curvature of spherical or other curved surfaces.
Clocks that incorporate a device for recording times of arrival and departure of individuals, usually in the context of employment.

Pail-like or cone-shaped vessels, often having handles, made of bronze, silver, ceramic, glass, or another material. They were often decorated; used in the Iron Age, ancient Egypt, Asia, in the ancient Roman world, and in Christian religious rituals.
Formal arrangements of letters or words with particular attention to overall design and composition, as on the spines or covers of books or on signs.
Instruments for measuring vapor pressure.
Calibrated instruments for measuring electric power in watts.
Receptacles in the shape of a tower, located near Christian altars, for the reserve of the Eucharist; may also be set on top of altarpieces.
Barrel-shaped containers used to hold liquids, up to 30 gallons, having a taphole on top and a bunghole in the body.

Ancient Greek drinking vessels featuring a deep, footed bowl set on a tall footed stem and two vertical side handles extending from the bottom of the vessel to the rim. The kantharos is intimately associated with the wine god Dionysos, who is often depicted on vases holding a kantharos of type A or a rhyton.
Refers to the style and culture of the Kabardino-Balkariya republic of modern day Russia, located in the North Caucasus, which is comprised largely of the Kabardin and Balkar peoples.

In bookbinding, free-swinging joints produced by setting the boards a slight distance, about 1/8" to 1/4", away from the backing shoulder, creating a space into which the covering material is pressed, forming a gully or groove. It is one of the more obvious characteristics of library bindings. It allows relatively thick covering material, such as buckram, to be used while still allowing the covers to open easily. Distinct from "tight joints," in which the board lies with its back edge flush against the shoulder, making for a comparatively rigid joint with no gully.

Baskets or hampers of various shapes and sizes in different regions, particularly referring to large round wicker baskets used to transport or weigh items such as grain or coal, often by default utilized as a unit of measurement.

Containers for the chrism and consecrated oil used in Christian ritual. The term usually refers to vessels, either having one containing unit or, in some designs, having three flasks, for the oil for baptism, confirmation, and anointing of the sick. The term is also used for a small container or opening built into the interior church architecture, where the consecrated oil is stored.

Bead-like pieces of pure gold, typically incuse with designs or markings, used as currency and said to have facilitated specific transactions such as in rituals, religious or high value settings. The coins were used in the Mataram kingdom in Java, Indonesia and found subsequently in neighbouring polities such as Bali and Philippines. These coins have also been found in Southern Thailand. Piloncitos is a term given to these coins retrospectively.
Fabrication attribute of items that are offered for sale in a complete and finished state, ready for use, as opposed to items that are custom-made or made-to-order.
The activity of killing cattle, sheep, or other animals, usually for food.

Visual works in the shape of two intersecting bars, usually an upright one traversed by a horizontal one, especially those used as Christian symbols. For motifs consisting of two intersecting lines, with many variations in the shapes of the arms, use "crosses (motifs)."

Components of works or sometimes stand-alone works that are made of strips of cane, which is the long, hollow, pithy, jointed stem of certain plants, such as bamboo, rattan, sugarcane or certain palms. Examples of canework include furnishings, such as  the woven seat of a chair.
Small wood caps with a blow hole on top, used to enclose and support the reed of some single or double reedpipes.

Paintings or carvings consisting of or mounted on three attached panels, often hinged so that the outer wings fold over the central portion; a common form for altarpieces. Also used for other works having three related images side by side.
Engravings, drawings, photographs, or other images that are shaded off gradually at the edges.

Wooden discs in which figures have been applied in high relief that depict proverbs and sayings. They are mainly used to discuss a disagreement between spouses or to advise children. This custom is mainly found among the Bantu people of Central Africa.
Caucasian flat-woven rugs from Karabagh with weft-float brocading.
Mythical celestial bird-man and minstrel; celestial musician; celestial birdman playing instrument.
Marksmen of accurate aim; in naval and military use and also extended to those engaged in sport or exhibition.
Lighting devices designed to hang on a wall having one or more candle sockets or lamp holders; often ornamental and frequently incorporating a reflector.

Materials or items left of a thing or things after other parts have been removed, used, or destroyed. Examples include substances of organic origin that are entirely or partially preserved, often in the earth, in a conserved or fossilized condition, including what is left of a person or animal when life is extinct. May also include artifacts, ruins, and other remanants of a person or civilization.

An efflorescent salt found on excavated limestones that have been stored or displayed in the presence of acetic acid vapor. Thecotrichite is composed of calcium acetate nitrate chloride hydrate. It is only formed under very specific conditions in which a calcareous stone that contains chloride and nitrate ions is put in an environment with acetic acid vapors and moisture. Mitigation involves any or all of the following: 1) desalination, 2) decreasing relative humidity, or 3) elimination of acetic acid vapors.
Joints between two separately cast metal elements in which one element slots into the hollow “sleeve” of the other. The joint is generally further secured using pins, rivets, or by soldering.
Sculptured representations of the deceased on a tomb.
People of either sex who run their own household as their primary job or activity.
Any of varied devices that absorb mechanical shocks, sudden impulses or dampen vibrations, especially on vehicles.

A technique of elemental analysis in which a small area on a surface is bombarded with charged particles (non-electrons, usually protons) to produce fluorescent X-rays specific to an element. The method is used in conservation science, archaeology, and geology to obtain an elemental map which may guide research regarding dating, provenance and authenticity.

Packets of promotional materials for distribution to the press, as at a press conference. For official or authoritative statements distributed to the press typically by a public relations firm or government agency, use "press releases."

The action or condition of causing something, such as a group of people or a settlement, to exist. Founding usually involves official documents and official naming, and occurs on a specific date. For reference to less formal beginnings of groups of people or other things, use "establishment (action or condition)."
