Sheets of paper or tissue, usually blank, placed, adhered, or bound in between leaves of text or illustrations for protective or decorative purposes or for taking notes.

Engraved design motif or pattern featuring bold, angular lines contrasted with delicate, organic shapes. They are found on canoe prows, headrests, bamboo quivers, and on korwar carved figures, which often have enlarged heads in proportion with their squatting bodies. Objects bearing korwar style designs are often used during funerary rites in order to maintain contact with ancestors.
Founders or leaders of heresies or heretical sects.

Templates made of a variety of materials with engraved or cut-out  images of letters that are used to create uniform characters by following the guide directly with a writing implement or through the use of a pantograph.
Those parts of the flanking walls of the cella of a temple that project beyond its front or rear, often terminating in antae.

Synthetic elastomeric fiber or fabric composed largely of alternating rigid and flexible segments of polyurethane. It is used in the clothing industry, especially for hosiery, underwear, swimwear, and other close-fitting garments. Spandex is the generic name in the United States and Canada. Elastane is the generic name used elsewhere. Lycra is a proprietary name for this material.
Small, club-shaped tools with rounded ends, used to grind or pound the colored pigments required to make paint. Frequently used in conjunction with a mortar.

A decorative motif in the form of a stylized iris or lily, usually with three curled petals, but occasionally with five, one of which forms the central axis to the symmetrical design. The design is based on an iris, which was equated with the lily and had the same symbolic references as the lily; it probably developed from the honeysuckle design motif.
Supports, usually pilasters or colonettes, engaged to a wall, that carry one end of an arch, a groin, or a vault rib.
An elephant band motif in base.
Establishments primarily engaged in producing surfaced lumber, by cutting, smoothing, and matching wood.
Areas within an ornamental scheme, usually rectangular and enframed. In bookbinding, also includes spaces on the sides of a book or between the bands on the spine.

Alphabetical lists of terms related to a particular subject or area of interest, including definitions or explanations of usage. Glossaries are typically part of a larger work and generally exclude pronunciation and etymological information.
Legal instruments in which a person declares the disposition of his/her property, to take effect after his/her death, and which is revocable during the lifetime of that person.

Recommendations and often examples, laying out best practice or advice regarding a certain procedure, activity, or topic. For documents containing more prescriptive instructions, use "rules (instructional materials)." For more prescriptive instructions, prefer "rules."
Collections of tools and materials that are kept together in a receptacle for a variety of needlework practices.
Apparatus that allows separation of ions in a single drop of solution; used for analysis of minute samples. Vaporizarion of solvent from filter paper is effected, leaving the solute in a ring shape.

Millinery tools consisting of cast-iron, egg-shaped balls of various sizes mounted on metal shanks and fixed to a short wooden handle. Used to iron the inside of convex surfaces on bonnets, sleeves, bows, or waistbands.
Guiding tools such as stencils, patterns, or overlays used for duplicating shapes or designs in sculpting, woodcrafting, creating architectural details, graphic arts, sewing, and other activities.
General term for various devices used to cut wood.

Fine clay which, when mixed with water, results in a fluid with a creamlike consistency, used in casting, glazing, decorating, and repairing ceramic wares; in its natural state, it contains sufficient flux to be used for glazing and decorating without the need of additives. For ceramic glaze with a high content of slip, use "slip glaze."

The process of shedding the values, practices, effects and influence of colonization within a formerly colonized culture, people or a former colonial power. This includes the changes in thought processes, attitudes, assumptions, power structures, and institutions of the colonized and colonizer respectively.

Religious order of nuns, established under the rule of St. Augustine in 1572 from a company founded at Brescia in 1537, for the teaching of girls, nursing of the sick, and the sanctification of the lives of its members.

Christian sect centered along the Malabar Coast of southwestern India, said to have origins in the Christianization efforts of the apostle St. Thomas. The origins of the sect are uncertain, though they seem to have been in existence before the 6th century and probably derive from the missionary activity of the East Syrian (Nestorian) Church, which held that the two natures of Christ were two persons joined in a moral union. In geographic isolation from Syria, the sect has nonetheless retained the Chaldean liturgy, Syriac language, and fraternal ties with the Babylonian (Baghdad) patriarchate; their devotional practices also include Hindu religious symbolism.
Caps worn underneath other headwear, often plain, and not intended to be seen, but some exhibiting embroidered or jewelled borders. These have been made in a variety of materials.
Shoes made at least partially of wood, especially those carved from a single block of wood; worn originally by farmers and other workers in the Netherlands, France, and Belgium.
Boots whose upper part reaches to the thigh.
Popular family carriages, with four wheels, drawn by one or two horses or ponies, and usually having a top; developed in the United States in a variety of styles during the late 19th century.
Caps of fantastic shape, often garnished with bells, formerly worn by court fools or jesters.

Variants of air-breathing jet engines that do not include a rotary compressor; relying instead on the engine's forward motion to compress the incoming air. These do not function at zero airspeed and cannot be used to power aircraft through all phases of flight.
The arrangement of masts and sails on boats or ships.
Farmer's two-wheeled carts that can be converted to four-wheeled wagons.
Components of garments, such as shirts, nightgowns, or dresses, consisting of a neck and shoulder piece.
Costume indicative or characteristic of a calling, rank, or function.
Open-faced helmets with cheekpieces and a closely fitting skull, at first made of two and later of only one sheet of bronze. They originated in the Peloponnese in the early 7th century BCE.
Toys that children use for modeling clay and other malleable materials as well as supplies such as modeling tools or molds.
Accessories worn to commemorate a deceased person or group of individuals. Examples include armbands worn around the upper arm or pins and ribbons worn on the chest.
Use to distinguish any type of binding in which the covers are not stiff; may be of various materials, including vellum, paper, cloth, or plastic.

Bindings, usually of calfskin leather, decorated with patterns and motifs derived from Etruscan pottery, including key patterns, vases, and palmettes. They were popularized in the mid-18th century by the bookbinders of Halifax, Yorkshire, England, notably the Edwards family.
Gliding toys or sporting items that are generally made of injection molded plastic and roughly 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) in diameter. These have an aerodynamic profile in cross-section.
Water-soluble anionic surfactant used in detergents and other cleaning products such as toothpaste. In conservation, used in the aqueous cleaning of painted surfaces.
Large wooden puck-like objects used in the Dutch game of platte bol and for other traditional Dutch games. For similar objects used for ice hockey, use "hockey pucks."

Suits, generally intended for men, worn on formal occasions and at ceremonial events. Contemporary versions consist of a tuxedo-like suit with a tail coat, a starched shirt and collar, a white vest, white bow tie and black trousers with single or double stripe of satin running the length of the leg.
Skirts that are cut to be full at the waist and over the hips, but narrow at the hem.
Close-fitting trousers with a strap passing under the instep; worn especially in the 19th century.
General term for long capes worn by cardinals, bishops, and other Christian prelates.
Main garments of varying length extending from the waist or hip and covering a part of the lower body. Also, the lower part of a dress, coat, or other garment.
Soft coverings for the head and neck, and sometimes extending to the shoulders, either separate or attached to a garment.
Refers to a woman's corset, or corset-like undergarments that shape the body by a variety of means.
Frames or oval hoops worn to extend a woman's skirt at the side.
Arrangements of flowers to be worn as costume accessories, as on the bodice or at the wrist.
Ladle-like culinary tools with pierced or screened bowls to allow liquid to drain through while retaining larger solids.

Traditonal Korean bridal robe, a topcoat with flowing sleeves made of embroidered silk. It has been a culturally significant article of female wedding apparel since the early Choson dynasty. The hwalot evolved from Chinese costume styles.
Originally applied to various types of loose-fitting cloaks and coats for men and women.  In the 19th century applied to women's fitted jackets worn over a garment with a crinoline or bustle.
Perforated utensils, usually having a handle, used to skim liquids.
Rotating stand used to serve condiments or food.
A rounded script developed in the 13th century used mainly in southern Europe.

Common soldiers' armor worn during the 15th and 16th centuries, typically sleeveless and of waist-length or slightly longer. One form had small overlapping iron or horn plates fixed inside between layers of fabric by trellis-pattern stitching.

Bottles, usually made of glass or stoneware, made to protect individuals and locations from witchcraft. Contain various combinations of pins, nails, plant material, bodily fluids, and or human organic materials (nail clippings, hair, etc.) After preparation, bottles were placed inside building foundations or concealed in outdoor locations such as churchyards. Commonly practiced in England in the 17th century, though some examples have been found in the United States dating from the mid-19th century.
Late Roman and Early Byzantine silver coins issued between the late 3rd and early 7th centuries.
Any of various German, then Central European, silver coins equivalent to groats and gros tournois and introduced in the 13th century.

Scripts used for writing by the Syriac Christians from the 1st century ad until about the 14th century. Using a Semitic alphabet, it is descendent Aramaic cursive with 22 letters, all representing consonants, and was typically written from right to left, although occasionally vertically downward. Diacritical marks used to represent vowels were introduced in the 8th century and two systems of vocalization were developed, one similar to the system in Arabic, and one using small Greek letters above or below the line.
Chants based in ancient Hebrew music, following well-established modal patterns.
Books of responsories for religious service.
Sharp, broad-bladed and often short-handled knives used for cutting large pieces of meat into joints or roasts.
Large rectangular pans without lids, slightly deeper than baking pans, intended for roasting meat and poultry in an oven. For enamel pans with lids, use "roasters (cookware)."

Flags, banners, figures, or other objects displayed or carried as an identifying symbol or rallying-point of a leader, public officer, organization, etc. Examples include  banners of noble houses, flags of nations, and the colors of a military unit.
Stoves designed and used primarily for cooking and baking, rather than only for heating a space.
General term for literary works written and published for children, including fiction and non-fiction.

Process developed by Lea and Luis Remba with Rufino Tamayo that produces embossed or dimensional prints in color with handmade paper. This is achieved with inked plates moulded from a model created by an artist into which is pushed raw paper pulp under great pressure.

Small to medium-sized receptacles made of leather or other flexible material and frequently having several inner compartments, used for carrying money and other personal items, fastened with a zipper, clasp, press stud, etc., and carried as a ladies' handbag or shoulderbag.

Term generally applied to any bowl used to serve or display real or artifical fruit. Prefer "compotes" for bowls, usually set on a high footed stem and sometimes having a cover, used to serve fruit, compotes, nuts, or sweets.
Vessels made to hold liquid foods, usually shallow and round.

Earthenware vessels, shaped much like tea kettles, but generally larger, with a canted spout and handles. Found in Barbados, Jamaica, Nevis, and Antigua as early as the 18th century and still made today.  Also made in the American south (particularly in the Carolinas and Tennessee).
Tall cups consisting of a bowl of varying form resting on a stem and usually having a cover; often used for ceremonial purposes.
Cups of various forms designed for drinking wine, made of glass, metal, or ceramic. The bowl may rest on a stem; the cup may have a lid.
Jar designed or used for storage of tobacco.
In Indian architecture, a measuring cord.

Paper sleeves that house phonograph records dating from the late 19th century and originally meant for 78 rpm discs. These are often decorative, square paper sleeves, usually with center-cut holes that reveal the label on the disc.
Boxes, bags, or other receptacles designed to contain and transport neckties for safe keeping.
Containers made of woven plant material of varying shape. Some examples contain lids or hoops for carrying poles. Made to carry various personal materials.
Pouring projections formed by eversion of the rim of the mouth or spout of a vessel.

Bodies, typically tending to spheroidal shapes, that are produced by the female of birds, reptiles, fish, amphibians, and other animal species. Eggs are the organic vessels in which an animal embryo develops enclosed within a shell or membrane. For the egg cells of mammals and other animals, use "ova."

Devices with firm, rigid frames equipped with slot-hole configurations through which yarn is threaded to create a warp. Considered one of the simplest styles of looms to use, these devices are known for their combined heddle, beater, and reed elements within one riddle heddle reed component, which is used to both raise and lower warp threads and beat weft yarn into place. To facilitate hand weaving, the device's riddle heddle reed is placed alternately in the up and down positions to create the sheds through which the shuttles are passed. When the heddle is in the up position, the threads in the holes are raised; when it is in the down position, the threads in the slots are raised. As compared to other types of looms, these devices are notably smaller and more portable. Though they are designed to produce plain weaves, these looms can also be manipulated to create more complex patterns.

Phylum of numerous marine invertebrates characterized by a series of vertical ciliary combs over the surface of the animal. Most species float through the water, although a few creep or are parasitic. Refers to solitary, hermaphroditic, marine invertebrates of the phylum Ctenophora, found worldwide, having an ovoid, gelatinous, bilaterally symmetical body with regular, comblike rows of beating cilia for propulsion, and two trailing tentacles with adbesive cells to trap planktoon.
Cylindrical cases to hold pins.
Any objects, tools, or printed matter used while conducting psychological examinations of individuals or groups.

Mechanized devices, typically comprising a series of two to four rollers, used to attenuate, straighten, comb, and combine the loose and inconsistent slivers produced through the carding process. As slivers are passed through the frames' rollers, which spin at increasingly rapid speeds, their individual fibers are made parallel and uniform for future usage. These devices are specifically designed to carry out drawing, doubling, and drafting processes. The device's original invention is credited to Lewis Paul and John Wyatt who developed the first drawing frame in the 1730s.
Salt or ester of boric acid. Borate has many applications, chief among them as wood preservative and corrosion inhibitor.

Style of textiles, particularly floor coverings, handwoven in the neighborhood of Melas, southwestern Turkey, on the Aegean coast. The rugs are characterized as being usually of small size, dating from the 19th century, and having unusually wide borders in relation to their narrow fields. In the prayer rugs, the arch (which indicates the direction of Mecca, the holy city) is straight-sided, with a triangular indentation below it on each side, the local reminiscence of a lobed-arch form used in the Ottoman court prayer rugs of the 16th and 17th centuries. The color scheme is unique among similar carpets: the field is usually a strong red, with yellow and violet together with a light blue that is quite variable owing to uneven dyeing. Examples that predate the use of chemical dyes are considered to be among the most attractive Turkish carpets.

A culture and style of pre-Muslim Central Asia, named after, but not restricted to the area of Sogdiana. Noted visual arts were created 5th/ 9th centuries. Many cultural streams united in the area of Sogdiana, including Sāsānian culture, post-Gupta India, and Sui and T’ang Chinese. Style is characterized in painting and carved wood.
Parts or components of vehicles.
Systems of posted signs arranged to communicate directions or essential information.
Action of offering incense as an act of devotion or cleansing.
Collections of books, periodicals, and other materials, organized to provide physical, bibliographic, and intellectual access by the public or members of a group.

Refers to minute parts of a larger structure, object, or image. For architectural drawings of design or construction details, use "detail drawings." For preparatory studies of pictorial or design details, use "detail studies."

Process of creating windows or other visual works using glass in cement or another matrix. Pieces of glass, usually slab glass, are laid out in a design or pattern; the pieces of glass may be cut, shaped, and chipped along the edges to resemble faceting. Cement or another material is poured between the pieces of glass, often with metal reinforcements, and allowed to harden.
Objects like carabiners that allow quick addition, removal, and storage of keys.
Handheld devices that deliver an electric shock, designed to be administered to the flanks of cattle to startle them into movement.
Artificial replacements for teeth, whether or not they are permanently anchored in the mouth.
Smoking apparatuses in which the smoke is drawn through a cnotainer of water and cooled before reaching the mouth.

Those whose occupation or profession it is to engage in a game played with a ball and rackets on a rectangular court consisting of a smooth grass lawn, or a floor of hard gravel, cement, or asphalt, divided with a net and outlined with smaller boundaries into which the ball is aimed.
Designation for various types of subdivisions in Italian cities.
Any drills for drilling or otherwise working stone or masonry.

Dependent communities, nations, or territories, which, by international treaty, are placed under the protection or domination of a foreign power or group of powers, typically entailing loss of control over such matters as defense and foreign relations.

Burnishers used primarily to work with etching plates to efface previously etched areas, and also to treat the edges of the plate. These come in a variety of shapes for differing purposes, straight, curved, ball-tipped, or twisted with an alternate needle point end.

Refers to relatively small household items, often collectibles such as ceramics, fans, or statuettes that are characterized by being ornamental, often having antiquarian interest, and typically being displayed on tables, shelves, or elsewhere in a living area. This term is generally not used for collections of natural history objects, coins, furniture, or fine art.
Ropes made of rice straw, hemp, or other fibers woven together, often used for ritual purification of sites. Strung across torii or Shinto shrines.
Tanks or artificial ponds used for immersing cattle in chemically treated water for the purpose of preventing disease.
Territories or domains ruled by an earl.
Refers to the material woven from the fiber of Pandanus leaves, used traditionally, for example, as sails for canoes constructed on the Society Islands of the South Pacific.

Used in the 18th and early 19th century to mean a closely woven linen tabby, first manufactured in Holland. In the mid- and late 19th century, also came into use for a heavily glazed starched cotton cloth, commonly used for window shades.

Woven textile in which the binding is achieved by a displacement of warp ends secured by the weft, resulting usually, though not always, in a very open weave; used particularly for surgical dressings and as backing for paper, especially maps.
The process of applying color or a glaze with a sponge to create a mottled effect; may be applied randomly or in a pattern.
The distortion of an object originally linear or planar so that it is curved or coiled in shape.
Covering or enclosing entirely or to a great extent with a flexible material, especially by winding or folding.
Term refers to the process of demagnetization, originally used in the context of warships, now extended to magnetic media such as audio tapes and computer storage media.
Describes processes that change the volume or length of an object resulting from temperature, moisture, or other environmental condition.

Foot-propelled vehicles with, usually, two wheels in tandem, a low footboard on which the rider stands set between the wheels, and a handlebar for steering, generally mounted on a vertical post; for similar, but larger and heavier, motorized vehicles, use "motor scooters."
The act or process of reducing a gas or vapor to a liquid or solid form.

Classes of magnitude or dimensions, typically numbered, into which articles are divided according to how large they are. Examples are in manufactured clothing, such as shoes, dresses, gloves, and hats.
In Indian architecture, having six śākhās.
Having a size greater than the size of life, or, with reference to visual representations of something, larger in size than the original.
The ability to bend without breaking or cracking.
Having an empty space or cavity within; not filled in with matter.

Games, existing in several variations globally and through history, having in common that they are all played on a board with two rows of 12 vertical points, and dice are rolled to determine the movement of pieces. Backgammon is a modern western variety of these games.
The state or quality of substances of being able to mix with other, usually specified, substances.

Some frames on early European panel paintings that were not only attached, or 'engaged,' but were made from the same piece of wood as the painting’s support where the grain of the upper and lower moldings match, visible if the gilding has been stripped away. These are found on small-scale Netherlandish panel paintings, which in some cases would be carved from a single plank, having either a raised profile only on the front of the panel and a flat surface on the reverse, or in some cases with raised frame projections on both surfaces. Examples of these exist from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century.

Zitherlike chordophones of Timor, the strings of which are either of copper, strung in pairs around the tubular bamboo or wood string bearer, or cut out and raised from the string bearer itself. The tube is surrounded by a palm leaf resonator. For similar chordophones from Madagascar, use "valihas."

Dolls with moving parts, similar to "jumping-jacks," particularly those used by children in ancient Greece. They were typically made of wood, bone, ivory, marble, cloth, wax, alabaster, or terracotta, with articulated arms and legs that were made separately and attached to the doll's body with cords, which allowed the limbs to move. Earliest examples date to about 800 BCE.
Five-string plucked lutelike chordophones of the Wolof people of Senegal and the Gambia, having a narrow boat-shaped soundbox and an unfretted cylindrical neck.

Compilations of separate articles, treatises, studies, or literary compositions of various kinds brought together into one volume. For compilations of brief extracts of works that are considered the best examples of an author, subject matter, or literary form, use "anthologies."
Small pocketable cards that are imprinted with the names of candidates, slogans or other promotional details for elections.
The quality of a substance of tending to evaporate rapidly.

Dresses open in front to show an underskirt or with a front gore of contrasting material, with collar and lapels and long sleeves. Bodice may be double-breasted and high-waisted; worn especially during the 1820s through the 1860s. For double- or single-breasted three-quarter length or full-length fitted overcoats with flared skirts, use "redingote (overcoats)."

A natural orange-red dye extracted from the root of the of the munjeet plant, Rubia cordifolia, indigenous to the mountainous regions of Asia. Munjeet is a lightfast dye that was historically used for dying cotton in Asia. The principle colorant is munjistin, an anthraquinone, and it also contains smaller amounts of purpurin, pseudopurpurin, alizarin, and xanthopurpurin.

Strong, tough, waxy, nonflammable synthetic resin produced by the polymerization of tetrafluoroethylene; has numerous applications. It is distinguished by its slippery surface, high melting point, and resistance to attack by almost all chemicals.
Books containing prayers and other forms of worship.

Various types of rural deities of Roman mythology. In early representations, they appear like men with horns and the tail of a goat; in later representations, they also have goats' legs like the satyrs.

Species of very large deciduous trees native to northwestern North America; planted elsewhere as an ornamental. In some classifications, a subspecies of Populus balsamifera. Noted as the first tree species for which the genome was sequenced. Used for timber and for extracts from the fragrant buds for use in perfume, medicines, and cosmetics. Native Americans of the Pacific Northwest used the inner bark as food and medicine, the anti-inflammatory, salicin, content making it useful for treating wounds and other purposes. The wood, roots, and bark were used for firewood, canoes, rope making, fish traps, baskets, and structures. The gum-like sap was used as glue and waterproofing.

Trademarked variety of fiberboards made from bagasse (sugar cane waste) or mineral fibers. Examples include insulating tiles and boards. Celotex products were treated to resist fungi, termites, and water. The boards had a rough, weblike surface that accepted paint well, but they became brittle and friable with age. Low-density Celotex boards were used in the 1930s for heat and sound insulation in such buildings as the White House, Washington D.C. and Rockefeller Center in New York City.

Species of ornamental and shade tree, often 30 meters (100 feet) in height, having graceful, drooping branches, many-lobed dark green leaves, and large, distinctive acorns about 5 cm (1.7 inches) long. The ash-gray to light-brown bark, slightly orange-tinted, is fissured in irregular cubes.

Genus containing various annual grasses of wide climatic adaptability that have been cultivated for food since prehistoric times and are now cultivated in most temperate areas for the grain they yield, particularly T. aestivum and T. turgidum. The tall stalks (about 1 m) have heads of grain that are primarily ground into flour for pasta and bread. Wheat grain is also used for making starch, alcohol (beer), and feeding livestock. It contains carbohydrates (70%), proteins (11-15%), minerals, and vitamins.  The wheat straw (stalks) are used for fodder, papermaking, and bedding.
Deities who are associated with a place, whether a natural place or an inhabited place.

Genus of flowering plant native to scrub and heathland in Europe, western Asia and North Africa, and is one of several genera in the tribe Genisteae which are commonly called brooms. These shrubs produce brightly colored, pea-like flowers that are often fragrant.

One of two  long-lived species of bristlecone pine (the other is Pinus aristata) that grow at high altitudes in the Western U.S. Pinus longaeva lives longer than any other tree. Dendrochronological studies have produced a continuous tree-ring sequence back to 6700 BC for a sample in the White Mountains of California. Like other bristlecone pines, its cones have long curving spines on each scale.
Unique names assigned to an information unit in a data system to identify it within that context.
Institutions owning or maintaining collections of photographs, sometimes including other visual resources in various formats and media, usually within larger libraries, archives, or collections.
Museums that are owned or administered by representatives of multiple nations, or that specializes in exhibitions from multiple nations.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of whitish colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of purple colors.

A range of purplish red or pink colors resembling the color of reddish lake pigments, which are organic pigments prepared by precipitation of a dye on a powdered, inorganic substrate. The color term "lake" refers particularly to the colors of cochineal, kermes, madder, lac, etc., which are all reddish in color and used in oil painting.
A range of yellow colors resembling the color of Indian yellow pigment, originally made from the urine of cows fed exclusively on mango leaves.
Variable shades of light gray.
A range of grayish colors resembling the color of the lustrous metal, silver.
Refers to a range of yellowish green colors, the name coming from the common Irish name "Kelly," referring to the association of Ireland with the color green.
Various tones of warm orangey pink, referring to the color of the flesh of the salmon fish.
Style of domestic architecture, particularly in North American 1940s-1950s. Characterized by having one-story and low-pitched roofs.

Colors in a range of a greenish blue, used in photography and color printing; it is one of the primary subtractive colors. The name is ultimately based on cyanine, which it resembles in color, although it is distinguished by its status as a primary subtractive color.

Suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of dog-like carnivorans, including dogs, bears, racoons, mustelids, pinnipeds, and related taxa. Feliformia stands in contrast to the other suborder of Carnivora, Feliformia, cat-like carnivorans.
Members of an order containing cicadas, hoppers, whiteflies, aphids, and scale insects.
Regarding personal names, assumed names under which people engage in combat or, by extension, in some other analogous activity or enterprise such as spying or courtship.

Order containing 309 species in five families including hawks, falcons, eagles, the secretary bird, Old World vultures, and condors. They are characterized by typically have a sharply hooked beak with a cere (soft mass) housing the nostrils, long and fairly broad wings suitable for soaring flight, strong legs and feet with raptorial claws and an opposable hind claw, most are carnivorous, hunting by sight during the day or at twilight, and being exceptionally long-lived with low reproductive rates. They date from the Middle Eocene.
Bladed tools designed to cut fruits and vegetables.
Educational institutions providing the first stage of compulsory education, generally extending from grade 1 through grades 6 or 8 and teaching the rudiments of learning; may house a kindergarten.

Refers to angles, quoins, corners, or corner projections of northern Indian temple structures. In Indian architecture, an angle; plain fillet (moulding); corner wall-division; corner-division of plan and elevation; corner; kōṇa; corner projection. In Indian architecture, a corner (Kaliṅga); karṇa; kaṇika-pāga (Oriyā).
Massive self-luminous celestial bodies of gas that shine by radiation derived from internal energy sources. There are tens of billions of trillions of stars composing the visible universe.
Bowl-shaped hollows that are partly surrounded by cliffs or steep slopes, and situated at the head of a glaciated valley.
Jar-shaped Chinese ritual bronze vessels used to hold wine. Appeared between the Erligang and Anyang period.
Large inlets of the sea, usually more enclosed and more deeply indented than bays.
Paper size, generally used in Great Britain, that measures one size larger than royal, or 19-21 by 27-28 inches.
Order containing five species in one family, characterized by long noses, mouse-like tails, long limbs, large canine teeth, and high-crowned cheek teeth like those of ungulates.
Genus of four species in Asia, including the leopard cat, flat-headed cat, and fishing cat.
Proofs, meeting the right to print impression, that are intended as gifts to groups or individuals.
Marbled paper prepared with a turpentine mix, as well as the added oil or gall. The color then breaks into fine holes.
Book size having height dimension of approximately 25 inches.
Feast in the calendar of several Christian denominations, observed on August 6. It celebrates an episode in the New Testament in which Jesus is metamorphosed into a radiant in glory upon a mountain.
Physical mark identifying a buddha, conventionally depicted as a cranial bump and said to possess magical properties.
Small stitches sewn in a line by passing a needle in and out of the fabric.
In Indian architecture, a round, mortar-based pillar.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in Sudan.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in Burkina Faso.
Having the form or outline of a semicircle, a plane figure which is the half of a circle divided by the diameter, or the half of its circumference.

Genre of  motion picture featuring action and adventure, usually though not always in a more or less accurate historical setting, with dashing and courageous protagonists who fight, often with swords, for some noble cause.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Sudan and Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Burkina Faso primarily, with smaller numbers in Togo.
Book cloth grain with honeycomb pattern.
Those who specialize in applying paint and gilding to sculpted or carved works.

Thin metal plates of tin or zinc used during pressing to ensure even distribution of pressure, to protect the textblock from moisture, and to prevent the indentations of the turn-ins from marking the textblock.
Nationality, styles, and cultures of the people of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Businesses involved in the distribution of products.
Use when describing the culture of or products from the chief fishing tribe of the same name from Madagascar, currently inhabiting its southwest coast.

Soft food product made with gelatin derived from animal collagen, pectin, or other substances, often with the juice or flavor of fruit added. This is prepared by by boiling and subsequent cooling, and displays a characteristic elastic consistency and translucence.
Mouthpieces of bridles, having fittings at each end to which the reins are fastened.

Embroidered badges awarded for completion or proficiency in a particular subject, activity, craft, or other event associated with a formal organization. These are normally worn on a recipient's clothing or uniform, or on a sash.

Strip of lace, cloth, leather, or another material that is gathered on one edge or cut on the bias, so that when attached to the hem, button placard, neckline, or wrist of a garment it produces an ornamental frill or flounce.

Note containing the name, brief biographical information, and roles (if necessary) of the named or anonymous individuals or corporate bodies responsible for the design, production, manufacture, or alteration of the work, presented in a syntax suitable for display.

Devices used in conjunction or as part of grain mills to automatically regulate the flow of grain into a mill, generally consisting of a receptacle into which grain is placed and a rotating cylinder that moves the grain into the next portion of the mill.

Small, long needles, equipped with pincers at each end, used to produce nets, filet-lace, and similar mesh-like materials. Netting thread is wound lengthwise on the needle between the two pincers, which increase the user's control of the thread before it is wrapped around the net gauge, thus lessensing potential tangling or knots.

Mechanized devices designed to utilize thermal techniques to produce non-linear, wavy, and zig-zagged ridges in man-made fibers. Taking advantage of the thermoplasticity of fibrous materials, these devices typically set fibers at a temperature near their softening point while simultaneously subjecting them to bending and twisting actions before lowering their temperature using cooling technologies. Because fibers are commonly heat stretched prior to crimping, they experience considerable thermoshrinkage when crimped using these devices. The primary function of crimping machines is to provide bulk to fibers, resulting in increased softness and resistance to wear and abrasion.
Devices used to measure the ability of textiles not to fade or change color after washing or dry cleaning.
Cylinders of wood or other materials, usually with short handles at each end, for rolling out dough.
Vessels in which brine is allowed to evaporate, leaving behind salt.
Devices used to clean milk bottles.
Devices used to vaporize substances by means of heat, and then condense the vapour by exposing it to cold, obtaining the substance or one of its constituents in a state of concentration or purity.
Meaning "wrote [it]," in printmaking indicates the one who physically wrote the lettering or passage. May be used for works other than prints.

Mancala is a generic name for a family of two-player turn-based strategy board games played with small stones, beans, or seeds and rows of holes or pits in the earth, a board or other playing surface. The objective is usually to capture all or some set of the opponent's pieces.
Paper or paper-like diagnostic tool used in dentistry to highlight occlusal contacts and the distribution of occlusal forces.
Mechanized devices designed to mantain yarn at a uniform degree of tension while it is being unwound from the warp beam for the purpose of sizing and dressing.
Telling or writing stories, especially recounting stories aloud to others, either from memory, ex tempore, or reading from notes or a book.
In cataloging art and cultural heritage, refers to the first known owner of the work, when the method of acquisition is unknown or not applicable.

The activity or process of assigning titles or names to works, including movable works and built works; may also be used for the process of giving names or titles to films, written works, music, dance, or other creative works or compilations of works.
Titles applied to archival groups, which are aggregates of items that share a common provenance.
System for tracking objects or animals using radio signals. Usually employed via a device such as a microchip which transmits radio signals.
Describes occurrences taking place during a particular interval of time relating to a judgment, the function of judging, the administration of justice.
Unit of French currency of varying value, known from the Middle Ages until the French Revolution.
Refers to varieties of Spanish spoken in Peru.

General term for a number of calendars used in ancient Greece, dividing the year into the 12 lunar months, in many examples having the intercalary month Embolimos. Independent of the division of a month into days, the month was divided into periods according to the waxing and waning of the moon.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 400-421; founded by Han Chinese Li family.
Refers to the numbers Frits Lugt created in his widely used reference works on provenance research.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1399 to 1300 (or 1400 to 1301) Before Common Era.
Machines employed to split hides that operate by seizing the skin and forcing it around a cylinder towards a knife that can be adjusted to different thicknesses.

Narrative ceremonial dance cycles practiced by the inhabitants of the eastern Kimberleys region of Australia. The narrative dance is based on the cyclone and serves as a way of explaining such events to the general population. Painted boards and threaded crosses are carried behind the dancers head while performing. The type of material utilized for the dances changes depending of the context of the story.
A milky beverage produced by soaking, grinding, and boiling dried soy beans. It is a traditional staple of Chinese and Japanese cuisine and has been promoted as a substitute for cow’s milk elsewhere.
Brand name of reusable plastic zipper storage bags and containers; developed by Dow Chemical Company in 1968; manufactured by S. C. Johnson & Son.
Language family, which along with Quechuan, is one of the primary language families of the indigenous central Andes.
Standard literary Arabic used across the Middle East, North Africa, and Horn of Africa; one of the six official languages of the United Nations.
Any of various devices by means of which sound vibrations are converted into a visible form for analysis.
Smooth features that slope away from the lower termination of canyons, on the sea floor.

In situations where one artist is copying or basing a work on another artist's work, the artist of the original work is referred to as the "original artist." An example of usage is when a printmaker engraves an image on a plate based on the original artist's painting.

Etruscan pottery made between the end of the 7th and the beginning of the 5th centuries BCE. Produced as a substitute for metalware, its forms, decorative motifs, black color, and polished finish mimic the style of metalware.
People who create architectural drawings or other images using CAD (computer-aided design).
Languages used as a means of communication between populations speaking vernaculars that are not mutually intelligible.
Artists who specialize in making concept art, which is art that conveys the plan or idea of a project, such as in animation, films, video games, comic books, or other media.

Culture, nationality, and styles of the Slavic linguistic and ethnic group that came from Asia in the third or second millennium BCE, spread steadily across eastern Europe, and played an important role in the Medieval world, particularly during the Slavic migrations.
The act of springing into the air.
The state or condition of being unoccupied or inactive, or a habitual avoidance of work.
In Indian architecture, a prati-kaṇṭha of the temple’s base or of hāra-base bearing makara-figures.
Semi-divine spirits who take the form of a maiden inhabiting the sea, rivers, mountains, woods, trees, or other natural places, and often portrayed in poetry as attendants on a particular god.
In architecture, measurements of height equivalent to one story.
Units of distance in English-speaking countries, equal to 1760 yards or approximately 1609 meters. It is derived from Roman units of distance of 1000 paces, or approximately 1618 yards.

An early style of gem cutting that is thought to have originated in India and to have been brought to Europe by the Venetians. The rose cut is recognizable by its flat bottom and a crown side with triangular facets that come together in a point. It started out as a relatively simple cut, but became more sophisticated over time.

Millet is the traditional staple of the Pinuyumayan people. Every July each tribe holds a harvest festival with different proceedings and denomination. In the tribe of Kapitol (Zhiben area), a pole known as talingel will be set up to mark the festival and the celebration involves wrestling (known as malalius) and street procession. Wrestling is also on the agenda of the tribes of Pinaski and Puyuma; the latter’s celebration, additionally, involves dancing and outings to Mount Dulan, Green Island and Orchard Island. In the Murivurivuk tribe at Chulu, the celebration entails drimiakulu (“swinging”) and dremadodas (“rattan ball piercing”).

Cultures and styles of the Thao people lived in Taiwan. The Thao people primarily live in Yuchi Township and Shuili Township, Nantou County. Thao used to be categorized as one of the branches of the Tsou people. In 2001 it gained official recognition as an indigenous people. Thao’s social organization revolves around patriarchal clans and families, passing on hereditary roles from generation to generation. Tribal politics, economy and religious office follow the organization of clans as well. The major festival of the Thao people is the worship of ancestral spirits in August in the Lunar calendar.
The state of an individual being unsure of their own gender or sexual orientation.
Textiles consisting of appliqued fabrics to create various images or patterns. Particularly created by Hmong women for bedspreads, quilts, and clothing.
General term for objects comprising or containing the image or represenation of a saint or other holy figure.
Flat, horizontal platforms used for water sports. Located near the rims of pools or other bodies of water.
Mines from which the primary extraction is tin, which is an element and a soft, pliable, silvery white metal.

A bright white and sparkling marble, sometimes with orange stains, that is quarried near Olympia in the Peloponnesus in Greece. Similar to Parian marble but with more compact texture and smaller grain, it is the only white marble that does not effervesce upon contact with nitric acid.

Acid that occurs in sour milk as a thick water-soluble liquid. It is induced by bacterial decomposition of sugar, a process of fermentation; it may also be found in molasses, many fruits, beer and wine. Lactic acid is used in dyeing and leather processing.

A copper-based mineral, copper carbonate hydroxide, that is often used in jewelry ranging from very deep blue to pale blue. Azurite is often found in association with the green mineral malachite, resulting from weathering and oxidation of copper sulfide.
Glass that is impenetrable by light, neither transparent nor translucent.
A brick or tile of normal face dimensions, having a nominal 2 in (5 cm) thickness.
Glass with a ruby color due to the presence of various materials, including colloidal gold, cadmium selenide, or copper and zinc sulfide.

Refers to cut crystal glass in which a decorative ceramic object is embedded, usually a medallion or cameo that has been carved into a white porcellaneous, heat-resistant material. A Bohemian invention of the 18th century, the technique was taken up in Paris but only became popular through English glassmakers in 18th- and 19th-century Europe. For glass characterized by a particular yellow or red color, use "cadmium sulphide glass."

An element, symbol Cl and atomic number 17, that is at ordinary temperatures a greenish-yellow gas, toxic and corrosive to the eyes and respiratory system. It becomes a liquid at -29 degrees Fahrenheit. It occurs in nature in great abundance in compounds, such as common salt.  Free chlorine is used as a sterilizing agent, such as for water.
Portland cement mixed with the existing soil to serve as a paving or surfacing material.
Motifs of a semicircle with projecting fanlike rays.
Crosses with arms terminating in potents, which are bars forming a T-shape.
Municipal areas having special administrative ranking. Examples are in Taiwan, the Netherlands, and Cuba.

Regions of land and settlements that are not governed as their own local municipality, but rather are administered as part of larger administrative divisions, such as a township, parish, borough, county, city, canton, state, province, or country.
Straplike elements that encircle moldings, such as those applied to the center or corner of 17th-century frames.
Gardens or landscapes designed for low water maintenance by plant selection, planting techniques, and irrigation systems tolerant of low water input.
Building or other facilities serving as a checkpoint along a roadway for the inspection of vehicular weights, usually limited to checking trucks.

Japanese bridge often found in decorative gardens made from eight narrow wooden planks arranged on supports to form a zigzag pattern. The term is used for all similar Japanese bridges, even if they have greater or fewer planks. The tradition of such bridges comes from the poem Ise Monogatari (The Tales of Ise) in which the story's protagonist and his companions stop to rest at a famous iris marsh traversed by an eight-planked bridge.
Designates multistory apartment or commercial buildings lacking elevators.
Buildings of assembly for Christian religious worship, typically not of ecclesiastical architecture, and especially in reference of meetings of Nonconformists.
A parish church is the principal church of a parish, serving the needs of religious administrative districts called "parishes."
In Indian architecture, a shrine located at the corner of a vimāna; karṇa-prāsāda.
In Indian architecture, a temple-type with openings at cardinals; four-faced; with four openings; caturmukha.

Places where medicines may be prepared on-site, dispensed, and or sold. Pharmacies are often sited within modern drugstores that sell a variety of products, though they may also exist outside of this context.
A building type found in gardens, built in secluded, quiet areas and used for studies or studios. Such buildings are generally enclosed and located deep within the garden.
Small, usually isolated, fortification works of any form, commonly square or polygonal in plan, used to defend a prominent point.
Buildings in which nursing is taught and student nurses are trained
Buildings housing businesses by which small, inexpensive goods of various kinds are sold.
Houses owned by a parish, especially the house used to accommodate the minister or clergy or for the parish poor.

Built works housing businesses that sell tools and other items and products needed for home maintenance and repair, such as hammers, saws, nails, plumbing supplies, paint, insecticides, etc. Originally referred to ironmongery shops, where tools made of iron were sold and often also made.
In Indian architecture, a octagonal śikhara-type.
General term for buildings in which instruction in the various humanities is carried out.

Subsidiary agricultural buildings for cooling, handling, and processing milk. For agricultural buildings for the making and storing of dairy products in general, use "dairies (non-mechanized)" or "dairy plants."
Large rooms where sails are cut out, fabricated, and maintained.

Entrance porches in early basilican churches, and for interior vestibules across the western end of later churches. For narthexlike spaces at the west end of some English and French Romanesque and Gothic churches, often used as chapels, prefer "galilees."
Very large, multipurpose, adaptable structures housing all or most of the functions of a city. For less comprehensive and dominating structures, use "multipurpose buildings."
Underground passages or chambers.
Designated spaces within wineries, breweries, or distilleries where visitors can sample the products made there.
In Indian architecture, a hall for mount/vehicle.
Storage area or structure containing shelves upon which books, boxes, and other materials are stored, such as in a libary, archives, or museum.

Basins or bowls containing holy water at the entrance of a church. The font may be of various forms, either built into the wall, standing on a pedestal, or as a bucket hanging from a fixture. Often richly decorated, they are typically used by worshippers to cross themselves upon entering and exiting the church. The holy water font evolved from the fountain for ablutions that was placed in the center of the atrium of the early Christian basilica, and is still placed there in Eastern rites. Before entering the church, worshippers washed their hands and feet in accordance with a rite derived from Judaism. When the atrium of the Christian basilica was reduced to the proportions of a narrow court or a simple porch, the fountain gave way to a smaller structure.
Series of rough or slightly raised strips of pavement on a highway, intended to slow down the speed of vehicles.
Rooms or areas in a structure that are allocated for storage.
In Indian architecture, a prati-kaṇṭha of a base bearing end-makaras and vyāla figure(s) between.
In Indian architecture, wall base moldings that have a curved shoulder like an inverted pot; vēdībandha’s second moulding in the sequence of five.
In Indian architecture, a pillar-bracket, a member of the capital-complex.
Minor defensive features established outside the principal fortification limits.
Pieces of metal, wood, or other material used to cover joints around doors and windows to prevent drafts and to keep out rain and snow.

Shutters having louvers or slats positioned vertically in a frame rather than horizontally; distinct from "vertical blinds," which have vertical slats or panels, but are typically lighter-weight and attached at the top rather than in a frame.
Deep concave moldings, especially one at the base of a column in classical architecture.
In Indian architecture, a framed niche.

Lankan gouchuang 闌檻鉤窗 (“balustrade bench and railing window”) is a kind of window supported by a balustrade-like series of posts crowned with a built-in bench for leaning or sitting (kanmianban 檻面版, “railing-top plate” or “railing cap”). Outside the window is an ornate railing supported by goose-neck (鵝項 e’xiang (arched)) balusters which are topped with small cloud-shaped brackets (yungong 雲栱) that hold the support rail (xunzhang 尋杖). This is called a “cloud-bracket goose-neck link-railing” (yungong e'xiang goulan 雲栱鵝項鉤闌).  Based on current knowledge, the only extant pre-modern use of this term is in the Yingzao fashi (1103; Li 2009, 7.3b-4b) where it is categorized under xiaomuzuo 小木作 (“small woodwork” or “fine carpentry”). The construction method of the lankan gouchang is recorded in detail in this text, including an accompanying drawing in later chapters (Li 2009, 32.7b).

Walls used jointly by two parties under easement agreement, erected upon a line dividing two parcels of land or between two dwelling units. Walls used jointly by two parties under easement agreement, erected upon a line dividing two parcels of land or between two dwelling units.
Masonry courses which form a continuous plinth.
In Indian architecture, flat ceiling-type.

Meaning literally interrupted or halted mountain (peak) (Kroll 2015, 503, 399), in an architectural context xieshan 歇山 is a form of traditional Chinese gabled roof with four ridges (two per side) framing the gable, above a lower hip roof with an additional four ridges above four corner beams supporting the hip (Qing gongbu 1773, 54.1b). Sometimes it is written as xieshan ding 歇山頂 (anonymous 1644-1911, 29a). The term is first seen in Qing dynasty texts and was only used for palace or other large-scale buildings. In modern research, xieshan also describes a roof form without obvious ridges but with four slopes and two gables in vernacular architecture.
Columns with shafts intertwined as if tied in a knot.
Capitals resembling the crown of a palm tree, the edge of the spreading top being scalloped to suggest the fronds, common in ancient Egyptian architecture.
Consecrated grounds that surround religious sites or places of worship.
Spanning members consisting of straight lintels carried on corbels projecting into the opening and usually cut into hollow curves under the projecting ends.
Building complexes focused on a mausoleum, but also containing other structures; mausoleums are generally large and ornate.

Refers to the work of a school of painters active in Nagasaki from the 17th century through the 19th century. Nagasaki was the only port open to foreigners during the Edo period (1600-1868), and consequently Nagasaki artists painted foreign subjects such as Dutch and Chinese residents of the city, often borrowing European or Chinese stylistic innovations. The style is evident in four main types: woodblock prints; official portraits painted by government artists; Chinese-inspired bird and flower paintings; and individualist work that often employed Western techniques of shading and perspective.

Refers to a style of pottery that is named for the city of Mishima in Shizuoka prefecture, Japan, although it was originally developed in Korea. It is created using a distinctive technique of decorating the ceramic piece with inlaid clays in contrasting colors, then generally covering the piece with a celadon glaze. The name "Mishima" dates from the 17th century, but the style dates to the Koryo Period (935-1392), when it was called "Korai" or "Zogan."

Refers to a Chinese dynastic culture, style, and period dating to 960 to 1279 CE. It was a time of social, economic, and artistic invention and transition; in particular, an unsurpassed refinement was achieved in many of the arts. As society shifted away from being one of aristocrats towards one of meritorious commoners, the ruling class sought to shore up their power. For instance, emperors promoted the painting of themes associated with dynastic legitimacy and stability. The Song emperors were among China's most culturally enlightened rulers and many were even accomplished artists in their own right. Since the Song emperors were less powerful than their Han and Tang predecessors and because they maintained a tenuous peace with their hostile neighbors, the art of this period is introspective. The Song period is best known for landscape painting, although ceramics, sculpture, and architecture also flourished. Clay and wood often replaced stone for sculpture, allowing for softer, more lifelike figures. Song architecture is notably elongated and thin with curved roofs and a distinctive Song spire. Pagodas were first constructed of masonry during this period. There are two divisions within this style and period: Northern Song, dating to 960 to 1127, and Southern Song, dating to 1127 to 1279.
Chinese painting style in monochrome ink, not color.
Refers to the culture and creative output and activity of residents of the United States, of Latin American, or Spanish origin.

Describes elements of the built environment, primarily in newly constructed suburban areas of the United States, characterized by a mix of land uses, spaces and buildings scaled to pedestrians, public green space, and an emphasis on mass transit rather than on automobiles, elements typical of traditional American small towns; popular from the 1980s. For the American planning movement incorporating neotraditional design principles, use "New Urbanism."

Refers to the style and culture of the Secwépemc (also Shuswap), an indigenous, Interior Salish people of present day British Columbia, though their ancestral land stretched from the Rocky Mountains in the east to Fraser River in the west.
Culture of an Algonquian indigenous tribe in the Commonwealth of Virginia, located on land granted to the tribe by an act of the Virginia General Assembly in 1658.

Refers to the culture of the Narragansett, an Algonkian-speaking Indian tribe that occupied most of what is now the state of Rhode Island west of Narragansett Bay. Today, the Narragansett largely live in southern Rhode Island as a federally-recognized tribe.

Refers to the style and culture of the Karuk Tribe, an indigenous people of California, whose ancestral land is located around the Klamath River in Northern California. The Karuk is the second largest tribe in California.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in southern central Tanzania.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a nomadic Berber group living in Mauritania and Mali.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Central African Republic and Democratic Republic of Congo.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Ethiopia.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting northwestern Tanzania.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Kenya.
Styles belonging to Upper Sangha River area cultures.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Democratic Republic of Congo.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northeastern Nigeria.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Cameroon.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name currently inhabiting the Ivory Coast.
Refers to depictions with a point of view from the side of the subject, as contrasted to depictions taken from the back or front. For views of figures taken from the side, use "profiles."
Portraits depicting two or more individuals.
Refers to visual works made of steel. With reference to architecture, use "steel frame construction."
Chemical additive that releases a gas to expand the material by forming closed bubbles; also used to cause a froth, as in detergent or fire-fighting foam.
Masonry, usually brickwork or stone, used as nonstructural fill in the spaces between major wood wall members in timber construction.
Roofing construction

Substances used to optically brighten or whiten materials including textiles and paper, or to give a blue tint to metal, particularly gunmetal. A variety of substances may be used as bluing including many pigments and chemical formulations.

An essential oil derived from steaming the leaves of the Australian tea tree. Tea tree oil is believed to have antibacterial properties and is used as a topical treatment for a variety of skin conditions. It is commonly found in skin products including soaps and lotions. In a conservation context it has been used to control fungi, bacteria, and other biodeteriogens on paper objects and in collection care.

A liquid or semi-liquid preparation obtained by the combination of a solid with a solvent, to form a homogenous mixture of two or more finely divided substances in which the particles are present at a molecular scale.
Sensitized flexible film in cut sizes.

Paper coated with a substance that may be imprinted on a surface by the application of pressure, moisture, or heat and pressure; it often has a backing of glassine paper. In general, it is any type of paper used to transfer an image to another surface.  Examples include decal paper, carbon paper, transfer lithography paper, and transferotype (a special bromide paper with soluble gelatin first made by Kodak in 1888 for transfering photographic emulsions). The term also refers to special papers used in the process of transfer lithography.
Popular drying oil used as a paint medium; hardens over several weeks as components of the oil polymerize to form an insoluble matrix.
An orange pigment comprising a mixture of cadmium yellow and Venetian red.
Fiber made from the inner bark of the mulberry tree, including species Broussonetia papyrifera and others.

Paper made of the pulp of wood. In 1854, a process was patented for the mass production of paper pulp from wood, which was inferior in quality and durability to earlier papers. Paper manufactured before the 1850s was made primarily from bast fibers obtained from linen, flax, rags, or cotton.

Refers to papers made by traditional papermaking traditions of Korea; may be made from a variety of materials, chiefly mulberry bark, but also hemp, bamboo leaves, rice-straw and pine-needles. Korean paper is typically denser than most Chinese paper and is known for its high purity and durability.

A natural inorganic blue pigment with slight red cast made from the ground, separated blue particles (lazurite) from the gemstone lapis lazuli. It has good fade resistance, fair transparency, but poor resistance to acids. It was the most expensive pigment in Western Medieval and Renaissance painting and manuscript illumination, generally reserved for the robe of the Madonna or another prestigious figure. It darkened with age, thus the synthetic variety was developed in the 19th century; blue deposits on the walls of lime kilns had been used earlier to produce a similar pigment, "artificial ultramarine blue."
Resin from true juniper trees, of the genus Juniperus. For the resin of the genera Callitris and Tetraclinis, which is sometimes called "gum juniper," use "sandarac."
Natural dyestuff used to test the acidity of chemical solutions; also used as a textile dye, wood stain, and food colorant.
Wood of the coniferous evergreen Juniperus virginiana species.
Wood from any of various coniferous trees from which pitch or turpentine can be obtained and which yield very resinous wood.

Wood that has been affected by water and fungus, often causing it to be brittle, short-grained, and easily broken. Spalted wood often has a greenish color. It is valued as an unusual material if the wood is still in a good enough state to be workable.

Wood that has undergone a process that uses vacuum and pressure to force chemical preservatives into the wood. The goal of process is to protect the wood from termites or other insects and fungal decay; the wood has been found to contribute to environmental pollution.

General term for wood of any species of evergreen oak native to the U.S., often either Quercus virginiana or Q. agrifolia. The light brown wood of live oak trees is strong and hard, once highly valued by shipbuilders. Now the trees are mainly grown as shade trees.

A flammable, colorless gas with a strong, suffocating odor; first synthesized in 1859, but it occurs naturally in coal and wood smoke, as an outdoor air pollutant in large cities, and found in indoor environments from items such as new particle board, freshly laid carpet, foam, adhesives, insulation, and new fabrics. Formaldehyde is a powerful reducing agent reacts with many materials on contact.
General term for wood of certain species belonging to the genus Shorea native to north Borneo; not true mahogany.
A red marble with large irregular stains of flinty blue that originates from the southeast of France.
Bars, or series of bars, usually across a door, used as a means of pushing a door open.
Pre-cut keys that fit multiple locks.

Preserved information constituting evidence about events, usually documents, collected and maintained by the congregation of a synagogue or community house of worship that serves as a place not only for liturgical services but also for the study of Judaism. Modern synagogue records chronicle the same functions associated with ancient synagogues but may reflect added social, recreational, and philanthropic programs.
Maps showing land or sea bottom relief in terms of height above or below a datum by any method, such as contours, hachures, shading, or tinting.

New impressions of an edition of a printed publication using the same setting-up of type or plates of the original, or articles, chapters, or other portions of previously published larger works, printed separately subsequent to the original publication, usually but not always from the original type or plates.

In bookbinding, labels made of paper or other material, other than leather, different from the book cover material, bearing the book title, often the author(s) name, and sometimes also date and publisher, afixed to the spine or front board. Sometimes such labels were printed on otherwise blank leaves, typically in vertical format, and bound into the book, so that book owners could cut them out and use them. For similar labels made from leather, use "lettering pieces."
Official documents related to the transaction and ownership of property.
Administrative records that document work processes through completion.
Written acknowledgment of the receiving or taking of goods or money delivered or paid.
Elementary books for teaching children to read.
Albums or scrapbooks containing photographs and other momentos of a wedding.
Small, usually rectangular pieces of stiff paper or similar material that carry illustrations and/or text as mementos or souvenirs of a particular occasion, exposition, or location.

General term for committees, offices, departments, or other branches or representatives that exercise powers of governing or government through statutory or other authority. For bodies that administer and manage, but do not  necessarily govern or are not representatives of government, use "administrative bodies."
Collections of people, groups, or nations that join for mutual protection or cooperation, or for another purpose.

People serving a prison sentence following conviction for a criminal offense. For those involuntarily confined in prison or kept in custody, use "prisoners." For those confined to an institutional facility voluntarily or involuntarily, use "inmates."

Persons who have engaged in advanced study and acquired expertise in some special field along with accuracy and skill in investigation and powers of critical analysis in interpretation of such knowledge.
General term for those who engage in research in or practice with a degree of doctor in any of the medical sciences.

Those who have roles in a story or drama. For performing artists playing roles, prefer "actors (performing artists)." For the lead characters in a story or main actors in performing arts, prefer "protagonists."
Authors ol compositions characterized by condensed language chosen for sound and suggestive power as well as meaning.

People who practice the performing arts, such as such as singers, actors, dancers, acrobats, magicians, circus performers, comedians, etc. For persons who make performance art, considered a fine art and often seen in a museum, see "performance artists."
Those whose occupation is to mend household items such as pots or utensils, and normally have no fixed shop, but travel door to door.
Refers to people who enact or create laws, especially members of legislative bodies.

Officials in any of the senior grades of the former imperial Chinese civil service. Mandarins were chosen by examination, and there were nine grades, each of which was distinguished by a distinctive round ornament or button on top of the official headgear.
In South Asia, people having a particular title of high rank, especially a prince.
People who sell or deal in tobacco, which is smoked, chewed, or otherwise ingested, and is derived from the leaf of any of several plants of the genus Nicotiana.
People who pour molten metal for casting.
People who make leather or articles from leather, or who decorate leather.

Those who oversee the art departments on films and television productions, including the design of sets, costumes, lighting, and makeup. For those who oversee the design of sets, costumes, etc. in the theater, use "scenographers."
Persons who engage the professional advice or services of others.
One who works with either a manual or mechanical hammer.
Those whose occupation is the preparation of plans and specifications related to the technology of nuclear fission and fusion, particularly in the context of power generation.
Those who make prints using vitreography.
Gouge-shaped bits for boring holes in wood.
Architects who specialize in the preservation and conservation of historic buildings.
Cutting tools or machines having one or more disc-shaped blades that rotate.
Parts or components of culinary tools.
Bipoint Paleolithic flaked tools, elliptical in shape and pointed at both ends.
Apparatuses for culturing cells and samples in sterile environments.
Portable devices, typically made up of burners and gas containers, used to ignite various materials such as fireplace logs or charcoal briquettes.
Devices that cause explosions.
Instruments that were historically used for measuring the diameter of the sun. In later use, heliometers were used to determine the angular distance between stars.
Tools with a long beak, used in making raised work on metal surfaces by repercussion.
Tongs primarily used by clock- and watchmakers to hold pins, arbors, or other small objects while they are being filed.
Devices used to hold two sections of film or recording tape in proper alignment while they are being spliced together.
Apparatuses for mixing drywall mud and exposed aggregate materials, consisting of two bladed wheels, an upper which cuts the material downward and a lower which cuts it upward.

A movement among French painters of the 1920s and 1930s that manifested in reaction to then current, modern movements such as Surrealism and Cubism. Essentially an attempt to bridge modernism with academicism with an emphasis on normally perceived reality, the movement was unofficially led by Dunoyer de Segonzac. Other artists associated with the movement were Robert Lotiron, Raymond-Jean Legueult, Charles Dufresne and Luc-Albert Moreau. Néo-Réalisme is not connected with the later movement known as Nouveau Réalisme.
Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Mustafa I. He ruled briefly 1617 to 1618 and then was deposed and reinstated from 1622 to 1623.

Refers to the style of European and American architecture and fine and decorative arts between the mid-18th century and the mid-19th century inspired by archaeological discoveries in the Mediterranean and Near East and characterized by the imitation of Greek and Roman forms and motifs.  Also considered a reaction to Rococo opulence, Neoclassical works are often linear, symmetrical, and even severe.

Refers to the 19th century style originating in France and spreading to other parts of Europe, England, and the United States, that revived Rococo forms and motifs in interior design and decorative arts.  Also applied to painting, it describes the work of artists who sought to recapture the lyricism, color, and vibrant surfaces of Rococo artists, particularly of Watteau.

Culture and ethnicity of nomadic, warlike, Asiatic pastoralist people, the Huns, who invaded southeastern Europe ca. 370 CE; through the mid-5th century, they built up an enormous empire reaching into central Europe. Appearing from beyond the Volga River some years after the middle of the 4th century, it is not known whether the Huns were a single people or a confederation of diverse ethnic groups.
The style and culture the originated with the Phocaeans, an ancient Ionian people from the Gulf of Smyrna, Anatolia (now the Gulf of İzmir, Turkey).

Refers to the period in the 8th century BCE during which the Phrygian kingdom flourished in western Anatolia particularly under the rule of king Midas. The art of the period is characterized by a mixture of local traditions and Neo-Hittite inspiration from eastern Anatolia and is known for its monumentality.

Refers to the historical cultures of the region of Western Asia immediately east of the Mediterranean. For the nationality of the modern nation of Syria, use "Syrian (modern)." For a general term referring to the ancient fertile crescent, use "Ancient Syrian."
Refers to the period in Mesopotamia roughly from the founding of the first dynasty of Babylon in 1894 BCE until the Hittite sack of Babylon in 1595 BCE.
Nationality, style, and culture of the area of ancient Erétria, Central Greece.

Refers to the style and period of Middle Angkor surrounding the reign of King Suryavarman II (1113-1150 CE). The style of this period is driven by the expansion of the Angkor empire and the foundation of the exemplar state temple Angkor Wat. Style of sculpture during this period features narrative low relief in continuous narrative sequences that represent passages from Hindu religious and mythical texts, and exhibits the predominant color red as a symbol of veneration. This use of shallow relief ensured the harmonious juxtaposition of the whirling, frenetic figures carved into the frieze and the distinct clean linearity of the architecture. Among the minor relief figures of deities decorating the walls of shrines, the element of sensuality dominates. Sculptural themes reflect narrative finesse, royal ambitions, kingly heroic deeds, and detailed characterization of just and wicked figures achieved through exaggerated proportions and intricate costume attributes.

Refers to the period named for the capital city of Thailand founded by Rama I (1782-1809 CE) in 1782. In architecture, the period is best represented by the various constructions and subsequent renovations in the Grand Palace (Phra Borom Maha Ratchawang) which includes the Amarin Winichai Hall, featuring a T-shaped plan, and the Dusit Maha Prasat Throne Hall (1789), featuring a Latin Cross plan, lacquered and gilded doors and windows, and gilded nine-tiered spires. Temples in this period feature main sanctuaries that house the Palladium of the kingdom and other revered Buddha images, altars depicting the Traiphum or realms of existence, friezes of gilded garuas, ubosots or elongated ordination halls, mother-of-pearl inlaid works, bronze lions, wihans or assembly halls, and multi-tiered roofs. Later in the 19th century, architectural styles reflected European colonial aesthetics. In sculpture and painting, works of this period display scenes from the Ramakien and from Hindu texts.

Refers to a Neolithic style and culture that developed in the Tisza river valley in eastern Europe in the fifth and fourth millennia BCE. It is characterized by an emphasis on fishing and hunting in addition to agriculture, creation of textiles, and distinctive clay figures that are decorated with complex, abstract designs, and are built up like pots, rather than being created through modeling.
Textile styles belonging to Indian cultures.

Refers to the style of Shinto architecture that developed around 300 BCE. The style is characterized by a type of shrine that is rectangular in shape, divided into two parts and constructed of rough unbarked wood. The roof is gabled with each end terminating in two crossed members, and is supported by large round posts.
Coating selected areas of a surface to prevent them from being acted upon, as in etching or screen printing.
Describes the activity of producing and repairing movable objects that support various human activities in in a dwelling, business, or public space.
The process of furnishing a building or other object with new parts or equipment not available at the time of its manufacture.
The rendering of a photographic plate developable by agents other than light such as a resin, metal, volatile liquid, or printing ink; Discovered by English chemist William James Russell in 1897.
