The measurement of light, specifically the intensity of a light source.
Image-making technique that uses smoke as a medium. Paper is held above candle flame and carbon deposits are allowed to collect on the paper, creating a smooth, slick texture.

Refers to a technique of drawing or sculpting in which the subject is directly transferred to the image or replica by comparing the measurements of the two, often with the aid of plumb-lines and calipers.

Process or technique of covering a dried painted surface with a thin coat of a different transparent color, usually in order to modify the tone without mixing. To cover with a transparent varnish for protection, use "varnishing."
Removal of stains from textiles and other materials.
General term for processes and techniques used for construction and assembling.
Watertight reservoirs or tanks that receive sewage and by sedimentation and bacterial action effect a process of clarification and partial purification.
Joints that are joined continuously with the members. An example is metal joints, such as on a bridge, or joints in plumbing.
Special-purpose short-threaded nails each having a large head and usually galvanized or aluminum with a neoprene or plastic washer to aid in fastening roof coverings.
Annular ring nails used for nailing into metal studs to hold gypsum board in drywall construction.
Devices that automatically switch lights off when a space becomes unoccupied or exterior lighting conditions brighten sufficiently.
Door hinges each having one plate surface-mounted onto the door leaf, and the other plate mortised into the jamb; the opposite of half-mortise hinges.
Factory assembled locks, requiring little or no alterations on installation.
Small objects carved in wood, ivory, horn, or sometimes wrought in metal; used as toggles for Japanese kimonos or pouches.

Works executed in the medium of wax (usually bees wax), particularly those representing objects or figures, including life-size effigies of persons, with head, hands, and bust of wax, colored and clothed to look life-like.
Sculpture in the form of a herm but usually depicting the Roman god Terminus; used by the ancient Romans as boundary markers.

Free-standing figures representing deities, most often carved in wood, found in Polynesia, particularly the Hawaiian Islands. The word 'tiki' is commonly used to refer broadly to these figures, but is technically incorrect. Use "Tiki" to refer to the popularization of Polynesian imagery in Post-WWII North American culture, and more specifically to copies of these figures.
Cloaks or capes made of animal skins or pelts; usually implies a cloak that is not a luxury item, for example, not made of mink pelts.
Close-fitting jackets with a standing, Mandarin-style collar.
Sculpture that is relatively small in size, often small enough to be held in the hand.

Goffered headdresses, which, when laid over the top of the head, formed a wide frill. The goffering might only extend to the eartip, but sometimes was carried down as far as the chin. Worn by women during the 14th century.
Plates intended primarily for serving an individual portion of soup, having a shallow well and usually a wide rim.

Drinking glasses having a small bowl and relatively short stem, intended for serving liqueurs, which are strong alcoholic drinks sweetened and flavored with aromatic substances. In a set of matching glasses, a liqueur glass is generally the smallest of the set, smaller than a port glass. While the meaning overlaps with "cordial glasses," cordial glasses typically have a very tall stem proportionally to the size of the small bowl, while liqueur glasses have a short stem. Modern liqueur glasses may lack a stem entirely.
Inserts or inlay surrounding keyholes. For larger plates surrounding keyholes, use "escutcheons (hardware)."
Fiddles of Sweden, known since the 15th century, with keys set in a frame along the neck which players press with the left hand as they bow with the right.
One or more mechanical figures, typically in armor, which strike the hours and sometimes quarters with a club or ax.
Small guitars with four strings and a fretted neck, developed in Hawaii.
Prints made from plaster casts of intaglio plates or the plaster casts themselves.

Circular, flat-sided bases, often made of wood; used in conjunction with gavels to communicate particular actions or to gather attention; accomplished by striking the gavel block with the mallet. Examples of use include court proceedings or auctions.
General term for tables of small size or certain types of stands.

Desks that close by means of a flexible shutter of convex shape and composed of horizontal slats of wood. Distinguished from "tambour desks" which close by means of upright reeded or slatted shutters.
Tables with surfaces adjustable for elevation and angles of incline.
Cabinets for radio receivers, often also having places for related audio accessories, such as record players.
Term used for chests having a base containing two or more drawers.

Tall case pieces generally having seven or more drawers divided by a cornice into two sections with the lower section supported on raised legs. For the equivalent American pieces, use "high chests of drawers."
Articles of furniture consisting of a flat, slablike top supported on one or more legs or supports.

Refers to a simpler type of bed that originated in France in the first half of the 17th century, replacing the massive carved frames of earlier beds. The frame of a lit à housse was a simple cubelike form, broken only by plumed finials at the corners of the tester, and covered entirely in fabric. This type of bed featured a deep valance and four curtains: two wide curtains went from the center of the foot of the bed round the outside of the footposts and to the center of the sides; two narrow curtains went from the bedhead to the center of the sides. Towards the end of the century the lit à housse became more elaborate and taller, although the frame continued to be entirely covered by fabric. Lits à housse are so-called because they resemble a grand state bed with its protective covers.
Large locking cabinets that store many keys securely for a building or institution. These usually have a range of hooks on which the keys are hung in order for ease of retrieval.
Chairs with interwoven splats in the form of interlaced ribbons, such as those popularized by Chippendale and appearing in mid-18th century England and America.

Term generally applied to a variety of chairs with adjustable back heights and sometimes adjustable or revolving seats intended for use while playing a musical instrument. Use "music stools" for similar seating with a revolving or adjustable seat but no back and intended for use while playing the piano or other musical instruments.

From the Latin for "chairs" or "seats," refers to ancient Roman chairs of heavy structure that were derived from the klismos, which is a lighter, more delicate chair developed by the ancient Greeks. For chairs used by bishops in Christian cathedrals, use "cathedrae (bishop's chairs)."
Lamps employing the principle of hydrostatic balance to deliver oil to the wick.
Lamps of any kind lit in recognition of a vow, prayer, or desire.

Lamps for lighting that use LEDs, organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), or light-emitting polymers consisting of semiconductors that convert electricity into light. Solid-state lighting is used in a variety of lighting applications because it is energy-efficient, environmentally friendly, and has longer life. They are also considered durable, intrinsically safe, and ideal for smaller, flexible light fixtures.
Devices used for reducing the brilliance of a light.

Curved swords derived from the sabres used historically by Egyptian Mamluk warriors. In the 19th century, several western armies, such as the French and the British, adopted these. The western version had a similar hilt, but the blade resembled that of contemporary western sabres.

Single-edged knives or short swords used by Saxon and Anglo-Saxon people during the Early Middle Ages. The shape and construction of this weapon varies widely; continental versions have a curved blunt edge while those found in England are straight-backed, with an angled point.
Devices that support or hold tapers.
Bent or curved devices used for suspending or fastening objects or for attaching objects to a surface.
Round pins used to fasten veneers until glue has set.
Paintings created with the medium tempera, which is paint formed of an emulsion of watery and fatty constituents, usually egg-based.

Final drawings from which a structure, object, or work of art is made. For drawings done in developing a work, use "sketches," "studies (visual works)," "preliminary drawings," "preparatory drawings," or "design drawings."

Representational drawings of scenes from the lives of 19th-century Plains Indians, with an emphasis on martial accomplishments. Ledger drawings were so named for the ruled ledger books in which they were often executed; these books were obtained from white soldiers or traders.
Letters on Roman and Byzantine coins indicating the particular workshop of a mint that produced the coins; used from the mid-3rd century to the early 8th century.
Chain lines in the paper that appear to run the wrong way for a particular format, for example, vertical chain lines in a horizontal format.
General term for the period of an early culture dating prior to the introduction of ceramic artifacts.

Used for reference to the regions in and around the Pacific Ocean, largest of the world's oceans and situated between North and South America to the east and Asia and Australasia to the west. For reference to the islands and cultures of this area, excluding the ocean itself, typically prefer "Oceanic (cultures)."
The nationality, culture, or style of Bosnia in southeastern Europe.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Idaho.

Refers to the cultures and styles that existed on the ancient Italian peninsula before the development and expansion of the Roman culture. It includes cultures of numerous tribes who spoke around forty different languages or dialects, and whose cultures varied greatly. The term excludes Greeks who colonized the area, and it generally excludes the Etruscans. In the strictest sense, the term only refers to cultures that spoke Italic languages, including Latin, Faliscan, Osco-Umbrian, South Picene, and Venetic, which are generally held to be Indo-European languages that share many common features, and are distinct from Etruscan and Greek. In some contexts the term includes Etruscans along with other pre-Roman cultures.
Nationality, culture, or style of Martinique Island or the dependency of Martinique, in the eastern Caribbean.
In Indian architecture, six-storeyed structures.

Juzhe, literally “raise" and "bend, bow” (Kroll 2015, 226, 596), is a method of positioning the purlins in relation to each other in order to manipulate the slope and curvature of the roof. In premodern literature, the term juzhe only appears in the Yingzao fashi. According to this text, a building’s juzhe is determined through a process called ding ceyang 定側樣 (deciding the side appearance) or dian caojia 點草架 (designating the rough structural frame). During this process, the roof frame would be drawn on a wall plane at a scale of 1:10 (Li 2009, 5.9b).
Areas of a site that have been landscaped.
Use to designate large rooms that are much longer than they are wide, such as the long galleries of Elizabethan country houses.

In medicine, direct examination of the interior parts of the body by an optical instrument introduced through insertion or ingestion, the endoscope; in conservation, endoscopy may be performed on objects with hollow bodies, such as musical instruments, globes, or mummies.

Frameworks of heavy timbers, steel, or reinforced concrete beams laid longitudinally and crossed by similar members laid on them to spread a heavy load over a larger area; includes similar structures used to distribute a concentrated load over the top of the footing.

A belief system, doctrines, or principles of a group active the late 16th and 17th centuries. It was a religious reform movement that sought to “purify” the Church of England of remnants of the Roman Catholic “popery” that the Puritans claimed had been retained after the religious settlement reached early in the reign of Queen Elizabeth I. Puritanism included varied and sometimes mutually inconsistent forms of belief.
Providing documents, published or unpublished, in hard copy or microform, upon request, either free of charge or for a fee.

Official ceremonial visits to a place by a dignitary, noble, pope, head of state, or other person of authority, often accompanied by a retinue in procession and ceremony, including a formal greeting by dignitaries of the visited location.

An indigenous Korean religion founded by Ch'oe Suun (1824-1864) as an attempt to directly appeal to the religious consciousness of the Korean people. Chondogyo was a reaction against Christianity and the traditional religions of Korea although it nevertheless contains elements of Confucianism, Taoism, Buddhism, shamanism, and Roman Catholicism. After Suun was executed by the government, his successors Ch'oe Si-hyong and Son Piyong-hi fostered the movement until it grew to become a major Korean religion. The Chondogyo scriptures are the writings of the three founders. The religion views humans as bearers of divinity and as such, humans must treat one another 'as God.' Chondogyo stresses the universality of God and calls for a cooperative kingdom of God on earth based on faith, simplicity, steadfastness, and sincerity. There is no concept of eternal reward because the religion's aim is solely to bring righteousness and peace to the world. There are five recommended practices: chanting of a formula every night at nine o'clock; the use of water as a symbol of purity; attending a Sunday worship service; offering rice to the church on a regular basis; and praying in different ways. Chondogyo had an important role in modernizing Korea after 1894. It also opposed Japanese imperialism after 1919 and did not acquiesce to communism in North Korea after 1945. By the late 20th century, there were approximately 3 million members.
Recognizing or establishing someone or something as being a particular person or thing.
In Indian architecture, a loti-formed crowning member.
Designates vertical enclosures in buildings containing a stairway and having a fire endurance rating high enough to qualify as fire escapes.
Games or toys that are played individually or in a group and are intended to transfer mathematical skills.
Process of raising money for nonpersonal, noncommercial purposes, such as for nonprofit organizations or political concerns.

Christian sacrament or ritual consisting of the anointment with oil or chrism, along with other activities such as the sprinkling of holy water, reception of confession, blessings, and recitation of prayer. Originally in the Roman church it was administered by a priest to a person in imminent danger of dying. The modern sacrament is usually called the "sacrament of the sick" or other such name, and is available for all who are seriously ill or elderly, not only those who are at the point of death.

Silent, immobile arrangements of one or more costumed performers, usually staged with appropriate scenery and props, to reproduce a scene from art, drama, literature, history, or the imagination. Enacted in ceremonial, theatrical, festive, or recreational contexts, in public or private, they may be presented on floats, on theatrical stages, such as at the end of an act of a play, or in any suitable private or public space. For the contemporary sculptural works composed of figures and objects arranged into a picturelike scene, use "tableaux (sculpture)."
Those who practice the telling of stories, as a livlihood or a skill.
In Indian architecture, a śākhā-jamb of the door bearing entwined nāga-nāginī pair (occurring in Karṇāṭan temples); śākhā with nāga pattern; jamb with snake pattern; cobra-ornamented śākhā.
Sudden calamitous events producing great material damage, loss, or distress.
The action or state of being two-sided or double-dealing in action or conduct, of acting in two ways at different times, either openly or secretly.
Unwanted or incidental sounds audible in a particular space or area.
The return of light, heat, or sound after striking a surface.

Imagined or real point in space from which a viewer of an art work would look at an object or visual field. Compositions and perspectival systems in works of Western art are often designed with the viewer's point of view in mind. The meaning overlaps with "station point," although "station point" is more often used in reference to perspectival conventions of architectural drawings, while "viewpoint" is used to refer to all art forms.
Uniformly distributed loads over part of or the whole of a length or surface.

The attribute or quality of an object reflecting light to a significant degree, and either giving back an image or reflection, for example as in mirrors, or more diffusely, for example as in desert sand.

The arrangement of elements on a page or other graphic design area, for example, the plan of a publication showing general arrangement of text, illustrations, etc., with indication of type styles and sizes.
Having a semi-circular form like a stylized fan, typically distinguished from "semicircular" shapes by being less regular than a semicircle or by having radiating elements, as the folds of a fan.
Refers to the variant stages of development of graphic and textual works.

The compilation of works of art, crafts, natural history, science, etc., along with associated research, materials, ideas, texts, and other intellectual property gathered around a particular theme and intended for public display. For the public display of such works as an event, prefer "exhibitions (events)." For published catalogs documenting the exhibition and related texts, prefer "exhibition catalogs."
The material property which is measured by the rate at which the stress in a material increases with strain.

Refers in a general sense to a spiritual quest for hidden truth, the goal of which is to be united with the divine. It also refers more specifically to a belief in the existence of important realities beyond perceptual or intellectual understanding that are accessible by subjective experience, such as by intuition or meditation. Forms of mysticism are found in all major religions as well as in secular experience.

Religious ideology based on the belief that God and the universe are ultimately identical, and therefore only the divine is real and sense experience is not. Pantheism is an important element of Hinduism and some schools of Buddhism.
The rate at which the position of something changes. It is a vector quantity, taking into account direction.
Use to refer to the influences of Greek culture as it spread to new areas following the conquests of Alexander the Great; use also for devotion to Greek culture and ideals in any later period.

Any organized body of ideas and attitudes, especially about the structure and working of human society, that comprehends a program of practical political and social action and is more or less institutionalized or shared with others. Originally used for a branch of knowledge dealing with the history and nature of ideas.
Property that is insured for a specific amount.
The sum of a sequentially ordered finite or infinite set of terms.
The management or administration of the money, financial resources, or material resources of a community, a nation, or the world.

Political ideology that advocates a transition to a socialist society, achieved gradually through the democratic process. Originally a form of Marxism, the movement grew out of the formation of the German Social Democratic Worker's Party in 1869, which eventually led to the Social Democratic Party of Germany. Its philosophy evolved and eventually rejected militarism, totalitarianism, and revolution as a means for political change. A main advocate of social democracy was theorist Eduard Bernstein, who parted ways with Marx and Engel, instead positing that democracy must be embraced in order to instill socialist changes. Following the Second World War, several social-democratic governments came to power, including those in West Germany and Sweden.
Real property held and occupied by two or more persons in undivided equal shares with the right of survivorship.

Biological characteristics and physiological traits that distinguish the males and females of a species. For the pattern of attitudes and behavior that in any society is deemed appropriate to one sex rather than another, use "sex role." For the sum of an individual's sexual emotions, ideas, and behavior, use "sexuality."
Clemency and compassion shown to a person who is in a position of powerlessness or subjection, or where severity is merited or expected, usually in giving legal judgment or passing sentence.

The condition whereby a person supplies compulsory labor to another, due to obligation, imprisonment, or another reason. In modern usage, does not include the condition of voluntary employment for domestic servants, whether past or present.
The practice of using a typewriter.

A method for dating fired clay objects, which is based on accurate measurement of the hydroxyl content of fired clays, as well as accurate determination of the chemical kinetics of rehydroxylation or chemical recombination of fired-clay ceramics with environmental moisture.
Lists of words, names, or phrases explaining or giving the value of conventions or symbols used on a map, chart, or other graphic document.
Category of sciences that deal with beings, objects, energy, and processes observable in nature, and with objectively measurable phenomena.

The process of reconstructing an existing object by starting with the final product and working through the design process in the opposite direction. It may involve disassembling and examining and analyzing the object or action in detail to discover the concepts involved in manufacture.

Management of cultural heritage and other protected sites (natural as well as man-made environments) which may include, but is not limited to, securing and maintenance of the site; ensuring its sustainability; outreach, tourism, and education.
The discipline and practice of designing and creating the sets, that is the physical surroundings in which the action takes place, for films, television, or theater.
The techniques or the activity of making spirit photographs.

Public archaeology, known as community archaeology in the UK, aims to engage the public by a wide array of means (books, television presentations, excavations open to visitors, and so forth) in order to share archaeological findings, promote interest in the discipline, and involve the community in archaeological matters that are relevant to them.

Technique of scattering a monochromatic light, such as a laser, changing the vibrational, rotational, or electronic energy of a sample, the results of which help determine its molecular structure. Discovered by Indian physicist Sir Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman (1888-1970).
Documents that are publicly announced or officially declared; especially a public notice by an official of some order, intended action, or state of facts.

Originally used in reference to sailing vessls, now used to refer to the state of people having come from a certain place. One common example of usage is when cataloging biographical information, the term is used to refer to a place where a person resided early in life, when the birth place is unknown or uncertain.
Shallow grooves sawn into the back of the text block near the head and tail to receive cords or the loops of stitches.
Type of woven design in which compartmentalized forms surround a large central floral motif in a diaper pattern that resembles lace or net; popular in England between 1690 and 1730.

Persons who maintain theological or religious opinions that vary from an orthodox doctrine, particularly that of the Christian Church, but also by extension any religious system, considered as established.

Styluses, rods, or wires of metal, usually held in a holder, used as a common tool for drawing. They were used for writing in ancient times. Metal points are typically used on a paper or parchment support, which has been covered by a ground. As the point moves across the ground, it leaves behind a thin layer of metal. The thin metal quickly oxidizes. For example, silver point becomes the brownish grey of tarnished silver and lead point becomes quite dark. Metal points are the predecessors of "pencils."
People or corporate bodies that make coaches, which are  carriages, usually drawn by draft animals.

Triangular gable walls above the horizontal cornice of a classically treated building; also, triangular or roughly triangular elements, sometimes curved, or broken at the center, surmounting porticoes or openings. Common also on furniture, including as bonnet tops.
Synthetic rubber made by the copolymerization of two compounds (one being butadiene) and a catalyst (sodium).
Boxed kits containing a range of pre-selected paint colors, typically designed for novice painters who want to mix myriad hues with minimal expenditure.

Decorative motif in the form of a carved or painted floral pattern, square in shape, employed in Gothic architecture. The fleuron was also used for decorative borders and to embellish frames, and as a decorative element at the center of each face of the Corinthian abacus. It is also employed on furniture. For printers' type ornaments, use "printer's flower."
Any wall facings over less durable or attractive substances or constructions.
In Indian architecture, a decorative band showing leafy vine motif.
In Indian architecture, an elephant’s palate; cusped ceiling-course; decorative motif of ceiling.
Establishments that specialize in making clay pottery, such as earthen pots or vessels.
Sources intended primarily for consultation that pertain to heraldry.

Generally meaning the state of being of mixed origin. In a social or cultural context, refers to the concept of individual or group self-identity or creative activity deriving from the interaction of two different societies or cultures, often within the context of Third World people encountering Western or Westernized people, or the formerly colonized meeting the colonizers.
A broad designation of mechanical and/or electrically powered devices used to decorate or assemble textiles.
Finely abrasive cloth manufactured by sprinkling powdered emery or aluminum oxide onto a thin cloth coated with glue and used either wet or dry for polishing metallic surfaces.
Implements of flat plastic, wood, or other material, made in a great number of triangular shapes and sizes; used as guides for drawing lines at various angles.
General term for adzes used in woodworking.
Refers to a white lead-glazed 'faïence fine' introduced by Jacques Chambrette at Lunéville in 1748 and there used unglazed for biscuit figures and groups and as a pipe clay.
The customs and course of living as to food and ways of feeding.

Refers to a Christian millenarian sect that arose in 1747 in England out of a group of radical Quakers that had adopted the French Camisards' ritual practices of shaking, shouting, dancing, whirling, and singing in tongues; the sect was later spread to the United States by Ann Lee and her disciples. The sect advocates communal living, productive labor, and celibacy. Shaker communities in the United States flourished economically and created a distinctive and influential style of architecture, furniture, and handicraft before the sect declined in the late 19th and 20th centuries. Shaker dances and songs are also admired as folk art and the Shakers are responsible for numerous important inventions.
Copying from an original by drawing over it onto a transparent or translucent piece of paper, cloth, or other material.
People who practice healing by the use of herbs.
Those who believe in or practice humanism.
Ancient pottery that is solid red in color, has a satiny gloss, and comes from Rome, the Near East, or Greece. To refer specifically to Roman red gloss ware, use "terra sigillata ware."
The reverent love and allegiance accorded a deity, idol, or sacred object, often expressed through ceremonies, prayers, or other religious rituals.
Place or state of extreme or eternal suffering, usually inflicted as punishment upon the wicked or the nonbelieving, common to many belief systems.
Lists or records of subscriptions and subscribers.
Photographic prints made by the platinum process.
African masks in the form of an elongated vertical plank, positioned in front of the masker's face, and projecting upwards. Worn in Burkina Faso among the Gurunsi, Mossi, Bwa, and others.
Small printed works consisting of one small-sized leaf of paper folded and not stitched or bound, containing printed matter, chiefly for gratuitous distribution.
Small-scale charts of the world designed to show the legal time on land.
References from one part of a book, catalog, file, or other document to another part where the same or related topic is discussed or recorded.
Discharging people from an institution, enterprise, or obligation.
Modifier describing a color of light intensity and light value; may be overlapping in meaning with the modifier "light," although typically "pale" suggests less intensity than "light."
In computing, collections of related records stored in digital form for use by a computer and able to be processed by it.
Motion pictures whose length is relatively short in comparison to feature films; they may range between a few minutes to one hour but 30 minutes is typical.
Photographs that have been altered through interference in the optical or chemical procedures, or physically altered, as for example, sewn, marked on, or torn.
Describes objects, structures, or spaces, or portions thereof, located to the left of an observer facing in the same direction as the object or space specified.

Type of bobbin lace made in Paris from the 18th century onwards. This firm lace, not fit for gathering, is characterized by its hexagonal mesh, which is formed by intertwining triangles. The pattern consists mostly of flowers, leaves or vines or occasionally animal figures.

Photographic processes in which the light-sensitive salt is formed in the fibers of the paper rather than in a binder. Sometimes designed to be developed out, as in the calotype process, and sometimes printed out, as when making salted paper prints.

A term referring to an artmaking practice or trend coined in the early 1990s. Context Art highlights the interaction between artists and social situations, and the formal, social, and ideological conditions of the artist's production, in contrast to the functions of traditional art. The term "Kontext-Kunst" was introduced by the Austrian curator Peter Weibel in an exhibition of the same name.
Bodies of water serving as ways or routes for travel or transportation.
Officially allowing a conditional release from prison.
Disseminating information to the public about some product, company, institution, individual, cause, or project.
Enclosed spaces with pens, stables, and sheds, where beef cattle are confined for fattening prior to market; usually associated with a railroad line.
That which evokes an awareness or feeling of deep revulsion or painfully disturbs a previously accepted aesthetic ideal. Can be considered as culturally defined or as an individual reaction.

Plan of a building or city that is arranged to most conveniently accommodate the flow of traffic, activities, or work that goes on inside it, instead of along an axis or radiating from a central point.

Refers to distinctive, rural fortified dwellings of relatively modest size; particularly, but not exclusively, those dating from the 13th century and later in northern Europe. These "stone houses" were typically owned by local minor lords or land holders; they were usually made of stone. Do not use this term to indicate common houses made of the material stone; instead, use material = "stone (worked rock)" plus work type = "house."
Structures marking or denoting burial sites.
In Indian architecture, a makara-bearing band in a base (in decorated Hoysaḷanāḍu temples).
Temporary structures roofed with branches and adorned with fruits or vegetables, built near a house or synagogue, and used as dining or living areas during the Jewish festival of Sukkot.
The seat of a patriarch, the capital of his area of jurisdiction.
Designates residential communities designed around golf courses.
Thin, flat, circular objects of any material.
Nationality, culture, and style of the city of Lucca in northwest Tuscany.
Solvent that has been treated or mixed with oxygen.
Fitted sleeves or covers worn on the forearm to protect a shirt sleeve.
Waterproof outer layers that are worn over an absorbent cloth diaper. These usually have the appearance of brief-style underwear.
Generally, any garment or costume accessory that supports; use especially for bands and similar devices, usually of elastic or cotton webbing, worn to support a part of the body.
Cases attached to belts or harnesses that support the poles of flags or banners while being carried in procession.
Ankle-length tunics worn by women in ancient Egypt; fringed at the hem and usually held with a girdle.
Voluminous squares of cloth draped around the body and worn by women of ancient Rome.

Utensils or devices used to retain or hold back solid pieces or particles while a liquid passes through. For bowl-shaped or conical devices with perforated or pierced walls used to drain or strain foods use "colanders."
Devices used to hold menu cards upright and visible to diners.
A majuscule book hand developed in the 1st century CE, having condensed letters with pronounced shading and prominent serifs.
Components of certain musical instruments, such as xylophones, musical bows, and lutes, which reinforce the tone by sympathetic vibration and impart much of its characteristic quality.
Protective garments often used as armor, in the form of a shirt, covering the torso and made of mail, which is metal fabric consisting of iron or steel rings riveted or pressed together.
Gold coins of the Roman and Byzantine periods from the early 4th until the 11th century.
Venetian large, silver coins issued from 1202 until the mid-15th century and valued as multiples of denari; later imitated throughout Europe as, for example, groats, gros tournoi, and groschen.
Traditional chants of the Maori culture of New Zealand.
Books containing the rites of the Latin church for the administration of the sacraments by parish priests.
Devices, usually of sheet metal, for cutting shaped forms for cookies, such as circles or stars, from rolled dough.

Flat-bottomed, metal pans with a long, straight handle and a cover intended primarily for cooking. Also, pans with vertical, bulging, or ogee-shaped sides and often a pouring lip used, for example, for making sauces, melting butter, or the like; generally of brass or copper; sometimes of silver when intended primarily for use as a serving receptacle.
Possessions or assets wthat confer prestige or are acquired as a symbol of high social standing or wealth.
Any of various utensils used in popping corn.

Large bowls, usually made of silver, ceramic, or glass, in which a beverage, such as punch or lemonade, is prepared and served. They are frequently accompanied by a ladle and sometimes a set of punch cups.
Bags of relatively small to medium size, closed at the mouth by drawing tight a thong or drawstrings.
Vessels to contain honey, usually glass, ceramic, or wooden, usually lidded.
Flat boards with raised rims used to carry and display small items used in food service.

Drinking vessels consisting of a wide flat or shallow bowl supported on a stem with a central knop, made with or without handles and rarely with a cover; used especially with reference to 16th-century forms. For dishlike vessels set on a high stem and used for serving food or drink, use "salvers."
Long, narrow, flexible strips of linen, steel, or wire-woven cloth graduated to measure distances and often stored coiled in a protective casing into which they can be rewound after use.
Cylindrical containers used in ancient Rome to hold papyrus rolls.

Vessels made from materials such as stone, glass, or clay used to store ointments and oils. Ancient Egyptian ointment vessels were often lavishly decorated or shaped as delicate animals or young women, symbolizing rebirth or regeneration.
Small bags, often with multiple compartments designed to carry small personal items.
Projections by which an object may be held or supported; may have a small opening for a suspensory strap.

Instruments for gauging the purity of milk, such as for ascertaining the comparative value of each cow's milk in a dairy. The instrument is made of glass with a weighted bulb at the end and a graduated stem at the top. If the milk sample is pure, the lactometer floats on it and if it is adulterated or impure, the lactometer sinks. It is often used with instruments to determine the percentage of butterfat in milk, "butyrometers."
Devices for measurement between two opposite surfaces.
Time-keeping devices designed for travel. These are often compact and have a folding or clamshell design so that they can be closed and stowed safely.
Vessels containing the hot water, also called zeon, that is poured into the chalice of communion wine during some celebrations of Christian mass, particularly the Rite of Constantinople.

Refers to the space allowed for each line of type on typewriters, typesetters, printers, or other devices not involving metal type. For the extra spacing between lines of metal type, use "leading (spacing)."

Receptacles used in religious contexts that are considered in essence the dwelling-place of the deity, intended literally or symbolically. In Christian contexts, tabernacles often have an architectural character and are located near the high altar of a church, set into the wall or free-standing; their purpose is to hold the consecrated Host. The term is derived from Latin, meaning a small dwelling.

Sacred gourds used in Luba villages in Central Africa by diviners to hold natural or manmade objects that are used in divination ceremonies. Distinct from "mboko (sculpture)", which are carved wooden figures of a woman carrying a bowl, used by the Luba people in ceremonies pertaining to divination or to the transfer of power.
Russian boat-shaped drinking vessels with a long handle at one end; possibly also used as ladles.
Refers to the style and culture of modern Kuwait.
Strips of paper or cloth, bound in a book and used to attach leaves or plates, or used to repair or reinforce the folds of gatherings.
Deep cylindrical basket made of palm leaves in postclassic central Mexico.

Late Neolithic Chinese jade or stone tubes having a squared exterior surface and a round, hollow interior. They are usually decorated at the corners with facial features, sometimes abbreviated to concentric circles or eye-like shapes, and embellished with incised horizontal bars on the planar surfaces. An ancient Chinese text called 'The Rites of Zhou' states that the cong was used as a sacrifice to the earth. Symbolic meaning may be a counterpart to that of the "bi (ceremonial object)," which represented the heavens. Similar vessels may date to later periods.
Coins that are impossible to identify and hardly recognizable due to wear or poor preservation, except by their shape.
Describes ceramic or objects of ceramic fashioned from a mixture of clay and crushed shell.
The action of scattering seed for the purpose of producing a crop or other plant cultivation.
In Indian architecture, a demigod figure, placed on top of the śikhara (Orissa).
Works or parts of works made with wood, especially such work used in the construction of buildings and other structures.
Works of art submitted by the artist to an academy for approval as part of the requirements for admission to membership.
Persian flat-woven rugs of blue and white cotton used as inexpensive floor coverings.
In Indian art and architecture, figures representing female celestial minstrels.

Soldiers from Switzerland, now exclusively used by the Vatican to guard the Pope, and the college of cardinals. Originally the soldiers were mercenaries used to guard various monarchs, and their most familiar uniforms were designed by Michelangelo during the Renaissance.
A burden carried on the shoulders.

A chemical compound; in conservation, a chelating agent of ammonium salt of citric acid used in solution for surface cleaning of paper, paintings, and other materials. May also be used as a buffering agent, preservative, and food additive.

Faintly raised lines that form at the joints between mold sections when a molten material or slurry is poured into a mold. Seam lines are found on plaster or wax casts as well as on bronzes cast in piece molds. In ancient Chinese bronzes, some seam lines were exaggerated and integrated into the design of the casts. The term also refers to the line along which the pieces of a refractorypiece mold join, which is the locus of the line that forms on a bronze. Depending on how well the piece mold pieces fit together, the seam line may be more or less raised. More extreme flashing occurs with ill-fitting pieces.

Small ancient Egyptian figures of stone, wood, or clay that were placed in tombs, often in large numbers, for the purpose of serving the deceased in the afterlife. The term is derived from ancient Egyptian and is usually translated as "answerer." During the New Kingdom (1539-1075 BCE) the figures were made to resemble the tomb owner by being fashioned in the form of a mummy bearing the owner's name.
Women whose occupation is the washing and ironing of clothes and linen.
Small holes, usually round and finished along the edge, as in cloth or leather for the passage of a lace or cord or as in embroidery for ornamental effect.
Wide straps that run over the back and under the belly of a horse or other animal to keep blankets or packs in place.
A substance or preparation that destroys or masks odor.
Athletes trained or engaged in the competitive sport of wrestling.
Regions in one country that are controlled by another country or power. An example of a historical controlled region was when the Dutch controlled Taiwan in the 17th century.
Hammers used to chip, pound, or otherwise work stone or masonry; may include automated hammers or hand held hammers.

In bookbinding, the process of shaping the back of a text block into a convex arc, as by light hammering or by putting it through a rounding or rounding and backing machine, before the block is cased-in; usually performed at the same time or just prior to backing.
Territories that have historical, geographical, or political special status within or outside a primary political entity; the special status may be established by treaty.
Objects that are made by humans rather than being natural. Used primarily in the context of distinguishing man-made objects from natural objects.

Designs created by pouring colored sands, powdered pigments from minerals or crystals, or pigments from other natural or synthetic sources onto a surface to make a fixed or unfixed image. They are often made on the ground or the floor rather than on a separate support. Unfixed sand paintings are created or used in religious and healing rituals by various groups, including Navajo, Pueblo, and Zuni in North America, Australian Aborigines, Tibetans, Japanese, and Hindus in various nations. Sand paintings may be fixed, often with works of relatively small size for sale to the tourist trade.
The bones of ritually killed animals, carved with script and used in ancient China for divination.
Principalities for which genealogical inheritance has been replaced by succession of a religious office.

Fine, lustrous, soft, sheer cloth originating in the Philippines, woven from piña fibers, from the pineapple plant. It is used for decorative handkerchiefs, trimmings, lingerie, accessories, and home furnishings.
Any woven figured textile produced on a Jacquard loom.
Ottoman textile material incorporating metal‑wrapped thread into a lampas, or multiweave fabric.

Marking the surface of an object by applying pressure with a tool, for example, transferring an ink mark to paper or embossing soft clay; also, applying preprinted labels such as postage stamps that substitute for official stamped marks. In bookbinding, distinguished from "blocking", in which pressure is applied by a machine.
The process or condition of making or having hollows or impressions in a surface, such as by a blow with a sharp or edged instrument.
Refers to the process of combining together separate constituents to form one cohesive substance or mass.
Removal of gum or gummy substance from a material, deglutination. In textile conservation, refers specifically to removal of sericin from  raw silk by various methods.
Process or action of setting, hardening, solidifying.

Wheeled, often collapsible, chairlike carriages designed primarily for pushing small children able to sit upright. For wheeled carriagelike or wagonlike conveyances used primarily to push or pull infants, prefer "baby carriages."
Transmission of energy, in the form of heat, sound, or electricity, through a conductor.
Use to describe a design or part of one, as on coins, that is rendered in intaglio rather than in relief.

The element to which a calculation is directed in an equation or ratio of size, dimensions, or other contexts. An example is in an equation of numeric scale, the right side of the equation is the target, 3/4 inch = 1 foot. For the left side of the equation, use "base (relationship indicator)."
In Indian architecture, a with thee planes of offsets in plan and elevation.

Refers to the resolution capability of electronic imaging devices such as computer monitors, digital cameras, televisions, or scanners, expressed as the number of pixels per linear distance (pixels per inch or pixels per centimeter). Pixel density can also describe the resolution of image files.
Characteristics and qualities of form.
Made of a liquid other than water or pertaining to an activity alternative to one that otherwise employs water: for example, nonaqueous cleaning.
Medium-sized end-blown straight brass trumpetlike aerophones of Tibet, of conical bore, used in pairs in Buddhist rituals.

Zitherlike plucked chordophones with metal strings raised above the fingerboard on a steel nut; the strings are stopped by the pressure of a steel bar held in the player's hand, which slides along the strings creating a wavering or glissando effect.
Dolls having heads, and sometimes neck, arms, feet, or body, made of porcelain, whether glazed or unglazed (bisque).
Two-string plucked lutelike chordophones of the Hausa people of Nigeria.
Documents distributed to the public by sale or other transfer of ownership, or by rental, lease, or lending.
Small objects backed with a pin, displaying images or text that advocate for a cause or person, usually affixed to clothing.
Use to describe things transported by or communicated by water.

Dresses with a tight bodice and a sack-back consisting of two box pleats, popular in the 18th century. These can be attached at the shoulders and hang freely to the ground or be stitched down on each side of the back seam from the neckline to the waist of the full skirt. Typically worn with a fichu.

A naturally occurring red colorant derived from any of several lichens. It was widely used in antiquity for textile dyeing. Orcein is the essential constituent of archil and is used as a biological stain.

A water-soluble polymer, commonly known as carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), composed of the sodium salt of modified cellulose. A viscous gel when dispersed in water at low concentrations, CMC forms a tough, non-soluble film in reaction with heavy metal salts. In conservation, it is used as an adhesive and as a poultice for cleaning stone.

Books or other document forms containing the Book of Psalms, which is composed of 150 psalms of the Old Testament. A psalter is usually divided into sections to be recited daily at Matins and Sunday Vespers, used as a liturgical book for the clergy in the Divine Office (forming the basis for the Breviary) or by the laity for private devotions. In addition to the psalms, psalters generally contain an ecclesiastical calendar, canticles, creeds, and the litany of the saints. King David and his court musicians were traditionally considered to be the authors of the psalms; the subjects of the psalms have to do with hymns in praise of God and pleas for help and mercy. In the Christian tradition, the psalms were interpreted with the Lord of the Old Testament understood to be Christ the Messiah. Various passages of individual psalms were seen as Christian metaphors and prefigurations. The Hebrew text of the psalms reached the Latin West by way of translations made by St. Jerome in the 4th century AD, two from the Greek version (the Septuagint) and one directly from the original language. The three versions, known respectively as the Roman, Gallican, and Hebrew Psalters. The psalter was one of the most frequently illustrated medieval texts in the West, beginning around 725 and flourishing between the 12th and 14th centuries. The text was often enhanced with precious ornament and images; however, psalms did not readily lend themselves to literal illustration, in contrast to the narrative portions of the bible. Consequently, their illustration was varied, both in format and in iconography. Most illuminated psalters were illustrated with decorated or historiated initials at the main divisions of the text.
Navy blue, knitted caps worn in inclement weather by seamen in the U.S. Navy.
Shoes which have pieces of leather sewn across the insteps, usually in a contrasting color.

Low, light, semi-open, four-wheeled carriages with an open perch in front for the driver and a seat for two passengers covered with a folding or half hood; developed in the second half of the 19th century and used mainly as park carriages. By extension, may also be used for semi-open touring automobiles with a folding top covering only the rear seat.
Woven or knitted caps that are relatively simple in structure, without a rim or visor; are often colorful, comprising woven designs.
Instruments which measure and indicate the rate of climb or descent of an aircraft.
Denotes any wooden support for the rigging of a vessel, including the booms, gaffs, masts, and yards.
Carts having three rather than two wheels.
Rear flaps of a man's coat, such as on a tail coat, cutaway, or the like.

Shirts or longer garments made of haircloth, which is a stiff, unsupple fabric. Hairshirts were worn next to the skin, sometimes under other clothing, by ascetics and penitents of several religions. They were also worn by certain ancient troops, to make them tougher.

Helmets widely used in Europe during the period of Roman domination, having a hemispherical, slightly bulbous skull topped by a small knob, and cheekpieces hinged to the sides and tied under the chin. Originating in Gaul, they were adopted by the Romans in the 6th century BCE.
Toys consisting of a toy gun in combination with one or more targets.
Articles of costume worn about the neck.
Bindings that permit the withdrawal and insertion of pages at any desired position by means of rings, posts, cords, or other type of fastener securing the margins of the individual leaves.

Bindings of a style originating in Paris in the 16th century having a design of interlaced ribbons, defined by a double line on one side and a single one on the other, which divide the cover into symmetrical compartments that are sometimes filled with gold tooling.
Toys comprising a icosidodecahedron structure (a type of polyhedron) that resembles a geodesic dome; it can be folded to a fraction of its extended form via scissor-like actions of its joints.

An inorganic compound used in the form of a white crystalline powder used variously as an antioxidant, a disinfectant, and a preservative in foods. In a conservation context, it has been used for removing rust stains from paper.
Specially designed circular metal rings, usually with one surface rounded and the other surface flat, tossed in the game of quoits. Based on the ancient throwing weapom, "cakras (weapons)."
Close-fitting straight-cut skirts, usually with the hemline at or below the knee.
Calf-length trousers worn by women and girls, originally worn while bicycling.
Liturgical shawls or sashes worn as a superhumeral over the shoulders, similar in form to a pallium.
Exposed bifurcated garments which extend from waist or hips to the ankle or sometimes to the knee or just below.
Labels for an information unit in a data system that is meant to be read by the end user.
Enterprises where scientific experiments or other research, testing, and investigations happen in a space equipped to facilitate these activities.
Libraries formed by the collections of individuals rather than as a public institution and often devoted to a particular subject or interest.
Museums dealing with the sea in general, navigation, or shipping, as distinct from "naval museums," which deal with navies, warships, or ships in general.
A range of colors resembling variations of yellow pigment.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of green colors.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of purple colors.
A range of colors resembling variations of pink pigment.
A range of purplish red colors resembling the color of magenta or fuchsine dye, which is a snynthetic aniline dye.
A range of yellow or greenish yellow colors resembling the color of the fruit of the lemon tree or any of several pigments called "lemon yellow."
Various colors ranging from a yellowish white to a slightly bluish medium gray, resembling the lustrous color of a pearl, which is an animal material that forms in the shells of certain mollusks.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.
A range of reddish brown colors resembling the color of Spanish red oxide pigment, which is an inexpensive colorant containing red iron oxide.
Refers to a range of yellowish greens resembling the color of the lime, the fruit of a tropical citrus tree.
Variable orange colors resembling the color of sandarac resin.

A generic style, particularly in the context of clothing fashion and interior design, characterized by harking back to a former style that is nostalgically retrospective, particularly styles from the mid-20th century. Differing from "old-fashioned" in not being antiquated in form or character, but having reference to a previous style that is both not from as distant a time as "old-fashioned" and is still considered desirable and popular.
Range of greenish gray or bluish gray colors, resembling the color of the ash-blue chemical product of copper and lime-water.

Suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of cat-like carnivorans, including cats, hyenas, mongooses, civets, and related taxa. Feliformia stands in contrast to the other suborder of Carnivora, Caniformia, dog-like carnivorans.
Members of an order of insects containing sawflies, wasps, bees, and ants.
Regarding personal names, assumed names used by authors rather than their real names.
General term referring to a large number of birds, most in Galliformes or Anseriformes orders, including the duck, chicken, turkey, pheasant, and many others.
Privately run schools with programs organized as an alternative to traditional public or private schools, usually with a highly flexible or voluntaristic framework.
In Indian architecture, a lateral porch of a maṇḍapa/ hall.
Groups of planets, meteors, or other objects that orbit one or more large stars.
Treeless areas located in forests.
Chinese bronze ritual vessels of rectangular shape, with lids, used to store food. This shape appeared during the late Western Zhou period.
A set of shared application programming interface (API’s) specifications that allows for the parsing and sharing of digital images and presentation metadata across the Web.
Narrow channels, such as branches of streams.
Ancient order of marsupial mammals containing one living species.
Genus of one African species.

Proofs designated for the printer who produces an edition of prints, occasionally marked P.P. Sometimes the same as the bon a tirer proof for the edition. Printers' proofs are generally identical to impressions of the regular edition except for annotations identifying them as a proof. They can also be used as galley or page proofs on which printers and typographers can make queries and corrections for the client or artist to check, mark, and return; for this use such proofs are usually stamped "MASTER PROOF" or "MARKED SET."

Japanese marbled paper created using the ancient technique of suminagashi, literally ‘ink dropped in water’; in which inks mixed with pine resin are dropped onto a bath of water in the marbling tray, and gently manipulated into a pattern then transferred to a sheet of plain paper.
Book size having height dimension of approximately 50 inches.
Christian holiday celebrated on celebrated on May 31 (earlier on July 2), recognizing the pregnant Blessed Virgin Mary visiting her cousin, Elizabeth, who was pregnant with John the Baptist.

Flat, parallel embroidery stitches worked on a ground fabric to fill a motif, and that imitates the shiny appearance of satin. It is the simplest of all embroidery stitches, but requires skill in uniformity and keeping the stitches flat and even to imitate the appearance of satin.
In Indian architecture, a octagonal pillar-type.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in southwestern Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Côte d'Ivoire.
Having the form or outline of a half of an ellipse that is bisected by one of its diameters.
Genre comprising accounts of travel presented as film, video, or illustrated lectures; usually with narration, intended to give information about and an overall impression of places visited.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting the Ubangi River region.
The style and culture of an East African tribe living between Lake Rudolph and the Nile.
Style and culture of the group of African peoples referred to by that collective name living in Burkina Faso between the Black Volta and the Red Volta  rivers.

Contemporary artists who create outdoor paintings, drawings, or three-dimensional works on walls, sidewalks, or street surfaces in public thoroughfares, sometimes intended to draw attention to urban issues. The term may also refer to anyone routinely creating works outdoors, for example painters who are set up on sidewalks to paint canvases or tatoo artists who decorate customers on sidewalks.
Style and culture of the nation of Dijbouti.
Businesses that employ engineers, who apply technical, scientific and mathematical principles to the design of structures, machines, and the like.
Food material made by emulsifying vegetable oils or animal fats with water or milk, originally as a butter substitute, used as a spread and as a cooking fat.
The joints between the fore- and the upper arm of humans or animals. For the similar joint on legs, use "knees (animal or human components."

Modern looms designed to draw the weft from a stationary supply through the warp yarn by means of projectiles, rapiers, or water/air jets, rather than traditional shuttles. Without the use of shuttles, these looms do not utilize the pirn winding process thus reducing manufacturing costs and auxiliary operations while increasing filling insertion speeds. Patened in 1928 by Rudolf Rossman, the shuttleless loom plays an important role in adjusting fabric structures, reducing fabric defets, improving fabric quality, and reducing machinery noises.

Phylum having members that are characterized by a hard, spiny covering or skin. Echinoderms have existed since the Lower Cambrian Period, and today comprise about extant 7,000 species that fall into five well-defined groups: Crinoidea (sea lilies and feather stars), Ophiuroidea (basket stars and brittle stars), Asteroidea (starfishes), Echinoidea (sea urchins, sand dollars, and sea biscuits), and Holothuroidea (sea cucumbers). In the 19th century, Echinodermata was recognized as a distinct group of animals that was occasionally associated with the cnidarians and selected other phyla in a division of the animal kingdom known as the Radiata, however the concept of the superphylum Radiata is no longer valid. Marine invertebrate animals of radially symmetrical structure, having a body wall stiffened by calcareous pieces that may protrude as spines, and tiny hydraulically-operated tube-feet.
Small tool having a sharp, pointed edge for unpicking sewn stitches.
Instruments for probing parts of the body. These are usually long and slender and have a slightly enlarged end. Similar in structure and purpose as a catheter.

Cylindrical vessels, typically made of metal such as lead, copper, or iron, used to facilitate the application of color to textile materials. The fabrics to be dyed are placed in the vessel and wet thoroughly with warm water before the colored dye is applied to create a dye bath. These vessels are often large in size to allow fibre bundles to be stock dyed, and are sometimes fitted with racks on which textile materials are hung while submerged in the dye bath.
A colorless, non-combustible gas which hydrolyzes when exposed to air. It is used to catalyze chemical reactions in industry, and as a detector of slow neutrons in radiation measurement.

Style of textiles, particularly floor coverings and prayer rugs, made in or associated with Mudjar, a village near Kirsehir in central Turkey. The rugs are characterizsed by usually having a deep border, an arch motif, and similar to desings of medieval stained-glass windows of European churches. The characteristic design in older examples, from the 19th century, is a prayer niche with a stepped arch crowned by a little turret form that is echoed in the crenellations of a narrow cross panel above. The niche is soft red, pale yellow, or green and may contain a skeleton tree or be perfectly plain except for an edging of small triangular indentations. The green spandrels (spaces between the exterior curves of the arch and the enclosing right angle) display stylized ewers. The broad stripe of the border is composed of varicoloured, carefully detailed squares, reminiscent of tilework, and the soft-blue inner stripe has a diamond pattern.
Parts or components of visual works.
Systems used for conveying rainwater, surface water, condensate, cooling water, or similar liquid wastes, exclusive of sewage or industrial waste, to the storm sewer or other legal place of disposal.
Playing a musical instrument by striking it with the hand or a stick.
Groupings into which items are divided to be sold or for another purpose.
Small ornament of shiny metal or plastic in any shape, but usually round, and having a hole in the middle for use in fastening to clothing to create decorative effects.
For art information, a brief statement indicating how the work came into the current or an earlier collection or how it came to be on view at the repository.
Devices for removing, by means of agitators and sieves, the flour that may cling to bran after it has passed the bolting-mill.
A broad category of small wares, especially cheap, useful articles, specifically for haberdashery or sewing; buttons, hooks, ribbon, and thread.

Mechanized devices designed to facilitate maximum shrink-resistance in woolen cloth by exposing the material to a steam atmosphere under controlled pressure. These devices are comprised of hot cylindrical drums around which the woolen cloth is continuously wound with minimum tension while being rotated and sprayed with atomized steam or hot water. Through this process, these devices ensure that the woolen materials experience maximum shrinkage thus preventing further shrinkage during subsequent processing and wearing.

Devices used to dry lettuce leaves and other fruits or vegetables using centrifugal force. These consist of colanders that fit inside a larger container with a lid; the lid contains a mechanism that turns the colander.
Machines that use rollers to express oils from oil-containing seeds.
Instruments for dividing straight or curved lines into smaller regular sections.
Devices for sterilizing milk cans using steam and boiling water.
Pumps that enable taking water from a source and depositing it into one or many receptacles based on timing, flow, or other measured parameters such as rainfall, water quality, etc.
Meaning "carved [it]," in printmaking indicates the one who engraved the plate or carved the wood block.
Instruments that allow the dentist to simulate the relationship of the temporomandibular joint with the jaws.

Devices, typically comprising a metal rotating framework with measured dimensions, used for both measuring the warp required to weave textile materials and marking the beginning/end of the warp thread to facilitate the weaving process.
Promises by one party to make a gift or gifts to another party at some future time. To be legally enforceable, a promised gift requires three elements: donative intent, delivery, and acceptance.

Titles or names of works that are written, stamped, or printed on the work. For works of art, it may include any part of an inscription that is clearly intended by the creator or publisher to serve as a title or that the cataloging institution wishes to record as a title. For manuscript or book cataloging, it is the title on the title page or found elsewhere in the book.
Identifying numeric or alpha codes found, usually on the spine, of a manuscript, book or other volume, giving the location where the item can be found in the library.
Events for relaxation and rest.
The standard unit of currency of the Eurozone, comprising member states of the European Union.
Refers to the variety of Spanish spoken in Puerto Rico, largely derived from Canarian Spanish and Andalusian Spanish.

The internationally most widely used civil calendar, named for Pope Gregory XIII, who introduced it in October 1582. It is typically used as a proleptic calendar, which means the dates are extended backward to dates preceding its official introduction in 1582. The Gregorian calendar was a refinement to the Julian calendar, correcting the length of the year by 0.002% through alteration of leap years.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 385-400 and 409-431; founded by people of Xianbei ethnicity.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 13,999 to 13,000 (or 14,000 to 13,001) Before Common Era.
Awls used to make holes in leather, typically to facilitate sewing.

Dances in which the participants move in a circular fashion; examples are folk dances in which the dancers form a circle, and ballroom dances in which couples move in circles round the ballroom, such as a waltz or polka.
Aromatic beverage prepared from selected dried leaves and buds of the tea plant, by infusion in hot water. For similar beverages made from various other plants and herbs, use "herbal tea."
United Nations scheme for Romanization of geographical names from Arabic letters to the Latin alphabet.
Instruments for transmitting sound by means of light, especially those invented by Alexander Graham Bell and Sumner Tainter in 1880.
Branches of canyons or valleys on the sea floor.

Artists who create artworks to be displayed or incorporated into public areas, having the purpose of beautifying and enriching public places, whether or not the works are also functional. The term is often reserved for use in modern contexts.

Hellenistic pottery, usually vessels such as cups, bowls, or lamp feeders, decorated with distinctive relief designs. The ware originated in Cales, Caserta, Italy. It is characterized by reliefs that imitate metal work, often taken from molds that copied contemporary Hellenistic and earlier prototypes. In other cases reliefs are appliqué work that has been applied to black-glazed vases of various shapes.
Artists who create collages, which are mixed media works in two dimensions or very low relief, made by gluing paper, fabrics, photographs, or other materials onto a flat surface.
Languages characterized by the existence of people still living who learned the language as a first language.
Those who specialize in creating embellishments, adornments, or ornamentation.

Cultures of several Latin peoples from what is now Romania, Moldova, and the southern Balkan Peninsula, south and west of the Danube River; the term was used by Germanic people to distinguish the Roman descendants from the indigenous people in this area.
The act or posture of falling or resting on one's knees.
The action of asking questions, typically in a pointed or aggressive manner.
Spirits or deities who inhabit the forest.
Order of flowering plants; some systems place families in this order within Gentianales order instead.
In Greek mythology and elsewhere, beings having human form but of superhuman stature, found frequently in mythic or pseudo-historical traditions and in romantic fiction.

A barrier film composed of a polymer matrix to which copper particles are bonded which blocks contaminants, ozone, bacteria, and corrosive gasses from passing through. It is used for protection and long term storage of a wide variety of metal artifacts.

Species of medium-sized oak tree native to lowland wetlands in the southeastern United States, from Delaware and southern Illinois south to northern Florida and southeast Texas. The common name refers to the acorn almost completely enclosed by the cup or its scale. The Latin name comes from the shape of the leaves, which resemble a lyre.
Genus of grasses containing five species.
Deities associated with, or personifications of, the planets, sun or other stars, or the moon.

Genus containing 100 to 600 species of medium-size trees, shrubs and lianas; the number of species classified here varies with the authority. The genus is native to tropical Central and South America, Africa, Madagascar, and southern Asia.

Species of large evergreen tree, growing to 20-55 m tall, native to Europe and western Asia. Its name, "black pine," is derived from the somber appearance created by dark green, sharp, rigid, rather long needles and deeply fissured bark. It is widely cultivated as an ornamental.
Extremely simplified form of the brilliant cut, used mostly for small diamonds. 8 facets surround the table and 8 facets form the pavilion.

Mirayon (the “flying fish festival”) of the Tao people begins on the first day of the month of Paneb. It involves nocturnal fishing carried out by large boats manned by six up to ten people. Every male member who can walk independently in the Tao society should come to the beach to attend the fish-summoning ritual. The first flying fish caught in Mirayon should be treated with procedures as follows: in Mirayon, as crews of every boat live together in panlagan, a communal house used during the month of Paneb, the family of one of the crews whose house contains more than three doors is to be chosen to cook the fish in their hearth; and the flesh of the first-caught fish should be shared by all of the fishing crews and members of the family in charge of cooking the fish.

Cultures and styles of the Truku people lived in Taiwan. The Truku people primarily reside in the Xiulin Township and Wanrong Township in Hualien County. It used to be perceived as identical to the Atayal people because of the kinship between their language and culture. However, considerable difference exists in these fields, leading up to Truku’s official recognition in 2004. The everyday praxis of Truku culture centers on the utux belief and the regulations set up by gaya.
A broad term used for a variety of non-binary sexual expressions of individual indigenous North American people. More specific terms are unique to language groups.

Projecting equipment that consists of a lens, an objective, and an illumination source that varies depending on the location where the apparatus will be used. The light source can be an oil lamp, acetylene, gas, limelight, incandescent light, arc lamp, or electric.
General term for decorative materials added to furniture, such as braids or tassels.
General term for lamps used in ceremonial or religious contexts.
Equipment comprising of a visor or goggles and a mask covering the nose; held in place by a headband. Used for diving, usually in conjunction with a breathing tube.

General term for wood of several species belonging to the genus Melanorrhoea, native to Borneo. It is not a true rosewood. It is deep-red in color with light and dark streaks and has a close texture suitable for carving.
A coarse, variegated marble from Hawkins County, Tennessee. It is dark chocolate brown or red in color with white streaks and masses throughout and it usually contains some fossils.
A white marble with a bluish tinge from the island of Thasos in the Aegean Sea; it has a compact texture and sparkling crystals.

A colorless or yellowish, fuming, caustic, corrosive, water-soluble liquid, HNO3, having powerful oxidizing properties, usually obtained from ammonia or from Chile saltpeter. It is used cheifly in the manufacture of explosives and fertilizers.

The most common barium mineral, barium sulfate (BaSO4), occurring in hydrothermal ore veins containing lead and silver, in sedimentary rocks such as limestone, in clay deposits formed by the weathering of limestone, in marine deposits, and in cavities in igneous rock in Spain, Germany, and in the southern Appalachian, central states, and California in the United States. It commonly forms as large tubular crystals, as rosettelike aggregates of those crystals, or as divergent plates known as crested barite. It is abundant. Ground barite is used in oil and gas well drilling muds, in the preparation of barium compounds, as a body or filler for paper, cloth, and phonograph records, as a base for white pigment, and as an inert body in colored paints.
A highly refined glass, usually a flint glass of special composition, or made from rock crystal, used for lenses and prisms.

Pure metallic element having symbol Li and atomic number 3; a soft, silver-white metal, the lightest element in the alkali metal series. It is obtained from minerals, such as spodumene, in which it occurs or as a byproduct of potash and borax. Use also for this metal as processed and formed for use as a heat transfer medium in nuclear reactors or as a strengthener in alloys and many manufactured products such as ceramics and glass. Its salt is used in psychiatric medications.
A brick, one side of which is beveled.
Powdered glass that is colored deep blue by oxide of cobalt. After cooling, the glass is finely pulverized for use as a pigment or for brightening whites in laundry.
Glassware with facets, grooves, and depressions produced by cutting with a rotating wheel of metal or stone.

Brownish-black crystals or powder, insoluble in water, synthesized by the oxidation of amorphous Cr(OH)3 with oxygen. Developed as rod-like particles for thin film deposition as magnetic recording material, and as a catalyst. Chromium dioxide is no longer widely used because of high production costs and toxicity.
Decorative motifs based on the hexagonal crystal formation of snowflakes.
Crosses with an X or several crossed lines placed over the point where the two bars of the cross intersect, symbolizing rays of light or a star.
Communities designed to provide telecomunications services for to people working at home, often including state-of-the-art techonolgy and located in rural areas.

Gardens, originally in Japan, comprising an outdoor space in which natural materials such as rocks, gravel, sand are arranged in lines and patterns, creating a serene environment designed to assist meditation.
In Indian architecture, a triple shrine, three-shrined temple.
Buildings having no windows.

Muslim places of worship. Public mosques consist of an area reserved for communal prayers, frequently in a domed building with a minaret, and with a niche (mihrab) or other structure indicating the direction of Mecca. There may also be a platform for preaching (minbar), and an adjacent courtyard in which water is provided for the obligatory ablutions before prayer. Since representations of the human form are forbidden, decoration is geometric or based on Arabic calligraphy.
Churches associated with a priory, which is a religious house ranking immediately below abbeys and presided over by a prior or prioress.
In Indian architecture, a rectangular miniature shrine.
Public urinals partly screened and located for easy access, usually at curbside; found in some European countries.
Small, earthwork fortifications in the form of an entrenched earthen rectangle, square, or pentagon that were used mostly in Northern Europe from the late middle ages until the 19th century.
Buildings housing educational institutions that focus entirely or partially on religious instruction and theology.
Buildings belonging to or used by members of professional, fraternal, or trades organizations.
Buildings housing businesses that sell home furnishings, carpets, draperies, or a variety of other goods to be used in the home.
In Indian architecture, a octagonal śikhara-type (South India).
Facilities designed to convey or control the flow of water, including channels, bridges, dams, and other such constructions.
Agricultural buildings designed to reduce labor, automate, and improve efficiency in milking cows. Several different designs are in use, but all parlors follow key components of milking procedures.
Rooms off the kitchen for storing and washing dishes and food.
Rooms in monasteries or convents where visitors may be received.
Buildings that physically illustrate their name or function in their plan or elevation, for example a dairy stand shaped like a milk bottle.
Rooms furnished for the use of persons waiting, as in railroad stations or medical offices.
An open, single-story hall often seen in gardens, generally built at minor scenic spots.

Stone basins with a drain, generally set near the sacristy, often in a niche. The piscina was used for the celebrant's ablutions and for washing the sacred vessels during the Mass. Piscinae drain into the ground, and some have a small upper shelf that serves as a credence. For pools in Roman or Medieval homes or public sites, use "piscinae (pools)."
Benches, signs, light fixtures, and receptacles provided as part of the design of a road.
In Indian architecture, a fillet with lotus-leaf pattern.
Slanted moldings, as in a pediment.

Yixinggong 異形栱 literally means “irregularly-shaped bracket arm,” and are different from regular arch-shaped bracket arms (gong 栱), the ends of which support small bearing blocks (dou 斗), as defined in the Yingzao fashi. Homophonous with “wing-shaped bracket arms” (yixinggong 翼形栱), the use of irregular (異 yi) instead of wing (翼 yi) was first seen in 1955 and became more widespread after 1978, but usage was not consistent in all sources.
