Plain knit fabric formed with knit and purl sides, usually referring to fine machine-knitted fabric generally. This type of knit was originally a staple industry of the British isle of Jersey.

Tapestry-woven textile of silk, or of silk and metal thread, woven in a pictorial design, commonly used for Chinese textiles. The term means "cut silk," referring to the visual illusion that is created by distinct, unblended areas of color resembling cut threads. The earliest surviving examples date from the Tang dynasty (618-907); it was popular during China's Southern Song period (1127-1279), and from the Ming period (1368-1644) through the end of the Qing dynasty in 1912. The kesi technique was often used to copy famous paintings.

Pendant trimming, decoration, or garment, comprising loose strands. Before the 20th century, usually a wooden mold covered with strands of silk or worsted; now often merely a bunch of threads, cords, or other strands gathered together at the top.
A description or quotation regarding the merit or significance of a particular work.
Grinders used to mill and process bran.
Tools used for embroidery or rug making that create a field of tightly-packed loops of thread or yarn on a woven fabric substrate.

Mechanized devices designed to process and condense large quantities of wool or other fiberous materials into felt material at high speeds. To automate the work of needle felting, the device exposes fiberous materials to a needle board or multineedle holder into which a large number of barbed needles are fixed. The needles rapidly move up and down so that they poke the fiberous materials and catch the scales of the fibers. This needling action interlocks and tangles the fibers to form a compacted felt fabric.
Devices used to dry wet lettuce leaves, consisting of a wire vessel with handles. Lettuce leaves are placed inside the vessel and shaken to remove water.
Machines or devices that are components of a milk cooling tank that removes heat from milk.
Devices for determining the amount of oil contained in any substance, or for the degree of purity of an oil.
Toys or sets where a ball has to be hit with rackets. Unlike professional sports equipment, this is marketed in all shapes and colors for recreational use.
Bands or small rings attached to teeth and used to secure or adjust during orthodontics, or otherwise to position dental work in the mouth.

Long, flat pieces of wood, ivory, iron or other durable materials, typically carved to a short point at the top and sometimes equipped with an arrowhead-like tip, used to beat the weft and secure it into place. When the batten is passed behind the warp, the entire set of warp strands is separated and prepared to receive the woof. This device is commonly associated with warp-weighted looms, traditional upright looms, backstrap looms, and several bone weaving tools. Traditionally carved with illustrations of creation myths, divination, marriages, conquest, and royal descent, these devices have long been used by Indigenous peoples in the Americas who imbued them with diestic, ritual, and spiritual meanings. The devices have also been discovered in the cemetaries and other archaeological remains of the Anglo-Saxons, dating to the early Middle Ages.
Method of acquiring property by payment of funds.
Titles or names that were originally assigned to a work or assigned soon after its creation. It may refer to a former title or to a title that has been translated.

Gatherings of people wearing masks, disguises, or costumes, often of an elaborate or fantastic nature; activities often include dancing. In Western cultures they tend to be simply recreational, while in others, notably African, they are important ceremonies.

Historical standard unit of currency of Florence, Italy, represented by a gold coin struck from 1252 to 1533, having 72 grains of nominally pure or 'fine' gold (3.5 grams, 0.1125 troy ounce). Since Florentine banks were international enterprises, the Florentine florin was the dominant currency of Western Europe for large-scale transactions for many years.
Refers to varieties of Spanish spoken in Venezuela.
General term for any of several luni-sidereal calendars traditionally used in Hinduism.
Culture, style, and period of a state of the Sixteen Kingdoms, flourished 407-431; founded by the Tiefu tribe.
Identifying numbers associated with the sequence of pages in books or other documents.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 399 to 300 (or 400 to 301) Before Common Era.
Hammers used as a handtool for leathercraft. Of varied design, but often with a slightly convex face on the hammerhead that helps prevent marring leather.
General term for dances intended to be performed by groups or couples for communal or recreational purposes.
Refers to several liquors made from a fermented mash of cereal grain; distilled chiefly from matted barley in Ireland, Scotland and in the British Isles; and from corn and maize in the US.
Instruments that allow changing the directionality of sound for analysis of the localization of sound.
Zones of irregular topography on the sea floor, which include ridges, escarpments, or troughs.
Artists with no formal training.

Hellenistic pottery characterized by very sumptuous decoration, combining plastic ornamentation with painted decoration in a technique where white slip covers the surface and design is added in tempera colors. It is named after the town of Canosa, Apulia, Italy.

Artists who work in the genre of conceptual art, which is the genre of art in which the ideas or concepts that a work expresses or refers to are considered to be its defining characteristic, and the finished material result, if it exists at all, is regarded primarily as a form of documentation rather than as the art work.

Languages made up of a mixture of elements from two or more languages, usually when one has been substantially influenced by another language. An example is English having been influenced by Norman French.
People who design representations that symbolize and suggest other objects or ideas, particularly popular as an occupation and hobby in Europe from the 15th through 17th centuries.
Human behavior that involves making the spontaneous sounds and movements of the face and body usual in expressing joy, mirth, or amusement.

The activity of putting to death, depriving of life, slaying, or slaughtering a living thing. Originally implied personal agency, often with violence or the use of a weapon, but later usage extends to ending life by any means or cause, including an accident, over-work, grief, drink, a disease, etc.
In Indian architecture, a flying celestial figure; angel; divinized warrior; angelic figure (possessing magical powers); flying (or gliding) semi-divine.
Measurements of length equal to 0.001 inch or 0.0254 mm. Specifically used for measuring thickness of materials.

Order containing 8 families, 151 genera, and about 1,000 species of flowering plants. All the families in Santalales are parasitic to some degree, attaching either to the roots or branches of their hosts. Members have a cosmopolitan distribution, but are most heavily concentrated in tropical and subtropical regions.
Mythical female beings having snakes for hair, and whose look turned the beholder into stone.

A registered trademark for a series of products made from a patented plastic barrier film. It is composed of a polymer matrix to which copper particles are bonded forming a reactive film that neutralizes all corrosive gases from passing through, neutralizes contaminants, blocks ozone and retards bacteria production. In conservation, can also be used to slow the degradation of cellulose acetate.

Species of white oak timber tree native to North America, found in eastern and midwestern United States and south-central Canada. It is also called "mossy-cup oak" for its heavily fringed acorn cups. It is a popular ornamental and shade tree in urban areas because of its resistance to insect and fungal attack, drought, and air pollution. Previously common in oak savannas and prairies, the tree is well adapted to fire with its corky, fire-resistant bark.
In Indian art architecture, a male Jaina presiding deity.
Genus containing around 12 species of locust trees.

Species of evergreen tree having long, tufted foliage and a tall, columnar trunk up to 35 m in height, found along the coastal plain of the southern U.S. from Texas to Virginia and Florida. The species is a principal source of turpentine, kraft paper, paperboard, and book paper made in the United States. The hard, stiff, durable lumber was also used for ships, boxes, flooring, heavy construction, and millwork.
Institutions that curate a collection of books, periodicals, and other materials, organized to provide physical, bibliographic, and intellectual access by the public or members of a group.
Libraries that are available to the public and typically maintained by public funds, as distinguished from libraries available only to a certain group or individual.
Museums of collections of weapons, armor, uniforms, ammunition, documents, maps, photographs, and other records and artifacts of military forces, leaders, wars, and battles.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of green colors.
A range of colors resembling variations of purple pigment.
A range of red colors resembling the color of the synthetic iron oxide pigment known as "Mars red."
A range of dark yellow colors resembling the color of the synthetic iron oxide pigment known as "Mars yellow."
A range of medium to dark bluish gray, greenish gray, and purplish gray colors resembling the color of slate, a metamorphic rock.

A gem or diamond cut style with a squared table, bordered by four long narrow facets that are step cut in the shape of equal isosceles trapezoids. When there are several rows of steps and the corners are chamfered, use emerald cut.

Palamal is a Sakizaya ritual that worships the Sakizaya ancestors and commemorates the historical trauma of Takubuwan Incident. In 1878, under the aegis of the policy of “opening up the mountains and civilizing the savages,” the Qing army entered eastern Taiwan and waged battles with the Sakizaya and Kavalan peoples who then dominated the Qilai plain in Hualien. During the invasion the Sakizaya chief Komod Pazik and his wife Icep Kanasaw were tortured to death and the Sakizaya people was set into a diaspora.In 2006, the Sakizaya people held a memorial ceremony at what used to be the site of Takubuwan tribe in Hualien city. “Fire,” as the ceremony pamphlet describes, “brought down the people, but also lit up the way out for the refugees.” The memorial thus held fire as its central theme and consecrated the chief and his wife as the lord and lady of fire who are the national heroes of Sakizaya.

Cultures and styles of the Tsou people lived in Taiwan. The Tsou people primarily reside in Alishan Township, Chiayi County; some of them can also be found in Xinyi Township, Nantou County. The Tsou people are historically known as Cou, and they are famous for Mayasvi, a festival honoring the war god. There are two kinds of Tsou tribes, hosa and denohiyu; hosa ranks higher than denohiyu and the former possesses kuba (“main hall”) as the symbol of its power. The Tsou society is patriarchic and the basic social unit is family.
Small bags of varied material, usually with a drawstring opening used to store tobacco before use.
Decorative elements added to furniture components.
General term for plaques intended for religious contexts.
Footwear used by divers to protect their feet. Generally made of waterproof materials; earlier examples were made of metal and leather.
Things used in the sport or entertainment of tossing and catching or manipulating objects in the air and/or keeping them in constant motion.

Strong fiber obtained from leaf stems of the species Musa textilis, native to the Philippines. Not related to true hemp. It was exported to Europe and elsewhere in the 19th century and is now cultivated in Central America. Fibers are lustrous and range in color from cream to light purple, brown, or black, varying in texture from silky to stiff. It is used for rope, especially in marine environments since it is buoyant and does not swell in water. Coarser fibers are used for heavy cordage, twine, hats, hammocks, manila paper, and tissue paper. Fine, glossy fibers are used for carpets, tablecloths, placemats, purses, rugs, and clothing. Waste fibers are used for papers with high wet strength, such as tea bags.
Wood in the state of small particles, detached from a tree, plank, etc. in the process of sawing.

Gum exudation of small evergreens native to the Mediterranean countries, soluble in both alcohol and turpentine; used for artists' paint and coating lacquer. Mastic varnish becomes yellow and brittle with age. Mastic was used in 16th and 17th century recipes for oil-resin varnishes; in the 19th century, mastic was a popular clear, glossy spirit varnish for oil paintings and was also used as an additive in oil medium. By the 20th century, its use was superseded by dammar.
A yellow natural dyestuff obtained from several East Indian mulberry trees and shrubs of the genus Morinda.
A compact close-grained fragrant yellowish wood that is yielded by trees in the genus Santalum, typically used for its essential oil.
Wood of the Pinus serotina, found in the wetlands of the southern United States, and is a valuable as a heavy, resinous wood used for lumber or pulpwood.
Flexible slender branches, stems, or twigs used for tying, binding, or weaving, especially in wickerwork, basketry, or to construct furniture such as chairs.
Wood of the species Quercus garryana, native to the western coast of North America, particularly common in the Willamette Valley. It has a compact texture and a straight grain.

Carbohydrate containing exudates obtained from some trees or shrubs belonging to the family Fabaceae of the pea order Fabales. Gum is insoluble in alcohol and either soluble or swellable in water. Some plant gums are used in the form of water solutions in the manufacture of cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and foods; when the water evaporates, a film having a considerable adhesive character is formed. Some gums, such as gum arabic, dissolve in water to give clear solutions. Other gums, such as gum tragacanth, form mucilages by the absorption of large amounts of water. May be distinguished from "resin" in that gum hardens in drying, but is usually soluble in water.

Dense, pale yellow wood from trees of the genus Buxus. Although difficult to carve, the wood has excellent dimensional stability and is very wear resistant. The hard, fine-grain wood is often used for printing blocks, rulers, mallets, architects scales, slide rules, modeling tools, musical instruments, engravings, inlays, small decorative items, and game pieces.
A fine-grained white marble from Vermont that is highly valued by sculptors; it may contain bluish-gray veins or clouds.

A coarse-textured white marble that is nearly pure calcium carbonate; it was used to build the first 152 feet of the Washington Monument in Washington, DC. It is quarried in Texas, Maryland, not in the state of Texas.

Any of a class of complex organic acids found in chromosomes of cells and viruses that store genetic information or translates the instructions inscribed in this information to the cell’s protein manufacturing sites. The two chief types of nucleic acid are DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid ) and RNA (ribonucleic acid).

A rare lead compound, a transparent to pale white mineral in the monoclinic system. It was first identified in the lead-antimony vein at the southwestern end of Bounds Cliff, Cornwall by Cornish mineral collector Richard A. Barstow. It has also been found as a corrosion product on lead artifacts.

Clear silicate glass that will form permanent three-dimensional color photographic images when subjected to x-rays or ultraviolet light through a negative. Photosensitive glass contains submicroscopic metallic particles; the high energy causes the particles to precipitate out of solution. The image is fixed by heating the glass to 540 C.

Pure metallic element having the symbol Mg and atomic number 12; the lightest metal that is stable under ordinary conditions, silvery white in color. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials.
A building stone or brick of special shape to be used at an oblique corner.
Refers to any of various green to brown silicate glass materials formed when a meteorite impact melts the local rock.

Flat pane glass characterized by straight ripples. Is made by an an ancient technique of blowing a large glass bubble and swinging it on a blow-pipe to form a long bottle, then cutting off both hemispherical ends. The resulting cylinder is then cut lengthwise and reheated after which it is flattened by a wooden plane or by being allowed to sink to a flat state. Traditionally, it was characterized by a great variability of texture, color, and thickness, though it is more regular when produced by modern methods. Cylinder glass largely replaced crown glass when the process of making it was mechanized.

Naturally occurring sediments that are produced by chemical actions resulting during the weathering of rocks. Clays are composed of hydrated aluminum silicates, such as Kaolinite, Illite, Palygorskite, Attapulgite, Bentonite, and Montmorillonite. Small amounts of other minerals can change the color (white, yellow, brown or red) and texture of the clays. Clays may include all earths that form a paste with water and harden when heated.
A mixture of lime and water with shell, gravel, or stone which, when dry, is as hard as rock; used as a building material.
In Indian architecture, a distinctively detailed vertical foliage pattern (decorative motif); coconut tree.
Crosses with arms having split and spayed terminations, resembling the arms of a traditional ship's anchor.

Motifs comprising circular representations of the points of the compass, often including both true and magnetic directions. Typically seen on maps and navigational charts; originally used to assist mariners in navigation, now most commonly decorative in nature.
In Indian architecture, a triple shrine; three-shrined temple.

Multistoried shrine-like towers of stone, brick, or wood, usually associated with a Buddhist temple complex and often crowned by hemispherical or bulbous stupa. A pagoda may comprise open stories of balconies or enclosed floors, generally of diminishing size from bottom to top, often capped with corbeled cornices and pent roofs; this form is seen particularly in Japan. The pagoda derives from the stupa of ancient India, which was a dome-shaped commemorative monument, usually erected over the remains or relics of a holy man or king.

Refuge churches are Protestant churches in Protestant areas in close proximity to recatholicized areas of Silesia. After the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) in the 17th and 18th centuries, they served not only the local population of the Protestant religion but also the faithful from abroad who did not have religious freedom in their territories.

Domestic shrines found in Roman homes, dedicated to the house gods, the Lares and the Penates. Its form varied greatly, from a simple wooden cabinet to a richly decorated miniature chapel. Found most often in the atrium.
Places that provide seclusion for the purposes of rest and relaxation, or for prayer and meditation, especially for religious groups.

Defensive barriers of stakes, piles, or other timber and often including loopholes for gun fire, placed across entrenchments and redoubts, a harbor or river, or around a building, village, or another area in need of fortification.

Buildings that house schools where equitation is taught; usually including an arena, seating, and housing for horses and equipment. For schools training horses, use "manèges."  For complexes offering training, board, and care, use "equestrian centers."

Structures that originated in Greek architecture, comprising freestanding colonnades or covered walkways, or long open buildings with the roof supported by one or more rows of columns parallel to the rear wall. Stoas surrounded marketplaces and sanctuaries, forming places of business and public promenade. Rooms could back onto the colonnade, and a second story was sometimes added. A famous example of a stoa was the great hall at Athens, which was adorned with frescoes of the battle of Marathon, and in which Zeno lectured, giving the name to his disciples, "Stoics."
Buildings housing businesses that deal in hose and frame-knitted or woven underclothing generally.

General term that groups all structures built for the purpose of industry. For buildings or groups of buildings intended to house the machinery and activities associated with modern industry and machine manufacture that arose after the Industrial Revolution, beginning in the mid-19th century, use "industrial buildings."
Agricultural buildings equipped with kilns for drying hops, typically circular in plan, with a conical roof and commonly found in Kent, England.

Rooms designed or used for sewing, which is the process of creating or mending clothing or other works by joining or decorating cloth, leather, or other flexible materials with thread by means of a needle. Sewing rooms may be furnished for hand sewing or machine sewing.
That part in the eastern arm of a church between the choir and the sanctuary, usually reserved for the clergy.
Circular columnar buildings that are roofed but have no cella.
In Japanese samurai or domestic architecture, a sitting room. If it features a raised floor, prefer 'jodan-no-ma.'
Rooms set apart for the storing of goods or supplies in a home, public building, or ship.

Elevated stands enclosed by a guardrail and a platform on which to rest a book, intended for clergy to preach to the congregation; usually situated within a church and may be fixed or movable (movable pulpit). It often has a staircase, a backboard, and a sounding-board.
Paved or planted islands in roadways designed to guide the flow of traffic.
In Indian architecture, cyma-fillet.
In Indian architecture, a minor sub-plinth moulding.

Yixinggong 翼形栱, which cannot be found in Chinese literature until 1930s, is a term coined by Liang Sicheng that combines yixing 翼形 (literally, wing-shaped (Hanyu dacidian, online; Kroll 2015, 551) and gong 栱 to refer to the wing-shaped brackets in Tang, Liao, and Song architecture. In terms of shape, yixinggong 翼形栱 is based on actual examples which were referred to as yixinggong 翼形栱 by Liang Sicheng. In terms of function, the two ends of yixinggong 翼形栱 do not support a bearing block and would therefore be considered more decorative than structural. With the publication of Liang Sicheng's investigation reports on Song, Liao, and Jin architecture in the Journal of the Society for the Study of Chinese Architecture (Zhongguo Yingzao xueshe huikan 中國營造學社彙刊) between 1932 and 1935, the term yixinggong 翼形栱 was used repeatedly and it gradually became a term with a much clearer definition which was adopted by other scholars. It is important to note that the consensus reached by later architectural historians about the meaning of yixinggong differs from Liang Sicheng's use of the term. The discrepancy mainly lies in different understandings of what is meant by “wing-shaped” (yixing). Prior to 1979, the term yixinggong 翼形栱 (“wing-shaped bracket arm”) was applied to all irregularly-shaped brackets. Now some scholars also use yixinggong 異形栱 (“irregularly shaped bracket arm”) instead; see yixinggong 異形栱.

The strongest and securist parts of Japanese castles, these tower-like structures were constructed both within other buildings and free-standing and were sometimes located within an inner compound called a "honmaru". They could exist alone or connected to other structures of the same type. For these types of fortification structures in western European castles, use "keeps".
In Indian architecture, an altar; group of wall mouldings (above the adhisthana); plank-moulding below the grīvā-śikhara.
In Indian architecture, a niche at the central-most face of the bhadra.

Windows formed by pieces of glass set into lead cames. While the glass may be colored, uncolored, or clear, the more specific "stained-glass windows" is typically used for windows in which all or most of the glass is colored.
In Indian architecture, a vertical salient flanking the bhadra-salient in the composition of śikhara.
In Indian architecture, a figure-bearing band; rūpadhārā; figural string-course.
Stucco ceilings consist of a layer of plaster or other mortar arranged on a ceiling or vault as a decorative whole.

Literally meaning “solid” or “rigid” mountain peak, yingshan is a technical term used to describe a traditional Chinese gable roof, in which the eaves of the gable are flush with the surface of the wall, in contrast to one where the eaves extend past the wall plane on the gable end (see xuanshan). The term yingshan first appeared in the literature of the Qing dynasty. In the narrowest sense, yingshan refers to a roof that has front and rear slopes, in which the purlins are sealed within the walls of the gable ends (Liang 2006, 84; Yao 1986, 40). More broadly, yingshan is regularly used to refer to a gable roof in which the top of the gable ends extend to the eaves tiles or, in some cases, can even extend above the level of the roof.
In Indian architecture, a mixed type; composite or polymorphic pillar-type, combining forms from square to polygonal to circular.
Capitals representing the heads and necks of animals, human heads or mythological creatures.

Fortified sanctuaries used as a refuge in times of war, situated on hilltops in eastern Kenya among the Mijikenda and related peoples. Many kayas are regarded as sacred sites. a primary division of a building’s elevation
Semicircular arches in which the rise is less than half the span.

Complexes of buildings comprising the permanent establishment of a Christian missionary post or station. Buildings may include the central church, structures for the housing of the friars or other personnell, kitchen, storage, barns, surrounding grounds, and possibly other buildings.
Sets or kits or implements used for dissecting biological specimens. These contents of these vary, but usually include scissors, forceps, and scalpels.
Magnetometers that record the direction and strength of the earth’s magnetic field.
Small anvils used for the working of thin sheet metal, so called because they are supported by a sharp vertical prop which is inserted into a hole in the workbench.
Pieces of rigid material with central holes cut into them through which lenses may be mounted and attached to large format view or process cameras, enlargers, or other optical devices.
Large tubs or vats used for mixing a material, such as plaster or cement.
Style of the 19th century provincial art movement in Britain.

Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the regin of Murad IV, who ruled from 1623 to 1640. The illustration of the poem "Pashaname" (1630), executed in vivid, cartoon-like miniature, was completed during his regin. Murad IV built two kioks at Topkapi to commemorate his capture of Erivan in 1635, and Baghdad in 1638.

Style of painting resulting from the technique of pointillism, which uses dots or short dashes of unmixed color to create images. Some scholars make a distinction between pointilism as a technique only, not using the term to designate the style per se of the Pointillist painters.

General term for art and architecture inspired by Venetian styles, which themselves encompass a cross-section of Byzantine, Venetian Renaissance, and other styles. The time periods when the revival styles may be found is great, from 17th through 19th centuries.

Refers to a period, culture, and style that developed first in Attica, but was eventually found throughout Greece, in Italy, and in the Levant. It is generally held to have occurred from around 900 BCE to around 700 BCE, though some classification schemes omit the Protogeometric period and begin the Geometric period at 1100 BCE. In pottery it is characterized by dark-on-light decorations arranged in regularly spaced horizontal bands, and differs from Protogeometric style in that the designs are busier and the bands cover nearly the entire vessel. Designs include zigzags, triangles, meanders, swastikas, and distinctive stylized, angular human and animal figures. Similar designs and figural types were used in sculpture and other arts.

Refers to the style of art and architecture found in southeast Anatolia and north Syria during the Neo-Hittite period from about 1000 to 750 BCE. The style is characterized by a combination of Hittite and Syrian traditions and Assyrian influences seen particularly in large-scale reliefs.
Periods related to prehistoric Mesopotamian cultures.

Refers to a Neolithic style and culture named for the round barrow near Avebury, Wiltshire, England. It is characterized by causewayed camps and distinctive pottery that is among the oldest found in Britain.
Culture and style of a widely distributed South Asian social and ethnic group living mainly in the area now comprising north-western India and Pakistan.

Refers to the style of architecture developed during the Song dynasty (970-1279 BCE) in China and introduced into Japan along with Zen Buddhism during the Kamakura period (1185-1333). The style is characterized by smaller, more structurally complex buildings than before, with strongly articulated bracketing.

Refers to a style of Japanese painting that flourished from the middle of the Edo period (1600-1868) to the Taisho period (1912-1926). It was inspired by the Chinese literati, or "Wen ren," scholar-painting tradition, intended for a small, intellectual audience. Unlike other styles that developed in major Japanese studios, Nanga style includes varying techniques, styles, and subject-matter, linked by a loose tradition rather than by standardized rules. It is generally characterized by the combination of painting, poetry, and calligraphy, with a preference for subtle brushwork, monochromatic or subdued coloring, and abstraction of natural forms to convey highly personal views of nature.

A type of Japanese folk, or mingei, ceramic first produced in the Edo period. Its name (“West Plate Mountain” in English) refers to its production area in Fukuoka prefecture.in northern Kyushu. A distinct ceramic style peculiar to the reddish brown stoneware soy sauce jars, sake flasks, and mortars manufactured by the kilns of Nishi Sarayama has been identified by scholars in recent years.

Refers to the culture, period, and styles associated with the Chinese dynasty dating from 1368 to 1644. It is characterized by being a period of stability, prosperity, and by a renewal of Chinese culture and national consciousness. Styles in this period developed largely  from a system of court patronage of the arts that generally encouraged a high level of workmanship, but conservatism in design and technique. The major art produced during this period includes cloisonné, enamelware, bronzework, lacquerwork, furniture, and small ornamental carvings of jade, ivory, wood, and porcelain. In ceramics, earlier styles, including, blue-and-white wares, were refined in technique and decoration. In architecture, the earlier experiments of the Sung period were abandoned, in favor of more traditional designs, including the construction of the Forbidden City in Peking. In painting, schools of professional academics/artists and "literati" encouraged independent, personal styles.
Refers to the work of a group of artists, lead by the late 16th and eartly 17th century painter Zhao Zuo.
The culture of Americans of Irish descent.

The planning movement in the United States of the 1990s espousing a return to traditional small-town design features for newly constructed suburbs or redeveloped urban neighborhoods. To describe the architectural elements of the movement, incorporating such features as pedestrian spaces, mass transit, and mixed land use, use "Neotraditional."
Style and culture of the Zia-speaking tribe of Pueblo people, today centered at Zia Pueblo Indian reservation in New Mexico.

Style and culture of a Native American tribe from southern Florida. Originally part of the Mvskoke (Creek) nation, the Miccosukee moved from Mvsoke territory in present-day Georgia and Alabama to Florida during the mid 1700s. Distinct from Seminole communities in both language and culture. In 1962, the Miccosukee were federally recognized and land designated for a reservation in southern Florida.

Refers to the culture of the Passamaquoddy, an Algonkian-speaking Native American/First Nations people who live on Passamaquoddy Bay, the St. Croix River, and Schoodic Lake on the boundary between what are now Maine and New Brunswick. The Passamaquoddy tribe belonged to the loose confederation of eastern American Indians known as the Wabanaki Alliance, together with the Maliseet, Mi'kmaq, Abenaki, and Penobscot.

The culture and style of an Athabascan-speaking tribe of Canada's north country. The name "Slave" is the translation of a Cree term, since these traditional enemies sometimes raided and enslaved them. Another name for them "Etchao-tine," is Chipewyan for "people dwelling in the shelter, or by willows." The Slavey historically occupy territory west of the Great Slave Lake and Mackenzie River in Canada's present-day Northwest Territories, Alberta, and British Columbia.

Designates an archaeological period, extending roughly from 6,000-1,000 BCE, when Native Americans of California turned towards a broader range of food resources, including plant matter, as reflected by extensive use of milling stones and other grinding technology.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in southern Africa in the border area between Malawi and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Style and culture of the Berber people of the same name living in northern Morocco.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Ethiopia and Eritrea.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Kenya.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Used to descibe works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Nigeria.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Chad.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Senegal and Guinea-Bissau.
Refers to dipictions with a vantage point below the subject, but not so low as in a worm's-eye view.

Portraits in which the likeness of the sitter is generally maintained but the features and other attributes are presented in a way considered more beautiful, younger, stronger, or otherwise better than warranted by the sitter's actual appearance.
Visual works made with wire, which is a filament or slender rod of drawn metal.

Any materials manufactured through advanced technology, that differ physically from materials known throughout human history, specifically before the 20th century. This term is most often used to describe various polymers and synthetic materials.
Material added to paint or varnish to increase gum or resin content or to increase rate of oxidation, so as to cause an increase in hardness of the drying film.
Building panels consisting of two high-density outer sheets, usually plywood, hardwood, or metal, bonded to a lightweight core material, often plastic foam, rubber, or honeycombed paper.
Any substance that in small amounts increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed itself.
Oil derived from turmeric (Curcuma longa), a tuberous rhizome of the ginger family.
A clear plastic or stiff foam, a polymer of styrene, used chiefly as an insulator in refrigerators, air conditioners, and for packaging.
Material taking the form of long, narrow pieces of one or more substances, such as fabric, plastic, metal, or paper. Examples of tape as material include as a matrix for adhesive or other fastener.

Paper so coated (as with lime, whiting, and size) that marks made on it with a metal point are indelible. Can also refer to either paper coated with finely flaked metal to give the appearance of a metallic surface or to paper to which a metallic foil has been laminated.
Paper discarded as superfluous or not fit for a particular use, although possibly regarded as valuable in other processes; also, blank paper.
A drying oil obtained from the kernel of the fruit of the oiticica tree that is similar to tung oil; used chiefly in varnish, paint, and printing ink.
Sculptures of the Archaic Greek period depicting standing nude male youths.

Large, rectangular items of woven material frequently decorated with a variety of designs made across Mesoamerica. Worn over the shoulders like a cloak, they were also a primary unit of trade used in the payment of tribute during the pre-Hispanic period.
Jackets of various design meant to be worn while mounted on horseback.

Large carved monolithic rings of the Taíno people, mostly limited to Puerto Rico. Many are elliptical with a thicker portion with two panels that exhibit decorative carvings. While their exact use is unknown, most archaeologists suggest they were worn on the hips for ceremonial purposes or ball games. They can be classified in at least two types: slender or massive.
Tall, cylindrical headdresses seen in ancient Greek representations of certain goddesses.

Millinery pieces that cover only a small part of the head, the front edge beginning above the hairline, and resting on the crown. Originally developed by Lilly Daché ca. 1940, these may be embellished with a variety of decorative elements.
Collector's term for a type of small plate made in pressed glass from the 1830s to the 1860s. They may have been used under a toddy glass or as a large saucer.
Tall slender glasses intended to be used for beer.
Bars or fences erected to prevent people from entering a prohibited area. These are often brightly colored and demountable.

Fiddles of northern India, Nepal, and Pakistan, with a short, thick, unfretted neck, waisted body with a skin belly, two or more bone bridges, three or four bowed strings, and a variable number of sympathetic strings. They are held upright when played.
Structures specifically designed to contain and protect the movements of timepieces.
Small, five-stringed guitars with convex-curved bodies and vaulted backs. Predominant in mariachi music.
Secondary prints pulled from a plate without reinking, made for any purpose. This technique produces a print with radically reduced tonality, as it is pulling only residual ink from the plate.

Pieces of furniture having hooks, used to receive  hats, coats, umbrellas, and scarves, and often having shelves, a seat, and mirror. Usually situated near the front door in the hall of the house. For upright postlike stands with pegs or hooks around the top, use "coat trees."

Boards, often carved in profile, that are components in chests or the support of stools or benches. Common support elements for stools in the Medieval period, and until the 17th century when legs became the norm.

Refers to tables having a set of cabinets above, used for writing. The form was popular in France, England, and America in the early 18th century. In modern usage, it is typically distinguished from an "escritoire" or a "secretary."
Surfaces used as supports for etching; users place their work on the tables for stability while working.
Pieces of furniture fitted with pigeonholes or compartments to hold paper; either resting on a specially made cabinet placed at one end of a bureau plat or on the top of the bureau plat itself.
Seaman's chests, generally used to store personal property.
Racks of various designs used for drying towels; may be attached to a wall or other surface, or standing on the floor.
French beds meant to have a separate canopy overhead; of a type made in the late 17th century.

Case furniture on low legs, popular during the Victorian period. It is characterized by being divided in half vertically, with one half comprising shelves enclosed by a wooden or glass-fronted door, for the storage of books, dishes, or curiosities, and the other side often comprising a secretary, cabinet, or some combination of mirror, drawers, and fold-down desk top. Distinguished from a chifforobe, which is case furniture also divided vertically, but typically characterized by placement in a bedroom, having a narrow clothes closet on one side, and a narrow chest of drawers with a mirror on the other side.
Chairs with horizontal slats across the back.
Chairs which served as models from which to work; frequently with arms or legs showing alternative forms and styles of decoration.
Floor lamps in which multiple lamp fixtures radiate from various positions on the pole. May also refer to lamp fixtures having a more realistic form of a tree, or to lamps hung from actual trees.

Cone-shaped devices used to extinguish flames on candles. For scissorlike devices with a boxlike receptacle attached to one blade, use "candle snuffers." For scissorlike devices with flat disc-shaped ends used for pinching out a candle flame, use "douters."
Military daggers from the 20th century on, having a strong, sharply pointed, double-edged stabbing blade and, in American models, a set of brass knuckles, designed for hand-to-hand fighting.
Platforms or racks on stands for holding votive candles, in churches or other devotional settings.
Objects of one material around which another material, as concrete, plastic, or metal sets or solidifies, especially to provide a means of attachment.

Works in which paint is applied on a textile support with only a thin glue preparation or no preparation; the painting surface remains flexible, and the works are often rolled and portable. These works were popular in Germany, the Netherlands, and Italy. For similar works on textiles having a thin gesso preparation, popular in Spain and its colonies, prefer "sargas (visual works)."
Drawings produced with the aid of instruments such as compasses or T-squares.

Official marks stamped on mail, sometimes serving as cancellations, that indicate the place, date, and sometimes the time that the postal system accepted custody of the item; use "cancellations" only for official defacements of postage stamps to prevent their reuse.
Large format maps painted on, or designed to be hung, on walls.
Reproductions, usually of documents, originally made with the Photostat (TM) machine, later also produced on similar machines.
Official records, in book form, of the pedigree of purebred animals.

HIstorically, sticks or rods made of wood or other materials, and marked with transverse notches for the purpose of counting or measuring a debt or payment. Some tallies were split, and a debtor and creditor would each retain halves of the sticks which would be cleft lengthwise across the notches, constituting legal proof of the debt.
Teaching aids in learning to read consisting of a board with ledges on which the letters of the word that is depicted above the ledge can be placed.
Bodies that exercise continuous authority on behalf of a nation, state, community, or other administrative entity over the actions of subjects or citizens, by authoritative direction or regulation.
Associations or bodies of people united by common interests, purpose, or profession.
Persons to whom anything is dedicated.
People who devote themselves to a particular occupation, activity, or branch of knowledge.

Scientists trained in or working with the laws determining the structure of the observable universe and the interaction between its fundamental constituents, such as matter and energy, with the broad goal of explaining natural phenomena.
Persons responsible for checking that a product or service meets required standards.
Authors of scripts and screenplays for motion picture production.
Those who project images or operate a film projector.
People who hold an office, function, or mandate within an organization or government, and who perform official duties as a representative of the organization or government.
Members of a small group holding power in a state.

Those who sell wool in its raw state for processing into products. Merchants historically have acted as purchasers, organizers, and sellers of finished textile material. For its manufacture, which required many processes, including cleaning the raw wool to final fulling and dyeing, merchants relied on an array of subordinate workers.
Refers generally to workmen and craftsmen who work with marble, including those who do any of quarrying, dressing, sculpting, mosaic, and masonry work.

Those who oversee the design and creation of the sets, that is the physical surroundings in which the action takes place, for films, television, or theater. For the broader role of overseeing the sets as well as other visual aspects of a production, prefer "scenographers" for theater productions or "production designers" for film and television productions.

Limited function wholesalers who take custody of but not legal ownership of the goods handled as part of a business transaction. They are paid either directly by the owner or by a share of the sale proceeds. Distinct from "brokers" in that they take the actual physical possession of the goods while brokers do not.
People who are notably skilled in the art of building, particularly those who have achieved proficiency in one of the building arts and are licensed or qualified to supervise construction.
Artists who specialize in painting or stamping designs or scenes on wallpaper, which is decorative paper made primarily for attachment to walls and ceilings.
People who engage in making wood engravings.
Bits shaped like a half cylinder, used with a brace for drilling dowel holes.
The people employed by or active in a business, organization, or service; it is a collective term and never refers to an individual.
Architects who guide, review, or approve the work of other architects, architectural design groups, or supervisory personnel.

Specialized hand-held tools designed for use in boating and sailing activities. Historically, these tools comprised a single pointed steel blade mounted on a wooden handle. Sailor's traditionally used these tools to rub light seams, carry out various cutting and chopping tasks, and eat or prepare meals while on board a ship. Modern sailmaker's knives, however, are designed to be increasingly versatile; these tools now often take the form of folding-knifes, equipped with multiple blades and additional tools including shackle openers and marlin spikes, amongst others.
Devices that attach to projectors that allow continuous strips of film to be projected, rather than individual slides.
Any of various tools for chasing or engraving, usually on metal, sometimes on wood. For the tools used in printmaking to engrave metal or end-grain wood blocks, prefer "burins."
Nationality, culture, or style of the historic region of Bretagne or modern Britanny, France.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Iowa.
The culture or style of the ancient Piceni, the Early Iron Age inhabitants of the Adriatic coast of Italy from Rimini to the Sangro River.
Nationality, style, or culture of Nevis, an island in the Caribbean Sea.
In Indian architecture, a three-storeyed or  three-floored vimāna.
Structures that provide protection from sun, weather, and other damaging elements for archaeological sites and other heritage sites.

Refers to the main central part of an interior divided into a high center with lower side portions divided by columns or piers, usually but not always in a church. Use also for the main part of a church without aisles but with a distinct chancel.

Experimental technique used to analyze short-lived chemical intermediates created when molecules are split by an intense flash of light. Analysis by spectrophotometry follows during a second, less intense, flash. This technique is useful in the study of the mechanisms of fast chemical reactions.

Blocks, strips, or pegs, usually made of wood, set into or onto construction, such as masonry or steel, to serve as surface into which nails may be driven. An example of use is to attach crown molding by nails.

The liberal Protestant movement that arose in Europe during the 16th century Reformation, was embodied in a church in Transylvania, and achieved denominational status in the 19th century in the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada. It is characterized by a denial of the orthodox Christian doctrines of the Trinity and the divinity of Jesus, the free use of reason in religion, and the belief that God exists in one person. In 1961, in the United States and Canada, it merged with the Universalist denomination to form "Unitarian Universalism."  Use also generally for the theological doctrines of the unified nature of God and the humanity of Jesus, first expressed in second- and third-century monarchism and in the teachings of Arius in the third and fourth centuries, and later in the radical Neoplatonist thinkers of the Reformation such as Michael Servetus, Faustus Socinus, and Ferenc David.
Collecting, preparing, altering, and arranging materials for publication or public presentation, including but not restricted to data, written materials, film, and tape.
Religious and philosophical system of the Druids, who were members of the learned priestly class among the ancient Celts. Frequented oak forests and acted as priests, teachers, and judges.
Explanation of what is not immediately plain or explicit, as in suggesting what meaning is to be found in a set of data or in a visual work.
Subordinate vertical structures, generally more or less tapering, rising above the neighboring parts of a building, and that may support a spire. Usually in Gothic architecture.
A game that occupies a single player who uses a small wood paddle to repeatedly hit a small rubber ball that is attached to the paddle itself by an elasticated string.
Committing funds to a project or enterprise in order to promote that project or to earn a return.

Treatment of a subject, in speech or writing, in which the various facts, opinions, and issues relating to it are considered, particularly in order to reach a decision or to exchange ideas with someone else.

Christian private or public devotions, special prayers, or services that are observed on nine successive days, or on the same day for nine successive weeks. The purpose of novenas is to request special graces of God or to express mourning; a novena is not, strictly speaking, a ceremony or liturgical event. The practice derives from Jewish tradition, although Jewish prayer periods were of seven days rather than nine. The tradition of nine days derives from the ancient Romans, who had official religious ceremonies that were nine days in duration.
In Indian architecture, a śākhā adorned with foliage; door-jamb with vine or leaf pattern.
Action or condition of being much talked about, chiefly in a good sense. Reputation derived from great achievements, celebrity, honor, renown.

Reduction of the concentration of ozone in the ozone layer as a result of the action of atmospheric pollutants. The thinning of the ozone layer and the appearance of a visible "hole" over the South Pole region has been the subject of extensive public policy discussions, media coverage, and national legislation and international treaties. Stratospheric ozone shields living organisms on Earth from the harmful effects of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation; even a relatively small decrease in the stratospheric ozone concentration can result in an increased incidence of skin cancer in humans and in genetic damage in many organisms. The prohibition of the manufacture or use of chlorofluorocarbons in the United States, and many other nations, is perhaps the most visible positive result to date of this debate.

Generally an array of the components of an emission or wave separated and arranged in the order of some varying characteristic, as wavelength, mass, or energy. Specifically, the colored band into which a beam of light is decomposed by means of a prism or diffraction grating.
Art that portrays forms recognizably derived from objective sources, in however altered or distorted form. Includes but not limited to representations of the human figure.
The quality or state of a substance or body of transmitting light, but without allowing clear visibility.
The reliance on line for the principal effect in a drawn or painted composition, rather than on color or tone.
Having a three-dimensional rounded shape, resembling a sphere but not necessarily with the geometrical precision of a true sphere.
Creative work in which is sought the unification of many art forms, including those from the visual, decorative, and performing arts, into a single total work.
Extreme form of skepticism that denies the objective reality of all values, beliefs, and truths.
The religious ideology that there are many gods, as opposed to monotheism. Polytheism is characteristic of primitive religions as well as the religions of ancient Greece and Rome.

A philosophy that asserts the essential dignity and worth of humanity and its capacity to achieve self-realization through reason; also (capitalized), the Renaissance movement characterized by the revival of classical letters.

In philosophical and religious traditions, the concept of or belief in the continued existence of a material thing into infinity, or of the existance of an immaterial soul or mind beyond the physical death of the body.
Physical quantities with magnitude and direction.
An interest, commonly expressed in money, which an owner has in property over and above all liens against the property.
Governing principles that serve as guidelines for decision-making and action as embodied in legislative and judicial enactments.

Meaning "joint rule" or "harmonious rule,” the term refers to several political ideologies, the most prominent of which were prominent in France in the 19th century and in Mexico in the 1930s. The term was used by Alexandre Saint-Yves d'Alveydre (1842-1909) in "La France vraie" to describe a form of government in reaction to the emergence of anarchist ideologies and movements; this political formula would include social differentiation and hierarchy, but with collaboration between social classes. It also refers to an ideology and political movement in Mexico beginning in the 1930s, historically originating in the Roman Catholic extreme right, and violently opposed to the populist and secularist policies of the revolutionary governments in power.
Statutory obligation requiring all individuals and organizations to submit one or more copies of a document or publication to a recognized national institution.
State of wistful yearning to return to a former place or time.
The theory describing various aspects of social disintegration involving individuals, groups or social classes.
Use collectively for the parts of a book that precede the main text, including, for example, title pages, prefaces, or tables of contents.
The branch of science dealing with the three dimensional interpretation of flat images, often sections or projections, using general principles of geometrical probability.
Branch of engineering involving the design of relatively large-scale, complex systems.
Refers to the practice of designing for Websites, including graphical functional, and structural considerations.

The art and process of making video recordings using a video camera. Light reflected from the subject is focused onto a camera tube or sensor whence it is converted into an electronic signal and recorded on magnetic tape or laser-beam disk.

Branch of archaeology that deals with the recovery of ancient objects found beneath the sea, as shipwrecks or remains from submerged human settlements, and with the techniques of underwater exploration, excavation, and retrieval.
The action or process of coating a surface such as a wall with whitewash: a powdered mineral substance such as calcium hydroxide or chalk suspended in water, often with size or other ingredients.

An analytical technique which measures quantifiable aspects of a stone’s porosity by forcing a non-wetting liquid, such as mercury, into the pores of the material using a porosimeter. The technique is used in archaeological conservation to determine the durability and behavior of ancient stone and the choice of conservation methods
Action or process of creating illumination, which comprises paintings and other adornments applied to books, scrolls, or other document types for the purpose of illustrating or decorating the text.
Often imitated painting technique associated with Rembrandt of gouging in wet paint with the wooden end of a brush or other utensil to create texture and manipulate tone.
The process of making free from living microorganisms.
Making or modifying something according to individual specifications or preferences.

Small electrical panels containing switches and fuses or circuit breakers. For larger panels, frames, or assemblies containing switches, fuses, instruments, and protective devices, use "switchboards."
Hinged joints by which two rods are connected.

Nails designed to fasten sheathing of wood or another material. Sheathing nails for wood sheathing have no points, but have square ends to punch out their own holes, driving a portion of the soft sheathing wood before them. Sheathing nails for metal sheathing are small sharp nails with a flat head. An example of sheathing requiring such nails is on a ship's bottom, where sheathing preserves the planks.

Small, short nails with broad heads, designed to nail leathers to wood. Examples of use are nailing leather onto scuppers, which are holes on ships or other locations to allow water run-off, or to attach leathers to blacksmith bellows.
Hinges that allow a door to swing into a pocket at a right angle to a door frame.
Locks which can be adapted to fit a door of either hand.
Small Japanese ornamental sculptures, displayed in the tokonoma alcove of a traditional Japanese house.

Term used to describe things produced by synthesis, the combining of elements, materials, or entities into a unified entity. Where the emphasis is a distinction from things natural, prefer "artificial."

Miniature scale houses or sets of rooms of various types, designed to display miniature furniture and furnishings, usually to be used in conjunction with like-sized dolls. Typically illustrate domestic interiors and activities. May be used as collectibles or childrens' toys; known since the 16th century.

Figures and ornaments made in plaster of Paris to imitate Staffordshire pottery and other works. The works were not fired but painted or left in their natural white color. The works were popular in the United States in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Visually-based works created or used within religious contexts.
In Indian architecture, a main enshrined deity.

Artistic concepts comprising proposed undertakings or creations, including the creation of works of art or architecture, or for the actual carrying out of such proposals. When emphasis is on specific conceptual schemes for the organization or appearance of graphic works, objects, structures, or systems, use "designs." For visual works and other physical items that are used to carry out the project, use "projects (object groupings)."
Layers of colored plaster in a casting mold that indicate the proximity of the cast surface; to prevent damage to the cast surface as the mold is chipped away from the cast.

A spectroscopic technique in which short pulses of terahertz radiation probe intermolecular interactions, allowing characterization of solid materials. The detection scheme is sensitive to the material's effect on both the amplitude and the phase of the terahertz radiation. In conservation science used as a nondestructive subsurface analysis of paintings which can reveal buried layer information such as underdrawings or highlight interfaces between layers in a stratigraphic buildup.

Documents containing affirmation of person's character or the value of a thing. Specifically, written declarations stating an individual's achievements or the usefulness of a product or service, such as a letter of endorsement.
The state that an information object possessed in the past, but that is no longer valid in a present context.

Individual sides of a leaf, recto or verso; the individual sides of leaves resulting from folding a sheet, as of paper or parchment, whether blank or containing writing, printing, or other matter. Distinguished from a "folio" in that a folio is numbered on only the front side.
Patterns having a watered or rippled look. To refer to the optical illusion of movement caused by intersecting lines, use "moiré effect."
People in a religious faith who are not part of the clergy.

Small, hand-held tools used to manually agitate paint components in a can or container. Specifically designed with the objective of mixing the liquid contents that rise to the top of the can with the pasty contents that accumulate at the bottom to create a homogenous paint consistency. While sometimes taking the form of stiff metal blades with holes or slots that reduce the resistance of the stirring movement, these tools are often cheaply made of wood or plastic. For the mechanical tools designed to blend paint colors or components, use "paint shakers."

Devices usually of ceramic consisting of a well for water in which a wheel is mounted to revolve that wets surfaces brought into contact with it. Used chiefly to moisten tape for drafting or for adhesive stamps for postage.

Refers to those who prepare food for consumption, especially but not exclusively by the use of heat. Includes those who prepare meals and dishes in a private home, public eating place, or institution, or who cook foods as a preparation stage in commercial food processing plants.

Horizontal, rectangular framed panels in Mesoamerican architecture, having their recessed surfaces often decorated with paintings or sculpture and the whole often cantilevered over sloping apron walls to form talud-tableros.
In Indian architecture, a wall-offset flanking karṇa; anuratha (Eastern India); wall projection flanking karṇa; wall-bay flanking karṇa (in caturaṅga plan).

Vulcanite is an old trade name for a dark, brittle, moldable hard rubber that was produced by heating (‘vulcanizing’) a preparation of india rubber and sulfur. It was marketed in the U.S. as vulcanite and in England as ebonite. Vulcanite was used for small items such as buttons, brooches, and combs, finishes on camera bodies, and for insulation.
The representation of the leaves of plants, usually used for decoration or ornament.
In Indian architecture, a floral band; minor band bearing floral (or vine) decoration.
Motif comprising figures of goblins or dwarfs in Indian art or architecture.
Mills or factories where wood is reduced to paper pulp.

Systematic guides to the contents of texts, files, documents, or collections, presented as a list, usually in alphabetical order, of persons and/or subjects referred to in documents, with location of references thereto.
The condition of combining two or more branches of academic, scientific, or artistic disciplines.
Thin paper used to create patterns for cutting textiles into pieces in the construction of garments or other items.
Finishing tools with a handle and a rotating wheel that has one or more raised bands on its edge for impressing a line or parallel lines; commonly used in bookbinding.
Pointed tools used for making holes in wood.
The sum of activities and status having to do with the home and household.

General term for businesses and people having occupations related to health and medicine. In a given region or community, the term may be by law reserved for a doctor of medicine or osteopathy, podiatrist, dentist, chiropractor, clinical psychologist, optometrist, nurse practitioner, nurse-midwife, clinical social worker who is authorized to practice medicine, or other defined specialists.
People who hoard wealth and are avaricious, grasping, stingy, and parsimonious; in the original meaning, such people live miserably in order to hoard wealth.

Refers to objects made of a fine white earthenware clay decorated with delicate, repeating, incised or impressed designs inlaid with different -colored slips, especially yellow ochre and brown. Favored designs were scrolls, coats of arms, a variety of popular abstract motifs, especially those used for ornamenting book covers. Motifs were generally derived from the pattern book "La Fleur de la science de pourtraicture" (1530) by Francesco Pellegrino. Relief work was often added. The thin, overlying lead glaze has the appearance of a varnish and gives the ware a cream color. Saint-Porchaire ware was made at Saint-Porchaire, France, and the surrounding area around Saintes in south-west France during the reigns of François I and Henri II, the period of manufacture lasting from ca. 1500 to ca. 1570. Due to the technical skill involved, only a small number were made (64 recorded). Such wares were imitated in the 19th century by such factories as the Minton Ceramic Factory in England.
Concepts related to the doctrine of Hinduism.
Lists of items lacking or needed, such as a list of books issued by a librarian or a list of objects wanted for a museum collection.
Photographic prints produced by the silver-dye bleach process.
All media used to record microimages.
Maps indicating patterns of weather, such as the movement of clouds or wind, high and low systems, and rain.

Documents, usually Greco-Roman and often inscribed on lead tablets, requesting that the gods, other spirits, or deceased persons cause another person to be affected negatively, typically asking that they be cursed with illness or misfortune.
Establishing or bringing into conformity with standards.
Modifier describing a saturated color of high intensity, and medium-light to medium-dark value.
Documents, of Pennsylvania German origin and common in the 18th and 19th centuries, often family records such as birth certificates, distinctive by a particular style of calligraphy and illumination.
Cinematic film with accompanying recorded sound. It may have synchronized sound, or sound technologically coupled to the image. The term is used to distinguish such films from silent films.
Photographic positives, usually a gelatin or carbon print, printed on or transferred to opaque, white glass.
For positional attributes of three-dimensional works or the illusionistic space of a composition, referring to the viewer's lower left-hand side of the work or composition.
Lace produced in Russia and characterized by a coiling tape forming elegant patterns in very simple to very elaborate designs.

Catalan avant-garde movement in art and literature, founded in Barcelona in 1948 and active until the early 1950s. It was a counter-movement that wanted to break open the imposed art under the Franco regime. The style is based on Surrealism and Dadaism, but combined with Cubism and contemporary post-war trends, which opened Spanish art to foreign influences and made it the precursor of Spanish informal art and Abstract Expressionism. The movement published a magazine with the same name.

Group consisting of two extant genera, Psilotum and Tmesipteris. They are chiefly tropical, clump-forming plants of skeletal appearance resembling whisk brooms. These plants are primitive in structure, lacking both roots and leaves, or having structures on the aerial shoot that are foliar. They are structurally similar to the fossil genus Rhynia. Recent molecular systematic studies suggest that the family is actually related to primitive ferns.
The action of making or transmitting signals, which are gestures or things that convey meaning.
Open spaces used for the movement of people or things from once place to another.

Materials derived from any of several species of sphagnum moss, particularly the polysaccharides known for strong antibacterial properties used medicinally. This extract has also been used as a fungal inhibitor in art conservation, and for other purposes.
Plan of a building or city that is arranged within a square, usually a centralized plan.
In India, a townhouse, mansion, or manor houses, typically relatively large with courtyards and intricate decorations.
Elaborations constructed over or around burial sites; for simple interments in the earth, use "graves."
In Indian architecture, a frieze of flowers fringed with pearl-strings.
Temples or shrines built over holy wells, places of pilgrimage and ceremonies.

Generally refers to small settlements of indigenous people; specifically may refer to settlements and tracts of land in the western United States that were federally recognized and allotted for Native Americans to live, primarily established between 1906 and 1910. These Native populations had been driven to near extinction, made landless and often homeless by non-native migration into the western states, especially after the mid-19th century.
In the context of archaeology, this term refers to thin, flat pieces of stone intentionally removed from a tool or core during the process of stone tool manufacture.

Ritual mud brick pits or holes dug at points of importance in Ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian temples or tombs during their construction. Votive offerings were set under the foundation of monumental buildings, or nearby, perhaps to commemorate or sanctify these structures. These may also have been made to identify the craft of a tomb occupant.
Nationality, culture, or style of The Marches region, Italy.
A fragrant, liquid, unsaturated hydrocarbon used chiefly in making synthetic rubber, resin, and plastic and in improving drying oil.

Periods and cultures between prehistory and history, during which a culture or civilization has not yet developed writing, but other cultures have provided written historical records for this people in a given area.

Use specifically for plucked chordophones developed in the European Renaissance, having a large pear-shaped body composed of thin, narrow ribs, a flat top, central circular soundhole covered by a rose, and from seven to ten frets on the neck. For the general class of all chordophones with the plane of the strings running parallel to the resonator and a neck that serves both as string bearer and as handle, see "lutelike chordophones."

Books produced by commercial publishers for sale to the general public primarily through bookstores, as distinguished from a textbook edition, subscription book, or a book meant for a limited public because of its technical nature, specialized appeal, or high price.

Notices, usually decorative or pictorial, intended to be posted to advertise, promote, or publicize an activity, cause, product, or service; also, decorative, mass-produced prints intended for hanging. For small printed notices or advertisements intended for distribution by hand, use "handbills."
The state or condition of having relatively high moisture content.

Dresses having a shirtwaist bodice, typically including a center front button or stud placket opening, cuffs, and a collar, imitating certain details of a man's shirt. The bodice is attached straight or full skirt, often having a belt at the waist.

Synthetic form of dihydroxyanthraquinone (alizarin) made from anthracene, a coal tar product, in 1868 by Carl Graebe and Carl Lieberman. Prior to that time, alizarin was obtained from the root of the madder plant.
Poems with a religious subject or spiritual theme.
Shoes, often laced over the instep and with rubber or rubberlike soles, made in a wide variety of forms. Originally designed for sports and now also worn for casual dress.
Caps with long visors, of the style worn by jockeys; also worn by light infantry from the mid-18th century.

Accessories used to lengthen the collars of garments. Can take varying forms; some consist of a button with a fabric loop which are inserted into the top buttonhole of a garment, while others are rectangular inserts which are buttoned along the inside of collars.
Originally a collective term for all the articles of linen, lace, etc. in a woman's wardrobe or trousseau. Now used for women's underwear and nightclothes, particularly high-end women's underwear.
Open helmets developed in the 16th century from the kettle hat, consisting of a skull with a broad curved brim, flat or turned down at the sides but sweeping upwards into a peak at front and rear.
Toy figures, usually from vinyl or rubber that make a squeak when they are pressed, often intended for young children or pets.
Long scarflike vestments worn by bishops of the Eastern Church during the celebration of Mass.
Bindings typically used for pamphlets that are expected to receive infrequent use. Typically they are side-stitched, sometimes with wire, and covered with boards.
Bindings of the style associated with Jean Grolier generally characterized by geometric patterns and arabesques, sometimes colored.
Toys that allow children to mimic household tasks, such as cooking and cleaning.
White hygroscopic crystals, the sodium salt of nitrous acid; used in dye manufacture, as a fixative for color photographs, a meat preservative, and as a corrosion inhibitor when applied to steel.

Plates, usually metal and either discs or rectangular in shape, decorated or inscribed, and surmounted on a pole to be used in sports shooting as a target pointer, an indicator of where the marksman was to stand, and to be carried in processions of archery or shooting clubs.
Main garments of varying length that extend from the waist or hip and cover a part of the lower body, and that feature a series of folds set into them either by pressing or stitching.

Trousers cut wide around the thighs and then tightly fitted from just above the knees to the calves; worn by men and women for horseback riding. For trousers cut full over hips and thighs and extending to the ankles, use "jodhpurs."
Vestments resembling a dalmatic worn by a bishop in the Eastern Orthodox Church during the liturgy.

Wide-brimmed, low-crowned sun hats thought to be Thessalian origin, worn by ancient Greeks, Etruscans, and Romans; considered traveling hats. The style was revived during the early Medieval period. These hats are believed to have been made of wool felt, leather, or straw, with a floppy brim. The god Hermes/Mercury was originally portrayed with wide-brimmed traveling hats; when his depictions were changed to winged hats, these were also often called "petasuses" even if they were close-fitting caps.
Brief-like undergarments meant to protect against the effects of incontinence. These are usually disposable and have absorbant qualities.

Ornaments such as bracelets, necklaces, and rings, of precious or semiprecious materials worn or carried on the person for adornment; also includes similar articles worn or carried for devotional or mourning purposes.
A book hand characterized by rounded majuscules, developed from the older Roman cursive; used especially in Greek and Latin manuscripts of the 4th to the 8th century.
Outer garments intended for women.
Hip-length, double-breasted, straight-hanging jackets, especially those worn by sailors.
Devices for holding cards marking the place at a dining table, or other location, where each diner or other participant is assigned seating.
Small gold coins worth one third of a gold solidus and used in the Roman and Merovingian territories from the late 4th until the 7th or 8th century.
General term for a number of historical gold coins of Germany and the Netherlands.
Chants of the Navajo culture.
Used broadly for books containing religious rites and sometimes hymns.
Tools of various forms used to cut soft curd into cubes to facilitate drainage of whey. Prefer "cheese knives (food preparation tools)" for large spatulas used to break up the curd for cheesemaking.
Cooking vessels with a perforated insert to hold food to be steamed.
Table or sideboard accessories used to keep dishes warm.
Treatises or series of comments that systematically explain or annotate another work.

Covered vessels for boiling water, usually having a short pouring spout, a bail handle, and a broad, flat bottom. Often used with but different from a teapot, in which the tea leaves are brewed or steeped.
Medium-sized bags suspended at the top corners from one or two long straps, designed to be suspended from one shoulder or across the chest.
Small vessels for serving jam or preserves usually having a cover, which often has an indentation for the stem of a jam spoon, and a fixed saucerlike stand. Sometimes a part of a breakfast service.
Vessels for holding pieces of ice, made in a variety of forms, sometimes having a cover or handles.

Term generally applied to vessels, often of silver, having two vertical handles and generally resting on a footed base and sometimes having a cover with a finial. For small two-handled cups typically made of silver and intended for caudle, use "caudle cups."
Accurate surveying instruments that measure distances by using modulated, continuous-wave radio signals.
Boxes for storing Buddhist sutra scrolls, often made of lacquered wood and highly decorated.

Term applied to a wide variety of bottles of different size and shape intended primarily for holding or dispersing perfume. Includes those made for sale to cosmetics manufacturers as well as those often decorative forms meant to be placed on the dressing table and sometimes part of a toilet set.
Small chests or boxes for holding objects of value such as money, letters, and jewels; usually of wood or metal and highly ornamented and often hinged.
Openings on objects such as vessels, through which the contents enter the cavity.

Vessels made of a refractory material, such as clay, graphite, or porcelain, or a relatively infusible metal, that may vary in size and that are used for melting, calcining, or filtering a substance at high temperatures.
Graduated cuplike vessels used for measuring ingredients, as for cooks or chemists.

Small, movable, graduated scales running parallel to the fixed graduated scales of precision instruments, such as sextants or transits, and designed to measure a fractional part of the smallest divisions on the fixed scales.
Areas on pages of printed or written matter, or on other sheets of text or images, between the information area and the outer edges of the page or sheet.

Receptacles of various types that contain holy relics. Usage has varied over time. In modern usage, the term refers to relatively small disc-shaped, glass-faced metal receptacles for relics, often designed so that they may be inserted into reliquary monstrances. In Early Christian usage, the term referred to cells or openings dug into walls to hold the corpse. For discs or clips that secure a host in a monstrance, use "lunettes (monstrance clips)."
Trays or containers for packing and conveying goods, such as portable platforms on which goods can be moved, stacked, or stored, especially with the aid of a forklift truck.

Drinking vessels in the form of a wide, flat-bottomed, shallow bowl; originally of wood (especially maple) and often having silver or gilt mounts. Many have a central ornamental print on the interior.
Nationality, culture, and styles of Oman, on the southeast coast of the Arabian Peninsula.
