Coverings for the head or tail of the spine of a book, formed by turning the material on the spine over the head and tail and shaping it.
Shallow oblong baskets made of wooden strips with a handle from side to side, chiefly used for carrying fruit, vegetables, or flowers.
Earthenware vessels, with or without a cover, of cylindrical shape.

Silver or copper coins, primarily of ancient India, struck with a variety of punches containing symbols rather than struck by regular obverse and reverse dies; in use at least between 500 BCE and CE 500.

In Britain, the class of schools founded in the 16th century or earlier for the teaching of Latin. Subsequently, they became secondary schools of various degrees of importance, sometimes ranking little below the level of the 'public schools.'
Molded pedestals, plinths, or bases of structures that support an image of a deity, or lingam.
Sources and upper parts of streams, including upper drainage basins; generally used in plural form.
High, steep ledges of rock.
Chinese bronze ritual vessels used to pour water during ablutions, and used with "pan." Employed during the late Western Zhou period.
In hypertext, embedded instructions or codes that connect units of data. Links may take the form of highlighted text, images, or other indicators.
Order of marsupial mammals containing six living species in one family. They have thin limbs, a long pointed snout, a thin hairy tail, and are largely carnivorous.
Genus of one Asian species.
In Chinese architectural tradition, pillars used to support the eaves, usually placed around the outer perimeter of a structure.
In printmaking, proofs pulled at various stages of the process, to test various aspects of the print during creation.
Marbled paper made in Sweden and having a characteristic spotted pattern.

Genre of motion pictures, television, and radio shows characterized by a setting in the American West during the time of western expansion, usually the 1850s through the early 1900s. May also apply to certain films with similar themes but set in Australia, Argentina, or other places.

Refers to the Friday before Easter during Holy Week. On this day the crucifixion of Jesus Christ is commemorated. It is a day of penance in liturgical churches. Good Friday and the following day (Holy Saturday) are the only days of the years on which mass is not celebrated in the Roman Catholic Church. The rite includes the veneration of the cross and communion with hosts consecrated on Maundy Thursday. Good Friday is kept as a feast rather than as a fast in some Protestant churches and is considered a special celebration of the Lord's Supper. The Three Hours Service is the main service of Good Friday in many denominations. The day is known as Great Friday in Eastern Orthodox churches. Some denominations come together to celebrate Good Friday as an expression of Christian unity.
Small, shallow overcast stitches arranged in a diagonal; used to bind pieces together or to secure small rolled-over hemming.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Sudan.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Bénin.
In the royal courts of China, assistant or apprentice painters.
Boards, usually with a right-angle projection on one end, used to protect the sides and fore edges of a covered book during tying up.
Style and culture of the people of Equatorial Guinea.
Businesses that sell furniture, which is movable objects or equipment for sitting, reclining, or storage, such as chairs, beds, tables, and cabinets.

The front part of the head of a human or animal; in vertebrates, the area of the head on which the sense organs of vision and smell as well as the mouth and jaws are located. In humans, the face extends from the forehead to the chin; the term may also be used to describe the part of the front of the head below the forehead, from the eyebrows to the chin.

Portable, human-operated devices used to weave narrow strips of fabric, roughly an inch wide, called tapes. These devices are typically made of wood and often comprise a paddle-shaped board equipped with alternating slots and holds (a rigid heddle) sometimes, but not always, attached to a box or frame. Designed to be held between the user's knees during operation, these devices required that the warp be stretched by the user's one hand to determine the correct degree of tension while the weft be picked with the user's other hand.
Describes groupings of a species from the Animalia kingdom.
Clamps of metal, wood, or plastic, used to hold work at one end so that it can be stretched.
Instruments used for examining the chest or other part by auscultation, the sounds of the heart, lungs, or other internal organs being conveyed by means of it to the ear of the observer.

Equipment used to evaluate the quality of textile products prior to their being released to the market. Such equipment is important to assure regulatory compliance and assess the performance of textile materials, as well as to provide insight into the physical or structural properties of materials.

A compound that appears as a white powder prepared by treating acetic acid with calcium carbonate or lime. It is a water-soluble compound that has been used for aqueous and nonaqueous neutralization and alkalization of paper. However, during the neutralization process, calcium acetate is converted to calcium carbonate with the release of acetic acid. Any residual calcium acetate will continue to release acetic acid. Calcium acetate is used commercially as a mordant in dyeing and printing textiles, for liming rosin, for curing and tanning skins, and as a metallic soap.

Generally, a style of textiles, particularly large, coarse carpets handwoven in western Anatolia and exported by way of Izmir (ancient Smyrna). Such carpets originally represented the production of the town of Usak, but in the late 19th and early 20th centuries large carpets from other centers were also called Smyrna, including those from Ghiordes, Kula, and Demirci. Specifically, the term refers to a particular pattern, usually seen in small examples and derived from a floral pattern used in the Ottoman court production of the 16th and 17th centuries.
Parts or components that are related to the phenomena of living organisms.

Physical works, such as drawings and written documents, that were used in the planning or execution of a definable physical work or set of works; also includes the finished works. Alternatively, a project may be planned, but unexecuted. For the conceptual activities of planning or carrying out of proposed undertakings or creations, use projects (artistic concepts).

Refers to terminal elements on which objects rest and that are small in relation to the body of the object. For relatively massive elements at the bottoms of structures or objects upon which the upper parts are supported, use "bases (components)."

Apparatus designed to manipulate the hand for physical therapy consisting of four clamps that are attached to the fingers, a palm rest and a crank. When cranked, the device moves the fingers in certain positions to increase their flexibility.
Particular areas into which a city or larger administrative entity are divided.

The process of covering a portion of the outside surface of the boards of a book with a material different from and contrasting with that already applied to the spine and part of the boards, as in half, quarter, and three-quarter binding.

Under the Charter of the United Nations, non-self-governing territories, primarily former mandates and colonies of the defeated powers of the Second World War, placed under the administrative authority of U.N. members and subject to regular inpection by U.N. missions.
Objects that occur in nature, not made by humans. Used primarily in the context of distinguishing man-made objects from natural objects.
In Indian art or architecture, an image; icon.

Objects routinely used by organizations, businesses, governments, or other corporate bodies in codified formal proceedings or ritual events. These objects sometimes serve to symbolize civic or corporate identities. This subclass does not include objects used to associate individuals with corporate bodies; these are organized under Personal Symbols.
Administrative bodies in the Islamic Middle East, often subject to an emir, or, as in the United Arab Emirates, a sheikh.
Textile made from silk fiber, which is a fiber derived from the cocoon of the silkworm moth.

Textiles produced by the Malay people in Southeast Asian countries, in which gold or silver coloured threads are woven into a base fabric, typically silk or cotton, creating raised patterns on the fabric. The textiles are usually decorated with geometric, floral or symbolic motifs which bear cultural meanings. Kain songket was historically worn only by royalty but has evolved to be worn as formal attire during festive events, traditional and religious occasions by Malays in Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.
Woven textile material characterized by a weave structure that uses a secondary or binding warp to bind the wefts that form the design, producing a double weave effect.
Intentionally leaving the marks of a tool on a surface, especially on leather or stone; produced during the finishing or dressing process.
Process or action of transforming a molecule into an isomer of itself, i.e. a molecule whose atoms remain the same but are differently arranged.

The action of joining two discontinuous lengths of material together into one, as in weaving together two ends of rope, making a joint in magnetic tape or film, or lapping two pieces of timber into a continuous length.
Removal of sizing from textiles.
The action of forming crystals, or a crystalline structure, through a purification process which takes place in many substances while cooling from a state of fusion or solution.
Used for objects, typically masks or figures, with two faces positioned front-to-back or side-to-side.
The quantity or mass of an object or material that occupies space.
In Indian architecture, a with three facets; tri-faceted (kumuda type); tri-faced.

The resolution of electronic imaging devices such as computer monitors, digital cameras, televisions, or scanners, expressed as the number of pixels per linear inch. Pixels per centimeter also describes the resolution of image files.
Characteristics and qualities that are related to the physical properties of the earth.

The capacity or tendency of a material to respond to light or similar radiation. Examples include inks, dyes, paper, fabric, glass, and other materials that undergo physical changes when exposed to light.
Jewish ritual instruments dating from Biblical times, consisting of a natural ram's or ibex horn, traditionally with no mouthpiece but simply a hole bored in the narrow end of the horn.

Zitherlike chordophones of Madagascar, varying regionally in form. The most common type is of bamboo with from seven to twenty strings raised at both ends by small bridges; the strings, traditionally cut from the outer layer of the bamboo, are nowadays of metal. They are plucked with the fingers while held in an upright position. For similar chordophones from Timor, use "sesandos."

Objects or sets of objects and supplies used for crafts, which may include pencils, shears, glue, and various forms of paper, often brightly colored. Used by children for hobby activities that involves making things skillfully with the hands.

Mechanized devices that utilize electrostatic applicators to adhere small fibers, or flocks, to a fabric's surface in order to create a soft, velvet-like finish. These devices facilitate the flocking process by electrically charging the flock particles causing them to attach to the fabric surface in an upright position, and then propelling and anchoring the particles into the adhesive at right angles. Through this process, these devices ensure that the flock application is both durable and permanent.

Refers to an embroidered or tapestry-woven inscription band in Islamic textiles, or fabric with an inscription band added in a technique different from the ground weave. Tiraz garments embroidered in silver or gold were a luxury good in Medieval Europe and are represented in portal sculptures on Chartres Cathedral.

An indication of the tribe, band, ethnic group, linguistic group, cultural group, civilization, religious group, nation, country, city-state, continent, or general region from which the work originated.
Tools and equipment used for sewing, which uses the process of joining, attaching, or decorating flexible materials with needle and thread.
Devices that grate ice into shavings via a perforated cylinder turned by mechanical action. Blocks of ice are pressed against the cylinder, shaving the ice when turned.
Devices used to keep milk cool in order to keep it from spoiling.
A class of instruments than can measure the quality or fact of being very small in diameter or thickness, often of fibers or particulate matter.

Tiddlywinks is a game where round chips or discs called "winks" have to be shot into a bin, pot or scoreboard. This is done by pressing a chip on the edge of another chip so that it jumps into the air.
Bibs placed below the chin during dental procedures to protect the patient's clothing and to maintain a sterile barrier.

Greek state religious festival that honored Athena. It was eventually celebrated every fourth year with great splendor, probably in deliberate rivalry to the Olympic Games. The festival consisted solely of the sacrifices and rites proper to the season (mid-August) in the cult of Athena, the city's protector. At the Great Panathenaea, representatives of all the dependencies of Athens were present, bringing sacrificial animals. After the presentation of a new embroidered robe to Athena, the sacrifice of several animals was offered. The great procession, which included the heroes of Marathon, is the subject of the frieze of the Parthenon. Musical contests were held, and portions of epic poems were recited, a long-standing accompaniment of the festival. The contests took place in the odeum, originally built for the purpose by Pericles himself.
Walking, dancing, or performing other balancing skills on a tightly stretched rope, wire, or wire cable for entertainment.
Method of acquiring property for temporary use under terms by which the party in possession of the property will pay a regular fee for having control of or occupying the property.
Titles or names that are used for a work or other entity in popular culture, but are not the official or repository title or name.
Strings of characters or numbers used to identify individual electronic resources online.
The standard unit of currency of France prior to adoption of the Euro.
Calendar of the Inca, comprising 12 months of 30 days, with each month having a festival.
Numbers or codes assigned to an individual person, used to identify the person and disambiguate him or her from other people. An example is a number used to validate electronic transactions.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 3999 to 3000 (or 4000 to 3001) Before Common Era.
Alcoholic beverage made from fermented grapes. The term has been used for beverages made from other fermented plants.
General term for knives used for cutting and working leather.

Dances involving rhythmical tapping of the toes and heels, in which a dancer wears shoes fitted with heel and toe taps that sound out audible beats when striking the floor or any other hard surface. Tap dances originated in the United States through the fusion of several ethnic percussive dances, primarily African tribal dances and Scottish, Irish, and English clog dances, hornpipes, and jigs.
Language family spoken in Colombia and Ecuador.

Instruments used to demonstrate the interference of sound, consisting of two U-tubes, one sliding into the other, with a Galton's whistle at one intersection of the tubes and a sensitive flame at the other. Air passes through the two bends of the tube to meet at the flame, and the flicker is analyzed against a scale on one of the tubes.
Linear, closed, and shallow depressions on the sea floor.

Hellenistic pottery characterized by the use of a combination of relief decoration and painted scenes, which are distinctive in depicting figures painted in various colors, imitating mural paintings. The name refers to a site at Centuripe, Sicily.
Artists that create works with the technology of copying machines.

Languages containing lexical and other features from two or more languages, characteristically with simplified grammar and a smaller vocabulary than the languages from which the pidgin language is derived. Pidgins have no native speakers, as the populations that use them during occasional trade contacts. The term originally referred to languages that developed out of sporadic and limited contacts between Europeans and non-Europeans.
Artists whose work aims chiefly at 'expression,' especially a visual artist, composer, writer, or other who exhibits the style or technique of Expressionism.
Actions or verbal expressions of scorn, derision, taunting, imitation, or hurtful mimicry.

Historical unit of measurement in France and other places, prior to the adoption of the metric system in the late 18th century. French units of measurement were based on the Carolingian system, in turn were based on ancient Roman measures. Equal to around 32.48 cm or around 1.066 feet.

Order of dicotyledonous flowering plants, consisting of 16 families, 112 genera, and nearly 2,500 species, encompassing a wide variety of plant types distributed throughout the world, including shrubs and trees, rock-garden plants, familiar garden ornamentals, and bushes that yield currants and gooseberries. It belongs to the core eudicots, and, although its phylogenetic position is not well resolved, it is probably sister to the Rosid group in the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group II botanical classification system.

Composite mythological creatures with the head and wings of a bird (usually that of an eagle) and the body and hind quarters of a lion. Was a favorite decorative motif in the ancient Middle Eastern and Mediterranean area, probably having originated in the Levant in the 2nd millennium BCE; the griffin had spread throughout western Asia and into Greece by the 14th century BCE. The Asiatic griffin had a crested head, whereas the Minoan and Greek griffin usually had a mane of spiral curls. It was shown either recumbent or seated on its haunches, often paired with the sphinx; its function was often protective. The Greeks believed griffins inhabited Scythia to keep jealous watch over the gold of that country.

Carbonated magnesium propylate dissolved in heptafluoropropane used in a nonaqueous impregnation process. The manufacturer distributes the formula as a deacidifying aerosol spray for mass deacidification in paper conservation.

Species of oak tree native to the southern Mediterranean, Morocco, and Asia Minor. The tannin extracted from the large acorn cups was used in the 18th century for tanning leather and for dyeing. The acorns, themselves called "valonia," are edible.
In Indian architecture, a female Jaina presiding deity.
Genus containing around 20 species in the legume family.
Species of white pine native to Japan, growing 15-25 m tall and typically as wide as it is tall. Needle-like leaves grow in bundles of five.

Institutions that maintain places where objects of value such as works of art, antiquities, scientific specimens, or other artifacts are housed and displayed for public benefit. An institution devoted to the procurement, care, documentation, study and display of objects of lasting interest or value.
Libraries, either general or specialized, that are organized for consultation and research; generally non-circulating.
Museums devoted to the art, history, and technology of motion pictures, television, and video.
The color of fabric stained by mauve dye, generally light shades of purple ranging between lilac and violet, but may also refer to deep purple tones.
Variable yellowish colors resembling the color of massicot, a pigment made of lead monoxide.

Color representing that portion of the spectrum that is intermediate between red and blue, with wavelengths between 380 and 420 nanometers. The term may refer to any of this group of colors that vary in lightness and saturation. Examples of violet color in nature are seen in certain plum fruits and in the bloom of the violet plant, Viola odorata. Violet is a secondary pigment color (made by combining blue and red). Spectral violet cannot be reproduced accurately in the RGB color model (used for computer screens).
Various colors ranging from reddish brownish gray to dark yellowish brown, from French and Latin words referring to the color of moleskin, which is the fur of the mole (animal).
Refers to a range of green colors resembling the green color used on some porcelain created during the Ming dynasty.
Variable orange colors resembling the color of xanthine, a secretion of various animal organs.

A style, particularly in the context of interior design, characterized by European or American antiques or replicas of antiques that that show evidence of wear and age, such as layers of paint that are worn and chipped and faded or muted fabrics. The style first developed in Britain. The term was coined in the "World of Interiors" magazine in the 1980s and has become a registered trademark for a US company.

A range of blue colors resembling the clear medium blues used in ceramics, named after the distinctive blue glazing used as backgrounds and other details in works by the studio of Renaissance ceramicist, Luca della Robbia.
Red slip ware produced in central, eastern, and southern Tunisia.
Members of an order containing cellulose-eating insects, the social system of which shows remarkable parallels with those of ants and bees, although it has evolved independently.

Names adopted by monarchs, popes, or other rulers during their reigns and by which they are subsequently referenced in history. Since ancient times, some monarchs have chosen to use a different name from their original name when they accede to the monarchy.
Order containing five species in one family in the northern hemisphere. Characterized as foot-propelled diving birds with webbed feet and pointed bills.
A gem or diamond cut style existing as early as the early fifteenth century. The natural octahedron was made flat on both the table and pavilion sides.

Palilin is a Kavalan family worship of ancestors held by female seniors during the new year celebration. In the tribe of Paterongan, Palilin takes on two forms known as the Kavalan and Torbuwan.The Kavalan-style palilin takes place at midnight on a date selected from December 26 to 28, with offerings including rak (“wine”) and sukue (“new year pastry”). Three rounds of libation should be poured, and the sukue is to be broken into smaller pieces while the prayer is being said as an act of offering. If there is a family member or friend visiting the household, the visitor should be invited to make his or her share of offering known as paspaw. The Torbuwan –style palilin underscores fasting and abstaining from sex. Spring onion, garlic, fish and pork are prohibited during this period. Before the ritual, the hostess should butcher a cock with a loud voice without shedding its blood as the sacrifice; on the following day only seaweed and fruits are allowed for consumption before noon. The cock may be eaten after the ritual is over.The difference between the two styles reflects the migration and evolution that the Kavalan culture has gone through, while both styles highlight continuity and sharing of blessing and good health through celebrating the new year.
Type of siding made from vinyl, often replicating the visual qualities of other materials such as stone or wood.

Objects originally created as distinct elements associated with sites, buildings, or parts of larger structures. Rather than functioning simply as parts of larger structures, site features are independent entities that complement other structures. This class includes such objects as birdbaths, flagpoles, gates, and fences.
General term for symbols having a religious context.

Equipment used for low-impact cardiovascular exercises. Consists of a base where two rotating platforms are attached and a handlebar; users use their feet to move the platforms and the handlebar for balance or added arm exercises.
Describes works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Nigeria.

Refers to views having a viewpoint well below normal eye level, typically depicted as if seen from the surface of the earth or the floor, as if the viewer is lying down and looking straight up. The horizon for a worm's-eye view is usually placed very low or outside the picture. For architectural drawings in precise perspective, use "worm's-eye perspectives."
Portrait to the knee, as opposed to a bust or full-length.

Indication of multiple materials being used for a group, set, or other configuration of multiple works, including visual works, audio works, written works, or other types of works. For the indication of multiple materials being used on one single work, use "mixed media."

Any hygroscopic additive used to promote moisture retention. Humectants are added to commercial products such as cosmetics, tobacco, baked goods, and to leather to restore suppleness. Glycerine is an example of a humectant.
The covering, usually wood boards, plywood, or wallboard, placed over the exterior studding or rafters of a building; provides a base for the application of wall or roof siding.

Organic chemical compounds capable of forming coordinate bonds with metals. Chelating agents are used to sequester or remove residual trace metal ions from materials to which they have attached. In a conservation context, uses of chelants include stabilizing of paper containing iron-gall ink, removal of iron residue from platinum prints; treatment of excavated copper objects.
Copolymer plastic composed of styrene and acrylonitrile that has high thermal resistance.

Material in the form of thin facing sheets intended to be used for a decorative purpose or to cover a cheaper material, glued to the surface of an inferior base material. Materials may include wood, brick, stone, plaster, ivory, tortoiseshell, brass, or other materials.

A type of handmade drawing paper that was textured and of high quality. It was a laid paper with a surface having rows of narrow parallel ridges on one side and a rougher, bumpy surface on the other side. A paper of this name is still produced by the Ingres paper mill, but scholars debate whether this paper is the same paper that was so prized by Seurat and other 19th-century artists.
Typically refers to strong paper usually made from mixed pulps that is used for packing or wrapping parcels.
Vegetable oil extracted from the ripe fruit of olive trees, and used mainly for food and cooking oil.
Natural fiber from the floss of the pod of the common milkweed. Compressed floss has a silky sheen and is added to nonwovens to enhance softness, insulating properties, absorbency, bulk.
Shingle or clapboard formed by splitting a short log into tapered radial sections.
General term for materials obtained from excretions from certain trees or shrubs. Natural resins are aromatic hydrocarbons that are generally soluble in alcohol or turpentine and insoluble in water.

One of the natural colorants extracted from madder roots and other Rubiaceae family plants. Purpurin forms a brilliant red color when mordanted with aluminum salts. It is not considered a permanent artists pigment.
Wood from any of species of the Sequoia genus or related genera.
Wood from any of various trees, usually pines or other conifers having reddish bark or wood.

Wood of the species Quercus lyrata, native to lowland wetlands in the southeastern United States, from Delaware and southern Illinois south to northern Florida and southeast Texas. It is used for flooring, furniture, and heavy construction.

General term used to refer to dense, compact dyewood from several (but not all) species of the Caesalpinia genus used in violins, bows, veneer, cabinetwork, and high quality furniture. It accepts a high polish. The wood contains the colorant brasilin, a hydroxyanthraquinone, that gives a deep red to brownish color.
Mixture of beeswax and lampblack used for making rubbings and polishing the shoes, particularly the edges of the soles.
A red and brown marble variegated with white dolomitic, quarried near Winooski, Vermont.
A bluish white marble that is slightly peppered brown and mottled; it is from Mount Lebanon, near Tyre (modern day Sur in Lebanon).

Refers to a strong organic acid derived from sorrel and other plants. A crystalline powder, oxalic acid lends itself to many commercial applications, principally as a bleaching agent and as a reducing agent to remove tarnish, rust and ink stains. In art manufacture and conservation, further uses include removal of paint and varnish, and cleaning of encrustations from sculptures and paintings.
A soft, aluminum-containing ore; it is an impure mineral that contains hydrous aluminum oxides and aluminum hydroxides. It is named for one location where it was mined, Baux, France, near Arles.

Pure metallic element having symbol Mn and atomic number 25; hard, brittle, silvery metal. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials.
Type of glass made from the inclusion of uranium in the batch and yellowish-green or greenish yellow in color.
Glass that is made by continuous drawing of the molten glass by a series of rolls on automatic machinery.

A hard, strong construction material comprising a mixture of sand, gravel, crushed rock, or other aggregate, held together, typically by a hardened paste of cement and/or lime. Several types of aggregate are used such as crushed stone, slag, cinders or gravel. Ancient Romans developed pozzolan cement about the 3rd century BCE. Modern concretes use various cements such as portland or hydraulic. Concrete is durable and relatively inexpensive, used for foundations, bridges, dams, walls, and highways. Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension so it is often reinforced with steel bars or wire netting. Once a concrete mixture is stirred with water and poured into a mold, it is allowed to cure slowly over about a week. Stresses, such as vibration, freezing, and rapid drying, will diminish the strength and durability of the concrete. As it ages, concrete is subject to erosion, spalling, and pollution. Poor mixing can cause erosion. Spalling can be due to freeze-thaw cycles of moisture and ice, salt crystallization, or corrosion of steel reinforcements. Acid rain can deplete the natural alkaline reserve of fresh concrete.
Conventionalized figures derived from astronomical stars, having radiating points of any number.
Crosses having a hook or bend in the end, ranging from a small point-like hook to a larger bend, as in the swastika.
Refers to shell-like motifs, especially of the Rococo period.

In Indian architecture, a temple-type having three sancta for enshrining the trinity (Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu/Sūrya, usually sharing a common hall); hall-temple enshrining the trinity Brahmā/Sūrya, Śiva, Viṣṇu
In Indian architecture, a symbolic representation of Jina’s three ramparted place of preaching as a structure with three concentric ramparts with fourfold images of Jina in Majesty.
Buildings housing churches that are under direct jurisdiction of the monarch rather than the ecclesiastical hierarchy.
In Indian architecture, a liṅga-shaped shrine-type described in early śilpa texts.

Rooms or offices where medical and paramedical professions, particularly those of general practitioners, are practiced, patients examined, and treatment prescribed. Originally, these may have been in private houses, now most often they are offices in urban districts.
Distinctive structures typically used as fortified collective storage bins or communal refuges in Berber settlements.
Buildings housing academic enterprises that prepare educators.
Buildings on a college campus dedicated to social and organizational activities of the student body.
Buildings that house businesses that sell or make jewelry.
Built works whose purpose is centered around the housing of, and the dissemination of, information.
Structure for the storage of harvested potatoes or sweet potatoes.
Buildings or spaces designed or used for audio recording, typically conforming to special acoustical requirements and having specialized equipment.
Refers to those areas of a church situated behind the high altar; often found in English Medieval architecture.

Meaning, literally, a "plaque" (-holding) "commemorative monument,"  paifang is a structure that functions to commemorate virtuous people and actions, markoff an area, and/or delineate space. Paifang adopt a wide variety of forms and are made of wood, stone, or brick. They are usually composed of two or more pillars connected by tie beams, which are covered by roofs called lou 樓. Paifang are often erected on streets and bridges, as well as near buildings such as government offices, schools, ancestral halls, temples, and tombs.  The name of each paifang and the reason for its establishment were often inscribed on a plaque affixed to the tie beam and were sometimes inscribed directly onto the tie beam itself.
Rooms or spaces that serve as storage places for valuable objects. For buildings designed for this purpose use 'treasuries (buildings).'

Posts, often fitted with horizontal rods, that enclose the ends of Christian altars, from which curtains are hung. The riddel posts may be surmounted by candleholders or sculptures of angels with instruments of the Passion.
In Indian architecture, a band, register; broad rectangular fillet.

Seen in the Yingzao fashi (1103 CE), referring to squared beams (fang 方) carved with bracket-arms in low relief, layered within the wall plane above pillar tops. Also called “superficial bracket arms” (fubigong).

In Indian architecture, basal wall-mouldings consisting primarily of khura, kumbha, kalaśa, sometimes  antarapaṭṭa, and kapōtapālī/kapōtapālikā (North Indian type); aggregate of five mouldings — khura, kumbha, kalaśa, antarapaṭṭa, and kapōtapālī — in the base or lower section of the wall of North Indian and a few Karṇāṭan temples; pābhāga (Oriyā).
In Indian architecture, a minor niche with Saṁvaraṇā roof; bell-topped miniature niche; a sort of Phāṁsa-kūṭa, carved (generally in series) on door-lintels, āsanapaṭṭa’s exterior face, etc.
Vertical slitlike windows; often found in Medieval structures.
In Indian architecture, a peripheral screen wall with lamps.

Horizontal bands of masonry, generally narrower than other courses, extending across the face of a wall and in some instances continuing across piers or engaged columns; may be flush or projecting and may be flat surfaced, molded, or otherwise shaped.
Nonstructural ceilings suspended below the overhead structural slab or from the structural elements of a building, and not bearing on the walls.
Columns shaped from a single block of stone.
Capitals in which the four sides are shaped into a series of curves resembling truncated cones.

Class of circular or radiating boulder outlines built by ancient North American Indian peoples of the Great Plains. These enigmatic archaeological features are believed to have some religious, astronomical, territorial, or calendrical significance.
Complexes planned or used for multiple purposes.
Books or other documents containing organized, prescriptive instructions regarding a certain procedure, activity, or topic.
People who are organized and united in purpose due to mutual or common activities or interest.
Groups convened to develop and promote standards for any particular technical field.
Personages holding high rank or office.
People who are attending school, or otherwise engaged in study.
Refers to enthusiasts of cinema: persons knowledgeable about motion pictures or filmmaking. Not used for people engaged in creating films such as directors, cinematographers, etc.
Authors who specialize in writing manuals, descriptions, reports, proposals, or other technical documentation, usually highly specialized or concerned with practical applications.
People who prepare the set for a film, theater production, etc. with props and furniture.
Refers to people who are actively involved in politics, particularly party politics, or, more specifically, to people who hold or seek political office.
Lords who are superior in rank to other lords or rulers, such as a supreme feudal superior.
Artisans who specialize in creating decorative borders, particulaly on framing mats.

People or corporate bodies who specialize in designing tapestries, which are heavy, woven textiles incorporating a design or scene, and used as wall hangings, curtains, upholstery, or for other purposes.
Individuals who purchase, use, and dispose of goods and services, the ultimate clientele of manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers, and service providers.
Officials, usually architects, who superintend building operations for a city, state, or project; typically used in historical connotations.
Artists who make zincographs, which are engraved or etched designs on zinc, or prints from such designs.
People who have left office, employment, or service permanently, especially when the person is older, has reached pensionable age.
Those design architecture, but have not completed the requirements for architectural registration, including having a valid license.

Short backswords, bayonets or choppers with a saw-back. Used by practically all armies during the 19th century, more often as a tool than as a weapon. Some fighting and survival knives are made as saw-backed knives.
Compressible piece of packing material (as of rubber) used to seal a joint and make it water- or airtight.

Tools in the shape of a nippers or pliers used to trim glass to a particular shape, as in making stained glass or sizing window glass. The tool is typically used after the glass has been scored to allow a neat trim.
Instruments used specifically for dissection of animals or plants for the purpose of scientific examination.
Historical term for telescopes, each equipped with a graduated circle, by which the right ascension and declination of stars can be observed in transit.
Tools used for various purposes but especially to set the teeth of saws, and in sheet metal work, hand tools used to shape material to the desired form.
Any opaque material used to block light or chemistry from exposing photosensitized material.
Motor-powered, portable pumps which feed plaster into a hose and onto the surface to be plastered without the use of hawks or trowels.
Use with reference to the 19th-century movement in photography.

Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Sultan Ibrahim, who ruled from 1640 to 1648. His best-known monument is the elegant, gilded, cupola-like 'bower' on the terrace of the Topkapi Palace. Ibrahim was a violent ruler who was assassinated in 1648.
Style of buildings that were constructed before 1939, arising during a population boom in Europe in the 1880s.

Refers to the ancient Greek period, culture, and art of ancient Greece that lasted from about 330 BCE to 31 BCE, when Augustus defeated Cleopatra and Mark Antony. It is characterized by an international culture that was ushered in by Alexander the Great's conquest of India, Egypt, and the Near East. In architecture and art, the style is marked by greater sophistication, complexity, and diversity than was known in earlier Greek styles. Architecture diverges from strict rules of earlier periods. Sculptors emphasized more realistic figures in a greater variety of poses than in earlier Greek art.

Culture and period of ancient Troy, associated with excavations at Hisarlık, Turkey. The nine major periods of ancient Troy are labeled I to IX, starting from the bottom with the oldest settlement, Troy I.
Refers to the style and culture of the area of southern Mesopotamia known as Sumer, now in modern Iraq, from at least 3500 to about 2000 BCE.

Refers to the style and period of the early Angkor empire associated with the rule of King Yashovarman I (889-900 CE). The style of this period is characterized by the prominence of religious temples as city centers and the embryonic development of the temple into five-tiered pyramid structures built of sandstone, surmounted by sandstone tower-sanctuaries in quincuncial arrangements, and featuring subsidiary shrines, libraries, galleries, and gopuras. Temples of this period also developed into complex structures whose design featured Indian-influenced chronological symbolism and seasonal cycles. Decorative arts and sculpture in the period exhibited the endeavors of Yashovarman I to represent his kingdom as a model of the cosmos and symbolic center of the world. Sanctioned artistic productions featured high relief sculptures of guardian figures and celestial beings and bas relief carvings of foliage swirls and jewel bands that surround figures of deities.

Central European Neolithic culture and style that probably developed from the influx of Neolithic peoples into Mesolithic cultures, and spread quickly from the Hungarian plain to Slovakia, Czech lands, Austria, Germany, Poland, the Low Countries, and eastern France between ca. 5,400 and ca. 4,900 BCE. It is characterized by the introduction of farming, animal husbandry, large longhouses, chipped stone tools, and distinctive pottery decorated with incised bands of lines, strokes, and indentations. "Bandkeramik" is sometimes used interchangeably with "Linienbandkeramik," however, according to traditional classification the latter is a variety of the former. "Danubian" was formerly more commonly used to refer to this culture, though "Bandkeramik" is more often used by modern scholars.
Chalcolithic culture active ca. 1500 BCE in Maharashtra.

The name given to naive narrative paintings of folk tales and religious subjects presented in illustrated books and scrolls that emerged in 16th century Japan. These are considered a popularized version of the Tosa style, and are characterized by a simplicity and a lack of illusionistic rendering.

Refers to the style of stoneware produced during the Momoyama and early Tokugawa periods. The style is characterized mainly by tea ceremony ware produced in the Seto region with rough surfaces and warm colored, simple glazes.

Refers to the the culture, style, and period associated with the reign of the Quing dynasty, dating from 1644 to 1911. Beijing remained the Chinese capital and was embellished with large scale, brightly colored buildings in brick and stone. In ceramics, contrasting styles of elaborate, opaque overglaze wares and monochrome wares were developed. In painting, an official academy was established, continuing the traditional landscape style of the Four Wangs.

Refers to a style of Chinese painting, the ideals of which were formulated in the eleventh century, though the tradition is evident from at least the tenth century to the twentieth century. It was created by scholars and gentlemen, as opposed to professional painters or craftsmen, for a small, well-educated audience. It is characterized by the combination of painting, poetry, and calligraphy, with a preference for subtle brushwork, monochromatic or subdued coloring, high literary content, and the abstraction of natural forms to convey highly personal views of nature. It inspired the Japanese "Nanga" style.
The culture of Americans of Italian descent.

Refers to the movement, centered mostly in the American Midwest among architects, notably Louis Sullivan and Frank Lloyd Wright, united by the rejection of revivalist styles and by the development of a new architectural vision based on the faithful expression of the natural qualities of a region or nation. The style generally favored elongated horizontal arrangements that blended naturally with the open American landscape.
Refers to the style and culture of the St'át'imc, an Interior Salish people indigenous to the southern interior of British Columbia, with many located in the town of Lillooet.

Refers to the style and culture of the Muscogee (also known as Creek), an indigenous people of the southeastern United States, and whose ancestral lands spans parts of present-day states Tennesee, Alabama, Georgia, and Florida.

Style and culture of a Native American tribe from coastal Virginia. Historically a member of the Powhatan paramountcy and ally to the Jamestown colonists. Today they are a state-recognized tribe known as the "Patawomeck Indian Tribe of Virginia."
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Tanzania and Zambia.
Style and culture of the Berber people of the same name living in the Aurès Mountains of Algeria.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting western Ethiopia.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in Kenya and in Uganda northeast of Lake Victoria.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Kenya and Uganda.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Democratic Republic of Congo and Angola.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting the Jos Plateau in northern Nigeria.

Refers generally to the belief that God only works in a person who is completely quiet and passive; religious followers should therefore withdraw from the everyday world and suppress their will. It also refers more specifically to forms of Christian mysticism, particularly to trends in the Middle Ages and 17th-century controversies in Spain and France.

Doctrine, practice, or attitude of one who destroys religious images or opposes their veneration. Use also for the specific period of Byzantine history. For opposition to the use of idols generally, use "aniconism."
Skill and diligence in working, often involving intellect, cleverness, ingenuity, exertion, and effort; the quality or practice of applying hard work or assiduity in the performance of a task.
Monetary assistance, generally used to support people or causes.
Secret organizations resisting authority, especially in occupied countries; most applicable to the underground movement to resist the Axis forces during World War II.

A form of government in which the political authority exercises absolute and centralized control over all aspects of life, the individual is subordinated to the state, and opposing political and cultural expression is suppressed.

The standing or position of affairs, according to the law, of a person, site, object, conceptual work, other thing, or activity. Included with status are often designated and defined various privileges, protections, obligations, restrictions, or powers. Examples could include the status of a building as private property, or the status of a person as citizen of a given nation.
The human ability to perceive specific or meaningful images in random or ambiguous visual patterns.

The condition in which different levels of caste, class, privilege, or status make up a society. A person's strata may be ascribed at birth or achieved. Factors involved in social stratification include gender, race, age, wealth, family relationships, education, occupation, marital status, and language.

Lists of the signatures of which books are compiled, often printed at the end of early printed books, particularly those printed in Italy, to asssist the binder in assembling and collating complete copies.
Use with regard to photography in war for the purposes of historical documentation. For military applications of photography, such as for mapping or training, use "military photography."
Refers to the study of the nature, collection, and management of data and information in automated environments.
Field of archaeology that recovers, preserves, and analyzes data from human settlements in order to study the history of city life.
Refers to the analytical technique which uses an instrument, a profilometer,to evaluate irregularities of a surface; e.g., measuring gloss and surface roughness of paint films.
The art or process of providing drawings or other pictures intended to elucidate a description, story, or other written material, usually in a book or periodical.
The removal of granulation by scraping or friction; in painting refers especially to the creation of forms and textures by scraping a wet painted surface.
The use of a vacuum cleaner to clean objects or surfaces by suction.
Refers to creation of molds for casting purposes. For the process of making a positive from material pressed into the mold use "molding," or "casting" for objects cast from liquid.
The process or activity of hurting, injuring, or otherwise causing damage, often in a way results in the lessening or loss of value of a thing.
Devices in which electromagnetic radiation is generated by a potential at a junction between two types of material, upon absorption of radiant energy.

Fittings or devices so designed and constructed as to provide, when properly vented, a liquid seal that will prevent the back passage of air without materially affecting the flow of sewage or waste water.
Tongue-and-groove joints between two matchboards, which are boards having a tongue cut along one edge and a groove cut along the other edge.
Nails of galvanized steel, aluminum alloy, or coated steel, often having a threaded shank.
Nails having with sharp points and flat shanks.
Strap hinges that form an "H" when open, and with the joint in the crossbar.
Door locks applied to the surface of a door with its strike applied to the face of the jamb.
Freestanding, cast brass shrine figures, symbols of the Ogboni society of the Yoruba people of Nigeria; they often occur in pairs. The name literally means "owners of the earth."

Monolithic stone figures carved of volcanic tuff, a soft volcanic stone. On average, the moai sculptures stand 13 feet high and weigh 14 tons. The moai represent the Easter Island ancestral chiefs whose supernatural power protected the community. The common structure of the moai consists of a trunk, engraved, inset arms and an angular head. Monumental moai figures are the most common and well known of Easter Island art, although various sizes and styles of moai do exist.
Coats made from nettles in postclassic central Mexico. Dyed black, lined in five places with eagle down balls, it was part of the array of Huitzilopochtli. Literally in nahuatl, "nettle mantle".

Lightweight outerwear garments with full or partial front openings, loosely sized to fit easily over other garments or layers. Typically constructed with features made to resemble shirts, such as turndown collars, button or zipper fasteners, and cuffs. Often feature unshaped hem finishes and are not designed to be tucked in.

Contemporary sculptural works that are composed of figures and objects arranged into a picturelike scene, which the viewer does not enter. For works that create surroundings that the viewer can enter, use "environments (sculpture)." For the silent, immobile arrangements of one or more costumed performers to reproduce a scene from art, drama, literature, history, or the imagination, use "tableaux (performances)."
Headdresses of the later Egyptian pharaohs, combining the white crown of Upper Egypt with the red crown of Lower Egypt.
Men's felt hats with a soft crown dented lengthwise and a slightly rolled brim.
Eight-inch plates, variously shaped, a size between dinner plates and muffin plates.

Small wine glasses of distinctive shape and size, designed for drinking port, a type of sweet, dark red fortified wine, originally from Portugal. Port glasses have a round foot, a stem, and small bowl of any of several shapes; in a set of glasses having similar-shaped bowls, a port glass is distinguished by being smaller than the sherry glass, but not so small as the liqueur glass.

Three-stringed fiddles of southern Afghanistan, India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, having a short unfretted neck surmounted by a pegbox and a deeply waisted body of irregular shape with a skin belly over the lower part, on which rests a wood bridge. They are played held upright, with a heavy, curved bow.
Keys used to wind the movements of timepieces.

Prints that are embellished with metallic leaf, spangles, or pieces of fabric. Examples are known since the 15th century, but the most common examples are 19th century popular plain or hand-colored prints representing theatrical figures.
Stands with pegs, hooks, or other devices for hanging hats, often also with places for coats or umbrellas. More elaborate and more likely to be freestanding furniture than "hat racks."
Multipurpose commodelike desks containing a set of drawers which could be mechanically raised from the back section of the piece.
Tables fitted with medical apparatus for doctors' use in examining patients.
Cabinets with the interior divided into nests of small drawers for holding spices.
Miniature chests consisting of innumerable small drawers for holding spices; intended to be placed on a table or chest of drawers.
Racks comprising a frame with compartments for holding bottles of wine.
Refers to beds in the shape of a shallow basket, primarily found during the period of the French Restoration in the early 19th century.

Large upright pieces of furniture fitted with hooks, pegs, or rods, used for hanging clothes, generally with two large doors and perhaps a drawer or drawers below. Although there may be a shelf in a wardrobe, the term is typically distinct from "clothes presses," in which clothes are stored exclusively on shelves rather than hanging.
Chairs whose backs are comprised of framed cylindrical bars or "spindles."
English type of upholstered armchair with wings and an arched top making a niche to screen the occupant from drafts; made from the mid-18th century onwards.

Armchairs with large backs which are hinged so that they can be swung forward to rest on the arms, converting the piece into a table. Chairs of this type were made from the Middle Ages to the late 17th century in Europe and until the late 19th century in America.
Lamps that employ mechanics or machinery in their design.
Transparent devices often of gelatin or glass which are placed in front of a light source and serve to diminish the intensity or alter the color of the light.
Light double-edged swords having a simple cross hilt with small quillons and sometimes a side ring. They were used chiefly in the third quarter of the 17th century.
A type of dagger or sword popular throughout the Ottoman Empire distinguished by a single-edged blade that curves slightly inward and by a hilt with no guard and two flared wings at the pommel.
Fasteners that are designed for impact insertion, usually slender, pointed, and headed.
Drawings made using as medium a metal wire or rod, usually in a holder, to make marks on a prepared support of paper, parchment, or wood support, or on ivory.
Printed numerals, letters, or symbols irregularly occurring in the lower margins of some hand-pressed books for the purpose of recording press practice.
Copies made by light-sensitive processes, often the diazo process, usually of line drawings, in which black or colored lines appear on a white background.
Collections of documents associated with the assessment and payment of taxes, including tax returns, tax bills, and warrant books.
Ledger-style documents that record tribute given by individuals or communities to a ruler, religious institution, government, or other entity. Examples are found in many ancient cultures.
Small, thin instruments with usually tapered edges and rounded or tapered ends used for folding, smoothing, burnishing, and other operations.
Axes, typically having a metal or stone head mounted to a wooden shaft, used for chopping, cutting, smoothing, and otherwise working wood.
Costume and manner of dressing required by custom or etiquette for certain occasions or times of day.

Members of a profession that emerged during the Middle Ages when the practice of surgery was not taught in universities. Barbers were called in by physicians in cases where razors or blood letting was deemed necessary. The organization of the United Company of Barber Surgeons of London in 1540 began the evolution toward qualifications for those who performed operations. This guild was the precursor of the Royal College of Surgeons of England.
Persons who believe in pacifism or are opposed to war or violence of any kind.

Ceramic ware of the late Middle Bronze Age first excavated at Tell el-Yahudiyeh in the eastern Nile Delta of Egypt, but of uncertain origin. The ware, generally black or brown juglets with incised or punctured decoration filled in with white chalk, are widely distributed in a large number of Levantine and Cypriot sites.
The concept that a spiritual being or deity may take human or other physical form.
Photographic prints that have been developed by using the sun as a light source, or prints that have been overexposed to light during development, resulting in bronze-tone shadows.
Blocks of blank or ruled paper bound together for the purposes of notetaking.
Maps that display area boundaries of zip codes.
General term for documents that have the function of declaring, setting forth, explaining, or affirming something, such as facts, laws, intentions, and many other topics.
Engaging in a temporary stoppage of work in order to bring about compliance with demands.
Modifier describing a color of high intensity and high to medium value, typically of a higher intensity than "brilliant."

Texts associated with exhibitions or other displays in museum galleries, usually displayed on the walls or in handouts. Gallery texts typically give the context of the works in the context of importance or history. For the short texts displayed with the work, listing title, artist, date, etc., prefer "tombstones (documents)."
For positional attributes of three-dimensional works or the illusionistic space of a composition, referring to the viewer's lower right-hand side of the work or composition.
Films paid for by a company or an organization for promotional purposes or communication.
Used to distinguish photographs that are created from the original negative or other master image, as distinguished from reproductive copies of original photographs.

Refers to a bobbin-made lace that is characerized by simple geometric patterns and relatively coarse designs. It typically made by peasants in many European countries; it is noted as one of the mainstays of the lace makers of the Austrian Tirol and as the type of lace on which apprentices generally begin learning lace-making.

Refers to a movement formed of a group of Austrian artists active in the 1960s. The style is characterized by violent and disturbing forms of expression such as actions or happenings, often involving nudity, blood, and the destruction of animal corpses.

A large group of around 20,000 species of flowerless, seedless vascular plants having true roots from a rhizome and fronds that uncurl upward, reproducing by spores. The ferns are an ancient lineage of plants, dating back to at least the Devonian; during the Palaeozoic, tree-ferns grew several meters tall. The ferns include three living groups (Marattiales, Ophioglossales, and leptosporangiate ferns) and two or more extinct groups. An additional group, the Psilotales, is tentatively included in the ferns, although the group is vastly different from living ferns and its relationships are uncertain. The ferns group is also referred to as Polypodiophyta or Polypodiopsida when classified as a subdivision of tracheophyta (vascular plants).
Expressing opinion or choice in a matter by some specific means, such as casting a ballot or raising a hand, among a group of other voters.
In Indian architecture, a lotus frieze; string-course with half-lotuses in series.
Material comprising the stem or main axis of a plant.
In India and other locations, mansions or palaces, or other buildings or sets of buildings used by certain organizations devoted to a particular activity, group, or concern.
Ancient Mesopotamian temple towers in the form of stepped pyramids.
Inhabited places in which a government, ruling house, or court is established or set up over a region or realm; often also the capital of the region or realm.
General term for any tool or instrument having a handle surmounted by prongs, usually two to six in number, used for digging, lifting, or securing food, earth, or many other substances.
Objects that are in the possession of one party, and transferred to another party without the expectation or receipt of an equivalent.
Nationality, style, or culture of Milan, Lombardy, Italy.
Generally, a class of hydrocarbons found  in the volatile oils of plants, especially the coniferous and aurantiaceous orders. Most  common is the chief constituent of turpentine, pinene.
Division of human prehistory into three ages: the Stone Age, the Bronze Age, and the Iron Age.

Refers to the culture of the modern nation of the United Kingdom. It also refers to the cultures of historical nations that had Great Britain as the central ruling power. For the culture of the ancient Britons, who were those tribes that spoke the Celtic (Brythonic) language, use "Ancient British."
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Kansas.

Ancient period, style, and culture dating from ca. 3200-2500 BCE in Tuscany and Latium. It is characterized by the development of copperworking, using minerals extracted from the Colline Metallifere. The type site for the culture is Rinaldone, Lazio.
In Indian architecture, resembling South Indian temple-type.

General term for vernacular forms of construction using entire logs. One of the oldest known methods of construction, log construction has been used for dwellings, fortifications, churches, bridges. Log walls are produced by stacking logs and filled with mud or other insulating materials. Structures made of logs are characterized by corner joints that interlock with a cross-lap connection, or with dovetailing.
Refers to the main rooms of ancient Greek houses and for similar rooms in ancient Roman houses used as reception areas.
A non-destructive testing method that is a form of themographic inspection involving imaging of the thermal patterns on a sample surface heated by a brief pulse of light.

Specifically the liberal Protestant denomination active in the United States and Canada, starting first as an organized movement in the 18th century and achieving denominational status in the 19th century. Its basic and defining belief was in the salvation of all souls, rejecting the Calvinist doctrine of the election of a few and the damnation of many. Other principles included the freedom of individual interpretation, tolerance of diversity, and the inherent worth and dignity of all human beings. In 1961 it merged with "Unitarianism" to form a new denomination "Unitarian Universalism." Use also generally for the doctrine of universal salvation that has appeared at various times in Christian history, starting with the writings of Origen in the third century.
The process or function of inserting material, typically used for material or data that was typed by hand.

Beliefs of the indigenous ancient Egyptians from predynastic times (4th millennium BCE) to the disappearance of the traditional culture in the first centuries CE. It included a complex system of polytheistic beliefs and rituals, focused on interaction with many deities who were believed to be present in, and in control of, the forces and elements of nature.
Examining the particulars in an attempt to learn the facts about something hidden, unique, or complex.
In Indian architecture, a pinnacle, crest.
Use to designate the elements connecting the central block with the outlying wings of a building of five-part Palladian form.

Games that require players to solve or navigate a challenge to progress to another more difficult challenge. These are usually single-player games, but may involve multiple players depending on the game type.
Giving or letting out a thing or funds for temporary use.
Occasions of the selection or drawing off of an individual from a larger group for some special purpose, most often for military service, but also found in sports.
Actions or processes surrounding the conferring of holy orders, or otherwise appointing or admitting a person to the ministry of a priesthood of the Christian church another another religion.

In Indian architecture, an unworked lower section of door-jamb; lower section of door-jamb bearing guardian and acolytic figures; lower block of door-jambs (often carved with figures of river-goddesses and door guardians); basal section of the aggregate of śākhā-doorjambs.
Of people or animals, the state or attribute of being savagely cruel or destructive.
The introduction of or condition of having harmful or otherwise undesirable substances or products in the environment; for the substances themselves use "pollutants."
All existing matter, space, time, and energy regarded collectively.

Genre including physical objects that are that are meant to be perceived primarily through the sense of sight, are of high quality, requiring refined skill in creation, and typically using the media of painting, drawing, or sculpture. It may also refer to architecture and design. Although there is overlap, fine art is generally distinguished from other art forms based on the media, extent of skill, and the level of formal training required. It is distinct from "decorative art" in that the fine arts are art in which the aesthetic or intellectual expression is more prominent than the utilitarian purpose. It is distinct from "crafts," which are handiworks of media such as ceramics, glass, needlework, or any medium other than painting, drawing, sculpture, or architecture. It is also distinct from "commercial art," which is created to serve commerce such as in advertisements or illustration. Avoid using "fine art" in a broader sense, to include the arts of poetry, music, and filmmaking.
The quality or state of a substance or body of transmitting light without appreciable scattering so that things lying beyond are entirely visible.
Describes the relationship between various masses or volumes of a building or structure.

A smooth, rounded shape that is convex on both sides; that is, the shape of a long oval that is indented on one side. Named for the shape of the glandular organs situated in the abdominal cavity, especially those of humans, cattle, sheep, and pigs.
The study and application of the methodological principles of interpretation and explanation; specifically the general principles of Biblical interpretation.

Theory that there are no universal essences in reality, that the mind can frame no single concept or image corresponding to any universal or general term, and that only individual concrete entities have existence.
Wooden or plastic disks, 6 inches in diameter and 1 inch thick, of various colors used in the game of shuffleboard.

Long, cloth skirts, often ankle-length, decorated with brightly colored ribbons. Primarily worn by Native North American women as everyday wear and as ceremonial garments. Ribbons are usually sewn in parallel bands near the hem, either overlapping or with thin margins between each ribbon. Likely developed from ribbonwork created by Native women during the 18th-19th centuries with French trade silk.

Loose, ankle-length trousers that are gathered or otherwise relatively tight around the ankles. They are worn by both men and women in India and Southeast Asia; often worn with a tunic-like over-garment.

Turbans worn especially in India, often of light material and with one end left hanging down in back. Also narrow lengths of cloth, usually of light material, worn around a helmet or hat and often with a piece left hanging down in back to protect the wearer's neck from the sun.
Garments for toddler-age children that are intended to ease the transition from diapers to toilet training.
Strings which guide and support children who are learning to walk.  Sometimes in the form of reinforced cloth attached to the shoulders and hanging to the ankles.
The characteristic script of Spain from the 8th to the 12th century, developed from the later Roman cursive.

Blanketlike garments, usually square or oblong with a slit in the center for the head, originating in South America. Also, similar garments used elsewhere, including those made of water-repellent fabric and usually having a hood, and when not worn, used as a blanket or tarpaulin.
Food service accessories used to hold a name card to indicate table seating arrangements. Often takes the form of a decorative loop or clip.
Ancient Greek coins valued at three obols or one half of a drachma.
Small silver coins of Germany and German-speaking territories issued from at least the 13th century until the 19th century in Germany and then as a copper coin in Austria into the 20th century.

The official monophonic unison chants, originally unaccompanied, of Christian liturgies. Music was developed for voice, based on a system of modes and performed in free rhythm corresponding at least in part to the accentuation of the words, though often with considerable elaboration of the melody. In usuage, often applied chiefly to the music of the Western Church, particularly chants of the 4th-century St. Ambrose and in the 6th-century by St. Gregory the Great.

A liturgical document such as the 'Synodikon of Orthodoxy.' read aloud at particular feasts, especially in the Eastern Orthodox Church. It can also refer to a letter written from one patriarch to another to circulate the decrees of a patriarchal synod, or council. More broadly, it is a declaration signed by members of a synod, affirming decisions.
Boards often of wood and sometimes of plastic or other synthetic material, used as firm surfaces for cutting food.
Relatively large vessels used for boiling or cooking; examples include wide, metal vessels with side handles, a bail handle, a lid, and sometimes small feet.

Rings, usually of plain gold or another precious metal, placed by the bridegroom on the finger of the bride as part of the marriage ceremony, and worn by her ever after to signify her marital status. In contemporary Western practice, the ring is placed on the third finger of the bride's left hand, and such a ring is similarly presented by the bride to the bridegroom, and worn afterwards by him. A bride's wedding ring may be, but is not necessarily, conjuncted with an engagement ring after the marriage.
Vessels for cooking or coddling eggs. For containers with a tight-fitting lid, and often an insert with separate wells, used to poach eggs, use "egg poachers."
Written compositions in which two or more characters are represented as conversing.

Covered vessels for brewing and serving tea, usually with one spout, which is often long and gracefully curved, and, on the opposite side of the vessel, one handle, and sometimes small feet. Distinguished from "teakettles" which usually have a short pouring spout, a bail handle, and a broad, flat bottom, and are used for heating water from which tea is made.
Cups or bowls made from the fruit of a calabash tree, or made of other materials to resemble such vessels.
Accessories comprlsing a saucer or small platter with a ring on the surface to hold in place a cup of hot chocolate.
See mānasūtra.

Cases designed to hold portrait photographs, usually daguerreotypes or ambrotypes. The case was customarily made of leather or another material, hinged, opening like a book, with velvet or another covering applied to the interior surface facing the image, and the outside surfaces decorated with relief designs. The design was patented in the United States by Samuel Peck in 1854.
Vessels with turned-in rim, high foot, and lid used for holding perfume for both personal use and religious rites.
Rectangular containers made to hold checkbooks, variously made of fabric or leather.
Relatively narrow, or constricted parts of containers, such as the slender portion of a bottle or vase between the mouth and the shoulders.
Containers for use in a kitchen, or for cooking.
Graduated pitchers marked for measuring liquids.

Basic organizational units of the comic. Often arranged sequentially, with an individual panel depicting a singular moment in the story. Panels may also be arranged in tabular fashion and vary in size to break up visual monotony and vary narrative emphasis.

Large baskets, bags, or boxes, often used in pairs, used for transporting objects. These may be carried by a beast of burden; on a person's shoulders or by hand, or mounted on bicycles or automotive vehicles.

Distinctive cantir-type containers originating in the Mapuche culture, having two openings, often of terracotta, and often in the form of animals. The vessels may be used for liquids; occasionally also to make music.
Nationality, styles, and culture of Qatar, on the Arabian Peninsula, on the west coast of the Persian Gulf.
Refers to linked stitches, often chain stitches, made by hand at the head and tail of a text block, joining each gathering to the one next to it.
Baskets used to winnow or separate threshed grain.

Used by modern scholars to refer to ancient Greek large, round-bottomed bowls that curve into a wide, open mouth, and that often stood on a stand. Metal vessels of this shape were probably used for cooking and those made of terracotta were used for mixing wine and date from the mid-seventh through the late fifth centuries BCE. They are distinguished from "lebetes" by their larger size. Some scholars hold that ancient literary evidence suggests that the term was originally applied to drinking cups rather than bowls, and that such bowls were at that time called "lebetes."
Wobbly, saucer-shaped coins; struck during the Byzantine period, especially in the 11th through the 13th centuries, and in India.
Use to describe items of clothing made by a tailor or having the appearance of being made by a good tailor.
Representations of the fall of cloth, as depicted in visual art.
Works in two dimensions or very low relief that were made by gluing paper, fabrics, photographs, or other materials onto a flat surface

Works in any medium of the visual arts that explore a subject or are preliminary to a separate, more finalized work; more finished than sketches. For representations or diagrams that clarify, usually accompanying a text, use "illustrations."
In Indian architecture, a dancing Śiva figure set in śukanāsa’s great nāsī, or occurring in the central box of a compartmental ceiling; as pantheonic image on the temple walls.

Generally, refers to all physical objects or physical phenomena not produced by humans. The universe of physical objects is often divided into realia, which are naturally occurring objects and phenomena, and "artifacts, " which are human-made objects and phenomena. Specifically, in library classification systems, realia are physical objects that are not the books, periodicals, or sound recordings typically cataloged by libraries. Specifically, in education, realia are objects from nature, home, or otherwise from real life that are used in classroom instruction.
Persons of any gender who keep buildings, shops, or equipment in good repair.
The study of emission and absorption spectra via absorption spectroscopy or reflectance spectroscopy over wavelengths in the ultraviolet and visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Documents in early modern institutions of higher education for announcing academic dissertations to be defended in public.These decorated broadsheets summarise the student’s conclusion. The aim of the engraved posters was mainly to advertise the disputation and to introduce the theses in question. The practice was mostly common in Catholic European countries: Italy, France, the Southern Netherlands, Germany and Austria.

A comprehensive and integrated strategy for the identification, assessment, conservation and management of historic urban landscapes within an overall sustainable development framework. The approach moves beyond the preservation of the physical environment, and focuses on the entire human environment with all of its tangible and intangible qualities. It seeks to increase the sustainability of planning and design interventions by taking into account the existing built environment, intangible heritage, cultural diversity, socio-economic and environmental factors along with local community values. The recommendation on the Historic Urban Landscape was adopted on 10 November 2011 by UNESCO’s General Conference. [derived from warrants #3 and #4]

In printing, a printer's unit, which is the full size of a piece paper when printed. The press sheet will be folded to form consecutive pages of a publication, or cut to form smaller units, for example with printing of postage stamps.
Ecclesiastics or lay people whose duty is to read the scriptures during services.

Solid nonmetallic mineral matter which, when ground, produces powder that can be used as paint pigment. If large quantities of paint are required, the stones are typically crushed using a paint pestle and mortar. For smaller quantities of paint, however, the stones can be dipped in water and rubbed in a paint dish from which the resulting pigment is captured by a paint brush.

Devices consisting of four strips of wood or some other material which are hinged together in a square so that they overlap and can be adjusted to the scale of the work being copied, enlarged, or reduced.
Persons who make or repair wooden vessels formed of staves and hoops, such as casks, buckets, tubs. Also shipboard artisans who repair casks and other containers.
Relatively narrow inclined bands of masonry found on walls of some northern Mesoamerican architecture since about 800 BCE; after around 300 CE often part of the talud-tablero architectural feature.
Stones used to form the corner of a wall of masonry, especially when accentuated by a difference in the surface treatment from that of the rest of the wall mass.

Stylized floral motif based on the palmette (of ancient Egyptian, Greek, and Roman art), which was seen by 18th-century architects and craftsmen to resemble flowers of the European honeysuckle, species Lonicera periclymenum. The honeysuckle motif is seen most often in architecture and furniture decoration. It is symmetrical with three or more curved members radiating from each side of a long central petal; it differs from the palmette in generally having thinner members.
In Indian architecture, a diminutive of ratnapaṭṭa; band of diamond pattern; maṇipaṭṭa, maṇipaṭṭikā; minor jewel-band .
Head of gandharva as a decorative motif, generally set inside the gāḍha of the nāsī/gavākṣa.

Buildings or other industrial installations where a material, such as sugar, oil, metal, etc., is refined, meaning it is purified, clarified, distilled, or otherwise treated, typically by a series of industrial processes, to make the material purer or of a finer quality.

Formal, machine-readable specifications of a conceptual model, in which concepts, properties, relationships, functions, constraints, and axioms are all explicitly defined.
