Refers to a compilation that is not technically a controlled vocabulary, but that uses one or more controlled vocabularies for a defined domain and expresses the vocabulary in a representative language that has a grammar for using vocabulary terms to express something meaningful. Ontologies generally divide their world into the following areas: individuals, classes, attributes, relations, and events. The grammar of the ontology links these areas together by formal constraints that determine how the vocabulary terms or phrases may be used together.
The way, model, or view in which something is represented. An example is when an architectural work is represented in an elevation or in a floorplan.
Tools used in sailmaking used to hold the canvas taught while sewing.

Proofs of prints having an image, but before the addition of title, artist's name, or other alphabetical content has been added; relevant when such printed matter exists on a later state. Such proofs are usually rare and valuable and thus command high prices.
Paper marbled to resemble tree calf, or tree marbled leather binding, which is decorated with marbling or staining in a tree-like branching pattern.

The evening before All Saints’ Day, observed on October 31. It initiates the season of All Saints, which lasts three days and concludes with All Souls' Day. In much of Europe and most of North America, the observance of Halloween is largely nonreligious and has taken on the customs of pre-Christian autumnal festivals, such as the festival of Samhain among the Celts of ancient Britain and Ireland.
The style and culture of the Mande people inhabiting northwest Sierra Leone and the southern coastal regions of the Republic of Guinea in West Africa.
Style and culture of the people of the modern nation of Eritrea, or to the ancient civilization that flourished in this region.
Business specializing in planning of gardens, which are open spaces where flowers, shrubs, trees, vegetables, or fruits are grown.

Refers to the style and culture of the Otoe (also Oto), a Siouan people. Historically a Great Lakes culture, migrations occurred in the 16th century toward the Minnesota and Iowa border. The Missouria Tribe, nearing extinction in the late 18th century, settled among the Otoe. Today the tribe is known as the Otoe-Missouria.
Paste or dough made of water and flour into various forms such as macaroni, spaghetti, and vermicelli; it can be dried for use later or made fresh.

The component structures of the outer covering and flight surfaces of all modern birds and some dinosaurs, apparently having evolved from the scales of reptilian ancestors. The many different types of feathers are variously specialized for insulation, flight, formation of body contours, display, and sensory reception. The typical feather consists of a central shaft (rachis), with serial paired branches (barbs) forming a flattened, usually curved surface (the vane). The barbs possess further branches, the barbules.

Small phylum that includes acorn worms and pterobranchs, characterized as wormlike marine invertebrates closely related to the chordates. While they are typically given phylum rank, some sources place the group at various other taxonomic levels with the other so-called protochordates. Hemichordates are so named for the Greek hemi, meaning "half," and chorde, meaning "string," thus, "half-chordate," which was first proposed because the buccal diverticulum, a tubular outgrowth from the mouth cavity forward into the proboscis, resembled a rudimentary notochord. This theory has since been rejected, however, because it has been determined that the diverticulum bears little resemblance in origin and function to the vertebrate notochord. Along with the proboscis, the body comprises a short collar, and a long, wormlike trunk.
Any of various machines for sewing material such as textile or leather, usually having needle and shuttle to carry thread and powered by treadle, waterpower, or electricity.
Tools and devices used to carry out surgeries, both invasive surgery or non-invasive surgery, including tools for modifying bodily tissue and providing access for viewing it.
Devices, both mechanized and manual, used to separate and partially clean baled cotton.
Organic compound used variously as a catalyst and also as a consolidant in stone conservation.

Style of textile, particularly carpets, made in the town of Ushak, the principal manufacturing center of large commercial carpets in Ottoman Turkey. It includes rugs created for palace and mosque use and for export. By the close of the 19th century the style had become coarser and rougher, with designs calculated to please European tastes. The best-known pattern among the older carpets is a scheme of large, rounded medallions of two types, alternating upon a field of brick red or dark blue. A second common pattern shows diagonal rows of eight-pointed star medallions alternating with diamonds. In the 18th and 19th centuries, a number of carpets with prayer-niche motifs in rows were made for mosque worship.

Refers to the style, culture, and period of the historic West Turkestani region before the Turkmen Soviet Socialist republic was formed in 1924. For the style and culture pertaining to the area of Turkmenistan after 1924, use "Turkmen."
Groups of objects, images, or data elements arranged in a specified order. For photographs taken in chronological order to record motion or change, use "chronophotographs" or "motion photographs."

Rings or bands, usually of metal, serving as fittings, adapters, or holders, as for example holding the bristles of a brush to the handle, or affixed to the body of a silver article for inserting a handle of another material, or on the handle of a utensil or tool into which is fitted the rest of the utensil or tool, or a plumbing fitting providing access to the pipe for maintenance.
Orthotic devices such as braces or sprints applied externally to the body which limit or control movement of a body part.
Slender pieces of board covered with emery, a coarse variety of corundum, used as an abrasive file most commonly for fingernails.
Political subdivisions in the modern day country of Greece.
Method of bookbinding in which the free edges of double leaves are sewn together as the binding edge, with the folds at the fore edges.

Territories that are defined in United States law as under the control of the government of the USA, and where fundamental rights apply as a matter of law, but certain other constitutional rights are not available. Examples are Puerto Rico and Guam.

Refers to small manufactured articles that are decorative or amusing and intended primarily for personal or household use. They are typically characterized by being of little utilitarian value and for being appealing primarily due to the newness of their design.

Folkloric objects associated with Appalachia. These are rounded clumps found inside feather pillows that are created by feathers that have formed into a halo shape. Death crowns mark the passing of a loved one.
Feudal estates or pieces of land which are held on the condition of service to a superior, under whose ownership the property remains.
Textile woven of synthetic fiber, plant fiber, or animal hair, used for awnings, tents, or other coverings.
A silk fabric of fine weave from Ghana. Long, narrow strips are hand-woven and then sewn together to form a pattern. Kente is typically found in delicate colors.
Sheer, lightweight plain-woven textile, originally of linen now also of fine combed cotton yarn, filled with starch or sizing. often used for handkerchiefs, aprons, and curtains.
Partial rising of a topcoat such as a paint, solvent, or varnish layer, due to the break in adhesion to the undercoat or surface layer.

A spontaneous phenomenon where a thin film on a surface ruptures into an ensemble of separated objects, like droplets, stripes, or pillars. This occurs when a liquid film retracts from a solid to form a bead-shaped drop.
Process of refining precious metals like gold and silver; the impurities are oxidized and partly absorbed into the cupel.
Use to describe objects embellished with precious or semi-precious stones.
The length of a straight horizontal line extending from one side to the other of a form. For the measure or distance of the extent across a surface, prefer "breadth," although usage overlaps.
In Indian architecture, with three minor offsets.
Size of pores in porous materials as related to porosity, pore structure, and pore size distribution; and as measured and described by techniques such as porosimetry and particle characterization.
Pertaining to the social movement centered on a concern for the environment and sustainable living.
The extent to which one substance will dissolve into another, usually specified, substance.

Horns, made of plastic though earlier models were metal, used as noisemakers at sporting events especially in South Africa. They may have originated with certain horns used in African villages to summon people for meetings.

Zitherlike plucked chordophones of ancient and modern India, composed of a hollow bamboo or wood tube to which one or more half-gourd resonators are attached, usually one at each end. Different regional types have varying numbers of frets and melody and drone strings. Medieval models had a single string supported by a rectangular bridge with a convex upper surface, which caused a buzzing effect when the string vibrated. The term is also used generically in India and other countries of southern Asia for chordophones of all kinds.

Multiple-necked plucked lutelike chordophones of Africa and Cuba, having from two to eight bowed necks of wood projecting from the back of the resonator, from each of which a string is stretched tautly to the front of the resonator.
Copies of a work in typewritten form, as distinguished from those in printed or handwritten form.
Models describing or illustrating what a product or service consists of or looks like.
Knitted or crocheted dresses.

Synthetic colorant made from anthranilic acid and chemically identical to natural indigo. Synthetic indigo was first produced in 1880 by Adolf von Baeyer. It has almost entirely replaced the natural dyestuff.

Objects containing sacred Jewish scriptures. The term Tanakh is an acronym based on the primary letters of the work's three major components: the Torah or Pentateuch, the Nevi'im (meaning Prophets), and the Ketuvim (meaning Writings). The Tanakh is also the source for the Old Testament, a component of the Christian Bible. Has been reproduced in the format of oral histories, scrolls, codices, and books. Some codices and scrolls, from the 11th century CE and earlier, are illuminated with scrollwork, geometric designs, and micrography.
Shoes with no obvious method of fastening.
Tall, flat-topped, brimless hats worn by some clergy of the Eastern Church.
Generally, the rear portions of watercraft.
Term used in the 18th and 19th centuries for a woman's bodice or upper portion of a dress or garment.
Clothing intended to be worn at home, designed to be comfortable, but often fashionable and sometimes worn in front of guests.

Helmets worn by parachutists; of metal with a liner system and chin strap. Often similar in appearance to the combat helmet, but with an extra liner system behind the head and an extra chin piece on the chinstrap.
Sets of dimensional letters or images, usually cast in rubber, with which children can make prints.

Small, rectangular, ribbon-covered pins of distinctive colors worn on military uniforms on prescribed occasions that represent the medals or decorations worn on dress uniforms on the most formal occasions.
Bindings in which the covering material is glued directly to the spine, or to a lining on the spine, of a book.
Bindings in which the spine and the corners of the cover are of one material and the remainder of the sides of another.

Items that are considerably smaller than the standard or usual size, especially objects that are accurate scale models of the original and intended as toys or collectibles. Miniatures are often manufactured at standard scales, for example, doll house furniture is often 1:12 scale and model trains may be 1:87 (HO) and 1:48 (O guage) scale.
Robes or loose light garments worn with a short cape or scarf over the shoulders; worn by clergy.

White, odorless, water-soluble crystalline powder found in almost all laundry soaps. It is a mild alkaline oxidizing agent which serves to increase detergency. It is also used as a deodorant and antiseptic. Dilute compounds of sodium perborate have been used in the conservation field to remove stains from textiles and other materials.

Mechanized devices designed to automate the process of folding open textiles, garments, and fabrics in half and harvesting fabric rolls and boards, thus facilitating subsequent storage procedures. Typically, the device's conveyor belt system carries the textiles through various folding rods and mechanisms, resulting in uniform folds.
A description of the current or last known location of the work.
Implements used to hold stitches in yarn while they are not being worked.
Mechanical devices that pull and aerate a soft candy base to make taffy. The machine has two or four arms that stretch and fold the material, giving it a satin look and mixing it with additives.
Devices used to remove some portion of the water content from liquid milk by boiling.
Devices that provide a measure of the consistency of bituminous materials, including asphalts and tar products.

Games where words have to be formed with letters. They are played for entertainment, can also be used for educational purposes. Some word games are simply played with pen and paper, others with adapted game material, and some popular television programs consist of word games.
Surgical blades specially made for dental procedures.
Occasions of celebration or merrymaking by groups of people. For larger and more formal occasions of celebration, use "festivals."

Genre of performing arts involving light popular songs, commonly of a satirical or topical nature, often together with a play or stage performance of a light and amusing character, often with other entertainments such a juggling, mime, etc. Particularly popular in the USA from the mid-1890s until the early 1930s.

The return of cultural property, such as looted artwork or historic artifacts, to its country or culture of origin. From the late 20th century into the 21st, the issue of and debates surrounding repatriation has grown as countries assess their laws related to cultural property, and their histories related to colonialism.
Descriptive text meant to identify collections of works or visual materials, often by an individual, such as photographs or prints, issued or housed together in a portfolio.
Numbers or alphanumeric codes that are not repeated within a given environment and used to unambiguously and uniquely identify an object, record, or data element.
Unit of German currency of varying value minted as gold coins by several German states from 1354.
Dating system used in much of the Islamic world, based on a year of 12 months, each month beginning approximately at the time of the new moon.
Numeric or alphanumeric codes included in mailing addresses to facilitate the sorting and delivery of mail.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1899 to 1800 (or 1900 to 1801) Before Common Era.
An alcoholic beverage made by mixing wine with fruit juice, and frequently also soda water and sugar; served chilled.

A language isolate, the only remnant of the languages spoken in southwestern Europe before the region was Romanized in the 2nd through 1st century BCE. At the beginning of the Common Era, dialects of Basque were probably spoken north and south of the Pyrenees and as far east as the Aran Valley in northeastern Spain. It is known in several dialects.
Mechanical or electronic devices designed to artificially induce the long-term sound propagation of enclosures, i.e.: echo and reverberation, usually to create effects for sound recording.
Narrow breaks in ridges on the sea floor.
Porcelain ware that is made and decorated in China to European order, as distinct from porcelain in native taste.
People who create costume.

Means of communication using facial expressions and bodily movements, especially of the hands and arms, as opposed to acoustically conveyed sound patterns. Used when spoken communication is impossible or not desirable, for example between speakers of mutually unintelligible languages or when one or more parties is deaf.
Persons who draw or paint illustrations of fashionable apparel and accessories, especially for advertisement.

The action of a human infant or other baby mammal taking milk by mouth from the breast or teat a female, usually their mother. For drawing milk from a breast or teat by hand or mechanically, use "milking."
The activity of saying farewell and going away from a person.

Historical unit of measurement meaning a "thumb"; used in France and other places, prior to the adoption of the metric system in the late 18th century. French units of measurement were based on the Carolingian system, in turn were based on ancient Roman measures. Equal to 12 lignes in  the old French measurement system. In modern systems, equal to around 27.07 mm or 1.066 inches.
Order containing 5 families with 165 genera and more than 4,000 species of flowering plants.
Fabulous marine animals resembling a sea horse or equine, having two front legs and a lower body ending in a dolphin's or fish's tail. Often accompanying the chariot of Neptune and other sea deities.

Trademarked general term for daylight fluorescent and glow-in-the-dark paints and pigments, including objects colored by the pigments. Originally used only for products manufactured by Day-Glo Color Corporation, Cleveland, although the term is commonly used generally for flourescent pigments.

Species of valuable North American bottomland timber tree of the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains and Mississippi Valley region, growing 24-36 meters in height, with branches rising at narrow angles from a columnar trunk to a round, compact head. It has silver-white, red-tinged bark and bright green, glossy leaves, velvety and whitish beneath, usually 20 cm in length and turning red in autumn. Swamp chestnut oak is often called "cow oak," because the acorns are eaten by cattle, or "basket oak" from local use of the wood strips for basket material. It was formerly considered a variety of Q. prinus ("rock chestnut oak" or simply "chestnut oak"). Q. michauxii is typically more massive than Q. prinus. A quick way to distinguish the two species is by habitat; if the tree grows on a ridge, it is probably Q. prinus; if it grows in wet bottomlands, it is probably Q. michauxii.
Deities who are the principal or most powerful gods in the pantheon of a religion.
Genus containing 16 species of evergreen trees native to tropical regions of Africa and South America, located primarily in swampy areas or near rivers or lakes.

Species of medium-sized tree native to the western and southwestern Mediterranean region. It is widely planted for timber in its native area, being one of the most important trees in forestry in France, Spain and Portugal. Also used as an ornamental and for medicine and turpentine.
Organizations that oversee and enable the production of operas, which are dramatic musical works in which singing forms an essential part.
Libraries consisting of specialized documents, and providing facilities for undertaking exhaustive investigation and research.
Museums that are owned or administered by representatives of a nation, or that specializes in exhibitions from a given nation.
A range of colors resembling variations of green pigment.
Variable red colors resembling the colors para red, a class of pigments created with paranitraniline, a coal tar derivative.
A range of yellowish colors resembling the color mustard, which is a powder obtained from the seeds of a mustard plant.
UCL (Universal Color Language) standard color name identifying a range of blue colors.
A range of reddish or orange brown colors resembling the color of the clay product, terracotta.
Refers to a range of cool green colors resembling either the dark green colors of the leaves of the aromatic mint plant or the light green colors of confections flavored with mint.

A generic style, particulary in the context of decorative arts and interior design, characterized by motifs and elements originating in New Mexico, Arizona, and nearby areas, including influences of Native American and Spanish design.
A range of purplish blue colors resembling the color of the fluorochrome, diaminophenyl oxydiazole, used to stain specimens and for other purposes.
Members of an order containing 155,000 species of butterflies, moths, and skippers.
Personal names acquired by a person when assuming religious orders or otherwise assigned to the person for religious reasons.

Order containing around 210 species in 11 families including rails, coots, and moorhens. They are morphologically diverse wading and terrestrial birds ranging from small quail-like hemipodes to large long-legged cranes, marsh-inhabiting rails, swimming coots and finfoots, and cursorial bustards.
Graduate schools that teach law and the legal profession, with the object of producing professional lawyers, scholars of law, or other professionals.
The high enclosure-walls of a south Indian temple structure, or the covered walkway that surrounds the temple boundary.
Floating masses of ice; detached portions of glaciers which have been carried out to sea.
Areas that are rich in coal deposits.
Includes all non-pantherine cats.

Chinese lidded ritual vessels with curved bodies and handles. Used from the latter part of the Shang to to the middle of the Western Zhou. Wine containers of various shapes, squat to long, may be called "you" if they lack other documented terminology and follow the general stereotype above.
Computer facility linked to the processor that holds data or program instructions until they are required.

Order containing 22 species in two families. Includes bandicoots and bilbies, all having a plump, arch-backed body with a long tapering snout, very large upright ears, relatively long, thin legs, a thin tail, fused second and third toes, and several pairs of lower front teeth.

Pas-taai is held every two years, and the celebration is carried out by representatives from communities from north and the south. The proceedings involve three stages. At the first stage, knots of silver grass will be tied on a long string to mark the total number of days in which Pas-taai takes place, and a committee of chiefs will be held. The second stage of Pas-taai, being the body of the festival, involves resolution of disputes, acknowledging the ancestors, sets of dancing addressing to the advent and departure of the spirit of Short People, and finally a thanksgiving banquet. The Pas-taai celebration ends with the seeing of Short People’s spirits on the eastward stream. The festive and ceremonial proceedings unify community-tribes on both sides by binding everybody’s fate together in a single rite shared by all Saysiyat people. Pas-taai consummates a symbolic unification of the Saysiyat society across the boundaries of bloodlines and tribe borders.
Balls used for exercise routines, usually made of plastic or other flexible material.
In Indian architecture, a smaller band; rectilinear fillet; kampa (South India) or auxiliary fillet; often top slab of an adhiṣṭhāna.
In Indian architecture, a narrow recessed moulding; gala.
In Islamic architecture, windows filled with screens or grilles of turned wood. For lattices or screens of perforated stone, in Islamic architecture, especially of Mughal India, use "jali."
In Indian architecture, a string-course bearing diamond pattern; faceted band.

Tianhua 天花 refers to a type of ceiling in traditional Chinese architecture, and its use was most common in the Ming and Qing dynasties. Literally meaning “heavenly flowers,” the semantic range for the compound is quite rich.
In Indian architecture, a pillarette with entwined half-human male/female snake deity (Kaliṅga).
Unadorned cushion capitals, characteristic of the Tuscan order.
Sites that contain prehistoric, megalithic monuments.
Buildings housing the offices, stages, backlots, sound stages, and other studios and operations of a motion picture studio company.

Refers to the work of a school of artists who re-established the literati tradition in painting in China during the late 15th and early 16th centuries. The style is characterized by balanced, harmonious landscape compositions, with an emphasis on sinuous lines and flattened space.
Style, culture, or ethnicity of American people of Japanese heritage.

Refers mainly to the style of architecture found in the Southwestern United States which draws its inspiration from the Pueblos and the Spanish missions in New Mexico. The style developed at the turn of the 20th century and reached its greatest popularity in the 1920s and 1930s, although it is still commonly used for new buildings. Pueblo Revival imitates the appearance of traditional adobe construction, however through the use of modern materials such as concrete and brick. Typical attributes include rounded corners, irregular parapets, and thick, battered walls used to simulate adobe. Roofs are always flat, and a common feature is the use of wooden roof beams that are often decorative rather than supportive.
Refers to the style and culture of the indigenous, First Nations, Interior Salish people residing in the Okanagan Valley of British Columbia and northeast Washington state.

Style and culture of a Native American tribe in Virginia, originally part of the Powhatan paramountcy in the 17th century. Achieved state recognition in 1985, and is known today as the "Nansemond Indian Nation."
Style and culture of the Paiute group from the Mono Lake area.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in southeastern Kenya.
Works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Tanzania.
Style and culture of the Berber people of the same name living in the High Atlas and Anti Atlas mountains as well as the Dra and Sous regions of Morocco, and in western Algeria.
Culture of the dynasty of 12th-13th-century Ethiopian kings who lived a nomadic military life and also left a legacy of important Christian monuments.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Uganda and Rwanda.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northeastern Nigeria.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in northern Cameroon.
Nationality, styles, and cultures within the secret Simo society of West Africa.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Nigeria.
Double portraits or companion portraits that depict partners in marriage. When depicted accompanied by children or other kin, use 'family portraits'.
Refers to materials whose particle constituents are of nanoscale dimensions, especially nano-engineered materials produced by nanotechnology.
Any substance which slows or prevents a particular chemical or biochemical process, reactant or catalyst.

A mixture of oil, usually olive oil, and balsam that is consecrated for use as an unguent in the administration of certain sacraments (baptism, confirmation, and ordination) and in the performance of certain ecclesiastical functions in the Catholic, Orthodox, and Anglican churches. It is consecrated on Maundy Thursday by bishops in the West and by patriarchs in the East. In Orthodox churches the mixture can also include other ingredients such as wine, nuts, and gum. The annointing with chrism is sometimes called chrismation, especially after baptism.
Woven reed, rattan, twigs, or other material, especially used to construct furniture.
Lightweight, highly finished transparent writing paper made transparent by hydration of the pulp in beaters.
Paper intended for writing upon with ink; usually finished with a smooth surface and sized.

Plant oil extracted from the mesocarp of the fruit of some palms, particularly the West African oil palm (Elaeis guineensis). The outer fleshy portion of the fruit is steamed to destroy the lipolytic enzymes and then pressed to recover the palm oil, which is highly coloured from the presence of carotenes. Palm oil is used in making soaps, candles, and lubricating greases and in processing tinplate and coating iron plates.

A pale yellow pigment used alone or mixed with other pigments, such as Prussian blue, barium yellow, and zinc yellow. It is used in oil paints, anticorrosive coatings, and pyrotechnics. It is not used often in watercolors due to its high opacity.

Bast fiber obtained from the bark species Edgeworthia papyrifera, native to China and cultivated in Japan. Mitsumata has been used for paper since about 1600 CE. The soft, absorbent fibers produce a paper that is weaker and less absorbent that kozo. Mitsumata paper also tends to shrink and expand with moisture content.
Wood in the form of relatively narrow strips that are used to build up a surface, often a curved suface, such as for a structure, cask, or barrel.
Exudate of pine trees, used for a variety of purposes, including as a sealant, incense, and in ancient Egypt, for embalming and preserving human bodies.

Flavonoid compound used as a yellow dye, obtained from the bark of the black oak, Quercus velutina, native to the eastern and midwestern United States. The outermost layer of bark gives a bright yellow dye while the inner bark gives a darker oranges and tans. Used to dye wool bright yellow or orange. At one time this colorant was used with cochineal to produce scarlets of particular brilliance. Quercitron was introduced in England in 1775 by Edward Bancroft as a substitute for weld.
Wood from any of the species of evergreen spruce trees, forming the genus Picea.
Wood from any of several pine trees of the southern United States, having foliage with a fragrance resembling the herb rosemary.

Wood from the species Quercus palustris, native primarily to bottomlands and moist uplands of eastern North America, but found as far west as Oklahoma and Ontario, Canada. It is a reddish brown hard wood that shrinks and cracks with drying; sometimes sold as red oak for flooring and lumber, but it is weaker and contains more knots.

Wood derived from either of two species in the Guibourtia genus of western Africa; it has a light red, brown, or violet background with evenly spaced pink or purple stripes. The wood is of medium texture and polishes to a high gloss. It is used, often as veneer, for cabinets, pianos, other furniture, and for smaller decorative items such as handles and boxes.

Any of numerous organic compounds that serve as chemical messengers. They are secreted by a gland or organ into the body fluids of an animal, particularly the bloodstream, by a gland or organ, are transported to another part of the organism, and trigger or regulate particular functions such as growth, metabolism, reproduction, and the functioning of various organs. The term may also refer to similar compounds produced by plants or produced synthetically. The term was coined in 1905 from the Greek "horman," meaning "to set in motion."
A white marble with black and gray blotches from Pickens County, Georgia; it is coarser than white marble from Vermont.
Any of the three acids, orthophosphoric acid, H3PO4, metaphosphoric acid, HPO3, or pyrophosphoric acid, H4P2O7, derived from phosphorous pentoxide, P2O5, and various amounts of water.
A hexagonal mineral, which includes several varieties of gemstone such as emerald and aquamarine.

Glass coated on one side with a transparent metallic coating that reflects light and radiant heat, particularly when used as window glass. Reflective glass is rated by the solar heat gain coefficient, ranging from 0.10 to 0.40.

Refers to various types of glass made in Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries using the techniques and styles that had been perfected in Venice, Italy, the name being French for "Venetian fashion."  It was produced in areas outside Venice, including other parts of Italy, France, Spain, Britain, Germany, and the Netherlands, and it evolved various local stylistic and technical traits over time.

A liquid silicate that hydrolyzes to form a colorless, transparent film of silica. Used, for example, as a source of colloidal silica in heat-resistant and acid-resistant coatings, as a protective coating for industrial buildings and castings, as a consolidant for stone, and as a bonding agent.

Crosses having arms terminating in steplike forms, in heraldry typically affecting all four arms. In other contexts, often a Latin cross with only the lower arm terminating in the steplike form, as if the cross were standing on a mount.

Motifs consisting of two intersecting lines or bars, with many variations in the shapes of the arms. For structures or objects of cross shape, especially those used as Christian symbols, use "crosses (visual works)."
In Indian architecture, a hall-temple enshrining the trinity Brahmā/Sūrya, Śiva, Viṣṇu.
Relic hall, where Buddhist relics are preserved and venerated. A  famous example is located on the grounds of Engakuji Temple in Kamakura.
Imitation grottoes representing the grotto in Lourdes, France where apparitions of the Virgin Mary were believed to have occurred in 1858.
Buildings  housing establishments where people may go for fitness, yoga, nutritional counseling, physical therapy, chiropractic care, preventative medicine, and eastern medicine.
Buildings housing educational institutions that focus on training, advising, and research on governmental systems and practical applications.

Dogon men's meeting houses used to discuss community issues. Togu na are characterized by millet-stalk roofs supported by wood pillars, which are typically carved with fertility symbols such as women's breasts or scenes from Dogon society.
Buildings that house businesses that sell alcoholic beverages.
Built works used by, or in support of, institutions.
Enclosed concrete rooms for retting flax, as part of a rottery.

Working places set aside for artists to work. The term is generally applied to workspaces used by artists creating fine art, particularly art dating from the 16th century to the present. The characteristics of a studio may be dictated by the practical requirements of adequate light, ample space in which to create the work of art, and storage of materials. Display of the finished art works and training may also be accommodated in a studio. Creation of an art work may require a range of artistic processes; therefore, separate areas of work may be delegated in the studio. The term may also refer to spaces used by dancers, singers, musicians, and other performing artists to create or practice. The term "workshops" is generally refers to spaces used by craftspeople, artists working prior to the 16th century, and industrial workers. For studios that are larger spaces or complexes, and are used to create films, television or radio programs, or other large scale productions, use "motion picture studios," "broadcasting studios," "sound studios," "recording studios," "radio studios," or "television studios."

Rooms in or attached to churches where the sacred vessels and other treasures are kept. Vestments may also be stored here and the space used by the celebrants to dress for the services. For rooms used primarily for dressing for the services, use "vestries (dressing rooms)," although in modern usage, particularly for newer and smaller churches, the vestry and the sacristy are often the same room.

Meaning, literally, "plaque" (-holding) "tower" (Kroll),  the pailou functions to mark specific locations, divide space, and commemorate virtuous individuals and actions. The ‘lou’ in pailou can refer to a roof or eaves (Guo 2002, 61), however, in Ming dynasty (1368-1644) literature, the term pailou was widely used and was often used interchangeably with the term paifang. For example, in the Jiajing Dezhou zhi 嘉靖德州志 (ca. 1545 CE), pailou are recorded under the chapter on paifang, indicating that pailou and paifang refer to the same objects (Zheng and He 1522-1566, 1.13a). The term paifang was often used to emphasize why the structure was erected, while the term pailou was used to emphasize the location. These structures were so symbolic in their appearance that they became the markers of specific places. Junctions composed of multiple paifang structures at road intersections were often found in cities, such as the “Four Pailou” and “Three Pailou” in Nanjing.
Refers generally to a cloakroom; use specifically for large rooms in monasteries or other buildings where garments are kept.
Platforms above rood screens or rood beams, from which choirs sing or readings are made.

Type of late-18th- and early-19th-century English drinking glass having a capacious bowl which rests on a short stem. Early examples have ovoid bowls of fairly thin glass; later ones are much thicker, straight-sided and stand on heavy, sometimes square, feet.
Rods affixed to the bases of stair risers that through pressure hold carpets designed for staircases securely in place, preventing slippage.
General term used to group instruments similar to, and including, violins.
Prints produced by vitreography.

Stands made to support hot water urns or teakettles. May be short-legged stands that are set upon a table, or taller stands with legs that reach the floor. For tables that support a tea service, use "tea tables." Use "teakettles-on-stands" for teakettles made en suite with a stand.
Elaborate mechanical tables that could sink or rise through the floor to be replenished with food.

Writing desks, generally fall-front desks sitting on top of a chest of drawers, having compartments, slots, and cubbyholes above. For secretaries surmounted by a bookcase, use "secretaries-bookcases." The term "secretary" originally referred to a small, portable writing desk, often with drawers, that was placed on top of a table. In modern usage, these small portable desks are generally called "escritoires," and the term "secretaries" refers to larger pieces meant to be placed against a wall.

Tables of various designs at which cards, dice, and other games are played. They may have tops marked as a game board for playing chess, backgammon, goobun, or other games; they may have tops edged with a railing. Distinct from "card tables" which have a smooth, undecorated top.
Furniture cabinets meant to hold and enclose television sets, presenting aesthetically pleasing screen views while hiding functional componets. For use in the home.
Specialized furniture form most popular in the American South; generally having a hinged lid on top covering a large divided storage chamber for brown and white sugar.
Beds for servants' use; term frequently found in 16th- and 17th-century inventories.

The name sometimes given to early 18th-century chairs in which the back has a gentle double curve designed to fit the back of the sitter. Also a mid-19th century chair with a rounded, waisted back and short legs.

Chairs that are designed or used to serve as both a chair and a pulpit or lectern in a relgious setting; found in the context of Buddhism, Islam, Christianity, and other religions. Examples are chairs having a tall back surmounted by a lectern, so that the chair could be used as a pulpit at open-air services or worship conducted at local houses.
Chairs, often upholstered, having a full-length leg rest and usually arms, designed for one person to recline on. For similar chairs used outdoors, use "deck chairs."

Lamps consisting of simple, open, shallow vessels into which fuel is placed. The wick rests in the fuel on the bottom of the pan; sometimes equipped with hangers so that they can be suspended from the ceiling, wall, or a lampstand.
Fuel containers that support the burner and receive the lower part of the wick and that are an integral part of the lamp.
Short blocks, usually metal, each having a threaded hole in the center for receiving a bolt or threaded rod.

Drawings that are a hybrid of drawing and printmaking. Oil transfer drawings are achieved by covering a surface, often a sheet of paper, with oil paint or printing ink, laying a clean sheet of paper over it, and drawing on top with a mark-making tool; the pressure of the tool causes the ink or paint from below to transfer to the back of the top sheet.

Emblematic designs or devices of a printer or publisher. The printer's mark as an identifying device was used in typographic books with the invention of printing in the 15th century; printers gradually added a blank piece of paper at the front of a book to protect the first page from soiling. The identifying device, monogram, or emblem was applied to this page or with a brief sentence at the rear of the book; when the printer's mark was incorporated into the colophon, it is sometimes itself known as a "colophon."
Copies made by xerography.
Official documents used during travel.
Documents in which are expressed security transactions.
Learning materials so designed that individuals can proceed to learn on their own with little or no personal supervision from an instructor or expert.
Groups of productive or profit-making enterprises or organizations that share a similar technological structure and that supply similar goods or services.

Refers to organizational, regulatory, or representative bodies for particular trades or occupations. These may promote and develop commercial and industrial interests, or advocate for the views of members on matters of common interest.
People undergoing training, especially for an occupation.
People who are abnormally small in stature.
Persons who train others, either for athletic contests or for intellectual examinations.
Authors who specialize in writing about traveling and travel destinations.
Performers who work along the streets or other public areas, typically hoping to earn tips from passersby for their performance.

Persons who keep official records, especially the officials at educational institutions who maintain students' personal and academic records, issue grade reports, and mail out calendars and other official publications.
Senior magistrates or governors, or those holding any of various positions of command or superintendence; especially as in the ancient Roman or medieval worlds.

People skilled in, or specializing in, the art of niello, which uses technique of decorating metal by engraving it with designs that are then filled with a black inlay. Prints are sometimes made from the engraved metal before inlaying.

People and corporate bodies who specialize in the design of textiles, which are materials produced by weaving, felting, knotting, twining, or otherwise processing natural or synthetic fibers. Included may be those who create designs for finished textile art works, or designs for the textile materials, such as patterns to be printed on fabrics.
Individuals or companies who buy and sell materials, such as antiques, works of art, or library materials.
The most common type of drill bit used for making holes in materials, such as wood, plastic or metal.
The people who perform labor in an economy. For the concept of the human activity that produces the goods or provides the services in demand in an economy, use "labor."
Small, thin-bladed, usually straight knives, sometimes with changeable blades, used for precise cutting or delicate removal of one material from another.

Toothed wheels, cones, or cylinders, or other machined elements that are designed to mesh with other similarly toothed elements for purposes which include the transmission of power and the change of speed or direction.

Cutting instruments consisting of a blade with a sharpened longitudinal edge fixed in a handle, either rigidly as in a table-, carving, or sheath-knife, or with a joint as in a pocket- or clasp-knife. Knives may be used to cut food, especially in serving and eating, as weapons, and for other purposes. The blade may be of steel or another metal or stone, as in the flint knives of early man, or of another material such as ivory or wood (as with a paperknife). The term also refers to tools that are shaped or used as knives, even if the edge is not particularly sharp or actually used for cutting.
Boxes where seeds are sprouted to determine the amount of seeds able to grow.
Tools made for gardens and gardening, and by extension with the range of tools made for agriculture and horticulture.
Historic instruments for making observations of celestial objects.
Cutting tools consisting of a rotary blade mounted in a handle to enable cutting compound curves into photographic prints.
Knives, the blade of which is usually curved on one side and straight on the other, used to apply and smooth plaster.
Term coined to describe a variety of styles and movements post WWI that were influenced by expressionism but rejected the movement's aesthetic.

Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Mehmed IV, who ruled from 1648 to 1687. Artistic achievements during his reign include additions to the Topkapi Palace and the completion of the Yeni Valide Mosque in 1683.
Styles having elements that anticipated and had a profound influence on Expressionist art, literature, and dramatic arts.

Nationality, culture, and style of one of the four major divisions of the ancient Greek people, along with the Aeolians, Achaeans and Doric. the Ionians were an ancient Hellenic people inhabiting Attica, parts of western Asia Minor, and the Aegean Islands in pre-classical times.

Refers to culture and period from about 850 to 590 BCE during which the kingdom of Urartu ruled the part of eastern Anatolia centered around the area of Lake Van. The art and architecture of the period is characterized by distinctive bronze artifacts and fortresses of fine ashlar masonry.
Refers to a style in Mesopotamia that is characterized by a synthesis of Sumerian and Akkadian culture.

Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age cultures that lived in the fourth millennium BCE. The name is derived from the inverted-cloche form of the characteristic vessel. Bell Beaker vessels occur in a variety of styles with specific regional distributions and chronological limits. The beakers are typically decorated in bands of incised and corded decoration and frequently occur in graves associated with wristguards of polished and perforated stone and V-perforated buttons. While earlier generations of archaeologists attributed the beakers to a particular "Beaker folk" who originated in Spain and spread to central and western Europe carrying bronze technology to the British Isles, scholars now tend to think that the beakers were prestige items whose popularity spread over time among existing peoples as symbols of social rank.
Culture of a dynasty that ruled in west central India 6th-7th centuries.

Refers to the work of a school of painters whose careers spanned the Edo period (1600-1868) to the early part of the Meiji period (1868-1912). The style is characterized by the use of traditional Japanese materials and techniques such as black or colored ink made from minerals, shells or plants and painted on paper or silk.
Refers to the style of early glazed wares of the Nara period (645-794 CE), produced directly under government control. The style is characterized by green glazes.

Culture and period of ancient nomadic people who formed a state in Mongolia north of the empire of the Han Dynasty. What little is known of the culture is offered by Chinese literary sources and a few archaeological sites and artifacts.

Communities of any size that hold a market or otherwise provide a variety of retail functions for the surrounding area. For larger centers of business and commerce on a grander scale, use "commercial centers (inhabited places)."

Objects comprising a length of metal, wood, plastic or other material, bent back or otherwise fashioned with a sharp angle, often having a C-shape. Typically hooks form a part of something else, such as a pole, chain, or the like, adapted for catching hold, dragging, sustaining suspended objects, or another purpose.

Shaped supports for the head either made as separate objects, as used in ancient Egypt and other African cultures, or as attachments to other objects, such as used on the backs of motor vehicle seats or barbers' chairs.
Nationality, culture, and styles of the city of Modena, Emilia-Romagna, Italy.
Quaternary ammonium salt used as a basic solvent.

Refers to the culture of the modern nation of Bulgaria, or in general to cultures that have occupied the area of modern Bulgaria in the Balkans in modern history. For the culture of the ancient Bulgars, use "Bulgar."
Nationality, style, and culture of Saint Lucia island, in the eastern Caribbean Sea.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of  the U.S. state of Kentucky.

Refers broadly to the period, styles, and culture of the state centered on the city of Rome from the period from the founding of the city ca. 700 BCE through the events leading to the founding of the republic in 509 BCE, the establishment of the empire in 27 BCE, and the final eclipse of the Empire of the West in the 5th century CE. Ancient Rome became a powerful force and supplanted Greek and Etruscan influence on the Apennine peninsula. Its rule and influence gradually encompassed a wide area in Europe, northern Africa, the Middle East, and Asia Minor. Its influence was wide in scope, including sculpture, painting, architecture, engineering, language, the road system, law, and many other areas of culture. Roman art and architecture is characterized by early derivations from Greek art and architecture, but it gradually developed into a style of its own, absorbing characteristics of styles from the far flung regions under its control.

Processes or techniques for construction of buildings or engineering works, using primarily individual units of masonry laid in and bound together by mortar Typical materials for masonry construction include stone (including marble, granite, travertine, limestone, etc), brick, cast stone, concrete block, glass block, and cob. For construction techniques using unfired earth, use "earth construction."

Rooms that are a few steps higher than the front of the house or from the other rooms on the same floor. The original form is typically Dutch, seen in the Netherlands, Belgium, and in locations where the Dutch colonized.
A minimally non-destructive technique used to assess in situ the mechanical properties of masonry walls and the local average compressive stress.
Curved wall surfaces which form a transition between a dome (or its drum) and the supporting masonry.
Function involving the showing or presenting works or other things to public view. For events at which works are exhibited, prefer "exhibitions (events)."

Religion of the ancient Etruscans, involving complex rules regulating a large number of rituals. Heavily based on influences from Greece in its orientalizing period, but the religion of Etruria proclaims a very un-Greek view of the abasement and nonentity of man before the gods and their will. Known from the Mediterranean Iron Age in the second half of the first millennium BCE.
The analytical division of time into defined periods, especially the grouping of historical and cultural events into periods for purposes of discussion and criticism.
Components of Buddhist stupa architecture that surmount the dome and represent the world axis.
Parts of a building that project beyond the rest.
The sport or game of throwing rings of flattened iron, rope, or rubber at a target; typically throwing or aiming such rings at a peg placed in the ground or at another target.
Activity by which the transfer of title or possession of goods or the supplying of services from seller to buyer is effected, including advertising, shipping, storing, and selling.
The action or condition of finding or meeting, with reference to a person, thing, or experience. May imply difficulties or opposition surrounding the meeting, but this is not necessarily the case.
Ceremonies that make a person or thing ritually clean. An example is the ritual cleansing of a woman after childbirth in accordance with Jewish religious laws.

In Indian architecture, an unworked lower section of door-jamb; lower section of door-jamb bearing guardian and acolytic figures; lower block of door-jambs (often carved with figures of river-goddesses and door guardians); basal section of the aggregate of śākhā-doorjambs.
State, aspiration, or condition of harmony within a community or group having similar goals.
Changes in relative humidity, particularly in the context of collections care and collections environment and historic sites.
A periodic motion or oscillation about equilibrium.

Art and crafts that exist outside the received canons of taste established by academic art, that are produced in culturally cohesive communities or contexts, and that are guided by local traditional rules or procedures. Included are paintings, ceramics, textiles, sculpture, and other art forms. It is generally distinct from "naive art," which is created by those without formal training, but not necessarily within a cohesive cultural community. It is also distinct from "outsider art," which usually refers specifically to art created or collected according to a philosophy of avoidance of traditional training.
In textile chemistry and conservation: the quality, condition, or degree of whiteness in dyed, undyed, and whitened textiles.
Describes the impression of grandeur, nobility, permanence, and often, though not necessarily, size in a work of art or structure.

Shape or form delimited by two curves intersecting so as to delimit a space that is overall narrow but wider in the middle and tapering to a point on both ends (sometimes only on one end), thus resembling a spear or lance-head. For similar forms that are overall wider, use "almond-shaped."

Refers to the philosophy of Plato or to any philosophy inspired by Plato, especially to Plato's idea that the phenomena perceived by the senses are an imperfect and transitory reflection of the ideal forms of an unchanging and eternal reality. This absolute reality (or realities) gives value and meaning to everything's existence, particularly to human life.

Refers generally to the religious practices of some northern Asian peoples who believe that good and evil spirits inhabit the world and can be summoned or heard through inspired priests acting as mediums. Shamanism is also found amongst the pre-Chrisitian Lapps, the Inuit, the Plains Indians of North America, some Australian Aborigines, and some other peoples. The term was originally used by the Tungus people of Siberia.
Belief in or claim to personal intellectual, cultural, or spiritual superiority not accessible to mankind in general.
The quality or state exhibited by soundness of moral principle, uprightness, honesty, sincerity, and uncorrupted virtue, particularly regarding truth and fair dealing.

Adjustment of a loss when cargo on board a ship belonging to one or more owners has been sacrificed for the safety of the whole, whereby the amount of the loss is shared by all who have cargo on board the vessel.
Supreme and independent authority of a political unit to make and apply laws within its own boundaries and to conduct international relations.

Form of rule in which power is maintained by a tyrant, who holds vast or absolute power, and exercises power oppressively, cruelly, or unjustly. For forms of rule in which power is absolute and the element of arbitrariness is present, prefer "despotism."
Systems of procedures or processes for interpreting and enforcing the law, elaborating the rights and responsibilities involved.
The process of becoming aware of objects, qualities, or relations via the sense organs; involves the reception, processing, and interpretation of sensory impressions.
Describes a condition of hatred or fear of transgender people, and by extension discrimination based on those with transgender identity.

Complementary parts or sections added to serial or monographic books or documents to give further information, update information, or correct errors. Includes separate sections devoted to special subjects inserted into newspapers or periodicals. Supplements may be issued with the text or separately.

Area of knowledge or study of the principles and regulations established in a state or community by some authority and binding on its people, whether in the form of legislation or of custom and policies recognized and enforced by judicial decision. Also the professional practice that deals with these principles and regulations and legal procedure.
The building and repair of stringed instruments, particularly of the violin family.
The branch of science that deals with the detection or measurement of radiant photomagnetic energy.

In the context of art and cultural heritage, the process of making an image or images, including all depictions and representations in two or three dimensions of an object, building, person, animal, plant, place, or phenomenon, whether the optical counterpart exists in reality or only in imagination.
Application of paint in thick, opaque masses, usually with a well-loaded brush or a palette knife.
Cleansing with water or other liquid.

Process of making a cast or an impression from a ready made or natural object, particularly part of the body; plaster of Paris frequently used in this technique; sometimes used for creating life masks and death masks.
Refers to the dissipation of energy in motion of any type, especially oscillatory motion, and the consequent reduction or decay of the motion.
Terminals of an electricity system made to receive the pins of a plug or other means of supplying current to an appliance or device.
Appliances to make hot water, usually consisting of an electrical or gas heating unit under a tank in which water is heated and stored.
Corresponding nob and grove which hold the parts of a mold in alignment.
Relatively short, stout nails made of copper or another nonferrous metal, designed for nailing down slates to a slate roof.

Mechanical contrivances that allow swinging motion in a single plane of one of the members to which they are attached, such as a door, and in which water or some other liquid is employed in the mechanism to control the speed at which the hinge moves; usually to slow the motion of a closing door.

Locks of various designs that are key operated or keyless letter-combination type, originating in China. When they are locked, the sliding bolt is trapped by the opening springs against the inner wall of the lock-body. They are often decorative objects as well as utilitarian.

Large standing wooden bird sculptures with long curved beak, rounded head, prominent belly, and sharp-cornered rectangular wings, usually standing on a hollow base. They are made for use primarily in central Senufo rituals, including Poro male initiation rites and funeral ceremonies for dignitaries.
Ancient Egyptian sculptures depicting a standing or kneeling male figure proffering a naos, which is a small room of shrine for a deity.
Patterned cloaks worn by women and men from Thrace.
Sports jackets or coats, typically made of tweed or wool, and worn when shooting or hunting.
Poles carved and painted with a series of totemic symbols, erected before the homes of Native Americans of the northwestern coast of North America.

Native American headgear, part of ceremonial regalia, and made from the hair of deer, porcupine, and occasionally moose or horse. The roach headdress is held in place by a scalp lock, which is a small lock of hair braided on the crown of the wearer's head.
Hats designed or used for the activity of hunting, which is chasing game or other wild animals, for sustenance, profit, or sport.

Vessels intended to hold or dispense tea, of varying form but having a spigot rather than a spout; usually supported on legs or a stand and may have a heating device. May be part of a tea service. Prefer "hot water urns" for urnlike vessels intended to hold or dispense hot water in connection with the serving of tea and which also may be part of a tea service.

Wooden containers, usually made of birch bark and sewn together with basswood bast, made to store maple sugar. Particularly made and used by Anishinaabe, Potawatomi, and other Great Lakes Native North American tribes. Sometimes decorated with quillwork, braided sweetgrass, or incised designs.

Large circular or oval bowls with scalloped rims used to cool inverted wine glasses or punch cups, usually six or more. Often made of silver, but also of earthenware, porcelain, or other metals. Those with detachable, scalloped rims also served as punch bowls. For small vessels that hold one wine glass, use "wine-glass coolers."
Small containers for fragrant spices or perfumes originally intended to be carried to ward off infections. Perforated and usually globular, apple-shaped, or composed of fitted sections.
Flat, thin containers, usually made of paper or plastic, with circle-shaped indentations to hold coins. Used for both storage and display.
A type of base on a glass vessel made by applying an additional gathering of molten glass to the bottom and spreading it out to form a ring.
Containers or devices that hold and dispense something in small amounts.
Spoons of different marked sizes, usually part of a set, for measuring small amounts of ingredients.
A distinct passage or section of a text, usually composed of several sentences, dealing with a particular point, a short episode in a narrative, a single piece of direct speech.
Metal, earthenware, or plastic containers, generally for domestic use, that are usually broad, shallow and open.
Vessels of Celtic tradition, particularly Irish, used for drinking mead, often communally.These often have squared sides and handles, and may be made of wood or ceramic.
Culture of the of the Quraish tribe.
Refers to the leaf of a book's endleaves that is pasted to the cover.
Large, spherical or cylinder-shaped earthenware vessels with wide necks used for the conservation or transportation of goods, such as wine, oil, or grain, during the Roman Empire.

Describes gathered matter collated but never bound, such as items left in sheets, gatherings, or signatures. To describe gathered matter that has been removed from its binding in preparation for rebinding, use "pulled" (alternate of "pulling.)" To describe sections of gathered matter from a composite volume that have been removed to stand alone thereafter, use "disbound" (alternate of "disbinding").
Visual works with subject matter or form that is fantastical, fabulous, imaginary, unreal, or whimsical.
Visual works, including architecture, that are made of concrete, which is a hard, strong construction material comprising a mixture of sand, gravel, crushed rock that may be poured into molds.
Visual works submitted for decision or consideration, such as for a commission or entrance into a competition.
In Indian architecture, a figure of a female dancer showing abhinaya-expressions.

Refers to a class of manufactured articles, generally of utilitarian type, usually specified by its material, use, style name, or other characteristic, such as ceramic ware or kitchenware. In archaeology, refers to distinct groups of pottery types classified according to characteristics of temper, hardness, type of paste, and surface treatment, rather than by shape or decoration, such as Kamares ware.
Women who have charge of the domestic arrangements of institutions such as hospitals, schools, and prisons.

Method of infrared spectroscopic analysis that measures the ways a molecule can vibrate. Radiation is passed through a sample and its absorption is detected in terms of characteristic frequencies associated with normal modes of vibration of molecules.

Collective concept referring to the types of living arrangements of a particular group. For the specific structures or groups of structures designed for these arrangements, use the descriptors collocated under "dwellings", <housing complexes>, or "settlements."
Ribbons attached to books, used for for marking a place by insertion between the leaves. Distinguished from "bookmarks," which are unattached.

The characteristic pattern known from plaid textiles, consisting of bars or stripes of various colors crossing each other at right angles over a contrasting background color, whether or not the pattern exists on a textile or another material. Plaid patterns were known from ancient times in many cultures.
In Hinduism and Buddhism, regents or guardians of one of the four principal quarters.

Containers, commonly made of aluminum or plastic, designed to both facilitate the even application of paint onto a commercial paintroller and hold unused paint during the painting process. Such containers comprise a centralized paint well or reservoir into which the paint may be added, as well as roller ramps to engage the roller, one or more side walls fitted with end wipers to remove excess paint, a drainage spout, and four outboard legs to support the device while in use.

Implements comprising rods of a marking substance, enclosed in wood, plastic, or metal, and used for writing or drawing. Common examples of materials used in pencils are graphite, lead, and pigmented wax.
Those who make, sell, or repair knives and other cutting implements.

Sections of hide or cloth that are attached to the tipi poles, often by rawhide strips or buffalo hair rope. Several liners were typically overlapped to provide coverage of the entire interior space. Tipi liners may be painted or decorated with quillwork or beadwork.
In Indian architecture, a recess between wall-bays.

Motif resembling a string of buds, wheat husks, or bell flowers nestled each against its neighbor to form a string or festoon. Examples include late 18th-century Neoclassical furniture, ceramics, and other works.
In Indian architecture, a band with figures; figural or narrative band.
Hindu decorative motif of a man-eagle, representing a mythical bird that is Viṣṇu's vāhana.
Buildings containing facilities for the recovery and reuse of materials and energy from waste.
Books of designs or plans circulated or published to enable widespread copying. May also be used for unbound collections of drawings or prints which serve as artists' models.
A body of methods, procedures, working concepts, rules, and postulates employed by a science, art, or discipline.
Awl-like devices used in the fabrication of sails.
Tools used for embossing, as in the stamping of linen book bindings, or gold leaf surfaces.
Chisels used in woodworking.
The state of being under the influence of an alcoholic liquor to the extent that it affects self-control.

Historically, those who prepared and sold drugs for medicinal purposes, this business being conducted by a druggist or pharmacist since ca. 1800. From about 1700 apothecaries began to act as general medical practitioners. Modern apothecaries hold this status legally in some places by examination and licence, but in popular usage the term is archaic.
Those who love, support, and defend their country and its interests with devotion.
General term for earthenware having a white, shiny, opaque glaze comprising lead with tin oxide. On this white background are typically brightly colored patterns, scenes, or other decoration.
Remission of the punishment, including purgatorial atonement, due by divine justice for sins whose guilt has been pardoned by the reception of the sacrament of penance.
Photographic prints made by the stabilization process.
Fragments of pottery or stone containing inscriptions.
Authors' notes prefixed to works, offering them to friends or patrons as marks of esteem, affection, or gratitude, or as pleas for patronage.
Concluding or discontinuing an activity, program, or job position. For the act of dismissing an employee, use "firing (managing)."
Modifier describing a color of any intensity or value, having overtones of red, orange, or yellow.
Documents that contain graphics.
The position or condition of being external to a reference point.
Short works promoting new coming attractions such as feature films or television mini-series, usually containing scenes from them. They are shown in theaters and on television.

Photographs produced without a camera, usually by placing an object directly on sensitized paper and exposing it to light. Includes Talbot's first photographs, which he called photogenic drawings. In the early 20th century the term was sometimes used to mean all photographs.
Lace originally manufactured in the town of Valenciennes, in northern France.
Photographic processes using two colors, usually red and green or orange and near-cyan, to synthesize the full color spectrum; may be additive or subtractive.

Modern art tendency attributed to Daniel Spoerri, who opened the Eat Art Gallery in Dusseldorf in 1970. The gallery was dedicated to works made from food materials, or that represented the acts of serving or consuming food. Artists associated with this movement initially were Dieter Roth, Joseph Beuys, Richard Lindner, Ben, and the Nouveaux Réalistes Arman, César and Niki de Saint Phalle, and Spoerri himself, whose "snare paintings" consisted in the fixed remains of meals, presented as tableaus. The term has been applied to contemporary artists working in a similar mode.

Class including about 4,100 species of predominantly marine algae often found attached to other shore plants. Their morphological range includes filamentous, branched, feathered, and sheetlike thalli.
Constructions, such as bridges or tunnels,  that allow animals to pass over or under a roadway.
In Indian architecture, a flower garland; floral frieze.
Material comprising stems, which are the ascending parts of a plant, supporting the leaf, flower or fruit.

Stiff dough made from flour, salt, and fat; usually in the form of butter, and some liquid. Also collectively, articles of food of which pastry forms an essential part, specifically pies or tarts after being baked.

Parts of a human's or an animal's body, usually having toes, located below the ankle joint of the legs, with the main function of supplying support and locomotion. For the truncating components of arms, use "hands (animal components)."

Slender, pointed needles designed for sewing, to pierce and draw thread or other fiber through cloth or another flexible material. They generally have one or more holes or eyes at one end for thread to pass through; they are now usually of polished steel.

Cylindrical instruments, most often consisting of a tube mounting a piston, or a tube with a rubber bulb attached, used to draw in liquid, and to eject it in a stream or jet for making injections, taking samples, cleansing, or for other purposes.
Tool with hinged top for breaking the wooden core of flax stems.
An aqueous solution of calcium carbonate dissolved in carbonic acid. Calcium bicarbonate has been used as a neutralization and alkalization agent in paper conservation. Chemical formula: Ca(HCO3)2.
The style and culture of the Uzbek khanate, refering to any of the three states that ruled Transoxania, in present-day Uzbekistan, before it came under Russian rule in the 19th century.

A conceptual grouping of visual arts works, literary works, or performance art created in succession by the same author, artist, or studio and intended by the creator(s) to be seen together or in succession as a cycle of works. Works in a series typically share the same or related subjects, the same or similar media, or other characteristics, but their defining characteristic is that they were intended to be conceptually related as a series. Individual items in a series may be cataloged separately and linked to the series.
Projecting rims, collars, or rings, providing added strength or a place to attach something, as for example on a pipe, on a machine housing, or on a container or its lid.
Rectangular frameworks usually made of wood or aluminum designed to be worn on a person's back to support a burden.
Administrative territories having the primary purpose of containing the federal capital. Examples are in Nigeria and Pakistan.

Process of attaching a worked headband to the text block, by looping the thread used in forming the headband down the back to a point below the kettle stitch, through the fold of the gathering, and then back up to be wound around the core of the headband; it may be done through all or only every few gatherings.

States that are subordinate to the ruler of another state, usually providing military assistance or tribute to the dominant state. Examples are Troy, which was a vassal state of the Hittites, and historical Tibet, which was a vassal state of China.

Works of fine or decorative art, typically in the context of collectables and of relatively small size, rather than museum objects or large in size. In English, use of the French term "objets d'art" emphasizes this meaning. For fine art, generally prefer the term "works of art" rather than "art objects," although usage overlaps. When referring to the study or practice of the fine arts or the fine and decorative arts together, use "art."
Wreaths made of human hair that are commemorative of a loved one. These are usually a product of the Victorian era, and would be displayed in glass cases as decorative objects.
Territories that are ruled by a grand duke or grand duchess.
Textile made from the animal hair wool.
Cloth of cotton, wool, or a blend, often of a serge weave, characterized by a dull brownish color and originally referring to cloth used for British field uniforms of the 1880s.
Fabric with open spaces between the yarn or wire. A mesh fabric may be knit, woven, or knotted.
The process by which something becomes firm and rubbery; particularly used to describe the hardening of oil paints in the tube or can caused by impurities.
Intentionally loading with additional weight; with regard to fibers and textiles, the addition of a substance to increase the weight or bulk of the fibers.
The process of taking apart, whether by damage or intentionally; examples are when folios of manuscripts are cut out of the volume for redistribution separately.
The removal or reduction of acid content by neutralizing the acidic components in a material, often paper, and providing an alkaline buffer to counteract acidic build-up in the future.

Having a pattern or design in relief; or protruding above a surface to which it is attached or is a part. For the relative positional attribute describing individually discrete things raised in relative position to other things or places, especially above the ground or other surface, use "elevated".
In Indian architecture, a plan/wall with three bays; with three projections.

Refers to the dimensions of an object that are visible to the eye, as distinct from the actual size of the object. It is typically used to describe the dimensions of the portion of a two-dimensional work of art that are visible within the window of a frame or mat, not including those parts of the work that are hidden by the rabbet of the frame or the area of the mat. It may also be used to describe the frame or mat itself, referring to the size of the opening through which a work of art would be seen.
Materials not containing hydrocarbons or their derivatives.
The quality or degree of being poisonous.
Zitherlike chordophones of Korea, similar to a dulcimer. They are in a trapezoidal shape, and usually have fourteen strings.
Long-necked plucked lutelike chordophones of the Tadjiks, Uighurs, Kazaks, and Uzbeks of Central Asia, varying in size, shape, and materials from one group to another.

Lettered notices or other displays that bear names, directions, warnings, advertisements, or symbols that are displayed or posted for public view. For smaller, less public identifying notices, use "labels (identifying artifacts)." For systems of signs arranged to communicate directions or essential information, use "signage."

Long dresses with butterfly sleeves, considered part of the national costume for women in the Philippines, and made of jusi or polyester organza. Unlike the barong Tagalog worn by males, terno are worn mostly during special occasions.
An unstandardized hue name for either a madder obtained from the Near East or any synthetic colorant of the same hue.

Numerous texts dealing with the esoteric practices of some Indian sects. In Hindu tradition, Tantras cover theology, yoga, construction of temples and images, religious practices, spells, rituals, and symbols. Buddhist Tantras cover philosophy, symbols, guidance for complex rituals, and application of sacred powers for mundane purposes.
Women's dress shoes or pumps with very narrow high heels, which became fashionable from the 1950s.
Small military caps with a nearly horizontal visor and a rigid crown that slopes toward the front; most popular in the French and United States armies, later adopted for civilian use.
Rails or parapets above and around a ship's stern, especially on sailing ships; often carved or otherwise decorated.
The parts of a hat or other headgear covering the crown of the head. For head-encircling devices signifying rank or used as ornament, but not part of a hat, use "crowns (headdresses)."

Refers to coverings for all or part of the face, usually with openings for the eyes and sometimes the mouth. They are worn to hide or alter the identity of the wearer or for protection. Masks as cultural objects have been used throughout the world in all periods since the Stone Age. Masks are extremely varied in appearance, function, and fundamental meaning. They may be associated with ceremonies that have religious and social significance or are concerned with funerary customs, fertility rites, or curing sickness. They may be used on festive occasions or to portray characters in a dramatic performance and in re-enactments of mythological events. They may be used for warfare and as protective devices in certain sports. They are also employed as architectural ornaments.
German spiked helmets before and early during WWI. They were made ​​of pressed leather, pressed horsehair, or metal. A metal spike or sphere was mounted on the top of the helmet.
Decorative devices intended to shape or knot a scarf in order to keep it in place.

Bindings in a simple style featuring tooled republican motifs and symbols, commissioned in large quantities by the English republican Thomas Hollis, who gave away collections of books bound in this way to universities and libraries in Europe and America to disseminate and promote republican beliefs.
Small vehicles based on full-sized models, often to scale.

Liturgical vestments worn by all three classes of the Orthodox Church (deacon, priest, bishop). These correspond to the Western alb, but, unlike it, sticharions may be of any colour. The sticharion of the deacon is an open vestment, held together by buttons.

A colorless, solid, water soluble carbonate perhydrate, sodium percarbonate is a highly concentrated source of anhydrous hydrogen peroxide used as a bleaching agent in many applications including paper and textile conservation.
Cone-shaped objects, usually feathered and with rubber or cork tips, volleyed back and forth in badminton.
Long, wraparound skirts worn by women for sidesaddle horseback riding.
Term generally applied to trousers worn for informal wear.
