Old Egyptian protective amulets, usually hung at the back of the neck as a counterpoise part of a necklace with a corresponding front plate, or "aegis." It was frequently made of glazed ware and was often found buried with the dead, and it was a symbol of divine protection.

Men's robe-like outerwear of cotton or silk, usually heavily embroidered with symbolic imagery around the neck and down the front; worn originally by the Hausa and primarily by the aristocracy, as a symbol of status, power, or wealth.
Round, perforated plates, usually ceramic or metal, for serving food with excess liquid or juices. Designed to be set over a larger dish to allow liquid to drain away.

Use both for Sicilian bronze coins valued at one twelfth litra and issued during the 5th century BCE and for later Roman, bronze struck coins equal to one twelfth as and issued during the Republic until the 2nd century BCE.
Heavy silver Byzantine coins worth six scruples, one twelfth of a gold solidus, and issued from the early 7th to the early 8th century.
Religious chants based on the use of divine words and phrases, that were conveyed to the Prophet Muhammad by the archangel Gabriel or at times directly by God.

Books of tropes, which are introductions to liturgical chants or interpolations or elaborations to the text of the Catholic Mass. They were discontinued when the Roman Missal was revised under Pius V (1566-1572).

Culinary hand tools for cutting and dividing dough, blade along one edge and a wooden or rolled metal handle along the opposite edge. Used to cut, pick up and portion dough and to clean the kneading surface.
Large pots in which stock for soup or sauce is made or kept.
Heated compartments for warming plates prior to food service.
Genre comprising the portrayal of fictional or non-fictional events meant to be delivered through the performance of written dialog or actions, staged by actors before an audience.
A textual description of the work or other entity, including a discussion of issues related to it.

Tools used for bead or French embroidery beading, as well as decorative chain stitch embroidery called tambour embroidery. These have a small, bent tip similar to a crochet hook or rug hooking tool. The hook catches the thread on the backside of the fabric, pulling it to the front side to create loops or attach beads or sequins.
Tools for tying poultry in preparation for cooking. These are usually made from steel, have a sharp end and an end with an eye. They are made in various lengths.
Devices used to heat milk.
Devices that measure the concentration or quality of specific gaseous compounds within a mixture of multiple gases, to register qualitatively the proportions of gas within a system.
Devices of various designs that are applied to the teeth, used in orthodontics to align and straighten teeth.
Events that are held, or occur, in relation to politics and political activity.
Method of transferring loaned property back to the original owner or custodian.

Titles or names that have been used to refer to the work in publications. For works of art and architecture, examples are titles or names in catalogs or journal articles that are not necessarily a title by which the work is normally known. For books, the term may be used to distinguish the final published title from an original unpublished or working title.
The standard unit of currency of modern Greece prior to adoption of the Euro.
The lunisolar calendar used today predominantly for Jewish religious observances, including dates for Jewish holidays and dates for reading from the Torah and other texts.

Numeric, alphanumeric, or other identifying codes of various types assigned to an art object, book, other item, or group of works by the repository that holds that item or group. Any item or group in a repository may have multiple types of repository numbers. For numbers specifically assigned at the time of accession by a repository, prefer "accession numbers."
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 899 to 800 (or 900 to 801) Before Common Era.
A category of pliers intended to be used for leather craft.
Dialect cluster spoken in Indonesian Papua Province.

Acoustic devices composed of a toothed spinning wheels that create tones if a blade or plectrum is held against them. Tones varying due to the speed or size of the wheel. Invented by French physicist Félix Savart. His invention was later adapted as a component of the tone wheel organ.
Hills on the sea floor with elevations, usually rising less than 500 meters.

Ware, originally produced in South China but later found elsewhere in China, in Japan, Vietnam, and elsewhere in Asia. It includes green-glaze ware and other color-glaze wares with distinctive low relief decoration. Objects include tea ware, decorations for the walls and roof ridges of temples, and figures, including human figures, animals, birds, and flowers in bright, glossy colors.
Visual artists who specialize in the medium of pigments incorporated in wax crayons; crayons are often known as a children's medium in current usage.
The oral manifestation of languages; language produced by articulate sounds, as opposed to a written language. Many languages have no written form and so are only spoken.
Artists of any medium who specialize in depicting the human body and figures.

Activities involving an expression of sorrow for sin or wrongdoing, self-mortification, or the undergoing of some penalty as as a token of repentance and as a means of satisfaction for sin. Penance may be imposed by ecclesiastical or other authority or voluntarily undertaken.

Various activities or disciplines concerning combat and self defense that arose as the fighting arts of the warrior and are now often practiced as sport. They include both armed and unarmed forms of combat, as well as non-combative styles. Martial arts traditionally emphasize control, spiritual training, and the unity of body and mind. Many are of East Asian origin.

Measurements of length equal to 5.5 yards, 16.5 feet, or about 5.03 meters. Also used as area measurements where square rods are equal to 30.25 square yards or about 25.3 square meters. Rods are also called poles or perches.
Supernatural beings not subject to death, as applied to mythological deities.
Trademark for a series of extremely tough and stiff acetal homopolymer resins manufactured by DuPont and used in injection molded parts.

Species of spreading oak tree that is native to North American, in the greater Midwest, ranging downward to the deep South and over into the eastern edge of the Great Plains of the U.S. When in the open, it grows to 60 feet in height by 80 feet in width, often with wide-spreading lower branches of great diameter. Chinquapin oak prefers moist, well-drained, deep, rich, alkaline soils, but is often found near the summit of hills or uplands in dry soils that may be rich, clay, sandy, or rocky. It also tolerates neutral to acidic soils. It thrives in full sun to partial sun (but is shade tolerant in youth).
In Māori tradition, beings living in deep water or dark caves, sometimes taking the form of a giant sea creature.
Genus of flowering plants in the legume family.

Pine tree native to the Mediterranean region, occurring in Southern Europe, North Africa, and the Levant, known for its edible seeds, which are also used for a variety of products including pine seed oil used in painting.

Institutions, groups, or other corporate bodies who oversee the finances, management, and maintenance of a park, which is a reserved recreation area, usually with open space or natural features; generally reserved for those managing a large public or private park. For groups with broader authority to oversee and fund multiple parks for an area, prefer "parks commissions."

Privately owned libraries established, supported, and administered by a business firm, private corporation, association, government agency, etc., to meet the needs of its members or staff in pursuing the goals of the organization.

Museums containing collections dealing with the properties of natural objects, plants, or animals, such as preserved specimens of birds, mammals, insects, and plants; rocks, minerals, and fossils. These museums have their origins in the cabinets of curiosities built up by prominent individuals in Europe during the Renaissance and Enlightenment.
Variable red colors resembling the color of pigments called "permanent red."
Variable yellowish colors resembling the color of Naples yellow (antimony yellow) pigment.
A range of colors resembling variations of blue pigment.
Any of several brown colors, originally referring to the color of umber pigment, which is derived from earth.
Refers to a range of bright green colors resembling the color of Paris green, a very poisonous copper-based powder that is used as an insecticide and pigment.
A generic style, particularly in the context of interior design, characterized by the use of long-established and common styles of furniture, wall and window treatments, etc.

A range of blue colors resembling the color of French blue pigment, which is synthetic ultramarine blue, the name originating in the early 19th century when the pigment was first imported from France.
Members of an order containing nearly 3000 species of chewing lice.
Regarding personal names, names not having particular religious signficance, used to distinguish such names from names assigned to a person for religious reasons.
Order containing 18 species in one family of fruit-eating large birds with brilliant purple, green, and crimson plumage and a prominent crest.

Second-level educational institutions, in France or based on a similar system, where the school is maintained by the state in contradistinction to a college or secondary school maintained by a municipality.
Entablatures that form the transition from wall to roof in a Dravida temple.
Depressed areas on icecaps.
Chinese bronze ritual vessels with a basin shape, similar to gui, but without handles, common to the Erligang and Anyang period. The style ends in the Western Zhou.
Text elements that act as containers or environments created to hold a logical grouping of unique identifiers, as for a scheme or concept.

Order containing around 15 species of mammals in three families, including horses, asses, zebras, rhinoceroses, tapirs, and kin, characterized as browsing and grazing animals, with an odd number of toes on each hoof, usually large in size, having relatively simple stomachs and being hindgut fermenters, digesting plant cellulose in their intestines rather than a stomach.
Proof, similar to an artist's proof, which is retained by the publisher. Can also be used in reference to any three-dimensional object.
Marbled paper showing black veins with orange, yellow and white portions. The dominant color is applied last, which pushes the other colors into fine veins.
In the Christian calendar, the week immediately preceding Easter Sunday.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in the Sudan.
Book cloth grain pattern in use from ca. 1833-1866.
Style and culture of the people of the modern nation of Ethiopia or of the ancient peoples known as the AEthiopes.
Businesses focused on selling, and often making, hats and other headgear.
Otoe and Missourias were known to live in the Nebraska region in the mid-19th century. Now located in Oklahoma; traditionally spoke Chiwere, of the Siouan language family.

Pas-vake is part of the traditional Saisiyat agricultural ceremony. It takes place twice a year; the first festival comes after the sowing is over, addressing to the ancestral spirits that the task has been completed, and the second one happens after the harvest. The significance of Pas-vake is twofold: in religious terms the festival invites the ancestors to share the food with the living Saisiyat people through rituals and asks for the ancestors’ favor at the same time; for economic purposes Pas-vake is an occasion in which people supplicates for good fortune in farming and hunting. Pas-vake also confirms and consolidates the identity conferred by the Pas-vakean to its members as a way to come to terms with and symbolically transcend the difference of backgrounds and geographical origins.
General term for equipment used for various kinds of health exercises.
Small beds for baby dolls, often with rockers.

Mechanized devices designed to increase the thickness, compactness, and consistency of woolen fibers by subjecting woolen cloth to moisture, heat, friction, and pressure. Woolen cloth is first submerged in a vessel where it is treated with liquid; the wet cloth is then removed from the vessel by means of cylindrical rollers which agigate and beat the cloth before transferring it to a fulling box to be shrunk.

A strong yellow pigment made by mixing powdered lead chloride with lead carbonate, then fusing. This yellow pigment was used for a short time in oil paints, but its sensitivity to light and sulfur fumes limited its use and it was replaced by chrome yellow pigments.

Fiber product used by Maori in weaving. It is prepared by scrapping, pounding and washing New Zealand flax, which are plants of the Phormium genus, not true flax. Muka is a key material in Maori traditional textiles where it is usually used in tāniko or twined weaving.
Any object made from wood: from "tree."

The solid, brittle, clear resinous residue left after the distillation of turpentine from balsam, having a color ranging from yellow or reddish-brown. It becomes sticky when warm and has a faint pine-like odor. Primarily composed of abietic acid (about 80%), rosin reacts in hot alkaline solutions to form rosin soaps. Rosin weathers poorly, becoming oxidized and brittle with age. It also has poor moisture resistance. Although many of its aging properties are undesirable, rosin is or was used as an ingredient in paints, varnishes, inks, adhesives, sealing wax, soldering fluxes, sizing paper, and linoleum. Because it increases sliding friction, it is commonly used for coating bows of some stringed instruments, and as a slip preventative on the floors of stages and shoes of dancers. The inexpensive resin is also used for sizing paper.
A fugitive yellow natural dyestuff prepared from the dried flowers of Crocus sativus.
Wood of trees of the genus Taxus.

Wood from the Pinus sylvestris, native to Eurasia and imported to North America. The Scotch pine has tough, light brown wood. Its lumber is used for millwork and it is an important conifer for timber in Europe.

Hard, close-grained, durable wood of the species Quercus stellata, native to sandy soils of the central and southern United States. It is tough and rot-resistant, used for fence posts, rough construction, and as a fuel for barbequing meat.

Wood of the species Cinnamomum camphora, native to southeastern Asia. Camphorwood has a pungent smell, reddish-brown streaks, and irregular grain, and has been used for small carvings and decorative items, clothes chests, trunks, wardrobes, and coffins.

A member of a large group of organic chemicals, containing only the elements hydrogen and carbon. They are major constituents of crude petroleum and natural gas, from which certain fractions are extracted for use as fuel and as raw materials for the chemical industry.
A major fiber-associated component of wheat bran and legumes responsible for the storage of phosphorus. In paper conservation, it has been used as a treatment for iron-catalyzed oxidation.
A secondary mineral found in the oxidized zones of antimony-bearing lead deposits.

A material composed of two sheets of plate glass with a sheet of transparent resinoid between, the whole molded together under heat and pressure. It will crack without shattering when subjected to a severe blow.

Pure metallic element having symbol MO and atomic number 42; a gray silvery metal. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make objects and materials.

Any glass, usually blown glass, made with colorless, white, or colored canes to form a linear pattern in the glass. One method of production is by placing side by side a series of transparent rods or canes, each containing a twisted thread of colored or milk-white glass. The rods are then heated until they are fused into a single sheet.
In Indian architecture, a palm-leaf (decorative pattern); palmette design.
Crosses with vertical and horizontal arms of equal length.
A motif of hair on crown; finial, crest.
In Indian architecture, a a Jaina temple with three sanctuaries.

Community places for the regular assembly or congregation of Jews for liturgical services, assembly, and study apart from the service of the temple; since the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem, worship at the synagogue is the sole place of public worship.
In Indian architecture, a vimāna with a solid ground floor.
Structures or parts of structures equipped for taking X-rays for medical diagnosis or other purposes.
Buildings in which science is taught, often containing laboratories or other hands-on learning and research facilities.
Building used for union gatherings.
Lots or buildings used for storage, cutting, and sale of lumber and wood-related products, particularly lumber used in construction and home improvement.
General term for built works containing facilities for laundering clothing, linens, and other textiles.
Buildings enclosing a natural spring; sufficiently cool for use as a storehouse of milk and other dairy products.

Refers to public or private spaces set aside for manual or light industrial work. It may be used to refer to spaces in which fine art was created, particularly regarding art dating prior to the 16th century. It may also refer to spaces in which woodworkers, furniture makers, pottery makers, glass makers, and other craftspeople work. In the most general sense, it refers to spaces where goods of any type are made, prepared for sale, or sold. In modern usage, the term "studios" is generally used to refer to spaces for creating fine art dating from the 16th century to the present.
Transverse arms of cruciform buildings, usually churches.
In Indian architecture, a five-spired structure.

In Christian churches, rooms or separate buildings in which the celebrants, other clergy, and acolytes may dress prior to the mass or other services. The room may also be used for storage of liturgical vestments, sometimes for storage of vessels, and other items, and for meetings. For rooms serving more for the storage of sacred items, use "sacristies," although modern usage of the two terms broadly overlaps.
In Indian architecture, a oversailing rectilinear fillet.
In Indian architecture, a square or rectangular tenon-moulding between the abacus and the capital of the pillar.
Narrow windows having a single light; may be decorated with pilasters and topped by an arch.

Courses of stone projecting beyond the face of a wall to guide water away from the face of the wall. Courses of stone projecting beyond the face of a wall to guide water away from the face of the wall.
In Indian architecture, a triangular decorated ceiling-slab at sub-cardinal position.
Columns depicting serpents, features of Toltec architecture.
Long, thin swords with blunt ends, used by the Tuareg and other Saharian peoples.
Objects that hold pieces of paper together or affixed to another surface.

Drawings using ink as the primary medium and pen as the primary implement, usually on paper but may be on another support. Such drawings have a distinctive, linear appearance. For drawings that use pen and ink as well as washes, prefer "pen and wash drawings." For drawings or paintings using ink applied with brushes, use "ink wash paintings."
Marks on base metals, silver plate, and American silver in imitation of hallmarks; pseudohallmarks are not required by law and do not always have the same significance as true hallmarks.

Generally, records of organizations which are vital to the continuity of a business in case of emergency or after a disaster. For public records of life events generated under government or other authority, use "vital statistics records."
Books designed to teach spelling; often employing lists of selected words and sometimes including exercises.
Groups who work to promote or accomplish stated goals through projects or other activities.

Groups consisting of a particular library's target clientele plus any others who actually use the collection or services of the library. Also, formal or informal groups of people who use a particular database or retrieval product.

In a society, people who are successful in military endeavors and hold high status due to this, especially when they represent a relatively small percentage of the population; usually refers to historical rather than modern societies.
People who depart from their native or usual country or region to live elsewhere. For those who come into a country or region from another to settle there, use "immigrants."
Generally, a person who collects specimens, works of art, curiosities.
People who appear often on television and are known to the public primarily through that medium. They include actors, announcers, hosts of shows, and religious leaders.
Refers to people who rule or govern, specifically sovereigns.
People who claim or aspire to a title or a throne, often when considered to have no just title or otherwise did not achieve the position.
People who polish surfaces, often a craftsperson in the production process.

People who coat the surfaces of walls, furniture, vehicles, or other things with paint, which is pigment suspended in liquid, with the primary goal of protecting or giving simple color to the surface. For people who apply paint to a surface to create an expressive or communicative image, see "painters (artists)."
People who design websites, particularly with a focus on aesthetics, content, and ease of use.

People responsible for spreading out or dispersing products, such as a film, book, or other work, available in a certain situation or venue. For those who place work on the market for sale or distribution to the public, use "publishers.".
Small, tempered-steel knives with slim handles and oblique cutting edges used for precise, delicate cutting, as of friskets and stencils for printmaking.
General term for cutting tools designed for use with leather.
Instruments, dating from the early 20th century, used for measuring grain.
Prisms located in the lenses of refracting telescopes, which enable images to be seen as spectra.
Vented cabinets equipped with suspending rods for drying films after processing.
Blades of various shapes without a cutting edge that are used for applying putty.

Refers to a movement of Western art that existed from the late nineteenth century through the early twentieth century. The term was coined by art critics Roger Fry, Clive Bell and others to refer to art that chronologically followed the Impressionist movement but was distinct from Neo-Impressionism. It is characterized by widely differing, highly personal artistic styles.
Refers to the style and period that coincided with the reign of Süleyman II, 1687 to 1691.

Refers to the European movement affecting visual arts, literature, music, and to a lesser degree architecture from the mid-18th to the mid-19th centuries. Viewed as a reaction to Neoclassical formality, it stressed emotion and the right to individual expression. Works encompass a range of styles but in general are painterly, dynamic, and reflect an interest in color over line.
Nationality, culture, and general style of ancient Laconia, a region in the southeastern part of the Peloponnese peninsula, for a time having its capital at Sparta.

Refers to the culture in northern Europe dating from late 5th millennium BCE and beyond; named for the distinctive vessels that are sometimes shaped like funnels. Although the culture is classified as early Neolithic, it has much in common with the late Mesolithic. The culture varies from region to region, but it is generally characterized by early domestication of animals and plants, polished stone and flint tools, collared flasks, buckets, bowls, funnel beakers decorated with horizontal and vertical grooves, and megalithic burial monuments in some regions.
Style and culture of the area around Kushinagara, Uttar Pradesh.

Painting style from the Heian period (794-1185) that may have referred specifically to the work of professional painters of the imperial court and was notable for its ink-line drawing and action packed scenes. This style, considered masculine, was sometimes contrasted with "onna-e," feminine painting.

Refers generally to a variety of styles of ash-glazed pottery produced at the Sanage kilns east of the present-day city of Nagoya, throughout the Heian period (794-1185). Productions typically included bowls, jars, dishes and vases.
Period, style, and culture of historicTangut state, occupying an area in what is now northwestern China, that flourished from ca. 997 until 1227 when it was conquered by Genghis Khan.
Refers to the work of a school of artisst founded by Wu Wei (1465-1508). The style is characterized by rapidly sketched compositions, with loose and forceful brushstrokes.

Style of art and approach to pop culture in general that challenges the validity of a high or established art aesthetic. Critics disagree as to its relationship with the fine art world, and if it is to be considered a "legitimate" art movement on its own. The term was coined by artist Robert Williams in 1979 to refer to the populist nature of his own work. The style is characterized by both its influences, such as comic books, tattoos, and hot-rod street culture, and it approach, which is typically bright, garish, and infused with a sense of humor.

Revival style found in the United States in the 1930s, that employees elements of Georgian and Regency style prototypes, usually resulting in buildings two stories high with a hipped roof, and brick walls with quoins at the corners and sometimes at the main entrance. Its also often features double-hung windows with shutters; an entrance porch, and a small octagonal window above the door.

Style and culture of an Iroquoian-speaking Native American tribe in southern and coastal Virginia. Related to the Meherrin and Tuscarora communities in North Carolina and southern Virginia. Today the Nottoway are recognized as two different tribes, the "Nottoway Indian Tribe" and the "Cheroenhaka (Nottoway) Indian Tribe."
Culture of a First Nations band government in the Canadian province of British Columbia; the only First Nations band within the boundaries of the City of Vancouver.

Refers to the culture of the Nisenan, a group indigenous to Northern California, specifically areas along the foothills of what are today Nevada, Sierra, Yuba, Sutter, and Placer counties. While historically the Nisenan have been classified as part of the Maidu people, the tribe corrects this mis-identification in their literature.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Kenya.
Works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Tanzania.
Use to describes works produced by the Berber people of the same name living in the Egyptian oasis of Siwah.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northern Nigeria.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Cameroon, southwestern Chad, and western Central African Republic.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group collective of the same name living in eastern Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, and western Guinea.

Portraits, usually photographs in any format, that depict members of a profession, either singly or in groups. Those depicted are most often wearing clothing associated with that profession, or display tools or other paraphernalia associated with it.
Substances which absorb or release large amounts of so-called ‘latent’ heat when they go through a change in their physical state, i.e. from solid to liquid and vice versa.
Any substance or agent that ceases chemical or electrical reactions.
A framework of interwoven rods, poles, or branches; used with daub as a building material.
Compounds that lower the surface tension of water so that soils may be dislodged, and that suspend soil particles to be flushed away.

Generic term for materials derived from vinyl chloride, vinyl acetate, or vinylidene chloride. Commonly used with reference to all polymers and copolymers of which vinyl chloride is a constituent. Use more precise terminology for known materials such as "polyvinyl chloride" or "polyvinyl acetate."
General term for materials comprising fibers or other components that are created by weaving. Includes, but not limited to, woven textiles.

General term for a heavy type of paper that is at least 0.012 inches thick. Some paperboards are made from thick paper pulp castings that are milled or pressed into a hard, stiff sheet, while others are made from several laminated sheets of paper adhered together.
Vegetable oil extracted from the seed kernel of the peanut. The oil is edible and used for cooking, but is also used in soaps and fuels.
Refers to the interior portions of buildings or other structures fully separated and divided off from the other portions by a floor, ceiling, and walls or partitions.

A technology that provides rapid multi-parametric analysis of single cells in solution. Flow cytometers utilize lasers as light sources to produce both scattered and fluorescent light signals. Cell populations can be analyzed and/or purified based on their fluorescent or light scattering characteristics.
The process or function of copying or taking material or data from one place for use in another; for example, copying data out of a database for reconfiguration in a publication.

Pre-Christian and pre-Islamic religious beliefs and practices of the Finno-Ugric peoples, who inhabit regions of northern Scandinavia, Siberia, the Baltic area, and central Europe. In modern times the religion of many of these peoples has been an admixture of agrarian and nomadic primitive beliefs and of Christianity and Islam.
The activity of determining objectives and outlining or arranging the procedures and resources for attaining them, especially in a formal project proposal or scheme.
Board games where the objective is to move game pieces from a start to a finish point. These may have linear tracks or other designs that form a guide for the advance the player's pieces.
Conveying property to a creditor as security for the repayment of a loan.

Sudden outbreaks of a disease in people, animals, or plant populations in a region where the disease was not previously recognized or where a rapid increase in the number of new cases of a previous existing endemic disease occurs in the area.
Religious ceremonies featuring music and dance traditionally performed by African Americans in coastal Georgia and South Carolina, derived from African practices.
In Indian architecture, a door-jamb bearing pramathas or amorini figures.

The state or condition associated with male, female, neutral, or other social or cultural distinctions and differences, rather than strictly biological ones. Although gender may be based on sex, for biological and physiological traits that distinguish the males and females of a species, prefer "sex (biological characteristic)."
Describes concepts related to resources located in or produced by the natural environment.
Art produced for rituals commemorating the dead and for art produced as an individual expression of grief.
Term used to describe soft, delicate and often exaggerated blending in oil paint, particularly when applied to flesh tones; art historical term used primarily in the 18th century.

Forms or outlines created by two curves that intersect in such a way so as to combine characteristics of oval and almond-shapes, being rounded on one end and pointed on the other. Examples include leaf-shaped arrowheads. To designate a plant or other thing that is composed of or possesses leaves or parts that resemble leaves, use "foliose."

Philosophical theory that recognizes more than one ultimate reality or value, each capable of rational support and all appropriately included as options for individual choice. For the cultural movement promoting the full participation of diverse ethnic, racial, religious, or social groups within the larger community, use "multiculturalism."

Religious ideology based on numerous texts dealing with esoteric practices originally of some Indian sects. Among other practices, noted for sexual and meditative rituals and techniques concerned with divine creative energy (shakti) and supranormal mystical goals. Tantrism appears in both Buddhism and Hinduism and has also influenced a number of other religious movements and trends since the 5th century.
Belief that the only or the highest values or objectives in life lie in material well-being and pleasure, and in the furthering of material progress.
The quality, faculty, or aptitude for creating unique solutions to problems, or of inventng new things, language, art, etc.
Refers to organized activity in which capital and labor are utilized for some useful purpose or to manufacture goods or to manipulate or process a product.
Money compulsorily levied by the state or local authorities on individuals, property, or businesses.

Declarations of laws, regulations, fund allocations, international treaties, etc., having the force of authority by virtue of their passing or enactment by an official organ of a state or other governing body.
In written or printed works, a list of the work's parts in sequence, usually with a page number or other symbol indicating where each part begins.
The aggregate of real things and actual existence as opposed to what is theorized, imagined, or desired. Reality is that which underlies and is the truth of appearances or phenomena.

Refers to the condition of urban areas characterized by general deterioration in the quality of existing buildings and infrastructural systems, often caused by adverse economic, environmental, or zoning forces.

Disciplines that focus on forming plans regarding human habitats or humans’ effects upon other habitats, typically disciplines that deal with the design, sustainability, or control of development regarding urban, economic, regional, environmental, community, health-related, and transportation concerns.
Any process of measuring sensitivity.

The process of obtaining or generating a visual representation of something by means of photography, radar, ultrasound, X-rays, or other technique, typically for a purpose such as examination, research, medical diagnosis, or reconnaissance.

Technique of blowing for the purpose of coloring or decorating. An example is in decorating porcelain, where powdered pigment is blown through a hollow tube, passing through a piece of gauze attached at the other end to ensure that the pigment spreads evenly.

Any of various aqueous treaments to remove dirt or other unwanted surface materials. In commercial garment cleaning, the term is used interchangeably with "green cleansing" to describe gentle, environmentally friendly aqueous cleansing. In conservation context: washing of textiles.
Giving a smooth finish to metal by striking lightly with a smoothly faced hammer, or to metal or other materials by passing through rolls.

The process of embellishing architecture, furniture, or other objects. In reference to specific forms of decoration, such as fluting, finials, or monograms, that embellish and are part of the building or object, but are not structurally essential to it, use "ornaments"
Electrical connections used in telephones, computers, network cabling, and other contexts; characterized by solid copper wires having been punched down into short open-ended slots.
Short spouts, pipes, or channels designed to convey water outward and away from vertical surfaces, as from gutters, parapets, cisterns, or basins of fountains.
Joints in wood, metal, and other materials that are held secure by driving or inserting dowel pins or other pins into holes drilled into the joint.

Nails of various types used for wooden trunks, both to hold panels together and to attach leather or thin wooden supports to the face of panels. When attaching supports, the nails were driven part way into the panel and then a piece of iron was held against the interior, so that the nail hit the iron and clinched or curled back into the wood, in order create a smooth interior surface.
Hinges that employ a pin in one leaf of the hinge and a socket in the other, allowing the joint to be disengaged simply by being lifted out.
Locks for use on metal doors of the small chests or boxes within a fireproof safe.

Refers to small objects of prehistoric art, especially of the Upper Palaeolithic, that could be carried from place to place, as opposed to cave art. Examples include small figures, carved tools, or pieces of jewelry.

Small Christian devotional statues that are typically carried as amulets in a pocket or elsewhere on a person's clothing. For items having a similar function but in the shape of a disc, use "devotional tokens."
Men's loose-fitting jackets, often of a heavy fabric and trimmed with a braid, worn for smoking or lounging at home.

Refers to carved wooden sculptures depicting stylized heads and necks of birds. The larger sized style features a very long, usually pointed beak and a face that may include features of a crocodilem, a horned figure, or a D'mba figure; the arching neck piece is mounted on a detachable spherical base. The other main style. is smaller, made from one piece of wood, is more compact,with a shorter beak, is less elaborately carved, and mounted on a concave base. They serve mainly as shrine pieces, representing both the Supreme God and the spiritual protector of the family lineage. Alternative uses are as dance headresses and divination implements for such rituals as male and female initiation and harvest, healing, judiciary, and funerary ceremonies.
Greek headdresses as depicted on Attic vases, often appearing with dotted motifs or patterns.
Large, ornately trimmed hats as worn in the musical show The Merry Widow in 1907.

Small wine glasses of distinctive shape and size, designed for drinking sherry, a fortified wine of Spanish origin. Sherry glasses have a round foot, a stem, and small bowl; a common design has a tapering bowl that is colored at the lip and fades to a light color or clear at the top of the stem.
Fiddles having a hollow soundbox curving inwards at the waist like a violin but with a flat back, and frets on the fingerboard. They are played held downwards on the lap or between the legs.
Supports for a person's feet, as for example an attachment to a barber's or a reclining chair.

Elevated stands with a sloping top and usually a ledge at the bottom of the slope designed to support a book or script in a convenient position for a reader standing before it. A lectern may be placed on a table or mounted on a pedestal. A lectern In a church is usually situated in the chancel, sometimes inside a rood screen or tribune.
Small, low tables with box stretchers and, generally, turned legs and overhanging tops; designed for a variety of domestic uses, not necessarily exclusively for taverns.
Desks that resemble spinets, the keyed musical instruments which are closely related to harpsichords.
Large tables situated in the main room or great hall of a manor house or other large, stately home.
Cabinets that hold spools of thread on spindles. Holes are drilled in the fronts of the cabinets where thread can be pulled out.
Paneled chests often used as cabinet stands.
Beds with two or four posts approximately four feet in height.
Use with reference to chairs with a square back such as those popularized by Sheraton and appearing from the late 18th century.

Chairs with a low seat and a tall sloping back, used as a prayer seat or stool; the form was seen in the 17th century, but became particularly popular during the Gothic Revival of the 19th century. For kneelers of similar form having a support for elbows and bookshelf, but not in the form of a chair, use "prie-dieus (benches)." For chairs with a very similar design, particularly those dating to the 18th century, but intended for use by females watching card games, use "voyeuses à genoux." Prie-dieu chairs may be made of humble materials, such as a wooden frame with a rattan seat-kneeler, or they may be upholstered; they may include a shelf for prayer books. They are found in private chambers and occasionally in churches. If they are part of a set, it is usually a bedroom set. Voyeuses à genoux are always upholstered, and are generally part of a larger set along with voyeuses intended for males to sit astride while watching card games.

Enclosing devices of glass used to protect the light source within, diffuse or redirect its light, or modify its color; also such devices used to increase the draft to the flame in an open-flame lamp or candle.
Upholstered chairs with low seats and very high backs placed either beside or in front of the fire.
Small oil lamps consisting essentially of a font and burner with a short rounded stub on the bottom for insertion into a socket of a candlestick, sconce, or chandelier; usually of metal or glass.
Small bags with secure closings intended primarily for holding coins.
Relatively small, squat lidded boxlike vessels for holding cosmetics and toilet articles in ancient Greece. Generally cylindrical in shape. Often found in the graves of women and warriors.
Rough place on a blown glass piece where the pontil rod has been broken away. May be ground or ground and polished to form a smooth circular depression.
Bags used by doctors to carry equipment, particularly when making house calls.
Photoelectric instruments used for measuring the amount of sediment in liquids; often used in the process of papermaking, to gauge opacity.

Headings, initials, titles, catchwords, marginal index words, or other text printed or written in red (the remainder of the text being in black), or otherwise distinguished in lettering, as guides to the contents of pages.
Tin vessels with compartments used to carry food, originally for field workers. The lids of these vessels could be used as plates.
Small vessels used to serve heated milk and sops, or small pieces of bread, which were dipped into the bowl.
Refers to the style and culture of modern Saudi Arabia.
In bookbinding, cords, tapes, or thongs placed against the back of a text block around which the sewing passes. They may also be used as a means of board attachment.

Tall, wide-mouthed vessels, generally having a pouring lip, and that have a deep bowl on a stemmed base and a single vertical handle. The bowl is usually cylindrical, baluster-shaped, or helmet-shaped.
Produced or shaped by beating with a hammer, as iron or silver objects. For commercially pure iron of a fibrous nature made by melting white cast iron use "wrought iron."
Decorations designed or used for festivals, which are any gala occasions devoted to community observances.
Works of art produced using the technology of copying machines.
Visible signs (which can include figures, such as personifications, or objects) that stand for something else, often something abstract or invisible.
In Indian architecture, a seated male figure as personified wealth or treasure (auspicious decorative motif): Types: Śaṅkhanidhi, Padmanidhi, etc.; mythical treasure, sometimes personified.
People whose work involves transmitting messages and parcels or performing errands.

Deterioration caused by agents present in a material itself. This may be the a result of short-lived, temporary, or impermanent materials, or the structural nature of a material. This fault or defect may lead to natural deterioration or make an object more susceptible to external agents of deterioration.
Places on the back of a text block where the sewing needle emerges from or passes into the leaves or gatherings, generally designated during marking up.
A pattern consisting of five elements arranged at each of the four corners of a square or rectangle, and one in the center. Often used in series as a motif in a border or field in textiles.
Indian Buddhist masters who have attained superhuman abilities through tantric practices. Many schools of Tibetan Buddhism trace the origins of their teachings to the eighty-four mahasiddhas.

Tools having very flexible blades, used by artists to mix colors or spread paint; sometimes used to apply paint or to clean the palette. Palette knives resemble knives, but do not have sharp edges and are not used for cutting.
Equipment used to sharpen pencils against a cutting edge.
Those who make dies, which are stamps used for impressing a design upon a softer material. Die making may involve forging and engraving.
Writing shelves, characteristic of Shoin style architecture, that projected out, sometimes from a bay window, onto the surrounding porch.
Setbacks in the face of a wall or in an earthen embankment; also, footings or ledges formed by the setting back of a wall.
Motif found in Maōri art depicting an unfurling fern frond.
In Indian architecture, a narrative episode (carved on decorative bands).
In Indian architecture or sculpture, a gorgon face or gorgon head; kīrttimukha; gorgonoid head-mask.

Reference sources detailing drugs, medicines, and their preparations, use, and dosage, especially those recognized as official or standard. For non-standard references setting out the ingredients and amounts to be used in pharmacological preparations but not including any recommendations for use and dosage, use "formularies."
General term referring to people, places, things, events, activities, or attributes that are not firmly established or can be any of various options.
Hand tools used in the fabrication of sails used to smooth and flatten seams.

Tools used by shoe makers to add lustre to leather. These consist of  relatively large beak-shaped, iron heads attached to a wooden heft. The head, which is hot and is covered in wax or another polishing material, is rubbed over the surface of the leather.
Cutters of various types used in woodworking.
The perception of identity, distinctiveness, and significance of a group that shares a linguistic group, religious belief, nationality, cultural tradition, or perceived physiological characteristics.
People skilled or trained in physiotherapy, which is the treatment of injury, disease, or pain by physical methods, such as manipulation, massage, exercise, and application of heat or cold.
Those who favor or advocate the legal prevention of the manufacture, sale, or transportation of alcoholic beverages.
Pottery characterized by a fine-grained matrix encorporating rock fragments that cause the surface to feel gritty. Used generally to refer to materials from different periods and regions.
Concepts related to the doctrine of Jainism.

Complete, nonperiodical printed works generally of fewer than 80 pages, often with a paper cover, sometimes short treatises on arguments or topics of current interest. For smaller printed works, of one sheet folded and not stitched or bound, use "leaflets." An independent publication consisting of a few leaves of printed matter fastened together but not bound.

Navigational maps that primarily display traffic roads but also commonly include administrative boundaries, and points of interest for travellers. Since the mid-20th century these have been primarily intended for use by motorists.
Written, digital, spoken, or signed representations of the attributes or qualities of something or someone.
Modifier describing a color that is not saturated and of low intensity.

Portable books, treatises, or compendiums, covering one or more subjects, arranged for quick location of information and of a size such as may conveniently be held in the hand. Examples are instructional manuals and guides to museums' collections.
Extending in the same direction and everywhere equidistant; usually said of lines and linear objects and structures. For the corresponding noun, use "parallelism."

Early cinema works that relied on the technology of the camera or editing techniques such as split-screen, stop-motion, double-exposure, or substitution shots as special effects to create surprising or seemingly magical tranformations onscreen. These works first appeared in the late 19th century, created by Georges Méliès, the French showmen Émile and Vincent Isola, the British magicians David Devant and John Nevil Maskelyne, and later by American cinematographers Billy Bitzer and James Stuart Blackton. The term is reserved for a genre of early cinema distinct from contemporary films that may also employ special effects.
An assemblage of photographic prints pieced together to form a continuous panorama or aerial view.

Refers to the style predominantly of sculpture that first appeared in an art exhibition in 1966. Named by critic Lucy Lippard, the style is characterized by a rejection of Minimalist formalism, with an emphasis on experimental form and the use of soft materials such as rubber, vinyl, plastic and polyester resin.
Process of making photographic prints using a printing-out paper that has light-sensitive salts of uranium and silver in a collodion binder.

Large group containing between 5,000 and 10,000 species, depending upon the classification, of mostly multicellular, marine algae, including many notable seaweeds and coralline algae. They are characterized by having eukaryotic cells without flagella and centrioles, using floridean starch as food reserve, having phycobiliproteins as accessory red pigments, lacking external endoplasmic reticulum, and using sexual reproduction.
In Indian architecture, a jewel frieze.
Dried stalks of cereals or other grasses, used for many purposes, including weaving, plaiting, and braiding.
Thin pieces or plates of any substance, but often of metal. Examples are the relatively pliable metal plates often used in making armor pieces.

Objects of any material, such as pieces of wood, bone, paper, straws, etc., used in methods of random selection to secure a decision. Examples of use include in resolving disputes, dividing goods, choosing people for an office or duty, or choosing a course of action. The use of the objects may be seen to appeal to chance or to a divine agent believed to be involved in the results of chance.
Nationality, culture, or style of the city of Naples, Italy, and its historic kingdom.
A liquid compound used as an anesthetic in obstetrics, and in conservation as a degreasing solvent.

Refers to the styles and cultures developed by the peoples dwelling in the range of mountains extending northeast from the modern central Czech Republic to the Polish-Czech border and into Romania and the Ukraine.
Style and culture of the dependency of Saint Martin, the French depency on the island of Saint Martin.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Louisiania.
Provincial styles belonging to Roman cultures.
Describes construction that utilizes prefabricated units, based on the combination of similar subcomponents.

Scissors, which comprise a pair of pivoted blades attached to handles, designed for tasks involved in sewing, including cutting thread and clipping seams. For scissors to cut lengths of fabric, use "sewing shears."
Hand tool in wood with finger-thick teeth for untangling scutched flax.

Calcium stearate is a white, waxy powder, insoluble in water, created by heating calcium oxide and stearic acid. It is used industrially as a water repellent, as in paints and emulsions, and as a food additive.
Historic styles belonging to West Turkestani cultures.

Assemblies of items that the creator intended to be kept or seen together, cuch as a tea set, a desk set, or a pair of terrestrial and celestial globes. A set differs from a collection in that it is typically smaller and it was intended by the creator to be grouped together. It is useful to catalog the set as a whole when the items in the set will not be cataloged separately or when there are characteristics of the whole set that may not be apparent in the individual records for the parts.
Components which are broad, limber, or flat, usually hanging or working on a hinge.

Rods, sticks, or shafts used to point to text or other material. Typical use of a pointer is by teachers or lecturers to indicate something on a blackboard, map, diagram, or other visual material. For pointers that use a laser light rather than a rod, use "laser pointers."
Objects or textiles specifically designed to clean eyeglasses.

Territories that are ruled directly by a central government within a federation. Examples are in Venezuela and Malaysia. For entities that are part of a federation and that share sovereignty, use “federated states.”

Gifts presented by the groom’s family to the bride’s family during a betrothal ceremony, as part of pre-wedding customs. In Asian cultures, the gifts serve as a token of appreciation to the bride’s family for raising their daughter, and a show of the groom’s sincerity in marrying her. Betrothal gifts typically have symbolic and auspicious meanings associated to them, and may include food items, tea, jewellery and bride price.

The bookbinding process of wrapping cord tightly around a book held between specially shaped boards, the cords running over the spine on either side of the raised bands, over the boards, and under the fore edge of the book, for the purpose of making the covering adhere securely to the boards. May refer also for the process of wrapping cord from head to tail at the spine of a book in order to pinch the headcaps.
Refers to works in any medium intended for use by or the appreciation of a general audience, as opposed to works intended for the appreciation or use of specialists, experts, or critics.
Administrative bodies under the authority of an intendant.

A mesh fabric made from threads or cords that are knotted or woven at regular intervals. Nets were originally made by hand, but are now typically machine woven. Net may range from a lace-like fabric to coarse nets used for sports equipment and hunting. For the objects consisting of meshed arrangements of threads, cords, or ropes that have been twisted, knotted, or woven together at regular intervals, use "nets (objects)."
To become opaque, darken and lose clarity, mist up. In conservation context, refers to opacification of stained glass and enamels.
Causing a liquid to spread over a given surface or to penetrate into a given material.
Taking apart or removing significant pieces, especially to reduce or disable the function.
The process of dispersing particles and breaking up lumps within a substance in order to create greater fluidity; frequently used in ceramics to convert clay into slip.
The outline, form, or characteristic configuration of an object, including its contours; the external form or outer boundary of the object.
In Indian architecture, a three-celled structure.
The quality or state of lacking stability, of tending toward changeability, or of readily decomposing or changing chemically.

Having a surface that resists but is not impervious to water. To describe materials or surfaces impervious to water, use 'waterproof' (ALT of "waterproofing"). For the state or quality of having little or no affinity for water, especially on the molecular level, use "hydrophobicity."

A zither is a musical instrument introduced into England and America ca. 1850 from Austria, and having thirty to forty strings let into the lower rim of a shallow wooden resonance-box. It bears fretted melody strings of metal, usually five in number and tuned by machine screws, and unfretted strings of gut or nylon, sometimes numbering thirty or more, tuned by metal wrist pins. It is played by striking with the fingers and thumb. In modifications of the instrument a fretted finger-board is fitted across a resonance-box shaped like a heart (bow zither) or like a viola (viola zither), and the instrument is played with a bow.
Okinawan musical instruments whose name literally translates to "three strings," typically covered with snakeskin. It was the precursor to the mainland Japanese shamisen.

Small printed sheets, and later cards, bearing tradesmen's advertisements, often including an engraved illustration; produced from the 17th through the 19th century. For cards made later, bearing the name and address of a business concern and the name of its representative, and intended more for information than for advertising, use "business cards." For cards made later and distributed for advertisement, use "advertising cards," and for those made later and issued primarily to be collected, with or without advertisements on them, use "collecting cards."

Cloth dresses typically worn by Native North American women from the Plateau region (including Yakama, Cayuse, and Umatilla communities, amongst others.) Derived from pre-contact buckskin dresses, wingdresses today are usually made from cotton fabric, sometimes decorated with florals. Sleeves are cut to drape over the arms, mimicking the form of a bird's wing. Usually worn for various ceremonies, such as the Fancy Shawl Dance.

A wine-colored organic colorant from various sources; originally made with cochineal or brazilwood dye. In the 19th century, aniline dyes were used to make Vienna lake. None of the colorants are permanent and are usually restricted to interior house paints.
One of four genres of text that together constitute each of the Vedas, the sacred scriptures of most Hindu traditions.
Shoes with a strap around the ankle or instep, with an extra strap that comes out of the vamp (as to form a 'T') with the strap around the ankle.
Headwear of varied design, often in the form of a scullcap formed from a knitted tube shape.
Rear frames of square-ended watercraft terminating at the stern. Use also for the individual planks or boards forming the sterns of square-ended watercraft.

Any of various folds in the fabric or applied or detached bands that serve as a finish or trimming on the arms or legs of items of costume such as blouses, coats, trousers, gloves, or boots, or as costume accessories. Includes cuffs made as separate items in addition to those made as component parts of garments. In an example in a military context, sleeve cuffs may be employed to designate unit or rank.
Womenswear designed to be worn during pregnancy.

Ancient Etruscan helmets derived from the widely used Corinthian helmets of Greece and Italy, with the skull covering the head to the eyes only, and having either a short tail at the back or a flared circular brim all round to protect the neck and cheeks.
Objects of adornment worn on an individual's shoulders.
Bindings of a style originating in France in the late 17th century characterized by outside covers of austere plainness and elaborate doublures or inside covers.

Miniature reproductions of cars (whether or not they exist) that can be played with. Model cars are often classified by scale, but also by brand. Some have become a collector's item and thus some models are also marketed specifically to collectors.

Ecclesiastical vestments worn by bishops and priests consisting of a long narrow strip of silk, linen, or other cloth worn around the neck and falling from the shoulders to the knee or lower. In the Western church, the sides of the stole are crossed over the chest.

A super-absorbent polymer, the sodium salt of polyacrylic acid, with broad commercial applications. In a conservation context, it is used as a moisture buffer material for humidity control in museum exhibit cases and in historic structures.
Firearms used for recreational purposes; for military projectile weapons, use terms found under "<projectile weapons>."
Apron-shaped garment components that may be worn with dresses that open at the front.

Headdresses consisting of a tight-fitting cap around which is wound a long cloth, originating in eastern Mediterranean and southern Asian countries. Also, headgear of similar appearance which may be constructed differently.

Large pieces of square, oblong, or triangular cloth used as garments traditionally for women worn over the shoulders, covering the back, chest, and, sometimes, head. Shawls can be made from cotton or wool, and can be plain or patterned.
Conical containers, usually made of metal, made to hold small floral arrangements. Worn by individuals attached to a buttonhole or lapel for ornamentation.

Type of ladies' garment that first developed in the 1670s in Europe; they were relatively loose, gown- or coat-like garments worn belted at the waist with a long train draped at the hips to reveal the front of the matching petticoat below. This style replaced the earlier stiff, constricting boned bodice-and-skirt style previously worn by women. As the style evolved, the pleats at the front were reduced in number and the bodice was opened, with the torso now covered by a stiffened piece of fabric known as a stomacher. Originally an informal style, the mantua gradually developed as formal dress and the skirt grew to extraordinary proportions. The mantua was thought to display silk designs to their best advantage, as they were draped rather than cut; as such, it is believed the garment was named after Mantua, Italy, where expensive silks were produced. However, it has also been suggested that the name derives from manteau, the French term for a coat.
Rectangular, sloping slabs to be placed under one end of a platter, so causing gravy to flow to the opposite end.
Roman silver coins of uncertain value issued between roughly 211 and 170 BCE and characterized by a depiction on the reverse of Victory placing a wreath on a trophy.
Aluminum-bronze coins of the Soviet Union valued at one hundredth of a ruble and Russian silver or copper coins issued since 1534.
General term for the vocal music of the various Syrian Christian churches, including Eastern Orthodox churches such as the Jacobites and Nestorians, and the Eastern churches in union with Rome.
Books containing rules and rubrics for the religious services of the Eastern Church year.
Sheet tin utensils with vertical sides and an inner and outer ring used to shape doughnuts, often with an attached handle.
Pots, usually terracotta, with conical lids, traditionally used in North Africa to slowly simmer sweet and spiced fruit, vegetables and meat, or other foods.
Apparatuses for making coffee by forcing boiled water under pressure through finely ground coffee. They are used primarily for making espresso and other traditional Italian coffee-based beverages.
In modern usage refers to literary art forms, such as prose, poetry, plays, films, and other works where the story has a theme of grandeur and heroism.

Machines that knead and/or form dough or pastry into sheets of consistent thickness between horizontal steel rollers. These devices have been made in two forms: simple and return; the second is able to reverse the motion. The distance between rollers is reduced to bring the dough to a desired thickness.
Pottery drinking or serving vessels in the form of a human figure, usually a stout seated man holding a mug and wearing a three-cornered hat, first manufactured in England in the 18th century.
Manufacturers' term used in the 19th century to describe a small bowl in any shape. Some nappies are covered, while others look like small compotes.
Rings or bands through which a folded napkin is inserted, often as part of a place setting.

Devices that filter undesirable elements from drinking water. These come in various forms, often tall, cylindrical ceramic containers, fitted with a filter on the inside and consisting of a porous wall, sometimes lined with a charcoal or sand.

Drafting tools for drawing straight parallel lines, generally consisting of ungraduated strips of wood, metal, or plastic guided along drafting boards and held parallel by wires or strings passing through the ends of the rules; may or may not slide on rollers. For a set of two attached and pivoting rulers used often as navigational aids to transfer parallel lines, prefer "parallel rulers."

Devices used to homogenize milk by forcing milk through a small opening at high pressure. This reduces the size of the fat globules found in the milk, preventing them from clumping and allowing the fat to remain evenly distributed throughout the milk.
Instruments for measuring the forms and angles of salts and  crystals.
Brackets used on a fixed orthodontic appliance to secure wires and archwires.

Spoken or visual representations of information, such as speeches, demonstrations, and slide shows, for the purpose of achieving favorable visibility and persuading an audience to believe or support the presentor's ideas, projects, or goals.
Method of acquiring property by legally conferring existing ownership to another person or institution; it does not necessarily involve benefactors.

Titles preferred by the repository of a work. For example, in cataloging works of art, the title assigned by the repository that houses the work is often given preference over other titles for the same work.
Numeric identifiers which indicate unique iterative states of an object.

General term for unit of currency of various values, used in Germany and Austria before the establishment of the present monetary systems; based on a small silver coin that equaled a portion of a thaler.
Calendar introduced by Julius Caesar in 46 BCE (708 AUC) as a reform of the Roman calendar.

Numbers that firms such as commercial art dealers or galleries may assign to objects when taking them in to stock. These are typically written or affixed on the objects themselves, and can be used to associate particular objects with entries in a stock or sales book. These numbers are not necessarily unique, and objects may have multiple stock numbers.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 8999 to 8000 (or 9000 to 8001) Before Common Era.
A broad category of punch types used to cut holes in leather.
Family of Native American languages, spoken in parts of the Great Plains, from North Dakota to Oklahoma.
Small depressions on the sea floor.
Any of various devices used to study or illustrate musical intervals or the relationship between a vibrating string and the sound it produces.
Pottery made by slaves, frequently found at plantation sites in South Carolina, Virginia, and several Caribbean Islands.
People who cut and carve the material fo crystal.
A vernacular language is the local, native, or indigenous language of a country, district or other area, or of a given culture.
Artists who specialize in painting flowers.
The activity of using using rope fixed at a higher point to make a controlled descent of a vertical drop, such as a rock face or tall building.
The action of celebrating, revelling, and conviviality, often accompanied by drinking alcohol; engaging in a festive occasion or party.
Units of length comprising 3 feet or 36 inches; by international agreement in 1959 standardized as exactly 0.9144 meters.

Fabulous beasts of composite form in Buddhist and other Japanese and Chinese art; in typical examples, they have the head of a dragon, body and legs of a stag or horse, tail of an ox or lion, single horn on the forehead, and parti-colored or scaly body.
Brand name roofing systems.

Species of tall, pyramidal tree native primarily to bottomlands and moist uplands of eastern North America, but found as far west as Oklahoma and Ontario, Canada. It is distinguished by having clusters of short, spiky twigs and leaves with bristle-tipped lobes, thus accounting for the common name "pin oak."

Refers to God, divinity, or a deity in Nahua culture. A term generally translated as "god" or "deity" usually referring to members of the Nahua pantheon. Caught in a constant process of movement, these forces or powers are associated with different areas of action, predispositions and shared or exclusive prerogatives. As a prefix, the root of the term, teo-, enters into the composition of a number of words designating substances, plants, birds or instruments whose translation is often complex.

Genus containing 14 living species and several extinct species of trees, most native to tropical America, but at least one native to the east coast of Africa. The trees are used for edible fruits, leaves to make tea, a dense wood used in making ships and furniture, thick bark to make canoes, seeds containing large amounts of a highly viscous polysaccharide used for food, paper, cosmetic and pharmaceutical, and hard resins used for varnish. Resin is gathered from living trees and as found in the ground, deposited by lost specimens of living species or extinct species.
Species of  widespread and variable pine native to western North America and widely cultivated elsewhere for its timber and for ornament.
Institutions that maintain spaces for devices that project celestial images onto the interior of a dome for public viewing.
Libraries maintained by state funds, whose broad function is to preserve state records and publications for the use of state officials and citizens.
Museums dealing with collections having to do with navies, warships, or ships in general; distinct from "maritime museums," which deal with the sea in general, navigation, or shipping.
The color of pink roses, which may range from pinkish to reddish, typically with overtones of mauve.
A range of brownish colors resembling the color of natural or synthetic Vandyke brown pigment, also known as "Cassel brown."
Refers to a range of light green colors resembling the color of the peridot stone, which is a light green variety of olivine that is used as a gem stone.
Typically used with reference to collectibles and desirable objects not so old as an antique (100 years old), usually reserved for objects dating between the 1940s and 1970s.
Range of strong blue colors, resembling the color of artificial ultramarine blue pigment, also known as "French ultramarine."
Order of insects containing 2,400 species and about 430 genera in 15 families, found in temperate and tropical habitats globally.
Regarding personal names, assumed names used by actors and other performers rather than their real names.
Subclass of birds having a well-developed sternum, a relatively short tail, forelimbs modified to wings, and  teeth replaced by horny rhamphoteca over bill.

Institutions devoted to the instruction of adults. Types of lyceums include specific literary institutions established in the early 19th century and those established later to provide popular lectures on literary and scientific subjects, public discussions, concerts, and other activities for furthering general education. In some nations, the term is used for universities or colleges. The term is derived from the proper name of a garden with covered walks in Athens where Aristotle taught philosophy.
Balustrades or railings enclosing a sacred object or places of veneration in Indic religious structures, the railing-formed blind dado of a pillared porch/raṅgamaṇḍapa; blind railing-enclosure.
Elevated areas on ice caps.
Conical landforms made of volcanic material or mud.

Chinese bronze ritual vessels of jar shape with a wide lip, supported by a tall ring, and used to hold wine. In the latter half of the Shang period, this shape was replaced with a taller profile based on the "gu." The term "zun" is also sometimes used to describe an animal-shaped vessel.

System of interconnected computers or any instances of two or more organisations or individuals engaged in a common pattern of information exchange through automated, online, or on air communications links.

Order containing seven living species in one family, characterized by unique large keratin scales covering their skin, and being nocturnal animals that use their well-developed sense of smell to find insects.

Refers to prints having remarques, which are doodles or sketches by the artist outside the main design. While remarques were originally used to test the strength of the acid on a plate and then burnished away, since the nineteenth century they are sometimes deliberately kept in printed editions to produce rarities for collectors.
Marbled paper produced usually with two colors, usually a light and dark of the same color. Similar to Spanish marbled paper, but without the wave design.
Year designated by the Pope, during which special indulgences are granted and ceremonies held; in modern times, usually once every 25 years.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name currently inhabiting southern Sudan.
Describes works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Burkina Faso.
Book cloth pattern introduced ca. 1836.
Style and culture of the inhabitants of the nation of Gabon.
Businesses that sell home furnishings, carpets, draperies, or a variety of other goods to be used in the home.
Baked foods made by lining shallow dishes with pastry and filling this with a sweet or savory filling. The filling is often finished with a pastry crust on top.
The terminal parts of the hand of a human or an animal, usually numbering five (as in humans) or four.

Creatures, spirits, or other living entities that are imaginary, fictitious, or belonging to myth or legend. For human or human-like entities of legend, myth, or religion, prefer "legendary characters" or "religious characters."

Qatapan used to be the celebratory singing and dancing after satapan (“head hunting”). Over the years its religious significance takes up a festive and performative turn. Qatapan is now regularly put on show in tribes, local chapels, Kavalan societies, campaign gatherings and national concert halls. Upon their return, the head-hunters dressed in straw cape and with a walking stick hang the heads on a long rod, circled by warriors and seniors chanting spaw and toasting. Legend has it that it will rain after the chanting to purge the people. The Japanese rule severely proscribed the Kavalan’s head hunting and the ritual was thus suspended. By the 1970s the nature of Qatapan shifted significantly as the Kavalan people tend to organize harvest festival together with the Amis as their long-established matrimonial kin. Even if the festival bears the same name, the head hunting hymn of spaw is no longer sung. With the campaign for recognition in the 1908s, the revival of the traditional ritual took up the form of circular dancing around a type of tree called Palaquium formosanum, and one of the hymns known as miomio has been adapted with modified lyrics as a precious cultural heritage constituent of the Kavalan identity.
Rectangular, padded floor coverings used to provide a barrier between the floor and the user; used for exercises.

Mechanized processing machines designed to convert textile waste or cheap raw materials into usable fibers for yarn spinning and other textile applications. Strongly resembling carding machines, these devices are made of large metal cylinders with fine spiral grooves cut into their surfaces; rigid blades are wound into the groves. Carding elements, such as wire teeth or rollers, can also be mounted to the surface of the cylinders in lieu of the grooves and blades. As the cylinders rotate, raw or scrap materials are fed into the device. The carding elements or blades on the rotating cylinders work to open, separate, and align the materials' fibers, removing impurities and creating a uniform batt of fibers. These devices provide a sustainable solution for recycling textile waste.

Information about the dimensions, size, or scale of the work, presented in a syntax suitable for display to the end-user and including any necessary indications of uncertainty, ambiguity, and nuance. It may include the scale of the work. It may also include the number of the parts of a complex work, series, or collection.

Refers to third millennium Chalcolithic culture of the ancient Baden region which spread over much of central Europe, and developed out of late Stone Age Lengyel culture. It is characterized by metal objects such as axe handles and plain, dark pottery. Images of domesticated horses are appear in artifacts as are four-wheeled carts.
Culture, ethnicity, style, or historical period occurring just before or after European colonization in India.

Refers to the style of folk painting that developed in Okiwake from the Kan'ei era (1624-44). Popular with pilgrims to the nearby temple of Midera and other travellers, the style is characterized by works drawn in ink and plain colors, often illustrating popular folk tales or common religious beliefs. During the Meiji period (1868-1912), their quality declined and production dwindled.

Refers generally to a variety of styles of ceramics used for tea ceremonies and every-day use, made at kiln sites in Kagoshima Prefecture (formerly the Satsuma domain) in southern Kyushu, from the early 17th century to the present. Styles range from "sharkskin" ware with a grayish, light sepia or yellowish glaze and fine granular surface to fine iron-glazed teawares in the first half of the 17th century, copies of Sawankhalok ware, a Thai ware decorated with underglazed iron-oxide painting, from ca. 1700, and overglaze enamels from the late 18th century.
Longest-lived and most powerful of the northern Chinese dynasties that existed before the reunification of China under the Sui and Tang dynasties, 386-534/535 CE.

Style and culture of a Native American tribe in central North Carolina. Descended primarily from Occaneechi communities that have lived in the area since European contact; Eno, Saponi, and other Siouan-speaking tribes also comprise modern Occaneechi identity.
Use to describe the works produced by the Algonquian-speaking tribe of the same name, who inhabit Southern New England.
Refers to the style and culture of the Nisga'a, an indigenous people who have traditionally lived in the Nass River Valley of Northwestern British Columbia.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name, a Berber people of central Morocco and Algeria.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Uganda and Kenya.
An African people living in the Jos Plateau of Nigeria.
Describes works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting mainly northern Nigeria with some population in Cameroon.
Portaits in any medium that focus on the head and face of the sitter, omitting all or most of the body.
Material that causes illness or death when absorbed, inhaled, or ingested by a living organism.
Any substance added to another to mask unpleasant odors, such as essential oil to paint.
Designates heavy metal wire welded together in a grid pattern and used as reinforcing in concrete slabs.
Use generally for any substance spread over a surface, usually for protection or decoration.

A thick paper formed from multiple sheets adhered with an adhesive then pressed to produce a hard, stiff board. Pasteboard was used for book boards and playing cards in Europe from the early 16th to the late 18th centuries. It is now primarily used for making boxes and cartons.
Drying oil used in house and industrial paint, linoleum, and printing ink.
An unstandardized name referring barium yellow, calcium chromate, and several other pigments.

Fibers from plants of the nettle family, cultivated for centuries in Europe and Asia for making ropes and sails. Nettle fibers are light-color, soft, and strong They are used for twine, rope, canvas and sailcloth. Nettle fibers are also used as substitutes for flax and hemp.
