With carbohydrates and proteins, lipids are one of three types of materials that compose living cells. The structure of lipids range from simple straight chain hydrocarbon to complex ring structures. They can be subdivided as 1) fatty acids, 2) neutral fats, 3) phospholipids, 4) glycolipids, 5) aliphatic alcohols and waxes, 6) terpenes, and 7) steroids. Any of the large group of fats, oils, waxes, sterols, and triglycerides that occur in living organisms and are characteristically soluble in certain organic solvents but only partially soluble in water; they are oily to the touch. With carbohydrates and proteins, lipids are one of three types of materials that compose living cells. The structure of lipids range from simple straight chain hydrocarbon to complex ring structures. They can be subdivided as 1) fatty acids, 2) neutral fats, 3) phospholipids, 4) glycolipids, 5) aliphatic alcohols and waxes, 6) terpenes, and 7) steroids.
Any of a group of astringent vegetable principles or compounds, chiefly complex glucosides of catechol and pyrogallol, used for their tanning properties.
A common rock-forming mineral, usually white or gray, it is the chief constituent of limestone and most marble.

Pure metallic element having symbol Pd and atomic number 46; a rare, lustrous silvery white metal found in platinum ore. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials.

A type of deeply etched, crystalline glass developed by Bernard O. Gruenke and his son, Bernard E. Gruenke, Jr., in the 1970s. The glass was inspired by a Czechoslovakian etched glass exhibit they saw at the World's Fair in Osaka, Japan; they called their glass "leptat," a word derived from the Czech meaning "to etch," in honor of its inspiration. The etching technique was later patented.
Titanium ore found in igneous rock and supplies a major portion of the world's titanium; source for titanium white pigment and used in ceramic glazes.

Crosses having four splayed arms; it is an eight-pointed cross comprising four deep V-shapes joined together at their apex, so that each arm has two points. The cross was originally the symbol of medieval Amalfi, a small Italian republic. The form has been in use since the First Crusade, when the eight points represented the eight facets of courage: loyalty, piety, honesty, bravery, honor, fearlessness, charity, and obedience to the church.
Humorous designs in the margins of Medieval manuscripts or in inconspicuous parts of wood or stone carving in Medieval buildings.
In Indian architecture, a circular temple-type; bull figure on roof; bull figure on roof corner; Nandi.

Nigerian Igbo votive shrines constructed as part of complex festivals of life and sacrificial rituals, often highly ornate and filled with sculpture; prior to the 1960s, built of perishable materials and once erected are left to decay.

Buildings that house schools offering instruction in one or more skilled or semiskilled trades or occupations. For educational facilities traditionally training technicians in business, industry, and commerce, usually for an immediate local area, use "polytechnics."
Structures built and used by military forces.
In Indian architecture, palaces, mansions; or temples.

Fillet moldings that are produced by cutting a groove in a plane surface. Distinguished from "fillets (motifs)" which are an impressed line, either gilt or blind, created by the finishing tool, the fillet.

Windows of large size, characteristic of Renaissance and later classicizing styles, divided by columns or piers resembling pilasters into three lights, the middle one of which is usually wider than the others and is often arched. Named for Veneto architect Andrea Palladio, or in reference to Sebastiano Serlio, who wrote an architectural treatise describing arches of ancient Rome.
In Indian architecture, a trident-bearing, free-standing column.
Sites that contain evidence of prehistoric human activity, often through archaeological investigation.
Arches comprising lobes or sub-arches.
Building complexes focused on one or more pyramids, but containing other structures such as palace, temples, solar boat pits, and other features. The complex at Giza, Egypt, is an example.

Sunny rooms or balconies designed for exposure to the rays of the sun. In ancient Greek and Roman houses, solariums were open sunporches or apartments on the roofs of buildings. In modern usage, may also refer to rooms having large windows, particularly rooms provided for patients in hospitals or clinics.

The use of an optical interferometer for a wide variety of metrological and spectroscopic applications that study the interference pattern (or "fringe") established when a single beam of light multiply divided into beams traveling unequal paths is reunited.

The term pingzuo 平坐 (also written pingzuo 平座; lit. “level” “seat” Kroll 2015 346, 636) has a variety of meanings in classical Chinese literature beyond the scope of architecture, including a sitting posture (Li 1995, 36), a certain kind of sitting apparatus (Xu and An 2004, 2444; Zhou 2000, 12515), and a base (Gu 1984, 12.186). In the Ming and Qing dynasties (14th-20th centuries), pingzuo was also used to refer to a seat or throne (Zhang 1981, 58). All these meanings emphasize that pingzuo is a structure designed to provide a level base for whatever is on top of it. Current architectural historians focus on the use of pingzuo as described in the Song court architectural manual Yingzao fashi (1103 CE) in the context of timber-framed structures. Here the basic characteristic of pingzuo is a platform supported by bracket sets on top of pillars, providing a level foundation for a building constructed above it. The pillars supporting the pingzuo can be erected on top of a lower story, directly into the ground, in the water, or on top of city walls.
The process or function of copying or otherwise inserting data or material, such as files or a data, from one location into a database or other location by using automated methods.

General term for various systems of beliefs and practices of the eastern Mediterranean peoples under Hellenistic influence from 300 BC to 300 BCE. Characterized by a spiritual revolution in the Greek and Roman empires, when old cults died or were fundamentally transformed and when new religious movements came into being.
Planning how to conduct affairs by assessing, minimizing, and preventing potential losses, injuries, or other damages.
In Indian architecture, a minor offset demarcating planes; minor facia in plan and elevation; chamfered subdivision or indentation in a ratha-buttress and in śikhara.
Games that are played on tables, either generic tables or tables designed specifically for play of a particular game.
Acquisition of goods or services through purchase, lease, hiring, or trade.
Occasions of prolonged, extreme, and general scarcity of food in an area.
In Japan, ceremonies for the preparation and consumption of green tea, according to strict rules of ceremony as an expression of Zen Buddhist philosophy.
In Indian architecture, a decorative door-band; door-jamb.
An auspicious state, typically with reference to the life of a person, resulting from favorable outcomes.

Art or architectural elements that are associated with urban design, planning, and preservation of a city, town, or district. For art having the purpose of beautifying and enriching public places, but not necessarily located in a city or associated with urban design, use "public art." For art created in urban environments, but not necessarily sanctioned or legally displayed, prefer "urban art."
The formal concept of the layout of spaces and elements in the built environment, such as of a building or city.
Having a form or outline delimited on at least one end by two intersecting lines, that is, tapering to or ending in a point or apex.

Designation applied to artistic or literary material, produced to appeal to popular taste, and marked especially by sentimentalism, sensationalism, or slickness. For the related concept applied to taste, use "camp."
A theory that reason is in itself a source of knowledge superior to and independent of sense perception.

Socio-political movement and critical theory asserting the collective rights and identities of Indigenous people, primarily in the United States and Canada. First formulated in the early 20th century with the development of Native-led political organizations like the National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) and the American Indian Movement (AIM).

Refers to the concept of the physical world, including the forces at work in it and the nonhuman life inhabiting it, perceived by human beings as separate and independent from themselves, their activities, and civilization. For aggregates of physical things, conditions, and influences surrounding and affecting given organisms or communities of organisms at any time, use "environments (object groupings)." For the branch of biology dealing with the relations and interactions between organisms and their habitat, use "ecology."

Contractual business transaction between two or more parties that is restricted to specified undertakings during a particular time frame. It differs from "partnership (legal concept)," in that partnership is a long-term agreement.

An association of two or more people formed for the purpose of carrying on a business that does not have a legal personality of its own, and therefore partners must agree on the method of distribution of profits and losses and are liable for the debts of the firm.

The consciousness of perceiving or seeming to perceive a condition of one's body or its parts or of the senses as messages from the body's sensory receptors register in the brain as information about the environment.
The art of making puppets, which are representations of figures, animated by strings, by hands inside the figure, rods, or another manual method.
The measuring of viscosity.

Refers to the technique of making compositions from portions of existing images, such as drawings or photographs, arranged into somewhat unified images. When pieces of various relatively flat materials are pasted together to form less unified images, use "collage." Used also in film when two or more shots are superimposed to form a single image.
Dressing or trimming so as to allow the creation of a lapped joint, where pieces overlap rather than abutting.
Migration of ions in an electric field under the influence of an electrical potential difference.
A resistor that functions through manual or mechanical means to vary the flow of electrical current, or resistance, to a source.
Joints which allow rotations to occur freely except in the direction perpendicular to the support.
Greek archaic rudely carved cult statues, originally of wood, and later copied in stone. Scholarship suggests that only stone or marble copies of originals in wood have survived to the present day.
Devices that consist of a heavyweight hinge with an added pivot using the same pin. The leaves of the pivot interlock with the hinge leaves. Two conventional hinges are required to complete the set.
Locks having for obstacles, projections cast in the keyhole opening or on the inside of the case.

South Australian carved sculptures made of wood, gypsum, and ochre, which function as direction-markers. These sculptures were placed in the ground to indicate which particular tribal group inhabited the site or in which direction they could be found. The aboriginal Australians named Diyari constructed these innovative signposts at the Lutheran Mission at Killalpaninna between 1903 and 1906. Toas are not a traditional form of sculpture; it is believed that the production of toas was by the request of Europeans interested in aboriginal culture. Toas were only produced in the South Australian state.
Lightweight, short jackets that are zipped up the front, sometimes with closefitting waistband and cuffs to protect against the wind. These are worn as sports and leisure wear.
Women's hats of various materials having a wide brim which frames the face; derived from similar hats depicted in portraits by Gainsborough and Reynolds.

Drinking glasses, usually crystal or glass, in the shape of a handbell, having a bell-shaped bowl, a stem without a foot, and often a clapper. The bell is rung when the glass has been emptied. The glass can only stand when empty and turned upside down. For bells found on tables to call attendants during meals, use "table bells (clapper bells)."
Shaped tops on cabinet pieces.
Furniture in the form of pedestals with an an inclined, sometimes moveable frame; used to hold scores or sheet music in position for reading.
Small, portable desks, designed to be sutiable for use while traveling; typically equipped with a wrting surface and containers for pens, ink, and paper.
Tables used for the activity of knitting, typically outfitted with drawers or cubbyholes to hold wool or other supplies.
Chairs with compartments for smoking equipment.
Wooden beds with spool-shaped turnings in the spindles and usually in the rails and posts of the headboard and footboard.
Shades which protect candles from drafts.

Collector's term for square low-back chairs, often without arms, having turned legs and stretchers; this type, covered in leather or turkey work, long antedated the period of Cromwell but became widely popular in England in the mid-1600s.
Lamps which are fixed to a spring-loaded, adjustable pole which fits between a ceiling and floor.
Elastic, ring-shaped rubber or latex loops usually used as temporary binding devices for paper or other objects.

Drawings in charcoal or, less commonly, pastel on board painted white and coated with marble dust, which gives the finished drawing a sandpaper-like sparkle and texture, and effects of light and dark similar to those in engravings. Popular in the mid-19th-century United States.

Authority that creates and puts into circulation, according to its instructions and in an official manner, the currency and paper money of legal tender in some territory. Depending on the political context, the issuer may be an individual (such as a king, an ecclesiastical leader, or a military commander) or a geopolitical entity (such as a republic, a state, or a city-state).
Use for references to identities assigned to people who did not exist; examples are false names assigned to a forged work of art and fictitious literary characters.
Persons or organizations to whom goods are consigned by consignors.
Governors of a province, particularly as under the ancient Persian monarchy.
Carpenters or metalworkers who line out the details of the work.
People who create or sell perfumes, which are liquids or pastes containing aromatic ingredients.

People who make themselves available to be engaged for work on particular assignments or projects, rather than being engaged on a long-term or permanent basis by a single employer. In original usage, referred specifically to military adventurers who offered services to states or individuals for payment, rather than fighting for their own lord.
Builders who specialize in, or who have a role as, reconstructing a destroyed or damaged work.
Case or covers, usually rigid, that enclose and protect mechanisms or apparatus.
Double-edged hand tools having an axe blade on one side and a pickaxe or wide chisel on the opposite side.
Centrifuges used to train and prepare astronauts for the acceleration forces in spaceflight.

Flat mirrors, often mounted to telescopes, which are rotated to compensate for the daily rotation of the celestial sky, therefore directing light from celestial objects under observation to the same position.
Glass or plastic rods often having a thick disc at one end for crushing tablets or crystals; used to stir solutions while dissolving chemicals.
A variety of hand tools used to scratch a plaster surface to increase bonding of the successive coat.

Veils or shawls worn across the shoulders of altar servers, to cover their hands when carrying the mitre and crosier during liturgical functions and processions. For veils that are similar but larger, and worn by the priest or other celebrant, prefer "humeral veils."

A white, powdery inorganic compound, the sodium salt of the polyphosphate penta-anion. It is manufactured for use as an emulsifier and chelating agent in water softeners and detergents. In conservation it has been used as a sequestering agent for the treatment of excavated copper and bronze objects, a chelating agent in the conservation of paper objects, and as a surfactant in the cleaning of photographs. It has been suspected of contributing to water pollution.
Nets or sheets of strong canvas supported by strings and tightly stretched across a metal frame mounted on legs, used as a springboard in gymnastics or acrobatics.

Skirts designed to clear the floor evenly in the front and back, cut approximately 5 inches from the ground to lessen the garment's weight and allow the wearer increased leg mobility. Often worn for practical and comfort purposes when walking, hiking, or traveling.

Short sleeveless or short-sleeved garments consisting of front and back panels and open at the sides, worn over other garments, sometimes to display heraldic devices, by knights, heralds, or civilians, especially during the 12th to the 14th centuries. For padded or quilted protective garments worn over metal armor embellished with heraldic devices, use "coat armors."
Devices attached to or inserted into the openings of pockets either to keep objects from falling out or to protect garments from stains and wear.
Loose-fitting gowns or lounging robes made of lightweight fabric, being short, unwaisted, and usually narrowing at the hem.
Refers to a unit of currency in circulation in Bhutan from 1974, equal to 100 chetrums.
Tools used to mince, chop, or shred food.
Electrically operated ovens using high-frequency electromagnetic waves, used to heat, cook, or thaw food.
Short literary compositions on single subjects, often presenting the personal view of the author.
Culinary utensils with broad, flat usually flexible blades used to blend or spread soft food or to remove food from bowls and other utensils.
Large bowls intended primarily for serving salad.  Also, small bowls used for an individual portion of salad.

Vaselike forms, typically made of glass, which resemble celery glasses but which usually have a scalloped rim and are frequently made to match tableware patterns; intended to be used on the dining table to hold spoons. For similar vessels, typically of glass, also used on the dining table and intended to hold stalks of celery, use "celery glasses." For vaselike forms made of glass, wood, or bone and intended to be placed near a fireplace or lighting device, use "spill holders." For footed vessels in the center of which is a column with a pierced gallery for the suspension of spoons, use "spoon stands."
Boxes intended for toilet articles and sometimes writing materials, often fitted with drawers, trays, or partitions and usually a mirror; often especially for travel.

Dishlike containers for holding soap, especially bathroom or kitchen accessories or fixtures; may be lidded. For small boxes or perforated globular containers used to hold a ball or bar of soap, use "soap boxes."
Steplike changes in the contour of an object, such as the transition part of a bottle between its narrow neck and wider body.
Decorated cosmetic containers made by African Akan metalsmiths from imported sheet brass and primarily used to store shea butter and sometimes, to store gold weights, gold dust, and other valuables.

Narrow rectangular wooden rods, varying in length from about 16 1/2 inches to 24 inches, with a small brass projection for positioning the rod in the bung hole of a cask, designed to measure the wantage or shortage of partially filled casks; usually calibrated with tables for casks of various capacities.
Representations of speech, song, or other sound in two-dimensional visual works.
Large containers or structures for holding liquids or gases.
Scottish drinking vessels in the form of a small, shallow bowl typically with two, but sometimes with three horizontal handles; generally made of wood, pewter or silver.

Culture and style that developed beginning in the early-14th-century among the ruling elites of successor states of the Mongol Empire; retained Mongol political and legal institutions, but adopted Turkic languages and religions such as Buddhism and Islam.
Stitches that secure a worked headband to the text block.
Bronze Age Aegean vessels generally made in a flat, open dishlike form with incising on one side. Their use is uncertain.

Statues in the shape of a lion or a lion-dog, usually of terra cotta, stone, or wood, particularly such statues placed in pairs as guardians at the entrances of tombs, palaces, and government offices in China and other Buddhist sites in Asia and elsewhere. They represent the "Dog of Fo," a mythical beast that was half lion and half dog. The figures first appeared in Han China in the late third century BCE, probably developing from Indian depictions of the lion as the protector of dharma.

Visual works produced by drawing, which is the application of lines on a surface, often paper, by using a pencil, pen, chalk, or some other tracing instrument to focus on the delineation of form rather than the application of color. This term is often defined broadly to refer to computer-generated images as well.
In Indian architecture, a courtier figure; gaṇa; member of the assembly; attendant.

Persons employed to carry baggage for patrons at a hotel or transportation terminal. For those stationed at a door or gate of a public or private building to admit or assist those entering or exiting, use "doorkeepers." May also be used more generally as persons whose occupation is to carry loads; a carrier.
The action of placing or determining the place of something, or the state of existing in a place.
In Islam, public criers who proclaim the regular hours of ritual prayer from the minaret or the roof of a mosque, recite in services, or perform other speaking duties.
Having a whirlpool design.
Technical drawing leads for use on drafting film.
People who create, decorate, or paint designs or scenes on fans, which are hand-held implements used to produce a current of air or that serve as purely decorative accessories.
In Indian architecture, a upper register of the temple wall; upper jaṅgā (in North Indian temples).

Motif derived from the the boteh, copied from Kashmiri shawls by the woollen manufacturers of Paisley, Scotland in the 19th century, and becoming popular in Britain, France, and North America. It occurs in many variations and with numerous ancillary motifs, particularly in textile patterns.
In Indian architecture, a series of joist-ends.
In Indian architecture, a paired geese decorative motif.
Factories in which ceramic tile is manufactured.
The state or action of taking or maintaining possession, controlling, or inhabiting something, such as a structure or land area.

Machines for turning fiber into thread or yarn, in which the formation of the thread is performed by the help of a wheel worked either by a hand or foot pedal that spins the thread onto a single spindle. Said to have been invented in India, they were introduced into Europe via the Middle East in the Medieval period, and were in common use there and in North America after colonization into the 18th century. For spinning machines developed in the 18th century having more than one spindle, use "spinning jennies."
Heatable devices usually with a flat metal base of some weight that are used to smooth, finish, or press cloth.
Punches used in woodworking.

Transfer of property from one individual or group to another, made gratuitously to the recipient, bestowed voluntarily and without monitary compensation. In various societies, gift giving is associated with status, ritual, and tradition for various occasions and circumstances. Reciprocal gifts may be expected, resulting in an exchange of gifts rather than unilateral giving.
Those who believe in or adhere to spiritualism.

State or place of spiritual cleansing and purification, allowing a purging of sins. A notable example is in the doctrine of the Roman Catholic Church, where it is defined as  a state where the souls of those who die in grace undergo such punishment as necessary to expiate their unforgiven venial sins before entering heaven.
Long strips of flexible material used for written documents and rolled for ease of handling and storage. For paintings on either hanging scrolls or handscrolls, use "scroll paintings."
Tributes or laudatory speeches written in praise of a person or thing; often, but not always, refers to tributes in honor of the deceased.

Books containing accounts of an individual's or organization's occurrences or transactions, including records of financial transactions. Use "diaries" when referring to personal accounts of the writer's experiences, attitudes, or observations.
Describes objects, structures, or spaces, or portions thereof, located to the right of an observer facing in the same direction as the object or space specified.
Photographs converted to electrical signals, transmitted over wires, and then reformed into images.

The movement associated with the Gutai Art Association: a collective of vanguard artists founded in Ashiya in Japan 1954 and disbanded in 1972 after the death of its leader Yoshihara Jirō. Gutai in Japanese means ‘embodiment’ or ‘concreteness’. The group’s primary goal was to seek an “international common ground” of new art that would transcend modernist painting. Gutai’s experimentalism encompassed both painting (gestural abstraction in the 1950s and hard-eged abstraction in the 1960s) as well as such innovative forms as performance art (on the stage and for the press), installation art (both indoors and outdoors), land art, sound art, intermedia art, and conceptualism, among others, through which the group prefigured what to come in the 1960s. Gutai was known internationally from the late 1950s, and its legacy and reception underwent multiple periods of revival and discussion.
In Indian architecture, a register of vyālas; vyāla frieze; band of vyāla figures.

Objects consisting of meshed arrangements of threads, cords, or ropes that have been twisted, knotted, or woven together at regular intervals. For the open weave textile made of twine or strong thread or yarn, usually of silk, cotton, nylon, or rayon, with fine to coarse meshes of fixed dimension, used to make various items from veils and trimming on clothing to tennis nets and fish nets, use "net (textile)."

Decorative forms or embellishments that are an integral part of a building or object but are not essential to its structure. Refers also to decorative objects attached to or worn by humans and animals. For objects signifying an honor bestowed upon an individual, usually worn on the person, see "decorations." Regarding techniques of embellishment in general, see "decoration (process)."
Nationality, culture, or style of Perugia, Umbria, Italy.

Refers to the culture of the modern nation of Croatia, or in general to the cultures that have occupied the area in central Europe corresponding to the modern nation. It may refer broadly to the culture of the Slavic Croat peoples who came out of the Ukraine in the seventh century CE.
Nationality, styles, and culture of Trinidad, the southernmost island in the Caribbean.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Michigan.

Culture and style of the ancient Siculi people who inhabited eastern Sicily, and for whom the island is named. They may have been relative latecomers to Sicily, arriving from mainland Italy. They are hard to identify archaeologically, although some words of their Indo-European language are known.

The term paishan goudi 排山勾滴 combines the words paishan, referring to the practice of aligning rooftiles (pai 排) along the slope of the gable end (shanmian 山面, lit. “mountain (peak)” “side”), and goudi, which refers to the goutou 勾頭 and dishui 滴水 capping tiles. In placing more emphasis on practice of paishan, it is also called “capping the gable-end tiles” (lingdang paisha 鈴鐺排山; lit. aligning bell clappers along the gable end) (Liu 1932, 193; Wang 1995, 31).
Long, typically curved, awls with a blunted end used primarily in saddlery to insert stuffing, or "flock" into cart-saddle panels or the peaks of riding saddles.
Language family comprising one endangered language and one extinct language, so far as is known; spoken in northwestern Washington state.
Axial depressions of the mid-oceanic ridge system.
Artists who specialize in works created with edible materials.

Artists in any media who specialize in scenes depicting historical events.Lake: Adrienne Martyn : Waikato Museum of Art and History Artist in Residence. Adrienne Martyn, John Hurrell, Waikato Museum of Art and History, 2001 - Taupo, Lake (N.Z.) Waikato Museum of Art and History - 2001

The action of a person or animal using their legs to go faster than a walk, specifically to go steadily by springing steps so that both or all feet leave the ground for an instant in each step. May be employed as a competitive sport.
The actvity of visiting monuments, landscapes, and other places of interest in a particular location.

Mythical creatures that are part animal and part human, or combine elements of two or more animal forms; frequently of great size and ferocious appearance. May also apply to any imaginary creatures that are large, ugly, and frightening.
Trademarked roofing systems of the Duro-Last company.

Species of large oak tree native to most of Europe, Anatolia, the Caucasus, and parts of North Africa; growing 25-40 meters in height, and having a bark that is grayish brown in color and having deep fissures with aging. The tree is valued for brown wood with a coarse but straight grain. The bark is used for tanning and dyeing.
In India, demigods or nature spirits, often inoffensive tutelary guardians of a place, such as spirits of trees, mountains, streams, and forests.
Genus of flowering plants.
Species of large pine tree native to eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Minnesota and Manitoba, and south along the Appalachian Mountains to Georgia.

Museums containing collections dealing with the development and application of science, scientific ideas, technology, and instrumentation. Like museums of natural science and natural history, science museums have their origins in the Enlightenment. Some of them developed from the collections of learned societies, others from private collections
Variable red colors resembling the color of scarlet vermilion pigment.
A range of yellow colors resembling the color of the mineral, sulfur.
Variable color in the range of bright yellowish greens, resembling the color of Scheele's green pigment, a hydrated form of copper arsenite.
Refers to a range of dark grayish blue colors resembling the color of blue ink used for writing.
Members of an order containing around 4,000 species of lacewings, mantidflies, antlions, and their relatives.
Order containing one living family of flamingos.

Educational institutions that train people for careers in the armed forces and for private schools organized following the discipline and dress codes of military life; both offer courses in military training and both are generally at university level with degree-granting programs.
Generally used for narrow openings of rivers into riverbanks or lakes and seas into shores.
Narrow gorges or passes between mountains.

Refers to tools, usually a combination of software and database accessible through the World Wide Web, which enable persistent computer-mediated relationships that encompass social networking, blogs, wikis, and social or collaborative tagging. For specific activities that use social media, use relevent terms such as "social networking."

Order containing four living species in one family. Characterized as huge quadrupeds having long curving ivory tusks, a prehensile trunk or proboscis, columnar legs, a huge head with temporal glands, and wide flat ears. There were at least 170 fossil species, such as mammoths and mastodons.
Refers to proofs that are corrected by hand by the artist.

In the Christian church, a festival observed on the 7th Sunday after Easter, in commemoration of events described in Acts 2 when the Holy Spirit is reported to have descended upon the disciples during the Jewish festival of Pentecost (Shavuot).

Style and culture of people of the modern nation of Guinée (Republic of Guinea) or of the historical people of the broader region of forest and coastal areas of western Africa between the tropic of Cancer and the equator known also as "Guinea."

Businesses formed by one or more lawyers to engage in the practice of law, which entails advising and representing in civil or criminal law cases, business transactions, and other matters for which legal advice is required.

Refers to the culture of the Sioux, a North American Plains Indian people, or confederation of peoples, of Siouan linguistic stock. Sioux is an abbreviation of Nadouessioux, a name originally used to refer to them by the Ojibwa; the word Dakota means "allies." There are three main divisions of the Sioux: Santee, Yankton, and Teton, calling themselves, respectively, Dakota, Nakota, and Lakota.

A prepared foodstuff made from maize dough wrapped in a corn or banana leaf and steamed. Often with meat, or vegetable filling, and sometimes cheese after dairy was introduced to the Americas. Can also be sweet.

Parts of a human's or an animal's body, usually having fingers, located below the wrist joint of the arms, characterized by being routinely used for purposes other than support and locomotion. For the truncating components of legs, use "feet (animal components)," "paws (animal components)," "hooves (animal components)," or another appropriate term.
Round or ham-shaped pads for pressing clothing during sewing or maintenance.
Phylum of about 70 wormlike species of ancient, terrestrial invertebrates with short, thick legs and a dry, velveteen-like body.
Large containers or casks into which woven cloth is immersed and washed, tanned, or beat for the purposes of cleansing and/or thickening.

Material having the formula Co3(AsO4)2, used as a colorant in paints, glass, glazes, and enamels. It occurs in nature as cobalt bloom or erythrite; it was synthetically produced in 1880. It is highly toxic by ingestion, inhalation, and skin contact.
Those portions of, or attachments to, objects that are designed to be grasped by the hand.
Short light sticks, typically capped at both ends with metal or covered with leather and intended for carrying in the hand, often by military officers.
Small mechanical devices for clipping fingernails or toenails.
Political divisions of nations or other adminstrative entities, where the division is totally or primarily comprised of an island.
Territories under the sovereignty of feudal lords; also designate  specific districts or provinces.
Cut-thread and pulled-thread cloth made and used by the Kalabari peoples of the Niger Delta, Nigeria, Africa.

Soft, thin woven, and usually unbleached fabric woven from uneven threads of raw silk, cotton, or artificial fibers. It is often piece-dyed or printed. The term, of Chinese origin, means 'woven at home'.

Creating marks on the surface of a hard material, such as metal or glass, by incising with a sharp tool, when the designs or images created are for their own sake and not to be printed from. For printing processes that involve this technique plus intaglio printing from the surface, use "engraving (printing process)."

In plaster, the appearance of small, cone-shaped holes up to a quarter inch in diameter; caused by the expansion of lime or foreign material and occurring between three months and up to one year after the plaster has set.
Removal of salts, as from water or soil.
Use to describe objects supported by three legs.
In Indian architecture, elliptical; elliptical temple-type.
Characteristics or qualities of living organisms.

Iranian lutelike chordophones having a small pear-shaped body, long neck with movable frets and three or four metal strings. Originating from the 15th century or earlier, it had three strings until the mid-19th century, when a fourth was added.
Pieces of self-fabric pleated and puckered, such as on a gown, petticoat or scarf, in the form of a flounce or swag.
Close-fitting caps of linen or muslin, especially those worn by elderly women.

Reform dress was a reaction to the perceptions of discomfort surrounding women's clothing at the end of the 19th century. These movements campaigned in different countries to ban the corset, garters, tight bodices, and the train. Dress reformers championed garments that do not restrain the body, but let it move freely, during both work and leisure.

Lightweight infantryman's helmet, characterized by an almond-shaped bowl, a short brim, with a distinctive turned-back point at the apex. They are more similar to "cabassets" than "morions." However, they were called "Spanish morions," referring to their being preferred by Spanish troops, although usually manufactured in Italy.

Paper toys and models shaped more or less realistically like airplanes and generally intended to glide through the air with impetus from the human hand. Simple models are folded from virtually any kind of paper by people with no special training into a long, delta-wing shapes. More elaborate and often more lifelike models are carefully crafted from special stiff, lightweight paper, and often painted or otherwise decorated with military insignia and other symbols and designs.
Two supporting bands of elastic, leather, or cloth, worn across the shoulders and fastened at the waistline to trousers, a skirt, or a belt.
Bindings in a style made from the mid-eighteenth to the early nineteenth century, with decoration featuring Masonic symbols tooled in gold.
Foliage pressed flat between or inside a stable medium, such as glass or resin.

Mechanized devices, comprising pull levers or pedals; a large rotating dial; and a series of looping points (needles), designed to smoothly fuse two parts of a knitted garment or stocking together in a flat and invisible seam. By piercing each garment parts' looping line, or line of stitches along which the seams must be set by the looping machine, the device allows users to precisely trim any surplus stock away from the loops before executing the seam.
A description including the title or name of the exhibition, its location, and other pertinent information.
Instruments intended to divide lines into equal parts, measuring angles and polygons within a circle.
Devices used to heat raw milk and hold it at temperature for a certain period of time in order to destroy microorganisms, making it safer to consume.
Racks designed to support one or more Imhoff cones, which typically have no foot for support, and make comparative analysis easier.
Handpieces designed to hold a dental bur, which is a cutting device.
A formal procedure or act in a religious or other solemn observance or ceremony, carried out according to established and prescribed rules.

In book cataloging, the title proper is the primary name of a bibliographic item, including any alternative title but not parallel titles and other title information. The title proper is entered in the title and statement of responsibility area of the bibliographic description. The title proper is usually found on the chief source of information.
The standard unit of currency of Italy prior to adoption of the Euro.
General term for the calendar of ancient Rome, that in fact changed in scheme several times between the founding of Rome and the fall of the Roman Empire.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 699 to 600 (or 700 to 601) Before Common Era.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name living in Tanzania.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northern Nigeria.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living on the Jos Plateau in Nigeria.
Any material, compound, or system, though generally a clay or silicate, that can provide a sorption function such as adsorption, absorption, or desorption.
Liquid or solid that dissolves in or is compatible with a resin, gum, or other material, and renders it plastic, flexible, or easy to work.
Liquids or gases used to cool and lubricate a tool, engine, or nuclear reactor.
Paper made from high-grade rag pulp with a treated surface generally in imitation of parchment.
An oil obtained from seeds of the mustard family.

Bast fiber obtained from the stems of several varieties of the species Boehmeria nivea, native to tropical Asia but cultivated in China, Japan, Europe, South America, and the United States. The Ramie has been used in China for paper and fabric since prehistoric times. Its use spread through Europe in the Middle Ages. It is white or green in color, depending upon the variety. It is soft, fine, and durable fiber that is very lustrous and dyes well, used for twine, fishnets, sewing thread, and fabric for clothing, summer suits, dresses, canvas, tablecloths, and upholstery. Ramie has also been used to produce strong paper for linings, banknotes, and cigarettes.

A combination of wax and resin used as a preservative, adhesive, and in thermal transfer technologies. In the conservation of paintings, it has been used reinforce works by applying a paper or fabric lining attached with a wax-resin.

Bright yellow natural dyestuff extracted from the flowers, leaves and stems of the dyer's rocket plant, Reseda luteola. Weld has been used since Roman times and was widely cultivated in Europe during the Middle Ages. It was the most popular yellow dye until it was replaced by quercitron, made from oak bark, in the 18th century, and then by synthetic dyes in the 19th century. The primary coloring matter in weld is luteolin, which is extracted in a hot alkaline solution made with boiling water and potash. Depending on the mordant, weld produces colors ranging from bright yellow (using tin) to gold (using aluminum) to green (using iron). Although weld has the best lightfastness of any natural yellow, it still is not permanent. Weld was used to dye wool and silk, stain wood, and make lake pigments used in miniature paintings.
Wood from Pinus lambertiana, the largest living pine tree.

Light red wood with a coarse grain, of the species Quercus falcata native to the southeastern United States, but found from New York to Florida, Missouri, and Texas. The strong wood is used for lumber, furniture, cabinetwork, and flooring.

Wood of the genus Castanea; several species produce a light reddish brown wood that is relatively weak with a coarse grain. It is a soft light wood that splits easily but does not turn well. It is used for general construction, framing, fencing, poles, barrels, and veneer. Chestnut wood was commonly used for painted panels, especially in Italy.
Pungent yellow powder of the seeds of any of several common mustard plants, used as a condiment, dye, or in medicine as a stimulant and diuretic, an emetic, or a counterirritant.

Any of a class of sugar acids occuring in various polysaccharides and in urine with both an aldehyde and a carboxyl group. It is the product of a monosaccharide in which the terminal group has been oxidized.

A salt of oxalic acid, calcium oxalate can form naturally on calcareous stones as a reaction to oxalic acid excretions of mosses and lichens. In a conservation context, calcium oxalate is generally considered in its role as a form of bioterioration but its cultivation as a protective film for limestone surfaces has been investigated as well.

Pure metallic element having symbol Pt and atomic number 78; a lustrous, malleable, ductile, silvery white metal, considered a precious metal. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make objects and materials.
Glass decorated with haphazard streaking of two or more colors to resemble marble.

A nonmetallic element of the halogen family with atomic number 53 and symbol I. It is a dark crystalline solid used as an additive to salt to prevent iodine insufficiency and is used in dyes, photographic film, x-ray contrast media, and other applications.

Crosses incorporating the chi-rho symbol, which is formed by the first two Greek letters in the name of Christ, where the "X" shape is imposed on the bar of the "P" shape rather than across it, forming a cross topped with a right facing loop.
Earring-shaped motifs that may represent marriage.
In Indian architecture, a circular temple (in basal configuration).
Sanctuaries particularly designed or used to honor the god Mithras, often comprising an underground chapel or a series of artificial caves illuminated from above by light shafts.

Buildings that house either Hebrew-English day schools providing both secular and religious instruction, usually operated under Orthodox Jewish auspices, or for schools providing training in Talmudic law and which may ordain rabbis. For educational facilities specifically devoted to the training of rabbis, use "rabbinical seminaries." For buildings that house day schools operated under Reform or Conservative Jewish auspices, use "Hebrew schools."
Buildings that house businesses that sell shoes.

Refers to buildings designed and fitted with machinery for the purpose of performing some task or making a product, including grinding of grain into flour or running a loom to make fabric. For the machinery itself, independent of the building, use "mills (equipment)."
Prefabricated buildings with a semicircular cross section, generally built of corrugated metal and provided with thermal insulation.
The flat bands above the uppermost moldings or cymas of cornices, or the small bands above and below the scotia of an Attic base.
Outsize windows placed to frame or as if to frame a desirable exterior view; it may be placed between two narrower windows, typically in a living room or other such room in a home.
In Indian architecture, a column/tower of victory.
Sites that contain evidence of protohistoric human activity, often through archaeological investigation.
In Indian architecture, a tōraṇa-arch adorned with haṁsas.
Areas equipped with targets for practice in shooting weapons; when possible use a more specific term.

Tic-tac-toe is a simple two player game. It can be played on a sheet of paper, or with objects. The game is played on 3 by 3 fields, which are all empty at the start. One player puts a 'cross' (Xs) and the other player a 'circle' (Os). Whoever has three of their own characters in a row, which may be diagonal, vertical or horizontal, is the winner.
Acknowledging in writing the payment of a bill, or the delivery of money, articles, or goods.
Occasions, usually religious, where the tone is solemn and activities are marked by abstaining from food and drink for all or most of the day or series of days.
In Indian architecture, a śākhā/jamb in the form of a pillar; pillaret-formed jambs.
The quality or condition of feeling or expressing appreciation of kindness received, involving a feeling of goodwill towards the benefactor and a desire to do something in return; gratefulness.
Art that depicts mythological subjects or figures drawn from oral or written tradition, regardless of culture of origin.
Forms or outlines delimited by lines defining a sector equal to one quarter of a circle or half a semicircle, having an arc of 90 degrees.
Relation between respective parts or between parts and the whole, in a building or any work of art, whether considered purely visually or numerically.
The concept of the few outstanding works in which the artistic personality of a great artist finds its fullest expression.

In philosophy, a theory that holds that in human knowledge objects are grasped and seen as they really are in their existence outside and independently of the mind. It is opposed to idealism, the theory holding that spiritual and ideal is of central importance in the interpretation of experience.

The dance, literature, music, theater, cinema, television, language, fashion, and other cultural indicators intended for or appreciated by the mainstream public rather than an elite audience. Popular culture reflects changes of style, fads, nostalgia, critical revivals, popular institutions, and forms borrowed from elite art, folk art, or foreign culture.
Purely animal or physical part of human nature; the senses and appetites of the physical body.  Also, gratification of the senses, self-indulgence, or the quality of being lascivious.

Processes and their accompanying technologies that can construct physical models from three-dimensional design data. It is an additive process, created by adding layers of paper, wax or plastic with the end result being a solid, 3-D object. Rapid prototyping processes are generally used by industrial designers to create prototypes of their designs both for displaying and testing.

Refers to the practice of painting scenes while outdoors, rather than in a studio from sketches that may or may not have been made outdoors. It is often used to refer to impressionistic painting originating in France in the late 1860s that attempts to capture the transient effects of atmosphere and light by direct observation from nature.
To form with right angles and straight edges.
Movement of molecules of a liquid through a semipermeable biological membrane from a less concentrated field into one of greater solute concentration under the influence of an electric field.
Refers to a device used to interrupt electric current, now used historically.

For joining two narrow boards. Both boards are planed smooth, coated with glue, and rubbed together until all air pockets and excess glue are expelled from the joint. No clamping is necessary and the joint is extremely strong.
Hinges containing one or more springs to move a door into a closed position. They may be either single- or double-acting.

Thin carved tools with decorative handles used by the Taíno people. These are typically made of wood, shell, or bone. They were used to induce vomiting for cleansing purposes related to the cohoba ritual, in which hallucinogenic powder was inhaled.
Low, circular, brimless hats.
Drinking glasses of apparently normal but actually minute capacity originally used by 18th-century toastmasters.
Vertical sliding pieces that when pulled out support the fall front of a desk or secretary.
Stands or racks designed to store collection bags or other receptacles that are used to gather offertory gifts in churches.
Desks designed to be mounted on the surface of walls with no secondary support. These usually incorporate a folding or sliding work surface incorporated into a cabinet for storage.
Altars used at religious sites for liquid offerings, which are poured over it, often through rhytons. These may slope down toward a basin to collect the liquid, or have carved depressions.
Chairs convertible into a stepladder.
Grand, lavishly upholstered beds intended for princes and noblemen.
Flexible cords from lamps, usually coated with rubber. They generally run through the base of a lamp, and connect at the socket where the bulb is screwed in.
Term first used by Sheraton to describe armchairs having a semicircular back and elongated seat, the shape suggesting an open carriage.

Oil lamps which incorporate a spring-loaded pump mechanism to force oil from the reservoir in the base through a tube to the burner at its top when the tube is pushed down; usually pewter and of French manufacture.
Cylindrical or slightly tapering fasteners having a loop or eye for the head.

Elaborate flourishes, often resembling animals, humans, or plants, produced by calligraphers to decorate calligraphic works. They were especially common in European copybooks of the 17th and 18th centuries, and were made, or made to look if they were made, with a single unbroken line.

Refers to national and international voluntary groups and organizations, unaffiliated with any government and usually nonprofit, such as the UN (from which body the term originated), charity groups, etc.

In general, men of distinction in a society without precise designation of rank. May be used to mean specifically men in a society who are entitled to bear arms, though not ranking among the nobility.
One who consigns or dispatches goods to another, to be sold, rented, or loaned to third parties.
Chiefs of an Arab family or tribe, the headmen of an Arabian village, or other types Arab rulers.
Workers who are charged with tending fires or furnaces for steam-powered tools or on vehicles such as locomotives and steamships.

People or corporate bodies who specialize in making or finishing works or architectural elements with plaster, which is a soft, plastic material mixture of water, lime, and sand, often combined with other materials, such as animal hair. For workman who apply plaster but not for artistic effect, use "plasterers."
People who arrange services for the dead. For people who prepare the dead for burial, use "undertakers."
A person who engages in the setting of rivets.
Reservoirs used to store and supply ink as part of a pen assembly.

Tools, usually hand-held or hand-powered, having a sharp edge, used for punching out holes or designs in paper or other such materials. Punches are standard office supplies and used in papercrafts and leather crafts. For punches having a shaped tip at one end and struck by a hammer, designed to make an indentation rather than cutting out holes or shapes, use "punches (marking tools)."
Needles that are used to introduce cells or organisms into a culture medium for growth or observation.
Instruments which capture images of the sun by using only particular wavelengths of light, specifically Balmer emission lines of hydrogen.

Electric, straight-handled irons used for dry mounting photographs by holding paper, dry-mounting tissue, and cardboard in place until they are put in a dry-mounting press, where they are thoroughly bound.
Flat hand tools having a broad steel blade; used to apply, spread, and shape plaster or mortar or to smooth the surface of unformed concrete.

Refers to the international intellectual movement centered mainly in Paris from the 1920s to the late 1940s. Adopting some of the aesthetic experiments of Symbolism and the attitudes of Dada, the movement is characterized by an emphasis on exploring the limits of experience by fusing reality with the instinctual, the subconscious, and the realm of dreams, in order to create an absolute reality.

Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the rule of Osman III, who ruled from 1754 to 1757. He completed the construction of the Nuruosmaniye mosque after the death of his brother, Mahmud I. Also during this period, the sultan had a small wooden kiosk built for himself at Topkapi over looking the Bosphorus.
Nationality, style, or culture of the island of Rhodes, now in Greece, in the Aegean Sea off the southwest coast of Turkey.

Nationality, style, and culture of Magadha, an ancient kingdom of northeastern India, situated in what is now west-central Bihar state, in northeastern India. It was the nucleus of several larger kingdoms or empires between the 6th century BCE and the 8th century CE.

Refers to the works of a school of painters who specialized in ink painting, active from the 15th century to the 18th century. Centered around the Kyoto temple of Daitokuji, the schools important paintings include panels for the subtemple Shinjuan, as well as numerous scrolls in a wide variety of subject matter, including bird-and-flower paintings, portraits of the Zen master Ikkyu Sojun, and ink landscapes.

Refers to a variety of styles of ceramics produced in the Mino Province from the 7th century to the present. Early wares can be traced from Sue ware, but in the 12th century under the influence of the Sanage kilns, productions included large-mouth jars, small-mouth jars, and mortars. From the 15th to the mid-16th century, ash-glazed and iron-glazed utensils were produced. By the end of the 16th century, production was revolutionized by the introduction of multi-chambered kilns, resulting in tea ceremony wares that included green glaze and feldspathic glaze, with a wide variety of painted shapes and decorations. By the 19th century, underglazed blue decorated wares were produced.
Culture of Americans of Romanian descent.
Architectural style of North America that uses elements of the Spanish Baroque.
Refers to the style and culture of the Yakama Nation (formerly spelled 'Yakima'), an indigenous people whose ancestral land primarily spans areas of eastern Washington State.
Skirts constructed of a long panel of fabric that wraps around the body, and fastens at the hip or back, often with buttons or ties.
Jewels or ornaments attached to a long pin; also tufts or bunches of ribbon, velvet, flowers, or threads of silk, worn in the hair, on a cap, or dress.
Main garments consisting of five to seven yards of lightweight cloth draped around the body so that one end forms a skirt and the other a head or shoulder covering.
English gold coins introduced in the mid-1340s by Edward III and issued until the mid-15th century.
Machines designed to automatically cut a variety of foods into slices of variable thickness.
Pedestals designed as cupboards lined with tin and fitted with racks and a heater.
Fictitious narratives usually with animals or inanimate objects as protagonists, intended to convey a hidden meaning regarding human conduct.
Syringe-like tools used to force liquid seasoning into raw meat.

Flat, dishlike serving vessels, sometimes having a high stem, used for a variety of purposes, especially presentation of food or drink. For drinking vessels with a wide, shallow bowl, especially 16th-century examples, use "tazzas."
Footed vessels in the center of which is a column with a pierced gallery for the suspension of spoons. For vaselike containers with a scalloped rim in which spoons are held, use "spoon holders."
Large, often cylindrical bags; made of canvas, rubberized fabric, or other materials, used to carry personal belongings.

Type of receptacle for a toilet sponge in the form of a sphere divided horizontally midway, the lower half resting on a spreading base and the upper half being a hinged lid having a pattern of pierced work.
A type of valve or cock used to control the flow of liquid through a tap, as found on coffee urns, tea urns, wine fountains, and the like.
Containers primarily intended for holding glue or in which glue is melted.

In the context of an individual page or sheet, such as a poster the main body of type or written matter, as opposed to the illustrations, margins, borders, headings, or other features. With reference to a book or periodical, refers to the main body of the writing, as distinct from front matter, notes, index, appendix, and bibliography.
Containers of a particular type, usually made of reeds and leather; found in Latin American cultures.

Vessels from Ancient Greece, eastern Europe, or the Middle East that were typically made as a closed form with two openings, one at the top for filling and one at the base so that liquid could stream out. They are often in the shape of a horn or an animal's head, and were typically used as a drinking cup or for pouring wine into another vessel. Drinking was done by holding the rhyton above the drinker's head and catching the stream of liquid in the mouth.
Nationality, style, and culture of Yemen, Western Asia.

In bookbinding, the type of joint formed by the juncture between the board and the book shoulder. The board lies with its back edge flush against the shoulder, creating a relatively rigid joint and leaving a thin crease instead of a gully, as compared with "French joints."
Small, usually ceramic vessels with narrow mouths, especially ones used by apothecaries to hold medicines.
Pictorial or three-dimensional representations in any medium of an event or story, including historical and fictional events.

Art works that are made, partially or entirely, of edible materials. Included are works considered fine art as well as works intended for display at meals or feasts. For the art and practice of preparing and cooking foods, prefer "culinary art."
In Indian architecture, a side or secondary divinity figure; attendant divinity (in Orissa, a synonym for parivāradēvatā).
Domestic officers who are responsible for procuring or requisitioning provisions for the household, usually for a monarch or other high-ranking person.
The action or practice of observing, watching, or noticing.

Followers of mysticism, such as beliefs in the existence of important realities beyond perceptual or intellectual understanding that are accessible by subjective experience, such as by intuition or meditation.
Decorative pattern consisting of wavy lines or other series of generally wavelike forms. For the specific running patterns of successive, connected spirals, use "wave scrolls."
A piece of lead used by scribes after the 12th century to create rules or sketches of layouts on parchment pages.

Generally any craftsperson involved in the manufacture of felt. The Worshipful Company of Feltmakers was one of the Livery Companies of London, makers of felt hats, incorporated in 1604. Current usage most often refers to artists and craftspeople who create sculptural or wearable objects from felted fibers, usually wool. For those who create works from fibrous material in general, use "fiber artists."
In Indian architecture, a frontal part of nālambalam.

Motif resembling a stylized erect leaf divided into lobes, in the form of a fan or palm leaf, often supported by spirals. Its origins are obscure, but similar motifs are first recorded in Syria and Mesopotamia and in the islands of the eastern Mediterranean by the 2nd millennium BCE. As the name suggests, it may have been derived from representations of palm-trees, especially in view of the belief that a tree cult may have existed in western Asia in association with the introduction of the cultivated date-palm; however, it has much in common with other early floral and spiral motifs. The motif is common in classical and classicizing styles, used either individually or along with other conventionalized flower or foliage forms, for example, in an anthemion.
In Indian architecture, a band carved with creeper design.
A motif of a female elephant in Indian tradition.
Indication in texts, databases, tables, and lists when the topic or element for the instance at hand is some value beyond the specific values provided.
Hand tools used for mending or creating sails. Sail twine is wrapped around the shaft of the heaver several times, and the handle is turned accordingly to tension stitching or seizing.
Machines that use heat and pressure to permanently sandwich paper documents between thin plastic sheets to protect them from tearing, moisture, or other degradation.
Rasps of various designs for woodworking.
The status and dignity of deities.
People who have visions, or have unknown things revealed to them in visions.
Expiation or atonement for a crime, sin, or offence, including a release from punishment. In theology, deliverance from sin and damnation by atonement or, in Christianity, by the salvation of Christ.

Single pieces of paper, other than broadsides, used as a support with material written, printed, or drawn on one or both sides. The term is often used to refer to the support as contrasted to the image made on the support.
Written questions or exercises testing knowledge, aptitude, or skills.
Transcribed collections of numbers, names, or other text indicating tallies of concepts collocated for any particular purpose.
Use to describe objects mounted directly onto a ceiling, wall, or other surface.

Refers to the paintings of a group of West Coast artists working in the 1960s. Named by critic Jules Langsner in 1959, the style is characterized by the use of large shapes with sharp outlines that extend across the canvas from edge to edge, painted in two or three saturated hues.
In Indian architecture, a register of vyālas; vyāla frieze; band of vyāla figures.

The compilation of an object or group of objects packed, wrapped up, or tied together, generally restricted to relatively small or medium- sized compilations of objects. May refer to physical objects and also to digital objects.

Usage extended from the original Greek or the Latin "palimpsēstus," which refers to parchment that has been reused to inscribe a second text, see "palimpsests (manuscripts)"; as the general object genre, the meaning is extended to refer to other objects, such as brass plates or stained glass that have been erased or turned over to be re-inscribed or re-painted on the reverse, or structures characterized by superimposed features produced at two or more distinct periods.
Nationality, style, and culture of Piedmont, Italy.

Refers to the culture of the modern nation of the Czech Republic, or in general to cultures that have occupied the area of the modern nation in central Europe. It is also used to refer broadly to the culture of the Bohemian people.
Nationality of Trinidad and Tobago, in the Caribbean.

Culture or residency of the Midwest, which is the north-central USA, including the states of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Iowa, Minnesota, and usually Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska, Kentucky, and the Dakotas.
Nationality, culture, and style of the city of Venice and also of its historic Republic, which flourished from the late 7th century until 1797.
Construction technique using palm fronds and other parts of the palm, sometimes with materials from other plants. Examples are the structures made from date palms in the Middle East.
Certain upper floor rooms in Medieval houses that are smaller than halls and reserved for private family use. The form grew out of the Greek and Roman "solariums (building spaces)."

Refers to analysis of materials on a microscopic or macroscopic scale using a beam of positively charged light ions. Ion beam analysis (IBA) techniques are often used to study works of art,  because of their noninvasive and nondestructive character. These techniques exploit the products of interactions between beams of accelerated charged particles and the target in order to determine its elemental composition.

Rectangular or square supporting elements or lower blocks, as for columns, pilasters, or door framing; also solid monumental bases, often ornamented, used to support statues or memorials. For the bases of external walls or the platformlike base courses of buildings, use "plinth courses."

Refers to the process of making an audio master disc or tape from which multiple copies will be made. Mastering may incorporate a variety of functions, excluding recording. The term is frequently extended to videodisc technology.

Faiths that occurred in the early years of Buddhism, in South and Southeast Asia. In Hindu-Buddhism, ideas and dieties of the two faiths were combined, as Buddhism first grew out of Hinduism in India in the 6th century BCE.
In the sciences, taking of samples for technical analysis.
In Indian architecture, an architectural division carrying vertical facias.

Anvils on which a shoe may be held in place while a shoemaker performs work. These have varied form, some resembling an upended foot on an arm and others having two or three arms conjoined, ending in varied shapes.
Small family of Native American languages in Colombia and Panama.
Depressions that may not be continuous, located at the base of many seamounts, islands, and other isolated undersea landforms.

Any of various devices that create audible sound waves, usually electronically and/or digitally. These may incorporate oscillators, modulators, or amplifiers or all of these combined to create a synthesis.

Pottery characterized by a gray or brownish-gray color, having a relatively simple design that is painted or imprinted. It is common in ancient India, Korea, Native American culture, Greek, Minoan, Roman, Middle Eastern, and many other cultures.
Artists that produce raised letters or designs on a surface, typically by means of stamping or molding.

Sculptors in colonial Latin America who created religious figures, usually representations of Christ, the Virgin, saints and angels for altars, processions, nativity, and passion scenes. Imagineros worked with a variety of materials including stone, bone, ceramic and shell, but primarily with polychromed wood.
General term for sexual activity or behavior of any type.
Recreational activity in which a person rides a skateboard, a narrow board mounted on roller-skate wheels, usually in a standing position.

Legendary creatures, from the Greek meaning "every wild beast," that often take the form of a large cat with a multi-colored coat, but may also be in the form of another animal or a composite creature. The ancient Greeks believed the panther was one of the favored mounts of the god Dionysus. In Medieval legend, the panther would sleep in a cave after feasting upon prey, and after three days emitted a sweet odor from its mouth, to draw additional prey into the cave.
Brand name for a board comprising polystyrene between two coated papers, often used for mounting or backing works of art. Manufactured by Monsanto.

Species of oak native to northeastern United States and southeast Canada, but found north in Nova Scotia, south to Georgia, and west to the Great Lakes. It is used for timber but often cultivated as an ornamental; it grows rapidly into a round-headed, wide-spreading tree about 25 m (80 feet) in height, with leaves that turn red-orange in autumn and persist into winter.
Genus of legume consisting of approximately 150 species found in tropical and subtropical regions.
Describes institutions that specialize in the history, objects, vehicles, and other materials associated with transportation.
Species of evergreen coniferous pine tree growing up to 25 m in height, having a broad range in Eurasia; it is cultivated in North America and New Zealand. Many varieties exist.

Separate, independent, and generally self-sufficient institutions engaging in basic or applied research under contract or as nonprofit organizations. For institutions that support research conducted as part of a larger organization, use "research centers."
Variable red colors resembling the colors of red in the spectrum, which is the colored band into which a beam of light is decomposed by means of a prism or diffraction grating.
Any of various brownish-gold colors resembling the topaz mineral.
Colors in a range of a bluish grayish green, resembling the color of certain patches feathers of the teal (a river duck).
Variable color in the range of brilliant greenish blues, resembling the color of the kingfisher bird.

Members of an order of containing at least 5,000 living species of insects with adults that are easily recognized by their two pairs of narrow, transparent wings, sloping thorax, and long, usually slender body; the abdomen is almost always longer than any of the wings. They are large, active by day, and often strikingly colored.

Order containing around approximately 400 species in six families including jacamars, puffbirds, barbets, honey guides, and toucans. Characterized as forest dwelling, hole-nesting birds that feed upon insects and fruit, having outer toes able to face rearward, some are specialized for climbing, and some that are brood parasites.
Independent professional schools of music emphasizing advanced instruction in performance for singers, conductors, and musicians; usually granting certificates.
Bodies of shallow water separated from the sea by a barrier, such as a sandbar or coral reef.
Low areas that are surrounded by higher land and usually characterized by interior drainage.

A standard peripheral interface for connecting devices such as mice, keyboards, cameras, etc. to personal computers. The term "USB" is used to refer to the standard as well as the cable device and port.

Order containing more than 2,050 species in 27 families characterized by having no canine teeth and strong incisors, the upper and lower pairs of which are ever-growing and rootless, including rats, mice, porcupines, beavers, squirrels, marmots, pocket gophers, and chinchillas.
Proofs produced as part of the creation process in printmaking, used as the artist or craftsman creates the plate or screen, and makes decisions regarding alterations or next steps.

Christian holiday celebrating the birth of St. John the Baptist, held on June 24. It may include festivities, lights, and fireworks, reminiscent of the earlier feasts of Midsummers for the summer solstice, which occurs at around the same time (on a day between June 21 and 24).
Style and culture of the Ivory Coast.
Bussiness enterprises providing modes of transportation for hire, most commonly automobiles and boats.

Refers to the style and culture of the Stoney Nakoda, an indigenous people of Canada and the United States, particularly Montana. They are culturally connected to the Assiniboine and usage overlaps. The Stoney Nakoda Nations are: Bearspaw First Nation, Chiniki First Nation, and Goodstoney First Nation.
Plants that are cultivated for food, typically restricted to the edible parts of a herbaceous plant (such as leaves, stems, or roots) that are traditionally served as a savory course of a meal.

The anterior parts of the body of humans and animals containing the mouth, special sense organs such as the eyes, nose, and ears, and the brain; typically separated by a neck or otherwise distinguished from the rest of the body.

Phylum including several tube-dwelling, worm-like marine invertebrates characterized by a horseshoe-shaped lophophore, which is a characteristic feeding organ. Wormlike marine invertebrates of the phylum Phoronidea, having a true body cavity divided into compartments, a cluster of tentacles at the upper end, a circulatory system, circular and longitudinal muscles, and a nervous sytem beneath the epidermis; ranging up to 15 feet in length, each individual lives in a chitinous tube which it secretes, the lower end of which is buried in the mud or sand at the bottom of shallow seas while the tentacles extend out of the t to gather food.

Mechanized devices designed to arrange worsted wool fibers in parallel order, eliminate minor impurities in the wool, and ensure that the fibers are blended uniformly. While these devices can come in many forms, they are typically composed of a pair of feed rollers and a series of moving pins or combs which act upon the wool in a combing action. The wool is first feed onto the feed rollers and is then carried through the pins and combs, which arrange and blend the fibers at rapid speeds.
Material with formula Co3(PO4)2∙8H2O that is used in painting porcelain and coloring glass, glazes, enamels, and plastics.

Large and small items that are necessary to attach, anchor, hold, or join materials and components of structures, furniture, and other objects. Also, items used in the finishing of buildings and objects, such as hinges and knobs.
Small files of metal or cardboard, for trimming, smoothing, or shaping the fingernails and sometimes having a point for removing the dirt from under them.
Administrative divisions of Russia. Similar to oblasts, but generally covering larger territories.
Administrative bodies subject to a margrave.

Stiff, durable textile characterized by corded effects in either the warp or weft, originally made in white cotton, later also in rayon or silk, and printed or in colors; used for dresses, blouses, trousers, sports clothing, purses, and neckwear.
Plain-woven fabric of any fiber or blend, with crosswise ribs that typically gives a corded surface.
Refers to the action of effacing, rubbing out, or removing something written, drawn, engraved, or recorded on any media.
The act or process of reducing to powder, pulverization; in conservation science context refers to granular disintegration of stone and pigments.

The process in which a material leaves the surface of the solid into which it was absorbed or adsorbed; it is the reverse of those processes. In conservation, adsorption may refer as well to intentional removal of absorbed or adsorbed material from a substrate through increased heat, decreased pressure, or other measures.
Having the two dimensions of length and width, but not height.
The quality of being closed or covered in Indian architecture.
The characteristics of a material or object that concern its degree of magnetism and the magnetic phenomena it evinces.
Plucked lutelike chordophones of Japan having three strings of nylon or silk, a long unfretted neck, a bridge, and a small square soundbox covered with cat or dog skin.
Interior components of garments stitched inside clothing to provide support and warmth, or simply as a finish.
Headwear with a stiff visor at a right angle to the forehead. The crown is wider than the head. The shape is held by internal stiff support material.
Sealed and pressurized suits designed to allow the wearer to leave a pressurized cabin in outer space or at extremely high altitudes within the atmosphere.

Steel helmets of a distinctive style developed by the Imperial German Army to replace the traditional boiled-leather "pickelhaubes" (spiked combat helmets) in 1916 during World War I. Stahlhelms comprised a steel outer shell with a liner made of a headband and padding materials.

Toy versions of irons with which children can learn to iron or pretend to be ironing. With older versions it was possible to really iron by placing the iron on a stove or by means of electricity. Often sold in combination with a toy ironing board.

Narrow pieces of lace, lawn, or other soft cloth worn by women inside or around the neck opening when wearing a low-cut bodice, especially from the 17th to the early 19th century. For more shaped accessories or main garments made with or without sleeves and worn especially from the 19th to the early 20th century, use "chemisettes."
Bookbindings decorated with painting, often along with gilding or other decoration.
Apparatus consisting of a short horizontal bar attached to the ends of two suspended ropes and used in gymnastics and acrobatics.
Refers to work created by thread embroidered through punched holes in paper supports.
Toys or sets of objects designed for a form of play in which divination is performed.

Mechanized devices, typically comprising an automated range of stenter chains for tension control, designed to facilitate the application of a caustic soda chemical treatment on cotton fabrics to prepare the fabrics for subsequent dying and chemical finishes. By providing a temperature and tension controlled surface upon which the wet textile process of mercanization is carried out, these devices give fabrics a lustrey finish, increased tensile strength, and greater absorptive properties, creating a foundation for finishing treatments.
Content of information artifacts such as audio-visual recordings or printed matter that is unsuitable for all users. This refers most often to sexual or violent subject matter.
Devices used to pump milk from one vessel (such as a tank) to another in a dairy.
Instruments for determining the strength of an indigo solution by volumetric analysis.
Instruments for finishng an amalgam for filling.
