Generally, practices or patterns of behavior regularly performed in a set, precise manner, for either personal or public purposes. Specifically, particular activities performed during a designated event, often a ceremony.
In book cataloging, titles comprising the title proper along with any other information, such as general material designation.
The standard unit of currency of Japan.

Dating system based on a cycle of 60 Tibetan years, each of which usually has 354 days (12 cycles of the phases of the Moon). Adjustment to the solar year of about 365 days is made by intercalation of an extra month every three years. It is based on the Chinese calendar.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 6999 to 6000 (or 7000 to 6001) Before Common Era.

Fiber derived from leaves of the species Agave sisalana. The fiber has been used since pre-Columbian times; the Aztecs are known to have made clothing from it. From the late 1930s sisal has been cultivated commercially in Central and South America as well as in Africa. It is a strong, stiff fiber with a pale cream color. Sisal is typically dyed bright colors with direct or acid dyes. Sisal is used for cordage, ropes, sacks, brushes, upholstery padding, rugs, matting, handbags, hats, dartboards, and in papermaking.
Pale, soft wood from any of many species of North American pines, generally native to eastern and central parts of the continent.

Wood of the species Quercus bicolor, native to eastern North America. It is a strong, hard, heavy wood used in shipbuilding and furniture. Wood of the species Quercus bicolor, native to eastern North America. It is a strong, hard, heavy wood used in shipbuilding and furniture.

Wood from the species Brya ebenus native to Central America and the Caribbean islands. It comes from the black or rich brown heartwood. It is brittle, very heavy, exceedingly hard, having a fine uniform texture, and capable of receiving a high polish. It is used for inlays, brush backs, parquet, and musical instruments. Not a true rosewood.
Any of various preparations made from the seeds, fruits, leaves, or bark of the neem tree, used for medicinal purposes, as an insecticide, and for other purposes.
A mold inhibiting calcium salt used as a food preservative. In conservation, used for reduction of acidity and fungi in aged paper documents.

Radioactive, soft, metallic chemical element, atomic number 88; a member of the group of the alkaline earth metals. It occurs in small amounts in pitchblende and other uranium ores. It undergoes spontaneous disintegration to form Radon gas and alpha rays. Bright white radium was formerly used to make luminous paints used in clock dials, doorknobs, and other glow-in-the-dark items prior to the 1970s.

Glass made with slices of colored canes embedded in clear molten glass, usually creating flowerlike designs. Distinguish from "mosaic glass" which uses slices of colored canes as inlays for walls and furniture, beads, jewelry, and to form vessels when arranged in molds and fused together.
Any of a large group of substances that typically show a characteristic luster, are good conductors of electricity and heat, are opaque, can be fused, and are usually malleable or ductile.

Crosses having three crossbars on a longer vertical bar, where the upper bar represents the INRI title of the cross, the second longer crossbar designating arms of the cross, and the lowest crossbar, which is always inclined at an angle, signifying the suppedaneum or foot rest.
Nahua symbol having a curl shape or spiral shape, representing the cross-section of a Strombus gigas or Turbinella angulata conch shell.
Siamese Buddhist temples; may also be used for Siamese Buddhist monasteries.
In Indian architecture, a main temple as opposed to subsidiary shrines in a complex; main shrine; shrine proper.
Buildings housing businesses specializing in the retail sale of sporting equipment, such as rackets, balls, clubs, etc., and specialized clothing designed to be worn while playing sports.
Buildings planned or used for multiple purposes.
Earthen enclosures of relatively small size, usually circular and possibly serving as fortifications or chiefs' residences. Examples are found in Wales, Ireland, India, and elsewhere.
Narrow raised bands, particularly the topmost members of the Doric architrave.
Windows designed for use in mental institutions, characterized by heavy intermediate sections, restricted glass sizes and ventilator heights, plus special screens and hardware.
Arches that are curved in the shape of a parabola, following a plane curve that is mirror-symmetrical and is approximately U-shaped.

Sites upon which one building is built, altered through major accretion to become a different building, or rebuilt as a different building over time, but still retaining the same function and often the same name. The term is often, but not exclusively, used for archaeological sites having this characteristic; refers to both the site and the sum of structures that have occupied the site over time. Examples include the Aztec Templo Mayor, which was rebuilt six times on the same site, and the Temple of Jerusalem, also rebuilt several times on the same site, and Stonehenge, altered through accretion over centuries. To refer in general to a site where a building is or was located, whether or not the building is under construction, use "building sites."
Land and water spaces and associated structures set aside for recreation.

An expression of the ratio between the size of the representation of something and that thing, such as the size of the drawn structure in an architectural drawing and the actual built work. May also refer in general to the concept of relative size.

The state or process in which events or conditions transpire, a tendency, or a trend evident at a particular time or in a particular sphere, particularly a course or series of actions and endeavours on the part of a group of people working towards a shared goal or to advance a shared political, social, or artistic objective.

The philosophical systems and speculative tendencies of various Medieval Christian thinkers, who, working against a background of fixed religious dogma, sought to solve anew general philosophical problems (as of faith and reason, will and intellect, and the provability of the existence of God), initially under the influence of the mystical and intuitional tradition of patristic philosophy, and especially Augustinianism, and later under that of Aristotle.
The quality of belonging to a dialectal, idiomatic, local group.
Concept concerning the ability to recognize and follow the most suitable or sensible course of action, utilizing good sense, discretion, circumspection, caution.

Ownership or control that permits domination of the means of production or the market in a business or occupation, usually in order to control prices; it is achieved through an exclusive legal privilege, control of the source of supply, or combination or concert of action.
Land owned and controlled by the state or federal government. Also, the status of publications, products, and processes that are not protected under patent or copyright.

Generally used for the sum of an individual's sexual emotions, ideas, and behavior. For the pattern of attitudes and behavior that in any society is deemed appropriate to one sex rather than another, use "sex role." For the concept of the physiological traits that distinguish the males and females of a species, use "sex."
Refers to the manufacture of rope and the stages of that process, from spinning through twisting or braiding.

Painting technique whereby tones and hues are obtained by applying regular small dots or touches of unmixed pigment on the canvas so that they combine optically. The French critic Félix Fénéon coined the term "peinture au point" in 1886 after seeing Seurat's "La Grande Jatte." Paul Signac offered the alternative term of "divisionism" in his book "D'Eugène Delacroix au Néo-Impressionnisme (1899), although in modern usage "pointillism" is reserved for the technique involving dots applied in a controlled manner, while "divisionism" refers to use of marks of unmixed color in Italian painters’ works.
Forming objects by applying pressure with a tool, for example, shaping metal, including coins, with dies. For stamping that creates surface designs, use "stamping (marking)."

Large panels, frames, or other assemblies on which are mounted switches, fuses, instruments, and protective devices; for smaller panels containing switches and fuses or circuit breakers, use "panelboards."
Hinges, often ornamental, mounted on a face of a door rather than the edge.

Sculptural works that may be worn on the human body. These are usually meant to be activated or completed by the movement of a wearer in performance situations, though they are frequently exhibited as static objects. Costume or apparel works are often referred to as wearable art, though a distinction should be made between streetwear, costume, and 'wearable art,' here scoped as sculpture.
Women's hats with a soft, circular crown enclosed by a stiffened, turned up brim; worn in the 19th century.
Drinking vessels without a stem, foot, or handle and traditionally having a rounded bottom; also includes similar forms with heavy, flattened bottoms.
Name given to the bosses on large stretchers linking and strengthening the legs of a table or secretaire; often very richly carved and pierced.
In Christian churches or places of other religious services, stands or tables used for the collection plate or other offertory gifts.
Term used loosely to describe Wooton cabinet office secretaries and rotary desks, each invented by William S. Wooton. Whenever possible use more specific term.
Tables incorporating a translucent screen illuminated from underneath, for tracing, viewing slides, and other activities.
Chairs having one flat arm wide enough to use as a writing surface, or with a small table surface attached to one arm.
Term used by Chippendale for low beds without any superstructure, generally used by servants.

Modernist chair designed for Knoll International in 1952 by Harry Bertoia. The basic form of the chair is constructed from wire rods welded together. There are many variations in upholstery and finish.
Argand lamps without a separate reservoir and with burners that have low dome deflectors with circular openings.  The font, if not the entire lamp, is made of metal, commonly brass.
Cylindrical fasteners having a head with a slot or recess and helical or spiral threading, to be inserted by rotating, as with a screwdriver.
Drawings executed in silverpoint on pigmented, prepared paper and highlighted in white, where the range of the three resulting tonal values is exploited to depict three-dimensional form.

Organizations no part of the net earnings or income of which is distributed or inures to the benefit of any private individual, but is applied to the stated purpose of the organization, such as charity, community service, or research.
In general, women of distinction without precise designation of rank. Women considered by the society to be of good birth or breeding.
Those who take part in a conspiracy.
Hereditary commanders-in-chief of the Japanese army; until 1867, the virtual rulers of Japan.
People skilled in the practice of taxidermy, which is the preparation of lifelike representations of animals by stuffing the skin or molding it around a model of the specimen.
People or corporate bodies who make or decorate visual works made of porcelain, which is an impermeable translucent ceramic material.
People who own or run art galleries, or those who promote artists by exhibiting in galleries.
People who construct or repair roofs as an occupation.
Assemblages of systematically arranged keys by which a machine is operated.
Instruments or apparatuses that aid the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of diseases and injuries used in the practice of medicine.
Files with projecting teeth for rough work.
Handheld tools that end in small, wire loops. These tools are sterilized, then used to streak bacterial samples in Petri dishes, or to transfer microorganisms between test tubes.
Models of the skies used for teaching nautical astronomy.

Refers to the international intellectual movement that was first applied to literature in the late 19th century, spreading to painting and theater, and influencing European and American literature from the 20th century to the present.  Affecting later movements such as Surrealism, it is characterized by a complex synthesis of psychology, mystical and occult practices, and linguistics used to challenge traditional relationships between representation and meaning.

Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Mustafa III, who ruled from 1757 to 1774. He founded The Laleli Mosque, which recalls the design of the Nuruosmaniye Mosque with its raised platform and approaching flight of steps.
Nationality, styles, and culture of ancient Sicyon, in the northern Peloponnesus.

The style or culture of the  Marathi people, also rendered as Marathis or Maharashtrian, an ethnolinguistic group who speak Marathi, an Indo-Aryan language. They inhabit the state of Maharashtra as well as districts bordering the state, such as Belgaum of Karnataka and the state of Goa in western India as well as districts of southern Gujarat and parts of Madhya Pradesh. In the 17th century the Marathas, under Shivaji Maharaj, established the Maratha Empire, which is credited to a large extent for ending the Mughal rule.

Refers to the work of a school of painters begun around 1600 by Sōtatsu and his contemporary Hon'Ami Koetsu, revised in the 18th century by Korin and again in the 19th century by Saki Hoitsu. The alternate name for the school, "Rimpa" is devised from the last syllable in Korin's name (rin) and the word school (ha). The style is characterized by an adherence to the classical Japanese sense of decorativeness, delicate coloring, and a keen observation of the natural world.  Precious materials such as gold and silver along with colors were used on folding screens, fans, and other objects. Subject matter was taken from medieval literature as well as nature. Although the style did not last past the Edo period (1600-1868), it influenced 20th century Japanese painting.

Refers to a style of gray stoneware manufactured from the 5th to the 10th centuries. Originating in the southern part of the Korean peninsula, the style immigrated to Japan in the 5th and 6th centuries, where it was called iwaibe doki or Chosen doki, until the 1950s. The style is characterized by the production of coil-made vessels fired at temperatures exceeding 1,000 degrees centigrade (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit) resulting in a gray color. Sue wares are typically unglazed except for the natural ash glaze occurring during the firing process and decorated with simple combed or punctate designs. In the Hein period (794-1185), productions included new glazed versions using native ash glaze and green or three-color glazing techniques.
The culture of Americans of Russian descent.

Style of American architecture inspired by built works of Spain and Latin America, blending elements of Moorish, Mediterranean, and Spanish Colonial elements. The style is particularly prevalent in Florida.

Style and culture of Siouan people of North Carolina and Virginia. Historically located near the Blue Ridge Mountains prior to European contact, the Sappony moved to the Piedmont region of North Carolina and northern Virginia in the 1700s. Today, the tribe is state recognized by both North Carolina and Virginia, and are known as "Sappony."

Style and culture of an Algonquian-speaking Native American tribe located in Long Island, New York. Have also been referred to as the "Poospatuck" in reference to the reservation the Unkechaug live on (Poospatuck Reservation, NY).
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in Tanzania.
Style and culture of the African people of the same name living in  the Democratic Republic of Congo west of Rwanda and Burundi.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting northern Nigeria.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Nigeria.
Anaerobic bacteria which obtain energy by converting sulfate compounds into sulfide compounds.

A substance that adds oxygen or removes hydrogen in chemical reaction with another compound. Used as bleaches that whiten or decolorize in conjunction with oxidizing agents. Examples of reducing agents include: sulfites, bisulfites, dithionite, and sodium borohydride.

Substances of animal, vegetable, mineral, or synthetic origin that are used as an ingredient in pharmacy, in the prevention or treatment of disease, as a medicine, or to otherwise obtain a physiological effect on a living organism. Also includes substances having intoxicating, stimulant, or narcotic effects.
Paper treated with a coating of wax.
Vegetable oil obtained from rice bran and used in cooking.
Air tight devices for quick cooking or preserving of foods by means of superheated steam under pressure.
Narratives set in the distant past recounting events impossible in the real world, often magical and with fairies, but with humans as heroes and heroines.
Devices used for circulating air through milk. Often used to remove animal heat, gases, and odors from fresh milk before canning.
Boat-shaped vessels, usually with a long pouring lip at one end and a handle at the other or two pouring lips and a central handle, used for serving sauces, gravies, or the like.
Covered boxes of varying shape intended primarily for holding and serving sugar; often made en suite with one or two tea caddies.  Sometimes containing a sugar spoon for serving.
Small cases, usually ornamental, meant to contain personal articles, such as bodkins and toothpicks. Formerly, also cases for surgical instruments.

Containers probably used to hold ointments and perfume. Early ceramic examples found at Petra (probably 4th-century BCE) were in the typical Hellenistic form of the spindle bottle, but this form was later completely replaced by a series of high-necked types with round to ovoid bodies of varying and apparently standardized forms (from the 1st century BCE onwards). The number of unguentaria found at Petra suggests that they were made locally; their manufacture would have been linked to the myrrh and other unguents that the Nabataeans traded. They have also been found at western sites. Pear-shaped glass unguentaria were later made at various locations in the Arabian peninsula.
Tubular protruberances through which the contents of a vessel may be poured or sometimes drunk.

Ancient Greek vessels in a shape reminiscent of an oil lamp. They feature prominent spouts and seem to have been specialized containers designed for the refilling of oil lamps with a fresh supply of olive oil. Most lamps were made with a hole in the discus (the round sealed cover of the reservoir) so that the refilling did not need to disturb the wick that emerged from the spout.
Written or printed characters or combinations of characters ordinarily appearing as a unit, when in a sentence or phrase, between spaces or between a space and a punctuation mark.
Term applied to tinplate containers with a cover or lid used for packaging biscuits, crackers, tobacco, or the like.
Small cups or shallow bowls used for drinking the Japanese fermented rice wine called sake.
The extra length and width of the covering material of a book overlapping the head, tail, and foredge of the cover, which is turned over the edges of the board and adhered to the inside surface.

Vessels partly in the shape of a moldmade head or face. For aryballoi, kantharoi, mugs, oinochoai, and rhyta, the head usually constitutes the body of the vessel. All other parts of a head-vase (except for the handles) are wheelmade. Animal heads are most popular for rhyta while human heads or faces are characteristic for other vessel types.

Ephemeral works or more substantive works that are displayed specifically during a holiday period for interior or exterior decoration, including garlands, ornaments, candles, electric lights, hangings, and many other types of works.
Images recorded and stored in computer and video systems.
In Indian architecture, a ghoul figure.
People of any gender whose occupation or business is making repairs.
The state or activity of having or causing a beginning or a bringing into existence.

People, usually priests, who makes statements prompted by his or her deity. This was especially common in ancient times, sometimes in a specific sacred place. The oracle's utterances serve as a directive to the inquiring party.

Type of pattern common on late 18th and 19th century ceramics, derived from Chinese sources, depicting a willow tree, a pagoda, a bridge with figures, two birds flying, and a small boat; most commonly blue figures on a white background.
Tools similar to a flat file having a coarse side and a fine side; used for pointing pencils, charcoal, crayons, and pastels.
Artisans who make artificial flowers, often in the media of silk or ceramic. For those who paint two-dimensional images of flowers, prefer "flower painter."
Walkways, typically behind the parapets, along the tops of defensive fortications such as those found in castles or as part of city walls.
In Indian art and architecture, a leafy scroll; vine, leaf, or floral-band motif.
In Indian architecture, a creeper-bearing band.
In Indian architecture, a fantastic or imaginary animal, often in part composite as a decorative motif; imaginary hypostatic animal.

Inclusive of all, both physical and conceptual; indication of the inclusion of everything between the extreme points, measured from end to end, or including the whole range of components, features, or aspects.

Refers to examples of the knitting machine invented by William Lee of Cambridge, England in 1589. It produced net composed of the basic looped ‘stocking stitch’ and thus superseded hand-knitting. The introduction of this technology initiated the process of mechanizing the textile industry.
In stained glass work: hand-held implements used to open the grooves of lead cames and to smooth them over cut pieces of glass.
Reamers used for woodworking.
Originally, a supporter of the international movement for the establishment of a Jewish nation in Palestine, and later for the State of Israel itself.
The state or condition of being in agreement, accordance, being consistent and congruous, as related to another person, animal, nature, or other thing or condition.

The doctrinal concept that some aspect of the self or soul can be reborn any number of times in a new body (animal or human) after death. Fundamental to a number of Eastern religions such as Hinduism and Buddhism, this belief is also found in some modern Western belief systems such as theosophy.
Information as displayed on a computer screen, or that cannot be read without the aid of electromechanical devices.

A short tale, often of a fantastic or artificial nature, used as an example to illustrate a moral point; developed, cultivated, and popular in the Middle Ages, exempla were often incorporated into sermons.

Printed matter of any kind, or written works in digital form. Examples are tales and writings of a nation, region, period, or language, of a particular form or genre, on a particular subject, or for a particular audience. For the written works produced by an individual or specific group of individuals, use "writings". For the discipline of the humanities dealing with written or oral verbal literary works, use "literary studies."
Connected to a support located above, often reserved for describing the position of an object hanging with empty space beneath it.

Refers to the movement or style evolving from Photorealism in the United States and Europe. Historically the term has often been used interchangeably with Photorealism. Hyperrealism may now be considered a separate idiom, particularly since the early 2000s. Hyperrealist works use photographic images as sources to make even more exacting renderings of subject matter. Hyperrealist painting and sculpture often incorporates narrative, emotive, or political content, unlike Photorealist works, which attempted to eschew subjectivity through precise rendering of the photographs themselves.
In Indian architecture, a vyāla frieze; vyālamālā; band of vyāla figures.

Small compilations of things that are bound or packed together. For the bag or envelope for packing small compilations of things, use "packets (containers)." An example of a packet is the stack of gold called a "mold" compiled at one stage of the gold beating process.

General concept for flat, relatively thin sheets or disks of a rigid material such as metal or glass that have a uniform surface and thickness, used to make a work in multiples. Examples are copper or steel plates that are etched or engraved and used in printmaking, and thin sheets of metal or glass used in photography to make positive or negative images.
Nationality, culture, and style of the city and territory of Pisa, central Italy.
Refers to the style and culture of the former nation of Czechoslovakia (1918-1993).
Nationality, culture, and styles of the Virgin Islands, in the Caribbean, the westernmost islands of the Lesser Antilles; today they are divided between Great Britain and the United States.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Minnesota.

The culture and style of the ancient Venetii, people of northeastern Italy who arrived about 1000 BCE and occupied an area stretching south to the Po river and west to the Vero river. This culture is unrelated to the ancient Celto-Venetic culture of Britanny.

Sensitive technique for detection and measurement of radioactivity using a detector which flashes when substances known as 'scintillator' materials, incorporated into solid plastics or liquid solvents, convert radiation into flashes of light. The resulting photons are amplified after being converted into electric pulses, and are finally displayed as individual counts.

Timber frame construction in which the upright posts are raised above damp ground on individual foundation blocks to avoid rotting the frame members and to facilitate replacement of foundation pieces without rebuilding the frame; common in the vernacular architecture of the Lower Mississippi Valley.
Interior spaces, usually in dwellings, designed to allow entry of sunshine through large windows. For ancient sunporches or modern sun lounges in hospitals, use “solariums (building spaces).”

Holes in the ground used to hold the foot of post components of fences or other structures. In the context of archaeology, these are recognizable as circular patches of darkened earth, where wood has decayed, or the hole has later been filled with a different material. Postholes are important to archaeologists to plot the layout of former building structures.
Observing and collecting information about something over time or distance for some specific purpose.

General term for the set of intellectual and philosophical tenets and highly diverse beliefs and practices that define the civilization, art, literature, society, and politics of the Indian subcontinent. Hinduism is not a common set of rigid beliefs , but varies significantly between different regions; it includes Shaivism, Vaishnavism, Srauta, and numerous other traditions. Among other practices and philosophies, Hinduism includes a wide spectrum of laws and prescriptions of "daily morality" based on karma, dharma, and societal norms. The highest divine powers are seen as complementary to one another and not exclusive. Hinduism does not have a particular founder or central authority. Hindu literature is rich and varied, with no one text considered uniquely authoritative. The Vedas, dating to the Vedic period (ca. 1200-500 BCE), are the earliest extant writings. Religious law books and epics such as the Ramayana and the Mahabharata have been and continue to be highly influential.
In archaeology, a dating technique which places artifactual samples in serial order according to prescribed typological criteria.
In Indian architecture, an internal covering slab in śikhara, below skandha; plank or slab sealing the garbhagṛha/śikhara.
Games in which the pieces used to play are small rectangular pieces (tiles).
The restriction of rent that may be charged for the occupation or use of certain premises in a municipality, usually residential, by local law.
Events where something is totally or partially consumed by fire, whether intentionally or by accident. For the process of altering, injuring, or consuming something by fire or heat, see "burning."
In Indian architecture, a śākhā/jamb carved with creeper design; śākhā with vine pattern; creeper-bearing door-jamb.

The knowledge held in an organization by its employees including personal information that provides an understanding of the history and culture of the organization, especially undocumented anecdotes that explain the logic behind certain decisions or procedures.

Refers to art created by non-professional artists or artisans who have not had formal training and are often self-taught; also art in the naive style created by formally trained artists. It typically displays a child-like rendering of anatomy, perspective, and other pictorial elements. Media may include painting, sculpture, embroidery, quilts, toys, ships' figureheads, decoys, painted targets, and other objects; often refers to such objects created specifically in 19th- and 20th-century Europe and North America. Distinguished from "outsider art," which is based on a philosophy of the avoidance of, rather than simply a lack of, traditional training. It is also usually distinct from "folk art," which is created according to specific cultural traditions.
Shape resembling or suggestive of a rose.
Fissures or systems of fissures without complete separation into pieces.
Low rounded hills located on the sea floor.
Devices that analyze the presence or volume of auditory signals.
Pottery, usually large buff ware vessels, from 5th millennium BCE in Anatolia, distinguished by thick walls and a gritty face.
Artists who work in the medium of enamel.

Painters who endeavor to express the general impression produced by a scene or object, to the exclusion of minute details or elaborate finish. The term is also used for writers who practice a similar method in prose or verse.
The action of removing the hair from the head or face with a razor.
The activity of riding to and fro on a swing.

Mythical birds resembling an eagle but having red and gold plumage. The phoenix was said to live for hundreds of years, then it would burn itself in a funeral pyre or temple sacrifice, only to rise from the ashes with renewed youth. Variations of the myth place the birds in the deserts of Arabia or in ancient Egypt.

A nonwoven, low melt synthetic polyester, manufactured by Wonderflex, that softens and shrinks when heated, transforming into a rigid 3-D structure upon cooling that can be cut and sewn. In conservation, it has been used for constructing mannequins and mounts for textiles, costumes, and other objects.

Species of large oak native to the Atlantic Coastal Plain of the U.S., in the Mississippi and Ohio river valleys. It is also found in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Maryland, and Ontario, Canada. It is used for shade, for timber, and the acorns and leaves are food for various birds and mammals.

Genus containing around 450 shrubs, undershrubs, climbers, or trees native to tropical and subtropical areas throughout both hemispheres. They are so named from the movements of the leaves in certain species that mimic animal sensibility, including rapidly moving when touched. Certain plants called "mimosa" were formerly assigned to this genus, including Albizia julibrissin (silk tree) and Acacia dealbata (silver wattle).
Virtual representation of a physical museum, or of a collection without physical counterpart, accessed through electronic media.

Species of pine tree native to the southeastern United States, from Texas to Florida and Delaware. It grows to 30-35 m (98-115 feet) tall. The needles usually fall only every two years, giving the species an evergreen character. The word "loblolly" refers to a low wet place, although the trees grow in other habitats as well.
Enterprises where scientific experiments and research take place, in in a space equipped to facilitate these activities.
Variable purple or reddish color resembling garments dyed with Tyrian purple dye, obtained from marine gastropods of the genus Murex.
A range of yellow colors resembling the color of Turner's yellow pigment, which was made by mixing powdered lead chloride with lead carbonate, then fusing.
Variable green color resembling the color of verdigris pigment, which is composed of basic copper acetate.
Range of blue or greenish colors resembling the color of the lapis lazuli gem, which is a semiprecious stone that is usually rich blue in color.
Members of an order of insects including grasshoppers and crickets.
Order containing 22 species in one family, two species having recently gone extinct. Characterized as  foot-propelled diving birds with lobed toes, minute tails, and silky plumage.
Educational institutions, generally associated with universities, sponsoring degree-granting programs in a broad range of subjects pertaining to the field of music.
Large natural depressions in the earth's surface that contain water, usually salt water, including oceans and seas.
Broad category of dry regions occurring where rainfall is less than 50 cm per year; usually barren and treeless.

Order containing 17 species in one family, characterized as slender animals with long tails and soft gray or brown fur, with tterrestrial species larger than the arboreal forms with larger claws, which they use for digging up insect prey.

Christian feast day celebrating the 4th-century Nicholas of Myra, a bishop and saint from Roman Asia Minor. In the western church, his feast is celebrated on December 6, coinciding with the first days of the Christmas season, which begins with Advent. In some traditions, gifts are given to children on the eve of the Saint Nicholas' Day.
Style and culture of Kenya.
Businesses that focus on processing or shaping products out of metal.
Light, flat pastries with a typical honeycomb pattern, made with a batter of flour, milk and eggs and baked in a waffle iron.
In bipedal and quadrupedal animals and in humans, the projecting part of the body on each side formed by the lateral expansions of the pelvis and upper part of the thigh bone.

Instruments used for pushing needles forcefully through leather or canvas, composed of a leather or canvas strap that is worn on the hand into which is set a metal thimble impressed with cavities that fit the heads of needles.

Phylum of flat soft-bodied invertebrates that include tapeworms and flukes. The flatworms are free-living as well as parasitic and lack respiratory, skeletal, and circulatory systems. The body is not divided into true segments, but rather has spongy connective tissue called parenchyma filling in the space between organs. Flatworms are hermaphroditic and are the lowest invertebrates to possess three embryonic layers of endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm. Bilaterally symmetrical worms of the phylum Platyhelminthes, having a soft, solid, usually flattened body without an internal cavity.

Driven rollers or wheels, typically tubular in shape and mounted to rotating spindles, around which the filaments of textile fibers are drawn during the manufacturing process. These devices may be heated and are often tapered at one end. The name, godet, refers to a triangular piece of material inserted in a garment to create a flared shape; its application to these textile devices is thought to have originated from the rollers' tapered geometery. Historically made from glass, the rollers are oftentimes components of larger spinning machines.

A coloring agent found in pyrotechnics and in many pigments. It occurs naturally in crystalline form as blue colored azurite and green hued malachite. Copper carbonate is synthesized by adding sodium carbonate to a solution of copper sulfate; the product is then filtered and dried resulting in a colored powder.
The striking part of a percussion, edged, or projectile tool or weapon, or the part of an explosive projectile weapon carrying the live explosive.
Rectangular pieces of cloth, paper, or other absorbent material, used for wiping or drying.
Adhesive strips worn on the outside of the nose to improve breathing.
The constituent political and administrative divisions of the modern federal nation of Germany.
Political entities having governments in which the political power resides with the military.
Coarse homespun cloth, usually reddish or brownish in color.

African textile material of Ewe origin but adapted and varied by other peoples, woven on a loom in narrow strips to produce strong patterns. A popular cloth, it is traded all around the Niger Delta region.

Creating marks on the surface of a hard material such as metal or glass, by the controlled corrosive action of acid. Use "etching (printing process)" for the series of steps that includes printing from a bitten plate.

The action of making a substance more physically soft or pliable; to lessen hardness or rigidity. This may refer to applications of softening agents or processes in treatment of materials such as leather or parchment to increase softness, smoothness, or plasticity.
The process of freeing a material or object from infusion of sulphur.
With reference to physical objects, having the lines intact and whole, not broken or fractured.
The quantity of matter in a body, as distinct from its weight.

Large, fretted lutelike chordophones of India, having a pear-shaped body made of a gourd or of hollowed-out wood, and a long hollow neck. They are important instruments in the Indo-Muslim style of Hindustani music.

Variously shaped inserts, as of cloth or leather, placed in a seam, as in a sleeve or glove, to strenghten or enlarge some part; also, pieces of chain mail or plate at the openings of the joints in a suit of armor.

Term applied to conical caps or bonnets with the peak bent or turned over in front. It originated in the ancient country of Phrygia in Asia Minor and is represented in ancient Greek art as the type of headdress worn by Orientals. In Rome the Phrygian cap was worn by emancipated slaves as a symbol of their freedom. During the 11th and 12th centuries, it was again extensively used. For similar caps worn in the French Revolution and identified with the cap of liberty, use "liberty caps."
Garments and accessories designed to be worn while engaged in a specific active sport.

Simple, close-fitting metal helmets of the 17th century covering the crown of the head, typically worn under a felt hat, by civilians as well as soldiers. Generally made in one piece, a variation made of riveted strips of metal is also known.
Toy versions of kitchens intended for children's play.
Small fabric inserts, worn with main dress to simulate a vest.
Sports and athletic equipment used in conjunction with water sports.

Traditional Arab robes or over-garments worn throughout the Arabian Peninsula, made of loose wool, cotton, polyester, or other material covering the body to the ankles. Typically long-sleeved and white in color, but the garment's specific style varies between regions.
Ornaments or badges made from ribbon or silky material arranged to resemble a rose and worn on clothing to signal membership in an organization, or as the symbol of an award.
Long, loose robes, with or without sleeves, worn by Greek and Roman women.
Silver, nickel, or cupronickel decimal coins, valued at 100 avos, of the Portuguese territory of Macao, in southern China.
Devices used to cut large quantities of potatoes into a shape appropriate for making french fries.
Visual works constructed from assemblages of seeds and grains.
Plastic or metal support made to strengthen flower stems in floral arrangements.

Mechanized devices, typically comprising vibration-withstanding frames, tension controls, single or double padded (nip) rollers, fabric guiders, and a dye trough, designed to facilitate the continuous textile dyeing process by infusing fabrics with chemcial dying solutions. Fabrics are passed into a chemical dyeing solution under the device's submerged roller and subsequently squeezed to remove excees solution. These devices are specifically designed to allow for even coloration of fabrics, maximum dyestuff yield, minumum rest liquor, and shade reproducibility.
A prose description of the process, manner, or style in which a thing is made, including the materials and workmanship.
Devices used to gather a representative sample of a large quantity of milk in order to subject the sample to testing.
Laboratory apparatuses of glass used to condense vapors to turn them into liquids by cooling them down. These may be single- or double-walled.

Cutting instruments designed to fit in a dental handpiece; may be made from hardened steel, stainless steel, tungsten carbide, or coated with diamond particles, may have straight or parallel surfaces.
Meetings conducted by a medium, who is person believed to be in contact with the spirits of the dead, in attempt to communicate with the deceased.
Titles or names that have been translated into a language other than the original language, or expressed in a writing system other than the original.
General term for the principal monetary unit of Denmark and of Norway.
Reckoning of days, months and years in the calendar used by adherents of the Zoroastrian faith.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1599 to 1500 (or 1600 to 1501) Before Common Era.
Hand tools fitted with a blade used to thin leather or skins, often at the edge.
Group of languages spoken by indigenous people of Argentina and Chile, in Tierra del Fuego and Patagonia.
Round buildings, especially those that are round both outside and inside and covered by domes.
In Indian architecture, a upper fillet moulding (South India).
Window openings cut in the form of a quarter-circle, commonly found in Federal and Greek revival houses.

Sites considered in the past or present as consecrated or important to a deity or a religion; sites include natural features, such as springs and caves, as well as sites upon which built works have been constructed, such as standing stones and pilgrimage churches.
Groupings of diversified religious buildings and related facilities.
Process of cutting solid materials, such as stone, into certain shapes or figures.
The process, manner, or style in which a thing is made, including the materials with which it is made and workmanship.
Hats with a wide brim turned up at the sides and projecting to front and back.
Drinking glasses intended for water; also a term applied in 18th-century England to a glass of cylindrical form to distinguish it from a tumbler, which has an incurving base.
Open-fronted storage units in the well of a desk.
Stands of various designs for supporting one or more pipes.

Boxlike nests of drawers enclosed in the front by a flap that drops down to form a writing surface. For flat-top desks on long legs, generally taking the form of a table with one long drawer in the apron, use "writing tables."
Preparation tables, usually with a cutting surface of wood or other material for cutting or chopping meat products.

Late 19th- and early 20th-century chairs intended primarily for tourists' use on boardwalks. Use "invalids' chairs" for chairs with ratchet mechanisms for raising or lowering arms, back, or footrest or with large wheels and designed especially for those who are sick or disabled.
Portable, lightweight beds or cots that can be folded for transport and carried with handles, resembling a suitcase. The beds may include attached light bedding, or may be only the bedframe.
Bulb-shaped dilatations of glass tubes used as the container of an incandescent filament or fourescent light, typically placed in a fixture or lamp that is connected to electricity.
Folding portable chairs usually with a wood frame and canvas seat and back originally used on the sets of motion pictures as seating for actors or directors.
Lamps in which the wick or wicks are enclosed in an up-curving or slanting tube attached to the side of the font.
Fastening devices that close with a click when the two parts are fitted tightly into each other.
Small, brief, concise drawings.
Departments or administrative entities, often governmental, responsible for particular activities or duties, having a head and senior officials.
Females who succeed or are designated to succeed to property or rank, either by will or law, upon the death of the former possessor.
People who make copies, especially those who copy manuscripts, music notation, other documents, or art works by hand.
Historical leaders having a high rank, especially the chief magistrates of the Dutch republic; earlier viceroys or lieutenant governors of a province or provinces in the Netherlands.
Craftsmen who shape objects by means of cutting tools while the piece of wood from which the objects are made rotates rapidly on a lathe.
People who decorate textiles or other objects by decorative arrangements of quills derived from feathers.
Tradespeople who specialized in the storage of grain for distribution.
Those whose business or trade it is to erect scaffolds.
Parts or components of land vehicle equipment.
Blades, often disposable or replaceable, used with a razor, for cutting or shaving.
Devices used to perform Kahn tests which determine the reactions for the diagnoses of syphilis.
Instruments that combine the functions of microscopes and telescopes (now rarely used).

Refers to the French artistic and literary movement founded in 1908 by Jules Roman that influenced the Abbaye, a community of young artists and writers living in Paris.  The movement is characterized by an emphasis on group consciousness and collective emotion and the need for the artist's work to reflect this experience.

Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Abdülhamid I, who ruled from 1774 to 1789. During his reign, he constructed the village of Beylerbey along the Bosphorus with a line of raised up royal apartments.
Nationality, styles, and culture of ancient Sparta, a prominent city state in ancient Greece on the banks of the Eurotas River in Laconia, in the southeastern Peloponnese.
The culture and style of a group of people of mixed ethnic heritage who speak Malayalam, in the Indian state of Karala and elsewhere.

Refers to the style of ceramics produced at sites in or near present-day Nogata and Fukuoka, Fukuoka Prefecture, from 1601 to almost the end of the Edo period (1600-1868). The style is characterized by the production of everyday utensils and tea ceremony ware. Early wares are characterized by thick-walled everyday ware with sea slug glazes or opaque white-straw or wood-ash glazes. During the Enshu period (1630-1665), productions focused on elegant, thin-walled tea ceremony ware with a characteristic toffee-brown glaze.

Style of architecture and design reaching its height in the late 1930s in the United States. In architecture, it is characterized by the use of horizontal lines, round corners, and sometimes nautical elements, such as railings and porthole windows. In design, these elements were expressed in a variety of new materials, such as Bakelite (TM) and chrome.
Architectural style of North America that uses elements of Romanesque styles of Spain and Italy.
First Nations and Native American confederation of five principal nations: the Mi'kmaq, Maliseet, Passamaquoddy, Abenaki, and Penobscot,

Refers to the culture of the Shasta Native Americans. The Shasta have historically inhabited the highlands of interior northern California, in the basins of the Upper Klamath and the Scott and Shasta rivers. The main subdivisions are the Shasta, New River Shasta, Konomihu, and Okwanuchu. The Achomawi and Atsugewi were formerly included with the Shasta but are now usually classified separately.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northern Nigeria.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northeastern Nigeria.
Compound able to reduce the surface tension of liquid to which it is added.
A crystalline phenol, obtained naturally from various types of resin or artificially; used especially in making dye, pharmaceuticals, and resin.
A solution of gum arabic and acid used in desensitizing lithographic plates and stones.
A pale, non-yellowing drying oil of good film-forming properties and excellent color retention.

General term for wood from any of several pines. In America, it refers to wood of several closely related species of North American pine with yellow tinted wood. In Great Britain, the term is used in the timber trade to refer to the wood of several additional pines as well.
Wood of the species Quercus macrolepis, native to the southern Mediterranean, Morocco, and Asia Minor, although the tree is primarily used for tannins from its acorns.

Smooth, lemon yellow colored wood of the species Calycohyllum candidissimum, native to Cuba, Mexico, Columbia, and Venezuela. It is used for structures, millwork, carving, fishing rods, archery bows, and tool handles.

Any greasy substance that is liquid at room temperature and insoluble in water. Fixed (nonvolatile) oils have the same chemical composition as fats: they consist chiefly of glycerides, resulting from a reaction between glycerol and fatty acids. Oils may be divided by function and type: mineral (e.g., paraffin), vegetable (e.g., linseed), animal (e.g., fish), essential (e.g., turpentine), or edible (e.g., olive).

Any silicate of calcium as occurs crystallized in diopside and other minerals. Hydrated calcium silicate with inorganic fiber reinforcement is commonly molded into a high temperature insulation material, a safe alternative to asbestos. Calcium silicates are also used in the manufacture of materials such as glass, porcelain, and cement, and as fillers for plastics and paper.

A rare silvery-white hard ductile metallic element of the transition series, atomic number 45; Symbol Rh. Rhodium is resistant to acids, and may occur naturally in pure form, but is normally obtained from nickel ores. It is used especially as a catalyst and in platinum alloys.

Glass made with slices of colored canes which can be used as inlays for walls and furniture, fashioned into beads and various kinds of jewelry, or arranged in molds and fused together to form vessels. Distinguished from "millefiori glass" which is glass made with slices of colored canes embedded in clear molten glass, usually creating flowerlike designs.

Naturally occurring inorganic element or compound having an orderly internal structure and characteristic chemical composition, crystal form, and physical properties; use also for synthetically derived equivalents.

Crosses having three crossbars, with the longest near the middle and the two others above successively shorter (having a conifer-tree-like silhouette). The three bars represent the papal realms of authority: the church, the world, and heaven.
Rug motif in the form of a stylized water vessel with a handle and long spout.
Grave shrines used in Ancient Greece, which may frame individual statues.

Buildings housing businesses where tea leaves are sold and where brewed tea is sometimes also served. For establishments that do not sell tea leaves, but instead contain tables and specialize in serving brewed tea, coffee, and other light refreshments, use "tea rooms."
Structures or edifices of importance or historical interest, typically erected in memory of the dead or of an important event.
Small cases of varying form and material intended primarily for holding eyeglasses. May be quite decorative and sometimes suspended from a chain so they can be worn on the person.
Large bowls or basins for washing one's hands and face, usually accompanied by a pitcher.
Protruding ledges or rings near the top of the neck of a bottle or jar.
Devices or contrivances by which, or containers in which, something is held.
Open, variously shaped containers of wood, metal or other rigid material with a flat bottom and a low rim for holding, carrying, or exhibiting articles.

A type of drinking vessel in the shape of a deep cup, usually with two horizontal handles attached to the lip and a small integral foot. In all-black or unglossed plain wares the skyphos was the most common type of cup.
Containers, usually of metal, especially silver, that are hollow, such as drinking, serving, and display vessels, and that have significant depth, as distinguished from flatware and cutlery.

Creative works, usually two-dimensional, depicting an outdoor scene dominated by the land, hills, fields, sky, trees, fields, rivers or other bodies of water, and other natural elements. Landscapes may include a near point of view in the foreground, but also usually depict a view into the distance. Landscapes may contain architecture or figures, but the primary focus remains the land. When an ocean, sea, or other large body of water dominates the picture, use "seascapes." For actual areas of land rather than depictions, use "landscapes (environments)."
Works comprising primarily raised letters or designs on a surface, typically by means of stamping or molding.
In Indian architecture, a goblin; gaṇa, bhūta; or dwarf figure.
Generally in historical usage, for people who are privately employed to perform personal or household services.
The activity or state of abiding in a particular place for any length of time.

A class of Haitian Vodou priest, who perform a role as ministers to the lwas. They are often the heads of Vodou temples, though these may also be led by their female counterparts, known as manbos or mambos.
Cigar-shaped implements often pointed at both ends, consisting of tightly rolled leather, paper, or felt; used in drawing to blend or smudge charcoal, soft pencil, pastel, chalk, or crayon.
General term for all those engaged in the production, repair, and refurbishing of furniture.

Decorative motif that resembles stylized fruits of the species Ananas comosus. Examples include finials on Rococo furniture and tableware. On book bindings they are typically placed in the lozenge compartments of a panel divided by diagonal fillets.
In Indian architecture, a broad band carved with floral scroll.
Motifs representing a symbol of a hand with the index finger extended, used to draw attention to a specific area of interest on a printed page.
Belonging to or affecting only a part of something; not universal; not applicable to all of a given class.

Wooden instruments resembling a sword, paddle, or butcher's knife, used for beating and scraping flax, hemp, cotton, or other fibrous plant material in order to separate the fibers from woody or coarse particles.The tools may be hand-held or attached to a wheel.

Smoothing and polishing tools of various designs, often made of ivory or bone, but also of smooth stone or wood. Often used in the context of archaeology, where the style of the tool could indicate the culture that used it.
Saws designed for use with wood.

Describes the fashionable world of dressmakers and dressmaking establishments collectively, including all that contributes to it culturally. For the practice and industry of dressmaking associated with these houses, use "couture."

Religious tenet of the rising of the dead, the restoration to life of a dead person. It is a standard eschatological belief in the Abrahamic religions and in a number of other ancient religions; it is at the core of Christianity, in the belief of the physical resurrection of Jesus.
Adhesive-backed slips of paper or similar thin material, usually bearing messages or designs.
Books containing accounts of such events as festivals, parades, or ceremonial entries.
Short poems or prose compositions in which text is arranged so that letters other than the first or last in each line form another word, phrase, or motto.
Use to describe objects in a state or condition of being inclined or diverted from a horizontal or vertical position.

Refers broadly to artworks in a variety of styles that incorporate some aspect of motion, including machines, mobiles, and actual objects in motion. Orginating between 1913 and 1920 with the works of Marcel Duchamp, Naum Gabo, and Vladamir Tatlin, the style reached its peak in the 1960s.
In Indian architecture, a register of vyālas.

Poles, rods, sticks, or stakes placed in a horizontal position and used for any of various purposes, typically as a prop or support. Examples include bars provided as resting places for birds, rods supporting the body of a cart, bars on which to hang clothes or other things, and bars over which pieces of cloth or leather are secured for working.
Merchandise offered in addition to or in combination with a product for the purpose of attracting purchasers.
Nationality or culture of the city of Rome and surrounding areas in modern times.

Nationality, culture, and styles associated with the eastern portion of Europe; in modern times defined by the United Nations as including Belarus, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, and Ukraine.
Cultures and styles belonging to the West Indies, a crescent-shaped group of over 1,200 islands separating the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea from the Atlantic Ocean.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Mississippi.

Refers to the Iron Age style, period, and culture named after the site at Villanova, near Bologna, Italy. It is evident in northern and central Italy and Campania in the ninth and eighth centuries BCE, continuing in northern Italy until the sixth century BCE. The culture varied in different areas and at different times, but it is generally characterized by distinctive cemeteries, armor, weapons, jewelry, and grave urns and other pottery, including double-coned and house-shaped urns, decorated with geometric designs produced by scratching and stamping. Many scholars believe that the Villanovan culture probably developed from a branch of the Urnfield cultures of eastern Europe that moved into Italy, and were eventually confronted with advancing Etruscans. Others classify Villanovan as the beginning of Etruscan civilization.
Medical procedure that examines breasts by means of x-rays; chiefly used for early detection of cancer.
The making of components, usually standardized and factory-made, that are later assembled during the construction of an object or structure.
Rooms located at the far end of the atriums in ancient Roman houses.

In architecture or other construction, refers to stiff, vertical, relatively isolated members of considerable length. Posts are typically round, square, or rectangular in cross-section and are used in building as supports for a superstructure or to provide a firm point of lateral attachment. They are characteristically relatively undecorated and made of a single timber, but may be made of stone, metal, another material, or composite materials. The term is particularly used for any main vertical support in a timber frame structure. For square uprights in classical style, and for square and rectangular masonry uprights, use "piers (supporting elements)"; for most cylindrical uprights, and for all uprights in steel and concrete frames, use "columns (architectural elements)."
The actions, functions, or event of issuing printed, taped, or otherwise reproduced records of knowledge or visual works in any medium for sale or distribution to the public.

Term used to designate the system of folk medical and magical practices originally developed by enslaved people in North America, particularly on the plantations of the old South. Hoodoo melds traditional West and Central African traditions with Native American and colonial European ethno-pharmacopeias and ritual knowledge. Its practitioners embrace natural reverence and engage in practices including herbal healing, ancestor worship, counterclockwise circle dancing (Ring Shout), water immersion, sacred music, and charm use. While united by common elements, Hoodoo is geographically distinct and best described as a body of personalized practices transmitted through apprenticeships. It has been assimilated into, but is distinct from, Voodoo practices in the Mississippi River Valley. For the African diasporic structured religion of the Mississippi River Valley, use “Voodoo.”
Identification of the sex of human or animal subjects, typically prenatal or as remains.
Continuous pedestals or bases of buildings; appropriate for such elements in Roman or Etruscan temples. For similar features found in Greek temples prefer "stylobates."

Various interactive computer games in which a player controls electronically generated images on a video display screen; usually restricted to those written after the late 1970s for microcomputers, arcade systems, or dedicated consoles.
Seeking or examining merchandise or property offered for sale, especially but not exclusively by visiting shops.
Sudden occurrences of bursting inward or interior collapse, intentional or accidental, including the collapsing of buildings as a means of demolishing them.
In Indian architecture, a door-jamb bearing vidyādharas (often with vidyādharīs or consorts in medieval Karṇāṭan temples).
Verbal or written communication from one person to another as a means of acquainting one of the people to a third person.

A genre of art-making practice involved with electronic media such as video, robotics, computer coding, and digital media in general. The term new media has been in use since the 1960s when it was applied to any non-traditional medium, initially video, which then was newly available to artists. With the rapid expansion of digital technologies, the term has come to refer to art that is by its nature electronic or digital and not merely made with with recent technological techniques.
Forms or outlines having a degree of curvature approximating that of a circle or sphere.

In art and architecture, a compositional element comprising the two- and three-dimensional areas around, above, below, beside, between, and within objects, whether the area is actual or simulated. Included is space occupied by architecture, a work of art, other object, or things depicted in a work.
The disputatious comparison of the various arts, popular in Renaissance Humanist circles.
Use with reference to endeavors to communicate with the souls of the dead or other spirits.

Refers to the way of thinking, prominent in the 1960s and 1970s in America, associated with the rejection of stable, middle-class values and conservative attitudes in regard to fashion, politics, musical tastes, education, and social values. The movement is generally characterized by radical political beliefs, sexual liberation, provocative fashion styles, and drug use. In a limited sense, the movement also catalyzed the spirit of the civil rights and environmental movements of the 1960s.

The quality of being worthy of attention; importance, or consequence. In the conservation and management of cultural heritage contexts, significance is a paradigm of preservation which focuses on the cultural meaning and integrity of what is being preserved.
The supporting of artists and buying or funding of their work.
The welfare or well-being of the general public.
The act of expressing or describing thoughts, feelings, or perceptions by the articulation of words.

Technique or painting on paper, ceramics, or another surface, where the design is created through application of a temporary protective layer of paint, wax, or another material. The surface is then coated with ink, glaze, or another material. When the work is fired or washed, heat or the action of water removes the excess coating, and protective layer has allowed the underlying colors or design to remain pristine;  uncovered areas have absorbed the color of the coating. For resist work done on textiles, use "resist dyeing."
Mountain ranges located beneath of the surface of the ocean.

Devices which do not produce sound themselves but modify the sound produced by something else, such as human breath. For equipment that transmits and reproduces sound, without necessarily modifying it, see "sound transmitting and reproducing equipment."

Stoneware manufactured from the early 17th century in Nagato Province, now Yamaguchi Prefecture. It is distinguished by having thickly formed bowls, typically for tea, flaring from foot to lip and set on a sometimes notched foot rim and covered with a semi-transperent feldspathic glaze. It was called Matsumoto ware or Fukawa ware until 1668.
Contemporary artists who specialize in works that are usually created outdoors and on a grand scale, typically incorporating features of the site itself.

Artists whose work incorporates concepts and research from mathematics, the physical sciences, biology, kinetics, telecommunications, or digital systems including computer coding. Works may be fashioned from pieces of found data or from archived and manipulated information. The final form of an information artist's work may or may not be a physical object, but one that incorporates some form of data. A genre of art that may incorporate concepts and research from mathematics, the physical sciences, biology, kinetics, telecommunications, or digital systems including computer coding. Works may be fashioned from pieces of found data or from archived and manipulated information. The final form of an information art work may or may not be a physical object, but one that incorporates some form of data.
The act of placing oneself upon an object or the ground so that the weight of the body is on the posterior. Term may modify a representation of a figure in a seated posture.
Activities that are intended to be pettily irritating, annoying, playfully taunting, or vexing to another person.

Mythical animals with a single horn, sometimes identified as a type of unicorn. In legend, the appearance of the qilin coincided with the birth or death of a great ruler or sage, such as Confucius. Representations of qilin often appear on a spirit way, lining the path to a tomb.
Tradename for Fujifilm film. There were two lines of daylight-balanced color reversal films, Provia and Velvia, which require an E6 process.

Hard, close-grained, durable wood of the species Quercus stellata, native to sandy soils of the central and southern United States. It is tough and rot-resistant, used for fence posts, rough construction, and as a fuel for barbequing meat.
Genus containing one species, and two varieties, of South American trees valued for aromatic resin and for dark brown wood and deep red heartwood.

Museums that specialize in works made from wax, often realistic duplications of actual objects or sculptural portraits of people, especially historical characters. Human figures in wax museums are often dressed in real clothing and posed as if carrying out representative activities.
Species of medium-sized pine tree native to the U.S., in poorer soils from Long Island, New York, through the Appalachian Mountains to western Tennessee and Alabama.
Various bright scarlet reds of varying degrees of value, resembling the color of the pigment vermilion, which is synthetic red mercuric sulfide.
A range of greenish yellow colors resembling zinc yellow pigment, which is derived by reacting zinc oxide with potassium dichromate solutions.
Variable green colors resembling the color of viridian pigment, which is composed of hydrated chromium oxide.

A range of purplish or bluish colors resembling the color of flower of the lavender plant, which is a Mediterranean mint widely cultivated for its narrow aromatic leaves and spikes of flowers that are dried and used in sachets.
Members of an order of insects including stick and leaf insects.
General term referring to domestic birds, including chickens, ducks, geese, turkeys, etc., which are raised for their flesh, eggs, or feathers, but usually excluding wild game birds.

Educational institutions for children, having facilities and structured program activities devoted to play, often convening only in the summer; established as an emergency measure during World War I; used both as places for children of working parents and as places for parents and teachers to study the playing habits of children.
Broad, curving, generally looplike bends in rivers or streams.
Areas where ditches enter lagoons, lakes, or bays.

Order containing four living mammal species in two families, characterized by being fully aquatic, herbivorous, inhabiting  rivers, estuaries, coastal marine waters, swamps, and marine wetlands. The order evolved during the Eocene epoch, more than 50 million years ago.

In the western Christian liturgical calendar, the first Sunday after Pentecost; in eastern Christianity, the Sunday of Pentecost. Instituted to honor the Holy Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting northern Ghana and Burkina Faso.
Style and culture of any of the ethnic groups of Lesotho, particularly the Sotho.
Film production companies that create and distribute motion pictures.
The feet of a quadrupedal animal, usually reserved for feet having a keratinized sheath covering the toes or lower part of the foot, as is typical of ungulates such as horses, cows, pigs, and goats.
Small bell-shaped covers worn over the fingertip to protect it when pushing a needle through material in sewing.

Phylum of marine invertebrates that live a sedentary life in long, protective tubes on seafloors throughout the world and often possessing a beard-like mass of feather-like tentacles at the anterior end. An intestine, which forms in embryos, disappears as development progresses; they are the only multicellular animals that have neither mouth nor anus.

Manual wool carders used in the spinning of cotton, wool, and other natural fibers. These hand-held devices are typically made of sharp wire or steel teeth adhered to layered leather and mounted on rectangular wooden frames a thin handles. To carry out the manual carding process, users hold a card in each hand with the teeth pointing towards each other. Wool or other fibers are placed between both cards, which are dragged lightly over the wool to disentangle and smooth the fibers.

A bright blue-green gel or light blue powder. Cupric hydroxide will decompose with time or heat to form black copper oxide. It is used as a source for copper salts and as a mordant in dyeing textiles. Copper hydroxide reacts with Ammonium hydroxide to form the cuprammonium that is capable of dissolving Cellulose. It is used in the manufacture of rayon. Copper hydroxide has also been reported as a component in marine corrosion crusts on copper alloys.
Any liquid, gaseous, or solid foreign body enclosed within the matrix of another material.
Straps passed across the forehead or chest and secured to a bundle to help support a load carried on a person's back.
Clip to hold the nostrils closed, usually used when swimming or otherwise in water.
Particular type of administrative territorial subdivision. Examples are in Grenada.
Political entities having a government with a single, usually hereditary, chief of state with life tenure who may exercise governmental powers varying from nominal to absolute.

Woven fabrics with ribbed or corded effects in either the warp or filling direction. Warp faced rib weave has a fine warp covering a thicker weft. In weft faced rib weave, a thin weft completely covers a thicker warp.
Generally, the action or process of digging out a hollow or hollows in the earth. Specifically, refers to the systematic digging and documentation of an archaeological site.
Creating separations in a flexible material by pulling or wrenching part from part.
Refers to the removal of water from a site to maintain a dry and stable condition during construction.
Of limited size or comparatively restricted dimensions, especially in comparison with other things of the same kind.
Properties that involve relationships between stress and strain or that involve reactions to applied forces.

Long-necked, fretless, plucked lutelike instruments of the Indian subcontinent, with a round-backed resonator and, traditionally, four metal strings, used exclusively to provide a humming drone accompaniment to vocal and instrumental melodies.
Bands encircling the crown of a hat; sometimes worn as a badge of mourning.

Small, cloth caps worn high on the head by women and sometimes young girls in the 17th and 18th centuries; early examples were made with lappets and later ones often were trimmed with ruffles or lace.

Protective headwear for tank crews, in a variety of designs since the advent of the tank as a modern war machine during WWI. Meant to protect against bumps and projectiles; more recent versions are provided with fixtures for the attachment of communication devices.
Term for clothes worn by infants that restrict movement to some extent, including either clothing consisting of narrow strips of cloth used to swaddle an infant or an infant's long clothes.
Malleable non-drying, re-usable material for children to knead and play with.
Bindings stamped with designs by means of relatively large engraved blocks or plates that require a mechanical press; popular in the 15th and 16th centuries and revived in the 19th century.
Sports and athletic equipment used in conjunction with winter sports.
Blankets that are worn loosely draped on the body.

Refers to long bands or strips of fabric wrapped around the waist or worn over the shoulder or hips and typically tied, rather than secured with fasteners. They are worn as accessories, honorary symbols, or as part of a military uniform to denote rank or affiliation.
Sets of two or more garments made to harmonize or match in color. Also, any costume designed to be worn for a special purpose or under particular conditions, such as a space suit or a snowsuit.

English bronze coins minted after 1971 and valued at 2.4 old pennies or one hundredth of an English pound. Prior to 1971, the pre-decimal penny (1d) was a coin worth 1/240 of a pound sterling, its symbol was "d," from the Roman denarius.
Any of various tools for grating, powdering or shredding food or other materials handled in a similar way, such as pressed blocks of tobacco or cosmetics.
Metal utensils for baking or roasting having one open side that is placed close to a fire.
Literary genre in which works are of a whimsical or visionary nature, having suppositions that are speculation or resting on no solid grounds.
Instruments or devices for cracking the shells of nuts.
Bowls intended primarily for serving an individual portion of soup; made with or without handles and sometimes accompanied by a saucer or cover or both.
Low, flat utensils having short legs, upon which to rest a teapot in order to protect the surface below from the heat.
Instrument for exposing visual stimuli used in the study of visual attention.

Toys in the form of a transparent globe, often made of glass or plastic, containing a liquid and particles simulating snowfall when shaken. Often contains small figures inside to create particular scenes.
Containers of varying material (often paper or plastic) used to hold gifts. Usually have handles and are large enough to obscure the gift inside.
Coin-shaped metal objects that are worn to communicate opinions about political causes, issues, or candidates for office. These may have an attached loop, hole, or pin for suspension from clothing.
Mechanized devices designed to rapidly cut scalloped, notched, or zig-zagged edges into fabric seems for decorative purposes or to prevent fraying.
A statement about the way the text is paginated, or the page range of the thing within a larger text.
Scales used to weigh milk. They often take the form of spring scales with a hook from which a bucket of milk can be hung.
Scales for measuring chemical equivalents.
Dental instruments having a sharp-edged working end, specialized for removing excess materia, contouring surfaces, and carving.

Informal and isolated displays of works of art, motion pictures, or other items; may include displays of works in a gallery. For more formal, organized, usually named, temporary public displays of works, prefer "exhibitions (events)."

In book cataloging, a uniform title is the distinctive title selected for cataloging purposes to represent a work issued under more than one title, usually in more than one expression or manifestation. For example, uniform titles are commonly used to catalog sacred texts and liturgical and musical works.
General term for any of a number of monetary in use in France between the 8th and 18th centuries.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 599 to 500 (or 600 to 501) Before Common Era.

Machines used in paring or thinning leather or skins. These involve feeding the material through rollers toward a knife edge, and were first operated mechanically via a crank, though now they are often automated.
Language family of northeastern Siberia, where traditionally the speakers are indigenous hunter-gatherers and reindeer herders.
Ridges or grooves produced in flexible materials by, for example, folding or pressure against a hard edge. For the parts of something that fold onto themselves, use "folds."

Long, sharp-pointed pieces of metal or other hard material, usually non-circular in cross-section, used for fastening things securely together. In the building and railroad industries, spikes have a head, for impact insertion. For similar fasteners, but smaller and round in cross-section, use "nails (fasteners)."
Drawings in which surfaces and planes are indicated by contrast between different tones or values, rather than by lines.
Describes defined groups of individuals within an organization.

Refers generally to those who succeed or are designated to succeed to property or rank, either by will or law, upon the death of the former possessor. Use specifically in a legal context for those who inherit from an intestate person by operation of law. The term may refer to males or females, but to distinguish only females, use "heiresses."

People or organizations who communicate with others by correspondence. For people employed by a newspaper or broadcasting company to contribute regular news reports or interpretations from a location distant from the home office, use "correspondents (reporters)."

Types of feudal lords to whom vassals paid tribute. If the vassal broke the feudal contract, the suzerain regained his fief by escheat. For the entities in modern international relations, where state has supremacy over another state which possesses its own ruler or government but cannot act as an independent power, use "suzerains (states)."
Persons who produce scrimshaws; originally whalers who carved whale teeth and baleen while aboard ship.
Persons employed in the construction of ships.
Clamps used to hold an object with radial symmetry, especially cylinders. In a lathe, it holds a rotating workpiece.
Cutting tools having thin, flat metal blades, bands, or stiff plates with cutting teeth along the edges. Used to cut wood, metal, or other materials.
Devices used to determine the oxygen consumption of animals.
