Instruments that combine the functions of telescopes and polariscopes (now rarely used).

Refers to the style of architecture that coincided with the reign of Selim III, from 1789 to 1807. His reign saw a mix of Islamic and Rococo styles with his salon at Topkapi constructed of richly gilded wood, panels of tiles, and mirrors.
The culture and nationality of ancient Troy.
Culture of an empire dating ca. 321-185 BCE, known as the first pan-Indian empire.

Refers to the work of a school of painters active in the 17th -19th centuries, as an ofshoot of the Tosa school. The school was founded by Sumiyoshi Jokei, who was appointed head of the Office of painting of the Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. The style is characterized by the continuation of the miniaturist tradition of the Tosa school, with small format albums and picture scrolls, typically showing man in nature.

Refers to the style of ceramic produced in the southwestern part of the ancient province of Tamba (present-day town of Konda, Hyogo Prefecture). Archeological data is limited but productions appear to have begun as early as the Kamakura period (1185-1333), continuing to the present. Early productions are characterized by thick, asymmetrical storage vessels produced by the coil method, with an accidental greenish glaze, resulting from falling wood ash. During the 17th century, improved technology increased speed of production and resulted in more variety and finer shapes. Wares from this period are characterized by reddish brown, black or amber glazes and simple designs. During the Edo period (1600-1868), productions included elegant tea ceremony wares.

Refers to an American variation of Art Nouveau, named after the lighting fixtures and interior designs of Louis Comfort Tiffany, which featured mosaics of opalescent glass and were based on natural forms.
Style of American architecture inspired by built works of the Spanish Renaissance.
Refers to the culture and style of the indigenous Shapra people of Peru.
Style and culture of the Algonquian-speaking, Native American people of Rhode Island, southeastern Massachusetts, and the eastern shore of Narragansett Bay.

Refers to the style and culture of the Tsnungwe, a federally-recognized tribe indigenous to parts of what is today Trinity and Humboldt counties, California; specifically, the Tsnungwe are indigenous to areas along the South Fork Trinity River, Willow Creek, Salyer, Burnt Ranch, and New River. The name of the tribe in their local language is tse:ningxwe. "tse:ning" refers to Ironside Mountain.
Style and culture of the small African highland society inhabitng the Mandara highlands in Adamawa state in Nigeria.
Fluid that is used with a solvent when cleaning or stripping oil paintings to reduce the strength and slow down the activity of the solvent.
A pale yellow drying oil obtained from soya beans. It is frequently used in paint and varnish, and sometimes mixed with linseed oil.

In the lumber trade, a general term for wood of many species of oak belonging to a subgroup of oak trees, including Q. alba and others, all characterized by having acorns that mature in six months, are sweet or slightly bitter, and have a hairless inside shell. Trees are native to Europe, Asia, north Africa, and North America.

Wood of trees belonging to the genus Cornus. Although dogwoods are primarily grown as an ornamental trees, their fine-grained wood is hard and heavy, ranging in color from yellow to pinkish-brown, and has been used for small ornamental items and utilitarian objects such as skate rollers, golf club heads, pulleys, hammer handles, and in the textile industry for shuttles and spindles.
A mineral found as efflorescence on some calcareous specimens and archaeological ceramics stored in oak museum cases. Its name alludes to its components: calcium, chlorine, and acetate.

Pure metallic element having symbol Rb and atomic number 37; soft, silvery white, and very reactive, rubidium is found as a trace constituent of various alkali minerals. It is used in photoelectric cells and as a catalyst.

Refers to a type of glass that was invented during the Gothic Revival in the 19th century and is characterized by an uneven thickness that is thicker in the center, and thinner on the edges. It is made by blowing the molten mixture into a rectangular mold, or by blowing and molding a bubble of glass into a box shape, then cutting the sides of the box to form rectangles of glass. The glass may be clear or colored.
Inert gaseous element with symbol Ne and atomic number 10; used as the medium in some electric discharge lamps.

Crosses having two crossbars of which the lower is the longer and intersects the upright above or at its center, the upper bar representing the INRI inscription traditionally placed above Christ's head.
Rug motifs that are cuff-shaped, in which each cuff appears as a triangle with a narrow link between the two hypotaneuses. In some cases, the "cuff" is surrounded by a diamond, which may be stepped.
In Indian architecture, a subsidiary shrine.
Buildings housing businesses whose primary commodities are tobacco products and smoking accessories.
Use only for buildings designed to be flexible enough to serve different purposes at different times.

Medium- or high-rise buildings having smaller depth compared to their length and usually to their height; use to distinguish from "point blocks" which are usually towerlike in form and built around a central circulation core.
In Indian architecture, a projecting upper band (South India); above kampa or paṭṭikā; fillet.
In Islamic architecture, windows projecting from an upper story and, when opening onto public spaces, enclosed by privacy screens.

Locations where, usually very destructive, weapons are exploded distant from an observation point; also, where scientific field explorations or investigations are conducted, as in archaeology or geology. For complexes where weapons are tested under close scrutiny, use "proving grounds."
Building or complex where activities having to do with any branch of science take place.
Men or women employed by restaurants, other eating and drinking houses, hotels, caterers, and similar establishments to wait upon the guests at table.
To go back or revert to a previous owner; the act or action of return.
Those whose occupation or function is to proclaim or set forth religious doctrine in public, particularly but not exclusively those who preach the Christian gospel.
People who make objects that are spherical representations of the earth or of celestial stars and constellations with its map on the surface.

Relatively small pencil-shaped instruments with a hard point, often metal or bone, used for marking, writing, or drawing. Among uses for styluses are for incising lines on a soft surface such as wax, for transferring drawings through tracing with pressure, with inked ribbon as a tracing-point in devices such as a seismograph or telegraph receiver, and as an indicator on touch-sensitive electronic devices.

Ornamental motif in the form of a stylized flower, foliage, diamond, star, or other graphic shape cast as a single unit in letterpress, used to separate paragraphs, indicate notes, etc., and which can be repeated to form a decorative border.
In Indian architecture, a jamb decorated with fantastic animals; śākhā/jamb decorated with vyālas.
In Indian art and architecture, a goblin motif or figure.
A rate, number or proportion considered in its quantitative relation to the whole; usually a quantity or amount reckoned as so many hundredth parts of another.
Iron tools consisting of a long handle terminating in a ball-like or bulblike end that is heated to melt tar or to warm liquids. Most commonly used by shipbuilders to melt pitch.
Scrapers used for finishing in woodworking.
Concept concerning efforts to preserve and protect the artistic, historical, and natural heritage of a given region.

The doctrinal concept of the deliverance of man or his soul from evil or sin by religious means, the restoration of people to their true state, and the attainment of eternal and blessed life. God's intervention is responsible for salvation in theistic religions while in Buddhism salvation comes from escaping the cycle of birth and rebirth, thereby reaching nirvana.
Flat surfaces or slabs, either portable or mounted on a wall or other structure, bearing or intended to bear inscriptions or pictures; also, thin, rigid slabs used as writing surfaces.
Documentary audio recordings, often for professional or research purposes, which are generally made outside a professional sound studio or venue.
Brief statements of a fact or experience, written down for review, or as an aid to memory, or to inform someone else; also includes short, informal letters.
Situated or passing above the level, surface, or base of measurement of something else.

Refers to the international avant-garde art and poetry movement based in Paris and begun by Romanian writer Isidore Isou in 1945. In the visual arts, the style is characterized by the use of letters, numbers, and signs as motifs, rather than elements of language.
In Indian architecture, friezes containing images of the spirits, yakṣas.
Tubular conduits, generally leakproof, for the transport of liquids or gases. For assemblies of pipes, tubes, and fittings in plumbing systems, use "piping (plumbing system components)."

Articles intended to be given as a gift or on a special occasion, usually inscribed with information regarding the giver, the recipient and/or the occasion; often articles of silver, or pottery, or coins or medals specially struck. For copies of books or other publications, including prints, similarly intended and inscribed, use "presentation copies."
Styles and cultures found on the island of Sardinia and territories within its domain, including ancient and modern cultures.
Nationality, culture, or style of Estonia, a country stretching along the south coast of the Gulf of Finland.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Missouri.
The culture and style of the Volsci, an Italic tribe documented in the first century of the Roman Republic, when they inhabited the area south of Latium.
Analytic technique by which chemical substances are identified by the sorting of gaseous ions in electric and magnetic fields according to their mass-to-charge ratio.
The process and technique of cutting architectural works or large sculptures out of living rock rather than assembling the works from processed blocks of stone or other materials.
In Maori architecture, central support pole of a meeting house; often carved.
Creating a record of data or information in some lasting form, such as writing on paper or electronic signals on magnetic tape.

General term for the belief systems of thousands of small-scale societies who have distinct languages, kinship systems, mythologies, ancestral memories, and homelands, but whose religious and spiritual beliefs fall outside the realm of world religions such as Buddhism or Christianity. Central to indigenous religious traditions is an awareness of the integral and whole relationship of symbolic and material life, often incorporating ritual practices and cosmological ideas.
The areas or compilations of changes, up to and including the complete replacement of a built work.
The clandestine transport of goods to avoid payment of duties, or transport of goods that are illegal, particularly across national, state, or district borders.
Courses of travel, having a beginning and end in space and time, and and taken as a whole. Extended to excursions, expeditions or tours.
The action or fact of the adaptation of a global culture or something such as a product, application, or document to meet the language, cultural and other requirements of a specific locale.

Art that presents a visual form with no specific reference to anything outside itself, in contrast to art that depicts subjects found in nature or elsewhere in the real world. To refer to the particular style of contemporary art displaying some of these characteristics, use "Nonobjective."

Forms or outlines consisting of a curved line that winds or meanders in multiple directions but does not cross or intersect itself. An example is when describing furniture pieces, the fronts of which are shaped in alternating concave and convex curves. For other features, such as arches or moldings, composed of flowing, wavelike curves, use "undulating." For features consisting of or bounded by curved lines in general use "curvilinear."

Refers to a philosophy of the absurd, or knowledge that eludes rational notions of causation or scientific inquiry. Coinage of the term is attributed to the writer Alfred Jarry to describe a "science of imaginary solutions." The concept, though originally speculative or fictional, has inspired publications, artworks, a literary school, and a society known as the Collège de 'pataphysique.

A philosophical movement that flourished in Greek and Roman antiquity.  Stoics have always believed that the goal of all inquiry is to provide humanity with a mode of conduct characterized by tranquility of mind and certainty of moral worth, and urged participation in the affairs of humankind. Thus, moral worth, duty, and justice are singularly Stoic emphases, together with a certain sternness of mind.
The adherence to the doctrines or practices of a tradition based on beliefs often opposed to modernism, liberalism, and radicalism.

The state or fact of the continuance of anything after the end of other like things within the same context, as after some event. The persistence of a living thing, custom, or observance, after the circumstances or conditions in which it originated or which gave significance to it have ceased.
Sum of money or its equivalent that is paid or payable, usually in return for goods or services, or in discharge of a debt.
The sending or bringing back of persons to their country of citizenship or of legal or cultural property to its country, land, or culture of origin.

The greater part of the psychic apparatus accumulated through life experience that is not ordinarily integrated or available to consciousness, considered by many psychologists to be a powerful motive force in overt behavior.

Refers to the process or branch of fine art concerned with creating sculpture, which are three-dimensional works. It refers particularly to carving or engraving a hard material, or with molding or casting a malleable material, so as to produce designs or figures in relief, in intaglio, or in the round. It is typically used to refer to the production of large or medium-sized objects in stone, clay, or bronze. The production of small objects in bronze or stone is typically referred to by a specific term, such as "stone carving" or "die sinking." The production of sculpture in wood or ivory is typically referred to as "carving," even though the finished work in these materials may be called "sculpture (visual work)."
The technique of applying a coat of opaque or semiopaque color to a painting with a nearly dry brush to make an image less defined or brilliant.
Architectural project management technique whereby construction is allowed to begin before the design and specifications are completed.
Electric devices for introducing mutual coupling between circuits, generally used to convert a power supply at one voltage to another voltage.
Men's felt hats with a round crown and a wide brim, sometimes turned up on one side; worn from the 18th century onward and adopted for military use.
A short, squat drinking glasses without a stem used for serving whiskey. Their volume capacity is around 10 ounces, but they are traditionally filled with only about 2 ounces of whiskey.
Hinged flaps in a desk which pop up to provide a slant top reading or writing surface.
Relatively small table-like or shelf-like pieces of furniture used to hold or display potted plants, or sometimes containers of cut flowers.

Flat-top desks on long legs, generally taking the form of a table with one long drawer in the apron. Use "writing desks" for similar forms having a superstructure with pigeonholes for writing materials.

Side or serving tables arranged with compartments or drawers for bottles and decanters, and a flat work space for mixing drinks. It may be marble-topped and have a roll top that descends to cover the marble slab when not in use.
Revolving chairs, usually with a spring back, made for office use.
Low bedsteads specifically designed so that they can be moved under another bed when not in use.
Lighting device components that obscure or diffuse the source of light in a lamp.
Armchairs with an upholstered frame and projecting wings for protection against drafts.

Lamps produced by Tiffany Studios beginning in 1895 having shades made of various types of stained glass, sometimes set in intricate leaded patterns. Other lamps have shades resembling flowers made of iridescent glass. Lamps produced by Tiffany Studios beginning in 1895 having shades made of various types of stained glass, sometimes set in intricate leaded patterns. Other lamps have shades resembling flowers made of iridescent glass.

Blue-and-white Japanese porcelain manufactured at the Mikawachi kilns for the Prince of Hirado. Productions are usually small and of fine quality with the finest pieces made between 1751 and 1830. Only low-grade pieces made after 1843 are marked.
Artists who produce landscape images, which are outdoor scenes in which the primary subject is the land, bodies of water, or other natural elements.
Slight bounds or springs performed in succession.
To draw or drag a something, often a vehicle, by another conveyance under power by a connecting member or hitch.
In Indian architecture, a lion-monster; a tiger-vyāla.

A proprietary name for a breathable waterproof material used chiefly for outdoor clothing. It is the a Teflon (TM)-based membrane filled with many minute pores which make it breathable yet waterproof and vapor proof. Its most common use is as a laminate between layers of cloth in all-weather clothing and footwear.

Genus containing around 25 species of medium- to large-sized trees native to tropical regions of Central and South America. Valued for hard wood that becomes dark purplish brown upon exposure to UV light.

Species of medium sized evergreen oak native to southwest Europe and northwest Africa, cultivated in Spain, Portugal, France, Italy, Morocco, Tunisia, and Algeria. The tree has a thick, insulating bark that helps it to recover quickly after forest fire; branches, having been protected from the fire by cork, quickly resprout and recompose the tree canopy, while other trees regrow from shoots or seeds. The lightweight, buoyant outer bark of the cork oak is used for stopping bottles, flooring, and many other purposes commercially. No trees are cut down during the harvesting process: the outer bark is stripped about every 10 years, and a new layer of cork grows.
General term referring to any of various coniferous trees from which pitch or turpentine can be obtained and which yield very resinous wood.

Corporation or other corporate body engaged in securing, managing, and maintaining mass transportation of passengers, generally limited to buses, trains, and other ground or underground transportation methods in an urban area.
A range of purplish blue colors resembling the color of the aromatic blooms of the lilac plant, a European shrub that is also cultivated in North America.

Members of an order of containing at least 1,700 recorded living species of insects, named because larvae are found under stones in streams. All species are intolerant of water pollution, thus their presence in a stream or still water is considered an indicator of good water quality.

Order containing 368 species in two families, 10 species have been extinct since 1600.  Characteraized as often brightly colored, strong-flying, seed-, fruit-, or nectar-eating birds with very stout, hooked bills and feet with the outer toe facing rearward.
Educational institutions for training individuals to become policemen, usually in accordance with state requirements.
A navigable narrow part of a bay, strait, or river.
Lines of high ground that separate adjacent drainage basins.

Order containing around 370 species in three families of shrews, moles, and kin. Moles (family Talpidae) are sometimes classified with hedgehogs in Erinaceomorpha. It is now often classified as a biological clade within the class of mammals, because members apparently are paraphyletic (i.e., a taxonomic group which does not include all the descendants of an ancestral taxon).
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Togo.
Style and culture of the nation of Liberia, a West African state founded in 1822.

Business enterprises, including private companies and those owned by nations or international organizations, that gather, write, and supply news reports and photographs fom around the world or a nation to newspapers, magazines, radio and television broadcasters, government agencies and other users who subscribe to their services.

The non-deciduous excrescences, often curved and pointed, consisting of an epidermal sheath growing about a bony core on the head of certain mammals such as cattle, sheep, goats, and antelopes, or formed from matted hair on the rhinoceros. Horns serve as displays and as weapons of offence or defense.
Cards on which thread or yarn is wound for sale and for use, usually made from cardboard and decorated with advertising.

Phylum of primitive multicellular aquatic animals. There are approximately 5,000 described species and inhabit all seas, where they occur attached to surfaces from the intertidal zone to depths of 29,000 feet or more. Early naturalists regarded the sponges as plants because of their frequent branching form and their lack of obvious movement. The animal nature of sponges was first described in 1755, and was confirmed in 1765 after observations revealed movement of their openings. In structure, function, and development, however, sponges are distinct from other animals. Many zoologists regard sponges as occupying an isolated position in the animal kingdom and classify them in the subkingdom Parazoa. Other sources consider sponges relatives of the invertebrate animal group coelenterates. Aquatic, chiefly marine animals of the phylum Porifera, varying greatly in size, shape, and color, and having a porous body and siliceous or calcareous internal framework, living permanently attached singly or in groups, feeding b filtering food particles from the water that enters their internal body channels through their pores. They are very simply organized with no mouth, digestive cavity, nerves, muscle, or true behavior, and sometimes are considered to be colonized protozoans rather than single multicellular organisms. For the light, porous, yielding fibrous skeletal matter of these animals, use "sponge (material)."

Long iron hooks, often used in pairs, designed to secure cloth to a cropping board or padded bench in order for the cloth's nap to be sheared. Used in the finishing process of fulled cloth, these hooks are comprised of sharp barbs that attach to cloth and hold it taut over a board or bench, stabilizing the cloth for subsequent fabrication activities. Often, these hooks are secured with a central block on their lengh, which acts as a grip to facilitate manual attachment or removal. Though its name has changed over the centuries, a version of this tool has been utilized in the textile production process since the medieval period.
A yellow-orange compound of copper and vanadate. Used as a pigment; and a member of the vanadium group of natural and synthesized pigments.

Areas where lacunae, gaps, cracks, pores, holes, or other losses or differences in grade have been filled or leveled with a filling material, such as in paintings, mosaics, frames, sculpture, architectural elements, landscape surfaces, and other objects of many kinds.
Portable, usually waterproof canopies consisting of a frame with hinged ribs radiating from a center pole with handle, carried for protection against the weather.
Devices used for splitting solid pills or tablets in half when only half a dose is required.
Particular districts that include limited local areas, as opposed to bigger areas. The term is often used in a generic sense.
Political entities in which a small group of people rule, usually a a few people or families. In later usage, frequently restricted to rule by the wealthy elite.

Woven textile characterized by a basic binding system or weave with smooth, shiny surface formed by long warp floats. Generally, each warp end passes over four or more adjacent weft picks and under the next one.
The act of digging up or otherwise removing a body from a grave, disinterment.

The process of separating, shredding, pulling asunder, carding, or back-combing fibers or hairs in order to draw fibers or hairs in a given direction for the purpose of separating, forming a nap, or increasing volume. Examples of use of the term include in fiber processing, weaving textiles, and in hairdressing.
The physical and chemical changes occurring in sediments between the times of deposition and solidification.

Formats of paintings, prints, photographs, sculptures, or other works or other things that fall within a small range of size for the norm. For example, the term is used to describe photographic film formats 35mm and smaller.

The quantity of water in a given substance; its weight as a percentage of the total dry weight of the material (as measured on the dry basis) or percentage of the weight per unit mass of the wet material (the wet basis).

Long-necked plucked lutelike chordophones of Iran and the Caucasus with a deeply curved, figure-eight shaped soundbox with a belly of animal membrane, movable frets, and six strings in three courses of two; Caucasian models may have sympathetic strings as well.
Small, indoor caps with a single or double frill as a border to the front only, ending at the ears; worn by women in the 18th century.
Ribbons decorating hats, as hat bands, bows, or in other decorative arrangements.
Clothing designed for playing tennis.
Constructed units, often temporary or demountable, designed for children to play in or on.
Bindings in which the spine is of a material different from that of the sides of the book cover and the spine material extends up to one-eighth of the width of the boards.
Pieces of cloth made in varying widths and lengths and worn for decoration or warmth across the shoulders, around the neck, over the head, or about the waist.
General term for coins with a penny denomination.
Punches, resembling cookie-cutters, designed specifically to cut round wafers for hosts from a larger piece of wafer material; the hosts are used in Christian eucharistic liturgies.
Cooking appliances fitted with a spit on which food is rotated before or over a source of heat.
Traditional stories or legends in a given culture that are passed down over time, often orally.
Smooth, flat boards of wood, stone, or plastic on which dough is rolled or kneaded.
Bowls supported by a stem and foot; used especially with reference to those used for serving fruit or sweetmeats.
Racks with vertical partitions for holding and serving several (usually four to eight) slices of toast on edge.
A receptacle, often rectangular or cylindrical, for storing large quantities of liquid foods.
Packs strapped to the waist and used to carry personal items.
Tubular devices inserted into a vessel that permit the outflow of the liquid contents, usually with a spigot to control the rate of the flow.
Containers used in the context of gardening and the cultivation of gardens.

Long, narrow, open receptacles, usually boxlike in shape. The term is used chiefly in the context of holding water or food for animals, but may be extended to any large tank or vat of similar shape used for other purposes.

Tall glasses, usually conical, footed beakers of clear glass, intended for serving milkshakes or sodas in ice-cream shops or soda fountains, and in many restaurants. These are common in the United States.

Vessels or other receptacles, usually two in number, used for storing the sacred oils used for baptism and ordinations, and for the annointing of the sick. Typically placed with a third vessel, for the holy chrism, which is a mixture of oil and balsam. Set of three containers for the holy oils in a case or box used for the anointment Sometimes provided with three matching spoons.
Visual works in Hindu art and architecture, representing Shiva's phallic pillar. These objects are generally three-dimensional, in the shape of a phallus and worshipped as a symbol of the god Shiva.

Visual works in the medium of enamel, which is a semi-transparent or opaque vitreous, porcelain-like coating; enamels are typically set into a metalwork support. Often reserved for works that depict figures or scenes. For vessels and other objects that are coated with protective enamel but are generally not considered art works, use "enamelware."
In Indian architecture, an attendant, door-guardian figure.
Embroidered textiles depicting narrative scenes. Examples include cloths woven by Hmong women depicting war and refugee scenes.
Ribbons, made of fabric, paper, or plastic, used to decorate gifts and gift containers. Tied in knots with two loops and two ends.
Objects that are worn to communicate opinions about political causes, issues, or candidates for office.

Mechanized devices, comprising a series rollers and gears/ blades, designed to produce uniform and precise folds in fabric. Once fed into the device, the fabric is first folded and pressed in a controlled manner using pressure from the gears or blades. The resulting pleats are then typically fixed in place by heat exposure as the fabric passes through a set of rollers.
A description of the political, social, economic, or religious events or circumstances associated with the work over time.
Devices used to stir fresh milk in order to quickly cool the "animal heat" (residual heat from the body of the cow from which the milk was obtained).

Instruments that contain a combination of colored glasses that transmit only red light, used for viewing colored flame to detect the presence of potassium or other substances, by the red light that they emit.
Cases designed to organize and carry dental instruments.
Titles applied to a volumes, which are objects comprising sheets of paper, vellum, papyrus, or another material that are bound together.
General term for units of currency based on gold coins of France issued in the reign of Louis XIII and subsequently till the time of Louis XVI.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 5999 to 5000 (or 6000 to 5001) Before Common Era.
Leatherworking hand tools used for burnishing or scraping the surface of skins.
Family of languages that were spoken on the southern California coast and islands; languages are virtually extinct, but well documented.
Physical injury to a thing, such as impairs its value or usefulness.
Prominent elevations, typically pointed, located beneath the surface of the ocean.

Devices comprised of one or two pendant bobs suspended from a steel piller that strike a block affixed to the base. A graduated arc emerges from block that marks the arc of the pendulum. This measures the instensity of sound in relation to speed and distance of the pedulum strike.
Extensions attached to a compass to extend the length of one of the legs; used to increase the radius of an inscribed arc or circle.
Cutting tools consisting of two bevel-edged cutting blades and handles, and being movable past one another on a pivot in the center by which they are held together.
Instruments for detecting and measuring odors.
Instruments that combine the functions of telescopes and spectroscopes (now rarely used).
Refers to the style of art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Mustafa IV. He reigned briefly from 1807 to 1808.

Refers to the style of ceramics produced from the early half of the 12th century to the first half of the 16th century, with some production continuing to the present. The style is characterized by strong, heavy wares, such as wide-mouth jars, bowls, and vases of dark reddish brown with a dark olive, natural ash glaze.
Culture or style of an ancient Indian people of pre-Aryan origin, now living scattered in central India and in a region extending from east central India towards Bangladesh.

Refers to the works of a school of Buddhist painters active from the mid-12th century to the late 14th century. The style is characterized by the use of bold brushstrokes inspired by Chinese works of the Song Dynasty (960-1270).

A style reminiscent of the cultures of the islands of the South Pacific. Evident after World War II, its popularity is often attributed to returning U.S. soldiers who were exposed to authentic Oceanic culture during wartime service. The term is variously used to describe architecture, interior design, sculpture, and industrial design. The style peaked in the 1950s, but became resurgent as a fad in the early 21st century. For the small greenstone carvings of the Maori culture, use 'hei-tiki'. For authentic free-standing Oceanic sculpture of deities, use 'ki'i.'

Refers to the theory coined by Vincent J. Scully in 1949 to address the style of mid-19th century American timber-framed domestic architecture and to correlate the desire to express structure with an externally conspicuous and organic wooden frame. The style reflects European traditions based on half-timbered Late Gothic domestic architecture of England, France, and Germany, on Swiss chalet styles, and on Scandinavian and Slavic vernacular building designs.

Refers to the style and culture of the Sinixt, an indigenous First Nations people in eastern Washington state and British Columbia. The Sinixt primarily live on the Colville Indian Reservation and are part of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation. However, the Sinixt state that they were driven to the Colville Reservation from their indigenous lands in British Columbia. In 2017, the government of Canada officially recognized the tribe.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in western Uganda.
Refers to works produced by the African ethnic group of the same name, inhabiting Nigeria.
Describes works produced by the African people of the same name living in northeastern Nigeria.
Material applied as outer layer of a surface for protection or decoration, in architecture and other contexts.

Vegetable oil obtained from a tree cultivated in China valued for its drying properties and is probably the traditional material used by Chinese artist to grind vermillion. It was formerly used as an adulterant in Chinese tung oil.

A sticky, black residue obtained from the distillation of coal tar, petroleum, or pine tar. Pitch is used as a sealant and wood preservative as well as a component in roofing, paving, and water proofing.

A heavy, metallic, hard tin dioxide, chemical formula SnO2, that is the major ore of tin. It is colorless when pure, but brown or black when iron impurities are present. Commercially important quantities occur in placer deposits, but cassiterite also occurs in granite and pegmatites.

Rare-earth metallic element having symbol Sc and atomic number 21. Scandium is a soft, silvery-white metal which does not tarnish in air. It was discovered in 1879 but predicted a decade earlier and given its initial name, ekaboron.
Term used in the glass trade for a glass made to resemble onyx either by the addition of metal and metallic oxide that impart a silver luster upon heating, or by mixing glass of contrasting colors.
Crosses in the form of the letter X, used as a heraldic symbol in the form of a diagonal cross or letter X and as a symbol for Saint Andrew, who is said to have been martyred on such a cross.
Small ancient Roman shrines, usually built as enclosures open to the sky.
Buildings constructed or used primarily for offices, which are spaces where business, administrative, or professional activities are conducted.

Denotes semi-underground buildings forming self-contained structures without a built floor, common to England and northern Europe throughout the first millennium CE and used variously for such functions as houses, storehouses, and workshops; use "pit dwellings" for prehistoric houses whose floors are generally deeply set below ground level.
Several windows set directly adjacent, without intervening wall space, so as to form a horizontal band of fenestration; found in buildings of Modernist style.
Places where residential garbage and commercial wastes are collected, compacted, or baled for transport to a processing facility or landfill; may be fixed or mobile.

Pieces of land or other physical positions on which something is located, particularly where human habitation or activities have taken place. Examples include sites that have archaeological or other historical context.
People who make or sell gloves.
Motif in the form of a stylized rose with petals radiating from the center, or for similar circular ornaments having a design radiating from the center.
In Indian art and architecture, a tortoise motif.

The position from which something, such as the subject depicted in a visual work, is seen or viewed, or the perspective from which a subject or event is perceived. An example is when the subject of a visual work is seen as a bird's eye view.
Frames used for the manufacture, processing, or embellishment of textiles.

Wood planks, with an integral handle, most often with detailed decorative carving on one side, used to press and smooth linen. Examples date from the 16th century, and are common to northern European countries such as Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Holland.
Quality or condition of being impure or of containing something foul or unclean.
The doctrinal concept of divine manifestation, especially the appearance of a god to a human.
Sheets torn from a publication, usually to send as proof of insertion to an advertiser whose advertisement appears on it.
Descriptive catalogs or classifications of the plants of any geographical area, geological period, etc., whether in book form, an online site, or other medium.
Portions of documents or other written works, either included as discrete sections in an extant document or detached from the original document.
For positional attributes of three-dimensional works or the illusionistic space of a composition, referring to the viewer's upper left-hand side of the work or composition.

Refers to a form of minimalism credited to Southern California artists of the 1960s and 1970s characterized by a preoccupation with light, transparency, reflectivity, and color. These artists used glass, resin and cast acrylic, often forming site-specific installations.
Ornamental bands decorated with human figures or animals.
Communites of any size that have shipbuilding as a major industry.
Flat, thin, usually small objects, made of metal, clay, ivory, glass, or basketry, sometimes set into a surface for decoration or to bear an inscription.
Things or substances that are generated or produced, by human activity or by natural processes.

Nationality, culture, and style of the inhabitants of the island of Sicily, the largest in the Mediterranean, separated from the SW tip of Italy by the narrow Strait of Messina. Strategically positioned between Africa and Europe, Sicily has long been a center of trade routes between East and West and a crossroads for races, peoples and cultures.
Nationality, culture, or style of the Faröe Islands, an autonomous dependency of the kingdom of Denmark situated between Great Britain and Iceland.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Montana.
Process where the owner or inhabitant has directly organised the design and construction of their own home or other building.

Generally, the action or process of determining or calculating a length, quantity, value, magnitude, extent, or other designation of dimensions, size, weight, number, or volume of an object or group of objects, person, animal, plant, plot of land, or other thing, typically by the application of an instrument or device marked in standard units.
Pieces of lumber used as temporary supports, as when in an oblique position to hold a wall under pressure or as a component of formwork.

Making a legal or official record or list of people or objects. Specifically, in museology, creating a written record for an object in a collection in order to identify the object and to record information about it such as provenance, condition, or value.

Systems of diverse beliefs and practices of the culturally and linguistically related group of ancient peoples who inhabited the Iranian plateau and its borderlands, as well as areas of Central Asia from the Black Sea to Khotan (modern Hotan, China). In religion and culture, both the northern and southern Iranians had much in common with the ancient Indo-Aryan-speaking peoples of the Indian subcontinent, although there was much borrowing from Mesopotamia as well.
Refers to the act of assigning and enhancing value. In a heritage management context, valorization is used in the sense of highlighting and promoting aspects of cultural patrimony.

The function of watching or guarding people, activities, or situations, usually having a connotation of spying on a suspected person or a prisoner, or observing in order to provide supervision for direction or control.
The areas or compilations of changes made to renew and improve a built work.
Periods of restricted movement, physical interaction and access into common and/or public spaces enforced by an authority to contain emergencies for public safety and health.

The political, economic, and social principles advocated by Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels, and their followers; it includes the labor theory of value, dialectical materialism, economic determination of human actions, and class struggle as a fundamental force in history.

Refers to art created or collected according to a philosophy of avoidance of the conventional fine art tradition. The concept generally refers to art that fits the ideal described by Jean Dubuffet, who posited that art should be inventive, non-conformist, unprocessed, spontaneous, insulated from all social and cultural influences, "brut," created without thought of financial gain or public recognition, and based upon autonomous inspiration, in direct contrast to the stereotypes of the traditional or official artistic culture. Dubuffet sought such art in the work of psychiatric patients and other insulated individuals. It is generally distinct from "naive art," which is created by those without formal training, but not necessarily in accordance with the principles described above. It is also typically distinct from "folk art," which is made according to the rules and traditions of a particular culture.
Parallel relationships to a vertical axis in designs for graphic works, objects, and structures.

The length of time during which something runs its course, characterized by some prevalent or distinguishing condition, circumstance, or occurrence, or by the rule of a particular government or dynasty; a distinct historical or cultural portion or division of time.
Reconciliation or union of conflicting (as religious) beliefs or an effort intending such.
A property of beliefs, propositions, and linguistic statements, being that they conform with fact or agree with reality.
The amount of money or a material equivalent expected, required, or given in payment for a commodity or service.
Any people or corporate bodies, occasionally also animals or inanimate things, that cause, own, oversee, or are otherwise responsible for a thing, person, animal, condition, status, or action.
The craft or business of building ships.
A method of painting which produces soft stains or blots of color through the use of heavily diluted paint on unsized canvas.

The process of extending something flexible, such as a cord or piece of fabric, from one point to another, across a space, or over a form, for the purpose of drawing it taut or rigid or for making it larger.
Semiconductor devices used to amplify, control, or modify electrical current. Transistors perform the same function as a vacuum tube while requiring less power and producing less heat.
Hats, usually felt, but also of straw or cloth, with a brim designed to be arranged at various angles; popular especially during the second quarter of the 20th century.

In a general sense, refers to all drinking glasses intended for wine, made in various shapes (usually stemmed), sizes, and styles; each is said to be most suitable for a particular type of wine. In a specific sense, the term refers only to glasses intended for use at table for wine to accompany the meal, and excluding champagne glasses and other specialty glasses. In this sense, in a matching set of stemware, the wine glass is smaller than a goblet for water, but larger than glasses for sherry, port wine, or liqueur. In such a set, there may be separate glasses of distinctive form for white and for red wine. For similar but smaller drinking glasses used for serving other beverages, use "gin glasses" or another specific term.
Stands for holding large prints; generally having a front which falls down and often having a lock.
Small tables made to stand beside a bed; includes those having a cupboard to hold a chamber pot and those with a close stool that pulls forward in the lower part.

Chairs having a rather low seat and a padded top rail, designed to allow male spectators of card games to astride while resting their arms or elbows on the top rail. The term is derived from the French verb "voir," "to see." First made in France about 1740 and later in England. For a lower-seated variant of this chair designed for women, use "voyeuse á genoux."
Beds having a liquid-filled rubber or plastic mattress in a rigid, often heated, waterproof frame and providing a surface that conforms to the sleeper's body in any position.
Modernist easy chair design created by Arne Jacobsen in 1958 for the SAS Royal Hotel in Copenhagen.

Hollow cavities, parts, or pieces, usually long and narrow and of cylindrical or shaft form, constructed to receive an element and hold it in place; examples include sockets for candles or light bulbs.
Floor lamps having its source of lighting in a reflecting bowl that directs the light upward.
Double-pointed, U-shaped pieces of metal used to attach separate articles together.
Images made by tracing, which is copying from an original by drawing over it onto a transparent or translucent piece of paper, cloth, or other material.
Those who choose to live in seclusion and solitude. Examples are those who do so for religious motives.
People who commit acts that are forbidden by, or who omit duties that are required by, public law and that make the offender liable to punishment by that law.
Nahua elites or lords.

People whose employment is staining, particularly those who color wood or other building or furniture materials with pigments that penetrate below the surface. Stainers belonged to special guilds in Europe from the Middle Ages onward. For those who apply pigment to cloth, use "dyers."

People active in public distribution or sale of property as the official recorders of the transaction and prices paid. In certain cases, this person may have worked with the "commissaires-priseurs," or may have been in charge of recording as well as valuing the works for sale, adjudicating, and bringing down the hammer for the sale.
Workers who build or install shores, which are pieces of lumber used as temporary supports.

Refers to painters; usage is generally limited to painters of miniatures or of portraits. Usage is slightly different depending upon the period of art cited. For art of the European Middle Ages, the term refers to manuscript illuminators, who were creating miniature paintings and other decoration. For art from the 16th to the 19th century, the term typically refers to painters of miniatures, particularly miniature portraits. In Colonial and 19th-century America, it generally refers to itinerant painters who were trained craftsmen and naive portrait painters, producing both miniatures and full-size portraits.
Describes the state, condition, or appearance of being asleep, the natural physiological period of rest.
Fictitious woodland creatures, partly human and partly bestial, often having the body of a lion, the tail and horns of an antelope, and the face of an old man.

A cushioning system of cored-out hexagonal recesses developed by Reebok for use in shoes. Its honeycomb structure is made of rubbery thermoplastic urethane. Hexalite has been adapted for use as a support for wallpapers and textiles in museum display.

Genus containing around 45 species of spiny, deep rooted trees and shrubs found in subtropical and tropical regions of the Americas, Africa, Western Asia, and South Asia. They form extensive thickets in areas from South America into the southwestern United States. Two races occur, one low (called running mesquite) and the other often growing into trees 15 m (50 feet) tall.

Species of medium-sized, fast-growing oak tree distributed on rocky hillsides and sandy ridges throughout the eastern and Midwestern United States, having a black or dark brown bark. While the tree is occasionally used for lumber, its most important commercial product is a yellow dye obtained from the bark.
General term referring to many species of trees, usually pines or other conifers having reddish bark or wood.
Institutions or departments in institutions that exclusively or primarily store, maintain, care for, and make available images in various formats, including slides, photographs, and digital images.
A range of blackish blue to blackish red colors resembling the color of logwood colorant, a dye made from an American tree.
Members of an order containing around 150 species of tiny, pale, wingless, blind, primitive insects that live in damp humus and soil and feed on decaying organic matter.
Order containing 16 species in one family of stocky, pigeon-like ground birds with short legs, fast flight, and feeding upon seeds and insects in the deserts of Africa and Asia.
Private schools intended to prepare students for more advanced formal education.
Large areas of thin sheets of floating ice driven together by wind or currents to form a mass covering the entire sea surface with little or no open water.
Open expanses of elevated land, most often used in the plural. Examples are the treeless undulating chalk uplands of the southern England.

With the platypus, Tachyglossa are the only egg-laying mammals. The female lays a single soft-shelled, leathery egg, deposits it directly into her pouch, where there are no nipples, but after hatching the young echidna sucks milk from the pores of the two milk patches.
Style and culture of inhabitants of the large ancient country, Libya, in North Africa, or of the modern state of Libya.
Associations of persons carrying on commercial enterprises focused on the discovery, development, and manufacture of pharmaceuticals, which are medicinal drugs.

In vertebrates, the lower part of the alimentary canal extending from the pylorus to the anus. In biology, may also refer to the whole alimentary canal from the mouth downward, especially in invertebrate animals. The intestines are the site of most chemical digestive processes and the place where digested food materials are either absorbed for use by the body or collected into feces for elimination.
Phylum of 15 species of predatory, marine, mud-inhabiting, unsegmented worms. They are sometimes classified as a class.

Small cards, often rectangular in shape and made of wood, into which a series of holes are punched corresponding to a row of textile pattern. These cards are designed to control the operation of Jacquard looms by dictating the movement of the loom's needle in accordance with the predesigned pattern. Laced together by rope into long rows, the cards are fed onto the Jacquard loom's perforated, cylindrical feeder, which moves them towards the needle board until they come in contact with the needle. Joseph Marie Jacquard is credited with inventing these cards, and the Jacquard looms they control, in 1801. These cards not only increased the efficiency of the weaving process, but are also considered to have laid the foundation for modern computer programming technology.
Compounds that provide a chemical bond between two dissimilar materials, usually an inorganic and an organic material.
Frameworks used to assist mobility for the disabled or infirm, or designed to support babies learning to walk.
Regions administered by local government agencies rather than larger entities. The term is often used in a generic sense.
Hand-held sticks designed for digging in the earth, to expose roots or tubers, and for planting.
Administrative bodies subject to a lord superior or a supreme lord, such as a feudal superior.
Strong closely woven textile, traditionally woven in a striped cotton or linen twill, used for mattress and pillow covers, upholstery foundations, and, in lighter weights, for clothing.
Ottoman compound-weave fabric woven with silver and gold metallic threads.
Signifies the act of drawing forth a material from that which holds it.
Vertical displacement between layers resulting in converging sides that resemble a tent.
Processes in which particles are selectively removed from a liquid by means of their unequal diffusion through membranes.
Printing format, used especially for newspapers, in which pages are half the size of those of the average broadsheet.
Refers to the physical form of a thing or a material, often regarding shapes and arrangements of parts.

Long-necked lutelike chordophones having two pegboxes, one for the strings running along the fingerboard which were stopped by the fingers while played, and another positioned above and to the side of the first, for the long off-board strings which are not stopped when plucked.
Military-style caps with a tall rigid crown and a visor, typically worn by soldiers and members of marching bands.
Small, metal plates attached to the heel of a shoe to protect it from  wear.
Identifying garments or styles of dress worn by the members of a given profession, organization, or rank.
Miniature race tracks on which toy cars or other toy vehicles can drive.
Bindings in which the spine and approximately one third the width of the boards are covered, usually in leather or cloth, with disproportionately large corners of the same material.
Pouch bags used as purses, worn hanging from a belt at center front; used especially with reference to those worn in Scottish Highland costume.

Simple slip-on garments made with or without sleeves and usually knee-length or longer and belted at the waist; especially those worn by men and women of ancient Greece and Rome. Also, garments extending from the neckline to the waist or longer, usually high-necked and worn over other garments.

A number of different coins minted by countries formerly ruled by Spain; for trade coins of dollar size valued at eight reales and issued by Spain and Spanish America between about 1500 and 1900, use "Pieces of Eight."
Sharp-pointed tools for chipping or cutting ice.

Pointed rods for thrusting through and holding meat and other foods while cooking before or over a source of heat; sometimes made as a component part of rotisseries and other cooking and heating devices. Use "skewers" for long pinlike utensils used to hold small pieces of food while cooking or dipping.
Prose tales of the supernatural in which the living encounter manifestations of the spirits of the dead.
Chambers used for preserving food by exposing it to smoke.
Bowls of varying form but usually lidded, intended primarily for holding and serving sugar; made as an individual piece, to match a creamer, or as part of a tea or coffee service.
Small, open containers of varying form used to hold or dispense toothpicks.
Receptacles that are typically wider than high, for storing food.
Bags for garments on hangers while in storage or when traveling. Made of cloth, paper, or plastic, often with a zipper down the front and a closed bottom.

Refers to threads of glass that are applied as a decoration, generally on the body, foot, or handle of a vessel. The threads may be laid down in straight rows or in a pattern or chain. Trailings were first seen in ancient Roman glass, and were also popular in medieval and later glass.  They are distinct from "threadings," which are independent designs that are often partially free-standing.
Containers used for the maintenance of a household.
Wide, low containers originally made of wooden staves held together by hoops and sometimes having a lid or wire handles or both. Also, similar containers made of metal or plastic.
Vessels, often made of silver and similar in form to tankards, having one or two handles and a spout and usually a lid with a finial. Used for feeding invalids and babies.

Ancient Greek or Roman vessels for water with three handles: two horizontal side handles for lifting and one vertical back handle for holding and pouring. Many hydriae were also made in bronze in addition to terracotta and, unlike the metal versions of other shapes, a good number survive.

Works of a specific iconographic type, depicting the Virgin Mary and Christ Child enthroned in the center with saints and angels in adoration to each side. The type developed in Italy in the 13th century and was based on earlier Greek types. Works of this type are typically two-dimensional, including painted panels (often altarpieces), manuscript illuminations which imitate panels, and occasionally low-relief carvings that also imitate the panels.

Vessels, plates, and other typically utilitarian visual works that are coated or painted with enamel, which is a vitreous protective coating. For works that are set into a metalwork support and depict figures, scenes, or are otherwise primarily decorative rather than utilitarian, generally use "enamels."
In Indian architecture, a female door-guardian figure.
People who set up machinery, equipment, or other items in preparation for a job or task.

General term for representations of nude, chubby toddlers, typically male and often with wings, derived from personifications of Eros in Greek and Roman art and Cherubim of Christian tradition. They most frequently appear in both mythological and religious art of the Renaissance, Baroque, and Victorian periods.
Small, carved items or designs usually made from a single block of wood.
Containers made and used to hold gifts. Sometimes decorated with ribbons, bows, or other elements.
Toys made of plastic or other materials that are designed to be inflated with air.

Mechanized devices, comprising a series of rotating stranders and a take-up package mounted on a rotating frame, designed to produce three- or four-strand ropes out of synthetic, natural, and other types of fibers. To produce the rope, fiber strands are fed into the device's rotating stranders which are then fed into the take-up package which carries out a two-for-one twisting action.

Refers to text-based description of images. These texts offer the equivalent information that a sighted reader would get when looking at a picture, but intended as an accessibility aid for those who are blind or visually impaired. Image descriptions may be in an image caption, in a text post, or shared in a text link for extended descriptions.
Devices used to achieve duration and very controlled temperatures for heating of materials, or for other purposes for analysis in a laboratory context.
Machines or devices for mixing casting materials for dental casts.
Titles used temporarily while a more permanent title is devised.  An example is the title provided by an author at the time a manuscript is submitted to the publisher.
The standard unit of currency of Mexico.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 999 to 900 (or 1000 to 901) Before Common Era.
Tools for roughening the surface of leather or other materials, such as the soles of shoes before they are cemented. Farriers and woodworkers may use this tool for varied tasks.

Language family of the indigenous people of south Texas and adjacent Mexico; it is uncertain how closely or if these languages were all actually related, because documentation is scarce. However, the term is still used as a term of convenience for the languages of this region.
The state of an artifact, structure, or atmosphere when it contains moisture, usually meaning more than a desirable amount of moisture.
High, narrow, tower-like formations of rock or coral, located beneath the surface of the ocean.

Devices constructed for the study of the localization of sound. These consist of a spherical cage constructed of circular wire components that divide it into eight equal parts. This is suspended by two lateral poles and is large enough to accommodate a seated adult with the upper part of the body inside of the cage. The blindfolded participant is exposed to sounds and indicates from which quadrant it appears to be emanating from. Used as a study or laboratory device.
Used generally for porcelain produced in Hizen province (now Saga prefecture), Japan.
Refers to artists who produce art within the context of a culturally cohesive community, generally guided by traditional rules or procedures.

Refers to the style and culture of the Wolastoqiyik, also known as Maliseet or Malecite, a First Nations indigenous people belonging to the Wabanaki Confederacy, together with the Passamaquoddy, Penobscot, Mi'kmaq, and Abenaki Indians. The Wolastoqiyik mainly live in Canada, especially New Brunswick, with one group across the border in nearby Maine.

Describes works produced by the African people of the same name living mainly in Burundi and Rwanda, including traditional crafts of weaving, pearl bead-making, and basketry. The Tutsi monarchy had rich traditions of dynastic poetry and courtly music. The Tutsi are an ethnic group of probable Nilotic origin who came into the area in the 14th or 15th century. They were nomadic herders and warriors who gradually dominated the resident Hutu through generally peaceful infiltration and the establishment of a feudal system headed by the Tutsi king and aristocracy, at the same time adopting the Hutu's Bantu languages. The European colonial period created tensions between the two groups that remain problematic.
Substance added to, for example, food, paint, or a chemical compound, to prevent deterioration, the breaking down of an emulsion, or the loss of desirable properties.
Material that is added to soil or other growing media to supply chemical elements needed primarily for plant nutrition.
A pale yellow drying oil with a pleasant odor and taste obtained from the large seeds of the common sunflower plant.

A hard, heavy, durable heartwood wood yielded by various trees of the genus Diospyros in tropical Asia and Africa, valued for its dense, smooth-grain from the earliest times; was imported to Egypt from Nubia and the Sudan. It is extremely durable, resistant to rotting, fungi and powder post beetles, but difficult to work and carve. It has been used for decorative items, inlay work, black piano keys, musical instruments, and tool handles. Several other dark, heavy woods from unrelated species are also called ebony because of their color, including cocuswood, coffeewood, blue ebony, and African blackwood.
In physics, plasma is an electrically conductive gas of low density, affected by magnetic fields. It is fully ionized and contains approximately equal numbers of positive and negative ions.
A soft, gray-green, iron silicate mineral that was first described in 1847 near Verona, Italy. It is a mica type mineral that has been found as a pigment in some Chinese and Indian paintings.

Refers to glass created by a technique in which ground glass is made into a paste and molded into a vessel or figure, and then the design is refined by carving. Glass created by this method was known in ancient times and revived in France in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, notably in the studio of glass and jewelry designer, René Lalique.

Cross in the shape of the Greek letter tau, that is, T-shaped. In Christianity and other ancient societies, the tau cross symbolized life, resurrection, reincarnation, and blood sacrifice. Used in the crux ansata or ankh of ancient Egyptian symbolism, in heraldry, on a St. Anthony's cross as a sacred symbol, and by St. Francis of Assisi as the symbol of his order.

Impressed lines, either gilt or blind, created in leather or other semi-hard surface materials by finishing tools also called fillets; most commonly used in bookbinding. For similarly shallow recessed moldings in other plane surfaces, use "sunk fillets."
In Indian architecture, the shrine where a figure of the deity resides.
Built works used for arts and public performance.
Use to designate circular buildings of classical date, with or without a peristyle.

Circular windows containing patterned tracery, particularly stained glass windows that are divided into compartments by mullions radiating from a center, or filled with tracery suggestive of the form of a rose or wheel.

In archaeology, geology, and related disciplines, sites having features or characteristics that are used to define, or are paradigmatic of, a culture, stratigraphic level, or other pertinent feature or characteristic. For example, in archaeology, a type site could contain artifacts in an assemblage that are typical of that culture. The type site is often the eponym for the culture or feature, that is, the site after which the culture or feature is named.
Building complexes focused on one or more tombs, but also containing other structures.
Indication in texts, databases, tables, and lists when information for the instance at hand is possibly applicable, although not all facts or scholars agree.
General term for a variety of storage devices designed to hold textilemaking tools and materials.
Rollers comprising tubes with a fiber surface, that are mounted on a roller and handle, and used to apply paint.
The office and dignity of royalty, especially of a king or queen and their reign.

A deep pit or distant land located under the earth or in a dark precinct where humans and other creatures exist after earthly death, common to many mythologies. The nature of the place varies from a dreary land where the dead are gathered and from which only a few exceptional human heroes are permitted to enter heaven, to a terrible precinct where sinners pay for misdeeds. In many religions, it is from the underworld that dreams, ghosts, and demons originate.

Refers to Inca designs comprising geometric forms enclosed in squares, believed to be used primarily on textiles. It is believed that the designs were a system of pictographs, perhaps an ancient ideographic form of writing (perhaps representing the names of cities or kings) or a mnemonic system. Tocapu was apparently used only on the garments of chiefs and other individuals of high rank. See also "khipu," which was a mnemonic system made of knotted strings.

Books, usually illustrated literary anthologies, intended to be given as gifts and often published annually; popular in the 19th century. For works produced to mark an occasion, use "keepsakes (books)."
Books of images with little or no text, especially those intended for children or beginning readers.
For positional attributes of three-dimensional works or the illusionistic space of a composition, referring to the viewer's lower right-hand side of the work or composition.

Refers to certain works that continued Abstract Expressionism into the 1960s and 1970s (e.g., by Guston, Frankenthaler). For the French painting of the late 1940s sometimes called Abstraction Lyrique, use "Tachiste."
Communities of any size that have shipping as a major industry.
Flat surfaces, blocks, or floors, generally raised above the adjoining  floor.

All movable physical objects used on a motion picture, television, or stage set that are not costume or structurally part of the set, such as furnishings, decorations, and objects held or touched by actors.
Nationality, style, and culture of Siena, Tuscany, Italy.

Refers to the culture of the southern Netherlands, roughly corresponding to modern Belgium, Luxembourg, and part of France, particularly during the historical period when Flanders was an independent principality.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Nebraska.
Construction method using as building materials blocks of soil held together by grass and the grass' roots. Blocks of sod were placed grass-side down to create thick walls.

Testing techniques that cause minimal damage to the sample. The designation is the middle term in characterizing destructivity of scientific analysis, falling between ‘destructive testing’ and 'non destructive testing’.

Blocks, usually plain, forming the low pedestals of statues or columns, and also for the plain faces at the lower part of walls or pedestals. [Savannah: Could refer to a hoof, clogs, or an architectural base. Would need more context to assign a value.]
The function, act, and process of making a new, amended, improved, or up-to-date version of something, such as data, a document, building plan, etc.

Refers to the religion and philosophy founded in India in the sixth century BCE by Vardhamana, one of the religious figures who protested and repudiated the orthodox doctrines of the Vedic cult. It is characterized by an aversion to rites of sacrifice prevalent in Vedic traditions, by the belief in the ethical doctrine of ahimsa, advocating non-injury to all living creatures, and by the struggle for the consummate ideal of human perfection achieved through monastic and devout living.
Examining and measuring critically the qualities or abilities of something or someone, often with reference to established standards.
The areas or compilations of changes to fix, correct, and repair a work of art or architecture.
Customary or social occasions of taking food, typically at an approximately fixed time of day, such as breakfast, dinner, etc.
Circumstances, events, or conditions that are adverse, particularly those that are caused by, or are perceived to have been caused by, bad luck.

Art in which people are socially or physically engaged directly in an artwork, allowing them to become creative participants in a work or action, to the extent that they may be considered co-authors, though usually anonymous. This type of work is considered incomplete without the interaction of viewers or audience. For technological works that require physical manipulation, or that are directed by formal instructions given by the artist, use "interactive art."

An outline or form combining elements of oval and triangular, typically having three sides, often rounded, with the form being wider at the top and tapering to a point at the bottom; the name refers to a common shape of medieval shields or escutcheons. The term is used, for example, with reference to the backs of Federal and similar types of chairs, and for a certain shape for cut gems.
The history of the ownership and transmission of an object, including previous locations of a work.

A philosophic movement based on an idealistic belief in the essential unity of all things, the innate goodness of man, and the supremacy of insight over logic and experience in understanding reality and ascertaining truths. It is considered to be a part of the Romantic movement and had a powerful impact on the arts, particularly literature. The term generally refers to 19th-century transcendentalism in New England although the movement was found in other countries including Germany and England.
Moral standards or principles held by a person, community, or participants in an enterprise which may philosophically inform the activities that these parties plan and undertake.
Wealth or success.

The action of restoring or giving back something to its rightful owner, or of making reparation for a loss previously inflicted; restoration of a thing lost, taken, or damaged. In the context of cultural property, this refers to returning cultural property to an individual, whereas "repatriation" refers to returning cultural property to a country or culture.
Preparing lifelike representations of animals by stuffing the skin or molding it around a model of the specimen.
Chinese painting techinque using broad full strokes and no outline, often with the side of the brush. Used often during the Southern Sung period.

The technique, technology, science, and practice of copying and reproducing documents or graphic materials in facsimile form by means other than conventional printing, for example photocopying, microfilm, and digitalization.
High-crowned hats made of felt or straw with a very wide brim usually rolled at the edges, worn especially in the American Southwest and Mexico.
Boards, planks, or slabs of wood or any other rigid material fixed in a horizontal position to a wall or in a case, to hold books or other objects as in a bookcase or cabinet.

Stands with adjustable mirrors and a small table surface at chest-level, used by men to hold the implements required for shaving. The form appears in Europe in the 17th century, and was common in Britain and North America through the early 20th century.

Tables or other platforms in temples and churches upon which offerings to divinities are set. Not specific to geographic location, religious culture, or historical period: there are Ptolemaic, Shinto Buddhist, Vaishnav, Christian and Jewish offering tables. Examples are the blocks of sculpted stone or wood, intended to be placed in front of the false doors or statues of Egyptian tombs. These held food, drink, or other offerings to the dead and deities. For similar objects used specifically for liquid offerings, use 'libation tables.'
Term for the earliest type of bentwood chairs; patented by Samuel Gragg in 1808.

Poles, masts, or structures mounted with one or more electric lamps of high wattage. Generally permanently fixed for use in stadiums, light towers also exist as mobile units used in the construction industry.
Lamps formed from drinking glasses by the addition of pierced, domed covers and carrying handles and the insertion of a lamp or candleholder.

Strips of flexible material, especially leather, used for fastening or holding things together. May have a buckle or other fastener attached. For strips that pass over the shoulder, use "shoulder straps (object components)."
Abstract wordless images made on paper using a typewriter as a mark-making device. Coined by Edwin Morgan to describe the works of Dom Sylvester Houédard.
Organizations working for political purposes or goals.
Men who in the opinion of others have performed heroic acts or services and are regarded as ideals or role models.

Those who engage in aggressive movements or enterprises against some public evil or some institution or group considered an evil. Includes specifically those who take part in wars or fighting expeditions instigated and blessed by the Church.
Historical Roman rulers of one of four divisions of a country or province; at a later period applied to subordinate rulers generally, especially in Syria.
Generally, craftspeople or industrial workers engaged in any or all of the processes involved in textile manufacture.
Refers to people engaged in bringing articles of trade or commerce into a country from abroad for sale or exchange.
Those whose occupation it is to climb steeples, chimneys, or other tall structures, and to repair them.
Parts of looms.
Tools used to penetrate materials, such as awls.

Hand operated cutting implements resembling scissors but of larger size, or any other cutting instruments that similarly operate by the simultaneous action of two blades on opposite sides of the material to be cut. The term may also be used for various machines used for cutting that are more or less analogous to shears in manner of operation.

Instruments that measure the rate of photosynthesis in plants, specifically by measuring the volume of gas produced by aquatic plants in varying temperatures and with varying levels of light intensity.

Refers to the style of architecture that coincided with the reign of Mahmud II, who ruled from 1808 to 1839. Mahmud broke the power of the janissaries, whose reactionary views were in part responsible for the Ottoman military decline. In the arts, he was a major force in Europeanizing Ottoman art and architecture, building structures in the Baroque and Rococo styles, as well as the Neo-classicism of Napoleonic France. His Nusretiye or Divine Victory mosque was built in the late Baroque style with undulating, curving walls and large open courtyards. Under Mahmud II, court artists were sent to France to learn scientific methods of painting and drawing and rules of linear perspective.

Refers to the style of stoneware produced in Seto and southward onto the Chita Peninsula in the 12th century. The style is characterized by the production of everyday ware such as bowls, jars and motors.
Culture of a dynasty that ruled in what is now the Indian state of Tamil Nadu, including Tanjore, Trichy, and Pudukottai 600-900 CE.

Refers to the work of a school of painting that specialized in the native Yamoto-e style from the early 15th to the later 19th century. Tosa School painters worked primarily for the imperial court and specialized in courtly themes and scenes from classical literature. The style is characterized by fine, delicate lines, attention to detail, lavish color, and flat, decorative compositions. The Tosa style exerted a wide influence on other schools of painting, especially during the Edo period (1600-1868).
A genre of graffiti art with interlocking, highly stylized and often cryptic lettering.

Architectural style originating in the American Southwest, characterized by squared-off adobe construction, brick coping at the top of the structure, square beams rather than round vigas, and relatively formal Victorian-style windows.

Trademarked name for a series of glass fiber reinforced aluminum honeycomb boards used for sailboat contruction; and in art conservation as support panels for objects such as mosaics and wall paintings.

Genus of tropical trees containing over 30 species noted for their broadly winged circular fruits and including many kinds valued for their hard, often red, wood, some of which are padauk, amboyna, mukwa, barwood, or narra. Some species are used produce a fugitive red dyestuff containing santalin that has been used for textiles and tanning leather. The dye is soluble in alcohol, but insoluble in water. It was used commercially to produce mock turkey red dyes.  The scientific name is a Latinized ancient Greek term meaning "winged fruit," in reference to the shape of the seed pod.

Species of evergreen tree native to the southeastern and gulf area of the United States into Mexico, and Cuba, having a coarse, reddish brown bark and reaching 50 feet in height. Valued for its hard, durable wood, formerly used in shipbuilding; today most often used for shade trees. It is readily hybridized, and thus confusion regarding varieties and certain common names has arisen.
General term for any of several pine trees of the southern United States noted for foliage having a fragrance resembling the herb rosemary.
