Grouping consisting of placental mammals and all extinct mammals that are more closely related to living placentals than to living marsupials.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name, a subgroup of the Gur living in northern Benin.

Style and culture of a people of mixed Arab-Berber descent inhabiting the Western Sahara, neighboring parts of Morocco, Mali, Algeria, and the Islamic Republic of Mauritania. To refer to the products, style and culture of people living within the boundaries of Mauritania proper use "Mauritanian."

Business enterprises that provide and oversee the physical and technical means allowing the creation or manifestation of a thing or event. Examples are production companies for the creation of film, television, radio, performing arts, new media art, etc.
The female gametes or reproductive cells in animals, usually produced by an ovary and capable of developing into a new individual after, or in some cases without, fertilization by the male sperm.
Frames, devices, or machines of various designs, used for interlacing at right angles two or more sets of threads or yarns to form a cloth.

A volatile, organozinc liquid compound used in mass deacidification of library materials. Because it ignites upon exposure to air, diethyl zinc can only be used in conservation under controlled conditions, released within a specially designed vacuum chamber from which oxygen has been evacuated.

Lateral flat parts on either side of a hinged joint, as on diptychs, door hinges, folding doors, and table tops; by extension, for tables, may also be used for similar but removable components, whether originally hinged or separate. For the lateral components of polyptychs specifically, prefer "panels (wood)" (ALT of "panel (wood)").
Pads or towels worn by women to absorb menstrual flow.
Generic term for subdivisions under the level of nation.
Crisp textile, typically in plain weave, sometimes with a fine crosswise rib and a smooth lustrous surface on both sides, originally of silk, now of various fibers.
Political entities having a strong monarch in the executive branch, but also having a parliament.
Pulverizing, polishing, wearing down, or sharpening by friction.
Refers to a natural or manmade soil moisture regime and its effects on the physical, chemical, and biological properties of irrigated soils.

The passage of an electric current through an electrolyte with subsequent migration of positively and negatively charged ions to the negative and positive electrodes. In conservation used for cleaning off surface deposits.
The properties of light and its interaction with matter.
Small, brimless caps or hats worn by men or women in various different eras and countries.
The two parts of a garment folded back on the chest, especially a continuation of a coat collar.
Clothing designed for or worn while working, differing in style depending upon the job, such as manual labor, crafts, or office work.
Three-dimensional representations of a circus consisting of various parts such as the tent, track, benches, acrobats, clowns, and circus animals, intended for children's play.
Small, thick, Anglo-Saxon silver coins of the 7th and 8th centuries; predecessors of the penny.
Utensils consisting of a crescent-shaped blade with a handle at each end; the blade is rocked to chop ingredients.
Devices or appliances used to brown breads or other foods by exposure to heat.
Genre of literature native to India concerning the previous births of Gautama Buddha. These are the stories that tell about the previous lives of the Buddha, in both human and animal form.
Deep vessels of varying size and shape, and usually having a cover; used for serving soup, sauce, stew, or other such foods.
Metal frames, sometimes gold, intended to hold a ceramic, usually porcelain, cup for coffee.

Boxes, usually made of wood, made to store liquor. Often containing various compartments to hold singular bottles, secured with a lock. Commonly used in the 19th century to store liquor for medical and personal use.

Accessories used to hold handkerchiefs for personal use; some examples take the form of a chain with a ring for the handkerchief to be looped and knotted through. Others take the form of a rectangular wallet, with the handkerchief stored inside.

Earthenware pots common to Southeast Asia, particularly Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam. These are often decorative or formed in the shape of an animal and would be part of an ensemble of accessories related to the ritual of betel chewing.

Tall, one-handled drinking vessels, usually with a hinged lid and often a thumbpiece; generally made of silver or pewter, but sometimes made of glass. Tankards were formerly made of wooden staves and hooped; used chiefly for drinking beer.

A Cycladic vessel featuring a globe-shaped body, tall neck, pedestal foot, and four pierced lugs on the body. The pierced lugs would have held cords for securing a lid to the vessel. Kandilai take their name from their resemblance to modern Greek church lamps; they would have been used to hold liquids such as oil or wine. The kandila form was very common, made in both marble and clay and in a wide range of sizes. The gradual elimination of a foot or base may represent a step in the transition from the kandila to the spherical pyxis form that later became popular.
Group portraits, usually paintings, representing members of the civil militia or civic guard. The genre was common in the Netherlands of the 16th and 17th century.
Works that include the act of sending materials via facsimile transmission; may also be applied to the materials themselves.
Figures used to discourage birds from damaging crops, usually in the form of a man dressed in old clothes or rags, placed in fields or gardens.
People who function as doorkeepers and escorts, responsible for guiding and seating people in a theater, church, courtroom, or other place of assembly.
The ability or permission to, or the method or manner of employing, occupying, applying or exploiting the value of something.
Assistants at Mass or other liturgy who arrange the altar, assist the celebrant, and make the responses.

People or corporate bodies who specialize in making lamps, which are lighting devices of relatively small size and used in households or public buildings. Examples include those having a vessel to contain fuel used as a source of illumination, or those using a candle, oil, gas-jet, or incandescent wire inside a light bulb, often having a decorative shade to shield users from direct light.
A forest-creeper motif in Indian architecture.
In Indian art and architecture, a representation of the face of a divine female minstrel.
The status or condition of a thing, being, or information being available to only a chosen audience, but concealed or safeguarded from general view or knowledge.
Finishing tools consisting of a handle and a brass wheel, the circumference of which is engraved so as to impress a continuous repeating pattern, called a roll, as it revolves under pressure.
Freedom from work or other obligatory activities.
Pictorial records of events kept by Lakota and other Plains Native tribes, usually on a yearly cycle. Primarily painted on buffalo hides. Some of the earliest winter counts date from the 1600s.
Print or nonprint materials used for the purpose of imparting knowledge, attitudes, or skills to others.

Post-1945 art movement building upon some of the aesthetic principles of Constructivism. Began in Russia, organized by Lev Nusberg (born 1937), Francisco Infante (born 1943) and Vyacheslav Koleychuk (born 1941).
Communites of any size known for the production of textiles and fabric.
Objects based on an interior cylinder, usually with flanges attached, around which flexible materials may be wound for storage or supply uptake.
Emblems, symbols, or paraphernalia indicative of a royal state or of an office or membership in a group.
Nationality, styles, and culture of Taranto, Apulia, southeastern Italy.

Refers broadly to the culture and styles associated with the area of southeast Europe comprising the southern Balkan peninsula, Peloponnese, and various offshore islands, as well as other territories that were colonized or held by Greece during various periods of history.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of New Jersey.
Building technique in which structural elements, roofing, or other loads are suspended from cables, ropes, or chains attached to natural or constructed supports.
Testing and evaluation techniques that do not require touching the sample, as when there is a distance between the probe and the tested object.

World Wide Web-based activity conducted through Web sites that enable members to create profiles of personal details, maintain lists of contacts, and send messages to other members. Establishing relationships for play, business, or action with others with similar interests is the primary goal.

Areas in a building, usually a tall building, where there is a step-like recession in a wall or building profile in order to reduce the obstruction the upper stories offer to sunlight and air reaching the lower stories and street.
Fitness equipment made to improve hand strength; consists of two handles held together by thick wire. Users squeeze the handles together when exercising.
Pieces or lengths of fine fabric, such as silk or satin forming a narrow strip or band, awarded for competition or merit.
Self-contained sets of supplies that children can use to learn tricks, illusions, or sleight-of-hand. These may include items of dress such as magic wands, or capes.

An indication of the substances or materials used in the creation of a work, as well as any implements, production or manufacturing techniques, processes, or methods incorporated in its fabrication, presented in a syntax suitable for display to the end-user and including any necessary indications of uncertainty, ambiguity, and nuance. For works on paper, descriptions of watermarks may also be included.

Mechanized devices designed to uniformly and gradually stretch cotton goods and other textile fabrics that have contracted through the course of bleaching, dyeing, printing, and other textile fabrication processes. Specifically, these devices carry out a textile finishing process that prepares materials for the market by laying their warp and woof yarns in parallel poisitions. The machines typically comprise a series of large rubber-covered stretching pulleys mounted on a driving shaft, a traveling belt, and two pairs of corrugated wheels. As fabric is fed into the device, it is held under the pulleys by the pressure of a traveling belt acting against the lower half of each pulley; when the wheels move the pulleys, the fabric is likewise pulled to achieve to the user's desired width.
Instruments that measure the duration of phosphorescence in varied materials or substances.
Dental surgical clamping devices used to achieve compression.
From 1924 to 1948, used as the official designation of the German currency. Later historical use chiefly refers to this official designation during this period.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1299 to 1200 (or 1300 to 1201) Before Common Era.
Chisels, shaped like a small pitchfork, used in leatherworking to make holes specifically for sewing or lacing.
Family of languages spoken in Greenland, Canada, Alaska (United States), and eastern Siberia (Russia), by the Eskimo and Aleut peoples.
Visible impressions, markings, tracks, or traces on a surface, produced by natural phenomena, by man or another living creature, or by other means.
Series of associated undersea ridges or seamounts.
Megarian-style ceramics, often moldmade bowls, produced in central Italy and elsewhere.
Artists who specialize in creating drawings, prints, or other pictures intended to elucidate a description, story, or other written material, usually in a book or periodical.

Artists in any medium whose primary subjects concern the armed forces, including uniforms, equipment, and other topics. Such artists may or may not themselves be members of the military. For artists specializing primarily in battles and war, use "battle artist."
The action of tightly wrapping a  newborn child in cloth bands or other swaddling clothing.
Imaginary species of sea serpent, derived from the Latin vulgate of a passage in Isaiah. Also generic, imaginary sea creatures who are part woman, including the Sirens of Classical mythology.

Trade name for a purified and standardized form of funori, a Japanese glue extracted from the red algae genus Gloiopeltis. It was developed specifically for use by conservators for the consolidation of matte paint.
Genus of flowering plants containing around 20 species of trees native to India, China, Ceylon to Malaysia, and Sulawesi.
General term referring to any of many species of pine, spruce, and hemlock.
Members of an order containing over 5,000 species of  tiny, slender insects with fringed wings.
Self-conscious use of earlier styles in new works of visual art, architecture, literature, or theatre, on a scale broader than quotations or pastiches, generally to the point of an artistic movement.
The state or realm of existence, particularly of the physical.
Taxes or imposts paid to a prince or state, by another prince or state or by vassals, in homage, acknowledgement of submission, or as the price of peace, security, and protection.
Property ownership arrangement in which persons or groups of persons share ownership or rental, usually of vacation housing, and each owner holds title for a specified time each year.

Painting technique in which wet paint is applied to a dry ground. Given that this is the more usual way of applying paint, the term is typically used only when needed to distinguish it from painting techniques that apply wet paint to a wet ground or wet paint. For example, with the art of Jackson Pollock, where the artist used both methods.
Working out or recording the chief features of a visual form, usually but not necessarily by drawing.
Women's low-crowned straw hats having a brim turned up behind and held in place by a bandeau, which is usually decorated with flowers; similar to hats depicted in paintings by Watteau.
Upper surfaces of tables, placed upon legs or other supporting elements.

Stands for holding turbans. Prime examples were created in the Ottoman Empire, where court officials and members of the elite classes wore elaborately shaped turbans that indicated rank and position, wound accordiing to precise clothing regulations. The turbans were placed on turban stands between wearings.
Tables with slate surfaces covered with cloth, having six pockets and surrounded by cushioned rails. Distinct from "billiard tables" which do not have pockets.

American adaptations of late Sheraton-Style, open-backed side chairs. These are usually painted black with stencilled decoration that emulated gilt and lacquered furniture imported from Europe, and were developed and sold by Lambert Hitchcock in Connecticut in the mid-nineteenth century.
Devices incorporated into the stems of candleholders for the purpose of adjusting the candle in the holder and ejecting the stub.
Lamps having a holder or support for the wick, frequently a half tube, attached to the bottom of the reservoir.
Devices that fasten or hold together separate parts of objects made from textiles.

Organizations that support religious activities by providing places of worship or schools and the payment of salaries to religious leaders. Some religious organizations also establish doctrine, determine qualifications for membership, appoint religious leaders, discipline members regarding religious law, and other duties.
People who enter a country or region from another to settle there. For those who depart from their native or usual country or region to live elsewhere, use "emigrants."
Lovers of the fine arts. Also, people who are interested in an art or science on a superficial level.
Local rulers in various parts of southeastern Europe.
People who conduct meetings or ask questions of another person. Examples occur in journalism and in interviews for a job.
Parts of compasses or other devices designed for holding pencil leads and attached to a compass leg.
Devices that shake test tube cultures and specimens, often for the purpose of aeration.

Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Abdülhamid II, who ruled from 1876 to 1909. During his reign, he constructed a mosque at Yaldiz with miniature lakes, fountains, waterfalls, and bridges. Great attention to patterning and inlays is evident in the sultan's own tables at Yaldiz, which were set with mother-of-pearl.
An Iron Age Indian culture of the western Gangetic plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley on the Indian subcontinent; named for the pottery associated with the culture.

Refers generally to any Japanese variety of the visual arts that uses Western Techniques. The term came into usage during the Meiji Restoration (1868-1912) to distinguish Western-style art from traditional styles of Japanese painting. Western style painting was first know in Japan in the 16th century, but interest faded with the policy of National Seclusion during the reign of the Togukawa shogunate (1603-1867). In 1855, the shogunate set up a research bureau for Western studies, with the Technological Art School established in 1876. During the 1880s, there was a reaction against Western-style painting and a revival of interest in traditional arts.

Style and culture associated with a Siouan-speaking Native American people of North Carolina. Originally known as the "Waccon" or "Waccamassus" by Euro-American settlers, the Waccamaw first resided in southern North Carolina and northern South Carolina. During the early 1700s, the Waccamaw moved to the Green Swamp area of North Carolina, where they reside today. State recognized in 1971.
Any of various inorganic compounds composed of titanium oxides, or the salts of titanic acid, made by heating a mixture of an oxide of carbonate of metal and titanium dioxide.
A yellowish drying oil used especially for artist's paint.
Wood from any fruit-bearing tree. Use a more specific term, if possible.

General term for solid or semisolid organic substance usually obtained from plant secretions, but sometimes obtained from insects or synthetically produced. It is soluble in organic solvent but not in water, and is commonly used in varnish, printing ink, and size. It is distinguished from "gum" by not being dissoluble in water. To distinguish between natural and synthetic resins, use the narrower terms "natural resin" or "synthetic resin."
A very soft mineral, composed of silver chloride, ranging in color from a white to pale-yellow or gray.
Glassware decorated with a matte finish.
An element with symbol P and atomic number 15.
In Indian architecture, a chain of bells or chain interspersed with bells as a decorative motif.
Buildings or groups of buildings owned and operated by a governing body, carrying out official duties, and often occupied by a governmental agency.
In Indian architecture, a window.
Order containing 47 species in one family of ground-dwelling birds resembling quails or pheasants with flat, elongated, and rather weak bills and very small tails.
Schools where equitation is taught; usually including an arena, seating, and housing for horses and equipment.
Steep slopes in front of fortifications. Also, long, steep cliffs or slopes resulting from erosion, and which separate two comparatively level surfaces.
Grouping consisting of about 4,700 living species in 20 orders, characterized by the fetus being nourished during gestation by a placenta.
Describes works created by the African people of the same name living in northwestrn Ghana.
Style and culture of the modern African nation of Mauritania.
Businesses that make books and other works of writers and songwriters available to the public, traditionally through books or other printed materials.

The feet of a quadrupedal animal, characterized by being relatively compact feet with pads and claws, often configured so the weight of the animal is placed on the pad and toes rather than on a heel; examples are the feet of a bear, dog, or cat.

Mechanized devices designed to change the synthetic tow, or coarse fibers that have been removed during textile processing, into sheets of fibers cut into predetermined lengths. These devices then transform the cut fibers into slivers to be used in subsequent drawing processes. Ideal for blending disparate types of synthetic and natural fibers, the devices were popularized in the English, French, and American textile industries due to their effeciency and ability to by-pass opening, picking, carding, gilling, and combing processes. Introduced to the textile industry in 1949, these devices fueled the application of tow-to-top conservion systems throughout the world.
Polymerizable liquid used in the manufacture of rubbers, ion-exchange resins, polyesters, and other polymers. It consists of two vinyl groups bonded to a benzene ring.

Pieces of glass, crystal, plastic, or other transparent substance characterized by having two curved surfaces or one plane and one curved surface, serving to cause regular convergence or divergence of the rays of light passing through it. Lenses may be components of a larger object or objects in themselves. They are used for magnifying vision in eyeglasses, binoculars, telescopes, microscopes, cameras, and for directing or magnifying light in lighting devices such as flashlights or lighthouses.
A preparation for cleaning, especially for hair or fabric.
Provinces or regions within Russia. Also used for administrative divisions within republics of the former Soviet Union.

Refers to a woven textile characterized by parallel diagonal ridges or ribs, produced by passing the weft threads over one and under two or more threads of the warp, instead of over and under in regular succession, as in plain weaving. Regular twill features a diagonal line that is repeated regularly, usually running from the left to right at a 45-degree angle and upward. The weave may be varied in several ways, including changing the angle or direction of the twill line, as exemplified in herringbone twill.
Administrative bodies under the authority of a prefect.
Sharpening edged tools with or as if with a whetstone.
The formation of small ridges or furrows on a formerly smooth surface.
The process of separating out finer particles in a mixture from courser ones by washing or decanting; often used in ceramics to create more finely grained clay body.

In the general sense, describes substances containing carbon compounds, ultimately derived from living organisms. In a more specific sense, with reference to food and other consumer products, produced with no artificial materials, fertilizers, or additives, and, with regard to livestock, in a nonfactory setting with room to move around.
Caps of white or navy blue cloth with a flat crown and stiff, dark-colored visor, and usually decorated with an insignia on the front and a braid; patterned after naval officers' caps.
Streamers, often of lace, ornamenting a headdress, cap, bonnet or the like, which either hung down or along the side of the face or which were pinned up.
Clocks with which children learn to tell the time in a playful way.
Use both for German silver coins issued from the 15th through the mid-19th century and for certain Austrian coins of the 20th century.
Kitchen tools, often having a swiveling, protected blade, for removing the peel or outer skin of a vegetable or fruit.
Utensils, usually ceramic, and often decorative, in several parts used for keeping warm the contents of a bowl, teapot, or cup which rests on a hollow pedestal containing a heat source.
Something written, said, or done to excite laughter or amusement.

Objects made from bison or other large-animal hides, particularly shields, trunks, or containers made by the North American Plains Indians. Examples are large, folded, rectangular envelopelike containers, characteristically decorated with painted designs, and used for the packing of dried meat and other dried foods, blankets, or clothing, for example.

Boxes intended primarily for holding hats while in storage. Also, pieces of hand luggage that are usually round and deep, have handles, and are designed especially for carrying hats, though are often used as traveling bags by women.
Receptacles or formed or flexible coverings designed to hold, store, or ship letters, packages, etc., delivered to or intended for particular addresses or individuals.
Scottish drinking vessels having a lid with a knob, typically made of pewter.
Broad, shallow, open tubs or vessels, especially ones used for cooling liquids.

Visual works or parts of works, such as elements of costume, furnishings, ceremonial objects, or decorations, that are made of feathers. Generally the feathers are either adhered to a solid support or tied individually to a woven support. Important examples of featherwork are found in Mexico and South America.
In Indian architecture, figure riding on a lion mount.
In pricing studies, largest amount of money that a defined number of consumers is prepared to pay for a product or service.
Those who act as intermediaries between the natural and supernatural worlds, serving as healers and priests, foretelling the future, and controlling spiritual forces for the welfare of the community.
Those who make, design, or repair stringed instruments of the lute, harp, viol, and violin families, such as guitars, frame harps, violas da gamba, and violins.
In Indian art and architecture, a long garland worn by Viṣṇu.

In Indian architecture, a stylized elephant-eye motif; perforated decorative design; a serrated orthogonal decorative design; patterned square with recesses (decorative motif); screen type formed by the conjoined chains of this motif.

Condition or characteristic in which an official body has conferred a special status, usually a legally binding status, upon for a site, structure, environment, species, culture, or other thing or entity in an attempt to secure its continuation or and protect its well-being.

Stones used for rubbing or otherwise applying friction to another surface. Examples of use are for smoothing tiles or other surfaces, sanding or burnishing surfaces, treating animal skins, or processing grain or pigments.
The ability to read and write.
Engraved, printed, or written expressions requesting a person's company at a certain event at a given time and place.

Documents containing a set of questions for submission to a number of persons in order to obtain statistically useful information. Use "surveys" for documentation of inspections conducted to achieve a comprehesive view.

Refers to the style of painting and sculpture inspired by the Dada movement, and first seen in the works of artists Jasper Johns and Robert Rauschenberg in the late 1950s. The style is characterized by the use of ready-made motifs such as flags, maps, and numbers, popular images such as comic strips, and mass media images. The style has been seen as the prototype to Pop Art.
Use with reference to the unsold or unused end of piece goods.
A sample is a part of anything taken or presented for inspection or shown as evidence of the quality or composition of the whole. For instances that represent a class, use "specimens."
Nationality, styles, and culture of Torino, Piedmont, Italy.
Nationality and culture of the island or dependent state of Greenland, in the Arctic and Atlantic Oceans.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of New Mexico.
Technique for face brick in which bricks are laid in a decorative pattern with a combination of horizontal, vertical, and diagonal elements. An example would be a basket-weave pattern.
Testing techniques that do not damage or destroy the sample.
Supporting frameworks consisting of inclined upright pieces with diagonal braces; used in architecture, furniture, and for other purposes.

The decentralized practice and method by which individuals and groups create, manage, and share terms, names, etc. (called "tags") to annotate and categorize digital resources in an online "social" environment. This method is not necessarily collaborative because the effort is typically not organized, individuals are not actually working together or in concert, and standardization and common vocabulary are not employed.

Refers to the religion based on devotion and worship to Mithra, the Iranian god of the sun, justice, contract, mediation, and war in pre-Zoroastrian Iran. Also refers to the religion in the Roman Empire during the second and third centuries centered around the worship of  Mithras, the patron deity of loyalty to the emperor. This religious practice dissipated with the recognition of Christianity by emperor Constantine in the fourth century.
Occurances and happenings related to one's occupation or status.
The quality or condition of having strong moral principles, integrity, good character, honesty, and decency.

An outdated designation formerly used for the art of certain people considered to be outside the spheres of influence of other, politically dominant cultural groups; was used especially concerning communities in sub-Saharan Africa, the Pacific Islands, and native tribal groups throughout the Americas. Use instead "indigenous art," "tribal art," or the most specific name known for the culture of origin. Distinct from "primitivism," a term sometimes used for artistic styles or movements intended, often romantically or sentimentally, to emulate the appearance of art made by people operating outside of mainstream art markets.
Having a straight, uncurved and unbent front, particularly as used in reference to the fronts of case furniture, legs of furniture, and architecture.
General term for exercise equipment built for use in the home, as opposed to equipment made for fitness center or gymnasium use. They are often comprised of several different fitness machines in one.
The kind of object or work described, e.g., painting, book, cathedral.

Mechanized devices designed to fill pillows, cushions, stuffed animals, or other textile objects with opened fibre or crushed material such as latex, foam, or viscoelastic. These devices typically utilize suction turbines or compressed air to facilitate the stuffing process.

Laboratory apparatuses used for collecting samples of pure gases such as hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen. These are of varied size and made from glass, metal, or plastics, and depend on the transfer of gas from one vessel through water contained in another. The original concept was developed by Reverend Stephen Hales ca. 1727.
Air compressors designed to run dental devices; produces high-quality, high-pressure air, which runs through specialized lines..

General term for unit of currency of various values, used from the late 16th to the mid-19th centuries in various European countries, particularly in the Netherlands, the Holy Roman Empire, the Austrian Empire, Sweden, Denmark, and Scotland.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 12,999 to 12,000 (or 13,000 to 12,001) Before Common Era.
Language family of the savannah areas of the Orinoco River region in eastern Colombia and southwestern Venezuela.

Condition caused by the early stage of growth of any of several types of mold or fungi, appearing as a white to black downy and often smelly film on the surface of organic materials such as cloth, wood, leather, and paper. The two most common species are Aspergillus glaucus and Penicillium glaucum. Mildew is most often found in warm, damp, dark areas and can often look like dirt. It excretes damaging organic acids, such as citric, oxalic, gluconic, etc., that can discolor dyed textiles, paper, paint and leather.
Small canyons, located on the sea floor.
Devices used in noise reaction experiments in which a ball is released from an adjustable height and falls upon a rubber block and thence either makes or breaks a contact that generates a sound.

A kind of fine stoneware developed by Josiah Wedgwood. White in its natural state, it is stained with metallic oxide colouring agents to achieve shades of pale blue, dark blue, lilac, sage green, black, and yellow, though blue and white ware is most common. Used for cameos, vases, plaques, tableware, furniture mounts, and portrait medallions. The earliest formed was stained integrally and was known as “solid,” Later varieties had surface coloring and were known as “dip.” Decorations, in the Neoclassical style and usually white, were made in separate molds and applied to the body of the piece.
People who create art, usually dating from the 1960s or later, that uses the exhibition space as part of the design.
Artists in any media whose primary focus in subject matter is mythology and mythological characters.
Erotic embrace of a sex act. The term is used in art history, classical studies, and archaeology to refer to explicit depictions of complex and unusual sexual positions, or unusual pairings.
Mythical creatures having a lion's body and a human head. Originating in Egypt, probably as a type of the king, the Sphinx became known early to Syrians, Phoenicians, and Mycenaean Greeks.

Trademarked name for a series of glues and impregnating resins made from urea, melamine and/or phenol with formaldehyde. In conservation, Kauramin (TM) impregnating resins are used for consolidation of archaeological wood.
Genus of flowering plants. Until 2005, species were considered members of Acacia.
General term for many species pines generally native to eastern and central parts of North America.
Members of an order of containing approximately 370 species of small primitive, wingless insects having three slender, bristlelike appendages at the tip of the abdomen.

In two-dimensional representation such as drawing or painting, the depiction of figures and objects in perspective with their gradations of light and shadow, using such techniques as hatching; applies particularly to architectural rendering that depicts shadows cast at a particular angle.
Methods used in the arrangement or placement of lighting devices, for desired effects.
Hats made of white canvas or duck with gored crown and stitched brim, worn by enlisted navy personnel.

Refers to the fixed soft coverings for furniture, especially seating and reclining furniture. Originally referred to all the textile components of a room supplied by upholsterers, including wall hangings, bed hangings, window curtains, and table coverings.
Stands used to hold or support typewriters.
Furniture consisting of a flat, slablike top mounted on legs, designed specifically to support large radio sets.

Armchairs that are stuffed or have a loose cushion to support the back, and wooden legs and a slide-out frame in the front upon which to rest the feet. In many versions, the slide may extend to full length so that the occupant may recline. Popular in the late-18th- and early-19th-centuries, the name refers to the chairs having been common in hunting lodges.
Devices with a reflecting surface, often of metal, glass, or fabric, used behind or in front of a light source to redirect light.
Decorative strips or loops, as of cloth, cord, or metal, designed to hold a curtain or drapery back to one side, so that it is draped in a partially open position.
Ministerial offices, branches of public employment, or bodies of public servants concerned with some particular kind of work or the supply of some particular need in a society.

People confined, voluntarily or involuntarily, to an institutional facility. Use "prisoners" for those involuntarily confined in prison or kept in custody. Use "convicts" for those serving a prison sentence following conviction for a criminal offense.

People or groups of people who finance or who give, such as items or art works to a collection. For those who make a partial contribution to a larger whole, use "contributors." For those who sponsor the broader work of people such as artists and writers, use "patrons." For supporters who assume primary responsibility for projects or activities, use "sponsors."
Military commanders or commanders-in-chief. They may work in the service of a king or emperor, or they may have a regional power base that is ruled independently of the central government.
Individuals whose principal business consists of advising others, either directly or through publications, on their investments and on investment opportunities.

Refers to masses, usually long in relation to their width, suspended from a fixed point, and often having a weight on the free end, and able to swing in an arc back and forth by the actions of gravity and acquired momentum; sometimes used for regulating the speed of clock mechanisms.
Tools that act as levers in order to force or pry open, out, or up.
Pencils specifically for marking the skin, usually used by medical professionals during physical examinations.
Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Mehmed V, who ruled from 1909 to 1909. During this period, Turkey fought in World War I on the side of Germany.

Style or culture of a Lushootseed-speaking Native American nation, whose ancestral lands are located in central Puget Sound in Washington state. Their endonym derives from a Lushootseed phrase meaning "people of the clear salt water."
Additive used in concrete admixtures to alter the amount of water required to produce flowing concrete.
A substance used to increase the durability or stability of another substance, such as pigment on paper or dye in textiles.
General term referring to dark, tropical hardwoods of various species in several genera, including Dalbergia, Passiflora, Platymiscium, Miconia, and Brya.

Any of a group of glycosides obtained from plants that gives a soapy lather with water. Saponin is obtained from several unrelated species, including the bark of the soap bark tree, the roots of the soap plant, the fruit of the soapberry tree, and the leaves of the soapwort plant. Saponins have been used since ancient times as a natural cleaner. Uses include in solution as a mild detergent for cleaning dirt and smoke from paintings. It is poisonous to fish or if injected into the bloodstream.

A natural fine-grained, greenish-blue corrosion product associated with cuprite and atacamite observed on ancient Egyptian bronzes. The formation of chalconatronite seems to have been due to the presence of hydrated sodium carbonates in the arid soils of certain parts of Egypt.

Pure metallic element having symbol Ti and atomic number 22; a hard, lustrous, silvery metal. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials.
Refers to glass blown with double walls and sealed after silvering of the enclosed surfaces; used to produce ornamental wares.

In painting, sculpture, and artistic image-making of various kinds, representations of radiant light or luminosity emanating from divinities, holy persons, and other divine beings or objects, such as the Christian Lamb of God or the word "God." Sometimes used by extention to refer to the entire ensemble of light and beings or objects.

Communal men's houses built and used by Yup'ik men for daily activities (eating, sleeping, bathing). Also used as a communal dance hall for masked dance performances; during these dances the house is open to all individuals. Usually contains a firepit for steam baths and benches.
Small windows or other openings, sometimes closed by grilles, forming places of communication; typically placed in another window or opening. Examples are windows in banks for cashiers or tellers.

Order containing 37 species in one family, characterized with extremely soft-plumaged arboreal birds that feed on insects and small fruit, and having weak feet with the first and second toes directed backward.
Educational institutions located in sparsely populated nonurban areas to provide public, usually elementary, education to local residents.
Points where rivers open into larger bodies of water.
Fractures in the crust of a planet, accompanied with a displacement of one side of the fracture compared with the other, usually in a parallel direction to the fracture.

Subclass of primitive mammal including monotremes and their extinct relatives, characterized by being egg-laying, having hair, mammary glands without nipples, a pectoral girdle, and separate oviducts that open into a cloacal chamber that is shared with excretory ducts. Most of the animals in this group are extinct, known from fossils of the Cretaceous and Cenozoic periods. They are represented today by the monotremes, platypus and several species of echidna.
Style and culture of the African ethnic group of the same name inhabiting Bénin.
The style and culture of the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean.
Companies that equip and operate ships, for sea or inland navigation.
The complex, translucent, colorless, colloidal material comprising the living part of a cell, including the membrane-bound cytoplasm, nucleus, and other organelles.
Devices used in weaving, comprising a comb-like bar with evenly spaced pins along the long side, used to space the warp threads.

Any of a class of three-membered cyclic ring ethers including ethylene oxide, propylene oxide, and butylene oxide. Epoxides have been used as a permanent wood preservative treatment based on the chemical modification of the wood components.
Lengths of film or magnetic tape whose ends have been sliced together, so as to project or play back the same material continuously.
A preparation that is lathered and applied to a surface in order to soften and condition the area for shaving.
Particular type of administrative territorial subdivision. Examples are in Germany.
Thin, lightweight, sheer, or semi-transparent fabric usually made of cotton, silk, wool, or other synthetic fibers.
Administrative bodies under the authority of a president.
Chipping stone, especially flint, with sharp, quick blows to manufacture tools through a process of lithic reduction.
The process by which any substance is converted from a liquid state into a vapor or gaseous state.

Portions of a whole, including subtances in the context of being combined with other substances, portions of temporal works, or portions of literary or dramatic works. For parts of visual works and other objects, prefer "components (object parts)."
Toy and miniature versions of musical instruments for children to learn how to make music while playing.
General term for coins with a shilling denomination.
Scissorlike tools with one tip for digging out the eyes on a pineapple and the other tip for snipping them off.
Devices or receptacles designed for incubating yogurt cultures. These have a variety of designs, some powered and others using insulation to keep the incubated material at a uniform temperature.

Genre of highly stylized Sanskrit literarature employed in the court epics of India from the early centuries CE. Characterized by an elaborate poetics of figures of speech, among which the metaphor and simile predominate. Other characteristics of the style are hyperbole, the careful use of language to achieve a particular effect, a sometimes ostentatious display of erudition, and an adroit use of varied and complicated meters. Topics are usually traditional subjects and themes derived from early popular epics.
Bags of distinctive shape used to store salt, grain, or the like; used especially with reference to woven bags used by nomads.
Containers made to store hatpins; generally in the form of a hollow cylinder or rectangular box with holes in the top to hold the pins.

Cases used to contain the mezuzah parchment and that are thus attached to the doorframe of a Jewish home. The cases are usually of linear, tubular design and of various materials, including wood, silver, gold, ceramic, or plastic.
Hand-sized cups having a bowl shape, usually without a handle, used for drinking tea; sometimes accompanied by a matching saucer. Often, but not always, from Asia or having an Asian theme.
Water vessels with bulbous spout and elongated neck with flared rim; of Malay origin and found throughout Southeast Asia.

Visual works or parts of works, in any medium, having subject matter that provides a visual representation of a story. Stories may be based on literary works, myths and religion, historical events, or any story.

Visual works made primarily of felt, which is a dense textile constructed usually of wool and fur fibers that are held together by heat, moisture, and pressure without weaving or spinning. The term is usually reserved for artistic or decorative works having felt as the medium and support (if any); clothing made of felt is not called "felt work."

Refers to small figures, animals, and other small details added to enliven a painting or drawing of a landscape or architectural composition. Staffage was often painted by specialist artists, for example, in the northern Netherlands in the 17th century. The term may also refer to painted, gilded, or other small accents or embellishments added to decorate porcelain, furniture or other decorative arts.
The essential, immaterial, or spiritual part of people or animals, as opposed to the physical.
People who specialize in making mirrors, which are objects with a highly polished surface designed to reflect images; often intended for those who make mirrors of glass.
In Indian art, a pear-shaped citrus as a motif.
In Indian architecture, a tortoise motif.
The source or quarter of origin or derivation. For the history of the ownership and transmission of an object, including previous locations of a work, use "provenance (history of ownership)."
Machines designed to smooth wood and remove saw or lathe marks and other imperfections; ranging in size from hand-held to large drums or belts capable of surfacing a full-size panel.
Means of communication designed to reach large numbers of people, such as hardcopy or online newspapers, radio, and television, regarded collectively.

Works produced to mark the occasion of a gathering or event, distributed to those in attendance and not usually otherwise available. For 19th-century books intended to be given as gifts, usually illustrated literary anthologies, use "gift books."

Composite volumes comprising two or more works, whether printed, manuscript, or both, that were created separately and later bound together, sometimes with additional pages tipped in. A Sammelband differs from an anthology, which contains intellectual content from multiple works, but which is typically originally made as a single physical object. For volumes containing separate treatises or other works, but having parts that were not necessarily physically created separately, use "miscellanies."

Refers to the style of art, predominantly of painting, inspired by German Expressionism that gained popularity in Italy, Germany, and America in the late 1970s and early 1980s. The style is characterized by large, figurative works, crudely and rapidly painted, often with objects imbedded in their surfaces, such as broken plates or straw.
Circular objects made of various materials and in various sizes, used in many different contexts and applications.
Thin, often tapered pieces of material such as wood, metal, or stone that are used to fill space between things for support, leveling, or adjustment of fit.
Nationality, styles, and culture of Trieste, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Italy.
Nationality or culture of Herzegovina, a country in southeastern Europe, now part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of New York.
Construction system of interlocking patterned concrete blocks especially associated with Frank Lloyd Wright who built four textile-block homes from 1923-1925.
Testing techniques that do not penetrate or alter the sample.
Segments of vaults used externally as the supports of projecting features.
Examining the content of documents, either textual or pictorial, in order to determine what they are about or of.

The body of mythical stories or traditional beliefs belonging to a particular religious or cultural tradition; usage often differs from standard religions only in that the belief system is no longer extant.
Events by which something new is put officially into operation, often but not always formal, public, and invitational.

Occupations or other recurring activities that require an expert level of knowledge and achievement in some subject, field, science, or discipline, especially those activities that involve prolonged training and a formal qualification. For recurring jobs or livlihoods that do not necessarily involve this same high level of expertise, use "occupations."

Art and architectural elements having the purpose of beautifying and enriching public places rather than private spaces, whether or not the works are also functional. For art undertaken in conjunction with particular communities, usually to produce an effect or inspire response specifically within those communities, use "community art." For art associated with urban design, planning, and preservation, use "municipal art."
Having the shape or consisting of three round projecting parts.

Group or succession of persons with their own identity, arising from shared theory or practice, from being disciples of the same master, or from a similarity of principles, methods, or artistic style.

The worth of a thing based on estimating or fixing the monetary value. Valuation is not tied only to the market value of the thing; it may record the cost or price paid for the thing, or calculate intangibles such as scarcity, popularity, and the likelihood of value increasing. For the records of valuation, use "appraisals (financial records)."
Private or civil injurious actions or breaches of duty, other than breaches of contract, intentional or not, for which the law will award a remedy in the form of damages.
Painting technique in which paint is applied to a wet ground or onto wet paint.
Games in which wins or losses depend on the motor dexterity of the player.

Machine simulating the experience of riding a bull; a motor is used to manipulate the item. The bull facsimile usually depicts the head and upper body. Riders sit on the top of the bull and attempt to stay on the item for as long as possible. Usually a soft mat is placed around the machine to break riders' falls.

Spinning plates are those specially made for a kind of juggling, specifically by spinning the plates on the end of a thin dowel. These plates often have a central well at the bottom that allows them to spin on a central point.
A description of the way the work of art is meant to be seen or has been displayed. For the arrangement of archival materials, prefer "arrangement description."

Mechanized devices designed to pass fabrics through either one or two sandpaper-covered or emery rollers in order to raise the short fibers on the fabric's surface, thus producing a soft nap finish on the fabric similiar to suede. Factors dictating the sueding process, including the speed and direction of the rollers, coarseness of the sandpaper, and pressure between the fabric and the rollers, can be individually manipulated using this device to precisely determine the appearance and feel of the fabric's suede finish.
A variant form of polariscope used for testing sugar solutions under polarized light.
Gauges used to measure the size and shape of a tooth or a dental crown.
The standard unit of currency of Russia.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1199 to 1100 (or 1200 to 1101) Before Common Era.
Native North American language family comprising the Muskogean languages and a few extinct language isolates.
Long narrow elevations with steep sides, located on the sea floor.
Telecommunications devices that produce radio frequency alternating current via an antenna.

Japanese porcelain produced in the Arita district of Hizen province by the Sakaida family during the Tokugawa period. Wares were generally of hexagonal, octagonal, or square shape. They initially featured an underglaze blue-and-white, and later a polychrome overglaze technique.
Artists who specialize in intarsia, which is art comprising designs or patterns assembled from small pieces of veneer in various shapes.
Artists in any media that focus on subjects depicting natural objects and beings, for example from the realms of zoology, botany, and minerology.
Activity, status, or expression of thankfulness or gratitude for a blessing or good fortune.
In Indian architecture, a heavenly damsel; apsarās; celestial damsel.

Trademarked name for a synthetic, layered clay composed of sodium magnesium lithium silicate. Combined with water, Laponite (TM) forms a gel used to stabilize emulsions in paints, cosmetics, and other industrial products. It is also used as a film forming agent to produce conductive, antistatic, and barrier coatings; and, in conservation, as a poulticing material for cleaning paper and stone and ceramic objects.
Genus of the Fabaceae family whose sole species is Spartium junceum (Spanish broom).
General term for any of several species of North American and European pines.
Members of an order containing small moth-like insects having two pairs of hairy membranous wings, closely related to moths and butterflies.
Variable color in the range of strong greenish blues, resembling the color of a peacock's neck.
Cords, bands, or similar flexible devices used for fastening, especially by interlacing, such as in a knot or bow.

Organizations that provide instruction and practice of fine arts, crafts, performing arts, or other physical discipline. In the context of the visual and decorative arts, refers to groups comprising a master artist or architect and his or her assistants. A studio typically includes a number of assistants and pupils, who were usually talented or adept artists who were honing their skills under the direction of the master. The term is typically applied to groups active in the 17th century and later. The meaning of the term overlaps with "workshops (organizations)," although there is often a subtle distinction in usage: "Workshops (organizations)" typically refers to groups active prior to the mid-17th century, where the emphasis is on organized collaboration, smooth teamwork, a division of labor, and where apprentices are learning a trade rather than being trained as "artists" in the modern sense of the term. "Studios (organizations)" typically refers to later groups in which the master artist or architect took on pupils rather than apprentices, and the emphasis of the pupil was on honing his native artistic skills rather than on learning a trade. The phrases "studio of" or "workshop of" are often used to signify a work produced by persons in an artist's studio or workshop, but without the direct participation of the master's hand.

General term for a person, group of people, places, things, or concepts that are invented for a particular reason, but not identified or accepted in reality. In the context of art, an "invented entity" could refer to multiple creators that are known by a single pseudonym for a collective project or work.

General term referring to people who are qualified to participate and have registered to vote in an election. For the individual people who cast votes in an election, prefer "voters," although usage overlaps.
Persons who seek to commit funds for profitable return, such as by purchasing bonds or shares in companies.

A pen point is the tip of a pen that touches the writing surface and distributes ink from a reservoir in the pen or adhering to the tip itself. The design may vary, including a simple tip, a split tip, a ball point, a stylograph, or another design.
Tools used in the art of decorative wood-burning, or pyrography.
Casts of biological specimens used for scientific study.
Refers to the art and architecture that coincided with the reign of Mehmed VI, who ruled from 1918 to 1922.
Nationality, the part of the Punjab that lies within India.
Chemical compound used for converting soluble scale-forming solids in water into insoluble form.
A substance added to a solid to increase its fusibility.

General term for wood of any of several species of trees of the genera Eucalyptus, Corymbia, and Angophora that exude copious sap or gum from any break in the bark. It is tough, has an interlocking grain, and is used for mallets, furniture, and bottle cases.

A water-dispersible cleansing and emulsifying agent produced by the saponification reaction of long chain fatty acids, such as found in oils and fats, with an alkali, such as sodium hydroxide or lye. Soaps made from animal fat and wood ashes have been used since antiquity. Although soap was made at home for laundry purposes from the European Middle Ages to early modern times, cake soap was a luxury product that came into common use only in the 19th century.

A common, bright brass-yellow mineral with a metallic luster and greenish or purplish iridescence, constituting the most important ore of copper and composed of copper iron sulfide. Chalcopyrite is mined in North and South America and in Europe.

Pure metallic element having symbol W and atomic number 74; a heavy white metal with a specific gravity of 19.6 and the highest melting point of any metal. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials, particularly alloy steel and magnets, and in electronic applications.

Refers to glass of various colors created by adding metallic oxides to the molten glass; different oxides create various colors. Stained glass may be conbined with painted glass, which involves fusing pigment onto the surface.
Naturally formed aggregate of one or more minerals. For processed or dressed rock use "stone."
In Indian architecture, a wave design as decorative motif.
Built works used for purpose of recreation.
Geological formations comprising a narrow, residual wall of hard sedimentary rock that remains standing after surrounding rock has been eroded away along parallel joints or fractures.

Grouping of mammals including all placental and marsupial mammals, characterized by having mammary glands with nipples, functional teeth, oviducts that are partly fused, may have a cloaca, and having a uterus and vagina, giving birth to live young (viviparous).
Style and culture of the nation of Morocco or its historical counterparts.
Retail businesses that sell merchandise or services, usually relatively small in scale.
Container for dipping flax bundles when retting in running water.

Chemical compound, originally developed for hair-perming preparations, used in conservation of paleontological artifacts. It is applied in solution to fossil materials for neutralization and removal of sulfates and pyrite oxidation products.
Long, regular channels or projections used for finishing and decorative purposes.
Small bags or cases containing the accoutrements of shaving facial or body hair, usually intended for travel. These normally contain a razor, some form of shaving cream, a brush, etc.
Particular type of civil administrative divisions. Examples are in the United Kingdom and in the US state, Louisiana.

Woven textile weave developed by Navajo weavers in the 19th century, consisting of alternating triangular designs. Weave is placed diagonally with the weft doubling the amount of warp threads covered with each pass.
Administrative bodies subject to a prince or princess.

Stone knapping technique used in the Palaeolithic period which involved the striking off of flakes from a prepared core to be used as scrapers of knives. This procedure was more sophisticated than earlier techniques. Named after an archaeological site near Paris.
The proccess or act of forming into a gel.

Measurable properties that can be experienced through sight, sound, touch, taste, smell, or detected through a measuring tool, including color, brightness, length, height, width, mass, volume, density, hardness, solubility, ductility, malleability, heat conduction, melting and boiling points, electrical properties, etc.
Long, pipelike extensions of the hood, worn in the 14th and 15th centuries by men. For long, narrow streamers of cloth attached to or part of a garment use "tippets (costume accessories)."
Toy versions of kitchenware including pots, pans, appliances or ovens that are intended for children's play. For toy dinner, tea or coffee sets, see toy tableware.
Silver alloy coins of France minted in the 18th century primarily for circulation in French colonies.
Implements used to cut pizza, usually a rolling wheel-shaped blade on a handle or a mezzaluna.
Single-strapped bags worn over one shoulder, used originally for carrying soldiers' rations and other supplies.

Small boxes which contained the powdered tea used in the tea ceremony. These containers were made from a variety of materials including wood, dry lacquer, ceramic, metal, and black quartz. They were decorated in a variety of ways and were only used during the summer months.
Vessels, commonly of metal, for boiling water or other liquids over a fire or other source of heat; includes covered metal vessels with a spout, used to boil water for domestic purposes.

Paintings with subject matter of interest to women, particularly romances such as the Tale of Genji. There are few if any contemporary definitions of the term, resulting in ambiguity about the style of painting or the gender of the artists creating these works. This term was used in the Heian period (794-1185). For paintings or prints that depict the beauty of women, see also "bijinga," a term coined in the Edo (1615-1868) or Meiji (1868-1912) period.
Freestanding carved full-length human figures, usually at the front apex of a Maori house and named after an ancestor.
Incorporeal or immaterial beings, as opposed to beings having body and matter; used especially in theology. For spiritual beings who were once human or animal, see "souls."

Motif particularly associated with a style of Romanesque and Early Gothic capital that is formed of broad, smooth leaf-shapes (typically four in number), unribbed except for a central fold, which curve upward and outward before curling over at the tips where they meet the square or octagonal abacus. The curled tip of the waterleaf may be small and neat or large and bulbous; it usually curves inward towards the abacus, but may occasionally turn outwards. Developed as a fanciful interpretation of the Corinthian order; the names refer to various types of leaves that the motif was thought to resemble: waterleaf plant, lily leaf, and hart's tongue fern.

Motif in the form of the head of a lion, usually a maned African lion. Examples occur in Western and Asian art, for example in carpet designs, spouts and other elements on pottery, and ornamental elements on architecture or furniture.
The status or condition of a thing, being, or information being open to general observation, view, or knowledge, or of activties existing, performed, or carried out without concealment.
Devices which hold a piece of sandpaper for sanding by hand.

A process by which an object is removed or detached from its original context and introduced into the collection of a museum, leading to an alteration in the status of the object. This process includes acquisition, documentation, preservation, and often exhibition.
Documents stating rules of action or conduct prescribed by controlling authority and having binding legal force.
Plans of procedure, showing the sequence of items or operations and the time allotted for each.

Refers to the work of a group of artists exhibiting in New York in the mid-1980s. Incorporating ideas from earlier movements such as Dada, Hard-Edge, and Pop, the work is purposefully calculating and intellectual and includes paintings in flat, Dayglo colors, kitsch objects, and sculpture made out of consumer products.
Straight, slender, usually cylindrical stick staff or wand.
Objects serving as tokens of remembrance of some person, place, or event.
Styles and culture of Tuscany, central Italy. For the culture of the ancient people who inhabited this and surrounding areas, use "Etruscan."

Refers to the culture of the modern nation of Hungary, or in general to the cultures that have occupied the area of modern Hungary in central Europe. More broadly, it may refer to the culture of the Magyars, a Finno-Ugric people who settled in the middle basin of the Danube River in the late ninth century CE.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of North Carolina.

Tailiang is one of the two main systems of traditional Chinese timber-frame structures. The term was coined by architecture historians in the 1940s in contrast to chuandou 穿鬥. “Tailiang” can also be called liangzhushi 梁柱式, jialiangshi 架梁式, dieliangshi 叠梁式, zhuliangshi 柱梁式 and is a system in which beams are as structurally important as pillars and posts in supporting purlins. Literally, “tailiang” means fitting beams on top of the pillars, and fitting posts on top of the beams. Consequently, in this system there are fewer pillars with the building interior. To further distinguish it from chuandou, tailiang is interpreted as a framing system in which beams are supported on top of the pillars, and purlins are extended across the beams. It is usually considered to be the standard timber-frame structure of traditional official buildings in northern China.
In nuclear magnetic resonance imaging, the measurement of the time it takes for excited nuclei to return to their relaxed base state.

Writing of manuals, reports, proposals, descriptions, or other documentation, usually highly specialized or concerned with practical applications, used for scientific engineering, business, or other technical purposes.

Parts of buildings with walls rising considerably above the rest, usually with vertical proportions, and to some extent architecturally distinct. For usually detached or isolated buildings or other structures high in proportion to their lateral dimensions, use "towers (single built works)."
Religious beliefs and sacramental practices of the indigenous peoples of the United States and Canada, excluding the Eskimos and Aleuts.
Events related to the life cycles of human beings.
The action or condition of preserving someone or something from harm, danger, or damage, or providing guardianship, care, patronage, shelter, or defense.
Use broadly for art depicting religious subjects or for art used in worship.
Having a form or outline comprising two crossed bars or lines, with one line meeting the second at a right angle in the center of the second line, resembling the uppercase letter T.
Configuration of artistic elements that together constitute a manner of expression peculiar to a certain epoch, people, or individual. A distinctive appearance or manner; a visual language.
An amount, as of goods, services, or money, considered to be a fair and suitable equivalent for something else.
Legal concepts related to land use and planning restructions.
Method of Chinese painting by free sketch or freehand brushwork, usually done in ink.
The procedure of marking or coloring the skin by pricking in coloring matter so as to form indelible marks as figures or by production of scars.

In an optical system, use of magnifying lens or other technology to increase the apparent size of an object. The term may also be used to designate a measurement of degree along a spectrum of enlargement and reduction within an optical system; the size of an image relative to the size of the object creating it.

Skull racks or similar constructions used in Mesoamerica to display the heads or skulls of sacrificed human victims, or platforms carved with human skulls to resemble such a rack. Tzompantlis were usually placed near temples or ballcourts. Those displaying real skulls comprised a wooden framework supporting skulls skewered on horizontal poles run through holes drilled through the temples. Tzompantlis took a variety of forms and seem to have served several functions: altars and venues for ritual; displays of Aztec prowess; and to terrorize subjugated populations.
Small tables supported on legs, pillar, or tripod, with an adjustable top, hinged to fold flat. GLOAG.
Chairs that incorporate latticework adapted from Chinese sources in the back or arms. Coined by Thomas Chippendale.
Lighting device components used to redirect the light from a source, primarily by the process of refraction.
Various materials used for celebrations, such as weddings or birthday parties.
A statement about the way the text is paginated, or the page range of the thing within a larger text.

Mechanized devices designed to expose textile surfaces to a stiff-bristeled brush thus creating a soft, uniform surface finish and removing dust or impurities accumulated during previous steps of thetextile  manufacturing process. Though this device is commonly used as a surface finishing tool in textile production, its application is also relevant for the fabrication of wood, metal, and other similar materials.
Devices that measure for total sediment in residual fluids.
Presses that were historically used to form hollow metal shells used by a dentist as temporary crowns.
General term for units of currency based on English silver or cupronickel coins valued at twelve pence and minted from the mid-16th century until 1970.
Language of the ancient Akkadians.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 11,999 to 11,000 (or 12,000 to 11,001) Before Common Era.
Small language family of indigenous Harakmbet people of Peru.

The condition of providing access and being unblocked. Typically relating to an object or environment that has both an open and closed state, such as a book, box, vessel, garment, gate, window, room, or the like.
Broad elevations on the sea floor that gently rise.

Devices used to teach the deaf to regulate vocal tones. These incorporated a spinning disk on which fifteen rings of alternating black and white spaces were displayed, the white spaces on the inner ring numbering 8, and on the outer ring 32, with intervals between. The numbers of the white spaces correspond to the vibrations of a diatonic scale. Alternating rings would appear as the user spoke, activating the flicker of a flame, causing a strobe effect as visual feedback.

Middle Minoan pottery found mainly at Knossos, Phaistos, and the Kamáres cave sanctuary, for which it is named. It is characterized by a dark lustrous ground to which ornament is added in red and white, with sophisticated designs in curvilinear abstract patterns, and stylized plant, marine, and figural motifs. It often employed the distinctive compositional device of torsion, where the balance of opposing compositional forces was emphasized, for example, with two opposed diagonal compositions twisting around the vase. The potter's wheel was generally used for smaller vessels, and larger vessels were made by hand using the older method.

Artists whose work synthesizes two or more fields or branches of study to create something new, as a mix of theory and practice, and that may integrate two or more elements of expression, such as sound, image, movement , text, etc.. Interdisciplinary artists may work in many genres, or combine fields such as painting, photography, filmmaking, literature, or philosophy.
Artists, usually painters or photographers, who specialize in panoramas, which are pictorial representations with very broad horizontal ranges of view.
Activities surrounding washing and attiring oneself.
Mythological canines that resemble raccoons. In Japanese folkore, tanukis are tricksters and sources of amusement.
Methyl methacrylate made by E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company, Inc., marketed in rolling powder and in rolls, tubes, and cast and molded sheets.
Genus of legumes, ranging from trees to shrubs, that are native to the New World Tropics.
Members of an order containing one family and two genera of insects, one extinct and one living.
A range of purplish blue colors resembling the color of the blooms of periwinkle plants, which are evergreen trailing subshrubs and herbaceous perennials with flattish flowers and glossy leaves.

General term referring to members of 22 species of large, carrion-eating birds that live predominantly in the tropics and subtropics of the New World and Old World. Although they superficially resemble each other, they are only distantly related, the similarities between Old World and New World groups due to convergent evolution.

Two or more public schools cooperating in a system that is under the administration of an executive officer and approved by a dedicated commission to provide schools and education to all residents of the designated area.
Saline lakes, often with no outlet to the sea so that salts brought in by rivers accumulate, especially when the water is not particularly alkaline.
Architectural style that developed in Istanbul in the 18th century, drawing upon European Baroque models.

An artistic movement in India that took place in Bengal between 1895 and 1910. Revivalism meant the rebirth or return to traditional Indian culture. Indigenous artistic styles and motifs with a focus on non-Western artistic values such as spirituality were emphasized. This movement was undertaken in opposition to Western style naturalism taught in the art academies.
Any material that can be digested or absorbed by the body of a human or other animal and used as a source of energy or some essential nutrient, to build and replace tissue, or to relieve hunger.
Wood of trees of the genus Celtis, used for lumber.

Thick, viscous, brown or black, inflammable liquid residue resulting from the partial evaporation or distillation of wood (such as pine, fir, or larch), sugar, tobacco, peat, coal, or other organic substance. It contains hydrocarbons, resins, alcohols, and other compounds; it has a heavy resinous or bituminous odor. It is used as an antiseptic, for coating asphalt roads, preserving timber, caulk on wooden sailing ships, waterproofing for roofing papers, insecticide, in disinfectant soaps. Some tars, such as those obtained from pine or beech wood, have been mixed with linseed oil to form a dark brown glaze and for other purposes.

A hydrous silicate of copper having a green or sky-blue, a shining luster, often opal-like in texture, and used as a gemstone. It has been gathered or mined as a semiprecious stone since 3000 BCE. The translucent to opaque stone is typically greenish or sky-blue in its natural state, but appears true green when ground into a fine powder, which is used as a pigment.

Pure metallic element having symbol U and atomic number 92; a radioactive, silvery metal. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials.

Refers to a type of glass that is blown from two colors combined in the molten state, creating streaks of various colors. It is often used to make windows, but may also be used to make vessels. It differs from "reamy glass" in that reamy glass generally contains white streaks and has the distinctive appearance of a colored liquid having been stirred into cream.
Any substance resulting from the combination of negative ions from acids and usually metal ions. For common table salt, or NaCl, use "sodium chloride."
In Indian architecture, a bull's eye; jāla/jālī design as motif.
Built works designed and used specifically for research.
The layer of tissue forming the external covering of the body in vertebrates.

Mechanized devices designed to draw out, attentuate, and twist wool, cotton, or other types of sliver in preparation for subsequent spinning processes. Historically fueled by leather belts transferring power from a mill's steam engine, these devices drastically expedite the roving process in a factory-based textile manufacturing system.

Compound known as a hygroscopic, blue-gray powder that occurs naturally as the mineral "vivianite (mineral)." Used in the pigment "blue ocher"; has been found in Roman paint residues. Ferrous phosphate is also used as a colorant in ceramics.
Projecting aperatures used to direct the flow of fluids or air or to change the velocity of the flow, especially such aperatures that taper or have a constriction as on the end of a hose or bellows.
Sticks of soap or emollients used for shaving.
Particular type of administrative subdivisions. Examples are in Spain.
Administrative bodies subject to a satrap, being divisions of ancient Persia under the Achaemenian Empire and later administrations.

A technique for cleaning of flesh and grease from skeletal remains of vertebrate specimens for study or display. Bones are steeped in a liquid, usually a chemical or enzymatic solution, for several days to allow soluble matter to dissolve.
Technical term used in wood pulp and paper research that refers to the stiffening of the polymer structure that takes place in lignocellulosic materials upon drying or water removal.
Ornamental trimmings around the lower sections of sleeves.
Toy versions of an intelligent electromechanical machine with an often human or animal appearance or a simple toy figure that looks like a robot.
Various large silver coins of Central Europe minted from the late 15th to the mid-19th century primarily for trade and commemorative purposes; the origin of "dollars (coins)."
Tools for cutting up either raw or cooked poultry.
Literary works that are presented as the work of an author by whom they are not written, with the intention to deceive.
Maori woven bags, such as tote bags, having a decorative pattern.
Bags woven by central Asian nomads, intended to secure the tips of a bundle of strut poles.
Drinking vessels that are designed to challenge the skill of the drinker, or make drinking impossible.
Small ancient Greek covered vessels with an inturned rim; they were used for cosmetics, oils, and perfumes.

Distinctive processional statues depicting Jesus on a donkey, mounted on a wheeled platform. Typically life-size or nearly so, they were common in Palm Sunday processions in certain regions of Catholic northern Europe from the 10th century; found also in southern Europe and South and Central America. Smaller versions were made in imitation of the life-size statues.
In Indian art or architecture, a bifacial (figure).
General term for beings who inhabit the spiritual or otherworldly realms, or who inhabit the physical world but have powers and abilities of the supernatural.

Those who construct models, generally from hard, nonmalleable materials such as wood or stone, such as scale working or display models of three-dimensional objects or models to produce molds for cast products. For those who create models of clay, wax, or other malleable material, see "modelers".
Motif on bone china comprising formalized flowers, foliage, and peaches in blue underglaze; first introduced at Meissen in 1739, and copied extensively by other manufacturers.

Motif often serving as a framing architectural device, generally combined with lintels of free-standing gateways supported by carved pillars set on molded bases. Based on ancient mythical animal, the "makaras (legendary animals)," of Indian origin and used throughout Asian art.
Indication of the reason for which something is done or made, for which it exists, the result or effect intended or sought, or the aim to which an object is directed.
