Any of various tools used for scraping, producing a clean or a smooth finished surface, cutting grooves, or shaping objects by scraping away superfluous material.
Hurried or negligent and irregular writings, or irregular and unmeaning marks. For casual drawings, use "doodles."

Letters, packages, and other physical materials delivered to or intended for one individual or for one address, usually but not always delivered by an official postal system. For electronic mail, prefer "electronic mail."
Postmodern movement in the visual arts of the 1980s in which artists were influenced by pop art.
Broad, thin objects or layers, rigid or flexible.

A specimen is an individual instance that represents a class. A good specimen shows the character of the thing or material, useful for close study and permitting exact identification. For parts of anything presented as evidence of quality or composition, prefer "specimens."
Nationality, culture, or styles of Umbria, Italy. The term is typically used for periods from the Middle Ages forward. For the ancient cultures in this area, use "Ancient Umbrian (culture or style)."

The style and culture of the Iberians, a prehistoric people of southern and eastern Iberian Peninsula, who arrived 8th-6th cen. BCE. The term may also refer to the culture of the modern nations of Spain and Portugal together.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of North Dakota.
Refers to the method of constructing walls and partitions, sometimes floors, by pouring concrete or assembling wooden sections on site in a horizontal position, and then tilting them into place.

Evaluation tests used for museum storage materials in order to detect any emission of faint amounts of chemicals that can damage objects over time. Created in 1973 by conservation scientist Andrew Oddy.The test material is enclosed in an airtight reaction vessel with three small metal coupons: copper, silver and lead. The container is sealed with a small amount of water to maintain a high humidity, then heated at 60 degrees Celsius for 28 days. An identical container with three metal coupons acts as a control. At the end of the trial, the metal coupons are monitored for corrosion effects.
The activity of comprehending, analyzing, and expressing written or spoken material in a different language from the original.
In Indian architecture, a bamboo-sheath/nodes; outer nodal sheath of curvilinear spire, usually showing karṇāṇḍakas/bhūmi-āmalakas.

General term for several spiritual movements that attempt to revive the ancient polytheistic religions of Europe and the Middle East. They strive to revive authentic pantheons and rituals of ancient cultures.
Events which are advance showings of a performance such as a film, play, or exhibition, before being made available to the public.
The socialogical concept of sacrificing of oneself or one's own needs; the giving up of one's own interests, happiness, desires, and even life, for the sake of duty or the welfare of others.
Paintings or carvings worked on living rock.

Having the shape or outline of a hollow cylindrical vessel; differs from "cylindrical," in that "tubular" may be used to describe objects with curved surfaces rather than straight, and tubular objects are typically quite narrow.
The study of society as a complex arrangement of elements, including individuals and their beliefs, as they relate to a whole (e.g., a country).
All property or resources that have monetary or exchangeable value or economic utility.

The art or practice of the accurate graphic delineation of the natural and man-made surface features of a specific urban area, tract of land, or other place, especially so as to show their relative positions and elevations. For the relief features or surface configurations of a place or object, including its natural and man-made features, use "topography (attribute)."
General term for the techniques and processes used in the manufacture of goods, materials, or other things.

Stands or receptacles for holding umbrellas, generally located inside a home or other building near an exterior door. The term is used for stands of metal or wood construction as well as for large cylinder-shaped vessels of ceramic, metal, or another material, designed and used for holding umbrellas.

Late 18th- and early 19th-century circular or octagonal pedestal tables which have a deep top with numerous drawers in the frieze. Often the drawers are marked with days of the week or dates, as such tables were used by landlords for filing collected rents.
Ancient Greek chairs having a deep top rail curving forward from the back and sabre legs; usually undecorated. Imitated during various classical revivals, especially in the 19th century.

Fuel containers which do not bear burners; for fuel containers that support burners, use "fonts (lighting device components)." Some lamps have both fonts and reservoirs, in which case fuel is supplied automatically or manually from the reservoir to the font.

Tensile units adapted to holding concrete forms secure against the lateral pressure of unhardened concrete, with or without provision for removal of metal to a specified distance from the finished concrete surfaces.

It the context of visual and decorative arts, refers to groups of artists or craftsmen collaborating to produce works, usually under a master's name. The workshop typically included trained artists as well as a number of apprentices, who were learning a trade by practicing progressively more sophisticated tasks associated with the production of art works or decorative objects. Different people in the workshop generally performed different tasks associated with producing a work; for example, one person would apply the gilded background of a painting and another would paint the primary figures. The term is typically applied to groups active prior to the mid-17th century. The meaning of the term overlaps with "studios (organizations)," although there is often a subtle distinction in usage: "Studios (organizations)" typically refers to groups active in the 17th century and later, when the master artist or architect took on pupils rather than apprentices, and the emphasis of the pupil was on honing his native artistic skills rather than on learning a trade. "Workshops (organizations)" typically refers to earlier groups where the emphasis is on organized collaboration, smooth teamwork, a division of labor, and where apprentices are learning a trade rather than being trained as "artists" in the modern sense of the term. The phrases "studio of" or "workshop of" are often used to signify a work produced by persons in an artist's studio or workshop, but without the direct participation of the master's hand.
Those who own, rent, or otherwise have a legal right to occupy land.
People who ride horses.
Buyers and sellers of commodities for profit.
Refers to any one-dimensional array of hundreds or thousands of photodiodes. Photodiode arrays are used as position sensors and incorporated in UV detectors.
Devices used for reading.

Noisemaker used during celebrations; usually made of paper or plastic, with a hard mouthpiece and flexible tube which is curled when not blown into. When used, the tube fills with air and unfurls, creating a noise.
Description of salient aspects of the physical appearance of the work and its decoration, including design elements and pattern names.

Mechanized devices designed to modify the physical form of synthetic textile materials by introducing twists, loops, coils, or crinkles into the fiber's filaments, thus improving textile appearance, increasing warmth and absorbency, and lessening pilling. Because there are myriad texturing methods, these devices vary slightly. While some utilize friction disks or spindles and heat to twist fibers, others utilize air streams and high pressure to facilitate the texturing process.
Devices used to determine soundness of cement by measuring its expansion when heated in an atmosphere of steam or boiling water.

Tooth-shaped caps that restore a decayed, broken, weak, or worn-down tooth; the caps are placed over a natural tooth or part of a tooth, to replace the crown of the tooth, which is the exposed portion of the tooth above the gum line.
The standard unit of currency of Singapore.
Language of the ancient Akkadians in transliteration.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1999 to 1900 (or 2000 to 1901) Before Common Era.
Family of languages spoken in southern China, northern Vietnam, Laos, and Thailand.
An aged appearance caused by environmental factors, acquired naturally or artificially induced; used especially with regard to a surface layer on metal caused by oxidation or corrosion.
Low parts of the sea floor that resemble a saddle, located on undersea ridges or between contiguous seamounts.
Instruments for measuring the frequencies of tones or exact pitch, as a set of graduated tuning forks. An advancement of Reed's tonometer, providing more tones.

Glazed pottery manufactured at Karatsu, Hizen Province, in the late 16th century. Early productions are typically untensils for everyday use, grainy in texture and painted with neutral feldspathic glaze. Later productions, after Korean potters were brought to Japan, were mostly fine tea sets with contrasting glazes, underglaze painting, and inlay designs.
Artists who specialize in art interventions, which are works or performances designed specifically to interact with an existing structure or situation.
Those who make portraits in any medium.
The act of discharging urine, which is liquid excretion of metabolic waste in vertebrates.
Imaginary, partly human sea creatures with the head and trunk of a man, usually bearded, and the tail of a fish or cetacean; in Heraldry and elsewhere, often holding a trident and a shell-trumpet.

A registered trademark for a type of hardboard building material first made in 1924 by William H. Mason. Masonite is a wet process fiberboard composed of fine wood fibers compressed into a dense, rigid sheet with heat. The fibers are held together by the natural binders from the pulp with no additional adhesive. Masonite boards do not bend or warp easily but the sheets are brittle and break under pressure.
Genus of flowering plants. Until 2005, species were considered members of Acacia.
A range of blue colors resembling the color of artificial ultramarine blue pigment, also called "permanent blue."

Educational institutions for the level between primary or elementary education and the higher or university level education, usually including the last three or four years of the twelve-year school education program. In most systems, secondary schools include the last years of middle or junior high school and all of high school.

The shallower salt water areas of the earth lying on the margins of continents; loosely applied as a proper name to any specific bodies of water. For the main water areas of the earth, lying in basins, use "oceans."
Cracks in the earth associated with volcanic activity.

Refers to an subclass (or "superorder" or "magnorder") containing the orders Cingulata and Pilosa, currently including 29 species among five living families.  It includes the living anteaters, tree sloths, and armadillos, as well as the extinct ground sloths, glyptodonts and pampatheres. Xenarthrans were formerly grouped with pangolins and collectively referred to as edentates (a former order, Edentata), which alludes to the absence of teeth in some members.
Style and culture of the nation of Mozambique.

Associations of persons carrying on commercial or industrial enterprises focused on the development and manufacture of software, which includes computer system programs, procedures, and associated documentation concerned with the operation of data processing systems, and which require hardware for use to be made of them.
Sheets of thin plastic used to cover food.
Wood of the small tree or shrub belonging to the genus Crataegus.

Any solid or semi-solid substance that is slightly greasy to touch, usually solid, translucent, and has a low melting point; waxes are not a chemically homogeneous group. Waxes are composed of long chain hydrocarbon compounds, and may contain esters of fatty acids and alcohols, are thermoplastic and melt at low temperatures of between 40 and 100 C. In general, waxes are water-repellent, smooth, soluble in organic solvents, and classified as animal (e.g., beeswax), vegetable (e.g., bayberry), mineral (e.g., paraffin), or synthetic (e.g., polyethylene). Waxes are used for polishes, candles, crayons, sealants, coatings, adhesives, waterproofing, carbon paper, media in encaustic and wax emulsion paintings, and as repellents in wax-resist watercolor paintings.

Pure metallic element having symbol V and atomic number 23; a pale gray metal with a silvery luster. Use also for this metal as processed and formed, usually in combination with other substances, to make various objects and materials, particularly steel.

A soft, dense, red, native ore composed of mercuric sulfide, found in deposits in veins near volcanic rocks or hot springs around the world. Cinnabar was mined in the Roman Empire for use as a pigment and for its mercury content; it has been the main source of mercury throughout the centuries. The toxic stone was also used for decoration and a talisman in Mayan tombs, as a colorant in Chinese carved lacquerware, in ink used by high officials in the Byzantine Empire, and other applications. Cinnabar is chemically identical to synthetic red mercuric sulfide, which is called vermilion.

General term for any glass used as a material that is not "blown glass," that is not shaped by blowing air through a blowpipe into a glob of molten glass. The term is used in situations where it may be assumed that the glass normally would be blown, but is not; also used to refer to glass as a raw material prior to being blown.
Nonmetallic element with symbol Se and atomic number 34, obtained chiefly as a by-product in copper refining.
In Indian architecture, a decorative motif showing bell with a hanging chain dangling from a grāsa-mask.

Built works that provide shelter and accomodations for the basic physical functions of life for an individual or family; may also include spaces for dependents animals. Among the functions provided for are a place to sleep, prepare food, eat, and sometimes to work, usually having doors, windows, or other sources of light and with protection from the weather.
Colorless liquid, an aldehyde of furan, which is used chiefly as a solvent, a biocide, and in the manufacture of synthetic resins.
General term for object parts, including both physical and illusional aspects of works.
Instruments with a curved blade, used by ancient Greeks and Romans to scrape sweat and dirt from the skin after exercise or while bathing.

The constituent political and administrative divisions within various sovereign states, including historic ones such as the Roman Empire and modern nations under a federal system such as Canada and Spain.
Administrative bodies in the Arab world subject to a sheikh.
Processes for changing the size or shape of a workpiece by means of machine-operated cutting tools.

The process of raising the level of relative humidity in a closed environment, such as a building or room; use also for the treatment of items by making them moist, such as by the application of steam.
The presence or manifestation of two opposite or contrasting principles or tendencies, as for example in electric batteries and in magnets.
Colorful, multilayered appliqué panels created by the Cuna Indians and usually applied to the front or back of women's blouses.
Sewing machines tailored to children, with which textiles can be sewn.
Italian, medium-sized silver coins used from 1475 until 1846.
Tools used to reduce a large loaf or cone of sugar into suitable size pieces.

General term for the genre of works, written or oral, that are the result or product of literary activity. Included are written works considered collectively; a body of literary works produced in a particular country or period, or of a particular genre.
Small cases in which keys are carried.
Flexible packaging, closed at one end and with a removable cap at the other, usually made of metal or plastic, for storing and dispensing artist's colors such as oil paint.
Large, ceramic, muglike drinking vessels usually having two or four handles, but sometimes as many as twelve; use especially for those made in England in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Any of various large ancient Greek wide-mouthed vessels with two side handles, usually horizontal, generally used for mixing wine and water.

Art that has as its subject peasant life, usually in the media of painting, prints, or sculpture. For art that is created by local artists in local traditions, regardless of subject matter, use "folk art."

Temporary decorations or pictorial works made either in interior or exterior spaces with colorfully arranged flowers or petals on the surface of the ground. Most often these are done in public squares or in churches as part of a festival, and may be of very large scale.
In Indian art or architecture, a figure with with erect phallus.

Nahua priests. Literally, "one who guards the deities" in Nahuatl. Part of a complex group of ministers of worship, each of whom engaged in very specific tasks such as rites of incense, or sacrifice as well as activities related to the maintenance and offering of fire. All generally wore long hair, anointed their bodies with black charcoal pigment, and performed frequent penances such as fasting and self-sacrifice. Each type of priest had a specific name, while in the colonial period, missionaries used the term teopixqui to designate the office of a Christian priest.
People or corporate bodies who specialize in making sound-producing apparatuses with the primary function of playing music.
In Indian architecture and art, the figure of a goddess riding on a makara; Gaṅgā.
The parts, activities, and duties held in life and society by a person or entity; includes significant roles or characteristics of a person or a function or purpose of a corporate body.

Hand-held tools, typically comprising a hardwood or plastic rolling device mounted to a handle, used to flatten, press, or obscure the seams between connected strips of material. Commonly utilized, for example, by wallpaper hangers, tailors, seamstresses, quilters, and leather workers.

Identification of a person with a particular state or nation. In a modern sense, the it is the legal status of being a citizen or subject of a particular state, usually involving mutual obligations of support and protection.
Stylized forms of graffiti using names or initials as markers. These are considered the most basic form of graffiti art.

Writings in which important or memorable events, jubilating institutions or important people are commemorated by describing those events, institutions or persons or recording memories of them in order to save them for posterity.

Refers to the work of a group of artists that was formed in Germany in1949. Rejecting Nazi artistic ideals, the style is typically characterized by simple, un-idealized portraits and landscapes showing the destruction in Germany during World War II.
Broad, flat, somewhat thick, and usually rigid, objects; thicker than sheets, wider than slats or boards.
Architectural materials reused; usually pieces built into a new fabric. A term used especially for ancient and Medieval instances of the practice.
Nationality, culture, and styles of the Veneto region, Italy.

Refers to the culture of the island of Ireland, which is located west of England on the Irish Sea and is currently divided administratively between the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. It often refers specifically to the Celtic culture of the island of Ireland.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of f the U.S. state of Ohio.
Building technique in which major structural elements are trusses and arches.
Nondestructive analytic technique used to monitor oxygen consumption. It is based on the dynamic quenching of the fluorescence or phosphoresence of luminescent dyes by molecular oxygen.
The process or function of augmenting, revising, or otherwise bringing material up-to-date.
The western ends of certain Carolingian and Ottonian churches, having an entrance hall, upper-level chapel, and towers.

Ancient Greek practices and philosophy stressing a movement in the world from cosmic order, represented mythologically by an original primordial egg, to a gradually developing disorder. Most scholars agree that by the 5th century BCE the Orphic movement existed, with travelling priests who offered teaching and initiation, based on a body of legend and doctrine said to have been founded by Orpheus.
Actions intended to bring something or someone into renewed existence; rebirth or restoration of a person, thing, geographical area, etc. by improvements.
Sexual attraction and sexual behavior, usually also including sexual identity, romantic attractions, and romantic behaviors. It may also include membership in sexual communities.
Refers to art created by artists who do not have formal training.

Having a form or outline forming a series of wave-like curves, a succession of gently rounded heights and hollows. Used, for example, with reference to architectural features such as arches, moldings, and tracery. For furniture pieces, the fronts of which have alternating concave and convex surfaces, use "serpentine (shape)." For features consisting of or bounded by curved lines in general, use "curvilinear."
The manner in which an artist or craftsman uses the technical elements of a medium to achieve a desired aesthetic effect.
Ordinances that outline how land developers may be granted concessions in exchange for providing amenities a community feels are desirable, such as low-income housing.
Refers generally to objects designed specifically to support vessels such as Roman kraters or Chinese bronze ritual vessels.
Tables of various designs used for displaying and serving food in a dining room. In modern usage, for case furniture used for serving food and displaying dishes, use "sideboards (furniture)."

Refers to a traditional Norwegian chair made from a solid log, produced by hollowing out a tree trunk so that the lower portion retains the cylindrical shape of the trunk. The kubbestol is typically decorated with traditional Norwegian painting and carving.
Sheet iron cylinders 8 to 10 inches in diameter and about a foot high, pierced all over with regularly spaced holes. Placed over burning rushlights or rush candles at night for safety.
Long pins of hardwood used for fastening planks or timbers in some post-and-beam construction.
Refers to persons who are currently alive.
Persons or corporate bodies who participate in the exhibition of objects, documents, or information at fairs, conferences, shows, or other events, public or private.
People of great wealth and typically of great influence and prestige in society. Those whose assets are worth at least a million pounds, Euros, dollars, or another roughly equivalent currency.
The large pointed blade components of plows, attached to a colter, with a sharp edge to cut the earth while plowing.
Equipment used for the reproduction of graphics through photomechanical or electronic means.
Wooden boards used by entomologists for setting insect specimens.
Style that developed in Greece and Turkey in the 18th century, drawing upon European Rococo style.
Culture of a dynasty that ruled parts of eastern India  6th-8th centuries.
Fine-grained abrasive commercially available in the form of blocks, bricks, or rods of solidified or semi-solid abrasive paste.
Conical hats, usually brightly colored or patterned, worn at celebrations. Usually made of paper or plastic.
The prose description of the provenance or history of the owners or others in possession of a work of art or other property.

Manual or mechanized devices designed to twist raw silk filaments into a unified thread to be used for weaving. While these devices vary, they typically comprise a twisting frame that rotates a series of spindles which twist skeins of raw silk and winds them onto bobbins. The first evidence of these devices can be traced back to either 1272 -1276 CE in Lucca, Italy or 1313 in China, though the devices could have been in use much earlier.
Instruments for revealing radium emanations visible to the naked eye.
Hand-held tools that were historically used to slit the axial surface of a dental crown to facilitate its removal.
The standard unit of currency of South Africa.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 2799 to 2700 (or 2800 to 2701) Before Common Era.
Grouping of around 12 small language families that were spoken mainly in California, Arizona, and Baja California. Different versions of the Hokan hypothesis include different member languages.
The capacity or tendency for any material such as paper, metal, or plastic to show effects of past treatment or for returning to a former condition or shape.
Lines along which there are marked increases of slope, at the outer margins of continental shelves or island shelves.

Instruments used to study human sensitivity to changes in pitch. Originally invented by William Stern in 1897 for psychological research. These consist of a brass resonator tube that is supplied with a flow of air across its top end while an interior piston may be raised or lowered, or in some cases mercury introduced, changing the volume of the chamber, thus altering the pitch of the tone of the resonator. A circular scale attached to the front indicates the audible resonance frequency.

Japanese porcelain ware that was developed in the 18th century in modern-day Hakoda, within the city of Kasama. Ware includes a household goods, kitchen containers, mixing bowls, and jugs; after WW II, export goods such as tea vessels, flower vases, and sake containers were manufactured.
Artists who specialize in creating art that incorporates movement, particularly mobiles or similar works.
People who make illustrations for printed materials, including newspapers and magazines.

Traveling on foot at a moderate pace, proceeding by steps, and moving the feet alternately so that there is always one foot on the ground in bipedal locomotion and two or more feet on the ground in quadrupedal locomotion.

Fabulous and legendary animals usually regarded as having the body of a horse with a single horn projecting from the forehead. The unicorn has at various times been identified or confused with the rhinoceros, with various species of antelope, or with other animals having a horns or a horn-like projection from the head. The horn of the narwhal was passed off as unicorn horn; the unicorn horn was valuable, reputed to possess medicinal or magical properties
Melinex is the trademarked name for one in a series of clear polyethylene terephthalate (PET) polyester films produced by DuPont.
Refers to a range of bluish gray colors resembling the color of pewter, an alloy of tin.
Schools that award general education degrees in a wide variety of subjects that are not part of graduate education.
Portions of bodies of water that are shallow.
Low-lying flat or level ground, usually associated with wetlands and river valleys.

Formerly used to refer to what was considered an order of mammals characterized by either the complete lack of teeth, or teeth that are small and few, such as in armadillos and anteaters. It was subsequently realized that Edentata was polyphyletic, meaning it contained animals that were actually members of unrelated families; thus the order is now considered invalid by cladistic standards.
Style and culture of the people of the nation of Namibia or of the Namib desert.
Retail businesses selling various articles.
The male gametes or reproductive cells in animals, especially in vertebrates, which fertilizes the female gamete, the ovum.

Components of scouring machines, typically made of cast iron and equipped with a perforated bottom and sequeeze rollers, designed to wash shorn wool to remove unwanted contaminents. Specifically, these bowls are filled with a mixture of water, detergent, and sodium carbonate or another alkali acting as a detergent builder to achieve grease emulsification. Typical scouring machines incporate two to four bowls, on top of which wool is fed by sets of harrows as a saturated mat. As both water and the wool are fed into each bowl at the same time, in the same direction, the wool fibers are agitated and dirt or grease is freed from the surface of the wool. In conjunction with a heating component and a series of rinsing bowls, these bowls then utilize squeeze rollers to remove persistent grease from the wool materials.

Refers to distinctive glass made in Venice, Italy. It can refer to early glass made from about 450 CE when glass-makers from Aquileia fled there and were soon joined by others from Byzantium. In addition, the term is particularly used to refer to glass made on the Venetian island of Murano from before 1292 to the present day. It is generally a sodiac type of glass; soda glass is light in weight and highly ductile. Venetian glass incorporates a number of styles and techniques although Venetian glass-makers particularly excelled in the making of colored glass, agate glass, opaque white glass (lattimo), cristallo, filigrana, and millefiori. Engraving is rarely found while enameling and gilding are common, particularly in fifteenth- and sixteenth-century specimens. In order to protect their profits and the secrets of Venetian glass, the Venetians confined glassmakers under pain of death to the island of Murano; however, the techniques were eventually imitated in "Altare glass" and "façon de Venise." For glass made exclusively on Murano, see "Murano glass."
An alkaline solution of soda ash, borax, or ammonia, used as a cleanser and stripper. Sig water was formerly made from a solution of stale urine.
In Indian architecture or sculpture, a decorative motif of jingle bells suspended from a chain dangling from a gorgon-mask suspended from grāsamukhas (gorgon faces).
Structures housing facilities and institutions dedicated to science.
Binary compound formed from a halogen and another element.
Generally, any thing laid over something else, more specifically a transparent sheet placed over an image, text, map, diagram, or artwork, to form a composite.
Small medicated sticks that help to stop the bleeding of small cuts in the skin, as from shaving.
Particular types of subdivisions of towns or cities, particularly where there are four divisions total. Examples are in Italy.

Implements consisting of a wooden staff or handle, at the end of which a stouter and shorter staff or club, called a swingle or swipple, is so hung as to swing freely. One example is used for threshing corn.
Administrative bodies subject to a sultan.
Process or action of digging to extract metal, coal, or other substances, or to create a tunnel, such as under a wall, fort, mountain, or another thing.
Refers to he incorporation and absorption of water.
Attributes relating to position, which include context, orientation, portions of a whole, or relative to other properties.

Cloth covering attached to Native North American cradleboards, often decorated with floral or iconographic beadwork. Designed to hold babies to the cradleboard; moss is usually placed in the bottom of the bag to cushion the baby and act as a diaper. Name is derived from this moss.
Miniature scale railroad steam engines, which are usually a part of sets of other railroad cars and accessories.
French silver coins of varying values used in the 16th century.

Aparatuses of various designs for slicing, chopping, or cutting vegetables or fruit. An example consists of a flat, rectangular piece of wood with raised edges on the upper surface; equipped with an angled slot inset with a metal blade in the middle and sometimes a handle at one end.
Traditional maxims of a religious teacher or sage. An example of usage is with reference to the sayings of Jesus.
Small locking receptacles that provide secure storage for keys that need to be made available to multiple people. These are usually secured by a combination lock.
Cups which attach to a painter's palette and are used for holding small quantities of medium or solvent.
Bowls of varied shape and materials, used for serving wine.

Refers to ancient Greek small, deep bowls that curve in sharply at the shoulder and have a distinct neck with overhanging lip and round bottom designed so the bowl could sit on a stand, although some had feet. A lebes may be equipped with a pair of upright handles at the shoulder and often with a domed cover topped by a tall, stemmed handle. Bronze lebetes were used for cooking and those made of terracotta were used for mixing wine. They are distinguished from "dinoi" by their smaller size. Many scholars in the past have used the term to refer to both the dinos and lebes, because they thought that the term dinos referred to a cup.
Visual works, usually paintings or sculptures, that depict the Virgin Mary holding the dead body of Christ, generally on her lap.

Carved geometrical patterns of intersecting lines, either pierced or in relief; in the late 19th century applied especially to openwork patterns carved out of thin pieces of wood with a fretsaw. For similar patterns confined to a continuous band, use "frets (patterns)."
In Indian art and architecture, a courtesan figure.
Specialists in the study or science of theology, or religious doctrines and practices, generally from the viewpoint of religious believers.
People who make music boxes, which are mechanical musical instruments that incorporate tuned steel prongs and moving parts driven by a clockwork mechanism.
In Indian art and architecture, a garland-bearing person/vidyādhara/angel motif.

Authoritative instructions for conduct or prescriptive instructions regarding a certain procedure, activity, or topic. Examples are instructions governing procedure in documentation or cataloging, for a legislative body, game, sport, or contest. For less prescriptive recommendations, use "guidelines."
Implements used for spraying paint or other substances over large areas.

Artifacts, institutions, persons, literature, and other entities regarded as emblematic and valuable in representing a nation's cultural heritage and identity. The identification of such works may be codified in law or statute.
In general, an orderly classification for a defined domain. More specifically, a classificatory nomenclatures of real objects, organisms, or phenomena, especially for living and extinct organisms.
Books containing written or printed music.
Refers to the style of painting popular in the early 1960's in Paris, London and New York. Reacting against Absract Expressionism, the style is characterized by a return of figurative images.
Strips of stiff material, such as wood or metal, for example used as louver boards or in chair backs.
General term for screens, sheets, louvers, parasols, or other devices or objects used for protection of a building, person, or other entity from the heat and light of the sun.
Nationality, styles, and culture of Verona, Italy.
Refers to the culture of the modern nation of Italy, or in general to cultures that have occupied the boot-shaped Italian peninsula in the Mediterranean Sea.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Oklahoma.
Building technique in which structural elements comprise girders of open framework.

Peptide mass fingerprinting (PMF) is an analytic technique for protein identification. Proteins extracted from the proteome of a sample are individually digested using a protease into a series of smaller peptides. The set of masses of these peptide fragments is then measured with a mass spectrometer, forming a peptide mass fingerprint of the protein which can then be compared with known protein sequences for this organism in a protein sequence database.
Subsidiary parts of buildings extending out from the main portion.
Periods of withdrawal to a place of seclusion for the purpose of spiritual rest and restoration.

Theory in sociology that sociocultural advance is the product of intergroup conflict and competition and that therefore the socially elect classes (those possessing wealth and power) possess biological superiority in the struggle for existence.
Works of art created as a series, a popular genre since the late 19th century, especially in Minimal art of the 1960s.
Having the outline of the uppercase letter U, or for a three dimensional form, when in cross-section resembling a U.

Refers to a philosophical or critical concept that supposes that humanity's attempt to find meaning are doomed due to the chaotic and inexplicable nature of the universe in which we live. The concept was thought to have been embodied in the Theatre of the Absurd, a dramatic genre of the 1950s and 1960s, exemplified in the work of Samuel Beckett and Eugène Ionesco, among others.
Forming or producing letters to record the ideas which characters and words express or to communicate the ideas by visible signs.
Techniques related to music arrangement.
Furniture combining features of a table and cupboard and used to hold articles (as a pitcher, basin, and towel) for washing the hands and face.
Term generally applied to small, portable tables designed to hold food or drink for one person.

Open-arm chairs with upholstered seats and backs, popular in the 18th and 19th centuries in North America. Seats are generally low and shallow, and the backs are high and often have serpentine cresting.

Devices which make it possible to burn the last inch of a candle. Includes small pans or short cylinders, usually metal, with one or more pins or adjustable arms at the top for holding a candle stub, and some with a peg to fit into a candleholder.
A link with a screw-thread at one end and a swivel at the other, used for tightening a rod or stay.

People who hold an office or position temporarily, as substitutes in place of the person to whom the office belongs. For those who assume the position of head of a monarchy in the minority or disability of the rightful monarch, use "regents." For those who claim a title or throne to which they have no just right, use "pretenders."
Those who perform exorcisms.
Historically, people who change money from one form to another, as a profession.
Parts or components of printing presses.
Instruments or apparatuses used to immobilize or confine a human being or animal.
Devices that assist in staining, increasing visibility and contrast in microscopic samples for scientific analysis.
Style and culture of one of the largest Indian scheduled tribes; the Santal are a Kolarian people of northeastern India and Bangladesh.

Refers to the artwork of the North American Indians of the Northwest Coast who traditionally lived on the mainland and islands around the Skeen and Ness rivers and Milbank Sound in what are now British Columbia, Canada and Alaska. They speak any of three Tsimshian dialects: Niska, coastal Tsimshian, and Kitksan (or Gitksan). Tsimshian is classified as a Penutian language.
Material used to produce heat or power by burning.

Wood of the tree belonging to the genus Carya, valued because it is strong, elastic, and shock resistant. The reddish brown wood has a straight grain and a fine texture that polishes well; used for flooring, tool handles, farm implements, chairs, wheel spokes, golf clubs, baseball bats, and for flavoring smoked food. It is also split into thin canes for weaving. The heartwood is white.

Rare metallic element, the penultimate in the lanthanide series, having the symbol Yb and atomic number 70. Ytterbium is a soft, lustrous silver-white metal. Some of its isotopes generate gamma rays when irradiated and are used as a radiation source-substitute for portable X-ray machines.
Any mineral that occurs as minute sheetlike or fibrous crystals in clay; it is a hydrated aluminosilicate having a layered crystal structure.
Kits for making scale models of buildings or vehicles. They consist of loose parts that must be assembled or glued together.

Element for identifying materials that have an association to the materials being described. May be used to identify associated materials in the same repository or elsewhere. These materials may be related by sphere of activity, subject matter, or other characteristics.

Manual or mechanized devices, comprising rows of pulsating needle-like devices operating along a series of rollers, designed to manufacture carpet or other upholstory products by inserting loose pile yarn into a pre-woven carrier/backing material, thus creating a patterned or looped surface. As yarn is individually fed to each of the needles in the needle row, an additional set of tufting needles is inserted into the backing cloth; before the former row of needles retracts, loopers pick up the yarn in a repeated process that creates a series of loops on the surface of the carrier material.
Heating devices used for evaluating the fire resistance of materials and objects.
Cups used for rinsing the mouth in a dental office or at home when brushing teeth.
The standard unit of currency of South Korea.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 2499 to 2400 (or 2500 to 2401) Before Common Era.
Language isolate having several dialects, spoken by indigenous people of the Pacific coast in the Mexican state of Oaxaca.
Devices designed to visualize audio waveforms, particularly the human voice. Vibrations were conducted through solid or liquid media, and either projected or photographed to view the result.
Surface damage produced by grinding contact; sharp-edged, narrow furrows often involving loss of surface material.
Areas of broad elevation that rise gently, and generally smoothly, from the sea floor.

Attic Greek red-figure pottery, primarily vases, found at Kerch in the Ukraine and North Africa. It is characterized by the adoption of new techniques, the use of gold and other colors, and tall figures. The term was first applied in the 19th century, but is rarely used by modern scholars, who generally do not feel that the common characteristics of the individual painters are distinctive enough to define a separate style.
People who make lacquerware, which are objects, usually made of thin wood, that are coated and decorated with layers of lacquer, a particular paint or varnish that dries with a high gloss.
Artists in any media who focus primarily on religious objects and subjects in their works.
The act of speaking very quietly, without vibration of the vocal chords.
In Indian art and architecture, an animal vehicle, an animal or bird mount that carries a deity.
Trademarked name for a series of polyvinyl acetate emulsions used in conservation as paint binders, coatings, consolidants, and adhesives.
A range of blue colors resembling the color of phenyl blue dye, a dark blue dye which is a phenylimide derivative of a quinone.

Degree-granting institutions that may include liberal arts undergraduate colleges, graduate schools, and undergraduate or graduate professional schools. A university is a group of schools for studies after secondary school, with at least one of these schools being a college where students receive a bachelor's degree.
Areas of permanent snow and ice forming the accumulation area at the head of a glacier.
Natural or man-made basins that control the runoff from large storms.

In former classifications, referred to a major division of Mammalia comprising all hoofed mammals, which are now divided into the orders Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates) and Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates).

A theater production system based on a permanent association of actors, and often a particular location or theater structure. Professional theater companies evolved during the Renaissance in response to urbanization in the major countries of Europe. Modern theater companies follow the same model as the earliest ones: a group of actors, scenarists, and technicians devoted to presenting theatrical performances.

The posterior extremities of animals, in position opposite to the head and forming either a distinct flexible appendage to the trunk (e.g., in a dog or cat) or a continuation of the trunk behind the anus (as in a dolphin). In vertebrates, the tail contains an extension of the vertebrae beyond the backbone.

Automated feeders comprising a series of scouring bowls and squeeze heads, which carry wool materials from one bowl to the next to facilitate the grease emulsification and scouring processes. These feeders are typically linked to an incline dryer and woolgrease recovery system within a larger scouring machine.
A plug, typically of cotton, used in cases of hemorrhage or to absorb menstrual flow.
Administrative divisions or districts of the former Soviet Union, and presently used in other Eastern European countries, such as Moldova.

States a people is a tributary to a suzerain ruler, or in more recent history, to a more powerful state that controls its foreign affairs while allowing the tributary vassal state some limited domestic autonomy. An historical example is the Ottoman Empire and its surrounding regions.

The making of holes through an object; may be done purposefully, either when the object is made or later, or may be the result of natural processes. Having a hole, as a result of the drilling process.
The phenomenon of weak linking between molecules, particularly water molecules or other molecules with a hydroxyl group, such as alcohols.
The quality or condition of tending to react, especially the tendency of a substance to undergo chemical reactions.
Ornamental bands or borders, especially on an ecclesiastical vestment.
Toy versions of stoves with for children's play. On older versions, cooking could actually be done on charcoal or by using electricity.
Byzantine gold coins used between the 10th and 12th centuries.
General term for culinary knives and other blades of various designs used specifically to slice vegetables or fruit.

Rules or principles of conduct, morality or prudence, expressed in sententious form. It is often used specifically for precepts of morality or prudence occurring in Old English verse, or for self-evident propositions assumed as a premiss in mathematical or dialectical reasoning. The meaning of this term may overlap somewhat with "aphorisms."
Bags of canvas, nylon, leather, or other flexible material worn on the back by means of a strap over each shoulder.
Vessels used to hold paste, often including compartments for water in an effort to keep the paste from hardening.

Ancient Greek vessels in the form of a shallow bowl with two horizontal handles and a lid. Such vessels are often depicted on vases in connection with weddings, as containers for articles used by women for dressing and grooming, and as containers for small items such as toys, spices, or thread. Lekanai were also used for serving food.

Representations of real individuals that are intended to capture a known or supposed likeness, usually including the face of the person. For representations intended to be anonymous, or of fictional or mythological characters, see "figures (representations)."

Electronic art that incorporates process in the creation of the work. The work itself is usually experienced through time and space, and may include sound, motion, animated graphics, sculptural elements, or any combination of these. Generative art has a performative aspect. For visual art that incorporates algorithms to produce static visual works, use "algorithmic art."
In Indian architecture, a ghoul figure.
Ecclesiastics or lay attendants who carry burning incense in religious ceremonies.
Those who make or sell eyeglasses and contact lenses in accordance with the prescriptions of eye specialists such as optometrists and opthamologists.
In Indian art and architecture, a flying celestial angelic male figure carrying garland; garland-bearing heavenly warrior.

Designation indicating something, someone, a characteristic, or an activity belongs to the second class in respect of importance, is not chief or principal, is of minor importance or subordinate, or is occurring or existing second in a sequence.
Small binder's finishing tools consisting of a usually brass shank or head cast in designs of varying complexity, set into a wooden handle.
The absence of clothing, leaving those parts of the body that, in the cultural traditions of the viewer, are usually covered, exposed to view.
Short poems or prose compositions in which text is arranged so that the last letters of each line form a word, phrase, or motto.
Published notices of a death, usually with a brief biography of the deceased.

Refers to the style of painting and sculpture popular in the  late 1970's in Europe and the United States.  Reacting against Conceptualist Art, the style is characterized by a fusion of abstraction and figuration and an emphasis on the creative process of manipulating images.
Object genre for any close-fitting protective covers or cases, particularly objects that are closed around all sides except for a slit or opening at one or two edges or sides.

Works in any medium, typically of relatively small size, and usually but not always cut, engraved, or inscribed with prayers, astrological signs, or magical symbols, intended to heal or keep the bearer from harm. For talismans or other objects worn on the person, with or without inscriptions, use "amulets."
Nationality or culture of the island of Jersey and surrounding islands, off the coast of Normandy, France, currently a dependency of the United Kingdom.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Oregon.
Technique using thick joints of lime-rich mortar that serves as a flexible gasket when laying irregular bricks to the line, level, and overall gauge required for a wall or facade.
The practice of measuring phosphates in soil from archaeological sites to map the boundaries of settlements and agricultural areas.

An atheistic religion established in the 1970s by Claude Vorilhon, known as Raël, who is held by his followers to be a prophet along with Buddha, Mohammed, Moses, and Jesus Christ. Among its basic tenets are that life on Earth was created through genetic engineering by extra-terrestrials and that life may be continued after death through cloning, citing as proof an interpretation of certain scientific material, the Bible, and other religious texts.
Sudden headlong rushes or flights of herds of animals, especially cattle and horses, usually due to fright.
Important subjects of debate or litigation having to do with an organized and interdependent community.
Art works, especially paintings and prints, designed for popular taste and marketed as home furnishings.
Having an outline or form that is higher than it is wide, swelling symetrically outward at or near the middle and narrowing at top and bottom, resembling the contours of a vase.
An underlying intent or meaning in a work of visual or literary art; also a motif, subject, or idea repeated in a number of artistic works.

Tables on which the game of table tennis or ping-pong is played. These are 9 feet or 2.74 meters long by 5 feet or 1.525 meters in width. The playing surface is at a height of 2.5 feet or 76 centimeters. These may be made from a variety of materials, and may be either portable or fixed.
Armchairs with adjustable backs and loose cushions, of a type first produced by William Morris, Philip Webb, and the firm Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Co. about 1866 in England.
Supports for the shade of a lamp, consisting of a ring-shaped channel, a wire frame, or both.
Flattened rings, usually made of metal, that are used in joints in order to relieve friction and prevent unsteadiness.
Collectively refers to the non-noble people in Nahua culture. Frequently associated with commoners, vassals, or peasants from the colonial period forward.
People who explore, usually by traveling, in search of scientific, geographical, or other types of information.
People who lend money at interest on the security of an article deposited in their possession.
Disks or drums with an attached abrasive for power tool application in sanding.
Instruments for measuring and determining the configuration of and measuring angles of the chest.
Culture of a dynasty that ruled in the Deccan region late second century BCE- early third century CE.
Style or culture of a Native North American tribe located in Washington State.
The materials or formula of ingredients from which paper is made.

Wood from the genus Ilex, white or grayish-white in color and having a fine uniform texture with an irregular grain pattern. It has been used for sculpture, carvings, veneer, marquetry, engraving, and burning.

Chemical  element having symbol Y and atomic number 39. Yttrium resembles lanthanide metals very closely and is often classified as a ‘rare earth element.' Yttrium’s most important use is for making the phosphors used in television screen displays and in LEDs. Yttrium phosphors emit a clear red light when excited by electrons.
A green mineral occurring commonly in slender prisms or acicular crystals and composed of sulphate and chloride of copper.
The dioxide form of silicon, SiO2, occurring in quartz sand, flint, and agate. It is used chiefly in its prepared white powder form in the manufacture of glass, ceramics, and abrasives.
In Indian architecture or sculpture, a chain of grāsas; grāsahāra, grāsapaṭṭī.
General term for structures providing some degree of protection, refuge, or defense; if possible, use a more specific term.
Documents that ratify or identify the belonging of an individual to an official group.

Identification of citations to sources of textual information related to the work of art or architecture being described, including published bibliographic materials, Web sites, archival documents, unpublished manuscripts, and references to verbal opinions expressed by scholars or subject experts.
Devices for noting the tithonic or chemical effect of rays of light.
Dental equipment incorporating a bulb or lamp that is used for polymerization of light-cure resin-based composites, and for other purposes.
The standard unit of currency of Spain prior to adoption of the Euro.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 2099 to 2000 (or 2100 to 2001) Before Common Era.

Family of languages spoken in most of Europe and areas of European settlement and in much of Southwest and South Asia. The well-attested languages of the Indo-European family fall into 10 main branches documented in sizable texts.

Devices comprised of acoustic receivers positioned at right angles to one another and attached to a shaft that is held by the user. The sound collected by these horns is conducted to ear-pieces through rubber hoses. Developed to discover the position of the source of sounds in space, as invented ca.1880, particularly for use on ships to locate the position of foghorns.
Narrow ridges or lines which indicate that an object has been made by molding.
Valleys on shelves on the sea floor; generally the shoreward extensions of canyons.

Japanese porcelain manufactured in Kaga Province, now part of Ishikawa Prefecture from 1655 to 1704 and again from 1807 to the present. Older productions are typically tableware in dark overglazed enamels, the bodies being coarse-grained and the glazes varying from dull to shiny. Later productions feature more eclectic, colorful, and intricate designs.
Refers primarily to Native American draftsmen and painters of the 19th century who used account ledger books or similar lined or bound paper to record vignettes of the Plains Indian.
Photographers who specialize in creating works that copy existing works, including other photographs.
Involuntary deep inhalation with the mouth open, often accompanied by the act of stretching.
In Indian art or architecture, a horse-faced female nature-spirit, generally malevolent; female yakṣa; female divinity associated with Jina and guardian deity of Jaina church; generally mare-faced.
Registered trademark for a series of optically clear, colorless, thermoplastic polyester films. First introduced in the early 1950s, Mylar is composed of polyethylene terephthalate.

Various colors ranging from pale or grayish blue to a deep blue, named for the color of powdered smalt that was formerly used in washing clothes as a bluing agent and in coloring porcelain; the smalt powder is deep blue, and the smalt diluted in water is a pale blue color.

Educational institutions offering instruction in one or more skilled or semiskilled trades or occupations. For educational facilities traditionally training technicians in business, industry, and commerce, usually for an immediate local area, use "polytechnics."
A long arm of the sea or relatively narrow channel between the mainland and an island or islands or connecting two larger bodies of water.
Landforms which are the result of water moving over the earth's surface, shaped by erosional and depositional processes.
Style and culture of the western African country of Niger, formerly part of the Federation of French West Africa.

Corporations originally formed for the purpose of exercising the functions of a trustee, such as managing property for the benefit of other organizations or individuals, now usually engaging in other financial activities as well, such as banking.

Bone-like structures found in the mouths of many vertebrates, used for biting and chewing. Some also use teeth for hunting and defensive purposes. The roots of teeth anchor the teeth in the jaw; they are covered by gums. Teeth are not technically made of bone, but rather of multiple tissues of varying density and hardness. The cellular tissues that develop as teeth originate in the the ectoderm. The general structure of teeth is similar across the vertebrates, but there is variation in placement and form. Monophyodonts develop only one set of teeth for use in adulthood, while polyphyodonts develop many sets of teeth.

Hand-held wooden tools, comprising a cylindrical head with a semi-circular groove cut along its length attached to a thin handle, designed to pass serving (typically spunyarn or twine) around a rope. To facilitate serving, a method of protecting rope ends from damage by wrapping them in yarn or twine, the rope is fitted into the tool's groove and the yarn/twine is wound tightly around its head and handle. As the tool is rotated around the rope, the serving material is fed in such a way that allows it to be kept taut thus ensuring maximum tightness. Resembling a mallet, this tool is most often used by ship crews to manage rope while sailing.

Hydrazine is a hydronitrogen compound and a powerful reducing agent. It is a colorless liquid synthesized for use in pesticides and as a corrosion inhibitor in boilers. It is also a component in rocket fuels. In conservation, hydrazine has been used to reduce manganese content in medieval stained glass and thus to lighten browning.

Any of various horizontal structural members in a frame or paneling, as in a window sash, paneled door, or chest of drawers, or joining the vertical posts of furniture, as in the crest rail of a chair.

Political entities have a government in which the supreme rule is intended to be God or a god directly, or through a priestly order. Also, one whose government is heavily influenced by religious leaders.
The process of making or forming a hole by piercing or probing with a pointed instrument.

The chemical reaction of water and any other compound substance to form two or more new substances. This involves ionization of the water molecules as well as splitting of the compound hydrolized. For example, when a salt is hydrolized, the result is a slightly acid or alkaline solution.
Patterns or passages intended to be repeated. Examples are a decorative pattern that is repeated uniformly over a surface, or a passage repeated in music.
Sections of a garment set in vertically and usually stitched on two sides or strips of cloth attached at the top and allowed to hang freely from a garment.
Toy versions of dining, tea or coffee sets tailored to children or dolls. Older dinner sets are usually made of porcelain, earthenware or tin.. Modern versions are usually made of plastic.

Narratives or histories autobiographical in nature or stressing the author's personal experience of the events. For works that are written daily or on a frequent basis, laying out a day's events and experiences, use "diaries."

Boxes with small interior compartments for storing pieces of lace. The term is popularly applied to wide and shallow boxes, often decorated with marquetry, made in the late 17th-century in England; such boxes, however, were not necessarily intended to contain lace.

Covered containers in the shape of a vase or jar and characterized by pierced decorations on the shoulder or cover, or both. They were intended primarily for liquid or dried potpourri, which is a mixture of flower petals, spices, fruit juices, or other aromatic substances. For similar containers, often vaselike in form, in which aromatic pastilles may be burned or liquid perfumes evaporated, use "cassolettes."
Ancient Greek vessels set on a high foot or pedestal and with a bulbous body and a disk-shaped rim around the mouth.
In Indian art or architecture, a erotic depiction; erotic act.
Visual works made of glass. Examples are tableware of glass used in serving food and drink.
In Indian architecture, a female vidhyādhara figure.
The wise people of Nahua societies, who were said to be the owners of painted books and possessors of knowledge.

People who make wooden panels to be used for panel paintings. For example, in Europe, In the Middle Ages and beyond, the panel maker was a skilled craftsman who belonged to guilds and signed his work.
Motifs representing grotesque or otherwise caricatured faces of humans or animals, usually viewed frontally; found in various architectural and decorative arts contexts.

The details, manner, or position in which anything is set, fixed, or placed. Examples include the props and surroundings of a figure in a portrait or the literary framework of a narrative or other composition. For the sets or aggregates of physical things, conditions, and influences surrounding and affecting an organism, object, or structure, use "environments (object groupings)."
The transmission of facts and cultural knowledge, rules, beliefs, and stories in oral rather than written form.

Master documents containing a standard or preset design, layout, format, and sometimes style, but lacking some or most content. Templates are intended to be used for creating content according to a prescribed and repeatable formula in electronic or paper media. Examples of the use of templates are to create form letters, pages in printed media, and HTML pages on a Web site.
Brief, formal, written compositions, often designed for publication, generally presented orally at a public venue. Examples include writings on art historical, scientific, or historical topics.
Refers to a style of painting that combines ideas of science and art, and mythology and history, updating 16th-century Mannerism's use of distorted bodies and space.
Stout, sharp-pointed pieces of metal, wood, or other hard material, or stout sharp-pointed projecting parts of an object.

Objects or other gifts given to a person or place, or exchanged between two parties, as a sign of esteem and honor. May involve ritual and ceremony; in historical contexts, may involve slaves or animals.
Nationality or culture of the region or nation of Kosovo in southeastern Europe.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Pennsylvania.
Construction consisting of upright posts or stakes interwoven with twigs or tree branches and plastered with a mixture of clay and straw.

Predictive modeling refers to any process used to create a statistical model of future behavior. In archaeological predictive modeling,  analysis of quantifiable attributes from land that has undergone archaeological survey, such as soil types, vegetation, geomorphology, etc., is used to predict the archaeological sensitivity of unsurveyed areas.

A religious and political movement originating in Jamaica in the 1930s that identifies the former Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia as the Messiah, and Africans as the chosen people of the Bible. Rastafarians, or Rastas adhere to codes of behaviour and dress, including the wearing of dreadlocks, the smoking of cannabis as a sacrament, and a diet that excludes pork and shellfish.
Instances or events where enemies or adversaries are overcome in battle, usually by force of arms.
Changes in the social status of individuals or groups.

Generally, any item created by soldiers, prisoners of war, or civilians from any kind of material, as long as it and they are associated in time or place with armed conflict or its consequences. Specifically, objets of metal, cloth, bone, or wood made as remembrances either during or after World War I or World War II.

Having an outline or form comprising or in cross-section delimited by two straight sides that are wider on one end and intersect or come to a near-point on the other end, resembling shape of the letter V.

Describes phenomena that are not media-specific or can be realized in a large number of media, such as literature, art, film, or music. Transmedial phenomena can occur with narrative or conceptual content in the form of myths, legends, or cultural symbols that have become part of common discourse and lost their connection to any specific medium.
Process of applying oil on or to; rubbing, smearing, covering, moistening, or lubricating with oil.

Term applied to small tables of various designs, intended to hold a tea service, or part of the service, and other articles used for serving tea; may have a top so made that it could be lifted off for separate use as a tray.

Refers to a series of cantilevered chair designs by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe first realized ca. 1927. the structure is of tubular steel and is regarded as a prime example of this type of furniture design emerging from the Bauhaus in the 1920s.
Devices, usually glass, suspended above lighting devices with an open flame to protect the ceiling from soot deposits.
Those who sacrifice their lives for the sake of religion or principle.
Those who establish or originate things such as cultures, movements, institutions, or communities.
Parts or components of scaffolds.
Instruments or apparatuses that convey notice or warning.
Specimens of tissue taken for scientific analysis or testing.
Culture of the fourth dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, 1414-1451; founded by Khizr Khan.

Grains or pieces of gum and sometimes spices that are burned to produce a fragrant odor. Incense is frequently used as an oblation, or in religious ritual. The term can also refer to the smoke produced by the burning of incense.
Wood of the genus Carpinus, used for turned and machined parts in windmills, pool cues, drumsticks, and piano actions.
A very hard crystalline mineral made of aluminum oxide, used chiefly as an abrasive.

Semi-metallic element, having symbol Si and atomic number 14, in amorphous and crystalline forms, occurring in a combined state in minerals and rocks and constituting more than one fourth of the earth's crust. The chemical industry uses the term "silicon metal" and "silicon" interchangeably, and anything but pure silicon is generally referred to in this context as "semiconductor-grade silicon."
In Indian architecture, a band of gorgon faces in series; band of grāsa motifs; band showing grāsa heads in file.
Objects worn on the shoulders, usually as part of a uniform that indicate membership or rank within a group.
Identification of iimages that depict the work of art or architecture being described.

Instruments used for measurement or analysis by the process of determining the concentration of a solution or its constituents by adding measured volumes of a reagent until a reaction just begins or ceases to occur.

Appliances comprising a thin sheet of rubber, pierced by a dental dam punch to allow the crowns of one or more teeth to protrude, with the purpose to provide moisture control, operator visibility, and hygienic conditions.
General term for unit of currency of various values, historically used in the Netherlands and Belgium; based on a small coin, originally silver.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 2399 to 2300 (or 2400 to 2301) Before Common Era.
Family of around 16 North American indigenous languages spoken in the Middle Atlantic and South USA.
Instruments developed for counting the frequency of vibrations of tuning forks, and later used to make vibrations visible in materials such as textiles.
Ceramic glaze defect stemming from poor glaze fit or high compression and causing pieces of glaze to flake or raise off the clay body; frequently occurs along ridges and rims.
Zones adjacent to continents (or around islands) that extend from low water lines to a depth at which there are marked increases of slopes towards oceanic depths.

Ware produced by the earlier phase of Bandkeramik culture, characterized by pottery decorated with scratches, grooves, and relief patterns arranged in bands of meanders, curves, spirals, and wave-shapes.

Creators of Christian devotional images in sculpture and painting, called "retablos" and "bultos", active in Mexico from the Spanish colonial period, and later in the Spanish-speaking United States, to the present day.
Artists who create works featuring light as an artistic medium.
Female practitioner of yōga, endowed with supernatural power.
Produced by Markal, Paintstik is a solid paint marker in the form of a large cylindrical crayon, and is intended mainly for industrial mark-making.
Colors in a range of bright, deep geenish blues, resembling the color of the pigment of the same name that originally consisted chiefly of ferric ferrocyanide.
A narrow waterway, usually narrower and less extensive than a sound, connecting two larger bodies of water.
Low places located in ridges, and not used for transportation.
Nationality, styles, and culture of Réunion, Africa, located in the Indian Ocean, east of Madagascar.
Businesses that specialize in urban planning, which concerms the designing and improving the spacial organization and content of urban areas.
The digits of the foot of a human or an animal.
Implements which are inserted into the warp threads as they are prepared for the loom, and keep the different sheds separate while the loom is being threaded.

Binary compound of oxygen and iron as occurs naturally, for example, in the mineral hematite. There are sixteen known iron oxides and oxyhydroxides. The corrosion product rust is a form of iron oxide. Iron oxides have many applications including chemical catalyst, pigment and colorant.

Any form of recess made in one member of wood, metal, stone, or another material, particularly when the recess is made in order to receive another member. Included are rabbets, which are channels or grooves cut along the edge or face of a member, or rectangular recesses made along a projecting angle to form a step or shoulder.
Equipment or apparatuses that involve ultraviolet radiation or chemical means to produce a cosmetic tan on skin.
Governing entities that encompass and serve a multi-jurisdictional regional community.
Agricultural tools consisting of a long straight handle, furnished at the end with two or more large prongs, and used for carrying, digging, lifting, or tossing.

The capability of being changed back to a previous status or condition; the quality of being not irrevocably permanent, but of being easily and safely disassembled, for example to correct an error in conservation treatment or to replace worn components.
Loops of fabric or leather worn around on the outside of pant legs to protect the fabric from wear.
Toy versions of telephones intended for children's play.
Rabbinic homiletic commentary on a text from the Hebrew scriptures, characterized by non-literal interpretation and legendary illustration.
Small cases, boxes, or racks designed with compartments to hold correspondence, documents, or other papers.
Any of various types of receptacle used for sorting loose items, components, or foodstuffs.

Small, extremely rare egg-shaped vessels of ancient Greece, found in both black- and red-figure. The specific use of oa is not determined although real eggs as well as marble and ceramic ones were placed in graves. Lidded oa might have held scented oil (perfume). Lidless oa were probably not containers since they either have a small hole at one or both end or no opening at all.

Creative works that depict the ocean or other large body of water where the water itself dominates the scene. When lesser bodies of water are depicted, use "landscapes (representations)." When ships, shipbuilding, or harbors are depicted, use "marines (visual works)."

Works, such as keepsakes, made from hair; usually from human hair but occasionally also from the hair of a beloved pet. The hair is often braided and arranged in decorative patterns, entwined over wire forms, etc. While hair is the primary medium of such works, seed pearls, glass beads, ribbons, dried flowers, and other materials may be included. Hairworks are often memorials, typically worn or displayed as a mourning ornament in memory of the donor of the hair. However, they may also be made from the hair of living individuals, such as the members of a family or of a church congregation. Hairwork was popular during the Victorian era.
In Indian architecture, god or guardian figures or images on vimāna walls.
Practitioners of Haitian Vodou, residing in both Haiti and the diaspora, who self identify as servants of the Vodou spirits (or lwa).
People or corporate body who make products that are intended to be assembled or compiled as part of a larger product.
In Indian architecture, a fabulous figure in the form of dolphin with elephant-trunk; decorative figure, sometimes used for temple conduits (Kaliṅga); karimakara.
Gestures, actions, sounds, visual stimuli, or objects acting as the prompt for a particular action or a sign to convey warning, direction, or other information.
The condition or state of mental or physical harmony, tranquility, or serenity, or mutual concord between individuals or groups.
Written or printed words, phrases, or sentences arranged to make a communication. Includes oral verbal communications set down in writing or print.
Documents that provide authorization or permission.

Refers to the international movement in architecture begun in the late-1970s. The style is characterized by a combination of a Late-Modernist emphasis on function, technology and purity with Deconstructionist notions of complexity and displacement.
Cylindrical devices on which something is wound.

Objects taken as spoils in war or in hunting, or awarded as prizes for victory in contests; typically include such things as armor and weapons taken from an opponent in battle, stuffed and mounted skins, heads or other portions of a slain animal, and elaborate silver pieces awarded as contest prizes. Distinct from "trophies (monuments)", which are monuments erected as permanent reminders of military victories, usually  containing images of the spoils of battle,.
Nationality, culture, or style of the historical region of Languedoc in southern France.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Rhode Island.

Construction method where a structure or superstructure is built directly on the earth or slab, with no underground foundation to provide stability and support. Structures built upon  piers or pilings may also be withouit foundations.

Measurement of character and extent of respiration by using a respirometer, a tool which monitors the concentration of a gas contained within an enclosed space into which the material being monitored is respiring.

Beliefs and practices of the inhabitants of the Italian peninsula from ancient times until the ascendancy of Christianity in the 4th century CE. It is influenced by religions of ancient Italic cultures, especially those of other Latin tribes, of the non–Indo-European Etruscans, as well as by that of the Greek colonizers of Sicily and southern Italy.
Collective action undertaken by people, who may or may not be formally organized, for the purpose of promoting or resisting an aspect of social change within a society.

Refers to the art and certain artifacts of small-scale societies, even when the societies are not strictly speaking tribal in social structure. The rubric is typically applied to works of Native Americans, Oceania, and sub-Saharan Africa. The characteristics that define creators of tribal art are 1. isolation, politically and economically, from advanced civilizations; 2. oral traditions in rather than literacy; 3. small, independent population groupings, usually in villages of no more than a few hundred inhabitants who live a life of face-to-face social interaction and informal social control; 4. a low level of labor and craft specialization; 5. subsistence by hunting, fishing, and gathering and/or small-scale agriculture; 6. little technology beyond hand tools, often of stone rather than metal; and 7. slow rates of cultural change prior to European contact.

Having the form or plan of two intersecting bars or lines of equal length, in which the intersection does not necessarily form right angles, and where the bars run diagonally across the vertical plane, that is, the base of the form rests on two arms that are not at right angles with the horizontal base plane. Resembling the letter "X." Use "cruciform" for forms or plans having two intersecting lines or bars at right angles, whether or not the bars are of equal length, and where the base of the form is perpendicular to the horizontal plane.

The total of images, objects, and other visuality that has been built up by a group of people and transmitted from one generation to another. It includes art media such as painting, drawing, prints, and installations; architecture and design; utilitarian artifacts of a culture such as tools and costime; media such as photography, film, television, and digital media, covering topics of news, popular culture, advertising and consumerism, politics, law, religion, and science and medicine.
The action of rendering a metal inert in order to inhibit corrosion; in electronics, coating of semiconductors for this purpose.
Tables or other platforms on wheels used in serving tea and light refreshments; may have attached platforms or storage attachments.
Chairs constructed of a molded shell mounted on a single support on a flared base.
Automatic switches forming part of the auxiliary circuit of some fluorescent lamps, which enables heat to travel to electrodes for a discharge to occur after a period of inactivity.
Female heads of families, tribal lines, or entire social orders, classes, or peoples.
People who play games as a profession or pastime. For people who play athletic games, usually prefer "athletes."
Refers to those who own businesses or commercial establishments. For those who generally have legal title to something, see "owners."

Long, straight parts of various types of tools, machines, and weapons, such as the rods that transmit power or motion from one part of a machine to another, or the slender sticks that constitute the main bodies of arrows.
