Devices for watering lawns, crops, or recreation fields, for fire control, or for another purpose, where a flow of water is passed through holes in the device to spread water over a wide area.
Devices, now historic, used to determine the volume of carbon dioxide and oxygen molecules in blood samples.
Culture of the dynasty that ruled the Jaunpur Sultanate; of Abyssinian origin, founded in 1394.

Style and culture of a group of Native Americans Chinook who are closely related to the Wishram, both being Plateau tribes that share many cultural aspects of the Northwest Coast tribes. When Europeans arrived, the Wasco lived along the banks of the Columbia River, near The Dalles. Today the tribes are part of the Warm Springs Reservation in Oregon and Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation in Washington.
Substance or molecule, other than the reactant, that starts a chain reaction (as in polymerization) and is usually consumed in the reaction.

Wood of the genus Aesculus, native to North America, southeastern Europe, and eastern Asia. While primarily grown as an ornamental tree, horse chestnuts have light, soft, tough, fine-grained wood used for artificial limbs, splints, brush handles, boxes, crates, and paper pulp.

Zirconium is a metallic element having symbol Zr and atomic weight 91.22. It is obtained from zircon and other minerals and is commercially the most important ore. A hard metal resistant to heat and corrosion, it is much used in nuclear reactors, in alloys, refractories, and ceramics.

A mineral consisting of lead chromate that occurs in the oxidized zone of lead mineral veins. It is compositionally identical to the pigment chrome yellow but only secondarily related. The element chromium was found in this rare secondary mineral in 1787 and became the basis for the pigment which was subsequently produced synthetically.
An inorganic sol-gel material developed as a consolidant for loose paint layers on stained glass windows. When added to glass or ceramics, SZA forms an irreversible bond.
Domestic architecture designed for a single, extremely specialized purpose or activity, rather than for general or broad use.
Objects worn as a non-political social statement of greeting, opinion, or support.
Identification of works of art or architecture related to the work being described; may include a description of the relationship between the works.
Devices that measure or monitor changes in volume in a substance or solution.
Devices designed to reduce the presence of fluids and dehydrate the mouth for a dental procedure.
The standard unit of currency of Sweden.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 2899 to 2800 (or 2900 to 2801) Before Common Era.
Language family spoken on Japanese and other islands; developed from common ancestral language, Proto-Japonic.
Breaking or chipping of masonry or pavement at joints, cracks, or edges, usually resulting in fragments with feather edges.
Areas or mounds of unconsolidated material undersea.
Celadon stoneware produced in kilns in the town of Longquan (province of Zhejiang), China, from the Song to the mid-Qing dynasties (roughly from the 11th to the 18th century).
Commercial artists who render images to illustrate scientific concepts.
Artists who create mail art, which is usually in post card format, typically intended to be mailed to other artists and then shared or displayed.

Trademarked name for a moldable, self-sealing plastic film composed of polyolefins and paraffin wax which is permeable to oxygen and carbon dioxide and resistant to many common reagents. It is used as a moisture barrier film for short-term storage. In conservation it has been used to repair splits and as temporary backing for ivory miniatures; and tested as an adhesive for strip lining of twentieth century paintings.
Range of vivid deep purplish blues, so-named because the color is sometimes associated with clothing of kings, or resembling the color of ultramarine blue, which was also called "royal blue."
Depressions in the earth that contains water.
Landforms resulting from glaciers.
Nationality, culture, or styles of the historical area of Rhodesia, Africa. For the nationality of the modern nation, use "Zimbabwean."
The central portions a human's or animal's body, not including head and limbs.

Devices of various designs, often a slender bar-like object, used in weaving or netting. In weaving, it passes the thread or yarn of the weft to and from one edge of the cloth to the other between the threads or yarns of the warp.
Class of compounds derived from isocyanic acid used in manufacture of polyurethane resins for use in foam, coatings, and adhesives.
Generally, the lines of junction formed by the abutment or attachment of two edges, especially the edges of two portions of a single object, such as a garment or metal cylinder.
Particular subdivisions under a region. Examples are in Greece.
Administrative and governing entities of tribes, whether or not the entities enjoy the privileges and immunities of external sovereign status.
Puncturing or perforating, as to create a decorative pattern by removing small pieces of the material, usually metal; original technique done with a chisel but later with a small saw.

The condition of low oxygen; it is typically defined as a level below 20.9% in an atmospheric environment and in the range between 1%-30% saturation in an aquatic environment. Hypoxic conditions are detrimental to living organisms. In a conservation context, hypoxia may be deliberately induced as a means of preservation of materials or pest control. For the extreme condition in which oxygen is below 0.1% or absent, use "anoxia." For a medical condition characterized by low blood oxygen, use "anoxemia," for which "hypoxemia" is a used for term.
The quality or condition of accompanying or varying with particular seasons of the year.
Short, skirtlike sections of a costume attached at the waistline, such as on a bodice or jacket, and usually extending to cover the hips.
Literature that is a burlesque imitation of the heroic style, employing the imitation of a heroic character, manner, or actions, usually for humorous effect.
Containers, often set into a wall, used for safekeeping or storage and usually capable of being locked, such as those used in schools and gymnasiums for storing clothing and other valuables.
General term for containers that store materials.
Ancient Greek one-handled vessels used for ladling and pouring wine or water; made in a variety of jug- and pitcherlike forms.
Japanese erotic prints and paintings.
Advertising signage or structural objects which have been installed with electrical or other power for the purpose of illumination.
In Indian architecture, a vidhyādhara semi-divine figures in the act of lifting up or defending the kūṭas and śālās of a temple.

Individuals, known in several cultures, who perform the ritual duties of a priest as well as accompanying troops or taking part in war. Examples are in the Aztec culture, where warrior priests carried sacred idols and conducted human sacrifices on the battlefield.
In Indian architecture, a fish-wheel decorative motif.
The originating cause or substance of some material thing or physical agency, or the conceptual inspiration for a conceptual thing.

Altruistic concern for human welfare and advancement usually as manifested by the donation of money, property, or work to needy persons, by endowment of institutions of learning or health care, or by generosity to other socially useful purposes.

Standardized displays of information about an art object or other cultural material that include specific data elements that uniquely identify and describe the object, often the name of creator, title, date of creation, materials, dimensions, location and unique identifying number (such as an accession number), and copyright and credit line. Tombstones are used in wall labels, captions under illustrations in publications, etc.
Includes any written requests and lists of signatures submitted to an authority to appeal for the performance of specific action.

Describes a photographic movement identified in an exhibition organized by William Jenkins at the International Museum of Photography at George Eastman House, Rochester, NY (Dec 1975–Feb 1976). Included were ten photographers: Robert Adams, Lewis Baltz, Bernd Becher and Hilla Becher, Joe Deal, Frank Gohlke, Nicholas Nixon , John Schott, Stephen Shore, and Henry Wessel Jr. Jenkins posited that these photographers observed the American landscape with a clinical objectivity rather than a Romantic or Symbolist sensibility that had marked earlier representations.
Elastic bodies, often strips or wires of steel coiled spirally, that recover their shape after being compressed, bent, or stretched.

Object genre including items, equipment, accessories, and other things that are utilitarian in purpose rather than purely decorative. Objects having a primary purpose of being useful and used, rather than purely decorative.
Nationality, culture, or style of Latvia, in the Baltic region of northern Europe.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of South Carolina.

Process of analysis done by transversing the scanned subject by a detector or an electromagnetic beam; scanning is done to determine the nature, qualities, measurements, etc. of an object, living subject, area, or other thing; the analysis may involve the recording of information derived from the scanning.

The belief system, teachings, and practices of the Worldwide Brotherhood or Rosicrucians, first documented in 1614. The legendary founder was named Christian Rosenkreuz, said to have been born in 1378. The name probably actually derives from the order’s symbol, a rose on a cross, which is similar to the family coat of arms of Martin Luther. Rosicrucian teachings are a combination of occultism and other religious beliefs and practices, including Hermeticism, Jewish mysticism, and Christian Gnosticism. The core of their beliefs is that they possess esoteric wisdom handed down from ancient times.
Concepts related to the acknowledgement of status or merits, usually but not always positive recognition.

Art that is created for and about large cities and city life, often done by artists who live in the city and sometimes having a distinctive rough style. Examples are graffiti and street performances. The art is often, but not always, displayed in or on public spaces; it may be uncommissioned and illegally created. The term is typically reserved for modern contexts; it typically refers to visual arts, but may be applied to other art forms as well.  For art or architectural elements that are sanctioned or commissioned by the authorities and associated with urban design, prefer "municipal art."
Technique for altering any plain configuration, surface decoration, or structural composition with a repeated motif, especially for textiles.
Furniture designed specifically to support analog telephone sets. These usually include compartments or drawers for telephone directories, notepads, or writing utensils.
Term used by Chippendale for small painted chairs with rush seats used at general entertainments.

Disc-shaped wheels on lighting device burners at the outer end of a shaft by means of which the shaft and its wick wheel or wheels can be turned manually; in some burners a simple loop of the shaft replaces the wheel.
Married women of mature years, usually with connotation of social rank, dignity, and propriety; often, but not ecessarily , associated with the mother of a large family.
People or organizations who receive others into a house or other venue, either actual or virtual.
People who own and manage restaurants.
The stems or straight parts of any tool or equipment, such as of a nail, needle, tongs, or other items.
Equipment used to hammer or pound materials.
Culture of a dynasty that ruled in the present-day Odisha in eastern India 9th-12th centuries.
Substances or mixtures applied to leather generally to clean, preserve, or maintain its strength and flexibility.

General term applied to wood from several Brazilian species in various genera of the laurel family or of the borage family, all producing moderately heavy wood resembling walnut, the heartwood ranging in color from olive to chocolate brown and with a medium luster; valued for joinery, flooring, and furniture.

The cubic crystalline form of zirconium dioxide (ZrO2). As a synthetic gem it is often used as an inexpensive replacement for a diamond. Color most often ranges from white to light yellow and brown, but as a synthetic, can be produced in a large variety of colors. Its refractive index and colour dispersion are fairly close to the diamond, but its hardness is lower and its specific gravity much higher.
Ornamental motifs including fanciful human and animal forms and floral ornament, based on the decoration of Nero's Domus Aurea in Rome, discovered in 1488.
Buildings or other structures designed or utilized primarily for storage.
Watercraft, largely made of inflatable material such as plastic. Standard form is a horizontal platform, but many variations exist in shape and size.
Miscellaneous notes or comments pertinent to information in a record.

Devices for monitoring the equilibrium of water, and that can supply an index useful in controlling anti-corrosion treatment. This is in respect to its degree of CaCO3 saturation. If a water has a negative Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) value, it is under-saturated with respect to calcium carbonate and is potentially corrosive.
Devices used to organize and distribute dental materials, including cotton rolls, cotton balls, or other small items used during dental procedures.
The standard unit of currency of Switzerland.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 2199 to 2100 (or 2200 to 2101) Before Common Era.
Small language family of northern Peru and eastern Ecuador.
Separations in a flexible material caused by pulling or wrenching part from part.
Low parts of an underwater gap that are separated by basins; includes similar features at the mouthes of fjords.

Pottery that existed during the third and second centuries BCE, and was first found at Megara, but later in Attica and numerous other places. It is generally found on bowls, and is characterized by relief decoration on the exterior, created by a combination of wheel work, stamping, and molding. The surface may be covered with glaze that is also ornamented in black or red. Themes are usually of flowers, with occasional figures and narrative scenes.
People who specialize in creating painted set designs.
Artists who specialize in Matter art, which is painting characterized by thick, crusted paint and the incorporation of discarded materials such as scraps of wood.
A non-woven, acid free viscose fabric stabilized by acrylic binder. It is used for gentle aqueous cleaning of water-sensitive articles, such as paper objects, via capillary action.
Range of pure bright blues or purplish blues resembling the color of the sapphire gem.
Fields or areas of crushed rock.
Bodies of water that flow in a constant circular motion in opposition to the main current.
Nationality, style, and culture of Rwanda, in central-eastern Africa.

Long pointed teeth, particularly such teeth that project beyond the mouth, as in the elephant, wild boar, and various other animals. Tusks are generally seen in living mammals, but existed in other extinct animals. Tusks are used by the animal for mating competition, display, defense, offensive fighting, digging, and occasionally for hunting.

Mechanized devices, typically comprising a yarn creel, a yarn guidance system, and a sizing delivery system, designed to apply a sizing agent to warp yarn in order to add strength/stiffness and reduce absorbency of the textile material. To facilitate the sizing process, yarn is wound on section beams and fed through the device's sizing delivery system, comprising a size box containing the sizing agent. After soaking in the agent and passing through the device's squeeze rolls, which rid the yarn of execess chemicals, the yarn is dried in the device's drying cans using hot air.

An aromatic liquid phenol, isoeugenol is a constituent of the essential oils of several plants including nutmeg. It may also be synthesized from closely related eugenol by isomerization with alkali. Isoeugenol is used in perfumery and in the synthesis of vanillin.
Parts or subdivisions separated or divided off from the remainder; portions into which a thing is cut or divided.
Soft, porous, disposable papers used for personal hygeine.
The constituent political and administrative divisions of the modern nation of Italy.
The dominions of a tsar.
A process for smoothing the surface of wood or another material by shaving off small fragments.

Reciprocal and reversible transfer of ions of the same charge between a solution and a relatively insoluble solid in contact with it. Cation exchange and anion exchange are, respectively, the exhange of positively and negatively charged ions. Ion exchange is used in such applications as kidney dialysis, water purification, and chemical analysis.
Train-shaped toys specially made for children's play. For scale models of life-sized trains that run on powered tracks, use 'model trains.'

Separate treatises on a particular subject, typically written expositions of a subject narrow enough in scope to exclude all but a single aspect of the subject, for example, a study of the works of a single artist. In book cataloging, non-serial bibliographic items complete in one part or in a finite number of separate parts.
Containers of varying form and size intended primarily for a traveler's belongings.

Receptacles for holding square decanters (or up to four such decanters placed in a line), having an overhead hinged frame that can be locked when vertical and swung sideways when unlocked to permit removal of the decanters.
Large, bulbous, usually wide-mouthed earthenware or woven vessels used for holding water or food or for cooking; may have handles.

Works of art, traditionally from the 18th and 19th century in Great Britain, that depict "country pursuits" such as game hunting, fishing, dog racing, horse racing, and pugilism. The genre is sometimes expanded to works of art that depict any kind of amateur or professional sport.

Displays of lights intended to be seen primarily at night, incorporating candles, lamps, electric lights, or other types of lights. Illuminations display lights in a decorative way, arranged in artistic designs, and usually in token of festivity or rejoicing. For displays primarily featuring fireworks, use "fireworks (visual works)"; however, fireworks may be incorporated as a feature of larger illuminations.
Devotees or ascetics who practise the system of yoga, as evolved in India.
People who specialize in making pipes for smoking.
In Indian art or architecture, a peacock motif.
Physical extent or area, in two or three dimensions, in the natural world or built environment. Typically used in the context of space being applied to or sufficient for a purpose or action.

The historical-political-cultural nexus of the global colonial experience and its aftermath in the late 20th century and beyond; it embraces the colonial past, the present time following the end of colonial status in a given region, the exile and diaspora of colonized and colonizing peoples, and the politics of multiculturalism.
Sheets or small books printed by printers, type founders, or publishers to show what types are available and their appearance.

Registries made of metal plates, usually round or rectangular and of relatively small size, into which the hallmarks of registered metalworkers are stamped with the maker's original stamp. The metal plates were easily transportable, and could be used to validate authenticity of works of gold, silver, and other metals.

Use with reference to mostly French art of the 1960s that is realist in the sense of appropriating materials from the environment or staging actions or happenings. This movement was announced by the publication of a short manifesto in Paris, 1960; authored by Pierre Restany, and signed by the artists Arman, François Dufrêne, Raymond Hains, Yves Klein, Martial Raysse, Daniel Spoerri, Jean Tinguely and Jacques de la Villeglé.
Piles, heaps, or groups of things, particularly such a piles having their constituents arranged in an orderly fashion, such as a stack of wheat or goods.

Objects that are specifically designed to be heavy in order to hold down or provide resistance. Examples include round disks designed to be used in lifting to improve physical strength, paperweights, sinkers used for fishing, and pieces of metal or ceramic sewn into a costume or drapery to weigh down a hem or sash.
Nationality, culture, and styles of the landlocked German-speaking alpine country and a microstate in Central Europe.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of South Dakota.
Technique for evaluating basic structural properties of paper using wet and dry paper strips over a range of short spans from 0 to 1 mm.

Religious tradition of African origin that was developed in Cuba and then spread throughout Latin America and the United States. Santería was brought to Cuba by the people of the Yoruban nations of West Africa, who were enslaved in great numbers in the first decades of the 19th century.
The relative prestige of an individual or group and the hierarchical position of a social role in a social structure or stratification system.

Art produced by artisans trained and working within a local client economy according to local tastes, as opposed to "academic art."  It differs also from "folk art," in that vernacular art is defined in terms of its creators (rather than the response of its viewers), and is not so much bound to the biographical details of an individual craftsman.
Collocates descriptors for processes of physical and/or chemical change in a material or object.
Small tables or supported planks dedicated to pork-salting or producing other pork products.

Cantilever chairs that are considered a major development in modern furniture. Mart Stam created the first experimental models with gas pipes and flanges and developed the principle of cantilevering chair supports without four legs. Later innovations allowed the use of tubular steel. Others such as Marcel Breuer and Mies van der Rohe designed their own variations on the principle.

Pointed implements used to adjust the wicks of simple lamps; may be in the form of a short length of wire attached to the lamp or a separate wire mounted in a handle of wood or ivory fitted into a matching stand.
Those who have membership in an organization, community, joint enterprise, or other group.
People who study or practice hypnotism, which is the science of inducing an artifically induced trance-like state.
People who examine, revise, or give an opinion on a publication, exhibition, etc.
Parts or components of stoves; the constituent elements or parts of apparatuses for heating.
Equipment used to provide strength to structures.
Dynasty of an Afghan family that ruled in northern India from 1540 to 1556.
Layer of material used to line the inner side or surface of something to reinforce or protect it.

Wood of any of several trees in the genus Chlorophora, native to the west coast of Africa. It is tough, dense, and very durable, often used in cabinetmaking and paneling as a substitute for teak. Iroko is a medium weight wood with an open-grain texture. The color is a brown with yellow streaks; used in structures, ship building, joinery, benches, and flooring.
A mineral Pb4Cu4Cl8(OH)8.H2O consisting of a basic lead-copper chloride occurring in deep blue tetragonal crystals. Used as a pigment.

In the design of Turkoman rugs, a large, usually eight-sided geometrical motif (although it may be hexagonal or lozenge-shaped), "gul" originally from the Persian for "rose." It originally represented a stylized rose but subsequently was modified in ways characteristic of various tribes. The motifs constitute the primary decorative elements of Turkoman weavings.

Set comprising a board with letters, numbers, or other signs around its edge, at which a planchette (movable pointer, upturned glass, etc.) points supposedly in answer to questions from users; used by attenders at a seance. Popular from the 19th century.
Notes included in a data field that provide descriptive information about a concept or expands upon information recorded in other fields.

Rotary instruments used to remove tooth substance, particularly in the treatment of caries. Historically, the drill was hand-operated or pedal-driven. Modern dental drills operate by an electric motor; they consist of a dental handpiece that may be fitted with variously shaped burs.
General term for units of currency based on various large silver coins of Central Europe minted from the late 15th to the mid-19th century.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 2699 to 2600 (or 2700 to 2601) Before Common Era.
Family of languages that are spoken south of the chief range of the Caucasus mountains.
Haziness of a fluid caused by sediment or other particles in suspension.
Slopes that run seaward from the shelfs edge to the beginning of continental rises, or to points where the slopes are reduced.
Ceramic ware produced in the Mino Province from the 7th century to the present. Included are large-mouth jars, small-mouth jars, mortars, ash-glazed and iron-glazed utensils, and tea ceremony wares.

Artists who specialize in creating silhouettes, which are portraits or other shapes cut from paper and mounted on a contrasting background. The art form was particularly popular in Europe and the United States during the 18th and 19th centuries.
Artists who create or compile images, animation, video, audio, print, and digital media to create advertisements, television shows, websites, or other media productions.

Trademarked commercial name for a series of paraxylylene-based polymers used as a vapor-formed conformal coating highly resistant to organic solvents, inorganic reagents, and acids. Among its applications, Parylene is used as a protective coating in conservation of paper, photographs, book bindings, and other archival materials.
Range of deep blue colors resembling the color of smalt, which is a deep blue paint and ceramic pigment.
Small, commonly V-shaped channels carved in the land by fluvial action and through which water flows only occasionally or seasonally.
The style and culture of the people speaking the Bantu Rwanda language of East Africa, or of any of the inhabitants of the country of Rwanda.

Organs of flight of any flying animal, such as a bird, bat, or insect.In birds the wings are specially modified forelimbs; in bats (and the extinct pterodactyls, etc.), extensions of the skin attached to modified parts of the forelimbs; in insects, membranous expansions attached to the thorax in addition to the limbs.

Mechanized devices, typically comprising a wooden frame, a sloping apron or feeding cloth, and a series of drawing and winding mechanisms, designed to lightly twist and further reduce the thickness of cardings or slubbings. The resulting product is thus strengthened to better withstand subsequent spinning processes. Developed as an offshot of the spinning jenny, these devices have the capacity to draw out entire rows of carding or slubbing simultaneously due to the presence of 30 to 50 spindles on which drawn out cardings/slubbings can be wound onto bobbins. However, due to the labor intensive nature associated with operating these devices, they were largely superceded by more techologically advanced wollen condensers in the 1850s.

The most important of the lithium compounds, lithium hydroxide is a white crystalline powder. Among its applications, it is a sorbent for carbon dioxide, an additive to storage batteries, and is used in the manufacture of alkyd resins and other lithium salts.
Strips of leather, cloth, or other material that pass over the shoulder and from which an article is suspended. For strips used for fastening, use "straps."
General term for various articles, cosmetics, or products used in washing, dressing, and hygiene.
Particular districts or administrative divisions, particularly divisions of towns and cities in Italy.

Refers to districts or provinces ruled by a viceroy, who is a person acting as the representative of their sovereign or king. Viceroyalities are often on frontiers or in provinces distant from the seat of power of the state.
The process by which electrons are lost from or transferred to neutral molecules or atoms to form positively or negatively charged particles.

Continuous, unbounded, or unlimited extent in every direction, without reference to any matter that may be present; this is regarded as an attribute of the universe, describable mathematically (in modern science usually conflated with time, time-space).
Ornaments made of feathers, silk, hair or other relatively delicate materials, worn or displayed as decoration or as symbols of honor or rank.
Straps used to keep multiple pieces of luggage together as a unit, or to secure a piece of baggage to prevent its opening.

Boxes used to store tinder, which is a flammable substance that readily takes fire from a spark and burns or smolders such as partially charred linen or corkwood. The box also typically contained the flint and steel with which the spark was struck, and sometimes the brimstone matches.
In Indian architecture, lotus vine; lotus-creeper motif.

Images, often paintings, in which the focus is a depiction of inanimate objects, as distinguished from art in which such objects are subsidiary elements in a composition. Common examples of still lifes are depictions of fruit, flowers, meat or dead game, vessels, eating utensils, and other objects, including skulls, candles, and hourglasses, typically arranged on a table. Such images were known since the time of ancient Greece and Rome; however, the subject was exploited by some 16th-century Italian painters, and was highly developed in 17th-century Dutch painting, where the qualities of form, color, texture, and composition were valued, and the images were intended to relay allegorical messages. The subject is generally seen in oil paintings, though it can also be found in mosaics, watercolors, prints, collages, and photographs. The term originally included paintings in which the focus was on living animals at rest, although such depictions would now be called "animal paintings."

Works dating from the 1960s or later that use their exhibition space as part of their design. Demanding a viewer's active engagement, installations are often created by artists in direct opposition to the notion of permanent artwork, or art as a commodity.
Persons who are excessively or fanatically devoted to a cause or ideal, especially a religious or political one.
People who specialize in making puppets, which are representations of figures that are designed to be animated by human effort, including the use of strings, wires, sticks, or directly by the hand.
In Indian architecture, an auspicious couple motif.
Criteria, rules, procedures, or devices approved by official authority or general consent, that serve as examples to be followed or as measures for evaluation or comparative judgment.
The property of strength, influence, and dominance over others, which can be personal, political, or national.
Works designed as a volume, but which remain without binding, or with only a paper binding.
Solemn promises, usually in writing and signed, to do or refrain from doing something, such as to support or contribute towards a cause, fund or allegiance.

Refers to the international art movement that flourished in Europe and America in the mid-1960s. The style is charcterized by the careful manipulation of bold, sharply contrasting shapes and colors in order to create vitural movement, vibration, or chromatic tension.
Stout sticks or posts with a pointed end for driving into the ground as to mark a boundary or site, to support a plant or part of a framework, or used as tethering rods.
Nationality, culture, or styles of Limburg, an area western Europe in the modern Netherlands and Belgium.
Architectural style of North American incorporating elements of the Southern US states, often including antebellum.
Includes the complete examination, investigation, and testing of surface and subsurface soil and conditions at a site.

Refers to the religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard in the 1950s, based on the principles of Dianetics, which is a form of psychotherapy for ridding the psyche of painful experiences or engrams. It includes a highly structured system of beliefs, including the role of the thetan, which is comparable to the soul or life energy, in the physical universe. It views Jesus Christ as an important teacher, values self-determination, and has the stated goal of building a planet populated by happy, fulfilled people.
The enduring, orderly and patterned relationships between elements of a society.

Genre including physical objects that are meant to be perceived primarily through the sense of sight, were created by the use of skill and imagination, and possess an aesthetic that is valued and of a quality and type that would be collected by art museums or private collectors, including drawings, painting, sculpture, architecture, and decorative arts. Performance art is considered a visual art, but the performing arts and literature are not.
Causing a liquid, fluid, or anything in loose particles to flow or fall.
Italian type of small, spindly three-legged tables, especially popular in 18th-century Venice.

Portable chairs borne on two long poles; generally with elaborate upholstery and decoration. For conveyances for one person consisting generally of canvas or similar material stretched or laid across a frame for transporting the sick, wounded, or dead use "stretchers (conveyances)." For more elaborate conveyances boxlike in form and often enclosed by curtains and carried on poles by people or animals use "litters."
Those elements in lighting devices, usually cords, ribbons, or tubes of loosely woven, twisted, or braided fibers, that draw fuel to the flame by capillary action.
People, usually creators, whose name is unknown, but whose identification in association with their works is known only by their initials, usually seen in signatures in monogram.
People who guide or inspire others, or who affect others by ascendancy, sway, control, or authority, especially when not formally or overtly expressed.
Individuals working in stores who serve the customers and process sales, returns, and refunds.
The projecting shank, prong, fang, or tongue of a metal tool, weapon, or instrument, as a chisel, file, knife, or sword, by which it is secured to its handle, hilt, or grip.
Nationality, styles, and culture of the Tamil people, originally of southern India and speaking Tamil, one of the principal languages of the Dravidian family.

Fluid that smoothes motion or reduces friction between surfaces. Lubricant occurs in nature as synovial fluid in the joints of vertebrate animals. Various artificial lubricants have been used since prehistory, including mud and animal fat. Since the 19th century, crude oil has become the chief source of lubricants for most applications in industry.
General term for exceptionally tough or hard wood from any of numerous species of trees and shrubs, such as ebony, hornbeam, or acacia.
A glassy blue mineral, named for its copper content and its similarity to rivaite, that is a component of the artificial inorganic pigment, Egyptian blue.
Any salt or ester containing three phosphate groups.

Motifs in carpets and other contexts often consisting of a vertical row of triangles, diamonds or lozenges with a bar between each extending to the sides with another diamond on the end. There are usually diamonds or bars on the top and bottom of the motif. It represents a desire to marry.
Structures of any kind that serve the transportation and transport of goods and passengers.
Statement or account that describes the seller in an acquisition event, listing characteristic features, or significant details.

Instruments used in dental extractions to loosen teeth prior to forceps extraction; they may be used to remove roots or impacted teeth, when teeth are badly compromised, or when teeth are malpositioned and cannot be reached with forceps.
The standard unit of currency of Turkey.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 2599 to 2500 (or 2600 to 2501) Before Common Era.
Language family in Brazil comprising of two languages.
Damage or deterioration occurring gradually as a result of continuing use or exposure, usually a gradual diminishing from such actions as rubbing, scraping, or washing.
Subordinate elevations, ridges, or rises on the sea floor that project outward from larger features.
English ware produced by Thomas Minton in Staffordshire beginning in 1793, including majolica, Parian ware, Palissy ware, and blue-printed earthenware.
Artists who specialize in depicting scenes in space, planetary bodies, space settlements, space vehicles, etc.
Artists who create works in miniature, such as paintings, photographs, furniture, and other objects. For those who paint or draw pictures or other decorative forms in manuscripts, see "illuminators."
Polymeric emulsifier used in art conservation to clean painted surfaces.
Refers to a range of bluish colors resembling the color of the metal alloy, steel, particularly the bluish colors taken on by steel while being tempered.

High projections of land extending into a large body of water beyond the line of the coast. For lower land areas projecting into the sea and marking a notable change in coastal direction, use "capes (landforms)."
Style and culture of the nation of São Tomé and Príncipe.
The carpus joints that connect the arm with the hand of humans and other animals, or the leg with the foot of a bird.

Mechanized devices that utilize multiple sets of rollers to straighten, draw out, and add a small amount of twist to cotton fibers prior to spinning, thus transforming slivers into slubbing. This is the first machine that the sliver is exposed to after leaving the drawing frame. In order to produce slubbing, cans containing slivers are placed in the rear of the device and, after passing through the device's rollers, are carried on a revolving spindle and ultimately wound onto a bobbin. Slivers can pass through these devices multiple times, depending on the desired refinement of the cotton thread. The process carried out by this device resembles the drawing process, through which the sliver is incrimentally transformed into smaller and smaller dimensions.
Organic compound used as a catalyst and as an ingredient in consolidant in stone conservation.
Boards, often removable, forming the sides or parts of the sides of structures, as on beds, such as hospital or childrens' beds, or carts and carriages to increase their carrying capacity.
Slender pointed implements used after eating to remove bits of food lodged between the teeth.
Particular districts comprising areas outside of urban areas, often in agricultural regions.
Hand-held rakes of moderate size, used in gardening and landscaping.
Administrative bodies subject to a voivode, including semi-independent districts or provinces of Eastern European countries.
Enlarging a round hole, as in a piece of metal, by means of a revolving-edge tool.
Active, passive, or facilitated movement of salts and other electrolytes in the form of ions across energy-transducing cell membranes.
The quality of being not likely to give way, deteriorate, decompose, or otherwise change.
Flat pouchlike components stitched into or onto a garment, accessible through a finished opening typically convenient to the hand.
Toys that imitate the look and feel of weapons.

Genre and tradition concerning the study of a culture's body of myths, belonging to a particular religious or cultural tradition in an authoritative and official fashion and through symbolic narrative, iconography, or characterization, usually through the forms and personalities of deities.
Art works comprising designs or patterns assembled from small pieces of veneer in various shapes, often applied to furnishings.
Makers of distinctive clothing worn and ornaments. Examples are Native American artists who make regalia.
Anatolian rug motif symbolizing a dragon, which frequently looks like a line with a row of protruding hooks.
In the visual arts, oral works, music, performing arts, and literature, the topics, themes, or other visual, oral, or written content of the work. It includes what the work is of or about.
Collective term for news-producing media and news organizations as well as the people who define and establish the news like reporters, editors, commentators and photographers or photojournalists.
Variants or special forms of documents.

Versions of scholarly or scientific documents or manuscripts that have been peer reviewed, revised and accepted for publication, but that have not been formatted for final printing, presentation, or distribution.
Movement of Matisse-influenced decorative painting in New York in the 1970s.
Short pieces of wood, especially pieces cut or shaped for a particular purpose.
Refers to the culture of the modern nation of Lithuania, or in general to cultures that have occupied the Eastern European state on the Baltic sea.
Culture or residency of the Southwest USA, which typically includes the states of Arizona, New Mexico, Oklahoma and Texas.

Sample extraction technique used for chromatographic analysis of dilute solutions in difficult matrices, liquid and gaseous. Solid-phase microextraction (SPME) has two discrete steps. Extraction is achieved by solute absorption from the sample matrix into a thick layer of silicone or related adsorptive material. Analytes are then transferred into a chromatography inlet system by gaseous or liquid means.

The indigenous Japanese religious beliefs and practices as distinguished from Buddhism, which had been introduced into Japan in the sixth century. In general, it is characterized by its lack of official sacred scripture and specific formal dogma and by the veneration of small images set in particular Shinto shrines. The religious system is categorized into three interconnected sects: Shrine Shinto (Jinja Shinto), which constitutes the main currents of Shinto tradition; State Shinto (Kokka Shinto), based on the unification of religion and state and practiced by the Japanese Imperial family; and Sect Shinto (Kyoha Shinto), a movement consisting of sects that originated in Japan around the 19th century and after World War II, each organized by a founder into religious associations in which members are known as parishioners (ujiko) of a particular shrine.

Concept about the practice or habit of restraining oneself in provocation, passion, desire, and exercising rational self-restraint and moderation in action, expression, particularly self-control, restraint, or forbearance when provoked to anger or impatience.
The action or process of making something ready for use or service or of getting ready for some occasion, test, or duty.

Refers to any low pressure suction table whether equipped with heating, air circulation, or humidification capabilities. Vacuum tables are used in conservation science to carry out tasks such as relining and relaxing canvases, cleaning paper and textiles, mending tears in various materials.
Term generally applied to a wide range of chairs without arms to distinguish them from armchairs.
Implements used to cut and shape the ends of wicks, particularly the ribbon wicks of kerosene lamps.
Members of a people or group who have no permanent residence or settlement but move about in regular seasonal or cyclical routes to obtain sustenance.

Generally, those who inform others of some fact or occurrence. In the context of law enforcement and the judiciary, connotes those who lay information against other persons. In the context of anthropology, linguistics, art history, and other cultural studies, refers to those who assist investigators by providing information from their specialized or native knowledge.
Representatives or proxies who act for others who intend to sell something, most often real estate, but may be extended to those performing this role in any transaction of goods or services.
Containers composed of toner and mechanical components used to print images within laser printers.
Describes equipment used for critical examination or evaluation.
Refers to the style and culture of the historical and linguistic region of peninsular India, comprising the north-central and northeastern portions of present-day Andhra Pradesh state.
Substances, usually taken internally or applied topically, having the primary purpose of curing or alleviating symptoms of illness or injury.

Hard, heavy wood from the Brazilian species Mezilaurus itauba, having uniform texture and color, greenish olive in color when cut but becoming dark chestnut color over time. It has been used in construction, for shipbuilding, bridges, posts, beams, door and window sills, floorboards, and furniture.

Monoclinic crystalline mineral with a combined salt of sodium sulfate and sodium nitrate. Darapskite is found naturally in nitrate ores and in limestone caves. It is more rarely found as a strong saline efflorescence on surfaces of walls and buildings.

A liquid made up of molecules of hydrogen and oxygen (HO2). When pure, it is colorless, tasteless, and odorless. It exists in gaseous, liquid, and solid forms; it is liquid at room temperature. It is the liquid of which seas, lakes, and rivers are composed, and which falls as rain. Water is one of the most plentiful and essential of compounds. It is vital to life, participating in virtually every process that occurs in plants and animals. One of its most important properties is its ability to dissolve many other substances. The versatility of water as a solvent is essential to living organisms. The term "water" is typically used to refer to the liquid form of this compound; for the solid or gaseous forms, use "ice" or "water vapor."
Refers to the highly conventionalized figure based on the shape of the human heart.
Buildings that act as workshops for specific crafts or industries.

Objects originally created to communicate a particular personal belief, opinion, achievement, status, rank, occupation, membership, office, or identity. This class includes articles of adornment or clothing worn primarily for their symbolism.
Horizontal, curved boards used to exercise muscles used for balancing one's body.
Numeric or alphanumeric values that govern the sort order of data in databases, spreadsheets or other datasets.
General term referring to the combination of all the electric, pneumatic, and other power sources used to operate the dentist's tools.
The standard unit of currency of the United States of America, containing 100 cents.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 2299 to 2200 (or 2300 to 2201) Before Common Era.
Small ridges or furrows in a formerly smooth surface.

Group of African languages spoken mainly in southern Africa, with two outlying languages found in eastern Africa. Although they seem to have no direct relationships, they are unified by use of click consonants and they do not belong to other language families.
Flat horizontal or gently inclined surfaces on the sea floor, often long and narrow, and which are bounded by steeper ascending and descending slopes.

Ware produced on the Greek mainland and dating from the Middle Helladic, characterized by wheelmade, angular shapes, and unornamented surfaces. The pottery was named by Schliemann after the legendary inhabitants of Orchomenus in central Greece, where he first came upon it; today it is believed unlikely that the Minyans were the original creators of Minyan ware
Artists in any media who focus primarily on subject matter having to do with sports and sports players.
People who produce work in the visual arts using mixed media, which is any combination of a variety of materials plus the associated techniques, used in the making of a single work of art.

Commercially produced, British acrylic plastic consisting essentially of polymerized methyl methacrylate. Polymethyl methacrylate was discovered in the early 1930s by British chemists at Imperial Chemical Industries in England and trademarked the name Perspex.
Range of deep greenish blue colors resembling the pigment phthalocyanine blue.
Upland moors or sandy areas dominated by low shrubby vegetation including heather.
Style and culture of the people of Senegal.

A water-soluble compound created by bubbling carbon dioxide through a suspension of magnesium carbonate in water. In conservation, magnesium bicarbonate solutions are used for deacidifcation of paper.
Slender parts of objects, such as the vertical support of a vessel which unites its bowl to its base or the tubelike portion of a pipe that fits snugly into the bowl.
Whisks, typically consisting of birch twigs, used in traditional Finnish saunas to gently stimulate the skin and muscles.
Particular administrative districts. Examples are in Puerto Rico.
Taking away or getting rid of something.
Refers to the technique of exposing something to radiation, whether of x-rays, ultraviolet light, or other type.
The elements or parts of an entity and their interrelations, often with reference to the manner in which they are organized or constructed.
On shoes, leather strips typically found between the sole and the upper. Phased out by the end of the 18th century.
Vehicles made for children's play.
Literary works emphasizing a story or sequence of events, given in order and with the establishing of connections between them.
Small bags composed of a pile-woven front and weft-faced plain weave on the back.
Textiles or other materials used as wrappings for parcels, gifts, or articles that need to be put away or carried from one place to another.
In Indian architecture, a door-jamb showing lotus-garland as decoration.
Depictions of people and activity on urban streets.
The state or quality of being morally or spiritually pure, sinless, or free from ritual pollution.
Commercially published groups of photographs of one place, event, or activity, sometimes spiral bound or accordion folded.
Versions of scholarly or scientific documents that precede formal peer review or publication, but that may be distributed for assessment.

Refers to the international movement in painting and sculpture that became popular in the late 1960s and early 1970s. The style is characterized by the precise, objective rendering of subject matter, often street scenes or portraits, taken from actual photographs or direct casts from human figures.
Long, narrow pieces of rigid or flexible material, of generally uniform width.
Nationality, culture, and style of Livonia, a historic region on the eastern shores of the Baltic Sea, located in present-day Latvia.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Tennessee.
Statistical technique in which the spatial locations, distributions, and relations of designated factors are analyzed.

Religious tradition formulated in ca. 700s CE Japan, comprising beliefs from Shinto, Shingon Buddhism, and Taoism. Developed by legendary Buddhist monk En no Gyōja (ca. 634-701), also known as En the Ascetic. Particularly focuses on completing challenging physical feats, such as reciting sutras under waterfalls or fasting, as well as seclusion from worldly desires in mountain and forest temples.
The customs, tendencies, and routines attributed to how people exist.

The process of performing actions to halt damage or to keep any object, material, or system from injury or destruction. For example, it may refer to the preservation of food or an ecological system. For the function of preservation, use "preservation (function)" or a specific type of preservation, such as "historic preservation." For the discipline of involving treatment and long-term preventive care of cultural and natural heritage objects and systems, use "conservation."

Small bedroom tables, often of trestle form, with deeply rimmed tops and sometimes one or more shelves designed to hold the contents of a man's pockets when he undresses. First made in France in the 1720s and popular there and in England in the late 18th century.
Upholstered armchairs, often with a button-tufted back, having a single piece forming a high sloping back and a concave seat; of a type made in America in the mid-19th to early 20th centuries.
Circular or flattened-ovoid tubes extending through the base plate of a lamp and housing the wick; combustion of fuel and wick takes place at the top of the tube.
Unnaturalized foreign residents of a country, nation, or state who do not hold official citizenship status within that place. Noncitizens may or may not possess residence documentation.

Persons who assign or address a work of art or literature, in a style less formal than that of a dedication; also, persons who mark a surface with words or characters, especially in a durable or conspicuous way.

Generally, those employed in the business of making a consumer product directly or indirectly available to consumers; includes everyone in the chain of production and distribution, such as the manufacturers, wholesalers, distributers, and retailers.  Specifically in the construction business, those who provide materials, equipment, and prefabricated parts to contractors, subcontractors, or owners, but who usually do not do any installation or labor.
Handles on tools.

Generally, devices that can transform an input of physical quantity, usually coming from an energy source, into an output quantity typically of a different kind, for instance, converting solar heat into electricity, or pressure into hydraulic energy. Many devices, such as phonograph pickups, microphones, thermometers, loudspeakers, and light meters, can be termed transducers.
Culture or style of the group who speak the Telugu language and are from the Indian areas of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Yanam in Puducherry.

Correctly, wood from various trees of the genus Jacaranda, native to the West Indies, tropical Americas, Florida, and California. Jacaranda is a fragrant ornamental wood has been used for carvings, small decorative items, pianos, knife handles, cabinets, and expensive furniture. The term is also commonly used as a general term for Jacaranda as well as various varieties of rosewood, which itself is a general term referring to various species of the genera Dalbergia or Melanorrhoea.
A carbonate of sodium and aluminum found as a low-temperature hydrothermal mineral in shale. It crystallizes in the orthorhombic crystal system. It is not mined for ore.
A heavy inert noble gas with symbol Xe or X and atomic number of 54, used principally in lamps, lasers, and as a general anaesthetic.
Any emblem or device occupying the field of a shield, such as a geometric design or the image of a person, animal, plant, or other object.

Ancient structures using evaporative cooling systems, employing windcatchers and water brought from nearby springs to produce cold or even freezing conditions for storing food or ice. Developed in ancient Persia; yakhchals had a domed-shape structure above ground and a large subterranean storage space.
Watercraft propelled by the wind, consisting of a horizontal platform for the rider and a single large sail. Riders use a bar attached to the sail to both maneuver the craft and to stay on the board.
Indicators describing the status of the item described or of the record itself.
Organizers, tubs, cases, and other containers or spaces for holding and storing dental equipment.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1700 to 1799 (or 1701 to 1800).
Family of languages spoken by indigenous Native Americans in New Mexico, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas.
Tongue-like extensions of a flat sea floor into adjacent, higher features.

Japanese porcelain ware produced at the Nabeshima clan’s kiln at Ōkawauchiyama from ca. 1677 to 1871. Production consisted of sometsuke (underglaze cobalt blue, blue-and-white), aoki (celadon), and iroe (polychrome overglaze enamel) wares. In addition to developing original decorative processes, the kiln copied the Chinese doucai techniques.
Artists in any medium whose primary subject matter is still life, which depicts inanimate objects such as bowls of fruit, bottles, and flowers, which are often arranged in an aesthetic composition.
Craftsmen or artists who decorate surfaces with patterns or pictures composed of small, regularly-shaped pieces of colored durable material, such as stone or glass.

Proprietary name for polymerized methyl methacrylate, used as a substitute for glass in products such as windows, skylights, illuminated signs, and aircraft. Plexiglas was trademarked by Rohm and Haas AG in Germany ca. 1930s.
Refers to a range of bluish and greenish colors resembling the turquoise mineral, typically a light to moderate greenish blue.
Mountainous or elevated lands.
Style and culture of the nation of Seychelles, an island republic in the western Indian Ocean, comprising about 115 islands.

Thimble-sized dies, caps, or plates equipped with myriad small holes through which a plastic melt base material or polymer spinning solution is forced, thus enabling the extrusion of long filaments for spinning into yarn and other man-made fibers.  Akin to a shower head through which water is forced by pressure, these devices likewise utilize pressure to force the solution through its many circular or oval-shaped openings. Each hole on the die forms a single filament; the combined filaments produced by the totality of holes form filament yarn. Typically made of stainless steel or platinum, these devices can comprise myriad sizes and shapes depending upon the resulting filament's desired appearance and surface area. However, these devices are conventionally circular in shape and produce fibers that are round in cross section.

Powdery alkaline compound used in paper pulp manufacture and mass deacidification treatments. Magnesium hydroxide is found in nature as the mineral brucite. It is used medicinally as a laxative and antacid. As a suspension in water it is commonly known as milk of magnesia.

Various types of small flaps, loops, or other devices projecting from an object, usually to facilitate identification, grasping, or fastening or that serve as decorative elements on the edges of costume.
Small pieces of cloth used for washing one's face and body.
Roman provinces during the Principate where the Roman Senate had the right to appoint the governor or proconsul.
Archaeological term for the secondary shaping of a stone core or implement after initial manufacture. Small fragments are removed to sharpen, straighten, or thin the core.
The transformation of a substance from a solid or gaseous state to a liquid state.
Tactile surface characteristics. For the visual characteristics of an artistic composition, use "texture (visual characteristics)."
Ornamental clips made to hold sashes or scarves around the wearer.
Any of various toys whose primary components spin or whirl.
Literature about  natural objects, beings, and phenomena.
Small cases or pieces of luggage specifically designed to store toiletry items and make-up.
In Indian architecture, a pearl-festoon with half-lotuses within its loops as a decorative motif.

Refers to pictorial or photographic representations that faithfully (though not necessarily with total accuracy) depict actual locations. May be "landscapes (representations)," "cityscapes (visual works)," or "townscapes (representations)," though those terms tend to imply invention whereas "topographical views" implies recording of appearances. For faithful drawings of individual buildings, use "measured drawings," "record drawings," or "as-built drawings."

Works that merge already known art forms to inaugurate a new type. If a resulting art form gains currency and acquires a name, it becomes a new medium and is no longer intermedial art. For works that employ several distinct art forms, such as sculpture and music, see "multimedia works." To indicate that works are composed of a variety of materials, see "mixed media."
Refers to people in Spain and Latin America who work with sacred art and the carving of retables. Because of their drawing skills they were also known historically as “professors of architecture.”
Representations, realistic or stylized, of a penis, usually erect; often seen as a symbol of the generative power in nature, venerated in various religions.

Objects comprising sheets of paper, vellum, papyrus, or another material that are bound together. Volumes may include printed books, manuscripts, sketchbooks, or albums. Where the parts of a historical volume have been dispersed, records for the individual sheets may be linked as a historical volume for research purposes. Given that an album contains individual drawings, prints, or other art works that have been mounted, the drawings, etc. in an album may be cataloged as items and linked to the record for the volume. For intact books, manuscripts, and sketchbooks, the illuminations or other parts may be better cataloged as components rather than items. The term may also refer to a separately bound portion or division of a written work or series that is divided into two or more sections, each contained in a separate binding; generally, multiple volumes of the same work or series are of similar dimensions and contained in similar bindings.

Source material that is derived directly from a person or project without secondary interpretation or commentary. Used especially for unique, unpublished materials, but it may also refer to published materials, including transcriptions of interviews. Other examples of primary sources include correspondence, diaries, unique handwritten archival documents, works of art, manuscripts, etc.
Refers to the historicizing, classicizing movement in Italian painting of the 1980s.
Genre of objects comprising narrow, flexible strips, as of cloth, paper, plastic, or metal.
Ethnicity, culture, and styles of the Lorraine region, currently in present-day northwestern France.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Texas.

Means of measuring wavelengths of the rays of a spectrum. To refer to the observance of how a substance transmits, emits, or responds to various wavelengths in the electromagnetic energy spectrum, use "spectroscopy." When the word is used in a bound compound term, it may form a synonym for spectroscopy, because the process of observing is not distinguished from the process of measuring; examples are "infrared spectrometry" and "infrared spectroscopy," which are considered synonyms.

Refers to the Indian religion that blends together Islamic and Hindu elements, founded by Nanak Sikhs, disciples of Nanak and his nine successors known as the Ten Gurus, in the Punjab region of India in the late 15th century. Its characteristic principles include the idea that there is one God, who is not represented by idols or images; the individual's responsibility in leading an obedient life dominated by prayer and the reading of the Granth; and the striving for transmigration where the individual exists in communion with God. Prominent features of this belief system are the lack of a professional priesthood and the eligibility of adults of either sex to conduct religious ceremonies.
Strong heavy waist-high tables on which the work of mechanics, machinists, and carpenters is performed.
Term generally applied to any of several varieties of chairs having a seat and back formed from a single sheet of canvas, leather, or the like, and hanging loosely on a frame.
Persons who  live at, occupy, or have possession of a building, a unit within a building, a plot of land, or any other property for a significant period of time.
People of superior intellect, particularly those who pursue academic or cultural interests.
People who make a copies of a work in writing, or to copy out from an original.
Metal points which may be attached, for example, to rules, steel squares, or beam compasses in order to scribe large circles.
Tools used in the process of covering and stuffing furniture.
Style and period of the Utpala dynasty, a Hindu kingdom that ruled over the Kashmir region from 8th to 10th century CE.
The red-coloured wood of the mahogany gum-tree (Eucalyptus marginata) of West Australia that is strong, hard, reasonably fire-resistant and rot resistant. Known to be used for flooring.
A highly transparent and exceedingly hard mineral of carbon; it is the hardest known substance.

An infusible, insoluble white solid oxide of zinc (ZnO) in the form of a fine white powder used in compounding rubber, as a fungicide, as an absorber of ultraviolet radiation, in pharmaceuticals, in cosmetic preparations, in pigments, as a component in paint to toughen and prevent yellowing, as a semi-conductor, in photocopying processes (related to its photoconductivity), and in ceramic glazes, printing inks, glass colorants, enamels, and lubricants. Zinc oxide is prepared in either of two ways: by the oxidation of pure zinc or by roasting zinc ore. Zinc oxide has been used for various purposes since the Middle Ages, but was rarely used in making pigments until the 19th century.
In Indian art and architecture, a moon-arch decorative motif : candraśālā; candraśālikā; gavākṣa.
A prose description of the salient characteristics of a work in relation to a particular style, historical period, group, school, or movement.
Equipment including a motor and a variety of handpieces and tips, using air and suction to dry and clean the mouth of saliva and debris during dental procedures.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 700 to 799 (or 701 to 800).
Small language family spoken by people in northern Papua New Guinea; the validity of this family is disputed among scholars.
Deep, narrow, asymmetrical depressions on the sea floor, with somewhat steep sides.
Pottery objects from the northern and central Pre-Columbian Andes that uses a negative painting technique, in which the design is reserved in unpainted areas against a colored background.

Artists, particularly painters, who specialize in a style emphasizing shadows, darkness, or night effects; particularly used for artists having this style in 17th-century Europe and as influenced by Caravaggio.

Artists that create works, such as in cinema, opera, or performance art that fuse aesthetic disciplines into a singular artistic experience. Working collaboratively, each individual draws on distinct fields of knowledge to create what is usually a single work, or activity. Bound by these distinct distinct fields, as in, for example in cinema, where photographers, writers, editors, and musicians work together to create a whole, singular piece. The term 'multidisciplinary artist' is often used to mean artists that work in multiple disciplines, but for artists that create works in many disciplines or that individually create works drawing on multiple fields, use 'interdisciplinary artists.'
Trademarked name for an aqueous wax emulsion used as a protective coating for metals.

Variable color in the range of vivid and bright cool blues, resembling pigment derived originally from the mineral lapis lazuli and named with reference to the foreign ("overseas") origin of this mineral.
Elevation of earth's surface, smaller than a mountain.
Style and culture of the nation of Sierra Leone.

The general term for a range of mechanized devices equipped with long rows of spindles designed to spin and twist cotton fibers into yarn. Lancashire entrepreneur Richard Arkwright is credited with inventing the first spinning frame in 1767, contributing to the Industrial Revolution-era transition to factory-based textile manufacturing. Historically leveraging water power, these machines made it possible to mass produce strong yarn and reduced the need to spin cotton by hand.

A colorless crystalline solid used industrially as a crosslinking agent to form stable alcohol gels. Dissolved in methanol or Freon and deposited on paper as an aerosol spray, has been used as a nonaqueous deacidication treatment.
Projections on the hinged lids of some drinking vessels used to open the lid with the thumb while grasping the handle.
Supports consisting of a base, a short shaft, and a top, on which wigs are placed when not in use.
Particular subdivisions of a city or town, particularly when there are six districts total. Examples are in Italy.
Process of removing an outer layer by drawing the edge of some instrument held nearly perpendicularly across the surface.
The process or action of rendering magnetic; the condition of being magnetized.
The quality or state of being theatrical in action, appearence, or style.
Ornaments, made of varying materials, made to hold scarves in place around the wearer. Usually ring-shaped, which allows the scarf to be pulled through.
Short prose tales popular in the Renaissance and for later prose narratives intermediate between novels and short stories.
Re-useable small receptacles of varied design that keep matches dry and stored for use, often used in military or outdoor contexts.
In Indian architecture, a series of lotuses; loti-formed vessel.

Creative works that depict settlements that may be considered towns or villages. For creative works depicting settlements that may be considered cities, use "cityscapes." For images that seem more documentary than creative, prefer "views." To designate the actual built forms of towns or cities as perceived visually and aesthetically, use "townscapes (built environment)."
Paper stencils, created by a traditional Japanese method; used primarily to stencil on fabric, but the cut paper itself may be considered an art work.
Those whose occupation is to fabricate cordage formed by twisting or braiding natural or artificial fiber.
Motifs representing chubby, sometimes winged and naked figures of little boys, derived from Greco-Roman depictions of Eros. Common in art from Renaissance through the 18th century.
Objective goals to be achieved, or quantities to be attained through action or development.

Identification of a group of people as distinct from other groups on the basis of physical or socially defined characteristics, such as the color of skin, language, nationality, ethnic group, or a combination of multiple characteristics. More recently race has been considered an obsolete or non-scientific system of classification though it is widely and commonly used for categorization still in contexts such as a census.

Includes offers by one person or organization to another of terms and conditions with reference to some work or undertaking and plans or schemes put forward for consideration, discussion, or adoption.

Refers to the international art and cultural movement that flourished in Britain and America in the 1950s and 1960s. Influenced by Dada, the movement advocated the use of everyday imagery, such as advertisements, signs, and comic strips, executed in the techniques and graphic styles of mass media. The movement respresented a move toward a more objective, immediate art form after the dominance of Abstract Expressionism.

Relatively small, flat objects, often rectangular, used to cover roofs, floors or walls, as game pieces, as lids, or for other purposes. Originally referred to such objects made of baked earth or earthenware, but modern usage includes such items made of other materials, including metal or plastic.
Nationality, styles, and culture of Luxembourg in western Europe.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Utah.

Means of observing the way a substance transmits, emits, or responds to various wavelengths in the electromagnetic energy spectrum. To refer to measurement of wavelengths (rather than only looking at them) of a spectrum, and not necessarily wavelengths only of electromagnetic energy spectrum, use "spectrometry." When the word is used in a bound compound term, it may form a synonym for spectrometry, as process of observing and measuring are not distinguished; examples are "infrared spectrometry" and "infrared spectroscopy," which are considered synonyms.
Beliefs and practices of the ancient Slavic peoples of eastern Europe, a large branch of the Indo-European family of peoples.
The action of transforming, altering, or treating a thing by using a special process or technique, including operating upon the thing mechanically or chemically.

Sturdy tables of relatively substantial size, used for various tasks, from kitchen work to carpentry or other heavy work. For table-like structures of waist height, typically used for heavy work while standing, prefer "work benches."
High-backed, low-seated chairs without arms and often upholstered; intended for bedroom use.
Children deprived by death of one or usually both parents. The term is sometimes extended to children who are abandoned or unsupported by living parents.
Persons who by creative imagination create a new device or process.

People who prepare the dead for burial. For people who arrange the funeral, use "funeral directors." In small communities or former times, the arrangement of the funeral was also often done by the undertaker.

Strips of woven ribbon or other material that is either impregnated with ink or coated in a transferable medium, used to offset pigment to paper in various devices for impact printing. These are part of standard designs for manual or electric typewriters. Typewriter ribbon most commonly comes wound onto spools or reels, but may also be found in cassettes or other forms.
General term for tools and equipment used for wallpaper hanging.
Style and culture of the area around ancient Vaisali, in Bihar, India, important to Buddhism and Jainism.
A medicinal or cosmetic preparation, in the form of a viscous or semisolid paste, applied to the skin; formerly used for ceremonial or sacramental anointing.
Wood of the species Dyera costulata. Grows in Malaysia, Borneo, and other regions of Southeast Asia.

A green, calcium magnesium silicate mineral sometimes used as a gemstone; a pyroxene-type mineral with short, monoclinic crystals. The transparent to translucent crystals have either a square or octagonal cross section. The color of diopside crystals ranges from light to dark green. Powdered diopside is used as a matting agent in ceramic glazes.
In Indian art and architecture, a garland of mesh design or motif.
A description of the subjects depicted in, on, or by the work.

Specialized instruments designed to remove carious dentin from the tooth surface. Typically is a double-ended instrument with an angled working-end, shaped to access the problematic parts of the mouth.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1000 to 1099 (or 1001 to 1100).
Small language family spoken in central New Guinea, along the left bank of the May River.
Depressions on the sea floor with characteristically flat bottoms and steep sides; usually more shallow than undersea trenches.

Refers to the characteristic pottery produced by the Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) culture, an Iron Age culture in north India from ca. 700 BCE-ca. 200 BCE. The ware is recognizable by its black or bluish lustre.

Artists, usually printmakers or painters, who specialize in Ukioyo-e, a genre that developed in the Edo period, Japan, and is characterized by a mixture of the realistic narrative of brothels, kabuki theaters, and other such places, with a distinctive decorative style.
People who make contemporary works of art that employ several distinct art forms, such as sculpture and music or painting and light art.
Trademarked name for a series of low molecular weight, hydrogenated hydrocarbon resins. In conservation, it is used as a varnish for furniture and pictures.
A range of greenish blue or green colors resembling verditer pigment, which is prepared by adding chalk or whiting to a solution of nitrate of copper, often used in making crayons and water colors.
Rock pinnacles, pillars, or columns of rock having fantastical shapes, formed by erosion or other natural agency. Hoodoos generally form within sedimentary rock and volcanic rock formations.
General national designation of the nation of Somalia, the Somali Democratic Republic.

Machines equipped with many spindles designed to simultaneously draw out, twist, and wind (or spin) multiple spindles of fibers to form yarn. A modification of the spinning jenny, these machines were equipped with spindles mounted on an enlarged moving portion of the machine, rather than on a stationary frame. The modern spinning machine is often considered to be a power-driven instantiation of these manually-operated devices. The first reference to this device is thought to be in approximately 1802, when James Scholfield installed the spinning machine in his North Andover textile mill.

Oxide of magnesium, a highly refractive, white, powdery material used in ceramic glazes, bricks, magnesia cement, and other industrial processes. In paper conservation, magnesium oxide has been used as a nonaqueous alkalization agent.
Rows or ranks of objects arranged one above the other, as amphitheater seats, beams, or oars on galleys.

Refers to particular administrative units, defined differently in different jurisdictions, for example a province or district under the rule of a governor, archbishop, sheriff, or steward. Refers to particular administrative units, defined differently in different jurisdictions, for example a province or district under the rule of a governor, archbishop, sheriff, or steward.
Devices in which seeds are sprouted.

Generally, the process of cutting or scraping the surface of something with a sharp-edged tool so as to remove a thin layer or unwanted extra material. In the context of skin and hide preparation, denotes the beamhouse operation of removing hair or excess dermal material to create an even thickness. In the context of bookbinding, for the removal of a small amount of material from the edges of a book, use "trimming."
Processes by which minerals are introduced into other matter, such as into rock to form ore deposits or into organic components to form fossils.

Fasteners, made of various materials, used to hold shirts in place on the wearer or to group together loose fabric of a shirt. Clips do not pierce the fabric but instead have a loop or bar to weave the shirt through.

Invented prose narratives of considerable length and a certain complexity that deal imaginatively with human experience through a connected sequence of events involving a group of persons in a specific setting.
Small portable cases or pouches that are designed to accommodate a variety of medicines for travel.
In Indian architecture, lotus foliage, lotus leaf; series of lotus petals carved on the external-most jamb.

Views that are realistically conceived but having elements that are completely imaginary. For scenes of accurately rendered buildings grouped in an arbitrary, imaginary arrangement, use "capricci (visual works)."
Italian imitation of Asian lacquer work in which the relief decorations are formed by cut-out prints stuck to the surface and varnished.
People who make, repair, or sell saddles, bridges, and other eqipment for horses, particularly riding horses.
