A diamond shaped figure with hooks projecting from the outermost diamond; a rectangular figure with lateral projecting hooks; or a triangular figure with a projecting hook serving as the tail.
Body of generalizations and principles developed in association with practice in a field of activity and forming its content as an intellectual discipline.

Interaction, communication, artifacts, and customs related to written texts. This includes reading, but also buying, lending, giving and owning books (both read or unread), the attitude of individuals, groups and society as a whole towards the reading of books, literacy, acquiring reading, reading behavior, reading habits, reading clubs, library patronage and other aspects. Reading culture is researched with the help of egodocuments such as diaries, literary criticism, research on traces of reading such as marginalia and underscorings, and iconographic analysis.
Hypertext documents of text or images that are accessible via the World Wide Web, hosted on a web site.

Hollow, usually cylindrical objects, long in proportion to their diameter, sometimes flexible; in varied forms these may be used for conveying or containing fluids or vapor, or for containing other materials such as paper or textiles.

Describes the culture and style related to the modern Republic of North Macedonia in southeastern Europe. The republic changed its name from "Macedonia" to "North Macedonia" in 2019, putting an end to a dispute over the name with Greece. However, North Macedonia prefers "Macedonian" as an adjectival form to describe anything related to cultural or ethnic identity. This is distinct and separate from the adjective "Macedonian" used in Greece.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Vermont.
In chemistry, a rapid identification technique which introduces a drop of reagent into a drop of an unknown mixture held on a “spot plate”, on paper or on a microscopic slide.

Religion and philosophical tradition originating in China, generally emphasizing individual freedom and spontaneity, laissez-faire government and social primitivism, techniques of self-transformation, mystical experience, and individual and government ethical responsibility. It is founded on the texts of the Tao-te Ching, Chuang-tzu, and Lieh-tzu. Later, the tradition diverged, resulting in strictly philosophical Taoism on the one hand, and religious Taoism on the other. The governing principle of the latter is the struggle to reach a state of 'immortality' through a strict regimen of dietary restrictions, breath control, meditation and visualization of the gods that inhabit the body, sexual control and discipline, the practice of theoretical internal alchemy (nei-tan) used to energize the Yin and Yang forces within the body, and the use of magic talismans. Successful devotees were known as hsien (Immortals).
Modernist chair designed ca. 1958. The chair features a foam and upholstery-covered molded shell of synthetic material on an aluminum swivel base.
People awaiting or under medical care and treatment.
Owners or holders of land or houses which are leased or rented to others.
Refers to persons or agencies who offer goods and services for sale, especially those who create, market, and sell computers, software, automated systems, databases, and services.
In archaeology, stone tools from which flakes have been removed from only one side of an edge.
Equipment that allows a stream of high-pressurized water to be projected at particular speed and flow, typically used for cutting or cleaning purposes.
Culture of a dynasty in the Indian subcontinent that originated from the Deccan, from mid-3rd century CE.

Any materials added to increase optical density and make opaque. In ceramics, opacifiers are substances added to glaze or enamels for this purpose. They include tin oxide, titanium dioxide, and lead chromate.

Rare and expensive wood figured with golden markings, from the species Dalbergia cearensis native to South America, mainly Brazil. The sapwood is white in color, with clearly defined variegated colored heartwood. It is varied from violet-brown to almost black, and streaked with violet brown, black, blackish-violet, or golden yellow. Because of the small size of the trees, its uses are restricted to decorative work, such as inlay and turnery.
A pearly sedimentary mineral composed of calcium-magnesium carbonate.
In Indian art and architecture, a water-leaf decoration on the inverted laśuna of the wall’s serried shafts.
Equipment used to assist divers with breathing when underwater by regulating the pressure of one's oxygen; usually consists of several tubes, a valve, and a pressure regulator.
The titles or names given to a work of art, architecture, or group, as well as the type of title, and the dates when the title was valid.
Diagnostic tools, typically having a hook on one end for caries detection and a an angled probe on the other end.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1400 to 1499 (or 1401 to 1500).
Language family comprising languages spoken near the mouth of the Mamberamo River, along the northern coast of Papua province, Indonesia.
Relatively shallow, wide depressions, usually with continuous gradient, and located on the sea floor.

Pottery from Paestum, Italy, characterized by vases of various shapes decorated with distinctive motifs and scenes such as women's daily life and Dionysiac subjects. Distinctive palmettes that are placed below the handle often serve as a frame for the figural scenes.
Landscape and view painters who specialized in "vedute," which are largely factual topographical views, especially 18th-century Italian paintings, drawings, or prints of cities.
Artists that use new means of mass communication to create their work, specifically electronic and digital technology, inclusive of video and other forms of graphic, motion picture, and sound media.
Trademarked name for an impregnating agent, an acetal copolymer used in conservation of damaged and acid paper.
A range of clear blue colors, resembling the blue in the coat of arms of the British royal Windsor family.
Relatively undissected uplands located in between adjacent stream valleys.
Style and culture of the people of South Africa.

Early spinning machines having more than one spindle, enabling a person to spin a number of yarns simultaneously. The characteristic feature of these devices is the fact the the spindles are fixed upon a stationary frame, rather than being placed on a moving portion of the machine. For an earlier type of spinning machine, involving a hand- or foot-pedaled wheel and a single spindle, use "spinning wheels."
A brown-black insoluble compound used as an oxidant, a depolarizer of battery cells, for paint pigments, to decolorize glass, and in manufacture of ceramics and glass.
Administrative areas of particular kinds. An example is in Nairobi.
Process of removing the fleshy parts of leaves, seeds or other vegetation to reveal only the most durable fibers.
Any natural aging process and its effects on materials. In conservation science refers to effects on paper and other materials; as opposed to accelerated (or "artificial") aging.
A  thread count is a measurement technique that determines the compactness of a fabric by counting the number of warp yarns and filling yarns in 1 square inch of fabric.
Removable fasteners usually of metal and often inset with precious stones, or other material. These are passed through eyelets in a shirt in order to fasten the shirt front.
Tales in rhymed verse for children.
Curved, thin pieces of metal used to hold banknotes together. Sometimes engraved with decoration.
In Indian architecture, a lotus vine motif; padmalatā.

Portayals of the navel of Vishnu or other form or symbol of the female organ of generation, used as an object of veneration among Hindus and others; often used in conjunction with the male symbol, the lingam.

Visual works made of or decorated with lacquer, which is paint or varnish that dries with a high gloss. Works are usually made of thin wood, then coated and decorated with lacquer applied in several coats. This dries to a very hard and smooth surface layer which is durable, waterproof, and attractive to feel and look at. Works of lacquer may be painted with pictures, inlaid with shell and other materials, carved, or dusted with gold and given other further decorative treatments.
In Indian architecture, a lion (decorative motif).

Generally, the comparative study and analysis of the characteristics of things, including their grouping into classes on the basis of common characteristics; also includes the analysis of the origin and meaning of Biblical types, especially in comparing the Old and New Testaments.
Occupations, amusements, or physical activities carried out by humans and animals for their own sake or for relaxation and entertainment.

Broadly used for the written works by an individual or a specific group of individuals. For the body of writings of a particular nation, region, period, or language, of a particular form or genre, on a particular subject, or for a particular audience, use "literature (writings)."

Documents designed to inform prospective investors or patrons, consisting of a formal summary of a proposed commercial, literary, or other venture, or a description of the features or services of an institution or business.
Chairs with tall legs and a high seat, such as those used at counters.

Founding fathers or male heads of families, tribal lines, or entire social orders, classes, or peoples. Use also for the high-ranking prelates of that title in certain Christian churches, such as the Greek Orthodox, Russian Orthodox, and Coptic Churches.
Those who take the lead in any enterprise or movement, or who guide the actions and opinions of followers.
Parts or components of wells.

Period and culture that flourished in India ca. 1500 BCE-ca. 500 BCE, developing due to an influx of nomadic and pastoral peoples who spoke Indo-European languages and followed the early religion of Vedism.
Any material used to protect, cushion, or brace objects for safe shipment or storage. For packing material that carries information or otherwise conveys a message about the product, use "packaging."
Wood of Paulownia tomentosa, used in China, Korea and Japan to make objects including musical instruments.
A mineral of the pyroxene group consisting of magnesium silicate varying in color from grayish white to olive green and brown.
In Indian art and architecture, the depiction of a crown of matted locks; motif of arranged mass of matted locks.
Iron hooks or spars.
Containers, usually made of metal, used to hold gases necessary for breathing when conducting underwater activities.
Toys where young children knock rods or balls through a cavity, causing them to fall out again.
An expression of the value of the work or entity, including currency and amount.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 400 to 499 (or 401 to 500).
Family of distantly related languages in northern Argentina.
Italian red-gloss pottery dating to before the flourishing of terra sigillata in the first century BCE.
Artists who make found object sculptures.
Acrylic resin emulsion of the Rhom & Haas Company, used in paint, textile finish, and adhesive.
Narrow strips of land connecting two larger land masses separated by the sea, such as the Isthmus of Panama.
Style and culture of the people of the Sudan.

Tool comprising two sticks with an adjustment mechanism in the center to control width.  Their ends are stuck into the selvedge and the mechanism is then locked so that the weaving is locked at the desired width.  Sometimes, a needle or hook may be inserted in the selvedge and tied to the frame to maintain width and tension.

Compound of sulfur and manganese. It occurs naturally as the mineral alabandite. It may be synthesized by reacting ammonium sulfide with a manganese salt. Compound of sulfur and manganese. It occurs naturally as the mineral alabandite. It may be synthesized by reacting ammonium sulfide with a manganese salt. Found as in inclusion in cast iron to which it has been added to aid in solidification.
The constituent political and administrative units of various nations under a federal system of government, such as Australia and the United States of America.
Removing a substance from the surface of a liquid.
In chemistry, processes involving an acid and a base in which the net result is neither acid nor alkaline.
Characteristics and qualities that are time-related.
Any of the various parts that make up the construction of footwear.
Minor works of literature or music.
Fob-like objects that attach to a baby's clothes with a clip, to prevent the pacifier from being lost.

Typically cylindrical or nearly cylindrical vessels, generally of metal or plastic, for catching, holding, or carrying liquids or solids and usually having a bail handle or other handle and sometimes a removable cover.

In general, paintings and calligraphy by Zen Buddhist priests of China, Korea, and Japan. More specifically, may refer to work by Japanese Zen priests from the Edo period (1600-1868). The content of the work is focused on teachings of the Dharma. Aesthetically this style is known to be bold, spontaneous and even amateurish in execution and light-hearted in tone. The term literally means "Zen painting." For the practice of painting as a Zen activity, use "gazen."
Works or parts of works made of stones, particularly precious or semi-precious stones.
People who make seals, artifacts bearing monograms, writing, numbers, or designs in intaglio for making an impression in relief on some soft, tenacious substance such as clay or wax.
In Indian architecture, a siṁhavaktra; lion-head nāsī-top; frontal lion-head.
Indication in texts, databases, tables, and lists when information for the instance at hand is not readily available.
State or condition of existing or operating in the country as opposed to a town or city.
Polls taken by sampling a cross section of the public in an effort to predict election results or establish public attitudes.
Nationality, culture, or style of the island Mallorca, located in the Mediterranean Sea.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. District of Columbia.

Analytical method used in archaeology and petrography that characterizes stones by comparing isotopic ratios of elements such as oxygen, carbon, or sulfur. SIA has been used in geological evaluation of environmental variables impacting the chemical characteristics and isotopic composition of stone samples.

Liberal denomination founded in the United States and Canada in 1961 through the merger of the Unitarian and Universalist denominations. Its characteristic principles include the responsibility of each individual for her or his own religious beliefs and ethics, the inherent worth and dignity of every human being, the value of religiously-motivated action for social reform, democratic method in church governance, and respect and regard for a diversity of religious traditions. There is no creed to which members must subscribe.

In general, people of high social status, especially those from an established wealthy family. Examples are members of the privileged citizen class of ancient Rome; or to holders of high rank and title in the Byzantine Empire; in several Italian republics (Venice, Genoa, etc.), or in the Free Cities of the German Empire.
Those who lecture or give formal discourses designed to instruct, usually in a college or university, but may be extended to professional people who give lectures for hire.
Circular frameworks of wood, metal, or other hard material often with cogs or teeth on the rim used to transmit or modify force and motion in machinery or a mechanical contrivance.
Any soft material or mass that serves to cushion, protect, fill out, or heighten.

Wood of the trees of the genus Laburnum, having a striking, dark greenish brown or reddish brown color, fine grain, and capable of taking a high polish. It is typically used for cabinetmaking and inlay.
A yellowish green mineral consisting of a silicate of calcium, aluminum, and iron and occurring massive or in grains, columns, and monoclinic crystal.
In Indian art and architecture, a crown of matted locks; arranged mass of matted locks.

Exercise equipment built to simulate the movements made during skiing; often used in physical therapy and in rehabilitation for elderly individuals. Consists of a platform on a raised, curved track and a handlebar. Users stand on the platform and use their legs to move back and forth across the track.
Evidence, assurance, or guarantee of a fact by supplying a source for the verification of a piece of knowledge.
Files used in dental work, including files used by hand or rotary files mounted in a dental handpiece.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1 to 99 (or 1 to 100).
Language group including families in Brazil and parts of Argentina, Paraguay, and Bolivia.

Minoan pottery from Crete dating to the Late Neolithic and Early Minoan periods. It is characterized by a surface fired to a dark brown or black and burnished with a smooth pebble or wooden burnisher to produce a linear decoration.

Creators of ornament, which includes decorative forms that are an integral part of a building or object but are not essential to its structure. The term is especially used to refer to those artists who specialize in engraved designs of ornament.

Printmaking paper, with trademarked brand name by Rives Papers; made with 100% cotton and no optical brightening agents. It is bright white in color, smooth, soft, and pliable, having an absorbent wove surface.

Distinctive landscapes, usually located on soluble rock such as irregular limestone, and characterized by caverns, sinkholes, fissures, ridges, and underground drainage. The term is derived from the Karst region of Slovenia.
Style and culture of the people of mixed heritage, predominantly Nguni, inhabiting the kingdom of Swaziland (independent since 1968) and parts of eastern Transvaal in the Republic of South Africa.

Mechanized devices consisting of a confined box chamber, which may be heated, cooled, or exposed to a steam injection, designed to crimp, fold, bulk, and bend the individual fibers of a tow, converted tow, sliver, or similar assemblage of filaments. To facilitate this method of texturing, these devices are attached to a series of either feed rollers or fluid jets onto which textile fibers are packed or compressed; these rollers then force the fibers into the stuffer box chamber where they are exposed temperature changes while being pressed into a zig-zag pattern. Though this device was originally created for crimping carpets, it was eventually adapted to the textile industry by Joseph Bancroft & Sons.

A thiol used as a corrosion inhibitor or a sulfide mineral flotation collector. In conservation science, used in treatment of metal artifacts of archaeological origin to treat tarnish and as a fungicide in paper.
Areas of various kinds designated as significant due to high population density, economic significance, or other reasons. They may be administrative areas, or the term may be used in a generic sense.
The process of removing the outer layer of something, such as the removal of original paint when restoring a painting.
Processes involving changes in atomic nuclei.

Relief features or surface configurations of a place or an object, including its natural and man-made features. For the art or practice of the accurate graphic representation of the topography of a specific urban area, tract of land, or other place, use "topography (image-making)."
Works that record interviews conducted to preserve the recollections of persons whose experience or memories are representative or are of special historical or social significance.
Bags or containers of varied form designed to carry objects by one person.

Ancient Roman containers in the form of a shallow bowl without handles, often with a base whose center is pushed up into the body; used for offering libations at religious ceremonies or for drinking. For similar ancient Greek containers, use "phialae."
Visual works that utilize lasers.

Craftsmen who make and sometimes also design shoes, boots, and other footwear, as well as repair or refinish them. For those whose primary work is to repair or refinish footwear, and sometimes also other items such as handbags, luggage, and belts see "cobblers."
In Indian architecture, a lion's head; lion’s mouth holding water-chute.

Indication in texts, databases, tables, and lists when information for the instance at hand is not determined. For information that is unavailable to the cataloger or other information provider, rather than being in general undetermined, prefer "unavailable."
The quality or state of being hidden or concealed.

Recorded information, often standardized in format and content and treated as a unit. Records include such compilations of data regardless of medium, that are created, received, and maintained by a project, agency, institution, organization, or individual in pursuance of legal obligations, in the transaction of business, for the storage of research and knowledge, or for other purposes.

Refers to art in which the process of creating it becomes the subject matter, first applied to the practice in Action Painting and Tachisme in the 1940s and 1950s, and later to the work of a group of artists working in the late 1960s. The style is characterized by the introduction of time, change, and chance, often resulting in documentation about the artwork's creation.
Nationality, styles, or culture of Malta, a southern European archipelago and currently a nation in the Mediterranean Sea.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Washington.
Auxiliary technique of analysis which artificially colors (with stain or dye) portions of the organic material examined to provide contrast between parts, thus facilitating examination.

Term used to designate the syncretic Afro-Creole religion of Haiti, which melds elements of Roman Catholic ritual with traditional West African magical and religious rites. Adherents commonly embrace spirit possession, animal sacrifice, altar worship, and ceremonial participation to serve the Vodou spirits (or Iwa). While rooted in the Vodún religious practices indigenous to Dahomey, Vodou signifies a specific New World transformation of Vodń as realized by West Africans enslaved on the plantations of Saint-Domingue (modern-day Haiti) during the Atlantic slave trade. Vodou provided a means for enslaved peoples’ liberation and identity-making. The religion played a significant role in facilitating the Haitian Revolution and continues to thrive as a popular folk religion both in Haiti and the diaspora. For the traditional religion of the Fon and Ewe people in Dahomey (modern-day Benin), use “Vodún.” For the African diasporic religion of the Mississippi River Valley, use “voodoo (Mississippi River Valley) .”
The process of setting upright or causing to stand up. For the process of lifting something into the air from the ground, use "lifting (transporting)."
Refers to a variety of 19th-century chairs with nautical motifs and often a tablet top and a backrail incorporating cable molding. Made after the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805.
Characters or figurative masks that performing artists, such as actors, writers, or singers, take on in order to perform. The persona may have a different name from the actual person.
People who are in love or who have sexual intercourse.

Current usage refers generally to liquid containing aromatic ingredients in an alcohol base; used as a personal toiletry item. Originally any substance that emits a pleasant smell when burned, primarily incense, from the Latin term referring to smoke or burning, "per fumum."

Tough, elastic, heavy wood obtained from various species of different genera of the Annonaceae family, native to the West Indies, Jamaica, Cuba, Hispainola, and Guiana, used for wheel spokes, carriage shafts, fishing rods, and archery bows.
Hydrous magnesium sulfate mineral usually found as a crust, efflorescence, or tiny crystals on mine and cave walls. Neutralized and purified, epsomite is sold as epsom salts.
The flower of the banana plant or plantain motif.
A description of watermarks, which are marks inherent in or applied to the material before it was fashioned into the work, including watermarks and stationers' stamps or marks.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1 to 999 (or 1 to 1000).
Language family in Brazil, Colombia, and Venezuela.

Pottery, primarily household wares, characterized by a brown glaze, originally made by the Rockingham Ceramic Factory in Yorkshire, England. Similar wares called "Rockingham ware" were later made in the United States in Chelsea, Massachusetts, Baltimore, Maryland, and elsewhere.

People who practice the art of painting, which is applying pigments suspended in liquid to a surface to create an expressive or communicative image. For people who apply paint primarily to protect or give simple color to a surface, use "painters (tradespeople)."
Trademarked name for a series of styrene acrylate and pure acrylate aqueous dispersions used for preservation purposes in libraries and archives.
Connections between two land masses, usually used in a prehistoric context.
Style and culture of the East African state of Tanzania, formed in 1964 by the union of the republics of Tanganyika and Zanzibar.

Hand-held tools, typically comprising a series of teasel seed pods mounted onto a wooden frame and handle, used to brush the surface of woven cloth in order to raise the naps of the wool. Beginning in the 1860s, growing textile manufacturing mills began to replace these tools with automated napping gigs.

White, crystalline compound formerly used extensively as wood preservative, antiseptic and disinfectant, insecticide, and, in archival conservation, a fungicide for paper and books. Due to its toxicity mercuric chloride's use is now restricted in the U.S.
Divisions under the jurisdiction of a nation, not vested with the full authority of provinces or states, but having some degree of local governing and legislative power.
Cultivating implements used primarily for pulverizing or smoothing the soil, sometimes for mulching, covering seed, or removing weeds.
The process of removing an outer layer of material.
The process or result of combining with oxygen; sometimes contributing to the degradation of a surface, such as in corrosion.
The state of not being finished or completed. Includes the sense of intentionally not being brought to what is usually considered to be a final state of completion.

Slits in costume used as a form of decoration to reveal a lining or undergarment often of a contrasting color, used especially on doublets, hose, sleeves, and shoes of the 15th through the 17th century.

Literature, stories, and oral traditions having to do with the beginnings of a culture, civilization, peoples, land, deity, hero, or other entity; often associated with religious beliefs or mythology. Origins stories are most often literary or legendary; they are typically not historical, in that they are not documented and not considered true by those outside the culture or belief system.
Flat, folding cases for holding banknotes and papers, and typically of a size designed to fit the inside pocket of a man's jacket of the 19th and early 20th centuries.

Ancient Greek containers in the form of a shallow bowl without handles, often with a base whose center is pushed up into the body. It is used for drinking or pouring libations of wine or olive oil in ancient Greek ritual; the libations were poured over an altar to honor the gods or a burial site to satisfy the souls of the deceased. For similar ancient Roman containers, use "paterae (containers)."
Works or parts of works made of leather, particularly worked and decorated leather.
Painters and other artists who make signs, which are lettered notices or other displays that bear names, directions, warnings, advertisements, or symbols that are displayed or posted for public view.
In Indian architecture, a tōraṇa with a crowning gorgonoid or leonoid head.
General term referring to a person, people, place, or thing for which the identity has not been established .

The state or condition of a group of humans living in company with other people; the system of customs and organization adopted by a group of people for harmonious coexistence or mutual benefit. May also apply to the social life of animals that are not human.
Citations or other sets of bibliographic elements that refer to a published or other work and are complete enough to provide unique identification of the work for a particular bibliographic function.

Refers to the art and cultural movement of the mid- to late 1960s that was international in scope, but flourished mainly on the American West Coast. The movement advocated the exploration of the subconscious mind through drugs, sensory deprivation, and a total immersion of the senses through music and light shows. In the visual arts, the style is characterized by obsessively detailed images, ambiguous representations of space, and acidic colors.
Nationality, style, and culture of Moldova in eastern Europe.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of  Wisconsin.

Term used to designate the syncretic Afro-Creole religion developed along the lower Mississippi River and its tributaries, most notably New Orleans. The evolution of Voodoo was strongly influenced by Haitian immigration to Southern Louisiana in the early 19th century; the diaspora melded its Vodou practices with elements of neo-African counterculture religions, Native American traditions, and traditional folk healing. Voodoo practitioners centered spirits of the dead, embodied by the almighty God figure Li Grand Zombi. While variations of Voodoo are still practiced today, it is widely understood to be a historical religion that died out by the 1940s due to increased persecution of worshipers. Nonetheless, it continues to be associated with the culture and identity of the Southern Louisiana region. In addition to its usage in the specific context of southern Louisiana, the term 'voodoo' is often used as a racialized and pejorative umbrella term for all Black peoples’ religious and spiritual practices. When used outside the context of the Mississippi River Valley, voodoo represents a colonial misunderstanding of Black religion that ignores the distinct histories of Vodún, Vodou, and Voodoo. For the Afro-Creole religion of Haiti, use "Vodou." For the traditional religion of the Fon and Ewe people in Dahomey (modern-day Benin), use “Vodún.”
The process of rejoining and fixing a part or parts of a whole that have become detached.
Late-19th-century, richly upholstered armchairs with little or no frame exposed and usually mounted on a spring platform or having a spring back.
People who drive elephants, especially in south Asia.
Refers to the class of materials and material products used in the processing of photographs, including the constituent parts of the photograph itself.

Wood obtained from any of several species of the genus Shorea; sold as Philippine mahogany on the American market. It is a reddish- brown wood resembling mahogany in texture, weight, and strength, but it is not dimensionally stable with changes in relative humidity. Lauan wood is used for furniture, cabinetry, veneers, and boat building.

A secondary mineral produced by the surface oxidation of primary cobalt. Erythrite is a violet to peach red arsenate once used as a pigment in paints, glass, and ceramics; replaced for these purposes by its synthetic form, cobaltous arsenate.
Four opposing sets of rams horns, usually with a diamond in the middle.  The four sets often appear within a gül.
A short breathing tube used by swimmers and divers, often used in conjunction with a diving mask or physically attached to a diving mask.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1300 to 1399 (or 1301 to 1400).
Small language family of closely related languages of Paraguay.
Chinese porcelain in a famille rose style, painted with ruby ​​red enamel on the underside. It was first manufactured during the reign of Emperor Yongzheng (1723-1735).
People who create works using primarily paper, which is thin matted or felted sheets or webs of fiber, as both the support (if any) and the media. For people who make paper, use "papermakers."

Trademarked name for a sheer openweave monofilament polyester fabric produced until 2004. Stabiltex (TM) has been used as a support fabric in textile conservation, a polyester crepeline for covering fragile textiles. Tetex TR (TM), produced by Sefar, is essentially the same material.
Relatively large areas of land that have boundaries formed by oceans, seas, or other bodies of water.
Nationality, style, or culture of the West African state of Togo (formerly Togoland).
Compound HgI2, in the form of a dense, bright red powder that is used as a paint preservative and as an antiseptic.
Principal governing bodies of a town.
The shaping of objects by means of cutting tools while the material from which the objects are made rotates rapidly on a lathe.

Treatment or impregnation of a substance or compound with ozone. Ozonation may be part of a purification process or used to induce a change in color as in ozone treatment of resonant wood to obtain the appearance of old wood, desirable in restoration of violins as well as for production of new musical instruments.
In art context refers to modern paintings with matte surfaces and rough, unvarnished finishes.
Pleated or crimped cuffs or frills worn at wrist or forearm.
Short, fictitious stories that illustrate a moral attitude or religious principle.
Shallow bowls made to store rings when not in use. Some examples include cylindrical protrusions to hang rings on as well as being placed in the dish.

Vessels, generally of ceramic, glass, metal, or plastic, that have a wide mouth with a broad lip and usually a handle at one side, but sometimes having two ears; includes those accompanied by a washbowl and used for personal hygiene.
Artwork featuring light as an artistic medium.
People or corporate bodies who specialize in designing and constructing staircases and their components.
In Indian architecture, a lion-crest.
Appearances or outward aspects of things or situations.

Pervasive, oversimplified, culturally contingent, and often inaccurate characterizations of particular social groups, rooted in assumption or perception rather than empirical data. Such assumptions are often deeply embedded within power structures and social institutions. The study of stereotyping within the social sciences is widely traced to Walter Lippmann, who coined the social use of the term in his 1922 book "Public Opinon."
Sources intended primarily for consultation rather than for consecutive reading.

Theorized by French curator and critic Nicolas Bourriaud in the late 1990s, relational art describes a set of art practices in which the production of human relations and their social context are privileged over a discrete, portable, autonomous work. The artist, acting as a facilitator, establishes spaces, situations, or "platforms" designed to host social activities and information exchange between audience participants. Participatory in nature, a relational work emphasizes the social interactions created by the installation or event and conceives the audience as a community. Key practitioners include Liam Gillick, Pierre Huyghe, Maurizio Cattelan, Carsten Höller, and Rirkrit Tiravanija.
Nationality or culture of Monaco, a small independent principality on the Mediterranean coast of France.
Culture or condition of citizenship or residency of the U.S. state of Wyoming.
The process of studying and interpreting the land surface and subsurface conditions of a geographical area using, for example, aerial photography or computer models.

Popularized, general term for varied belief systems or rituals derived from African diaspora religions practiced in the Caribbean or southern United States, or in West Africa itself that combine elements of Roman Catholic ritual with traditional West African elements. It is recommended to avoid use of this term, but instead to reference more specific concepts such as Vodou, Vodun, or Voodoo (Mississippi River).

Any correction or removal of errors. In techniques such as photogrammetry and aerial photography, rectification refers to compensation for predictably distortive data routinely added to procedures in order to produce correct results.

A chair designed by Marcel Breuer ca. 1925 that features a tubular chromed-steel structure and strips of leather used as seat, back, and arm support. This chair is often used as a prime example of the design aesthetic of the Bauhaus during this period, and of mid-20th century modernist design in general, due to the innovation of the use of tubular steel in its construction.
People who journey a great distance, particularly those who travel to a sacred place as an act of religious devotion.

Material that causes illness or death when absorbed, inhaled, or ingested by a living organism; particularly when the substance is able to kill by rapid action and when taken in small quantity. For a toxic material secreted by an animal and injected into a victim, use "venom."
Wood of trees belonging to the genus Laurus, native to India, West Pakistan and Burma. It is used extensively for making furniture, cabinet-making, interior joinery, and staircases.
Mineral used to create chromium oxide pigment.
In Indian art, a representation of an earring, an earring motif.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 300 to 399 (or 301 to 400).
Language family consisting of other families, spoken in Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Bolivia.

Pottery originating in Samos, an island in the Aegean Sea. May refer to Roman pottery made on Samos or of clay from Samos, as a variety of Terra sigillata pottery. May also refer to Greek Geometric and Orientalizing pottery made or excavated on Samos.
Artists or craftsmen who use papier mâché, which is a composite material made of repulped or pulverized paper and a liquid adhesive binder, as their primary material.

Registered trademark for foamed polystyrene that was developed in the 1940s. Polystyrene expanded into a multicellular mass that has one-sixth the weight of cork and will withstand temperatures above 170 degrees Fahrenheit.
Large masses or areas of solidified, or flowing, erupted magmas.
The style and culture of the central African State, Uganda.

Devices designed to dry and stretch wet woven cloth to a desired width under tension. These devices have been used since the 14th century, during which time they comprised large wooden frames equipped with an array of equidistantly mounted tenterhooks on which wet cloth was fastened and held taut. Mechanized devices now exist, however, characterized by pairs of continuous traveling chains fitted with hooks on horizontal tracks. The chains diverge as they pull the fabric forward through the device, stretching the fabric on all edges. After traveling half the length of the mechanized frame, fabric is exposed to water through the device's spray pipe components and subsequently carried through a heated chamber component to dry.
A non-aqueous deacidifying agent applied to paper via spray or immersion.
Political entitites officially bound in agreement to a joint action or policy. The European Union is an example.

Agricultural implements having a thin, flat blade usually set transversely at the end of a long handle; used for such activities as breaking up or loosening the surface of the ground, dislodging weeds, and covering plants with soil.
Forming or paring something, especially wood, by cutting off bits with a knife.
The process of piercing or passing into or through a body, form, or substance.
Use to describe things perceptible by vision, usually to the unaided eye, but may be under other circumstances, such as through a microscope.
Shaped coverings for the arm. Originally made separate from the main garment and attached by lacing through eyelets at the shoulder; later, often made as component parts of garments.
Narrative accounts of the suffering or martyrdom of Jesus Christ, a saint, or other character.

Literally "hanging objects", these containers were used in conjunction with "netsuke" to suspend personal items such as tobacco, pipes, brushes and money from the waist sashes, or "obi", of Japanese men. The most common sagemono were boxes made of lacquer, called "inrō".
Vessels supported by two, three or four small legs, often refers particularly to Middle American archaeological objects and also the European Beaker culture of the Neolithic and Early Bronze Age.

Translucent porcelain plaques produced from 1830 to ca. 1900, most in Germany by the Royal Porcelain Manufactory in Berlin and by Meissen, and in England by Minton and Copeland. Relief molds of decorative motifs, usually based on paintings, were impressed into hard-paste porcelain while in its soft state so that after firing the image would be visible by transmitting light through the plate. These objects were typically hung in windows, placed on stands as screens, or incorporated into lamp shades. The process was invented by Baron Paul de Bourgoing and patented in France in 1827.
People who specialize in making sundials, which are instruments that indicate approximate time of day from a shadow cast in sunlight.
In Indian architecture, a lion-crest.

General term referring to systems of quantities taken as unified standards of measure, usually represent a uniform system established by a nation. The regulation of weights and measures is necessary for science, industry, and commerce.
Culturally imposed prohibitions often supported by supernatural authority, which, if violated, result in punishment.
General term for texts of religion, sacred beliefs, or related to religious beliefs and practices.

An aesthetic trend in the post-Stalinist Soviet Union (late 1950s – 1970s) often referred to as ‘the official art of the Khrushchev thaw’. The term was coined by the art critic Alexander Kamenski in 1969. Developed as a reaction to the Stalin era ‘colorful’ Socialist Realism, Severe Style emphasized simplified expressive outline and utilized a simple palette of muddied greys browns and earth tones. The style’s aesthetics was influenced by the early Soviet realism of the 1920s-1930s and medieval Russian icon and church fresco painting. On the conceptual level the artists of the ‘severe style’ strived to reveal the ‘unvarnished truthfulness’ of the rigorous reality. The most common subject matter of their paintings was people of labor (workers, builders, geologists, cultural workers). In Central Asia artists turned to the aesthetics of the Severe Style in late 1960s – 1970s.
Nationality, style, and culture of Montenegro in southeastern Europe.
Methods of analysis that characterize material by examining how it responds to heat.

General term for organized belief systems having large numbers of adherents world-wide. The twelve religions typically included among the world religions are the following: Baha'i, Buddhism, Christianity, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, Jainism, Judaism, Shinto, Sikhism, Taoism, and Zoroastrianism.

The action of saying or doing something over again which one has already said or done. The term may be used in the context of visual images, the spoken or written word, performances, music, and other contexts.

Angular lawn chairs, similar in form to Adirondack chairs, but constructed of boards rather than slats and heavier and more amply proportioned; older than the classic Adirondack chairs, patented by Harry C. Brunnell, and manufactured between 1904 and 1930.
In Nahua society, persons belonging to the noble class who performed state functions and ruled the macehualtin, or common people.

General term for those who bring about or construct artifacts directly by their own labor, especially as their craft or profession; also, those who construct intangible works, such as music. For industrialists who own or run a manufacturing plant, use "manufacturers." For those who practice an occupation, trade, or pursuit requiring manual dexterity or artistic skill, use "craftsmen."
Wood of the Citrus limon, or lemon tree. A hardwood with fine grain that can be carved into small tools or objects.

A mineral composed of aluminum sulfate and hydrous basic calcium often formed by the reaction of sulfates and concrete or mortar. Ettringite crystal formation induces sulfate decay in the cement paste matrix. Conservation interventions seek to remove ettringite or limit its attack.
In Indian architecture, a miniature bell, generally suspended from chain (decorative motif).
Concave, circular-shaped sleds, usually made of metal or plastic.

Sets of various items, such as instruments, tools, hardware and other components, usually in a scaled-down size and sometimes requiring assembly. It includes instructions. Used to teach children how apply knowledge about the science fields, usually by performing various experiments.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1800 to 1899 (or 1801 to 1900).
Family of languages spoken by people indigenous to southern Mexico, Guatemala, and Belize; Mayan languages were also formerly spoken in western Honduras and western El Salvador.

Ceramic wares made at kiln sites in Kagoshima Prefecture (formerly the Satsuma domain) in southern Kyushu, from the early 17th century to the present. Wares include items used for tea ceremonies and everyday use, such as "sharkskin" ware and copies of Sawankhalok ware, a Thai ware decorated with underglazed iron-oxide painting.
Artists who specialize in making pastels, which are works of art created with colored crayons made of ground pigment mixed with a small amount of binder, either oil or water and gum.
Brand name for a fast-setting adhesive based on ethyl-2-cyanoacrylate polymers, with stabilizers, thickeners, and catalysts.
The style and culture of  the south central African country, Zambia (formerly Northern Rhodesia).

Hand-held devices fitted with a series of metal teeth, which are designed to eliminate neps and impurities in fibers, as well as to ensure that fibers lay parallel to one another. While these devices can take many forms, they are typically utilized to create cleaner, finer, stronger, and more lustrous fibers.
Simple unpolymerized compounds, having low molecular weight as distinguished from dimers or polymers.
Particular types of administrative divisions. Examples are in India.
The action of removing a coating, as of paint or ink, from the surface of a support with a cloth or similar material to leave empty zones or a film behind as an effect, to efface, or to clean.
Refers to a class of techniques used to generate selective, permeable membranes. These processes rely on the phase separation of polymer solutions producing porous polymer films.
Glasslike in appearance or composition.
Strips, originally of bone, now usually of plastic or metal, used to stiffen various elements of costume, such as women's foundation garments, strapless bodices, and shirt collars.
Genre designating single or collected dramatic works, intended to be acted on the stage.
Bags used primarily for carrying books and school supplies.
Cylindrical or rounded containers, often of metal or earthenware and varying in size; used chiefly for domestic purposes.
Visual works created using materials that are considered to be precious or rare, such as gold, gemstones, ivory, etc.
Craftsmen who make swords.
Nahua designs composed of repeating figures of skulls and bones.

The action, condition, or cultural concept of visiting different cities, countries or regions, especially distant or unfamiliar places, whether by necessity or for pleasure or education. One common purpose of travel is to see different sights and acquaint oneself with cultures different from one's own.
Official or formal records of a special investigation, in the form of documents containing presentations of facts, proceedings, investigations, or events.

Refers to the work of a group of avant-garde artists and cultural theorists active in several European countries from 1957 to 1972. Known formally as the Internationale Situationniste, the group was influenced by Dada, Surrealism, Marxism, and anarchism. The movement was highly politicized and often defaced appropriated imagery and comic strips with revolutionary slogans. Founded by Guy Debord, Situationists were influential in the developments of the general strike in Paris, May 1968.
Refers to the style and culture of the Mordvin people of the middle Volga region in modern western Russia.
Any number of methods for determining volumetrically the concentration of a desired substance in solution by adding a standard solution of known volume and strength until the reaction is completed.

In Indian Philosophy, a spiritual and ascetic discipline having the goal of spiritual purification and self-understanding leading to union with the divine (samadhi). It is one of the six orthodox systems of Indian philosophy, and a system of meditative discipline.
Subjecting something to a special process again.

Chairs having a seat that is a shaped and contoured plank drilled with sockets on the upper and lower surfaces to anchor the back and undercarriage and having the rear legs and a back that are separate rather than continuous members. The elements of the back are vertical, horizontal, or curved, and spindles may or may not be present. Chairs using bentwood back frame and legs pegged directly into the seat instead of being framed with aprons. The style is so named for chairs originating around Windsor Castle in England between 1700 and 1725, and was made by wheelwrights or turners, rather than cabinetmakers.
In Roman society, commoners, as opposed to privileged patricians; plebeans could be prominent citizens and wealthy.
Persons engaged in the physical production of coins. For officials in charge of and responsible for coin production or content, use "mintmasters."

Refers to a mixture of flowers, herbs, spices, fruit juices or other aromatic substances that are typically aged, fermented, or stored in a jar and used for scent. Although the term originally referred to the jar (or "pot") that stored the fermenting mixture, it is often now used to refer to the aromatic mixture itself.

Grotesque animal heads or masks resembling the form of a lion that are used as decorative devices on some temples, common in India and Southeast Asia. They may appear with horns, pearl festoons, or floral garlands erupting from the mouth; grāsamukha; demon head.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 800 to 899 (or 801 to 900).
Small family of languages spoken by indigenous Native American peoples on the east coast of Nicaragua and nearby areas.

Pottery found predominantly in the Diyala region of Mesopotamia at the start of the Early Dynastic period from about 2900 to 2750 BCE; characterized by generally large, broad-shouldered pots with painted red designs, often outlined in black, on a buff or yellow ground.
Highly trained experts who work with pearls, their main task being to peel away the multiple skins of a natural pearl layer by laye to uncover a series of tints.

A trademarked name for polytetrafluoroethyelene (PTFE) which was discovered by Roy Plunkett 1938 and first marketed as Teflon (TM) by DuPont in 1943. This fluorinated polymer is known for its resistance to adhesion, heat, oxidation, light, and chemicals. It is used chiefly for molding articles and for nonstick cookware.

Relatively small, usually isolated, masses of land with level or nearly level tops, standing distinctly above the surrounding countryside, and having steep erosion scarps on all sides; smaller than plateaus, and larger than buttes.
The style and culture of Zimbabwe or of Black Rhodesians in the former Rhodesia.

General term for the mechanical equipment used to remove superfluous moisture content from fabrics or garments, comprising a broad range of devices utilizing a range of drying methods. Most typically, this equipment uses hot air to evaporate the fabric's liquid content.
A salt or ester of nitric acid.
Particular types of local administrative divisions that have a single tier and are often responsible for all local government functions within their area. Examples are in the United Kingdom.
Increased rate of chemical reaction caused by radiant energy in the form of light.
The distance between successive peaks of a wave or wave-like formation.
Ornamental fastening that secures one half of a sweater or jacket to the other, usually through a buttonhole.
Bags used to protect shoes while in storage or when traveling.  Often made in pairs and generally of a soft fabric with a drawstring closure.

Vessels often made of bronze, with dual spouts; one on each side of the reservoir, that were usually suspended within a niche, and used to dispense water by tilting to one side or the other. Used before the advent of running water, most date from the Middle Ages.
Works produced by artists, often in post card format, specifically when intended to be mailed to other artists or to be displayed in an exhibition; may be unique works or multiples.
In Indian architecture, a bull’s head motif.
In Indian art or architecture, the quality of being terrifying.
Recorded results of diligent and systematic inquiry or investigation into a subject made to discover or revise facts, theories, or applications.

Movement centered around artist Otto Peine, as well as artists at the Center for Advanced Visual Studies at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Sky artists have utilized modern technologies such as laser projections and solar-tracked holograms, as well as simpler techniques such as kite-flying, to produce temporary artworks in sky space, both urban and rural.

Refers in general to cultures that have occupied the same area as the modern nation of the Netherlands in northwestern Europe along the North Sea, as well as the territory extending through medieval Flanders, which is the area of modern Belgium and part of France. For the culture of the modern nation of the Netherlands, prefer "Dutch (culture)," although usage overlaps.
Analysis to determine how a tool was used and what materials were worked on by examining its wear.

Designates the ancient pre-Islamic religion of Iran, founded by the Iranian prophet Zoroaster in the sixth century BCE, featuring both monotheistic and dualistic features that later influenced Judaism, Islam, and Christianity. The religious society is divided into a three-part class structure consisting of chiefs and priests; warriors; and husbandmen and cattle breeders. Gods or daivas are often associated with each class, though Zoroaster rejected the cults of all gods except the one of Ahura Mazda (the Wise Lord). Its characteristic principle is the belief that the origin of evil began in the exercise of free will at the nascent stage of creation in which the twin sons of Ahura Mazda, embittered in rivalry, chose different moral paths: Spent Mainyu (Bounteous Spirit) choose good; Angra Mainyu (Destructive Spirit) chose evil.
The process of converting or adapting a thing or material for a different purpose or for use in a different way.

Wide, contoured chairs consisting of a molded plastic shell covered with foam rubber padding and wool cloth set on a tubular steel frame; designed by Eero Saarinen and introduced in the mid-1940s; usually accompanied by a matching upholstered footstool.

Persons involuntarily confined in prison or kept in custody. Use "convicts" for those serving a prison sentence following conviction for a criminal offense. Use "inmates" for those confined, voluntarily or involuntarily, to an institutional facility.

Generally refers to people who serve as objects for artists (especially painters and sculptors) to copy. May also refer to people employed in that profession, or people employed to display clothes or fashion.

A moist, usually heated mass of a substance with a soft, absorbent, or pasty consistency, applied to the skin of a person or animal, or to another surface for the purpose of cleaning, drawing out abscesses, increasing circulation, or relieving swelling or pain.

Wood derived from trees of the genus Guaiacum; it is generally the heaviest, hardest, and most dense type of commercially available wood, black to brownish green in color. It is tough and difficult to carve, but valued for its fine grain that polishes to a high gloss. It is naturally resistant to fungi. It is used to make pulleys, shafts, axles, and bowling balls. The wood is relatively waterproof because of its high fat content.

Vitreous green iron silicate mineral, a member of the olivine group, named for the type locality, Fayal Island, Azores. The brittle stone was also produced synthetically as a component of slag separated in smelting at ancient iron working furnaces.
Ornamental motifs resembling cords which are interlaced.
Dental equipment for holding a dental bur or file. Usually made of corrosion-resistant materials to allow sterilization; may be high-speed or low-speed.
Languages of the native peoples of the Americas.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 100 to 199 (or 101 to 200).
Language family comprising living languages spoken on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Mexico, and surrounding areas.

Painted ware of mid-late Neolithic widely diffused in southern Italy during the fifth millennium. It is named for a site near Matero and is characterized by necked and flat-bottomed vessels with distinctive spiral handles. Serra d'Alto ware, which is often found among grave goods, may have been created as a prestige item intended for trade.
People who formulate works of performance art.  For people in the traditional performing arts, use "performing artists."
Trademark for a highly durable low-permeability polyethylene plastic used for storage containers.

Areas of uncultivated dry or wet land that are populated with low vegetation, such as grass and shrubs, and often flat with poor drainage systems. Often associated with regions within the British Isles. Distinct from "bogs," in which the land is regularly wet and comprised of peaty soil.

Large containers or casks in which textile materials are soaked in reducing baths, which utilize reducing agents like sodium hydrosulfite to convert water-insoluble vat dyes into a soluble form, as a means of altering the color of fibers for aesthetic purposes. When textile materials are exposed to dyes in these containers for prolonged periods of time, their individual fibers are impregnated with the dye color; the dyes, now infused in the fibers, are then oxidized back to their original insoluble forms for increased color brilliance and light fastness. First used in medieval Europe, these containers derived their names from the large vats once used in the reduction of indigo plants through fermentation.

In chemistry, refers to a large class of compounds containing at least one molecule of carbon. The only carbon compounds not considered organic are its oxides and carbonates. As distinct from "inorganic compounds".
Particular subdivisions of an urban area Examples are in the United Kingdom.

Preservation or conservation technique used for biological specimens that replaces fluids and fat with synthetic materials such as polyester polymers, epoxy resins, and silicone rubber. The technique has been used for the consolidation of organic archaeological materials. Plastinated specimens can be cured with gas, heat or UV- light in order to harden them.
Measurement of the relative heaviness of an object or other body; the force with which a body is attracted toward the earth or a celestial body by gravity.
Extended parts of a skirt, gown, or state robe that lie on the floor and trail behind the wearer, either separate or attached.
Aggressive, forcefully presented arguments, often disputing a policy or opinion.
Boxes in which shoes are packed.

Tall, multitiered vessels consisting of three globe-shaped bottles, each meant to be filled with a different colored liquid (usually water); set in windows or on the counters of apothecary shops in the 19th century to attract customers.

Visual works, or parts of works, where the image or design is made with small pieces of specially shaped wood, ivory, or other materials, often incorporated into a suface of decorative veneer in furniture or interior surfaces. Distinguished from "inlays (decorations)," where decorative pieces are set into a solid ground; in marquetry work, the entire surface is veneered. For less complex designs made of veneer, prefer "veneering (visual works)."
People who specialize in making tiles, which are small, flat objects, often rectangular and decorated, used to cover roofs, floors, or other surfaces.
In Indian art and architecture, a vyāla head.
In Indian art or architecture, the quality of tormentation.
Periodicals, reports, or essays giving critical estimates and appraisals of art, a performance, or event. For other critical descriptions and analyses, prefer "criticism."

Refers to the works of art associated with the aesthic doctrines developed by Argentine-Italian artist Lucio Fontana (1899-1968). The style is characterized by a desire to end the separation of architcture, painting and sculpture by synthesizing elements such as color, sound, space, motion and time into a new kind of total art. Notable are Fontana's canvases with have holes or slits, that cast shadows upon the surface.

Cultures and styles of the northern area of the continent of Europe in historic or current times; in the modern world, defined by the United Nations to include Denmark (with Faroe Islands), Estonia, Finland (with Åland), Iceland, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway (Svalbard and Jan Mayen), Sweden, and the UK (with Guernsey, Isle of Man and Jersey.
Examination with the naked eye, to distinguish from more technical modes of analysis employing tools or apparatus.
Chairs with X-shaped frames; often designed to fold.
The realm, group, or groups of ordinary people in general, or of a given community united by common ideas, ideology, or hobbies; distinguished from groups comprising the elite or a chosen few.
Those who practice or espouse an ethically righteous way of life.
Fine powders of various materials used to treat or protect the surface of a drawing or of parchment, or to transfer a design through a pricked drawing.

Wood of the species Terminalia superba, native to West Africa. It ranges in color from pale straw to dark irregular grey markings; it is used for making solid parts of furniture, paneling, inlay, and musical instruments, famously the Gibson guitar. It is prized for its workability, color, and finish.

General name for a large group of aluminum silicate minerals, usually white or flesh-red in color, occurring in crystals or in crystalline masses. Feldspars are divided into three primary groups: potassium aluminum silicates (orthoclase, microcline), sodium aluminum silicates (albite, anorthoclase), and calcium aluminum silicates (anorthite). A few of the feldspars are found as gemstones such as moonstone, sunstone, and Amazon stone, but most are found in mineral structures, such as granite and diorite. They are used in the production of clays, ceramics, glass, concrete, abrasives, for cleaning, as a flux in ceramics, glazes, and glass, in fertilizer, and in granular roofing material.
In Indian architecture, a ridge-plate; decorative pattern at kapōta corners.

Exercise equipment consisting of a single wheel propelled by the user using two pedals while straddling a frame. The wheel and all elements are attached to a base, preventing locomotion. Handlebars are also sometimes present to provide support.

Puzzles that challenge the user to slide (frequently flat) pieces along certain routes (usually on a board) to establish a certain end-configuration. The pieces to be moved may consist of simple shapes, or they may be imprinted with colors, patterns, sections of a larger picture like a jigsaw puzzle, numbers, or letters.
Millennium in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1000 to 1999 (or 1001 to 2000).
Language of South America, having several dialects; not clearly related to any other South American languages.
Japanese pottery of all types. The term is derived from the city of Seto, an important producer of utilitarian wares in the early modern period.

Individuals who specialize in creating photographs, which are still images produced from radiation-sensitive materials, typically by means of the chemical action of light on a sensitive film, paper, glass, or metal.
Trademarked name for water soluble polymers composed of cellulose ethers used as protective colloids. In conservation, Tylose (TM) has been used to resize brittle paper.
A series of mountains or mountain ridges closely aligned in formation, direction, and age.
Any of a class of binary chemical compounds in which oxygen combines with another element or with an organic radical.
Particular subdivisions comprising an urban area. Examples are in colonial Australia.

In molecular biology a technique for rapidly replicating a sequence of genomic DNA by a simple enzyme reaction. The process is used to produce a sufficient quantity of DNA for detailed analysis and manipulation.
Projecting pieces of headgear that shade or protect the eyes, entire face, or neck. Also, separate pieces of headgear attached to a stiffened headband, worn to protect the eyes or face.
Literature intended for the general audience, rather than for specialists and not having the goal to attain critical acclaim.
Strong bags, usually paper or plastic, with handles, used to carry purchases or belongings.
Trade term for vessels, generally of glass or crystal, usually having a bowl mounted on a footed stem; especially those used for serving beverages and desserts.
Visual works that are the products of working any kind of metal, particularly metal objects of artistic merit.
Anatolian rug motif said to represent the highly stylized mouth of a wolf, orignally an amulet of herdsmen for protection against wolves.
State or condition of existing or moving in a city or other urban area.

Growing out of Constructionism, Structurism is the style and movement that emphasizes the underlying structural forms and processes found in nature, particularly as illustrated in the painted reliefs developed by the U.S. artist and theorist Charles Biederman (1906-2004).
Nationality and culture of Northern Ireland, the part of the United Kingdom in the northeast of the island of Ireland.

Electroanalytical technique used in analytical chemistry to determine the chemical makeup of small concentrations of metals in a substance by measuring electrical activity on electrodes placed in the substance.
Process or technique of using or creating mechanisms using ropes to allow access to high locations, particularly for the inspection, maintenance, and repair of built works or features.

Modernist chair designed by Hans J. Wegner ca. 1950, and manufactured by Carl Hansen. The frame is of beech and the seat is constructed of woven paper cord. Part of the backrest is in the form of the letter 'Y,' from which the chair derived its name.
Persons known of by the general public who have a role of special social, cultural, or political prominence as monarchs, state leaders, mayors, ministers, artists or musicians.
People who feel or express grief or sorrow.

Substance added to materials, natural science specimens, or foodstuffs to preserve them against deterioration, discoloration, or spoilage. In paint or adhesive, prevervatives are nonvolative chemicals added to prevent fermentation and mold growth.

Light-brown wood from of any of several trees of the genus Tilia, having a straight grain and easily worked. Linden wood is used for furniture and cabinets.  Its particular structural character lends itself well to carving, allowing tools to be used both along the grain and to some extent axially. Because linden wood is soft and workable, it has been used since the 1500s for decorative items with intricate carvings, such as picture frames and sculptures. Despite its relative cost, it was the most common wood used for sculpture in Germany. During the late 15th and early 16th centuries limewood was the preferred material for the genre of the winged altarpiece.
Comparatively rare rock-forming mineral related to feldspar but containing less silica.
In Indian architecture, a miniature kūṭa-shaped decorative motif; resembling square aedicula.

Exercise equipment used to provide aerobic exercise and endurance training. Generally consists of two parallel platforms attached to a base, with handlebars for stability. Users step on the platforms to simulate the motion of walking up stairs. Some machines use a staircase that moves in a continuous path.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 1600 to 1699 (or 1601 to 1700).
A language of Amazonas, Brazil, having one remaining dialect. Linguistically it is characterized by agglutinativity, a small number of phonemes, whistled speech, and the use of tone.

Japanese glazed ceramic ware produced in Seto by one of the so-called Six Ancient Kilns, dating from the 12th century to the end of the 15th century. Included are ash-glazed bottles, bowls, dishes and jars with four small handles, new shapes, patterns, iron glazed-wares and utensils for Buddhist rituals, and items household use, typically tea ceremony ware.
Artists who create photomontages, which are combinations of photographic images, or of photographic and other images such as architectural drawings, usually arranged into a somewhat unified image.

Trademarked name for series of spunbonded sheet products made of olefin fiber. This durable, tear resistant, waterproof polyethylene fabric has many applications. These include use as paper, garments, a protective liner in packing crates and display, and is widely used as a material in book conservation.

Prominent landforms rising considerably above the surrounding area, typically having steep slopes, a sharp summit area, and large mass. Mountains rarely occur individually, and in most cases, are found in ranges, chains, or systems.
General term for the mechanical equipment used to manufacture textiles and fabrics, comprising a broad range of devices that are essential to various phases of the production process.

Colorless crystalline alcohol used in making synthetic resins, paints, adhesives, and varnishes. Reacting pentaerythritol with nitric acid creates pentaerythritol tetranitrate (PETN),  a highly explosive organic compound related to nitroglycerine.
Particular subdivisions comprising an urban area, usually under the administration or government of a prefect. Examples are in Japan and ancient Rome.
The process of joining two or more molecules of the same kind to form a more complex molecule with different physical properties.
Bands encircling the waist, especially as a part of a skirt or pair of trousers.
Reverent petitions made to a deity or other spiritual entity.
Large two-handled open-topped bags, often of canvas, used especially for carrying small packages. Also, handbags or luggage of leather or another material, having the same basic design.
Ancient Aegean vessels with a false spout rising on top to support two stirrup-shaped handles and having a narrow, easily sealed spout further down on the shoulder.
Visual works created using multiple media.
Those who make or sell toys.
Relative worth of a thing, idea, place, or person based on esteem and judged in terms of importance, usefulness, or desirability.

Works including books, journal articles, speeches, reviews, research reports that analyze, assess or interpret an historical event, era, or phenomenon, by someone who did not experience first-hand or participate in the events or conditions, and generally utilizing primary sources to do so. Secondary sources often offer a review or a critique.  Also included would be reference sources like encyclopedias.

Refers to the art group co founded in 1999 by British artists Charles Thomson and Billy Childish, along with eleven other artists. The term 'Stuckist' was derived from fellow artist Tracey Emin's criticisms of Childish's paintings as 'Stuck! Stuck! Stuck!' The movement calls for a return to painting and the authenticity of direct expression. Rejecting postmodernism as a marketing tool that denies emotion or content, the Stuckists promote a form of 'Remodernism', where spirituality can counteract prevalent skepticism and nihilism.
Nationality, style, and culture of the people inhabiting the shores of the Baltic Sea east of the Vistula up to the 17th century, related linguistically to the Lithuanians and Latvians.
The action, process, or technique of making slight linear abrasions on a surface of any kind. May refer to damage, or to a technique for creation of art, such as in printmaking.

Persons who have fled their native country or usual country of residence to escape danger or persecution. For persons who have withdrawn voluntarily from their native country, especially those who have renounced allegiance to it, use "expatriates."
People who commit unlawful killings of human beings with malice aforethought.
Wood of trees belonging to the genus Robinia, ranging in color from yellow with a greenish tint to medium golden-brown, and used for making wheel spokes, ladder rungs, and occasionally furniture.

Multi-colored transparent or translucent material containing calcium fluoride, commonly occurring in massive crystalline cube form with perfect octahedral cleavage, used as flux, as a source of fluoride compound, and in the preparation of opalescent and opaque glass, vitreous enamel, and a purple pigment.
In Indian architecture, a miniature curvilinear or pyramidal shrine-model placed over a pillaret; decorative motif arranged in vertical chains in the formation of Bhūmija superstructure.
Tools, equipment, and supplies originally created for capturing terrestrial animals by any means other than weaponry. This subclass does not include objects used for the trapping of household pests.

Triangular, flexible appendages built to improve underwater movement, worn on the feet and sometimes also attached to the ankles with a single loop. Usually made of rubber. Commercial swim fins were first patented by Owen Churchill (1896-1985) in the 1930s.
Century in the proleptic Gregorian calendar including the years 600 to 699 (or 601 to 700).
Language family of the Native Americans of the southeastern United States, consisting several other language groupings.

Japanese stoneware found  in the Shigaraki valley, Southern Shiga prefecture,1185-1333. Included were vessels for domestic use such as narrow-mouthed jars and mortar bowls. In 1632, Shigaraki ware became the official ware for tea storage vessels for the Tokugawa Shogunate. Since the 19th century, production has shifted to various wares such as planters, braziers and sake jugs. Typically, the style is characterized by reddish brown and coarse grained wares, with white specks of feldspar or quartz that melt during firing and protrude from the surface.
An exponent of photorealism; an artist working in a photorealist style.

A trademarked translucent, white petroleum jelly first manufactured in 1870 by Robert Chesebrough, an English-born chemist. It is composed of a mixture of aliphatic hydrocarbons ranging from about C15 to C20; used as an ointment, lubricant, water repellent, release agent, and temporary adhesive. It is not recommended for contact with any art object.
Groups of mountain ranges with similarities in form, and thought to have originated from the same geologic events.

Magnifying tools, comprising a rotatable magnifying lens mounted a fixed distance above a platform on which textile materials can be examined, designed to count woven fabric threads within a given space or texture. To measure the thread count of a fabric sample, these optical  devices work to enlarge the user's view of the fabric's warp and weft threads so the fabric quality can be more easily determined.

Crystalline ester prepared from salicylic and carbolic acids, also known as salol; it is an ultraviolet-absorbing compound used in sun screen preparations and as a stabilizer for cellulosic and vinyl plastics.
Generic designation for divisions of an urban area.
A reaction or reaction mechanism step in which a proton is removed from one species (the acid) and accepted by another species (the base).
Bands on a sleeve, especially on a shirt sleeve, that cover the wrist.
Literary works in prose, but having the concentrated rhythmic, figurative, sonorous language characteristic of poetry, written as a continuous sequence of sentences without line breaks.
Containers, of varying sizes and materials, made to store knickknacks or other small items.
Works produced by the technique of montage. If photographs dominate the composition, use "photomontages."
Persons who make or sell wine.

Evil, immoral, or wicked habits or conduct, resulting in a state of depravity or corruption of morals, and sin. The number and type of vice varies by culture. In traditional western or Christian culture, as outlined by Dante, they include pride or vanity, envy or jealousy, wrath or anger, sloth or laziness, avarice, gluttony, and lust; others could include blasphemy, indifference, and hatred.
Books or pads of blank sheets used or intended for sketching, which are informal or rough drawings.

Refers to the works of a group of photographer working in Western Europe in the 1950's who were influenced by the teaching of Professer Otto Steinert. Emphasizing experimentation and the creative impulses of the photographer, the style is characterized by the subordination of the subject matter and an emphasis on pattern and form, in a manner akin to graphic art.

Nationality and culture of territories over which the Pope had sovereignty, generally referring to those held from 756 to 1870 in central Italy, but technically encompassing more lands and a longer historical period.
The process of removing rough or unsuitable parts of a material during processing. Examples of use are in reference to processing fibers, tanning of leather, processing bark, or processing stone.
People, or sometimes animals, who occupy, dwells, or have an abode in a given place, typically on a long-term basis.
Those who deliver speeches, are skilled in eloquence and rhetorical skill, or are proficient in public speaking.
In chemistry, a substance for use in chemical reaction to detect or test or produce other substances.

Wood of the species Heritiera javanica, native to West Africa, Thailand, and most notably the Philippines. The sapwood is pale yellowish-red with a light red to reddish-brown heartwood. It is used in the construction of cabinets, flooring, doors, boat ribs, and planking.
A principal ore of lead; lead sulfide (PbS). Often contains silver.

Motifs depicting on a flat surface a path that twists around itself but never crosses itself, usually leading from an outer edge to the center. Common in Roman mosaics and inlaid in Medieval church pavements.
